*On the Workmanship of God*, or *The Formation of Man.* We restore this double title, in imitation of Plato, from Jerome, Honorius of Autun, the old editions of Lactantius, and very many manuscript codices. In some manuscripts there is only *On the Workmanship of God*; in others, merely *On the Workmanship of Man*; while in two more recent ones—an Oxford manuscript and a Colbert manuscript—and in *Divine Institutes*, book II, chapter 9, one reads: “The Work of the World and the Workmanship of God.” Theodoret also discusses excellently all parts of the human body in Sermons 3 and 4 *On Providence*. See further, if desired, Gregory of Nyssa, *On the Creation of Man*.—The book *On the Workmanship*, which is the most corrupted of all Lactantius’s books, and which I should wish to be more carefully collated against the manuscripts, was published separately at Cologne from the Quentell press in 1506 (following the Venice edition of 1497), then with the notes of Desiderius Erasmus at Basel in 1529, Paris in 1529, and with those of Willichius in 1542. FRITZSCHE.

To Demetrianus, his pupil. That this book was addressed to Demetrianus is indicated by Lactantius himself below, at the beginnings of chapters 1 and 20, and in *Divine Institutes*, book II, chapter 10, after the middle; and by Jerome, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. Nearly all editions and many manuscripts likewise agree: it is not addressed to Demetrius, nor to Donatus, as one learned man thought.

“How far from tranquil I am.” Whenever *quam* intensifies, it is elegantly prefixed to superlatives, as in *quam plurimis*, “with very many” or “with as many as possible.” But when it is used for *quantum*, “how much,” I do not recall its being joined, among authors who speak correctly, except with positive forms. Thus in this passage I would have said, “how far from tranquil I am,” or “how little tranquillity I have.” ERASMUS.

“And amid the greatest necessities.” Erasmus notes that in some manuscripts *etiam* is wrongly read for *et*. This indicates that the latter particle is present in others. That *quam* is required here is inferred from the fact that it is not new for a man situated amid the greatest necessities, or persecutions, to be very far from tranquil; whereas, if the conjunction *et* is retained, only what was previously said will be repeated, in the sense: “and how I am.” SPARK.

Accordingly we restore *et*, as required by the sense and supported by the editions of Graphius, Gymnicus, Cratander, and Isaeus, and by the Erasmus manuscript and one Colbert manuscript. In the latter *et* is written by the first hand, while *etiam* has been written above it in a later and darker ink, indicating that the second hand read *etiam*, as in most manuscripts and editions—unless one prefers to read *et jam*, “and already,” with another Colbert manuscript. In a third Colbert manuscript there is *etc.* with an abbreviation mark. I shall publish it. The Regius-Puteanus manuscript and three recent manuscripts have *extundam*, “I shall hammer out”; not badly.

“Philosophers.” Erasmus here forgot that Justin Martyr, Clement of Alexandria, and others also call Christian doctrine “philosophy” and Christian teachers “philosophers.” Kortolt demonstrated this at length in his commentary on Justin Martyr. BUN.

“Of our sect.” He elegantly, but not very theologically, noted Christians as “philosophers,” because he composed this little book almost wholly in a philosophical style, as Boethius did his book *The Consolation of Philosophy*. He used *secta* in a favourable sense, as Tertullian occasionally does, since among the Greeks *hairesis* means what *secta* means for us; and he calls the devout “wise,” piety “wisdom,” the new profession “Christianity.” ERASMUS.—But as alien doctrines proliferated in the Church, the term “sect” began to become odious.—“Of our sect.” Elsewhere our author used “sect” in a bad sense, for example in *Institutes*, book IV, chapter 30, and *On the Wrath of God*, chapter 2. Here he takes it in a good sense, as Tertullian does in the *Apology*, chapters 1, 21, and 40: “the origin of the Christian sect.” BUN.

“And are chastised.” He said *castigare*, not in the sense of “to correct,” but of “to rebuke” or “to scourge.” ERASMUS.]

LUCIUS CAECILIUS FIRMIANUS LACTANTIUS, ON THE WORKMANSHIP OF GOD, OR THE FORMATION OF MAN: A BOOK ADDRESSED TO HIS PUPIL DEMETRIANUS. (C)

[Col. 0009A] CHAPTER I. Preface and exhortation to Demetrianus.

How far I am from tranquil, even amid the greatest necessities, you may judge from this little book, which I have written out for you, Demetrianus, in almost unpolished language, according to the capacity allowed by my modest talent. It is intended that you may both know my daily occupation and not lack me as your teacher even now, though now of a more honourable matter and a better teaching. For if, in literature—which furnishes nothing but language—you have shown yourself a sufficiently diligent pupil, how much more teachable ought you to be in these truths that concern life? Before you I now declare that I am hindered by no necessity, whether of circumstance or time, from producing something by which the philosophers of our sect, which we defend, may henceforth become better equipped and more learned, although they are now spoken ill of and publicly chastised because they live otherwise [Col. 0011A]

[Note: [Col. 0011C] [Variant Notes on columns 11–12]

“Those.” This is absent from the Bovian manuscript, and fittingly so.

“As.” Thus I restored it from the excellent manuscripts Regius-Puteanus, Gothicus, Emmeramensis, Merton, Christ Church, two Colbert manuscripts, Brunensis, and Bovianus, and from the editions of Graphius and Cellarius, with Walch’s approval. In eleven recent manuscripts and almost all printed editions, it was *sic*, “thus.”

“In.” This is absent from the Bovian manuscript, and correctly so.

“Mind.” Virgil, *Aeneid* I.608.

“To flow prosperously.” Thus in Cicero, *On Duties*, book I, on courage: “Even in prosperous circumstances, and in those flowing according to our wish, we must earnestly flee pride, disdain, and arrogance.”

“Creeps in.” The simple verb is used for the compound *irrepat*, a usage familiar to Lactantius. Thus *irrepat* was wrongly substituted in six recent manuscripts and gradually intruded into five others and into recent editions. I deleted it as a superfluous adverb, since *paulatim*, “little by little,” which means the same, immediately precedes. In the Bovian manuscript one reads *manum tuam repat*, “it creeps upon your hand,” but this is an error. There too *sensim*, “gradually,” has been removed, correctly.

“And, repeating it, again and again I shall warn you.” Lipsius 2 and some editions, for example Venice 1493 and 1497, read: “and repeating it, again and again I warn,” in the present tense, as Cellarius wishes. Parrhasius, Aldus, Cratander, Fasius, Gryphius, Tornesius, Thomas, Thysius, and Gallius: “Repeating it, again and again I shall warn.” Venice 1471 and Rostock omit all this. BUN.

“Think that you possess.” Seneca aptly says in Letter 8: “Stand suspicious and fearful before every chance good. Do you think they are Fortune’s gifts? They are traps.” BUNEMANN.—“Think that you possess.” Here Erasmus marks Lactantius with his censorious pen, as though he had spoken harshly, because *habere te credas* sounds the same as *credere te credas*, “think that you think.” But, with due respect to so great a man, I consider that Lactantius uses the verb *habere* in its common meaning, “to possess.” SPARKIUS.

“Step by step.” That is, cautiously. The words “therefore the highest prudence is” precede. Donatus on Terence, *Phormio* III.3.19: “Step by step: cautiously, from the feet and from testing.” Cicero, *Against Verres*, Action I, chapter 7: “step by step and cautiously”; *For Cluentius*: “cautiously and step by step.”

“To proceed.” Thus we restored it from the best and oldest manuscripts, Bononiensis and Regius-Puteanus, Bovianus, and eleven others. [Col. 0012C] Two recent manuscripts and the common editions read “to walk”; four recent manuscripts read “to go”; in two others the word is absent.

“Lies in wait for safety.” Thus read the two Bononiensian manuscripts, Erasmus manuscript, Emmeramensis, and almost all editions. This is the good reading and is approved by learned men. Twenty-one manuscripts and two editions read “a leap lies in wait”; four Regius manuscripts and the Bovian manuscript, and the Graphius edition, read “a leap will strike.”

“Stumbling-blocks.” An unusual word for “offence”; here it is taken actively.

“Secretly.” A word used by Cicero and Ovid. Cyprian aptly says in *On the Unity of the Church*, Oxford and Bremen edition, fol. 804: “The enemy is more to be feared and guarded against when he steals up secretly, when, deceiving through an appearance of peace, he creeps forward by hidden approaches … This is always his cunning, this his blind and shadowy deceit in surrounding man. Thus from the beginning … with lying words he deceived inexperienced souls through unwary credulity; thus he secretly approached the Lord himself …”

“Prosperous.” Thus I emended from four Oxford manuscripts and the Bovian manuscript and the editions of Cratander, Graphius, Gymnicus, Tornesius, [Col. 0012D] and Walch. Seven Regius manuscripts, Claromontanus and Brunensis, four Colbert manuscripts, and seven editions have “one’s own.” See what follows; but Cicero also has *prospera res*, “a prosperous circumstance,” *For Cluentius* 12.

“In what state you have enrolled your name.” That is, in what state you have been initiated by baptism. In two Bononiensian manuscripts, two recent Regius manuscripts, Taxensis, two Colbert manuscripts, and Baluze, “into what state.”

“The arrangement is thus constituted.” All editions read “therefore constituted.” I wrote “thus constituted” from the Gothicus manuscript. Heumann also correctly conjectured this. Compare book II, chapter 12; book VI, chapter 1.

“The body is indeed in some fashion a vessel,” etc. Thus the Bovian manuscript; others read, “The body is indeed in some fashion a clay vessel,” but less well.

“Made.” Bononiensis, Taxensis, Buneman: “made [masculine].”

“Smallness.” A word little used among approved authors.

“In the book *On the Republic*.” This book has perished; Cicero had written it in imitation of Plato. But Basil the Great and Ambrose in their *Hexaemeron*, and Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, in his books *On Providence*, treat the same subject as Lactantius; and in more recent times Granatensis in his *Catechism*, and the illustrious Fénelon, archbishop of Cambrai, in his outstanding French treatise *On the Existence [Col. 0013B] of God*.]

as befits wise persons and conceal, under the cover of that name, vices which they ought either to cure or wholly avoid, so that by a life conforming to their precepts they might vindicate the blessed and incorruptible name of wisdom itself. Yet, in order to instruct both ourselves and others together, I refuse no labour. For I cannot forget myself, especially at a time when it is most necessary to remember; just as you too, I hope and pray, do not forget yourself. For although the necessity of public affairs turns you away from true and just works, nevertheless it cannot happen that your mind does not from time to time look up to heaven:

> A mind conscious of what is right.

For my part, I rejoice that all things regarded as good are flowing prosperously for you, provided only that they change nothing in the disposition of your mind. For I fear lest little by little habit and the pleasantness of those things—as commonly happens—creep into your mind. [Col. 0011B] Therefore I warn you,

> And, repeating it, again and again I shall warn you

not to think that these delights of earth are great or true goods. They are not only deceptive because uncertain, but also treacherous because sweet. For you know how crafty that wrestler and adversary of ours is, and at the same time how violent, as we now see. He regards all things capable of enticing as snares, [Col. 0012A] and indeed as snares so subtle that they escape the eyes of the mind and cannot be avoided by human foresight. The highest prudence, therefore, is to proceed step by step, since on either side he lies in wait for one’s safety and secretly places stumbling-blocks in one’s path. Accordingly, I advise you, in keeping with your character, either to despise, if you can, or not to admire greatly the prosperous circumstances in which you now live. Remember both your true parent, the state in which you enrolled your name, and the rank to which you belonged. You certainly understand what I mean. For I do not accuse you of arrogance, of which there is not even the slightest suspicion in you. Rather, what I say must be referred to the mind, not to the body, whose entire arrangement is thus constituted: that it may serve the mind as its master and be governed by its command. The body is indeed in some fashion a vessel in which the mind—that is, the true man himself—is contained, [Col. 0012B] and it was made not by Prometheus, as the poets say, but by that supreme founder and artificer of things, God, whose divine providence and utterly perfect power can neither be comprehended by perception nor described in speech.

Yet, since mention has been made of body and mind, I shall attempt to explain the constitution of each, so far as the smallness of my intelligence can perceive it. I judge this task especially worth undertaking because Marcus Tullius, a man of exceptional talent, attempted it in the fourth book of *On the Republic* [Col. 0013A]

[Note: [Col. 0013C] [Variant Notes on columns 13–14]

“He accomplished absolutely nothing; for.” Thus I restored it from two Bononiensian manuscripts, two Regius manuscripts, Taxensis, two Colbert manuscripts, Baluze, and Claromontanus in the margin. Those words are absent from sixteen manuscripts and from Fritzsche’s edition itself. In nearly all common editions, “and” stands instead of “for.”

“Lightly plucking the highest points of each matter.” Thus the common manuscripts and editions; but the Bovian manuscript reads, “lightly gathering the chief points of each matter.”

“Scipio.” Here, according to Cicero, *On Laws* I.6, he had written six books on the best republic.

“To be touched by the eyes.” This is the sound reading of all editions and manuscripts except the Bononiensian manuscript, which reads “to be viewed,” and Cellarius’s edition, in which he restored “to be surveyed,” without any manuscript authority. Against this correction—or rather corruption—the learned Heumann rose up and showed from various passages of ancient authors, namely Tacitus, *Annals* III.12; Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VI, fable 7; Augustine, Letter 3; Gregory Nazianzen, First Theological Oration; [Col. 0013D] Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* III; and Chrysostom, Homily 3 to the People of Antioch, that this is a sound, indeed elegant, mode of expression. It is accepted not only among Latin and Greek writers; we French also say *faire toucher une chose au doigt et à l’oeil*, “to make a thing touchable with finger and eye.” Lactantius uses the same mode of speech in *Divine Institutes* V.21, near the end.

“Put forward.” Thus I restored it from the old editions and Cellarius. All manuscripts except two recent Colbert manuscripts, one Brunensis, and Bovianus read “assert,” as also do the recent editions.

“To examine.” Thus I restored it from two Bononiensian manuscripts, Taxensis, two Colbert manuscripts, and one Regius manuscript, supported by Regius-Puteanus and another Regius manuscript, which read “to look down upon.” In eleven more recent manuscripts and in the editions, “to inspect.”

“Whatever has been made.” An elegant reading, which I restored from five editions and two Bononiensian manuscripts, two Regius manuscripts, Taxensis, Peniensis, Caucasianus, Ultramontanus, four Colbert manuscripts, Baluze, Claromontanus, and Brunensis; joined by Regius-Puteanus, Gothicus, and Emmeramensis, in which one reads “whatever has been made.” In four recent Regius manuscripts, two Colbert manuscripts, Marmoutier, and eight editions, “what each person has become.”

“Gave.” This chapter together with the following one is wholly directed against Lucretius, who charges Nature with injustice in making man.

“That artificer.” *Ille*, “that,” is often elegantly added, as in chapter 1, “by that supreme … artificer God”; *Institutes* VI.23, “that adversary of ours.” BUN.

“Perception.” That is, mind or intellect. See the note on chapter 1, “comprehend by perception.” Compare *Institutes* VI.2; Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* II, p. 279: “And while I debate this religious scruple in my mind.” BUN.

“That rational power.” Thus one reads in nine editions and in the old and excellent manuscripts Regius-Puteanus, Caucasianus, and Erasmus; Gallaeus and Walch approve this reading. Fifteen recent manuscripts and seven common editions have “life”; one Leipzig manuscript and Bovianus have “that rational life.”

“Provided beforehand.” The most learned Francius suspected that *apte*, “fittingly,” should be read instead of *ante*, “beforehand.”

“For he clothed all with hairs from themselves.” Thus have the old and excellent Bononiensian and Caucasian manuscripts and the editions of Graphius, Cratander, and Spark, which Erasmus approves: hairs that are born with the animals themselves. Twenty-one manuscripts and nine editions have “skins”; Emmeramensis and Bovianus read “he clothed [them] from their own skins.” The reflexive pronoun is used harshly here; for it does not refer to God but to the living creatures. Further, not every animal is covered with hair or even with skins: some are protected by a shell, such as oysters and tortoises; some by a hard covering, some by hide, others by scales, feathers, bristles, spines, stings, shaggy hair, crusts, plates. These matters are treated at length by Aristotle, *Parts of Animals* IV.10; Pliny, preface to book VII; and Gregory of Nyssa, *On the Workmanship of Man* chapter 7.—“Yet, in what manner … he provided beforehand. For he clothed all,” etc. Aristotle likewise, *Parts of Animals* IV.10; Lucretius V, “for whatever things you see,” etc.; Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II; Plutarch, *On Fortune*; Pliny, preface 7; Maximus of Tyre, Discourse “On Socratic Love”; Gregory of Nyssa, *On the Workmanship of Man*, chapter 7. ISAEUS.

“To endure the force of frosts and cold.” Thus I restored from the very oldest and best manuscripts: two Bononiensian, Regius-Puteanus, three other Regius, four Colbert, Baluze, Claromontanus, Taxensis, Peniensis, [Col. 0015C] Brunensis, and Bovianus. Yet in three recent Regius manuscripts, two Colbert manuscripts, and the common editions: “to endure the force of frosts and cold [plural].” But Cicero has “the force of cold.”]

but achieved absolutely nothing; for he confined an extensively broad subject within narrow limits, lightly plucking the highest points of each matter. And lest there should be any excuse for his not having carried out that passage, he himself testified that neither willingness nor diligence had been lacking to him. For in the first book of *On Laws*, when he was treating this same topic in outline, he says: “Scipio has adequately, as it seems to me, set forth this subject in those books which you have read.” Later, however, he tried to pursue this same subject more extensively in the second book of *On the Nature of the Gods*. But since he did not adequately set it forth even there, I shall undertake this task and boldly take upon myself to explain what that most eloquent man almost left entirely untouched. Perhaps you may criticize me for attempting to discuss something amid obscure matters, when you see that men commonly called philosophers have existed with such great rashness [Col. 0013B] that they investigate things which God intended to be wholly hidden and concealed, and seek out the nature of heavenly and earthly things—things far removed from us, which cannot be touched by the eyes, handled by the hand, or apprehended by the senses. Yet they argue about the nature of all those things as though they wished what they put forward to seem established and known. Why, then, should anyone judge it blameworthy in us if we wish to examine and contemplate the constitution of our own body? It is not wholly obscure, because from the functions of the limbs themselves and the uses of the individual parts we may understand how great a force of providence made each thing.

CHAPTER II. On the generation of beasts and man.

For that artificer and parent of ours, God, gave man perception and reason, so that it might thereby be evident that we have been generated by him, because he himself is intelligence, perception, and reason. Since he did not attribute that rational power to other living creatures, he nevertheless provided beforehand for the greater security of their lives. For he clothed all with hairs from themselves, so that they might more easily endure the force of frosts and cold. For every kind he established its own appropriate defences against external assaults, [Col. 0014B] so that they may either resist stronger creatures with natural weapons; or, if weaker, withdraw themselves from dangers through swiftness of flight; or, if they need both strength and speed, protect themselves by cunning; or fortify themselves in hiding places. Thus some are lifted aloft on light feathers; others are supported by hooves or equipped with horns; some have weapons in their mouths, teeth, or hooked claws on their feet. No creature lacks a means of protecting itself.

[Col. 0015A] [Note: [Col. 0015C] [Variant Notes on columns 15–16]

“They have been banished into that region.” Thus many manuscripts and editions. Lactantius elsewhere likewise uses the ablative for the accusative case, and conversely. Some have “bound in a region”; some “bound by religion,” as the Bovian manuscript does, but wrongly.—“They have been banished into that region.” Erasmus in the Froben edition of 1529, Gymnicus, Tornesius, Betuleius, and Paris 1561: “They have been banished into that region.” Rostock wrongly has “bound.” Gothicus, Leipzig, Reimmann, 1465–1524, Thomasius and later editions: “They have been banished in that region.” *Relegare* means “to remove,” “to send away,” “to separate.” It is more often joined with the dative. Thus Lactantius from Virgil, *Institutes* I.17:

> The nourishing goddess hides [him] in secluded  
> abodes, and relegates [him] to the nymph Egeria and the grove, etc.

BUN.

“If in man.” Thus I restored it from the oldest and best manuscripts: two Bononiensian, Regius-Puteanus, two other Regius, Taxensis, two Colbert, and Baluze. Eleven recent manuscripts and the editions have “if to man.”

“Who would not perceive?” Thus I restored it from all manuscripts and the old editions: Rome, Gymnicus, Graphius. In eleven recent editions one reads “perceives.” The former is Lactantius’s correct reading.

“Whom.” Thus it should be written, according to Heumann from the editions of 1472, 1478, 1513, and 1515; others read “because,” which seems less good. “Philosophers”: namely Leucippus and Democritus, whom Epicurus followed, and Lucretius, who followed Epicurus.

“Indivisible,” etc.: namely, atoms.

“May come to be and have come to be.” Thus, and excellently, the Bovian manuscript and editions of 1472, 1476, and 1478.

“Things pertaining to the world itself.” Thus with almost all editions: two Bononiensian manuscripts, Regius-Puteanus, Taxensis, Ultramontanus, Emmeramensis, and Claromontanus in the first hand. But Erasmus read in a manuscript he saw: “pertaining to the world itself,” deleting *quae*, “things which.” In six Colbert manuscripts, Marmoutier, Brunensis, [Col. 0016C] and three editions, “pertaining” is absent.

“They complain that man is born too weak and fragile.” Namely Lucretius V, near the beginning; Pliny, preface to book VII—yet wrongly and foolishly, as Aristotle says, *Parts of Animals* IV.10; Seneca, *On Benefits* IV.18; Galen I, chapter 2 and following; Plutarch, *On Fortune*; Basil, Homily 10 on the *Hexaemeron*; Gregory of Nyssa, *On the Workmanship of Man*. ISAEUS.

“Too weak … than other animals.” That is, “in comparison with other animals”: an unusual manner of speaking, which one will scarcely find in any author.—“Too weak … to be born, than.” Sparkius also calls this construction unusual. Reiher, indeed, in his *Theatre of Plautus*, explains *nimis quam cupio*, “I desire excessively,” as “more than I desire”; but it rather means “very much,” “exceedingly.” More on the expression *nimis quam* in Gronovius on Gellius V.14, p. 328, and Burman on Quintilian, *Institutes* IV.2, p. 336. BUN.

“As soon as they are brought forth … immediately.” *Ut … protinus* is elegant, as in Cicero, Caesar, and Livy: *ut … statim*; *ut … confestim*; *ut … continuo*; *ut … extemplo*; *ut … subito*. See Tursellinus, *On Particles*, ed. II, Schwartz, p. 1099 and following. BUN.

“Immediately … suitable, because.” Sublacensis, Rostock, Venice 1471, 1472, both editions of 1478–1515, Paris, Cratander, Froben, and Gymnicus: “immediately … suitable, than.” Erasmus says that he again used the expression *statim quam*, “as soon as,” in a novel manner, instead of “as soon as.” I should not reject the term that Erasmus calls novel, remembering that our author said in *Institutes* VII.5: “not as soon as he is born.” BUN.

“Man, by contrast, naked,” etc. Tertullian, *On the Flesh of Christ*: “You surely recoil from an infant poured forth and besmeared with its own impediments.” Seneca, *To Marcia*: “What is man? A weak and fragile body, naked and by its own nature unarmed.” PRICAEUS.

“When he has been poured forth.” Birth is elegantly said to be “poured” or “poured forth.” *Institutes* III.19: “the place in which each person is poured forth from the womb.”]

But if some succumb as prey to larger creatures, still, lest their race should perish utterly, they have either been banished into a region where larger creatures cannot exist, or have received abundant fecundity for breeding; so that beasts feeding on blood might have a sufficient food supply from them, while their own multitude might nevertheless overcome the destruction inflicted, preserving the race. Man, however, although granted reason and the power of perception and speech, God made devoid of those things attributed to other animals, because wisdom could supply what the condition of nature had denied him. He determined that man should be naked and unarmed, because he could be armed by ingenuity and clothed by reason. Yet how wonderfully those very things given to dumb creatures and denied to man contribute to human beauty cannot be expressed. For if he had added to man the teeth of a wild beast, or horns, or claws, [Col. 0015B] or hooves, or a tail, or hairs of varied colour, who would not perceive how ugly an animal he would have become, just as dumb creatures would be if they were fashioned naked and unarmed? If you remove from these creatures either their body’s natural covering or those things with which they arm themselves from their own substance, they could be neither beautiful nor safe. Thus they appear wonderfully equipped, if you consider usefulness, and adorned, if appearance: so remarkably does usefulness agree with beauty.

But man, whom he fashioned as an eternal and immortal animal, he armed not outwardly, like other creatures, but inwardly. He placed his protection not in the body [Col. 0016A] but in the mind, because it was superfluous, after granting him what was greatest, to cover him with bodily defences—especially since these would impair the beauty of the human body. Hence I am accustomed to marvel at the madness of the philosophers who follow Epicurus. They criticize the works of nature in order to show that the world was neither equipped nor governed by any providence; instead, they assign the origin of things to indivisible and solid bodies, through whose chance collisions all things may come to be and have come to be. I pass over the criticisms which they make concerning matters pertaining to the world itself, in which they are absurdly mad. I take up the point pertinent to the matter now under discussion.

CHAPTER III. On the condition of cattle and man.

[Col. 0016B] They complain that man is born too weak and fragile compared with the way other animals are born. As soon as these are brought forth from the womb, they immediately rise onto their own feet and leap about in running; and, since they come forth into the light protected by natural coverings, they are at once suited to endure the air. Man, by contrast, is cast forth naked and unarmed, as though from a shipwreck, into the miseries of this life, and driven out—unable either to move himself from the place where he has been poured forth, to seek the nourishment of milk, or to endure the injury of the weather. Thus they say that nature is not the mother of the human race but its stepmother, since, though she has treated dumb animals so [Col. 0017A]

[Note: [Col. 0017B] [Variant Notes on columns 17–18]

generously, has poured man forth in such a way that, needy, weak, and requiring every assistance, he can do nothing except foretell the condition of his frailty by his weeping and cries:

> To whom there remains in life only a passage through evils.

When they say these things, they are thought exceedingly wise, because everyone is thoughtlessly ungrateful for his own condition. But I maintain that they are never so foolish as when they speak in this way. For, considering the condition of things, I understand that nothing ought to have been done otherwise—not to say that it could not have been, since God can do all things—but that so provident a majesty necessarily accomplished what was better and more right.

I should therefore like to ask these critics of divine works what they think is lacking in man because he is born weaker. Are human beings for that reason less fully reared? [Col. 0017B] Do they less fully advance to the highest strength of age? Does weakness impede either growth or health? For reason compensates for what is lacking. “But,” they say, “the upbringing of a human being entails the greatest labours. Surely the condition of cattle is better, since all of them, once they have brought forth offspring, attend only to their own feeding. From this it follows that, with their udders swelling spontaneously, they provide their offspring with the nourishment of milk, and, compelled by nature, the offspring seek it without the solicitude of mothers.” What of birds, whose manner is different? Do they not undertake the greatest labours in rearing their young, so that at times they seem to possess something of human intelligence? For they build nests either with mud or from twigs and leaves; they sit upon eggs without food; and, because they are not permitted to nourish their offspring from their own bodies, they gather food and spend whole days in this running about. At night they defend, warm, and protect them. What more can human beings do—except perhaps only this: that they do not drive out their young when adult, but keep them joined to themselves by a lasting bond and tie of affection? Moreover, the offspring of birds is much more fragile than that of man, because birds do not nourish the creature itself from the mother’s body; rather, that which, warmed by the brooding and warmth of the mother’s body, becomes a creature—yet when it has been endowed with breath, that featherless and tender thing lacks not only the use of flight but even [Col. 0018B] the use of walking. Is not he, then, utterly foolish who thinks nature has treated birds badly, first because they are born twice, and then because they are so weak that they must be fed by their parents with food acquired through labour? But these people choose the stronger examples and pass over the weaker.

Therefore I ask those who prefer the condition of cattle to their own what they would choose if God offered them the choice: would they prefer human wisdom with weakness, or the strength of cattle with their nature? Certainly they are not such cattle themselves that they would not prefer even a more fragile [Col. 0019A]

Elephants are called “Lucanian oxen” (*boves lucae*) because they were first seen in Lucania, according to Varro, *On the Latin Language*, Book VI: “the Lucanian ox, the elephant.” Others, not understanding this, altered *lucas* into *vaccas* (“cows”), as happened in three Regius manuscripts, three Vatican manuscripts, three Colbert manuscripts, one Sorbonne manuscript, one Clermont manuscript in the second hand, and in the Roman editions of 1468 and 1470, Aldus, Paris 1525, Cratander, Fasitelus, and Thomas. Or when do wolves serve? Thus Lucretius:

> In towered body, to endure the wounds of war.

much more than it is now, provided it be human rather than that irrational strength. Yet these supposedly wise men wish neither for human reason together with frailty, nor for the strength of dumb creatures without reason. For nothing is so inconsistent or contrary that every animal must necessarily be equipped either by reason or by its natural condition. If it is equipped with natural defenses, reason is superfluous. For what will it devise? What will it do? What will it undertake? Or in what will it display that light of intelligence, when nature of its own accord grants those things which reason can provide? But if it is endowed with reason, what need will there be of bodily fortifications? Once reason has been granted, it can perform nature’s office. Reason indeed has such power for adorning and protecting man that nothing greater or better could have been given by God. [Col. 0019B]

Finally, although man has neither a large body nor great strength and is of feeble health, nevertheless, because he has received that which is greater, he is both more equipped and more adorned than the other animals. For though he is born fragile and weak, he is safe from all dumb creatures; and all things born stronger, even if they stoutly endure the force of the heavens, cannot nevertheless be secure from man. Thus reason contributes more to man than nature contributes to dumb creatures, since in them neither greatness of strength nor bodily robustness can prevent them from being either overpowered by us or subjected to our power.

Can anyone, then, when he sees even Lucanian oxen—that is, elephants—or horses, with bodies and strength of the greatest enormity, serving man, complain of God, the maker of things, [Col. 0019C] because he has received only moderate strength and a small body? Such a person does not assess the divine benefits bestowed upon him according to their worth, [Col. 0020A] which is the mark of an ungrateful person—or, to speak more truly, of a madman. Plato, I suppose, in order to refute such ungrateful people, gave thanks to nature that he had been born a human being. What sort of statement that itself is need not be considered here. How much better and sounder is the person who judges the human condition better than those who would rather have been born cattle. If God should perhaps transform them into those animals whose lot they prefer to their own, they would certainly at once wish to migrate back, and with loud cries demand their former condition. For bodily strength and robustness are not so valuable that one should lack the service of speech; nor is the free roaming of birds through the air so valuable that one should need hands. Hands accomplish more than lightness and the use of wings; the tongue, more than the strength of the entire body. What madness, then, is it to prefer things which, if they were given to you, you would refuse to accept?

## Chapter IV. On Human Frailty

These same people complain that man is subject to diseases and untimely death. Clearly they are indignant that they were not born gods. “Not at all,” they say, “but from this we show that man was made without any providence, because he ought to have been made otherwise.” What if I show that this very thing was wisely provided: namely, that he could be harassed by diseases, and that life could often be broken off in the middle of its course? Since God knew that the living creature he had made would of itself pass over into death, so that it might be capable of death itself—which is the dissolution of nature—he gave it frailty, through which death might find an entrance for dissolving the living creature. For if it had been made of such strength that disease and sickness could not approach it, then death could not approach it either, since death is the consequence of diseases.

But how could untimely death be absent from one for whom mature death had been appointed? Of course, they do not wish any human being to die until he has completed his hundredth year. How can reason remain consistent for them amid so great a contradiction of things? For in order that no one may be able to die before a hundred years, some strength that is immortal must be attributed to him. Once this is granted, the condition of death must necessarily be excluded. But what sort of thing could that be which made a human being solid and invulnerable against diseases and external blows? Since he consists of bones, sinews, internal organs, and blood, what among these can be so firm as to repel frailty and death? Therefore, if man is to be indissoluble until the time which [Col. 0021B] they think should have been established for him, from what material will they assign him a body? All things that can be seen and touched are fragile. It remains for them to seek something from heaven, since on earth there is nothing that is not weak.

Since, then, man was to be formed by God so as to be mortal at some time, the matter itself required that he be fashioned with an earthly and fragile body. Therefore he must be capable of receiving death at some point, since he is bodily; for every body is dissoluble and mortal. Most foolish, therefore, are those who complain of untimely death, because the condition of nature makes room for it. It will consequently follow that he is subject to diseases as well; for nature does not allow weakness to be absent from a body which is at some point to be dissolved. But let us suppose it possible, as they wish, that man should not [Col. 0021C] [Col. 0022A] be born under the condition of being subject to disease or death, unless, after completing the span of his age, he has reached extreme old age. They do not see, then, what follows if this has been established: that for all the remaining time he would by no means be able to die. But if another person can prevent him from food, he can die; therefore the matter requires that a man who cannot die before a fixed day should have no need of nourishment, since it can be withdrawn. If he has no need of food, he will no longer be a man but a god. Thus, as I said above, those who complain of human frailty chiefly complain that they were not born immortal and everlasting. No one, except an old man, ought to die. Surely he ought to die for this reason: because he is not God. Yet mortality cannot be joined with immortality. For if he is mortal in old age, he cannot be immortal in youth; nor is the condition of death foreign to one who is someday to die; nor is there any immortality for which a limit has been set. Thus it comes about that immortality, excluded forever, and mortality, admitted only for a time, place man in the condition that he is mortal at every age.

Necessity, therefore, fits on every side: it ought not to have been otherwise, nor was it permissible for it to be otherwise. But these men do not see the logic of the consequences, because they have erred once for all in the fundamental point. For once divine providence had been excluded from human affairs, it necessarily followed that all things arose of themselves. From this they devised those impacts of tiny seeds and their chance collisions, because they did not perceive the origin of things. Having thrown themselves into these straits, necessity now compelled them to think that souls are born with bodies and likewise perish with bodies. For they had assumed that nothing is made by a divine mind. For they had assumed that nothing is made by a divine mind. They could prove this only by showing that there are some things in which the plan of providence seemed deficient. They therefore criticized those very things in which providence has most wonderfully displayed its divinity: the matters I have mentioned concerning diseases and untimely death. They ought instead to have considered what would necessarily follow from these assumptions—and the consequences are those I have stated—if a human being did not admit disease and needed neither shelter nor clothing. Why would he fear winds, rains, or cold, whose force consists in bringing diseases? For this reason he received wisdom: that he might defend his frailty against harmful things. It necessarily follows that, since he contracts diseases in order to preserve reason, he must always also admit death; because the one [Col. 0023B] to whom death does not come must necessarily be robust. Weakness contains within itself the condition of death; but wherever robustness exists, neither old age nor death, which follows old age, can have a place.

Moreover, if death were fixed for a definite age, man would become most arrogant and would lack every humane quality. For almost all the laws of human fellowship by which we are bound together arise from fear and awareness of frailty. Finally, all weaker and more timid animals gather together, so that, because they cannot protect themselves by their strength, they may protect themselves by their numbers. But stronger creatures seek solitude, because they trust in their bodily power and strength. If man likewise possessed a ready strength for repelling dangers, [Col. 0023C] [Col. 0024A] and needed no help from any other person, what fellowship would there be? What order? What humanity? Or what would be more dreadful than man? What more savage? What more brutal? But because he is weak and cannot live by himself without another human being, he seeks fellowship, so that common life may become both more civilized and safer.

You see, then, that the entire rationale of man especially rests in this: that he is born naked and frail, that he is afflicted by diseases, that he is punished by untimely death. If these are taken away from man, reason and wisdom must also be taken away. But I have argued too long over matters that are evident, since it is clear that nothing has ever been made, or could have been made, without providence. If I now wished to discuss all its works in order, the material would be infinite. But I have undertaken to speak only of the one body of man, in order to show in it how great the power of divine providence has been, [Col. 0024B] and only in matters that are comprehensible and evident; for the matters belonging to the soul can neither be subjected to the eyes nor comprehended. We are now speaking of the very vessel of man that we see.

## Chapter V. On the Forms and Limbs of Animals

In the beginning, when God was forming living creatures, he did not wish to gather and compress them into the round shape of a ball, although in this way they might readily move for walking and bend themselves in any direction. Instead, from the very top of the body he extended the head; likewise he extended certain limbs farther out, called feet, so that, fixed upon the ground by alternating movements, they might carry the living creature wherever the mind led it or the necessity of seeking food prompted it. [Col. 0025A] [Note: [Col. 0025C] [Notes of the Variants on columns 25–26]

For cattle and wild beasts. These words are absent from the Bovian manuscript.

But for making and regulating. This, in my opinion with Cellarius, is the true Lactantian reading, found in four Regius manuscripts, Caucianus, Gothanus, three Colbert manuscripts, Navarrus, Victorinus, Ultramontanus, Lipsiensis, one Brunensis manuscript, and the Roman editions of 1470 and 1474; and in Betuleius with one Colbert manuscript and Marmolita, in which there is “for regulating,” with “but for making” omitted. The Rome 1468 edition has “for repairing” for “regulating”; not understanding this word, many copyists substituted “for holding,” as in two Bologna manuscripts, two Regius manuscripts, two Colbert manuscripts, Tacinensis, Bodleianus, one Sorbonne manuscript, Clermontensis, Baluzius, and one Brunensis manuscript; this has the same sense. But what do the several other editions mean, in which there is “but for making and working,” as though making were not the same as working?

Larger and short bones. Brunensis manuscript and the edition of Betuleius: “larger and shorter bones.”

Soft. One Bologna manuscript, two Regius manuscripts, two Colbert manuscripts, Baluzius: “softer.” The rest agree with all editions, as in our text.

Solid latticework. Virgil, *Aeneid* XII.508:

> He drives the sword through the ribs and latticework of the breast.

Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VIII.806:

> And the breast to be held only by the latticework of the spine.

*Metamorphoses* XII.370:

> Which [the spear] broke through the latticework of the sides.

BUN.

Or for making. Added from all manuscripts and fourteen editions; absent from Thysius and Gallaeus.

And few. Likewise added from fourteen printed editions and all manuscripts save one Colbert manuscript, which has “and small.” It is absent from the editions of Thysius and Gallaeus. [Col. 0026C]

He finished. Bovian manuscript: “they finished.”

He formed. Restored from the older editions and all manuscripts, except two recent Colbert manuscripts, which have “he re-formed,” and one likewise recent Regius manuscript, which, like the recent common editions, has “he made,” of the same sense. Lactantius often uses compound verbs for simple ones and simple verbs for compound ones; later editors, attempting to correct them, altered them wrongly.—He formed: he aptly used a compound for a simple verb, as in chapter 8: “God did not wish to form [the ears] with soft skins”; chapter 12: “both, having been coagulated, to be formed”; chapter 19: “the formation of the body.” BUN.

The limbs needed only to bend. The Venice 1472, both 1478, 1493, 1497, Pierius, Parrhasius, Paris, and Juntine editions wrongly insert: “the limbs needed to bend in every direction,” inconveniently repeated from what precedes and contradicted by “only.” BUN.

From the place from which they arise, in every direction, etc. Thus restored from the older editions and very many manuscripts. Five others and recent common editions omit *from there* and add “from the body” after “arise,” superfluously.

Would seem like a trunk. A *proboscis* is the elephant’s hand, by which it is said to remove whatever objects lie in its way. Since it is flexible like a serpent, Lucretius called elephants *anguimanus* (“snake-handed”) in Book II and Book V. Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II, Aristotle, *Parts of Animals* II.16, and Isidore, Book XII, chapter 2, likewise discuss it. The elephant’s trunk is called *promuscis*, by which it brings fodder to its mouth, and it is serpent-like. RITTERSHUSIUS.—Seven manuscripts have “like a proboscis”; eight, with the Rome 1470 edition, “like a promuscis”; two recent Regius manuscripts and Marmolita, “like a promoscis.”]

From the very body he made four projections: two behind, which are feet in all creatures; and likewise two near the head and neck, which provide animals with various uses. In cattle and wild beasts they resemble the hind feet; but in man they are hands, which were born not for walking but for making and regulating.

There is also a third kind, in which those front members are neither feet nor hands but wings, in which feathers set in order provide the use of flight. Thus one act of formation has diverse forms and uses. And in order to hold the very bulk of the body firmly together, he joined together larger and shorter bones, like a keel, which we call the spine. He did not wish to make it from one continuous bone, lest the animal lack the ability to walk and bend itself. [Col. 0025B] From about its middle he extended ribs—that is, transverse and flat bones—in opposite directions; by their gentle curvature and their drawing together upon themselves almost into a circle, the internal organs are covered, so that those things which needed to be soft and less strong might be protected within the embrace of that solid latticework. At the very summit of this structure, which we said resembles a ship’s keel, he placed the head, in which the governance of the whole living creature might reside. According to Varro’s letter to Cicero, it received this name because the senses and nerves take their beginning from it.

The parts which, as we have said, were extended for walking, making, or flying, he wished to be neither excessively long, lest they impede swift movement, nor excessively short, lest they lack firmness; rather, he wished them to consist of few and large bones. For they are either two, as in man, or four, as in a four-footed creature. Yet he did not make them solid, lest sluggishness and heaviness delay movement, but hollow and filled within with marrow, to preserve bodily vigor. Nor did he end them in uniform extensions; rather, he gathered their outermost portions into thicker knots, so that they might more readily be bound by sinews and turned more safely—whence they are called joints (*vertibula*). He covered these firmly compacted knots with a certain smooth covering called cartilage, so that they might bend without friction and without any sensation of pain.

Yet he did not form them all in one fashion. He made some simple and rounded in a circle, only in those joints in which the limbs needed to move [Col. 0026B] in every direction, as in the shoulders, since it is necessary for the hands to be moved and turned either way. Others, however, he made broad, even, and rounded in one direction, precisely in those places where the limbs needed only to bend, as in the knees, elbows, and the hands themselves. For just as it was at once beautiful and useful for the hands to move in every direction from the place where they arise, so indeed, if the same thing also happened with the elbows, movement of that sort would be both superfluous and ugly.

For the hand, having lost the dignity which it now possesses, would through excessive mobility seem like a trunk (*proboscis*), [Col. 0026C] and man would plainly be “snake-handed” (*anguimanus*), as has been wonderfully effected in that [Col. 0027A] [Note: [Col. 0027C] [Notes of the Variants on columns 27–28]

Most enormous. A frequent epithet for elephants; hence in chapter 8 he said: “Lucanian oxen with most enormous bodies.”

For God, who. This is the reading of all manuscripts and editions, except one Regius manuscript and the editions of Gallaeus and Spark, in which there is “because.”

That not. Thus I restored it from seventeen manuscripts and the editions of Betuleius and Cellarius. In six manuscripts and many editions there is “so that.”

But, as usual. All books read “but, as usual”; likewise Book I of the *Institutes*, chapter 12: “the Stoics, as usual”; Book VII, chapter 7: “as the Academics are accustomed.” With the Paris 1513 edition, I placed “as usual” in parentheses. BUN.

To make room for his atoms. Common editions add several words which occur neither in the manuscripts nor in the Roman edition. And shortly thereafter recent editions add “in which the principle of reproduction had failed.” But *reproduction* is absent from the old books as well. CELL.

Flying through infinite void. These words are absent from fifteen manuscripts and the Roman edition. They occur, however, in the remaining editions and in two Bologna manuscripts, two Regius manuscripts, three Colbert manuscripts, Sorbonicus, Caucianus, Tacinensis, Penzianus, Ultramontanus, and Baluzius.—“Flying through infinite void.” These words correspond to Lactantius’ style in Book III, chapter 17: “It is not the work of providence. For there are seeds flying through the void”; and *On the Anger of God* 10: “Indeed atoms fly through the void.” Heumannus: “through infinite void.” BUNEMANNUS.

What folly—damn it!—was that. Thus read the codices: two Bologna manuscripts, two Regius manuscripts, Caucianus, Erasmus, one Colbert manuscript, Baluzius, and the common printed editions of Cratander, Betuleius, Antwerp 1570, Tornesius, Soubron, two Paris editions, Isaeus, Spark, and Gallaeus. Erasmus approves this reading, calling the sentence like the Terentian “what, damn it! …” For *malum* here has the force of an interjection. The remaining manuscripts and editions have “what evil of folly was that,” incorrectly, as Erasmus rightly held. In Lipsiensis: “what, an evil of folly was that”; in one Colbert manuscript: “what great folly was that.” Our reading is confirmed by Latin authors. Thus Quintus Curtius, Book VIII: “What madness, damn it, compelled you to test the fortune of war?”; Plautus, *Menaechmi* v. 242: “What, damn it, is this impudence?”—“What folly, damn it, was that.” Thus Cicero, *First Philippic* 6: “What, damn it, is that voluntary servitude?”; *On Duties* II.15: “What reason, damn it, he says, led you into that hope?” Add *For Roscius the Actor*, at the end. Livy, Book V, chapter 54: “What reason, damn it, is this?” Seneca, *To Marcia* 3: “For what madness, damn it, is this?” BUN.

In which the principle of reproduction. This word *reproduction* is wrongly omitted in twenty manuscripts and many common editions; it is read in one Regius manuscript, one Bologna manuscript, Tacinensis, one Colbert manuscript, Baluzius, and other best witnesses, and also in the editions of Thomas, Isaeus, Thysius, Gallaeus, and Spark.

Had failed. Thus I emended from one ancient Bologna manuscript, one Colbert manuscript, Marmolita, and Clermontensis. This reading seemed to us better than “would fail” in the rest.

Nothing wholly devoid of reason could have been generated. That is, nothing could have been generated in which the reason and providence of the creator did not in some manner shine forth. ISAEUS.

For first. Thus I restored it from two Bologna manuscripts, two Regius manuscripts, four Colbert manuscripts, and many others. In six manuscripts and an equal number of common editions there is “but for”; in Ultramontanus, “or for”; in one Regius manuscript and one Colbert manuscript, “indeed for.”

Through the union of bodies. Thus all witnesses. Some have approved the word from Pacuvius and Pliny; rarer forms from ancient glosses are *abjugassere*, *abjugare*, *abjugus*. BUN.

Where a mass of a great work. One ancient Bologna manuscript: “of a burden.”—“Of a great work.” Bologna manuscript in Isaeus wrongly has “of a great burden”; so shortly below, “for the completed work”; Book VII, chapter 1: “firm and suitable foundations … for bearing the work.” Seneca, *Letters* 55: “caves … of great work.” More in Gronovius on Livy, Book XXI, chapter 57. BUN.

Provides for in advance. Thus I restored it from Bologna manuscript, four Regius manuscripts, five Colbert manuscripts, Marmolita, Baluzius, Brunensis, the Roman edition, Cratander, and Cellarius. This reading suits better with the following “provided beforehand” than “foresees in advance,” found in two manuscripts and nine editions. In ten editions there is “perceives in advance.”

In constructing animals. I supplied *in* from all manuscripts and the editions of Rome, Gymnicus, and Walch. It is absent from eight common editions.

For he said. These words are from Lucretius, Book IV. Lactantius already discusses this in Book III of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 3.]

most enormous beast. God, who wished to display his providence and power through the marvelous variety of many things, had not extended that animal’s head far enough for it to touch the ground with its mouth, since that would have been hideous and dreadful. And because he had armed its very mouth with protruding teeth in such a way that, even if it could reach the ground, the teeth would nevertheless take away its ability to graze, he extended from between them, from the top of the forehead, a soft and flexible member, by which it could grasp and hold anything whatever, so that neither the protruding size of its teeth nor the shortness of its neck might impede its means of taking food.

## Chapter VI. On Epicurus’ Error and the Limbs and Their Use

I cannot refrain at this point from again exposing Epicurus’ [Col. 0027B] folly. For all the nonsense that Lucretius talks is Epicurus’ own. In order to show that animals were born not through the workmanship of a divine mind but, as usual, by chance, he said that at the beginning of the world there had been born certain innumerable living creatures of marvelous form and size, but that they could not survive because they lacked either the ability to procure food or the means of mating and reproducing. Clearly, in order to make room for his atoms flying through infinite void, he wished to exclude divine providence. But when he saw that a marvelous rational design of Providence exists in all breathing things, what folly—damn it!—was it to say that there had been prodigious creatures in which the principle of reproduction failed?

Since, therefore, everything we see has been born with reason—for reason alone can bring about birth itself—it is clear that nothing wholly devoid of reason could have been generated. For in the formation of each individual creature provision was first made both for its use of the service of its limbs in the necessities of life and for the preservation of every kind of living creature through offspring produced by the union of bodies. If a skilled architect decides to make some great building, he first considers above all what the completed building is to be like; and beforehand he measures what place will bear a light weight, where the mass of a great work will stand, what intervals there will be between the columns, and what, or where, will be the courses, outlets, and reservoirs of falling water. [Col. 0028B] These things, I say, he provides for in advance, so that whatever will be necessary for the completed work may be begun together with the foundations themselves. Why, then, should anyone think that God, in constructing animals, did not provide in advance for what would be necessary for life before giving life itself? Life certainly could not subsist unless the things by which it subsists had first been made.

Epicurus therefore perceived in the bodies of living creatures the ingenuity of divine reason; but, in order to establish what he had previously assumed imprudently, he added another absurdity consistent with the former. For he said that eyes were not born for seeing, nor [Col. 0029A] [Note: [Col. 0029B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 29–30]]

“Nor ears for hearing.” These words, absent from the editions of Thysius and Gallæus, I have restored from the other printed editions and all manuscripts. And rightly so. See a little below: “the use of seeing, hearing, and walking,” to which these three bodily members correspond. In manuscripts 1 Sorbonne, 2 Colbert, and Baluze, *nec* occurs in both places instead of *neque*.

“I fear lest . . . seem no less foolish.” Lipsius, third edition; Reimmannus wrongly reads: “I fear lest . . . seem not too foolish.” Erasmus says: “The sentence seems incomplete unless you add ‘than to say,’ or something similar.” But everything here is sound and complete. In the same way, *On Anger*, ch. 10: “I fear lest he who thinks these things need refutation seem no less mad; nevertheless, let us reply,” etc. Compare book VII, ch. 12. BUN.

“They are not.” Thus nearly all manuscripts and printed editions. We have removed the *if* prefixed in manuscript 1 Bologna, Lipsius, and five recent editions.

“For the sake of what thing they were born.” From all the manuscripts and old printed editions I restored *were born*. In the more recent common editions it is *may be born*.

“Orderly.” Thus all manuscripts; but Bov. has “orderly arranged.” — “So orderly.” I confirm this from book III of the *Institutions*, ch. 17: “How the world was made so orderly, so well arranged.” BUN.

“Wild beasts for savagery.” He seems to refer to the Ode of Anacreon. — “Birds . . . wild beasts for savagery,” etc. He seems to have had in view Quintilian, *Institutes*, book I, ch. 1: “Just as birds are born for flight, horses for running, wild beasts for ferocity, so the activity and ingenuity of mind are native to us.” BUN.

“For which each was generated.” Thus I emended from all manuscripts and many editions. Seven recent common editions read “each was generated,” but corruptly: for to what does “for which” refer—to wild beasts? to living creatures?

“The very summit of truth.” I added *very* from the editions of Isaeus and Cellarius and from all manuscripts except one recent Royal manuscript, in which, as also in ten common editions, it is lacking.

“Would smell.” Thus I restored from manuscripts 6 Royal, 1 old Bologna, Cauc., 4 Oxford, 3 Colbert, Em., Clermont, Brun., and the Roman edition and six others. Seven manuscripts have “or would smell”; manuscript 1 Royal, 3 Colbert, Cant., Marm., and eight common editions have “smells.”

“Position.” That is, situation, disposition. Book III of the *Institutions*, ch. 17: “They fit together by varied order and arrangement.” BUN.

[Col. 0030B]

“They leave untried.” Eight recent manuscripts: “tried.” — “They leave no kind of position untried.” “Commonly,” says Cellarius, “it is wrongly ‘untried.’” I wish that most distinguished man had not pronounced so. I confirm it from *On Anger*, [Col. 0030C] ch. 10: “The atoms . . . leave no position which they do not try.” But just as “to leave nothing tried” can scarcely be said, the other expression occurs very frequently. Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.415:

> She who was about to die left nothing untried in vain.

Ovid, *Heroides*, epistle 20, v. 42:

> My passion will allow nothing to remain untried.

Curtius often uses the phrase thus; book III, ch. 6: “Nor did Philip omit anything untried.” BUN.

“All the members likewise.” Thus most manuscripts and all editions more correctly than Bologna’s “every member whatsoever.” BUN.

“Structural supports.” I have not encountered this word in earlier writers; lexicons add Augustine. Our master Arnobius, book II, said “solidified bones.” BUN.

“He bound with sinews,” etc. See Galen, who says that there are two kinds of sinews, and Aristotle, *History of Animals*, book III, ch. 5.

[Col. 0030D]

“To resist.” That is, to stand firm, the opposite of the preceding “run forth.” See note on *On Anger*, ch. 4: “He halted at the final step.”

“With even the slightest nod.” Thus in manuscripts 5 Royal, 4 Colbert, Em., Brun., Clermont, and all editions; in some, *even* is absent. Seven manuscripts read “motion.”

“He covered with flesh.” *Viscera* means not so much the entrails as whatever is made of flesh and covered with skin. Ovid uses it thus in the epistle of Penelope:

> Our flesh is torn apart by your power.

Hence the “distribution of flesh,” mentioned in Cicero’s *On Duties*, as the interpreters say. BETULEIUS.

“As each place required.” Four recent manuscripts and three editions: “as every place,” etc.

“So that the solid things, enclosed, might be covered.” Thus the ten better and older manuscripts, with four editions. Ten recent manuscripts with seven editions read: “and so that the solid bones, enclosed, might be covered”; three editions have “might cover.” The Lipsius manuscript: “indeed solid.”]

for seeing, nor ears for hearing, nor feet for walking, because these members were born before there was any use of seeing, hearing, and walking; but that all their functions arose from things already born. I fear that to refute such monstrosities and absurdities may seem no less absurd. Yet I am pleased to be absurd, since I am dealing with an absurd man, lest he think himself excessively clever.

What do you say, Epicurus? Were eyes not born for seeing? Why, then, do they see? “Their use,” he says, “appeared afterward.” Therefore they were born for seeing; for they can do nothing other than see. Likewise, the use itself shows for what purpose the other members were born. And this use could in no way have existed unless all the members had been made so orderly and so providently that they could have a use.

[Col. 0029B] For what if you were to say that birds were not born for flying, wild beasts for savagery, fish for swimming, or human beings for wisdom, when it is apparent that living creatures serve the nature and function for which each has been generated? But plainly, one who has lost the very summit of truth must always wander. For if all things are born not by providence but by the chance collisions of atoms, why has it never happened by chance that those principles should so combine as to produce [Col. 0030A] a creature of such a kind that it heard with its nostrils, smelled with its eyes, and saw with its ears? For if the first principles leave no sort of arrangement untried, such monsters ought to be generated daily, in which both the order of the members was reversed and their function wholly different. But since all kinds of creatures, and likewise all their members, preserve their own laws, arrangements, and allotted functions, it is plain that nothing has been made by chance, because the constant ordering of divine reason is maintained. But we shall refute Epicurus elsewhere; now, as we began, let us discuss providence.

## Chapter VII. On all the parts of the body

[Col. 0030B] Therefore God bound and fastened together the structural supports of the body, called bones, by means of joints and connecting sinews, so that the mind, if it wished to run forth or to resist, might use them as restraints; and this without any labor or exertion, but with even the slightest nod might govern and bend the mass of the whole body. He covered these with flesh, as each location required, so that the solid parts, being enclosed, might be covered. He also mingled veins among the flesh itself, like streams [Col. 0031A] [Note: [Col. 0031B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 31–32]]

“Through which.” Thus I restored it from manuscripts 2 Bologna, 2 Royal, 2 Colbert, Tax., Baluze, Marm., Clermont in a second hand, and five editions. Correctly, as I think, if referred [Col. 0031C] to the veins; nor is “through which,” found in ten common editions, bad if referred to the streams. Ten manuscripts with the Roman edition read “through which things.”

“He covered with bristles.” Reimmannus wrongly: “he sufficiently fitted.” Betuleius: “he covered.” Book VII, ch. 27: “covered over.”

“Distinguished.” Absent from the Bov. manuscript.

“Of image.” Seven manuscripts with the edition of Isaeus have “of image.” One Colbert manuscript reads “images,” corruptly. The other manuscripts and printed editions have “of animals.” What if one read: “displays innumerable varieties of images”? For in most codices *animals* stands, perhaps in place of *images*; and below one reads “a manifold diversity of formed things.”

“Displays.” Thus I restored it from seven editions and all manuscripts except one Royal manuscript, which, like ten common editions, has “carries through”; one Colbert manuscript has “brings forth.”

“The same sequence and order of members exists.” This is a Lactantian phrase which takes a similar construction. Below, ch. 10: “two feet and likewise hands.” Another would have said: “and the same order of members . . . and likewise two hands.”

“Connected below.” Two Bologna manuscripts: “supported below.”

“Thighs.” I have no doubt that Lactantius wrote this: [Col. 0031D] for who would have changed *femora*, a word known to everyone—which is the reading of nine recent manuscripts and the editions—into *femina* [woman], as in 3 Royal, 2 Bologna, Cauc., Tax., 1 Colbert, Baluze, Brun.? In Marm. and Clermont it is *femoralia*, corruptly. See also “the length of the thigh,” below, ch. 13, shortly after the beginning.

“Only.” But the Bov. manuscript has “alone,” and this is quite suitable.

“In it.” Very aptly in the greater number of manuscripts and older editions. Five recent manuscripts and ten editions read “in the mouth,” with an unpleasant repetition, since “the mouth also” has just preceded.

“Of formed creatures.” Thus I restored from manuscripts 4 Royal, 6 Colbert, 4 Oxford, Coth., Lipsius, Clermont, Em., Cambridge, Marm., Brun., and older editions; in 2 Royal and Baluze and many common editions, it is “of forms.”

“In its own genus and species.” We restore *its own* from older editions and manuscripts 6 Royal, 5 Colbert, Cauc., Pen., Ultr., and 1 old Bologna, in which it reads “in the species of its own genus.” Five recent manuscripts and almost all common editions have “in its genus and species.” The conjunction is absent in three manuscripts and two editions.

“Nothing more obstructive for usefulness, nothing more misshapen in appearance.” [Col. 0032B] Lactantius often places adjectives of this kind thus. In this book, ch. 8: “For appearance no number is more perfect.” Again: “than which nothing could be more hideous in appearance, more useless in function”; ch. 10: “manageable for the use of the fingers”; again: “That is wonderfully suited for use”; *On Anger*, ch. 10: “Than which nothing can be either more orderly in arrangement, more suitable for usefulness, more elegant in beauty, or greater in mass.” BUN.

“Presents.” Bunemann reads “required,” and gives this explanation of the variant. — “Required.” Thus I print it from Bologna, Tax., and Isaeus, which Spark and Heumann approve. Reimmannus and the rest: “presents,” having the same force as “displays” above. BUN.

“Backs marked with spots.” A Greek construction: “marked in respect to their backs.”

“Supported by the smoothness of their scales.” Cellarius doubts whether this is sound. Yet all read thus, with the better spelling *laevitate* [smoothness] with *ae* in Parrh., Betuleius, and Torn. 1587. So in *On Anger*, ch. 10, *laevitudo*, as here *laevitate*, “into slippery courses.” So Pliny, book II, ch. 3, attributes to serpents a body slippery through smoothness. Nor should “supported” be suspect. Our author, ch. 2: “supported by hoofs.” BUN.

[Col. 0032D]

“He sharpened.” On this word consult Savaron, who collected many examples in his notes on Sidonius, book VII and book VIII.

“If you take away.” Thus I restored from all manuscripts and five editions. Eleven common editions have “if you will take away.”

“Each in its own genus.” Thus I emended from the Bologna manuscripts, 4 Royal, Em., Brun., and the Roman, Graph., Betuleius, Tornes., Soubron., 2 Parisian, Isaeus, Cellarius, and Walch editions, with the approval of Betuleius and Francius. The others read “also.”

“Can.” I corrected this from the manuscripts and almost all editions. Five recent common editions have “could.”

“But nevertheless since.” The *but* was added from manuscripts 2 Royal, 2 Bologna, Tax., 2 Colbert, Baluze, Clermont in a second hand, and five editions. It is absent from the rest. “But although the very nakedness of man,” etc. Perhaps from this comes the Greeks’ approval of naked statues, because they conceal nothing. Pliny, XXXIV.5: “Nude statues also pleased them,” he says, “holding a spear, modeled from youths in gymnasia; these they call Achilles-statues. It is Greek practice to conceal nothing; Roman and military practice to add breastplates.” And Pliny the Younger, book III, epistle 6, not only excuses but celebrates this nakedness in a bronze statue of an old man which he bought, in these words: “For it is nude and neither conceals faults, if any exist, nor displays its merits too sparingly.” EDMUND FIGRELLIUS.]

running throughout the whole body, through which the circulating moisture and blood might irrigate every member with vital juices. And he covered those organs, formed in the fashion suited to each kind and location, with skin laid over them; this he adorned either with beauty alone, or covered with bristles, or fortified with scales, or embellished with distinguished feathers.

But this is a marvelous contrivance of God: that one disposition and one bodily configuration displays innumerable varieties of image. For in nearly all breathing creatures there is the same sequence and order of members. First comes the head, and joined to it the neck; likewise, the breast is joined to the neck, and from it project the shoulders; the belly adheres to the breast; likewise, the genitals are connected below to the belly; in the last place, the thighs and feet.

[Col. 0031B] And not only do the members preserve their own tenor and position in all creatures, but so do the parts of the members. For on the head itself the ears possess a fixed place, the eyes a fixed place, likewise the nostrils, and the mouth also, and in it the teeth and tongue. Although all these are the same in all living creatures, there is nevertheless an infinite and manifold diversity of formed beings, because the things I have named are either longer or shorter, encompassed by features differing in varied ways.

And is it not divine that, amid so great [Col. 0032A] a multitude of living creatures, every animal is most beautiful in its own genus and species? Thus, if something should in turn be transferred from one to another, it would necessarily seem nothing more obstructive to usefulness, nothing more misshapen in appearance: for example, if you gave an elephant a long neck, or a camel a short one; or if you added feet or hair to serpents, whose evenly extended bodily length serves no other purpose than that, their backs marked with spots and supported by the smoothness of their scales, they may glide in slippery courses with sinuous bends.

But in quadrupeds the same craftsman drew the structure of the spine from the top of the head, extended it farther beyond the body, and sharpened it into a tail, so that the shameful parts of the body might be covered because of their ugliness, or fortified because of their tenderness; and so that certain small and harmful creatures might be driven from the body by its motion. If you take away this member, the animal becomes imperfect and weak. But where there are reason and hands, it is no more necessary than a covering of hair. So fittingly does each thing agree in its own genus that nothing more ugly can be imagined than either a naked quadruped or a clothed human being.

But although the very nakedness of a human being contributes wonderfully to beauty, it did not suit the head as well; [Col. 0033A] [Note: [Col. 0033B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 33–34]]

“For how great a deformity there would be in it is evident from baldness.” These words are absent from the Goth., 3 Colbert, Lipsius, Clermont, Brun., and Bov. manuscripts, and from the Roman edition and four other older editions. Compare Theodoret, Discourse 4, *On Providence* (*peri pronoias*), and Histories 51 and 53, narrated by Isidore of Pelusium. [Col. 0033C] PRICAEUS. — Yet this is peculiar to the human being, unless it is innate. Pliny frequently discusses the ugliness of baldness among authors. Hence the praise of baldness, an *adoxos* [paradoxical, “unregarded”] argument. Moreover, on the beauty of hair, read ch. II of the First Epistle to the Corinthians. Christ’s own saying testifies that God’s providence appears even in hairs, when he says that not even a hair of the head falls without the Father’s will. Theodoret should be consulted—that great admirer of Providence—in his fourth discourse on the Providence of God, where he considers the rationale of hairs. Later he speaks of the use and adornment of hair. Then he treats at length the disgrace of baldness.

“The highest summit of the structure.” Thus in ch. 10: “The head is, as it were, the summit of the whole divine work.” Thus in ch. 8 he calls the head “the highest peak”; our author and others gladly add “highest” to the terms *summit* and *peak*. So Livy, book I, ch. 34, calls the head “the highest summit of man”; and Lactantius, book VI, ch. 13: “to the highest summit”; book VI, ch. 24: “the highest peak.” BUN.

for how great a deformity there would be in it is evident from baldness. Therefore he covered it with hair; and because it was to stand at the top, he adorned it as though it were the highest summit of a building. This adornment was not forced into a circle or made round in the shape of a cap, lest it be unsightly through the bareness of certain parts; rather, it is spread out in one place and drawn back in another according to the suitability of each location. Thus the forehead, encircled all around, the hair flowing from the temples before the ears, their upper parts bound about in the fashion of a crown, and the whole back of the head covered, display an appearance of marvelous beauty.

Moreover, it is incredible how much the rationale of the beard contributes, whether to discerning the maturity of bodies, to distinguishing the sexes, or to the beauty of manhood and strength. Thus the design of the whole work would plainly not have held together if anything had been made otherwise.

## Chapter VIII. On the parts of the human being: the eyes and ears

[Col. 0033B] Now I shall set forth the design of the whole human being, and explain the uses and configurations of the individual members, whether exposed or covered in the body. Therefore, when God had decided to make from among all animals only the human being heavenly, and all the rest earthly, he raised this one erect for contemplation of heaven and made him two-footed, so that he might look toward that place from which his origin comes. But he pressed the others down to the earth, so that, since they have no expectation of immortality, cast with their whole bodies upon the ground, they might serve their bellies and fodder.

Accordingly, the upright arrangement and lofty stance of the human being alone, and a countenance shared with and akin to God the Father, bear witness to his origin and his Maker. His almost divine mind, because it has received dominion not only over the living creatures on earth but also over its own body, is placed in the highest head and, as though in a lofty citadel, surveys and beholds all things. He formed this palace of the mind not drawn out and extended, as in dumb animals, but like a circle and globe, because every roundness is characteristic of perfect reason and form. Therefore the mind and that divine fire are covered there as though by heaven; and when he had covered its highest [Col. 0035A] [Note: [Col. 0035C] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 35–36]]
