summit with its natural covering, he also equipped and adorned at once the front part, called the face, with the necessary functions of the members.

And first, he enclosed the globes of the eyes in hollow cavities. Varro thought that the forehead (*frons*) was named from this boring (*foratus*). He willed that they should be neither fewer nor more than two, because for appearance no number is more perfect than two. So also with the two ears, whose duality displays an incredible degree of beauty: both because each part is adorned by its similarity to the other, and because voices approaching from opposite directions may be more readily gathered. Their form itself is also made in a marvelous manner, because he did not wish their openings to be bare and unprotected, which would have been less beautiful and less useful. For a voice could pass beyond the narrowness of simple [Col. 0035B] cavities unless the openings themselves held it in, once [Col. 0036A] received through the hollow windings and retained by reverberation. They are like the small vessels set upon vessels with narrow mouths, by which the latter are customarily filled.

Therefore God the craftsman did not wish the ears—so named from receiving voices, whence Virgil says:

> . . . and with these ears I drank in the voice;

or because the Greeks call the voice itself *audē* [“utterance,” *αὐδή*], and from hearing (*auditus*), through alteration of a letter, ears (*aures*) are named as though *audes*—to be fashioned from soft skins, which, hanging and flaccid, would diminish beauty; nor from hard and solid bones, lest, immovable and rigid, they be unfit for use. Instead, he devised something intermediate between these, so that a softer cartilage might bind them and they might possess strength at once suitable and [Col. 0036B] flexible. In them the function of hearing alone is established, [Col. 0037A] [Note: [Col. 0037B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 37–38]]

“He covered them with translucent membranes.” Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II. ISAEUS.

“So that images of objects placed opposite, gleaming as though in a mirror, might penetrate to the inner sense,” [Col. 0037C] etc. He touches upon that celebrated and difficult question concerning the manner and mechanism of sight, over which the leading philosophers of various schools labored: some asserting that vision occurs through inward reception; others through the influx or efflux of material and bodily things; others through that of spiritual and immaterial things. On this subject see Plato, *Timaeus*, on the eyes; Aristotle, *On the Soul* II, text 66 and following, and *On Sense and Sensible Things*, ch. 2; Lucretius IV; Plutarch, *Opinions of the Philosophers* IV.13; Gellius V.16; Macrobius, *Saturnalia* III.14; Galen X.12 and *On the Opinions of Hippocrates and Plato* VII.9 and following; Averroes, *Colliget* III.38. What Lactantius thinks is not sufficiently clear. From the words placed above, he seems indeed to assert that images of things penetrate to the inner sense—that is, are received inwardly—which very weighty scholars have maintained was taught not only by Aristotle but also by Plato: Leonicus, in the introductory statements of his commentary on *On Sense and Sensible Things* and its second book; Scaliger, *On Subtlety against Cardano*, Exercise 325, ch. 5; and others. ISAEUS.

“That sense which is called mind,” etc. In accordance with the common saying of Heraclitus, mentioned by Aristotle, *Problems*, section 11, problem 33: “Mind sees; mind hears.” But he would have spoken better had he said “soul” or “spirit,” for I said above, *Institutions*, book VII, ch. 12, that Lactantius understands *mind* and *soul* very differently from their true meaning. ISAEUS.

“Sees through what is outside.” Lipsius, second edition: “perceives through.” I alter nothing. He imitates Lucretius IV.272–279: “things outside . . . are seen through.” BUN.

“That we see through the impact of images.” Thus we read in all editions and manuscripts except 1 Colbert, which has “impacts”; manuscripts 2 Bologna, 2 Royal, Tax., 2 Colbert, Baluze, Clermont have “collisions.”

“As the philosophers have said.” Manuscripts 2 Colbert, Em., Brun., and the editions of Betuleius and Cellarius: “discuss.” The rest as in the text.

“Or through the tension of air, with the visual ray,” etc. This opinion does not send forth rays, but holds that the air near the pupil is driven against the things seen by rays from the pupil, and that vision thus occurs with the aid, as it were the support and conveyance, of the air itself. For the struck air that touches the pupil is supposed to be driven toward the object, where it forms the base of a cone whose apex is in the pupil itself. Lactantius’ reasoning shows this invention not merely empty, but also false because we see no worse when we step backward, though this impulse cannot occur while retreating, but only while standing still or moving forward. Moreover, air will not penetrate beneath water, though things placed at the bottom of water are seen. ISAEUS.

“Or through the emission of rays.” This was the opinion of all opticians and of most philosophers down to Aristotle. Averroes afterward reproves those whom Galen followed; compare Julius Caesar Scaliger, *On Subtlety*, Exercise 298, ch. 16, with any of the ancients. ISAEUS.

“We would see the ray toward which we direct our eyes.” Thus 3 Royal, 2 Colbert, and the old Roman, Tridentine, and Florentine editions. The other printed editions and manuscripts—except 1 old Bologna, which has “eyes”—read: “we would see more slowly than we direct our eyes.” But our reading gives a much clearer sense.

“That it is the mind which, through the eyes,” etc. Salvian, *On Providence* III.7: “Knowing that the light of the eyes are, in a way, windows of our minds.” Others have called the eyes the gates of the soul; Origen Adamantius, *Physiognomy* I.1; Cicero, *On the Orator*, calls them indicators of the soul. just as in the eyes the function of seeing is established. Their subtlety is especially inexplicable and marvelous, because he made their globes, displaying the likeness of gems, covered on the side from which sight was required with translucent membranes, so that images of objects placed opposite, gleaming as though in a mirror, might penetrate to the inner sense. Therefore, through these membranes, that sense called mind sees through the things outside.

Lest perhaps you suppose that we see through the impact of images, as the philosophers have said—since the function of seeing must be in that which sees, not in that which is seen—or through the tension of air, together with the visual ray or the emission of rays: for if that were so, we would see the ray toward which we direct our eyes, until the tense air with its visual ray, or the emitted rays, reached the object to be seen [Col. 0037B].

When we see at the same instant of time—and often while occupied with something else—nevertheless all the things placed before us, it is truer and more evident that it is the mind which sees through the eyes the objects opposite it, as though through windows covered with shining glass or mirror-stone. Therefore the mind and the will are often discerned from the eyes.

In order to refute this, Lucretius employed an utterly foolish argument. “For if,” he says, “the mind sees through the eyes, then, when the eyes have been torn out and gouged away, it would see more clearly; since doors removed together with their doorposts admit more light than when they are shut.” Clearly he—or rather Epicurus, who taught him—had eyes gouged out, so that he did not see that gouged-out eyeballs, ruptured fibres of the eyes, blood flowing through the veins, flesh growing from the wounds, and finally scars drawn over them can admit no light; unless perhaps he wished eyes to arise like ears, so that we might see not so much with eyes as with holes [Col. 0038B]—than which nothing could be more ugly in appearance or more useless in function. For how little could we see if the mind, from the innermost recesses of the head, attended through tiny fissures of cavities; just as [Col. 0039A]

**“If anyone wishes to see through a reed-pipe . . . let him see.”** From almost all manuscripts I have restored *wishes* (*velit*), which agrees better with *let him see* (*cernat*) than *would wish* (*vellet*), found in all editions and in 2 Reg. and Em., in the latter of which stands *would see* (*cerneret*). if someone should wish to look through a reed-pipe, he would certainly see no more than the capacity of the pipe itself could contain. Therefore, for seeing, organs gathered rather into a rounded form were necessary, so that sight might be spread broadly and, being attached upon the foremost face, might freely behold all things. Thus the ineffable power of divine providence made two very similar orbs and bound them in such a way that they could not be turned completely around, yet could nevertheless be moved and bent within limits. He willed the orbs themselves to be full of pure, clear fluid, and in their middle part to contain enclosed the sparks of light which we call pupils; in these pure and subtle parts reside the faculty and principle of sight. Through these orbs, therefore, the mind directs itself in order to see; and, by a wonderful arrangement, the sight of both lights is blended and joined into one [Col. 0039B].

## Chapter IX. On the Senses and Their Power

At this point I am inclined to criticize the folly of those who, wishing to show that the senses are false, collect many instances in which the eyes are deceived—among them also the fact that to madmen and drunkards everything appears double, as though the cause of that error were obscure. It happens because there are two eyes. But learn how it happens.

The sight of the eyes consists in the mind’s attention. Therefore, since the mind, as has been said above, uses the eyes as windows, this occurs not only to drunkards or madmen [Col. 0040A], but also to people who are healthy and sober. For if you bring something too close, it will appear double; for there is a definite interval and space at which the visual rays of the eyes converge. Likewise, if you call the mind backward, as if to think, and relax the mind’s attention, then the visual ray of each eye is drawn apart, and each begins to see separately.

If you direct the mind again and focus the visual ray, whatever appeared double converges into one. What wonder, then, if the mind, loosened by poison and the potency of wine, cannot direct itself toward seeing, just as neither can the feet toward walking when the numbed sinews are weak? Or if the force of madness raging in the brain separates the harmony of the eyes? This is so true that one-eyed persons, if they become either mad or drunk, can in no way [Col. 0040B] have anything appear double to them. Therefore, if the reason why the eyes are deceived is evident, it is plain that the senses are not false: either they are not deceived when they are sound and unimpaired, or, if they are deceived, the mind is nevertheless not deceived, since it knows their error.

## Chapter X. On the External Members of the Human Being and Their Use

But let us return to God’s works. Therefore, so that the eyes might be better protected from injury, he covered them with the shelter of eyelashes—whence Varro thinks they were called *oculi* (“eyes”). For the eyelids themselves, which possess mobility and have also given the name to fluttering (*palpitatio*), being bordered with hairs standing in a row [Col. 0041A]

> [Note: [Col. 0041B] [Various Notes on columns 41–42]
>
> **“Bordered.”** Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II: “The eyelids too are fortified, as if by a rampart of hairs, so that, even with the eyes open, anything that fell upon them might be repelled; and when they were closed in sleep, when we had no need of our eyes for seeing, they might rest as though wrapped up.” This passage is falsely cited by Nonius Marcellus as from *On the Orator* II. These remarks are drawn from Plato, and Galen speaks similarly.
>
> **“And dry out.”** Cellarius, from the Gothic manuscript and the Leipzig edition, printed *and dry out*; and so I found it in the Reimm. manuscripts. Parrh., Paris., Junt., Ald., Crat., Erasm., Gymn., Fasit., Gryph., Torn., Bet., Thomas., Isaeus, Gall., and Spark prefer *and dry thoroughly*. I judged this compound to be authentic, and did not dare prefer the less ancient manuscripts to so many almost equally ancient editions, derived from very ancient manuscripts.
>
> **“The heights of the eyebrows . . . lest anything . . . fall upon [them].”** Apuleius, *On the Doctrine of Plato* I, p. 16: “The hedge of the eyebrows fortifies the eyes in advance, lest what falls from above disturb the tender and delicate vision.”
>
> **“Rising gently.”** Thus 3 Reg., 2 Bonon., 1 Colbert., and other manuscripts, with almost all common editions. In Regio-Put., 3 other Reg., 4 Colbert., 5 others, the Roman edition of 1470, and Gymnic., *lightly* is read; in 1 Colb., *gentle*; in Marm., *light*. I prefer *gently*, with Cellarius and other learned men, based on Latin idiom, as in Pliny, *Letters* V.6: “The villa, set upon the lower slope of a hill, rises so gently and gradually, the ascent deceiving one, that, though you do not think you are climbing, you realize that you have climbed.” And Calpurnius, *Eclogue* 7.25:
>
> > And gently reclining slopes.
>
> Thus too Julius Caesar, *Gallic War* II: “a gentle ridge of a mountain.”
>
> **“Prominent [parts].”** Heumann thinks that *prominent things* should be read.
>
> **“As far as.”** Absent from the Bov. manuscript.
>
> **“But the lower part softened by adhering cartilage, so that,”** etc. Thus I emended from Regio-Put., 2 other Reg., 2 Colb., Baluz., Clarom., and Sangerm. manuscripts. This seems to me by far the best reading of all. See what precedes. Other manuscripts support it—4 Reg., 4 Colbert., Goth., Em., Cant., Lips., Marm., Brun., and the Roman edition of 1470—in which stands, corruptly, “cartilage adheres, softened.” Almost all common editions divide it as “soft in this manner,” likewise corruptly; Spark has “it adheres to soft cartilage, so that.”
>
> [Col. 0042C]
>
> **“Through its cavities.”** *Its* has been supplied from manuscripts and many editions.
>
> **“Which God himself.”** Thus I corrected it from manuscript 7 Reg., Ultr., Baluz., Brun., the Roman edition of 1470, Graph., Cellar., and Walch., most properly. Thus the author himself below: “the opening itself of the nose,” and “by that very duality.” In manuscripts rec. 1 Colb., Marm., Clarom., and twelve editions, “which God himself” is masculine.
>
> **“By how wonderful.”** Thus I restored it from manuscripts 7 Reg., 5 Colb., Ultr., Baluz., Brun., the Roman edition of 1470, Graph., Cellar., and Walch. Rightly so: our author below says, “how useful, how becoming.” In rec. manuscripts 1 Colb., Clarom., Marm., and eleven common editions, “by so wonderful.”
>
> **“If one single opening.”** The very oldest manuscripts—Regio-Put., 2 Bonon., Tax.—and the editions of Thomas., Is., Thys., and Gall. prefer this reading; Lactantius uses the same wording shortly afterward when he says “one simple structure.” The words *one single* are absent in twenty-four recent manuscripts and thirteen common editions.
>
> **“From which we understand.”** Thus restored from the older editions and from all manuscripts except 1 Reg., in which, as in eight printed editions, stands “from which it is understood.”
>
> **“Therefore.”** Absent in Bov., contrary to the authority of the other manuscripts.
>
> **“Into two parts.”** Galen called them κοιλίας, that is, “cavities” or “ventricles”: “The brain has two κοιλίαι.” He also acknowledges that there are two, according to some, where the ruling faculty of the mind resides. Vesalius certainly adds a third ventricle in figures 5 and 6 of Book VII. Aristotle, *History of Animals* I.16.
>
> **“Yet it has two inner chambers.”** Pliny, *Natural History* II.37: “Within itself it provides the first dwelling-places for mind and blood in a cavernous hollow—threefold in large animals, and in none fewer than two; there the mind dwells,” etc. Hippocrates, in *On the Heart*, calls these chambers γαστέρες; Julius Pollux calls them κόλποι. BETUL.
>
> **“In which are contained the living sources.”** From this source two great veins run toward the front and back; branching into smaller veins, they irrigate all the limbs with vital blood. Pliny. These branches are described by Vesalius in the first and second figures of chapter 15, Book III. BETULEIUS.]

provide a most becoming barrier for the eyes. Their unceasing motion, converging with incomprehensible speed, neither interrupts the continuity of sight nor fails to refresh the gaze. For the visual ray—that transparent membrane—unless it is continually cleansed with moisture so as to shine brightly, dries up, withers, and grows dim. What of the very heights of the eyebrows, adorned with short hairs? Do they not, as if with embankments, both protect the eyes from anything falling from above and at the same time provide beauty? From their meeting-point the nose rises and, extending as though by an even ridge, both separates and protects the two visual rays. Likewise, the becoming swelling of the cheeks below, rising gently in the likeness of hills, makes the eyes safer on every side; and the supreme artificer has provided that, should some more violent blow occur, it may be repelled by these prominences.

The upper part of the nose [Col. 0041B] is formed solid as far as the middle; the lower part, however, is softened by attached cartilage, so that it can be handled for the use of the fingers. Yet in this member, though simple, three functions are established: one, drawing breath; another, receiving smell; a third, allowing the discharges of the brain to flow down through its cavities. God has fashioned these themselves by how wonderful, how divine [Col. 0042A] an arrangement, while ensuring that the very opening of the nose should not deform the appearance of the face. This certainly would have happened if one single opening had stood open. But he separated and divided it, as though by a wall drawn through the middle, and by that very duality made it most beautiful. From this we understand how much the dual number, united in a single and simple structure, contributes to the perfection of things.

For though the body is one, it could not consist wholly of simple members unless there were parts either right or left. Accordingly, just as the two feet and likewise the hands contribute not only some utility and function, whether of walking or making, but also a wonderful form and beauty, so in the head—which is, as it were, the summit of the whole divine work—the supreme artificer has divided hearing into two ears, sight into two visual rays, and smell [Col. 0042B] into two nostrils. For the brain, in which lies the faculty of sensation, although one, is nevertheless divided into two parts by an intervening membrane. And the heart, which seems to be the dwelling-place of wisdom, though one, nevertheless has two inner chambers, divided by an intervening partition, in which are contained the living sources of blood; so that, just as in the world itself the supreme totality of things is either a duality from a simple principle or a simple unity from a duality, and governs and holds together the whole, so in the body, all things formed from two might display an indissoluble unity.

> [Col. 0043A] [Note: [Col. 0043B] [Various Notes on columns 43–44]
>
> **“In . . . the world, the supreme totality of things . . . from a simple principle a duality.”** Thysius and Heumann interpret this as referring to God the Father and the Son. To me it seems to concern the two principal elements, fire and water, from whose discordant concord he shows more fully in *Institutions* II.9 that the world consists. Add the doubtful passage from *Institutions* II.8 in the notes: “By whose mixture and tempering the world and all things in it might consist.” Certainly I do not recall Lactantius anywhere calling God “the totality of things.”
>
> **“The tongue enclosed within, which by its movements distinguishes voice into words.”** Plato, *Timaeus*; Xenophon, in the place cited above; Aristotle, *On the Soul* III at the end, and *History of Animals* IV.16–17; Cicero, in the place cited above; Galen VIII.5, IX.8, II.10, XVI.3. ISAEUS.
>
> **“Unless with the help or impact of the teeth.”** Thus I restored it from manuscripts 3 Reg., 1 Colb., Clarom. in the first hand, Marm., Brun., and Bov., as well as two old Roman editions and Cellarius; manuscripts Goth., 3 Colb., and Leipzig have the corrupt reading *life* instead of *help*. In manuscripts 3 Reg., 2 Colb., Baluz., Clarom., and Sangerm. in the second hand, and in the Aldine and Parrhasian editions, stands *assisted*, which the rest followed, perhaps because it seemed more usual. Yet the simple word is not unusual; for Tacitus says at the beginning of *Annals* XIV.4: “Skill was pleasing, and was in time also helpful.”
>
> **“Returned to infancy.”** Lips. 3 and Reimm. read “dissolved into infancy,” wrongly. *Institutions* VIII.15: “As though returned to a second infancy.” *Institutions* VII.22: “To be returned again to the womb and to go back to infancy.” BUN.
>
> **“In which, among all,”** etc. Thus the common editions, the Bov. and Sangerm. manuscripts, and many others read. But Regio-Put. and one Bolognese manuscript have “which, among all.” The Erasmus manuscript has “which among human beings.” “The tongue performs the function of gathering food in all mute animals, but in this alone, since in the human being it provides a double use.” ERASMUS.—Heumann, however, reads: “which it uses not only in human beings, but also in mute animals.”
>
> **“Therefore Varro [derives it] from binding,”** etc. Isidore, *Origins* II.1, reports that Varro thought *lingua* (“tongue”) was named not from binding food, as Lactantius says, but from licking food; others derive it from binding utterances, because it binds words through articulated sounds. ISAEUS.
>
> [Col. 0044B]
>
> **“May flow out.”** Thus I restored it from the manuscripts, except 1 Bonon., which has “may flow back,” and 2 Reg. and the common editions, which have “may flow down.”
>
> **“And God surrounded it with the fences of teeth,”** etc. Thus I restored it from the Roman edition of 1470, Is., Cellar., Walch., and all manuscripts except Cauc., in which, as in ten printed editions, is read: “and God, enclosing it with the row of teeth.”—“And God surrounded it with the fences of teeth as with a wall.” Gellius, I.15, writes that Homer said the teeth were set as a rampart against the wantonness of words, and he quotes Homer’s verses. ISAEUS.
>
> **“Fixed in a row in a wonderful manner.”** Though recent manuscripts Angl., Goth., Lips., Reimm., and printed editions from 1465–1566 lack these words, and Cellarius and Walch again remove them, this is Lactantius’ genuine reading, attested by the two oldest Bolognese and Taxaq. manuscripts. From these Thomas., Isaeus, Gall., Sparkius, and Heumann rightly judged it should be accepted. In a similar way our author says in chapter 5: “Feathers fixed in a row.” BUN.—Thomas restored these five words rightly from the best manuscripts, 2 Bonon. and Tax.; they are absent from the other manuscripts and common editions, except Is. and Spark.
>
> **“And then adorned [them] with the coverings of the lips.”** The lips are fashioned both to guard the teeth and for the use of speech: Aristotle, *Parts of Animals* II.16. ISAEUS.
>
> **“As in a millstone,”** etc. Hence molar teeth, to which he seems to allude; they are also called jaw-teeth.
>
> **“For grinding.”** Thus 2 Bonon., 7 Reg., 5 Colb., Tax., Pen., Clarom., Brun. manuscripts and the old editions read. In some manuscripts and five common editions *or* is read; in 1 Colb. and Marm., *etc.*
>
> **“The faculty of taste [is] in the palate,”** etc. Aristotle is therefore mistaken, Pliny is mistaken, and with them all antiquity—even learned antiquity—is mistaken. For this word, like *throat*, is often used metonymically by authors for pleasure. Cicero, *On Ends* II, speaking of Laelius’ wisdom: “It does not follow that one whose heart has taste has no taste in his palate”; and Quintilian, I.2, complains that “the palate of children is trained before their speech.” Favorinus in Gellius XV.8 rebukes the governors of cookshops who say that those have no palate who eat the upper parts of birds and fattened fowl. Horace, *Epistles* II:
>
> [Col. 0045B]
>
> > My three guests seem nearly to disagree,
> > demanding very different things according to varying palate.
>
> Philosophers, however, assign the sense of taste to the tongue together with the palate, or throat: Aristotle, *Problems* section 28, and Gellius XIX.2. BETULEIUS.]

The appearance of the mouth also, and its opening spread transversely, cannot be sufficiently described as useful and becoming. Its use consists in two functions: taking nourishment and speaking.

The tongue, enclosed within, distinguishes voice into words by its movements and is the interpreter of the mind. Yet it cannot by itself fulfill the office of speech unless it strikes its point against the palate, unless with the help or impact of the teeth, or the compression of the lips. The teeth, however, contribute more to speech; for infants do not begin to speak before they have teeth, and old people, when they have lost their teeth, stammer so that they seem to have returned [Col. 0043B] once more to infancy. But these things belong only to the human being or to birds, in which the pointed and vibrating tongue, moved in fixed ways, produces innumerable inflections of song and varied modes of sound.

The tongue has, moreover, another function, which it uses in all animals, yet in mute creatures alone: it gathers food crushed and ground by the teeth, presses it together by its force [Col. 0044A], and transmits it to the stomach. Hence Varro thinks that the tongue received its name from binding food together. It also aids beasts in drinking: extending and hollowed, they draw up water; and, so that the water held in the hollow of the tongue may not flow out through delay or lingering, they strike it swiftly against the palate. The tongue is therefore covered by the hollow of the palate as by a shell; and God has surrounded it with the fences of teeth as with a wall.

The teeth themselves, fixed in a row in a wonderful manner, lest, bare and exposed, they should be more frightening than ornamental, he adorned with soft gums—so called from producing teeth—and then with the coverings of the lips. Their hardness, as in a millstone, is greater and rougher than in the other bones, so that they might suffice for grinding food and fodder. The lips [Col. 0044B] themselves, which previously seemed, as it were, to adhere together, he separated most becomingly. The upper lip, directly beneath the middle of the nostrils, he marked with a slight hollow, as if with a valley; the lower, for the sake of beauty, he unfolded gently outward.

For as regards perceiving taste, whoever supposes that this sense resides in the palate is mistaken; it is through the tongue that tastes are perceived—yet not through the whole tongue. Its parts [Col. 0045A]

> [Note: [Col. 0045B] [Various Notes on columns 45–46]
>
> **“Nothing from any substance.”** Thus I restored the reading from the very oldest and best manuscripts: 2 Bon., Regio-Put., 3 other Reg., Cauc., 2 Colbert., and Baluz. The remaining manuscripts and printed editions have “from whatever substance.”
>
> **“The acquisition of smell takes away.”** Thus 2 Bon., Regio-Put., 2 other Reg., Cauc., Baluz., 3 Colb., Clarom. in the margin, and the editions Graph., Thom., Is., and Cellar. read. This reading is, as is evident, not at all corrupt; Lactantius uses here a rare but proper term. *Capio, capionis* means “taking” or “acquisition,” a noun often used by jurists, as in *usucapio* (“acquisition by use”) and *pignorum capio* (“taking of pledges”), in Book VII of the Theodosian Code, “On Exactions,” and the title “On the Sale of Pledges.” Gellius VII.10 teaches that Varro called it *pignoris-capio*, just as Lactantius here speaks of *odoris capio*, “the acquisition of smell.” In the remaining manuscripts and editions *capio* is absent, apparently wrongly, to the detriment of the clarity of the sentence. Thys. and Gall. have, corruptly, *captio*. 
>
> **“The chin gently drawn down from the cheeks,”** etc. Sidonius requires not the milk-white skin of a fat chin, but that of a succulent one; Apuleius too, in his description of Bathyllus, calls for a moderate chin in a face. Anacreon, in his portrait of a beloved woman, asks for a delicate and soft chin. Varro, cited in Nonius, *On Softness*. Arnobius, Book III, calls those *mentiones* whose chin projects more than is proper. FRANC. F. F. JUNIUS.
>
> **“Stiff.”** That is, straight, upright. I noted this at *Institutions* II.1: “stiff and standing”; II.17; and *On the Workmanship*, chapter 8. BUN.
>
> **“The vigorous strength of the projecting muscles, marked by prominent swellings,”** etc. Thus I emended from the very oldest and best manuscripts: 2 Bonon., Regio-Put., 5 other Reg., Cauc., Goth., 5 Colb., Baluz., Ultr., Lips., Em., 1 Sorb., Brun., and Thomas.’ edition. In four recent manuscripts and many editions is “the immense strength of extended muscles”; Marm. has “from so great”; Clarom. “projecting.” See shortly below: “the thumb has two projecting joints.” Hercules is especially praised for his muscles, just as Apollo is for his hair, according to the verse appended to Virgil:
>
> > Apollo is long-haired; Hercules is muscular.
>
> Learned writers also write *thori* (“swellings”). Vesalius, Book II, chapter 2, in discussing muscles, says that a *thorus* is simple flesh covered with fibres. These swellings are especially in that part of the arm beginning at the shoulders and ending at the elbow. Therefore, contrary to the grammarians, *lacerti* must be the upper part of the arm. It should also be noted from passages already cited above that authors rarely mention either *tori* or *lacerti* unless strength is meant, just as the word *brachium* in the Bible corresponds to ὁ βραχίων in the Septuagint. BETULEIUS.
>
> **“What shall I say of the hands,”** etc. Aristaenetus, Book I, letter 16: “I saw the extremities of the hands and feet, the splendid tokens of beauty.” Lactantius here praises broad hands, as does Sidonius; Apuleius likewise makes Bathyllus’ hands tender and somewhat long: “His hands,” he says, “were tender.” Ovid too, *Amores* I.4, does not seem to disapprove of soft hands. Soft and tender hands are contrasted with:
>
> > Hands worn and hardened by Tuscan wool.
>
> From Juvenal, *Satires* V.
>
> **“Spreads out earlier.”** That is, it extends. Thus I corrected it from the best manuscripts—1 Bon., Regio-Put., 1 other Reg. in the second hand, 3 Colb., Clarom., Marm., and Baluz. in the first hand. That is, the thumb indeed begins at the hand, but spreads in another direction earlier, or sooner, than the other fingers. Recent manuscripts 3 Reg., Em., Cant., Brun., and all printed editions have “splits earlier”; 2 Reg., 1 Colb., Baluz., “the hand splits”; 1 Colb., 1 Bonon. rec., and four recent common editions, “the hand spreads.”
>
> **“Which presents itself, as it were, opposite.”** Theodoret, in his fourth discourse *On Providence*, describes the extremely skillful structure and manifold use of the hands in Greek no less elegantly than Lactantius does in Latin.
>
> **“Among the rest.”** Heumann believes Lactantius wrote “above the rest,” that is, “before the rest”; as in *Institutions* I.6: “the Erythraean, who is regarded as more celebrated and more noble among the others.” BUN.
>
> **“Not, like the others, three each.”** From manuscripts 1 Bonon. old, Regio-Put., 5 other Reg., another Reg. in the second hand, Goth., Tax., Lips., 6 Colbert., Clarom., and the Roman edition of 1470, Betul., Tornes., Soubron., Cellar., and Walch., I have restored this reading. In 1 Bon. rec., 1 Reg. in the first hand, Brun., and eleven editions stands *threefold*.—“Three each.” I retain *three each*. Our author seems to have observed Pliny, *Natural History* II.43.99: “The fingers of a human being have three joints each; the thumb two, and bends opposite all the fingers, while by itself it extends obliquely.” BUN.
>
> **“But one is joined to the hand by flesh for the sake of beauty.”** In two very old manuscripts, Cauc. and Reg.-Put., this is written continuously and without any contraction of words, except that the latter has *of the hand*. Eighteen manuscripts have “is joined to the hand by flesh”; and Hecquet, a Parisian physician, thinks this should be read, persuaded by the situation and position of the part. Gaudefridus, a physician of Orléans, would prefer, with six manuscripts and nine editions: “But one is joined to the flesh of the hand for the sake of beauty”; this seems to him our author’s genuine meaning, since Lactantius in this work attends especially to the elegance and beauty of the body. Otherwise “is joined to the hand” would please him more. It would also please Eustachius, a physician of Orléans, who nevertheless prefers, with the Pen. manuscript, “is clothed with flesh at the hand.” He warns that Lactantius errs in saying that the thumb has only two projecting joints, when it has three; the first is not one of the bones of the hand, which have no perceptible motion, whereas the motion of the first joint is most manifest. Thus our Firmianus, as seems inferable from the middle of chapter 5, recognized two kinds of joints in the thumb: two, namely, projecting and visible; the other joined to the hand and concealed by muscles, which is the third: “One indeed is clothed with flesh at the hand.” Jo. Cauci: “is covered with flesh.”]

on either side, being more delicate, receive taste through extremely subtle senses. And although nothing is diminished from either food or drink, nevertheless the flavour penetrates to the sense in an indescribable manner, by the same principle by which the acquisition of smell takes nothing away from any substance.

How beautiful the remaining parts are can scarcely be expressed. The chin gently drawn down from the cheeks and so enclosed below that a lightly impressed division seems to mark its extreme point; the straight and smooth neck; the shoulders lowered from the nape like gentle ridges; the arms strong and braced with sinews for strength; the vigorous power of projecting muscles marked by prominent swellings; the useful and becoming bending of the elbows. What shall I say of the hands, ministers of reason and wisdom? The most skillful artificer formed them with a flat, moderately hollow palm, so that, if anything must be held, it may suitably rest there, and terminated them in fingers. In these it is difficult to determine whether beauty [Col. 0046A] or usefulness is greater.

For the number is complete and full, their arrangement and gradation most becoming, the curvature of the paired joints flexible, and the rounded form of the nails, enclosing and strengthening the tips of the fingers with hollow coverings so that the softness of the flesh should not give way in holding, provides great ornament. But this is wonderfully suited to use: one finger, separated from the others, rises with the hand itself and spreads earlier in another direction. Presenting itself, as it were, opposite the others, it alone—or above all—possesses the entire faculty of holding and making, like the ruler and governor of all; whence it also received the name *pollex* (“thumb”), because it is powerful in strength and authority among the rest. It has indeed two projecting joints, not three each like the others; but one is joined to the hand by flesh for the sake of beauty [Col. 0046B]. For if it too had been divided into three joints, an ugly and ungraceful appearance would have taken away the hands’ beauty.

Already the breadth of the chest, raised aloft and exposed to the eyes, displays a remarkable dignity of appearance. The reason for this is that God seems to have formed the human being alone as if lying on his back (for scarcely any other animal can lie upon its back), but to have fashioned the mute animals as though lying upon one side, and pressed down toward the earth. Therefore their breast is narrow, withdrawn from sight, and cast down toward the ground; but that of the human being is open and erect, because, being filled with reason bestowed from heaven, it ought not to be lowly or unseemly. The nipples also, gently projecting and encircled by darker, small rings, add no little grace: in women they are given for nourishing offspring; in men, for ornament alone, lest the breast should seem shapeless and, as it were, mutilated. Beneath this lies the flat expanse of the belly, which the navel marks almost at its center with a not unseemly sign [Col. 0047B], being made for this purpose: that through it the fetus, while in the womb, may be nourished.

[Col. 0048A] CHAPTER XI. On the intestines in the human being, and their use.

It necessarily follows that I should begin also to speak of the internal organs. To these, since they are hidden, beauty has not been assigned, but an incredible usefulness; for it was necessary that this earthly body should be nourished by some juice derived from foods and drinks, just as the earth itself is nourished by rains and frosts. The most provident craftsman made in its middle a receptacle for foods, so that, when these had been digested and liquefied, he might distribute their vital juices to all the limbs. But since the human being consists of body and soul, the receptacle of which I have spoken supplies nourishment to the body alone; for the soul he gave another seat.

For he made a kind of organ, soft and [Col. 0048B] porous, which we call the lung, into which breath might pass in reciprocal alternation; and he did not fashion it in the manner of a womb, lest breath should be discharged all at once or inflated all at once. Thus he made it not even a solid organ, but one capable of inflation and of receiving air, so that gradually [Col. 0049A]

> [Note: [Col. 0049B] Notes of Various Scholars on Columns 49–50]

**“The alternation of exhaling, inhaling, and the process of breathing,” etc.** For this reason it is compared to a bellows; or rather, human art has imitated natural ingenuity. See Theodoret, *Third Discourse on the Providence of God*. The word *flandi* (“exhaling”) is read in MSS 2 Reg., 2 Bon., 2 Colb., Baluz., and in nearly all the common editions. It is absent, however, from 15 manuscripts and also from the Roman editions and Cellarius; but it must be retained. *Flandi*, that is, giving out air drawn in by the breath . . . *spirandi*, that is, admitting air drawn in by the breath: for the whole process of breathing consists in this reciprocal movement of admitted and discharged air, that is, the entire business of respiration. Accordingly, one should read “the alternation of exhaling and inhaling,” omitting the comma placed between *flandi* and *spirandi*; it will be better placed after *spirandi*, since the alternation discussed here is not that of exhaling only, but also of inhaling. HECQUET.

**“Sustains life,” etc.** Yet in such a way that whatever useful and necessary to life has been processed in the lungs is conveyed to the left ventricle of the heart; whatever is useless is breathed out by the way through which we inhaled. On this matter see Theodoret, who discusses it with admiration. BETULEIUS.

**“Which nourishes the soul.”** Do not understand here the rational soul, but that vital soul which we share with brute animals. ISAEUS.

**“So that the neck may be bent and moved easily.”** These words are absent from 19 manuscripts and from the two old Roman editions and Cellarius. In 3 Colbert manuscripts and in Baluz., *facillime* (“very easily”) stands in place of the adverb *facile*.

**“There must be two tubes through the neck . . . one for food and one for breath.”** That which Lactantius calls the food-tube is the gullet [*gula*], called οἰσοφάγος (*oesophagus*) by the Greeks. Some also call it στόμαχος (*stomach*), including Celsus and Galen themselves. The breath-tube is the τραχεῖα ἀρτηρία, “rough artery,” of the Greeks, because it consists of cartilaginous rings. Our author calls it the *gurgulio* [windpipe]. BETUL.

**“For that passage which is from the mouth.”** Thus restored from all printed editions and manuscripts, except one recent Colbert manuscript and the Gallic edition, in which the reading is *Illi enim qua*.

**“In the manner of a reed.”** Virgil, *Eclogue* 2:

> I have a pipe made fast  
> Of seven unequal reeds.

**“And this passage is always open.”** Thus the manuscripts; the editions have *hinc* (“from here”).

**“The nostrils,” etc.** Galen enumerates the instruments of breathing: nostrils, mouth, throat, windpipe, and lungs; and the vessels of nourishment: mouth, teeth, stomach, belly, jejunum, and small intestines. Besides, according to Festus, there is another derivation of *nares* [nostrils]: namely, because through those openings of the nose we become aware of every odor. BETUL.

**“Or breath does not cease to flow through the nostril.”** Thus Festus and Isidore, *Origins*, book XI, chapter 1, who have *manare* (“to flow”) for *nare*; but the latter must here be restored. ISAEUS. Here *nare* means the same as “to flow.” **“Which are, as it were, the entrances of this tube.”** These words had to be restored to Lactantius from Bonon., Tax., Pen., Lips.; they are lacking in the others.

**“It also opens through to the mouth.”** I have thus emended from MSS 2 Bonon., Tax., Regio-Put., 3 other Reg., 5 Colb., 4 Oxon., Goth., Pen., Lips., Em., Gat., Marm., Sorbon., [Col. 0050C] Vict., Baluz., Clarom., the edition of Cellarius, and Walch, with better sense than the words found in 4 recent manuscripts and the editions, *verba iter patet*, which cannot accord with the syntax in any way. He said *interpatet* (“opens through”), because it does not proceed straight to the mouth but toward the nostrils. It is, however, somewhat open toward the mouth and also has a passage to it. This word is sufficiently Latin. Thus Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book VII, chapter 15, said that the lung “opens through with fissures.” This is partly from THYSIUS. Nor is our Lactantius the author of this word; it occurs also in others.

**“The hills of the throat.”** Johannes Caucus and Isaeus think *tolles* should be read, a reading I have found in no manuscript. In one recent Colbert manuscript is *calles faucium* (“paths of the throat”); in 2 recent Reg. manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1474, Venetian of 1490, Florentine, Juntine, and Graphian editions, *folles faucium* (“bellows of the throat”). But in MSS 2 Bonon., Regio-Put. and 4 other Reg., 7 Vatican, 5 Colb., Sorbon., Ultr., Cant., Em., Cant., Gat., Marm., Vict., Clarom., Baluz., Brun., and in 14 common editions, the reading is *colles faucium*. Let the reader consider whether *tolles* should be read in place of *colles* and *folles*. For *tolles* are glands, so called from a certain resemblance to an acorn. *Tolles* or *toles* is (as Festus observes) a swelling in the throat; by diminution they are called *tonsillae* [tonsils]. Pliny, book II, chapter 37: “tonsils in the human being, glands in the sow.” But *tolles*, or tonsils, which Celsus calls glands, are called *amygdalae* [almonds] by later physicians and *paristhmia* by the Greeks. They are called *tolles* from *tollere*, “to raise,” because they raise a part into a swelling. Perhaps, however, it would be preferable (says Hecquet) to read *tolli* rather than *tollere*. The passage would then be restored thus: “Where the *tolles* of the throat, facing the uvula, begin to be raised into a swelling.” If only the manuscripts favored this reading; against their testimony I have wished to alter nothing. For nothing prevents a swelling of the throat from being called a hill, and the most expert physicians Gaudeffridus and Eustachius do not object.

**“If, as the passage of the gullet.”** Thus I have restored from the oldest and best manuscripts of all, 1 Bonon. and Regio-Put., and from the edition of Isaeus. This reads better than *sicut gulae iter* (“just as the passage of the gullet”), the reading of 12 recent manuscripts and the editions. Supporting our text also are 2 Colb., Baluz., Brun., in which only *sicut gulae iter* is read, with *si* deleted. [Col. 0051C]

it might receive breath as the vital air is diffused through that porousness, and gradually give it out again as it issues from it. For that very alternation of exhaling and inhaling, the process of breathing, sustains life in the body.

Since, then, there are two receptacles in the human being, one for air, which nourishes the soul, and the other for food, which nourishes the body, it is necessary, so that the neck may be bent and moved easily, for there to be two tubes through the neck: one for food and one for breath. Of these, the upper carries from the mouth to the stomach, the lower from the nostrils to the lungs. Their function and nature are different. The passage from the mouth is made soft and such that it always remains closed and joined together, like the mouth itself, because drink and food, being bodily things, make room for their passage when the gullet is moved aside and opened [Col. 0049B]. Breath, on the other hand, being incorporeal and subtle, could not make room for itself; it therefore received an open way, called the *gurgulio* [windpipe]. It consists of flexible, soft bones, like rings fitted together and joined one to another in the manner of a reed; and this passage is always open.

For breath can have no rest from moving, because it continually passes back and forth; by the useful lowering from the brain of that part of the organ called the uvula, it is checked, as by a kind of obstacle, lest, coming with force and drawing in pestilential air, it corrupt the tenderness of its dwelling, or convey all the violence of its harmfulness to the internal receptacles. For this reason also the nostrils are opened narrowly. They are so called because through them either odor or breath does not cease to flow; they are, as it were, the entrances of this tube. Yet this breath-tube opens not only toward the nostrils but also through to the mouth, at the furthest regions of the palate, where the hills of the throat, facing the uvula, begin to raise it into a swelling. [Col. 0050B]

The reason and rationale for this are not obscure. We would not have the faculty of speech if, just as the passage of the gullet opened only toward the mouth, so the windpipe opened only toward the nostrils; [Col. 0051A]

> [Note: [Col. 0051C] Notes of Various Scholars on Columns 51–52]

**“Nor could breath issuing from it produce speech without the service of the tongue.”** These words have been supplied from MSS 2 Bonon., 1 Reg., Tax., 3 Colb., Baluz., Sorbon., Clarom. in the margin, and the editions of Isaeus and Spark, where they are lacking in the others and in the edition of O. F. Fritzsche itself.

**“For whoever thinks otherwise is mistaken,” etc.** Therefore Hippocrates, prince of physicians, is mistaken when, in Aphorism 59 of book VII, he says that those whose brain has been shaken from some cause must immediately become mute; and in Aphorism 5 of book V he indicates that this evil may also arise from drunkenness, and that it is so deadly, if the person has convulsions, unless seized by fever. See Vuilichius on these matters. BETUL.

**“Through their nostrils, as though lowing.”** I have added *quasi* (“as though”) from the manuscripts.—“They pour forth as though lowing.” The cause of the condition and injury is nearly the same in the mute and the deaf. See Aristotle, *Problems* 2 and 4, section 33; Alexander of Aphrodisias, *Problems* 138. IS.

**“Of speakers.”** *De* stands for *ex* (“from”). This is frequent in Lactantius and in Ovid, Florus, and Justin; Burmannus identified their passages in his notes on Ovid, *Amores*, book I, 10.8:

> And whatever love wrought from great Jupiter. BUN.

**“Hearing too,” etc.** Experience proves the contrary. Indeed, those born deaf must necessarily be mute.—**“Hearing too must be obstructed.”** This is so if it has occurred naturally and from birth; but if it comes later through some illness, physicians state that it is not necessary, as Aphrodisias reports in the passage cited above. IS.

**“May not even be able to admit [sound].”** From 21 manuscripts and 10 old editions I have deleted the word *auditum* (“hearing”), which seems quite superfluous, since the discussion concerns emitting a voice and admitting a voice—though some understand it otherwise. *Ne auditum admittere quidem possit* (“may not even be able to admit hearing”) is wrongly read in 2 Bonon., Tax., and 6 more recent common editions.

**“We may draw air.”** Thus I have restored from the most ancient MSS 1 Bonon., Reg., Put., Cauc., Ultr., 3 Colb., Baluz., Vict., Brun., and the Roman edition of 1470. That this is the proper reading is clear from what precedes. In 2 recent Reg., 3 Colb., Clarom., and many printed editions occurs *possumus*, wrongly. [Col. 0052C]

**“Breath be strangled.”** Isaeus and Gaudeffridus think that *strangulemur* (“we be strangled”) should be read, because strangulation pertains to the human being, not the air. But the manuscripts and editions, except Isaeus, oppose this. One may, however, say that air is strangled—that is, compressed in the throat.

**“Their juice,” etc.** This is not the function of the belly but of the intestines, which preserve for a while the juice received from the stomach, until, conveyed through the mesenteric vein to the liver, it is converted into blood, and thence all the limbs of the body are nourished. BETUL.

**“The many coils of the intestines,” etc.** Especially of that which is called εἰλεοί (*eileoi*, ileum), namely, the slender intestine. Pliny calls them “most winding circles,” Celsus “folds.” BETUL.

**“And yet constricted by one bond.”** Thus 15 manuscripts, two of which are the most ancient, and 8 editions. In 10 recent manuscripts and 7 recent printed editions: *et uno tantum* (“and by one only”). Both readings are sound and come to the same thing. [Col. 0052D]

**“And yet lest they perhaps adhere anywhere.”** Thus I have emended *necubi*, meaning *ne alicubi* (“lest anywhere”), from the oldest and best MSS 2 Bonon., Regio-Put., 1 other Reg., 3 Colb., Baluz., Tax. In 7 recent manuscripts: *ne cui*; in six recent manuscripts and common editions: *ne qui*.

**“He coated.”** This is the correct reading, which I restored from the Tornesian and Erasmus manuscripts and from the Graphian and Betuleian editions. The same statement, Erasmus attests, occurs in Aristotle and Pliny. In 9 manuscripts and 6 recent printed editions: *opplevit* (“he filled up”), wrongly.

**“Might glide.”** Thus I have emended from the most ancient MSS 1 Bonon., Regio-Put., 4 other Reg., Pen., Goth., 4 Colb., Vict., Gat., Marm., Clarom., Brun., and the old editions 3 Rom., Aldine 1515, Paris 1525, Parrhasian, Florentine, Graphian, Isaean, and Cellarian; this is more correct than *mitterentur* (“might be sent”), found in 9 recent manuscripts and 6 common editions.

**“The bladder, the use of which birds,” etc.** Pliny: “Below the belly on the fore part is the bladder, which belongs to none of the animals that lay eggs except the tortoise [thus far from Aristotle], to none except those having a blood-filled [i.e. vascular] lung, to none of those lacking feet,” etc. BETUL.

nor could breath issuing from it produce speech without the service of the tongue.

Therefore divine ingenuity opened a route for the voice from that breath-tube, so that the tongue might perform its function and, by its movements, divide the unbroken stream of voice itself into words. If this passage is obstructed in any way, it must produce muteness. For whoever thinks that people are mute for another reason is certainly mistaken. They do not, as is commonly believed, have a tongue bound fast; rather, they pour forth that vocal breath through their nostrils, as though lowing, because the voice has either no passage at all to the mouth or not one so open that it can emit a full voice. This generally occurs by nature; sometimes it also happens by accident, when, through some illness, this entrance is blocked and does not transmit voice to the tongue [Col. 0051B], thus making speakers mute. When this happens, hearing too must necessarily be obstructed, so that, because the person cannot emit a voice, he may not even be able to admit one.

This passage, then, was opened for the sake of speech. It also provides this: in taking baths, because the nostrils cannot endure heat, hot air may be drawn through the mouth; likewise, if perhaps the passages of the nostrils are blocked by the phlegm of a cold, we may draw air through the mouth, lest, when the faculty of passage is obstructed, breath be strangled. But when foods received into the belly and mixed with the moisture of drink have already been cooked by heat, their juice, spread throughout the limbs in an indescribable manner [Col. 0052A], moistens and invigorates the whole body.

How marvelous, too, is God’s work in the many coils of the intestines, their length wound back upon itself and yet constricted by one bond! For when the belly has discharged from itself the foods reduced to a soft mass, they are gradually forced through those winding recesses of the internal parts, so that whatever nutritive juice they contain may be distributed to all the limbs. And yet, lest they perhaps adhere anywhere and stop—something that could occur because of the bends of their coils repeatedly returning upon themselves, and could not occur without harm—he coated them within with a thicker juice, so that those excretions of the belly might more easily glide through the slipperiness toward their exits.

There is also a most subtle design in this: although the bladder, which birds do not have, is separate from the intestines and has no tube [Col. 0052B] through which to draw urine from them, it is nevertheless filled and distended with fluid. How this happens is not difficult to see. The parts of the intestines which receive food and drink from the belly are more open than the other coils and much thinner. These surround and enclose the bladder. When food and drink, mixed together, reach these parts, the thicker matter becomes excrement and passes on, while all the fluid is filtered through that delicate substance; and the bladder, whose membrane is equally thin and fine, absorbs and collects it in order to discharge it outside through the outlet which nature has opened.

[Col. 0053A] CHAPTER XII.

> [Note: [Col. 0053B] Notes of Various Scholars on Columns 53–54]

**On the womb, etc.** Cellarius says that what is set forth in this and the following chapter concerning the formation of the human being in the womb contains much popular opinion, which it would have been better and more decorous for Lactantius also to pass over in silence. Whoever wishes to learn truer things should turn to philosophers who investigate nature.

**“Understanding.”** Thus the Sangerman and Bov. manuscripts; the editions have the less satisfactory *sensus* (“senses”). Heumann considers our reading the true one.

**“Which contains the seed.”** Thus I have restored from MSS Regio-Put., 2 other Reg., Brun., and the edition of Betuleius, supported by MSS Bodl., Baluz., 3 Colb., Clarom. in the margin, in which is *quae seminum rationem continet* (“which contains the principle of seeds”); in 3 Reg., 2 Colbert from the first hand, and the Roman edition of 1470, *quae semina continet* (“which contains seeds”); in Marm., *quae semina continent*; in one recent Colbert manuscript and many editions, *quae semen continet*.

[Col. 0053C]

**“Thus.”** So MSS Bov.; the rest have *itemque* (“and likewise”).

**“The two seminal veins.”** These are described in medical definitions thus: Παραστάται (*parastatai*, “standing beside”; Philip translated it *vasa assistentia*, “attending vessels”). Observe in passing that he again insists on the dual number. Yet from Vesalius’s description I do not find two channels for semen in the penis. BETUL.

**“Yet joined in one structure.”** Thus I emend from the old MSS 2 Bonon., Cauc., 6 Reg., 4 Colb., Tax., Pen., Ultr., Vic., Gat., Marm., Brun., and the two old Roman editions, Fasitel., Betul. In 4 recent manuscripts and 9 printed editions is *in una tantum* (“in one only”); in 4 recent common editions, *una tantum*, without the preposition.

**“When cut open.”** Heumann correctly judges that *intersecta* (“cut open”) should be read, because this is a matter of anatomy.

**“Are opened.”** That is, “are cut open.” FRANCIUS.

**“The right contains male seed,” etc.** Plutarch and Censorinus make Anaxagoras and Empedocles authors of this view. Read Aristotle, book IV [Col. 0053D] *On the Generation of Animals*, chapter 1. It is Aphorism 48 of Hippocrates. BETUL.

**“And indeed throughout the whole body.”** I follow the greater part of the oldest and best manuscripts, along with Isaeus, Grapheus, and Cellarius. *Et ideo* (“and therefore”) is read in 10 recent manuscripts and 13 editions: both readings are good.

**“Some think [it comes] from the marrow alone; some.”** Thus MSS Bonon., Regio-Put., 1 other Reg., 2 Colb., 1 Sorb., and nearly all editions; but the recent MSS 4 Reg., 4 Colbert., Goth., Lips., Em., Cant., Vict., Gat., Marm., Clarom., Brun., the two Roman editions, and Cellarius, omitting the five preceding words, have: “some say [it comes] from the entire body.” This, moreover, is Plato’s view in the *Timaeus*, lightly sampled, evidently by someone attending to something else. Censorinus attributes this doctrine to Hippo. BETUL.—**“Some think [it comes] from the marrow alone.”** Aristotle said that it flows down from the brain through the spine, *Problems* 56, section 10.—**“Some [think it comes] from the whole body,”** as Aristotle reports, book I *On the Generation of Animals*, chapter 17; he refutes the opinion in chapter 18. ISAEUS.

[Col. 0054B]

**“Are folded about.”** The word is attested in Faber from Prudentius alone, apart from its occurrence in our author; I have also observed it in Gellius, book XVII, chapter 9. BUN.

**“Like the horns of a ram.”** Let us first hear Pliny on the names of the womb. “Women,” he says, “have all these things, except the little sac joined to the bladder, whence it is called *uterus* [womb], though they also call it *loci* [places]. In other animals, it is the *vulva*.” For the ram’s horns, and thus the form of the womb, read Vesalius, book V, chapter 15, as well as figure 25 of that book and several following in order. BUNEMAN.

**Varro.** Perhaps in the book which Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, attests was written by Varro himself, *On Human Origin*. It no longer exists. ISAEUS.

**“Varro and Aristotle.”** Aristotle expressly denies these matters in book I *On Generation*, chapter 20. There was once controversy among authors on this subject. I shall add Censorinus’s words: “This also makes the opinion among authors uncertain: whether offspring are born from the father’s seed alone, as Diogenes, Hippo, and the Stoics wrote; or also from the mother’s, as Anaxagoras, Alcmaeon, Parmenides, Empedocles, and Epicurus held. Pythagoras,” Plutarch says, “Democritus, and Epicurus thought that women too emit seed. For they have reversed seminal passages” (ἔχει γὰρ περαστάτας ἀπεστραμμένας, “for they have reversed passages”), “and for this reason,” they say, “have a desire arising from sexual intercourse.” Aristotle and Plato say that women emit a moist substance (ὕλην ὑγράν, “moist matter”), like sweat from exertion in wrestling, but not at all seminal substance. Hippo says that women do indeed emit seed, no less than men, but that it does not contribute to generation because it falls outside the womb (διὰ τὸ ἐκτὸς πίπτειν τῆς ὑστέρας, “because it falls outside the womb”); whence some women often emit seed without any intercourse, especially widows. Some maintain that bones come from the male, flesh from the female. Hippocrates in the book *On Generation* (whether it is the work of his disciple Polybus) asserts that women too eject seed suitable for generation.” BETUL.—**“And Aristotle.”** But he seems rather to deny this in book I *On the Generation of Animals*, chapter 18 and following, with whom St Thomas agrees in *Third Part*, question 31, article 5, reply to 3. Yet, because some other very celebrated authors defend the contrary view, Cajetan, who discusses the question extensively, should be consulted: 2–2, question 154, article 2. ISAEUS.

**“They say not only.”** Five recent manuscripts and 14 editions have *Aiunt enim* (“for they say”).

**“And hence offspring are generally born resembling their mothers.”** It would take too long to report in detail what philosophers thought about the resemblance of offspring. We shall indicate only some passages of authors. See Aristotle, book IV *On the Generation of Animals*, chapter 3, and book VII *History of Animals*, chapter 6; Plutarch, *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*, book V, chapters 11 and 12; Stobaeus, in the *Physical Eclogues*; Galen, book II *On Semen*; Pliny, book VII, chapter 12; Solinus, chapter 5; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, περὶ τῆς τῶν λογ` ἐξετ. [title abbreviated and materially uncertain in the source]; Strabo, book XV; Augustine, book V *Against Julian*, [Col. 0055B] chapter 9; Isidore, book II *Origins*, chapter 1; Pedro Mexía, book I *Various Readings*, chapter XIII; Levinus Lemnius, book I *On the Hidden Miracles of Nature*, chapter 4; Johannes Riolanus, *On Human Procreation*, chapter 12; Franciscus Bonamicius, *On Foods*, chapter 34; Balduinus Ronsseus, *On the Origin of Human Life*, chapter 10. LINDENBROGIUS.

On the womb, conception, and the sexes.

Since we are speaking of internal things, it is necessary also to speak of the womb and conception, lest we seem to have omitted anything. Although these matters lie hidden in concealment, they cannot lie hidden from understanding and intelligence. In males, the vessel which contains the seed is double, somewhat farther inward than that receptacle of obscene fluid. For just as there are two kidneys, so there are two testes, and likewise two seminal vessels, yet joined together in one structure. This we see in the bodies of animals when they are cut open. But the right-hand vessel contains male [Col. 0053B] seed, the left-hand female seed; and indeed [Col. 0054A] throughout the whole body the right side is male, the left female.

Some think that the seed flows to the genital vessel and is there formed, from the marrow alone; others, from the whole body. But how this occurs the human mind cannot comprehend. Likewise, in women the womb divides into two parts, which spread and bend in different directions, winding around like the horns of a ram. The part which turns toward the right is male; that which turns toward the left, female.

Varro and Aristotle judge that conception occurs thus. They say that not only males but females also possess seed, and that hence offspring are generally born resembling their mothers [Col. 0054B]; but that their seed is purified [Col. 0055A]

> [Note: [Col. 0055B] Notes of Various Scholars on Columns 55–56]

**“But that their seed is purified blood.”** Aristotle writes thus, and thus I write with five old editions and nearly all manuscripts; and three very expert physicians whom I consulted think this should be read. One recent Reg. manuscript, one Colbert manuscript, and 11 printed editions have *sanguine* (“with blood”), wrongly. For ancient physicians thought, says Hecquet, that menstrual blood entered into the formation of the human being.

**“And first, indeed, the human heart,” etc.** The conjunction *et* (“and”) has been added from the manuscripts and editions, except Gallic and Spark, in which it is lacking. Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, chapter 5, reviewing many opinions of many persons, says that in this matter Empedocles’ doctrine followed Aristotle. No other passage of Aristotle occurs readily to me except perhaps that in book III *On the Parts of Animals*, chapter 2, according to Theodore’s division 4, where indeed he does not make it the first of the parts of the human body: ἀλλὰ ἔναιμος πρώτη γινομένη τῶν μορίων ἁπάντων, “but [it is] the first of all the parts to become blood-filled.” He supports this with plausible reasons: namely, because it is the source of blood, and for this very reason because it diffuses itself from almost the middle of the body into the whole body. Perhaps Pliny also, as usual, followed Aristotle. His words are: “They relate that the heart is formed first in those being born in the womb, then the brain, and the eyes last of all.” But in Plutarch and Galen, ὀσφύν, that is, “the loins,” like a ship’s keel, are attributed to Aristotle as being formed first; the heart, however, according to physicians, inasmuch as the origin of veins and arteries is in it. Yet Galen, in *On the Formation of Fetuses*, says that it is formed after the liver, refuting the doctrines of Chrysippus and the Stoics. BETULEIUS.

**“Be formed.”** Thus I have restored from 19 better and older manuscripts and the edition of Cellarius. In 9 recent manuscripts [Col. 0055D] and 15 common editions is *confingi cor hominis* (“that the human heart be formed”). On this matter see Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, chapter 5, where he reviews philosophers’ opinions about the formation of the human being.—**“And first, indeed, the human heart be formed.”** Aristotle gives the reason, and Pliny, book X, chapter 53, reports this is considered true in all animals. Censorinus, chapter 5, gives various opinions. ISAEUS.

**“All life.”** Thus I have restored from 21 superior manuscripts and the editions of Cellarius and Walch. In 5 recent copies and 14 printed editions is *vita hominis* (“the life of the human being”).

**“And wisdom.”** In accordance with the opinion of those who hold that the mind is located in the heart; on this more fully below, chapter 16. ISAEUS.

**“The whole work.”** One Colbert manuscript and Brun., and the edition of Betuleius, have *totum corpus* (“the whole body”). Both readings are sound; the same variation occurs below in chapter 13: “The whole work is completed on the fortieth day.” Plutarch, book V *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*: Hippocrates thought that a male’s formation occurred in 30 days, a female’s in 42. Aristotle, however, book VII [Col. 0056B] *History of Animals*, chapter 3, set a longer period, namely 40 days for males and three months for females. LINDENBROGIUS.—There is nevertheless a different account for each sex. For Pliny, book VII, chapter 6, assigns movement in the womb to males on the fortieth day, to females on the ninetieth. Perhaps he transferred these statements from Aristotle, as he did most things, having nonetheless omitted or changed certain matters. See also Plutarch, book V *Opinions*, chapter 13. BETUL.—**“Finally, the whole work is completed on the fortieth day.”** Pliny indeed says this, book VII, chapter 6; Plutarch, *Opinions*, book V, chapter 21, however, reviews opinions. Gellius, book III, chapter 10, reports that Varro wrote not forty days, as Lactantius here reports, but forty-nine. ISAEUS.

**“That the eyes are formed first,” etc.** William Harvey demonstrates excellently that this conflicts with experience in his most learned little book *On the Generation of Animals*; one should not hesitate to consult his outstanding observations on this subject. GALLAEUS.—Aristotle also says in *On Generation* II that the eyes of all animals are formed late, without exception.—**“Yet in avian fetuses the eyes are formed first.”** Almost everyone opposes this opinion, as Pliny reports in the chapter cited, chapter 53. ISAEUS.

**“May take its beginning.”** As in book I of the *Institutes*, chapter 2: *principium sumere* (“to take a beginning”). Macrobius, *Dream of Scipio*, book I, chapter 18: “Let us take our beginning from one [source].” BUN.

**“Resemblances,” etc.** On this read especially Hippocrates, περὶ τοῦ θόνου [reading uncertain; perhaps *On the Seed*]; Galen, *On the Formation of Fetuses*; Aristotle, book IV *On the Generation of Animals*, chapter 3. Seek the doctrines of philosophers on this matter in Censorinus, Plutarch, and Galen, in the passages already cited above. BETUL.—**“But they think that resemblances in the bodies of children occur thus,” etc.** That is, certain persons, against whom Aristotle argues, book I *On the Generation of Animals*, chapter 3; he subsequently states his own opinion in the same book, chapters 17 and following, and book X *On the Generation of Animals*, chapter 3. ISAEUS.

**“If the male [seed] prevails,” etc.** These things do not always apply. See Hippocrates, Galen, Aristotle.

[Col. 0056D]

**“To result resembling the father.”** Recent MSS 1 Reg., 1 Colb., Gat., Brun. have *pervenire*; Marm., 1 recent Colb., and the edition of Isaeus, *provehi*. The great majority of the rest have the text’s reading.

**“Occurs.”** MSS Gat., Marm. and many editions wrongly add *solet* (“usually”), which the remaining manuscripts and the two Roman editions and Cellarius reject.

**“Equal.”** That is, “equal in amount,” as in the note on book II of the *Institutes*, chapter 8; Livy, book II, chapter 3, end: “to live under equal law with the rest.” BUN.

**“From equal seed.”** The better manuscripts—Reg.-Put., 2 other Reg., 2 Colb., Clarom., Brun.—and the Roman edition of 1470 and Graph., supported by one other Colb. manuscript which has *sementa*, prove that Lactantius wrote this. In 3 Reg., 3 Colb., Marm., Baluz., and 13 editions: *semine*, a more usual term substituted by later copyists.

blood; and that, if it is rightly mixed with the male seed, both are united, coagulate together, and take form. First, indeed, they hold that the human heart is formed, because in it are all life and wisdom; finally, that the whole work is completed on the fortieth day. These things have perhaps been inferred from miscarriages. Yet in the fetuses of birds it is beyond doubt that the eyes are formed first, as we often discover in eggs. Hence I think it cannot be that formation does not take its beginning from the head.

They think that resemblances in the bodies of children occur thus. When the seeds, mingled with one another, unite, if the male seed prevails, the child results resembling the father, whether male [Col. 0055B] or female; if the female seed has the greater force, the offspring [Col. 0056A] of either sex corresponds in appearance to the mother. Of the two, that which is more abundant prevails; for in some manner it embraces and encloses the other. Hence it generally happens that the offspring displays the features of one parent only. But if there is an equal mixture from equal seed, the forms too are mingled, so that the joint offspring seems to resemble neither parent, because it does not possess the whole from either one, or both, because it has borrowed a part from each. For in animal bodies we see either the colors of the parents blended and a third color produced, resembling neither parent, or the features of both so expressed that a harmonious mixture is varied throughout the body by differently colored limbs. In this way natures that differ are also [Col. 0056B] [Col. 0057A]

> [Note: [Col. 0057C] Notes of Various Scholars on Columns 57–58]

**“Properly produced.”** Thus I have restored from 20 manuscripts, eight old editions, and Cellarius. In six recent manuscripts and as many common editions: *recte pervenire*.

**“How marvelous an ordinance of God!”** In accordance with nearly all manuscripts, I have deleted after *Dei* (“of God”) the word *est*, which occurred in 11 common editions. In 13 manuscripts and the two old Roman editions: *constitutum Dei* (“an ordinance of God”); in the Graphian edition: *constitutum Deo* (“ordained by God”).

**“Successive offspring.”** Thus with all printed editions, MSS 3 Reg., 1 Colb., Vict., Brun., and correctly. In 2 Bonon., Pen., Tax., Cauc.: *successiva soboles*; in 3 Reg., 3 Colb., Gat., 1 Sorbon., Clarom. in a second hand: *subsiciva*; five others corruptly: *subscina*, *subvicina*, etc.; 1 Reg. Put.: *sicut soboles*, corruptly. “Successive offspring might be produced”: this is the true reading, approved by three most learned physicians. Six manuscripts have *pararetur*, and not improperly.

**“Thus a man,” etc.** Cicero likewise affirms the same thing in the second book of the *Tusculan Disputations*: “Courage is most properly a man’s characteristic; its two greatest functions are contempt for death and pain. We must therefore employ these if we possess virtue—or rather, if we wish to be men; because *virtus* [courage/virtue] has borrowed its name from *viri* [men].” Thus also the Greek ἡ ἀνδρεία (*andreia*, courage), from ἀνήρ (*anēr*, man). BETUL.

**“Likewise, woman [mulier], as Varro interprets, [is named] from softness [mollitia].”** Six recent manuscripts and 12 common editions add *est dicta* (“is so called”), but needlessly. See what precedes. These two words are absent from the old and best MSS 1 Bonon., Regio-Put., 4 other Reg., 4 Colbert., Pen., Vict., Gat., Marm., Clarom., Brun., and seven old editions. All attribute this derivation to Varro; yet this word is more commonly used to distinguish a woman who has known a man from a virgin, especially among jurists. Nearly the same distinction exists among the Greeks, who call her παρθένον (*parthenon*, virgin) who has not had a man; νύμφην (*nymphēn*, bride) who has had a man but has not borne a child by him; γυναῖκα (*gynaika*, woman/wife) who has also borne a child; and γραῦν (*graun*, old woman) who has ceased to bear: this distinction appears in Isaac Tzetzes’ commentary on Lycophron. In Sacred Scripture, ἡ γυνή (*hē gynē*) is generally used in place of ἡ ἄλοχος (*hē alochos*, wife). BETUL.

**“For the nourishment of the newborn, with milky springs.”** Thus I have emended from the oldest MSS 2 Bonon., Cauc., Regio-Put., 3 other Reg., 6 Colb., Tax., Pen., Ultr., Em., Vict., Gat., Marm., Clar., Baluz., Brun., and the edition of Betuleius, supported by 1 Sorbon. manuscript in which occurs *ad nutrimenta nascentibus fontibus lacteis*; in 2 Reg. and 14 common editions: *nascentis fontibus lactis*; in 3 other editions: *nascentibus fontibus lactis*. The editions of 1472 and 1478 also have *fontibus lacteis*.—**“Milky springs.”** Thus he calls the breasts; Gellius too, book XII, chapter 1, calls them “that most holy spring of the body, the nourisher of the human race,” etc. Basil, *Homily 9 on the Hexaemeron*: ἐπιζήτει δὲ τὰς οἰκείας πηγὰς τοῦ γάλακτος, “seek the proper springs of milk,” etc. Augustine, *Confessions* I, chapter 7. If the seed of male stock should happen to fall into the left-hand part of the womb, the belief is that a male is indeed conceived; but because he was conceived in the female part, he has something feminine in himself, beyond what masculine dignity permits: exceptional beauty, excessive fairness, bodily lightness, delicate limbs, short stature, a slender voice, a weak spirit, or several of these. Likewise, if seed of the female sex flows into the right-hand part, a female is indeed produced; but because she was conceived in the male part, she has something of virility in herself beyond what the nature of her sex permits: strong limbs, excessive height, a dark complexion, a hairy face, an unbecoming countenance, a powerful voice, a bold spirit, or several of these.

But if the male seed reaches the right side and the female seed the [Col. 0057B] left, both offspring develop properly, so that women retain in every respect the beauty proper to their nature, while men preserve masculine strength in both mind and body. How marvelous, moreover, is this very ordinance of God: for the preservation of each kind, he devised the two sexes, male and female, so that, when they were joined to one another through the enticements of pleasure, successive offspring might be produced, lest the condition of mortality extinguish every kind of living creature. But greater strength was assigned to males, so that women might more readily be compelled to endure the marital yoke. A man (*vir*) was therefore so named because there is greater strength (*vis*) in him than in a woman; and from this *virtue* (*virtus*) received its name. Likewise, *woman* (*mulier*), as Varro interprets it, [Col. 0057C] derives from softness (*mollities*), with a letter altered and removed, [Col. 0058A] as though *mollier* (“softer”). When she has conceived a fetus and childbirth has begun to approach, her swelling breasts are distended with sweet fluids, and her fertile breast overflows with milky springs for the nourishment of the child being born. For it was fitting that a rational creature should draw nourishment from the region of the heart. This too was most skillfully arranged: that a bright white and rich fluid should moisten the tenderness of the new body until it is furnished with teeth and strengthened with vigor so as to receive stronger foods. But let us return to our subject, so that we may briefly explain the remaining matters.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Lower Limbs

I could now explain to you the marvelous design of the genital [Col. 0058B] organs themselves, were modesty not to recall me from discourse of this kind. Accordingly, let the things that are shameful be veiled by us with the covering of modesty. As far as this matter is concerned, it is enough to complain that impious and profane human beings commit the greatest sacrilege when they turn the divine and marvelous work of God—provided and accomplished by an inconceivable design for perpetuating succession—either to the most disgraceful forms of gain or to the shameful acts of obscene lust, so that from a most sacred thing they now seek nothing other than empty and barren pleasure. What of the remaining parts of the body? Are they devoid of design and beauty? How well suited to the function of sitting is the flesh gathered into the buttocks! And it is firmer there than in the other limbs, lest it yield down to the bones beneath the pressure of the body’s [Col. 0058C] mass. Likewise, the elongated length of the thighs, strong with broader [Col. 0059A] [Note: [Col. 0059B] [Various Editors’ Notes on columns 59–60]

In French too it is called *péritoine*. From BETULEIUS.

By which the abdomen is enclosed as in a net. That is, the abdomen is enveloped by that membrane as by a net. That membrane, or peritoneum, embraces the stomach, intestines, omentum, mesentery, liver, spleen, kidneys, both bladders, the womb, and finally every vessel situated between the diaphragm and the legs. What of the spleen? Since many arteries are scattered through the spleen, it receives heat from the heart, by which it more thoroughly cooks that dreg-like and muddy blood, and it takes from it something by which it is nourished. BETUL.

What of the liver? What, Lactantius? Do you not know that this is a noble organ? Do you not know that it is foremost among the organs of the nutritive faculty? Do you not know what Plato says: Ὅτι τὸ ἧπαρ πέφυκε χάριν τῆς μαντικῆς (*Hoti to hēpar pephyke charin tēs mantikēs*, “that the liver was naturally formed for the sake of divination”)?
