From agitated blood. This at least is true: the substance [Col. 0060D] of the liver is extremely similar to recently congealed blood. BETUL.

What of the gall, etc. Yellow bile—whose vesicle is called the *bile sac* by the Latins and χοληδόκος (*cholēdokos*, “bile-receiving”) by the Greeks—does indeed assail health in an extraordinary way; nevertheless, it too has its benefits. For, in order that the blood may be purified, an excess of yellow bile must be diverted elsewhere. For bile is, as Pliny says, nothing other than the refuse of the worst blood. There must therefore be a receptacle in which the bile both warms the liver and preserves it from putrefaction. It also drives nourishment into the intestines and wipes away the filth of the intestines. See Vesalius discussing this fully in chapter 8 of Book V; and Pliny, Book XXVIII, chapter 9, enumerating medicines derived from animals: “Among all things,” he says, “the bile of animals is more outstanding in its effect. For its power is to heat, bite, split, draw out, and disperse,” etc. BETULEIUS.

What of the globe of the heart? Likewise, the lower legs were not fashioned with a uniform shape, lest an unbecoming configuration disfigure the feet; rather, with rounded calves gently projecting and gradually tapering, they have been both strengthened and adorned.

In the soles of the feet there is indeed the same design as in the hands, yet one markedly different. Since they are, as it were, the foundations of the entire body, the marvelous craftsman did not fashion them in a rounded shape—lest a human being be unable to stand, or need other feet for standing, as quadrupeds do—but made them more extended and longer, so that by their flatness they might render the body stable; from this [Col. 0059B] their name, *plantae*, was given to them. There are likewise as many toes as fingers on the hands, displaying beauty rather than greater usefulness; they are therefore joined together, short, and arranged in graduated order. The largest of them, because it did not need to be separated from the others as in the hand, was brought into line with them, yet in such a way that it appears to differ from the others in size [Col. 0060A] and by a small interval. This graceful brotherhood of the toes gives no slight support to the feet’s exertion; for we cannot be impelled into a run unless, with our toes pressed into the earth and braced against the ground, we gather momentum and spring forward. I appear to have explained everything whose rationale can be understood. I now come to those matters that are either doubtful or obscure.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Unknown Rationale of Certain Internal Organs

It is agreed that there are many things in the body whose power and rationale no one except their maker can discern. Does anyone think that he can explain what utility or function belongs to that thin translucent membrane by which the abdomen is enclosed as in a net and covered? What is the purpose of the kidneys’ paired resemblance? Varro says that they were so named because streams (*rivi*) of obscene fluid arise from them; but this is very far from the truth, since they adhere to the spine on either side when one lies supine and are separated from the intestines. What of the spleen? What of the liver? These viscera appear to have been congealed, as it were, from agitated blood. What of the extremely bitter fluid of the gall? What of the globe of the heart? Unless perhaps we think we must believe those who hold that the emotion of anger is located in the gall, fear in the heart, and joy in the spleen. They maintain that the function of the liver itself is to digest the food in the abdomen by embracing and warming it; some think that desires for sexual acts are contained in the liver.

First, the keenness of human perception cannot discern these matters, because the functions of these organs lie concealed, and they do not reveal their uses when exposed. For if it were so, perhaps all the gentler animals would have either no gall at all or less of it than wild beasts; the more timid would have had more heart, the more lustful more liver, and the more playful more spleen. Therefore, just as we perceive that we hear with our ears, see with our eyes, and smell with our nostrils, so surely we would perceive that we grow angry with our gall, desire with our liver, and rejoice with our spleen. But since we do not in the least perceive whence those emotions arise, [Col. 0061B] it is possible both that they arise elsewhere and that those internal organs accomplish something other than what we suppose. Yet we cannot prove that those who debate these matters [Col. 0062A] are speaking falsely. But I judge that everything pertaining to the movements of the mind and soul is of such obscure and profound rationale that clearly to perceive it lies beyond humanity. Nevertheless, this should be regarded as certain and indubitable: so many things, so many kinds of internal organs, have one and the same function—to contain the soul within the body. But who except the craftsman, to whom alone his work is known, can know what particular function has been assigned to each?

## CHAPTER XV. On the Voice

What account, moreover, can we give of the voice? The grammarians and philosophers define the voice as air struck by breath; from this, they say, *words* (*verba*) received their name—a claim that is manifestly false. For voice is not generated outside the mouth but within it. The more probable opinion is therefore [Col. 0062B] that compressed breath, when it strikes against the obstruction of the throat, produces the sound of the voice. In the same way, when we send breath down into an open reed-pipe held beneath the lip, [Col. 0063A] [Note: [Col. 0063B] [Various Editors’ Notes on columns 63–64]

While on meeting the descending breath it returns. In several printed editions *while* was missing; I have restored it from the MSS., nine of which have *returns*, while another has *brings back*. Ten MSS. and 14 [Col. 0063C] printed texts read: *by meeting it, it sends the descending breath back*; wrongly.

It has therefore not been comprehended, etc. On the contrary, it has been comprehended sufficiently. Both are produced by respiration, as Aristotle’s definition has taught us. Among the διαλεκτικά (*dialektika*), that is, the instruments of speech, Galen, in the first book of *Affected Parts*, assigns first place [Col. 0063D] to the tongue, which he calls the κυριώτατον ὄργανον (*kyriōtaton organon*, “most authoritative instrument”); then the nostrils, lips, and teeth. By their impacts these cause the otherwise open voice to hiss with consonants and render it ἔναρθρον καὶ ἐγγράμματον (*enarthron kai engrammaton*, “articulate and expressible in letters”). Aristotle makes the throat and lungs the instruments of respiration. BETUL.

At all. I have retained in the text this word, which occurs in the oldest and best MSS.—Regius-Puteanus, Bonon., and others—and in nearly all the printed editions, although it is absent from 15 recent MSS. and 2 Roman editions.

Various things, therefore, have been debated by the philosophers concerning its nature and location. Some affirm that its location is the heart, as Aristotle and Chrysippus do; others the head, as Plato and Galen, who treats this question fully throughout [Col. 0064B] Books II and III of *The Opinions of Hippocrates and Plato*. See Lucretius, Book III; Plutarch, Book IV of *Opinions*, chapter 2 and following. ISAEUS.

Some wished the seat of the mind to be in the breast, etc. Parmenides and Epicurus, namely ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ θώρακι (*en holō tō thōraki*, “in the whole chest”); the Stoics unanimously place the entire mind in the heart. Diogenes places it in the arterial ventricle of the heart, which according to Plutarch is the animal—that is, spiritual—ventricle. Those who called prudent people *cordati* (“men of heart”) appear to have held this opinion. On this matter let us hear Cicero’s discussion in Book I of the *Tusculan Disputations*: “There is great disagreement over what the mind itself is, where it is, and whence it comes. To some the heart [Col. 0064C] itself appears to be the mind; from this people are called *excordes*, *vecordes*, and *concordes*. Empedocles, however, judges that the mind is the blood suffused about the heart. To others, a certain part of the brain appeared to hold the mind’s governing power. Others were satisfied neither that the heart itself nor that a certain part of the brain was the mind; rather, some said that the seat and location of the mind was in the heart, others in the brain,” etc. Many expressions occur everywhere in the authors by which deliberation and thought are placed in the breast and heart. But leaving those aside, let us see what Holy Scripture says, in which the term νοῦς (*nous*, “mind”) is used in various senses. Paul also uses it for the governing part of the mind, which they call the ἡγεμονικόν (*hēgemonikon*), Romans 7:23. Christ calls the mind “light,” Matthew 6:22. *Soul* and *spirit* signify the mind more than once, as in these words of the blessed Virgin in Luke 1:46–47. Νοῦς is used for the understanding in 1 Corinthians 14:15. Moreover, that the language of Scripture makes the heart the seat of the mind and, as it were, a kind of workshop of thoughts and deliberations cannot be at all obscure to those who are not [Col. 0064D] drowsily engaged with it. “With the heart one believes unto righteousness,” says Paul. Believing, however, is a function of the mind—and indeed of a mind purified and illuminated through the Holy Spirit. It would be an endless task to collect testimonies on this matter; let this one therefore suffice: the Lord is called καρδιογνώστης (*kardiognōstēs*, “knower of hearts”) in Acts 1 and 15. The authority of Scripture must therefore be thrust upon and set before those who, relying on arguments, maintain doctrines that conflict with one another. Theodoret, Discourse III *On Providence*, assigns to the heart command or government over the whole body; and Jerome asserts this in many places. Yet there is no lack of scriptural testimonies by which it can be demonstrated that the heart is the seat of the emotions. For the Lord searches the kidneys no less than the heart; and when he examines the heart, he tests whether it is sufficiently contrite and humbled, or seethes with envy or hatred. For here the law of the flesh holds sway for the most part. BETUL.

Its seat in the brain. Plutarch: Πλάτων, Δημόκριτος, ἐν ὅλῃ τῇ κεφαλῇ, Στράτων ἐν μεσοφρύῳ (*Platōn, Dēmokritos, en holē tē kephalē, Stratōn en mesophryō*: “Plato and Democritus place it in the whole head; Strato between the eyebrows”). See the quite lengthy discussion in Vesalius’ anatomical work, Book VI. BETUL.]

the breath, beaten back within the hollow of the pipe and turned around from its bottom, while on meeting the descending breath it returns, produces a sound as it strives toward the outlet; rebounding into vocal breath, the wind is of itself given life. Whether this is true, God the craftsman will know. For the voice appears to arise not from the mouth but from the innermost breast. Indeed, even when the mouth is closed, such sound as can be made is emitted from the nostrils. Moreover, even by the greatest breath, with which we pant, no voice is produced; yet by a slight and unconstricted breath it is produced whenever we wish. It has therefore not been comprehended how it is produced, or what it is at all. Nor should you suppose that I am now slipping into the position of the Academy, since not all things are incomprehensible. For just as it must be admitted that many things are unknown because God willed them to exceed human understanding, so nevertheless there are many things that [Col. 0063B] can both be perceived by the senses and comprehended by reason. But we shall have a separate and complete disputation against the philosophers. Let us therefore finish the course that we are now running.

[Col. 0064A]

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Mind and Its Seat

Who does not know that the rationale of the mind too is incomprehensible—unless he has no mind at all—when it is unknown where the mind itself is located or what sort of thing it is? Various things, therefore, have been debated by the philosophers concerning its nature and location. But I shall not conceal what I myself think—not because I affirm that it is so, which is what a foolish person does in a doubtful matter, but so that, once the difficulty of the matter has been set forth, you may understand how great is the majesty of divine works. Some wished the seat of the mind to be in the breast. If that is so, how marvelous a thing it is that something situated in a dark and shadowy dwelling should move amid so great a light of reason and understanding! [Col. 0064B] And then there is the fact that sensations reach it from every part of the body, so that it seems to be present in every region of the limbs. Others said that its seat was in the brain. [Col. 0065A] [Note: [Col. 0065C] [Various Editors’ Notes on columns 65–66]

To dwell as though in a citadel. So 2 Royal MSS. and Cant. together with nearly all editions. Twenty-five MSS., among them two of the oldest, have *in the citadel of the body*; but wrongly, since the word *body* occurred immediately before in the preceding line.

Since the organs serving hearing, sight, and smell are located in the head. Three recent MSS. and all printed editions read *are*. The best MSS., the Regius-Puteanus and 13 others, have the subjunctive *should be*; rightly. See the preceding expressions: “that it should possess . . . that it should govern.”

But when it is engaged in some thought. I have restored this from the oldest MSS., the Regius-Puteanus, Bonon., Cauc., and 16 others. Three recent MSS. and the common editions read: *but whenever it is engaged in some thought*.

To withdraw. I have restored this from all the MSS. and the old printed editions. Three recent common editions have *to yield*.

[Col. 0065D]

When from the brain to the breast, etc. Therefore, Lactantius, by your judgment Pythagoras was far astray when he established the heart and brain as the boundaries or limits of the soul’s dominion. God is spirit; the mind is something divine. From this it follows that the mind or soul is ἀσώματον (*asōmaton*, “incorporeal”). The mind therefore has no need at all of spatial circumscription. I pass over the fact that the brain, the seat of the mind, not only prepares the animal spirit in such subtle form that it is fit for carrying out divine operations, but also distributes the instruments of the senses through the nerves as though through cords. The senses do not merely obey the commands of either part of the soul; at their nod all the particles of the body stand on guard, awaiting an order. For if the will—that is, the dictate of right reason—commands that something be seen, the eyes’ function is then immediately at hand. The same rationale applies to the other sensory organs, limbs, and remaining members. BETULEIUS.

But if it is not so. I have restored this reading from the oldest MSS.—the Regius-Puteanus, 2 Bologna MSS., Cauc., and seven others. In [Col. 0066C] the others the last two words are missing, and in some only the last; four old editions read: *But if it is not so, this nevertheless*. The Bov. MS. has, quite correctly: *But if it is not, it is nevertheless no less marvelous*.

Which is called mind or soul. Lactantius therefore takes *mens* and *animus* as referring to the same thing. So Lucretius often does in Book III, and Cicero in the *Dream of Scipio*, where Macrobius should be consulted at the cited chapter 14. ISAEUS.

Power. In the Bov. MS., *virtue*.

Bound. So the Bov. MS.; others have *entangled*, less correctly.

In any way. In the Bov. MS., *by any means*, and that is quite good.—Bunemannus has *by any means* and supplies the following note.—*By any means.* So Goth., Lips., and Reimm. Editions before Cellarius have *in any way*. I prefer the former here because *means* follows below in the phrase “by what means.” Our author is fond of fullness of expression. In the Venice editions of 1471, 1493, and 1497, and in Pier., the reading is *by no means*. BUN.

[Col. 0066D]

Confined. In the Bov. MS., *infused*.

The soul does not see itself, etc. According to Plotinus it will be able to do so when purged and purified; according to Catholics, however, when the soul has been freed from the body. BETUL.

Which is also possible. I restore this from the better MSS. and the edition of Graph. Others have *which also indeed* or *and which indeed*.

Xenocrates. Cicero, Book IV of the *Academic Questions*, enumerating the various opinions of various thinkers: “Or, as Xenocrates holds, is the mind devoid of any body—a thing whose nature can scarcely be understood?” etc. Moreover, Xenocrates’ argument, as reported by Nemesius, is this:

> Every body is nourished.  
> The soul is not nourished;  
> Therefore the soul is not a body.

BETUL.

Neither what the mind itself is nor of what sort. I have added *itself* from the oldest and best MS., the Regius-Puteanus, as well as another Royal MS., 2 Colbert MSS., Em., Brun., and the edition of Graph.]

And indeed they used plausible arguments: namely, that what possessed governance of the whole body ought rather to dwell at its summit, as though in a citadel; and that nothing is more exalted than that which governs the whole by reason, just as the lord and ruler of the world himself is at the summit. Then there is the fact that all the sensory organs—that is, the members serving hearing, sight, and smell—are located in the head, and that all their pathways lead not to the breast but to the brain. Otherwise we would necessarily perceive more slowly, until the faculty of sensation descended by a long journey through the neck all the way to the breast. Those men, then, are either not greatly mistaken or perhaps not mistaken at all.

For the mind, which holds dominion over the body, appears to be established at the summit of the head, like God in heaven; but when it is engaged in some thought, it appears to travel to the breast [Col. 0065B] and withdraw, as it were, into some hidden inner sanctuary, so that it may draw out and bring forth counsel as from a concealed treasury. For this reason, when we are intent upon thought, and when the occupied mind has hidden itself in the depths, we are accustomed neither to hear the things sounding around us nor to see those standing before us. If this is so, it is certainly marvelous how it occurs, since no path lies open from the brain to the breast. But if it is not so, it is nevertheless no less marvelous that, by some divine rationale unknown to me, it comes to appear so. Can anyone fail to marvel that this living and heavenly sense, which is called mind or soul, possesses such mobility that it does not rest even when lulled to sleep; [Col. 0065C] and such speed that in a single point of time it surveys [Col. 0066A] the whole heaven and, if it wishes, flies across the seas, travels through lands and cities, and finally sets before its own sight anything it pleases, however far and widely removed?

And does anyone marvel if the divine mind of God, extending throughout every part of the world, ranges through it and rules all things, governs all things, present everywhere and diffused everywhere, when so great is the power and potency of the human mind confined within a mortal body that not even the barriers of this heavy and sluggish body, to which it is bound, can in any way restrain it from granting itself, impatient of rest, the free capacity to wander? Therefore, whether the mind dwells in the head or in the breast, can anyone comprehend what power of reason brings it about that this incomprehensible sense should cling either within the marrow of the brain [Col. 0066B] or within that divided blood which is confined in the heart? And can he fail to infer from this very fact how great is the power of God, since the soul does not see itself—what sort of thing it is or where it is—and, even if it could see itself, still could not perceive by what means an incorporeal thing has been joined to a corporeal thing? Or perhaps the mind has no location, but, dispersed throughout the whole body, ranges through it—a thing which is also possible and was argued by Xenocrates, Plato’s disciple—since sensation is immediately present in every part of the body. Yet neither what the mind itself is nor of what sort can be understood, since its nature is so subtle and fine that, infused into the solid internal organs, it mingles with all the limbs by a living and, as it were, burning sensibility.

[Col. 0066C] But take care never to suppose it at all likely to be true, [Col. 0067A] [Note: [Col. 0067C] [Various Editors’ Notes on columns 67–68]

What Aristoxenus said, etc. The first part of this doctrine is attributed more often to Dicaearchus than to Aristoxenus; nevertheless, it is attributed to both. Cicero, Book I of the *Tusculan Disputations*: “Dicaearchus indeed and Aristoxenus, because it was difficult to understand what the soul was or of what sort, said that there was no soul at all.” But a little earlier in the same work: “Let us omit Dicaearchus, together with Aristoxenus, his contemporary and fellow student—learned men, certainly—of whom the former appears never even to have felt pain, since he does not perceive that he possesses a soul; while the latter is so delighted by his own melodies that he attempts to transfer them even to this subject,” etc. BETULEIUS. On the opinion of Aristoxenus, see Lactantius, Book VII of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 13. *At all.* Missing from the Bov. MSS.

Namely. Restored from all the MSS. and 8 old editions. Five common editions read *as it is*.

what Aristoxenus said, namely—
Source/review notes: The supplied source itself ends mid-sentence after “Magna”; the retained “Great” is the inherited boundary fragment.

Just as strings are properly stretched for a harmonious sound. Thus I have restored the text from the most ancient manuscripts—Caucasian, Regio-Palatine, five other Royal manuscripts, four Colbertine, Victorine, Taxaquian, Emmanuelean, Cambridge, Gatakerian, Marmoutier, Clairvaux, Brunellian—and ten old printed editions and two recent ones, Cellarius and Walch. In seven manuscripts and six common editions it reads: “just as strings properly stretched produce a harmonious sound.”

Broken. Thus I restored it from the aforementioned manuscripts and from the editions of Betuleius and Cellarius. In six recent manuscripts and fourteen common editions it is *interceptum*, “interrupted.”

Contracts a defect. The more familiar expression is “to make a defect.” Cicero, *Topics* III: “If those buildings collapsed and developed a defect.” See chapter 4, and Rhellicanus, Glandorp, and Brant on Caesar, *Spanish War*, ch. 19: “The tower developed a defect from its foundation.” BUN.

To kill sensation. That is, the mind. FRANC.

Not harmony. Nine manuscripts, and especially the Bolognese manuscript examined by Thomasius, together with the Graphian edition, read “never harmony.” The remaining manuscript and printed witnesses read as in the text.

A likeness of a living being. That is, a likeness with a living being. FRANC.

Without the touch of an artist. Thus eleven manuscripts and fifteen printed common editions; in seven manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1468 it is *tractu*; in six others, *tractatu*.—“Without the handling of an artist.” Thus I edit from the Bolognese and Taxaquian manuscripts, with Heumann’s support. Parrhasius and later editors substituted *tactu*, a more familiar word, for the rarer one. *Tractare*, *tractabilis*, and *tractatus* sometimes mean the same as *tangere*, *tangibilis*, and *tactus*. See Pierius on Virgil, *Georgics* III.302:

> The hide, hard to the handling, resists the handler.

Compare the note on Lactantius, *Institutes* VII.21 and V.21: “tangible to eyes and hand.” BUN.

Others, fire. Zeno, namely, as we cited above from Cicero; hence for the Stoics, *δερμὸν πνεῦμα* (“dermal breath”; the reading is uncertain). But in Nemesius fire is the soul for Democritus; in Plutarch, for Demetrius; in Macrobius, for Hipparchus; just as water is for Hippo. Hence Virgil’s words in *Aeneid* VI:

> A fiery vigour and a heavenly origin are theirs.

(Also in *Aeneid* IV.)

Which in Greek is “wind,” *ἄνεμος*. For another reason, we call the soul either *spiritus* (“spirit”) or *flatus* (“breath”): not because it is some kind of air, such as the breath which we draw by breathing, but “spirit” because it has a certain proper nature, free from body, and a substance superior to all the elements of the material mass. Thus Augustine, Letter 28. We call it “breath” because it was created by God’s breathing-in, as is clear from Moses, Book I, ch. 2, v. 7. The same in *City of God* XIII.24. Lactantius certainly holds the precise opposite of the Stoics, because they maintained that the soul enters the body at birth; Lactantius himself notes this, as does Aristotle, *On the Soul* I.5. Even the Latin *animus* and *anima* derive from *ἄνεμος*. Servius on *Aeneid* I. GATAKER.

When that has been consumed. The Clairvaux manuscript reads “when the oil has been consumed”; and Francius preferred that reading.

Is nourished. Thus the Bovine manuscript, more correctly according to Heumann, from the edition of 1472. Other witnesses have “is fed,” less well.

Endowed with sensation. That is, it is endowed with sensation; the opposite is “it needs sensation.” See the note on *Institutes* II.5: “To be sentient is to generate what is endowed with sensation, and to have sensation is that whose part is endowed with sensation.” BUN.

…what Aristoxenus said: that there is no mind whatsoever, but that, as it were, a harmony in strings, the capacity for sensation arises from the construction of the body and the arrangement of the internal organs. Musicians call the tension and concord of strings, sounding together in complete modes without any discord, “harmony.” They therefore maintain that the soul consists in man by a similar principle to that by which harmonious modulation consists in strings: namely, that the firm union of the individual parts of the body and the united vigour of all its limbs produce that sentient movement and compose the soul, just as strings properly stretched produce a harmonious sound.

And just as, in strings, when something is either broken or slackened, the whole art of playing is disturbed and dissolved, so in the body, when some part of the limbs contracts a defect, the whole is destroyed; and when all things have been corrupted and disturbed, sensation dies [Col. 0067B], and this is called death. But if he had possessed any mind, he would not have transferred harmony from strings to man. For strings cannot sing of themselves, so that there can be any comparison or likeness in them to a living being. The soul, however, both thinks and moves of itself. But if there were anything in us resembling harmony, it would be moved by an external stroke, just as strings are by hands; without an artist’s touch and the striking of fingers, they lie mute and inert. Yet doubtless he himself had to be struck by a hand in order that he might at some time feel, because his mind was numb through limbs badly put together.

[Col. 0068A] CHAPTER XVII. On the Soul, and the Philosophers’ Opinion Concerning It.

It remains to speak of the soul, although its principle and nature cannot be apprehended. Yet we understand nonetheless that the soul is immortal, because whatever is vigorous and moves of itself always, and can neither be seen nor touched, must necessarily be eternal. But what the soul is has not yet been agreed among philosophers, nor perhaps ever will be. For some have said that it is blood, others fire, others wind—whence *anima* or *animus* received its name, because wind is called *ἄνεμος* in Greek. Yet none of them seems to have said anything.

For if the soul appears to be extinguished when blood is shed through a wound or consumed by the heat of fevers, it does not immediately follow that the nature of the soul must be placed in the material of blood [Col. 0068B]. It is as if the question arose what the light we use is, and one answered that it is oil because, when the latter is consumed, the light is extinguished—although they are certainly different things, one being the nourishment of the other. The soul, then, seems to resemble light: it is not itself blood, but is nourished by the moisture of blood, just as light is nourished by oil.

Those, moreover, who considered it fire used this argument: that the body is warm when the soul is present and grows cold when it departs. But fire needs sensation, is visible, and burns by touch. The soul, however, is endowed with sensation and cannot be seen [Col. 0069A], nor does it burn. From this it is evident that the soul is something resembling God. But those who consider it wind are deceived because, drawing breath from the air, we seem to live. Varro defines it thus: “The soul is air taken in through the mouth, warmed in the lungs, made hot in the heart, and diffused through the body.” These things are most plainly false.

For I do not say that the explanation of matters of this kind is so obscure to us that we cannot even understand what cannot be true. If someone were to tell me that the sky was made of bronze, or glass, or, as Empedocles says, frozen air, should I immediately assent because I do not know of what material the sky is made? For just as I do not know this, so I know that. Therefore the soul is not air taken in through the mouth, because the soul is generated much earlier than air can be taken in through the mouth. For it does not enter the body after birth [Col. 0069B], as some philosophers think, but immediately after conception, when divine necessity has formed the fetus in the womb. For it lives so fully within the mother’s entrails that it grows with growth and strains to emerge by frequent impulses. Finally, an abortion must occur if the living creature within has died.

The remaining parts of the definition aim at making us appear to have been dead during the nine months in which [Col. 0070A] we were in the womb. Therefore none of these three opinions is true. Yet those who held them should not be said to have been so wrong as to have said absolutely nothing; for we live at once by blood, heat, and breath. But although the soul plainly consists in the body when all these are united, they did not properly state what it was, because it can no more be expressed than it can be seen.

[Col. 0069B] [Various Notes on Columns 69–70]

The soul is something resembling God. Thus a great many, and the better, manuscripts and seven printed editions transmit it; four recent manuscripts and twelve printed editions have *similem*. These matters must be understood soberly.—“The soul … resembling God.” Augustine aptly writes on Psalm LXII: “Since God is the life of the soul, and the soul the life of the body, just as the body cannot live without the soul, so the soul cannot live unless God is present.” BUN.

They think it wind. Nine manuscripts and five recent editions add “to be,” wrongly. It is absent from the others. See above: “they considered it fire.”

We seem. Thus three recent manuscripts and all printed editions. See above: “that the body is warm … and grows cold when it departs.” Seventeen manuscripts read “we are seen”; Cambridge has “they seem.”

Varro thus defines. Thus I restored it from the old manuscripts: two Bolognese, Caucasian, Regio-Palatine, another Royal, three Colbertine, Leipzig, Utrecht, Clairvaux, Victorine, Brunellian; and the editions of Betuleius and Cellarius. Nine recent manuscripts read, “and thus defines.”

“The soul is air taken in through the mouth, warmed in the lungs, made hot in the heart.” This is the true reading according to Vossius and three highly expert physicians whom I consulted. In most other authors who cite that passage from Varro, the soul is said to be “air received through the mouth, warmed in the lungs, kindled in the heart, diffused through the body.” This is the same thing. Warmth belongs to the lungs, heat to the heart; whatever heat the lungs possess is adventitious to them, as proceeding from the heart. For the heart was regarded by the ancients as the storehouse or workshop of vital heat. Thus twenty-seven manuscripts wrongly read, “cooled in the lungs, tempered in the heart”; the Marmoutier manuscript, “moistened in the lungs, tempered in the heart”; and two Royal manuscripts and sixteen editions, “cooled in the lungs, warmed in the heart.” See Vossius, *On Idolatry* II.83. The Bovine manuscript has: “cooling in the lungs, tempered in the heart.”—Buneman, however: “cooled in the lungs, tempered in the heart.” Sublacensian, Rostock, Venice 1471, 1493, 1497–1519, Tornesian, Betuleian, Thomasius, Isaeus, Thysius: “cooled in the lungs, warmed in the heart.” But because Vossius, *On the Idolatry of the Gentiles* II.83, judged that the nature of the matter itself requires “warmed in the lungs, made hot in the heart,” Gallaeus and Sparkius, moved by the authority of such a man, admitted this emendation into the text; and Heumann says: “I too agree, the subject matter itself supporting this wording.” Since learned men expert in anatomy and natural philosophy establish nothing certain here, I thought it safer to present the reading of the Bolognese, Taxaquian, Penian, Utrecht, Bodleian, Cottonian, Merton, Balliol, Corpus Christi College, Emmanuelean, Wolfenbüttel, Gotha, three Leipzig manuscripts, Reimannian, Venice 1472, both editions of 1478, and Cellarius: “cooled in the lungs, tempered in the heart.” BUN.

Of this kind. Strains to emerge by frequent impulses. That is, to leap out, spring out from the womb. Two Epicurean poets. Lucretius is certain; I shall append his lines from Book III:

> Now I say that mind and soul are held  
> Joined together, and from themselves compose  
> One nature; but that the ruling head,  
> Dominant throughout the entire body, is  
> Deliberative faculty, which we call mind and intellect.

Some refer to this the saying of Actius: “We think with the *animus*, we enjoy with the *anima*; without the *animus*, the *anima* is weak.” Cicero, recounting philosophers’ doctrines concerning the soul in the first *Tusculan Disputation*, writes among other things: “Our countrymen also commonly indicate that *animus* is called *anima*. For we say ‘to act out one’s last breath’ and ‘to breathe out,’ and ‘spirited’ and ‘well-disposed,’ and ‘according to one’s mind.’ *Animus* itself, however, is named from *anima*.” Nonius Marcellus presents a saying like that of Actius: “The *animus* is that by which we think; the *anima*, that by which we live.” Cornelius Fronto: “The *animus* is the quality of a living being; the *anima*, the cause of life.” But let us hear someone from among the Catholics—Augustine, indeed, long engaged in philosophical studies. In *On Spirit and Soul*, ch. 34, he writes: “*Spiritus* is used for the spiritual soul, or for that which breathes in the body. Likewise, we call *animus* the same thing as *anima*; but *anima* pertains to life, *animus* to deliberation. Hence philosophers say both that life remains without *animus*, and that *anima* endures without mind, as in the insane. For it seems to belong to mind to know; to *animus*, to will.” BETUL. Lactantius is believed to have meant Virgil as the other Epicurean poet. For in verses 3–4 of the *Ciris*, Virgil professes himself an Epicurean. Hence Fabricius, *Greek Library* III.33, counted Virgil [Col. 0071D] among the Epicureans. Others nevertheless think he meant Horace, whom they number among Epicurean poets, especially from *Odes* I.3 and *Satires* II.3.

[Col. 0069A] CHAPTER XVIII. On the Soul and the Mind, and Their Affections.

There follows another question, itself inextricable: whether soul (*anima*) and mind (*animus*) are the same, or whether that by which we live is one thing, while that by which we feel and think is another. Arguments are not lacking for either side. Those [Col. 0070B] who say they are one follow this reasoning: that neither can one be alive without sensation, nor can there be sensation without life; and therefore that what cannot be separated cannot be different, but whatever it is has both the function of living and the faculty of sensation. Accordingly, two Epicurean poets use *animus* and *anima* indifferently.

But those who say they are different [Col. 0071A] argue thus: it can be understood that mind is one thing and soul another because, while the soul remains unharmed, the mind may be extinguished, as commonly happens to the insane; likewise because the soul is put to sleep by death, the mind by sleep—and in such a way that it not only does not know what is happening or where it is, but is even deceived by the contemplation of unreal things. How this happens cannot be fully perceived; why it happens can be. For we can in no way rest unless the mind is held occupied by images of visions.

The mind lies hidden, oppressed by sleep, like fire slumbering beneath a covering of ashes; if you stir it a little, it burns again and, as it were, awakens. It is therefore diverted by phantasms until the limbs, refreshed by sleep, regain strength. For the body, while sensation is awake, though it lies motionless, is nevertheless not at rest [Col. 0071B], because sensation burns and vibrates within it like a flame, and holds all the limbs bound to itself.

But after the mind has been drawn away from attention to contemplate images, then at last the whole body is relaxed into rest. The mind is drawn away by blind thought when, as darkness compels it, it has begun to be alone with itself. While it is intent upon the things [Col. 0072A] of which it is thinking, sleep suddenly steals upon it, and thought itself gradually turns aside into nearby forms; thus it begins also to see what it had previously set before its eyes. Then it goes further and finds distractions for itself, lest it interrupt the body’s most healthful repose.

For as the mind is diverted by true visions during the day lest it fall asleep, so it is diverted by false ones at night lest it awaken. For if it saw no images, it would necessarily either remain awake or be lulled into perpetual death. Therefore the capacity for dreaming was granted by God for the sake of sleeping, and indeed in common to all living creatures. But this is especially characteristic of man: when God gave him this faculty for rest, He retained for Himself the ability to teach man future things through dreams. For histories often attest dreams whose outcome was immediate and astonishing; and the utterances of our prophets have partly consisted in dreams. Therefore dreams are neither always true nor always false, as Virgil testifies, who wished there to be two gates of dreams. But those which are false appear to exist for the sake of sleeping; those which are true are sent by God, so that through this revelation we may learn impending good or evil.

[Col. 0071D] [Various Notes on Columns 71–73]

Another thing, the soul. Thus the Bovine manuscript; printed editions read, less well, “another thing to be the soul.”

May occur. The Bovine manuscript has “may do.” BUN.—“What it may do.” Rostock, Venice 1471 and 1472, both editions of 1478–1515, Parisian, Juntine, Cratandrian, Gryphian, Thomasius, Isaeus, Gallaeus, Sparkius: “what may occur,” approved by Heumann. But Emmanuelean, Cambridge, Gotha, Leipzig, Reimannian: “what it may do.” BUN.

Unless the mind, etc. For, as Cicero teaches somewhere, the mind has an incredible desire to behold truth. But that part which the Greeks call *φαντασία* and the Latins *imaginatio* (“imagination”), being liable to errors, often drags the mind along with it into error. Lactantius says that the soul is deceived by contemplation of unreal things, and also by dreams. Lactantius calls a phantasm “blind thought.” BETUL.

[Col. 0073A] CHAPTER XIX. On the Soul, and Its Being Given by God.

It may also become a question whether the soul is generated from the father, rather from the mother, or from both. But in this doubtful matter I claim the right to decide that none of these three is true. For souls are sown neither from both nor from either one. A body can be born from bodies, because something is contributed by each; but a soul cannot come from souls, because nothing can be taken away from a thing so subtle and incomprehensible. Therefore the principle for the generation of souls belongs to God alone.

Finally, we are all sprung from heavenly seed:

> He is the same father of all,

as Lucretius says [Col. 0073B]. For nothing but what is mortal can be generated from mortals. Nor should one be considered a father who does not at all perceive that he has transfused or breathed out a soul from his own substance; nor, if he did perceive it, could he comprehend in his mind when or how this occurs.

From this it is evident that souls are not given by parents, but by the one and same Father of all, God, who alone possesses the law and method of generation, since He alone brings it about. For the earthly parent’s part is nothing except to emit or receive the bodily fluid [Col. 0074A] in which lies the material of generation, accompanied by the sensation of pleasure. Apart from this act, a human being goes no further and can do nothing more; and therefore parents desire children to be born to them because they do not themselves make them.

All the rest now belongs to God: conception itself, the forming of the body, the breathing-in of the soul, safe birth, and whatever thereafter serves to preserve a human being. It is His gift that we breathe, live, and flourish. For besides the fact that by His benefit we are sound in body, and that He supplies us with food from diverse things, He also grants wisdom to man, which an earthly father cannot possibly give. Accordingly, foolish people are often born from wise parents, and wise people from foolish ones; something which some attribute to fate and the stars. But this is not the place to discuss fate.

It is enough to say that even if the stars contain causal efficacy over events, it is nonetheless certain that all things are done by God, who both made and arranged the stars themselves. Therefore those who take this power away from God and attribute it to His work are foolish.

God wished that whether or not we use this heavenly and illustrious gift should lie in our own power. For by granting this, He bound man by the solemn obligation of virtue, so that he might attain life. Great

None of these three is true. You see that throughout this chapter the propagation of souls through descent is denied. Lactantius denies it, most correctly. For the contrary assertion has been condemned. When nevertheless, or how. *Tamen* is absent from six manuscripts and four editions; three have *quantum* (“how greatly”) for *quando* (“when”); the Penian manuscript has “by what method nevertheless.” Souls are not given by parents. It is certain that God is called the Father of spirits because He Himself creates souls and infuses them into bodies. A rational soul cannot be produced by generation in any way, for a bodily power such as generation cannot rise to the production of a spiritual thing. This argument also proves the matter: whatever comes to be either comes from some pre-existing matter, comes from nothing, or—in the opinion of those who posit modes as intermediates between being and nothing—comes from the modes of a thing. But the soul does not come from matter, because it would thus be bodily, which conflicts with its actions, which it produces independently of matter; nor does it come from modes, for modes produce nothing. At least this is certain: that what itself persists after the body’s death cannot produce a spirit. It remains, therefore, that it comes to be from nothing; but man cannot produce anything from nothing, because between being and nothing there is an infinite distance, which cannot be crossed except by infinite power. After these words an oration written in the lower margin of the book occurs in six Royal manuscripts, eight Vatican, six Colbertine, two Sorbonne, four Oxford, and fifteen others; in eight old Roman editions, Aldus 1515, Paris 1525, and ten others. Yet because it is absent from the most ancient and best manuscripts—Bolognese, Regio-Palatine, Caucasian, and others cited by Thomasius and Gallaeus—and from several printed editions, and because it contains much that smells of Manichaeism, of the kind which we have previously noted to have been inserted into Lactantian writings by these forgers, we have relegated it from the text to the lower margin as added by an adulterating hand, lest we seem to have acted in bad faith when we accuse those who received Lactantius by such unworthy means of the same crime. The oration runs thus:

> He gave him and appointed for him a most wicked and deceitful spirit as adversary, with whom he might struggle in this earthly life without any respite of security. Why God appointed this tormentor for the human race, I shall explain briefly.  
>   
> (Here chapter 20 begins in the common editions.) Before all things He wished there to be diversity; and therefore He did not disclose truth openly to the multitude, but revealed it to very few. This diversity contains the whole secret of the world. For it is that which produces virtue, which without it could not merely not exist, but could not even appear; since virtue cannot exist unless there is some opponent in overcoming whom it either exercises or displays its strength. For just as victory cannot exist without contest, so virtue itself cannot exist without an enemy. Therefore, because He gave virtue to man, He appointed for him, on the opposite side, an enemy, lest virtue, growing numb in idleness, should lose its nature. Its whole principle lies in this: that, shaken and weakened, it may be strengthened, and cannot otherwise reach its highest summit unless, ever exercised by a prudent hand, it establishes itself for its own safety by the continuous course of struggle.  
>   
> For God did not wish man to arrive at that immortal blessedness by an easy path. Therefore, intending to give virtue, He first gave an enemy who would introduce desires and vices into human minds, who would be the author of errors and contriver of all evils; so that, since God calls man to life, he on the contrary may seize and lead him away to death. This is he who either entices or deceives those who strive for truth, or, if he cannot prevail by deceit and schemes, assumes a courageous spirit in order to try to weaken the strength of those who aspire to higher things, devising unspeakable and abominable acts: he harasses and kills them. Yet as he casts down many, so he departs conquered and cast down by many.  
>   
> These are the things inserted here by an alien hand.

Whoever sees a man’s body also sees, and can touch, something of the man. Lactantius therefore asserts too generally that the body is only man’s receptacle. GALLAEUS.
