is indeed man’s strength, a great rational principle, a great mystery. Whoever has not fallen away from it, nor betrayed his faith and devotion, must be blessed—must, in short, to conclude briefly, be like God. For whoever measures man by the flesh is mistaken. This little body with which we are clothed is man’s dwelling-place. Man himself can neither be touched, seen, nor grasped, because he lies hidden within that which is seen. If he has been more delicate and soft in this life than his rational nature requires; if, scorning virtue, he has enslaved himself to the desires of the flesh, he will fall and be pressed down to the earth. But if, as he ought, he has promptly and steadfastly defended the condition which he rightly received upright; if he has not served the earth which he ought to tread underfoot and conquer, he will deserve everlasting life.

## CHAPTER XX. Concerning Himself and Truth

These things, Demetrianus, I have for the present set forth to you briefly, and perhaps more obscurely than was fitting, because circumstances and the time required it. You ought to be content with them, since you will receive more and better things if heavenly indulgence is granted to us. Then, therefore, I shall exhort you more fully and more truly to the teaching of true philosophy. For I have resolved to commit to writing as many matters as I can which concern the condition of the blessed life, and indeed against the philosophers, since they are harmful and formidable for the disturbing of truth.

For the force of eloquence and the subtlety of argument and disputation are incredible, and may easily deceive anyone. We shall refute them partly with our own weapons and partly with weapons drawn from their mutual conflicts, so that it may appear that they have introduced error rather than removed it.

Perhaps you will wonder that I dare so great an undertaking. Shall we then allow truth to be extinguished or overwhelmed? For my part, I would rather fail even beneath this burden. For if Marcus Tullius, the unique model of eloquence itself, was often overcome by unlearned and ineloquent men who nevertheless strove on behalf of truth, why should we despair that truth itself will prevail against deceitful and sophistical eloquence by its own inherent power and clarity? They indeed commonly profess themselves advocates of truth; but who can defend a matter which he has not learned, or make clear to others what he himself does not know?

I seem to promise much; but a heavenly gift is needed, that ability and time may be granted us for pursuing our purposes. And if life is to be desired by a wise man, I would certainly desire to live for no other reason than to accomplish something worthy of life, and something which may bring benefit to readers—if not eloquence, since in us the stream of eloquence is slight—yet at least benefit for living, which is most necessary. When this has been accomplished, I shall judge that I have lived enough and fulfilled the duty of a man, if my labour has freed some men from errors and directed them toward the heavenly way.

# [BOOK ON THE WRATH OF GOD]

[Col. 0077]

# ANALYSIS OF THE BOOK ON THE WRATH OF GOD

[Col. 0077C] The question of this book: Does God truly become angry?

Certain philosophers denied this, because they maintained either that God is a merely beneficent nature, or that he cares for absolutely nothing. Lactantius, on the contrary, demonstrates in this book that God truly becomes angry, by the following arguments:

I. Either wrath must be attributed to God and favour withdrawn; or both must be withdrawn; or wrath must be removed and favour attributed; or both must be attributed. The first is false, because no one ever said of God that he is moved only by anger and not by favour. The second is Epicurean. For Epicurus maintained that in God there is neither anger nor favour, since he cares for absolutely nothing; but falsely. For God would not be God unless he were moved; nor can any administration more worthy of God be assigned than the government of the world. Nor is there any blessedness in an immobile thing. The third is Stoic: that favour is in God but anger is not; this too is false. For if God is not angry with the impious, neither does he love the pious. The fourth therefore remains, and it is true: namely, that both wrath and favour must be attributed to God (chapters 1–6).

[Col. 0077D] II. Every opinion that removes religion is empty and false.

The opinion which takes from God either favour, anger, or both, removes religion; therefore that opinion is empty and false.

He proves the major premise in chapter 7: namely, that religion cannot be abolished, because it is proper to man. He confirms the minor premise in chapter 8. For if God grants no good thing to anyone, it is foolish to worship him.

Some object: Certainly it is useful to believe this, but for the sake of utility rather than truth, so that consciences may be frightened, which laws are able to punish.

Lactantius denies this, and maintains in chapters 9–11 that religion was instituted not merely for utility but for truth.

III. If there are good and evil things in human affairs, God must necessarily be moved toward each side: toward favour when he sees just deeds done, and toward anger when he perceives unjust ones.

[Col. 0078C] The former is true, as is shown in chapters 13–15; therefore so is the latter.

Epicurus’s objection: If there is in God an affection of joy for favour and of hatred for anger, he will therefore also have fear, lust, and desire.

Reply: It does not follow. For favour, anger, and compassion have in God material—that is, a cause; the remaining affections do not have it. God is free from those because they are affections of vice; he has the others, such as these, because they are of virtue (chapter 16).

Another objection: God is blessed because he is always at rest; therefore he neither becomes angry nor is moved by favour.

Lactantius replies that God is not at rest, because he neither sleeps nor dies. Therefore he cares for human life and, by force of consequence, becomes angry with the wicked and favours the good. Further, just as it belongs more to cruelty than to piety if a man does not avenge insults, so, he says, it does not belong to virtue in God not to be moved by things done unjustly (chapter 17).

[Col. 0078D] Objection: Yet God can correct sins without this affection.

Reply: The very sight of sin is worthy of indignation. For one who is not moved either approves offences altogether or avoids the trouble of punishing them, both of which are vicious. Here he censures the saying of Archytas of Tarentum, who, when he had discovered that everything on his farm had been ruined, reproaching the fault of his steward, said: “Wretch, I would have killed you with blows by now, if I were not angry.” For he teaches that because of the greatness of anger the punishment should not have been remitted but postponed (chapter 18).

IV. If God established the most holy law of life and willed all men to be innocent and beneficent, he certainly cannot fail to become angry when he sees his law despised. The former is true; therefore so is the latter.

V. If he is administrator of the world, he certainly does not disregard that which is greatest in the world.

VI. If he is Father and God of all, he surely both delights in human virtues and is moved by vices; [Col. 0079A] therefore he loves the just and hates the impious (chapter 19).

VII. If he can forgive, he can also become angry; but he can forgive, because he is himself the arbiter and judge of his law; therefore he can also become angry (chapter 20).

They objected: Why, then, are those who sin often happy, while those who live piously are often miserable?

Reply: Because fugitives and disowned sons live freely, whereas those who are under a father’s discipline live more strictly and frugally. Further, virtue is tested through evils, vice through pleasure. Besides, the happiness of the wicked is not everlasting.

Further objection: If God becomes angry, he ought immediately to take vengeance.

Reply: If he did this, no one would remain alive, nor would any sinners be converted (chapter 20).

[Col. 0080A] Objection: God forbids man in his law to become angry; therefore he himself does not become angry.

Reply: The law restrains man’s unjust anger; nor does it forbid anger altogether, because this affection was necessarily given; rather, it forbids remaining in anger. Indeed, God commanded anger; therefore he too becomes angry (chapter 21).

VIII. All the prophets, filled with the divine Spirit, speak of nothing other than God’s favour toward the just and his anger against the impious.

IX. The Sibyls likewise attribute anger to God, as does Apollo of Miletus (chapters 22–23).

The conclusion is exhortatory, urging all to love God because he is Father, and to fear him because he is Lord. —SCULTETUS.

[Col. 0079]

# BOOK ON THE WRATH OF GOD, ADDRESSED TO DONATUS

[Note: [Col. 0079C] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 79–80]

**Book on the Wrath of God, addressed to Donatus.** Thus most manuscripts and printed editions entitle it. In an older Bologna manuscript: “The eighth book of Lucius Caelius Firmianus Lactantius on the Wrath of God begins.” In the Regius-Puteanus manuscript: “The seventh book of the Divine Institutions of Caelius Firmianus, On the Blessed Life, ends; the eighth book on Divine Wrath begins.” In one Oxford manuscript it is also called *On Divine Wrath*. In sixteen manuscripts, “addressed to Donatus” is absent.

A distinguished testimony of blessed Jerome concerning this book survives in his commentary on chapter 4 of the Epistle to the Ephesians, in these words: “Our Firmianus composed a book *On the Wrath of God* in a style equally learned and eloquent; whoever has read it, I think, will find it sufficient and more than sufficient for understanding anger,” etc. He calls the same book “most beautiful” in his *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Firmianus. Nevertheless, one must beware of its theme, which is *On the Wrath of God*. For throughout the book he teaches that the affection of anger, and certain others, are found truly and properly in God, especially in chapters 15, 16, and 17; he also maintained this in book II of the *Divine Institutions*, chapter 18. See this passage. —ISAEUS.

**“I have often observed, Donatus.”** This imitates Cicero, who begins his *Paradoxa* thus: “I have often observed, Brutus.” —“Donatus.” Some judge this to have been the confessor Donatus to whom Lactantius dedicated his book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*. Others would have him be Donatus, heresiarch of the Donatists; still others Aelius Donatus, the grammarian and teacher of St Jerome. Since this can be guessed rather than known with certainty, I leave examination and judgment to the reader.

**“Many think this.”** Thus the two old editions, Roman and Betuleius, with all manuscripts except two Bologna manuscripts and the Taxianus, in which stands *aestimare*, “to judge.” Other editors rejected *id* (“this”) as useless.

**“Must be refuted by us.”** The preposition *a* is absent in one old Bologna manuscript.

**“Lest you too be deceived.”** *Et* (“too”) has been added from all manuscripts and the old Roman edition of 1470.

**“Yet we are not so arrogant.”** *Tam* (“so”) is absent from twenty-one manuscripts and three old editions.

**“Enclosed within the dark dwelling of the body.”** This is Platonic; Plato elsewhere calls the body “the soul’s tent” (*τὸ σῶμα τῆς ψυχῆς σκῆνος*), elsewhere its “vehicle” (*ὄχημα*), elsewhere a “prison” (*φυλακή*); Cicero calls it now a vessel, now a receptacle. More has been said on this in the *Divine Institutions*. Paul’s philosophy has a more magnificent view of the dignity of the human body. Thus he writes to the Corinthians, 1 Corinthians 3:6: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” Again: “Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?” chapter 5, verse 15.

**“Far removed from the perception of truth.”** Thus most editions and nearly all manuscripts, with Thomasius, and rightly. In five recent manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470, “from the perfection of truth,” wrongly; in six printed editions, “from the perception of God,” corruptly. For Lactantius does not intend there to discuss the knowledge of God, but to show that God is the author of the knowledge of truth. —GALLAEUS. On this opinion see book II of the *Institutions*, chapter 9.

**“Humanity.”** Here *humanitas* does not denote the virtue which a human being properly shows to another human being, but human nature—man himself. Minucius Felix, in the *Octavius*: “They have utterly removed all fear by which humanity is governed.”]]

(C)

[Col. 0079B] ## CHAPTER I. Concerning Divine and Human Wisdom

I have often observed, Donatus, that many think this—as some philosophers also have thought—that God does not become angry, either because the divine nature is only beneficent and it is fitting for the highest and best power neither to harm anyone; or certainly because he cares for nothing at all, so that no good comes to us from his beneficence and no evil from his maleficence. Since their error is very great and tends to overthrow the order of human life, it must be refuted by us, lest you too be deceived by the authority of men who think themselves wise.

Yet we are not so arrogant as to boast that we have comprehended truth by our own intellect; rather, we follow the teaching of God, who alone can know and reveal secrets. Deprived of this teaching, philosophers supposed that the nature of things could be discovered by conjecture. This is in no way possible, because the mind of man, enclosed within the dark dwelling of the body, is far removed from the perception of truth. Divinity differs from humanity in this: ignorance belongs to humanity, knowledge to divinity.

Therefore we need some light to dispel the darkness that overspreads human thought, since,

[Note: [Col. 0081C] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 81–82]

**“By our own senses.”** Seven manuscripts prefix *de* (“by”).

**“And Socrates was right.”** Francius suggests perhaps *Itaque* (“therefore”). In Em. it is *Recte ergo* (“therefore rightly”).

**“Ignorance” (*inscitiam*).** Reimm. has *justitiam* (“justice”), wrongly. Pierr. and Parrh.: *insaniam* (“madness”). Rostock, Venice 1471, both 1478 editions, Paris, Aldine, and all more recent editions: *inscitiam*. London, Regius, Gothic, and Venice 1493: *inscientiam* (“unknowingness”). I have adopted a word favoured by Cicero and our author. See book V; compare Gronovius on Livy XXII, chapter 25. —BUNEMANN.

**“That he knew nothing.”** In Plato, *Apology of Socrates*, near the beginning, and Cicero, *Academic Questions*, book I.

**“They think.”** Thus the Bovianus manuscript, a reading Heumann approves; others have “they thought.”

**“He himself feigned this doctrine.”** Seven manuscripts have *ipse* (“himself”). Nine manuscripts and two old Roman editions have *dissimulavit ipsam* (“he concealed it itself”).

**“Some portion of the truth.”** London and Regius: “some truth in some respect.” Not badly. The others have “in some respect,” as in book III, chapter 3: “It may be that all have erred in some respect and in some respect touched truth.” The same author has, from Cicero, “in some respect,” in book III. —BUNEMANN.

**“And he testified.”** *-que* is absent from one Colbert manuscript and nine editions. Plato wrote an *Apology* for Socrates, as Xenophon and Lysias did also. In it Plato presents Socrates defending his case against his accusers; and, in order to diminish the inflated estimate of one who prided himself on the title of wisdom, he prefers his own wisdom to that man’s by a most elegant and modest comparison: he himself claimed no wisdom, whereas the other, though knowing nothing, wished nevertheless to appear wise. Aristophanes the comic poet, bribed with money by Socrates’ rivals, attacks him outrageously in a stage play, among other calumnies alleging that, as a *merimnosophistēs* (μεριμνοσοφίστης), he taught right and wrong for payment. The commentator faithfully refutes this calumny, as he does the others. —BETULEIUS.

**“By Plato.”** Plato, in the *Apology*.

**“So greatly [did he despise] learning.”** Thus all manuscripts and most editions. Six printed editions have *adeoque* (“and so greatly”).

**“In him alone is truth.”** One recent Regius manuscript and seven editions: “in whom alone.”

**“To keep a firm footing.”** Lucan, book I: “Keeping his steps unshaken in an uncertain course.” Seneca, *Thyestes*, 5: “To set a firm step upon level ground.” Compare the note below. —BUNEMANN.

**“Fashioned.”** That is, of gods. Thus I emended from almost all manuscripts and the editions of Gymnicus, Isaeus, Cellarius, and Walch, much better than *fabricatos* (“fashioned”) of four recent manuscripts and eleven editions. For what sense is there in “the cults of gods fashioned”? But above, book VII of the *Divine Institutions*, [he speaks] of impious cults of gods made by hand. —“Cults of gods fashioned by human hands.” I do not think that the words *humana manu*, which occur in all [the manuscripts], should be disturbed; Latin writers willingly join these words. I note on Lactantius, book V, chapter 22: “Not to sacrifice to stones made by human hands”; book VII, chapter 11: “wrought by human hands.” —BUNEMANN.

**“To know his minister and messenger,” etc.** Namely, the angel of great counsel. For the Lord himself says, John 17: “This is eternal life, that they may know thee, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom thou hast sent.” If sent, therefore ambassador, messenger, angel, or apostle, yet with divine majesty unimpaired. Likewise minister, in the same respect. Romans 15.

**“Entangled.”** Bovianus manuscript.

**“But.”** The Bovianus manuscript reads “true.”

We have already refuted their ignorance in the second book of the *Divine Institutions*. From this it is evident that the books of the *Divine Institutions* were written before the book *On the Wrath of God*.

**“When they recognize.”** Thus emended from almost all manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470 and Gymnicus. See what follows. One recent Regius manuscript and the Cratander edition: “when they recognize.” Many printed editions: “when they agree.”]

while we live in mortal flesh, we cannot divine by our own senses. But God is the light of the human mind. Whoever has known him and admitted him into his breast will, with heart illuminated, recognize the mystery of truth; but once God and heavenly teaching have been removed, all things are full of errors.

And Socrates was right: although he was the most learned of all philosophers, yet in order to expose the ignorance of the others, who imagined that they possessed some knowledge, he said that he knew nothing except one thing: that he knew nothing. For he understood that that learning had in it nothing certain, nothing true. Nor, as some think, did he feign this doctrine in order to refute others; rather, he saw some portion of the truth. And, as Plato relates, he testified even at his trial that there was no human wisdom. So greatly did he despise, ridicule, and reject the learning in which philosophers then gloried that he professed as the highest learning precisely this: that he had learned to know nothing.

If, therefore, there is no human wisdom, as Socrates taught and Plato handed down, it is evident that there is divine wisdom, and that the knowledge of truth belongs to no one other than God. God, therefore, must be known: in him alone is truth. He is the Father of the world and Creator of things, unseen by the eyes and scarcely discerned by the mind. His religion is commonly attacked in many ways by those who have been unable either to possess true wisdom or to comprehend the reason of the great and heavenly mystery.

## CHAPTER II. Concerning Truth, Its Stages, and God

For since there are many stages through which one ascends to the dwelling-place of [Col. 0082A] truth, it is not easy for everyone to be raised to the summit. For those whose eyes are dazzled by truth’s brightness and who cannot keep a firm footing roll back down onto the plain. The first stage is to understand false religions and reject the impious cults of gods fashioned by human hands. The second is to perceive in the mind that there is one supreme God, whose power and providence made the world in the beginning and will govern it hereafter. The third is to know his minister and messenger, whom he sent to earth, so that, taught by him, freed from the error in which we were entangled, and formed for worship of the true God, we might learn righteousness. From all these stages, as I have said, falling is easy and a downward slide to ruin, unless one’s feet are planted with unshaken steadiness.

[Col. 0082B] We see men shaken from the first stage who, though they recognize what is false, nevertheless do not find the true. Despising earthly and fragile images, they do not devote themselves to worshipping God, whom they do not know; but, marvelling at the elements of the world, they worship heaven, earth, sea, sun, moon, and the other stars. But we have already refuted their ignorance in the second book of the *Divine Institutions*.

We say that men fall from the second stage when, though they recognize that there is one supreme God, they are nevertheless ensnared by philosophers and caught by false arguments, and think otherwise concerning that single majesty than truth permits. They either deny that God has any form [Col. 0083A]

[Note: [Col. 0083B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 83–84]

**“Who either deny that God has any form.”** “No one has ever seen God.” What, then, is that form in whose likeness, you will say, man was created? Yet it too does not come before human eyes, which, as you yourself admit, is scarcely conceived even in the mind. We acknowledge no form of God. See Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, and Basil, Homily 10. —“That God has a form.” Elsewhere he indeed maintains that God is incorporeal, for example book VII, chapter 3, and elsewhere; nevertheless he attributes form to God. Compare chapters 11 and 18, in which he erred along with others. —BUNEMANN.

**“Or is moved by no affection.”** So I read with seven Vatican manuscripts, the Regius-Puteanus, two other Regius manuscripts, five Colbert manuscripts, Marmoutier, one Claromontanus, Brun., and four printed editions. An error entered three Regius manuscripts, two Vatican manuscripts, one Colbert manuscript, and many editions, where *ullo* (“any”) is read in place of *nullo* (“no”), which the subject itself rejects; for Lactantius attacks those who think God is moved by no affection.

**“The builder of the divine and immortal temple.”** Namely, of the temple built of living stones, 1 Peter 2, whose dedication is the work of the divine Spirit. But the priest is the same as the builder: namely, that eternal one according to the order of Melchizedek, as is written to the Hebrews. —BETULEIUS.

**“Whom in part.”** Two manuscripts read *quod*, “which.”

**“Aforementioned.”** See the note on this word, book VI, chapter 5. Vopiscus uses it in the *Aurelian*, chapters 9 and 36, though it may quite suitably be two words. —BUNEMANN.

**“And we shall refute [them] later,” etc.** Lactantius seems to have intended to answer all sects then arising in Christianity. —RIVETUS, in manuscript notes.

**“While they dispute.”** Janus Gulielmus, on Plautus, *Menaechmi*, chapter 4, testifies that some copies read *dum dissipant*, “while they scatter,” and he approves that reading. —ISAEUS. Bunemann likewise has and approves this latter reading. —“They lost truth while scattering it.” Lactantius repeatedly stresses this, especially regarding the sects to which he refers. He said in book IV, chapter 30: “They would make dissension and scatter the Church, in which truth is found”; book II, chapter 10: “Truth is accustomed to be corrupted when scattered by varied discourses”; book VII, chapter 22: “An opinion of truth altered truth itself, scattered through different mouths and varied discourses.” —BUNEMANN.

**“They lost truth while they dispute.”** Thus most manuscripts and the printed editions read. But Janus Gulielmus prefers *dissipant*, “scatter,” with his old codices, similar to the Ultramontanus, Em., Br., two Regius, and three Colbert manuscripts. His reason is that truth is found, not lost, through disputation. But I judge that nothing should be changed, for the reading is elegant and suited to the purpose. —GALLAEUS.

[Col. 0084B]

**“But others remove anger.”** The text itself suggests that this should be read, as in all manuscripts and six printed editions, rather than “They, however,” as in twelve editions.

**“That it ought to be beneficent, just as it ought not to be maleficent.”** London, Regius, Gothic, Leipzig, and two Reimm. manuscripts: “that it ought not to be maleficent.” Cantabrigiensis—that is, Sublacensis—Rostock, Venice 1471, both 1478 editions, 1493, 1497, and Parrhasius: “and that it ought not to be maleficent.” Paris 1513: “that it ought to be excellent, not maleficent.” —BUNEMANN.

[Col. 0084C]

**“And the following division must be made.”** So I read from the older and better manuscripts: two Bologna, Regius-Puteanus and two other Regius, three Colbert, and many others. In six Regius manuscripts and printed editions stands *exsequenda*, “to be carried out,” which means the same thing; for *sequi*, “to follow,” is read in Cicero in the sense of *exequi*, “to carry out.”

**“Both alike must be withdrawn.”** From all manuscripts and thirteen old editions I have added *pariter*, “alike,” which is absent from the other printed editions.

**“Or both must be attributed.”** Thus the better and older manuscripts. In one recent Regius manuscript and many printed editions: “or neither must be attributed.” Very many manuscripts and the two old Roman editions and Betuleius have: “or neither must be withdrawn.” —“Or both must be attributed.” This reading, or the reading of another less ancient manuscript of St Saviour, Tax. and P., “or neither must be withdrawn,” which has the same meaning as the former, must be retained. But if one reads, as in the Aldine and other editions, “or neither must be attributed,” this fourth member would be identical with the one placed second, namely “or both alike must be withdrawn.” Thomasius observed this also in his notes. —ISAEUS.

[Col. 0084D]

**“Unsuitable to God.”** Two Bologna manuscripts, one recent Regius, Tax., one Sorbonne, two Colbert, and the editions of Betuleius and Isaeus prefer *inconveniens Deo*, “unsuitable to God,” as an emendation. But *disconveniens*, found in the remaining manuscripts and twelve editions, is Ciceronian, as certain grammarians think. —“Unsuitable to God.” Thus Bunemann, who supplies the following note: English manuscripts also, London, Regius, Gothic, Guelferbytanus, Memb.: “incongruous to God.” I know Horace’s *disconvenit* and Tertullian’s *disconvenientia*, noted by others. Thus book I, chapter 11: “How much more unsuitable to God!” The Turin manuscript has, they think, *inconveniens*. —BUNEMANN.

**“If God is the author only of evils?”** Theologians distinguish evil of punishment from evil of fault; God is the author of the former, not of the latter. —GALLAEUS. —“If God is the author only of evils?” He speaks of the evils of punishments which God inflicts in anger, and even St Thomas admits that God is their author and cause, *Summa Theologiae*, I–II, question 49, article 2. —ISAEUS.] 

or think that he is moved by no affection, because every affection is weakness, of which there is none in God. But others are hurled down from the third stage: though they know the envoy of God and the builder of the divine and immortal temple, they either do not accept him or accept him otherwise than faith requires. We have already refuted them in part in the fourth book of the aforementioned work, and shall refute them more carefully later, when we begin to answer all the sects which lost truth while they dispute.

But now we shall argue against those who have fallen from the second stage and hold perverse opinions concerning the supreme God. Some say that he neither bestows favour on anyone nor becomes angry, but, secure and at rest, enjoys the blessings of his immortality. Others remove anger but leave favour to [Col. 0083B] God; for they hold that a nature excelling in the highest virtue ought to be beneficent, just as it ought not to be maleficent. Thus all philosophers agree concerning anger; concerning favour they disagree.

But so that the discussion may proceed in order to the subject proposed, we must make and follow the following [Col. 0084A] division, since anger and favour are different and opposed. Either anger must be attributed to God and favour withdrawn; or both alike must be withdrawn. Or anger must be removed and favour attributed; or both must be attributed. Beyond these alternatives nature can comprehend nothing further, so that the truth which is sought must necessarily be found in one of them. Let us consider each, so that reason and order may lead us to the hidden places of truth.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning Good and Evil in Human Affairs, and Their Author

No one has ever said this first thing concerning God: that he becomes angry only and is not moved by favour. For it is unsuitable to God that he should be endowed with such a power [Col. 0084B] as enables him to harm and injure, while making him unable to help and do good. What reason, then, what hope of salvation is held out to men, if God is the author only of evils? If this were so, that venerable majesty would be reduced, not to the authority of a judge, who is permitted to preserve and set free, [Col. 0085A]

[Note: [Col. 0085B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 85–86]

**“Certainly, if God is the author of evils, there must be another who does things contrary to God.”** Thus I have restored the text from two Bologna manuscripts, one Regius, three Colbert, one Sorbonne, Tax., and the editions of Thomasius and Walch. In eleven manuscripts and five editions: “Certainly, if God exists, there must be another author who …”; in three recent editions: “Certainly, if God does not exist, there must be another who …”; in nine manuscripts and as many printed editions: “Certainly, if God does not exist, there must be another author who …” —“Certainly, if God exists … who does things contrary to God.” I retained the common reading, although B. and T. have: “Certainly, if God is the author of evils, there must be another who does things contrary,” etc. “If God,” he says, “is not the author, namely both of good and evil, so as only to harm men, another author of benefits must then be established, since we experience both good and evil. But no other besides God can be established; therefore the same God is the author both of evils—that is, punishments—and of goods—that is, benefits and rewards.” —ISAEUS.

**“Able to harm, unable to benefit.”** The last three words are absent from twenty manuscripts and three editions.

**“Since this is agreed.”** That is, because all agree on this; compare our author’s *On the Workmanship*, chapter 17: “Since this is agreed among philosophers.” So Cicero, *On Invention*, book I, chapter 9: “It is agreed what has been done”; *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, chapter 32: “Let this also be agreed.” —BUNEMANN.

**“To do harm.”** Lactantius uses this below in chapter 5, and all manuscripts read it, except two recent ones, which have “to do evil,” as in the printed editions. —But Bunemann: “To do harm.” I restore from Bon., Tax., London, Regius, Gothic, Leipzig, two and three Reimm., with Heumann agreeing, *malefacere*, as in chapter 3: “Why is he who does evil more renowned than he who does good?”; chapter 5: “nor does he do anything evil”; chapter 1: “from maleficence.” Venice 1693–97: “evil, which”; the rest: “to do evil, which.” Book III, chapter 17, according to Epicurus’s opinion: “It belongs to the wise man … to do harm … God does not become angry at anything.” —BUNEMANN.

**“And to injure.”** These words, as hardly necessary, are deleted by Emm., Cant., London, Regius, Leipzig, two and three Reimm., Subl., Rostock, Venice 1471, 1472, both 1478 editions, 1493, 1497, Pierr., Parrh., Paris, and Isaeus; they are added by Ald., Crat., Gymn., Fasit., Torn., Betul., Thomas., Thys., Gall., Spark., Cell., Walch., and Heumann. —BUNEMANN.

**“From this, he says.”** Lucretius, book I, verse 56:

> “For the entire nature of the gods must necessarily  
> enjoy immortal life with the highest peace,

[Col. 0086B]

These verses are Lucretius’s, but the opinion is Epicurus’s. For Lactantius reminds us, *On the Workmanship*, chapter 6, that everything Lucretius raves is Epicurus’s; and Cicero likewise attributed this error to Epicurus, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I. This is the first of the *Principal Doctrines* (*τῶν κυρίων δόξων*). “Although,” Cicero says, “I see that some think Epicurus, lest he incur the Athenians’ displeasure, left the gods in words but removed them in fact. Thus, in those selected and brief propositions of his which you call *κύριαι δόξαι* [principal doctrines], this, I think, is the first proposition: ‘That which is blessed and immortal neither has business itself nor gives business to anyone,’” etc.

Tertullian’s passage on this subject, from *Apology*, chapter 46, should be added and noted: “Some assert [God to be] incorporeal, others corporeal, as do both Platonists and Stoics; others [derive him] from atoms, others from numbers, as Epicurus and Pythagoras; others from fire, as Heraclitus thought. The Platonists indeed make him concerned with affairs; the Epicureans make him idle and inactive and, so to speak, a nobody as regards human affairs, but placed outside the world,” etc. In the first clause the Platonists and Stoics might seem to make God corporeal, although both make him incorporeal. For Plato called God *asōmatos* (*ἀσώματον*), “incorporeal.” But why should I be harsher with Tertullian for saying that Stoics make God corporeal, when Origen says the same in *Against Celsus*? Add that the Stoics call God fire, and fire is a body. —BETULEIUS.

**“Nor is moved.”** See below, “no motion.” Lactantius, book II, chapter 8: “The power of doing something cannot exist except in that which feels, is intelligent, thinks, and is moved … That which is insensible always lies inert and torpid, and nothing can arise from that in which there is no voluntary motion.” —BUNEMANN.

**“Which is proper to God.”** As above, in the preceding line, “which is proper to a living being.” Three recent manuscripts read “proper to God.”

**“Than the government of the world.”** Recent manuscripts and editions add, “than care for living beings,” which does not cohere with Lactantius’s other words and is absent from the older Regius-Puteanus, Bologna, and Taxianus manuscripts.

**“Lies torpid and immobile.”** See notes on book II, chapter 8. Compare the note on book VI, chapter 17: “the immobile stupor of the mind”; *On Wrath*, chapter 17: “Those who make God immobile.” —BUNEMANN.

**“But if he cares for nothing.”** This is absent in many manuscripts, but is found in one Regius, two Bologna, two Colbert, and others, and in nearly all printed editions. See below: “therefore there is neither care for any thing nor providence in him.”

**“Divinity.”** One Bovianus manuscript has “dignity.”

**“God’s substance.”** Heumann thinks one should read “the substance of God.” The books read “God’s substance.” So Salvian, book IV, chapter 9: “For whoever asserts that nothing is seen by God is close to taking away even substance from him from whom he removes sight; and whoever says that he sees absolutely nothing also says that he does not exist at all.” —BUNEMANN.]

But since we see that in human affairs there are not only evils, but also goods, then, if God is the author of evils, there must be another who does what is contrary to God and gives us goods. If there is, by what name is he to be called? Or why is he who does us harm better known to us than he who does us good? But if nothing can exist besides God, it is absurd and vain to suppose that the divine power—than which nothing is greater, nothing better—is able to harm but unable to benefit. Therefore no one has arisen who would dare say this, because it has no rational basis and cannot in any way be believed. Since this is agreed, let us pass on and seek truth elsewhere.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning God and His Affections, and the Refutation of Epicurus.

What follows is from the school of Epicurus: just as there is no anger in God, so neither is there even favour. For since Epicurus thought it alien to God to do evil and [Col. 0086A] harm—which for the most part arises from the emotion of anger—he also stripped Him of beneficence, because he saw that it followed that, if God has anger, He also has favour. Thus, lest he concede a vice to Him, he made Him incapable even of virtue. “For this reason,” he says, “He is blessed and incorruptible: because He cares for nothing, has no business Himself, and imposes none upon another.” Therefore God does not exist, if He is not moved—for movement is characteristic of a living being—nor does He do anything impossible for man—for this is characteristic of God—if He has absolutely no will, no action, and, finally, no administration worthy of God. And what administration greater or worthier can be assigned to God than the governance of the world, and especially of the human race, to which all earthly things are subject?

[Col. 0086B] What blessedness, then, can there be in God, if He always languishes in repose and immobility? If He is deaf to those who pray and blind to those who worship Him? What is so worthy, so proper to God, as providence? But if He cares for nothing and provides for nothing, He has lost all divinity. Therefore, he who removes the whole power, the whole substance of God—what else does he say [Col. 0087A]

“Impunity,” etc. No one can hope for this who knows God to be all-knowing and most just. “The Stoics are thought,” etc. He rebukes the Stoics because they attribute favour to God and imagine for themselves a God only gentle, not likewise stern, depriving Him of anger. The chief argument on which he relies is this: whatever is moved is moved in both directions; therefore, if God is moved by favour, He is also moved by anger. I would grant this if the bodily sense partook of the two opposed affections, as: whatever feels heat also feels cold. But no passion can befall God, because He is incorporeal. Anger is a passion and therefore a weakness. Favour, however, is not merely not a passion, but is besides a virtue, indeed a divine virtue; for it is a part of *chrēstotēs* (χρηστότης, “kindness”), which is rightly attributed to God alone, not as an accident but as a proper and inseparable attribute (*achōriston*, ἀχώριστον). From this it appears that favour and anger in God are not, as in a magistrate or prince, diametrically opposed. BETULEIUS.]

—unless that God does not exist at all? Finally, Marcus Tullius reports Posidonius as saying that Epicurus held there to be no gods, but that the things he said about the gods were said to ward off hostility. Thus, in words he left the gods, but in reality abolished them, since he attributed to them no movement and no function. But if this is so, what is more deceitful than he? Such conduct ought to be alien to a wise and serious man. But if he thought one thing and said another, what else is he to be called but a deceiver, double-tongued, wicked, and consequently foolish?

Yet Epicurus was not so cunning that he would say these things from a desire to deceive, when he also committed them to writing for everlasting remembrance; rather, he erred through ignorance of the truth. For, having from the beginning been led by the plausibility of a single proposition, he necessarily fell into the conclusions which followed. [Col. 0087B] For the first proposition was that anger is unfitting for God. Since this seemed true and unassailable to him, he could not reject the consequences; for once one emotion had been cut away, necessity itself compelled him to remove the remaining emotions from God also. Thus, one who does not grow angry is certainly not moved by favour either, since favour is the opposite of anger. And if there is in Him neither anger nor favour, then certainly neither fear, nor joy, nor grief, nor compassion. For all emotions have one principle, one agitation, which cannot befall God. [Col. 0088A] But if there is no emotion in God, because whatever is affected is weak, then there is in Him neither concern for anything nor providence.

Thus far the argument of this wise man proceeds; he kept silent about what follows: namely, that if there is in Him neither concern nor providence, then there is neither any thought nor any sensation whatsoever in Him; whence it follows that He does not exist at all. Thus, when he had descended step by step, he halted at the lowest step because he now saw the precipice. But what good was it to have remained silent and concealed the danger? Necessity compelled him to fall even unwillingly. For he said what he did not wish to say, because he arranged his argument so that he necessarily arrived at what he sought to avoid. You see, then, to what point he arrives once anger has been abolished and taken away from God. Finally, either no one believes this, [Col. 0088B] or very few do—and those wicked and evil persons who hope for impunity for their sins. But if this too is found false, that there is neither anger nor favour in God, let us come to that which was placed third.

“Very agreeable.” Thus the most ancient and best manuscripts: Regio-Put., two Bologna, three Colbert, Tax., Pen. Our author uses *favorabilis* actively, which is rare. *Admodum* (“very”) is absent from ten manuscripts and thirteen editions.

“A popular discourse.” That is, one pleasing and acceptable to the people, which conforms to the people’s will. WALCH.

“Littleness of spirit.” Six recent manuscripts and three editions: *pusillanimitatem* (“faintheartedness”).

“For anger is an agitation of the mind.” Let it suffice to have observed once for all that whenever we attribute anger to God, we understand it in the sense in which Durandus, Book II, distinction 30, question 2, says: “God is said to be angry, not according to emotion but according to effect, insofar as He prepares punishment for someone or inflicts it.” For Lactantius speaks somewhat harshly when he affirms that the emotion of anger properly belongs to God insofar as it impresses some movement upon Him. SPARKIUS.

“For when it enters anyone’s mind,” etc. Jerome, in his letter on Titus, chapter I, concerning an angry man: “With grim countenance, trembling lips, wrinkled brow, unrestrained abuse, and face changing between pallor and redness.” Seneca, *On Anger*, Book I, chapter 1: “There is much redness over the whole face, as blood boils up from the depths of the breast; the lips quiver, the teeth are clenched, the hair bristles and stands erect; the breath is constrained; there is the grating sound of joints twisting themselves, groans and bellowings, speech broken by words insufficiently articulated, hands repeatedly clapped, the ground struck with the feet, and the whole body in commotion and issuing great threats—a countenance foul to behold and dreadful, distorted and swollen by its own deforming passions.” ELMENHORST.

“Raise waves.” Francius: *excitat* (“raises”).

“Let the eyes blaze.” See Seneca, *On Anger*, at the beginning of Book I, chapter 1.

“Alternately.” *Alternis* is elegantly used absolutely for that which happens by turns. Lucretius I.1010:

> Thus it may render all things infinite in alternation.

Pliny, *Letters* V.18: “Things which I sometimes do alternately and sometimes at the same time.” BUN.

“It would be credible that He would have destroyed the universe.” I added the last two words from almost all manuscripts and twelve old editions. They are absent, however, from five manuscripts and an equal number of printed editions.—“Would be credible”: these words seem necessary. For as he said just above, “But if it does not become a man . . . how much less does it become God,” so too in the application. BUN.

“Does evil.” Three manuscripts: *malefacit*; Claromontanus: *malefaciet*.

“Nothing else remains.” Thus I read from two Bologna manuscripts, one Royal manuscript and others, and the Isaeus edition. The preceding context plainly shows that this must be read. In many manuscripts and printed editions, *abest* (“is absent”) is read.

“The common father of all.” As in Book V, chapter 8: “God, the common father of all.” A Terentian elegance. See note on Lactantius, Book III, chapter 18. BUN.

“And best and greatest.” Thus five Royal manuscripts, among them the ancient Regio-Put., and the Roman edition of 1470, Cellarius, and Walch. Others have “and truly greatest.”—“Greatest”: the Bovian manuscript has *maximusque* (“and greatest”).

“Is honoured.” Thus, with the Roman edition of 1470 and Cellarius, all manuscripts except two recent ones, which have “is honoured,” as do many editions.

“Is celebrated with every blessing and prayer.” Thus I read with the editions and all manuscripts except two recent ones, which have “is adorned with blessings and celebrated with every prayer.”

“In part.” London and Royal manuscripts: *in partem* (“into a part”). But the former is more correct. Book III, chapter 6: “they had removed in part”; Book VII, chapter 22: “they have corrupted in part . . . they agree in part.” BUN.

“The nature of the matter.” Francius: perhaps *Dei* (“of God”) should be read. Claromontanus manuscript: *rerum* (“of things”).

“Thus one who loves the good,” etc. Three Royal manuscripts reject the following words: “and hates the wicked,” and “and one who does not hate the wicked.”

“These things are connected by nature.” London, Royal, Reims, Gothic manuscripts: *Natura ista connexa est*, as though *natura* were nominative; but it is ablative. He imitates Quintilian, whom he cited in Book VI, chapter 23: “Things which are connected with one another by nature.” BUN.]

better view of the Divinity, when they say that there is favour in God but no anger. It is a highly agreeable and popular doctrine: that this littleness of spirit does not befall God, so that He should think Himself injured by anyone, though He cannot be injured; that that calm and holy majesty should be aroused, disturbed, and maddened—which belongs to earthly frailty. For anger is an agitation and disturbance of the mind, which is alien to God.

But if anger does not become even a man who is merely wise and serious—for when it enters anyone’s mind, like a savage storm it raises such waves that it alters the mind’s settled condition: the eyes blaze, the mouth trembles, the tongue stammers, the teeth chatter, and, alternately, now a spreading redness, now whitening pallor, stains the countenance—how much less does so foul a transformation become God? And if [Col. 0089B] a man who has command and power can through anger inflict widespread harm, shed blood, overthrow cities, destroy peoples, reduce provinces to desolation, how much more credible would it be that God, who holds power over the entire human race and over the world itself, would have destroyed the universe if He grew angry?

Therefore such a great and destructive evil ought to be absent from Him. And if anger and agitation are absent from Him because they are both ugly and harmful, and because He does harm to no one, nothing else remains but that He be gentle, tranquil, favourable, beneficent, and a preserver. Thus alone can He be called both the common father of all and the best [Col. 0090A] and greatest, as divine and heavenly nature demands. For if among men it is considered praiseworthy to benefit rather than harm, to give life rather than kill, to save rather than destroy; and if innocence is rightly numbered among the virtues; and if one who has done these things is loved, preferred, honoured, celebrated with every blessing and prayer, and finally judged, on account of merits and benefits, to be most like God—how much more fitting is it that God Himself, surpassing in divine and perfect virtues and removed from every earthly stain, should win over the whole human race by divine and heavenly benefits?

These statements are made attractively and in a manner pleasing to the people, and they entice many into belief. Yet those who think thus come nearer indeed to the truth, but they err in part because they give too little consideration to the nature of the matter. For if [Col. 0090B] God is not angry with the impious and unjust, neither surely does He love the pious and just. Therefore the error of those who remove both anger and favour is more consistent. For in matters that differ, it is necessary either to be moved in both directions or in neither. Thus, one who loves the good also hates the wicked; and one who does not hate the wicked does not love the good. For loving the good arises from hatred of the wicked, and hating the wicked descends from love of the good. No one loves life without hating death, nor desires light unless he flees darkness. So closely are these things connected by nature that one cannot exist without the other.

“In Him.” Three Colbert manuscripts, Claromontanus in a second hand, and the Gymnasium edition: “in it.” Claromontanus in a first hand: “in which.”

“For no honour can be owed to God,” etc. In a similar way, Origen in Jeremiah calls God gracious, lest we despair; stern, lest we despise His graciousness. But how, as Cicero teaches in *On Duties*, can a good man not sin even when impunity is set before him? For good men hate to sin through love of virtue; contrariwise, evil men hate to sin through fear of punishment. Moreover, does not Paul also say that the law is not laid down for the righteous? God’s graciousness does not generate contempt of Him; rather, if we believe Paul, God most fully commended His love toward us when we were still sinners. Further, if this judgment of either Lactantius or Origen were valid, Paul’s entire argument concerning predestination would be invalidated. For “But” is absent in twelve manuscripts and four editions. In Em. it is “to anyone.” Heumann also thinks the full stop after *versatur* (“turns”) should be deleted.

“If He is not angry,” etc. Many passages of Scripture testify that God is angry. Yet it should be noted that anger in God is not a violent passion, but a will to punish, and that it is attributed to God effectively, not affectively, as they speak; that is, God does what angry persons do, but is not therefore affected by any disturbance of mind, as angry men are. GAL.

“So that he wanders.” Ultramontane and Brunswick manuscripts: *ut evagetur* (“so that he wanders about”). Editions—Aldine, Fasitel, Tornesius—have *ut vagatur* (“as he wanders”).

“There is no difference between man.” Thus two Bologna manuscripts, Tax., three Colbert manuscripts, and the same number of editions. Elsewhere the corrupt reading “there is not no difference” occurs, contrary to Lactantius’ meaning.—“There is no difference between man,” etc. Thus B. T.; in some sources it is corruptly read “there is some difference,” contrary to Lactantius’ meaning, since at this point he recants the error he formerly held, namely that reason exists also in dumb animals; he discussed this in Book II of the *Institutions*, chapter 3. ISAEUS.

“Rational animal,” etc. Not unlike are the things which Aristotle, in the first book *On the Soul*, reports to have been Anaxagoras’ doctrines: namely, that all animals, both greater and lesser kinds, possess mind—though not the mind to which prudence is attributed, which is not present even in all human beings. Plutarch says nearly the same things about Anaxagoras in Book V of the *Opinions*, chapter 20. BETULEIUS.]

and a bad slave, he certainly does not either hate both or pursue both with benefits and honour; for if he does this, he is both unjust and foolish. Rather, he addresses the good servant kindly, honours him, and puts him in charge of his house, household, and all his possessions; but he punishes the bad servant with curses, beatings, nakedness, hunger, thirst, shackles—so that the former may be an example to the rest not to sin, and the latter an inducement to earn reward; so that fear may restrain some and honour may spur others on.

Therefore, one who loves also hates, and one who hates also loves; for there are people who ought to be loved and people who ought to be held in hatred. And just as one who loves confers good things upon those whom he loves, so one who hates inflicts evils upon those whom he holds in hatred. Since this argument is true, it cannot be overthrown in any way. Therefore their opinion is empty and false: those who attribute one of these to God while taking the other away from Him, [Col. 0091B] no less than those who take away both. But the latter, as we have shown, are not wrong in every respect, but retain the better of the two. Those, however, whom the reasoning and truth of this argument lead, having adopted an entirely false proposition, fall into the greatest error.

For they ought not to have argued thus: “Because God does not grow angry, therefore neither is He moved by favour”; but thus: “Because God is moved by favour, therefore He also grows angry.” For if it had been certain and beyond doubt that God is not angry, then it would have been necessary to proceed to the other conclusion. But since anger is more doubtful and favour almost manifest, [Col. 0092A] it is absurd to wish to overthrow what is certain by means of what is uncertain, when it is easier to establish uncertain matters from what is certain.

## Chapter VI. That God is angry

These are the philosophers’ opinions concerning God. No one has said anything else besides. But if we find that these things which have been said are false, there remains that one final conclusion in which alone truth can be found—a conclusion which has never been adopted or ever defended by philosophers: that God consequently grows angry because He is moved by favour. This is the proposition we must uphold and affirm. For upon it turns the entire sum and hinge of religion and piety. For no honour can be owed to God if He bestows nothing upon one who worships Him; nor can there be any fear if He is not angry with one who does not worship Him.

[Col. 0092B] ## Chapter VII. On man, brute animals, and religion

Although philosophers have often, through ignorance of the truth, departed from reason and fallen into inextricable errors—for this commonly happens to them as to a traveller who does not know the road and will not admit his ignorance: he wanders because he is ashamed to ask passersby—nevertheless no philosopher ever asserted that there is no difference between man and beast; nor has anyone at all, provided he wished to seem wise, equated a rational animal with dumb and [Col. 0093A]

“Equated.” Thus I restored the reading from manuscripts and the old Roman, Florentine, Juntine, Isaeus, and Cellarius editions. Other printed editions have *coaequaverit* (“has equated”); and for “similar,” two Bologna manuscripts, one recent Royal manuscript, two Colbert manuscripts, and Tax. have “very similar.”

“Equal.” Most manuscripts delete “us”; six of them—namely Regio-Put., one other Royal manuscript, two Colbert manuscripts, one Claromontanus manuscript, and eight Brunswick manuscripts—read: “the form of the face declares that [man] is not equal to dumb beasts.”

“Has.” Four recent manuscripts: “have . . . behold.” Francius: perhaps “have . . . behold” should be read.

“But man, in upright posture.” Lactantius above, *Divine Institutes*, Book VII, chapter 9: “His body, raised up from the earth, his lofty face, his upright posture seek their origin.” When he says, “he sets his countenance alongside God’s,” understand that, when he meditates on the likeness which he has in common with God, he says this, Walch maintains.

“He sets his countenance alongside God’s.” Walch’s emendation, “he turns his countenance toward God,” is not to be admitted in a sound passage, especially since Lactantius employs the same phrase in Book II, chapter 2: “You received an upright body so that you might set your eyes and minds alongside Him who made you.” BUN.

“And reason recognizes reason.” Francius preferred “and reason recognizes reason by reason.”—“Reason recognizes reason”: the sense is that human reason—that is, the rational human being—recognizes divine Reason, that is, God, who is Himself also called Reason in Book I, chapter 5. BUN.

“To be proper to man.” The reading is “proper to man,” etc., and the following note is offered.—“To be proper to man”: thus immediately, “speech is proper to man”; later, “laughter too is proper to man”; finally, “what is so proper to man?” and in the parallel passage, Book III, chapter 10: “which are thought to be proper to man.” BUN.

“Similar.” Seneca, *On Anger*, chapter 3: “Dumb animals lack human emotions, but have certain impulses similar to them.” Add the remaining material, and Arnobius, Book 7, and Vossius, Book III *On Idolatry*, chapter 44. BUN.

“Yet there is in them also some likeness of speech.” Francius: “yet there is.”

“This is because they recognize one another by their voices; and, when angry, they utter a sound.” Fourteen manuscripts and two old Roman editions read: “For they are recognized, [and] utter a sound.” Less well; the sense is incomplete.

“To us . . . their voices . . . seem unformed.” Rostock, Venice 1471 and 1472, both editions of 1478, 1493 and 1497, Pierius, Parrhasius, Paris: “unknown,” as Seneca, *On Anger* I.1, “voices insufficiently articulated.” BUN.

“Which understand one another.” *Quae* is correct, for he speaks of dumb animals. But there is an error in eight editions and twelve manuscripts, where *qui* is read.

“In every emotion.” Six editions: *effectu* (“effect”).

“They lower their ears.” That is, they let them droop. Horace, Book II, Ode 13:

> Spellbound by those songs,  
> The hundred-headed beast lowers its black ears.

TURNEBIUS.

“Providence for the future.” And below, “they provide for the future.” Francius: perhaps “foresight . . . and they foresee.”

“A huge heap of grain,” etc. Virgil describes the labours of creatures by this comparison in the first *Georgics*:

> And the weevil devastates a huge heap of grain, as does the ant, fearing a needy old age.

See Horace, *Satires* I, addressed to Maecenas:

> Just as the little ant—for she is an example of great industry—

Solomon too urges the sluggard to labour by the ant’s example, Proverbs chapter 6; and in chapter 30 he gathers examples also of animals’ industry. Besides, Aesop has a fable about the ants’ industry. On their nature consult Pliny, Book XI; Aelian, Book VIII; Aristotle, Book I *History of Animals*, chapter 11. BETULEIUS.

“When they ravage.” From the very ancient and excellent Regio-Put. manuscript I restored *cum populant*; nor is Virgil read otherwise, *Aeneid* IV.403 and *Georgics* I.185: *populat*, by archaism, since the ancients used *populo* actively, as Servius observes. Is. Nonius, chapter 7, no. 26. From WALCH.—In the other manuscripts and editions of Lactantius, *comportant* (“carry together”) is read. Aristotle, Book I *History of Animals*, chapter 1. BETULEIUS.

“It would be long, if I wished to set it all forth.” Not inelegant. “In dumb animals too.” That this is the correct reading is shown by almost all manuscripts and by the text itself. In four recent manuscripts and in the editions, through a scribal error, “in many” is read.

irrational creatures. This is done by certain ignorant persons, themselves like beasts, who, wishing to give themselves over to the belly and pleasure, say that they were born by the same principle as all breathing creatures. It is impious for a human being to say this. For who is so unlearned as not to know, or so imprudent as not to perceive, that something divine exists in man?

I do not yet come to the virtues of mind and intellect, through which man has a manifest kinship with God. Does not the posture of the body itself and the form of the face declare that we are not equal to dumb beasts? Their nature is bent down toward earth and fodder; nor do they have anything in common with heaven, which they do not behold. But man, upright in posture and lofty in countenance, raised to contemplate the world, sets his countenance alongside God’s; and reason recognizes Reason.

[Col. 0093B] Therefore there is no animal, as Cicero says (*On the Laws* I), other than man that has any awareness of God. For man alone is furnished with wisdom, so that he alone understands religion; and this is either the chief or the sole difference between man and dumb creatures. For the other things thought proper to man, even if dumb creatures do not possess them as such, can nevertheless be seen to have analogues among them.

Speech is proper [Col. 0094A] to man; yet there is also in them some likeness of speech. For they recognize one another by their voices; when angry, they make a sound resembling a quarrel; and when they see one another at a distance, they declare by voice the office of mutual greeting. To us their voices seem unformed, just as perhaps ours do to them; but to creatures which understand one another, they are words. Indeed, in every emotion they express definite vocal signs by which they show the disposition of their minds.

Laughter too is proper to man; yet we see in other animals certain signs of joy when they are eager for play: they lower their ears, draw back the mouth, smooth the brow, and let their eyes relax into playfulness. What is so proper to man as reason and foresight for the future? Yet there are animals which make several different exits from their hiding-places, so that if [Col. 0094B] danger arises, escape may lie open to those besieged; and they would not do this unless intelligence and thought were present in them. Others provide for the future, as:

> The ants, mindful of winter,  
> When they ravage a huge heap of grain, store it away beneath cover;

as the bees, which:

> Alone have known their homeland and fixed dwellings.  
> Mindful of the coming winter, in summer they undergo labour  
> And lay up in common what they have gathered.

It would take long, if I wished to set forth the things that are customarily done by the individual kinds of animals that closely resemble human ingenuity. But if, among the dumb animals too, a likeness is found of all those things that are ascribed to man, it is apparent that religion alone is that of which neither any trace nor any suspicion can be discovered among dumb animals. For justice is peculiar to religion, and no other animal attains to it. Man alone exercises dominion; the rest have been made subject to him. But the worship of God belongs to justice; whoever does not embrace it is alien to the nature of man and will live the life of beasts under a human appearance. Since, moreover, we differ from the other animals almost in this one respect alone—that we alone of all beings perceive the divine power and authority, whereas in them there is no understanding of God—it certainly cannot come about that, in this respect, either dumb animals are wiser or human nature is foolish; since to man, on account of wisdom, both all breathing creatures and the whole nature of things are subject. Therefore, if reason and the power of man excel and surpass other living creatures in this respect, that he alone receives knowledge of God, it is apparent that religion cannot in any way be destroyed.

[Col. 0096A] CHAPTER VIII. On religion.

Religion, however, is destroyed if we believe Epicurus when he says:

> For the nature of the gods, each in itself, must needs  
> Enjoy immortal life with the most perfect peace,  
> Removed from our affairs and far withdrawn.  
> For, free from every pain, free from dangers,  
> Strong in its own resources, needing nothing from us,  
> It is neither won by favours for services rendered, nor touched by anger.

When he says these things, does he think that any worship ought to be paid to God, or does he overthrow all religion? For if God bestows no good upon anyone, if he returns no favour for the obedience of one who worships him, what is so vain, so foolish, as to build temples, offer sacrifices, present gifts, and diminish one’s estate, in order to obtain nothing? [Col. 0096B] “But,” it may be said, “an excellent nature ought to be honoured.” What honour can be owed to one who cares for nothing and is ungrateful? Or can we be bound to him by any tie, when he has nothing in common with us? “God,” says Cicero, “if he is such that he is bound by no favour or affection for human beings, farewell to him. For why should I say, ‘May he be propitious’? He can be propitious to no one.” What could be said more contemptuously about God? “Farewell,” he says—that is, let him go and depart, since he can benefit no one. But if God neither possesses nor displays concern, why then should we not do wrong whenever we can escape human notice and evade public laws? Wherever an opportunity for concealment smiles upon us, let us look to our own interest; let us take what belongs to others, either without bloodshed, or even with bloodshed, if beyond the laws there is nothing further that ought to be revered.

[Note: [Col. 0097C] Various Notes on columns 97–98]

**“An opportunity … smiles upon us; let us look to our own interest.”** These last two words are absent from fifteen manuscripts and from the old Roman edition.

**“That ought to be worshipped.”** Thus nearly all manuscripts and the older printed editions. In four recent manuscripts and many printed editions, *that ought to be feared*. Both readings are good. Two recent manuscripts, with a very slight alteration, have *that ought to be lamented*.

**“Epicurus holds this view.”** Two Regius manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470 read, “Lucretius holds this view.” And indeed Lucretius is an echo of Epicurus.

**“Will follow.”** Thus all manuscripts, except two recent ones, which have *ut*; in the printed editions, *sequitur*.

**“So that wisdom also.”** “By which we differ from beasts, and justice.” These last four words are lacking in twenty manuscripts and seven editions.—“By which we differ from beasts, and justice.” Book III, chapter 10, and especially book III, On Anger, chapter 11: “We have said that, religion having been removed, neither wisdom nor justice can be maintained, since the understanding of divinity, by which we differ from beasts, is found in man alone.” These words plainly refer to our passage. BUN.

**“Not for the sake of truth,” etc.** For Valerius teaches by examples that Numa, Scipio, and others feigned religion. BETULEIUS.—And this in order that they might compel unruly peoples, through fear of the gods, to observe the laws.

**“But for usefulness.”** Regio-Put. has *for usefulness*; thirteen manuscripts, *by usefulness*.

**“Terror hangs over.”** Thus almost all manuscripts and six editions. Three recent manuscripts and seven printed editions wrongly have *impendat*; two recent Regius manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470 have *hinders*. One Colbert manuscript has “the executioner hangs over.”

**“They have been invented.”** I have restored this from almost all manuscripts and three editions. Ten manuscripts and twelve printed editions read “they have been completed.”—“They have been invented.” As Arnobius, book VII: “Numa, an artificer in devising religions.” Lactantius imitates Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, chapter 52: “What of those who said that the entire belief concerning the immortal gods had been invented by wise men?” BUN.

[Col. 0098C]

**“Although briefly.”** Thus nearly all manuscripts and six older printed editions, and Cellarius and Walch; in three recent manuscripts and ten printed editions, *however briefly*.

**“Protagoras,” etc.** See Laertius. Protagoras was discussed in book I of the *Institutes*, chapter 2. Arnobius also reports this in book VIII *Against the Nations*. Similar catalogues occur in Cicero’s first book *On the Nature of the Gods*; and among ecclesiastical writers, in Epiphanius’s *Epitome*, Eusebius’s *Preparation for the Gospel*, book XIV, chapter 1, and Irenaeus, book II, chapter 19. Irenaeus calls Anaxagoras *atheos* [ἄθεον, “godless”], unless the reading is corrupt; but I do not think it is. BETULEIUS.—Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, chapter 23: “Protagoras of Abdera, perhaps the greatest sophist of that age, having stated at the beginning of a book: ‘Concerning the gods, I am unable to say either that they exist or that they do not exist,’ was, by decree of the Athenians, expelled from city and territory, and his books were burned in the public assembly.”

[Col. 0098D]

**“In the time of Socrates.”** According to Laertius, he flourished in the seventy-fourth Olympiad. But Eusebius in his *Chronicle* places this burning of the books in the third year of the eighty-fourth Olympiad; Socrates was certainly then flourishing, and Plato’s dialogue entitled *Protagoras* also testifies that he was Socrates’ contemporary. Yet a question concerning this is discussed in Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book I, chapter 1. BETULEIUS.

**“And his books in the public assembly,” etc.** See what we said above on chapter 22 of book I. From this passage a passage in Minucius Felix must be corrected, where some read *they mocked at his writings*; one must read *they burned them*. This is clear from Lactantius and also from Diogenes Laertius, who discusses the whole matter. See also Cicero, book I, *On the Nature of the Gods*.

**“And Plato, his pupil,” etc.** How inconsistently he discoursed concerning divine matters is objected not only by Velleius the Epicurean in Cicero, but is also demonstrated clearly and evidently by Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book XIII, through a careful comparison of Plato’s own writings. BETULEIUS.

**“Indivisible.”** That is, atoms.

While Epicurus holds these views, he utterly destroys religion; once it is removed, confusion and disorder of life will follow. But if religion cannot be removed, if we are to retain both wisdom, by which we differ from beasts, and justice, by which common life is made safer, how can Religion itself be maintained or guarded without fear? For what is not feared is despised; and what is despised is certainly not worshipped. Thus it happens that religion, majesty, and honour consist in fear; but there is no fear where no one is angry. Therefore, whether you take away God’s favour, or his anger, or both, religion must necessarily be removed; and without it human life is filled with folly, crime, and savagery. For conscience greatly restrains men if we believe that we live in the sight of God; if we think that not only the things we do are seen from above, but also the things we think or say are heard by God. “But,” it is said, “it is useful to believe this, as some think, not for the sake of truth but for usefulness; because laws cannot punish conscience unless some terror from above hangs over us to restrain sins.” Therefore all religion is false and there is no divinity. But everything has been invented by prudent men, in order that life may be lived more rightly and more innocently. This is a great question, and one foreign to the subject we have proposed; but because it necessarily arises, it ought to be touched upon, although briefly.

[Col. 0098A] CHAPTER IX. On God’s providence and opinions opposed to it.

Since the opinions of philosophers in earlier times agreed concerning providence, and there was no doubt that the world had both been ordered by God and reason, and was governed by reason, Protagoras was the first of all to arise, in the time of Socrates, who said that it was not clear to him whether there was any divinity or not. His discussion was judged so impious, and so contrary to truth and religion, that the Athenians both expelled him from their borders and burned in the public assembly the books in which these matters were contained. There is no need to dispute about his opinion, because he pronounced nothing certain. After this, Socrates and Plato, his pupil, and those who flowed out from Plato’s school like streams in different directions—the Stoics and Peripatetics—held the same opinion as their predecessors.

Later Epicurus said indeed that God exists, because there must be something in the world eminent, excellent, and blessed; but he denied all providence. Thus he said that the world itself was equipped by no reason, no art, no craftsmanship, but that the nature of things was formed into a mass from certain minute and indivisible seeds. I do not see what could be said more contradictory than this. For if God exists, he is certainly provident, insofar as he is God; nor can divinity be attributed to him otherwise than if he both knows the past and foresees the future. Since, therefore, he removed providence, he also denied that God exists. But when he professed that God exists, he at the same time conceded that providence exists. For the one can neither exist nor be understood at all without the other.

[Note: [Col. 0099B] Various Notes on columns 99–100]

**“But when he professed that God exists.”** *But* has been added from all manuscripts and many printed editions, where it was lacking in the others. One ancient Bologna manuscript reads *confessed*.

**“Had declined,” etc.** Diagoras, however, is placed by Eusebius in the same Olympiad in which, as we said above, Laertius places Protagoras, namely the seventy-fourth. Theodorus, however, is placed in the one hundred and eighteenth Olympiad, although Epicurus was scarcely a few years earlier; for Laertius places his death in the one hundred and seventh Olympiad, although Eusebius reports that he flourished in the one hundred and eighteenth. BETULEIUS.

**“Melius Diagoras.”** “Melius” from his homeland, just as Theodorus below is called Cyrenaean. One ancient Regius manuscript has *Aetlius*; one older Bologna manuscript and eight others, with two old Roman editions, *Alius*; Regio-Put., one other Regius, two Colbert manuscripts, Goth., Navar., Gat., Marm., Ultr., Pen., Brun., *Aelius*; the Tornesian manuscript and the Geneva edition have *Metius*, which I think was corruptly written by a copyist for *Melius*, as he is called by Cicero, book I, *On the Nature of the Gods*. The Baluzian manuscript and fifteen printed editions have “A certain Diagoras arose at Athens.” Nor is this reading to be despised; for Suidas, under “Diagoras,” reports that Diagoras, after the capture of Melos—whence he was called Melius—withdrew to Athens. One recent Regius manuscript, Clarom., one Sorbonne manuscript, and three Colbert manuscripts read, “There arose a certain godless man, Diagoras,” except that the particle *and* is absent from the first two. Concerning this Diagoras, moreover, see the notes at the beginning of chapter 2, book I of the *Divine Institutes*.—“A certain Diagoras at Athens.” This is the received reading of almost all books, from which I have not dared depart. P., however, has “A certain Aelius Diagoras,” and B. “a certain other man,” whence one might suspect that it should be read: “A certain Melius Diagoras”; for Cicero indeed calls him Melius at the beginning of book I *On the Nature of the Gods*, where he treats these very matters, as do Plutarch, *Opinions*, book I, chapter 7; Sextus Empiricus, *Pyrrhonian Sketches*, book III, chapter 24; Arnobius, book IV; Minucius; and others. But when Lactantius and many others of our writers call Diagoras, Theodorus, and the others—also discussed in book I of the *Institutes*, chapter 2—*atheoi* [ἀθέους], that is, “without God,” it must be considered whether perhaps the ancient slander of the pagans against good and learned men is being imported even by Christians against these same men. For when they mocked the multitude of gods and so many monsters and prodigies that foolish paganism worshipped, they were thought to be *atheoi* [ἄθεοι], and to have believed in no god at all; and Clement of Alexandria certainly complains of and wonders at this. ISAEUS.

**“The Cyrenaean Theodorus.”** He too earned the epithet *the godless* [τοῦ ἀθέου], according to the testimony of Epiphanius. And I judge that Eusebius’s *Chronicle* should be read thus where “Theodorus of Athens” is found; nor do the dates oppose me. Augustine, *Against the Letters of Petilianus the Donatist*, book II, thinks that the saying of this Psalm was directed against this Theodorus: “The fool has said that there is no God.” BETULEIUS.

**“They preferred even against truth.”** *Even*, here meaning “also,” French *même*, is absent from ten manuscripts and as many editions.

**“To deny this.”** Two Bologna manuscripts, one recent Regius, two Colbert manuscripts, Tax., and Baluz. read *to deny it*.

**“Which, through so many ages and by so many intellects.”** This reading occurs in four old editions and all manuscripts, except one recent Regius manuscript, which, like fifteen editions, has “through ages and intellects.”—“Through so many ages, by so many intellects.” I take *through so many ages* in the ablative of removal, and *by so many intellects* in the dative, for *by so many intellects*. Book IV, chapter 2: “Wisdom sought with utmost zeal and labour by so many intellects and through so many times.” *Epitome*, chapter 40, at the end: “Truth sought by so many intellects, through so many ages.” BUN.

**“By the authority of eminent men.”** These were leaders of the greatest schools, whom he brings forward below before the end of chapter 10 and in chapter 11. Twelve manuscripts, with the Roman edition of 1470, read *truth*, another *virtue*.

**“By both.”** Thus manuscripts and printed editions. Francius thinks perhaps *by each* should be read.

**“May wander.”** Thus nearly all manuscripts with seven editions; in the other received editions, *may wander abroad*; in one recent Regius manuscript, *may roam*; in one Colbert manuscript and Clarom. from the first hand, *may be directed*.

**“Strato.”** Strato of Lampsacus, son of Arcesilaus and pupil of Theophrastus, was tutor to Ptolemy Philadelphus: a man of keen intellect who, having neglected the part of philosophy most necessary, that which lies in virtue and morals, devoted himself entirely to the investigation of nature, whence he obtained the surname “the Physicist.” He flourished in the 123rd Olympiad. Laertius writes his life in book V. He is frequently mentioned throughout Cicero, from whom these things too have been transcribed; for they are found almost word for word in the first book *On the Nature of the Gods*. BETULEIUS.—See also Cicero in *Lucullus*, near the end.

**“A power of generating and diminishing.”** Cicero states it more fully, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, chapter 13: “Nor should Strato, who is called the Physicist, be heard; he thinks that all divine power is situated in nature, which has causes of generating, increasing, and diminishing, but lacks all sensation and form.” BUN.

**“By a chance concurrence.”** *Chance* is absent from thirteen manuscripts and two old Roman editions. But it occurs in the others, in Lactantius himself, *Epitome*, chapter 36, and in Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, chapter 24, or section 66.
