**“The whole world came together.”** Good, as is evident from what precedes and follows. Eleven manuscripts and the edition of Isaeus have *cohered*. Both readings are good.

**“Did Leucippus alone have eyes?”** Francius:

> “Or do you alone, Paris, have eyes?”

Although Laertius makes no mention of atoms in connection with Leucippus, and Plutarch assigns them to Democritus as their author, Aristotle nevertheless frequently joins Democritus and Leucippus in this doctrine in the first book *On Generation*. Cicero does likewise in the first book *On the Nature of the Gods*: “These abominations of Democritus, or indeed earlier of Leucippus: that there are certain smooth particles, others rough, some round, others partly angular, some pyramidal, some curved and as though hooked; from these heaven and earth were produced, with no nature compelling, but by a certain chance concurrence.” Epicurus later also adopted this doctrine, just as there was nothing in Epicurus’s physics that he did not derive from Democritus. Yet, as Cicero writes in book I *On Ends*, the things Epicurus wishes to correct in Democritus appear to be corrupted by him. Thus Democritus’s atoms have motion from eternal time, while the Epicureans have deviation. Augustine also mentions this difference where he writes of empty and useless questions. BETUL.—See book III of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 17.—“Did Leucippus alone?” Cicero reports this in *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, chapter 24: “These abominations of Democritus, or indeed earlier of Leucippus: that there are certain smooth particles, others rough, some round, others partly angular, some curved and as though hooked; from these heaven and earth were produced, with no nature compelling, but by a certain chance concurrence.” CELL.

But in later times, when philosophy had already declined, a certain Melius Diagoras arose, who said that there was no God at all and, because of this opinion, was called *atheos* [ἄθεος, “godless”]; likewise Theodorus of Cyrene. Since both could discover nothing new, everything having already been said and discovered, they preferred, even against truth, to deny that in which all their predecessors had agreed without hesitation. These are the men who slandered providence, established and defended through so many ages and by so many intellects. What then? Shall we refute these petty and feeble philosophers by reason, or by the authority of eminent men? Or rather by both? But we must hasten, lest the discourse wander too far from the subject.

CHAPTER X. [Col. 0100A] On the origin of the world, the nature of things, and God’s providence.

Those who do not wish the world to have been made by divine providence say either that it was formed from first principles casually combining with one another, or that it suddenly came into existence by nature; and that nature, as Strato says, has within itself a power of generating and diminishing, but has neither sensation nor form—so that we may understand that all things have been generated, as it were, of their own accord, without artificer or author. Both positions are vain and impossible. But this happens to those ignorant of truth: they devise anything whatever rather than think what reason demands. First, I ask where those minute seeds are, or whence they come, by whose chance concurrence they say the whole world came together. Who has ever seen them? Who has perceived them? Who has heard them? Did Leucippus alone [Col. 0100B] have eyes? Alone have mind? He was surely alone of all men blind and senseless, to utter things which no sick man in delirium could rave, nor a sleeping man dream.

[Note: [Col. 0101D] Various Notes on columns 101–102]

**“Could dream.”** Thus I have restored it from five old editions and all manuscripts except one Colbert manuscript, which, with twelve editions, has *can*.

**“The four elements,” etc.** Not all philosophers agree on this. Empedocles and Anaxagoras were the first to maintain four elements; yet they held that these endure and are dissolved by concord and discord. This does not escape Aristotle’s criticism, who himself also maintains a fifth essence. BETULEIUS.

**“Smooth and rough,” etc.** These are Cartesian particles.

**“And angular and hooked.”** *And angular* is absent from four recent Regius manuscripts, four Colbert manuscripts, Goth., Lips., Marm., one Sorbonne manuscript, Clarom., and Brun. But it ought to be present, as will shortly be evident to the reader.—“And round, angular, and hooked.” I have accepted this reading because it agrees better with what follows, where these five are repeated: “If they are smooth and round, rough, angular, and hooked.” Again, *Epitome*, chapter 36: “If they are hooked and angular, then they are divisible.” Our author has it from Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, chapter 24: “There are certain smooth particles, others rough, some round, partly angular, hooked.” BUN.

**“Speaking something.”** Twelve recent manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470 have *speaking some things*.

**“They are smooth and round.”** Three Regius manuscripts, four Colbert manuscripts, and printed editions have *light*, wrongly.

**“The smoothness itself of the grains.”** Thus restored by me from nearly all manuscripts and the old Roman edition. Four recent manuscripts and nearly all printed editions have *lightness*.

**“If they are rough, angular, and hooked,” etc.** Thus the oldest manuscripts, two Bologna and Regio-Put. Twelve others and two editions add “he says”; with them, another eight manuscripts and ten printed editions omit *if*.

**“For hooks … and angles.”** I have restored the accusative case from many older and better manuscripts and the old Roman edition and Cellarius. In the other printed editions and five recent manuscripts, it is “with hooks … and angles.”

**“Minute particles of dust.”** Seven manuscripts have *crumbs*.

[Col. 0102D]

**“Perfect madness.”** Six manuscripts have *carefully covered*; one other, *protected*.

**“Nothing seems capable of being said further.”** More correctly, I think, according to two Bologna manuscripts, one Regius, two Colbert manuscripts, and Baluz., than to add the reading of the others; for with the verb *to add*, *further* would be useless.

**“That he might add.”** Thus restored from manuscripts. Printed editions have *what*.

**“To be empty.”** That is, to be void. FRANCIUS.

**“That worlds are innumerable.”** The phrases *many worlds* [πολλοὺς κόσμους] in Philo, *infinite worlds* [ἀπείρους] in Laertius and Plutarch, and *an infinite world* [κόσμον ἄπειρον] in Epiphanius gave rise to the proverbial Democritean worlds. Plutarch, *Opinions*, book II, chapter 1: “Democritus, Epicurus, and their pupil Metrodorus said that worlds were innumerable in the infinite expanse extending without limit throughout its whole extent.” BETULEIUS.

**“And first I ask.”** Eight manuscripts: “But first I ask.”

**“The nature or origin of those seeds,” etc.** Virgil and Lucretius also called the atoms [τὰς ἀτόμους] “seeds”; Lucretius, not far from the beginning of book I.

The ancient philosophers taught that all things consist of four elements. He did not wish this, lest he should seem to tread in another’s footsteps. But he wished there to be other first principles of the elements themselves, which can neither be seen nor touched nor perceived by any bodily part. “They are so small,” he says, “that no edge of iron is so fine that they can be cut or divided by it”; whence he gave them the name atoms [ἄτομα, “indivisibles”]. But there confronted him the objection that, if all had one and the same nature, they could not produce diverse things with the great variety which we see in the world. He therefore said that they are smooth and rough, round, angular, and hooked. How much better it would have been to remain silent than to have a tongue for uses so wretched and empty! And indeed I fear that one who thinks these things need refutation appears no less mad. Yet let us answer him as though he were saying something. If they are smooth and round, they certainly cannot grasp one another so as to form any body; just as, if someone wished to compress millet into a single compact mass, the smoothness of the grains themselves would prevent them from coming together into a lump. If they are rough, angular, and hooked, so that they can cohere, then they are divisible and capable of being cut; for hooks and angles must necessarily project, so that they can be cut off.

[Col. 0102A] Therefore, whatever can be cut off and torn away can also be seen and held. “These,” he says, “fly through the void in restless motions and are carried here and there, just as we see minute particles of dust in the sun when it has sent rays and light through a window. From these trees, grasses, and every kind of crop arise; from these animals, water, fire, and all things are generated, and again into these they are resolved.” This can be tolerated so long as small things are being discussed. But from these the world itself also was formed. He filled up the measure of perfect madness; nothing seems capable of being said further. Yet he found something to add: “Since,” he says, “the whole is infinite and nothing can be empty, worlds must necessarily be innumerable.” What force could there have been in atoms, that masses so immeasurable should be gathered together from things so minute? And first I ask what is the nature or origin of those seeds. For if all things are from them, from where, then, shall we say that they themselves exist? What nature will supply such an abundance for making innumerable worlds? But let us concede that he has raved with impunity about worlds; let us speak about this world in which we are and which we see. He says that all things are made from indivisible particles.

If this were so, no thing would ever need the seed of its own kind. Birds would be born without eggs, and eggs would be produced without being laid; likewise all other living things without intercourse. Trees and the things that grow from the earth would not have their own seeds, which we handle and sow every day. Why does a crop spring from grain, and grain again from a crop? Finally, if the conjunction and clustering of atoms made all things, everything would solidify in the air, since atoms fly through the void. Why, without earth, roots, moisture, or seed, can neither grass, tree, nor crops arise and grow? From this it is apparent that nothing is made from atoms, since each thing has its own definite nature, its own seed, its own law given from the beginning. Finally, Lucretius, as if forgetful of the atoms that he maintained, used arguments against those who say that all things are made from nothing which would have force against himself. For he said:

> For if things came to be from nothing, from all things  
> Every kind might arise; nothing would need seed.

And later:

> Therefore it must be acknowledged that nothing can be made from nothing,  
> Since things require seed, through which each created thing  
> May be brought forth into the gentle breezes of the air.”

Who would think that this man had a brain when he said these things and did not see that they were contrary to himself? For that nothing is made by atoms is apparent from the fact that the seed of each thing is definite—unless perhaps we are also to believe that the nature of fire and water comes from atoms. What of this: when substances of the hardest rigidity collide with a more violent blow, fire is struck out. Do atoms lie hidden in iron or flint? Who enclosed them? Or why do they not flash forth of their own accord? Or how could seeds of fire remain in the coldest material? [Col. 0103C]

[Note: [Col. 0103C] Various Notes on columns 103–104]

**“Not grass.”** Thus I have restored it from manuscripts and the old Roman, Gymnic, and Cellarius editions. The other editions read *not grasses*.

**“Can arise and grow.”** Fourteen manuscripts and thirteen editions have *or can be generated*.

**“To be made from nothing.”** Lips. 2, Reimm., Rost., and Venice 1471 have *from no thing*. Bologna, Goth., both Venice editions of 1478, Betul., Torn., and Walch have *from nothing*. The latter conflicts with the verse; the former is Lucretius’s *nilum*, who willingly contracts *nihilum* into *nilum*, for example:

> “… that all things return to nothing [nilum],”

and verse 674:

> “Lest all things utterly return to nothing [nilum].”

**“It must be acknowledged.”** Two Bologna manuscripts, one recent Regius, three Colbert manuscripts, Pen., and Clarom. have *it must be thought*; one Sorbonne manuscript, *it must be known*.

**“Who would think that he had a brain?”** Thus restored from nearly all manuscripts; four recent manuscripts and printed editions have *thinks*. “To have had a brain,” that is, reason and a sound mind; for the ancients said that the seat of the soul was in the brain. Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, book I, chapter 9.—“Had a brain.” Elegantly said, as Phaedrus says of a mask, book I, 7, 2: “What a great appearance, yet it has no brain!” See Bunemannus there in his new commentary. Again Lactantius, *Epitome*, chapter 54: “Men of empty brain”; and *On the Workmanship*, chapter 16: “Others have said that its seat”—that of the mind—“is in the brain.” BUN.

**“We shall believe.”** One Colbert manuscript has *we believe*; another Colbert manuscript and Brun., *may we believe*.

**“Fire is struck out.”** All manuscripts and printed editions have this, except the first Venice edition of 1478, which has a faulty form. I would prefer, if the books allowed it, *is struck forth*, as Virgil, *Aeneid* I.174:

> “And first Achates struck forth a spark from flint.”

BUN.

**“A glass globe,” etc.** This is the nature of crystal, which is nothing other than water frozen into the hardness of stone through cold and age. See Marbod with his commentators. A book by Theophrastus on the nature of fire survives. Similar methods of producing fire occur in Pliny and Lucretius himself, and also in Seneca’s *Natural Questions*. BETULEIUS.

**“It must be believed.”** Five manuscripts have *they believe*.

**“But fire cannot be kindled from the sun,” etc.** Lactantius is mistaken: experience establishes the contrary.

[Col. 0104D]

**“If you breathe upon wax.”** One recent Regius manuscript, three Colbert manuscripts, and Baluz. have “If [you breathe] upon wax in beehives.”

**“A light vapour.”** Goth. has *gentle*; one ancient Bologna manuscript, *gentle* in the neuter.

**“Or of the sea.”** Six manuscripts have *and of the sea*.

**“Why should I.”** This is to be read from the old manuscripts, one Bologna and Cauc. The others and printed editions have *therefore*; Brun., *then*.

**“Then.”** Thus restored from all manuscripts except three recent ones, which have *finally*, as in the printed editions.

**“If things which are not seen arise from invisible things, does no one see [those things which are seen]?”** Thus it should be read from both Bologna manuscripts, three Colbert manuscripts, Baluz., and Tax., not as the others have it: “If things which are seen arise from invisible things, why then does no one see?” He employs an argument from opposites: if things not seen flow from invisible bodies, then things seen come forth from visible ones; why, then, are those not seen? ISAEUS.

**“Let him consider.”** Seven manuscripts have *consider*.

**“Tangible.”** Sixteen manuscripts, including Regio-Put., have *touchable*; ancient Bologna, *capable of touch*; two Colbert manuscripts, *touchable*; two recent Regius manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470, *untouchable*; another Roman edition of 1474, *incapable of touch*; the other Roman edition of 1468, with the remaining printed editions and manuscripts, *tangible*, as in the text. Hence it is clear, as from other variant readings, that the three Roman editions differ from one another. Elsewhere Lactantius writes, *Divine Institutes*, book V, chapter 22, “tangible to eyes and hand”; see the note on *On the Workmanship*, chapter 1, “to handle with hand and eyes.”

[Col. 0104A] I pass over flint and iron. If you hold in the sun a glass globe full of water, fire is kindled from the light reflected by the water, even in the hardest frost. Must we also believe that fire exists in water? Yet fire cannot be kindled from the sun even in summer. If you breathe upon wax, or if a light vapour touches anything, whether a marble crust or a metal plate, water gradually gathers through the tiniest dewdrops. Likewise, mist arises from the breath of the earth or sea; either, dispersed, it moistens whatever it covers, or, gathered together and carried aloft by wind into high mountains, it is compressed into a cloud and pours down the heaviest rains. Where, then, do we say that liquids are born? In vapour? In exhalation? In wind? Yet nothing can subsist in that which neither can be touched nor seen. Why should I speak of animals, [Col. 0104B] in whose bodies we see nothing formed without reason, order, usefulness, and beauty of form? So much so that the most ingenious and diligent arrangement of all their parts and members repels chance and fortune. But let us suppose that limbs, bones, sinews, and blood can solidify from atoms. What of sensation, thought, memory, mind, and intelligence? By what seeds can these be joined together? “By the smallest,” he says. Then there are others larger. How, then, are they indivisible?

Then, if things which are not seen arise from invisible things, it follows that things which are seen arise from visible things; why, then, does no one see them? But whether one considers the invisible things in man or the tangible things which come under sight, who does not see that both consist by reason? How, then, can things coming together without reason produce anything rational? For we see nothing—

[Note: [Col. 0105C] Various Notes on columns 105–106]

**“The outer lineaments of the body.”** Lond., Reg., Reimm., and all the books have *outer*. Bouhier therefore rightly warns against Davisius on the basis of this passage; likewise in Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, chapter 44: “Only the outer lineaments must be preserved.” Lactantius similarly says in book V, chapter 2, “the lineaments and the general outline.” BUN.

**“I pass over.”** One ancient Bologna manuscript has *I omit*. In place of *the use of seeing*, the Venetian, Tridentine, and Florentine editions have *the sense of seeing*, wrongly, for the word *sensation* has just preceded.

**“Production.”** A rare word, but one found in Cicero, *On Ends*, book II, chapter 45, and book III, chapter 24: “the production of art.” **“For if the gods too had been constituted from them.”** Thus I have restored it from very many manuscripts, among which are the oldest, one Bologna and Regio-Put. Six manuscripts and printed editions read, “if the gods too had constituted [themselves] from them”; three recent Regius manuscripts, Clarom., and the Roman edition of 1470 have “if the gods … had constituted.”

**“Capable of dispersal.”** This word scarcely occurs among other writers; nevertheless it is found in Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book III, chapter 12: “Air is by nature most yielding and capable of dispersal.”

**“Returning.”** Two Bologna manuscripts, Tax., and one Colbert manuscript have *running back*.

**“Those first principles would generate.”** One ancient Bologna manuscript has *would have generated*.

[Col. 0106C]

**“Had not built.”** Seven manuscripts and four editions have *did not build*.—“I ask why they had not built.” Rost., Venice 1471–1515, and Paris have: “I ask … why they did not build.” Not badly, in Heumann’s judgment, who thinks the earlier form too not unworthy of Lactantius from the passages above mentioned. To me only the earlier form seems worthy of Lactantius, who, when uncorrupted, always uses the subjunctive after *I ask why*. Thus in book II, chapter 4, I restored: “I ask why they had not punished sacrileges”; book III, chapter 13: “They are accustomed to ask why … they are found.” Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, chapter 9: “I inquire why the builders of the world suddenly arose … I ask why your Providence has ceased”; *On Fate*, chapter 8: “I ask … why they cannot.” BUN.

[Col. 0106D]

**“The earth should be gathered into a mass.”** Thus the older and better manuscripts, Bologna, Regio-Put., and others, and the edition of Isaeus. But twelve recent manuscripts and printed editions have “the earths should be gathered into a mass.”

**“More subtle, minute.”** Bunemannus indeed reads *more subtle, minute*, and appends the following note to this expression.—“More subtle, minute.” Betul., Torn., 1587–1613, Geneva 1630, and Walch have “subtle and minute.” Lond., Reg., and Goth. have “subtle, minute.” Arnobius uses this frequently, Minucius more frequently, and Lactantius scarcely once or twice. Thus Goth. has “lesser, lowly,” where more witnesses have “lesser and lowly”; hence I followed the London and Goth. manuscripts: “more subtle, minute,” in place of “most subtle, most minute.” BUN.

**“So subtle.”** Six manuscripts and two editions add “and so wonderful”; Cauc. and nine editions have “so subtly formed by unfeeling nature.”

**“If it has no mind.”** Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book II, describes different opinions or definitions of nature: one of those who think nature a certain force, without reason, producing necessary motions in bodies; another of those who define it as a force sharing in reason and order, advancing as though by a road and declaring what each thing produces for what cause, what follows, and whose ingenuity no art, hand, or craftsman can attain by imitation. BETULEIUS.

…to exist throughout the whole world which does not contain within itself the highest and most wonderful rational order. Since this is above human perception and intelligence, to what can it more rightly be ascribed than to divine providence? Reason and art fashion a likeness and statue of a human being; shall we suppose that the human being himself comes to be from fragments randomly coming together? And what resemblance to truth is there in an imitation, when the highest and most excellent craftsmanship can imitate nothing but a shadow and the outward contours of the body? Could human ingenuity bestow upon its work either any motion or sensation? I pass over the function of seeing, hearing, smelling, and the marvelous utilities of the other limbs, whether visible or hidden. What craftsman could make either the human heart, or voice, or wisdom itself? [Col. 0105B] Does any sane person therefore think that what a human being cannot accomplish by reason and deliberation could have been accomplished by the random concurrence of atoms adhering together everywhere? You see into what ravings they have fallen, because they refuse to attribute the making and governance of things to God.

Let us nevertheless grant them that earthly things are made from atoms: are heavenly things made so as well? They say that the gods are incorruptible, eternal, and blessed; and they grant immunity to the gods alone, so that they may not appear to have been compacted by the concurrence of atoms. For if the gods too had been constituted from these, they would be liable to dissolution, once their seeds were at some time dispersed and returned to their own nature. Therefore, if there is anything which atoms have not produced, why do we not understand everything else in the same way? But I ask: before those first principles generated the world, why did the gods not build themselves a dwelling-place? Evidently, unless the atoms had united and made the heaven, the gods would still be hanging in the midst of the void. By what plan, then, by what rational principle did the atoms gather themselves out of a confused heap, so that from some of them the earth was massed together below, while heaven was stretched out above, distinguished by so great a variety of stars that nothing more ornate could ever be conceived? Can one who sees things so great and such as these suppose that such miracles were made by no design, no providence, no divine reason, but were compounded from fine, tiny atoms? Is it not like a prodigy that a man should have been born to say these things, or another should have existed to believe them—such as Democritus, who was his pupil, or Epicurus, into whom all folly flowed from the fountain of Leucippus?

But, they say—as others do—that the world was produced by nature, which lacks sensation and form. This is far more absurd. If nature made the world, it must have made it by deliberation and reason; for one who makes something possesses either the will to make or knowledge. If it lacks sensation and form, how can that be made by it which has both sensation and form? Unless perhaps someone thinks that the organism of living creatures, so subtle, could have been formed and endowed with life by something insentient; or that this appearance of heaven, so providently adapted to the needs of living beings, emerged suddenly by some unknown chance, without a creator, without an artificer.

“If there is anything,” says Chrysippus, “which can accomplish those things which a human being, though endowed with reason, cannot accomplish, that thing is certainly greater, stronger, and wiser than man.” But a human being cannot make heavenly things; therefore that which makes or has made them surpasses man in skill, deliberation, prudence, and power. What, then, can it be except God? But nature, which they imagine to be, as it were, the mother of things, if it does not possess mind, will never accomplish or undertake anything. For where there is no thought, there is no motion and no efficacy.

[Col. 0107C] **Variorum Notes to Columns 107–108**

**“Nor motion,” etc.** Yet Nature, in Zeno’s view, is an artificer, maker, counsellor, and provident provider for every utility and convenience of the world; it possesses all voluntary motions, impulses, and appetites, which the Greeks call *hormai* (ὁρμάς). Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, II. BETULEIUS.

**“By deliberation.”** Seven manuscripts add *his own*, absent from the others and from the printed editions, as also from the remaining members of the period.

**“Made.”** Two Colbert manuscripts, Claromontanus, and the editions of Gymnicus and Spark read *makes*.

**“Why could it make heaven . . . but not a city?”** These words resemble Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II.37: “If the concurrence of atoms can make the world, why can it not make a colonnade, a temple, a house, a city—things less laborious and indeed much easier?” BUNEMANN.

**“Yet the atoms ought not.”** Thus restored from the most ancient manuscripts and from the best copies—two Bononienses, three Regii, five Colberti, Claromontanus, Baluzius, Brunck—and supported by three others in which the negation is absent. In three recent manuscripts and ten editions, *could have* stands for *ought to have* [Col. 0107D]; in four other printed editions, *could*.

Bunemann reads *ought to have*, omitting *not*: “The printed editions,” he says, “have *yet they could have*. London, Royal, Gotha, Leipzig 2 and 3, Reimann: *yet they ought not to have*. Then *not* should be read for *surely not*. But Bononiensis, Taxensis, Penuensis, Emmanuellensis: *Yet they ought to have*.”

**“No arrangement.”** *On the Workmanship*, ch. 6: “If first principles leave no kind of arrangement untried.” BUNEMANN.

**“So far as earthly frailty could receive.”** Thus restored from all manuscripts and ten editions. The other printed texts read *desired*.

**“Necessary for . . . uses.”** He regularly joins the words thus. Book I: “having left the things necessary for the protection of life”; *Epitome*, ch. 56, beginning: “necessary for salvation”; Seneca, *Letters* 8: “Many things necessary for daily use are needed.” BUNEMANN.

**“Soul . . . ruler of the body.”** Book II, ch. 12; book VI, ch. 1; *On the Workmanship*, ch. 1; Sallust, *Jugurtha* I.3. BUNEMANN.

**“For his own uses.”** I follow the older and better manuscripts [Col. 0108B]—two Bononienses, Regio-Putianus, many others—and the editions of Isaeus. The remaining editions and ten recent manuscripts have *for the uses of his own*.

**“The human body was fashioned from earth.”** Thus all manuscripts, with the old Roman edition, except one recent Royal manuscript and the first hand of Claromontanus, which have, as do the printed editions, *was made*. See below, *to have been fashioned*.

[Col. 0108C]

**“From which man received his name.”** This is an allusion, not a true etymology, which must be sought from Hebrew, FRANCIUS.—See Lactantius above, *Divine Institutes* II.11, and Vossius, *Etymology of the Latin Language*. In seven editions *man* is absent.

**“Marcus Cicero, in the Tusculans and in the Consolation.”** In *Tusculan Disputations* I.27 Cicero quoted the following words from his *Consolation*. For he says: “Having followed this view, we expressed the following in the *Consolation* in these very words: ‘No origin of souls on earth,’” etc. CELLARIUS.

**“For there is.”** In twelve recent manuscripts and seven editions *for* is absent; it occurs in the remaining codices and in Cicero’s fragments of the *Consolation*.

**“And fashioned.”** Thus the manuscripts, the edition of Betuleius, and Cicero himself. In two recent Royal manuscripts and the printed editions: *made*.

**“Nor indeed anything moist.”** Thus Cicero. Supporting manuscripts are two ancient Royal manuscripts, five Colberti, Baluzius, and Brunck, which read *nor indeed anything moist*; the ancient Bononiensis and four others have *or indeed anything moist*.

[Col. 0108D]

**“Airy.”** That is, consisting of air. FRANCIUS.

**“For in these natures there is nothing.”** Thus the manuscripts with the old Roman edition of 1470 and the Venetian edition of 1490. Two Colberti, Baluzius, and ten printed editions read: “For nothing is innate in these.”

**“For in these natures.”** London, Royal, Gotha, Leipzig 2, with Cicero, elegantly read *in these natures*. BUNEMANN.

**“Which,” etc.** Thus with two Bononienses, Taxensis, two Colberti, Baluzius, Claromontanus in the second hand, and the editions of Cratander, Grynaeus, Cellarius, Walch, and Cicero himself. The rest read *whence, and*.

**“Foresees.”** So I read with the first ancient Bononiensis, Penuensis, and Cicero himself. Claromontanus in the first hand reads *perceives through*. The rest: *provides for*.

**“Nor can it ever be discovered.”** Thus consistently in all manuscripts and printed editions, except four recent editions which have *will be discovered*, as in Cicero. Bunemann, however, reads *will be discovered* and gives this following note: “Nor will an origin ever be discovered. Many books had ‘they are discovered ever’; Betuleius alone, ‘nor are they discovered anywhere.’ I wrote, with Cicero, Isaeus, Spark, and Heumann, ‘Nor will [it] be discovered,’ namely the origin; for above he had said, ‘No origin of souls on earth can be found.’” BUNEMANN. But if it employs deliberation to begin something, reason to arrange it, art to accomplish it, strength to bring it to completion, and power to govern and preserve it, why should it be called nature rather than God? Or if the concurrence of atoms, or nature lacking mind, made the things which we see, I ask why it could make heaven but could not make a city or a house; why it made mountains of marble but did not make columns and statues. But surely the atoms ought also to have converged to make these things, since they leave no arrangement untried. As for a nature which has no mind, it is no wonder that it forgot how to make these things.

What then is it? Surely God, when he began this work of the world—than which nothing can be more ordered for arrangement, more fitted for usefulness, more beautiful in appearance, or greater in bulk—himself made those things which could not be made by man. Among them he made man himself, to whom he gave a share of his own wisdom; and he equipped him with reason, so far as earthly frailty could receive it, in order that he might himself produce the things necessary for his own uses.

[Col. 0108A] But if in this commonwealth of the world, so to speak, there is no providence to govern it, no God to administer it, and indeed no sensation whatsoever prevails in this nature of things, whence, then, is the human mind believed to have arisen—so ingenious, so intelligent? For if the human body was fashioned from the earth—from which man (*homo*) received his name—then the soul, which is wise, which is the ruler of the body, whose limbs obey it as a king and commander, which can neither be seen nor grasped, could not have come to man except from a wise nature. But just as every body is governed by mind and soul, so too is the world governed by God. For it is not likely that lesser and lowly things should have a government, while greater and highest things should not have one.

Finally, Marcus Cicero, in the *Tusculan Disputations* and in the *Consolation*, says:

> “No origin of souls can be discovered on earth. For there is nothing in souls mixed or compounded, or which appears to have been born and fashioned from the earth; nor indeed anything moist, airy, or fiery. For in these natures there is nothing which possesses the power of memory, mind, or thought—which retains the past, foresees the future, and can comprehend the present; and these things alone are divine. For it is never discovered whence these things can come to man except from God.”

Therefore, apart from two or three empty slanderers, since it is established that the world is governed by divine providence, just as it was made, [Col. 0109A]

[Col. 0109C] **Variorum Notes to Columns 109–110**

**“And the other philosophers.”** Thus with nearly all manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470. But the most recent manuscripts—one Royal, two Colberti, Baluzius—and the printed editions insert *most eminent*.

**“Invented.”** Thirteen recent manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470 read *argued fictitiously*.

**“But let them have been wise.”** The word *wise* is absent in Colbertinus and Penuensis. In the Caucasian manuscript and seven common editions one reads, “but even if they were.”

**“And Pythagoras.”** First ancient Bononiensis: “as Pythagoras.”

**“In preserving their arrangements.”** Twelve recent manuscripts: “in maintaining.”

**“Could at first.”** Two Bononienses, Taxensis, two Colberti, Baluzius: “could only then.” [Col. 0109D]

**“Without a skilled and sentient ruler.”** Thus restored from the oldest and best manuscripts—Regio-Putianus, Caucasianus, two other Royal manuscripts, three Colberti, Ultramontanus, Claromontanus, Emmanuellensis, Brunck—and the edition of Betuleius. See below, “of a sentient . . . than God.” Two Colberti and Baluzius: “and a wise [ruler]”; two Bononienses, five other recent manuscripts, and six editions: “and a knowing [ruler]”; these words are absent in seven printed editions.

**“Of a sentient and wise nature; but a sentient and wise nature.”** These words are absent from the London, Royal, Leipzig 2, and Reimann manuscripts, likewise Rostock, Venice 1471, both editions of 1478, 1493, and 1497, so that the passage runs: “But reason can be nothing other than that of a sentient and wise nature.” Parrhasius and Paris read: “Reason can be nothing other than from a sentient and wise nature.” Gotha, Leipzig 3, Aldine, Cratander, Gymnicus, Fasti, Grynaeus, Tornesius, Betuleius, Thomasius, Isaeus, and the rest read as printed, except that Tornesius, Betuleius, and Walch lack *other*. BUNEMANN.

**“Has been established.”** Bunemann has *is established*. London, Royal, Gotha, Leipzig, Reimann, and all printed editions: *has been established*. Emmanuellensis: *is established*, which I prefer; Heumann likewise restores it. It is Lactantius’s usual usage. Compare ch. 10, “since it is established,” and III.11 and III.13. BUNEMANN. [Col. 0110C]

**“To belong to many.”** Three manuscripts and four editions insert *gods*; five recent manuscripts read “should be believed to belong to many.”

**“We have shown in our Institutions.”** Ten manuscripts read *we have taught*. Hence it is apparent that Lactantius composed the books of the *Divine Institutes* before *On the Anger of God*.

**“If divine force and power be distributed among many.”** All printed editions and manuscripts except seven, which read *scattered among many*.

**“It must necessarily be diminished; but whatever is diminished is certainly also mortal; yet if.”** Thus two Bononienses, many others, and some editions; it is more elegant than the other reading: “it is certainly diminished and mortal; yet if.”

[Col. 0110D]

**“There cannot,” etc.** By an argument from analogy and a kind of Socratic induction he establishes the divine monarchy. To confirm this point Philo the Jew uses a Homeric verse, which he believes said no less of the heavenly monarchy than of political monarchies.

**“In a herd or flock.”** Reimann: “in herd and flock.” Heumann restores “nor in herds of cattle,” because in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* 37 there is “herds of cattle,” and in the *Epitome* 2: “if there are many leaders in a herd.” Minucius, however, distinguishes them as in our passage, ch. 18: “One king among bees, one leader among flocks, one ruler among herds.” BUNEMANN.

**“Nor many kings in one swarm.”** This should be read thus from nearly all manuscripts and printed editions. Since he previously gave examples from human beings and then descends to dumb animals, it must plainly be understood of a swarm of bees, each swarm of which has its own king. Seven manuscripts and four printed editions read *government*.

**“Nor many kings in one swarm.”** This is the truest reading of both Bononienses. I confirm it from the very ancient Taurinensis in *Epitome* 2: “If there are many kings in a swarm of bees.” BUNEMANN. and since no one would dare prefer the opinion of Diagoras and Theodorus, or the empty fiction of Leucippus, or the frivolity of Democritus and Epicurus, to the authority either of those seven earlier men called sages, or of Pythagoras, Socrates, Plato, and the other philosophers who judged that Providence exists—false, therefore, is also that opinion by which they suppose that religion was instituted by wise men for the sake of terror and fear, in order that unlearned people might refrain from sins.

If this were true, then we have been made fools of by the ancient sages. If they invented religion for the purpose of deceiving us, and indeed the whole human race, then they were not wise; for lying does not belong to a wise person. But let them have been wise: what extraordinary success in lying was this, that they should so easily deceive not only the uneducated but Plato and Socrates as well, and Pythagoras, Zeno, Aristotle—the founders of the greatest schools? Divine providence therefore exists, as those men whom I have named believed; by whose force and power all the things that we see have both been made and are governed. For such greatness of things, such order, such constancy in preserving their arrangements and seasons, could neither at first have arisen without a provident artificer, nor have endured through so many ages without a powerful inhabitant, nor be governed forever without a skilled and sentient ruler. Reason itself declares this. For whatever possesses rational order must necessarily have arisen from reason. But reason belongs to a sentient and wise nature; and a wise and sentient nature can be nothing other than God. Since the world possesses reason, by which it is both governed and held together, it was therefore made by God. And if God is the creator and ruler of the world, religion has rightly and truly been established, since honour and reverence are owed to the author of things and common parent.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning God, who is one, and by whose providence the world is governed and held together.

Since providence has been established, it follows that we must teach whether it should be believed to belong to many, or rather to one. We have sufficiently shown, I think, in our *Institutions*, that many gods cannot exist. For if divine force and power were distributed among many, it would necessarily be diminished; but whatever is diminished is certainly also mortal. Yet if it is not mortal, it can neither be diminished nor divided. God, therefore, is one, in whom power and force are complete and can neither be diminished nor increased. But if there are many, while each has some share of power and divinity, the total itself decreases; nor can each possess the whole which is held in common with many. Each will lack as much as the others possess.

There cannot, therefore, be many rulers in this world: no more than many masters in one house, many helmsmen in one ship, many leaders in a herd or flock, or many kings in one swarm. [Col. 0110C] [Col. 0111A]

[Col. 0111B] **Variorum Notes to Columns 111–112**

**“Could.”** Thus the manuscript. Printed editions: *will be able*.

[Col. 0111C]

**“And if,” etc.** From the authority of Maro; for these verses are from *Aeneid* VI.726. But Lactantius, in book VII, ch. 3, twists these verses to another purpose: he rebukes the Gentiles because they made God the mind and the world the body of God. BETULEIUS.

**“Inhabitant of the world.”** Leipzig 2 and 3 read *governor*, apparently more fittingly, because in ch. 10 God is “creator and ruler of the world.” But the reading *inhabitant* is defended by the following words, *to inhabit*. So in *Institutes* IV.29: “This world is one house of God, and the Son and Father, who dwell together in harmony in the world, are one God.” Perhaps one should read *inhabitant and governor*. BUNEMANN.

**“Or described in words.”** Before Lactantius, Minucius Felix similarly wrote: “He cannot be seen, being brighter than sight; he cannot be grasped or estimated, being greater than the senses: infinite, immeasurable, known to himself alone in the full measure of what he is.”

**“Persuasion.”** Francius suspected that *and persuasion* should be read.

**“Persuasion.”** Heumann ingeniously thinks *persuasion or*, that is, “or persuasion,” should be read. In Reimann the traces of letters are such that *persuasion* may be read. Certainly the ablative fits poorly here, although it is in all printed editions. BUNEMANN. [Col. 0111D]

**“Those worshipped as gods were human beings.”** Nearly the same occurs in *Divine Institutes* I.15. Theophilus, *To Autolycus*: “And the names of those whom you say are worshipped as gods are names of dead human beings” (Καὶ τὰ μὲν ὀνόματα, ὧν φῆς, σέβεσθαι θεῶν, ὀνόματά ἐστι νεκρῶν ἀνθρώπων). He then adduces a long array of examples. BETULEIUS.

**“By which they had benefited.”** Thus two Bononienses and many others. See below, *by which*. Twelve manuscripts and the printed editions read *because*.

**“Immortal remembrance.”** Seven manuscripts: “remembrance of immortality.”

**“Euhemerus.”** He has been discussed in *Divine Institutes* I.11.

**“They set forth . . . tombs.”** Thus two Bononienses and several others. Many manuscripts and editions read *statues*, which would prove little or nothing.

**“Yet he himself . . . could introduce.”** Francius: perhaps, “but truth [could not];” otherwise the sense does not cohere.

[Col. 0112B]

**“Can never be extracted.”** Thus many manuscripts, including the very ancient two Bononienses and Regio-Putianus. Eleven manuscripts with the editions read *cannot*.

**“Achieved.”** Most manuscripts read *willed*. Seven recent ones have *could*; two recent ones and the editions, *was able*.

**“As Plato in the Timaeus.”** Cicero translated his words thus in *On the Universe*: “To find the maker and father, as it were, of this universe is difficult; and, when you have found him, to declare him openly to the multitude is forbidden.” ISAEUS.

**“Hermes bears the same witness.”** Namely Mercury Trismegistus, whose saying to Tatium is found in Stobaeus, *Selections*, Discourse 80, on gods and the nature of heaven and world: “To think of God with the mind is difficult; to utter [him] is impossible.” ISAEUS.

**“Cicero.”** That is, Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* III, as in *Institutes* I.6.

**“Called Trismegistus.”** The edition of Gymnicus reads *is called*. Trismegistus means “thrice greatest,” as three recent manuscripts explain for interpretation’s sake. Trismegistus in Stobaeus, Discourse 80, *On Gods*.

**“And he lived not only,” etc.** Moses is said to be much later, as Marsilius indicates from Augustine. For when Moses was born, Atlas the astronomer flourished, brother of Prometheus the natural philosopher and maternal great-grandfather of the greater Mercury, whose son this Trismegistus was. BETULEIUS.—Others, however, not without reason consider this Trismegistus much earlier than Moses.

**“In Xenophon,” etc.** In Xenophon, *Memorabilia* IV, Socrates, disputing with Euthydemus, says not only that the God “who orders all things” is invisible (τὸν οἰκονομοῦντα ἀόρατον), but also affirms that the ministers of the gods are invisible. A little below, he teaches that our souls partake in something of divinity. See these words of Xenophon in *Memorabilia of the Sayings and Deeds of Socrates* IV, about the middle; see Plato, *Laws* VII, and Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I.—**“In Xenophon,” etc.** These are his words in *Memorabilia of Socrates* IV: “Therefore, Euthydemus, you too will know that gods exist and care for human beings, if you do not wait until you see the forms of the gods; it will be enough to revere and honour them by considering their works,” etc. ISAEUS. Nor indeed could there be many suns in heaven, just as there cannot be several souls in one body. So completely does universal nature agree in unity. And if:

> A spirit within sustains it, and a mind infused throughout its limbs  
> Moves the whole mass and mingles with the mighty body,

then the poet’s testimony makes clear that God, the single inhabitant of the world, is one; since no entire body can be inhabited and governed except by one mind. All divine power, therefore, must necessarily reside in one being, by whose nod and command all things are governed; and he is therefore so great that he can neither be described in words nor measured by human senses.

Whence, then, did the persuasion concerning many gods reach humankind? Certainly all those who are worshipped as gods were human beings, and indeed the first and greatest kings. Who does not know that after death they were honoured with divine honours either because of the excellence by which they had benefited the human race, or because of the benefits and discoveries by which they had refined human life, and so obtained immortal remembrance? Nor were they men only, but women also. This is taught both by the most ancient Greek writers, whom the Greeks call *theologoi* (θεολόγοι, “theologians”), and by Roman writers who followed and imitated the Greeks—especially Euhemerus and our own Ennius. They set forth the births, marriages, offspring, reigns, deeds, deaths, and tombs of all these gods. Following them, Tully, in the third book of *On the Nature of the Gods*, dismantled the public religions; yet he himself, and no one else, could introduce the true religion, which he did not know. Thus he himself testified that falsehood indeed appears, but truth remains hidden. “Would that,” he says, “I could discover truth as easily as I can refute falsehood!”

He declared this not disingenuously, as an Academic, but truly and from his heart; because truth can never be extracted by human senses. Human providence achieved all it could achieve: it exposed falsehoods. For whatever is fabricated and invented, because it has no support in reason, is easily dismantled. One God, therefore, is the ruler and source of things, as Plato both believed and taught in the *Timaeus*; and he declares that God’s majesty is so great that it can neither be grasped by the mind nor expressed by speech.

Hermes bears the same witness—he whom Cicero says is reckoned among the gods by the Egyptians: namely, the man who was called Trismegistus because of his excellence and knowledge of many arts, and who lived not only long before Plato, but even before Pythagoras and those seven sages. Socrates, disputing in Xenophon, says that “the form of God ought not to be investigated”; [Col. 0113A]

[Col. 0113B] **Variorum Notes to Columns 113–114**

**“And Plato in the books of the Laws,” etc.** In *Laws* VII we read, under the person of the Athenian Stranger: “We say that one ought neither to seek the greatest god and the whole cosmos, nor to pry into their causes” (Τὸν μέγιστον θεὸν, καὶ ὅλον τὸν κόσμον φαμὲν οὔτε ζητεῖν δεῖν, οὔτε πολυπραγμονεῖν τὰς αἰτίας ἐρευνῶντας). There are some similar passages also in book X, but they do not belong here.

**“Pythagoras also,” etc.** Something similar occurs in Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I: Pythagoras held God to be a mind extended and passing through the whole nature of things, from which our souls were drawn. Yet Velleius the Epicurean also criticizes this view, and not without reason. The cruder account found in Epiphanius, and plainly different from ours, makes Epicurus hold God to be not mind but body. Yet from Plato, *Laws* X, the same Epicurus makes the stars not bodies of gods but gods themselves: consult Plato’s book. We cited this definition above in *Institutes* I.5, as also the following one of Antisthenes. BETULEIUS.

**“Incorporeal.”** Pythagoras in Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I.

**“Diffused and extended.”** Lactantius, *On the Workmanship* 16: “The divine mind of God, extended through all parts of the world, ranges about . . . diffused everywhere.” Minucius Felix 19: “For Pythagoras, God is a mind passing through and extended over the whole nature of things, from which also the life of all animals is received.” Compare Lactantius, *Institutes* I.5: “Although he had extended himself through the whole body.” BUNEMANN.

[Col. 0113D]

**“Antisthenes, moreover, in the Physical Treatise.”** See *Institutes* I.6. The words are Cicero’s, *On the Nature of the Gods* I.13: “Antisthenes, in the book entitled *Physical*, while saying that the popular gods are many but the natural god one, destroys the force and nature of the gods.” CELLARIUS.

**“Physical Treatise.”** Antisthenes had a book of that name.

**“Their own local gods.”** Nine manuscripts add *gods*.

**“Aristotle with his Peripatetics,” etc.** Book I, ch. 5. Lactantius has admitted that Aristotle disagrees with him, yet agrees on the main point, that Mind presides over the world. On that disagreement itself, see Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I. BETULEIUS.—On Aristotle and Zeno, see Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I.

**“And Zeno,” etc.** See especially Lactantius himself and Cicero in the passages already repeatedly cited, where these points, left suspended here in the middle, are examined more carefully.

**“Converged.”** Thus restored from many editions and all manuscripts except one recent Colbert manuscript, which, like five printed editions [Col. 0114B], reads *converge*.

**“Detestable wisdom.”** Francius preferred to read *shamelessness*. But one should read, with Regio-Putianus and ten other manuscripts, and two old Roman editions and Betuleius, *wisdom*: that is, the wisdom or knowledge of Gentile philosophers, as Cicero uses the word in this sense.

**“Because wisdom is the understanding of divinity.”** I follow the reading of the oldest and best manuscripts—two Bononienses, three Colberti, Baluzius—and the Plantin edition, approved by Thomasius in his notes, Isaeus, and Spark. The others vary widely: some read *while*; others, “while the understanding of divinity . . . justice is found”; others, *justice*; most reject this last word.—**“Because wisdom is the understanding of divinity,” etc.** I followed the reading of the best manuscripts and the approved Plantin edition, as explained by Thomasius in his notes. Antonius Augustinus preferred, instead of “justice is found in man alone,” “justice is found in man alone.” Nearly all printed books have: “Since the understanding of divinity, by which we differ from beasts, is found in man alone, unless desires . . .”; all, I think, understand that this reading is mutilated and does not cohere well with what precedes. BUNEMANN. [Col. 0114C]

**“Justice is found.”** Thus two Bononienses, three Colberti, and Baluzius. In the others: *may be found*.

**“Unless our desires.”** Thus I read with two Royal manuscripts, three Colberti, Christianus, Mertonensis, Leipzig, Ultramontanus, Emmanuellensis, Brunck, and the editions of Fasti, Basel 1532, and Egnatius. Others: *because*.

**“We shall live wickedly and impiously.”** Thus all manuscripts and old Roman editions, not *we should live*, as in the printed editions; for he had said, “will have restrained.”

**“Actions.”** Used for *action* also below, ch. 17: “he observes the actions of individuals.”

**“When religion and justice are removed.”** This is Lactantius’s expression, frequently found in his writings. Two Bononienses and five other recent manuscripts have *having been removed*.

**“We fall.”** Thus restored from all manuscripts and common printed editions; it is more Latin and more rounded than *we roll*, found in several editions.

**“Once fear of the higher power has been removed.”** Thus Bunemann, who gives the following note: “Most manuscripts: ‘fear from the higher [power]’; all printed editions, ‘higher fear.’ So Cyprian, *Letter to Donatus*: ‘there is no fear from laws; no dread of an investigator, no terror of a judge.’ Silius Italicus 17.394: ‘A fierce terror from a great name.’” BUNEMANN.

**“Through it.”** London, Royal, Leipzig 2, and Reimann: *through which*, namely fellowship. Gotha, Leipzig 3, and the printed editions: *through it*, namely fear of God. BUNEMANN. and Plato, in the books of the *Laws*, says that “what God is at all ought not to be sought, because he can neither be found nor described.” Pythagoras also confesses one God, saying that he is an incorporeal mind, diffused and extended throughout the whole nature of things, which bestows vital sensation upon all living beings. Antisthenes, moreover, said in the *Physical Treatise* that there is one natural God, although peoples and cities have their own local gods. Aristotle with his Peripatetics, and Zeno with his Stoics, say nearly the same. It would be tedious to recount the views of every individual: though they used different names, they nevertheless converged upon the one power which governs the world.

Yet although philosophers, poets, and even those who worship gods frequently acknowledge a highest God, no one has ever investigated or discussed his worship and honours. This is because of the conviction by which they have always believed him beneficent and incorruptible, and have supposed that he is neither angry with anyone nor in need of any worship. Religion cannot exist where there is no fear.

[Col. 0114A] ## CHAPTER XII. Concerning religion and the fear of God.

Now, since we have answered the impious and detestable wisdom—or rather madness—of certain persons, let us return to our subject. We have said that, once religion is removed, neither wisdom nor justice can be maintained: because wisdom is the understanding of divinity, by which we differ from beasts; and because justice is found in man alone. Unless God, who cannot be deceived, restrains our desires, we shall live wickedly and impiously. Therefore, that our actions are observed by God pertains not only to the usefulness of common life, but also to truth. For when religion and justice are removed, we fall either, reason having been lost, into the stupidity of cattle, or into the savagery of beasts—indeed, into something worse. For beasts spare animals of their own kind. What will be more savage or more cruel than man, if, once fear of the higher power has been removed, he can either evade or despise the force of laws? The fear of God alone, therefore, preserves human fellowship with one another; through it life itself is sustained, [Col. 0115A]

[Col. 0115B] **Variorum Notes to Columns 115–116**

**“Fear will be removed.”** The same expression occurs above. Four editions read *would be removed*. In twenty-one manuscripts and the Roman, Florentine, and Isaeus editions: *fear is removed*.

**“Reason itself and truth to us.”** *To us* is absent from many manuscripts and editions, but occurs in the oldest and best manuscripts, Regio-Putianus and two Bononienses, and in five common editions. [Col. 0115C]

**“How true the opinion of the Stoics is.”** Especially Chrysippus’s, as Cicero indicates in *On Ends* III and *On the Nature of the Gods* III. Quintus Lucilius Balbus treats the matter at length; according to Cicero, he advanced so far in Stoicism that he may be compared with the outstanding Greeks in that field. Among ecclesiastical writers, apart from those who wrote expressly on the work of the six days, Theodoret treated this matter most elegantly in the first two discourses *On Divine Providence*, and likewise the fifth. Besides establishing divine providence from the universe of things, he clearly teaches not only the utility that thereby arises for mortals but also its pleasantness. Our Lactantius too touches upon the same question in *Divine Institutes* VII.3. BETULEIUS.—**“Of the Stoics.”** The Stoics in Cicero’s *Lucullus*, as above in *Institutes* VII.4 and 7.

**“For our sake.”** Bunemann reads *for our sake* and supplies this note: “Respect must be paid to the antiquity of the Bononian manuscript, from which Isaeus adopted *for our sake* and Heumann approved it.” BUNEMANN. [Col. 0115D]

**“For the usefulness of man.”** Two Bononienses and four other recent manuscripts add *alone*. See below, “made by God for human use.”

**“For softening food.”** Thus I read from one Royal manuscript, two Colberti, and Baluzius; this word agrees better with the preceding *by fire* than *for grinding*, found in two Bononienses and Taxensis. Indeed Lactantius more idiomatically wrote *for softening* or *for making soft*. In Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II.134, one reads, “food is softened.” Scribes not understanding this changed it in recent manuscripts and printed editions to *for cooking*; Ultramontanus and Brunck: *for boiling*.

**“Variety of crops.”** Six recent manuscripts: “abundance of crops”; first ancient Bononiensis and Ultramontanus: “variety of fruits.”—**“Variety of crops.”** Bunemann has *variety of fruits* and offers this variant: “Bononiensis, Ultramontanus, Isaeus, and Heumann approving, ‘variety of fruits.’ Excellent, lest *abundance* occur twice in one number. Thus he imitates Cicero, *For the Manilian Law* 6: ‘Asia is so fertile that in both abundance of fields and variety of fruits it easily surpasses all lands.’” BUNEMANN.

[Col. 0116C]

**“Plains for grain.”** In fifteen manuscripts and three editions, *plains for grain* is absent.—**“Woods; plains for grain.”** Although these words, *plains for grain*, are absent from the English manuscripts and others, I judge them genuine, not only because Thomasius and Isaeus did not report them as lacking in their most ancient manuscripts, but also because they are beyond the capacity of a glossator and otherwise something would be missing from the enumeration of parts. The words “earth for receiving a variety of fruits” concern fruits only; but *plains* is elegantly said of fields, as I noted in *Institutes* VII.3: “the plains of the fields.” Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II.60: “Human beings have dominion over every earthly advantage. We enjoy plains and mountains; rivers and lakes are ours; we sow crops, we plant trees,” etc. BUNEMANN.

Abundance. Below: “an abundance of goods and resources.” Compare chapter 23. Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, II.60: “It provides great advantages for building ships, by whose voyages all resources necessary for life are supplied from every quarter.” [Col. 0116D] Pliny, *Letters*, VI.28: “So great an abundance . . . of resources, both urban and rural.” BUN.

Abundance of every kind of fish. Thus nearly all manuscripts and editions, better than the two Bologna manuscripts and Tax., “for variety.” For what can “the variety of every kind of fish” mean? Does not every kind of fish signify variety of fish?

Draws over. Manuscripts: one recent Royal and Claromontanus, “draws back over” (*superrinducit*). BUN.

Grow soft. Elegantly so, as often in Columella, III.1: “whose . . . grapes . . . as others grow soft in the heat.” III.2.15: “they grow soft more quickly.” IV.20.4: “before the grapes grow soft.” BUN.

Blind nights with dreadful darkness. Darkness is elegantly called dreadful. I have made further observations on Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, II.5: “lest excessively blind night should weigh heavily upon the earth with dreadful darkness.” BUN.]

is protected and governed. But that fear will be removed if a man has been persuaded that God is free from anger; yet common advantage, reason itself, and truth persuade us that he is moved and indignant when unjust things occur. Again, we must return to the foregoing points: since we have taught that the world was made by God, we must teach why it was made.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the benefit and use of the world and of the seasons

If anyone considers the entire ordering of the world, he will certainly understand how true is the opinion of the Stoics, who say that the world was constructed for our sake. For everything of which it consists, and everything which the world generates from itself, has been adapted to human use. [Col. 0115B] Man uses fire for warmth and light, for softening foods, and for working iron; he uses springs for drinking and bathing; rivers for irrigating fields and marking boundaries between regions; earth for obtaining a variety of crops; hills for planting vineyards; mountains for the use of trees and timber; plains for grain; he uses [Col. 0116A] the sea not only for commerce and for conveying resources from distant regions, but also for the abundance of every kind of fish.

And if he uses these elements nearest to him, there is no doubt that he also uses the sky, since the functions of heavenly things too have been ordered toward the fertility of the earth, from which we live. By unceasing courses and unequal intervals the sun completes its yearly circuits: rising, it brings forth the day for labour; setting, it draws night over for rest. Then, by withdrawing farther toward the south and approaching nearer toward the north, it produces the alternations of winter and summer, so that the earth may be enriched into fruitfulness by winter moisture and frosts, and that in summer heat either grassy crops may be hardened by ripeness, or things growing in wet places, unripe and heated, may grow soft. [Col. 0116B]

The moon also, ruler of the nighttime, regulates the monthly periods by the changes of light lost and regained, and illuminates blind nights with dreadful darkness by the brilliance of her radiance, so that summer journeys, expeditions, and works may be accomplished without strain or inconvenience. For indeed:

> By night light stubble, by night dry meadows  
> Are better cut.

[Col. 0117A]

For aids to work. Here, *kat’ exochēn* [κατ’ ἐξοχήν, “pre-eminently”] means agricultural work, farming, as Lactantius teaches most clearly in II.10: “So that animals might be useful to men, some . . . for food, others indeed for clothing; while those of great strength might help in cultivating the earth.” BUN.

To furnish and adorn life. Here refer to Seneca, *To Marcia*, 18: “You will learn and teach arts: some which furnish life, some which adorn it, some which govern it.” BUN.

that all living things are either useful, harmful, or altogether useless and contemptible. There is a definite rationale for useful things; harmful things discipline us because of sins. Our own times are not without examples, nor are the books of the Old Testament; and even in things which seem to us wholly remote from every use, there arises material for us to praise God even in the lowliness of ants. In sum, he infers from this that the completeness of the universe is thereby made whole. Basil applies this to morals. For, even on Solomon’s testimony, they can rouse us from idleness to diligence; although that creature also possesses its own natural virtues. Christ too commends wisdom to us by the example of serpents, etc. BETULEIUS.

In things that grow, and in the number of animals. All books read “in things that grow” (*in gignentibus*). In mice. Nor is this little creature so insignificant that it has not deserved notice even from the best writers. During the siege of Marseilles, according to Strabo, Pliny, and Valerius, it sold for two hundred coins. This also occurred during the sieges of Paris in 1590 and La Rochelle in 1628. I say nothing of its medicinal value: they relate that ash from the heads and tails of mice brings brightness to the eyes if applied with honey. For more of its properties consult Pliny, both elsewhere and especially [Col. 0118D] *Natural History*, XXIX.6; also Sextus the philosopher, who flourished in Hadrian’s time, chapter 21. BETUL.

Cockroaches. Both Aristotle and Pliny number them among insects. Aristotle calls his *prasokouridai* [πρασοκουρίδες], for Gaza translated the term thus; but he says that they are born from beetles, whereas Gaza says that they are born from beehives, so that the passage seems suspect to me. Pliny says that his are born from damp vapour. Virgil in *Georgics* IV and Columella in book X call them light-shunning; Pliny too says that they flee light and calls their life a foster-child of darkness. There is another kind, which the Greeks call *mýlochos* [μύλοχος], or, as others prefer, *sílphē* [σίλφη], a little worm troublesome to books and scholars. I think the remedy reported by Pliny toward the end of book XXIX should be assigned to the first kind, where he says that one variety is effective if its head is pulled off. For, he says, when crushed with rose-oil, it greatly benefits the ears, etc. Therefore cockroaches too have some use beneficial to mortals in medicine. BETULEIUS.

In serpents. Everyone knows that theriac [*theriacon*], very useful to man, is made from them. GALL.]

The other stars too, whether by their rising or their setting, at fixed stations supply the opportunities of the seasons. They also provide guidance to ships, lest they wander in a straying course across the immensity, when the helmsman, duly observing them, may be carried to the harbour of the shore for which he is bound. Clouds are drawn together by the breath of winds, so that crops may be watered by rain, vines may overflow with their produce, and orchards with fruit. And these things are provided throughout the world in turn, lest at any time there should be lacking what sustains human life.

“But,” one may say, “the same earth nourishes the other living creatures, and dumb animals too feed upon its produce. Did God labour even for the sake of dumb creatures?” By no means, because they lack reason. Yet we understand that they too were made by God in the same way for human use: some for food, some for clothing, some for aids to work, [Col. 0117B] so that it may be clear that divine providence intended by an abundance [Col. 0118A] of things and resources to furnish and adorn human life; and for that reason it filled the air with birds, the sea with fish, and the earth with four-footed animals.

But the Academics, arguing against the Stoics, commonly ask why, if God made all things for the sake of men, so many things opposed, hostile, and destructive to us are found both in sea and on land. The Stoics, failing to look to the truth, answered this most foolishly. For they say that among growing things and among the number of animals there are many whose usefulness still remains hidden, but that it is discovered in the course of time, just as necessity and use have already discovered many things unknown to earlier ages. But what usefulness can be found in mice, cockroaches, or serpents, which are troublesome and destructive to man? Is some medicine hidden in [Col. 0118B] them? If so, it will someday be discovered, [Col. 0119A]

They could therefore have answered more briefly and more truly in this way. When God had formed man as it were in His own image, which was the summit of divine workmanship, He breathed wisdom into him alone, so that he might subject all things to his command and dominion and enjoy all the benefits of the world. Yet He set before him both good and evil, because He gave him wisdom, the entire principle of which consists in distinguishing evils and goods. For no one can choose better things and know what is good unless he knows at the same time how to reject and avoid what is evil. The two are mutually connected, each with the other, so that when one is removed, [Col. 0119B] both must necessarily be removed.

Therefore, once goods and evils have been set before it, wisdom at last performs its function: it seeks good for advantage and rejects evil for safety. Thus, just as countless good things were given to man for his enjoyment, so too were evils, against which he might be on guard. [Col. 0120A] For if there were no evil, no danger—in short, nothing that could harm man—all matter for wisdom would be removed, nor would wisdom be necessary to man.

For if only good things were placed before his eyes, what need would there be for thought, understanding, knowledge, or reason? Whatever he stretched out his hand toward would be suited and adapted to nature. It would be as if someone wished to set before infants, who as yet have no understanding, an exceedingly lavish meal: each of them would surely seek whatever his impulse, hunger, or even chance had drawn him toward, and whatever they took would be life-giving and healthful for them. What harm, then, would there be in their remaining as they are and always being infants, ignorant of things? But if you mix in bitter, useless, or even poisonous things, they are certainly deceived through ignorance of good and evil unless wisdom is added, by which they may reject evils [Col. 0120B] and choose goods.

You see, therefore, that we have greater need of wisdom because of evils. Unless evils had been set before us, we would not be rational animals. If this reasoning is true—which [Col. 0121A]

the Stoics could in no way perceive—the argument of Epicurus is also refuted. God, he says, either wills to remove evils and cannot; or can and does not will; or neither wills nor can; or both wills and can. If He wills and cannot, He is weak, which cannot apply to God. If He can and does not will, He is envious, which is likewise foreign to God. If He neither wills nor can, He is both envious and weak, and therefore is not God. If He wills and can, which alone befits God, whence then are evils? Or why does He not remove them?

I know that most philosophers who defend providence are usually troubled by this argument and are almost compelled against their will to confess that God cares for nothing, which is precisely what Epicurus seeks. But once we have grasped the reasoning, we easily refute this formidable argument. For God can do whatever He wills, and in God there is no weakness or envy; therefore He can remove evils. But He does not will to remove them, and yet is not therefore envious. For this reason He does not remove them: because He also bestowed wisdom, as I have taught, and there is more good and pleasure in wisdom than trouble in evils.

For wisdom enables us even to know God and, through that knowledge, to attain immortality, which is the highest good. Thus, unless we have first come to know evil, we cannot know good. But Epicurus and no one else saw this: if evils are removed, wisdom too is removed with them, and no traces of virtue remain in man, whose principle consists in enduring and overcoming the bitterness of evils. Thus, for the slight gain of evils removed, we would lack the greatest, true, and proper good. [Col. 0121C] It is established, therefore, that all things, evils as well as goods, have been set before man for his sake.

[Col. 0122A]

## CHAPTER XIV. Why God made man

It remains for me to show why God made man himself. As He fashioned the world for man’s sake, so He made man for His own sake, as the priest of a divine temple and spectator of His works and heavenly things. For man alone, being sentient and capable of reason, can understand God, admire His works, and discern His power and might; for this reason he has been endowed with deliberation, intellect, and intelligence. Therefore he alone, beyond the other living creatures, was made with an upright body and bearing, that he might seem roused to contemplate his parent. Therefore he alone received speech and a tongue, the interpreter of thought, [Col. 0122B] that he might recount the majesty of his Lord. Finally, for this reason all things were subjected to him: that he himself might be subject to God, his maker and craftsman.

If, therefore, God wished man to be His worshipper and accordingly bestowed upon him so great an honour that he might rule over all things, it is altogether most just both to love Him who has bestowed such great things and to love man, who is joined with us by fellowship in divine right. For it is not lawful that a worshipper of God should be harmed by a worshipper of God. Hence it is understood that man was fashioned for the sake of religion and justice.

Marcus Tullius is a witness to this, saying thus in his books *On the Laws*: “But of all matters discussed in the disputations of learned men, surely nothing is more excellent than clearly to understand that we are born for justice.” If this is most true, then God wills all men [Col. 0122C] to be just: that is, to hold God and man dear—to honour God as a father, [Col. 0123A]

## CHAPTER XV. Whence sins came to man

Perhaps someone may here ask whence sins came to man, or what depravity distorted the rule of the divine institution toward worse things, so that, though he was born for justice, he nevertheless performs unjust deeds. I have already explained above that God set good and evil before us together: good indeed to be loved, and evil, which is opposed to it, to be hated. But He permitted evil so that good might shine forth, since we understand that the one cannot exist without the other, as I have often taught.

Finally, the world itself was formed from two opposing elements, joined together reciprocally—fire and water—and light could not have come into being unless darkness also existed, because there can be no upper without lower, no east without west, no hot without cold, no soft without hard. So too we are composed of two equally opposed things, soul and body. One is assigned to heaven because it is subtle and intangible; the other to earth because it is tangible. One is solid and eternal; the other frail and mortal. Therefore good adheres to one, evil to the other; to one, light, life, and justice; to the other, darkness, death, and injustice.

From this arose in human beings a corruption of their nature, so that it became necessary to establish a law by which vices could be forbidden [Col. 0123C] and the duties of virtue enjoined. Since, therefore, there are goods and evils in human affairs, the rationale of which I have explained, God must be moved in either direction: toward favour when He sees just things done, and toward anger when He sees unjust things.

But Epicurus confronts us and says: “If God has an affection of delight leading to favour, and of hatred leading to anger, [Col. 0124A] He must also have fear, desire, longing, and the other affections that belong to human weakness.” One who is angry need not fear; one who rejoices need not grieve. Indeed, the irascible are less fearful, and those naturally cheerful grieve less. Why need we speak of human affections, beneath which our frailty succumbs?

Let us consider divine necessity; for I do not wish to say “nature,” since our God is never believed to have been born. The affection of fear has grounds in man; in God it has none. Because man is subject to many accidents and dangers, he fears that some greater force may arise to strike, despoil, tear, afflict, or kill him. But God, to whom neither need, injury, pain, nor death [Col. 0124B] can happen, cannot possibly fear, because there is nothing able to inflict force upon Him.

Likewise, the rationale and cause of desire in man are plain. Since he was made frail and mortal, it was necessary that another and different sex be constituted, by whose union offspring might be produced to maintain the perpetuity of the human race. But such desire has no place in God, because both frailty and destruction are alien to Him; there is no woman with whom He could delight in union; and He needs no succession, since He will always exist. The same may be said of envy and covetousness, which occur in man for definite and manifest reasons, but in no way in God.

But favour, anger, and compassion do have grounds in God; and that supreme and singular power rightly employs them for the preservation of things.

[Col. 0124C]
