to repel injuries from them. Therefore he has reason to pity; for he is not so harsh and contemptuous of humankind as to deny help to those in distress. Likewise, many are persuaded that justice is pleasing to God, and they venerate him as the lord and father of all; with constant prayers and frequent vows they offer gifts and sacrifices, pursue his name with praises, and endeavour to win his favour by just and good works. Therefore there is a reason why God both can and ought to bestow favour. For if nothing is so fitting to God as beneficence, and nothing so alien as ingratitude, it follows that he must grant something to the services of the best and those who live holy lives, and return a recompense, lest he incur the fault of ingratitude, which is blameworthy even in a human being. Conversely, there are others, criminal and impious, [Col. 0125B] who defile everything by their lusts, afflict others with slaughter, deceive, rob, commit perjury; who spare neither kinsfolk nor parents, and disregard laws and even God himself.

Anger therefore has matter in God. For it is not right that, when he sees such things being done, he should not be stirred and rise up to punish the wicked and destroy the pestilent and harmful, in order to provide for all the good: so much so that even in anger itself there is beneficence. Therefore the arguments prove empty and false, both of those who, though unwilling that God should be angry, wish him to bestow favour—because not even this can occur without anger—and of those who think that there is no movement of the mind in God. And because there are certain affections [Col. 0126A] which do not apply to God—lust, fear, avarice, grief, envy—they have said that he is wholly devoid of every affection. He is indeed devoid of these, because they are affections of vice; but those which belong to virtue—that is, anger toward the wicked, love toward the good, compassion toward the afflicted—because they are worthy of divine power, he possesses as his own, just, and true. Unless indeed he possesses them, human life will be thrown into confusion, and the condition of things will come to such disorder that, laws having been despised and overcome, audacity alone will reign, so that in the end no one can be safe unless he prevails by strength. Thus the whole earth will be ravaged as though by universal brigandage. But now, because the wicked hope for punishment, the good for favour, and the afflicted for help, there is room for virtues and crimes are rarer. Yet, it may be said, often the criminal are more fortunate [Col. 0126B] and the good more wretched, and the just are wrongfully afflicted by the unjust with impunity. We shall consider later why these things occur. Meanwhile, let us explain concerning anger whether there is any in God; whether he cares for nothing at all and is not moved by things done impiously.

## Chapter XVII. Concerning God, care, and anger

“God,” says Epicurus, “cares for nothing; therefore he has no power.” For one who has power must necessarily care; or, if he has it and does not use it, what cause is so great that, not to mention our race, even [Col. 0127A]

but even the world itself should be vile to him? “For this reason,” he says, “he is incorruptible and blessed: because he is always at rest.” To whom, then, has the administration of such great affairs fallen, if the things which we see governed by supreme reason are neglected by God? Or how can one who lives and perceives be at rest? For rest belongs either to sleep or to death. Yet even sleep has no rest. For when we are asleep, the body indeed rests, but the mind is restlessly agitated: it forms for itself images which it may behold, in order to exercise its natural motion through the variety of sights; and it draws itself away by false things, while the limbs are refreshed and gain vigour from rest. Therefore eternal rest belongs to death alone. But if death does not touch God, God therefore is never at rest. What action, moreover, can God have except the administration of the world? But if he administers the world, [Col. 0127B] then God cares for human life, takes notice of the acts of individuals, and desires them to be wise and good. This is the will of God, this the divine law; whoever follows and observes it is dear to God. It follows, then, that anger must be stirred against one who has either violated or despised this eternal and divine law. “If God harms anyone,” he says, “he is no longer good.” Those who defame correction, [Col. 0128A] whether human or divine, under the name of harshness and malice are grievously mistaken, imagining that one must be called harmful who inflicts punishment on wrongdoers. If this is so, then we have harmful laws, which have prescribed punishments for sinners; harmful judges, who inflict capital punishment on those convicted of crime. But if a law is just which both gives the harmful person what he deserves, and a judge is called upright and good when he punishes evil deeds—for he protects the safety of the good who punishes the wicked—then God too, when he opposes the wicked, is not harmful. Rather, he himself is harmful who either harms the innocent, or spares the harmful person so that he may harm more people.

I wish to ask those who make God immovable: if someone possesses an estate, a house, a household, and his slaves, despising their master’s patience, have seized everything, [Col. 0128B] themselves enjoy his goods, are honoured by his household, while their master is despised, mocked, and abandoned by all—can one be wise who does not avenge such insults and permits those over whom he has power to enjoy his possessions? Thus in ch. 18: “From this one daily leaps forth into monstrous crimes”; and below: “They will proceed to a greater evil.” *Epitome*, ch. 61: “From this one leaps forth into monstrous crimes.” Everywhere, moreover, it is *ad*, not *in*, as Parrhasius has it; hence twice in book VI, ch. 5, and book VI, ch. 18: “to leap forth to doing harm.” BUN.
>
> **Incapable of injury** (*illaesibilis*). A rare word, which I have been unable to find anywhere else.—Bunemann reads “he is stable,” and supplies the following note:—“He is stable.” All editions: “incapable of injury”; likewise two Wolfenbüttel manuscripts: “incapable of injury,” followed by “injury.” The word *illaesibilis* had long seemed suspect to me, because he always abstains from it elsewhere; hence in ch. 17: “There is nothing that can inflict force upon him [God]”; and in ch. 5: “who cannot be harmed.” This reasoning is excellently opposed to the following one, “because he is fragile.” Thus ch. 15: “In a human being … because he is fragile and mortal … [this] has no place in God, because both fragility and destruction are alien to him … who will always exist, that is, is stable.” The same contrast occurs in *Institutions*, book V, ch. 21: “The body … weak, fragile, mortal … the mind stable and constant [Col. 0130D] and everlasting.” Again concerning God, *Institutions*, book VI, ch. 15: “That the same [God] may be always stable, immutable, and unshaken.” Yet, lest the lexicons suffer any loss from proscribing this word—which Walch calls exceedingly rare and says he could find nowhere else—in support of Lactantius I shall cite Tertullian, who said in *Against Valentinus*, ch. 27: “The Father, impassible, incapable of injury.” BUN.

Six manuscripts and fourteen printed editions have *irritat* (“provokes”). But below he says, “it branded pain upon [one],” ch. 18, near the middle.

>
> **“Such as slaves, children, wives, and pupils.”** The manuscripts have both distinction [of categories] and conjunction. CELLARIUS.—Relevant here is book VI, ch. 19: “The affection of anger [exists] to restrain the sins of those who are in our power, so that younger age may be formed toward uprightness and justice by stricter discipline.” You know the rest. which Cicero speaks of? “For indeed I ask: if some head of a household, after his children had been killed by a slave, his wife murdered, and his house burned, should not have inflicted upon the slave the most severe punishment possible, would he seem merciful and compassionate, or inhuman and utterly cruel?” But if forgiving crimes of this sort belongs to cruelty rather than compassion, it is therefore not a virtue in God not to be moved by things done unjustly. For the world is like God’s house, and human beings are like slaves. If his name is a mockery to them, what patience—of what kind or extent—is it for him to yield his honours, see crooked and unjust things done, and not be indignant? Indignation is proper and natural to one to whom sins are displeasing. Therefore anger is rational: for offenses are removed and license is restrained, which is certainly done justly and wisely. [Col. 0129B]

But the Stoics did not see that there is a difference between right and wrong, between just and unjust anger; and because they did not find a remedy for the matter, they wished to extirpate it utterly. The Peripatetics, however, said that it should not be extirpated but moderated; we have sufficiently answered them in the sixth book of the *Institutions*. That philosophers did not know the rationale of anger is apparent from their definitions, which Seneca listed in the books he composed *On Anger*. “Anger,” he says, “is the desire to avenge an injury. Others, as Posidonius says, [define it as] the desire to punish one by whom you think yourself unjustly injured.” Some defined it thus: “Anger is an incitement of the mind to harm one who either has harmed or wished to harm.” Aristotle’s definition is not far from ours. For he says that anger is the desire to repay pain. This is the unjust anger of which we spoke above, which exists even in dumb animals; in a human being, however, it must be restrained, lest through rage it leap forth into some very great evil. It cannot exist in God, because he is incapable of injury; but in a human being it is found because he is fragile. For injury brands pain upon one, and pain produces the desire for revenge. Where, then, is that just anger against wrongdoers? It is certainly not the desire for revenge, because injury does not precede it. I do not speak [Col. 0130B] of those who sin against the laws. Though a judge may, without fault, be angry with them, let us nevertheless suppose that he ought to be calm in mind when he subjects the guilty person to punishment, because he is the minister of the laws, not of his own mind or power; for this is what those who attempt to root out anger maintain. But I speak especially of those who are in our power—slaves, children, wives, and pupils—when we see them doing wrong and are aroused to restrain them.

For the good and just person must necessarily be displeased by things which are wrong, and one to whom evil is displeasing must be moved when he sees it done. Therefore we rise to correction, not because we have been injured, but that discipline may be maintained, conduct corrected, and license restrained. This is just anger, which, as it is necessary in a human being for correcting wrongness, is certainly also necessary in God, from whom the example has come down to humankind. For just as we ought to restrain those subject to our authority, so God ought to restrain the sins of all. In order to do this, he must be angry, because it is natural for a good person to be moved and stirred by another’s sin. Therefore they ought to have defined it thus: anger is a movement of the mind rising up to restrain sins. For Cicero’s definition, “Anger is the desire for revenge,” does not differ greatly from the preceding ones. But anger—which we can call either rage or irascibility—[Col. 0131B] ought not to exist even in a human being, because it is wholly vicious. Yet the anger which pertains to correcting vices ought neither to be taken from a human being nor can be taken from God, because it is useful for human affairs and necessary.

## Chapter XVIII. That sins cannot be punished without anger

“What need,” they ask, “is there for anger, when sins can be corrected without this affection?” Yet there is no one who can see a sinner calmly. Perhaps one who presides over laws can do so, because the crime is not committed before his eyes but reported from elsewhere as uncertain, and [Col. 0132A] no crime can ever be so manifest that there is no room for a defense; therefore a judge may remain unmoved against one who may be found innocent. And when the discovered crime has come to light, he acts no longer by his own judgment but by that of the laws. It may be granted that he does what he does without anger, for he has a rule to follow. But certainly, when wrongdoing occurs in our household through our own people, whether we see it or learn of it, we must be indignant; for the very sight of sin is unworthy. For one who is not moved at all either approves offenses—which is more disgraceful and unjust—or avoids the trouble of correction, which a composed spirit and tranquil mind rejects and refuses unless anger has spurred and incited it. But one who, though moved, nonetheless forgives through ill-timed leniency—either more often than necessary or even always—plainly destroys both the lives of those [Col. 0132B] whose boldness toward greater crimes he nourishes, and furnishes himself with an everlasting source of troubles. Restraining one’s own anger in the case of sins is therefore vicious.

Archytas of Tarentum is praised because, when he discovered that everything on his farm had been ruined, he rebuked the fault of his steward and said: “Wretched man, I would now have killed you with blows, if I were not angry.” They regard this as a unique example of self-control; but guided by authority, they do not see how foolishly he both spoke and acted. For if, as Plato says, no wise person punishes because a sin has been committed, but so that it may not be committed, it is clear what a bad example a wise man [Col. 0133A]

The rest as in the text.—“Brand pain upon [him].” Our author seems to have had in view Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, book III, ch. 9: “It is characteristic of an angry person to wish to brand the greatest possible pain upon the person by whom he thinks himself injured.” BUN.

The contrary appears in book II, ch. 9 and book VI, ch. 25, where he rightly held concerning God.—“But what we say concerning a human being we say also concerning God, who made humankind like himself. I pass over speaking of God’s form,” etc. Lactantius seems in many places to assert that God is endowed with a bodily [Col. 0134C] form, although in *Institutions*, book II, ch. 9; book VI, final chapter; and book VII, chs. 3, 9, and 21, he truly and rightly acknowledges that God is devoid of body. Writers thus readily sometimes both say and think things contrary to themselves. This was asserted not only by certain philosophers—as Aristotle writes, *Metaphysics*, book III, text 7—namely the Epicureans, concerning whom see Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, and Galen, *Philosophical History*, ch. 29; but also by some Jews and certain heretics among us, such as Tertullian, whom nevertheless St Augustine interprets piously in *On Heresies, to Quodvultdeus*, ch. 86; likewise the Vadiani and Manichaeans, as is found in Augustine, *Confessions*, book III, ch. 7. All these acquired from that error the surname Anthropomorphites. On them see what Nicephorus writes, book II, ch. 14, and book XIII, ch. 10. Cassian writes, *Conferences*, 10, ch. 1, that almost the whole body of monks dwelling in Egypt was once infected by it as well. For because Scripture says that human beings were created in God’s image and likeness, they attended to the lowly sound of the letter and conceived that error. But there likeness and image are understood not bodily but spiritually: whether we embrace the view of the Latin Fathers, that this image is said with respect to the human mind and its three powers, by which the most holy Trinity is in some fashion represented, as St Augustine teaches in *On the Trinity*; or that of the Greek Fathers, that this image and likeness concern the dominion one possesses not only over all earthly things, as Chrysostom understood in Homily 8 on Genesis, but also over one’s own affections and motions, insofar as they oppose reason, through freedom of choice—as Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, VI; Basil, Homily 10 on the *Hexaemeron*; Chrysostom, Homily 23 on Genesis; Plato in the *Phaedo*, according to Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book II, ch. 14; and Porphyry, as Eusebius likewise attests, maintain. Against that heresy see the Fourth Lateran Council [Col. 0135B] under Innocent III, ch. *Firmiter*, “On the Supreme Trinity”; St Augustine in the passage cited above, and *Confessions*, book II, ch. 10; *On Genesis according to the Letter*, book X, ch. 25; *On Christian Doctrine*, chs. 6 and 8; and St Thomas, *Against the Gentiles*, book I, ch. 21, and *Summa Theologiae*, part I, question 3, article 1. ISAEUS.

has set before them. For if slaves perceive that their master is savage when he is not angry, but sparing when he is angry, they will assuredly not commit slight offenses, lest they be beaten; rather, as far as they can, they will commit the gravest ones, so that they may provoke his anger and depart unpunished. I, however, would praise him if, after becoming angry, he had allowed time for his anger, so that when the swelling of his mind had subsided through an interval of time, his punishment might be measured. Therefore punishment was not to be remitted because of the greatness of anger, but postponed, lest he either brand greater pain than justice permits upon the offender or frenzy upon the one inflicting the punishment. But now what equity or wisdom, then, is this: that someone should be punished for a slight offense, but not punished for a very great one? If he had learned the nature and causes of things, he would never have professed such untimely restraint that a worthless slave might congratulate himself that his master had been angry with him. For [Col. 0133B] just as God has equipped the human body with many and varied senses necessary for the use of life, so too he has bestowed varied affections on the mind, by which the order of life might be sustained: [Col. 0134A] as he gave lust for the sake of producing offspring, so he gave anger for restraining offenses.

But those who do not know the limits of goods and evils, just as they use lust for corruptions and pleasures, so use anger and affection to do harm, while they are angry with those whom they hate. Therefore they are angry even with those who do not sin, even with equals or even with superiors. From this one daily leaps forth into monstrous crimes; from this tragedies often arise. Archytas, then, would deserve praise if, when angry with some citizen and equal who had wronged him, he had nonetheless restrained himself and softened the onset of rage by patience. This restraint of oneself is glorious, by which some imminent great evil is checked. But not restraining the offenses of slaves and children is a sin, for through impunity they will proceed to a greater evil. Here anger is not to be restrained; rather, if it lies dormant, it must even be aroused. What we say concerning a human being, moreover, we say also concerning God, who made humankind like himself. I pass over speaking of God’s form, because the Stoics deny that he has any [Col. 0135A]

…God’s form; and abundant further material would arise, if we wished to refute them. I speak only of the mind. If it belongs to God to think, to be wise, to understand, to provide, and to bestow, and if among all living creatures man alone possesses these things, then he has been made in God’s likeness. Yet he therefore falls into vice because, being compounded with earthly frailty, he cannot preserve incorrupt and pure what he received from God, unless he is instructed by that same God in the precepts of justice.

## Chapter XIX. On the soul and body, and on Providence

But since, as we have said, he is compounded of two things, mind and body, virtues reside in the one and vices in the other, and they struggle against one another. For the goods of the mind, which consist in restraining desires, are opposed to the body; and the goods of the body, which consist in every kind of pleasure, are hostile to the mind. But if the virtue of the mind resists desires and suppresses them, it will truly be like God. From this it is apparent that the human soul, which receives divine virtue, is not mortal.

But the distinction is this: since virtue has bitterness and pleasure has a sweet allurement, very many are overcome and drawn away toward sweetness. But those who have devoted themselves to the body and earthly things are pressed down to earth and cannot attain the grace of the divine gift, because they have defiled themselves with the pollutions of vices. But God acknowledges as like himself those who have followed God and obeyed him, who have despised bodily desires and, preferring virtue to pleasures, have preserved innocence and justice.

Since, then, he has established a most holy law and wishes all persons to be innocent and beneficent, can he fail to be angry when he sees his law despised, virtue rejected, and pleasure sought? And if he is the governor of the world, as he ought to be, surely he does not disregard that which is perhaps the greatest thing in the whole world. If he is provident, as God ought to be, he surely provides for humankind, so that our life may be more abundant, better, and safer. If he is Father and God of all, he certainly delights in human virtues and is moved by vices; therefore he loves the just and hates the impious.

“There is no need,” someone says, “for hatred; for he has once for all appointed reward for the good and punishment for the evil.” But if someone should live justly and innocently, and yet neither worship nor concern himself with God at all, as Aristides and Timon and the other philosophers did, will he escape with impunity because, although he has obeyed God’s law, he has nevertheless despised God himself? There is therefore something for which God may be angry: namely, when someone, trusting in his own integrity, rebels against him. If he can be angry with such a person because of pride, why not still more with the sinner who has despised the law together with its very lawgiver? A judge cannot remit sins, because he serves another’s will. But God can, because he himself is the arbiter and judge of his own law; and when he established it, he certainly did not deprive himself of all power, but retains the freedom to forgive.

## Chapter XX. On sins and God’s mercy

If he can forgive, then he can also be angry. “Why, then,” someone may ask, “are those who sin often prosperous, while those who live piously are often miserable?” Because fugitives and disowned children live freely, whereas those under the discipline of a father or master live more strictly and frugally. For virtue is both tested and established through evils; vices, through pleasure. Yet the person who sins ought not to hope for perpetual impunity, because no prosperity is perpetual:

> But surely a human being’s final day must always  
> Be awaited; and no one ought to be called happy  
> Before death and the last funeral rites.  
> —Ovid, *Metamorphoses* III.135–137

So says the poet, not without charm. The outcome is what tests prosperity; and no one can escape God’s judgment, whether alive or dead. For he has power both to cast down the living from the heights and to afflict the dead with eternal torments.

“But,” he says, “if God is angry, he ought immediately to exact vengeance and punish every person according to his deserts.” Yet if he did so, no one would remain alive. For there is no one who sins in nothing, and there are many things that incite one to sin: age, drunkenness, poverty, opportunity, reward. So subject to sin is the frailty of the flesh with which we are clothed that, unless God spared this necessity, perhaps far too few would live. For this reason he is most patient and restrains his anger. Since virtue is perfect in him, his patience also must be perfect; and patience too is a virtue. How many sinners later became just, evil persons good, and wicked persons self-controlled! How many who in early life were disgraceful and condemned in everyone’s judgment afterward proved praiseworthy! This certainly would not happen if punishment followed every sin.

[Col. 0138B] Public laws condemn manifest criminals; but there are very many whose sins are concealed, very many who suppress an accuser either by entreaties or reward, and very many who evade judicial proceedings through favour or power. If divine judgment condemned all who escape human punishment, humanity would be either scarce or altogether nonexistent upon the earth. Indeed, that one cause alone could justly have sufficed for destroying the human race: human beings, despising the living God, render divine honour as though to heavenly beings to earthly and fragile images, worshipping works fashioned by human fingers. Though God the craftsman has formed them with uplifted face and upright posture for contemplating heaven and knowing God, they have preferred to bend down toward the earth in the manner of cattle.

**“Resisted desires.”** This is the reading of the most ancient and best manuscripts: two Bologna manuscripts, the Regio-Putianus, Caucasianus, and another Royal manuscript; two Colbert manuscripts, the Leipzig manuscript, Baluze’s manuscript, and fourteen printed editions. In thirteen later manuscripts and two old Roman editions and the edition of Isaeus, the reading is “pleasures” (*voluptatibus*). Bunemann likewise prints this reading and supplies the following note:

**“Resisted pleasures.”** Others read “resisted desires.” Heumann prefers the former. “That word seems more appropriate to me here, because he continually uses this term in this sense”: Book IV, chapter 17: “They employ lust to attain pleasures.” *Epitome*, chapter 61, beginning: “Lust seeks pleasures.” Compare below. What he discusses concerning pleasures in Book VI, chapters 20–23, may serve as a commentary. —BUN.

**“And suppressed them.”** One Colbert manuscript has “overpowered them”; two Bologna manuscripts and the Taxaquet manuscript, “restrained them.” See below, at the beginning of chapter 21: “his fury had to be moderated and suppressed.”

**“And suppressed them.”** To restrain is too little, since they must be suppressed. I observe the distinction from Cicero, *First Oration against Catiline*, chapter 12: “With this one man killed, I understand that this plague of the republic can for a while be restrained, but cannot be suppressed forever.” —BUN.

**“Will truly be like God.”** Thus the ancient manuscripts Regio-Putianus and Caucasianus, two other Royal manuscripts, the Colbert manuscripts and many others, as well as thirteen printed editions. Two Colbert manuscripts read, “will indeed be like God”; two Bologna manuscripts, the Taxaquet manuscript, and Baluze’s manuscript read, “will be found truly like God”; one later Royal manuscript, one Colbert manuscript, and four common editions read, “is found.” Bunemann also adds this word, as in the following note:

**“Is found truly like God.”** Others: “will truly be like God.” Quite good. Thomas, Thysius, Gallæus, and Sparkius: “is found truly like God.” The Bologna and Taxaquet manuscripts and Isaeus: “will be found truly like God.” I preferred this because of the antiquity of the manuscripts and because the other reading—“has suppressed, will be”—seems to contain something awkward. Otherwise the sense comes to the same thing. *On the Workmanship [of God]*, chapter 19: “This person is blessed; this person must necessarily be like God.” Book II of the *Institutions*, chapter 18: “This person will be judged worthy of heaven.” Book VI, chapter 18: “Because nothing can be found more worthy than a human being endowed with virtue.” —BUN.

**“Those who have devoted themselves to the body.”** Six manuscripts and the old Roman editions have “because,” which follows shortly afterward.

**“The divine gift.”** I have restored this from very many manuscripts, among them the very ancient and best two Bologna manuscripts, Regio-Putianus, Caucasianus, and the editions of Betuleius and Cellarius. Three later Royal manuscripts, four Colbert manuscripts, and thirteen common editions have “the divine deity”; Claromontanus has “name,” wrongly.

**“Have defiled themselves.”** I read thus with almost all manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470, the Florentine edition, and Isaeus. But the other common codices, together with one later Royal manuscript, two Colbert manuscripts, and Claromontanus, read “defiled.”

**“And if he is governor of the world.”** One later Bologna manuscript reads “who.”

**“If he is provident.”** Thus, with the old editions, all manuscripts except one later Royal manuscript and Caucasianus, which have “provident” [*providens*], as do fifteen printed editions.

**“He says.”** The Emmanuscript and the editions of Cellarius and Walch read: “someone says.”

**“Aristides.”** No room remains for me to doubt that Aristides should be read here: both from Cicero, who cites him for irascibility and Timon for hatred, and from the most ancient and best manuscripts—one Bologna manuscript, Regio-Putianus, one Vatican manuscript, one Colbert manuscript, Bodleianus, and Claromontanus in the margin—which later manuscripts and printed editions corrupted into “Aristotle.” Aristides, moreover, was an Athenian Greek, whose virtues, sayings, and examples Cicero recalls in *Tusculan Disputations* V.106, *On Duties* III.44, *Orator* 32, and *For Publius Sestius* 141: “If among the Athenians, Greek men, that Themistocles, saviour of his country, was not deterred … by the exile of Aristides, who alone of all is said to have been most unconquerable … with so many examples of anger set forth,” etc.

**“And Timon.”** According to Cicero, he too was an Athenian; according to Laertius, a worthy man, fond of solitude and gardens, and a hater of humankind. Cicero reports his sayings in *Tusculan Disputations* IV.25 and 27, and *On Friendship* 87. Timon is absent from eleven manuscripts and three editions. Others maintain that this was Philigismus, a disciple of Pyrrho.

**“As Aristides and Cimon.”** One Vatican manuscript, Aldus, Cratander, Gymnicus, Fasius, Gryphius, Tornæsius, Betuleius, the Paris edition of 1561, Thomas, Thysius, Gallæus, and Sparkius read “Timon.” For in the most ancient Bologna and Turin manuscripts, the capital letters *c* and *t* are almost one and the same in form. Nepos speaks plainly of Aristides in *Aristides*, chapter 2: “Many things remain in memory concerning his justice, fairness, and innocence.” Lactantius praises his justice in Book III, chapter 19; add Book VI of the *Institutions*, chapter 6. But what decisively led me to emend to “Cimon” was the genuine passage of Lactantius, *Institutions* VI.9:

> Whoever does not know God must necessarily be ignorant of justice itself. But let us suppose it possible that someone, through natural and inborn goodness, may attain true virtues; such, we have received, was Cimon at Athens, who gave alms to the needy, invited the poor, and clothed the naked. Yet because that one thing, which is greatest—the recognition of God—is lacking, all those good things are already superfluous and empty, and he has laboured in vain to attain them. For all his justice is like a human body without a head.

You see that our author here too is speaking of Cimon and the philosophers. —BUNEMANN.

**“Rebelling.”** Thus read thirteen manuscripts, including Regio-Putianus. Two later Royal manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470 read “of rebellion”; two Bologna manuscripts and five others read “while rebelling”; almost all printed editions read “for rebellion.”

**“If, then, he can also be angry.”** Thus I read with Regio-Putianus, four other Royal manuscripts, two Colbert manuscripts, Baluze’s manuscript, and Claromontanus. In the two Bologna manuscripts, Taxaquet, one Colbert manuscript, and the edition of Isaeus, *then* is absent; common editions lack *also*. One Royal manuscript, three Colbert manuscripts, two Leipzig manuscripts, Brunensis, and the Roman editions of 1470 and 1474, the Tridentine and Florentine editions, read: “If, then, he can be angry, why then?”

**“Disowned.”** That is, rejected.

**“Tests prosperity.”** That is, demonstrates or proves it. Minucius Felix, chapter 36, at the end: “Thus, as gold is tested by fires, so we are tested by adversities.” Jerome, letter to Paula: “Humility of dress tested not their swollen minds.” —BUN.

**“Drunkenness.”** I emended this from almost all manuscripts, including two Bologna manuscripts, Regio-Putianus, two other Royal manuscripts, three Colbert manuscripts, four Oxford manuscripts, Taxaquet, Emmanuscript, Cantabrigiensis, Brunensis, the Roman edition of 1470, and Cellarius. Johannes Caucius and Francius also suspected that this was the proper reading, and Heumann approves it. But three later Royal manuscripts, three Colbert manuscripts, Marmoutier, Claromontanus, and thirteen printed editions have “violence.”

**“Whose sins are concealed.”** Thus restored from the Gymnicus edition and the manuscripts, except two later Royal manuscripts and three Colbert manuscripts, which have “are hidden,” as do most printed editions.

**“Or even none at all.”** *Even* is added on the authority of nearly all manuscripts and the Gymnicus edition; it is absent from the other printed editions and four later manuscripts.

**“Wrought.”** Francius: perhaps “elaborately made.” Yet *laboratus* is used in the same sense by Cicero, *Letters to Atticus* XIII.3 and *For Cælius* 54.

**“They preferred, in the manner of cattle.”** Thus I restored it from the old Roman editions and twelve other printed editions, and from Regio-Putianus and fourteen other manuscripts. The Caucasian and Claromontanus manuscripts and twelve printed editions read “in the custom” [*more*] instead of “in the manner” [*modo*]. One Royal manuscript, the Bologna, Taxaquet, and Leipzig manuscripts add “to creep on the ground”; five manuscripts read “to creep into [the ground].”

[Col. 0139A] …one who, turned away from the sight of heaven and God the Father, worships earthly things which he ought to tread underfoot—that is, things moulded and fashioned from earth. Therefore, amid such great impiety and so many sins of human beings, God’s patience achieves this: people themselves correct their errors after condemning their former life. Finally, many are good and just; abandoning earthly cults, they acknowledge the unique majesty of God. Yet although God’s patience is greatest and most beneficial, he punishes the guilty, however late, and does not permit them to proceed further when he perceives that they are incorrigible.

## Chapter XXI. On the anger of God and of man

One final and ultimate question remains. For someone may perhaps say that God is so far from being angry that even in his commandments he forbids a human being to be angry. I might say that human anger had to be restrained because people often become angry unjustly; and it has an immediate impulse because it is temporal. Therefore, lest those things be done in anger which humble persons, persons of middling rank, and great kings do, its fury had to be moderated and suppressed, lest, out of control of its mind, it commit some inexpiable crime.

But God does not become angry for the immediate present, because he is eternal and of perfect virtue; and he is never angry except deservedly. Yet the matter is not quite so. For if he altogether forbade anger, he would in some sense be reproving his own workmanship—he who from the beginning placed anger in the human liver; for the cause of this agitation is believed to reside in the moisture of the gall. He therefore does not wholly forbid anger, because this passion was necessarily given; but he forbids remaining in anger. For the anger of mortals ought itself to be mortal; if it remains, enmities are confirmed unto everlasting destruction.

Further, when he commanded us indeed to be angry, but not to sin, he certainly did not root out anger entirely, but moderated it, so that in every act of correction we might observe measure and justice. Therefore, he who commands us to be angry is himself surely angry; he who commands us to be quickly appeased is himself surely appeasable. For he commanded those things that are just and useful to the common good.

But because I had said that God’s anger is not temporal, [Col. 0140B] like a human being’s, who burns with a momentary agitation and cannot easily govern himself because of frailty, we must understand that, because God is eternal, his anger likewise remains eternally. Yet again, because he is endowed with the greatest virtue, he has his anger in his own power: he is not governed by it, but himself moderates it as he wishes. This certainly does not conflict with what was said above. For if his anger were wholly immortal, there would be no room for satisfaction or favour after a transgression, whereas he himself commands people to be reconciled before sunset. But divine anger remains eternally against those who sin eternally. Therefore God is appeased not by incense, not by a sacrificial victim, not by costly gifts—all of which are perishable—but by moral amendment; and whoever ceases to sin makes God’s anger mortal. For this reason he does not punish every offender at once: so that a human being may have the opportunity to come to his senses and correct himself.

## Chapter XXII. On sins, and on the verses of the Sibyl recited concerning them

These are the things I had to say about God’s anger, most dear Donatus, so that you might know how to refute those who make God immovable. It remains for us to use, in Cicero’s manner, an epilogue for the peroration. Just as he did when discussing death in the *Tusculan Disputations*, so in this work we must employ divine testimonies that may be believed, in order to refute the persuasion of those who believe that God is without anger and thereby dissolve all religion. Without religion, as we have shown, we are made equal either to beasts in savagery or to cattle in folly; for wisdom exists in religion alone—that is, in the knowledge of the highest God.

All the prophets, filled with the divine Spirit, speak of nothing except God’s favour toward the just and his anger against the impious. Their testimonies are certainly sufficient for us. But because these people do not believe them—people who parade wisdom in their hair and clothing—we also had to refute them by reason and arguments. For matters are perversely arranged when they grant human things authority over divine things, whereas they ought rather to grant divine things authority over human things. Let us now omit these, lest we accomplish nothing among such persons and the subject extend to infinity. Let us therefore seek testimonies which they may either believe or at least not oppose.

Very many and very great authorities have reported that there were Sibyls: among the Greeks, Aristo of Chios and Apollodorus of Erythrae; among our own writers, Varro and Fenestella. All of these record that the Erythraean Sibyl was eminent and renowned above the others. Apollodorus indeed boasts of her as a fellow citizen and compatriot. Fenestella also reports that envoys were sent by the senate to Erythrae in order to bring this Sibyl’s verses to Rome and, when the Capitol was then being restored under the direction of Quintus Catulus, that the consuls Curio and Octavius arranged for them to be deposited there.

In her, the following verses concerning the supreme God and creator of all things are found:

> Imperishable Creator, eternal, dwelling in the ether,  
> Bringing good to the good—a far greater reward—  
> But stirring up wrath and anger against the evil and unjust.

Again, elsewhere, enumerating the crimes by which God is most greatly provoked, she added these lines:

> Flee unlawful forms of worship; serve the living God.  
> Guard yourself from adultery and from the unclean bed of a male.  
> Nourish your own offspring; do not kill.  
> For the Immortal One will be angered with whoever sins.

Therefore, he is indignant against sinners.

## Chapter XXIII. On God’s anger and the punishment of sinners; on Sibylline verses recited concerning it; and, further, on correction and exhortation

But because, as I have shown, the most learned authorities report that there were several Sibyls, the testimony of one alone should not be sufficient to confirm the truth which we intend to establish. The Cumaean volumes, in which the destinies of the Romans were written, are indeed kept secret; but the booklets of nearly all the rest are not forbidden from being available to everyone. From these, one Sibyl, proclaiming to all nations the anger of God because of human impiety, began in this way:

> When great anger comes upon a disobedient world,  
> I disclose God’s messages for the final age,  
> Prophesying to all people, city by city.

Another likewise said that, through God’s indignation against the unjust, the deluge occurred in the former age in order that the wickedness of the human race might be extinguished:

> When the heavenly God was angered  
> At the cities themselves and at all human beings,  
> The sea, bursting forth in a flood, covered the earth.

In a similar way she foretold a future conflagration, by which human impiety would again be destroyed:

> And one day God, no longer soothing his anger,  
> But making it heavier and destroying the race  
> Of human beings, will lay all waste beneath a conflagration.

Accordingly, Naso says this of Jupiter:

> He remembers, too, that it is in the fates that a time will come  
> When sea and land and heaven’s seized palace  
> Will burn, and the massive structure of the world will be in travail.

This must necessarily happen when honour and worship of the highest God have perished among human beings.

Yet the same Sibyl, declaring that he is appeased by repentance for deeds and by self-correction, added this:

> But turn in mercy now, mortals; do not lead  
> The great God into wrath of every kind.

Likewise, a little later:

> He will not destroy, but will again cease from anger, whenever all of you  
> Practise precious piety with one mind.

Then another Sibyl declares that the begetter of heavenly and earthly things must be loved, lest his indignation rise up to destroy humankind:

> Lest perhaps the imperishable God, angered, destroy  
> Every race of human beings—their life and shameless stock—  
> One must love God the wise begetter, who exists always.

From these things it is apparent that the arguments of the philosophers are empty, who remove from God anger—the very thing through which majesty itself is maintained—and thus remove what is most salutary for human affairs.

**“Turned away, [he worships] earthly things which he ought to tread underfoot.”** Correctly so. See what follows. Regio-Putianus and one other Royal manuscript, the Roman edition of 1470, Aldus, Fasius, and Betuleius read: “turned away, [he worships] the earth which he ought to tread underfoot.” Thirteen manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1468 read: “turned toward the earth which he ought to tread underfoot.”

**“They acknowledge the unique majesty of God.”** Lactantius uses this expression frequently elsewhere as well. See the note on Book I, chapter 1 of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*. Emmanuscript reads “of the heavenly God”; two later Royal manuscripts, three Colbert manuscripts, Claromontanus, and two old Roman editions read “recognize.”

**“One final and ultimate question remains.”** This is the reading of the older books, both manuscripts and printed editions. Many printed editions add “greatest” after *one*; one Colbert manuscript has “very greatest”; four later manuscripts read “one and greatest.”

**“That even in the commandments.”** I restored *even* from the editions of Cratander and Cellarius and all manuscripts, except four later manuscripts, in which, as in the other printed editions, *and* is read; Emmanuscript has “he himself.”

**“Had to be.”** I restored this from the old Roman editions and Isaeus, and from very many manuscripts. Caucasianus and eight printed editions have “had”; five manuscripts and four common editions have “should have had.”

**“Lest, out of control of its mind, it commit some inexpiable crime.”** Fourteen manuscripts, including Regio-Putianus, and one seen by Janus Gulielmus, together with the Roman edition of 1468, read: “lest [it commit] something impossible of mind,” without sense. Hence Gulielmus and Gallæus believe that one should read, “lest, out of control of its mind through bile,” or “in bile.” Two Bologna manuscripts, one later Royal manuscript, Taxaquet, two Colbert manuscripts, one Sorbonne manuscript, Baluze’s manuscript, and Claromontanus in the margin read, “lest after [it has committed] some…” One Colbert manuscript reads, “lest after anger [it commit] some…”

**“Who from the beginning.”** Fourteen manuscripts and as many printed editions have “because in the beginning.”

**“Had placed anger in the human liver.”** Two Royal manuscripts and four Colbert manuscripts have “anger in the human liver”; Emmanuscript, “in the human gall.”

**“Had placed anger in the human gall.”** Bunemann reads “anger in the human gall” and supplies this note:

**“Had placed anger in the human gall.”** All printed editions have “anger in the liver.” I wrote “anger in the gall” from Emmanuscript. The following words recommend it: “in the moisture of the gall”; and *Institutions* VI.15: “The passion of anger is in the gall, that of lust in the liver”; and *On the Workmanship [of God]*, chapter 14: “The passion of irascibility is located in the gall … the lusts of sexual things in the liver.” —BUN.

**“Further.”** Thus restored from the Bologna edition of 1470, Betuleius, and Cellarius. One later Royal manuscript and twelve printed editions have “finally.”

**“When he commanded us indeed to be angry, but not to sin, he certainly…”** Three later manuscripts and fourteen editions read, “he commanded him to be angry…”; three later manuscripts read, “commands.”

**“But not to sin,” etc.** In Psalm 4, the Septuagint indeed reads, “Be angry, and do not sin” (*ὀργίζεσθε, καὶ μὴ ἁμαρτάνετε*). But the Hebrews translate, “Tremble”; the sense is that we should shrink from sins. —BETULEIUS.

**“Who commands himself to be appeased.”** Thus I corrected it from all manuscripts and many editions; some printed editions read “to appease.”

**“Commands more quickly.”** Thus I read from very many of the most ancient and best manuscripts, with Francius approving; this corresponds to the earlier phrase, “commands.”

**“For he commanded those things.”** Thus restored from all manuscripts and the old Roman edition. Twelve printed editions read, “for indeed he commands.”

**“And cannot easily govern himself because of frailty; we must understand,” etc.** All manuscripts and five editions preserve this reading. It is the true and genuine reading of the Tridentine and Florentine editions and the Venetian edition of 1490. The reading in the other printed editions, “therefore not to understand,” is corrupt and contrary to Lactantius’s purpose, as Thomasius and Isaeus rightly observed.

**“His anger remains eternally.”** That is, from omnipotence and God’s other attributes it necessarily follows that he hates all who have sinned against his majesty with an obstinate mind. Conversely, from God’s infinite mercy follows his allowing those to return into favour with him who, as our author says below, make good use of the granted opportunity to come to their senses and correct themselves. —SPARKIUS.

**“Or room for favour after a transgression.”** One ancient Bologna manuscript reads, “or a fixed place for favour.”

**“Before sunset,” etc.** This is not Christ’s saying but Paul’s, Ephesians 4. Thus he attributes so much authority to Paul’s writings that he holds them in the place of an oracle, as dictated by divine inspiration.

**“The opportunity to come to his senses and correct himself.”** *And correct himself* is absent from twenty manuscripts; but twelve have “the opportunity to come to his senses himself,” although *himself* cannot be construed with *coming to his senses*. The edition of Betuleius has “a human being [has] the opportunity to receive himself.” But these words of Lactantius are taken from Cicero, where one reads “the opportunity to come to one’s senses and correct oneself.”

**“You might refute.”** One ancient Bologna manuscript reads “you refute.”

**“Let us refute their persuasion.”** Thus I restored it from almost all manuscripts, the Venetian, Tridentine, Florentine, Isaeus, and Cellarius editions. Brunensis reads “by persuasion”; one Colbert manuscript, Marmoutier, and Claromontanus read “persuasions”; one later Royal manuscript reads “let us thoroughly conquer their persuasion”; Caucasianus, one Colbert manuscript, and fourteen printed editions read “let us conquer [their] persuasion.”

**“Refute.”** Excellent. *Institutions* I.16: “What kind of proof should we employ against them more than to refute them by the testimonies of their own gods?” *On the Workmanship [of God]*, chapter 10: “We shall refute those whom … [we arm] with weapons taken from their own mutual conflict,” and often elsewhere. —BUNEMANN.

**“These persons do not believe them.”** Book I, chapter 5: “But let us omit the testimonies of the prophets, lest proof from persons wholly disbelieved seem less suitable.” —BUN.

**“Who parade wisdom in their hair and clothing.”** For those professing wisdom wore their hair long and dressed themselves in cloaks, as we said in Book III of the *Institutions*, chapter 25. —ISAEUS. See also Book V, chapter 2.

**“Had to be refuted.”** Heumann reads “had to be.” The books read “had been.” A similar passage occurs in Book V, chapter 4: “[Cyprian] did not use the material as he ought. For [Demetrian] had not been refuted by testimonies of Scripture, which he regarded as fabricated … but by arguments and reason.”

**“They grant human things authority over divine things, whereas they ought rather [to grant authority] to divine things over human things.”** Almost all manuscripts, including the most ancient, and seven old editions read this. In five manuscripts and many printed editions the text is corrupt: “that they grant human authority to divine things, whereas they ought rather [to grant] divine [authority] to human things.” One Colbert manuscript reads “they have granted.”

**“Sibyls.”** Four later manuscripts and sixteen editions add “there were many,” words absent from the others. For what we have said about the Sibyls, see volume I, Book I, chapter 6. Suidas, doubtless drawing upon records of very ancient writers, confirms Lactantius’s view in the many things he relates. He affirms that there were ten, at different times and places. But Sebastian Castellio maintains that everything attributed to the Sibyls proceeded from one woman; he has almost brought me over to his opinion, supported by arguments that are not merely plausible in appearance but fortified by certain sound reasons. Yet the authority of antiquity induced me to weigh the arguments more carefully.

First, the incredible longevity of the Sibyl, whom he makes one out of many, stands in the way: namely, from the Flood down to the age of the Tarquins, a span of about 1,770 years. Although the Sibyl’s longevity once passed into a proverb, an age so prodigious, as no writer records in such extent, surpasses belief. Next, the diversity of names stands in the way—not names varying merely according to different nations, but chiefly proper names. Finally, I can scarcely be induced to believe that in Noah’s time they wrote in Greek, and indeed in heroic verse, flowing so easily with the charm of Homer, Hesiod, or, if you prefer, the older Orpheus. And as I readily believe that there were not ten Sibyls, so I prefer to agree with those who posited only two or four. —BETULEIUS. But whatever Betuleius says here, see what we have said concerning the Sibyls in Book I, chapter 6.

**“Aristo of Chios.”** Thus several manuscripts and almost all editions; Cicero calls him no differently in *On the Laws* I.78, where he reports his doctrines, and Minucius Felix in the *Octavius*. Therefore “Aristochius” in two Colbert manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470 is corrupt; “Aristonicus” in Regio-Putianus, Caucasianus, and seven others is worse; Marmoutier reads “my Aristo” instead of “Aristonicus”; one ancient Bologna manuscript reads “Aristo the Stoic”; one later Royal manuscript, two Colbert manuscripts, and the Roman edition of 1468 read “Aristoricus”; some editions read “Aristarchus.” This Aristo was a native of Chios, a Stoic philosopher; see Diogenes Laertius, Book VI at the end, and Book VII at the end of the life of Zeno.

**“Apollodorus of Erythrae.”** Also cited in Book I, chapter 6. —CELL.

**“To Erythrae.”** Thus most manuscripts and all editions. Others vary: Baluze’s manuscript reads “to Erythrae”; Regio-Putianus, “Erythraea [sent] by the senate”; two later manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1468, “to the Erythraeans”; one Colbert manuscript, “Erithros”; Bologna, one Royal manuscript, and Brunensis, “Erythro”; one Colbert manuscript, “Erithreo”; another Colbert manuscript, “Eritheo.”

**“To bring [them] away.”** Or, “to transport them.”

**“The consuls Curio and Octavius.”** The third Leipzig manuscript, Reimmann, and Rost read “Octavianus.” Incorrectly. Curio and Octavius were consuls in the year 678 from the founding of the City. —BUN.

**“Quintus Catulus.”** Thus the manuscripts and most editions; Cicero likewise in Books II and III of *On the Orator*. Others read “Catullus.”

**“Imperishable,” etc.** Latin translation:

> The incorruptible Creator, eternal, dwelling in the ether,  
> Bringing good to the good, a much greater reward;  
> But stirring up wrath and fury against the evil and unjust.

**“To the good, good.”** One later Royal manuscript, one Colbert manuscript, and seven editions read “to the harmless, harmless.” The others agree with Autolycus, as in the text.

**“She added these.”** Thus I restored it from all manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470 and Betuleius. The other common editions read “she reported.”

**“Flee…”** In Latin:

> Flee impious religions, and serve the living God.  
> Abstain from adultery and from an unclean union with a male.  
> Nourish your own generation of children, and do not kill;  
> For the Immortal One is angered with whoever has sinned.

**“Your own generation.”** Lactantius’s Regio-Putianus manuscript represents this in capital letters as: `ΘΗΝΔΙΔΙΑΝ ΘΗΝΔΗ`.

**“Therefore he is indignant against sinners.”** I added this from all manuscripts and the three old Roman editions, the Florentine edition, Betuleius, and Cellarius; it is absent from the other printed editions.

**“As I have shown.”** Chapter 22 and *Institutions* I.6 and following. —BUN.

**“Fates.”** I retain *fates*, whence, as Heumann aptly observes, Livy calls the Sibylline books “fatal books” in V.14–15 and XLII.2. I add that Fulvius Sabinus, in Vopiscus’s *Aurelian* 19, said from Aurelian’s letter that “the fatal books should be consulted.” Suetonius too, in *Caesar* 79, calls these verses “fatal books”; in *Augustus* 31, “prophetic books.” —BUN.

**“Proclaiming.”** Concerning matters of the greatest seriousness and threats. Compare below, *Institutions* II.16; VII.13 and 16. Cicero, *Letters to Atticus* II.23, at the end: “He casts terrors and makes threats.”

**“When great anger comes…”** At the beginning of Book VIII. In Latin:

> When great anger comes upon the disobedient world,  
> I disclose God’s messages for the final age,  
> Prophesying to all people city by city.

**“When…”** At the beginning of Book IV. In Latin:

> When the supercelestial God was angry  
> At the cities themselves and all human beings,  
> The sea, bursting forth in a deluge, covered the earth.

**“Cities.”** Two Royal manuscripts have *πόλιεσιν*; one other Royal manuscript and the Roman edition of 1470, *πολέεσι*.

**“And one day…”** At the end of Book IV. In Latin:

> And one day, God no longer soothing his anger,  
> But making it heavier and destroying the race  
> Of human beings, will lay all waste by conflagration.

**“Soothing.”** Regio-Putianus has the passive *πραϋνθέντα*, wrongly.

**“Naso.”** *Metamorphoses* I.256.

**“But in mercy…”** Book IV. In Latin:

> But turn in mercy now, human beings; do not lead  
> The great God into wrath of every kind.

**“He will not destroy…”** Book IV. In Latin:

> He will not destroy, but will again cease from anger, whenever all  
> Of you practise precious piety in your hearts.

For *εὖτ᾽ ἂν ἅπαντες*, Regio-Putianus has *ἢν ἄρα πάντες*; one Colbert manuscript and the Roman edition of 1470, *ἐπὰν ἅπαντες*; another Colbert manuscript, *ἐπειδὴ πάντες*. Some manuscripts and editions have *περὶ θυμῷ*. Printed editions of the Sibylline books have *περίψιμον*; one Colbert manuscript, *περίθυμον*. But Regio-Putianus most correctly has *ἐρίτιμον*, with Opsopoeius approving.

**“Lest perhaps…”** In Latin:

> Lest the imperishable God, angered, destroy  
> Every race of human beings, their life and shameless stock;  
> One must love God the wise begetter, who exists always.

**“Without anger.”** Heumann reads “to be without anger.”

**“They remove … that by which majesty itself is maintained.”** Thus read both Bologna manuscripts, Taxaquet, and Penia. In Leipzig, the two Brunensis manuscripts, Ultrajectinus, and others, the passage is mutilated and reads: “they remove that which is contrary to majesty itself.” “This kingdom.” —ISAEUS.

In the very ancient Regio-Putianus the reading is: “they remove that which is maintained by majesty itself.” The words between the first *which* and the third *which* are missing. Here an error of the copyist is apparent, caused by the omission of a line. Lactantius seems to refer to what he says at the end of chapter 17 above concerning anger: that it is useful and necessary for human affairs.

**“They remove that which is most useless, taking away from him that which is most salutary for human affairs, by which majesty itself is maintained.”** I did not venture to reject this reading of the most ancient manuscripts of all—namely, the two Bologna manuscripts, Taxaquet, and Penia—which Thomasius, Isaeus, Thysius, Gallæus, Sparkius, and the Cambridge edition received into the text.

**“And God…”** In Latin:

> And God, king and begetter of all,  
> Whom earth, heaven, and sea tremble before,  
> Whom Tartarean recesses and demons dread—  
> Ministers of so great a power.

Baluze’s and Brunensis manuscripts and the Roman edition of 1470 read “before all things” instead of “of all.”

**“Ministers of so great a power.”** Heumann reads, not inelegantly, “of Tartarean power,” which is expressed by the Greek word *ταρτάρεοι*. I retain “so great,” namely, of divine majesty. For below he says: “of this so great power,” namely, “that the ruler of things may have true and eternal power over all.” Compare above. Demons of this so great power are called ministers of the kingdom. —BUN.

It rests upon fear. You may say this of earthly rule, which rests upon laws and fear; yet Livy says in Book II: “The powers of laws are stronger than those of men.” This is not the case with heavenly rule, which is maintained by love and hope rather than fear. Penal law and fear in religion exist only for the unjust, since the righteous person is guided by grace and love, or filial fear.

“Wherefore,” etc. Here Chapter XXIV begins in four Colbert manuscripts, the Clairmont manuscript, and the Roman editions of 1470 and 1474, Parrhasius, and Isaeus; the others connect it with the preceding chapter.

“Empty talk” (*vaniloquentia*). In Reimmann it is emended from “vain eloquence” (*vana eloquentia*) to “empty talk” (*vana loquentia*). The received word occurs in Plautus, Livy, and Tacitus. BUN.

“Both capacities in him are worthy of reverence.” That is, we must revere him not only as a beneficent father, but also as a severe lord. Lactantius had already said this at the beginning of *Divine Institutes*, Book IV, chapter 4, where he says: “Since God sustains both capacities, that of Father and that of Lord, we must love him because we are children, and fear him because we are servants.” HEUMANN.

“Himself possesses.” Heumann reads “possesses.”

“If you consider God.” Thus indeed all the books read; I should prefer, with Davies on the *Epitome*, chapter 70, “if you consider the Lord”; for shortly afterwards there is mention of lord and parent. Compare Book I, chapter 7. BUN.

“Dutiful.” Supply “household.” HEUMANN.

“Knowledge.” γνῶσις, “knowledge.” See the note on *Institutes*, Book II, chapter 15, and Book V, chapter 14. BUN.

“Let us meditate upon heavenly, divine, and everlasting things.” Thus the manuscripts and printed editions. Francius read “and everlasting,” as also Heumann, who thinks *divina* (“divine”) ought to be omitted.—“Heavenly, divine, everlasting things.” Thus all the books; I should prefer that the *et* be removed: “heavenly, divine, everlasting”; unless perhaps you explain “everlasting” as “the things which are everlasting.” BUN.

“And he must be loved.” This is absent from fourteen manuscripts, among them the Regio-Putianus, and from ten common editions. Yet it must be restored and retained from the others, so that there may be reference to the three following expressions; and the two very ancient Bolognese manuscripts have it in the text as we have written it. Thomasius rightly defends this reading from this very passage of Lactantius: “God must be followed, because he is the cause of things; worshipped, on account of the reason of virtues; loved, because he is the source of goods.”

“The material of things.” That is, the cause of things. SPARK.

[Those] who think that God is without anger, and among his other praises set down that which is most useless, taking away from him that which is most salutary for human affairs, through which majesty itself is maintained. Unless fear preserves this earthly kingdom and dominion, it collapses. Take anger away from a king: not only will no one obey him, but he will even be hurled down from his height. Indeed, remove this feeling from any humble person: who will not despoil him? Who will not mock him? Who will not inflict injury upon him? Thus he will be unable to possess either clothing, a dwelling, or food, since others will seize whatever he has; much less should we suppose that the majesty of heavenly rule can stand without anger and fear.

Apollo of Miletus, when consulted concerning the religion of the Jews, gave this response:

> And God—the king and begetter before all things—  
> whom earth and heaven and sea tremble before,  
> and the Tartarean recesses and the demons shudder at.

If he is as mild as the philosophers would have him, how is it that at his nod not only demons and the ministers of so great a power, but heaven, earth, and the whole nature of things tremble? For if no one serves another except under compulsion, every dominion therefore rests upon fear; and fear rests upon anger. For unless someone is moved against one unwilling to obey, that person cannot be compelled to obedience. Let each person consult his own feelings: he will then understand that no one can be subjected to rule without anger and punishment. Therefore, where there is no anger, neither will there be rule. But God has rule; therefore he must necessarily have the anger by which rule is maintained.

Wherefore, let no one, led astray by the empty talk of philosophers, train himself to despise God; this is the greatest impiety. We must all both love him, because he is a father; revere him, because he is lord; honor him, because he is beneficent; and fear him, because he is severe: both capacities in him are worthy of reverence. Who, without forfeiting piety, would not love the parent of his soul? Or who could with impunity despise him who, as ruler of all things, possesses true and everlasting power over all?

If you consider him as Father, he supplies us with our birth into the light which we enjoy; through him we live, through him we entered the lodging of this world. If you consider God, he nourishes us with innumerable resources; he sustains us; we live in his house; we are members of his household. And if we have been less obedient than was fitting, and less dutiful than the immortal merits of our Lord and Parent required, nevertheless it greatly helps us to obtain pardon if we retain his worship and knowledge; if, having cast aside humble and earthly things and goods alike, we meditate upon heavenly, divine, and everlasting things. And in order that we may do this, God must be followed, God worshipped and loved; because in him are the cause of things, the reason of virtues, and the source of goods.

For what is greater than God in power, more perfect in reason, or more splendid in brightness? Since he begot us for wisdom and brought us forth for righteousness, it is not permitted for a human being, abandoning God, the giver of understanding and life, [Col. 0147A]

to serve earthly and perishable things, or, clinging to the pursuit of temporal goods, to defect from innocence and piety. Vicious and deadly pleasures do not make one happy; nor does wealth, the instigator of lust; nor empty ambition; nor fleeting honors. Entangled by these, the human soul, enslaved to the body, is condemned to eternal death. Rather, innocence alone and justice alone make one happy; and their lawful and worthy reward is immortality, which God established from the beginning for holy and incorrupt minds that preserve themselves whole and inviolate from vices and from every earthly stain.

Those who have defiled their conscience by crimes, frauds, robberies, and deceptions, and who by injuries to others and wicked deeds have branded themselves with stains that cannot be washed out, cannot share in this heavenly and everlasting reward. Therefore all who wish deservedly to be called wise, who wish deservedly to be called human beings, must despise frail things, trample earthly things underfoot, and scorn humble things, so that they may be united to God in a most blessed bond.

[Col. 0148A] Let impiety be removed; let turbulent and destructive discord and dissensions be quieted, by which human societies and the divine union of the public covenant are broken, divided, and scattered. Let us resolve, so far as we can, to be good and beneficent. If we have any wealth or resources at hand, let it be distributed not for the pleasure of one person, but for the welfare of many. For pleasure is as mortal as the body to which it renders service. But justice and beneficence are as immortal as the mind and soul, which by good works attain likeness to God.

Let God be consecrated for us not in temples, but in our heart. All things made by hand are destructible. Let us cleanse this temple, which is defiled not by smoke or dust, but by evil thoughts; which is illuminated not by burning candles, but by the brightness and light of wisdom. If we always believe that God is present within it, to whose divinity the secrets of the mind lie open, we shall so live that we may always have him favorable and never fear him as angry.

[Col. 0147]

# DISSERTATION ON LACTANTIUS’S BOOK *ON THE ANGER OF GOD*

By Dom. Le Nourry, O.S.B.

## CHAPTER I. Analysis of this book

At the beginning of this book (chapter 1), he declares that he wrote it in order to refute the error of very many people, including certain philosophers, who denied that God becomes angry. Yet he admits that he has not reached such a degree of arrogance as to suppose himself, by his own intelligence, to have comprehended the truth which, according to Socrates’s testimony, no human being can attain alone by himself. Rather, he professes that he follows the teaching of God, who alone has the power to disclose hidden truth.

There are, he says (chapter 2), three steps by which one ascends to this truth. The first is to recognize false religions and reject the impious worship of gods. The second is to know the true, one, and supreme God, who created all things by his power and governs them by his providence. The third is to acknowledge God’s ambassador and messenger, who, having freed human beings from their errors, formed them for the worship of this true God and for righteousness. He briefly indicates, moreover, where he has refuted, or will subsequently refute, those who have gone astray in explaining this threefold stage of truth.

Having set this forth by way of preface, he teaches that a fourfold question may be raised concerning God’s anger. First, whether anger should be attributed to God and favor denied him. Second, whether both should be denied him. Third, whether favor should be ascribed to him and anger removed. Fourth, whether both should be attributed to him. Of the first question, he says (chapter 3), there can be no dispute. For what could be more absurd to say than that God, the author of good, benefits and does good to no one, but harms everyone and is angry with all?

The Epicureans, however, had plainly dreamed that in God there is no movement either of favor or of anger (chapter 4). But few people held this utterly false opinion, and they were wicked people. For if God, as they babbled, is unmoved—if he lies inactive, motionless, without any will or providence—then he is certainly not God. Therefore, if this is Epicurus’s opinion, he undoubtedly asserted the existence of God not in reality, but merely in word.

The Stoics and some others thought (chapter 5) that favor exists in God, but that there is never any stirring of anger. For just as kindness and beneficence, they said, ought to be in God, so every disturbance of mind must necessarily be wholly absent from him. Lactantius, by contrast, says: If God is moved by favor, then he is also moved by anger. Indeed, one who loves the good and pious is angry with the impious and unjust. Love of the good flows and proceeds from hatred of evil, and hatred of evil from love of the good. Therefore, one who by a movement of favor does good to the good is also angry with the wicked, and corrects and punishes them according to their deserts.

Accordingly, our author judges (chapter 6) that the only opinion consonant with truth is that which maintains that God is in reality moved both by favor and by anger. He considers the whole sum and hinge of religion to be involved in this matter (chapter 7). He demonstrates this because, although human beings have many things in common with brute animals, or similar to them, they are distinguished from the others by wisdom and especially by religion—that is, by knowledge and worship of God. But religion cannot stand without sincere fear of God as offended and angry toward sinners. The Epicureans therefore wrongly attempted to remove God’s anger (chapter 8), asserting foolishly that he cares for nothing. For temples are built and sacrifices offered in vain to one who cares for nothing and has nothing in common with us. No honor is due to such a being. Moreover, if God is not angry, he is surely not feared; if he is not feared, neither is he worshipped. Indeed, human beings, restrained by no curb of conscience, will wallow in every kind of crime.

They responded, however, that religion and fear of divinity had been invented by prudent men not for truth’s sake but for usefulness, so that others might live with greater innocence and integrity of character. Lactantius admits that this response presents him with a great subject for disputation, and one remote from his purpose; nevertheless, he touches on it briefly. Thus he relates (chapter 9) that Protagoras first of all called into doubt whether any God exists; then that Epicurus taught, in an open and utterly absurd contradiction, that there is some divine nature, but one without providence; and finally that Diagoras and Theodorus wholly denied the existence of any God.

In order completely to overthrow these false opinions, he shows with various and powerful arguments (chapter 10) that those are utterly mistaken who dreamed that the world arose by its own nature, without any providence of God, formed from minute and indivisible particles, as Leucippus, Democritus, Epicurus, and Lucretius supposed. With no weaker force and arguments of no less weight, he attacks and destroys the error of Strato, who foolishly proclaimed that nature, lacking sensation and form, was generated of its own accord, without any artificer or author. By other arguments he most clearly demonstrates that the human being, who derives his name from the earth, along with his soul and the entire world, was created by God and governed by his providence. Therefore, he says, all those were utterly mad who maintained that religion was instituted for the sake of fear and terror.

Thereafter, by many examples and arguments, he most clearly demonstrates (chapter 11) that this God can be only one. Having uncovered the origin of the impious worship of many gods, he confirms this by the public and certainly unquestioned testimony of Plato, Trismegistus, Socrates, Pythagoras, Antisthenes, and Aristotle. Yet these men, he says, like the poets and other pagans, even though they conceded that there is one God, nevertheless believed that he is never stirred to anger because they established nothing concerning the worship of him whom they thought beneficent. From what has been said thus far, he concludes (chapter 12) that the response of those who contended that religion was introduced solely for the sake of usefulness has been completely overthrown.

Yet he establishes by further arguments that God truly becomes angry. In order to make this still clearer to all, he vividly shows (chapter 13) that God made the world not for mute animals, but for human beings.

“But if this is so,” the Academics asked, “why are so many things found which are harmful and destructive to humanity itself?” The Stoics replied that their hidden usefulness could later be recognized, and that a remedy for the poisons of these animals could be found in the animals themselves. Lactantius refutes them, because many things appear to have no use, and it would be better that no harmful or deadly things existed than that one should seek from them a remedy against themselves. Therefore he replies that God gave wisdom to the human being alone among living creatures, so that he might distinguish good from evil, choose the former, and avoid the latter and whatever is harmful to himself.

By the same reasoning he overthrows another argument which he himself proposed in this form: Either God can remove evils and does not wish to do so, in which case he is envious; or he wishes to do so and cannot, in which case he is weak. Therefore he will not be called God. Lactantius grants that God can remove evil, but says that he did not remove it because, as stated, he gave human beings wisdom by which they can recognize evil and attain the highest good, that is, blessed immortality.

Just as God created the world for the sake of humanity, so he created humanity for his own sake: that he might be known by human beings and worshipped with due reverence. From this he aptly infers (chapter 14) that the same human being was created for the sake of religion and, as Cicero says, justice. But if anyone asks whence sins came to humanity, Lactantius replies (chapter 15) that he has already answered this question when he said that God set before humanity good and evil, and permitted the latter, which he hates, in order that the former, which he loves, might thereby shine forth. Since, however, humanity, no less than the world, is composed of contrary and conflicting elements—namely, a substantial and eternal soul and a fragile, mortal body—hence arose both the corruption of its nature and the vices which had to be forbidden by God’s laws. God is therefore moved by favor toward good people who obey those laws, and by anger toward transgressors.

Nor could Epicurus object that God ought likewise to have feelings of fear, lust, and desire. For these and similar motions arise from human fragility and cannot belong to God, who is immortal and needs nothing (chapter 16). Anger against wicked human beings, by contrast, love toward the good, and compassion toward the afflicted are feelings entirely worthy of God, and have their proper ground in him. Otherwise every kind of crime would inundate the world with impunity.

Epicurus insisted that God is blessed, therefore tranquil and caring for nothing. But, Lactantius argues (chapter 17), he certainly feels and always lives. Therefore he acts. And what is God’s action, if not the administration of the world? But if he has care for the world and for humanity, he surely wishes human beings to observe his law and is angry with its transgressors.

Nor, indeed, should Epicurus still press the claim that one who harms another is not good. For those who exact due punishments from the guilty and unjust do not harm them.

Then, from the various definitions of anger advanced by the Stoics and others, Lactantius plainly shows that they did not understand the difference between just and unjust anger. Having supplied the true definition of just anger, he infers (chapter 18) that it can be removed neither from human beings nor from God himself. “What then?” they asked. “Cannot sins be corrected without the feeling of anger?” Lactantius replies: rightly so, if the crime is concealed or is guarded against by human law. But when it is known and manifest, it is necessary for its judge to be indignant. Otherwise, he would approve the offense and open a safe road to greater crimes.

Nor does he permit the example of Archytas to be brought against him: because Archytas was angry with his offending steward, he was unwilling to punish him. For this is a single example which, as he seeks to establish by Plato’s testimony and various arguments, no one ought to imitate. But the same, he says, must be said of God—though he says nothing of God’s form—as of the human being whom God made like himself.

But because human beings consist of soul and body, by which they are borne either toward virtues or, contrary to the law established by God, toward vices, God, the father and ruler of all, delights in human virtues and is moved by vices; he loves the good and hates the unjust (chapter 19).

“But,” they asked, “what need has one who has established a reward for the good and a punishment for the wicked of hatred?” Because, Lactantius says, if anyone lives justly and rightly but neither worships nor cares for God, then God himself does not allow that person to go unpunished, and anger is stirred against him because of his pride. Therefore, just as he can forgive, so he can also become angry.

To the question why those who sin are often happy and those who live piously are often miserable, our author replies (chapter 20) that children placed under their father’s discipline live more strictly and frugally than other persons who are runaways and disowned. Then, he says, those who sin will not escape God’s judgment, and will someday pay the deserved and everlasting penalties for their crimes.

They pressed further: Why, if God is angry with sinners, does he not punish them immediately? Lactantius replies that, given human frailty such that no one does not sin, very few would remain alive.
