Moreover, many wicked and immoral persons become righteous and self-controlled, and many worshippers of idols have recognized the true God. Therefore God’s patience is most useful: though he punishes the guilty late, he nevertheless does not permit those who stubbornly refuse correction to advance too far.

But others pressed even more sharply, saying that God is so far from being angry that he actually forbids human beings to be angry at all. Lactantius easily resolves this (chapter 21). God forbids human beings to be angry because their anger is very often unjust; but God himself is never moved by anger except justly. Moreover, God did not forbid human beings to be touched by any movement of anger whatsoever, but forbade them to remain in it. Therefore he commanded it to be restrained, and commanded a person to be reconciled with his brother before sunset. Though God himself is eternal, he nevertheless holds the movement of his anger so within his power that he is eternally angry only with those who always sin.

Our author again proves (chapters 22 and 23) that God is truly moved by this anger—not, indeed, by the testimonies of our sacred prophets, which pagans rejected, but by those of others, and especially the Sibyls and Apollo of Miletus, whom pagans could not contradict at all. He adds that rule cannot stand without fear, nor fear without anger. But God has rule; therefore he has anger as well, and for this reason demons and all other things tremble at his nod.

Finally, Lactantius concludes this book with an epilogue, in which he concludes that God must be loved because he is the best Father; feared because he is a severe Lord; and honored because he is a most beneficent God. He concludes, therefore, that one must obey him, bid farewell to fleeting and fragile goods, pleasures, and vices, and devote oneself to works of justice, innocence, beneficence, and the other virtues, so that, united to God himself in a most blessed bond, we may always have him favorable and no longer fear him as angry.

## CHAPTER II. On the author, title, subject, date, and manner of composition of this book; and how he imitated Cicero

That this book proceeded from our Lactantius is so certain and established that there never has been, nor can be, any debate or controversy on the matter. For in his own words he reveals himself as the author of this book which he had promised to write. In the second book of the *Divine Institutes*, when he came to speak about the anger of God, he says: “Let this subject of discussing God’s anger be set aside for the present, since it is a fuller matter and must be pursued more extensively in a work of its own.”

He himself expressly indicates that he kept his promise. For in this book he refers us repeatedly to the second, fourth, and sixth books of his *Divine Institutes*, openly acknowledging that he was the true father of all these books. Thus, to assemble more testimonies of other writers concerning a matter so clear and so plainly acknowledged by our author himself would be as easy as it would be superfluous.

Yet we cannot wholly omit Jerome, both on account of his antiquity and because of the judgment he gives concerning this book. In writing to Magnus, an orator of the city of Rome, he first wrote thus of this book: “Lactantius composed two volumes, *On the Anger of God* and *On the Workmanship of God*. If you wish to read them, you will find in them an epitome [ἐπιτομή] of Cicero’s dialogues.” In his catalogue of ecclesiastical writers, when he comes to Lactantius himself, he says: “We have his book, a most beautiful one, *On the Anger of God*.” Finally, in another work: “Our Firmianus composed a book *On the Anger of God* in a style at once learned and eloquent; whoever has read it, I think, can gain from it more than sufficient understanding of anger.”

Whether this judgment of Jerome concerning the book is fair and approved by all, we shall examine below. For the present, from the words cited from Jerome and from our Lactantius, we infer that Lactantius is its true and genuine author.

No less clearly do we see that he entitled it *On the Anger of God*. For although Jerome and Lactantius himself had been wholly silent about this title, the entire book itself, in all its extent, proclaims and establishes it. Lactantius had no other aim or end in writing it than to make publicly known to all that God truly becomes angry. Indeed, almost nothing other than God’s anger is treated throughout this book, and everything is referred to that subject. This will become quite clear and manifest to everyone from the analysis we have provided, or even from the most cursory reading of the book itself.

Finally, from the same passages of Lactantius which we cited, it is demonstrated with equal clarity that he composed and published this book after the seven books of the *Divine Institutes*. It may reasonably be said that no long interval of time elapsed between them. For when he wrote the second book of the *Divine Institutes*, he promised, as we observed shortly before, that he would write this book. But that he fulfilled his promise quickly may be inferred from the fact that he was fully persuaded that this question concerning God’s anger was of the greater importance because religion was wholly overthrown by very many writers—as we have said—and by not a few, nor obscure, pagan philosophers who denied it. And, burning as he was with zeal to defend truth, as we have seen, he could not delay long in freeing others from error and instructing them in true doctrine.

Moreover, Lactantius, as Jerome says, “in extreme old age was tutor in Gaul to Caesar Crispus, son of Constantine.” Crispus waged war in Gaul about the year 320 and died in 326, when he had barely reached his thirtieth year. But Lactantius, as we have said, was engaged in writing the books of the *Divine Institutes* about the year 321, already advanced in age. Therefore not long afterwards he composed, as he had promised, this book *On the Anger of God* and issued it publicly.

No one who has read this and his earlier books, even cursorily, will deny that he wrote it in the same style and by the same method of composition. Everywhere there shines forth in it the same mode of argument as in the others, the same elegance of language, the same cultivation, ornament, and brilliance of expression. Why, then, would it be anything other than superfluous to prove this at greater length, as if bringing light to the noonday sun?

It will not, however, be entirely unworthy of notice that Lactantius indicates in the peroration of this book that he had proposed to imitate Cicero. Hear, please, his words: “It remains for us to employ an epilogue in the manner of Cicero, to bring our discourse to a close: just as he did when discussing death in the *Tusculans*, so we ought in this work to adduce divine testimonies that may be believed.” There he indicates the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, whose epilogue he not unjustly professes to imitate.

“But,” someone may ask, “was it not for this reason that Jerome wrote to Magnus that an epitome [ἐπιτομή] of Cicero’s dialogues is found in this book?” Not at all, in our opinion. For Lactantius indicates that he imitates the Latin orator only in the epilogue, and he did not make an abridgment of what Cicero said; indeed, he uses testimonies wholly and entirely different from those employed by Cicero. Therefore the word ἐπιτομή is used by Jerome in the sense in which we explained it above, unless we are mistaken.

## CHAPTER III. What reasons induced Lactantius to compose this book; who was the Donatus to whom he dedicates it; the division of the book into chapters and their arguments; the manuscript and printed witnesses; and various observations upon it

The chief reason which seems to have prompted Lactantius to write this book was that he judged the whole sum and hinge of religion and piety to depend upon the assertion of God’s anger, which he had discovered was denied by many. For when this was removed, he thought, as we said shortly before, that true religion itself was utterly removed, destroyed, and extinguished. Therefore, seeing that this anger of God was denied by many persons of no low reputation, and by very celebrated philosophers, he decided that all of them ought to be refuted in a public book.

For he knew that the Stoics, whose authority was exceedingly great, had openly asserted that God is moved by favor indeed, but by no means by anger. Nor was he less aware that Seneca had published books in defense of this opinion, which he himself calls “favourable,” and which, because of Seneca’s reputation for learning and fairness, Lactantius thought might lead many into error. Finally, he knew with absolute certainty that the opinion of the Epicureans was the worst of all: they proclaimed that God is stirred neither by anger nor touched by favor. Therefore, lest anyone be further deceived by the extreme impiety of the Epicureans or the false piety of the Stoics, he published this book in order to refute both groups and establish what he regarded as the true view of God’s anger.

Nor does he conceal this. At the beginning of the book he addresses Donatus and, under his name, all others with these words: “Their error, which is the greatest and tends toward the overthrow of human life, must be refuted by us, lest you too be deceived, swayed by the authority of men who think themselves wise.” Again, in the epilogue of the book: “This is what I had to say concerning God’s anger, dearest Donatus, so that you may know how to refute those who make God immovable.” There he principally designates the Epicureans, who, with the founder of their school, as Lactantius himself says, taught that God is incorruptible and blessed because he is always at rest and therefore never becomes angry.

As you have just heard, he addresses Donatus at the beginning and end of this book, which he sent and dedicated to him. But who this Donatus was is certainly very difficult to say. Some conjecture either that he was the father and founder of the Donatist sect, or Aelius Donatus, Jerome’s teacher. But these notions are invented gratuitously, without any given reason or even a conjecture resembling truth.

Some writers of our age, certainly not insignificant, have thought that this Donatus was the same person to whom Lactantius had earlier directed another book, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, under the title *To Donatus the Confessor*. It would certainly be desirable if those learned men had supplied some sufficiently strong reason for their opinion. For they rely on nothing but similarity of name, by which they thought it could be established, as they greatly desired, that Lactantius was the author of that book. But here we wholly miss their customary acuteness.

For there is a very great difference between the two Donatuses. The one to whom *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* is dedicated was, as we have shown elsewhere, older than the other and a very celebrated martyr. We read that the author of that same book wrote of him: “Nine times subjected to torments and diverse tortures, nine times you conquered the adversary by your glorious confession.” The other Donatus, to whom *On the Anger of God* is dedicated, was still a novice and not yet sufficiently trained in Christian doctrine. As we saw from Lactantius’s words cited shortly above, Lactantius feared that he might be imbued with and deceived by the false philosophical opinions concerning God’s anger.

As famous as the former Donatus was through the most noble triumph of martyrdom, so entirely unknown is the latter to all. For we know nothing else about him except what we learn from Lactantius’s statements: namely, that he was most closely joined to Lactantius by friendship and was his pupil. Since no more certain information about him is available to us, we judged it preferable to remain with those things alone which are certain rather than, by seeking further, indulge in vain conjectures.

Certainly, it is established that this book *On the Anger of God*, like the preceding works, was written by Lactantius [Col. 0156C] without any division into chapters. For not only the most ancient manuscript codices prove this most clearly, but the printed editions as well. We know indeed that the Roman edition, and another prepared in the same city by Isaeus, present twenty-four chapters; but others contain only twenty-three. Who, then, would deny that this varying division did not originate with Lactantius? If therefore this book was not divided by him into chapters, still less did the chapter headings—which are likewise different in the printed editions—proceed from him. Since, then, all these things were added in later times and arranged badly, anyone is free to restore them to a better order.  
> **Note:** Since the most learned le Nourry has published numerous and very lengthy dissertations on every individual work of Lactantius—dissertations which alone could easily fill one of our volumes—the kindly reader will understand more than sufficiently how necessity compelled us, here and elsewhere, to commit to print only excerpts from these dissertations. EDD. [Col. 0156D]

## [BOOK ON THE DEATHS OF THE PERSECUTORS.]

## PRELIMINARIES TO THE BOOK *ON THE DEATHS OF THE PERSECUTORS.*

[Col. 0157]

## LENGLET’S NOTICE

[Col. 0157A] This golden little book is composed and executed with such sincerity that one sees in it not only the distinct events of the persecution—its disastrous beginning, its dark course, and its happy outcome—but also, everywhere, the avenging hand of the Almighty standing forth against the tyrants, and the manner in which God everywhere shows himself the defender of piety and the repeller of wrongs inflicted upon his worshippers by evil rulers.

Conversely, it shines forth with what care and zeal the Supreme Divinity cherished those rulers who were well disposed toward the faithful, such as Constantine always was; or those who were at least so moderate as to grant Christians freedom to practise their religion without molestation, such as Licinius then appeared to be.

[Col. 0157B] It is my view that this book is the genuine offspring of Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius. All the more learned scholars have held this opinion, and we ought not depart from their judgment. The most distinguished Stephen Baluze discovered it in a manuscript codex of the Colbertine library, formerly belonging to the ancient monastery of Moissac in the diocese of Cahors. For many centuries that treasure had lain unknown, hidden away in the recesses of this monastery’s library. Hardly had it come to light when learned men of every nation eagerly received it for careful reading; the English and the Swedes also saw to its republication, and it was translated into French and English. Very learned men, whether French or Dutch, illustrated it with scholarly notes.

In 1710 Dom Nicolas le Nourry, a Benedictine monk of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, again published it; [Col. 0157C] but he not merely doubted, he even asserted that this book was not by our Lactantius but by some unknown writer called [Col. 0158A] Lucius—or rather Lycius—Caecilius. Yet Nourry brought only a few, that is, three or four, to his opinion. Indeed, certain more learned men refuted his error more sharply than was fitting and attacked him so vigorously that no room remained for an open and plausible response. Nor, certainly, was the refutation difficult: Lactantius’ style, his genius, and distinctively Lactantian turns of expression are found everywhere scattered through this little work. Only one manuscript codex survives: it is complete and ancient, but is so disfigured through the incompetence of the copyist and by certain gaps that conjectures, or even divinations, must very often be employed in explaining it.

But since we think it worth while to refute the arguments of Nicolas le Nourry, although [Col. 0158B] they are of slight weight, we have caused to be printed here the learned dissertation of the most distinguished Nicolas de Lestocq, doctor and fellow of the Sorbonne, dean of the Church of Amiens, and abbot of Saint-Acheul, with whom I have maintained an old association and close friendship for more than fifty years.

Yet let no learned reader think that this edition lacks anything because I have omitted the preface by Dom Thierry Ruinart, Benedictine monk of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, to the *True and Sincere Acts of the Martyrs*, published by him in 1689 and repeatedly reprinted at Amsterdam, Venice, and Paris, and translated into French. That preface is indeed excellent; but although Paul Baudri printed it at the end of his edition of Lactantius, I nevertheless did not think it useful to print it yet a seventh time, since once rather scarce, it is now commonly in [Col. 0158C] everyone’s hands and contributes little or nothing to an understanding of our author.

[Col. 0157]

## INQUIRY CONCERNING THE AUTHOR OF THE BOOK ENTITLED: “THE BOOK OF LUCIUS CAECILIUS ON THE DEATHS OF THE PERSECUTORS,” WHICH IS USUALLY ATTRIBUTED TO FIRMIANUS LACTANTIUS

By Nicolas de Lestocq, Doctor and Fellow of the Sorbonne, Dean of the Cathedral Church of Amiens, Vicar-General of the Bishop of Amiens, and Abbot of Saint-Acheul.

[Col. 0157C] A book bearing this title was discovered by the most learned Stephen Baluze in a manuscript codex of the Colbertine Library, now the Royal Library: “The book of Lucius Caecilius on the Deaths of the Persecutors.” He ascribed it to Firmianus and arranged for it to be printed at Paris in 1679, by order of Jean-Baptiste Colbert, in the second volume [Col. 0159A] of his *Miscellanies*, with this heading prefixed: “The book of Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius on the Deaths of the Persecutors.”

Later, other editions of this book appeared in various parts of Europe; with general agreement, the names Firmianus Lactantius were prefixed in their titles to the words Lucius Caecilius or Caelius.

But Dom Nicolas le Nourry, a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict, certainly a most learned man, through whose study and labor a new edition of the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* was produced at Paris in 1710, retained only the names Lucius Caecilius in the title and did not add the words Firmianus Lactantius. He did this both because the manuscript codex lacks the names Firmianus Lactantius, and because he judged the arguments by which this book is attributed to Lactantius to be weak; moreover, he believed that other arguments were available, and not insignificant ones, by which it should be denied to him.

[Col. 0159B] On this point Stephen Baluze and Dom Nicolas le Nourry agree: the manuscript codex—the sole surviving one, from which this book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* was printed—is, besides having several breaks and lacunae, infected with many errors. Dom le Nourry further showed that there are many passages in this codex which have been wholly corrupted not merely by the copyist’s usual inattention, negligence, or excessive haste in writing, but also, as he says on p. 119, by profound ignorance of the Latin language.

Therefore, whatever in the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* is written feebly, crudely, obscurely, or incorrectly, and appears foreign to the clarity and elegance of expression, or even to Lactantius’ opinions, must be attributed to the scribe and not to the author; nor should the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* be taken away from Lactantius on account of faults of this sort. Nevertheless, the learned religious man from the Benedictine fraternity seizes on this as an opportunity to prove that this book is not Lactantius’.

[Col. 0159C] With this one preliminary observation, however, it will be manifest even to a casual reader that several arguments by which Dom le Nourry tries to overthrow the opinion attributing the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* to Lactantius collapse and are dissolved.

Already in 1715 M. de la Crose had attacked Dom Nicolas le Nourry more harshly than was proper in his *Critical Observations*, [Col. 0159D] which he caused to be published in the first part of volume VII of the *Journal Littéraire* (*Journal Littéraire* for 1715, The Hague), where he learnedly overturns the principal arguments of Nicolas le Nourry; but our inquiry will be much more peaceable.

With these preliminary remarks, which support the common opinion concerning the author of this book, I shall at the same time examine among the arguments which Dom le Nourry thinks oppose it those which seemed to me to require a particular reply.

1. The title of the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* bears the names LUCIUS, or LYCIUS, CAECILIUS, which appear [Col. 0160A] to be two of the forenames of Firmianus Lactantius. For although Lactantius is commonly called Caelius and the names Firmianus Lactantius are absent from the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, in several manuscripts of Lactantius’ undisputed works he is named Lucius Caecilius; and in certain other manuscripts the names Lucius Caelius are lacking, as Dom le Nourry admits. We shall deal with this at the end of the present inquiry. Further, no ecclesiastical writer other than Lactantius is listed as Lucius Caecilius; absolutely unknown is any other person of this name to whom the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* could be ascribed.

2. Saint Jerome, in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, mentions one book of Lactantius *On Persecution*. This book *On Persecution* does not appear [Col. 0160B] to be different from the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*. For this book is one book, as is the book *On Persecution*; and it does not deal only with the deaths of the persecutors but also with the harsh persecution stirred up against Christians by various emperors. Thus it could bear either title. The difference between these two titles is indeed very slight: one who speaks of persecution must also treat of persecutors, for these are certainly connected with each other. Lactantius himself did not distinguish them in this way in chapter LIII of the *Epitome*, where he speaks together of persecution—that is, of punishments inflicted upon Christians—and of the deaths of the persecutors.

3. The book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* is dedicated to Donatus; Lactantius also dedicated the book *On the Anger [Col. 0160C] of God* to Donatus. The author of both books calls Donatus “dearest.” Therefore it appears to be one and the same Donatus to whom each work is dedicated. Yet Dom le Nourry maintains that the Donatus to whom Lactantius addresses the book *On the Anger of God* differs from the Donatus to whom the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* is dedicated. He proves this as follows.

Donatus, to whom Lactantius dedicated the book *On the Anger of God*, is expressly called by him a novice entangled in worldly affairs and not sufficiently imbued with Christian doctrine. But when Lactantius wrote the book *On the Anger of God*, he could not have called Donatus a novice entangled in worldly affairs and insufficiently imbued with Christian doctrine if he were the same Donatus to whom the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* is dedicated. For the book *On the Anger of God* was written many years after the end of the persecution, [Col. 0160D] during which Donatus had been kept in chains and prison for Christ’s name for six years, had fought against tyrants nine times, and had stood unconquered, as is stated in the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*. Who could believe that such an outstanding confessor could afterward be called a novice, entangled in worldly affairs, and insufficiently imbued with the Christian religion?

But this argument is not so well established as would support the conclusion and opinion which Dom le Nourry seeks to establish. For nowhere in the book *On the Anger of God* is Donatus expressly called by Lactantius a novice entangled in worldly affairs and insufficiently imbued with the Christian religion. Not only is this nowhere expressly said of Donatus [Col. 0161A] by Lactantius; nothing at all occurs in him from which anyone might suspect that he held such an opinion about Donatus.

Lactantius addresses Donatus directly in only two passages in the book *On the Anger of God*: namely, in chapter I, where he writes:

> “I have often observed, Donatus, that very many think that God is not angry . . . . . . . . Since their error is very great and tends to overthrow the condition of human life, it must be refuted by us, lest you yourself be deceived through the authority of men who think themselves wise.”

The other passage is read in chapter 22, where Lactantius says:

> “These are the things which I had to say concerning the anger of God, dearest Donatus, so that you might know how to refute those who make God immovable . . . . . All the prophets, filled with the divine Spirit, speak of nothing other than the favor of God toward the righteous and the anger of God against the impious. Their testimonies are sufficient for us; but because those men who parade their wisdom in their hair and dress do not believe them, they had also to be refuted by us through reason and arguments.”

From these passages it is clear that Lactantius’ purpose was to instruct Donatus concerning God’s providence so that he might refute, by the force of rational arguments, the philosophers themselves who denied it. But so far is he from calling him a novice entangled in worldly affairs and insufficiently imbued with Christian religion that Lactantius’ words imply that Donatus was not ignorant of what all the prophets said concerning God’s favor toward the righteous and his anger against the impious; thus their testimonies were known to Donatus and were sufficient for him, just as [Col. 0161C] they were sufficient for Lactantius himself: “their testimonies,” he says, “are sufficient for us.”

I think, indeed, that there have been many outstanding martyrs sufficiently imbued with the Christian religion, and that there are still some Christians conspicuous for piety who nevertheless could not disentangle themselves by reason and arguments from the philosophers’ arguments against God’s providence, as Lactantius attempted to do in the book *On the Anger of God*. Such, indeed, are these arguments that Lactantius says in chapter 13 that most philosophers who defend providence are usually troubled by them and are almost forced against their will to confess that God cares for nothing.

Dom le Nourry seems through a lapse of memory to attribute to Donatus what Lactantius says to Demetrianus in the book *On the Workmanship of God*. Lactantius had, namely, dedicated that book *On the Workmanship of God* to Demetrianus and addresses him as a kind of novice:

> “As your teacher,” he says in chapter 1, “even now, though in a more honorable matter and in the teaching of something better . . . I advise you again, and shall advise you again, not to believe that these delights of earth are great or true goods.”

And in the final chapter:

> “If God grants it,” he says, “I shall exhort you more fully and more truly to the teaching of true philosophy.”

These words are certainly those of Lactantius the teacher addressing a novice not sufficiently imbued with the Christian religion; but they concern Demetrianus, not Donatus.

4. Lactantius is proved to be the author of the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* because he too was living in Nicomedia in Bithynia, as was the author of the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, at the time when persecution was raging against Christians and the temple of God was destroyed. Lactantius himself testifies to this in book V, chapter 2, of the *Institutions*, where he says:

> “When I had been summoned to teach rhetoric in Bithynia, it happened that at the same time the temple of God was destroyed.”

Lactantius does not name the city in which he taught; but Jerome did not omit it. For he says in the passage cited above [Col. 0162B] that Lactantius taught rhetoric at Nicomedia. The author of the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* does not actually say that he too remained at Nicomedia while the persecution raged and while the temple of God was leveled to the ground; but he narrates the whole event in section 12 in such a way that it is understood to have taken place before his eyes:

> “Suddenly, while daylight was still uncertain, [the prefect] came to the church . . . The doors having been broken down, the image of God is sought; the Scriptures that are found are burned; plunder is given to all. There is seizure, panic, running to and fro. The emperors themselves, however, from their lookout—for the church, situated on high ground, could be seen from the palace—debated long among themselves whether fire ought rather to be applied. Diocletian’s opinion prevailed, since he feared that, if a great fire were started, some part of the city might burn. Accordingly the Praetorians came in battle array, with axes and other tools; breaking in from every side, they leveled that very lofty building to the ground in a few hours.”

And in section 13:

> “On the next day an edict was posted, providing that persons of that religion should be deprived of every honor and dignity, should be subject to tortures . . . One man, though not rightly, yet with great courage, tore down and shredded this edict . . . He was immediately brought forth and not only tortured but also duly roasted, and finally burned, with admirable endurance.”

Further, the contents of section 17 concerning the illness which afflicted Diocletian at Nicomedia, and of section 35 concerning Galerius’ edict posted at Nicomedia and the day on which Galerius’ death became known at Nicomedia, sufficiently prove that the author of this book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* lived for some time at Nicomedia.

5. The style of the author of the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* is the same as Lactantius’ style. That this may be clearer, I have here transcribed both matters, thoughts, and expressions—especially those distinctive and proper to Lactantius—which are found similarly in the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* and in Lactantius’ other undisputed works, and have placed them side by side.

> **Note [Col. 0161]:** In Migne, the sections of text “Haec leguntur . . . Geminis Consulibus” and “Haec leguntur . . . esse cruciatum” are printed in parallel.

[Col. 0161D] The following is read in section 2 of the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*:

> “In the final period of Tiberius Caesar, as we read in Scripture, our Lord Jesus Christ was tortured by the Jews on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, when the two Gemini were consuls.”

[Col. 0162D] The following is read in book IV of the *Institutions*, chapter 10:

> “Under the reign of Tiberius Caesar, in his fifteenth year—that is, when the two Gemini were consuls—on the seventh day before the Kalends of April” [thus many editions], “the Jews crucified Christ.”

And in chapter 22 of the same book:

> “He will cease to wonder that God was tortured by men.”

[Col. 0161D] The text of the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* agrees with the two texts set beside it insofar as it states [Col. 0162D] that Christ was tortured by the Jews under Tiberius Caesar, when the two Gemini were consuls.

[Col. 0163A] But there are two points in which the text of the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* appears to conflict with the text of book IV, chapter 10, of the *Institutions*.

The first is that, according to the text of the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, Christ was tortured in the final period of Tiberius Caesar; whereas, according to the text of book IV of the *Institutions*, in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar. But since Tiberius ruled for twenty-two years, if Christ was tortured in Tiberius’ fifteenth year, he was not tortured in the final period of Tiberius.

The response is that the author of the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* spoke thus because Tiberius’ fifteenth year tended more toward the end of his reign than toward its beginning; nor is this a matter of an exact reckoning of years.

[Col. 0164A] The other point in which these two texts seem to conflict is that the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* reads that Christ was tortured “after the tenth day before the Kalends,” while the *Institutions* reads “on the seventh day before the Kalends.”

The response is that the notes to the text of Lactantius’ *Institutions* in the edition of 1660 observe that certain manuscripts read “on the tenth day before the Kalends”; and those notes adduce these words of the jurist Paulus: “On the tenth day before the Kalends and after the tenth day before the Kalends: by either expression the eleventh day is indicated.” If this is so, all conflict between these texts disappears. Still, it cannot be denied that some error concerning the number of days has entered those texts; [Col. 0164B] but it must be attributed to the copyists.

> **Note [Col. 0163]:** In Migne, the sections of text “Haec leguntur . . . fundamenta miserunt” and “Haec leguntur . . . ubique posuerunt” are printed in parallel.

[Col. 0163B] The following is read in the same section 2 of the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*:

> “When he had risen on the third day, he gathered together the disciples whom fear of his arrest had driven into flight; and, having remained with them for forty days, he opened their hearts and interpreted the Scriptures, which until that time had been obscure and veiled. He appointed and instructed them for the preaching of his dogma and teaching, establishing the solemn discipline of the New Testament. When this office had been completed, a storm-cloud enveloped him and, withdrawing him from human sight, carried him away into heaven. And from there the disciples . . . were scattered over all the earth . . . and laid the foundations of churches through all provinces and cities.”

[Col. 0164B] The following is read in book IV of the *Institutions*, chapter 19:

> “On the third day . . . he came forth alive from the tomb and went into Galilee to seek his disciples.”

And in chapter 20 of the same book:

> “When the disciples had been gathered again, he opened the sacred writings of Scripture, that is, the hidden meanings of the prophets, which could in no way be understood before he suffered . . . The writings composed after his resurrection are called the New Testament.”

And in chapter 21 of the same book:

> “Having arranged for his disciples the preaching of the Gospel and of his name, a cloud suddenly surrounded him and bore him up to heaven on the fortieth day after his passion . . . But the disciples, scattered through the provinces, set the foundations of the Church everywhere.”

[Col. 0163C] That text of the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* is similar to the parallel texts of Lactantius, both in subject matter and in wording. Yet Dom le Nourry concludes from the words of the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, “they laid the foundations of churches,” that this book was not written by Lactantius. “For what author of good Latin,” he asks, “ever said *mittere fundamenta*, ‘to cast foundations’? Lactantius certainly did not; he wrote better, *fundamenta Ecclesiae ubique jecerunt*, ‘they threw the foundations of the Church everywhere.’”

To refute this argument, it should first be observed that the text of chapter 20 of book IV of Lactantius’ *Institutions* does not read *fundamenta Ecclesiae ubique jecerunt*, “they threw the foundations of the Church everywhere,” but *posuerunt*, “they set them.” Secondly, Cicero uses *jacere* and *mittere* in the same sense in the book entitled *The Orator*, where he says that an orator employs wit in “throwing and casting a joke” (*in jaciendo mittendoque ridiculo*). Further, Horace uses *mittere*, “to cast,” for *jacere* and *ponere*, “to throw” and “to place,” in *Satires* II.3:

> “To cast myself, head covered, into the river.”

And in Satire I of the same book:

> “He would cast the dice at Pyrgus.”

And in the *Art of Poetry*:

> “Verses launched upon the stage with great weight.”

Indeed Lactantius himself uses *mittere*, “to cast,” interchangeably with *jacere*, “to throw,” in book I, chapter 21, of the *Institutions*, where he says:

> “Saturn was worshipped in Latium by the same kind of sacrifice—not indeed so that a human being was sacrificed at the altar, but so that he was cast into the Tiber from the Milvian Bridge . . . But this sort of sacrifice is said to have been abolished, though the rite remained, so that images were thrown in place of actual men.”

Lactantius confirms this from Ovid, citing the following verses, in which *mittere* and *jacere* are used indiscriminately in the same sense:

> “That the Quirites cast straw figures into the water;  
> By Hercules’ example, cast false bodies.
>
> Then too, the maiden customarily casts  
> Reed effigies of ancient men from the oaken bridge.”

> **Note [Col. 0163]:** In Migne, the sections of text “Haec leguntur . . . et mugit” and “Haec leguntur . . . malas de terra” are printed in parallel.

[Col. 0163D] The following is read in the same section 2 of the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*:

> “The disciples . . . were scattered throughout all the earth to preach the Gospel, as that MASTER, THE LORD, had commanded; and . . . through all provinces and cities they laid the foundations of churches. And when Nero was already emperor, Peter came to Rome and, having performed certain miracles—which he wrought by the power of God himself, through authority given him by God—converted many to RIGHTEOUSNESS and established for God a FAITHFUL and stable temple. When this was reported to Nero . . . he sprang up to destroy the heavenly temple and to obliterate RIGHTEOUSNESS. And he was the first of all to persecute the servants of God: he fastened Peter to a cross and killed Paul. Yet he did not go unpunished . . . Cast down from the height of imperial power and hurled down from his summit, the uncontrolled tyrant suddenly appeared nowhere, so that not even a place of burial for so evil a BEAST appeared on earth.”

And in section 3:

> “After him came another tyrant, no less great . . . He reigned for a very long time, secure, until he stretched out impious hands against the Lord. But after he was stirred up by the instigation of demons to persecute the RIGHTEOUS PEOPLE, he was then delivered into the hands of enemies and paid the penalty.”

And in section 4:

> “Who but an evil man persecutes RIGHTEOUSNESS?”

And in section 9:

> “Maximian . . . worse than all the evils that had been. This BEAST possessed a natural barbarity.”

And in section 21:

> “The bodies already burned, their bones gathered and crushed to powder, were thrown into river and sea.”

And in section 32:

> “The BEAST grieves and bellows.”

[Col. 0164D] These passages, I think, prove more than sufficiently that the words *fundamenta miserunt*, “they laid foundations,” are not only good Latin but also accord with Lactantius’ style.

The following is read in book IV of the *Institutions*, chapter 21:

> “But the disciples, scattered throughout the provinces, set the foundations of the Church everywhere, themselves also performing great and almost incredible miracles in the name of the MASTER, GOD, because at his departure he had equipped them with power and authority . . . Peter and Paul preached at Rome . . . when Nero had killed them, etc.”

From chapter 14 of the same book:

> “It is clear that all the prophets foretold concerning Christ that someday he would . . . establish for God an eternal temple, which is called the Church . . . This is the FAITHFUL house, this the IMMORTAL TEMPLE.”

From book V, chapter 1, of the *Institutions*:

> “They torture the worshippers of the highest God—that is, righteous men.”

[Col. 0166A] And in chapter 2 of the same book:

> “At that very time the righteous people were wickedly torn to pieces.”

And in chapter 7 of the same book:

> “Righteousness is nothing other than the pious and religious worship of the one God.”

And in chapter 11 of book V of the *Institutions*:

> “They violently exercise their impiety against the RIGHTEOUS, and not without reason are called BEASTS by the prophets . . . For what Caucasus, what India, what Hyrcania ever bred BEASTS so savage, so bloodthirsty? . . . That is the true BEAST, at whose single command
>
> Dark blood is shed everywhere; everywhere cruel mourning,  
> Everywhere terror, and countless forms of death.
>
> No one can adequately describe the savagery of this great monster, which, lying in one place, nevertheless rages throughout the whole world with iron teeth. It not only tears apart men’s limbs, but crushes their very bones and raves even against their ashes, so that no place for burial may remain.”

And in chapter 23 of book V of the *Institutions*:

> “Let the most unjust persecutors . . . not think that they will go unpunished . . . For they will be punished by God’s judgment . . . Therefore he promises that he will swiftly avenge himself upon them and exterminate the evil BEASTS [Col. 0166B] from the earth.”

[Col. 0165B] The meanings and expressions in these texts agree. The persecutors of the Church are called beasts in both; the bones of martyrs are said to be crushed into ashes. Further, attention should be given to these similar expressions in each: [Col. 0166B] *Master Lord*, *Master God*; *faithful and stable temple*, *eternal temple*, *faithful house*; “to establish for God,” “to constitute for God”; *righteous people*, *the righteous*, for worshippers of the true God; *righteousness*, for the worship of the one God.

> **Note [Col. 0165]:** In Migne, the sections of text “Haec eodem . . . opera mitesceret” and “Haec lib. VII . . . Deo serviant” are printed in parallel.

[Col. 0165B] The following is read in the same section 3 of the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*:

> “The Church . . . in the following times, when good rulers held the helm and government of the Roman Empire . . . stretched out its hands to East and West, so that there was now no corner of the earth so remote that God’s religion had not entered it, and indeed no nation living in manners so savage that it was not softened, after adopting the worship of God, to works of righteousness.”

[Col. 0166B] The following is read in book VII of the *Institutions*, chapter 15:

> “Rome . . . after the destruction of Carthage, which for so long had rivalled the Roman Empire, stretched out its hands across the whole world by land and sea . . .”

And in book V of the *Institutions*, chapter 13:

> “But since the divine law has been adopted from the rising of the sun to its setting, and every sex, every age, nation, and region serve God with united and equal minds . . .”

[Col. 0165B] According to these texts, there is no people, no nation, that has not adopted the worship of God; and the greatness of the Church and of the Roman Empire is described in the same words. [Col. 0166B]

> **Note [Col. 0165]:** In Migne, the sections of text “Haec num. 9 . . . verberibus animadverti” and “Haec lib. IV . . . IMMORTALE munierit” are printed in parallel.

[Col. 0165C] The following is read in sections 9 and 10 of the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*:

> “Diocletian . . . But I shall explain what reason he had for persecuting. Being, through fear, an investigator of future events, he sacrificed animals and sought what was to come in their livers. Then certain servants, knowing the Lord, as they stood by while he sacrificed, made upon their FOREHEADS the IMMORTAL SIGN. When this was done, the demons were put to flight and the sacred rites disturbed. The haruspices were alarmed and did not see the usual marks in the entrails; and, as though the sacrifice had not been accepted, they sacrificed repeatedly. But the repeatedly slaughtered victims revealed nothing, until that master of the haruspices, Tagis, whether from suspicion or from vision, said that the sacred rites did not answer because profane persons were present at the divine ceremonies. Then, in wrathful FURY, he ordered not only those who ministered at the sacrifices but all who were in the palace to sacrifice; and, if they refused, to be punished with beatings.”

[Col. 0166C] The following is read in book IV of the *Institutions*, chapter 27:

> “When they sacrifice to their gods, if someone bearing a marked forehead stands by, the sacred rites are in no way accepted:
>
> Nor can the consulted seer render an answer.
>
> And this was often the principal reason why evil rulers persecuted righteousness. For when some of our servants stood by rulers while they sacrificed, having placed the sign upon their FOREHEADS, they drove away their gods, so that they could not depict future events in the entrails of victims. When the haruspices understood this, prompted by those same demons to whom they sacrifice, and complaining that profane men were present at the sacred rites, they drove their rulers into fury, so that they might storm the temple of God and defile themselves with sacrilege, which was to be expiated by the most grievous punishments of the persecutors. But since they cannot approach those . . . whom the IMMORTAL SIGN has fortified . . .”

[Col. 0165C] In both texts not only is the same cause of persecution assigned, but the matter is also set forth in the same manner and in almost the same words. [Col. 0166C]

> **Note [Col. 0165]:** In Migne, the sections of text “Haec num. 16 . . . inaudita excogitabantur” and “Lib. V . . . excogitata sunt” are printed in parallel.

[Col. 0165D] The following is read in section 16 of the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*:

> “Therefore the whole earth was afflicted, and, except for Gaul, three most bitter beasts raged from East to West.
>
> Though I had a hundred tongues, a hundred mouths,  
> An iron voice, I could not encompass every form of their crimes,  
> Or recount every name of the punishments
>
> which the judges inflicted upon the righteous and innocent throughout the provinces.”

And in section 15 of the same book:

> “Men of every sex and age were dragged away to burning . . . unheard-of kinds of tortures were devised.”

[Col. 0166D] The following is read in book V of the *Institutions*, chapter 11:

> “It is impossible to recount what each man did throughout the whole world. For what number of volumes could contain such infinite and varied kinds of cruelty? Having received authority, each raged according to his own character . . . Thus it cannot be said how numerous and grievous were the kinds of tortures that judges of this sort devised.”

And in book VI, chapter 17:

> “Throughout the world there have been seen, and are still seen, punishments of the worshippers of God, for whose tormenting new and unheard-of tortures have been devised.”

[Col. 0165D] The fury of the persecutors is identical in the texts on both sides and expressed in nearly the same manner.

> **Note [Col. 0165]:** In Migne, the sections of text “Haec num. 38 . . . sceleris magnitudo” and “Et lib. VI . . . sceleris magnitudo” are printed in parallel.

The following is found in section 38 of the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*:

[Col. 0167A]

> “But as for that ruinous, surpassingly corrupting desire—beyond that of all who have existed—what can I say? I do not know, unless that it was blind and unbridled; and yet, in his indignation, he cannot express it in these words. The magnitude of the crime exceeds the capacity of speech.”

[Col. 0166D] And in book VI of the *Institutions*, chapter 23:

> “What shall I say of those who practise not an abominable lust but rather madness? . . . By what words, or with what indignation, can I pursue so great a crime? The magnitude of the crime surpasses the capacity of speech.”

[Col. 0167A] In these two texts wholly similar expressions occur. Yet the text of the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* is corrupt. But if the word *mens* (“mind”), which could have been omitted through the copyist’s fault, is added, it should read [Col. 0168A]:

> “And yet the mind cannot express it in these words, in proportion to its indignation.”

The sense will then be plain and clear. All the more learned editors have emended it thus.

> **Note [Col. 0167]:** In Migne, the sections of text “Haec num. 5 . . . in scutis” and “Haec cap. 1 . . . contineret Caesar” are printed in parallel.

The following is read in section 5 of the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*:

> “Is it not astonishing that anyone should have dared . . . to devise plans against the majesty of the one God who governs and contains all things?”

And in section 12:

> “They leveled the temple to the ground in a few hours.”

[Col. 0167B] And in section 15:

> “Constantius . . . allowed the meeting houses—that is, the walls, which could be rebuilt—to be destroyed.”

Section 16:

> “The originator and counsellor in making the persecution”—this is said of Hierocles.

In the same section: “You triumphed over the age with its terrors.”

In the same section: “The impious command having been disregarded.” *Jussio* (“command”) is a Lactantian word.

In the same section: “Let no snare lead [him] in.”

Section 18 of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*: “He would have incurred the hatred of many.” A Lactantian expression, in place of *acquisivisset* (“had acquired”).

In the same section: “Precisely so.”

*On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, section 21: “Let them consign themselves INTO SLAVERY”; that is, into servitude.

*On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, section 23: “He killed [them] contrary to every law of humanity.”

*On the Death of the Persecutors*, section 24: “The judgment of God has now drawn near to him.”

In the same section: “He handed over the empire to him.”

*On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, section 26: “He sought how.” *Quatenus* is used here in the sense of *quomodo* (“how”).

*On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, section 27: “Inflamed with anger”; likewise above, section 14: “Inflamed with anger.”

*On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, section 28: “Like another Superbus, he was expelled.” He speaks of Tarquin.

*On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, section 30: “He got away with it unpunished.”

And section 33: “God struck him with an incurable plague.”

[Col. 0167D] In the same section: “Outwardly”; an unusual word.

In the same section: “An inestimable swarm surged forth.”

*On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, section 36: “For the present.”

And section 38: “He gave noble-born girls, violated, to his slaves.”

Section 44 of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* reads as follows: “And although Maxentius remained in Rome, because he had received the response that he would perish if he went outside the gates of the city . . . Constantine was warned in a dream to mark the heavenly sign of God upon the shields.”

These words occur in chapter 1 of Book I of the *Institutions*: “You have both recognized and honored the majesty of the one and true God.”

And in Book IV of the *Institutions*, chapter 21: “They declared that it would come to pass that . . . he would level their cities to the ground.”

And in Book V of the *Institutions*, chapter 11: “One man in Phrygia . . . burned the entire people together with the meeting-house itself.”

[Col. 0168B] Book V of the *Divine Institutions*, chapter 11: “Another wrote more bitterly on the same subject, who was then among the number of the judges, and who was above all the instigator OF BRINGING ABOUT THE PERSECUTION.” This too concerns Hierocles.

Book IV of the *Divine Institutions*, chapter 26: “He would triumph over death WITH ITS TERRORS”; and Book VI, chapter 23.

Lactantius, *Institutions*, Book IV, chapter 15, uses the same word *jussio* (“command”); also Book V, chapters 11 and 13.

Lactantius, *Divine Institutions*, Book I, chapter 21: “Let them be led into the same snares.”

Thus Lactantius, *Divine Institutions*, Book I, chapter 20; Book II, chapter 12; Book IV, chapter 1; Book V, chapter 1; Book VII, chapters 11, 14, and 15; and the *Epitome*, chapters 4, 20, and 27: in all these places, *quaerere* (“to seek”) is used for *acquirere* (“to acquire”).

Lactantius, *Divine Institutions*, Book I, chapter 11; Book II, chapter 2: “Precisely so,” in the same manner.

Lactantius, *Epitome*, chapter 52: “He will hand over entire nations INTO SLAVERY,” in the same sense.

Lactantius, Book V of the *Divine Institutions*, chapters 19 and 22: “Contrary to the law of humanity”; [Col. 0168C] Book VI, chapter 10: “Contrary to the law of humanity and every sacred right, they despoil, torture, kill, and exterminate.”

Lactantius, *Divine Institutions*, Book VII, chapter 14: “I shall show that the time of this judgment is drawing near”; and chapter 24: “And now that final day of the ultimate consummation is drawing near.” Lactantius likewise uses *propinquare* (“to draw near”) in the *Epitome*, at the beginning of chapter 71.

Lactantius, *Divine Institutions*, Book II, chapter 4: “He lived to old age and handed over the kingdom to his son.”

Lactantius, *Divine Institutions*, Book II, chapter 21, where *quatenus* is likewise taken in the same sense; as also in Book IV, chapter 27, and Book VII, chapter 6.

Lactantius, *Divine Institutions*, Book VII, chapter 17: “Inflamed with anger.”

Lactantius, *Divine Institutions*, Book IV, chapter 14: “Proud Tarquin was expelled.”

Lactantius, *Epitome*, chapter 53: “He got away with it unpunished”; and chapter 55, “Getting away with it unpunished.”

And Book VII of the *Institutions*, chapter 15: “God struck Egypt with an incurable plague.”

[Col. 0168D] Lactantius, *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 2: “Outwardly,” in the same sense.

Lactantius, *Divine Institutions*, Book I, chapter 16; *On Anger*, chapter 10; *Epitome*, chapter 72: *inaestimabilis* (“inestimable”), in the same sense.

Lactantius, *Divine Institutions*, Book VII, chapters 6, 10, and 15, and *On Anger*, chapter 22: *ad praesens* (“for the present”) is employed in the same sense.

And Book I of the *Institutions*, chapter 10: “I pass over the girls whom he violated.”

Book II of the *Institutions*, section 7, reads as follows: “For Jupiter is said to have appeared in a dream to Tiberius Attinius, a man of the plebeian class.”

And afterwards, speaking of Augustus, he says: “An appearance of Minerva presented itself to his physician Artorius, warning Caesar not to remain in camp because of his bodily weakness.”

Let these similar expressions in the two texts be noted: “He remained in Rome”; “he remained in camp”; “he was warned in a dream”; “appearing in a dream, warning.”

[Col. 0169A] [Note: In Migne, the sections “*On the Deaths of the Persecutors* . . . *they did, received*” and “Lactantius, *Divine* . . . *his reward*” are printed in parallel.]

*On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, section 44: “And his own particular [property]”; expressions wholly characteristic of Lactantius.

*On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, section 47: “They were able”; a word frequent in Lactantius.

And section 49: “He was carried away by unbearable pain even to madness of mind.”

And section 52, which is also the last: “God deigned to restore and gather together again his flock, partly ravaged by rapacious wolves and partly scattered, and to root out the evil beasts.” — And section 50: “Thus all the impious, by the true and just judgment of God, received the same things which they had done.”

[Col. 0170A] Lactantius, *Divine Institutions*, Book III, chapter 10; Book IV, chapter 14; Book V, chapter 11; *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 2, where *suum proprium*, *suo proprio*, and *sua propria* are always used.

Lactantius, *Divine Institutions*, Book II, chapter 5; Book V, chapter 22, where *quiverunt* and *quiverint* (“they were able,” “they will have been able”) are also employed with the same meaning.

And Book VII of the *Institutions*, chapter 16: “This man will afflict the world with unbearable tyranny.”

And Book V of the *Institutions*, chapter 23: “They will be punished by the judgment of God . . . he promises that he will swiftly exact vengeance upon them, and will exterminate the evil beasts from the earth . . . their reward will come, will come, upon the rabid and ravenous wolves.”

[Col. 0169A] These texts agree on both sides. It should be noted that this word, [Col. 0169B] *insustentabili* (“unbearable”), is perhaps found in no other author.

Doubtless Dom le Nourry had not compared with sufficient care these forms of expression, which represent one and the same author; otherwise, I think, he would not have adopted so freely an opinion from which all the most learned men wholly dissent. Moreover, if he had resolved to embrace this view, he ought not to have employed flimsy, trivial, and vain arguments; rather, he should have adduced strong—indeed, most weighty—reasons capable of moving learned men away from their former judgment. Nor should Nourry say that similar expressions were found in the two authors only by chance and accident. That may indeed happen once or twice, but not everywhere, and forty times or more, as occurs in a little book of about sixty pages; especially when the question concerns [Col. 0169C] expressions so distinctive that one can scarcely find them in any writers.

From these passages, therefore, which I have excerpted not only from the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* but also from the undisputed works of Lactantius, it is clear that the style of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* is the same as that of Lactantius.

The book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* displays an eloquent writer, fluent, polished, and clear in expression, who has thoroughly read the authors of liberal learning—qualities which are also Lactantius’s.

Finally, further support for attributing *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* to Lactantius lies in the fact that, just as the author of that work teaches in sections 1 and 50 that all persecutors of the Christian name were defeated by the most high God and destroyed by deserved vengeance, so Lactantius, in Book V of the *Institutions*, chapters [Col. 0169D] 22 and 23, relates that God avenged the afflictions of his people upon evil rulers and utterly unjust persecutors, and that it has always occurred that vengeance followed.

Anyone who has considered these reasons together will not wonder that, as soon as *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* came to light, the judgment of all learned men was that it should be ascribed to Lactantius.

Let us now deal with Nicholas le Nourry’s principal argument. The manuscript codex of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, he says, bears the name of LYCIUS, or LUCIUS CAECILIUS; therefore it is not Lactantius’s. I am surprised that the learned editor here did not remember what he himself nevertheless admitted: that the copyist who wrote this codex, through carelessness and negligence, excessive haste in writing, and even ignorance of Latin, had corrupted many things in this book and [Col. 0170A] thoroughly ruined them. This being so, could not that scribe [Col. 0170B] have omitted the final two names from LUCIUS CAECILIUS LACTANTIUS FIRMIANUS? But nowhere, says Dom le Nourry, can Lactantius be found distinguished by the forenames LYCIUS COELIUS or LUCIUS CAECILIUS. But this, certainly—these are the editor’s words—will be found still less in the title of any book written by him. Who would not believe a man so highly religious as he is learned when he makes such an assertion? I myself would swear by the words of the learned editor that he had collated all the manuscript codices that could be found in our country, and that in none of them had he read the names Lucius Coelius and Lucius Caecilius attached to Lactantius. Yet the case is altogether otherwise.

When Dom le Nourry published *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, he was then living in Paris. Why, then, did he not examine the Library of the Most Christian King? In that royal treasury he himself saw many codices, and calls them such in his *Apparatus to the Library of the Holy Fathers*, volume II. Why did he not inspect them more curiously and carefully? Let us now perform more accurately what Nourry neglected through carelessness.

The first codex, nine hundred years old, number 1662, has these words on folio 25:

“The first book of CAECILIUS FIRMIANUS, *On False Religion*, ends.

“The second book of Lactantius CAECILIUS FIRMIANUS, *On the Origin of Error*, addressed to the Emperor Constantine, begins.”

At the end of the seventh book it is written thus: “The seventh book of CAECILIUS FIRMIANUS’s *Divine Institutions*, *On the Blessed Life*, ends.”

On folio 179 verso one reads: “The seventh book of CAECILIUS FIRMIANUS, *On Divine Anger*, ends.”

On folio 191: “The eighth book of CAECILIUS FIRMIANUS, *On the Workmanship of God*, ends.”

The forename LUCIUS has indeed been omitted in these places.

Thus, in manuscript codex number 1664, at the end of the third book, one reads: “Of L. COELIUS FIRMIANUS,” with the name Lactantius omitted.

At the end of the sixth book there stands: “The sixth book of CAECILIUS FIRMIANUS LACTANTIUS, *On True Worship*, ends.”

Codex 1663 reads: “The book of FIRMIANUS’s *Divine Institutions* begins.” But in the margin of the codex, in uncial letters, one reads: “Of CELIUS FIRMIANUS, *On Religion and Divine Matters*, addressed to the Emperor Constantine.”

At the end of the first book, moreover, it is written: “The first book of L. CAELIUS [Col. 0171A] FIRMIANUS’s *Divine Institutions* happily ends.”

At the end of the fourth book one reads: “The fourth book of CAELIUS FIRMIANUS’s *Divine Institutions* ends.”

At the conclusion of the fifth book it is written: “The fifth book of L. CAELIUS FIRMIANUS’s *Divine Institutions*, *On Justice*, ends.”

Royal manuscript number 1673 reads: “The first book of LUCIUS CAELIUS LACTANTIUS FIRMIANUS’s *Divine Institutions against the Gentiles*, addressed to the Emperor Constantine.”

At the end of the manuscript codex, however, one finds: “The seventh and final book of L. CAELIUS LACTANTIUS FIRMIANUS’s *Divine Institutions against the Gentiles*, addressed to the Emperor Constantine, happily ends.”

Thus in codex 1671 of the same library one reads: [Col. 0171B] “The Preface to the Emperor Constantine of the first book, *On False Religion*, of L. CELIUS LACTANTIUS FIRMIANUS’s *Divine Institutions against the Gentiles*.”

The Colbertine codex, now number 1667 in the Royal Library, has prefixed to it an inscription in these words: “The book of LUCIUS CAECILIUS FIRMIANUS LACTANTIUS against the Gentiles begins.”

In the Lactantian codex in the library of Marmoutier near Tours, at the beginning of the first book one finds: “The rubrics of the first book of LACTANTIUS FIRMIANUS CAECILIUS, *On the False Religion of the Gods*, begin.”

At the end of the second book one reads: “Of FIRMIANUS LACTANTIUS CAECILIUS.”

Finally, at the end of the sixth book it is written: “Of CAECILIUS FIRMIANUS LACTANTIUS,” etc.

[Col. 0171C] In these places the forename LUCIUS has been omitted through carelessness.

Indeed, in the ancient Bolognese codex, though its first two leaves are missing, one nevertheless reads at the end of the first book: “The first book of L. FIRMIANUS LACTANTIUS, *On False Religion*, ends”; at that point, that is, the name CAELIUS or CAECILIUS is omitted, though it is found in the other books.

At the end of Books II, III, and VII there stands: “Of L. CAELIUS FIRMIANUS LACTANTIUS,” etc.

But at the end of Book IV one has: “Of L. CAELIUS LACTANTIUS FIRMIANUS,” etc.—the order being reversed, as you see.

At the end of *On the Anger of God*, moreover, one reads: “Of LU. CAELIUS LACTANTIUS,” the name FIRMIANUS having been passed over.

But why did Dom Nicholas le Nourry not inspect the manuscript codex of Lactantius that was in the Library of Saint-Germain, where he then resided? There he would doubtless have read, at the end of *On the Workmanship of God*: “Of L. CAELIUS FIRMIANUS LACTANTIUS, *On Reason*, addressed to Demetrius, ends.” Yet in the books of the *Institutions* he is called only [Col. 0172B] FIRMIANUS LACTANTIUS three or four times.

From what source, pray, did so many editors of this author copy the forenames and surnames LUCIUS CAELIUS FIRMIANUS LACTANTIUS? Surely from the manuscript codices they used? For they neither invented them nor published them by chance and accident. It follows, therefore, that Nicholas le Nourry wrote more negligently and confidently than was proper when he said that Lactantius was nowhere distinguished in manuscript codices by the names LUCIUS CAELIUS or LUCIUS CAECILIUS. On the contrary, it is established that he is called by these first names, so that he is recognized just as readily under the name Lucius Caelius or Caecilius as under that of Firmianus Lactantius.

Therefore, once Dom le Nourry’s principal argument has been removed, his entire opinion collapses; nor is there any obstacle to assigning the little work *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* to Lactantius, even though it bears only the names LUCIUS CAECILIUS—especially since we have shown quite adequately, and by many reasons, that this elegant and highly useful little work can be ascribed to Lactantius alone.

[Col. 0171]

## APPENDIX ON TWO PASSAGES OF THE MANUSCRIPT CODEX OF *ON THE DEATHS OF THE PERSECUTORS*, IN WHICH CERTAIN WORDS HAVE BEEN ALTERED IN THE TEXT OF DOM LE NOURRY’S EDITION

[Col. 0171D] I. The first passage occurs in section 2, column 196, where the text of Dom le Nourry’s edition reads as follows concerning Nero:

“First of all persecutors, he persecuted the servants of God, fastened Peter to a cross, and killed Paul; yet he did not get away with it unpunished, for God looked upon the affliction of his people. Therefore, cast down from the summit of empire and hurled from on high, the powerless tyrant suddenly appeared nowhere, so that not even a place of burial on earth might be found for so evil a beast. Hence certain madmen believe that he was removed and kept alive. The Sibyl declares that the matricide, a fugitive, will come from the frontiers, so that, because he was the first to persecute, he may likewise be the last to persecute, and may precede the coming of Antichrist.”

Dom le Nourry noted that the manuscript reads [Col. 0172D] *deleri* [“to be destroyed”], and, since this word does not cohere with the rest and its meaning there is not understood, he judged that the word *deliri* (“madmen”) ought to be placed in the printed text. But this emendation ought not to be accepted, for it wholly opposes the author’s meaning. Lactantius certainly does not say that the opinion held by certain persons about Nero—that he was removed and kept alive—is his own; but he sets it out in such a way that it is manifest that he does not reject it at all, since he supplies plausible reasons for that opinion of certain persons.

First, he relates that it arose from Nero’s having suddenly appeared nowhere, so that a place of burial could not be found for so evil a beast. Next, he teaches that this opinion was supported by the authority of the Sibyl, which was then very influential, and he reports her words. He also assigns the reason why Nero was thought to have been preserved: namely, that he might become the forerunner of Antichrist, and that he who had been the first persecutor might likewise be the last to persecute. Finally, he recounts examples of two prophets who were translated alive.

The author’s intention, therefore, was not to call mad those who held this opinion. This is all the less likely because this author did not say that Nero had been killed or had died; and in the same age this opinion had seized the minds of very many Christians, learned persons, and saints—that Nero had been preserved. Severus Sulpicius testifies to this in Book II of his *Sacred History*, section 40, speaking of Nero:

“He proved to be worthy—not, I would say, of kings, but of all human beings, and even of savage beasts—the foulest of men, to begin the first persecution of Christians; I do not know whether he also completed the last. For many have accepted the opinion that Antichrist himself will come”; and in section 42: “Meanwhile, however . . . he is removed from human affairs . . . certainly his body was slain [reading uncertain]; whence it is believed . . . that, his wound having been healed, he has been preserved, according to what is written concerning him: ‘And the wound of his death was healed,’ to be sent at the end of the age, that he may exercise the mystery of iniquity.”

The same Severus Sulpicius, in Dialogue 2, *On the Virtues of Blessed Martin*, says on this subject:

“Moreover, when we asked him—that is, Blessed Martin—about the end of the age, he told us that Nero and Antichrist would come first: Nero would rule in the western region, after subduing ten kings . . . and Nero himself would finally be killed by Antichrist.”

Saint Augustine, Book XX of *The City of God*, chapter 19, writes as follows on the various opinions about Nero:

“Some suppose that he himself will rise again and become Antichrist; others, however, think that he was not killed, but rather withdrawn so that he might be thought killed, and that he is hidden alive . . . until . . . he is restored to the kingdom. But I am greatly astonished at the excessive presumption of those who hold such opinions.”

Yet how false all these reports about Nero were is clear from Suetonius, Book VI of *The Caesars*, where he recounts Nero’s manner of death, the arrangements and expenses of his funeral, and the location and construction of his tomb:

“He drove a sword into his throat, aided by Epaphroditus, his secretary for petitions . . . He had demanded nothing sooner or more insistently from his companions than that no one should gain possession [Col. 0173D] of his head, but that he should somehow be burned whole. Icellus, Galba’s freedman, permitted this . . . His nurses Ecloge and Alexandra, together with Acte, his mistress, laid his remains in the family monument of the Domitii, visible from the Campus Martius,” etc.

Although I think that the word *deliri* should be removed from the text of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, I nevertheless have absolutely no idea what the word *deleri* means in that place; and I do not wish to seem, alone among others, to know what I do not know.

II. The other passage in which certain words of the manuscript codex of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* have been altered in the text of Dom le Nourry’s edition occurs in section 52, page 99, where the text of the aforesaid edition reads [Col. 0174A] (page 250 in ours): “I speak all these things according to the testimony of those who know them, and I judged that they should be committed to writing as they happened.”

Dom le Nourry notes that the manuscript has: “I speak all these things according to the end, for I speak to one who knows, and I judged that they should be committed to writing as they happened.” I maintain that the words “for I speak to one who knows” should not have been altered. For they have a plain and clear sense, wholly consistent with the author’s intention. Lactantius is addressing Donatus, to whom he had dedicated *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, when he says, “for I speak to one who knows.”

Indeed, the word *finem* (“end”), the meaning of which does not immediately appear, gave grounds for suspecting that something in this phrase should be altered. But if this word *finem* was to be altered because it seemed obscure, the following two words, whose sense is altogether clear, ought not on that account to have been altered. Let us suppose that *finem* ought to be emended, as it was in the printed text: nothing further ought to have been changed. For it yields a phrase that wholly recalls Cicero’s style, as follows: “I speak all these things according to the evidence, for I speak to one who knows, and I judged that they should be committed to writing as they happened.” It is as though he had said: “I judged that all these things should be committed to writing according to the truth of the matter, as they happened—a fact which you, Donatus, certainly know.”

According to Cicero, in the fourth letter of Book III to his brother Quintus, to speak *secundum fidem* (“according to the evidence”) is to speak or say according to the facts of the case. Here are Cicero’s words: “It pleases me that, when I had given testimony most solemnly according to evidence and conscience, the defendant said,” etc. No one fails to see that to give testimony *secundum fidem* is the same as doing so according to [Col. 0174C] the truth of the matter.

We must now consider whether the word *finem* should be changed in that passage. It certainly ought to be retained if an appropriate sense can emerge from it. If retained, it may have this sense: *secundum finem*, that is, near the end of the world; so that the sense is: “I judged that all these things should be committed to writing as they happened, with the end of the world impending—a fact which you yourself, Donatus, know.”

It is established that ecclesiastical writers sometimes use the word *finis* (“end”) for the end of the world, from Tertullian, chapter 39 of the *Apology*, where he says: “We pray for the emperors, for their ministers and authorities, for the condition of the age, for peace in affairs, for the postponement of the end.” In that passage of Tertullian, to pray for the postponement of the end is to pray that the end of the world may be delayed. What he there calls “the end,” he had called “the conclusion of the age” in chapter 32 of the same *Apology*, in these words:

“There is also another, greater necessity for us to pray for the emperors, indeed for the whole condition of the Empire and Roman affairs, because we know that the immense force threatening the whole world, and the very conclusion of the age, menacing dreadful calamities, is delayed by the continuance—that is, duration—of the Roman Empire. Therefore, we do not wish to experience it; and while we pray that it may be deferred, we favor Roman continuance.”

The ancient author of the *Commentaries on the Epistles of Saint Paul*, published at the end of the works of Saint Ambrose, writes as follows on the words in chapter XV of the First Epistle to the Corinthians, verse 24: “Then comes the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father”: “Then comes the end: he says this because, once the kingdom has been delivered over, the end of the world will come.”

[Col. 0175A] It is well known that in the first centuries of the Church many Christians held the view that the end of the world was drawing near. That this was Lactantius’s own view is evident from Book VII of the *Institutions*, chapter 16, where he teaches that the Roman name will shortly be removed from the earth; and in the *Epitome*, chapter 10, he teaches that the destruction of the world must occur when six thousand years have been completed. “This,” he says, “is near at hand, so far as can be inferred from the number of years and from the signs foretold by the prophets.” And in chapter 25 of the aforementioned Book VII of the *Institutions*, he says: “Yet the entire expectation seems to extend no more than two hundred years, although the histories differ concerning the number of years from the beginning of the world.”

Saint Cyprian had affirmed the same thing no less explicitly before him in writing to the Thibaritans: “For you ought to know and hold that the day of tribulation has begun to hang over [Col. 0175B] your heads, and that the decline of the age and the time of Antichrist have drawn near.” And in his book addressed to Demetrianus, he teaches that the entire world itself is already in decline and at its end.

Blessed Martin too was so persuaded of this that, according to the testimony of Sulpicius Severus, in Dialogue 2, *On the Virtues of Blessed Martin*, section 16, Blessed Martin, discussing the end of the age, said that there was no doubt that Antichrist was then in childhood and would assume imperial power upon reaching lawful age. Sulpicius Severus adds: “It is now the eighth year since we heard these things from him. You yourselves, however, consider on what a precipice the things to come stand.””

Nor should it seem surprising if Lactantius, in the epilogue of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, turning his discourse toward Donatus, made some mention of the end of the age, which neither Lactantius nor that most distinguished confessor Donatus doubted was imminent.

[Col. 0176]

## HENRY DODWELL’S DISSERTATION ON *RIPA STRIGA*

[Col. 0175C] On Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, § XII.

§ I. This *ripa* was not the shore of a sea, but of a river. — § II. *Striga* is a term of surveying and military encampment. — § III. Roman camps were generally square. The front of permanent camps faced east; that of mobile camps, the enemy. — § IV. Accordingly, the ancients called the front of a camp a *striga*, its side a *scamnum*. — § V. Roman colonies were laid out according to military discipline. The defensive frontiers of colonies were *strigae*. — § VI. The boundaries of fields, camps, and especially Roman provinces were rivers. — § VII. The Danube was the boundary of the Illyrian defensive frontiers. The Riparian Illyrian provinces derived their name from the bank of that same Danube. — § VIII. This is proved also from the very frequent permanent camps on the bank of the Danube and from history. What fortifications Roman defensive frontiers had. Tertullian is explained against Rhenanus. — § IX. The same conclusion from Attila’s province taken from the Romans. — § X. The Romans sometimes crossed the bank of the Danube, but rarely. — § XI. Their belief in the fated bounds of empires prevented them from crossing it often. Yet in Diocletian’s age they retained no trans-Danubian province. — § XII. This mention of a *ripa striga* accords with Diocletian’s plan and route.

[Col. 0175D] § I. “Thus, when summer had passed, he came to Nicomedia by way of a circuit of the RIPA STRIGA,” etc. The distinguished editor of Lactantius suspects an error in *RIPAM STRIGAM*, mentioned by Lactantius in Diocletian’s journey from Ravenna toward Nicomedia; or, if it really is Lactantius’s text, he thinks it means the shore of the Propontis along which Diocletian travelled. The most learned man is mistaken on both points.

Learned persons will readily grant that among pure authors of the Roman language the shore or coast of the sea is called *litus*; nor is it difficult to allow that perhaps, though rarely, the bank of the sea may also sometimes be called *ripa*. Yet *ripa* is far more common with rivers than with the sea. It is therefore most probable that the *ripa* called *Striga* was the bank of a river, not of the sea or the Propontis.

There remains, however, the further difficulty: what Lactantius means by the name *Striga*, how it can apply to a river, and which river he intended to designate. Once this is determined, we shall have Diocletian’s route established beyond doubt.

§ II. *Striga*, then, is a surveying or land-surveyors’ term, first derived from the laying-out of camps and subsequently transferred and applied to the lands of colonies, which were customarily measured and distributed according to the model of camps. Charisius teaches us most explicitly that it is a military term. Nor should anyone suppose that this is exceptional in the case of this word. The same judgment must be made of the whole skill of the land-surveyors and likewise of all the terms of that discipline.
