Hyginus calls the place at the entrance of the praetorium the *groma*, and gives the same work the title *Gromaticus* which he wrote on the method of laying out camps. The same Hyginus testifies that the practitioners of this discipline were called *Gromatici* from the military *groma* that I have mentioned. Therefore, from the military use of this word we must wholly determine every secondary use.

§ III. Although no one doubts that the Romans sometimes used for camps a shape other than a square, no one doubts that the square was by far the most frequent of all. Nor should we doubt that the soldiers were arranged in camp in the same order as in battle. It is established that they marched in a square formation whenever danger from a nearby enemy threatened. They evidently believed that form best suited to fortifications. The Pythagoreans regarded the number four as unfallen or unyielding (*aptōton*); and philosophers commonly call a man of invincible steadfastness “four-square” (*tetragōnon*). We shall therefore rightly establish this form as the standard of the surveying art.

Now a square figure has two kinds of boundary: one in length and another in breadth. It is certain that they called one of these *striga*, the other *scamnum*. There were, moreover, two dispositions of camps: one, uncertain and mobile, according to circumstance and the demands of war; the other, fixed and immovable, as in permanent camps. In a fixed arrangement, the Praetorian Gate faced east; in a mobile arrangement, it faced the enemy. This is how I understand Hyginus and Vegetius. In facing their camps eastward, as I think, they had regard to healthfulness. Agricultural writers commend that orientation as the healthiest of all. But the enemy was doubtless a more important consideration than the east. Still, whenever no danger was feared from another quarter, they preferred the east to the other regions of the sky. I wished only to observe here that, among the surveying writers, east has the same force in a permanent position as the enemy has in a mobile one; hence the boundary which in a permanent arrangement they would face toward the east, they would in a mobile arrangement face toward the enemy.

§ IV. Thus we shall understand what orientation *striga* and *scamnum* held in military discipline. Aggenus Urbicus calls a field *strigated* when it runs lengthwise from north to south; he calls it *scamnated* when it extends in this fashion from west to east. Phalanxes thus laid out lengthwise from north toward south would have their faces turned toward the east rather than the north. They would thus face the standards and the Praetorian Gate in the fixed camp-plan. Frontinus himself says no differently: “Whatever, under this arrangement, is marked out in length is called by STRIGAE; whatever by breadth, by SCAMNA.”

These remarks of Frontinus concern the division of fields—not the individual lots and portions of individual colonists, whose boundaries could vary greatly from one another, but the fields enclosing the boundaries of the colony as a whole, or whose total measure is allotted to the community. Therefore, we need not doubt that a field of this kind includes boundaries of the same kind and conforms to camp-laying practice. It is established, moreover, that in accordance with the discipline of laying out camps, the battle line was usually presented to the enemy in its greatest length at the front, so that it could not be outflanked. Finally, these words of Hyginus also support this: “Whenever we distribute by STRIGAE, they should not be divided into more than three parts.” I take this threefold distribution to be none other than the very familiar Roman military division into hastati, principes, and triarii. Yet this threefold battle line faced the enemy.

Therefore, the boundary called IN FRONTEM (“at the front”) in sepulchral inscriptions is called STRIGA by the land-surveyors in laying out camps; conversely, what the land-surveyors call SCAMNUM is customarily designated IN AGRUM (“into the field”) in inscriptions. The meaning of *scamnum* among agricultural writers agrees with this too. If any ground was left untouched by the plough during ploughing, they regarded it as a *scamnum*. Therefore, the orientation of a field along the second furrow is called *scamnated*; an orientation transverse to the furrows will be called *strigated*. But an orientation transverse to the furrow represents the faces of soldiers standing in battle line.

§ V. Now the same rules that prevailed in camps prevailed also in colonies and frontier garrisons. For these were founded not only to cultivate the land but also to defend borders. This is sufficiently evident from the very terms of agricultural surveying. For them, *territorium* denotes all that is established for frightening the enemy. “Ager arcisinius,” says Frontinus from Varro, “is so called from keeping enemies at bay.” Thus frontier colonies were a kind of large camps; consequently, there is no reason at all to wonder if they were arranged according to the custom and discipline of camps.

They certainly use terms proper to camps—centuries, measuring-rods, and innumerable others—so that we understand that colonists, in allocating fields, looked toward one another in the same manner as soldiers in battle line. Writers on agricultural surveying also represent colonies by the square shape of camps. Moreover, the very term *praetentura*, which Ammianus uses with reference to frontier garrisons, makes it wholly impossible for us to doubt that colonies standing guard for the safety of the republic performed the function of camps, and that in those great, as it were, camps of the whole republic they occupied especially the position which *strigae* occupied in camps.

For among the surveying writers, those squadrons that occupy either side of the praetorium are said to *tendere* (“extend”); perhaps those behind it *retendere* (“extend behind”); but certainly those placed before the praetorium, facing the enemy and the Praetorian Gate, *praetendere* (“extend in front”). It follows, therefore, that whatever boundary they had at the front must likewise be called a *striga*.

§ VI. Furthermore, Siculus Flaccus counts streams among field boundaries, and Frontinus rivers—statements to be understood chiefly of the boundaries of private colonists. Yet this was necessary for a much stronger reason in camp-laying and frontier defensive lines. A river offered a double advantage to a camp: water and fortification. Therefore, skilled emperors took care, even in temporary camps, that at least one boundary of the camp should be washed by a river. In permanent and frontier camps, however, whose location could be chosen and which were founded for defense rather than attack, it is still much more probable that the ancients observed this rule.

For rivers are certain natural boundaries of provinces, established by divine providence itself; and an enemy could be overwhelmed more easily in the very act of crossing a river than if he had to be met in open and unobstructed country. It is certain that the ancients fortified river-fords just as they fortified other difficult places. The larger and less fordable the river, the more defensible and more suitable for repelling enemies they thought it; and, if the enemy crossed it, the easier they found the retreat of their own forces into fortified places.

There is therefore no need for us to ransack geographers’ archives for rivers that form provincial boundaries. Examples occur everywhere. Not to go farther afield, we have notable rivers as the boundaries of the Roman Empire with which we are concerned. The Rhine defended Gaul against the Germans and marked its boundary; the Euphrates, Syria against the Parthians. Why, then, should we not say that the Danube was the boundary of the Illyrian defensive frontiers, and that no other river need be sought whose bank Lactantius called *Striga*? For the Illyrian defensive frontiers had the Danube set before them at the front, facing the enemy.

### § VII

Most ancient authorities certainly recognized the Danube as a boundary of the Roman Empire. Strabo: “Of the three continents, they possess almost the whole of Europe, except the region beyond the Ister, and the peoples dwelling by the Ocean between the Rhine and the Tanais.” King Agrippa in Josephus: “For the whole Euphrates toward the east did not suffice them, nor the Ister among the northern regions,” etc. And, after some intervening words: “Dwelling by the Ister, they are held in check by not merely two detachments, with which they themselves repel the assaults of the Dacians.” Tacitus: “Two legions in Pannonia and two in Moesia held the bank of the Danube, with an equal number stationed in Dalmatia, which lay behind them by the position of the region.” [Col. 0178C] Appian: “In Europe two rivers, the Rhine and the Ister, chiefly mark the boundaries of the Roman dominion.”

Thus, even after Diocletian’s time, Festus Rufus extends the frontier of the Roman Empire as far as the Danube, and always identifies the Danube itself as the boundary of the frontier provinces. Hence we have so many provinces on that side called Riparian, evidently so named in order to distinguish them from inland provinces of the same name. All recognize Riparian Dacia, to which the *Notitia of the Empire* adds Valeria and Noricum, likewise expressly as Riparian. There was also Savia, or Pannonia Secunda, called Riparian, I think, from the Riparian garrisons. For those garrisons occupied the bank of the Danube.

Under the command of the duke of Riparian Valeria we read of Dalmatian cavalry at a place called Ripa Alta, doubtless from that bank of the Danube. Under the command of the duke of the province of Raetia I and II: “the prefect of the Third Italic Legion, of the upper division assigned to the First Bank, at Submontorium.” On that bank, certainly, Galerius kept watch under Diocletian. Thus Lactantius represents him complaining that fifteen years had elapsed since he had been relegated to Illyricum, or to the bank of the Danube, to struggle with barbarian peoples, while others ruled delicately within broader and quieter lands. [Col. 0178D]

By the same pattern Tacitus mentions a prefect of the bank of the Rhine. The same Tacitus shows that the two legions to whose protection those frontiers were entrusted, as both he and King Agrippa testify, had been stationed in Pannonia. Thus we need not wonder that Pannonian soldiers in particular, as the most ancient defenders of those frontiers, were called *Riparii*, “men of the bank.” Accordingly that Pannonia was called *Ripariensis*, rather than *Ripensis*.

### § VIII

The very numerous permanent camps on the Danubian bank with which we are concerned indicate the same thing. Those camps established for repelling enemies necessarily had to be close to the enemy’s boundaries. The histories themselves show the same. When the Goths had been driven out by the Huns, they did not dare cross the Danube until they had first obtained permission from the Roman emperor Valens. [Col. 0179A] Clearly the frontier garrisons were what made them hesitate. Eunapius calls those stationed on the banks “Romans assigned to the banks”; Tacitus calls them prefects of the bank. Thus those garrisons held that bank in such a way as to leave no crossing-place unoccupied.

For this was how the Roman imperial frontiers were usually enclosed by *praetenturae*, defensive frontier-lines. We learn it from the anonymous tract *On Military Matters*. Its words are:

> Moreover, among the useful advantages of the commonwealth is the care of the frontiers, which everywhere encircle the side of the Empire. Continuous fortlets will better provide for their protection, so that, at intervals of a thousand paces, they may be erected with a permanent wall and very strong towers. These fortifications should be established by the apportioned responsibility of landholders, without public expense, with watches and agricultural services performed in them, so that the tranquillity of the provinces, surrounded by a kind of girdle of defence, may rest secure.

On this condition, therefore, the *duumviri* distributed the lands of colonies: that at the colonists’ own expense the boundaries of the colonies should both be fortified and defended. This was, indeed, nearly the same law of Roman colonists as that of the *timariots* among the Turks and, among ourselves, military service. [Col. 0179B]

Perhaps this was peculiar to the Romans: that they fortified all the boundaries of their empire with stronger defences than we fortify our camps even when battle is imminent—namely, with a permanent and stable wall, and with towers or very strong fortlets at every interval of a thousand paces. We have fortifications of this kind in Britain even today, in the walls of Hadrian, Antoninus, and Severus. Our later Offa likewise imitated this in that frontier rampart, still bearing his name, between England and Wales.

I would refer to the same system Tertullian’s words: “The nation of the Moors and the barbarism of the Gaetulians are besieged by the Romans.” The most learned Rhenanus understands this as referring to some war then in progress when Tertullian wrote. Yet the writers of that age are wholly silent concerning such a war. The siege was established not to enclose enemies within their own boundaries, but rather to exclude them from Roman territory: “lest,” says Tertullian, “they should exceed the boundaries of their own regions” [Col. 0179C]; and therefore the Romans fortified their Empire with the garrisons of their legions.

Here Tertullian altogether presents the form of the *praetenturae*, as I have said; yet this did not differ altogether from the arrangement of siege-camps. For siege-camps performed the twofold function which I mentioned: not only to confine besieged enemies, but also to exclude reinforcements from external enemies. Thus the Romans regularly fortified the outer boundary of such camps, so as easily to repel an enemy from that direction as well, even one otherwise equal in strength. In this way they repelled Hannibal himself during the siege of Capua, and Caesar repelled the very numerous Gallic army during his siege of Vercingetorix at Alesia. For they also had that outer boundary strongly fortified with a rampart and with towers answering one another at fixed intervals. The *praetenturae*, therefore, resembled the outer boundary of siege-camps.

### § IX

[Col. 0179D] So long as that discipline of the *praetenturae* flourished, the Roman frontiers remained unharmed and withstood even the fiercest barbarian enemies. Valens removed them and entrusted the frontier to the Goths; thereafter he exposed the Romans as easy prey to barbarians. Yet traces of the old frontiers remained even amid the inundation of enemies that followed.

Priscus thus describes the province recovered by Attila from the Romans: “Its length lay along the current of the Ister, from the Paeonians as far as Novae of the Thracians; its depth was a journey of five days.” The Danube, therefore, ran along the length of the Roman province; and we have said that the boundary of this length was called *striga*. Accordingly Attila also moved the place of commerce, according to the same Priscus: “And he ordered that the market in Illyricum should not be held beside the bank of the river Ister, as formerly, but at Naissus, which he established as the boundary, as it were, of Scythian and Roman territory, after it had been devastated by him.”

Who cannot see that these places of trade were established on the very frontiers of the Empire, when Attila designated Naissus itself for this commerce because it was the boundary of his new province? [Col. 0180A] And who therefore cannot see that, since the old place of trade had been the bank of the Danube, this was because it had also been the ancient frontier of the Empire? The Oxford Father therefore rightly conjectures that the name of the city Strigonium preserves even today the memory of the *ripa striga*, “the strip-like bank”; that city too is situated on the bank of the Danube.

### § X

Although this was so, I nevertheless acknowledge that Appian cautiously added: “These are the continental boundaries, as nearly as one may approach exactness.” For the Romans at times crossed the Rhine, the Euphrates, and the Danube itself. When Appian wrote, they held Dacia beyond the Danube, conquered by Trajan. Marcus added the Marcomanni and Quadi, whom he had also occupied with garrisons. Yet Commodus removed Marcus’s garrisons immediately after Marcus’s death. Trajan’s province endured much longer. But Aurelian, before Diocletian, voluntarily stripped even it of garrisons, transferring its colonists elsewhere.

Thus nothing prevented the bank from being called a *striga* with the greatest accuracy under Diocletian. [Col. 0180B] Even so, the Romans could only very rarely advance beyond the established boundaries of the *praetenturae*. Tertullian observed this concerning the African frontier-lines, in the passage already cited: “Nor can they extend the forces of their realm beyond these peoples.” If this was true even in Africa, it was certainly true with much greater reason on the bank of the Danube.

Aurelian undoubtedly held this view, though coins and inscriptions call him, and rightly, most victorious. Such a great emperor, adorned with the spoils and triumphs of so many barbarians, nevertheless judged that the territories beyond the Danube could not even be defended. For nowhere did the Romans endure more frequent or stronger barbarian attacks; and the hazard of war was extremely uncertain.

### § XI

Moreover, at that very period, was there not in force an opinion—or rather a superstition? Whatever its character, it certainly prevailed: that, just as estates, so too empires possessed sacred and fated boundaries which no one could violate with impunity. Thus Capaneus was struck by lightning because he dared to be the first to burst through the sacred walls of Thebes [Col. 0180C]; Protesilaus was slain because he was the first of the enemy to leap upon shores sacred to Neptune.

A man was believed to incur sacrilege, to rouse a certain sacred Nemesis or Adrasteia, and to provoke the resentment of the deity, not easily appeased, if he crossed the limits fixed for humankind. The same opinion concerning the boundaries of the Roman Empire was generally accepted. The very brave emperor Carus was therefore thought to have been struck by lightning because he had crossed that fated boundary of the Empire, the Euphrates. For they regarded this punishment by lightning as the clearest possible sign of divine displeasure.

When the example of Carus made soldiers less eager to venture forth on another Persian expedition—whether that of Galerius Maximianus or, perhaps more probably, Julian—Vopiscus consequently judged that this opinion had to be refuted. Perhaps this explains why good emperors were unwilling even to extend the boundaries of the Empire. We have Tacitus as authority that the policy of confining the Empire within its boundaries proceeded from Augustus. It is also probable that Hadrian was of no other mind when, without any enemy compelling him, he voluntarily abandoned to freedom from garrisons provinces already conquered by Trajan. [Col. 0180D]

I am not unaware, however, that historians explain these matters otherwise; but they conjecture it from disposition rather than from any documentary evidence of established trustworthiness. If, therefore, the Diocese of Illyricum ever had any boundary other than the Danube, it is nevertheless likely that this was rare. The bank of the Danube which I have mentioned was thus the fixed and permanent boundary of those regions. On it were the *praetenturae* and their permanent fortifications. On it were the rampart and fortlets answering one another at fixed intervals of the rampart. Were all other evidence lacking, these facts would amply suffice for this bank rightly to be called a *striga*. The Danube was the permanent boundary of very many frontier provinces. But we have already shown that in Diocletian’s age it was the boundary of all.

### § XII

Moreover, this reference to the *ripa striga* accords exactly with Diocletian’s purpose and journey. Lactantius says that he had contracted an illness already mild and persistent—plainly a chronic illness, not an acute one. [Col. 0181A] For chronic illnesses, especially when declining, Celsus teaches that conveyance is most beneficial, provided that sufferers are free of fever. Such was Diocletian’s illness.

Among kinds of conveyance, Celsus includes both that in a litter and that in a ship, whether in a harbour or on a river; he even declares the latter the gentlest of all. Accordingly our emperor was conveyed for much of the way from Rome to Ravenna in a litter. From there perhaps he travelled in a litter to the Danube; then the rest of the journey by ship, following the current of the Danube, through the Euxine Sea to Nicomedia. That entire route was exceedingly healthful for a weakened body; nor can we find any other so safe and harmless, or less wearisome while preserving health over so long a journey. [Col. 0182A]

Since, as rivers commonly do, the Danube often bent this way and that, he is said to have reached Nicomedia by a circuit of the *ripa striga*. Nor did this journey serve merely for bodily recovery; it was also imperial business. Thus he could inspect the frontier garrisons, particularly in regions where danger from the enemy was most pressing. Many laws issued in Illyricum, and the appointment there of Caesar, the most warlike of all men, testify to his concern for those regions.

[Col. 0181]

# HENRY DODWELL’S CHRONOLOGY OF THE PERSECUTIONS, TOGETHER WITH STEPHEN BALUZE’S DIOCLETIANIC CHRONOLOGY, INTERMIXED AS THE ORDER OF TIME REQUIRED. IN ADDITION, THE CONSULS OF EACH YEAR AND OTHER EVENTS HAVE BEEN ADDED.

[Col. 0181B] **A.D. 64.** In the sixty-fourth year of the Lord according to the Common Era. Consuls: C. Lecanius Bassus; M. Licinius Crassus. Pagi: Nero’s persecution of the Christians; according to Tacitus, he charged them with the fire which he himself had set at Rome. DODWELL.—19 June: Saints Gervasius and Protasius crowned with martyrdom at Milan.

**66.** Consuls: C. Suetonius Paulinus; L. Pontius Telesinus. Saints Peter and Paul sentenced to death on 29 June: the former by the cross, the latter by the sword. LENGLET.

**95.** Consuls: Domitian Augustus XVII; T. Flavius Clemens. Pagi: Domitian’s persecution began after 13 September, according to Bruttius. DODWELL.—In this persecution T. Flavius Clemens, consul, was put to death by Domitian because of religion.

**96.** Consuls: C. Fulvius Valens; C. Antistius Vetus. Pagi: shortly before 18 September Domitian recalled the Christians from exile. For the exiles had not yet returned before Nerva’s new edict. DODWELL.

**97.** Consuls: M. Cocceius Nerva III; T. Virginius Rufus. The emperor Nerva removed all statues of Domitian. He acquitted persons accused of Christianity and forbade anyone to be accused under that name. LENGLET.

**107.** Consuls: C. Sosius Senecio IV; L. Licinius Sura III. Pagi: persecution under Trajan, in which Ignatius suffered, according to his acts. Saint Simeon, bishop of Jerusalem, is subjected to martyrdom. Peace was restored in this very year. The persecutions of Pliny and Arrius Antoninus perhaps also occurred in this same year. DODWELL.

**108.** Consuls: Ap. Annius Trebonianus Gallus; M. Atilius Metilius Bradua. Pagi: after Ignatius’s death, which occurred on the twentieth day of December in the preceding year, Polycarp wrote to the Philippians when he had received news of the death in Asia, though he had not yet received a verified account of Ignatius’s acts. DODWELL.—Pope Evaristus is crowned with martyrdom.

**109.** Consuls: A. Cornelius Palma; C. Calvisius Tullus. Onesimus, disciple of Saint Paul and bishop of the Ephesians, is cast into prison and crushed beneath stones at Rome. LENGLET.

**116.** Consuls: Aemilianus; L. Antistius Verus. Pagi: Simeon son of Cleophas suffered, and the family of David became extinct. DODWELL.

**153.** Consuls: C. Bruttius Praesens; A. Junius Rufinus. Pagi: an edict of Antoninus Pius in favour of the Christians, if indeed it was Pius’s. DODWELL.

**161.** Consuls: M. Aelius Aurelius Verus Caesar III; L. Aelius Commodus II. Pagi: the same edict, if it is rather to be attributed to Marcus than to Pius. DODWELL.

**167.** Consuls: L. Aurelius Verus Augustus III; Quadratus. Pagi: persecution of the Gauls of Lyons and Vienne under Marcus. DODWELL.

[Col. 0183A] **168.** Consuls: L. Vettius Paulus; T. Junius Montanus. Pagi: Athenagoras’s embassy on behalf of Christians after Lucius’s return. DODWELL.

**170.** Consuls: M. Cornelius Cethegus; C. Erucius Clarus. Pagi: apologies of Melito of Sardis and Apollinaris of Hierapolis. DODWELL.

**202.** Consuls: L. Septimius Severus Augustus III; Aurelius Antoninus Caracalla Augustus. Pagi: Severus’s persecution began after 6 April and before the solstice. The seventeenth year of Origen’s age. DODWELL.

**203.** Consuls: L. Fulvius Plautianus; P. Septimius Geta. Pagi: the eighteenth year of Origen’s age, the second of this persecution. DODWELL.

[Col. 0183B] **204.** Consuls: L. Fabius Cilo II; M. Annius Libo. Pagi: at the beginning of the secular year, this persecution of Severus ceased. DODWELL.

**235.** Consuls: Severus; Quinctianus. Pagi: Maximinus’s persecution toward the end of the year. Persecution in Asia. DODWELL.

**236.** Consuls: C. Julius Verus Maximinus Augustus; Julius Africanus. Pagi: at the beginning of the year, the persecution ended. The Gordians revolted in Africa in May; the Senate did so in Italy. DODWELL.

**237.** Consuls: L. Ovinius Cornelianus; P. Titius Perpetuus. Pagi: the Gordians were killed in Africa in June. In July Maximus and Balbinus assumed imperial power as Augusti; Gordian III assumed Caesarian power. DODWELL.

**238.** Consuls: Pius; Pontianus. Pagi: during the Capitoline Games, before 22 June, Maximus and Balbinus were killed. Gordian assumed imperial power. DODWELL.

**248.** Consuls: M. Julius Philippus Augustus III; M. Julius Philippus Augustus II. Pagi: Alexandrian persecution at the end of the year. DODWELL.

**249.** Consuls: Fulvius Aemilianus II; Vectius Aquilinus. Pagi: toward the end of the year Decius’s persecution began together with his reign. At least in Africa, this persecution was thus far bloodless. DODWELL.

**250.** Consuls: Cn. Messius Quintus Trajanus Decius Augustus II; Annius Gratus. Pagi: at the beginning of April the persecution in Africa proceeded to executions, but it promptly became milder. The greater part of the second year of the Alexandrian persecution falls in this year. DODWELL.

**251.** Consuls: Cn. Trajanus Decius Augustus III; Q. Herennius Etruscus Decius Caesar. Pagi: third year of the Alexandrian persecution. The persecution was relaxed both at Alexandria and in Africa. DODWELL.

**252.** Consuls: C. Vibius Trebonianus Gallus Augustus II; C. Vibius Volusianus Caesar. Pagi: plague under Gallus, and his very brief persecution. DODWELL.

**257.** Consuls: P. Licinius Valerianus Augustus IV; P. Licinius Gallienus Augustus III. Pagi: at the beginning of August, Valerian’s persecution, but without martyrdoms. DODWELL.

**258.** Consuls: M. Aurelius Memmius Tuscus; Bassus. Pagi: at the beginning of August, Valerian’s edict concerning capital punishment. DODWELL.

**261.** Consuls: Gallienus Augustus IV; Petronius Volusianus. Pagi: Aemilianus seized the purple in Egypt. Gallienus revoked Valerian’s persecution in the rest of the Empire. DODWELL.

**262.** Consuls: P. Licinius Gallienus Augustus V; Faustinus. Pagi: Gallienus revoked the same persecution in Egypt, Aemilianus having already been captured. DODWELL.

**275.** Consuls: L. Domitius Aurelianus Augustus IV; T. Avonius Marcellinus. Pagi: at the beginning of the year, toward the end of Aurelian’s reign, he issued edicts of persecution. DODWELL.

**284.** Consuls: Emperor M. Aurelius Carinus II; Emperor M. Aurelius Numerianus II. SPARK. Substituted consuls according to Lydiat’s calculation:

| Date | Consuls |
|---|---|
| 1 May | Valerius Diocletianus |
| or October | Annius Bassus |
| 1 September | M. Aurelius Valerius Maximianus |
| or November | M. Junius Maximus |

SAME AUTHOR. Diocletian was raised to the imperial office on 17 September. In this year begins the Diocletianic Era, or Era of the Martyrs, on the twenty-ninth day of August, on which the Egyptian year begins; the Egyptians still use that era. LENGLET.

**285.** Consuls: Valerius Diocletianus II; Aristobulus. SPARK. Maximian Herculius is created Caesar by Diocletian.

**286.** Consuls: M. Junius Maximus II; Vettius Aquilinus. On 1 April Maximian Herculius is created Augustus and accordingly is called by Diocletian into partnership in the Empire. Maximian grants the Theban Legion martyrdom. LENGLET.

**292.** Consuls: Annibalianus; Asclepiodotus. On 1 March Diocletian and Maximian adopt Constantius surnamed Chlorus and Galerius Maximianus surnamed Armentarius, and name them Caesars. Constantius repudiates Helena, by whom he had begotten Constantine, afterward surnamed the Great, and marries Theodora, the stepdaughter of Herculius. Galerius likewise, having repudiated his wife, takes as wife Valeria, daughter of Diocletian and the empress Prisca. BALUZE.

**293.** Consuls: Emperor Valerius Diocletianus V; Maximian Herculius IV. Constantius Chlorus expels the Franks from Batavia and Belgium and settles them among the Suessiones and Remi. LENGLET.

**297.** Consuls: Maximian Herculius V; Galerius Maximianus Caesar II. SPARK. Narseus, king of the Persians, defeats and puts Galerius to flight in Mesopotamia, and afterward in Armenia. Diocletian comes to Nisibis. Narseus is defeated and routed by Galerius; his wife and daughters are captured and preserved under the strictest guard for chastity, to enhance the splendour of the triumph. A great quantity of booty is captured, with immense spoils. BALUZE.

[Col. 0185A] **301.** Consuls: Postumius Titianus II; Flavius Popilius Nepotianus. SPARK. Diocletian’s first persecution of soldiers. DODWELL. Constantius defeats the Germans at Langres, which they had reached.

**302.** Consuls: Flavius Valerius Constantius Caesar IV; Galerius Maximianus Armentarius IV. Diocletian departed from Nicomedia, where the imperial residence then was, for the East, and remained there until winter. Then, returning to Nicomedia, he consulted there with Galerius concerning making war upon Christians. BALUZE.

Narseus, king of the Persians, defeated by Galerius. DODWELL.

**303.** Consuls: Emperor Valerius Diocletianus VIII; Maximian Herculius VII. SPARK. First year of the persecution, begun at Nicomedia on 23 February. DODWELL.

A persecution against Christians was stirred up in this year, the most savage of all that had ever occurred. It began at the city of Nicomedia, whose church was demolished on the seventh day before the Kalends of March, on the very day of the Terminalia. On the following day an edict of the emperors and Caesars against Christians was posted, requiring them to sacrifice throughout the whole world. BALUZE.

Diocletian proceeds to Rome, celebrates there his twentieth anniversary and holds a triumph over the Persians. Soon peace was made, which endured, remaining in force until the time of the divine Constantine; the Persians restored Mesopotamia together with the five districts beyond the Tigris, the boundary of the empires being set upon the bank of the Tigris. SAME AUTHOR.

The Goths, having crossed the Ister, invaded a neighbouring province and expelled the inhabitants. SAME AUTHOR.

Diocletian, offended by the excessive witticisms of the Romans, departs immediately after completing his twentieth anniversary celebrations and leaves for Ravenna on 20 December. SAME AUTHOR.

[Col. 0185C] **304.** Consuls: Emperor [al.], Diocletianus IX; Maximian Herculius VIII. SPARK. First year of the persecution completed; second begun, though its first according to Eusebius. DODWELL.

Diocletian enters upon his ninth consulship at Ravenna. Afterwards he fell into a severe illness, the force of which unsettled his mind and rendered him insane; and after the summer he reached Nicomedia. There he dedicated the Circus in the year after his twentieth anniversary had been completed; and on the Ides of December, when his breath was cut off, he appeared to have died. BALUZE.

At the same time when Diocletian entered upon his ninth consulship at Ravenna, Maximian Herculius entered upon his eighth at Rome; and afterwards, on 1 April, he entered the twentieth year of his reign. Then, in the summer of that year, he was in Campania. SAME AUTHOR.

At the end of the year Galerius Maximianus Caesar came to Diocletian at Nicomedia, to compel him to resign the Empire, having previously persuaded Herculius to do the same. SAME AUTHOR.

**305.** Consuls: Constantius Chlorus V; Galerius Maximianus Armentarius V. SPARK. Second year of the persecution completed; third begun, though its second according to Eusebius. Diocletian and Maximian laid aside the purple. Then a new and harsher persecution was renewed in the East by Galerius and Maximinus, against all Christians henceforth, whereas previously it had been directed only against clergy. A five-year contest at Caesarea. Persecution ceased in the West. DODWELL.

On 1 March Diocletian appeared in public at Nicomedia to prove to the people that he was alive. BALUZE.

On 1 May, Diocletian near Nicomedia and Maximian Herculius at Milan lay aside the purple and name Constantius and Galerius Augusti—Diocletian naming Galerius, Herculius Constantius. SAME AUTHOR.

On the same day Severus and Maximinus Daza were made Caesars: they were named by Galerius, but Severus was invested by Maximian and Maximinus by Diocletian. Then Diocletian returned to his native country, that is, Dioclea in Dalmatia, where he grew old in distinguished retirement. Herculius withdrew to Lucania.

**306.** Consuls: Constantius Chlorus VI; Galerius Maximianus Armentarius VI. SPARK. Third year of the persecution completed; fourth begun. At Caesarea the new persecution of Maximinus began, compelling all to sacrifice. DODWELL.

The emperor Constantius demanded back from Galerius his son Constantine, whom Galerius held as a hostage. Constantine therefore departed for Gaul and reached his father, who was at the point of death, on 21 July. Four days later Constantius died at York in Britain. Constantine succeeded him, both by his father’s final will and by the agreement of the soldiers, who invested him with the purple. BALUZE.

A laureate image of Constantine is conveyed to Galerius. He, however, sent Constantine the purple and named him Caesar on 25 December, having either on that same day or shortly before named Severus Augustus. SAME AUTHOR.

Constantine issues an edict favourable to Christians.

Meanwhile, when images of Constantine had been brought to Rome, Maxentius, son of Herculius, seized imperial power on 27 October, while his father long hesitated. Calling his father to himself, who was then in Campania, and twice naming him Augustus, he made him partner in the Empire. SAME AUTHOR.

Maxentius usurps the Augustan purple and brings Rome and Italy under his power on 28 October.

**307.** Consuls: Maximian Herculius IX; Constantine Caesar. SPARK. Fourth year of the persecution completed; fifth begun. Mutilations began in place of executions. Death of Urbanus, persecuting prefect of Palestine. DODWELL.

Galerius Maximianus orders Severus Augustus, to whom the protection of Italy had been entrusted, to lead an army against Maxentius. Severus immediately besieges Rome, flees to Ravenna, and dies, as it seems, near the month of April, at the Three Taverns.

> **Note [Col. 0186D]. At the Three Taverns.** That is, as Zosimus, writing in Greek on the same subject, says in Book II of his *History*: “Having come to a place called Three Inns.” Literally, therefore: when he had come to a certain place whose name was, or is, “Three Inns.” For *kapēleion* is invariably, among all learned writers, ancient and modern whom I have been able to consult, an inn or eating-house. Nor does the recent interpreter of our Diocletianic Chronology translate otherwise here: *meurt aux trois Tavernes*, “he dies at the Three Taverns”; nor do Isidore of Pelusium and Grotius on Acts 28:15: “They came out to meet us as far as the market of Appius and the Three Taverns.” Yet the Genevan French versions customarily render Luke’s “three taverns” simply as *trois boutiques*, “three shops,” rather than, with the Louvain versions and others, as *trois tavernes*, “three inns”: “They came to meet us at the market of Appius and at the Three Shops.”

Maximian Herculius, twice Augustus, departs for Gaul, where he names Constantine—who until then had been content with the title Caesar—Augustus on 31 March, and gives him his daughter Fausta in marriage. BALUZE.

Meanwhile Galerius Maximianus leads an immense army into Italy to avenge Severus’s death. He vainly besieges Rome and returns ingloriously to Illyricum. SAME AUTHOR.

Then Herculius, returning from Gaul, attempted in an assembly to strip his son Maxentius of imperial authority; but he received the insults of the soldiers and was expelled from the city and Italy. He then again made for Constantine in Gaul. After remaining there for a short time, he proceeded to Carnuntum in Pannonia to Galerius, found Diocletian there, and was present on 11 November when Licinius was named Augustus, Galerius Maximianus appointing him in Severus’s place. When he had vainly urged Diocletian to resume the Empire, he was rejected by him and returned to Gaul, where he again laid aside imperial power and afterwards spent the remainder of his life. SAME AUTHOR.

**308.** Consuls: Maximian Herculius X; Galerius Maximianus Armentarius VII. Fifth year completed; sixth begun. Constantine is declared Augustus. Firmilian, governor of Palestine, persecuted by mutilations rather than executions. The persecution was relaxed from August until November, and renewed at the end of this year by a new edict of Maximinus; yet in December the persecutors returned to mutilations. DODWELL.

Maximian Herculius X and Galerius Maximianus VII were consuls, reconciliation having now been established between them and Maxentius. BALUZE.

On 20 April Maxentius is declared consul at Rome. With Romulus, Herculius flees to Gaul, where he plans disturbances against Constantine.

**309.** Consuls: Licinius Augustus; or, after the consulship of Herculius X and Galerius Maximianus VII, Maxentius II and Romulus II. Sixth year completed; seventh begun. On 7 March Eubulus, the last of the Caesarean martyrs, suffered. Thereafter, through the negligence of the pagans, peace returned to Christians. DODWELL.

**310.** Consuls: Maxentius III, without colleague. SPARK, according to Lydiat. Consuls: Galerius Maximianus Armentarius VIII, with Licinius Licinianus Augustus substituted. SAME AUTHOR. Seventh year completed; eighth begun. A new persecution of Christians arose again from pagan hostility; but it was very brief and a single outbreak. DODWELL.

When the Franks disturbed the condition of Gaul and Constantine was considering how to suppress them, Herculius—always restless, deceitful, and faithless—urged him not to take the entire army with him, since the barbarians could be overcome by a few troops. Constantine trusted both the old man and his father-in-law. Meanwhile, Herculius, spurred by desire for the Empire and thinking Constantine farther away, solicited the soldiers to revolt by gifts and promises, seized the treasuries, and for the third time put on the purple in Belgica. When Constantine returned with remarkable speed, Herculius, fearing what he deserved, fled to Narbonensis Secunda and shut himself within the walls of the city of Arles. Then, as Constantine’s army approached, he hurried to Marseilles. There he was besieged by Constantine, captured, and granted life after being rebuked. But shortly afterward, by Constantine’s order, he was strangled, having been discovered in the plot which he was preparing to kill Constantine. BALUZE.

In the same year Galerius Maximianus fell into a grave and dangerous illness, by which he was afflicted throughout the whole year; this disease attacked him as he entered the eighteenth year of his reign. SAME AUTHOR.

**311.** Consuls: Galerius Maximianus Armentarius VIII; Maximinus II. Eighth year completed; ninth begun. Galerius’s edict for peace, between 1 March and 30 April. That peace did not last even six whole months: persecution returned toward the end of October, but it too was a single, bloody outbreak. Maximinus received the first embassies of cities at Nicomedia. DODWELL.

Galerius, continually ill and warned that this illness had come upon him because of the evils he had inflicted on Christians, ordered by a posted edict that the persecution should cease in the eighth year after it had begun. Then the prisons were opened, and the Christians detained there were permitted to depart. Shortly afterward Galerius died at Sardica, apparently in May, having first commended and entrusted to Licinius his wife Valeria and his son Candidianus. But because they unhappily preferred Maximinus’s following, they met a pitiable fate, as will later be said. BALUZE.

Maxentius declares war on Constantine, allegedly to avenge the death of his father Herculius.

Then there is war between Licinius and Maximinus, rivals for imperial power. But peace and friendship are arranged on specified terms at the Thracian Bosporus, where the boundary of the two empires is established. SAME AUTHOR.

Afterward Maximinus withdraws the indulgence granted to Christians by the common agreement of the rulers, having procured embassies from cities requesting that Christians not be allowed to erect meeting-houses within their cities. Thereupon harsher violence was inflicted on them, until Maximinus was deterred by Constantine’s letters. SAME AUTHOR.

In this or the following year the cross appears in the sky to Constantine.

**312.** Consuls: Flavius Valerius Constantine Augustus II; Licinius Augustus II. SPARK. Ninth year completed; tenth begun. Second embassies of cities, with decrees against Christians. Maximinus’s rescripts to them, ordering Christians expelled from those cities and their territories, after May. A new persecution began, but only of mutilations, and was immediately calmed by Constantine’s threats and letters as he moved against Maxentius. Constantine crosses the Alps and defeats and routs Maxentius’s forces at Turin and elsewhere. At last, near Rome, on 27 October, a cross was shown him from heaven as a sign of victory, on the day before he joined battle; in that battle Maxentius himself was defeated on 28 October and drowned in the Tiber. Constantine enters the City as victor. The Senate decrees to Constantine the title of First Augustus. Maximinus’s first edict for peace. DODWELL.

Valeria, Galerius’s widow, was cast into exile by Maximinus’s order together with her mother Prisca, relegated to deserted Syrian wildernesses, and informed her father Diocletian of her misfortune through secret messengers. But when her father demanded her return, Maximinus refused. BALUZE.

At the same time statues of Maximian Herculius were removed by Constantine’s order; images of Diocletian too were taken down because he had been depicted with Herculius. Hence Diocletian’s grief, and shortly afterward, exhausted by hunger and anguish, he died on 3 December. SAME AUTHOR.

Maximinus secretly sends ambassadors to Maxentius at Rome and makes friendship with him. SAME AUTHOR.

The beginning of the indictions: either 1 or 24 September.

**313.** Consuls: Flavius Valerius Constantine III; Licinius Augustus III. SPARK. Tenth year completed; eleventh begun. Maximinus is defeated by Licinius at the Plain of Serenus on 30 April. The edict of Constantine and Licinius for peace is posted at Nicomedia on 13 June, at which point Lactantius ends this ten-year persecution, §48. Then Maximinus’s second edict in favour of Christians. DODWELL.

After affairs in the city had been settled, Constantine departed from Rome about 18 January and made for Milan, where he celebrated the marriage of his sister Constantia to Licinius. When this business was completed, Constantine returned to Gaul, Licinius to Illyricum. BALUZE.

Meanwhile Maximinus moves his army from Syria, intending to make war upon Licinius and occupy his provinces. Licinius meets him in Thrace. Battle is fought on 30 April in the plain called Serenus, namely between Hadrianople and Heraclea. Victory belonged to Licinius. SAME AUTHOR.

Diocletian dies in this year, perhaps in May.

Maximinus fled with the utmost speed to Nicomedia, thence into Cappadocia, and finally into Cilicia, where he perished at Tarsus by a pitiable and dreadful manner of death. SAME.

After Maximinus had been routed and put to flight, Licinius led his army across into Bithynia; and, entering Nicomedia on the Ides of June, he ordered an edict concerning the restoration of the Church to be posted, and also exhorted orally that the places of assembly be restored to their former condition.

Peace was granted to the Church after the ten-year war. SAME.

Licinius ordered Valerius, Candidianus, the son of Galerius Maximinus, Severianus, the son of Severus, and the children of Maximinus to be put to death. SAME.

**314.** Consuls: Volusianus II and Annianus.

Constantine’s first war against Licinius: Licinius was defeated at Cibalae in Pannonia on 31 October. They fought again at Mardia in Thrace, but with equal success.

Peace between Constantine and Licinius.

Valens is chosen Caesar by Licinius; afterwards, by the mutual agreement of the Augusti, he is expelled and deprived of his rank.

**315.** Consuls: Constantine IV and Licinius IV. Valeria, daughter of Diocletian, and Prisca, his wife, are beheaded at Thessalonica. In this year Lactantius published his book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*.

**317.** Consuls: Gallicanus and Bassus. Crispus and Constantine, sons of Constantine the Great, are created Caesars, as is Licinianus, son of Licinius. Constantius, another son of Constantine and Fausta, is born. At the close of this year, as we suppose, Lactantius is summoned from Nicomedia into Gaul.

**318.** Consuls: Licinius Augustus V and Crispus Caesar. [Col. 0189C]

**319.** Consuls: Constantine Augustus V and Licinius Junior Caesar. In this year Licinius Augustus removes Christians from his palace. Arius falls into heresy and is condemned in a council of one hundred bishops.

**320.** Consuls: Constantine Augustus VI and Constantius Caesar II. The Licinian persecution, according to Eusebius in the *Chronicle*. Crispus Caesar defeated the Franks and Alamanni in battle. In this or the following year Lactantius published his *Institutions*.

[Col. 0190A] **321.** Consuls: Crispus Caesar II and Constantine Caesar. Nazarius delivers at Rome a panegyric upon Constantine on the Kalends of March. The Donatists are expelled from Rome. Constantine promulgates an enactment concerning the observance of the Lord’s day.

**322.** Consuls: Petronius Probianus and Anicius Julianus. Constantine subdues the Sarmatians in Pannonia, where their king Rausimondus fell.

**323.** Consuls: Acilius Severus and Junius (or Vettius) Rufinus. Constantine’s second war against Licinius: on 3 July the latter is defeated by Constantine at Adrianople. Licinius is again defeated by Constantine on land near [Col. 0190B] Chrysopolis and Chalcedon, and at sea by Crispus Caesar in the Hellespont. Licinius flees to Nicomedia and begs pardon for the past, at the intercession of Constantia, his wife and Constantine’s sister. He is admitted to Constantine’s table and sent into exile at Thessalonica; there, after some months, his throat is bound with a noose because of the revolution he was plotting, while Martinianus, created Caesar by Licinius, is slaughtered in Cappadocia. (See Tillemont, vol. IV, *Emperors*, p. 195.) Constantius, son of Constantine, is chosen Caesar.

**324.** Consuls: Crispus Caesar III and Constantine Caesar III. Constantine writes to Arius in order to recall him from error.

**325.** Consuls: Anicius Faustus Paulinus and [Col. 0190C] P. Cejonius Julianus. The first ecumenical synod is convened at Nicaea in Bithynia, from 18 or 19 June until 25 August; Arius is condemned there. On 25 July Constantine celebrates his twentieth anniversary.

**326.** Consuls: Constantine Augustus VII and Constantius Caesar. Constantine goes to Rome; and about the month of July orders Crispus Caesar to be executed, on a charge of a false crime. Fausta, Constantine’s wife, is likewise condemned to death.

**362.** Consuls: Flavius Mamertinus and Flavius Nevitta. Julian’s persecution, while he was at Antioch, toward the end of October, when the image of Olympian Jupiter had burned, as is inferred from Ammianus, XXII. DODWELL.

[Col. 0189]

# LUCIUS CAECILIUS FIRMIANUS LACTANTIUS, BOOK ADDRESSED TO DONATUS THE CONFESSOR, ON THE DEATHS OF THE PERSECUTORS

[Note: [Col. 0189C] *Notes of Various Scholars on columns 189–190*

**To Donatus.** An eminent confessor of those times, who nine times endured various tortures for Christ’s name, having been held in prison for six years, [Col. 0190C] from which he was released in the final period of Galerius Maximianus, as is read below, chapters 16 and 25. BALUZE.

**On the Deaths of the Persecutors.** See our Dissertation [Col. 0191B] on the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*. Lactantius likewise used *deaths* in the plural above, *Institutions*, book V, chapter 20; and “from deaths,” book VII, chapter 10. Thus two deaths are set forth.

**“Which in his sight . . . have sought.”** Earlier editions read: “You pour them out throughout every hour of the whole day, and [those] of our other brethren, who,” etc. But from the surviving traces of letters we infer that the reading should be as we have indicated in the text.—In the Colbert manuscript the passage stands mutilated thus: *Quas in conspectu ejus cons . . . . . m . . . S Sim m qui glosa fessione sepit . . . . . pro fidei . . . . . rittis.* O. F. Fritzsche restored it in his edition of Lactantius’s works, already cited by us: “Which, standing in his sight, you are accustomed steadfastly to pour forth, and indeed also the prayers of the most holy martyrs, for their everlasting crown, by the merits of their faith.” Similarly, Lactantius says in the final words of his *Epitome of the Divine Institutions*: “that, with God as judge, he may obtain, **for the merits of his virtue**, either **the crown of faith** or the reward of immortality”; and in book VII, chapter 14: “they sought not immortality for themselves, but death through sins and lusts.”—**They sought** (*quaesierunt*): for “they acquired.” So too Lactantius, *Divine Institutions*, book I, chapter 20; book VII, chapter 14; and elsewhere. See below, note on chapter 18.]

(C, S)

## I

[Col. 0189C] The Lord has heard your prayers, dearest Donatus, [Col. 0190C] which you constantly pour forth in his sight every day, and those of our most beloved brethren, who by their glorious confession [Col. 0191A]

[Note: [Col. 0191C] *Notes of Various Scholars on columns 191–192*

**Will be added** (*addetur*). Thus in the manuscript, instead of *additur*; and that this is the proper reading here is confirmed by the preceding perfect tense, “has heard,” and the following words, “rises again” and “is built.” Yet the most learned Jean-Baptiste Cottelerius, *Monuments of the Greek Church*, vol. II, p. 528, suggested that one should read *atteritur* (“is crushed”), because of the neat antithesis between “is crushed” and “rises again”; but this is less satisfactory.

**The adversary.** That is, the devil; Lactantius so calls him in *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 1: “For that wrestler and **adversary** of ours—you know how cunning he is—regards as snares the things that can entice.” — O. F. Fritzsche: “Behold, all adversaries having been destroyed.”

**And restored throughout the world.** The manuscript lacks *and*, but the space for this syllable remains blank. It then reads “with peace restored throughout the world,” but through a scribal error, where *restituta* (“restored”) was written *restituto*.

**The Church, lately overthrown.** Lactantius says in *Divine Institutions*, book V, chapter 2, “to overthrow wisdom”; and in chapter 4, “I should overthrow all . . . with one assault.”

**The temple of God, which had been overthrown by the impious, is built by the Lord’s mercy.** The temple at Nicomedia, of which Lactantius speaks in chapter 13 and in *Institutions*, book V, chapter 2: “When I had been summoned to teach rhetoric in Bithynia, it happened that at the same time **God’s temple was overthrown**.” Do you see the same expression? Cuper and Baluze, however, in the second edition understand “temple” as the Christian community; yet one cannot say of a society of believers being restored that it “is built.” This verb is intelligible only of material construction, not of a congregation of believers and its union in Christ under its chief shepherd.

**Rulers.** Constantine and Licinius. See their decree below, no. 48.

**Who annulled the wicked and bloody rule of the tyrants.** Lactantius, *Divine Institutions*, book V, chapter 11: “The wicked rescript of rulers”; book VII, chapter 26: “You who were able in true piety to **annul** the evil counsels of others.”

**Of the past** (*transacti*). Colbert manuscript: *trisansaru*; Buneau: *tristi nefarii*. O. F. Fritzsche agrees with us in reading *transacti*. Shortly after, where the manuscript has *postatae*, Buneau reads *post atrae*; we, with O. F. Fritzsche, preferred *post tantae*.

**By prayers.** We added this word in order to bring out the meaning more clearly.

**And the afflicted.** But the manuscript reads “that the afflicted.”

**Raises up. Behold now.** Other editions read, “He raised up. Now.” But on closer and more scrupulous inspection of the manuscript codex, the reading is “He raises up. Behold now,” which is more elegant.

**Will wipe away; and those who.** Earlier editions have “wiped away”; but with light brought close, we read “will wipe away,” and *luii*, etc., which final word the editors correctly interpret as *qui* (“who”).

**Those who had struggled against.** The manuscript reads *illustrati*; but by changing one letter I read *illuctati*, as though one said “those who had opposed.” The latter word appeared in earlier editions: “those who had struggled against God lie low.” Thus I have restored it. The participle *illuctans* occurs in Statius. As to the construction of this word, below, chapter 18, one also finds *luctari* with the dative; likewise *reluctari* in chapter 11, and *obluctari* in Virgil, *Aeneid* III. Lactantius often uses *luctari*, *reluctari*, *luctatio*, *eluctatio*, and *eluctari*: book II, chapter 20; book III, chapter 11 twice; book IV, chapters 25 and 30; book V, chapter 21; book VI, chapters 18, 23, and 24. Moreover, the word “lie low” most aptly corresponds to the preceding “had struggled against.” In the same sense our author said in *Divine Institutions*, book VII, chapter 26: “Those who wished to abolish the worship of the heavenly and singular God lie low, overthrown.”

**The righteous.** That is, Christians. Lactantius calls them this in book I, chapter 1, and book V, chapter 11.

**They tortured to the utmost** (*excarnificaverunt*). Thus in the manuscript; other editions also have *excarnificaverunt*. We judged that nothing should be altered.

**Though late indeed.** The manuscript corruptly reads *Seruit . . . . . Destulerat*. In the first edition and those following it: *profuderunt . . . . . Distulerat*. The remaining words had been omitted; Nourry was the first correctly to restore them from the manuscript. O. F. Fritzsche prints: “Late indeed.”

**That posterity might learn.** Thus the manuscript codex reads; therefore after *quibus* (“by which”) I deleted *et* (“and”), which appears in all printed editions.

**And that he is the same avenger, namely, [one who inflicts] worthy punishments, etc.** We judged that the passage should be restored thus; for the manuscript reads: *et eumdem vicucem digna vid . . . supplitia*, etc. But the first edition had: “and that the same death [inflicts] the proud and impious with worthy vengeance”; these words do not agree with the manuscript writing. The text of other editions is therefore exceedingly corrupted, and here we bring it into conformity with the manuscript. In place of *Vicucem* we supplied *Vindicem* (“Avenger”), because at the beginning of *Divine Institutions*, book V, chapter 21, one reads: “God himself will be the **avenger**.”

**It pleased [me] to bear written witness concerning their end.** The manuscript reads: *de quo exitu . . . . . tificari placuit*. But since the phrase is incomplete, we restored it thus: *quorum* (“of whom”) in place of *quo*, and after *exitu* added *scripto tes.* (“to bear witness in writing”), because this little book ought to instruct both exiles or those removed afar and posterity. [Col. 0193A] Nourry restored: “to bear open witness concerning their end,” etc. But *openly* is less suitable; *in writing* is more fitting in that place. *Exitus* (“end”) is equivalent to “death.” Thus below, chapter 50, near the middle: “when the news of his death was heard, he immediately fled.”]

have sought for themselves an everlasting crown by the merits of their faith. Behold, to all these things the adversary will be added; and, peace having been restored throughout the world, the Church lately overthrown rises again, and with greater glory the temple of God, which had been overthrown by the impious, is built by the mercy of the Lord.

For God has raised up rulers who have annulled the wicked and bloody rule of the tyrants and provided for humankind, so that now, as though the cloud of the past time had been scattered, a pleasant and serene peace may gladden the minds of all. Now, after the violent whirlwinds of so great a storm, the calm air and the longed-for light have shone forth. Now God, appeased by the prayers of his servants, raises up with heavenly aid those who lie low and are afflicted. Behold now, with the conspiracy of the impious extinguished, he will wipe away the tears of those who mourn; and those who had struggled against God lie low; those who had overthrown the holy temple fell by a greater ruin; those who tortured the righteous to the utmost poured out their guilty souls under heavenly blows and deserved torments—late indeed, but grievously and deservedly.

For God had delayed their punishments, so that he might furnish great and wonderful examples in them, by which posterity might learn both that God is one and that he is the same avenger, namely, one who inflicts worthy punishments upon the impious and persecutors. It pleased me to bear written witness concerning their end, [Col. 0193A]

[Note: [Col. 0193B] *Notes of Various Scholars on columns 193–194*

**Those who were removed far away.** The manuscript reads only *procul moti fuerunt* (“were moved far away”), that is, driven into exile or banished; therefore I judged that the letter *a* should be supplied, so that it reads *amoti* (“removed”). Thus a clearer sense emerges. So in Tacitus, “to be removed to an island” means “to be driven into exile.”

**Those who will be hereafter.** The manuscript reads only *p . . . turi sunt*. We supplied the words according to the space displayed in the manuscript. Others read “those who will be after us”; others, “those who will live after us.” But we chose simple words which represented the best sense in accordance with the manuscript’s space.

**His power and majesty.** And below, chapter 5: “Against the majesty of the singular God.” Lactantius, *Divine Institutions*, book I, chapter 1: “You have known the majesty of the singular and true God,” etc.; book III, chapter 4; book II, chapter 1: “to assert the majesty of the singular God”; twice, book IV, chapter 26: “to interpret the power and majesty of the singular God”; [Col. 0193C] book VI, chapter 9: “he recounts the power and majesty of the singular God”; book V, chapters 15 and 22; book VII frequently; book IV again, chapter 29; book VI, chapter 17; *On the Anger of God*, chapter 20: “having cast aside earthly cults, they acknowledge the majesty of the singular God”; *Epitome*, chapters 3 and 4; and elsewhere throughout.

**In cutting down and destroying, etc.** The manuscript reads *in e . . . . . dis delendisque*. After the letter *e*, the middle portion of the letter *x* appears; hence we supplied *exscindendis* (“cutting down”), a word our author uses below, chapter 2, near the middle: “Nero sprang forth to cut down the heavenly temple and destroy righteousness.” Or supply *extinguendis* (“extinguishing”); at the beginning of chapter 46 he joins the expressions thus: “that he might extinguish the name of Christians and utterly destroy it.”

**The Most High God.** And in chapter 47. You will encounter these words a hundred times among Lactantius’s writings: *Divine Institutions*, book I, chapter 1: “The Most High God raised you to the blessed summit of imperial power”; likewise chapter 5 and chapter 6; book II, chapter 1; book III, chapter 11; book IV, chapter 4, twice in chapter 6, chapters 10, 13, and 16; book VII, chapter 27; *Epitome*, chapters 12, 28, 43, and 49; twice in *On the Anger of God*, chapter 2; and elsewhere throughout. Indeed, there can be no doubt that these epithets too, *singular* and *most high*, among others (says Baudry), indicate that Lactantius is the author of this little book.

**May show.** Perhaps one should read “has shown”; see what precedes.

**It is therefore useful, if.** The manuscript reads only *Vincta . . . . est, si*, from which we formed the sense in this manner: “It is therefore useful, if,” etc.; and this accords with the manuscript’s space.

**Who the persecutors may have been.** The manuscript has *qui fuerint . . . . ecutores*, with four letters missing before *ecutores*. I therefore think that the passage should be restored: “who the persecutors may have been.” The Paris edition of 1710 has *fuerunt* (“were”), contrary to the manuscript codex, and it cannot stand with the following *vindicaverit* (“may have exacted vengeance”). That edition reads “were the authors,” but incorrectly. For the manuscript clearly writes *fuerint*; then it wrongly writes *auctores*, when the lower part of a *p* and the upper part of an *s* are visible. [Col. 0194A] Therefore one must read *persecutores* (“persecutors”). See the specimen printed above.

[Col. 0194B]

**Upon them . . . may have exacted vengeance.** Our Lactantius, *Divine Institutions*, book II, chapter 4: “They exacted vengeance upon the sacrilegious”; and book IV, chapter 17: “I shall exact vengeance upon him.”

**Jesus Christ . . . was tortured.** That is, fixed to the cross. Lactantius employs the word in the same sense in *Divine Institutions*, book I, chapter 16: “having been subjected by men to an extraordinary punishment and tortured”; book IV, chapter 18, and *Epitome of the Divine Institutions*, chapter 18: “and they tortured him in great humiliation”; book IV, chapter 22: “that, having been killed as mortal . . . God was tortured by men”; and *Epitome*, chapter 18: “Since therefore he sits at God’s right hand, he shall tread down his enemies who tortured him.” So too book IV, chapter 16, *cruciando* (“by torturing”), in the same sense.

**After the tenth day before the Kalends of April.** The manuscript has *Aprilium*, not *Aprilis*. Lactantius, *Divine Institutions*, book IV, chapter 10: “Under the consulship of the two Gemini, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, the Jews fixed Christ to the cross”; which is the same thing. See above, note on book IV at the end of chapter 10. It is an elliptical expression, which [Col. 0194C] one may supply as “after the rising of the tenth day before the Kalends of April,” or “after that day had begun.” Thus Christ’s words, “After three days I shall rise,” Mark 8:31, are explained by most learned persons as “on the third day,” or “after the third day has come.” In part from JEAN COLUMBUS.

But “after the tenth day before the Kalends of April” and “before the tenth day before the Kalends of April” are the same as “on the tenth day before the Kalends”; this we shall demonstrate abundantly from Lactantius himself and others later in our Dissertation on this book. Do not hesitate to consult it.

**Under the consulship of the two Gemini.** He assigns this in *Institutions*, book IV, chapter 10, to the fifteenth year of Tiberius. This indeed agrees with the consulship of the two Gemini. But observe, reader, how monstrously he is thereby mistaken. Tiberius began the fifteenth year of his reign in the year 28 of the common era. In this very fifteenth year of Tiberius, John the Baptist, as we read in Luke 3:1, 2, 3, began to preach repentance. According to our Lactantius, it was Tiberius’s fifteenth year . . . Therefore Christ, baptized on 6 January under the consulship [Col. 0194D] of the two Gemini in the year 29 of the common era, and suffering on 23 March of the following year, accomplished in no more than two and a half months all that is reported from his baptism to his death. This is monstrous to say, although it was incautiously asserted by many other ancients and inserted into the Idatian Fasti. For what, then, will become of the four Passovers by which the Saviour’s ministry is distinguished in the Gospels? And so forth. Thus the most learned Nicolas Toinard of Orléans.

**Arrest.** You will find *comprehensi* (“having been arrested”) and *comprehendat* (“may arrest”) twice in the same sense, *Divine Institutions*, book VII, chapter 17, and below, chapter 15.

**And he appointed and instructed them for the preaching of his doctrine and teaching.** Lactantius, *Divine Institutions*, book IV, chapter 21, and *Epitome*, chapter 47: “But, having arranged the preaching of the Gospel and of his name for his disciples”; or, according to the Juenian and Gothic manuscript codices, “having arranged evangelical teaching for his disciples”; and shortly after, “they preached.”]

so that all who had been removed far away, or who would be hereafter, might know to what extent the Most High God would show his power and majesty in cutting down and destroying the enemies of his name. It is therefore useful, if I set forth from the beginning, from the time when the Church was established, who the persecutors may have been and by what punishments the severity of the heavenly Judge may have exacted vengeance upon them.

## II

In the final period of Tiberius Caesar, as [Col. 0194A] we read written, our Lord Jesus Christ was tortured by the Jews, after the tenth day before the Kalends of April, under the consulship of the two Gemini. When he had risen on the third day, he gathered together his disciples, whom fear of his arrest had driven into flight; and, having remained with them forty days, he opened their hearts and interpreted the Scriptures, which until that time had been obscure and veiled. He appointed and instructed them for the preaching of his doctrine and teaching, establishing the solemn discipline of the New Testament.

[Col. 0195A]

[Note: [Col. 0195A] *Notes of Various Scholars on columns 195–196*

**Having been fulfilled** (*repleto*). This is more easily read in the manuscript than *expleto* (“having been completed”), which appears in printed editions; therefore the editors ought not to have changed anything.

**He snatched [him] up into heaven.** Lactantius, *Divine Institutions*, book VII, [Col. 0195B] chapter 17: “He shall be snatched up into heaven.”

**Matthias and Paul having been taken in the place of Judas the betrayer.** Do not infer from these words that Paul, together with Matthias, was substituted for Judas by the apostles. Lactantius merely intended—writing somewhat carelessly—to indicate that two others performed the apostolic office in Judas’s place: Matthias, chosen by lot (Acts 1:26), and Paul, chosen by Christ himself. TOINARD.

**To preach the Gospel.** Lactantius, book IV, chapter 21: “Peter and Paul preached at Rome.”

**The Lord, their master.** Lactantius, book IV, chapter 21: “In the name of God the Master,” and chapter 26, as well as book VI, chapter 8; and elsewhere throughout.

**And for twenty-five years, etc.** From the consulship of the two Gemini, or from the year 29 of the common Christian era, when, according to Lactantius’s hypothesis, the apostles preached the Gospel everywhere after Pentecost, twenty-five full years extend to 13 October in the year 54, when Nero succeeded Claudius; but from the year 33 of the Christian era, when Christ actually suffered, to 58, there are twenty-five years.

Perhaps from these twenty-five years, which belong equally to the preaching of all the apostles, arose the opinion of the twenty-five years attributed by certain ancients and an innumerable host of moderns to Saint Peter the Apostle in the Roman see . . . But if it were permissible to depart from the common opinion, ingrained in human minds, I would gladly prefer Lactantius’s: that is, I would readily grant that Peter preached the Gospel at Rome, not under Tiberius Claudius, as people commonly suppose, but under Nero Claudius. For once this most true opinion, as I think, has been established, the entire dispute is immediately settled without any detriment to the authority of the Roman pontiff. For it was not a long succession of years during which Peter was bishop of Rome that established the primacy of that Church, but Peter’s person, who placed his chair there and strengthened and confirmed it with his blood. From BALUZE.

**They laid the foundations of the Church.** That is, “they placed”; *mittere* (“to send”) for “to place.” Surveyors frequently use it: *limitem mittere*, “to set a boundary-marker”; *mittere murum aut vallum*, “to set a wall or rampart,” in Lampridius, *Life of Septimius Severus*. So also in Cicero, *Against Verres* I, *mittere in possessionem*, “to put into possession”; in Seneca, *mittere in Acta*, “to enter in the records”; in Livy, *mittere urbes in servitutem*, “to place cities in servitude”; in Statius, *corpus mittere sepulcro*, “to place a body in the tomb.” In Sidonius Apollinaris, book II, letter 11: “the foundations of a striving friendship once laid.” In the old translator of our Vulgate: “they put new wine into new wineskins,” etc., Matthew 9:17 and 15:26.—“They laid the foundations of the Church.” “What author of good Latin,” says Nourry, “ever said *mittere fundamenta*?” Certainly not Lactantius, who wrote better: “they everywhere cast the foundations of the Church.” Columbus, however, correctly upheld the phrase *fundamenta mittere*. Jerome, *Life of Hilarion*: “they did not permit him to depart before he should lay out the plan of the future [Col. 0196A] Church”; and Ambrose, *On Duties*, book I, chapter 29: “Behold, I place a stone in the foundation of Zion”—that is, Christ as the foundation of the Church—which he immediately explains: “Paul laid Christ as the foundation.” Also the translator of Irenaeus, book III, chapter 28: “I place a precious stone in the foundations of Zion.” So too Cyprian, Erasmus’s book II *Against the Jews*, chapter 16, where Pamelius has: “I place into the foundations.” Curtius also, book V, section 4: “the foundations of the towers were sunk thirty feet into the earth.” BUNEAU.

**And when Nero was now ruling, Peter came to Rome.** Many assert two arrivals of Peter in the city of Rome, under Claudius and Nero; others acknowledge only one, under Nero; while certain heterodox enemies of the Apostolic and Roman Church deny both. They have been very solidly refuted by men of the same religion, John Pearson in his posthumous works and Samuel Basnage, *Historical Exercises*, on the year 44, no. 25. TOINARD.

**He converted many to righteousness.** Thus below he says “to destroy righteousness,” that is, the religion and worship of the true God. Lactantius says in the same sense, book V, chapter 7: “Righteousness was indeed restored to earth, but assigned to few; it is nothing other than the pious and religious worship of the one God”; and book V, chapter 12: “as righteousness gains strength”; book VII, chapters 16 and 26; in the Epilogue to Constantine: “The Most High God raised you to restore the dwelling-place of Righteousness”; and book I, chapter 1: “Through whom . . . righteousness and wisdom have been restored.”

**And established for God a faithful and stable temple.** Below, concerning Nero: “He sprang forth to destroy the heavenly temple and abolish righteousness”; and chapter 15: “For Constantius . . . kept unharmed the true temple of God, which is in human beings.” Lactantius, *Divine Institutions*, book IV, chapter 14: “The true temple of God, which is not in walls but in the heart and faith of people who believe in him and are called faithful”; and the following chapter: “The eternal and immortal temple of God”; and chapter 24: “that it may have root and foundation, and remain stable and fixed among people.” Also book IV, chapter 10: “that he might establish a temple for God and teach righteousness.” **Faithful temple.** Here and below “heavenly temple” means the Christian religion or the Christian assembly, as is correctly interpreted from the accompanying words “faithful” and “heavenly.”

**An accursed and harmful tyrant.** Thus below, chapter 4: “The accursed beast Decius.” *Nocens* means wicked and impious. The word *execrabilis* is frequent in Lactantius. See book I, chapter 21; book III, chapter 18; book VI, chapters 17 and 23; book VII, chapter 16, etc.; *Epitome*, chapter 63.

**To destroy the heavenly temple.** Our Lactantius says in *Divine Institutions*, book III, chapter 26, “to cut out vices”; book VI, chapter 15, “they utterly cut out vices”; book V, chapter 3, “to utterly cut out truth”; and *On the Anger of God*, chapter 17, “they wished utterly to cut it out.”

**And to abolish righteousness.** That is, the Christian religion and the worship of the true God.

**The first of all to persecute God’s servants.** So Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 5; Saint Augustine, book II *Against the Letters of Petilian*, chapter 92; Sulpicius Severus, book II, speaking of Nero: “He proved worthy to be the first to begin persecution against Christians.” After *omnium* (“of all”), Lactantius should, with Eusebius, have added *imperatorum* (“emperors”), or “since the Church was established.” For the martyrdoms of Saints John [Col. 0197A] the Baptist, James, and Stephen had preceded, at the time when, according to Acts chapter 8, there was a great persecution at Jerusalem. In the Colbert manuscript, *persecutos* occurs instead of *persecutus*, incorrectly.]

When he had completed that office, a whirlwind of cloud enveloped him and, taking him from the sight of men, snatched him up into heaven. Then the disciples, who were eleven at that time, having taken Matthias and Paul in place of Judas the betrayer, dispersed through the whole earth to preach the Gospel, as the Lord, their master, had commanded them; and for twenty-five years, until the beginning of Nero’s reign, they laid the foundations of the Church in every province and city.

And when Nero was now ruling, Peter came to Rome; and, having performed certain miracles which he did by the power of God himself, granted to him by God, he converted many to righteousness and established for God a faithful and stable temple. When this was reported to Nero, and he perceived that not only at Rome but everywhere a great multitude was daily abandoning the worship of idols and, rejecting antiquity, passing over to a new religion, he, being an accursed and harmful tyrant, sprang forth to destroy the heavenly temple and abolish righteousness. The first of all to persecute God’s servants, Peter [Col. 0197A]

[Note: [Col. 0197B] *Notes of Various Scholars on columns 197–198*

**Yet he did not go unpunished.** Thus the Colbert manuscript has *habuit* (“he had”), as also below at the beginning of chapter 30, where the same manuscript likewise reads *habuit impune*. At the latter place the Paris edition of 1710, and at the former earlier editions, substituted *abiit* (“he went away”); but wrongly. Lactantius uses the same expression in *Epitome*, chapter 53: “Nor did anyone go unpunished who injured God”; and chapter 55: “Why do the Egyptians go unpunished, who worship cattle and beasts of every kind?” *Habuit* is written between the lines in the manuscript, but entirely in the same hand.

**For God regarded the affliction of his people.** Suetonius: “When Nero was sought by the Senate for punishment, fleeing from the palace, at the fourth milestone from the City, on the suburban estate of his freedman between the Salarian and Nomentan roads, he killed himself at the age of thirty-two.” This occurred in the year of Christ 68, on 9 June. TOINARD.

**He suddenly appeared nowhere, etc.** Saint Augustine, *City of God*, book XX, chapter 19: “Some hold that Nero himself will rise again and will be Antichrist; others think that he was not even killed, but rather removed so as to be thought killed, and hidden alive in the vigor of the age in which he was when he was believed to have perished, until in his own time he is revealed and restored to the kingdom.” It was the opinion of many even in the third and fourth centuries that Nero would come before the end of the age, and that he himself would either be Antichrist or rage in the West at the same times at which Antichrist would rage in the East. This was also the opinion of Saint Martin of Tours and Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogues* 2 and *Sacred History* II. “But great,” says Augustine in the passage cited above, “is the presumption of those who think this.” Against the opinion of Lactantius and Sulpicius is the account given by Plutarch in the *Life of Galba*; above all, what Suetonius says, book VI, chapter 50: “He was buried at an expense of two hundred thousand [sesterces], in white coverings interwoven with gold, which he had used on the Kalends of January. His nurses Ecloge and Alexandria, together with his concubine Acte, laid his remains in the monument of the Domitii, visible from the Campus Martius, situated on the hill of the gardens. In that monument is a sarcophagus of porphyry marble, surmounted by an altar of Luna marble and enclosed with Thasian stone.” TOINARD.

**So evil a beast.** He uses the same expression below, chapter 4, writing of tyrants; and in chapters 9, concerning Maximian Galerius: “This beast possessed a natural barbarity and savagery”; and in chapters 16, 25, 32, 39, and 52. In *Divine Institutions*, book V, chapter 11: “That is the true beast,” etc.; and chapter 23: “Afterward God promises that he will exact vengeance upon them and exterminate evil beasts from the earth”; also book VI, chapter 9. He also calls them wild beasts in book V, chapter 11, and book VI, chapter 17.

**Madmen.** The manuscript has *deleri*.

**They believe that he was removed and preserved alive.** A fable whose origin is not obscure. For there were several false Neros: the first on the island of Cythnus, Tacitus, *Histories* II, chapter 8; the second, named Terentius Maximus, Zonaras under Titus; the third under Domitian, twenty years after Nero’s death, Suetonius, at the end of *Nero*.
