For various reports circulated concerning his end, many inventing and believing that he was alive. BUNEAU.

**The Sibyl saying.** Lactantius is accustomed to cite the Sibylline books in this way, though he knew that they belonged not to one Sibyl but to several. Thus he himself says in *Divine Institutions*, book I, chapter 6: “There are separate books belonging to each of them; because they bear the name of Sibyl, they are thought to be the work of one [woman]. But we too shall speak indiscriminately of ‘the Sibyl’ wherever we make use of their testimonies.” These passages seem to be from books V and VI of the Sibylline Oracles. See Baluze’s notes. **From the borders.** The most learned Janson van Almelove says that *terrae* (“of the earth”) should be added, which he thinks has fallen out.

**May persecute.** Thus the manuscript, but in abbreviated letters; this agrees better with the preceding clause.

**Therefore it is permissible to believe.** I restored this reading, observing very carefully the manuscript writing, in which only *fas* (“permissible”) is read quite fittingly; a space of five or six letters precedes it, whence I supplied *itaque* (“therefore”). This word can fill the space. Other editions have *nefas est credere* (“it is impious to believe”). But the reading we follow seems to me more consonant in the text with the manuscript and with the author’s subsequent words.

**Two.** The manuscript has “two [feminine],” but wrongly.

**Into the last times, and the beginning of Christ.** After “last” at least two words have been erased in the manuscript. But since, upon careful inspection of the writing, the final three letters of *atque* (“and”) can be read, I thought that *tempora atque* should be supplied. The two prophets mentioned here are Moses and Elijah.—**Into the last . . . beginning of Christ.** Into the final age. “The beginning of Christ” seems to mean the beginning of the millennium, which Lactantius maintained in various places. CELLARIUS.—**Into the last . . . beginning.** Two or three words have been erased there, according to Nourry. Whether these things are to be understood of the millennium is uncertain, because the passage is defective; and Baudry doubts it because “everlasting” follows. BUNEAU.

**Which the Sibyls foretell will come to pass.** After *coeperit* (“shall have begun”), about ten letters are missing in the manuscript, down to *um pronuntiant*. I thought they could be supplied by these words, which in abbreviated letters may fill that space. Other editions have *pronuntiant* (“they declare”), a word which may be read in abbreviation as *praenuntiant* (“they foretell”). Concerning these Sibylline prophecies, see *Institutions*, book VII, chapters 15–20.

**As a forerunner, etc.** Here the manuscript reads only *cursor* (“runner”), and three or four letters are missing before that word, which we supplied as *ut praecursor* (“as a forerunner”), or *qui praecursor* (“who [is] a forerunner”).

**Of the human race.** In the manuscript the final two letters of *humani* and the first two of *generis* are missing; thus they were not difficult to supply.

**Some.** The manuscript reads *aliquod* (“some [neuter]”), a frequent error in that book.]

Another tyrant, no less great, arose. “Arose,” that is, he began to reign: Domitian, the last of the twelve Caesars. TOINARD.—Domitian was called “Bald Nero” by Juvenal; Tertullian, in the *Apologeticum*, ch. 5, calls him “a portion of Nero in cruelty”; and Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* III.17, “the successor of Nero’s impiety and hatred toward God.” BALUZ.

“Unjust.” This can be read in the manuscript; the other editions have “hated” [Col. 0199B].

[He] crucified [Peter] and killed Paul. Yet he did not go unpunished; for God regarded the affliction of His people. Cast down from the summit of empire and hurled from on high, the powerless tyrant suddenly appeared nowhere, so that not even a place of burial on earth was visible for so evil a beast. Hence certain madmen believe that he was removed and kept alive, citing the Sibyl’s saying that the matricidal fugitive would come from the ends of the earth; so that, since he was the first persecutor, he might also be the last to persecute, and might precede the coming of Antichrist. Thus they think it permissible to believe that, just as [Col. 0198A] two Prophets were transferred alive to the last times and to the holy and everlasting beginning of Christ when He begins to descend—as the Sibyls foretell will happen—so Nero too will come, to be the devil’s forerunner and the advance herald of one coming for the devastation of the earth and the overthrow of the human race.

III. After him, when some years had intervened, another tyrant, no less great, arose; and although he exercised unjust [Col. 0199A]

[Note: [Col. 0199B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 199–200]

“He pressed upon the necks of his subjects.” Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* V.5: “They would press only upon things hidden away”; and ch. 9: “They press upon them with all the strength of their butchery”; VII.19: “Having captured the world, he will press upon it with great armies of brigands.”

“Handed over into the hands of his enemies, he paid the penalty.” Domitian began to rage in February A.D. 94. He was killed in A.D. 96, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October (that is, 18 September), as is universally agreed. TOINARD.—Likewise Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* VII, concerning Antichrist: “And, captured, he shall at last pay the penalty for his crimes.” The same, *Epitome*, ch. 68.

“Killed at home.” We preferred to read this, with the most learned Cuper, rather than, with the others, “killed, at home.”

“The memory of his name was erased.” And below, ch. 52, “and he erased [it] from the earth.” Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.12: “Domitian had appropriated October under his own name; but it was decided that the ill-omened word should be erased from every bronze or stone.” BALUZ.

“Since he had constructed many remarkable works.” Suetonius, *Domitian*: “He restored very many and very extensive works destroyed by fire, including the Capitol, which had again burned; but all under his own name alone and with no memory of the former founder.” BALUZ.

“Neither of his images nor of his inscriptions,” etc. Eusebius says the same, *Ecclesiastical History* III.20. Suetonius: “The Senate was so delighted that, crowding eagerly into a packed Curia, it did not refrain from tearing the dead man with the most insulting and bitter kind of acclamations; it ordered ladders brought in, his shields and images removed before its eyes, and there fastened to the ground; finally it decreed that his inscriptions everywhere be erased and all memory abolished.” FROM BALUZ.

“Should leave.” Manuscripts: “should leave” [plural].

“Most severe.” The manuscript has *gravissime*, with a capital initial letter and a preceding full stop, wrongly.

“With the tyrant’s acts annulled.” See above, note on ch. 1. [Col. 0199D] “Not merely.” Thus the manuscript, with abbreviated letters *ttm*; printed editions wrongly have “not only.”

“The Church restored.” Dio, in Xiphilinus, relates that Nerva acquitted all those accused of impiety toward the gods, recalled exiles to their homeland, and by an additional edict forbade anyone thereafter to accuse another either of impiety or of the Jewish sect—thus they then called the Christian religion. On that occasion the apostle John, whom Domitian had banished to the island of Patmos, was released from exile and returned to Ephesus, as Eusebius reports from Clement of Alexandria, Book III, ch. 23.

“And.” Heumann thinks this conjunction should be deleted, so that the sentence may flow better.

“Good emperors.” Though pagans: namely Nerva, Trajan, the Antonines, and so on, who did not promulgate edicts against Christians. Lactantius, at the end of Book VII of the *Divine Institutes*, to Constantine: “Since you alone of all men have arisen to furnish outstanding examples of virtue and holiness, by which you not only equal, but even—what is greatest—surpass, the glory of the ancient emperors, whom fame nevertheless numbers among the good,” etc. On the good emperors, who both permitted our people freedom of belief and used their service in the palace and provinces, raising them to the highest dignities, see Eusebius at the beginning of Book VIII of the *Ecclesiastical History*. BALUZ.—“Good emperors.” Zosimus I.7: “From this time good men” (*ἐντεῦθεν ἄνδρες ἀγαθοὶ*) “obtained the principate—Nerva, Trajan, and after him Hadrian and Antoninus Pius, and that pair of brothers, Verus and Lucius—and corrected many abuses.” Lactantius, VII.16, in the notes, has an excellent passage: “Whom fame nevertheless numbers among the good, whom you not only equal, but even—what is greatest—surpass.” BUN.

“Suffering no assaults of enemies.” That is, almost none, or none of serious consequence. “She stretched out her hands toward East and West.” Lactantius, [Col. 0200C] *Divine Institutes* VII.15: “Rome … after Carthage had been overthrown, stretched out her hands over the entire world by land and sea.” *Epitome* 51: “She stretched out her wings toward East and West.”

“No corner of the lands was so remote that the religion of God had not penetrated it.” Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* IV.26: “Rather, the cross was chosen, signifying that He would be so conspicuous and so exalted that all nations from every part of the world would come together alike to know and worship Him. Finally, there is no nation so barbarous, no region so remote, to which either His Passion or the sublimity of His majesty is unknown.” BALUZ.

“Where not.” In the manuscript, *co n*.

“Finally, a nation.” In the manuscript, *denique di natio*.

“No nation finally,” etc. In the manuscript, after *denique*, stands *di natio*. It is either *mundi* (“of the world”) or *Dei* (“of God”); BALUZ says that the word, as superfluous, ought to be deleted.

“After many years the execrable beast Decius arose,” [Col. 0200D] etc. That Decius raged as soon as he became emperor is also taught by the *Paschal Chronicle* in these words: “At the beginning of Decius’s reign, a persecution against the Christians having been stirred up …” It is established that Decius perished near the end of A.D. 251 at Abrittium or Abrittum, in battle against the Carpi, and reigned more than two years: namely, from some point between 17 June and 19 October A.D. 249 until the end of November A.D. 251, and thus two years and about five months. TOINARD.

“For who but an evil man persecutes righteousness?” By “righteousness” understand here the righteous people, the people of God, the servants of God.

“He had been raised to that sovereign height.” And below, ch. 18, “the lofty height,” namely imperial rank. Likewise Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* VII.26, near the end, in the epilogue to Emperor Constantine: “The providence of the highest divinity has raised you to the sovereign height.” Do you see [the similarity] of the author of the two works?—[[Col. 0200] This break marks the end of column 200. There is no continuation of this note on column 201.]]

rule, nevertheless he pressed upon the necks of his subjects for the longest possible time and reigned securely, until he stretched forth impious hands against the Lord. But after he was, at the prompting of demons, incited to persecute the righteous people, then, handed over into the hands of his enemies, he paid the penalty. Nor was it sufficient for vengeance that he was killed: even at home the memory of his name was erased. For although he had constructed many remarkable works, although he had built the Capitol and other famous monuments, the Senate pursued his name so thoroughly that it left no trace either of his images or of his inscriptions, branding him even after death, by the most severe decrees, with a mark for everlasting disgrace. Therefore, after the tyrant’s acts had been annulled, not merely was the Church restored to its former condition [Col. 0200A], but it shone forth far more brightly and flourishingly; and in the times that followed, when many good emperors held the helm and governance of the Roman Empire, it suffered no assaults of enemies and stretched out its hands toward East and West. Thus there was now no corner of the lands so remote that the religion of God had not penetrated it; nor any nation living by manners so savage that, upon accepting the worship of God, it did not grow gentle for works of righteousness. But afterward the long peace was broken.

IV. For after many years the execrable beast Decius arose, to harass the Church. For who but an evil man persecutes righteousness? And as though he had been raised to that sovereign height for this very purpose, he immediately began to rage against God, so that he might immediately fall. For he set out against the Carpi, who at that time occupied Dacia and Moesia; and, immediately surrounded by barbarians and destroyed with a great part of his army, he could not even be honored with burial. But stripped and naked, as befitted an enemy of God, he lay as fodder for wild beasts and birds.

V. Not long afterward Valerian too, seized by a rage not unlike this, directed impious hands against God and shed much righteous blood, though for a short time. But God inflicted upon him a new and extraordinary kind of punishment [Col. 0201B], so that he might be an example for posterity that the adversaries [Col. 0202A] of God always receive a recompense worthy of their crime. Captured by the Persians, he lost not only the empire which he had used insolently, but also the freedom which he had taken from others, and lived most shamefully in slavery. For Sapor, king of Persia, who had captured him, whenever he wished to mount either a carriage or a horse, ordered the Roman to bend down for him and present his back; and, setting his foot upon Valerian’s back, he said that this was the true kind of triumph, reproaching him with laughter—not the kind which Romans painted on tablets or walls. Thus he, most deservedly triumphed over, lived for some time, so that for a long while the Roman name might be a mockery and derision to barbarians. This too was added to his punishment: although [Col. 0202B] he had a son who was emperor, he found no avenger for his captivity and was not reclaimed at all.

[Note: [Col. 0203B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 203–204]

“Utmost.” Manuscript: *extremaeme*, wrongly.

“His skin was torn away.” Thus the manuscript, but wrongly. *Diripere* means to plunder: to plunder fields or cities. Here I would prefer, with the most learned Nicolaus Heinsius, *derepta* (“stripped away”). *Deripere* means to pull off, remove, as he shows in his notes on Ovid, from this verse of the *Metamorphoses*, 388:

> “The skin was stripped away over the uppermost limbs of the crying man.”

“And he was not reclaimed at all.” The most learned Nurrius extends this passage too far. But Pollio, contrary to the opinion of our Caecilius, presents three letters in which Kings Betsoldus and Artabandes demanded Valerian’s freedom from Sapor. Therefore these letters seem to have been wholly unknown to Caecilius, unless one can establish that his words mean nothing else than that Valerian was not reclaimed by any Roman name or Roman subject. What if one explains it most simply of the son, of whom alone the preceding passage spoke, so that the pronoun is understood, as often: “he found no avenger [for him], nor was he reclaimed [by him].” BUN.

“Is.” This word is not read in the manuscript; there is only a certain small stroke.

“Most illustrious triumph.” Manuscript: *Karissimi*.

“Displayed.” Thus the manuscript; printed editions have “for display.”

“Of the emperor.” Manuscript: “emperors,” wrongly.

“Among their gods.” That is, in the temple of their gods.

[Col. 0203D]

“Aurelian, being such as he was.” Thus the Colbert manuscript. Almeloveen suggests perhaps “when he was”; quite acceptably.

“Mad and headlong.” From Flavius Vopiscus: “Aurelian was a severe, savage, bloodthirsty emperor.” From Eutropius IX, concerning the same man: “A man powerful in war, but of unrestrained spirit and rather prone to cruelty.” And *praeceps* (“headlong”) is not distinctly read in the manuscript, but there is a small stroke with the word *prebs*, which could equally mean “a mad emperor.” Nevertheless, *praeceps* in the printed editions is not unsuitable; Livy elegantly says “a spirit headlong into greed and cruelty.”

“He was killed at the very beginning of his fury.” Thus he stirred up persecution only near the end of A.D. 274 or at the beginning of the following year. For he was killed in April A.D. 275; see Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VII.30.

“Caenophrurium.” Midway along the sea-route between Heraclea and Byzantium. Flavius Vopiscus, *Aurelian*: “But while he was traveling, he was killed at the station of Caenophrurium, which lies between Heraclea and Byzantium, through the malice of his secretary and by the hand of Mucapor.” See Eutropius IX. BALUZ.

“Not merely.” It is not absent from the manuscript.

“They did.” That is, they acted.

“Diocletian.” He was called Diocles before becoming emperor, as appears from the end of ch. 9.

“Contriver of evils.” Thus Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* VII.24: “the CONTRIVER of all EVILS.”

“Not even from God.” I would prefer to read *ne* (“not even”), as at the beginning of ch. 6: “but he was not even permitted to accomplish what he had intended.”

“The world.” Understand the immense extent of the Roman Empire.

“Greed.” On this, see Vopiscus, *Numerian*, and below Baluzius’s notes on this chapter.

“Fearfulness.” By this he made three men participants in his reign: Maximian, surnamed Herculius, in A.D. 285; Constantius, surnamed Chlorus; and Galerius Maximian, surnamed Armentarius, in A.D. 293.

“Into four parts.” Diocletian ruled the East; Maximian Herculius, Italy and Africa; Constantius Chlorus, the provinces beyond the Alps; and Galerius Maximian, Illyricum and Thrace. Diocletian’s imperial residence was Nicomedia in Bithynia, Herculius’s Milan, Constantius’s Augusta Treverorum, and Galerius’s Sirmium in Pannonia.

“Had begun to be greater.” Manuscript: “had begun to be greater” [plural], wrongly.

“By the enormity of the *indictiones*.” Manuscript: *inhormitate*. *Indictiones*, that is, taxes imposed outside the ordinary order at the victor’s discretion or according to the needs of the state. COLUMBUS.

“The provinces too were cut into pieces.” From this we see the origin of the multiplication of provinces, which was not otherwise clearly known. The new number of provinces is presented by the *Notitia* of each empire, by another list of bishoprics, by Schonovius’s *Little Book of Provinces*, which we recently published with Sextus Rufus, and, in the Western Empire, by Sextus Rufus himself, or Rufus Festus. CELL.

“Offices.” That is, prefects, or those who hold offices. On them see Pancirollus on the *Notitia Imperii*, ch. 9, and Vossius, *On the Faults of Speech* III.30.

“To press upon the cities.” Thus Lactantius also, *Divine Institutes* VII.19: “Indeed, having captured the world, he will PRESS UPON it with great [Col. 0205B] armies of brigands”; V.11: “lying back in one place.”]

Afterward, when he had ended his shameful life in that disgrace, his skin was torn away; and, stripped of its entrails, the hide was dyed red, in order that it might be set up in the temple of the barbarian gods as a memorial of the most illustrious triumph, and might always be displayed to our envoys, lest Romans place too much confidence in their strength when they saw, among the gods of the barbarians, the spoils of a captive emperor. Since, then, God exacted such punishments from sacrilegious men, is it not astonishing that anyone afterward dared not merely to do, but even to conceive, anything against the majesty of the one God who rules and sustains the universe?

VI. Aurelian, who was by nature mad and headlong, though he remembered Valerian’s captivity, nevertheless forgot his crime and punishment and provoked God’s anger by cruel deeds. Yet he was not even permitted to accomplish what he had intended; rather, at the very beginning of his fury he was immediately killed. His bloodstained letters had not yet reached the more distant provinces, and already at Caenophrurium [Col. 0204A], a place in Thrace, he himself lay bloodstained upon the ground, murdered by his friends through a certain false suspicion. Such and so many examples ought to have restrained later tyrants. But they were not merely undeterred; they acted even more boldly and confidently against God.

VII. Diocletian, the inventor of crimes and contriver of evils, while he was ruining everything, could not keep his hands even from God. He overturned the world at once through greed and fearfulness. For he made three men partners in his rule, dividing the world into four parts and multiplying the armies, because each of them strove to have a far greater number of soldiers than earlier emperors had possessed when they governed the state alone. So much greater had the number of receivers become than that of contributors that, their strength exhausted by the enormity of the *indictiones* [Col. 0204B], the farmers abandoned their fields and cultivated lands turned into forest. And, so that everything might be filled with terror, the provinces too were cut into pieces: many governors and more numerous offices pressed upon the individual regions, and almost now upon the cities; likewise *rationales* [Col. 0205A]

[Note: [Col. 0205B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 205–206]

“*Rationales*.” That is, procurators of the imperial treasury sent into the provinces; thus Lampridius, *Alexander* 45: “Procurators, that is, *rationales*.”

“I shall not say frequent, but unceasing.” So also Lactantius, [Col. 0205C] *Divine Institutes* III.22: “I SHALL NOT SAY of dumb creatures, BUT of cattle and wild beasts”; and II.4: “who had held the gods not merely in contempt, but openly in derision”—omitting only *solum* (“merely”) and *etiam* (“also”).

“And neither can those things be endured.” The preceding words require: “injuries not to be borne,” etc. The manuscript has “these also.” The most learned Almeloveen and Baudri observed that *nec* should be read.—“And neither can those things be endured.” Manuscript: “These also.” “And neither” is substituted for that reading. But to what end? Has he not already spoken above of the *indictiones* in connection with soldiers? It is clear what he means: these things could indeed still have been endured, if his insatiable mind had stopped here. Mieg, cited by the illustrious Van Mastricht, who approved Mieg’s opinion. BUNEMAN.

“Concerning the provision of soldiers.” Either for supplying actual persons for military service from every district, as is commonly done today; or, more probably, for providing soldiers’ pay, food, and the other necessities of life. Thus Justin II.9.2: “to provide with provisions,” and XI.10: “to provide life.”

“Concern.” Manuscript: “await.”

“Through fear.” Heumann reads “then,” correctly.

“The law [was dissolved] by necessity itself.” Baluz[ius]: “For laws are enacted with the purpose that they may benefit, not harm,” as Pope Symmachus writes to Avitus, bishop of Vienne.

“Here.” Used distributively: “elsewhere.”

“Mint.” Here it means the building in which coins are struck.

“A great part of the city is made to depart.” Namely, of Nicomedia, where Diocletian lived and which, as Lactantius will immediately say, he sought to make equal to Rome. In French we similarly say, *toute la ville est sortie*, *tout Paris est sorti*, etc. *Exceditur*, or “people depart”: in other words, by the construction of such vast buildings very many citizens are compelled to yield their places and leave the city, seeking other dwellings outside. Lactantius uses *exceditur* here as he uses *acceditur* below at the beginning of ch. 47. Thus the received reading may be accepted. Heumann reads *exciditur* (“is demolished”) in place of *exceditur*: that is, old houses are destroyed so that room may be opened for new palaces.

“He said.” Manuscript: “he did,” wrongly.

[Col. 0206C]

“Thus he was always mad.” Thus the manuscript; not “was made mad,” nor “was always changing,” as some learned men have thought. He was so foolishly extravagant. BAULDRI. The French translator Maucroix: “Thus his mania for building had no bounds.” *Dementabat*, that is, “he was insane.”

“To make equal.” Manuscript: *quo equare*, wrongly.

“Almost permitted by custom.” The comedy *Querolus*: “For I readily understand a jesting perjury; what do you think? Yet let us pass it over, because, as I see, custom has already made it trivial.” St Ambrose, Letter 66: “Is something permitted merely because it is not forbidden?”

“What of his brother Maximian, who was called Herculius?” His brother not by nature but by imperial rank, namely Diocletian’s, of whom we have spoken in the preceding chapter. In French: *son associé à l’empire*, “his partner in the empire.”

“Who was called Herculius.” Manuscript: *Que dictus Irculius*. In this manuscript the letter *h* is often entirely omitted.

“To remain united in so faithful a friendship.” Manuscript: *fidele quo erere*, wrongly.

“One mind.” Manuscript: *mensura*. But an *n* is added above the *r*, by the same hand and in the same ink.

“One had more greed than the lesser, but less than the greater; but more fearfulness, and yet more courage—not for doing good, but for doing evil.” Lactantius appears here to say that Herculius was more greedy than Diocletian. The passage appears corrupt. Some wish to remove the words “greater” and “lesser” as marginal matter intruded into the text, and read *avaritiae* (“of greed”). A passage extremely similar in word order and figure occurs in *Divine Institutes* IV.3, from which it may be established that this passage too is genuinely Lactantian: “In that former part, as there is less danger, so there is more difficulty, because the obscure nature of the matter compels different opinions. Here, as there is more danger, so there is less difficulty, because the actual experience of things and daily trials can teach what is truer and better.” Partly from COLUMBUS.

The most learned Almeloveen deleted *altero* (“than the other”); and after “fearfulness” read: “but the other had more courage.”

“[The] very.” Manuscript: “the very” [feminine], wrongly.]

many *magistri* and vicars of prefects. For all these men civil cases were exceedingly rare; there were only frequent condemnations and proscriptions, exactions of innumerable things—not, I say, frequent, but unceasing—and in those exactions intolerable injuries. Nor can the things required for supplying soldiers be endured either. The same man, in insatiable greed, never wished his treasuries to be diminished, but always heaped together extraordinary wealth and largesses, so that he might keep undiminished and inviolate the things which he stored away. The same man, while by various injustices he caused immense dearness, attempted to fix by law the prices of merchandise. Then, over trifling and cheap articles, much blood was shed; nothing for sale appeared because of fear; and dearness flared up much worse, until the law was dissolved by necessity itself after many people had perished [Col. 0205B]. To this was added a certain boundless passion for building, and exactions from the provinces no less burdensome for providing laborers, craftsmen, wagons, and every other thing needed for constructing works. Here were basilicas; here a circus; here a mint; here an arms factory; here a house for his wife; here one for his daughter. Suddenly a great part of the city was made to depart. Everyone migrated with wives and children, as though the city had been captured by enemies. And when these things had been completed at the ruin of the provinces, he said, “They have not been done properly; let them be done another way.” Again they had necessarily to be torn down and changed, perhaps to fall again. Thus he was always mad, seeking to make Nicomedia equal to the city of Rome. I pass over now how many perished for the sake of possessions or wealth. For this was customary and almost permitted by the custom of evils. But in his case this was especially characteristic: wherever he had seen a more cultivated field or a more splendid building, an accusation and capital penalty for its owner were already prepared, as though he could not seize another’s property without bloodshed.

VIII. What of his brother Maximian, who was called Herculius? He was not unlike him. For they could not have remained united in such faithful friendship unless in both there had been one mind, the same thought, an equal will, an identical judgment. They differed only in this: one had more greed than the lesser, but less than the greater; but more fearfulness, and yet more courage—not for doing good, but for doing evil. [Note: [Col. 0207B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 207–208]

“Either Africa or Spain.” Thus the manuscript. Either *vel* here stands for “and,” or these words were inserted into the text from the margin.

“And.” Heumann wishes *at* (“but”) to be read.

“By informers.” That is, by accusers or denunciators.

“So that the lights of the Senate were continually put out.” Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* VII.26, on Rome: “And we must pray to and worship the God of heaven, if indeed His decrees and purposes can be deferred, lest that abominable tyrant come sooner than we think, who may devise so great a crime and put out that light, at whose destruction the world itself will fall”; and V.12: “let eyes be gouged out”; and below, ch. 36: “Thus the eyes of confessors were gouged out”; and *On the Workmanship of God* 8.

“Pestilential.” Manuscript: *pestiphero*. Some would prefer to read *pestifera*, referring it to the word “lust.”

“To corrupt males.” Victor also records this: “For Herculius was driven by such lust that he did not restrain the stain of his mind even from the bodies of hostages.” This was observed by the learned Cuper. Moreover, who does not see that *mares* (“males”), not *mores* (“customs”), must be read after this, as in the manuscript, since lust concerns not people’s customs but the use of the body? Add the antithesis, “the violation of daughters”; add that he calls it hateful and detestable. ALMELOVEEN.

And although (says Burnet) the gradation may seem less fitting from the crime of sodomy to the abduction of virgins, among the Romans this crime was nevertheless considered the greater; perhaps because in abduction violence was inflicted upon daughters, but not upon males, who had been enticed and won over by entreaty, payment, and other seductions.

“Hateful.” Manuscript: *otiosum*, wrongly.

“To be violated.” Manuscript: *volandas*, wrongly.

“Wherever.” Manuscript: *quecumque te*.

“Constantius.” That is, Chlorus, the father of Constantine the Great, a most excellent and kindly emperor.

“Since.” Manuscript: *qm*. The expression would be more elegant if it said “how unlike,” etc., by way of exclamation.

“The other Maximian.” His praenomen was Galerius and his cognomen Armentarius, because he had been a herdsman. He was Diocletian’s son-in-law, because he had as his wife Valeria, Diocletian’s daughter, a most chaste and most unhappy woman. But we shall speak more fully of her later. BALUZ.

“Son-in-law.” See Eutropius IX.

“BEAST.” Thus he calls Galerius Maximian and the other persecutors of Christians. They think that what Lactantius writes in *Divine Institutes* V.11 can be applied to this Galerius: “For what Caucasus, what India, what Hyrcania ever nourished BEASTS so savage, so bloodthirsty? For the rage of all wild beasts reaches only the satisfaction of their belly and, when hunger is assuaged, immediately rests. That is the true BEAST, at whose single command dark blood is shed everywhere, cruel mourning everywhere, fear everywhere, and the manifold image of death. No one can adequately describe the savagery of so great a monster, which, though lying in one place, yet rages with iron teeth throughout the whole world; and not only tears apart human limbs, but crushes the very bones and rages into ashes, lest any place for burial remain.” BALUZ.—Likewise, ch. 24: “He will exterminate evil BEASTS from the earth.”

“Native barbarity.” Heumann reads *natalis* (“by birth”), not badly.—“Native.” Thus Julius Capitolinus, *The Two Maximini* 20: “The Senate, fearing Maximian’s native and necessary cruelty.” Casaubon illustrates the force of *naturalis* from Persius, *Satires* II, p. 225. BUN.

“And ferocity.” Manuscript: *efferitas*.

“Since his mother … had fled.” Here *cum* means “because.” In the same way, ch. 17 says: “Since he could not endure the liberty of the Roman people, he broke forth”; and ch. 18: “Since from there … he saw that nothing accrued to him but the name, he answered”; following Terence, who writes: “And since he was afraid to wrong this most excellent young man, was he not afraid?” From Paulus BAULDRI.

“Beyond the Danube.” Thus the manuscript, with *v* for *b*, as among ancient Latin writers and more recent Greeks.

“Having crossed over.” Manuscript: *trasjecto*.

“Lofty stature.” Syntax and sequence certainly require this to be written: “huge body, etc.; lofty stature.” For if one reads *statu celsus*, as in the manuscript, to what does *celsus* refer—to a noun of neuter gender, *corpus*? But we likewise read in Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* II.1, *status celsus*, and III.1, *status rectus*, and elsewhere. In these places *status* means “stature.” Cicero, *On the Orator* 18: “an upright and lofty stature.”

“He feared most keenly.” From Virgil, *Aeneid* I.366: “or fear was keen.”]

For, although Italy itself, the seat of empire, lay under his control, and the richest provinces were subject to him—either Africa or Spain—he was not so diligent in guarding his wealth, of which he had an abundant supply. And when there was need, the wealthiest senators were not lacking, who, through suborned informers, were said to have sought imperial power, so that the lights of the Senate were continually put out. The most bloodthirsty treasury overflowed with ill-gotten wealth. Now lust in this pestilential man extended not only to the corruption of males—which is hateful and detestable—but also to the violation of the daughters of leading men. For wherever he traveled, virgins torn from before their parents’ eyes were immediately at hand. In these things he judged himself happy; in these he thought the felicity of his empire consisted: if he denied nothing to lust and evil desire.

“Stirred up … by examples.” Compare Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* VI.23: “Stirred up by the example itself.” BUN.

“And his mind shattered.” Thus in the manuscript; not *deiectus* (“cast down”), which would be better. In this manuscript one often finds *dis-* and *di-* in compound words in place of *de-*. ALMELOV. — Columbus and Tollius read *deiectus*.

“The example of Valerian.” [That is,] captured by the Persians and carried off into slavery.

“By his stratagems.” Tollius wishes it to be rewritten: “using stratagems” (*insidiis usus*).

“Hampered.” The manuscript: “unskilled, and occupied with baggage”; corrupt.

“Not with difficulty.” A rare word, but it is nevertheless read in Cicero, *Academica* IV.

Africa or Spain was not so diligent in guarding its wealth, of which he had an abundant supply. And whenever need arose, there was no lack of extremely wealthy senators who, on the basis of suborned accusations, were said to have aspired to imperial power; thus the eyes of the Senate were continually gouged out. The bloodiest treasury overflowed with ill-gotten riches. Already the lust of this pestilential man extended not only to corrupting morals—which is hateful and detestable—but even to violating the daughters of the foremost men. For wherever he had travelled, virgins torn from their parents’ sight were immediately made available. By such things he judged himself blessed; in them he thought the felicity of his rule consisted, if he denied nothing to lust and evil desire.

I pass over Constantius, since he differed from the rest and was worthy to hold the world alone.

## IX

[Col. 0207B] The other Maximian, whom Diocletian had adopted as his son-in-law, was worse not merely than these two whom our own times experienced, but than all who had ever existed. [Col. 0208A] This beast possessed an inborn barbarity and a savagery alien to Roman blood. Nor is this surprising, since his mother, a woman from beyond the Danube, had fled into New Dacia after crossing the river when the Carpi were making incursions. His body too was suited to his character: lofty stature, enormous flesh, spread out and swollen into a frightful bulk. In short, in speech, action, and appearance alike he was an object of terror and dread to all. His father-in-law also feared him most intensely.

The cause of this fear was as follows. Narseus, king of the Persians, stirred up by the domestic examples of his grandfather Sapor, was eagerly bent upon seizing the East with great forces.

Then Diocletian, being—as he was in every disturbance—fearful and broken in spirit, and at the same time afraid of Valerian’s example, did not dare to advance to meet him. Instead, [Col. 0208B] he sent this man through Armenia, while he himself remained in the East and awaited the outcome of events. By his stratagems, he overwhelmed without much difficulty the barbarians—whose custom it is to proceed to war with all their people—hampered by their multitude and encumbered with baggage. Having put King Narseus to flight, [Col. 0209A] he returned with immense booty and spoils, bringing arrogance to himself and fear to Diocletian.

[Col. 0209B] *Notes of the Variorum on columns 209–210*

“Was exalted.” Heumann thinks Lactantius wrote “was carried away” (*elatus est*).

“Would reject.” Thus this manuscript; elsewhere, *detractaret*.

“When he had heard in letters sent to him.” Diocletian heard it from Galerius’ letters. CELL. — Rather, Galerius had heard, or seen, it. BUN.

“How long [shall I remain] Caesar?” For Galerius was ambitious to be called and to be Emperor and Augustus—that is, to hold the first rank; for Caesar held only the second rank.

“That he had been begotten by Mars.” He imitated Diocletian, who called himself Jovian, and the other Maximian, who called himself Herculean, as though [they were descended] from divine ancestors. On Galerius, Victor’s *Epitome*, ch. 57: “He dared insolently to assert that his mother, after the manner of Olympias, mother of Alexander the Great, had been embraced by a serpent and had conceived him.” [Col. 0209C] CELL.

“Romula.” This was Galerius’ mother, after whom the town of Romulianum was named.

“For afterward.” Thus ch. 5: “But afterward”; *Institutes* IV.15: “But afterward things were perceived than …” BUN.

“His father-in-law having been stripped [of office].” That is, after Diocletian had laid aside the purple, abdicated the Empire, and Galerius became Emperor. We French use the same manner of speaking, commonly saying: *Cet homme s’est dépouillé pour son fils* [“That man has stripped himself for his son”]. So also below, ch. 10. Or rather, “his father-in-law having been stripped [of office]” means after Galerius forced Diocletian to yield the empire, as below, ch. 18 at the beginning; which is more correct.

“Thus.” We have supplied this particle with Cuperus; without it the sentence is defective. Thus below, ch. 19: “Diocletian threw upon him his own purple, which he had put off; he became Diocles again.”

“Of persecuting.” Add “them,” that is, “the righteous,” a designation which immediately precedes.

[Col. 0209D]

“While he was acting.” Lactantius likes this expression in this sense: *Divine Institutes* IV.27, where the same matter occurs, and IV.23. BUN.

“Through fear.” Emend: “because of fear,” that is, because of timidity.

“Some of the attendants, etc.” This passage too clearly shows that this book is Lactantius’s. For he has entirely similar words in *Divine Institutes* IV.27: “For when they sacrifice to their gods, if anyone bearing the marked forehead stands by, the rites by no means succeed, nor can the consulted seer give replies.” And this was often the principal reason why evil rulers persecuted righteousness. “For while certain of our attendants stood by their masters as they sacrificed, having placed the sign upon their foreheads, they drove away their gods, so that they could not portray the future in the entrails of victims. When the haruspices understood this, prompted by those same demons whom they propitiate, they complained that profane persons were present at the sacred rites; they drove their rulers into frenzy, so that they might attack [Col. 0210B] the temple of God.” BALUZ.

“Knowing the Lord.” Thus Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* VII.20: “Therefore those who knew God will be judged”—that is, Christians. — “Knowing the Lord.” III.29: “Those who know God”; and *Institutes* VII.20: “Those who knew the Lord,” that is, the faithful. BUN.

“The immortal sign.” Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* IV.27: “[those] whom the immortal sign has fortified as though by an impregnable wall,” etc. There Lactantius recounts in nearly the same words the miracle of demons being put to flight by the sign of the Cross. On the power of this sign, St Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 13: “The saving trophy of Jesus, the Cross … heals diseases, puts demons to flight,” etc. Likewise, *Catechesis* 13: “Since this grace is from God—the sign of the faithful and the terror of demons”; and *Catechesis* 4: “Mark the Cross openly upon your forehead, so that the demons, seeing [Col. 0210C] the royal sign, may flee trembling far away. Use this sign when eating and drinking, sitting and lying down, rising from bed, speaking, walking; and, to say it once for all, in every matter and every undertaking.” St Ignatius Martyr: “The sign of the Cross is a trophy against the power of the ruler of this world; seeing it, he is terrified, and hearing of it, he is afraid.” See St Augustine, *Exposition* 4 on Psalm XXX, and on Psalm L, no. 1: “If perhaps Christians are frightened in the circus itself for some reason, they immediately make the sign and stand there bearing on their foreheads that from which they would depart if they bore it in their hearts.” Also *City of God* XXII.3. Theodoret too says, *Ecclesiastical History* III.3: “When these demons appeared in their customary form, fear compelled Julian to place the sign of the Cross upon his forehead.” On the sign of the Cross, its power and efficacy, see further Origen, Tertullian, Basil, Athanasius, *On the Incarnation of the Word of God*, vol. I, p. 73; Gregory Nazianzen, poem 61, vol. II, p. 142, and *Oration* 3 against Julian, p. 206; Ambrose, Paulinus, and other holy Fathers. — “They placed upon [Col. 0210D] their foreheads the immortal sign.” See my notes on Lactantius, IV.26. Nourry, on these words of Caecilius, p. 183, completely distorts Lactantius’s passage. — “So says—or, more truly, so dreams—Bunemannus.” I am astonished at how fiercely the non-Catholics are agitated in this place; for they leave nothing untouched in order to eliminate the force of this Lactantian testimony, which greatly favors the orthodox rites of the Catholic Church. Bunemannus refers that “immortal sign” to Christ alone. But let him read the passage; let him read attentively, and he will see that demons were not only driven away by Christ through the sign placed upon Christians’ foreheads, but that the attendants of Diocletian—who perhaps stood by at sacrifices—then drove demons away from themselves as soon as they themselves placed upon their foreheads the immortal sign, that is, the sign of the Cross, as was the practice in the ancient Church at that time. See what we have noted on this chapter of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* and on chapter 27 of book IV of the *Divine Institutes*.

For after that victory he was raised to such heights of pride that he now disdained the name Caesar. When he had heard this in letters sent to him, he would cry out, with a grim expression and a terrible voice: “HOW LONG [SHALL I BE] CAESAR?” Thereupon he began to act most arrogantly, desiring both to seem and to be called one begotten by Mars, as though he were another Romulus. He preferred to disgrace his mother Romula by alleging her violation, so that he himself might appear to spring from the gods. But I defer speaking of his deeds, lest I confuse the chronology.

For after he received the title Emperor, when his father-in-law had been stripped [of power], only then did he begin to rage and despise everything. For before he became emperor he was called Diocles. Although he was overthrowing the commonwealth by such counsels and such associates, although he deserved every punishment for his crimes, nevertheless he reigned in the highest prosperity for as long as he did not stain his hands with the blood of the righteous. I shall now explain what reason he had for persecuting them.

## X

While he was in the eastern regions, being—as he was through fear—a searcher into future events, he sacrificed cattle and sought coming events in their livers. Then some attendants who knew the Lord, standing by while he sacrificed, placed the immortal sign upon their foreheads. When this was done, the demons were driven away and the sacred rites were thrown into confusion. The haruspices were alarmed and did not see the customary marks in the entrails; and, as though they had not sacrificed successfully, they sacrificed repeatedly. But again and again the slaughtered victims disclosed nothing, until that master of the haruspices, [Col. 0211A] Tagis, whether from suspicion or from sight, said that the rites did not answer because profane persons were present at the divine ceremonies.

[Col. 0211B] *Notes of the Variorum on columns 211–212*

“Tagis.” Others have *Tages, -etis*. He was Etruscan and the first of all haruspices. See Arnobius, *Against the Nations* II. Either Tagis was the title of the office of the man who presided over the discipline of haruspicy, or, as our Baluzius says, the author speaks rhetorically because Tagis was once a great Etruscan haruspex and teacher of haruspices. Besides Arnobius, see Cicero, *On Divination* II; or else, as Heumann thinks, the word *Tagis* was transferred from the margin into the text.

“Profane persons.” Christians, who were called profane, impious, and irreligious by the pagans.

“In wrathful rage he ordered not only … to sacrifice.” An excellent reading of the manuscript, why it was altered in printed editions, and even in old codices, I do not know. What could be clearer than this wording, and the words shortly afterward: “Thus far his frenzy and wrath proceeded”? Other editions have “his wrath raging”; but I follow the manuscript. Nourry has in the lower margin of his edition “wrath for rage.” But the manuscript has “wrath of rage,” as if one said “wrath full of rage”; so Plautus has “full of age,” and Livy “full of spirit.” We say this so that the text may not be altered.

“If they should refuse.” Heumann rightly observes that one should read “those who should refuse.”

“Commanders.” These were military prefects, ranking after tribunes but nevertheless commanding a cohort just as tribunes did, as Henri Valois observes on Ammianus Marcellinus. Lactantius, ch. 46, mentions commanders and tribunes together. From their number came that St Dorotheus whose encomium Eusebius recounts in *Ecclesiastical History* VIII.1.

“The soldiers were to be compelled,” etc. Besides Lactantius, Eusebius notes that this persecution began with them, *Ecclesiastical History* VIII.1, and that at that point it went no further.

“Thus far.” The manuscript has *ac tenus*, but incorrectly.

“After an interval.” The manuscript: *interdicto*, incorrectly. “Bithynia.” The manuscript: “Bethany,” corruptly.

“Maximian Caesar.” Namely, Galerius.

“He arrived inflamed with wickedness.” Thus Cicero, fifth accusation against Verres: “He himself came into the forum inflamed with wickedness and fury.” Thus Lactantius, *Institutes* VII.1: “Inflamed with love of power”; and ch. 17: “The impious king, inflamed.”

“The foolish old man.” He means Diocletian.

“His mother.” Namely, the mother of Galerius Maximian, whom he above called Romula. [Col. 0212B]

“A woman exceedingly superstitious.” “Since she was,” etc. The passage is corrupted or confused. Should it be read with an inversion of words: “Since she was a superstitious woman”? Or, with Tollius: “Since she was at Nicomedia”? Or should it be understood with Columbus thus: “Since she was [eating],” that is, when she ate or dined?

“She supplied her deputies with her own feasts.” Almeloveen and Gallius perhaps read “feasts.” I suspect that some error lies beneath the text. Some wish to read “she entertained villagers with feasts”: “villagers,” they say, meaning inhabitants of the same place. Others read: “she supplied her deputies with her own feasts.” And this would indeed be a sound reading; for in Justin IX.2 we read: “Let him not enrich the Scythians with estates, but scarcely supply them with provisions.” *Exhibere* means “to support”; “deputies” means courtly or household attendants.

“To remove.” Namely, from the midst, or to kill. Thus our Vulgate, John XIX.15: “Take away, take away, crucify him.” Thus in Justin’s history XXXVIII, “to be removed” means “to be killed.”

“Men.” The manuscript has *omines*, incorrectly.

“The old man.” Diocletian.

“His.” Namely, Galerius Maximian’s.

“The world.” That is, the Roman Empire, as I noted above.

“Palace officials.” That is, the grandees of the palace.

“Of the headlong man.” Galerius, of whom, above at the beginning of ch. 6, it is said that he was headlong—that is, acting without consideration and rashly. [Col. 0212D]

“For.” The manuscript has “not,” incorrectly.

“Would be attributed to the fault of others.” Thus Eutropius says of Diocletian, *History* IX.16: “He was cunning in disposition and wished to carry out his severity through another’s unpopularity.”

“By their own hatred against Christians.” The manuscript has “their own hatred,” corruptly. Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* V.11, speaking of this very persecution: “Others through their own hatred against the righteous.” For Lactantius, “the righteous” means Christians.

“Who otherwise.” The manuscript has “in what manner,” incorrectly.

“Fearing.” Lactantius in the same place, *Divine Institutes* V.11: “Others, through excessive timidity, ventured further than they were commanded.”

“Wishing to oblige.” The same author, there: “Some, in order to please and to fortify by this service their path to higher things.”

Then in wrathful rage he ordered that not only those who ministered at the sacred rites, but all who were in the palace, should sacrifice; and that, if they refused, punishment should be inflicted upon them with scourges. In letters sent to the commanders, he further ordered that the soldiers too be compelled to perform the impious sacrifices, so that those who did not obey should be discharged from military service. Thus far his frenzy and wrath proceeded; nor did he do anything further against the law or religion of God.

Then, after some time had passed, he came to Bithynia to winter there. At the same time Maximian Caesar too arrived, inflamed with wickedness, to urge the foolish old man—who had already made a beginning—to persecute the Christians. I have learned that the cause of this fury was as follows.

## XI

[Col. 0211B] His mother was a worshipper of the gods of the mountains, a woman exceedingly superstitious. Being such a woman, she offered sacrifices with banquets almost every day and supplied her attendants with feasts. The Christians abstained; while she feasted with the pagans, they persisted in fasting and prayer. Hence she conceived hatred against them and by womanly complaints incited her son, himself no less superstitious, to remove these people.

Accordingly, after they had held counsel together throughout the whole winter, with no one admitted, while everyone supposed that matters concerning the highest condition of the commonwealth were being discussed, the old man long resisted his fury. He pointed out how ruinous it was to disturb the whole world and to shed the blood of many; that they were accustomed to die willingly; that it was enough if he merely forbade palace officials and soldiers from that religion. Yet he could not turn aside the madness of this headlong man.

It therefore pleased him to test the opinion of his friends. For this was characteristic of his malice: whenever he had resolved to do something good, he did it without consultation, so that he himself might be praised; but whenever he intended something evil, because he knew it was blameworthy, he called many into consultation, so that whatever wrongdoing he himself had committed might be ascribed to the fault of others. [Col. 0212B] A few judges and a few military men were therefore admitted, and, according to the precedence of their rank, were questioned. Some, from their own hatred of Christians, judged that the enemies of the gods and foes of public religions ought to be removed; and those who thought otherwise, having understood the man’s will, either through fear or wishing to oblige him, concurred in the same opinion. Not even thus, however, was the Emperor [Col. 0213A] persuaded to give his assent; but he decided that the gods should be consulted above all, and sent a haruspex to Milesian Apollo. Apollo responded as an enemy of the divine religion. Thus he was drawn away from his purpose.

[Col. 0213B] *Notes of the Variorum on columns 213–214*

“Emperor.” Diocletian.

“Milesian.” See above, book IV, ch. 13, and Eusebius, *Life of Constantine* II.1.

“Caesar.” Galerius.

“Terminalia.” A Roman festival day in honor of the god Terminus. On the god Terminus see Lactantius, *Institutes* I.20; Florus, *History* I.7; Cicero, *Letters to Atticus* VI, at the beginning.

“Are selected.” The manuscript: “are delegated,” incorrectly.

“On the seventh day before the Kalends of March.” That is, 23 February, A.D. 303. See Tillemont, vol. 4, *History of the Emperors*, article 10; also his *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. V, article 8 and note 7, p. 598, col. II; and Baluzius’s note.

“So that, as it were, a boundary might be imposed on this religion.” “Who,” Bauldrius asks, “besides this author, used *terminum imponere*, ‘to impose a boundary,’ in the sense of ‘to set an end’?” But Lactantius is recognized once more in this phrase. For I find in *Institutes* IV.19: “And therefore the Sibyl said that after a sleep of three days he would impose a boundary upon death.” Apuleius similarly uses the simple expression, *Metamorphoses* IV: “And he indeed set a limit to life worthy of his virtues.” Eutropius, IV.11.6: “And he set an end to the war.” Lactantius again, VII.2: “That this unjust age … might receive its end,” meaning “might receive its conclusion.” Thus “to have an end” in VII.5 and VII.10. BUN.

[Col. 0213D]

“Church.” Namely, that at Nicomedia; thus Christians commonly called the building designated for sacred observances. — “To the church”: the house of Christian assembly, the Christian temple in the city of Nicomedia. And not only Christian writers of those times, but even pagan writers speaking of Christians, use this word. Zosimus, V.24: “Secretly, therefore, having set fire to the church by night … and the whole CHURCH was burned.” CELL.

“Prefect.” We are compelled to read this. The manuscript has “professed,” which gives no sense, for nothing agrees with that word. Bunemannus, however, reads “having set out.”

“The image of God is sought.” By the pagans, who thought temples could not exist without images. Lactantius, II.2: “The image of God is not that.”

“The Scriptures found are burned.” From this arose the term *traditores* (“handers-over”), applied to those who, through fear of punishments, surrendered the sacred Scriptures to imperial judges.

“They themselves.” Diocletian and Galerius.

[Col. 0214B] “Whether it ought.” Add “rather than be demolished,” for a clearer sense.

“That very lofty shrine.” The manuscript has “nevertheless,” which yields no sense. With the most learned Tollius, Paul Bauldri, and others, I substitute *fanum* (“shrine”) for *tamen* (“nevertheless”), since the words have the same number of letter-strokes. Paul Bauldri observes in the notes to his edition that *fanum* is used of a temple or larger church; see him below.

“Every legal action against them should remain in force.” Thus consistently the manuscripts, not “should prevail.” Here *caleret* is correctly said in Latin by Lactantius; it is not, as some suppose, a case of his making Latin from Greek words, such as *sophia* for “wisdom,” III.16; *anastasis* for “resurrection,” VII.23; *antitheus*, II.10; etc.

“Someone tore down and shredded that edict.” Who he was is not established. From the silence of Lactantius, who was then at Nicomedia, it is sufficiently understood that the man’s name was unknown, because he was doubtless one of the common people. Others wrongly say that he was named St John, martyred on 7 September; others St George the martyr, who suffered on 23 April. From Lactantius and Eusebius it is certainly inferred that this man was immediately brought forward and immediately delivered to death, and therefore died at the end of February. From BALUZIUS.

“Tore down.” Thus it should be read, not “tore off.”

[Col. 0214D]

“Posted.” Learned men prefer this to “set before,” which is in the manuscript.

“Stretched on the rack.” A word he uses below, ch. 27.

“Lawfully cooked.” That is, over a slow fire, such as that by which meats are roasted: first cooked, then burned. From CUPERUS. — Others would have “very slowly cooked,” as below, ch. 21: laws having been issued that those condemned after torture should be burned by slow fires. “Lawfully cooked,” that is, scorched. The method of cooking Christians alive is explained below, ch. 21: “Then burning torches, extinguished and relit, were applied to their individual limbs … until finally, after their entire skin had been cooked away over much of the day, the force of the fire penetrated to the inner parts.” He called him “lawfully cooked” because he had been cooked according to laws issued by the Augusti, just as in *Institutes* V.11 and VI.9 the expression is used in the same sense. From BALUZIUS and TOINARD.

“With remarkable endurance,” etc. Eusebius says of him, *Ecclesiastical History* VIII.5: “He preserved joy and tranquility of spirit until his last breath.”

And because he could resist neither his friends, nor Caesar, nor Apollo, he attempted to maintain this moderation: that he should order the matter to be conducted without bloodshed, whereas Caesar wished those who resisted sacrifice to be burned alive.

## XII

A suitable and auspicious day for carrying out the affair was sought; and the Terminalia were selected above all, falling on the seventh day before the Kalends of March, so that, as it were, a boundary might be set to this religion.

> That day was the first cause of death, and the first cause of evils

[Col. 0213B] which befell both themselves and the whole world. When that day dawned, while the two old men were holding the consulship for the eighth and seventh times, suddenly, while the light was still uncertain, the Prefect came to the church with commanders, tribunes, and financial officers. The doors having been torn off, the image of God was sought. The Scriptures found were burned; plunder was given to everyone. There was seizure, panic, running to and fro.

[Col. 0214A] The two rulers themselves, however, watching from a lookout point—for the church stood on high and could be seen from the palace—debated long between themselves whether fire ought rather to be applied. Diocletian’s opinion prevailed, since he feared that, if a great blaze arose, some part of the city might burn. For many great houses enclosed it on every side. Accordingly the Praetorians came in battle array, with axes and other tools; sent in from every side, they levelled that very lofty shrine to the ground in a few hours.

## XIII

On the following day an edict was posted, providing that persons of that religion should be deprived of every honor and rank; that they should be subject to tortures, from whatever order or grade they came; that every legal action against them should remain in force; that they themselves could bring no action for injury, adultery, or stolen property; in short, that they should possess neither liberty nor voice. Someone tore down and shredded that edict, though not rightly, yet with great courage, saying mockingly that victories over the Goths and Sarmatians had been posted. He was immediately brought forward, stretched not only on the rack but also lawfully cooked, and finally burned, with remarkable endurance.

## XIV

[Col. 0215A] *Notes of the Variorum on columns 215–216*

“Caesar.” Galerius; he was not yet Augustus.

“Is.” Heumann thinks this little word should be deleted.

“Fire.” Eusebius also mentions it, *Ecclesiastical History* VIII.6.

“The Christians were accused as public enemies,” etc. Pagans, in order to incite hatred against Christians, falsely attributed crimes to them and charged them with every calamity that befell the entire world, because, they said, their gods were not worshipped by us. Arnobius, St Cyprian in *Treatise* 1, *Against Demetrianus*, and St Augustine, *City of God* I, sharply reproach the pagans on this matter; consult them if you wish.

“Hostility.” The manuscript: “vidia,” incorrectly, through error.

“Of Christians.” Heumann, following Tertullian, *Apology* V, reads “the Christian name,” not badly.

“By their counsel.” The manuscript: “by that counsel,” incorrectly.

“Burned.” A verb such as “was reported” or “was said” seems to be missing. ALMELOVEEN.

“Inflamed with anger.” In Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* VII.17: “Inflamed with anger he will come with a great army.”

“To torture all his own people.” His courtiers or household. The manuscript has “to be tortured,” which the following verb “began” does not permit.

“Began.” Thus restored from the manuscript. Printed editions: “ordered.”

[Col. 0215D]

“He himself sat.” Diocletian.

“All the judges,” etc. Diocletian had a great number of Christians among his household. From them not only the masters of the palace, but all the judges themselves were tortured, authority having been granted to others to judge them; for if they were judges, there was no necessity to grant them authority to judge. I do not see why *coepit* (“began”) was changed to *praecepit* (“ordered”), and *torquebantur* (“were tortured”) to *torquebant* (“were torturing”), which produces a wholly different sense, since no one tortured the household of Caesar Galerius. Relevant here seem to be the words Lactantius writes, *Divine Institutes* V.24: “Necessity made them ministers of another’s madness, satellites of an impious command. For that honor or advancement in rank was not … What number of volumes could contain such infinite and diverse kinds of cruelty? Once authority had been received, each raged according to his own character,” etc.

“They competed,” etc. In place of “they were competing,” or “there was competition,” etc. In French: *On cherchait à l’envi* [“They strove with one another”]. It cannot be said how many and how severe kinds of tortures judges of this sort devised. Thus in devising kinds of punishments they think of nothing but victory. For they know that it is a contest and a battle. Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* V.11.

“Of Caesar.” Galerius.

“He himself was present.” Galerius Maximian.

“To let the anger of the thoughtless old man burn itself out.” That is, to cool, diminish, decline. In Livy XL: “Let your anger burn itself out.”

“The more quickly.” Thus the Aboensis edition and Heumann; the others have “but.”

“Emperor.” Diocletian.

“He compelled his daughter Valeria and his wife Prisca to be defiled by sacrifice.” Perhaps they were Christians. Valeria had been married to Caesar Galerius Maximian since A.D. 292. See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VIII.1.

“Formerly powerful eunuchs.” Among them was Peter. See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VIII.6.

“Through whom the palace itself had formerly stood.” Some read: “Through whom he himself had formerly set the palace ablaze”; others: “through whom it was established that he had formerly governed the palace.” But the manuscript’s reading is more pleasing.

“Ministers.” Deacons.

“Without any proof or confession.” The manuscript has “and confession,” incorrectly; I read “or confession,” that is, in French, *sans aucune preuve de témoins, et sans être convaincus d’aucun crime par leur propre aveu* [“without any witness-proof and without being convicted of any crime by their own admission”]. [Col. 0216D]

“But they were scorched in groups with fire set around them.” Thus I read *sed* (“but”) for *et* (“and”), which seems to have arisen in the manuscript from *set*. *Circumdare* and *ambire* mean the same thing: what sense is there in the printed reading “they were surrounded with fire and surrounded”? Read *amburebantur* (“were scorched”), a verb Lactantius uses in more than one place, especially *Divine Institutes* VII.17: “Fire will proceed from his mouth and scorch him,” and ch. 21: “They will be touched by fire and scorched.”

“Lest anyone casually,” etc. *Temere*: through inadvertence; in French, *par mégarde, sans y penser* [“by mistake, without thinking”]. Lest judges might unknowingly hear and adjudicate some Christian’s case. On this see the *Acts of Crispus* in Mabillon, *Analecta*, vol. 3. “In the secretariats”: in judicial courts. For *secretaria* properly were places where judges heard civil or criminal cases and sat in judgment. BAULDRI. — On the *secretaria*, see *Code* III.24.3.

But Caesar was not content with the provisions of the edict. He prepared to assail Diocletian in another way. For, in order to drive him to the design of a most cruel persecution, he secretly set fire to the palace through agents. When some part had burned, the Christians were accused as public enemies; and amid immense hostility, the Christian name burned together with the palace. It was alleged that, after taking counsel with the eunuchs, they had planned to destroy the rulers, and that two emperors had almost been burned alive in their own house.

Diocletian, however, who always wished to appear shrewd and intelligent, could suspect nothing; but, inflamed with anger, he immediately began to torture all his household. He himself sat and burned the innocent with fire. Likewise all the judges, indeed all who were masters in the palace, having received authority, [Col. 0215B] were tortured. They competed to see who would discover something first. Nothing whatsoever was found, since no one tortured Caesar’s household. He himself was present and pressed them on, nor did he allow the anger of the thoughtless old man to burn itself out.

But after an interval of fifteen days, he contrived another fire. It was detected more quickly, yet its author did not appear. Then Caesar, having prepared for departure in midwinter, burst forth, declaring on that very day that he fled lest he be burned alive.

## XV

The Emperor therefore now raged not merely against his own household, but against everyone; and first of all he compelled his daughter Valeria and his wife Prisca to be defiled by sacrifice. Eunuchs formerly powerful, through whom the palace itself had previously stood, were killed. Presbyters and ministers were arrested and, without any proof or confession, condemned and led away with all their households. Men and women of every age were dragged away to be burned; and, because the multitude was so great, they were not burned individually but scorched in groups with fire set around them. Household servants, with millstones fastened to their necks, were drowned in the sea.

Nor did persecution descend with less violence upon the remaining populace. Judges scattered throughout all the temples compelled everyone to sacrifice. The prisons were full. Unheard-of kinds of tortures were devised; and lest justice be administered inadvertently to anyone, altars were set up in the judicial secretariats and before the tribunal, so that litigants should first sacrifice and then state their cases. Thus people went to judges as though to [Col. 0217A]

*Notes of the Variorum on columns 217–218*

“Also.” Thus the manuscript; but the printed editions have “and now,” which Heumann considers less good.

“Was not expected.” That is, “was not being expected.” The manuscript reads *spectata*.

“The old Maximian.” Namely, Maximian Herculius.

“Not so merciful.” On the harshness and cruelty of Maximian Herculius, see Eutropius, books IX and X.

“Constantius.” He governed Gaul and Great Britain.

“To dissent.” The manuscript has *desentire*.

“Of the greater [rulers].” That is, of the Augusti, who were superior to the Caesars.

“He allowed the walls … to be demolished.” Thus he allowed churches in certain parts of Gaul to be demolished, but ordered it by no edict. Thus Eusebius does not contradict Lactantius, as Baluzius thought. See his note.

“But the true temple of God.” That is, the Christian person. See Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* V.8 and VI.25: “Finally, let him always have God consecrated in his heart, since he himself is the TEMPLE OF GOD.”

“The whole earth.” That is, the Roman Empire.

“Three most bitter beasts were raging.” Thus in Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* VI.6, “bitter dominations,” and VII.9, “bitter censuses.” These three most bitter beasts were Diocletian, Maximian Herculius, and Galerius Maximianus. He does not count Constantius, who ruled Gaul, among the persecutors. Lactantius, V.2: “Nor without reason are they called BEASTS by the prophets … They disdain the bodies of wild beasts, though they themselves are MORE SAVAGE. For … what Hyrcania ever nourished such savage, such bloodthirsty BEASTS? … That is the true BEAST, at whose single command black blood is everywhere shed,” etc. See above, note on ch. 9.

“Not.” Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.625.

“Could I.” Thus I restored it from the Colbert manuscript, and thus I read it with Virgil, elegantly indeed, in place of *possem*, which all editions of Lactantius give; for example: “if you should be here, you would think otherwise,” in place of “if you were here, you would think otherwise.”

“Donatus.” This Donatus was the friend of our Lactantius, an illustrious confessor of Christ, who, tortured nine times under three judges, triumphed over the devil and was released free from prison.

“Flaccinus the prefect.” Namely, the prefect of Bithynia.

“Hierocles.” The governor of Bithynia.

“Author and adviser for carrying out the persecution.” *Persecutionem facere* (“to carry out a persecution”) was a phrase of those times. Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* V.11: “Another wrote on the same subject more bitterly, who was then among the number of judges and WHO WAS IN THE FIRST PLACE THE AUTHOR OF CARRYING OUT THE PERSECUTION.”

“Priscillianus.” Governor of Bithynia, according to the Greek Menologion for 12 June.

“Zabulum.” That is, *diabolum* (“devil”). Nothing is more common in ancient manuscript books than *zabuli* or *zaboli* for *diaboli*, and *zabolici* for *diabolici*. Thus everywhere among the holy Fathers. See note 2 to the new edition of the works of St Paulinus of Nola by J. B. le Brun, Paris, 1685.

“You have triumphed over the age with its terrors.” To triumph with the accusative is also Lactantian usage: *Institutes* IV, “he might triumph over death with its terrors”; VI.23, “he will triumph over this earth”; *Epitome* 46, “he will triumph over captives”; ibid. 51, “when they see their gods triumphed over by men through the Cross”; and finally ch. 66, “the age having been triumphed over.”

“How pleasant was that spectacle to God!” Cyprian, Epistle 9: “O what a spectacle that was to the Lord!”

Elephants. For the ancients also yoked elephants to a chariot, as is evident from Lampridius in the *Life of Antoninus Heliogabalus* and from other passages. Flavius Vopiscus reports that, in the triumph which Aurelian celebrated over Zenobia and Tetricus, twenty elephants marched in procession. See Bulenger, *On Triumphs*, ch. 21.

“Yoking . . . they were yoked.” Although these words displease the most learned Nicolaus Heinsius, they are nevertheless Lactantian; for thus he says in *Divine Institutes*, book VII: “[Col. 0218D] Aristippus, therefore, was mistaken, who YOKED man, like a beast, to pleasure—that is, to evil.”

“When rulers are ruled.” Here *dominari* has a passive sense, as in Cicero, *On Duties*, book I: “O ancient house, alas, how unlike the master who rules thee!”

“By a wicked command.” Thus Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, book IV, ch. 15: “He acted by word and COMMAND”; and book V, ch. 13: “not tyrannical COMMANDS”; and ch. 11 of the same book: “That is the true beast, by whose single COMMAND black blood is everywhere shed.” And shortly afterwards: “those whom necessity either found or made ministers of another’s fury, attendants of an impious COMMAND.” According to Cange, *jussio* denotes a command, especially that of a prince.

“Bugbears” (*terriculae*), that is, terrors. Livy, book XXXIV, ch. 11: “They were moved by no threats, by no terrors.” On this word consult Nonius. COLUMBUS.

“Nothing could the claws…” The claws (*ungulae*) were a certain kind of iron pincers, formerly used among instruments of torture. For their shape see [Col. 0219C] Gallonius, *On the Torments of Martyrs*, ch. 5, and others who have written on the martyrs.

“...the gods might be approached.” Letters had also been dispatched to Maximian and Constantius, that they should do the same. Their opinion was not awaited in matters so grave. And indeed old Maximian willingly obeyed throughout Italy, being a man not especially merciful. Constantius, however, lest he should appear to dissent from the injunctions of his superiors, allowed the meeting-places—that is, the walls, which could be rebuilt—to be demolished; but he preserved unharmed the true temple of God, which is in human beings.

## XVI

Thus the whole earth was harassed; and, apart from Gaul, from east to west three most savage beasts raged.

> Though I had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths,  
> A voice of iron, I could not comprehend every form  
> Of their crimes, or recount every name of their punishments,

[Col. 0217B] which the judges inflicted upon the righteous and innocent throughout the provinces. But what need is there to relate those things, especially to you, dearest Donatus, who beyond others experienced the storm of the turbulent persecution? For [Col. 0218A] when you had encountered Flaccinus the prefect—not a petty murderer—then Hierocles, formerly vicarius and now governor, who was author and counsellor in bringing about the persecution, and finally Priscillian, his successor, you furnished all with an example of unconquered courage. For nine times subjected to tortures and various torments, nine times you overcame the adversary by glorious confession. In nine battles you defeated the devil (*zabulus*) with his attendants; by nine victories you triumphed over the world (*saeculum*) with its terrors.

How delightful a spectacle was that to God, when he saw you victorious, yoking to your chariot not white horses or huge elephants, but pre-eminently the triumphant conquerors themselves? This is the true triumph: when rulers are ruled. For they were conquered [Col. 0218B] and yoked by your courage; since, scorning their wicked command, you overthrew all the machinery and terrors of tyrannical power by steadfast faith and strength of spirit. Neither blows, nor claws, nor fire, [Col. 0219A]

>
> “That is, a soldier of Christ.” Thus the manuscript. Shortly afterwards it reads: “That is to be a disciple of God”; here, for *est* (“is”), I would prefer *esse* (“to be”), or else that “that is” should be repeated.
>
> “Let no snare ensnare.” The same expression occurs in Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, book VI, ch. 24, after the middle: “they are ENSNARED IN the same SNARES.”
>
> “Of the Lord.” Thus in the manuscript, *Dni*; when the true name of God is written there, *Di* is read. Yet the other printed editions have “of God,” contrary to the authority of the manuscript.
>
> “Of Diocletian.” Thus the manuscript; the printed editions, however, have “Diocletian.”
>
> “Vicennalia.” Emperors celebrated quinquennial, decennial, and vicennial festivals at great expense.
>
> “Since he could not endure the freedom of the Roman people.” Here *cum* means “because,” and therefore does not govern the subjunctive. “Freedom”: the manuscript has *libertate*, wrongly.
>
> “He contracted an illness that was slight, but lasting.” With learned critics I read *at traxit* (“but contracted”) for *ac*, which is found in the manuscripts. *Traxit* stands for *contraxit* (“contracted”). A simple verb for a compound one, as Lactantius commonly does.
>
> “By a circuitous route along the Istrian shore.” The manuscript has *ripae Strigae* (“shore of Striga”). Many learned men suspect an error in the manuscript’s word *Strigae*. They read *Istricae*, that is, “along the shore of the province of Istria,” which Diocletian should have sought when, leaving Ravenna, he went to Nicomedia. For why should he have made the longer journey toward the Danube, when a shorter and easier route lay along the coast of Istria and of Dalmatia, Diocletian’s own homeland, then through Illyricum, where there were military roads by which he might reach Byzantium and afterwards sail past to Nicomedia? He says “by a circuitous route,” because, in seeking the Istrian shore, he had to go around the northern part of the Adriatic gulf. Whoever desires more may read Henry Dodwell’s dissertation *On the Shore of Striga*, at the end of this volume.
>
> “Wherever he saw himself pressed.” Correctly, by metathesis, for *quoque cum se premi videret* (“whenever he saw himself pressed”). Similarly: “we shall have made sufficient satisfaction to God,” *Divine Institutes*, book IV, ch. 17.
>
> “Overcome.” Supply “he was,” which Lactantius often leaves implicit.
>
> “And.” The manuscript has *ad*, erroneously.
>
> “Changed.” Heumann wishes to read *mutati*.
>
> “Until the Caesar…” That is, Galerius Maximianus should arrive.
>
> “The whole.” The manuscript has *tota*, erroneously.
>
> “Stunned.” In the printed editions *morte* (“by death”) is prefixed, though it is absent from the manuscript. Some prefer *morti*, others *morbo*; but wrongly. For, as the most learned Graevius rightly observes, those are called *sopiti* (“stunned,” “benumbed”) who, through a fainting fit, lose for a time both consciousness and bodily sensation, and lie as though dead. Livy, book I: “Tanaquil addresses the people and orders them to be of good courage: the king had been stunned by a sudden blow; the weapon had not penetrated deeply into his body; he had already returned to himself.” This passage is nearly parallel to Lactantius’. “He had recovered his spirit” is the same as “he had returned to himself.” Those benumbed by sleep, a wound, or illness awaken and return to themselves; those benumbed by death sleep that iron sleep from which they are never awakened in this world. GRAEVIUS.
