>
> “The Caesar.” Galerius Maximianus.
>
> “Not in order to congratulate his father.” He was Diocletian’s adopted son, and also his son-in-law: see ch. 9. For Galerius had married Galeria Valeria, Diocletian’s daughter. TOINARD.
>
> “To compel him to yield the empire.” The manuscript, here as below, has *imperium credere* (“entrust the empire”).
>

>
> “He therefore approached Diocletian, saying that he was now an old man,” etc. Here begins the dialogue between Diocletian and Maximian Galerius: the latter, Diocletian’s son-in-law, pressing him to surrender imperial power, the former resisting. This point must be carefully noticed. For until now we have supposed Diocletian’s abdication to have been voluntary and long contemplated; and this certainly seemed most clearly deducible [Col. 0221B] from ancient authors who wrote only the public histories and did not know the secrets of affairs. But Lactantius, who had been summoned to Nicomedia by Diocletian and was frequently at court, could know this entire history better than those who later turned their minds to writing histories. BALUZE.]

neither iron nor the various kinds of torture had any power against you. No force could take from you faith and devotion. This is to be a disciple of God; this is to be a soldier of Christ: one whom no enemy storms, no wolf carries away from the heavenly camp, no snare entangles, no pain conquers, no torment afflicts. Finally, after those nine most glorious contests, in which the devil was defeated by you, he did not dare to engage you any further, having learned through so many battles that you could not be overcome. And when a victorious crown was prepared for you, he ceased to challenge you further, lest you should now receive it. Though you have not received it in the present life, it is nevertheless kept whole for you in the kingdom of the Lord, in accordance with your courage and merits. But let us return to the order of events.

## XVII

[Col. 0219B] This crime, then, having been committed, Diocletian—since prosperity had now departed from him—immediately proceeded to Rome, in order to celebrate there the day of his vicennalia, which was to fall on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December [20 November]. When these solemnities had been celebrated, since he could not endure the freedom of the Roman people, impatient and sick at heart, he burst forth from the city as the Kalends of January approached, on which his ninth consulship was to be conferred. He could not endure thirteen days, so as to enter upon the consulship at Rome rather than Ravenna. But setting out in winter, scourged by severe cold and rain, he contracted an illness slight but lasting; and, harassed throughout the entire journey, he was carried for the most part in a litter. [Col. 0220A] Thus, after the summer had passed, he came to Nicomedia by a circuitous route along the Istrian shore, his illness now growing severe. Wherever he saw himself pressed, he was nevertheless carried out, in order to dedicate the circus which he had built, when the year after his vicennalia had been completed; then he was so overcome by weakness that prayers for his life were offered to every god, until on the Ides of December [13 December] there were suddenly mourning in the palace, grief and tears, the alarm of the judges, and silence. The entire city was already saying that he was not merely dead but even buried, when suddenly, on the following morning, a report spread abroad that he lived, and the faces of the household and judges changed to joy. There were not lacking those who suspected that his death was being concealed until the Caesar should arrive, lest perhaps the soldiers undertake some innovation. This suspicion prevailed so strongly that no one believed him alive until he appeared on the Kalends [Col. 0220B] of March [1 March], scarcely recognizable, since for almost an entire year he had wasted away through illness. And on the Ides of December he had been benumbed and recovered his spirit—but not all of it. For he became insane, so that at fixed hours he raved and at fixed hours recovered his senses.

## XVIII

And not many days later the Caesar arrived, not to congratulate his father, but to compel him to surrender imperial power. He had recently clashed with old Maximian and frightened him by raising the spectre of civil war. He therefore approached Diocletian, first gently and amicably, saying that he was now an old man, and now less vigorous, [Col. 0221A]

> “At the same time he advanced Nerva’s example,” etc. This is altogether false; for Trajan, adopted by Nerva, did not reign until Nerva had died. It should be observed, however, that this is not asserted by Lactantius on his own authority, but is reported in Lactantius as spoken by Maximian in his own interest. For he wished to misuse this example before Diocletian, [Col. 0221C] a man uneducated and ignorant of history, but then also hard pressed, in order to induce him to abdicate the empire. TOINARD.
>
> “But he said that it was also unbecoming.” I have restored *et* (“also”) from the manuscript. I have no doubt that Lactantius wrote it thus. Otherwise he would have written *sibi* (“for himself”), as below, not *ei* (“for him”), as in the printed editions: “Diocletian said.”
>
> “Had fallen.” The manuscript has *decidisse* (“to have fallen”).
>
> “Had acquired.” The manuscript has *quaesisse*, that is, “had acquired”; or it may be understood from the certain fact that no one voluntarily incurs the hatred of many people, but always suffers it unwillingly. Likewise, above at the beginning of this book and below, ch. 31 after the middle, *quaesierunt* means “they acquired,” and *cibos labore quaesitos* means “food acquired by labour.” Lactantius customarily employs the verb *quaerere* in the sense of *acquirere*, a simple verb for a compound one: *Divine Institutes*, book I, ch. 20, and *Epitome*, ch. 20: “Flora, having ACQUIRED great wealth by the trade of prostitution”; book II, ch. 12: “Through his divine and unique name he SEEKS mercy for himself”; book IV, [Col. 0221D] ch. 1: “They ACQUIRED eternal death for themselves, together with the gods and bodily goods”; book V, ch. 1, near the end, speaking of St Cyprian: “He had ACQUIRED great glory for himself from the profession of oratory”; book VI, ch. 12: “Shall I destroy the family property ACQUIRED through my own labour or that of my ancestors?”; book VII, ch. 11: “They ACQUIRED an indelible name for their courage”; likewise ch. 14: “By their merits they ACQUIRED for themselves not immortality but death through sins and lusts”; likewise ch. 15: *male quaesitum*, “badly acquired”; and *Epitome*, ch. 27.

and unfit to administer the Republic; that he ought to rest after his labours. At the same time he brought forward the example of Nerva, who had handed over the empire to Trajan. But Diocletian said that it was also unbecoming, after so great a splendour of lofty rank, to have fallen into the obscurity of humble life; and less safe, because during so long a reign he had acquired for himself the enmities of many. Nerva, however, after ruling for one year, because he could not bear the weight and care of affairs so great, whether by reason of age or inexperience, had laid aside the helm of the Republic and returned to private life, in which he had grown old. But if he desired to obtain the title of emperor, nothing prevented all from being called Augusti.

But Galerius, who had already embraced the whole world in hope, seeing that there would come to him either nothing beyond the title or not much [Col. 0221B] more, replied that Diocletian’s arrangement ought to be preserved perpetually: that there should be two greater men in the Republic, holding the supreme power, and likewise two lesser men [Col. 0222A] to assist them; that harmony could easily be maintained between two, but by no means among four equals. If Diocletian refused to yield, he would look to himself, so that he should no longer be the lesser and lowest-ranking. Fifteen years had now passed, he said, since he had been banished into Illyricum—that is, to the bank of the Danube—to struggle with barbarian peoples, while others ruled luxuriously within lands more spacious and tranquil.

When he heard this, the feeble old man, who had now also received letters from old Maximian, reporting whatever Galerius had said to him, and had learned that he was increasing his army, said tearfully:

**DIOCLETIAN.** “Let it be so, if this pleases you. It remained for Caesars to be chosen by the common counsel of all.”

**GALERIUS.** “What need is there of counsel, when those two must approve whatever we do?”

**D.** “Yes, precisely. For it is necessary that their sons be nominated. [Col. 0223A]

> “He had recently ordered him to be called Maximian after his own name.” Baluze, a most distinguished man, acknowledges in his notes that here and almost always elsewhere the old manuscript reads *Maximianum*. Hence I suspect that Daza was called Maximianus by Galerius Maximianus from the latter’s full own name, not Maximinus. For in two inscriptions from the Baths of Diocletian in Gruter, p. CLXXXVIII, nos. 2 and 7, after Constantius and Maximianus Augusti and Severus Caesar, there is named Maximianus Caesar, who can be none other than Daza. > “Diocletian had changed his name in part, for the sake of an omen,” etc. Toinard thinks one should read *nomen ex fratre mutuaverat, ominis causa* (“he had borrowed the name from his brother, for the sake of an omen”). For, he asks, can anyone be said to change another’s name in part who adds to it an entire name, as this *Maximiani* was imposed upon Galerius by Diocletian? Lactantius here uses *mutuaverat* for *mutuatus fuerat* (“had borrowed”), as in Priscian, book VIII, on the verbs *meto* and *metor*, *mutuo* and *mutuor*, and in Nonius, ch. 17, no. 48. To understand the basis of this emendation, it must be known that Maximian Herculius had been called Diocletian’s brother, namely by partnership in the empire. TOINARD.—“He had changed [his] name in part.” That is, Galerius had been ordered to lay aside his old praenomen and thereafter be called Maximianus Galerius. Thus Diocletian had changed his name not wholly but partly. Had this interpretation occurred to Toinard, he would not have laboured so vainly to prove that one should read “he had borrowed the name from his brother.” HEUMANN.—“For the sake of an omen.” [Col. 0225B] The manuscript has *hominis* (“of a man”), wrongly. With learned men—Cuperus, Toinard, and others—I write *ominis*. He says “for the sake of an omen” because, he says, he hoped Daza would prove as faithful to him as Maximian Herculius was, whose name he gave to the other.]

Caesars. Maximian had a son, Maxentius, son-in-law of this same Maximian, a man of destructive and wicked disposition, so proud and obstinate that he was accustomed to adore neither his father nor his father-in-law. Constantius also had a son, Constantine, a most upright young man and most worthy of that high position, who, because of his notable and distinguished physical appearance, military ability, good character, and singular graciousness, was loved by soldiers and desired also by private citizens. >
> “You shall see.” A formula of disapproval. These and all the words to the end of the chapter are Diocletian’s.—“You shall see . . . it will not be.” Diocletian speaks, with whose words Lactantius concludes this conversation. The very learned Nourry judged this dialogue to contain such great difficulties that, without intense application and weighing every single word, no one could readily determine what Diocletian or Galerius had said; and because of these great difficulties he says that interpreters supplied distinct initial letters to the different words of the interlocutors, whereas the author himself ought to have prefixed such marks. Further, if the matter had been so difficult, perhaps the interpreters would have erred here in assigning the speakers. But since, with the exception of Bauldrius alone, all have correctly indicated the words of Diocletian and Maximian Galerius, this very agreement attests the clarity of the dialogue. Indeed Baluze, Columbus, Cuperus, and others supplied no marks at all for the speakers. Where this has been done by Toinard, Cellarius, Walch, and ourselves, it was done not because of such great obscurity but for the benefit of those who are either hurried, excessively dull-witted, or eager to have their own opinion confirmed by others. If certain things seem less clear, it happens because this conversation is unknown to all other historians. But Lactantius, as Baluze rightly judged, having been summoned to Nicomedia by Diocletian and being frequently at court, could know this history better than those who later turned their minds to writing histories. BUNEMANN.
>
> “Will occur.” Thus the manuscript, not *acciderit* (“will happen”), although Heumann, with Gale, preferred *acciderit*.
>
> “On the Kalends of May.” Hence it is established that Diocletian and Maximian Herculius laid aside the purple on the Kalends of May in the year 305.
>
> “The foremost soldiers.” Thus the manuscript. Some would prefer *primores militum* (“the chief men among the soldiers”), just as “chief men of cities” occurs below in ch. 21. But both readings are good. See Cuperus’ note and Cange’s *Glossary*.
>
> “Outside the city.” Near Nicomedia.
>
> “At the summit of which Maximian…” Namely Galerius Armentarius.—“Maximian himself.” Nourry, p. 258 and p. 279, with some others, takes this to refer to Maximian Herculius; but it seems more correctly taken of Galerius Maximian, for this chapter speaks below of him, and the pronoun *ipse* requires this, just as in ch. 18 it is used in the same way of Galerius Maximian. BUNEMANN.
>
> “An assembly of soldiers is called.” “The old man says.” The passage is thought corrupt. Yet the manuscript reads *inquit senex* (“the old man says”). Some think it should be restored as *in qua senex* (“in which the old man”); others, *convocetur, inquit senex* (“let an assembly be called, says the old man”). But whether one reads *inquietus senex* (“the troubled old man”), following the editions, or *inquit senex*, or even “Let an assembly of soldiers be called, says the old man, with tears,” etc., the sense is much the same.
>
> “Maximinus.” Namely Daia. In the manuscript he is always called Maximianus. Greek and Latin writers often confuse the two names. We have everywhere restored “Maximinus,” lest any difficulty delay the reader.
>
> “Constantine stood by.” As tribune of the protectores and carrying out his duties; for by what reason would he have been absent from so celebrated an event?
>
> “Upwards” (*susum*). For *sursum*; it occurs in Plautus, *Cistellaria*, act II, scene 3, v. 78.
>
> “To hesitate.” The manuscript has *stare* (“to stand”); but in the margin, in the same hand and ink, *esitare*, which is nothing other than *haesitare* (“to hesitate”), and gives the correct sense. The printed editions have *sciscitari* (“to inquire”), also a good sense. The most learned Baluze therefore substituted *sciscitari* for the manuscript’s *stare*, and *esitare* in the margin for *haesitare*. But the learned Paul Bauldri suspected that *susum stare* should be read *susurrare* (“to whisper”), which suits this place as well as *sciscitari*.
>
> “Among themselves.” Understand: asking one another. “Maximian”: Galerius.
>
> “Having stripped him.” Daia: thus Baluze corrected it in the errata, and syntax requires it, not *exuto* (“having stripped”), as in the manuscript.—“Having stripped [him of] private clothing.” Spark and Bauldrius prefer “of private clothing.” But the manuscript reading, *exuto*, is foolish. I note on Lactantius, book IV, ch. 14: “Clothed in filthy garments.” BUNEMANN.
>
> “The East to tread underfoot.” Cicero, *Philippics* II, ch. 23: “when Caesar had given him Italy to trample underfoot.” Lactantius, book VI, ch. 18: “We tread underfoot pain and death.” BUNEMANN.
>
> “Disturbed by the unforeseen novelty of the event.” This is how it should be emended. The manuscript reads: “by the inspired novelty of the event,” wrongly.
>
> “Diocletian threw his own purple upon him.” Diocletian clothed Maximian Daia as Caesar in his own purple garment; whence one may infer that the garments of emperors and Caesars were then the same.
>
> “Diocles became himself again.” That is, he returned to private life, as before he had undertaken the government of the empire.]

because Maximian had shown loyalty with the utmost conscientiousness.

**D.** “Who is this whom you offer me?”

**G.** “My kinsman,” he said.

**D.** But he groaned: “You are giving me men not fit to be entrusted with the guardianship of the Republic.”

**G.** “I have tested them,” he said.

**D.** “You shall see, since you are to assume the government of the empire. I have laboured enough, and have provided that, while I reigned, the Republic should stand unharmed. If anything adverse should occur, it will not be my fault.”

## XIX

When these arrangements had been made, he came forth on the Kalends of May [1 May]. All watched Constantine. There was no doubt. The soldiers who were present, the foremost soldiers chosen for the occasion [Col. 0225B] and summoned from the legions, fixed upon this one man, rejoiced, wished for him, and offered prayers. There was a high place about three miles outside the city, at the summit of which [Col. 0226A] Maximian himself had assumed the purple; and there a column had been raised bearing the image of Jupiter. They proceeded thither. An assembly of soldiers was called. The old man spoke with tears and addressed the soldiers: he was infirm, he sought rest after his labours, he was handing over the empire to men stronger than himself, and was appointing other Caesars. All waited in the highest expectation to see what he would bring forth.

Then suddenly he proclaimed Severus and Maximinus Caesars. All were astonished on the tribunal. Constantine stood by, looking upward. They hesitated among themselves, wondering whether Constantine’s name had been changed, when, before the eyes of all, Maximian stretched his hand backwards, drew Daia forward from behind—Constantine being thrust aside—and, stripping him of his private clothing, placed him in the middle. All wondered who he was and whence he came. Yet no one dared object, all being disturbed by the unforeseen novelty of the event. [Col. 0226B] Diocletian threw upon him his own purple garment, which he had taken off, and Diocles became himself again. Then they descended; and the veteran king was conveyed out by carriage through the city. [Col. 0227A]

> [Note: [Col. 0227B] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 227–228]
>
> “Homeland.” Salonae in Dalmatia, whose ruins lie opposite the city of Spalato, near the fortress of Clissa. Spalato was Diocletian’s estate, where he died. Thus St Jerome says of him in the *Chronicle*: “Diocletian dies not far from Salonae, at his estate of Spalato.”
>
> “Guardsman” (*scutarius*). That is, an ordinary soldier.
>
> “Protector.” That is, a member of the emperor’s bodyguard serving in protective custody.
>
> “Maximian.” Galerius.
>
> “After the old men had been expelled.” Diocletian and Maximian Herculius.
>
> “And accomplished.” Perhaps *effecit* (“accomplished”). Thus Lactantius, book VI, ch. 14: “We shall see whether they accomplish what they wish.”
>
> “He believed himself to be.” The manuscript reads *esse ferebatur* (“he was said to be”). Some read *esse se rebatur* (“he believed himself to be”); the printed editions read *esse ferebat*.
>
> “Health.” Thus the manuscript. Consult Dausqueius, *On Orthography*, under *valitudo* and *valetudo*.
>
> “Had died.” Manuscript: *novisset* (“had learned”); wrongly.
>
> “By three.” Namely Galerius, Severus, and Maximinus.
>
> “He himself.” Maximian Galerius.
>
> “Or.” After *nominaret* (“he might name”), the manuscript has a blank space for two letters, which I believed to have been *ut*, because of the line drawn above; as I have represented it here. If one wishes the letters to have been *et*, that too is possible.
>
> “He might call [him] Augustus and brother.” As above in ch. 8, and in laws where Marcus and Lucius Antoninus are called “the divine brothers.” Yet this was not permanent; for Augusti also made their sons Augustan emperors, as Severus, Philip, and Theodosius did. CELLARIUS.
>
> “Then indeed he himself.” Galerius himself, delighting in this plan. CELLARIUS.
>
> “His own son.” Candidianus, born of a concubine. For he had no son by his wife Valeria, Diocletian’s daughter, who was barren, as Lactantius teaches below in ch. 50.
>
> “He himself should lay down [the empire].” Galerius too should lay down imperial power, following the example of Diocletian and Maximian Herculius.
>
> “Candidianus.” Galerius’ son, then nine years old. CELLARIUS.
>
> “With an impregnable wall.” Lactantius commonly writes thus: book IV, ch. 27, “as though an impregnable wall.” BUNEMANN.
>
> [Col. 0228B]
>
> “These plans showed them.” With learned men I read *consilia* (“plans”). The manuscript has *consilio eis* (“by counsel to them”), namely to Galerius and Licinius, whose advice Galerius, as we have seen above, employed in governing everything. The printed editions read “his plans showed.” The most learned Graevius judges that one should read: “His plans tended to this.”
>
> [Col. 0228C]
>
> “Having therefore obtained…” Galerius.
>
> “The defeated Persians.” See above, ch. 9.
>
> “They commit themselves to slavery.” Here *servitium* stands for *servitus*, as in Lactantius, *Epitome*, ch. 52 at the beginning: “he shall hand over all nations INTO SLAVERY”; *Divine Institutes*, book II, ch. 1: “They DEVOTE themselves wholly to lusts”; book VI, chs. 20 and 23: “because they had DEVOTED themselves to the body, in which death has power.” On this Persian institution or custom, read Brissonius.
>
> “Household.” That is, servants or slaves, as among the Persians. The manuscript has only *milia* (“thousands”), and lacks *fa-*.
>
> “The land.” The manuscript has *era*.
>
> “Thus he acted, that he himself…” Heumann: “He did this, so that in fact…” I myself would prefer: “Thus he acted, so that he might silently take freedom away from men.” BUNEMANN.
>
> “The decurions were tortured.” Under Roman civil law it was not permitted to torture decurions, as is evident from Constantine’s letter to Probianus, proconsul of Africa. Later, however, Constantine enacted a law permitting decurions to be tortured in cases of forgery. BALUZE.
>
> “Of the cities.” The manuscript has *civitatis* (“of the city”), with *u* written above the final syllable.]

Egregii ac perfectissimi viri. “Distinguished” and “most perfect” men: honorary ranks, concerning which see Law 1 of the Theodosian Code, *On Honorary Diplomas*. Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, V.14: “No one is distinguished unless he has been good and innocent; no one most illustrious unless he has lavishly performed works of mercy; no one most perfect unless he has fulfilled every degree of virtue.” The rank of *perfectissimus*, as Valesius says in his note on Book XXI of Ammianus Marcellinus, was lower than that of *clarissimus*; and, as the *clarissimi* assembled before the Prefect of the City, so the *perfectissimi* before the Vicariate Prefecture.

Noble matrons were carried off into the *gynaeceum*. *Gynaecea*, as the word itself indicates, were places assigned to women’s work, into which both men and women were sometimes cast as a punishment. See Valesius’s notes on Eusebius, p. 211, and Cange’s *Glossary*.

[Col. 0229B]

*Gynaeceum.* In the manuscript, *Geniceum*.

“is transported and sent back to his homeland. But Daia, recently raised from cattle and forests, was immediately a guardsman, then at once a protector, soon a tribune, and the next day Caesar; he received the East to tread down and crush—being a man who knew neither military service nor the commonwealth, now a shepherd not of cattle but of soldiers.”

XX. Maximian, after expelling the old men, had done whatever he wished and believed himself now the sole master of the whole world. For he despised Constantius, although he necessarily had to be named first, because Constantius was mild by nature and impaired in bodily health. He hoped that he would soon die; and, if he did not die, it seemed easy to strip him of office even against his will. For what could he do if three men compelled him to lay down the imperial power? He himself had Licinius, a friend from their old companionship and an intimate from his first military service, whose counsel he used in governing everything. But he did not wish to make him Caesar, lest he should name him his son, or later proclaim him Augustus and brother in Constantius’s place; while he himself would then retain the supreme power, rage over the world at his own discretion, celebrate his twentieth anniversary, and, having substituted his own son as Caesar—who was then [Col. 0228A] nine years old—would himself lay down office. Thus, while Licinius and Severus held the highest power, and Maximinus and Candidianus held the second title of Caesars, protected by an impregnable wall, he might spend a secure and tranquil old age. To this end their plans tended. But God, whom he had made hostile to himself, frustrated all his designs.

XXI. Having therefore obtained the highest power, he bent his mind upon harassing the world which lay open before him. For after the Persians had been conquered—whose custom and practice is to devote themselves to service under their kings, and for kings to use their people as though they were a household—this wicked man wished to introduce that custom into Roman territory, and from the time of that victory shamelessly praised it. And because [Col. 0228B] he could not openly command it, he acted so as himself to deprive men of liberty. First, he took away their honors. Under him not only decurions but also leading men of cities—distinguished and most perfect men—were tortured, and indeed in trivial civil cases. If they seemed deserving of death, crosses stood ready; if not, fetters were prepared. Freeborn and noble matrons were carried off into the *gynaeceum*. If anyone was to be flogged, four posts stood fixed [Col. 0229A]

[Note: [Col. 0229B] [Various Notes to columns 229–230]

*In the stable.* Thus the manuscript, not *sabulo*, as some preferred. Here understand *stabulum* not as a stable for horses, but for racks and similar apparatus, where people stood fastened to posts and nearly suspended. Thus Plautus has *stabulum ferriterium*, “an iron-rack stable,” in *Persa*, Act III, scene 3, line 13, according to Gronovius’s emendation. COLUMBUS.

“To which no slave had ever been customarily stretched.” Thus the manuscript. Some would prefer to read “unless a slave.”

*Lusorium.* A theatre or amphitheatre where public games were presented, as Cange demonstrates at greater length. Salvian, Book VI, p. 123 of Baluze’s second edition; *Acts of Saint Seraphia, Virgin and Martyr*. BALUZ.

*Ferociae.* The manuscript has *Ferocia*, incorrectly.

“And very like himself in ferocity and size.” Lactantius uses *similis* with the dative in *Divine Institutes*, IV.24, *hominum simillimum*, “most like men”; III.20, *suorum simillimus*, “most like his own”; *On the Wrath of God*, 18, “he made man LIKE HIMSELF”; and 19, “God recognizes these as LIKE HIMSELF”; *On the Workmanship [of God]*, 16, “LIKE THE TRUE.”

*Elegerat.* He had selected bears larger-bodied, more monstrous, and fiercer than others.

*Nominatim.* Perhaps the tyrant had given each bear a particular name.

“But to be sucked dry.” Bears are accustomed, that is, to lick and suck blood and so consume the body; hence Eusebius rightly classes them among “blood-devouring beasts” (*αἰμοβόροις θηρσί*) in *Ecclesiastical History*, VIII.7. *Obsorbere*, moreover, occurs also in Plautus, *Truculentus* 2.3.30: “which suck up whatever comes within the bars”; and *Miles Gloriosus* 3.2.21, “because I sucked it up.” From Virgil, *Georgics* IV and *Aeneid* II.

*Objectabantur.* For *objiciebantur*, “were thrown before.”

“Men . . . whose limbs, when they were torn apart.” A Lactantian expression, *Institutes* V.11: “No one can adequately describe the ferocity of so great a beast, which . . . with iron teeth . . . not only TEARS APART THE LIMBS OF MEN, but,” etc.

“And this he first, etc.” Thus I read with the most learned man. The manuscript reads: “and he had first permitted exile against Christians, laws having been issued.” Should one read *promserat*, “had promulgated”? Cicero, *On the Laws*, I.22.

*Deligati.* The same as *ligati*, “bound.” The manuscript: *Delegati*.

*Callum solorum.* Cicero speaks of this hardened skin of the feet in Book V of the *Tusculan Disputations*.

“Breath might be restored.” Lactantius, *Institutes* V.11: “They therefore strive to prevail, inflict exquisite pains upon bodies, and avoid nothing so much as having those tortured die.” And shortly after: “But they, with obstinate folly, order careful treatment to be applied to the tortured, so that their limbs may be renewed for further tortures and fresh blood restored for punishment.” BALUZ.

*Accidebat.* The manuscript has *Accedebat*.

“When throughout much of the day, etc.” With the approval of all learned men, I read *cum* (“when”) for *tunc* (“then”), which occurs in the manuscript, followed by the same number of strokes.

“Bones gathered and crushed into powder.” Relevant are the words of *Institutes* V.11: “No one can adequately describe the ferocity of so great a beast, which, lying in one place, nevertheless rages with iron teeth throughout the whole world and not only tears apart the limbs of men [Col. 0230C] but crushes even the bones themselves and raves them into ashes, so that no place for burial may remain—as though those who confess God desired people to come to their graves.” Here *legere ossa*, “to gather bones,” means to collect them. BUN.

“Into river and sea.” Thus the manuscript, and it should not be read otherwise. For formerly, as in Ovid and Varro, *mare* was written in the sixth case; and with the preposition *in*, used in place of the fourth case, you will find it more than once in Lactantius. See Columbus’s note on this passage. *Jactabantur*, “were cast,” for *jaciebantur*. Heumann, however, wishes “into a river and sea” (*in flumen ac mare*) to be read.

“No punishment with him was light.” In the old copy it reads, *nulla penis eum levis*. A very bad reading has pointed us to the good one. BALUZ.

*Insulae.* The manuscript: *Insolae*.

*Carceres.* The manuscript: *Incarceris*.

“Those . . . daily.” The manuscript: “That . . . daily.”

*Facilia.* That is, readily granted. ALMELOV.

*Domestici.* These were men divided into various corps who served more intimately within [Col. 0230D] the palace, though some were nevertheless sometimes sent into the provinces. BUN.

*Administratores.* Officials serving in the court.

“In the council chamber, capital punishment and execution by the sword.” Thus I read, with the approval of the most learned man, with no alteration or only the slightest. For the manuscript reads: *In ca poena capitis et animadversio gladii*, incorrectly. Printed editions have: “In a capital case and execution by the sword,” omitting *poena*, “punishment.”

“As though a favor.” Thus I read with two learned men, instead of *beneficii*, which is in the manuscript; there is no need to add the word *loco*, “in place.”

“A good death.” That is, not one compelled by the violence of tortures, nor a shameful and ignominious death upon a public gallows, but an easy and private one—such as the opening of veins or poison—often granted at the pleasure of defendants. See below, chapter 26, at the end. In the manuscript: *bona morte*.

“Now these things had been light to him.” I restore *huic*, namely Galerius, in place of *his*. See the preceding: “he had learned . . . he practiced . . . in him.”

*Execrati.* Passive, as below, *metiebantur*.

in the stable, to which no slave had ever customarily been stretched. Why should I relate his playground or delights? He had bears very like himself in ferocity and size, which he had selected throughout the time of his reign. Whenever he wished to amuse himself, he ordered some particular one of them to be brought. Men were thrown before these bears not to be eaten outright but to be sucked dry. When their limbs were torn apart, he laughed most pleasantly; nor did he ever dine without human blood. For those without rank, the penalty was fire; and this he had first permitted against Christians, laws having been issued that, after torture, the condemned should be burned by slow fires. Once they had been bound, a gentle flame was first applied beneath their feet for so long that the hardened skin of their soles, contracted by the fire, was torn away from the bones. Then lighted and [Col. 0229B] extinguished torches were applied to every limb, so that no place on the body was left untouched. Meanwhile the face was drenched with cold water, and the mouth washed with liquid, lest, as the throat dried from thirst, breath should quickly [Col. 0230A] be given up. This finally occurred when, after much of the day, all the skin having been boiled away, the force of fire had penetrated to the innermost organs. Thereupon a pyre having been made, the bodies, already burned, were burned; the bones were collected, crushed into powder, and cast into river and sea.

XXII. Therefore, what he had learned in torturing Christians, he practiced against everyone through force of habit. No punishment was light with him: not islands, prisons, or mines; but fire, the cross, and wild beasts were for him daily and easy things. Members of the imperial household and administrators were corrected with the spear. In the council chamber, capital punishment and execution by the sword were awarded to very few as though a favor—those who, because of former merits, had obtained a good death. By now these things had been light to him. Eloquence was extinguished; advocates [Col. 0230B] were removed; jurists were either exiled or killed. Learning was counted among the evil arts; and those who knew it were crushed and cursed as enemies and foes. License in all things, the laws having been dissolved, was assumed

[Col. 0231A]

[Note: [Col. 0231B] [Various Notes to columns 231–232]

*Assessoribus.* That is, advisers.

“Was of all.” Thus the manuscript. Two learned men suspect that *initium*, “the beginning,” should be read in place of *omnium*, “of all.”

“Sent once.” Those two learned men prefer *simul*, “together,” in place of *semel*, “once.” The two are often confused in the manuscript.

*Glebatim.* Thus in the manuscript: that is, from clod to clod, plot by plot. ALMELOV.

[Col. 0231C]

*Metiebantur.* “Were measured,” passively; so also in Arnobius and Quintus Curtius, Book III. In the manuscript: *mitiebantur*.

*Scribebantur.* That is, they were entered on record; their number and kind were recorded in registers so that a tax might be paid on their account. Thus *scriptura* is more than once used by Cicero for a tax.

*Adunatae.* Lactantius also uses this word near the end of *On the Workmanship of God*, 17.

*Fora omnia.* The manuscript: *Foras omnia*, incorrectly.

*Suspendebantur.* Add: from the rack.

“The most faithful slaves were tortured against their masters.” Contrary to the legal rule that forbids slaves to be examined in a case against their masters.

“If everything had failed.” Thus the manuscript. Some learned men wish to read: “if tortures, or instruments of torture, had failed.” I should prefer: “if all these things had failed.”

“They themselves were tortured against themselves.” That is, they were driven by tortures to accuse—and as it were convict—themselves. [Col. 0231D] Lactantius likes such conceits. Thus *Divine Institutes* V.2: “himself a stern censor against himself and a most severe accuser”; VI.6: “they cut off the steps by which they ascended, lest anyone be able to imitate them against themselves”; I.18, II.1, and VI.8: “he will flee himself.”

*Adscribebantur.* That is, even possessions that were not possessed were entered on the rolls, so that they might assign those possessions, or their value, to the treasury.

*Valitudinis.* Thus the manuscript. One must supply *nulla*, “no,” or *aut*, “or,” which has fallen out of the manuscript. Heumann writes: “or of health.”

“Years were added to little children; years were taken away from old men.” Here is the reason for both practices from Ulpian, *On Censuses*, *Digest* L.15, § [where he says]: “In making a census it is necessary to state age, because age grants some persons exemption from the burden of tribute. Thus among Syrians males from fourteen years and females from twelve years until the sixty-fifth year are liable to the poll-tax. Age, moreover, is assessed at the time of census-taking.” BAULDRI.

[Col. 0232B]

—“Years were added to little children, so that they could be tortured, or rather so that they might pay tax. For imperial laws provided that those, for example, who were not ten years old, and those born more than sixty years earlier, were not bound to pay poll-tax, as is clear from Book III of the *Digest*, *On Censuses*, and Books IV and 6 of the Theodosian Code under the same title, where Jacobus Gothofredus may be consulted.”

[Col. 0232C]

“What the ancients.” Namely, the Romans. I find no reason for changing this reading, which occurs in the manuscript and can stand. The editors, following Baluze, substituted “conquerors.”

*Haec illae.* The manuscript: *Et ille*, wrongly written by the copyist.

*Parentes.* That is, ancestors, because of his mother from beyond the Danube.

*Daciis.* Thus the manuscript, with a double *i*. For there were two Dacias, upper and lower; so too in Paulinus of Nola, Bishop, poem 17, to Nicetas, line 249: “and each is a Dacian.” See above: “the census was sent into the provinces.” Therefore I wished to change nothing. Either reading is good.

*Post hoc.* Heumann reads *post haec*, “after these things.”

*Hisdem.* Read *iisdem*, “the same.”

*Mortales.* Lactantius uses this word for “human beings” in *Divine Institutes* I: “a work which he himself granted to mortals for propagating offspring”; VII.15: “the works of mortals are mortal”; VII.14: “certain mortals”; and elsewhere [Col. 0232D] frequently. Likewise *mortalitas*, “humanity,” in the same sense, IV.24.

“And nothing the less.” Almeloveen, Gale, and the Abo edition: “and nevertheless.”

“Whom misery and misfortune had made safe from every kind of injury.” Lactantius, *Epitome*, 59, near the end: “they might make themselves safe from injuries.” Yet a certain learned man wished the manuscript’s reading: “the injury of the age,” or “of the times,” in French, *par le malheur des temps*, “by the misfortune of the times.” — “Misery and misfortune.” In the manuscript: “of misery and misfortune,” incorrectly.

“An impious man.” Thus the manuscript. I should prefer, with certain learned men, “a pious man,” ironically, because the word “compassionate” follows in the manuscript, not “pitiless.”

“Thus, while he took care.” Some would read “takes care,” because “may evade” follows in the manuscript; or else one should read “might evade.” Thus Tollius, Columbus, and Heumann.

“Of wretched men.” Thus the manuscript. I should prefer “of truly wretched men.”

“He killed, contrary to every law of humanity.” So too Lactantius, [Col. 0233B] *Divine Institutes* V.19: “Are minds evil in those who are mangled contrary to the law of humanity, contrary to every sacred right?” and 22: “nor does he covet anything belonging to another, lest his speech harm anyone contrary to the law of humanity”; VI.10: “therefore those who injure men, who plunder, torture, kill, and exterminate contrary to the law of humanity and every sacred right, must be considered savage beasts.” See also chapter 20, if you wish.

“and granted to judges.” Military judges, uneducated in humane letters, were sent into the provinces without advisers.

XXIII. But this was the public calamity and the common grief of all: a census, sent once into the provinces and cities, with census commissioners scattered everywhere and throwing everything into turmoil; it was like a hostile uprising and the dreadful appearance of captivity. Fields were measured plot by plot; vines and trees were counted; animals of every kind were registered; the heads of human beings were recorded. In the cities, urban and rural populations were assembled; all forums were filled with crowds of households; everyone was present with children and slaves. Tortures and beatings resounded; sons were suspended against their parents; every most faithful slave was tortured against his master. [Col. 0231B] If everything had failed, they themselves were tortured against themselves; and when pain had prevailed, things not possessed were entered on the rolls. There was no exemption for age or health. The sick and weak were brought forward; the ages of individuals were assessed; years were added to little children and taken away from old men. All was full of mourning and grief. What the ancients had done to the conquered by right of war, [Col. 0232A] he dared to do to Romans and subjects of Rome, because his ancestors had been subjected to the census which Trajan, after conquering the Dacians repeatedly in rebellion, imposed upon them as a penalty. After this, money was paid for heads, and payment was made for life. Yet the same census commissioners were not trusted: others were sent over and above them, as though they would discover more. The amount was always doubled—not because the officials found anything, but because they added whatever they pleased, lest they seem to have been sent in vain. Meanwhile the animals diminished and human beings died, yet taxes were paid none the less for the dead, so that it was no longer permitted either to live or even to die free of charge. Only beggars remained, from whom nothing could be demanded and whom misery [Col. 0232B] and misfortune had made safe from every kind of injury. Yet that impious man took pity on them, so that they might not be in need. He ordered them assembled, transported in little boats, and drowned in the sea—so compassionate a man, who had ensured that no one, while he ruled, should be miserable. Thus, while he took care that no one might evade the census through a pretence of beggary, he killed a multitude of wretched men contrary to every law of humanity.

XXIV. [Col. 0233A]

[Note: [Col. 0233B] [Various Notes to columns 233–234]

“Now God’s judgment drew near to him.” The author seems to have had in mind 2 Maccabees 9:18: “For the just judgment of God had come upon him.” The verb “draw near” is poetic, from Plautus’s *Truculentus*, Act II, scene 6, or from Virgil; it also occurs below at the beginning of chapter 46. It is found also in Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* II.8: “The corruptible cannot draw near to the incorruptible”; VII.14: “I shall show that the time of that judgment is drawing near”; and below in the same Book VII.24: “And now that supreme day of the final consummation is drawing near”; also II.9 and *Epitome* 71.

“His affairs began to dissolve and ebb away.” He alludes to Virgil’s familiar line, *Aeneid* II.169:

> From that time the hopes of the Greeks began to ebb away  
> and, slipping back, to be borne backward.

*Laboraret.* Add: “from illness.”

“And indeed long before.” With the approval of the most learned man, I preferred to restore *quidem*, “indeed,” in place of *quem*, by a slighter alteration than adding the two words “in vain he had repeatedly demanded,” since no lacuna exists in the manuscript.

“For also in plots.” The manuscript has the preposition *in*.

[Col. 0233D]

“The hand of God protected the man.” Lactantius likewise, *Divine Institutes* II.15: “Whom the mighty and exalted hand of God protects.”

“At the very hinge.” That is, at the very crisis or opportunity for liberation, at the final and decisive moment. BAULDRI. From Virgil, *Aeneid* I.676.

“At the very hinge.” Lactantius likewise, *Divine Institutes* II.8: “This therefore is the hinge of things; here everything turns.” Similarly III.7 and *On the Wrath of God* 6: “For in it the whole sum and hinge of religion and piety consists.” COLUMB.

“For, when he could not kill him for a long time.” I think no word should be added, nor *diu*, “for a long time,” changed to *diutius*, “for a longer time,” nor *necare*, “kill,” to *negare*, “refuse.” He had long wished to kill him secretly but could not, no suitable opportunity having arisen; for openly he did not dare, as above.

*Sigillum.* That is, a letter of dismissal secured with a seal. See Cange’s *Glossary*.

“Having received instructions.” Which, I think, he was to carry to his father Constantius.

[Col. 0234B]

*Teneretur.* That is, “be detained” by Severus. For one traveling from Nicomedia to Gaul had to go through Italy, where Severus ruled. The *Fragment on Constantius Chlorus*, p. 471: “That he might avoid Severus while passing through Italy, he crossed the Alps in utmost haste, having cut the post-horses’ hamstrings behind him, and came to his father Constantius at Boulogne.”

*Sublatis.* Zosimus in Book II relates that Constantius, fearing that he might perhaps be caught while fleeing, mutilated and left useless the post-horses maintained by the state as soon as he reached any stable; and, doing this as he traveled from place to place, prevented his pursuers from proceeding farther. Nearly the same is read in the epitome of Victor.

*Evolavit.* Read with Heumann *avolavit*, “flew away,” a word Cicero uses in *Tusculan Disputations* I.43: “I shall fly away hence,” he says.

“The public post was stripped bare for him.” Thus the manuscript: that is, no public horses for travel remained at the stations, because Constantine had mutilated them.

*Ei.* In the manuscript *eis*, incorrectly.

“He handed the imperial power to him through his hands.” Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* II.4: “For he lived until old age and handed the kingdom to his son through his hands.”

“Having commended him to the soldiers.” For he received the imperial power both by his father’s will and by the unanimous agreement of the soldiers. CELL.

“He received the repose of life in his bed.” The Fasti of Idatius, under the consulship of Constantius VI and Maximian VI: “Under these consuls Constantius died, and Constantine was afterwards elevated on the eighth day before the Kalends of August.” Eusebius’s *Chronicle*: [Col. 0234D] “Constantius died in Britain, at York, in the sixteenth year of his reign; and he was buried there,” if what the most learned William Camden recounts about his tomb on p. 572 of *Britannia* is true. This occurred in the year of Christ 306, as Valesius rightly maintains against Petavius in his notes on Eusebius—indeed on the eighth day before the Kalends of August. BALUZ.

“He did nothing before restoring Christians to their worship and their God.” Thus the manuscript, by a Hellenism. Otherwise one should read: “than that he should restore.” Lactantius, in the preface to Book I of the *Divine Institutes*, addressed to Constantine: “For when that most blessed day had dawned upon the world, on which the highest God raised you to the blessed summit of empire, you inaugurated a saving and universally desired rule with a splendid beginning, restoring justice which had been overthrown and removed, and expiating the most foul crime of others.”

“His first enactment, of holy religion restored.” Thus the manuscript, *restitutae*, “restored,” for *restitutio*, “restoration.” So *missa* is used for *missio*; *relata* for *relatio*; *ascensu* for *ascensio*; *defensa* for *defensio*; *accessa* for *accessio*; *exposita* for *expositio*; [Col. 0235B] and *remissa* for *remissio*, in Tertullian and Saint Cyprian, fellow-countrymen of Lactantius. — *Sanctio.* Heumann reads *functio*, “performance.” Nothing seems to require correction: thus chapter 48, “the form of the enactment of this our favor,” and again, “the enactment of this our favor.” Shortly afterward the manuscript has *restituta*, incorrectly. BUN.]

Now God’s judgment drew near to him, and the time followed when his affairs began to dissolve and ebb away. He had not yet turned his mind to overthrowing or expelling Constantius. He was occupied with the matters which I have set out above and awaited Constantius’s death; yet he did not think he would die so quickly. Since Constantius was seriously ill, he had sent letters asking that his son Constantine be sent back to him for a visit, and indeed he had done so long before. But the other wanted anything rather than this. For he had often also plotted against the young man’s life; because he dared do nothing openly, lest he stir up civil arms against himself and, what he feared most, the hatred of the soldiers. Under the pretext of exercise and sport, he had exposed him to wild beasts, but in vain, since the hand of God protected the man and delivered him from [Col. 0233B] his hands at the very crisis. For, when he had long been unable to kill him, as daylight was already declining he gave him a sealed permit and ordered him, having received instructions, to set out [Col. 0234A] the next morning; either intending himself to detain him on some pretext, or to send letters ahead so that Severus might hold him. But Constantine, foreseeing this, once the emperor had gone to rest, hurried after supper to depart; and, having removed all the public horses at many stations, he flew away. The next day the emperor, having deliberately slept until midday, ordered him summoned. He was told that Constantine had departed immediately after supper. He began to rage and fume. He demanded public horses in order to have him brought back. He was told that the public post had been stripped bare. He could scarcely contain his tears. But Constantine, traveling with incredible speed, arrived at his father, now failing, who, having commended him to the soldiers, handed over the imperial power to him through his hands; and so he received in his bed the repose of life, as he desired. Having assumed imperial power, Constantine Augustus did nothing before restoring Christians to their worship and their God. This was his first enactment: the restoration of holy religion.

XXV. [Col. 0235A]

[Note: [Col. 0235B] [Various Notes to columns 235–236]

“His laurel-crowned image was brought.” His means Constantine’s. Lactantius calls it a laurel-crowned image because those who announced joyful and successful events brought tablets wreathed with laurel, as Salmasius explains at length [Col. 0235C] in his notes on Lampridius, p. 235. BALUZ.

“To the evil beast.” Galerius Maximian, whom Lactantius calls an evil beast as a cruel persecutor. See above, notes on chapters 2 and 16 of the same book.

“His affair was.” The manuscript: “he was king.”

*Amici.* That is, those who were advisers.

*Flexissent.* For *deflexissent*, “had turned him aside”; a simple form for a compound, which, as we have often said, is familiar in Lactantius.

*Suscepturi.* The manuscript: *suscepturum*.

“About to rush to him with the greatest eagerness if he came armed.” The manuscript: *ad eum concursas alacritate summa, si invenisset armatus*.

“Turbatae rationes.* In the manuscript, *turba rationes*, through error.

“Nor could he name another outside the number.” That is, beyond four, lest he alter Diocletian’s arrangement, which he had himself declared must be carefully maintained above, chapter 18. BALUZ.

“He devised this.” Lactantius, *On the Workmanship of God* 3: “For what will he devise? What will he do? What will he undertake?”

“Not emperor, as he had been made.” That Constantine, from his father’s death until his marriage to Fausta, was not emperor but Caesar is proved both from coins in Cange and others and from the panegyric addressed jointly to Maximian his father-in-law and Constantine, chapters 1–5—if anyone should perhaps refuse to trust Zosimus on this point, Book II, chapter 9. CELL. — “Not emperor.” Authors differ. Eusebius agrees with our author. Nurr. carefully explains what should be thought of the other writers and the uncertain author of the panegyric. Shortly afterward the manuscript has, according to its usual practice, “with Maximian.” BUN.

*Maximino.* The manuscript always has *Maximiano*.

*Quodam modo.* The manuscript: *quo modo*.

*Allatus est.* Thus the manuscript. But below it has *allato*; I follow the manuscript.

“Maxentius was made emperor at Rome.” The learned Toinard wishes either to read or to understand “Caesar,” not “Augustus.” But the most learned men Baluze and Paul Bauldri maintain, on many excellent grounds and from Eutropius, Book X, that he was proclaimed Augustus by the Praetorians; consult those authors if you wish.

[Col. 0236B]

“To devour the world.” Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* VII.16: “They will destroy everything, crush it, and devour it.” So also *Epitome* 11: “Ten men will occupy the world, divide it, and devour it”; and shortly afterward, “he will devour the whole earth,” as all printed editions and manuscripts read, except the Turin manuscript, which has “he will harass.”

*Prosiluit.* Thus the manuscript, and correctly. Most printed editions have *prosiliit*. Both readings are good, and nothing should be changed.

[Col. 0236C] “From this captivity.” That is, from this tax; for a census was undertaken only in order to impose a revenue-payment.

“To register the population.” Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* I.22: “He registered the gods by households.” “He had abolished the Praetorian camp.” Not altogether; he had reduced it. Otherwise, how could the Praetorians, if none existed, have proclaimed Maxentius emperor? Aurelius Victor correctly says in his *Book of the Caesars*: “Hence the strength of the city was, as it were, curtailed, as the number of Praetorian cohorts and of the armed populace was reduced.” BALUZ.

*Nacti.* Bunemann has *nancti*. On this word he provides the following note: *Nancti.* Thus the manuscript, defended by Columbus and certain learned men. Thus the Florentine manuscript of the *Pandects*, I.2, “who acquired knowledge”; the Glossary of Cyril, *δραξαμένος*, “having obtained”; and Peter Daniel’s manuscript of Valerius Maximus, IV.4.6. *Nancti*, Torrens’s edition.

“Having killed the judges.” “After first killing Abellio,” says Zosimus, “because he, holding the office of Prefect of the City, seemed to oppose these designs.” BALUZ.

[Col. 0236D]

“They had clothed Maxentius in purple.” In the manuscript: “Maxentius had clothed [himself] in purple.” The two readings are not equally good. One indicates that Maxentius himself assumed the purple amid public upheaval; the other—and better—indicates that Maxentius was invested with purple by the soldiers.

“He was disturbed.” Galerius Maximian.

“Excessively frightened.” *Nimium*, that is, “very.” *Divine Institutes* V.10: “If they have been TOO pious”; and *On the Workmanship of God* 9: “If you bring something TOO near.”

“He could not make three Caesars.” Diocletian’s arrangement stood in the way. See above, chapters 18 and 25.

“He summons [him], and having exhorted [him].” Thus the manuscript. Yet one may read either *hortatus*, “having exhorted,” or *hortatur*, “he exhorts.” We have followed the reading that sounds better.

*Recipiendum.* That is, to be recovered.

*Maximiani.* Namely, Herculius.

*Maxentium.* The manuscript: *Maximianum*, incorrectly.

“There to live.” The manuscript: “that they might live.”

A few days later his laurel-crowned image was brought to the evil beast. He deliberated long whether he should accept it. The matter nearly came to the point that he would burn both the image and the man who had brought it, had not his friends turned him away from that frenzy, warning him of the danger: all the soldiers, against whose wishes unknown Caesars had been made, would support Constantine and rush to him with the greatest eagerness if he came armed. Therefore he accepted the image most reluctantly and sent Constantine the purple, so that he might seem to have voluntarily admitted him into partnership. His plans were now thrown into confusion, and he could not name another beyond the prescribed number, as he had wished. But he devised this: he proclaimed Severus, who was older, Augustus; but ordered Constantine to be called not Emperor, as he had been made, but Caesar along with [Col. 0235B] Maximinus, so as to cast him down from second place to fourth.

XXVI. His affairs now seemed in some way settled, [Col. 0236A] when suddenly another terror was brought to him: his son-in-law Maxentius had been made emperor at Rome. The cause of this movement was as follows. Having decided, by instituting censuses, to devour the world, he advanced to such madness that he did not wish even the Roman people to be exempt from this captivity. Census commissioners were already being appointed to be sent to Rome to register the populace. At about the same time he had also abolished the Praetorian camp. Therefore the few soldiers who had been left in the camp at Rome, having found an opportunity, killed certain judges and, with the people not unwilling—for the people had been stirred up—clothed Maxentius in purple. When this report was brought, he was somewhat disturbed by the novelty of the affair, yet not excessively frightened. He both hated the man and could not make three Caesars. It seemed enough to have done once what he had not wished to do. He summons Severus and, exhorting him to recover [Col. 0236B] the empire, sends him with Maximian’s army to attack Maxentius; and sends him to Rome, where those soldiers, having most often been received with the greatest indulgence, wished not merely that the city should be safe, but to live there.

And, having carefully made ready the hostile measures he had undertaken. Thus the manuscript. The passage is somewhat obscure; nevertheless I think that nothing should be altered. I would render it in French, “by enterprises which announced or declared war.” For *coeptis* some propose *aptis*.—*Instructis.* Some read *instruens*.

At the wedding of his younger daughter. The manuscript has, “at the wedding of his lesser family,” which the printed editions rightly altered. I am surprised that none of the learned men has investigated who Fausta’s elder sister was, and whether she ever existed; for I have been unable to find any such person among the writers of Roman history. Yet the manuscript reading was rightly altered, nor could it stand as it is in Lactantius. Maximian Herculius had no children by his wife Eutropia except Maxentius, mentioned in chapter 26, and Fausta, mentioned in chapter 30. But Eutropia, before her marriage to Herculius, had a daughter Theodora, whom Constantius Chlorus, Constantine’s father, had married. Herculius undoubtedly regarded Theodora, Eutropia’s daughter, as his own. Thus Lactantius could say of Fausta that she was Herculius’ younger daughter.—And, having carefully made ready the hostile measures he had undertaken. For *instructis*, Bunemann has *instruens*, and offers the following note on this passage:

> “And, having carefully equipped the measures … [Col. 0238D] I suspected, because of the similarity of letters, that one should read: ‘Having fortified the city, and having carefully equipped the hostile resources and forces,’ that is, he sets out after making preparations. On this interpretation everything is complete. After the city had been fortified and the resources and forces carefully prepared and equipped, he sets out. For everyone knows that *instructus* is elegantly used for ‘prepared,’ and that the terms are therefore often joined.” BUN.

Meanwhile, he: Galerius Maximian.

“To besiege the walls.” In the manuscript, *circumsedendam*; an error for *circumsedendum*. The editions have *circumsedenda moenia*, “the walls to be besieged.”

“The cities which he knew.” Thus in Virgil’s *Tityrus*:

> The city which they call Rome, Meliboeus, I, in my folly,  
> Thought like our own . . . .

“Detesting the crime.” The manuscript has *detestande*. Perhaps one should read *detestatae*, “having detested.”

“They abandoned the empire.” Namely, Galerius’ empire. Perhaps one should read [Col. 0239B] “the emperor.” See below, because they were soldiers who had deserted Severus.]

Maxentius, conscious of so great a crime, although by right of inheritance he could win over to himself his father’s soldiers, nevertheless reflected that Maximian, his father-in-law, might fear precisely this and leave Severus in Illyricum, while himself coming with his own army to attack him. He therefore sought how he might fortify himself against the impending danger. To his father, who after laying down the imperial power was staying in Campania, he sent the purple robe and for a second time called him Augustus. The latter, both eager for revolution and having laid it down reluctantly, gladly seized it.

Meanwhile Severus advanced and came armed to the walls of the City. Immediately the soldiers raised their standards, departed, and surrendered themselves to the man against whom they had come. What remained for the deserted man but flight? But Maximian, now having resumed imperial power, was already approaching. At his arrival Severus fled to Ravenna and shut himself up there with a few [Col. 0237B] soldiers. When he saw that he would be handed over to Maximian, he surrendered himself and returned the purple robe to the same man from whom he had received it. By this act he obtained nothing except a good death. For, after his veins had been opened, he was compelled to die gently. From this point he began to persecute his own people.

## XXVII

[Col. 0238A] But Herculius, knowing Maximian’s madness, began to consider that, upon hearing of Severus’ death, he would come in anger, aflame with rage, accompanied perhaps by Maximinus, and with forces doubled, which could in no way be resisted. Having fortified the city and carefully made ready the hostile measures he had undertaken, he set out for Gaul, to win Constantine to his side by the marriage of his younger daughter.

Meanwhile the other, having assembled an army, invaded Italy and approached the City, intending to destroy the Senate and slaughter the people. But he found everything shut and fortified. There was no hope of breaking in; a siege was difficult; he did not have sufficient [Col. 0238B] forces to besiege the walls, since he had never seen Rome and supposed it was not much larger than the cities he knew. Then certain legions, detesting the crime that a father-in-law should attack his son-in-law, and that Roman soldiers should attack Rome, transferred their standards and abandoned the empire. And now the remaining soldiers [Col. 0239A] were wavering, when he, his pride broken and his courage cast down, fearing Severus’ end, threw himself at the soldiers’ feet and begged that he not be surrendered to the enemy, until by immense promises he bent the minds of some of them, turned the standards back, and in panic took to flight. In that flight he could most easily have been overwhelmed, if anyone with a few men had pursued him.

Fearing this, he gave the soldiers permission to scatter as widely as possible and plunder or despoil everything, so that anyone wishing to pursue would have no provisions. Thus that part of Italy through which that pestilential column marched was laid waste: everything was plundered; women violated, virgins ravished; fathers and husbands tortured so that they might betray their daughters, their wives, and their possessions. Herds and beasts of burden were driven off as though from barbarians. In this manner he withdrew to his own headquarters, after he who had once been a Roman emperor, now a ravager of Italy, had devastated everything in hostile fashion. Formerly, indeed, as soon as he received the title of emperor, he had declared himself an enemy of the Roman name, whose designation he wished to change, so that the empire might be called not Roman but Dacian.

[Note: [Col. 0239C] Variorum Notes to columns 239–240]

“Were wavering.” The manuscript: *mutabantur*, “were changing.”

“And their spirits cast down.” Perhaps one should read *demissisque animis*, that is, “with their spirits dejected.” Cicero uses this expression in various places. ALMELOV.

“And.” From the manuscript, but omitted in the editions.

“He bent the minds of some.” The manuscript has *felix animus quorum*. The editors restored *flexit animos eorum*. By writing *quorumdam*, “of some,” I have adhered to the manuscript reading by adding a single syllable; I consider both the word and the reading genuine.

“Could have been overwhelmed.” For *potuisset*. Thus in *Institutes*, VI.24: “he could have been a true worshipper of God, if someone had shown him.” Compare *Institutes*, II.4, *oportuit*. BUN.

“Would have no provisions.” *Utensilia* are provisions, supplies necessary for sustenance.

“Through which.” *Qua*, according to Tollius and Heumann.

“He withdrew to his own headquarters.” Galerius Maximian.

“Had devastated.” Baluze thinks that one should read *vastasset*, “had laid waste.” Yet below, chapter XXXI, the author speaks of “the oppression of the human race.”

“Dacian.” Thus I read with the manuscript, as in Vopiscus, *Aurelian*, chapter 38, rather than *Dacicum*, as most editions have it. *Daciscum*, because he himself was born in Dacia.

“The other Maximian.” Namely, Herculius.

“Gaul.” The manuscript has *Gallie*, erroneously.

“Since the son’s authority was earlier and greater.” Heumann: “since it was earlier and greater.” But Lactantius elsewhere too omits the substantive verb after a preceding *cum*. Compare *Institutes*, VII.2. BUN.

“The son’s authority existed.” I have added *esset*, “existed,” lacking in the manuscript but necessarily to be added.

“Who also.” The manuscript has *et ea*.

“That.” The manuscript has *quos*, erroneously; perhaps *quae vellet*, “what he wished.”

“The soldiers were his own.” Namely, the soldiers of Emperor Maximian Herculius. With the most learned Gisbert Cuper and Paul Bauldri, I add *sui*, “his own”; the sense altogether requires this reading, and its truth is clear from chapter 44. The similarity of the letters in *sui* and *qui* may have caused that word to drop out. From CUPER.

“Author of evils, leader of disasters.” Similarly Lactantius, *Epitome*, chapter 72: “the prince of demons himself, author and contriver of evils.”

[Col. 0240C]

“The disasters which the commonwealth endured.” Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, VI.8: “to endure all evils”; and chapter 18: “Let us bear with one another and endure the evils of this life by mutual assistance.” COLUMB.

“He tore the purple robe from his shoulders.” Thus the manuscript. One ought properly to say *deripuit*, that is, “he tore it down from his son’s body,” whereas *diripere* means “to tear into pieces.” Thus Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, IV:

> . . . . . Procne  
> Tore the coverings from her shoulders.

From CUPER.

“Stripped.” The manuscript: *exsutus*.

“He was expelled like another Superbus.” That is, Tarquinius Superbus, the last king of the Romans. Lactantius, *Institutes*, IV.14: “Tarquinius Superbus was expelled.” BALUZ.

“To the enemy of his son, Maximian.” That is, Herculius set out for Galerius, the enemy of his son.

“And to discuss matters with him.” Thus the manuscript. The editions omit *et*, and rightly so. *Disputaret* means “to confer,” “to negotiate with him.” [Col. 0240D] Thus in Cicero, *Letters to Friends*, II.8, and the *Speech for Caelius*.

“Under the pretext of reconciliation.” The preposition *per* here retains something of ancient elegance, as in Livy and Seneca’s *per fidem*, a usage which Davies also vindicated for Caesar or Hirtius, *Gallic War*, VIII.48.3. BUN.

“Wherever he came.” “Diocletian was present there.” Bunemann, however, does not place a full stop after *venisset*, and reads thus: “Wherever he came, Diocletian was present,” etc., adding the following note:

> “An anonymous critic punctuates thus: ‘Excluded by his own [people]. Wherever he came, Diocletian was present there.’ This pleases Heumann and me.” BUN.

“Diocles was present there.” He was with Galerius Maximian, his son-in-law, by whom he had recently been summoned.

“Appointed in place.” In the manuscript one may read either *substituto* or even *substituturo*.

“In Severus’ place.” Thus the manuscript. Learned men prefer to write “into Severus’ place”; but either reading can be defended.

“With both present.” Namely Diocletian and the aged Maximian Herculius.]

## XXVIII

After this man’s flight, when the other Maximian had returned from Gaul, he held the imperial power jointly with his son. But the young man was obeyed more than the old, since [Col. 0240A] the son’s authority was earlier and greater, and he had also restored imperial power to his father. The old man bore it with resentment that he could not freely do what he wished, and in childish rivalry envied his son. He therefore planned to expel the young man, that he might reclaim his own power. This seemed easy, because the soldiers who had deserted Severus were [his own]. He called together the people and soldiers, as though intending to deliver a public address concerning the present evils of the commonwealth. After saying much about these matters, he turned his hands upon his son; declaring him to be the author of evils and the leader of the disasters which the commonwealth endured, he tore the purple robe from his shoulders. Stripped of it, the latter cast himself headlong from the tribunal and was caught by the soldiers. The impious old man, disturbed by their anger and shouting, was expelled from the city of Rome like another Superbus.

## XXIX

[Col. 0240B] Returning again to Gaul, where he stayed for some time, he set out for Maximian, his son’s enemy, ostensibly to negotiate with him concerning the restoration of the commonwealth, but in truth to kill him under the pretext of reconciliation and seize his kingdom. Excluded by his own people, wherever he came, Diocles was present there, recently summoned by his son-in-law, so that, in Diocles’ presence, he might do what he had not done before: make Licinius emperor, appointed in Severus’ place. Thus it came about with both present.

At one time there were six. Therefore, his designs having been frustrated, the aged Maximian planned a third flight also. He returned to Gaul, full of evil intent and crime, to entrap by wicked deceit Constantine the emperor, his son-in-law, the son of his own son-in-law. To make deception possible, he laid aside his royal garment. The Frankish people were under arms. He persuaded Constantine, who suspected nothing, not to take his entire army with him, since the barbarians could be defeated with few soldiers; thus he himself would have an army which he could seize, while Constantine could be overwhelmed because of the small number of his soldiers. The young man trusted him as an experienced and elderly man, obeyed him as a father-in-law, and set out, leaving behind the larger part of his soldiers.

After waiting a few days, when he thought Constantine had entered the barbarians’ territory, Maximian suddenly assumed the purple robe, seized the treasuries, and distributed lavishly, as was his custom; he invented accusations against Constantine which immediately recoiled upon himself. The acts that had occurred were swiftly reported to the emperor. With remarkable speed Constantine flew back with the army. The man was surprised unexpectedly, not yet adequately prepared; the soldiers returned to their emperor. He had occupied Massilia and barred the gates. The emperor approached nearer and addressed him standing upon the wall, not harshly or as an enemy, but asked what he intended, what he lacked, and why he was doing what was especially unbecoming to him. But from the walls he hurled insults. Then suddenly the gates behind him were opened and the soldiers admitted. The rebel emperor was dragged before the emperor: an impious father, a treacherous father-in-law. He heard [Col. 0242A] the crimes he had committed; his garment was removed, and, after being reproached, he was granted life.

[Note: [Col. 0241C] Variorum Notes to columns 241–242]

“At one time there were six.” Thus the manuscript. Some would prefer *praefuerunt*, “were in command.” That is, there were six rulers of the commonwealth, emperors or Caesars: Herculius, Galerius, Maximinus Daza, Constantine, Maxentius, and Licinius.

“Therefore.” From Terence, *Andria*, act III, scene 5.

“Maximian.” Namely Herculius. “Planned”: that is, prepared. *Aeneid*, II.108.

“Intent.” Thus the manuscripts, and rightly. Early editions have *contagionis*, “contamination,” perhaps because at the beginning of Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, V.12, one reads “to keep the breast pure from every contamination of crime.”

“Constantine the emperor, his son-in-law.” For he had married Fausta, Maximian Herculius’ daughter. TOINARD.—Toinard erroneously reads “Constantius.”

“The son of his son-in-law.” Constantius Chlorus, to whom Flavia Maximiana Theodora, Herculius’ stepdaughter, had been married. Thus Constantius, having married his stepdaughter, is regarded as his stepfather’s son-in-law. TOINARD.

“By wicked deceit.” We now use *dolus* only of evil; among the ancients it was also used of good actions, whence we still say *sine dolo malo*, “without malicious fraud,” because one also used to say *bonus dolus*, “good craft.” BUN.

“The Frankish people were under arms.” Eusebius perhaps refers to this Frankish war in *Life of Constantine*, I.25.

“He persuades.” That is, Herculius persuades Constantine, who suspects nothing.

“Could.” The manuscript: *possit*.

“Small number.” The manuscript: *paucitate*; perhaps *paucitatem*.

“Thought.” Learned editors read *existimaret*.

“He invents accusations against Constantine,” etc. That is, he pretends that Constantine has been overwhelmed by enemies, just as he himself was soon afterward overwhelmed by his son-in-law’s unexpected return. CELLARIUS.

“To the emperor.” Namely Constantine.

“Flies back.” Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, VII.12: “until the soul, released from the body’s prison, flies back to its own abode.” You will find this expression in no other Christian author; our Firmianus, an imitator, took it from Cicero and Virgil, *Georgics*, I.361.

“The man.” The aged Herculius.

“Especially unbecoming.” Because Constantine was Herculius’ son-in-law, and it was in some sense unbecoming for a father-in-law to wage war upon his son-in-law.

“Behind him.” That is, the gates which were behind Herculius.

“The soldiers.” Constantine’s soldiers.

“Impious father.” Father, namely, of Fausta, whom Constantine had married; impious because inhuman.

“He hears the crimes he committed.” Elegantly said of one charged with wrongdoing. Thus Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, V.19: “He hears what God threatens against him.”

“His garment is removed.” Namely the imperial garment, that is, the purple.

“Unable to endure humiliation.” That is, unable to endure an abject and lowly condition. Thus in the manner of the ancients, Cicero, chapter 18, chapter 43, and book VI, chapter 4. BUN.

[Col. 0242D]

“He plotted, because once he got away with it unpunished, he summons [her].” I have punctuated with Gabo, Boherellus, the anonymous critic, and Heumann. Previously the text was printed: “He plotted; because once he went away unpunished, he summons [her].” BUN.

“Got away with it unpunished.” The manuscript reads no differently, as does Lactantius, *Epitome*, chapter 53, “he got away with it unpunished,” and chapter 55, “they get away with it unpunished.” Here the editions read *abiit*, “he went away.”

“Scene.” The manuscript: *schena*, as though it were pronounced *chena*, in the Italian manner.

“To his son.” That is, to his son-in-law, Constantine, because he was the husband of Maximian Herculius’ daughter.

“Sprang out.” It would be better as *prosilit*, “springs out.”

“The manifest murderer freezes.” Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, I.7: “as though all routes had been removed and exhausted, he stops, freezes, fails.” From Plautus, *Aulularia* and *Trinummus*.

“As though.” Virgil, *Aeneid*, VI.471.

“And.” The same author, XII.603.

“Interval.” The manuscript: *intervallo*.]

## XXX

Thus, having lost the rank of emperor and father-in-law, unable to endure humiliation, he again plotted other snares. Because he had once gotten away with it unpunished, he summoned his daughter Fausta and solicited her, now with entreaties, now with caresses, to betray her husband. He promised her another husband more worthy than Constantine; he asked her to allow the bedchamber to be left open and guarded less carefully. She promised to do it and immediately reported the matter to her husband. A scene was arranged by which the crime might be manifestly established. A certain lowly eunuch was substituted, to die in the emperor’s place.

He rose in the dead of night and saw everything favourable to the plot. The guards were few and indeed farther away; yet he told them that he had seen a dream which he wished to report to his son. He entered armed; having cut down the eunuch, he sprang forth exultantly and declared what he had done. Suddenly Constantine appeared from the other side with a band of armed men. The corpse of the slain man was brought forth from the bedchamber. The manifest murderer stood frozen, dumb with astonishment:

> As though a hard flint or a Marpesian cliff should stand.

He was reproached for his impiety and crime. At last he was granted the free choice of death:

> And from a lofty beam he fastens a noose of shameful death.

Thus he, the greatest emperor of the Roman name, who over a long interval of time celebrated the vows for twenty years with immense glory, ended his detestable life by a shameful and ignominious death, his most arrogant throat crushed and broken.

[Note: [Col. 0243B] Variorum Notes to columns 243–244]

“Vows for twenty years.” That is, the *vicennalia*, which he celebrated at Rome with Diocletian. BALUZ.—See Valesius on Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, IV.47.

“Shameful.” The manuscript has *turbi*, with *p* changed to *b*, an error often made by scribes.

“An ignominious death.” On this, see Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, VIII.13. He was strangled at Massilia, namely, according to Eusebius’ *Chronicle*.

“The other Maximian.” That is, from Maximian Herculius to Maximian Galerius, surnamed Armentarius.

“Author.” That is, one of the authors of the persecution; [Col. 0243C] see above, chapter 2, “the persecutors.” He was not its sole author, but one of several.

“Also the power.” Thus I read from the manuscript, in which there is *et . . . em*, with a blank space of seven or eight letters; I believe it cannot be read otherwise. All editions have *etiam vim*, “also force,” which cannot accord with the rest of the manuscript writing. In this manuscript *etiam* is commonly written in four letters. Our reading is confirmed by the wording in chapter I: “that he might display his own power and majesty in extirpating and destroying the enemies of his name.” Likewise Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, IV.26: “to expound the power and majesty of the one God”; and VI.9: “he declares the power and majesty of the one God.”

“And that.” After *cogitabat*, “he was planning,” four letters are missing in the manuscript, which I judged should be supplied as *et ut*.

“Repay.” The manuscript has *rediret*, erroneously.
