“Also, under the name of the vicennalia, he inflicted a second axe.” Graevius considers that these exceedingly corrupt words should be emended thus: “What he had promised to repay, he repaid, and under the empty name of the vicennalia he inflicted a second axe.” It seems to mean that, by a new assessment under the name of the forthcoming *vicennalia*, he oppressed the provinces so that things necessary for the preparations and splendour of the games might be procured.—“Also in the name of the vicennalia.” I read *etiam nomine vicennalium*, “also under the pretext, under the cover, of the vicennalia.” The final *m* of *etiam* or the first letter of the following word seems to have intruded. BUN.

“He inflicted a second axe.” Thus the manuscript, equivalent to “he struck with a second axe.” Indeed our author had in view Cicero, *For Gnaeus Plancius*, chapter 9: “For what heavier axe could those judges have inflicted upon the commonwealth?” “Who can worthily recount?” The manuscript has *et quis*. I have written *ecquis*, with the slightest—almost no—alteration, since *t* and *c* are similar or nearly similar in most manuscripts.

“Soldiers of all offices.” That is, the soldiers of all magistrates, or soldiers who assisted magistrates.

“No pardon for those unable [to pay].” Thus I read it, so that the sense is: “there was no pardon for those who did not have the means to pay.” The manuscript has *veniam non habentibus nullas abstinendi multiplicis cruciatus*; a corrupt passage which nevertheless may be emended with very slight alteration. In *veniam*, the *m* is erroneous and superfluous; likewise the *s* in *nullas*, which I suspect begins the following word *abstinendi*. Thus one has *nulla sustinendi*, or *sustinendi multiplices cruciatus*, “enduring multiple tortures,” all of which gives an excellent sense.

“Was produced.” Supply “the tax,” which they were unable to pay.

“Although these things are intolerable, [namely] to snatch from men’s mouths food acquired through labour.” With the approval of certain learned men I emended this passage thus. The manuscript has “how tolerable these things are,” an erroneous sense, for it is not tolerable. One must also read *ab ore*, “from the mouth,” with learned editors, in place of *labore*, “through labour,” which has entered the manuscript from the word *labore* immediately following. Moreover, *quaesitos*, “sought,” here means “acquired,” as I showed above in the Notes on chapter 18; Lactantius frequently uses the simple word for the compound. *Divine Institutes*, VI.12: “Shall I destroy family property acquired through my own labour or that of my ancestors?” *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 3, near the middle: “food acquired through labour”; and *On the Anger of God*, chapter 23: “in seeking temporal goods.”

“Bearable.” Thus the manuscript. Early editions have *tolerabile*, which means the same; Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, VII.16, similarly said *insustentabili dominatione*, “an unbearable domination,” for “intolerable.” Perhaps *sustentabile* should be *sustentabantur*, “were sustained.” The preceding number is plural.

“By hope of future things.” The learned Paul Bauldri wished to read [Col. 0244D] *spe foeturarum*, “by hope of offspring,” or the increase of living creatures; for *foetura*, he says, denotes among the Latins both the increase of animals and the offspring itself. “What of clothing of every kind?” Supply “is demanded,” or “is taken away.” Paul Bauldri thought some verb had fallen out, such as the one we supply.

“For a vow.” Thus they called festivals in which vows were made for the safety and long life of rulers; and, just as they celebrated the *vicennalia*, so they prayed the gods to grant that they might likewise celebrate their *tricennalia*. BALUZ.

“Which he was not going to celebrate.” This passage is of great importance, since it certainly follows from it that Galerius Maximian did not reach the twentieth year of his reign; for, as the most learned BALUZ notes, he perished earlier from a foul disease.

“Maximinus.” The manuscript, as usual, has “Maximian.” Moreover Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, VIII.13, confirms our author; and again in our present book, chapter 44, Maximinus claimed for himself the title of the first name. BUN.]

## XXXI

From this man God, the avenger of his religion and people, turned his eyes to the other Maximian, author of the impious persecution, so that in him too he might show the power of his majesty. He too was now planning the celebration of his *vicennalia*; and, having long since afflicted the provinces by assessments of gold and silver, he inflicted a second axe, under the very name of the *vicennalia*, in order that he might repay what he had promised.

Who could worthily recount the exactions imposed by that oppression of the human race, especially those for the grain supply? Soldiers of every office—or rather executioners—clung to each individual; it was uncertain whom one should satisfy first. There was no pardon for those unable to pay; they endured manifold [Col. 0243B] tortures unless what did not exist was produced immediately. Surrounded by many guards, there was no opportunity [Col. 0244A] to breathe freely; at no time of year was there even slight respite. There was continual conflict over the same persons, whether by the judges themselves or by the soldiers of the judges. No field was without its tax collector, no vintage without its guard; nothing was left to those labouring for their sustenance.

Although such things are intolerable—to snatch from men’s mouths food acquired through labour—yet they were in some way bearable through hope for the future. But what of clothing of every kind? What of gold? What of silver? Must not these necessarily be obtained from the sale of produce? From where, then, O most demented tyrant, shall I furnish these things, when you take away all produce and violently seize everything that grows? Who, then, was not ruined in his possessions, so that the wealth which existed under his rule might be scraped together for the vow which he was not going to celebrate?

## XXXII

[Col. 0244B] Licinius having therefore been proclaimed emperor, Maximinus was angry and was unwilling either to remain Caesar or to be named in third place.

[Note: [Col. 0245B] Variorum Notes to columns 245–246]

“He therefore sends envoys to him repeatedly.” Galerius Maximian sends them to Maximinus, to placate him.

“But he.” Maximinus, namely.

“By priority.” The manuscript: *praescriptionem*.

“Despises.” Thus I emend from the preceding and following verbs, which are in the present tense. The manuscript: *contempsit*.

“The beast is pained.” Galerius Maximian. Lactantius thus calls the emperors who persecuted Christians evil beasts.

“And bellows.” Thus the manuscript. Some prefer “roars.”

“Since.” The manuscript has *eum*, in place of which I have written *cum*, because the following *is tamen*, “yet he,” requires it.

“Vanquished by obstinacy.” The sense is that Maximinus, carried away by the force of his obstinacy, did not obey Maximian’s reasonable request. TOINARD.

“He abolishes the title of Caesars.” Of three men, namely Maximinus, Constantine, and Maxentius. TOINARD.

“Maxentius and Constantine, sons of Augusti.” I fully agree with Baluze’s suspicion that *Maximinum*, “Maximinus,” should be read, not *Maxentium*. Galerius hated Maxentius as a public enemy and could not have included him in this arrangement, nor omitted Maximinus, who, though not born to an Augustus as father, had nevertheless been adopted by an Augustus.

“Maxentius.” Granvillius corrects this to “Maximinus” and discusses it at length in the letter on the coin of Maximinus appended to Banduri’s *Bibliotheca Nummaria*, edition of J. A. Fabricius, pp. 278–281. Add Heumann. BUN.

“In the Campus Martius.” Here *Campus Martius* is not the name of a place such as the one at Rome, but rather, so to speak, a military assembly at which the army was reviewed. Whether it was held at fixed times or whenever the emperor commanded is not clear. TOINARD.

“Proclaimed.” The manuscript: *nuncupato*.

“He commands all four to be counted as emperors.” Add a comma after “four” and read “named” instead of “counted.” Thus: “he commands all four to be named emperors,” namely Licinius, Maximinus, Constantine, and Maxentius. Here “emperors” means Augusti. TOINARD.

“Counted.” Perhaps one should read “named.” Yet Heumann thinks, from Cicero, that “counted” is to be read, as it stands in the manuscript.

“God struck him.” Namely Galerius Maximian. “With an incurable blow.” Thus Lactantius, *Institutes*, VII.5: “God struck Egypt with an incurable blow.”

“In the lower part of the genitals.” See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, VIII.16, and *Life of Constantine*, I.57; Rufinus, VIII.18; the *Fragment on Constantius Chlorus*, p. 472; and also Paul Orosius, VII.28.

[Col. 0246B]

“The physicians cut and treat [it].” Thus the manuscript. The *medici* are wound-doctors, now called surgeons. Some wish to read from Celsus, “they cut, they cauterize.” But nothing below concerns cauterization; it speaks only of cutting and treating.

“The wound cuts open the scar already formed.” Thus Celsus, IV.26, “by which a scar is formed.” The most learned Graevius thinks that *rescindit*, “cuts open again,” should be read, and not badly; for Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, VII.24, says “to pour out destruction from reopened wounds.” Johannes Columbus reads *scindit se*, “it splits itself,” as in Virgil, *Aeneid*, I.571: “the cloud splits itself.” Some read: “when the scar had already formed, the wound is cut open.” The manuscript agrees, except that it has *scindit*, not *scinditur*.

“Yet.” Immediately before occurs *tamen*. I would prefer *tandem*, “at last.”—“Scarcely yet.” Heumann, Boherellus, and Gale rightly restore, says Bunemann, *vix tandem*, “scarcely at last.” Propertius, III.20.7: “Scarcely yet does she admit [him] even once, though she has often refused.” Ovid, *Heroides*, “Orestes’ Letter”: “I scarcely remember indeed; yet I remember.” Phaedrus, IV.5: “received with difficulty—that is, scarcely—yet they escaped death.” BUN.

“Movement.” Thus I restored it: after the initial letter *m*, five or six letters are missing in the manuscript. The editions read *motu*, “by movement”; that word cannot belong here, since only three letters follow the *m*.

“Is wounded.” The manuscript: *vulneratus*, erroneously; I do not see to what it could refer. Some prefer *vulnerato*, and this reading should not be rejected.

“He becomes pale.” That is, he turns pallid, as Lactantius in *On the Anger of God*, chapter 5, speaks of a whitening pallor.

“Grows thin.” That is, his fat disappears; for, as said above in chapter 9, he was “a huge and swollen mass of flesh.” From Virgil, *Georgics*, III.129.

“Nearest.” The manuscripts have *promaxima*, erroneously.

[Col. 0246D]

“Rages.” Heumann thinks *serpit*, “spreads,” should be read.

“Phillyrides,” etc. This verse has been restored from Virgil, since the Colbert manuscripts read it wholly corruptly: *Phyllides Cirona, Metonius Melamphius*, contrary to the laws of metre.

“Are summoned.” That is, called in.—“Distinguished physicians are summoned.” Cellarius explains: “are called in,” correctly. Thus Lactantius, I.17: “he summoned a physician to treat the young man.” Nurrius says, p. 328: “He did not badly say *trahuntur*, ‘they are dragged,’ that is, unwillingly and reluctantly.” For, as Eusebius’ translation, *Ecclesiastical History*, VIII.18, end, has it: among the physicians, some who could not bear even the severity of the stench were killed; others, because they could furnish no remedy, were likewise put to death for that very reason. BUN.

“Human hands.” Cicero himself does not avoid this sound, as I noted on Lactantius, *On Anger*, chapter 2, “by a human hand.” BUN.

“Asclepius.” Gronovius observed that Lactantius preferred the Greek name to the Latin one, *Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 182. This too seems to contribute something to confirming this work’s author, since within it we see the term *Asclepius* recur, rather than *Aesculapius*, in I.17.]

He therefore repeatedly sends envoys to him: he begs him to obey, maintain his arrangement, yield to age, and show honour to grey hairs. But Maximinus more boldly raises his horns and contends, on grounds of priority, that he ought to rank first because he first assumed the purple. He despises Galerius’ entreaties and commands. The beast is pained and bellows, because, having for that very reason made him Caesar from an obscure background so that he would be obedient to him, this man nevertheless, forgetful of so great a benefit, impiously resisted his will and entreaties.

Vanquished by obstinacy, he abolishes the title of Caesars and calls himself and Licinius Augusti; afterward Maximinus writes that Maxentius and Constantine are sons of Augusti, as though announcing that, at the Campus Martius most recently celebrated, he had been proclaimed Augustus by the army. The other received this sadly and resentfully, and commanded all four to be counted as emperors.

## XXXIII

[Col. 0246A] The eighteenth year was now in progress when God struck him with an incurable blow. A malignant ulcer arose in the lower part of his genitals and spread more widely. Physicians cut and treat it. But the wound cuts open the scar already formed; and when a vein ruptures, blood flows to the danger of death. Yet with difficulty the bleeding is stopped. Treatment begins anew from the beginning. Nevertheless, it is brought to a scar. Again, through a slight movement of the body, it is wounded; more blood runs out than before. He himself turns pale, and, his strength exhausted, grows thin; and then indeed the stream of blood is checked. The wound begins not to respond to treatment: a cancer attacks everything nearest it; and the more it is cut around, the more widely it rages; the more it is treated, the more it grows.

> The masters gave way—  
> Chiron, son of Philyra, and Melampus, son of Amythaon.

Distinguished physicians are summoned from every side. Nothing of human [Col. 0247A]

When these had been unbound. Those animals were not placed upon the wounds without bandages, by whose aid they might be applied more effectively to the ulcerated parts and remain in their proper place. The animals were therefore bound to the wounds; and when afterwards the bandages were removed, the animals themselves were also unbound. For *resolvere* in a thousand passages means to unfasten what had been bound. Our author, ch. 46: “Licinian’s soldiers lay down their shields and unfasten their helmets.” Lactantius, *Epitome*, ch. 72: “But the prince of the demons himself . . . bound with fiery chains,” etc.; “but when the thousand years had elapsed and the prince of the demons had been unbound.” BAULDRI.—You will scarcely, I think, find this word used in this sense in any other Christian writer.

An inestimable swarm welled forth. That is, a swarm of little worms. *Inaestimabile* [“inestimable”] stands for *innumerabile* [“innumerable”], a word peculiar to Lactantius; *Divine Institutes*, I.16: “For since the number of human beings is scarcely credible and inestimable”—in French, *une quantité innombrable* [“an innumerable quantity”]; *On the Anger of God*, ch. 10: “that masses of atoms, so inestimable, should be gathered from things so minute”; and *Epitome*, ch. 72, “an inestimable multitude of angels.”

The destruction of wasting entrails. Thus the manuscript. Some prefer *tabescentium* [“of those wasting away”]; some, *tabe exesorum* [“eaten away by decay”]—in French, *un ulcère dans les entrailles* [“an ulcer in the entrails”]. In the same sense Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, VI.24: “to pour forth destruction from reopened wounds,” as we noted above.

Fruitful. Earlier editions: *secunda* [“favourable,” “prosperous”].

Different. Heumann reads *disperso* [“scattered”]. Perhaps *adverso* [“opposed,” “contrary”] should be read.

They had lost. In the manuscript, *admiserant*.

Pallid far away. In the manuscript, *luride longe*.

Had swollen apart. Thus the manuscript: *discreverat*, from *discresco*, not from *discerno*. A rare word. *Discresco* stands for *distendo*; *discrescere*, “to stretch further,” or “to stretch out,” more properly “to be stretched out”—in French, *étendre davantage* [“to extend further”]. Many wish to read *increverat* [“had increased”].

For a full year. That is, an entire, whole year. So also Lactantius, VII.26: “Then for seven full years the woods will remain untouched.”

[Col. 0248D]

He was compelled to confess God. See the similar history of Antiochus, 2 Maccabees, ch. 9; Rufinus, VIII.18; Orosius, VIII.28.

Of a new and pressing pain. Heumann reads: “for, under the pressure of the force of pain.”

The temple of God. Namely, at Nicomedia.

That he would make sufficient satisfaction for his crime. So also Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, V.13: “that he might make satisfaction for his crime”; VII.1: “Let us do enough also for this part”; and IV.17: “If, having confessed our sins, we have made satisfaction to God.” Note the words divided into two parts.

He issued an edict. That is, he published it. It survives in Eusebius, VIII.17, translated by him from Latin into Greek, and then translated from Greek into Latin by Rufinus, as he himself explains: “What had been translated from Latin into Greek, we in turn rendered into Latin.” Therefore, what we now read first in Latin is owing to Lactantius. BALUZE.—For the date on which the edict was issued, see the note at the beginning of ch. 35.

[Col. 0249B]

Edict. On this edict see Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, VIII.17.]

They extend their hands. Recourse is had to idols. Apollo and Asclepius are invoked; a remedy is demanded. Apollo provides treatment. The disease is aggravated much more grievously. Destruction was now not far off, and it had seized all the lower parts. The entrails rot externally, and the whole seat dissolves into corruption. Yet the unhappy physicians do not cease, even without hope of overcoming the malady, to foment and treat it. When the marrow had been driven back, the disease returned inward and seized the internal parts; worms are generated within. A smell, moreover, issues not merely through the palace, but pervades the whole city. Nor is this surprising, since the passages of excrement and urine had by then become confused. The body, eaten by worms and dissolved into putrefaction, comes apart amid unbearable pains.

> At once he raises dreadful cries to the stars,  
> [Col. 0247B] like the bellowing uttered by a wounded bull. [Col. 0248A]

Cooked and warm animals were applied to the flowing sore, so that their heat might draw out the little worms. When they had been unbound, an inestimable swarm welled forth; and yet the fruitful destruction of the wasting entrails had generated a much greater abundance. By now, through a different malady, the parts of his body had lost their form. The upper part, as far as the wound, had dried up, and, through pitiable emaciation, the pallid skin had sunk far in among the bones. The lower part, lacking all shape of feet, had swollen out like a wineskin. And these things continued for a full year; until at last, subdued by his sufferings, he was compelled to acknowledge God. Under the intermittent pressure of a new pain he cried out that he would restore the temple of God and make sufficient satisfaction for his crime. And now, failing fast, he issued an edict of the following kind.

### XXXIV. [Col. 0249A]

> [Note: [Col. 0249B] Notes of Various Commentators on columns 249–250]

That they might return to sound minds. That is, by renouncing the Christian religion in favour of paganism, since for Galerius the only sound religion was paganism. BAULDWIN.—Lactantius, V.19, perhaps referring to this edict: “But this very ignorance causes them to be so evil in persecuting the wise, and to pretend that they are consulting their interests and wishing to recall them to a sound mind.”

First. Earlier editions: *primi* [“the first”].

The same. Or *eisdem* [“the same”]; Eusebius has Ἕκαστος, “each,” and therefore appears to have read *cuique*, “to each.”

Various. Add: “places.”

Finally. Heumann reads *proinde* [“therefore”], because Eusebius has τοιγαροῦν, “therefore.”

Driven away. Eusebius reads ταραχθέντες παντοίους θανάτους ὑπέφερον, “having been harassed, they endured deaths of every kind.” Lactantius therefore ought to have written: “they were troubled and subjected to various deaths.” HEUMANN.

Observe. Supply: “openly.”

By reason of. This is the reading to adopt. The manuscript has *vero contemplatione* [“indeed, by reason of”].

Among these. Scholars read only *tantum his* [“only to these”].

We have believed. Manuscript: *credimus*, “we believe.”

Let them establish their meeting-houses. Some understand this of rebuilding Christian churches; others, more correctly, of holding their assemblies—thus in French, *tenir leurs assemblées* [“to hold their assemblies”].

That they do nothing contrary to discipline. Pliny, I [Book X], ep. 82 (79): “If any have acted contrary to discipline,” that is, “have acted.” BUNEMANN.

But by another letter. Manuscript: *aliam autem epistolam*, “but another letter”; either *per* must be prefixed, or it must be read as restored in the text.

We shall signify. Rufinus wrongly has “we have indicated,” narrating the matter as though already completed, whereas it refers to the future. Nor should this be ascribed to a printer’s error, since three ancient manuscript codices of the Colbert Library exhibit this reading. Christophorson and Valesius correctly translated, “we shall signify.” BALUZE.

May it remain. Manuscript: *perstetur*, erroneously.—Yet Bunemann has *praestetur incolumis* [“may it be kept safe”] and supplies the following note.—“May it be kept safe.” Printed editions have *perstet* [“may it remain”], while the manuscript has *perstetur*; hence, conveniently, as also seemed right to the anonymous Critic and to Heumann, *praestetur* should be adopted. For Eusebius translates παρασχεθῇ, “may it be granted/preserved.” Yet if anyone prefers *perstet*, let him compare the end of ch. 18: “The state might stand unharmed.” BUNEMANN.

In their own homes. Rufinus translates “in their households,” as is read in one Colbert manuscript. But other manuscripts and editions have “in their labours.” Christophorson translates “among their own families”; Valesius, “in their own dwellings.” BALUZE.

[Col. 0250C]

This edict was posted at Nicomedia on the day before the Kalends of May. Since Galerius Maximianus is called in the heading of the aforesaid edict holder of tribunician power for the twentieth time, it is clear that it was issued after the Kalends of March in the current year (311), on which Galerius himself had entered upon his twentieth tribunician power. That it was issued after that day is also made certain by Greek coins in Goltz. For the last coin on which the year of his Augustan rule is marked bears the characters L. Z., that is, year seven. For, since, according to Lactantius’s testimony, he was proclaimed Augustus on the Kalends of May in the year 305, on the Kalends of May in the current year of Christ he began the seventh year of his Augustan reign. Therefore, since the same emperor promulgated that edict when he was already failing, it is apparent that Lactantius’s account of Galerius Maximianus is corroborated by the coins, and that Valesius in his notes on Eusebius, and other learned men, wrongly wrote that the edict had been issued before March (Pagi, *Critica Baroniana*, on the year of Christ 311, nos. 12 and 13).

[Col. 0250D]

At last, when the eighth year of the persecution had been completed and the ninth had begun, Galerius’s edict appeared, by which the persecution was wholly extinguished, between the Kalends of March—on which he had begun his twentieth tribunician power—and the day before the Kalends of May, on which Lactantius says it was posted at Nicomedia (Dodwell, *Dissertation on Cyprian*, XI.82).

Himself. Namely Galerius Maximianus. Manuscript: *ipsa*, “herself.”

When he was consul for the eighth time, and Maximinus for the second. Namely in the year 311; manuscript: *Maximiano*, “Maximian.”

From custody. Manuscript: *et custodia*, “and custody.”

May have been. Or “had been.”

Into [his] hand. For *in manum*, accusative, with the ablative used in place of the accusative; below, ch. 39, near the beginning: “he seeks her in marriage”; and frequently in Lactantius: III.3, “which fall within the order of things”; IV.17, “cast upon the ground with his whole body and face”; *On the Workmanship of God*, ch. 2, “they are banished into that region.”

The limbs were wasting away. Some would prefer *diffluerent*, “were dissolving,” as in *Divine Institutes*, III.1: “what is corrupted vanishes and dissolves”; and ch. 20: “a body abandoned by the soul dissolves.” In both places the recent manuscripts and almost all editions have *defluit*, “wastes away.”]

## EDICT OF GALERIUS

Among the other measures which we always ordain for the advantage and benefit of the state, we had indeed previously wished, in accordance with the ancient laws and the public discipline of the Romans, to reform everything and to provide that the Christians also, who had abandoned the sect of their ancestors, might return to sound minds. For such a great desire had seized those same Christians, and such folly had occupied them that they did not follow the institutions of the ancients, which perhaps their own parents had first established; but according to their own judgment, and as it pleased them, they made laws for themselves, which they might observe, and gathered together various peoples in different places.

Finally, when our command of this kind had been issued—that they should betake themselves to the institutions of the ancients—many were overcome by danger, and many also were driven away; and since very many persisted in their resolution, and we saw that they neither rendered to the gods the worship and religion due to them nor worshipped the God of the Christians, having regard to our most gentle clemency and the perpetual custom by which [Col. 0250A] we are accustomed to grant pardon to all people, we have judged that our most ready indulgence should be extended to these also, so that they may again be Christians and organize their assemblies, provided that they do nothing contrary to discipline. But by another letter we shall signify to the judges what they ought to observe. Therefore, in accordance with this our indulgence, they ought to pray to their God for our safety, that of the state, and their own, so that the state may remain unharmed in every respect and that they may be able to live securely in their own homes.

### XXXV.

This edict was posted at Nicomedia on the day before the Kalends of May, when he himself was consul for the eighth time and Maximinus for the second. Then, when the prisons had been opened, dearest Donatus, you were released from custody together with the other confessors, [Col. 0250B] although prison had been your dwelling for six years. Yet by this act he did not receive pardon from God for his crime. Rather, a few days later, after entrusting his wife and son to Licinius and delivering them into his hand, when the limbs of his whole body were already wasting away, he was consumed by a dreadful decay. And this became known at Nicomedia on the Ides of the same month, [Col. 0251A]

> [Note: [Col. 0251B] Notes of Various Commentators on columns 251–252]

Ides of the same month. Since here, before *mensis* [“month”], the manuscript has a blank space of only two letters, I believed that no word other than *Id.* could be substituted: *Id.* for *Idibus mensis eiusdem Maii*, “on the Ides of the same month of May,” in which month Galerius died in the year 311 of the Common Era.—“At Nicomedia . . . of the same month.” The manuscript reads: “And this became known at Nicomedia, indeed in the month, when the vicennalia were to occur, with the Kalends of March impending.” BUNEMANN.

With the Kalends of March impending. Namely, of the following year, 312.

[Col. 0251C]

Maximinus. Manuscript: *Maximianus*.

He hastened through. Heumann reads *provolavit*, “he rushed forth,” because Livy has: “the two Fabii rush forth with hostile spears.”—*Pervolavit*. Heumann: *provolavit*. Good, except that *pervolavit* indicates diligence in hastening on the journey, since the prefix *per-* strengthens the force of the verb; hence the French translator: *se rendit en diligence dans l’Orient* [“he proceeded with all speed into the East”]. BUNEMANN.

The Chalcedonian strait. That is, the Thracian Bosporus, on which Chalcedon in Bithynia lies.

For the moment. Lactantius, *Institutes*, VII.6: “And other things which avail only for the moment”; ch. 10: “All vices are temporary; they are stirred for the moment”; ch. 15: “Although for the moment he displayed God’s power to humankind”; *On the Anger of God*, ch. 22: “He does not punish every offender for the moment.” COLUMBUS.

Raises. Heumann reads *sustulit*, “raised.”

Discord. Manuscript: *discordiam*, “discord.”

Almost. Manuscript: *pena*, incorrectly.

Opposite shores. That is, the shores of the Chalcedonian strait.—“Opposite shores.” Armed forces held the shores of the strait: Maximian’s on the Bithynian shore, Licinius’s on the Thracian. CELLARIUS.

Armed [men]. Manuscript: *armata*, feminine/neuter.

In the strait. Manuscript: *fretu*.

He returns. Namely Maximinus.

Under a joint title. The most learned men Cotelerius, Du Cange, Cuper, and Columbus judge that this should be read. For Lactantius refers to the constitution issued in ch. XXXIV, which, according to the custom then received, was headed with the names of Galerius Maximianus and Maximinus Daia—that is, under a joint title. The manuscript corruptly has *tutelo*.

That Christians should not be permitted to build meeting-houses. *Conventicula*, that is, churches.

So that he might appear to act under compulsion and persuasion of a formal proposal. Thus the manuscript, and rightly, I think. *Sausu* is from *suadeo*. To propose a law, moreover, is to seek a law through the collective votes. In French I would say, *porter tout son suffrage sur une loi* [“to cast all one’s vote in favour of a law”]. Thus, *ut suasu coactus* means, as it were: “as though he had been led to it by the votes of all the [Col. 0252B] cities requesting this law.”

Chief. Manuscript: *Maximus*.

Gods. Manuscript: *dos*; perhaps even *domos suas*, “their own homes,” which yields a good sense. Choose.

Through all their gods. That is, through all the temples of their gods, or in all temples.

Supported by the ministry. Manuscript: *subnexi*.—“Supported by the ministry.” In Lactantius’s customary usage: *Institutes*, IV.10, “supported by jurisdiction”; IV.10, “supported by power”; V.6, “supported by the power of swords.” BUNEMANN.

They should make it their business that Christians neither build. Supply *ut*, “that.” “I should like you to do [it],” for “I should like that you do [it].” [Col. 0252C] “How I wish you had remained at home,” for “that you had remained at home.”

Should worship. I would prefer, with Gale, the anonymous Critic, and Heumann, *coirent*, “should gather together.” BUNEMANN.

Those apprehended. Manuscript: *comprehensus*, singular.

Should compel. Manuscript: *cogeret*, singular.

This was not enough, unless also. Behold Lactantius’s style: I.10, “It seemed insufficient unless also”; V.9, “They do not have enough . . . unless also”; VII.3, “And this is insufficient . . . unless also.” BUNEMANN.

Set over. This verb, says Columbus, was very common in that age; he adds that it also occurs in Minucius Felix. Lactantius himself, II.2: “Why do you heap earth upon your heads?” BUNEMANN.

In white cloaks, etc. That is, priests wore garments of white colour, except those who conducted rites for the dead, as is very well known. Porphyry, *On Abstinence*, IV.19, specifically teaches that the prophets of Jupiter in Crete wore such garments. Silius, III, attributes a snow-white garment to a priest; Pliny, XVI, final chapter, a white one to Druids; and Apuleius, II, white linen to officiants at sacred rites. CUPER.

Which long since. This adverb is absent from earlier printed editions but is read in the manuscript.

Clemency only in appearance. Nothing is more frequent in Lactantius than these words thus joined; nor, I think, is there any need to copy out examples. But amid so many kinds of cruelty, the worst is that kind to which a false appearance of clemency gives a flattering guise: that executioner is the more grievous, the more savage, who resolves to put no one to death. Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, V.11.

He ordered [them] to be maimed. That is, mutilated, as, for example, those confessors whose left knees were maimed with red-hot iron. See Eusebius, VIII.12, and *Life of Constantine*, I.58, where the name Licinius has mistakenly entered Valesius’s translation in place of Maximinus.

By letters. Manuscript: *litteras*, accusative. On these letters see Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, IX.9.]

of that same month, when the vicennalia were to take place on the impending Kalends of March.

### XXXVI.

When Maximinus heard this news, he hastened through from the East by arranged relays, in order to occupy the provinces and, while Licinius delayed, to claim everything for himself as far as the Chalcedonian strait. Having entered Bithynia, in order to win favour for himself for the moment, he abolished the census to the great joy of all. There was discord between the two emperors, and almost war. Their armed forces held opposite shores. But peace and friendship were arranged on specified terms; a treaty was made in the strait itself, and right hands were joined. He returned secure and became once more the man he had been in Syria and Egypt.

First of all, he revoked the indulgence granted to Christians under a joint title, having instigated embassies from cities [Col. 0251B] to request that Christians should not be permitted to build meeting-houses within their cities, so that he might appear to act under compulsion and persuasion of their proposal, though he was going to act voluntarily. [Col. 0252A] Granting their request, by a new practice he appointed one chief priest in each city from among its leading men, who should both perform sacrifices daily through all their gods and, supported by the ministry of the former priests, make it their business that Christians neither build nor worship publicly or privately, but should compel those apprehended, under their own authority, to sacrifice or bring them before judges.

Nor was this enough, unless he also set over the provinces, one by one, men of a higher rank of dignity, as though they were pontiffs; and he ordered both groups to go about adorned in white cloaks. He was also preparing to do what he had long since done in the eastern regions. For, though he professed clemency only in appearance, he forbade the servants of God to be killed, but ordered them to be maimed. Accordingly, the eyes of confessors were gouged out; their hands were cut off, their feet mutilated, [Col. 0252B] and their noses or ears sliced away.

### XXXVII.

While he was planning these measures, he was deterred by Constantine’s letters. [Col. 0253A]

> [Note: [Col. 0253B] Notes of Various Commentators on columns 253–254]

Were drowned. Manuscript: *mergebantur*, plural.

The palace. Manuscript: *palatium*, accusative.

Tasted. It was a portion of a prepared meal which they plucked off and offered to the gods. They also customarily made libations from food. Silius Italicus, VII:

> First he rendered Vesta her due honour,  
> and cast libations from every side into the midst of the flame.

Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities*, IV, calls this “making libations of the first portions of meals.” GRAEVIUS.

Sacrificed. That which had been cut from a victim offered to the gods for a feast; as they customarily cut away and burn a portion of victims, reserving another portion for the meals of priests and sacrificers. GRAEVIUS.

Drenched with unmixed wine. Namely, wine with which they customarily made supplication, so that these foods might be made, as it were, sacred. For who does not know that the ancients customarily made supplication with incense and wine, even during meals? Horace, *Odes*, IV.5, concerning Augustus:

> At their tables they receive you as a god.  
> With many a prayer they attend you, with wine  
> poured from the bowl; and with their household gods  
> they mingle your divine power.

GRAEVIUS.

Like his master. Namely, Galerius Maximianus. So above, ch. 21: “men very like his greatness.”

Remained. Heumann deletes this word.

Storehouses. That is, wine-cellars; for this word see Phaedrus, IV.4.

Debts. Heumann adds “taxes.” Hence famine, though the fields bore crops. Thus the manuscript; nothing should be changed. “Though the fields bore crops,” that is, although the fields bore crops. See the preceding words: “he swept away . . . private granaries were shut,” [Col. 0253D] etc. Printed editions read “when the fields did not bear crops,” less well.—“Hence famine, though the fields bore crops.” Others correct it to “when the fields did not bear crops”; others, “when the farmers did not bear [the burden].” Nurrius correctly says: “Although the fields bore abundant produce, people nevertheless died of hunger, because Maximinus’s attendants took away with savage cruelty all wines, all grain, and whatever the fields bore, in order to sell them in other regions for the benefit of the public treasury.” BUNEMANN.

Herds, etc. All this is very corrupt, both in the manuscript and in the printed editions, so that it can scarcely be understood. I have judged, however, that it should be read as follows: “Herds of cattle and flocks were carried off from the fields for daily sacrifices, by which he had corrupted his courtiers so thoroughly that they despised grain-rations, and they scattered [the sacrificial meat] everywhere without discrimination or measure, while he decked out (that is, gratified) all his attendants, whose number was immense, with costly garments and gold coins, gave silver to common soldiers and recruits, and honoured barbarians with every kind of largesse.”

[Col. 0254B]

Them. Or “his own,” that is, his courtiers.

Had corrupted. Because it had already become customary for banquets to offer meats that had been presented to idols.

They scattered. Others: “he scattered.”

Attendants. The manuscript has *lites*, with no gap at all; but, with the most learned Toinard and Tollius, I have restored *satellites* [“attendants”]. This correction is confirmed both by the following “he gave gifts to his own” and by Rufinus, VIII.17: “Whence he lavished, so to speak, mountains of gold gathered together upon his household retainers and attendants”; and by Lactantius below, ch. 38, near the end: “surrounded by these attendants and protectors.”

[Col. 0254C]

Deck out. Manuscript: *expungerent*, plural.—“Deck out with gold coins.” That is, [he decked out] his attendants with costly garments and gold coins. It is a manner of requital, immediately returning one thing for another. Seneca, *On Benefits*, IV.40: “To send [a gift], and to requite a gift with a gift.” BUNEMANN.

Should honour barbarians with every kind of largesse. Manuscript: *omni genere largitionibus*.

According as. It is lacking in the manuscript.—“He gave, as each person.” Earlier printed editions: “he gave according as each person.” In the manuscript, according to the anonymous Critic: “each person was given”: hence that critic more correctly reads, “it was given, as each person”—I add that I have observed *prout* nowhere else in Lactantius. BUNEMANN.

I do not know whether I should think that thanks were not due to him. With Cuper, I read *an non* [“whether not”], which is irony. *Non* is not absent from the manuscript.

In the manner of merciful bandits. Thus Salvian: “Bandits customarily use this proverb, saying that they have given life to those from whom they do not take it.”

Capital. Manuscript: *capitali*, ablative/dative.

And. Thus the manuscript. Others have *ei*, “to him,” in place of *et*, “and.”

[Col. 0254D]

What can I say, I do not know. Lactantius, I.21: “For what can I say concerning infants who were sacrificed to Saturn because of Jupiter’s hatred?”

It cannot be expressed in words because of his indignation. Manuscript: *exprimere*, “to express.” If this is read, *mens* [“mind”] appears to be missing; and it would have to be read: “and yet [the mind] cannot express it in words because of its indignation.” So Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, VI.23: “With what words or with what indignation shall I pursue so great a crime? The magnitude of the crime surpasses the office of the tongue.”

Women of noble rank. The outrage was increased by their noble status. For to be inspected in this manner was wholly servile and abhorrent to free persons. Slaves were customarily displayed thus for inspection by slave-dealers to prospective bidders. COLUMBUS.—Rufinus, VIII.17: “Among other things, this was also a particular object of his zeal: that he should pass by no city, indeed not even a small town, without the adultery of noble matrons found in its places or the corruption of virgins.” In Latin, *foeminae* means not only women joined to husbands, but also virgins. Labbe’s glossaries: *Foemina*, θήλεια [“female”], which they commonly explain by *foeminea*, that is, “what belongs to the female sex,” and this is proper to virgins as well. BAULDRI.]

Woman. In the manuscript, *femina*.

Without precedent. We have one example of a second marriage among Augustan women: Lucilla, wife of Lucius Verus, whom, after her husband’s death, her father Marcus Antoninus gave, though unwilling, to Claudius Pompeianus, an old man and the son of a Roman knight. See Capitolinus, *Marcus*, ch. 20.

The man. For “to him,” namely Maximinus.

Their garments were stripped off—likewise those of virgins—and they were inspected limb by limb, lest any part of their body should be unworthy of the imperial bed. If any woman refused, she was put to death in water, as though chastity under that adulterer were a crime against majesty. Some men, when their wives had been violated—wives whom they held most dear because of their chastity and fidelity—and were unable to bear the grief, even killed themselves. Under this monster there was no integrity of chastity, except where marked ugliness repelled barbarous lust.

Finally, he had by now introduced this practice: no one might take a wife without his permission, so that in every marriage he himself might be the first taster. He gave freeborn virgins, after violating them, as wives to his slaves. His companions too, under such a prince, imitated [this example and violated the beds] of their fellow-citizens with impunity. For who [Col. 0255B] would exact punishment? He carried off the daughters of persons of middling rank whenever it pleased him. The daughters of leading families, whom he could not carry off, were sought as rewards for services; refusal was not permitted when the emperor endorsed the request: one had either to perish or to accept some barbarian as a son-in-law. For scarcely anyone stood in attendance at his side except men of the race of those who, driven from their lands by the Goths at the time of the vicennalia, [Col. 0256A] surrendered themselves to Maximian—to the misfortune of humankind—so that they, fleeing barbarian servitude, might exercise dominion over Romans. Surrounded by these attendants and protectors, he made the East his plaything.

### XXXIX.

Finally, having granted his lusts this law—that he judged lawful whatever he desired—he could not restrain himself even from the Augusta whom he had recently called mother. After Maximian’s death, Valeria had come to him, thinking that she would live more safely among his fathers, especially because he had a wife. But the accursed creature immediately burned with passion. The woman was still in black clothing, the time of mourning not yet completed. Having first sent envoys, he sought her in marriage, intending to divorce his wife if he obtained her. She alone was able to reply freely: [Col. 0256B] first, that she could not discuss marriage in that funeral attire, while the ashes of her husband—his father—were still warm; secondly, that he acted impiously in repudiating a wife faithful to him, since he would surely do the same to her; and finally, that it was unlawful for a woman of that name and rank, contrary to custom and without precedent, to take a second husband.

The man was informed of what she had dared to say. Lust [Col. 0257A]

> [Note: [Col. 0257B] Notes of Various Commentators on columns 257–258]

Companions. Here feminine in gender.

[Col. 0257C]

He banishes her herself together with her mother. Namely Valeria together with Prisca, Diocletian’s wife, of whom more has been said in the notes on ch. 15. Manuscript: *ipsa*, “she herself.”

Her female friends. Namely, Valeria’s.

Afflicted. Manuscript: *afflicto*, corrupt.

He suspects. Thus in the manuscript; printed editions have *suspicabatur* [“he suspected”]. That is, Maximinus suspects.

Eratineus. The passage appears corrupt. It is the name of a provincial governor. BALUZE.—Perhaps *Eratinus*, so that it is Greek ἐρατεινὸν, “lovely,” equivalent to ἐράσμιος, “beloved.” Yet Heumann suspects that *protinus*, “immediately,” should be read in place of *Eratineo*, a word familiar to Lactantius, as appears from chs. 29, 30, and 39 of this work.

A maidservant. Some wish to read: “a daughter by right and merit.”

Of a fugitive woman. Manuscript: *furtive*, incorrectly.

Not very close to the Augusta. Thus the manuscript. Some wish to read “not less”; others, “not at all.”

Was killed. Manuscript: *necabantur*, plural.

“A certain Jew is found,” etc. This was not first devised by Maximinus. Nero, a man of good example, had preceded him when he wished to divorce his wife Octavia to please Poppaea. See Tacitus, *Annals*, XIV.

An impartial and diligent judge. Said ironically.

May he be stoned. Namely by the citizens, who knew their innocence; or perhaps lest the Jew himself be stoned for false testimony.

“He had been ordered to speak; these women were not to speak.” Thus the anonymous Critic restored the passage, having inspected the manuscript in which about fourteen letters are missing. Others read *iussus clam erat, palam*, and the most learned Nicolaus Heinsius conjectured that this should be read. But the manuscript reads *loquerentur* [“they should speak”] and *coercentur* [“they are restrained”], which I did not wish to alter.

They are ordered. Add: “to execution.”

So great. Manuscript: *tanti*.

Had assembled. That is, had summoned together as a spectacle.

With hands. Manuscript: *manus*, nominative/accusative.

Promoted. Or “advanced”; or, as some maintain, military commanders promoted to higher ranks.

[Col. 0258B]

Instructed light infantry and archers escort them. Thus I read, with Baluzius among the errata to his edition, since the manuscript has *instructibile mens essagittari*, which is meaningless, though it contains the same number of letters. For here, he says, light infantry and archers are rightly joined, since both are lightly armed soldiers.

“And they would have lain.” Thus the manuscript, rightly. The word *-que* is absent from the early editions.

“The adulterer.” That is, the Jew. In the manuscript, *adulterio*, “adultery.”

“He revealed.” Heumann reads “he reveals.”

“He says.” The manuscript has *in quod*. This verb is superfluous, or should be altered as we have done by adding the missing conjunction *ac*, “and,” as though he said: “with his last breath he spoke,” or “he told all who saw that the innocent women had been put to death, and testified that they had been innocent.”

“Empress.” Namely Valeria, widow of Galerius Maximianus.

“Aware.” The manuscript wrongly has *magnarum*.

“Of her misfortune.” In the manuscript, *calamitates*, “misfortunes.”

“May entreat.” The manuscript has *deprecatur*, “he entreats.” — “May entreat”: may entreat earnestly. Cicero, *Letters*, II.24: “He had sent ambassadors of the senate not to entreat for peace, but to declare war.” — “May entreat.” The manuscript has *deprecatur*. The former is more correct, in the sense of *precetur*, “may pray/entreat,” from Lactantius’s usage; examples are indicated at *Institutes*, III.17. BUN.

“His embassy having failed.” Thus the manuscript. Some scholars wished to read “his embassy having been completed.” Bunemann strongly approves the latter reading, offering the following note: — “His embassy having been completed.” This must certainly be read with Heinsius in place of the editions’ manuscript reading, “his embassy having failed,” unless one prefers “now that the embassy had been completed.” BUN.

“At the same time.” Thus the manuscript. Two learned men would prefer “at that same time also.”

“Of the old man.” In the manuscript, “the old man.”

“Of Maximian.” Namely Herculius.

“The statues of the old man Maximian … were torn down.” This is confirmed by Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, VIII.13, and *Life of Constantine*, I.47; Baluzius and Nurrius discuss these passages. BUN.

“The images of the man with whom he had been portrayed.” Thus the manuscript, without any gap. After “images,” *of that man* seems to be missing.

…was changed into wrath and fury. At once she proscribes the woman, seizes her property, removes her attendants, kills eunuchs under torture, and banishes her herself, together with her mother; and not to a fixed place, but drives her headlong from place to place in mockery, and condemns her friends on a fabricated charge of adultery.

XL. There was a woman of very distinguished rank, who already had grandchildren from her grown sons. Valeria loved her as a second mother and suspected that it was through her advice that she had been refused. She commissions the governor Eratineus to put her to death dishonourably. Two other women, equally noble, are joined to her. One of them had left at Rome a virgin attendant, a Vestal, who was intimate with Valeria in her flight. The other had had a husband who was a senator, not especially close to the Empress. [Col. 0257B] Yet both were put to death because of their exceptional bodily beauty and chastity. The women are suddenly seized—not for a trial, but for brigandage. For no accuser appeared. A certain Jew, guilty of other crimes, is found; induced by hope of impunity, he lies against the innocent women. The fair and diligent judge delivers his judgment outside the city, under guard, lest he be stoned. This tragedy was enacted at Nicaea. Tortures are inflicted on the Jew so that he may say what he had been ordered to say; the women, lest they speak, are restrained by the torturers’ fists. The innocent women [Col. 0258A] are ordered away to execution. There is weeping and lamentation—not only from the husband who was present for his deserving wife, but from all whom the outrageous and unprecedented event had drawn together. And lest they be snatched from the executioners’ hands by the people’s onrush, light infantry and archers, equipped in military fashion, escort them. Thus, amid ranks of armed men, they are led to punishment. And they would have lain unburied, their household having fled, had not the clandestine compassion of friends buried them. Nor is the promised impunity paid to the adulterer: fastened to a gibbet, he revealed the whole mystery; and with his last breath he told all who saw—and testified—that the women killed were innocent.

XLI. The Empress, however, having been banished into certain deserted wildernesses of Syria, secretly made her father Diocletian [Col. 0258B] aware of her misfortune. He sends envoys and asks that his daughter be returned to him. He achieves nothing. Again and repeatedly he entreats. She is not returned. Finally, he dispatches a certain relative of his, a soldier and man of power, to entreat him, after reminding him of his benefits. He too reports that his pleas were fruitless, his embassy having failed.

XLII. At the same time, by Constantine’s order, the statues of the aged Maximian were torn down, as were the images of the man with whom he had been portrayed [Col. 0259A].

[Notes: Variorum Notes to columns 259–260]

“Both old men.” Namely Diocletian and Maximian Herculius.

“Since he saw it while alive.” Diocletian, whose images were being taken down during his lifetime, because they were joined with [Col. 0259C] images of Herculius.

“No one.” The manuscript has *nulla*, “no [woman/thing].”

“By a double grief.” Namely because of the insult inflicted both upon his daughter and upon himself. HEUM.

“His soul.” In the manuscript, “his soul” in the accusative.

“Through grief.” That is, from grief or because of grief.

“Sighs.” Cuspinianus, in his *Diocletian*: “Some say that, worn out by mental stupefaction and prolonged illness, he breathed out his soul amid sighs.” FROM CEDRENUS.

“So greatly.” Learned men read “by God.”

“Cast down into hatred of life.” Thus the manuscript, although *deiectus*, “cast down,” has just occurred. Therefore several would rather read *devectus*, “brought down”; others *adductus*, “brought into,” as Cicero uses “to bring into hatred,” “into ill repute.” — “Brought into hatred of life.” Bunemann reads *deductus*, “led into,” and gives the following note: — “Led into hatred of life.” Graevius so corrected it. Lactantius, *Institutes*, II.1: “led into the utmost necessity of begging”; II.1: “led into … blindness.” Valerius Maximus, I.1: “Regulus, reduced to the condition of a captive.” The phrase itself is scarcely to be found. BUN.

“He was consumed by hunger and anguish.” Others report that he died of dropsy, others of poison; Suidas, by hanging. However the matter stood, it is agreed that he died in 312, before the marriage of Licinius and Constantia. PAGIUS.

“One remained.” Namely Maximinus, surnamed Daza or Daia, who still governed the East.

“Because.” The manuscript has *qui ad*.

“That.” In the manuscript, *ut* is repeated twice.

“Constantine’s sister.” Constantia, who afterward so favoured Arius that she even urged her brother to protect him. BALUZ.

“Betrothed.” That is, promised in marriage.

“To request.” The manuscript reads *postulatam*; the printed editions have *postulans*. We have written *postulatum*, which seems more correct.

“Familiarly.” That is, amicably.

[Col. 0260B]

“The death of his father.” Of Maximian Herculius, whom Constantine had ordered strangled at Massilia. Zosimus, II: “Maxentius sought occasions for making war against Constantine, pretending that he grieved over his father’s death, for which Constantine had furnished the cause.” BALUZ. “That old man”: Maximian Herculius.

“So destructive.” I have restored *tam exitiabilem*, since the manuscript has *xtabilem*, lacking three or four initial letters. One may also read *detestabilem*, “so detestable,” if one deletes *tam*, “so.”

“He feigned discord.” Eutropius, X: “He then departed for Gaul, having contrived a deception, as though he had been expelled by his son.” BALUZ.

“To cut down.” The manuscript has *succedendos*.

“Civil arms had already been set in motion between them.” Between Constantine and Maxentius, from the year 311.

“An oracle.” Namely, from an oracle.

“Commanders.” The manuscript has “to lead.”

“And his own proper [army].” A Lactantian expression: *Institutes*, IV.14, “his own proper”; III.10 and IV.40, “by his own proper [means]”; V.2, “others, by their own proper hatred toward the just”; and *On the Workmanship [of God]*, 2: “For each kind [of creature] he established its own proper defenses for repelling external assaults.”

“From Moors and Italians.” Heumann thinks—and rightly—that “from Moors and Gaetulians” should be read, the Gaetulians being near the Moors. — “From Moors and Italians.” Heumann ingeniously reads “from Moors and Gaetulians.” For neighbouring peoples are thus joined. Yet the manuscript’s received reading can be tolerated: it was especially necessary to assemble, for the march toward Rome, an army drawn even from Italians, since they were nearer. BUN.

“A battle was fought,” etc. Heumann reads, “A battle was fought.”

“Ready for either outcome.” Understand: a decisive result—swift death or joyful victory. In Virgil, *Aeneid*, II.61:

> Confident in spirit, and ready for either outcome.

“The Milvian Bridge.” I follow the manuscript, which has no other reading. The printed editions have *Mulvii*, the correct name; today, Ponte Molle.

[Col. 0261B]

“The day on which Maxentius had seized imperial power … the sixth day before the Kalends of November,” etc. As is clear from Lactantius, Maxentius was proclaimed emperor at Rome on 27 October, the sixth day before the Kalends of November. Constantine defeated Maxentius on the sixth day before the Kalends of November, according to the same Lactantius.

…with him, were taken down. And because the two old men were generally depicted together, the images of both were taken down together. Thus, when he saw while still alive what had happened to no emperor before, afflicted by a double grief, he decided that he must die. He tossed himself to and fro, his soul seething with pain, taking neither sleep nor food. Sighs and groans, frequent tears, continual rolling of the body—now on the bed, now on the ground. Thus the emperor who had been most fortunate for twenty years, reduced so utterly to a lowly condition, trampled by insults, and cast down into hatred of life, was finally consumed by hunger and anguish.

XLIII. One alone now remained among the adversaries of God; I shall now append [Col. 0259B] the end and ruin of this man. Though he had a rivalry with Licinius because Maximian had preferred Licinius to him, and though he had lately confirmed friendship with Licinius, nevertheless, when he heard that Constantine’s sister had been betrothed to Licinius, he believed that this alliance of the two emperors was being joined against himself. He too secretly sends envoys to the City, to request alliance and friendship with Maxentius. He also writes in friendly terms. The envoys are received kindly; friendship is made; [Col. 0260A] images of both are displayed together. Maxentius gladly embraces this as divine assistance. For he had already declared war on Constantine, as though intending to avenge the death of his father. Hence a suspicion had arisen that that exceedingly destructive old man had feigned discord with his son, in order to make a way for himself to cut down the others; once all had been removed, he would claim the empire of the whole world for himself and his son. But this was false. For his purpose was that, after both his son and the others had been destroyed, he and Diocletian should be restored to sovereignty.

XLIV. Civil arms had already been set in motion between them. And although Maxentius remained within Rome, because he had received an oracle that he would perish if he went outside the city gates, war was nevertheless conducted through capable commanders. Maxentius had greater forces, because he had received from Severus both his father’s army and, recently, had drawn out his own proper army from Moors and Italians. A battle was fought, and Maxentius’s soldiers prevailed, until later Constantine, his courage strengthened and ready for either outcome, moved all his forces nearer to the City and encamped opposite the Milvian Bridge. The day was imminent on which Maxentius had seized imperial power: it was the sixth day before the [Col. 0261A] Kalends of November, and his quinquennial celebrations were ending.

[Notes: Variorum Notes to columns 261–262]

“Warned in sleep.” This is a distinctive word. Those to whom God commands something in a dream are said to be “warned.” See ancient inscriptions. TOLLIUS.

“The heavenly sign.” Elsewhere Lactantius calls it the “immortal sign,” *Institutes*, IV.27: that is, the sign of the cross. This passage is of great importance. For it specifies both the place and the day on which the cross by which Constantine was to conquer was shown to him. Since Eusebius testifies that he received it from Constantine’s own mouth—that at midday, as the sun inclined toward setting, Constantine saw in heaven the trophy of the cross; and that, as he wondered what this apparition meant, Christ of God appeared to him while asleep in the following night with the sign which had been shown in heaven, and ordered him to construct a military standard resembling that which he had seen in heaven and to use it as a saving protection in battles—it is certain that both visions occurred in one place and within the span of a few hours.

“And with the transverse letter X, its upper point bent around.” He marks Christ upon the shields. The manuscript has *Christo*, “Christ.” This must be understood to mean that Christ’s monogram was bent around [Col. 0261D] at the top of the Labarum, as we see on ancient coins.

“Without the emperor.” Without Maxentius.

“They engage.” *Concurrere* commonly means to advance to combat or battle. Here I understand it as engaging in equal battle line: going to meet the enemy with the same confidence and eagerness with which they approach you. Or, if preferred, all engage in an equally drawn-up line. The manuscript has “they engage”; others read “they engage.”

“Flight was known neither to these nor to those.” These words of Virgil, preserved in the most ancient manuscript of Lactantius, confirm Pierius’s assertion on *Aeneid* X.757: *neque … neque* should occur twice, not, as today, *neque nec*. BUN.

“The leader is rebuked.” Maxentius.

“On his birthday.” That is, on the day when he became emperor.

“He was giving.” The manuscript has “and when … and due,” without sense. Instead of “and due,” I read *edebat*, “he was giving,” with some learned men—Maxentius, namely. For the manuscript’s *cumque*, “and when,” I read *tumque*, “then”; others read *cunctus*, “the whole [people].”

“It is cut.” On the cut bridge see Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, IX.9, and Zosimus, XI.15.

“The battle line was prevailing.” This seems a biblical phrase: Exodus 17:11. Perhaps *suberrat aciei* should be read, says Bauldri—that is, it stretched itself here and there through the ranks of combatants, secretly exerting its force against Maxentius’s soldiers. For *acies* often means battle or combat; and “to move stealthily beneath the battle line” is like Claudian’s “to move stealthily beneath the mountains.” But Heumann thinks that this should be read: “But, as the hand of God prevailed, Maxentius’s battle line was routed.”

“Maxentius’s [soldier] is routed.” Thus the manuscript: Maxentius’s soldier, that is. Others want “Maxentius’s battle line,” while some prefer “Maxentius’s men are routed.” If anything were to be altered, I should prefer “Maxentius is crushed.” *Proterrere* means to drive into flight by terrifying.

“And.” In the manuscript, “this.”

“Finally.” The manuscript has “however.”

“The title.” Namely, “greatest.” After Galerius’s death, Maximinus, because he had been the earlier Caesar, although last to become Augustus, claimed precedence for himself in titles and honours among the Augusti of that time, Eusebius says, *Ecclesiastical History*, IX.10. But the Senate decreed that Constantine should be first among the Augusti.

[Col. 0262D]

“He claimed.” Perhaps “he had claimed.”

“Against the greatest emperor.” Against the son of an emperor, who held the provinces beyond the Alps by inheritance, and Italy and Africa by conquest. For it is not likely that the Senate’s decree then bestowed the surname “Greatest.” See Cuper. CELL.

“Proceeds.” This word is defective and almost worn away in the manuscript, and can scarcely be read.

“A wife.” Namely Constantia, Constantine’s sister.

“Which.” Heumann thinks this little word should be deleted.

“Double stages.” That is, in one day he travelled only as far as two stopping-places on the imperial road lay from one another. He rested not at the first but at the second. CELLAR. “He hastens into Bithynia.” Thus the manuscript. Some prefer “he runs to”; Almeloveen, “he ran.” For *cu* could easily have become *cum* and then *con*.

Warned in sleep, Constantine marked the heavenly sign of God upon the shields, and thus engaged in battle. He did as he had been commanded, and by a transverse X, with its upper point bent around, he marks Christ upon the shields. Armed with this sign, the army takes up the sword. The enemy advances to meet them without the emperor and crosses the bridge. The battle lines engage in equal array. The fighting is intense on both sides. Flight is known neither to these nor to those. A sedition arises in the City, and the leader is rebuked as a deserter of the public safety. Then suddenly the people—for he was giving Circensian games on his birthday—cry aloud that Constantine cannot be defeated.

Alarmed by this cry, he rushes away and, summoning certain senators, orders the Sibylline books to be consulted. [Col. 0261B] In them it was found that on that day the enemy of the Romans would perish. Led by this response into hope of victory, he advances and comes into battle array. The bridge is cut behind him. At the sight of this, the battle grows fiercer, and the hand of God prevails over the battle line. Maxentius’s soldier is routed; he himself, turned to flight, hurries to the bridge, which had been broken, and, pressed by the crowd of fugitives, is thrown into the Tiber. When the exceedingly bitter battle was at last concluded, the Emperor Constantine was received with great rejoicing by the Senate and people of Rome. [Col. 0262A] He learns of Maximinus’s treachery, intercepts letters, and finds statues and images. The Senate decrees to Constantine, in reward for his valour, the title of first rank, which Maximinus claimed for himself. When the news of the victory that had liberated the City was brought to him, he received it no differently than if he himself had been defeated. Then, when he learned of the Senate’s decree, he burned so with grief that he openly professed hostilities and uttered insults, mingled with jokes, against the greatest emperor.

XLV. When affairs in the City had been settled, Constantine proceeded to Milan in the following winter. Licinius also arrived there to receive his wife. When Maximinus learned that they were occupied [Col. 0262B] with the wedding ceremonies, he moved his army from Syria during the severest winter weather and, making double stages, hastened into Bithynia with his column weakened. For in the greatest rains, snow, mud, cold, and exertion, pack animals of every kind were lost; their pitiable carcasses strewn along the road announced to the soldiers an image of the coming war and a like disaster. Nor did he remain within his own borders.

[Notes: Variorum Notes to columns 263–264]

“Immediately after crossing the strait.” Namely the Thracian Bosporus.

“For such contingencies.” In the old manuscript it reads, “stationed by Licinius for such a cause.” Our correction is sound. In ancient manuscripts *causa*, “cause,” is often written for *casus*, “contingency,” as in St Ambrose, Letter 43: “In nature there is contingency; in choice, judgment”; in the very ancient manuscript of the Church of Beauvais, however, *causa* is written, though incorrectly. BALUZ.

“To entice.” In the manuscript, *illicire*.

“Yet neither force nor promises accomplished anything.” Thus the manuscript.

“The emperor.” Namely Licinius.

“Distrusting their small number.” Galerius preferred “weakened by their small number.” Nothing should be changed. Thus Tacitus, *Histories*, II.23: “distrusting the small number of cohorts,” as Jacob Gronovius restored from the Oxford manuscript. Conversely Livy, VI.23: “trusting in the number of soldiers.” The phrase is Lactantian: *Institutes*, VIII.1: “while he distrusts … the heavenly reward.” BUN.

“Heraclea.” The manuscript has *Heracliam*. That is, the city in Thrace, also called Perinthus below. Zosimus, I.62.

[Col. 0263D]

“Received in surrender.” Thus the manuscript. It ought to be “into surrender”; but, as I have already noted above, Lactantius speaks thus.

“Perinthus.” The manuscript has *Perentho*.

“Licinius already occupying the second station, at the same distance in miles.” Thus I read with Vossius and Baluzius. The manuscript has, quite erroneously, “occupying the second station, distant.”

“Who, having gathered.” With Vossius I read “who”—Licinius, that is. The manuscript has “and.”

“As many as.” In place of “how many.” For he—Maximinus, that is.

“He himself scarcely.” Licinius.

“Approaching.” A poetic word, as I observed above at the beginning of chapter 24; it is also found in Lactantius.

“If he had gained victory.” That is, won it. What else can “to gain victory” mean except what the Latins commonly called “to bring back,” “to obtain,” or “to achieve” victory? Yet who besides our author has used “to gain victory”? For I have observed no example anywhere. No manner of expression is more common in Lactantius, whose writings—especially Book VII—frequently contain “to gain courage,” “to gain wisdom,” “to gain origin,” “to gain fruits,” “to gain knowledge”; *On the Wrath of God*, 7, “to gain diseases”; *On the Workmanship [of God]*, 4, “to gain death.” Ibid.

“Would extinguish the name of Christians.” Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, I.18: “He extinguished a great part of humankind.”

“Sleeping.” That is, asleep. Compare Lactantius’s most elegant passage in *On the Workmanship of God*, 18: “For although the body lies unmoving while sense is awake, it is nevertheless not at rest; … lest it interrupt the body’s most healthful rest.”

“God most high.” When referring to the true God, scarcely any epithet is more frequent in Lactantius’s undisputed works, including chapters 1 and 47 of this work and elsewhere. Indeed, this among other points makes it impossible to doubt that Lactantius is also the author of this little work. BAULDRI.

[Col. 0264D]

“If he did so.” Heumann says that one should rather read, “if he did this.”

“A secretary.” That is, one of the confidential secretaries.

“To be summoned.” The manuscript has *asciri*.

“All.” Heumann thinks “our” should be written.

“On little documents.” That is, on shorter written sheets; so the very learned Heumann after Gisbertus Cuper.

“Commanders.” The *praepositi* were leading officers who commanded legions, as is evident from certain inscriptions collected by Gruter.

“All.” Namely all Licinius’s soldiers.

“The emperor fixed the battle for the day of the Kalends of May.” The emperor appears to be Licinius. Maximinus had been made Caesar on the Kalends of May.

“Day.” Scholars think “for a day” should be written; not wrongly.

But immediately after crossing the strait, he approached the gates of Byzantium under arms. There were garrison soldiers there, stationed by Licinius for such contingencies. He first attempted to entice them with gifts and promises; afterward to intimidate them by force and siege. Yet neither force nor promises accomplished anything.

Eleven days had already been consumed, during which there had been time to send messengers and letters to the Emperor, when the soldiers, distrusting not their loyalty but their small number, surrendered themselves. From there he advanced to Heraclea and, detained there for the same reason, lost several days. By then Licinius, hastening his march, had arrived at Adrianople with a few men; while Maximinus, having received Perinthus in surrender and lingered there for some time, advanced to a station eighteen miles away. For he could go no farther, since Licinius already occupied [Col. 0263B] the second station, at a like distance; Licinius, having gathered from the neighbourhood as many soldiers as he could, was marching to meet Maximinus, more to delay him than with a purpose of fighting or a hope of victory. For Maximinus was leading an army of seventy thousand armed men, while Licinius had scarcely assembled thirty thousand. The soldiers had been scattered among different regions, and the shortage of time did not allow all of them to be brought together.

XLVI. [Col. 0264A] As the armies therefore approached, battle seemed likely to occur soon. Then Maximinus made the following vow to Jupiter: if he gained victory, he would extinguish and utterly destroy the name of Christians. Then, on the following night, an angel of God stood beside Licinius as he slept, warning him to rise quickly and pray to God most high with his whole army; victory would be his if he did so. After these words, when he seemed to himself to have risen and to stand with the one who was warning him, that one then taught him how and in what words he should pray. Then, when sleep had been dispelled, he ordered a secretary to be summoned and dictated the following words exactly as he had heard them:

> God most high, we beseech you.  
> Holy God, we beseech you.  
> We entrust to you all justice;  
> we entrust to you our safety;  
> we entrust to you our empire.  
> Through you we live; through you we become victorious and fortunate.  
> Most high, holy God, hear our prayers.  
> We stretch out our arms to you.  
> Hear us, holy, most high God.

These words are written on many small documents and sent out through the commanders and tribunes, that each might instruct his own soldiers. The courage of all increased, since they believed victory had been announced to them from heaven. The emperor fixed the battle for the day of the Kalends of May, which completed the eighth year [Col. 0265A] of Maximinus’s accession, so that he might be defeated especially on his own imperial anniversary, just as that other man had been defeated at Rome.

[Notes: Variorum Notes to columns 265–266]

“His.” Namely Maximinus. — “Of his accession.” The day on which Maximinus had been created Caesar. The anniversary, therefore, is that of his rule, not his birth. Licinius was acting so that he might defeat Maximinus on Maximinus’s own anniversary, just as Maxentius had been defeated on his own. CELL. — Soon afterward the manuscript wrongly has “they will complete.” BUN.

“They completed.” The manuscript has “they will complete.”

“So that he might be defeated especially on his own anniversary.” Maximinus, plainly.

“Just as that other man was defeated at Rome.” That other man, namely Maxentius.

“It is announced in the camp that [Maximinus] has moved.” Namely in Licinius’s camp. So Cicero, *For Milo*: “it was announced into the gardens”; and *On Illustrious Orators*: “gladiatorial hissing was announced to me at Tusculum.”

“Barren.” The manuscript has *sterelis*, incorrectly.

“Serene.” Near Resiston, a place in Thrace between Adrianople and Heraclea, contrary to Zosimus, who reports this battle as fought in Illyria. FROM BALUZIUS. — “Which they call serene.” Most print it with a capital letter or in distinct type, as if *Serenum* were a proper name; but every plain bare of trees was called *serenus*, “clear, bright.” Thus Lactantius, *Institutes*, VI.3: “to have a level road, a bright and pleasant plain.” BUN.

“Both battle lines.” The manuscript has “both.”

“They unfasten their helmets.” That is, they loosen the fastenings by which helmets were fitted and bound to the head lest they fall off. Thus the soldiers said the prayer they had been taught only after removing their helmets and consequently uncovering their heads, either in accordance with the angel’s instruction, who had dictated the prayer, or in accordance with the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 11:4 and 7: “Every man praying with his head covered dishonours his head … for a man ought not to cover his head.”

“And they say the prayer after the Emperor.” Thus I read. The manuscript has *p imperatore prc dicunt*. The first *p* is written with a transverse line beneath it, which I think signifies *post*, “after”; then *imperatore* has a transverse line above its final *e*; and finally there are two lines above *p* and *c*, making *precem*, “prayer.” Thus also in *Divine Institutes*, I: “when he uttered a prayer.” Cellarius nevertheless thinks “for the emperor” should be written, but less correctly.

“Courage.” That is, martial valour, as below.

“They raise their shields.” That is, lift them up.

“Maximinus could not be brought [to peace].” The manuscript has *ferre*, a less Latin expression. — “Could not be brought.” Heumann corrects it to “could not be induced.” Our author indeed said with Cicero, *Institutes*, V.16, “to be carried toward one’s own advantages”; but this is less appropriate here. I would prefer, closer to the manuscript letters, “he could not be bent toward peace.” BUN.

“Stingy.” Eusebius proves by many examples that Licinius was greedy, *Life of Constantine*, I.55. Fragment on Constantius Chlorus, p. 474: “Licinius raged in crime, greed, cruelty, and lust.” BALUZ.

“Army.” In the manuscript, accusative “army.”

“They were able.” Lactantius likes this verb, and I recall reading it in many places in his works: above, chapter 18, near the beginning, “might be able”; *Divine Institutes*, II.5, “were able to understand”; V.10, near the middle, “he may not have been able to restrain wrath”; V.22, “if they should not have been able to accomplish this”; VI.2, “cannot behold.” Likewise VII.7 and *On the Workmanship [of God]*, 4. But the manuscript wrongly has “they rested.” 

“Was mowing down.” The manuscript has “was being feared.” But “was mowing down” must be read. Thus Silius Italicus, IV.464:

> Sheltered by a heavenly shield,  
> he mows down the ranks and strikes them down, etc.

Thus Lactantius himself, *Institutes*, VII.15: “Then destruction will range over the world, mowing down everything.” CELLAR. — “Was mowing down.” Thus it has rightly been corrected from the manuscript’s erroneous “was being feared.” I explained *metere* in this sense at *Institutes*, VII.15. BUN.

“To a devoted death.” Here a *devoted death* is a destined death, as in Virgil, *Aeneid*, I.716 … in French, “to a voluntary death.” MAUCROIX. — That is, to a voluntary death, with the sense felicitously explained. BAULDRI.

“God most high subjected [them].” The Martyrdom of St Basil, bishop of Amasea: “Licinius therefore, aided by the almighty hand of our Lord Jesus Christ, won victory over Maximinus.” BALUZ.

[Col. 0266D]

“Thought.” Read rather “had thought,” following HEUMANN.

“Having put on a slave’s garment.” Eusebius confirms this account, *Ecclesiastical History*, IX.10, and *Life of Constantine*, I.58. BALUZ.

“He crossed the strait.” That is, the Thracian Bosporus, sailing from Europe to Asia.

“But in the army.” With Tollius I read *at*, “but,” for the manuscript’s *ac*, “and,” which has also just occurred. Almeloveen read, “and thus half the army was destroyed.”

“But one part.” Add “the other.” — “But one part.” Heumann corrects “the other part”; I change nothing, but supply from the foregoing “but the other half.” BUN.

“In one day.” After these words, scholars think the name of the station to which he had gone that day is missing, since on the following night he made for Nicomedia. Perhaps *Melantiada* is missing. — “In one night and one day … Nicomedia.” The name of the station from which he reached Nicomedia on the next night appears to be absent. Columbus thinks “fleeing,” or something similar, is required. CELL.

Maximinus wished to advance sooner. At dawn on the preceding day he drew up his battle line, so that on the following day he might celebrate his anniversary as victor.
