It is announced in the camp that Maximinus has moved. The soldiers take up arms and march out to meet him. Between them lay a barren, treeless plain, which they call the Serene [Plain]. Both battle lines were now in sight. Licinius’s men lay down their shields, unfasten their helmets, stretch their hands toward heaven, and, led by their commanders, say the prayer after the Emperor. The army about to perish hears the murmur of those praying. They, having said the prayer three times and now filled with courage, replace their helmets upon their heads and raise their shields. The emperors advance for a conference. Maximinus could not be brought to peace. For he despised Licinius and believed that he would be abandoned [Col. 0265B] by his soldiers, because Licinius was stingy in giving while he himself was lavish. He had therefore begun the war with the intention that, after receiving Licinius’s army without a battle, he should proceed immediately against Constantine with doubled forces.

XLVII. [Col. 0266A] So they draw nearer; trumpets sound; standards advance. Licinius’s men, charging, attack their opponents. But they, terrified, could neither draw their swords nor throw their missiles. Maximinus circles the battle line, now trying to win over Licinius’s soldiers with entreaties, now with gifts. He is heard nowhere. An attack is made upon him, and he flees back to his own men. His battle line was cut down without resistance, and so great a number of legions, so great a mass of soldiers, was mown down by a few. No one remembered his name, his courage, or his former rewards; as though they had come to a death doomed in advance, not to battle, so God most high delivered them up to be slaughtered by their enemies. An immense multitude already lay fallen. Maximinus sees that events are turning out differently from what he had thought. He throws away the purple and, putting on a slave’s garment, flees and crosses the strait. But in the army one half was destroyed; the other either surrendered or fled. For the emperor’s desertion had removed the shame of deserting. But he reached Nicomedia on the Kalends of May—that is, after one night and one day, [Col. 0266B] and on another night.

The highest divinity. Nor does Lactantius use it otherwise in the *Divine Institutes*, book VII, chapter 26, in the Epilogue addressed to Emperor Constantine near the end: “May the providence of the highest divinity have raised you to the chief eminence.” And in book V, chapter 10: “Divinity, offended by the crime of wrongly religious men, smites them with grievous misfortune.” And above, “reverence for divinity.” Note that Lactantius uses *divinity* for God.—The highest divinity. Jupiter is not meant, as some suppose, but the supreme God. Compare Nurr., p. 371. Lactantius often writes thus: book IV, chapter 3, “Divinity which governs this world”; book V, chapter 10, “Divinity offended,” etc. BUN.

[Col. 0268D]

His customary favour. The manuscript: “his customary fervour.”

Dedication. That is, “your devotedness.” See, if you wish, Du Cange’s Latin Glossary. Eusebius has “Devotion.”—Dedication. Thus, instead of the other readings’ “your devotedness,” it should be restored from the manuscript. “*Dicatio*,” says Nurrius, “is a title of honour given to bishops and proconsuls.” BUN.

In letters issued to your office. Instead of “to your office,” Eusebius reads, “to your devotedness.”

“Seemed to concern the name of the Christians, now truly and simply each person.” The text should be supplied and corrected from Eusebius’s Greek, book X, chapter 5: “All the conditions concerning the name of the Christians which were contained therein, and which seemed altogether sinister and alien from our clemency, are to be removed; and now freely and simply each person.” See below the observation of the learned Paul Bauldri from the Utrecht edition.

For “now truly,” Eusebius has “freely”; the manuscript has “now beware.”

Any disturbance. The manuscript: “that disturbance.”

when the battlefield was one hundred and sixty miles away; and, having carried off his children and wife, together with a few companions from the palace, he made for the East. But in Cappadocia, having gathered soldiers from among the fugitives and from the East, he halted. Thus he resumed his imperial robe.

XLVIII. Licinius, however, having taken and distributed a portion of the army, crossed with his forces into Bithynia a few days after the battle. Entering Nicomedia, he gave thanks to God, by whose aid he had conquered; and on the Ides of June [13 June], when Constantine and he himself were each consul for the third time, he ordered the following letter, issued to the governor concerning the restoration of the Church, to be posted.

## LETTER OF LICINIUS

“When I, Constantine Augustus, and likewise I, Licinius Augustus, had met successfully at Milan, [Col. 0267B] and were considering all matters pertaining to public advantage and security, we judged among the measures that seemed likely to benefit many people that these matters, above all, ought to be arranged: [Col. 0268A] namely, those by which reverence for divinity was maintained. Thus we resolved to grant both Christians and all others free authority to follow whatever religion each person wished, so that the divinity dwelling in the heavenly seat might be appeased and favourable to us and to all who are established under our authority.

“Accordingly, we judged that this course should be undertaken with salutary deliberation and the most proper reasoning: that we should think no one at all ought to be denied the opportunity, whether he had committed his mind to the observance of the Christians or to that religion which he himself felt best suited to him; so that the highest divinity, whose worship we follow with untrammelled minds, might in all things extend to us its customary favour and goodwill.

“Therefore it is fitting that your Dedication should know that it has pleased us that, once [Col. 0268B] all conditions whatsoever which previously seemed to concern the name of the Christians in letters issued to your office have been removed, each and every one of those who hold to the same purpose of observing the Christian religion may, without any disturbance [Col. 0269A] [Note: [Col. 0269C] [Various Notes on columns 269–270]

Most fully. In the manuscript, “most full.”

The same. In the manuscript, “the same.”

Your Dedication. Eusebius: “your devotedness.”

“So that, in worshipping whatever each person has chosen.” Thus I read with the most learned Graevius, making a slight alteration. The manuscript has: “so that, in worshipping what each person might cherish, he may have free authority, who.”

“Because we do not wish anything to be taken away.” The manuscript has “who”; in its place I have put “because,” and supplied from Eusebius the two missing words, “we do not wish anything to be taken away.”

In the person. Heumann, following Eusebius, reads “to the person.”

The same. “Their,” according to Heumann.

“To which previously.” The manuscript: “to which q. previously.”

Were accustomed. Tollius reads “have become accustomed.”

Some persons. Thus I restored it from the manuscript. Eusebius has “if any persons, whether from our treasury.” All printed editions have “something.”

Be restored. Thus the manuscript. Earlier printed editions have “restore.”

[Col. 0269D]

Had been. Read “may have been,” from Eusebius’s Greek.

Had received as a gift. Thus the manuscript; [the printed editions have] “gave.”

If they should request. I am certain that Lactantius wrote this, following Eusebius—not “if they thought,” which is corruptly found in the manuscript and gives no sense. And shortly afterward Eusebius likewise has: *prosélthōsi tō epi topōn eparchō dikazonti*, “let them approach the prefect of the districts who administers justice.” Therefore here one must certainly read “let them apply to the Vicar,” with a capital V. The printed editions corruptly have “if they thought.”

Let them apply to the Vicar. That is, let them go to our Vicar, following the Greek of Eusebius. Others think the text should read: “if they request from our benevolence some equivalent, let them apply,” so that they too, etc. *Vicarium* means an item of equivalent value.—“Let them apply to the Vicar.” Diazius and Tollius understand *aliquid vicarium* as an equivalent thing, as compensation for restitution; the latter also reads “if they should desire” for “if they should think.” But Cuperus and Baluzius interpret *Vicarius* as the provincial Vicar, an office known from the imperial *Notitia*. CELL.

Whereby. In the manuscript, “co.”

[Col. 0270C]

To the body. That is, to the corporate association.

The same persons. Manuscript: “the same.”

Not only those places. Manuscript: “not in those places.”

They were accustomed. Manuscript: “they were accustomed”; as in note 7, “they had been accustomed.” HEUMANN.

“As we have set forth above.” Or, according to Eusebius’s Greek, “as has been set forth above.” HEUMANN.

The same. Manuscript: “the same.”

May restore. Manuscript: “restore.”

“In such great . . . matters.” That is, in so many matters. Eusebius: *en pollois*. BUN.

Conveyed. In the manuscript, *Plata*, meaning *perlata* (“conveyed”), not *prolata* (“published”), as in the printed editions; for *pro* in this manuscript is represented by p with a transverse stroke beneath the letter.

To bring . . . to knowledge. Pliny, book X, letter 15: “I did not think that these things should not be brought to your notice.” Cyprian, book I, letter 3: “Things to be brought to your notice.” BUN. [Col. 0270D] He exhorted. Licinius. “Is” is absent from the manuscript.

In. Absent from the manuscript.

Ten years, etc. That is, from the Kalends, or 1 March, of the year 303 to 13 June 313. Thus there were ten years, three months, and thirteen days.

“Then Licinius, etc. . . . breaking through.” Heumann reads these four lines thus: “Then Licinius, pursuing with his army, the tyrant Maximinus fled and withdrew, and again sought the narrow passes of Mount Taurus; fortifications and towers having been built there, he attempted to block the road. But as the victors broke through on every side, everything, etc.” From the words “then to the right” Heumann accordingly makes “on every side,” an expression Lactantius used above, no. 34, at the end.

The tyrant. Maximinus.

Withdrew. That is, yielded the ground, or made room for him by departing.

Sought. Correctly so. The manuscript has “seeks,” incorrectly.

Fortifications. In the manuscript, “monuments.”]

and inconvenience, strive to observe that religion. We judged that these matters should be communicated to your diligence most fully, so that you might know that we have granted these same Christians free and unrestricted authority to practise their religion.

“Since you perceive that this has been granted to them by us, your Dedication understands that an equally open and free opportunity of practising their own religion or observance has also been granted to others, for the peace of our times; so that in worshipping whatever each person has chosen, he may have free authority, because we do not wish anything to be taken away by us from the honour due to any person or any religion.

“Further, we have judged that the following provision should be made with respect to the Christians: if the same places in which they had formerly been accustomed to assemble—the places concerning which a fixed form had also previously been set forth in letters issued to your office—appear to have been bought in the former [Col. 0269B] period by certain persons, whether from our treasury or from any other person whatever, they are to be restored to the Christians without payment and without any demand for compensation, all evasion and ambiguity set aside. Those also who received them as gifts shall likewise restore them to these same Christians as soon as possible. And if either those who bought them or those who received them as gifts request something from our benevolence, let them apply to the Vicar, so that provision may be made for them too through our clemency.

“All these things must immediately be delivered to the corporate body of the Christians through your intervention and without delay. And since the same Christians are known to have possessed not only those places in which they were accustomed to assemble but also other things [Col. 0269C] belonging to the legal right of their corporate body—that is, of the churches, [Col. 0270A] not of individual persons—you shall order all these things, under the rule which we have set forth above, to be restored to these same Christians, that is, to their corporate body and congregations, without any ambiguity or controversy whatever; while the principle stated above is to be maintained, namely, that those who restore the same things without payment, as we have said, may expect indemnification from our benevolence.

“In all these matters you must provide your most effective intervention on behalf of the aforesaid corporate body of the Christians, so that our command may be fulfilled as soon as possible, and so that public tranquillity may thereby also be provided for through our clemency. Thus it shall come about that, as has been set forth above, the divine favour toward us—which we have experienced in such great matters—may continue throughout all time to bring prosperous success to our undertakings, together with the blessedness of our public welfare.

“Moreover, so that the form of this ordinance of our benevolence may reach the knowledge of all, you should arrange for these written provisions, conveyed by means of your proclamation, to be posted everywhere and brought to everyone’s knowledge, so that this ordinance of our benevolence cannot remain unknown.”

After this letter had been posted, he also exhorted them verbally to restore the meeting places to their former condition. Thus, from the destruction of the Church to its restoration, there were ten years and approximately four months.

XLIX. Then, as Licinius pursued the tyrant with his army, the latter fled and withdrew; and again he sought the narrow passes of Mount Taurus. [Col. 0270C] Having constructed fortifications and towers there, [Col. 0271A] [Note: [Col. 0271B] [Various Notes on columns 271–272]

To block the road. Naturally, against Licinius.

To the right. Manuscript: “to the left.”

There. In the manuscript, “Here,” incorrectly.

Would be sought. I believe Lactantius wrote this, as does the most learned Graevius. Nor does the blank space in the manuscript permit a longer word: scarcely five or six letters occur after the initial p, and not without abbreviation, so that it would have been written *petetur* in place of *peteretur*.

“First he stuffed himself with food and gorged himself with wine, as those persons are accustomed to do,” etc. Examples occur in Florus, book II, chapters 18, 4, 2, and 12. Of remarkable relevance here is another passage of Lactantius, *On the Blessed Life*, book VII, at the end: “As each person sees, with advancing years, that he is approaching the day on which he must depart from this life, let him consider how pure he leaves, how innocent he comes before the judge; not as some do, relying upon blinded minds, who, now that the body’s strength is failing, are reminded by this final necessity only to devote themselves more greedily and ardently to the indulgence of lusts.”

And so. That is, then.

He swallowed poison. Thus he did not die a simple death, as the Epitome of Victor reports.

Driven back. The manuscript has “driven back [masculine],” incorrectly.

For the present. That is, at that present time.

Changed. In the manuscript, “changed [masculine].”

“By whose force, as his vital organs raged.” The manuscript has *furens* (“raging”); but this is, I think, an error of the copyist for *furerent* (“raged”). The printed editions have: “by whose force, as his vital organs burned”: perhaps this too is satisfactory. We alter nothing beyond what we can; and whatever can be achieved by a slight change, we choose in preference, provided that the best sense is obtained. “His vital organs raged under the force of the disease” may correctly be said, that is, they were scorched by the force of the illness.

Unbearable. Learned men admit that they do not know who before our author spoke in this way. Lactantius himself is the one who says in the *Divine Institutes*, book VII, chapter 16: “he will harass the world by unbearable tyranny.” *Insustentabilis* means intolerable. Who would not persuade himself that Lactantius was the author of this work too?—“Unbearable pain.” I also find this expression in the Vulgate version, Prayer of Manasseh, attached to book II of Chronicles, chapter XXXVI: “For the magnificence of your glory is unendurable, and the wrath of your threatening is unbearable.” BUN.

Driven by madness. Thus we have emended it, whereas the old manuscript reads “struck by madness.” Lactantius, *Institutes*, book I, chapter 9: “Driven by frenzy and madness, he killed his wife together with his children.” BALUZ.

Earth scooped up with his hands. That is, dug up. Caesar, *Gallic War*, book V, chapter 42: “They were compelled to remove the earth with their hands and cloaks.” Statius, *Thebaid*, book III, verse 50: “and sand scooped up,” that is, taken. See the Scholiast and Barth, p. 685. BUN.

He dashed his head against the walls. This is one of the “abominable,” as Cicero calls them in the third *Tusculan Disputation*, kinds [Col. 0272B] of mourning. See Casaubon’s notes on Julius Capitolinus.

His eyes sprang from their sockets. Eusebius says the same in *Ecclesiastical History*, book IX, chapter 10, and *Life of Constantine*, book I, chapter 59; likewise Eutychius, Theophanes, and Anastasius. St John Chrysostom also mentions it in his Oration on St Babylas, and St Jerome on Zechariah, as we shall see in note I on chapter 50. BALUZ.

White-robed attendants. That is, God surrounded by white-robed attendants, or his angels. See Paul Bauldri on this passage.

He confessed. Add: “that he had done it.”

Weeping. Heumann: “imploring.”

“He breathed out his guilty spirit in an abominable manner of death.” Maximinus died in the year in which peace was granted to the Church, the same year in which Lactantius brought this work to an end; and the persecution began in 303, at the end of February. It is therefore clearer than daylight that Maximinus was extinguished in 313, the tenth year from the beginning of the persecution. BALUZ.

He defeated the persecutors. Lactantius, *Institutes*, book VII, chapter 26: “For those who wished, in order to defend impious religions, to abolish the worship of the heavenly and unique God, lie defeated.” Eusebius makes the same observation in *Life of Constantine*, book I, chapter 3; so do the author of the *Fragment on Constantius Chlorus*, p. 475, and Jerome on Zechariah 14. Consult Baluzius, if you wish.

Stock. Manuscript: “of stock.”

Root. In the manuscript, “radis.”

Valerius, whom. Thus the manuscript: namely, Valerius Valens, of whom Pagius speaks as follows at no. 15 under the year 306. “At the same time when Alexander, who held the office of Praetorian Prefect of Africa, was made emperor at Carthage, Valens was created emperor,” says Victor in the *Epitome*; after recounting Maximinus’s death, he adds: “Valens was put to death by Licinius.” Lactantius speaks of this Valens in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 50, as the most learned Abbot Louis Du Four de Longuerue first observed in letters written to Pagius. There Lactantius says of Maximinus’s death: “Licinius, having gained supreme power, first ordered Valerius to be killed, whom Maximinus, in anger, had not dared to kill even after his flight, when he saw that he himself must perish.” Nor can it be doubted that this Valerius is the same as the Valens mentioned by Victor, since Goltz, among the coins of the Thirty Tyrants who afflicted the Roman commonwealth during Gallienus’s reign, records this one: “ΑΥΤ. Κ. ΠΟΥ. ΟΥΑΛΕΡ. ΟΥΑΛΕΝΣ. ΣΕΒ. L. A.” That is: “Emperor Caesar Publius Valerius Valens Augustus, year one.” PAGIUS.—Yet Baluzius, on reconsideration, reads with the learned Cuperus and other critics: “Valeria, whom.”—Bunemannus agrees with this.

In anger. Namely because she had refused him marriage, if one reads “Valeria” above.]

he attempted to block the road; but as the victors broke through everything on every side, he finally fled to Tarsus. There, since he was now pursued by land and sea and hoped for no refuge, in anguish and fear he had recourse to death as though to a remedy for the evils which God had heaped upon his head. But first he stuffed himself with food and gorged himself with wine, as those who think that they are doing this for the last time are accustomed to do. Then he swallowed poison.

Its force, driven back by his full stomach, could not prevail at once, but changed into a grievous wasting illness resembling pestilence, so that, with his breath prolonged, he might suffer torments for a longer time. The poison had now begun to rage within him; and by its force, as his vital organs raged, he was carried by unbearable pain to madness of mind. Thus for four days, driven by insanity, he devoured the earth scooped up with his hands [Col. 0271B] as though hungry. Then, [Col. 0272A] after many severe torments, while he dashed his head against the walls, his eyes sprang from their sockets. At last, having lost his sight, he began to see God judging him, surrounded by white-robed attendants. He cried out, therefore, as those under torture are accustomed to cry; and he said that it was not he but others who had done it. Then, as though compelled by tortures, he confessed, repeatedly beseeching Christ and weeping that He would have mercy on him. Thus, amid groans such as he uttered as though being burned alive, he breathed out his guilty spirit in an abominable manner of death.

L. In this way God defeated all the persecutors of His name, so that neither stock nor root of theirs remained. For Licinius, having gained supreme power, first ordered Valerius put to death—Valerius whom Maximinus, in anger, had not dared to kill even after [Col. 0273A] [Note: [Col. 0273C] [Various Notes on columns 273–274]

Likewise Candidianus. Manuscript: “the same Candidianus.”

“But the woman, when she learned that he was alive.” Thus the manuscript. See Columbus and Paul Bauldri. “The woman” means Valeria.

Who because. The manuscript omits “who.”

End. That is, death.

Besides Valeria. Manuscript: “before Valeria.”

Willing. The most learned Cuperus considers that “unwilling” should be read. Manuscript: “willing.”—Cuperus is followed by Bunemannus, who presents the following reading: “She, unwilling, [to yield] to Licinius.” Manuscript: “she, willing, to Licinius.” Not badly, in Nurrius’s judgment, p. 272, deriving this sense: Licinius wished to seize all the inheritances of Galerius, and Valeria consequently fled from him at once in order to seek safer refuge with Maximinus, who had a wife. BUNEMANN.

Over all. Manuscript: “over all things.”

The son of Maximinus, then eldest. The manuscript has “his own” for “then”; add “by birth” to “eldest.”

Their mother. The wife of Maximinus, whose name is unknown.

She was cast into the Orontes. Thus the manuscript. Most have conjectured that “into the Orontes” ought to be restored, since it is established that a river is meant here; the most distinguished Cuperus has indeed demonstrated this learnedly with many arguments. But because he himself reports that some ancients called the river which the rest commonly call the Orontes “the East” (*Oriens*), I did not wish to alter the text.

Is. Absent from the manuscript.

There she often. Thus the manuscript, not “he.”

In plebeian dress. That is, in plebeian clothing. With her mother. Namely Prisca, Diocletian’s wife.

Those women. Manuscript: “there.”

Thus their chastity and status caused their destruction. The manuscript has “to their status,” incorrectly. It caused their destruction because Valeria refused to marry either Licinius or Maximinus. TOLLIUS.—Accordingly, even in that age it was regarded as part of chastity, for instance for women, to have been the wife of one man only. For it is well known from Tertullian’s treatise *On Monogamy* that in his own time he and the Montanists required monogamy in both sexes. It should meanwhile be observed that the rank which our author mentions here applies equally to mother and daughter—that is, to Prisca and Valeria; but the added mention of chastity pertains especially to Valeria. BAULDRI.—I wonder that Lactantius did not say that the sacrifices by which, at the compulsion of her father Diocletian, she had been defiled, although a Christian, chapter 15, caused Valeria’s destruction. TOINARD.

“According to faith—for I speak to one who knows.” The manuscript has near the end: “according to the end, for I speak to one who knows,” etc. The printed editions have “I speak according to the faith of those who know,” etc., but wrongly. I think nothing should be altered except *finem* (“end”), in whose place we write *fidem* (“faith”). “For I speak to one who knows” is enclosed in parentheses. Here our author addresses Donatus near the end of the book, as he did at the beginning; and the discourse thus proceeds correctly. For Donatus himself had shared in the persecution, since the persecutors had raged against him for several years. I am therefore surprised that this reading, so easy and so ready to hand, was not detected by earlier editors of this book.

Might perish. Manuscript: “to perish.”

[Col. 0274D]

Should corrupt the truth. The manuscript has “not” prefixed, wrongly.

Sins. Manuscript: “look.”

Against. Manuscript: “opposed.”

Eternal. Heumann reads “paternal.”

Mercy. Manuscript: “of mercy.” *Pietas* means kindness, clemency.

Evil beasts. The tyrants, persecutors of Christians, of whom above in the note to chapter 2 of this book: “and evil beasts.” “And” is absent from the manuscript.

Magnificent. Manuscript: “magnificence,” corruptly.

Became contemptible. From *vilesco*. The manuscript has “flourished,” but less well.

Them. Manuscript: “it.”

Let us celebrate. This word occurs twice in the manuscript; therefore we write it twice, and in that place it contributes considerably to the elegance.]

his flight, when he saw that he must perish. He also ordered Candidianus to be killed, whom Valeria had adopted, though born of a concubine, because of her barrenness.

But when the woman learned that he was alive, she changed her dress and mingled with his retinue, in order to discover Candidianus’s fate. Since he had presented himself at Nicomedia and appeared to be held in honour, fearing nothing of the kind, he was killed. When she heard of his death, she immediately fled.

Likewise he put to death by capital sentence Severianus, the son of Severus, now a vigorous adult, who had followed Maximinus from the battle line during his flight, on the ground that after Maximinus’s death he had contemplated assuming the purple. All of these had long preferred to be with Maximinus, as though fearing Licinius as an evil, except Valeria; for she had been willing to yield to Licinius her legal claim [Col. 0273B] to all the inheritances of Maximian, but had refused the same to Maximinus.

He also destroyed Maximinus’s son, then the eldest, eight years old, and his seven-year-old daughter, who had been betrothed to Candidianus. But first their mother was cast into the East [i.e. the Orontes; the reading is uncertain]. There she had often ordered chaste women to be drowned. Thus all the impious received, by God’s true and just judgment, the very things that they had done.

LI. Valeria too, having wandered in plebeian dress through various provinces for fifteen months, was finally recognized at Thessalonica and arrested with her mother [Col. 0274A] for punishment. The women were therefore led to execution amid a great spectacle and compassion for so great a reversal of fortune; their heads were cut off, and their bodies cast into the sea. Thus their chastity and rank caused their destruction.

LII. I believed that all these things, according to truth—for I speak to one who knows—should be committed to writing just as they occurred, lest either the memory of such great events should perish or, should anyone wish to write the history, he should corrupt the truth by keeping silent either about their sins against God or about God’s judgment against them.

We ought to give thanks to His eternal mercy, because at last He looked upon the earth and deemed it worthy to restore and gather together again His flock, partly ravaged by ravening wolves and partly scattered, and to root out the evil beasts which had trampled the pastures and destroyed the resting places of the divine [Col. 0274B] flock. Where now are those magnificent and famous surnames of the Jovians and Herculians among the nations, names first arrogantly assumed by Diocletian and Maximian and afterward transferred to their successors, but which have become contemptible? Assuredly, the Lord has destroyed them and erased them from the earth.

Let us therefore celebrate God’s triumph with exultation; let us honour the Lord’s victory with praises; let us celebrate it with prayers by day and night—let us celebrate it so that He may confirm forever the peace granted to His people after ten years. You especially, dearest Donatus, who deserve to be heard by God, beseech the Lord that [Col. 0275A] [Note: [Col. 0275A] [Various Notes on columns 275–276]

Eternal. Thus I read with the learned Boherellus and other learned men, instead of “and so,” which is in the manuscript. Perhaps “and indeed” was first written, which in abbreviated letters is *aeternam*.

“So that he may guard the flourishing churches in perpetual peace.” Thus I read this passage as Baluzius himself corrected it in the index of errors to his edition, and as others have read after him. The manuscript has, corruptly: “so that he may guard the flourishing Church in perpetual peace”; or, with Heinsius and Graevius, one could correctly read: “so that he may guard the perpetual peace of the flourishing Church.”]

He may preserve His eternal mercy, favourable and gentle, for His servants; that He may ward off from His people every snare and assault [Col. 0276A] of the devil; that He may guard the flourishing churches in perpetual peace.

[Col. 0275]

# FRAGMENTS OF LACTANTIUS FIRMIANUS

[Note: [Col. 0275C]

The fragment “On the Last Judgment” (“No one either denies or doubts . . . that these things are to come”), which Stephen Baluzius found appended to book VII of the *Institutes* in Colbert manuscript 1095 and attributed to Lactantius, is Augustine’s, *City of God*, XX.30. It is also read in some other manuscripts under Augustine’s name, and a certain pious man appended it so that the reader might beware of Lactantius’s errors concerning the millennial kingdom.

I further cite the following testimonies of Damasus and Jerome concerning Lactantius’s lost letters: “I confess to you that I do not readily read the books of Lactantius which you gave me some time ago, both because very many of his letters run to a length of as many as a thousand lines and because they seldom argue about our doctrine. Thus their length produces weariness in the reader; and whatever is brief in them is more suited to schoolmen than to us, discussing metres, the situation of regions, and philosophers” (or: “persons discussing”). (Damasus, letter to Jerome XXXV, *Works of Jerome*, ed. Vallarsi, I.1, p. 159.)

“Many, through ignorance of the Scriptures—as Firmianus does in the eighth [Vallarsi emends: second] book of his letters to Demetrianus—assert that the Holy Spirit is often called the Father and often the Son; and, though we plainly believe in the Trinity, they remove the third person, wishing his existence to be not a substance but a name.” (Jerome, Commentary on Galatians 4:6; add his letter to Pammachius and Oceanus, LXXXIV, ed. Vallarsi I.1, p. 528; *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 80: “we have . . . two books of letters to Demetrianus, his pupil.”) O. F. FRITZSCHE.]

(C)

I. Fear, love, joy, sorrow, desire, longing, anger, compassion, jealousy, wonder—these movements or affections of the soul were created by the Lord at the beginning of humankind and beneficially and healthfully implanted in human nature, so that by governing himself through them in an orderly and rational manner, a human being might be able to exercise good virtues by acting courageously, and through these might justly deserve to receive perpetual life from the Lord. For these motions of the soul, confined within their proper bounds—that is, situated on the good side—produce good virtues in the present and eternal rewards in the future; but when they overflow their limits—that is, incline toward the evil side—they become vices and iniquities and bring forth eternal punishments. V. Muratori, *Antiquities of the Italian Middle Ages*, III, p. 849.

II. “In our own time Lactantius also [wrote] concerning metres: ‘the pentameter,’ he says, ‘and the tetrameter.’” Marius Victorinus, *On Heroic Verse*, chapter 5, p. 1957, Putsch. (Cf. Jerome, *Catalogue*, chapter 80: “we also have another book entitled *The Grammarian*.”)

III. Firmianus says as follows to Probus concerning the metres of comedies:

> “For as to what you asked about the metres of comedies, I know that many people think that especially the plays of Terence have no metre—the Greek comedy, that is, of Menander, Philemon, and Diphilus, being composed of trimeter verses. Our ancient writers of comedy, however, in setting plays to rhythm preferred to follow Eupolis, Cratinus, and Aristophanes, as has been stated.”

Let those who maintain that there is metre—that is, *metron* (μέτρον)—in the plays of Terence, Plautus, and the other comic and tragic poets be Cicero, Scaurus, and Firmianus. Rufinus the grammarian, *On Comic Metres*, p. 2712 ff., Putsch.

IV. We shall set forth the words which our Lactantius expressed in the third volume to Probus concerning his view of this people:

> “The Gauls were anciently called Galatae from the whiteness of their bodies; and the Sibyl calls them so. The poet wished to signify this when he said, ‘Then milky necks are encircled with gold’ (*Aeneid* VIII.660–61), though he might have said ‘white.’ Hence comes the province of Galatia, into which Gauls once came and mingled with Greeks. Therefore that region was first called Gallo-Greece, afterward Galatia. Nor is it surprising if he should have said this of the Galatians, and related that western peoples, passing over such vast stretches in the middle of the lands, settled in the region of the East.”

—Jerome, Commentary on Galatians, book II, *Works*, ed. Vallarsi VII.1, p. 426. (Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 80: “we have four books of letters to Probus.”)

[Col. 0277]

# THE PHOENIX ATTRIBUTED TO LACTANTIUS, BY AN UNKNOWN AUTHOR

[Note: [Col. 0277C] [Annotations on columns 277–278]

By an unknown author. I have found these poems, which in printed books are attributed to Lactantius, in no ancient manuscripts. We nevertheless read them in a Saint-Germain manuscript, though it is not ancient. The poems on the Phoenix are not believed to be Lactantius’s; they are at least by a Christian, although written by some highly elegant poet, whom I nevertheless certainly believe not to have been a Christian. For he calls the Phoenix a priest of the Sun; and he speaks of that grove and Phoebus as though Phoebus were truly a god, possessed that grove as especially dear to him, and had it dedicated to himself. The poems on the Resurrection, or Easter, cannot be compared in elegance with those on the Phoenix; moreover, the poems themselves plainly show that their author was not the same. I found the latter among the minor works of Venantius Fortunatus, a Christian poet, in the Vatican Library, having been alerted by the excellent and learned Antonio Girona; I shall later make some observations on them. Nowhere could I find any trace of that third poem, *On the Passion of the Lord*; but not many errors occur in it, and consequently much effort of correction was not necessary. THOMAS. Erasmus judges that the poems on the Phoenix are not inelegant, but no one can affirm that they are Lactantius’s, since Jerome does not mention them when treating of our author’s works. Nicolaus Heinsius recognizes and extols in them a genuine offspring of Lactantius.

Phoenix. This entire story of the Phoenix must be counted among fables. Nevertheless, we did not wish to omit it, lest anything be lacking from our edition; and we collated these poems with the Saint-Germain manuscript.

Verse 1. “In the first, distant East.” That is, in Arabia, where they tell tales that the Phoenix dwells. Many, however, say that the Phoenix has its home among the Indians; on this question see Ausonius and Claudian.

Verse 2. “Where lies open.” Read Ovid, at the beginning of book II of the *Metamorphoses*, for an exceedingly elegant description of the Sun’s palace.

In the same place. “The greatest gate of the eternal heaven.” Thus the Saint-Germain manuscript. The printed editions have “the lofty portal of heaven,” but this seems less good because “lofty ridges” occurs in verse 7.

Verse 4. “But where.” In the Saint-Germain manuscript, “in which.”

[Col. 0278C] Verse 6. “No hill rises, nor does a hollow valley gape.” Therefore all is level and the site offers no opportunity for deceit. For according to Virgil, *Aeneid* II:

> There is a valley, with winding bend, suited to deceit.

Verse 9. “Stands.” Thus Nicolaus Heinsius and Heumann read. Other printed editions read “and.”

Verse 10. “Flourishing in the splendour of perpetual foliage.” Because leaves are the ornament and beauty of a tree. The Saint-Germain manuscript and the editions of 1472, 1478, 1497, and others read *virens* (“flourishing”); the common printed editions read *viret* (“flourishes”).

Verse 11. “Phaethonian.” For this myth see Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book II.

Verse 14. “It rose above the waters.” This is false if understood of the universal Flood, which rose above even the highest mountains. The reference, however, is solely to Deucalion’s flood, which was not universal.

Verse 15. “Hither.” Thus the Aldine edition; but the editions of 1472, 1478, 1497, and 1513 read “this.”

In the same place. “Bloodless diseases.” A common epithet for diseases. Thus Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book XV:

> And pale bodies were squalid with bloodless disease.

Verse 18. “Or Mars,” etc. The Saint-Germain manuscript reads:

> Or fear, or ardent frenzy yields to love,

and this is less good, for the poet has just spoken of fear.

Verse 22. “Frost covers the earth with chilly dew.” On the distinction between dew and frost, see Aristotle, *Meteorology*, book I, chapter 10.

Verse 25. “But there is a spring,” etc. This spring is distinguished by many names: it is living, clear, gentle, and sweet.

Verse 27. *Mensum*, for *mensium*: “of months.”

Verse 31. “The only one.” Thus of the Phoenix; hence the proverb, “Rarer than a Phoenix.”

Verse 32. “But it lives renewed by its death.” On this see below, Riddle XXXI, where it says of the Phoenix: “Death is life to me,” etc. On the Phoenix’s resurrection see Ovid’s *Metamorphoses* and Tzetzes, *Various History*.

Verse 33. “It obeys Phoebus.” Antiquity believed that birds, like trees, were consecrated to gods: thus the eagle to Jupiter, the dove to Venus, and so the Phoenix to Phoebus.]

(C, G, S)

[Col. 0277A] There is a blessed place in the farthest eastern region,

Where the greatest gate of the eternal heaven lies open;

Yet it is not close to the summer or winter risings,

But where the Sun pours forth the day from his vernal course.

[5] There a plain extends in open reaches;

No hill rises, nor does a hollow valley gape.

But that place towers above our mountains,

Whose lofty ridges are thought high, by twice six cubits.

Here is the Sun’s grove: a sacred wood, planted thick with many trees,

[10] Flourishes in the splendour of perpetual foliage.

When the sky had blazed with Phaethonian fires,

That place remained unharmed by flames.

And when the flood had drowned the world beneath its waves,

It rose above Deucalion’s waters.

[15] No bloodless diseases come hither, nor afflicted old age,

[Col. 0277B] Nor cruel death, nor harsh fear;

Nor unspeakable crime, nor the mad desire for wealth,

Nor Mars, nor frenzy burning with the love of slaughter.

Bitter grief is absent, and poverty clothed in rags,

[20] and sleepless cares, and violent hunger.

[Col. 0278A] There is no storm there, nor does the dreadful force of the wind rage;

nor does frost cover the earth with chilling dew.

No cloud spreads its fleeces over the fields;

nor does troubled water fall from on high.

[25] But in the middle there is a spring, called “living” by name,

clear, gentle, abundant in sweet waters.

Bursting forth once in each month’s cycle,

it waters the entire grove twelve times with its streams.

Here a race of trees rises with lofty trunk,

[30] bearing mild fruit that will not fall to the ground.

This woodland, these groves, are inhabited by the one bird, the Phoenix:

one, yet renewed by its own death it lives.

It obeys Phoebus, a servant worthy of remembrance:

mother Nature granted it this office,

[35] [Col. 0278B] when first the rising yellow dawn turns red,

when first it puts the stars to flight with rosy light:

three and four times it dips its pious body into the waters;

three and four times it sips water from the living pool.

It rises and settles on the summit

[Col. 0279A] [Note: [Col. 0279B] **Notes to columns 279–280**

**Verse 40.** *Despicit.* Because, in a certain sense, the other trees are lower than this one.

**Verse 44.** *Aura levis.* Thus Ovid:

> *Et levis impulsos retro dabat aura capillos.*  
> “And the light breeze blew back her wind-tossed hair.”

**Verse 46.** *Movere.* Thus the Sangerman manuscript. The printed editions have *ciere*. The manuscripts nevertheless vary. Heinsius thinks that *fovere* should be read.

**Verse 47.** *Quam nec Aedoniae.* The passage is corrupt. The Sangerman manuscript has *Idoneae*; the printed editions read *Julaeae*. Yet, following Gallaeus, Frideric, Gronovius and Heinsius emended it to *Aedoniae*.

**Verse 48.** *Cyrrhaeis.* That is, in Castalian musical modes, or those of the Muses and Apollo; for Cyrrha is a town at the foot of Mount Parnassus.

**Verse 50.** *Cyllenaeae.* As though he said “Mercurial,” because Mercury was born on Cyllene. Hence Claudian, in Book I of *The Rape of Proserpina*, himself calls Mercury *Cyllenius*.

**Verse 51.** *Postquam Phoebus equos, etc.* That is, after the sun has risen above the horizon. On the story of Phaethon, see Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*.

**Verses 53–58.** *Illa ter alarum*, etc., up to *Antistes nemorum*. The Sangerman manuscript reads these four verses as follows:

> *Illa ter alarum repetito verbere plaudit,*  
> “Three times she claps her wings with repeated beating,”  
>
> *Igniferumque caput ter venerata, silet.*  
> “And, having three times venerated her fire-bearing head, she falls silent.”  
>
> *Atque eadem celeres etiam discriminat horas*  
> “And by the same sounds she also distinguishes the swiftly passing hours,”  
>
> *Non errabilibus nocte dieque sonis.*  
> “With notes that do not stray, by night and by day.”

But, as I think, this is less satisfactory. *Celeres horas*—for Ovid makes the hours companions of the sun.

**Verse 59.** *Jam mille peregerit annos.* Claudian likewise extends the Phoenix’s life to a thousand years; Pliny, however, limits it to 660, although he considers the whole matter fabulous. Others assign it an even shorter span.

**Verse 61.** *Lapsum fatis.* We have emended this with Gallaeus and from the Sangerman manuscript. The printed editions had *lassum spatiis*, but that gives no sense.

**Verse 66.** *Venus.* Thus Heumann read it. She was worshipped in Syria Phoenicia. The printed editions have *vetus*.

**Verse 69.** *Sublimem Palmam.* Pliny counts this tree among those produced by Syria, namely in Book XIII, chapter 4.

**Verse 71.** *Et qua nulla nocens animans, etc.* This is how the Sangerman manuscript reads. The ordinary printed editions have:

> *Quam nec dente nocens animal perrumpere possit.*  
> “Which no harmful creature could pierce with its tooth.”

Heumann, however, has:

> *In quam nulla nocens animans perrumpere possit.*  
> “Into which no harmful creature could pierce,”

following the editions of 1472, 1478, 1513, and 1515; this agrees with our reading.

**Verse 74.** *Flabris.* That is, “with blasts” or “with winds.”

**Same passage.** *Purpureum aera.* Perhaps he means the morning hours, which we call dawn.

**Verse 75.** *Noto.* This wind gathers clouds. Yet Pliny calls it sultry.

**Same passage.** *Per inania coeli.* That is, through the middle region of the air.

**Verse 77.** *Sepulcrum.* On the tomb that the Phoenix builds for itself, see Claudian’s *Epigram on the Phoenix*, in these words:

> *Arentes tepidis de collibus eligit herbas,*  
> “It chooses dry herbs from the warm hills,”  
>
> *Et cumulum texens pretiosa fronde Sabaeum,*  
> “And, covering the mound with precious Sabæan foliage,”  
>
> *Componit, bustumque sibi partumque futurum.*  
> “It constructs both a funeral pyre and its future offspring for itself.”

**Verse 80.** *Opulentus Arabs.* Thus Horace speaks of the Arabs:

> *Otia divitiis Arabum liberrima cantat.*  
> “He sings of leisure freer than the riches of the Arabs.”

Understand this, however, as referring to Arabia Felix.

**Verse 81.** *Pygmeae gentes.* Some of the ancients place these peoples in India, others beyond Arabia; but the stories told about this people are fabulous.

**Verse 82.** *Terra Sabea sinu.* Thus Virgil, in Book I of the *Georgics*:

> *India mittit ebur, molles sua thura Sabaei.*  
> “India sends ivory; the gentle Sabaeans send their fragrant incense.”

**Verse 83.** *Cinnama.* The Sangerman manuscript reads this verse as follows:

> *Cinnamum hic avisque procul spirantis amomi.*  
> “Here are cinnamon and the far-off breath of fragrant amomum.”

**Verse 85.** *Casiae mitis.* The cassia of the ancients is not the same as that of more recent writers.

[40] of a tall tree, which alone looks down upon the whole grove;

and, turned toward the new risings of newborn Phoebus,

it awaits the rays and the emerging radiance.

But when the sun has struck the thresholds of the shining gate,

and the light breeze of the first light has flashed forth,

[45] it begins to pour forth the melodies of its sacred song

and to stir the new day with a wondrous voice—

a voice which neither the songs of Aedonian birds nor the musical pipe

could equal in the Castalian modes of Cyrrha;

nor, it is thought, can the dying swan imitate it,

[50] nor the tuneful strings of the Cyllenian lyre.

After Phoebus has sent back his horses across the open heaven

and, proceeding, has led forth the whole circuit of the world,

three times it claps its wings with repeated beat,

with sounds unerring by night and day.

[55] [Col. 0279B] It also distinguishes the swift hours;

and, having thrice worshipped its fire-bearing head, falls silent—

priestess of the groves and venerable priestess of the sacred wood,

Phoebus, alone privy to your mysteries.

When it has now completed a thousand years of life

[60] and long time has made it heavy,

to renew the lifetime exhausted under the pressure of fate,

it abandons the sweet bed of its accustomed grove.

And when, eager to be reborn, it has left the holy places,

then it seeks this world, where death holds dominion.

[65] [Col. 0280A] Long-lived, it directs its swift flight toward Syria,

to which Venus herself gave the name Phoenicia;

and through trackless wilderness it seeks secluded groves,

where a remote forest lies hidden among the woodland glades.

Then it chooses a palm lofty in its airy crown,

[70] which has the pleasing name “phoenix” from the bird;

and which no harmful creature can penetrate—

no slippery serpent, nor any predatory bird.

Then Aeolus shuts the winds in their hanging caves,

lest they violate the purple air with their blasts,

[75] or lest clouds gathered by the South Wind drive away,

through the voids of heaven, the sun’s rays and harm the bird.

It then builds for itself either a nest or a tomb;

for it dies in order to live, yet itself creates itself.

Then it gathers juices and scents from the rich forest,

[80] [Col. 0280B] which the Assyrian gathers, which the wealthy Arab;

which either the Pygmy peoples or India plucks,

or which the Sabaean land produces in its gentle bosom.

Thereupon it heaps up cinnamon and fragrant amomum, breathing scent from afar,

and balsam mixed with foliage.

[85] Neither mild cassia nor the twig of fragrant acanthus,

nor tears of frankincense and rich drops, is absent.

To these it adds the tender spikes of downy nard,

and joins to myrrh pastures exceedingly pleasant. [Reading uncertain.]

[Col. 0281A] [Note: [Col. 0281C] **Notes to columns 281–282**

**Verse 88.** *Et sociat myrrhae.* The Sangerman manuscript has:

> *Et sociam myrrhae vim Banachea tuam.*  
> “And your Banachean power, companion of myrrh.”

Others have:

> *Panathea thure.*  
> “Panathean incense.”

**Verse 89.** *Mutabile.* The Sangerman manuscript has *motabile*.

**Verse 90.** *In talique thoro.* Thus the Sangerman manuscript. The printed editions have:

> *Vitalique thoro membra quieta locat.*  
> “And lays its resting limbs upon a living couch.”

**Verse 95.** *Genitali morte.* An antithesis.

**Verse 96.** *Aestuat.* In truth, a dead body does not burn so as to generate a flame; Claudian therefore gives the better account, referring the flame to the sun’s rays:

> *Fervet odoratus telis (id est radiis) coelestibus agger,*  
> “The fragrant mound seethes beneath the heavenly shafts—that is, rays—”  
>
> *Consumitque senem.*  
> “And consumes the old one.”

**Verse 97.** *Aethereoque.* Thus the Sangerman manuscript; the printed editions, however, have *Aer ioque*.

[Col. 0281D]

**Verse 99.** *Quos.* Thus the Sangerman manuscript; the printed editions have *Hos*.

**Verse 100.** *Conflat.* In the Sangerman manuscript, *constat*.

**Verse 102.** *Vermi.* Thus the Sangerman manuscript; the printed editions have *Vermis*. Pliny speaks of *vermis*, not Claudian.

**Verse 103.** *Crevit.* Perhaps *crescit* should be read.

**Verse 104.** *Ovi.* Claudian says nothing about an egg.

**Verse 107.** *Ac velut agrestes, cum filo ad saxa tenentur, Mutari tineae papilione solent.* The very learned Didacus Covarruvias, bishop of Segovia, pointed out to Thoma­sius that in the second verse *tineae* should be written in place of *pennae*; this is highly commendable. For *tineae* are those worms from which silkworm butterflies are born. Here the poet seems to have wished to imitate Ovid, in the last book of the *Metamorphoses*, who speaks of this same transformation as follows:

> *Quaeque solent canis frondes intexere filis*  
> “Those rustic moths which are accustomed to weave leaves with gray threads,”  
>
> *Agrestes tineae, res observata colonis,*  
> “A phenomenon observed by farmers,”  
>
> *Ferali mutent cum papilione figuram.*  
> “Change their form together with the deadly butterfly.”

And indeed I do not doubt that *tineae* should be read in place of *pennae*. But in the preceding verse, *illa: filo ad saxa tenentur*—“they are held by a thread to the rocks”—seems to me not sufficiently consistent with the actual matter, since those threads are attached rather to leaves or branches than to rocks. For that reason I think *taxa* should be read rather than *saxa*. Thus Thoma­sius.

**Verse 109.** *Non illi cibus.* On the Phoenix’s food, see Claudian’s *Epigram on the Phoenix*, verse 13 and following.

**Verse 111.** *Ambrosios.* Among poets, ambrosia is the food and nectar the drink of the gods. Thus Martial:

> *Jupiter Ambrosia satur est, et nectare vivit.*  
> “Jupiter is sated with ambrosia and lives on nectar.”

**Verse 112.** *Tenues.* That is, “delicate dews.” So reads the manuscript cited by Gallaeus. The printed editions have *teneri*, referring it to the dews and producing an elegant sense. *Polo* means “the sky.”

**Verse 113.** *Alitur mediis.* Thus the Sangerman manuscript and the editions of 1472 and 1478. The common editions read *mediis alitur*, but incorrectly.

[Col. 0282D]

**Verse 114.** *Perferat.* Thus the Sangerman codex and others. The printed editions, however, have *proferat*, but less satisfactorily.

**Verse 116.** *Patrias domos.* Thus the Sangerman manuscript; others have *primas domos*.

**Verse 117.** *Ante tamen, etc.* On this matter, see Claudian’s *Epigram on the Phoenix*, verse 72, which agrees with what is said here.

**Verse 125.** *Sub cortice laevi, Mitia quem croceum.* Thus Heumann emended it from the correction of Nicolas Heinsius. The printed editions, however, have *qualis sub sydere coeli*.

**Verse 128.** *Cum pandit vestes Flora rubente polo.* We have emended this partly from the Sangerman manuscript and partly from the printed editions. The manuscript has:

> *Cum pandit vestes flore rubente polo.*  
> “When Flora spreads her garments beneath the flowering red sky.”

But the printed editions read:

> *Cum pendens vestit sole rubente polus.*  
> “When the hanging sky clothes itself in the reddening sun.”

**Verse 129.** *Fulgent.* The manuscript has *Fulget*.

Straightway in the spread nest it places its changeable body,

[90] and lays its resting limbs upon such a couch.

Then with its beak it pours juices around and over its limbs,

to linger in its own funeral rites.

Then amid varied scents it commends its soul;

nor does it fear for the trustworthiness of so great a deposit.

[95] Meanwhile the body, destroyed in life-giving death,

grows hot, and the heat itself begets flame;

and from the far-off ethereal light it conceives fire.

It burns, and, scorched, dissolves into ash.

These ashes, gathered as though into a mass in death,

[100] it compacts and they acquire the likeness of seed.

From this, it is said, an animal first arises without limbs;

[Col. 0281B] but the worm, it is said, is of milky color.

In a fixed time it suddenly grows to an immense size,

and gathers itself into the shape of a rounded egg.

[105] Then it is re-formed in the figure it possessed before,

and the Phoenix springs forth when its coverings burst.

And just as wild moths, when held to rocks by a thread,

are accustomed to change into a butterfly—

it is not granted the food of our world;

[110] nor is anyone concerned to feed it while featherless.

It sips ambrosial dews with heavenly nectar,

thin dews that have fallen from the star-bearing sky.

[Col. 0282A] It gathers these; amid these scents the bird is nourished,

until it attains its mature form.

[115] But when it has begun to bloom in its first youth,

it flies back, now to return to its ancestral home.

Yet first whatever remains of its own body—

its bones, ashes, and its cast-off remains—

it embalms with balsamic ointment, myrrh, and dissolved frankincense,

[120] and gathers them into a rounded form with pious beak.

Carrying this in its feet, it hastens toward the rising sun

and, sitting upon the altar, places it in the sacred shrine.

It makes itself a wonder and spectacle to the beholder;

there is such beauty there, such abundant majesty.

[125] Its color first is like that which, beneath smooth bark,

mild pomegranate seeds take on—a saffron hue.

Such is the color in the leaves borne by the wild poppy,

when Flora spreads her garments beneath the reddening sky.

With this covering its shapely shoulders and breast gleam;

[130] with this its head, neck, and upper back shine.

Its tail extends, distinguished by tawny gold,

and in its markings purple glows with mingled red.

Above, among the feathers, is a bright emblem, such as Iris

is wont from on high to paint upon a cloud.

[135] A conspicuous greenish emerald gleams white;

[Col. 0283A] [Note: [Col. 0283B] **Various Readings for columns 283–284**

**Verse 136.** *Et puro cornu, etc.* He says that its beak is horn, but so bright that it appears to be a gem.

**Verse 137.** *Ingentes oculos credas, etc.* Read this way on the authority of the Vossian manuscript.

**Verse 139.** *Corona Phoebei verticis.* That is, the solar rays.

**Verse 142.** *Roseus.* The Sangerman manuscript has *Roseo*.

**Verse 144.** *Phasidis avem.* That is, the pheasant, named from the Phasis River of Colchis and brought to us by the Argonauts. See Martial, *Epigrams*, Book XIII, 72.

**Verse 145.** *Magniciem.* What bird this is is unknown; or perhaps the word stands for *magnitudinem* (“size”).

**Verse 151.** *Huc venit.* Thus the Sangerman manuscript; the printed editions, however, have *convenit*.

**Verse 153.** *Exsculpunt.* Thus the Sangerman manuscript and others; the printed editions instead read *Inscalpunt*.

**Verse 155.** *Genus omne volantum.* On this matter, see Claudian, verse 76 and following.

**Verse 157.** *Alituum.* For *alitum*. Thus Virgil, *Aeneid* 8:

> *Alituum pecudumque genus sopor altus habebat.*  
> “Deep sleep held the race of winged creatures and cattle.”

**Verse 158.** *Munere laeta pio.* That is, rejoicing in the duty of piety and reverence toward a bird of such dignity. Heinsius wrongly emends *munere* to *murmure*.

[Col. 0284B]

**Verse 160.** *Mox redit ista suis: conditur ille locis.* We read this in the Sangerman manuscript and in another old manuscript cited by Gallaeus. The printed editions read:

> *Mox redit illa; suis conditur inde locis.*  
> “Soon she returns; thereafter he is buried in his own places,”

and this is not a bad reading.

**Verse 161.** *At fortunatae sortis filique volucrem.* This is Heinsius’s emendation, referring *filum* (“thread”) to the Parcae,

> *Quae dispensant mortalia fila sorores.*  
> “The sisters who allot the threads of mortal life.”

But the Sangerman manuscript reads:

> *At fortunatae sortis, felixque volucrum.*  
> “But [he is] of fortunate destiny, and the happiest of birds.”

Gallaeus thinks that the reading should be:

> *O fortunatae sortis, fatique volucrem.*  
> “O bird of fortunate destiny and fate.”

The printed editions have:

> *Haec fortunatae sortis, fatique volucris.*  
> “This bird is of fortunate destiny and fate.”

**Verse 163.** *Foemina sit, vel mas, seu neutrum, seu sit utrumque.* We have emended this from the Sangerman manuscript and Heumann’s edition. The common editions have:

> *Foemina vel mas haec, vel neutrum sit mage felix.*  
> “Whether female or male, or neuter, may this one be happier.”

**Verse 169.** *Quae est ipsa.* Thus the Sangerman manuscript. The printed editions have *quia et ipsa*.

and a jewelled point of pure horn opens forth.

You would think its enormous eyes twin hyacinths;

from their midst a bright flame flashes.

A radiant crown equals the whole head,

[140] representing the lofty splendor of Phoebus’ brow.

Scales, distinguished with yellow metal, cover its legs;

but a rosy color adorns its claws with glory.

Its appearance is seen to combine the form of a peacock

[145] The *magnicies*—a bird produced in Arabian lands—

can scarcely equal it, whether beast or bird. [The name is uncertain.]

Yet it is not slow, like birds which, with large bodies,

rather, it is light and swift, full of royal splendor.

[150] [Col. 0283B] Such it continually presents itself to human sight.

Egypt comes here for the marvel of so great a spectacle,

and a rejoicing throng salutes the rare bird.

Straightway they carve its likeness in consecrated marble

[Col. 0284A] and mark both the event and the day with a new inscription.

Every kind of flying creature gathers itself into an assembly;

none remembers prey, nor is any afraid.

Accompanied by a choir of birds, it flies through the heights;

the flock follows with the glad office of reverence.

But after it has reached the breezes of the pure ether,

[160] this one soon returns; that one is buried in its own place.

O bird of fortunate lot and thread of fate,

to which God himself granted that it should be born from itself!

Whether female or male, neither sex, or both,

blessed is it, which observes none of Venus’ unions.

[165] Death is Venus to it; in death alone is its pleasure:

so that it may be born, it first desires to die.

It is its own offspring, its own father, and its own heir;

itself its own nurse, ever its own nursling.

It is itself indeed, but not the same self that it is; nor is it itself,

[170] having gained eternal life through death’s benefit.

## POEM ON THE PASSION OF THE LORD, BY AN UNCERTAIN AUTHOR

(C, G, S)

[Col. 0283D] Whoever you are, who stand present and enter the threshold of this middle temple,

pause a little and look upon me, innocent though suffering for your crime.

Keep me in your mind; preserve me in your breast.

I am he who pitied the bitter misfortunes of humankind.

[5] I came here as interpreter of the promised peace, and as broad

forgiveness of the common guilt. Here the brightest light from on high

was restored to the earth; here is the nourishing image of salvation.

Here I am your rest, the straight way, true redemption,

God’s banner and the memorable sign of destiny.

[10] For your sake and for your life I entered the Virgin’s womb,

[Col. 0284D] became human, and endured dreadful

deaths. Nowhere within the bounds of earth

did I find rest, but everywhere threats, everywhere labors.

The first dreadful shelter afforded me on earth was the Judaean hut

[15] at my birth, shared with my mother.

There, among dull brute beasts, dry grass spread out for me

my first bed in a narrow manger.

I lived my first years in Pharian regions,

a fugitive from Herod’s kingdom; having returned, I spent the rest in

[20] Judaea, always pursuing fasts, always embracing extreme

[Col. 0285A] poverty and the lowliest condition;

punishments and lifted up far from my sweet mother—

from head to foot. Look: behold hair

[40] clotted with blood, and neck bloodied beneath the hair;

a head pierced by cruel thorns; divine blood raining everywhere

over my living face.

Observe my closed eyes, bereft of light,

my afflicted cheeks; behold my dry tongue

[45] poisoned with gall, and my countenance pale in death.

See hands fastened with nails, arms stretched out,

and the vast wound in my side; see the bloody flow from it,

my pierced feet and bloodstained limbs.

[50] [Col. 0285C] Bend the knee and, weeping, adore the venerable wood of the cross;

[Col. 0286A] with humble lips, kiss the earth wet with innocent blood,
and bathe it with tears as they arise;

and sometimes bear me and my counsels in your devoted heart.

Follow the footsteps of my life;

[55] and, contemplating the punishments themselves and the harsh death

of my body, while recalling the innumerable pains of my soul,

learn to endure adversity and to watch over your own salvation.

If at any time it pleases you to turn these memorials over in your mind,

if you have any faith in your heart to bear my sufferings,

[60] if due devotion and gratitude worthy of my labors

should arise, they will be true spurs to virtue; they will be shields

against the enemy’s plots, by which you will be safe in every bitter

contest and bear away the victor’s palm.

If these memorials turn your thoughts away from friends

[65] of the unstable world and from the fleeing shadow of worldly beauty,

[Col. 0286B] they will ensure that, caught by empty hope,

you do not dare to trust in the shifting things of failing fortune

or to place hope in the fleeting years of life.

But assuredly, seeing such transitory things as these,

[70] secure and stripped of love for a better homeland,

the world’s riches, the use of possessions, and the aspirations of the devout

will raise you through sacred character, and amid harsh punishments

will cherish you with heavenly dew and feed you with the sweetness

of the promised good.

[75] Until, after the body has been left behind at the final fates,

great grace will recall your purple-clad soul to the lofty breezes.

Then, freed from every labor, joyfully beholding

the angelic choirs and blessed ranks of saints,

you will reign with me, forever happy, in the pleasant court of eternal peace.

[80] [Col. 0286C]

[Col. 0285]

## VENANTIUS HONORIUS CLEMENTIANUS FORTUNATUS, ITALIAN PRIEST, TO BISHOP FELIX, ON EASTER

[Note: [Col. 0285D] [Annotations on columns 285–286]

“Venantius … to Bishop Felix.” In the poems on the Resurrection, since it was plainly discovered to whom they belonged, the entire title was changed and the title found in those little works was added: “Of Venantius Honorius,” etc. These are in the Vatican Library; from them many readings in the printed books are corrected. Yet many were left unchanged, because the common reading seemed preferable to that of the Vatican manuscript. For that manuscript is very corrupt; nevertheless, it can assist one who uses it with judgment. And certainly those who undertake the task of correcting the books of ancient authors ought often to make one excellent text out of several bad manuscripts. THOMASIUS.]

(G, S)*

[Col. 0287A] [Note: [Col. 0287D] **Variant Readings for columns 287–288**

**Verse 23.** *Acer nux.* Others read *acernus*.

**Verse 42.** *Cuncta.* Others, *Puncta*.

**Verse 46.** *Has inter, etc.* Alternatively:

> *Has inter minimus passer amore cano.*  
> “Among these I, the smallest sparrow, sing of love.”

**Verse 50.** *Patris ore.* Others, *Penetrare*.

**Verse 59.** *Funeris, etc.* Alternatively:

> *Funeris exequias pateris vitae auctor et orbis.*  
> “You endure the funeral rites, author of life and of the world.”

**Verse 60.** *Intra.* Others, *Intras*.

**Verse 61.** *Tristia cessarunt.* Others, *Tristia cesserunt*.

[Col. 0288D]

**Verse 64.** *Aeternae.* Others, *Et terrae*.

**Verse 65.** *Sollicitam.* Others, *Pollicitam*.

**Verse 68.** *Non.* Others, *Nec*; others again, *Neu*.

**Verse 80.** *Raperet.* Others, *Rapuit*.

**Verse 82.** *Abis.* Others, *Adit*.

**Verse 87.** *Iste.* Others, *In te*.

**Verse 89.** *Trophaei.* Others, *Triumphi*.

**Verse 95.** *Concors.* Others, *Consors*.

[Note: [Col. 0287D] **Notes to columns 287–288**

**Verse 39.** *Salve festa dies, toto venerabilis aevo, Qua Deus infernum vicit et astra tenet.* On the authority of the Vatican manuscript, this verse has been moved so that it follows twenty couplets, which is certainly where it belongs. For before this, nothing is said about Christ’s Passion or Resurrection; rather, spring itself is praised for the many gifts proper to its nature. But after the Resurrection has been mentioned, the following is rightly added:

> *Salve festa dies, etc.*  
> “Hail, festal day, revered throughout all ages, on which God conquered hell and holds the stars.”

The following couplet is also properly attached immediately to it:

> *Nobilitas anni, mensum, lux alma dierum,*  
> “Nobility of the year and months, nourishing light of the days,”  
>
> *Horarum splendor, stridula puncta favent.*  
> “Splendor of the hours: the shrill moments give their favor.”

For *nobilitas* (“nobility”) must be read on the authority of the Vatican manuscript, so that some praise may be attributed to that day, which the poet wishes to praise; whereas from *mobilitas* (“changeability”), as it formerly stood, no praise can attach to any particular day, since this quality is common to all. In the second verse, *stridula puncta* (“shrill moments”) must likewise be read, so that everything refers to the day. Several other passages in these poems have also been altered, though they have been improved; anyone comparing this book with others will be able to understand this. — THOMASIUS.

[Col. 0285D] The seasons gleam, distinguished by flower-bearing serenity;

the gate of heaven stands open in greater light.

The orbit of heaven carries the fire-bearing sun higher,

as it wanders out from and enters the Ocean’s waters.

[5] Armed with rays and surveying the melting elements,

in this short night it stretches the day across the world.

The shining ether displays a cloudless face,

and the bright stars show their joy.

Fruitful earth pours forth its little gifts in varied adornment,

[10] when it has well put on spring; the year too restores its riches.

Soft violet beds paint the field purple;

the meadows are green with grass, and the grass flashes with leafy blades.

Little by little the starry lights of flowers emerge;

all the grasses smile upon their own flowers.

[15] Once seed is deposited, the crop springs up broadly in the fields,

promising the farmer that he may overcome hunger.

The vine-shoot, leaving its trunk, weeps its joys:

whence it will furnish wine, the vine now gives water.

Rising from the bark of its mother with tender down,

[20] the swelling bud prepares its bosom for fruit;

and beneath winter’s season, when its leafy hair has been shed,

the green woodland now restores its leafy roofs.

Willow, fir, hazel, siler, elm, maple, and walnut mingle together;

each lovely tree applauds with its own foliage.

[25] Here the bee, about to construct honeycombs, leaves its hives

and, humming among flowers, gathers honey with its legs.

The bird returns to song, which, its music stopped,

had been mute and sluggish in winter cold.

Here Philomela attunes her instruments to her reeds;

[30] and the breeze becomes sweeter through the echoed melody.

Behold: the grace of the reborn world bears witness

that all gifts have returned with their Lord.

For, after Christ’s triumph over grim Tartarus,

the woodland everywhere rejoices in leaves, the grasses in flowers.

[35] [Col. 0287B] With the laws of hell overthrown, light, heaven, fields, and sea

rightly praise God as he passes above the stars.

He who was crucified—behold, God reigns over all things;

all created things offer prayer to their Creator.

Hail, festal day, venerable through every age,

[40] on which God conquered hell and holds the stars.

The changing course of the year, the months, the gracious light of days,
the splendor of the hours—all shrill things give favor.

Here the woodland applauds you with its foliage; here the field with its ears of grain;

here the vine gives thanks with silent shoot.

[45] Here now the shrubs resound for you with the murmur of birds;

among them the sparrow sings with excessive love.

Christ, salvation of the world, good creator and redeemer,

only offspring from the Father’s divinity,

flowing unutterably from the parent’s heart,

[50] [Col. 0287C] the subsisting Word, mighty in the Father’s utterance,

equal, harmonious, companion, coeternal with the Father,

through whom the world received its beginning from its ruler:

you suspend the heavens, heap up the earth, pour out the seas,

and make flourish in due order all that dwells in their places.

[55] Seeing the human race sunk in the abyss,

you too became human in order to rescue humanity.

You did not merely will to be born from our body,

but, flesh, endured both birth and death.

You, the new creator of the Father and of the world, endure the funeral rites,

[60] entering upon death’s path in order to give salvation’s aid.

[Col. 0288A] The sad bonds of hell’s law have ceased;

Chaos was terrified to be pressed by the face of light.

The darkness perishes, driven away by Christ’s radiance;

the thick coverings of eternal night fall.

[65] But restore anxious faith, I pray, gracious Power.

The third day has returned: rise, my buried one.

It is unfitting that a cheap tomb cover your limbs;

that cheap stones press down the price of the world.

It is unworthy that he whose fist encloses all things

[70] should be enclosed by a stone’s forbidding rock.

Remove the linen cloths, I pray; leave the burial cloths in the tomb.

You are enough for us, and without you there is nothing.

Release the shades chained in hell’s prison

and call back upward whatever has fallen to the depths.

[75] Restore your face, that the ages may see the light;

restore the day which fled from us when you died.

But indeed, returning as a pious victor, you have filled heaven:

Tartarus lies crushed and no longer retains its laws.

Hell, opening its hollow jaws insatiably,

[80] which always sought to snatch away, is your prey, O God.

You rescue an innumerable people from death’s prison;

freed, it follows where you, its author, go.

The savage monster fearfully vomits forth the people it swallowed;

and the Lamb withdraws the sheep from the wolf’s jaws.

[85] Then, returning from Tartarus to the tomb and reassuming flesh,

as a warrior you bear abundant trophies to heaven.

Those whom punitive Chaos possessed, it has now given back;

and those whom death sought are held by new life.

Holy King, behold, a great part of your trophy shines forth,

[90] [Col. 0288C] when sacred washing blesses pure souls.

A white host comes forth from glittering waters,

and cleanses old corruption in the new stream.

A white garment also marks the shining souls;

and the shepherd has joy from the snow-white flock.

[95] To this concordant reward is added Felix the priest,

who wishes to give his Lord double talents.

Drawing toward better things those wandering in gentile error,

he fortifies God’s sheepfold lest the beast snatch them away.

Those whom harmful Eve had formerly infected, he now restores

[100] to the Church’s breast with its fertile milk, as shepherd.

[Col. 0289A] **[Variorum Notae]**

**Vers. 101. _Mitibus._** The following verses were added from the Vatican codex by Thomasius, whose words are as follows:

“In this poem I added ten verses from that codex, which agree excellently with the actual matter and explain why Venantius wrote those poems to Bishop Felix—who certainly is no Felix among the Roman Pontiffs [Col. 0290A], but was one of those early bishops of the Saxons. For when the Saxons had been defeated by Charlemagne after a war lasting thirty years and more, they accepted the Christian religion; among the Roman Pontiffs, however, the last to bear this name was Felix IV, who lived long before Charlemagne. I therefore judged that those ten verses should be added, because they agree excellently with the subject under discussion, and because at the end of the poem the number of verses, **CX**, had been added, so that precisely ten were lacking to complete the number.”

[Col. 0289A] By cultivating rustic hearts with gentle speech,

a crop born from bramble springs up through Felix’s gift.

The harsh Saxon people, living almost by a savage custom,

made holy by your healing, returns the beast as a sheep.

[105] A harvest remaining with you through the ages in a hundredfold return

fills granaries with abundant produce.

May this spotless people be cherished in your arms,

and may you bear a pure pledge to God amid the stars.

May one crown be given and granted to you from on high;

[110] another, gained from your people, may bloom.

[Col. 0289]

## RIDDLES OF CAELIUS SYMPHOSIUS

[Note: [Col. 0289D] [Notes of Various Scholars on columns 289–290]

“Caelius Symphosius.” As far as I know, Christopher Heumann was the first to attribute these verses, which Saint Jerome indeed mentions, to Lactantius. They had earlier been published under the name “Caelius Firmianus Symposius the Poet” by Nicolaus Caussinus of the Society of Jesus and appended to Horapollo’s *Hieroglyphics*. Already in 1533 Joachim Perionius had made these riddles public under the name “the poet Symphosius.” Others, however, called him not *Symphosius* but *Symposium*. Heumann undoubtedly found occasion to ascribe these riddles to Lactantius because in some editions they bear the heading “Caelius Firmianus”; and he thought that the poet’s name, Symphosius, ought to be written *Symposium*, that is, “Banquet.” Thus some modern scholars also published them as *Table Talk*. Nevertheless, all learned men, and especially Johann Albert Fabricius, did not adopt Heumann’s opinion.

“Sweet things of the table.” Hence it is evident that these verses are nothing other than table-talk; therefore *Symposium* is the title of the work, not the poet’s name.]

(C, G, S)*

[Col. 0289B] Symphosius too played these games in trifling verse;

thus you teach, Sextus; thus, with you as my mad master, I rave.

When Saturn’s annual festive season returned,

a celebration always observed among us with uninterrupted sport,

[5] after joyful feasting and the sweet cups of the table,

among babbling old women and talkative boys,

when the eloquence of wine-soaked tongues resounded far and wide,

then the wordy company, eager for foolish conversation,

devised at random, from some great theme, I know not what trifles,

[10] and spoke much nonsense at length.

Nor was it a slight likeness of a great contest

to propose different things or solve each in turn.

But lest I alone seem shamefully to have kept silent,

having brought with me nothing I could say,

[15] I composed these verses at once in the verse-form of riddles.

Among madmen one need not be sane.

Grant pardon, reader, if my drunken Muse lacks wisdom.

### 1. Stylus or writing-needle

Flat at the top, but not flat at the bottom,

I am turned in either direction by the hand and perform opposing offices;

one part undoes whatever the other part has done.

### 2. Reed

[Col. 0289D] I always love shores near the deep banks,

singing sweetly for the Muses; steeped in black color,

I am the messenger of speech, marked by my master’s fingers.

### 3. Ring with a gem

[Col. 0290B] I cling to an extremity of the body, no great weight;

you would call me inborn, so little does anyone feel burdened by my weight;

yet one face is destined to bear many figures.

### 4. Key

I bring great powers from small strength.

I open closed houses, yet again close open ones;

I guard the house for its master, but in turn am guarded by him.

### 5. Chain

Bound, I am linked with iron, destined to bind many.

I myself am first bound, but, bound, I in turn bind.

And I have released many, though I myself have not been released.

### 6. Roof-tile

[Col. 0290C] Earth gave me my body; fire gave me strength.

I seek a high house, yet my seat is always at the bottom.

I am drenched with liquids, but the moisture quickly leaves me.

### 7. Smoke

I have tears, yes, tears, but no cause of grief.

My path is to heaven, but heavy air hinders me;

and he who gave me birth is not himself born without me.

### 8. Mist

I am night in appearance, but not black in color;

yet I bring darkness with me into the middle of day.

Neither stars give me light, nor Cynthia her radiance.

### 9. Rain

[Col. 0290D] I come from on high, fallen in a long descent.

I fell from heaven, sent through the middle airs;

and the bosom that received me simultaneously received itself.

### 10. Ice

[Col. 0291A] I was once water, which I believe I shall soon become again.

Now I am bound in the hard chains of the rigid sky;

I can neither endure being trodden upon nor be held naked.

### 11. River and fish

There is a house on earth that resounds with a clear voice.

The house itself sounds, but its silent guest makes no sound;

yet both run together, guest and house alike.

### 12. Snow

A fine dust of water, fallen with slight weight,

wet in sunlight, flowing in summer, dry in cold,

destined to make rivers, I first cover whole lands.

### 13. Ship

Long, swift, I am the daughter of the beautiful forest,

with an innumerable company of companions surrounding me together;

I travel many roads, leaving no tracks.

### 14. Chick in the egg
