I shall tell you the wondrous beginnings of our life.

I was not yet born, nor was I then in my mother’s womb;

after the offspring had been laid aside, no one saw me born.

15. Viper.

I cannot be born unless I kill my mother.

I have killed my mother; but the same end awaits me.

My death undergoes what my origin has already done.

16. Bookworm.

A letter fed me, yet I do not know what a letter is.

I have lived in books, and am no more learned for it.

I have devoured the Muses, yet have not myself improved.

17. Spider.

Pallas taught me to know the labour of weaving.

[Col. 0291C] Neither the threads of a robe nor the warp-threads of a loom are required by me.

I have no hands, yet everything is done by my feet.

18. Snail.

I carry my house with me, always ready to migrate;

and, though I change my ground, I am no wretched exile,

but my counsel is born from heaven itself.

19. Frog.

I am hoarse-sounding, a vowel amid the waters;

yet my voice sounds in praise, whereby it praises itself as well.

And though I sing continually, no one praises my songs.

20. Tortoise.

Slow in slow step, endowed with a handsome back,

indeed taught by study, but ruined by a cruel fate:

while alive I said nothing—I who, now dead, sing thus.

21. Mole.

[Col. 0291D] My blind face is obscured by black darkness.

Day itself is night, nor do I behold any sun.

I prefer to be covered by earth: thus no one will see me either.

22. Ant.

I make provident provision for life, not idle in hard work,

myself bearing on my shoulders the rewards of a secure winter.

Nor do I carry much at once, but gather much in turn.

23. Fly.

I am shameless, I confess; for what disgrace does the belly fear?

I was avoiding the cold, which now I return to in summer;

but I am quickly driven away, alarmed by a false wind.

24. Weevil.

No good guest to farmers, nor useful to crops;

not large in form, nor called by a proper name;

[Col. 0292A] unwelcome to Ceres, nor do I take a small meal.

25. Mouse.

My house is small, but its door is always open.

At little cost I live on stolen fare.

The name which is mine was borne by a consul at Rome as well.

26. Crane.

I am a letter of the sky, flying on written wings,

waging bloody wars, the winged formations of Mars;

nor do I fear battles, provided that the enemy is not longer.

27. Crow.

I live nine lives, if Greece does not deceive me;

and I am always black, compelled by no grief.

And, unangered, I utter insults unbidden.

28. Bat.

Night gives me my name from the first time of night.

[Col. 0292B] I have no feather, though I have the wing of a flying creature.

But I return amid darkness, and do not entrust myself to the day.

29. Hedgehog.

A house full of spines, tenant of a small body,

its back uninjured though pierced by sharp weapons.

An unarmed inhabitant bears armed crops.

30. Lice.

There is a new capture of creatures marked for all:

so that, if you catch anything, you refuse to carry it away for yourself,

and yet carry back with you what you have not caught.

31. Phoenix.

Life is death to me: I die if I begin to be born;

but the destiny of death precedes the origin of light.

Thus, alone, I call the Shades themselves my parents.

32. Bull.

[Col. 0292C] I was the king’s adulterer, yet I followed wooden limbs;

I am a mountain of the Cilicians, yet not by name alone;

I am borne in heaven, and walk upon the very earth.

33. Wolf.

With mad teeth I am he who conquers sheep,

seeking bloody prey and bloodstained food

with much frenzy; I can raise my voice as well.

34. Fox.

My body is small, but my heart is greater than my body.

I am crafty in deceits, shrewd in subtle intelligence;

and I am a wise wild beast—if any wild beast may be called wise.

35. Goat.

Kindly nurse of Jupiter, clothed in long hair,

roaming heights difficult and steep of step,

I answer the keeper of the flock with trembling tongue.

36. Pig.

[Col. 0292D]

Born in the fruitful womb of a bristle-bearing mother,

from above, from on high, I await green food;

having a god in my name, if its first letter should perish.

37. Mule.

Unlike my father, different in appearance from my mother,

offspring of a mixed kind, a progeny unfit for procreation:

I am born from others, and nothing is born from me.

38. Tiger.

I am named from a river, or the river is named from me;

and I am joined to the wind, swifter than the wind itself;

the wind gives me offspring; I seek no husband.

39. Centaur.

Distinguished by four feet and two hands,

[Col. 0293A] I am unlike myself, because I am not one and one;

and I both ride and walk, because two bodies bear me.

40. Poppy.

My head is large, but my limbs within are small;

I have one foot only, but that one foot is exceedingly long;

and sleep loves me, though I do not sleep with my own sleep.

41. Mallow.

I do not deny that feet like those of a goose are mine;

nor are there merely two, but you see more in a row;

and yet I carry all these very feet upside down.

42. Beet.

I am called “whole” in Greek, but am not whole in Latin;

yet written before the middle of the innkeeper’s tavern.

I am born in the earth, washed in water, anointed with olive oil.

43. Gourd.

[Col. 0293B] I hang while I am born; again, by hanging I swell.

Hanging, I am moved by winds and nourished by waters.

If I am not hanging, I am no longer—and am about to be.

44. Onion.

I bite those who bite, yet I bite no one unprovoked;

but many are ready to bite the biter.

No one fears my bite, because I have no teeth at all.

45. Rose.

I am the purple of the earth, suffused with beautiful colour;

and, fenced about lest I be violated, I am defended by sharp weapons.

O happy one, if I could live by a long destiny!

46. Violet.

I am indeed not large, but the greatest strength is in me.

My fragrance is great, though in a small body.

[Col. 0293C] My bud has no blemish, nor is my redness a fault.

47. Frankincense.

The sweet scent of the grove is wearied by flame and smoke;

and this pleases the gods above: that I am sent into the midst of fires,

although nature has denied me any capacity for sinning.

48. Myrrh.

From tears and for tears my origin began.

I flowed from eyes, but now I am born from a tree:

a joyful honour to the foliage, yet a sad image of grief.

49. Ivory.

I am a great god, related to Eastern peoples.

Now through my forefathers I have passed into many bodies;

my strength remains no longer, but the grace of form has remained.

50. Hay.

Formerly I was grass from the green turf of the earth;

[Col. 0293D] but, soft, cut by the hard metal of steel,

I am pressed by my own mass, enclosed beneath a lofty roof.

51. Millstone.

We are both stones; we are one; both of us lie down.

How idle is one; the other goes, scarcely less sluggish.

This one remains motionless; that one never ceases to move.

52. Flour.

I was among stones which crushed and pressed me;

yet, bruised in every marrow, I scarcely escaped.

And now my form is smaller, but my quantity greater.

53. Vine.

I do not wish to be joined in marriage, though I like being a bride.

I do not want a husband in my bridal chamber: through me my offspring is born.

I do not wish to suffer tombs; I know that I shall be buried beneath the earth.

54. Fishhook.

[Col. 0294A]

A small body, with the curve of a hooked point,

I bear deceptive baits amid the flowing water.

I flatter in order to harm; I send food before death.

55. Needle.

Long but slender, drawn out from thin metal,

I draw soft bonds following light iron;

I restore form to things torn and binding to things loosened.

56. Boot.

Long ago I was much greater, while life remained;

but now lifeless, torn, bound, and pulled away,

I am given to the earth, yet not buried in a tomb.

57. Boot-nail.

I enter into a head, though I hang from a foot alone;

with my crown I touch the ground; I mark the footprints of the head.

[Col. 0294B] Yet many companions suffer the same fall.

58. Hair.

None can split me; many can cut me off.

Yet I am of changing colour, someday to become white.

I prefer to remain black: I shall fear the final fates less.

59. Ball.

I am not surrounded by a mane, nor adorned with hair;

for within I have hairs which no one sees.

Hands throw me, and by hands I am sent back into the air.

60. Saw.

I am full of countless teeth throughout my body;

with sharp bite I consume the leafy-haired offspring;

yet I chew in vain what I reject as the reward of my teeth.

61. Bridge.

A grove stands in the waters; a forest stands in the deep whirlpool,

[Col. 0294C] and immovable timber remains amid the waters.

Yet the earth sends forth what provides the earth’s gifts.

62. Sponge.

I am not heavy in myself, but the weight of water clings to me;

my entire inner parts swell, spread through open cavities.

Water lies hidden within, but does not pour itself out of its own accord.

63. Trident.

I have three teeth, which one arrangement holds;

moreover, there is one god, alone in the depths;

a divine power holds me, the wind fears me, the waters heed me.

64. Arrow.

Fenced with heavy iron, surrounded by light feathers,

I strive through the middle air in a winged course;

and, sent away, I return with no one sending me.

65. Whip.

[Col. 0294D] From the back of a beast I frighten all beasts,

rendering obedience under the rule of measured pain.

I do not wish to be despised, yet conversely I do not wish to harm.

66. Lantern.

Fitted with hollow horns, transparent in a rounded ring,

having within it light like a divine star,

in the midst of nights I do not lose the face of day.

67. Window-pane.

I am seen through entirely, nor do I block the sight of light,

transmitting eyes moving through my substance;

winter does not pass through me, but the sun shines within me.

68. Mirror.

I have no fixed form, no foreign form.

Within is a radiance flashing with brilliant light,

[Col. 0295A] which shows nothing unless it has first seen something.

69. Water-clock.

I am a good law of speaking, and a stern law of silence also;

the right of a greedy tongue, an end to endless talking;

flowing myself, while words flow, so that the tongue may rest.

70. Well.

Water, sunk far beneath the earth in deep ground,

can emerge only through veins that have been bored through,

and is drawn upward, led by another’s labour.

71. Pipe.

Earth covers the trunk; waters lie hidden in the soil.

It is a small channel, having no banks at all.

It is conveyed in the middle of a piece of wood which conveyed timber.

72. Bellows.

I do not immediately die when breath goes out;

[Col. 0295B] for it returns continually, although it often withdraws.

Now I have great power of breath, now none at all.

73. Stone.

I survived the cruel flood of Deucalion,

akin to earth, yet far harder than it.

Let one letter be removed: I shall also have the name of a bird.

74. Lime.

I escaped flames; I fled the torments of fire.

My own remedy fights against my contrary fate.

I burn from water; I am kindled amid waters.

75. Flint.

Fire is always in me, but is rarely seen.

For it lies hidden within, but comes forth only at blows;

it needs neither wood in order to live nor water in order to die.

76. Wheels.

[Col. 0295C] Four equal sisters run by art,

as though competing, although the labour belongs to all alike;

they are close together, yet cannot touch one another.

77. Ladders.

We are those which stretch upward, seeking heaven,

whom one harmonious arrangement holds in construction,

so that, joined together, ascent to the air may be made by us.

78. Broom.

Great mother of cleansing, joined by a firm binding,

attached to level ground and grasped by two hands,

I am drawn everywhere following, and all things follow me as well.

79. Bell.

I am fashioned from curved bronze into an open circle.

Within is the movable likeness of a clattering tongue;

when set down it does not resound, but when moved it often rings.

80. Spiced drink.

[Col. 0295D]

Once we were three, joined in one name.

From three comes one, and three are mixed in one;

each is good by itself; better is that which contains them all.

81. Wine turned into vinegar.

Nothing has been taken away; nothing added from outside;

yet I do not find whatever I myself formerly left.

What had been is not; what was not has begun to be.

82. Apple.

Having a Greek name, the great contention of goddesses,

the deception of the handsome youth, concern of many sisters,

the destruction of Troy, while I brought bloody wars to completion.

83. Ham.

I derive noble lineage from the race of great Cato.

[Col. 0296A] I have one sister, though many think there are several.

My appearance is from smoke; my wisdom was born from the sea.

84. Hammer.

I do not claim strength for myself from my entire body,

but in the contest of heads I refuse to yield to anyone.

My head is large; indeed all my weight is in it.

85. Pestle.

I crush all things together with great strength of force.

I have one neck, but the form of two heads.

A head serves as feet; for the remaining parts of the body are absent.

86. Strigil.

Red, curved, capacious, moist with another’s drops,

counterfeiting the colour of gold with false gleams,

devoted to sweat, I yield to slight labour.

87. Bath.

[Col. 0296B] Harmless fire enters throughout the whole house.

There is great heat in the midst, which no one fears.

The house is not naked, but the naked guest comes together there.

88. Die.

I am always committed to chance, uncertain of the future;

I am thrown into doubtful outcomes by varying whirl;

now sorrowful in misfortunes, now happy in favourable circumstances.

89. Money.

At first I was earth, concealed in the hiding-places of earth;

now flame has given me another value and another name.

Nor am I now called earth, though land is bought with me.

90. A woman bearing twins.

I bore more than one body ought to have borne.

I had three souls, all of which I held within.

Two departed, but the third almost followed them.

91. A gouty soldier.

[Col. 0296C]

Formerly mighty in war, feared in savage arms,

I had five feet, which no one ever denied;

now I scarcely have two: abundance has made me poor.

92. A one-eyed man selling garlic.

It is now right to see what you can scarcely believe lawful to believe.

There is one eye, but many thousands of heads.

He who sells what he has—how shall he procure what he does not have?

93. Tightrope-walker.

Between the light-bearing heaven and the earth lying below,

a traveller passes through the middle air by skilled art;

but the path is narrow and does not suffice even for his feet.

94. Shadow.

I fear no snares from hidden deceit,

for God has bestowed upon us these gifts of form:

[Col. 0296D] that no one moves unless he himself has first moved.

95. Echo.

A very modest maiden, I faithfully keep the law of chastity.

I am not wanton in speech, nor rash in tongue;

I do not wish to speak first, but give answers to one speaking.

96. Sleep.

Coming of my own accord, I display various images.

I fashion empty fears without distinction from reality.

But no one sees me unless he closes his own eyes.

97. Monument.

Bearing a man’s name, I remained after his final fate;

the empty name remains, but sweet life has fled.

Yet life survives death after the times of life.

[Col. 0297A] 98. Anchor.

My double point is joined to hooked iron.

I struggle with the wind; I fight the deep whirlpool.

I search the midst of the waters; I bite the earth itself as well.

99. Jug.

Earth was my mother; Prometheus himself was my father,

[Col. 0298A] and ears encircle and govern my hollow belly.

When I fell unhappily, my mother broke me apart.

100.

Now believe me that what is denied to be possible can happen.

You hold eight in your hands; but, with me as your instructing guide,

when seven have been raised, six will remain for you.

> **Note:** [Col. 0297A]  
> Heumann spoke at length in explaining this riddle and adduced various interpretations. Heynazius explains it thus: “The ancients counted on their fingers: they signified six by extending all the fingers of the left hand except the ring finger, that is, the finger next to the little finger; seven by depressing the little finger alone; eight by depressing the ring finger and little finger, or auricular finger. Therefore, if they raised the little finger expressing seven, the ring finger remained depressed; hence the number six.”  
> Moreover, neither this nor the following riddle is found in Perionius’s edition, whereas it appears as no. 100 in Lemaire’s edition; consequently, it is wrongly said that Reusner copied this from that edition. The riddle is:
>
> **Cuckoo.**
>
> I depart in the cold; I return when warmth returns.  
> I abandon what I have laid, yet another mother brings it up.  
> What more do you want me to say? My own voice reveals me.

[Col. 0297]

# Notes of Stephen Baluze of Tulle on the Book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*

[Col. 0297B] Among the many and various manuscript codices which Jean-Baptiste Colbert—a man most devoted to letters and to men of learning, and most distinguished in every kind of excellence—collected from all Europe, Asia, and Africa for the public benefit of scholarship, there was found one worth its weight in gold. It contains the book of Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius on persecution, or *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, of which the Church had hitherto been deprived.

He does not behave as most people do. When they obtain an unpublished work of some ancient writer, however slight and thin it may be, they carefully conceal it, as though it shone more brightly in darkness, so that they may boast that they alone possess what everyone would wish to possess; and they take the greatest care that it cannot come into others’ hands. The spirit of this most illustrious man is too liberal and too lofty to be held by that false glory. Thus, when he learned that this book of Lactantius existed among the ancient manuscript codices of his library, and had fully established how much benefit would accrue to the Church if it were published, although previously [Col. 0297C] he had frequently ordered that anything unpublished appearing in those ancient codices should all be committed to the press, on this occasion he nevertheless gave a special command; and, with his customary greatness of spirit, immediately ordered that this book of Lactantius be brought into the clearest light.

We therefore publish it from manuscript 1297 of the Colbert Library (now in the Royal Library, quarto, no. 2627), which appears to be about eight hundred years old: complete indeed, but written by an unskilled hand and consequently infected with many errors. Those errors whose correction was easy and obvious we have freely corrected; but we have left untouched those in which boldness in correction was not free from danger. Perhaps others will be more fortunate.

The book was composed and completed in that year when, after the persecutors had been destroyed, the Church of Christ heard the sweetest and most beautiful name of peace, and tranquillity and freedom to speak and write were restored to our people. For who would write a history of this sort [Col. 0298B] in the midst of a most atrocious persecution? Lactantius certainly wrote the books of the *Divine Institutions* while persecution raged, at its very beginning, as may be inferred from chapters 2 and 4 of Book V; but he did not publish them, being impeded, evidently, by the necessity of circumstances and time, as he himself says at the beginning of *On the Workmanship of God*. But when peace had been granted, and every fear had been driven from Christian hearts by the beneficence of the Emperor Constantine the Great, then ecclesiastical writers, availing themselves of the indulgence of that most gracious prince, turned their minds to writing, which previously they had not dared to do.

Accordingly, Lactantius then revised the books of the *Divine Institutions*, in which certain passages occur here and there that plainly were written after the war had been calmed and extinguished. He added much, especially what is said at the beginnings of the books and in the epilogue to Constantine. Some wrongly judge these passages spurious and interpolated, so much so that Joseph Isaeus, relying on their prejudice, who issued the latest Roman edition of Lactantius, deleted everything [Col. 0298C] that is read in other editions as written to Constantine. Yet I think it cannot truly be doubted that these are Lactantius’s, since they are in the same style as his other works, and since certain expressions found there are the same as those in various passages of this history and of Lactantius’s other writings.

But undoubtedly there were two ancient editions of the *Divine Institutions*: one issued almost immediately after peace had been granted to the Church, while Lactantius was still in Bithynia; the other after the wars of Cibalae and Mardia, when he had gone to Gaul on account of Crispus, Constantine’s son. Those who used the earlier edition certainly did not have the material later added concerning Constantine; and thus it is no wonder that it is absent from certain copies.

But to return to the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, from which the occasion for discussing the time when the books of the *Divine Institutions* were written has led us aside: it is certain that the author wrote it at Nicomedia in Bithynia, where he lived throughout [Col. 0299A] the period in which persecution raged in the East; and that it was completed after the battle at Campus Serenus in Thrace, after which the Church’s peace was entire, Maximinus—an especially bitter enemy of our religion—having been overthrown and dying shortly thereafter.

This is gathered from several passages of the same history, but chiefly from the epilogue, in which the author indicates in the clearest words that he wrote this after peace had been granted to the people of God, who for ten years had been partly devastated and partly scattered. Add that he dedicated his book to Donatus, the distinguished confessor of those regions, whom he also addresses in the middle and at the end of the work. These facts indicate that they were then together, or at least not separated by any great distance. It should also be carefully observed that in this work he transcribed only those edicts issued in favour of Christians that were posted at Nicomedia; he makes no mention of others, since he naturally reports only what he himself saw posted and could therefore readily obtain.

[Col. 0299B] I see that there are various opinions concerning Lactantius’s homeland. The weaker seems to be that which maintains that he was born in the town of Firmum in Picenum because he is called Firmianus. I prefer the view that he was African. For he had Arnobius as his teacher in Africa; and when summoned by Diocletian to Nicomedia to teach rhetoric there, as he himself writes, he seems to have come from nowhere but Africa, since Jerome, in his book *On Illustrious Men*, records that Lactantius described in hexameter verse his *Hodoeporicum*—his journey—from Africa all the way to Nicomedia.

He was at Nicomedia during the persecution under Diocletian which shook the whole Church, and remained there when peace was granted. For what is said in the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* concerning the Constitution of Constantine and Licinius posted at Nicomedia, and concerning Licinius’s arrival in that city, certainly could not have been written by anyone other than one who had seen with his own eyes what he wrote.

Later, after Constantine had concluded the war of Cibalae in the year of Christ 314, on 8 October [Col. 0299C], and set out for Thrace and Macedonia, Lactantius undoubtedly came to him from Nicomedia, whether known to him already or then perhaps for the first time; afterwards, at Constantine’s command, he went to Gaul, where he instructed Crispus, Constantine’s son, in Latin literature.

The most learned François Chifflet thought that Crispus was educated by Lactantius in the year of Christ 312, at the very time, as he says, when Constantine first, and soon afterwards his mother Helena, acknowledged Christ, having been taught the mysteries of our faith by Eusebius, bishop of Besançon; and that Crispus was left at Besançon with Helena and Lactantius by Constantine when he set out for Italy against Maxentius. But the narrative from which Chifflet constructed this history is a writing of a later and inferior age and deserves no credit. Moreover, it is certain that Lactantius was still in Bithynia when war against Maxentius was being prepared, and for some time afterwards.

Lactantius therefore came to Gaul—as I see was also the opinion of the illustrious Jacobus Gothofredus—only in the year 315, when peace had been established after the battles [Col. 0299D] of Cibalae and Mardia between Constantine and Licinius, and Constantine the Great returned to Gaul. That he returned to his wife is readily inferred from Zosimus and the Epitome of Victor, where it is written that Constantine’s son, Constantine the Great’s son, recently born in the town of Arles, was made Caesar together with Crispus and Licinianus, Licinius’s son; and the Fasti of Idatius teach that this occurred on 1 March 317. For since the battle in Pannonia occurred at the end of 314, and Constantine, Constantine’s son, was born in Gaul at the beginning of 317, his father must have been in Gaul in the intervening period, and therefore have returned there after peace was made with Licinius.

On that occasion it is probable that Lactantius, the most learned man of his age, as Eusebius says, was brought by Constantine into Gaul in order to imbue Crispus with knowledge of history and of the other liberal studies. And indeed I readily agree [Col. 0300A] with the most learned Christophorus Brower and Aegidius Bucherius, who state as certain that Lactantius spent his final old age at Trier while he devoted himself to Crispus’s education, and there probably composed the books of the *Divine Institutions* for the Emperor Constantine.

But Chifflet, led by an honourable and becoming love of his native country, distributes this honour equally between the people of Trier and those of Besançon: conceding to Bucherius that Crispus was educated by Lactantius at Trier, but wishing this to have happened at Besançon as well. Yet that conjecture has absolutely no foundation beyond the goodwill of that most illustrious and excellent man, and his inclination toward his fellow citizens of Besançon.

Moreover, Lactantius himself, writing to Constantine at the beginning of Book I of the *Divine Institutions*, teaches that he was elsewhere than in Licinius’s empire when Licinius appeared openly hostile to Christ’s religion, and hence that he was then in Gaul. “For the evils,” he says, “which still rage against the just in other parts of the earth, the same omnipotent [Col. 0300B] God will repay the more violently, the later he does so.” Licinius began openly to persecute Christians in the year 320, as most learned men have shown by certain arguments. From this it may be inferred that Lactantius was still alive at that time.

Indeed, he himself seems to show at the end of Book IV of the *Divine Institutions* that he lived beyond that year, where, among the various sects of heretics, he counts Arians also. For, since they did not become fully known throughout the world until after the Council of Nicaea had been held, Lactantius appears to have survived that council, if the reading is genuine.

I know that the most illustrious and learned Michael Thomasius removed the name of the Arians from that passage in the edition of Lactantius’s works which he prepared, and that Joseph Isaeus supported his opinion. But since they have only a few old books asserting and defending that position, while the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius testified that nine Vatican manuscripts and two from the Vallicellian Library contain this clause; [Col. 0300C] since I further knew of one manuscript from Bologna, seen by both Thomasius and Latinus Latinius; also of four Royal Library manuscripts, or Colbert manuscripts, and of the old editions—that is, those preceding Thomasius’s edition; since, I say, I knew that so many old codices and editions mention Arians here, and that very few old copies were produced in which this name was absent, I was not unwilling to agree with Baronius in criticizing Thomasius for corrupting Lactantius’s text against the testimony of almost all ancient manuscripts and editions, without adding any reason, even a slight one, why he had done so.

But now, reflecting that the codices which mix Arians among the heretics mentioned by Lactantius are not particularly old, whereas the two very ancient and excellent Royal Library manuscripts numbered 3735 and 3736, as well as that very ancient manuscript from Bologna used by Thomasius, make no mention of Arians, I am compelled to doubt whether Thomasius’s emendation should be retained against the testimony of so many manuscript copies. For it is certain that in matters of this kind the multitude of witnesses, who may have been corrupted and falsified through scribes’ ignorance and recklessness, must sometimes yield to the worth and authority of a few more ancient witnesses.

However the matter stands, since it is established that Lactantius was Crispus’s teacher in his extreme old age, he must have died around the time when Constantine celebrated the twentieth anniversary of his reign. Whether he died at Augusta Treverorum [Col. 0300D] or elsewhere is not known. I am strongly inclined to agree with Bucherius that he both died and was buried in that city, since his very advanced old age, which Jerome teaches that he spent in Gaul, readily persuades one of this.

**Lucius Caecilius.** In the old codex the title of this work is simply phrased: “Of Lucius (or rather Lycius) Caecilius. The book to Donatus the confessor, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, begins.” [Col. 0301A] That this is Lactantius, whose seven books of the *Divine Institutions* and certain other smaller works survive, is supported by arguments so numerous and manifest that the matter seems to lie beyond all controversy. For the style is wholly Lactantian, as competent judges of such matters will readily recognize; the author also inserts Virgilian verses into this work from time to time, as Lactantius customarily does; finally, most of what is read there is found almost word for word in his other books, as we shall note in the appropriate places below. Add the authority of Saint Jerome, who, in his catalogue of illustrious men, lists among Lactantius’s works one book *On Persecution*—namely, this work of ours.

Nor should anyone be troubled because Lactantius is called not Caecilius but Caelius in editions circulating among learned men, as though it could thereby be inferred that Lucius Caecilius, author of this book, was different from Lactantius. For although it is true that he is always called Caelius in editions bearing his forename, as all the later editions do, nevertheless [Col. 0301B] in the Roman edition of 1470, prepared by John Andrew, bishop of Aleria, he is called simply Lactantius Firmianus, without any forename. And in manuscript 1975 of the Colbert Library, containing the received writings of Lactantius, he is explicitly called in the title “Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius”; while in manuscript 3736 of the Royal Library, “Caecilius Firmianus.”

Indeed, since I see him called merely Firmianus in manuscripts 3737, 3738, and 3740 of the Royal Library, and in manuscripts 3573, 4095, and 4495 of the Colbert Library, and also in the excellent and very ancient manuscript copy of Oxford University, I am readily led to believe that most old copies of his writings have neither the forename Caelius nor Caecilius, and nevertheless that his true name was Caecilius. For he is consistently so called in the title of this history in Royal Library manuscript 3736 and in Colbert manuscript 1975, as we have noted.

Although, it must be admitted, “L. Caelius Firmianus” is always written in Royal manuscript 3735, which we have said is extremely ancient and excellent. Why the true name of Lactantius—last among the four assigned to him—was omitted in the title of the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* and in that Royal manuscript must, as Sirmond observed in a similar case concerning Sidonius, be attributed to the scribe’s carelessness. Not wishing, in the interest of brevity, to write all the names of this author, he ignorantly chose, instead of the last name, which was his proper one, the name that occurred first.

**To Donatus, the distinguished confessor of those times**, who endured torture nine times for Christ’s name, being held in prison for six years, from which he was released in the final period of Galerius Maximianus, as is read below in chapters 16 and 35 of this work. Lactantius also dedicated to him the book *On the Wrath of God*, written after peace had been divinely granted.

**On the deaths of the persecutors.** In Jerome one reads simply that Lactantius wrote one book *On Persecution*. But we have retained the reading of the old manuscript, because it is manifest that the author’s purpose and plan was to describe the miserable ends of those who had stirred up persecution against Christians. He used *deaths* (*mortes*) as Cicero does in Book II of *On Ends*: “The deaths of commanders are glorious.” Likewise, at the end of Book I of the *Tusculan Disputations*: “Deaths endured for one’s country are ordinarily regarded as not only glorious to rhetoricians but blessed.” Tacitus, *Annals* XI: “And many deaths were carried out at Messalina’s command”; and Book XIV: “The deaths of illustrious men follow.” The same author, *Histories* III: “The varied manner of those perishing, and every image of deaths”; likewise, Book I: “Their ends equal to the praised deaths of the ancients.” And Statius, in Book IX of the *Thebaid*:

> And he bore away forsaken deaths without burial.

And shortly afterwards:

> There is no need further to try arms and waste deaths.

Saint Augustine, Letter 68: “Moreover, if they voluntarily inflict upon themselves any [Col. 0302A] deaths, they wish them to be odious to us.” The same author, Book I against Gaudentius, chapter 6: “Such is the innocence of Donatus’s party: that you do this, adding your own deaths, which you assert that at Carthage also, to our discredit, you did concerning basilicas that were yours, as far as you could and with whom you could, without your own deaths.”

# Chapter I

**God raised up rulers.** That is, Constantine and Licinius, who, when Lactantius wrote this, had granted peace to the Church; persecution against our people had not yet been stirred up by Licinius.

**“Who struggled against them,” or “who opposed them.”** The old book reads *illustrati* (“illuminated”), which we altered because the emendation was certain.

**“The holy temples overthrown.”** In the first edition I wrote that chapter 13 of this book and chapter 11 of Book V of the *Divine Institutions* show that the reference here is to the church at Nicomedia, destroyed by Diocletian and Maximian. Later, when I saw that the most illustrious and learned Gisbert Cuper had offered another interpretation of this passage, which seems consonant with the truth, I gladly adopted it. He thinks that Christian religion in general should be understood here, since the ancients, after the apostle, commonly call the body of Christians the temple of God, as we observe in our note on chapter 2.

**“They poured out guilty souls.”** Namely Diocletian, Maximian Herculius, Galerius Maximianus, and Maximinus Daza, whose dreadful deaths are described in this book.

**“The power and majesty.”** Lactantius, *Institutions*, Book IV, chapter 26: “to set forth the power and majesty of the one God”; and Book VI, chapter 9: “he recounts the power and majesty of the one God.”

# Chapter II
After the tenth day. This passage above all confirms that this book is genuinely Lactantius’s. For he himself, in Book IV of the *Divine Institutions*, ch. 10, speaking of the Jews, says: “From then on they had tetrarchs down to Herod, who lived under the rule of Tiberius Caesar; in whose fifteenth year—that is, in the consulship of the two Gemini—the Jews crucified Christ on the tenth day before the Kalends of April.” Thus it is read in all ancient manuscript copies of Lactantius, in the Roman edition of 1470, in the Venetian edition of 1521, and in Paul of Middelburg’s *Paulina*. Xystus Betuleius, however, maintains that the better editions of Lactantius read “on the seventh day before the Kalends,” and attacks that Roman edition which has “on the tenth.” But in 1650 Josephus Isaeus at last restored the ancient reading to that passage, on the authority of a great many old copies; and it is now confirmed by this further work of Lactantius. See, moreover, the notes of the most learned Michael Thomasius on that passage in Book IV of the *Divine Institutions*.

After the tenth day. In Book IV of the *Institutions* one reads “before the tenth day.” Yet this discrepancy entails no contradiction. For *post diem* [after the day] and *ante diem* [before the day] have the same force, as Paulus observes in the law *Anniculus*, 132, Digest, *On the Signification of Words*: “A child of a year old is lost if he dies on the last day of the year.” And ordinary usage declares this to be so: “the tenth day before the Kalends,” “the tenth day after the Kalends.” But this passage of Paulus is not without difficulty. For Marcellus Francolinus, in his treatise *On the Time of the Canonical Hours*, ch. 73, contends that here the words *post diem* cannot denote one of the days before the Kalends, but rather the tenth day after the Kalends—that is, the ninth day of the month—and he attempts to support this with several examples. In vain. For since Lactantius, recounting the same event in two passages, says in one “before the tenth day” and in the other “after the tenth day,” it is evident that the expressions must have the same meaning. Moreover, the Romans never reckoned from the Kalends the days following the Kalends, but only those preceding them, as is plain to anyone moderately learned.

[Col. 0303A] He gathered the disciples. Lactantius, *Institutions*, Book IV, ch. 20: “When the disciples had again been gathered together, he opened to them the writings of Holy Scripture—that is, the mysteries of the prophets—which could in no way be understood before he suffered.” And in ch. 15: “So too the utterances of the Prophets, though read by the Jewish people for fifteen hundred years and more, were nevertheless not understood until Christ had interpreted them both by word and by deeds.”

He appointed. Lactantius, ibid., ch. 21: “Having arranged for his disciples the preaching of the Gospel and of his name, a cloud suddenly enveloped him and bore him up into heaven.”

For 25 years. Lactantius says that the Apostles, including Matthias and Paul, who had been added to the others after the death of Christ the Lord, preached the Gospel throughout the whole earth for twenty-five years, down to the beginning of Nero’s reign; and that Peter went to Rome while Nero ruled there. Although Eusebius later held otherwise than some ancient writers concerning Peter’s journey to the city of Rome, it is highly probable that this was then the common opinion, since Lactantius raises no controversy on the matter. Perhaps, then, from these twenty-five years—which equally concern the preaching of all the Apostles—arose the opinion that assigns to the holy Apostle Peter twenty-five years in the Roman see, an opinion held by certain ancient writers and by an innumerable host of modern ones.

Certainly, although I judge that some have vainly and superfluously denied his arrival in the city of Rome—a fact established by the most illustrious testimonies of the ancients—I nevertheless have great doubts about the date, seeing how many and how great difficulties attend the opinion of those who maintain that he came to Rome under Claudius. They have been compelled to double his journey to the city and likewise to invent a double contest with Simon Magus: first in Claudius’s time, then under Nero’s rule. How absurd this is, since no ancient writer has transmitted it in written memory, is clear to those skilled in these matters. For what a later author puts forward without the authority of any older source is disregarded, as the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius observed.

Accordingly, if it were permissible to depart from the common opinion, deeply rooted in human minds, I should gladly prefer the Lactantian view: that is, I would readily concede that Peter preached the Gospel at Rome, not under Tiberius Claudius, as is commonly thought, but under Nero Claudius. Once this, in my opinion most true, view is established, the entire dispute at once comes to rest, without any detriment to the authority of the Roman Pontiff. For it was not a long sequence of years during which Peter was bishop of Rome that established the primacy of that Church, but the person of Peter, who placed his chair there and made it firm and confirmed it by his blood.

They laid foundations. That is, they set them down, as Lactantius himself wrote in the passage cited a little earlier: “But the disciples, scattered through the provinces, everywhere laid the foundations of the Church, themselves also performing great and almost incredible miracles in the name of their divine master.” Writers on agriculture use *mittere* [to cast, lay] for *ponere* [to place], as the most distinguished Nicolaus Rigaltus shows at length in his *Glosses*.

He turned many to righteousness. That is, to the worship of the true God, as Lactantius says in Book VII of the *Institutions*, ch. 17. The same author, Book V, ch. 7: “Righteousness has indeed been restored to the earth, but assigned to few; and it is nothing other than the pious and religious worship of the one God.” Lactantius regularly employs this word to signify the Christian religion in this book and in his other writings. Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History*, Book II, speaking of Romans gathered to hear Paul: “When they had understood the truth, and had been moved by the miracles of the Apostles, which they then frequently performed, they gave themselves to the worship of God.”

A faithful and stable temple. Namely, the Church, which is the true temple of God—not in walls, but in the heart and faith of those who believe in him and are called *fideles* [the faithful]—as Lactantius says in Book IV of the *Institutions*, ch. 14. In the following chapter he calls the Church [Col. 0304A] “the eternal and immortal temple of God”; he also repeats this in ch. 2 of the book *On the Anger of God*. Hence below, in this very book, concerning Nero: “He sprang forth to destroy the heavenly temple.” And in ch. 15: “For Constantine, lest he should seem to dissent from the injunctions of his forefathers, allowed the meeting-houses—that is, the walls, which could be restored—to be torn down; but he preserved unharmed the true temple of God, which is in human beings.” Hence, in Book IV of the *Institutions*, ch. 10, he says that the Son of God had necessarily to descend to earth in order to establish a temple for God and teach righteousness.

He established it firmly. Lactantius, *Institutions*, Book VII, ch. 10: “He established for himself a permanent dwelling.”

The first of all to persecute. Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 5: “Consult your records. There you will find that Nero was the first to rage with the sword of Caesar against this sect, then especially flourishing at Rome. Yet we even glory in such an inaugurator of our condemnation.” Petilianus, bishop of Constantine or Cirta, of the Donatist party, in Augustine, Book II *Against the Letters of Petilianus*, ch. 92: “I shall pass over Nero, who was the first to persecute Christians.” Sulpicius Severus, Book II, speaking of Nero: “He, not to say the vilest of kings, but of all human beings and even of savage beasts, proved worthy to be the first to begin persecution against Christians.”

That he might have no place of burial. Suetonius, on the contrary, teaches that Nero was buried at an expense of two hundred thousand, and that his remains were placed in the tomb of the Domitii, visible from the Campus Martius and situated on the hill of the gardens; and that for a long time there were persons who adorned his tomb with spring and summer flowers.

Reserved alive. Some ancient persons were persuaded that Nero had not died but was still living, and would come before the end of the age; and that he himself would either be the Antichrist, or would rage in the West at the same time as the Antichrist in the East, as Casaubon observed on Suetonius. On this subject see also the *Ecclesiastical Annals* of the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius. But Lactantius held another view: he declares that those who think so are delirious. Therefore Josephus Isaeus’s conjecture is wholly false. In his notes on Book VII of the *Divine Institutions*, ch. 16, he suspects Lactantius to have held that the most powerful king who will be established ruler of all at the end of the world would be Nero; and on that account he charges Lactantius with error.

The Sibyl speaking. Lactantius customarily cites the Sibylline books in this manner, although he knew that they belonged not to one Sibyl but to several. Thus he himself says in Book I of the *Divine Institutions*, ch. 6: “There is one book for each [Sibyl]; but because they bear the name Sibyl, they are believed to belong to one woman. Yet we too shall speak of ‘the Sibyl’ collectively whenever we need to employ their testimonies.” There are, however, two passages in the commonly circulated Sibylline Oracles to which I think Lactantius referred here. The first occurs in Book V:

> “A mother-killing man will come from the ends of the earth,  
> A fugitive, pondering a sharp device;  
> He will overthrow the whole earth and rule over all things.”

Thus Sebastian Castellio translated it into Latin:

> “A certain slayer also of his mother, from the ends of the world,  
> Will come, a fugitive, breathing monstrous threats and raging;  
> He will lay waste all lands and conquer all things.”

The second passage, in Book VIII of the Sibylline Oracles, reads:

> “. . . so that, when he returns,  
> The fugitive slayer of his mother, coming from the ends of the earth,  
> Bestowing these things upon all, will make Asia greatly rich.”

> “So, when the fugitive slayer of his mother returns  
> From the furthest edge of the world,  
> Bestowing these things on all, he will richly enrich Asia.”

## CHAPTER III

Another no less great. That is, Domitian, called “the bald Nero” [Col. 0305A] by Juvenal, whom Tertullian in the *Apology*, ch. 5, calls “a portion of Nero in cruelty,” and Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, ch. 17, “the successor of Nero’s impiety and hatred toward God.” Tertullian: “Domitian also had attempted it—a portion of Nero in cruelty—but, being a human being, he readily checked what he had begun, even restoring those whom he had banished.” Thus the old editions and two ancient manuscripts of the Colbert Library read. Later editors preferred *qua* [“whereby”]; let others judge how well. Moreover, Francis Zephyrus interprets Tertullian’s statement concerning the Christians restored from banishment as meaning that Domitian, since he had not cast off all humanity and saw that Christians did not deserve exile or another penalty, checked his attack and himself restored those whom he had already banished to islands and various other places.

I once thought this false, since it is clear from Dio and Clement of Alexandria, and also from Lactantius, that Christians were not recalled from the islands before Nerva’s reign. But I now think this contradiction can be reconciled thus: Domitian did indeed recall Christians who had been transported to islands or other places of exile, but they could not enjoy his clemency before Nerva’s reign, because Domitian seems to have died immediately after granting it. This reconciliation, moreover, is not mine but that of the most learned Henry Dodwell.

It was erased. Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book I, ch. 12: “Domitian had appropriated October for his own name; but it was decided that, as an ill-omened designation, it should be erased from every bronze inscription and stone.”

He had constructed many remarkable works. Suetonius, on Domitian: “He restored many very great and magnificent buildings consumed by fire, including the Capitol, which had burned again; but all were restored under his name alone, with no memory whatever of their former founder.”

Nor his images nor inscriptions. Eusebius says the same, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, ch. 20. Suetonius: “The Senate, on the other hand, rejoiced so greatly that, when the curia had been filled in a rush, it could not refrain from lacerating the dead man with the most insulting and bitter kind of acclamations. They even ordered ladders brought in, and his shields and images taken down before their eyes and dashed to the ground on the spot; finally, they decreed that his inscriptions everywhere should be erased and all memory of him abolished.” See also Xiphilinus on Nerva, and Procopius of Caesarea, *Secret History*, p. 37 of the Lyons edition.

The Church restored. Dio, as preserved in Xiphilinus, relates that Nerva acquitted all who had been charged with impiety toward the gods and recalled the exiles to their homeland; moreover, by edict he prohibited anyone henceforth from being accused either of impiety or of the Jewish sect—thus they then called the Christian religion. On that occasion the Apostle John, who had been banished by Domitian to the island of Patmos, was released from exile and returned to Ephesus, as Eusebius records from Clement of Alexandria, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, ch. 33.

Good emperors. Although pagans. Lactantius, at the end of Book VII of the *Divine Institutions*, addressing Constantine: “Since you alone of all men have arisen to furnish the foremost examples of virtue and holiness, by which you have not merely equaled the glory of ancient rulers—whom fame nevertheless counts among the good—but even, what is greatest, surpassed it. They perhaps resembled the just merely by nature. For one who does not know God, the governor of the universe, may attain a likeness of justice, but cannot attain justice itself.” For good rulers who both allowed our people freedom to believe, employed their service in the palace and provinces, and raised them to the highest dignities, see Eusebius at the beginning of Book VIII of the *Ecclesiastical History*.

No corner of the earth. Lactantius, *Institutions*, Book IV, ch. 24: “For since he who is suspended on a cross is both visible to all and higher than the rest, the cross was chosen, signifying that he would be so conspicuous and so exalted that all nations from every part of the world would flock alike to know and worship him. Finally, no people is so barbarous, no region so remote, that either his passion or the sublimity of his majesty is unknown to it.”

No nation, finally. An old manuscript reads: “No nation of God, finally.” But we have removed the word *God*, which was altogether superfluous here. The passage from Lactantius just cited confirms our correction.

## CHAPTER IV

The imperial summit. Lactantius, in the epilogue of Book VII to Constantine: “The providence of the highest divinity has raised you to the imperial summit.”

Against the Carpi. Constantine, in his *Oration to the Assembly of the Saints*, ch. 24, calls them Getae or Goths; the author of the *Alexandrian Chronicle*, Franks; Zosimus, in Book I of his *Histories*, Scythians—whom Cuspinianus also interprets as such. Indeed Constantine writes in the same oration that Decius perished in the Scythian plains. This matter can be reconciled as follows: because the Carpi and Goths had the same origin, and because both had settlements by the river Ister, as Zosimus teaches, their names could easily be interchanged; thus one writer may refer to the Goths what elsewhere is said of the Carpi and Scythians. I would have the same understood concerning the Franks, who were of the same origin as the Carpi and Goths.

Nor burial. The epitome of Victor: “In barbarian territory, amid confused masses of troops, he was drowned in the floodwaters of a marsh, so that not even his body could be found.” The author of the *Alexandrian Chronicle* relates the event very differently, writing that Decius, together with his son, was slain at Abrittus by one of the leaders. Eusebius in the *Chronicle*: “Decius with his son is killed at Abrittus”; see there the notes of Joseph Scaliger.

## CHAPTER V

Valerian. Trebellius Pollio records remarkable things about Valerian’s moderation, gentleness, and other outstanding virtues [Col. 0306C]. These are also confirmed by Eusebius, who in Book VII of the *Ecclesiastical History*, ch. 10, especially commends him because he was exceedingly gentle and kindly toward Christians; and adds that none of the preceding emperors—not even those who are said to have been openly Christian—embraced our people with such humanity and goodwill as Valerian showed at the beginning of his reign. His entire household was filled with Christians, so that it seemed to be God’s Church. But later, utterly changed from what he had been, he raged most cruelly against Christians; and God’s hand swiftly followed, grievously afflicting him.

To bow the Roman for himself. *Acts of Saint Pontius the Martyr*, ch. 24: “The emperor Valerian, having been led captive by Shapur, king of the Persians, received, not by the sword but by mockery, the reward merited by his deeds on every day of his life. Whenever King Shapur wished to mount his horse, Valerian did not offer him his hands, but, bending his back and placing the king’s foot upon his neck, gave his limbs to the horse.” Valerian therefore did not perform for Shapur the office of a groom; rather, he plainly acted as a footstool or ladder for him as he mounted his horse, as Salmasius rightly observed from this passage in the *Acts of Saint Pontius*—whose author he identifies as Eutropius—in his notes on Trebellius Pollio, p. 276.

His son as emperor. Namely Gallienus, of whom the same Pollio relates that, when he learned of his father’s captivity, he rejoiced at it, so far was he from avenging it. Trebellius adds shortly afterward: “And although very many mourned his father’s captivity, he rejoiced beyond measure, under the appearance of decorum, because his father seemed to have been deceived by devotion to virtue.”

His skin was stripped away. That is, Valerian’s. The emperor Constantine confirms this story in his *Oration to the Assembly of the Saints*, ch. 24: “You also, Valerian, when you had displayed the same cruelty toward the servants of God, set the righteous judgment of God before the eyes of all. Captured by enemies and led about in chains with purple cloak and the rest of your imperial attire, you finally furnished an everlasting spectacle, a trophy of your misfortune: Shapur, king of the Persians, had your skin stripped off and ordered it preserved.” This passage receives illumination from Lactantius. See further what the most distinguished Henry Valesius notes there.

For the memorial of triumph. This is the trophy which Constantine, in Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, Book IV, ch. 11, writes was so greatly boasted of by the Persians before their king Shapur.

## CHAPTER VI

Mad and headlong. Flavius Vopiscus: “Aurelian, which cannot be denied, was a severe, savage, bloodthirsty emperor.” Eutropius, Book IX, on the same man: “A man powerful in war, but of excessive spirit and rather inclined to cruelty.”

He was slain. The same Constantine states it elegantly in the same ch. 24: “You likewise, Aurelian, torch of every vice—by what immediate and manifest vengeance of the divine power, while driven by madness you traversed Thrace, were you struck down in the middle of the public road and filled the furrows of the public embankment with impious blood!”

At Coenophrurium. Between Heraclea and Byzantium. Flavius Vopiscus, *On the Deified Aurelian*: “But while he was traveling, at the posting-station of Coenophrurium, which lies between Heraclea and Byzantium, he was killed through the malice of his secretary and by the hand of Mucapor.” See Eutropius, Book IX.

Through false suspicion. The same Vopiscus recounts that story at length; consult him.

## CHAPTER VII

Avarice. The same Vopiscus, *On Numerian*: “When Diocletian, while still serving in lesser positions, was staying at a certain inn among the Tungri in Gaul, and was settling the account of his daily board with a certain Druidess, and she said, ‘Diocletian, you are excessively avaricious, excessively sparing,’ Diocletian is said to have replied in jest, not seriously: ‘I shall be generous when I am emperor.’”

Three partners in the rule. Maximian, surnamed Herculius, in the year of Christ 285; Constantius, surnamed Chlorus, and Galerius Maximianus, surnamed Armentarius, in 293. “Four rulers of the world,” says Vopiscus in *Carinus*, “strong, wise, kind, and very generous, thinking as one in the state.” But these words were written of emperors still alive, and flattery lay beneath them, as is plain from the emperor Julian’s book *The Caesars*. The *Alexandrian Chronicle* states that Diocletian shared the empire with Maximian Herculius in the third year of his reign, and that Maximian Jovius and Constantius were admitted into partnership in the empire at Nicomedia on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, in the ninth year of Diocletian’s reign—that is, in the year of Christ 292, according to Baronius’s interpretation, or rather 293. But later we shall discuss the beginnings of Maximian Herculius and the others. For now it will suffice to note that the author of the *Alexandrian Chronicle* is gravely mistaken when he relates that Maximian Jovius and Constantius were made Caesars on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June; for it is beyond all controversy that they were raised to the imperial summit on the Kalends of March.

The enormity of the *indictions*. That is, taxes. Salvian, Book V, p. 105 of our second and third editions: “For by what else did the Bacaudae come into being than by our iniquities, the wickedness of judges, and the proscriptions and plunderings of those who converted the name of public exaction into profit for their own gain and made tax-assessments their own booty?” And p. 107: “New obligations are decreed for them; new tax-assessments are decreed.” Likewise p. 108, at the end: “For just as they burden the poor under the weight of new tax-assessments, so they support them by the aid of new remedies; just as those of lesser means are especially crushed by new taxes, so they are especially relieved by new remedies.”

The fields were abandoned. The same Salvian, p. 103: “But indeed, what is this, how customary among the Romans, that they proscribe one another by exactions?” Likewise p. 104: “Meanwhile the poor are devastated, widows groan, orphans are trampled down—to such a degree that many of them, even those born of no obscure family [Col. 0308A] and liberally educated, flee to the enemy, lest they die from the affliction of public persecution”; and what follows.

*Rationales*. That is, the procurators of the emperors, whose responsibility it was to claim for the treasury, in the provinces, escheated and vacant property, as the most learned Henry Valesius observed on Ammianus Marcellinus and Eusebius. *Rationales* were appropriately sent at this time because much property lay vacant owing to the abandonment of fields.

For furnishing soldiers. That is, for providing pay to soldiers. For in civil law *exhibere* means to supply maintenance and the other necessities of life, as in law I, Digest, *On the Office of the Prefect of the City*, and law XXXIV, Digest, *On Affairs Conducted*. So too in canon law. In Book III of the *Extravagantes communes*, under the title *On Rents*, there is a constitution of Benedict XII in which *exhibere* is used in the sense of *procurare* [to provide], as the gloss there notes—that is, to furnish sustenance. Indeed, in Acts ch. 8 it is read in the same sense: “Now in those places there were estates belonging to the chief man of the island, named Publius, who, receiving us, entertained us kindly for three days.”

The law concerning the price of things for sale. Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXII, p. 226 of Henry Valesius’s edition, speaks very aptly to this passage, when discussing the emperor Julian: “Among his principal and serious actions, however, this seemed superfluous: from a love of popularity undertaken without any sound reason, he sought cheapness in goods for sale, which, when regulated other than it ought to be, can sometimes produce scarcity and famine.” The ancients called it *vilitas* [cheapness] when goods cost little, as Valesius shows at length on this passage of Ammianus. Arnobius, Book I *Against the Nations*: “Very often there were the greatest yields of grain, and such cheapness and abundance of goods that all commerce was astonished, the established scale of prices having been overthrown.”

The law by its own necessity. Because laws are enacted with the purpose of benefiting, not harming, as Pope Symmachus writes to Avitus, bishop of Vienne. L. Valerius, in Livy, Book XXXIV, speaking of the repeal of the Oppian law: “Who does not see that this law was written because of the poverty and distress of the state, since the money of all private persons had to be converted to public use, and that it would remain as long as the reason for writing the law remained?”

A large part of the city. Of Nicomedia, where Diocletian lived, a city which he was eager to make equal to Rome, as Lactantius will say immediately. So Constantine the Great desired to make Constantinople equal to Rome. The fragment concerning Constantius Chlorus and Constantine the Great, published by Henry Valesius after Ammianus Marcellinus, p. 475: “Constantine named Byzantium Constantinople because of the distinction of his victory; he adorned it as though it were his homeland with great cultivation, and desired it to be made equal to Rome.” Eutropius, Book X, speaking of Constantine: “He was the first to undertake to raise the city bearing his name to such a height as to make it Rome’s rival.”

Permitted by custom. From the comedy *Querolus*: “I do not easily understand what you mean by playful perjury. Yet let us pass it by, since, as I see, custom has now made it slight.” St Ambrose, [Col. 0308D] Letter 64: “Is something permitted because it is not forbidden?”

## CHAPTER VIII

His brother. These words should not be understood as though Maximian Herculius were Diocletian’s brother by nature, but rather his brother in imperial rule, as the emperor Severus elegantly says in a letter to Albinus cited by Julius Capitolinus. This followed the custom of kings, who are accustomed to call one another brothers, as the most learned Charles du Fresne shows at length on Anna Comnena, p. 274. For it is plain from the panegyric delivered by Mamertinus to Herculius that he was Diocletian’s brother not by nature but by choice, to use the words of St Ambrose in Letter 63. Mamertinus says: “You have mingled different bloods by your affections. Your brotherhood is not accidental, but chosen.” Eumenius also confirms this in his first panegyric to Constantine the Great, where, after praising Diocletian’s firmness in retaining private life, he adds: “Thus he whom that man had adopted as a brother was ashamed to imitate him.” Finally, Diocletian was a Dalmatian; Maximian was a Pannonian. Add that no historian relates that they were brothers by nature.

In the same way Galerius Maximianus, since he had been made Caesar together with Constantius, is called Constantius’s brother by Trebellius Pollio in *On the Deified Claudius*: “I have set these things down so that it may be clear to all that Constantius, a man of divine stock, a most holy Caesar, belonged also to the Augustan family and would produce from himself many Augusti—Diocletian and Maximian being safe as Augusti, together with Galerius, his brother.” Indeed, those who held the same or an equal magistracy in the state were called brothers, as is clear from St Augustine’s Letter 160.

Moreover, learned men hold varied and widely divergent opinions concerning the determination of the beginning of Maximian Herculius’s reign; Dionysius Petavius enumerates them in Book XI of *The Doctrine of Times*, ch. 31. He places it in the year of Christ 285, in which Diocletian entered upon the second year both of his tribunician power and of his empire. This most learned man infers from the fact that the anonymous author of the panegyric delivered to Maximian and Constantine affirms that Maximian experienced imperial vigils and cares for twenty years, and in his twentieth year was emperor and in his eighth consul; and also because Aurelius Victor reports that he had power for one year less than Diocletian.

Certainly, the years of Maximian’s rule follow this fixed rule, in my view: the twentieth year of his reign must coincide with his eighth consulship. Since it is certain that his eighth consulship fell in the year of Christ 304, and since from the Fasti of Idatius we know that his reign began on the Kalends of April, it follows that Diocletian made him emperor on the Kalends of April in 285, when Diocletian had already been ruling since the preceding November. For Eusebius too, in the *Chronicle*, says that Maximian was admitted to partnership in rule in Diocletian’s second year—not in Scaliger’s edition, indeed, but in three ancient manuscript copies in the Colbert Library, one of which is extremely ancient and excellent; also in that old Venetian edition, and in the edition which Arnaldus Pontacus, bishop of Bazas, issued corrected according to ancient copies.

This should not, however, be understood as though Maximian were admitted to partnership in rule after Diocletian had ruled for a full year, but in the second year after Diocletian’s elevation, counting from the Kalends of January, when they used to begin the year. The words of Aurelius Victor—that Maximian had power for one year less than Diocletian—must likewise be referred to this rule: namely, a year begun, not completed. For, as I have said, it is a fixed rule that the twentieth year of Maximian’s reign cannot be separated from his eighth consulship.

The words of the panegyric must be understood as follows: “Again, in your twentieth year as emperor and eighth as consul, Rome wished to detain you in a certain embrace, so that she seemed already to foretell and fear what came to pass.” We must say that Maximian remained at Rome after Diocletian’s departure, entered upon his consulship there on the Kalends of January 304, at the end of the nineteenth year of his reign; began his twentieth on the Kalends of April, which fell within his eighth consulship; then, on departing from Rome in the year in which he was consul for the eighth time, aroused the complaints and suspicions of Roman citizens, as though they were already foretelling and fearing what came to pass—namely, the abdication of imperial power. This occurred in the following year after his eighth consulship, when he entered upon the twenty-first year of his reign.

Thus Diocletian held imperial power only four months and twelve days longer than Maximian. He ruled for twenty years, five months, and twelve days; Maximian, however, for twenty years and one full month. Here another difficulty again presents itself: namely, whether Diocletian first made Maximian Herculius Caesar [Col. 0310A], and Augustus in the following year; or whether he was immediately styled Augustus and brother, without passing through the title of Caesar.

Some have raised this controversy from an argument drawn from Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXVII, ch. 6. There, after saying that Gratian, while still a boy, had been made partner in imperial rule by his father Valentinian—an event occurring in 367—he adds that this was done contrary to the custom established in antiquity, because Valentinian had not first made Gratian Caesar, but had immediately named him Augustus. From this, most learned men inferred that Maximian, who had been elevated to imperial rank long before Valentinian’s time, was first made Caesar by Diocletian, especially because they saw that Eutropius called him so in Book IX, where he discusses the Bacaudae subdued in Gaul.

Eutropius then adds that Diocletian, at one and the same time, made Maximian Herculius Augustus from Caesar, and made Constantius and Galerius Maximianus Caesars. But the most learned Henry de Noris, in his dissertation *On a Coin of Diocletian and Maximian*, ch. 2, maintains that Eutropius erred even in this passage, because Maximian’s inauguration as Augustus preceded the appointment of the Caesars by a full five years. Antony Pagi, likewise a most expert student of these matters, understood the force and weight of that argument; and, in order to weaken it, says that Eutropius, as is his custom, briefly summarizes events of different years. That reply would certainly be excellent if Eutropius had not there observed the chronological order.

But since he says that Maximian was made Augustus after Carausius had occupied Britain, the Quinquegentiani had harassed Africa, Narses had brought war into the East, and Achilleus had revolted in Egypt—events which Eusebius’s *Chronicle* teaches occurred in the third, fourth, and fifth years of Diocletian’s reign—it is clear that he indicates the time when Constantius and Galerius Maximianus were made Caesars. Thus the most distinguished scholar correctly observed that Eutropius erred in this passage. From this we certainly conclude that this passage has no force for establishing the opinion of those who think that Herculius was first made Caesar [Col. 0310C] and then Augustus by Diocletian.

That he was immediately named Augustus is proved by several laws issued under the consulship of Diocletian and Aristobulus, whose heading bears the names of Diocletian and Maximian as Augusti; among them is one issued on the Nones of August. Since Maximian was admitted by Diocletian to partnership in the empire in that year, and the public laws bear his name as Augustus rather than Caesar, there seems to be no room for doubt concerning his rank. Nor should those who compiled the Code of Justinian, in which those laws are reported, be accused here of negligence or error. Their diligence in making these distinctions should rather be praised.

For example, they ascribed a law issued by Diocletian when Carinus was consul for the second time and Numerian was consul—who were consuls in the year when Diocletian was elevated emperor—to Diocletian alone. But they give the heading of a law issued in the fifth consulship of Diocletian and fourth of Maximian, when Constantius and Maximian were Caesars, as follows: “The emperors Diocletian and Maximian, Augusti, and Constantius and Maximian, most noble Caesars.” Similarly, a further law issued by Constantius and Galerius Maximianus after the abdication of the former Augusti is headed not only with the names of those who issued it, but also with those of Severus and Maximian, or Maximinus, most noble Caesars, who were raised to that rank at the same time that Constantius and Galerius Maximianus attained the highest grade.

Therefore those numerous laws found to have been issued by Diocletian and Maximian as Augusti under the consulship of Diocletian and Aristobulus show that Maximian Herculius was made Augustus in the same year in which Diocletian made him a partner in his rank and power.

In both, one mind. That is, in Diocletian and Maximian: the ancients note that they were harmonious as equal partners in power, and that Maximian always complied with Diocletian in everything. Mamertinus, in the panegyric which he delivered to Maximian, says: “This concord of yours, most invincible princes, [Col. 0311A] causes Fortune also to correspond to you in so great an equality of successes. For you govern the commonwealth with one mind; nor is the great distance of places such that you do not govern, as it were, with joined right hands.” The same author, in the *Genethliacus*, says: “For we understand, most sacred princes, that a twofold agreement resides in you, though you differ in age; nor is he slower than you, but you imitate one another and emulate one another’s years. Thus you are younger, both older. Neither favours his own disposition more. Each wishes to be what his brother is.” Flavius Vopiscus, speaking in the life of Carinus about Diocletian and Maximian, Galerius Maximian and Constantius, says: “Certainly four rulers of the world—brave, wise, kind, and exceedingly generous—are of one mind in the commonwealth.” Yet I see that the Emperor Julian thought otherwise. In his book *The Caesars* he says that the gods admired their concord, but that one of them, behaving harshly and intemperately, desirous of innovations and full of treachery, and not harmonious in every respect with the tetrachord, was not admitted by Silenus [Col. 0311B] to the banquet of the emperors. It is sufficiently clear that Maximian Herculius is meant in this passage.

One [was] less avaricious than the other. These words are certainly corrupt and depraved. For Lactantius seems here to say that Herculius was more avaricious than Diocletian; yet shortly afterward he writes that Herculius was not especially careful to preserve the wealth supplied to him by Africa and Spain, the richest provinces. And below, chapter 29, speaking of the same man, he says: “He seizes the treasuries and, as is his custom, gives lavishly.” From this one may infer how much trust should be placed in the *Acts of Saint Mauritius and his Companions*, composed by Eucherius, where Herculius is described as fierce in disposition and cruel through avarice.

Distinguished scholars have attempted to emend this passage, namely Sparkius and Columbus. Columbus thinks it should be read thus: “They differed only in this: the one who had the greater avarice had more of it, but also more timidity; the one who had less had less, but more courage—not for doing good, but for doing evil.” Sparkius, however: “They differed only in this: the one with less avarice [Col. 0311C] had more [of courage] (the one with greater avarice had less, but more timidity), but more courage—not for doing good, but for doing evil.” He further reports that the very learned Bishop of Asaph considered that it should be read: “the one with less avarice had more, but more timidity; the one with greater avarice had less, but more courage.”

Neither of these emendations satisfies me. Yet if one of them had to be accepted, I should prefer the one which we said was Sparkius’s; but only if it were read simply as we have printed it, except that *avaritiae* should be restored in place of *avaritia*. In that case the passage should be understood as follows. Diocletian was indeed so avaricious that, in his insatiable greed, he never wished his treasures to diminish; rather, he continually amassed extraordinary wealth and largesses, so that what he stored away might be kept whole and untouched. Maximian too was avaricious, but not so careful in guarding his wealth; and therefore he may be called more avaricious than Diocletian, because, while squandering his resources, he was compelled daily to devise new means and new arts of exacting and amassing money [Col. 0311D]—perhaps for this reason those *Acts of Saint Mauritius* written by Eucherius call him cruel in avarice.

It is equally plain that the timidity there attributed to one of the emperors must apply to Diocletian. Thus far, I think, everything can fit properly. Afterwards, however, something is lacking, as I judge, to complete the comparison. For what follows certainly does not pertain to Diocletian, but to Maximian.

Wealthy senators. Following, evidently, the example of the divine Aurelian, of whom Vopiscus writes in his life: “He is further said to have been of such cruelty that he would lay a fabricated charge of conspiracy and usurpation upon many senators, so that he might more easily put them to death.”

Their eyes should be gouged out. Lactantius, *Institutes*, book VII, chapter 26, says of Rome: “The God of heaven must be entreated and worshipped by us—if indeed His decrees and determinations can be delayed—that that abominable tyrant may not come sooner than we think, a man who would undertake so great a crime and gouge out that light [Col. 0312A] at whose extinction the world itself is destined to fall.” Mamertinus, speaking of this same Roman Senate in the birthday panegyric for Maximian, writes: “Rome herself also, mistress of nations, uplifted by the immeasurable joy of your nearness, sent forth the lights of her Senate.”

Constantius. Surnamed Chlorus, father of Constantine the Great, a prince most excellent and most kind—as he is deservedly called in an unpublished ancient inscription from Nicomedia. Some years ago the most distinguished John Vaillant, royal antiquarian, copied it in that city from an ancient stone found in the courtyard of the New Mosque, and most graciously shared it with me. It reads thus:

> TO THE MOST EXCELLENT  
> AND MOST KIND PRINCE,  
> FLAVIUS VALERIUS  
> CONSTANTIUS, MOST NOBLE CAESAR,  
> GERMANICUS MAXIMUS, CONSUL.  
> THE COLONY OF THE NICOMEDIANS,  
> DEVOTED TO HIS DIVINITY AND MAJESTY.

[Col. 0312B] This inscription was erected after the victory won by Constantius over the Germans or Alamanni, after he had been called *Germanicus*, in A.D. 294, when he and Galerius Maximian were consuls. Eutropius speaks of this victory in book IX as follows: “At the same time Constantius Caesar fought in Gaul near Langres. Within one day he experienced adverse and favourable fortune. For when the barbarians suddenly attacked, he was forced by so urgent a necessity to take refuge inside the city that, the gates having been closed, he was hauled up onto the wall by ropes. Yet scarcely five hours later, when his army arrived, he killed about sixty thousand Alamanni.” If anyone wishes to assign the title *Germanicus* added to Constantius to the period after the defeat of the Franks, that opinion too may be sound.

## CHAPTER IX

Maximian. His personal name was Galerius, his surname Armentarius (“the Herdsman”). He was Diocletian’s son-in-law, because he had married his daughter Valeria, a woman most chaste [Col. 0312C] and most unfortunate. But we shall speak more fully of her later.

This beast. Lactantius commonly calls the persecutors of Christians by this name. He gives the reason for this designation in book V of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 11: “What Caucasus, what India, what Hyrcania ever nourished beasts so savage, so bloodthirsty? For the rage of every wild animal rages only until its belly is filled; hunger once assuaged, it immediately rests. That is the true beast, at whose single command black blood is shed everywhere, cruel mourning everywhere, terror everywhere, and the image of death in countless forms. No one can adequately describe the savagery of so great a monster, which, though lying in one place, rages throughout the entire world with iron teeth; and it not only tears apart human limbs, but crushes the very bones and rages even against ashes, lest any place for burial remain.”
