The distinguished Ezechiel Spanheim understood that this passage had been found through the aid of our index, in his notes on the *Caesars* of the Emperor Julian, p. 52. There, after setting out the words of Lactantius explained here [Col. 0312D], he adds that Lactantius somewhere gives the reason why he calls those emperors beasts. It would not be an unreasonable conjecture to suppose that these words too are directed against Galerius Maximian, a most cruel man, whom Lactantius and other writers call the author of the persecution stirred up against Christians, as we shall observe below. On the same grounds Sulpicius Severus, in book II of his *Sacred History*, calls Nero “the filthiest of savage beasts”; and Victor, in book V on the Vandal persecution, likewise calls King Huneric a beast.

His mother. Romula, of whom shortly.

New Dacia. That is, Aurelian’s Dacia: namely, the part of Moesia into which Aurelian had transferred the peoples whom he had led away from Trajan’s Dacia. That region had been lost under Gallienus, but brought back under Roman rule by Aurelian, and afterwards abandoned by him again because he despaired of retaining it. The Romans removed from it were settled in central Moesia, as Eutropius relates in book IX. [Col. 0313A] Flavius Vopiscus, in the life of the divine Aurelian, says: “When he saw Illyricum devastated and Moesia lost, he abandoned the province of Dacia, established by Trajan beyond the Danube, together with its army and provincials, despairing that it could be retained; and he settled the peoples removed from it in Moesia, calling it his own Dacia, which now divides the two Moesias.” Therefore Romula, Galerius’s mother, who was from beyond the Danube, had undoubtedly fled into New Dacia.

Having crossed the river. That is, the Danube, where the boundary between the two Dacias of that period had been established.

A huge body. Eusebius relates facts consistent with Lactantius in *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, chapter 16, and in book I of the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 55: Galerius Maximian, even before the illness by which he died, had grown through excessive consumption of food into an enormous mass of fat.

Through Armenia. Greater Armenia, as Sextus Rufus teaches. [Col. 0313B] There were therefore two Armenias, separated from one another by the river Euphrates. Lesser Armenia bordered Cappadocia; Greater Armenia lay adjacent to the Persian kingdom. Thus, when war was being prepared in Greater Armenia, the armies were far from Nicomedia, and Diocletian was therefore secure from fear of the Persians.

Sextus Rufus accordingly relates that Maximian Caesar, after being defeated by the Persians in the first engagement, scarcely obtained from Diocletian permission to try the fortune of Mars again with an army reconstituted from the frontier forces of Dacia. In Greater Armenia the emperor himself reconnoitred the enemy with two cavalrymen; then, arriving unexpectedly at the enemy camp with twenty-five thousand men, he suddenly attacked innumerable Persian ranks and slaughtered them to extermination. Narses, king of the Persians, escaped. His wife and daughters were captured and kept under the strictest protection of their chastity. In admiration for this, the Persians acknowledged Roman superiority not only in arms but also in morals; they restored Mesopotamia together with the five districts beyond the Tigris. This is a remarkable passage, deserving transcription here.

[Col. 0313C] Narses having been routed. Henry Valesius argues at length in his notes on Eusebius, p. 170, that these events occurred in A.D. 298; consult him. Yet it must be admitted that the victory of Galerius over the Persians is expressly dated to the seventeenth year of Diocletian’s reign in that excellent and most ancient Eusebian Chronicle of the Colbert Library; whereas the old Venetian edition assigns it to the fourteenth year. The triumph for the defeat of Narses was celebrated at Rome at the time of the twentieth anniversary festivities, in A.D. 303, as we shall show below at chapter 17.

He resisted the title of Caesar. He was not the only man who preferred possessing imperial power to awaiting it. Julian Caesar followed his example: not content with the title of Caesar, he both wished and permitted himself to be called Augustus. When this was reported to the Emperor Constantius, he resolved, as Ammianus Marcellinus relates in book XX, to dispatch his quaestor Leontius swiftly into Gaul with letters to Julian, ordering him—if he cared for his own safety and that of his associates—to lay aside his swelling arrogance [Col. 0313D] and keep within the authority of Caesar. But Julian resisted, asserting, as Victor’s *Epitome* relates, that under the title of the lofty imperial office he would obey much more dutifully.

Diocles before his accession. Below, chapter 19: “Diocletian threw upon him his own purple robe, which he had put off, and Diocles became once more.” Victor’s *Epitome* says: “Diocletian, a Dalmatian and freedman of the senator Anulinus, was named Diocles after both his mother and his town, Dioclea, until he assumed imperial power; when he acquired dominion over the Roman world, he converted his Greek name into Roman form.” See Valesius’s notes on Eusebius, p. 165. Flavius Vopiscus must therefore be corrected in the passage quoted above from the life of Numerian: it should read “Diocles, excessively avaricious,” rather than the extant “Diocletian.”

He reigned with the greatest good fortune. See what we note below at chapter 17.

## CHAPTER X

[Col. 0314A]

Investigator of future events. Aurelius Victor: “For, as an investigator of impending events, when fate [foretold] internal disasters,” etc.

Certain attendants. This passage too openly shows that this book is by Lactantius. For he has an entirely similar passage in book IV of the *Institutes*, chapter 27: “For when they sacrifice to their gods, if someone bearing the marked forehead stands by, the rites in no way obtain a favourable result, nor can the consulted seer give answers. And this was often the chief cause of persecuting righteousness among evil rulers. For when certain of our attendants stood by their masters as they sacrificed, having placed the sign upon their foreheads, they put their gods to flight, so that they could not portray future events in the entrails of victims. When the haruspices understood this, urged on by those same demons whom they propitiate, they complained that profane persons were present at the rites and drove their rulers into a frenzy to assault God’s temple.”

Here, to note this in passing, Josephus Isaeus gravely erred in thinking that this concerns a temple of Jupiter, Apollo, or some other demon which had been cleansed; whereas the passage must be understood as referring to the Church, or the body of Christians, as the above-mentioned Cuperus correctly explains. For at the time when the rulers were driven into frenzy to assault God’s temple, Diocletian was not at Nicomedia but in the East, as Lactantius teaches. What Lactantius says in book IV concerning the assault upon God’s temple, he explains by the ruinous and unjust edicts of Diocletian, who ordered not merely those performing sacred offices but everyone in the palace to sacrifice, and commanded even soldiers to be compelled to participate in abominable sacrifices.

Thus the first persecution of soldiers fell in A.D. 302. Nor, certainly, is frenzy needed to cleanse a temple, but rather piety; yet for assaulting the temple—that is, the body of Christians—frenzy gave them courage, because the God worshipped in the Christians’ temple had disturbed the rites to which the emperors devoted themselves. Thomasius did better in retaining here the word *expugnarent* (“assault”), rejecting the alternative reading, since if we read *expurgarent* (“cleanse”), God’s temple would have to mean that of Apollo or another such deity—which Lactantius would have called not God’s temple but the profane dwelling-place of a demon. Yet he did not attain the meaning of the passage either. For he thinks that “the temple” here means the individual Christians present at the sacrifices, who suffered martyrdom because of the complaints of the demons and their priests; whereas it is certain that the Church as a whole is in view.

The occasion of error was the word *expurgarent*, which some editions print instead of *expugnarent*. That *expugnarent* must be read is demonstrated by six ancient manuscripts of the Royal Library, as many of the Colbert Library, and two further ancient Bolognese manuscripts, seen by both Thomasius and Isaeus; as Latinus Latinius attested in the margin of his Lactantius, which my most distinguished and learned countryman Anthony Faure, Doctor of Theology of Paris and provost of the Church of Reims, generously shared with me. Peter Ciaconius likewise advised this reading in the margin of his Lactantius [Col. 0314D], which the same distinguished man lent me for use. So indeed do the old Roman edition, the Venetian edition of 1521, and the Basel edition of Xystus Betuleius read.

The immortal sign. Lactantius, *Institutes*, book IV, chapter 27: “Those whom the immortal sign has fortified as an unconquerable wall.” Elsewhere he calls it the heavenly sign.

Tages. I think this is said in an oratorical manner, because Tages the Etruscan was formerly a great haruspex and teacher of haruspices. Arnobius, *Against the Nations*, book II: “Before Tages the Etruscan beheld the regions of light, did any human being know, or take care to learn and know, whether the fall of thunderbolts or anything in the veins of entrails signified something?” See there the observations of Gebhart Elmenhorst. Hence Ammianus Marcellinus, book XVII, p. 101: “It is read in the Tagetic books that those about to be struck by the thunderbolt of Vejovis are at once so stupefied that they can hear neither thunder nor any louder crashes” [Col. 0315A]. Henry Valesius emended this passage thus, where previously *Tagetis Thusci* had been read. In an old manuscript of the Colbert Library, it is written *Tagetinicis*.

Prefects. This is the title of a military rank, indeed one below tribunes, though they commanded a cohort just as tribunes did, as Henry Valesius observes on Ammianus Marcellinus. Lactantius, chapter 46 of this history: “These things are written in numerous letters and sent through the prefects and tribunes.” Among their number was that Dorotheus whose encomium Eusebius recounts in *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, chapter 1, as Valesius himself inferred from the Acts of the martyrs Indes and Domna.

Soldiers being compelled. Eusebius therefore rightly notes in the same first chapter of book VIII that the persecution first began with those in military service. Nor did it then proceed further.

Bithynia. An old manuscript reads *Bethania*, by an obvious error. For it is certain that the events narrated next took place at Nicomedia, the metropolis of Bithynia [Col. 0315B].

## CHAPTER XI

His mother. That is, the mother of Galerius Maximian, whom he above called Romula.

A worshipper of mountain gods. Commodianus, book I, chapter 21: “You call [them] mountain gods.” Thus it is read in the very ancient manuscript of Saint Albinus at Angers, from which Jacobus Sirmond copied the *Instructions* of Commodianus, although both editions of Rigault read: “You call mountains and gods.” Incorrectly. For even the title, inscribed “To the Montensians,” warned that the reading of the old exemplar should be retained.

It is difficult, however, to interpret who the mountain gods were. [Col. 0315C] For an old Roman inscription, in which these gods are mentioned, makes their explanation more difficult. It is found in Gruter, p. 21:

> ALTAR TO JUPITER THE LIGHTNING-BRINGER,  
> IN ACCORDANCE WITH THE COMMAND  
> OF THE MOUNTAIN GODS.  
> VALERIUS CRESCENTIUS, FATHER  
> OF ALL THE GODS,  
> AND AURELIUS EXUPERANTIUS,  
> PRIEST OF SILVANUS,  
> DEDICATED [IT]  
> WITH THE BROTHERS AND SISTERS.

Moreover, there were other Montenses, mentioned by the *Praedestinatus*, book I, chapter 69, and in a constitution of the Emperor Honorius published in the appendix to the Theodosian Code, title XII. Saint Augustine, in his letter to Quodvultdeus, calls them Montenses, as do many others listed by the distinguished Charles du Fresne under the word *Montenses*. These were Donatists, as is well known even from book II of Optatus of Milevis.

They persisted in fasts. Thus Maria, servant of the chief official Tertullus, in her Acts: “While Tertullus celebrated his son’s birthday and sacrificed victims to impure idols and vain images, Maria devoted herself to fasting.”

Between themselves. That is, between Diocletian Augustus and Maximian Caesar, as what follows shows.

That they gladly die. Sulpicius Severus, speaking of this very persecution in book II of his *Ecclesiastical History*, says: “Then men rushed eagerly into glorious contests.” [Col. 0315D] Nothing is more common in the acts of martyrs than such voluntary cries: “I am a Christian; I wish to die,” and similar words. Hence that holy envy of Christians toward the dead, because they had not been judged worthy to share in their death, as in the case of Valerius in the Acts of Saint Pontius the martyr. Hence also the ardent zeal and, if I may say so, pious frenzy of some who voluntarily offered themselves to death and torture. Against these Mensurius, bishop of Carthage, was incensed, as Saint Augustine testifies in the *Brief Account of the Conference with the Donatists*, book III, chapter 13. He teaches that Mensurius wrote to Secundus, bishop of Tigisis, a letter in which it was read: Mensurius disapproved of those who, though not arrested, offered themselves for persecutions and volunteered that they possessed scriptures which they would not surrender, although no one had asked them this; and he forbade Christians to honour them. Canon 60 of Elvira also concerns this matter.

Elegant and especially memorable is the passage of Pontius the Deacon in the *Life of Saint Cyprian*. Speaking of Cyprian’s flight when he was sought for martyrdom, he says [Col. 0316A]: “That fear was indeed fear, but just fear: fear of offending the Lord; fear that preferred obedience to God’s commands to receiving a crown in that manner. For a mind devoted to God in all things, and faith made subject to divine admonitions, believed that, unless it obeyed the Lord then commanding concealment, it would sin even by suffering itself.” Hence, finally, the prayers of some addressed to martyrs, asking that they might be found worthy to share martyrdom—such as those of Eulampia in the Greek Menologion for 10 October, in volume II of Henry Canisius’s *Ancient Readings*. These examples, from many and almost innumerable others that could readily be cited, are sufficient.

He ascribed it to another’s fault. Eutropius, book IX: “Diocletian was crafty and shrewd in conduct, exceedingly subtle in intellect, and wished to exercise his severity through another’s unpopularity.” Suidas relates the same concerning him, saying that he was variable and crafty in disposition, but often concealed the defects of his nature by singular prudence and acuteness, transferring all harsher measures to others.

[Col. 0316B] His own hatred of Christians. Lactantius, *Institutes*, book V, chapter 11, speaking of this very persecution: “Others, from their own personal hatred against the righteous.”

That they should be removed. *Acts of the Passion of Saint Salvinus, Bishop and Martyr*: “The greater part of the people cried out, saying: ‘Let the Christians be removed’; and their pleasure is assured.”

The fearful. Lactantius, in the same place: “Others, through excessive timidity, ventured beyond what was commanded.”

Those wishing to curry favour. The same author, in the same place: “Some, in order to please and to fortify through this service their path to higher positions.”

[Col. 0316C] The Milesian Apollo. Eusebius recounts this story in book II of the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 1, but does not explain to which temple of Apollo it pertains. Pausanias, in the *Arcadica*, relates that Xerxes, son of Darius, took away from the Milesians the bronze Apollo which was at Branchidae, and that many years later Seleucus restored it to them. Branchidae, moreover, was a place in Milesian territory above the harbour of Panormus, renowned for Apollo’s oracle, which the Ionians and Aeolians formerly consulted, as Henry Valesius observes from Herodotus, book I, in his notes on Ammianus Marcellinus, p. 382. Lactantius, *Institutes*, book VII, chapter 13: “A certain Polytes consulted the Milesian Apollo.” Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book I, chapter 17: “Maeandrius writes that the Milesians sacrifice to Apollo Oulios (Ἀπόλλωνι οὐλίῳ) for their safety.”

As an enemy of the divine religion. That is, he said that righteous men living on earth—namely Christians—hindered him from speaking true prophecies, and that false oracles were therefore being issued from the tripod, as Eusebius teaches in book II of the *Life of Constantine*. The author of the *Acts of Saint George the Martyr* in Surius copied these words and made them his own.

## CHAPTER XII

[Col. 0316D] On 23 February. Correctly so. For the Terminalia are marked on this day in the old Roman Calendar, published in Constantine’s time and made public by Herwart and Bucher. Saint Augustine, *City of God*, book VII, chapter 7: “They say that the Terminalia are celebrated in February, when the purificatory rite called *februum* takes place.” The first day of this persecution, therefore—and this should be noted—was the seventh day before the Kalends of March, the very day of the Terminalia. This is also demonstrated by chapter 48, as will be observed there.

While the consuls were performing the rites, the old men offering sacrifice. That is, Diocletian and Maximian Herculius, who are known to have been consuls for the eighth and seventh times in A.D. 303. These words certainly establish the date of this persecution, over which learned men dispute so fiercely. Onuphrius, Baronius, and Petavius—to name no others—contend that it began in A.D. 302; Scaliger, Valesius, and many others say the following year. That their opinion is correct is proved by this passage of Lactantius. For it is also clear from chapter 17 that these events occurred shortly before Diocletian went to Rome. Yet it is certain that he departed for Rome toward the end of the nineteenth year of his reign and there celebrated a triumph over Narses, king of the Persians, as Joseph Scaliger correctly notes on Eusebius’s Chronicle.

[Col. 0317A] Moreover, Lactantius below, chapter 48, reviewing the history of this persecution, says that Constantine’s and Licinius’s edict in favour of Christians, by which peace was granted to the Church, was posted at Nicomedia on the Ides of June, when Constantine and Licinius were consuls for the third time; and he says that from the destruction of the Nicomedian church to its restoration there were ten years and approximately four months. But if one calculates from 23 February 303, when the Nicomedian church was demolished, to 13 June 313, one finds that ten years, three months, and nineteen days elapsed from the destruction of that church to its restoration.

Finally, that the persecution began in 303 may also be proved from Eusebius, book VII, chapter 16, where he says that it began to relax somewhat after the eighth year. For if one counts from the Easter festival of 303 to April 311, when Galerius Maximian, at the point of death, ordered the persecution to cease, one readily finds that eight complete years had elapsed from its beginning and the ninth had begun [Col. 0317B]. Thus it began to relax after the eighth year, as Eusebius observed. Therefore the arguments which Petavius adduces in book XI of *On the Doctrine of Times*, chapter 32, from Sulpicius Severus in order to prove that the persecution began in 302 are plainly weak, since they rest upon the premise that it ended in 312, whereas it is certain that it did not cease until the following year.

An image of God is sought. Namely, in the manner of pagans, who did not think temples could exist without images. Yet Pliny, book II, chapter 7, had said: “I consider it a mark of human weakness to seek God’s likeness and form.” Christian churches therefore lacked images, as Desiderius Heraldus discusses at length in his notes on Arnobius, book VI. See also Casaubon’s notes on Aelius Lampridius’s *Alexander Severus*.

[Col. 0317C] The Scriptures are burned. Eusebius recounts these things in *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, chapter 2, as do many others whom it would be superfluous to name. The matter is very well known. From this arose the contemptuous term *traditor* (“surrenderer”) against those who, through fear of punishment, had handed over the divine books to imperial judges. On this subject one should consult especially African writers, above all that Donatist who recorded the *Acts of the Holy Martyrs Saturninus, Dativus, and Their Companions*. Nor should the proceedings for the vindication of Caecilian, bishop of Carthage, and Felix, bishop of Aptunga, be omitted.

## CHAPTER XIII

On the following day. That is, 24 February. On this day, therefore, the edict of Diocletian and Maximian against our people was posted at Nicomedia, the persecution having already begun. Eusebius, however, writes in *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, chapter 2, that it was posted in March, as the festival day of the Lord’s Passion approached; and the author of the Alexandrian Chronicle says that it was posted on 25 March, the very day of Easter. These statements may, I think, be reconciled as follows: the edict was first posted at Nicomedia, as in the imperial city, on 24 February; it was then sent to the other cities of the empire, posted in March [Col. 0317D] in the place where Eusebius then lived, in Palestine in April, and at Alexandria or elsewhere on Easter Day itself.

They should be deprived of every honour. Rufinus expresses this in Eusebius, book VIII, chapter 2: “If any among our people was protected by the prerogative of any office, he should remain dishonoured after that prerogative was removed.”

They should not have freedom. These words are explained more clearly by Eusebius, book VIII, chapter 2, according to Rufinus’s translation. The other interpreters have not grasped the sense of the law sufficiently well. Rufinus reads: “If any slave remained a Christian, he could not obtain freedom.” Penalties were first prescribed against persons of rank, then against the common people, and finally against slaves; all hope of freedom was removed from the latter if they persisted in professing the Christian religion.

Accordingly, the otherwise learned Henry Valesius is mistaken when, in his notes on [Col. 0318A] Eusebius, p. 164, he says that Rufinus’s interpretation cannot stand. Nicephorus Callistus wandered still farther from the truth: in book VII, chapter 3, he understood the edict to mean that slaves were granted freedom if they renounced Christianity. Yet although the distinguished Gisbertus Cuperus thinks Lactantius is not here referring to slaves’ freedom, and approves Valesius’s view so thoroughly that he considers it beyond doubt, Rufinus was both proficient in each language and close to the period in which these measures were enacted. It is therefore highly probable that he knew both the force of Eusebius’s words and the actual course of events in Diocletian’s persecution. Moreover, the condition of slaves would have been better than that of persons of rank if no penalties had been prescribed against them. The opinion of the distinguished Dodwell, who interprets the passage as concerning freedmen, might appear more likely; but the authority of Rufinus always prevents me from embracing it.

[Col. 0318B] As for the man who [acted against] the edict. Lactantius’s silence, though he was then at Nicomedia, sufficiently indicates that this man’s name was unknown, because he was undoubtedly of the common people. For if he had been an illustrious man, conspicuous for the prerogative of secular offices—as Eusebius describes him, whether by hearsay or from the tradition of his elders—Lactantius would neither have been ignorant of his name nor omitted it, and it would also have reached Eusebius. It concerned the Christian community that the name of the man who had dared that great deed should become known to all the churches.

[Col. 0318C] For this reason, I view with great suspicion what is read in certain old martyrologies under 7 September: after reproducing Rufinus’s words translating Eusebius, they say that these acts were committed by a certain blessed John. Since Lactantius and Eusebius certainly establish that this man was immediately brought forward and immediately put to death, and thus died at the end of February, how can his feast day fall in September, so far from the beginning of the persecution? Indeed, although the authority of those martyrologies carries little weight with me, I nevertheless cannot agree with the distinguished Godfrey Henschenius, who in volume III for February, p. 107, contends that this history must be understood as concerning Saint George the martyr. He says that George suffered at Nicomedia in A.D. 303, on 23 April, with the solemnity of the Lord’s saving Passion imminent.

For, apart from the certainty that the persecution began at the end of February and that the man who tore down and shredded the edict was killed in the same month—thus two months before 23 April—the *Acts of Saint George* published by Henschenius do not say this, and are so full of fables and prodigious narratives that it is entirely clear that nothing sound or reliable can be drawn from them. The story of the Empress Alexandra alone—said to have been a Christian and condemned to be beheaded by Diocletian himself pronouncing sentence—surpasses every poetic invention, since it is certain, as we shall say shortly, that Diocletian had no wife throughout his entire reign other than Prisca.

Furthermore [Col. 0318D], since Henschenius himself writes that Easter fell in A.D. 303 on 18 April and the Lord’s Passion Sunday on the sixteenth, it is clear that this history cannot concern Saint George. If George suffered in the year in which Easter fell on 18 April, as Henschenius wishes, he certainly did not suffer with the Paschal solemnity approaching, but after the feast days had passed. Yet that was Henschenius’s strongest argument, taken from the preface to Eusebius’s book on the Martyrs of Palestine, where it is written that the edicts for destroying churches and burning sacred codices were posted in Palestine in April, as the day of the saving Passion approached. This may be true with reference to Palestine, but is false with reference to Nicomedia, where it is certain that the edict was posted eleven days before the Kalends of March, on the day after the Terminalia.

[Col. 0319A] Although not rightly. Ruffinus in Eusebius, book VIII, chapter 5: “Inflamed by too great a zeal of faith, as though he reproved that imprudent and untimely ardour for faith in Christ.”

Victories over Goths and Sarmatians. Because the emperors called themselves Gothic and Sarmatian in the heading of the edict, as in an old inscription reported by Cuspinian in his book *On the Caesars*, p. 135. In the heading of the edict were placed not only the names of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, but also those of the Caesars Constantius and Galerius Maximian, as may readily be inferred from the account of the passion of the holy martyrs Saturninus, Dativus, Felix, and their companions, and from the martyrdom of the holy women Agape, Chionia, and Irene.

“lawfully cooked.” The manner of cooking Christians alive is explained below, chapter 21. He called him “lawfully cooked” because he had been cooked according to laws enacted by the Augusti; just as in *Institutions* V.11 he calls those rites “lawful” (*legitima sacra*) which were performed according to ancient custom, because custom has the force of law. For the same reason he says, in VI.9, that injuries are lawfully inflicted upon enemies—namely, after war has been announced and declared through envoys, with the law of war observed [Col. 0319B]. Josephus Isaeus is therefore gravely mistaken here in supposing that the word *legitime* is used ironically in this passage, because he evidently did not understand its true meaning.

“With admirable patience.” These are the words of Rufinus translating and explaining Eusebius: “Immediately raging against him with every form of cruelty, they could not even achieve this alone: that anyone should see him dejected amid his punishments. Rather, with a cheerful and glad expression—even when his inner organs had already failed under the tortures—his spirit nevertheless rejoiced in his face. Hence his torturers themselves were more grievously tormented, because they exhausted every kind of punishment upon one whom they could not render even sorrowful by them.”

## CHAPTER XIV

“He set fire to it.” Eusebius, VIII.6, discussing this fire, confesses that he does not know by what accident it was kindled. Others write that the palace was struck by lightning and burned down [Col. 0319C], as Constantine does in his *Oration to the Assembly of the Saints*, chapter 25.

“All his own … immediately …” An old manuscript reads: “he immediately seized all his own people.” We have emended it.

“Power having been granted.” Lactantius, *Divine Institutions* V.11, speaking of this very persecution: “For, once authority had been received, each man raged according to his own character. Some, through excessive timidity, ventured beyond what had been commanded. Others, through their personal hatred of the just; some through the natural savagery of their disposition; others in order to please, and by this service to secure for themselves a path to higher office. Some proved headlong in killing, as did one man in Phrygia, who burned the entire population together with the very place of assembly.”

“They tortured.” Thus it is written in the old book; but above the final line, as often happens, a sign was added to indicate that *torquebantur* (“were tortured”) should be read—a manifest error. We have often found in manuscripts that this is the source of very many errors occurring in ancient authors. Copyists first transcribed books [Col. 0319D], which were then passed on to correctors. These, however, frequently changed a good reading into a bad one under the appearance of correction.

“They competed.” Lactantius in the passage cited shortly before: “Thus, in devising kinds of punishments, they devise nothing but victory.”

“The household of Caesar.” That is, of Galerius. It therefore pleased him to exempt this household, as though it were abominable to suspect any crime against Diocletian in Caesar’s household; and so that the authors of the fire, who had come from his own house, might not be discovered, if an opportunity for investigation had been allowed.

“His departure prepared.” At that time there was no war, so far as I know. But this man of frenzied and savage spirit acted so obstinately and arrogantly that by this manner of proceeding he more forcefully impelled Diocletian toward the destruction of the Christian religion, although he saw him hitherto applying himself mildly to so great an undertaking.

## CHAPTER XV

[Col. 0320A]

“His daughter Valeria.” She was married to Galerius Maximianus Caesar. After her husband’s death she lived an unhappy life and perished, together with her mother, by a pitiable death under the rule of Licinius, as Lactantius teaches at the end of this work. This account wholly destroys the conjecture of the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius, who, under the year 294, writes that Diocletian’s daughter, who was joined in marriage to Galerius Maximianus, did not long survive her wedding, since no mention of her occurs in earlier monuments, nor is any offspring recorded as having been born from her. He then adds that the father, wishing to consecrate for eternity the memory of his deceased daughter, desired that a part of Pannonia be established and named after her; and he cites Ammianus Marcellinus, book XIX, to that effect.

But Marcellinus does not say this. He says only that that part of Pannonia was established in honor of Valeria, Diocletian’s daughter, and thus named. I shall quote his very words: “He came to Valeria, formerly a part [Col. 0320B] of Pannonia, but established in honor of Valeria, daughter of Diocletian, and thus named.” Moreover, Aurelius Victor teaches in his *Book of the Caesars* that it was neither established nor named by Diocletian, but by Galerius Maximianus: “He named the province Valeria after his wife.”

Having established these points as though they were certain, Baronius adds that, when the affinity contracted between Diocletian and Galerius had been dissolved by Valeria’s death, Diocletian hastened to join in a marital compact with him a maiden from his own kindred, related to him more closely by degree: namely Susanna, daughter of Gabinius, the brother of Pope Caius. Both were related to Diocletian by blood, as being born of the brother of that same Diocletian, as appears from the Acts of the same Saint Susanna. But this whole history collapses when the foundation upon which it rested collapses—that is, the death of Valeria, who is known to have long outlived Galerius. Indeed, the errors of great men are so dangerous that this slip of Baronius has drawn in its wake many learned men: Odoricus Raynaldus, John Bolland, and others [Col. 0320C].

“His wife Prisca.” While her husband was still alive, she was later driven into exile by Maximinus together with her daughter Valeria; at last she was beheaded by command of Licinius, as Lactantius will teach at the end of this work. But here a great difficulty presents itself. In the ancient Acts of Saint Susanna the Virgin, who is written to have completed her martyrdom at Rome under Diocletian’s rule, mention is made of the Augusta Serena, wife of that emperor, who was secretly Christian; her feast-day is there assigned to the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September [16 August].

It would indeed be a serious difficulty if the truth and authority of those Acts were established. But although they bear many, and weighty, signs of fabrication, they are proved false particularly on this ground: that they would have Serena to be Diocletian’s wife. For I shall show that throughout the whole period of his rule Diocletian had no wife other than Prisca. If Prisca was Valeria’s mother, as indeed she was, she must necessarily have married Diocletian before he became emperor [Col. 0320D], that is, before AD 284, since Valeria was joined in marriage to Galerius Maximianus in the year 293, at no less than her twelfth year of age. It is also certainly inferred that Prisca, her mother, was then alive, because she survived long afterward and was put to death only in 313, after Licinius’ victory over Maximinus.

These monuments had not been known to the most illustrious founder of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, Cardinal Baronius. Yet he suspected that there would be those who called into question the story of the Augusta Serena, since no mention of her whatsoever is found elsewhere, neither in pagan writers nor in ancient inscriptions. As though he had settled that most difficult question, he asks the “little scholars,” if the name Serena Augusta displeases them, to say by what other name Diocletian’s wife, the Augusta, is found called by earlier writers; and, since they will not find one, not to make a controversy about the name. Thus his question has been answered most abundantly [Col. 0321A].

That supposititious wife of Diocletian having therefore been rejected, let us see whether Eleutheria, whom the very distinguished Hadrian Valesius inferred to have been Diocletian’s wife from the *Life of Pope Vigilius* found in the *Pontifical Acts*, commonly attributed to Anastasius the Librarian, was truly Diocletian’s wife. Vigilius had come to Constantinople at the command of Justinian and Theodora; and, when he was compelled to do things he did not wish to do, he said: “As I see, the most pious rulers Justinian and Theodora have not made me come to them, but today I know that I have found Diocletian and Eleutheria.” From this passage that very distinguished man inferred that Eleutheria was Diocletian’s wife, because it is certain that a comparison is instituted there between Justinian and Diocletian, and between Theodora, Justinian’s wife, and Eleutheria, therefore Diocletian’s wife.

But from the arguments adduced against Serena it follows also that Eleutheria—whether Lutheria, as in the very ancient manuscript 417 of the Colbert Library, or Leuthere, as it is written in manuscript 733 of the Royal Library [Col. 0321B]—was not Diocletian’s wife, since, as I said before, it is certain that he had no other wife than Prisca throughout the whole duration of his reign. Vigilius therefore erred in the history, or the book of the *Pontifical Acts* is corrupt in this place. Indeed, manuscript 736 of the same Colbert Library reads: “But today I know that I have found Diocletian and Decius, or Leutherius.” Thus that woman has now been changed into a man.

Furthermore, from what has been said thus far about Serena and Eleutheria, anyone may easily infer what credence ought to be given to the history of Saint George the Martyr, in which it is written that the Empress Alexandra, Diocletian’s wife, on seeing a remarkable miracle performed in the person of the Martyr, acknowledged the truth—that is, embraced the faith of Christ. This, evidently, is Alexandra, Diocletian’s wife, mother of Maximian’s wife, as is reported in the Life of the same George, a fragment of which Godefridus Henschenius published in the third volume for April, p. 103 [Col. 0321C]. Nicephorus Callistus, VII.15, relates that the same woman, after dying, was recalled from the underworld by the prayer alone of that same George.

“He compelled [them] to be defiled.” From this passage the most learned Henry Dodwell inferred in his *Cyprianic Dissertations* that Diocletian’s wife Prisca and his daughter Valeria were Christians; and he confirms that opinion by Eusebius’ authority. In *Ecclesiastical History* VIII.1, recounting the circumstances which preceded Diocletian’s persecution, Eusebius says that the wives of emperors were openly and publicly Christian, and had received from the emperors themselves the liberty of freely practicing, in their presence, what belonged to their religion, both in word and deed. Although he does not name the emperors who granted their wives this liberty, these words of Lactantius nevertheless seem to imply that Diocletian and Galerius must be meant.

But if these women were truly Christians, how can they be thought to have been defiled by sacrifice, even under compulsion? Who would believe that imperial women, placed in so exalted a position, did not dare to resist [Col. 0321D], when boys and insignificant women, as Lactantius says in *Divine Institutions* V.13, did not yield to tortures; while eunuchs preferred to be killed rather than deny the faith of Christ or have it defiled by an impious sacrifice? Moreover, wherever Prisca and Valeria are discussed in this book, there is no trace of their religion—though Lactantius would nevertheless have mentioned it, at least in chapter 2, where, describing their end, he says that their chastity and condition caused their destruction.

“The eunuchs were killed.” Among them was Peter, whose martyrdom Eusebius describes in VIII.6; likewise Indes, as the Acts of his martyrdom relate.

“They were dragged off to be burned.” Eusebius confirms this in the same place, writing that, by imperial command, all the worshippers of God at Nicomedia, gathered in masses with their households, perished—some consumed by the sword, others by flames.

“They were drowned in the sea.” Eusebius in the same place: “The executioners also threw countless others, bound and placed in boats, into the deep sea” [Col. 0322A]. In his book *On the Martyrs of Palestine*, chapter 6, recounting the martyrdom of Agapius, he says that he was sunk in the middle of the sea with stones hung from his feet.

“A man not so merciful.” Ancient writers report that Maximian Herculius was harsh, cruel, and inhuman. Eutropius, IX: “Herculius, openly savage and uncivil in character, signifying his harshness even by the terror of his expression.” Again, X: “A man inclined to every harshness and cruelty, faithless, troublesome, wholly lacking in civility.” Even Diocletian, who had shared supreme rule with him, was accustomed to criticize his harshness, as Flavius Vopiscus teaches in his *Divine Aurelian*. See also the Emperor Julian in his *Caesars*.

“He allowed the walls to be torn down.” On the contrary, Eusebius, VIII.13, explicitly writes that Constantius neither demolished church buildings—or places of assembly, as Lactantius calls them here [Col. 0322B], and Rufinus likewise in his translation of this Eusebian passage—nor undertook anything against our people.

“The true temple of God.” That is, the Christian person. Lactantius, *Institutions* V.8: “His temple is not stones or clay, but the person himself, who bears God’s image; this temple is adorned not with corruptible gifts of gold and gems, but with the eternal gifts of virtues.” Again, VI.25: “Temples are not to be built for him from stones piled to a height: he must be consecrated in each person’s own breast.” And below: “Finally, let each always have God consecrated in his heart, since he himself is God’s temple.” Again, II.2 and VI.10, he says that man is God’s image.

## CHAPTER XVI

“Except Gaul.” In the petition presented to Constantine the Great by the Donatists, in Optatus of Milevis, I: “We beseech you, most excellent Emperor Constantine, since you are of a righteous stock, whose father, among the other emperors, did not exercise persecution, and Gaul is free from this crime, that your piety command judges to be given us from Gaul.” Gaul, therefore, was exempt from this persecution because the most kindly Emperor Constantius ruled there. As Eusebius relates, he was entirely free from the persecution stirred up against us; he preserved the worshippers of God dwelling under his rule safe from every harm and injury, neither demolished church buildings nor enacted anything new against us.

Indeed, Eutropius, at the beginning of book X, seems to say that no Gallic blood was shed in this persecution. Speaking of Constantius, he says: “He was not only beloved but also revered by the Gauls, especially because they had escaped, under his rule, Diocletian’s suspected prudence and Maximian’s bloody recklessness” [Col. 0322C]. Yet against this protest the histories of certain Gallic cities and provinces, which proclaim that their martyrs were conveyed to God in this persecution—so much so that scarcely any city in Gaul is not said to have then been soaked with Christian blood.

These facts may be reconciled as follows: at the beginning, Gaul was not altogether exempt from the persecution; Constantius was occupied against the barbarians, namely, as the most illustrious Bishop of Montpellier, François Bosquet, says in book IV, chapter 2, of his *Histories of the Gallican Church*; and, in accordance with custom and the habitual fury of the pagans, many Christians were killed in Gaul. Eusebius confirms this at the end of his book *On the Martyrs of Palestine*: “For the regions lying farther on—namely all Italy, Sicily also, Gaul too, and all those extending toward the setting sun: Spain, Mauretania, and Africa—although they experienced the fury of the war scarcely during the first two complete years of persecution, soon obtained the most immediate help of the divine power and peace.”

The most learned Dodwell, however, wishes this passage in his *Cyprianic Dissertations* to be understood thus: that Eusebius, by naming the principal provinces, designated the region of the Western Empire, and indicated that the persecution itself did not continue throughout that whole region beyond the second year; while Gaul nevertheless remained exempt from it in the meantime. Certainly his argument has much appearance of truth, and I should readily adopt this view, were it not established that Eusebius intended expressly to name Gaul [Col. 0323A].

“The three beasts.” That is, Diocletian, Maximian Herculius, and Galerius Maximianus. Lactantius therefore persists in his view and does not number Constantius, ruling Gaul, among the persecutors.

“Flaccinus the prefect.” Of Bithynia, in which Hierocles held the governorship before administering the prefecture of Egypt, an office which Henry Valesius, in his annotations on Eusebius, p. 177, shows that he held. Flaccinus’ cruelty is inferred from Lactantius’ calling him “no small murderer.” At the same time Flavianus, prefect of Egypt, lived; he is mentioned in the Greek Menologion for the eighth day of July, published by Henry Canisius in the second volume of *Antiquae Lectiones* [Col. 0323B].

“Hierocles.” This passage confirms the conjecture of the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius, who thought that the following words of Lactantius, which we shall transcribe from book V of the *Divine Institutions*, should be understood of Hierocles. Hierocles was governor of Bithynia, as has already been said, and he practiced much slaughter upon Christians.

“Author and adviser.” Lactantius, *Institutions* V.2: “Another wrote on the same subject more bitterly; he was then among the number of judges, and was one of the chief instigators of carrying out the persecution.”

“Priscillianus.” Governor of Bithynia, as is read in the Greek Menologion for the twelfth day of June: “On the same day, Saint Antonina the Martyr. At Nicaea in Bithynia, under the Emperors Diocletian and Maximian, Priscillianus being governor, Antonina, persevering steadfastly in confessing the Christian faith, was at last struck by the sword and crowned with martyrdom” [Col. 0323C]. The same appears in the Roman Martyrology.

“You have conquered the adversary.” Cyprian, Epistle 7, to Rogatianus and the other confessors: “As much as we grieve for those whom the hostile storm has overthrown, so much do we rejoice because of you, whom the devil could not overcome. Yet we exhort you, through our common faith and through the true and sincere affection of our heart toward you, that, having conquered the adversary in this first contest, you may maintain your glory with courageous and persevering strength.”

“Zabulum.” That is, the devil. So in Commodian, II.17: “All [things] from the pomp of Zabulus”; and chapter 18: “Or the whole pomp of Zabulus”; and I.35: “Avoid utterly the Zabulean law.” Again, II.31: “Crowd, bow down so that you may act under Zabulean seed.” We cite these passages according to the authority of an old manuscript, for the printed edition differs. Nothing is more common than the word *Zabulus* in ancient books. For the same reason they wrote *Zaritorum* for *Diaritorum*, as in the first Conference of Carthage, chapter 139.

Because Papirius Masson did not notice this [Col. 0323D], he wrote *Hyppensis Zaritorensis* here in place of *Hipponensium Zaritorum*, which is the correct reading; Peter Pithou retained this reading in his edition of the Carthaginian Conference. Therefore, in the ancient *Notitia of Africa*, published by Sirmond and afterwards by Chifflet, instead of the reading there, *Marianus Hippzaritensis*, one ought to write *Marianus Hipponensium Zaritorum*, that is, of the Diaritans or Diarrhytans, as in Pliny, *Natural History* V.4. So too in Commodian, *Zacones* for “deacons.” I have also read *Numizia* for Numidia in an old manuscript of the Colbert Library.

“You triumphed.” Lactantius, *Institutions* IV.26: “Finally, he did not refuse even to undergo death, so that, under that leader, man might triumph over death, subdued and chained, together with its terrors.”

“A delightful spectacle.” Cyprian, Epistle 9: “O what a spectacle that was for the Lord—how exalted, how great, how acceptable to God’s eyes through the mystery and devotion of his soldier!”

“Elephants.” For the ancients also harnessed elephants to a chariot, as appears from Lampridius’ *Life of Antoninus Heliogabalus* and other passages. Flavius Vopiscus reports that twenty elephants preceded the triumph which the Divine Aurelian celebrated over Zenobia and Tetricus. John, abbot of Biclar, under the ninth year of the Emperor Justin, notes that Justinian, commander of the Roman army, sent twenty-four elephants to Constantinople for the triumph to be celebrated over the conquered Persians. See Sirmond’s notes on Sidonius’ panegyric of Anthemius, and Bulenger, *On Triumphs*, chapter 21.

“Rulers are ruled.” In a passive sense, as in Cicero, *On Duties* I: “O ancient house, alas, how ruled by an unequal master!” Vergil, *Aeneid* II: “having been ruled for many years.”

“He ceased to provoke.” Donatus was released from prison in the final period of Galerius Maximianus, as is stated below, chapter 35.

## CHAPTER XVII

[Col. 0324B]

“Prosperity departed from him.” That is, from Diocletian, whom ancient historical writers report to have been fortunate throughout the entire twenty years of his reign. There is no need to adduce the testimony of each writer. A single author, the panegyrist who addressed Maximian and Constantine at the marriage of Fausta, will suffice. Thus he says: “But indeed this was brought about by the very changefulness and nature of Fortune, which had been unable to alter anything while you held the Empire, so that that unbroken prosperity of twenty years might be distinguished by some interval.”

“He went to Rome.” Diocletian went for two reasons: to celebrate his *vicennalia*, and to celebrate a triumph over Narseh, king of the Persians, whom he had defeated some years earlier. For the triumph was celebrated in this year, not in the eighteenth year of his reign, as Henry Valesius thought. Valesius therefore connected with the triumph the cheapness of grain which the Idatian Fasti report the emperors ordered, as though this had been instituted by them after the triumph in favor of the Roman people [Col. 0324C].

Scaliger therefore rightly observes in his notes on Eusebius’ *Chronicle* that the triumph was celebrated by Diocletian and Maximian in the twentieth year of their reign, some months before they laid aside the purple. But the last point is false, for they still retained imperial power for almost a year and a half, as we shall see later. That the triumph was celebrated at the time of the *vicennalia*, which is what we must prove, is evident from Lactantius, chapter 10. After recounting the victory over the Persians, he says that Diocletian departed for the East and spent there the year preceding the persecution; then he came to winter in Bithynia, where the plan to destroy the churches was adopted, and the persecution began in the following February. It is therefore certain that Diocletian was not at Rome in the eighteenth year of his reign, in which Valesius, following Eusebius, maintains that he celebrated a triumph, for which Joseph Scaliger reproves him.

Certainly, what cannot be denied is that in the common editions of Eusebius’ *Chronicle*, and in most ancient manuscripts, that triumph is entered under Diocletian’s eighteenth year. But in the very ancient and excellent Colbert manuscript, and in other ancient manuscripts seen by Pontacus, it is placed in the nineteenth year, though in the wrong order, since it precedes the account of the persecution. This was the occasion of the distinguished Valesius’ error. It is probable, moreover, that Diocletian delayed the triumph over the Persians for so long in order to join it to the festivals of the *vicennalia*, rendering them thereby more splendid and celebrated.

Now Eusebius’ words must be quoted: “The Augusti Diocletian and Maximian triumphed at Rome in splendid pomp, with Narseh’s wife, sisters, children, and all the booty with which they had despoiled the Parthians preceding their chariot.” Eutropius says the same at the end of book IX, where he says that Diocletian and Herculius laid aside the purple after the celebrated triumph which they celebrated at Rome over many nations, with the splendid procession of platforms, in which Narseh’s wives, sisters, and children were led before the chariot [Col. 0325A]. But Eutropius must be corrected here, where he speaks of Narseh’s wives being led before the chariot. Sextus Rufus in two places, and Eusebius in the *Chronicle*, who seems to have drawn from Eutropius, speak of only one wife of Narseh.

Diocletian, then, was in the East in the year 302, and toward its end came to Nicomedia. At the beginning of 303, once the persecution had begun, he afterward went to Rome, to celebrate the triumph and the *vicennalia*.

“The day of the *vicennalia*.” These were to be celebrated at the beginning of the twentieth year of the reign, and not on one day alone, but over successive days, as is also evident from what Eusebius recounts of the Roman martyr in his book *On the Martyrs of Palestine*. With respect to Diocletian’s celebrations, it is certain that they were observed at Rome for a full month, since Lactantius says that, when those solemnities were completed, he broke abruptly out of the city, impatient and distressed in spirit, and could not endure thirteen days so as to enter office as consul at Rome rather than Ravenna.

Moreover, this passage alone proves that Diocletian celebrated the *vicennalia* in the same year in which the persecution against Christians began; and they were celebrated in the year in which he held his eighth consulship. For he broke out from the city a few days before the Kalends of January, when his ninth consulship was being conferred upon him [Col. 0325B].

“The Kalends of December.” Since Diocletian’s reign is the foundation of this history, the matter seems to require that we establish its beginning in a brief account, in order finally to put an end to the disagreements which have arisen over this question among learned men. As to the year in which he entered upon the administration of the state, I do not think it can now be disputed, since Dionysius Petavius, a man most skilled in this and many other matters, has demonstrated clearly in *On the Doctrine of Times* XI.30 that it was AD 284.

Finally, if the persecution against the Church was stirred up in AD 303, as many passages of this work of Lactantius, quoted above by us, make certain, and if it was stirred up in the nineteenth year of Diocletian’s reign, as all agree, it cannot be denied that his principate began toward the end of 284. The greater difficulty, therefore, lies in determining the day on which he was made emperor. Before Petavius, learned men were persuaded that he had been hailed emperor by the soldiers on the Palilia themselves—that is, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May [21 April]. This view, as false, is deservedly refuted by that same most learned man, who adds: “Let all chronologists henceforth come to their senses, unlearn this assumption (*prolēpsis*) about the first day of Diocletian’s reign, supported by so slight—indeed by no—argument, and replace it with a better one.”

Thanks, however, are due to that Alexandrian Chronicle, whose author, from public records, identifies for us the day on which Diocletian was first called emperor at Chalcedon: namely, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October [17 September]. If Petavius were now alive, I am certain that, as a most devoted lover of truth, he would restore to Lactantius the credit for establishing that day, which he falsely assigned to the author of the Alexandrian Chronicle, and would change “the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October” to “the twelfth day before the Kalends of December” [20 November], the day which Lactantius teaches was the anniversary of Diocletian’s accession, on which he was to celebrate the *vicennalia* at Rome.

In this way the difficulty noted by Valesius in his annotations on Eusebius, p. 175, is resolved: Eusebius says that Romanus completed his martyrdom on 17 November while Diocletian’s *vicennalia* were being celebrated; if this is true, it seems to follow that the first day of Diocletian’s reign fell in November, not in September, as the author of the Alexandrian Chronicle relates [Col. 0325D]. It therefore fell in November, but later than the seventeenth day of that month.

Against this, however, the very distinguished Antonius Pagius objects that the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, assigned by Lactantius to Diocletian’s *vicennalia*, was not his anniversary, but that of Maximian Herculius. He also proves this from the fact that book III of Justinian’s Code contains a law of Diocletian given on the Ides of October, when Carinus was consul for the second time and Numerian was consul—that is, in the year in which we too have written that he was made emperor. Therefore, it is certain that he had been raised to supreme authority long before the twelfth day before the Kalends of December.

I confess that this point carries great weight, if the reading is certain. But because only one such law is found in Justinian’s Code, and thus cannot derive authority from other laws of the same time; because four ancient manuscripts of the Royal Library, seven of the Colbert Library, and three which belonged to the very distinguished Peter Pithou do not give the time at which it was issued; and because one Royal manuscript, one Colbert manuscript, and three Pithou manuscripts call it a law of Diocletian and Maximian, Augusti and Caesars—it is clear that nothing sound or secure can be obtained from this evidence for establishing the beginning of Diocletian’s reign. Even after Pagius’ observation, therefore, we are free to hold true the opinion we derived from Lactantius concerning the day on which that Augustus first attained imperial power—especially since the Idatian Fasti teach that Maximian was elevated emperor on the Kalends of April [1 April], not on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December [Col. 0326A].

“He could not endure the freedom of the Roman people.” Namely, their unrestrained freedom, all the more biting because it had been interrupted. The Roman people’s boldness and freedom of speech must indeed have been great, since they compelled Diocletian, otherwise a fairly good prince—if one excepts the persecution stirred up against our people—to leave the city so precipitately. The same license moved Constantine also to leave Rome and transfer the seat of empire elsewhere, as Zosimus relates in book II of his histories. Though another reason for transferring the empire is given in the Donation of Constantine.

“He broke out from the city.” On the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January [20 December], after the *vicennalia* had ended. For the festivals of the *vicennalia* lasted a full month, as we have already said.

“His ninth consulship.” These facts also prove that the persecution was stirred up in AD 303, since he says that Diocletian’s ninth consulship was appointed for the Kalends of January next following the outbreak of the persecution. Diocletian’s ninth consulship fell in AD 304.

“Was being conferred.” By the Senate, of course. But this must be explained [Col. 0326C]. For it is certain that the nomination of consuls was then wholly in the emperors’ power. The Senate, therefore, did not designate consuls as it had once done, but declared them, handed them the insignia of the consulship, and thus seemed in some sense to confer and bestow the consulship. The Emperor Valerian teaches us this in his speech to Aurelian, later emperor, in Flavius Vopiscus: “For today I designate you consul, writing to the Senate that it may assign you the sceptre and also the fasces. For the emperor does not customarily give these; rather, when he becomes consul, he receives them from the Senate.”

Diocletian therefore had appointed the consulship to himself for the following year; and, if he had remained at Rome, he would have received its insignia from the Senate in accordance with consular custom. But because of the excessive license of the Roman people, he could not endure thirteen days in order to receive them.

“At Ravenna.” On leaving Rome, Diocletian therefore went to Ravenna, the direct route toward Illyricum and Bithynia.

“That he might enter office as consul.” Aelius Lampridius, in *Heliogabalus*: “Finally, on the Kalends of January, when they had at the same time been designated consuls, he refused to enter office with his cousin.” The Idatian Fasti, under “Diocletian II and Aristobulus”: “In their consulship Carinus Margo was killed, who in that same year had entered office as consul with Aristobulus.” The Alexandrian Chronicle, p. 641: “The Emperor Diocletian was proclaimed at Chalcedon on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October; he entered Nicomedia clothed in the purple on the fifth day before the Kalends of October; and on the Kalends of January he entered office as consul” [Col. 0326D].

The procession of ancient consuls, in my judgment, as indeed almost all beginnings, was modest and simple. Later vanity and ambition added many things, which afterward exceeded all measure. Hence Flavius Vopiscus’ complaint in his *Divine Aurelian*: “We recently saw the consulship of Furius Placidus celebrated in the Circus with such extravagance that it seemed not prizes but estates were being given to charioteers, when semi-silk tunics and linen garments with gold embroidery were given, and even horses were given, to the groaning of frugal men. For the consulship has become a matter of wealth, not of men; for if it is conferred for virtues, it ought not to despoil the giver. Those chaste times have perished, and will perish still more through popular ambition.”

The lavish generosity of many persons in staging a consulship elicited various imperial laws intended to place a limit upon the immensity of such gifts. This is evident from Justinian’s Novel 105, which enumerates seven consular processions per year and determines how they are to be celebrated. For the munificence of that same Justinian in staging his first consulship, see Marcellinus Comes.

Departed in winter. Henri de Valois, in his notes on Eusebius, p. 168, arguing against Joseph Scaliger, who maintained that Diocletian’s triumph was celebrated at Rome in the twentieth year of his reign, some months before he laid aside the purple, says—while arguing against him—that this opinion cannot be sustained, because it would follow that Diocletian celebrated his triumph in the winter season and departed from the city of Rome in the middle of winter, arriving at Nicomedia. [Col. 0327B] “Neither of these,” he says, “is probable, since Roman emperors were not accustomed to celebrate triumphs during winter, nor could Diocletian’s age and health have endured the labor of so long a journey in the winter months.” Yet these things which seemed absurd to that most distinguished man are true; and he himself would have recognized them as true had he seen this work of Lactantius, composed by lamplight. For it is certain both that the triumph was celebrated at the same time as the vicennalia, and that Diocletian departed from Rome in winter, while the cold was severe, and afterward arrived at Nicomedia—not indeed in that very winter, but after the following summer. Nor is what Valois shortly afterward adds true: namely, that the illness by which Diocletian was somewhat deranged in mind first seized him at Nicomedia shortly after he had initiated the persecution. Constantine does not say this either. The illness seized him after the triumph and the vicennalia, while he was on the journey, as Lactantius writes here.

The bank of the Striga. When we published this book of Lactantius, [Col. 0327C] we observed that either this passage lay under a textual corruption, or that by the name “bank of the Striga” the shore of the Propontis around Nicomedia must be understood. That our conjecture was true did not seem so to the most distinguished Thomas Spark; and he therefore published a learned and indeed elegant dissertation to show that anything rather than the shore of the Propontis was meant by “bank of the Striga.” After lengthy digressions on the meaning of the word *Striga* and on the bank of the Danube, he declared that the bank of the Danube, or Ister, was meant here, along which, he says, the sick Diocletian was conveyed as far as the Euxine Sea.

But Lactantius does not say that he completed his journey by ship, but “by a circuit along the bank”; this plainly proves that it was made by land, since, according to Ulpian, Book LXVIII *On the Edict*, what is done “on a bank” is not regarded as having been done “in the river.” Diocletian therefore completed his journey by land, namely through those places which are described in the Antonine Itinerary along the bank from Viminacium to Nicomedia—this being the very bank of the Ister, mentioned also by [Col. 0327D] Ovid, Book I *Letters from Pontus*, Elegy IX:

> An ancient city stands upon the bank of the neighboring Ister, bearing its name.

By this place the poet means Antonine’s Istrum, or the Istropolis of Pliny, Ptolemy, the Peutinger Table, and others. Indeed, the legions stationed on the bank of the Ister were called *riparienses*, as is clear from the *Notitia of the Empire*. The Ister, moreover, is the same river which, rising from the ridge of Mount Abnoba, is called the Danube until it reaches Axiopolis; there, Ptolemy relates, the Danube takes the name Ister. Furthermore, that Axiopolis was situated between Sucidava and Capidava may be seen in that same Ptolemy, in the Antonine Itinerary, and in the Peutinger Table.

Accordingly Diocletian, having left Ravenna and set out after winter, reached Nicomedia by the public road described in the same Itinerary and in the Peutinger Table near the end of November: that is, by way of Verona, Altinum, Concordia, Aquileia, Sirmium, Taurunum, Viminacium, [Col. 0328A] and thence along the bank of the Striga, or the Istrian bank, through Cuppae and the remaining places as far as Dorostolum, Sucidava, Axiopolis, Capidava, Istrum, Develtum, Burtudizum, Drizipara, Heraclea, Byzantium, Pantichium, Libyssa, and thence directly to Nicomedia. I have named these places because, among those on the Istrian bank, they enjoy greater renown, and because a large part of them is noted in certain constitutions of Diocletian contained in Justinian’s Code, which appear to show the progress of his journey.

For from the constitution issued at Ravenna on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April in the year 304, it follows that he did not leave Ravenna before March; and another law enacted there on that day shows that he was at Verona on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June. From there he went to Aquileia, Sirmium, Taurunum, and Viminacium, where he seems to have remained for some time, as may be inferred from laws issued or subscribed there from the end of August until the Kalends of October. He was then at Dorostolum on the twelfth and eleventh days before the Kalends of November. On the third day before the Kalends he was at Develtum; on the third day before the Nones, at Burtudizum; [Col. 0328B] on the sixth day before the Ides, at Heraclea; and on the fifth day before the Kalends of December, at Nicomedia. These matters, as I have said, may be gathered from Diocletian’s laws preserved in Justinian’s Code.

I would not, however, insist that these things are true in every respect, since I know that he could have been in the same places on the same days in other years. I offer only my conjecture, which seems sufficiently probable to me. Yet if anyone does not approve it, he may reject it as false and enjoy his own judgment, especially if he has clear grounds for dissent.

That he might dedicate a circus. At Nicomedia, which this man, exceedingly eager for building, was endeavoring to make equal to the city of Rome.

When the year after the vicennalia had been completed. That is, in my judgment, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December. For the sense requires this. Lactantius afterward, at some interval, mentions the Ides of the same month. Diocletian therefore did not lay aside the purple in A.D. 304, as learned men have thought, but in the year after the triumph had been celebrated and the [Col. 0328C] vicennalia observed: that is, in A.D. 305. Scaliger is therefore more correct when, in his annotations on Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, he says that Diocletian laid aside the purple somewhat later than learned men commonly judge. Among other arguments, he adduces that Diocletian is known to have held his tenth consulship, and that it cannot be said that he was consul after laying aside the purple. For Cassiodorus says that Diocletian and Maximian laid aside the purple in the year when Diocletian was holding his tenth and Maximian his seventh consulship. The same is read in a very ancient manuscript of the royal library, written in uncial letters, entitled *Chronicles of George, Bishop of Amiens*.

Although, to speak the truth, that tenth consulship of Diocletian seems highly suspect to me, and I strongly incline to think it was produced by error from the words of the *Fasti*: “likewise for the tenth time, and Maximian for the seventh,” which should be referred to Maximian Herculius and Galerius Maximianus. These considerations nevertheless do not prevent the abdication from being said to have occurred in the year 305, especially since the same fact is established by further evidence. For since Zosimus writes that one hundred and one years elapsed from the consulship of Chilo and Libo—in which Severus exhibited the secular games—to the year in which Diocletian and Maximian abdicated, a year which he wrongly identifies with Diocletian’s ninth and Maximian’s eighth consulship; and since by the agreement of all writers those secular games were celebrated in A.D. 204; it is clearer than daylight that the event which took place in the one hundred and first year afterward occurred in A.D. 305.

So true is this that Johann Friedrich Herwart, having cited this passage of Zosimus at the head of chapter 230 of his chronology and having held that Diocletian abdicated in 304, was compelled to interpret the one hundred and one years that passed from Severus’s games to the year of abdication so as to assert that both endpoints were included in the number—namely, 204 and 304. For he saw that, if he began with 205, [Col. 0329A] as he should, the number of one hundred and one years would not accord with the year of abdication from imperial rule, which, as I have said, he thought occurred in 304. But if he had known that it was accomplished only in the following year, he would not have been driven into these straits.

Moreover, that the abdication occurred in the year we have stated is also proved by chapter 44 of Lactantius, where he writes that the eighth year from the designation of Maximinus, surnamed Daza, was completed on the Kalends of May in the year in which he fought with Licinius. Since that battle was fought in 313, it follows that Diocletian abdicated and Maximinus was designated Caesar on the Kalends of May in 305.

That his death might be concealed. As was formerly customary after the deaths of emperors. Tacitus relates this of Augustus in the first book of the *Annals*, and Rufinus of Constantine in Book I, chapter 11, of the *Ecclesiastical History*. Other examples may also be found. But these are of no great importance.

The Kalends of March. Of the following year, namely 305. For since it is certain that Diocletian celebrated the vicennalia [Col. 0329B] at Rome in 303, departed thence in the middle of December, arrived at Nicomedia after the summer of 304, and dedicated the circus when the year after the vicennalia had been completed—that is, in November—and then fell so ill that he was believed dead on the Ides of December, it is evident that the Kalends of March immediately following those Ides fell in 305, and that Diocletian was still emperor at that time. But shortly we shall see him deliberating with Galerius about laying down the empire.

He became deranged. Eusebius, Book VIII, chapter 13, rightly says that this illness of Diocletian, by whose force he was removed from his soundness of mind, occurred after the vicennalia had been celebrated and after the persecution against our people had been set in motion. He is right indeed. Yet he must be corrected on the point that he says the vicennalia were completed before Diocletian made war on the Christians, whereas from Lactantius, an eyewitness, it is evident that the persecution was initiated first and the vicennalia celebrated afterward, at the close of the year. Chrysostom also mentions [Col. 0329C] Diocletian’s madness in his oration on the holy martyr Babylas.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Nerva’s example. Nerva, burdened by old age and therefore seeing that he was held in contempt, adopted Trajan and on the same day designated him Caesar in the senate, as Xiphilinus reports from Dio. Pliny gives the same cause for the adoption in his *Panegyric*:

> O new and unprecedented path to sovereignty! Not your own ambition, not your own fear, but another’s advantage and another’s fear made you prince.

And below:

> That an emperor who had lost reverence might be able to bestow the empire, it was brought about by the authority of him to whom it was bestowed. At once son, at once Caesar; soon emperor and partner in tribunician power.

That it was unbecoming. Here begins the dialogue between Diocletian and Galerius: the latter pressed his father-in-law to lay down the empire, while the former resisted. This deserves close attention. For hitherto we had thought Diocletian’s abdication voluntary and long [Col. 0329D] contemplated, which certainly seemed most clearly inferable from ancient authors who wrote merely the commonly circulated histories and did not know the secrets of affairs. But Lactantius, who had been summoned to Nicomedia by Diocletian and was frequently at court, could know this entire history better than those who later turned their minds to writing histories.

“He had invaded” or “He had coveted.” In the old manuscript, *invenerat* (“he had found”) is read.

The arrangement. The plan for constituting or governing the commonwealth. The word was then in common use. In the letter of Aurelian to Flavius Arabianus, preserved in Flavius Vopiscus: “Now it is your duty, most agreeable Arabianus, to take care that my arrangements do not come to nothing.” In Valerian’s letter to Ragonius Clarus, preserved in Trebellius Pollio’s *Thirty Tyrants*, chapter 17: “Carry out the arrangement of Balista.” In this sense you see the term applied to the commonwealth. See Lactantius, Book II of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 16; [Col. 0330A] Book III, chapters 7 and 10; and Jacques Godefroy on the title *Concerning the Proximate Officials* in the Theodosian Code.

That the arrangement might be preserved. Since he himself had first divided the Roman world into four parts, two of which he had ordained to be held by two Augusti and the remaining two by two Caesars admitted in hope of the empire, he should now himself, without altering but rather preserving this arrangement, yield the empire along with the aged Maximian, call himself and Constantius—who were then Caesars—Augusti, and appoint two new Caesars in their place. Thus he would give posterity an example of how the immense body of the commonwealth ought to be preserved.

Concord between the two. Galerius was silently proposing the example of Diocletian and Maximian Herculius, who had held the empire for so many years in remarkable harmony, to show that this was not difficult. But in truth harmony is most difficult, particularly where supreme power is concerned; and Tacitus rightly writes in Book IV of the *Annals* that power and harmony can scarcely exist in the same place. In Book XIII, speaking of Seneca and Burrus, the directors of the youth of the emperor Nero, [Col. 0330B] he observes, as something difficult and extraordinary, that they were harmonious in an equal partnership of power. Finally, the discord which later existed between Constantine and Licinius, who held the Roman Empire with equal authority, proved that harmony is difficult to preserve between two emperors.

Inferior and last. Below, chapter 20: “For he despised Constantius, although he necessarily had to be named first.” These passages show that Constantius was given the first place in the adoption, doubtless because of the nobility of his lineage, which he traced to the emperor Claudius. But more on this later.

“Illyricum or.” The old manuscript has *Illyricum*. But in this passage *vel* (“or”) has the same force as “that is.” For Cuper’s observation is not correct, that Illyricum was not on the bank of the Danube but on the Adriatic Sea. Both Moesias, which lie on the Danube bank, belonged to Illyricum, as is well known. The Carpi and Bastarnae, [Col. 0330C] whom the same distinguished man afterward says were defeated by Galerius, were beyond the Danube.

“Precisely so.” A phrase familiar to Lactantius. Book I of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 11: “Precisely so. For he had never spared either virgins or married women.” And Book II, chapter 11: “Precisely so: just as the common people think that the souls of the dead wander about the tombs and the remains of their bodies.”

That their sons should be called [Caesars]. What Diocletian proposed was indeed fair and consonant with reason: that Maxentius, the son of Herculius, and Constantine, the son of Constantius, should be made Caesars, lest emperors’ sons live as private persons. But obstinate Galerius prevailed, appointing other Caesars even in Constantine’s presence.

Not even his father. The same things are related about Maxentius in the *Epitome* of Victor: “This Maximianus” (read *Maxentius*, as is clear also from Book XI of the *Miscellaneous History*) “was never beloved by anyone, not even by his father or his father-in-law Galerius.” He is commonly written to have been the son of Maximian Herculius. Yet shortly before, in the same *Epitome*, these words are found: [Col. 0330D] “By Eutropia, a Syrian woman, he begot Maxentius and Fausta, Constantine’s wife; to whose father Constantius he had given his stepdaughter Theodora. But they report that Maxentius was substituted by a woman’s contrivance, to retain the affection of her husband, who was captivated by the prospect of a most welcome child conceived by a boy.” For I deservedly, as I think, prefer this reading to the others.

This history is confirmed by the anonymous panegyric addressed to Constantine after Maxentius’s defeat, whose author the most learned Pierre Pithou thought to be Nazarius: “For, not to mention those things which ought not to be compared, he was a substitute-child of Maximian, while you were the son of pious Constantius; he [was] of the most contemptible depravity” (read *parvitatis*, “littleness,” rather than *pravitatis*, “depravity”), “with limbs twisted and slackened, and even his very name mutilated by an abusive appellation; you—enough to say it—are so great and such a man.” The author of the fragment on Constantius Chlorus and Constantine says: “When inquiry was made concerning his origin, his mother, having confessed that he had been begotten by a certain Syrian, replied…”

[Col. 0331A] Drunkard, drunken.
