The same author says: “Caesar Severus, obscure both in character and birth, was drunken, and for this reason a friend of Galerius.” The author of this fragment thought Galerius to have been a drunkard, though elsewhere he is not easily found accused of habitual drunkenness. Thus that author says: “Galerius was so drunken that, when in his cups he ordered things that ought not to be done, he established, having been admonished by the prefect, that no one should do anything by his command after dinner.” Doubtless the author of the fragment confused Galerius Maximianus with Galerius Maximinus, of whom Eusebius says in Book VIII, chapter 14, that he was so given to drunkenness and gluttony that he became mad and raged at drinking-parties, and while drunk ordered things which he regretted on the following day when sober.

This is how the Greek words of Eusebius were translated by Christophorson and Valois. But Rufinus gave them another sense, saying that Maximinus was so drunken that he was thought mad and mentally deranged by wine-fury, and that while drunk he ordered things to be done which on the next day he did not know he had ordered. The *Epitome* of Victor says the following of the same man, which agrees more closely [Col. 0331B] with the interpretation of those distinguished men: “He was excessively fond of wine; when drunk, with his mind corrupted, he gave certain harsh orders, and when the deed displeased him, he decreed that what he had ordered should be deferred until a sober and morning hour.” Finally, after his defeat by Licinius, when he had gone to Tarsus and hoped for no refuge, in anguish and fear he fled to death as a remedy for his evils; and first he stuffed himself with food and gorged himself with wine, as Lactantius will say below in chapter 49.

“I sent him to Maximian.” Galerius was indeed exceedingly bold: before consulting Diocletian, he had sent Severus to Maximian in order that he might be made Caesar by him. This passage also shows how rash and mad Galerius was, and how little free and voluntary Diocletian’s abdication was.

“That he might be clothed by him.” Namely, with the purple, which was the insignia of the imperial rank. Thus Severus, later defeated by Herculius and brought to Ravenna, returned the garment and purple to the very man from whom he had received them, as Lactantius says below in chapter 24.

Pointing out Daia. Or Daza, the son of Galerius’s sister, and for this very reason called Galerius Maximinus at his adoption. The *Epitome* of Victor: “Galerius Maximinus, born of the sister of the Cattleman, and before his accession called by his true name Daza.”

“He had ordered Maximinus.” In the old manuscript, both here and almost everywhere, *Maximianus* is read—the customary error of Greek and Latin copyists, who very often confuse the names Maximianus and Maximinus. But because it is certain that this man was called not Maximianus but Maximinus, we have corrected it everywhere, lest any difficulty delay the reader.

Of a man. Cuper and Spark observe that *ominis* (“of an omen”) should be read; I strongly approve this.

## CHAPTER XIX

They proceed on the Kalends of May. In A.D. 305, as we have said. Therefore Zosimus and the Idatian Fasti are in error, where these things are said to have occurred under the consulship of Diocletian IX [Col. 0331D] and Maximian VIII, on the Kalends of April. Others place the emperors’ abdication on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, at the Palilia themselves; Labbe places it on the Kalends of August, on what authority I do not know. But now it is not permissible to dispute either the year or the day, after so clear and precise a history of that abdication as Lactantius gives us.

“Constantine, looking upon…” From this passage and several other testimonies of ancient writers, it can be proved that Constantine was with Diocletian at the time these events took place. Therefore there must be an error in the fragment on Constantius Chlorus and Constantine, p. 472, where it is written: “Severus and Maximinus were made Caesars, Constantine knowing nothing of anything of the sort.” Here *Constantio* must be read, “Constantius,” without whom both the abdication was performed and the Caesars appointed, as Lactantius teaches.

Maximianus himself. Galerius, surnamed the Cattleman.

[Col. 0332A] He had assumed the purple. These words are highly important and must not be passed over lightly. For they indicate the place where Galerius Maximianus was adopted by Diocletian: namely, near Nicomedia. The ancient writers of history are wholly silent about this matter, except that the Alexandrian Chronicle says that Maximian Jovius and Constantius were admitted into partnership in the empire at Nicomedia. Sigonius, in Book I *On the Western Empire*, thinks this was done in Illyricum. But this passage of Lactantius proves him wrong.

Here again it should be noted: just as Diocletian and Maximian laid aside the empire on one and the same day—the former near Nicomedia, the latter at Milan—so also on one and the same day Caesars were adopted by them: Galerius by Diocletian near Nicomedia, and Constantius by Herculius in Italy, perhaps even at Milan.

To seek rest. From this doubtless arose the common opinion that Diocletian, once willing and acting voluntarily, divested himself of the empire because of old age and failing health, [Col. 0332B] and that he did this after long deliberation. Learned men infer this, and rightly, from the ancient panegyric addressed to Maximian Herculius and Constantine after the marriage of Constantine and Fausta. But Lactantius disclosed the secret of this history, which Eusebius confesses that he did not know in Book I of the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 18, where he says that the elder Augusti somehow or other abdicated the empire.

Rufinus, Book VIII, chapter 15, says that Diocletian Augustus reached such a pitch of vanity and madness that, having laid aside together with his colleague Augustus the insignia of royalty, they lived after their reign as private men and commoners. But Constantine, in the *Oration to the Assembly of the Saints*, chapter 25—to whom Eusebius, Book VIII, chapter 13, seems to lend support—expressly affirms that Diocletian voluntarily abdicated the empire because of mental derangement. Valois refutes him in his annotations, and rightly. Yet Valois himself was wrong when he said that Diocletian formed his plan of abdicating the empire long before the persecution, namely when he triumphed at Rome over the Persians and other barbarian nations. For the sequence of this work of Lactantius shows that the plan of abdicating the empire was formed after the persecution had been stirred up, after Diocletian’s return from Rome, after the vicennalia had been completed, and therefore after that severe illness through whose force Diocletian seemed, according to Eusebius, to have been removed from his soundness of mind. Moreover, the triumph was not celebrated before the persecution, as has been shown above.

Severus and Maximinus. The Idatian Fasti, under the consulship of Diocletian IX and Maximian VIII: “Under these consuls Diocletian and Maximian laid aside the purple and became private persons, and clothed Severus and Maximinus: Herculius [clothed] Severus at Milan, and Diocletian [clothed] Maximinus near Nicomedia.” But Eusebius’s *Chronicle* is wrong, where it is written that Galerius alone held the imperial power as Augustus for two years, and that in the year after the elder Augusti’ abdication, Maximinus and Severus were made Caesars by Galerius Maximianus. Thus it stands in most editions. But in the Venetian edition of 1483, [Col. 0332D] in the ancient manuscript codices cited by Pontacus, and also in the very ancient and excellent Colbert manuscript, the words stating that Galerius alone held the empire for two years are absent, and the substitution of Severus and Maximinus as Caesars is placed in the very year in which the abdication occurred.

Petavius nevertheless defends the common reading of Eusebius’s *Chronicle* in Book XI, chapter 34, of *The Doctrine of Times*, and interprets the words concerning Galerius’s two years thus: that he ruled alone for two years, that is, before Caesars had been created; but that the Caesars were chosen in the year in which Constantius died. Accordingly, in Book XIII, which is chronological, he says he infers from the fragment of an anonymous writer published after Ammianus Marcellinus in Valois’s edition that Severus had commanded troops in Italy for some time before becoming Caesar, and that he did not attain that rank so quickly, but at almost the same time as Constantine, son of Constantius. Petavius would surely have recognized all these things as false if he had seen this book of Lactantius.

Severus and Maximinus. It is certain that these things were done at Nicomedia, where Diocletian and Galerius Maximianus then were. Yet Socrates, at the beginning of his history, as Musculus, Christophorson, and Valois translate him, says that Galerius, after the abdication of Diocletian and Maximian Herculius, went to Italy and appointed two Caesars, Maximinus in the East and Severus in Italy. Epiphanius Scholasticus translates otherwise, and more consistently with historical truth: “When Diocletian and Maximian Herculius had chosen private life, and Maximian Galerius, who had ruled with them, holding Italy, had made two Caesars—Maximinus in the East and Severus in Italy—then Constantine, after his father’s death in Britain, was appointed emperor.”

However the matter may stand, it is plain that Socrates thought Maximinus and Severus were made Caesars after Italy had passed into Galerius’s dominion, whereas at the time of the abdication it had fallen to Constantius. Eutropius seems to have held the same opinion at the beginning of Book X, where he writes that Galerius, when he perceived that Italy also had been added to his administration with Constantius’s consent, created two Caesars. Both are therefore mistaken, since Lactantius shows that the Caesars were made near Nicomedia at the same time as the elder Augusti laid aside the empire. [Col. 0333B] The occasion of their error, in my judgment, was this: Maximian Herculius abdicated at Milan in the presence of Severus, whom he made Caesar and from whom he received the purple; therefore they doubtless believed that both Caesars were made in Italy by Maximian, failing to distinguish Maximian Herculius from Galerius Maximianus. But this could not have happened except after the abdication. See Sigonius, Book II *On the Western Empire*.

“Susum.” “In the upper part, in the marked place,” as Papias says. The ancients used *susum* for *sursum* (“upward”), as the most distinguished Charles du Fresne shows at length in his *Glossary*. Rigaltius too, on Book II, chapter 28, of St Cyprian’s *Testimonies to Quirinus*, where “he called heaven upward” is read, notes that *susum* is found in the Beneventan and Veronese manuscripts.

“To inquire” or “to hesitate.” In the old book *stare* (“to stand”) is written, and *haesitare* (“to hesitate”) in the margin, apparently as an emendation. I think both readings false, and that *sciscitari* (“to inquire”) better suits this passage.

With Constantine rejected. This passage alone, even though other arguments are not lacking, shows that Constantine was not made Caesar with Severus and Maximinus. The same is established by the silence of writers of that age and by certain ancient inscriptions written after Diocletian’s abdication and before Constantius’s death; in these, after the names of Constantius and Galerius as Augusti, the names of Severus and Maximinus as Caesars are inscribed, with Constantine’s name omitted. One of these is presented by Onofrio Panvinio in Book II of the *Fasti*, another by Gruter, p. 178.

Moreover, this was the arrangement introduced by Diocletian in the administration of the commonwealth, which Galerius insisted ought to be preserved permanently: that there should be only four rulers, two senior ones holding supreme power, and likewise two junior ones serving as assistants, as Lactantius teaches in chapter 17 of this work. Consequently, when Galerius later received news of Constantius’s death and of Constantine’s installation in his place, though he greatly wished to hold the empire alone and yet did not wish to alter the established constitutional order, he preferred to take an Augustus as colleague rather than designate a third Caesar beyond the proper number, as Lactantius says in chapter 25 of the same history. From what has been said thus far, it is plainly inferred that Constantine was not made Caesar with Severus and Maximinus.

Yet the following occurs in the *Epitome* of Victor: “Constantius, father of Constantine, and the Cattleman are called Caesars [and] Augusti; Caesars having been created—Severus for Italy, Maximinus, the son of Galerius’s sister, for the East—and at the same time Constantine is made Caesar.” It certainly cannot be denied that Constantine [Col. 0334A] was Caesar, since many coins attest it, on which his laureate image is seen with this inscription: “CONSTANTINE, MOST NOBLE CAESAR.” On one, even Constantine’s forenames are read as follows: “FLAVIUS VALERIUS CONSTANTINE, MOST NOBLE CAESAR.”

The most learned man, relying on the authority of Aurelius Victor, believed that Constantine received the rank of Caesar from Augustus Maximian, his father-in-law, in the same month in which his father Constantius was proclaimed Augustus. Against him, Joseph Scaliger, in his annotations on Eusebius, p. 247, maintains that Constantine was not Caesar under his father but under Galerius, although he subsequently notes that no history reports that he was called Caesar by Galerius. Had this history of Lactantius been known to learned men, they would doubtless have refrained from writing things not consonant with truth. For first, as we have said, it is certain that Constantine was not made Caesar with Severus and Maximinus. Next, he could not at the same time have been made Caesar by Maximian Herculius, since he was not with him but with Diocletian. Nor was Herculius then his father-in-law, because Constantine married Fausta, Herculius’s daughter, only after Constantius’s death, as we shall say in its place. Finally, we shall see below that Lactantius teaches Constantine was called Caesar by Galerius—a fact found in no historian in Scaliger’s time.

He cast the purple upon him. So that he might clothe and invest with imperial dress the man whom Galerius had stripped of private attire. For *to clothe* was the term by which the insignia of supreme authority were then denoted. The Idatian Fasti: “They clothed Severus and Maximinus.” And Lactantius in this chapter, speaking of Severus: “I sent him to Maximian, that he might be clothed by him.”

The veteran king. He aptly calls Diocletian a veteran king because he had reigned for twenty complete years, as though thereby he had earned privileges like those granted to soldiers who had served for twenty years in a legion or vexillation.

He is sent home. That is, to Dioclea, a town near Salona in Dalmatia, where he grew old in distinguished retirement.

Shield-bearer. There were various kinds of shield-bearers in the palace of the Roman emperors; Henri de Valois discusses them in his notes on Ammianus Marcellinus, p. 33.

Protector, then tribune. Constantius had reached the empire by the same ranks, though not so quickly. A fragment published by Henri de Valois, p. 471: “Constantius, nephew through a brother of the divine Claudius, that excellent emperor, was first a protector, then a tribune, and afterward governor of the Dalmatias.” They were called protectors because they protected the emperor’s side and were selected to guard his person. Some remained in his retinue; others were sent to the provinces with counts and masters of soldiers; some from that corps were even assigned to guard the frontier. Henri de Valois treats them more fully in his notes on Ammianus Marcellinus, pp. 33, 46, 152.

## CHAPTER XX

The old men having been expelled. That is, Diocletian and Herculius: the former withdrew to Dalmatia, the latter to Lucania, as most writers report.

The sole lord of the world. Not because he was truly the sole emperor, since he had Constantius as colleague, but because, despising him, he regarded him as nothing. Socrates too, Book I of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 11, writes that Galerius Maximianus held the helm of the entire empire. Henri de Valois says this must be understood generously: “For Galerius did not truly hold the helm of the whole empire, since at the same time there were two other Augusti, Constantine in Gaul and Maxentius at Rome. Yet he is said nonetheless to have administered the supreme power because he was the senior Augustus and was honored by the junior Augusti as a father.”

This observation of the most learned man has something of truth, but not everything. For although I should grant that Galerius was honored as a father by Constantine, who was a man of great courtesy, it is certain that he was not so honored [Col. 0335A] by Maxentius, though Galerius was his father-in-law. Indeed, they were never on good terms, even while Diocletian lived, and a most serious war existed between them from the time Maxentius assumed the purple until Licinius’s reign.

Named first. Above, chapter 18, Galerius Maximianus says to Diocletian: “If he himself should refuse to yield, I would look to my own interests, lest I remain any longer inferior and last.” Eusebius, Book I, chapter 18, of the *Life of Constantine*, says that, when the elder Augusti abdicated the empire, Constantius was proclaimed the first Augustus and was called the first Augustus among the four subsequently appointed. He is always named in the prior place in the Idatian Fasti, by Zosimus, Eutropius, in Justinian’s Code, in an ancient inscription concerning the dedication of Diocletian’s Baths, and in several other inscriptions printed by Gruter, pp. 58, 159, 161, 164, 279, 1063.

Yet Aelius Spartianus in *Aelius Verus*, and Flavius Vopiscus in *Carinus*, name Galerius Maximianus before Constantius, even during Diocletian’s lifetime. It certainly seemed fair that the man adopted by Diocletian, and married to his daughter Valeria, should have precedence over the man adopted by Maximian, the emperor of second rank. Conversely, it accorded with reason that a man of great nobility, such as Constantius, should not be placed after a rustic, a herdsman, but should have him after himself in the administration of the commonwealth.

I would judge that the testimonies of Spartianus and Vopiscus should yield to the authority of ancient inscriptions and of those authors who expressly say that first place was given to Constantius—especially because those who assign it to Galerius did not treat this history systematically, but only in passing and while pursuing another subject. The same must be said of the author of the *Life of Saint Procopius the Martyr*, found in the fourth volume of Surius, where Galerius is named first before Constantius.

From the three. That is, from Galerius, Severus, and Maximinus.

[Col. 0335C] Licinius, a man of the rank *vir clarissimus*, his friend. Socrates reports the same (Book I, chapter 2), where he says that Galerius Maximianus departed this life after first making Licinius emperor—his old friend and tent-companion, who was of Dacian origin.

Lest he call him his son. I think this is the sense of these and the following words. Although Galerius had Licinius as an old friend and tent-companion, a good soldier, to use Tacitus’s expression, and a partner in victory, whose counsels he employed in the governance of everything, he nevertheless did not wish to make him Caesar, lest he should call as his son one with whom he had lived throughout his life as with a brother. Instead, by casting his plans far ahead, he contemplated putting him in the place of Constantius—who would either soon die or at least certainly be driven out by force—so that he might thus call him Augustus and brother. For those made Caesars were counted among the sons and were called sons of the Augusti. But those proclaimed Augusti were called brothers of the emperors, as we saw above concerning Maximianus Herculius.

[Col. 0335D] He might celebrate his vicennalia. In imitation of Diocletian, who, after completing nineteen years of his reign, came to Rome and celebrated the beginning of his twentieth with such magnificence that Sextus Rufus therefore said that the triumphal pageant of the victory won over the Persians under Diocletian was famous. But at that time Galerius was still far from his vicennalia. For chapter 35 of this book shows that they ought to have been celebrated on the Kalends of March following his death. He therefore died at the beginning of the nineteenth year from his being made Caesar, since he died in May, the month immediately preceding the day of the vicennalia. He died, moreover, while holding his eighth consulship, as is written in this history and in the Fasti of Idatius. But if these things are true, how can Galerius have ruled for twenty-one years? For that is the total counted from the consulship of Tiberianus and Dio, in which Galerius is said to have been made Caesar, to his eighth consulship.

Further, Lactantius himself, in chapter 18 of this book, [Col. 0336A] teaches that at the time when he was urging Diocletian to abdicate, he had already struggled for fifteen years in Illyricum, on the bank of the Danube, against barbarian peoples, while others meanwhile ruled luxuriously within more spacious and peaceful lands. Certainly, if one adds the six years during which he administered the commonwealth after Diocletian’s retirement to the fifteen which had elapsed when these words were spoken by Maximianus, it will be evident that he died in the twenty-first year of his reign, as is read in the common editions of Eusebius’s Chronicle. Yet in the very ancient and excellent manuscript of the Colbert Library, and in various old copies which Pontacus attests that he saw, only this is read: “Galerius Maximianus dies.”

But since Lactantius’s authority is such that he cannot be contradicted, and Aurelius Victor writes that Galerius held the power of Caesar for thirteen years and the imperial power for five, while Eutropius at the beginning of Book IX and the author of the Alexandrian Chronicle, p. 651, teach that Constantius, who was made Caesar with Galerius, [Col. 0336B] died at York in Britain in the thirteenth year of his rule; and since, moreover, the fragment on Constantius Chlorus, p. 472, reads that Galerius ruled for nineteen years, we must accept the view which confines his authority within nineteen years. The fifteen years during which he fought barbarian peoples must be understood partly of wars he waged there while still a private person, partly after he was made Caesar; and the beginnings of his principate must be reckoned from the Kalends of March in the year 293, so that he can thus be said to have been Caesar for [OCR uncertainty: “135” probably requires correction] years in the year 315, when Diocletian laid down the imperial power.

His own son as Caesar. Galerius’s son, I suppose: below, in chapter 35, Galerius commends his wife and son to Licinius. Nowhere else do we read that Galerius had a son. Certainly, if he had one, he would have had him by an earlier wife. In that case he would not have sought two Caesars outside his own family, but would at least have named his own son in the first place. He had none by Valeria, for she was barren, as Lactantius teaches below in chapter 50. These words, therefore, must be understood of Candidianus, who is named shortly afterwards and whom Lactantius notes below in the same fiftieth chapter to have been born of a concubine, adopted because of Valeria’s barrenness by Valeria, Galerius’s wife, and betrothed to the seven-year-old daughter of Maximinus Augustus. Thus the father intended to make him Caesar after celebrating the vicennalia. Candidianus was killed by Licinius in A.D. 313, at the age of sixteen.

He himself might lay down. The imperial power. Galerius therefore contemplated withdrawing from public affairs after the celebration of the vicennalia, in imitation of Diocletian’s fortune. But God frustrated all his plans. He neither celebrated the vicennalia, nor made Candidianus Caesar, nor attained the sweetness of leisure.

## CHAPTER XXI

The decurions were tortured. Lactantius notes this as an act contrary to law and custom. Under Roman civil law it was not permitted to torture decurions, [Col. 0336D] as is clear from Constantine’s letter to Probianus, proconsul of Africa. Hence Baronius, under the year 314, warns that the Acts of the exoneration of Felix, bishop of Aptunga, are corrupt at the place where the proconsul Aelianus says to Ingentius: “Do not therefore flatter yourself because you tell me that you are a worshipper of God and for that reason cannot be tortured.” Here “decurion” ought to be read in place of “worshipper of God.” Yet afterwards, as Baronius observes there, Constantine enacted a law permitting decurions to be tortured in a charge of forgery.

Men of the rank *perfectissimus*. Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, Book V, chapter 15: “No one is most perfect unless he has fulfilled every grade.” The dignity of *perfectissimus*, as Valesius says in his note on Book XXI of Ammianus Marcellinus, was lower than that of *clarissimus*; and just as the *clarissimi* assembled before the prefect of the city, so the *perfectissimi* assembled before the vicariate prefecture. See also Baldwin’s notes on Eumenius’s oration on the restoration of the schools; Juretus, in his notes on letter 40 of Book X of Symmachus; and Jacobus Gothofredus, on the Theodosian Code, vol. III, p. 418.

*Gynaeceum*. *Gynaecea*, as the word itself indicates, were places assigned to women’s work, to which both men and women were sometimes consigned as a punishment. The most distinguished Charles du Fresne made many observations on such *gynaecea* in his Glossary; so did we in our notes on Regino, p. 568, and on the Capitularies, p. 1009. See also Valesius’s annotations on Eusebius, p. 211.

*Lusorium*. A theatre or amphitheatre where public games were presented, as the same Du Fresne shows at length. Salvian, Book VI, p. 122 of our second edition: “Indeed, since it would take too long now to speak of everything—amphitheatres, odea, *lusoria*, processions, athletes, and so forth.” The Acts of Saint Seraphia, virgin and martyr, chapter 3: “But on the third day the governor prepared a *lusorium* beyond the bridge over the arch of Albinus, where theatrical performances were customarily held.”

The *lusoria* in Vopiscus are something else: namely, the vessels which the Romans kept on rivers [Col. 0337B] separating the Roman Empire from barbarian peoples, always fitted out and ready to prevent their crossings and incursions, as Salmasius explains in his notes on the same Vopiscus, p. 475. Jacobus Gothofredus also discusses them at length in his commentary on the title of the Theodosian Code, *On the Danubian Lusoriae*. Elsewhere *lusorius* means the same as “mocking,” as in Book XLIII of the Digest, last law, *That Nothing Be Done in a Public Place*, where it reads: “He who builds contrary to the praetor’s edict must remove the building. Otherwise the praetor’s authority will be empty and ludicrous.” Likewise Seneca, *On Benefits*, Book V, chapter 8: “Like a jesting name, it immediately passes away”; and Letter 80: “A spectacle neither faithful nor serious, but ludicrous.”

So too in Pope Gelasius’s letter to Euphemius, bishop of Constantinople, where the common text reads: “Or you will be known to cast these accusations against me in excuse of luxury.” In the very ancient and best manuscripts of the Church of Beauvais and the monastery of Corbie, however, I saw written: “Or grant pardon: you will be known to cast these accusations against me in mockery (*lusorie*).” [Col. 0337C] Nor is this error unusual. For Salmasius observes in the passage cited shortly before that, in place of what he himself printed in Vopiscus—“the barbarians burned the Roman *lusoriae*”—the common text was accustomed to print “Roman luxuries.” And Jacobus Gothofredus, in the passage just cited, mentions three places in the Theodosian Code where *luxuriis* is written for *lusoriis*.

That breath might be restored. Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, Book V, chapter 11: “They strive, therefore, to prevail, and inflict exquisite pains upon bodies; and they avoid nothing except that the tortured should die.” And shortly after: “But with obstinate folly they order careful treatment to be given to those under torture, so that their limbs may be renewed for other torments and fresh blood restored for punishment.”

## CHAPTER XXII

No punishment in his power. In the old copy one reads, “No punishment light for him.” A very bad reading has pointed us to the good one.

In a capital case. This correction too is ours. [Col. 0337D] For the old manuscript has: “In a case, punishment of the head and the penalty of the sword for very few,” etc. Clearly the word *poena* crept into this place from above.

A good death. That is, a death not compelled by the force of tortures, but easy and without suffering, such as opening the veins, strangulation, and poison. Below, chapter 26, concerning Severus: “By this action he gained nothing except a good death. For, when his veins were opened, he was compelled to die gently.” And chapter 30, concerning Maximianus Herculius: “Finally, he was granted the power of a free death, and he tied the knot of hideous death from a lofty beam.” But here Lactantius has Tacitus against him in saying that Severus was compelled to die gently after his veins were opened. For Tacitus, *Annals*, Book XVI, in his final discussion of Petronius, who perished by that sort of death, says: “Then the slowness of death brought grievous sufferings.”

## CHAPTER XXIII

A census into the provinces. A census declaration comprised two things: [Col. 0338A] the extent of lands and the number of persons, both free and servile, as Henry Valesius explains extensively and with his customary learning in his note on Ammianus Marcellinus, p. 167. Moreover, this passage of Lactantius confirms the conjecture of the very learned Jacobus Gothofredus, who inferred from Book II of the Theodosian Code, *On the Census*, that Galerius Maximianus made some change throughout Lycia and Pamphylia after Diocletian’s abdication—namely, subjecting the urban populace to the poll-tax. That law certainly receives much light from this chapter of Lactantius.

Slaves against their masters. It is a rule of law, as Casaubon says in his note on Flavius Vopiscus, that a slave cannot be questioned in a case affecting his master’s life. But a constitution of Severus made exceptions for several crimes: adultery, evasion of the census, and treason. Emperor Tacitus therefore annulled that constitution by his law. Galerius restored it—I do not know whether by enacting a law, but certainly in practice. Paulus, *Sentences*, Book I, title 13: “Neither slave nor freedman may be questioned in a case affecting the life of master or patron.”

[Col. 0338B] Which the victors. At first, following the old copy, we published: “Which the ancients.” Afterwards the correction suggested itself. Then we also restored *ea* (“those things”) in place of *et* (“and”).

Trajan and the Dacians. For Galerius Maximianus was born in Dacia Ripensis, in a place which he himself called Romulianum after Romula, his mother; it lay not far from Sardica, as Eutropius and Eusebius teach in the Chronicle. Trajan made two expeditions against the Dacians: the first in his fourth consulship, the second in his fifth, when he had already been reigning six years, as Casaubon observes on Spartianus. Xiphilinus, indeed, from Dio records both of Trajan’s expeditions against the Dacians, but nowhere mentions a tribute imposed upon them. He says only that Dacia was made a province, as Flavius Vopiscus also reports in his *Divine Aurelian*. But since it was a fixed and constant Roman rule that every people reduced to provincial status was tributary and obeyed a magistrate of the Roman people, as Sigonius observes in Book I, *On the Law of Provinces*, there can be no doubt that Dacia was tributary—especially since Lactantius expressly affirms it.

Protected from injuries. The old book wrongly reads *injurietatis*, and so we first printed it. But in the final page we observed that *injuriae tutos* (“protected from injury”) ought to be read; since the correction is certain, we have now transferred it into the text.

## CHAPTER XXIV

That he might send Constantine away. Zosimus, an enemy of Constantine, treats this history differently from Lactantius. He attributes Constantine’s departure from Galerius’s side not to Constantius’s commands but to Constantine’s ambition and desire for power, already long meditated in his mind. When Constantine saw Severus and Maximinus made Caesars, he resolved to leave the places where he was staying and set out for his father Constantius, who was among the Transalpine peoples and usually lived in Britain.

Aurelius [Col. 0338D] Victor says the same in the *Book of the Caesars*. He writes that Constantine, even from boyhood stirred by a lofty and powerful spirit with the ardour of ruling, could not endure that Severus and Maximinus had been made Caesars while he himself was passed over. By the pretext of flight—which is also found in Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, Book I, chapter 20—he reached his father Constantius in Britain as the latter was approaching the end of life; after his father’s death, with the efforts of all who were present, he assumed imperial power.

But in the Epitome of Victor, where the same matters are repeated, it is wrongly written that the young Constantine was held hostage by Galerius in the city of Rome under the pretext of religion. This is what Baronius, Camden, and Morinus also wrote after that Epitome. Yet Galerius had not at that time seen Rome, as may certainly be inferred from chapter 27 of this work, and he never set foot in the city. Further, all writers agree that Constantine was with Diocletian and Maximianus, namely in Bithynia, where Diocletian resided. Praxagoras in Photius, codex 62, expressly teaches this; it is also inferred from the *Polity of Saints Metrophanes and Alexander* in Photius, codex 264, and from Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, Book I, chapter 19.

If what Nicephorus Callistus reports concerning Constantine, Book VII, chapter 18, were true, this discrepancy could readily be reconciled. For he says that Constantius, whom he calls Constans, arranged for the boy Constantine and his mother to be brought to Rome. Fearing, however, that something improper might happen to him through jealousy and marital rivalry on the part of Theodora, his lawful wife and Constantine’s stepmother, he sent him to Diocletian at Nicomedia, where Diocletian was with his son-in-law Galerius Maximianus; there Constantine lived in the imperial palace.

Before leaving this matter, the reader should be warned that Baronius has forced this passage from Victor’s Epitome into a foreign meaning. When the Epitome says that Constantine was held hostage by Galerius “under the pretext of religion,” Baronius interprets this as the Christian religion: either because the young man, born to Helena, a Christian mother, and to Constantius, a father more favourably disposed to Christians, had given some indication that he favoured that religion; or because Constantius’s marked favour toward our people led Galerius to suspect him of abandoning ancestral superstition. [Col. 0339B] Baronius therefore judges that Constantine was kept under guard at Rome by Galerius as a hostage, so that, using religion as a pretext, he might prevent this exceptionally gifted young man from succeeding his father.

But no such circuitous explanation was needed for the Epitome’s passage, whose narrative is simple and plain. The author meant only that Constantine was held by Galerius as a hostage under the appearance of religious devotion—that is, under the appearance of special affection and duty—as though Galerius had requested him from his father for instruction in military affairs and in the art of governing the commonwealth. For Helena was not yet Christian at that time, nor did Galerius, a superstitious man, charge Constantine with Christianity, when Diocletian judged that the sons of Herculius and Constantius ought to be created Caesars. Galerius tried to remove the young man from the highest station by other devices: namely, plots, exposing him to various dangers.

He had long sought him back in vain. These words are absent from the old manuscript. Since, however, the sense was defective and it was clear that something was missing here, we added these two words on the authority of the Fragment on Constantius Chlorus, which reads: “Constantine, a hostage with Diocletian and Galerius, served bravely under them in Asia; after Diocletian and Herculius had laid down the imperial power, Constantius sought him back from Galerius. But Galerius first exposed him to many dangers.” Nevertheless, if anyone thinks that the gap cannot be filled with these words, he may substitute “had not seen him” or something similar.

He had attacked him with plots. The same Fragment: “But Galerius first exposed him to many dangers. For, while serving as a cavalryman against the Sarmatians, the young man had seized a fierce barbarian by his flowing hair and brought him captive before the feet of Emperor Galerius. Then, when Galerius sent him through a marsh, he entered on his horse and made a path for the others to the Sarmatians; after many of them had been struck down, he brought victory to Galerius.” Galerius then sent him back to his father. See also Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, Book I, chapter 20, and the Annals of Zonaras.

He had exposed him to wild beasts. Praxagoras, in his book *On the Deeds of Constantine*, says that Galerius Maximianus set traps for the young man and arranged that he should enter into combat with a fierce lion; Constantine overcame and killed the beast. Zonaras says the same under the reign of Diocletian.

The seal. That is, a letter of release secured with a seal. See Du Fresne’s Glossary.

That he might be detained by Severus. For one traveling from Nicomedia to Gaul had to pass through Italy, where Severus ruled. The Fragment on Constantius Chlorus, p. 471: “In order to avoid Severus while passing through Italy, he hurried with the utmost speed, cutting the post-horses’ hamstrings behind him; having crossed the Alps, he came to his father Constantius at Boulogne.”

Having removed the public horses. Zosimus, Book II, relates that Constantine, fearing that he might perhaps be captured while fleeing, mutilated and rendered useless the stable horses maintained by the state as soon as he reached any posting station. By doing this from place to place as he travelled, he prevented pursuers from proceeding further. Nearly the same account is found in Victor’s Epitome.

The public post. See Casaubon’s notes on Spartianus, where he discusses the public and fiscal post extensively and learnedly.

He reached his father. On the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, in my opinion. For in the old calendar published by Herwart, the following is written for that day: “The arrival of the Divine One,” that is, plainly, of Constantine. For that calendar was written under his rule. Those who think that he reached his father on the eighth day before the Kalends of August have been misled because Aurelius Victor [Col. 0340B] in the *Book of the Caesars*, and other ancient writers, say that he came to his father Constantius in Britain as the latter was approaching the end of life. They interpret these words as though one near death must necessarily have died immediately after Constantine’s arrival. On his arrival to his father Constantius and on the events concerning Constantine at that time, see Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, Book I, chapter 21, and the *Polity of Saints Metrophanes and Alexander* in Photius. He came to his father from Nicomedia, not from Rome, as Camden falsely wrote in his *Britannia*, p. 52, misled by the author of Victor’s Epitome.

He handed over the imperial power through his hands. Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, Book XI, chapter 4: “For he lived to old age and handed over the kingdom through his hands to his son.”

He handed over the imperial power. Eusebius says the same in *Life of Constantine*, Book I, chapter 25. Joseph Scaliger therefore wrongly rebukes the author of the *Polity of Saints Metrophanes and Alexander* in his notes on Eusebius’s Chronicle for writing that the dying Constantius designated Constantine as successor in the imperial power. Nor does that unanimity of the soldiers, to which Scaliger assigns the beginning of Constantine’s reign, prejudice at all the statements of the author of the *Polity*. Eumenius proves this in his panegyric on Constantine: after saying that Constantine was chosen emperor by the manifest decision of his father, he immediately adds: “Good gods, with what happiness did you endow pious Constantius even at his departure! An emperor about to pass into heaven saw the heir whom he was leaving behind. For immediately after he had been removed from earth, the entire army united in your favour; the minds and eyes of all singled you out.”

Likewise Emperor Julian, in his first oration to Constantius: “Why should we recount in greater detail how your father, after his own father’s death, acquired imperial power not only by his father’s judgment but also by the vote of all the armies?” Orosius, Book VII, chapter 26: “Constantius Augustus, a man of the highest gentleness and civility, died in Britain; he left Constantine, his son born of the concubine Helena, as emperor of the Gauls.”

He received the repose of life. The Fasti of Idatius, under the consulship of Constantius VI and Maximianus VI: “Under these consuls Constantius died, and Constantine was afterwards raised on the eighth day before the Kalends of August.” Eusebius’s Chronicle: “Constantius died at York in Britain in the sixteenth year of his reign; he was also buried there,” if what the very learned William Camden relates of his tomb in *Britannia*, p. 572, is true. This occurred in A.D. 306, as Valesius rightly maintains against Petavius in his annotations on Eusebius. Then, as Socrates says, Constantine was made emperor in place of his father Constantius, who had departed life on the eighth day before the Kalends of August. This, therefore, is the first year of Constantine’s reign. Thus the very ancient calendar in Herwart and Bucherius reads: “8 Kalends of August: birthday of the Divine Constantine.” It is therefore wrong for Book I [Col. 0341A] of the *Tripartite History* and Book XI of the *Miscellaneous History* to state that Constantine was made emperor on the sixth day before the Kalends of August. Eumenius, in the panegyric cited above: “O Britain, fortunate and now happier than all lands, which first beheld Constantine as Caesar!”

To restore Christians to worship. Lactantius, in the preface to Book I of the *Divine Institutes*, addressed to Constantine: “For when that most blessed day had dawned upon the world, on which the supreme God raised you to the blessed summit of empire, you inaugurated a saving and universally desired rule with a splendid beginning, restoring justice after it had been overturned and removed, and expiating the most shameful crime of others.”

Restored. I think *restitutio* (“restoration”) should be substituted, so that it reads: “This was his first enactment: the restoration of the holy religion.” Columbus substitutes *restitutae*.

## CHAPTER XXV

His image was removed. Eumenius, in his panegyric on Constantine: “And although you had referred to the senior emperors what they wished to be done concerning the supreme government, they nevertheless anticipated you by their enthusiasm—an action which they soon afterwards approved in judgment.” The most distinguished Hadrian Valesius, in Book I of his *Frankish History*, p. 20, understands “the senior emperors” here to mean Diocletian, Maximianus Herculius, and Galerius Maximianus, whom he says approved the action of the soldiers who had put the purple upon Constantine.

The very learned man will permit me to depart from that opinion, since it is certain that Diocletian and Herculius then had no role in the commonwealth, and consequently there would have been no point in Constantine’s referring to them the imperial power offered him. By “senior emperors,” therefore, I understand Galerius Maximianus Augustus, Severus, and Maximinus Caesar. Yet I am strongly inclined to think that the report was made to Galerius alone, who was then sole master of affairs; but that Eumenius, in the manner of orators, spoke according to a formula and referred to all emperors matters that ought to have been said of one only.

Lactantius called it a laurelled image because those who announced joyous and successful events brought laurelled tablets, as Salmasius explains at length in his notes on Lampridius, p. 235.

He sent the purple. A mark of royal dignity, as Lactantius says, *Divine Institutes*, Book IV, chapter 7: “Among the Romans the garment of purple is now the mark of assumed royal dignity.” Constantine did not need purple to be sent to him by Galerius, since he had received it from the soldiers at the beginning of his reign. Eumenius, in the passage cited just above: “The soldiers, serving the public advantage more than your inclinations, cast the purple upon you at once, as soon as your father’s passing made this necessary, while you wept.” Thus Probus received the purple. Flavius Vopiscus, in his *Life* of Probus: “He was also clothed in a purple mantle taken from a statue in a temple.” Likewise, the same author on Saturninus: “There, however, when he began to think that it was unsafe for him to live as a private person, he took down the purple from the statue of Venus; clothed in his wife’s *cyclas* by the surrounding soldiers, he was clad and acclaimed.” On this matter see Casaubon’s notes on Capitolinus.

But it was more fitting when purple was conferred by an emperor. Thus Severus received it from Herculius, Maximinus from Diocletian, and Herculius again from his son Maxentius, then ruling at Rome. For this showed agreement in accepting the new emperor.

Outside the number. That is, beyond the four, lest he alter Diocletian’s arrangement, which he himself had said ought so carefully to be preserved.

That he should proclaim Severus Augustus. It is certain that this Severus was proclaimed Augustus, as coins found in Adolf Occo demonstrate. The time when he assumed the title Augustus is not so certain. “There are those who write,” says Panvinius in Book II of the *Fasti*, “that as he came with an army against Maxentius, he called himself Augustus.” Tristan de Saint-Amant adopts this opinion. There can be no doubt that this happened shortly before he marched to Rome against Maxentius. But it did not happen because Maxentius had assumed imperial power; rather, it occurred when Constantine was declared Caesar by Galerius after Constantius’s death, that is, in my opinion, late in A.D. 306. This will be discussed below.

Moreover, it may also be inferred that Severus was invested with the dignity of Augustus from the fact that when Galerius gave imperial power to Licinius—that is, made him Augustus—Lactantius writes in chapter 24 that he was substituted for Severus. This plainly would not be true if Severus had not been Augustus. Occo reports that he was called both Caesar and Augustus by Galerius, but does not note the date.

But Caesar. We have already shown that Constantine was not made Caesar together with Severus and Maximinus. Yet because coins establish that he was Caesar, and learned men have hitherto sought in vain the time when he was raised to that dignity, it seems worth pausing here briefly in order to establish the beginning of this proclamation. For although the author of the panegyric addressed to Maximianus and Constantine after the marriage of Fausta teaches that, when his father left him the imperial power, Constantine was nevertheless content with the title Caesar and preferred to wait for the same man to declare him Augustus who had honoured his father Constantius with that title, he does not say when this happened. The question is therefore open to us, as though we lacked the authority of that ancient writer.

We must accordingly determine the matter thus. Constantius died in A.D. 306, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August. Constantine succeeded him immediately; and when his laurelled image had been brought to Galerius, Galerius proclaimed Constantine Caesar, so as to cast him down from the second rank which he held as replacement for his father, into the fourth and thus final place. That Constantine was then proclaimed Caesar by Galerius is also clear from the following chapter. It is written there that, when news reached Galerius that Maxentius had been made emperor at Rome, he summoned Severus and, because he could not make three Caesars, urged him to reject imperial power. From this a wholly certain inference follows: there were already two Caesars in the imperial government, namely Maximinus and Constantine. For Severus had been proclaimed Augustus after Constantius’s death and thus is not there counted among the Caesars.

The words which immediately follow confirm this interpretation: “It seemed sufficient,” he says, “to have done once what he did not wish”—that is, to have named Constantine Caesar. Otherwise, until that day he had done nothing that he had not wished; indeed, he had done everything he wished. I therefore think that Constantine was declared Caesar by Galerius late in that same year, A.D. 306. For in the old calendar written during Constantine’s reign, first published by Herwart and afterwards by others, one reads: “8 Kalends of January: Birthday of the Invincible One.” This cannot appear to refer to any day other than that on which Constantine was proclaimed Caesar. For the most distinguished Peter Lambecius, in Book IV of his *Commentaries on the Viennese Library*, p. 298, refers this birthday to Constantius on the authority of the Fasti of Idatius; but he is refuted by the very words of those Fasti. Vetranio, indeed, is said to have been deposed on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, but Constantius was raised as Caesar only on the following Ides of March, which is Constantius’s birthday.

Moreover, whenever the name “the Divine One” or “the Invincible One” is read simply in this calendar without another name added, it is certain that Constantine the Great must always be understood. A wholly new opinion, however, is that of the most distinguished Peter Francis Chifflet, who in his notes on Vigilius of Tapsus, p. 134, believes that Constantine was created Caesar by Galerius Maximianus on the eighth day before the Kalends of August in A.D. 305, while residing in his court as a hostage given by his father; and was afterwards again declared Caesar at York in Britain in the following year, after the death of his father Constantius. But this opinion lacks truth.

Later Constantine was proclaimed emperor by Maximianus Herculius, twice Augustus, in A.D. 307, when he was about to marry Fausta, Herculius’s daughter. The author of the panegyric cited shortly before teaches us this: “Although very many have said, and many will say, those things by which all your deeds and the merits of your highest virtues are praised, most sacred emperors Maximianus—Augustus forever, whether you wish it or not—and Constantine, emperor in your rising; nevertheless, I am resolved in this discourse especially to embrace those matters proper to this particular rejoicing: that to you as Caesar was added the title of imperial power, and that the celebrations of these heavenly nuptials are being held.” And shortly afterwards: “What could you, Maximianus, have given more dearly, or you, Constantine, have received more dearly, when by this kinship, Maximianus, your youth has been renewed through your son-in-law, and, Constantine, your imperial title has been enlarged through your father-in-law?”

These things are indeed certain and plain. Labbe, however, in Part I of his *Historical Chronology*, p. 223, cites Eusebius and Zosimus as witnesses to the same matter; I have been unable to find anything of this sort in either. Therefore, as is recorded in the old calendar, Constantine had four birthdays: the third day before the Kalends of March; the eighth day before the Kalends of August; the eighth day before the Kalends of January; and the day before the Kalends of April. The first, as the very learned Charles du Fresne rightly observed, pertains to Constantine’s actual birthday, the day on which he was born; the second, to the day on which he succeeded his father Constantius; the third, to the day on which he was proclaimed Caesar by Galerius; and the fourth, finally, to the day on which he received the designation emperor and Augustus. The fifth, which the Calendar of Philocalus places on the third day before the Kalends of April, I do not think differs from that which other editions place on the third day before the Kalends of March. For this reason I judge that the edition of Philocalus should be corrected.

## CHAPTER XXVI

Maxentius was made emperor. Fragment on Constantius Chlorus, p. 472: “Suddenly, in the city of Rome, the praetorian soldiers made Maxentius, son of Herculius, emperor.” Eutropius, Book X: “Meanwhile at Rome the praetorians, having stirred up a tumult, proclaimed Augustus Maxentius, son of Herculius, who was staying not far from the city on an imperial estate.” Eusebius writes the same in the Chronicle. He was the son of Maximianus Herculius and son-in-law of Galerius Maximianus, as Lactantius teaches here, above in chapter 18, and shortly below in chapter 27. This is also conveyed in Victor’s Epitome: “That Maximianus [read: Maxentius] was never dear to anyone, not even to his father or to Galerius, his father-in-law.” And the Fragment on Constantius Chlorus, p. 472: “Son-in-law with father-in-law”—that is, Maxentius with Galerius. I therefore wonder that the very learned Joseph Scaliger, in his notes on Eusebius’s Chronicle, wonders why, since Maxentius was the son of Maximianus Herculius, his coins nevertheless read: “Emperor Maxentius: to the Divine Maximianus, father-in-law, eternal remembrance.” This coin was minted not in memory of Maximianus his father, but of Galerius Maximianus his father-in-law.

He had abolished the praetorian camp. Not entirely, but had reduced it. Otherwise, how could the Praetorians, if none existed, have proclaimed Maxentius emperor? Aurelius Victor rightly says in the *Book of the Caesars*: “Hence the city’s strength was, as it were, curtailed, the number of praetorian cohorts and of the populace under arms having been diminished.” Here perhaps one should read: “and of the unarmed populace.”

The judges having been killed. “Abellio having first been murdered,” says Zosimus, “because, while holding the office of urban prefect, he seemed to oppose their designs.”

He was disturbed. Galerius Maximianus.

There could not yet be three Caesars. This was prevented by Diocletian’s arrangement, who had established that there should be two Augusti and two Caesars; and Galerius had observed this arrangement when he received the title of Augustus. Later, however, three Caesars were made by Constantine and Licinius in A.D. 317: namely Crispus and Constantius, sons of Constantine, and Licinianus, son of Licinius. Then, after Licinius had been defeated and killed, and Crispus and Licinianus likewise removed, Constantius and Constans, the younger sons of Constantine, were made Caesars at different times. To these times must be referred Eutropius’s observation in Book Ten: “At that time the Roman state was under one Augustus and three Caesars—which had never otherwise occurred—when the sons of Constantine governed Gaul, the East, and Italy.” [Col. 0344A]

Maxentius. In the old manuscript Maximianus is read, plainly erroneously, just as we have just seen that the same error was made in Victor’s Epitome.

His father’s soldiers. Those who were in Severus’s army, as is said a little above.

In Campania. All the other writers agree that Maximian Herculius was then in Lucania, whither he had withdrawn after his abdication—Eutropius, Zosimus, and Suidas. The matter must therefore be understood thus: Herculius did indeed retire to Lucania when he laid aside the imperial power; but, when these events were taking place, he came into Campania, so that from there, as from nearby, he might test and solicit the dispositions of the Praetorian soldiers stationed at Rome, and, if the opportunity were given, either resume the empire which he had unwillingly relinquished or secure it for his son Maxentius. For Aurelius Victor, in his book On the Caesars, shows that these schemes had been pursued by Herculius over a long period:

> Meanwhile at Rome the populace and the Praetorian companies confirm Maxentius as emperor, while his father Herculius deliberates long.

[Col. 0344B]

I am astonished, however, that Santamantius, a man celebrated for his knowledge of numismatics, has forced this passage into an altogether contrary meaning, as though Maxentius had been made emperor while his father objected—that is, resisted. I see that this interpretation also pleased the most learned Hadrian Valesius. But they were undoubtedly misled by the erroneous note of Andreas Schott, who writes here that *retractante* has the same meaning as *detrectante*. *Retractare* means the same as *tractare*, “to handle” or “consider.” Lactantius, Divine Institutes, Book IV, chapter 28: “Those who reconsidered all matters pertaining to the worship of the gods, and as it were reread them, were called religious.” And shortly afterward: “They are called religious from rereading, because they carefully reconsider those things which pertain to the worship of the gods.” Hence Saint Augustine’s books of Retractions. These examples suffice.

Accordingly, after Maxentius had become emperor, Maximian, immediately summoned by him, set out for Rome and shortly afterward delivered Severus to death. Soon thereafter [Col. 0344C] he went into Gaul, where he celebrated the marriage of his daughter Fausta to Constantine, in the summer when Galerius led his army into Italy against Maxentius, as we shall see later. Petavius was therefore extraordinarily deceived by the authority of the anonymous Writer on Constantius Chlorus, who does not recount events in the order in which they occurred. Thus Petavius writes in Book XIII of The Doctrine of Times, p. 713, that Galerius Maximian came flying to Rome with vast forces in A.D. 307; that, despised and abandoned by most of his own men, he departed for Illyricum; that he made Licinius Caesar and returned to Sardica; then that Maximian Herculius, encouraged by hope of recovering his former eminence, came flying from Lucania to Rome and exhorted Diocletian to do likewise; later that he deceived Severus by perjury, delivered him into custody, and slew him; then, when he plotted against Maxentius, that he was driven from Rome and came into Gaul to Constantine, gave him his daughter Fausta in marriage, and bestowed upon him the title of Augustus. There can be no doubt that all this is written not indeed contrary to the truth of history, but in an utterly disordered sequence of times [Col. 0344D] and events.

Sethus Calvisius erred still more grossly, writing that Maxentius did not seize the empire until after Constantine had been created Augustus by Maximian Herculius, and that Maximian, persuaded by the Romans, resumed the empire in the following year. But how could one who was neither emperor nor Augustus declare Constantine Augustus?

Eager for revolutions. Julian the Emperor says the same of Herculius in The Caesars.

He had laid it aside unwillingly. This is the settled view of all writers, except the uncertain panegyrist who pursued the praises of Maximian Herculius and Constantine. At the marriage of Constantine and Fausta, I say, all writers agree that this Maximian laid aside the empire unwillingly. Yet they recount this history otherwise than Lactantius. For Lactantius, in chapter 18, teaches that Herculius was compelled by Galerius to abdicate and [Col. 0345A] was frightened by him through the threat of civil arms. The others, on the contrary, write that Diocletian, feeling himself, as age pressed upon him, insufficiently fit to govern the empire, advised Herculius that they should retire into private life; and that Herculius obeyed his colleague reluctantly, but nevertheless obeyed.

He eagerly seized it. That is, the purple which he had laid aside. The anonymous panegyrist cited above says:

> Rome herself acted in accordance with the majesty of her name, to show that she could rule even emperors. She withdrew her armies and restored them to you; and when you brought the authority of a private ruler to calm their minds, stretching forth suppliant hands to you—or rather, complaining—she cried: “How long, Maximian, shall I endure this?” etc.

And shortly afterward:

> Long ago you ruled at your brother’s request; rule again at your mother’s command.

Herculius readily resumed the purple, since he is found to have assumed it three times. This most pernicious precedent caused the death of Licinius. When Constantine had defeated him and granted him life, he later ordered him killed at Thessalonica, upon the demand of a military tumult, lest, following the example of his father-in-law Maximian Herculius, he should again [Col. 0345B] assume the purple he had laid aside to the ruin of the Republic. This is recorded in the Fragment on Constantius Chlorus, p. 475. Likewise Boniface VIII, fearing that Celestine V, if he were allowed liberty, might resume the pontificate which he had abdicated, ordered him kept in custody. Callistus II had provided a precedent in his treatment of Burdinus.

He fled to Ravenna. Zosimus, in Book Two, writes that Herculius, having ensnared Severus by oaths, persuaded him to leave Ravenna, whither he had retired, and to come to Rome; and that, as he proceeded there and reached a certain place called the Three Taverns, he was seized by the ambushes which Maxentius had placed there and killed with a noose fastened around his neck. The anonymous panegyrist addressed to Constantine after his victory over Maxentius says:

> Severus had led a great army, and, abandoned by treachery, armed his own enemy.

The author of the Fragment on Constantius Chlorus, p. 472:

> Severus, deserted by his own men, fled to Ravenna. Summoned there by his son Maxentius—for so it should be read—[Col. 0345C] Herculius came, deceived Severus by perjury, delivered him into custody, led him into the city in the garb of a captive, and had him guarded in the public villa at the thirtieth mile of the Appian Way. Later, when Galerius was advancing into Italy, he was slain; afterward he was brought back to the eighth milestone and buried in the monument of Gallienus.

From this passage Henricus Valesius concluded that Eutropius and Aurelius Victor were mistaken in writing that Severus was killed at Ravenna. Learned men thus dispute over the place where Severus ended his life. Scaliger, in his notes on Eusebius, says that he does not doubt that these Three Taverns were in the district of Ravenna, nor that anything else can be inferred from Zosimus’s words. Valesius, on the contrary, maintains that the Three Taverns were on the Appian Way near Rome. But the conclusion which Sigonius draws from Zosimus in Book Two of The Western Empire is scarcely probable: that Severus, trusting Maximian’s good faith, left Ravenna and betook himself to the Three Taverns, in the undoubted hope that he would be restored to the city through Maximian’s agency. Hieronymus Rubeus followed this opinion of Sigonius [Col. 0345D] in Book Two of his History of Ravenna.

With his veins cut. On the contrary, Zosimus, Book II, and the author of the Fragment on Constantius Chlorus write, as we have just seen, that Severus died with his neck broken by a noose.

## CHAPTER XXVII

Maximinus added. By surname Daia or Daza, who administered the East.

He proceeds into Gaul. Zosimus also supports the credibility of this narrative, though he errs in the order of events. He says that Herculius, frustrated in his attempt to draw Diocletian into resuming the empire, turned back across the Alps to meet Constantine, who was staying there; he promised him his daughter Fausta, and, after fulfilling that promise, attempted to deceive the man. Zosimus errs, I say. For chapters 27 and 29 of Lactantius [Col. 0346A] show that Herculius went into Gaul twice before he sought Carnuntum, and that he did not see Diocletian until after the marriage of Constantine and Fausta.

Yet Lactantius and Zosimus say that Herculius promised his daughter to Constantine; whereas the panegyric by the anonymous author delivered at the marriage of Constantine and Fausta reads otherwise, stating that Constantine requested her from Maximian:

> But assuredly, Constantine, just as divinity was first reconciled to your father-in-law before you asked from him the pledge dearest to himself, so now also in this congratulation those matters must first be mentioned which that great man—author both of your father’s empire and of your own—rejoiced to see in you when he rejoiced at what you requested.

Meanwhile, it should be observed that the writer of this panegyric calls Herculius the author of Constantine’s imperial power. On this point see what was said above on chapter 25.

His younger daughter. Here it should be noted that the old manuscript erroneously reads, “thus, of his lesser household.” He means Fausta. But the time when the marriage of Constantine and Fausta was celebrated [Col. 0346B] must be investigated. It is certain that the Emperor Severus was put to death early in A.D. 307, though the month is uncertain. Thereafter Maximian Herculius, Fausta’s father, proceeded into Gaul in order to win Constantine to his party, promising him marriage to his younger daughter Fausta. And, when this promise had been fulfilled, as Zosimus says, he tried to persuade Constantine to pursue Galerius Maximian as he departed from Italy. From these words it is inferred that the marriage was celebrated while Galerius was in Italy, or at least when he was preparing for the Italian expedition.

But since he returned from Italy into Illyricum in the same year, 307, before September, in my view; and since chapter 27 of this work of Lactantius establishes that Herculius went to Rome again after Galerius’s flight, and that, when he returned again to Gaul in the same year, he remained there for some time and afterward came into Illyricum to Carnuntum, the Pannonian city; and since he was there on 11 November, the day on which Licinius was made emperor by Galerius, [Col. 0346C] it is clear that the marriage of Constantine and Fausta was contracted a considerable time before September of A.D. 307.

If the statements concerning Constantine’s beginnings made by Father Peter Francis Chifflet in his notes on Vigilius of Thapsus were certain, there would be no need for the investigation with which we have thus far occupied ourselves. He maintains that Constantine’s marriage to Fausta, and the beginning of the Augustan dignity conferred upon him by his father-in-law Maximian, occurred on 25 July A.D. 307. He relies upon the same authority by which he writes that Constantine was first made Caesar by Galerius in A.D. 305, on 25 July, and again declared Caesar on 25 July A.D. 306, after his father’s death. But because these claims are not proved by that most distinguished man, the care which we have taken in investigating the date of this marriage was necessary.

He meanwhile. Galerius Maximianus. Moreover, Zosimus summarizes Galerius’s entire preparation in these few words:

> Since Maximian Galerius bore with displeasure what had been inflicted upon Severus Caesar, he decided to proceed from the East to Rome and impose upon Maxentius the punishments deserved for his crimes. But when he arrived in Italy and found the soldiers’ dispositions toward him insufficiently loyal, he returned to the East without engaging in battle.

[Col. 0346D]

He intended to massacre the people. Fragment on Constantius Chlorus, p. 472:

> Then Galerius came to Rome with immense forces, threatening the destruction of the city, and pitched camp at Interamna on the Tiber. He then sent Licinius and Probus as envoys to the city, seeking by conference that the son-in-law should obtain from the father-in-law—that is, Maxentius from Galerius—by entreaties rather than arms what he desired. When he was scorned, he learned that his own men had deserted his cause through Maxentius’s promises. Disturbed by this, he turned back; and, to provide his soldiers with whatever plunder they might find, he ordered the *flamminia* to be carried off.

Henricus Valesius confesses that he does not know what *flamminia* means in this passage, and thinks that something is missing here concerning Maximian Herculius. [Col. 0347A] I would rather think that these final words belong with those to which they are joined, so that the meaning is that Galerius, in order to furnish his soldiers with every sort of booty—that is, to grant them unrestricted license to plunder, restrained by no law—ordered even those things which could not be carried away to be delivered to the flames, so that any pursuer should lack provisions, that is, necessities of life, as Lactantius will shortly say. I therefore judge that *flammis omnia* (“everything to the flames”) should be written instead of *flamminia*, because of the common scribal error of frequently omitting the first syllables of words.

Perhaps the error was introduced by someone who, seeing *flammonia* or *flammomnia* written here and not understanding sufficiently what word it was, knew besides that the ancients had used *flamonium* for *flaminium*, and thought the word should be corrected and restored to its origin. For the ancient glossaries of Isidore and others, Sidonius, and two ancient inscriptions copied by Jacobus Gothofredus from Gruter’s Thesaurus in his note on Theodosian Code 12.1.21—one of which is also given by Savaro, and Sirmond in his notes on Sidonius—use *flamonium* for *flaminium*. [Col. 0347B] I know that this is an altogether inelegant expression, and that one does not ordinarily say that a thing is “carried off to the flames.” But elegance of diction is not to be sought in the author of excerpts.

Yet I readily conclude that my conjecture is not correct from the reading which Carolus du Fresne, Sieur du Cange—a man most expert, as our friendship has allowed me to learn, in this and very many other branches of learning—communicated to me: he thinks that *flammula* should be read here instead of *flamminia*, that is, military standards. When these are raised, soldiers must stand in battle-line; when they fall, they are readily scattered. See the Latin Glossary of the same du Fresne.

He bent the minds of those whom. We formerly noted that this should be corrected thus, when we first printed *felix animus quorum*.

He took to flight. Hadrian Valesius, in Book One of Frankish History, writes that Licinius was created Caesar by Galerius in A.D. 308 and assigned the guardianship of Illyricum; that Galerius entered Italy with very great forces, besieged his son-in-law Maxentius at Rome, and was repelled from the city by the stratagem of Maximian Herculius. [Col. 0347C] We shall show later that Licinius was made emperor after Galerius’s return from Italy. For the moment it need only be observed that what this distinguished man says—that Galerius was repelled from the city by the stratagem of Maximian Herculius—seems scarcely probable, since chapters 27 and 28 of Lactantius establish with certainty that Herculius was in Gaul with Constantine during the entire time Galerius was in Italy. This may also readily be inferred from Zosimus’s words.

He could have been overwhelmed. In Zosimus, Herculius is said to have wished to persuade Constantine to pursue Galerius as he departed from Italy. But since Herculius was by nature restless and faithless, it is no wonder that Constantine rejected his counsels.

He had harassed. I think *vastasset*, “had devastated,” should be read.

The title to be changed. These things are not read elsewhere. And it is surprising that they were passed over by other historians.

Dacian. Because he himself had been born in Dacia.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

[Col. 0347D] The other Maximian. By surname Herculius, who had resumed the empire and held it jointly with his son Maxentius.

The son’s power was prior. Namely, in view of the new empire. For the father had previously laid aside imperial power and retired into private life. Later he had been admitted by Maxentius into partnership in the empire, since Maxentius sent him the purple and twice named him Augustus.

The soldiers, etc., remaining from Severus. That is, soldiers from the former army of Maximian Herculius, sent by Galerius with Severus to subdue Maxentius. Having transferred their standards and deserted Severus, they had surrendered themselves to Maximian. Since they had formerly been his men, Maximian supposed that they would adhere to him.

He tore away the purple. Eutropius, Book X:

> Yet after these events Maximian Herculius attempted, in an assembly of the army, to strip his son Maxentius of power, but suffered mutiny and the soldiers’ insults.

The anonymous panegyrist addressed to Constantine after Maxentius’s defeat:

[Col. 0348A]

> Finally, he who was believed to be that man’s father attempted to tear the rent purple from his shoulders, etc.

In Socrates, Book I, chapter 2, we read that Herculius, seized by a desire to recover the empire, attempted to kill, or remove from the way, his son Maxentius. This is the rendering of Christophorson and Valesius, owing to the word ἀπολέσαι (*apolesai*), which has various meanings. Epiphanius Scholasticus renders it better, in my judgment: “Thereupon his father, from a desire to rule, wished to deprive his son of the kingdom.” For that interpretation accords better with the narrative of Lactantius and of the others.

The other Proud One. That is, Tarquinius Superbus, the last king of the Romans. Lactantius, Divine Institutes, Book IV, chapter 14: “Tarquinius Superbus was expelled.”

## CHAPTER XXIX

Maximian. Galerius.

Diocles was present there. Aurelius Victor, speaking of Severus’s flight and end, says:

> Galerius, more fiercely aroused by this, summoned Jovius into council and, on account of their long-standing friendship, made Licinius Caesar and Augustus; leaving him to guard Illyricum and Thrace, he marched upon Rome.

[Col. 0348B]

But Victor is proved mistaken when he says that Licinius was created Augustus after Severus’s death and before Galerius led his army into Italy against Maxentius. On the contrary, the testimony of Lactantius and others establishes that Licinius was made emperor in Severus’s place after Galerius’s return from Italy; and that Galerius’s intention in conferring the empire upon Licinius was to employ him in the war he had undertaken against Maxentius. Zosimus says:

> Maximian Galerius made Licinius, his intimate friend from their former association, emperor, because he intended to pursue Maxentius in war with his assistance.

The author of the Fragment on Constantius Chlorus, p. 473:

> Licinius, therefore, of humble origin from New Dacia, was made emperor by Galerius, as though about to fight against Maxentius.

Yet Victor says that he was left in Illyricum at the very time when Galerius was especially contemplating the Italian war. This too must be false, since the author of the same Fragment, p. 472, writes that Licinius was in the army of Galerius while he besieged Rome and was sent by him with Probus into the city to discover some means of agreement between father-in-law and son-in-law. These facts also prove that he was still a private citizen and hence not yet emperor. It is therefore very surprising that the most learned Hadrian Valesius should have followed Victor rather than the other authorities agreeing with the author of this Fragment in writing this history.

What he had not done before. Namely, make Licinius emperor. He could already have done this when he made Severus and Maximian Caesars; but he had not wished to do so, for the reasons set out above in chapter twenty.

He should give the empire to Licinius. Learned men dispute among themselves in determining the year in which Licinius was made emperor: some hold that it occurred in A.D. 307, others in the following year. I shall present the arguments of both parties.

Those who defend the earlier opinion employ, or may employ, these arguments. In A.D. 307 arms were taken up against Maxentius, who had seized the empire at the end of the preceding year; and Caesar Augustus Severus, sent by Galerius Maximian to Rome to subdue him, was repulsed and finally put to death by a miserable mode of execution in the second year of his reign, as is read in Eusebius’s Chronicle—that is, in A.D. 307, before the Kalends of May, two years after he had been made Caesar by Maximian Herculius. Thus Onuphrius Panvinius, in his commentary on Book Two of the Fasti, under the year A.U.C. 1059, corresponding to A.D. 308:

> In this year, about the Kalends of May, Severus, whom Galerius had made Caesar over Italy and Africa, came to Rome with an army against the rising of the Praetorians and Maxentius; abandoned by the treachery of his soldiers and himself fleeing, he was killed at Ravenna in the second year of his empire.

Galerius, inflamed by this disgrace, which recoiled upon him as author of the war, flew with incredible speed from Illyricum to Rome with an immense army; and, ingloriously, flew back from [Col. 0349A] Italy to Illyricum, traversing that entire extent of territory twice within no more than five or six months. He thought all the more eagerly of punishing and expelling Maxentius because he, who had been accustomed to conquer, was now compelled to turn his back in great disgrace. For this reason, after his return from Italy, he created Licinius emperor, assigning him to Italy against Maxentius. These things occurred on 11 November, as is read in the Fasti of Hydatius and in the Alexandrian Chronicle.

But although these two books agree on the day, they do not agree on the year. The Alexandrian Chronicle assigns the beginning of Licinius’s reign to the year in which Flavius Constantine Augustus was sole consul; the Fasti to the following year, marked thus: “Again, for the tenth time, and Maximian for the seventh.” Incidentally, the Greek word παλινδεκατου (*palindekatou*) in the Alexandrian Chronicle must be translated in this manner, rather than as Raderus translates it, *Palindecato*, being compelled to note in the margin that it must be understood of Diocletian’s tenth consulship. In this the most learned man certainly erred. For if Diocletian was consul ten times, his tenth consulship fell in A.D. 305, as we saw above. [Col. 0349B] Therefore this passage must be understood of the tenth consulship of Maximian Herculius, who had then resumed the empire.
