But, passing over these matters, to which we have paid attention only incidentally and, as it were, while engaged in another task, let us pursue the arguments by which it may be proved that Licinius was made emperor in A.D. 307. It is certain that Constantine was made emperor after his father’s death in A.D. 306, at the end of July. Thus the first year of his reign ended in the same month of July in the following year. Since Eusebius in his Chronicle places Licinius’s imperial rank in the second year of Constantine’s reign, there can be no doubt that, according to Eusebius’s testimony, its beginning should be assigned to the end of A.D. 307.

Finally, if the tribunician power of the emperors of that age was reckoned from the day on which they obtained the empire, as most learned men hold, this too confirms that Licinius was made emperor [Col. 0349C] in A.D. 307. For in the edict which Galerius, about to die, issued in A.D. 311 in favor of the Christians—and which was posted at Nicomedia on the day before the Kalends of May—the fourth year of Licinius’s tribunician power is recorded by Eusebius in Valesius’s edition and by Nicephorus. Yet if you count Licinius’s years and begin them in November 307, you will readily find that A.D. 311 was the fourth year of his tribunician power, and therefore also of his reign. These are the arguments that may be advanced to confirm the opinion of those who judge that Licinius was raised to imperial dignity in A.D. 307.

But against these arguments it may be replied that the authority of the Fasti of Hydatius is great, for they assign this history to the following year, and rightly so. First, Galerius Maximian could not have proceeded into Italy so swiftly and precipitately with enormous forces, besieged Rome, and led the army back to Illyricum, that all these things might be said to have occurred within five or six months. Thus Galerius’s departure from Italy [Col. 0349D] seems more probably to have occurred in A.D. 308. Moreover, it is not credible that Maximian Herculius, an old man who was at Carnuntum with Diocletian when Licinius was made emperor, should have traversed Italy and Gaul within six months, celebrated the marriage of Constantine and Fausta, returned again to Italy after Galerius’s flight, then again gone into Gaul, and from there proceeded into Pannonia to Diocletian. Finally, Victor’s Epitome states that Maximinus Daia was Caesar for four years and Augustus for three. Since he was made Caesar on the Kalends of May, A.D. 305, it follows that he retained the name of Caesar until the end of A.D. 308. Otherwise he would not have been Caesar for four years, but three, if Licinius had been made emperor in the preceding year.

These points indeed at first sight appear to carry great weight. But if we consider the condition of the commonwealth at that time; the fierce, [Col. 0350A] irascible, headlong, and proud character of Galerius; and the instability, faithlessness, and fickleness of Herculius—vices which indeed always precipitate those in whom they adhere, because in human minds they are more powerful than virtues, as Lactantius says in Book One of the Divine Institutes—we shall readily understand that things which at first glance seem nearly impossible could nevertheless have been done by restless men eager to retain supreme power.

For example, Illyricum, where Galerius resided, adjoins Italy. Thus he could readily enter Italy and afterward withdraw, even with an army, within the six-month interval mentioned, especially since from Zosimus and the author of the Fragment on Constantius Chlorus we learn that he departed Italy without engaging in battle—that is, that he remained in Italy only briefly. And who should wonder that Herculius, eager for the empire which he had unwillingly laid aside, made so many journeys with such speed, since there can be no doubt that he made them with every hesitation and delay cast aside? He sailed from Rome and, crossing the sea, upon reaching Massilia quickly proceeded to Augusta Treverorum, [Col. 0350B] where Constantine’s seat was. All these journeys can certainly be completed within a month by an energetic man. Thereafter he was with Constantine for some time on the occasion of the marriage. Then he needed another month to return to Italy, from which he was soon expelled. Add another month for the second journey into Gaul, where he did not remain long, and a month for the journey from Augusta Treverorum to Carnuntum in Pannonia.

It is now clear that this entire number of months agrees sufficiently with the interval which elapsed from Severus’s death—for it was then that Herculius first proceeded into Gaul—until 11 November, the day on which Licinius was made emperor. Indeed, I suspect that Severus was killed long before the Kalends of May, namely in February. For in the old calendar published by Herwartus, Constantine’s *natalis* is marked on the day before the Kalends of April. Since a learned man judged that this should be interpreted as the day on which he was made Caesar, I would rather believe it refers to the day on which [Col. 0350C] Maximian Herculius proclaimed him Augustus. That this occurred in A.D. 307, in my opinion, admits no room for doubt.

Accordingly, if Maximian declared Constantine Augustus at the end of March, we have nearly nine months rather than the six that we had counted from Severus’s death to Licinius’s accession—within which both Maximiani could readily make the journeys and expeditions of which we have spoken. Further, I think it may be inferred that Constantine’s *natalis* on the day before the Kalends of April cannot refer to the day when he was made Caesar because he was either made Caesar together with Severus and Maximinus, or when he reached his father, or at least when he was proclaimed Caesar by Galerius. But we have already shown that he was not made Caesar with Severus and Maximinus. Even if he had been, that *natalis* could not agree, since it is certain that Severus and Maximinus were made Caesars not on the day before the Kalends of April but on the Kalends of May. Nor can it agree with the time when he succeeded his father, since that occurred at the end of July. It could therefore agree [Col. 0350D] only with the time when Constantine was made Caesar by Galerius.

But neither did that occur on the day before the Kalends of April. For it cannot be doubted that Constantine’s laureate image was conveyed to Maximian as soon as he succeeded his father Constantius, that is, at the end of July, just as his image was immediately brought to Rome; and this was the occasion of Maxentius’s seizure of the empire, as Zosimus teaches in Book Two. But if news of Constantine’s acquisition of the empire was brought to Galerius at the end of July, and Lactantius does not teach that there was any delay in sending the purple to Constantine, it is reasonable to believe that he was both made Caesar and sent the purple within the same year in which his image was brought, and therefore long before March. Certainly it accords with reason that the day on which he received the supreme dignity should have been marked in the calendar; if one does not assign it to the day before the Kalends of April, no record is found anywhere of the day on which [Col. 0351A] Constantine was declared emperor and Augustus.

As to the evidence cited from Victor’s Epitome, it does not obstruct what has thus far been said. For there are many things in that Epitome which do not cohere, especially in this passage, where it assigns only seven years of reign to Maximinus, although it is certain that he ruled for eight full years and some months. Finally, we must return to the tribunician power, which carries great weight in this question. Henricus Valesius, understanding this, yet maintaining that Licinius was made emperor only in A.D. 308, went so far in his notes on Eusebius, p. 171, as to admit that the observation concerning the tribunician power harmed his opinion about Licinius’s accession. He was also compelled to assign that edict, in which the fourth year of Licinius’s tribunician power is noted, to the end of A.D. 311, thereby finding that year to be Licinius’s fourth year of tribunician power. But that conjecture collapses, since Lactantius establishes that the edict was posted at Nicomedia on the day before the Kalends [Col. 0351B] of May and that Galerius died shortly afterward.

Thus, even from that most learned man’s observation, we infer that the opinion of those who believe Licinius was made emperor in A.D. 307 is entirely true. I think this may further be confirmed by the fact that Maximian Herculius and Galerius Maximian are found to have held the consulship together in the following year, and that no war was subsequently waged against Maxentius, Herculius’s son. For the reconciliation later existing between them must have been established when Herculius and Galerius were together at Carnuntum, since we see that Galerius was then actively considering war against Maxentius when he intended to raise Licinius to the chief eminence, and that this ardor immediately cooled after Licinius’s promotion. If the consulship was undertaken by Herculius and Galerius—as cannot be denied—by mutual agreement after their friendship had been cemented at Carnuntum, and if it fell in A.D. 308, it is evident that Licinius was made emperor at the end of A.D. 307. [Col. 0351C]

These points having been established, it remains to say something about another difficulty occurring here: whether Licinius was first made Caesar and afterward Augustus, as some have thought, or whether he was Caesar and Augustus at one and the same time, as others maintain. The matter can easily be decided by the single testimony of Lactantius, who writes that the empire and the first place after Galerius were given to Licinius, even above Maximinus. This is also confirmed by Eusebius’s authority, as we shall show shortly. Thus the difficulty requires no fuller examination. It arose from a misunderstanding of a passage of Aurelius Victor where he deals with Licinius’s creation as Caesar and Augustus. See Scaliger’s notes on Eusebius’s Chronicle.

With both present. That is, Diocletian and Maximian Herculius, as we shall say presently. Herculius had come to Diocletian, who, as Zosimus says, was then staying at Carnuntum, in order to urge him to resume [Col. 0351D] the empire; but he had come from Gaul, as Lactantius teaches, not from Italy, as Cluverius supposed. In chapter 5 of his book on Vindelicia and Noricum, Cluverius writes—on the authority, as he says, of Zosimus—that Herculius set out from Lucania, a region of Italy, for Diocletian at Carnuntum, and passed through Ravenna both going and returning. Both assertions are undoubtedly false. For, as I have said, Herculius departed from Gaul for Carnuntum, where he found Diocletian; and, leaving him, returned to Gaul. This may also be inferred from the panegyric delivered by Eumenius to Constantine, where he recounts Herculius’ various errors in their proper sequence as follows:

> The necessity of fate brought it about that he should render this return for your dutiful devotion: you received into your provinces, your forces, and your palace the man whom you had driven from the City, expelled from Italy, and rejected by Illyricum.

Correctly said, I maintain. For when he wished to strip his son Maxentius and deprive him of his kingdom, he was driven from the City and expelled from Italy, and fled to Constantine. Then [Col. 0352A] he proceeded into Pannonia, a province of Illyricum, to lay snares for Galerius. There he urged Diocletian to resume the empire—having previously, as may be inferred from Eutropius, tried him unsuccessfully by letters. Since he achieved nothing by his persuasions, and his plans had been thwarted, he planned, as Lactantius says, a third flight and returned to Gaul. Lactantius proves that these events occurred as they are read in the panegyric.

Especially memorable is Diocletian’s saying when he rejected the empire, as Herculius and Galerius urged him to resume it. The Epitome of Victor says:

> While he was being urged by Herculius and Galerius to take back the empire, he replied, detesting it as though it were some plague: “If only you could see at Salona the vegetables cultivated by my own hands! You would surely never judge this attempt worth making.”

Thus, from this passage of Lactantius, we learn something we did not previously know: the year in which Herculius went to Diocletian—namely, that in which Licinius was made emperor.

Moreover, it should here be observed that Arnaud Pontac, Bishop of Bazas, erred in his notes [Col. 0352B] on Eusebius’ *Chronicle*, p. 678, as did Joseph Scaliger in Book V of *The Correction of Times*, p. 497 of the last edition. Rebuking Zosimus, who had said that Diocletian was met by Herculius at Carnuntum, a town of the Celts, they assert this to be false, since Diocletian, after his abdication, never set foot in Gaul—indeed, never left Salonae in Dalmatia. The first part of the observation is true: Diocletian never set foot in Gaul after abdicating the empire. Yet he was at Carnuntum in Pannonia, where Herculius met him. And that he did leave Salonae is clear from his reply, quoted shortly above: “If only you could see at Salona the vegetables.” For if he had been at Salonae when he said this, there would have been no place for such an exclamation. Therefore, he was far from Salonae.

The most learned Jean Morin errs even more seriously in Part II of his book *On the Church Liberated through Constantine*, ch. 1, pp. 126, 129, and ch. 3, p. 153. There he writes that Maximian [Col. 0352C] Herculius wrote to Diocletian what, as we have already seen, was spoken rather than written; he invents a long letter allegedly written to him, of which no trace survives among the ancients; and he claims that Diocletian, having received that letter, honored it with the brief reply which we quoted from Victor’s Epitome.

These points having been established, we must consider whether the statements made by the eminent Hadrian Valesius in Book I of his *Frankish History*, p. 22, concerning Maximian Herculius’ departure into Illyricum and his subsequent departure, can be true. He says that Herculius, seeing that all the provinces of the Roman Empire were held by Galerius, Maximinus, Maxentius, and Constantine, and that accordingly there was nowhere for himself to take a stand, nor any way for him to sustain imperial rank for long without provinces and an army, again resigned the empire after retaining the insignia of the principate for about two years. Knowing himself to be hated by Maxentius and his soldiers, he allegedly asked Galerius to permit him to live out the rest of his life as a private person in Illyricum, having been expelled by his son from the City and Italy. Rejected by [Col. 0352D] Galerius, he supposedly left for Gaul in the second year after his own tenth consulship and Galerius’ seventh, under the pretext of duty—namely, of visiting Constantine, his son-in-law—pretending that Maxentius had driven him out. These are, indeed, the eminent man’s exact words.

First, his assertion that Herculius resigned the empire before leaving for Illyricum cannot stand, since Lactantius teaches that he did so after returning from Illyricum to Constantine. Next, it is certain that he set out for Galerius within the first year of his resumed rule, not after retaining the insignia of the principate for about two years. For he resumed the purple at the end of A.D. 306, and in the following year he set out for Illyricum, in a month—October, as will appear later. As for the assertion that he asked Galerius for leave to live out the remainder of his life privately in Illyricum, since I find this nowhere else, I think Valesius drew it paraphrastically from Eumenius’ words [Col. 0353A] that Herculius had been “rejected by Illyricum,” as though he could not have been rejected otherwise than by being denied residence in Illyricum. But the true sense of Eumenius’ words, as I judge, must be that he is called rejected by Illyricum because there, as we have said, he could not by his persuasions bring Diocletian to resume the empire.

Nor did that rejection occur in the second year after Herculius’ tenth consulship—that is, A.D. 310—as Valesius thinks, but immediately after imperial rank had been conferred upon Licinius. For Lactantius writes of his departure from Illyricum as of a desperate flight, and thus as a sudden departure and precipitate journey. Finally, Valesius narrates Herculius’ return to Constantine as though he had not yet seen Constantine after being driven from Rome, and therefore had not complained to him of his son’s cruelty towards him; whereas we know with certainty from Lactantius that Herculius, fleeing Rome, came first to Constantine in Gaul, then from there went to Galerius and Diocletian in Illyricum, and, rejected by the latter, returned to Constantine in Gaul [Col. 0353B].

With both present. That is, Diocletian and Maximian Herculius. One question here requires examination: whether their presence should be taken to imply consent, especially since these measures were taken by Galerius, a most obstinate and proud man, accustomed, as it were with drawn sword, to demand rather than entreat; and whether that consent should in turn be extended to the others in whose hands lay authority over the state. For Eusebius, Book VIII, ch. 13, seems to say this:

> Λικίνιος δὲ ἐπὶ τούτοις ὑπὸ κοινῆς ψήφου τῶν κρατούντων αὐτοκράτωρ καὶ σεβαστὸς ἀναπέφηνε.

“Besides this, Licinius was proclaimed *autokrator* [emperor] and *sebastos* [Augustus] by the common vote of those in power.”

The interpreters have rendered this passage in various senses. Rufinus translates: “And Licinius, admitted to imperial power by the common judgment of all, is proclaimed Augustus.” Musculus: “Licinius, moreover, is by common judgment of the potentates himself made emperor and Augustus.” Christophorson: “Thereupon Licinius is declared emperor and Augustus by the common vote and consent of those in whose hands lay supreme power.” Finally, Valesius: “Licinius was declared [Col. 0353C] emperor and Augustus by the common vote of the emperors.”

Rufinus, then, leaves uncertain whom he means. Nor does Musculus explain more clearly what he intends by the term “potentates,” leaving it uncertain. But Christophorson and Valesius plainly declare that this was done by the common vote of the emperors, or of those in whose hands lay supreme authority. Yet this interpretation has very great difficulty. Since this council was, evidently, hastily convened by Galerius, the shortage of time did not permit the consent of the Caesars in the provinces to be sought; nor was this Galerius’ custom. Moreover, as we shall say later, it may be certainly inferred from Eusebius and Lactantius that neither Maximinus nor Constantine was consulted. Nor is it likely that Maxentius’ consent was requested, against whom war was being prepared. It remains, therefore, that this passage of Eusebius be understood of the emperors—namely, Diocletian [Col. 0353D], the retired sovereign; Maximian Herculius, who had then resumed the empire; and Galerius Maximian. For these three were at Carnuntum when Licinius was made Augustus. Therefore Eusebius is not altogether correct here when he says that Licinius was made emperor and Augustus by the common consent of those who then possessed the state.

There were six. Namely, Maximian Herculius, Galerius Maximian, Maximinus surnamed Daia or Daza, Constantine, Maxentius, and Licinius.

His son-in-law. Constantine, who had shortly before married Fausta, the younger daughter of the elder Maximian, in the same year, namely, in which Severus was killed and Licinius made emperor. The anonymous panegyric addressed to Maximian and Constantine on the marriage of Fausta says:

> O Maximian, how divine was your judgment! You chose that this man should be to you a grandson by right of adoption, a son by rank of majesty, and also a son-in-law.

[Col. 0354A] The son of his son-in-law. For Constantius, Constantine’s father, having repudiated Helena as he was ordered to do, married Theodora, whom some report to have been Herculius’ daughter, others his stepdaughter.

He lays aside the royal garment. That is, the purple; and so he again returned to private life. Hadrian Valesius writes, in Book I of his *Frankish History*, p. 21, that Herculius did this before leaving for Illyricum, that is, at the end of A.D. 307. But Lactantius contradicts this opinion, explicitly assigning Herculius’ second abdication to a later time, though he does not name the year. It is nevertheless probable that it occurred not long after he had returned from Illyricum to Constantine, that is, at the beginning of A.D. 308, when he himself was consul for the tenth time and Maximian for the seventh. For thereafter no mention is found of his crimes until A.D. 310, when he died; and a man most eager to mark the years by his consulships is not thereafter found to have been consul.

Leaving behind part of the soldiers. [Col. 0354B] In the power of his father-in-law Maximian. But the treacherous man incited them to revolt. Besides Lactantius, Eumenius is a witness in the panegyric later delivered to Constantine. Having said that Maximian had broken faith with his son-in-law, he immediately adds:

> Is this the loyalty, is this the religious reverence devoted to the inner sanctuaries of the imperial palace: that slowly and hesitantly—now, to be sure, after plans of war had been made, the journey completed, and the supplies of stopping-places consumed, so that no army might be able to pursue—this purple-clad man suddenly takes his seat within the walls, and, having twice laid aside the empire, claims it for a third time; sends letters to stir up the armies; attempts to unsettle the soldiers’ loyalty by displaying rewards; intending, of course, to employ without fear an army whose hands he had taught to be for sale?

Livineius says that the sense of this passage is that Maximian Herculius resumed the purple at Arles, after Constantine had received him when he had been driven from the City, fled Italy, and been rejected by Illyricum. This is right enough as to the history. But I do not know where he found that these things took place at Arles. Eumenius does not say so; he says only that Herculius shut himself up in the city of Arles, whither Constantine’s army pursued him [Col. 0354C], and that from there he later fled to Marseilles.

It seems certain to me that Herculius resumed the purple, which he had laid aside twice, in the city of Trier itself or not far from it. I think I infer this from Lactantius’ words, where he says that a few days after Constantine had departed against the Franks, Herculius, having seized the public treasuries, suddenly assumed the purple, believing that Constantine had entered barbarian territory. For the frontier of the Franks lay around the Danube. And the public treasuries which Herculius then seized could have been nowhere other than in the emperor’s palace, that is, in the city of Trier. Thus Herculius could not have resumed the purple at Arles within a few days, since that city is a long distance from Trier.

Which was itself unfitting. Eumenius, in his panegyric of Constantine:

> While you were occupied with matters so conducive to the public advantage and dignity, new disturbances caused by that man, who ought above all to have favored your successes, diverted you to himself.

## CHAPTER XXX

[Col. 0354D]

She reports it to her husband. Eutropius, Book X:

> Therefore, when the plot had been discovered through his daughter Fausta, who had disclosed the deceit to her husband, Herculius fled to Marseilles; there he was overcome and paid the penalty by a most just end.

Eutropius is mistaken. For Herculius had fled to Marseilles before he devised this plot, as is clear from Lactantius. Zosimus erred more seriously, saying that Herculius, because Fausta had forestalled his attempt and reported the entire matter to Constantine, was reduced to despair of all his affairs and died of illness at Tarsus. He plainly confuses Maximian with Maximinus, who held the East and, after being defeated by Licinius, finally died at Tarsus in Cilicia, as will be noted below. Yet neither of them explained the plot; they appear to have referred it to the seizure of imperial power.

Eucherius alone, bishop of Lyons, noted in his history of the Martyrs of Agaunum that Maximian Herculius laid snares for Constantine [Col. 0355A] in order to take his life:

> When, having arranged his plots, he was planning the death of his son-in-law Constantine, then ruling the kingdom, the deceit having been discovered, he was captured near Marseilles and not long afterwards strangled; subjected to this most shameful punishment, he ended his impious life by a death he deserved.

This is correct and in agreement with Lactantius. Eusebius also recalls this perfidy and then the death of Herculius in Book I of the *Life of Constantine*, ch. 47, writing that one of those who had abdicated imperial power, while preparing plots for Constantine’s death, was discovered and perished by a most disgraceful kind of death. Eusebius plainly indicates Maximian Herculius.

But because Eusebius immediately relates that all the images and statues everywhere of the man whom he says died thus were thrown down, and describes this death at a considerable interval after the chapter in which he treated the overthrow of Maxentius, Valesius in his *Annotations* went so far as to suppose Eusebius’ text corrupt and in need of correction so that Maximinus should be understood here—the Maximinus who was made Caesar together with Severus. [Col. 0355B] For Maximinus died after Constantine’s victory over Maxentius, and by a most disgraceful kind of death, as Valesius says may be inferred from Eusebius, Books VIII and IX. These are the comments made by that most learned man on this passage, but I think they conflict with the truth of the history.

For first, it is certain that Eusebius speaks of one of those who had abdicated imperial power. This cannot be understood of anyone other than Maximian Herculius, who held second place in the empire and abdicated with Diocletian. It cannot in any way be said of Maximinus, who is nowhere said to have abdicated. Secondly, the man of whom Eusebius speaks died after being discovered preparing plots to kill Constantine. It is no less certain that this history must be referred to Herculius than that Constantine was attacked by the plots of Herculius; Lactantius in this book and all the other historians unanimously report this. Certainly the images of both men were thrown down after their deaths, as is clear from Eusebius. Moreover, the narrative of Maxentius’ slaughter, which precedes the account of Herculius’ death, does not damage this view. For Eusebius—as Socrates observes at the beginning of his history—in the books he composed concerning the life of Emperor Constantine only touched most matters incidentally. His greater concern, as commonly happens in encomia, was to weave together the emperor’s praises and a panegyrical discourse, rather than to record events accurately. But in Book VIII of the *Ecclesiastical History*, ch. 13, where he follows chronological order and recounts the same matters concerning Maximian that are also read in the *Life of Constantine*, he teaches that they cannot and ought not be understood of anyone other than Herculius, since at the beginning of the following chapter he says that Maxentius was the son of the man of whom he had spoken before [Col. 0355C].

The scene is arranged.

[Col. 0355D]

The manuscript reads *schena*. The correction was easy. In Tacitus, *Annals*, Book XIII, Agrippina, Nero’s mother, speaks thus: “Now, through his male concubine Atimetus and the actor Paris, he arranges matters like stage plays.” In the Acts of the Vindication of Felix, bishop of Aptunga: “Falsehood has always thus been enacted through terror, through a scene, through an irreligious mind, by those unwilling to agree with the Catholic religion.”

Vows for twenty years. That is, the *vicennalia*, which he celebrated at Rome with Diocletian.

With his throat crushed. The Epitome of Victor says:

> Maximian Herculius was besieged by Constantine at Marseilles, then captured, and paid the penalty of death by a final kind of punishment, his neck broken by a noose.

Orosius, Book VII, ch. 28:

> Maximian Herculius set out for Gaul in order, equally joined to his son-in-law Constantine by treachery, to take away his empire; but discovered and betrayed through his daughter, he then took flight, was overcome at Marseilles, and killed.

All historians err on this point, and Lactantius sets them right. Suidas is especially mistaken in writing that Diocletian was killed by the Senate, whereas Maximian hanged himself. The death of Maximian Herculius is said in the Fasti of Hydatius to have occurred in the second year after his tenth and seventh consulships, corresponding to A.D. [Col. 0356A] 310. But Maximian was not killed by Constantine because he had assumed the purple for the third time, as the most learned Hadrian Valesius supposed, but because, after violating his oath, stirring up civil war, and soliciting the soldiers, he had finally wished to kill Constantine—and would have killed him, had Fausta agreed with him.

## CHAPTER XXXI

The other Maximian. Galerius, surnamed Armentarius.

The author of the persecution. Eusebius says the same in Book I of the *Life of Constantine*, ch. 58; Rufinus, Book VIII, ch. 15: “But he who was second to him in honor, and afterwards his successor even in the first rank, who had also proved the instigator and standard-bearer of our persecution.” And ch. 28: “For divine vengeance seized the very author of the crime.” The Fragment concerning Constantius Chlorus, p. 472: “Then Galerius made Licinius Caesar in Illyricum. Leaving him in Pannonia, he himself returned to Serdica; seized by a grave illness, he so wasted away that he died with his belly open and putrefying, [Col. 0356B] as the most just punishment for the most unjust persecution returned upon the author of the criminal decree.” See Lactantius above, ch. 1 and following. Scaliger therefore vainly says in his *Annotations on Eusebius’ Chronicle* that Galerius Maximian never persecuted Christians, but was a good and praiseworthy prince, an outstanding and brave warrior. Petavius rightly rebukes him here in Book XI of *The Doctrine of Times*, ch. 34, and Book XIII, p. 714.

Even the force of majesty. In this passage several letters are missing in the old copy, which reads: “that in him also . . . the force of majesty might be displayed.” From the traces of letters that have disappeared, we conjectured that it should be read as in this edition. Lactantius himself confirms our conjecture. His words in Book I of the *Divine Institutions*, ch. 3, are: “What of the fact that the supreme power of things and divine force cannot even once be divided?” And in Book III, ch. 17: “They did not understand the force and majesty of the true God.” Elsewhere he used *virtus* [Col. 0356C] for *vis* [force], as in Book IV, ch. 26: “To set forth the power and majesty of the one God”; and Book VI, ch. 9: “He recounts the power and majesty of the one God.”

Concerning the celebration of the *vicennalia*. In imitation of Diocletian, whom he so sought to imitate that he even at some point contemplated laying aside the empire. Yet he did not celebrate the *vicennalia*, having died before the time came for their celebration.

They have no pardon. We had first printed: “For those having no pardon, no [means] of avoiding manifold tortures.” Although the archetype unquestionably reads so, I nevertheless do not doubt that the reading now established is the true one.

How tolerable these things are. The old manuscript reads: “How tolerable these things are: to snatch away from men’s labor food gained by labor.” We have restored the final part correctly, I think. We have not dared to alter the former part, though we once thought it could be replaced by: “Although it is intolerable.” Sparkius proposes: “Since these things are intolerable.” Columbus preferred our conjecture [Col. 0356D].

Vow. They called by this name festivals at which vows were made for the safety and long life of rulers: thus, just as they celebrated, for example, the *vicennalia*, so might the gods grant that they should celebrate the *tricennalia*. But I need not say more on this subject, since two most learned men, Charles du Fresne and Henry Noris, have recently treated it fully: the former in his dissertation on the coinage of the lower age, published after the third volume of his *Glossary*; the latter in his chronological dissertation on decennial vows, published together with his dissertation on the coins of Diocletian and Licinius. See also Casaubon’s notes on Spartianus.

Which he was not going to celebrate. This passage is of great importance, since it certainly follows from it that Galerius Maximian did not reach the twentieth year of his reign.

## CHAPTER XXXII

[Col. 0357A]

Maximinus was angry. Eusebius, Book VIII, ch. 13, after saying that Licinius had been made both emperor and Augustus, adds:

> This Maximinus took most grievously, since until then he had been called by everyone only Caesar. Therefore this man, endowed above the rest with a tyrannical disposition, proclaimed himself Augustus.

He therefore sends. Galerius sends to Maximinus, to placate him.

Let him preserve his station. Because he had made Licinius, his old tent-companion and comrade in victory, emperor of the second rank.

Let the old man yield. This was said concerning Galerius, who was old. It cannot be understood of Licinius, since he was not yet sixty when he died. The Epitome of Victor says: “Licinius was killed about the fifteenth year of his rule, nearly at the sixtieth year of his life.” In the Fasti of Hydatius he is said to have been killed under the consulship of Paulinus and Julianus, which falls in A.D. 325. He died, however, [Col. 0357B] near the end of the year. In the Fragment concerning Constantius Chlorus he is said to have reigned nineteen years, leaving behind a son and wife. This is not wholly true. For from the end of A.D. 307 until A.D. 324, when, defeated by Constantine, he returned to private life in October, only seventeen years are counted. If, then, in A.D. 324, while he was in the seventeenth year of his reign, he had not yet reached his sixtieth year, it is clear that he became emperor at about forty years of age. Thus what is said here about grey hairs cannot be referred to him.

He removes the name of Caesar. Not indeed in order to abolish the name of Caesar, which the emperors always retained, but so that thereafter those adopted in expectation of imperial power should refrain from it, and Maximinus should thus be excluded. This, I think, is the sense of the passage. Against this, Antoninus Pagi, a man distinguished for religious devotion and learning, thinks in his consular dissertation, p. 138, that Lactantius’ words have another meaning and must be referred to Galerius [Col. 0357C] Maximinus surnamed Daia, not Galerius Maximian. But Jean Columbus, in his notes on this passage, says that he is astonished Antoninus Pagi takes these words of Maximian Daia, when the sequence of the words and the matter itself teach that they must be understood of Galerius Maximian. For the latter, already a veteran, cannot be called insubordinate toward the newly made emperor Maximinus, since insubordination belongs to an inferior toward a superior. I judge that Columbus rightly rebuked Pagi here.

Maxentius. Either I am greatly mistaken, or the name Maxentius is wrongly placed here, as in the Alexandrian Chronicle, instead of Maximinus. For there is no mention in this context of Maxentius, whom Galerius Maximian, his father-in-law, hated and had shortly before attacked in war as a public enemy. But the eminent Jean Columbus retains the name Maxentius here and adds the name of Maximinus Daia, which he believes was omitted by a sleeping copyist; he says the four emperors named shortly afterwards are Licinius, Maximinus, Maxentius, and Constantine. [Col. 0357D] It seems much more likely to me that this passage should be understood thus: the four whom Galerius ordered to be called emperors were Galerius himself first, as was proper, then Licinius, next Maximinus, and finally Constantine. For, as I said before, there is then no mention of Maxentius, and it is certain that Maximinus could not have been passed over, since he had a strong army.

Constantine, son of Augustus. From this passage especially I infer that Constantine’s consent was not sought when Licinius was made emperor. For it is not likely that one who had been called emperor and Augustus by Herculius; who was the son and son-in-law of Augusti; who was also a man distinguished in military service, commander of most valiant armies, and illustrious for many victories—would have allowed a new man to be preferred before him. Indeed, I do not know whether this arrangement succeeded in every respect. For in the edict of A.D. 311, in which three emperors are named, [Col. 0358A] Galerius’ name is placed first as senior emperor, then Constantine’s, and Licinius’ last. This indicates that Licinius’ rank met with some opposition from Constantine, which was settled only by relegating Licinius to third place.

Having called himself Augustus. There is an outstanding passage entirely consistent with Lactantius’ account in Rufinus, Book IX, ch. 5. Speaking of the same Maximinus, he says:

> Although he was permitted to do everything as he pleased, since he had already presumptuously appropriated to himself the rank of Augustus, he nevertheless wished to appear to act in these matters for certain just reasons.

Eusebius confirms this in Book VIII, ch. 13. After saying that Licinius had been declared emperor and Augustus, he adds: “This Maximinus took most grievously, since until then he had been called by everyone only Caesar. Therefore this man, endowed above the rest with a tyrannical disposition, proclaimed himself Augustus.”

## CHAPTER XXXIII

[Col. 0358B]

The eighteenth year. This is A.D. 310, as the date of Galerius’ death shows. For since he began to be ill in the eighteenth year of his reign, remained ill for a full year, and died in May A.D. 311, it is clear that the eighteenth year of his reign corresponds to A.D. 310.

An incurable plague. Lactantius, *Institutions*, Book VII, ch. 15: “God struck Egypt with an incurable plague.”

In the lower parts of his genitals. See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VIII, ch. 16, and *Life of Constantine*, Book I, ch. 57; Rufinus, Book VIII, ch. 18; the Fragment concerning Constantius Chlorus, p. 472; and Orosius, Book VII, ch. 28.

The scar having now formed. The manuscript reads: “But, the scar having now formed, the wound cuts.” From this we initially made: “But the wound cuts the scar now formed.” Now, however, we see that the reading of the old book should be retained, except that *scindit* [cuts] should be replaced with *scinditur* [is cut open]. Lactantius, *Institutions*, Book VI, ch. 24: [Col. 0358C] “To pour forth destruction from wounds torn open.” A little later there is a lacuna, which, as we formerly noted, might perhaps be supplied thus: “Wounded again by a slight movement of the body.” Here Columbus says *vulnerato* should be read.

Asclepius. So also in *Institutions*, Book III, ch. 19: “He evidently feared that before Rhadamanthus, collector of the vow, he would be made a defendant by Asclepius.” This is the reading of the most ancient manuscripts of Lactantius, though the common editions read “by Aesculapius.” Slightly earlier in that passage the printed text has *pro se sacrarent*. In my judgment, Royal Manuscript 3735’s *prosecrarent* is better. Manuscript 3736 of the same library likewise first had this reading, though the syllable *sa* was subsequently added above the line. Thus the common edition was established. Below, Book IV, ch. 27: “At the instigation of the same demons to whom they consecrate.”

Worms are generated within. See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VIII, ch. 16, and Orosius, Book VII, ch. 28. An altogether similar story concerning Julian, uncle of the Apostate, is told by St John Chrysostom in his oration on St Babylas, Sozomen, Book V, ch. 8, and Theodoret, Book III, ch. 13.

[Col. 0358D]

Odoritatem. It is certain that this passage is corrupt. I therefore conjectured that it might be restored thus: “A foul odor [spread] not merely through the palace.” Sparkius subsequently judged that, by an easier correction as he himself says, one should read: “But the odor.” Cuperus: “A foul odor.” Columbus: “The odor was so foul.” What if one were to substitute: “The dreadfulness of the odor”?

He was compelled to confess God. What Rufinus relates at this point, Book VIII, ch. 18, is memorable. I shall quote his words:

> Finally, he orders many of the physicians killed because they could neither offer any remedy for the disease nor endure the force of the stench. Among them, when one man was standing by, about to be executed rather than to give treatment, he said, inspired by God: “Why, emperor, do you err and think that what God inflicts can be recalled by men? This disease is not human, nor is it cured by physicians. But remember how greatly you have acted against the servants of God, and how impious and profane you have been toward the divine religion, and you will understand [Col. 0359A] from whom remedies must be sought for you. For I, indeed, can die with the rest; but you will not be cured by physicians.” Then for the first time Maximian understood himself to be a man, etc.

Orosius, Book VIII, ch. 28, briefly touches upon the same story, as does the author of the *Miscellaneous History*, Book XI, drawing from him. But Eutychius in his *Annals* relates that Maximian voluntarily recognized and said that he suffered these things because he had killed Christians, and that he sent letters into all his provinces ordering Christians in prison to be released. Yet he grievously errs in writing that Maximian recovered from this illness through Christian prayers, and later lapsed into a greater degree of impiety than before, ordering Christians everywhere to be killed and utterly exterminated. This error came from confusion of the names Maximian and Maximinus, when he attributed to one what is known to have been done by two. Sethus Calvisius also errs in thinking that the ten-year persecution ceased after that edict and Galerius’ death, when only the eighth year of the persecution had elapsed, as we said above.

[Col. 0359B] He issued an edict. It survives in Eusebius, Book VIII, ch. 17, translated by him from Latin into Greek, and then translated from Greek into Latin by Rufinus, as he himself states: “Having translated these things from Latin into Greek, we have again rendered them into Latin.” Therefore, the original Latin that we read today is due to Lactantius.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

They return to sound minds. Lactantius, *Institutions*, Book V, ch. 19, perhaps referring to this edict: “But this very ignorance causes them to be so evil in persecuting the wise, and to pretend that they are consulting for them, wishing to bring them back to a sound mind.” The Acts of Saints Saturninus, Dativus, and Felix, ch. 7: “You ought to have brought others back to a sound mind, and not acted contrary to the commands of the emperors and Caesars.”

So that they do not follow their former institutions. He reproaches Christians because they had departed from the ancient simplicity of their ancestors. Eusebius indeed, Book VIII, ch. 1, describing the wretched state of the Church [Col. 0359C] in that age—jealousies, slanders, something like civil wars among Christians, contests of bishops against bishops, and the other things that provoked God’s wrath against them—says that from this arose the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian against the Church. See also Rufinus, Book VIII, ch. 1, and Lactantius at the beginning of *On the Workmanship of God*.

We shall signify. Rufinus wrongly renders this “we have indicated,” narrating the matter as if already done, whereas it refers to the future. Nor should this be attributed to printers’ error, since three ancient manuscript codices of the Colbert Library contain that reading. Christophorson and Valesius correctly translate: “we shall signify.”

And their own. Rufinus omitted these words; the others rightly restored them.

In their dwellings. Rufinus translates “in their homes,” as is read in one Colbert manuscript. But the others and the editions have “in their labors.” Christophorson translates “in their own households”; Valesius, “in their own residences.”

## CHAPTER XXXV

[Col. 0359D]

It is posted at Nicomedia. Galerius Augustus was, of course, absent, being ill at Serdica. Thus the assertion by the very learned Henry Valesius in his notes on Eusebius, p. 171, that this edict was issued after the beginning of A.D. 311 but before March cannot be true. For the imperial years of Galerius began on the Kalends of March.

He himself consul for the eighth time, and Maximinus for the second. In the Fasti Maximian is called consul for the eighth time, alone. The anonymous author on the consuls and the author on the Roman pontiffs, cited by Cuspinian, report the same. But here Maximinus is added as consul for the second time. This is very remarkable, especially since no mention of his first consulship is found anywhere. Yet one cannot doubt that he was consul for a second time, since Lactantius’ testimony about it is most explicit.

The prisons having been opened. Rufinus, Book IX, ch. 1:

> [Col. 0360A] The judges, sending edicts through each city and publishing the law, ordered all those detained in prison, in the mines, or kept in any bonds whatsoever, to depart free.

With his wife. Valeria, the daughter of Diocletian. She did not, however, remain at the court of Licinius because of his fierceness, but fled to Maximinus, where she was treated most harshly, as we shall see below, ch. 39.

With his son. Candidianus, of whom mention has been made above, ch. 20.

Consumed by a dreadful wasting disease. Rufinus, book VIII, ch. 15, says that Galerius was afflicted by so many and various diseases, by bodily wasting and by mental derangement, that after long and intractable languors, driven by the furies of his crimes, he voluntarily surrendered his impious life—that is, as Orosius explains in ch. 28 of book VII, he laid violent hands upon himself. But these things are not true. He died in the year of Christ 311, when he had entered upon the nineteenth year of his reign. This is established above all from the most clear testimony of Lactantius. For since it is evident from [Col. 0360B] ch. 33 that Galerius began to be ill in the eighteenth year of his reign, that his illness lasted a whole year, and that thereafter, as he was failing, he sent out an edict in the following year permitting Christians publicly to worship God, and since he died when the vicennalia were about to take place, with the Kalends of March imminent, it is clear that he did not attain the twentieth year of his reign, but died in the nineteenth.

Aurelius Victor agrees with Lactantius in his book *On the Caesars*, where he says that Galerius bore the authority of Caesar for thirteen years and held the imperial power for a quinquennium: “His imperial power of five years,” he says, “was for Constantius but one year,” although indeed both had borne the authority of the Caesars for thirteen years. This is confirmed by the authority of Eutropius at the beginning of book IX and by the Alexandrian Chronicle, p. 651, where it is written that Constantius, who was made Caesar together with Galerius and was proclaimed Augustus on the same day as Galerius, died at York in Britain in the thirteenth year of his principate [Col. 0360C]—that is, after completing it, since some months earlier he had entered his fourteenth.

But above, ch. 17, we proved that Diocletian and Maximian laid down the imperial power in the year of Christ 305, on the Kalends of May. Therefore, he who was then Caesar for thirteen years had been adopted in the year of Christ 293, on the Kalends of March. If you add a quinquennium—or rather, a sexennium—of imperial rule, you will readily find the total of nineteen years, during which he is inferred from Lactantius to have ruled. For the author also of the fragment concerning Constantius Chlorus, p. 492, reports that this same Galerius ruled for nineteen years.

When the most distinguished man Henry Valesius saw this, yet was convinced that he had reigned for twenty-one years, he interpreted the passage in the fragment so as to say that Galerius had indeed ruled for nineteen complete and full years, but besides these, two half-full or hollow years. Yet in the constitution which Lactantius described above, issued shortly before his death, he himself calls himself *imperator XIX* in Eusebius and Rufinus. I know that the same most learned man whom [Col. 0360D] I just named interprets these matters so that in this place the word *Imperator* does not signify Augustan rank; for, he says, it has one meaning in imperial titles when it stands first, another when it is appended to the other titles. For the word *imperator*, when placed second, denotes the emperors’ victories and indicates how many times, after victory had been won, they had been hailed by the army as imperatores, as Dio teaches. I do not wish here to dispute against this interpretation of that most distinguished man. I wished only to note that Galerius is called *imperator XIX* in the heading of that edict.

Galerius died, as may be inferred from Lactantius, in May at Sardica. Onuphrius Panvinius, however, in his commentary on the second book of the *Fasti*, reports that he died about September. Sigonius does better in the second book *On the Western Empire*, where he writes that Galerius departed this life not long after the eleventh day before the Kalends of May. Yet in this he errs: he thinks that Licinius was then made partner in the Empire and proclaimed Augustus by Galerius at Carnuntum, when he perceived himself unfit to manage the Empire. For that was not the reason for associating Licinius in the imperial partnership, but so that Galerius might rely on more defenses and employ him in war against Maxentius. Moreover, this did not occur in Galerius’ last days, but four years earlier, as was shown above.

The occasion of this error was that most ancient writers state that Galerius’ death followed after imperial rank had been bestowed on Licinius. Eutropius, book X: “At this time Licinius was made emperor by Galerius, a native of Dacia, known to him through long acquaintance and esteemed for his vigorous labors and services in the war which he had waged against Narses. The death of Galerius immediately followed.” Zosimus, book II: “Maximianus Galerius, from the fellowship of former times, made his friend Licinius emperor, intending to pursue war against Maxentius with his assistance. After Galerius, while entertaining these plans, had exchanged life for death through an incurable wound, Licinius also claimed the Empire for himself” [Col. 0361B]. Orosius likewise, book VII, ch. 28, and the author of the Fragment concerning Constantius Chlorus, p. 472, narrate the history in such a way that Galerius’ death immediately follows Licinius’ elevation. And Aurelius Victor, who says that Licinius was made emperor before Galerius went into Italy, writes that Galerius was consumed by a pestilential wound shortly after he had departed Italy. In Victor’s *Epitome*: “This Licinius is killed about the fifteenth year after the beginning of his rule,” counting, of course, from Galerius’ death. Socrates too, book I, ch. 2, says that Maximian departed life after first making Licinius emperor. Guided by these authorities, Sigonius erred; Morinus followed him.

Of the same month. That is, May.

The Kalends of March. For on that day Galerius Maximianus had been made Caesar with Constantius; accordingly, the years of his reign always began on the Kalends of March, and the vicennalia ought to have been celebrated on the Kalends of March in the approaching year, which was to be the twentieth year of his reign. The Fasti of Idatius, under the consuls Tiberianus and Dio: “In that year Constantius and Maximian were elevated as Caesars on the day of the Kalends of March.” Eumenius’ panegyric addressed to Constantius: “O Kalends of March, once the auspices of emperors making vows for years, now of emperors eternal!” But here again there arises a difficulty concerning the years of the reign. For if it is true that Galerius was made Caesar under the consulship of Tiberianus and Dio, and if their consulship corresponds to the year of Christ 311, as is commonly thought, it will follow that he died at the beginning of the twenty-first year of his reign. Since, however, the arguments drawn from Lactantius cannot be contradicted, some way must be sought by which we may extricate ourselves from these difficulties. And indeed it is certain that those excellent Fasti of Idatius are not free from blemishes and errors, as could readily be proved.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

While Licinius remained. He was then in Mediterranean Dacia, at Sardica or not far away. For Galerius had died there.

[Col. 0361D] The Chalcedonian strait. Maximinus wished to establish this as the boundary of the Eastern Empire, so that Bithynia too, as far as Chalcedon, might lie within it; while the provinces beyond the Chalcedonian strait should belong to the Western Empire, so that the imperial seat, then at Nicomedia, should belong to him, as the one first made Caesar, and not to Licinius.

Bithynia. In the old manuscript one reads *Bhyaniam*. That the correction is certain is proved first by Maximinus’ journey, as he hastened from the East to Chalcedon; then by Maximinus himself, who in the letter written the following year to Sabinus, quoted by Eusebius, teaches that he had been at Nicomedia in the preceding year: “When in the preceding year,” he says, “I had happily entered Nicomedia, the citizens of that city came to me while I was staying there.” Hence Henry Valesius rightly observed in his *Annotations on Eusebius*, p. 185 ff., that after Galerius’ death [Col. 0362A] Maximinus occupied Asia and Bithynia, which Galerius had retained for himself together with Illyricum and Thrace.

The opposite shores. That is, clearly, Maximinus held the Bithynian shore, Licinius the opposite one, on which Byzantium stood.

A treaty in the strait itself. Undoubtedly at the mouth of the Thracian Bosporus, between Byzantium and Chalcedon. That Bithynia passed into Maximinus’ legal authority and dominion may be inferred from the martyrdom of St Lucian of Antioch, narrated by Eusebius, book IX, ch. 6.

Indulgence. That is, peace, a cessation from persecution. Above, ch. 34, in the edict: “We believed that our indulgence ought to be extended”; Rufinus and Valesius rightly retained this word in their translations, while Christophorsonus wrongly omitted it. Lactantius, *On the Wrath of God*, ch. 20: “If indulgence comes to us from heaven.” Acts of Saints Saturninus, Dativus, and Felix, ch. 13: “Whoever among you wishes to attain indulgence, so that he may be saved, let him make profession.” Optatus of Milevis, book I: “The storm of persecution was completed and ended. [Col. 0362B] At God’s command, Maxentius sending indulgence, liberty was restored to the Christians.” St Augustine frequently uses this term against the Donatists when speaking of the imperial rescripts by which those same Donatists had been granted liberty for their doctrine.

By a common *tutelo*. It is certain that Lactantius is speaking here of the edict issued in Galerius’ final days in favor of Christians. By *communi tutelo*, however, he meant “by common agreement.” I have found this expression nowhere else. Perhaps it is corrupt. My most learned and intimate friend Jean-Baptiste Cotelerius, whom we recently lost to the great detriment of letters and the Church, considers, in vol. III of the *Monuments of the Greek Church*, p. 662, that *titulo* should be restored. Cuper and Columbus are of the same opinion. Sparke, however, prints *tutela*, while noting that a certain learned man among his associates thinks that *titulo* should be read. The most learned Charles du Fresne du Cange thinks that *titulo* must certainly be read—and rightly. For Lactantius refers to the constitution published in ch. 34 [Col. 0362C], which, according to the custom then received, bore the names of Galerius Maximianus and Maximinus Daza—that is, a common title.

By staged embassies. Eusebius explains this more fully, book IX, ch. 2, saying that it began with the Antiochenes: “And likewise,” says Rufinus, “he incites the most depraved citizens in each city to a similar crime, and arranges for an embassy of this kind to be sent from all the provinces.” I have quoted these words because they are clearer than Eusebius’ Greek.

High priests. This is confirmed by Eusebius, book VIII, ch. 14, and book IX, ch. 4. See Valesius’ annotations on the same Eusebius, p. 169.

Adorned with white cloaks. Eusebius, in the passages just mentioned, notes that Maximinus added ornaments to the priests established throughout the provinces, whom he attached to a military retinue—that is, to lictors and attendants; on this see Valesius’ annotations. But Lactantius adds that he ordered [Col. 0362D] those pontiffs who were over the provinces to go about adorned with white *chlamydes*. Here I take *chlamys* to mean a military cloak (*paludamentum*), as in Nonius; or rather, a kind of white tunic, sometimes edged with gold, used only by imperial officials, concerning whom Salmasius says more in his Notes on Lampridius, p. 241. Thus Maximinus shared the garments of palace officials with the high priests whom he appointed throughout the provinces. This perhaps explains the passage in Trebellius Pollio’s *Divus Claudius*: “two cloaks edged with true light,” where Salmasius interprets “true light” as the color purple.

He ordered them to be maimed. See Eusebius, book VIII, ch. 12, and book I of the *Life of Constantine*, ch. 58, where the name Licinius has intruded into Valesius’ translation in place of Maximinus.

Their eyes were gouged out. I would not have noted these things, also mentioned by Eusebius, unless I wished to point out [Col. 0363A] that Suidas attributes this cruelty to Diocletian and Maximian, and that here, as he often does in historical matters, he has erred.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

By Constantine’s letters. After defeating Maxentius, Constantine had met with Licinius at Milan and issued a constitution highly favorable to Christians; he sent it to the East to Maximinus, so that he might arrange for it to be posted in his provinces. Eusebius, book IX, ch. 9, is the authority: Maximinus at first groaned deeply at this; but afterward, since he neither wished to appear to have yielded to Constantine and Licinius nor, through fear of those who had commanded it, to suppress what had been ordered, he wrote a letter to Sabinus the prefect as though on his own initiative and by his own authority. In it he established nearly the same provisions concerning Christians as were contained in that constitution of Constantine and Licinius. Constantine had also added letters to Maximinus, which Eusebius mentions in the final part of the same chapter.

That sacrifice be offered by priests. What Lactantius says here about Maximinus eating sacrificial food daily, Eusebius says was established by him through a public edict in his book *On the Martyrs of Palestine*, ch. 9: all persons, men and women alike, together with servants and infants, were to be compelled to sacrifice and pour libations to the immortal gods, and to eat the flesh of animals offered in sacrifice; and everything offered for sale in the market was to be defiled by the libations of sacrifices. The Acts of the Passion of the holy martyr Lucian of Antioch, whom this same Maximinus put to death, teach the same thing: “Indeed he proceeded to such cruelty that he spared not even infants, but killed them too, because he could not persuade them to taste what had been sacrificed to demons.”

The Acts of the holy martyrs Agape, Chionia, and Irene, who completed their martyrdom at Thessalonica in the second year of the persecution, under the consulship of Diocletian IX and Maximian VIII, show that Maximinus followed in this the footsteps of his master Galerius. For in those Acts, Cassander the *beneficiarius* wrote thus to Dulcetius the governor: “Know, my lord, that Agatho, Agape, Chionia, Irene, Casia, Philippa, and Eutychia refuse to eat things sacrificed to the gods.” The same occurs in the Acts of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, who suffered under the same Maximinus; likewise in the Acts of the holy martyr Varus and his companions, and in the Acts of Theodore of Amasea, surnamed Tyro. Indeed, I find that this practice had been adopted long before in the Acts of Saints Terentius, Africanus, and their companions, where it is written that the Emperor Decius had sent an edict throughout all the provinces of the Roman Empire, so that all Christians might be compelled to sacrifice and eat things sacrificed to idols.

Therefore, when Lactantius says that Maximinus first devised this arrangement—that all animals he ate should be sacrificed at altars, not by cooks but by priests—he must not be understood to mean [Col. 0363D] an edict or general law, since this had been established many years earlier by Decius and Galerius Maximianus, but the private use of food in the imperial household. Moreover, the Acts of St Saba the Goth, who completed his martyrdom in Cappadocia on the day before the Ides of April, under the consuls Modestus and Arintheus—that is, in the year of Christ 372—show that this practice extended even into regions beyond the boundaries of the Roman Empire. But it is more widely known than needs confirmation by ancient testimonies that the Church always abhorred such sacrificial foods, which they called *idolothyta*.

Drenched with unmixed wine. Lactantius, book VI of the *Divine Institutes*, ch. 1: “Men, neglecting justice, though stained by every shameful act and crime, think themselves religious if they have bloodied temples and altars with the blood of victims, if they have soaked hearths fragrant with the pouring out of old wine. They even prepare sacred banquets and exquisite feasts, as though offering something to beings who would drink libations from them.” And in the following chapter: [Col. 0364A] “Thus they slaughter the best and fattest victims for God as though he were hungry; they pour out wines as though he were thirsty.”

Hence the famine. Eusebius describes the cruelty of that famine, book IX, ch. 8. Rufinus should also be consulted, for he contains some matters not found in Eusebius. Eutychius of Alexandria also mentions this famine in his *Annals*.

He gave them to his own as gifts. Rufinus, book VIII, ch. 16: “And thus he bestowed, so to speak, mountains of gold amassed upon his intimates and attendants.”

After the manner of merciful robbers. Salvian, at the end of book VIII of *The Governance of God*, p. 191: “Robbers are accustomed to use this proverb: they say that they have given life to those from whom they do not take it.”

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

Duty prevails. The very same words occur in book VI of the *Divine Institutes*, ch. 23.

Women of noble rank. Rufinus, book VIII, ch. 17: [Col. 0364B] “Among his other qualities, he had this singular zeal: never to pass by—not merely any city, but even a small town—without adultery with the noble matrons found there or the corruption of virgins.”

Food-taster. This is a metaphor drawn from food and drink, also used by Cicero in his speech *For His House*: “You, of course, to the foulest glutton, the taster beforehand of your lusts, Sextus Roscius, a most needy and most criminal man,” etc. A *praegustator*, therefore, is one who tests foods and drinks by tasting them, especially for eminent men, lest perhaps they ingest poison with food or drink. For that reason Antony, fearing the wicked cunning of Cleopatra, took no food except after it had been tasted, as Pliny teaches, *Natural History*, book XXI, ch. 3. Suetonius, *Claudius*, ch. 44: “It is agreed that he was killed by poison; but where it was administered, and by whom, is disputed. Some report that it was by the eunuch Halotus, his food-taster, while he was dining in the citadel with the priests.” Tacitus, *Annals*, book XIII: “There, while Britannicus dined, because a select servant [Col. 0364C] tested his food and drink by tasting.” Pope Gregory XI, in a letter written to Charles V, king of France, and his wife Joanna, published in vol. IV of D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, p. 300: “Furthermore, by these presents we grant that those who prepare such eggs, milk, butter, and cheese, or dishes from them, and also those who serve them to you, may, solely for the purpose of making a trial, taste them.” What Gregory here calls *pro proba facienda*, we now say, *pour faire l’essai*. Evodius of Uppsala, book II of *The Miracles of St Stephen*, ch. 3: “He orders his wine-taster.”

Violated beforehand. I once thought this passage corrupt and conjectured that *invitas* (“unwilling women”) should be restored. Later the most distinguished Sparke and Columbus advised me that the reading in the old manuscript should be retained, because the word *imminutas* means nothing else than “tasted beforehand” or “deflowered”; Columbus demonstrates this by several examples, especially by Lactantius himself, book I of the *Institutes*, ch. 10: “I pass over the virgins whom he violated beforehand.”

[Col. 0364D] They violated beds with impunity. Rufinus, book VIII, ch. 17: “Flowing in pleasures, luxury, and every sort of licentiousness, he set the most shameful examples for his soldiers. Finally, whatever had been done wantonly, insolently, or luxuriously by governors either of soldiers or of provinces went unpunished because of the emperor’s example.”

Driven out by the Goths. When Diocletian set out for Italy to celebrate the vicennalia, the Goths, or peoples inhabiting the bank of the river Ister, took advantage of the occasion, invaded some part of the neighboring province, and expelled its inhabitants. These, driven from their homes, fled to Galerius Maximianus Caesar and later attached themselves to Maximinus, whom Galerius had adopted; they were enrolled among his attendants and protectors.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

Not even by the Augusta. Valeria, Galerius’ widow, who after her husband’s death had gone to Maximinus’ court, rejecting Licinius, to whose care Galerius had entrusted her.

Her father. Galerius, who had adopted Maximinus and made him Caesar.

Her, together with her mother. Diocletian’s wife, of whom more was said in the notes on ch. 15. Octavius Strada says that she died several years before her husband. But Lactantius’ authority proves Strada mistaken, for below, ch. 39, he will say that she was beheaded in the year 313, after Diocletian had already died in the preceding year.

## CHAPTER XL

Eratineus. The passage is corrupt. It is the governor’s name. What if the name Flaccinus should be restored here—the man whom our author in ch. 16 calls no small murderer?

Not less. This correction is not mine but Columbus’. For the old manuscript has *nimis* (“too much”). It is certain that these words were often interchanged in ancient books.

A certain Jew. This was not first devised by Maximinus. The exemplary Nero had preceded him when he wished to repudiate his wife Octavia for Poppaea’s favor. On this matter see Tacitus, book XIV of the *Annals*.

Armed light troops. In the old manuscript it is written *instructibile mens essagitari*. This is certainly an error; but a definite correction did not immediately present itself and was only finally found after the edition had been completed. Columbus, however, prefers *vigiles* (“watchmen”) to *velites* (“light troops”).

## CHAPTER XLI

But the Augusta. Valeria. It should be noted here that nothing is now said about her mother, nor that she was reclaimed by Diocletian when Valeria was reclaimed. Yet she was still alive, as is clear from ch. 31.

## CHAPTER XLII

The statues of the aged Maximian. Rufinus, book VIII, ch. 16, says that Maximian Herculius, disgracefully caught in the plot which he was laying against Constantine, perished even more disgracefully, [Col. 0365C] so that after his death his statues and images were removed, and the names derived from his name were changed in public buildings. In Eusebius, book VIII, ch. 13, the story is described as though Herculius had been the first whose statues and images were destroyed. Since Christophorsonus saw this to be false, he translated Eusebius so as to make him say that this insult was inflicted while Herculius was living. That this is not true is clear from Lactantius’ following words, where he says that no emperor before Diocletian had experienced the destruction of images of a living ruler.

Henry Valesius therefore took another course: Herculius was not the first of all emperors from the beginning of the Empire to have this disgrace branded upon him, but the first among those who had administered the commonwealth in that age. Thus Trebellius Pollio, in *The Thirty Tyrants*, ch. 28, says that the image of Celsus was raised upon a cross by a novel kind of outrage; although, as Casaubon notes here, Greeks and Latins had been accustomed to cast down, smear with mud, break, cast upon the Gemonian stairs, [Col. 0365D] and subject to every kind of indignity the images of condemned persons. He proves this also by Plutarch’s authority.

While alive, he saw it. Diocletian, whose images were being taken down while he was alive because they were joined with the images of Herculius.

Sighs. Cuspinianus, in his *Diocletian*: “Some say that, worn out by mental stupor and a long illness, he breathed out his soul amid sighs.” I think he derived this from Cedrenus.

Worn out by hunger and anguish. Others report that Diocletian was destroyed by another kind of death: some by dropsy, others by poison; Suidas, by hanging. See also what is said below on ch. 50. He died not far from Salona in Dalmatia, at his estate at Aspalathus, where he was also buried. See Henry Valesius’ notes on Ammianus Marcellinus, p. 112. Learned men hold various opinions concerning the year in which Diocletian died: some think it happened [Col. 0366A] in 313, others three years later. The authority of the Fasti of Idatius has led the latter to this opinion; in them it is written that Diocletian died at Salona on the third day before the Nones of December, under the consuls Sabinus and Rufinus.

But it is now established that the author of those Fasti falsely wrote these things, since Lactantius teaches that Diocletian died before the marriage of Licinius and Constantia, and before Maximinus Daza. Since, therefore, he died after Galerius and before Maximinus, at the end of a year, it is evident that he died at the end of the year 312. For Maximinus perished in the following year, as I shall show. Therefore, what is read in Victor’s *Epitome* is not true: that Diocletian spent almost nine years in private life. From the Kalends of May in 305 to the third day before the Nones of December in 312 are only seven years and seven months and some days.

But against this may be said what I see has pleased some: that Diocletian could not be said to have died in 312, since in law 2 of the Theodosian Code, *On the Census*, issued in 313 on the Kalends of June, Constantine calls him [Col. 0366B] “lord and parent,” whereas he would have called him *divus* if he had died. But that argument is false is proved by the letter of the Augustus Maximinus to Sabinus in Eusebius, book IX, ch. 9. There he still calls Galerius Maximianus, whom it is certain had died in the preceding year, his “lord and parent”; yet in the edict preserved there by Eusebius he calls that same Maximianus and Diocletian his deified parents.

Moreover, since this passage of Lactantius establishes that Diocletian died before the marriage of Licinius and Constantia, it follows that what is read in Victor’s *Epitome* is false: namely, that he was consumed by death, as was sufficiently apparent, through voluntary fear. “For, when summoned by Constantine and Licinius to the wedding festivities, he excused himself on account of old age, as unable to attend; having received threatening replies, in which he was reproached for having favored Maxentius and for favoring Maximinus, and suspecting a dishonorable death, he is said to have taken poison.” It is scarcely probable that he who had refused to return to the government of the commonwealth, and who had preferred private life to imperial rule by the memorable and most wise maxim which we quoted above from the same *Epitome*, p. 73, should have been suspected of favoring Maxentius and Maximinus—especially Maximinus, by whom he knew that grievous insults had been inflicted upon his daughter Valeria and wife Prisca, and by whom he had himself been treated with contempt when reclaiming Valeria; an event too recent for him so quickly to have forgotten.

## CHAPTER XLIII

One remained. Namely, Maximinus surnamed Daza. Lactantius calls Diocletian, Herculius, Galerius, and Maximinus “adversaries of God.” He does not include Maxentius in the same number because, though cruel and savage, he nevertheless appeared to favor Christians. Nor does he number Licinius among them, because when Lactantius wrote these things, Licinius seemed to be a friend of Christians. Later he revealed himself.

[Col. 0366D] A recent friendship. That is, the time when peace was concluded between Licinius and Maximinus on the Thracian Bosporus, shortly after Galerius’ death.

Constantine’s sister. Constantia, who afterward favored Arius so strongly that she even induced her brother to defend him.

He sent secretly. Eusebius, book VIII, ch. 14, mentions this same thing: namely, that Maximinus secretly made an alliance with Maxentius.

He had declared war on Constantine. From this passage and from book II of Zosimus it appears that the plans for waging war did not originate with Constantine, but with Maxentius; and thus Constantine sprang to arms, as it were, unwillingly, and was later invited to do so by the Romans, who bitterly endured Maxentius’ tyranny. Yet the most distinguished Hadrian Valesius, in book I of his *Frankish History*, p. 23, imputes that war to Constantine’s arrogance: he says that Constantine took so ill the overthrow at Rome, by Maxentius’ order, of his statues that he thought the injury should be avenged by arms. Valesius sharply and insultingly attacks Constantine’s memory because, after ordering the statues of his father-in-law Maximian to be overthrown in Gaul, he could not endure a like injury inflicted upon himself by Maxentius, Maximian’s son.

Love of truth and the memory of a great prince require us to observe here that there is an immense difference between these two acts. Constantine had overthrown the statues of an enemy, but one already dead, and therefore unable to avenge the insult done to him. Maxentius, however, had cast down, as Nazarius says, the venerable images of a living ruler and commander of most valiant armies; accordingly, Constantine both could and ought to punish the man by whom he had been injured with such great disgrace. Indeed Diocletian, Lactantius writes below, was so moved when he saw his own statues overthrown—though joined to Herculius’ statues, and although this was not done deliberately against him but out of necessity—that he thereby received great and incredible grief [Col. 0367B], and consequently resolved that he must die.

Yet Constantine, in his greatness of spirit, was prepared to forgive Maxentius that injury if he would have accepted equitable terms of peace. But Maxentius despised Constantine: “He fled from, rejected, and abhorred his approach”—these are Nazarius’ words. When his desire for peace had been set aside, he advanced to such madness, says the same Nazarius, that he even provoked without cause the man whom he ought to have courted. It is therefore clear that Constantine is unjustly accused of arrogance here. Had he not avenged his injury upon a fierce enemy who mocked his kindness, he would surely have incurred from forgetting that insult a greater disgrace than words could possibly express.

The death of his father. Of Maximian Herculius, whom Constantine ordered strangled at Massilia. Zosimus, book II: “Maxentius sought occasions for waging war against Constantine, pretending to grieve for the death of his father, to whose death Constantine had supplied the cause.”

Detestable or ruinous. In this passage several letters are missing in the old copy, where only *xtabilem* is read. From this we concluded that *intestabilem* should be restored. *Intestabilis* means the same as *detestabilis*, “detestable,” and *invisus*, “hateful.”

He feigned a quarrel. Eutropius, book X: “From there he departed for Gaul, with a plot contrived, as though he had been expelled by his son.”

## CHAPTER XLIV

Between them. Between Maxentius and Constantine.

He had received an answer. The anonymous panegyric addressed to Constantine after Maxentius’ defeat: “That foolish and wicked animal did not dare to go anywhere beyond his walls. For he was moved either by portents or by forebodings arising from his own fear.”

Six days before the Kalends of November. This, therefore, was the first day on which Maxentius was seen as emperor, contrary to other writers, who state that he seized imperial power on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, the day before he was killed [Col. 0367D]; neither assertion is true. For he was slain on his birthday, as Lactantius and the author of the panegyric mentioned shortly above teach. Yet this writer is mistaken in saying that Maxentius marked the day of his birth by his own slaughter, lest he should violate, even at its beginning, that sacred and religious number seven. For if he was slain on the very day of his birthday, it is evident that he was slain on the day upon which he had assumed imperial power. For the ancients called this day the birthday of emperors. Thus Maxentius was killed in the year of Christ 312, six days before the Kalends of November, after the completion of the sixth year of his reign, at the very beginning of the seventh. In this sense, then, Aurelius Victor and the author of the Alexandrian Chronicle are to be understood when they say that he perished in the sixth year of his tyranny. Eutropius, however, says that Constantine commenced war against Maxentius in the fifth year of his reign. He did indeed commence it, but did not complete it.
