Accordingly, the words of the old calendar published by Bucherius—“On the fifth day before the Kalends of November [Col. 0368A], the defeat of the tyrant; on the sixth, the entry of the Deified One”—must be understood of Maxentius and Constantine, as the most learned Petrus Franciscus Chiffletius and Henricus Noris rightly judged; but in such a way that the fifth day before the Kalends refers not to the day on which Maxentius died, as they supposed, but to the following day, on which his body was found, as the author of the fragment concerning Constantius Chlorus teaches, the day on which victory became certain; and that the sixth day before the Kalends refers to the day on which Constantine the victor entered the city of Rome. These matters seem certain and wholly beyond controversy.

Nevertheless, the very distinguished Petrus Lambecius, in the fourth book of his *Commentaries on the Viennese Library*, p. 298, refers that “defeat of the tyrant” to the time when Licinius, driven by Constantine from Byzantium and Chalcedon, withdrew to Nicomedia and was there besieged as well. Despairing of his situation, as Zosimus says, because he knew that no forces sufficient and properly equipped for battle remained to him, he left the city, submitted himself to Constantine, called him emperor and lord when the purple robe was brought forward, and begged pardon for his past actions [Col. 0368B]. All this occurred in the year of Christ 324, when Crispus was consul for the third time and Constantine for the third time, as appears in the Fasti of Idatius. But Lambecius’s opinion cannot be true, since it is established that the words of the old calendar must be understood of the overthrow of Maxentius. Moreover, nowhere is it recorded that Licinius’s surrender fell on the fifth day before the Kalends of November; and this would above all need to be demonstrated. Indeed, it seems possible to infer that it occurred somewhat earlier from Zosimus’s statement that, after Chalcedon had been taken—that is, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October, as is read in the Fasti—Licinius, his army routed and surrendered, withdrew to Nicomedia with his remaining cavalry and a few thousand infantry. Anyone even slightly acquainted with geography readily understands how brief an interval was required for a victorious army to reach Nicomedia.

For this reason I strongly suspect that the departure of the Deified One, which the old calendar marks on the fifth day before the Kalends of October, should be understood as [Col. 0368C] Constantine’s departure from Chalcedon for Nicomedia. Since the route from there is definite and not long, it will not be an unreasonable conjecture to say that Licinius surrendered a few days later, that is, about the beginning of October. For Zosimus makes clear that he did not long endure the siege of Nicomedia; and from the fragment concerning Constantius Chlorus published by Henricus Valesius it may be inferred that Constantia, Licinius’s wife, came to the camp of her brother Constantine on the day after his arrival.

Nor is the point of great weight which the same distinguished man notes here: that in the Theodosian Code Licinius is called tyrant *kat’ exochēn* (κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν), that is, “pre-eminently.” For we also read that Maxentius was called tyrant in the panegyric delivered by Nazarius to Constantine. Speaking there of Constantine’s actions at Rome after Maxentius’s defeat, he adds: “By the marvel of these deeds all were so won over that they grieved not so much that they had endured that tyrant for so long, as that they had come so late to enjoy such a prince.” And above, concerning the same [Col. 0368D] Maxentius: “That tyrant himself was betrayed not by a manly death but by shameful flight.” Likewise: “This foulest head of the tyrant himself followed his retinue.” The fragment concerning Constantius Chlorus, p. 475: “Meanwhile Constantine, having defeated the commanders of the tyrant at Verona, advanced upon Rome.” An ancient inscription erected in Constantine’s memory after victory over Maxentius: “Because, by the prompting of divinity and by greatness of mind, with his army he avenged the republic at one time by just arms both upon the tyrant and upon all his faction.” Prudentius, Book I *Against Symmachus*: “The Mulvian [bridge], hurling the tyrant received into the Tiber’s pools.” Indeed, Maxentius is also meant by “the tyrant” in the Theodosian Code, in the sole law *On Freeborn Persons Who Served in the Time of the Tyrant*, and in Book I *On Cohortales*.

The five-year vows were being concluded. It is certain that Maxentius celebrated his quinquennial festival. Lactantius’s authority is plain. Moreover, Occon, p. 541, preserves [Col. 0369A] a coin of Maxentius, on whose reverse are written: “VICTORY OF OUR LORDS, THE AUGUSTUS AND CAESAR; VOWS FOR FIVE YEARS, FOR MANY [YEARS] UP TO TEN.” Therefore, there can be no doubt that Maxentius celebrated his quinquennial vows, and that he did so after the completion of the fifth year. I ask only how it can be that rites performed according to custom on the first day of the sixth year were concluded at the end of that same year. I know that those vows were celebrated with great display, that the festivities lasted many days, and that they were observed not only in the imperial city but also in the provinces. Yet this does not resolve the difficulty.

Unless we say that Maxentius, a man given to pleasure and fond of idleness, as he is described, wished to make his quinquennial celebrations notable by a new custom, and for this reason continued them for an entire year; but this seems scarcely probable. Or perhaps, just as the first day of the year, on which the quinquennial vows were celebrated, was spent in games and sacrifices, so the same solemnities were repeated on the final day of that year, in order that the quinquennial celebration might end in the same manner in which it began—much as the processions of consuls occurred seven times in a year, as appears from Novella 105 of Emperor Justinian [Col. 0369B].

What if emperors’ birthdays were feast days whenever they recurred in each month? For in the Acts of Saint Marcellus the centurion, who suffered martyrdom in the city of Tingis under Diocletian’s rule, I find that the twelfth day before the Kalends of August was a feast day in the Roman Empire: “Now, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August,” he says, “beside the standards of this legion, when you celebrated the feast day of your emperor, I publicly declared that I am a Christian.” Diocletian, to be sure, was made emperor on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December. Thus certain people formerly sacrificed to Epicurus on the twentieth day of the moon and kept monthly observances called *Icades*, as Pliny says in Book XXXV, chapter 2, of his *Natural History*.

The heavenly sign. The “immortal sign,” as Lactantius calls it elsewhere: that is, the sign of the cross. This passage is of great importance. For it identifies both the place and the day on which the cross by which Constantine would conquer was shown to him [Col. 0369C]. Since Eusebius, who says that he received the account from Constantine’s own lips, establishes that Constantine saw the trophy of the cross in the sky at midday, while the sun was declining toward the west; and that, while he was wondering what this apparition meant, Christ the God appeared to him in a dream on the following night with the sign that had been shown in heaven, and commanded him to fashion a military standard in the likeness of that which he had seen in the sky and to use it as a saving protection in battle—it is certain that both visions occurred in one place and within the space of a few hours.

If this is so, as certainly it is, learned men now have grounds finally to end the famous controversy regarding the place where the sign of the cross was shown to Constantine, and to establish the credibility of the author of the Life of Saint Artemius, on the authority of the commander of Egypt. The very learned Petrus Franciscus Chiffletius sought, by circuitous argument and evasion, to weaken and diminish that author’s authority. These are Artemius’s words, defending Constantine’s memory before Emperor Julian: “He turned to Christ when summoned by Him, when he undertook the most difficult battle [Col. 0369D] against Maxentius. Then at midday there appeared to him the sign of the cross, brighter than the rays of the sun, and in golden letters announcing victory in war. For we ourselves also saw the sign when we were engaged in the war, and read the letters. Indeed the entire army witnessed it, and many witnesses of this event are in your army.” In Surius, 20 October.

Perhaps someone may be surprised that Artemius here says that many witnesses of this event were then in Emperor Julian’s army. For if these words were spoken toward the end of the year of Christ 342, fifty years had passed since Maxentius’s death, and it is difficult for many soldiers to have survived from the army that then fought against him. But this ought not at all to seem surprising. For in the *Dialogue on Distinguished Orators*, whose author most suppose to be Quintilian, others Tacitus, and some Suetonius—in that dialogue, I say, written in the sixth year of Vespasian’s principate—the author testifies that he saw in [Col. 0370A] Britain an old man who declared that he had been present at the battle in which the Britons attempted to bar Caesar, as he brought arms against them, from their shores and to drive him back; this had occurred almost one hundred and twenty years earlier. And Saint Jerome, in his *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, which Baronius considers to have been written about the year of Christ 382, says that there were still then living persons who had attended the Council of Nicaea, though few because of their age.

Accordingly, to return to our subject, it must be established that the vision of the cross shown to Constantine occurred in the camp while he was besieging Rome, on the seventh day before the Kalends of November in the year of Christ 312. Jacobus Oiselius was indeed far too audacious when, in his *Treasury of Ancient Coins*, p. 463, he said that anyone who attributed the whole affair of the cross shown to Constantine to pious frauds of the ancients would not depart far from the truth. For what thereafter will be judged true, if it is permissible to count this history—which rests upon the testimony of Lactantius, Publius Optatianus Porphyrius, Eusebius, and ancient coins—as one of the fables and, as he calls them, pious frauds [Col. 0370B] of the ancients? Such matters must be handled more reverently, and such irreverent rashness must be far from Christian hearts.

With Christ bent around it. These words must be understood to mean that Christ’s monogram was bent around the top of the Labarum, as we see on ancient coins.

To consult the Sibylline books. Zosimus, Book II: “Maxentius, shut up [in Rome], sacrifices victims to the gods and consults soothsayers concerning the outcome of the war, after also investigating the Sibylline oracles themselves. When he discovered an oracle indicating that it was fated that whoever planned matters tending to the ruin of the Roman people would perish by a miserable death, he interpreted the oracle as applying to himself, as though he were repelling those who attacked Rome and intended to capture it. But the outcome confirmed what was true.” These statements agree entirely with Lactantius’s narrative.

## CHAPTER XLV

The winter immediately following. That is, the winter which immediately followed Maxentius’s death [Col. 0370C]. But Maxentius perished in 312, six days before the Kalends of November. Therefore Constantine departed for Milan at the end of that year or, as I rather believe, at the beginning of the following one. For Nazarius, in the panegyric which he delivered to Constantine, speaks of the delay Constantine spent at Rome in such a way as plainly to establish that he remained there for two months: “What the deadly domination had inflicted throughout six whole years, a care of nearly two months healed.” It is not probable, however, that one so close to the Kalends of January would have left Rome while they were impending, in order to enter upon the consulship somewhere other than Rome.

Moreover, there survives in Book XI, title 57, of the Code of Emperor Justinian a law given by Constantine at Rome on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, when he and Licinius were consuls for the third time—that is, in January immediately after Maxentius’s death. From this it may be inferred that Constantine did not leave Rome before the day on which that law is said to have been issued. If so, Nazarius’s words should be understood in the manner in which Saint Augustine, in Book *To the Donatists after the Conference*, chapter 33, says that Aelianus the proconsul heard the case of Felix, bishop of Aptunga, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, nearly four months after Caecilian had been judged by Miltiades; although from the sixth day before the Nones of October, when he was judged, to the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, when Felix’s case was heard, four and a half months had elapsed [Col. 0370D]. By the same reasoning Pope Saint Leo, writing in his fifty-second letter to Ravennius of Arles and the other bishops of Gaul, says that the Council of Chalcedon consisted of nearly six hundred bishops, although the constant judgment of virtually all writers is that 630 bishops attended it.

Constantine therefore reached Milan near the end of January. Licinius also came there to marry Constantia, Constantine’s sister. Zosimus likewise records these events [Col. 0371A], rightly noting that they occurred after Maxentius’s defeat and before war broke out between Maximinus and Licinius. Thus the most learned Joannes Morinus is evidently mistaken when, in his book *On the Church Liberated through Constantine*, p. 328, he writes that Licinius came to Milan to Constantine after Maximinus had been defeated and killed, and there took Constantia in marriage. “When this had been accomplished,” says Zosimus, “Constantine returned to the Celts, and Licinius to Illyricum,” as the author of the *Fragment concerning Constantius Chlorus*, p. 473, relates. But before they left Milan they promulgated the law in favor of Christians which will shortly be reproduced.

Certain most learned men believe that the marriage of Licinius and Constantia was celebrated at Milan in March, drawing their argument from the first law of the Theodosian Code, *On Vacant Property*, which is written as having been issued by Constantine at Milan on the sixth day before the Ides of March, Constantine Augustus being consul for the third time and Licinius consul. Morinus, however, in his *On the Church Liberated through Constantine*, p. 329, thinks that March must be changed to May in that constitution, because, as he says, Constantine fought against barbarians in Germany in March of that year. Certainly—an observation that it is enough to make once here—nothing certain can be inferred from the subscriptions of laws contained in the Theodosian Code. Consequently, one cannot conclude from them that Constantine was at the places where the laws are said to have been issued at the stated times [Col. 0371B].

For if this were certain, it would likewise be certain that within six days he was at Heraclea in Macedonia or Thrace and at Milan in Italy: for the law of which we have spoken is read as issued at Milan on the sixth day before the Ides of March, while the first law *On Agents* is said to have been issued at Heraclea on the third day before the Nones of March, under the same consuls. An even stronger example may be drawn from Law 2, *On Penalties*, and Law 1, *If a Co-heir in a Petition Dies without an Heir*. The former is said to have been issued at Chalon, the latter at Antioch; both on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, when Constantine Augustus and Licinius were consuls for the fourth time.

The most learned Jacobus Gothofredus saw that there is a difficulty in the subscription of the latter law, and either declared that it should be attributed to Licinius, who held the East, whose principal city was Antioch, or proposed that Antigonia near Stobi in Macedonia should be restored in place of Antioch, since it fell to Constantine when peace was concluded between him and Licinius after the battle at Cibalae. But these explanations do not resolve the difficulty. For it will always be difficult to reconcile this discrepancy, since it is certain that Constantine could not have been in Gaul and Macedonia on one and the same day.

Again, how can the same man who was at Chalon and Antioch on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April have been at Thessalonica in that same year on the eighth day before the Ides of March, and two days later, on the sixth day before the Ides, at Rome? This follows from the subscriptions of Law 1, *On Various Offices*, and Law 2, *On the Julian Law concerning Public and Private Violence*. Then, on the Ides of September in the same year, he would have to be thought at Rome, and six days later at Naissus in Dacia. For the first law *On the Right of the Fisc* is said to have been issued at Rome on the Ides of September, and the first law *On Centonarii* [Col. 0371D] at Naissus on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October. Finally, if this rule were certain, Constantine would in the following year have been at Sardica on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May, yet at Rome on the Kalends of May itself, within twelve days; this may be inferred from the subscriptions of Laws 2 and 3 *On Donations*. Further examples could be adduced, but these suffice. It must therefore be concluded, as we said above, that no certainty can be inferred from the subscriptions of laws in the Theodosian Code for identifying the places at which Constantine resided during the various periods of his reign. Consequently, the arguments that the most learned men have drawn from them to confirm and establish their historical conjectures are weak.

For such contingencies. In the old manuscript the reading is: “for such a cause, Licinius having been posted.” Our emendation is good. In ancient manuscripts one often finds *causa* written for *casus*, as in Saint Ambrose, Letter 43: “In nature there is contingency; in choice, judgment” [Col. 0372A]. In the very ancient manuscript of the church of Beauvais, however, *causa* is written in place of it, though incorrectly.

At Perinthus. That is, Heraclea. For Heraclea in Thrace is so called in distinction from other cities of the same name, as Henricus Valesius rightly observed on Book XXII of Ammianus Marcellinus. The Greek Menologion for the tenth day of May: “Perinthus, a city of Thrace, which is now called Heraclea.” In Canisius, vol. XI, *Ancient Readings*, p. 768.

Eighteen thousand. Near Resiston, the first place encountered in the Antonine Itinerary by those traveling from Heraclea to Hadrianople, although there it is said to be twenty-two Roman miles from Heraclea.

The second station. The reading of the old exemplar must again be presented; it runs thus: “Holding the second station, being distant with soldiers and with an equal number collected.” We once conjectured that the reading should be: “Holding the second station, distant with an equal number of soldiers and collected troops.” Later I observed that the British conjecture is not only clearer but correct, and therefore transferred it into the text, although Columbus does not approve the conclusion which we had drawn from that emendation [Col. 0372B].

## CHAPTER XLVI

Most high God. The very distinguished Joannes Columbus thinks that Eusebius refers to this prayer in Book IV of the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 19, when he writes that Constantine, by a law, commanded those soldiers who had not yet received the teaching of the divine faith to go out on Sundays into an open field and, at a signal, all together offer to God the prayer they had previously learned. Immediately afterward, in the following chapter, he gives its formula. But that prayer differs greatly from the one which the angel taught Licinius; and it is highly probable that Constantine’s soldiers had often recited the former earlier, since Books II, chapters 4 and 12, of the *Life of Constantine* establish that he always offered prayers to God before coming to blows and battle.

The Kalends of May [Col. 0372C]. For on that day he had been made Caesar in the year of Christ 305, as we saw above. This also confirms what we have said concerning the year in which Diocletian laid down the empire. For if the eighth year from Maximinus’s proclamation was completed on the Kalends of May 313, as Lactantius says, it necessarily follows that he was proclaimed Caesar on the Kalends of May 305. Those who think that he held imperial power for only seven years—four as Caesar and three as Augustus in the East—are therefore mistaken. For he ruled for eight full years and some part of a ninth.

Like that man. That is, Maxentius, who was defeated on the very day of his birthday.

They call it the Serene [Plain]. Near Resiston, as we have said: a place in Thrace between Hadrianople and Heraclea. It was indeed a plain rendered famous by this battle, which brought peace to the afflicted Church. Zosimus is therefore mistaken in believing that the battle was fought in Illyricum. These are his words: “When civil wars had been kindled between Licinius and Maximianus, and a sharp battle was fought in Illyricum, Licinius at first appeared to be defeated; but immediately, when battle was renewed, he put Maximianus to flight” [Col. 0372D].

Tenacious. Eusebius, Book I of the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 55, proves by many examples that Licinius was greedy. The fragment concerning Constantius Chlorus, p. 474: “Licinius raged in wickedness, greed, cruelty, and lust.”

## CHAPTER XLVII

The supreme God. The martyrdom of Saint Basileus, bishop of Amaseia: “Licinius, therefore, aided by the almighty hand of our Lord Jesus Christ, gained victory over Maximinus.”

Having put on a servant’s garment. Eusebius confirms this narrative in Book IX, chapter 10, of his *Ecclesiastical History* and Book I, chapter 58, of the *Life of Constantine*.

He crossed the strait. The battle was therefore fought in the part of the empire held by Licinius, that is, between Heraclea [Col. 0373A] and Hadrianople, in a plain called Serene, as Lactantius said in the preceding chapter. It was sixty Roman miles from Nicomedia.

He made for the East. Zosimus: “Departing through the East toward Egypt, in hope of assembling forces sufficient for conducting war.”

He resumed his garment. Namely, the purple, the emblem of imperial majesty.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

Having entered Nicomedia. Joannes, presbyter of Nicomedia, mentions Licinius’s arrival at Nicomedia in the *Life of Saint Basileus, Bishop of Amaseia*. From it we learn that Constantia, Licinius’s wife, also came with him to Nicomedia after Maximinus’s defeat: “Therefore, after Maximinus’s just punishment and the divinely inflicted wrath, Licinius, having all the East under his authority, came with great pomp to Nicomedia, the city of our region, together with his wife, in order to reside in the imperial palace and govern the empire of the East. Then suddenly a certain profound peace was brought, by Licinius’s will and action, over the whole region of the world, after those violent agitations and conflicts stirred up by mad idolatry.” Although some consider these Acts of Basileus false and spurious, it is sufficiently clear that they are genuine at this point [Col. 0373B].

On the day of the Ides of June. These words must not be understood of the day on which the edict was issued, but of the day on which, by Licinius’s order, it was posted at Nicomedia.

Constantine and he himself being consuls for the third time. That is, in the year of Christ 313.

The letter. Eusebius reproduced it in Book X, chapter 5, but translated, as he says, from the Roman language into Greek. We owe its present Latin form, as it was first issued, solely to Lactantius’s diligence. He, however, omitted the preface found in Eusebius.

That the highest divinity may be able to favor us. Eusebius translates: “that whatever divinity and heavenly being there may be” (ὅπως ὅ τι ποτὲ ἐστι θειότης καὶ οὐρανίου πράγματος). Valesius says that this reading is unsound. Certainly it does not agree with the words of the edict [Col. 0373C].

Whose religion we follow with free minds. Eusebius did not render these words in Greek.

Dication. That is, “condescension” or “gracious regard.” For I see these terms used interchangeably and without distinction. A little later in this letter one reads: “Your dication understands.” The same word occurs in the first Conference of Carthage, chapters 10 and 19; in the report of Anulinus, proconsul, to Constantine Augustus, in the third Conference, chapter 220; and in Saint Augustine, Letter 68. Whoever seeks more examples should consult Du Fresne’s glossary.

Conditions. Eusebius translates *tōn haireseōn* (τῶν αἱρέσεων). This word has caused learned men much trouble, as appears from Valesius’s annotations on this passage. Now, however, the meaning of this place will be easy. Greek jurists called *haireseis* (αἱρέσεις) what we call conditions, as may be seen in various passages of the *Basilica*, especially Book XLIV, title 19, section 30 and the following sections, in the Graeco-Roman Code of Law, and elsewhere. Constantine Harmenopulus, Book V, title 8: “Unlawful and ridiculous conditions in testamentary appointments and legacies are treated as not appended, and these are therefore provided without such a condition.” Joannes Mercerus translates the passage correctly thus: “Conditions which are contrary to law or absurd are deemed not appended in testamentary appointments and legacies, and these are consequently conferred without such a condition.” In Laws 9 and 10 of the Theodosian Code, *On the Estates of Shipowners*, *haeresis* means a naval duty or condition: “We order that the naval obligation be maintained in every respect, so that all estates sold by auction up to twenty years ago and separated from the naval obligation because of a public contract, if they are shown previously to have been subject to this burden, shall again remain liable to the required public duty” [Col. 0373D].

Because . . . honor. These words are corrupt in Eusebius, where the translation of Valesius reads: “And this has been done by us so that it might not appear that anything has been taken away by us from any divine worship or honor” [Col. 0374A]. This is certainly better than Musculus and Christophorsonus.

Having issued letters. He speaks of the earlier constitution of Constantine and Licinius, enacted shortly after Maximinus’s defeat. See Valesius’s annotations.

Those who bought [them]. Constantine renewed this constitution after his victory over Licinius, as appears from Book II, chapter 41, of Eusebius’s *Life of Constantine*, in Valesius’s edition.

A deputy. Since Eusebius wished to speak Greek and had no word to express the office of *vicarius*, he used translation and circumlocution. Eusebius’s translators then rendered it “prefect,” who administers justice in that province or district.—(See below, col. 370, the two letters of Baluzius on this passage.)

He urged [him]. Namely, Licinius.

Ten years. This passage shows—and we said above—that the persecution began on the seventh day before the Kalends of March, the day on which the church of Nicomedia was destroyed. For if one counts from 23 February 303 to 13 June 313, when the edict concerning the restoration of churches was posted at Nicomedia, one finds that ten years, three months, and nineteen days elapsed: that is, as Lactantius says here, ten years and approximately four months [Col. 0374B].

## CHAPTER XLIX

The narrow passes of Mount Taurus. Or “the defiles,” as others call them. They lie between Cappadocia and Cilicia. Lactantius teaches in chapter 47 that Maximinus, in flight, passed through Cappadocia. And certainly the direct route from Bithynia to Cilicia is through Cappadocia. I therefore think that the narrow passes were located where the Cilician Gates are marked on geographical maps.

He fled to Tarsus. Lactantius testifies in chapter 47 that the Serene Plain, where Maximinus was defeated and routed by Licinius’s army, was 160 Roman miles from Nicomedia. In the Bordeaux Itinerary, however, the distance from Nicomedia to Ancyra in Galatia is recorded as 258 Roman miles, and from Ancyra to Tarsus as 343. The total is 761 Roman miles [Col. 0374C]. I know that Maximinus fled with the greatest haste until he reached Nicomedia. But afterward, I think, his mind recovered somewhat and the ardor of flight cooled for a time. Thus, since he still had 601 Roman miles to travel to reach Tarsus, the Cilician city; since he gathered soldiers from his flight and from the East; since he first halted in Cappadocia and then in the defiles of Mount Taurus, where he built fortifications and towers to repel the attacks of Licinius’s pursuing forces—it could not have been possible for one who arrived at Nicomedia on the Kalends of May to have reached Tarsus before the following July.

I have thought it worth noting this because I see that most hold that this Maximinus died in June, while Henricus Noris, otherwise a most learned man, maintains in chapter 2 of his dissertation on a coin of Licinius that Maximinus died at the beginning of spring in 314. We shall consider the year later. Meanwhile, it should be observed that Maximinus did not die immediately upon arriving at Tarsus. Rather, he survived his disgrace for some time and long endured the most severe pains, so that one may rightly affirm that he did not die before August [Col. 0374D].

Driven by madness. We emended the text thus, since the old manuscript reads *insania percutis*. Lactantius, Book I of the *Institutions*, chapter 9: “The same man, driven by rage and madness, killed his wife and children.” Saint John Chrysostom, in his oration on Saint Babylas, speaking of the deaths of the persecutors, says that one of them, still alive, had the pupils burst from his eyes—that is, Maximinus—and that another, driven by madness, and another overcome by some other affliction, met death. Henricus Valesius interprets what is here said of madness as referring to Diocletian, whom he infers from Eusebius and Constantine to have died insane. But Eusebius and Constantine do not say this; they state only that in the final year of his reign he was deprived of soundness of mind by the force of illness. And Lactantius, who describes his illness, records nothing about insanity or madness. Had Chrysostom not explained himself, I would readily believe that what he says concerning the emperor driven mad ought to be referred to Maximinus because of this passage in Lactantius [Col. 0375A].

He struck his head against the walls. This is one of the “detestable” forms of mourning, as Cicero calls them in the third *Tusculan Disputation*. See Casaubon’s notes on Julius Capitolinus.

His eyes burst forth. Eusebius says the same in Book IX, chapter 10, of his *Ecclesiastical History*; Book I, chapter 59, of his *Life of Constantine*; and likewise Eutychius, Theophanes, and Anastasius. Saint John Chrysostom also mentions it in his oration on Saint Babylas, and Saint Jerome in his commentary on Zechariah, as we shall see shortly.

As though he were being burned. In the *Annals* of Eutychius it is written that Maximinus fell into an illness in which his body was so burned that it became like charcoal [Col. 0375B]; that he was so scorched that his entrails burst from the heat he felt within; that his eyes fell out and dropped to the ground; and that his burned flesh separated from his bones. But Anastasius the librarian explains these matters better in his *Ecclesiastical History*, in these words: “The divine wrath that had gone before seized him. For a flame kindled from the midst of his entrails and marrow threw him face downward upon the ground, gasping in intolerable pain, so that both his eyes burst forth and he was left blind—as was fitting for one truly wicked. Then, as his flesh decayed and fell away because of the immeasurable burning of his bones, he gave up his life while fighting against God.” It is plain that Anastasius took these statements from Theophanes.

He breathed forth his guilty spirit. In Victor’s *Epitome* it is written that he perished by a simple death—that is, a natural death, or by his fate. Eutropius likewise relates that he forestalled his imminent destruction by an accidental death. Both statements are true. The common opinion of learned men [Col. 0375C] is that this death occurred in the year of Christ 313. Petavius, however, in book XI of *The Doctrine of Times*, chapter 34, writes that, on the authority, as he says, of Eusebius in the *Chronicle*, with Victor and Eutropius concurring, Maximinus was destroyed in the second year after Galerius Maximianus perished—that is, in the year of Christ 312. But since it is certain that he died in the year following the slaughter of Maxentius, Henry Noris rightly rebukes Petavius at this point. Yet Noris himself is shown to be mistaken in this: following Baronius, he maintains that the death of Maximinus occurred in 314, at the beginning of spring. For since the final chapters of Lactantius establish that he perished in the year in which peace was granted to the Church, the year in which Lactantius also brought this work to its conclusion; and since we have shown that the persecution began in 303, at the end of February, it is clearer than daylight that Maximinus was destroyed in 313, the tenth year from the beginning of the persecution.

The learned man indeed relies upon an argument plausible in appearance: namely, certain words of Maximinus in the edict which, shortly before his death, he issued in favour of the Christians [Col. 0375D] in Eusebius, book IX, chapter 10. There he says that in letters issued in the preceding year to the individual governors of provinces, he had ordained the same measures as were contained in the letters of Constantine and Licinius. Since, then, that constitution of Constantine and Licinius was promulgated at the beginning of 313, it seems altogether evident that this one, issued in the following year, must be assigned to 314, and therefore that in that year the tyrant lost both empire and life. A weighty argument indeed, if it were established that Maximinus counted his years from the Kalends of January. But since the eighth year of his reign was completed on the Kalends of May 313, as Lactantius teaches, an edict issued by him some months later falls in the following—that is, the ninth—year of his reign, but not in the year of Christ 314; especially since Eusebius’s narrative establishes that it was issued shortly after his defeat by Licinius. Thus Baronius, joining together Licinius’s victory and Maximinus’s end, writes that these happened [Col. 0376A] in the year of Christ 314—an error of one year.

For what the most learned Henry Noris adds from coins concerning the sixth year of Maximinus Augustus does not at all militate against the opinion of those who assign Maximinus’s death to 313. For he who had assumed the title of Augustus at the end of 307, or at the beginning of the following year, could have counted the sixth year of his reign in 313. That he died in that year may also be proved by the authority of Aurelius Victor, who writes that, after a reign as Augustus of two years—that is, two years after the death of Galerius—he was defeated and put to flight by Licinius and perished at Tarsus. For since Galerius died in May 311, Maximinus, dying in 313, is rightly said to have reigned in the East for two years; whereas, if he had died only in 314, he would have exceeded the two years attributed to him by Aurelius Victor.

I had thought these things true, or at least probable, because I could find no other means of escaping that difficulty except the method of counting Maximinus’s years from the Kalends of May. Afterwards Henry Dodwell, a man of extensive reading [Col. 0376B] and refined judgment, judged my explanation unsound, because it was not accepted usage in that age to reckon emperors’ years from the anniversary of their accession; although he declared himself inclined to accept that opinion if the practice could be confirmed by some suitable example of established authority.

He therefore follows another path, and refers the edict of the preceding year mentioned by Maximinus to the end of the year of Christ 312. His argument is drawn from a law of Constantine published in the Theodosian Code, which, he says, Constantine issued at Rome near the beginning of December, but when about immediately to depart from Rome. Accordingly, he thinks that the edict of Constantine and Licinius concerning peace for the Church, issued at Milan, reached Maximinus about the middle of December, in the same month; and that Maximinus could have issued the former edict, mentioned in the second, in that same year. He then adds that no one should wonder at these arrangements if he considers the speed of the imperial couriers and Maximinus’s own impetuous character [Col. 0376C].

I trust that the modesty and even temper of this man will make him not take it ill if I here note the difficulties that occurred to me upon a serious examination of his words—not because I wish to set myself above him or even on a level with him, but that through friendly disputations we may seek truth from one another, which ought to be the sole aim of our studies.

First, I admit that it was not then customary for years to be counted from emperors’ accession-days, but from the Kalends of January, from the procession of the consuls, who marked the calendars and gave their names to the years, to use Lactantius’s words from book VI of the *Institutions*, chapter 4. Yet, if anyone wished to contend for this here, he might bring forward against it the observation of the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius, who notes in the *Ecclesiastical Annals* that Diocletian instituted the practice that years thereafter should be counted from the first day of his reign, and that Maximinus, who succeeded him, counted his years in the same manner by that example. But let us set aside these claims, which are unsupported by ancient testimony.

The most distinguished man says that Constantine entered Rome on 29 October and did not complete two months there; this he derived from the panegyric delivered to Constantine by Nazarius. But if he left Rome at the beginning of December, as the most learned man thought could be inferred from the law cited above, then that two-month administration praised by Nazarius disappears. On that account Constantine would scarcely have spent a full month at Rome. But the point which strikes at the throat is this: as we have said, there survives in the Code of the Emperor Justinian, book XI, title 57, a law issued by Constantine at Rome as the month of January was drawing to its close—the January immediately following Maxentius’s destruction. This law, I think, plainly shows that Constantine did not depart Rome before the end of January. Moreover, the distance from the city of Rome to Milan is immense and cannot be covered in a short interval, since the *Itinerary of Antoninus* counts 528 Roman miles; and from Milan to Nicomedia there are 1,476,000 paces [Col. 0377A]. It is impossible that a law issued at Milan about the middle of December could have been conveyed to Nicomedia in that same month, however swift the couriers or rapid their horses. Nor does Maximinus’s impetuous character have any bearing here, since Eusebius, in book IX, chapter 9 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, reproaches him instead for slowness in this affair.

With these matters thus duly established, I think it can no longer be doubted that we must return to our explanation: the first edict of Maximinus was issued in 313, apparently in April; the later one, in which he recalls the former as having been issued, as it were, in the preceding year, was promulgated about September. Or certainly—and this seems more probable—we must say that Maximinus counted years in the Greek manner, and that September was consequently the beginning of his year. If this explanation is admitted, it will no longer be difficult to understand how a constitution issued in April of the Roman year 313 could be described as having been issued in the preceding year by one who began the year [Col. 0377B] in September, according to Greek practice.

## CHAPTER L

He defeated the persecutors. Lactantius, *Institutions*, book VII, chapter 26: “For those who wished to abolish the worship of the heavenly and unique God in order to defend impious religions lie overthrown.” Eusebius observes the same in book I of the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 3, as does the author of the *Fragment concerning Constantius Chlorus*, p. 475. Jerome, on Zechariah XIV: “Let us read the ecclesiastical histories: what Valerian, what Decius, what Diocletian, what Maximian, what Maximinus, most savage of all, and recently Julian suffered; and then by events we shall prove that even according to the letter the truth of the prophecy has been fulfilled: that their flesh has rotted away, their eyes have wasted away, and their tongue has dissolved into stench and pus.”

Scaliger, in his annotations on Eusebius, p. 248, interprets this passage so as to think that Jerome places Maximinus among those whose flesh rotted away. But I think this is not Jerome’s meaning. [Col. 0377C] He first speaks of the miserable death of Valerian and Decius, but does not specify its kind; for the words of the prophecy, which he had undertaken to interpret, could not be applied to the manner of death by which those two emperors perished. He then refers the rotting of flesh to Maximian, the wasting of the eyes to Maximinus, and the stench and pus of the tongue to Diocletian—if the reports concerning him by Eutychius of Alexandria and George Cedrenus are true: namely, that, near death, he cast forth from his throat a multitude of worms together with the tongue itself, which had rotted.

Valeria. Since I saw that an old manuscript distinctly read “Valerius whom,” I did not dare change it in the first edition of this book, fearing, of course, that perhaps some person of that name might be lurking somewhere. But afterwards I observed that there can be no doubt that the old manuscript is corrupt at this point and that the name Valeria must be restored here. I have therefore restored it.

When she learned that he was alive. Columbus conjectures that one should write: “when she learned that he—that is, Licinius—had issued an edict.” But I think that absolutely nothing should be changed. The sense is this: Licinius ordered Candidianus to be killed. Since the command was not immediately carried out, Valeria, when she learned that he was still alive at the time when he had been ordered killed, joined Licinius’s retinue in order to watch Candidianus’s fate.

Their mother. That is, Maximinus’s wife, whose name learned men admit they do not know.

Into the Orient. Most have conjectured that it should be corrected to “into the Orontes,” because it is certain that a river is denoted in this passage—a point most learnedly demonstrated with many arguments by the distinguished Cuperus. Yet because he himself relates that some ancients called that river “the Orient” which others commonly call the Orontes, I did not wish to alter the text, although that same distinguished man does not doubt that Lactantius wrote “Orontes,” and that “Orient” intruded in place of the true name through copyists at an age when they spoke in that way.

## CHAPTER LI

[Col. 0378A]

Corrupts truth. Lactantius, *Institutions*, book III, chapter 1: “God wished the nature of the thing to be such that plain and naked truth should be more splendid; for it is sufficiently adorned in itself, and therefore, when painted over with embellishments added from without, it is corrupted.”

Jovian and Herculean. Thus were called the households of Diocletian, who styled himself Jovian, and of the elder Maximian, who was called Herculean, as though they derived their lineage from Jupiter and Hercules, as the most learned men have observed. Aurelius Victor notes that from this name was given a designation to the outstanding military auxiliaries in the army: namely, that they should be called Herculiani. Hence Ammianus Marcellinus, books XX and XXII, mentions the Joviani and Herculiani.

And here at last let there be an end to our notes on Lactantius’s book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*. Aurelius Victor, if the report is true, had written a work on the same subject, comprising a history of the Church’s persecutions down to Diocletian. Marianus Victorius, in his notes on Jerome’s twenty-first letter, addressed to Paul the Concordian monk, testifies that this work existed in his day in the Vatican Library. Jerome had requested from him “the commentaries of Fortunatianus and, for knowledge of the persecutors, the history of Aurelius Victor.” Yet I greatly doubt whether it can truly be said that Aurelius Victor, a man by no means Christian, wrote a history of that kind. For that passage of Jerome is corrupt in the received editions and so intricate that it drove the most learned Andreas Schott into terrible windings as he sought an Aurelius Victor who wrote about the persecutions of the Church; he was compelled to descend to the opinion that there had been several Victors, writers of Augustan history, and that one of them had even given his name to Christ.

For if that history had existed in the Vatican Library in the period when Victorius wrote his scholia on Jerome, it certainly would not have escaped [Col. 0378C] the learned and diligent hands of Baronius, nor of so many most learned men, deeply devoted to ecclesiastical antiquity, who lived at Rome after the pontificate of Pius V and the time of Marianus Victorius, and who rendered praiseworthy service in publishing, revising, and correcting the works of writers—especially ecclesiastical writers. Indeed, the unanimous and constant silence of so many eminent men on a matter of such consequence, men who nowhere make even a passing mention of any history by this Aurelius Victor, compels me, unwilling and reluctant though I am, to suspect either that Victorius’s memory failed him or that he was deceived. This is especially so because Jerome’s words do not permit the inference that Aurelius Victor wrote a history of the persecutions, but only that his history—which treats of the lives of emperors down to Julian—is useful to one who wishes to know the persecutors: that is, those emperors who persecuted the Church of God.

For here *persecutors* must be read, not *persecutions*, as is shown especially by manuscripts 173 and 2789 of the Royal Library, another old manuscript of the same library formerly belonging to the distinguished Claude Puteanus, then manuscript 305 of the Colbertine Library, the first Roman edition of 1468, the Venetian edition of 1488, and the Lyons editions of 1508, 1513, and 1518. Erasmus was the first of all to restore *persecutions*, doubtless on the authority of some ancient exemplar, since manuscript 4110 of the same Colbertine Library also reads thus. Victorius followed him. But from what has thus far been said, it is sufficiently clear that this reading is unsound and that the one presented by the old manuscripts and editions must be retained, since it entails no difficulty. Let us, moreover, give thanks to the immeasurable kindness of God, greatest and best, who has restored to us after so many centuries this book of Lactantius; and let us use it for His greater glory and for the benefit of the holy Church, for whose sake this labour was undertaken.

[Col. 0379]

## TWO LETTERS OF STEPHEN BALUZE, EXPLAINING AND ELUCIDATING TWO PASSAGES FROM LACTANTIUS’S BOOK *ON THE DEATHS OF THE PERSECUTORS*

(A remark by a most learned man upon one of the same passages is prefixed at the beginning.)

## [OPINION]

[Col. 0379A] Opinion of the most illustrious Peter Valerius Diaz, councillor to the King of Spain in the Supreme Council of Aragon, concerning a corrupt passage in Lactantius.

In Lactantius’s book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, which the learned world recently saw restored through the learning and ability of the most illustrious Lord Stephen Baluze, there is a passage especially badly corrupted on p. 43, where we see the following printed (col. 269):

> “Even those who bought, or who shall have acquired by gift, if they shall think something from our benevolence, let them request the Vicar, so that provision may also be made for them through our clemency.”

I judge that this passage must be cleansed by three corrections and written in this form:

> “And now even those who bought, or who shall have acquired by gift, if they should desire something in compensation from our benevolence, let them request it, so that provision may also be made for them through our clemency.”

First, it is sufficiently clear that the Greek τὸ, “the,” represented here by *etiam* (“even”), does not suit this part; by a slight division it must be replaced with *et jam* (“and now”), which has the same force as “then,” “soon,” or “afterwards.” Thus Plautus, in the final scene of the *Truculentus*, said: “Now you are going away after obtaining the gold.” For the emperors’ intention in the proposed edict was that property should be restored to Christians as quickly as possible without any payment, and that afterwards, as they subsequently say, the matter of compensation should be considered, if they desired it.

Second, *putaverint* (“shall have thought”) was introduced by an easy scribal error through interchange and transposition of the letters *o* and *u*. The sense of the expression is entirely sound if one reads *optaverint* (“shall have desired”). For lower down in the same constitution it is said: “let them hope from our benevolence.” These two verbs, “to desire” and “to hope,” frequently occur together; and Cicero, in the twenty-seventh speech *To the Quirites*, said: “Besides, we have attained many things desired from the immortal gods.”

But our principal observation concerns *Vicarium* (“the Vicar”), which Lord Baluze caused to be printed with an initial capital letter, perhaps because he had found it so in the Colbertine manuscript, or, as I think more likely, because he added it himself, judging that the dignity of a Vicar was meant here. He followed the ancient reading and interpretation of Eusebius, which he had seen expressed in their translations both by the earlier translator Christophorson and by the latest—and far more learned and accurate—Henry Valesius. Yet Eusebius was mistaken, if I may say so without offence, and led others into error; Lactantius’s passage reveals this to us. For in this imperial edict, which Lactantius transcribed in Latin as it had been drafted, there is no mention of a governor, a Vicar, or another provincial judge. Rather, *aliquid vicarium* means some compensatory thing: something to be returned by the emperors in the stead and place of that which had been restored to the Christians. This is demonstrated by the following reasons.

For Lactantius expressly said that these imperial letters were addressed to the Governor, not to the Vicar; and their entire tenor is directed to that same person to whom the execution of the restoration was entrusted. It would thus be wholly absurd for the emperors’ words to be directed to some other official exercising jurisdiction in that province.

Now this mode of expression—to desire [Col. 0380A] and request something compensatory (*aliquid vicarium*)—is elegantly used by Latin writers. Indeed, in Holy Scripture we read of rendering something compensatory: Leviticus, chapter XXIV, verse 19: “He who has struck an animal shall render a substitute,” that is, life for life; and below, in verse 21: “He who has struck a beast of burden shall render another.” At this point Cornelius a Lapide, to omit other sacred critics, interprets it as a living animal in place of the animal killed by him. Lorinus says: “A substitute animal means another which supplies the place of the one struck or killed.” He then adds: “I find the translator’s use of the noun *vicarius* only in this passage.”

To the most illustrious and learned Peter Valerius Diaz, royal councillor, Stephen Baluze of Tulle.

From the letter which you sent last year to the illustrious abbot-chamberlain of renowned name, I learned, most illustrious sir, that you are well and that you make mention of me—not unpleasantly nor without advantage. For you speak of me and my studies not only kindly and honourably, but also advise me what in your opinion should be corrected in a certain constitution of Constantine the Great found in Lactantius’s book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*. I embrace both with the reverence and grateful acknowledgment due from me to you, most learned man. I therefore thought it my duty to send you this letter, both to thank you for this favourable disposition toward me and, through this occasion, to enjoy the acquaintance of a man whom the man with whom I passed the better part of my life—the Peter de Marca, Archbishop of Paris, of immortal memory—highly esteemed and was accustomed to compare with Antonio Agustín.

As you see, most illustrious sir, I call you back to the rocks of Brescon, where your association with that great man began. When he was afterwards taken up to heaven, you were deprived of a great friend and I of an excellent patron.

I now come to the passage of Lactantius whose correction you have attempted. It is sufficiently evident that it is obscure and mutilated, namely through the absence of one word. Once that word has been supplied, no difficulty will remain, at least in my judgment. Lactantius’s own words seem sufficiently to indicate what it is; but Eusebius’s Greek translation makes it clearer. From this we infer that the word *poscendum* (“to be requested”), or something similar, must be added here, and that the passage should be read thus:

> “Even those who bought, or who shall have acquired by gift, if they shall think that something is to be requested from our benevolence, let them request the Vicar, so that provision may also be made for them through our clemency.”

This restoration is confirmed by the words of the first law of the Theodosian Code, *On the Office of the Provincial Governor*: “If they shall think that anything is to be requested concerning civil cases.”

But you, most learned man, judge that the text should be read and punctuated thus:

> “And now even those who bought, or who shall have acquired by gift, if they should desire something in compensation from our benevolence, let them request it, so that provision may also be made for them through our clemency.”

Your conjecture is indeed worthy of a learned and erudite man and has much plausibility. For the ancients elegantly spoke of vicarious service, substitute hands, reciprocal love, vicarious punishment, vicarious death, and other such things. Yet your opinion, if you permit me to speak frankly, is not without difficulty. Besides the fact that you do not supply the word missing there and change *putaverint* into *optaverint*, which is not permissible without the clearest necessity, the sense appears to require that the Emperor designate the person to whom the provincials who had been despoiled should present their petitions. Since the Vicar was charged with the entire business of receiving and forwarding petitions, as one reads in the title of the Theodosian Code *On the Office of the Vicar*, Constantine did nothing foreign to that office when he ordered that those who thought they had something to request from his benevolence for the property which they had been compelled to return to the body of Christians should approach the Vicar, so that he might report to the Emperor whatever that thing might be.

But you, most learned man, say that Lactantius expressly stated that these imperial letters were addressed to the Governor, not to the Vicar, and that their whole tenor was directed to the same person to whom execution of the restoration was entrusted; and that it is wholly absurd for the Emperor’s words to be referred to some other official exercising jurisdiction [Col. 0381B] in that province. But here, unless I am mistaken, it should be observed that the Governor’s name was not placed at the head of the constitution, since general edicts were customarily inscribed with the names of the Praetorian Prefects, although it was sent to him by Licinius.

For Licinius, after winning victory over Maximinus with the manifest aid of the divine power, sent those letters to the Governor as soon as he afterwards entered Nicomedia, in order that they might be posted in that city under the Governor’s care, to render thanks to the supreme God. Since the title “Governor” is general and applied to all those who governed the provinces of the Roman Empire, Lactantius seems there to have understood by “Governor” either the Vicar of the Pontic Diocese or the consular governor of Bithynia, which is known to have been under the jurisdiction of that same Vicar. Therefore, since the Vicar of Pontus was the highest magistrate in that region after the Prefect, it seems that his authority was preserved in the edict ordered to be posted in the city of Nicomedia, and consequently that the received reading of this passage in Lactantius should be retained.

I disclose my mind to you, most learned man, and entrust to you my conjectures, readily to embrace whatever opinion you prove true. For some time I have heard of the letters of Antonio Agustín, which rumour had it you were going to publish. There is great reverence and authority among us for that man, and we seize upon his writings most eagerly. Therefore, if that edition has not yet been made, I ask you, most illustrious man, in the name of all who love humane letters, not to prolong our expectation any longer. I do not doubt that among the letters of Latino Latini you have read several addressed to that same Antonio, others speaking of him, and even one from Antonio himself to Latini.

Besides, it must be investigated whether the suspicion of Latini, writing to Metellus, is true: namely, that Antonio’s mind had been alienated from him because, though occasionally writing to him, he had not bestowed upon him the most ample titles of “most illustrious” and “most reverend,” in which the Spaniards greatly delighted. For I have observed [Col. 0381D] that Agustín despised vanities; accordingly, I suspect there were other reasons why he interrupted the correspondence which he had with Latini. I leave the whole matter to your judgment, most learned man, and wish you a long and prosperous life.

Paris, on the Kalends of May, 1683.

To the distinguished Henry Noris, Augustinian, Stephen Baluze of Tulle sends greetings.

Two years ago, when our most learned friend Antonio Magliabechi, a man most devoted to you, to me, and to our shared studies, sent me your work, most learned man, in which you elucidated the Pisan cenotaphs of Gaius and Lucius Caesar, I had resolved to write to you concerning a controversy which I see has arisen between us over certain obscure words of the jurist Paulus. I intended, however, to leave the whole matter to your judgment. But because at that time I was much occupied with publishing the first volume of my *Councils*, and consequently suffered from a lack of leisure, I was compelled to abandon that plan, or at least defer it to another time.

Meanwhile that great patron and supporter of my studies, Jean-Baptiste Colbert, departed this life. With his fall, I confess, my mind was so cast down and shattered by grief that, although I sought refuge and consolation in my books, I thought of nothing less than offering the appearance of a playful contest; and so I lost even the memory of our controversy, which I mentioned just now.

It was recalled by letters which that friend of ours sent me on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February this year, and which I received rather late, namely on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of April. For by mentioning in them a new work published by you, which he promises to send, he revived the memory of the Pisan cenotaphs [Col. 0382B] and of your dispute with me. At last, therefore, I come forward as the advocate, such as I am, of what I believe to be a good cause, most learned man, to plead it before you—I mean, to have as judge the man whom I have previously experienced as an adversary. Nor need I fear under such a judge, who, besides being my friend and just and steadfast in what is right, will with the utmost fairness of mind sustain three roles in one, as Cicero said of himself: his own, that of adversary, and that of judge.

These, then, are the words of Paulus in the editions commonly published by printers, now in learned men’s hands:

> “A child under one year is lost who dies on the last day of the year. And customary speech shows that this is so: ‘before the tenth day of the Kalends,’ ‘after the tenth day of the Kalends.’ For by neither expression are eleven days denoted.”

I interpreted this passage in my annotations on Lactantius’s book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* as meaning that the same day is denoted by the two modes of speech adduced by the jurist. You, on the contrary, most distinguished man, think that the former expression should mean the ten days preceding the Kalends, while the latter means the ten days following the same Kalends—that is, the tenth day of the following month. Although Rebuffus wrote that this question involves more subtlety than usefulness, and Budé and Alciati thought that Paulus intended rather to amuse and detain the reader with this riddle than to teach him, so that it may seem pointless to investigate further the true sense of those words, I shall nevertheless endeavour, according to the measure of my powers, to show what the jurist meant and at the same time confirm my opinion about Lactantius’s words.

In antiquity there were two versions of Paulus’s words, in which the whole difficulty lies and which have tormented learned men. Some manuscripts have: “For in either expression the eleventh day is equally denoted”; others, by contrast: “For in neither expression is the eleventh day denoted.” The former version, embraced by Paul of Middelburg, Valla, Budé, Alciati, Rebuffus, and Denis Godefroy, rests upon the authority of old manuscript exemplars—one in the Royal Library and the rest in the Colbertine Library. The manuscript of Germain Colladon, cited by Godefroy himself, also agrees with them. The latter version, which Cujas, Antonio Agustín, Marcellus Francolinus, and Denis Petau preferred to follow, has in its support two old books of the Royal Library, one of which formerly belonged to the most learned Aymar Ranconet; nor have I found it elsewhere. Whether the authority of the Florentine Pandects supports it, we shall see later. For the moment, let us examine both versions, affirmative and negative, as some have called them.

The affirmative version is found, as I have said, in eight old exemplars of the Royal and Colbertine Libraries. In the Royal manuscript marked 4673, the reading is: “For in either expression the eleventh day is equally denoted.” Colbertine manuscripts [Col. 0383A] 524, 529, and 2608 read: “For in both expressions the eleventh day is equally denoted.” Manuscript 743 reads: “In both expressions the eleventh day is denoted.” Manuscripts 397 and 461 read: “For in either expression the eleventh day is denoted.” Finally, manuscript 583 reads: “In either expression 11 days are denoted.” By contrast, Royal manuscript 4672 reads: “For in neither expression is the eleventh day denoted.” In the manuscript formerly belonging to Aymar Ranconet: “For in neither expression is the eleventh day denoted.” It should be noted that above the line in this last manuscript was anciently written: “Elsewhere *utro* is read for *neutro*.” This reading more closely approaches that presented by the Florentine manuscript, in which, as you yourself testify, the reading is: “For by neither expression are eleven days denoted.”

We must now investigate whether that reading of your manuscript is sound, and whether it supports the negative version, as some think, or should rather be restored to the reading preferred by so many old exemplars. At first sight, that manuscript of yours, unquestionably the most ancient now extant, appears to show that the eleventh day before the Kalends is denoted by neither of these modes of speech—as is likewise written in the Royal manuscripts, and as Antonio Agustín says he read in yours—and must therefore be judged to confirm the reading called negative.

But if we consider the entirely true observation made by the most learned Nicolas Rigault in his notes on Tertullian, that utterly false readings are sometimes maintained by the authority of ancient books, and if we set against it the agreement of so many old manuscripts favouring the affirmative reading, we shall rightly and properly hesitate whether to rely on your exemplar or embrace the reading presented by the remaining manuscripts, which cannot be denied to have been drawn from older exemplars. Nor perhaps would he be mistaken who thought that *neque* (“neither”) was written in your manuscript by error for *aeque* (“equally”). Thus, in the fragment of St Ambrose reported in the acts of the First Synod of Ephesus, Colbertine manuscripts 1363 and 1600, together with very ancient exemplars of the old Latin translation of that same synod, have “Not the letter itself,” in place of what is read in editions of St Ambrose’s works, “This very letter,” and in Marius Mercator and the Contian edition of the same synod, “And the letter itself”—as I recently noted while revising that same ancient translation.

Moreover, who could bring himself to believe that Paulus, a serious jurist, wished to employ a negation in order to establish a point that most needed affirmative proof? For it had to be proved that someone who dies on the final day of the year should be counted as a child under one year old, whether that day has begun or has ended. Therefore, wishing to demonstrate this by analogy, the jurist says that just as the same day is denoted whether one says “before the tenth day of the Kalends” or “after the tenth day of the Kalends”—that is, whether before the day is completed or after it is completed—so also one who dies on the final day of the year must be counted as under one year old, whether that day is completed [Col. 0383D] or not completed.

Further, when learned men interpreted the words “before the tenth day of the Kalends” as meaning something done before the tenth day was completed and ended, they gave us grounds to interpret “after the tenth day of the Kalends” as referring to the tenth day before the Kalends itself, yet after it had passed and ended. Since these two modes of speech were used interchangeably and without distinction by the people, custom brought it about that the same day was understood by either expression: whatever was done within the twenty-four hours of day and night was regarded as though done at any hour of daylight. So teaches Paulus himself in book XIII *To Sabinus*: “By Roman custom,” he says, “the day begins at midnight and ends at the middle of the following night. Thus whatever is done in these twenty-four hours—that is, in the two half-nights and the intervening daylight—is as though done at any hour of daylight.”

Censorinus confirms this, chapter 23; I transcribe his words:

> “The Romans considered a day to extend from midnight to midnight. The public sacred rites and also the magistrates’ auspices furnish evidence: if anything is done before midnight, it is assigned to the day which has passed; but if anything is done after midnight and before dawn, it is said to have been done on the day following that night. The same point is shown by the fact that those who are born between midnight and the next midnight, during these twenty-four hours, have the same birthday.”

It seems to me that one may infer from this that, although the Romans began the day at midnight, in ordinary speech they nevertheless called “day” that interval which lies between sunrise and sunset, that is, the natural day; and what was done very early in the morning, or before daylight, they called, as Joseph Scaliger previously observed, “before the Kalends,” whereas what was done after sunset they called “after the Kalends.” But subsequently the same time was gradually denoted by both forms of expression, because the populace—in whose hands lie the judgment, right, and norm of speech—did not attend to the distinction [Col. 0384B] formerly made in this manner between a day beginning and a day completed.

Thus Cicero, writing to Tiro—a passage which, most learned sir, you have adduced in support of your opinion—says that on the Nones of November he was at Alyzia and, setting out from there before daylight, sent this letter “on the eighth day before the Ides of November” (Cicero, *Letters to Friends*, book XVI, letter 3). Although this can be understood of any hour of the day, it is more natural to interpret it of the day beginning, since Cicero writes that he sent the letter as he was departing from Alyzia, which was before daylight. In the same way Seneca reports that the emperor Claudius, who, he says, began to expire when the sun was hastening toward its setting, between the sixth and seventh hour, died “on the third day before the Ides of October”; whereas Suetonius writes that he expired near daylight, that is, at the beginning of the natural day. This may also be confirmed from Tacitus’s words: after explaining that Claudius’s death had been concealed for some time, he adds that Nero emerged before the cohort in the middle [Col. 0384C] of that same day.

Therefore, to return to the point from which we digressed: when the ancients said, “before the tenth day of the Kalends” or “after the tenth day of the Kalends,” they intended by both expressions the tenth day of the Kalends, the Kalends themselves being included in the count. The most learned fellow-countryman of mine, Simeon Bosius, also derived this interpretation from the reading of your manuscript; in his notes on the first of Cicero’s letters to Atticus, he says that by either manner of speaking the tenth day of the Kalends themselves is meant.

Cujacius, on the contrary (*Digest*, book XIII, *On Verbal Obligations*), holds indeed that the tenth day is denoted in both expressions, but interprets “the tenth day which is called after the Kalends” as the tenth day of the month following the Kalends. To speak frankly, Cujacius has in agreement with him an old interlinear gloss in manuscript 524 of the Colbert Library: above the words “before the tenth day of the Kalends” is written, “namely, preceding the Kalends”; and above the words “after [Col. 0384D] the tenth day of the Kalends” is likewise written, “namely, following the Kalends.” Yet both this ancient glossator and Cujacius himself, and others, were driven to that interpretation by the obscurity of this passage, being without a parallel example such as is found in Lactantius. Had they possessed that example from Lactantius and considered attentively that it was not Roman usage to attach the days following the Kalends to the Kalends, but rather to the Nones or Ides, they would never have twisted Paul’s words into that sense.

For if it were permissible to interpret the ancients in this way merely by conjecture, without any example or authority, I should prefer to say either that Paul believed the eleventh day of the Kalends to be meant by both forms of expression—as most old copies read—or that the copyist who first recopied this passage, from whom the others received it, mistakenly wrote “eleventh” for “tenth,” rather than force readers into that interpretation [Col. 0385A] which all earlier antiquity opposes. For in obscure matters, as the same Paul teaches, one ordinarily considers what is more probable, or what generally occurs.

I know that you are accustomed to rely upon a passage of Cicero—or rather of M. Caelius writing to Cicero—from which you infer that he divided times into before and after the Kalends, because he reports Pompey as saying that before the Kalends of March he could not decide about Caesar’s provinces without injustice, but that after the Kalends of March he would not hesitate (*Letters to Friends*, book VIII, letter 8). Yet that passage concerns an undetermined and indefinite time; it does not in any way assist your opinion, nor does it weaken that which I maintain. For no one denies that one may very properly say that something cannot be done before the Kalends but can be done after the Kalends. But this does not prove that the days following the Kalends were customarily connected with the Kalends, so that, for example, events occurring on the fourth day before the Ides of January could also be said to have occurred after the tenth day before the Kalends of January.

[Col. 0385B] But Plutarch, in his *Life of Cicero*, says that Cicero was born on “the third day of the new Kalends” (*hēmerā tritē tōn neōn Kalandōn*), and Franciscus Fabricius translates this as “after the third day of the Kalends of January,” since Cicero himself and Aulus Gellius establish that he was born on the third day before the Nones of that month. Therefore, the third day before the Nones is also the third day of the Kalends. I grant that the third day before the Nones is the same as the third day after the Kalends. But although Fabricius interpreted Plutarch’s passage in this way, saying that Cicero was born after the third day of the Kalends of January, this does not harm our case. For Fabricius has no authority from antiquity and therefore carries no weight in showing that days following the Kalends were customarily joined to the Kalends in the reckoning of days. Plutarch, a Greek, spoke in Greek fashion; Cicero and Gellius in Latin fashion. I prefer to follow Cicero writing in Latin concerning himself, rather than Plutarch speaking in Greek concerning Cicero.

Indeed, Plutarch’s very words do not much favor your opinion, since nothing else can be inferred from them [Col. 0385C] than that Cicero was born on the third day of the new Kalends, which had begun—or rather ended—on the first day of January.

The authority of the jurist Gaius is also raised against us. His words are: “After the Kalends of January, on the third day, vows are undertaken for the emperor’s welfare.” You rightly observe that this expression means the third day before the Nones of January. But I have already answered this objection in the discussion concerning Cicero’s birthday; moreover, it is certain that Gaius’s words do not concern our controversy. For he does not say, “after the third day of the Kalends of January,” as he would have had to say in order to support your opinion; rather, he says, “after the Kalends of January, on the third day.” This we freely concede to be true.

Before I put an end to this discussion of mine, I see that I must return to the final part of Paul’s passage, which I know well may be objected against me even after all that I have said thus far. For even if [Col. 0385D] you grant me that one and the same day is indicated by these two expressions, “before the tenth day of the Kalends” and “after the tenth [Col. 0386A] day of the Kalends,” it will nevertheless always remain true that neither of them means the eleventh day of the Kalends; and from this you will infer that the reading called negative is more correct.

I admit that this difficulty is great and cannot easily be answered. Yet, because it does no harm to our case but rather seems to confirm it, I have no intention of pursuing it further. If we accept the negative reading as true, I think Paul’s words should be understood as though he meant to say that one may infer from this that by these two expressions the tenth day of the Kalends is meant, according to the Roman custom of reckoning, because neither expression signifies the eleventh. Thus the negative proposition will be converted into an affirmative one.

I have shown sufficiently, I think, what is the sounder explanation of Paul’s words, which have exercised very learned men. To strengthen my proofs, I shall also bring forward Lactantius’s authority. Just as I formerly used Paul’s testimony to show [Col. 0386B] that the discrepancy in Lactantius’s words entails no contradiction, so now I shall use Lactantius’s words to prove that Paul’s words contain no contradiction. For since their manner of expression is altogether alike and similar, it is clear that they shed light upon one another, and that what is obscure in one may be made clearer with the help of the other.

Lactantius says, then, in book IV, chapter 10, of the *Divine Institutes*, that Christ was fastened to the cross by the Jews “before the tenth day of the Kalends of April”; but in the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* he says that Christ was tortured by the same Jews “after the tenth day of the Kalends of April.” You, most distinguished sir, judge these expressions to differ in meaning: the former, you hold, should mean 23 March, and the latter 10 April. But I ask you whether it is probable that Lactantius, a learned and educated man, wrote things contrary and contradictory to himself—especially since in his age it was commonly believed that Christ suffered on the tenth day before the Kalends [Col. 0386C] of April, while no one up to that point had written that he suffered on 10 April.

I do not think anyone can resist this argument, since it is most strong and cogent. Accordingly, I believe one may safely affirm that Lactantius intended to express precisely the same thing by these two forms of speech: namely, that Christ was fastened to the cross on the twenty-third day of March. If this is so—as certainly it is—it is now established that Paul’s words also must bear one and the same meaning, and that both the former and latter expression must mean the tenth day preceding the Kalends, in no way the tenth day following the Kalends.

These things, most learned sir, I have set forth before you in defense of my opinion with all the brevity I could. Henceforth, as I said at the beginning, it will be for your judgment to determine what should be thought about the whole matter. In your kindness, bring me back to the road by showing me what is truer, if perhaps you discover that I have passed beyond the boundary of truth. Meanwhile, farewell; and continue to esteem me as one most devoted to your name [Col. 0386D].

Paris, 10 April 1684.

[NOTES OF JOHANNES COLUMBUS ON THE BOOK *ON THE DEATHS OF THE PERSECUTORS*]

[Col. 0385]

NOTES OF JOHANNES COLUMBUS ON LACTANTIUS

Johannes Columbus sends greetings and every good wish to the most illustrious and eminent Lord Gisbert Cuper, delegate of the Estates of Overijssel (Transisalania) to the assembly of the most illustrious and mighty States General of the United Netherlands, and consul of the renowned republic of Deventer.
