Although I rejoice that my own country also produces great and illustrious minds which love humane letters, receive them with exceptional generosity, and in many ways foster and adorn even my own efforts, I should nevertheless say that this little work, of its own accord, was eager to fly away from this soil, across the sea, into your embrace, most eminent sir—or rather, to return there. Certainly, unless I had first sent to you this whatever-it-is, and had ensured that its very frontispiece bore your [Col. 0387A] most illustrious name, I should have thought it scarcely possible to escape several serious charges.

For either I should be a plagiarist, laying hands upon a body owed to you; or I should in some fashion be liable for peculation, even akin to the crime of a *quadruplator* (a common informer entitled to a share), if I diverted into a private title so many excellent things of yours intended for public use. Nor could I have avoided the mark of ingratitude, equally hateful and detestable to all good people, unless I acknowledged that this advance of mine was received from you, from your labor and aid.

My plan for publication was not yet sufficiently settled and fixed when you, now praising this work of Lactantius, now approving my emendations, now correcting them and bringing them back to the right path, and finally sharing your own observations—which by themselves alone would add considerable value to my edition—brought it about that I persisted in my undertaking. And this you did for my sake amid the greatest cares and affairs, upon which the safety of peoples depends and by which the duties of your most important office generally occupy you. Finally, by your customary generosity you secured that a copy of the British edition, long but vainly awaited from our booksellers, should be delivered to me by the public post.

It is therefore no wonder if I resolved to send these efforts of mine—indeed, yours, and far more successful ones—to no one before you, together with the whole little work. It was also right and proper that readers should know from the very threshold to whom they would be indebted for each thing. If, however, the edition itself does not satisfy your refinement, I ask you to pardon my absence; because of it I further fear that some materials sent too late have been deferred to another time. Yet there remains some hope that the time will soon come when it will be permissible to bring those things also into the light. Certainly, as long as I live, with God’s good help, I shall labor to make known and attest that none of the materials which your great kindness deigned to share with me has perished through any fault of mine. Farewell, distinguished sir, and judge my efforts kindly. Written at Uppsala, the day before the Kalends of July, 1684.

[Col. 0387C] TO THE BENEVOLENT READER, GREETINGS

From the time when a distinguished man did not hesitate to point out to me, among books then being brought before the public, this little work, which seemed undoubtedly to bear Lactantius’s name as author, I confess that I burned with no slight desire to know it more deeply. When at last I obtained it together with the other volumes published by the celebrated Baluzius, the work did not seem to fall short of expectation, nor did its composition appear alien to that lucid and polished thread of Lactantian style. Many other features, above all the unusual nature of its material and either its trustworthy agreement with other accounts or, at times, even its less suspicious divergences from them, lent some credibility to the claim that no empty commodity was being sold under so great a name.

I also thought I had found this genre employed among the ancients: in the three books of C. Fannius, in which he narrated the ends of those killed or exiled by Nero, books which Pliny the Younger, *Letters*, book V, letter 5, calls subtle, diligent, and Latin, and intermediate between dialogue and history. Trebellius Pollio also seems to have followed this genre: he says, with sufficient modesty, that he had written several books in a style neither historical nor eloquent, but plain. I further recognized certain things derived from biblical books, especially from Second Maccabees—which I believe was fabricated after Christ’s time, in times of persecution; for its reliability in historical matters has long been questioned by learned persons—and likewise from blessed Cyprian and other Fathers. According to my ability, I have tried to indicate these matters here and there.

Concerning this same little work, which blessed Jerome designates by the simple title *On Persecution*, as he also mentions Tertullian’s book, which Tertullian himself more fully entitles *On Flight in Persecution*, I shall, God willing, speak more extensively some day—especially if resources hitherto sought in vain come into my hands, such as the little work of John of Salisbury on the same subject. John himself says in *Polycraticus*, or *The Trifles of Courtiers*, book VIII, chapter 20, p. 648: “What can the little book entitled *On the End of Tyrants* more fully disclose, though in concise compass, concerning its view of tyrants?” But whether that little book survives, I confess I do not know with sufficient certainty. If it does survive, I hope that some light will thereby be added to the present work.

I further confess that, while collating this work with Lactantius’s writings already long published, I encountered rather many points that seemed to agree. Of these, I placed beside the relevant and very similar passages those which could be extracted with less labor and placed them beside passages which, if I judge rightly, were fitting and very similar, so that this little grove of parallels might be available either to those wishing to form a judgment from comparison or to assist young people pursuing, together with memorable subject matter, traces of purer diction everywhere. Yet I cannot conceal that the old refrain of Epimachus kept ringing again and again in my ears: “Be sober and remember to distrust” (*Nēphe kai memnēs’ apistein*).

Above all I wished that the celebrated Baluzius had informed me more concerning the manuscript that alone preserves this treasure—especially where it had previously lain hidden, and from the cabinet of what person or institution it had passed into the library of the most illustrious Colbert. Other thoughts also came to mind, tending much in this direction: perhaps this resemblance to Lactantius’s style had been laboriously drawn; perhaps those remarkable arrays of facts had been composed as a kind of stage-set for winning applause. In the manuscript itself some things appeared artificially dirtied, gnawed, and perforated—everything designed to counterfeit the appearance of antiquity. Long ago, the ambition of persons with excessive leisure had produced similar fabrications: people eager either to imitate other men’s minds and abilities or, under their names, to play upon others’ credulity.

Yet I admit that these and other thoughts of this sort were nearly overcome by the evidence favoring the opposite side. I saw the integrity and candor of the celebrated Baluzius, no less than his learning, praised by men of keen discernment. I then found men of uncommon distinction more inclined to think that such tricks were less likely to have been played here. The exceptional quality of certain information not casually discoverable elsewhere—of some matters I speak—and other evidence of no slight weight also counted for much. Supported and encouraged by these considerations, I persisted in my undertaking, and also wished to offer something to those who put the removal of stains of antiquity and similar matters almost on the same level as attention to hangnails and nail-parings.

But, hastened too quickly, after the letters of the most illustrious Lord Cuper arrived, and finally the Oxford edition also, trusting that at least a few persons more acquainted with these matters would not reject critical skirmishes, I completed what you see here. Enjoy it, if you please, my reader; but expect greater and more exact things from those to whom it has been granted to restore and reform the now declining study of letters with greater success. Among these you have the most celebrated Graevius, whose promised emendations of this little work I await eagerly, almost impatiently.

In the aforementioned British edition I do not so much regret that certain matters were anticipated from Lord Cuper’s conjectures and mine as rejoice that, through the concurrence of great men’s studies, strength and credibility accrue even to these conjectures and authority to the work itself. I have no time now to extract those emendations; I hope this will be done shortly, and I shall share them more fully in another pamphlet. But lest young people absorb any error from these pages, whenever this author inveighs too vehemently against the pursuit of arms and military service—which was necessary in Diocletian’s case—let them remember that Lactantius elsewhere, in a most serious error, condemns wars among Christians altogether. See book VI, chapter 20, p. 648. Who, then, would wish to follow him as a guide in so absurd a matter? But perhaps I shall discuss these points more fully elsewhere. Meanwhile, farewell, my reader; and grant me, if anywhere I have erred, the pardon which you yourself expect from others.

TESTIMONIES AND SOME JUDGMENTS CONCERNING THIS BOOK

Jerome, in the *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*:

“Among Lactantius’s other works, he mentions one book *On Persecution*.”

Freculphus, [Col. 0389A] Honorius of Autun, Abbot Trithemius, and others follow Jerome.

From a letter of Nicolaus Heinsius, written from Vienne to Lecca, 20 January 1680, to J. C. at Uppsala:

> “I have recently received from France several books by no means contemptible, among them a most elegant little book of Lactantius on the dreadful and violent end of those Roman emperors who, from Nero’s reign to his own times, had persecuted Christians. The celebrated Baluzius first published it by inserting it in a volume of his *Miscellanies*.”

From a letter of Gisbert Cuper to Constantijn Huygens, secretary to the most exalted and serene Prince of Orange, dated 30 December 1682:

> “That book of Lactantius is very elegant; and because its novelty and the variety of its very famous matters pleased me wonderfully, I began to examine various passages more carefully, etc.”

The same man, in a letter to J. C., written at The Hague, 3 October of the same year:

[Col. 0389B]

> “You are right to consider publishing Lactantius, for his little book is worthy even of being read by young people, that from an early age they may see that Christ, God thrice best and thrice greatest, truly is Savior, Defender, Champion, Protector, and Preserver—titles wrongly given to the fictitious gods of the Gentiles—of the Church which he redeemed by his blood.”

Stephanus Baluzius, in the preface to the second book of his *Miscellanies*:

> “We offer you, reader, the second book of our *Miscellanies*, in which the first and deserved place belongs to Lactantius’s book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, now published for the first time from a very ancient manuscript of the Colbert Library. At present it is unnecessary to say more about the excellence of this book, since our notes upon it have sufficiently addressed this matter.”

The same, at the beginning of the notes:

> “Among the numerous and varied manuscripts which Jean-Baptiste Colbert, a man most devoted to letters and men of letters and most outstanding in every kind of distinction, collected from all Europe, Asia, and Africa for the public benefit of learning, one was found worth its weight in gold, containing the book of Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius *On Persecution*, etc.”

Ludovicus Moreri, in the *Historical Lexicon*, published in French at Lyons in 1681:

> “M. Baluze published in the second volume of his *Miscellanies* a treatise of Lactantius that we had lost. It is the book addressed to Donatus the Confessor, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*. He added very fine notes of his own.”

Antonius Pagi, in the *Hypatic Dissertation, or On Imperial Consuls*, repeatedly calls upon this book’s testimony, and nowhere doubts that it is Lactantius’s.

From the preface to the reader in the Oxford edition:

> “We present, that is, our Lactantius’s book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, worth its weight in gold, which, having been desired for more than a thousand years, we have very recently recovered through the efforts of the most learned Baluzius. And, badly mutilated and frequently gaping with lacunae as it was, we have from time to time restored it partly from our own conjectures and partly from those of the most learned men, the bishop of St Asaph and Isaac Vossius, etc.”

[Col. 0389]

NOTES OF JOHANNES COLUMBUS ON THE BOOK *ON THE DEATHS OF THE PERSECUTORS*

[Col. 0389]

ON THE TITLE

[Col. 0389C]

“L. Caecilius Lactantius Firmianus.” Here, as in most other respects, I have followed the Paris edition, in which the author is called not L. Caelius, as in his works previously published, but L. Caecilius Lactantius Firmianus. This was changed by the celebrated Baluzius on the authority of that ancient manuscript of the Colbert Library which preserved this work for us; it bears this title: “The book of Lucius Caecilius to Donatus the Confessor begins, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*.” Another manuscript of the same library supports this, containing the other surviving works of Lactantius, where he is likewise called L. Caecilius Lactantius Firmianus.

“To Donatus the Confessor.” The book *On the Wrath of God*, highly praised by blessed Jerome, is likewise addressed to him. But which Donatus this was among the great multitude of persons mentioned by that name among ancient writers is difficult to say. Yet since below, in chapters 16 and 35, he is said to have suffered nine times various tortures and torments for the sake of heavenly truth, and also to have been held in prison for six years without being overcome, it is clear that Baluzius rightly celebrates him with the praise of an illustrious confessor of those times.

For in that period “confessors” were called martyrs “designate,” as Tertullian calls them: persons grievously afflicted in various ways who persevered courageously in confessing Christ’s name but had not yet been taken to death. Thus blessed Cyprian, letter 52 to Antonianus: “With the presbyter Moses subscribing, at that time still a confessor, now also a martyr.” Today, adherents of the Roman pontiff call “confessors” persons not agitated by any storms of persecution, but nevertheless conspicuous above other mortals for holiness of life, as they themselves maintain.

“On the Deaths of the Persecutors.” Vossius, *On Analogy*, book I, chapter 40, and Baluzius at the beginning of his notes on this book, have shown with many examples that the plural *mortes* (“deaths”) was commonly used by Cicero and other writers of the best standing. Not a few more examples could be added if needed, such as this from Prudentius, *On the Crowns*, hymn V:

> No force exerted through  
> So many deaths of guilty men  
> Prevails in this contest;  
> Even the art of inflicting pain is defeated.

And indeed Lactantius, book VII, chapter 10: “For just as two lives are set before a human being, one of the soul and the other of the body, so two deaths are set before him.”

ON CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0390D] “The Lord heard your prayers.” I suppose this alludes to 2 Maccabees 1:5: “May he hear your prayers and be reconciled to you.”

“For the merits of his faith.” Johannes Vorstius, on Sulpicius Severus’s *Sacred History*—a work of Sulpicius which young people read regularly, rightly, and profitably—book I, chapter 23, on the words “by the merit of faith he averted the night,” notes:

> “Wherever the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews says *pistei*, ‘by faith,’ or *dia pisteōs*, ‘through faith,’ our author says *merito fidei*, ‘by the merit of faith.’ And *merito* is almost superfluous, as in chapter 12: ‘By the merit of the blessing he had preferred the greater to the lesser,’ that is, ‘by the blessing’ or ‘through the blessing.’”

See also his notes on chapter 47. Sulpicius likewise uses *fidei merito* in *Dialogue* II, chapter 11. For *mereri* is often used in the sense of attaining, obtaining, or receiving by lot, so that it denotes an outcome rather than a right and worthiness—or an outcome as well as, not merely, right and worthiness—according to the great Gronovius, *Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 7, p. 76, where see what he adduces from Plautus, Terence, Cicero, and others. Thus in prayers of the ancient Church: “That, through his coming, we may be granted to serve you with minds purified.” Nothing is more frequent in writings of these times.

“An avenger shall be added to all these.” An avenger is set against the pagans, who had previously seemed to rage against Christ’s flock with impunity, in order to restrain them. Thus Virgil, *Georgics* II:

> Shall I recall the harbors and the barriers added to Lake Lucrinus?

And *Aeneid* VI, in the Sibyl’s words:

> Nor shall Juno, joined against the Trojans,  
> Be absent anywhere.

[Col. 0391B] See Servius there, and especially Macrobius, *Saturnalia* VI.4.

“Recently overthrown.” Thus Lactantius, *Institutes* V.2: “For when the professor of wisdom, Epicurus, strove to overthrow wisdom.” Chapter 4: “That I might overthrow in one attack all those who everywhere accomplish the same work.” The same word must be retained in Lactantius, book VI, chapter 23: “He plunged souls born for holiness as though into a whirlpool of filth, extinguished shame, and ruined chastity.” Thus several manuscripts, both handwritten and printed, according to Servatius Gallaeus; his edition, however, reads *flagitavit*; he himself preferred *flagitiavit*. Neither of these can there be supported by sufficiently firm arguments. For the proper use of this word, young people should consult Gellius, book VI, chapter 23.

“Now, appeased, the God of his servants …” The word *precibus* (“by prayers”), or another similar word, seems to have fallen out. If restored, the sentence will be fuller and much more elegant. Thus *On the Wrath of God*, chapter 21: “God is appeased not by incense, not by sacrifice, not by costly gifts, but by the amendment of character.” Sulpicius Severus says that the Lord, appeased by Moses’s prayers, turned aside the calamity. Yet 2 Maccabees 1:2 introduces some uncertainty. I know well what standing that book has among learned people; nevertheless, Christians in times of persecution seem to have read it continually because of the suitability of its subject. It will become sufficiently clear below that the author of this work echoed certain words from it in several places.

The sequence of the words is more obscure; but I think they should nevertheless be joined so that God is called “the God of his faithful servants,” just as in the sacred Scriptures God is very frequently called the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Examine it, please, and decide for yourself, my reader, which reading you think should be chosen.

“God had deferred their punishments.” Gregory of Nazianzus speaks forcefully on a similar subject, *Invective* III against Julian:

> “At first, while God still endured and deferred his anger on our behalf, and had not yet kindled all his zeal, but still held his hand high against the impious and had bent and made ready the bow—yet restrained it forcibly—and, like some hidden and malignant disease, waited for wickedness first to discharge all its evil. Such is the law of God’s judgment: either that it may save by repentance, or punish more justly.”

But to set forth this doctrine from the divine Scriptures and their faithful interpreters, ancient or modern, is not my purpose. Apart from those sources, from which it ought chiefly to be drawn, neither should one wholly despise the utterances of those outside the faith (*hoi exō*) who spoke under the guidance of the law of conscience given to them, or who were taught by others. Such is Andromache’s question to Menelaus in Euripides:

> “Do you not believe in divine things, nor think that justice exists?”

Likewise the chorus in another tragedy by the same poet:

> “Though far away, yet nevertheless the heavenly ones,  
> Dwelling in heaven, care for mortal affairs.”

How outstanding also are these lines from his *Antiope*, preserved for us by Stobaeus:

> “Justice indeed is slow;  
> Yet even so, when she falls upon … [the text is fragmentary]  
> You do not notice when she has you,  
> Whatever impious mortal you may be.”

That is, in the translation of the distinguished Grotius:

> Though justice comes late,  
> Yet it is justice, imposing  
> Upon the impious the penalties  
> They deserve; it lies in wait as from ambush.

Here *Dikē*, or Justice, denotes the goddess of the pagans; she is the same as Astraea, Themis, Erigone, Nemesis, and Adrastia, or at least not very different. On her Samuel Bochart, a man of uncommon and truly abundant learning, writes at length in *Hierozoicon*, part II, book V, chapter 2. There he examines and elucidates learnedly and skilfully the rash judgment of the Maltese concerning St Paul: “Justice does not permit him to live” (Acts 28:4).

Since many more utterances of this sort occur here and elsewhere throughout Euripides, both in dialogue and in choruses, where the poet commonly speaks in his own person, it may seem surprising, not without reason, that Plutarch and perhaps Sextus Empiricus should not hesitate, in verses transmitted to us in a better text by the most learned Petrus Petitus, to attribute to Euripides himself the impious and sacrilegious opinion uttered in the person of Sisyphus, although he was so diligent and skilled an investigator of human affairs. But it is unnecessary to inquire more deeply into these matters now.

In any event, that everlasting power of justice watches—watches the perpetual eye, judge and avenger of events; sometimes late, but a scrupulous examiner of what has been done rightly or wrongly, as Ammianus Marcellinus more or less says. Yet by however slow a step it advances to avenge itself, it compensates the delay of punishment by its severity, as Valerius Maximus has it. The theologians treat this subject more clearly and at greater length. But neither should the writings of outsiders on this topic be wholly disregarded, especially those of Seneca and Plutarch, nor the things various authors have collected to the same effect: Erasmus, *Adages*, “The gods have woolen feet”; “God finds out the guilty man”; Mornay, *On the Truth of the Christian Religion*, chapters 12 and 24; Lipsius, *On Constancy*, book II, chapters 13–15; Barthius, *Adversaria*, p. 2907; Christoph. Ad. Rupertus on Valerius Maximus, p. 31; etc.

“Concerning whose end.” The missing words may perhaps be supplied thus, says the most eminent Cuper: “Concerning whose end of empires it pleased [the subject is lost in the source] to bear witness, so that all who were removed afar off, or who should come after us, might know to what extent God most high displayed his power and majesty in destroying and annihilating the enemies of his name.” The same scholar, shortly afterward: “Authors … Perhaps ‘of such great crimes,’ or ‘of the persecution,’ has fallen out.”

I agree with the most eminent man in the rest; but instead of *imperiorum* (“of empires”), which he supplies, I think “of cruel rulers” or “of tyrants” would be more suitable. John of Salisbury likewise later published a book *On the End of Tyrants*; and the distinguished Nicolaus Heinsius seems, from the words quoted above, to have called the present little work, and perhaps thought it should be called, not very differently.

I admit, too, that I formerly understood the following words differently. By “those removed afar off” (*moti procul*), I understood those removed or separated far from the truth, as similar words are commonly rendered in the Psalms; likewise Christians called “lapsed” those who failed in those most severe contests of persecution and either returned altogether to paganism or committed a single offense by casting incense upon an idol’s altar. If any weight is to be given to this conjecture, the whole passage should be established as follows: “It pleased [the subject is lost in the source] to bear witness concerning the end of the most savage rulers, so that all who had been removed afar off, or who should later go astray, might know to what extent God most high displayed his power and majesty in destroying and annihilating the enemies of his name.”

Moreover, the discussion will proceed rightly and in order if, from the beginning, [the missing continuation is not recoverable from the supplied text] who were the authors of the persecution and by what punishments, etc.

“Who were the authors.” Both the logic of the syntax and the following verb *vindicaverit* show that Lactantius wrote *qui fuerint auctores* (“who may have been the authors”), not *qui fuerunt* (“who were the authors”).

[Col. 0393A] “May have exacted vengeance upon them.” Lactantius, book II, chapter 4: “But they themselves too often exacted vengeance upon the sacrilegious.” Similarly, the same author in chapter 4 of that book and book IV, chapter 17; likewise Hegesippus—or Ambrose, if, as a certain great man seems rightly to have concluded, that is he—or someone else; also the Latin ecclesiastical Fathers, Vegetius, Gellius, Julius Capitolinus, and others frequently.

ON CHAPTER II

“Was tortured.” Labbaeus’s glosses: “He tortures and crucifies,” *stauroî*. Lactantius, *Institutes* I.16: “He was subjected by men to an infamous punishment and tortured.” And shortly afterward: “They formed an impious plan to remove and torture him.” Chapter 18: “And they tortured him in great humiliation.” Chapter 21: “He will cease to wonder that God was tortured by men.”

After the tenth day before the Kalends of April. An elliptical expression, which may be supplied as: “after the tenth day before the Kalends of April had dawned,” or “after that day had begun.” Thus Christ’s words, μετὰ τρεῖς ἡμέρας ἐγείρομαι, “after three days I rise,” are explained by most learned men as “after the third day has arrived.” So in Mark, chapter II, verse 2, “after six days” means “when the sixth day had begun.” On this and more besides, after Antonius Augustinus and certain other interpreters of law, see Scioppius and Wisembachius on Law 122, *On the Signification of Words*; and, more recently, Philippus Munckerus’s useful work *On Intercalation*, for understanding ancient writings—see him on Book I, chapter 2, no. 4.

With the two Gemini as consuls. It is not my purpose to resolve the chronological problem concerning the year, month, and day on which Christ the Lord redeemed humankind by his saving Passion. Anyone undertaking it would require a work of considerable scope, both to examine the differing opinions of the ancients and to calculate those of modern writers. For the present it will suffice to observe that many Fathers held the view followed by Lactantius: namely Tertullian, Julius Africanus, Jerome, Augustine, Sulpicius Severus, and Paulus Orosius; indeed also more recent writers, Glareanus and Haloander. They held that Christ preached the Gospel in its fuller sense for one year only, and, when that had ended, suffered and died in the following year, under the consulship of C. Rubellius Geminus and Fusius Geminus.

Among those now treating this question carefully, preference seems due above all to those who agree with the ancients that Christ was baptized in the fifteenth year of the emperor Tiberius—as Luke expressly says in chapter III—namely under the consulship of Appius Junius Silanus and P. Silius Nerva; that thereafter he celebrated four Passovers, or at least underwent that great sacred event, venerable to all devout persons of every age, before the fourth; and consequently that this was accomplished under the consulship of Sergius Sulpicius Galba and L. Cornelius Sulla. This is Scaliger’s opinion, joined by those among us who arrange the chronology of these times more successfully. Those seem to have come nearest after them who add one year, judging that the Son of God died that death salutary for humankind before the fifth Passover; the rest depart further afield.

As to the month and day, sacred history sufficiently establishes that Christ suffered and died on the fourteenth day of Nisan, at the first full moon after the equinox: that is, if we follow Scaliger, on the third of April. But if we think one year must be added to Scaliger’s reckoning—namely a lunar year, since the intercalation customarily made three times in an eight-year cycle does not appear to have fallen in that year—the day of the crucifixion (σταυρωσίμως) would have been the tenth day before the Kalends of April, on or about which day the calculation, or the tradition following earlier writers, of several ancients comes to rest. But I gladly leave these matters to others for fuller and more polished treatment.

Having fulfilled that office. He elegantly uses *officium* for administration. Nothing is more familiar or usual in speaking of companions of the imperial court, governors, and judges of provinces, indeed even their attendants; perhaps I shall cite some examples below. The Greek Fathers likewise call Christ’s ministry οἰκονομία, “dispensation” or “administration.”

A cloudstorm. The illustrious Cuperus rightly warns that one should not depart from the guidance of the divine writings. Certainly, the careless mingling of those external darknesses with heavenly light did no small harm to certain Fathers of the early Church. Here too I fear that the notion (ἐννόημα) that Christ was snatched from his followers’ sight through the sudden intervention of a storm-cloud adhered to Lactantius from what is read concerning Romulus in Livy and other Roman historians—not to mention Homer’s or Virgil’s clouds, by which they conceal their gods or heroes. Not much better, in Book IV, chapter 21, he says that the cloud suddenly enveloped him; whereas from the divine Scriptures the event is gathered to have occurred calmly and gently, like most of Christ’s acts upon earth. Blessed Cyprian, near the end of his tract *On the Vanity of Idols*, puts it rather more simply and correctly: “Then,” he says, “he was raised into heaven, a cloud having surrounded him.”

They laid foundations. Sidonius Apollinaris, Book II, Letter 11: “Nor would I cease to build up, by various kinds of honours, the foundations once laid of our striving friendship.” Agricultural writers say in much the same way “to lay down a line” or “a boundary,” “to lay down according to the written rule of an estate,” and the like. You find “to put forth a root” in the old translator of the Bible, 2 Kings 19. Lampridius, in the *Life of Septimius Severus*, chapter 12, says “to construct a wall or rampart”; older writers said “to drive in a root” or “to draw a wall.”

Peter came to Rome. The truth of the story concerning Peter remains doubtful.

And firm. Lactantius himself uses the expression in this way; for example, Book IV, chapter 24: “May it have a root and foundation, and remain firm and fixed among men”; and Book VII, chapter 10: “But when he established for himself a permanent dwelling,” etc. What he calls “faithful” means the same thing; the latter term explains the former. I think it is a Hebraism and refers to God’s words to Jeroboam through the prophet Ahijah, promising him, on condition that he acted piously and kept God’s laws, a firm and permanent house, 1 Kings 10:38: “I shall be with you, and I shall build you a faithful house, as I built a house for David.”

As the illustrious Cuperus observed on the preceding chapter, the holy Fathers commonly call the true Church of God the house or temple of God, following the guidance of the sacred writings. Lactantius too does so in many places. Thus, in Book IV, chapter 10, he says that “the Son of God descended to earth in order to establish God’s temple and teach righteousness.” Likewise chapter 11: “Therefore, wishing to send the surveyor of his temple to earth, God did not wish to send him in heavenly power and glory.” And chapter 13: “The Church is the true temple of God, which is not in walls, but in the heart and faith of those who believe in him and are called faithful; but that Solomonic temple, because it was made by hands, fell by hands.” Add the beginning of chapter 14, where there is much that is excellent. Likewise in *On the Anger of God*, chapter 2, where he similarly calls Christ the founder of the divine and immortal temple. I refrain, for brevity’s sake, from gathering more examples from others.

To a new religion. It is true that men everywhere hurled this reproach at Christians; Galerius does the same in the edict which appears in Greek in Eusebius and Nicephorus, and in Latin below, in chapter 34 of this book. As to the meaning of Julius Capitolinus’s words, if I too must take a side, I confess that I incline to Casaubon. The other great man, confronted with a knot which he himself admits is difficult, seems to resort to emendation as a rather poor poet resorts to a theatrical machine. Yet let love of truth excuse this remark about a man whom I otherwise, as is fitting, admire and esteem.

To destroy the heavenly temple. Thus Lactantius, Book V, chapter 3: “Since he had endeavoured utterly to destroy the truth.” So too “to destroy vices,” Book III, chapter 26, as two older manuscripts read there; likewise Book VI, chapter 15, and *On the Anger of God*, chapter 17.

He nowhere suddenly appeared. We shall be somewhat less surprised that the author of this little work reports this, if we remember that Tacitus, *Histories* II.8, relates that long after Nero’s death a rumour circulated about him as though he were alive: “At about the same time,” he says, “when Vespasian held supreme power, Achaia and Asia were terrified by a false alarm, as though Nero were approaching; reports of his end varied, and thus many imagined and believed that he was alive.” He then recounts the disturbances caused by a worthless fellow who pretended to be Nero; consult the historian himself, or Casaubon’s notes on Suetonius.

Certain Fathers of the early Church, together with our Lactantius, mention and refute the error apparently strengthened by these false rumours and attached to many Christians of those times: that Nero either survived, or would return to life in the last times in order to rage against the entire Christian name. Such are Jerome on Daniel 11; Augustine, *City of God* XX.119; Ambrose on 1 Corinthians 4:9. Others likewise suspected that Nero was either a type of Antichrist, or Antichrist himself, and would be so in the future. See Chrysostom on 2 Thessalonians 2, Homily 4, p. 1504; the sermon *On Almsgiving*; Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History* II.29 and *Dialogue* II, final chapter; etc.

When he shall begin to descend . . . Lactantius’s readers observe that he loves old formulas and elegances of expression; an eminent man rightly notes the same in the use of *descensor* or *descendere*. Consult also, if you please, Adrianus Turnebus, *Adversaria* IX.9; Virgil’s commentators on *Georgics* II.326; and Torrentius on Horace, *Epodes* 13.

And they bring down Jupiter with rains and snows. Regarding the restoration of gaps in a page perforated by moths or damaged by age around this passage, I have nothing to add, except that I think it may be read with a smaller alteration: “and in the last age”; and then, as the distinguished Cuperus proposes: “or even into the last centuries, they announce that, when the holy and everlasting beginning of Christ shall begin to descend, they will return.”

Some ancients thought that Enoch would return with Elijah, as Augustine testifies, *On Genesis according to the Letter* IX.6. Others have already cited his words and shown what Gregory the Great thought on the same subject. Andreas of Caesarea also seems to incline this way in his commentary on the Apocalypse, p. 45, published by Sylburgius together with certain books of Chrysostom; not to mention the words of Tertullian, much older than these, known through the work of others, which are read in his *On the Soul*, chapter 50, where Pamelius gathered several further passages of nearly the same opinion.

Indeed, certain heterodox writers of our time have attempted to support this very claim from Sirach 44:11, aided less by the Greek words of Sirach than by the Latin translator’s rendering: “Enoch pleased God and was translated into Paradise, that he might give repentance to the nations.” In Hoeschel’s Greek edition, corrected from very ancient copies, it reads: “Enoch pleased the Lord and was translated, an example of repentance for the generations” (Ἐνὼχ εὐηρέστησε Κυρίῳ, καὶ μετετέθη, ὑπόδειγμα μετανοίας ταῖς γενεαῖς).

But on these matters it will be far better to consult the renowned Helmstedt theologian Dr. Georgius Calixtus, in that part of his treatise *On the Last Judgment* which deals with the signs preceding that decisive day. In the judgment of Johann Heinrich Boecler, a most celebrated and learned man, this error was refuted by him excellently; see *Universal History*, p. 210.

## On Chapter III

No lesser tyrant. This was Domitian, whom Ausonius says Rome called “the bald Nero”; Tertullian, in the *Apology*, called him “a portion of Nero in cruelty,” and in *On the Pallium*, “a sub-Nero.”

He pressed upon their necks. Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* V.9: “But upon those worshippers of God who have not denied him, they press with all the forces of their slaughterhouse.” VII.19: “For once he has seized the world, he will press upon it with great armies of brigands.”

Even the memory of his name was erased. Dio Cassius, Herodian, and the Latin writers of the *Augustan History* mention this practice in many places. Lactantius himself alludes to it in the last chapter of this work.

He had constructed public works. Symmachus, Book I, Letter 52: “I was raising urban works to the highest summits.” Spartianus, *Life of Hadrian*, chapter 19: “Although he had everywhere completed innumerable works, he never inscribed his own name, except in the temple of Trajan his father.” But the usage is exceedingly common. Domitian’s works are listed by Suetonius, Eutropius, and most fully by Eusebius in the *Chronicle*, no. 2200: the restored Capitol, the Odeon, the Forum Transitorium, the Stadium, the pepper warehouses, and more besides. Consult the eminent men who have elucidated the writers mentioned with notes.

He persecuted his name. Tertullian, *On Patience*, chapter 2: “Persecuting the name together with his whole household.” Aurelius Victor, *On the Caesars*, chapter 3: “They persecute the entire family and kinship with arms.”

He stretched out his hands. Lactantius, Book VII, chapter 15: “For when Carthage had been destroyed, he stretched out his hands over the whole world, by land and sea.”

## On Chapter IV

For who but an evil man persecutes justice? Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 5: “Such have always been our persecutors: unjust, impious, shameful men—men whom you yourselves are accustomed to condemn, and those condemned by whom you have been accustomed to restore.” Compare Book I *Against the Nations*, chapter 7, and many other sayings of others to the same effect. For pious persons of every age truly glory that they are hated by evil people alone; but to cite their words would be a lengthy task.

Having set out against the Carpi. The author of this book names the Carpi alone, although it is certain that other peoples far more numerous than the Carpi were present: the Borani, the Goths, the Urugundi—as Zosimus usually calls them—and indeed the Astringi, Taifali, and many others whom Jordanes lists in this history. Lactantius nevertheless names the Carpi alone, because they were better known to the Romans than the others through their frequent incursions. Jordanes likewise, *The Gothic History*, chapter 16: “Three thousand of the Carpi also arrived, a people exceedingly ready for war and often hostile to the Romans.” Add the observations of the most learned men: Cellarius on Zosimus I.28, and Baluzius on this passage of Lactantius.

It is well known that emperors not infrequently took a cognomen from a people scarcely conquered, much less completely subdued; likewise, that tyrants bore titles from peoples whom they had not even attacked in war. But perhaps more on this elsewhere.

## On Chapter V

He said that it was true. I hesitated somewhat whether a word had dropped out here—perhaps “yoke,” “trophy,” or something similar. But the most distinguished and learned Cuperus, consulted on the matter, removed this doubt from me. I do not think the Romans ought to be blamed because they customarily committed their deeds to memory through paintings or engraved stones. How many most beautiful achievements would be better known to us if other peoples too had cultivated this practice! Read, if you wish, what Pliny relates in Book XXXV, chapter 4, about Messalla, L. Scipio, Hostilius Mancinus, and especially Augustus; likewise what Aurelius Victor says of L. Aemilius publicly displaying a painted panel of his triumph over the Ligurians, and other passages scattered among other authors.

Nor did they only paint: they also most frequently engraved achievements in marble. Caesar Bulengerus demonstrates this in his commentary *On Triumphs* from Marius’s marble trophies, which still survive, from the triumphal arches of Constantine and others, and from other monuments. Coins too, as the illustrious Cuperus has already observed, everywhere show with what zeal they laboured to make their victories known to posterity. Among them are not merely many imperial coins depicting trophies, but also some struck under the free Republic, on which the victor presses the neck or back of the conquered. An example is that of Paulus Aemilius in Goltzius, in which the victor insults the conquered not much differently from Sapor.

Casaubon does not conceal, in his notes on the *Life of Pescennius Niger*, chapter 6, that the Romans nevertheless laboured to excess in representing all their deeds through painting and similar arts, especially in the age of the emperors here mentioned; I would have the reader consult him.

But now, I think, the reader demands that I give the words of Nazianzen commended above by the distinguished Cuperus:

> “It is a royal custom—I do not know whether among all peoples subject to kingship, but certainly among the Romans it is a matter very zealously pursued—that rulers be honoured by public images. Crowns, diadems, the splendour of purple, the laws that are counted, taxes, and the multitude of subjects do not suffice to sustain their sovereignty. They require worship too, by which they may seem more august—not only that they themselves may be worshipped, but also those represented in forms and colours—so that the reverence paid to them may be more insatiable and more complete. To these images they delight in adding different adjuncts at different times: some depict the most splendid cities bringing gifts; others Victories crowning them above the head; others officials paying homage and being honoured by the insignia of offices; others killings in the hunt and skill in aiming; others barbarians defeated, cast beneath their feet, or slain—manifold forms, on account of which they think highly of themselves. For they love not only the realities of their achievements, but also their representations.”

Thus spoke that holy writer truly. It would be easy to illustrate every point individually; but since anyone not wholly ignorant of Roman affairs can do the same, I shall for the present merely note that the practice of victors trampling necks or backs seems to have originated in the East and to be extremely ancient. At Joshua’s command, the leaders of Israel placed their feet upon the necks of conquered kings, Joshua 10:24. From this very ancient and well-known practice the phrase συντρίβειν ὑπὸ τοὺς πόδας, “to crush under the feet,” or *conculcare*, “to trample,” seems to have arisen. It signifies subduing, taming, or reducing an enemy to order, and setting him a limit so that he may do no harm thereafter. You find it in Genesis 3:15; Psalms 119 and 118; Romans 16:20. Several other biblical sayings agree with these. Though all are most sacred and plainly mystical, they nevertheless show the custom of Eastern peoples. But others discuss this more fully.

## On Chapter VI

Mad and headlong. Among other things, this is sufficiently shown by his assumption of the title “Lord and God”; see the illustrious Spanheim, *On the Excellence and Use of Coins*, p. 729. On the persecution initiated by him, see what Antonius Pagius collected in his learned dissertation *On the Caesarean Consuls*, p. 380.

Caenofrurium. Paeanius calls it καινὸν φρούριον, “new fortress”; therefore Scaliger thought it worth noting that it should be written with AE.

Killed by his friends. Learned men have shown that kings call “friends” those whom they admit to their inner circle and keep close for more secret counsels; this is Aristotle’s friendship καθ’ ὑπεροχὴν, “by superiority.” To forestall the threats of Aurelian, a bloodthirsty emperor, Mnestheus, one of his freedmen—called Eros by Zosimus and described as τῶν ἔξωθεν φερομένων ἀποκρίσεων μηνυτὴς τεταγμένος, that is, Master of Offices—incited several men to murder him, partly through true and partly through false alarms; exactly as Commodus later provoked his own associates against himself, according to Spartianus, *Commodus*, chapter 9. See Vopiscus, *Aurelian*, chapter 36; Aurelius Victor, *On the Caesars*, chapter 35; *Epitome*, chapter 50; Eutropius IX.9.

They acted against God. Caelius in Cicero, *Letters to Atticus* X: “Now to act against Caesar the victor is the height of folly.” So that unworthy prelate or bishop in Optatus of Milevis: “I killed this man; and whoever acts against me, I shall kill.”

## On Chapter VII

To confirm what he said above—that Christians were hated only by evil men—he is about to speak of Diocletian and his partners in the Empire. He teaches that they acted perversely in many matters and attacks their conduct and institutions severely. Yet although those tyrants deserved hatred for the most savage and atrocious slaughter of Christians of any age, which has occurred since then and may occur hereafter, if God so wills, those who know those times should consider whether Lactantius here sometimes serves his own purpose in certain details, and does so in such a way that he sometimes censures things whose rationale is different and which other writers report and explain very differently.

Inventor of crimes and contriver of evils. Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* VII.24: “The prince of demons, who is the contriver of all evils.” Thus Virgil calls Ulysses an inventor of crimes, and Claudian calls Rufinus so.

For three partners in rule. Claudian, *Against Rufinus* II:

> He rebukes Augustus: let him mount the lofty tribunal;  
> let him declare him partner of the sceptre, companion in honour.

Likewise Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXVI, says that Valentinian brought forward his brother Valens as a lawful partner in power, though obedient after the manner of an attendant. And the author of the *Life of Septimius Severus*, chapter 8: “When Pescennius Niger summoned Severus to participation [in power], he was scorned.”

To say something briefly about Diocletian’s arrangement for the benefit of youth, nothing is more familiar than Homer’s saying: “Rule by many is not good; let there be one ruler” (οὐκ ἀγαθὸν πολυκοιρανίη, εἷς κοίρανος ἔστω). This has been confirmed by the agreement of very many others, such as the chorus in Euripides’ *Andromache*, Act II:

> “The power of one man sustains houses and cities.”

So too Seneca, both philosopher in Book I of *On Clemency*, chapter 4, and poet in *Medea*; Lucan, Book I; and those mentioned there by the illustrious Grotius. Jerome likewise writes to the monk Rusticus: “Even dumb animals and herds of wild beasts follow their leaders. Bees have their rulers; cranes follow one in ordered formation. There is one emperor, one judge in a province,” and so on. Add Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 289, and Minucius Felix, who borrows his words; from this the emendation of Fulvius Ursinus is also confirmed, reading *desiit* (“ceased”) for *discessit* (“departed”). There you will find several authors cited to this effect by the most eminent and learned Ouzelius, p. 139. Nor should our Lactantius be passed over: *Institutes* I.3 and 5.

Truth itself approves the judgments of these and others. Diocletian would undoubtedly have acted more prudently if, instead of gradually raising Maximian to equality with himself and then adding others, thereby opening a broad window onto future civil discord, he had selected suitable ministers and deputies everywhere, retained the supreme power in all its parts, and provided more securely for the peace of his subjects. Thus our Firmianus judges, and rightly. Yet I know that certain others take an altogether different view.

Ammianus, Book XXVI, certainly praises Valentinian because, seeing himself overcome by the magnitude of urgent business, he believed that no delay should occur before he proclaimed his brother Augustus. Zonaras likewise declares concerning Diocletian, *Annals* II: “Looking to the excessive magnitude of the Empire, he took a partner in it in the fourth year of his rule—or, according to others, in the second.” But Mamertinus speaks excessively in the manner of a panegyrist: “You, who have bounded the Empire not by regions of earth but of heaven, share between yourselves so great a force and power; this is assuredly a confidence divine and immortal, which greed may disturb.” *Panegyric to Maximian*, chapter 10. You find similar, or even grander, statements in the birthday oration, chapter 6.

What then shall we say about this tetrachord, greatly praised by Julian the Apostate and others? Our writer answers even here: its concord was not sincere, but a partnership somehow preserved for the sake of circumstances; not friendship born and cultivated from virtue as mother, but a conspiracy such as arises among brigands and μονοπωλίται, “monopolists,” for mutual assistance. It is surely worth observing that they had very similar faces as well—look at the coins of both men—whom nature had so aptly matched in character, fortune, lot, life, habits, and actions.

But if we consider the other two, Constantius, owing to gentleness and affability of disposition, did not approve the conduct of that most cruel pair; but he endured it as best he could, since he could not correct it. In Galerius, however, the tetrachord was too discordant: he was otherwise a terror to those two elder men, and in the end compelled his father-in-law Diocletian to abdicate the Empire, an example later followed by Herculius. But enough of this; for if anyone should prepare a serious examination of the matter, it would furnish material for a dissertation neither unpleasant nor perhaps unprofitable.

Indictions. At first, indictions appear to have been imposed irregularly, at the conqueror’s discretion or according to the needs of the commonwealth; Asconius seems to have held this view when he distinguished them from the regular assessment and contribution. Later, however, these too were assigned fixed times. See the jurists. The translator of the Bible likewise says, 2 Kings 15: “Menahem imposed silver upon Israel, upon all the powerful and wealthy”; and chapter 18: “The king of Assyria imposed upon Hezekiah king of Judah three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold.” Add the end of chapter 23.

Many governors. Eutropius touches lightly on this matter, Book IX, chapter 15, and simultaneously shows the opportunity Diocletian used to accomplish these measures: wars and victories. Having gained these, he regulated and arranged each province according to his own will and discretion. Egypt is an example, after Achilleus had been overthrown there: “He used victory cruelly; he defiled all Egypt with severe proscriptions and slaughter. Yet on that occasion he established its order and wisely arranged many things that remain to our own age.” Paeanius speaks more clearly and appropriately:

> “Diocletian himself, having defeated Achilleus in Egypt, put him to death and pursued his victory with every cruelty, slaughtering some Egyptians and imposing upon the rest taxes as heavy as possible. For this reason he imposed contributions upon all the subjects of the Empire, after measuring the land and recording everything in a census; and this arrangement has continued to the present.”

Therefore all things agree well with this account, and it appears that the fuller details given by that epitomist are not always so unhistorical, whether he added them himself or used a more extensive Eutropius than we have today. I think I have also observed traces of the matter discussed here in the laws of those and subsequent times, but I do not presently have sufficient leisure to collect them.

Our author rightly calls them *praesides*, “governors,” because they were sent and appointed by the emperor. See Lipsius, excursus on Tacitus, *Annals* I.75 and XII.60; Salmasius on Spartianus’s *Hadrian*, chapters 13 and 33; Spanheim, *On the Excellence and Use of Coins*, p. 572. By *officia* he here understands the attendants of governors and judges—that is, lesser magistrates with soldiers—who approximately occupied the place of those whom an earlier age called *accensi* and *statores* (though the later age too had its *statores*), and, when they attended the highest magistrates, *lictors*; later writers called them collectively *officiales*. Nothing is more frequent in the Acts of Martyrs, the laws of that age, the *Notitia of Both Empires*, and other writings. Gronovius, “the very learned,” even shows that Suetonius speaks in this manner in his *Vespasian*.

Thus a certain Count of the East had six hundred men in his office; the praetorian prefect of Africa had 388; others more or fewer, as circumstances seemed to require. See what Pancirollus collected on these matters in his notes to chapter 9 of the *Notitia of the Eastern Empire*. If anyone should contend that Lactantius here means rather the governors themselves, as a single expression for two things (ἓν διὰ δυοῖν), or those somewhat higher, equal, or subordinate to them, I shall not strongly object. For I remember that these too are called *officia*, especially with reference to emperors. Thus Trajan writes to Pliny: “By the diplomas which I gave to your office,” final letter, Book X. Thus Licinius writes elsewhere to the governor of Bithynia, in chapter 48 of this book: “By letters given to your office.” But this may already be known.

Many rationales. The *rationales* established in provinces also had an *officium*, or staff, as the most learned Valesius demonstrates from Law 7, *On Cohortales*, and Laws 2 and 4, *On Vacant Estates*, in the Theodosian Code. They seized the property of condemned persons and those proscribed by judicial sentence. Consult Valesius on Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXVIII. Indeed, *rationales* were imperial procurators who collected whatever provincial revenues belonged to the emperors. Add Du Fresne’s *Glossary*.

And masters. The term *master* has a broad range; for anyone is so called who either directs people and regulates their life and conduct, or presides over affairs. Thus Cicero himself calls the Roman consuls “masters of the people.” Censors are commonly called masters of morals. In the old Bible translation, Exodus 1, there are masters of works—called *Arbetes Fougtar* in our language and ἐργοδιώκται in Greek. Those appointed under a praetor’s authority to supervise the division of property, and many others, were likewise called masters.

Festus, and Gronovius following him on Livy XXXIV.25, list more properly so-called masters: masters of districts, companies, villages, colleges, cavalry, games, moreover banquets, and finally teachers of arts. The dignity of all these was a *mastership*, not a magistracy. Later the word became common in imperial courts: there were masters of soldiers; see the same Gronovius, *Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 217. There were likewise masters of offices; consult Corippus the African, Book III, verse 172, and the learned notes there, especially Salmasius on Julius Capitolinus’s *Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher*, chapter 8, and Valesius on Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXVI.

There were also masters of letters, memory, petitions, arrangements, census, linen clothing, private clothing, and other matters. Consult the *Notitia of Both Empires* and the notes of men renowned for uncommon learning on the *Augustan History*.

Civil acts. *Actus* for “actions” was common in that age. Lactantius likewise says in *On the Anger of God*, chapter 12: “Our acts are watched by God”; and chapter 17: “He observes the acts of individuals.”

Exactions. Hence *exactores*, ἐπιστάται, “overseers,” who exact either taxes or compulsory labour. See the interpreters of Moses on Exodus 5:6 and 14: “Those who had charge of the labours of the children of Israel were flogged by Pharaoh’s exactors.” But such matters are also found everywhere else in sacred and secular literature.

Frequent wars troubling the whole world during Diocletian’s reign offer some excuse for these exactions. To omit their very beginnings: the Bagaudae troubled Gaul; Carausius, with the inhabitants of that island, Britain; the Persians, the East; Achilleus, Egypt; Julianus and the Quinquegentian peoples, the rest of Africa. Hence the author of this writing says below: “These too can be endured—the demands related to furnishing soldiers.” On this census or assessment, especially the poll tax, see Lipsius on Tacitus, *Annals* I.31.

A law regulating the prices of goods for sale. In former times the greed of sellers was restrained by the aediles, whom the Greeks call ἀγορανόμοι, “market-supervisors.” See what Piccartus collected on Aristotle, *Politics* VI.8, unless you prefer to examine the archives of the Romans and of other nations.

Until the law was dissolved by necessity itself. With excessive cheapness imposed by decree, all sellers act in concert, as though in Plautus’s oil-dealers’ market, and make goods disappear so that they are sought in vain. For this and other reasons, experience, the corrector of laws, rebukes many laws after testing them, as Livy says approximately in Book XLV, chapter 32. This should especially be understood, among other things, of laws concerning price controls. For price is more uncertain than spring winds. See Boecler’s dissertation *On the Measure of Price*, and the eminent authorities cited there.

Here, “mint” (*moneta*). Ancient glosses: “Mint: τόπος, the place of stamping”; likewise, “Mint: the place where coin is struck” (τόπος ἔνθα τὸ νόμισμα χαράσσεται). Thus the “mint of Trier” is mentioned in a mutilated stone inscription in Gruter, p. 93, no. 3. Thus Ausonius celebrates the temples that stood at Milan, “the palatine citadels, and the wealthy Mint.” Ferretius shows in *Lapidary Muses*, Book IV, memorial 21, that several verses of this poem survive in an ancient marble inscription.

The emendation of the learned man who, in notes on Ausonius, reads *et laeti mores*, “and cheerful customs,” where previously *antiqui mores*, “ancient customs,” was read, is not supported by that marble. And indeed Ennius’s well-known phrase, “By ancient customs,” repeated twice by Plautus and cited also by the emperor Vespasian in Tacitus, *Histories* III.57, and by Marcus Antoninus the philosopher-emperor in Volcatius Gallicanus’s *Life of Avidius Cassius*, chapter 5, seems to fit that Ausonian poem well enough.

Thus he was always deranged. That is, he was mad, frenzied, and insane. Hincmar, *On Lothair’s Divorce*: “Some have been deranged by drink, others by food, through sorcerers.” Latin-Greek glosses: *dementat*, “he drives out of his mind” (ἐξίστησιν). Tertullian used *dementire*, as did Lactantius himself in the *Institutes* and others. Cuperus.

Lactantius’s words, Book IV, chapter 27, are: “Behold, someone stirred by the prompting of a demon loses his mind, is carried away, goes mad.” Corresponding are these words in Book I, chapter 21: “For, with their shoulders cut and swords drawn in each hand, they run, are carried away, go mad.” This reading must certainly be retained, not the *efferantur* forced upon us against the manuscripts by Dempster and Gallaeus. Lactantius imitates Cicero, as he often does elsewhere. *For Caelius*, chapter 9: “The injured grieve; the angry are carried away.” *Against Rullus*, chapter 35: “But they will certainly be restrained; they will advance farther; they will be carried away.”

But to return to the present passage: *dementare* is used here as *efferare* is in Hegesippus: “Herod had become savage against all.” See Gronovius, *Observations on Ecclesiastical History*, p. 71. Such verbs as *ponere*, *mutare*, *movere*, *praecipitare*, and many others are sometimes used intransitively—or, rather, elliptically—so that *se* is understood. Let well-born young men consult Vossius, Book III *On Analogy*, chapter 3.

## On Chapter VIII

His brother Maximian. Maximian Herculius was Diocletian’s brother not by nature but by partnership in imperial rule. This use of the term was common among historians and panegyrists of that age. See Baluzius, or rather Mamertinus himself, whom he cites, and the others.

Herculius. That is, just as Diocletian represented Jupiter, so Maximian represented Hercules bringing his father aid against enemies; hence the names Jovians and Herculians, prolonged down to posterity, of which this writer speaks below at the end of this book. See Mamertinus’ panegyric, especially the earlier one, addressed to Maximian. Yet many princes of old seized upon the names and honours of gods with remarkable insolence. Thus Antigonus; thus Antiochus, one of the sons of Grypus; likewise Mithridates; and after them M. Antonius, and also C. Caligula, strove to resemble Bacchus; Menecrates, Mercury; Themiso, Alexander, Pyrrhus, Commodus, and this Maximian, Hercules; indeed Maximinus the Elder likewise the same god. Augustus played Apollo, though he did not always decline the name of Jupiter; certainly Ovid and others call him this more than once, as you may sometimes read also of the rest. Andreas Schottus, *Observations on History*, III.3, and the distinguished Spanheim, *On the Excellence and Use of Coins*, in several places, have demonstrated this at greater length. [Col. 0401D]

“There was more avarice in the lesser [emperor], but less in the greater; yet more cowardice, but more spirit—not for doing good, but for doing evil.” The eminent Baluzius admits that this passage is corrupt and distorted; nor does the most distinguished and learned Cuper conceal that the passage is difficult. Yet I shall attempt what I can. I think it may be restored thus:

> They differed only in this: the greater had more avarice, but also more cowardice; the lesser, less [avarice], but more spirit—not for doing good, but for doing evil.

Historians everywhere relate that Diocletian was cowardly and cunning, and also avaricious. (Indeed, he is the more timid who fights not with strength but with deceitful arts; and avarice is commonly compatible with both faults.) Such, I say, was Diocletian. Maximian, however, was driven by luxury, by the passion for lavish expenditure and reckless giving, to plunder and other injuries; so that it is not surprising that he too is called avaricious, though less so than the other. Men of this sort compete in scattering what they have seized and recovering with rapacious avarice what they have scattered, as Seneca says, *On Benefits* I; or, as Ovid says:

> They strive to seek in order to consume, and to seek again what has been consumed;  
> And the very vices themselves provide one another’s nourishment.

Likewise Manilius, IV.25:

> We purchase luxury with profits, and plunder with luxury;  
> And the highest price of wealth is to pour wealth away.

Add, if you wish, Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics* IV.3. But to return to these passages of Lactantius: a passage very similar in verbal arrangement and figure occurs at IV.3, from which it may be established either that these too are genuinely Lactantius’ words, or that the author of this writing imitated him rather closely. In the former part there is less danger, but more difficulty, since the obscure logic of the matters compels differing opinions. Here there is more danger, but less difficulty, because the use of things itself and daily experience can teach what is truer and better. [Col. 0402A–B]

“Immediately at hand.” Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I.38: “What of the fact that, as soon as I please, an image is at hand?”

“I pass over Constantius.” These words seem more properly to belong to the ninth section, or chapter.

## On Chapter IX

“Cruelty alien to Roman blood.” Write also “and cruelty” (*et feritas*): thus below, ch. 40, *essagitarii* for *sagitarii*. The most distinguished Cuper writes most kindly that he accepts this and my two following emendations.

“Tall in stature.” Thus the Paris edition; but that one must read *status celsus*, “lofty bodily bearing,” is taught by several similar passages in Lactantius: *Divine Institutes* II.2: “But to us an upright bearing and elevated countenance were given by the Creator”; ch. 2: “that you might despise the earth placed beneath your feet, while preserving the posture of your body”; ch. 17: “We have received an elevated stature”; III.1: “whose bodily bearing is upright”; VII.9: “whose body, raised from the shoulder, elevated countenance, and erect posture seek its origin.” *On the Anger of God* 7: “With upright posture and elevated face.” *On the Workmanship of God* 8: “Thus in man alone are reason upright and stature elevated.” Similarly Minucius Felix, p. 138; and, among older writers, Plautus, *Amphitryon*: “I assumed this man’s form and bearing.”

“And cast down in spirit.” I write *dejectus*, “cast down,” as in Claudian—now a more carefully corrected work—*Rape of Proserpina* III.297:

> Supplicant and cast down, I cast myself  
> At your knees.

Elsewhere too the same poet spoke of a “cast-down client”; as do Statius, Silius, Prudentius, and others. The Glosses likewise: *deicio*, “I cast down”: *katapherō*; *kataballō to phronēma*, “I cast down the spirit”; *kataballō*.

“To go to war with all his own people.” Of the Eastern nations when they enter battle—

> Their movement is most fierce, with no  
> Order, and with unexpected returns,

as Claudian says. There is no reason why I should heap together here matters observed by ancient and modern writers. Let whoever wishes consult Julius Caesar, *Gallic War* III.3; Herodian IV, last chapter; Seneca, *On Anger* III.3; Florus III.3, no. 5; and so forth. Modern Turks also retain this custom of their ancestors. [Col. 0402C–D]

“So that he now began to refuse.” Thus in Minucius Felix, p. 260, “scattered falsehoods”; in Symmachus VI, last letter, *commandare*; and in other authors, *contractabil[.....]*, *impartire*, *obaudire*, *circumsedere*.

## On Chapter X

“He was, through fear, an investigator of future events.” *Prae timore* or *prae metu*, “from fear,” is certainly more usual. Yet I think *pro timore* can be said, as in the translator of the Bible, 2 Kings [4 Kings] VI: “And the heart of the king of Syria was troubled on account of this matter”; and as Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History* I.9: “After their father’s death, he treated his brothers kindly, as they feared because of their conscience.” He speaks learnedly: superstitious divination arose from the fear and anxiety with which we turn our minds beforehand to future events. Arrian, *Discourses of Epictetus* II.7:

> What then drives us continually to seek oracles? Cowardice—the fear of outcomes.

Lucian, *Alexander the False Prophet*:

> They perceived that human life is tyrannized over by these two greatest powers, hope and fear . . . For in both cases—in the fearful man and in the hopeful man—they saw foreknowledge to be most necessary and most desired; and that Delphi had therefore long been rich . . . and Delos, and Claros, and Branchidae—

and the rest, which will be read more accurately in Lucian himself. Valerius Flaccus too speaks gracefully, IV:

> But the blinded mind cannot trust; and, however near  
> Phasis and that supreme labour of their undertaking may be,  
> The nearer dangers trouble them all the more; nor are the seers  
> Mopsus and Idmon now enough for me.

“Tagis, master of the haruspices.” I think *Tagis* may be retained even in the nominative case, after the Greek usage, among whom occur Tagis the Pythagorean, mentioned by Stobaeus, and likewise Agis, Bacis, Betis, Datis, Lysis, Eupolis, and other masculine names so ending. But, not to conceal anything, I suspect the word *aruspicum* (“of the haruspices”) to be a gloss; I conjecture that here there originally stood “interpreter of Tagis,” or something similar. Compare the highly similar account in Prudentius, *Apotheosis* 467:

> And the crafty interpreter marked  
> The last throbs of life in the cooling heart  
> By their number and their end.

Add what Gregory Nazianzen and Theodoret relate about the same Julian; from which it may be established that those impious pagan rites were frequently disrupted by Christian intervention. [Col. 0403A–B]

“Profane men.” Just as that most wicked impostor of whom Lucian speaks did in a fictitious matter, others did in real matters: they accused Christians—who alone were truly pious—of impiety and sacrilege. Thus against Flavius Clemens (the Leunclavius edition wrongly calls him Fabius), Roman consul, and his wife Domitilla, relatives of Domitian’s wife, “an accusation of impiety and atheism was brought against them both” (*amphoin asebeias kai atheotētos enklēma epēnechthē*). For their punishments one may consult Dio’s Book LXVII, unless one prefers to consult the Christian martyrologies themselves. Add Baluzius on the words in the third chapter, “the Church restored.” [Col. 0403B–C]

## On Chapter XI

“Worshipper of the gods of the mountains.” The distinguished Baluzius, to whom the republic of letters owes this book as its first defender and editor, by no small service, does not doubt that these “gods of the mountains,” whom Commodianus also touches upon as “mountain gods” (*deos monteses*, as he thinks one should read), and likewise the “mountain gods” (*deos montenses*) to whom was dedicated, by their command, the altar in Gruter whose inscription we shall give shortly, are the same gods. Yet he confesses that it is not clear to him who they are, or what their names may be. And indeed the subject is not without obscurity. Let us nevertheless see what path our Cuper, a man most distinguished alike in learning and rank, marks out for us here.

From his notes on the *Apotheosis of Homer*—a work now, as I hear, hastening to completion and eagerly awaited by students of ancient elegance—the celebratedly humane scholar shared with me, in his customary generosity, the following extracts. After beginning to discuss a painting of Homer placed upon a lofty mountain, he says: “Mountains were once held in great veneration; and, as sacred and profane history abundantly shows, altars and temples were built upon them for many divinities. Hence, in Philostratus, the Indians call Caucasus ‘the house of the gods’ (*Theōn oikon*); the Persians in Herodotus, ‘ascending to the highest peaks of the mountains’ (*epi ta hypsēlotata tōn oureōn anabainontes*), sacrifice victims to Jupiter. Montinus, the god who presides over mountains, occurs in Arnobius; Galerius Maximian’s mother is called by Lactantius a woman most superstitious, a worshipper of the gods of the mountains. The Mountain Gods are celebrated in an inscription in Gruter, p. 21. Since it was discovered at Rome, they seem to signify the gods presiding over the seven hills, in whose honour perhaps the festival of the Septimontium was established. It was celebrated by the *montani*, that is, those inhabiting the hills, not by the whole people, as may be read in Varro, *On the Latin Language* V. In seven places also, according to Festus, they made sacrifice to the presiding gods, I think; just as the *flamen Palatualis* was appointed to sacrifice to the goddess under whose protection they believed the Palatine stood.”

He then continues his discussion of Mount Argaeus, the god Penninus, and Jupiter worshipped on mountains; these matters are more correctly sought from the book itself, shortly to appear for public use. But in another letter, which conveyed to me the notes of that eminent man now enjoyed here by readers, he added the following: “I wrote earlier on this subject; but since they worshipped not mountains alone as gods, see whether one should rather read *omnium*: ‘worshipper of all the gods.’ Thus ch. 36: ‘who also performed sacrifices daily to all his gods.’ But perhaps she especially worshipped Elagabalus and other gods worshipped in the form of a mountain. For Elagabalus was so called as though ‘god mountain’ or ‘god of the mountain,’ as Salmasius teaches on the *Historia Augusta* after Fuller; and it is clear from Herodian and coins that his image was nothing other than a great stone. Relevant here is the Mother of the Gods, or Cybele, whom Maecenas in Diomedes III, p. 514 calls the ‘wild goddess of mountains,’ either because she was worshipped on mountains or because she was an unformed stone cut from a mountain. Certainly Maximus of Tyre, Dissertation XXXVIII, writes that the inhabitants worshipped Mount Atlas as a god, and that for the Cappadocians the mountain was ‘both god, oath, and statue’ (*kai theon, kai horkon, kai agalma*).

“More might be noted on this subject; but take, on the occasion of the Mother of the Gods, two emendations which I submit to your judgment. Strabo X, p. 469, writes that the Phrygians call her *pylinēn* from a place; but Pylene is a city of Aetolia, according to Stephanus and Statius. I therefore write *Sipylēnēn*, ‘Sipylene,’ a name given to the Mother of the Gods; and so on the Arundelian marble the Magnesians and Smyrnaeans swear ‘by the Sipylene Mother’ (*mētera tēn Sipylēnēn*). The other passage is from Varro in St Augustine, *City of God* VII.24:

> They call her the Great Mother because she has a drum, signifying that she is the globe of the earth; because she has towers on her head, [signifying] towns; because she is represented seated around them, although all things move, while she herself does not move.

Restore the last words thus: ‘because she is represented seated, while all things move around her, and she herself does not move.’ That is, the goddess is represented seated, as is clear from very many coins, because she herself—that is, the earth—does not move, although everything moves around her. This is not the place to investigate the doctrines of philosophers who taught either that the earth moves or that it remains motionless.” [Col. 0403D–0404C]

Lactantius rightly says “worshipper of the gods”; and likewise “worshippers of Mars” (*Marticultores*) occur in an ancient inscription in Gruter. I long ago emended what follows thus: “when she attended banquets, she sacrificed almost daily and offered feasts to her deputies.” From the final letter of *cum* and from the abbreviated manner of writing *ir* for *inter*, this preposition has been omitted; and the phrase itself shows that *epulas*, “feasts,” must be read. Thus she offered feasts to her deputies—that is, to courtly attendants, companions, prefects, who were around her—and, as follows, Christians abstained from them. Clearly, when she wished to offer banquets, she also sacrificed and ordered the remnants of the sacrifices (*leiphana*) to be brought to the tables. These were food offered to idols, from which Luke and Paul teach how Christians ought to abstain. I could note several things on this question, not obvious to everyone; but time does not permit. I shall only point out that Maximinus used the same fraud against Christians below, ch. 37.

These are the remarks of the most distinguished and learned Cuper. Since they offer a sufficiently clear explanation of this passage and are exceedingly pleasing in their elegance, I shall compress my own reflections on them into a few words. Those two emendations—of Varro’s words in St Augustine, and of Strabo’s phrase on the Idaean or Sipylene Mother—please me greatly; nor do I doubt that they will commend themselves to men much more learned than I. Nor does it seem wrong to substitute, for “of the mountains,” “worshipper of all the gods”; and indeed many altars were once dedicated to “all gods and goddesses,” “Jupiter and all gods,” “Silvanus and all gods,” and many similar formulas. Yet, since it is safer to adhere to the reading of the ancient manuscript, I interpret “gods of the mountains” as gods worshipped by the profane Gentiles. For Moses himself says that they placed their gods upon high mountains, hills, and beneath every leafy tree, Deuteronomy XII.2. Add 2 Kings [4 Kings] XVII.11 and other passages. Such testimonies and formulas from Holy Scripture seem to have been before Lactantius when he was composing a consolatory work for Christians, since nothing is thought more effective for their consolation or more powerful for assuaging the bitterness of events; he therefore often fashions his style upon them.

Nevertheless, nothing prevents us from including under these words either the gods of the Septimontium—whom Tertullian too, *To the Nations* II.15, expressly calls gods of the mountains: “of Arquis and Janus and the mountains of the Septimontium” (where perhaps one should read “of the Septimontium”)—or the gods of the Roman mountains, which were in Picenum in the district of Reate (mentioned by Siculus Flaccus and the other writers on agrarian matters), or other mountain gods. Except that the Silvanus, guardian of boundaries, did not admit the sacrifice of that Romulan woman: for it was forbidden that he should be worshipped in this manner by a woman. Yet I think Silvanus should by no means be excluded from the assembly of mountain gods mentioned by the inscription, nor from the company to which Commodianus points. For that Exuperantius boasts himself priest of Silvanus; and it seems likely to me that Commodianus here especially alludes to that priestling, Silvanus, and his fellow-altar and fellow-temple deities (*symbōmous kai synnaous*)—that is, Rustic Hercules, Father Liber, nymphs, and similar monsters—since he was devoted alike to their rites and to nocturnal warnings supposedly given to himself or others. [Col. 0404D–0405B]

But here is the inscription of that crude marble altar found on the Quirinal Hill:

> TO JUPITER THE LIGHTNING-BEARER. BY COMMAND OF THE MOUNTAIN GODS. VALERIUS CRESCENTIO, FATHER OF ALL THE GODS, AND AURELIUS EXUPERANTIUS, PRIEST OF SILVANUS, DEDICATED [THIS] WITH THE BROTHERS AND SISTERS.

Here *PATER* stands for *PATRI*, through the stonecutter’s error; and other faults also occur, but they are easily detected. The form *MONTENSES*, however, seems to designate specific mountains here, just as they called Diana of Nemi “Arician,” and in the same formation Ammianus has *Fretentes*, *Fabricenses*, and *Comitatenses*.
