It therefore seems safer to say that these were unknown gods, whose number or names people did not dare to investigate, worshipped nevertheless on identifiable mountains—just as *Campestres* are named in another inscription in Gruter, p. 1015, no. 2—or as they commonly worshipped the Genius, Tutela, and presiding gods of places.

Refer here the little story of the voice saying “I say”; likewise the formulas “whether god or goddess,” “to all gods,” “to the gods present,” “to the god, genius, and tutelary deity of this place,” “to the presiding gods of this place,” and many others, in which people carefully guarded against overlooking anyone improperly. To return, then, within definite limits: I think Lactantius and Commodianus refer to all the gods of the Gentiles, especially those commonly worshipped at Rome, or to those of the Septimontium, whom, as we have seen, Tertullian expressly calls gods of the mountains. But I think that inscription dedicated the altar only to those gods present upon the mountains where it had been consecrated.

The words “when she was,” with the following words, I conjecture to be sound if assisted by punctuation, thus: “Therefore, when she was [at table], she sacrificed at banquets daily.” *Cum esset* means “when she ate” or “dined.” Thus Valerius Maximus IV.3 at the end: “do not eat those things”; and Hyginus, *Fables* 139: Saturn asked Ops “that she might eat what she had borne.” The distinguished Heinsius pointed out both passages to me on Ovid, *Art of Love* III.757. “To sacrifice at banquets” is as in Lactantius I.21: “In which the priests themselves sacrifice not with their own blood but another’s”; and VI, final chapter: “Therefore one ought to sacrifice to God with the Word, since God is Word.” In Plautus’ *Mostellaria*: “If I had sacrificed silver to supreme Jupiter.” Understand “deputies” in a priestly matter. Thus the emperor Marcus Antoninus is said by Capitolinus, ch. 2, never to have performed a sacrifice through a deputy except when ill. [Col. 0405C–D]

“For it was his malice.” Eutropius IX.16: “Diocletian was crafty in character; moreover shrewd and exceedingly subtle in disposition, and desirous of satisfying his own severity through another’s unpopularity.” Read similar things in the excerpts of John of Antioch edited by Valesius. Diocletian seems to have observed Simonides’ precept given to Hiero in Xenophon, but extended it beyond proper bounds:

> A ruler should command others to inflict what necessity requires, but should dispense rewards himself.

“And as they thought.” The distinguished Baluzius saw in the addenda that one must read: “And those who thought otherwise.”

“Milesian Apollo.” On the oracle of Milesian Apollo, or of the Branchidae, see Strabo IX and what scholars have collected on the Oxford Marbles. Above all consult Valesius on Ammianus Marcellinus XXIX, and Isaac Vossius on Mela I.17, who offers few but excellent remarks.

## On Chapter XII

“On the seventh day before the Kalends of March.” Consider whether there is here an ellipsis of the word *diem*, “[on] the day,” a usage common even now in ordinary speech. Moreover, not only the calendar mentioned by Baluzius places the Terminalia on the seventh day before the Kalends of March, but other calendars no less ancient do so as well, including that celebrated one frequently published by Ciacconius, Paulus and Aldus Manutius, and later others. If certain calendars seem to differ, that results from the intercalation known to have been made in that month. Nor are those greatly mistaken who say that the churches were destroyed at Easter-time. For after the persecution began at the Terminalia, the tyrants pressed on fiercely in the following spring—indeed throughout the whole year. [Col. 0406B]

“While the old men held the consulship.” These words establish with certainty the time concerning which some scholars inquire with no slight dispute, as Baluzius also properly observes: namely, the time when the persecution began, the year of Christ 303, as Scaliger and Valesius correctly judged. See how Baluzius, Pagius, and others who undertook to examine these matters carefully infer this. According to Scaliger, it was the Antiochene year 351 of Christ; the Dionysian year 303. The Golden Number was XIX; the solar cycle IV. [Col. 0406B–C]

“Having gone to the Church.” One must certainly write “the prefect [having gone]”—that is, the prefect of the praetorian guard; otherwise the sequence of words will remain gaping and broken. The subsequent words prove it as well: the praetorians are said to have destroyed the church, while both emperors were watching.

“Yet that most lofty [defence].” I think one should write *tutamen*, “protection.” Virgil, Livy, and Arnobius, Lactantius’ teacher, use this word in a manner not much different from Lactantius here. Arnobius speaks of animals, II, p. 55, Leiden edition: “Do we not see some construct for themselves dwellings in the most suitable sites for nests; others shelter and fortify themselves upon hanging rocks and cliffs; others dig out the soil and prepare for themselves protections and beds in excavated burrows?” And p. 17: “Nor would they seek for themselves the protections and coverings of houses or garments.”

## On Chapter XIII

“Finally, that they should have neither liberty nor a voice.” A similar complaint occurs in St Gregory Nazianzen, *First Invective*:

> These measures were: that Christians should be deprived of every freedom of speech; that they should be excluded from every assembly, market, public festival, and even from the law courts themselves. For no one who had not burned incense before the altars set before him, and paid a great price for so great and serious a matter, was permitted to make use of these things.

To this may be added what our author relates below, ch. 15.

“Although not rightly.” No one should suppose that this phrase merely expresses slight disapproval. The old translator of the Bible uses it of things farthest removed from what is right and pious: 2 Kings [4 Kings] VII.9: “We do not act rightly; this day is a day of good news.” Ch. XVII.8: “And the children of Israel provoked the Lord their God with unrighteous words.” 1 Chronicles XXI, at the end: “And he walked not rightly.” Wisdom II.1: “For the ungodly said, thinking not rightly.” And ch. VI: “For, being ministers of his kingdom, you did not judge rightly.” So too older authors everywhere; for example Cicero, *For Gnaeus Plancius* 6: “That man rather than I? Either I do not know, or I do not say; or finally—what it would be most grievous for me to say, though I ought nevertheless to say it without fear—‘not rightly.’” Lactantius himself has spoken so above, ch. 7; elsewhere he says “not piously,” “not perfectly,” “not with an unblemished conscience.” [Col. 0406D–0407A]

“Yet with great spirit.” For the wise, nothing is great except what is also good; but they sometimes follow ordinary usage, at least in speech. Thus Cicero praises greatness of spirit in *For Milo*. Thus Seneca reproves Livy because he distinguishes a man of good spirit from a man of great spirit, *On Anger* III, final chapter. Yet Seneca himself, *To Marcia* 16, says: “Even one who has denied that the Gracchi were good will admit that they were great.” I seem to have read similar remarks in Hegesippus’ *Destruction of Jerusalem*. Certainly well known is Ovid’s phrase: “Yet he fell through great ventures.” It appears to be taken from that old iambic line read in Dionysius Longinus:

> To fail greatly is a noble error.

Scholars will determine whether it is more correctly read: “To fail in great matters.” [Col. 0407A–B]

“Cooked lawfully.” I think these words contain something like the words of St Lawrence in Prudentius:

> Turn over the part of my body  
> Already sufficiently roasted;  
> And test what your burning  
> Vulcan has achieved.  
>
> The prefect orders him turned.  
> Then he says: “It is cooked; devour it;  
> And make trial whether it is raw  
> Or more pleasantly roasted.”

“Cooked lawfully,” he says—that is, as I interpret it, cooked according to the lawful or customary manner of those handling pagan rites, or even culinary matters. Our people would say, “cooked in the ordinary way,” or “like another roast.” Thus “a lawful sacrifice” often occurs in sacred and secular books. Ovid has “lawful words”:

> Then the greatest Curio proclaims the Fornacalia  
> In the prescribed words.

Vegetius I.24 has “a lawful trench.” Hence Lactantius himself says “lawful rites,” V.2.

## On Chapter XIV

“He immediately ordered all his own people to be tortured.” Baluzius admits that the ancient manuscript has not *praecepit* (“ordered”), but *coepit* (“began”). I think the author left it so to cast odium on the tyrant: “He immediately began to torture all his own people.” For he adds: “He himself sat [there],” and the rest. Understand “all his own people” as courtiers serving him; in ch. 15 he calls them *domestici*, as the most distinguished and learned Cuper rightly observes. For in the period immediately following, *domestici* was the particular name for guards of the emperor’s person—both cavalry and infantry: those stationed at court were called *domestici*, while those in military service were *protectores*. [Col. 0407C]

“They were contending.” This is a figure of *macrologia*, or expansion, on which see Buchner, *On the Altered Mode of Speech* I.21. This kind is extremely frequent in Greek and Latin Bibles. Lactantius too writes thus, II.13: “The nations began to be wandering from the knowledge of God.” Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II.8: “For all these things are better than those which lack them.”

“But more swiftly observed.” In place of the preceding *sed*, “but,” *id* seemed to require restoration by a conjecture not open to doubt.

## On Chapter XV

“With millstones fastened to their necks.” Were those burned by fire the same persons who were afterwards drowned in the sea with millstones tied to them? No, indeed; they were others. Yet the preceding words cohere rather poorly. I judge that it should be corrected thus: “Lest they be dealt with one by one, since the multitude was so great, they were burned in groups with fire surrounding them; the *domestici*, with millstones fastened to their necks, were submerged in the sea.” Thus VII.21: “Then those whose sins have prevailed in weight or number will be touched by fire and burned.” Cyprian, *On Works*, etc.: “And they will go into eternal burning.” Ammianus Marcellinus XXX: “Their internal parts were burned by excessive heat.” Thus an ancient inscription in Antonio Agustín, Dialogue X: “WITH THE BODY BURNED,” that is, consumed by fire. Other authors say the same everywhere.

Yet if someone, because many preferred fire to death by suffocation in water—thinking that flame, kindred to souls, purified and cleansed them, whereas water crushed and extinguished them—should say that pagan emperors granted this as a kind of indulgence to the *domestici*, that they might be consumed by fire, while the others were annihilated by water as wicked and sacrilegious persons, I shall not strongly resist; I grant that one may read: “The *domestici* were burned in groups with fire surrounding them; the others, with millstones tied to their necks,” and so on. But for the moment I choose the former reading, since it does not displease the illustrious Cuper. [Col. 0407D–0408A]

“Altars in the courtrooms.” A *secretarium*, or *secretum*, is a place in which judges sit upon the tribunal. See Hesychius under *Sekreton*, and Suidas under *Stēlē*. Valesius on Ammianus Marcellinus XV: “From this custom of secular judges there seems to have arisen the practice that bishops and presbyters had *secretaria* in churches, where they were free to hear the affairs of the brethren.” So Valesius. Sulpicius Severus also mentions them, *Dialogue* 2.1 and Letters 1 and 3, *On the Life of Martin*; consult Vorstius’ notes there as well.

Altars insidiously placed by pagans are mentioned in more than one place in the ancient annals. Thus Symmachus laboured vigorously to have the altar of Victory placed in the Senate. Thus Julian, when about to distribute a donative to the soldiers, ordered that each man receiving gold should cast a few grains of incense upon the altars—so slight an act that it deceived many Christians who did not know what they were doing.

“Letters travel back and forth.” Symmachus I, Letter 91: “Because my letters are welcome to you, they will travel more frequently.”

“But the true temple of God.” Lactantius, *Epitome* 8: “Let the heart be emptied of every stain, so that it may be a temple of God, which is made bright not by the gleam of gold or ivory, but by the splendour of faith and chastity.” Jerome, *To Nepotian*: “Many build walls and erect columns for the church: marbles shine, ceilings gleam with gold, the altar is distinguished by jewels; but there is no selection of Christ’s ministers.” [Col. 0408B–C]

## On Chapter XVI

“Three most bitter beasts.” Thus “bitter truth,” Lactantius IV.26; “bitter dominations,” VI.6; “bitter taxes,” VII.9.

“Then against Hierocles.” This is that Hierocles who afterwards governed Egypt. When he cruelly persecuted Christians by disgraceful means, Aedesius—after he had publicly confessed his name among the other martyrs—met him with harsh words and struck him with his fist. See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.5. Different from him, and somewhat older, was the Hierocles of whom Dio Cassius speaks in the Valesian excerpts, Elagabalus’ foulest slave; and distinct again from both was Hierocles the philosopher, no more favourably inclined toward Christian truth, who under Julian the Apostate disseminated most virulent writings. Consult Jonsius, *On the Writers of Philosophical History* III.18.

“Priscillian.” Prefect of Bithynia after those men mentioned above. See Baluzius’ notes.

“You defeated the adversary nine times.” Tertullian, *Apology* 27: “And we never triumph over those demons more than when we are condemned for the obstinacy of faith.” Similar statements occur in Cyprian, Ambrose, Prudentius, and likewise in the martyrologies.

“Zabolus with his attendants.” Aeolians change Delta into Zeta: *zanyktos* for *dianyktos*; *zaballein* for *diaballein*; hence *zabolos* for *diabolos*, a form used also by Cyprian, Hilary, and others. Indeed Paulinus scarcely ever says anything other than *Zabolus*. Similar is *zeta* for *diaeta*. Thus Vossius, *On the Art of Grammar* I.21; Gronovius, *Observations* IV.13, p. 208. [Col. 0408C–D]

“How delightful that spectacle [was] to God . . .” Cyprian, Letter 9 to the Martyrs: “O what a spectacle it was to the Lord! How sublime! How great! How acceptable to God’s eyes through the sacrament and devotion of his soldier!” Add what Lipsius adduces from Minucius Felix and Epictetus on those noted words of Seneca, *On Providence* I.2: “Behold a spectacle worthy for God, intent upon his work, to look upon; behold a thing worthy of God’s equal—a brave man matched against adverse fortune.”

“When rulers exercise rule.” Cyprian, Letter 6: “Now is the time that they should fear the adversary more as he lies in wait; for he attacks every stronger man more fiercely, and, made keener by the very fact that he has been defeated, strives to overcome his conqueror.” And Letter 34, on Celerinus the Martyr: “Amid punishments he lay stronger than his punishments; enclosed, greater than those enclosing him; lying down, loftier than those standing; bound, stronger than those binding him; judged, higher than those judging him.”

“By a wicked command.” Thus *Divine Institutes* IV.15: “He acted by word and command”; V.13: “They do not tremble at tyrannical commands or the swords of governors.” See more in Elmenhorst on Arnobius II, p. 67.

“And bogeys.” See Nonius on this word. Moreover, from Naevius they cite “an empty bogey,” and from Seneca’s lost works, “Mock all his bogeys.” Livy too has it, XXXIV.11: “They were moved by no threats, by no bogeys.”

“With steadfast faith.” I suspect that one word has slipped out: perhaps, “with steadfast faith and unconquered strength of spirit.”

“Nothing [could] the claw.” *Ungulae* are a kind of iron pincer formerly employed among instruments of torture. For their form see Gallonius, or the materials appended to Magius’ book *On the Rack*, pp. 176 and 81.

## On Chapter XVII

“The day of the vicennalia.” Although the origin and rationale of the solemn vows—namely the quinquennial, decennial, and thereafter—have been transmitted by learned scholars, I shall nevertheless recount them briefly for the benefit of those for whom books of this kind may not be readily at hand. When Caesar Augustus, after restoring and settling the Roman state following the greatest upheavals and disturbances, had governed for ten years, whether because he was worn down by protracted ill health and the cares and labours of empire and seriously considered restoring the republic (as Suetonius seems to affirm in *Augustus* 28), or merely pretended to do so for reasons set out at length by Dio, he summoned the Senate and rendered an account of his administration of the empire in such a way that, as though by the Senate’s decree, he retained for the next five years the power to settle the republic.

When this period had elapsed, another five years were again decreed; after the ten-year period, and after its completion, another period once more. Thus, through uninterrupted decades, he retained supreme power throughout his life. His successors in some measure followed this example: although imperial power had been conferred upon them not for a fixed period but for their whole lifetime, they nevertheless celebrated a festival at every ten-year interval for its renewal. Dio, Book LIII, and later writers following him relate this approximately thus. It was first done under Augustus in his seventh consulship and Agrippa’s third. Subsequent emperors accordingly celebrated these festivals every ten years—called by Xiphilinus *dekaetērides*, “decennial celebrations”—at which vows were paid to the gods, and at the beginning of each decade vows were thereafter customarily made solemnly. A donative was given to soldiers, and grain-distributions and circus-games to the people.

Indeed, this began subsequently to be repeated at each *lustrum*, or five-year period. Thus quinquennial vows were undertaken in the first year of an office; but they were paid when the five-year period had passed. Then decennial vows were pronounced, to be paid only after the second five-year period had been completed. Vicennial vows were undertaken in the fifteenth year of an emperor’s reign; but the festival itself was celebrated in the twentieth, when gifts also customarily were sent to the emperor. On this see Symmachus X, Letter 26. Moreover, prisoners were released from confinement, thanks were given to God, money was distributed through the cities, and public rejoicing was displayed in many ways. Coins teach this more fully in Adolphus Occo, Erizzo, and Chaluce; others confirm or repeat it, such as Charles du Fresne, *Dissertation on Coins of the Lower Age*, p. 29. Henry Noris likewise treated the same subject with great care in his *Dissertation on Decennial Vows*, and Antonius Pagius in his *Hypatic Dissertation, or On Caesarean Consulships*. [Col. 0409B–0410A]

“On the twelfth day before the Kalends of December.” On this passage see Antonius Pagius, pp. 90, 92, and 93 of the work just mentioned. He maintains that Diocletian did not celebrate his *vicennalia* on this day because it was the anniversary of his accession, but because Maximian Herculius had then been proclaimed Caesar. This sometimes happened, certainly after the time of Constantine the Great: when some reason intervened, a festival of this kind was celebrated not on the birthday of the principal emperor himself, but on that of his partner—that is, the day upon which the partner had assumed imperial office.

“By whatever means he was being pressed.” I read: “So that, however, he was being pressed” (*quo utcumque se premi*).

The soul . . . yet not the whole of it. That is, life, or the vital spirits. Thus the old translator of the Bible, II Sam. 1:9: “For distress has seized me, and yet my whole [Col. 0410B] soul is still in me.” Usuard’s Martyrology, 30 January: “And there they expelled the spirit that remained in him.” See Barthius, *Adversaria*, p. 1682.

## ON CHAPTER XVIII

“He said it was unbecoming to him.” Write: “He said it was also unbecoming,” so that this clause may answer the following one, “and less safe,” more neatly.

“He had incurred the hatred of many.” Lactantius, book II, ch. 12: “Through His divine and unique name he seeks for himself the mercy of men.” And book IV, ch. 1: “They sought perpetual death for themselves, together with the gods and bodily goods.” Add Gronovius on Seneca, *Hercules Furens*, v. 285.

“But Nerva, having reigned for one year.” The requirements of syntax prove that it should be written: “But Nerva, reigning for one year.”

“He himself had already longed . . .” I read: “He had already longed in hope, since he saw that from that source nothing, or not much beyond the name, accrued to him.” Nothing—or very little—seemed to accrue to Galerius if the two senior emperors retained supreme power while he, content with the name of Caesar, held third or fourth place.

“Fifteen years had now elapsed.” Lactantius, book III, ch. 17, expressing the adversaries’ view: “Let us not allow a single day, indeed not a single instant of time, to pass from us without pleasure.”

“Fifteen years, into Illyricum.” He seems to have had in view Livy, book VII, ch. 38: “Was it fair that their surrendered subjects should enjoy that good fortune” (Leiden edition, 1634: “enjoy that fertility and pleasantness”), “while they, wearied by military service, struggled in the pestilential and arid soil around the city?”

“To be called sons.” *Institutes*, book I, ch. 8: “Whom the ignorant and foolish both call and worship as gods.” So book IV, ch. 4: “to call father,” “to call lord,” though in a somewhat different sense. For here *nuncupare* means to proclaim someone Caesar, and consequently to call him to the inheritance and right of one day obtaining the empire.

“Most holy young man.” That is, of the most upright and innocent life. Thus Lactantius says of pagans, book V, ch. 10: “Although they may live with holy morals, in the highest faithfulness and innocence, nevertheless, because they worship gods, they are alien from justice and from the name of true piety.” This word is very frequent in Symmachus, who, I suppose, was emulating Christians. In his fifth book alone see how often he repeats it: Epistle 15, “To holy Lampadius, your brother”; Ep. 20, “Holy Aurelius”; Ep. 29, “The holy philosopher Asclepiades”; Ep. 39, “Holy Sabius”; Ep. 49, “From your most holy and eloquent mouth.” I shall not heap up further examples.

“He rendered faithfully.” Cuper’s earlier interpretation of this passage is wholly correct. Thus in the Latin Bible, II Chronicles 31:18: “Food from the things that had been consecrated was faithfully supplied to the priests by families and to the Levites.” Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXVIII: “Because they refused to supply the necessities for expeditionary purposes.” They similarly said “to supply suitable things,” “to supply what is due,” “annual supplies,” “daily supplies,” and the like. Lactantius, *Institutes*, book IV, [Col. 0411A] ch. 8: “That we may render to God, who begot us, just and due works.”

“That he might be clothed by him.” Others used *vestire*, “to clothe [with office],” as Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXVI: “If you love your own, best emperor, you have a brother; if the republic, seek one whom you may invest.”

“Daja, a young man.” I suppose he was so called because he derived his origin from the people of the Dahae—not so much that people situated near the Caspian Sea, known from writers on Alexander’s exploits, as the European, and indeed Germanic, people. See what Cluverius collected concerning them in *Germanic Antiquities*, Freinshemius on Curtius, and Dausqueius on Silius Italicus.

## ON CHAPTER XIX

1 May. Baluze noted that Zosimus and the Idatian Fasti say this occurred on 1 April, while others place it even further away; nevertheless Antonius Pagius thinks there can likewise be no doubt that Lactantius’s date, 1 May, must be retained. See the same author, p. 239 of the dissertation mentioned, and several other passages.

[Col. 0411B] “And the foremost of the soldiers.” I think one should read *primores militum*, “the leading men of the soldiers,” as Livy, Tacitus, and others very frequently do. Lactantius too said “the leading men of the Jews,” book IV, ch. 16; Hegesippus, *On the Destruction of Jerusalem*, book II, ch. 15: “Even certain leading men of the soldiery being afflicted.”

“The old man says.” I emend to “in which the old man,” namely in the assembly, “receives”; for what a very learned man suggests, namely that it should be joined with the following “he addresses,” cannot suitably fit here.

“He addresses the soldiers.” Properly so, as others have noted; hence *allocutiones*, “addresses,” occur often on coins.

“All on the tribunal.” Punctuate: “All are astonished. Constantine stood above on the tribunal.” For not only those standing on the tribunal were astonished, but the others as well. You have *susum*, “upward,” in Plautus, *Cistellaria*, Act II, scene 3, v. 78:

> Why do you now, lying on your back, look upward into heaven?

Thus indeed two ancient manuscripts read, according to Paraeus in the *Analecta*, and Gruter printed it twice in this manner. Cato too uses it at the end of *On Agriculture*, ch. 157. So in the decree concerning the arbitration of boundaries between the Genuates and Veiturians, printed in Gruter’s collection, p. 204:

> There the boundary stands; thence, up the stream toward the River Lemuris; thence up the River Lemuris as far as the Comberanean brook; thence up the Comberanean brook as far as the Caepetiam valley.

The same word remains in compounds: *sustollo*, *suspendo*, *suscipio*, *sustineo*, and similar words. Ducange offers more in his *Glossary*.

“Immediately a guardsman, forthwith a protector.” These are ranks of honorable military service, on which learned men have written abundantly. Above all see Valesius on Ammianus Marcellinus, book XIV. He shows that among the Palatine schools there were some of guardsmen (*scutarii*), others of archers, and others of mailed cavalry (*clibanarii*); that the *protectores* guarded the emperor’s side; and that some remained in the retinue, while others were sent with counts and masters of soldiers into the provinces. Constantius Chlorus, nephew through a brother of the deified Claudius, that excellent emperor, was first a *protector*, then tribune, and later governor of Dalmatia, as the extracts published by Valesius show [Col. 0411D].

## ON CHAPTER XX

“What he wished, he did.” I think the author wrote *effecit*, “he accomplished.” Thus *Divine Institutes*, book VI, ch. 14: “We shall soon see whether they accomplish what they wish.” An inscription of the same times in Adolphus Occo, p. 11, no. 3, in Commelin’s edition:

> To the Emperor Maximian Hercules Caesar Augustus, Constantius having been made Caesar in the West, and the empire of the republic having been enlarged far and wide, and he also having been made colleague at the same time with Diocletian, the unconquered prince.

“He represented himself as lord.” I suspect *esse*, “to be,” was added by a copyist. Velleius Paterculus, book I, ch. 11: “Who represented himself as Philip and of royal stock.” Tacitus, *Annals*, I.2: “Presenting himself as consul.”

“His son Caesar.” Candidianus, born of a concubine, but also adopted by his wife Valeria, as our author will relate below, [Col. 0412A] ch. 50. I think Baluze interpreted this quite correctly.

## ON CHAPTER XXI

“Let them devote themselves.” *Divine Institutes*, book II, ch. 1: “They devote their whole selves to lusts.” Book VI, chs. 20 and 23: “Because they had devoted themselves to the body, in which death has power.” On this Persian institution or custom, read Brissonius.

“Thus he acted.” Unless you add “thus he acted secretly,” or “by arts customary to himself,” or something similar, there will be nothing clearly answering the preceding passage.

“Men of most distinguished and most perfect rank.” Not merely town councillors, who indeed were not called men of distinguished and most perfect rank, but also persons of higher standing: such as duumvirs, defenders of cities, priests, curiales, and anyone among or beyond these who, by diplomas issued by emperors, had obtained the honors and insignia of the ranks *egregius* and *perfectissimus*. Without any regard for those dignities—and thus after they had been stripped from them—they were subjected [Col. 0412B] by him to torture. For more on these and other titles see Pancirollus on the *Notitia of the Empire*.

“Fastened in a stable.” Here understand *stabulum* not as a stable for horses, but for racks and apparatus of that kind, where people stood fixed to stakes and nearly suspended. Thus you have *stabulum ferriterium*, “an iron-mongers’ workshop,” in Plautus, *Persa*, Act III, scene 3, v. 13, according to Gronovius’s emendation.

“What a place of sport!” *Lusorium* means an amphitheatre, if we follow Salmasius on Spartianus. Yet from this passage one may infer that the term denotes a building specifically assigned to the emperor’s amusement in watching the slaughtering of beasts, or the butcheries perpetrated by them. The scholiast on Juvenal, Satire IV, v. 100: “In the young Caesar’s *lusorium* this youth often killed bears as a hunter.” Salvian too lists a *lusorium* as distinct from an amphitheatre, in words cited by Du Fresne, where see more. Indeed Seneca, *Letter* 80: “I reflect how many exercise their bodies, how few their minds; what a crowd gathers for a spectacle neither genuine nor serious, but sporting; [Col. 0412C] and how great is the solitude around the noble arts.”

“He kept bears.” Ammianus Marcellinus says not dissimilar things of Valentinian, book XXIX: “When he had two savage, man-devouring she-bears, Golden Mica and Innocence, he took especial care that their cages should be set near his own bedchamber, and that faithful keepers should be assigned, who would diligently ensure that the deadly fury of the beasts did not break loose by some accident. Finally, after seeing many burials of corpses mangled by Innocence, he released her unharmed into the woods as one who had deserved well.”

“And of exile.” This is a difficult passage, and I should gladly see it restored by others; nevertheless I shall attempt it myself. I think the scribal abbreviation *cros*, which ought to have denoted “the others,” was changed into *Christianos*, “Christians”; and that *exilii* was written in place of *exilium*, just as in the following chapter *beneficii* stands for *beneficium*, and *imperii* for *imperium* in Aurelius Victor, *On the Caesars*, ch. 35, as Schott rightly conjectured—the copyist’s hand sometimes, evidently, faltering. With these observations in mind, I write: “For those without rank, the punishment was fire; or, if the mention of Christians is thought altogether necessary, because the chief discussion concerns them: ‘For Christians without rank the punishment was fire; for the leading men he had permitted exile’”—meaning Roman leading men, for the municipal decurions were previously discussed—“against the others he had issued laws, so that after torture they should be burned by slow fires.” Cyprian, Letter 82, recounts a not wholly dissimilar series of punishments, which you may more properly read there.

“Throughout much of the day.” Thus it had already been printed at Åbo, I suppose through the conjecture of a very learned man who did not disdain to oversee the labor of having this little work correctly published there. Subsequently the letters of the most distinguished Cuper confirmed it. The Paris edition had: “What was added at last. Then through . . .” For “into river and sea,” perhaps “into rivers and sea” has also rightly been restored; for I can readily believe Lactantius wrote thus. Yet “they were thrown into the river” is not entirely unprecedented. In the *Passion of Bishop and Martyr Savinus*, ch. X, you have: “He ordered everything to be broken up and thrown into the river”; and Lactantius also uses it not rarely, as I shall show below [Col. 0413A]. Ovid too has *mare* for *mari* in several passages, and before him each Varro did so, as others have observed. I shall therefore not oppose anyone who insists that the reading of the first edition should be retained.

## ON CHAPTER XXII

“No punishment was light in his hands.” I agree with the learned Baluze in making *penes* from what was *poenis* in the manuscript. But since the word *poena*, “punishment,” occurs below, according to his own testimony, I think this should be arranged thus: “No punishment was light in his hands.”

“They were corrected with a spear.” I think this kind of penalty was a form of beating, as our Cuper also believed; and that a spear was used in place of a rod, as less disgraceful. Apuleius, book X, ch. 1: “A spear conspicuous for its very long shaft, which he had set up, not at that time for the sake of discipline, but in order to terrify the wretched travelers . . .” You find “to reform the Roman state by laws” and “to reform cities by judicial decisions” in Horace and Quintilian [Col. 0413B].

“In the place of a benefit.” I said in the preceding chapter that there is no need to insert *loco*, “in the place of,” and that one should write *beneficium*, “a benefit.” Dio, book LVIII, p. 634: “And he made life a punishment for some, and death a benefit.” So too others.

“A good death.” That is, an easy death, free from torment. Pliny, book II, final letter: “How long do you torture the wretch? Why do you begrudge him a good death, when you cannot give him life?” Add Gruter and Buchner on that passage. Publilius Syrus:

> A good death for a man is that which takes away the evils of life.

## ON CHAPTER XXIII

“Census officials scattered everywhere.” Haste does not permit me to set forth what I have discussed concerning the method of the provincial census, or assessment (*censitio*), and its difference from the urban census. It is known to everyone that Augustus likewise surveyed the provinces in this way. Later Vespasian, [Col. 0413C] Constantine the Great, Arcadius, Justinian, and others did so as well, as the laws expressly show.

“All the marketplaces.” Thus I emended it, with the approval of the most learned Cuper. The Paris edition read: “all outside places.”

“They themselves were tortured against themselves.” That is, they were compelled by tortures to accuse and, as it were, convict themselves. Lactantius likes such conceits. Thus *Divine Institutes*, book I, ch. 18: “inferior or uglier than himself”; ch. 22: “But though he deceived others, he nevertheless did not deceive himself”; book II, ch. 1: “to restore themselves to favor with themselves, lest they despise themselves so greatly”; likewise: “therefore they renounce themselves.” Still more apposite are these: book III, ch. 27, “They were so uncertain, and often argued things contrary to themselves”; book V, ch. 2, “Himself a severe censor and most vehement accuser against himself”; book VI, ch. 6, “And they cut off the steps by which they ascended, lest anyone be able to imitate them against themselves”; book VII, ch. 2, “opinions contrary to themselves.” Others offer similar examples, among them Ovid, wittily:

> Against yourself, ingenious human nature, you have acted,  
> And have been too inventive in devising your own harms.

Cicero speaks quite similarly, and equally in forensic matters. *For Roscius the Actor*, ch. 6: “What do you, Saturninus, who come against this man, think otherwise?” Ch. 13: “You—yes, you, Fannius—I shall summon from your own benches as a witness against you”; ch. 14: “He will never give testimony against himself.” And elsewhere similarly. The particle *contra*, “against,” is very common in legal proceedings and has the flavor of legal formulae. Julius Capitolinus, *Antoninus Pius*, ch. 6: “He gladly heard complaints against his procurators.” The older writers too frequently use it thus, as when Cicero says “to defend a case against another advocate,” “to argue against,” and the like.

“What conquerors [did] against the conquered.” Read with Baluze in the addenda: “what conquerors [did] against the conquered.”

“They paid for their heads.” It is well known that the ancient Romans did not reject the capitation tax, among whom the poorer were *capite censi*, “assessed by the head.” Constantine exempted only the Roman plebs from this tax. See Franciscus Balduinus, *On the Laws of Constantine*, p. 154.

[Col. 0414A] “Not even to die for nothing.” He alludes to the proverb κᾷν ἀπὸ νεκροῦ φέρει, “to carry away something even from a corpse,” found in Aristotle, *Rhetoric*, book II, ch. 6 [elsewhere 14].

“But surely, an impious man.” Others would prefer always to write this separately, *at quin*. See Brissonius, *Parerga*, or Isaeus on Lactantius, book I, ch. 4. Lactantius himself, book IV, ch. 12: “But surely the prophet comprehends both His comings in a few words.” Thus the manuscript of Franciscus Pena, according to Servatius Gallaeus. More necessary is the correction in book V, ch. 9, where it is now read: “Likewise it cannot happen that those who err throughout life should err also in religion.” There perhaps one should read: “should not err also in religion.” Unless, on the traces of the Bologna manuscript, which has *atquin* for *aeque*, one should write: “But it cannot happen that those who err throughout life should not err also in religion.” The sense certainly is that persons driven by error through their whole life cannot keep the straight path of religion either. Moreover, since the tyrant is here being ridiculed, it is probable that he was called not “an impious man” but “that pious man,” ironically. For it is known that in that age merciful or kindly inclined emperors were called *pii*, “pious,” as in Claudian:

> Be pious above all; for though we are surpassed in every  
> Gift, clemency alone makes us equal to the gods.

On this manner of speaking see Augustine, *City of God*, book X, ch. 1, and among modern writers Scaliger on Ausonius. A similar irony occurs in Terence, *Andria*, 5.2: “O Chremes, the piety of your son!”

“Such a merciful man.” Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, book I, ch. 21: “Men so barbarous, so savage, that they called their own parricide a sacrifice.” Cicero, book V, letter 11: “A serious man and an outstanding citizen.” See more in Gronovius on Seneca, *Consolation to Marcia*, ch. 9.

“Thus, while he took precautions.” More correctly, “takes precautions,” since “he may evade” follows.

“Against every law of humanity.” Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, book V, ch. 19: “Is there an evil mind in those who are torn to pieces against the law of humanity, against every divine right?” Ch. 22: “Nor does he covet anything belonging to another, lest his speech injure anyone against the law of humanity.” He discusses the same law more fully in book VI, chs. 10 and 20 [Col. 0414C].

## ON CHAPTER XXIV

“The judgment of God.” He seems to have had in mind II Maccabees 9:4: “He being pressed hard by heavenly judgment”; and v. 18: “For the just judgment of God had come upon him.”

“His affairs were dissolving and slipping away.” He refers to Virgil’s familiar words, *Aeneid* II:

> From that point the hopes of the Danaans began to ebb,  
> And, slipping backward, to be borne away.

“Often in ambushes.” Perhaps *in* should more properly be deleted.

“The hand of God protected the man.” Lactantius, book II, ch. 15: “Whom the mighty and exalted hand of God protects.”

“At the very turning-point.” Thus *Divine Institutes*, book II, ch. 8: “This, therefore, is the hinge of things; here all things turn.” Similarly book III, ch. 7, and *On the Anger of God*, ch. 6.

[Col. 0414D] “Since he had long been killing.” Baluze rightly emended *necare*, “killing,” to *negare*, “refusing,” in his second recension. And perhaps, moreover, *diu*, “long,” should be changed to *diutius*, “for longer.”

“He gave him a seal.” *Sigillum* may mean an order, letter, diploma, or the letter itself furnished with a seal; so a *bulla* is a diploma equipped with its own seal. The Greek-Latin glossaries: σύνθημα, “seal; travel warrant.” These matters and more are treated by Carolus Du Fresne, a man exceptionally learned in this field. Nor must it be denied that, in the age of Augustus and the emperors immediately following, diplomas granting use of the public post were countersigned by the emperor himself or by some proconsul or governor. Yet Budaeus seems not wrongly to have concluded that in some age only tokens bearing the emperor’s seal were valid; Scheffer, our countryman, confessed that he inclined to this opinion in the first book of his work *On the Vehicular Service*, ch. 18, p. 264. Jerome calls it a *synthema* in his letter to Julian: “When the *synthema* had now been sent down, the public horse was saddled, and a belt encircled the noble [Col. 0415A] youth, clothed in a purple tunic.” Livy calls the *synthemata* also mentioned by Polybius—though these are undoubtedly different from the former—secret signs through which the recipients might recognize that the sender’s instructions were genuine. Add Lipsius on Tacitus, *Annals* XIII.2; Casaubon on Aeneas Tacticus; Salmasius on Julius Capitolinus, *Pertinax*, ch. 1. Nor would it be absurd to say that these contained a kind of signs called *sigla* by Emperor Justinian, used by *semeiographers* or *tachygraphers*, that is, writers in signs or shorthand writers. Nicolaus Heinsius, an illustrious man, refutes in a letter to my late father-in-law—long ago kindly shared with me by him—those who understood these *sigla* to be individual letters, as Valerius Probus held. Had the matter been within my own power, that letter would long since have been published. The same I wish said of no few other writings that now lie hidden in the papers of my late father-in-law, wholly against my will and desire.

“Rest from life, as he wished.” The author of the *Polity of Metrophanes and Alexander*, cited by Photius, reports his most elegant words:

> Now death is sweeter to me than life, since I receive as my greatest funeral gift your rule, my son. For to leave upon earth an emperor able to wipe away the tears of Christians and to halt the unjust slaughter which Maximian does not cease to perpetrate against Christians already grants me a blessed end.

“To render [him] to his God.” Perhaps Concinnius: “that he might render [him] to his God.”

“The restoration of holy religion.” I think it should rightly be emended thus, since the Paris edition has merely *restituta*, “restored.” So below, ch. 48: “the sanction of this our benevolence.” That age uses this construction very frequently. Yet, if this brevity does not please someone sufficiently, one might read: “This was his first enactment: holiness restored to religion.” Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, I.4: “Holiness is knowledge of worshipping the gods”; II.2: “The worship of the gods and the sanctities of religions,” likewise joined together. Indeed Lactantius himself similarly says at the beginning of the *Divine Institutes*: “Through whom justice and holiness were restored to human affairs.” For him “holy religion,” “man, a holy animal,” “holy writings,” and the like are quite common [Col. 0415C].

## ON CHAPTER XXV

“His laureate image.” Laureate—or, as they were later called, laurate—images had various uses; but their chief use was at emperors’ inaugurations. For immediately after they had attained the Augustan rank, their statues were sent into the provinces as a sign of the dignity acquired and so that they might be received by the peoples. Philostorgius, book XII, ch. 10: “The images of Constantine, as was customary for those who had newly entered kingship, are sent to the East.” These matters, and more to the same effect, are in Ducange’s most learned glossary; much else could be added from other sources if necessary. See below on ch. 42.

“His accounts were thrown into confusion.” Disordered or confused accounts are contrasted with accounts that are clear and readily settled. Thus Petronius has “to throw a census into confusion” and “to throw foreign luxuries into confusion”; on these see Gronovius, *Observations* 3.11. Unless you prefer to refer this to disordered arrangements of landed estates, of which agricultural writers speak, and on whom Rigaltius and Goesius, very learned men, comment.

“But he devised this.” Lactantius, *On the Workmanship of God*, ch. 3: “For what will he devise? What will he do? What will he contrive?”

## ON CHAPTER XXVI

“To devour the world.” The old translator of Isaiah, ch. 24:6: “Therefore a curse shall devour the earth.” Lactantius, book VII, ch. 16: “They will destroy all things, crush them, and devour them.” The *Epitome*, ch. 11, also speaks thus twice, leaving aside older writers.

“To register the populace.” Lactantius, *Institutes*, book I, ch. 22: “He registered the gods by households.” It is a very common word concerning the census or assessment; similarly among the Greeks, ἀπογραφή and ἀπογράφειν, “registration” and “to register.”

“Having obtained an opportunity.” I would not have changed *nancti*, which is in the Paris edition. And learned editors ensured that Livy, book XXV, ch. 30, should read: “Having found Mericus without arbiters.” The glosses: *nanctus*, δραξάμενος, “having seized.” It also appears in ancient books among other writers [Col. 0416A].

“Excessively terrified.” *Nimium* means “very,” ἄγαν. *Divine Institutes*, book V, ch. 10: “If they have been excessively pious”; *On the Workmanship of God*, ch. 9: “If you bring anything too close”; where one should read *nimio propius*, “too much closer.” Thus Livy, book I: “More than was sufficiently safe for the inhabitants.” Horace:

> And glory, raising its empty head too high.

Plautus said *nimio satius*, “much more suitably,” and others use expressions not unlike it.

“He sought how.” In that age *quatenus* more often means “how.” Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, book I, ch. 21: “The Egyptian rites of Isis concern how she lost or found her little son”; book IV, ch. 27: “He who sees will know how those adjured through Christ flee from bodies”; book VII, ch. 6: “How, or why, human beings were begotten.”

“To protect himself against the impending danger.” Lactantius, *Epitome*, [Col. 0416B] ch. 6: “Our life is protected by the most severe laws”; *On the Workmanship of God*, ch. 4: “That it might protect its frailty against harmful things”; ch. 10: “That the eyes might be more protected against injury.”

“Meanwhile Severus goes.” This wording seems less fitting to the elegance of our Firmianus: “Severus goes and approaches the walls.” I think it should be written: “Meanwhile Severus invades Italy.” It is no objection that these words are repeated shortly afterward, namely in the next chapter. For we see Lactantius frequently use habitual verbal formulas, provided this could be done without tiring readers.

“And the garment and purple.” Is this a hendiadys? I would rather believe that both an inner and an outer garment are meant, since each bore some insignia of imperial majesty.

“From this head [he began] to pursue his own.” Even very learned men acknowledge the difficulty of determining what these mutilated words mean. I suspect the author of this work briefly says that Max. Galerius made a beginning, or *caput*, of persecuting his own people from Severus—whether you take *caput* for “person” or “beginning.” Thus Ovid:

> Looking up at this [place], and from it beholding the Capitol.

Curtius, book V, ch. 2: “After these came Antigonus, and from him Amyntas the Lyncestian.” Florus, book III, ch. 18: “So that victorious Asia and Europe might seek Rome from Corfinium.” And others similarly, not infrequently [Col. 0416C].

## ON CHAPTER XXVII

“With the city fortified and rendered hostile to the enterprises begun.” I think it read: “With the city fortified and rendered hostile to the enterprises begun, he carefully prepares war and departs for Gaul.” The enterprises were those undertaken by Severus and, after his death, by Galerius; by these actions, that is, machinations, he made the city hostile. You also find “to prepare a contest” in Lactantius, book VI, ch. 22.

“With their spirits cast down.” More fittingly, I think, “with their spirits lowered.”

“A spirit elated by immense promises.” With Baluze one should write: “Until by immense promises he bent their minds”; or, as I prefer: “until, having bent the minds of certain persons by immense promises, he turned the standards back.”

“But Dacian.” The Paris edition had *Daciscum*, which I would not lightly change. For you find *Dacisci* for Dacians even in Vopiscus, *Aurelian*, ch. 38 at the end; Salmasius shows that he similarly said *Hunnisci*, *Teotisci*, and *Maurisci*.

## ON CHAPTER XXVIII

“The other Maximian.” Herculius, who, as was said above in ch. 26, held the resumed imperial power jointly with his son Maxentius.

“The prince of calamities.” Thus Jupiter is “prince of religions” in *Divine Institutes*, book I, ch. 21; and there likewise the “princes” are to be understood as the divine Curetes; the Pythagoreans, Stoics, and Peripatetics are “princes of every discipline,” book II, ch. 8.

“What the republic might endure.” *Divine Institutes*, book VI, ch. 8: [Col. 0417A] “For the sake of which it is so great a thing both to forgo pleasures and to endure every evil”; ch. 18: “Let us endure one another and bear the evils of this life through mutual assistance.”

## ON CHAPTER XXIX

“When he had stayed a little, he departed.” Punctuate: “When he had stayed a little, he departed . . .”; or: “He departed against the enemy of his son . . .” Below, I think *in Severi locum*, “into Severus’s place,” was written, not merely *loco*, though I do not forget that examples of the latter usage are also found.

“What he had not previously done.” Antonius Pagius, *Hypatic Dissertation*, p. 245, understands *ante*, “previously,” of the time when he proclaimed Severus Augustus or Licinius Caesar. Moved by the authority of what the most distinguished Cuper cited in his support, I do not think Licinius was declared Caesar in such a way as to have been fully adopted into the immediate expectation of imperial power. Yet where Aurelius Victor, according to Schott, ch. 40, and the anonymous author of the *Life of Constantius Chlorus and His Son Constantine the Great*, say that Galerius made him Caesar, I conjecture that this is like what is said above, ch. 18, of Maximinus: “Diocletian had now also changed his name in part”—that is, some rank had been conferred on him through the favor of Galerius, so strongly disposed toward him, but he was not declared Caesar in the full sense.

“Thus there were six at one time.” From this one may infer that Diocletian, or Diocles, should not be counted among them. Antonius Pagius nevertheless thinks that Aurelius Victor says he held the empire for twenty-five years because even in this year he took part in public deliberations; and this passage makes that sufficiently clear. Without him there were certainly six, namely, as the learned Baluze also lists them: Maximian Herculius, Galerius Maximianus, Maximinus, Constantine, and Licinius. Herculius indeed was not then ruling in good faith; nevertheless I would sooner believe that he completed this number than Diocles.

“Full of evil contagion and crime.” This manner of speaking is frequent in sacred and secular writings. Thus Joshua 7 says that Israel was defiled by the accursed thing, and Achan contaminated by crime. Lactantius said “to be contaminated and bound by inexpiable crime,” book V, ch. 1, and *Epitome*, ch. 6. Solomon speaks somewhat differently, Proverbs 5:22: “His own iniquities seize the wicked man, and he is bound by the cords of his sins.” The Greeks express it very elegantly: “Lawlessness ensnares a man, and he is bound fast by the cords of his own sins.” Add Salmasius on Solinus, p. 1091 [Col. 0417C].

“He flies back with the army.” Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, book II, ch. 12: “Until, released from the prison of the body, it flies back to its own abode.”

“He hears of the crimes that he committed.” Elegantly said of one liable to punishment. Thus *Divine Institutes*, book V, ch. 19: “He hears what God threatens him with.”

## ON CHAPTER XXX

“He summons his daughter Fausta.” Her image on a coin may be found in the most illustrious Spanheim, *On the Use and Excellence of Coins*, p. 639. She later died in a bath overheated beyond measure; pagans alleged that this was done at her husband’s command. But the very learned Cellarius rightly regards this as suspect in his notes on Eutropius, book X, ch. 4, no. 13. Such fortunate names, as Tacitus calls them, were much loved, not only for men but also for women. Hence Felicitas, Fausta, Faustina, Faustilla, Fortuna, Felicissima, Tyche, Callityche, Profutura, and others already listed by eminent scholars.

“He promises [her] a worthier husband.” This may quite properly be understood of dignity of honors. Thus Lactantius, book III, ch. 11: “But nothing more beautiful than virtue, nothing worthier than wisdom, can be found.” Usuard in the *Martyrology*: “And he was buried at the church where he had been appointed a worthy minister.” Others, especially ecclesiastical writers, use it similarly very frequently. The old writers of our own language do likewise; for example King Birger, in the preface to the Laws of Uppland, elegantly calls an archbishop *Baerdogan Verra*. Yet in this passage of Lactantius perhaps *dignum* is more correctly understood in relation to this condition of marriage: [Col. 0418A] as in Tibullus, book IV, elegy 7:

> . . . . . Since I shall be said to have been worthy of the worthy.

“By which he would be manifestly implicated in the crime.” Jurists explain what it is to be *manifesto teneri*, “caught in manifest guilt.” See Brissonius and others.

“The manifest murderer is stuck.” Lactantius, book I, ch. 7: “As though all routes had been withdrawn and exhausted, he stops, sticks fast, fails.” Ancient glosses: *haereo*, ἅπτομαι, ἐνέχομαι, “I cling; I am entangled.” A “manifest thief” occurs in Plautus’s *Aulularia* and *Trinummus*. Later writers preferred to say *manifestum*; the Greeks, ἐπαυτοφώρῳ, “in the very act.”

“Vows for twenty years.” Against Norisius, Antonius Pagius teaches in the *Hypatic Dissertation*, p. 157, that Maximian did not anticipate his *vicennalia*, but celebrated them at the lawful time, since he had been proclaimed Caesar two years before he received the purple. Let him be consulted.

“He ended by death.” Other writers, especially Zonaras, have accounts highly consonant with these; so much so that even the things by which he thinks the earlier authors came to disagree among themselves are plainly true and become much clearer from this remarkably lucid narrative. But to bring them forward here would be an excessively lengthy undertaking [Col. 0418B].

## ON CHAPTER XXXI

“Though he too was to celebrate the vicennalia.” Not because their time had then come for Galerius, but because emperors thought that several years’ work was required for the preparations. Consult the recently cited Antonius Pagius, who treats this subject carefully, *Hypatic Dissertation*, p. 188. The same author, p. 247, shows that this is an excellent passage for demonstrating the magnitude of expenses incurred on such occasions.

“Who long ago.” In this small gap I think there is lacking: “that he might render to his gods,” namely what he had promised; words which immediately follow.

“He struck with a second axe.” A very learned man thinks that one should read “a second security,” namely an emperor; I confess that I do not grasp this, since the matter here concerns not Emperor Diocletian but the provinces. Nor do I doubt that he had in view Cicero’s words *For Gnaeus Plancius*, ch. 29: “What heavier axe could those judges have inflicted on the republic than when they expelled from the city the man who, as praetor in a neighboring war and as consul in a domestic war, had liberated the republic?” Moreover, although the reading now printed is much more common, I would prefer that the form found in the French edition, *securem*, should have been retained in accordance with the usage of that age. Prudentius likewise, in the *Passion of the Martyr Prudentius*, v. 328:

> Does yielding gentleness thus blunt  
> The public axe?

Ammianus too, book XXX, p. 430: “Papirius Cursor, dictator at that time, ordered the axe to be made ready through a lictor . . .” But such forms ought not to be imitated by our young men, although *sitem* is also read in Prudentius and Boethius, *cutem* in Cornelius Celsus, indeed even *turrem* in Vergil if we follow Charisius, and other forms in other writers.

“Let an exaction be carried out.” Optatus of Milevis, book III: “Whenever some action has been conducted in public courts”; book V: “When he saw such mighty acts performed by the Son of God,” that is, works of such divine power produced; book VII: “No judgment was conducted, but the effect of the sentence was carried out.”

“For those not having pardon, none.” Read with Baluze at the end of the second volume: “For those who had no permission to refrain, there were manifold tortures”; or, as I prefer, “No permission [was granted] by those who did not possess it [for] refraining.” The sense is that the magistrates sent for this purpose were not allowed to withhold tortures from provincials, even though they had nothing to furnish.

“No threshing-floors without an exactor.” The ancients sometimes kept grain on the threshing-floors until it had been threshed and cleaned, and then stored it in granaries and storehouses. See the agricultural writers. Livy too, book XXXIV, ch. 9: “It happened to be the time when they had grain on the threshing-floors.”

“What things are tolerable.” Emend with Baluze: “Although it is intolerable to snatch from men’s mouths food [Col. 0419A] acquired by labor,” unless *quaestos*, “acquired,” may seem allowable in accordance with archaic usage. Similar in rhetorical form is Lactantius, book V, ch. 9: “But this is beyond telling, which is done against those who do not know how to do wrong”; while similar in sense is Livy, book XXI, ch. 13: “Although these things are grievous and bitter, your fortune counsels you.”

O most demented one. This passage recalls to me another which now stands in Lactantius undoubtedly corrupt. Namely, Divine Institutions, book V, chapter 10: “What can be more demented than this piety: to sacrifice human victims to the dead, and to feed fire with the blood of men as though with oil?” Here madness is first ill opposed to piety; then the two words “than this piety” cause the following clause, “than to [sacrifice] human [victims] to the dead,” etc., to lack anything to which it can suitably correspond. Servatius Gallaeus attests that, in place of *dementius* (“more demented”), one old manuscript reads *inclementius* (“more cruel”); hence I infer that the true reading is this: “What can be more cruel than this piety? What more demented than to sacrifice human victims to the dead [Col. 0419B], and to feed fire with the blood of men as though with oil?” The meaning then is: nothing is more cruel, and therefore nothing more unworthy of Aeneas, who boasted of being dutiful (for clemency too is called *pietas*, as was shown earlier), than cruelly to slaughter and burn innocent persons; nothing less fitting for an experienced and prudent leader than to believe that the dead are nourished by human blood. Let others judge whether Lactantius can seem to have written thus.

Overthrown by his own possessions. He imitates Cicero, who likewise says that someone is overthrown by his possessions, or by his fortunes, as others have noted.

## ON CHAPTER XXXII

He therefore frequently sends envoys to him. Galerius, of course, to Maximinus. See Eusebius, book VIII, chapter 13, whose words several others have already cited.

By prescription of time. Because Maximinus had assumed the purple long before Licinius.

Vanquished in obstinacy. I am surprised that Antonius Pagius [Col. 0419C] takes these words of Maximinus Daia, or Daza, when both the sequence of the words and the matter itself teach that Galerius is meant. For how could Galerius, already a veteran emperor, be called obstinate toward the newly elevated Daia? Obstinacy belongs, surely, to an inferior toward a superior. Further, Maximinus Daia would have shown no soundness of mind if, while Galerius lived, he had tried to abolish the title of Caesars and, alone, to throw everything into confusion at his own discretion rather than truly to govern it.

But Pagius insists: “What, then, became of Maximinus? Did Galerius deprive him of every rank?” First I could reply that he is not named at this point, since he was already Galerius’s enemy and wholly hateful to him; later mention is made of him, once regard could no longer be withheld. Then, if you wonder that Daia was passed over by Galerius, how much more shall I wonder that Galerius was passed over by Daia? Yet could Daia on that account have cast him down from his eminence? But, to deal more seriously, I think that the name of Maximinus Daia has here been omitted by a drowsy copyist, and that one should write: “Maximinus, Maxentius, and Constantine, sons of the Augusti.” Thus [Col. 0419D] everything will certainly be entirely clear, and it will be evident that Baluze rightly interpreted these words of Galerius.

What follows confirms it. Lactantius says that he ordered all four to be counted as emperors: namely Licinius, Maximinus, Maxentius, and Constantine. He proclaimed all these four emperors; for no one doubted concerning Galerius himself, who had already ruled for so many years. I hope that those who weigh these matters more carefully will join me in this, and especially you, most eminent and learned Cuperus. Should this happen, I shall not take it ill if some disagree.

Sons of the Augusti. Thus Julius Capitolinus, in *Verus*, chapter 3: “No other honorific addition was attached to his name except that he was called the son of Augustus.”

## ON CHAPTER XXXIII

Now the eighteenth year. The eighteenth year of Galerius Maximianus began on the Kalends of March in the year 309; toward its end, or thereabouts, he was afflicted by that disease, continuing until the end of the following year and the beginning of 311. After the Kalends of March, having assumed the twentieth tribunician power—see the heading of the edict given below in the next chapter, in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, chapter 17—he issued an edict in favor of the Christians. After the Kalends of May in that same year, with his vicennalia due on the Kalends of March 312, he breathed out his wretched soul. These matters, and more, are in Antonius Pagius, *Dissertationes Hypaticae*, p. 159, whom I think should be followed in this matter.

God struck him with an incurable blow. He had in mind 2 Maccabees 9:5: “But the Lord God of Israel, who watches over all things, struck him with an incurable and invisible blow.” Thus Eusebius and Nicephorus speak of Herod: “A heaven-sent scourge seized him and drove him to death.” And those consulted by Herod concerning his illness declared this of him: “God exacts from the king this penalty for his great and impious conduct.” Delete the particle *καί* with Nicephorus and certain manuscripts: *τὸ πολὺ δυσσεβές* means “great impiety.” See whether the reading may have been *τὸν θεόν* [Col. 0420B]. That is: God exacts from the king this punishment for manifold impiety.

Many examples teach that this is the customary punishment either of monstrous sacrilege and impiety or of other atrocious crimes. I shall now, in haste, recount a few. Pheretima, more than a woman in exacting punishments from her enemies, swarmed alive with worms, as Herodotus testifies at the end of book IV. Aelian, *Various History*, book IV, chapter 28, and Pliny, book VII, chapter 51, will relate how shamefully Pherecydes of Syros perished—whether through lice or serpents generated from his very body—he whose tongue was most unrestrained and foul against the gods. Sulla, a man of notorious cruelty, died of phthiriasis, as Plutarch reports; and Eunus too suffered from the same disease, the slave and wonder-worker, the dreadful torch of the savage Sicilian slave war against Roman masters.

Herod the Great, of whom I began to speak, was carried off by an inflammation (the Greek words *τοῦτε ἤτρου* are corrupt or uncertain) and a putrefaction of the genitals producing worms—evils plainly twin to those of Galerius. On these, Eusebius and the earlier Josephus should be consulted. His grandson Agrippa also died worm-eaten (*σκωληκόβρωτος*), he who was likewise called Herod, Acts 12:23. Claudius Herminianus in Cappadocia, after treating Christians cruelly, when he alone in his praetorium had been devastated by plague and swarmed alive with worms, said: “Let no one know, lest the Christians rejoice in hope.” Later, having recognized his error—that by tortures he had made certain persons fall away from their resolve—he died almost a Christian. This is Tertullian’s account, *To Scapula*, chapter 3, where more may be seen.

Arius, the head of the heretics, seized by a dreadful kind of disease, and emitting his foul soul after his intestines burst and poured forth—his stench being intolerable even to sewers—is described by Socrates Scholasticus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book I. Julian, Parabates’ uncle, should also be counted among these; see those cited by Baluze. More examples will be supplied by Plutarch in the *Life of Sulla*; Helladius in Photius, p. 870, Schott edition; and Schott himself in his notes on Aurelius Victor’s *Sulla*. Still more are given by the admirable Samuel Bochart, part II, book IV, chapter 18 of the *Hierozōicon*. Saint Jerome discusses these and similar accounts with weighty judgment on Zechariah, chapter [Col. 0420D] XIV, verse 12: “Their flesh shall waste away,” etc.:

> “But we shall say that all persecutors who afflicted the Church of God, to say nothing of future torments, have received even in this present age what they did. Let us read ecclesiastical histories: what Valerian, Decius, Diocletian, Maximian, Maximinus—the most savage of all—and lately Julian suffered; and then by facts we shall prove that, even according to the letter and the truth of prophecy, it has been fulfilled: their flesh wasted away and their eyes rotted.”

I shall add only this passage of Saint Gregory Nazianzen, *Invective* 11: “Who could adequately dramatize the deserved diseases of the impious—Hervagius’s edition has, by an astonishing error, *εὐσεβῶν*, ‘the pious’—their conspicuous ruptures, their many other wounds and scourges resembling the deeds they dared to commit; deaths not gladly suffered in the ordinary manner; confessions made amid their very sufferings and fruitless repentances; chastisements through dreams, and waking apparitions?”

[Col. 0421A] A malignant ulcer. Eusebius, book VIII, chapter 16, says that it was first an abscess, then a fistulous ulcer in the lower part. He himself provides more.

The physicians cut, treat. These words are too weak unless you write: “The physicians cut, cauterize, treat.” Celsus, book VI, chapter 18, no. 3, discussing maladies of this kind in those parts: “If medicaments are defeated, here too whatever is corrupted must be cut away with the knife, in such a way that it carries off with it some sound tissue. It is likewise an invariable rule that, once the cancer has been excised, the wound must be cauterized.” Add what follows, concerning movement and the blood flowing from it. Saint Pacian, in the *Paraenesis*: “Prudent sick people do not fear physicians, even when they are to cut and cauterize the hidden parts of their bodies. We remember persons who did not blush to expose even the remote and shameful parts of the body, and who endured the knife, cautery, and that grievous biting power of powder. And how small is what human beings have endured! Shall the sinner be afraid? Shall the sinner blush to purchase eternal life with present shame? Shall he withdraw wounds badly concealed from the Lord who holds out his hands?” Below he also employs this same comparison more than once.

The wound cuts through the scar. Baluze attests that an old book had, “but after a scar had already formed, the wound cuts through,” where he thinks one should write *scinditur*, “is cut through.” I should prefer *scindit se*, “it cuts itself open,” as Vergil: “the cloud parts itself.”

At a slight movement of the body [source defective]. Baluze seems rightly to restore *motu*, “movement”; but the syntax further requires that one write *vulnerato*, “when wounded”: namely, when Galerius was wounded, blood ran more freely.

He himself grows pale. That is, he becomes pallid, just as “whitening pallor” is spoken of in *On the Anger of God*, chapter 5.

He grows thin. As Vergil:

> “But of their own will the cattle grow lean through wasting.”

The masters yielded. The most eminent Cuperus writes, in his commentary on the *Apotheosis of Homer*, that he emended the text thus and that its meaning is: the most excellent physicians present could not cure Galerius, and therefore others were summoned from other regions. He also says that elsewhere Lactantius called the master of the haruspices of his own time by the name of their inventor—or at least of an ancient haruspex—Tages. I confess that at first glance I recognized those Vergilian verses which are read near the end of book III of the *Georgics*.

Distinguished physicians are brought from every quarter. Lactantius, *Institutions*, VI.4: “Whom greed or pleasure drags headlong.” Ammianus, book XXVIII: “Many are drawn from widely separated regions by diverse prejudgments.”

Apollo and Asclepius. The very learned Gronovius observed in his *Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 182, that Lactantius even in printed editions preferred to use the Greek name rather than the Latin. This too seems somewhat to support the attribution of this work to its author, since here we see the same term recur in the same form, *Asclepius*, not *Aesculapius*.

The malady recedes inwardly. Lactantius, VI.17: “For nature does not seem capable of receiving anything that recedes into its opposite.”

[Col. 0421D] Stench. I think Lactantius wrote either “the odor was so foul” or “the stench of the smell.” Hegesippus, book V, chapter 2: “All the limbs of the slaughtered citizens stank with a dreadful odor.”

Eaten by worms. Baluze reads: “… and the urinary passages, namely, eaten by worms.” But the most eminent Cuperus has: “he is eaten by worms; and in ….” These seem to me to be joined more suitably with what follows if we write *comestur*, “is eaten”; for this responds better to the words “is dissolved” and “removes.” Cicero also used *comest* actively, according to Nonius, with whom see more. The grammarian Diomedes likewise teaches that the passive form I have now used was common: “In the passive one declines *edor, ederis, estur*; likewise *ambedor* and *comedor*.” The simple *estur* occurs in Plautus, Ovid, and Columella.

Cooked and warm animals. Perhaps one should read “uncooked and warm animals …,” that is, still alive but opened by cutting, such as I recall physicians sometimes applying. But I do not strongly contend for this.

Inestimable. Thus Lactantius, book I, chapter 16: “Since the multitude of human beings is incredible, their number is inestimable.” Similarly, “inestimable heaps,” “an inestimable multitude of barbarians,” and expressions very frequent among writers of that age, for whom *aestimare*, “to estimate,” sometimes meant nearly the same as to count, or rather to make a conjecture about the number; as Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXXI: “They were slain in such numbers that from the aforesaid number no more than five thousand, as was estimated, escaped.”

The force of the wasting entrails. I do not see by what rule or analogy *tabescendorum* (“of things to be wasted”) can be said. Someone might perhaps prefer *tabidosorum*, a word occurring in Tertullian’s *Apology*, chapter 14. But Lactantius, who long taught the art of speaking, wrote far more correctly in most matters. I therefore judge it more likely that *tabescentium*, “of wasting [entrails],” can be restored; as Cyprian, *On the Good of Patience*: “There is added the vastness of the wounds, and the punishment of ravenous worms consumes the wasting and flowing limbs.” Or, if this too does not sufficiently please, “of entrails eaten away by decay” (*tabe exesorum*).

[Col. 0422B] Fruitful destruction. Elegant and proper; for *pernicies* is said from the destruction either of parts or of the whole body. Hence it is often joined with plague and opposed to health. Thus *Divine Institutions*, book VI, chapter 24: “Therefore it is better either to pour out one’s conscience, or voluntarily to open our own mind and pour out destruction through reopened wounds.”

It had diminished when swollen. That is, it had decreased, becoming more contracted or shorter. The ancient glosses: *discrescere*, “to diminish” (*ἀπομειοῦσθαι*).

A whole year. Lactantius, book VII, chapter 26: “Then for seven whole years the forests will remain untouched.” You also have the expression in Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue* I; Mamertinus several times in the panegyrics; and others.

Of a new pressing pain. I think one should write: “by a new force of pressing pain,” or “pressing at intervals.” Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*: “Then I should have had to be tortured; then I should have had to be driven by the force of pain to confess the crime.” Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXXIX [the supplied citation is uncertain or erroneous]: “He perceived, amid a certain immense pressure of diseases, that the appointed term of final necessity was at hand.”

And to make sufficient satisfaction for his crime. Lactantius, book V, chapter 13: “That he might make satisfaction for his deed”; book VII, chapter 1: “Let us also do sufficient justice to this part.”

## ON CHAPTER XXXIV

The first … had established. Not because they had been the first authors or founders, but because they had earlier confirmed and sanctioned these things with the others. For *constituere* often means to restore things which have been scattered and to strengthen them in a firmer condition. Hence Eusebius translates: “as perhaps their parents too had previously established [them].”

That they might make laws for themselves. There are two heads of accusation which he brings. First, that in religious matters they followed certain laws of their own, rejecting and condemning the public ones. Second, that they formed associations, or assemblies—wholly harmless and indeed holy in themselves, but utterly hateful to emperors, to whom nothing was more suspect than a gathering of people held without their command, whatever its designation. I agree with the most eminent Cuperus that the preceding words concern the secession made from the pagans, while the following words, “nor observe the God of the Christians,” refer to heresies.

Which they might observe. This term pertains to religious practice. Cyprian, Epistle 10: “Having despised the law and observance of the Lord, which those same holy martyrs and confessors command to be maintained.” Arnobius, book I: “Without any anxious observance of sacred rites.” See Heraldus’s notes there, pp. 41–42.

Many, subdued by danger. Eusebius: “Therefore, since such an ordinance had followed from us—so that they should [the following Greek clause is materially corrupt: *ἐπὶ τὰ τῶν ἀρχαίων κατασταθέντα ἑαυτοὺς ταμεθήσαιει*]—many, having been subjected to danger, and many having been disturbed, endured deaths of every kind.” Here *οἱ ὑποβληθέντες κινδύνῳ* does not mean “those exposed to dangers,” as [Col. 0423A] translators render it, but, as Lactantius—or rather Galerius himself—has it, “subdued by danger”: that is, thoroughly conquered, cast down from the degree of constancy, and shamefully overcome. For *ὑποβάλλεσθαι* sometimes has this sense, as is also clear from Pollux, who joins *ὑπωθεῖν*, “to thrust down,” *ταπεινοῦν*, “to humble,” and *ὑποβάλλειν*, book IV, chapter 6. Examples of speakers using it thus have been supplied by others.

The ancients use the word “to cast down” in the same way. Among them Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXIX: “He departed innocent, rescued by the philosopher Pasiphilus; to overthrow him from the station of a resolute mind by unjust falsehood, he was cruelly tortured, but could not be cast down.” The rest, harassed, afflicted, and troubled—I think this is how *τοὺς ταραχθέντας* should be interpreted—remained in their position; or, as he himself says, “they endured deaths of every kind,” which may simply be translated, I think, “they underwent diverse deaths,” or, if you prefer, “various punishments.” But since it is not likely that Eusebius, who rendered the rest of this edict so aptly, departed far from it in this one point, I think that *indeturbati*, “not cast down,” should be read instead of *deturbati*, “cast down,” or at least that several words have fallen out.

Consideration of our clemency. Cyprian, Epistle 54: “We believe that this too will please you in consideration of paternal mercy.” Pacian, Epistle I: “Let no one despise a bishop in consideration of human dignity; he is esteemed worthy of honor.” And thus people commonly spoke in that age.

## ON CHAPTER XXXV

And Maximinus again. To reconcile this passage with the other writers—some of whom say that Maximianus Galerius alone was consul in this year, while others say that Licinius was his colleague—I have so far found nothing more suitable than what Antonius Pagius, investigating these matters carefully, sets forth. If it pleases, then, let us follow him here: at the beginning of the year Galerius is to be said to have entered upon the consulship alone; shortly afterward he added Licinius as colleague; on the Kalends of May he admitted Maximinus, because the consulship ought to be a certain addition to imperial majesty. This consulship was therefore not ordinary [Col. 0423C] but suffect, as Licinius’s had been earlier. Indeed, Maximinus’s earlier consulship was also suffect, held after Constantius Chlorus and Maximianus Galerius became the new Augusti and ordinary consuls in 306. Whether we accept all this, I say, or only some of it, there nevertheless remains this new and almost singular feature in this passage: that the status of a suffect consulship is reckoned in such a way that Maximinus is called consul “again” on account of it. But perhaps elsewhere I shall deal with these matters more laboriously.

Prison … as a dwelling. Lactantius, book VI, chapter 10: “But they had leaves and grass for beds, caves and caverns for homes.”

Handed over into the hand. This construction is extremely common in the old Latin version of the Bible.
