Genesis 30:35: “But he handed over the entire flock of one color into the hand of his sons”; chapter 39: “Who handed over into his hand all the prisoners who were kept in custody”; 1 Samuel 24:11: “Because the Lord handed you over into my hand”; 2 Chronicles 34:10: “They handed [it] into the hands of those set over the workmen.” It is well known, however, that Cicero too said *veni in senatu*, “I came in the senate,” and Varro *qua in Caelio monte itur*, “where one goes on the Caelian Hill”; such expressions, nevertheless, should not be imitated rashly by young people. They became much more frequent in later centuries, and Vorstius notes several in the very elegant writer Sulpicius Severus. Thus Lactantius too does not avoid them: book III, chapter 3, “which fall in the nature of things”; book IV, chapter 17, “cast upon the ground with all his body and face”; *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 2, “they have been banished in that region.”

The limbs might waste away. *Institutions*, book III, chapter 1: “Falsehood indeed pleases by another’s appearance, because, corrupt in itself, it vanishes and wastes away unless adorned from elsewhere”; chapter 20: “The body abandoned by the soul wastes away.”

At Nicomedia, in the middle of the same month. Read: “And this became known at Nicomedia in the middle of the same month.” The eminent Cuperus later confirmed this in his letter.

With the Kalends of March impending. Baluze rightly teaches [Col. 0424A] that the Kalends of March of the following year are meant, provided we maintain that the narrative given in this chapter is complete. For if the terrible death of Galerius became known at Nicomedia in May, the Kalends of March could still be impending in that year. I note this because of the doubt of a most polished gentleman, who admits that he was hasty in this matter. It may be that I have not yet sufficiently grasped his meaning.

## ON CHAPTER XXXVI

For the present. Lactantius, book VII, chapter 6: “And other things which have force only for the present”; chapter 10: “All vices are temporary; they are stirred for the present”; chapter 15: “Although for the present he displayed God’s power to men”; *On the Anger of God*, chapter 21: “He does not punish every harmful person for the present.”

He abolishes the census. I thought *sustulit*, “he abolished,” should be restored, since “that he might reconcile” precedes. Yet I now think it makes little difference, since the verb is very customary in Lactantius; for example, book II, chapter 5: “And so many philosophers abolished religions”; book III, chapter 5: “Therefore he abolished the disciplines of others by what was right.”

Armed men held the opposite shores. Note that the shores of the Propontis, especially at the narrows of the Bosporus, are called “banks.” Thus Pliny, book IX, chapter 15: “The tunny-fish enter by the right bank and depart by the left.” See more in the eminent Heinsius’s added notes on Ovid, *Heroides* 6.54.

By common protection. Baluze comments: “I find this word nowhere else; perhaps it is corrupt.” I too judge it wholly corrupt, and think that *titulo*, “under the title,” should be written in its place. For this peace was granted to Christians in the joint name of the emperors, as is clear from the edict at the end of Eusebius’s eighth book. Ovid:

> “It is enough for you to have the title of my death.”

And elsewhere:

> “Let the benefit be yours; let the title be given to your friend.”

[Col. 0424C] The author of the elegy addressed to Livia:

> “The leader bore the title of war from his brother, the leader.”

For titles of enacted laws see Tacitus, *Annals* I.8; for “the title of administration,” Symmachus, book X, letter 4; and similar passages in others.

High priests. I was preparing to explain rather more fully who the Asiarchs of that age or earlier were who were *στεφανοφόροι ἀρχιερεῖς*, “crown-bearing high priests,” or *sacerdotes maximi*, “high priests.” But other academic labors now keep me tightly occupied. Much has already been accomplished on these matters by men far more learned: Selden, on the origins of Eutychius and on the recension of the Smyrnaean donor-inscriptions; others on the Arundelian, or Oxford, marbles; Dionysius Gothofredus on Law 8, Digest, title *On Exemption and Excusal from Public Duties*; and Pancirollus on the *Notitia of the Eastern Empire*, chapter 105.

He might set [them] over provinces. This verb is very common in that age; it occurs also in the highly elegant Minucius Felix, p. 152: “That Epicurus nonetheless sets nature above.”

In appearance only. Nothing is more frequent in Lactantius than these words joined thus; I think there is no need to copy out instances. On this type of cruelty, however, in which a false appearance of clemency flatters, Lactantius himself says more in book V, chapter 11.

## ON CHAPTER XXXVII

That all animals. He distinctly said “all.” Earlier men too employed such devices, but nevertheless allowed other kinds of meat as well; this man allowed only meat polluted by superstition. He is said to have been the first to devise this practice.

Storehouses. Among the ancients an *apotheca* was a larger wine-cellar, or another capacious storehouse. Storehouses for grain, wine, and oil occur in 2 Chronicles 32. Arnobius also uses the word, book VIII. Others have collected more instances from earlier writers.

By which he had so corrupted them. I read: “by which he had so corrupted his own [men].” I at once had no doubt that *soldiers* should be restored [Col. 0425A], understanding persons of higher rank, or palace guards, as very learned men have already shown that the term was often used in that period. He calls the soldiers corrupted by the daily sacrifices because of the sacred feasts; fattened by these, they disdained cheaper and truly military foods. Nazianzen reports precisely the same thing about Julian; and I have no doubt that that deserter—or, if you prefer, turncoat—imitated much from Diocletian and the emperors contemporary with him. This is clear from the invectives of the holy Father whom I mentioned.

Moreover, the reading should be *expungeret*, “he might strike out,” not *expugnaret*, “he might storm,” as the most illustrious Cuperus also perceived—and as has long been printed under my supervision. That names or debts are “struck out” when discharged, and that persons themselves are thus “struck out,” is well known from Tertullian, who speaks this way very frequently, and also from earlier writers; the very learned Gronovius demonstrated it in his *Observation on Ecclesiastical Writers*. Thus too Saint Cyprian, Epistle 38: “And since I sent you as my representatives in my place, so that you might discharge the needs of our brethren from the funds … he intervened so that no one could be discharged, nor could those matters which I had requested be distinguished through careful examination; he even threatened our brethren who had first come forward to be discharged.”

## ON CHAPTER XXXVIII

I do not know what to say. Lactantius, book I, chapter 21: “For what am I to say of the children sacrificed to Saturn because of Jupiter’s hatred?” Book VI, chapter 23: “With what words, or with what indignation, can I pursue so great a crime? The magnitude of the wickedness surpasses the capacity of speech.”

To express according to indignation. I read: “These things cannot be expressed according to [their] indignation.” CUPERUS.—This conjecture, which seems true and certain, can indeed be sufficiently attractive; but the words “according to his indignation” stand in the way. For one could not conveniently say, “Desire cannot be expressed according to its indignation,” unless perhaps, in place of *indignatione*, we read *indignitate*, “outrageousness.” But it seemed to me that, with a smaller alteration, one should read—provided we remember that *ais*, “you say,” was written for *his*, “these,” that is, “mind”—“And yet the mind cannot express the matter in words [Col. 0425C] according to its indignation”; or, “the mind [cannot express it] in these words,” and in place of the lacuna, “the foulest thing,” or something of that kind. Thus I thought before the letter arrived from our excellent and most learned benefactor. Now I leave the whole judgment to him and to readers.

Noble women. The fact that they were noble increased the outrage of the matter. For to be examined in this way was utterly servile and detestable for free persons. Slaves were customarily inspected thus by slave-dealers and displayed to bidders. See what the most learned and celebrated D. Rappoltus adduced from Suetonius and Martial on Horace, p. 600, to this effect.

Defiled virgins. Baluze emends in the final book to “unwilling virgins,” which does not please me. For Lactantius says of that filthy Jupiter of the pagans, book I, chapter 10: “I pass over the virgins whom he defiled”; and you will find similar expressions in Plautus and Roman law. Cicero himself even said “to violate and diminish right and duty.”

They imitated [him] under such a prince. Supply “the example,” and “of his friends,” according to Cuperus; or: “They violated with impunity the morals of their master and the beds of his household.” Thus Lactantius says of the same Jupiter, book V, chapter 6, and of his household: “Since to imitate the morals and vices of a king is judged a form of obedience, they all cast aside piety, lest, if they lived piously, they might seem to reproach the king with his crime.”

## ON CHAPTER XXXIX

Whom she had recently called father. For her husband, Maximianus Galerius, had adopted him, as we saw above in chapter 18. She therefore hoped that her protection would be safer with him than with Licinius, to whom Galerius had entrusted her. Coins preserve for us an image of this Valeria, Diocletian’s daughter: one is displayed by the eminent Spanheim in his work *On the Excellence and Use of Coins*; another by D. Patin, among the Roman imperial coins in medium and small bronze, p. 452, etc. In her honor a part of Pannonia was named Valeria, as Ammianus Marcellinus testifies, book XIX.

[Col. 0426A] He asks [for her] in marriage. Thus Sulpicius Severus: “And asking her from her father in marriage for himself, he bound himself to seven years’ service.” A learned man there restores *in matrimonium*, “in marriage,” yet admits that such expressions are common elsewhere in Sulpicius. See my note above on chapter 35, “handed over into the hand.”

Her female friends. Note that just as these are called friends of emperors, so here the friends of Augustae may be called *amicae*. Return to chapter 6. The female companions mentioned below have the same reference.

## ON CHAPTER XL

By whose counsel it was denied to him [source defective: *sibi neg.*]. The most eminent Cuperus seems rightly to emend: “By her counsel [it was] denied.”

To the governor Eratineus. Perhaps *Eratinus*, so that it is the Greek *ἐρατεινόν*, equivalent to *ἐράσμιος*, “lovely” or “beloved.”

No less close to the Augusta. In the Paris copy, incorrectly, “not too close.” But *proxima* is used as in Lactantius, book I, final chapter: “Ulysses was nearest in the same rank.” So too Apuleius, “humanity very close to a town,” and similar expressions. See the notes of my blessed father-in-law on Phaedrus’s verse [Col. 0426B]:

> “She denied that she was close to guilt.”

While he was ordered. Perhaps the words “ordered by the evil beast, he was speaking” have fallen out. CUPERUS.

Promoted in military fashion. I thought these should be joined as though he meant that they were led forth in military fashion, just as soldiers under a tribune or centurion were accustomed to lead condemned persons. I shall not now object if someone prefers, “equipped in military fashion,” on account of what follows.

[Corrupt or uncertain reading: “Bile mens essagitarii.”] Baluze’s earlier conjecture, “soldiers and archers,” sufficiently refutes itself, since it would be irrelevant to say that soldiers had been brought forth or equipped in military fashion for such an act; this could readily be understood on its own. I confess that for some time I held the alternative, “light-armed troops and archers,” because Pacatus in his panegyric, chapter 35, and Ammianus Marcellinus in several passages mention them as forces of no small use in warfare even in that age. More than anything, this appeared relevant because that historian, book XXIV, pp. 264 and 271, says that Julian’s attendants were light-armed troops. At present, however, I prefer: “equipped in military fashion, watchmen and archers,” or “watchmen and Cretan archers” (or something else in that place). Watchmen were recruited from various bodies of craftsmen, as is clear from Roman laws, which may be found in Pancirollus on the *Notitia of the Eastern Empire*, chapter 27, and other legal authorities. They are therefore aptly said to be promoted or equipped in military fashion, since they were not themselves soldiers, though archers were attached to them. And I seem elsewhere to have read that half of those who performed watch-duty or frontier-watch in the provinces were Roman soldiers, while the rest were gathered from townspeople or other provincials. But I now hasten to other matters.

## ON CHAPTER XLII

Of the aged Maximian. Just as images of those who had already assumed imperial power were sent into the provinces [Col. 0426D] and received with reverence by magistrates and peoples—as was said above on chapter 25, and could be established by many proofs—so Zosimus, book II, chapter 9, says that when Constantine’s image was displayed at Rome “according to custom,” it stirred Maxentius’s anger; and in chapter 12 he relates that the same man, when he thought his empire secure, sent persons into Africa to carry his image about. Other examples might be brought from other sources. Likewise, more than a few report that the images of those whose conduct had greatly displeased, and whose memory was condemned after death, were removed from military standards and that their statues were thrown down.

Herodian, book VIII, chapter 5, tells this of Maximinus Thrax and his son; and Julius Capitolinus repeats it from him in *The Maximini*, chapter 23, and *The Gordians*, chapter 9. Eusebius, at the end of book VIII, reports it of Maximianus Herculius, as though this disgrace had first befallen him; but Valesius thinks this should be understood of rulers of those times. In the same way, therefore, I think it may be maintained that our author says this first happened to Diocletian: that while alive he saw his images and statues destroyed. For that this is not simply true is evident even from Tacitus, *Histories* III.13, who relates that Vitellius’s images were torn down, and III.85, that Vitellius himself was compelled, among other humiliations, to behold his own statues falling.

But, to deal rather with what seems pressing, I do not think these words have escaped unhurt from moths and decay. The same thing is said twice, that both men’s images were taken down, and the rest does not seem sufficiently apt or well joined. They will stand somewhat better if we read: “His images, with the man with whom he was painted”; and in place of “and because,” “for indeed the two old men were generally painted together.” Perhaps at the beginning also, in place of “at the same time,” one should write “at that same time.”

Cast down into hatred of life. Lactantius certainly did not write, in one and the same place, “cast down to a humble life” and “cast down into hatred of life.” Sleepy copyists sometimes repeat words when another of similar sound ought to follow. In the latter place, therefore, restore “led” or “brought,” as Cicero said “to lead someone into weeping and pity.”

## ON CHAPTER XLIII

Only one now remained. That Maximinus is meant is sufficiently clear from what follows. But whether Antonius Pagius’s argument is compelling—that Maximinus died in A.D. 313, not, as others say, in 314, because Lactantius treats of Maximinus’s death only after recounting Diocletian’s end, although Maximinus is known to have outlived Diocletian—I leave others to examine. Consult, if you have leisure, the work cited, p. 248.

Since he had rivalry. Lactantius, *On the Anger of God*, chapter 13: “Unless wisdom is added, through which they may have rejection of evils.” Jerome, *To Nepotianus*: “Possess prudence, justice, temperance, courage.” Spartianus, *Hadrian*, chapter 5: “He had so great a zeal for clemency.”

And he too [sent] envoys. I suspect the reading was: “Therefore he too secretly sent envoys to the city.” “He too,” that is, no differently from Constantine and Licinius, who had conspired together as allies.

## ON CHAPTER XLIV

He had recently drawn [troops] from the Moors and Italians. More customary would be *contraxerat*, “had assembled.” Yet I think the other reading also has some warrant somewhere.

Prepared for either event. Vergil:

> “Confident in spirit and prepared for either event.”

*Aeneid* II.61. The other line—

> “… Flight was known to neither these nor those”—

which follows shortly afterward, is found in *Aeneid* X.755.

Warned in a dream, Constantine. The most learned Cuper has much to say on this passage; and, since I do not doubt that it will please curious readers, the fewer things will now be added by me. As for the truth of this history, I do not wish to draw out a long saw of dispute with anyone, being well mindful both of what Eusebius relates that he heard from Constantine himself and of what is piously said by those who urge that it should be held quite probable that God, as he assisted the first beginning of the Christian religion by many miracles, so also assisted, by at least this one miracle if not more, its extraordinarily wide propagation under Constantine. Nevertheless, in such matters I think that one must look solely to what seemed good to God, not to what seemed likely to the weakness of human judgment; and consequently to what is reported as having truly happened in histories of unquestioned reliability, not to what the weakness of human judgment supposes would have been fitting.

Therefore, with the good leave of those who think otherwise, if I may venture some assertion on this point, I judge that two apparitions, very different in place, manner, and time, are being combined into one. When Julian, that impious deserter of the heavenly sacrament, was laying waste the Lord’s flock with equal cunning and extreme cruelty, and was also stirring up Jewish fury against it, authors of no slight credibility report that the sign of the cross flashed forth—not only on men’s garments, as very many testify, but also in heaven—and indeed in a most brilliant form. Let us hear, if you please, one of them: Nazianzen, that Father of distinguished holiness and steadfastness. In his Second Invective against Julian he speaks thus:

> But what was still more astonishing and conspicuous than this: a light stood in heaven, outlining the cross; and that which had formerly been dishonoured on earth by the godless, both in form and in name, was now displayed in heaven equally to all, and became for God a trophy of victory over the impious, a trophy loftier than every other. What will the wise men of this age say to these things?

[In the Paris Greek-Latin edition of 1630, the word τούτου, “than this,” is absent.] The same edition here has τροπαίου, “of a trophy,” for τρόπαιον, “a trophy”; and φήσουσι, “will say,” for φήσονται.

Had Gregory written this contrary to truth, at almost the very time when these events were said to have occurred, how badly would he have served Christian piety! My opinion, therefore, is that Constantine did indeed see the figure of the cross, namely in a dream, and certainly by divine agency. But if he had also seen it in heaven, Nazianzen would scarcely have been silent at so opportune a point [Col. 0428B]; Lactantius would scarcely have omitted it; or at any rate he would have narrated it more clearly and explicitly.

One might also say that God judged it sufficient to admonish and encourage, through a gracious apparition during sleep, the pious emperor who was zealously doing everything to foster the holy religion; whereas greater terror was needed for pagans and Jews, to overthrow their impious designs. But let those accustomed to investigate and scrutinize such matters more deeply pardon me if I seem insufficiently skilled in treating them.

When I happened to read Eusebius’ fuller account of that vision, I seemed to myself to see the time when it befell Constantine indicated by Eusebius’ own words more plainly than it has appeared to interpreters, men much more learned than I in many respects. Eusebius says, in Book I of the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 28, that it was shown to the emperor “about the midday hours of the sun, when the day was already declining” (Ἀμφὶ μεσημβρινὰς ἡλίου ὥρας, ἤδη τῆς ἡμέρας ἀποκλινούσης). Nicephorus, Socrates, and Zonaras say little differently.

These two expressions seem to conflict: “at midday,” or “about the midday hours,” and “when the day was declining toward evening,” though they are the same thing. For Isidore, Book XX, chapter 3, expressly says that the period after midday is also called *meridies*; and Censorinus, in the last chapter of *On the Natal Day*, says that what occurred before *suprema*—that is, as most explain it, before sunset—is said to have occurred *de meridie*. For the Twelve Tables contained the words: “Let sunset be the final time.” Yet the Plaetorian law (others read “Praetorian”) prescribed as the final time that at which the praetor in the assembly pronounced *suprema* to the people, as Varro testifies in *On the Latin Language*, Book V.

Hence Ammianus Marcellinus says that the day was “turning toward midday,” Book XVI, in Julian’s Address. The same author, Book XXXI, p. 455: “And when battle had begun, as the day was turning toward midday, nocturnal darkness took possession.” From these passages it is clear that Eusebius did not write contradictory things there; rather, among the ancients *meridies* was also said of the hours nearer to sunset. But I wish these remarks only to establish what time Eusebius designates. To discuss the vision itself at greater length is neither presently possible nor perhaps relevant.

[Col. 0428D]

“And when suddenly the people…” What the most learned Cuper notes occurred to me, I confess, before his letter reached me—except that, in place of *cumque*, “and when,” I conjectured *cum*, with the enclitic particle deleted, and, in place of τοῦ, I was led by my conjecture to *suggerebat*, “suggested,” or *edebat*, “produced,” whereas that most learned man restores something else [materially uncertain in the surviving OCR]. If the latter reading should please anyone, then in place of *debita* perhaps *elata*, “raised,” or *sublata*, “removed,” should be read.

Now circus-games were the customary offering on the birthdays of emperors, whether the emperors themselves gave them to the people or the senate and people dedicated them in the emperors’ honour. Julius Capitolinus, *Antoninus Pius*, chapter 5: “He did not refuse the circus-games dedicated to his birthday, though he declined other honours.”

“The hand of God was over the battle-line.” This seems to be a biblical phrase. See Psalm XXXVIII [Latin XXXVII], 2; Psalm XXXIX, 11; etc.

“He is routed.” I think that the word *miles*, “soldier,” should be restored here.

“The title of first rank.” Of the conjectures advanced by the most learned Cuper on this passage, I embrace that which assigns Constantine and his name the first place among those Augusti. [Col. 0429A]

## On Chapter XLV

“While winter was raging as fiercely as possible.” Quite often, with *illo* removed or understood, writers say *cum maxime*, meaning “at present,” “at this time,” as the most learned scholars maintain. Yet I think this reading may also be borne, elliptically: “while winter was raging as much as possible.”

“With doubled stages.” That is, they completed each day as much of the journey as they would ordinarily complete in two days. For a *mansio*, “stage,” was usually taken as a day’s journey, since the relays of post-horses and the lodging places were arranged according to a fixed calculation of stages, so that one stage corresponded to one day’s journey—except that the watering-places for camels sometimes varied. But see Salmasius’ fuller explanation, *Exercises on Pliny, on Solinus*, pp. 494–495.

[Col. 0429B]

“Force or promises.” I suspect Lactantius wrote: “Yet neither force nor promises availed anything.”

“Now holding the second stage.” The illustrious Baluze would prefer: “now holding the second stage, at a distance …” I do not agree at all. For I understand the phrase “Licinius holding the second stage” in the manner of Livy, Book XXXII, chapter 7: “Where there were cliffs cut sheer, a station of a few armed men held [the place].” That Livy spoke thus elsewhere too has been shown by the most excellent Gronovius on Book XXIV, chapter 3. In the remaining words the conjecture of the first editor seems somewhat more successful; and I think the entire passage should be recast thus:

> For he could go no farther, Licinius now holding the second stage, at the same number of miles’ distance. Therefore, having gathered from the neighbourhood as many soldiers as he could, he proceeded to meet Maximinus.

*Quantis*, “as many,” stands for *quot*, “how many,” as was said very frequently not only in that age but also by Propertius in his own:

> But what countless thousands of cares she will give you!

Book I, Elegy 5.

## On Chapter XLVI

[Col. 0429C]

“He ordered a notary.” The very accurate Valesius teaches, in his note on Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XIV, that in the age of the Augusti *notarii* were called *exceptores*, those who wrote down the official acts of governors. See him there for more.

“Supreme God.” Am I mistaken, or does Constantine refer to this in Eusebius, Book IV of the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 19, when by enacted law he ordered soldiers who had not yet accepted the saving doctrine of the Christian faith to go out on Sundays into an open field and, at a signal, all offer together to God the prayer which they had previously learned? Certainly the sense of the prayer formula is not far different:

> You alone we know as God; you we acknowledge as king; you we call upon as helper; from you we have received victories,

and the rest.

“In several written notices.” *Libelli* are shorter sheets; and in this age they were sometimes used for letters, as the same Valesius observes on Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XVI, unlike their usage in Cicero’s time, as Paulus Manutius notes on Cicero’s letters, Book II, letter 11. [Col. 0429D]

“Through the *praepositi*.” Most learned men think that these men were set over cohorts, like tribunes, but ranked below tribunes, as they infer from Vegetius, Book II, chapter 12. Josephus translates the term χιλιάρχους, “commanders of a thousand”; Apuleius likewise calls them commanders of a thousand armed men. Others provide further discussion.

“The emperor set the battle for the day of the Kalends of May.” Perhaps he meant “for the day” or “on the day.” What if we read: “The emperor set the day of the Kalends of May for battle”? Yet I think the transmitted text can somehow be tolerated too: “to appoint a battle for that day,” that is, “to appoint battle for that day.”

“Whom they call Serene.” That is, calm, still, free of winds. Claudian, *Rape of Proserpina*, Book III, verse 232:

> … when, serene with dew,  
> the field gleams white.

[Col. 0430A] There *serenus* is similarly explained by Guillaume Pyrrhon as *placidus*, “calm.” So too the ancient glosses: *serenus*, νήνεμος, “windless.”

“Spoken three times.” The ancient Christians seem to have favoured the number three in prayers, not so much through an improper imitation of pagans as for remembrance of the most holy Trinity in God; Cyprian expressly says this in *On the Lord’s Prayer*, and I seem to have read it in others too. That boy mentioned by Nicephorus, Book XIV, chapter 46, also heard it sung three times. After the dreadful terrors of earthquakes, when Christians had assembled for supplications, he was snatched up aloft and shortly afterward restored to the company of mortals, but then again taken away from it through death. He heard sung three times, I say, these words:

> Holy God, holy Mighty One, holy Immortal One, have mercy on us.

Nearly the same is sung even today by the Orthodox Church, and in our own language. The Latin Church also possessed it.

## On Chapter XLVII

“He was mown down by a few.” I judge this reading entirely correct. Lactantius, Book VII, chapter 15: “Then destruction will range through the world, mowing down all things and laying everything low like a harvest.” Jerome to Heliodorus: “Behold, the double-edged sword proceeding from the mouth of the king mows down everything in its way.” Virgil, *Aeneid* X:

> He mows down all that is nearest with his sword, and, blazing,  
> drives a path through the broad battle-line with steel.

For more see the distinguished Heinsius on Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book V, verse 104. [Col. 0430B]

“No one remembered his name…” In battles, commanders used, when affairs seemed to be proceeding too sluggishly, to address their own men by name, so as to show that each of them was known to them and that praise and rewards would not be lacking, according to the valour and merit of each. But here, when all were trembling in divinely sent terror, that device achieved nothing.

“In one night and one day.” Supply “fleeing”; for without that or a similar word, this does not cohere with what follows, where he is said to have arrived at Nicomedia on another night, that is, the second or following night. [Col. 0430C]

## On Chapter XLVIII

“That indeed the divinity…” That this is unsound may be seen even from the fact that the words do not agree: “That indeed the divinity may become appeased and propitious.” I think it should be written: “That whatever divinity there might be in the heavenly abode…” Eusebius has:

> That whatever divinity and heavenly reality there may be may be able to be kindly disposed toward us and toward all who live under our authority.

One seems to have to read in Eusebius ὅ, τιποτέ ἐστι θειότητος, “whatever there may be of divinity.” When I pointed this out to the most learned Cuper, and confessed that I doubted whether Lactantius’ wording could somehow be tolerated—“that whatever divinity there might be in heaven might be propitious to us,” as though he meant, “Whether one ought to think about the nature of the godhead with these people or those, the divine power should in any case be favourable to us”—he replied:

> You rightly perceived that a defect lies hidden in the words “that indeed the divinity …” First, the genius of the Greek language persuades us that Eusebius wrote no otherwise than θειότητος, “of divinity”; then, following your traces and Eusebius’ words, I restore in Lactantius: “that whatever divinity there might be in the heavenly abode.” For if the nominative *divinitas* is retained, “appeased and propitious” can refer to no word; and the emperors speak thus because they mean both the God of the Christians and the gods of the heathen. Thus shortly afterward: “That the supreme divinity, whose religion we obey with free minds, may be able to afford us in all things its accustomed favour and goodwill.” That is, both Christ and the deities of the Gentiles.

So he spoke. But Nicephorus raises another difficulty. As he follows Eusebius in most other matters, so also in this edict, which he reports in Book VII, chapter 41, he more rarely departs from him. He frames the words thus: ὅ, τι ποτέ ἐστι θειοτάτου καὶ οὐρανίου πράγματος, “whatever there may be of a most divine and heavenly reality.” Yet I incline rather to think that θειότητος, “of divinity,” should also be read in Nicephorus. For I see that he is corrupted in very many places, doubtless by the fault of copyists; and I wonder that those who published him so splendidly did not compare him more carefully with Eusebius, nor correct at least the places where the errors are manifest. But this should be reckoned a lighter loss in a writer whose reliability is not everywhere of the best. Let us return, therefore, to Lactantius.

Let younger readers note in Lactantius that *divinitas*, according to the usage of that age, is used for God or a divine being. This is very frequent in Tertullian’s works, especially those discovered later, which he entitled *To the Nations*. Thus Constantine wrote on his triumphal arch that he had, “by the prompting of DIVINITY, avenged the republic with just arms upon the tyrant and all his faction.” Among many others, Salvian also speaks thus in *On the Government of God*, Book II: “The sight of propitious divinity is the gift of human preservation.” I shall add also this passage from Tertullian just mentioned, *Apology*, chapter 34, since it bears upon the subject itself:

> See whether this charge of irreligion does not also apply: to take away freedom of religion and forbid choice of divinity, so that I may not be permitted to worship whom I wish, but may be compelled to worship what I do not wish.

The emperor Jovian held the same view in Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III: “that it should be permitted to worship as each person wishes.” But it belongs to others to pursue this question more fully; therefore I refrain from adducing more about it. [Col. 0431B]

“With all restrictions entirely removed.” The restrictions here called *conditiones* are called αἱρέσεις, “provisions” or “exceptions,” in Eusebius, as Baluze has admirably observed; see him.

“Now to provide for [them] freely and simply.” An attentive reader will easily recognize that these words too are corrupt—indeed mutilated. Their sense is this (for I would not venture to supply the words; all learned men would rightly disapprove if anyone presumed to thrust his own words in place of the ancients’):

> Therefore your devotedness ought to know that it has pleased us, after all the restrictions contained in our earlier letters sent to your office concerning the Christians have been wholly removed—restrictions which seemed altogether perverse and alien to our clemency—to provide now that freely and simply, etc.

Here I have printed in a different style or type of lettering only those things added from the Greek. To make it clearer whether this was done suitably, I shall give a somewhat fuller Greek text:

> Accordingly, it was consistent for us to write back that, once the restrictions entirely removed which were contained in our earlier letters sent to your devotedness concerning the Christians, and which seemed altogether improper and foreign to our mildness, have been taken away, each of those who have adopted the same resolve to preserve the Christian religion may now freely and without deviation maintain this very thing without any disturbance.

“Which … honour.” Or perhaps: “Because…” I conjecture that the reading was:

> This has been done by us in order that it may seem that nothing has been taken away or diminished by us from anyone’s honour or religion,

or something of that sense. Eusebius’ Greek is:

> This has been done by us so that nothing may seem to have been diminished by us from any honour or any religion.

“Something in the earlier time.” Read *aliqui*, “some persons.” Eusebius has: “so that those who either [received something] from the treasury …” [Col. 0431D]

“Let them restore [it] as quickly as possible.” Vossius and Borrichius, two eminent men, numbered *quantocius* among non-Latin words. Yet it is read in Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue* III, chapter 4: “Depart as quickly as possible, lest heavenly wrath consume me because of your injury.” The old translator of the Bible also has it at Genesis XLV, 9. Labbe’s glosses: *quam ocius*, τὴν τακίστην, “with the greatest speed”: write *quantocius*.

“Even those who bought [them].” I separate this from the preceding words and restore each in its proper place thus:

> … let them restore [them] as quickly as possible. Even those who either bought [them] or received [them] as a gift—if they think that they have any claim upon our goodwill—should petition the vicar, so that they too …

*Postulare* in this sense means to state one’s request, or that of a friend, before the person who presides over jurisdiction, as Ulpian teaches in Book I, *On Petitioning*. See Brisson, *On the Meaning of Words*.

## On Chapter XLIX

“But Licinius, following…” It seems necessary that we should shortly read: “he sought the passes; and the fortifications …”

[Col. 0432A]

“With unbearable pain.” Thus in Book VII of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 16: “He will afflict the world with unbearable domination.” Lactantius luxuriates in such formations: similarly *inextricabilis*, “inextricable”; *inexcogitabilis*, “unthinkable”; *illibabilis*, “unimpaired”; *inviolabilis*, “inviolable”; *ineluibilis*, “inescapable”; *incomprehensibilis*, “incomprehensible”; *cruciabilis*, “torturing”; *dissipabilis*, “destructible”; *ineloquibilis*, “inexpressible”; and you will find many others, some of which occur in other authors as well.

## On Chapter L

“When he learned that he was alive.” The wording is awkward. “When he learned that he, Candidianus, was alive, she joined his retinue in order to watch Candidianus’ fortune.” For otherwise one cannot understand *vixisse*, “to have lived,” except euphemistically of Candidianus, who was already marked for death; but the rest protests too strongly. More correctly, therefore: “When she learned that he, Licinius, had issued this edict, she joined his, that is, the emperor’s, retinue.” If shortly afterward you read, “Because he had presented himself at Nicomedia,” those words too will be easier.

“Living in the years eight.” Perhaps read: “Living in Cilicia for eight years.” Lactantius certainly uses the expression thus: Book V, chapter 22, “He who lives amid prosperity is impatient”; Book VI, chapter 2, “Like one living in darkness”; *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 1, “Your affairs, in which you now live.” “He lived his life for so many years” appears in an ancient inscription:

> Tigrinianus made this for Profutura, his most deserving wife, who lived with me twenty-five years. She lived her life fifty-eight years. In peace.

[Col. 0432B]

“She was cast headlong into the Orient.” From a letter of the most illustrious Cuper to a man likewise resplendent in his own and his family’s distinctions, Constantijn Huygens, secretary to the most exalted Prince of Orange:

A few days ago, when I enjoyed conversation with you and your brother and we were discussing various antiquities, the book of Lactantius *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* came up, as often happens. Stephen Baluze inserted it in volume II of his *Miscellanies*, thereby earning great merit for ecclesiastical history. Your most learned brother maintained that a dispute had been raised against a man in France over these words in chapter 50: “But first their mother was cast headlong into the Orient,” whereas reason and the context plainly advise that a river is indicated here and that *Orontem*, “into the Orontes,” should be read.

I immediately thought that further deliberation was needed, and stated that I had read that the Orontes was called the Orient. But because I remembered only the references, receive what I have noted at home on that passage. I certainly never doubted that Lactantius, the most eloquent of the Fathers, wrote *Orontem*. Yet *Oriens*, “Orient,” crept into the place of *Orontes* through copyists, undoubtedly in an age when they spoke thus; nor did that most learned man act so badly in retaining the spelling found in ancient manuscripts. For one and the same river is meant; and Hegesippus, Book III, chapter 5 of *The Destruction*, and Isidore, *Origins*, Book XIII, chapter 21, testify that this river was called *Oriens*. Hence Eustathius, bishop of Thessalonica, in his commentary on Dionysius Periegetes, interprets Orontes as Ἀνατολικός, “eastern”:

> Others say that Caesar Tiberius renamed it Orontes from Dracon, which among the Romans means “the Eastern [river].”

But just as it is contrary to truth that Tiberius, successor of the emperor Augustus—unless, however, some later Tiberius is meant—named this river Orontes from Dracon, though Orontes is mentioned already in Polybius, so Eustathius undoubtedly refers to the word *Oriens*. Along with other authors he thus somehow defends the common reading, which clearly teaches that Hegesippus and Isidore did not without reason report that the Orontes was called the Orient.

These were his words there. In a letter sent to me last autumn, however, that most learned man added:

> This is what I think of the passage; I sent it before. To add this: Propertius celebrates Orontean myrrh, because it was brought from Arabia to Antioch, the most famous market-city of Syria, situated on the river Orontes. Gaspar Hofmann, *Various Readings*, Book III, chapter 4, thinks that the myrrh is named not from the river Orontes but from Cyprus, where Cinyras, Myrrha’s father, reigned; that Cyprus was once part of Syria, according to Pliny, II.88; and accordingly that in Ovid, *Metamorphoses* X, one should rewrite:

> > … Princes chosen from every side  
> > desire you, and the youth throughout the whole Orontes,

> as “throughout the whole Orient.” Nor, he says, should anyone be troubled that the first syllable of *Orontes* is short. Finally, he thinks that this aromatic was always sought from the Arabs, that the Orontes are Arabian peoples according to Pliny, VI.26, and that the myrrh was named from them. I shall not waste time refuting these things. The Orontes are not a people in Arabia, but neighbours of the Gordyaeans in Mesopotamia. And although Arabs lived in that region, and the name Arabia sometimes extends so far, myrrh does not grow there. Columella, Book X, celebrates Achaean myrrh because, according to Dioscorides, it grows also in Boeotia, which, as you know, is included under the name Achaia together with neighbouring regions.

Thus far the most learned Cuper. That the diligent reader may lack nothing that can presently be adduced, I shall give Hegesippus’ words from Book III, chapter 5, where he describes Antioch:

> A river runs through the middle of it, which, rising from the sunrise, empties into the sea not far from the city; the ancients called it Orient from the course of its source, so that people generally suppose it gave its name to the regions, whereas it received it from them. By the very force of its colder currents, and by the zephyrs continually blowing through those places, the whole city is cooled at almost every moment, so that it hides the Orient in the regions of the Orient.

The same may be read in Isidore, Book XIII, chapter 21. Since these matters have been splendidly explained by a man of the highest rank and most abundant learning, I have nothing to add but applause. I judge Eustathius’ words undoubtedly corrupt. Strabo reports that Typhon was called Orient; but I do not recall having read anywhere, except here, that it was named Dracon. I do have a conjecture: ἐξ Ὀρόντου αὐτὸν Ὀριέντην μετωνόμασε, “he renamed it Orient from Orontes.” But since it is credible that Cuper also readily saw this, yet rejected it as too bold, perhaps it is better to await more certain assistance from others. Everything concerning the name of that region mentioned by Hegesippus may be known from Constantine’s *On the Themes*.

## On the Final Chapter

[Col. 0433C]

“That he might not corrupt the truth.” *Ne*, “lest,” preceded; therefore I judge that *non* [Col. 0434A], added by a copyist, should be deleted.

“He looked upon the earth.” This elegant mode of speaking is not merely very common in secular literature, as learned men have sufficiently shown, but also in sacred writings. Deuteronomy XXVI, 7: “He heard us and looked upon our humiliation, labour, and distress”; and verse 15: “Look down from your sanctuary and lofty dwelling-place of heaven, and bless your holy people.” Thus the Virgin *Theotokos*, “God-bearer,” in that admirable hymn: “For he looked upon the lowliness of his servant” (Ὅτι ἐπέβλεψεν ἐπὶ τὴν ταπείνωσιν τῆς δούλης αὑτοῦ), where Pricaeus collected further examples.

Eusebius uses it also of this very restoration of peace to the Church, which this writer treats, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VIII, chapter 16: “For the divine and heavenly grace showed its kindly and gracious oversight toward us” (Ὡς γὰρ τὴν εἰς ἡμᾶς ἐπισκοπὴν εὐμενῆ καὶ ἵλεω ἡ θεία καὶ οὐράνιος χάρις ἐνεδείκνυτο). Unless you prefer there to derive the metaphor from inspection or visitation carried out by the ἁρμοστῆρες, “commissioners,” who were sent to investigate and regulate the affairs of allies or provincials. On this see the most learned and celebrated Buchnerus, on the Nativity Hymn sung by Prudentius to Christ the Saviour.

“That he may guard the flourishing churches in perpetual peace.” Two most learned men thought one should read: “That he may guard the flourishing churches in perpetual peace.” It seems to me more possible, according to the usage of those times, that it was written: “That he may guard the perpetual peace of the flourishing Church.” For he is speaking only of the one true Church. The rest too would better suit Lactantius’ style: Book VI, chapter 10, “That he might secure for himself the safety of night’s rest”; Book VII, chapter 2, “When the souls of the pious have been restored to blessed life, may a tranquil, peaceful, golden age—as poets call it—flourish, with God himself reigning.” The pleasing name of peace, moreover, was greatly loved by Romans and Roman emperors, as coins show and others have demonstrated. Constantine the Great also loved it, among others—not to mention pagans—being called on his triumphal arch and coins “Liberator of the City” and “Founder of Peace,” and elsewhere displaying the most welcome names, “Public Peace” or “Public Tranquillity.” May God, best and greatest, grant that all bearing the Christian name, and in particular our country with its pious, brave, and fortunate KING, may flourish forever in firm and enduring peace and tranquillity, together with the goods already named and other blessings proper and perpetual. [Col. 0434C]

[Notes of Nicolas Toinard on the Book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*]

[Col. 0433]

## Nicolas Toinard’s Notice to the Reader

Since those things which I wrote in these notes on chapter 4, concerning Holy Saturday and the passions of the blessed Polycarp and Pionius, largely for my own satisfaction, have been committed to print, I have thought it worthwhile to state that the following two opinions seem to me highly probable—opinions which I shall elsewhere set out more fully: namely, that Polycarp suffered martyrdom on the Jewish Great Sabbath itself, that is, the Sabbath immediately preceding the fourteenth paschal moon, on 26 March [as in the Acts], in the year of Christ 147; and that Pionius was arrested likewise on the Great Sabbath, 22 March 251, and suffered martyrdom on the twelfth day of the seventh Asian month, which in the aforesaid year 251 fell on a Sabbath, 5 April.

Those who defend this opinion need pay no attention to the consulships, since they have been wrongly appended to the proconsular Acts.

[Col. 0433]

## Notes of Toinard of Orléans on the Book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*

### On Chapter I

[Col. 0433D]

“Behold, an adversary shall be added to all these; and, once tranquillity has been restored throughout the world, the Church lately overthrown rises again.” The distinguished Jean-Baptiste Cotelerius, editor of the *Monuments of the Greek Church*, published at Paris in 1681, p. 528, directs in his notes that the text should be read: “Behold, an adversary is crushed by all these”; the sense, he says, thus becoming plain and the antithesis between “is crushed” and “rises” being apt. I have thought it right to present here, at the head of my notes and under a good omen, this excellent emendation of a most learned man once closely associated with me, lest it remain unknown to students of Lactantius while hidden in an unfamiliar place. [Col. 0435A]

### On Chapter II

“In the final times of Tiberius Caesar, as we read in Scripture, our Lord Jesus Christ was tortured by the Jews, after the tenth day before the Kalends of April, under the consulship of the two Gemini.” In these few words there is more than one error. The first is due to a copyist’s carelessness: *post*, “after,” has crept in for *ante*, “before.” For I think it should here be read *ante diem decimum*, as Lactantius himself has elsewhere, namely in the *Institutes*, Book IV, chapter 10, where he says of the Jews:

> From that time they had tetrarchs down to Herod, who lived under the rule of Tiberius Caesar, in whose fifteenth year—that is, under the consulship of the two Gemini—the Jews fastened Christ to the cross on the tenth day before the Kalends of April.

The illustrious Stephen Baluze, most diligent editor of this great treasure, in his notes on the preceding chapter 2, published at Paris in 1679 [Col. 0435B], denies that there is any contradiction between the two formulations, “after the tenth day” and “before the tenth day,” relying on the authority of the jurist Paulus, *Digest*, “On the Meaning of Words,” law *Anniculus*, Book 132. See his words.

But the illustrious Henry Noris, in the great work *Pisan Cenotaphs*, published at Venice in 1681, p. 345, refutes this opinion. From the autograph manuscript of the Pandects preserved at Florence, he supplies the genuine reading of Paulus’ words:

> “The tenth day before the Kalends” [and] “the tenth day after the Kalends”: by neither expression are eleven days meant.

He then says:

> From this genuine reading of the text, Riccioli’s opinion is refuted … For Paulus’ statement has an excellent and entirely true sense, although not expressed in the jurist’s identical words. For in Book 134, *Digest*, “On the Meaning of Words,” he says: “A child is called one year old not immediately upon birth, but on the three hundred and sixty-fifth day, which is beginning but plainly not completed.” Therefore one who dies on the final day of the year, once it has begun, is said in Book 132 to be lost as an *anniculus*, a child in its first year. He proves this by an argument drawn from common usage: when we say “on the tenth day before the Kalends,” we count the terminal day itself, namely the following first day of the Kalends, not the eleventh day which follows the Kalends, namely the second day of the month.

> Therefore, says the jurist, the *anniculus* is likewise lost when it is lost on the very three hundred and sixty-fifth day, which has begun but has plainly not been completed; it need not be lost on the first day of the following year. Thus it is established on the authority of the most celebrated jurist that the common phrase “on the tenth day before the Kalends” does not signify eleven days but only ten, with the Kalends themselves included in the reckoning.

[Note: “The eleventh day which follows the Kalends, namely the second day of the month.” With all respect to the most learned Noris, it seems one should write: “The tenth day which precedes the Kalends, namely the tenth day before the end of the month.”]

Finally, on the following page, after recounting Baluze’s reconciliation of Lactantius’ two passages, Noris adds:

> But the most learned interpreters understand Paulus’ text differently. Antonio Agustín, Book IV of his *Emendations*, says concerning Paulus’ cited law: “It is found that *ante diem tertium nonas*, ‘on the third day before the Nones,’ and *tertio nonas*, ‘on the third [day] before the Nones,’ and *die tertio post kalendas*, ‘on the third day after the Kalends,’ are the same.” I once noted these words of Cujas in his *Adversaria*: “*Post diem decimum kalendarum* signifies the tenth day after the Kalends, with the Kalends themselves included in the reckoning. Therefore *post diem decimum kalendarum Ianuariarum* is the fourth day before the Ides of January.” Paulus Manutius rightly notes in the twelfth letter of Book III of Cicero’s *Letters to Friends* that the ancient Latins said *ante diem tertium nonas*, that is, “on the third day before the Nones”; for when *tertio nonas* is said, the phrase is compressed, since *die ante*, “on the day before,” is understood, and the suppressed preposition governs *kalendas* in the accusative. Therefore *post decimum diem kalendarum Aprilis* is the same as “on the tenth day after the Kalends of April” …

> Nor does Paulus support the aforementioned opinion of the most learned Baluze. For he writes that neither formula, “the tenth day before the Kalends” and “the tenth day after the Kalends,” signifies the eleventh day, but the tenth—not, however, of the same month, but in the one case the tenth day before, that is, preceding the Kalends, and in the other the tenth day after, that is, following the Kalends. Thus Gaius the jurist says in the same Digest, Book L, law 233: “On the third day after the Kalends of January vows are undertaken for the emperor’s welfare,” namely on the third day before the Nones of January. Hence it is evident that these phrases signify entirely different months: “the tenth day before the Kalends of April” and “the tenth day after the Kalends of April.” The former designates 23 March; the latter, however, [Col. 0436A] the tenth day after the Kalends of April.

[Note: “The day after the tenth day before the Kalends of April.” Write: “The tenth day after the Kalends of April,” namely the tenth day of April.]

> Therefore Lactantius’ formula of words has the support of no ancient Latin author and is rejected by the most learned modern scholars. I know that astronomers reckon a day from the preceding noon to the noon of the following day. Hence, in their terminology, 23 March after noon is called “after the tenth day before the Kalends of April.” To indicate the time of day at which the Lord suffered, namely the afternoon of 23 March, Lactantius wrote according to astronomers’ manner of speaking. Yet I wish that these remarks be regarded not as objections to the most learned Baluze but as proposals submitted to his judgment.

Thus far the illustrious Noris, whose passage I have given almost entire, both because of its own excellence and because the *Pisan Cenotaphs* are not in everyone’s hands. [Col. 0436B]

I wholly accept Noris’ opinion, so that by the words *post diem decimum kalendarum Aprilis*, “after the tenth day before the Kalends of April,” the tenth day of April is meant, with the Kalends themselves included in the count.

But the most celebrated author vainly calls astronomers to Lactantius’ aid in excusing or interpreting him. For what has Lactantius to do with astronomers in a matter not at all astronomical, that we should resort to such subtleties, which Lactantius never thought of?

Moreover, if that astronomers’ manner of speaking had any place, it would follow that, because the tenth day before the Kalends of April had, according to astronomers, ended at noon on 23 March and the ninth had consequently begun, Lactantius said that Christ was crucified after noon on that day. For, in the author’s own words in chapter 2 of this book, he “was tortured after the tenth day before the Kalends of April,” and this expression signifies “was fastened to the cross.”

But Lactantius does not write separately about a part of the day, but only generally about the day itself on which Christ underwent the cross. Hence nothing at all is easier than to say that *post* in this passage is a copyist’s error and that *ante* should be substituted for it. This is all the more so because, in the passage from the *Institutes*, Book IV, chapter 10, where *ante diem decimum* is correctly read, some editions—such as the Lyon 1548 duodecimo and the Antwerp 1555 octavo—read *ante diem septimam*, “on the seventh day before,” for *ante diem decimum*, “on the tenth day before,” as is generally found in numerous ancient manuscripts and corrected editions.

Just as, therefore, the word *septimam* has been placed for *decimum* in the passage from the *Institutes*, so in this work *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* the word *post* has plainly been written wrongly for *ante*.

Joannes Columbus, who illustrated this same book in notes published at Åbo in Finland in 1684, has the following remarks on this passage: see his words, col. 363.

Thus far Joannes Columbus, whose opinion is more than sufficiently refuted by what Norisius and I have adduced above.

Moreover, that learned man did not observe that, in the other example, Mark IX.12—though it is in fact Matthew XVII.1—the sixth day cannot possibly be understood as having begun, but as having elapsed. For in the parallel passage in Luke IX.28, “about eight days” (ὡσεὶ ἡμέρᾳ ὄκτω) are counted. Thus in Matthew and Mark the six days must be reckoned as complete, [Col. 0437A] so that the following seventh comes nearer to the eight mentioned in Luke.

I said above, at the beginning of chapter 2, that Lactantius’s words contain several errors. The copyist’s error having therefore been dealt with, attention must now be turned to Lactantius himself.

He says that Christ suffered in the last times of Tiberius Caesar, during the consulship of the two Gemini. In the other passage of the *Institutions*, namely Book IV, chapter 10, he assigns those last times of Tiberius to Tiberius’s fifteenth year. This indeed agrees with the consulship of the two Gemini. But observe, reader, how grossly he is thereby mistaken.

Tiberius began the fifteenth year of his reign in A.D. 28, on 19 August. In this very year of Tiberius, John the Baptist, as we read in Luke III.1–3, began to preach repentance. According to Lactantius, this was the fifteenth year of Tiberius in progress, since, according to the same author, Christ suffered in Tiberius’s fifteenth year, which continued until 19 August of A.D. 29.

[Col. 0437B] Therefore, if Christ was baptized on 6 January, in A.D. 29 under the consulship of the two Gemini, and suffered on 23 March following, he accomplished all that is related from his baptism to his death in no more than two and a half months. This is monstrous to say, although it has been rashly asserted by many other ancients and inserted into the Fasti of Idatius.

For what, then, is to become of the four Passovers by which, as the most learned Hardouin himself admits in the index to his *Antirrheticus*, published at Paris in 1689, the Saviour’s ministry is distinguished in the Gospels? What Philolaus or Ptolemy, what Copernicus or Tycho, will find in that year A.D. 29 the calendrical conditions fitting the day of Christ’s Passion—namely, a Friday coinciding with the day of Passover?

And yet this is the very Lactantius who, together with other authors of the same sort—that is, equally heedless of chronology and evangelical [Col. 0437C] history—is pressed into service by those who deny that Christ was crucified in A.D. 33, on the fourteenth of Nisan, or 3 April.

But far be it from me to wish any diminution of the authority of Lactantius and other ecclesiastical writers on that account. This alone I maintain: the more they are celebrated for their antiquity, the less credit ought to be given them in chronological matters. For, knowing and teaching only Christ, and him crucified, they did not preserve the sequence of events with such precision.

The most distinguished Joannes Hardouin, in his *Antirrheticus*, p. 67, decides this question in the following terms: “Finally, we understand that the Lord Jesus suffered in A.D. 29, at the third Passover after undertaking the office of preaching, as the most ancient of the Fathers have handed down with unanimous consent, under the consulship of the two Gemini.”

Then, in the Addenda at the end of the book, he adds: “For both the rites of the Jews and astronomical [Col. 0437D] tables, as we shall say elsewhere, agree with that year.”

Then, rising against the most distinguished Joannes Vaillant on the same p. 67, he says: “Had you suspected anything of these matters? Or did anyone inform you of them before us?”

Thus far the distinguished Hardouin. I do not know what could be produced to establish this opinion. For I am by no means altogether unacquainted with Jewish rites; nor can any device ever extract from astronomical tables a Friday and a Passover day jointly occurring in A.D. 29, on which Christ suffered.

“Matthias and Paul were taken in the place of Judas the traitor.” Do not infer from these words that Paul, along with Matthias, was appointed by the apostles in Judas’s place. Lactantius, writing somewhat carelessly, meant only to indicate that in Judas’s place two others performed the apostolic office: Matthias, chosen by lot, Acts I.26, [Col. 0438A] and Paul, chosen by Christ himself.

“And for twenty-five years, down to the beginning of Nero’s reign, they laid the foundations of churches in every province and city.” From the consulship of the two Gemini—that is, from A.D. 29, in which, according to Lactantius’s hypothesis refuted above, the apostles, after Pentecost (Acts II.1; cf. Mark XVI.20), preached the Gospel everywhere—twenty-five full years extend to 13 October A.D. 54, when Nero succeeded Claudius. But from A.D. 33, when Christ truly suffered, there are only twenty-one.

“And when Nero was already reigning, Peter arrived at Rome.” In the short register of the deposition of martyrs, published by Aegidius Bucherius at Antwerp in 1634 in his commentary *On the Doctrine of Times*, one reads: “On the eighth day before the Kalends of March” (that is, 22 February), “the feast of Peter’s Chair.” According to Lactantius’s reckoning, this occurred in A.D. 55, while Nero’s first year was in progress from 13 October of the preceding year.

But if the opinion of the most learned men Godfrey [Col. 0438B] Henschenius, at the beginning of the first volume of the Saints for April, published at Antwerp in 1675, and Daniel Papebrochius, in the *Propylaeum* to the *Acts of the Saints* for May, published there in 1685, be accepted—the same opinion embraced by the distinguished Antonius Pagi in the *Baronian Critique*, published at Paris in 1688—namely, that Peter was martyred at Rome on the third day before the Kalends of July, under the consuls Nerva Silianus and Vestinus Atticus, that is, 29 June A.D. 65, Nero’s twelfth year, then Peter lived no more than ten years, four months, and eight days after the establishment of his chair at Rome.

From Flavius Josephus, and likewise from coins—as I shall show in my treatise *On the Coins of the Herodians*—it must be established that A.D. 43, Claudius’s third year and Agrippa the Elder’s seventh and final year, was the year when Peter was divinely delivered from chains at Jerusalem, and afterwards Agrippa, struck by an angel, died at Caesarea in Palestine (Acts XII.3, 23), where he was presenting games in honor of Claudius Caesar at a festival instituted for the emperor’s safety. Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book XIX, [Col. 0438C] final chapter.

If, therefore, as above, the feast of Peter’s Chair on 22 February of some year is accepted, and Peter was crucified in A.D. 65, it is altogether necessary that he should have come to Rome once at least two years before Agrippa imprisoned him in A.D. 43; and that this should have occurred at the beginning of Claudius’s first imperial year, and in the waning month after Caligula’s murder on 24 January A.D. 41; and that he should then have returned to Judaea, so as to establish his see at Rome twenty-five years before his death.

But if this journey of Peter is thought insufficiently probable because it appears inconsistent with the sequence of events narrated in Acts through chapter XII, then his first arrival in the City could not have occurred at the earliest before A.D. 44, under Claudius, on 22 February, as above, from the register of the deposition of martyrs. From that date to A.D. 65 and 29 June, when, according to the opinion of Henschenius, Papebrochius, and Pagi reported above, Peter was killed at Rome during Nero’s violence, [Col. 0438D] no more than twenty-one years, four months, and eight days can be counted.

And certainly, since in the Paschal Chronicle—recently republished at Paris by the distinguished Carolus Du Cange, and formerly but wrongly called Alexandrian—nothing is written concerning the death of Peter and Paul in A.D. 66 or thereafter, it is to be understood that its author assigned this event to some earlier year. But which year that was cannot be determined because of a gap occupying fully twenty years in this Chronicle between A.D. 45 and 66.

I do not linger over the Fasti of Idatius, printed third at the end of the same Paschal Chronicle, which say that Peter and Paul suffered under Nero III and Messalla as consuls—that is, in A.D. 58. Who in his right mind could tolerate this? Even if Tacitus’s passage, which I shall cite below, were not at hand, it proves that Nero did not rage until A.D. 64.

“Yet he did not escape unpunished. For God looked upon the affliction [Col. 0439A] of his people . . . so that not even a place for the burial of so evil a beast appeared upon the earth.” Nero immediately persecuted the Christians after Rome had been burned. Tacitus explicitly states this in *Annals*, Book XV, chapters 38 and 44.

Suetonius also treats of this fire in *Nero*, chapter 38, as does Dio, p. 708. According to Tacitus himself, *Annals* XV.33, it occurred under the consuls C. Lecanius Bassus and M. Licinius Crassus, that is, in A.D. 64. It began on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of Sextilis, or 19 July, and ended only on the sixth day, that is, 24 or 25 July, according to Tacitus, ibid., chapter 44, where he adds: “Therefore, to suppress the rumor, Nero fastened guilt upon and inflicted the most exquisite punishments upon those whom the populace, hated for their shameful acts, called Christians.”

Let us therefore grant Nero the remaining seven or eight days of July to devise a plan for transferring to the Christians the odium for the burning of the City. It follows that the persecution began about the opening of August in A.D. 64. Now A.D. 68 and 9 June are marked by Nero’s death. The interval before divine vengeance: three years, ten months, and about nine days.

[Col. 0439B] From these considerations and those stated above, the blessed Apostles must have suffered martyrdom at the end of the eleventh month after the persecution was stirred up. For from the beginning of August A.D. 64 to the end of June A.D. 65, the eleventh month elapsed.

## On Chapter III

“After him, some years having intervened.” Namely, thirty years besides six months, as will be stated below.

“Another tyrant, no less great, arose.” Domitian, the last of the twelve Caesars.

“Yet he lay upon the necks of his subjects for a very long time and ruled securely, until he stretched out impious hands against the Lord.” Domitian succeeded his brother Titus in A.D. 81, on 13 September. If he began to rage against Christians in about February A.D. 94, as I judge, he had then ruled before the persecution for twelve years, four months, and more than a half.

[Col. 0439C] The Paschal Chronicle connects the beginning of the Domitianic persecution with A.D. 92, not 93 as the distinguished Antonius Pagi thinks in his *Hypatic Dissertation*, published at Lyons in 1680, p. 110, and in the *Baronian Critique* at A.D. 90, no. 5, p. 86. There he further says that the author of this Chronicle follows the Eusebian method in calculating Olympiads, that is, anticipates them by one year, though in fact the Chronicle’s author anticipates them by two years. For he places their beginning in Julian Period 3936, whereas they began only in 3938.

None of this, nor many other things, was perceived by the person whose chronological works the distinguished Du Cange used in adding chronological identifiers to the Paschal Chronicle.

In the aforesaid edition of that Chronicle, there is such confusion—arising, shall I say, from ignorance or carelessness?—that the year in which Domitian stirred up the persecution is left uncertain on p. 250 between A.D. 93 and 94. Nor is the first year of the 218th Olympiad, [Col. 0439D] which there is Domitian’s thirteenth year, marked by any chronological identifier whatsoever.

We must now inquire at what earliest time Domitian vexed the Church.

The distinguished Antonius Pagi, in the *Hypatic Dissertation*, p. 110, and in the *Baronian Critique*, p. 85, no. 4, places this at the end of A.D. 93, on the basis of a passage of Tacitus which, at the end of the *Life of Agricola*, declares Agricola fortunate because he died under the consuls Collega and Priscus—that is, in A.D. 93—on the tenth day before the Kalends of September, or 23 August, and thus escaped that final period in which Domitian drained the commonwealth, not now by intervals and pauses, but continuously and, as it were, with a single blow. From this Pagi infers that the persecution began at the end of A.D. 93.

But in my judgment, it follows only that Domitian did not rage until after Agricola’s death. Since it is uncertain at what later time [Col. 0440A] this occurred, and since moreover the commonwealth appears to have been ill-treated first and then the Church, this passage of Tacitus contributes nothing at all to fixing the persecution in A.D. 93.

Henry Dodwell, an Englishman, a distinguished man, in his eleventh Cyprianic Dissertation, published at Oxford in 1684, to which he affixed the heading *On the Fewness of Martyrs*, most unworthy of anyone calling himself a Christian, much less a learned author, contends from Bruttius’s words in Eusebius, *History*, Book III, chapter 18, that the Church was not vexed by Domitian until A.D. 95, because in the fifteenth year of his reign Flavia Domitilla, niece through his sister of Flavius Clemens, then consul, was banished to the island of Pontia for confession of Christ.

But the whole of Dodwell’s dissertation has been excellently refuted not only by the distinguished Antonius Pagi throughout the *Baronian Critique* and by Theodoric Ruinart, a Benedictine monk, in the preface to the *Genuine and Select Acts of the Martyrs*, published at Paris in 1689; this argument too, advanced to establish the brevity of the Domitianic [Col. 0440B] persecution, has been answered: nothing follows from it except that the persecution was most intense in A.D. 95.

And indeed, in the Paschal Chronicle, under Domitian’s fourteenth year, these words occur: “Brutus reports” (read Bruttius, Βρούτιος) “that many Christians suffered martyrdom in Domitian’s fourteenth year” (ἱστορεῖ ὁ Βροῦτος … πολλοὺς Χριστιανοὺς κατὰ τὸ ιδ` ἔτος Δομιτιανοῦ μεμαρτυρηκέναι).

But in order to extract from that passage of Bruttius anything on which we may rely, certainties must be separated from uncertainties, and the following established:

First, Domitian began his twelfth year in A.D. 92 on 13 September, while the fourth year of the 217th Olympiad was running.

Second, the 218th Olympiad began at the summer solstice of A.D. 93.

Third, Domitian’s thirteenth year ran from 13 September A.D. 93, while the first year of the [Col. 0440C] 218th Olympiad was running.

Finally, his fourteenth year began in A.D. 94, while the second year of that same 218th Olympiad was in progress.

It follows that the author of the Paschal Chronicle errs by two years when he links Domitian’s thirteenth year with the first year of the 218th Olympiad and with Indiction 5. For, according to this author’s own method and assumptions, the 218th Olympiad and Domitian’s thirteenth year would have begun in A.D. 91.

I do not pause over the fact that the consulates in Domitian’s later years were incorrectly assigned by the author of the Paschal Chronicle. That is irrelevant to the present matter. I assume only what is reported there from Bruttius’s history: that many Christians suffered martyrdom in Domitian’s fourteenth year. Since scholars agree that Domitian did not vex the Church until, after Agricola’s death on 23 August A.D. 93—as noted above from Tacitus—he drained the commonwealth continuously and, as it were, with a single blow, I think I shall take the safest middle course if I say [Col. 0440D] that the Domitianic persecution began in February of the following year, 94; and consequently that in that same year, on 6 May, the apostle John was put into a vat full of boiling oil and then banished to the island of Patmos. This agrees with Jerome, who says in his catalogue of ecclesiastical writers that this happened in Domitian’s fourteenth year, when Domitian, initiating the second persecution after Nero, was moving against Christians.

Thus from the Neronian persecution, which, as I showed above, began around the opening of August in A.D. 64, to the Domitianic persecution there were thirty years besides six months—namely, from the beginning of August A.D. 64 to the end of January A.D. 94.

“But after he had been incited by the prompting of demons to persecute the righteous people, he was then delivered into the hands of his enemies and paid the penalty.” Domitian began to rage in February A.D. 94, as just stated. He was killed [Col. 0441A] in A.D. 96 on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October, or 18 September, as all agree. The interval before divine vengeance: about two years and seven and a half months.

## On Chapter IV

“For after many years there appeared that accursed animal Decius, to vex the Church. For who but an evil man persecutes justice? And as though he had been advanced to that supreme station for this very purpose, he immediately began to rage against God, so that he might immediately fall.” That Decius raged as soon as he came to power is likewise taught by the Paschal Chronicle in these words: “At the beginning of Decius’s reign, when persecution against the Christians had been stirred up, Flavianus—read Fabianus (Φαβιανὸς)—bishop of the Romans, suffered martyrdom.” We must now inquire when this occurred.

Decius succeeded Philip, who was still reigning on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, or 18 June, Aemilianus and Aquilinus being consuls, in A.D. 249, according to the Code of Justinian, Book VIII, [Col. 0441B] title 56, *On Revoking Gifts*, law 1. But the name of Decius Augustus is prefixed under the same consuls on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November, or 19 October, in the same Code, Book IV, title 16, *On Hereditary Actions*, law 2. Therefore Decius obtained the empire between 17 June and 19 October.

If we grant that he began to rule at the end of June or the beginning of July, as will be said below, then from the Domitianic persecution, which I assigned to February A.D. 94, to the Decian persecution there will be 156 years, besides about five months; and Lactantius rightly calls these “many years,” because the ensuing persecutions were almost contiguous with one another.

But Lactantius’s statement that Decius fell immediately after he vexed the Church does not describe exactly the same duration as elapsed from Domitian’s stirring up the persecution to his death—namely, from February A.D. 94 to 18 September A.D. 96. That interval is two years and about seven and a half months; that it was somewhat [Col. 0441C] shorter in Decius’s case is shown as follows.

From what has been said, Decius ruled in A.D. 249 between 17 June and 19 October. He ceased to rule in A.D. 251, in which he entered upon his third consulship with his son Decius Etruscus as colleague. For in the following year, 252, Trebonianus Gallus, successor to both, already Augustus, appears in the Fasti, with his son Vibius Volusianus, already Caesar, as colleague.

At what season of the year the Decii died may be inferred from Trebellius Pollio in his *Valerian*, where these words are found: “Under the consulship of the two Decii, in A.D. 251, on the sixth day before the Kalends of November, or 27 October, when the senate was meeting in the Temple of Castor at Rome because of imperial letters, and each senator’s opinion was being asked as to whom the censorship ought to be conferred—for the Decii had placed this matter in the power of the most august senate—… Valerian being absent, for he was on campaign with Decius, all with one voice said, interrupting the customary procedure for delivering opinions: ‘Valerian’s life is a censorship’ … When this had been said repeatedly, all added their assent; and so the meeting was adjourned. When Decius received [Col. 0441D] this decree of the senate, he summoned all the courtiers and ordered Valerian himself also to be invited.” Thus far Trebellius Pollio.

From this it is clear that, after the absent Decii had referred to the Senate the authority to choose a censor, Valerian—also absent—was elected censor at Rome on 27 October.

Valerian was stationed on the Moesian frontier with the Decii, who were killed there before the end of that year. Let us allow about a month both for reporting that decree of the Senate to Moesia and then for engaging in the battle in which both Decii fell: the Decii were killed at the end of November.

This occurred at Abruttus, or Abyrtus, or Abrittus, as Victor in *On the Caesars*, Dexippus in Syncellus, p. 376 of the royal edition of 1652, and the Paschal Chronicle under A.D. 251 attest; besides Jordanes, *On Gothic Affairs*, chapter 18, where one reads: “Coming to Adabritto [or *abrupto*], a city of Moesia, he is surrounded by the Goths and himself perishes.” The distinguished Antonius Pagi noted in the *Baronian Critique*, p. 51, at A.D. 251, that [Col. 0442A] *Abrutto* should be read; but it is better to read *ad Abrittum*. Read likewise *Abrutti* in Victor, *On the Caesars*, instead of *Bruti*.

Victor, *On the Caesars*, says simply that Decius ruled for two full years; the other Victor says thirty months. But those thirty months cannot be found in Decius’s reign unless we admit that Philip died immediately after 17 June A.D. 249, when his name was entered in the law mentioned above, and that Decius perished in battle against the Carpi at the end of A.D. 251. Thus the thirtieth month would be included.

Meanwhile, these facts establish that the Decii ruled more than two years: namely, from a point between 17 June and 19 October A.D. 249 until the end of November A.D. 251, and therefore for two years and about five months.

[Col. 0442B] That the Decii reached the third year of their reign is taught by various inscriptions in which tribunician power III is assigned to Decius the Elder: one at Feltre in Gruter, CCLXXXIII.6; another at Vintii in Gaul, where it still survives and is reported by the distinguished Antonius Pagi, *Hypatic Dissertation*, Part I, chapter 7, p. 64, and more correctly in the *Baronian Critique* at A.D. 251, p. 52.

The author of the Paschal Chronicle wrongly confines Decius’s reign within the span of one year and connects the persecution with A.D. 251. This is correct indeed as regards the consulship of the two Decii, but contrary to the chronological indicators of Pionius’s martyrdom which are there supplied.

It may not be irrelevant to reproduce the very words in which I suspected two errors lay concealed, and to propose their correction. They are:

> Καὶ ἐν Σμύρνῃ τῆς Ἀσίας Πιόνιος . . . . ἐπὶ Πρόκλου Κυντιλλιανοῦ ἀνθυπάτου τῆς Ἀσίας, πρὸ δ` εἰδῶν Μαρτίων [Col. 0442C] ὅ ἐστι κατὰ Ἀσιανοὺς, μηνὶ ἕκτῳ, ιβ` σαβάτου ὥρᾳ δεκάτῃ.
