“And at Smyrna in Asia, Pionius … under Proclus Quintilianus, proconsul of Asia, on the fourth day before the Ides of March; which, according to the Asians, was the sixth month, the twelfth day, on the Sabbath, at the tenth hour.”

It occurred to me that, instead of δ` εἰδῶν Μαρτίων, “four days before the Ides of March,” and μηνὶ ἕκτῳ, “in the sixth month,” one ought to read δ` εἰδῶν Ἰουλίων, “four days before the Ides of July,” and μηνὶ αὐτῶ, “in that very month,” or “in the same month.”

As to the first correction: after δ` εἰδῶν, “four days before the Ides,” I proposed substituting Ἰουλίων, “of July,” for Μαρτίων, “of March,” because in Decius’s entire reign no Sabbath that was the twelfth day of a month coincides with any fourth day before the Ides of March. Only the fourth day before the Ides of July and the twelfth day of the month in A.D. 251 coincide with a Sabbath. This is shown as follows.

As stated above, Decius ruled at the latest after 17 June A.D. 249 until the end of November A.D. 251. In these years, and in the intervening year 250, a Sabbath fell upon a fourth day before the Ides of some month as in the following table, which also indicates [Col. 0442D] what day of the month the fourth day before the Ides was.

In A.D. 249, dominical letter G:

- Fourth day before the Ides of February: the tenth day of the month.
- Fourth day before the Ides of May: the twelfth day. This would fit excellently for correcting the Paschal Chronicle, since τωῦ Μαίων, “of May,” can easily be changed into Μαρτίων, “of March”; but Decius was not yet ruling in that May, as shown above.
- Fourth day before the Ides of November: the tenth day.

In A.D. 250, dominical letter F:

- Fourth day before the Ides of August: the tenth day of the month.
- Fourth day before the Ides of October: the twelfth day; but Ὀκτωβρίων, “of October,” is too unlike Μαρτίων, “of March.”

In A.D. 251, dominical letter E:

- Fourth day before the Ides of July: the twelfth day of that same month of July. For the Ides fall on 15 July. Therefore I conjectured that the Paschal Chronicle should read Ἰουλίων, “of July,” [Col. 0443A] instead of Μαρτίων, “of March,” so that the fourth day before the Ides and the Sabbath would coincide with the twelfth day of the month, and thus Pionius’s passion would fall in A.D. 251.

Thus far concerning the first correction.

As to the second, in which αὐτῷ, “itself,” is substituted for ἕκτῳ, “sixth,” the sense would be that the day before the Ides is included in that same month whose twelfth day is indicated there.

For although among the Romans counting backward from before the Nones or Ides is undertaken, just as from before the Kalends, there is this difference: days counted backward from before the Kalends belong to the month preceding the designated Kalends, and thus to a different month from the Kalends themselves. It is otherwise with days counted backward from before the Nones or Ides: they belong to the same month as the Nones and Ides from which they are counted back.

Therefore the author of the Paschal Chronicle, in Pionius’s martyrdom, by the above words μηνὶ αὐτῷ ιβ`, “in the same month, the twelfth day,” would indicate that the fourth day before the Ides of July was the twelfth day of July itself according to the Asians, because Asians count the days of months in direct order from the first day, but not [Col. 0443B] backward from the following Nones or Ides as Romans do; among the Romans, when counting proceeds backward from before the Kalends, the designated day is not in the same month as the Kalends.

It would therefore be vain henceforth to seek, in accordance with those corrections, a sixth month in March in the Paschal Chronicle and in the Latin Acts of Pionius’s Passion, as others formerly did.

Yet, to speak the truth, the alteration of Μαρτίων, “of March,” to Ἰουλίων, “of July,” seems rather too bold to me, especially since I am led to believe that Pionius suffered in A.D. 250, as the second consulship of Decius, with Gratus as colleague, recorded in the Acts of his Passion teaches.

Accordingly, I should judge that the author of the Paschal Chronicle actually wrote πρὸ δ` εἰδῶν Μαρτίων, that is, “before the fourth day of the Ides of March”; but that March should there be understood as Xanthicus, which in the solar year of the proconsular Asians is the sixth month, when counting begins from the month Dios. As Dios began on 24 September, so Xanthicus began on 22 February.

Moreover, since St Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, suffered on the second day of Xanthicus, on the seventh day before the Kalends of March, on the great Sabbath, at the eighth hour—as we learn from the letter of the Church of Smyrna concerning the martyrdom of St Polycarp, published by Ussher, and from Greek menologies—and since elsewhere in the Acts of Pionius’s Passion the following is related: “On the twenty-third day of February, when the great Sabbath was impending—that is, was present—the birthday [feast] of the blessed martyr Polycarp, while the Decian persecution was raging, the presbyter Pionius and Sabina … were arrested”; which words in the Acts of the same Pionius published by the distinguished Theodoric Ruinart, p. 123, appear thus: “Therefore, on the second day of the sixth month, which is the fourth day before the Ides of March, on the great Sabbath, while celebrating Polycarp’s birthday [feast], etc.” From these indications of 23 February and the Sabbath, it necessarily follows that Pionius was arrested in A.D. 250.

[Col. 0443D] But since he suffered on the twelfth day of the following March, or Xanthicus, which fell on a Tuesday in that year, everyone will recognize that the word σαββάτου, “of the Sabbath,” was wrongly added both in the Acts of Pionius and in the Paschal Chronicle by some petty scholar. Remembering that Pionius had been sent to prison on a Sabbath, indeed a great Sabbath, and that he had suffered martyrdom on the twelfth day of March, or Xanthicus, he rashly attached to the twelfth day of Xanthicus the Sabbath indicator proper to 23 February, without distinguishing the days on which Pionius was arrested and suffered; although in the same year 23 February and 22 March cannot both fall on a Sabbath.

Whence that Sabbath, which fell on 23 February Julian in A.D. 166, when Polycarp suffered martyrdom, and in A.D. 250, when Pionius was arrested, should be called “great,” I do not know whether anyone has hitherto discovered; nor am I confident that I have discovered it. Yet let it be permitted to investigate the matter and thereby stir the ingenuity of others.

In those two years, A.D. 166 and 250, Easter fell on 7 April, and thus the first Sunday of Lent fell on 24 February. Hence the Sabbath preceding that first Sunday of Lent could have been called “great” by the proconsular Asians, who, being Quartodecimans, had much in common with the Jews in matters relating to Easter.

Among the Jews, moreover, the Sabbath immediately preceding Passover is called great. Since the time for beginning Lent depends upon the following Easter and reminds Christians of Easter, the Smyrnaeans may therefore have given the Sabbath before the first Sunday of Lent the same designation which the Jews give to the Sabbath before Passover.

It is irrelevant to the present matter that the Smyrnaeans, with the Quartodecimans, celebrated Easter on the fourteenth moon itself—that is, in A.D. 166 and 250, on Tuesday 2 April—unlike other Christians. For the Quartodecimans and other Christians had the same beginning of Lent.

[Col. 0444B] I noted above that the word *instaret* in the Acts of Pionius’s Passion, after *cum sabbatum magnum*, means “was present.” For it was rendered from ἐνισταμένου, incorrectly understood after σαββάτου μεγάλου as though it spoke of an impending great Sabbath, although it indicates a Sabbath which had already arrived.

Among Latin authors, indeed, *instans* often denotes the time lying between past and future; but because its meaning is ambiguous, such a mistaken interpretation has sometimes given less learned readers occasion among various authors to misunderstand matters.

The distinguished Theodoric Ruinart, mentioned above, reports various Latin Acts of Pionius’s Passion from published and manuscript codices among the *Genuine and Select Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 138. There, omitting the twelfth day found in the Paschal Chronicle, “four days before the Ides of March,” or “of March,” is usually joined with the sixth month, except in one Bollandist manuscript, which reads: “Before the fourth day of the Ides of March, in the Roman manner; but in the Asian manner, on the eleventh day of the seventh month, on the Sabbath, at the seventh hour.”

It is not known why in that Bollandist codex the seventh hour is read instead of the tenth; nor can one conjecture how, in those same Latin Acts and in Greek menologies, Pionius is said to have suffered on the eleventh day. But I suspect that “seventh month” was deliberately placed instead of “sixth month,” because the numbering of the months there began with Hyperberetaeus, which among various peoples and authors is the beginning of the civil year. Thus Xanthicus is made the seventh rather than the sixth month; although in other contexts it is first when compared with April, as in the Paschal Chronicle’s author in passages where he himself speaks.

I do not pause over the fact that, in the passages cited above, the months are called, without any other designation, by their ordinal place in the year: Xanthicus, for example, is called [Col. 0444D] the first, and so the rest. Yet perhaps it will not be irrelevant to offer from Flavius Josephus, who calls the Jewish lunar months by the names of Syro-Macedonian months, a similar example containing an error.

It is in Book V of *The Jewish War*, chapter 25 in the Greek, or Book III in the Latin copies, p. Gr. Lat. 888D, where Vespasian is said to have entered Gadara on the fourth day of the month Dystrus (τετάρτῃ δύστρου μηνὸς); yet Dystrus precedes Xanthicus. But shortly before, namely p. 887F, the Sicarii are said to have invaded the little town of Engaddi at the feast of Unleavened Bread, celebrated in the middle of Xanthicus. Read therefore, with a slight alteration, δευτέρου, “second,” for δύστρου, “Dystrus”; thus it will read τετάρτῃ δευτέρου μηνὸς, “on the fourth day of the SECOND month.” Accordingly, Vespasian entered Gadara on the fourth day of Artemisios, the month immediately following Xanthicus, nineteen days after the Sicarii had plundered Engaddi. Artemisios also is simply called Δεύτερος μὴν, “the second month,” in 1 Maccabees XIII.51.

[Col. 0445A] Furthermore, in the same Latin Acts of Pionius’s Passion, Decius is said in various ways to have been consul with Vizetus Gratus, Vicius Gratus, or Vitius Tratus as colleague; hence the true name of that Gratus cannot be ascertained.

Here, incidentally, having been given the opportunity, I would warn jurists or any other readers of the Code of Justinian who are less devoted to precise chronology that, down to Diocletian’s time, an anachronism of one year is committed in the A.D. dates appended to those laws in which consuls are named—for example, in the laws cited above, enacted under the consuls Aemilianus and Aquilinus. For A.D. 250 is appended instead of 249.

The error was first made by the illustrious father of the Fasti, Onuphrius Panvinius, and then by his copyist. Panvinius, thinking that the Saviour’s birth must be moved back by one year, inserted into his Fasti, without distinction, both Christ’s age and the Christian era; and he had as imitator the person who undertook to append years of Christ to the consulates specified in the Code.

Cardinal Baronius further increased Panvinius’s error by one year in his ever-praiseworthy *Annals*, as chronologists have commonly noted. But, what is most astonishing, amid such great chronological learning, the distinguished Carolus Cointius, recent author of the *French Annals*, stumbled on the same stone. Now from this side-path back to the road.

In Du Cange’s edition of the Paschal Chronicle, p. 270, by the same fate and the same error as with the year of the Domitianic persecution discussed above, the year of the Decian persecution too is left bare and uncertain between A.D. 253 and 254, through a double error.

First, because Decius’ reign is marked by no chronological indicators whatsoever. Secondly, because, if the year of Christ 253 is there connected with the last year of the emperor Philip, the Decian persecution must necessarily have begun at the earliest in the year of Christ 254; whereas it is altogether certain [Col. 0445C] that Decius died before the year 252. For in that year 252, as I noted above, his successor Trebonianus Gallus entered upon his second consulship, already Augustus, with Vibius Volusianus, his son, already Caesar, as colleague.

I am not at all surprised that the most distinguished Du Cange was frequently mistaken in registering events of this sort: for, just as he possessed an exceedingly extensive reading in varied and most recondite matters, so he had very little—indeed almost no—command of chronology.

“For he set out against the Carpi, who had then occupied Dacia and Moesia.” The most distinguished Du Cange demonstrates, in his notes, p. 547, on the passage of the *Paschal Chronicle* mentioned above, that the Carpi in this passage of Lactantius, the Franks in the *Paschal Chronicle*, the Getae or Goths in Jordanes, and the Scythians in Zosimus, are the same people.

## ON CHAPTER V

“Not long afterward, Valerian.” Seven years later: for in the year of Christ 257, the fifth of his reign, he punished bishops and presbyters [Col. 0445D] with exile, as is clear from Cyprian’s life, acts, and letters. In the following year, 258, the sixth of his reign, he raged about the summer, as the aforementioned Cyprian teaches in his letter to Successus. Hence Lactantius says here that Valerian shed much righteous blood, though for a short time—that is, within the space of a single year; for he was captured by the Persians in the following year, 259.

## ON CHAPTER VI

“Aurelian was destroyed amid the first beginnings of his madness.” He therefore set persecution in motion only toward the end of the year 274, or at the beginning of the following year. For he was slain in March 275.

## ON CHAPTER XI

“And he sent a soothsayer to Milesian Apollo.” That the Milesians worshipped Apollo is shown, besides by Strabo, book XIV, p. 634, and Pausanias in the *Attica*, p. 15, by several coins. [Col. 0446A] Among these is a large bronze coin in the Royal Cabinet, of the emperor Julius Verus Maximinus, as follows:

> ΑΥ. Κ. Ι. ΟΥΗΡΟΣ. ΜΑΞΙΜΙΝΟΣ.  
> (Radiate head.)  
> ΑΜΙΚΟΥ ΕΛΕΥΘΕΡΑΣ ΕΤ . ΣΞΗ.  
> (Apollo seated, holding a *tyra* in his right hand; Serapis standing, with a modius on his head, ears of grain in his right hand and a spear in his left.)  
> Below, between the two figures, a globe. At the bottom: ΑΜΙΣΗΝΩΝ ΜΙΛΗΙΩΝ.

That is:

> Emperor Caesar Julius Verus Maximinus.  
> Of free Amisus, year 268. Of the Amisenians, Milesians.

From this coin you will understand that Serapis was worshipped by the Amisenians, just as Apollo was worshipped by the Milesians.

[Col. 0446B] As will appear from the observations below concerning the second Amisenian era, it was struck in honour of Maximinus in the year of the Julian Period 4950, A.U.C. 990, A.D. 237, after the death of both Gordians.

Taking occasion from the numeral letters inscribed upon it, I shall say briefly that Amisus had at most two eras.

The first was reckoned from the year of the Julian Period 4667, A.U.C. 707, 47 before Christ, when Julius Caesar rewarded the Amisenians with freedom (*ἐλευθερίᾳ ἠμείψατο*), according to Dio, book XLII, p. 207. This was because Pharnaces, the parricidal son of Mithridates, had deprived them of their manhood, as Hirtius teaches, *Alexandrian War*, chs. 41 and 70, together with Appian, book II of the *Civil Wars*, p. 484, and Dio, book XLII, p. 206. In Dio, where the text reads, “he killed all the adult males in it” (*τοὺς τε ἡβῶντας ἐν αὐτῇ πάντας ἀπέκτεινε*), one should read, on the evidence of the other two authors, “he cut them off” (*ἀπέτεμε*); in Appian, “he made them eunuchs” (*τομίας ἐποιήσατο*). I am astonished that this error has hitherto remained unnoticed.

[Col. 0446C] This first era of Amisus is displayed by a coin of Hadrian—if indeed it is genuine—cited by Joseph Scaliger, *Canones Isagogici*, book III, p. 301, Amsterdam edition, no. XC:

> ΑΥΤ. ΚΑΙΣ. ΑΙΛ. ΑΔΡΙΑΝΟΣ. ΣΕΒ. Π. Π. ΥΠ. Γ.  
> ΑΜΙΣΟΥ ΕΛΕΥΘΕΡΑΣ ΕΤΟΥΣ . ΡΠΓ  
> (incorrectly, ΓΠΓ)

That is:

> Emperor Caesar Aelius Hadrian Augustus, Father of the Fatherland, consul for the third time.  
> Of free Amisus, year 183.

There Scaliger interprets ΥΠ. Γ, “consul III,” incorrectly, not merely as “third,” when it means “three times”; he also errs when he says that those 183 years end in the year of the Julian Period 4833, to which he assigns Hadrian’s third consulship. For Hadrian entered upon his third and final consulship in the year of the Julian Period 4832, A.U.C. 872, A.D. 119. Thus, on either reckoning, the era would have to be counted back, without any foundation whatsoever, from the year of the Julian Period 4650 or 4651—that is, from 64 or 63 before Christ.

[Col. 0446D] But I strongly suspect that on that coin one ought to read ΡΞΓ, 163, just as another silver coin of the same Hadrian in the Royal Cabinet bears:

> ΑΥΤ. ΚΑΙ. ΤΡΑ ΑΔΡΙΑΝΟΣ . ΣΕΒ. ΥΠ. Γ.  
> (Laureate head.)  
> ΑΜΙΣΟΥ ΕΛΕΥΘΕΡΑΣ ΕΤΟΥΣ . ΡΞΓ  
> (Pallas standing, holding a small Victory in her right hand, resting her left upon a shield.)

As we shall see from the following era, it was struck in the year of the Julian Period 4854, A.U.C. 885, A.D. 132, the fifteenth year of Hadrian’s reign. For Hadrian, after Trajan’s death, obtained the empire in A.D. 117, on the tenth day of August.

The second era, marked by the numeral letters ΣΞΗ, 268, on the aforementioned coin of Maximinus, must be reckoned from the very beginning of the year of the Julian Period 4683, A.U.C. 723, 31 before Christ, when the Amisenians, after killing or expelling the tyrant Strato, won freedom for themselves by arms. But where Strabo, book XII, p. 547, says that freedom was restored to them by Caesar Augustus after the battle of Actium, this must be understood as meaning that it was confirmed.

[Col. 0447A] The same era appears on a medium-sized bronze coin of Diadumenian, preserved in the museum of the most learned and courteous Franz Dronius:

> Μ. ΟΠΕΛ. ΑΝΤ. ΔΙΑΔΟΥΜΕΝΙΑΝΟΣ ΣΑΙΣΑΡ.  
> (Bare head.)  
> ΑΜΙΣΟΥ ΕΛΕΥΘΕΡΑΣ ΕΤΟ . ΣΜΘ.  
> (Eagle with wings spread.)

That is:

> Marcus Opellius Antoninus Diadumenianus Caesar.  
> Of free Amisus, year 249.

It was struck before June of A.D. 218; for in that year the emperor Macrinus was killed together with his son Diadumenian at the beginning of June.

[Col. 0447B] Here the reader must be warned that the coin of Aelius Caesar which the most distinguished Antonius Pagi says, in the additions to his *Critica Baroniana*, p. 305, was sent to him by me from the Royal Cabinet, bearing the letters PZE, 165, does not belong to Aelius Caesar and is not in the Royal Cabinet. I do indeed remember writing this to that most distinguished man, as he presents it; but I had earlier received the same information by letter from a friend, deceived without malicious intent.

The coin is in fact one of Sabina, Hadrian’s wife, found on p. 307 of the *Thesaurus Palatinus*, published by L. Beger at Heidelberg in 1685. Thus falls the third Amisenian era which Antonius Pagi, in the same place in the additions, erected upon that false attribution of the coin.

[Col. 0447C] Nor should it be omitted that Holstenius too, in his notes on Stephanus of Byzantium, under the entry Ἀμισός, incorrectly reports a coin of Caracalla struck at Amisus, on which, he says, are the letters CNE, 255, which fit neither era. The letters on it are CME, 245, as they are read on a very large bronze coin in the Royal Cabinet, as follows:

> ΑΤ. Κ. Μ. ΑΥΡ. ΑΝΤΩΝΙΝΟΣ. ΓΕΡΜ.  
> (Radiate head.)  
> ΑΜΙΣΟΥ ΕΛΕΥΘΕΡΑΣ.  
> (Victory in a two-horse chariot, holding a crown in her right hand and a palm in her left.)  
> At the bottom: ET. CME.

That is:

> Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Germanicus.  
> Of free Amisus, year 245.

Caracalla did not assume the title Germanicus until the course of his sixteenth tribunician power, as may be seen in coins in Occo, p. 377, and Mediobarbus, p. 293. Tribunician power was conferred upon Caracalla in A.D. 198; and thus in A.D. 213 he entered upon his sixteenth tribunician power, during the course of which alone he styled himself Germanicus.

[Col. 0447D] That coin was therefore struck in A.U.C. 967, A.D. 214, not in A.U.C. 961, A.D. 208, as the most distinguished Pagi judges on the same p. 305 in the additions, where, led into error by Holstenius, he reckons the letters CNE, 255, from the earlier era of Amisus—that is, from A.U.C. 707.

## ON CHAPTER XIII

“Lawfully cooked.” That is, burned, as in ch. 21: “Then lighted and extinguished torches were applied to the individual limbs.” This happened finally, when, after the entire skin had been seared away over much of the day, the force of the fire had penetrated to the innermost parts.

## ON CHAPTER XV

“The emperor therefore raged now not only against members of his household, but against everyone; and first of all he compelled his daughter Valeria and his wife Prisca to be defiled by sacrifice.” They were therefore Christians. That they were Christians, and had not always been treated so badly, may be learned from this passage of Eusebius, rendered word for word (*Ecclesiastical History*, VIII.1, at the very beginning):

> What need is there to speak of those who were in the imperial households, and of those who ruled over all? They allowed those of their own household to conduct themselves openly [Col. 0448A] before them, in matters divine, both in word and in manner of life—their wives, children, and servants—almost permitting them even to boast of the open profession of their faith; and they considered them especially acceptable, and more so than their fellow-servants. Such was Dorotheus, most well-disposed and most faithful toward them all; and for that reason distinguished above those in offices and commands, together with the renowned Gorgonius associated with him.

[Col. 0448B] I may be permitted to append two other translations of this text, published by distinguished men: one by John Christophorson, the other by Henry Valesius. By comparing them with the foregoing version, the reader will understand how great and how insane is the licence of certain translators, who, in rendering authors, turn everything upside down and stuff in innumerable words—mostly trifling and useless ones—even without any distinction of characters. Such, for the most part, are the things which I have taken care to enclose in brackets in these two versions.

I present first, as the older, that of John Christophorson. It is as follows:

> What need is there to speak of those who were in the emperors’ palace [and had attained great dignity], and finally of the emperors [themselves], who permitted their household [members], while they themselves looked on, freely and openly to speak for the propagation of the divine word and to pursue [a pious] manner of life; and who granted their [own] wives, children, and servants permission, as it were, openly to glory and exult in the [wonderful] freedom of the faith? These they certainly held dearer and more especially beloved than [the remaining [Col. 0448C] multitude of servants]. Such was that Dorotheus, who showed toward them, beyond the rest, the greatest goodwill and no less fidelity, and who accordingly attained a most eminent degree of honour above the others who held magistracies and prefectures in the empire. Such was Gorgonius, who shone with a not dissimilar reputation [and renown].

Thus far Christophorson, whom you see took τῷ θείῳ as an adjective; for he renders it “divine” and joins it to λόγῳ, “word.” But wrongly: it must be taken substantively and rendered “the divine being” or “divine matters.” Hence Valesius rendered it as “the things pertaining to their religion.” His complete translation is as follows:

> What need is there to speak of those who [were employed] in the emperors’ palaces, or of the emperors [themselves]? They gave their household [members], and their wives, children, and servants, permission to perform freely before [the emperors themselves] the things that pertained to their [own] religion, both in words and in deeds; in some fashion allowing them, on account of this freedom of their [own] faith, to glory [and display themselves], and embracing them with a special [sort of] affection above all the other [ministers]. Such was Dorotheus, who showed the greatest goodwill and fidelity toward them [Col. 0448D] and, for that reason, earned great honour above [all] magistrates and governors of provinces. To him should be joined that most celebrated Gorgonius.

Thus far Valesius. In his notes the following is read:

> Γαμεταῖς. Christophorson understood these words of the emperors’ wives, to whom, that is, the emperors permitted the free profession of the Christian faith. But what follows openly refutes this sense.

[Col. 0449A] But the distinguished man ought to have attended not to what follows, but to what precedes. For from the word οἰκείοις, occurring in the preceding phrase and rendered by me “their own people,” he would have perceived that the three kinds of persons found in the imperial palaces were comprehended under that generic term: namely, γαμετάς, παῖδας, and οἰκέτας—wives, children, and servants—assuredly all belonging to the emperors. Dorotheus and Gorgonius, however, pertain immediately only to the third kind or class just mentioned, namely τῶν συνθεραπευόντων, “those who serve together,” which I rendered in one word as “fellow-servants.” For Dorotheus was among those entrusted with prefectures of the empire; whence Valesius notes, from the *Acts of the Martyrs Indes and Domna*, ch. 23, that he was distinguished by civil rank, as one called *praepositus* by the Italians.

## ON CHAPTER XVII

“Thus, after the summer had passed, by a circuit of the bank of the Striga.” Restore *Istricae*, that is, “of the Danubian [bank],” from *Ister*, the Danube. For corruption from *Istricae* to *Stricae*, and then to *Strigae*, was easy, the first letter having fallen out of use among copyists. Thus *Strix* from *Histrix*; hence *Striculus* in Arnobius for *Histriculus*, and *Strionem* for *Histrionem*. Isidore and the ancient glossaries: “*Strio*: a mime, an actor.” These examples, with many others, are supplied by the great Salmasius on Spartianus, ch. 27, in the *Hadrian*.

[Col. 0449B] Henry Dodwell, in his dissertation *On the Bank of the Striga*, appended to the works of Lactantius published at Oxford in 1684, indulges himself when he says:

> “In this passage of Lactantius, *Striga* is a term of the land-surveyors, or *gromatici*, first derived from the laying-out of camps, then transferred and applied to the lands of colonies, which were customarily measured and distributed according to the pattern of camps.”

After the very learned man has maintained this with great exertion, he finally concludes as follows:

> “Accordingly, our emperor Diocletian was conveyed for most of the way from Rome to Ravenna in a litter. From there perhaps in a litter to the Danube; then the remainder of the journey by ship, going downstream on the Danube, through the Euxine Sea as far as Nicomedia.”

But what sane person could admit that an emperor sick in body and mind undertook a long and most dangerous voyage through the cataracts of the Danube and the shoals and storms of the Euxine Sea? It would therefore be preferable to say that Diocletian was carried in a litter to the Drava or the Sava, at the place where they first become navigable; and that from there, going downstream on that river and likewise on the Danube, he arrived in those regions nearer Hadrianopolis, whence he would again have set out by direct road toward Nicomedia in a litter.

[Col. 0449C] But Lactantius’ text stands against this view, though more plausible, just as much as against Dodwell’s; for the emperor is nowhere said to have used downstream rivers in making the aforesaid journey. The interpretation must therefore be sought elsewhere: namely, in the itinerary called that of Antoninus, in which it may be seen that there were two routes from Viminacium, situated in Moesia, as far as Nicomedia.

Diocletian therefore came from Ravenna to Viminacium, a city long dear to him, as various laws issued there by him show; there he had two routes, one of which he might take.

The one was indeed very short: on it, through Municipium and Hadrianopolis, only twenty stopping-places are listed as far as Ostudizum, where the two routes converge. But I judge that Diocletian avoided and left this route on his right, because it was extremely difficult and required the crossing, by this shortcut, of many mountains, especially Haemus.

[Col. 0449D] It is described on p. 30 of the *Itinerary of Antoninus*, Cologne edition of 1600. I thought it worthwhile to place it before the eyes, without listing every locality or giving the distances, neither of which concerns the present matter.

| Route |
|---|
| Viminacium |
| Municipium — 18 Roman miles |
| Idimum — 17 Roman miles, etc. |
| Burditpa |
| Hadrianopolis — 24 Roman miles |
| Ostudizum — 18 Roman miles, etc. |
| Byzantium (Constantinople) |
| Chalcedon |
| Crossing into Bithynia — 4 Roman miles |
| Pantichium — 15 Roman miles |
| Libyssa — 24 Roman miles |
| Nicomedia — 22 Roman miles |

[Col. 0450A] The other route, in which the phrase *per Ripam*, “by the Bank,” is to be noted, runs from the same terminus at Viminacium to the same terminus at Ostudizum. It is found on p. 49 and is entitled as follows:

| Route |
|---|
| Ister |
| Likewise, by the Bank from Viminacium to Nicomedia: 12 [sic] — 72 Roman miles |
| Cuppae — 24 Roman miles |
| Novae — 24 Roman miles |
| Ratiaria, Legion XIV *Gemina* — 18 Roman miles |
| Oescus, Macedonian Legion — 12 Roman miles |
| Novae, Legion I *Italica* — 17 Roman miles |
| Across the Murisca |
| Candidiana — 13 Roman miles |
| Teglicium — 12 Roman miles |
| Dorostorum, Legion XI *Claudia* — 12 Roman miles |
| Sucidava — 18 Roman miles |
| Axiopolis — 12 Roman miles |
| Trosmis, Legion I *Iovia*, Scythia |
| Arrubium — 9 Roman miles |
| Diniguttia — 9 Roman miles |
| Noviodunum, Legion II *Herculea* — 20 Roman miles |
[Col. 0450B]

| Tomi — 36 Roman miles |
| Sadame |
| Tarpodizum — 18 Roman miles |
| Ostudizum — 32 Roman miles |
| Byzantium |
| Pantichium — 15 Roman miles |
| Libyssa — 24 Roman miles |
| Nicomedia — 22 Roman miles |

Note that in this second list Chalcedon and the crossing into Bithynia are omitted by the author, although they occur in the first.

The route just described was indeed extremely long, having fifty-three stopping-places, as anyone counting them in the *Itinerary* itself will see; but it was the most convenient for an emperor in poor health, because it ran over level ground, following the Istrian Bank—that is, the bends of the lower Danube.

[Col. 0450C] For in the Latin manuscripts of Ptolemy, in the place where the Greek is lacking, p. 57 of Bertius’ Greek-Latin edition of 1618, one reads: “The bend near the city of Axium,” that is, Axiopolis, “and from there as far as the mouths it is called the Ister.” Add p. 53 of the same *Itinerary*: the route from Taurunum into Gaul as far as Legion XXX is said to run “by the Bank of Pannonia,” not simply “by the Bank,” because that designation belongs to the Ister *κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν*, “preeminently,” on p. 49.

Diocletian chose this latter route, not only as more convenient than the other, which was a shortcut, but also because on it, if his health permitted, he would fulfil the functions of an emperor: namely, by repeatedly inspecting the various legions mentioned above, stationed on the frontiers of the empire, whereas none were on the other route. In particular, he could inspect Legion I *Iovia* at Trosmis or Trosmi, and Legion II *Herculea* at Noviodunum. Both were named from the cognomina of Diocletian and the elder Maximian, and endured until the time of Honorius, as Claudian testifies in his *War against Gildo*:

> The king of the gods calls the Herculean cohort his own Alcidean cohort,  
> and the Jovian cohort his own.

[Col. 0450D] You now understand, I think, reader, what Lactantius means by “the circuit of that Istrian Bank,” by which Diocletian came from Ravenna to Nicomedia: namely, a land journey through the various bends of the lower Danube, nearly as far as its mouths, and then to Ostudizum.

I received this excellent observation from a most illustrious abbot, whose modesty, no less than his astonishing learning, is such that he wishes his name to remain concealed.

## ON CHAPTER XVIII

I here present the entire chapter, divided not only into numbered sections but also by the addition of the names Diocletian and Galerius Maximianus. Moreover, for greater distinction, the words of each are printed in italics. It would be desirable for the books of all authors, especially ancient ones, henceforth published to be similarly divided by numbered sections. Their passages could then be cited with the greatest convenience to the reader.

### Chapter XVIII

[Col. 0451A] 1. Not many days later Caesar arrived, not to congratulate his father, but to compel him to relinquish the empire.

2. He had recently come into conflict with the elder Maximian and had frightened him by raising the spectre of civil war.

3. He therefore approached Diocletian, first gently and amicably, saying that he was now old, now less vigorous, and incapable of administering the commonwealth; that after his labours he ought to rest.

4. At the same time he adduced the example of Nerva, who, he said, had handed over the empire to Trajan.

5. But he replied that it would be unbecoming, after the splendour of so lofty a summit, to fall into the obscurity of a humble life; and that it was less safe, since in so long a reign he had acquired the hatred of many.

6. Nerva, he said, having reigned for one year, because through age or lack of experience he could not bear the weight and care of such great affairs, had laid down the helm of the commonwealth and returned to private life, in which he had grown old.

7. But if he desired to acquire the title of emperor, there was nothing to prevent all from being called Augusti.

[Col. 0451B] 8. But he, who had already greedily fixed his hopes upon the whole world, seeing that from this he would gain either nothing beyond the name or not much, replied that Diocletian’s arrangement must be preserved permanently: there should be two senior rulers in the commonwealth, holding supreme power, and likewise two junior rulers as their assistants.

9. Concord could easily be preserved between two; among four equals, by no means.

10. If Diocletian did not wish to yield, he would look to his own interests, lest he should continue to be junior and last in rank.

11. Fifteen years had now passed since he had been relegated to Illyricum or to the bank of the Danube, struggling with barbarian nations, while others ruled luxuriously in broader and more peaceful lands.

12. On hearing this, the feeble old man, who had already received a letter from the elder Maximian reporting all that had been said, and had learned that Galerius was increasing his army, wept.

13. **DIOCLETIAN.** “Let it be so,” he said, “if this pleases you. It remained for the Caesars to be chosen by the common counsel of all.”

14. **MAXIMIAN.** “What need is there for counsel, when the two of them must approve whatever we do?”

[Col. 0451C] 15. **DIOCLETIAN.** “Precisely so. For their sons must be appointed.”

16. Now Maximian had a son, Maxentius, the son-in-law of this very Galerius Maximian, a man of destructive and evil disposition, so proud and obstinate that he was not accustomed to pay reverence either to his father or to his father-in-law, and was consequently hated by both.

17. Constantius also had a son, Constantine, a most excellent young man and most worthy of that eminence, who, because of his remarkable and handsome bodily appearance, military energy, upright character, and singular affability, was loved by the soldiers and desired by private persons.

18. He was then present, having long before been made tribune of the first rank by Diocletian.

19. “What, then, shall be done?”

20. **MAXIMIAN.** “That man,” he said, “is not worthy. For if, while a private man, he despised me, what will he do when he has received imperial power?”

21. **DIOCLETIAN.** “But he is lovable, and he will rule in such a way that he will be judged better and more merciful than his father.”

[Col. 0451D] 22. **MAXIMIAN.** “Then it will come about that I shall be unable to do what I wish. Therefore those must be appointed who are in my power, who fear me, who do nothing except at my command.”

23. **DIOCLETIAN.** “Whom, then, shall we make Caesars?”

24. **MAXIMIAN.** “Severus,” he said.

25. **DIOCLETIAN.** “That dancer? That drunkard and tippler, to whom night is day and day night?”

26. **MAXIMIAN.** “He is worthy,” he said, “because he has served the soldiers faithfully; and I have sent him to Maximian, that he may be clothed by him.”

27. **DIOCLETIAN.** “So be it. Whom will you give as the other?”

28. **MAXIMIAN.** “This man,” he said, pointing to Daia, a certain half-barbarian young man whom he had recently ordered to be called Maximinus after his own name.

29. Diocletian himself had also taken a name from his brother, for an omen, because Maximian observed loyalty with the utmost scrupulousness.

30. **DIOCLETIAN.** “Who is this man whom you offer me?”

31. **MAXIMIAN.** “My kinsman,” he said.

[Col. 0452A] 32. But Diocletian groaned:

> **DIOCLETIAN.** “No,” he said, “you are not giving me men to whom the protection of the commonwealth can be entrusted.”

33. **MAXIMIAN.** “I have tested them,” he said.

34. **DIOCLETIAN.** “You must see to it, since you are about to undertake the government of the empire. I have laboured and provided enough for the commonwealth to remain secure while I ruled. If anything adverse happens, it will not be my fault.”

The notes on this chapter now follow.

“Father.” He was his adopted son. He was also his son-in-law. For Galerius Maximian had married Diocletian’s daughter, Galeria Valeria.

“Old man.” Perhaps one should read “to the old man.”

[Col. 0452B] “At the same time he adduced the example of Nerva, who had handed over the empire to Trajan.” This is altogether false. Trajan, though adopted by Nerva, did not rule until Nerva’s death. Yet the illustrious William Lloyd, bishop of St Asaph in Wales, agrees with this view after the distinguished Henry Dodwell, in the appendix to the *Dissertations on Cyprian*, no. XL, as is taught by Lloyd’s most learned and painstakingly written *Canon of Nerva and Trajan*, which I carefully preserve in my possession until it appears in the chronological work that all scholars daily await from so great a man.

It should be observed, however, that this is reported in Lactantius not as Lactantius’ own assertion, but as Maximian’s statement made to serve his purpose. By this example he wanted to impose upon Diocletian—who was not only ignorant of history but was also then in difficult circumstances—in order to induce him to abdicate the empire. But in that state of affairs Diocletian did not dare distrust Galerius Maximian; and hence below, in §6, whether from ignorance of the matter, as an uneducated man, or rather from fear of Maximian’s fierceness, as a timorous old man, he did not at all expose the falsity of the example.

How Nerva entered upon the empire, however, and how, after adopting Trajan, he ended his life, it will not be altogether irrelevant to explain briefly here.

[Col. 0452C] After Domitian had been killed on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October—that is, on 18 September—in A.D. 96, Nerva became emperor. On that same day long before, namely in A.D. 56, Trajan had been born, as appears in Pliny, book X, letter 28, and in the old calendar published by Bucherius and Lambecius. Hence in ch. 92 of his *Panegyric*, Pliny calls that day joyful with a threefold gladness: it removed the worst prince, Domitian; gave the best, Nerva; and produced one better than the best, Trajan.

Then, shortly after Nerva adopted the absent Trajan at the end of October in A.D. 97, Nerva died—namely, in A.D. 98, on 27 January. For according to Dio, p. 771B, he reigned no longer than one year, four months, and nine days.

Certainly, that Nerva did not survive long after Trajan’s adoption is clear from Pliny, *Panegyric*, ch. 10, where he says of Nerva:

> “The gods claimed him for heaven, lest after that divine and immortal act he should perform anything mortal; for this reverence was due to so great a work, that it should be his last, and that its author should immediately be consecrated, so that posterity might one day ask whether a god had done it.”

Thus far Pliny the Younger.

[Col. 0452D] Moreover, since Aurelius Victor in the *Epitome* fixes at three months the time Nerva lived after adopting Trajan, Trajan’s adoption is suitably assigned to the end of October 97, specifically to the fifth day before the Kalends of November—that is, 28 October. The fifth day before the Kalends of any month was sacred for comparable actions of emperors, as the distinguished Antonius Pagi teaches in the *Hypatic Dissertation* and in the *Critica Baroniana*.

If Nerva had truly abdicated the empire, who could have known it better than Pliny the Younger? Yet in his letters and in Trajan’s very panegyric there is not merely profound silence on the matter; the exact contrary is asserted in them.

[Col. 0453A] Aurelius Victor wrote this in his book *On the Caesars*, where the following words occur concerning Nerva:

> “When he perceived that the empire could not be administered except by men stronger in body and mind than his predecessors, in the sixteenth month he abdicated himself.”

What authority should be accorded to this writer on Nerva’s abdication of the empire is shown by the writer himself when he says, concerning Nerva’s accession:

> “For what was wiser or more restrained than Nerva of Crete, who, in extreme old age among the Sequani, whither he had withdrawn through fear of the tyrant, assumed the empire by the will of the legions,” etc.

Concerning these words Joseph Scaliger, no. 2113 of Eusebius, rightly says: “Everything is false and monstrous.”

The source of Victor’s error in the *Caesars* may have been either this passage of Lactantius, in which Galerius Maximian presses this example upon Diocletian, or another passage from the same Pliny, likewise misunderstood. Speaking of Trajan’s adoption in ch. 8 of the *Panegyric*, Pliny says of Nerva:

> “Then, as though he had laid down the empire, with what security, [Col. 0453B], with what glorious joy—for what little difference is there whether you lay down or share the empire, except that the latter is more difficult—relying upon you as though you were present, and sustaining himself and the commonwealth upon your shoulders, did he grow strong through your youth and your strength?”

From this, the author ought to have understood that, although in Pliny’s rhetorical speech laying down and sharing the empire are nearly the same thing, Nerva nevertheless did not lay it down, but merely shared it.

Indeed, Eutropius’ words, speaking of Diocletian himself, are:

> “Alone of all men, after the foundation of the Roman empire, he returned from so great an eminence to the status and civil condition of private life.”

This is partly false: Diocletian shared this with his brother Maximian Herculius; and both acted under compulsion, not from free choice, as we learn from this book of Lactantius, chs. 18, 19, and 20.

“But he replied.” Diocletian.

“And.” I have restored this in place of the particle *ei*, following the indication of Johannes Columbus—unless one prefers to take *ei* as equivalent to *sibi*, “to himself.”

[Col. 0453C] “Nerva, having reigned for one year.” One should read this in place of “But Nerva, reigning for one year.” Nerva had in fact ruled about one year and six and a half months when he adopted Trajan; this is the interval from the middle of September A.D. 96 to 28 October A.D. 97.

“Returned to private life, in which he had grown old.” From what has been said above it is clear that Nerva lived and ruled for three months after Trajan’s adoption.

“The title of emperor.” In this sense it was used of Augusti alone. Thus in ch. 9 of this book: “After he received the title of emperor.” Then in ch. 25: “Constantine, however, not emperor, as he had been made, but Caesar.” Likewise in ch. 27: “Formerly, indeed, when he had received the title of emperor.” Then in ch. 29: “Constantine emperor.” Further, in ch. 30: “having lost the honour of emperor.” Finally, in ch. 32: “Licinius having been named emperor”; and at the end of the same chapter: “he orders all four to be called emperors.”

“All.” The other two, namely Constantius and Galerius Maximian himself, who were Caesars.

“But he.” Maximian.

[Col. 0453D] “Hope.” The autograph wrongly has *ipse*, as Johannes Columbus rightly observed.

“Or not much.” I have added *haud*, “not,” before *multum*, as necessary; but not *non*, since *haud* seems rather to have been absorbed into the preceding word *aut*.

“He would look to his own interests, lest he should continue to be junior and last.” Galerius Maximian was junior to the Augusti, Diocletian and Maximian Herculius, since he was only Caesar; and he was the last of the Caesars because he ranked below Constantius. He had long endured this most unwillingly; for after Narses, king of the Persians, had been put to flight, he cried out with fierce countenance and terrible voice: “How long [am I to remain] Caesar?”

[Col. 0454A] “Let it be so,” he said, “if this pleases you. It remained for the Caesars to be chosen by the common counsel of all.” These are continuous words of Diocletian himself, not, beginning with “It remained,” intermediate words of Lactantius, as they might appear at first sight. For *supererat* is used in place of *superesset*, just as *erat* is used for *esset* in Cicero’s speech *On the Manilian Law*: “But if Gnaeus Pompeius were at Rome at this time as a private citizen, he nevertheless was to be chosen and sent for so great a war.” Other examples also occur.

“By the common counsel of all.” That is, a counsel in which Maximian Herculius Augustus and Constantius Caesar ought to have shared.

“The two of them.” Maximian Herculius and Constantius.

“Precisely so. For.” Again, *nam*, “for,” in place of *autem*, “but.”

“To be appointed.” Namely, as Caesars.

“Now there was.” From the beginning of §16 to the end of §18 is a single parenthesis containing Lactantius’ words.

After “Maximian,” “a son” has been added, as in §17 after “Constantius” . . .

The first Maximian mentioned there is Herculius; the other is Galerius.

[Col. 0454B] “What, then, shall be done?” These are Diocletian’s words, immediately following his final words in §15.

“That man.” Constantine, whom Maximian then, in §18, was contemptuously indicating as present.

“That he may be clothed.” With the purple by which Caesars were distinguished.

“Whom he had ordered to be called Maximinus after his own name.” The distinguished Baluze acknowledges in his notes that here, and almost always elsewhere, an old manuscript reads *Maximianum*. Hence I suspect that Daia was called *Maximianus*, not *Maximinus*, by Galerius Maximian after his own full name. For in two inscriptions from the Baths of Diocletian, in Gruter, p. 183, nos. 2 and 7, after Constantius and Maximian, Augusti, and Severus Caesar, there is listed Maximian Caesar, who can be none other than Daia. Add that Greek writers too indiscriminately call him Maximianus.

I would therefore judge that, since there were now two Maximiani—Herculius and Galerius—it became customary among the populace, for the sake of distinction, to call Daza not *Maximianus* but *Maximinus*, as he is styled in Greek and Latin coins.

Further, Galerius Maximianus must be held to have adopted Daza at the same time as he ordered him to be called after his own name; for in chapter 39 Daza is said to have called Valeria, the wife of Galerius Maximianus, “mother,” and Galerius Maximianus is there likewise called Daza’s father.

“And he himself also.” Galerius Maximianus Armentarius.

“Diocletian had borrowed the name from his brother, as an omen, because Maximianus performed loyalty with the highest scrupulousness.” I have restored this in place of what was written: “He had altered it in part, on account of the man,” etc. For can anyone be said to alter another’s name “in part” who adds to it an entire additional name, such as this name of Maximianus, bestowed upon Galerius by Diocletian?

It could perhaps in some fashion be said that Galerius’s name was altered in part by Diocletian [Col. 0454D], had Galerius been called *Galerianus* by the termination of adoptive names—just as Octavianus comes from Octavius, Valerianus from Valerius, and many similar cases. But when the name Maximianus was imposed, there is no trace among Galerius’s appellations of a name altered, but plainly of one added.

Perhaps someone will object that Galerius’s name was changed because he was called Maximianus instead of Armentarius. But this does not succeed very well. For *Armentarius* is not a name but a nickname bestowed in jest, like those of Caligula, Caracalla, and Tarantus; these were used only in popular speech and would not be found inscribed on public monuments, such as edicts, stone inscriptions, and coins. Further, Galerius did not cease, after he began to be called Maximianus, also to be called Armentarius, as may be seen in each of the two Victors and elsewhere.

Anyone with even a moderate knowledge of Latin will understand that Lactantius here uses *mutuaverat* [Col. 0455A] in the sense of *mutuatus fuerat*, “had borrowed.” For Priscian, Book VIII, *On the Verb*, says: “The ancients similarly used many verbs with a twofold termination in one and the same meaning: *partio* and *partior*, *meto* and *metor*, *modero* and *moderor*, *mutuo* and *mutuor*.” Thus far Priscian, whose authority alone may count for that of many. Lactantius himself, in chapter 16 of this very book, has: “This is a true triumph, when rulers rule; for they have been conquered and subjected by your power.”

At present, examples of this usage in the verb *mutuo* do not occur to me, apart from that in Matthew 5:42: “Do not turn away from one wishing to borrow from you” (*mutuare*, δανείσασθαι); and another in Nonius, among the authors of the Latin language, chapter 17, no. 48, p. 751.

“Let him borrow” (*mutuet*): let him take a loan. Caecilius, *The Spendthrift*: “He will run to a friend to borrow; let him borrow for my sake.” Here one should read *currat*, “let him run,” and *causa mea*, “for my sake.”

To these two examples add, if you wish, Pliny, Book II, chapter 9, saying: “The other stars are governed by the brilliance of the sun, since throughout they shine by light borrowed from it” [Col. 0455B].

But, in order that the rationale of this correction may be understood, it must be known that Maximianus Herculius was called Diocletian’s brother, namely by reason of their partnership in the empire.

Thus at the very beginning of chapter 8 of this book, where Diocletian is under discussion, we read: “What of HIS BROTHER Maximianus, who was called Herculius?” Likewise, in an inscription of the Baths of Diocletian in Gruter, CLXXVIII, 7, after the names of Diocletian and Maximianus (Herculius), Constantius and Maximianus (Galerius), Severus and Maximinus (Daza) have been given, one reads:

“THE HAPPY BATHS, CONSECRATED IN THE NAME OF DIOCLETIAN AUGUSTUS, HIS BROTHER,” etc.

Here, after the word *FELICES* (“Happy”), either the stonecutter’s or the copyist’s carelessness omitted *MAXIMIANUS AUG.*, that is, the name of Herculius, as appears in another similar inscription, which is presented there as mutilated, no. 8.

I shall attempt partly to supply it, in the matters relevant to the present purpose [Col. 0455C], as follows:

> SENIORES AUGG. *Read: D. D.* C. N. N. CONSTANTIUS ET MAXIM. THERMAS FELIC[ES]. The senior Maximianus Augustus … ordered [them] to be made by the presence of his majesty and consecrated [them] to the name of Diocletian.

There you see that *MAXIMIANUS AUG.*, which is missing in the first inscription, is added in this one after *THERMAS FELICES*, because Herculius had consecrated them to Diocletian, his brother.

Moreover, in chapter 20 of this very book we learn that the Augusti were brothers to one another, while the Caesars were called sons by the Augusti, in these words: “But he did not wish to make him [Licinius] Caesar, lest he call him SON, so that afterwards he might be named AUGUSTUS and BROTHER in Constantius’s place.”

[Col. 0455D] The same brotherhood of Diocletian and Maximianus Herculius is proclaimed by an inscription set up in the forum of Tyre, reported in the Jerusalem Talmud, tractate *Avodah Zarah*, chapter 4, fol. 39 verso, col. 2, line 17, in this form:

> “I, the emperor Diocletian, who built this forum of Tyre for the fortune of Herculius, MY BROTHER, in eighty days.”

This is from Bomberg’s Venetian edition, which is far more elegant and correct than that Cracow edition of the Jewish year 367, or A.D. 1706.

Lactantius therefore means that Diocletian, whose brother was Maximianus Herculius, borrowed—or had borrowed—the name of his brother Maximinianus Herculius, as the text reads, in order to give it to Galerius Armentarius.

The reason for giving the name is then added: as an omen, because Maximianus Herculius performed loyalty with the utmost conscientiousness. Diocletian, that is, sought an omen from the name, thinking that Galerius, whom he was creating Caesar, would be loyal to him [Col. 0456A] if he bore the name of the emperor Maximianus Herculius, his brother, who was loyal to him. In Victor’s work *On the Caesars*, too, Maximianus Herculius is said to have been faithful to Diocletian in friendship.

IN CHAPTER XX.

Maximianus, after driving out the old men and accomplishing what he wished, represented himself as now lord of almost the whole world. He must then be thought to have wished to alter the title of the Roman Empire, so that it should be called not the ROMAN but the DACIAN Empire.

“And, having substituted as Caesar his own son, who was then nine years old.” He was therefore born in A.D. 296, after the month of May, or in 297, before that same month. For the old men were expelled on the Kalends of May in A.D. 305, the year which immediately followed Diocletian’s ninth consulship.

Candidianus. This is the name of the son of Galerius Maximianus, begotten from a concubine and adopted, because of her barrenness, by Valeria, wife of that same Maximianus. Since his father [Col. 0456B] waged war for fifteen years in Illyricum or along the Danube bank, one might not altogether inappropriately say that Candidiana—whether town or posting-station—which, according to the Antonine Itinerary, p. 63 cited above, lies between Transmarisca and Teglicium, received this name because Candidianus was either born or raised there.

IN CHAPTER XXIV.

“Having taken up the empire, Constantine Augustus did nothing before restoring Christians to their worship and their God.” He therefore acted at once as Augustus, though never previously Caesar, and held second place in the empire, as chapter 25 states at its end. Eusebius too, *Life of Constantine*, Book I, chapter 22, says that Constantine was called Augustus immediately after Constantius’s death. Unless one prefers to say that Lactantius calls Constantine Augustus proleptically; for he did not claim this title, if the author of the Panegyric of Constantine and Maximinus is trustworthy, until after receiving it from Maximianus Herculius, who, having resumed the purple, came into Gaul [Col. 0456C] in A.D. 307 to give his daughter Fausta in marriage to Constantine.

But whence then come so many varied coins—gold, silver, and bronze—on which CONSTANTINE is styled CAESAR? Must this be attributed to Constantine’s moderation, since some were struck in the provinces under his control? Or were they in the greater part struck in obedience to Galerius Maximianus rather than Constantine, in those regions subject to Galerius Maximianus, so that, by coins scattered throughout the empire, Constantine might be deprived of the title Augustus?

The reason for this view is that Galerius Maximianus ordered Constantine to be called emperor, as he had been made, but Caesar together with Maximinus, at the end of chapter 25. This may also be inferred from chapter 26, in which that same Maximianus is said not to have been able to make Caesars—namely Maxentius, added to the two others, Maximinus and Constantine.

IN CHAPTER XXV.

[Col. 0456D] “In order to cast him down from second place to fourth.” Constantine, in chapter 24, had been commended by his father Constantius, near death, to the soldiers and had been made Augustus; accordingly he was Galerius Maximianus’s equal and second in the Roman Empire. But Severus and Maximinus had been made Caesars by Galerius Maximianus (chapter 18, verses 24 and 28–34) before Constantine obtained any rank. Again, once Severus was now called Augustus and Maximinus had attained third place, since he had previously been made Caesar, Constantine necessarily had to yield his place to both, if he had been called only Caesar; and so he would have been cast down from the second place granted to him by the soldiers after his father’s death, as noted above at the end of chapter 24, into fourth.

IN CHAPTER XXVI.

“Maxentius was made emperor at Rome.” Do not understand *emperor* here in the sense of Augustus, as Maxentius himself afterwards was made [Col. 0457A] (at the end of chapter 32). Here it means nothing other than Caesar; for below, with Maxentius counted in, one reads: “And Maximianus hated the man and could not make three Caesars.”

“And he names him Augustus twice.” That is, again or anew.

IN CHAPTER XXVII.

“With Maximianus added.” That is, Maximinus. For by Lactantius Daza was called indiscriminately Maximianus and Maximinus. See the note on chapter 28, verse 28.

“At the marriage of his younger daughter.” Fausta.

“He.” Galerius Maximianus.

“Felix animis quorum.” Read: *flexis animis eorum*, “with their minds bent.”

IN CHAPTER XXIX.

“There were six.” Diocles is not included in the number, but Maximianus Herculius is, to whom, while he remained in Campania, his son Maxentius had sent the purple and had twice—that is, anew—called Augustus, so that father and son [Col. 0457B] held the empire jointly.

“Constantine the emperor, his son-in-law.” For Constantine had married Fausta, daughter of Maximianus Herculius.

“The son of his son-in-law.” Constantius Chlorus, to whom Flavia Maximiana Theodora, stepdaughter of that same Herculius, had been married. Thus Constantius, having married the stepdaughter, is regarded as the son-in-law of the stepfather.

IN CHAPTER XXX.

“His son.” Thus, in the Constantius inscription in Gruter, p. CLXVI, 7, Constantius is called the son of Maximianus Herculius, though he was only the husband of his stepdaughter, as was just noted.

IN CHAPTER XXXII.

Maximinus was angry and did not wish to be called either Caesar or third in rank. From this you will understand that Maximinus placed himself before Constantine. For if he had regarded Constantine as holding the rank of Augustus, as he had been made, then he himself could have been named only fourth. But this does not conflict with what I noted above on chapter 24 [Col. 0457C].

“He therefore repeatedly sends envoys to him.” That is, Galerius Maximianus to Maximinus.

“He asks him to obey, to preserve his arrangement.” Namely, the arrangement by which he had given the empire to Licinius, substituting him for Severus.

“Let him yield to age and grant honor to grey hairs.” Licinius, made Augustus, was older than Maximinus; Galerius Maximianus regarded him as a friend from their former shared military service and an intimate from his earliest military career.

“The beast is distressed.” Galerius Maximianus. So also at the beginning of chapter 25: “the evil beast.”

“Overcome by obstinacy.” I wholly subscribe to the view of the distinguished Antonius Pagi, who says in his *Baronian Criticism* under A.D. 307 that these words must be understood of Maximinus; and he demonstrates this from Eusebius, where, in Book VIII, chapter 13, after Licinius was named Augustus by Galerius Maximianus, Maximinus is said to have proclaimed himself Augustus.

[Col. 0457D] These words, “overcome by obstinacy,” mean the same as “unequal to obstinacy,” not another’s obstinacy but his own. The sense is that Maximinus, carried away by the force of his own obstinacy, did not obey Maximianus, who was making a fair request. Let it be permitted to illustrate this idiom with several examples, drawn especially from Flavius Josephus; for this author has become somewhat familiar to me.

Plato, at the beginning of the *Hipparchus*, calls lovers of gain, φιλοκερδεῖς, “inferior to gain,” ἥττους τοῦ κέρδους—literally “lesser,” that is, overcome by gain. In Herodian one finds ἥττων ὀργῆς καὶ ἐρῶτος, “inferior to anger and love.”

In *Antiquities*, Book XXII, chapter 3, p. 401, Onias the priest is called χρημάτων ἥττων, “inferior to money,” that is, avaricious; this vice is in the same passage called by Josephus φιλοχρηματία, “love of money.” Then, Book XVII, chapter 10, p. 600, concerning Herod: ὀργῆς μὲν ἥσσων, κρείσσων δὲ τοῦ δικαίου, “inferior indeed to anger, but superior to justice.” Finally, Book XVIII, chapter 11, p. 613, concerning Gaius Caligula: [Col. 0458A] ἥσσων μὲν τοῦ αἰσχροῦ, κρείσσων δὲ τοῦ βελτίστου, “inferior indeed to what is shameful, but superior to what is best,” that is, to uprightness.

Further, in these passages of Josephus, and in Book XIV, chapter 17, p. 484, where the just man Sameas is called τοῦ δεδοιέναι κρείττων, “superior to being frightened,” that is, above terrors, κρείσσων means “one who despises.” For in Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, Book VII, Tlepolemus uses a Greek idiom in Latin: “Greetings, clients of most valiant Mars, and comrades-in-arms now loyal to me; receive willingly a man of high-spirited vitality who comes willingly, who more readily receives wounds in his body than gold in his hand, and who is SUPERIOR even to death itself, which others fear.”

Thus, in Tacitus, *Annals*, Book XIII, chapter 46, Poppaea is said to have pretended that she was unequal to desire and captivated by Nero’s beauty; and in Victor’s *Epitome*, Julian the Apostate is said to have been overcome by a burning desire for glory. Conversely, Marcus Porcius Cato is called by Livy, Book XXXIX, 40, a man with a spirit unconquered by desires; the same Julian the Apostate is, in Victor’s *On the Caesars*, conqueror of all food, lust, and every desire [Col. 0458B]; and the emperor Gratian, in Victor’s *Epitome*, conqueror of wine and lust. Finally, Cicero, *On Ends*, says: “Those who retain their own judgment, lest, conquered by pleasure, they do what they think ought not to be done.”

From these passages it is clear that the words “overcome by obstinacy” are not said here of another’s obstinacy; those who have attributed them to Galerius Maximianus have therefore thus far been mistaken, since they are said of Maximinus.

“He removes the name of the Caesars.” Of the three: that is, of himself, Constantine, and Maxentius.

“Maxentius and Constantine, sons of the Augusti.” Maxentius and Constantine were naturally sons of Augusti, namely of Maximianus Herculius and Constantius; but this was a title of rank with which Maximinus distinguished both. There is reason, however, to suspect that he wished by this title, merely honorific, to reduce them to a lower class; for those called Sons of the Augusti possessed no, or very little, power in the empire. Hence [Col. 0458C] Capitolinus, chapter 3, concerning the emperor Lucius Verus, adoptive son of Antoninus Pius, says: “Before he became emperor, no other honorific addition to his name was given him than that he was called Son of Augustus.”

I further suspect that the coin of Constantine the Great which Mediobarbus displays on p. 459—if indeed it is genuine—with the legend CONSTANTINUS FIL. AUGG., that is, “CONSTANTINE, SON OF THE AUGUSTI,” namely Constantius and Maximianus Herculius, was struck deliberately and by Maximinus’s order somewhere in his territories, in order that this ordinance, whereby Maximinus wished Constantine to be regarded as only SON OF AUGUSTUS, might be promulgated through the medium of coins.

“In the recently celebrated Campus Martius, he was proclaimed Augustus by the army.” Campus Martius here is not the name of a place, as it was at Rome, but rather, so to speak, of military assemblies at which the army was reviewed. Whether a Campus Martius was celebrated at fixed times, or whenever the emperor ordered it, is not clear.

It is probable that Maximinus, who governed Syria and Egypt, chapter XXXVI [Col. 0458D], assembled the legions of these provinces in camp, so that, proclaimed Augustus by the soldiers themselves as the authors of the title, he might secure himself against the consequences of the designation which he had seized.

Nor was a Campus Martius celebrated only among the Romans; in imitation of them it was also celebrated among the Franks. Hear Gregory of Tours, Book II, chapter 27, speaking of King Clovis: “When the year had passed, he ordered the whole phalanx to come with its equipment of arms, to display in the Campus Martius the brilliance of its arms.” This confirms what I said above: the celebration of the Campus Martius was a review of military forces. Clovis’s event, moreover, occurred at the beginning of spring, when armies customarily march out for war.

“He orders all four emperors to be numbered.” Add a comma after “four,” and read *nominari*, “to be named,” instead of *numerari*, “to be numbered,” thus: “He orders all four emperors to be named”—namely Licinius, Maximinus, Constantine [Col. 0459A], and Maxentius. Here, however, “emperors” means Augusti, as noted on chapter 18, verse 7.

IN CHAPTER XXXIII.

“Having struck back the marrow, the evil falls back inward.” Who has ever heard or read of marrow being struck back? Add a comma after *malum* (“evil”), therefore, and write: “The evil, repelled by remedies, falls back inward.” For *medelis* is used for *medicinis*, “medicines.” Thus above: “The wound begins not to feel the medicine.” If you approve this emendation, reader, ascribe it to a distinguished man who forbade me to praise him as its author.

IN CHAPTER XXXVII.

“Without measure, with soldiers.” Read: “with guards” (*satellites*). Thus at the end of chapter 38: “Surrounded by these guards and protectors.”

IN CHAPTER XXXIX.

[Col. 0459B] “Finally, that it was unlawful for a woman of that name and station, contrary to custom and precedent, to try a second husband.” Valeria said this either because she was truly ignorant of the matter, or in pretence, so that Maximinus might be diverted from his purpose by the exceptional character of the precedent. For an old example of such a marriage was available from 142 years earlier in Lucilla Augusta, daughter of Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher—that is, Marcus Aurelius—and widow of the emperor Lucius Verus. Capitolinus testifies in *Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher*, chapter 20, in these words: “As he departed for the German war, he gave his daughter, before the period of mourning had elapsed, to Claudius Pompeianus, the aged son of a Roman knight, of Antiochene stock and not sufficiently noble; him he later made consul twice, though his daughter was Augusta and the daughter of an Augusta.”

This occurred, I say, 142 years earlier; for that number of years from Lucilla’s mourning to Valeria’s mourning is demonstrated as follows.

Galerius Maximianus died in his eighth consulship, in May, chapter 21; thus Valeria became a widow in A.D. 311.

[Col. 0459C] Lucius Verus ended his life in midwinter, as Galen testifies, *On Prognosis*, Book I, chapter 10. That winter occupied the end of A.D. 169 and beginning of 170.

At present I do not discuss whether Lucius Verus died before the end of 169 or after the beginning of the following year, although I think it occurred near the end of 169. In either case it follows that from then to May of the aforesaid year A.D. 311, when Maximianus died, the 142nd year was running.

That Lucius Verus died near the end of 169, or at latest lived until the beginning of the following year, may be established from the beginning and end of his reign.

Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus both acquired the empire, in an unprecedented arrangement, after the death of Antoninus Pius, who departed this life in A.D. 161—according to Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 25, and Dio, p. 814—on 17 March.

If this is granted, since Lucius Verus did not reach the tenth year of his reign, he must have died before the seventeenth day [Col. 0459D] of March in A.D. 178. Otherwise he would have reached the tenth year of his reign.

That he reached only the ninth, and not the tenth, year is established chiefly by two arguments, which I shall briefly explain.

The first is provided by coins, both Greek and Latin, none of which at all displays a date beyond L. Θ, that is, year 9, or beyond TR. P. 9.

The second is found in the Paschal Chronicle, where under the first year of the 237th Olympiad, indiction VI, consuls Apronianus and Paulus, Lucius Aurelius Commodus is said to have died, ἄρξας ἔτη θ, “having reigned nine years.”

This testimony of the author of that Chronicle is not for that reason to be rejected, because it dates Lucius Verus’s death two years earlier than it should, namely in A.D. 168. For in this anachronism it is consistent with itself, since it carries the beginning of Lucius Verus’s reign back to A.D. 159 [Col. 0460A]. Both facts are plainly shown by the carefully supplied indiction numbers in this Chronicle; as is also another and continual error of the same author, an anticipation by two years in fixing Olympiads, as I noted above, p. 151.

If someone asks me why, then, Capitolinus says in his life of Lucius Verus that Lucius Verus reigned with his brother Marcus Aurelius for eleven years, he will receive the answer that the word *undecim* (“eleven”) arose there from the two numeral letters XI, transposed from the two letters IX, by which nine is signified; so that from XI, “eleven” was then fully written out and flooded all manuscripts of Capitolinus which have hitherto reached our hands.

Nor should it surprise anyone that Victor the Epitomator, Cassiodorus, and Eutropius likewise read “eleven.” For all of them, once the source had become corrupted, imbibed the same poison.

In Cedrenus the correction of the same error is easier. There one reads, p. 250 of the Royal edition of 1647: [Col. 0460B] Μάρκος Ἀντωνῖνος ἐβασίλευσεν ἔτη ιθ΄, μετὰ μὲν Βήρου (incorrectly Σεβήριου), τοῦ γαμβροῦ αὐτοῦ, ἔτη ι΄ καὶ μῆνας θ΄: “Marcus Antoninus reigned nineteen years; with Verus indeed (incorrectly Severus), his son-in-law, ten years and nine months.” For instead of ἔτη ι΄ καὶ μῆνας θ΄, “ten years and nine months,” one should either read simply ἔτη θ΄, “nine years,” or restore η΄ after ἔτη in place of ι΄—that is, 8 in place of 10—because η΄ was changed into ι΄ by an easy scribal slip, both because of similarity of shape and because, among some persons, the two letters had the same pronunciation. Thus Lucius Verus, who began to rule in mid-March of A.D. 161, died according to Cedrenus in 169, before he had entered the tenth month of the year, by the arrival of mid-December.

Let it therefore stand that Lucius Verus reigned only nine years and ended his life at the end of A.D. 169 or the beginning of 170. Hence, by A.D. 311, when Maximinus sought marriage with Valeria after Galerius Maximianus’s death, the 142nd year was in progress.

I shall add, since this too contributes to establishing [Col. 0460C] the chronology of Lucius Verus, that Capitolinus, chapter 2 in the life of Lucius Verus, must furthermore be corrected where it reads: “He lived forty years less two,” that is, thirty-eight. This agrees very well with the birth-year of Lucius Verus during his father’s praetorship, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January, in Capitolinus, chapter 1. But on this elsewhere.

Nor can I omit an excellent example supporting the proposed correction of the letters XI to IX, advanced by the most learned Johannes Hardouin in *Illustrated Ancient Coins*, published at Paris in 1684, p. 316, under the entry ΜΑΣΣΑ, from Pliny. In Book XVIII, section 69, Pliny directs, after the years have been transposed, that one read “the 516th year of the City” (*Urbis an. DXVI*) in place of DXIV.

I have collected from Greek and Latin authors very many examples not only of similar transpositions but also of numeral letters misunderstood and then the numbers themselves written out in full; I shall someday present them in a suitable place.

Among them is one especially notable example, if any is, in Flavius Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book XVII, chapter 10, Greek p. 600, E, line 9, where Herod’s funeral is said to have proceeded from Jericho to Herodium σταδία ὄκτω, “eight stadia,” whereas in the parallel passage, Book I of *The Jewish War*, chapter 21, p. 774, third line from the end, it is said to have occurred σταδίους διακοσίους, “two hundred stadia” [Col. 0460D].

The reconciliation of these two passages led astray three authors otherwise most acute: Wilhelm Lange, Book II, *On the Years of Christ*, chapter 18, p. 350, Leiden edition of 1649; James Ussher, *Annals*, latter part, Julian period year 4711, p. 536, London edition of 1654; and Christian Noldius, *History of Idumaea*, p. 71, Franeker edition. I once devoted considerable effort to refuting their views. For the present I shall say only that the reading ὀκτω, “eight,” in the *Antiquities* is wrong: it was written out in full from η΄, the sign for eight, whereas η΄ had been wrongly formed or read from σ΄, the symbol for two hundred. It must be observed that numbers in the books of the *Antiquities* are almost universally expressed in abbreviated form by numerical letters [Col. 0461A], unlike the books of *The Jewish War*, where the numbers themselves are written in full.

Further, in that account of Herod’s funeral procession in the books of *The Jewish War*, the same letter η is wrongly read for σ—namely, p. 744, sixth line from the end, in the word Προῆγε, “went before,” in place of Πρόσγε, “furthermore.” For the passage reads:

> Προῆγε δὲ ἡ λοιπὴ δύναμις·  
> “And the remaining army went before.”

This is wholly contrary both to the sequence of the narrative, as will be clear to the reader, and to the corresponding passage in the *Antiquities*, p. 600, E, line 6:

> Τούτων δὲ κατόπιν ἤδη πᾶς ὁ στρατός  
> “After these came now the entire army.”

IN CHAPTER XLIV.

“Civil arms had already been set in motion between them. And although Maxentius kept himself within Rome.” This was in A.D. 312.

The Senate decreed to Constantine, as a reward for his valor, the title of the first name, which Maximinus claimed for himself. The title [Col. 0461B] is *Maximus*, which is observed at the end of this chapter and afterwards on Constantine’s coins. Constantine had received it in Gaul in the preceding year, as the most illustrious Mediobarbus has very well observed from coins, p. 462 of his excellent work, on which occur: IMP. CONSTANTINUS MAX. P. F. AUG. SM. H. ER. VOTIS V. MVLT. X. VICTOR. AVG. P. TR.

The final three letters, P. TR., mean “struck at Trier”—with *coinage* understood.

Yet coins or inscriptions have not so far shown that Maximinus used the title *Maximus*, which, according to Lactantius, he claimed for himself. Thus the learned man thought that in this passage the “title of the first name” must mean the designation of “first emperor,” which Maximinus claimed for himself by priority in time, since he had been made Caesar (chapter 18) long before Constantine.

IN CHAPTER XLVI.

“Just as he was defeated at Rome.” Maxentius, as in chapter 44.

IN CHAPTER XLVIII.

[Col. 0461C]

“What indeed is divinity in the heavenly seat.” Read: “Whatever divinity and heavenly reality there is,” from Eusebius, Book X, chapter 5, and Nicephorus, Book VII, chapter 41, where θειότητος must be read instead of θειότης in Eusebius and instead of θειοτάτου in Nicephorus.

“They appeared regarding the name of Christians, now let each person take care freely and simply.” Supply and correct from Eusebius’s Greek, Book X, chapter 5: “Let the restrictions imposed regarding the name of Christians be removed; likewise let those things which appeared wholly adverse and foreign to our clemency be removed; and now let each person freely and simply…”

IN CHAPTER L.

“First of all, Valerius.” Certainly he is the man of whom Sextus Victor, *Epitome*, no. 55 says: “Valens is created emperor”; and in no. 56: “Valens is punished with death by Licinius.” Occo, p. 480, gives his coin:

> ΑΥΤ. Κ. ΠΟΥ. ΟΥΑΛΕΡ. ΟΥΑΛΕΝΣ. ΕΥ. ΣΕΒ. Λ. Α.

[Col. 0461D] That is: “Emperor Caesar Publius Valerius Valens, Pious Augustus, Year 1.”

The most illustrious Count Mediobarbus, p. 387, did not rightly assign this coin to Valens, the usurper under Gallienus. For that Valens, whom Pollio mentions in no. XVIII, was called Valens Thessalonicus, as Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXI, chapter 16, informs us, not Valerius Valens with a doubled name. Rather, another coin in Occo, p. 528, belongs to him, in this form:

> ΑΥΤ. ΚΑΙ. Γ. ΙΟΥΛ. ΟΥΑΛΕΝΣ. ΣΕΒ. Ε. Α.

That is: “Emperor Caesar Gaius Julius Valens Augustus, Year 1.”

Therefore Occo there wrongly judges that this Valens was put to death by Licinius, since he belonged to the time of Gallienus.

Further, Valerius Valens inscribed on the first coin cannot be the Valens whom Licinius, after war had broken out [Col. 0462A] between himself and Constantine, created Caesar, but not Augustus. For that Valens, once Caesar, was later, after peace had been made between the two emperors, merely reduced in rank, not killed, as the Anonymous writer of Sirmond in Valesius’s edition of Ammianus, p. 659, and Peter, *On Embassies*, in the *Excerpts*, vol. I of Byzantine History, p. 27, testify. Nor should Zosimus be heard, Constantine’s most hostile enemy, when he relates—yet does not affirm, as the Greek word οἶμαι, “I think,” which he uses sufficiently indicates—that this Caesar Valens was killed by Constantine’s will and command.

The other Valens, an Augustus, was killed at almost the same time as Maximinus perished; and once these had been removed, the rights of empire came into the hands of Constantine and Licinius, as Sextus Victor writes. The rights of empire came to Constantine and Licinius in A.D. 313. Therefore Valens—or Valerius Valens—mentioned by Victor perished then; for Lactantius writes that he was killed first by Licinius.

[Col. 0462B] Nor is this Valerius Valens Valeria Augusta, as has been corrected in the Oxford notes; for Valeria was killed last, not first, by Licinius, as chapter 41 expressly states.
