This, among many other things, was formerly taught me by the most illustrious and learned Abbot Louis Du Four de Longuerue. The most distinguished Antonius Pagi recently inserted what he had received from him into his *Baronian Criticism*, under A.D. 306, no. XV, p. 20, candidly acknowledging, as befits an honest man, from whom he had learned it.

IN CHAPTER LI.

“Thus their chastity and rank were their ruin.” I wonder that Lactantius did not say that the sacrifices by which Valeria, though Christian, had been defiled under compulsion from Diocletian, her father, were her ruin, as I discussed in chapter 15.

IN CHAPTER LII.

“Where now are those magnificent and famous throughout the nations surnames of the Jovii and Herculii, first arrogantly assumed by Diocletian [Col. 0462C] and Maximianus and afterwards transmitted to their successors, which flourished?” That is, the Lord has obliterated and erased them from the earth. Lactantius wrote this rhetorically and contrary to historical fact, unless one says that he placed the concluding flourish upon the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* at some intermediate time after all persecutors of the name of God had been defeated, before the following coins were struck, on which both Licinii are inscribed as Jovii.

The first is displayed with its type in the *Byzantine Families* of the most distinguished Charles du Cange, published in Paris in 1680, p. 25, as follows:

> D.D. N.N. IOVII. LICINII. INVICT. AVG. ET CAES.

A gemmed head. Busts of Licinius Augustus and Licinius Caesar, each holding in his hands Victory, who extends a laurel wreath to each.

Two others are cited by Mediobarbus, p. 455, in these words:

> D.D. N.N. IOVII. LICINII. INVICTI. AVG. ET CAES.

The laureate heads and busts—that is, the figures to the waist—of the Licinii, father and son, facing one another, hold Victory in their right hands; she, with arms outstretched, holds a separate wreath in each hand [Col. 0462D].

This coin appears to be the same as the preceding one of du Cange.

There follows there in Mediobarbus another final coin:

> D.D. N.N. IOVI. LICINII. INVICT. AVG. ET CAES.

The laureate heads of the Licinii hold in their right hands the figure of Fortune, namely a figure with the head adorned by a *calathus*, holding a rudder in her right hand and a cornucopia in her left.

Moreover, legions, cavalry wings, and cohorts continually bearing the names Jovii and Herculii remained in existence even under Constantine himself and down to the emperor Valentinian III, as can be seen throughout the *Notitia Dignitatum* of the empire.

Farewell, reader. May fortune answer your wishes; such are my wishes.

NOTES OF GISBERT CUPER.

[Col. 0463]

Preface.

[Col. 0463A] Some years ago, at the request of the late Johannes Columbus, a learned man, I hastily put onto paper certain observations which I thought might serve to elucidate one or two passages of this golden little work. They were published at Åbo, the capital city of the Finns. Yet, just as I readily believe that they were not wholly approved by learned men, so I ask them to be persuaded that I did not then wish to make anything else public. Columbus had informed me that he had many annotations upon Lactantius; I therefore did not wish to put my sickle into his harvest. But, to oblige my friend—the son-in-law of the most distinguished Scheffer, a man of exceedingly elegant learning—I sent notes which were published in the furthest North.

What a man more worthy of a long life might have achieved is evident. And since I observe that not a few things remain which deserve fuller elucidation, and since some of my own work—for I am not ashamed to admit it—now pleases me less, I began to examine this most elegant little work more carefully and, where this could conveniently be done, to insert among these new notes my own remarks which Columbus published with his, so that all may, as it were, come under a single view by this route; and so that those who desire to know my opinion may not be obliged at every moment to consult the labours of that eminent man. From this arose annotations far more extensive. The most eloquent of the Fathers prompts me to publish them; the splendid matters which he teaches us prompt me; and finally the subject of the work prompts me—a subject whose revival today we behold and wonder at, and which is the principal theme of all discussion, at least among those who reflect upon ancient times, the wounds inflicted upon the Church, and the tragic ends of the persecutors, and who are touched and tormented by the Church of God, afflicted in ways so miserable, so horrible, and perhaps so incredible to posterity.

If I shall have produced anything worthy of Lactantius and acceptable to learned men, there will certainly be cause for me to rejoice seriously; if the contrary happens, and if men of captious disposition, to whom nothing pleases unless it proceeds from themselves, think that they can find many things displeasing to them, let that be so as far as I am concerned. For I devote my time free from public business [Col. 0463B] not to disputes and commissions, but to genuine learning and humane letters, and to the relaxation of a mind which must sometimes be allowed recreation.

I would bid you farewell, reader, were it not that Constantine the Great, the glory and ornament of the little work composed by Lactantius which I elucidate with notes, laid his hand upon me. Since he must often be summoned into the discussion, and since I offer many observations concerning him when occasion presents itself, I judged that I should not act without purpose if I investigated the birthplace of this most illustrious prince. I see men of eminent learning differing enormously among themselves: some think that that great emperor was born in Thrace, others in Britain, others elsewhere—he who is called on coins, not without reason, “Conqueror of All Nations,” “Most Foresighted Prince,” “Victor Everywhere,” and “Founder of Peace”; to whom on the same coins are attributed “the Happiness of the Age,” “Blessed Tranquillity,” and also “the Security of the Commonwealth.”

Baronius, Pomponius Laetus, the Archbishop of Armagh in his *Antiquities of the British Churches*, and recently Stillingfleet in his *Origines Britannicae*, judged that this prince was born in Britain. Others make Helena, his mother, the daughter of some king of Britain—an absolutely sheer invention. The chief support of the former opinion, however, is the panegyric delivered by Eumenius to Constantine: “O fortunate Britain,” he says, “and now happier than all lands, which first beheld Constantine as Caesar!” To this must certainly be added the panegyric, by an unknown author, addressed to Maximian and Constantine, in which occur these words: “He freed the Britains from slavery; you made them noble by your origin there.”

But, with all due respect to such great men, I think entirely otherwise. I judge that Constantine the Great was born in Illyricum, taken in the broad sense, or in Mediterranean Dacia, and specifically in the city of Naissus. Constantine Porphyrogenitus certainly teaches this without ambiguity, *Themes*, book II, chapter 9: “The prefecture of Mediterranean Dacia under a counsellor: five cities—Pantalia, Germanus, Naissus, the homeland of the great Constantine.” Stephanus—or his epitomizer Hermolaus Barbarus—testifies to the same thing under Ναϊσσός: “Naissus, a city of Thrace, a foundation and homeland of the emperor Constantine.” I think Julius Firmicus likewise transmits this in book I of the *Mathesis*, and that there [Col. 0464A] one should read with Valesius, from the manuscripts, *Naisus*, not *Tarsus*, which is what the printed books preserve: “Constantine, born at Naissus, holding the reins of empire from the first stage of life.”

But the strongest argument is supplied by the author of the *Extracts concerning Constantius Chlorus and Constantine the Great*, whose words are these: “Thus Constantine was born at the town of Naissus, his mother Helena being of the lowest condition.” Nothing can certainly be said more clearly. I would pass on to other matters, were it not that I judged it in the interest of the republic of letters to submit a conjecture that conveniently occurred to me, and which I also mentioned in my note on chapter 26—not because I wish to impose it upon others, or even wholly to embrace it myself, but so that more diligent scholars may have something upon which to exercise themselves.

It is known that Helena is called the concubine of Constantius by some. Yet no one, so far as I know, has been found to call her a woman of the lowest condition, except the author of the *Extracts*—who perhaps did not write this, since it is not likely that a Christian would speak thus of one so devout and venerable, who, as she is called on coins, was Augusta. What then? Hesitantly and with complete uncertainty, I say that perhaps the text originally read: “at a most insignificant town” (*vilissimo in oppido*). For this town seems not to have been very distinguished or large; and immediately afterward the same *Extracts* state that Constantine adorned it marvellously. Stephanus calls it his “foundation” (*κτίσμα*); and since it was splendidly adorned thereafter, it is no wonder that Ammianus Marcellinus, XXI.10, calls it a populous town.

I am surprised, however, that some learned men believe this city to be identical with Nastos and Nestos—the former of which Stephanus makes a city of Thrace and says is also spelled Νεστόν, while the latter is a city and river of Illyria—and record that no ancient writer mentions the Illyrian city and river Nestus, whereas Mela, Pliny, and Solinus mention Nestus, the very celebrated river of Thrace. For I indeed judge that Pliny, VIII.16, mentions no other Nessus than the Illyrian one, when he observes that in Europe lions occur only between the rivers Achelous and Nestus. Scylax of Caryanda—or the geographer published under his name—mentions in Illyria the “Nestrian gulf” (*κόλπον Νεσταῖον*) and a city, or river—for he does not add [Col. 0464B] which of the two—called Νεστόν.

Indeed, Apollonius Rhodius, IV.1215, also assigns the Nestaeans to the same region; and the words of the scholiast deserve notice:

> “Scylax says that the Nestaeans are an Illyrian people; from them there is a voyage of one day into the gulf. Eratosthenes also, in the third book of his *Geographical Matters*, says: ‘After the Illyrians come the Nestaeans, near whom is the island Pharos, a colony of the Pharians.’”

There was therefore in Illyria a city and a river Nestus; there was a Nessus, or Nestus, river in Thrace; and finally there was Naissus, the city which was Constantine’s homeland, which Stephanus too calls a Thracian city, the name of that region evidently being taken broadly. Unless someone wishes, with Valesius, to emend the text to Δακίας, “of Dacia,” and understand Mediterranean Dacia—a matter on which I offer sufficient instruction in the notes.

Constantine, then, was born in the town of Naissus and afterwards called Great on account of the glory of his deeds. It seems to have been insignificant and small because Constantine adorned it marvellously, in order, presumably, to make his birthplace more illustrious. It is therefore called “most insignificant” by the author of the *Extracts*, if indeed my conjecture is true. I was unwilling to press it longer even for this reason: that low status may be removed from Augusta Helena, which I do not recall ever having been alleged against her by any ancient writer—unless it be that Eutropius relates that Constantine was Constantius’s son by a less distinguished marriage. This could certainly have been said by him in comparison with the second marriage which Constantius contracted with Valeria, daughter of the emperor Diocletian.

But to continue: chronology allows in no other way that Constantine could have been born in Britain. For he was born in A.D. 272, under the consulship of Aurelian and Bassus, long before his father was adorned with the rank of Caesar, which occurred in A.D. 291. Constantius did not enter that island before becoming Caesar, and earlier he doubtless spent most of his time in Illyricum. For, as the author of the *Extracts* says, Constantius, nephew through his brother of the divine Claudius, that excellent prince, was first a Protector, then a tribune, [Col. 0465C] afterwards governor of the Dalmatias; and he received his final office from Carus, who began to reign in 282, or at least held it under him, as is clear from Vopiscus in the *Life of Carinus*.

Nor does Eumenius assist those eminent men in any respect. I judge that the cited words have a quite different sense: Constantine first saw Britain as Caesar, not because he was born there, but because, after his father’s death, he was made Caesar by the army. That this is true is more than sufficiently clear from what I observed in the notes. Nor does the other panegyrist establish anything by saying that Constantine made the Britains noble by originating there. For people are said to “originate” (*oriri*) when they are born and enter into life, and an origin (*ortus*) is attributed to them; but the same words are also used, with singular elegance, of those who become kings, emperors, or Caesars.

Thus Gaius and Lucius, adopted by Augustus and designated princes of the youth, are called “rising youths” (*orientes juvenes*) by Velleius Paterculus, II.99. Pliny, XXXIII.3, speaks of “the rising” (*exortus*) of the emperor Vespasian, referring to the beginning of his reign. Curtius, X.9, also speaks, as many believe, of him:

> “Therefore the Roman people rightly and deservedly professes that it owes its salvation to its prince, for whom a new star shone forth in the night which we had almost regarded as our last. By Hercules, this man’s rising—not that of the sun—restored light to the darkened world.”

Nor do panegyrists speak otherwise. Chapter 1 of the panegyric addressed to Maximian and Constantine: “Most sacred princes—Maximian, Augustus forever whether you will or no; and Constantine, emperor in his rising (*oriens*).” Chapter 8: “This is he who, at the very rising (*ortus*) of his divinity, restored Gaul, made savage by the wrongs of earlier times, to obedience to the commonwealth”—that is, as soon as he became emperor, at the beginning of his reign. Eumenius, chapter 10 of the panegyric delivered to Constantine: “I suppose that some undistinguished band of barbarians, by a sudden attack and unforeseen brigandage, attempted the auspices of your rising (*ortus*).” The same author, in another panegyric, chapter 2, calls the day on which Constantine was proclaimed Caesar “the divine rising of his majesty.”

Thus, when Constantine is said to have made Britain noble by originating there, [Col. 0466A] nothing else can certainly be inferred except that he assumed the purple there and was made Caesar or emperor. This is also the opinion of Justus Lipsius in the *Admiranda* and of Johannes Livineius. The mode of speech is drawn from the sun or stars, to which emperors used to be compared. Britannicus is called by his sister Octavia, in Seneca, “the star of the world.” Antoninus the Philosopher calls himself an old setting sun, but Commodus a rising sun (*ἀνατέλλοντα*). Geta and Caracalla, on a very rare Ephesian coin in Spon and Morell, are called “New Suns” (*ΝΕΟΙ ΗΛΙΟΙ*).

What I think of the *Acts of Pilate* I made clear in my note on chapter 36. Later I came upon the posthumous works of the Bishop of Cistercia and noticed that the illustrious man observes on p. 51:

> “The *Acts of Pilate*, full of impiety against Christ, fabricated by the order of the tyrant Maximinus, were publicly posted both in the countryside and in the cities and handed over to schoolmasters to be learned by children; the Romans made use of these under Diocletian and Maximinus in order to recall Christians from martyrdom, as the words of Maximinus testify in the Passion of Saints Tarachus, Probus, and Andronicus: ‘Most unjustly, do you not know whom you invoke—Christ, a certain man, placed under the custody of Pontius Pilate, whose acts are deposited [the printed editions read otherwise]?’”

If the illustrious bishop means by Maximinus Galerius Maximinus, under whose rule Eusebius testifies that these acts were fabricated, the Romans could certainly not have used them under Diocletian and Maximinus—or rather Maximian—for they had laid aside the purple before these acts were published. Further, the quoted words in the Passion were not uttered by the emperor Maximinus, as the bishop seems to suppose, but by Numerianus, the chief governor, who brought the martyrs to trial under Diocletian and Maximian Herculius, consuls for the second time, as the *Acts* testify, although I do not find that they held their second consulship together. Incidentally, the translator of Theodore Metochites wrongly makes three emperors out of them—Diocletian, Maximian, and Herculius—when the text itself has “Diocletian and Maximian Herculius” (*Διοκλετιανὸς καὶ Μαξιμιανὸς ὁ Ἑρκύλιος*).

Moreover, Eusebius attributes these utterly filthy acts, as I noted, to Galerius Maximinus; hence in book I, chapter 9, he writes that they were fabricated “only yesterday and the day before” (*χθὲς καὶ πρώην*). A learned man who recently published a dissertation on the Thundering Legion writes that Diocletian and Maximinus produced these acts, although Diocletian, after laying aside the empire, was living at Salonae. He also judges that the *Acts of Pilate* cited by Justin Martyr, Tertullian, and others are forged. The Bishop of Cistercia, however, opposes this opinion; I leave that controversy for others to examine.

In the same chapter 36, I explain that by “the high priest” in Prudentius one should understand not the Roman pontifex maximus, but the priest of Cybele. And undoubtedly he was the first among Cybele’s priests and the head of the rest, just as Apuleius in book I calls the priest of Isis “chief priest”: “And when we had now reached the temple itself, the chief priest and those who carried forth the divine images … duly arrange the statues.”

It is also worth observing that Lactantius, chapter 4, relates that Valerian’s skin, “torn off” or “stripped off,” as I judge one should write, was dyed red and placed in the temple of barbarian gods in commemoration of a most illustrious triumph, and was always displayed to Roman envoys. For the author of the Alexandrian Chronicle relates similar things concerning Carinus: namely, that after being defeated he fled to Carrhae, was captured by the Persians, then killed; and that they made a sack from his stripped skin and, having embalmed or anointed it (*σμυρνίσαντες*), preserved it “for their own glory” (*εἰς ἰδίαν δόξαν*).

I am entirely ignorant of the source of this story. No other author recorded anything of the kind about Carinus, since he was defeated and killed in the battle which he fought against Diocletian near the Margus in Moesia. Thus the author of that Chronicle must be read with great caution. In that very passage he makes Carus the uncle of Carinus, though Carus was the father both of Carinus and Numerian:

> “King Carinus, having set out, fought against the Persians, against his uncle Carus” (*Κάρινος ὁ βασιλεὺς ἀπιὼν πολεμήσας κατὰ Περσῶν κατὰ τοῦ θείου αὐτοῦ Κάρου*; the transmitted Greek is problematic, since the author renders it “with his uncle Carus”).

He not only makes him an uncle on the father’s side, but also writes that Carinus accompanied his father when the latter set out against the Persians. On the contrary, Carinus governed Gaul, while Numerian undertook the eastern expedition with his father, according to Vopiscus. If the word *αὐτοῦ*, “his,” were absent, or had been added by ignorant copyists, *θείου Κάρου* could be rendered “of the deified Carus,” as Carus is called not only on coins but also by Nemesianus in the *Cynegetica*, written for Carinus and Numerian:

> Soon shall I undertake with a better lyre  
> to celebrate your triumphs, most valiant pledges  
> of the deified Carus.

On chapter 16 I noted that the distinguished Casaubon made a human error when he wrote that Constantius defeated the Persians in war. Yet the author of the Chronicle just mentioned reports this too, p. 642: “The Persians,” he says, “were set in motion in full force by Constantius and Maximinus Jovius” (*Πέρσαι … κατὰ κράτος ἐκινήθησαν ὑπὸ Κωνσταντίου καὶ Μαξιμίνου Ἰοβίου*); the accompanying Latin gloss reads: “The Persians were defeated in a very great war by the Caesars Constantius and Maximinus Jovius.” These events are said to have occurred under the consulship of Maximian Herculius for the fifth time and Maximian Jovius Caesar for the second, in the year 1050 from the founding of the city and A.D. 297, when Galerius Maximian certainly overcame Narses. But Constantius was fighting in Britain. Further, “Maximinus Jovius” is Galerius Maximianus Jovius, since Gaius Valerius Maximinus had not yet been made Caesar at that time.

I had thought—see the note on chapter 29—that Aurelius Victor ought to be corrected by inserting the particle *and*. Yet even the received reading indicates that Licinius was made Caesar and Augustus at the same time, although ordinarily princes first received the Caesarian rank and afterwards the name Augustus.

I discussed cremation of corpses—see the note on chapter 39—and thought that the words *CORPUS INTEGRUM CONDITUM*, “the body buried whole,” in two inscriptions indicated that the body had not been cremated but interred. I do not yet reject that conjecture. Learned men should nevertheless consider whether those who set up the monuments rather wished to indicate that the bodies had been buried not mutilated but whole. For the pagans held a powerful religious concern that this should occur; and it was great consolation to them if they bade farewell to human affairs while their limbs were flourishing and intact. Statius, *Silvae* II.1.156:

> Yet, Fates, it is welcome that no lingering death,  
> as he lay, consumed the boyish beauty, and that he went below  
> to the shades whole, his body violated by no injury,  
> as he had been …

Gevartius aptly relates to this the action of Augustus, who on his last day, having asked for a mirror, ordered his hair to be combed and his drooping cheeks corrected, as Suetonius testifies. They were persuaded, of course, that shades moved about in the underworld as their bodies had left life, as Deiphobus in Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, and Laius in Statius, *Thebaid* II, show, not to summon further examples. Hence Cornelius Severus, quoted by Seneca, *Suasoriae* VII, inveighs so severely against Antony for ordering Cicero’s head and hand to be cut off:

> Neither the merciless victory of the Persian at Emathia,  
> nor you, dire Syphax, over your enemy Philip,  
> nor all the outrages inflicted upon conquered Jugurtha,  
> nor fierce Hannibal, falling beneath our anger,  
> bore his limbs, nonetheless inviolate, beneath the Stygian shades.

Perhaps Nero also has this in view when, according to Suetonius, “he demanded nothing earlier or more insistently from his companions than that no one should gain possession of his head, but that he should somehow be cremated whole” (*totus*). Though he may have had before his eyes the possibility of mockery and of a head fixed on a spear, as was customary. Pagans therefore desired to enter the underworld whole, so that with limbs likewise whole they might engage in dances and banquets in the Elysian field. Hence, I think, the limbs of the slain were carefully fitted together so that they might be buried as though whole. Statius, *Thebaid* III.132:

> They fill deep wounds with tears. Some, vainly sparing the right hand,  
> draw out the spears; others gently fit  
> severed arms into place and restore faces to necks.

They likewise bound up wounds, as in Euripides, *Phoenician Women*, v. 1663, where Antigone asks Creon that she may bind the wounds of her slain brother Polyneices:

> “But let me cast bandages about the savage wounds”  
> (*Ἄλλ᾽ ἀμφὶ τραύματ᾽ ἄγρια τελαμῶνας βαλεῖν*).

In the same chapter I offered certain remarks, for elucidating Tertullian, concerning “the king of this age,” and later suspected that one might quite suitably write, “namely, in emulation of the devil, king of this age.” For the devil is called in the New Testament—and specifically in the Gospel of John—“ruler of the world” (*ἄρχων τοῦ κόσμου*), and in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians “the god of this age” (*ὁ θεὸς τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου*). Or the received reading may be explained thus: the pontifex maximus is, in imitation of the devil, king of this age.

Finally, it should be added that Freher, a very learned man, treats with great erudition of the various kinds of taxes in the dissertation which he composed on the Coin of the Census; and Lactantius’s third and twentieth chapters are greatly elucidated by his following words:

> “It must certainly be maintained that the land-tax, that is, the tax upon fields, was levied according to their extent and size, as Ulpian teaches in *On Censuses*—or rather according to their fertility. For stipend and tribute are burdens upon produce: Digest VII, *On Usufruct*; Digest, *On Expenditures Made upon Dotal Property*. Hence Maecenas in Dio: ‘Having imposed a tax generally upon all things that yield some profit to their owner’ (*Φόρον ἐπιτάξας πᾶσιν ἁπλῶς τοῖς ἐπικαρπίαν τινὰ τῷ κεκτημένῳ αὐτὰ παρέχουσι*). Taxes were imposed not only on land, but also on other property—coined and uncoined gold, ready money, slaves, and herds—according to their amount. As this differed between the rich and the poor, so did the burden of tax; nor was this very much to be feared by the poor. But the poll-tax was one and the same for all free persons alike—for slaves had no taxable heads, but, like cattle, a tax was paid by their master on their value together with his other property—the rich and the poor, married and unmarried, parents and those without children. I shall not distinguish young men and old, because a limit was fixed in this matter, so that one was not liable to the poll-tax before his twentieth year and old age had its own exemption—except that in Judaea even this was made somewhat more burdensome, as Ulpian states in Digest III, *On Censuses*.”

As I wished here to leave you again, reader, behold: a consular letter from Henricus Noris, certainly a most celebrated man, to whom the study of antiquity owes a great deal, was brought to me from Italy—a letter which he had sent me as a gift. In my note on Lactantius chapter 10, I teach that Caesars were wholly subject to the power of the Augusti, and that it is therefore no wonder that Galerius Maximian ran to Diocletian’s carriage. My view and that of others are strongly confirmed by this most eminent man, who on p. 177 of the cited letter teaches that the title Caesar was no indication of any imperial power. Antonius Pagi, likewise a very learned man, repeatedly speaks of Caesarian power; others rejected this, and he introduces them as speaking thus:

> “We plainly do not know what this Caesarian power of Domitian and Commodus is which your author invents. For Dio, book LIII, discussing imperial titles, testifies that the designation Caesar signified no special power, but only succession in the family line. And, not to depart from Domitian, Tacitus at the end of *Histories* III writes that, after Vitellius’ death, Domitian was hailed Caesar by a numerous soldiery. At the beginning of book IV he says: ‘Domitian had received the name and seat of Caesar.’ Yet it is clear from what he immediately adds that no imperial power was conferred upon him by that title: ‘The praetorship and consular power are decreed to Domitian.’ The praetorship conferred on Domitian no imperium, but only the power of jurisdiction. But so that he, as Caesar and son of Vespasian Augustus, might possess some authority and power above private praetors, consular imperium was decreed to him by senatorial decree; the bare title Caesar conferred no imperium upon him. Marcus Aurelius made his sons Caesars while they were still boys, sharing with them no imperium, of which they were not yet capable because of their age. After the ninth year, however, he granted proconsular imperium to Commodus, who before this had been merely Caesar, without any imperium. For the Augusti, retaining authority and imperium for themselves within the city, invested their sons as Caesars with proconsular imperium outside the city. Therefore Commodus and the remaining Caesars, before receiving proconsular imperium, were considered devoid of all imperium. Thus, when in 175 the senate received news of the death of Avidius Cassius, among the festive acclamations addressed to the absent Marcus Aurelius they said: ‘We ask lawful imperium for Commodus; we ask tribunician power for Commodus.’ Commodus was therefore without imperium, although he had been Caesar since 166, designated indeed for imperium, which he finally received in 175 together with tribunician power. The same Albinus, after Commodus had honoured him with the name Caesar, later said as emperor in an address to the people: ‘I did not despise Commodus’ gift of the Caesarian name.’ He did not say ‘Caesarian imperium,’ but simply ‘the Caesarian name.’ Capitolinus is the authority for these matters in chapters 2 and 3 of the *Life of Albinus*.”

These matters are read in that exceptionally distinguished man, the corrector and creator of the *Fasti*, whose friendship, kindness, and learning I esteem most highly. From them, reader, you may also perceive that Julian rightly called himself a faithful attendant; that Galerius Maximian had reasons, in Lactantius chapter 9, for refusing the title Caesar and, on hearing it in letters addressed to him, exclaiming with grim expression and terrible voice, “How long [shall I be] Caesar?”; and why Galerius Maximinus in chapter 32 wished neither to be Caesar nor to be named in third place.

I had just arranged these matters when, behold, a letter from that most eminent man was brought to me. Since it more fully elucidates the Caesarian rank, as well as the year in which Constantius and Galerius were designated Caesars, I thought fit, reader, with your kind permission, to add it.

[EPISTLE.]

To the Most Illustrious Lord, the most learned and renowned man, Lord GISBERT CUPER, most distinguished senator of the Mighty States of the United Netherlands.

When I dared to send you my consular letter, most illustrious sir, I did not hope that you, entangled in the affairs of the Mighty States of the United Netherlands amid difficult circumstances, and especially amid the upheaval of Europe shaken by French arms, would turn your eyes toward it. For, having been enrolled in the supreme senate of the Belgian provinces, you must attend with counsel and foresight to present matters and to contingencies which may arise in diverse ways, rather than call your mind back to ages that have slipped away.

But such is your genius: when in the senate you deliberate upon matters of the greatest importance and publicly sacrifice to Consus, afterwards at home you perform the sacred rites of Minerva. To execute both with distinction is granted only to those whom impartial Jupiter has loved. Hence you praise the *Fasti* of the nation victorious over peoples, corrected by me, while you yourself, on account of the distinguished volumes published by you, are most highly praised in the *Fasti* of the republic of letters.

I am very glad that you intend to elucidate the golden book of Lactantius with new notes in addition to those of Baluze. For there many matters unknown to our forefathers are explained, and the chronology of Diocletian’s reign—which escaped Scaliger, Panvinio, Baronius, and others—is most correctly set out. Nicolas Toinard of Orléans long ago asked my opinion about the year in which, according to Lactantius, Constantius and Galerius were designated Caesars, since Baluze thinks this took place in the year 293 of the common Christian era. I replied that Baluze admits an anachronism of a year.

For Galerius Maximianus, in the heading of the edict promulgated for Christians in A.D. 311—the year in which that same Augustus gave up his life amid torments—is styled “holding tribunician power for the twentieth time, consul for the eighth time” (*TRIB. POT. XX COS. VIII*). But if he had received tribunician power in A.D. 293, that tribunician power would only have begun to be counted for the twentieth time on the Kalends of March in A.D. 312. Panvinio writes that they were designated Caesars in A.D. 291, as the Idatian *Fasti* had previously reported, adducing also a solar eclipse in the same year. But with Baronius that designation of the Caesars must be assigned to the Kalends of March, A.D. 292.

For after Lactantius had written of Galerius in chapter 33: “The eighteenth year was now passing when God struck him with an incurable disease,” etc., he adds: “And these things continued for a whole year, until at last, overcome by his sufferings, he was compelled to acknowledge God,” etc.; and now dying, he issued an edict of this kind. Accordingly, he began to be ill in the latter part of the eighteenth year of his reign, or of his eighteenth tribunician power, and was afflicted by the disease throughout the nineteenth; but at the beginning of the twentieth tribunician power—namely after the Kalends of March in A.D. 311—he issued the edict.

Now if he had promulgated the edict in that same year 311 before the Kalends of March, at the end of the twentieth tribunician power first assumed in A.D. 291, as Panvinio thinks, he would have been ill for a full two years before promulgating the edict: namely, during the latter part of the eighteenth tribunician power and again throughout the nineteenth and twentieth, when, as consul for the eighth time, that is, in 311, he issued the edict. Astronomical tables should be consulted to determine whether an eclipse occurred in 292, as the cited *Fasti* report. Petavius places an eclipse in A.D. 291 on 15 May, at the third hour after noon. But Idacius incorrectly recorded both that eclipse and the designation of those Caesars in the same year 291, whereas the creation of the Caesars occurred in the following year, if Lactantius is to be trusted.

Concerning the imperium of Caesars under Augusti, this is my view. Some were merely Caesars, without any imperium, such as Gaius and Lucius, sons of Augustus, immediately after their adoption; and Nero before he was endowed with proconsular imperium in A.U.C. 804. Commodus and his brother Annius Verus likewise were so when they were children. But certain others received imperium together with the Caesarian rank. Thus Constantius and Galerius, as soon as they were made Caesars, received proconsular imperium.

Vopiscus, chapter 6 of the *Life of Carus*, says that Carus had intended to take from Carinus “Caesarian imperium”; for, as he writes at the beginning of the *Life of Carinus*, Carinus held Caesarian imperium, by which he was able to conduct war in the West. See my writings, p. 189, *Cenotaphium Pisanorum*. Since Constantius and Galerius were called Caesars as future commanders of wars, they likewise assumed proconsular imperium together with the name Caesar. Hence in very many rescripts of the Code of Justinian, the Augusti Diocletian and Maximian and the Caesars are named in the headings of laws, namely on account of proconsular imperium outside the city. Thus under Valerian and Gallienus, Caesar Valerian is also placed at the head of rescripts there, as is Philip Caesar with his father Augustus.

But in the same Code, wherever rescripts of the Deified Brothers are cited, Marcus Aurelius Caesar is never added. From this I infer that, while Antoninus Pius was alive, he was merely Caesar. See Code II, titles 1, 13, and 38; Code VI, title 26. Nor is Commodus named together with his father Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus in Code III, title 31; Code V, title 25; Code VI, title 26. I therefore think that some Augusti transferred proconsular imperium to their Caesars, while others shared with sons, whether by nature or adoption, a Caesarian dignity wholly bare of imperium.

But I submit all this for examination by your singular learning, with the intention that I am ready to go over to whatever opinion you may hold; for you are a senator and, in my eyes, hold the first consular opinion, as they once said. Farewell, most learned sir, glory and safeguard of letters in Belgium. Written at Florence, on the tenth day before the Kalends of December, 1688.

The most humble and devoted servant  
of Your Most Illustrious Lordship.

These things that illustrious man in learning sent to me. If they please you, reader, as much as they please me, they will certainly please you greatly. Farewell.

[Col. 0471]

NOTES ON LACTANTIUS.

[Col. 0471A] *On the Deaths of the Persecutors.* From the examples noted by Baluze and Columbus, it is sufficiently clear that the ancients frequently used *deaths* in the plural. Manilius speaks no differently, I.887:

> The office of tears had ceased, and funerals were lacking  
> for deaths, and tears.

Seneca, *Suasoriae*, at the end: “Juba and Petreius met in mutual wounds and lent deaths at interest.” To these should be added Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* II.675.

Moreover, I too should very much like what Columbus desired: that the little work of John of Salisbury, which he himself testifies in the *Nugae Curialium* to have entitled *On the End of Tyrants*, might come into public view. For I think that he mentioned the deaths and ends of Diocletian, Maximian, and other tyrants and fighters against God (*θεομάχων*). Since he was accustomed to read ancient authors, and lived in the twelfth century, when a much greater abundance of manuscripts survived, he may perhaps have consulted this very little work of Lactantius. The credit for discovering and publishing this work is reserved for the English or the French, since he spent his life in both kingdoms. Men eminent in learning should certainly leave no stone unturned so that this work of John of Salisbury may at last come to light. According to Bale, it is entitled *On the Evil End of Tyrants*. Among the manuscripts of the Bodleian Library his *Nero* is mentioned; Graevius judged that it was the same little work, entitled *Nero* after the first and most savage tyrant and persecutor, and *On the End of Tyrants* from its subject. That mode of entitling books is ancient, as is clear from Cicero and Varro.

CHAPTER ONE.

To all these will be added. Unless I am mistaken, the devil is meant, who is the chief adversary and enemy of the faithful, and whom he says will at last also be conquered, just as his instruments, the persecutors, were overcome: ch. 14: “For having been subjected nine times to tortures and various torments, nine times you conquered the ADVERSARY by glorious confession” [Col. 0471C]; shortly afterwards, repeating the same thought, he calls him Zabulus, or the devil: “In nine battles you vanquished Zabulus with his attendants,” that is, the persecutors. And although Maxentius in ch. 43 is said to be one among the adversaries of God, yet he and all the other persecutors had been removed by the time Lactantius wrote these things; hence ch. 50: “In this way God conquered all the persecutors of his name, so that neither stock nor root of theirs remained.” Yet to all these the adversary is added, that is, the devil; as is also indicated at the end of this little work: “That he may ward off from his people all the snares and assaults of the devil, and preserve the flourishing churches in perpetual peace.” If this happens, the devil has certainly been conquered and is added to the other adversaries who have been trampled down. Thus the devil is said to prepare contests for the martyrs. In the *Passion of Saints Perpetua and Felicitas*: “But for the young women the devil prepared an exceedingly fierce cow, procured contrary to custom for this purpose, vying even through the beast against their sex.” The Greeks similarly call this adversary ἀντικείμενον, “the opposing one,” as Chrysostom, on chapter XII of the Second Epistle to the Corinthians [Col. 0471D], citing 3 Kings IV, explains οὐκ ἦν Σατὰν ἐν ἡμέραις αὐτοῦ, “there was no Satan in his days,” as τουτέστιν ἀντικείμενος, “that is, no adversary.” So too ὁ ἀντικείμενος in the Epistle to the Thessalonians is God’s adversary, or Antichrist, who continually and perpetually attacks God.

**Peace having been restored throughout the world.** They spoke elegantly in this way, because wars were compared, as is well known, with storms and tempests. Hence on a coin of Antoninus in Tristan, vol. I, p. 576: *TRANQUILLITAS AUG.*—“the Tranquillity of Augustus”—indicating that Antoninus, through his prudence and courage, had given peace and tranquillity to the Roman Empire. [Col. 0472A] On other coins occurs *SERENA TRANQ.*, “serene tranquillity”; and accordingly Lactantius shortly afterwards calls peace pleasant and serene.

**The temple of God, which had been overthrown by the impious.** The most learned Baluzius thinks that the temple at Nicomedia is meant, which was destroyed by Diocletian and Maximian, as appears from ch. 13. But I think that Christian religion in general, or Christians formerly harassed by bitter persecution and now restored through Constantine to peace and repose, should be understood. Thus nothing immediately follows about constructing a building, as would certainly have been necessary; rather, it concerns minds gladdened by pleasant and serene peace. That this refers to what precedes is abundantly clear from the particle *enim*, “for.” Nor does what follows seem to me to require another interpretation: “Those who had overthrown the holy temple fell by a greater ruin; those who had tortured the righteous.” For this must in general be referred to the persecutors, who certainly had not all ordered the Nicomedian temple to be destroyed. Indeed, at the beginning of the chapter he calls that temple—that is, the congregation of believers—the Church: “Peace having been restored throughout the world, the Church lately laid low rises again” [Col. 0472B]; although I do not overlook that in ch. 12 he uses the same word for a meeting-house.

Moreover, the Fathers used to call the sanctuaries of pagan gods *temples*, and the places in which Christians assembled *churches*, or *meeting-houses*, etc. Lactantius himself does so in chs. 5, 15, 35, and 36; this is also clear from the letter of the emperor Aurelian in Vopiscus, and has been sufficiently demonstrated by men of outstanding learning. And just as believers in the New Covenant are called ναὸς Θεοῦ, “the temple of God,” so the Latin Fathers called them the holy, faithful, steadfast, heavenly temple of God. Lactantius himself does this in chs. 2 and 15, and also in *Divine Institutes* IV.25: “Complaining that profane persons were taking part in sacred rites, they drove their rulers into frenzy, so that they might storm the temple of God.” Here I think Lactantius refers in no way to the Christian temple at Nicomedia, but to the faithful whom they tried to assault throughout the Roman Empire. And this expression can aptly be used not of the destroyed meeting-house, though soldiers had set their hands to the work, but of Christians afflicted by persecution. [Col. 0472C] Thus in *Institutes* V.2, the addition of *Dei*, “of God,” seems to indicate that believers are to be understood there too, just as in ch. 33 below, since the edict which shortly follows concerns all Christians.

**They provided for humankind.** Relevant here are coins inscribed *PROVIDENTIA AUG.*, “the Providence of Augustus,” and *SAPIENTIA PROVIDENTISSIMI PRINCIPIS*, “the Wisdom of the Most Provident Prince.” By *humankind* it is customary to understand the Roman Empire; hence on these same coins occurs *SALUS GENERIS HUMANI*, “the Safety of Humankind.”

**Now appeased.** I had thought that *Deus*, “God,” ought to be placed after *placatus*, “appeased,” and that Lactantius had used *jacentes et afflictos servorum*—“prostrate and afflicted of [his] servants”—for “wretched and afflicted servants.” But Columbus’s reading *precibus* (“prayers”) now does not displease me; it also occurred to learned Englishmen.

**Concerning whose end.** The words which have fallen out may perhaps be supplied thus: “Concerning the end of the impious, it pleased [me] to bear witness, so that all who were far removed, or who should come after us, might know to what extent God Most High displayed his power and majesty in destroying and annihilating the enemies of his name.” Shortly afterwards, after *auctores*, “authors,” I think *tantorum scelerum*, “of such great crimes,” or *persecutionis*, “of the persecution,” has fallen out. [Col. 0472D] The English supply the passage somewhat differently, as does Columbus; if anyone prefers their conjectures to mine, I shall not take it ill.

## CHAPTER II

**He was crucified.** That is, fastened to a cross, as Columbus shows from Lactantius’s *Institutes*; nor did Hegesippus speak differently, book XVIII: “Innumerable persons were captured; nearly five hundred were crucified each day.”

**Under the two Gemini.** How differently others think is well known; see Scaliger, Petavius, Bucherius, Onuphrius, Langius, Christmann, Thomas Lydiat, and others. [Col. 0473A]

**A storm-cloud.** He says more than Holy Scripture does; for there is only mention of νεφέλης, “a cloud,” and the ascension itself is expressed by ἀνελήφθη εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν, “he was taken up into heaven.” This mode of expression entirely excludes a storm and teaches that the Lord Jesus Christ was taken peacefully into heaven.

**Peter comes to Rome.** Lactantius also relates this in *Institutes* IV.21. The miracles undoubtedly concern the story told about Simon Magus, narrated by Arnobius and others.

**And steadfast.** That is, firm and enduring. Thus on coins occur *TELLUS*, or *TERRA STABILITA*, in Erizzo, p. 386; by this the emperors undoubtedly signify that they had given lasting and firm peace to the world.

**From the worship of idols.** Lactantius speaks here as a Christian; for pagans said “the worship of the gods.” An inscription in Gruter reads:

> DIOCLETIAN. CAES. AUG. GALERIO. IN ORIENTE. ADOPT. SUPERSTITIONE. CHRIST. VBIQ. DELETA. ET. CULTU. DEOR. PROPAGATO.

“Diocletian Caesar Augustus [to] Galerius, adopted in the East: Christian superstition having everywhere been destroyed and the worship of the gods promoted.” [Col. 0473B]

And, as is abundantly clear from innumerable Greek and Latin authors, as well as martyrologies and acts of the martyrs, pagans designated statues representing gods by the names of the gods themselves.

**To a new religion.** This too was continually objected to Christians, as appears abundantly from Arnobius, book I, p. 34; book II, pp. 92, 93, and 94; and others. Hence the pagan Asclepiades in Prudentius, Hymn 10, *Peristephanon*, v. 580, first celebrates ancient rites and then reproaches Christians with a novel doctrine. Tristan, following Baronius, vol. I, p. 698, understands by the “boys and girls of new men” in Capitolinus’s *Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher* the children of Christians; though I think Casaubon and Salmasius give a truer account. [Col. 0473C]

**First of all.** All narrate this with one voice. Although Christians seem to have been treated badly by Claudius, just as the Jews were—for in the earliest period of the nascent Church Christians too were included under that name, as is elegantly shown by Sulpicius Severus II.99—nevertheless that disturbance was not counted among the persecutions. Blessed Luke in the Acts of the Apostles relates that Claudius ordered the Jews to leave Rome; and Suetonius speaks thus of the same matter, ch. 24: “He expelled from Rome the Jews, who were continually rioting at the instigation of Chrestus.” By *Chrestus* he undoubtedly means Christ our Lord; they called him so because Chrestus was a common Roman name, as is clear from inscriptions and Cicero, *Letters to Friends* II.8. I think the pagans thus named our Lord through error regarding the name, rather than as an insult, though learned men think otherwise. For it does not seem to me any insult to call someone *Chrestus*, that is, good, kind, gracious, though the pagans erred greatly when they thought this was our Savior’s name. [Col. 0473D]

But Christ could not have incited the Jews, since he was received into heaven under Tiberius. Rather, I think the matter must be interpreted thus: some Jews said that our Christ was the Messiah, while others denied it; and hence disturbances arose among them, both privately and publicly. Yet Claudius did nothing other than expel them all from Rome; and at that time Christians too undoubtedly shared the same fate. Since they were compelled only to change their place of residence, while retaining their property and religion, Claudius was not numbered among the persecutors.

**So evil a beast.** Lactantius most deservedly calls Nero, Diocletian, and the other persecutors by this name, as Baluzius observed. See chs. 4, 9, 16, 25, 32, and 39, where one finds now “execrable animal,” now “wicked [animal],” now “evil beast.” The Latin Pacatus calls Maximus a raging beast; Livineius there observes similar expressions from Rutilius and Seneca. Nor do Livy, XXXIV and XXXIX; Cicero, *On Duties* I and III; Lucian, pp. 1015, 1016, 200, and 206, Bourdelot edition; Dio Cassius, end of book LXXVII; Arnobius V, p. 115; and Asterius, Homily 1, speak differently concerning tyrants and impious rulers. To these may be added Rittershusius, *Sacred Readings* IV.9; and in the Passion of Seraphia, Helpidius is called a most rabid dog.

For sometimes they were not satisfied to apply the general designation of beast or animal, but cast upon foul persons whatever animal seemed most fitting, or was thought fitting, to them. Thus Lycophron, p. 20, calls Helen a κύνα, “bitch,” on account of her shamelessness; and at p. 170, Clytemnestra a δράκαινα διψάς, “thirsty she-dragon.” Meursius, on Lycophron, p. 125, observed that persons endowed with savage and harsh dispositions were called ὄφεις, “serpents,” δράκοντες, “dragons,” and scorpions. Thus Asterius, p. 72, does not hesitate to call an adulteress an ἀσπίς καὶ ἔχιδνα, “asp and viper”; and in Livy XXXIX.11 Hispala, a woman insufficiently modest, is called an *ex(c)etra*, a poisonous serpent. Thus Julian, Epistle 23, calls Constantine a πολυκέφαλος ὕδρα, “many-headed hydra”; from which one may clearly perceive [Col. 0474B] with what hatred that Apostate persecuted Christians.

**The coming . . . sacrilege.** I think this can be supplied thus: “which it is sacrilege to believe.” Just as they declare that two prophets, translated alive, will precede the holy and everlasting beginning of Christ in the last age, when he begins to descend, so too they think Nero will come, who is to be the forerunner of the devil. Lactantius rightly says first that it is sacrilege to believe Nero will return and precede the coming of Antichrist; and shortly before he calls certain persons mad. Hence it is clear that our author, as Baluzius did not fail to observe, does not accept the opinion of those who thought Nero had not died but was still alive and would come before the end of the age, either himself to be Antichrist or to rage in the West at the same time as Antichrist in the East. More on this may be seen in Casaubon on Suetonius.

Commodianus, *Instructions* 41, sings that Nero will return from hell; and his verses should be supplied here [Col. 0474C], because that little work is extremely rare and because they also mention Elijah’s coming:

> Isaiah said: “This is the man who shakes the world  
> And so many kings, under whom the earth shall become desolate.  
> Hear, because the prophet foretold concerning him.  
> I have invented nothing, but have spoken without care [i.e. plainly].  
> Then indeed the world ends, when he appears;  
> He himself will divide the world among three rulers.  
> But when Nero has been raised from hell,  
> Elijah will come first to mark the beloved.  
> Things which the region of Africa and the whole northern nation—  
> For seven years the earth shall tremble on every side—  
> But Elijah shall hold half the time, Nero the other half.  
> Then Babylon the harlot, reduced to ashes,  
> Thereupon the Latin victor shall proceed to Jerusalem.  
> Then he will say: ‘I am the Christ whom you have always prayed for.’”

By the two prophets translated alive, Enoch and Elijah are meant, as is clear from John of Damascus, *On the Orthodox Faith* IV.27; although some mention only Elijah as destined to return, as Commodianus too does, as appears from the cited verses. [Col. 0474D] Moreover, Lactantius seems to look to Christ’s millennial kingdom, on which see also *Institutes* VII, end of ch. 1, and ch. 14, and elsewhere in the *Divine Institutes*; Commodianus may be added.

As in this place he says Christ comes by descending, so he speaks no differently of his birth in *Institutes* IV.10: “That, as the end of the age drew near, it would be necessary for the Son of God to descend to earth.” The Greeks call this καταβαίνειν, “to descend,” and Jupiter Καταβάτης, “the Descending One,” occurs on coins. With that title the Athenians, prone to flattery, honored Demetrius Poliorcetes, as though Jupiter, transformed into him, had descended to earth.

In my judgment Tristan, vol. II, p. 571, not cautiously enough explains this as Jupiter hurling a thunderbolt down to earth. For although Jupiter hurling thunder, and when it rains, may be called καταβαίνειν and “descending”; although the thunderbolt itself, or σκηπτός, is called by Lycophron, p. 67, καταιβάτης, “descending”; and although, at p. 199, Ζεὺς καταιβάτης is said to burn enemies’ houses with lightning; although places struck by lightning were consecrated to Jupiter, according to the author of the *Great Etymologicum*, s.v. Ἐνηλύσια, and Pollux, book IX, ch. 5—nevertheless I think Demetrius was so called because flatterers wished to appear persuaded that he himself was Jupiter. Thus Jupiter too is said to descend when it rains. Virgil, *Georgics* II.324:

> Then the almighty father, in fruitful rains,  
> Descends widely from heaven into the lap of his spouse.

Perhaps this mythology is represented on a coin of Antoninus Pius in Seguinus, p. 197, in which Jupiter is suspended in the air, holding a winged thunderbolt in one hand and pouring from a cornucopia with the other either dew or rain.

## CHAPTER III

**Until impious hands.** The Vulgate translator of Isaiah XIV.26: “And this is the hand stretched out over all nations.” Lactantius, in the following chapter: “He stretched impious hands against God.” [Col. 0475B] These expressions signify nothing else than attacking someone. In a Latin inscription in Gruter I.830, Procope is said to have raised his hand against God because he killed an innocent person, with an image of two raised hands added. For she testifies that she died innocent and accuses God of cruelty, because she was so quickly removed from human affairs.

**Killed at home. Also in memory.** I almost distinguish the words thus: “Killed. At home also,” that is, at Rome, by decree of the Senate, as appears from what follows and from Suetonius. On the practice of condemning someone’s memory, see Lipsius on Tacitus, *Annals* VI, and Rad. Fornerius, *Everyday Matters* II.17–18. Related to this is that the coins of such emperors were also destroyed and melted down, as Dio says happened after Caligula’s death; or that they were of no value, as Arrian teaches concerning Nero in *Epictetus* IV.5. But how much better for good rulers to possess the ἀγαθὴ μνήμη, “good memory,” which Themistius ascribes to them in his ninth Oration!

If this distinction is not to be admitted, Lactantius undoubtedly means by *domi*, “at home,” that Domitian was killed in his palace, and by his own people, as is clear from Suetonius, ch. 17; and this now seems preferable to me. [Col. 0475C]

**To its former state.** That Lactantius thinks this was done under Nerva, not while Domitian was still alive, I believe is sufficiently clear from the preceding words, “the acts of the tyrant having therefore been annulled”; for that certainly could not happen until after Domitian’s death. Yet he did not persecute the Church for long. Indeed, restored to a better mind, he ceased persecuting Christians and recalled exiles, as is not obscurely evident from Tertullian: “Domitian too had attempted it, a portion of Nero in cruelty; but since he was also human, he easily checked what he had begun, even restoring those whom he had banished.” Hegesippus in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* III.20, reports similar things.

## CHAPTER IV

**The execrable animal Decius.** If martyrologies deserve credit, Christians nevertheless stood nearest to him: for Trofonia, or Tryphonia, or Tryphaena, wife of his son Caesar, whose commemoration is celebrated in the recently published German Martyrology on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November [18 October], and Cyrilla, daughter of that same Caesar, were initiated into the same sacred rites, according to Ado in the *Martyrology*, pp. 159, 174, and 178. But books of this sort must be read with careful caution. [Col. 0475D]

**For after him arose the execrable animal Decius.** Hardly any passage in this entire little work is equally noteworthy. For from it we learn that Christians did not suffer persecution in the times of Nerva, Trajan, the Antonines, and so forth, through imperial edicts promulgated and posted, and thus by the emperors’ own command. Hence in the preceding chapter Lactantius calls them good princes, which he certainly would not have done if the Christian cause had sustained from them as much harm as the martyrologies claim. It is especially worthy of note that Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* II.669, joins the Decian persecution to the Neronian, omitting not only the persecutions attributed to the Antonines and other good princes, but even that in which Domitian raged against the pious. [Col. 0476A]

> At his instigation Nero first, having murdered his mother,  
> Drank apostolic blood and polluted me with the slaughter of the pious,  
> And cruelly branded me with his own crime.  
> After him Decius, reveling amid opened throats,  
> Soon fed his insane madness; and a thirst  
> Like that of many burned within him.

Prudentius undoubtedly had his own reasons for preferring to veil Domitian’s cruelty in silence rather than recount it. That persecution did not last long, and he changed his purpose for the better. For he began to rage against Christians in the fourteenth year of his reign; and since he was killed in the fifteenth, he could certainly not have done this for many years. This will appear more clearly from Tertullian’s testimony that he easily checked what he had begun, even restoring those whom he had banished. Nor should it be omitted that Tertullian uses the word *tentaverat*, “had attempted”: “Domitian had attempted [it]”; [Col. 0476B] and that Lactantius in the preceding chapter writes that Domitian had long sat upon the necks of his subjects and had ruled securely until he stretched impious hands against the Lord, and that he was delivered into the hands of his enemies when he was incited to persecute the righteous people. Such modes of expression abundantly indicate that Domitian stirred up persecution at the end of his reign. Indeed, the word *tentare*, “attempt,” seems somewhat to soften the matter and indicate that it was only begun.

Furthermore, Prudentius speaks of the tortures and killings with which Nero and Decius raged against Christians. But Domitian put to death only those who said that they were descended from Judah and related to Christ; the rest he banished, as is not obscurely clear from Eusebius III.20. Hence he too is said by Tertullian to have restored those whom he had banished; and Nerva permitted those who had been ἀδίκως ἐξεληλαμένοι, “unjustly driven out,” to return to their country.

Henry Dodwell, Dissertation XI on Cyprian, expends much effort in establishing the small number of martyrs; following Lactantius, he rejects the persecutions attributed to Hadrian and the Antonines. John Mabillon, in his *Italian Journey*, tries to refute his opinion by means of Prudentius, Hymn XI, *Peristephanon*, where he celebrates the countless ashes of martyrs, and by two inscriptions. The first testifies that a certain Alexander suffered martyrdom under Antoninus; the second, that Marcus, a young man and military commander, suffered martyrdom under Hadrian. But even if these inscriptions were genuine—something others may perhaps judge differently—two martyrs could not greatly increase their number, nor would they prove that Hadrian and Antoninus put to death at Rome as many Christians as are recalled in the martyrologies. [Col. 0476C] Further, the question is not whether some Christians suffered under them at Rome or in the provinces—for harsher prefects or governors, more devoted to pagan superstition, could have done this—but whether those good emperors ordered such things. This I certainly find difficult to believe. Finally, Prudentius wrote after the very severe persecutions of Diocletian and others, through whom more persons certainly suffered martyrdom at Rome; and poets must be allowed something when they seek to heighten a matter.

**For he set out against the Carpi.** Philip, who ruled before Decius, fought them and, if coins are to be trusted, defeated them; for a bronze coin bearing his portrait, according to the distinguished Spanheim, is inscribed *VICTORIAE CARPICAE*, “Carpian Victories.” But either they had not been properly subdued or they rebelled, since Decius set out against them; and on his coin in Tristan, vol. II, p. 578, one reads *VICTORIA CARPICA VOTIS X*, “Carpian Victory, [for] Ten-Year Vows.” From the vowed decennial vows it is quite clearly apparent that in the first year of his reign Decius fought successfully against the Carpi; and he seems to have waged war for the entire two years against the Carpi and other barbarians.

Indeed, Zosimus I.2 testifies that, having been raised to the imperial power, he compelled the enemy to retreat to the bank of the Tanais and expelled them from Moesia and Dacia, which they had occupied. Hence one undoubtedly sees on his coins *DACIA CAPTA*, “Dacia Captured,” and *DACIA FELIX*, “Prosperous Dacia.” Yet the Carpi did not remain quiet: Lactantius and Zosimus, who gives a fuller account, testify that Decius was slain by them. Aurelian, having defeated the same people, was called Carpicus, as Vopiscus relates. Thereafter Diocletian removed them from their ancient seats and resettled them in Pannonia, according to Ammianus Marcellinus XXVIII.1, Jerome, *Chronicle*, p. 178, Eutropius IX.15, Aurelius Victor 39, and others.

From them, without doubt, the village of the Carpi in Moesia received its name; Ammianus mentions it at XXVII.5, where Valesius notes that the Carpi were defeated by Galerius and, after their surrender, were all transferred to Roman soil under the consuls Tuscus and Anullinus. And for his defeat of the Carpi, Galerius is called δὶς Καρπῶν μέγιστος, “twice greatest victor over the Carpi,” in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VIII.17. On this occasion I propose to learned persons for elucidation the cities called Carpiae, mentioned by Menander Rhetor, book I, ch. 15, *On the Epideictic Genre*: [Col. 0477A] Τοῦ δὲ ἀναγκαίου, ὡς κατὰ τὰς πόλεις τὰς κατὰ τὸν ποταμὸν ὑπὲρ Ῥωμαίων κατοικισθείσας τὰς καλουμένας Καρπίας, ὡς μὴ διαβαίνοντες οἱ βάρβαροι κακουργεῖν.

“And concerning what was necessary: as regards the cities along the river, founded by the Romans and called Carpiae, [this was done] so that the barbarians might not cross over and ravage.” Natalis Comes renders the Greek: “Concerning what was necessary, namely the cities built by the Romans along the river, called Carpiae, so that barbarians crossing over might not harass [the country].” Let others investigate what these cities were, and whether they were those called Carpiae or Carpicae, which the Romans built on the bank of the Danube against the incursions of the Carpi. If so, the Romans must initially have feared these barbarians greatly. Ptolemy places a town, Κάρπιν, Carpin, on the Danube.

**Not even burial.** Lactantius also counts this among the punishments inflicted on Decius. It is well known that pagans greatly desired the burial of corpses or remains because they believed that the souls of the unburied did not rest and were not received by the gods above or below. Christians also, although Augustine says it makes no difference whether one decays in the ground or elsewhere, were very concerned with burial; pagan judges often denied it to martyrs, as is abundantly clear from their histories. Thus it is not surprising that Lactantius notes this, especially in the case of an emperor, for whom otherwise perhaps a mausoleum would have been erected.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0477C]

**He said that that was true.** These words are entirely sound, and nothing is to be supplied, as a learned man thought. Romans, of course, used to paint emperors on walls or panels trampling the necks and backs of conquered enemies and kings. Coins are certainly indisputable witnesses of this custom; and an elegant passage of Gregory Nazianzen, *Invective I against Julian*, teaches that emperors were so depicted. The king of the Persians therefore says that the Roman paintings, in which the emperor trampled the necks of kings—and perhaps of Sapor himself—were fictitious and imaginary; but that it was true that he trampled Valerian’s back.

To understand this passage clearly, it must be noted that the saddles of the ancients lacked stirrups, the instruments which we now use in mounting horses and in which riders in some manner stand. Hence they mounted horses either by a leap, or were lifted up and placed upon them with the assistance of others. Virgil, *Aeneid* XII.287: [Col. 0477D]

> Others rein in the chariots, or by a leap  
> Throw their bodies up upon the horses, and stand by with drawn swords.

Even in Vegetius’s time, as appears from book I, ch. 18, “recruits learned not only to leap up and down from the right side, but also from the left.” The *desultores* of Livy and others, nor the paired horses of Festus, invoked by Stewechius, have any relevance to this.

Thus those who dismounted from horses were said *equis delabi*, “to glide down from horses,” *desilire*, “to leap down,” and *defluere*, “to flow down,” as is clear from Justin I.10, Virgil, *Aeneid* XI.501, and Furius in Macrobius, *Saturnalia* VI.14. The Greeks likewise used ἀποπηδᾷν in the same sense, that is, “to leap down,” as appears from Themistius, Oration 6. I think *desilire* is to free oneself from the horse with a single leap; *defluere*, however, is to descend slowly, as it were across the horse’s body. Thus Furius spoke of a wounded man; Livy does the same in book II: “The dying Roman, not at all hindered by the rider’s wound, with his arms slipping over his body, flowed down to the ground.” Hence Virgil, by *desilire*, may seem to ascribe greater agility to Camilla than to her troop, which he says *defluxisse*, “glided down.” [Col. 0478A]

Others, and more distinguished persons, were lifted onto horses by attendants. Livy VI.24: “When Camillus, lifted onto his horse by the bystanders, had swiftly been brought to the supporting troops, he said: ‘Soldiers, this is the battle you demanded.’” They had *stratores*, so called from grooming or preparing horses, who lifted their masters onto them. Spartianus, *Caracalla* IV: “Finally, while his STRATOR was lifting him, [the assassin] pierced his side with a dagger.” Ammianus Marcellinus XXXVIII: “When the horse he had mounted did not lift him up, raising its forefeet unusually high, he ordered the right hand of the soldier STRATOR to be cut off.” Observe here that soldiers rendered this service to emperors, for he speaks of Valentinian. So in XXII.1, concerning Julian: “The soldier who raised him with his right hand as he was about to mount the horse slipped.”

In an inscription in Gruter, no. 7, ch. 1, appears: *MATERNIUS PERLETUS, SOLDIER OF LEGION VII, PRIMA PIA FIDELIS, STRATOR*; and in no. 2.389: *SILIUS HOSPES, HASTATUS OF THE TENTH GEMINA LEGION, HIS STRATOR*, or [the strator] of the governor Titus Claudius Candidus. I do not know whether the term occurs in the same sense in an inscription in Spon, *Miscellanea*, p. 233:

> DIOMEDES AP. STRATOR FAUSTAE HEDIAE.

For the learned man explains it as “the road-builder of the Appian [Way],” who paved that road and repaired its surface where it failed. [Col. 0478B] If this Diomedes lifted Fausta Hedia onto a horse, we would have striking proof that women too had their own *stratores*. But, to tell the truth, I prefer the interpretation “road-builder of the Appian Way,” who perhaps preserved the memory of his wife; and thus Virgil uses *strata*, and Suetonius *stratura viarum*, “road-paving.”

Among the Greeks, a man who performed the same service for those mounting a horse was called an ἀναβολεύς; Suidas explains him as ὁ ἐπὶ τὸν ἵππον ἀνάγων, “one who lifts [a person] onto a horse.” He confirms this with an example taken from some unknown author: ὁ δὲ βασιλεὺς τὸν ἀναβολέα προσκαλεσάμενος, καὶ ταχέως ἀναβὰς ἐπὶ τὸν ἵππον, ᾔτησε πιεῖν· “The king, summoning the *anaboleus*, and quickly mounting the horse, asked for a drink.” Nor did Plutarch speak differently in his *Crassus*: “When a horse with golden reins was brought to Crassus, καὶ οἱ ἀναβολεῖς αὑτὸν ἀράμενοι παρεβίβασαν, the attendants lifted him up and placed him upon it.” From this it is likewise clear that several persons sometimes performed this office together for one and the same person.

The Persians too, as is clear from Xenophon’s account of Tiribazus in book IV and from his *Hipparchicus*, p. 956, did not know stirrups and had servant-attendants who lifted riders. From this I am inclined to infer that *stratores*, still unknown to the Greeks at that time, and the custom itself, came from the Persians. Xenophon writes that younger horsemen should learn to leap onto horses; but for those advanced in age it would be very useful τὸν περσικὸν τρόπον ἀναβάλλεσθαι ὑπ᾽ ἀλλήλων, “to be lifted up by one another in the Persian fashion.” Magius showed in his *Miscellanies* that the Scythians did not use them.

Therefore, in order to mount his horse, Sapor used not *stratores* but Valerian, who did not even perform the office of a *strator* for him, but rather served as a stirrup; for he placed his feet on Valerian’s back, as the distinguished Salmasius rightly observes on the *Historia Augusta*. [Col. 0478D] The author of the *Passion of Saint Pontius* in Baluzius did not fail to note this: “Valerian, namely, emperor, taken captive by Sapor king of the Persians, received, not by the sword but by mockery, a deserved recompense for his deeds throughout all the days of his life: whenever King Sapor wished to mount a horse, he set his foot not in Valerian’s hands—behold the office of a *strator*—but upon his bent back and neck, where he served as a stirrup, and so placed his limbs upon the horse.” Hugo of Fleury’s *Chronicle* reports similarly: “At last Valerian himself, deprived of God’s protection, was captured by Sapor king of the Persians and grew old in shameful servitude among him; and as long as he lived he constantly bore this punishment of an infamous office: crouching upon the ground, he raised the king who was about to mount, not with his hand but with his back.”

Since the use of stirrups was unknown to the ancients, the coin of Alexander the Great shown by Laurenberg in *Ancient Greece* is certainly either spurious or incorrectly illustrated, because it depicts his feet placed in such instruments. An exactly similar coin appears in Lazius, book I of *Greece*, but stirrups do not hang from the horse’s sides. [Col. 0479A]

Spon, vol. II, p. 386, therefore rightly rejects the saddle or horse-cloth which the Helvetians attribute to Julius Caesar. Yet the origin of these instruments should be investigated. Carolus Pagius, p. 333, makes them very recent indeed. Scaliger likewise declares them a novelty and, for this reason, judges a very large silver coin of the emperor Constantine to be modern. Others, by contrast, including Magius, contend that the practice is ancient, though not extremely ancient; they cite an ancient inscription, whose ending is:

> CASU. DESILIENS. PES. HAESIT. STAPIAE. TRACTUS INTERII. IN. REM. TUAM. MATURE. PROPERA. VALE.

“By chance, while dismounting, my foot caught in the stirrup; dragged along, I died. Hasten quickly to your own affairs. Farewell.”

[Col. 0479B] But first, nothing is established concerning the age of this monument; secondly, various considerations suggest that it is either of the latest period or a forgery. Hence Janus Gruter also included it among spurious inscriptions. Yet it cannot be denied that this implement is mentioned by Eustathius, who flourished in the time of Manuel Comnenus, about A.D. 1150, and likewise under Alexius Comnenus and Andronicus, in his commentary on the *Odyssey*: “*Anaballein* [ἀναβάλλειν] also means to raise someone onto a horse, to make him mounted; whence *anaboleus* [ἀναβολεύς] signifies not only the iron into which some put their feet in becoming mounted, but also a person who assists in such a task.” That is: “ἀναβάλλειν means to lift onto a horse and make a rider sit upon it; hence ἀναβολεύς denotes not only the iron into which some place their feet in mounting their horses, but also the man who serves for the same purpose.”

Before Eustathius, Suidas, who lived in the time of the earlier Alexius Comnenus, about A.D. 1080, mentions the same implement: “ἀναβολεύς: also what the Romans call a *skala* [σκάλα], ladder.” He seeks to establish this by adducing testimony [Col. 0479C] from an anonymous author: “But Massias, when old, mounted his horse without an *anaboleus* [ἀναβολεύς].” Salmasius, in his *Letter on the Cross*, and Reinesius, *Various Readings*, III.2, rightly emend this to *Massanissas* [Μασσανίσσας], i.e. Masinissa. Salmasius understands by *anaboleus* not a ladder but a groom (*strator*), who offered his hand to his master mounting a horse. The distinguished scholar thinks this perhaps a fragment of Polybius; Reinesius believes that Suidas drew this expression from it. But Lipsius rightly observes that its author is Appian, since in his *Punic Wars*, p. 107 of the latest edition, he speaks thus of Masinissa: “He was of great and robust body even into old age [ἐς γῆρας πολύ]; until death he took part in battles, and mounted a horse without an *anaboleus* [ἵππου δὲ χωρὶς ἀναβολέως ἐπέβαινε]”—that is, he mounted a horse without a groom (most badly rendered “without saddle-cloths”).

Thus, although ladders were in use by some in the time of Suidas, they are in no way to be sought in the quoted words, since in earlier times they were wholly unknown. The Emperor Leo, surnamed the Philosopher, who assumed the empire upon the death of his father Basil the Macedonian in 886, also mentions these implements in *Tactics*, I.6: “for the saddles, two iron ladders” [εἰς δὲ τὰς σέλλας δύο σκάλας σιδηρᾶς]. Indeed, before him Maurice, who is said to have lived in A.D. 491, uses the same words in book I, chapter 2 of his *Tactics*. Even in the age of St Jerome, who flourished in 408, these ladders seem to have been in use. For, according to Magius, Jerome says in his Letters: “If memory does not fail me, when he received certain letters and was about to mount a beast of burden, he already had his foot in the *bistapia*.” Indeed Vossius, *On the Latin Language*, I.7, relying on the ancient inscription previously cited by me, judges that their use may perhaps have been somewhat earlier; but, from what I have observed, it is clear that this is a weak argument.

From these facts it will certainly be clear that Hugo, *On Equestrian Warfare*, I.5, wrongly thinks that no mention of this implement survives except in Eustathius, the interpreter of Homer. It should, however, be carefully noted that Eustathius says that some used this iron; and the eminent Salmasius believes that, in the time of Emperor Leo, riders did not have their feet placed in these iron ladders [Col. 0480A] while riding. Rather, they served only for mounting the horse, after which they were drawn up and stored under the saddle. If that is true, riders were already riding without these ladders in Leo’s time, and the use of our stirrups was still unknown—though Jerome’s *bistapia* and Leo’s “two iron ladders” (for one would have sufficed for a person mounting) seem to acknowledge them.

For the prefix *bi-* in *bistapia* undoubtedly denotes the dual number, as in other compounds. Thus in Prudentius, *Hymn* 12, a *bifestus dies* is a day sacred to two apostles, Paul and Peter; *bipalium* in Varro, *On Agriculture*, I.24; *bicinium*, where two sing; *bilorus*, *biblex*; and *bisellium*, elucidated by Chimentelius, which also occurs in the school dialogue published with glosses by Vulcanius: “Give him seats, chairs, a bench, a *bisellium*” [Δότε ᾧδε θρόνους, δίφρους, βάθρον, διέδραν]. And in the Notes of Tiro, p. 164: “Chair, chair-maker, couch-feast, double-seat, bench-seat, two-day feast, three-day feast,” where read “double couch, triple couch” (*biclinium, triclinium*).

Be that as it may, the certain origin of this practice can scarcely be drawn from darkness into light. Casaubon, on Athenaeus VI.16, writes that he has shown elsewhere that the most ancient Rabbis mention stirrups. And if the coin published by Tristan is genuine and is to be assigned to Chosroes, king of the Persians and contemporary of Justinian, then this custom may perhaps be traced to the Persians. For Chosroes sits on horseback in the guise of the Sun—Persian kings called themselves brothers of the Sun and Moon—adorned with rays; and his feet rest in stirrups, as is evident from the cast.

But since not everyone had grooms, C. Gracchus, in the free Republic, in order to provide for the convenience of the common people and win the goodwill of the Italians, paved many roads and set up stone columns to indicate the mile-markers: “He also placed other stones, set a little distance apart from one another, on both sides of the road, so that those who had horses might easily mount them without needing *anaboleis* [ἀναβολεῖς].” [Col. 0480B] That is, “He placed other stones, spaced a little apart, on either side of the road, so that those who had horses could readily mount them without the assistance of grooms,” as Plutarch testifies in his *Life*. Since ladders were not then in use, there is certainly no reason why Lipsius should hesitate and suppose that those words can refer to a mounting implement. Xenophon also mentions somewhere, long before, the same measure taken by Gracchus.

**“With his foot placed upon his back.”** The authors of that and later times differ in describing the calamity inflicted upon Valerian, as may be seen in Barthius on Claudian and on Statius, *Thebaid* II.713. But, apart from Victor’s *Epitome* and the *Passion of St Sabinus*, Lactantius himself is a witness beyond all exception that Sapor trod upon his neck. A learned man illustrates, from both the Old Testament and secular authors, the custom of treading on the necks of the conquered; and from Corippus he shows that Roman emperors were depicted thus:
