> In the middle of the hall he had painted the conqueror himself,  
> Treading the savage neck of the Vandal tyrant.

From this he attempts to prove that the words, “For as long as the king of that province lived, he would customarily mount his horse by placing his foot upon the man’s neck as he bent down,” appended from elsewhere to Eutropius, are not found in the better manuscripts and were also omitted by the Greek translator. After setting out various accounts of Valerian’s misfortune, he also calls Eusebius as a witness; and from *Ecclesiastical History* VII.8—or rather from Dionysius, whom Eusebius follows—he teaches that Valerian grew old in imperial power, until weakened by age he handed over its administration to his sons. He adds that Eusebius passed over a matter disgraceful to the Roman name, whether from reverence for his own rulers, negligence, or some other cause; and that no one is unaware that he often goes astray in this manner along with his whole flock.

Certainly Valerian had two sons, Gallienus and Valerian: he made the former Augustus and the latter Caesar before he came under Sapor’s power. Yet I find in no other author that Valerian so grew old in the empire [Col. 0481A] that, weakened by age, he handed it over to his sons. First, he did not grow old in imperial office, but became emperor at the age of seventy. Since he bore his age extremely well and, endowed with many virtues, was worthy of empire, it surely cannot be said that he transferred the empire to his sons because of age—although, perhaps when absent on the Persian campaign, he made Gallienus Augustus at the beginning of his reign and the other son, Valerian, Caesar.

Barthius was undoubtedly misled by Christophorson, Eusebius’ translator, whom Valesius rightly notes to have understood the quoted words as referring to Valerian, although they must be referred to Macrianus, who had just been mentioned. Thus the passage is now translated: “Macrianus, burning with desire to rule, although unworthy of empire, could not himself assume royal power because of his bodily infirmity; so he set over the empire his two sons, who were to transfer their father’s crimes upon themselves.”

This accords perfectly with what Trebellius Pollio relates in Macrianus’ Life. Though he does not mention desire for empire, his counsel with Ballista—on which see the same author in the *Gallieni*—and Ballista’s immediately giving him his hand, make it sufficiently clear, I think, that they enacted this scene by common counsel and that Macrianus may thus be said to have coveted empire. The remaining particulars also fit extremely well. For Macrianus said: “I am not of an age for this; I am old; I cannot ride as an example [the reading *ad exemptum* is uncertain]; I must bathe more often and eat more delicately. My wealth long ago withdrew me from military service.” When Ballista understood that he was thinking of his sons, he said that he entrusted the commonwealth to Macrianus’ prudence: let Macrianus give us his sons, Macrianus and Quietus, most vigorous young men. Thus he was made emperor with his two sons, all the soldiers consenting.

But because Lactantius makes such notable mention of Valerian Caesar, I cannot refrain from examining Victor’s *Epitome*: “Licinius Valerianus, surnamed Colobius, ruled fifteen years. Though born of the most distinguished parents, he was nevertheless foolish and very indolent, fitted neither by counsel nor by deeds for any public office. [Col. 0481C] He made his son Gallienus Augustus, and Gallienus’ son Cornelius Valerian Caesar.”

What Victor says of Valerian’s character is sufficiently refuted at the beginning of Tristan, volume III, whose observations I judge most true. Moreover, Valerian did not reign for fifteen years, but at most six. For, as Trebellius Pollio testifies, he was made emperor at seventy; this occurred in A.D. 253, and he was captured by the Persians in 259, in the consulship of Fulvius Aemilianus and Pomponius Bassus. Learned men observe that he died a most cruel death, his skin being stripped from his neck to the soles of his feet by Sapor’s order in the seventy-seventh year of his age. This certainly excludes so many years of rule, even though the Alexandrian Chronicle likewise assigns him fourteen years.

The source of the error may perhaps be sought in those authors who wrote that Valerian and Gallienus ruled for the same number of years. Since this is true of Gallienus—for he held imperial power six years with his father and nine alone—others interpreted it also of Valerian. Trebellius Pollio speaks thus in the *Gallieni*: “Concerning the years belonging to the imperial reigns of Gallienus and Valerian, accounts are so uncertain that, although it is established that they reigned for the same fifteen years—that is, Gallienus reached the fifteenth year whereas Valerian was captured in the sixth—some commit to writing that Gallienus ruled nine years, others even ten.” It is evident from what the author of the *Epitome* next relates that he could have had no other meaning: “He reigned fifteen years”—namely Gallienus—“seven with his father and eight alone.” Hence Gallienus is called in Dionysius’ letter in Eusebius VII.23 “an emperor both old and young at once” [παλαιὸς ἅμα βασιλεὺς καὶ νέος].

As for the addition that Valerian made Gallienus’ son Cornelius Valerian Caesar, others, with better right, refer it to Valerian, Valerian’s son, who was born of a different mother from Gallienus, or of Mariniana, and was called Caesar by his absent father, as Trebellius Pollio testifies. In contrast, P. Licinius Cornelius Saloninus Valerianus, Gallienus’ elder son, was made Caesar by his father. The latter died [Col. 0482A] during his father’s lifetime and was deified; the former was killed with his brother Gallienus. Thus I wonder that Balerus, king of the Cadusii, and Artabasdes, king of the Armenians, in letters sent to Sapor and reported by Trebellius Pollio, mention only Valerian’s son and grandson: “Valerian has both a son who is emperor, Gallienus, and a grandson.” But I leave these matters for others to investigate. Nor should you regret, reader, consulting the most illustrious Spanheim, Dissertation VII; John Vaillant, a most learned man, in his *Coins of the More Notable Emperors*; and also Reinesius’ note on inscription XLI of class III.

**“With his foot placed upon his back.”** Athenaeus, VI, p. 256, records that certain women of Caria, summoned by the wives of Artabazus and Mentor, were called *Klimakides* [Κλιμακίδες, “ladder-women”], because they offered themselves as ladders, so that “the ascent took place upon their backs, and the descent upon those riding in the carriages” [ὥστε ἐπὶ τοῖς νώτοις αὐτῶν τὴν ἀνάβασιν γίγνεσθαι, καὶ τὴν κατάβασιν ἐπὶ ταῖς τῶν ἁμαξῶν ὀχουμέναις]: that is, they might climb by the women’s backs into the carriage in which they were conveyed, and descend from it in the same way. Casaubon observes that Eustathius, after citing Athenaeus’ words, remarks, p. [Col. 0482B] 1669, that this was also done in his own time: when a rider could not easily mount his horse, someone would bend over, and his neck would serve in place of a ladder or stirrup. This passage further teaches us that the use of those implements was not general in Eustathius’ time.

Moreover, the savagery of the Persians and eastern peoples should be noted, since they subjected so great an emperor to such shameful mockery. Here belongs the cruelty of Adoni-bezek, who cut off the thumbs and great toes of seventy petty kings and forced them to gather crumbs under his table, as the Book of Judges testifies. Here belongs the arrogance of Sesostris, who yoked conquered kings to his chariot whenever he entered a temple or city, as we read in Diodorus Siculus. Finally, no less savage was the act of Tamerlane, who carried about the Turkish emperor Bajazeth enclosed in an iron cage as an object of mockery, and even attached him to his chariot, if credence is to be given to Matthew Palmerius’ manuscript Chronicle, which Henry Copezius gave me to use:

> Tamerlane, an emperor of incredible power, dies. He had been born among the Tartars in humble circumstances and acquired such strength that he had more than twelve hundred thousand men in his camp. With this multitude, after crushing the Turks in war—he elsewhere also calls them Teucrians—he attached their emperor, bound in golden chains, to the chariot in which he rode, as though in triumph.

**“That he had a son …”** Gallienus, who did not persecute Christians and is therefore called by Dionysius of Alexandria, in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VII.23, “the most pious and God-loving emperor” [ὁ ὁσιώτερος καὶ φιλοθεώτερος].

**“His skin was stripped from him.”** That is, after death; this is also related by Peter the Patrician in the *Extracts on Embassies*, as Valesius notes on Eusebius, chapter 24 of Constantine’s *Oration*. Thus Cedrenus wrongly reports that Valerian was flayed alive: “He died after being flayed by Sapor” [ὑπὸ Σαπώρου ἐκδαρεὶς ἐτελεύτησεν]. And Barthius vainly calls this history into doubt in his note on Statius, *Thebaid* II.713. Agathias too, IV, states that Valerian’s skin was removed while he lived. After recounting that Nachoragan had been subjected by Chosroes to this punishment, and after assigning the story of Marsyas to fables, he adds that Sapor, who ruled long before Chosroes’ time, originated this punishment; that he was very unjust, prone to anger and cruelty; and that many histories testify that this penalty was inflicted by him upon Valerian. [Col. 0482D]

**“Of the unique God.”** That is, of the one God, who alone is God. In *Institutes* V.5 Lactantius calls him “the unique creator of things”; and in chapter 14 of the same book he says: “Those who had begun to defend true justice and serve the unique God.”

**“Containing all things.”** Cicero speaks similarly of the world in *On the Nature of the Gods* II: “The world restrains and contains all things within its embrace.”

## CHAPTER VII

**“He made three partners in his rule.”** Not simultaneously or at the same time. For Maximian Herculius was admitted by Diocletian into partnership in the empire and made Augustus in 285; then both of them made Constantius Chlorus and Galerius Maximian Caesars in 293. I think Eutropius errs when, in book XIV, chapter 13, he relates that Herculius was made Caesar, and in chapter 14 that he was made Augustus from Caesar, although Orosius VII.25 and Paul the Deacon, book X of the *Miscellaneous History*, follow him. The author of the *Epitome of Times* in Scaliger, p. 277, also errs, and does not write cautiously enough when he says that Herculius was made “partner in imperial authority” [βασιλείας κοινωνός] at the beginning of the third year of Diocletian’s reign. This occurred on the Kalends of April, A.D. 285, while Diocletian had assumed imperial power on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, 284, as Baluzius demonstrates in his chronology.

**“Of the indictions.”** That is, of taxes, as the same author teaches, and Du Cange confirms with many examples in his *Glossary*. Below, chapter 31, “indictions of gold and silver”; and they seem at first to have been imposed extraordinarily. Victor touches on the subject in *On the Caesars*, chapter 39: “Thereupon an immense evil of taxation was introduced into a part of Italy. For, since all bore the same burden, fixed—or, according to another reading, moderated—a new law imposing payments was introduced, so that the army and emperor, who were always or for the most part present, might be supported.” Asterius, *Homily on Avarice*, p. 28, calls them *epitagmata* [ἐπιτάγματα, “imposts”].

**“Many governors.”** A highly noteworthy passage, since it contributes greatly to understanding the beginning of the division of a single province into several, each having its own governors. These words deserve careful elucidation by someone with more leisure, since they will doubtless shed much light upon both ecclesiastical and secular authors.

**“Civil proceedings were rare.”** That is, these judges rarely gave attention to settling private lawsuits. Rather, they heard cases of heinous crimes, condemned persons to death, or proscribed them. In chapter 21 he called them “minor and civil cases.”

**“Here, a mint.”** The word is used for the building in which money or coins were struck. Ammianus Marcellinus XXII.121: “Because he had overturned an altar in the mint which he governed.” Sidonius, in his poem on Narbo:

> Hail, Narbo, mighty in healthfulness,  
> In gates, porticoes, forum, theatre,  
> Shrines, Capitols, mints,  
> Baths, arches, granaries, markets.

Others said *monetum*, as Du Cange teaches. That Diocletian built many splendid works is evident from this passage and from his baths at Rome, which are simply called the Baths of Diocletian. The scholiast on Juvenal, whose words Ferrarius cites, *Electa* I.6, says: “Sejanus first placed the camp beside the agger”—that is, above the Baths of Diocletian, which were called the Praetorian Camp; for that camp lay beyond these baths. Thus Vopiscus, in *Carinus*, chapter 19, testifies that Diocletian made more magnificent at Rome the stage which had been burned down.

**“An arms factory.”** Factories in which either every kind of weapon, or weapons of one or another kind, were made. Thus in the *Notitia Imperii*, the Master of Offices in the West is said to preside over eight factories in Gaul: at Argentoratum, of every kind of weapon; at Matisco, of arrows; at Augustodunum, of cuirasses; at Suessiones, of ballistae, shields, and heavy cavalry equipment.

## CHAPTER VIII

**“What of his brother Maximian?”** Namely, Herculius, whom Diocletian had made partner in imperial power and Augustus. Whether he held the rank of Caesar is a great controversy among scholars. Eutropius IX.13, Paul the Deacon in the *Miscellaneous History*, Hugh of Fleury in his Chronicle, and others—Tristan, III, p. 349, and Anthony Pagi, p. 157—record and maintain that Herculius was made Caesar before he was created Augustus. But Victor relates that Diocletian, when he learned that the Bagaudae, having ravaged the fields, were attacking most cities, immediately ordered Maximian to become emperor. Scholars write that the Bagaudae were defeated by him as Caesar. Further, the rank of Caesar appears in none of his coins collected by Mezzabarba.

Francis Angeloni does indeed list one whose obverse bears MAXIMIANUS NOB. CAES. and whose reverse bears PRINCIPI IUVENTUT.; but perhaps it should be referred to Galerius, whose coins are adorned with such inscriptions. Mamertinus also calls him Caesar in chapter 6 of the panegyric which he delivered at Trier: “We saw you, Caesar, on the same day both undertake vows on behalf of the commonwealth”; and shortly afterward: “We saw you, Caesar, in the most brilliant garb of peace.” Yet the oration was delivered to Maximian Herculius Augustus. Hence, in chapter 4, he calls him Diocletian’s brother; and in chapter 9 he says that they are brothers in virtues. Thus chapter 1: “Indeed, most sacred Emperor, anyone might rightly call you and your brother founders of the Roman empire”—words surely by no means appropriate to a Caesar. And since in chapters 2 and 5 he recounts various victories of Herculius, including those over the Burgundians, Alamanni, Chaibones, and Heruli, this panegyric could only have been delivered to an emperor and Augustus. For these peoples were defeated in 287, when Diocletian Augustus for the third time and Maximian Augustus were consuls; and, according to scholars, Maximian was made Augustus in 286, having been created Caesar in 285. Hence it appears that *Caesar* is, for the author of the panegyric, not a title of the second rank but, in the ancient manner, of the first.

**“His brother Maximian.”** Baluzius very well and truly observes that Maximian is called Diocletian’s brother not because they were born from the same parents, father, or mother, but because they were partners in imperial power, or both Augusti. As they were called brothers, so in relation to the Caesars they were called fathers, and conversely the Caesars were their sons, as is clear from chapter 20, which preserves an excellent trace of this custom. Diocletian and Maximian are even called fathers in relation to those whom they had made Augusti from Caesars, as is clear from inscription 7, p. 178, in Gruter:

> The lords Diocletian and Maximian, unconquered senior Augusti, fathers of emperors and Caesars; Constantius and Maximian, [Col. 0484C] unconquered Augusti; and Severus and Maximinus, most noble Caesars, consecrated and dedicated to their Romans the Fortunate Baths, in the name of their brother Diocletian Augustus, the structures having been begun and, in accordance with the magnitude of so great a work, completed with every adornment.

In this inscription one should further observe that Diocletian and Maximian Herculius, after laying down imperial power, are still called Augusti; and finally that Diocletian, who is shortly before called father by the emperors and Caesars, is called their brother. To illustrate this form of speech further after Baluzius, it should be noted that kings called one another brothers. In Ammianus Marcellinus XVII.5, Sapor calls Constantine Caesar his brother; Valesius proves from both sacred and secular writers that others did likewise.

Both Romans and Greeks also customarily described animate or inanimate things, provided they were of the same origin or alike, in the same way. The priests called the Arval Brothers are well known; inscriptions also contain “brother craftsmen,” namely those belonging to one guild of craftsmen. In the treaty in Polybius VII.2, the Carthaginians and Philip with the Macedonians call one another “friends, kinsmen, and brothers” [φίλους, καὶ οἰκείους, καὶ ἀδελφούς]. From panegyrics and inscriptions it is well known that the Aedui and Batavi were granted this distinction by the Romans. Harduin, p. 487, notes from Aristides and Dio of Prusa that other cities did the same; and in Polybius, chapter 25 of the *Extracts on Embassies*, the Rhodians testify that they and the Solenses derive from Argos and that there is therefore between them “a fraternal kinship” [ἀδελφικὴ συγγένεια]. Carthage and Utica are called sisters by Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, because both were said to have been founded by Phoenicians.

That inanimate things also were described by the name of kinship is taught by Mela I.5: “There are high mountains which, continuously and as if deliberately arranged in a line, are called Brothers because of their number, seven, and their resemblance.” Thus, because the ancients believed that the Euphrates and Tigris arose from the same source, as is clear, for example, from Lucan II.256, they were called brothers, or even, more strongly, twins. Mamertinus, in the *Genethliacus*, chapter 6: “For you, the Rhine and Danube and Nile, and the Tigris with its twin Euphrates.” Livineius interprets “twin Euphrates” as the Euphrates which joins the Tigris in Mesopotamia while otherwise flowing separately. But it is called twin because it rises from the same springs; hence Eumenius, in chapter 21 of the speech which he delivered for the restoration of the schools, also calls them the twin rivers of Persia. Yet if anyone here prefers to understand two rivers, as Virgil spoke of twin serpents, Manilius of the twin hinge of the world, and others similarly, I would not oppose him.

Moreover, in Stephanus the Euphrates and Araxes are called brothers because they arise from the same Armenian mountain; and the author of the *Great Etymologicum* explains *adelpha* [ἀδελφά, “sisters”] as *homoia* [ὅμοια, “similar things”]. The word is used in that sense in Aelian, *Various History* II.18 and XII.1. Lucian, *On Slander*, calls flattery the sister of slander; Petronius calls poverty the sister of good sense; Martial calls coverlets sisters; [Col. 0485B] and many others speak in this way.

**“Who was called.”** I punctuate this as follows: “Who was called Herculius? Not unlike him; for neither …” The interrogative mark has been transferred. Maximian, however, is frequently called Herculius in the Panegyrics and ancient inscriptions; Hercules appears on his coins, together with the inscription “To the Valour of Hercules,” as may be seen in Tristan, Spanheim, and others.

**“The lights of the Senate were continually dug out.”** He has imitated his Virgil:

> After he had reached the deep waters and come to the sea,  
> He washed away there the flowing blood of his gouged-out eye.

Though Virgil speaks literally and Lactantius metaphorically, precisely as Velleius II.52: “The two heads of the Republic collided, and one light of the Roman empire was gouged out”—that is, Pompey; though Scioppius would prefer *effusum*, “poured out.” As Lactantius calls the foremost senators “the lights of the Senate,” so Prudentius also, in *Hymn* 2, *On the Crowns*:

> Even the lights of the Senate,  
> Formerly Luperci and Flamines,  
> Kiss the lights  
> Of apostles and martyrs.

Cicero, *Second Catilinarian*, calls them “the lights of the state”; Velleius II.99 calls Tiberius “the other light of the Republic.” In Pacatus’ Latin panegyric, chapter 16, the two Theodosii are called “the hopes and eyes of the Republic,” and in chapter 46 the foremost senators are “the lights of the Senate.” Agamemnon is for Euripides, *Hecuba* 841, “the greatest light of the Greeks” [μέγιστον Ἕλλησι φάος]; Amphiaraus is for Adrastus in Pindar, *Olympian* VI, p. 47, “the eye of my army” [στρατιᾶς ὀφθαλμὸς ἐμᾶς].

Indeed this expression was transferred to other things as well. Athens and Sparta are, for Justin V, the two eyes of Greece; Plutarch in the *Political Precepts* relates that Athens was not destroyed by the Lacedaemonians lest Greece become “one-eyed” [ἑτερόφθαλμος]. This bears on Philo the Jew’s statement somewhere that Athens is in Greece what the pupil is in the eye, and reason in the soul. For Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* III, Corinth and Carthage are the two eyes of the coast; for Pindar, *Olympian* II, Agrigentum is “the eye of Sicily” [Σικιλίας ὀφθαλμός]; and finally Catullus, poem 27, calls a villa “the little eye of peninsulas and islands.”

**“For corrupting morals.”** The most learned Burnet rightly saw, as appears from his translation, that *mares* (“males”) should be read; Victor also reports this: “For Herculius was driven by such lust that he did not restrain the stain upon his soul even from the bodies of hostages.”

**“The happiness of the empire.”** This appears on coins of various emperors: “the happiness of the times,” and “the perpetual happiness of the age” on coins of Commodus, Geta, Caracalla, and others; indeed, on one coin, most elegantly, “the happy condition of the times.” He therefore thought himself to be happy and blessed, as the preceding text says. Thus “public blessedness” occurs below, chapter 48; “most blessed Caesars” in Nazarius, chapter 4; “most blessed victory” in the final Panegyric, chapter 32; “blessedness of the city,” chapter 33; and “a most blessed age” in Tacitus, *Agricola* 3. From these passages it is clear that the ancients used *beatus* in a different sense from that customary today.

## ON CHAPTER IX

**“But the other Maximian.”** Namely Galerius. From these names Jordanes wrongly makes two Caesars: “For these reasons Constantius, Galerius, and Maximian were assumed as Caesars into the realm.”

**“Narseus, king of the Persians.”** Diocletian had previously either defeated the Persians or they had made peace with him. For Mamertinus, in the panegyric which he delivered to Maximian Herculius before his quinquennalia, speaks thus in chapter 7: “I believe that the Euphrates likewise embraced in its own arms excellent and fertile Syria before the kingdoms of Persia voluntarily surrendered themselves to Diocletian.” Again, in chapter 10: “In the same way that king of the Persians, who had never before deigned to acknowledge himself a man, supplicates his brother and opens his entire kingdom if he should deign to enter it.” That Herculius himself waged war at the Euphrates may undoubtedly be inferred from chapter 2. Hence in chapter 5 of the *Genethliacus*: “I pass over the Franks who came with their king to seek peace, and the Parthian who flatters you with the marvels of gifts.” He also speaks of those gifts in another Panegyric, chapter 10.

Sapor, his grandfather. If we follow other authorities, Sapor was Narses’ great-grandfather. That is, Sapor was succeeded by his son Hormisdas; [Col. 0486B] this king of brief duration was followed by Vararanes, who, after reigning three years, left a son of the same name, seventeen years old, as king. He was followed by Vararanes III, surnamed Segansaa, because his father Vararanes had subdued that people, as may be seen in Agathias, book IV. The learned make Narses the son of Vararanes III; consequently, in their view Sapor was his great-grandfather.

Agathias, however, does not say that Narses was begotten by Vararanes III, although he succeeded him. And if Lactantius writes truly and Sapor was Narses’ grandfather, he may have been born to Hormisdas, and Sapor, because of his infancy, have been his uncle; afterwards Sapor’s sons were preferred to him. Yet Agathias says that our Narses reigned seven years and five months—a statement which can in no way be true if he had already held the kingdom in Probus’ time. Vopiscus, chapter 16 of his Life, speaks thus:

> It is also reported that his letter, rejecting the gifts which the king of the Parthians had sent, was addressed to Narses in the following terms.

Casaubon notes that this Narses was a petty king of Armenia, ordered by the Persian—or Parthian—king to convey these gifts to the Roman emperor; and that Aurelius Victor mentions him in his account of Diocletian. Certainly Victor mentions no Narses in his *Diocletian* other than this our Narses, king of the Persians and conquered by Galerius Maximianus. Thus it is more than sufficiently clear that this most learned man confounds both times and persons, and mistakenly thinks that Vopiscus’ Narses is praised by Victor in his *Diocletian*. For that reason he makes him a petty king of Armenia, whereas he seems to me also to be the king of Persia. But he may be confused with Vararanes, who reigned in Probus’ time, if Agathias’ warning is true. For if Narses brought gifts to the Roman emperor and thus performed an ambassadorial office, it is not likely that Probus would have given a letter to him in person; nor could he be said to have received letters, to have been “third,” and to have made peace—things all appropriate to the king of Persia or Parthia.

Perhaps, when writing this, Casaubon had before his eyes the Narses whom Sapor, nephew of our Narses, sent to Constantius in the year 357, as we read in Ammianus Marcellinus XVII.5; Ammianus nevertheless does not say that he was a petty king of Armenia. Moreover, Eutropius makes our Narses—or Narsetes, or Narses—the grandfather of Hormisdas and Sapor; this too must be examined. Agathias relates that after Narses his son Hormisdas reigned (perhaps bearing his grandfather’s name) for the same number of years and months; that he was succeeded by Sapor, a posthumous son, who ruled seventy years; and that after Sapor’s death the empire passed to his brother Artaxerxes. This I can scarcely comprehend. For if Hormisdas left his wife pregnant, and the child whom the queen should bear was to reign, as Agathias records, it is plainly evident that Hormisdas had no other sons and that Sapor had no brother.

Hence, when the Persians learned from the Magi that the queen would bear a daughter and successor [probably “a son and successor”; the transmitted reading is problematic], they placed a crown upon her womb and made king the child not yet born: this was Sapor, grandson of our Narses. Chevraeus certainly errs, book IV, chapter 3, when he writes that so fortunate an omen of future power befell the Sapor who conquered Valerian and treated him with such indignity, while he was not yet born. That event can by no means be attributed to this Sapor; rather, it must be referred to the other Sapor who lived in Julian’s time, as will be clear to anyone who consults Agathias.

This narrative, as I said, plainly excludes a brother; and these matters cannot be reconciled unless we say that Artaxerxes was born to a concubine of Hormisdas and was raised to the throne at more than seventy years of age. Yet it is strange that Sapor should have been succeeded by his brother, when Ammianus Marcellinus XXV.1 mentions two sons of the king—namely, our Sapor. But if we suppose that they died and that Sapor left no descendants, then his brother Artaxerxes, though born from a concubine, could succeed; for sons of concubines were excluded from the throne as long as legitimate children survived, as Brissonius noted from Herodotus. Agathias certainly testifies in explicit words that after Sapor his brother Artaxerxes reigned four years, and that he was succeeded by a son likewise named Sapor.

From this, moreover, I think it follows that Hormisdas, who fled to Constantine the Great, could not have been the brother of long-lived Sapor. Yet this is what most learned men maintain, including Henry Valesius on Ammianus XVI.18; he says that Hormisdas was royal, as Zosimus and Suidas call him the king’s son. But no one writes that he was descended from Hormisdas, son of Narses. Narses, namely, had four sons: Adanarses, Hormisdas, an unnamed son, and Hormisdas. Adanarses lost the kingdom because of his cruelty and savage utterance—though this differs from the saying uttered by Hormisdas. Hormisdas, after the death of his father Narses and the expulsion of Adanarses, was cast into chains because of the circulated story of Marsyas; released from them through his wife’s ingenuity, he fled to Constantine the Great. The kingdom was handed over to Hormisdas, who blinded his other, unnamed brother, as may be seen in Zonaras.

The ancients nevertheless seem to have thought that Hormisdas was Sapor’s brother and Narses’ grandson, as is apparent even from Eutropius’ words. Nor, certainly, can everything in so great a historical obscurity be fully and clearly elucidated. Two points remain to be explained: with whom Narses waged civil war, and whether he was captured by Galerius.

On the former Mamertinus speaks thus, chapter 17 of the *Genethliacus*:

> Ormies, the brother, attacks the Persians themselves and the king himself, having summoned Sacae, Russi, and Gelli—or Gethae; nor does he spare him either as a king, out of respect for majesty, or as a brother, out of affection.

Livineius writes “Ormies,” and notes that Eutropius makes Narses the grandfather of Sapor and Hormisdas. But if we examine the chronology, it will readily appear that Eutropius’ Hormisdas cannot have a place here. The panegyric was delivered, as its beginning shows, before the celebration of Herculius’ quinquennial festival, which fell in 288 or the following year. For if Narses reigned only seven years and some months, as Agathias records, and died in 302, as scholars think, he must necessarily have begun to reign in 295—after this panegyric had been delivered. Thus Narses’ grandfather or father, rather than Narses himself, must have undertaken this civil war.

Scholars also note that Narses was captured by Galerius together with his wife, children, and sisters, and cite Eusebius in the *Chronicle* and Eutropius as authorities. But Eusebius writes that Galerius, after overcoming Narses and capturing his wives, children, and sisters, was received by Diocletian with great honour. Eutropius writes that Galerius, after routing Narses, plundered his camp and captured his wives, parents-in-law, and children. From this it cannot in any way be proved that Narses himself fell into Galerius’ power. Aurelius Victor nevertheless relates this, and I am surprised that learned men have overlooked him:

> Finally, in the same place he brought King Narses under his power, together with his children, wives, and royal court.

Chevraeus likewise states this, book IV, chapter 3 of his *History of the World*. But both are mistaken; from all the other historians, and also from our Lactantius, it is plainly clear that the king escaped by flight.

After Narses had been routed. Yet Galerius was first defeated, as is clear from Victor, Rufus, and Jerome. The latter writes thus: “Galerius Maximianus, defeated by Narses, ran in his purple robes before Diocletian’s carriage.” [Col. 0488A] Ammianus Marcellinus IV.41 refers to this episode when he calls Galerius not merely Caesar but *purpuratus*, “clad in purple”; for those created Caesars were clothed in purple, as is clear from Lactantius, chapter 19, and Ammianus XV. Hence Julian, addressing the soldiers as Caesar in Ammianus XX.5, calls himself *purpuratus*.

But if we listen to Paul the Deacon, book X of the *Historia Miscella*, Galerius fought his first battle successfully; then, having engaged between Callinicum and Carrhae, he was repulsed, but afterwards fought successfully in Lesser Armenia and defeated Narses. If, however, we follow Hugh of Fleury, Galerius, having already fought two battles against Narses, was defeated in a third engagement; after losing his forces, he fled to Diocletian, and subsequently met with better fortune.

It is, moreover, highly worthy of notice that Diocletian was so arrogant and so cruel that he either permitted or commanded his Caesar to run before his carriage, clad in purple—that is, adorned with the insignia of his authority. History preserves comparable instances. Eutropius VII.5 relates that many kings came from their kingdoms to render obedience to Augustus, and, wearing Roman dress—that is, the toga—ran beside his vehicle or horse; but this was voluntary, whereas the other was regarded as a punishment. Galba, according to Suetonius, chapter 6, ran beside the carriage of the Emperor Gaius for twenty Roman miles, although he was descended from an ancient and noble family. Epictetus, bishop of Centumcellae, supplies another example of this arrogance in the *Book of Petitions* presented by Faustinus and Marcellinus to the Emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius:

> Finally, when Rufinianus persisted in the integrity of the faith, Epictetus—that cruel and dreadful bishop of Centumcellae—forced him to run before his carriage; and, after running for a long time, he expired on the road, his vital organs ruptured and his blood flowing.

Nor should anyone be surprised that Galerius obeyed Diocletian; Caesars were entirely subject to the Augusti. The latter supplied them with provisions, secretaries, and transport; the offices of the Caesars’ households depended upon their will, as is clear from various passages of Ammianus Marcellinus. Thus Julian Caesar calls himself, in Ammianus, “a faithful attendant.” [Col. 0488C]

With immense booty. Eumenius speaks elegantly of this and of the victories of other emperors and Caesars in the speech which he delivered for the restoration of the schools, chapter 21:

> There may be recalled, through representations of the various regions, the most beautiful achievements of the bravest emperors; while, amid the ever-warm and ever-arriving reports of victories, the twin rivers of Persia are revisited, the thirsty fields of Libya, the joined horns of the Rhine, and the many-mouthed shores of the Nile; while the mind of each observer imagines for itself, in these several scenes, Egypt resting after its frenzy beneath your clemency, Diocletian Augustus; you, unconquered Maximian, striking down the Moorish ranks like lightning; beneath your right hand, Lord Constantius, Batavia and Britain lifting their unkempt heads from forests and waves; and you, Maximian Caesar, trampling Persian bows and quivers.

All other writers likewise testify that Galerius acquired immense booty. It should especially be noted that the author of the *Collection of Histories* (*Synagōgē historiōn*), edited by Scaliger, p. 395, relates that he returned “having purses filled with precious stones and pearls” (*βαλάντια πεπληρωμένα ἔχοντα λίθων τιμίων καὶ μαργαριτῶν*). He says that Diocletian then first used clothing and shoes adorned “with precious stones and gold” (*λίθοις τιμίοις καὶ χρυσῷ κεκοσμημένοις*), and ordered that, abandoning the old manner of greeting, men should adore him.

But Eusebius assigns the beginning of this custom to the year 295 and Narses’ defeat to 303. Moreover, before Diocletian, Carinus wore gems on his shoes, used a jewelled clasp, and often a jewelled belt, according to Vopiscus, chapter 17. Indeed, before Carinus, Aurelian used gems and garments entirely gilded, which still seemed almost unknown to Roman customs, as we read in Victor’s *Epitome*. Thus Diocletian was not the originator of this practice, though he may have multiplied gems and added them to every garment. Tristan, vol. III, p. 325, notes from Eutropius that Diocletian had coverings for his legs of silk and purple: “even putting on stockings of silk and purple, says Eutropius”; yet I am still searching for this in Eutropius. [Col. 0489A]

With immense spoils. Furthermore, the Persians were compelled to cede Mesopotamia and the five Trans-Tigritane districts to the Romans, as Rufus Festus testifies. After Julian’s death Jovian was forced to restore these to them, as we read in Ammianus XXV.7, where Maximian Galerius is also mentioned. It is further worthy of notice that Ammianus XXIII.5 relates that, while Julian was waging war against the Persians, a dead lion was brought to him—just as a lion and a boar had formerly been brought to our Maximian. He discusses what these omens portended: death for Julian, victory for Galerius.

Fear of Diocletian. He undoubtedly did not wish to add new territories to the Roman empire, lest Galerius become more insolent. Victor says:

> So complete was the victory that, had not Valerius, by whose will everything was administered, refused—on an uncertain ground—the Roman fasces would have been carried into a new province.

From our Lactantius we may learn the reason which Victor confesses he does not know. Yet it is strange that Victor should relate such things, when what I have noted on this very chapter shows that Narses surrendered Mesopotamia and the dominion of the five nations settled beyond the Tigris. To reconcile these accounts, we must hold that the Romans recovered nothing except what Trajan had brought under their power. Under Trajan the eastern frontier had been established on the banks of the Tigris; under Diocletian Mesopotamia was restored and the frontier re-established on the Tigris, so that the Romans obtained dominion over five peoples settled beyond it. This treaty arrangement endured until the time of the deified Constantius, as Rufus Festus testifies. For the regions are called Trans-Tigritane in relation to the Persians, not in relation to the Romans, as Valesius showed in his note on Ammianus Marcellinus XXV. [Col. 0489B]

He claimed to be descended from Mars. That is, he wished to imitate Diocletian and Maximian, who were not merely called Jovian and Herculian, but also made Jupiter and Hercules their fathers. Hence Mamertinus, chapter 1 of the *Panegyric*, calls Hercules “the founder of Maximian’s race”; and shortly thereafter says:

> The very likeness of your lineage and the silent force of your nature make you so generous in honouring Rome’s natal day.

The same author, in the *Genethliacus*, chapter 2: “For you are acknowledged to have been born from gods—not merely by your divine titles, but much more by your virtues.” Chapter 3: “And especially your parents, who bestowed upon you both names”—Jovii and Herculii—“and empires, are occupied by the perpetual accomplishment of the greatest deeds.” Soon afterwards Jupiter is called the divine author of Diocletian; and he and Hercules are called parent gods by the anonymous author of the Panegyric of Hercules and Constantius, chapter 8. He speaks of the latter no differently:

> This is he who gave you the name which he had received from the god, the founder of his race; who proved himself to be the offspring of Hercules, not by flattering fictions, but by equal virtues.

But I am surprised that Lactantius does not criticize this arrogance of Diocletian and Maximian, when he censures the same thing in Galerius. [Col. 0489C]

His mother Romula. The author of Aurelius Victor’s *Epitome* likewise calls Galerius Maximianus’ mother Romula, adding that he dared insolently to claim that his mother, in the manner of Olympias, mother of Alexander the Great, had conceived him through intercourse with a dragon. Although this differs considerably from Lactantius’ account, it equally displays the man’s arrogance. This name was given to other women as well: *Petronia Romula* occurs in an inscription in Reinesius. Sometimes the word is adjectival: we find *Romula gens* in Horace, “Romulan sceptres” in Prudentius, and “Romulan speech” in the ancient grammarians in Pithoeus’ *Catalecta*.

At the beginning of the chapter this woman is said to have been Trans-Danubian and to have fled into New Dacia. First, the spelling *Transdanuviana* should be observed, since the river is otherwise almost always written *Danubius*. Yet precisely the same spelling, *DANVVIVS*, occurs on a coin of Trajan in Tristan I, p. 393, and likewise in inscription 3, CCCCXLVIII, in Gruter. Next, some remarks must be made about New Dacia. It is mentioned also by the author of the Valesian Excerpts:

> Licinius, therefore, of lowly origin from New Dacia, was made emperor by Galerius.

This is Aurelian’s Dacia, as Baluzius rightly teaches. I think that the author of the *Description of the Whole World*, edited by Gothofredus, chapter 6, had this before his eyes when he writes that the Dacians lived on that side of the Danube where Pannonia and Thrace are.

Victor’s *Epitome*, followed by Paul the Deacon, relates that Armentarius was born in Dacia Ripensis and buried there, and that the place was called Romulianum after his mother Romula. Scholars of the preceding century divided Trans-Danubian Dacia into Mediterranean, Ripensian, and Alpine Dacia. If that distinction is correct, Armentarius was born before his mother migrated into New, or Cis-Danubian, Dacia. Yet I have so far found no ancient author who mentions Alpine Dacia. Ripensian and Mediterranean Dacia are mentioned, but they lay on this side of the Danube, in Moesia and Dardania; I discuss this more fully on chapter 35.

These are the two Dacias enumerated by Rufus Festus in the *Breviary*:

> Trajan conquered the Dacians under King Decebalus and made Dacia beyond the Danube a province in barbarian territory, with a circumference of one million Roman paces. But it was lost under the Emperor Gallienus; and under Aurelian, when the Romans were transferred from there, two Dacias were created in the regions of Moesia and Dardania.

One of these Dacias was called Ripensian because it lay nearest to the Danube; the other Mediterranean because it lay farther from it and inland. That New Dacia lay near the Danube is clear from Eutropius, book II, chapter 9:

> He removed the Romans from the cities and fields of Dacia and settled them in the middle of Moesia; it lies on the right side, where the Danube flows into the sea, whereas before it had lain on the left.

Paul the Deacon, book X of the *Historia Miscella*, follows this and adds: “He settled them in the middle of Moesia and called it Dacia, which now divides the two Moesias.” The distinguished scholar wrongly attributes these words to Eutropius. They are drawn from Vopiscus, chapter 39 of the *Aurelian*, where the eminent Salmasius rightly interprets them as Dacia Ripensis and Dacia Mediterranea.

It ought not to be objected that Aurelian is said by Vopiscus, Eutropius IX.9, Jordanes, and others to have been born in Dacia Ripensis, since this seems to imply that Dacia, or part of it, was already called Ripensis before his reign. For these authors commit an anachronism: what was called Moesia when Aurelian was born was later called Dacia Ripensis. Hence some ancient author stated that he was born in Moesia. I am surprised that Vopiscus did not understand this, since the same writers assert both that Aurelian was born in Dacia Ripensis and that he was born in Moesia. [Col. 0490C]

After casting off his father-in-law. This is a most elegant mode of expression. For one is said to “cast off” someone—for example, a father-in-law—when one puts aside a father-in-law’s disposition and no longer conducts oneself towards one’s son-in-law as a father-in-law. Thus Statius and Quintilian say “to cast off the human being,” that is, to desert, as it were, human nature and become savage and barbarous; Seneca, *Epistle* 95, says “to cast off the woman”; Haymo, book VIII, chapter 2 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, “to cast off the prince and put on the raging tyrant”; Valerius Maximus, “to cast off the father”; Hesychius, in the *Lives of the Philosophers*, *ἐκδῦναι τὸν ἄνθρωπον*, “to put off the human being”; and Tacitus, *Annals* VI, “to put on the traitor and enemy.”

But in this place the expression cannot be explained thus, because Galerius was not Diocletian’s father-in-law, but his son-in-law. Therefore “after casting off his father-in-law” means nothing other than after Diocletian had been removed from power, or after Diocletian had laid aside the purple and abdicated the empire, and Galerius had become emperor or Augustus: then at last he began to rage. It is well known that the purple garment or purple military cloak was the insignia of both Caesarean and Augustan rank. Hence those created Caesars or Augusti were simply said to be “clothed,” whereas those who laid down, or were compelled to lay down, sovereignty were said to be “stripped.” Lactantius, chapter 18: “And I sent him to Maximian, that he might be clothed by him”; and chapter 29: “Stripped of office, he hurled himself headlong from the tribunal.” Thus the following words fit together very well, in which Diocletian, now a private person, is called Diocles; and I judge that they should be written thus: “Diocles—for such was his name before his accession—when the commonwealth . . . . .” [Col. 0491A]

## Chapter X

While he was acting in the regions of the East. At the very beginning of the *Notitia Dignitatum* we read, “Register of offices in the regions of the East,” where all the provinces of the eastern empire are designated, of which the East was one part. Like Lactantius, Trebellius Pollio also speaks in this manner in the *Gallieni*, according to Salmasius’ correction: “When Odaenathus had seized power in the regions of the East”; and elsewhere: “Therefore Macrianus, having collected armies from every quarter, made for the regions of the East.” In these places “the East” must mean a portion of the eastern empire, because Odaenathus brought it, or a part of it, under his power, and Zenobia held it after his death.

Undoubtedly this mode of speaking arose because, first, the eastern empire was a part of the Roman empire; then because the empire was divided into as many portions as there were Caesars or emperors; and thirdly because the East itself was also a part of the whole body. Below, chapter 39: “After Maximian’s death Valeria came to him, believing that she might remain more safely in his regions”; that is, in the part of the Roman empire which he governed.

In this chapter Lactantius distinguishes Bithynia, and in chapter 9 Armenia, from the East. It is therefore worth investigating what provinces fell under that name. Learned men judge it uncertain what part of Asia was so called, and suppose it lay towards Parthia, Assyria, and Lesser Armenia. I think that, if not all, at least most of the regions listed in the *Notitia Imperii* were included in that name: Palestine, Phoenice, Syria, Cilicia, Cyprus, Arabia, Isauria, Palaestina Salutaris, Palaestina Secunda, Phoenice Libani, Euphratensis, Syria Salutaris, Osrhoene, Mesopotamia, and Cilicia Secunda.

Ammianus Marcellinus XV.8 describes the eastern provinces, beginning with Cilicia and Isauria. He then says that these regions are separated from the eastern world by Mount Amanus, and that the frontier of the East stretches long and straight from the banks of the Euphrates to the heights of the Nile, adjoining the Saracen peoples on the left. Within the frontier of the East he includes Commagene, Euphratensis, Syria, Phoenicia, Palestine, Arabia, and Cyprus; so that Cilicia, Isauria, and Mesopotamia themselves do not fall under that designation.

Basil also mentions the East, book I of the *Life of Thecla*: “That city, Iconium, is in Lycaonia, not far from the East” (*Πόλις δὲ αὐτὴ Λυκαονίας, τῆς μὲν ἑῴας οὐ πολὺ ἀπέχουσα*); yet it lies more towards Asia and at the very entrance of the country of the Pisidians and Phrygians. Here “Asia” means Asia Minor lying towards the Hellespont, to which Iconium was nearer than to the East beyond Mount Amanus.

But since Diocletian is said in chapter 9 to have halted in the East, we must see where he spent the summer. Aurelius Victor writes that Jovius set out for Alexandria, the province having been entrusted to Maximian Caesar; there he defeated Achilleus, who had assumed the purple, as Victor himself, Eutropius, and Suidas under *Diocletianus* record. Lactantius, chapter 36, says that Maximinus arranged his march from the East and soon became such as he had been in Syria and Egypt, from which he had presumably come. Thus by the East in which Diocletian halted, Egypt seems to be meant, since, according to Ammianus Marcellinus, the frontier of the East extended to the River Nile.

Valesius, in his note on Ammianus XIV.7, wonders that Egypt should be numbered among the provinces of the East, since the *Notitia* and innumerable authorities establish that Egypt was separate from the provinces of the East. But he adds that he ceased to wonder after learning that Egypt and Mesopotamia had formerly been under the administration of the Count of the East. He adduces an ancient inscription:

> M. MAECIUS MEMMIUS FURIUS BALBURIUS CAECILIANUS PLACIDUS, *vir clarissimus*, Count of the East, Egypt, and Mesopotamia.

Certainly Egypt is separated from the East by Vopiscus in the *Probus*, chapter 9; by the *Book of Petitions* offered by Faustinus to Valentinian, etc., p. 20; and by Haymo, book VIII, chapter 2 of the *Ecclesiastical History*. Therefore I still do not see that it was included under the name “East”; for if it were, it would surely not be distinguished from the East in the cited inscription. “Eastern provinces,” then, is one thing; “the East” and “provinces of the East” another. They may be used in two senses: either for provinces generally lying towards the rising sun, or for provinces included within the East properly so called. Ammianus says that he is enumerating eastern provinces, under which designation Mesopotamia and Egypt were certainly included, although they were distinct from the East, or from the provinces of the East in the strict sense. This must be carefully noted.

Since Lactantius expressly writes that Diocletian halted in the East and watched for the outcomes of events, he may first have halted at Antioch, the capital of the East, and then proceeded to Egypt. Or rather, the periods must be distinguished: both may have occurred during the Persian war, but not in the same year. For war was waged against the Persians in 294, 295, 296, and 297; Achilleus was defeated, scholars think, in 295. Thus in the final year, when Narses was defeated, Diocletian seems to have halted in the East—indeed at Antioch. [Col. 0492B]

Searcher of future events. Thus Aurelius Victor calls Diocletian “searcher of impending things.” Because he consulted the entrails of sacrificial victims and so diligently worshipped the pagan gods, I think that Zosimus II.10 reports that he refused to resume the purple because he foresaw disturbance in public affairs: *οἷα καὶ τῇ περὶ τὸ θεῖον ἀεὶ προσκείμενος*, “as one ever devoted to matters divine”—that is, a diligent worshipper and consulter of the gods. Likewise Ammianus Marcellinus XXII.1 relates that Julian continually examined entrails and watched birds, hastening to foreknow the outcome of events.

The rites were disturbed. That is, the sacrifices could not be performed properly; an evil omen confronted them. Vergil, *Aeneid* III.407:

> Let no hostile face appear amid the holy fires, in honour of the gods, and disturb the omens.

The master of those haruspices, Tages. He certainly calls him the chief of the haruspices, because Tages is said by Cicero and others to have invented that art, and therefore to have written on haruspicy, if Fulgentius is to be trusted in his *Explanation of Ancient Speech*. Thus in chapter 33 he designates the physicians of his own time by the ancient names Chiron and Melampus. Nor is it unusual for heads of sacred colleges to be called *magistri*, “masters.” In inscriptions occur “master of the college of the Arval Brethren,” of the priestly order of the Unconquered Sun Mithras, and of the Salii. Indeed, “Master of the Public Haruspices” is itself found on a stone in Reinesius, verse 13:

> L. FONTEIUS FLAVIANUS, HARUSPEX OF THE TWO AUGUSTI, PONTIFEX, DICTATOR OF ALBA, PUBLIC MASTER OF THE HARUSPICES, TO THE ORDER OF HARUSPICES, EX D.D. [abbreviation uncertain].

[Col. 0492D] I do not know whether the Greeks sometimes rendered this term by *didaskalos*, “teacher.” Certainly Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VII.10, speaks of “the teacher and chief of the synagogue of the magi from Egypt” (*ὁ διδάσκαλος καὶ τῶν ἀπ’ Αἰγύπτου μάγων ἀρχισυνάγωγος*), who incited Valerian to persecute Christians. With Valesius, I do not think that this can in any way mean Macrianus, who later seized the empire. For he is said to have been *katholikos*, that is, the emperor’s rationalis or financial administrator, and to have returned an outstanding favour to “them”—or “to the men themselves,” namely Valerian and the chief of the synagogue. At least this must be so unless other matters preceded, since these things are not narrated in unbroken sequence; and this does not favour Valesius’ opinion either. It is safer to understand the passage with the eminent Franciscus Spanhemius as referring to a Jew, since the titles chief of synagogue and teacher were peculiar to them.

Profane persons. Christians, whom the pagans therefore excluded from their rites and called atheists, impious, and irreligious, because they condemned the worship of the gods, as is clear from Lucian’s *Alexander the False Prophet* and Arnobius. [Col. 0493A]

He ordered that soldiers be compelled to impious sacrifices. Baluzius rightly notes that Eusebius VIII.1 records the same thing. Eusebius also elegantly describes the origin of the evils that followed this edict; it is worth adding his words so that each person may draw an example from them:

> God began gradually and moderately to visit punishment upon us, beginning the persecution with those in military service. But when we were wholly devoid of sense and did not even consider appeasing God; when, rather, like certain impious persons, we thought that human affairs were governed without any care or providence, and daily added one crime to another; when the shepherds, disregarding the rule of religion, contended among themselves with mutual disputes, striving only to increase quarrels, threats, rivalries, hatreds, and reciprocal enmities, and claiming primacy for themselves with the utmost contention as though it were a kind of tyranny—then at last, according to Jeremiah’s saying, “the Lord darkened in his wrath the daughter of Zion,” etc.

The same author, chapter 4, teaches that Christian soldiers who would not sacrifice were dismissed from military service. There it should be noted that the *stratopedarchēs*, whoever he was, was the first to persecute the soldiers. He undoubtedly acted at Diocletian’s command, if we follow Lactantius; but Eusebius attributes the action to Maximian Galerius. For in book VIII, p. 317, he says that Galerius, long before the other emperors, persecuted Christians in the army and at court, and was the author of the lamentable persecution.

Christians were compelled to sacrifices because there was no more evident sign of worshipping the gods. Hence *Pietas* is represented on coins with instruments customarily used in sacrifice, as I show in my note on Homer’s apotheosis, p. 288. Because Christians refused to do this, they were called atheists. Arnobius, book VI, near the end:

> Since it has been sufficiently shown, as the matter allowed, how vainly images are made, the order of discussion now requires that we say, as briefly and without any circumlocutions as possible, something of priests, slayings, and sacrifices of victims, of wine, incense, and all the other things performed in this department. For in this matter you are accustomed to stir up the most tumultuous hostility against us, call us ATHEISTS, and inflict upon us, because we attribute least to the gods, even punishments of death through the cruelties of beasts.

[Col. 0493C]

## Chapter XI

Worshipper of mountain gods. What I think of this passage will be apparent from what I sent to Columbus *ton makariton* (“the blessed”), which could not conveniently be transferred here from the notes of a learned man. I am now persuaded that this reading is correct, and that Galerius’ mother worshipped mountains as gods; or at least that she especially worshipped gods whom people believed to dwell in mountains as their seats. Rigaltius observed that “mountain gods” (*Monteses deos*) are so called in a copy of Commodianus, although he prefers the reading:

> You call mountains and gods,

either because *Montes* is written for *Montenses*, just as *NEMORESIS DIANA* in Gruter, inscription 7, p. XLI, means *Nemorensis Diana*, “Diana of the grove,” or because it is written thus in the idiom of that age. Thus “gods of the mountains” occurs in the Vulgate translation, 3 Kings 20:23:

> The servants of the king of Syria said to him: Their gods are GODS OF THE MOUNTAINS; therefore they defeated us. But it is better for us to fight on the plains.

The Septuagint retains the singular: “The God of Israel is a god of mountains and not a god of valleys” (*θεὸς ὀρέων Θεὸς Ἰσραήλ, καὶ οὐ θεὸς κοιλάδων*). The Syrians mean that the gods—or god—worshipped by the Israelites dwell and exercise dominion in the mountains. So Ovid sings:

> We are rustic gods, and we who rule in the high  
> Mountains; over his own dwelling Jupiter holds dominion.

Not only rustic gods may be called mountain gods, but also those worshipped in mountains and others believed to dwell there, such as Diana, who hunted wild beasts in the mountains and was therefore called *montivaga*, “wandering the mountains.” Indeed Cybele is called “goddess of the mountains” by Maecenas in Diomedes, book III, p. 514:

“Be present,” he says, “O Cybele, fierce goddess of the mountains.” Thus Galerius’s mother worshipped gods of the mountains, or gods that were mountains; and if anyone prefers the latter interpretation, I certainly shall not object. For she was of Dacian origin, perhaps born of Dacian parents and brought up there; hence it should occasion no surprise if she followed their superstition. For it is established that the Getae, or Dacians, worshipped a certain mountain as a divinity. Strabo, book VIII: “Among the Getae the priest was called god. And the mountain was left sacred, and they call it thus.” Among the Getae, the priest is called a god, and the mountain is regarded as sacred and is so named. Scholars think that Statius celebrates the “sworn summit” because the Dacians, when about to wage war, assembled on that mountain and bound themselves by an oath. Yet Strabo’s mountain may have been deemed sacred merely because the priest lived there, who was called θεός (“god”), following the example of Zamolxis; and because that cave-like place was inaccessible (ἄβατον) to all others, except the king and his attendants, as we read in the same author. This excludes the notion of Dacians binding themselves by an oath there. Perhaps the word ἱερόν should be translated “temple,” just as Maximus of Tyre, Dissertation 38, writes that the inhabitants of Libya regarded Mount Atlas as “a temple, a god, an oath, and an image” (ἱερόν, καὶ θεόν, καὶ ὅρκον, καὶ ἄγαλμα). Whatever the case, Lactantius must be understood to mean either gods that were mountains or gods of the mountains.

But when I call this superstition to mind, I cannot help first lamenting that humankind could venerate as divinities masses which, though arranged, were nevertheless rough and shapeless; and that it bestowed the same honour upon unformed stones, whitewashed tree-trunks, and columns bearing no human figure. Because of the similarity of the subject, I shall add here, though at some length and though not everything is new, what I have noted upon this matter, so that this foul and insane superstition may be set most clearly before our eyes.

Stones [Col. 0494C], therefore, or rocks, were worshipped by the pagans with divine honours—that is, they were anointed, crowned, and adored—as is evident from Arnobius, book II: “Whenever I saw painted ribbons upon ancient trees, a slippery stone smeared and soiled with olive-oil, I worshipped it, addressed it as though a present power dwelt within it, and sought benefits from an insensible trunk.” The commentators may be consulted there. Lucian, in *Alexander or the False Prophet*, observes that whenever Rutilianus saw “a stone that had been anointed or crowned” (λίθον ἀληλιμμένον ἢ ἐστεφανωμένον), he immediately fell to his knees, worshipped it, made vows, and requested favourable outcomes from it.

And I think that eminent scholars rightly observe that superstitious people imitated Jacob, who poured oil upon a stone at Bethel, Genesis XXVIII. Yet, as Augustine testifies, he did not pour oil upon the stone in the manner of idolatry, as though making it a god; nor did he worship the stone or sacrifice to it. Certainly the Arabs bordering Palestine worshipped a stone as a god. Maximus of Tyre, Dissertation 38: “The Arabs reverence a certain being—whom, I do not know; but the image which I saw was a square stone.” Among the same people, seven stones set in the middle were anointed with the blood drawn by a sharp flint from the great fingers, or thumbs, of persons entering into a treaty; and Bacchus and Urania were invoked, according to Herodotus III.8.

The god whom they worshipped in the form of a stone was, I think, Bacchus, called by another name Δευσάρης [Dusares]. For Suidas is not to be followed when he changes this into θεύς, that is, θεὸς Ἄρης (“the god Ares”), as the illustrious Bochart observed. Yet he rightly describes its image: “The image is a black square stone, without sculpted form, having no figure, four feet high and two feet broad, placed upon a golden base.” Thus in Tertullian’s *Apology* the god of Arabia is called Dysares; and in Hesychius we read: “Dusares: Dionysus among the Nabataeans.” Indeed Stephanus writes that Dusares is a crag and a very lofty summit in Arabia, and has its name from Dusares, the god worshipped by the Arabs.

The most distinguished Vossius, *On the Idolatry of the Gentiles* VI.39, thinks that the square stone mentioned by Maximus of Tyre was the top or summit of a high place, which the Arabs worshipped as a divinity, because Stephanus calls it a crag and summit; and shortly afterward adds that Stephanus, or Hermolaus, plainly reports that a ridge or the highest place in Arabia was called Dysares and was held as a divinity by the Arabs as well as the Dachareni. In making these observations, the most learned man makes a human error. For Stephanus merely says that the summit or crag took the name Dusares from the god Dysares; and we have learned from Suidas that its image—not the mountain—was a square stone.

Porphyry, *On Abstinence* II, seems to be explained with reference to this Arab divinity: “The Dumatae of Arabia annually sacrificed a boy, whom they buried beneath the altar which they used as an image.” The Dumatae also, a people of Arabia, annually sacrificed a boy and buried him beneath an altar which they used in place of an image. For since the god of the Arabs was a square stone, according to Maximus of Tyre and Suidas; since very many altars have that shape; and since this altar served the Arabs as an image, I see no reason why Porphyry cannot be explained thus.

This superstition seems also to have passed to the Saracens, although the stone which they worshipped had the features of a head if one examined it more carefully, according to Euthymius Zigabenus in the *Panoply* edited by Sylburg. Indeed, even today the Mohammedans, in a small temple which they fabulously say Adam built after his expulsion from Paradise, and in which Abraham, Ishmael, and Mohammed, if we follow their account, offered their prayers, worship and kiss the stone called *al-ḥajar al-aswad*, which they call Brachtan. They absurdly claim that Gabriel carried it from Paradise to Abraham, that it was originally whiter than snow and milk and shone like the sun, but became black because of human sins, as Chevraeus teaches in his *History of the World*.

Perhaps Antoninus the Martyr speaks of this stone in his *Itinerary*: “On a part of that mountain the Saracens have placed their marble idol, white as snow. There a priest remains, clothed in a dalmatic and a linen pallium. [Col. 0495C] But when the time of their festival comes, as the moon runs its course, before the priest enters for their feast-day, that marble begins to change colour; and while they worship the idol, the marble becomes black like pitch. When the time of the festival has ended, it returns to its former colour; at which we were greatly astonished.” Thus the words are cited by others.

And as the Arabs, or Ishmaelites, poorly imitated the patriarchs, so the Phoenicians consecrated stones which, according to Damascius in Photius, they called Baetylia or Baetyls. The Greeks gave the same name to the stone which Rhea is said to have given Saturn to devour in place of Jupiter, as Selden, Vossius, Bochart, Salmasius, and Reinesius have shown from Hesychius, Priscian, and others. Looking to this story Lycophron, in *Cassandra*, p. 70, calls Jupiter “the greatest disk,” that is, the greatest stone. For, as Tzetzes observes: “By ‘disk’ he means Zeus, because of the stone wrapped in swaddling-clothes by Rhea in place of Zeus and swallowed by Cronus.”

Moreover, “divine stones” occur in Lampridius, *Heliogabalus*, ch. 8: “He wished to bring the stones called divine from their own temple, and Diana of Laodicea from her inner sanctuary, where Orestes had placed it.” Salmasius supposes that the divine stones were in the inner sanctuary of Diana of Laodicea; and Casaubon notes that the famous image carried off from Tauris by Orestes and Iphigenia is called “divine stones.” Rubenius, *Electa* II.31, understands the divine brothers, that is, the Castors, whose temple Domitian restored; but he at once admits that he remains uncertain and that further deliberation is needed. He ends the sense after *templo* (“temple”) and inserts *simulacrum* (“image”) after *Laodiceae*.

Certainly these stones could not have been in Diana’s inner sanctuary, nor have they anything in common with that goddess’s statue; nor can they in any way be referred to the Castors, because a separate temple is expressly assigned to the divine stones, and because Lampridius is discussing new gods whom Heliogabalus wished to transfer to Rome from other cities. Noticing this, Tristan, II, p. 324, supposes that the divine stones [Col. 0496A] were none other than the thirty square stones which stood at Pharae in Achaea around the statue of Mercury, each of which, according to Pausanias VII, bore the name of a god. But a separate temple in which the divine stones were placed prevents me from accepting this explanation also.

Tristan indeed assigns a temple to these stones on Pausanias’s authority; but I find nothing of the kind in Pausanias. He merely reports that at Pharae there was water sacred to Mercury, that the spring was called Hama, that the inhabitants spared fish because they regarded them as sacred to the god, and that nearly thirty square stones stood near his statue. What then? I think that these stones must be sought in the East and Syria; and that whether one writes *divi lapides* (“divine stones”) or, with the illustrious Salmasius, *vivi* (“living”), Baetyls are meant. The Greeks called these not only “animated stones” (ἐμψύχους λίθους), but also told many marvels concerning them, as may be seen in Photius’s Damascius. Somewhere in the East, Heliogabalus’s homeland, perhaps at Hierapolis, they had a separate temple constructed for them.

And it is quite evident from the relative pronoun *id* (“it”), which otherwise cannot suitably refer to any preceding word, that *simulacrum* or *signum* (“image” or “statue”) has dropped out, or is to be understood, as Obrecht supposes. Thus, in my opinion, Lampridius’s words should be punctuated: “He wished to bring the stones called divine from their own temple; [and] the image of Diana of Laodicea from its inner sanctuary, where Orestes had placed it.”

But, to continue: it must be carefully observed that Dio Chrysostom, Oration 12, expressly states that many barbarians, through poverty or because they knew no sculptural art, considered mountains to be gods, “and unwrought trees and unmarked stones,” that is, shapeless stones. Pausanias writes in the *Achaica* that it was ancient Greek custom to pay honours due to gods to “unwrought stones” (ἀργοῖς λίθοις) instead of images (ἀντὶ ἀγαλμάτων); and in the *Corinthiaca* he notes that before the temple of Diana Lycaea lay a stone called sacred, upon which nine men of Troezen purified Orestes from the murder of his mother.

Further, Pliny II.58 records that in his time a small stone was worshipped in the gymnasium at Abydus—the stone which Anaxagoras had predicted would fall in the middle of the earth, that is, from the sun. Another was worshipped at Cassandria, formerly called Potidaea; and Anaxagoras had at another time again predicted that a stone would fall from the sun. This occurred by day in that part of Thrace near the river Aegospotami, and the stone was displayed, of the size of a wagon and burnt in colour. Since such things are related of Anaxagoras, it is surely no wonder that Ammianus Marcellinus, XXII.16, writes that he predicted stones would fall from heaven. I am surprised that Pliny’s words escaped the most learned commentator, who writes that Philostratus and Tzetzes agree with Ammianus, but that all the others say Anaxagoras predicted only one stone would fall. For he predicted it twice; and those who write that the philosopher predicted stones would fall could join the two stories, or, if persuaded that it happened only once, could have used the plural for the singular, in a most common manner of speaking. Thus Ammianus himself, ch. 8 of the same book [Col. 0496D], says that Anaxagoras predicted at Aegospotami that stones would fall from heaven, although there was only one.

There also presents itself the Mother of the Gods, whom Livy XXIX.11 writes was a sacred stone, and whom Arnobius, book V, records as having been formed from a rock of unprecedented vastness, called Agdus, in Phrygia; when Pyrrha and Deucalion cast stones over an earth empty of mortals, this rock was divinely shaped and endowed with life. Thus the mountain from which the Mountain Goddess, or “mountain deity” (ὄρειος θεός), namely Rhea, derived her origin was called Agdus. Reinesius, *Various Readings* III.17, thinks that this word should be restored in Isidore, whose Glosses read *Agadir*, or, as Vulcanius printed it, *abadir lapis* (“the stone Abadir”).

The most learned man rightly censures Barthius, who seeks this stone in Germany; but wrongly supposes that Agdir, Agadir, or, if Arnobius is uncorrupt, Agdus, was a stone; and likewise that the goddess worshipped in the form of a great black stone transported from Phrygia to Rome was that same stone. For Agdus was not a stone but a rock or mountain. Next, Abdir, Abadir, Abaddir is a baetyl-stone (βαίτυλος), as scholars have noted from Priscian, who says in book I, “Abdir is a kind of stone”; in book V, “Abadir is a god; the stone which Saturn is said to have devoured in place of Jupiter is also called by this name, and the Greeks call it Baetylus”; and in book VI, “Abdir also, and Abaddir—the baetyl of this Abaddir.”

The stone believed to be the Mother of the Gods seems to have had the features of a woman’s face, features which Zigabenus also attributes to the Saracens’ stone. Prudentius, Hymn 10, v. 155:

> A dark little stone, to be borne in a carriage,  
> Sits enclosed in silver, with a woman’s face.

Unless the poet means that the silver casket in which the stone was enclosed bore a woman’s face, so that it was enclosed in silver fashioned with a woman’s face. I ask more learned persons to examine this.

Alagabalus too was a stone-god. Herodian, book V, calls it “a very great stone, rounded below and tapering to a point”; he adds that it had a conical shape (κωνοειδὲς σχῆμα) and a black colour, that certain protuberances and forms or markings (τύποι) appeared upon the stone, that it was an image of the sun not wrought by human art, and finally that it had fallen from heaven. This god is seen on a coin of Heliogabalus; and the notable stone appears with an eagle and three stars in Spanheim’s commentary on Julian’s *Caesars*.

Moreover, on coins of Seleucia in Pierian Syria, struck in honour of Trajan, a mountain is represented whose summit has an opening, or else a stone set in the middle of a temple, with the inscription ΖΕΥΣ ΚΑΣΙΟΣ, “Zeus Casius.” Hence distinguished scholars rightly think that Jupiter Casius is represented, or that this mountain itself was believed to be Jupiter Casius, since, according to Ammianus Marcellinus XXII.14, it rises in a smooth rounded mass to a height, precisely as it is portrayed on the coin.

On a coin of Philip the father, there is likewise a temple and, in its centre, a rock or mountain, with the inscription ΚΑΙ ΤΗΣ ΑΡΤΕΜΙΔΟΣ ΠΕΡΓΑΙΑΣ, “[the temple] also of Artemis Pergaea.” This is no empty indication that the rock [Col. 0497C] or mountain was worshipped with special honour and was sacred to Diana. On another coin of Caracalla, a round stone tapering to a point occupies the centre of a temple, with the inscription ΚΟΙΝ. ΔΕΙΗΩΝ. Hardouin thinks this stands for Διήων and refers it to Dium, a city in the Decapolis region of Syria mentioned by Pliny and Stephanus. Tristan and Holstenius refer it to Dia, a city of Arabia, and think Venus is represented, whom, they show from Clement of Alexandria, Maximus of Tyre, Arnobius, Dio Chrysostom, and Pausanias, was worshipped in that form.

But Clement, Maximus of Tyre, Arnobius, and Dio do not name Venus; they celebrate only a stone, a square stone, or a shapeless stone. They may have referred to the square stone worshipped by the Arabs, of which I mentioned earlier. Perhaps Tristan perceived this; and, to prove that this stone was Venus Urania, he adds that Pausanias, book I, reports a temple at Athens dedicated to Venus Urania, whom they said was the most ancient of the Fates, “in which there was a stone made in the form of a Hermes, or boundary-marker, whose inscription indicated that it was the image of Venus Urania.”

The Greek reads: “The image of Urania is square, in the same manner as the Herms” (Οὐρανίας ἄγαλμα τετράγωνον κατὰ ταὐτὰ καὶ τοῖς Ἑρμαῖς). In these words I find no pointed stone, but a square statue of Venus in the manner of Herms—that is, it had a head and the remainder of the body was square and without arms, and so forth, as Herms were usually made.

Venus Paphia belongs entirely to this topic. Her image, according to Tacitus in the *Histories*, was not in human form but “a continuous round mass, rising from a broad base into a narrow circumference in the fashion of a cone; the reason is obscure.” Maximus of Tyre, Dissertation 38, writes that her statue could be compared to nothing except “a white pyramid” (πυραμίδι λευκῇ). Such an image appears on a coin of Drusus in Patin, of Trajan in Tristan, and others in Jacob Gutherius, *On Pontifical Law* III.5, who wrongly refers these coins to Diana Paphia.

In the same place that learned man emends Lampridius’s words quoted a little earlier: “He wished to remove from its own temple the Diana of Lycaea, and from its inner sanctuary at Laodicea the image which Orestes had placed there”; and he understands the stone which, according to Pausanias, lay before the temple of Diana Lycaea and was called sacred. He adds that the Laodiceans obtained from Seleucus the image of Diana transported from Brauron, and that this was the goddess’s statue which Orestes and Iphigenia had formerly taken from Tauris.

But first, the divine or living stones are one thing, and the stone lying before Diana Lycaea’s temple at Troezen is another. The former had their own temple; the latter was placed not even in a temple, but before the shrine of another divinity. Secondly, Pausanias does not teach that the statue of Diana transported from Brauron into Persia and given by Seleucus to the Laodiceans of Syria was Diana Taurica. On the contrary, in book III he refutes this with various arguments and teaches that the image of Diana Orthia, worshipped at Limnaeum in Laconian territory, was rather that which Orestes and Iphigenia had taken from the barbarians.

Nor do I approve what Gutherius adds, namely, that the statue was an ancient work of Praxiteles, who was reputed fortunate and famous in marble. Since Praxiteles lived in the time of Gnaeus Pompey the Great, he certainly could not have made the image of Diana Taurica. Pausanias writes in the *Attica* that at Brauron there is a shrine of Diana Brauronia and an image, the work of Praxiteles; but he adds: “And at Brauron there is the ancient wooden image, Artemis, as they say, the Tauric Artemis.” It is therefore clear that there was there another, far more ancient image of Diana Taurica. Because the learned man did not distinguish them, he fell into error.

But to continue: Selden, from Suidas and Hesychius, observes that the statue of Apollo Agyieus was a stone upon a circular base tapering into a cone. Yet those authors, no less than Harpocration, the scholiast on Aristophanes, Stephanus, the author of the *Great Etymologicum*, and Eustathius, p. 166, unanimously report that an Agyieus was an altar before doorways, “in the form of a column,” or “a column tapering to a point,” placed before doors; or a conical column sacred to Apollo, Bacchus, or both. At the same time, these sources show that Apollo was called Agyiatēs and Agyieus, that is, “of the way” or guardian of roads. But I have not yet been able to learn from these authors that Apollo himself was worshipped in such a form; indeed Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.9, plainly hands down the contrary:

> For, as Nigidius also reports, among the Greeks Apollo is worshipped under the name Thyraeus (“of the door”); and they honour his altars before their doors, showing him to have power over departure and entrance. The same Apollo is also called among them Agyieus, as being set over city streets. For they call the roads within the sacred boundary ἀγυιαί.

For Apollo is expressly distinguished from the altar.
