Moreover, Pausanias, in the *Megara*, writes that there was a stone “having the shape of a not-large pyramid,” called Apollo Carinus; and in the *Corinthiaca* he records that the images of Jupiter Meilichius and Diana Patroa were made by no art, the former resembling a pyramid and the latter a column. Thus the author of the *Phoronis*, cited by Clement of Alexandria, calls the statue of Argive Juno a column for no other reason, as Scaliger notes on Eusebius. Bacchus too, according to the same Clement, was worshipped in the form of a column. Dickinson, ch. 10 of his *Delphic-Phoenician* work, refers this to the column which, in the Old Testament, went before Moses—out of whom they made Bacchus—and the Israelites. Nor without reason does Clement himself say that columns were formerly worshipped as images: “Before the forms of images had been precisely fashioned, the ancients set up columns and worshipped them as dedications of the god.”

The disk which I show in Harpocration to have been worshipped by the Paeonians as the sun might also be referred here; as might the Penates of Lavinium, whose form and figure Timaeus, cited by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book I, says were “iron and bronze caducei and a Trojan potsherd,” unless one prefers, with Baudelot de Dairval, I, p. 199, to translate τὸ κέραμον as “lamp.” Finally, the Saxon idol Irminsul belongs here, and Meibom devoted a separate book to it.

This worship of shapeless stones and rocks lasted long, and the Christian common people in country districts were infected by it. Ivo of Chartres, part II, ch. 38, reports a canon of the Council of Nantes ordering that stones which people venerate in ruined and wooded places be dug up entirely. And in ch. 57 he cites a canon of the Council of Agde decreeing that inquiry be made whether anyone makes vows at trees, springs, or certain stones as if at altars. From these facts, I think, it is more than sufficiently apparent that Greeks, Syrians, and other peoples worshipped shapeless stones as gods.

We must now consider whether the people of Romulus and the toga-clad nation likewise advanced to this madness. It is known that they worshipped the Mother of the Gods and Elagabalus, and also anointed stones; but my purpose is to examine whether they venerated any native divinity in this form. Certainly Tristan, I, p. 427, observes that Jupiter was called ἐπάκριος, not only because he was worshipped on mountain summits, but because the mountain or rock itself was thought to be Jupiter—the very Jupiter surnamed Lapis, mentioned by Cicero; other celebrated antiquaries follow his lead.

But the most ancient Roman rite, as Apuleius calls it, of swearing by Jupiter Lapis [Col. 0499B], or the most sacred oath, as Gellius I.21 calls it, has no relevance here. For, as Turnebus and Sanctius have shown from Festus and Polybius, the expression is elliptical. Those who swore by that rite held a flint stone and said: “If knowingly I deceive, then may Diespiter cast me out from my goods, saving the city and citadel, just as I cast out this stone.” From this it is evident that the Romans did not worship Jupiter in the form of a stone.

They nevertheless paid honour to shapeless stones—for example, to the *manalis lapis*, or stone of rain, which was a rock, according to Festus, outside the Capena Gate beside the temple of Mars. When they dragged it into the city because of excessive drought, rain immediately followed; and because it caused waters to flow, they called it the *manalis lapis*. And just as the stone whose fall Anaxagoras predicted was worshipped, so in the territory of Crustumerium, according to Livy XLI.9, a stone that fell into the grove of Mars was regarded as sacred—if the same author in ch. 13 is speaking of the same stone and not another: “At Crustumerium a woodpecker, as it is called, dropped a sacred stone from its beak.”

But, to turn to another branch of the matter, it should be noted that pagans also worshipped bare tree-trunks as gods. The spears of which I spoke in connection with Homer’s apotheosis belong here. The image of Ephesian Diana, when it first fell from heaven, or when it was consecrated by the Amazons, was a pointed elm trunk, as Scaliger notes on Eusebius. If this is true—for Petitus holds otherwise in ch. 30 of his highly polished book on the Amazons—Peter Faber was not sufficiently cautious when, *Semestria* I.3, he wrote that the image of Diana consecrated by the Amazons was in the ancient and customary form of a huntress. He is equally wrong in trying to prove that Ephesian Diana was not made with many breasts and spikes; this, however, is so clear that it requires no proof.

But, to return to the subject, Arnobius, *Against the Nations* VI, must be heard:

> You laugh at the Persians of ancient times for worshipping a river, as memorial writings indicate; at the Arabs for worshipping a shapeless stone; at the nations of Scythia for worshipping a sword; at the Thespians for worshipping a branch as Cinxia; at the Icarians for worshipping an unworked piece of wood as Diana (others read Carians, and understand Caryan, or Caryatid Diana, worshipped by the Lacedaemonians); at the Pessinuntians for worshipping a flint as the Mother of the Gods; at the Romans for worshipping a spear as Mars, as Varro’s Muses indicate; and, as Aethlius records, before the use and art of sculptors, at the Samians for worshipping a bench as Juno. Yet you refrain from laughter when you pray to little images of men and human forms as immortal gods?

These words set this foolish superstition most clearly before our eyes. Thus Clement of Alexandria calls the image of Cinxia, or Juno, “a cut-off trunk”; that of Diana, “unworked wood”; and that of Juno, “a plank,” as scholars have observed. Nor does Callimachus, cited by Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* III.8, describe Samian Juno or Lindian Minerva otherwise, as Vossius learnedly shows in his commentary on Catullus.

Tertullian speaks elegantly of statues of this kind, *To the Nations* I.12: “What difference is there, when Attic Pallas and Pharian Ceres are distinguished from the upright beam of a cross, although they are represented without form, by a rough stake and merely the standing support of unshaped wood?” For the phrase should be read *rudi palo*, “a rough stake,” with Stephen le Moyne, a most learned man. By the upright beam of the cross he means the vertical timber of the cross, which Justin calls ὄρθιον ξύλον (“upright wood”). Lipsius wrongly infers from this that a cross sometimes consisted solely of one upright piece of wood. The sense is that pagans ought not to wonder that Christians prize the cross, since they themselves worship Pallas at Athens and Ceres or Isis in Egypt under the form of a stake or standing support—that is, an upright pole, which is part of a cross.

For Tertullian had said earlier in the same chapter: “The nature of the cross is a sign made of wood; among yourselves too you worship something made of material, together with an image. Yet as yours has a human form, ours has its own proper form. Let the outlines now be considered, provided that the substance is one; let the form be considered, provided it is the very body of the god.” The most learned Gothofredus thinks these words may settle the agitation of those inquiring whether, in Tertullian’s time, an image of the crucified one was added to the cross. He adds that Tertullian explicitly establishes this difference between pagan and Christian crosses: the former, namely, had a human image, while the latter possessed its own form—not a human image or human features, but were “unadorned,” bare of an image. What precisely this means, I scarcely understand.

For I do not think that one can find in the Fathers or elsewhere that pagans worshipped any one of their gods affixed to a cross, or paid honour to a cross—unless perhaps some except the Egyptians, whose hieroglyphic signs include a figure resembling a cross. Nor is this Tertullian’s meaning. Rather, he argues thus: the Christians’ cross is a sign made of wood; pagans also worship what is material, or made from wood; therefore the quality of both is the same. The pagans’ pieces of wood represent human figures, that is, are statues; while the cross likewise has a figure, not human but its own and proper figure. Hence Minucius Felix writes in the *Octavius*: “We neither worship nor desire crosses. You, indeed, who consecrate wooden gods, perhaps worship wooden crosses as parts of your gods.”

Tertullian therefore adds that no account should be taken of outlines, or that statues should not be preferred to a cross, because they are made of wood; and he then says that, even if we grant there is a difference here, Attic Pallas differs in no way from the upright stake of a cross. Perhaps this was the Pallas which Eusebius, in the cited place, reports the Autochthons to have set up from wood.

This superstition was common in the countryside, where Terminus was worshipped in the form of a stone or trunk. Prudentius first teaches us, *Against Symmachus* II.1005:

> We enjoy the country’s yield, and we do not disdain  
> To exercise our hands in tilling it; and if there stands  
> An ancient stone which error had been wont to bind about  
> With little fillets, or to entreat with a hen’s lung,  
> It is broken, and no Terminus is profaned by entrails.

Ovid teaches the latter at the same time, *Fasti* II:

> Terminus, whether you are a stone or a trunk  
> Buried in the field, you too have been a divinity from ancient times.

Tibullus I.1 calls it an abandoned trunk—an expression which some emend and others explain, as may be seen in Scaliger on Varro, *On Agriculture* I; Barthius, *Adversaria* IV.2; Vossius II.7.21, *Harmony of the Gospels*; Giphanius in the index to Lucretius; Jacob Loensis, *Miscellanies* II.18; and the commentators on the poet—and Prudentius, in the hymn on the Roman martyr, calls it an unhewn trunk.

They called such a trunk a *delubrum*. Festus: “They called a stripped trunk a *delubrum*, that is, a trunk from which bark had been removed, which they worshipped as a god.” The most learned Vossius thinks that the final words are Paul’s, who everywhere takes care not to seem favourable to pagan religion. Although I am by no means opposed to that view, I think I can raise some difficulties. Since *delubrum* is used only of a sacred object or religious place, Festus would have said nothing unless he had added the last words; and every stripped trunk, every trunk fixed in any place for any reason, would have been a *delubrum*.

Massurius Sabinus, cited by Servius on *Aeneid* II.225, explains *delubrum* as an image, from stripping bark, because the ancients made branches of fortunate trees into images of gods after removing their bark. Servius himself, on book IV, observes that an image is called a *delubrum* because it is made from *liber*, that is, stripped wood, and is called in Greek ξόανον (“carved wooden image”). Some, finally, cited by Asconius, agree exactly with Festus—for Servius’s passages may also be explained concerning statues. There are also those who think *delubra* were stripped, that is, barkless, pieces of wood placed in the old manner as images of gods; but wrongly. For where Festus says “in the manner of the ancients,” he seems to express this by “which they worshipped.”

Hence in the Glosses *delubrum* is explained as καθίδρυμα, ξόανον, ἀνάθημα—“a consecrated object,” “a wooden image,” “a votive offering”—and elsewhere as ξόανον, *delubrum*. The spear worshipped by the Romans in place of Mars, according to Arnobius and Plutarch, also belongs to this superstition. Perhaps Servius on *Aeneid* II.325 should be explained from this: “Others hold that those Penates were Apollo and Neptune; others say that they were Astatae and were placed in the royal palace.” For either *Hastatos* should be read, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus describes the Penates, or *Hastas, et positas* (“spears, and placed [there]”); and the spears of Mars should be understood, which Julius Obsequens testifies were kept in the royal palace.

These observations will suffice to illustrate that foul superstition and to elucidate certain passages of authors. I hope that the fair-minded reader will receive this work, whatever its worth, kindly.

**Worshipper of the gods.** Thus Statius, *Silvae* V.1.193, calls Priscilla Caesar’s especial worshipper; and in inscriptions in Gruter we find worshippers of Hercules, Jupiter, the Lares, and other gods, signifying that they venerate those gods with particular devotion. I have shown in my notes on the *Apotheosis* that gods were worshipped on high mountains, that Jupiter was therefore called Acraean (Ἀκραῖος), and that he appears thus on a coin of the Smyrnaeans. I hope, reader, that you will be very pleased if I share with you a very elegant inscription, recently sent to me from Smyrna with other excellent specimens, which preserves the memory of the same Jupiter:

> ΕΚ. ΤΟΙ. ΕΙΣΑΧΘΕΝΤΟΣ ΥΔΑΤΟΣ . ΕΠΙ. ΤΟΝ. ΔΙΑ ΤΟΝ ΑΚΘΑΙΟΝ . ΕΠΙ. ΟΥΛΠΙΟΥ ΤΡΑΙΑΝΟΥ ΤΟΥ ΑΝΘΥΠΑΤΟΥ ΕΝ ΤΑΙΣ ΣΤΠΑΤΗΓΙΑΙΣ ΤΑΙΣ . ΜΑΠΚΩΝ. ΙΟΥΝΙΩΝ ΥΙΟΥ . ΚΑΙ. ΠΑΤΡΟΣ.

[Materially uncertain Greek inscription as supplied: “Upon water having been brought in for Zeus Actaeus, under Ulpius Trajan the proconsul, during the στρατηγίαι (‘generalships’ or ‘magistracies’) of Marcus Junius, son and father.”]

**To Apollo of Miletus.** The fame of this oracle seems to have been great at that time. Thus Licinius, when about to wage war against Constantine, consulted, according to Sozomen, I.7, the oracle at Miletus of Didymaean Apollo. The author of the *Tripartite History* translates it thus: “They say that he then experienced divination at Miletus, of the Twin Apollo.” Moreover, from this passage, from Ammianus Marcellinus, who at XIV.6 relates that Serenianus sent one of his household to a prophetic temple, and from other authors, it is apparent that the oracles had not yet entirely fallen silent through age, or that the frauds of the priests had not yet been exposed to every eye.

## CHAPTER XII

**A suitable and fortunate day.** That is, a day which was not forbidden, black, or unlucky for undertaking affairs. It is well known that pagans did nothing on forbidden, ominous, or Egyptian days; but if they wished to undertake anything, they selected favourable and fortunate days. On this subject I could, if it were my purpose, bring forward several observations, and observations by no means commonplace.

**On the seventh day before the Kalends of March.** I should not mention the most familiar point—that it should be written with the letters separated, *a. d.*, that is, *ante diem* (“before the day”)—unless I saw that the same error remains in chapters 17 and 44. For the various opinions concerning the beginning of Diocletian’s persecution, see Velser’s notes on the conversion of St Afra.

**As though a boundary-marker.** Sacrifices to Terminus were performed in February, which was considered the final month of the year in ancient times. Ovid, *Fasti* II.47:

> Yet lest you err through ignorance of the ancient order:  
> January’s month, though it is first, was formerly before [it].  
> The month that follows Janus was the last of the old year:

You too, Terminus, were the end of the sacred observances. Indeed, Ovid seems to indicate that, after the Terminalia, or rites performed for Terminus, no further day in that year was celebrated as sacred to any god. Certainly, in the calendars, after the Terminalia no festivals are mentioned [Col. 0502A], except those introduced after those earliest times of which Ovid speaks. Yet I do not think that the last five days of February were sacred to Terminus; for, if that were true, five—indeed six—days would have been assigned to Terminus. Moreover Dionysius of Halicarnassus assigns a fixed day, or *hēmeran takten* (ἡμέραν τακτήν), to the Terminalia (book II, p. 133); and Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.13, writes that the Romans intercalated not after February was completed, but after its twenty-third day—once the Terminalia had of course been completed—and then appended the remaining five days of February after the intercalation. By a certain fiction, the day of the Terminalia was regarded as the final day of the year. Varro, *On the Latin Language*, book V: “Terminalia, because that day was established as the year’s last. For February is the twelfth month; and when an intercalation is made, the final five days are removed from the twelfth month, so that these five days, together with the intercalary days, are not counted as part of February.”

“Having set out.” Columbus very rightly judges that *praefectus* (“the prefect”) should be read. For the emperor did not go personally to the church [Col. 0502B], as is clear from what follows: he himself was on the watchtowers. That the praetorian prefect is meant is evident from the commanders and tribunes accompanying him, and also because the praetorian soldiers demolished the church.

“Drawn up for battle” (*acie strunta*). Either *instructa* should be read, or, just as *strumentum* is used for *instrumentum*, as Du Cange teaches in his Glossary, so they also used *struere* for *instruere*. Virgil too, if I remember correctly, somewhere says *struere aciem*, “to draw up a battle line.”

“That very lofty shrine.” At first Christians met in private houses to worship our Lord Jesus Christ, as is abundantly clear from the New Testament. There Paul too, in the last chapter of First Corinthians, mentions “the church, and the house of Aquila and Priscilla” (*kai oikon Akylas kai Priskillas*, καὶ οἶκον Ἀκύλας καὶ Πρισκίλλας). Later, since pagan emperors and magistrates did not forbid them, and because a multitude was daily taking Christ’s name, they erected spacious and large buildings in individual cities, as is evident from Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VIII.1, and also from this passage of Lactantius, in which the church is called “most lofty”—that is, a building. But when shortly before he said that many large houses enclosed the church on every side [Col. 0502C], this seems to mean that the church was surrounded everywhere by private dwellings, so that it could not be seen by persons walking through the streets. This was doubtless done to avoid pagan hostility; just as today we see older monasteries enclosed on every side by houses, so that their extent cannot be seen.

## CHAPTER XIII

“They were subjected to tortures.” For, as Roman law establishes, not everyone could indiscriminately be tortured. Thus in chapter 21 Lactantius notes, as something unusual, that decurions and leading citizens—excellent and highly distinguished men—were tortured.

“Every legal action might be in force.” I do not reject this reading, since Cicero says that trials *calere*, that one is *calere in agendo*, and that a charge *calere*; nevertheless, *valeret* (“might be valid”), as jurists speak, strongly commends itself.

“They should finally have neither freedom nor voice.” That is, they could not bring actions concerning injury, adultery, and other insults, nor lodge a complaint before a judge [Col. 0502D]. Nor do I think Lactantius refers to the freedom of slaves, as Baluzius supposes. I judge that Rufinus here translated Eusebius correctly: *hoi en oiketiais* (οἱ ἐν οἰκετίαις) undoubtedly means slaves; and those whom Eusebius elsewhere calls *hoi en basilikais oiketiais* (οἱ ἐν βασιλικαῖς οἰκετίαις) are certainly none other than the emperors’ attendants, those belonging to the household or palace and serving there, even though they are not slaves in the strict sense.

“The victories over the Goths and Sarmatians.” Namely, those whom they had defeated. Hence the coins of Diocletian and Maximian bear VICTORIA SARMATICA; and that the Goths had been conquered by them is evident from Mamertinus’ *Genethliacus*. That Christian therefore wishes to indicate that the emperors, having destroyed Christians, ought to assume a title from them, just as they were called Gothic after the Goths and Sarmatian after the conquered Sarmatians. And although Eusebius seems to praise this man [Col. 0503A], I nevertheless think that Lactantius takes the better view in writing that this was not rightly done.

“Cooked according to rule” (*legitime coctus*). Gallonius and Sagittarius, in their works on the tortures of martyrs, say nothing about those “cooked according to rule.” I now think that he was first cooked over a slow fire, such as is ordinarily used for roasting meat, and then burned through; for Galerius’ savagery toward Christians is evident from chapter 21, where among other things we read, “with all the skin cooked away over a long day.” Eusebius VIII.6 likewise significantly says that a certain Peter was roasted in fire like meat prepared for food, or, in Lactantius’ language, “cooked.” Thus one may certainly explain *legitime* conveniently with Columbus. Yet I would not oppose those who explain it as “according to laws enacted by the Augusti”; just as Petronius calls oil *legitimum*, the oil with which wrestlers were anointed according to the law and custom of the palestra, as the most learned Gronovius showed in his notes on Statius.

## CHAPTER XIV

[Col. 0503B] “By hidden agents.” Perhaps this stands for “through hidden agents”; or it means Diocletian’s servants and household attendants, without whose knowledge or notice he caused the palace to be set on fire.

“Two emperors.” Yet only one was emperor; the other was Caesar. This must be noted carefully, because this manner of speaking occurs in other writers too, and because Eusebius likewise calls them *basileis* (βασιλέας, “kings/emperors”). Lactantius distinguishes these things correctly in chapter 18, where Diocletian addresses Galerius Maximianus, who was Caesar: “But if he desired to obtain the title of emperor, nothing prevented all from being called Augusti.”

“All his own people.” That is, the courtiers serving him; in chapter 15 he calls them his household. It should be observed that many in the palace had taken Christ’s name, and that our Lord granted this favour to the courtiers—and indeed the intimate associates—of the most cruel persecutors. Thus at the end of his Epistle to the Philippians St Paul mentions “the saints who are of Caesar’s household” (*tous hagious, tous ek tēs Kaisaros oikias*, τοὺς ἁγίους, τοὺς ἐκ τῆς Καίσαρος οἰκίας) [Col. 0503C]. Eusebius’ words, *Ecclesiastical History* VIII.1, are especially worthy of notice:

> The emperors’ kindness toward our people may serve as proof: they even entrusted provinces to them for administration, freeing them from every fear of sacrificing because of the singular goodwill with which they were disposed toward our religion. What need is there to speak of those who lived in the imperial palaces? Or of the emperors themselves, who allowed their household servants, and their wives, children, and slaves, freely to carry out before their very eyes, both in word and deed, whatever pertained to their religion—permitting them even, on account of this freedom in their faith, to glory and in some manner display themselves?

Likewise, VII.10, he writes that Valerian at first embraced Christians warmly, and that his whole house was full of *theosebeis* (θεοσεβῶν, “god-fearing persons”), so that it appeared to be a Church of God (*ekklēsia theou*, ἐκκλησία θεοῦ).

## CHAPTER XV

[Col. 0503D] “He compelled them to be defiled by sacrifice.” What I think of this passage I explain at chapter 1.

“Through whom [he controlled] the palace.” That is, those who possessed the greatest influence with the emperor. The *Historia Augusta* supplies many examples of this. And “formerly” (*quondam*) should not be understood of a long interval of time, but of a short one—namely, that preceding the edict.

“Presbyters and ministers.” That is, presbyters and deacons. Isidore, cited by Gratian: “These Levites are called in Greek *diakonoi*, in Latin *ministri*.” Canon 18 of the Council of Elvira concerns priests and ministers if they have committed adultery; Canon 33 concerns bishops and ministers, requiring them to abstain from their wives. More on this may be found in Gaspar Ziegler, *On the Deacons and Deaconesses of the Ancient Church*, and in Du Cange’s Glossary. Sulpicius Severus, II.43, uses the term generally: “I would certainly not pass over this example in silence, and would gladly press the reading MINISTRIS ecclesiarum, ‘ministers of the churches.’”

But since the Council of Elvira has been mentioned, I must, with the reader’s kind permission, discuss Januarius, bishop of Sibariensis—or, as others write from manuscripts, Salariensis—who is mentioned there [Col. 0504A]. Mendoza testifies that the codex of the Church of Toledo reads *Januarius de Fiblaria*, and *Fibularia*, and writes that this reading ought not lightly to be rejected, since Pliny testifies that Calagurris Fabularia was so called by the ancients. I therefore judge that *Fibulariensis* should be written, because Liutprand, no. 226 of the *Adversaria*, expressly preserves that name: “In the gorges of the Fibularian forest is Fabularia, which the Moors call Xergal, an episcopal see.” Thus, in the fourteenth place of the Council of Elvira, Januarius is confirmed as bishop of Fibularia; so too in certain manuscripts. From this it follows either that the names of the bishops were arranged in a different order in some codices, or that the number XIV must be changed to XVII, where in the printed editions the name of that Januarius is recorded. Gonzalez also cites this passage in his notes on that council, but does not observe that it pertains to the Januarius mentioned; and he wrongly tries to prove from it that, beyond the bishops listed, the bishop of Fibularia also attended and subscribed to the council.

[Col. 0504B] “With all his own.” Namely, household members, children, and slaves; for he immediately continues, “and no less among the rest of the populace.”

“The prisons were full.” Above all, it should be noted that Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VIII.6, writes that at the beginning of the persecution innumerable Christians were put to death; but that an edict was soon posted commanding that all heads of churches be bound and shut up in prisons, because some men in Melitene and others in Syria were seizing imperial power. The prisons, he says, were filled with bishops, presbyters, deacons, readers, and exorcists. Afterwards another edict was posted: anyone who sacrificed might go free, but whoever refused would be subjected to severe tortures. Valesius, from Libanius, notes that the man who seized power in Syria was called Eugenius; but it is a great loss to history that we do not know what occurred in Melitene or Lesser Armenia. Would that Lactantius, who could have known everything accurately, had supplied this deficiency! [Col. 0504C]

“Lest anyone rashly…” That is, lest judges perhaps pronounce judgments in favour of Christians, which was forbidden by the laws, as is clear from chapter 13.

“From the commands of their superiors…” That is, of Diocletian and Herculius, who were Augusti, while he himself and Galerius were only Caesars: with Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* IX.1, you might say *tōn kreittonōn* (τῶν κρειττόνων, “their superiors”). Constantius certainly showed great favour to Christians; and in Gaul, Britain, and neighbouring places, no one seemed to be a Christian in violation of the law, as Cassiodorus testifies, *Tripartite History* I.7. The memorial of the Donatists presented to Constantine, preserved by Optatus of Milevis, says: “Your father, among the other emperors, did not carry out the persecution, and Gaul is free from this crime. For Gaul and Britain had fallen to Constantius.” In Gaul he fought bravely near Langres and killed many Alamanni, according to Eutropius IX.15; whence Vopiscus, *Carinus* 18, says that he restored Gaul to Roman laws [Col. 0504D]. Here Casaubon certainly suffers a human lapse when he notes that our Constantius defeated the Persians in war.

## CHAPTER XVI

“Zabulus.” He calls him “the adversary” shortly afterwards and in chapter 1, as I showed there. Martyrs who resolutely endured tortures were customarily said to conquer the devil, because he is the leader and emperor of those who persecute Christ’s Church. To this belong the visions recounted in the passions of Saints Perpetua and Felicity. When Perpetua refused to put on the dress consecrated to Ceres, she is said to have already trodden upon the head of the Egyptian—that is, the devil.

“Not white horses, nor monstrous elephants…” Evidently, both formerly and then, white horses were harnessed to the chariots of triumphing generals. Ovid, *Art of Love* I:

> Golden, you will go in a chariot with four snow-white horses.

[Col. 0505A] Therefore Claudian, *The Gothic War* V.127, attributes snowy quadrigae to them:

> Who drove captive kings in snow-white four-horse chariots.

So too Plautus, *Asinaria* II.2.13, “white quadrigae.” The precedent was Camillus, although the act brought him resentment because he seemed to wish to imitate Jupiter and the Sun, as Livy, the author of *On Illustrious Men*, Plutarch, and others testify. Nor do I follow the distinguished Freinshemius, who comments on Florus and Curtius that this did not arouse resentment against Camillus because white horses formed part of the ceremonial of a triumph. It did indeed become so later; but Camillus provided the first example, and the novelty of the thing incurred resentment against him. Nor do I agree with Plutarch when he says that no later emperor so triumphed, since the contrary may easily be proved from Roman history.

“Not white horses.” Their precedent, as I noted, was Camillus. Livy speaks of him thus, V.23: “He himself was most conspicuous, entering the city [Col. 0505B] in a chariot drawn by white horses; and this seemed scarcely civil, indeed scarcely human. They construed it in religious terms: that the dictator was equating himself with the horses of Jupiter and the Sun.” Scheffer, the distinguished scholar, in *On Vehicles* I.18, emends this to “the horses of Jupiter alone.” Livy continues: “For this one reason especially, the triumph was more brilliant than welcome.” And in chapter 28: “Camillus became conspicuous for justice and fidelity by a far better reputation than when white horses carried him through the city in triumph.” Varro, to cite no other testimonies, states in Gellius X.15 that white victims were sacrificed to Jupiter; Curtius III.3 reports that Jupiter’s chariot among the Persians was drawn by white horses. An elegant passage in Eratosthenes—whom, incidentally, the scholiast on Germanicus often follows closely—also teaches us that horses of this colour were consecrated to the Sun, *Catasterisms* 13:

> This is Erichthonius, son of Vulcan and Earth. Jupiter, they say, when he saw that he was the first among men to harness horses to a chariot, marvelled because he had made an imitation of the chariot of the Sun, harnessing white horses (*hoti tē tou hēliou antimimon epoiēsato diphreian, hypozeuxas hippous leukous*, ὅτι τῇ τοῦ ἡλίου ἀντίμιμον ἐποιήσατο διφρείαν, ὑποζεύξας ἵππους λευκούς).

The scholiast just cited refers this to a four-horse chariot: “He first taught men to make horse-drawn chariots like the Sun’s quadriga.” Hyginus says similar things in his *Poetical Astronomy* [Col. 0505C].

“The little terrors of tyrannical power…” That is, terrors; Lactantius speaks thus also in chapter 47. Lucilius, cited by Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* I.21—if Barthius is to be trusted in his notes on Statius V.68—writes:

> Little terrors, Lamiae, which the Fauns and the Numas of Pompilius  
> Instituted…

Barthius explains this as idols that instilled terror in children or others. But printed editions circulate “Terricolous Lamiae”; and the illustrious Huet, in the *Evangelical Demonstration*, emends it to “Tower-dwelling Lamiae,” because Tertullian proverbially called Lamiae “the towers and combs of the Sun.”

“Claws…” These were iron instruments resembling birds’ talons, whence they received their name. By them people were torn, usually while stretched upon the rack. Besides Gallonius, Magius, and others, Ferrarius discusses them in *Electorum* I.6. Prudentius states it clearly, Hymn 5, *Peristephanon*, v. 337:

> He traces with kisses  
> The double furrows of the claws.

He calls them double because one claw made two furrows at a single stroke.

## CHAPTER XVII

[Col. 0505D] “Ninth consulship…” Zosimus II.7 writes that this fell in the one hundred and first year after Severus had celebrated the Secular Games; that the time when these should have been celebrated fell in the third consulship of Constantine and Licinius; and that, because those games were neglected, the Roman Empire was unfortunate. This passage must be carefully noted because of its chronological indication.

“The consul would proceed.” This is a technical expression, as Baluzius showed. Hence on a coin cited by Spanheim, dissertation 8: FELIX PROCESSUS COS. VI, AUG., or AUG. COS. VI; add Wilthemius on the Liège Diptych [Col. 0506A] and Henry Noris, in his dissertation *On the Decennial Vows*. Emperors were accustomed to assume the consulship as soon as they entered upon imperial power. Hence perhaps CONS. on Aurelian’s coin denotes “consul,” although I explain it otherwise on the Gemma Augustea. On that same coin the Sun may be called DOM. IMP. ROM., since, as Vopiscus testifies, Aurelian honoured the Sun with great reverence. This explanation seems all the more compelling because CONS. on coins sometimes denotes consul. Sirmond comments on Epistle 12, book II of Sidonius:

> The obverse displays Valentinian’s face with the usual inscription, D. N. PLA. VALENTINIANUS P. F. AUG.; the reverse, Maximus seated in a curule chair in senatorial dress, holding a scroll in his right hand and an eagle-topped sceptre in his left, with this inscription: PETRONIUS MAXIMUS O. C. CONS.

Wilthemius illustrates this coin more fully in the book cited. This expression is generally used when emperors came forth in public with ceremony and on a solemn day. Thus in chapter 19, where Lactantius narrates that Diocletian and Herculius abdicated and created new Augusti and Caesars: “When these arrangements had been made, they proceeded on the Kalends of May.” Diocletian entered upon his ninth consulship at Nicomedia, and Herculius upon his eighth at Rome [Col. 0506B]. Baluzius notes that the latter spent the summer of 304 in Campania. Indeed, I think I can affirm from the Passion of St Felix that he was at Nola: “After twelve days the praetorian prefect ordered him to sail after the emperors”; and shortly afterward: “Fasting, he came to Nola.” For though the emperors are mentioned and the prefect wished to send to both, Felix was presented to Herculius alone, because Diocletian was at Nicomedia. The author of the Passion, undoubtedly ancient, correctly writes that the edict ordering the persecution of Christians was promulgated when Diocletian was consul for the eighth time and Maximian for the seventh—that is, in 303, not 304, as is marked in the margin of the book. In the latter year Felix suffered capital punishment. Yet a great difficulty arises because Felix is said to have been beheaded on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February [Col. 0506C; 15 January], since in February 304 Herculius was still at Rome and there, as Baluzius notes, entered upon the twentieth year of his reign in April. I can scarcely see how this knot can be untied, unless we suppose that at the beginning of 305 Herculius still remained in Campania and that Felix was then put to death by the sword. I should like others with more leisure to examine this more carefully.

“Along the circuit of the bank of the *striga*.” The highly distinguished and learned Heinsius once informed me that *ripae Histriae*, “the shore of the Hister,” or *Histricae*, “Histerian,” should be written; just as *striculus* occurs for *histriculus*, *Spania* for *Hispania*, and other such forms are found in Salmasius’ notes on Tertullian’s *Pallium*. If this emendation is correct, the meaning is not straightforward [materially uncertain]. Diocletian went to Nicomedia by a route that took him round the shore of that region, or of Histria. Or perhaps the bank of the Danube must be understood, since the Danube is also most commonly called Hister. Certainly he used a circuitous route. Thus Victor too speaks of Carinus, who was in Gaul: “He hastily sought Italy by a circuitous route through Illyricum.”

## CHAPTER XVIII

[Col. 0506D] “He had recently fought with the elder Maximian.” Either he follows Greek usage, or the particle *cum* (“with”) has dropped out; or *Maximiano seni* should be written, just as some have said *certare* without *cum*. Virgil, *Eclogue* 5:

> Amyntas alone may contend with you on our mountains.

In Catullus we read, “do not fight two [men],” and in Ammianus Marcellinus XV.4, “to engage barbarians”; though the particle *cum* may be understood.

“That fifteen years had now passed…” *Quibus* seems to have fallen out, so that Lactantius wrote: “that fifteen years had now passed during which [he had been sent] into Illyricum,” etc. Otherwise nothing need be changed with Baluzius. For Illyricum in the strict sense did not extend to the bank of the Danube but to the Adriatic Sea, which is also called Illyrian; moreover not merely Illyricum but the whole tract as far as the Pontus was entrusted to Galerius. Aurelius Victor: “The Illyrian coast as far as the strait of the Pontus was entrusted to Galerius; and after defeating Narseus he conquered the Carpi and Bastarnae dwelling on the Danube.” [Col. 0507A] I know that Illyricum extended far and wide in those times, especially in subsequent times; the most illustrious bishop Peter de Marca teaches this in his dissertation *On the Patriarchate of Constantinople*, and Baluzius can thus defend his emendation. But why change anything beyond necessity?

“Now Maximian had a son, Maxentius.” Maxentius was therefore the son of Herculius. Yet Trist., tome III, p. 376, notes from Julian, *Oration* I, p. 9, that Eutropia, when asked whether Maxentius was her son, replied that he had been born to her by a certain Syrian. If this is true, Maxentius was not the son but the stepson of Herculius, or was passed off as Herculius’ son. Yet I find nothing of the kind in Julian. He says only that some Easterners related that they had given the grandmother of Constantius, son of Constantine the Great, in marriage to his maternal grandfather—that is, Herculius—because Eutropia was Syrian and Herculius had Fausta by her, the wife of Constantine the Great [Col. 0507B]. I shall discuss this more fully at chapter 39.

“Was accustomed to adore.” Diocletian, of course, was the first to demand that he himself be adored, whereas emperors had previously merely been saluted. Eutropius IX.16: “Diocletian was the first, in the Roman Empire, to introduce the form of royal custom rather than Roman liberty, and ordered himself to be adored, whereas before him all had been saluted.” Jerome, *Chronicle*: “Diocletian was the first to order himself to be adored as a god and to have jewels set in his garments and footwear; whereas before him all emperors had been saluted in the manner of magistrates and had worn the purple cloak as the chief distinction from private dress.” You may read similar things in Jordanes and other writers. Herculius and Galerius undoubtedly followed Diocletian’s customs. Nor does Maxentius seem blameworthy for refusing to render divine honour to emperors, any more than the Macedonians who likewise refused to flatter Alexander the Great in this way. Thus I cannot see why Lactantius calls him proud and obstinate in this respect, unless perhaps the practice of adoration begun by Diocletian became customary and was used also by Constantine and others [Col. 0507C].

“Detested by both.” The same is reported in the Epitome of Victor: “This Maximian was dear to no one ever, not even to his father or to Galerius, his father-in-law.” It is certain that *Maxentius* should be read here, from Paul the Deacon; Valesius noted this in his remarks on the excerpts published with Ammianus Marcellinus.

“Constantine…” It is no wonder that Diocletian favoured him, since his father Constantius had sent him to Nicomedia to be educated (*paideuthēsomenon*, παιδευθησόμενον), according to Praxagoras cited by Photius; or so that in the emperor’s court and, as it were, under the eyes of the prince—whom Eutropius calls most diligent and energetic—he might learn what would one day be necessary for his own rule. Others report that he was a hostage; and he may indeed have been regarded as such. The Excerpts of Valesius state:

> Constantine was born at Naissus to Helena, a woman of very humble birth, and reared there; he afterwards magnificently adorned that town. Poorly instructed in letters, he was a hostage with Diocletian and Galerius, and under them served bravely in Asia.

This undoubtedly occurred when Galerius was warring against Narses and Diocletian was recovering rebellious Egypt. For we read in the *Polity of the Holy Fathers Metrophanes and Alexander*, cited by Photius, p. 1406, that Constantine accompanied Diocletian: “[He] related that he had seen Constantine *en tois ephēbois telounta* (ἐν τοῖς ἐφήβοις τελοῦντα, ‘among the young men’) in Palestine, when he was present with Diocletian as he made war upon Egypt.” That war had been provoked by a revolt, as Paul the Deacon, book X, also reports, as well as Eusebius, *Life of Constantine* I.19, who records that he himself saw him there [Col. 0507D].

“Most virtuous young man.” That is, a man of upright and honourable life, who observed justice and was endowed with good character. In Velleius II.53 Pompey is called *sanctissimus et praestantissimus vir*, “a most upright and eminent man,” in this sense; and in chapter 29, “outstanding in innocence, pre-eminent in uprightness.” Very many examples could be adduced from authors and inscriptions, but that would be an abuse of leisure. In these inscriptions one often finds “a most upright husband” and “a most upright wife” [Col. 0508A]; by this encomium spouses attest that the deceased had lived continently, honourably, and chastely. Nor do I agree with the learned man who, in the Grenoble inscriptions, thinks that a certain Valerius consecrated his wife Valeriana and therefore calls her SANCTA. For this epithet signifies nothing else than that the woman had lived chastely, just as Catullus calls Juno the holy wife of Jupiter.

“For he who despised me while I was a private man…” Yet he had already been raised in rank: he was tribune of the first order and at the same time son of a Caesar. We certainly would not today call such a man a private person. An especially elegant passage relevant to this is Horace, *Odes* III.8, which I think very learned men have not sufficiently understood:

> Since you disregard whether the people suffer any misfortune,  
> Spare yourself, a private man, excessive caution;  
> Joyfully seize the gifts of the present hour,  
> And leave stern cares behind. [Col. 0508B]

The poet celebrates the Kalends of March, because he had nearly been killed by a tree on that day, as is evident from II.13. He exhorts Maecenas to cheer himself on that anniversary because his friend survived, and to set aside civic concerns for the city. This is all the more appropriate because the Dacians and Cantabri had been defeated, the Medes and Parthians were rushing upon one another with hostile arms, and the Scythians were preparing for conquest. Such being the case, he adds: *parce privatus nimium cavere*—that is, do not be excessively intent upon the safety of the city and Empire, or fear too anxiously for the city, as he says elsewhere, since you are not emperor or the person in whose hands supreme power rests, but a private man.

Once Roman affairs had been concentrated in one man, all others, though adorned with the highest offices and honours, were called private persons in relation to the princeps. This is what Claudius repeatedly asks in Tacitus, *Annals* II.31: whether he himself possessed the Empire, or whether Silius was a private person—that is, whether Silius had not yet been made emperor. Thus “private spectacles” in Suetonius, *Nero* 21, are rightly explained by Torrentius and Casaubon as spectacles presented by persons other than the emperor, even though they held magistracies [Col. 0508C]. In the same sense Tacitus, chapter 39, calls Agricola a private man, although he governed Britain with imperial authority. Under the free Republic, a private man was one who did not hold *imperium*, or had laid it down, even if he held other offices, as Suetonius, Caesar, Cicero, and others establish. Since Caesars or emperors alone held *imperium*, while the rest bore delegated standards, as Statius elegantly sings, and magistrates received their jurisdiction from the Princeps, they were rightly called private persons.

Therefore, Maecenas, since care for the Empire does not belong to you but to Augustus, spare yourself such continual concern to provide against any harm befalling the Roman people through negligence. I interpret “the negligent people” as a people negligent of its own safety, given over to leisure, games, and idleness. It is well known that Tacitus, at the beginning of the *Annals*, observes that Augustus, having won over the soldiers with gifts, the populace with grain, and all with the sweetness of peace, drew the functions of senate, magistrates, and laws to himself, with no one opposing him. Juvenal, *Satires* 10, sings:

> Long since, from the time when we sold our votes to no man,  
> That people has cast off its cares; for the people that once bestowed  
> Empire, fasces, legions—everything—now restrains itself  
> And anxiously desires only two things:  
> Bread and circuses. [Col. 0508D]

It should further be noted that *privatus* is sometimes opposed to a soldier, and then means civilians, or persons who have not entered military service. Lactantius himself taught me this shortly before: “He was loved by soldiers because of his honourable character and singular courtesy, and desired by civilians.” On this occasion I cannot refrain from also elucidating Cicero. Those who have written on pontifical law ask whether the Pontifex Maximus of ancient Rome was a private person; and Muretus discusses the question at length in his notes on the first Catilinarian, where Cicero says: “Did that most distinguished man P. Scipio, Pontifex Maximus, kill Tiberius Gracchus, who was moderately shaking the state of the Republic, as a PRIVATE person?” Leaving the question to Muretus, Gutherius, and Bosius, I think he struggles in vain: Cicero never intended in this passage to say that the Pontifex Maximus was a private person. Rather, P. Scipio—who afterwards became Pontifex Maximus—suppressed the sedition of Gracchus while he was still a private man. Cicero makes this clear and unambiguous in *On Duties* I: “The singular Africanus, both as a man and as a commander, did no more service to the Republic in destroying Numantia than P. Nasica did at the same time as a PRIVATE person when he killed Tiberius Gracchus.”

Although Appian, *Civil Wars* I, writes that Scipio the Pontifex Maximus led the Romans—“and first among them the man called the chief priest, Cornelius Scipio Nasica, led the way” (*kai prōtos autois ho megistos archiereus legomenos exērche tēs hodou Kornēlios Skipiōn ho Nasikas*, καὶ πρῶτος αὐτοῖς ὁ μέγιστος ἀρχιερεὺς λεγόμενος ἐξῆρχε τῆς ὁδοῦ Κορνήλιος Σκιπίων ὁ Νασικᾶς)—and says that the Gracchans gave way before so great a man, or *kat’ axiōsin andri aristō* (κατ’ ἀξίωσιν ἀνδρὶ ἀρίστῳ, “in deference to an excellent man”), the opposite seems plainly true to me. Velleius’ authority is greater. He writes, II.3, that P. Scipio Nasica did these things as a private citizen and in a toga, and that because of these virtues he was the first of all men to be made Pontifex Maximus while absent [Col. 0509A]. Scipio therefore suppressed the sedition as a private man and deserved the supreme pontificate through so outstanding an act. Since he obtained that office shortly afterwards [Col. 0509B], writers who did not properly distinguish the times wrote that he killed Gracchus while he was Pontifex Maximus.

P. Licinius Crassus Dives, Pontifex Maximus, died while conducting war against Aristonicus. The Epitome of Livy, book 59: “P. Licinius Crassus, consul, although at the same time Pontifex Maximus—which had never before occurred—set out beyond Italy, was defeated in battle, and was killed.” According to Julius Obsequens, chapter 87, this was in the consulship of Appius Claudius and M. Perpenna—that is, A.U.C. 623—when Crassus had been consul in the preceding year and had set out for the war in that same year, in which some also maintain that he died. Therefore Scipio could by no means have held the supreme pontificate during the sedition of Gracchus, which was suppressed in 620 or 621. But after Licinius Crassus was killed, that office was first offered to him, and while he was absent; for, to remove him from public hostility, he had been sent to Asia under the pretext of an embassy, as the author of *On Illustrious Men* testifies.

“He faithfully supplied.” Namely, pay and military provisions, what various authors call *praebenda*. I confess that I doubted whether *praefuit* (“he presided”) could be read; but Columbus, not unwillingly on my part, adopts the former explanation. Still, the passages he cites have attached to them the thing supplied, as similar instances occur in Terence, Cicero, Horace, and others. Yet just as *praebere* is used absolutely here, so too in the Theodosian Code *praebitores* are called provincials who furnished compulsory services and vehicles for the public post in certain provinces, as Jacob Gothofredus explains [Col. 0509C].

“Let him be clothed.” Namely, in the purple, which was the sign of imperial and Caesarean rank. Thus in chapters 20 and 28 Lactantius uses *exuere*, “to put off,” absolutely in the opposite sense, for “to lay aside imperial power.”

“He had changed the name in part…” This passage is obscure and, so far as I can see, corrupt; yet it may be restored by a very slight change. Lactantius says that Galerius changed the name of his relative Daia or Daza to Maximianus, because Diocletian had earlier changed Galerius’ own name. I therefore write: “whom he had recently [Col. 0509D] ordered to be called Maximinus after his own name. For Diocletian had also changed his name in part for the sake of an omen, because Maximianus displayed loyalty with the highest devotion.” Galerius Maximianus had formerly been called Galerius and surnamed Armentarius, “the cattle-herd,” because, born to farming parents, he had been a herdsman. Hence Aurelius Victor, *Caesars*, gives him this cognomen: “For these reasons he created Julius Constantius and Galerius Maximianus, whose cognomen was Armentarius, Caesars”; and the Epitome: “He created Constantius and Galerius Maximianus, surnamed Armentarius, Caesars.”

Though the sources do not expressly state that Galerius was called Armentarius before becoming Caesar, I do not hesitate to affirm it. It is improbable that anyone would have dared so to surname him after he had been raised to that pinnacle of honour, although I do not deny that later in the same Epitome he is so called while already Caesar. Diocletian therefore changed only part of the name—namely the cognomen Armentarius—and, retaining Galerius’ name, called him Maximianus. He did so as an omen, hoping that he would be as faithful to him as Herculius Maximianus, whose name he gave to the other. Victor speaks thus of Herculius’ loyalty: “He immediately commands Maximian—faithful in friendship, though half-rustic, yet good in military service and ability—to be emperor.” Yet the Epitome says that he was dear to no one, not even to his father or father-in-law Galerius. But since Herculius was not Diocletian’s son and did not have Galerius as a father-in-law, the text must certainly read: “This Maxentius was dear to no one ever,” as I mentioned above and as not only Valesius but Baluzius also showed [Col. 0510A].

“For the sake of the man” (*hominis causa*). Corrupt, as we have already indicated, for *ominis causa*, “for the sake of an omen.” The same error occurs in the scholiast on Juvenal, *Satires* II.142: “Barren women offered themselves to the Luperci during the February rites and were struck with a rod. On account of this man who…” There write: “were struck with a rod under this omen; who…” The remaining words do not seem capable of restoration without the aid of manuscripts [Col. 0510B].

“He is my relative.” This word is used loosely for “son of a sister.” The same usage occurs on a coin published by Du Cange in *Byzantine Families*: IMP. MAXENTIUS. DIVO. CONSTANTIO. ADFINI. Maxentius was the maternal half-brother of Flavia Maximiana Theodora, wife of Constantius.

## CHAPTER XIX
On the Kalends of May. Baluzius rightly observes that this was the actual day on which Diocletian and Herculius laid down the imperial power. Eusebius confirms this to some extent; for, after relating that Dionysius was beheaded on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, he adds, ἐν τούτῳ, that is, “during,” or “about,” the same time, that a change of emperors took place. Idatius is therefore mistaken in the Fasti, where he writes that this happened on the Kalends of April. He may not have understood Eusebius sufficiently well, and may have referred that ἐν τούτῳ to the Kalends of April, as the nearest date; but Lactantius makes it clear [Col. 0510C] that a longer interval is meant.

Columbus noted that Zosimus relates the same event, although it appears nowhere in him. I think that this distinguished man did not grasp Baluzius’s meaning, since he writes that there is indeed an error in Zosimus and in the Fasti of Idatius, where these events are said to have occurred when Diocletian was consul for the ninth and Maximian for the eighth time, on the Kalends of April. But I think the eminent man means that Zosimus relates the event as occurring under the consulship of Diocletian IX and Maximian VIII, while Idatius names the same consuls and the Kalends of April. Moreover, the author of the panegyric addressed to Herculius himself and to Constantine, ch. 8, also testifies that Maximian divested himself of imperial power in his eighth consulship; and shortly afterward he tells us that Diocletian was then weakened by illness and age, whereas Maximian retained sound and unimpaired strength.

The leading men of the soldiers . . . Thus *prior civitatis* (“leading man of the city”) occurs in the Passion of St. Mammarius in Mabillon, *Annals*, IV, p. 94; likewise *priores scrinii* (“chiefs of the bureau”) in the Theodosian Code, and *prior loci*, *prior scholae*, and similar expressions occur in Du Cange’s *Glossary*.

A column bearing Jupiter’s image. The ancients customarily erected columns in public places [Col. 0510D] and at places made solemn by some public celebration, placing upon them statues either of gods or of emperors. This could be established by many examples, were that my present task; but I shall merely note that a statue of the Emperor Marcian was placed upon the column at Constantinople which still survives there, with the following inscription, as Spon reports:

> BEHOLD THIS STATUE OF THE EMPEROR MARCIAN; [AND] THE FORUM [the inscription reads *torumque*; the proposed reading is *Forumque*]; TEREIUS VOWED [IT]; TATIANUS—THE WORK [text incomplete/uncertain].

A learned man supposes that Marcian’s heart was placed in a square vessel set atop the column, and that perhaps his body lay beneath the column. But scholars should consider whether *Forumque* ought rather to be written. Here, perhaps, a statue of Jupiter was placed because Diocletian wished to be regarded as descended from Jupiter; hence he was called Jovius, as is very well known.

Tristan, vol. III, p. 332, seems to suggest [Col. 0511A] that Diocletian laid down the purple in Jupiter’s temple. He certainly writes that Maximian too used these words when laying down the purple: “Receive, Jupiter, what you desired.” “What Diocletian did at Nicomedia, and Maximian at Milan, in Jupiter’s temple, both using these words: *Recipe*, etc.” But the author of the panegyric, ch. 12, from whom these details are drawn, does not even mention a temple; moreover, he speaks of Maximian alone, without mentioning Diocletian.

Eumenius, however, in ch. 13 of the panegyric addressed to Constantine, quite plainly suggests that Herculius laid down the imperial power in the temple of Jupiter—indeed, of Capitoline Jupiter. For, after praising Diocletian because he refused to resume the empire, he adds: “Thus he who had been adopted by him as a brother was ashamed not to imitate him; he regretted having sworn to him in the temple of Capitoline Jupiter.” That is: Herculius did not imitate Diocletian, and regretted having sworn to Diocletian, in Jupiter’s temple, that he would in good faith lay down imperial power following his example.

These things, however, were done by Herculius at Milan, [Col. 0511B] lest anyone perhaps understand Rome because Capitoline Jupiter is mentioned. For, following Rome’s example, Capitolia also existed in other cities: Suetonius attests this of Capua, *Tiberius*, ch. 40; the Passion of St. Saturninus in Chifflet and Ado in the *Martyrology*, p. 193, of Toulouse; Ado, p. 118, of Ravenna; Eumenius, in the oration on the Restoration of the Schools, of Augustodunum; and Pausanias, of Corinth. On this matter one may also consult Velser, book IV of *Rerum Augustanarum*, and his commentary on the conversion of St. Afra.

Now “column” in Greek is called στήλη (*stēlē*), a word that very often also means “statue,” a fact scholars frequently fail to notice. In the *Anthology*, book IV, ch. 8, under the heading εἰς εἰκόνας (“on images”), there occurs Posidippus’s epigram εἰς στήλην Ἀλεξάνδρου τοῦ Μακεδόνος (“on a statue of Alexander of Macedon”), which is wrongly translated “on Alexander’s column.” This is surely remarkable, since the poet celebrates a statue of Alexander made by Lysippus. Likewise, the στήλην Ἀμαζονίδα (*stēlēn Amazonida*) celebrated by Plato in the *Axiochus* should, I think, be translated not “a column of an Amazon” but “a statue of an Amazon.” Plutarch’s translators make the same error [Col. 0511C] in the *Life of Theseus*: for he calls the woman whom Theseus possessed Hippolyte, not Antiope. Some say that she fell while fighting Theseus, pierced by a javelin thrown by Molpadia: καὶ τὴν στήλην παρὰ τὸ τῆς γῆς Ὀλυμπίας ἱερὸν ἐπὶ ταύτῃ κεῖσθαι—“and that her statue, the one standing beside the sanctuary of Olympian Earth, was set up in her honor”; it is commonly but wrongly rendered, “that a column was erected.”

Diocletian cast his own purple upon him. Namely, upon Maximinus Daza or Daia. Yet I should like to ask scholars whether they think there was any distinction between the purple of an emperor and that of a Caesar. This passage certainly suggests the contrary, since Diocletian, an Augustus, clothed Maximinus, a Caesar, in his own purple. This in turn raises a question deserving inquiry: by what badge were emperors distinguished from Caesars? For coins show that both Caesars and emperors wore diadems, as the distinguished Spanheim, Dissertation 8, and Du Cange, no. 16 of his dissertation on coins of the lower age, have demonstrated; though at times the Caesarean dignity was bestowed χωρὶς τοῦ διαδήματος, “without the diadem,” as the latter notes from Chrysostom.

In this manner Demetrius, king of Syria, had Myrmes of Samos as his κοινωνὸν ἔξω τοῦ διαδήματος, “partner apart from the diadem,” according to Athenaeus, book XIII. Likewise Philostratus, at the end of book VII, contrasts ἐν Καίσαρος σχήματι (“in the guise of Caesar”) with ἐν διαδήματι (“with the diadem”): he writes that Julian lived five years in the dress of Caesar, but, after Constantius, two and a half years with the diadem. Hence it is perfectly clear that at that time the diadem was reserved for Augusti alone, although coins exist on which Julian appears diademed with the inscription **D. N. JULIANUS NOB. CAES.** From the other side’s inscription, **VOT. V. MULT.**, it is clear that they were struck in the final year of his Caesarean rank. Otherwise, on most coins Caesar Julian appears without a diadem or laurel crown.

Thus, when Julian was proclaimed Augustus by the soldiers while Constantius was still living, he was crowned with a diadem, or with a neck-chain because no diadem was at hand, in order that, by being crowned, he might at least display an indistinct semblance of the higher authority [Col. 0512A], as Ammianus Marcellinus testifies, book XX, ch. 4. It should also be noted there that Caesar Julian testifies that he had never possessed a diadem. It is therefore certainly strange that, while still Caesar, he appears diademed on coins—unless the coin was struck at the very time when he was proclaimed Augustus, since, as the same author testifies, book XXI, he was already celebrating his quinquennalia as Augustus; or, more probably, this should be attributed to the mint officials.

Otherwise Constantius Chlorus, Constantine, the younger M. Licinius, Crispus, Constantine the Younger, Constantius, and Decentius, as Caesars, appear on coins in Du Cange either with radiate crowns, laurel crowns, or bare heads. The exception is one coin on which **CONSTANTINUS JUN. NOB. CAES.** is also encircled by a diadem, though one not adorned with gems.

Aurelius Victor says that Gaius Caesar, or Caligula, was the first Roman emperor to assume the diadem: “He was the first, placing a diadem upon his head, to order himself to be called Lord.” But greater credit should be given to Suetonius, who writes that he came very near to assuming the diadem and converting the appearance of the principate into the form of kingship, ch. 22. [Col. 0512B] Indeed, Victor forgets himself in the *Epitome*, where he attributes this to Aurelian: “He was the first among the Romans to bind the diadem around his head.” Since Cedrenus and others make Constantine the Great the originator of this custom, either one must say with Valesius, on Ammianus Marcellinus XXI.1, that Aurelian did not use it continually, but only on feast days and more solemn occasions; whereas Constantine was the first to wear a permanent diadem, and from that time it was counted among the insignia of Augustan power and was not granted to Caesars; or else that Aurelian bound a diadem around his head without gems, while Constantine added gems to it—as indeed this adornment appears on coins.

Aurelian is not seen wearing a diadem, except that Tristan, vol. III, p. 211, mentions a coin on one side of which Vaballathus appears and on the other Aurelian, adorned in this way. He thinks this coin was struck in the East by Vaballathus to indicate that he submitted his imperial power to Aurelian, and that the diadem signified this, since the Romans had not yet at that time encircled their emperors’ heads [Col. 0512C] with it. On a coin published by Patin that is entirely similar, Aurelian is encircled by a laurel crown and Vaballathus by a diadem.

But before Aurelian, Antoninus Caracalla used a diadem, if Greek coins are to be trusted. Tristan, vol. II, p. 215, published one which on one side shows a trireme and beneath it **ΑΝΤΩΝΕΙΝΙΑΝΗΣ ΣΕΥΗΡΑΣ**, and **ΤΑΡΣΟΥ ΜΗΤΡΟΠ.**; on the other, according to his interpretation, Caracalla encircled by a diadem, with **ΑΥΤ. Κ. Μ. ΛΥΡ. ΕΥΗΡΟΣ. ΑΝΤΩΝΕΙΝΟΣ**. Unless we say that the people of Tarsus did this in the manner of Eastern kings, and that Caracalla never used a diadem.

Indeed, before Caracalla, Heliogabalus used a diadem, and a jeweled one at that, as the illustrious Salmasius notes, *Exercises on Pliny*, p. 370: “The royal diadem was a broad white band; such were the sacred fillets of priests . . . Such was the diadem of Roman emperors, which Heliogabalus was the first to use adorned with gems. Caligula had tried to use a diadem after Julius Caesar; but after Diocletian all used a jeweled one.” I wish that this great man had explained this to us more clearly.

Herodian, indeed, writes in book V that Heliogabalus adorned his head with στέφανον λιθῶν πολυτελῶν χροίᾳ διηνθισμένον, “a crown blooming with the colors of precious stones,” and elsewhere that he wore εἰς εἶδος θιάρης στεφάνην χρυσῷ καὶ λίθοις ποικίλην τιμίοις, “a crown in the shape of a tiara, distinguished by gold and precious gems.” But this was not properly a diadem; moreover, Heliogabalus wore it not as emperor but as priest of his god, as will be clear to anyone who consults Herodian.

But, leaving the diadem and returning to the purple, I think it first established that in Diocletian’s time nothing besides the investiture with purple was required to declare someone Augustus or Caesar; and that, if the diadem had also served that purpose, Lactantius would not have passed it over in silence. Secondly, the purple was the badge of so lofty a rank. Therefore Galerius sent purple to Constantine, whom the soldiers had made Augustus upon his father’s death, so that he might seem voluntarily to have admitted him into partnership, below, ch. 25. Maxentius likewise sent purple to his father, who was staying in Campania after laying down the imperial power, and twice called him Augustus, ch. 26. Hence those divesting themselves of imperial authority delivered their purple to the victor: ibid., “He surrendered himself and returned the garment and purple”—that is, the purple garment, the purple military cloak—“to the same man from whom he had received them”; again: “The people, who had been aroused, clothed Maxentius in purple, not against his will”—namely, the soldiers. Similar passages may also be seen in chapters 28, 29, 32, 47, and 50. But these matters are known; and some things concerning this purple may be consulted in Rad. Fornerius, *Rerum Quotidianarum*, V.30.

And he is sent back to his homeland. That is, to Dioclea near Salona, a town of Dalmatia, where, as the most learned man notes, he grew old in distinguished leisure. Aurelius Victor declares that Dioclea was Diocletian’s native place, and Paul the Deacon, book XI, follows him. Eutropius, book X, and Zonaras, however, write that he withdrew to Salona; so that *in patriam*, “to his homeland,” may be understood as “to Dalmatia,” or [Col. 0513B] “to Salona,” as now seems to me.

Aurelius Victor certainly says that Illyricum was the homeland of Diocletian, Herculius, Galerius, and Constantius. Constantine Porphyrogenitus, *Themes*, II.9, makes Diocletian native ἀπό τινος χωρίου Σαλώνας, “from a certain place, Salona.” Either he calls Salona a *chōrion*, “place,” though it had at that time been ravaged and destroyed by the Slavs; or he denotes the territory adjoining Salona; or *chōrion* means a city, in which case Diocletian was born in Salona itself. For Zonaras says: Διοκλητιανὸς ἐν Σάλωνι πόλει τῆς Δαλματίας διῆγεν, ἥτις ἦν αὐτῷ καὶ πατρίς—“Diocletian lived in the city of Salona in Dalmatia, which was also his native city.”

Dioclea, or Diocla, lay toward Epirus and far from Salona; nor do I think there were several cities by that name. That Diocletian withdrew to Salona is shown not only very clearly by his answer to Herculius and Galerius when they urged him to resume imperial rule—“Would that you could see at Salona the vegetables planted by our own hands! You surely would never judge this undertaking worth attempting”—but also by Diocletian’s palace, which was near Salona and is today called Spalato [Col. 0513C], as the late Spon (ὁ μακαρίτης), and George Wheler, an English knight, have clearly demonstrated in their most careful descriptions.

Indeed, Diocletian died in this palace or villa. Jerome in the *Chronicle*: “Diocletian dies not far from Salona in his villa at Spalato (according to others, Aspalato), and alone among all men is enrolled among the gods after dying a private citizen.” If all these words came from Jerome, then certainly this palace was called Spalatum or Aspalatum more than four hundred years ago. But, when I considered the Latin of Jerome’s age, it seemed to me that this word was at times added in the margin, as they say, and then found its way into the author’s text. This appears less contrary to truth because Eutropius—whom Scaliger reasonably suspects Jerome to have drawn upon—writes: “Diocletian, as a private citizen, grew old in distinguished leisure in a villa not far from Salona.”

Yet the same word also occurs in the *Notitia Imperii*: “Procurator of the Jovian weaving-house in Dalmatia, at Aspalato.” Accordingly, I would not oppose those who make this word more than four hundred years old, unless one thinks that here also it was added for explanatory purposes. Diocletian therefore had his villa or palace near Salona; he died there and perhaps was also buried there. Ammianus Marcellinus XVI.8 mentions his tomb: “He concealed, with certain accomplices, a purple veil stolen from Diocletian’s tomb.” The very learned Valesius believes that the underground vaulted chambers, elegantly constructed, described by Constantine Porphyrogenitus at Aspalathus, are Diocletian’s tomb itself. Yet it seems safer to me to judge that these are remains of the whole palace, which Spon shows to have been extremely vast.

Not only was Diocletian buried there; he was also enrolled among the gods. Valesius thinks that the purple veil laid in his tomb is the surest evidence of his consecration. I know that Eutropius and Jerome relate [Col. 0514A] that no one born after mankind’s beginning, except Diocletian, received the distinction of being enrolled among the gods despite dying as a private citizen. Yet I do not see what evidence a purple military cloak could furnish of that honor, since it might rather have been placed upon his bier or tomb to indicate that he had been emperor.

Furthermore, it seems very strange to me that no one except the authors just cited speaks of Diocletian’s consecration, nor does it occur on coins or marbles, although living emperors customarily attested their devotion toward the deceased through such monuments. What I should truly say on this matter I scarcely know, since it does not seem likely to me that Constantine or Licinius conferred this honor upon Diocletian: they thought that he had favored Maxentius and Maximinus, as is clear from Victor’s *Epitome*; and Constantine even allowed Diocletian’s images, together with Maximian’s, to be taken down, as Lactantius testifies, ch. 42.

Nevertheless Galerius Maximinus, in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* IX.10, calls Diocletian and Maximian θειοτάτους, “most divine,” which may aptly be translated *Divi*, “deified ones.” Yet a persecutor of Christians might have addressed them thus as a title of honor although they had not been consecrated. This honor, however, was granted by Maxentius to Maximian Herculius—if Herculius, rather than Galerius Maximianus, is meant.

But to return to Diocletian’s native place: I think he was born at Salona, or near Salona, that is, in the suburban territory of that city, because Lactantius says that he returned to his homeland and because it is established that, after laying down imperial power, he lived as a private citizen near Salona. Yet Victor mentions Dioclea, a city near Epirus: “Diocletian, a Dalmatian, the freedman of the senator Anulinus, [was called] Diocles from his mother and likewise from the town named Dioclea, deriving his names from both until he assumed imperial power.” Victor uses no circumlocution and clearly says that Diocletian, or Diocles, drew his name from his mother and the town in which he was born. What can I set against so ancient an authority? Scarcely anything—unless we say that Victor was deceived by the similarity of names, [Col. 0514C] or that the words have been dislocated and moved from their proper position.

Others, I think, will agree with me that this difficulty is not groundless when they examine the words of Paul the Deacon, who everywhere follows Victor: “From [his] mother, likewise from the town named Dioclea, he was called Diocles until he assumed imperial power.” A very different meaning arises from this. If we follow Paul, Diocletian was not born in the city of Dioclea; rather, his mother, born there into the daylight of life, bore the same name, and from her—as also from the town from which she sprang—her son was called Diocles. She could have given birth near Salona, or in the city itself, though she was native to Dioclea.

But since a new edition of Lactantius is still sweating beneath the press, I cannot refrain from adding some observations to what I have noted about the city of Dioclea, in case Diocletian’s history may thereby be more fully illuminated. I observe, then, that some relate Diocletian’s mother to have been native to that city, and others that Diocletian himself was born there. But the Emperor Constantine intervenes: in ch. 29 of *On the Administration of the Empire*, he writes that the κάστρον Διοκλείαν, “fortress of Dioclea,” which in his own time was inhabited by the Διοκλητιανοί, “Diocletians,” was built by Diocletian; and in ch. 35 he writes that the region called Διοκλέα derived its name from the fortress built there by Diocletian, which, though then still empty of inhabitants, was called Dioclea.

Moreover, in chapters 31 and 35 he testifies that Diocletian settled many Romans who had left Rome in Dalmatia. Undoubtedly he then also built Dioclea, or rather transferred a colony there, and adorned and enlarged the place from which his mother originated. For just as Constantine, ch. 30, writes that Salona was a fortress, ἔργον Διοκλητιανοῦ βασιλέως, “the work of Emperor Diocletian,” although it is certain that the city was far more ancient and thus could only have been adorned, enlarged, or fortified by Diocletian; so I think that Dioclea too was adorned and enlarged by that emperor—what the Latins expressed by *condere*, “to found,” and the Greeks by κτίζειν and οἰκοδομεῖν, “to build.”

It should also be observed that Aspalathus is mentioned twice in the same book. For in ch. 29 the emperor states that Diocletian built τοῦ Ἀσπαλάτου κάστρον ὅπερ παλάτιον μικρὸν ἑρμηνεύεται, “the fortress of Aspalathus, which is interpreted ‘little palace’”; that he possessed it as a kind of house, constructed his own court and palaces there, and that most of them had perished; that there remained the ἐπισκοτεῖον τοῦ κάστρου, “the episcopal building of the fortress,” and the church of St. Domnius, which had been the emperor’s bedchamber; that beneath were round vaults, which had been prisons into which he cast saints cruelly tortured by himself; that this fortress was built not of brick or *enchoregon*—a kind of material—but of squared stones joined together with iron and molten lead; that there were several columns with epistyles, upon which Diocletian wished to build vaults and cover the town; and, above these, houses of two or three vaulted stories—for this, I think, is how the Greek words should be translated. The city walls had no περίπατος, “walkway,” nor battlements, but only high walls, καὶ τοξικὰς φωταγωγούς, with openings for shooting out.

In ch. 30 he again writes that Salona and Aspalathus were built by Diocletian, and that his palace was there. Some of these things, I certainly think, should be counted as fables. First, it is scarcely credible that Diocletian wished to cover an entire city with vaults and place houses upon them. Secondly, what is related concerning the tortures of martyrs is empty, since none of the ancients mentions that Diocletian, after withdrawing to Salona upon laying down the purple, acted cruelly against Christians. Finally, I greatly doubt whether Aspalathus means “little palace.”

Furthermore, Constantine Porphyrogenitus, ch. 30, places Dioclea near the towns of the territory of Dyrrachium; he mentions no other city of that name, and therefore doubtless only one city so called existed in that region. Finally, in ch. 53 he consistently calls Constantius, the father of Constantine the Great, Constans; and there relates that, when he was a Τριβοῦνος, “tribune,” he led an army against the Sarmatians at the river Halys by Diocletian’s command—thus he himself served in Asia before becoming either Caesar or Augustus.

[Col. 0515C] The East must be trampled down. That is, devastated, destroyed, trodden underfoot. Thus they spoke of a conquered people, upon whom emperors therefore set the soles of their feet on coins. Justin, at the end of book XII, said “to trample down a people”; Corippus, “to trample down tyrants”; Julius Firmicus, “to trample down death”—and in the latter, by a harsher metaphor, one also reads “to trample the waves beneath the oars.” To this Ovid refers in *Tristia* IV.2:

> Behold, Germania too, her hair unbound, is said  
> To sit in mourning beneath the invincible leader’s foot.

And in *Epistles from Pontus* II.2:

> Nor did she disdain, once Illyrian arms were cast aside,  
> To bear the Caesar’s foot upon her submissive head.

Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* I.462 and II.748, speaks similarly; Lactantius, ch. 38, explains how Maximinus destroyed and ravaged the East.

## Chapter XX

[Col. 0515D] His nature was gentle. This was also apparent, if Orosius is to be trusted, VII.25, because he yielded Italy and Africa to Galerius and was content with Spain and Gaul. But I do not know whence Orosius derived this, since Diocletian retained for himself and Galerius the East in its broad sense; assigned Britain, Spain, and Gaul to Constantius; and Illyricum, Italy, and Africa to Maximian Herculius, as the illustrious bishop P. de Marca explains at the beginning of his dissertation on the Patriarchate of Constantinople.

But in Socrates, whom Orosius cites, I find nothing else than that Diocletian established τὰ βασίλεια, that is, the imperial residence, at Nicomedia. Victor speaks thus of the matter: “As though the empire had been apportioned, everything in the Gauls beyond the Alps was entrusted to Constantius; Africa and Italy to Herculius; and the Illyrian coast as far as the strait of Pontus to Galerius. Valerius retained the rest.” This clearly shows that Orosius was completely asleep when he wrote these things.

Lest he call him son. Caesars were thus called by [Col. 0516A] Augusti, as Baluzius shows on ch. 8. The uncertain author of the panegyric addressed to Maximian Herculius and Constantine, ch. 3: “O divine judgment of yours, Maximian, you who wished this man to be your grandson by right of adoption, your son by rank of majesty, and even your son-in-law!” Herculius, of course, had adopted Constantius, Constantine’s father, who thereby became his grandson; his son by rank of majesty because he was made Caesar by him, or because he had at that time been proclaimed emperor by him. That this was sometimes done I show from an ancient inscription on ch. 8. Maximinus, in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* IX.10, calls Diocletian and Maximian θειοτάτους γονέας, “most divine parents,” because they had made him Caesar.

## Chapter XXI

They treat them as household property. That is, as slaves, who are denoted by *familia*. Phaedrus, Fable 58: “Aesop, when he was his master’s only *familia*”—that is, when his master had no other slave than Aesop. Fable 46: “The *familia* throws scraps.” But these matters are known. Brissonius, book I *On the Kingdom of the Persians*, demonstrates by many examples that the kings of Persia regarded all their subjects as slaves.
