He removed their honors. Perhaps for this reason: that they might be tortured. For otherwise decurions and men of rank were exempt from torture by Roman laws, as Baluzius notes on this passage. Hence Ammianus Marcellinus XXVIII.7 writes of Valentinian:

> When he learned these things, he became enraged; being a more vehement enemy of vices than a severe judge, by a single proclamation in cases of this sort—which he arrogantly mixed with a charge of injured majesty—he decreed that all whom the justice of ancient law and the decisions of the deified emperors had exempted from bloody examinations should be subjected to torture if the case required it.

But later, when envoys sent by decree of the nobility begged that punishments not be more severe than offenses and that no senator be exposed to tortures by an unprecedented and unlawful practice, “the cruel order was amended,” as the same author says. Men of rank were tortured only in charges of treason, as Valesius and, before him, Fornerius, *Rerum Quotidianarum* III.8, teach. Thus Lampadius was first stripped of the dignity of the prefecture before he was tortured, according to Ammianus Marcellinus, book XV. More on this matter may be found in Langlaeus, *Semestria*, XIII.1.

To this belongs in some degree the elegant passage in the *Petition of Faustinus*: “But Clementinus, although he was not a Christian, nevertheless showing reverence for the episcopal name—especially in the case of a man whom he saw holding it reasonably and faithfully—replied to Hosius: ‘I do not dare,’ he said, ‘to send a bishop into exile so long as he remains under the name of bishop. But first pronounce sentence yourself, deposing him from the honor of the episcopate; then at last I shall carry out against him as a private person what you desire to be done by the emperors’ command.’”

A sport. Fighting bears and other wild beasts was considered a sport and was among the exercises of young men. Below, ch. 24: “Under the pretext of exercise and SPORT he had exposed him to wild beasts.” Perhaps *lusorium* derives its name from this: those trained for it seemed to play with wild beasts, eluding their attacks by leaps or other means, as is very clear from the Liège Diptych and Wilthemius’s notes upon it; to these may be added Bulenger, ch. 29, *On Circus Hunting*.

He ordered them to be brought by name. These beasts evidently had their own names, just as in Marcellinus XXIX one of the she-bears kept by Valentinian was called Golden Mica and another Innocence. In the collection of Leonardo Agostini, the foremost antiquary of Rome, part II, no. 32, there is a gem on which one sees a man holding a whip and soothing with it a she-bear leaping upon him. Around it is the inscription **ΕΥΤΥΧΙ ΜΛΡΚΕΛΛΕ**, and above the beast’s back **ΕΙΡΗΝΗ**. The latter is evidently the proper name of the she-bear, while with the former the man leading the beast seems to pray for good fortune. Similarly, it is established from Suetonius, Dio, and ancient inscriptions published by both Gruter and Spon that individual circus horses had their own names.

[Col. 0517A] Not exactly for eating, but for swallowing up. Bears customarily lick and suck blood, and thus consume a body; hence Eusebius rightly counts them among αἱμοβόροις θηρσίν, “blood-devouring beasts,” *Ecclesiastical History* VIII.7. *Obsorbere*, “to swallow up,” also occurs in Plautus, *Truculentus* 2.3.30: “Those things which swallow whatever comes within the bolts”; and *Miles Gloriosus* 3.2.21: “For I swallowed it up, because it was very hot and burned my throat.”

But since bears have been mentioned, I shall attempt to explain one or two passages in the Passion of Saints Perpetua and Felicitas, which are exceedingly elegant and, so far as I know, have not been adequately explained. Xiphilinus, drawing from Dio, relates that the Emperor Commodus devoted careful attention to hunts and slaughterings of beasts, and among other things uses these words:

> Διείληπτο γὰρ τὸ θέατρον πᾶν συμπήκτοις τισὶ διαμέτροις τήν τε στέγην περίδρομον ἔχουσι, καὶ δίχῃ τέμνουσιν ἄλληλα, ἵν’ ἐξ ὀλίγου πανταχόθεν τετραχῇ τὰ θηρία μεμερισμένα ῥᾷον ἀκοντίζηται.

“For the entire amphitheatre was divided by certain joined diameters, having a roof around which one could walk, and cutting one another in two, so that beasts divided into four parts might more easily be struck with missiles from every side out of a confined place.”

Lucas Holstenius, a man comparable to few, thinks that Xiphilinus speaks of the bridges of the amphitheatre, mentioned in the Passion of Saints Perpetua and Felicitas. He comments:

> “Since bridges are mentioned a little earlier, this seems to have been done according to Commodus’s arrangement, namely, that there should be bridges in the amphitheatre. For Xiphilinus relates under Commodus that this emperor constructed BRIDGES across the arena of the amphitheatre in order to dispatch beasts from them.”

But I am persuaded that Commodus’s arrangement has nothing in common with these bridges; and I hope others will agree who are willing to compare and examine the words of Dio and the most ancient Passion. Commodus divided the amphitheatre by συμπήκτοις τισὶ διαμέτροις—that is, by joined boards raised upright—which cut the arena into four equal parts in the following manner. That these structures were wooden is sufficiently indicated by πήγνυμι, since that word is almost always used properly of such material. Πήκτη δωμάτων, “joined house-doors,” are doors made by fastening several boards together; πῆγμα (*pegma*) is a wooden apparatus in an amphitheatre, concerning which scholars have said enough.

Moreover, the diameters were enclosed by a στέγῃ περιδρόμῳ, by which Dio means that a covered portico was constructed around the amphitheatre, through which the emperor could walk around and from which he could dispatch beasts very conveniently with missiles. The translator wrongly ascribes the roof to the diameters; the following diagram will plainly show that this is wholly contrary to the author’s meaning.

A. Amphitheatre.  
B. περίδρομος (*peridromos*), surrounding walkway.  
C–D. First diameter.  
E–F. Second diameter, both cutting one another at right angles.

This is fully confirmed by Herodian, who, speaking of the same matter in Book I, says: “For Commodus a **peridromos** (περίδρομος), a circuit all around, had been constructed, so that he might not run the risk of fighting the beasts at close quarters, but, hurling missiles from above and from a safe position, might display skill in throwing rather than courage”; that is, in Angelo Poliziano’s translation [Col. 0517D]: “When the day of the spectacle had arrived,”, and the amphitheatre was full, a peridrome had been built for Commodus, by which he could run around in a circuit, lest he should be endangered by fighting the beasts hand-to-hand; rather, by casting weapons from above and from a secure place, he might exhibit his skill in missile-throwing rather than his bravery.” A little later he says that Commodus himself, running in a circuit, pierced the noblest animals from above with missiles: “running around, he hurled missiles from above” (περιθέων ἄνωθεν κατηκόντιζεν).

Herodian too records the peridrome, or portico; but Dio adds further, “and [the diameters] cut one another in two” (καὶ δίχη τέμνουσιν ἄλληλα), or, as I should translate it, “and intersected one another equally.” Aristotle speaks thus in *Politics*, Book VI: “If the court be divided equally into two” (Ἐὰν δίχα γένηται δικαστήριον). Nor indeed can any other division be understood, since shortly afterward he says that the animals were divided into four parts; and *diameter* is scarcely used except where a whole is divided into two equal parts, as is readily apparent from the diameter of the terrestrial globe and of other circles: drawn through their centre [Col. 0518A], it makes two equal parts.

In this amphitheatre there were two diameters: one drawn across the breadth, the other across the length. Thus that structure was divided into four equal parts, as is plainly apparent in the figure set forth. Dio gives the reason: “so that the beasts, divided fourfold on every side, might more easily be struck with missiles from a short distance” (ἵν᾽ ἐξ ὀλίγου πανταχόθεν τετραχῆ τὰ θηρία μεμερισμένα ῥᾶον ἀκοντίζηται); or, as I judge it should be translated, “so that they might more easily be struck with missiles from every side in a short time.”

Yet one may properly ask by what means spectators could have watched the killing of the beasts if the peridrome had been constructed from boards from top to bottom. For, if it had that form, people could in no way have enjoyed the spectacle. I therefore think either that this peridrome and the diameters were not so high, and that the lower seats were left vacant; or that, although the diameters were indeed raised high, the lower portion of the peridrome was open to sight, and that it existed only in its upper part—so that Commodus could go around and throw missiles at the beasts, while the spectators could take in everything with their eyes [Col. 0518B].

The *pontes* (“bridges”) praised in the Passion have nothing in common with this arrangement of Commodus. I shall show, more clearly than daylight, that they had another use—yet on this condition and qualification: I shall advance nothing regarding their origin, which is wholly unknown. The *PONTES*, then, were elevated platforms in the form of bridges: one end rested on the ground, while the other was raised on wooden supports, or supports made of some other material. Upon them those condemned to the beasts were stationed or bound, so that the beasts might rush upon them with greater force and that the tearing or “tormenting” (*vexatio*), as they called it, might be visible to all. There was then no division of the amphitheatre; rather, in the open arena, exposed to every eye, the *PONTES* were erected approximately, I think, in the following manner.

Certainly the author of the Passion confirms this explanation: “And when he had been bound beneath the bear upon the bridge, the bear refused to come forth from its cage.” That is: when the martyr, bound to the bear, was placed upon the bridge so that the bear might rush at and rage against him [Col. 0518C]—what shortly before he called “binding and presenting him to the boar”: “Accordingly, when he was being presented to the boar, the hunter rather, who had bound him to the boar, was gored by that same beast and died after the days of the games.” That is: while he was laid down bound upon the bridge, or certainly in the arena, and offered to the boar to be torn apart.

This *PONS* is called a *pulpitum* (“platform”) in the same Passion. “Accordingly, when recalled for the contest of the spectacle, having encountered the leopard, he was also tormented by the bear upon the platform.” That is, placed upon the platform or bridge, he was first tormented by the leopard and then by the bear—that is, bitten and torn, which is the usual sense of this word. Arnobius and Lactantius, in Book VII of the *Institutions*, attribute *vexationes* to beasts; and the Greeks call this treatment “the tearing of beasts” (ἑλκυσμὸν τῶν θηρίων).

Indeed, martyrs are said to “ascend” with reference to these platforms or bridges, as appears from the same Passion: “The others indeed received the sword motionless and in silence; but much more [was this true of] Saturus, who, as he had ascended first, was the first to yield up his spirit.” He had ascended, namely, onto the platform or bridge. Although I would not deny that the *spoliarium* may also be understood here [Col. 0518D]. Since it was like an underground cave—Cassius Severus calls it a *specus*, Pliny a sinister receptacle—and since Saturus came from it into the theatre by steps, he is not inappropriately said to have ascended. This is my opinion on the matter; I am nevertheless ready to change it if anyone offers a better explanation.

## CHAPTER XXII

**They were corrected with the spear.** As punishment by the sword was more honourable than punishment by the axe, so correction by the spear seems to have been more honourable than chastisement with clubs; and I suppose that both sword and spear owe their origin to military service. Yet I do not think that Apuleius, Book X, mentions this custom, as a learned man supposes; and by *disciplina* there I understand military discipline, according to whose prescription an army on the march had to arrange its baggage.

In the Passion of Saints Perpetua and Felicitas [Col. 0519A], Perpetua sees in a vision a ladder of marvellous size, in whose sides every kind of iron implement was fixed—swords, spears, hooks, daggers. But these spears, I think, are mentioned because martyrs were sometimes pierced through with them. After this word had been borrowed from the Spaniards, as Gellius testifies, XV.30, it began to be used frequently; and certain soldiers armed in this fashion were called *Lancearii*, as is clear from the *Notitia Imperii* and from Gruter’s inscription 3, p. 495, in which a prefect of the *Lancearii* seems to be mentioned. The petition of Faustinus also mentions them: “And first indeed he torments [them] through public authorities, so that on several occasions he has had [a man] seized only in the dead of night and carried away from the city by lance-bearers.” Before the tent of the camp prefect a spear was planted, according to Obsequens in the final book of *Prodigies*, perhaps so that it might be distinguished from the others.

**A good death.** This expression also occurs in Publilius Syrus; but in his latest edition it is wrongly written [Col. 0519B]:

> A good delay is for a man that which extinguishes the evils of life.

For one must read either *hour* (*hora*) or *death* (*mors*). Syrus generally calls a death good when it removes someone wretched and unhappy from life. The most distinguished Baluzius also counts strangulation among good deaths, because persons who end life in that manner die without agonies and tortures. Lactantius, chapter 30, calls it a shapeless death, after Virgil’s example, and a foul and disgraceful death, in view of the dishonour attending such an end. The medieval writer Widukind calls it a bad death in Book III: “Three leaders of the Hungarian nation were captured and presented to Duke Henry; they were punished with a bad death, as they deserved: for they burst asunder by hanging.” For everyone will readily concede that strangulation and such hanging should be reckoned one and the same thing.

Long ago Homer, at the end of *Odyssey* X, called death by hanging “not a pure death” (μὴ καθαρὸν θάνατον). Eustathius notes [Col. 0519C] that “a pure death” (καθαρὸν θάνατον) was considered death by the sword (τὸν διὰ ξίφους), but that death by hanging (τὸν ἀγχονιμαῖον) was polluted or abominable; on this matter he should be consulted in full at *Odyssey* XI, p. 1678. Before Eustathius, Hesychius observed the same distinction in explaining this Homeric passage: “Certainly not a pure death, through hanging. Death [by hanging] is not pure, but [that] through the sword [is]; hence they do not even perform funeral rites for those who have hanged themselves” (Μὴ μὲν δὴ καθαρῷ θανάτῳ δι᾽ ἀγχόνης . θάνατος οὐκ ἔστι καθαρός, ἀλλ᾽ ὁ διὰ ξίφους . ὅθεν οὐδὲ ἐναγίζουσι τοῖς ἀπηγξαμένοις). He further teaches us that not even funeral offerings were made for those strangled.

Xenophon, at the end of Book II of the *Anabasis*, recounting the death of Meno of Thessaly, plainly testifies that beheading was regarded as the most honourable death: “But after the other generals had already been killed, he too was punished with death by the king—not, indeed, as Clearchus and the other generals, whose heads were cut off, ‘which death seemed the noblest’” (ὅσπερ κάλλιστος θανάτων ἐδόκει εἶναι); “but, as a wicked man, he is said, after being tortured alive for a whole year, finally to have expired.” Seneca somewhere testifies that men die more gently by no manner of death than when the neck is cut by the sword.

Conversely, Latinus Pacatus calls strangulation an infamous and womanish death, chapter 28 [Col. 0519D]:

> One of them, after the highest magistracies, consular purple robes, and a kind of senate of honours accumulated within one household, was compelled to renounce life; the other had his throat broken at home by the hands of British guards, and the disgrace of a womanish death was branded upon him—as though a man especially fond of the sword had preferred to perish by a noose rather than by the sword.

From Tacitus and Suetonius, the most distinguished Scheffer observes that women were subjected to this form of punishment. It should further be noted in passing that Tacitus, at the end of Book XVI of the *Annals*, where he narrates that the slowness of death brought grievous sufferings to one dying with his veins opened, speaks not of Petronius, as Baluzius supposes, but of Thrasea Paetus.

**A good death.** That is, an easy death, without agonies and tortures; in this sense Baluzius observes in chapter 26 that opening the veins is called a good death. It also seems to have been considered more honourable to end life by a blow from the sword than by one from an axe. At the end of the Republic punishment by the sword was not yet in use [Col. 0520A], as Casaubon rightly observes from Lucan; but under the emperors it began to be employed. And just as lictors used the axe, soldiers removed the heads of condemned persons with the sword, so that this custom seems to have derived its origin from them.

A soldier skilled in decapitation is mentioned by Suetonius in *Caligula*, chapter 32; and Antoninus Caracalla rebuked Papinian’s killer for striking him with an axe rather than a sword, according to Dio and Spartianus, whose words are: “Papinian was struck with an axe and killed by soldiers; after this had been done, [Caracalla] said to the executioner: ‘You ought to have carried out my order with a sword.’” From this it is quite clear that soldiers ordinarily employed the sword and that its punishment was considered more honourable than that of the axe.

And although Lactantius calls decapitation a good death because it is gentler, it too may sometimes have its own agonies and pains—namely, when the soldier, or “cutter of necks,” as Cicero says in the speech for Roscius, inflicts several blows. Latinus Pacatus, chapter 41:

> Unless indeed another’s hand is gentler than one’s own, or private death fouler than public death, or it is a longer punishment to bend beneath the sword [Col. 0520B], to burden the body with the wound, and to receive death all at once rather than divide the punishment—to bend the knee, to stretch out the neck for perhaps more than one blow.

Hence the relatives of condemned persons gave money to the lictors, so that, to alleviate suffering, they might remove their heads with a single blow, as is clear from Cicero’s Fifth Speech against Verres. From that passage, no less than from Suetonius’s *Life of Caligula*, chapter 30, we infer that the populace did not take up weapons against an executioner if he inflicted several blows on the condemned man. Indeed, later it was established by law or custom that after the third blow the executioner dared not strike further, if credit is to be given to the history of the Passion of Blessed Cecilia, Valerian, Tiburtius, and others, published by Bosius. On p. 26 occur these words:

> When the executioner had struck her with a third blow, he could not sever her head; thus the bloodstained executioner left her half-dead. For among the ancients a law had been imposed upon him: if he did not decapitate [a person] in three blows, he did not dare strike further [Col. 0520C].

**Advocates were removed, and jurists either exiled or killed.** He rightly distinguishes these groups, because the former pleaded cases in the forum or courts, while the latter gave opinions on points of law, as is clear even from Cicero and from Hotman’s little work entitled *The Jurist*.

**Letters were counted among the evil arts.** By “evil arts” I understand magical arts, forbidden by imperial edicts, which are called *artes malae* and *artes Dardaniae*, as I show in my notes on Homer’s *Apotheosis*, p. 271. Ammianus Marcellinus, XXIII.6, calls them “secret arts”; Statius, Book I of the *Thebaid*, calls them the “Thracian art.” I once thought that Proclus, in his encomium of Blessed Chrysostom, called magic the art of Midas; but now I embrace exclusively what Johann van Haarsholten, a man of distinguished nobility, suggested to me in conversation. At that time he was delegated, on behalf of the Frisians, to the assembly of the most powerful States General. I believe that there one should read: “he stripped Artemis naked” (*Artemida nudavit*) or “he drove Artemis away” (*fugavit*).

**Military judges, unlearned in humane letters, without assessors.** That is, governors, proconsuls, dukes, counts, and others [Col. 0520D] who commanded military affairs in the provinces administered justice to provincials without employing assessors or jurists, as emperors themselves had formerly also been accustomed to do, according to Fornerius, Book IV of *Everyday Matters*, chapter 10. These men were, as it were, advisers to judges; hence, in an ancient inscription, C. Calpurnius Asclepiades is said to have sat with the magistrates of the Roman people. Since this Asclepiades is said to have been a physician, it seems that persons other than jurists were also employed—unless we suppose that he simultaneously devoted himself to law.

From this period, I think, the custom gradually prevailed that ordinary or civil judges were disregarded and cases brought before military jurisdiction. Constantius, Arcadius, Honorius, and Marcian prohibited this by laws, as Gothofredus teaches in his notes on vol. I of the *Theodosian Code*, p. 86.

Under Μαξιμῖνος (*Maximinus*), Suidas relates that, once he had become emperor, he immediately dismissed all the friends who had been intimate with Alexander and all those [Col. 0521A] who were called σύνεδροι, “assessors,” by the Senate; and that, while he ruled in the East, he perpetrated many impious acts, persecuted Christians, and at last fell into a most serious disease: his flesh melted like wax, his body seemed to burn as though in a fire, and human form itself was destroyed. From this it is evident that he too dismissed assessors. Yet this must be understood to mean that he dismissed only those who were friends of Alexander.

Suidas drew the earlier part of this narrative from the beginning of Book VII of Herodian. Thus one should first read ἐπιλεχθέντες, “chosen,” or *electi*; next, those words refer to Maximinus, who succeeded Alexander Severus. But what follows concerning his death must be referred to Gaius Valerius Maximinus Daza, of whom Eusebius, at the end of Book IX, and Lactantius, chapter 49, narrate precisely similar things; or else to Maximian Galerius, of whom chapter 33 treats.

## CHAPTER XXIII

**With census officials dispersed everywhere . . .** Thus in chapter 26 and chapter 6 [Col. 0521B]: “Yet no trust was placed in these same census officials.” Those, namely, who conducted the census in the provinces were called *censitores*, not *censores*. Hence an inscription mentions a *censitor* of the province of Hither Spain, and *censitores* of other provinces occur on the same stones. They were stationed in towns or communities, and those who lived in the countryside had to come there with their children and slaves. Thus all the forums of towns or communities were filled with crowds of slaves, and urban and rural commoners were gathered together in the communities, as Lactantius immediately says.

**Animals of every kind were registered.** That is, they were entered in writing and recorded in their registers. He speaks significantly and properly; for the tax paid in the free Republic for grazing livestock was called *scriptura* (“registration”). Hence, according to Festus, a *scripturarius ager* is grazing land, and tax-farmers are called *scripturarii*, as is well known.

What I once added—that Jews paid a tax for trees, as on this occasion, by Galerius’s order [Col. 0521C], vines and trees were counted—I now retract. I think that Juvenal, *Satires* III.15, generally censures Roman greed and contempt for the ancient religion, since they leased the grove of the Camenae to Jews.

**They were suspended . . .** Namely, from the rack (*equuleus*). Prudentius, in the hymn on the Roman martyr:

> Inflamed by this, Asclepiades ordered  
> The body, to be disembowelled, to hang  
> Suspended from the distant rack . . .

The same author elsewhere:

> Do you think me wretched because I hang,  
> Stretched out with arms twisted backward? . . .

The Passion of Saint Tarachus: “Strip him, bind him, and suspend him.” Again: “When you are suspended, consent and sacrifice.” These two passages agree exactly with Lactantius, no less than another from Ammianus Marcellinus, XIV.9: “Eusebius, boldly denying the accusations, remained steadfast in the same degree of constancy while suspended.” For this he says elsewhere, XIX.12: “Certainly clinging to the rack for a long time.”

The word *equuleus*, I think, is corrupted [Col. 0521D] in Ado’s *Martyrology*, p. 38: “Then he was chained and sent into exile, in which he was again beaten for a long time with clubs.” The sense requires that one read *equuleum*, “the rack.” How martyrs or criminals were stretched and suspended upon the rack may be seen in Magius, Gallonius, and others.

**Sons were suspended against their parents; every most faithful slave was tortured against his master.** That is, children were suspended on the rack in order that they might give testimony against their parents—namely, that they had not properly declared their property. For the same reason slaves were questioned under other and doubtless more severe tortures. Lactantius expresses this elegantly through the word *vexabantur* (“they were tormented”). For this word conveys the sense of a great calamity; and, as Gellius says, II.6, one who is carried, dragged, and pulled this way and that is properly said to be *vexari*.

To this may be added Asconius on the Second Speech against Verres. Lactantius, chapter 27: “Now the despoiler of Italy had ravaged everything as an enemy,” that is, plundered and laid waste it. In this sense the word is frequent [Col. 0522A] in Justin, Florus, and others; add Servius on Virgil’s *Eclogues* VI and the eminent Salmasius, p. 787, *On the Method of Interest*. Holstenius, in his notes on the Passion of Saints Perpetua and Felicitas, has shown that the word was also applied to arena contests, and that those whom beasts wounded with horn or mouth, without killing them, were said to have been “tormented” (*vexati*) by beasts. Perhaps by *vexatio* in Suetonius, *Tiberius*, chapter 61, tortures should be understood.

**Years were added to little children.** Either this was done so that they could be tortured, just as Lipsius, on Tacitus, *Annals* V.9, notes that a certain boy was ordered by the triumvirs during the proscription to put on the manly toga so that he could lawfully be killed; or, more likely, so that he might pay the tax. For imperial laws provided that, for example, those under ten years of age and those over sixty were not obliged to pay the poll tax, as is clear from Law III, *Digest*, *On Censuses*, and Laws IV and VI of the *Theodosian Code* under the same title, where Jacobus Gothofredus may be consulted.

**Payments for heads.** In this chapter Lactantius sharply attacks Galerius Maximian, because, by his order, the *censitores* searched out and investigated everything [Col. 0522B]. He reports that they measured the fields clod by clod, and so forth, as though all these practices had then been introduced for the first time. But matters stand very differently. For Ulpian, who lived in Hadrian’s time, writes in his book *On Censuses* that fields, arable lands, vineyards, olives, meadowland, pastures, coppice woods, the number of vines, slaves and their ages, duties and occupations, fishponds, harbours, saltworks, and tenants were entered in census registers. Thus Galerius introduced nothing new, and he can be blamed either for excessive harshness, or because he revived an abandoned practice, or because he introduced this tax into provinces that had not formerly paid it.

For this reason Lactantius narrates, as though it were unusual, that urban and rural commoners were gathered together in the communities. As I have already noted, the *censitores* in the communities prepared census registers, and the fields situated in the territory were recorded there, as is clear from Law IV, §2, *Digest*, *On Censuses*. Likewise, the persons of country dwellers inhabiting the territory of some town were recorded [Col. 0522C]. Yet I do not see what new and unusual practice Galerius introduced, unless Lactantius means that citizens and country people were compelled indiscriminately to pay the poll tax, whereas formerly the *honorati* and *decuriones* had been exempt from this payment, and, in eastern provinces, even the urban populace itself, as Valesius teaches in his notes on Ammianus Marcellinus, XVI.5; to him may be added Contarenus, chapter 18 of *Various Readings*.

## CHAPTER XXIV

**He had exposed him to beasts.** Baluzius rightly observes from Praxagoras that it was a lion, and, agreeing with Tristano, vol. III, p. 528, that the memory of this event is preserved on a coin [Col. 0522D]. He further reports that Pomponius Laetus relates the same story, and thinks that Laetus drew it from some author other than Praxagoras—perhaps Zonaras, in whom the same story is also found. But I do not find in Praxagoras that Constantine defeated the lion *corps à corps*, so as to crush it, nor that he lacked weapons. He may have been portrayed so on coins because, after Hercules’ example, he conquered a lion; legendary history relates that Hercules crushed the lion with his breast, as Statius sings, or slew it unarmed in the clasp of his arms.

**At the very turning point.** At the very critical moment, because dangers still awaited him and because he was about to see his father alive.

**Having received the commands . . .** Which, I think, he was to carry to his father Constantius.

**The public post was stripped bare before him.** That is, there were no horses at the stations, because it precedes that all public horses had been removed from many posting-stations. Florus, II.15: “The port of work stripped bare.” Cicero, *Letters to Atticus* XIII: “Stripped of protection.” The author of the Epitome of Victor speaks thus of this matter:

> While still a young man, he was detained by Galerius in the city of Rome under pretext of religion; taking flight, and, in order to frustrate his pursuers, killing the public beasts of burden wherever his route led, he reached his father in Britain.

There he wrongly writes that Constantine had been held hostage in Rome. Paul the Deacon also errs when, in Book X, he relates that Diocletian wished to kill Constantine by treachery because he saw him advancing in intelligence, bodily strength, and aptitude for learning [Col. 0523A], and perceived that he would be the destroyer of tyranny and of Diocletian’s system. For all this applies to Galerius, nor is it credible that Diocletian pursued such a design, since he wished to make Constantine Caesar. Hence I also think Philostorgius errs, I.5, where he writes that Constantine fled “the plot of Diocletian” (τὴν ἐπιβουλὴν Διοκλητιανοῦ).

**He could scarcely restrain his tears.** Therefore the author of the Valesian Excerpts is mistaken in writing that Galerius sent Constantine back to his father after he had caused the victory that Constantine won over the Sarmatians.

**He reached his father . . .** Doubtless at York in Britain, where he lay ill and died on the fourth day after Constantine’s arrival, as Baluzius thinks. But the author of the Excerpts diverges widely from this, writing that Constantine, in utmost haste, crossed the Alps on post-horses after cutting their hamstrings behind him, and came to his father Constantius at Boulogne [Col. 0523B], formerly called Gesoriacum by the Gauls; and that, after a victory over the Picts, his father Constantius died at York.

But he is undoubtedly mistaken. Constantine found his father sick and near death not in Gaul but in Britain, as all the other writers unanimously testify. Next, according to the opinion of scholars, Constantius crossed into Britain in the year of Christ 305 to wage war against the Picts, and died at York on the eighth day before the Kalends of August [25 July] in the year 306.

Yet Eumenius, or another author of the Panegyric addressed to Constantine, chapter 7, greatly confuses the question:

> For already then you were called by heavenly votes to the safety of the Republic, when, at the very time your father was crossing into Britain, your sudden arrival shone upon the fleet already setting sail; so that you seemed not to have been conveyed by the public post, but to have flown there by some divine swiftness.

For he also plainly implies that Constantine sought Britain from Gaul together with his father Constantius, or saw his father setting sail. He seems unlikely to have said such things before Constantine himself if they were untrue. The panegyrist therefore recounts almost the same things as the author of the Excerpts [Col. 0523C], but plainly rejects the subsequent victory over the Picts, because the same and the following chapter establish that Constantius did not survive long after his son’s arrival. This is particularly shown by these words:

> Good gods, with what felicity did you endow Constantius Pius even in his departure! The emperor, about to pass into heaven, saw the heir whom he was leaving behind.

I leave it to others to reconcile these accounts.

**He delivered [it] into his hands.** In the *Life* of the holy Fathers Metrophanes and Alexander, in Photius, p. 1406, we read that Constantine was instructed in the Christian sacred rites by his father, was proclaimed Caesar by him, and was called βασιλέα, “king” or “emperor,” by his dying father. But Photius writes that he does not know from where these things were drawn, because he knew, of course, that they were contrary to truth.

The same Acts recount the words spoken by Constantius to his son while dying. If these events really took place as narrated, then Lactantius’s statement that Constantius received rest from life will receive no slight illumination. Accordingly, the same work reports [Col. 0523D] that Constantius died in the third year of the persecution. Yet this is not so if we make an exact calculation: the persecution began at the Terminalia, or 23 February, in 303; from there to March 306 are three years. But Constantius died on the eighth day before the Kalends of August [25 July] in 306, when the fourth year of the persecution was already under way.

**The holy religion restored.** Either one must write *restitutio*, “restoration,” or, with Columbus, *restitutae*, “restored,” so that Constantine may truly be called *Restitutor Religionis Christianae*, “Restorer of the Christian Religion.” Thus Aurelian and Carus are called *Restitutor Orbis*, “Restorer of the World”; Probus, *Restitutor Exercitus*, “Restorer of the Army”; Alexander Severus, *Restitutor Monetae*, “Restorer of the Coinage.” On another coin of Aureolus occurs: *LEGIO I MINERVA RESTITUTA*, “The First Minervan Legion Restored.”

## CHAPTER XXV

**His laurelled image.** It received this name, I think, because it was encircled by a laurel crown. See Meursius in the Graeco-barbarous Glossary under λαβράτον, and Du Cange in the *Glossary of the Middle Ages*, concerning the expressions “laurelled letters,” “laurelled doorposts,” and others [Col. 0524A].

**But Constantine—not emperor, as he had become, but Caesar.** The authors disagree. Some say that after his father’s death he was made emperor; others that he was made only Caesar by the soldiers. Lactantius follows the former view, as does Eusebius, Book VIII, chapter 13, and Socrates, Book I, chapter 2. But Zosimus, II.6, relates that the soldiers assigned Constantine “the rank of Caesar” (Καίσαρος ἀξίαν); and the Valesian Excerpts testify that he was made Caesar with the consent of all the soldiers.

Eumenius says no differently in chapter 11 of the panegyric which he delivered to Constantine Augustus: “O fortunate Britain, and now more blessed than all lands, which first beheld Constantine Caesar!” Eumenius certainly would not have said this—especially given what seems to be implied also in the preceding chapter—if the matter had been otherwise.

Hugh of Fleury, though a writer of later times, follows the same view [Col. 0524B], and relates in his *Chronicle* that Constantius appointed Licinius Caesar of the Spanish provinces and his son Constantine Caesar of the Gallic provinces. The former assertion, however, is wholly contrary to truth. That Constantine was Caesar is entirely certain, and coins attest it: on them he is called not only Caesar, but also *filius Augustorum*, “son of the Augusti,” as Caesars are known to have been called.

The words of the panegyric addressed to Maximian Herculius and Constantine, chapter 5, deserve attention:

> Although, why should I employ in your case a designation of age rather than of gravity? Such is your maturity that, when your father had left you the empire, you nevertheless preferred, content with the title of Caesar, to await the same man who had declared him Augustus declaring you Augustus. For you judged that the empire itself would be more splendid if it did not grow by hereditary succession, but came to you as due to your virtues, having been earned from the supreme emperor.

I do not know how a very learned man could have found in these words that, after marrying Fausta, Constantine, although his father had left him the empire, was content with the title of Caesar. For that is not the panegyrist’s meaning, and he is not speaking here of events after Fausta’s marriage [Col. 0524C]. Rather, he says that, although Constantine had received the empire from his father Constantius, he did not wish to take the title Augustus, but was content with Caesarian rank, in order that the same person who had called his father Augustus might also call him Augustus—namely, Maximian Herculius, who made him emperor at the very marriage of his daughter Fausta to Constantine.

At the beginning of the same panegyric:

> Most sacred princes, Maximian—Augustus forever, willing or unwilling—and Constantine, rising Emperor: yet I have resolved in this discourse especially to embrace those things which belong to this particular joy, in which the name of empire has been added to you as Caesar and the festivals of this heavenly marriage are celebrated.

Constantine, then, was made Augustus at the time of the wedding. It should be noted in passing how eagerly the panegyrist flatters the emperors when he says that Constantine waited to be called Augustus by the same person who had made his father Constantius Augustus. For this could not have entered Constantine’s mind, since Maximian Herculius, when Constantius died, was living as a private man in Campania after resigning the empire—or, as Eutropius relates, in Lucania [Col. 0524D].

**But Caesar . . .** Baluzius not improperly refers the words of the ancient calendar, “Eighth day before the Kalends of January: Birthday of the Unconquered One” (*VIII Kal. Jan. Natalis Invicti*), to the time when Constantine was named Caesar by Galerius. Yet an apparent difficulty arises: Constantius died in July 306; Constantine immediately sent his laurelled image to Galerius in the customary fashion; and yet Galerius first recognized him as Caesar only in December of the same year.

Still, as I have said, this conjecture is not displeasing and should be preferred to Petavius’s explanation [Col. 0525A]. That most learned man, on the end of Julian’s Fourth Oration, understands games celebrated in honour of the unconquered Sun. Certainly the unconquered Sun occurs very frequently on coins, and on one coin of Victorinus is called simply “the Unconquered One.” But even if this interpretation could be entirely valid, I nevertheless do not see in what sense it would be called the Birthday of the Sun. Further, if games in honour of the Sun are assigned to that day, they immediately follow the final day of the Saturnalia; yet it is gratuitously asserted that an eighth day was added to the Saturnalia in Constantine’s time.

For the final day of the Saturnalia is the tenth day before the Kalends of January [23 December], while the Birthday of the Unconquered One falls on the eighth day before those same Kalends [25 December]. But if perhaps Constantine Caesar’s birthday was celebrated on that day, it follows that the Sun’s games fell on the ninth day before the Kalends of January [24 December]. On that very day the calendar notes: *munus consummat[um]*, “the gladiatorial exhibition completed”; and this seems to indicate that no further gladiatorial shows were celebrated in that year.

Since Julian writes in the passage mentioned that after the contest celebrated in honour of the Sun [Col. 0525B] it was unlawful to exhibit any “gloomy spectacles” (σκυθρωπῶν θεαμάτων), I have come to suspect that games were consecrated to the Sun on this day by the institution of Julian or some other emperor. For they immediately followed the final day of the Saturnalia: “But,” he says, “the Helia are joined in regular succession immediately to the final Cronia” (Ἀλλὰ τοῖς Κρονίοις οὖσι τελευταίοις εὐθὺς συνάπτει κατὰ κύκλον τὰ Ἡλιαῖα); and a little earlier: “Immediately before the new moon, after the final day of Cronus, we hold for Helios the most illustrious contest” (πρὸ τῆς νεομηνίας εὐθέως μετὰ τὴν τελευταίαν τοῦ Κρόνου ἡμέραν—thus perhaps one should read—ποιοῦμεν Ἡλίῳ τὸν περιφανέστατον ἀγῶνα).

But I should like others to examine these matters more carefully. The illustrious Spanheim, distinguished in rank and learning, will be particularly able to do so; he promised us a more corrected Julian, and his notes on that emperor’s *Caesars* abundantly demonstrate the extent of his learning.

## CHAPTER XXVI
Maxentius was made emperor at Rome. Eutropius, book X, chapter 2, writes that Maxentius had been staying not far from the city in a *villa publica*. There was at Rome a *villa publica* in the Campus Martius: it was a large house in which sumptuous hospitality was provided for ambassadors of foreign peoples, as Nardini and Donatus teach. [Col. 0525C] That place should not be understood here, but rather a praetorium, or country house, which, I think, is called public because it belonged to the emperors and the state—just as beasts of burden are called public when they were used for the public post. For the Epitome of Victor teaches us that Maxentius was in a villa six miles from the city, on the Labican road; and you will find the same words in Paul the Deacon, who nevertheless also calls the villa public. Thus on the Appian Way there was another public road. The author of the Valesian Excerpts writes: “Herculius, summoned thither by Maxentius his son, came; by perjury he deceived Severus, delivered him into custody, led him to the city in the guise of a captive, and had him guarded in a *villa publica* at the thirtieth milestone of the Appian Way.” Eutropius likewise, X.2, relates that Constantine the Great died at Nicomedia in a *villa publica*. The Greek translator rendered this, ἐν Νικομηδικῳ χωρίῳ, “on an estate near Nicomedia”; just as, certainly, Plutarch writes that the slaughter committed by Sulla occurred ἐν χωρίῳ μικρῷ, “in a small estate,” that is, in a country house, as Latin speakers express it. For χωρίον signifies not only a field, but also a villa or a house built in the countryside outside cities. [Col. 0525D] And when Constantine Porphyrogenitus, *Themes* II.9, says that Diocletian was born ἀπό τινος χωρίου Σαλῶνος, “from a certain estate of Salona,” he may mean that he was born in the territory or at the villa near Salona, at the very place where he later built his large palace. On this matter, see what I note on chapter 19. Certainly Maximian Herculius built a palace not far from Sirmium at the place where his parents performed hired labour, according to the Epitome of Victor and Paul the Deacon. Constantine also magnificently adorned the town of Naissus, where he was born and brought up, as we read in the Excerpts so often cited: “Constantine, born of Helena, a most low-born mother, in the town of Naissus, and brought up there, afterwards magnificently adorned that town.” If anyone judged that this should be corrected to “born of Helena, in the most lowly town of Naissus,” he would surely remove the lowliness of birth from Helena.

He was made emperor at Rome. It is especially worthy of notice [Col. 0526A] that Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VIII.14, relates that Maxentius at first pretended to be a Christian, ἐπ’ ἀρεσκείᾳ καὶ κολακείᾳ τοῦ δήμου Ῥωμαίων, “for the gratification and flattery of the Roman people”: that he might accommodate himself to, and ingratiate himself with, the Roman populace. From this, I think I can affirm that the number of Christians at Rome was immense at this time, and perhaps exceeded that of the pagans. For, turn the matter whichever way I may, I can find no other reason why a new emperor, most devoted to pagan superstition and pursuing Christians with hatred, should have sought the favour of Christians.

He had also dismantled the praetorian camp. Aurelius Victor teaches us that these forces had been reduced by Diocletian and Herculius—or at least by the former:

> Herculius was driven by such lust that he did not restrain the stain upon his mind even from the bodies of hostages; Valerius had too little honourable loyalty toward his colleagues, undoubtedly through fear of dissensions, while he thought that the tranquillity of their partnership might be disturbed by informers. Hence also the city’s strength was, as it were, curtailed, the number of Praetorian cohorts and of the populace under arms being reduced—by which, indeed, very many hold that the empire had been established. [Col. 0526B]

I think the sense of this passage is that Diocletian seldom met with the other emperors because he feared dissensions arising from such meetings and had no trust in them; he thought their partnership could be maintained through intermediaries whom they sent to one another; and he reduced the number of praetorian soldiers because he feared that another might use them to wage war against himself. Diocletian’s wary prudence is well known from Eutropius. By “the populace under arms” one might perhaps understand the urban cohorts, which seem at that time to have been recruited from the common people; or, with the illustrious Baluze, one should read *inermis vulgi*, “of the unarmed populace,” since a great multitude of common people also commonly furnishes occasion for seditions.

What this emperor did Lactantius ascribes to Galerius—unless he later also reduced the number of praetorians. For although he relates that Galerius dismantled the praetorian camp, this is not altogether true, since Constantine the Great did this later, according to Zosimus II.17. Valesius, on Ammianus Marcellinus XIV.9, teaches that Constantine greatly diminished the power of the praetorian prefects [Col. 0526C]. Constantine, however, abolished the camp because the praetorian soldiers, by Maxentius’ command, had at a fixed time killed all whom they encountered in Rome and perpetrated a vast slaughter, as Eusebius VIII.14 and Paul the Deacon, book XI, report; and because they were suited to fostering factions. Victor writes:

> He had afflicted them—the senate and the people—to such an extent that he once permitted the praetorians to massacre the populace; later, owing to hatred of them, the praetorian legions and auxiliary troops, better suited to factions than to the city of Rome, were utterly abolished, together with their arms and the use of military dress.

Yet not many praetorian soldiers seem to have survived when Constantine abolished them, because a great part fell in the battle in which Maxentius was defeated. For I think the words of the anonymous author of the panegyric, chapter 7, should be understood thus:

> The enemies were terrified and put to flight, and were shut in by the narrowness of the Milvian Bridge, except for the principal authors of that banditry, who, despairing of pardon, covered with their bodies the place which they had chosen for battle.

For I understand these to be the praetorians who had made Maxentius emperor and had ravaged the Romans with massacres [Col. 0526D].

He could not make three Caesars. This was prevented, of course, by Diocletian’s law, as Baluze explains very well. Mention of this law, or arrangement, occurs in chapter 18: “But what follows—that it seemed sufficient to have done once what he did not wish to do—refers to Constantine,” whom he unwillingly admitted as Caesar.

He summons Severus. Victor relates that Severus happened to be near the city—namely Rome—and that Galerius ordered him promptly to take up arms against the enemy. Certainly Severus held Italy and could have been near the city; but he seems to have been summoned thence into Illyricum by Galerius, who then urged him to recover the empire.

To recover the empire. That is, Italy, which together with the West had fallen to Severus Augustus and which Maxentius, made emperor by the praetorian soldiery, had seized. But if we follow Zosimus, Severus was only Caesar, not Augustus, since at II.10 he relates that Galerius took badly τὰ ἐπὶ τῷ Καίσαρι Σεβήρῳ γενόμενα, “what had happened in the case of Caesar Severus.” [Col. 0527A] But Zosimus is mistaken; and because Severus had been placed at the summit of power for a very short time, he undoubtedly calls him Caesar. For in the preceding chapter Lactantius expressly writes that Severus was created Augustus, and his coins bear the inscription: *IMP. C. SEVERUS P. F. AUG.* Tristan, vol. III, p. 437, observes that he was made Augustus with the consent of Constantius and Galerius. Yet, as is clear from Lactantius, only after Constantius’ death was Severus made Augustus by Galerius, when he had learned that Constantine had been clothed in purple by the soldiers in Britain.

Whether Galerius, upon receiving this news, immediately called Severus Augustus, or instead did so only after learning of Maxentius’ attempt, is uncertain; learned men support each opinion. Lactantius establishes that Severus was created Augustus when Constantine’s laureate portrait had been brought to Galerius; and Zosimus testifies, II.9, that Maxentius was made Augustus when such a portrait of Constantine had been displayed at Rome. Thus it is clear that the learned men do not differ greatly from one another, [Col. 0527B] and that both events could have occurred at nearly the same time—although there is no need to believe that Galerius knew what was being done at Rome when he proclaimed Severus Augustus.

I observe that coins of Severus as Caesar represent his head laureate, whereas those of Severus as Augustus show it helmeted—perhaps to indicate that, as soon as he had become Augustus, he set out against Maxentius. To this belongs the fact that the coins of Severus Augustus bear the legends *CONCORDIA* or *FIDES MILITUM*, which do not at all appear on his Caesarian coins.

With his veins cut. The *Life of the Holy Fathers Metrophanes and Alexander*, in Photius, p. 1407, is therefore mistaken in stating that Severus died of illness; perhaps it attributes to this Severus what belongs to Severus, successor of Niger. If we follow the Valesian Excerpts, he was murdered by having his throat cut, and not immediately, but later, as is clear from the words which I have just cited. They also teach us that Herculius deceived Severus and violated his oath.

## Chapter XXVII

[Col. 0527C]

The city having been fortified, and hostile undertakings begun. The passage is not only difficult but, so far as I can see, corrupt. Perhaps one should read *rebus captis inimici*: “carefully equipping and fortifying himself with the resources which he had seized from the enemy Severus.”

He lacked equipment. That is, things necessary for carrying out the pursuit. Peter Damian, cited in the most learned Du Cange’s *Glossary*: “Spurs, whip, and whatever other *utensilia* belong to riding”—that is, implements.

## Chapter XXVIII

Because they were soldiers who had deserted Severus. The sense absolutely requires the reading: “because they were his soldiers, who had deserted Severus”; and that this is correct is evident from chapter 44, while the similarity of the letters could have obscured the word.

He tore the purple from his shoulders. If we wish to speak Latin correctly, [Col. 0527D] it should be *deripuit*, that is, “he pulled it down from his son’s body”; whereas *diripere* means to cut into pieces, as I show in *Observations* IV.5. Thus Ovid, chapter 7:

> Procne tears the garments from her shoulders.

And Virgil: “They strip the hides from the ribs.” In Socrates, where this attempt of Herculius is discussed, we read ἀπολέσαι, which may most conveniently be translated “to destroy.”

## Chapter XXIX

While he was conversing with him. That is, while he was talking, discussing, or negotiating with him. Cicero, *Letters to Friends* III.8: “Thus I think that I argued at great length before the tribunal at Synnada.” In the *Oration for Caelius*: “Know, judges, that the desires and pursuits of which I speak cannot easily exist in the same man”; and frequently elsewhere.

Excluded from his own [territory]. Namely, that which, before he had become Augustus a second time, [Col. 0528A] while Diocletian was still reigning, he had possessed, as is clear from chapters 7 and 8; and to govern which he had now been summoned by his son Maxentius, chapter 28.

Diocles was present there. A learned man observes that Herculius did not at this point truly reign; nevertheless he, rather than Diocles, completes the number six. Certainly Diocles, or Diocletian, could not be counted among the six rulers, since he never resumed the purple—although Herculius and Galerius had urged him to do so, as Zosimus and Eutropius testify. Herculius, on the contrary, truly reigned: for Maxentius Augustus had sent him the purple, and, having become emperor for the second time, he even called Constantine emperor, though Constantine was only Caesar. I admit that the effective power of the empire lay with men other than Herculius; nevertheless Diocletian cannot be compared with him in this respect.

That he should give the empire to Licinius, who was substituted in Severus’ place. Therefore Licinius was immediately made Augustus; for, as [Col. 0528B] is evident from chapter 25, Severus had been designated Augustus by Galerius. The anonymous author of the *Life of Constantine* writes that Galerius made Licinius Caesar in Illyricum; Tristan, vol. III, p. 482, follows him—as do Oiselius on Table XIII and Antonio Pagi in the *Hypatic Dissertation*. Tristan also observes there that Licinius first assumed the title emperor after Galerius’ death, which is very far from the truth.

But Lactantius, especially chapter 20—where he expressly relates that Galerius had refused to make Licinius, his friend from old comradeship and companion from his earliest military service, Caesar, lest he should have to name him son and later proclaim him Augustus and brother in Constantius’ place—together with the observations of Henry Noris in his *Explanation of the Coin of Diocletian and Licinius*, p. 38, seems to establish the contrary. Yet on a coin in Strada one sees the laureate bust, προτομή, of Licinius the father, [Col. 0528C] with the inscription: *LICINIUS. NOB. CAES.* On the other side: *CONCORDIA. AVGG. DD. NN. AET.* And on another coin in Angeloni, his laureate head appears with: *D. N. VAL. LIC. LICINIUS. NOB. C.*

Noris, in the passage cited, observes that Licinius was designated Caesar and Augustus at one and the same time, and that this is sufficiently clear from Eusebius and the inscriptions of coins. If what that most learned man observes is true, one might suppose that no one at that time was made Augustus without first having been created Caesar; and that those who were to be made Augusti were called Caesars merely as a formality at the very same time at which they were proclaimed Augusti. Thus Licinius, substituted for Severus, will have been made Augustus; but, in order that everything might be carried out in due form, Caesarian rank was first conferred upon him.

The same seems to be true of Maxentius, whose coins also bear: *M. VAL. MAXENTIUS NOB. CAESAR.* The Licinian coins cited refute Scaliger’s insufficiently cautious assertion that Licinius is not called *NOB. CAES.* on coins. Moreover, Aurelius Victor confirms that Licinius was made Caesar and Augustus simultaneously, if the word *et* is inserted:

> Galerius, more incensed, having called Jovius into counsel, made Licinius—known to him from an old friendship—Caesar and Augustus.

[Col. 0528D] I admit that *et* does not appear in the editions; but perhaps it was absorbed by the final syllable of the preceding word. Nor do I think Victor would have omitted first to record that Licinius had been made Caesar, if he had thought that Licinius had first been Caesar and was then made Augustus. Moreover, Victor’s manner of speaking would have required him to write, “He makes Licinius Caesar, known from an old friendship, Augustus,” if he wished to indicate that Licinius at that time was made Augustus from being Caesar.

The Frankish people. The most learned Baluze observes that the Franks’ frontier was around the Danube. But they inhabited the region near the Rhine, which Constantine undoubtedly crossed; from there they spread widely, as is clear from the Peutinger Table and various authors. Further, if they lived on the Danube, Constantine could not have entered their territory within a few days, something which is nevertheless clear from this chapter [Col. 0529A] that he did. Constantine defeated the Franks on another occasion as well: hence on one of his coins a captive sits, with the inscription *GAUDIUM ROMAN.* and *FRANCIA*, in the illustrious Spanheim.

## Chapter XXX

Because he once went away unpunished. Phaedrus speaks in precisely the same manner, Fable 8:

> Since he can no longer afterwards depart unpunished.

Terence, Cicero, Catullus, and Seneca speak no differently.

To have seen a dream. He speaks properly; hence the frequent epigraphic formula *EX VISU*, “in consequence of a vision.” The old translator of Genesis 41.1: “After two years Pharaoh saw a dream.”

With his most proud throat crushed and broken. The most learned man, intending to elucidate Herculius’ death, observes that Suidas writes very badly that Diocletian was killed by order of the senate, whereas Maximian hanged himself. Certainly Diocletian was not killed by order of the senate; yet Herculius, [Col. 0529B] being allowed his choice of death, chose hanging, as is perfectly clear from this chapter of Lactantius. Suidas reports the same; thus I do not see why he should be criticized. He is mistaken, however, in calling Maximian Herculius, who ended his life by hanging, γαμβρός, “son-in-law,” of Diocletian; for that was Galerius Maximianus. That many men in antiquity were granted choice in the manner of their death is more than sufficiently clear from Tacitus, Suetonius, and others.

He ended [his life] by death. At Massilia, namely. Baluze rightly notes that Zosimus, confusing Maximinus with Maximian Herculius, writes that the latter died of illness at Tarsus. Socrates I.2 commits the same error, as does Cassiodorus, *Tripartite History* I.4:

> Hence his [Maxentius’] father, in his desire to rule, wished to deprive his son of the kingdom, but could not do so; after this he died at Tarsus in Cilicia.

## Chapter XXXI

That he might pay what he had promised. This passage is exceedingly difficult [Col. 0529C], and I scarcely see what meaning it contains. It seems to say that Galerius imposed burdensome exactions so that he might hold and celebrate splendidly the *vicennalia* which he had promised.

He struck them with a second axe. Here too I scarcely satisfy myself. If the sense is, as Columbus thinks, that Galerius struck or inflicted a second axe-blow upon the provinces, I would readily believe that Lactantius indicates a new exaction and distinguishes it from the former one mentioned in chapter 23. Thus the name *vicennalia* will mean nothing other than that the vicennalia were already being spoken of, much discussion of them was occurring, and the things necessary for their celebration were being prepared. Perhaps the lacuna may be supplied thus: “He was considering—as one who had long since …”

Soldiers of all offices. At that time *officium* meant a staff or the men attending an illustrious man; hence in the *Notitia Dignitatum*: “the staff of the illustrious prefect of the praetorium of the East: chief clerk, cornicularius”; elsewhere, “the staff of the illustrious praetorian prefects [Col. 0529D] through Illyricum.” Moreover, the offices themselves were also designated by this name. Suetonius, *Nero* 15: *praeterito quaestoris officio*, “having passed over the office of quaestor,” that is, having passed over the quaestorship; inscription I.361: *PERFUNCTO OFFICIO PRAEFECTURAE PRAETORIO*, “having discharged the office of praetorian prefect.” Below, chapter 48, *ad officium tuum*, “to your office,” that is, to you as judge. Thus “soldiers of all offices” may suitably be explained as soldiers of all magistrates, whom he soon calls soldiers of judges.

Threshing floor. Namely, the place where grain was cleansed and separated from chaff. See the agricultural writers.

In hope of future things. Namely, crops growing in the fields, by which they could support themselves.

I shall provide. That is, I shall furnish or give. Thus in Suetonius, *Domitian* 9, *praestare* means to pay a fixed sum; Cicero: “I scarcely seem able to provide what I promised.” From this come *praestatio* and *legatorum praestatio* in legal language. Galerius seems to have exacted garments of every kind, tapestries, even gold and silver, to adorn the procession of the vicennalia. Hence Lactantius asks him: “From where shall I provide this for you, [Col. 0530A] or be able to give it, if you take away all the produce from the sale of which I must acquire such things?”

## Chapter XXXII

Neither as Caesar nor in the third place. Maximinus behaves almost as Galerius himself had behaved earlier, as is clear from chapter 9; and in some fashion we may observe the law of retaliation: that is, he was harassed by Maximinus Caesar just as he himself had harassed Diocletian and Herculius. Galerius Maximianus was first of the Augusti, Licinius second; Constantine, Maximinus, and Maxentius were regarded as Caesars. But Galerius was at last compelled, as is clear from the end of the chapter, to count four emperors, so that there were simultaneously five Augusti: Galerius, Licinius, Constantine, Maximinus, and Maxentius.

But in what position Maximinus’ name stood is not yet certainly established. He did not wish to be called either Caesar or Augustus in the third place; hence it is altogether clear that he considered the second place due to himself and wanted his name to be placed after Galerius’ name [Col. 0530B]. Certainly after Galerius’ death he wished to be first, as Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* IX.10, teaches: καὶ πρῶτον ἑαυτὸν ταῖς τιμαῖς ἀναγορεύειν, “claiming for himself the first place in titles and honours.” Valesius rightly notes that Maximinus placed his own name first in the inscriptions of public works and statues because he had been made Caesar before Constantine and Licinius.

From this one might perhaps arrive at the true reason why Maximinus’ name is not found in the edict in Eusebius VIII.17: namely, he wished to be named not in third but in second place after Galerius. Yet if the edict was promulgated under a joint title, as Lactantius teaches in chapter 36—that is, with the names of Galerius, Constantine, Licinius, Maximinus, and Maxentius written at its head—perhaps Christians omitted the names of the last two because they only briefly ceased persecuting them. Or Galerius, Constantine, and Licinius omitted them because friendship with them was not sufficiently secure; [Col. 0530C] perhaps also because Maxentius disputed precedence, since he had been made emperor by the praetorians before Constantine, Maximinus, and Licinius. The edict could also have been sent to Maximinus and Maxentius for each to publish under his own preceding name; and that it was sent there is clear because Maximianus in the East, which he ruled, refused to promulgate it, as Eusebius IX.1 testifies.

Let him preserve his arrangement. That is, what he established, decreed, or laid down as though a law. Chapter 18: “His arrangement ought to be preserved for ever”; chapter 34: “What we ordain for the perpetual advantage and benefit of the commonwealth.” An ancient inscription: “It is commanded that the form of this interdict and arrangement be observed under threat of the sword.”

He raises his horns more boldly. He takes greater courage, becomes bolder and more arrogant. [Col. 0530D] Ovid, *Art of Love* I.239:

> Then laughter comes; then the poor man takes up horns.

The same, *Tristia* IV.9:

> Now I am borne into battles and have not yet taken up horns;  
> nor, I would wish, may there be any reason for taking them up.

In the same sense Micyllus, in Lucian’s *Cock*, speaks of κέρατα εἶναι, “having horns.”

Sons of the Augusti. Columbus’ observation seems to me perfectly correct. Lactantius says that no one other than Galerius Maximianus was overcome by Maximinus’ obstinacy. Constantine and Maxentius were in fact sons of Augusti, and so are called by Eutropius X.3. But Maximinus Daza was a new man; nevertheless I think that he too received this title, since it is by no means likely that Galerius would have passed over altogether the man whom he himself had made Caesar.

At the recently celebrated Campus Martius. This passage has its difficulties, and I do not understand what “to celebrate the Campus Martius” means. Does it mean that military manoeuvres were held? Or that an *armilustrium* was performed? But [Col. 0531A] this was not celebrated in the Campus Martius, but in Region XIII of the City, where Publius Victor mentions the *Vicus Armilustri*. Furthermore, the *armilustrium* did not concern the whole army but only the *ancilia*, which, as I teach in my *Observations*, are called arms. Varro, *On the Latin Language* V: “At the Armilustrium, armed men playing with the ancilia went around.” Moreover Maximinus was not at Rome but in the East, as is clear from chapter 36. Thus we learn that other cities too, following Rome’s example, had Campi Martii.

I therefore think that all the soldiers had been assembled together, whether for exercise or for some other purpose, and that the day was solemn; for this reason Lactantius says that the Campus Martius had been celebrated. In much the same sense we read “the asylum is celebrated” in the Calendar published with Ovid’s *Fasti*: “A temple was built to Carmentis. The asylum is celebrated.” Ovid, if we follow some editions, expresses this thus: *vicini lucus celebratur asyli*, “the grove of the neighbouring asylum is celebrated”; for which Heinsius emends *Hylerni*. [Col. 0531B] To celebrate the asylum means to observe the day on which Romulus opened the asylum; to celebrate the grove of Hylernus means to observe a fixed day in honour of the deity presiding over that grove. Sacrifices may also have been offered to Mars in the celebration of the Campus Martius.

## Chapter XXXIII

God struck him. Job 2.7: “[He] struck Job with a most grievous ulcer”; Exodus 9.15: “I shall strike you and your people with pestilence”; Jeremiah 30.12: “Your fracture is incurable and your wound most grievous.” Immediately afterwards follows: “For I struck you with the wound of an enemy, with cruel chastisement.”

Cancer attacks him: gangrene, as is clear from the Latin physicians Celsus and Scribonius, and from Rhodius’ notes in the Lexicon of Scribonius.

The masters yielded. This is taken from Virgil, and should be written:

> The masters yielded—  
> Chiron, son of Philyra, and Melampus, son of Amythaon—

as I show on p. 4 of the *Apotheosis of Homer*.

[Col. 0531C] Apollo gives treatment. That is, by his oracle he prescribes what remedies should be applied. That sick persons often consulted gods or their oracles, so that the gods might provide them with treatment, is too well known to need proof. See Aristides in various places, and Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher, book V, §8.

The whole seat. Likewise below he calls *sedes fluens*, “the flowing seat,” that part of the body upon which we sit and through which excrement is discharged. The Greeks similarly called it ἕδρα, as is clear from Hesychius under Γαφανιδόσθηναι.

Foulness. I do not condemn Baluze’s reading, *odor taeter*, “a foul smell”; but we depart least from the received text if we read *odoritas tetra*, “foul odorousness.” Thus we find *prioritas*, *commodioritas*, and *superioritas*, noted by Meursius in chapter 32 of the *Avita Philologica*; nor is *uberitas* absent from coins, and somewhere I remember having read *differitas* for *differentia*.

Inestimable. That is, innumerable.

They had lost the form of the body. Suidas says precisely the same:

[Col. 0531D]

> Λαυρότερον δὲ φλογιζομένῳ καὶ αὐτὰ συνεφλόγησαν τὰ ὀστᾶ, ὥστε ἐξαφανισθῆναι καὶ τὸν χαρακτῆρα τῆς ἀνθρωπίνης μορφῆς.

> As he burned ever more fiercely, the bones themselves too were burned up, so that even the outline of the human form was completely obliterated.

I have shown in my note on chapter 22 that these words are to be understood of Maximinus, or Galerius Maximianus, not of Maximinus, successor to Alexander Severus.

A whole year. That is, an entire, complete year. The word occurs in this sense in Plautus’ *Amphitruo*, Justin V.7, and inscription II.164; thus Festus does not observe carefully enough when he says that poets alone used it.

Of the pressing new pain. Either he imitates the Greeks, who often use a genitive in place of an absolute dative, or some corruption is concealed here, which Columbus suitably removes by reading *per nova vi doloris*, “through a new force of pain.” Moreover Haymo, VIII.2, writes that Maximinus—thus he calls Galerius Maximianus—was suddenly swollen by distended entrails; afterwards, when the wounds had putrefied, worms swarmed forth and he gave off an intolerable stench. At the end of the following chapter [Col. 0532A] he writes that Maximinus Daza, seized by a violent illness and pains of the internal organs, and having also lost his sight through the disease, then more fully seeing what he had committed against Christ, ended his life after first issuing a law granting freedom to Christians.

## Chapter XXXIV

And benefit. This also occurs on a coin: on one side appears a laureate emperor with *MAXIMIANUS P. F. AUG.*; on the other, a robed woman holding a globe in each hand, with *UTILITAS PUBLICA*. It is found in Andrea Morelli’s highly learned *Specimen of the Whole of Ancient Numismatics*. Cassius’ well-known remark in Tacitus, *Annals* XIV.44, is relevant: “Every great example has something of injustice, which is compensated with respect to individuals by public benefit.”

According to the ancient laws and public discipline. That is, according to laws enacted long ago, rites accepted by use, or precepts observed in this period. Pliny X.82: “If any conduct themselves contrary to my discipline, [Col. 0532B] let them be restrained immediately.”

They might return to sound minds. Those are said to return to a sound mind who, abandoning wrong opinions, embrace better ones and return from error to the path. Cicero, in a letter to his friends, calls such people those who “return to sanity,” that is, to better counsels. *Bona mens* also occurs in Petronius: “Poverty is the sister of a sound mind.” By this he means that the rich rarely possess a healthy mind, since they are usually corrupted by luxury and other vices.

And might gather diverse multitudes in diverse places. Eusebius translates: καὶ ἐν διαφόροις διάφορα πλήθη συνάγειν, “and to gather various crowds in different places.” Some interpret this as: “in differing sects and opinions they might gather differing assemblies.” But I prefer: “in different places”; and I think Lactantius likewise used *diversa* in the sense of different places or towns.

Many subdued by danger. That is, many, subdued by the tortures and penalties which they were bound under our laws to endure, [Col. 0532C] renounced Christ. Many others did so without torture, provided that *deturbare* is used in the sense proposed by Du Cange. But the passages he adduces denote rather scattering or separating an assembled crowd than *détourner*, “turning aside.” Eusebius expressed the former by κινδύνῳ ὑποβληθέντες, “subjected to danger”; the latter by ταραχθέντες, “disturbed”—that is, dislodged—or those who, through fear of tortures, went over to the pagans. For ταράττειν, as is well known, means to frighten, alarm, strike with consternation, and also to dislodge or cast down. Cicero, *Letters to Friends* V.7: “But know this: your old enemies, now friends, lie greatly struck down by your letter and cast down from great hope.” Elsewhere: “Each man’s own crime drives him from health and soundness of mind.”

And not to observe the God of the Christians. Unless I am mistaken, these words refer directly to the heresies born in this or preceding centuries. After others, Frederick Spanheim, the most celebrated theologian among the Dutch, discusses them excellently in his *Introduction to Sacred Chronology and History*, whose second part is now being studied by learned men with great profit and pleasure. Among others, there were many who held Christ, or the God of Christians, [Col. 0532D] in derision and invented for themselves certain monstrous religions, as is clear from Augustine, Epiphanius, Damascene, the presbyter Timothy, and others.

This edict, however, has its difficulties; therefore I shall briefly state what seems to me the meaning of one point and another. By the words “those who had abandoned the sect of their parents,” I think Christians should be understood: those who had renounced the superstitions of their pagan parents and ancestors. He then adds that they had wished to call them back to a sound mind—that is, to make them worship the gods again and embrace the sect they had abandoned. He adds the reason: such ἄνοια, “folly” or “madness,” had overtaken them that each fashioned for himself, according to his own will, a religion and cult, abandoning the institutions of the earliest Christians, who worshipped God with one mouth and one heart. He then adds that he had ordered them to betake themselves to the institutions of the ancients: that is, abandoning such discordant opinions, to worship the gods of the pagans [Col. 0533A].

I think this is the true sense of these passages. Although I formerly suspected that the words “that they should not follow those institutions of the ancients which perhaps their first parents had established” also referred to pagan superstition, upon more careful reflection I change my opinion. I judge with Baluze, a man of outstanding learning, that Christians are censured for having departed from the primitive simplicity of their parents and divided themselves into very many sects. But what follows—“that they should betake themselves to the institutions of the ancients”—I understand of pagan superstition, to which Galerius had attempted to bring Christians back.

Our indulgence. This is the proper term and occurs on coins themselves. It signifies the emperors’ clemency and benevolence, whether in remitting arrears or in granting and conceding what was requested. Meursius thinks that it arose in the time of Ammianus Marcellinus because he writes in book XVI:

> Finally, we know that he observed this uniformly to the end of his reign and life: [Col. 0533B] he did not, through what they call indulgences, remit arrears owed to the revenue.

But I think nothing of the kind can be inferred from this, because Ammianus merely says that, if emperors remitted arrears of taxes, that act was called *indulgentiae*, as indeed it was. The term occurs in much older authors and denotes a favour or remission granted by emperors. Thus on a coin of Caracalla one reads *INDULGENTIAE FECUNDAE*, in Tristan, vol. II, p. 169; on another of Severus, *INDULGENTIA AUG. IN CARTHA.* Hence Eumenius in his panegyric often calls emperors “most indulgent princes”; and Ambrose, in his oration on the death of Theodosius, calls the promised but, because of death, unfulfilled remission of grain exactions “an inheritance of indulgences.”

Their meeting places. Thus in chapters 15, 36, and 49, where these are called the places to which they were accustomed to assemble. Cicero uses the term in the *Oration for the House* and the *Oration for Sestius* for an assembly or congregation.

But another letter [was sent] to the judges, etc. [Col. 0533C] Either he means that he would assign Christians specific places through the judges in which to assemble, or that he would order the judges to observe what was done in those places and to ensure that they entered into no plans against the state. For this liberty was granted them on the condition, as is clear from the words, “so that they do nothing against discipline”: that is, against the emperors’ commands, the imperial authority, or the laws.

In Eusebius we read: ὥστε μηδὲν ὑπεναντίον τῆς ἐπιστήμης αὐτοὺς πράττειν, which I do not think is satisfactorily rendered, “so that henceforth they should be compelled to do nothing contrary to their own discipline.” Christian liberty is granted on the condition that they commit no offence against laws and enactments. At the beginning he used the same sense in τὴν δημοσίαν ἐπιστήμην τὴν τῶν Ῥωμαίων, “the public discipline of the Romans”; Lactantius has: “according to the ancient laws and public discipline of the Romans.”

“their god …” In the free Republic, the Romans prayed to their gods for the welfare of the commonwealth, as is evident even from Velleius, book I, chapters 10 and 22, and other authors. The first was Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus, for whose safety all Italy undertook vows, as the same author testifies, II.48. After the force of imperial power had been transferred to one man, they likewise prayed to the gods for his safety, as the same writer teaches at the end of book II; Seneca, *Consolation to Polybius* I; Pliny at the end of the *Panegyric*; Aristides, vol. I, p. 50; and Julius Firmicus, book I of the *Mathesis*. Christians, with the fullest justification, imitated this practice; they also prayed to Christ for the safety of emperors, even though they were pagans, and did so by the command of St Paul, 1 Tim. 2:2, confirmed by Jer. 29:7.
