That they did this is shown by Theophilus, *To Autolycus*, book VII, p. 76; Athenagoras, at the end of the *Embassy for the Christians*; the *Passion of St Cyprian*, p. 11; the *Passion of St Victor of Marseilles*, published by the learned Colomesius; Tertullian, chapter 30 of the *Apology*; and, finally, Dionysius in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VII.1, where he relates that Gallus killed “the sacred men who were acting as envoys to God concerning his peace and health” (*τοὺς ἱεροὺς ἄνδρας τοὺς περὶ τῆς εἰρήνης αὐτοῦ καὶ τῆς ὑγιείας πρεσβεύοντας πρὸς τὸν Θεόν*). See also chapter 11 of the same book [Col. 0534A]. Thus today the Greek and Armenian patriarchs do the same for the emperors of the Turks, according to Ricaut in his *Life of Mahomet IV*. That Egyptian Christians still retain this ancient custom, and that orthodox Christians prayed to God for emperors infected with the Arian heresy, is evident from the Coptic liturgies, as well as from Cyril, *Catechesis* 4, and the letter sent by the Synod of Rimini to Constantius. Would that certain persons today, who wish to be considered Christians of the first rank and station, observed it!

## CHAPTER XXXV

“By a horrible wasting disease …” What sort it was is clear from chapter 33; and Baluzius rightly notes there that John Chrysostom tells a similar story about Julian, uncle of the Apostate. Philostratus VII.10 also relates the matter concerning this Julian, but omits the worms; these, however, are mentioned by the author of the *Passion of Theodore*, presbyter of Antioch, in Mabillon, vol. IV of the *Annals*, p. 133. Moreover, it should be noted that the statue of this Maximian, though a most cruel emperor, was still seen at Antioch in Julian’s time. Ammianus Marcellinus XXV.10: “For the statue of Caesar Maximian, which had been placed in the vestibule of the palace, suddenly lost the bronze sphere, formed in the likeness of the heavens, which it bore.” It either always remained there, or was restored by Julian, the most hostile enemy of Christ.

“He was consumed.” He died at Serdica, or near that city in Dacia Mediterranea, as Baluzius observes on the following chapter. Yet there is no Serdica in Dacia; that city must be assigned to Thrace. Nor are those authors mistaken who write either that Galerius was born in Dacia, not far from Serdica—as Eutropius does—or that he died at Serdica. For, as I showed above, Dacia beyond the Danube was a Roman province created by Trajan. After it could no longer be defended, Aurelian transferred its inhabitants to the other bank of the Danube and called that region Dacia. The part near the Danube was called Ripensis, while the interior was called Mediterranea.

Thus Ammianus Marcellinus XXI.10 writes that the summits of Haemus and Rhodope separate the Illyrians and Thracians: on this side adjoining the Dacians of the interior and Serdica; on that side looking down upon the Thracians and Philippopolis, large and noble cities. This can certainly be explained only of Moesia or a neighbouring region. Likewise, XXVI.5, he writes that Aequitius received a report from Antonius the tribune, commanding troops in Dacia Mediterranea; this too, as is clear from what follows, must be sought in Thrace or Moesia.

Following Ortelius, others think that Ammianus calls Serdica a city of Macedonia, at the end of book XXXI; but nothing of the kind is found in him, as the words themselves will show: “Those besieged at Hadrianopolis … having gone out at midnight, avoiding the public embankments, through wooded and trackless places, some hastened to Philippopolis and thence to Serdica; others to Macedonia.” So far from assigning Serdica to Macedonia, he rather plainly affirms the contrary. If some sought Macedonia from Hadrianopolis, while others sought Philippopolis and thence Serdica, Serdica certainly could not have been assigned by Ammianus to Macedonia [Col. 0534D]. Indeed, the most direct route from Hadrianopolis to Philippopolis and then to our Serdica runs westward, whereas Macedonia lay to the south.

Learned men also note that Nicetas Choniates mentions a Serdica situated on the bank of the Ister, and hence different from our Mediterranea. But all I find in him, p. 19, is that “the Huns, having crossed the Ister, ravaged Branitzoba and plundered Sardica.” From this one cannot in the least prove that a city of that name was situated on the Ister; for it is well known how great a distance those peoples customarily covered in a short time, since they were intent on nothing but carrying off plunder.

Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History* II.20, assigns Serdica to Illyricum. But this too does not make it different from ours, because the name Illyricum then extended very broadly. Appian extends Illyricum as far as the mountains of Thrace, including within it the Moesias and other regions. The *Notitia Imperii* shows that there were eight governors through Illyricum: of Thessaly, Old Epirus, New Epirus, Dacia Ripensis, Moesia Prima, Praevalitana, Dardania, and Macedonia Salutaris [Col. 0535A]. Rufus Festus assigns seventeen provinces to it. It is therefore unsurprising that authors of that age assigned this city to Illyricum.

Indeed, if we consider that the praetorian prefect of Illyricum presided over the two dioceses of Macedonia and Dacia, and that Dacia comprised five provinces—Dacia Mediterranea, Dacia Ripensis, Moesia Prima, Dardania, Praevalitana, and part of Macedonia Salutaris—it will readily appear that Serdica too lay within Illyricum in the broad sense. It is further established, and has been noted by learned men, that Illyricum was divided into Eastern and Western. The former comprised two regions, Moesia and Thrace; eleven provinces: Moesia Prima or Upper Moesia, Praevalitana, Dardania, Dacia Ripensis, Dacia Mediterranea, Moesia Secunda or Lower Moesia, Scythia, Thrace, Haemimontus, Rhodope, and Europa. Western Illyricum, however, comprised four regions [Col. 0535B]: Raetia, Noricum, Pannonia, and Illyris; and nine provinces: Raetia, Vindelicia, Noricum Mediterraneum, Noricum Ripense, Pannonia Prima, Pannonia Secunda, Savia, Valeria, and, in Illyris, the peoples of the Iapodes, Liburnians, and Dalmatians.

Thus Zosimus may be excused for writing that Licinius and Maximinus fought a battle in the Illyrias, although Lactantius and others establish that it was fought near Perinthus or Heraclea of Thrace. Learned men further observe, from Cedrenus and Curopalates—or rather from the older Procopius, *Buildings* IV—that Serdica seems to be near the Nessus in Serbia; and that Sigonius, in book V of his *Western Empire beyond the Ister*, places it in Dacia Mediterranea between the two Moesias. I cannot consult the earlier authors. But Sigonius thinks no differently from me, since he places that city on this side of the Danube and thus excludes trans-Danubian Dacia. Aurelian’s Dacia lay between the two Moesias and also included [Col. 0535C] Dardania, or Serbia, and perhaps part of Thrace—unless we say that Dardania too came under the name of Thrace.

For I acknowledge only one Serdica, situated in Thrace. Hence an inscription in Gruter, II, p. DXL: “A THRACIAN BY NATION, OF THE CITY OF SERDICA” (*NATIONE THRAX. CIVITATE SERDICA*). Since perhaps part of Thrace was later added to Dacia Mediterranea, or since, as I have said, Dardania too was counted as Thrace, it was said to be in Thrace and Dacia Mediterranea. And because Illyricum extended very widely, it was therefore said to be situated in Illyricum. Several learned men have thought that cities bearing that name were being mentioned; yet this is wholly contrary to reason.

Victor uses the term Illyricum in this broad manner when he writes that Diocletian, Herculius, Constantius, and Galerius had Illyricum as their homeland. Galerius was born in Dacia near Serdica, Diocletian in Dalmatia, and Herculius near Sirmium. Although Constantius’ birthplace is unknown, he was undoubtedly born in the same regions, since he fathered Constantine by Helena in the city of Naissus, according to the Valesian Excerpts.

I had made these observations when I came upon Sanson’s geographical map, in which that highly knowledgeable man delineated Illyricum. I noticed that he placed Sardica at the river Cebrus, on the side of Mount Haemus toward Dardania and the Adriatic Sea; whereas on Ptolemy’s maps it appears on the other side of that mountain, facing the Propontis. This view seems supported by Ammianus Marcellinus, whom we heard saying that the summits of Haemus and Rhodope adjoined, on the one side, the Dacians of the interior and Serdica, and looked down, on the other, upon the Thracians and Philippopolis. Thus no part of Thrace would have been contained in Dacia Mediterranea. Whatever the case, there was only one Serdica.

Ptolemy expressly encloses it within Mount Haemus, book III, chapter 11. First he writes that in the province there are districts “adjoining both Moesias and Mount Haemus, beginning from the west” (*στρατηγίας πρὸς μὲν ταῖς Μυσίαις καὶ τὸν Αἶμον τὸ ὄρος ἀρχομένοις ἀπὸ δυσμῶν*); and he counts Sardica among them. Then, among the inland cities of Thrace, he lists Deultum Colonia, Orcelis, Carpudaenum, Byzia, Sardica, Terta, Philippopolis, and others [Col. 0536A].

“At Nicomedia, in the same month …” I have no doubt that one must write: “at Nicomedia in the middle of the same month,” namely May. For the Edict could not conveniently have been published at Nicomedia any earlier, while Galerius lay ill at Serdica; and it was posted there before receipt of this report, on the day before the Kalends of May.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

“The Chalcedonian strait …” This too was the boundary of Maximinus’ empire, as is clear from chapter 45.

“By common protection …” One must certainly write *titulo* (“by title”), as I once sent to Colomesius. For this liberty was granted to Christians in the joint name of the emperors; hence the names of Maximinus and Maxentius also followed as headings to the edict, though they are not visible today. On this point see what I note on chapter 32. That peace was granted to Christians after this edict is clear not only from Lactantius but also from Eusebius, chapter 9 of *The Martyrs of Palestine*, where Maximinus’ many cruelties are described [Col. 0536B].

It should be noted, however, that Maximinus refrained from persecuting Christians for scarcely six full months, and did not promulgate the edict in the East, over which he ruled. He merely ordered his commanders to refrain from persecuting Christians; and the praetorian prefect Sabinus sent the emperor’s decision to the provincial governors. Finally, the first thing he did was to exclude Christians from the assemblies held “in the cemeteries” (*ἐν τοῖς κοιμητηρίοις*). Titles included names and honours. Suetonius, *Tiberius* 50, writes that “son of Augustus and Livia” was to be added to Tiberius’ titles; and, at the end of his *Domitian*, he says that the Senate decreed that Domitian’s titles should everywhere be erased and every remembrance of him abolished.

“High priests …” Valesius rightly notes on Eusebius VIII.14 that before this period there were *archiereis* (*ἀρχιερέας*) and provincial priests; Spanheim demonstrates the same at length in his *Dissertations* [Col. 0536C]. Nor should the notable passage in the *Chronology of the Monk of Auxerre*, p. 39, be omitted:

> There were also then, in the time of Commodus, in Britain twenty-eight flamens—that is, pontiffs of the pagans—and likewise three archflamens, to whose authority the other judges of morals and religious devotees were subject. These men were finally rescued from idolatry by apostolic command; and where there had been flamens they established bishops, and where archflamens, archbishops.

Although I am not unaware how reluctantly credence ought to be given to such monastic narratives, traces are nevertheless found there that pagans had priests appointed over provinces or cities. By *fanatici*, moreover, I understand priests or persons consecrated to the gods, as in inscriptions: “devotee of Isis Serapis,” “devotee from the district of Bellona,” and “from the temple of Bellona.”

“Should perform rites through all their gods …” That is, they should sacrifice to all the gods. It is an unusual expression, which I do not know whether it occurs elsewhere. In the following chapter he says, “to sacrifice every day.”

“By their own right …” Freely, without anyone hindering them, at their own discretion. Cicero, *Letters to Atticus* II.2; Florus I.17 and III.17 speak in no other way [Col. 0536D].

“From the rank of higher dignity he set individual men over them as though pontiffs …” The high priests were selected from among the leading men of the cities and presided over the other priests of the same city. But a pontiff was set over the entire province, and he was chosen from men endowed with a higher dignity than that of the leading citizens, such as provincial governors. Eusebius VIII.14 and IX.4 teaches this clearly, calling the high priests *hiereis* (*ἱερέας*) and the pontiffs *archiereis* (*ἀρχιερέας*). By *primores* one may suitably understand decurions or municipal magistrates, just as “leading men of the city” occurs in Digest XVI, *On Use and Usufruct*.

It should be observed, however, that the pontiff set over a province was also frequently called a priest of the province, as appears from law 46 of the Theodosian Code, *On Decurions*, in which the emperors determine that the priest of a province should be appointed only from advocates and their association; see Gothofredus there, as also vol. VI of the same Code, p. 254 [Col. 0537A]. Relevant here are the Asiarchs, concerning whom Salmasius on Solinus, Spanheim in the *Dissertations*, Augustine on Modestinus’ *On Exemptions*, Gothofredus’ *On the Prohibition upon Christians of Communion with Pagans*, Grotius on the New Testament, Rubenius’ *On Neocoran Cities*, and lastly Hardouin, p. 422 of the *Illustrations of Coins*, may be consulted. All these very learned men discuss the matter at length.

To these must be added the Galatarchs, who presided over the *Commune* of the Galatians and administered the solemn games. They are mentioned in an unpublished inscription in my possession, found at Ancyra:

> Γ. ΑΙΛ. ΦΛΑΟΥΙΑΝΟΝ ΣΟΥΛΠΙΚΙΟΝ . ΔΙΣ. Γ . . . ΛΑΤΑΡΧΗΝ. ΤΟΝ ΓΝΟΤΑΤΟΝ . ΚΑΙ. ΔΙ ΚΑΙΟΤΑΤΟΝ ΦΔΑΟΥΙΑΝΟΣ ΕΥΤΥΧΗΣ ΤΟΝ . ΓΛΥΚΥ ΤΑΤΟΝ . ΠΑ  
> ΤΡΩΝΑ. ΔΙΕΥΤΥΚΥ.
>
> “[Gaius] Aelius Flavianus Sulpicius, twice Galatarch, the most eminent and most just; Flavianus Eutyches [honours] his sweetest patron …” (The surviving text and names are materially corrupt at several points.)

And in Gruter, III. CCCCX and I. CCCCXV, T. Flavius Caius Antonius—for that man bore those names, as I shall show elsewhere from more complete inscriptions—is called *Galatarches* (*Γαλατάρχης*) and *Sebastophantes* (*Σιβαστοφάντης*). But because Ancyra was the metropolis of Galatia, I hope I shall not do the reader an unwelcome service if I append another, most elegant unpublished inscription that mentions it:

> ΚΑΛΠΟΥΡΝΙΟΝ ΠΡΟΚΛΟΝ . ΕΚ. ΣΥΝ ΚΛΗΤΙΚΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΥΠΑΡ ΧΩΝ . ΚΕΙΛΙΑΡΧΟΝ ΕΝ . ΔΑΚΙΑ. ΛΗΓΙΩΝΝΟΣ. ΙΓ. ΓΕΜΙΝΗΣ. ΔΗΜΑΡ ΧΩΝ . ΣΤΡΑΤΗΓΟΝ. ΡΩ ΜΕ . ΕΠΙΜΕΛΗΘΕΝΤΑ. Ο ΔΩΝ . ΗΓΕΜΟΝΛ. ΛΗΓΙΩ ΝΟΣ . Α. ΑΘΗΝΑΣ . . . [Col. 0537C] ΑΝΤΥΠΑΤΟΝ ΓΑΛ . . . ΑΣ. ΠΡΕΣΒΕΥΤΗΝ. ΚΑΙ. ΑΝΤΙΣΥΡ ΤΗΓΟΝ . ΒΕΛΤΙΚΗΣ. Π ΜΗΤΡΟΠΟ ΛΙΣ . ΤΗΣ ΓΑΛΑΤΙΑΣ ΣΕΒΑΣ ΤΗ . ΤΕΚΣΑΓΩΝ ΑΝ ΚΥΡΑ . ΤΟΝ. ΕΑΥΤΗΣ. ΣΩΤΗ ΡΑ . ΚΑΙ. ΕΥΕΡΓΕΤΗΝ
>
> “Calpurnius Proclus, of senatorial and consular rank, tribune in Dacia of the Thirteenth Gemina Legion, … commander at Rome, … governor of the First Legion at Athens, … proconsul of Galatia, legate and propraetor of Belgica. Sebaste Tectosagorum Ancyra, metropolis of Galatia, [honours] its own saviour and benefactor.” (Several offices and intervening words are materially uncertain because the supplied inscription is defective.)

But, to continue: women too were appointed priestesses of provinces. Inscription 8, p. CCCXXI:

> PORCIAE. M. F. MATERNAE O. SACER. DESI P. H. C. ET. POSTEA O. SACERD. CAESAR. M TARRAC. PERPETUAE L. NUMISIUS MONTANUS VXORI.
>
> “To Porcia Materna, daughter of Marcus, priestess-designate of the Province of Hither Spain, and afterwards perpetual priestess of the Caesarian [cult] of Tarraconensis; Lucius Numisius Montanus [set this up] for his wife.” (The abbreviated Caesarian title is uncertain.)

For learned men explain the abbreviations *P. H. C.* as *Provinciae Hispaniae Citerioris*, “of the Province of Hither Spain” [Col. 0537D]. It is worth noting that these provincial priests do not appear to have been priests of all the gods worshipped in that province, but of one god to whom the whole province offered sacrifice—especially, as Rubenius shows, of the Augusti. Thus inscription 10, p. CCCXXI, should be interpreted:

> “To Gaius Sempronius Speratus, flamen of the deified Augusti of the province of Baetica”  
> (*C. SEMPRONIO. SPERATO. FLAMINI. DIVORUM. AVGG. PROVINCIAE. BAETICAE.*)

This inscription further seems to teach that Speratus was flamen of all emperors who had been enrolled among the gods or who were worshipped there. Likewise, Victor says that throughout Africa a priesthood was decreed for the Flavian house, namely because Constantine was called Flavius. Relevant examples are the perpetual Augustal flamen in Baetica, the flamen of the Province of Hither Spain, and similar titles found in the same inscriptions; these teach us that flamens or priests were imposed upon provinces.

I grant, however, that their office differed from that of those whom Maximinus, according to Lactantius, established. For these presided over all the rest, while the others could only be called flamens or priests of the province because they administered the province’s common cult [Col. 0538A]. Yet “high priest” remains to be explained. Thus, as is evident from Lactantius and from what I have observed, the man called a high priest was set over the other priests in each city as their head. By the earlier priests we should understand those who had performed rites in those towns or cities before high priests were established.

That emperors were called *pontifices maximi* is too well known to require notice. Apart from them, high pontiffs or high priests occur rarely, though among Greeks *archiereis* (*Ἀρχιερεῖς*) are very frequent and sometimes designate the supreme pontificate of emperors and others, as the illustrious Spanheim excellently showed in Dissertation VI. In Reinesius, *Inscriptions* 58, class 5, there survives the memorial of a woman who was a *sacerdos maxima*:

> LABERIA. FELICIA SACERDOS. MAXIMA MATRIS. DEUM. M. I.
>
> “Laberia Felicia, chief priestess of the Mother of the Gods.” (The final abbreviation, *M. I.*, is unresolved.)

But I suppose she was so called because she surpassed the others in age, or because she was first admitted to the college. Festus testifies that the latter practice was customary at Rome. Among the lesser pontiffs, he is called *maximus* who entered that college first, and *minimus* who entered last. Similarly, the eldest Vestal virgin was called *maxima*, as Lipsius—certainly a very learned man who greatly illuminated antiquarian studies—has shown. Such a pontiff, priest, or Vestal virgin would nevertheless undoubtedly have surpassed the others in dignity and authority.

At Cephaloedium, a small Sicilian town near the river Himera, Cicero, *Second Action against Verres*, tells us that there was also a high priest: “The people of Cephaloedium have a fixed month in which a high priest must be created.” From what follows, it appears that he was annually elected from among the citizens in a popular assembly [Col. 0538C]. He was thus called high not because of age but because of authority, just as Festus testifies that some think the praetor *maximus* is so called because he possesses the greatest imperium, while others think it is because he is greatest in age.

Likewise the *curio maximus* is called such because the curiae and all the curiones are governed by his authority. Perhaps in relation to him the others were called lesser curiones, such as the one celebrated in Gruter, inscription 4, p. 305. Johannes Andreas Bosius also mentions an *augur maximus* in his very learned dissertation *On the Pontifex Maximus of Ancient Rome*, chapter 2; but, to speak truthfully, I have not yet seen him mentioned by any ancient author. Certainly he is not found in Festus under “praetor maximus.”

From these points, then, it is clear that the title *maximus* was given to some priests. But the question deserves examination whether Romans, besides their own *pontifex maximus*, called others by that name, whether at Rome or outside Rome. Gutherius thinks they did and believes that an ancient inscription mentions P. Vergilius as *pontifex maximus* of the Sabines. Bosius rejects this and, following Reinesius, supposes that it read *PONT. MAI.*, that is, *maiori*, “greater,” or *MAR.*, that is, of Mars [Col. 0538D]. But Reinesius himself later seems to have changed his opinion, since on p. 445 of the *Inscriptions* he notes that this Vergilius was called *pontifex maximus* among his own people and in the municipal college of pontiffs, just as at Rome there was also a chief among the lesser pontiffs. Bosius, however, thinks that he was either simply called *maximus*, or that the name of a scribe—or some other addition—has been inserted; for Bosius notes that lesser pontiffs were thus designated. Whatever the case, certainly other *pontifices maximi* besides the truly supreme pontiff of the Romans are mentioned very rarely.

I find *summus pontifex* in Prudentius, Hymn 10, *On St Stephen*, v. 223, where the Roman martyr addresses Asclepiades:

> “You sit as supreme pontiff, spectator of these things.”

I think he was a provincial pontiff. The same author also speaks of a *summus sacerdos*:

> “The supreme priest, to be consecrated, is immersed in a pit driven deep beneath the earth,  
> He is crowned with a mitre …”

Bulenger, Reinesius, p. 622 of the *Letters* and p. 77 of the *Inscriptions*, Sylburgius on Zosimus IV.36, and also a very learned man at p. 172 of the *Pisan Cenotaphs*, wrongly think that these verses describe a *pontifex maximus*. That supreme priest is the priest of Cybele, or Mother of the Gods, the first person consecrated in that manner. The illustrious Salmasius likewise judges that Prudentius is treating of these rites in his notes on the *Historia Augusta* [Col. 0539A].

“Individual men as though pontiffs …” I think I have shown that these were superior to the priests established in cities; nothing prevents the former from being called *maximi*, the latter simply pontiffs. For the name *pontiff* was always considered more dignified than *priest*: the former is general, the latter particular. Thus Velleius II.59 reasonably called the pontificate a priesthood. Indeed, the *pontifex maximus* is sometimes called simply *pontifex* in Latin, and *archiereus* (*Ἀρχιερεύς*) in Greek, with *megistos* omitted, as the illustrious Spanheim excellently shows in Dissertation 6. Thus Geta is called on coins sometimes *PONTIF.* and sometimes *PONT. MAXIMUS*. On a coin of Plautilla, Caracalla is called *ANTON. P. AUG. PONT. TR. P. V. COS.*, according to the famous antiquary and learned Johannes Vaillant. And in Cicero’s speech *On the Response of the Haruspices*, P. Lentulus the consul is called pontiff, though he was *pontifex maximus*.

And just as Eusebius calls Lactantius’ pontiffs *archiereis*, Plutarch likewise calls pontiffs nothing else in his *Numa*:

> “To Numa they also attribute the establishment and organization of the priests whom they call pontiffs, and say that he himself was the first among them”  
> (*Νουμᾷ δὲ καὶ τὴν τῶν Ἀρχιερέων, οὓς ποντίφικας καλοῦσι, διάτασιν καὶ κατάσταξιν ἀποδιδόασι, καί φασιν αὐτὸν ἕνα τούτων τὸν πρῶτον γεγονέναι.*)

This passage troubles me, because learned men think Plutarch relates that King Numa was *pontifex maximus*; Zosimus IV.36 confirms their opinion. But I am surprised that Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Livy, or another author older than Plutarch and Zosimus did not record this. I sometimes suspected that Plutarch should read *τὸ πρῶτον*, “at first,” that is, that he himself was initially one of them. Certainly I do not see how otherwise the word *ἕνα*, “one,” can have a place. Livy, directly relevant here, writes in I.20 that Numa himself performed many rites, especially those now belonging to the Flamen Dialis. Livy and others also testify that Numa Marcius, son of Marcius, was selected from the patricians as pontiff, and that all sacred ordinances, written down and sealed, were entrusted to him by King Numa. Zosimus’ authority does not move me in the least, since he relates other matters there incorrectly and may have been deceived by the name Numa [Col. 0539C].

“In white cloaks …” That is, priests wore garments of white colour, except those who served the gods below, as is very well known. Porphyry, *On Abstinence* IV.19, specifically teaches that the prophets of Zeus in Crete used such garments. Silius in book III gives a snowy garment to a priest; Pliny, book XVI, final chapter, a white garment to the Druids; and Apuleius, book XI, white linen to the ministers of sacred rites. And as a cloak is here assigned to priests, so Apuleius does the same in the cited book: “From his shoulders there hung behind his back a precious cloak.”

“The confessors had their eyes dug out …” This punishment was common, as were the cutting off of hands, feet, and noses, in ecclesiastical history. But it deserves notice that Eusebius VIII.12 relates that, during Diocletian’s affairs, after the judges had become satiated with tortures and blood, the emperors ordered Christians’ eyes to be plucked out and one of their legs to be disabled. Haymo VIII.1 records the same, and Suidas attributes it to Diocletian and Maximian, his son-in-law—namely Galerius—whom, as is clear from what follows, he confuses with Maximian Herculius.

He says that, overcome by the multitude of Christians who were being killed, they issued an edict that the right eye should be gouged out from all Christians wherever found, not only because of the severity of the pain but also because of the disgrace, “and because it was conspicuous and foreign to Roman civic order” (*καὶ προδηλον καὶ τῆς Ῥωμαίων πολιτείας ἀλλότριον*) [Col. 0540A]. Portus translates: “and conspicuous, and by reason of exclusion from Roman citizenship.” But Suidas seems to me to say that this punishment was alien to Roman custom, or not customary in the Roman commonwealth. This is certainly true; hence anyone could immediately recognize that they were Christians.

In the *Polity of the Holy Fathers Metrophanes and Alexander*, preserved in Photius, we read that Paphnutius, who attended the Council of Nicaea, had his right eye gouged out by the command of Maximian “the Christ-hater” (*τοῦ μισοχρίστου*) and the sinews of his left elbow cut: *καὶ τὴν λαιὰν ἐνευροκόπησεν ἀγκύλην*. But this should have been translated, “and he cut the sinews of his left ham,” because *ἀγκύλη* means both the bend of the knee and that of the arm, or elbow. Eusebius, after the words just cited, expressly writes that Christians’ right eyes were gouged out and that “their left feet were disabled at the hams with red-hot iron” (*τοὺς λαιοὺς πόδας κατὰ τῶν ἀγκύλων*) [Col. 0540B].

It is also not unworthy of notice that Eusebius IX.5, and Haymo VIII.3 after him, when dealing with this persecution of Maximinus, relate that the priests of the images were incited to hatred and slaughter of Christians. In order that this might seem to occur with some just reason, certain acts were fabricated as though they had taken place before Pilate concerning our Saviour, in which every blasphemy against Christians was set down. It follows that these forged Acts were made at the end of A.D. 311, because after Galerius’ death, which fell in May of that year, Maximinus refrained from persecution for scarcely six months.

Valesius thinks that these Acts had been mentioned earlier in the judicial records of Tarachus, Probus, and Andronicus, chapter 9: “You wickedly do not know,” says the chief governor, “the Christ whom you invoke: he was a man, placed under the custody of Pontius Pilate and punished; there exist Acts of his Passion.” These events occurred under Diocletian IV and Maximian III as consuls, that is, in A.D. 290. If the same Acts are intended, they certainly preceded the persecution. To reconcile the dates, Valesius thinks that one must write Diocletian IX and Maximian VIII, because those Acts mention an imperial command ordering all men to sacrifice to the immortal gods, and because the governor in chapter 9 says that the emperors had provided a long and profound peace, which had not occurred when Diocletian was consul for the fourth time [Col. 0540C]. He held his ninth consulship in A.D. 304; yet even thus the Acts of Pilate would have been forged before Maximinus’ persecution, whereas Eusebius expressly records that these spurious Acts were published at the beginning of that persecution.

I therefore think that the Acts of Tarachus do not refer to those Acts of Pilate. Either the governor Maximus alludes to Scripture itself, from whose history committed to writing by Christians it is established—not on Pilate’s authority but on Christ’s—that he was crucified; or he alludes to the Acts which Pilate sent to the Emperor Tiberius concerning Christ’s passion, resurrection, and miracles, and to which Tertullian, Eusebius, and others appeal. For if the impious crimes attributed to Christ by those wicked and godless men had then been read by pagans in the Acts of Pilate, Maximus would undoubtedly not have kept them silent, nor merely said that Christ was a man and had been punished.

“Earlobes …” That is, ears. The poet: “King Midas has the ears of an ass”; Arnobius, book VI, p. 240: “But now, because they see faces, eyes, heads, cheeks, ears, noses”; and Cicero’s well-known phrase, “the lowest part of the ear is softer.” Brissonius shows that these modes of punishment were frequently used among the Persians. The author of the *Great Etymologicum* derives *akrotēriazein* (*ἀκρωτηριάζειν*, “to mutilate extremities”) from the fact that the ancients cut off “the tips of the ears” (*τὰ ἄκρα τῶν ὤτων*) of criminals [Col. 0540D].

## CHAPTER XXXVII

“So that whoever had been invited to dinner might depart thence defiled and impure.” As I have already noted on chapter 11, as will appear from Colomesius’ notes, this must be referred to food sacrificed to idols (*idolothyta*). For the same reason Christians abstained from the feasts offered by Romula, Galerius’ mother. What was decided about such matters in the apostles’ time, and what Paul wrote to the Corinthians, is abundantly clear from the New Covenant.

When pagans sacrificed to their gods, they placed whole victims before the altars and consecrated them to the gods; yet they did not offer the entire animals, but a part served to entertain friends. Valerius Flaccus, *Argonautica* II.347:

> “While the first hunger is overcome by the sacred entrails …”

That is, by the flesh remaining from the sacrifice. The god to whom the offering had been made was thought to feed the guests. Hence Aristides, vol. I, p. 97, most elegantly calls Sarapis a host or entertainer (*ἑστιάτωρ*), as Salmasius excellently explains in his observations on Attic and Roman law.

Some were nevertheless frugal, seasoning at home with salt the remnants of sacrifices which they had carried back; others sold them to butchers, as Theophrastus teaches us in chapter 23 of the *Characters*; others, more respectable persons, to avoid expense, sent portions of the victims to friends, as learned men have shown from Theocritus and Plautus. But the person who divided them was not called *kalōkretēs* (*Καλωκρέτης*), as Castellanus supposes in the preface to his *Syntagma on Greek Festivals*. Rather, the sacrificer himself did this through a designated person, perhaps a slave. The *kalōkretēs*, on the contrary, was a treasurer of public money. Though he managed the expenses incurred in public rites and received the skins and remains of such victims, like the priests, as the scholiast on Aristophanes observes, it cannot in any way be inferred from this that he divided the remnants of sacrifices and sent them to the sacrificers’ friends [Col. 0541B].

Porphyry, *On Abstinence* II.8, testifies that in his time certain parts of animals were sacrificed and the rest used for feasting: “just as we now, after offering the first portion of animals, set the remainder as a meal” (*καθάπερ ἡμεῖς νῦν ἐπὶ τῶν ζώων ἀπαρξάμενοι γὰρ, τὰ λοιπὰ δαῖτα τιθέμεθα*). In §27, he thinks that people, having in ancient times offered the first fruits of crops to the gods and eaten the remainder, likewise tasted animals dedicated in sacrifice by the same precedent.

There were, however, sacrifices in which it was forbidden to eat what had been offered. Porphyry II.44: “For all theologians agree in this: that, in sacrifices intended to avert evil, the things sacrificed must not be touched, and expiatory rites must be employed” (*ὡς οὔτε ἁπτέον ἐν ταῖς ἀποτροπαίοις θυσίαις τῶν θυομένων, καθαρσίοις τε χρηστέον*). That is, in sacrifices made to avert some evil, the offerings must not be eaten; expiatory rites must instead be used.

The earliest Christians abstained from idol-sacrificed food. Besides examples collected by others, see Ado, *Martyrology*, pp. 80, 142, 148, and 181; Mabillon’s *Analecta*, vol. IV, p. 132—a singularly elegant passage—and p. 141. Conversely, the Nicolaitans and Valentinians ate such food, as Epiphanius and Augustine testify [Col. 0541C].

“In other respects also like his master.” I think Galerius Maximianus is indicated, unless someone supposes that one ought to write “like his masters,” since Diocles and Maximian are mentioned shortly afterward.

“From this came famine, the fields …” Haymo also mentions this, book VIII, chapter 3, but assigns other causes.

“They were dragged away to the daily sacrifices, by which them …” I formerly thought that *eos* referred to the fields; but I now reject that, because what follows plainly proves the contrary. Colomesius’ reading *suos* does not displease me: Lactantius would thus mean the courtiers or household servants of the emperor, who were so well filled with the remnants of sacrifices that they despised the grain-ration or provisions given them as worthless. This passage too concerns idol-sacrificed food and is nearly paralleled in Ammianus Marcellinus XXII.12:

> “Julian nevertheless drenched the altars with the copious blood of victims through excessive frequency, sometimes sacrificing a hundred bulls and innumerable herds of various cattle, as well as white birds sought from land and sea; so that almost every day soldiers, gorged with an overabundant supply of meat, living too dissolutely and corrupted by avid drinking, were carried through the streets on the shoulders of passers-by from the public buildings, where they indulged themselves in banquets requiring punishment rather than restraint, to their lodgings.”

By *annona* we must understand meat, oil, wine, and grain, as we learn from the Theodosian Code, *On the Distribution of the Military Annona*; see Gothofredus there, and Salmasius on the *Historia Augusta*. To these add Zosimus II.9, from which it is clear that there was one prefect responsible for providing pork to the praetorians.

And he scattered [it] everywhere . . . I judge that this should be written thus: “the grain allowance. And he scattered [it] everywhere without discrimination, without measure, when he stripped all the wealthy . . .” so that all this refers to Maximinus. Eusebius certainly, VIII.14 [Col. 0542A], relates that Maximinus despoiled every very wealthy man of his paternal and ancestral possessions, and bestowed “wealth in heaps and piles of money upon the flatterers about him” (*πλούτους ἀθρόως καὶ σωροὺς χρημάτων τοῖς ἀμφ᾿ αὐτὸν κόλαξιν*).

But to *expungere* someone of garments and gold coins means nothing other than to deprive someone of those things, to take them away from him. Yet the expression is remarkable, and I do not know whether it occurs elsewhere. *Expungere nomen* means to pay a debt; the poor are said to be *expungi* when they are paid what the Church owes them gratuitously for Christ’s sake, as the most distinguished Gronovius teaches in chapter 8 of his *Observations on Ecclesiastical History*. A *manipulus expunctus* is a soldier struck off the military roll and released from his oath; *rationes expunctae* are accounts cancelled and erased. None of these has anything in common with Lactantius’ phrase. And although someone might think that *emungerent* should be read, as Terence in the *Phormio* said of “milking an old man of money,” nevertheless I think Lactantius wrote *expungerent*, because Papinian uses almost exactly the same expression in law XV, *Digest*, *On Military Matters*: “A man marked for desertion and restored is struck off in respect of the expenses for the time during which he was in desertion” [Col. 0542B].

“I do not know whether they ought to be transacted . . .” I read: “whether they ought not to be transacted,” which Lactantius says ironically.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

“Through every limb . . .” Antony levels the same reproach against Augustus in Suetonius, chapter 69: “Negotiations were sought through friends, who would strip and inspect married women and adult maidens.” Casaubon notes there that male and female slaves were inspected naked by purchasers; Seneca also uses this term in book I of the *Controversiae*.

“He was drowned in water, as though it were a crime of treason.” This does not mean that drowning was the penalty for violated majesty; rather, that offence was capital—not indeed under the Julian law, but under the laws of later emperors. For whereas under the Julian law the penalty for such persons was exile, or interdiction from fire and water, as is also clear from Tacitus, the jurist Paulus nevertheless writes in his own time that those of lower rank were thrown to beasts or burned alive, while those of higher rank were punished [Col. 0542C] by decapitation. Consequently, in the following times—for Paulus lived under Alexander Severus—the death penalty was imposed upon those charged with treason.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

“Whom she had recently called mother . . .” Understand Valeria, widow of Galerius Maximianus, who had adopted Maximinus Daza. Yet it will be worthwhile to present briefly, as it were in a table, what wives Diocletian, Herculius, Galerius, and the others had, and who were born to them, so that clearer light may thereby be shed upon various passages in Lactantius.

That Diocletian had a wife named Serena is attested by Ado in the *Martyrology*, p. 135, Tristan, and others. Valesius calls her Eleutheria; others, Alexandra. But Lactantius, chapter 15, teaches that she was called Prisca, and all the earlier authorities seem to have erred—unless we say that she bore two or more names. Diocletian had by her Galeria Valeria.

As for Galerius Maximianus, Galeria Valeria married him. For Diocletian ordered this adopted son, after he had repudiated his former wife, to take her in marriage; hence in chapter 29 he is called Diocletian’s son-in-law. She was barren. Therefore she adopted Candidianus, born to Galerius by a concubine, whom he wished to make Caesar, as is clear from chapter 20; Lactantius teaches this in chapter 50: “Licinius ordered Candidianus, whom Valeria had adopted because of barrenness, though born from a concubine, to be killed.” When near death, Galerius commended her and his son Candidianus to Licinius and entrusted them to his care, chapter 35. But she left Licinius angry, as I suppose, because she would not marry him, and entrusted herself with her mother to Maximinus, although she had not been on sufficiently good terms with her husband, as is clear from chapter 32.

The reason why she left Licinius, I think, lies hidden in the words of this chapter: “After Maximianus’ death, Valeria came to him, thinking she would remain more safely in his territory, especially because he had a wife.” Licinius, of course, was unmarried [Col. 0543A], since later he took Constantia, Constantine’s sister, as his wife. It is highly probable that he had proposed marriage to Valeria and that she rejected him on the same ground on which she rejected Maximinus: that it was unlawful for a woman of such name and rank, contrary to custom and precedent, to take a second husband. Nor do I see for what other reason Lactantius would so pointedly have said that she entrusted herself to Maximinus especially because he had a wife. He did not dare to tell the matter as it stood because firm friendship existed between Constantine and Licinius when this little book was published.

Since, then, she also refused to marry Maximinus, he expelled her with her mother into exile and relegated her to certain desolate regions of Syria. Nor could she obtain pardon through Diocletian’s prayers, chapters 20 and 41. Finally Licinius ordered the heads of her and her mother Prisca to be cut off at Thessalonica, chapter 51; I shall emend the corrupt words there. It should be noted, moreover, that Ado of Vienne writes in the *Martyrology*, p. 105, that the emperor Diocletian’s daughter, troubled by a demon, was healed by St Vitus through prayer; indeed, on p. 70, that the same woman was called Artemia, was freed from the demon by Cyriacus, and was baptized. Then he himself adds that Maximinus killed his sister Artemia at that time. If there is any truth in these reports, Diocletian must have had two daughters. And if she who is said to have been killed is the same Artemia as the former one, “Maximianus” should be written—namely Galerius—since he had her sister Valeria in marriage and may be said to have killed his own [sister], by killing his wife’s full sister. But, to confess the truth, no great trust can be placed in authorities of this sort.

[Col. 0543B] Maximianus Herculius had as wife Valeria Eutropia. Before her marriage to him she had borne Theodora, or Flavia Maximiana Theodora, by a Syrian man; Theodora married Constantius Chlorus. After marrying Herculius, Eutropia bore Maxentius.

When Constantius Chlorus was made Caesar, he was compelled to repudiate Helena—whether concubine or wife [Col. 0543C]—by whom he had had Constantine, later called “the Great” because of the glory of his achievements. He married Theodora, Herculius’ stepdaughter; she bore him Dalmatius, Constantius, Hannibalianus, Constantia, Eutropia, and Anastasia. One of these married Licinius, as is clear from chapter 43: “When he heard that Constantine’s sister had been betrothed to Licinius, he believed that this alliance of the two emperors was being joined against him.” And because Maximus Herculius was Theodora’s stepfather, Constantius Chlorus is therefore called his son-in-law in chapter 29: “that he might treacherously ensnare Constantine the emperor, his son-in-law” (because of his wife Fausta), “the son of his son-in-law”—that is, the son of Constantius Chlorus, who had married Theodora, Herculius’ stepdaughter, and who was not Constantine’s mother but his stepmother.

Constantine the Great married Fausta, the younger daughter of Maximianus Herculius, as is stated in chapter 27, in the panegyric of an unknown author, and by others. This occurred after Minervina, his first wife, had died. It is sufficiently well known what children, and how many, he had; the illustrious Du Cange explains this admirably [Col. 0543D].

Maxentius was the son of Maximianus Herculius and Eutropia. Mamertinus praises him highly as a boy in chapter 14 of the *Panegyric*: “But surely the day will soon dawn when Rome shall see you victorious, and your lively son at your right hand—a son born, with every gift of intellect, for the most honourable pursuits, and whom some fortunate teacher awaits, knowing that he will have no labour in urging a divine and immortal offspring to the pursuit of glory.”

Yet the author of the *Epitome of Victor*, the author of the *Valesian Excerpts*, and Paul the Deacon report that he was imposed upon Herculius through Eutropia’s contrivance, in order to hold the affection of a husband whose hopes were bound up with the most welcome birth of a child long desired. The author of the anonymous panegyric, chapter 3, teaches the same: “At last, he who was believed to be his father attempted to pull the torn purple garment from his shoulders.” Behold: “believed”; therefore not his true father. Thus in chapter 4 the same author calls Maxentius Maximianus’ supposititious son. Tristan thought Julian reported the same, but I have shown, on chapter 18, that he was mistaken.

[Col. 0544A] Moreover, in the *Ecclesiastical Constitution of the Holy Fathers Metrophanes and Alexander* in Photius, Maxentius is called *adelphidous Maximianou* (*ἀδελφιδοὺς Μαξιμιάνου*), “Maximianus’ brother’s son.” I shall quote the entire passage, because it seems to me very tangled:

> “After Severus had died from illness, Licinius, who had as wife the sister of Constantius, ruled; Maximianus held the remaining part of the East. But Maxentius ruled the region around Rome, being Maximianus’ brother’s son; for the former was the son of the earlier Maximianus, while the latter was the son of Diocletian” (*Μαξέντιος δὲ τῆς κατὰ Ῥώμην ἦρχεν ἀδελφιδοῦς ὢν Μαξιμιανοῦ· καί γὰρ ὁ μὲν ἦν Μαξιμιανοῦ προτέρου, ὁ δὲ Διοκλητιανοῦ*).

I can scarcely extricate myself from this, and hope others may be found who will untie the knot. For I have never read that Maxentius was born of a brother or sister of Maximianus, since he was born to Herculius and the Syrian Eutropia. I have sometimes suspected that the passage is corrupt and that the words have been transposed; at the beginning, perhaps, it should read: “Maximinus held [the East], being Maximianus’ sister’s son” (*Μαξιμίνος ἐπεῖχε ἀδελφιδοὺς ὢν Μαξιμιανοῦ*). For Maximinus held the East and was born from the sister of Galerius Maximianus. Then Maxentius is called the son of Maximianus, namely Herculius; while the other—[Col. 0544B] Galerius Maximianus—was the son of Diocletian because he had been adopted by him and had Diocletian’s daughter as wife. But I define nothing certain and leave these matters for others to examine.

If we believe Tristan, Maxentius had as wife Magna Urbica, daughter of Galerius by his first wife; by her he had Romulus, who died and was consecrated while his father lived, and another son, said still to have been living with his mother two days before the disaster. Thus the panegyrist relates that Maxentius left the palace two days previously and voluntarily withdrew with wife and son to a private house.

Severus had a son Severianus, as is clear from chapter 50; the name of his wife and of his parents is unknown. Tristan thinks he was born of a sister of Galerius Maximianus; but Zosimus and Aurelius Victor, whom he cites, report this only of Galerius Maximinus, Daza before he became emperor. And if this had been true, I do not think Galerius Maximianus would have passed it over in silence when he addressed Diocletian and discussed with him the appointment of Caesars, chapters 18 and 19 [Col. 0544C].

C. Valerius Maximinus—whom Haymo wrongly calls Severus Maximinus in VIII.3—was born from the sister of Galerius Maximianus. The *Epitome of Victor*: “Galerius Maximinus, born from the sister of Armentarius, and called Daza by his true name before becoming emperor.” Therefore Galerius Maximianus calls him his relative in chapter 18; Paul the Deacon calls him Galerius’ sister’s son, though he incorrectly calls him Maximus. Tristan writes that Zosimus makes her the sister of Maximianus Herculius; but I find nothing of the sort in Zosimus, although Hofmann and Moreri report the same in their lexicons.

The name of his wife is unknown, chapter 39, and she herself was hurled into the Orontes, chapter 50. By her Maximinus had a son and a daughter, killed at Licinius’ command, in the same chapter. Yet in chapter 47 he attributes to him “sons,” not a son and daughter:

> “But on the Kalends of May—that is, in one night and one day—he reached Nicomedia in another night . . . and, having taken his children and wife and a few attendants from the palace, he made for the East.”

Indeed chapter 50 mentions his eldest son: “He also put to death Maximinus’ own eldest son, then eight years old, and his seven-year-old daughter, who had been betrothed to Candidianus” [Col. 0544D]. But if he had had several sons, Licinius surely would not have forgotten to kill them. Therefore, in the earlier passage the term “children” may perhaps include the daughter as well, as civil law shows it can. In the latter, moreover, *Maximus* is a proper name—unless we say that the younger child died during the flight.

For Eusebius appears clearly to teach that Maximinus had two sons, at the end of book IX of the *Ecclesiastical History*: “To all these were added Maximinus’ children, whom he had already made partners in royal honour and participants in the dedication of portraits and inscriptions” (*τούτοις ἅπασι προσετίθεντο καὶ οἱ Μαξιμίνου παῖδες, οὓς ἤδη καὶ τῆς βασιλικῆς τιμῆς τῆς τε ἐν πίναξι καὶ γραφαῖς ἀναθέσεως πεποίητο κοινωνοὺς*). I know that *paidas* (*παῖδας*) means children generally and can embrace Maximinus’ son and daughter. But Eusebius adds that they were depicted on panels and made partners in imperial power—things which, I think, do not apply to a daughter. I find no means of evading this difficulty except to say that Eusebius used the plural for the singular.

[Col. 0545A] These are the points I wished to note concerning the emperors, their wives, and their children. I also judged that readers would not find it unwelcome if, at the beginning of Lactantius’ little work, I displayed authentic likenesses of them and of the other persecutors, so that each might set before his eyes, as if in a single glance, the dreadful persecutions by which they afflicted the Church and the deserved punishments by which God afflicted them. I did not add Magna Urbica, because learned men doubt whether she was Maxentius’ wife. I included Licinius because Lactantius mentions him and because he later persecuted the Church; he therefore has his place among the Persecutors. I arranged for Constantine to be depicted in the centre of the table, surrounded by his father, mother, stepmother, and wife: because Constantius Chlorus favoured Christians, and because Constantine, conqueror of the tyrants, together with Licinius gave peace to the Church—which Licinius nevertheless afterwards disturbed, as I have noted.

[Col. 0545B] “He is inflamed.” That is, he is inflamed with lust, and is inflamed by looking.

“Before the period of mourning had yet been completed.” This was ten months; later, by the law of Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, it became twelve months, as learned men have noted. Thus these events happened late in 311 or early in 312, since Galerius died in May 311; and because Valeria complains that Maximinus had recently called her mother and that the ashes of her husband were still warm, I would willingly assign these matters to the year 311. From this it is likewise clear for approximately how long she remained with Licinius.

“In that funeral garb . . .” That is, black. Hence a little earlier: “the woman was still in dark garments.” Lipsius on Tacitus, followed by Kirchmann, II.18, *On Funerals*, thinks that under the emperors women wore white garments in mourning. That this did occur is clear from Herodian and Plutarch; but perhaps the custom had been abolished by Diocletian’s time, or was not observed by all, [Col. 0545C] indeed only in particular cases.

“With the still-warm ashes of her husband . . .” Therefore Galerius Maximianus was placed upon a funeral pyre, and at that time cremation was still in use among pagans—unless someone judges this merely a figurative manner of speaking, intended only to signify that Valeria’s husband had died recently. Learned men once attempted to prove, from Capitolinus, chapter 13 of the life of Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher, that cremation had been abolished under the Antonines; but their error has been corrected. That passage certainly teaches nothing else than that, after a great pestilence had arisen, the Antonines made some provision concerning the construction of tombs. What precisely that provision was, the most expert scholars in these matters—Salmasius, Casaubon, Jacob Gothofredus, and Obregthus—dispute among themselves; of these, Gothofredus does not seem to me wholly to have missed the truth.

But even if Capitolinus’ words did not refute that opinion, it plainly cannot be admitted because of the examples that follow. Among the least insignificant are the *Consecratio* with a pyre found on coins of L. Septimius Severus, Caracalla, and Caesar P. Cornelius Saloninus Valerianus, son of Gallienus Augustus; and Galerius Maximianus was cremated. I am persuaded that cremation was abolished through the passage of time, and I think learned men rightly judge that Christians were a major cause of this change. In the words of Minucius Felix, they feared no harm from burial, but followed the older and better custom of interment. Macrobius, *Saturnalia* VII.7, writes that in his own age—that is, under Theodosius the Younger—there was no practice of burning the bodies of the dead.

[Col. 0545D] That cremation was not an ancient institution, and that Sulla the dictator was the first member of the Cornelian clan to be cremated, is reported by Pliny and Cicero. Indeed, it is clear from Statius’ *Silvae*, where he describes Priscilla’s funeral, that in Domitian’s time burial, or the interment of corpses, was practised by some. Since the old custom increased more and more daily, and seemed the more humane even to pagans themselves, I think it came about that we sometimes read in ancient monuments that an entire body was interred [Col. 0546A]:

> To the Divine Manes. Of Lucius Julius Epigonus. He lived 26 years, 5 months, 12 days. The body was interred whole. Marcus Julius Hamus, father, for his most devoted son.
>
> Gaius Julius Hamus, to the Divine Manes of Lucius Julius Marcellus, his grandson. He lived 5 years, 41 days. The body was interred whole in a sarcophagus.

Nor does the opinion of a most learned and celebrated man displease me: that the catacombs were made by pagans and that corpses were placed in them. Yet I hope he will not take it ill if I add [Col. 0546B] what Giovanni Battista Doni thinks on this matter in the book entitled *On Restoring the Healthfulness of the Roman Countryside*:

> “Sand-pits,” he says, p. 52, “were subterranean chambers excavated in ancient times to extract sand for building purposes. Nowadays people do this differently, by digging from above into the earth, as is customary in trenching. Such chambers survive in great number not merely nearby, beneath vineyards near the city, but farther away also, in almost every direction as far as the sea and the Praenestine Mountains; and from another quarter of the sky, even very far into Etruria. Nor have some lacked the desire to investigate certain more hidden and deeply buried marvels of antiquity. Thus this whole suburban tract of Latium and Tuscia, whose lowest ground is everywhere by nature tufa and sand, may be considered thoroughly undermined and almost suspended. Hence it is scarcely ever shaken by internal tremors. Such long, manifold, and in various ways interconnected underground passages lie open in every direction that they present the appearance [Col. 0546C] of some immense labyrinth.
>
> “Subterranean chambers or tunnels of this kind, also simply called sand-pits (*arenariae*), are mentioned in ancient Acts of the Holy Martyrs; they are also called catacombs, because, during the raging persecution of tyrants, Christ’s innocent people chiefly hid themselves in these underground places by day, slept there, took food, and held sacred assemblies. Cemeteries differ from these as species from genus. They are generally near the city, beside the military roads—many survive—and extend through wider but shorter spaces, splendidly adorned with chapels, tombs, altars, and constructions of that kind. Something similar were certain underground monuments among the pagans, also called burial-vaults (*conditoria*), their circuit of walls supported by brickwork, containing numerous niches with urns and ossuaries belonging almost exclusively to a single family.”

Such is this very learned man’s opinion concerning these chambers and catacombs. I leave it to learned persons who live in Rome and can inspect its suburban countryside to examine it. [Col. 0546D] Yet I do not think the *puticuli* had anything in common with these chambers or tunnels. First, they were in one place outside the Esquiline Gate, whereas the catacombs and those sandy chambers are found around Rome. Secondly, it is in no way likely that the earth was excavated at such expense so that the corpses of poorer people might be buried there. Finally, a well—of which *puticulus* is the diminutive—is one thing; catacombs are another. The former lies open, whereas the latter are underground. Varro and Festus clearly teach that there were several wells in the place called the *puticuli*, and the very name *puticuli* appears to indicate nothing else.

Festus notes that *puticuli* was the most ancient kind of burial, because people were buried there in wells. These words seem to me to imply nothing else than that corpses were anciently laid in pits and covered with earth, and that those pits were called *puticuli*. Thus Varro, about to explain the reason for the name, writes [Col. 0547A] that people were covered there in wells—namely with earth, as is customary today. If we follow Aelius Gallus in Varro, corpses were thrown there, and the place was named from rotting (*putescere*). Festus also teaches this, adding after the words just quoted: “Such was the place outside the Esquiline Gate where corpses are now customarily thrown; because they rotted there, the name *Puticuli* arose.” The words both of Aelius Gallus and of Festus seem to teach that corpses were not even covered with earth, but simply thrown down, to dry out and be consumed by the air.

Horace plainly confirms this, *Satires* I.8, where he describes the gardens of Maecenas, situated on the Esquiline and at the *Puticuli*:

> But a reed fixed upon its summit terrifies the troublesome birds  
> and forbids them to settle in the new gardens.  
> Here formerly corpses, cast out from narrow cells,  
> a fellow-slave hired to be carried in a cheap coffin.  
> This was the common burial-place for the wretched populace,  
> for Pantolabus the buffoon and Nomentanus the spendthrift.  
> [Col. 0547B] A boundary-stone gave a thousand feet in frontage,  
> three hundred into the field, and forbade the monument to pass to heirs.
>
> Now one may live upon the healthful Esquiline  
> and stroll upon the sunny embankment, where before one viewed  
> a dismal field deformed by white bones.

From this we learn, first, that the bodies of slaves were cast out from hired coffins; secondly, that the graves of the lowest populace were also there; and finally, that bones of corpses lay scattered in the same place. All this suggests that many corpses were thrown into that spot, and that none, or only a few, were covered with a light layer of earth; and that perhaps the remains of the burned, namely bones and ashes, were not interred but left in the field. For public cremation grounds were also there. Porphyry, on Horace’s fifth Ode, notes that in the area of the embankment outside the Esquiline Gates the bodies of the poor were customarily either burned or thrown out. [Col. 0547C] The commentator published by Cruquius not only calls the *puticuli* pits, thus fully confirming my opinion, but also writes that there was a public cremation-ground there: “The place was called *puticuli* from wells, pits for burying the corpses of the poor; here also were public cremation-grounds.” I therefore think we may call these *puticuli* pits, trenches, or, in the Belgian idiom, *cuylen*, *groeven*. If these views displease others, I shall certainly yield at once if I am taught something better.

“Contrary to custom, contrary to precedent . . .” Therefore no Augusta, after her emperor-husband had died, married another man down to this time. This is abundantly clear from history itself. Statilia Messalina, Nero’s last wife, does not stand in the way: Otho had intended to marry her, according to Suetonius, *Life of Otho*, chapter 10, but the marriage was not contracted because death intervened.

Yet it is especially to be noted that learned men think Tertullian teaches, *Exhortation to Chastity*, chapter 13, that emperors, as pontiffs supreme, could not enter into second marriages by law. “The wife of a flamen,” he says, “is the wife of one man; such also is the law of the flamen. For even the chief pontiff himself is not permitted to marry twice; which surely is the glory of monogamy.” And in book I, *To His Wife*, chapter 7: [Col. 0547D] “Among the nations, priesthood belongs to widowhood and celibacy. In emulation, of course, of the devil: it is unlawful for the pontiff supreme, the king of the world, to marry again.”

In chapter 2 of his dissertation *On the Chief Pontiff of Ancient Rome*, Johannes Andreas Bosius alters the first passage to read “since even he himself,” and so removes the connection that the *nam* (“for”) has with what precedes. He then explains “king of the world” as the man who held supreme power among the pagans, that is, the emperor who exercised the chief pontificate. But there are so many examples of emperors who had several wives that we must either say that they disregarded the law or interpret these passages differently—especially since nowhere do we read that, under the free republic, a second marriage was forbidden to the chief pontiff.

I would rather therefore follow the learned men who understand by “chief pontiff” the *Flamen Dialis*, whom Gellius, X.15, records as supreme—that is, supreme among the flamines—and as a man of one wife. [Col. 0548A] This might perhaps also be referred to the priest of Cybele, whom I have shown in commenting on chapter 36 to have been called “supreme.” For Tertullian speaks no differently in the book *On the Prescription against Heretics*: “What? Does he not also ordain the chief pontiff to one marriage only?” Whatever the case, it is by no means likely that a Roman emperor can be meant. If Tertullian called either the *Flamen Dialis* or another priest “chief pontiff,” where he should have said “supreme,” as Prudentius did, this must be excused him.

He calls him “king of the world” not because he was ruler and emperor of the pagans, but because he was, as it were, the head of pagan superstition, which I think is denoted by *saecula* (“worlds”). Nor would I dispute if someone wished to understand a pontiff or some flamen who was set over the priests in Africa, or who was priest or provincial pontiff.

## CHAPTER XL

“A Vestal maidservant, a virgin . . .” She who is consecrated to a goddess is elegantly called the goddess’ maidservant, as Medea, priestess of Hecate, is called in Valerius Flaccus, VI.502 [Col. 0548B]:

> He shall know me as his mistress,  
> and shall feel grief at the shameful abduction of my maidservant.

The same author, VI.643:

> Her parents called her the maidservant  
> of Phasis, vainly, because of her uncut hair.

Again, VII.366:

> Then the maidservant was shown the field, where, by Phoebe’s lamp,  
> beneath the tenth yoke, she reaps the fruitful crop . . .

Oenomaus in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* V, calls the poet “servant of the Muses” (*Μουσῶν θεράπων*) because he is, as it were, consecrated to them. Indeed the Hyperborean people, *dāmos Hyperboreōn* (*δᾶμος Ὑπερβορέων*), is called Apollo’s servant (*θεράπων*) by Pindar, *Olympian* III, because it worshipped him especially. The Graces are Venus’ maidservants in the scholiast on Statius, *Thebaid* II—though I do not know why Barthius altered this. At last the same name was given to animals that carried out the commands of gods, such as the Calydonian boar in Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VIII.287:

> He is the servant and avenger of hostile Diana.

[Col. 0548C] Animals specially consecrated to gods were called by no other name; thus swans, partridge-hunters (*perdikothērai*, *περδικοθήρας*), and swift-winged creatures (*ōkypteroi*, *ὠκυπτέρος*) are called Apollo’s servants (*therapontes*, *θεράποντες*) by Aelian, *On the Nature of Animals* II.32, VI.19, and XII.4.

“No less close to the Augusta.” That is, she was as intimate with the Augusta as the other woman, who was always with her. I do not think *proxima* (“close”) refers to a degree of kinship, as it very frequently does, because the words “no less” refer to the intimacy mentioned immediately before.

“Lest he be stoned . . .” Namely, a Jew whom the people hated because of the false testimony he was about to give. Hence Lactantius ironically praises the judge’s equity and carefulness, because he defended from the people’s violence the man who ought to have been a witness in so grave a case.

[Col. 0548D] “Who, having been ordered . . .” Perhaps these words should be completed thus: “ordered by the evil beast,” or “by the wicked judge,” or something similar. Then perhaps it would also be better punctuated: “the innocent women are restrained and ordered to be led away.”

“They are restrained.” Namely, the two noble women who refuted the Jew. Thus in Eusebius, VIII.3, we read that soldiers restrained Christians with blows of the fist so that they might not speak or say that they had neither sacrificed nor would sacrifice; this is repeated in chapter 1 of *The Martyrs of Palestine*. It is very well known that accused and condemned persons are properly and absolutely said to be “led away” when they are conducted to prison or to the place of punishment.

“Deserving well.” Nothing is more common in ancient inscriptions than for a husband to be called by his wife, and a wife by her husband, “well-deserving” (*bene merens*, *bene merita*). By this form of speech pagans testified to marital love.

“Promoted men, equipped in military fashion . . .” Learned men attempt in various ways to repair this passage. Until others bring forward something more certain, I follow their traces and think it should be written: “Promoted men, equipped in military fashion, proceed as light-armed troops and archers.” The insertion of *ut* (“as”) seems necessary to me, because Lactantius does not say that soldiers accompanied those noble women, but that promoted officials were armed after the manner of light troops and archers. *Promoti* are officials of judges promoted to some rank, as is clear from law II of the Theodosian Code, *On the Julian Law Concerning Bribery*; see Jacob Gothofredus on law II of the same Code, *On Counterfeit Coinage*. But if, besides the promoted officials equipped in military fashion, light-armed troops and archers were present, *ut* may conveniently be omitted and *milites* (“soldiers”) read in place of *velites* (“light troops”); for on that reading it is not soldiers who are called equipped in military fashion, but the promoted officials.

“And not the adulterer . . .” Namely the Jew, who, under torture before the judge, had falsely confessed that he had had intercourse with the noble women and thereby had made himself an adulterer. These words show that what the preceding chapter relates is true: Valeria’s friends [Col. 0549B] were condemned on a fabricated charge of adultery. Moreover, the penalty inflicted upon the adulterer and adulteress should be noted: it was capital. The most learned jurists hold that under the Julian law the punishment for adultery was relegation, and that by Constantine’s law they were punished by the sword. But since Constantine’s law, law XXX of the Code *On the Julian Law Concerning Adultery*, was enacted in AD 326, while these events occurred in 312, it follows either that this penalty must be attributed to the character of the tyrant Maximinus or that capital punishment for adulterers had been established before Constantine’s law.

## CHAPTER XLI

“To certain desolate regions of Syria.” In what part of Syria these lay is indeed exceedingly difficult to say, since that region stretched far and wide and contained great deserts. The author of the *Life of Damasus* mentions one of them: “At the time when Blessed Damasus governed the Church, Blessed Jerome, a man praiseworthy for the splendour of his learning and holy life, was [Col. 0549C] in that desert of the eastern region which Syria bounds where it joins the frontier of Barbary.” Here perhaps he calls Arabia, or lands inhabited by Saracens, “Barbary.” Jerome himself speaks thus in the *Life of Paul the Hermit*: “In that part of the desert which lies next to Syria and joins the Saracens, I saw monks.” It is well known that *solum barbaricum* (“barbarian territory”), and indeed *Barbaria*, at that period denoted lands not subject to the Roman emperor.

“A military and powerful man . . .” That is, a man of great influence, adorned with great offices or dignities; in the same sense chapter 15 calls eunuchs “very powerful.”

## CHAPTER XLII

“The statues of the aged Maximianus . . .” That is, Herculius, who, together with Diocletian, is called a “Senior Augustus” in Gruter’s *Inscriptions*, p. 178. A coin of Maximianus Herculius himself bears the inscription: “To the most blessed Lord Maximianus, Senior Augustus” (*D. MAXIMIANO. BEATISSIMO. SEN. AUG.*). The statues of those who were stripped of imperial power [Col. 0549D] were thrown down; hence this was frequently the beginning of rebellion. See Ammianus Marcellinus XIV.7.

And the portraits in which he was painted were taken down as well. Lactantius immediately adds: “And because the two old men were for the most part painted together.” This gave rise in me to the suspicion that a slight defect lies hidden here, whose removal will yield a most elegant sense. Lactantius therefore distinguishes between statues, made of marble, bronze, gold, silver, or some other harder material, and images, painted on panels or shields and dedicated in temples, senate-houses, and other public places. I therefore think one should read: “And the images in which he too was painted were taken down.” This concerns Herculius; but what follows—“he bore Diocletian’s presence with difficulty, and because the two old men were for the most part painted together”—means that his images too, not statues, as must be noted, were removed together with the images of Herculius. So in chapter 44 he distinguishes statues from images: Constantine recognizes Maximinus’ treachery [Col. 0550A], discovers the letters, finds statues and images. And in chapter 43, by the images of Maxentius and Maximinus being placed together, nothing other than painted representations on shields can be understood; although I know well, and have indeed myself taught, that the word *imago* is also used of figures or statues made of marble or another material.

Thus Eusebius, speaking of Herculius, writes in VIII.3 that “the honorary paintings and statues” (*τὰς ἐπὶ τιμῇ γραφὰς καὶ ἀνδριάντας*) were thrown down. And there is an elegant passage to this effect in the same author, *Ecclesiastical History* IX.11:

> “Both all the pictures which had been set up in every city in honour of him and of his children” (*Γραφαί τε ὅσαι εἰς τιμὴν αὐτοῦ καὶ τῶν αὐτοῦ παίδων κατὰ πᾶσαν ἀνήκειντο πόλιν*).

That is: “But the images or paintings which had been set up in honour of him and his children”—he speaks of Maximinus—“and were seen in almost every city, were in some cases thrown down from on high and shattered; in others made useless, their faces being obliterated with black paint.” “Likewise, however many statues had been erected in his honour were thrown down and broken in pieces” (*ἀνδριάντων τὲ ὁμοίως ὀπόσοι εἰς τὴν αὐτοῦ τιμὴν διανεστὴκεσαν ὡσαύτως ῥιπτόμενοι συνετρίβοντο*). Just as Lactantius distinguishes images and statues, so Eusebius distinguishes *γραφαί* (“paintings”) and *ἀνδριάντες* (“statues”); [Col. 0550B] and he writes that some images were taken down and dashed upon the ground, while others were covered with black paint. He then relates that Licinius inflicted the final punishment upon Maximinus’ children: “whom he had already made participants in imperial honour and in dedication or consecration in painted panels and pictures” (*οὓς ἤδη καὶ τῆς βασιλικῆς τιμῆς τῆς τε ἐν πίναξι καὶ γραφαῖς ἀναθέσεως πεποίητο κοινωνοὺς*). This is how that passage should be translated.

Haymo, *Ecclesiastical History* VIII.4, rendered the former passage thus: “The images of the tyrant himself, whether sculpted or painted, are ordered to be cast down, or darkened with black, or obliterated with colours.” Yet, as is clear from the Greek, this translation is not altogether felicitous. Shields, upon which emperors were painted, certainly belong to painted representations. Suetonius, *Domitian* 23: “The Senate rejoiced so greatly that, when the senate-house was filled with its members competing with one another, it ordered even ladders to be brought in, and his shields and images”—that is, images painted on shields—“to be taken down before them and fastened to the ground there.” This passage teaches us that those shields were suspended on the walls of the senate-house in a higher position; hence Lactantius and Suetonius appropriately write that the images were “taken down” [Col. 0550C].

Nor does Justin speak otherwise, XXXVIII.9: “Then the people take down his statues and images.” Here likewise statues and images are distinguished. The same distinction is made by the jurist Venuleius Saturninus, Digest VI, *On the Julian Law of Majestas*, and Modestinus, Digest VII, §4, on the same title, as well as Suetonius, *Nero* 24. Venuleius speaks thus: “Those who melt down statues or images of the Emperor that have already been consecrated, or commit any other similar act, are liable under the Julian law of majesty.” From this we learn that images could be melted down: that is, the shields on which emperors were painted were often made of gold or silver. Thus Trebellius Pollio relates that the Senate placed a golden shield for Claudius in the senate-house. Further, statues or images of emperors, when solemnly installed and consecrated, were thereby made sacred and religious. For Marcianus testifies, Digest VII, *On the Julian Law of Majestas*, §2: “Severus and Antoninus replied to Pontius that it was not considered an offence against majesty if images of Caesar not yet consecrated were sold.”

But on this occasion I should like to ask learned men what they think the distinction was [Col. 0550D] between *ἄγαλμα* (*agalma*) and *ἀνδριάς* (*andrias*), and between an *ἀγαλματοποιός* (*agalmopoios*) and an *ἀνδριαντοποιός* (*andriantopoios*). Polybius, in the *Extracts on Virtues and Vices*, p. 1468, latest edition, distinguishes them where he speaks of Prusias despoiling Nicephorium: “He also plundered the statues and the stone objects among the *agalmata*” (*Ἐσύλησε δὲ καὶ τοὺς ἀνδριάντας, καὶ τὰ λίθινα τῶν ἀγαλμάτων*). The most learned editor translates this, “he began to despoil and plunder statues of the immortal gods”; yet he does not explain *τὰ λίθινα τῶν ἀγαλμάτων*, nor teach what the distinction was between *ἀνδριάς* and *ἄγαλμα*. And certainly I can find no reason why Prusias should have plundered only, and indeed carried away, the stone *agalmata*, while leaving those of silver and perhaps gold behind—unless we say that the statues made of more valuable material were transported to Pergamum when the enemy invaded their territory. For “the stone objects among the *agalmata*” seems to indicate that other images also stood in the same place.

Polybius thus distinguishes *agalmata* and *andriantes*; and the scholiast on Theocritus, [Col. 0551A] *Idyll* 5.105, presents their craftsmen as plainly distinct:

> “They say there were two men named Praxiteles: the earlier was an *andriantopoios*, the later an *agalmopoios*. The latter lived in the time of King Demetrius, concerning whom Theocritus speaks” (*Δύο δέ φασι Πραξιτέλεις· τὸν μὲν ἀρχαιότερον ἀνδριαντοποιόν, τὸν δὲ νεώτερον ἀγαλματοποιόν· οὗτος δὲ ἦν ἐπὶ Δημητρίου τοῦ βασιλέως, περὶ οὗ φησιν ὁ Θεόκριτος*).

Perhaps I err if I say that an *agalmopoios* made statues of gods, whereas an *andriantopoios* made representations of human beings. Yet this seems capable of some confirmation. Not only does Suidas explain *ἀγάλματα* as “representations of the gods” (*τὰ τῶν θεῶν μιμήματα*); Pausanias too distinguishes these words thus, I, p. 31: “There stand statues of the gods Eirene and Hestia, and other statues of men, including Autolycus the pankratiast” (*Καὶ θεῶν Εἰρήνης ἀγάλματα κεῖται καὶ Ἐστιάς, ἀνδρίαντες δὲ ἄλλοι τε καὶ Αὐτόλυκος ὁ παγκρατιαστής*).

I would not, however, affirm that either Pausanias himself or other Greek writers always observed this distinction. Nevertheless, when they distinguish the words so clearly, I think they also believed them to signify things distinct from one another; otherwise it would have sufficed to mention either *agalmata* or *andriantes*. Herodotus too, I.131, speaking of the Persians, joins “images, temples, and altars” (*ἀγάλματα καὶ νηοὺς καὶ βωμούς*); from which perhaps no idle argument may be drawn that *agalmata* were attributed to gods.

In Suidas, “a statue [Col. 0551B] of Athena,” Apollo, and Dionysus occurs under the entries “Statue of Apollo” and “Auxentius.” The interpreter joins all these under the former entry, where he renders the words “and there is in Antioch a statue, an abomination of desolation” (*καὶ ἔστιν ἄγαλμα βδέλυγμα τῆς ἐρημώσεως ἐν Ἀντιοχείᾳ*) as: “There is also at Antioch a manifest and abominable image of devastation and desolation.” This certainly cannot possibly be true. For first, one must write *ἐν Ἀντιοχεία*, or rather *Ἀντίοχος*: that is, this image occurs under that entry. And under the entry “Antiochus,” Suidas relates that Antiochus entered the Sanctuary and set up in it “an altar and an image, an abomination of desolation” (*βωμὸν καὶ εἴδωλον βδέλυγμα ἐρημώσεως*), that is, a statue of some god—undoubtedly Olympian Jupiter, to whom he was dedicating the Jerusalem temple. This statue was the abomination of desolation.

Eustathius on *Iliad* Δ, p. 456, teaches that *ἄγαλμα* is ordinarily used for a statue of gods or heroes [Col. 0551B–C]: “An ancient commentator writes thus: here *agalma* does not mean, as it commonly does, a statue of gods or heroes, but is used generally” (*Παλαιὸς δέ τις γράφει οὕτως· Ἄγαλμα οὐ συνήθως τὸ θεῶν ἢ Ἡρώων, ἀλλὰ κοινῶς*).

Ammonius establishes a quite different distinction among *ξόανον* (*xoanon*), *βρέτας* (*bretas*), and *ἄγαλμα*. He writes that the first is “the carved thing, of stone or ivory” (*τὸ ἐξεσμένον λίθινον ἢ ἐλεφάντινον*), glossed in the Latin as “carved, wooden, or ivory” [the discrepancy is probably corrupt]; the second, a likeness of a mortal, made of bronze or similar material; while an *agalma* is an image made of porous stone, that is, poros-stone—mentioned by Pliny—or of another kind of marble. Thus he restricts *agalma* to marble. If this is true, Polybius may be thought simply to have used “the stone objects among the *agalmata*” for marble statues, without regard to *agalmata* made of another and more valuable material. I leave this for discussion by others who have more leisure.
