Theocritus ascribes a bowl to Praxiteles, whom, in the scholiast’s view, he makes a contemporary of King Demetrius:

> “And there is a mixing-bowl,  
> the work of Praxiteles . . .”  
> (*ἔστι δὲ κρητὴρ, / Ἔργον Πραξιτέλους . . .*)

Since that bowl was carved and adorned with figures, let learned men see whether some difference may be discovered from this between an *andriantopoios* and an *agalmopoios* [Col. 0551D].

Accordingly, an *agalmopoios* would be a chaser or engraver, because the scholiast observes that the younger Praxiteles made that bowl. Praxiteles the sculptor, the “earlier” one, lived in the 104th Olympiad, according to Pliny XXXIV.8, who also lists his works at XXXIV.8 and XXXVI.5. But it is by no means certain whether he lived into the time of Demetrius and the first Ptolemies, under whom Theocritus flourished; and it may be that he was different from the man whom Theocritus celebrates as having chased the bowl. Thus the *agalmopoios* would be a chaser, and *ἄγαλμα* would signify “an ornament, anything in which someone takes delight and rejoices” (*καλλώπισμα, πᾶν ἐφ᾽ ᾧ τις ἀγάλλεται καὶ χαίρει*). By contrast, *ἀνδριάς* is ordinarily used only of figures or statues.

Or we must hold that Praxiteles lived until the time of King Demetrius and also chased certain works; or that Theocritus introduces the shepherd Comatas as mentioning him because the man’s fame was great, and in order to express the shepherd’s simplicity. But a different Praxiteles, very far removed from the earlier one [Col. 0552A], flourished at Rome in Pompey’s time. Loyd, Hofmann, and Morerius wrongly confuse him with the famous sculptor and assign him the works mentioned by Pliny XXXVI.5, though they undoubtedly belong to the earlier artist. Moreover, that Praxiteles was not a sculptor but a chaser of silver, as is clear from the same Pliny XXXIII.12 and Cicero, *On Divination* I. Cicero nevertheless does not call him a silversmith, as a recent translator does rather incautiously, citing Cicero’s words immediately afterward, although there is a great difference between a silversmith and a chaser of silver.

“An emperor most fortunate for twenty years.” Aurelius Victor writes that Diocletian ruled for twenty-five years; but he undoubtedly errs and has also counted the years in which, after laying down imperial power, he lived as a private person. For in the year of Christ 305 he put off the purple, and he died in 312, as Baluzius clearly teaches. Thus Zosimus II.8 and Suidas under “Diocletian,” who write that he lived only three years after abdicating the empire, ought not to be heard. But what is to be done with Tristan, who, following Victor, [Col. 0552B] writes that Diocletian survived nine years after laying down the empire, III, p. 325? If this were true, Victor himself ought already to have written that he ruled for twenty-nine years.

The learned man, I think, had before his eyes these words: “He lived sixty-eight years, of which he spent nearly nine in ordinary dress.” This passage certainly has its difficulties, because if we consider Diocletian’s whole life, he lived more than nine years in ordinary dress, that is, as a private individual. I have sometimes thought that one ought to write forty-nine, and that the preceding numeral mark has been effaced; if twenty years of imperial rule are added, he then lived sixty-eight years. But Paul the Deacon, following Victor’s tracks, records at the end of Book X that Diocletian lived sixty-eight years, of which he spent nearly nine after his rule in ordinary dress. He significantly adds “after his rule,” so that some seem to have believed Diocletian lived that many years after he laid aside the purple; yet this cannot be true.

Diocletian, although Herculius and Galerius urged it, refused to resume imperial power. Eumenius therefore praises him excellently in chapter 15 of the panegyric addressed to Constantine:

> “But that divine man, who was the first both to share and to lay down imperial power, does not repent of his counsel or his deed, nor does he think that he has lost what he voluntarily transferred. Truly happy and blessed is he whom your services, the services of such great rulers, honour. Sustained by an empire of many yokes, he too rejoices in the shelter of your protection; he knows that you have grown from his stock, and justly claims your glories for his own. Him, therefore, the man whom he had adopted as a brother was ashamed to imitate; to him, in the temple of Capitoline Jupiter, he repented of having sworn. It is no wonder that he also broke faith with his son-in-law.”

“He was consumed by hunger and anguish.” The most excellent Baluzius notes here and on chapter 1 that some relate Diocletian to have died of dropsy, others by poison, Suidas by hanging; while others attribute to him decay of the tongue, worms issuing from the throat, and pus. On chapter 30, the same scholar observes that Suidas relates [Col. 0552D] that Diocletian was slaughtered by the Senate and Maximian hanged himself, which certainly must be attributed to a failure of memory. I do not know whence Suidas drew this; but I do not recall any ancient writer relating that Diocletian or Maximian was slaughtered or killed by order of the Senate. It is, however, established that Herculius, when Constantine left to him the free choice of death, ended his life by hanging; hence *ὁ δὲ ἀπεπνίξατο* (“but he strangled himself”) suits him perfectly.

Others record that Diocletian died mad (*μανέντα*), driven by frenzy, as Henry Valesius notes from Eusebius, Constantine’s speech preserved in Eusebius, and Chrysostom’s homily on St Babylas. Eusebius VIII.13 writes that Diocletian, after celebrating his twentieth anniversary, fell into a grievous illness, “an unhappy disease” (*νόσον οὐκ αἰσίαν*), and was reduced from a sound state of mind. But he does not say that he died raving. Constantine, in chapter 25 of his speech, records that Diocletian, “through the harm of folly” (*διὰ τῆς ἀφροσύνης βλάβην*), that is, on account of the defect of madness, paid the penalty shut up in some mean dwelling [Col. 0553A]. I am persuaded this was said rhetorically rather than truthfully; and whatever the case, Constantine does not relate that he died seized by madness.

Chrysostom, I admit, testifies that Diocletian perished mad (*μανέντα*); but he may have exaggerated in the manner of rhetoricians, or may have referred to the illness which Eusebius mentions and Lactantius describes in chapter 37. For I cannot persuade myself that Lactantius would have failed to record and consecrate for posterity that Diocletian died driven mad, if this had been true. He could have known the entire affair, being a contemporary of those times. Yet he who describes the tragic and deserved ends of persecutors relates only that Diocletian was cast down into hatred of life, trampled by insults, and consumed by hunger and anguish. These words mean nothing other than that, as he says shortly before, worn out by a double sickness, Diocletian resolved that he must die. Everything related in this chapter proves that Diocletian ended his life through pain and anguish, [Col. 0553B] so great that he even rejected food. Thus, as Victor says, he was “consumed by a voluntary death through fear,” because, as follows, he suspected an ignominious death; hence he is also said to have taken poison.

Lactantius writes in chapter 17 that, during the illness into which Diocletian fell after celebrating his twentieth anniversary, he became deranged, so that at certain hours he was mad and at others recovered his senses. This may indeed have been so while he was distressed by illness, as occurs in many people; it may also have lasted for a time, even for the whole remainder of his life. Yet various circumstances, and indeed his death itself, seem to suggest the contrary. For he refused to resume the purple, though Herculius and Galerius earnestly requested it; and he replied wisely: “Would that you could see at Salona the vegetables planted by our own hands! You would surely never judge that this should be attempted.” Baluzius reasonably considers that this occurred at Carnuntum, on chapter 29.

For he had been summoned there [Col. 0553C] by Galerius Maximian, so that, in the latter’s presence, he might do what he had not done before: confer imperial power upon Licinius and deliberate with him concerning the supreme government of the state and the creation of Licinius as emperor, as Victor clearly teaches. He certainly would not have done this had he been reduced from a sound state of mind. Add that Eutropius writes that he grew old in distinguished leisure. Constantine’s account, though he could have known the matter, seems to require a grain of salt. For I think he is not speaking of Diocletian’s death, but merely implying that, having become deranged from illness, he laid down the empire and, shut up in a mean dwelling, paid the penalty for persecution. Yet this dwelling, or “despicable habitation” (*εὐκαταφρόνητος οἴκησις*), was not mean at all, but a vast and splendid palace, as Spon, most worthy of a longer life, has shown abundantly in his *Itinerary*.

If, however, anyone judges that Diocletian, after laying down the empire, was sometimes sane and sometimes not in his right mind throughout his life, and attributes everything Lactantius relates in this chapter to madness, I shall not oppose him [Col. 0553D]. Still, it seems to me punishment enough that, burning with fever, refusing food, drawing sighs, and fearing a miserable death, he should end his day in anguish and, as Eusebius writes at the end of Book VIII, “a prolonged and most grievous bodily weakness” (*μακρᾷ καὶ ἐπιλυποτάτῃ τῇ τοῦ σώματος ἀσθενείᾳ*). So also Maximinus, defeated and put to flight by Licinius, fled to death through mental anguish and fear.

Moreover, I do not know whence Jordanes drew the statement that Diocletian died in Cappadocia. I also think that the most learned Baluzius rightly rebukes Victor, who relates that Diocletian received threatening letters from Constantine and Licinius and therefore, suspecting an ignominious death, took poison. For although Paul the Deacon follows Victor, as he almost always does, at the end of Book X, I do not think Lactantius would have passed over a story that would have been especially noteworthy in narrating Diocletian’s death.

Moreover, on chapter 9 I observe [Col. 0554A] that Diocletian captured and killed Achilleus near Alexandria in Egypt after he had assumed the purple. Orosius adds that he employed his victory cruelly, gave Alexandria over to plunder, and defiled all Egypt with proscriptions and slaughter. Indeed, he seems besides to have held Alexandria in check by a fortress. Victor, bishop of Tunnuna, speaks thus in his *Chronicle*: “He is sent into exile”—namely Victor—“and, after the praetorian prison, is delivered to the prison of Diocletian’s fortress.” That this occurred in Alexandria is clear from what follows: “Victor and Theodore, the aforementioned African bishops, are removed from prison and, after fifteen consecutive days of disputations in the praetorium, are sent to another custody in the monastery of the Tabenesiots, which is at Canopus, twelve miles from the city of Alexandria.”

I thought it worth making this warning because Diocletian is mentioned so often in this little book; and I think that Victor should be read: “he is delivered, after the praetorian prison, to the prison of Diocletian’s fortress,” although the Latin of authors of that age cannot at all be brought into conformity with rule [Col. 0554B].

## CHAPTER XLIII

“Constantine’s sister . . .” Hence Licinius, in Photius’ *Acts of Metrophanes and Alexander*, p. 1407, is called “Constantine’s brother-in-law through his sister” (*ἐπ᾽ ἀδελφῇ γαμβρὸς Κωνσταντίνου*).

“The images of both are placed together.” Namely, on shields, just as those of Diocletian and Maximian Herculius in the preceding chapter; see the note there. So on one side of various coins we often see the joined faces of two emperors.

“As though his father’s death . . .” He rightly adds “as though,” because he had not loved him while alive; and Herculius had done things which would certainly have removed all affection and reverence, as appears from chapters 18 and 28. His father was therefore a pretext for war. Nor do I think Herculius was consecrated by Maxentius for any other reason, as the coins attest, inscribed: “To the deified Maximian, Senior, Best, Most Fortunate” (*DIVO MAXIMIANO SEN. OPT. FORT.*); for I do not think anyone other than his son did this.

[Col. 0554C] “This execrable old man . . .” Baluzius emends it thus, with my full approval; others wrongly think the phrase “execrable discord” (*discordiam intestabilem*) is meant.

## CHAPTER XLIV

“The response he had received . . .” Maxentius had indeed at first pretended to be a Christian, as Eusebius testifies, VIII.14; but afterward he showed abundantly that he embraced the foolish fables of the pagans. This is also unquestionably evident from the response received from the oracle and from his consultation of the Sibylline books. Yet it is strange—indeed more than strange—that Lactantius says nothing of his crimes, lust, and magical arts, all of which Eusebius vividly depicts, VIII.14, followed by Haymo VIII.2, Paul the Deacon, Book XI, and the frequently cited *Polity of the Holy Fathers* in Photius. Aurelius Victor himself touches lightly upon these matters: “At his death the Senate and people rejoiced with an incredible measure of delight and gladness, since he had afflicted them so greatly that he had once allowed the Praetorians to massacre the populace; and he was the first, by the worst innovation, under the pretext of the gods, to compel senators and farmers to contribute money to support his extravagance.” Here learned men not improperly emend “under the pretext of gifts” (*munerum specie*), but they incautiously cite the New Year’s gifts offered to Augustus and Caligula. For “gifts” must mean games and spectacles which he intended to stage magnificently, under which pretext he amassed and exacted immense sums of money.

Paul the Deacon also speaks at length in relating Maxentius’ cruelties and lusts. He adds that fields were abandoned and, all effort in ploughing and sowing having ceased, a great famine seized the City and every place. These things accord with what Lactantius ascribes to Maximinus Daza in chapters 37 and 38. The anonymous author of the panegyric addressed to Constantine also depicts Maxentius’ wicked character in chapters 4 and 14, calling him a most vile man, a stupid and wicked beast; see also Nazarius, chapter 31, who should certainly be consulted.

[Col. 0555A] “That he would perish, if . . .” This can be tolerated; perhaps, however, the word *se* has fallen out, and one should write: “that he himself would perish, if . . .”

“Concerning the Moors and the Italians . . .” In Africa Alexander had seized imperial power; but Rufus Volusianus, praetorian prefect sent by Maxentius, defeated him, according to Aurelius Victor, chapter 39, and Zosimus II.15. This Alexander appears to have been besieged in the city of Cirta. Victor says: “Then throughout Africa a priesthood was decreed to the Flavian house, and the town of Cirta, which had fallen in Alexander’s siege, was restored and adorned and given the name Constantina.” That is, this Numidian town had been ravaged and plundered while Alexander, who had assumed the purple, was besieged in it.

It may also have remained loyal to the emperors and been besieged and overthrown by Alexander, because Zosimus writes that he was defeated in the first encounter, captured, and immediately strangled. Tristan, however, adopts [Col. 0555B] the former view, III, p. 440, as appears from his words: “They [Volusianus and Zenas], having gone down into Africa, defeated Alexander at the first encounter and pursued him in flight so closely that they caught him in Cirta, which they took by force, and immediately strangled him.” Whatever the case, the devastated city rose again and received the name Constantina.

A learned man notes on Aurelius Victor that it was also called Nicephorium, because Alexander the Great had gained a famous victory there, and adds that in the *Notitia Imperii* it is called Nisibenian Constantina. But Alexander the Great never traversed Africa in victory. Further, Nicephorium was in Mesopotamia near Edessa, according to Stephanus and Pliny V.24; and Pliny testifies, VI.26, that it was founded by Alexander the Great: “Near the Euphrates is Nicephorium, as we have said, which Alexander ordered to be founded because of the site’s advantage.”

If Nicephorium, as Stephanus and Suidas following him write, bore the name Constantina, it seems to follow that it was formerly called Amida and received the name Constantina from Constantius, son of Constantine the Great, while he was still Caesar. For Ammianus Marcellinus XVIII.8–9 clearly testifies that he changed the name of Amida to Constantina—something which men eminent in learning do not seem to have noticed. But though I do not deny that Nicephorium could have been called Constantina, because Stephanus so states, it certainly has nothing in common with Amida or the Constantina praised by Marcellinus. Nicephorium was situated on the Euphrates, as Pliny and Ptolemy V.18 teach. But Ammianus’ Amida or Constantina lay near Nisibis, on the Tigris, according to Procopius, *Persian Wars* I; or it could be reached by a channel from the Tigris, as we read in Ammianus. To this may be added what the eminent Bochart notes, p. 21 of his *Sacred Geography*. Thus Stephanus’ words have nothing in common with Ammianus’ narrative.

That this city was near Nisibis is also clear from the *Notitia*, in which it is called Nisibenian Constantina, perhaps to distinguish it from another or other Constantinas in that region. One of these, if we follow Stephanus, was Nicephorium [Col. 0555D] on the Euphrates; another lay farther away in Arabia Petraea, as is clear from the subscription to the Council of Constantinople, published by the distinguished Pelletier from the code of canons restored by Pithou. There the bishops of the Province of Bostra are named: Elpidius of Dionysias, Chilon of Constantina, Uranius of Adrata or Adran, and Severus of Neapolis.

Although Constantius changed its name, it retained its old name as well. Procopius, in Photius, records that in the time of Emperor Anastasius, Amida was besieged by the Persians, and I am persuaded that its inhabitants are called Constantinians (*Κωνσταντιαίους*) at the end of the *Extracts*. For it is certainly clear that Nicephorium cannot be meant there, because Chosroes marched from it to Dara, which also lay near Nisibis and was called Anastasiopolis after Emperor Anastasius—unless indeed these towns were very close together, and one bore the name Amida, the other Constantina. For in the cited subscription bishops of the province of Mesopotamia are listed: Maras of Amida, Jobianus of Aemara, and Bathes of Constantina. I do not deny, however, that Bathes may have been bishop of another city in Mesopotamia which also bore the name Constantina, as Stephanus records of Nicephorium.

Dio, Book XL, and Strabo, Book XVI, also mention Nicephorium; and it is clear from the latter that it was near Carrhae. Scholars think that Jupiter Nicephorius, mentioned by Spartianus at the beginning of his *Hadrian*, was named from that city; and that great scholar doubted whether another city had that name, but considered Jupiter Nicephorius to have been named from the place. Yet Nicephorium was also a place or village near Pergamum, renowned for many temples and statues of gods. Polybius, in the *Extracts on Virtues and Vices*: “On the following day Prusias, having led his forces to Nicephorium, began to lay waste all the temples, to despoil and plunder the shrines, statues of the gods, and images.” There was also a grove planted by King Eumenes; hence Strabo, Book XIII, mentions “the grove of Nicephorus” (*τὸ Νικηφόρον ἄλσος*).

This is also clear from the Macedonian king’s reply to Titus Flaminius in Polybius, Book XVII. When the envoys of King Attalus, chapter 2, had requested that he restore “the temple of Aphrodite intact and Nicephorium, which he had destroyed” (*τὸ τῆς Ἀφροδίτης ἱερὸν ἀκέραιον καὶ τὸ Νικηφόριον, ἃ κατέφθειρε*), he replies in chapter 6: “Since I cannot otherwise restore Nicephorium and the temple of Venus, which have been devastated, to their former condition, I shall send plants and gardeners, whose concern it shall be to cultivate the places and foster the growth of Caesar’s trees.” Livy likewise relates this in Book XXXII, chapters 33–34, where the temple of Venus is similarly distinguished from Nicephorium.

From this I seem able to affirm that the grove received its name from the principal temple, which may have been that of Jupiter Nicephorus, and that it enclosed within its circuit or *peribolos* (*περιβολή*) the temples of Venus and other gods. Diodorus Siculus, p. 294 of the *Extracts*, certainly records that Philip destroyed “the sanctuaries around Pergamum, Nicephorium splendidly constructed, and the other [sanctuaries] possessing admired sculptures” (*τὰ περὶ τὸ Πέργαμον ἱερά, τό τε Νικηφόριον πολυτελῶς κατεσκευασμένον, καὶ τἄλλα γλυφὰς ἔχοντα θαυμαζομένας*). Again, p. 337, he says that Prusias, king of Bithynia, disappointed of the hope of capturing Attalus, damaged “the sacred precinct before the city called Nicephorium, and the temple” (*τὸ πρὸ τῆς πόλεως τέμενος τὸ καλούμενον Νικηφόριον, καὶ τὸν νεών*), as well as the statues, the images of the gods, and the celebrated statue of Asclepius (*τοὺς ἀνδριάντας, καὶ τὰ τῶν θεῶν ξόανα, καὶ τὸ περιβόητον ἄγαλμα τοῦ Ἀσκληπίου*), and finally plundered every sanctuary.

If anyone therefore thinks that Jupiter Nicephorius derived his name from this place and was so called because he held Victory in his hand, as he is very frequently seen on Greek and Roman coins, he is certainly free to do so.

But to return to Aurelius Victor: the learned man also notes that Cirta is written with a V in Strabo, and that Marcellinus, Book XX, mentions Virta as a town founded by Alexander. In Casaubon’s edition *Κίρτα* is written, which is a minor matter. But Virta, founded by Alexander the Great, has nothing in common with our Cirta and was not situated in Africa, but in the farthest part of Mesopotamia, as will be clear to anyone who consults Ammianus. Cirta in Africa, later called Constantina, was an ancient and celebrated city, once the seat of kings, situated far from the sea, according to Mela, I.6. Strabo, XVII, also places it inland (*ἐν μεσογαίᾳ*) and writes that it was a very strongly fortified city, excellently supplied with everything, especially by Micipsa, who settled Greek colonists there.

Leo Africanus relates at length that it flourished later under the Arabs, was celebrated in his time, and retained the name Constantina. The ambassador of the Emperor of Morocco, who not long ago was sent to the mighty Estates of the United Netherlands, likewise told me that the city was great and spacious, full of splendid ancient buildings and monuments inscribed with unknown letters—doubtless Greek and Latin—and situated far from the sea. We have just seen that Strabo and Mela also relate this last point.

Yet Sallust greatly confuses the location and seems to make the city near the sea, *Jugurthine War* 21: “Meanwhile, not far from the sea, near the town of Cirta, the two armies encamped.” How these statements can be reconciled, I scarcely see, since Constantina is even today far removed from the sea, nor was there a double Cirta in Africa—although Danaeus thinks so in his note on Augustine, *On Heresies* 69. I am surprised that this also occurs in Strabo’s index, when nothing of the sort is read in him. Since this city is little known, I think, reader, that I shall do you a welcome service if I append its drawing, which I owe to the most distinguished Witsius, councillor of the city of Amsterdam. Someone who spent three years there in harsh circumstances, but afterward in most splendid circumstances at Tunis, although he was a Christian, shared it with that distinguished man.

[Col. 0557A] Constantina, then, is set upon the summit of a nearly inaccessible mountain, further fortified by stones ten or twelve feet long and four or five feet broad. It is round and approximately the size of Rotterdam. Its buildings are of little account, according to the custom and character of the people; but the ruins and marble columns, everywhere dug up by those excavating the earth, are the surest indications that it was once splendid and magnificent. Such also it was in Leo Africanus’ time. “Costly buildings,” he says, “may be seen everywhere: among them the principal temple, [Col. 0557B] two colleges, three or four monasteries, and many other structures of this kind.”

This passage recalls to me that the city was formerly the metropolis of Numidia. Canon 86 of the Council of Milevis, “On the Archive and Register of Numidia”: “Then it pleased all the bishops who subscribed in this council that the register and archive of Numidia should be at the first see and in the metropolis, that is, Constantina.” Samuel Petit discusses this canon at length in *Various Readings* III.1; to him should certainly be added Louis du Pin, a man most learned indeed, *Historical Dissertation I on Ancient Church Discipline*. Constantina lies forty-five or fifty German miles from Tunis, twenty or twenty-five from Bona, and seventy from Algiers. The person who shared these facts with Witsius spent fourteen days travelling from the last-named city.

1. A high tower, from which burning lamps hang at night.

[Col. 0557C] 2. A fortress built in the middle of the city to protect the outlet of the old road, by which alone the city could be approached.

3. The road, or entrance to the city, cut through the rock, broad and high enough for horses and camels to ascend into the city by it. It is now filled with refuse, because supplying food to many lamps by day and night was judged too burdensome for the inhabitants; without them, indeed, this entrance could be of no use because of the darkness.

4. Fortifications—or rather a double wall fortified with towers—constructed to defend the approach. In the outer wall were two gates which led by a slanting road to the one gate in the inner wall; through this gate access was given to the rock-cut entrance into the city. Leo Africanus reports that there were two roads to the city: “There are only two very narrow roads leading into the city, one open from the east and the other from the west. It also has very large, spacious, and elegant gates.” But our eyewitness mentions only this one in his time; and, if the terrain had not prevented it, those two roads might have led to the two gates of the outer wall.

[Col. 0557D] 5. The present entrance to the city, made by the Turks out of the ruins of ancient buildings, but so difficult that one can use only one’s feet and cannot ride a horse. Thus Turks and inhabitants alike must dismount from camels and horses and lead them.

6. A fortress by which the new entrance is defended.

7. The baths of hot water, almost ruined, in which poor people now cleanse their bodies; and women, with the aid of a certain kind of earth possessing the force of lye-ash, which they call *to fill* [uncertain reading], make linen garments and other things bright. Leo undoubtedly speaks of these baths: “One descends to the river by certain steps cut into the rock; and in the river itself there is a building likewise cut from the rock, so that roof, columns, and walls form but one piece: here the women of Constantine customarily wash little cloths. Near this town there is also a bath of hot water, which spreads as it flows among the rocks.” [Col. 0558A]

8. Water-mills, built by the Moors expelled from Andalusia and Granada by Charles V.

9. The gardens and pleasure-grounds of those same Moors. Leo Africanus: “The river which flows past that plain has most fertile gardens on both banks, if they were properly cultivated.”

10. A cataract produced by a spring rising near the city toward the east and discharging a great quantity of water. It surrounds the city on its northern side, serves as a fortification, and pours itself with a great roar into a very deep valley. Leo Africanus: “It is enclosed by very high rocks; beneath it flows the river Sufegmate, itself also confined by rocks, so that the very deep river, together with the rocks set on either side, supplies Constantine with something like a ditch.”

11. A stream, or river, which rises from the aforesaid spring. As is plain, all these things agree almost completely. Yet it is strange that Leo makes no mention of the ancient approach to the city—unless perhaps he means the steps cut into the rock, by which one descended to the river. But enough of this. [Col. 0558B]

The Moors … They too were in Severus’ army, and doubtless passed over to Maxentius together with the other soldiers. For Zosimus, II.10, writes that Severus came “through the Moorish detachments” (*διὰ τῶν Μαυρουσίων ταγμάτων*). Nor is this surprising, since he had the army of Herculius, which, according to Eutropius, brought the war in Africa to a close, subduing the Quinquegentiani and reducing them to peace. Maxentius further increased these Moors; hence he is said recently to have drawn out an army of his own composed of Moors and Italians.

The soldiers of Maxentius prevailed. Lactantius indicates quite plainly that Constantine did not fight sufficiently successfully at the beginning. Eusebius, on the contrary, IX.9, relates that he defeated the tyrant’s first, second, and third battle-lines, and thus advanced to Rome to fight Maxentius himself. As is clear from the panegyric delivered to Constantine, the first engagement took place beneath the very ridges of the Alps, chap. 5; then in the plains of Turin, chap. 6; thirdly at Verona, chap. 8; and finally at the Milvian Bridge. On this matter Nazarius too may be consulted, chap. 17, 21, and the following chapters of his panegyric. Thus Orosius, VII.28, relates that Maxentius, worn down by many battles, was finally defeated and killed at the Milvian Bridge. Yet I do not think Lactantius would have committed such matters to memory if they had been wholly otherwise. The *Politia of the Holy Fathers*, in Photius, p. 1409, also supports him: it expressly relates that Constantine, unable to induce Maxentius to refrain from persecution, attacked him in war, and at first came very near to suffering defeat: “and when he joined battle, at first he came near to receiving the worse” (*καὶ συμπλακεὶς μάχῃ, τὰ πρῶτα μὲν ἐγγὺς γίνεται, τὸ λαβεῖν τὸ ἧττον*), as the Greek says. It then speaks of the cross seen in heaven, recounting the affair in almost the same way as Lactantius. [Col. 0558C]

The quinquennial festival was drawing to its close. Reader, see what the learned men Baluze and Pagi think of this passage in their notes here and on p. 248 of the *Dissertatio Hypatica*; you will learn that both hold Maxentius to have perished after the completion of the sixth year of his reign, at the beginning of the seventh. The author of the panegyric addressed to Constantine, chap. 16, confirms that view: “And, after six years consumed in idleness, he would mark the very anniversary day of his accession with a final slaughter, lest by even beginning he should violate that sacred and religious number seven.” I think the learned are not without reason in calling the sixth regnal year the quinquennial festival, because it was celebrated on the first day of that year. But there is no leisure to investigate this question more carefully; I leave the whole dispute to those who, both in France and in Italy, devote themselves to it with the highest credit.

Warned in a dream … If we follow Lactantius, it is certain that Constantine did not see this sign in heaven while awake. But I do not wish to examine a subject sifted by so many learned men. Consult Frederick Spanheim, a man highly expert in ecclesiastical antiquity, in his *Introductio Chronologica*, and Jacob Gothofredus on Philostorgius, book I, chap. 6. In what follows, however, one should write, as I noted [Col. 0559A] in passing in the *Dissertation on the Use which Princes May Derive from Coins*, “he marks Christ upon the shields”; that is, the name of Christ, which they expressed through the first two letters of the saving name. Prudentius speaks no differently in *Against Symmachus*:

> Christ, woven in sparkling gold upon purple,  
> Marked the labarum …

That is, the name of Christ, the monogram of Christ. And, if we follow Lactantius, it was arranged in this fashion, in the manner in which Baronius in the *Annals* and Gassendi in the *Notice of the Church of Digne* observe Christians to have marked themselves in the fourth century and thereafter. The first letters of the divine name occur likewise on a coin of Anastasius in the collection of Duke Arschotanus, plate LXVII. Others make it a cross; I, however, make it the name of Christ, because Christ, not the cross, is the saviour of the world, which is denoted by the globe. That monogram may also have been such as this [Col. 0559B], because it is expressed similarly on Constantine’s coins, and because Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, book I, chap. 25, writes that the first letters of Christ’s name were woven into the labarum, “the R being crossed in the middle” (*χιασομένου τοῦ Ρ κατὰ τὸ μεσαίτατον*). Yet these words may perhaps be interpreted of the former figure—which, I think, Lactantius indicates—since the Greek letter rho, if a line cuts it through the middle, is crossed. Certainly the learned author of the *Historical Dissertation on Constantine’s Vision* departs entirely from the truth and wrongly supposes that the ordinary mark of the circumflex accent was used in this form [Col. 0559C]. There is no need for a lengthy refutation, since I am sure that gentleman would abandon his opinion if he inspected the coins or encountered this note.

I should end here, were I not pleased to add what I sent to Columbus “the blessed” (*τὸν μακαρίτην*) to illustrate certain forms of crosses, since it has been included in his notes. These remarks, then, are as follows. [Col. 0559D] I shall not linger in examining what Charles Du Fresne notes in his *Dissertation on a Sixteenth Coin of the Lower Empire*, II.23; I shall merely observe that, in the cross designated by letter A, the upper transverse stroke denotes the tablet on which was inscribed “King of the Jews” (*βασιλεὺς Ἰουδαίων*), while the other represents the wood to which the hands of our Lord Jesus Christ were fastened. In that marked B, the uppermost and middle strokes must be understood in precisely the same sense, while the lowest stroke signifies the place to which the Saviour’s feet were fastened. In the third, designated C, the same things are denoted; but the crossed figures, as they are called, in the middle transverse stroke signify the places where the nails pierced the Lord’s hands for our sins. Finally, in the last cross, marked D, the upper circle must be referred to the title, the two parts of the transverse wood to the arms, and the lowest part to the pierced feet. Reason recommends all this, though I am wholly ignorant when such a manner of depicting crosses began; nor do I think the matter important enough that we should trouble ourselves over it in the least. [Col. 0560A]

The distinguished Du Fresne discusses the monogram of Christ as represented on coins in no. 24 of the dissertation just mentioned. Though elegant, I do not think he explains correctly the gem in which it is seen, together with the inscription *SAL. DO. N. ALEX. FIL. LUCE.* For it can in no way refer to Alexander, son of Mamaea; rather, it concerns Alexius, a name borne by several emperors in later times. *LUCE* may quite conveniently be expanded as *LUCEBIT*, “he shall shine,” so that prayers, as it were, are at the same time offered for Alexius, son of the emperor. Yet I would not reject *LUGET*, “he mourns,” because that occurs on other coins in Choul. Moreover, the monogram of Christ is seen on coins of Maxentius, p. 277, in the same author. But, to speak the truth, it does not at all seem probable to me that the divine character was placed or impressed on that coinage. If one considers the chronology, it could in no way have happened, since Maxentius died in that very battle in which Constantine first ordered this sign to precede his army. I therefore think Choul was deceived and attributed to Maxentius what Magnentius did, whose coins are known to have been marked thus. [Col. 0560B] The distinguished Mediobarbus sufficiently demonstrates this, and assigns to Magnentius another coin which Choul, p. 187, attributes to Maxentius.

I had thought that the distinguished Du Cange also cited a Delian coin notable for this monogram, and I had judged it spurious. But I now observe at last that the learned man means nothing else than that, on the gem displaying the monogram of Christ above Jupiter’s head, the heads of Jupiter, Apollo, and Diana are seen as they occur joined on a Delian coin in Goltzius, plate 18. I gladly confess that here I had been too hasty. How, however, that divine sign came to be placed upon Jupiter’s head is exceedingly difficult to say, and I certainly cannot extricate myself from this problem. For the added inscription, *VIVAS IN DEO F.*, that is, “May you live happily in God,” plainly seems to indicate that this gem was carved by a Christian—unless we say that some Christian later added the monogram and inscription to the heads of the gods, perhaps ignorant whose heads they were, or in order to convert a profane object, as it were, to sacred use. [Col. 0560C]

It should be noted that the monogram occurs on coins struck not only before Constantine but even before the saving advent of Christ. Scaliger on Eusebius and Rupertus in the historical orator Ptolemy Apion cite a coin on one face of which is seen a head with ram’s horns and a diadem; on the other, an eagle holding a thunderbolt in its claws. Beside it is a cornucopia; beneath the bird’s feet is this sign; around the coin: “Of King Ptolemy” (*ΠΤΟΛΕΜΑΙΟΥ ΒΑΣΙΛΕΩΣ*). They judge this sign to mean “[of] the oracle” (*ΧΡΗΣΤΗΡΙΟΥ*) of Ammon, near Cyrene, over which that king ruled. I should indeed like to inspect such a coin, for it must certainly be counted among the rarest. While I do not reject that interpretation, I remember reading somewhere that this sign on coins struck before Constantine denotes the name of the mint-master; though, to speak truthfully, that too has its difficulties. [Col. 0560D] Chi and rho occur almost similarly joined on a coin of Decius in Tristan, vol. II, p. 595, upon which is read:

“He marks Christ upon the shields …” Not, as I have noted, Christ’s image, but his monogram. Nor was even that done in Prudentius’ time. *Hymn* II, *On the Crowns* (*περὶ Στεφάνων*), v. 98:

> “Render to Caesar what you know is Caesar’s—  
> For I demand what is just.  
> Your God, unless I am mistaken,  
> Marks none of your coinage.”

Unless these words should be referred to the time of Lawrence, who suffered martyrdom in the year 254. Yet it was not done in Prudentius’ age either, since Justinian Rhinotmetus, who began to reign in 685, was the first of the Greek emperors to mark coins thus. [Col. 0561A] Du Cange therefore rightly rejects John Damascene, who writes that Constantine placed upon coinage “the then heaven-revealed sign of the saving cross, and the image of Christ, God-and-man, together with his own” (*τότε οὐρανοφανὲς σημεῖον τοῦ Σωτηρίου σταυροῦ, καὶ θεανδρικὸν Χριστοῦ χαρακτῆρα μετὰ τοῦ ἰδίου*).

Nor do I think Constantine marked coins with the faces of saints, although Andreas Mamora reports this in his *History of the Island of Corcyra*, published at Venice in 1672. He displays a coin on one side of which is seen Constantine’s head, encircled neither with a laurel nor any other crown; on the other, holy Corcyra, virgin and martyr, standing in a temple and holding a palm in her hands as a sign of victory, with the inscription “Of the Corcyraeans” (*ΚΟΡΚΥΡΑΙΩΝ*). They make this Corcyra the daughter of Cercillinus, prince of the senate of the Corcyraeans, converted to Christ by the activity of Jason and Sosipater, disciples of St Paul. But that bust (*προτομή*) has nothing whatever in common with Constantine’s countenance; moreover, those who can bring themselves to believe such things pleasantly deceive themselves, since they are wholly remote from the truth. [Col. 0561B]

“The army, armed with this sign, takes up the sword …” Zosimus, II.16, relates that Constantine observed not this, but another prodigy before drawing up his battle line and entering combat: namely, that owls flying in an innumerable multitude (*ἀπείρῳ πλήθει*) filled the walls. On seeing this, Constantine ordered his own men to take their positions (*τάττεσθαι τοῖς οἰκείοις*). This the pagans could invent in order to oppose something to the vision, “By this conquer” (*ἐν τούτῳ νίκα*). Perhaps this is also why an owl standing on a base appears on his coins, with a spear, shield, and helmet beside it, and the inscription *SAPIENTIA PRINCIPIS*, “the wisdom of the prince”; though all these things may conveniently be referred to Minerva, goddess and patroness of wisdom.

“And when suddenly the people …” I punctuate thus: “And when suddenly the people”—for they were holding Circensian games on his birthday—“and with a raised voice …,” so that *erant*, “were,” is understood. Yet I do not disapprove of Columbus’s *edebat*.

[Col. 0561C] Having summoned certain senators, he orders the Sibylline books to be consulted … It is well known that the Sibylline books were consulted first by the *duumviri*, then by the *decemviri*, and finally by the *quindecimviri sacris faciundis*. Learned men have noted that the *quindecimviri* continued down to the time of Theodosius, who abolished their priesthood together with the rites of the old superstition; likewise, that the Sibylline books were burned under Honorius by Stilicho. Yet here, by Maxentius’ order, not the *quindecimviri* but certain senators consult those books. From this one might perhaps infer either that by that time the *quindecimviri* no longer existed, or that the Sibylline books were consulted by men selected by the emperor. The former can scarcely be true, since, as the distinguished Salmasius notes on the *Historia Augusta*, Lactantius himself, *Institutes* I.6, assigns that office to the *quindecimviri* in the age of Constantine the Great. Vopiscus, in *Aurelian*, chap. 19, teaches that the pontiffs consulted the Sibylline books by decree of the senate and command of the emperor:

> “Come then, pontiffs: as pure, clean, holy, and suitably equipped in garments and minds for sacred rites, ascend the temple; [Col. 0561D] set out the laurelled seats; with venerable hands (others read ‘veteran hands’) unfold the books; seek out the eternal fates of the commonwealth.”

The same most learned man thinks that the *quindecimviri*, since many of them were also pontiffs, were called pontiffs by the more honorable title; nevertheless, they had charge of consulting and preserving the Sibylline books, not as pontiffs, but as *quindecimviri*. But I scarcely see how this can be reconciled with Lactantius’ mention here of certain senators, unless we either embrace the explanation advanced by me—that men other than the *quindecimviri* could consult the books when the emperor ordered it—or rather decide that these senators were themselves also *quindecimviri*. The address of Ulpius Sullani in Vopiscus seems also to suggest that those pontiffs were drawn from the senatorial order. For in ancient times the *decemviri* were created from the patricians, and later one half of them also from the plebs. Livy, VI.42: “Sextius and Licinius, the same men elected tribunes for the tenth time, carried a law that the board of ten for sacred matters should be created partly from the plebs. Five patricians and five plebeians were chosen; and by that rank a road to the consulship now seemed opened.” [Col. 0562A] I interpret this to mean that five of the *quindecimviri* were patrician senators and five plebeian senators; for it does not seem plausible to me that this priesthood was bestowed upon every member of the plebs. And it is established that senators were, for the most part, pontiffs and priests; Cicero alone, *Letters to Atticus* IV.2, teaches this: “All the pontiffs who were senators are summoned.”

“The enemy of the Romans …” This is ambiguous, as most such phrases are; and if Constantine had been defeated, they would undoubtedly have called him the enemy.

“The bridge behind him is cut through.” Apparently the Milvian Bridge, mentioned earlier. Victor says of this: “While, after the destruction of his battle-line, he was fleeing to take refuge in Rome, he was caught in crossing the Tiber by the snares which he had laid for the enemy at the Milvian Bridge.” I think Victor relates that Maxentius fell into the river from a bridge other than the Milvian. [Col. 0562B] The Milvian Bridge was built by Marcus Aemilius Scaurus, according to the author of *On Illustrious Men*, and was doubtless of stone. If Maxentius wished to secure his escape across it, it is highly probable that the bridge was cut through without his command. Although this is contrary to reason, Lactantius immediately relates that Maxentius tried to secure his escape by that route: “He himself turns in flight and hastens to the bridge, which had been broken; pressed by the multitude of fugitives, he is thrown into the Tiber.” Prudentius too celebrates the same bridge, *Against Symmachus* I:

> “The Milvian, hurling the tyrant whom it received  
> Into the pools of the Tiber.”

The anonymous author of the panegyric, chap. 17, writes that Maxentius’ soldiers, terrified and routed at the first charge of Constantine’s army, were driven by the narrowness of the Milvian Bridge and plunged headlong into the river. Eusebius, however, IX.9, testifies [Col. 0562C] that Maxentius joined boats across the Tiber and, when he wished to secure his flight across the bridge thus made, perished by his own snares. Praxagoras in Photius records the same, and Zosimus, II.15–16, narrates it more fully. Haymo, VIII.3, follows Eusebius, as usual: “And he plunges Maxentius the tyrant, preparing to engage, together with all the boats by which he had paved the river, into the deep.” Indeed, the *Epitome* of Victor and Paul the Deacon report that this bridge was a little upstream from the Milvian Bridge, and that Maxentius was submerged in the depths by the fall of his horse. But the assertion that the tyrant fell into the river through his horse’s fall is not found elsewhere—unless we judge that the *Excerpta Valesiana*, where we read that he was hurled down with his horse, mean the same thing. Zosimus says that the bridge’s timbers could not bear the multitude of fugitives and broke; and the *Politia of the Holy Fathers* in Photius, p. 1407, says that the deceptive bridge was broken, “their contrived bridge having burst” (*διαῤῥαγείσης αὐτοῖς γεφύρας σεσοφισμένης*). From this it is more than sufficiently clear what Victor means when he says that Maxentius was caught by the snares he had laid for his enemy at the Milvian Bridge. [Col. 0562D] He therefore fell into the river from the Milvian—or rather the wooden—bridge; and perhaps he had the Milvian Bridge cut through in order to draw Constantine into the trap, should he wish to cross the Tiber and seize Rome either during or before the battle. Yet the tyrant was not immediately drowned, but, riding his horse, attempted to escape; he was prevented by the higher and steep bank. The author of the panegyric, chap. 17: “The Tiber itself seized and swallowed in its whirlpool that very man, with horse and distinguished arms, vainly attempting to make his way up the steepness of the farther bank.”

“He is trampled underfoot.” Read “they are trampled underfoot”: namely, Maxentius’ army or soldiers, just as “the soldiers of Maxentius” occurred a little earlier—unless Lactantius means that Maxentius’ soldiers were terrified and routed by the first charge of Constantine’s army, as we have just heard the author of the panegyric say. Not only Terence and Plautus but also Virgil, *Aeneid* XII, whom Lactantius is accustomed to imitate, use the same word. [Col. 0563A]

“The title of first name …” I formerly wavered in various ways. Although I had thought that this title might be “the Greatest” (*Maximus*), because Constantine is so called on coins and inscriptions, and because Lactantius soon relates that Maximinus uttered insults mingled with jokes against the emperor Maximus, I now judge that nothing else is indicated than that Constantine’s name was placed first by decree of the Senate. Lactantius himself writes that Maximinus claimed the title of first name for himself; I show that Eusebius likewise reports this at chap. 32. Maximinus seems rightly to have been able to do this, because he had been made Caesar before Constantine.

## Chapter XLV

“At that very time …” I occasionally enjoy descending to minutiae. The words *quam cum maxime* indicate both time and the intensity of the cold, so that Lactantius says there was then extreme cold. Yet *nunc*, “now,” is often added; then the expression does nothing except intensify and augment. Cicero, *For Cluentius*: “A mother who for many years, and now more than ever, has desired her son murdered.” The books *On Old Age* put it somewhat differently: “I am now completing speeches on the distinguished causes, whatever ones I have defended, more than ever.” Nazarius, *Panegyric*, chap. 1: “For now more than ever he throws himself forward”; and before them Terence, *Phormio*: “But it is needed now more than ever.” [Col. 0563B]

“With doubled stopping-places.” That is, he covered in a single day as much distance as two stopping-places were apart from each other, and rested not at the first but at the second. The imperial roads were divided into *mansiones* and *mutationes*. At the *mansiones* travellers spent the night, the distance from one *mansio* to another being a day’s journey. At the *mutationes*, however, they changed horses and halted during the day to refresh themselves. For *manere* among the ancients meant “to spend the night.” Seneca, *On Benefits* III.16: “What woman will you find so wretched, so sordid, that one pair of adulterers is enough for her? Unless she divided them among the individual hours, and one day was not enough for them all; unless she was carried about with one and stayed with another”—that is, spent the night. [Col. 0563C] Cicero, *On Divination* I: “That bedroom where he was going to stay, if he had continued on his way, collapsed on the first night”; for which he said in book II: “He would have slept in that bedroom.” Suetonius uses the word likewise in *Augustus* 72, 78 and *Caligula* 55. Hence *mansiones* are places where someone spends the night. I show that “the stopping-places of the Salii” occurs in this sense in an ancient inscription, *Observations* IV.2. Thus *mansiones* are distinguished from *mutationes* not only in the Theodosian Code, the Bordeaux Itinerary, and elsewhere, but also a *mansio* is used for the journey of an entire day in Pliny, XII.14: “The incense-bearing region lies eight stages from the high mountain.” These *mansiones* were large buildings, so that emperors sometimes spent the night in them with their retinues, as is clear from Ambrose, *On the Death of Valentinian*, Suetonius’ *Titus*, and Vopiscus, *Aurelian* chap. 35. But granaries were also attached to them, or they performed the function of granaries; there the military grain-ration was stored for distribution to soldiers proceeding by military road on campaign. Eumenius calls that ration the “supplies of the stopping-places.” [Col. 0563D] But it would take too long to elucidate these words. I shall only note that a similar expression occurs in Justin, XIII.8: “Defeated, Neoptolemus fled to Antipater and Craterus and persuaded them, by continuing their stages without interruption, to come upon Eumenes, elated by victory and secure in his escape.” There is also an elegant inscription in Spon, *Miscellanies*, p. 302, in which the word *manere* likewise occurs:

> MERCURY HERE PROMISES PROFIT; APOLLO, HEALTH;  
> SEPTIMANUS, LODGING WITH LUNCH.  
> HE WHO COMES WILL FARE BETTER.  
> AFTERWARD, GUEST, LOOK TO WHERE YOU ARE TO STAY.

I confess that passage is obscure; if I make a human mistake in explaining it, I shall promptly follow others when better instructed. I think, then, that Mercury and Apollo were the signs of this inn; and hence Septimanus seizes the occasion to invite people to his lodging. Those, however, will make better use of it who bring lunch with them, or who come at the hour when lunch is taken; after lunch the guest must look to where he is to stay, that is, spend the night. [Col. 0564A]

“Perinthus having been received in surrender.” Learned men rightly note that Perinthus is Heraclea, which Lactantius shortly before related to have been besieged. Ammianus Marcellinus, XXII.2 and XXVII.4, and Procopius, *Vandalic History* I, observe that the city bore that name; Tristan, vol. II, p. 80, should certainly be added.

“Being equally distant in miles …” Following the conjectures of others, I read, “being equally distant by so many miles, and assembled there.” A most learned man notes that this happened around Resiston and that this place occurs first in the Antonine Itinerary for travellers going from Heraclea to Hadrianople. In the *Itinerary*, p. 37, I find Apros and Resiston listed between Trajanopolis and Heraclea; the former is twenty-three Roman miles from Trajanopolis, the latter twenty-two. Thus, if Resiston was the first stopping-place, Apros will certainly be the second, because Lactantius assigns equal mileages to both. But Lactantius mentions not Trajanopolis but Adrianople; and the author of the *Itinerary* describes quite different places between Adrianople and Heraclea: p. 30, Ostudizum, Bergulae, Drizipara, Izirallon; p. 51, he lists the same places with Heraclea; and p. 73, Hadrianople, Ostudizum, Burdidizum, Bergulae, Drusiparum, Tirallum, Perinthus, Heraclea. Conversely, on p. 75, he again enumerates Trajanopolis, Cypsela, Apros, Resiston, Heraclea. Thus it seems to me that the Campus Serenus mentioned in the following chapter must be sought elsewhere. [Col. 0564B]

## Chapter XLVI

“Through commanding officers and tribunes …” The designation *praepositus* is very general, as Gutherius teaches in his book *On the Offices of the Imperial Household*. Here they are set above tribunes. Yet Vegetius, II.12, writes that a tribune commanded the first cohort of a legion, while the remaining cohorts were commanded by tribunes or *praepositi*. [Col. 0564C] In inscriptions collected by Gruter occur: “commander of a cohort of the German expedition,” “commander of a legion,” “[commander] of units stationed in Pontus,” and “of the vexillation at Perinthus.” Thus no one will err who makes the *praepositi* here senior to the tribunes. So also in an unpublished inscription in my possession:

> To the divine shades. For Gaius Julius Candidus, commander of the Thirteenth Twin Legion. The heirs made [this] in accordance with the will.

For the double P.P. means *praepositus*. The abbreviations are sometimes wrongly expanded in Gruter’s index as *praefectus*; and more wrongly in Inscription VI, p. 277, as *pro praetore*, whereas it is the title *pater patriae* of the emperor Gaius. Likewise I, p. 278 must be explained thus: though *PRO. PR.* is there written out, it refers not to the emperor but to Marcus Aurelianus Valentinianus. But this by the way. [Col. 0564D]

“The battle on the day before the Kalends of May …” Either *diei* has been put for *die*, or one should write *diem*.

“The plain … called Serenus.” I think it was so called not because of the winds but because it lacked trees and bushes and was level. Such a plain, I think, is called by Eusebius, *Life of Constantine* IV.19, a “clear plain” (*καθαρὸν πεδίον*). He ordered soldiers who had not yet become Christians to go out into it every Sunday and, at a signal, all offer prayers to God together. For that plain was doubtless level and unobstructed by trees or other things, and I think soldiers also exercised there in arms. Livy, XXIV.14, says “a clear and open plain.” But the phrase “Serene Plain” causes me to mention that I have also read *serena militia*, “serene military service,” in Paul the Deacon, *Historia Miscella* X: “Carausius, though very low-born, had attained outstanding renown in the rank of serene military service.” I confess that I do not understand what “serene military service” is, unless someone supposes it so called in relation to emperors, who are called “Serene Lords” on a column still visible today at Constantinople. Let learned men consider whether one should rather restore *strenuae* or *severae militiae*, “energetic” or “strict military service.” The latter occurred to a learned friend: thus Carausius is said to have acquired renown by diligent observance of military discipline. [Col. 0565A]

“Stingy in giving …” Victor: “For the former”—Constantine—“was excessive in all else; in the latter”—Licinius—“there was only thrift, and indeed a rustic kind.” The author of the *Epitome* writes that he was the worst of all in his desire for avarice.

## Chapter XLVII

“He was mown down by a few.” That is, he was laid low, cast down, as we cut grass with a sickle. Columbus supplies examples; another occurs in the conclusion of Tertullian’s *Apology*: “Your more refined cruelty has accomplished nothing; it is rather an enticement to our sect. [Col. 0565B] We become more numerous whenever we are mown down by you; the blood of Christians is seed.” And in Silius Italicus, XIII:

> Scipio rushes into the opposing arms,  
> And insatiably mows down the hostile battle-line.

“God most high …” Our God is rightly so called. But pagans also used “the Most High” simply of the Greatest God whom they did not know. Statius, *Thebaid* IV.516:

> “And the Most High of the threefold world, whom it is forbidden to know.”

The scholiast notes: “He calls Demogorgon the Most High God, whose name it is not permitted to know.” Moreover, the Persian philosophers and magi maintain that, besides these known gods worshipped in temples, there truly is another ruler and greatest God, organizer of the other divinities, to whose race the sun and moon alone belong. The rest may be consulted: they are elegant, and Barthius attempts to emend them in his notes. Francisco de Cordova should be added; in chap. 25 of his *Didascalia Multiplex*, he restores *demiurgum*, “creator,” for *demogorgona*, and thinks that Demogorgon owes his origin to Boccaccio. But he wrongly doubts whether Lutatius or Boccaccio is the earlier, since nothing is more certain than that the former lived before the latter. [Col. 0565C]

## Chapter XLVIII

“The public security.” This appears on various coins in antiquarian collections: for example, in Erizzo, pp. 119, 413, 469, 497, 559; Tristan, vol. I, p. 630 and vol. II, p. 469; Patin, p. 73; the *Thesauri*; Vaillant, whose book on colonies we eagerly await; and others. Ammianus Marcellinus, XIV.6, also mentions “the security of Pompilian times.”

“We should have under consideration …” That is, we should consult and deliberate. See the relevant material in the often-cited glossary.

“Which indeed the divinity …” I think one should write: “whereby whatever divinity is in the heavenly seat …” See the notes of Columbus, that most learned man. The pagans spoke thus because they doubted what precisely the highest divine power was, who God was, and debated the matter among themselves. [Col. 0565D]

“For the tranquillity of the times …” That is: “that under my rule there may be rest and peace”; shortly afterward: “that by our clemency provision may also thereby be made for the public peace.” On a coin of Maximian Herculius in Tristan, vol. III, p. 372, a goddess is seen holding a measuring-rod in one hand and ears of grain in the other, with the inscription *QUIES AUG.* The emblem doubtless denotes that tranquillity, or peace, is the cause of abundance and grain supply. Ammianus Marcellinus, XIX.11: “Cherishing tranquillity as a saving goddess, they bore the burdens of taxpayers”; see Valesius there.

“Let them request a deputy …” This term is very general, so that one cannot assert with certainty what office this *vicarius* held here. Yet I do not think anyone would err who supposes that Maximinus designated any deputy whatsoever in his own province. Thus in the eastern regions there were four vicars: of the Asian diocese, Pontus, Thrace, and Macedonia; the *Notitia Imperii* may be consulted concerning these and the vicars of other provinces. In inscriptions published by Reinesius occur Flavius Rufus Sabinus Volusianus, vicar of Asia, and Virius Nicomachus Flavianus, vicar of Africa; and in the *Libellus Precum* of Faustinus, p. 14, occurs a vicar of Spain. In general, however, a *vicarius* is one who performs another’s office or serves another. Thus, according to Ulpian, a slave-deputy serves an ordinary slave. In inscription XII.580, *VICARIUS SUPRA COCOS* means one who presides over the cooks in place of him who had authority over them. Our vicars bear that name in relation to praetorian prefects or provincial governors whose office they administered. Hence Sextilius Agesilaus Aedesius is called on an ancient stone “Deputy of the Prefecture through the Spains”; and in Lactantius, chap. 16, Hierocles is said to have gone from deputy to governor—a term which the French wrongly translate *président*. [Col. 0566B] [Col. 0566A]

“To the right of their corporate body …” These are ecclesiastical possessions, and this passage clearly proves that before the law of Constantine the Great, Christian churches possessed what are called immovable goods. Julian prohibited this, as Ado testifies in his *Martyrology*, p. 108. Faustinus and Marcellinus would certainly have agreed with him, for in the *Libellus Precum*, p. 21, they say: “But the authority complained of that designation, even with every mark of disgrace, lest the Church’s possessions be taken from them. Would that the Church had never possessed them, so that, living in apostolic fashion, it might possess intact faith inviolate.”

“The right of their corporate body …” This edict of Maximinus permits everyone to worship whatever god he wishes. Since almost every pagan god had devotees gathered into a single corporate body, he therefore speaks similarly of Christians, who were devoted to the divinity and majesty of our Lord Jesus Christ. Ancient stones mention: “College of Aesculapius and Hygieia,” “Nauclerus, who was in the College of Serapis,” and “College of the Craftsmen of Venus.” There will shortly be an occasion to discuss these elsewhere. And just as these corporate bodies had their treasuries and estates from which they met expenses, Christians also possessed their own goods; yet they expended all revenues and all alms upon the poor, and did not feed idle bellies with them. [Col. 0566C]

“Public blessedness …” This too is a formal expression, occurring even on coins, and denotes a tranquil and fortunate state of the commonwealth. Tacitus calls it a “most blessed age,” *Agricola* chap. 3; Nazarius, “most blessed Caesars,” chap. 1 and the final chapter; and the panegyrist, “most blessed victory,” chap. 32, and “the blessedness of the city,” chap. 33.

With your proclamation posted . . . He indicates that the governor of a province ought publicly to announce in a written notice that he had received such an edict from the emperors and had been ordered to affix it. This passage certainly seems worthy of observation, because it teaches us that imperial edicts were not posted in the provinces unless the governors at the same time attested that edicts of this kind had been sent to them by the emperors. This was necessary in order to prevent forged edicts by which provincials might have been incited to innovations by turbulent persons. [Col. 0566D]

## CHAPTER XLIX

But Licinius following . . . I had thought that *sequente* should be written; but I now judge that Maximinus yielded before the following Licinius—that is, he did not wait for him, but fled as soon as he learned that Licinius was coming and approaching with an army. Cicero, *On the Orator* I: “When I have yielded to them, in order to discuss all these matters . . . yet I shall assign and grant that to the orator”; a passage which, if one considers the form of expression, is plainly similar to this of Lactantius.

The victors breaking through everything toward the right. After his forces had been slaughtered between Heraclea and Hadrianopolis, Maximinus first fled to Nicomedia, then thence to Cappadocia, as Lactantius testifies, ch. 47. When Licinius pursued him there, [Col. 0567A] he occupied the defiles of Mount Taurus; and, since mountains of this sort are not everywhere passable, I should readily believe that a definite place is meant—indeed, one by which Cilicia could be entered, since Maximinus is said to have fled to Tarsus. In Livy, XXXV.13, we read that Antiochus withdrew to Antioch by way of Cilicia, having crossed Mount Taurus. Alexander, in Justin, XI.8, fearing the defiles, crossed Taurus with great speed and arrived at Tarsus; Curtius, III.4, describes these defiles very well. From him we further learn that Alexander too sought Cilicia from Cappadocia, and that those passes or gates—for this might also be established from other examples—were so called. Licinius, however, took another route and crossed Taurus toward Pamphylia. Hence Maximinus, fearing lest his escape should be cut off, made for Tarsus, where he would of course be nearer to the East and Egypt.

As those are accustomed to do who think they are doing this as their final act. Thus surely the Numantians wished to rush into battle; and, when they could not do so, they killed themselves, Florus, II.18. Juba, after dining magnificently, handed himself over to Petreius to be killed amid the tables and drinking-cups, IV.2; and some of the Cantabrians, when they saw the extremity, forestalled death in rivalry—by fire, sword, poison, and amid feasting—IV.11. Moreover, persons condemned by a judge, to whom Lactantius perhaps alludes, and gladiators, were given a final *cena miscellanea*, a mixed last meal, so that they might fill themselves with a variety of foods and, well drunk, cast aside fear of death. Juvenal, *Satires* XI:

> Thus they come to the gladiatorial games’ *miscellanea*.

The commentator: “*Miscellanea*, that is, the gladiators’ last supper”; and he adds the reason: “It is called *miscellanea* because they mix together everything set before them, and so eat it.” Although others reject the poet’s interpretation, perhaps not without reason, and although it is not likely that all the gladiators’ foods were mixed together at the supper which they regarded as their last—rather, that they were filled by a variety of foods—the scholiast seems to preserve this custom for us. Among the Athenians, those condemned, or being led *ἐπὶ θάνατον*, “to death,” [Col. 0567C] were permitted to fill themselves with food and wine, *σίτου καὶ οἴνου πληρωθῆναι*, “to be filled with bread and wine,” according to Suidas, under *εἴποις τὰ τρία*, and the Vatican Appendix, Cent. I, Prov. 75. That a free supper was given to *bestiarii*, or those condemned to the beasts, and that they customarily dined most lavishly on the day before they fought, is clear from the Passion of Saints Perpetua and Felicity, as well as from what the most distinguished Henry Valesius observes in the preface. Indeed, the military breakfast seems pertinent here: it was so called because it prepares soldiers for war, that is, battle, according to Pollio in the life of Gallienus.

With white-clad attendants . . . I read, *cum candidatis*. In other formulas of speech, moreover, writers of that age omit this particle. Ammianus Marcellinus, XV.4, said *congredi barbaris*, “to engage the barbarians,” as I show at ch. 18. But since Ammianus has been mentioned, should not *ad damnandum*, “for condemning,” be written *ad amandum*, “for loving,” in the same author, XV.7? “Most just in judgment, benevolent by nature, though for the sake of maintaining authority he seemed harsh to some [Col. 0567D] and inclined toward loving.” This certainly seems right to me, because harshness and love do not fit well here; and from the same chapter it is clear that Leontius condemned men contrary to custom. The most illustrious Columbus judged this emendation necessary and correct.

With white-clad attendants . . . Thus, of course, the faithful are clothed in the Apocalypse and elsewhere, deservedly so, to signify purity and integrity of life. Prudentius, Hymn I, *Peri Stephanōn*, v. 67:

> There Christ presides over white-clad cohorts,  
> And, reigning from a lofty throne, condemns the infamous gods.

Praying continually to Christ . . . Eusebius, IX.10, near the end, reports the same. This remarkable example teaches us that the conscience even of the most savage persecutors has such power as to make them guilty in their own eyes. Relevant here is the fact that Maximinus, after being defeated by Licinius, granted freedom to the Christians by an edict which Eusebius, in the passage cited, preserved translated from Latin into Greek, and which Haymo also mentions, *Ecclesiastical History*, VIII.3. Yet it is strange that Lactantius preserved no memory of this matter.

He expired by a detestable kind of death . . . Eusebius, IX.9, writes that he died *αἰσχίστῳ θανάτῳ*, “by a most shameful death”; and the author of Victor’s Epitome says, “by a simple death,” which plainly conflicts with Lactantius and Eusebius. A simple death is attributed to those put to death without tortures or severe sufferings, as is clear from Suetonius, *Caesar* 74. Hence Prudentius, Hymn X, *Peri Stephanōn*, v. 877:

> Let us therefore first cut off some portion  
> Of the surviving body with the sword,  
> Lest this manifold criminal fall by a simple death,  
> Or the faithless man perish by a single slaughter.  
> As many limbs as he bears, by so many modes I wish him to perish.

But Maximinus endured the most severe pains, even though not inflicted by another. I think that writer contrasts a simple death with that by which someone is removed by another; it is as though he had said: “He was not strangled, [Col. 0568B] nor beheaded, but died his own death,” whatever its torments may have been. Paul the Deacon follows Victor—indeed, so faithfully that, following his example, he even praises this most savage man, writing that he was “by birth and upbringing a shepherd, but a devotee of every kind of wisdom and learning; of a quiet disposition, but rather too eager for wine, so that when drunk he sometimes commanded harsh measures with a disordered mind; when he regretted having done so, he decided that what he had ordered should be deferred until a sober morning.” But Lactantius teaches us something very different. I can tolerate a man of pagan religion praising a most vigorous defender of that religion; but such things are by no means to be pardoned in a Christian. Perhaps Victor calls him a devotee of every kind of wisdom and learning because he favored and cultivated pagan philosophers and priests, whom he judged far wiser than Christians.

He expired . . . He was buried in Cilicia; and Philostratus, VIII.1, records that Julian, Christ’s most hostile enemy, was buried by chance near him. [Col. 0568C]

## CHAPTER L

Valerius . . . Who this was, I cannot discover even by conjecture, since no one else mentions him; Baluzius rightly observed this as well. Nor do I think relevant what Paul the Deacon writes after recounting Maximinus’s death, XI: “Meanwhile Valens, proclaimed emperor in the East by the army, was put to death by the same Licinius. Then Alexander, who had been made emperor at Carthage, was slain by Constantine’s army.” For although Valens might at the same time have been called Valerius, he does not suit this period; and this author more than once suffers some human error in relating these matters. Valens was not put to death at that time. Rather, after Licinius had suffered defeat at Cibalae from Constantine, Valens was created Caesar by Licinius and was killed at Constantine’s demand when Licinius made peace with him, as Tristan, III, p. 472, shows from Victor [Col. 0568D] and Paul the Deacon. Yet from the same authors Tristan notes, not cautiously enough, that Valens rebelled against Galerius Maximianus. This is contrary to fact: Galerius Maximianus had already died when Valens was created Caesar by Maximinus’s consent, as the Valesian Excerpts establish, although Victor and Paul the Deacon call him emperor. The following claim, that Alexander was slain by Constantine’s army, likewise conflicts with historical truth. He was defeated by Maxentius through the praetorian prefect Volusianus and Zenas, as may be seen in Zosimus, II.14. Thus those two have nothing at all in common with our Valerius, whom I believe is found nowhere; and whom we can recognize only with the help of Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*. For just as Ovid sings of the virgin Iphis being changed into a male by Isis’s aid, so the suspicion has sometimes occurred to me that Valerius should, by the aid of textual criticism, be changed into Valeria. This will doubtless seem strange to others, because Lactantius in the following chapter relates Valeria’s death at greater length. Lactantius does indeed do this, I grant; but I think that in that chapter, and at the beginning of his account of the measures taken by Licinius after Maximinus’s defeat, he narrates the same matter in passing. Nothing did Licinius desire so ardently as to remove Valeria from the world. Nor do I see against whom he could have been angry except Valeria, who had rejected him, as is evident from ch. 39, and against whom he was doubtless hostile because of that injury. Hence I have sometimes suspected that this should be written: “first of all, Valeria, whom Maximinus . . .”; and the following fits extremely well, because he recounts that Valeria adopted Candidianus. And just as he presently describes in detail the death of Candidianus, whom he had said was killed, so in ch. 51 he recounts the deaths of Valeria and her mother Prisca, although they were not killed with Candidianus immediately after Maximinus’s death. I had reflected thus when I noticed that learned Englishmen had likewise emended this passage; I plainly attest that I had not consulted them beforehand. [Col. 0569B]

And he seemed to be held in honor . . . For he was the son of Galerius Maximianus by a concubine, and was adopted by his lawful wife Valeria, daughter of Diocletian; all of which could certainly have encouraged him. Thus, when at Nicomedia, the seat of the emperors, he carried himself too proudly and above a private station, he was killed at Licinius’s command, because, I suppose, he came under suspicion of revolutionary designs and perhaps contemplated assuming the purple—precisely what we shortly read was charged against Severianus, son of Severus.

Before Valeria, who was willing to yield to Licinius, by her own right, all the inheritances of Maximianus, but had denied the same to Maximinus . . . A very intricate passage. For if Valeria wished to yield to Licinius all the inheritances of Maximianus, it is in no way likely that she would leave him with her mother and entrust herself to Maximinus, if not her husband’s enemy, certainly not his friend, as is clear from ch. 39. These things certainly do not cohere; therefore I judge the passage corrupt. Lactantius relates that all whom he mentions feared Licinius as an evil and believed they would be safer with Maximinus; but he excepts Valeria and her mother Prisca, who, leaving Licinius by the example of the others, were unwilling also to be with Maximinus, to whom the rest nevertheless entrusted themselves. I therefore think Lactantius wrote, “who was unwilling to yield to Licinius . . .”; and thus the following, “but had denied the same to Maximinus,” fits perfectly. For this certainly would not be true if she had wished to give everything to Licinius. Valeria therefore did not wish to yield to Licinius the inheritances of her husband Galerius Maximianus. I am persuaded that Licinius had sought her in marriage before taking Constantine’s sister as wife, because Lactantius said so pointedly earlier that she had thought she would dwell more safely with Maximinus because he had a wife. This opinion is greatly confirmed by Lactantius himself in the following chapter, where he writes that their chastity and rank brought about their ruin: that is, they perished because Prisca was Diocletian’s wife, Valeria their daughter and Galerius Maximianus’s wife, and because this emperor’s widow was unwilling to marry either Licinius or Maximinus and, contrary to custom and precedent, enter upon a second marriage. Lactantius therefore praises these most illustrious women for their chastity; although he says that they suffered punishment, he seems to lament so bitter a fate: “The women were led to execution amid a great spectacle and pity for so great a calamity; their heads were cut off, and their bodies cast into the sea,” ch. 51. Nowhere does he criticize them, or even slightly suggest that Diocletian or Galerius Maximianus were incited by them to persecute Christians. Yet he does not forget to observe this concerning Romula, Galerius Maximianus’s mother, ch. 11; similarly, in this chapter he censures Maximinus’s wife because chaste women were drowned in the Orontes. Indeed, he separates them from the impious and persecutors. For after recounting in ch. 50 that all the impious had received, by God’s just judgment, the same things they had done, he immediately describes in the following chapter the death of Valeria and her mother Prisca. What then? Prisca and Valeria either were Christians or favored them. Lactantius himself inclines me to this view, ch. 15, where he speaks thus: “The emperor Diocletian now raged not only against his household, but against all; and first of all he compelled his daughter Valeria and his wife Prisca to be defiled by sacrifice.” Diocletian would not have compelled them to sacrifice, nor would Lactantius have written that they were defiled by sacrifice, unless they were Christians or had fallen under that suspicion with the emperor, even if they did not dare openly to embrace Christian doctrines. A pagan is not compelled to sacrifice; nor can such a person properly be said to be defiled by sacrifice. Rather, this is said of one who has given his name to Christ and returns to the superstition he had renounced. Thus, in the same chapter, *to compel* is used of Christians, whom they forced into temples and compelled to sacrifice: “And persecution no less violently fell upon the remaining populace”—from which, of course, he had distinguished presbyters and ministers—“for judges stationed throughout all the temples compelled everyone to sacrifice.” And Prudentius, Hymn II, *Peri Stephanōn*, v. 367, sings that the Jewish people were defiled by the golden calf.
