It is too well known to require proof that, to embrace the pagan religion, nothing else needed to be done than sacrifice to the gods and cast incense upon the altars. This opinion of mine is confirmed by various Acts and Histories which, in Baronius, Tristan, and others, make Diocletian’s wife a Christian, although they did not know her true name and relate much that departs from the truth; Baluzius also observes this. But if they were Christians, what reason is there why Lactantius does not report it in clear words, when, on the other hand, the Martyrologies for 16 August [*a.d. XVII Kal. Sept.*] report that Serena—this is the name they give Diocletian’s wife—died a martyr? To speak candidly, martyrdom seems to me to be counted among the other errors of the Martyrologies; nor is it likely that Lactantius would have passed it over had women so illustrious been executed on account of Christ. Indeed, their sacrifice offered to idols decisively excludes it. Even if they did this under compulsion, and perhaps afterward returned to sounder minds and erased that offense by tears, a chaste life, and genuine repentance, they were nevertheless not killed as Christians, because Licinius had granted Christians freedom by edict and had not yet resolved to harass an innocent people. For this little book was written before the war between Constantine and Licinius arose, while the Church enjoyed peace and tranquillity, as is most clearly evident from its end; and likewise from its beginning, where it relates that God raised up princes who overthrew the tyrants’ wicked and bloody governments—that is, Constantine and Licinius. I had reflected thus when it afterward occurred to me that Lactantius, as a Christian, could use the words by which he says Valeria and Prisca were defiled by sacrifice, and the word *compelled*, in the sense in which, in the same chapter, he says “they compelled [people] to sacrifice,” although, to speak candidly, these words signify force inflicted upon persons resisting it: “For judges stationed throughout all the temples [Col. 0570D] compelled everyone to sacrifice.”

But their mother had first been cast headlong into the East . . . Reader, see Columbus’s notes for my opinion on this passage. I thought it should remain there because it could not conveniently be transferred here. Yet lest I be wholly barren at a point where a famous river is mentioned, I shall try to remedy Josephus’s mention of the river Sabbaticus, *Jewish War* VII.24:

> It flows between the cities Arca and Raphanaea in Agrippa’s kingdom. It has a remarkable peculiarity. For when it flows, it is abundant and not sluggish in its course; then, wholly failing from its springs for six days, it leaves the place dry to be seen; thereafter, as though no change had taken place, it issues forth similarly on the seventh, and has always been observed to maintain this order exactly. Therefore they call it Sabbaticus, naming it after the Jews’ sacred seventh day.

That is, in Rufinus’s translation: “It flows [Col. 0571A] between the cities Arca and Raphanaea in Agrippa’s kingdom. It has, however, a certain peculiar marvel. For though, when it flows, it is very abundant and not sluggish in its course, yet after an interval of six days, failing from its springs, it presents a dry place to be seen. Then, as though no change had taken place, it rises similarly on the seventh day; and it has been certainly established that it always preserves this order. Therefore it is also called Sabbaticus, so named from the Jews’ sacred seventh day.” The passage is truly intricate and, in Casaubon’s judgment, was corrupt already before Rufinus, because all the rabbis disagree with Josephus and maintain that the river is called Sabbaticus not because it discharges its waters on the seventh day, but because it rests on that day. Pliny too says this, *Natural History* XXXI.11: “In Judaea a stream dries up every Sabbath.” Spizelius, in his dissertation *On the American Israelites*, judges that, according to Josephus, the river received the name Sabbaticus not because it rests every seventh day, but because it undergoes some remarkable alteration on every Sabbath. Manasseh ben Israel reverses the sense of the words so that it agrees in every respect with Pliny; Isaac Casaubon, however, restores the corrupted text in his *Exercises against Baronius* by transposing a few words and omitting others. But I am convinced that no words have been omitted, and I restored it thus:

> οὐ σχολαῖος ἓξ ἡμερῶν ἀριθμόν· ἔπειτα δὲ πᾶς ἐκ τῶν πηγῶν ἐπιλείπων, ξηρὸν παραδίδωσιν ὁρᾷν τὸν τόπον· εἶθ᾽ ὥσπερ οὐδεμιᾶς γενομένης μεταβολῆς, ὅμοιος μετὰ τὴν ἑβδόμην ἐκδίδωσι.

That is: “And it rushes with no gentle force for the space of six days; then, wholly failing from the very springs, it presents its channel dry to view; and afterward, as though no change had occurred, it bursts forth in the same manner after the seventh day.” For when he writes that the Sabbatic river was dry after the sixth day, and after the seventh burst forth as it had before the seventh day, he teaches clearly enough that it rested and was dry on every Sabbath. But let the learned judge, who have long promised us a much improved Josephus.

## CHAPTER LI

[Col. 0571C]

Valeria also, wandering through various provinces for fifteen months in plebeian dress . . . We must consider from what point the beginning of this wandering is to be reckoned. Licinius defeated Maximinus on 1 May, A.D. 313. If we calculate Valeria’s wanderings from that time, she must have been killed in June or July of A.D. 314. But if we begin to count them from the time when she was exiled by Maximinus, in A.D. 312, it follows that she was put to death not long after Maximinus’s defeat. This is by no means unreasonable, because Licinius especially desired to kill Valeria, if my conjecture is correct; and because Lactantius also states expressly, ch. 39, that Maximinus banished her with her mother—not to a fixed place, but drove them, headlong and in mockery, now here, now there. While she was compelled to endure that misfortune, she certainly wore only plebeian dress, although I do not deny that *pervagata*, “wandering through,” seems [Col. 0571D] to mean that she moved, not at the emperor’s command, but of her own accord, from one province to another in order to avoid her persecutors. If this book was published immediately after Maximinus’s defeat and before the war which broke out in A.D. 314 between Constantine and Licinius, this flight may conveniently be dated from Maximinus’s decree. Licinius was defeated in that war on 6 October of the same year; he obtained peace by surrendering Illyricum, and only in A.D. 319 returned to the gods—or rather showed that he had always been a pagan—by issuing an edict that bishops should not hold councils and persecuting Christians. If anyone thinks this book was published by Lactantius after the first war between Constantine and Licinius, he will easily see that its origin must be assigned to the period between A.D. 314 and 319. For the Church enjoyed peace when these matters were committed to memory.

[Col. 0572A] She paid the penalty . . . I do not think Lactantius means that they were punished as guilty persons, but only that they perished by a violent death.

## CHAPTER LII

All these things, etc. This will be entirely clear if one punctuates: “All these things—as I speak according to the testimony of those who know—I believed ought to be committed to writing just as they occurred.”

The illustrious titles of Jovians and Herculians, renowned among the nations, which were first insolently assumed by Diocletian and Maximian and afterward transferred to their successors, became worthless. Thus others after Diocletian and Maximian were called Jovians and Herculians. Galerius, Maximinus, and Licinius were certainly called Jovians, as Valesius teaches in his note on Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* IX.9, and Tristan, III, p. 433, though he does not adequately explain a most elegant coin. This Henry Noris, a most learned man, does in his explanation of the Licinian coin, where he also teaches that Constantius and Constantine were called Herculians. The author of the panegyric addressed to Maximian and Constantine, ch. 8, also mentions this: “This is he who gave you, Constantine, the name which he received from the god who is the founder of your race; he proved himself to be Hercules’ offspring not by flattering fables, but by equal virtues.” And in the *Epitome of Chronology*, p. 277, Maximinus Jovius occurs as *ἐπιφανέστατος Καῖσαρ*, “most illustrious Caesar”; Galerius Maximianus is intended. Conversely, Maximinus is sometimes called Maximianus by authors who confuse these names, or through scribal error.

The Lord destroyed them . . . God is most rightly called thus, since he is Lord of all things by the best right. Yet pagans also gave this splendid and illustrious title to their gods and goddesses. In Gruter, VI.68, occurs *Κύριος Ἀσκληπιός*, “Lord Asclepius”; and on a coin in Hardouin, *Θεὸς μέγας Κύριος Σάραπις*, “the great god, Lord Sarapis,” as the learned man reasonably suspects should be read with the letters separated. I have shown in Harpocration, p. 113, that the Sun was called *DOMINUS*, “Lord,” by the Latins and *Δεσπότης*, “Master,” by the Greeks. By *DOMINUS INVICTUS*, “the Unconquered Lord,” in Gruter XI.1066, either the sun should be understood, who is often called Unconquered; or the god whom Commodian, *Instructions* 13, calls simply *Invictus*, and who was Agdestis—to whom Arnobius attributes unconquered strength, and whom Rigaultius observes is confused with Mithras or the sun; or finally the god worshipped in that place is so called. Nor did goddesses lack this title. *Κυρία Ἄρτεμις*, “Lady Artemis,” occurs in an inscription in Gruter, XIII, p. 1066; *DOMINAE*, “to the Lady,” in another, p. 90, found at Alba Julia, by which the Mother Goddesses may perhaps be indicated; and *DOMINA HONOR*, “Lady Honor,” in an inscription, III, p. 100. This is noteworthy because *Honor* is masculine, yet is called *Domina*—if indeed no lines have been lost—because it was sometimes represented in the form of a goddess, as is clear from Galba’s coin inscribed *HONOS ET VIRTUS*, “Honor and Valor.” In Virgil, *Aeneid* III.113, Cybele, or the mother of the gods, is called in no other way:

> And the lions yoked to their mistress’s chariot passed beneath it. [Col. 0572D]

Although some in Servius think Cybele is called mistress of the lions, Servius nevertheless notes that she was properly called “mistress.” “They call goddesses *dominae*,” he says, “as elsewhere:

> These men, having undertaken to lead the mistress of Dis from her bridal chamber.”

Varro and the rest certainly affirm that the mother of the gods is properly called *domina*. For there too they say that Proserpina is called *domina* by Virgil because she is said to be the earth itself, like the mother of the gods. Servius then adds: “This same one,” namely Cybele, “is called *Era*, that is, Mistress.” Germanicus sings similarly in the *Aratea*:

> The Corybantes, servants of the Dictaean mistress, perform their rites—

that is, servants of the mother of the gods. Valerius Flaccus gives the same epithet to Juno and Diana, *Argonautica* IV.355 and VII.181. Indeed, the Arcadians worshipped with highest veneration a goddess called simply *Δέσποινα*, “the Mistress,” as is clear from Pausanias, book VIII. The interpreter, p. 499, makes her Proserpina, doubtless because she is joined with Ceres and because on p. 516 she is said to be her daughter. Yet there she is at the same time clearly distinguished from Proserpina, called daughter of Neptune and Ceres; and Pausanias further writes that he does not dare *ἐς τοὺς ἀτελεστέρους γράφειν*—“write [her name] for the uninitiated.” This certainly teaches abundantly that she was not Proserpina. But although pagan gods were so titled, our God is Lord by the best right. As he cast them down and trampled them, so I hope that at last he will look upon the most grievous calamities of the faithful people and restore peace to the true Church throughout the world. Roman emperors too were called *domini*, as is very well known; I would not mention it had I not seen that Caspar Gevartius does not adequately interpret the closing passage of Claudian in book I of Statius’s *Silvae*. For after showing that Domitian, Trajan, and others were called *domini*, he adds that he wonders at Claudian’s expressly writing, in *Praise of Stilicho* III, that the Romans first of all bestowed the appellation *dominus* on Stilicho, in these verses:

> But never did public favor pour itself forth with so great  
> A consent. For what ruler has obtained this by every service—  
> To be called lord and father—  
> As the vaulted spaces resound for you through unbroken days?  
> Hail, consul, in new titles: the warlike people confess  
> That you are lord, while Brutus does not object;  
> And what Roman liberty, compelled by no terror until now,  
> Has been able to endure, it has bestowed  
> Upon the love of Stilicho.

But I scarcely think this was Claudian’s meaning. Rather, I judge that he sings that the people, as though compelled and unwilling, had thus called emperors; which certainly follows if we admit Heinsius’s highly plausible conjecture, *princeps non omnibus emit obsequiis*, “no ruler purchased [it] by every service.” And [he sings] that the same people of their own accord and from affection called Stilicho lord; or that Stilicho was the first of the consuls to be called lord by the people. This is certainly confirmed by what follows, where he teaches that Brutus himself, the restorer of liberty, would not take it ill, because Stilicho, although called lord, nevertheless acted as the people’s father. [Col. 0573C]

To the most distinguished PAULUS VOET VAN WINSSEN, secretary to the high and mighty States of the Diocese of Utrecht, greetings from GISBERT CUPER.

If a new edition of Lactantius’s *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* had been completed, perhaps you would not be receiving this letter from me, most distinguished sir. For since various men of outstanding learning, besides Baluzius and myself—which gives me the greatest pleasure—have resolved to elucidate this little work, I scarcely doubt that the principal point of this letter will have occurred to one of them. It consists of a few words, in which at first glance scarcely anything worthy of observation presents itself. Hence, when I was arranging my Notes, I did not notice [Col. 0573D] what I now send you for the sake of informing you.

It is therefore established that the pagans compelled Christians to sacrifice to the gods, and demanded nothing else from them when they forced them to renounce the true religion. Very many passages in ecclesiastical history, in martyrdom accounts, and in the Fathers attest this abundantly. It is well known that Prudentius sings that Eulalia was told, Hymn III, *Peri Stephanōn*:

> “What labor is it, I ask, to escape these tortures?  
> If, with the tips of your fingers,  
> You should be willing, kindly maiden,  
> To touch but a little salt  
> And a small amount of incense . . .”

A severe penalty would have been far removed.

Diocletian in Lactantius, ch. 10: “In a furious rage, he ordered not only those who ministered at the sacred rites, but all who were in the palace, to sacrifice; and, if they refused, to be punished [Col. 0574A]. By letters sent to the commanders, he also ordered soldiers to be compelled to offer the impious sacrifices, and that those who did not obey should be discharged from military service.” Chapter 15: “The emperor therefore raged now not only against his household, but against everyone; and he compelled his first daughter Valeria and his wife Prisca to be defiled by sacrifice.” And shortly afterward: “For judges stationed throughout all the temples compelled everyone to sacrifice.”

I attempted in passing to explain these last words at ch. 1; but while I do not wholly reject that explanation, something greater and more deserving of annotation seems to lie concealed in them. For I think that Christians, oppressed by so bitter a persecution, attended the temples of the Gentiles together with the Gentiles—not in order to worship them, sacrifice to them, or render any honour to the fictitious divinities in any way, but in order to avoid the tortures and penalties which were continually ready for those deemed Christians who, after renouncing Christ, refused to sacrifice to the gods. Diocletian, informed of what was happening, ordered all found in the temples to sacrifice. It would by no means have been necessary to make such an order if no one other than Gentiles [Col. 0574B] entered the temples; and in this way Christians who sought to escape suffering were detected. Hence what follows shortly thereafter: “The prisons were full; unheard-of varieties of tortures were devised.”

And doubtless the Christians persuaded themselves that they were permitted to do this to avoid persecution and could nevertheless preserve the faith pledged to Christ, since, when entering the temples, they had no intention of worshipping idols. I shall not now say that the Nicolaitans taught people indiscriminately to do many things—to eat food sacrificed to idols, to be in temples, and openly to do everything in common—as the author of the *Index of Jewish Heresies*, commonly attributed to Jerome, expresses it. But I seem to have observed that the ancients distinguished those who entered temples for the purpose of worshipping idols from those who did not frequent them with that intention.

Canon 1 of the Council of Elvira reads thus: “It was resolved that, among those who, after the faith of saving baptism and at an adult age, has approached a temple in order to commit idolatry and has done so—which is the principal crime, since it is the highest wickedness—he should not receive communion even at the end [of life].” Thus Christians are distinguished: those who approach temples with the intention of worshipping idols, and those who actually did this and sacrificed. Since Christians seeking to free themselves from persecutions did neither, I seem not without reason to maintain that they had nothing in common with the others and that the canon of the council does not speak of them.

Thus Canon III distinguishes flamines who merely gave public entertainments celebrated in honour of the gods from those who also sacrificed: “Likewise, concerning flamines who have not sacrificed but have only given an entertainment: because they have abstained from fatal sacrifices, it was resolved that communion should be granted them at the end.” And Canon LV: “Priests who merely wear the crown, neither sacrifice nor provide anything from their own resources for idols, shall receive communion after two years.” There is also an elegant example in Cyprian, Epistle XXI, where he calls Candida *aecusa*—as Cestriensis emends it—because she counted out gifts on her own behalf, so as not to sacrifice. Yet she seems only to have ascended as far as the three *fata*, or [Col. 0574D] *dryphacta*—as J. F. Gronovius, a man of outstanding learning, rightly believes the reading should be restored, ch. 14 of his *Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers*—and then to have descended to the *dryphacta*, namely, the place where Christians were compelled to sacrifice before the governor. However far Candida may have gone, Cyprian nevertheless excuses her, because she did not defile herself with sacrifice.

And although, in my opinion, those who enter the temples of the Gentiles for this reason are by no means free from sin, they nevertheless seem capable of some excuse, because they did not do so with the intention of worshipping idols. Thus Canon 41 of the aforementioned council permits the faithful to have idols in their houses: “It was resolved that the faithful be admonished, insofar as they can, to prevent idols from being kept in their houses. But if they fear the violence of their slaves, let them at least keep themselves pure; if they do not do so, let them be considered alien to the Church.”

Nor is Albaspinaeus without reason in observing that these words establish beyond doubt that this council was convened in the most difficult times of persecution [Col. 0575A], and therefore before Constantine. For they would not have feared being denounced by their own slaves if, with immunity assured, they could at will embrace and defend whatever religion they pleased. Therefore, just as during persecution the faithful could keep idols in their homes and permit their slaves to worship them, lest they be accused by them, so they seem to have persuaded themselves that they could attend Gentile temples to avoid persecution. Nor could they easily be distinguished there, because the places were very spacious, adorned with colonnades and other structures in which they could walk about, doing none of the things the Gentiles customarily did in worshipping their divinities. This was all the more so because the latter often visited temples merely to greet the gods and did not always sacrifice.

I do not now wish to dispute whether Christians acted rightly or otherwise, or how grave this sin may be; nor do I wish to investigate what expiation is owed by those among us who enter the temples of those Christians merely to look at them, where statues and images have been arranged not only for decoration but also for worship [Col. 0575B]. But I cannot refrain from warning that the Gentiles demanded nothing else from Christians than that they sacrifice, without any concern for the intention with which people worshipped their gods.

> [Note: [Col. 0575D] A cruel slander. The Catholic Church chiefly requires the heart, but cannot search it. It compels no one. But its rulers, who do not bear the sword without cause, inflict deserved punishments upon rebels, sowers of discord, obstinate and turbulent persons, as persons harmful to the commonwealth.]

Would that the Roman Catholics did not imitate their example. They consider all those initiated into their rites whom they compel, by force, fear, penalties, and tortures, to participate in them. Julian the Apostate thought otherwise and forbade anyone to inflict injury or insult upon a Christian, **μηδὲ ἄκοντας πρὸς θυσίαν ἕλκειν**, “nor to drag unwilling persons to sacrifice”; rather, those who voluntarily approached the altars were first to propitiate the **Ἀποτροπαῖοι** (“Averting Gods”) and be purified by the expiations customary among them. For God demands for himself our better part—our mind and understanding—not our body.

But on this occasion I am pleased to call in an ancient inscription, from which I seem able to affirm that, in a time of persecution, Jews either renounced their religion or did certain things to avoid it, by which Gentiles could be persuaded that they were no longer Jews. Among the Oxford marbles, no. XXVIII, and in Reinesius III, no. LXVIII, there is an inscription containing the names of those who contributed money to adorn, apparently, the gymnasium at Smyrna. Among them Jews are listed: **οἱ ποτὲ Ἰουδαῖοι Μ. Α.**, that is, in the judgement of learned men, “those who were recently Jews, one mina.” But it seemed to me that these words should sometimes be rendered, “those who once were Jews.”

These things occurred at Smyrna in the time of Emperor Hadrian, when the Jews raised their most grievous insurrection and rebellion under Bar Kokhba, the false Messiah. Hadrian defeated them; all Judaea was devastated, and an innumerable multitude of that unhappy nation was slain. Since they undoubtedly suffered persecution throughout the Roman empire, it could readily have happened that some Smyrnaeans renounced God and embraced Gentile superstition, or contributed money for adorning the shrine of Fortune [Col. 0575D], so that Gentiles might suppose that they had crossed into their camp and thus free themselves from tortures. For that Jews could readily have done such things in accordance with their teachers’ judgement is clear from what Jacques Capellus observed on the books of Moses, p. 619 and following.

Nor indeed do I see why Jews who had recently arrived should give a mina for the adornment of a temple. It is not likely that Jews who had moved elsewhere, or gone away to another place, would contribute to the building of a temple at Smyrna; nor would they do the same if they dared openly profess themselves Jews, since they were by no means free from idolatry [Col. 0576A], from which that people, after the Babylonian captivity, had turned their minds altogether away.

This is my opinion concerning Lactantius’ passage and the ancient inscription. If you approve it, I shall think that I have rightly spent an hour in writing this letter to you. If otherwise, and my conjecture deceives me, I shall nonetheless rejoice that I have done this, because the scarcely consolable grief I conceived from the sudden death of my most beloved wife seems to be lessened while I converse with you. And this same cause does not allow me to put an end to the letter, but as it were bids me add one or two notes which ought to be joined to the rest.

To chapter 9, after *legimus*, I add: Augustine refers to this in *City of God*, IV, p. 29, where he mocks the god Terminus. For it is one thing not to have yielded, another to have returned from where one had yielded. “Yet afterward, in the eastern regions, by Hadrian’s will the boundaries of the Roman empire were changed. For he surrendered to the Persian empire three noble provinces—Armenia, Mesopotamia, and Assyria—so that that god Terminus, who according to these people defended the Roman boundaries and by that most beautiful omen had not yielded his place to Jupiter, seems to have feared Hadrian, king of men, more than the king of gods. When the aforementioned provinces were recovered at another time, almost within our memory, Terminus yielded backwards, when Julian, devoted to the oracles of those gods, with reckless daring ordered the ships carrying provisions to be burned, etc.”

On chapter 17 I note that the ancients said *certare alicui*, “to contend against someone,” and the like. I observe this form of speech also in Gruter’s Inscription CCCXXXIX:

> YOU CONTENDED AGAINST MANY.  
> POOR MAN, YOU FEARED NO ENVY.  
> HAVING ENDURED, YOU ALWAYS KEPT SILENT BRAVELY.

And in Apuleius, IV, p. 143: “When I saw dogs, both great and numerous, fit to fight bears and lions.”

To chapter 33 I noted that *odoritatem*, *prioritatem*, and the like occur; add *indulgitatem*. Junius Philargyrius on *Georgics* II: “He used *indulgentia* in a novel way. For the ancients said *indulgitas*, as Caelius in book VII: ‘by a wife’s customary indulgence toward her children.’”

To chapter 36, after “on the *Historia Augusta*,” add: Thus the chief priest of Isis is called the highest, principal, or foremost priest in Apuleius, II, pp. 264, 266, and 267, ed. Elmenhorst.

On chapter 40 I observe in what sense men or animals are called servants (*famuli*) and **θεράποντες**, “attendants,” of gods. Psyche, in Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* V, for this same reason entreats Ceres “by the winged chariots of your servant dragons”; and Plato used to call himself **τοῖς κύκνοις ὁμόδουλον**, “fellow-slave with the swans,” according to Olympiodorus in his *Life*, because swans were under Apollo’s protection or dedicated to him, and Plato himself was thought to have been born of that god. Moreover, those consecrated to gods or initiated into their rites were called servants.

Apuleius, II: “Hence I too ought to feel that I was being sought as a servant even of a great god, and to serve the same [gods].” Again: “And now dedicate yourself to the obedience of our religion, and voluntarily take on the yoke of service; for when you begin to serve the goddess, then you will feel more fully the fruit of your freedom” [Col. 0576D]. In Inscription XII.328 occurs *FAMULA BACCHI*, “handmaid of Bacchus”; and in Augustine, *City of God* IV.10, the Vestal virgins are called handmaids of Vesta, which accords admirably with Lactantius.

Strabo, XII.1.557, writes that at Ameria there was a temple of **Μήν**, having many **ἱερόδουλοι**, “temple-servants”; and on p. 577, at Antioch in Pisidia, a **ἱερωσύνη Μηνὸς Ἀρκαίου πλῆθος ἔχουσαν ἱεροδούλων**, that is, “a priesthood of Lunus, surnamed Arcaeus” (elsewhere called **Ἀσκαῖος**, and by Salmasius on the *Historia Augusta* **Ἀρχαῖος**), “having a multitude of hierodouloi,” or sacred servants. Under this term priests and persons consecrated to sacred service may be included. On p. 559 Strabo distinguishes **ἱερόδουλοι** from **ἱερεῖς**, “priests.”

I translated **μηνὸς** as *Luni* (“of Lunus”), and think that this should also be done on p. 580. I do not think that any month was worshipped by these peoples, but the god Lunus, who appears on coins of Antioch in Pisidia—not to speak of other cities—and who rides a horse on a coin of the Olbians, whose city was in Pamphylia. One may consult what I note on p. 17 of Harpocration, where I call Diospolis a city of Armenia which Strabo calls Diopolis; I thought this worth mentioning. It will also thereby become clear that “Month,” as learned men suppose, is not mentioned on the Antiochene coin, but that the reading should be “Antiochene,” not “of Month”: **COL. CAES. ANTIOCH.**, as I noted in passing in Harpocration and as Hardouin also approves in the *Antirrheticus*. And, if it is permitted to mix sacred things with profane, Christians—and the Apostles themselves—are called **δοῦλοι Χριστοῦ**, “slaves of Christ,” and a bishop in Inscription IX.1053, *FAMULUS CHRISTI*, “servant of Christ.”

On chapter XXXIX, and especially in the preface, I treat of the cremation of corpses and of bodies buried intact. Subsequently I observed that burial was also in use in Apuleius’ time, as is quite clear from the story of the boy believed to have been removed by poison, whereas the physician had actually mixed a sleeping draught for him, *Metamorphoses* X. Further, that the Gentiles held it a matter of great religious concern that bodies be buried intact is evident from their carefully guarding corpses laid out in houses, lest a sorceress take away any of their limbs. Apuleius recounts this at length, II, p. 124, and adds: “Ah! And what I almost passed over: if anyone does not restore a body intact in the morning, whatever has been cut off or diminished from it, he is compelled to make up the whole amount by cutting it from his own face.”

Whether true or invented, this nevertheless indicates the concern which the Gentiles had that bodies should be buried whole and should come whole to the underworld. Hence in book III Lucius’ grief, when he was summoned to trial for homicide and the Greek-style fire and wheel, then every kind of scourge by which he was to be torn apart, were brought forward: “My sorrow is greatly increased—indeed doubled—because I was not permitted at least to die whole.” In book VII, when, transformed into an ass, they wished to castrate him, he decided to throw himself headlong or die of starvation: “I shall die nevertheless, but I shall die whole.” Finally this is also clear from p. 199 of the same book: “The corpse, its parts scattered, was at last found whole, and, with difficulty pieced together, was buried there.”

On the same chapter I observe that no empress, after the death of her emperor-husband, entered a second marriage. There is an elegant passage on this subject in the Thirteenth Council of Toledo, held in A.D. 683. For the title of its fifth chapter reads: “That, after the death of the prince, no one should dare to unite his surviving consort to himself either in marriage or in adultery,” as is clear from the *Notice of the Councils of Spain* published in 1686 by Joseph Saenz de Aguirre. Although it is also certain that not all queens, either formerly or now, have observed this rule, as the example of Pythodoris in Strabo, XII, teaches us.

To chapter 46 add that Apuleius, at the beginning of *Metamorphoses* X, mentions a commander who held command over a thousand armed men, and that the same man is called a tribune on p. 244.

I noted on chapter 50 that Prisca and Valeria, Diocletian’s wife and daughter, were Christians, or at least favoured the Christian religion. Subsequently I observed that Henry Dodwell, a man of distinguished learning, in Dissertation XI on Cyprian, no. 66, affirms that they were Christians, as is clear from the words which follow:

> “Indeed, Christians moved freely even within the emperors’ palaces. Their wives themselves, their children, and their servants were Christians. (Such, it is established, were Diocletian’s wife Prisca and his daughter Valeria, and the wife of Maximian Galerius.) These [emperors] granted them the freedom to perform before them the observances of their religion, both in word and deed.”

This man, exceptionally skilled in these matters, relies on two authorities; these lead him to believe that the empresses professed Christ. One is Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VIII.1; the other Lactantius, ch. 15, whose words I too used, as it were, as the basis for proving the same thing at chapter 50. Yet Eusebius does not seem to me to speak of the emperors’ wives, but of the wives of household servants, courtiers, or those who frequented the palace [Col. 0578A], as will plainly appear if anyone wishes to consult the Greek. I myself therefore used the same words at chapter 14 to prove that Christians were often present in the palaces of Gentile emperors and indeed held the highest offices.

Christopherzon formerly thought that Eusebius spoke of the emperors’ wives, but Valesius corrected that error in his notes. I thought it necessary to point out that Dodwell had noticed before me that those empresses were Christians, lest anyone perhaps imagine that I claim another’s discoveries as my own. For I testify that, when arranging my notes, I had not observed those words, and that I would not otherwise have omitted to praise that very learned man on this account.

These are the matters which occurred to me and which friendship, and the very great and pleasant intimacy existing between us, caused me to share with you. If the printer—or rather the learned men whose notes, as I hear, he awaits—causes longer delays, you may perhaps receive from me another and longer letter [Col. 0578B]. For I have not exhausted all the material so completely that I could not compose more extensive dissertations on certain matters. Farewell. The Hague, 9 July.

This letter had scarcely been completed when Antony Pagi’s *Historical-Critical Chronology of the Annals of the Most Eminent Baronius*, by a most learned man and diligent restorer of chronology, was brought to me. Since he illuminates to an extraordinary degree the times of Diocletian and the emperors who reigned with him, it will be for you to judge whether the printer would not wisely serve his interests by extracting from that work the materials useful for elucidating Lactantius and appending them to the new edition. This certainly seems to me exceedingly useful and likely to be welcome to learned persons, both because that book is not in everyone’s hands and because in this way everything necessary for a better understanding of this golden little work would be collected into one small volume.

You are now wearied by the reading of so long and wordy a letter; yet I cannot dismiss you, and I ask pardon if I append a second one as prolix as the first. I see with the greatest pleasure that a man of distinguished learning agrees with me, under A.D. 306, that Constantine the Great was born in the town of Naissus, not in Britain; under A.D. 302, that Prisca and Valeria were Christians; and finally, under A.D. 306, that he refers **NATALEM INVICTI**, “the birthday of the Unconquered [One],” to the Sun. I therefore see no reason why Petavius’ opinion, which Hardouin also embraces in the *Antirrheticus*, should not now be followed: that day is rightly called the Sun’s birthday because then the sun first turns northward from the south, as Julian himself teaches in Oration IV. Hardouin judges that Christ’s birthday was first transferred at Rome to this day, so that while the Gentiles were occupied with their profane rites, Christians might freely attend to their own sacred observances.

But it seems more convenient to me to arrange under the order of the chapters the other matters I have noted in Pagi’s book—matters which either confirm my opinions or are worthy of examination [Col. 0578D]—so that you may more easily find and judge them all.

I discuss Domitian’s persecution at chapter 3 of Lactantius, and maintain that it was neither long nor severe. Pagi, by contrast, thinks that in the thirteenth year of his reign Domitian decreed a persecution against Christians; that it continued in the fourteenth year; and that it was intensified on the occasion of the quinquennial games in the fifteenth year, when, according to Suetonius, he was killed in his bedchamber, not in Jupiter’s temple, **ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ Διός**, as the author of the Alexandrian Chronicle writes.

To establish his view, the learned man writes that in the aforementioned Chronicle, under the consulship of Libo IX Asprenas and Marcus Arretinus Clemens, one reads: “Bruttius reports that a great multitude of Christians was put to death and martyred from the fourteenth year of Domitian.” He then observes that Eusebius, who had read Bruttius’ history, relates in the *Chronicle* that the persecution began in A.D. 93, confirms the same in his *History*, and in *Ecclesiastical History* III.17 speaks of the persecution under Domitian, while what he says afterwards in ch. 18 shows only that it was intensified in that year.

But the author of the Chronicle is assuredly not among the most exact writers. For he joins together the following consuls: Domitian XIII and Flavius Clemens; Asprenas and Lateranus; Domitian XIV and Clemens; finally Valens and Vetus [Col. 0579A]. To the first consuls he assigns the beginning of the persecution, and at that time writes that the apostle John was banished to Patmos and that Domitian resolved to extirpate David’s lineage. Under the next consulship he places Bruttius’ words; and in the remaining two years he makes no mention at all of persecution. We should judge similarly of Eusebius’ *Chronicle*.

And although, if we follow Bruttius’ authority, the persecution may have begun in the fourteenth year, it can be assigned as readily to the end as to the beginning of that year. If this is true, it will certainly differ little from the judgement of other learned men. But what Pagi attempts to prove from Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* III.17–18—that the persecution began in A.D. 93 and was intensified in A.D. 95—I cannot, to my astonishment, comprehend at all. For Eusebius did not arrange the chapters of his books by years; then he writes that Domitian persecuted Christians **τελευτῶν**, “toward the end,” that is, toward the end of his life. Chapter 18 connects what follows to the preceding matter in these words, **ἐν τούτῳ διωγμῷ**, “in this persecution.” Finally, the very words by which Pagi thinks it proved that the persecution was intensified in the fifteenth year are also connected with the preceding statements and indicate that Christians were harassed by persecution in that year. This seems to me a very firm argument that in his fifteenth year the emperor began to rage against an innocent people.

For, after saying that even pagan writers had not hesitated to hand down the Christian martyrdoms to memory, Eusebius adds: **οἵ γε καὶ τὸν καιρὸν ἐπ’ ἀκριβὲς ἀπεσημήναντο**, “for they also marked the very time of the persecution precisely.” But what was that time? Surely not the thirteenth year, nor the fourteenth, but the fifteenth. For they write that, in the fifteenth year of Domitian’s rule, Flavia Domitilla, niece through his sister of Flavius Clemens, who was then consul at Rome, was deported with very many others to the island of Pontia because of her confession of Christ [Col. 0579C].

Yet, as I said before, I do not intend wholly to oppose those who think that Domitian was already raging against Christians in the fourteenth year. For Cassius Dio, book LXVIII, after relating that Fabius Clemens, **ὑπατεύοντα**, “serving as consul,” and Flavia Domitilla were put to death, both charged with **ἀθεότης**, “impiety”—for that was how they spoke of Christians—adds that Domitian was killed **τῷ ἐξῆς ἔτει**, “in the following year,” under the consuls Gaius Valens and Gaius Antistius. And the words following Flavia Domitilla’s story make clear that in the preceding year other Christians also were either banished or put to death:

> **ἐπηνέχθη δὲ ἄμφοιν ἔγκλημα ἀθεότητος· ὑφ’ ἧς καὶ ἄλλοι ἐς τὰ τῶν Ἰουδαίων ἤθη ἐξοκέλλοντες πολλοὶ κατεδικάσθησαν· καὶ οἱ μὲν ἀπέθανον, οἱ δὲ τῶν γοῦν οὐσιῶν ἐστερήθησαν.**  
> “An accusation of impiety was brought against them both, Clemens and Domitilla; on this charge many others also, who had adopted Jewish customs, were condemned. Some died, while others at least were deprived of their property.”

Here “Jewish customs” means the Christian religion, not only in Dio but also in the author of the *Olympiads*, who writes that the charge of **Ἰουδαϊσμός**, “Judaizing,” was brought against them. For Jews and Christians were confused; and perhaps Dio spoke in this manner because Domitian ordered those descended from David’s stock to be killed. Even if I granted that the persecution began so early, it would not follow that it was either long or severe. I have scarcely any doubt that Domitian raged more cruelly against others, and that in this sense especially he may be called a portion of Nero in cruelty.

[Col. 0580A] On chapter 9 I observe that, before Narseus was defeated by Galerius Maximianus, the Persians had also been defeated by Diocletian, or had made peace with him; and that Herculius seems to have waged war against them. Antony Pagi, following Noris, another man of eminent learning, proves under A.D. 289 that Diocletian did indeed wage war against the Persians; Noris appears to do so in ch. 4 of Dissertation I on Diocletian’s coinage. Noris there also observes that Maximian Herculius never fought against the Persians, a conclusion which Pagi follows under A.D. 297.

The author of the Alexandrian Chronicle, to be sure, reports the contrary, and he also wrongly writes that Constantius waged war with the Persians. I observed on Lactantius ch. 15 that Casaubon likewise fell into this error. Perhaps he followed the author of the Chronicle, who says on p. 642: “The Persians were conquered in a great war by Constantius and Maximinus Jovius, Caesars.” In fact, Constantius never fought the Persians; after being created Caesar at Nicomedia, he immediately proceeded to the West. The other Caesar was also called not Maximinus but Galerius Maximianus. I show on Lactantius ch. 52 that this error occurs elsewhere in the same Chronicle—or *Epitome of Times*, as Scaliger calls it.

Yet Mamertinus, ch. 2 of the panegyric addressed to Emperor Maximian, speaks thus: “Shall I attempt to enumerate your achievements—what first standards inaugurated you under imperial auspices, what camps received a master they were to possess, what wars trained you, what victories increased you? I shall go, of course, tracing the steps of your courage along the whole boundary of the Danube, throughout the entire course of the Euphrates, and over the banks of the Rhine and the shore of Ocean.” I confess these words seemed to me to signify that Herculius had fought the Persians at the Euphrates; nor do I change my view. But this occurred before he was emperor, while he was serving in the camps of other emperors. Mamertinus here briefly recounts how Maximian spent his life before being raised to imperial power and what splendid proofs of courage he had given.

Nor do the gifts by which the Parthian, as one reads in ch. 5 of the *Genethliacus*, flattered Diocletian and Maximian prove anything; for Narseus did this after making a treaty with Diocletian, as is clear from ch. 10 of the panegyric I have cited: “In the same manner, that king of the Persians, who had never previously deigned to acknowledge himself a man, supplicates your brother, Diocletian, opens and offers his entire kingdom should he deign to enter it; meanwhile he sends various beasts of extraordinary beauty, content to obtain the name of friendship, and earns it by submission.” For without doubt he speaks of the same gifts.

Nor is it an objection that Maximian Herculius is called *Persicus Maximus* in inscriptions, because he acquired that surname from Diocletian’s victories. Diocletian was also called *Germanicus Maximus* from the victories of Herculius, as Noris notes, ch. V of Dissertation I on Diocletian’s coinage.

On chapter 18 I discuss whether Diocletian was consecrated. I now observe that Antony Pagi, under A.D. 316, establishes from the passage of Eusebius which I cited that he was enrolled among the gods by Maximinus.

On chapter 42, p. 494, I examine how many years Diocletian lived as a private person after abdicating the empire. What I note there should be recast thus: “He significantly says ‘after the empire’; and it is agreed that Diocletian survived for the same number of years after laying aside the purple, if we count among them the year in which he died. For he made himself a private citizen in A.D. 305 and died in A.D. 313; counting both years as complete, nine years result, as Pagi teaches under A.D. 316. But he did not wish, etc.”

On the same chapter I observe that Maximian Herculius was consecrated by his son Maxentius. Antony Pagi confirms this opinion from a coin in Mediobarbus bearing the inscription:

> **DIVO MAXIMIANO PATRI MAXENTIVS AVG. F.**  
> “To the deified Maximian, father of Maxentius Augustus.”

For this reason—and not because he had been consecrated by Constantine, his son-in-law—he is called *Divus* in a stone inscription in Nicolaus Bergerus 3.23 by Constantine the Younger, as Pagi elsewhere observes:

> **IMP. CAES. FL. VAL. CONSTANTINO. P. F. AVG. NEPOTI. DIVI. CONSTANT. AVG. PII. FILIO XXXIII.**  
> “To Emperor Caesar Flavius Valerius Constantine, Pious and Fortunate Augustus, grandson of the deified Constantine Augustus Pius, [in his] thirty-third [year].”

Unless we say that, at that time, living emperors intended nothing else by that word than to indicate that those whom they mentioned were dead. In this sense I thought, on chapter 19, that Diocletian and Maximian were called **θειότατοι**, “most divine,” by Galerius Maximianus in Eusebius.

On chapter 50 I showed that *Valerius* should be changed to *Valeria*. Pagi, under A.D. 306, no. 15, and 314, no. 12, writes that Valerius Valens was killed by Licinius. But I scarcely doubt that this man of rare learning would change his opinion if he encountered what I have noted concerning Valens’ death. As for the coin which in Goltz is inscribed in Greek **ΑΥΤ. Κ. ΠΟΠ** (Pagi has **ΡΟΥ**) **ΟΥΑΛΕΡ. ΟΥΑΛΕΝΣ CEB. L. A.**, it is highly doubtful whether it can be referred to Valens killed by Licinius, because Goltz lists another coin in which, in his opinion, that man is called **ΑΥ. ΚΑΙ. Γ. ΟΥΑΛΕΝΣ ΚΥ CEB. L. A.** To tell the truth, I should very greatly wish to see and handle those coins; they are extremely suspect to me—certainly one of them, since our Valens was never Augustus, but only Caesar.

Whatever the case, it is entirely clear that Valens was not killed by Licinius at that time but after the first war waged against Constantine, which fell in A.D. 317; for the events which Lactantius narrates in that chapter must be assigned to A.D. 314, Pagi himself arranging matters thus. I ask that what I noted on chapter 50 concerning Valens be recast in this way; for haste caused me not to attend sufficiently to what Tristan had noted:

> “For Valens, commander of the Dacian frontier—Pagi wrongly writes *militis*, ‘of the soldier,’—was not put to death at the same time, but Licinius created him Caesar after he had been defeated by Constantine at Cibalae. When both were again defeated in the battle fought on the plain of Mardia, which seems to have lain between Philippi and Hadrianopolis, Constantine made peace with Licinius on the condition that Valens should become a private citizen and be killed. This is noted by Tristan, vol. 3, p. 472, from the *Extracts on the Life of Constantine*, Zosimus, and Peter the Patrician. He also rightly reproves Victor, Paul the Deacon, and Occon for writing that Valens rebelled against Galerius Maximianus.”

For although I do not find this in the former two, it is nevertheless certainly true that Valens could not have rebelled against Galerius Maximianus, because Galerius had died when Valens was created Caesar by Licinius. Victor and Paul the Deacon call him emperor; and if they think that he was made Augustus, they are certainly wrong. Or one must conclude that in that age the title *imperator* was given indiscriminately both to Augusti and Caesars, just as, Pagi observes, Numerian is called on an ancient coin:

> **IMP. C. M. AVR. NUMERIANUS. NOB. C.**  
> “Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Numerianus, most noble Caesar.”

Yet I had thought that Numerian was sometimes at that period not Caesar but Augustus, because this would be the sole coin on which a Caesar was called *imperator*, a title which I do not see bestowed upon Caesars in other coins or inscriptions, except Inscription VII.275:

> **IMP. Q. IVLIO. FILIO. GALLIENI. AVG. ET. SALONINAE. AVG.**  
> “To Emperor Quintus Julius, son of Gallienus Augustus and Salonina Augusta.”

For he was made Caesar only. And the coin inscribed **IMP. ROMVLVS**, found in Tristan, vol. 3, p. 466, and attributed by Mediobarbus to Maxentius’ son—who in fact died a Caesar—is assigned by Tristan to Romulus called Augustulus, whom his father Orestes made Augustus or emperor. Nor does it seem an objection that Numerian is called *nobilissimus Caesar*, “most noble Caesar”; for Augusti sometimes retained this title, as is clear from Inscription IV.278:

> **IMP. M. AVR. CARINO NOBILISSIMO CAES PIO. FELICI. INVICTO AVGVST. PONT. MAXIMO. TRIB. POP. P. P. COSS. PROCOS.**  
> “To Emperor Marcus Aurelius Carinus, most noble Caesar, pious, fortunate, unconquered Augustus, chief pontiff, holder of tribunician power, father of his country, consul, proconsul.”

This is also clear from a coin in Mediobarbus on which Gaius Valens Hostilianus Messius Quintus is called both most noble Caesar and Augustus:

> **QVINTVS, NO. CAE. VALENS. HOSTIL. AVG.**

Thus Volusianus, Publius Licinius Valerianus, Herodianus son of Odenathus, Herennianus Maxentius, and Constantine the Great are called on coins **IMPERATORES AVGVSTI**, “emperors and Augusti,” and at the same time **PRINCIPES IVVENTVTIS**, “princes of the youth.”

[Col. 0582B] On the same chapter 50, I observe that Valeria and Prisca were Christians, or were very favourable to Christians. Antonius Pagius holds the same view, and attempts to confirm it also from Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, chapter 1; preferring, under the year 302, Christophorson’s translation to Valesius’s. As I examine Eusebius’s Greek words again and again, however, I cannot yet be convinced that he speaks of the emperors’ wives, since what follows plainly suggests the contrary, where Dorotheus and Gorgonius are mentioned. Surely it does not even seem doubtful that Eusebius would have named the Augustae and their children, once peace had been granted to the Church, if by these words γαμεταῖς καὶ παισὶ [“wives and children”] he had meant them. Indeed, when I inspect Eusebius more closely, I do not know how it comes about that I think neither Christophorson nor Valesius grasped the sense of these words, although I followed the latter’s translation in Lactantius, chapter 14. I shall set out my reasons, though I am ready to abandon them if another teaches something better, or if learned persons [Col. 0582C] judge them insufficiently sound.

Eusebius, then, relates that the Christian religion acquired great glory and freedom among Greeks and barbarians before Diocletian’s persecution; that this was demonstrated by the kindness of τῶν κρατούντων, that is, the emperors, toward Christians, since they granted them τῶν ἐθνῶν ἡγεμονίας, “governorships of nations.” Having thus discussed the emperors, he passes to others: τί δεῖ περὶ τῶν κατὰ τοὺς βασιλικοὺς λέγειν οἴκους καὶ τῶν ἐπὶ πᾶσιν ἀρχόντων; [“What need is there to speak of those in the imperial households and of the rulers set over all?”] Christophorson and Valesius interpret the latter words as referring to the emperors themselves; Pagius, to those who rule over all. But I judge that they should be translated thus: “What need is there to speak of those who are employed in the emperor’s palace? What of those who are set over all?” By these ἄρχοντες, “rulers,” I understand the Praetorian Prefects, or rather the chamberlains, or persons of similar rank, who presided over the rest who were employed in the palace and attached to the prince’s court.

Eusebius says that these were Christians and allowed their households—their wives, children, and slaves—to profess the Christian religion freely. Such was [Col. 0582D] Dorotheus, who was chief chamberlain, as Valesius shows; and such was Gorgonius, likewise another prefect in the palace; as were the rest who, with them, obtained equal distinction on account of τὸν τοῦ θεοῦ λόγον, “the word of God.” Finally, he adds that τοὺς καθ᾽ ἑκαστὴν ἐκκλησίαν ἄρχοντας, that is, the heads of the churches, were held in great honour παρὰ πᾶσιν ἐπιτρόποις καὶ ἡγεμόσιν—not, as they translate, “by all private persons and provincial governors,” but “by all the procurators of the Augusti and the presidents or governors of provinces.” Thus, in inscription II.595, Aufidius Julianus is called ὁ κράτιστος ἐπίτροπος τῶν Σεβάστων, “the most excellent procurator of the Augusti,” and in 459 T. Porcius Proclus, ἐπίτροπος Πρειουάτης διὰ Φλαμινίας, Αἰμιλίας, Λιγυρίας, “procurator of [uncertain provincial name] through Flaminia, Aemilia, and Liguria.”

These final words of Eusebius seem to me sufficiently to establish that he is speaking not about the emperors, but about those who held the foremost rank in their palaces and governed their households. The same is confirmed in chapter VI, where he treats περὶ τῶν κατὰ τοὺς βασιλικοὺς [Col. 0583A] οἴκους, “of those in the imperial households,” and there enumerates τοὺς ἀμφὶ τὸν Δωρόθεον βασιλικοὺς παῖδας, that is, the chamber-servants or similar persons over whom Dorotheus presided. Although they had been adorned by the emperors with the prerogative of the highest honour, and were loved by them no less than sons, they nevertheless chose to suffer indignities and tortures for the Christian religion. Soon after, he says that Dorotheus and Gorgonius were strangled.

And receive at last a thought which came to me while writing this. If you approve it, the entire dispute would plainly be removed. In chapter 6, as I have said, he mentions βασιλικοὺς παῖδας, the prince’s chamber-servants; and it will be for you to judge whether in chapter 1, instead of ἐπὶ πᾶσι, one ought to write ἐπὶ παῖσι ἀρχόντων, “rulers over servants,” with βασιλικοῖς, “imperial,” most conveniently understood from the preceding word. Since in chapter 7 he follows the same order, first recounting the steadfastness and martyrdoms of the βασιλικοὶ παῖδες, then of their own prefects Dorotheus and Gorgonius, and finally of Bishop Anthimus, I am increasingly confirmed in this opinion. I think that Gorgonius also held a prefecture in the palace, and perhaps was the father or grandson of the Gorgonius who, in the time of Constantius Augustus, according to Ammianus Marcellinus, XV.2, was likewise so called and was entrusted with the care of the Caesarian bedchamber.

For there were two chiefs of the sacred bedchamber, one for the Augustus and one for the Augusta, as appears from law V of the Code *On the Chiefs of the Sacred Bedchamber*; and Dorotheus and Gorgonius may have been adorned with both dignities. Yet I shall not dispute it if anyone thinks they held other offices in the palace; indeed, I shall entirely acquiesce if this conjecture displeases anyone—for I have nowhere else set down my emendations.

These are the matters, most distinguished sir, which I wished to communicate to you. It will now be yours to judge whether they are worthy of my leisure, and consequently of yours. Farewell most heartily.

The Hague, 15 July 1689.

Gisbert Cuper sends greetings to the most distinguished Voetius.

[Col. 0583C] What I often predicted would happen if Lactantius remained longer in the hands of the printers has now occurred. Here, then, is another note which the printer may easily insert somewhere among the others, if only you judge it worthy, most distinguished sir, of being made public.

Chapter 12. “He set out for the church while the light was still uncertain.” I observed that Christians first assembled in private houses; later, when emperors indulged and tolerated them, they built spacious houses in which they worshipped Christ our Lord, as it were publicly and openly. Eusebius, VIII.1, writes that, because of the countless multitude of believers, Christians were not content τοῖς παλαιοῖς οἰκοδομήμασι, “with the old buildings,” but built ἐκκλησίας εὐρείας εἰς πλάτος ἀνὰ πάσας τὰς πόλεις ἐκ θεμελίων, “spacious churches in breadth, from the foundations, throughout all the cities.” He adds that in the course of time these grew daily greater and better, no one begrudging them. Thus by παλαιὰ οἰκοδομήματα, “old buildings,” we may quite suitably understand private houses, or at least Christian meeting-places which differed in nothing from private dwellings; while by ἐκκλησίας εὐρείας εἰς πλάτος, “spacious churches in breadth,” we may understand larger structures, not so much long as broad and ample, in which almost anyone could know that Christians worshipped their God.

Lampridius, in my opinion, speaks of this kind of building in the *Life of Alexander Severus*, chapter 49: “When the Christians had occupied a certain place which had been public, and the tavern-keepers claimed in opposition that it ought to belong to them, he replied that it was better for God to be worshipped there in whatever manner than for it to be given over to tavern-keepers.” For although no clear mention is made of a building, it is nevertheless highly probable that Christians had constructed a meeting-place in that location, since by the emperor’s indulgence they could assemble without fear. From this we learn that Christians then had places where they assembled freely, and which lay open to all eyes.

Indeed, someone might think that this had been granted them even under Hadrian, because the same Lampridius, chapter 43 of the same emperor’s life, speaks thus:

> He wished to make a temple to Christ and receive him among the gods. Hadrian too is said to have contemplated this; he ordered temples to be built in every city without statues, which today are therefore called HADRIAN’S, because they contain no divinities. It was said that he had prepared these for this purpose.

Since Hadrian entertained this intention, as the great scholar P. Daniel Huetius proves at length in his *Evangelical Preparation*, it is not unreasonable to suppose that he favoured Christians and allowed them, as it were, to worship and adore Christ openly.

Scholars also believe, relying on Eusebius, III.37, that churches were built under Emperor Trajan. “At the same time Quadratus flourished, who is recorded as having been distinguished by prophetic grace together with the daughters of Philip. Besides these, several others also flourished at the same time, holding the chief place among the successors of the apostles: οἵ καὶ ἅτε τηλικῶνδε ὄντες θεοπρεπεῖς μαθηταὶ, τοὺς κατὰ πάντα τόπον τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν παρακαταβληθέντας ὑπὸ τῶν Ἀποστόλων θεμελίους ἐπῳκοδόμουν.” That is: “Being admirable and truly divine disciples of such great men, they built upon the foundations of churches which the apostles had previously laid in various places.”

Roman Catholics employ this argument to prove the antiquity of various churches. But, considering Trajan’s times, it seems to me wholly improbable that Eusebius could have had such a thing in mind. Trajan did not wish hetaeriae—associations, societies, or corporations—to be established in cities, because factions were everywhere stirred up by them, as appears from Pliny’s *Letters*, book X, letters 42 and 43. Christian assemblies fell into the same category, because the pagans too had sacred colleges devoted to a particular divinity; consequently Pliny, and doubtless other governors as well, forbade them to meet. For after, in Letter 98, he had related that Christians sang a hymn to Christ as to a god, bound themselves by an oath not to commit robbery or adultery, and then took ordinary and harmless food, he adds: “They had ceased to do even this after my edict, by which, in accordance with your commands, I had forbidden hetaeriae.”

Further, structures of that kind, [Col. 0584C] or churches, are opposed by the fact that Christians were accustomed to assemble on a fixed day before dawn, as the same Secundus says, and by Emperor Trajan’s decree that Christians were not to be sought out, but, if denounced and convicted, were to be punished. Since pagans pursued Christians with the utmost hatred and omitted no opportunity of accusing them, they could surely have done this most conveniently if Christians had assembled, as it were, before the eyes of cities. Nor do I think so poorly of the prudence and piety of the early Christians as to believe they knowingly and willingly exposed themselves to the gravest dangers.

Moreover, ancient monuments teach us, and the condition of the times itself confirms, that the faithful assembled in private houses, upper rooms, porticoes, crypts, and cemeteries. Indeed, whether temples or churches existed even in the third century is still disputed; on this question one may consult the exceptionally learned Frederick Spanheim, *Ecclesiastical History*. In short, I am persuaded that Eusebius’s translator, and those who follow him, most distinguished men though they are, did not understand the Greek words. For Eusebius is not speaking about buildings. He recounts that those successors of the apostles who were alive built upon foundations laid by the apostles for the churches; that is, they strengthened Christians’ faith, made many Christians, and enlarged their congregation or ἐκκλησία, “church.”

This manner of speaking is taken from the Apostle Paul, Ephesians II.20: Ἐποικοδομηθέντες ἐπὶ τῷ θεμελίῳ τῶν Ἀποστόλων καὶ Προφητῶν, ὄντος ἀκρογωνιαίου αὐτοῦ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ: “built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone.” In this sense ἐποικοδομέω, “to build upon,” and οἰκοδομή, “building,” are frequently used in the New Testament. Thus I am surprised that this did not occur even to the most penetrating Valesius.

Yet, although this is so, Roman Catholics nevertheless think and affirm that churches were constructed under Domitian and Trajan, works of a scale like those we see today. Minucius Felix speaks thus in the *Octavius*: “Why, indeed, do they labour so greatly to conceal and hide whatever it is that they worship? Honourable things always rejoice in public; crimes are secret. Why do they have no altars, no temples, no recognizable images?”

Upon these words the learned man who recently wrote on the true Christian origin of the Senones remarks, p. 40:

> “That these things were true in his time, insofar as public assemblies are concerned, when all things burned against Christians with slaughter and fire, I do not doubt at all. But after Nero and Domitian, under whom we place the era of the inauguration of the Church of Sens, dedicated to Christ by Savinian’s blood, had perished, and when affairs were for a time peaceful, no one can doubt that, following the imperial edicts mentioned above, Christians emerged from hiding-places and crypts, in which they were permitted to conceal themselves for reverence for their sacred rites and for their own protection, and erected churches of varied construction, or basilicas known to everyone, for their public use.”

Several things are to be noted here.

I. First, the period in which Minucius is said to have lived. His date is uncertain. The very learned Dodwell, p. 35 of his dissertation on Cyprian, thinks that he wrote toward the end of Marcus Antoninus’s reign. Balduinus places him later than Alexander Severus; Cardinal Bellarmine thinks he flourished under that emperor. But apart from that learned man, no one has been found who assigns him to the times of Domitian or Nero. For unless this is his meaning, I do not see how he can argue thus: in his own time Caecilius or Minucius truly says that Christians had no temples because emperors raged against the innocent people with persecutions; but after those emperors Nero and Domitian had died, this was no longer true because churches were being built. Further, if the Church of Sens was inaugurated under Domitian, and if Minucius wrote at that time, it follows that Minucius himself was mistaken when he reports that Christians under that same emperor had no temples or churches—for, to this learned man, these are the same thing—so incoherent are these claims.

II. He cautiously adds, “insofar as public assemblies are concerned,” so that he might silently impose upon us images and statues in that century. Yet it is altogether certain that Christians then knew nothing of them. Nor do I doubt that pagans would have dealt more mildly with Christians if they had worshipped statues, or possessed them for memorial purposes. Indeed, it would have been in Christians’ interest not to hide images, but to seek pagan favour through them. The pagans would readily have admitted them and allowed images to be worshipped publicly, because they would have imagined them similar to statues of their own gods, although worshipped in another manner and without incense being cast upon altars.

III. The Church of Sens could not have been inaugurated under Domitian, because Christians, as I have just proved, then assembled in private houses, and later in buildings either not at all, or only slightly, different from private dwellings. From the congregation of Christians meeting in them they called these ἐκκλησίας, “churches”; from the same congregation and their form, ἐκκλησιῶν οἴκους, “houses of churches”; and from their prayers, προσευκτηρίων οἴκους, “houses of prayer.” Later, when Christians enjoyed a freer life, they built basilicas. They did this, indeed, when leading men of abundant wealth embraced Christianity. They could do so without exciting pagan resentment, because the leading men among pagans also adorned their houses with basilicas, as Alexander Donatus teaches, and because people were accustomed to meet in basilicas.

For basilicas were magnificent buildings supported by many columns and having flat roofs. In them merchants not only sold their wares; judicial proceedings were also held, and perhaps recitations were sometimes given. I do not know why, but I greatly like to explain Juvenal, *Satires* I, in this way:

> Fronto’s plane trees and the shattered marbles  
> Ever cry aloud, and columns broken by the incessant reader.

[Col. 0586A] Though a portico may also be understood, anyone willing to consider how well suited private basilicas were to this purpose will, I hope, judge that it is not unreasonable to turn to them. However this may be, it is certain that public—and perhaps also private—basilicas always contained a great crowd of people, whether they were walking there, holding conversations, or doing something else. Hence, I think, Christians also met in them.

Ammianus Marcellinus, XXVII.3: “It is established that in the basilica of Sicininus, where there is an assembly for Christian worship, one hundred and thirty-seven corpses of those killed were found in one day.” This basilica was undoubtedly built by a certain Sicininus and perhaps joined to his house. There Christians could assemble even during persecution, under the pretext of doing something else, and sing a hymn to Christ. Others call it the Basilica of Liberius, not so much because Pope Liberius built a church there, as Valesius supposes, but because he converted it into a church. The former manner of speaking implies a new building; the latter does not.

That this was done appears from the Acts of Serotinus cited by Hugh Mathoud: “The noble man’s parents and relatives built over him, with marvellous workmanship, a basilica of beautiful construction, which the blessed bishop Potentian afterward consecrated as a church in memory of the martyr.” From this I think I may affirm that Christians first made basilicas, as public or private buildings, in places where martyrs had been buried, because it was permissible to adorn a city with works of that kind. These same basilicas were afterwards converted into churches, and they possess the name *basilica* from other works bearing the same name, not because they were dedicated to Christ, King of Heaven, as some suppose.

Since Roman basilicas were flat-roofed, as is clear from a coin of Lepidus inscribed *AEMILIA N. BASILICA, M. LEPIDUS REFECIT*, “New Aemilian Basilica: M. Lepidus restored [it],” and another of Trajan with the inscription *S. P. Q. R. OPTIMO PR. BASILICA ULPIA*, “The Senate and People of Rome [to the] best prince: Ulpian Basilica,” together with representations of those basilicas, as well as from Vitruvius, book V, chapter 1, and other authors, Christian basilicas undoubtedly had the same form. Pitched roofs could be placed on them when they were made into churches, so that Christians might imitate pagan temples and their splendour.

IV. Because Christians met either in private houses or in meeting-places which, externally considered, differed in no way from private houses, while pagan temples were extremely splendid, Caecilius therefore says that Christians had no temples. Temples and meeting-places are contrasted. Thus nothing prevents Christians from having assembled freely when this was written; Minucius need not be assigned to Nero’s or Domitian’s age. Thus Galerius, in Eusebius VIII.17, calls them οἴκους ἐν οἷς συνήγοντο, “houses in which they assembled”; Lactantius, chapter 48, “places to which they had been accustomed to assemble”; Lactantius himself, *Institutes* V.11, Arnobius, and others, call them *conventicula*, “meeting-places.” The Fathers frequently contrast temples and churches, assigning the former to pagans and the latter to Christians, as scholars have shown.

V. The cited imperial edicts contribute little to the argument. Those of Maximian were composed and promulgated long after the learned man supposes the Church of Sens to have been founded—and indeed at a time when Christians beyond doubt had spacious and conspicuous buildings, as is clear from Lactantius, and perhaps basilicas too.

These reflections, most distinguished sir, came into my mind; and I thought that I ought to communicate them to you, as one greatly devoted to refined studies. Farewell.

The Hague, 19 November 1679.

## Notes of Paul Baudri on the Book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*

[Col. 0587]

## Preface

[Col. 0587A] At last, learned reader, here is a new edition of the little book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, which you may rightly say has progressed with tortoise-like steps. How long it has been since it was begun matters little to know; many places in the work do not conceal the fact. Yet I shall say boldly that scarcely had I begun when I should gladly, had I been able, have obeyed Horace’s counsel: “Keep it back until the ninth year.”

Nor was this my only reason: it concerned the first offspring of my intellect, which above all others ought not rashly to be brought into the light. I had also observed that it is arduous to begin, and difficult besides lest those who hurry let various things escape which might better be recast at leisure. I myself often experienced this in the course of this edition, as printers pressed me contrary to expectation and desire.

Above all, there was the fact that the book which I had undertaken, so far as my powers allowed, to elucidate contained many exceedingly obscure passages here and there. Like other passages of that sort, I am accustomed to compare them with the darkest caverns, in which those who enter at first see nothing, but eventually see more or less if they remain longer and patiently inspect with attentive eyes. I do not wish to boast that, by such slow reflection, I have struck the mark, as they say, or, to speak more plainly, that I have successfully perceived what lies hidden in such great darkness. Away with it! We very seldom claim so much for ourselves. But even if I did not succeed, and accordingly the familiar line must more often be used:

> Either he sees, or thinks he sees the moon through clouds,

I nevertheless wished, diligent reader, to succeed for your sake and my own. Even if no certain hope of a favourable outcome existed, still, because of Peter’s example—who, as his most devout companion John testifies in the Gospel, chapter XX, saw more in Christ’s tomb than John, who had run ahead—there seemed no danger in delay. All the more because, when I seemed frequently to have abandoned this edition, I happened, while engaged upon another matter (for, lest you not know it, we have also very often, and, as friends partly know, seriously turned aside to other pursuits), to come unexpectedly upon confirmations or explanations of Caecilius’s narrative. But we linger too long among the old hindrances.

That this is a golden work, to which so many writings contained in this volume have been devoted, has been acknowledged almost without exception not only by all who have written, but also by all who have read it. And rightly so: both the matters, which are of the highest importance, and the author’s style, which is almost always polished and elegant, speak for it. But among all testimonies, the preface to the first Oxford edition is now especially notable, because it embraces in one sweep most matters relevant to the subject. We shall therefore reproduce it somewhat more fully:

> “We present our Lactantius’s book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, to be valued above gold, which, having been desired for more than a thousand years, we have very recently recovered through the zeal of the most learned Baluze. Mutilated and frequently gaping with lacunae, we have in part restored it from our own conjectures and in part from those of the most learned men, the Bishop of Asaph and Isaac Vossius. By means of this treatise, we are at last freed from the inveterate error concerning St Peter’s twenty-five-year pontificate. Moreover, we distinguish the sequence and dates of persecutions in the Church, and erase and reject the fictitious martyrdoms hitherto attributed to Diocletian before his eighth consulship. Finally, we now for the first time grasp the state of the Roman Empire during those dreadful times, historically narrated; and we understand that the purple which we vainly believed had been laid aside willingly by tyrants was surrendered reluctantly and not without tears.”

Here, beyond the book’s golden value and serious estimate of its worth, you see above all what we have said: that it was unequivocally assigned to Lactantius, the most polished writer of the third and fourth centuries, by the former most reverend Bishop of Oxford, John Felles, author of the preface. You see next how miserable the condition of that excellent product was once, even down almost to these times, in most copies; third, into what fortunate and skilled healing hands it at last came; and lastly, what remarkable matters it briefly contains.

As for us, and insofar as it is possible here to deal with matters which we have discussed elsewhere in their appropriate places, or of which it will be more fitting to speak shortly, we do indeed believe, because of Jerome’s authority cited in the note on the title, but especially because of the index we have begun to compile for our own use of words, phrases, and subjects shared by this author and Lactantius, that no one can be more suitably assigned the book than Lactantius. Yet, because of other matters which we have noted on that same title, we do not dare to put the question securely beyond every possibility of doubt.

But as to the old error just mentioned concerning St Peter’s long pontificate, and the claim that the intervention of the work before us finally freed us from it, it is worthwhile to relate what most recently happened to me. In his technical chronology, under the year of Christ 33, the industrious Philip Labbe assigns, in precisely so many syllables, the eclipse of the sun remembered by the three Evangelists Matthew, Mark, and Luke (Matt. XXVII.45; Mark XV.33; Luke XXIII.44) to 3 April of that year, as will be apparent to anyone consulting the passage. Likewise, in this very work, the most distinguished Toinard expressly maintains that Christ was crucified in year 33 of the common era, on the fourteenth day of Nisan, or 3 April.

Three days ago, believing that I could not fully regain the health lost through a very serious illness nearly three months previously if I lacked useful reading, I began to inquire which ancient author had joined the reported darkness with 3 April and at the same time with the death of Jesus Christ: whether pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite; or his commentator Maximus; or his paraphrast Pachymeres; or Phlegon, Hadrian’s freedman; or Eusebius and Philogonus, who cited Phlegon on the subject; or Methodius and Metaphrastes, who wrote Dionysius’s life; and so on through all who could come to mind or hand under any name.

But why say more? What I alone sought, I have so far been unable to discover anywhere. Yet what I sought concerning Peter’s first arrival in the city I found, contrary to expectation, in the martyrdom of Dionysius the Areopagite by Methodius—or, as others prefer, Methrodorus—and, according to the very interpretation of the Jesuit Peter Lansselius, as follows:

> “In the eight hundred and eighth year after the founding of Rome, when Nero Caesar, the fifth from Augustus, had gained the empire, the blessed apostle Peter, sent with the other apostles to preach the Gospel to the whole world, came. After many years of preaching, when the city of Rome had been taken and selected as his principal seat, he received there a divine commission to preach, in order that, having become as it were the summit and chief of the holy apostles in the order of apostolic office, he might be the first at Rome to become a companion and participant in the sufferings which Christ had endured. For that city, as it was involved in great errors, so needed greater remedies in order to be corrected, so that where error was most grievous, grace also might abound most greatly. Then the tyrant and impious Nero, hoping that he would subject land and sea to his tyranny, driven by the frenzy of his cruelty and the force of madness into fury, burned against Christ’s servants, and in the fourteenth year of his tyrannical reign condemned the blessed Peter and Paul to an unjust death.”
