This passage, which as other matters often do elsewhere, not only unexpectedly and remarkably confirms that the apostle Peter came to Rome when Nero was already reigning, as will be set forth below in chapter two, but clearly shows that we could have done without this little book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* in rejecting the contrary opinion, since we could already have condemned it by following Methodius. For if, according to Methodius, the apostle Peter, after Nero had already begun to reign, was sent with the other apostles to preach the Gospel throughout the world, and was beheaded at Rome only in Nero’s fourteenth year, after proclaiming Christian truth elsewhere for many years, how could he have served as bishop of Rome for more than about six or seven years? We come nearer to the point.

Many think that when some new work of the ancients, such as ours, is to be printed from a single manuscript codex which is not entirely sound, it should be published in every respect just as it stands written, lest the truth of the matter be concealed from anyone in any degree, or publication of readings in the author’s words where errors and lacunae occur make it less possible to think of new solutions. Otherwise, as the great Johannes Friedrich Gronovius declared in nearly these very words (*Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 8, p. 72), signs suitable for restoring the text and the author’s true hand will be lacking, and often better conjectures will not be capable of being proposed by others in place of earlier ones.

His words are:

> “Although I do not praise bold conjectures by which some have transformed ancient writing too greatly, and though it is safest to adhere to the manuscripts, nevertheless, if they offer anything harsh, rough, or thorny, I do not dislike that so much, because I know it certainly belongs to Minucius”—for he is speaking of Minucius Felix’s dialogue against pagans—“as because I do not despair that it can more easily be drawn out from what was the author’s own. For ancient codices are not without even monstrous errors; and our position is excellent when the signs for restoration and for the author’s genuine hand are sufficiently plain and certain. The rest will be supplied by a divine mind, by the greatest devotion to learning, and by a thoroughly known writer’s character and nature.”

And what he immediately adds:

> “In what is ours, I admit, it happens very often that we, whoever pursue these studies above the common level, are mistaken. Yet meanwhile we discover many splendid things. And just as of old one colleague generally mitigated the unfair censures of another censor, and another tribune helped against a tribune threatening force in the exercise of veto: so, if we have reconstructed anything badly, there arises and comes forth from this very order someone to correct our errors. Finally, time accomplishes the matter: what is not today will be tomorrow; thus life is driven onward.”

These words, I say, ought so far from discouraging us from faithfully reproducing ancient books like ours with all their faults that they make it more necessary for them to be reproduced openly. Since I thought exactly the same, I had believed that this little work could not be better communicated by my care to learned men than by being printed as closely as possible to the old exemplar. For that reason I restored to their places every reading which the first and most distinguished editor, Baluze, stated in his notes that he had rejected as corrupt; otherwise it was not permissible to consult the manuscript codex preserved at Paris.

But why delay? Such authority over another’s work was not granted to one requesting it by letter. Therefore, as regards the author’s text, we now reproduce for you above all the Paris edition pure and simple as it first appeared, altered only in those places which Baluze himself changed. Do not therefore, when—for example—near the beginning of the book you find freshly printed, on that most learned man’s correction, *qui adversati erant Deo, jacent*, “those who had opposed God lie fallen,” instead of the manuscript reading *qui illustrati erant Deo, jacent*, “those who had been enlightened by God lie fallen,” attribute the matter to any cause other than that which we have stated. Now concerning the notes.

As may be seen throughout the work, countless notes are quite short, or at least not so long that they could not conveniently be placed beneath what is called the text. On the other hand, there were other notes, not at all few, to which the same place could not be assigned: either because they were more extensive philological excursuses; or because, though they closely examined some difficulty of the author, they were themselves also rather long; or finally because it seemed easy to form from individual such discussions, or from several together, Caecilian dissertations after the model of the Cyprianic dissertations and Dodwell’s *On Ripa Striga*, in the prolegomena and especially in the second part of the book.

But for this to be done, three great bodies of work had to be cut into portions and fragments, without the approval of the most weighty authorities, nor, I think, of the authors themselves had they been alive: namely, the notes of the most learned Baluze, Cuper, and Colomiès. Therefore, changing our plan, we handed them over to the printers to be printed, each whole as far as possible—for the most distinguished Cuper had already separated his own notes from those of Colomiès. This was done so that, from all these, from Dodwell’s dissertation *On Ripa Striga*, and from all similar writings which might later be found—and such as in fact later appeared at Paris in 1690: the notes of the most distinguished Toinard on our little book, and the preface of the most learned Ruinart to the *Acts of the Martyrs*, described by him as genuine and selected—not only might the latter part of this edition be constituted, but also that in the first volume those items first published in it might be arranged in their proper order and fitting relation, which the French call, by a special name, *des renvois* [cross-references].

We did not then fail to know what a great harvest of such material would later arise. But beyond our already stated resolve always to preface something, where space permitted, lest the work be too dry or tedious—hence things of no great weight have sometimes been prefixed—we wished you, in reading the first part of the work, to be able quickly and easily, if you wished or the matter required, to read at the same time, for example, the learned notes bearing upon the course of the little book or upon the same passages of the author.

The most learned observations which today we publish together for the first time are recommended not merely by their old value. This additional new weight accrues to them: as commonly happens in second editions, the most learned men Baluze, Cuper, and Toinard have greatly enlarged their own contributions, whether by adding new annotations, revising old ones, or finally arranging them differently, as will become clear to those who compare them. For who could now indicate all these matters to you better?

In the second part we have gathered everything that remained to be placed beneath the text, whether conceived in different ways for the understanding of the author, or otherwise relevant to it. These are, first, the materials which the most learned and at the same time most friendly men Johann Georg Graevius—illustrious father of so many weighty and exquisite studies—and Elias Boherellus, from whom one might deservedly expect distinguished work every day, drew from their own stores at our request; next, those which we received, most kindly procured for us by our Boherellus while he was still living in England from the most distinguished Thomas Gale, Peter Allix, and Paul Colomesius, and for the most part laboriously copied out [Col. 0591A]; third, all the little notes which Colomesius likewise transcribed with his own hand, with the greatest care, from the margins of Vossius’s copy, and again sent to us through the same friend in his kindness; then those which, sooner or later, we obtained from the most learned men Jacob Tollius and the Abbé de Saint-Hilaire, canon of Beauvais, through the kindness of the most obliging Toinard or the efforts of our bookseller; finally, whatever we ourselves were able to contribute by our own exertions and from the already published works of others.

And indeed, since, both in themselves and because of their added notes, the three English editions could by no means be passed over, and since likewise two highly praised translations stood out for such material—the French one of the most distinguished Maucroix, canon of Rheims, and the English one of Gilbert Burnet, now the Right Reverend Bishop of Salisbury—as well as, lastly, Dodwell’s most learned Cyprianic dissertations and Pagi’s very learned *Criticism of Baronius’s Annals*, containing much that could most conveniently be referred to particular passages of the following little work [Col. 0591B], what else, I ask you, was to be expected in a book of this kind than that you should repeatedly see those works cited or excerpted? We hasten to the remaining matters.

We do not deny that our dissertation on the Ripa Striga, the preface to the *Acts of the Martyrs*, and, moreover, every individual passage which we have excerpted in so many places from Dodwell and Pagi, were published by us without consulting their most distinguished authors. But, in short, we did not think it at all unfair or discourteous to reprint and collect, even without the knowledge of those who had published them, many things which had already separately entered the public domain and bore upon our subject in whatever way—even though learned men may sometimes have clashed rather sharply with one another; for thus it will sometimes appear more clearly where the truth lies or is hidden. Nor do I think it should go unmentioned that the principal advocate of reprinting the preface was the eminent Cuper, who unexpectedly called the printer’s attention to the matter, for a fuller investigation of the truth.

We had almost given it the title [Col. 0591C] *On the Multitude of Martyrs*, chiefly because—owing to the deliberate suppression in their proper places of certain passages in which Ruinart gave a particular account of his latest edition of the *Acts of the Martyrs*—there would remain only what served with all its strength to establish the multitude of martyrs. But lest the plan of that preface should seem to have been rashly interpolated by us, its old title was retained; nor, I can honestly say, was anything at all removed from the entire work except that harsh appellation, “heretic”—the subject of controversy among learned men and, at the least, among members of both parties—by which Ruinart several times wished to stigmatize his opponent; in its place we substituted, more humanely, the certain and inoffensive designation “most learned,” or something of that kind.

Receive, then, in this manner, together with the noble monument of a most ancient Father of the Church, the fullest collection of all things that in any way pertained to it. And if, because of the many delays that intervened, you think no diligence in this matter deserves mention [Col. 0591D], hear at least further how faithfully we have wished to render to each his due.

First of all, since the observations of the first part which we received from others did not all come into our hands at once, but some sooner and some later, we placed the earlier ones here and there in the earlier position, unless by chance they were criticisms of the later ones. Next, we copied out every item that had to be transcribed from whatever source with such care that we omitted not even the circumflexes on ablatives and the grave accents on adverbs whenever we saw learned writers had used them; but we added none whenever, on the contrary, they had been omitted by them together with Johann Friedrich Gronovius (*Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 14, p. 152 ff.), as matters fit for beginners, children, or even old women. We thus preserved each person’s own manner of writing, even though this exactness generally made two utterly different and wholly incompatible kinds of orthography visible in this book. Then again, we also carefully appended the names of authors to their notes whenever possible [Col. 0592A]. Finally, because none of the three English editions made sufficiently clear which parents ought rather to be acknowledged by the little notes printed at the foot of almost every page, we named the editions themselves as parents of the notes.

This is all the more so because, although in the earlier Oxford edition, the mother of the other English editions, the above-mentioned Right Reverend author of the preface had simply written that he had, from time to time, restored Lactantius’s book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*—as badly mutilated and often gaping with lacunae—partly by his own conjectures and partly by those of the most learned Bishop of St Asaph and Isaac Vossius, he not only did not carefully distinguish, for example, his own conjectures from Vossius’s, but also, contrary to all expectation, mixed in several of Spark’s, as could easily be proved; indeed, he also included quite a number, as I have legitimate reason to suspect, of Gale’s, since in Gale’s transcript, with which that distinguished man favored us through our Boherellus, we found not a few deleted in no other manner than people customarily reject their own work. Add that the Cambridge edition [Col. 0592B], though it contains more little notes than the two Oxford editions, has an anonymous editor, or is *adespoton* (without an acknowledged master).

For the rest, I know that, however great our scrupulousness may have been in these matters, we shall doubtless appear insufficiently scrupulous in passages where we have so often attempted to render Caecilius’s words suspect, or to call into question and overthrow the conjectures and opinions of others by putting forward and supporting our own as best we can. But I shall say it in a word: as in religion, following the example of the earliest Christians, we are not devotees of the cross [Note: [Col. 0592D]

See Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 16. Tertullian does not say that Christians are not devotees of the cross; he says that they are thought such—“he who thinks us devotees of the cross”—and does not refute this, but explains it.

]; so neither are we devotees of crosses in authors. And as in religion we pursue truth above all things, so also always in critical studies and the sciences. Imitate us, even at the cost of undoing our work, if we have erred. For our own views are not oracles to ourselves, and we must all sacrifice to truth alone. And as we have often, when opportunity arose, freely and candidly reproved ourselves in this workshop, so we most willingly allow ourselves to be brought back by others from an erroneous path into the way, if candor and reason are kindly present in our study [Col. 0592C], and we rejoice greatly in it.

Indeed, trust that, if only you show, with superior authority or reason, why I have gone astray here or there, you will earn from me such gratitude as I would wish to earn from you, if—even merely because of the learned notes, in so great a number, partly recent and partly old, which we have collected and only now at last published—you could happily and safely on every side exclaim:

> One man, by delaying, restored the commonwealth to us.

But however much they may deserve esteem, how greatly one must fear that this task cannot be completed unless new manuscript codices are forthcoming! Farewell; and while, I hope, we undertake better things, take courage, if you can. For just as we do not preface certain matters whose explanation is easy to divine, so neither, I say again, do we wish all our own work to be considered highly commendable; and we shall always love to follow what we see and approve as better. Moreover, to our own notes or longer observations we do not append our name. Instead, a cross-sign is commonly prefixed [Col. 0592D]; for printers have omitted it in very many places.

[EPISTLE.]

To the most illustrious and most reverend man, Lord EMMANUEL DE SCHELSTRATE, canon of the Church of St Peter and first keeper of the Vatican Library, JACOB TOLLIUS sends greetings.

The praise owed to your distinguished studies and your consummate learning in ecclesiastical history, most illustrious and reverend sir, I shall defer to a more convenient time and a fitter opportunity. For the present, in a few words, I shall only show that my mind remembers your merits. For I willingly profess that I owe very much to your most generous humanity and kindness; but I am greatly grieved that I am unable to return to you [Col. 0593A], or to my other friends—whose most abundant and warmly disposed affection toward me I experienced on my journey through Italy—the deserved thanks, and thanks as great as I wish. But I shall attend to these matters later.

To your name, however, most illustrious and reverend sir, I wished to dedicate this, whatever it is, of my little notes on Lactantius’s *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*; although [Col. 0594A] they are scarcely worthy to come before your eyes. They are hurried and occasional works, briefly written without books, to oblige a bookseller friend. Yet I believe that they will please, because they are mine. For you love me; and I ask that you make that love perpetual. Farewell. Given at Amsterdam, 30 November 1688.

[Col. 0593]

PAUL BAUDRI’S NOTES [Note: [Col. 0593D]

It should be noted that Paul Baudri, to whom these notes belong, adhered to the Reformed religion and therefore cited passages of Holy Scripture according to Reformed versions.]

[Col. 0593A] *Lucius Caecilius.* The Colbert manuscript reads somewhat differently. For it has not *Caecilii* with *ae*, as Columbus incorrectly printed, but *Cecilii* with simple *e*, as the distinguished Baluze expressly stated, having seen it with his own eyes. Accordingly, on the first page of this edition and thereafter in these notes, partly for the sake of a certain scrupulous simplicity, partly so that those who wish may more readily deny this work to Lactantius, and finally because the spelling *Cecilii* with simple *e*, supplied by the ancient parchment, may perhaps not be such as should give rise to printing *Caecilii* with a diphthong.

Certainly the rhetorician Longinus, who first wrote *On the Sublime* (*Peri Hypsous*), is continually called Κεκίλιος, “Cecilius,” not Καικίλιος, “Caecilius.” And in every one of the many passages where he occurs, the Latin translator—whom the distinguished Tanaquil Faber, a man, if anyone ever was, of the keenest discernment, preferred to other translators—carefully rendered him *Cecilius* without a diphthong, not *Caecilius* with the first diphthong. And, to press the point further, in Dio Cassius, Book XLII, Κεκίλιος ὁ Μάρκος, “Marcus Cecilius,” is likewise the name of that Roman praetor who first of all dared to resist τοῖς τοῦ Καίσαρος, “Caesar’s interests,” as he puts it—not Καικίλιος, “Caecilius.” Yet in that passage, and always elsewhere, Dio wrote Καίσαρος, “Caesar’s,” from the Roman *Caesar*, not Κέσαρος; likewise, more than once, Αἰμίλιος, “Aemilius,” from their *Aemilius*, not Ἐμίλιος [Col. 0593C], and Αἴλιος, “Aelius,” from their *Aelius*, not Ἔλιος. Indeed, and most decisively, in Gruter’s inscriptions you will find Caecilia Progne, Caecilius Dexter, Caecilius Saturus, Caecilius Felix, and Quintus Caecilius, on Roman stones themselves, without a diphthong.

However this may be, the anonymous Cambridge editor followed neither spelling; but he changed both into *Caelii*, I think rather more confidently. I say this because two manuscripts, and not insignificant ones, formerly cited by Baluze, show that it is not unusual for Lactantius to be called *Caecilius*, not *Coelius*.

*Firmianus Lactantius.* Thus read the Paris, Oxford, and Åbo Latin editions, together with one or two translations. But all do so, if not somewhat too freely and incautiously, at least on mere conjectures. For in the old codex, says Baluze, the title of this work is stated simply thus: “The book of Lucius Cecilius to Donatus the confessor, on the Deaths of the Persecutors, begins.” If you do not see that reading at the head of this page as well, know that we are faithfully reproducing Baluze’s firstborn edition, so to speak, or rather that edition only insofar as he himself wished it to be modified by us. But the learned man sent us no alteration regarding the title. And as for that old Colbert leaf, we gave it above, wherever possible, so that it might not be banished altogether to the bad margins [Col. 0593D]. Now see Columbus, col. 389, but much more Baluze, col. 300, who gives a most learned account of various matters concerning Lactantius himself, his homeland, and the like.

*To Donatus the confessor.* For more on him, see chapter XVI of this book, Oxford and Cambridge editions. Correct—but there is still more at chapters 35 and 52. See also Baluze above, col. 301, and Columbus, col. 389. Indeed, both this Donatus’s piety before and after peace was restored to the Church, and Columbus’s observation on this part of the title, are relevant, lest we depart from the point even now. For today, as Columbus observed, those attached to the Roman pontiff call “confessors” persons who have been troubled by no storms of persecution whatever, yet who, as they maintain, are conspicuous above other mortals for holiness of life. But what the learned man did not mention is that the Church of that age wished those confessors of antiquity who had suffered affliction to be endowed with no lesser holiness either in the conflict or in peace; and for that reason it held out to them crowns to be obtained, either white through their work or purple through suffering and the perfection of virtue [Col. 0594B]. Those who have read Cyprian know what I mean; the blessed martyr’s own words will be transcribed later in a more suitable place.

Meanwhile, the very beginning and end of this little work proclaim that our Donatus, while he lived in the faith of Christ, was one of the holier confessors of the Church. Its beginning is: “The Lord has heard your prayers, dearest Donatus, which you pour out before him at every hour throughout the whole day.” Its almost final conclusion is: “You especially, dearest Donatus, who deserve to be heard by God, beseech the Lord.”

Moreover, if Beckius is to be heard in his *Martyrology of the German Church*, confessors in those times were properly Christians who, when questioned by a judge, had confessed Christ, yet had experienced neither prisons nor tortures, much less the punishment of death itself; thus they were called confessors solely from their confession of Jesus Christ. But this is stated too universally (*katholou*), and chapter 35 of this work plainly shows that the learned man is mistaken first about prisons. There our author says: “Then, when the prisons were opened, dearest Donatus, you were released from custody with the other confessors, though the prison had been your dwelling for six years.” Thus it is manifest, even if no other authorities were available, that confessors were sometimes thrown into custody.

Furthermore, Beckius is shown to have erred for the same reason concerning tortures, again by these words of the author: “But what need is there to recount those things, especially to you, dearest Donatus, who above the rest have experienced the storm of the turbulent persecution? … For nine times subjected to tortures and various sufferings, nine times you conquered the adversary by a glorious confession. … Neither blows, nor claws, nor fire, nor iron, nor the various kinds of tortures availed anything against you” [Col. 0594D]. Take care, therefore, whenever *confessor* or *confessors* are named in ancient books, not to understand them otherwise than the various circumstances (*peristaseis*) of matters, times, and persons require.

This is especially so because, beyond the three classes of ancient confessors easily gathered from the foregoing—the first, those simply questioned; the second, those thrown into prison; the third, those afflicted with tortures—the letters of Cyprian conveniently recall to our mind two further ranks of the same persons. One consists of those on whom judges formally imposed and inflicted the punishment of exile because they persisted in the confession of Christ; as happened very recently in our own country to so many of our most courageous brethren, whether preachers of the divine Word [Note: [Col. 0594D]

Or rather persecutors, at least in the Eucharist.]

or others: “I exult with joy and congratulate you, most courageous and blessed brethren, upon learning of your faith and virtue, in which Mother Church glories—and indeed recently gloried when, with confession persisting, she endured punishment that made confessors of Christ exiles” (Cyprian, Ep. 9) [Col. 0595A].

The other consists of those who were tested and proved not by judges but by God; that is, who were brought by divine providence to deliberate privately and before God whether they would abandon what was theirs or the Lord, or would rather follow the Lord and leave their own things behind. “We renounced the world when we were baptized; but now we have truly renounced the world, when, tested and proved by God, leaving all that is ours, we have followed the Lord and stand and live by faith and fear of him” (Cyprian, Ep. 7), written from his retreat, which he himself had chosen in order to withdraw from persecution in a similar manner.

*On the Deaths of the Persecutors.* See, by the complete agreement of all editions with the manuscript codex, what the subject of this book is. Except that in the Åbo edition, p. 78, Columbus introduces his notes thus: “Notes begin on the book of Lucius Coelius Lactantius Firmianus, *On Persecution, or On the Deaths of the Persecutors*,” evidently referring to those places in Jerome, Freculphus, and others where we read that Lactantius wrote one book, *On Persecution*. From this Columbus and the rest of the learned company at once did not hesitate to infer that this book’s title too had long ago simply been *On Persecution*, and that therefore the work itself cannot on this argument either be legitimately attributed to anyone other than Lactantius. But this is a rather weak defense.

Not every book *On Persecution* is immediately a book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*. For example, Tertullian’s book, which Jerome likewise cited in the same work as entitled *On Persecution*, does not discuss the deaths of persecutors by so much as a *gry* [a tiny amount], but expressly treats *On Flight in Persecution*—which is both its present title and its only title. Therefore, strictly speaking, nothing prevents Lactantius’s book *On Persecution*, mentioned a little later by Jerome himself, from having treated *On Flight in Persecution* too, with Tertullian; or *On the Causes of Persecutions*, or any other such subject that may come to mind—not at all the deaths of those who persecuted the Christian Church down to Constantine [Col. 0595B].

Nevertheless, far be it from me to undertake to maintain any one of these conjectures emphatically, still less to entertain each of them. I argue only that there is nothing in the words of Jerome and the others, “We have one book of Lactantius, *On Persecution*,” from which learned persons can clearly demonstrate what they wish concerning the genuine author of this book. Otherwise, just as we do not unwillingly concede that Lactantius was its author, so likewise we would not dare deny that the little work had two titles among the ancients. One, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, because it touched upon the manner in which most of the persecutors of the early Church ended their lives. The other, *On Persecution*, because of that persecution, so to speak, *kat’ exochēn*—the persecution par excellence, or ten-year persecution—upon which it particularly sought to discourse and which it narrates from chapter 20 through 52, the final chapter; indeed, it summarizes it in that last chapter in these words: “Let us celebrate the Lord’s victory with praises; let us honor it with daily and nightly prayers, that he may confirm forever the peace granted after ten years to his people.” Or rather, *On Persecution*, that is, on the various persecutions that arose against the earlier Christians down to the author’s own time [Col. 0595D]: in the same way in which *On Consolation* appears more than once in Seneca, likewise *On the Consolation of Philosophy* in Severinus Boethius, and *On Flight in Persecution* in Tertullian, and may most suitably be interpreted as *On Consolations* and *On Flights in Persecutions*.

Whatever the case, Baluze, col. 301, Cuper, col. 471, and Columbus, col. 390, teach by many examples how elegantly our author, following better writers, used *On Deaths*, a plural denoting multitude, in the former title. But what these most learned men, unless I am mistaken, forgot to observe is that the Greeks similarly said εἴκοσι θανάτους, “twenty deaths”; θανάτους ἀλλοκότους, “strange deaths”; ἐν θανάτοις πολλάκις, “often in deaths.” The Hebrews, moreover, say literally “deaths of sicknesses,” that is, most grievous sicknesses. Precisely as elsewhere it is certain that the Greeks used βίους, “lives,” and the Latins *vitas*, in a word of contrary meaning [Col. 0596A].

## CHAPTER ONE

“The Lord has heard your prayers.” It was a settled opinion of the ancient Christians—indeed, an entirely certain conviction—that whatever confessors and candidates for martyrdom asked from God would be granted. Hence our author at the end of this book says: “You especially, dearest Donatus, who deserve to be heard by God.” Therefore the Lapsed and others too employed them as intercessors; concerning this, several notable letters survive among Cyprian’s correspondence, and numerous examples occur in Ecclesiastical History.

As for the phrase, Horace likewise begins his address to Lyce in the same fashion:

> The gods have heard, Lyce, my prayers; the gods  
> Have heard, Lyce.

This belongs among the marks of an exulting spirit, whose joy it expresses most fully. TOLLIUS.—“The Lord has heard your prayers.” This manner of speaking has undoubtedly been drawn from common usage; or, if you prefer, from the whole Old Vulgate [Col. 0596B]. For why derive it rather from that clause in Maccabees, “May God hear your prayers and be reconciled to you,” as Columbus suspected, than from the innumerable expressions of this sort with which the sacred books are filled? For instance: “The Lord is far from the wicked, and he will hear the prayers of the righteous” (Prov. 15:29). Indeed, why not derive it specifically from Psalm 105, verse 44, where at the end, almost throughout as here, it says: “He heard their prayer”?

As to what that distinguished man just now asserted concerning the Lapsed—that they employed confessors most effectively as intercessors with God, and that some notable letters among Cyprian’s support this—letters 22, 13, and 14 of Pamelius’s edition strongly favor him, I do not deny.

The first does so because in it the confessor Lucianus, writing to Celerinus concerning peace granted to all the Lapsed at the command of the martyr Paul, says: “All whom the Lord has deigned to summon in so great a tribulation—we all, by common agreement, have granted peace to all.”

The second does so because likewise in it, according to the better editions of Cyprian, Cyprian himself, after the heading, “To the Clergy concerning the Lapsed and catechumens, lest they depart without communion,” says: “I think that provision must be made for our brethren”—speaking of the Lapsed—“so that those who have received certificates from martyrs and can be aided by their prerogative with God …” [Col. 0596C]

The last does so insofar as Cyprian also there, ending in almost exactly the same words and writing back to the clergy about those who were hastening toward peace, says: “Since you have indicated that some are immoderate, urgently demanding that communion be received quickly, and have desired that I give you a rule in this matter, I believe that I have written quite fully to you concerning this matter in the recent letter sent to you: that those who have received a certificate from martyrs and can be aided by their help with the Lord in their sins …”

But, to be brief, let learned scholars carefully consider whether those final two Cyprianic passages really support Tollius or only seem to do so. There are many reasons why, in my judgment, in both passages one should read *poscunt* (“request”) rather than *possunt* (“can be aided”), just as a little earlier there is *desiderastis dari* (“you desired [a rule] to be given”), and below *petierant dari* (“they had requested [it] to be given”), *postulastis dari* (“you requested [it] to be given”); this will shortly become clear. Cyprian is certainly speaking of certain Lapsed persons who had not merely received certificates from martyrs, but were immoderate and urgently demanding communion, or “hastening toward peace,” as the letter’s title puts it. Concerning them scarcely anything else seems to be determined than what we suggest: namely, that after their acts of apostasy they had, by every means, sooner or later obtained letters for themselves from martyrs or confessors, and then importunately demanded from bishops or other ministers of the Church and of divine reconciliation—to whom those letters were addressed—that through the aid of the martyrs or confessors who had written them they should be helped before the Lord in their sins. That is, that their denial might be forgiven through those persons’ prayers, and that they might at the same time be admitted to the holy Eucharist and to the peace of the faithful, coming in due time to the Lord with that peace [Col. 0597A]. This, then, the learned company must consider before all else.

Then, if they perhaps approve our corrections less, let those who are not very familiar with Cyprian’s text nevertheless beware of understanding Tollius’s words simply as they sound: that is, as though the Lapsed used confessors as intercessors with God, but not likewise with the governors of the Church. For the Lapsed also had recourse to confessors in order to receive their help before the latter. Nor did confessors entreat God alone for the Lapsed’ sake; they also entreated the sacred presidents (*proestōtas*) of the Church and of penitence.

Hence, in Cyprian’s letter to the martyrs and confessors who had requested that peace be given to the Lapsed—for that is the title of letter 11 in Pamelius’s edition—he says: “Since you have directed letters to me, in which you desired that your requests be examined and that peace be granted to certain Lapsed persons.” And again in letter 13, which we have just cited as written to the clergy concerning the Lapsed and catechumens, lest they leave without communion: “Since I see that there is not yet an opportunity of coming to you … I think provision must be made for our brethren … so that, after the hand has been laid upon them for penitence, they may come to the Lord with the peace which the martyrs, in letters written to us, desired to be given.”

Indeed, the aforementioned Lucianus, concluding his letter to Celerinus, says: “Therefore, brother, I ask that, when here the Lord begins to grant peace to the Church itself, according to Paul’s command and our arrangement, after the matter has been stated before the bishop and Numeria and Candida have made confession, they may have peace—not only these women, but also those whom you know concern our mind.” He is not obscurely asking that Celerinus ratify the peace which he himself, together with the remaining body of confessors, had already granted to Numeria and Candida. Thus confessors formerly interceded with bishops whenever time allowed, lest they seem of their own accord to invade the Church’s rights—even when peace had been granted to the Lapsed by confessors. This should be noted [Col. 0597B].

“Dearest Donatus.” Thus our author addresses this Donatus whenever he addresses him in this book, which he does four times. Compare chapters 16, 35, and 52. Nor should you forget that Lactantius likewise addresses as “dearest Donatus,” in chapter 22 of *On the Anger of God*, the Donatus to whom he dedicated that work. This too may, among other considerations, support the view that Lactantius is the author of this work.

“Who by a glorious confession have sought for themselves an everlasting crown, in accordance with the merits of their faith.” To this belong the final words of Lactantius’s *Epitome*: “that, with God as judge, he may attain, in accordance with the merits of his virtue, either the crown of faith or the reward of immortality.” GALE.

“By a glorious confession.” Not only did true glory return to confessors from that strength of spirit by which they despised the tortures tried in vain to shake their constancy; some also sought an empty and human glory, which Lucian wittily ridicules in Proteus. Our author uses the same expression in chapter 16: “Nine times you conquered the adversary by a glorious confession.” A glorious confession is opposed to one undertaken with great vehemence and ardor of mind, but without judgment and rashly, which afterward failed under tortures. Hence the sorrowful name of the Lapsed in the early Church, and the not insignificant example of Origen. It may also seem to be called “glorious” because through it Θεὸς ἐδοξάζετο, “God was glorified,” as in St John’s Gospel, 21:19. TOLLIUS.

That last explanation is indeed supported by Tertullian’s question: “How could martyrdoms occur for the glory of the Lord, if we compensated for the tax by procuring permission for the sect?” Not to adduce also from the same Tertullian this exhortation of the New Prophecy: “Do not desire to depart on beds, or in miscarriages and gentle fevers, but in martyrdoms, so that he who suffered for you may be glorified.” But, to say what is actually the case, I greatly doubt whether Caecilius’s phrase, “they have sought for themselves an everlasting crown,” means a confession glorious to God rather than to the confessors themselves. At least, the latter sense pleases me more.

And so, in my judgment again, our author below in chapter 16, and also Sulpicius Severus, Book II of the *Sacred History*, in these words: “At that time almost the whole world was drenched with the sacred blood of martyrs; for men rushed in rivalry into glorious contests, and martyrdoms were then sought by glorious deaths far more eagerly than bishoprics are now pursued by corrupt ambitions” [Col. 0598A]. This example seemed worth adducing above six hundred others also because the storm in which, according to Sulpicius Severus, men rushed in rivalry into glorious contests and sought martyrdoms by glorious deaths is the very one mentioned here: “The Lord has heard your prayers, dearest Donatus,” and those of our other brethren “who by a glorious confession,” and what follows. For these things truly belong to the recently concluded ten-year persecution of Diocletian; and immediately before the passage cited, the same author has: “After an interval of almost fifty years, under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, a most bitter persecution arose, which for ten continuous years devastated the people of God.” Thus, for our Caecilius and Sulpicius Severus, “glorious confession,” “glorious deaths,” and “glorious contests,” of which one speaks here and the other there, are plainly of the same time and meaning.

“In accordance with the merits of their faith.” Columbus, col. 390, tries altogether to remove the notion of merit from the meaning of this passage. How correctly he does so we shall examine elsewhere, God willing, and at length; for these words, together with the others to which they are connected, are truly notable for an honest understanding of several Ancients’ teaching on the reward and merits of good works.

“They have sought.” The Oxford and Cambridge editions read *quaesiverunt*, “they have sought”; but the change was unnecessary. The manuscript reading itself is also correct. Lactantius, *On the Blessed Life*, ch. 14: “They sought not immortality for themselves, but death for their sins and lusts.” Similarly, *quaesieris*, *quaesierat*, and *quaesisse* occur in approved authors, as does our author’s expression below, “when he had sought again with them.” As regards the sense, the translation of the Right Reverend Bishop of Salisbury reads, “who have acquired to themselves,” literally, “who acquired for themselves.” Excellent. For Caecilius does not say “who seek for themselves,” in the present tense, such that we should think of confessors still seeking [Col. 0598C]; but “who have sought for themselves,” in the past tense, such that we should think only of those who once sought and seek no longer—that is, those who have already acquired what they sought, at least in title. And that it is not contrary to this author’s practice to use the verb *quaerere* in the sense of “acquire” is attested by chapter 18, where he says of Diocletian: “But he said that it would be unbecoming if, after such splendor of the lofty summit, he fell into the darkness of a humble life, and less safe because in so long a reign he had sought for himself the hatreds of many.” Manifestly, for “had acquired,” as we shall establish in its place.

“Will be added.” Perhaps one should read *arcetur*, “is driven away.” See near the end: “May he drive away the assaults of the devil from his people.” In the same way here, “the adversary is driven away,” that is, the devil. Thus our Boherellus, a man worthy of every eminent encomium and indeed the delight of all learned and good persons who know him.

“The adversary is added to all these things.” This cannot be said of the pagans, of whom no mention has been made; rather, it must be referred to the prayers of Donatus and the other brethren, prayers which, having been heard, cause the adversary—that is, the devil—to be added by God, that is, restrained by divine grace and conquered through their prayers. Yet I would prefer to read here: “Behold, the adversary has been given,” or “handed over,” to all these persons. TOLLIUS.

“Behold, the adversary will be added to all these things.” I believe one should read: “Behold, with all these adversaries cast down.” ALLIX.

“Behold, he will be added.” I correct it: “He will be cut off,” that is, destroyed. Lactantius uses that word elsewhere in this sense. GALE.

What the learned man observes generally of the pagans—that no mention of them has been made in the whole preceding context of the book—is specifically true of the Persecutors also: they are not named even in the book’s title, such as some suppose is found in Jerome; for, as we saw above, it is simply *On Persecution*. Therefore I would not have learned readers refer this passage to them. It undoubtedly concerns the prayers of Donatus and persons like him. And nothing is more probable [Col. 0599A] than that, having once begun from the very frequent answering of their prayers—“The Lord has heard your prayers,” etc.—this author wished immediately to show in what matters they had been heard: “Behold, by all these things the adversary . . .” Would only Tollius have shown by some example that *addi*, “to be added,” or “the adversary to be added,” can mean “to be restrained and overcome”! Since he has produced none, we cannot but distrust his interpretation.

**“Will be added.”** This is the reading of the manuscript codex, followed by all the Latin editions except that of Åbo, where, whether deliberately or accidentally changing the tense, we find *additur*, “is added,” printed for *addetur*, “will be added,” both here and in the notes. But both were doubtless done deliberately. For Columbus’s explanation agrees: “*Additur*,” he says, “that is, it is appended.” Nor did Tollius and Boherellus read otherwise, each in his own way, using the present tense, though without stating the reason: the former, namely, *additur*, or *deditur*, or *traditur*; the latter, *arcetur*, “is driven back.” I approve—and also the translations which render it in the past tense [Col. 0599B]. For since the book begins, “The Lord has heard your prayers,” the author ought all the more to have supplied immediately a present or past example of that hearing—“Behold, the adversary is added,” or something similar—rather than a future and uncertain example of the same thing: “Behold, the adversary will be added.” Moreover, if we attend to what follows immediately, it reads: “and the Church rises again,” not “will rise”; likewise, “and the temple of God is built with greater glory,” not “will be built.” Both are no slight indication that some verb in the present, not future, tense stood at the beginning of the period. We should therefore most willingly prefer a present-tense verb.

Only, while the learned men whom I named above in honour propose, or have proposed, the aforesaid corrections as substitutes for the received reading on these unquestionably weighty grounds, I for my part prefer to read *abditur*: “Behold, by all these things the adversary is hidden away.” That is: behold, by the efficacy of all those prayers the devil—to whom it had been granted to come forth from the abyss [Col. 0599C] against Christians—is again thrust back and hidden in the darkness of the abyss. *Abdere*, “to hide, thrust back,” and *abditus*, “hidden, thrust back,” occur very frequently in Cicero, among others, in every variety of conjugation and construction.

“Do you hear this, Amphiaraus, hidden beneath the earth?” says Cicero, for example, after the *Epigoni* in the *Tusculan Disputations*; and in the second speech *Against Verres*: “The statues of the gods lie in darkness, thrust back and hidden away by that man,” concerning Verres. And, more importantly, we have learned not only from the Gospel that our Lord was once begged by a whole legion of demons not to command them to go into the abyss; John also says near the end of the Apocalypse: “Then I saw an angel descending from heaven, holding the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand. He seized that ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years; and cast him into the abyss, which he shut and sealed over him, so that he might deceive the nations no longer [Col. 0599D], until those thousand years were completed; after which he must be released for a short time.” Thus he is at times permitted, freed from prison, to traverse lands and air; at other times he is unwillingly hidden again in the abyss. Precisely as in Velleius Paterculus, Book II: “Nor was he more successful than his predecessors in concealing himself; and, shut up in prison, he met a death far more worthy than his life, together with his accomplices in the crime.”

Finally, the book’s colophon itself proves that this author could attribute all these things to the efficacy of the prayers of which he speaks: “Behold, by all these things the adversary is hidden away; and, peace throughout the world having been restored, the Church, lately overthrown, rises again, and the temple of God, which had been destroyed by the impious, is built by the Lord’s mercy with greater glory.” There, with no less solemnity: “You especially, dearest Donatus, who deserve to be heard by God, entreat the Lord that, gracious and gentle, he may preserve his mercy toward his servants; that he may drive away all the snares and assaults of the devil from his people [Col. 0600A]; and that he may guard the flourishing churches in perpetual peace.” Nor is this surprising, since James had long before led the way by testifying that the prayer of faith saves the sick, and that Elijah, though subject to passions like ours, prayed that it should not rain upon the earth, and it did not rain for three years and six months; and that he prayed again, and heaven gave rain.

**“Adversary.”** Against Columbus’s view, we have understood *adversarius* here without hesitation as the devil. We were led to this not only by the examples of very learned men who understand it in the same way, but especially by the weightiest arguments supplied for the matter by this writer’s style. The first is drawn from chapter 16 and was already adduced by the most distinguished Cuperus, col. 471. The second is that elsewhere, when our Caecilius discusses the persecutors of Christians, he calls them, collectively, “adversaries of God,” and calls Maximinus Daia, in chapter 43, one of the adversaries of God; but nowhere does he simply call a human persecutor “the adversary” (*ἀπλῶς adversarium*). The third and final argument is this: whereas Columbus understands “the adversary” not as some eminent persecutor of the faithful but, conversely, as some individual opponent of the persecutors who restrained and punished them, the words a few verses later strongly object: “God raised up princes who annulled the wicked and bloody reigns of the tyrants.” For there we have not this prince or that, but “princes,” in the plural; and chapter 48 does not simply begin the document concerning the restoration of the Church, “When I, the fortunate Augustus Constantine, . . .,” but rather: “When both I, the fortunate Augustus Constantine, and I, the fortunate Augustus Licinius, had met at Milan,” etc. Thus it is manifest that no human and individual avenger upon the persecutors is to be understood here by “the adversary.” It is not Constantine or Licinius, but, as stated, the great persecutor of the faithful, the devil—a point Cuperus admirably confirms below.

**“Throughout the world.”** It is remarkable how greatly, upon closer consideration, “throughout the world,” found here [Col. 0600C], may differ from “throughout all the earth,” found in the next chapter in another subject-matter; and likewise from “throughout all provinces and cities,” another expression in the same chapter and subject.

For there, since the Gospel of Christ is said to have been preached with the obedience of faith throughout all provinces and cities over a period of twenty-five years, nothing prevents—and, conversely, the passage itself, as will appear in its place, and the authority of many Fathers warn us—from understanding “throughout all the earth,” for example, broadly as the entire inhabited or habitable earth. That is, it includes not only everything contained within the boundaries of the Roman Empire, when it was at its greatest extent and height, from Augustus to Trajan; but also, for example, the whole of Scythia and India, neither of which, beyond all doubt, was any part of the Empire when Nero began to rule.

But here, since the subject is the restoration of peace lost throughout the world, and since that loss of public peace originated from nothing other than the emperors’ decrees against Christians [Col. 0600D], while those decrees had no force beyond the limits of the Roman Empire, the word “world” must certainly mean the Roman world alone—that is, the world subject to imperial laws—and by no means all regions not subject to the emperors. Thus in Julius Firmicus one may see “the whole world” restricted to the Roman world, in the most notable words imaginable: “Our Lord and Augustus, emperor of the whole world . . . Constantine the Great . . . upholds the Roman world by the salutary moderation of his government.” Nor need I add that *πᾶσαν τὴν οἰκουμένην* in this passage of Luke (Luke 2:1) has no broader meaning: “A decree went out from Caesar Augustus that all the world should be registered” (*Ἐξῆλθε δόγμα παρὰ Καίσαρος Αὐγούστου, ἀπογράφεσθαι πᾶσαν τὴν οἰκουμένην*). Indeed, as was excellently observed not long ago, ecumenical councils received that name in antiquity for no other reason than that those summoned and assembled for them came and were gathered [Col. 0601A] from each of those broader divisions of the inhabited world which were subject to the power and jurisdiction of the emperors.

**“Lately overthrown.”** See Columbus, col. 391.

**“The temple of God.”** This was the temple at Nicomedia. MAUCROIX.—That is, at Nicomedia, which Diocletian and Maximian destroyed. Oxford edition. These are almost the very words of Baluzius in the first edition, although on another passage.—At Nicomedia, namely (where Lactantius was then residing), which Diocletian, etc., as above. Cambridge edition.—Cuperus, col. 472, and Baluzius, col. 302, understand it differently, and not without reason.

**“Is built.”** A word familiar to this writer. Thus chapter 3: “When he had performed many wonderful works”; chapter 7: “Whatever was necessary for constructing works”; and chapter 36: “That Christians should neither construct . . .”

**“Princes.”** Constantine and Licinius. MAUCROIX, correctly.—Compare chapter 48 below.

**“They have provided for the human race.”** No one who consults the passage will deny that the coins praised by the most learned Cuperus, col. 472, concerning the emperors’ *providentia* are highly relevant here [Col. 0601B]. In addition, his interpretation here of “the human race” as the Roman Empire—whether from the same coins or others—strongly confirms our earlier observations concerning the peace restored throughout the world. But, I think, those coins would be wrongly applied to the devastation of the earth and destruction of humankind mentioned at the end of chapter 2.

**“They have provided for the human race.”** The connective *-que* might seem to have fallen out, were our author not often to speak in this fashion. TOLLIUS.—That he delights in asyndeton will be clear below from what is said on chapter 38. But here, unless I am mistaken, the omission of the conjunction is somewhat harsher.

**“The tranquil air.”** Lucretius, in Book I:

> “And the appeased sky shines with diffused light.”

TOLLIUS.

**“Now the appeased God of his servants . . .”** *For their prayers*, or *patience*, or some similar word seems to be missing. Oxford and Cambridge editions. Compare Columbus, col. 391, and Cuperus, col. 472.—“Now the appeased [God] of his servants.” Perhaps the word *groans* is missing. COLOMESIUS.—In my judgment, the question concerning this passage is not merely what is most plausibly missing and should be supplied; before all else, one must ask whether anything is actually missing, or whether rather a single letter is superfluous. For if from the end of *placatus* you erase the letter *s*, which may, as often happens, have intruded from the following word *servorum*, there remains with complete sense: *Nunc placatu servorum suorum Deus jacentes et afflictos coelesti auxilio sublevavit*: “Now by the appeasement of his servants God raised up those lying low and afflicted with heavenly aid.” That is, “Now God, by the appeasement of his servants . . .,” just as Cicero says: “What so great an appeasement of the gods has happened so suddenly?”—except that our author has used *placatus* for *placatio*. So below, chapter 48, he uses *tractatu* for *tractatione*, “negotiation.” Tertullian likewise uses *conculcatu* for *conculcatione*: “Then Jerusalem shall be for trampling by the nations.” And among the better writers *ejulatus* and *ejulatio*, *significatus* and *significatio*, *consolatus* and *consolatio* [Col. 0601D], *explicatus* and *explicatio*—not to accumulate more examples—are interchangeable. Therefore perhaps this passage may more properly be considered among the redundant than among the mutilated. Yet I affirm nothing.

I add only that, if it seems preferable to count it among defective passages, perhaps *causa* or *gratia* (“for the sake of”) is missing rather than *precibus* (“prayers”), *gemitibus* (“groans”), or something similar; so that the sense is: “Now God, appeased for the sake of his servants . . .” For in a very similar way, in 2 Maccabees it is evidently written: “And may God remember his covenant which he spoke to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, his faithful servants,” in place of: “And may God remember his covenant which he spoke to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, for the sake of his faithful servants.” Likewise in Greek, *πρὸς Ἀβραὰμ, καὶ Ἰσαὰκ, καὶ Ἰακὼβ τῶν δούλων αὐτοῦ τῶν πιστῶν*, in place of *πρὸς Ἀβραὰμ, καὶ Ἰσαὰκ, καὶ Ἰακώβ, τῶν δούλων αὐτοῦ τῶν πιστῶν χάριν*. Nor, I think, did Columbus intend anything else when, having begun his note on our Caecilius’s passage with these words—“The word *PRECIBUS*, ‘prayers,’ or another similar word appears to have fallen out; if you restore it, the sentence will be fuller and much more elegant”—he shortly afterward noted: “Yet 2 Maccabees 1:2 introduces some doubt.” However that may be, you have, beyond all certainty, the same ellipsis in Tertullian, *On Flight in Persecution*: “Whoever has been ashamed of me,” for “Whoever has been ashamed on account of me”; and again immediately: “And I shall be ashamed of him before my Father,” for “And I shall be ashamed of him on account of him before my Father.” Hence he immediately exclaims in fuller language: “Blessed are those who have suffered persecution for the sake of my name.” Add, among Latin authors, Horace singing in the *Art of Poetry*:

> “He crawls safely along the ground, excessively fearful of the storm.”

That is, learned men say, “fearful on account of the storm.” Among Greek authors, Homer, speaking of Juno, *Iliad* I, verse 56:

> *Κήδετο γὰρ Δαναῶν, ὅτι ῥα θνῄσκοντας ὁρᾶτο*  
> “For she was concerned for the Danaans, because she saw them dying,”

instead of: “concerned for the sake of the Danaans” [Col. 0602B]. Indeed, does not a direct and plain method of reasoning seem altogether to require that in that extremely difficult passage of Paul to the Galatians—*Φοβοῦμαι ὑμᾶς, μήπως εἰκῇ κεκοπίακα εἰς ὑμᾶς. Γίνεσθε ὡς ἐγώ, ὅτι κἀγὼ ὡς ὑμεῖς, ἀδελφοί, δέομαι ὑμῶν*—the Apostle wrote *δέομαι ὑμῶν* with a similar ellipsis, for *δέομαι ὑμῶν ἕνεκα* or *χάριν*: “Certainly, brothers, because of those observances of the ceremonial law, I fear for you—that I may in the end be found to have laboured among you, or for you, in vain. But become as I am. I say, you also fear this for me; because I myself, who fear on my own account lest I have preached the Gospel among you in vain, fear it also for you as for yourselves: thus I am concerned not merely for my own sake, but for yours also. Return like for like, then; and lest I lose the reward of my apostolate in regard to you, fear on my account.”

I know that *δεῖσθαι* more frequently means “to pray” than “to fear” in Greek; but in Plutarch it is certainly found more than once in the sense “to fear,” as in this apophthegm: *δεῖσθαι περὶ βίου, οὐ φοβεῖσθαι*, “to fear for one’s life, not to be afraid.” Indeed, what is more relevant, Hesychius plainly did not distinguish, in the terms *δεῖσθαι* and *φοβεῖσθαι*, between *δεῖσθαι* and *ἕνεκα*, but treated them, as Paul does here for us, as equivalent. Finally compare all those passages of the New Testament in which *ἕνεκα* or *χάριν* are left to be understood and are supplied daily by interpreters; for example, Matthew 11:1, *Μετέβη τοῦ διδάσκειν*, “He departed in order to teach”; Luke 24:29, *Εἰσῆλθε τοῦ μεῖναι σὺν αὐτοῖς*, “He entered in order to remain with them”; and so on through the rest, which are innumerable.

**“Those who had opposed God lie fallen.”** Thus all editors after Baluzius, with no slight confidence, as will soon appear.—“*Adversati*.” Read *insultati*. Isaac Vossius, in the margin of his own copy. For he had learned from Baluzius that the ancient reading was *illustrati*, and, judging it corrupt along with that eminent man, naturally thought it should be changed otherwise than to Baluzius’s *adversati*. Quite rightly. For though Baluzius called his emendation certain, Vossius’s conjecture is plainly much closer to the old codex than Baluzius’s, which thus begins to become uncertain.—“Those who were hostile to God lie fallen.” This is the conjecture of the most distinguished editor. The manuscript had: “Those who were *illustrati* to God lie fallen.” It will be closer to the traces of the old codex if one writes: “Those who had insulted God lie fallen.” Those are said to insult others who afflict them with every disgrace and treat them most indignantly. Caesar, according to Suetonius, when he had obtained what he desired against the groaning opposition of his adversaries, said that henceforth he would insult the heads of all. Nicolaus Heinsius, of blessed memory (*ὁ μακαρίτης*), conjectured: “Those who had mocked God lie fallen.” GRAEVIUS.—Very many passages in ancient writers indeed confirm the suspicion of that most celebrated and learned colleague. Minucius Felix: “This is to insult and mock: to serve defeated religions.” Claudian: “All insult the fugitive . . .” And many similar examples may also be found in the Vulgate translator. But what if we nevertheless resort to a simple transposition of a few syllables? Thus, instead of “Those who were *illustrati* to God lie fallen,” read: “Those who had mocked God lie stretched out and fallen”—*qui illuserant Deo, strati jacent*. Certainly the sense will be entirely clear. And that the great man just praised [Col. 0603A] will point out below, with Heinsius or on Heinsius’s behalf, that elsewhere *coepit* should be read for *capite*, and *cogitationis* for *contagionis*, by a not dissimilar method, at chapters 27 and 29; see those passages.

I add, lest perhaps, as once happened to someone, you too may find our reading less attractive because it is somewhat weaker than the following expressions: throughout the whole period one may readily discern a twofold gradation, both with respect to the wrongs of the persecutors and to their punishments, as follows:

> Those who had **MOCKED** God . . . lie **STRETCHED OUT AND FALLEN**.  
> Those who had **DESTROYED** the holy temple . . . **FELL** in a greater ruin.  
> Those who had **TORTURED** the righteous . . . poured forth their guilty souls amid deserved heavenly **SCOURGES** and **TORMENTS**.

Indeed, it may very readily be that at the beginning of the period this writer intended by that great and pre-eminent name, “God” (*κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν*), none other than our Lord Jesus Christ. Tertullian speaks of him in precisely the same way: “Read,” he says, “that God said: ‘Let him who can receive it, receive it,’” plainly indicating Christ by the word “God,” since it is certain from Matthew’s Gospel that Jesus once said, “Let him who can receive it, receive it”; and the whole passage in Tertullian reads: “Keep the virgin as a bride for Christ. Let no one make gain from her. These things, brother, may perhaps seem harsh and intolerable to you. But read that God said: ‘Let him who can receive it, receive it’; that is, let him who cannot receive it depart.”

But if we consider the matter itself, that pagans and persecutors of the Christian Church once mocked Christ whenever they wished to make an impious jest is shown even by these words of the same Tertullian in the *Apology*: “But a new representation of our God was recently displayed publicly in this city, since a criminal hired to bait beasts exhibited a picture with the following inscription:

> **THE GOD OF THE CHRISTIANS, ONONYCHITES.**

[Col. 0603C] He had ass’s ears, one hoofed foot, carried a book, and wore a toga. We laughed both at the name and the image.” As for the expression itself, not to speak further of the matter, consider, for example, Luke 22:63: “The men who held Jesus mocked him, beating him”; and 23:11: “Herod with his soldiers despised him and mocked him, clothing him in a white garment.” Moreover, perhaps the manner of expression which we suspect this author employed was suggested to him because, after Judas’s kiss, the agents of the Pharisees and priests—who by that kiss had deceitfully mocked Jesus—were cast to the ground, as it were by a single word, and lay stretched upon the earth for some time. Compare without fail Matthew 26:28 and Luke 22:47–48 with John 18:3–6.

At any rate, it is manifest that the following words, “those who had destroyed the holy temple,” do not conflict with this view, since they may also have been written in a tacit and not unattractive imitation of Christ’s reply: “Destroy this temple”—when, as John observed, he was speaking of the temple of his body. Compare above, col. 601. Finally, in our conjecture, “Those who had mocked God lie stretched out and fallen,” we are doing or proposing nothing that the distinguished Heinsius might not equally have thought in reading: “Those who had mocked God lie fallen.” Only, if the question concerns the origin and causes of so corrupt a transposition, perhaps—as we often say—we possess the Colbert manuscript copied from no other source than an exemplar in which one line ended in *Qui illus-*, the next began with *-erant*, while the word *strati* had immediately afterward been omitted from the text and then somewhat carelessly written in the margin, for example nearly opposite the *illus-*; so that a hasty and unlearned copyist wrote out, incorrectly, *Qui illustrati erant Deo jacent* for *Qui illuserant Deo, strati jacent*.

**“Those who had destroyed the holy temple,” etc.** See Cuperus, col. 472, and Baluzius, col. 302. Compare also our note, col. 601.

**“Those who had tortured the righteous.”** Thus Cicero, Book III, *On the Nature of the Gods*: “We have received that Anaxarchus the Democritean was tortured by the Cypriot tyrant.” And our author again, chapter 14: “Diocletian . . . immediately ordered all his household to be tortured.”

**“They poured forth their guilty souls.”** Baluzius, col. 302, lists the names of those to whom this happened. This author likewise uses a similar expression at the end of chapter 49: “He breathed out his guilty spirit in a detestable manner of death,” concerning Maximinus. Do not, however, understand anything slight by “guilty souls” and “guilty spirit” in the two passages; for in chapter 2 *execrabilis ac nocens*, “accursed and guilty,” are joined of the tyrant Nero.

**“For God had delayed their punishments.”** On punishments of this sort according to both pagan and Christian theology, see Columbus, col. 391.

**“So that posterity also might learn.”** The Åbo edition has *quibus posteri discerent*, “that posterity might learn,” without the conjunction; this is better.

**“To inflict death upon the impious and persecutors.”** Columbus’s edition has *irrogare*, “to inflict,” as Arnobius has *irrogare poenas capitis*, “to inflict capital punishment,” and Ambrose, *irrogare injuriam*, *irrogare vim*, *irrogare arma suis principibus*, *irrogare sibi manus*—“to inflict injury,” “violence,” “arms upon one’s own rulers,” “violence upon oneself”—and so forth, as the great J. Frid. Gronovius observed before us. Everywhere, as is clear, it means “to inflict”: death, capital punishment, injury, violence, and the rest.

**“Concerning whose end . . . it pleased [me] to bear witness.”** What is missing here, learned men have hitherto supplied in different ways in the common editions: the Oxford edition inserts *eorum*, “of them”; the Cambridge edition, *nobis*, “to us”; Cuperus once, if Columbus is to be believed, *imperiorum*, “of their reigns”; Cuperus himself, *impiorum*, “of the impious”; Columbus, in his first conjecture, *crudelium principum*, “of cruel princes”; Columbus’s supplement, *tyrannorum*, “of tyrants”; and his other supplement, *saevissimorum principum*, “of most savage princes.”

**“Concerning whose end . . .”** Read: “Concerning the dreadful end of whom it pleased [me] to bear witness”—that is, of the proud and impious princes, persecutors of the Christian name. For by these designations he particularly marks the pride of Diocletian and Maximian, both because they assumed the surnames Jovius and Herculius and because of their gold garments, jeweled crown, adoration, and so forth. Galerius Maximian too displayed immense and intolerable arrogance after defeating Narseus; our author discusses this below, chapter 9. Impiety, however, was common to them all, except that Maxentius appears to have surpassed the others. TOLLIUS.—First, since there is no gap in the manuscript after *de quo*, “concerning whom,” but only after *exitu*, “end,” we think there is no need, with Tollius, to turn *de quo* into *de quorum*, “concerning whose.”

Moreover, because we have not seen the blank space in the Colbert manuscript and do not know how many letters it can contain, or what traces of letters may remain there, we dare not choose from among so many learned supplements any one as indisputably genuine in preference to the others. Yet we may in the meantime be inclined toward the first, or something similar: both because it is simplest and because, since the immediately preceding word is *persecutoribus*, “persecutors,” and this author elsewhere uses *exitus* for death, the completed phrase would read: “Concerning their end,” that is, “concerning the death of the persecutors.” This is virtually the title of the book itself, and it is more than probable that our Caecilius wished to allude to it—especially since John of Salisbury mentions a work of his entitled *On the End of Tyrants*. Finally, that *exitus* here means death is amply established, apart from other evidence, by the other passage in chapter 50: “Candidianus, fearing nothing of the kind, was killed; and Valeria, when she heard of his end, immediately fled.” Here *exitus* clearly means “death.”—“Concerning whose end let [me] bear brief witness.” GALE.—“Concerning the end of the persecutors,” etc. ALLIX.—“Concerning whose end it pleased [me] to bear witness in this writing.” The Abbot of Saint-Hilary, Canon of Saint Peter at Beauvais.

**“That all who had been moved far away.”** Thus the manuscript codex and all editions alike. Only the Oxford and Cambridge editions note at the foot of the page that it may be emended: “that all who had been removed far away.” Or, if you prefer, the latter adds later: “that all who had been persecuted”; this too is found at the end of the work in the former edition, though proposed less plausibly.—“Who had been moved far away.” A confused reading. Write: “who had been driven by a storm.” ALLIX.—“*Moti*.” Read *nati*, “born.” VOSSIUS.—*Nati*, I say, not *noti*, “known,” as the most accurate eyewitness (*αὐτόπτης*) Colomesius took care, out of his zeal for sound learning, to inform us—and wished to have more carefully observed. But am I mistaken, or do the learned men trouble the received reading without cause? That *movere* occurs in Plautus, Cicero, and others in the sense of “to remove” or “to drive away” is beyond controversy and ought to be so. Plautus, for example: “Move delay away from yourself,” that is, “Remove” or “drive away delay from yourself.” Further, that *procul moveri* is very idiomatically said for “to be moved, removed, or banished far from one’s own home” is attested adequately even by these verses of Virgil:

> “And therefore they banish the bulls far away, to lonely  
> pastures.”

Compare in the same book:

> “She herself withdrew far away, dark amid the clouds.”

Thirdly, and far more importantly, after the tenth persecution had once begun, a great part of the faithful had been proscribed and sent into exile. This is not merely attested by Maximinus’s letter in Eusebius, writing among other things to the Tyrians: “If any persist in the detestable error of their own delusion, let them, as you requested, be separated and driven away as far as possible from your city and territory”—*ἐν πολλῷ πόρρωθεν τῆς ὑμετέρας πόλεως καὶ περιχώρου, καθὼς ἠξιώσατε, ἀποχωρισθέντες ἐξελαθήτωσαν*—but is stated much more explicitly shortly afterward by Eusebius himself: “Such letters against us were posted in every province”—*ταῦτα δὴ καθ᾽ ἡμῶν κατὰ πᾶσαν ἐπαρχίαν ἀνεστηλιτεύετο*. Moreover, in *On the Life of Constantine*, the same historian records two laws of that emperor: by one, all who had refused to betray the worship and faith of God and therefore, at any time, had been condemned by cruel judicial sentences and exchanged their homeland for foreign soil were to be restored to their ancestral estates; by the other, all who had likewise been relegated to islands and there confined amid rough mountains and surrounding sea were to be restored to themselves, their relatives, and friends. Finally, our Caecilius himself says below: “That all things might be filled with terror, provinces too were cut into fragments; many governors and many administrative staffs weighed upon individual regions and almost now upon cities; likewise many financial officers, masters, and deputies of prefects, whose civil proceedings were extremely rare, but their condemnations . . . and proscriptions frequent.” Hence chapter 52: “We must give thanks to the everlasting mercy of God, who at last looked upon the earth and deigned to restore and gather again his flock, partly ravaged by ravening wolves and partly scattered.” Clearly, he calls the Church of God a flock partly scattered and finally regathered for no other reason than that which we have thought worth mentioning. Therefore, if I have any judgment, this passage refers to no others “moved far away” than those faithful first proscribed and exiled but afterward recalled by Constantine’s edicts, as we have said; and for their benefit above all he undertook to write *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, so that they might learn of the things wrought by God’s power and majesty against the persecutors during their absence. See Columbus, col. 392.

**“Or those who . . . will be . . .”** Learned men have supplied this second gap in more than one way. We shall cite the conjectures: Cuperus, *post nos futuri* (“who will be after us”); Columbus’s first conjecture, *posthac aberraturi* (“who will hereafter go astray”); Oxford and Cambridge editions, first supplement, *procul i[ti]* [uncertain]; their second supplement, *perseca[tores]* [uncertain]; Vossius, *posthac futuri* (“who will hereafter be”).—“Or those who are yet to be born.” GALE.—“Or those who will exist afterward.” ALLIX.—“Or those who will come after us.” The Abbot of Saint-Hilary.—Of these supplements we judge only the first and last worthy of attention. But perhaps others not unlike either might afterward be admitted, for example: “or those who will live afterward.” Let those who have free access to inspect the manuscript see; the whole matter depends on the surviving letter-strokes, if any remain.

**“That he might display power and majesty.”** See Baluzius, col. 302. Meanwhile, at the end of chapter 5, our author calls the majesty of God singular, without any mention of divine power.

[Col. 0606A] **“In . . . them.”** Until now only one means of repairing this loss had been before learned men: *in [perden]dis*, “in destroying.” But now, behold, several more will not be lacking for the future.—“In . . . them, and in destroying them.” Perhaps *in [excinden]dis*, “in rooting them out,” as in chapter 2, where Lactantius joins *excindere* and *delere*. COLOMESIUS.—“In . . . them.” *In [punien]dis*, “in punishing them.” GALE.—*In [exscinden]dis*, “in extirpating them.” ALLIX.—*In [plecten]dis*, “in punishing them.” The Abbot of Saint-Hilary.—The learned man’s method is not displeasing and is excellent in itself. But perhaps then one ought also to read *in [extinguen]dis delendisque*, “in extinguishing and destroying them.” For in chapter 46 our author says: “If he had won the victory, he would have utterly extinguished and destroyed the Christian name.” Or perhaps again, *in [eraden]dis delendisque*, “in eradicating and destroying them.” For at the end of the work he says: “The Lord destroyed them and erased them from the earth.” Or finally perhaps *in [expugnan]dis delendisque*, “in overcoming and destroying them,” on account of Lactantius’s words in the *Epitome*: “for overcoming and destroying the nation of the saints.” Whatever you prefer, even this passing discussion shows more than sufficiently how perilous an undertaking it is to add to gapped and mutilated passages of ancient authors what seems more plausibly to be missing, when even the best method cannot be the safest.

**“Might show.”** In my opinion it would be much better to read “has shown.” Read the entire passage again.—“Might show . . . is, if.” The Oxford and Cambridge editions supply what is missing in the manuscript: “might show: [which will be clearer] if.” Columbus, however, supplies: “might show [but my discourse will proceed correctly and in order] if,” and what follows.—Let learned men who can inspect it determine whether the copyist wrote: “might show. [Which may succeed better] if . . .,” or something similar.—“Might show . . .” Read: “has shown . . .” GALE.—“Might show. [For this purpose it is worthwhile] . . .” ALLIX.—“He deigned to show . . .” The Abbot of Saint-Hilary.

**“If, from the beginning from which the Church has been established, who . . .”** Divide it altogether with Columbus: “if, from the beginning from which the Church has been established, who were the authors . . .” It is as though our Caecilius had written in full: “if, from the beginning—that is, from which the Church has been established—who they were,” etc. For, as will appear below, he meant to say that he would begin from the earliest origins of the Church, finally established in every respect through the apostles around the beginning of Nero’s reign, and trace what concerned the authors of persecutions and their punishments. But he did not mean equally to begin from the earliest origins of the Church’s establishment, whose foundations the apostles began to lay immediately after Christ’s ascension and, for twenty-five years until the beginning of Nero’s reign, spread throughout all provinces and cities, as he says in the immediately following chapter.

**“Who they were.”** This is the most consistent reading of the manuscript codex and of all editions prior to that of Åbo. Therefore I cannot understand what Columbus means below by “this *qui fuerint*,” unless, as is more than probable, he inadvertently took a typographical error of his own edition for the writing of the ancient manuscript.

**“Authors . . . and.”** After *auctores*, “authors,” the most distinguished Cuperus thinks *tantorum scelerum*, “of such great crimes,” or *persecutionis*, “of the persecution,” has fallen out. Columbus at one point assents to one or the other restoration, but later preferred *persecutionis*. The Oxford and Cambridge editions supply “of the persecution of the Church.”—“Authors . . .” “Authors of the persecutions.” ALLIX; likewise GALE and the Abbot of Saint-Hilary.—Supply: “of carrying out the persecutions.” Thus Lactantius, Book V, *On Justice*, chapter 2, says of Hierocles, though without naming him: “He was especially the author of carrying out the persecution.” COLOMESIUS.

**“And with what punishments the severity of the heavenly judge had avenged itself upon them, I shall set forth.”** See Columbus, col. 393.

“And with what punishments the truthfulness of the heavenly judge had avenged itself upon them, I shall set forth.” GALE.

## CHAPTER II
In the final period of Tiberius Caesar. Said too broadly.
