For from the event which this author here relates down to the death of Tiberius Caesar, eight full years, less a few days, elapsed: Jesus Christ having been crucified, according to the opinion of our writer, when the two Gemini were consuls, while Tiberius died under the consulship of Gnaeus Proculus Acerronius and Gaius Pontius Nigrinus. Indeed, we strongly incline to say that, in this place, by the latter [Col. 0607A] times of Tiberius Caesar should rather be understood the latter times of Tiberius’s life, since at the beginning of the consulship of the two Gemini he had already lived sixty-nine full years and more, than the latter times of his reign, since at the beginning of that same consulship Tiberius had entered only upon the fifteenth year of his reign and afterward reigned still eight years, as has now been said. The reverend Bishop of Salisbury, however, and the author of the highly polished Parisian translation take it otherwise; therefore we pronounce nothing.

As we read written. Does our Caecilius mean to suggest that the matters which he begins to narrate had been read by him in Lactantius, Book IV of the *Institutions*, chapter 10, in these words: “In the fifteenth year of that Tiberius Caesar, that is, when the two Gemini were consuls, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, the Jews fastened Christ to a cross”? Certainly he must either have had regard to those very words of Lactantius—which those who deny this work to Lactantius will undoubtedly maintain—or to words of some other writer or writers, which the illustrious Baluze will likewise [Col. 0607B] without doubt contend. But if to those Lactantian words, then our author will indeed have read there “on the tenth day before,” not “on the seventh day before,” as not a few editions and manuscript codices display. But then Lucius Caecilius Lactantius Firmianus will not be the true father of this work, but some other person designated only by the names Lucius Caecilius. If, however—which seems more probable to me—our author had before his eyes words and passages of some other writer rather than the foregoing words of Lactantius, then Lactantius may certainly easily have composed both the books of the *Institutions* and this *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, and thus have twice mentioned the same matter in different works from the records of others. Yet, whether we wish it or not, Baluze’s argument drawn from the συμφωνία, “agreement,” of the two passages will always remain rather weak; because, even if *ante diem decimum Kalendas Apriles* and *post diem decimum Kalendas Aprilis* are synonymous, nevertheless not all manuscript or printed copies in the foregoing section [Col. 0607C] (*περιοχή*) of the *Institutions* have *ante diem decimum*, but a considerable part have *ante diem septimam*: for example, the Basel edition of 1532, the Antwerp edition of 1587, the Leiden edition of 1652, the Cambridge edition of 1685, the Emmanuel manuscript codex praised in its preface; and so with the rest.

He was cruciated. Understand this, without impropriety, as “he was crucified”; and from the weightiest authorities brought forward on this point by the most learned Cuper, col. 472, and Columbus, col. 393, it is clear that not only should this passage from Book V of Hegesippus, chapter 18, be added: “Even the relatives of those who had departed were tortured, or the bodies of most of them, fastened to crosses, were displayed to those who had escaped”; but especially this passage of Plautus, *The Braggart Soldier*, Act II, scene 3, lines 7–8:

> SC. I am afraid. — PA. What are you afraid of? — SC. By Hercules, lest today, as many households as there are here,  
> We leap into the greatest torment of evil.

[Col. 0607D] For there, as Taubmann observed most aptly, “the greatest torment of evil” is what Plautus elsewhere calls “the greatest evil cross.” Thus this passage shows that even in purer Latinity it was customary to say *cruciari*, “to be tortured/crucified,” for *cruci affigi*, “to be fastened to a cross,” and *cruciare*, “to torture,” for *crucifigere*, “to crucify.” I think I once saw another passage matching this one of Plautus, if not even more explicit, in his same comedies. But it does not now come to hand.

After the tenth day before the Kalends of April. In Book IV of the *Institutions*, Lactantius has this: “On the tenth day before the Kalends of April the Jews fastened Christ to a cross”; so that it seems diametrically opposed to this passage. Yet Baluze contends, on the testimony cited from the books of the jurist Paulus, that there is no contradiction. He adds no other reason, however, except that the Romans never designated from the Kalends days which follow after the Kalends. That reasoning, more fully unfolded and explained, will readily reconcile these divided expressions. [Col. 0608A] For the same days may, in their natural sequence, be called “before the Kalends.” But if attention is given to the method of counting them—which, according to the Roman system of designation, begins from the Kalends—nothing prevents them from being counted among the later days by reckoning backward. Hence there is no danger of contradiction in using either expression. The Oxford and Cambridge edition follows this view.

The passage of Baluze to which the authors of the most recent observation had regard appears above, col. 302. It is certainly true that Baluze there adduces testimony from the writings of the aforesaid Paulus to prove that *ante diem Kalendas Apriles* and *post diem Kalendas Aprilis* have the same force. But that distinguished man does not directly and primarily deal with the expression of our Caecilius, but with that of the jurist Paulus, when he asserts that the Romans never designated from the Kalends days which follow the Kalends, but only those which precede them. Thus he intentionally refutes Marcellus Francolinus, [Col. 0608B] who had maintained that in the words of Paulus, *post diem decimum Kalendas*—for example, *Apriles*—one cannot understand any day of March, but expressly the tenth day after the Kalends of April, that is, the ninth of April. Nor was this the only reason Baluze offered to refute Francolinus; he also offered one which follows elegantly and naturally from Baluze’s hypotheses: since, according to Baluze, Lactantius related the same thing in two places and in one said *ante diem decimum Kalendas Apriles*, while in the other *post diem decimum Kalendas Aprilis*, it is evident that both expressions must have the same meaning; and therefore in Paulus *ante diem decimum Kalendas* and *post diem decimum Kalendas* cannot differ from one another, although Francolinus asserted that they differed as widely as heaven and earth. We thought this should not be passed over in the interest of truth, and also lest a matter already entangled in controversies should become still more complicated through the foregoing annotation, which was somewhat less [Col. 0608C] precise than it ought to have been. See Baluze again.

As for the remainder—that Columbus says, and not without force, that the expression *post diem decimum Kalendas Aprilis* is elliptical and may be supplied as *post exortum sive incoeptum diem decimum Kalendas Aprilis*, “after the rising or beginning of the tenth day before the Kalends of April”—this is of the greatest importance in the scholarly dispute in question. For if *post diem decimum Kalendas* can indeed sometimes mean, and must mean, “after the rising of the tenth day before the Kalends,” then it plainly cannot at all be understood of a twenty-four-hour, or civil, day, consisting of darkness and light and beginning for the Romans at midnight; rather, it must be understood strictly of that part of the civil day which the ancients distinguished from the preceding and following night, calling it now *dies*, “day,” now *lux*, “light.” Martial, for example, calls it *dies* when he sings:

> Phosphorus, restore the day. Why do you delay our joys?  
> Phosphorus, restore the day, for Caesar is coming.

Cicero, for example, calls it *lux* when [Col. 0608D] he writes to Lentulus: “I wrote this on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February, before daylight.” Thus we can readily understand how the Romans could properly and very aptly say, of one and the same civil day—say, the tenth day before the Kalends of April—both *ante diem decimum Kalendas Apriles* and *post diem decimum Kalendas Aprilis*. Namely, *ante diem decimum Kalendas Apriles* in this sense: on the tenth civil day before the full and civil day of the Kalends of April, the day of the Kalends itself being included in the count; but *post diem decimum Kalendas Aprilis* in this other sense: after the daylight had risen on the tenth civil day preceding the full and civil day of the Kalends of April, the day of the Kalends likewise being included—if, that is, they wished to speak more precisely of something done after sunrise. Such, beyond doubt, was our author’s meaning concerning the crucifixion of our Lord, which took place in daytime, as that famous darkening of the sun at Christ’s death and so many other Gospel passages do not permit us to doubt.

[Col. 0609A] But was Jesus Christ, then, crucified on the tenth day before the Kalends of April—that is, on the twenty-third of March? I reply: it is one thing to explain, or at least to conjecture as far as one can, a writer’s meaning; it is another thing to agree with him. Up to this point we have been concerned with the former; now we wish, with respect to the latter, chiefly for this reason to suspend judgment (*ἐπέχειν*): although at present we strongly side with those ancients and moderns who believe that Christ was crucified when the two Gemini were consuls, the very Fathers who assigned his Passion to the consulship of the two Gemini do not all assign it to the same day or in the same manner. Our author, for example, assigns it to *post diem decimum Kalendas Aprilis*; Lactantius, according to the variation of editions, sometimes to *ante diem decimum Kalendas Apriles*, sometimes to the seventh day before; Victor of Aquitaine consistently to the seventh; while Tertullian and Augustine each in his own way assign it to the eighth day before the Kalends of April. Which person, after carefully considering all the difficulties of the matter, would dare hope that he will clearly see what alone is true? At any rate, we have not thus far seen it. And if you consult Pagius on year 5525 of his Graeco-Roman Period, no. 6, I think you will even have reason to despair whether it can ever be known what is more probable.

Kalends of April. I should prefer *Aprilium*. For so the ancients spoke, and our author elsewhere also used the plural form of the name. TOLLIUS. — The received reading can very well be retained. For although this author, and perhaps other ancients, may have written *Kalendarum Aprilium* and similar expressions more frequently than *Kalendarum Aprilis, Maii, Februarii*, and so on, Pompey nevertheless once used *Kalendarum Martii*, not *Martiarum*, in his letter to Domitius. And Cicero, three times in one and the same letter to Pompey, wrote *Kal. Martii*, and to Atticus, *Id. Maii*, *Id. Quintii*. Indeed, elsewhere to the same correspondent, and likewise in a single letter, he uses *Non. Maiis* and *Kalend. Maii* indiscriminately, and that twice; and again, in another letter, now *Id. Maias*, now *Idus Maii*. It is therefore apparent that both usages were employed indiscriminately by the ancients, and that nothing here ought rashly to be altered. Especially since below, in chapter 44, we read *Kalendas Novembris*, not *Novembres*; and the passages already adduced from Cicero’s works are no slight obstacle to anyone’s maintaining that the received writing of our author, *Kalendarum Aprilis*, represents, in chapter 44, an ancient plural accusative of the adjectival form, *Novembris*, for *Novembreis* or *Novembres*—although I otherwise recall, among other examples, that Sallustian opening: “All men who strive to excel the other animals ought to exert themselves with the utmost effort . . .” But in a different matter a different explanation may readily apply.

When the two Gemini were consuls. Thus Tertullian, *Against the Jews*; Lactantius, Book IV of the *Institutions*; Sulpicius Severus, Book II of the *Sacred History*; Augustine, *City of God*; Prosper of Aquitaine [Col. 0609D] in his *Chronicle*, according to the more customary tradition, as he calls it; and finally his compatriot Victor in the Paschal Canon—all number among the other ancients whom we have seen speak explicitly on the matter. Yet, leaving Prosper aside, Bucherius, Labbe, and others rightly wonder “why Victor equated the first year of his Period—that is, the seventy-third Julian year, but the twenty-eighth common year of Christ—with the consulship of the Gemini, which is certainly known to fall only in the following year.” Among modern writers, moreover, the illustrious Pagius maintained that Christ suffered under the two Gemini in the Hypatic Dissertation, p. 199, and most recently in the *Critical Examination of Baronius’s Annals*, under year 5525 of his Graeco-Roman Period. Indeed, he says there, no. 3: “The ancient Fathers, Augustine, Jerome, and others, connected the consulship of the two Gemini, held in the twenty-ninth year of the Christian era, with [Col. 0610A] it. Eusebius was among the first to remove the Lord’s death from that year; Epiphanius in Heresy 51 and others later followed him, so that, once that door had been opened,” he continues, “some transferred the Passion to the thirty-first year of the Christian era, others to the thirty-second.” Pagius further concludes in the same terms that “from the eclipse seen when Christ suffered, no year other than the twenty-ninth year of the Christian era can be determined as the year of the Passion,” the year in which the two Gemini held the consulship.

[Col. 0610B] For our part, we have long followed the same opinion as Pagius; yet not on account of the authority of Jerome cited by him, nor because we believe the matter of the year of Christ’s death can be established as he sets it forth by the hypotheses and reasonings which he has prefixed to his conclusion concerning that eclipse. First, as to Jerome: how could he have been persuaded that the Passion occurred under the two Gemini, when in *On Ecclesiastical Writers* he explains the twenty-fifth year after the Lord’s Passion as the second year of Nero? Surely, if for Jerome the twenty-fifth year after the Lord’s Passion was only the second year of Nero’s reign, then Christ was not put on the cross in March or April under the consulship of the two Gemini; for from the time of their consular authority to the slightly begun second year of Nero’s reign there are twenty-six full years plus more than five or six months. Rather, with his Eusebius in the *Chronicles*, Jerome plainly places Christ’s Passion in the eighteenth year of Tiberius Caesar’s reign from the death of Augustus, when Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus and Marcus Furius Camillus Scribonianus were consuls. For if someone counts the years from the Passover of that year down to Nero’s second year, the twenty-fifth year after the Lord’s Passion will in fact coincide with Nero’s second year when it has at least somewhat advanced. Thus, although we regard the ancients as leaders of the opinion which we maintain with Pagius in this matter to the present day, we refrain from numbering Jerome among them. [Col. 0610C] Nor Jerome alone, but also Paul Orosius by name, contrary to the explicit opinion of Columbus. For since Orosius writes in Book VII, at the very beginning of chapter 4, that “Tiberius Caesar acquired the empire in the year 767 from the founding of the City, after the death of Augustus,” and subsequently adds that “in the seventeenth year of Tiberius’s reign Christ delivered himself to the Passion and was fastened to the gibbet,” that Passion can never fall under the consulship of the two Gemini, that is, in the twenty-ninth year of the Dionysian era, but only in that ὑπατεία, “consulship,” in which, two years later, Tiberius Caesar, with Aelius Sejanus as colleague, entered upon his fifth consulship; and therefore in the thirty-first year of the same era.

As for the eclipse seen at Christ’s death—for Thallus, Phlegon, and innumerable others called the dreadful darkness which then covered the earth an ἔκλειψις ἡλίου, “eclipse of the sun,” and we shall follow them in this manner of speaking, despite the objection of Syncellus—who can likewise say, even if the three passages of Africanus cited by Pagius are found somewhere in Greek in Syncellus, [Col. 0610D] that no year of the Passion other than the twenty-ninth year of the Christian era can be determined? Certainly, Julius Africanus is the principal—indeed, I might say the sole—authority for Pagius’s argument. Pagius says that Africanus stated in one passage in Syncellus that the eclipse happened in the fourth year of the 202nd Olympiad; in another, in the second year of the 202nd Olympiad; and in a third, that the eclipse recorded by Phlegon occurred in the second year of the 202nd Olympiad. In the first passage, says Pagius, there is an error and it should read “the fourth year of the 201st Olympiad,” while Africanus followed the common arrangement of Olympiads. But in the second and third, Pagius says, no error is present: for Africanus begins Olympiads and Olympiad years two years earlier than others do, so that the fourth year of the 201st Olympiad according to the common method, and the second year of the 202nd Olympiad according to Africanus’s own calculations, coincided; and the beginning of the consulship of the two Gemini fell in the middle of both divisions. [Col. 0611A] Everything may be seen exactly, in the appended diagram, in this way, so that both I and the matter itself may be better understood:

[Col. 0611C] +++ Of these three crosses, the first refers Christ’s death to the consulship of the two Gemini, the second to the second year of the 202nd Olympiad, the third to the fourth year of the 201st Olympiad.

But let it be granted, I say, that persons more fortunate than we will find all the passages of Africanus in question in the Greek *Chronography* of Syncellus. For until now we have nowhere been able to find the first, except in the Latin translation on page 323; but that is evidently corrupt, since in place of the Latin words “to the sixteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, which is equal to the fourth year of the 202nd Olympiad,” the Greek has: μέχρις ἕκτου καὶ δεκάτου Τιβερίου Καΐσαρος, ὅπερ ἦν Ὀλυμπιάδος σβ΄ ἔτος δεύτερον—literally, “to the sixteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, which was the second year of the 202nd Olympiad.” Indeed, let there later be as many as one pleases who wholly approve Pagius’s judgments about Africanus’s passages once discovered; nevertheless, no one is ignorant what Epiphanius long ago and Kepler and Petavius in our own age thought of the year of the Passion: namely, that Christ died in the year which is the thirty-first in the Dionysian era. [Col. 0611D] What if, then, one of their followers, wishing precisely this, should assert that the same passages of Africanus point to that result as well, because under the common hypotheses the second year of the 202nd Olympiad partly corresponds to the thirty-first year of the Dionysian era, and yet under Africanus’s peculiar calculations it was the fourth year of the same Olympiad? Then from that eclipse a year of the Dionysian era other than the twenty-ninth would be established as the year of the Lord’s crucifixion; and, what is more, this would be done without any correction of Africanus’s words and while otherwise following Pagius himself. If the matter is not yet sufficiently clear, the following diagram will make it clear and fully explained:

[Col. 0612B] + Christ crucified at the beginning of this year, according to Petavius and others.

We conclude, therefore, unless other considerations are summoned to aid, at most this: even if the passages which Pagius attributes to Africanus are Africanus’s, the learned man’s argument, drawn from that extraordinary eclipse and by which he believed it certain that the Passion belongs properly and uniquely to the twenty-ninth year of the Dionysian era, will always be ineffective.

But well then! Behold an opportunity, even now, for the whole force of Pagius’s argument to be preserved and restored unimpaired. Suppose that all and each of the matters which, long before the publication of Pagius’s recent volume on Baronius’s annals, we had publicly discussed and had also arranged in chronological tables, in order that a greater light might illuminate our arguments—matters which we rejoiced to find largely confirmed by him himself, but on which we nevertheless postponed giving our final opinion until we could obtain and weigh certain notable learned studies more or less favoring the contrary view—suppose, I say, that all these things, which we do not think, were nothing: [Col. 0612C] behold whence even now the whole efficacy of Pagius’s argument can be maintained intact.

In Jerome, Africanus says that Christ suffered not simply in the second year of the 202nd Olympiad, but also in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar.

First, then, I say, from the fact that according to Africanus Christ was crucified in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, it follows, whether one wishes it or not, that Christ died not in the thirty-first year of the Dionysian era, as Kepler and Petavius wished and as the second diagram seemed to demonstrate, but in the twenty-ninth, as Pagius held and as the first diagram based on Pagius sets before the eyes. The reason is evident: no fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar can fall in the thirty-first year of the Dionysian era; but it falls directly in the twenty-ninth year of that era if one counts, as is customary, from the death of Augustus.

Again, from the fact that according to Africanus Christ suffered both in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar and in the second year of the 202nd Olympiad, it follows no less incontrovertibly, I continue, [Col. 0612D] that wherever Julius Africanus assigns Christ’s death to the second year of the 202nd Olympiad, he does not reckon Olympiads in the customary manner, but in his own peculiar manner—and precisely in the manner first disclosed to the learned world by Pagius: that is, Africanus customarily anticipates by two years the accepted beginning of that Olympiad and of every other. The reason is equally clear: again, no fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar can be said to have coincided with the second year of the 202nd Olympiad under the ordinary reckoning. On the contrary, the fifteenth year of Tiberius from the death of Augustus almost entirely coincides with the second year of the 202nd Olympiad according to the regular anticipations of Africanus observed by Pagius.

That being so, it necessarily remains clear, against the view of Petavius and his like, that from genuine testimonies of Africanus compared with one another Christ suffered in the twenty-ninth year of the Christian era, when the two Gemini were consuls. Nor should we therefore, if Africanus is actually found [Col. 0613A] in Syncellus to have written the same thing that Phlegon wrote in Eusebius’s Latin *Chronicle*—namely, that a great eclipse of the sun, surpassing all others, took place in the fourth year of the 202nd Olympiad, or something of that sort—fail immediately to remember that, following Pagius, it must be corrected in both writers to the fourth year of the 201st Olympiad. Otherwise Julius Africanus would never agree with himself; nor would Julius Africanus and Phlegon ever agree with one another; or, worst of all, Africanus would have to be rejected, and, because of passages in Phlegon, Josephus, Dio, and others, we would have to say that Christ was crucified in the declining part of his thirty-seventh year of age. That opinion will always be most absurd, as we shall show elsewhere, God willing. Pagius’s indicated method must therefore be followed in the passage of Phlegon, for example, in Eusebius, and likewise in all passages of Africanus which at first glance lead elsewhere. But when you wish to consult the *Critical Examination of Baronius’s Annals*, p. 27, no. 10, and p. 28, nos. 13 and 14, for that purpose, we judge it useful for you that, for a fuller elucidation of the whole matter, [Col. 0613B] a third diagram should be printed in a more suitable place.

And what is here said concisely by our Caecilius, to say nothing of others, “when the two Gemini were consuls,” is stated more fully in Tertullian in these words: “This Passion was completed under Tiberius Caesar, when Rubellius Geminus and Rufius Geminus were consuls.” It was quite proper that he should add the names of the consuls by their cognomina for greater clarity and precision. Yet modern learned men remind us that the latter was called not Rufius, nor even Fusius, but Fufius, since he belonged to the Fufian family; nor perhaps did Tertullian write otherwise. Epiphanius certainly does very badly in Heresy 51, making two pairs of consuls out of that single pair: one from the two Gemini, the other from Rufus and Rubellio. Indeed, Tertullian does not merely say, “This Passion was completed under Tiberius Caesar, when Rubellius Geminus and Rufius Geminus were consuls,” but adds subsequently [Col. 0613C]: “on the eighth day before the Kalends of April.” Since his passage so reads, while ours says *post diem decimum Kalendas Aprilis*, it is therefore clear that the entire section (*περιοχή*) of our author was not copied from Tertullian, but from some other writer or writers of the first, second, third, or early fourth century. The most learned Cuper names many of those who do not agree concerning Christ’s crucifixion under the two Gemini, but are variously divided into contrary opinions; and Columbus, in his order, adduces and explains, among other matters, one or two of their principal views.

When the two Gemini were consuls, when he had risen . . . The Abo edition is much better, placing a full stop (*τελεία στιγμή*) after *consulibus*, thus closing the first period of this chapter and beginning the second: “In the latter times of Tiberius Caesar, as we read written, our Lord Jesus Christ was crucified by the Jews after the tenth day before the Kalends of April, when the two Gemini were consuls. When he had risen on the third day, he gathered together the disciples, whom,” etc. For it also punctuates after *discipulos*; [Col. 0613D] as does the Cambridge edition. Neither is wrong.

He gathered together the disciples. Namely, after giving the two Marys the command to announce his resurrection to the disciples and tell them to go into Galilee, where they would see him, Matthew 28:10–16. Mark, however, reports in chapter 16:14 that Christ came when they were already assembled, as does Luke in chapter 24:36. TOLLIUS. — Theodore Metochites has something similar in his *Roman History*, where he says: Καὶ πρῶτα μὲν ὤφθη δυσὶ γυναιξὶν ἡνίκα καὶ τοὺς πόδας αὐτοῦ κρατήσασαι κατησπάζοντο· ἔπειτα τῇ Μαγδαληνῇ μόνῃ ὀπτάζεται· μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα τῷ κορυφαίῳ Πέτρῳ: “And first he was seen by two women, when they embraced him, clasping his feet; then he appeared to the Magdalene alone; after this, to Peter, the chief.” This is the translation of the distinguished editor Johannes Meursius, although I would prefer “women” to “little women.”

But since, on the one hand, according to the Gospel of St John (chapter 20:11 ff.), Mary Magdalene was alone at the tomb [Col. 0614A] when Christ made his resurrection known to her and said: “Go to my brothers; tell them: I ascend to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God”; while, on the other hand, according to Matthew (chapter 28:8), the women were already far from the tomb when Christ, whose feet they embraced, gave them the command: “Go and tell my brothers to set out for Galilee, where they will see me”; and finally, according to Mark’s most explicit assertion (chapter 16:9), Christ, when he had risen early on the first day after the Sabbath, appeared first to Mary Magdalene: for these reasons, I say, it seems to me that she must be said both to have been the first of all to see the Lord risen from the dead, while she alone was at the tomb, and also to have been the first of all at that time to receive from him the command to announce his resurrection to the disciples. As to the phrase, Baluze notes and proves, col. 303, that it is Lactantian.

[Col. 0614B] Whom fear of arrest. It appears that, having recovered their courage after that first flight, the Apostles came together the following day and on the third day, anxiously and sorrowfully awaiting the outcome of this tragedy. See John chapter 20 and Luke chapter 24, where Christ is said to have come to them in the upper room at Jerusalem on the very day of the resurrection, while Cleopas and his companion were recounting Christ’s appearance to the eleven disciples and others. They had gone there and shut themselves in for fear of the Jews. This presents a great and almost inextricable discrepancy from Matthew and Mark: the former relates that the disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain indicated by Jesus; the latter that Christ appeared to the disciples after the two had recounted to others what had happened to them. TOLLIUS. — Those who consider all the matters embraced in the preceding observation of that most distinguished man at one glance, and as events of three Julian days—namely, the day of the Passion, on which Jesus Christ was placed in the tomb toward evening; the next day, on which he lay buried throughout; [Col. 0614C] and the day of the resurrection, at dawn of which he came to life again—will find Tollius’s earlier difficulty not merely great and almost inextricable, as he called it, but truly insoluble.

For thus, according to Matthew (chapter 28:1, 2, 5, 7), on that very day of the resurrection the angel said to the women at first light: “Go quickly; tell his disciples that he has risen, and behold, he goes before you into Galilee.” Then Jesus himself said a little later to the same women (ibid., 10): “Go, tell my brothers to go into Galilee; there they will see me.” Accordingly, they all went into Galilee that same day of the resurrection, to the mountain appointed by Christ, and there saw and worshipped the Lord. Yet, according to the other Evangelists, evening had already come (Luke 24:29, 33; John 20:2, 5, 7), and the Apostles were eating supper (Mark 16:14), if they had not already supped (Luke 24:41, 42), when Christ first showed himself to their company. When, then, did they set out for Galilee that day and behold and worship Christ on the mountain appointed for them? Finally, after supper, because not before? But before supper no reason other than that they might see Christ there had been conveyed to them by the women for going into Galilee. Why then would they have gone out after supper, at which time they had already seen him, for the sake of seeing him in Galilee? What, I ask, was the purpose of so untimely a departure? Since this is no insignificant knot, it is worth the effort, the occasion having been given, to untie it as far as lies in our power.

[Col. 0614D] So far as we can see, on the day of the resurrection Christ commanded the household of the apostles once (Matthew 28:2, 5, 7) and again (ibid., 10), through others, to set out εἰς Γαλιλαίαν, “into Galilee,” in order to see him. Since they doubted his resurrection from the dead, they neglected throughout the whole day to take the road in that direction. Therefore Christ finally came to them at night; nor did they any longer on that day, or on any of the immediately following days, think of going to Galilee because of Christ’s stated command, much less proceed there. This was consequently done by them only after at least eight days, [Col. 0615A] whether through mere chance, as we commonly say, or rather through a new command of Christ. Compare John 20:19, 26 with 21:1 ff. And when Christ was in Galilee at that time, he instructed them to assemble with him at a certain mountain in Galilee on a definite day, perhaps even at a definite hour, not while absent and by others’ agency, but himself and in person.

On that occasion the apostles, obeying their master’s words, went to the mountain of Galilee which he had designated for them, Matthew 28:16; and when they were still approaching it from a distance, most of them worshipped Jesus as soon as they saw him, verse 17. Some, however, refrained (ibid.) because they hesitated whether it was really he. That is, their sight was less sharp than that of the others; they were not calling into doubt anew his resurrection, which they had seen confirmed by so many most certain proofs, but only his presence. Unless they were entirely certain of it, they did not wish to show any religious honor to the man whom they beheld indistinctly and whom others, standing before them, worshipped as Jesus and as God. Compare John 16:4 ff. Thus the saying so often used by sacred chronologists must now be impressed upon us: “Distinguish the times, and you will reconcile the Scriptures.”

I admit that the matter would in some degree be clearer if, just as we read in Luke 24:36, Ταῦτα δὲ αὐτῶν λαλούντων, αὐτὸς ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἔστη ἐν μέσῳ αὐτῶν—“And while they were speaking these things, Jesus himself stood in their midst”—so Matthew’s words were: Οἱ δὲ ἕνδεκα μαθηταὶ ἐπορεύθησαν εἰς τὴν Γαλιλαίαν εἰς τὸ ὄρος οὗ ἐτάξατο αὐτοῖς αὐτὸς ὁ Ἰησοῦς: “But the eleven disciples went into Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus himself had appointed them to be present.” Yet, to say nothing else, no one even moderately learned in Greek will deny that the present reading has the same effect.

But as to that other question—how it can be true that Christ came to the disciples in the upper room at Jerusalem on the very day of the resurrection, while Cleopas and his companion were recounting to the eleven apostles and the others how Christ had appeared to them, whereas Mark reports the contrary [Col. 0615C], namely that Christ did not appear to the disciples until after the two had related to the others what had happened to them—here is how we untie this knot also, lest, when it is necessary and within our power, we fail Sacred History.

According to Mark (ch. XVI, 12), Christ appeared in another form than that to which he had been accustomed before his death, to two members of the body of believers who were going into the country. But these same men, if we turn to Luke (ch. XXIV), had scarcely recognized Jesus *in the breaking of the bread* (*ἐν τῇ κλάσει τοῦ ἄρτου*) and seen him vanish from their sight when they returned without delay to Jerusalem. There they found the apostles and their companions assembled, saying: “The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Simon.” Then Cleopas and his companion related what had also happened to them on the road and at supper, and at that moment brought their account to an end.

But now, if we return to Mark (ch. XVI, 12, 13, 11), very many of those to whom these things were being reported—who had previously heard similar accounts from others and had not believed them—did not believe even Cleopas and his companion. Hence all began again, and ever more earnestly, to discuss [Col. 0615D] and converse about these matters. And while they were thus speaking, says Luke (ch. XXIV, 36)—understanding by this both those whom Cleopas and his companion had met, and Cleopas himself with his fellow traveller—while they were discussing these same matters, Jesus himself stood in their midst. Thus Christ both presented himself alive and visible to the apostles a considerable time after the first account of Cleopas and his companion, and did so while they were all still discussing and disputing among themselves concerning the appearances mentioned by Mark.

If further proof is needed, three considerations establish this entire solution. First, that *ταυτὰ*, with a grave accent, often means not “these things,” but “the same things,” among competent authors—standing, that is, for *τὰ αὐτά*. Secondly, accents occur in none of the older manuscript codices of the New Testament; and therefore, if the sense of the passage or the demands of truth require it, one may as easily read *ταυτὰ* with a grave accent as *ταῦτα* with a circumflex. Thirdly, it is by no means likely [Col. 0616A] that at the first indication of the disbelief of the apostles or others, Cleopas and the man who was returning from the country with him—who had himself there seen Christ with his own eyes—would have fallen coldly silent, or turned the conversation to wholly different subjects, taking little concern for the truth and importance of the appearance granted to them. Rather, as the matter deserved, they would have persisted; as would likewise those who, when they entered the upper room, had said to them: “Christ has truly risen and has been seen by Simon.” I should therefore not hesitate to translate, as above: “While they were speaking of the same things”—that is, deliberating and disputing about them—“Christ himself stood in their midst.”

But these matters have led us too far afield. Let us return to our author. In speaking of Christ’s disciples, whom fear of his arrest had put to flight, he does not at all mean that the apostles feared Christ might be arrested; for it is certain from the Gospel that they fled only after his arrest. Rather, he means the fear that arose in them from the event of the arrest itself. See Matt. XXVI, 50, 56. Add [Col. 0616B] also what we shall note below at no. 36.

**“They were.” Read: “They had been.” BOHERELLUS.**—So far am I from opposing my most learned friend on this point that I have always thought it should be emended thus, being led both by the preceding words, “He gathered the disciples whom fear of his arrest had put to flight” (he uses the pluperfect, not the perfect), and especially by these words of Lactantius, *Institutes*, IV, ch. 20: “When the disciples had again been gathered, he opened the writings of Holy Scripture—that is, the mysteries of the prophets—which before he suffered could in no way be understood.” For there too one does not find “could have been understood.” But perhaps Columbus anticipated both of us in this correction. For this passage is printed no differently in the Abo edition, and it instructs us to read it as our conjecture proposes, although one looks in vain for the reason in his notes.

**“And he ordained them.”** They had already been ordained by Christ in Matthew ch. X, but with a mission restricted to the Jews. Therefore, in order that the word of God might also be preached to the Gentiles, they required a new [Col. 0616C] ordination extending to *all nations* (*πάντα τὰ ἔθνη*), Matt. XXVIII, 19; Luke XXIII, 47. TOLLIUS.—I approve this entirely; and, so help me God, I am glad to be able from this to recognize that most celebrated man. Whatever I have hitherto observed in disagreement with him, I have done neither out of malice nor envy—far from it—but solely from my supreme zeal and candour toward truth, as is permitted to scholars and critics.

Moreover, just as our author undoubtedly used “he ordained them” for what Paul would have called appointing them ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God, or something similar (see First Corinthians ch. IV, v. 1), so Suetonius, in *Vespasian*, ch. 23, writes: “When one of his dear attendants, having requested a stewardship for a certain man as though for a brother, had been put off, he summoned the candidate himself, exacted the sum which he had agreed with his patron, and without delay ordained him”—that is, plainly, he established or created him as a steward. Hugh of Fleury relates that Constantius “ordained Licinius Caesar of the Spains” [Col. 0616D]; and although that most eminent scholar pronounces the statement wholly remote from the truth, it is nevertheless an entirely certain example of the expression we have here, even though found in a writer of a later age. Baluzius supplies a third example from Lactantius.

**“The solemn discipline of the New Testament.”** That is, Baptism. For in the ancient Church its administration was solemn at Eastertide; on this matter see certain remarks in the notes on Ausonius’ Paschal poem. TOLLIUS.—The distinguished French translator, Maucroix, understood this of the whole discipline of the New Testament. But, in my opinion, wrongly. For, first, this writer touches in the preceding context only upon those things done by Christ after the resurrection. Yet he did not, for example, institute the Eucharist after his rising from the dead—he had done that before his death—but baptism, at least insofar as it concerned all nations, Matt. XXVIII, 19.

Moreover, when in our author, after “And he ordained them and instructed them for preaching his dogma and doctrine,” and again after the next words, “establishing the solemn discipline of the [Col. 0617A] New Testament,” there immediately follows, “When this office had been fulfilled, a storm-cloud enveloped him and bore him, withdrawn from sight, into heaven. And thence the disciples … were scattered through all the earth to preach the Gospel, as their Master and Lord had commanded them”: what could be more evident, first of all, than that “he ordained them and instructed them for preaching his dogma and doctrine” is precisely what we read in Matthew: “Jesus came to them and spoke, saying: All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me; therefore go and make disciples of all nations”? Then what could be clearer than that “thereupon establishing the solemn discipline of the New Testament” likewise is what immediately follows in the same Matthew: “Baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”? And finally, what is more obvious than that “when this office had been fulfilled, a storm-cloud enveloped him and bore him, withdrawn from the sight of men, into heaven” is again precisely what is written in Mark (ch. XXVIII, 19) [Col. 0617B]: “After he had spoken these things, he was taken up into heaven”; and in Luke in Acts: “And when he had said these things, while they were looking on, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him and took him from their eyes”? Therefore by that discipline, called here solemn and belonging to the New Testament, we see nothing that can better be understood—though not from Christ’s institution or the practice of Christianity’s earliest times, but from the usage, for example, of the fourth century in which our Caecilius was writing—than Baptism.

Take care, however, not to suppose, because the Paschal verses of Ausonius of Bordeaux begin:

> The holy solemnities of saving Christ return,

and because, in Thessaly of old, according to Socrates, baptism was administered only on the days of Easter, and because, according to Zonaras, the Church used to celebrate baptisms on Holy Saturday, and finally because Basil’s *Homily on Holy Baptism* does not point elsewhere, that baptism was not solemnly administered in the ancient Church at any other season of the year than Easter [Col. 0617C]. In very many places those baptized at Easter were also baptized at Pentecost, and in some places on the day of Epiphany as well—indeed, more frequently on Epiphany than at Easter, as we learn from the Decrees of Pope Leo I, title 7.

Only those who, following a particular rite received from their predecessors, more commonly baptized on Epiphany—or, as they call it elsewhere, “the Epiphanies,” and sometimes even “the Epiphanias”—were condemned by that pontiff, because, he says, they adopted an irrational novelty and, confusing the mysteries of the two seasons, believed there to be no difference between the day on which Christ was worshipped by the Magi and the day on which Christ rose from the dead. Indeed, Peter of Blois says: “The Church has forbidden under anathema anyone to baptize on the day of Epiphany, unless an emergency should intervene.”

The superstition of those who, like the Thessalians mentioned shortly before from Socrates, would not approach Baptism except *at Easter* (*ἐν τῷ Πάσχα*), has, so far as I know, been notably condemned by no council or bishop [Col. 0617D] of the Roman Church; but it was censured by John Chrysostom, *Homily 1 on Acts of the Apostles*. Those who customarily baptized on both Easter and Pentecost considered Easter the more solemn day; hence perhaps the “solemn discipline” of our passage is so called *pre-eminently* (*κατ’ ἐξοχήν*). Tertullian says: “Then Easter provides the more solemn occasion for Baptism, since … the passion of the Lord, in which we are baptized, has been fulfilled … Thereafter Pentecost is the most joyful”—or, as others read, “the most extensive”—“period for administering the washings.”

Finally, the custom by which both days were consecrated to baptism seems to us to have been by far the most common. It was received by the African churches, according to Tertullian’s testimony cited above; and Siricius states it expressly in his decretal letter to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona: “There follows, concerning the various times for baptizing, according to each person’s pleasure, a blameworthy and corrigible confusion, whereas the Lord’s Pascha, together with its Pentecost, particularly claims this privilege for itself, both among [Col. 0618A] us and among all Churches. On these days alone of the year it is fitting that the general sacraments of baptism be bestowed upon those coming to the faith.”

**“When this office had been fulfilled.”** I would prefer: “when it had been completed.” For this was why Christ had been sent by the Father into the world. “Faithful to him who made him” (*πιστὸς τῷ ποιήσαντι αὐτόν*), Heb. XI, 2, where he is also called “the apostle and high priest of our confession.” TOLLIUS.—The French language has very many expressions of this sort. For that reason, and because we must also acknowledge an infinite variety of Latin modes of expression, I would scarcely dare agree that there is an error in *repleto* (“fulfilled”); as for the sense of “office” here, see Columbus, col. 393.

**“A storm-cloud.”** This is Lactantius’ more rhetorical expression; he has not here forgotten the art that he taught, and it corresponds somewhat to Luke’s *was borne up* (*ἀνεφέρετο*), ch. XXIV, 51. TOLLIUS.

**“They were scattered over all the earth to preach the Gospel, as their Master and Lord had commanded them,” etc.** This passage is highly noteworthy, if we wish—as we may, and because of what was said above must—to ascertain more carefully what the author meant by “all the earth,” and shortly afterward by “all provinces and cities” [Col. 0618B]. “The disciples were scattered over all the earth,” he begins, “as their Master and Lord had commanded them.” But the Lord had not commanded the apostles to scatter for the sake of the Gospel merely among the peoples subject to the Romans; rather, he commanded them to go to all peoples without any limitation. Thus in Matthew XXVIII, 19: “Go,” he says, “teach all nations”; and more explicitly in Mark (ch. XVI, 15): “Go into all the world, preach the Gospel to every creature”—the Redeemer, that is, of the entire world, not merely of that portion subject to Roman rule.

Accordingly, when our author says that from the Lord’s ascension the apostles were scattered over all the earth to preach the Gospel, as their Master had commanded them, and immediately afterward says of them that “for twenty-five years, until the beginning of Nero’s reign, they laid the foundations of churches through all provinces and cities,” he means, in the broad sense, the whole inhabited earth and likewise all the provinces and cities of the whole earth—not strictly the Roman Empire, or simply all the provinces and cities of the Roman world.

This is exactly Theodore’s sense in his *Dialogue on the Laws*: “Those fishermen and tax-collectors of ours, and that cobbler of ours”—the cobbler (*ὁ σκυτοτόμος*) being Paul, thus designated—“brought the evangelical law to every nation. Not only did they persuade Romans and those who live under Roman rule (*καὶ τοὺς ὑπὸ τούτων τελοῦντας*), but also Scythians and Sarmatians, Indians besides, Ethiopians, Persians, Seres, Hyrcanians, Britons, Cimmerians, and Germans; and, to say it once for all, the entire human race and all nations, to receive the laws of the Crucified.”

[Col. 0618C] Add, if we descend briefly to certain particulars, that Scythia, for example, and India were never reckoned among the provinces of the Roman Empire under Nero’s predecessor Claudius. And among the other Fathers there are some who, though in some measure pseudonymous, have written not only that Philip, after the Saviour’s ascension, preached the Gospel among the Gentiles in Scythia for only twenty-one years, and then returned to Asia by revelation; but also, concerning Thomas, that the Gospel was preached by him to the Parthians and Medes, Persians, Hyrcanians, Bactrians, and Indians, while he held the eastern region and penetrated the interior of the Gentiles [Col. 0618D]—for the reading of Freculphus, which we follow, is far preferable to the Isidorian reading. They further state, what is more, that Philip was crucified and stoned in the twelfth year of Claudius. Indeed, some, under the name of Melito of Sardis, have handed down that in the second year after the Lord’s ascension the apostles were divided throughout the world and proclaimed the Gospel in foreign provinces.

The opinion of all these writers, therefore, must be either precisely that of this author or at least exceedingly similar: namely, that Christ’s faith was announced far beyond Roman borders before the beginning of Nero’s reign. Whether this was rightly or wrongly held would require a long inquiry; and [Col. 0619A] perhaps no one of even moderate prudence would dare define how far it had then reached. The subject is so obscure, and authorities disagree among themselves: for example, our Caecilius here; Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, III, ch. 1, compared with the end of book II; Origen, *Homily* 28 on Matthew; Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, in the section on Christ’s birth, near the end; and finally Augustine, in his eightieth letter to Hesychius, not far from the close. Let it therefore now suffice that we have, to the best of our ability, brought to light our author’s meaning, which will be explained still better in chapter three.

**“Master and Lord.”** This unquestionably refers to Christ. Columbus therefore preferred, without doubt, that both words begin with a capital letter. But that is of no consequence. Of some consequence, however, is the fact that Lactantius likewise calls him “Master God,” in these words: “The disciples, scattered through the provinces, everywhere laid the foundations of the Church, themselves also performing great and almost incredible miracles in the name of their Master God.” Thus the remarks cited by us above, col. 603, in support of this conjecture [Col. 0619B] are confirmed: “Those who mocked God lie prostrate.”

**“And for twenty-five years, until the beginning of Nero’s reign.”** The calculation is clear. For according to this writer Jesus Christ suffered on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, when the two Gemini were consuls; and under the same consuls, having remained with the disciples only forty days after the resurrection, he was taken up into heaven. Thereafter, according to the same author, the apostles, scattered over all the earth, laid the foundations of churches for twenty-five years, until the beginning of Nero’s reign. But from the season of the year in which Jesus Christ was received into heaven under the consulship of the two Gemini to the beginning of Nero’s rule, there are only twenty-five years, five months, and a few days. Our author has rounded the number, as is customary. The Abo edition rightly places a break after “for twenty-five years”; Baluzius has several remarks, not without importance, on these words, col. 303.

**“Through all provinces and cities.”** That is, if Maucroix’s French translation is to be followed, through all the provinces [Col. 0619C] and cities of the Roman Empire. Nor is there any doubt that below, ch. 23, “a census was once sent into the provinces and cities” is to be understood of a census sent into the provinces and cities of the Roman Empire; nor likewise that, in ch. 7, “provinces cut into fragments, individual regions, and almost cities themselves, crushed under many governors and still more offices,” means the provinces, regions, and cities of the Roman Empire.

But here, because of what was said above in col. 618, we cannot avoid supplying rather from the preceding phrase “all the earth,” taken broadly, as we have just observed. Thus, just as in our author “the Church established” must be understood differently in ch. 1 near the end and in ch. 12 about the middle, so likewise “through all provinces and cities” in one place and “everywhere into provinces and cities” in another signify different things according to the character of the contexts. Add what we shall say in this same chapter, col. 626, on the word “justice,” and also cols. 633 and 635, on “removed” (*translatum*, of Nero) and “removed” (*translatos*, of the two prophets). [Col. 0619D]

**“They laid the foundations of churches.”** See by all means both Lactantius’ words quoted above in col. 618, and Baluzius, col. 303, and Columbus, col. 394, on these words.

**“And when Nero had already begun to reign, Peter came to Rome.”** Here, reader, is a passage which we may rightly call combative and invincible against Baronius and countless other, more vehement defenders of the long twenty-five-year chair of St Peter in Rome. For Baronius says in the *Annals*, under the year of Christ 44, no. 13: “It is certain and well established by the testimony of all that Peter, prince of the apostles, came to Rome in the second year of that same Augustus, Claudius.” Our author, on the contrary: “Peter came to Rome when Nero had already begun to reign.” Hence, after this work was once discovered or published, those weighty judgments of learned Protestant and Roman Catholic writers which we hasten partly to quote and partly to indicate.

[Col. 0620A]

> “By the intervention of this Treatise, at last we are freed from the inveterate error concerning St Peter’s twenty-five-year pontificate.”

(*Preface to the Oxford edition—or rather, the preface of John Fell, the most pious and reverend bishop of Oxford while he lived. As his outstanding holiness of life, his most generous beneficence toward the poor, and his remarkable zeal for advancing sound learning have always commanded my just veneration, so may his memory, I pray, be eternally blessed.*)

> “The account that he gives of Saint Peter’s coming to Rome cuts off the fable of his being there for five and twenty years.”

(*The preface which Burnet, himself also afterwards, and with fullest right, bishop of Salisbury, then not yet a bishop, prefixed to his vernacular translation.*) Its sense is approximately this: What Lactantius recounts in this book about the blessed Peter’s arrival in Rome entirely deprives of further currency the fable by which they idly asserted that he sat in Rome for twenty-five years.

[Col. 0620B]

> “Eusebius in his *Chronicle* places Peter’s arrival at Rome in the second year of Claudius, an opinion followed by Baronius. But, as Valesius says in his notes on Eusebius, book II, ch. 16, this opinion seems refuted by the *Acts of the Apostles*, from which it is clear that Peter remained always in Judaea and Syria until the last year of King Agrippa. When Agrippa had imprisoned Peter at Jerusalem, he himself was shortly afterward destroyed at Caesarea by divine justice pursuing him, as Luke relates. Since Agrippa died in the fourth year of Claudius, as all agree, Peter could not have set out for Rome before that year. But the author of the Alexandrian Chronicle places Peter’s arrival in Rome still later. For he writes that Paul came to Jerusalem because of the controversy over circumcision in the sixth year of Claudius, and that in that year the Jerusalem council was held, the apostles not yet having separated from one another. Therefore, in his view Peter did not set out for Rome before the seventh year of Claudius. [Col. 0620C]

> “Finally Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, ch. 2, says that Peter came to Rome when Nero was already reigning, and this opinion seems more probable. For Eusebius is not to be given great credit in papal chronology, as we shall show below. It is better here to set forth the words of Lactantius just cited: ‘The apostles for twenty-five years, until the beginning of Nero’s reign, etc. … And when Nero had already begun to reign, Peter came to Rome, etc. …’ From these twenty-five years, which belong equally to the preaching of all the apostles, there seems to have arisen the opinion of the twenty-five years commonly attributed to St Peter in the Roman see. Those who wish Peter to have come to Rome in Claudius’ reign are compelled to invent a double journey of his to the City, and likewise a double contest with Simon Magus: first in the time of Claudius, then in Nero’s reign. Yet this has been handed down by none of the ancients, as Baluzius says in his notes on Lactantius. This opinion is also defended by Papebrochius in the chronological-historical essay appended to the catalogue of the ancient [Col. 0620D] pontiffs, and by Louis Du Four in his manuscript observations on papal chronology, which he kindly communicated to me.”

(Pagi, *Critique of Baronius’ Annals*, pp. 39–40, under A.D. 5536 of the Greek-Roman era, nos. 3–4.)

Would that he had indicated with equal precision the passage of Papebrochius that he had in mind. For so far we have been unable to find anywhere in the said essay, or in its appendices, a passage in which Papebrochius refutes or simply denies that double journey of Peter to the City. On the contrary, he says: “I shall therefore maintain,” p. 12, no. 4, “that Peter indeed came to Rome in the second year of Claudius (which fact deceived Eusebius), but that, because Simon Magus’ influence with the emperor prevailed … he soon returned to Syria and remained there until, by divine warning—if we believe Metaphrastes—or of his own accord, he again returned to Rome … Therefore I wish to suppose that the apostle flew to Rome at the beginning of the year 50, and that there in January [Col. 0621A] he established the Chair for himself and his successors.”

Papebrochius therefore doubles Peter’s arrival in the City in that passage, as is his custom, and indeed assigns both arrivals to the reign of Claudius: the first as early as Claudius’ second year, the second not earlier than his tenth. Where, then, is Papebrochius’ agreement with our writer and Pagi, who place Peter’s arrival at Rome only in Nero’s reign? Perhaps, however, Pagi means that whatever Papebrochius held concerning Peter’s two journeys to Rome under Claudius, he did not therefore agree with the common opinion that Peter presided as bishop in Rome for twenty-five years, but assigned him only fifteen, and thus, in his own words, deducted a full decade from the excessive number of twenty-five years. But if so, the most distinguished Pagi would have written somewhat differently from the way he did.

Baluzius’ note to which he referred stands in our edition, col. 303, on the words “for twenty-five years.” Because of this same passage, long before Pagi, the Oxford and Cambridge editions stated:

[Col. 0621B]

> “From this passage Baluzius refutes those who assign Peter twenty-five years of presidency over the Roman Church. When they saw that nearly every escape had been taken from them, they were reduced to inventing a double journey of Peter to Rome, one in the time of Claudius and the other in Nero’s reign, contrary to the testimony of all who have committed anything concerning it to writing.”

Let Cuper and Columbus now be consulted in their respective places, if anything remains to be said; but above all, when one wishes to investigate the truth of the matter more deeply, the truly learned and laborious dissertation of the most distinguished Friedrich Spanheim on Peter’s rashly credited journey to Rome, and the illustrious Salmasius’ treatise on the Primacy of Peter.

**“Peter came to Rome.”** See Scaliger on that arrival of Peter in his notes on the New Testament. TOLLIUS.—Scaliger’s passage concerns John XVIII, 31: “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death” (*Ἡμῖν οὐκ ἔξεστιν ἀποκτεῖναι οὐδένα*). There, with remarkable—not, I would say, confidence, but soundness of aim (*εὐστοχίᾳ*) and sagacity—the eminent man, to whom our author had never become known, anticipated near the end, in almost the same words, the very point which our author would later make: “From Christ’s reception into heaven to the fourth year of Nero it is absolutely certain that Peter did not come to Rome.”

**“And having performed certain miracles which, by the power of God himself and by authority given him by God, he performed.”** Before all else, it is better to punctuate with the Abo edition: “and having performed certain miracles which, by the power of God himself, and by authority given him by God, he performed …” I frankly confess that I do not know what miracles are here to be understood in the second place.

Perhaps it is because, whatever Arnobius, Sulpicius Severus, George Metochites, and others recount specifically concerning miracles performed by Peter among the Romans, our author descends to nothing of the sort, but refers only generally to “certain miracles performed …” Or perhaps because Arnobius and Sulpicius Severus mention only Simon Magus’ fall from heaven to earth, through Peter’s prayer to God—or even Paul’s—[Col. 0621D] whereas George Metochites expressly adds that at the entrance to that sorcerer’s house a dog was chained which devoured anyone entering to see its master without permission. Peter, wishing on one occasion to visit Simon Magus, ordered the dog to enter first and announce in a human voice to its master that Peter stood at the doors; and the dog immediately did so, to the astonishment of everyone in the house. Or, thirdly, because these miracles smell wholly of fable—whence the very learned Cuper below will call the first a fable, although he regards another explanation as more probable—whereas Christ had promised that miracles of a very different kind would be performed through the apostles, and such miracles they did perform, indeed such as the Fathers believed had been performed by them, as is evident from their homilies and commentaries on Acts. It is therefore quite possible, I say, that our Caecilius referred rather to miracles of better attestation performed at Rome through Peter than to those just recounted, which are not free from suspicion of falsehood. Or finally, although the Fathers ought to have credited only accounts of genuine and various miracles, they nevertheless accepted fabulous accounts more often than was fitting, as the same examples more than sufficiently show.

But whatever miracles our author may have intended, the Fathers certainly believed that even doubtful—or, if one prefers, plainly fabulous—accounts, when they accepted them as true without deceit, had been divinely performed, as was fitting. Nor does Peter speak otherwise concerning a true miracle in Acts—that is, after the famous healing of a certain man lame from his mother’s womb: “Men of Israel, why do you marvel at this? Or why do you fix your eyes upon us, as though by our own power or piety we had made this man walk? Through faith in the name of the Prince of life, his name has strengthened this man whom you see and know.” Likewise Orosius, concerning the miracles of all the apostles: “Pilate … reported to the emperor Tiberius and to the senate concerning Christ’s passion and resurrection, and the powers which followed [Col. 0622B], whether performed by Christ himself or performed by his disciples in his name.” Indeed, above all other testimonies, the preface attributed to Julius Africanus to the Apostolic History of Abdias says: “Whether the apostles displayed great miracles among the peoples or lesser ones, these are not to be attributed to human frailty; rather, we must faithfully confess that the one and same Lord Jesus Christ performs them, who dwells in them through good will and purity of mind.”

**“He converted many to justice.”** The expression is taken, unless I am mistaken, from Gabriel’s words to Zechariah concerning John the Baptist: “that he may convert … the unbelieving”—or, as others prefer, “the disobedient”—“to the prudence of the just.” Some may therefore perhaps at first glance suppose that “justice” here is nothing other than that same prudence of the just. But Baluzius, col. 303, better and beyond doubt teaches from Lactantius and Sulpicius Severus what should here be understood by the name “justice.”

[Col. 0622C]

**“And a faithful temple for God,” etc.** That is, the body of Christians. Oxford and Cambridge editions. Excellent.

**“When this was reported to Nero.”** Lactantius proceeds here in such a way that I find his good faith wanting. For the circumstances were very different from what he presents. The persecution occurred in order to divert onto Christians the odium of the burning of the city. Nor do the dates agree; indeed, to say it briefly, these statements are manifestly false. TOLLIUS.—Certainly correct, for those who have read Cornelius Tacitus and Sulpicius Severus and think them great authors—or the only authors to whom one may attend.

Tacitus, discussing the burning of Rome in the year 717 from the founding of the City, when Gaius Lecanius and Marcus Licinius were consuls, writes: “But neither human aid, nor the emperor’s largesses, nor propitiations of the gods removed the infamy that the fire was believed to have been ordered. Therefore, to abolish the rumour, Nero produced as culprits and subjected to the most elaborate punishments those whom the populace called Christians, hated for their crimes.” Similarly Sulpicius Severus: “When the multitude of Christians had now grown abundant, it happened that Rome was consumed by fire, while Nero was staying at Antium. But everyone’s opinion turned the blame for the fire against the emperor, and it was believed that he had sought the glory of rebuilding the city. Nothing prevented the belief that the fire had been ordered by him. Therefore he turned the odium onto the Christians, and most cruel tortures were inflicted upon the innocent; indeed, new kinds of deaths were devised: covered in the skins of beasts, they perished by the tearing of dogs; many were fastened to crosses or burned in flames; most were reserved so that, when daylight had failed, they might be burned for nocturnal illumination. This was the beginning of cruelty against Christians.”

Thus both writers. Yet it is already more than sufficiently clear from this alone that Cornelius Tacitus and Sulpicius Severus must in this matter be counted as only one and the same witness: the several words of Sulpicius enclosed in brackets are read in almost exactly the same number of syllables in Tacitus after the passage we transcribed from his *Annals*. We wish this to be observed before all else, lest anyone suppose that we are at present properly pressed [Col. 0623A] by a double authority rather than a single one.

Afterward, even if we were pressed by two witnesses, Tollius himself, I know, will admit that this author could never have encountered and read Sulpicius Severus’ *Sacred History*. Why? Because Tollius himself everywhere attributes this entire work, whatever it may be, to Lactantius; and he knows both when it was written—namely, when Licinius had not yet begun to rage against Christians, which he undertook only in A.D. 320—and how long Lactantius lived, approximately until 326; and finally after what definite year Sulpicius Severus completed his History—namely, not before the year 400, when Stilicho and Aurelian were consuls, nearly eighty years after Lactantius’ death. Thus there is, so far, no bad faith in our writer.

As for Tacitus, who was composing his *Annals* under the emperor Hadrian, our Caecilius could indeed have read him. But what if he nevertheless never saw him? Or [Col. 0623B] saw him indeed, but did not remember him when he ought? Or even read him and remembered him well when writing of the matters in question, but preferred to follow other authors? Whatever may be said of these three possibilities, will our author therefore rightly be found wanting in good faith, or shall the things read here be manifestly false? Let whoever wishes say so with that learned man; as I see the matter, I scruple to do so.

For, first, Suetonius, a writer as weighty and qualified as anyone else, records both that Rome was set ablaze by Nero and that Christians suffered persecution under him, yet not only does he fail to mention the two events together in one and the same chapter—or at least to mention the former event somewhere before the latter as something which afforded the occasion for it—but, on the contrary, he mentions the latter in chapter sixteen in these terms: “Christians, a class of men given to a new and harmful superstition, were subjected to punishments.” He mentions the former only in chapter thirty-eight, in these words: “But he spared neither the people nor the walls of his native city. When someone said in ordinary conversation, ‘When I am dead, let the earth be mingled with fire’ [Ἐμοῦ θανόντος γαῖα μιχθήτω πυρί], ‘Rather,’ he said, ‘while I am alive’ [ἐμοῦ ζῶντος], and he acted altogether accordingly. For, as though offended by the ugliness of the old buildings and the narrowness and winding courses of the streets, he set fire to the city so openly,” and so forth. In neither place, to put it briefly, does Suetonius give even the slightest indication that the persecution of Christians arose from that conflagration of Rome; he merely states generally in the first passage that Christians were afflicted under Nero as a class of men devoted, forsooth, to a new and harmful superstition.

Next, although in the Latin *Chronicle* of Eusebius—or rather, of Jerome—the two events are related in a different order, Jerome nevertheless assigns the fire only to Nero’s tenth year, with this note: “Nero, in order to behold the likeness of burning Troy, set fire to the greater part of the city of Rome.” But with respect to the persecution of Christians, we find it transmitted to posterity only in [Col. 0623D] the fourteenth year of that same Nero, and in this extremely simple account: “Nero was the first who, in addition to all his crimes, also instituted a persecution against Christians, in which Peter and Paul gloriously died at Rome.” Thus Jerome plainly relates the fire and the persecution as completely separate matters, which he judged to have had no relation of cause and effect [σχέσις] to one another.

Yet we shall undoubtedly understand this better if we turn, to continue speaking in this fashion, from Jerome’s Latin *Chronicle* to Eusebius’s Greek *Chronicle*, or even to Eusebius’s own *Ecclesiastical History*, in which men of outstanding learning rightly declare that he was more exact than in the *Chronicle*. There we shall first find the persecution under Nero alone mentioned in these words: “Nero, in addition to all his crimes, initiated the first persecution against Christians, at the time when the most divine apostles Peter and Paul, having borne witness for Christ, were crowned in the contest” [Νέρων ἐπὶ πᾶσι τοῖς ἀδικήμασιν αὐτοῦ τὸν πρῶτον κατὰ χριστιανῶν ἐνεδείξατο διωγμόν, ἡνίκα Πέτρος καὶ Παῦλος οἱ θειότατοι ἀπόστολοι τῷ ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ μαρτυρήσαντες ἐστέφθησαν ἀγῶνι]. We have just copied a sufficiently suitable translation of these words from Jerome.

But in the *Ecclesiastical History*: “There still remained, indeed, this one thing to be added to all his titles: namely, that he should be called the first Roman emperor hostile to the Christian religion … Thus Nero, chief and standard-bearer of all enemies of the divine Power, raged against the apostles themselves”—so Henry Valesius translates [Ἐνέδει δὲ ἄρα τοῖς πᾶσι …]—again with no mention whatever of the fire from which that persecution of Nero may have blazed forth.

Moreover, what of Orosius, who, as is certain, mentions both disasters in the same order as Jerome, and indeed in the same order in which Jerome does? Did Nero burst forth to persecute the faithful in order that the odium of the burned City might be turned against Christians? Not at all, as will be evident to everyone who has read even once chapter seven of book seven. There Orosius, after a lengthy enumeration of Nero’s crimes—at the end of which procession appear and are listed [Col. 0624B] above all the burning of the city of Rome; then an enormous sum of sesterces exacted from the senate for expenditures; next the plundering of very many senators; thereafter the despoiling of all merchants; then the slaughter of a great many of those same senators; further, the almost complete destruction of the equestrian order; and finally the parricidal murders of his mother, brother, sister, and wife, and the slaughter of all his other relatives and kinsmen—immediately adds:

“He increased this mass of crimes by the rashness of his impiety toward God. For he was the first at Rome to afflict Christians with punishments and deaths, and he commanded that they be tortured with like persecution throughout all the provinces; attempting to extirpate the very name itself, he killed the most blessed apostles of Christ, Peter by the cross and Paul by the sword.”

Accordingly Orosius assigns the whole cause and blame of the persecution of Christians so openly to Nero’s impiety toward God alone that anyone wishing to infer, from the sequence of events which we have set forth after Orosius, that Christians according to Orosius were harassed by Nero in order to divert against them the odium of the burned [Col. 0624C] City, might with like—indeed, better—right trace Nero’s parricides to that same end, since they are mentioned closer at hand in the cited passage [περικοπή] of Orosius.

Furthermore, while Tacitus and Orosius differ so widely from one another concerning the reason why Nero persecuted Christians, Pseudo-Hegesippus leads his readers in still another direction. He reports that Nero rose against Christians because Peter and Paul, teachers of the Christians, had made Nero hostile to them by the power of their deeds; that is, as he later expresses it, they had removed Simon Magus, who was useful to the emperor and necessary to the state.

Finally—and this is more significant—according to Theodore Metochites Nero had persecuted Christians long before the burning of Rome. That disaster occurred in the consulship of Gaius Licanius and Marcus Licinius, says Tacitus, at the time when Nero, Suetonius informs us, was in his twenty-seventh year. Yet according to Theodore Metochites, after Claudius Nero held the empire for fourteen years. [Col. 0624D] “And this utterly impure man, being about seventeen years old, first began the persecution” [ἐτῶν ὡσεὶ δέκα καὶ ἑπτὰ ὤν, πρῶτος τοῦ διωγμοῦ ἤρξατο]. Yet no one hitherto, so far as I know, has professed that the good faith of all these writers—Suetonius, I mean, Eusebius, Jerome, Orosius, and so on—ought to be called into question in this matter.

This being so, far be it from us to suspect, much less assert, that good faith is more lacking in this author; although it may easily happen that he received bad wares from others without bad faith, and afterwards displayed them as good in this very work. Why say more? At the end of this chapter he vigorously rejects madmen and their ravings. And at the beginning of chapter fifty-two: “I speak all these things,” he says, “according to the testimony of those who know; and I believed that they ought to be committed to writing as they occurred, lest either the memory of such great events should perish, or anyone wishing to write history should corrupt [Col. 0625A] the truth by suppressing either their sins against God or God’s judgment against them.” What better indications of good faith could one require in any author?

“But the dates do not agree,” the most distinguished man insists. Let that be so, I reply. Is that invariably a certain and unquestionable proof of bad faith, and never perhaps of involuntary lack of historical knowledge [ἀνιστορησία]? Certainly it proves the latter no less than the former. But besides, why should we grant that the dates do not agree? We cannot even conjecture what this objection means; and indeed they appear otherwise to agree quite well. For the four chronological points advanced here by our Caecilius—that Peter came to Rome when Nero was already reigning; that afterwards he converted many there to righteousness; that Nero then, first of all, after the Church had once been established, persecuted God’s servants; and finally, that Peter and Paul, servants of God, were put to death by Nero’s order in that persecution—not only all cohere with one another in this arrangement, but each is such that the author attaches none to any definite year. Thus, preserving the stated order, they may, if need be, be connected as well with this year as with that.

For example, Peter’s arrival in Rome may be connected with the fourth year of Nero’s reign, if it be altogether certain that Peter did not come to Rome from Christ’s reception into heaven until Nero’s fourth year—a view once maintained by Joseph Scaliger. For then Peter would fittingly have come to Rome for this writer “when Nero was already reigning.” Or it may be connected with the first year of Nero’s reign, if, according to the most recent opinion of Pagi, the first year in which Peter sat in the city of Rome must begin with Nero’s first year as emperor; for in that case too our author would quite properly have written: “When Nero was already reigning, Peter came to Rome.”

In a word, unless, for example, it is shown more clearly than the midday light that Peter was never in Rome—which Tollius does not seem to maintain—or that there was never any persecution under Nero—which Tollius does not deny—or that Peter and Paul never suffered martyrdom under it—which, I think, no one can prove—the dates, in my judgment, will always agree here sufficiently well.

**“With antiquity condemned.”** Not with antiquity simply and, as they say, without qualification, but with the antiquity of error, as Saint Cyprian spoke somewhere. Thus in the preceding century our forefathers, having condemned the antiquity of the errors of the Roman Church, passed over to that very new religion of which our Caecilius has just spoken. Let those, therefore, go their way who cry out that we or our forefathers condemned antiquity. We have reason, following their example and with the applause of the Fathers of the purer Church, to glory that we are Reformers, or sons of Reformers.

> [Note: Col. 0625D]  
> Therefore, by their own admission, they are Reformers and sons of Reformers. A splendid apology for the Roman Church: the religion of Christ, once established and essentially ignorant of error, has always condemned novelty in faith.

**“As he was an execrable … tyrant.”** Thus in chapter IV, Decius the emperor is called “an execrable animal.”

**“And criminal.”** We have already observed that, in the present case, no slight meaning is signified by this epithet; and not without reason, one may say.
