For besides being applied to a tyrant—to Nero, the tyrant of all tyrants and perhaps the greatest of all tyrants—it is preceded by another description of the same man, “execrable,” that is, the most hateful of all descriptions. Finally, Cicero says: “Yet as it must be avoided to turn eloquence to the plague and destruction of the good, so one must not scruple on occasion to defend a criminal man [nocentem], provided he be not wicked and impious.” Since no one can fail to see from this passage that among the Romans *nocens* was sometimes said of one who was wicked and impious, and since in our author “impious hands,” “sacrilegious,” and similar terms occur so often concerning persecutors, what could be clearer than that here *nocens* means the same as wicked, impious, sacrilegious?

Yet, lest you doubt, here is Martial’s most elegant epigram, in which the very word plainly denotes one who is impious [Col. 0626A] and sacrilegious—one might say, conspicuously criminal.

**ON THE FISH OF BAIAE**

Fisherman, we warn you: keep far from the Baian lake,  
lest you depart a guilty man.

These waters are swum by sacred fish,  
who know their master and lick  
that hand than which nothing in the world is greater.

What is more, each has a name and comes when summoned  
by the voice of its own master.

Once, while an impious Libyan, with trembling line,  
drew prey from the deep,  
he was suddenly blinded when his eyes were torn away  
and could not see the fish he had caught.

Now, hating sacrilegious hooks,  
he sits as a petitioner beside the Baian lakes.

But you, while you can, depart innocent;  
cast simple food into the waters  
and revere the consecrated fish.  
(Martial, *Epigrams*, book IV, epigram 30.)

Accordingly, in chapter 1, the “criminal souls” are impious and wicked souls of those who tortured the righteous and deservedly yielded them up amid heavenly blows and torments—souls which worshipped neither the true God nor his servants. Likewise, in chapter XLIX, the “criminal spirit” which Maximinus breathed out by a detestable kind of death was an impious and sacrilegious spirit.

**“To be cut down” (*excidendum*).** The Oxford and Cambridge editions have *exscindendum*. But the reading of the manuscript codex may stand very well. See Columbus, col. 394.

**“And righteousness to be destroyed.”** What our author properly understands by “righteousness” he explains in the following chapter in these words: “But after he had begun to persecute the righteous people,” etc.; and also by these words in chapter IV: “After many years there arose the execrable animal Decius, to harass the Church.” For who but a wicked man persecutes righteousness? Thus “righteousness” here is the Church, or the righteous people, whom you will shortly see called, in this very chapter, the people of God and servants of God.

Sons of rhetoricians know the figure of speech by which *crime* is used for a criminal person, and hundreds of similar instances are encountered every day in all authors. But here scarcely any example, I think, is more apt than Peter’s: “We await new heavens and a new earth according to his promise, in which righteousness dwells.” For there too, as the words stand, righteousness is nothing other than the righteous people of God.

But where shall we say that Nero’s attempted, if not completed, destruction of this righteousness took place? At Rome alone, with the most learned Dodwell in his *Cyprianic Dissertations*? Or throughout the Roman Empire, with the equally learned Pagi in his critique of Baronius’s *Annals*? Certainly, following Pagi’s opinion, we do not doubt that our author meant throughout all the provinces of the Roman Empire, because of this sequence of speech:

“When this was reported to Nero, and he observed that not only at Rome but everywhere a great multitude daily was abandoning the worship of idols and passing over to the new religion, having condemned antiquity, then, as he was an execrable and criminal tyrant, he rushed forth [Col. 0626D] to cut down the heavenly temple and destroy righteousness.”

For where in the world ought Nero to have been seen to cut down the heavenly temple and destroy righteousness, except where he understood that a great multitude daily was abandoning the worship of idols and passing over to the new religion, having condemned antiquity? But according to our author Nero observed this happening not only at Rome but everywhere. Therefore everywhere, and not at Rome alone, Nero, according to him, rushed forth through his edicts and prefects to destroy righteousness.

“But,” says Dodwell, “that persecution could certainly not have been of any Christians other than those living at Rome. For however unjust we may suppose persecutors to be, there was no reason, even in appearance, why the charge of burning the city should be brought against those who were absent from Rome. Therefore those who suppose that Christians other than those at Rome suffered in it must invent another persecution than that mentioned by Tacitus. But by what adequate testimony will they finally establish it?” [Col. 0627A]

But first, to begin where I properly should, here is Pagi’s recent answer to this:

“Dodwell,” he says, “in section 11, or rather 13, of the eleventh *Cyprianic Dissertation*, admits indeed that a great multitude suffered in Nero’s persecution, but only those Christians who lived at Rome, since there was no reason, even in appearance, why those absent from Rome should be accused of the burning of the city. But this is a weak argument. Nero, not the Christians, was the author of the fire; and therefore an edict was issued not merely to harass Christians living at Rome, but to abolish the whole sect throughout the Roman Empire, as we understand from these words of Lactantius, book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 2: ‘When Nero observed that not only at Rome but everywhere a great multitude daily was abandoning the worship of idols … he rushed forth to cut down the heavenly temple,’ etc. This persecution, therefore, was not local but universal. Nor does it matter that Tacitus says nothing about what was done against Christians in the provinces, since Suetonius, in chapter 16 of his *Nero*, does not restrict the persecution to the city of Rome. ‘Christians, a class of men given to a new and harmful superstition, were subjected to punishments,’ says Suetonius.”

These, then, are Pagi’s words, word for word, in the cited *Critique*, in their proper place.

Indeed, Gruter among others, and Joseph Scaliger—though Scaliger himself doubted its genuineness—have produced the following inscription. The former stated that it still existed in the ruins of a village in the Marquisate, in Lusitania; the latter, in Spain, at a place called Pisuerga:

> NERONI CL. CAIS. AVG. PONT. MAX. OB. PROVINC. LATRONIB. ET. HIS. QUI NOVAM GENERI. HVM. SVPERSTITION. INCVLCAB. PVRGATAM;

[Col. 0627C]

Or, as Scaliger published it:

> NERONI CLAVDIO CAESARI AVG. PONT. MAX. OB PROVINCIAM LATRONIBVS ET HIS QUI NOVAM GENERI HVMANO SVPERSTITIONEM INCVLCARANT PVRGATAM.

“To Nero Claudius Caesar Augustus, chief pontiff, because he cleansed the province of brigands and of those who had inculcated a new superstition upon the human race.”

Not content with the foregoing arguments against Dodwell, Pagi further maintains not merely that Scaliger’s doubt about the said inscription is vain, because Scaliger offered no reason whatever for his suspicion, but also that such doubt can never be advanced even on a sound basis. Elsewhere, too, Pagi observes that the general cruelty of Nero, which he posits against Christians everywhere, is undoubtedly indicated in that inscription because the Christian religion is there called a “superstition,” just as it is by Suetonius in the passage recently cited and in the ancient inscription concerning Diocletian. Therefore one must infer from it not merely that trophies celebrating the overthrow of Christ’s religion were erected in the Spanish provinces, but that this was likewise done in other provinces.

Especially since Orosius—“in book IX,” says Pagi, though book VII should have been said, chapter 7; and one should investigate elsewhere why the words of Orosius quoted by him differ so greatly at the beginning and end from the common editions—wrote of Nero:

“Finally, to all his crimes he added this also: that he was the first at Rome to afflict Christians with punishments and deaths, and he commanded them to be tortured by persecution throughout all the provinces; attempting to extirpate the very name itself, he fastened the most blessed apostle Peter to the cross and beheaded Paul with the sword.”

There Pagi again adds as a conclusion: “That martyrdom occurred in the following year; and therefore the persecution which began this year at Rome spread into the other provinces within that time—unless, what is more probable, the edict was immediately sent into all the provinces.” [Col. 0628A]

And now, to add something of our own to all these considerations, insofar as they strongly confirm that Nero burst forth to destroy God’s people everywhere, we think Dodwell has less to reply to them because, while arguing that there was no reason, even in appearance, why Christians absent from Rome should be accused of the city’s fire, he securely assumes on Tacitus’s authority, first, that the fire preceded Nero’s persecution of Christians, and then that it also furnished the occasion for that persecution.

But apart from the fact that this writer’s hypotheses are manifestly different from those of Tacitus, we have shortly before adduced much from Suetonius, Jerome, Orosius, and others which either makes Nero’s persecution earlier than the fire or makes it later indeed, but does not say that it arose from it. And even if we do not maintain that it was earlier, I confess that I do not see how anyone can neatly and clearly show it impossible that, after the burning of Rome, Nero persecuted believers everywhere throughout the Roman Empire merely on account of Christianity; or, if not merely on that account, then at Rome as guilty of arson because of Tacitus’s testimony, but elsewhere, as circumstances required, as persons devoted to a harmful superstition because of passages in other writers—even though they were in fact innocent of both charges.

It was precisely so that Haman, at Susa, decreed in the name of Ahasuerus that Mordecai should be killed for neglecting the duty of salutation, and that, when an occasion was given, all the Jews should be killed throughout the one hundred and twenty-seven provinces of Ahasuerus’s empire as a nation of men having laws different from those of all other peoples and refusing to obey the king’s edicts.

It must be carefully noted that what remains is that our author says of Nero, “He rushed forth to cut down the heavenly temple and destroy righteousness”; he does not say, “he cut down” [Col. 0628C] or “he destroyed.” For he truly wished to cut down and destroy. Indeed, to speak with Orosius, he “attempted to extirpate the very name itself”—but in vain. Such afterwards was Diocletian’s lot also, unless perhaps Nero achieved his end in that province of which the inscriptions cited above make mention. Let those who lately gloried, on the basis of coins and similar inscriptions, that the so-called Heresy had been extinguished, consider whether they too rushed forth in vain to cut down the heavenly temple.

**“And first of all Nero persecuted God’s servants.”** I shall speak plainly. Nothing could be less true, if one looks at the fact itself and attends to the particular examples which this writer adds. For why was Nero “first of all”—not, I say, first among emperors with Eusebius, for our author nowhere adds or implies that, but simply first of all, and hence among men—who persecuted God’s servants? Because, as follows, he fastened Peter to a cross and killed Paul.

Yet long before this, under Tiberius, Herod Antipas had most unjustly beheaded John the Baptist; and under the same emperor—or, as others wish, under Caligula—the Jews had stoned Stephen. Under Caligula, or, as others again hold, under Claudius, James, John’s brother, had been killed by Herod Agrippa, and Peter thrown into chains.

Indeed, if we pass from these individual martyrdoms or harassments of certain faithful persons to more general persecutions of the Church, in the reign of Tiberius—or certainly Caligula, if one prefers the common opinion—on the very day on which Stephen the protomartyr was stoned, “a great persecution arose,” says Luke in Acts 8:1, “against the Church which was at Jerusalem; and all were scattered throughout the regions of Judaea and Samaria except the apostles.” Hence George Syncellus, under the year of the world 5537, of the Divine Incarnation 37, and of Tiberius’s reign 20 or 21, says: “In this year a persecution having been stirred up against the Church, most of the faithful were scattered, to whom James, the brother of the Lord, wrote the Catholic Epistle, under the heading ‘To the faithful in the dispersion.’”

Moreover, to the highly distinguished Cuperus, and likewise to Lipsius on Tacitus’s *Annals*, it seems not without reason that the Christians who were living at Rome under Claudius are to be counted among those Jews who were badly treated by Claudius—that is, whom Claudius, as Luke (Acts 18:2) and Suetonius testify, compelled to leave Rome.

Why, then, did our Caecilius not count either disturbance among the persecutions, and why did he speak of Nero in no other manner, finally, than Sulpicius Severus did of the same man: “He was,” he says, “not merely the foulest of kings, but of all men and even of savage beasts, worthy to be the first to begin persecution against Christians”? Namely, because this author “had by no means undertaken to set forth persecutions of emperors or others of whatever sort, and their punishments, from the very time when the Church was to be established after Christ’s Ascension,” but only “from the beginning at which the Church was established.”

Now in this latter sense the Christian Church must be judged not to have been established before the apostles, for twenty-five years, until the beginning of Nero’s reign, had laid the foundations of the Church throughout all provinces and cities. Therefore Nero is quite properly said by our author to have been the first of all to persecute God’s servants, deliberately omitting the harassments inflicted by the other persecutors during those twenty-five years. Supply: “after the Church had once been established.”

Do you wish us to be pressed by an authority greater than ours? In Augustine’s *City of God*, book XVIII, chapter 52, there is a chapter with this heading: “Whether one should believe, as some think, that after the ten persecutions which have occurred, none remains except the eleventh, which will take place in the very time of Antichrist.” Read it, and when you come to these words, consider with yourself whether anything other than what we have just observed needs to be done:

“They count the first persecution from Nero … But … what will those who think this say concerning the persecution in which the Lord himself was crucified? In what number will they place it? But if, excepting this one, they think the others should be counted, as though those persecutions ought to be numbered which concern the body, not that in which the head itself was attacked and killed, what will they do with that which occurred at Jerusalem after Christ ascended into heaven—where the blessed Stephen was stoned, where James, John’s brother, was slain by the sword, where the apostle Peter was imprisoned to be killed and was delivered by an angel; where Saul, who later became Paul, devastated the Church; where he himself, now preaching the faith which he had persecuted, suffered the things he suffered, whether through Judaea or among other nations, wherever he preached Christ most fervently? Why then do they think the count should begin with Nero, when the Church, growing amid the most atrocious persecutions—of which it would be too long to tell all—had reached Nero’s time? And if they think persecutions carried out by kings ought to be included in the number, Herod was a king, who even after the Lord’s Ascension inflicted a most grievous persecution.”

Thus far Augustine.

[Col. 0629D] **“And first of all Nero persecuted God’s servants.”** Nor is what those compilers of martyrologies and menologies suppose true, that so many emperors were persecutors. Lactantius, who wrote under Constantine, lists only a few before Diocletian in the register of persecutors: Nero alone, Domitian, Decius, Valerian, and Aurelian. And Tertullian, in accordance with his own period, agrees with Lactantius; for he recognizes no emperors as persecutors before his own day except those recognized by Lactantius, Nero and Domitian. —DODWELL.

**“He fastened Peter to a cross.”** John, chapter 21, verse 19, seems to confirm this manner of punishment in Peter, referring to Christ’s words, “you will stretch out your hands” [ἐκτενεῖς τὰς χεῖράς σου]. For from “being girded and being led where one does not wish” [ἐκ τοῦ ζώννυσθαι καὶ τοῦ ἀπάγεσθαι ὅπου τις οὐ θέλει], no manner of death could otherwise be signified, but merely being cast into prison and chains, even without a capital punishment. —TOLLIUS.

**“And killed Paul.”** There are three reasons why it may not without reason seem that it was once written, “and killed Paul with the sword.” First, the common opinion of the ancients is that Paul died by the sword, his neck having been severed. Second, since our author knew the rules of rhetoric and, in the preceding words, when mentioning Peter’s martyrdom, named also the instrument of martyrdom—“he fastened Peter to a cross”—he could scarcely have failed to add immediately, “and killed Paul with the sword.” Especially since, according to such rules, we read in Sulpicius Severus: “Paul and Peter were condemned to death, the neck of the one being cut by the sword, while Peter was raised upon the cross”; and likewise in Orosius: “Nero killed the most blessed apostles of Christ, Peter by the cross, Paul by the sword”; and again in Pseudo-Hegesippus: “One was killed by the cross, the other by the sword”; while in Greek Theodore Metochites writes: “Nero crucified Peter, and brought Paul to his end by the sword” [Ὁ Νέρων τὸν Πέτρον ἐσταύρωσε, τὸν δὲ Παῦλον διὰ ξίφους ἐτελείωσεν].

Third and finally, so far are the Latin Fathers from using *interficere* or *interfici*, in an abbreviated expression, specifically and properly to mean “behead” or “be beheaded,” that they sometimes instead use *interficere* briefly to mean “crucify,” and *interfici* to mean “be cast into a river and killed by drowning.” Tertullian says of the Synagogue, which, as all know, did not strike Christ with an axe but crucified him: “The whole Synagogue of the children of Israel killed him [Jesus], saying to Pilate,” and what follows.

And the Latin *Chronicle* of Eusebius says of the martyr Quirinus, whom the pagans cast whole—that is, not first beheaded—into a river, and whom those or others afterwards killed by drowning: “Quirinus, bishop of Siscia, is gloriously killed for Christ. For, with a millstone tied around his neck, he was thrown from a bridge into the river; he floated for a long time and conversed with the onlookers, telling them not to be frightened by his example, and only with difficulty obtained, through prayer, that he should sink.”

Meanwhile, let learned readers consider, if it is not troublesome, whether the very fact that *interficere* is found used in the sense of crucifying and drowning—flowing, of course, from its general usage for killing and removing from the midst—means that this author too could have used *interfecit*, without any mention of a sword, of Paul beheaded with an axe, disregarding the stricter precepts of rhetoricians.

**“Yet he did not go unpunished.”** Our author uses a similar phrase below of the elder Maximian: “Because he once went unpunished,” etc., at the beginning of chapter 33.

**“For God looked upon the affliction of his people.”** I think that few, if they have not already understood it from the words themselves, will deny when reminded by me that there is an allusion here to Exodus 3:7: “I have seen, I have seen the affliction of my people.” This is all the more so because, when the Seventy long ago rendered the Hebrew words, “Seeing I saw the oppression of my people” [Ἰδὼν εἶδον τὴν κάκωσιν τοῦ λαοῦ μου], Beza in the preceding century rendered their translation in Acts 7:34 thus: “I have seen, I have seen the affliction [vexationem] of my people,” which perhaps was also the version of the old Italic edition.

Certainly, no one could doubt without injustice that the word *vexatio* still occurs in many places in the Vulgate, and, what is more, in a stronger sense—namely, for a grievous affliction and persecution. For in Jeremiah 29:18, for example, concerning Zedekiah and his princes, the Lord says: “I will give them over to affliction and distress among all the kingdoms of the earth.”

Thus elsewhere in our author—or at least in Sulpicius Severus, not to concern myself with testimonies from others—*vexatio* and *vexationes* mean persecutions; likewise *vexare* and *vexari* mean to persecute or to suffer persecution. Sulpicius himself, in book I of the *Sacred History*, says: “It seemed to me not absurd, when I had run through sacred history as far as Christ’s cross and the acts of the apostles, also … the destruction of Jerusalem and the afflictions of the Christian people,” etc., meaning the so-called ten persecutions.

Accordingly, after undertaking in book II to discuss each persecution individually and proceeding as far as the fourth, he says: “The fourth persecution is counted under Hadrian”; and immediately likewise of the fifth: “Under Aurelius, son of Antoninus, the fifth persecution was carried on.” Then he designates the sixth by the name *vexatio*, as though altogether synonymous: “The sixth affliction of Christians occurred under Severus.”

We know that the word *vexatio* elsewhere in this passage of Tertullian means illness: “I presume that many avoid this work of confession, or defer it from day to day, more mindful of shame than of salvation; like those who, having contracted an affliction in the more shameful parts of the body, avoid the knowledge of physicians.” But one must attend to what suits each passage.

And further, there is no room for doubt that in the passage actually before us our author said “the affliction of his people” in a passive sense, meaning “his afflicted people,” and that he said it of the Christian Church of God. This is clear both from chapter 4—“For the execrable animal Decius arose, to harass the Church”—and from Jeremiah 31:33: “I will be their God, and they shall be my people,” words which most certainly apply to the faithful of the new covenant. To think, I will not say of another interpretation, but even to dream of one, would be absurd.

Thus also above, in a passive sense: “Whom fear of his apprehension had turned into flight,” meaning, “Whom fear, when he had been apprehended, had driven into flight.”

**“He was therefore cast down from the height of empire.”** Beware lest, because of the words immediately following, “and hurled down from on high, the powerless tyrant,” you believe it necessary to read here likewise, “He was therefore cast down *from* the height of empire.” In better Latin authors, after this verb the preposition *de* or *ex* is often elegantly omitted and must be supplied. Cicero, in the speech for Murena: “He was cast down from the praetorship by these goatskins”; and in the second speech against Verres: “He promised whatever sum of money they wanted, if they would cast me down from the aedileship.” Elsewhere in the same work you will find *deicere honore*, as also more than once in Livy.

**“He suddenly appeared nowhere.” Fables.** “I wonder that ancient Christians were accustomed to lie so splendidly; if one wished to weave together a catalogue of their lies, whole wagonloads could be filled with them and sent, along with the Sibylline verses, to old women.” —TOLLIUS.

Although the things said here and immediately afterwards concerning Nero, not by our Caecilius alone but also by certain other Christians, whom nothing prevents us from considering his contemporaries, are such that I readily concede to the learned man that they are utterly fabulous, I nevertheless wish that he had not launched this sharp censure against our author and the other older ecclesiastical writers, or at least had postponed it to another, more suitable occasion. For now, if not from every direction, yet to no small degree an outstanding passage of Tacitus, which Columbus adduced from book II, chapter 8, of the *Histories*, defends both the candour and the honour of our author and of all other ancient Christians. Since the whole matter is not unworthy of being explained somewhat more carefully, it stands thus.

From this writer, Nero—or rather, to speak more accurately, the corpse of Nero, slain by his own hand—suddenly appeared nowhere, so that not even the place of burial of so evil a beast was visible upon earth. And that is indeed his sole and unqualified meaning. On the other hand, according to those certain Christians whom he censured, it was not the corpse of Nero, already dead, but Nero himself, alive and conscious, who suddenly appeared nowhere [Col. 0631D], and was carried away to a definite place, there kept alive in reserve.

But Tacitus says in the cited passage: “About the same time”—having not long before mentioned the oath of Otho, which both armies, namely that of Vespasian and that of Mucianus, had taken about the eighth month after Nero’s death—“Achaia and Asia were alarmed by a groundless fear, as though Nero were approaching; diverse rumours having arisen concerning his end, and many accordingly inventing and believing that he was alive.” Therefore, first of all, according to Tacitus, various reports concerning Nero were spread after his death, including one of such a kind that, should anyone have wished on that occasion to invent that Nero was still alive, he could readily have found credence with many. Secondly, those who invented this were found in the eighth month, more or less, after his death. Thirdly, several were discovered together who not only did not reject and refute the tale, but accepted it with such good faith that they were most miserably terrified, as though Nero [Col. 0632A] were approaching. Finally, those who then invented and began to believe this story were, for two reasons, by no means Christians, but plainly pagans. First, because it might indeed be in the interest of many pagans to invent that Nero still survived, but not likewise in the interest of Christians. Secondly, because Tacitus in the cited place makes absolutely no mention of Christians, but only of Achaia and Asia, in which several invented and believed that Nero was still alive after his death: from this it must plainly be inferred that pagans alone are meant. This being so, where, I ask, have our author’s Christians—whether madmen, of whom he will speak shortly, or otherwise—lied so splendidly?

In every case, if, as is proper, the question of the authors of the invention comes first, no share at all of that fault is to be assigned either to this man or to those others: it is, plainly, to be wholly imputed to the pagans. But if afterwards the question concerns the faith placed in the invention, we certainly acknowledge that this tale was believed—indeed, admitted with a very remarkable *epimetron* (ἐπίμετρον, “addition”)—by the deluded Christians of our Caecilius. [Col. 0632B] Yet, first, our author admitted neither the invention nor its addition; believing, in a word, that the corpse of Nero, once dead, had appeared nowhere, he denied both that Nero had never died in the earlier age of Christ and that he had still survived somewhere on earth in the fourth century. Thus, while denying both, he was so far from every splendid falsehood that he was fighting for truth itself against empty babblings.

Secondly, as regards his contemporaries who defended either tale, their case is certainly much less favourable. Nevertheless, if several pagans in Achaia and Asia, about eight months after Nero’s death, persuaded themselves that Nero was still alive—through excessive credulity indeed, but certainly with no deliberate purpose of lying splendidly, for, I think, they would by no means have wished to lie merely in order afterwards to be terrified by a false fear—why might Christians of that age, and others after them, not likewise have persuaded themselves of it? Through error, I say, rather than through any real fault of theirs. “Credulity is more an error [Col. 0632C] than a fault,” Plancus once wrote to Cicero, and it most easily creeps even into the mind of the best person; so that even here, where Christians are concerned, we must carefully avoid saying that they lied splendidly. How much more, then, where this author is concerned? Since he rejected the invention and the appendix to the invention with derision, his one evident error was that, among other reports concerning Nero’s end, he thought this one deserved belief: the report once spread abroad that Nero had suddenly appeared nowhere, which must undoubtedly be understood of Nero’s corpse; pagans, whose interest it was to exploit the ambiguity, soon after Nero’s death applied it to Nero himself, as though still alive, and Christians later followed their example for other reasons.

Add that, since even at Rome, according to the passage in Suetonius shortly to be set out in full, there were persons who, after Nero’s funeral, now displayed his images in the *praetexta* on the Rostra, now issued edicts as though he were alive and soon to return to the great ruin of his enemies, they could not say otherwise that Nero was still among the living [Col. 0632D] than by affirming at the same time that, while he was being sought in order to be punished according to ancestral custom, he had suddenly vanished, and that the funeral rites thought to have been rendered to Nero’s natural body had been rendered only to a substituted one. Nor could they make such assertions without giving Christians, living and destined to live later, too easy an occasion to believe and maintain such tales about Nero as our author states or attacks in this chapter.

“So that not even the place of burial of so evil a beast was visible.” This is contrary to Suetonius, who teaches that he was buried at an expense of two hundred thousand. Oxford and Cambridge editions.

The editions so styled derive this from Baluzius, as may be seen above, col. 304. Nor indeed can it be denied that Suetonius, in his *Nero*, toward the end of chapter 49 and at the beginning of chapter 50, expressly says:

> “Nothing had Nero demanded sooner or more urgently from his companions than that no one should obtain power over his head, but that by whatever means his whole body should be burned. Seius, Galba’s freedman, promised this. … He was buried at an expense of two hundred thousand, in white coverlets embroidered with gold, which he had used on the Kalends of January. His remains were laid by his nurses Ecloge and Alexandra, together with his concubine Acte, in the monument of the Domitii, which is seen from the Campus Martius, set upon the summit of the hill of gardens.”

Nor can it be denied that at the beginning of chapter 57 we likewise read:

> “He died in the thirty-second year of his age, on the day on which he had formerly killed Octavia. And he caused such public rejoicing that the people ran about the whole city wearing caps of liberty. Yet there were not lacking those who for a long time adorned his tomb with spring and summer flowers.”

But why say more? These facts do not, as someone might suppose, utterly destroy our Caecilius’s statement, “so that not even the place of burial of so evil a beast was visible.” For Suetonius immediately continues after the latter words, “Yet there were not lacking those who for a long time adorned his tomb with spring and summer flowers,” adding: “and who now displayed his images in the *praetexta* on the Rostra, [Col. 0633B] now edicts as though he were alive and soon to return to the great ruin of his enemies.” It is therefore clear that these persons regarded Nero’s tomb as a mere cenotaph. Consequently, the narrative of our author under discussion is not merely not destroyed but assisted.

“So evil a beast.” Orosius similarly says of the emperor Tiberius: “From a most gentle prince he flamed out into a most savage beast.” And Paul himself, as men of great distinction have long since said, meant none other lion than Nero in this passage of the Second Epistle to Timothy (4:7): “I was rescued from the lion’s mouth.” Hence, to omit others, Eusebius: “ἐῤῥύσθην, φησὶν, ἐκ στόματος λέοντος … τὸν Νέρωνα ταύτῃ ὡς ἔοικε διὰ τὸ ὠμόθυμον προσειπών”—“‘I was rescued,’ he says, ‘from the lion’s mouth’ … apparently calling Nero by this name on account of his cruel disposition,” as Valesius translates. We are prevented from adding more by what has been observed above by Baluzius, col. 312, and Cuper, col. 473; consult them therefore in their respective places.

[Col. 0633C] “Carried away.” Where? Here there is a remarkable brevity in our author, and this question, whether one wishes it or not, presents itself to attentive readers. I answer: to the ends of the earth, because of what follows. Read on.

“Kept alive in reserve.” See Baluzius on these very words; Cuper on that clause, “His coming … it is unlawful to believe”; and lastly Columbus again on this phrase, “He suddenly appeared nowhere.”

“The Sibyl saying, ‘a fugitive matricide.’” Some were persuaded that Nero himself would either be Antichrist, or would rage through the West during the same times in which Antichrist would ravage the East. Baluzius from Casaubon. The Sibylline verses cited by him are as follows:

> Ἥξει δ’ ἐκ περάτων γαίης μητροκτόνος ἀνήρ  
> Φεύγων ἠδὲ νόον (I think it should be corrected to νέων) ὀξὺ στόμα μερμηρίζων,  
> Ὃς πᾶσαν γαῖαν καθελεῖ, καὶ πάντα κρατήσει.

> “From the ends of the earth there shall come a matricidal man,  
> fleeing, and pondering in his mind [uncertain: perhaps ‘of youths’] a keen utterance,  
> who shall overthrow all the earth and rule all things.”

Thus the Oxford edition together with the Cambridge edition; except that the learned man who prepared the latter omitted altogether the conjecture enclosed in brackets [Col. 0633D], mentioning instead another conjecture without naming its author. We shall now identify him and introduce him as speaking; he testified that this reading too displeased him:

> Ἥξει δ’ ἐκ περάτων γαίης μητροκτόνος ἀνήρ.  
> Φεύγων ἠδὲ νόον ὀξὺ στόμα μερμηρίζων,  
> Ὃς …

“I read in the second verse:

> Φεύγων Ἠριδανοῦ ὀξὺ στόμα μορμυρίζον.

“The Po rises in the Alps. Aeschylus and Apollonius in the *Argonautica* identify it with the Eridanus, and they also confuse it with the Rhone. I understand the oracle to refer to Julius Caesar, who descended from Gaul into Italy by way of the Rhone and the Alps. ‘Matricidal one’: Julius Caesar.” —GALE.

The reverend gentleman judges that Julius Caesar is designated by this oracle, since the final word denotes a matricide, and therefore thinks the text should read [Col. 0634A]:

> Φεύγων Ἠριδανοῦ ὀξὺ στόμα μορμυρίζον.

He gives this reason for his conjecture: Eridanus is used by Aeschylus and Apollonius in the *Argonautica* for the Po, and the Po likewise for the Rhone, which Caesar crossed while making for Italy. But although this conjecture perhaps attains the sense of the oracle, it does not accord with Lactantius’s view, who expressly understands these words of Nero. Anonymous author of the Cambridge edition.

We are surprised that Lactantius’s view is invoked and pressed against the reverend gentleman’s emendation. For Lactantius—or our Caecilius, as we usually call him—was not one of the madmen whom he incidentally censured, but those who understood the praised verses of the Sibyl to concern Nero were such men. Therefore the most distinguished commentator on Iamblichus undoubtedly did not hold that, in the view jointly of the Sibyl and our Caecilius, these verses should be understood of Julius Caesar; rather, he held that the Sibyl’s oracle properly concerns Julius Caesar, yet that, according to this writer’s account, there were certain madmen who wrongly applied to Nero what the Sibyl had prophesied of Julius Caesar. [Col. 0634B] Thus the conjecture may stand perfectly well to that extent—a conjecture which the most eminent man most kindly permitted to be copied from his exemplar, together with those to be mentioned next, by Elias Boherellus, a very learned mutual friend of both him and our author. But we received them from England too late to mention some of them here in due time and place; since they have, greatly against our will, once fallen from their proper position, they must therefore be read only at the end of this little book. Meanwhile, we are glad that from what has just been said that celebrated man may understand how rightly he trusted that, when necessary, we would be candid interpreters of his thoughts.

“From the ends.” The word *earth* has fallen out. For the Greek has, “ἐκ περάτων γαίης,” “from the ends of the earth.” —TOLLIUS. “He is to come from the ends of the earth.” —GALE. No other reason is apparent. I entirely agree. For the Greek Sibylline verses contain the word γαίης, “of earth,” not once only, as might seem from what precedes, but twice.

[Col. 0634C] “Because he was the first persecutor.” I would prefer: “Because he persecuted the Church.” —TOLLIUS. I judge that the received reading should not be changed. For although our author wrote in this very chapter, “First of all he persecuted the servants of God,” and in chapter 2, “After he was incited to persecute the righteous people,” and shortly afterward again, “The senate thus persecuted his name,” and again in chapter 4, “Who but an evil man persecutes justice?”—and there are further examples of this kind, that is, where *persequi* occurs with an accusative immediately following or preceding it—yet at the end of chapter 9 there occurs another passage exactly like the one now under discussion, where the same verb is used absolutely, as grammarians say: “But what reason he had for persecuting, I shall explain.” There not even Tollius thought of reading anything else. Add that it was familiar to this writer to designate persecutors of the Church simply by the word “persecutors.” Thus, for example, the book’s title says nothing but *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, and chapter 1, “to inflict death upon the persecutors.” [Col. 0634D] Indeed, as will appear below, our author habitually uses without accusatives verbs which especially require accusatives to be joined to them, such as *agere*, “to do,” and *facere*, “to make.”

“His coming … it is unlawful to believe.” “His coming … to believe it is unlawful”: Cambridge edition, in the author’s words; but doubtless a typographical error. “His coming (which it is unlawful to believe)”: Oxford and Cambridge editions in the notes, with the parentheses that we reproduce. “His coming: which it is unlawful to believe”: Cuper, without parentheses. “His coming is not unlawful to believe”: Abbot of St Hilary.

For my part, to speak freely, I would prefer: “His coming. Others [say], which it is not lawful to believe.” For in this way the author censures two classes of madmen. One consists of those who, with gross and unpolished understanding, supposed that Nero had long ago, to speak with our author, been carried away and from that time kept alive at the ends of the earth, and that he would come thence “at the consummation of the age” (ἐν τῇ τοῦ αἰῶνος συντελείᾳ) to persecute the Church and precede [Col. 0635A] Antichrist’s coming. The other consists of those who sought to confirm the entire matter by what they regarded as an illustrious observation, though it was really futile: namely, that two prophets, Enoch and Elijah, had once been carried away alive to places from which they would return on the Day of Judgment to begin the holy and everlasting victory-song of Christ at the last trumpet when he should begin to descend; and that Nero would no otherwise go before the devil when he came to lay waste the earth and overthrow humankind, and would be his forerunner.

I acknowledge that we are thus relying upon several conjectures not yet set forth in their proper place, much less established by us beyond controversy to the extent of our powers. But we are hastening to them; meanwhile we most willingly grant everyone full liberty to prefer his own contributions to ours.

“As they declare that the two Prophets were carried away alive in the last … the beginning of Christ, holy and everlasting, when he shall begin to descend. …” This passage is shamefully mutilated and obscure. We judged it worth while to set below the ways in which others and we ourselves have completed and elucidated it, so that, reader, you may grasp more readily at once each person’s view of the whole clause and choose better whom to follow.

From the Oxford and Cambridge editions:

> “As they declare that the two prophets were carried away alive, and that they will precede, in the last ages, the holy and everlasting beginning of Christ, when he shall descend accompanied by his saints.”

From the most learned Cuper:

> “As they declare that the two prophets were carried away alive, and that in the last age they will precede the holy and everlasting beginning of Christ when he shall begin to descend.”

From Columbus:

> “As they declare that the two prophets were carried away alive, and that in the final age they will precede the holy and everlasting beginning of Christ when he shall begin to descend.”

From the same Columbus, by another construction:

> “As they declare that the two prophets were carried away alive, and that they will return in the last ages, when the holy and everlasting beginning of Christ [Col. 0635C] shall begin to descend.”

In our view:

> “As they declare that the two prophets were carried away alive, in order that at the last trumpet they may begin, or sing in advance, the holy and everlasting victory-song of Christ when he shall begin to descend.”

“Carried away.” Not, certainly, to the ends of the earth, as we explained “carried away” a little earlier, but out of the world, that is, into heaven—or, which must return to the same thing, into Paradise; or, if you prefer yet another expression, “to the divine” (πρὸς τὸ θεῖον). For what do sacred writers, their interpreters, and other such persons say of the two prophets undoubtedly intended here, Enoch and Elijah the Tishbite? Of Enoch: “He was translated into Paradise,” render the Arabic and Latin interpreters, the former at Hebrews 11:5 and the latter at Sirach 44:15. “He was translated into heaven,” has Vatablus (Genesis 5:24). Josephus says: “Ἀνεχώρησε πρὸς τὸ θεῖον, ὅθεν οὐδὲ τελευτὴν αὐτοῦ ἀναγεγράφασιν”—“He departed to God; hence they have not recorded even his death, or end” (*Antiquities*, book 1, chapter 4). As for Elijah the Tishbite, Tertullian says most elegantly in *On the Soul*: “Elijah will come not from the departure of life but from translation; he is not to be restored to the body from which he was not removed, but rendered to the world from which he was translated.” Sacred Scripture, moreover, says (2 Kings, 1:11): “Elijah went up in a whirlwind into heaven”; whence also 1 Maccabees 2:58: “Ἠλίας ἐν τῷ ζηλώσαι ζῆλον νόμου ἀνελήφθη ἕως εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν”—“Elijah, in his zeal for the law, was taken up even into heaven.”

“In the last …” The reason we think that not *ages* or *age*, with the learned men just cited, but *trumpet* should be supplied here, lies both in what we shall shortly say concerning the word *beginning* and especially in this passage of the Apostle:

> Πάντες μὲν οὐ κοιμηθησόμεθα, πάντες δὲ ἀλλαγησόμεθα ἐν ἀτόμῳ, ἐν ῥιπῇ ὀφθαλμοῦ, ἐν τῇ ἐσχάτῃ σάλπιγγι· σαλπίσει γὰρ, καὶ οἱ νεκροὶ ἐγερθήσονται ἄφθαρτοι, καὶ ἡμεῖς ἀλλαγησόμεθα.

“We shall not all indeed sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last—or, as the Vulgate translator has it, the final—trumpet. For the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall rise incorruptible, and we [Col. 0636A] shall be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:51–52).

Not to add that the Fathers were not infrequently accustomed to refer in writing to that same last trumpet. Tertullian, for example, in *On the Soul*: “Whither, then, will you breathe out the soul? Into heaven, while Christ still sits at the right hand of the Father? Before God’s command has yet been heard through the trumpet of the archangel? Before those whom the Lord’s coming finds in the world have been snatched—perhaps, ‘caught up’—to meet him in the air, together with those who are dead in Christ and will rise first?” For so we read and punctuate that passage.

But why rather, in our author, “in order that at the last trumpet,” than “at the last trumpet”? Partly because of the lacuna, no part of which seems to occur before *at the last*, while the whole occurs afterward; partly because of the nature of Latin, in which such transpositions are customary. Thus Cicero elegantly says against Verres, *vere ut dicam*, “truly, that I may speak,” for *ut vere dicam*, “that I may speak truly”; and in the letters to Atticus, *Quod vereor, tibi ipsi ut probem*, similarly for *Quod vereor, ut tibi ipsi probem*.

“The last beginning of Christ.” “The Last [Day] and Judgment of Christ.” —ABBOT OF ST HILARY.

[Col. 0636B] “The holy and everlasting beginning of Christ.” That is, as these good men thought, Christ’s millennial kingdom. The notion of this empty persuasion, which also prevailed among several of the Fathers, seems to have flowed from these words of Paul, 1 Corinthians 15:23–25:

> Ἀπαρχὴ [sc. ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀναστάσεως] Χριστός, ἔπειτα οἱ τοῦ Χριστοῦ, ἐν τῇ παρουσίᾳ αὐτοῦ. Εἶτα τὸ τέλος, ὅταν παραδῷ τὴν βασιλείαν τῷ Θεῷ καὶ Πατρί, ὅταν καταργήσῃ πᾶσαν ἀρχὴν, καὶ πᾶσαν ἐξουσίαν, καὶ δύναμιν. Δεῖ γὰρ αὐτὸν βασιλεύειν, ἄχρις οὖν ἂν θῇ πάντας τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ὑπὸ τοὺς πόδας αὐτοῦ.

For Christ’s *parousia* (“coming/presence”) precedes the *telos*, or end of the world, when he is to hand over the kingdom to God and the Father, and himself “will be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him” (ὑποταγήσεται τῷ ὑποτάξαντι αὐτῷ τὰ πάντα), as Paul says in verse 28. Between that *parousia* and the *telos* intervenes the *basileia*, that is, Christ’s kingdom, during which kingdom he “will abolish every rule,” etc., and “will place all enemies beneath his feet”; and death itself will be the last adversary. Thus thereafter the elect will always be victorious and, after Christ’s victory, will know death no more.

From this passage, therefore, the ancients extracted that kingdom of Christ on earth. They took its thousand-year duration from John’s Apocalypse 20:3, where the devil is said to be bound by an angel “for a thousand years” (χίλια ἔτη), and verse 4, where the holy martyrs and those who had not accepted the mark of the beast are said to reign (βασιλεῦσαι) with Christ for the thousand years, while the remaining dead did not come to life. That resurrection of the saints is there called the first; blessed and holy is the one who shares in it, since the second death will have no power over them. This agrees very closely with those words of Paul, where he says that death will at last be conquered and subdued.

As for the two prophets, Enoch and Elijah, forerunners of Christ descending from heaven to the millennial kingdom, they seem to me to be taken from Revelation chapter 11, where two witnesses are mentioned who will have power to shut heaven so that it may not rain—which chiefly concerns Elijah—and to turn waters into blood. Our Lactantius (*Divine Institutes*, book 7, chapter 17) attributes both powers to one man only, or one great prophet. [Col. 0636D] At last, after the devil and the principalities, dominions, and powers mentioned by Paul have been conquered and triumphed over—or after Gog and Magog have been consumed by heavenly fire, as John has it in Revelation 20:8–9—there follows the final judgment, or second resurrection, when earth, sea, and hell will give up their dead; and those then condemned will be cast with death and hell into the lake of fire, which is the second death.

From this vision of John there sprang so many waking dreams of men—and it suffices to read Lactantius, book 7, chapters 16–17—that the writer of the *Aeneid* did not send forth so many from the ivory gate of the underworld, nor did the sons of our Hermes scatter so many among all nations and peoples. But more fully on these matters elsewhere. —TOLLIUS.

Correctly so, I say, provided the most learned man remembers also to solve the two difficulties with which the interpretation he follows is burdened, and which he has hitherto left altogether untouched. One is how that future millennial kingdom of [Col. 0637A] Christ, to which this author seems to refer here, as does also the very learned gentleman, can suitably be called the *beginning of Christ*, when Christ, having once been raised and seated at the right hand of the Father, has already reigned in heaven and on earth for so many ages. The other is how the designation of an everlasting beginning can likewise truly suit that kingdom in a sound sense. For what is an everlasting beginning in a matter that will not have an eternal beginning, but, like other things, a transient and vanishing one, indeed an end after a thousand years?

Since I could not extricate myself otherwise from the profound silence of both eminent men on either difficulty, I long ago began to suspect some corruption in the word *initium* (“beginning”), asking, “What if *epinicium* should rather be read?” I then began to examine one by one how many things favour it, as follows.

First, John narrates in Revelation 7:9–12 that, after many other things which would come to pass in the course of ages, he once saw a great multitude, which no one could number, from all nations, [Col. 0637B] tribes, peoples, and tongues, standing before the throne and the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palms in their hands, and crying with a loud voice: “Salvation to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb.” All the angels, who at that time likewise stood around the throne, the elders, and the four living creatures, fell at these words upon their faces before the throne and worshipped God, saying: “Amen. Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honour and power and strength be to our God for ages of ages. Amen.”

Since palms were borne in the hands of the former group, these acclamations of both groups are no less truly an *epinicion* (ἐπινίκιον, “victory-song”) than the triumphal and laureate songs which the ancients sang to victors and called *epinicia*.

Next, those ancient songs were generally, as may be established even from Suetonius in his *Julius Caesar*, extremely impure and, if not always each confined to a single day, certainly to very few days at most. But the acclamations now under discussion are in every respect a holy *epinicion*, and truly everlasting to this extent: they belong to people who, as is clear from what follows, will worship God in his temple for all eternity.

Furthermore, among the other things which the Apostle joins in First Thessalonians with Christ’s descent from heaven, he expressly names a *keleusma* (κέλευσμα, “command-shout”):

> Αὐτὸς ὁ Κύριος ἐν κελεύσματι, ἐν φωνῇ ἀρχαγγέλου, καὶ ἐν σάλπιγγι Θεοῦ, καταβήσεται ἀπ’ οὐρανοῦ.

“[Col. 0637C] The Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a command-shout, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God.”

The Apostle undoubtedly alluded, when writing thus, to that kind of *keleusmata* which may be called military and which was formerly sung by victorious troops:

> “Raise a standard over the walls of Babylon; strengthen the watch; raise the guards; prepare ambushes; for the Lord has planned and done whatever he spoke against the inhabitants of Babylon. You who dwell by many waters, rich in treasures, your end has come, the measure of your cutting off. The Lord of hosts has sworn by his own life: Surely I will fill you with men like locusts, and over you a *celeusma* shall be sung.”  
> (Vulgate, Jeremiah 51:12–14.)

Even if Paul had instead alluded allegorically (ἀλληγορικῶς) to those ancient *celeusmata*, or exhortatory shouts, which were used in the treading of grapes and elsewhere in rowing, it is certain that the Vulgate translator elsewhere says of the former: “A *celeusma*, as of grape-treaders, shall be sung against all the inhabitants of the earth” (Jeremiah 25:30); and again, 48:33: “The grape-treader shall by no means sing the customary *celeusma*.” The nautical shouts, or those formerly given to rowers and called *keleusmata* (κελεύσματα) in a particular usage, were sometimes sung by young musicians and in a clear, projected voice (*assa vox*), as Paedianus testifies in his books on Cicero’s *On Divination*.

Moreover, the word *epinicium*, though Greek in origin, is sometimes used in Latin by the better pagan writers. Suetonius, for example, says in his *Nero*: “He declared … that on the following day, joyful among the joyful, he would sing the victory-songs (*epinicia*) which ought already to be composed for him.” On the undoubted authority of this usage, Laurentius Humfridus, at the end of his Origenic disputation on the resurrection translated from Greek: “The *Epinicion*, or triumphal acclamation, celebrated by Eutropius and, as appears, other hearers in praise of the victorious Adamantius: ‘O thou adorned with divine wisdom and every intelligence,’” etc.

Then, immediately after “the holy and everlasting beginning of Christ,” there follows in our Caecilius: “when he shall begin to descend.” These final words can never suitably refer except to Christ’s future descent from heaven, so often mentioned in the New Testament; and nothing can now fit that glorious descent of Christ better than, on the one hand, the last trumpet, which we have just recalled from Paul’s Epistles, and, on the other, the word *epinicium*, whose letters so largely occur in *initium*.

Finally, the Apostle denies in First Thessalonians [Col. 0638B] (4:15) that those whom Christ will find alive upon earth on the Day of Judgment will ever precede those who have fallen asleep in the Lord—that is, will be caught up earlier into heaven to go out to meet him. But nowhere does he, or any other sacred writer, deny that Enoch and Elijah, who were formerly carried alive into heaven, will descend from it on the same day in Christ’s company, so as to be his precursors and forerunners. Therefore the madmen whom this author mocks were all the more free to maintain that this would occur, and further to add that, at the last trumpet, they would sing in advance the praised victory-song of Christ, or something of the sort. Such, then, is the interpretation I have constructed of this passage, until we are taught something better.

“When he shall begin to descend.” Thus book 7, chapter 19: “Then heaven shall be opened in the middle of a dark and untimely night, so that throughout the whole world the light of the descending God may appear like lightning.” And shortly thereafter: “A sword shall suddenly fall from heaven, so that the righteous may know that the leader of the holy host is about to descend; and he shall descend, with angels accompanying him, into the midst of the earth.” —TOLLIUS.

That is, he understands our author as though he had written in so many words, “when Christ shall begin to descend.” I approve of nothing more. For what, for example, is Columbus’s construction: “When the holy and everlasting beginning of Christ shall begin to descend”? Especially if by Christ’s holy and everlasting beginning Columbus understood nothing other, as is likely, than Christ’s millennial kingdom. Kingdoms, or the beginnings of kingdoms, do not customarily move, descend, and ascend after the manner of human beings.

“When he shall begin to descend … they declare.” “When he shall begin to descend, they declare that they will go before.” —ABBOT OF ST HILARY. I wish he had indicated what meaning he drew from this passage with those supplements. I do not grasp it.

“They think that he will come … that he may be the devil’s runner and forerunner.” In brief, this is how learned men have hitherto completed the lacuna: “They think that he will come as one who is a forerunner.” Oxford and Cambridge editions. “They think that he will come, who will be a future forerunner.” Cuper. “They think that he will come as a forerunner.” Allix.

[Col. 0638D] “Of the human race.” Not now understood narrowly and improperly, as above, as meaning the Roman Empire—that is, all the provinces and all Rome, just as Aurelius Victor tacitly defines the Roman Empire in these words: “So greatly did all the provinces and all Rome rejoice at his destruction”—but understood beyond dispute most broadly and properly as the whole human race. Thus Florus (*Roman History*, book 4): “Everywhere,” he says, “there was either peace or treaty throughout the whole and continuous human race.” He meant not only all the nations which Augustus had formerly pacified in the west and south, likewise in the north within the Rhine and Danube, and in the east within Taurus and Euphrates, and which were consequently subject to the Roman people’s empire, but also the remaining nations which, as he continues, were free from Roman rule—the Scythians, Sarmatians, Seres, Indians, and Parthians—all of whom stood in peace in relation to the Roman Empire (ἐν σχέσει). See the passage, if you have leisure.

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0639A]

“After him.” Nero, of course. Hence the English translation of the reverend bishop of Salisbury, for greater clarity and in direct terms: “After Nero,” word for word, *Post Neronem*.

“After some years had intervened.” That is, thirteen. For precisely that many whole years, indeed with an additional three months and days, elapsed from the tenth day of June, when Nero miserably perished in the sixty-eighth year of the common Christian era, until the fourteenth day of September, when the other tyrant, of whom we shall speak shortly, began to reign in the eighty-first year of the Dionysian Christian era.

“Another tyrant, no less great.” “Domitian.” Maucroix’s French translation, in the margin. “Another Tyrant, Domitian, not much inferior to him.” The recently cited English translation, inserting Domitian’s name into the author’s words by way of commentary. “Domitian, whom his own Rome called the bald Nero.” Oxford and Cambridge editions, I suppose, from the appended verses of Ausonius:

> And Titus, fortunate in the brevity of his reign. There followed  
> his brother, whom his own Rome called the bald Nero.

Both ecclesiastical and secular history support all this. For among Nero’s immediate successors after Galba, Otho, and Vitellius—namely Vespasian, Titus, Domitian, and Nerva—none except Domitian fits what is related in this chapter. Compare Baluzius, col. 304, and Columbus, col. 395, but above all the chapter of Eusebius indicated by Baluzius.

“Tyrant.” Aurelius Victor likewise stigmatized Domitian with this description: “Therefore, from fear of Domitian’s cruelty and consciousness of their own danger, many conspired … and even admitted Domitia, the tyrant’s wife, to their counsel.”

“He arose.” This means “he began to reign,” interpreting our writer’s expression of the birthday of Domitian’s rule, not of Domitian’s birth strictly so called. That this must be done is strikingly evident from the fact that Domitian was so far from having been brought into the light after Nero’s death that he was already in his seventeenth year when Nero died. This passage strongly confirms, in my judgment, a view omitted by some chance from the most learned Cuper: when discussing Constantine’s birthday alone, he contended that the words *ortus* (“arisen”) and *oriri* (“to arise”) are not infrequently used with special elegance of those who become kings, emperors, or Caesars.

“He exercised a hated domination.” Namely, “displaying much cruelty against many persons, killing not a few members of the nobility and distinguished men at Rome without just judgment, and unjustly punishing countless other eminent men with exile beyond their native district and confiscation of their property,” as one may speak after Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History*, book 3, chapter 17): “Πολλὴν εἰς πολλοὺς ἐπιδεικνύμενος ὠμότητα, οὐκ ὀλίγον τε τῶν ἐπὶ Ῥώμης ἐπατριδῶν καὶ ἐπισήμων ἀνδρῶν πλῆθος οὐ μετ’ εὐλόγου κρίσεως ἀποκτείνων, μυρίους τε ἄλλους ἐπιφανεῖς ἄνδρας ταῖς ὑπὲρ τὴν ἐνορίαν ζημίαις φυγαῖς, καὶ ταῖς τῶν οὐσιῶν ἀποβολαῖς ἀναιτίως [Col. 0639D] [punishing].”

That is, if we imitate Valesius’s translation: “Giving many examples of his cruelty against many men, unjustly putting to death no small number of the noble and distinguished men of the city of Rome, and besides punishing innumerable other men of the highest rank, though innocent, by exile and confiscation of property.”

“Exercise domination,” incidentally, is one of those expressions which our forebears made French from Latin, of which we had previously said that there is an infinite multitude among our countrymen; we therefore did not readily concede to Tollius that *quo officio repleto* ought to be changed to *quo officio impleto*.

“He pressed upon their necks.” Thus chapter 7: “Many governors and numerous officials pressed upon individual regions and almost now upon cities”; see Tollius on those words. Compare chapter 15: “The persecution pressed violently upon the remaining people.”

As long as possible. Namely, for fifteen years and five months, if we are to follow the Greek Canon of Eusebius’ Chronicle, Jerome’s Latin version, and Jordanes, who is much later than both works. Thus, for example, the former says: Ῥωμαίων ἐβασίλευσεν θ Δομετιανὸς ἔτη ιε, μῆνας ε; that is, as Jerome translates and explains it: “The ninth ruler of the Romans was Domitian, Titus’s younger brother: 15 years, 5 months” [Col. 0640A]. Yet it would be surprising if Eusebius had not formerly written, instead of ἔτη ιε, μῆνας ε (“fifteen years, five months”), ἔτη ιε, ἡμέρας ε (“fifteen years, five days”). For Xiphilinus, excerpting Dio on Domitian, writes: Ἐμονάρχησε δὲ (Δομιτιανός) ἔτη πέντε καὶ δέκα, καὶ ἡμὲρας πέντε: “Domitian ruled fifteen years and five days.” Moreover, from 13 September in the year 81 of the Dionysian Christian era, when Titus, Domitian’s predecessor, ceased to live and rule, to 18 September in the same era-year 96, when Domitian exchanged life and sovereignty for death, only fifteen years and five days are to be reckoned—or at most, as Petavius preferred, fifteen years and six days. Indeed, the Epitome of Aurelius Victor records that Domitian ruled fifteen years; Suetonius, that he was killed in the fifteenth year of his reign; and Eusebius himself somewhere writes that he held power for fifteen years (πεντεκαίδεκα ἔτεσιν ἐπικρατῆσαι), without any mention of additional months or days. But they were undoubtedly rounding the number. Compare the Latin edition of Eusebius’ Chronicle, where, opposite A.D. 97 [Col. 0640B], the sixteenth year of Domitian is marked—since he had indeed entered upon it, however briefly. I add that the rounding of the number in Aurelius Victor’s passage under discussion is apparent also from the fact that, in place of his explicit words, “Domitian … ruled fifteen years,” another passage in the same author’s booklet *On the Caesars* reads: “He paid the penalty … in about the fifteenth year of his rule.” This cannot suitably be understood merely as “more or less the fifteenth,” but as “a little more than the fifteenth,” in view of the passage from Xiphilinus just cited.

Until he stretched out impious hands against the Lord. There is great diversity of opinion among chronologists regarding the year in which Domitian began to rage against Christians: some assign the beginnings of that persecution, in one way or another, to A.D. 90, others to 91, others to 93, others to 94, and still others to 95. We had here once proposed, with arguments that seemed not weak, to settle that controversy in Dodwell’s favour against Pagius and the rest [Col. 0640C], and the matter had long been finished. But, they say, what end will there be if we continue as we have begun? Henceforth we must grant to the greater number of our task-drivers (ἐργοδιώκται) that what we have annotated more fully upon this author, or still wished to observe, be reduced, as far as possible, into a few words. Cuper discusses this matter below in his first letter to Voetius, that eminent devotee of the more elegant Muses, p. 9 ff.; Dodwell in Dissertation XI on Cyprian, §16; and after him Pagius, under the years of Christ 90, §5–6; 91, §4; 93, §2; 94, §5; and 95, §2. On the expression employed here by our author, see Cuper, col. 475.

“And he ruled securely, until he stretched out impious hands against the Lord.” Domitian was the next after Nero to persecute Christians. … Yet there could not have been many who were crowned in that persecution. For it was extremely brief, so that it could scarcely have filled one year [Col. 0640D]. Lactantius implies that it was extinguished at once. “He ruled securely,” he says, “until he stretched out impious hands against the Lord. But after he was stirred up by the instigation of demons to persecute the righteous people, then, delivered into the hands of his enemies, he paid the penalty.” —DODWELL.

To persecute the righteous people. He explains what he had above meant by “destroying righteousness.” The distinguished English translator renders it “the holy seed,” that is, “the sacred seed,” as the Jews once called themselves (see 1 Esdras 9:2 and 3 Esdras 8:71).

He paid the penalty. Thus Aurelius Victor says of the same Domitian and in the same connection: “He paid the penalty in the forty-fifth year of his life.” Nor does Lactantius speak otherwise of Antichrist: “And when captured, he will at last pay the penalty for his crimes” (*On the Blessed Life*, ch. 19).

Killed at home. That is, in the palace. See what was said on chapter 14. That Domitian was killed in the palace which served as his home in the city of Rome, and where he even slept among other activities [Col. 0641A], is, in my judgment, beyond doubt. Eutropius, Jordanes, Suetonius, and Dio as excerpted by Xiphilinus report the matter with unanimous agreement against the author of the Alexandrian Chronicle, according to whom—cited before us by Cuper—Domitian was slain ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ τοῦ Διὸς, “in the temple of Jupiter.” “He was, on the contrary, killed in the palace by a conspiracy of his own people,” says Eutropius, for example. Suetonius and Zosimus also identify more precisely, each in part, the location in the palace where the murder was committed: Domitian’s bedchamber in the Palatine residence, in which he intended, as was his habit, to rest during the day, and at whose door Parthenius stood as supervisor of the chamber.

Even the memory of his name was erased. Aurelius Victor, *On the Caesars*: “The Senate decreed that Domitian’s funeral should be conducted—or, in the *Epitome*, carried out—in the manner of a gladiator, and that his name should be erased.” If you wish to see and know well how this was done, here is for you a notable example from Pagius’ *Historical-Chronological Criticism*, with the annotation of a very learned man:

[Col. 0641B]

A.U.C. 841. … BY DECREE OF THE SENATE, THE SECULAR GAMES WERE HELD.

“Domitian’s name is not found on that marble, because, as Suetonius says in his *Domitian* (ch. 23), the Senate decreed that Domitian’s inscriptions everywhere should be erased and every memory of him abolished.” —PAGIUS.

Add our author’s cry (ch. 52): “Where now are those magnificent and illustrious surnames of the Jovians and Herculians, celebrated among the nations—first arrogantly assumed by Diocletian and Maximian, and afterwards transmitted to their successors? The Lord has erased them and wiped them from the earth”—although that is indeed in a different sense from the present passage.

When he had constructed many remarkable works, etc. Behold, according to Cassiodorus’ *Chronicle*, not merely a very exact list of those works after Eusebius, whose similar catalogue is cited by Columbus, col. 395 [Col. 0641C], but also the consuls under whom each was built—a point omitted by Eusebius, or rather, to speak more truly, utterly confused by him.

Asprenas and Clemens.

> “Under these consuls many walls and most celebrated buildings were constructed at Rome: namely, the Capitol, the Forum of Passage, the Portico of the Deified [Emperors], the Iseum, the Serapeum, the Stadium, the Pepper Warehouses, the Temple of Vespasian, Minerva Chalcidica, and the Odeon.”

Domitian IX and Clemens II.

> “Under these consuls the most distinguished works were constructed at Rome: namely, Trajan’s Forum, Trajan’s and Titian’s Baths, the Senate House, the Morning School, the Golden Meta, the Sweating Meta, and the Pantheon.”

He had made noble monuments. Velleius Paterculus says of Publius Scipio Aemilianus: “He made a monument of his own valour, which had been a monument of his grandfather’s clemency.”

So that neither images nor inscriptions, etc. “The Senate was so delighted that, with the Curia filled in rivalry [Col. 0641D], it could not refrain from tearing the dead man to pieces with the most insulting and bitter kind of acclamations; it even ordered ladders to be brought in, his shields and images to be torn down before them and there dashed upon the ground, and finally decreed that his inscriptions everywhere should be erased and every memory abolished.” —Oxford and Cambridge editions, from Suetonius after Baluzius; see Baluzius, col. 305, for more.

Therefore, the acts of the tyrant having been annulled. This occurred under Nerva. “And Nerva released those being tried for impiety”—that is, Christians—“and recalled those who had fled” (Καὶ ὁ Νερούας τούς τε κρινομένους ἐπ’ ἀσεβείᾳ … ἀφῆκε καὶ τοὺς φεύγοντας κατήγαγε). —Oxford and Cambridge editions, from Xiphilinus following Dio, under Nerva.

“Therefore, the acts of the tyrant having been annulled, not only was the Church restored to its former condition, but it also shone forth much more brightly and flourished. … But afterwards the long peace was broken. For, after many years, there arose the execrable beast Decius, to afflict the Church.” If we follow Lactantius, there was no persecution whatsoever from Domitian until Decius. For he says: “Therefore, the acts of the tyrant”—Domitian—“having been annulled, not only was the Church restored to its former condition, but,” etc. From these words of his countryman we understand within what limits Cyprian’s “long peace” must be enclosed. —DODWELL.

“The Romans made void everything that Domitian had established.” —Jordanes, *On the Succession of Kingdoms*, I. And what our author here further says of the tyrant’s acts being annulled, he had above, in chapter 1, expressed in a similar phrase or sense as “annulling the tyrants’ commands.” “The Church was restored to its former condition.” How quickly this happened after Domitian, you have just now learned in two words from the Oxford and Cambridge editions, §17, at the beginning; Baluzius gives a fuller account, col. 305 [Col. 0642A].

Many good emperors. Nor is this according to historical truth. But he had to lie in order to prove that all persecutors met a miserable death, whereas Trajan and the Antonines died most peacefully. See John of Salisbury’s *Polycraticus* (VIII, p. 646 ff.). —TOLLIUS.

I was on the point of saying that the learned man had been engaged in something else when he wrote this [Col. 0642B]. Either because Zosimus, besides Eusebius and Lactantius—already cited for this purpose by Baluzius—testifies that many good emperors held the helm of the Roman Empire immediately after Domitian, in these words: “Domitian, slain by the freedman Stephanus … From this time good men (ἄνδρες ἀγαθοὶ) attained the imperial power: Nerva, Trajan, and after him Hadrian, Antoninus Pius, and the equal pair of brothers, Verus and Lucius.” Or because, even if Trajan and the Antonines died peaceful deaths—a fact I certainly should not wish to deny—our Caecilius did not thereby deny it any more, for he does not utter even a γρύ (“a word”) concerning their deaths, whether good or miserable. It therefore seems that he can only with the greatest injustice be said to have lied in order to prove that all persecutors met a miserable death. Especially since he placed neither Trajan nor the Antonines, nor any other Roman emperors from Domitian to Decius, among the persecutors, as what follows will establish [Col. 0642C].

But now I think that what displeased Tollius was precisely this: that our author, I say, called Trajan and the Antonines—whom Eusebius and others count among the Church’s persecutors—good emperors. The eminent man doubtless did not deny that they were good to the Romans and other pagans over whom they ruled, but denied that they were such to Christians. Nor did he imagine any other reason for that celebrated encomium than this author’s bad faith: since he could not show that they had met a miserable end, he lied that they were good. As though our author had undertaken to prove that the Lord always produced great examples in persecutors, rather than that “the adversaries of God often receive the reward their crime deserves,” as he will himself say in the proper place. Or again, as though, from Eusebius’ method of writing—where Hadrian is called, in Justin’s words, “most great and most illustrious” (μέγιστος καὶ ἐπιφανέστατος), although elsewhere he represents the same Hadrian not, with Sulpicius Severus, as setting up “images of demons in the temple and place of the Lord’s Passion, in order to destroy Christian faith” [Col. 0642D], but rather as “moved by a letter written in Christians’ favour by Serenius Granianus”; indeed, as so moved that he immediately wrote to the proconsul of Asia that Christians were not to be condemned without accusation of crimes; and who finally did not count a fourth persecution under Hadrian, in Sulpicius’ manner, but postponed mention of his fourth until the times of Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus—we should infer that Eusebius lied in all these matters and handled Hadrian’s affairs with evil intent alone.

Let, then, both our Caecilius and Eusebius rather be writers of good faith in these matters, yet writers to whom, for some serious reason, individual harassments of Christians did not seem worthy of inclusion in a catalogue of persecutions, nor even the individual emperors under whom, and sometimes because of whose rule, they occurred, worthy of enrolment in the register of persecutors. Precisely as Sulpicius himself says (*Sacred History*, II): “At that time Licinius, because he contended with Constantine for imperial power, ordered his soldiers to sacrifice; those refusing, he expelled from military service. But this is not counted among the persecutions, so slight was the matter that it did not reach the level of wounds upon the Churches” [Col. 0643A]. Or, to put it better, just as Jerome in his *Chronicle* recounts ten persecutions of the Church down to the time of Licinius, while Sulpicius in his *Sacred History* counts only nine—not even the same individual ones as Jerome’s; indeed, omitting among the others Aurelian’s persecution, which this author had justly rendered conspicuous by Aurelian’s bloody writings on one hand and cruel deeds on the other—yet was not therefore accused of bad faith because he undoubtedly had regard to Aurelian’s brief and ineffective attack, “who was not even permitted to accomplish what he had planned, being slain immediately at the outset of his rage,” as our author will shortly say.

Having suffered no attacks from enemies. Not that it suffered absolutely nothing from Domitian’s death until Decius. For it suffered, for example, under Trajan, Hadrian, Severus, and the Philips, as may be seen in Eusebius and others. Rather, the attacks made against it during those times were no attacks at all—that is, they were futile and of minor consequence [Col. 0643B], such as did not prevent “the Church from stretching out both hands simultaneously to East and West,” as our author puts it. Thus, altogether, in Cicero’s *Philippics* 5, he says, “These are no excuses”—not because he saw that no excuse at all was to be considered, for three immediately follow: “He is my friend. Let the fatherland come first. He is my kinsman”—but because, in his judgment, those three were worthless and trivial. Likewise, in *Philippics* 13: “What is it, wicked man, that makes you groan—that Dolabella, an enemy, has been judged so by the Senate, an order which you think does not exist at all?” Not that Antony likewise believed there to be no Senate in the city or the world; for, as follows, “he made it his cause for waging war to destroy the Senate utterly”; but because the Senate had no authority with Antony. On the subject itself, see Dodwell’s Dissertation XI on Cyprian, §§17–25 [Col. 0643C]. What if our author’s genuine text was perhaps, “having suffered some attacks from enemies” (*nonnullos inimicorum impetus passa*)—that is, a few and not very severe?

She stretched out her hands into East and West. Eusebius, discussing matters belonging to Trajan’s reign (*Ecclesiastical History* IV.2), says: Καὶ τὰ μὲν τῆς τοῦ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν διδασκαλίας τε καὶ ἐκκλησίας, ὁσημέραι ἀνθούντα ἐπιμεῖζον ἐχώρει προκοπῆς· “And the teaching and Church of our Saviour, flourishing more and more every day, advanced with continual increase.” Again, in the same book, ch. 7, speaking now of Hadrian’s times: ἤδη δὲ λαμπροτάτων δίκην φωστέρων τῶν ἀνὰ τὴν οἰκουμένην ἀποστιλβουσῶν ἐκκλησιῶν, ἀκμαζούσης τε εἰς ἅπαν τὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων γένος τῆς εἰς τὸν Σωτῆρα καὶ Κύριον ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν πίστεως … “Moreover, since Churches shining throughout the world like the brightest stars were now in bloom, and faith in our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ was flourishing among the entire human race,” and what follows [Col. 0643D]. On the expression, see Columbus, 396.

So that there was now no corner of the earth, etc. This writer therefore did not mean above, when he mentioned Christ’s disciples scattered immediately after His ascension into heaven and added that, while Nero had not yet begun to rule, they had founded the Church through all provinces and cities, to be understood as speaking of the entire inhabited earth without qualification. Rather, he excepted certain regions, more or fewer, in East and West, to which he thought Christ’s religion had not penetrated even under Nero’s entire reign; likewise, certain most savage nations which embraced the worship of God only long after Nero and were softened to works of righteousness. Hence also our qualifications in their respective places—“in a broad sense,” “widely”—when we discussed the author’s words concerning the whole earth having been evangelized (εὐηγγελισμένῃ) before Nero.

But did the Apostles, at least, on the hypotheses of our Caecilius, preach the Gospel before Nero’s rule in America generally understood? Pagius must affirm this after what he observed in his *Criticism* under A.D. 42, §2, both in the margin and elsewhere [Col. 0644A].
