But I would not hesitate to deny it; and Pagius himself must elsewhere deny it, since Lactantius—whom everyone, including Pagius along with all others, considers the true author of this book, and whom we too believe to be so—strongly attacks the doctrine of the Antipodes in *Divine Institutes* III.23. Thus there are among the ancients, without now amassing the authority of Augustine and others, those who would deny Pagius’ assertion that the Apostles proceeded to the utmost regions of the world. To follow my custom: Baluzius has something on this passage, col. 305.

Finally, no nation, etc. These things are said hyperbolically (ὑπερβολικῶς) and must be moderated by interpretation. Yet he speaks almost no differently in Book V, ch. 13, where he says: “Since the divine law has been received from the rising of the sun to its setting, and every sex, every age, nation [Col. 0644B], and region serve God with united and equal minds.” —TOLLIUS.

“Finally, no nation.” It would be preferable, I think, to read from an old manuscript, “finally, no nation of God,” on the basis of this passage of the Apostle, Romans 3:29: “Is he the God of Jews only? Is he not also of Gentiles? Yes, also of Gentiles.” Hence there is no nation in the world which is not God’s nation. Besides, when Paul proceeds, “Since God is one, who will justify the circumcision by faith and the uncircumcision through faith,” it follows that no nation could live in manners so savage as not to be softened to works of righteousness by the preaching of the Gospel and the worship of God.

Having received the worship of God. Lactantius has a similar expression in *On the Blessed Life*, ch. 27: “to receive wisdom along with true religion”; in *On Justice*, ch. 13: “to receive the divine law”; and in the final chapter of the *Epitome*: “to receive him whom God sent.”

But afterwards the long peace was broken. “Afterwards,” that is, under Decius, as is clear from what follows. The long peace is therefore approximately one hundred and fifty-three years. Only beware that, in light of what we said above [Col. 0644C], you do not understand this peace as βαθέα ἐν πάσῃ ἐκκλησίᾳ—“very deep throughout the entire Church”—such as Eusebius says Hegesippus found to have existed under Nerva. Our author instead speaks of a peace sometimes disturbed by a few minor persecutions, of the sort Sulpicius Severus had in view when he wrote: “Then, after thirty-eight years had intervened, Christians had peace—except that, in the intervening time, Maximinus harassed the clergy of certain Churches.” Here you see a peace of thirty-eight years, not pure and uninterrupted, but broken by some harassment; indeed, Jerome’s *Chronicle* plainly calls that interruption of peace under Maximinus the sixth persecution of the Church.

## CHAPTER IV

There arose, after many years. That is, after many years of tranquillity. —MAUCROIX, as his French version indeed reads. Undoubtedly, because of the recent mention of long peace, which he thought was to be supplied here in some measure from the common construction (ἀπὸ τοῦ κοινοῦ). But the complete phrase would therefore have to be restored thus: “after many years of long peace,” or “of tranquillity”—a mere tautology, since whoever says “peace of many years” thereby asserts that the peace was long. I would therefore prefer simply to understand “after many years” as referring to the many years that had elapsed, which, as we have now said, were one hundred and fifty-three.

The execrable beast Decius. Our author treated Nero with no different artifice (col. 196). But Cuper has something quite different about Decius’ immediate successors, col. 475.

For who—righteousness, etc. He returns to the mode of expression which we explained before, and which Lactantius uses similarly in these words: “This was often the chief cause of persecuting righteousness for evil kings.” For the rest, see Columbus, col. 396.

To that supreme eminence. Is it in the sense in which *principalis* sometimes means “first” and “chief”? Or in the sense in which, for example, Trebellius Pollio calls the power of Roman emperors “the highest summit on earth,” and our author below calls it “the lofty eminence” [Col. 0645A]? I would not think so, but rather in the sense in which *principalis auctoritas* (“imperial authority”) and *principalis notio* (“imperial cognizance”) in Zeno’s law concerning criminal cases properly signify the authority and cognizance of the emperor, in the second paragraph:

> “Only in cases of men of this kind will it be permitted to the deputy of the imperial auditor, if an accusation not brought before him has been disclosed, to refer it to the imperial cognizance; but the measure of punishment to be imposed on dignities so great shall rest only in the emperor’s discretion.”

And again shortly afterwards: “For in this case, concerning the restraint of the calumny of an accuser of this sort, imperial authority must not improperly be consulted.”

He immediately began to rage against God. It is certain that he began the persecution immediately upon assuming the empire. “As though he had been elevated to that supreme eminence for this very purpose, he immediately began to rage against God, so that he might immediately fall,” says Lactantius. And one and the same report brought the Alexandrians news both that Decius had succeeded to the empire and that he had issued edicts of persecution, as appears from Dionysius of Alexandria’s letter to Fabius of Antioch. He was himself at Rome toward the end of A.D. 249, beginning to rule about July; and Moses, Maximus, and Celerinus with their companions were the first of all to be arrested, while Decius was still residing at Rome. —DODWELL, Dissertation XI on Cyprian, §53, from which and the following five sections the remaining information concerning this persecution of Decius may be obtained.

“And as though he had been elevated to that supreme eminence for this very purpose, [he began] immediately to rage.” Thus Ammianus Marcellinus relates that “Caesar Gallus, advanced unexpectedly from the excessive squalor of miseries, in the first beginnings of the age granted [or: adult] to him, to the supreme height amid unlooked-for splendour, rushed beyond the bounds of his destroyed power and defiled everything by excessive harshness” [Col. 0645B].

For he set out against the Carpi. Constantine, in his *Oration to the Assembly of the Saints*, calls them Getae or Goths; Zosimus, Scythians. This can be reconciled thus: because the Carpi and Goths had the same origin, and because both had settlements beyond the river Ister, their names could easily be interchanged. —Oxford and Cambridge editions, from Baluzius, whom see for fuller annotation on this subject. See also Cuper, col. 475, and Columbus, col. 396.

And immediately, surrounded by barbarians, etc. Zosimus thus relates the manner of his death: “When Decius had signalled Gallus to rush upon them”—that is, the Scythians—“through the marsh, he attacked rashly through ignorance of the terrain, and, with the force accompanying him, was at once stuck fast in the mud. Being struck from every side by the barbarians’ missiles, he perished with those with him; no one was able to escape” (Τοῦ δὲ Γάλλου … μετὰ τῶν συνόντων αὐτῷ διεφθάρη, διαφυγεῖν οὐδενὸς δυνηθέντος). —Oxford and Cambridge editions [Col. 0645C].

He could not even be honoured with burial. I would prefer, “not even with burial” (*ne sepultura quidem*), since this is the common form of expression; so in ch. 6: “He was not even permitted to accomplish what he had planned.” Yet it must be admitted that the former construction occurs in ch. 7: “Though he was destroying everything, he could not refrain his hands even from God”; likewise in Lactantius, *On the Blessed Life*, ch. 1: “But those who, puffed up by ambition or inflamed by love of power, have devoted all their effort to obtaining honours, would not give credence even if we carried the sun itself in our hands”; and in Pliny (*Natural History* VIII.36), concerning bears: “They emerge in spring, but the males are very fat; the cause is not evident, since they are not fattened even by sleep except for fourteen days.” But the great Graevius, whom I consulted on these passages, among other things replied thus: “I think you have seen rightly in judging that *ne sepultura quidem* should be restored; and similarly in chapter 7, in Pliny, and in Lactantius’ *On the Blessed Life*. Copyists often confused *ne* and *nec*, although each has its proper place. I recall that Gronovius likewise corrected various passages in Suetonius.” —GRAEVIUS.

As befitted an enemy of God. Supply: “to be.”

For birds. “For vultures.” —MAUCROIX. As though our author had written *vulturibus* (“for vultures”).

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0646A]

Not long afterwards, etc. That is, not long after the emperor Decius. —English translation. In A.D. 251, Decius perished at Abritus, a city of Moesia; this occurred at the end of November or the beginning of December, as may be established from the observations of the illustrious Pagius. In A.D. 256, according to many, or at the latest, as Pagius preferred, in 257, Valerian’s persecution began. Thus, in truth, not long after Decius’ death, Valerian was seized by a similar frenzy of persecution. Our author, who omitted several others, also passed over in silence—as is clear—the persecution which Gallus and Volusian stirred up in A.D. 252 toward the end of June. But, to copy Pagius here deservedly, neither Eusebius in the *Chronicle*, nor Saint Augustine in *The City of God* XVIII.51—rather, 52—nor Sulpicius Severus counted it, since it was local and raised at Rome alone. Nor did Eusebius in his *History* record martyrs who suffered under Gallus and Volusian [Col. 0646B]. Indeed, Pagius continues, Orosius, who in Book VII compares the ten persecutions by which the Church was afflicted with the ten plagues by which Egypt was struck, derives the seventh plague under Gallus and Volusian from the pestilence which destroyed almost every kind of human being and beast, not from tortures inflicted on the faithful. Thus PAGIUS.

Valerian. Namely, the elder, who in A.D. 253, immediately after Gallus and Volusian were killed, was chosen emperor by the Norican and Raetian armies and soon made Augustus. He was at once father of Publius Licinius Valerian and grandfather of Publius Cornelius Valerian Saloninus. See Pagius under A.D. 259, §3–4, and 253, §8–9.

Valerian. “At the beginning of his reign he showed himself most kindly disposed toward Christians; then, with this disposition, he also changed his fortune.” —Oxford and Cambridge editions.

He directed impious hands against God. In chapter 3: “until he stretched out impious hands against the Lord.” The former expression is very frequent in Virgil, Tacitus, and others [Col. 0646C].

Although for a short time. That is, for about two years, according to Pagius’ calculation, which we consider sound. Not that Valerian ruled only two years; for he had begun his seventh year of rule when he was captured by Sapor; but because, with the Right Reverend Bishop of Salisbury, we believe the short time in question is to be understood of the duration of the persecution rather than, with Maucroix, of the duration of the reign. Compare Dodwell, Dissertation XI on Cyprian, §§59–60.

Of righteous blood. He understood much in view of the brevity of the time, much in view of the rank of those who suffered. —DODWELL.

Others differently, as appears from the same writer, whom you should consult. But, for example, why should the blood which the most learned man contends was shed in Egypt beyond the terms of the edict Valerian sent to the Senate—and whose substance Cyprian has preserved for us in his letter to Successus—not rather properly be said to have been shed under a special rescript to Aemilianus, prefect of Egypt? Dodwell argues from Valerian’s edict to the Senate alone. Yet besides that edict, indeed even before it—which was peculiar to the city of Rome, or at most Italy—very many other commands had been sent by the same Emperor Valerian to provincial governors, as is certain from Cyprian’s aforementioned letter. After setting out the substance of Valerian’s edict to the Senate, it continues: “Valerian the emperor also appended to his decree”—that is, to the law—“a copy of the letter which he sent to the governors of the provinces concerning us,” that is, Christians in general [Col. 0646D].

Moreover, not only does Aemilianus, prefect of Egypt, in Eusebius speak of “the command of the Augusti” (τῆς τῶν Σεβαστῶν κελεύσεως) sent to him, almost word for word; two facts among others show that this rescript was different from the one Valerian sent to the Senate. First, the one to the Senate was Valerian’s alone, if we heed Cyprian’s letter in more than one place; whereas the one to Aemilianus was not Valerian’s alone, but that of the Augusti—that is, Valerian and Gallienus. Second, by the command of the Augusti sent to Aemilianus, he was obliged, before all else, to banish the Christians of his province to a place in Libya called Cephro. Of this there is not one word in Cyprian’s account of Valerian’s rescript to the Senate; and rightly so, since this matter specifically concerned the prefect of Egypt, not the Senate, and Valerian had already written concerning Christians living in the provinces to their governors.

The public proceedings in Eusebius concerning the confession of Dionysius and others:

> “The prefect Aemilianus said: ‘I see that you are at once ungrateful and foolish, since you do not perceive the clemency of the Augusti. Therefore you will not remain in this city, but will be sent to the regions of Libya, to the place called Cephro. For I have selected this place by the command of our Augusti (ἐκ τῆς κελεύσεως τῶν Σεβαστῶν ἡμῶν).’”

Accordingly, some particular rescript had been conveyed to him by the emperors, and Valerian must therefore rightly be deemed to have shed, by that same command of the Augusti, the blood which he subsequently shed abundantly in Egypt [Col. 0647B]. Thus Valerian shed more blood, without bringing forward other evidence now, than Dodwell thought.

So that he might be an example to posterity, etc. Thus above, ch. 1: “God had deferred their punishments in order that he might produce in them great and remarkable examples, from which posterity also might learn … that God inflicts death, by worthy vengeance, upon the proud, the impious, and persecutors.”

The adversaries of God often, etc. Do you hear how, according to this author’s hypotheses, God’s enemies receive the reward deserved by their crime not always, but often? This passage therefore strongly confirms what we argued above against Tollius. Accordingly, our author could have counted Trajan and the Antonines among the Church’s persecutors even if they had died very peacefully, provided the persecutions occurring under them had flowed from their own edicts. But because they arose from elsewhere, those emperors were counted by our author among the company of good rulers [Col. 0647C]. That being so, I wish the most distinguished translators had not suppressed the word “often” (*saepe*).

He was captured by the Persians. The year in which Valerian was captured by Sapor has hitherto been disputed. … It is certain that, during A.D. 259, Valerian was reduced, in Zosimus’ words, to the condition of a slave, having entered upon the seventh year of his rule, approximately at the beginning of summer. —PAGIUS, whom one must by all means consult.

“He was captured at the end of A.D. 261.” —DODWELL, Dissertation XI on Cyprian, §59.

“Valerian, after setting persecution in motion against Christians, was immediately captured by Sapor, king of the Persians.” —JEROME, *Chronicle*, under A.D. 268 in Scaliger’s edition; but this contains more than one error. See above, §4, and Pagius in the relevant places.

Whenever it pleased him. “Whenever it had pleased him.” The Abo edition, whether by accident or design. Columbus says nothing about it in his notes. “More Latin would be *liberet*, or, closer to the writing of the old book, *libuerat*.” —TOLLIUS. I prefer the latter conjecture. For similarly in ch. 21: “As often as it had pleased him to take delight.” I have also considered whether our author’s fuller text perhaps read not, “whenever it had pleased him to mount either a carriage or a horse,” with a double *aut* (“or”), but with a single one: “whenever it had pleased him to mount a carriage,” etc. [Col. 0647D].

To mount a carriage or a horse. Thus Terence says *ascendere navem*, “to board a ship”; Caesar, *ascendere iugum*, “to climb a ridge”; and Livy and Suetonius, as here, *ascendere equum*, “to mount a horse,” without a preposition—although a preposition is usually used in such expressions, and Livy himself elsewhere says *ascendere in equum*.

To bow down to him, etc. Trebellius Pollio deliberately passes over this insult, mentioning no other affront than that Sapor spoke with the Roman king as with a cheap and contemptible slave—as though this disgrace had been confined to words alone. —Oxford and Cambridge editions.

“To bow down to him …” Eutropius, in the manuscript *Life of Pontius* from the library of the most learned P. Puteanus: “The Emperor Valerian, having been led captive by Sapor, king of the Persians, received the deserved recompense for his deeds throughout all his life, not by the sword but by mockery: whenever King Sapor wished to mount a horse, he raised himself onto the horse not by his own hands but with his back bent and his foot placed upon Valerian’s neck.” —GALE and BALUZIUS, though with several variant readings not to be despised [Col. 0648A].

The Roman. “The Roman Emperor.” That is, “the Roman emperor.” —English translation.

The Roman. Supply “king” from the common construction (ἀπὸ τοῦ κοινοῦ). That you may do so without hesitation, observe how Trebellius Pollio has long before led the way: “Valerian,” he says, “was defeated by Sapor, king of the Persians … and when Sapor, through the success of his glorious victory, treated him less honourably than was fitting, with proud and lofty spirit, and spoke with the king of the Romans as with a cheap and contemptible slave,” etc. Therefore, just as Greeks countless times called both Augusti—that is, emperors—and Caesars distinct from Augusti βασιλεῖς (“kings”), so Latin writers too, not uncommonly after the emperors of the first and second centuries, gave the name *reges* (“kings”) to Augusti and emperors; indeed, even one apparently much less noble, as we shall shortly see [Col. 0648B].

With his foot placed upon his back. A phrase for which no examples now occur to me except in the Vulgate: for instance, 2 Kings 12:30, “and the diadem was placed upon David’s head”; and Acts 15:10, “Why do you tempt God, to place a yoke upon the neck of the disciples?”

He said that this was the truth. I do not grasp the sense of the passage unless Lactantius means to suggest that what Sapor reproached him with was true: that Valerian belonged to him in the position of a slave, since he served as a ladder or stirrup—not, certainly, the things which the Romans paint upon tablets, that is, Persians conquered and triumphs won over them. Oxford and Cambridge editions, from which the author of the most elegant Paris translation does not greatly differ.—I should prefer: “He said that this was the true spectacle,” as in chapter 16: “This is the true triumph when,” etc. GALE.—“He said that this was the truth.” Namely, that he had placed his foot upon [Col. 0648C] Valerian’s back, and even as he spoke was pressing it there. For the whole sequence of the discourse is: “and, having placed his foot upon his back, he said that this was the truth . . . not what the Romans painted on tablets or walls”; so that our Caecilius, after Sapor, finally referred to that actual, not imaginary but truly enduring, position of both bodies, in which Sapor trampled with his foot upon Valerian’s back after he had once been commanded to bend down and offer his back. “Bend down before me and offer your back,” the king of Persia therefore said more imperiously to the Roman. When Valerian complied in deed with this command, Sapor immediately put his foot upon his back, saying: “This is the truth, not what the Romans paint upon tablets or walls.” As if he had said: “Your Romans once dared to depict the Persians as subjected to themselves in this fashion. But those things were fabricated at pleasure and wholly imaginary. Yet when I now put my foot upon you as you offer your back, this is pure truth, Valerian.” Thus, in my judgment, the entire difficulty of this passage arose because the author did not reproduce Sapor’s complete or exact words—which, I think, we have now supplied—but altered them and used expressions of his own.

**Reproaching him with laughter.** Much light and elegance, I think, may be brought to these words if they are joined with the immediately preceding and following words in this way: “He said, reproaching him and with laughter, that this was the truth, not what was painted upon tablets,” etc. Nor do I doubt greatly that this is the author’s own hand: that he did not, I say, write that Sapor reproached Valerian with laughter—for that expression is indeed obscure and less Latin—but that what Sapor said to Valerian was said to him in reproach and at the same time in mockery.

**Most deservedly led in triumph.** That is, as he deserved. For *dignus* and *digne* are so used by the ancients. Our author in chapter 1 says that God inflicts death upon the persecutors in deserved vengeance, and that in this very matter the enemies of God often receive a reward worthy of their crime. Otherwise one would have to read “most undeservedly.” Moreover, *triumphatus*, because of what follows, seems altogether to convey the sense of being led in a triumph, in remembrance [Col. 0649A] of that most famous triumph. Nor, in my opinion, is the English translation to be understood otherwise: “Being thus led about in triumph.”

**He lived for some time.** Valerian lived in that slavery until the year 269, according to the testimony of the author of the Alexandrian Chronicle, who deserves credit in this matter: “Under these consuls”—that is, Claudius and Paternus—“the Emperor Valerian, overwhelmed by the Persians, perished.” PAGIUS.—Namely, in A.D. 259, when Pagius is certain that Valerian was captured by Sapor. Thus Valerian’s servitude lasted ten years.

**Although he had a son as emperor.** That is, the elder Gallienus, whom he had already made his partner in imperial power in A.D. 251, and who, after his father’s capture, administered the supreme affairs alone for many years. To this belong these words of the English translation: “That he had a Son, upon whom the Empire had devolved by his misfortune.” Add Baluze, col. 306.

**The utmost slavery.** Doubtless in the same sense in which Livy uses “a man of the lowest talent” for a man of very mean talent, and “the lowest men” for the most lowly and humble persons [Col. 0649B].

**Nor was he recovered at all.** This is entirely true. Yet the Bactrians, Iberians, Albanians, and Tauro-Scythians wrote to the Roman commanders, promising aid to free Valerian from captivity, as Trebellius Pollio records in writing in his *Life of the Elder Valerian*.

**His skin was stripped off.** Nicolaus Heinsius thought that one should write *derepta est ei cutis*, “his skin was stripped off.” For in Latin *diripere* is one thing, as in plundering fields or cities; *deripere* is another, meaning to strip off or take away. That great man demonstrated this amply in his notes on Ovid, and confirmed it by the evidence and authority of very ancient manuscripts. GRAEVIUS. Compare Cuper, col. 482, and Baluze, 306.

**Dyed with a red colour.** “Which they painted red.” MAUCROIX.—As though our author had written *picta rubro colore*, “painted with a red colour.”—“And both it and its being tinctured with a red colouring.” English translation.—As though one now read in our author *tincta rubro colore*, and the subject concerned not Valerian’s skin alone but his entrails also. [Col. 0649C] I doubt whether the latter can readily be reconciled with the structure of the narrative: “and the skin, stripped of its viscera and dyed with red colour, was set up . . .” As for the rest, I scarcely dare determine which interpretation is preferable. Yet I think the second interpretation preferable because of this passage of Pliny: “Even women’s eyelids are, in a manner, dyed: so great is the pursuit of beauty that even the eyes are coloured.”

**Dyed with a red colour.** Just as votive images (*agalmata*) used to be covered with vermilion. On this subject see Servius on Virgil: “For red is a colour sacred to the gods, because of their fiery nature.” TOLLIUS.—I should willingly adopt the learned man’s view, were it not immediately followed by: “that it might be placed in the temple of the barbarian gods in memory of that most famous triumph.” But from the words “in memory of that most famous triumph,” I above all suspect that Valerian was clothed in a purple garment on the day on which Sapor triumphed over him—so that he might insult Valerian more bitterly and display before all eyes that he was celebrating a triumph over an emperor. Nor did Roman soldiers clothe Christ in a purple robe for any other reason, when they wished to mock him more intensely. Then I also suspect that Sapor was pleased to have the skin of Valerian, finally dead and flayed, dyed red for no other reason than that the memory might endure forever of that most famous day on which he had led Valerian, clothed in purple, in triumph. Compare Baluze on the same words, col. 306.

**The spoils of the captive prince.** Not therefore in the sense in which Virgil, *Aeneid* II, says:

> . . . clad in the spoils of Achilles;

but in the proper sense in which the same author has “the spoils of a serpent” in these verses:

> When, having cast off its old skin, new and bright with youth,  
> it coils itself.

Likewise Plautus uses “bovine spoils” for an ox-hide [Col. 0650A] or ox-skin; and again Accius in the *Bacchae*:

> Then fitting the painted spoils of beasts to his left side.

Let learned readers judge whether this passage can in any degree elucidate what has just preceded, “dyed with a red colour.” It does not seem so to me, but rather to concern the painted garments of the ancients. Moreover, our author, who shortly before silently bestowed the title “king” upon the emperor, now expressly calls him “prince”; this title, as I said, has at first appearance far less dignity. But do not attribute this to Valerian’s captivity. The highest dignity and authority of fortunate emperors was sometimes called the *principate* by the Romans, and they themselves were called *princes*. Hence our author in chapter 3 says: “Many good princes held the helm and governance of the Roman Empire.” Hence too, shortly afterward in chapter 4, he calls their *hyperochē* (“pre-eminence”) “that princely height.” So also in Pliny and others, “during the principate of Claudius” and “during the principate of the divine Augustus” mean while Claudius and the divine Augustus were ruling. Finally, concerning our very Valerian, while he was already captive, Balerus, king of the Cadusians, writing to [Col. 0650B] Sapor, says: “I do not sufficiently congratulate you upon the capture of Valerian, prince of princes”; so that even from this it may be clear what *princeps*, when said of a Roman emperor, signifies in the blind and perverse flattery of the pagans: precisely what is said of the Son of God in Revelation 1:5, “the prince of the kings of the earth.” Away with it!

**They might behold it among their gods.** There are countless examples in Latin authors in which “among me” and “in my house” mean exactly the same thing. Thus here “among their gods” and “in the temple of the barbarian gods,” which immediately preceded, have the same meaning for me.

**To act . . . against the majesty of God.** Here is what we said above: in our author *facere*, “to act,” is found absolutely, that is, without an accusative object. So too at the end of chapter 6: “they acted against God.” That this may seem less surprising, one should know that *facere* in both examples is nothing other than what we daily call *agir*, “to act,” used intransitively; the Greeks commonly use *politeuesthai* (“to conduct oneself”). In this sense too this author, speaking of Maximian in chapter 9, says: “thereafter he began to act most insolently.”

**The one God.** See Cuper, col. 482.

[Col. 0650C] **The all-containing [God], etc.**, in the same place.

## CHAPTER VI

**Aurelian.** The successor of the Emperor Quintillus—or Quintilius, according to Jerome’s *Chronicle*—who was killed on the seventeenth day of his reign; this was in November A.D. 270, or in the following month. The consular lists call him in several places L. Domitius Aurelianus; some inscriptions also call him Valerius Aurelianus, from the Valerian family to which he belonged by birth. See Jerome’s *Chronicle*, at A.D. 271; Pagius’s *Criticism* at A.D. 270, no. 3, and 271, no. 1; and finally Petavius, *On the Doctrine of Times*, at A.D. 274 and 275.

**Mad by nature, etc.** Aurelian was, undeniably, a severe, fierce, and bloodthirsty prince. Oxford and Cambridge editions, from Flavius Vopiscus. Add Baluze, col. 307, and Columbus, col. 397.

**Although he remembered the captivity of Valerian.** If anyone asks whence our author knew this, the answer is [Col. 0650D] ready. He could remember it because the event was so recent and notable that he could not fail to recall it; for Valerian had only lately died among the Persians after ten years of captivity—or, what is the same, only in A.D. 269. See above, col. 448.

**He provoked the wrath of God by cruel deeds.** Thus Aurelian’s persecution was not merely contemplated, as the most distinguished Dodwell thought, but put into execution, as Pagius says and proves by many arguments in his *Historical-Chronological Criticism*, at A.D. 272, nos. 5 and 6. Compare also the third and fourth arguments; indeed, Baronius at A.D. 273, nos. 9–10, and 275, nos. 4–5 and following. There, although the innumerable thousands of martyrs whom Leo the Great placed among those suffering in the eighth persecution under Aurelian are not enumerated, very many are at least named, together with their punishments, on the authority of martyrologies and similar writers.

**Aurelian . . . provoked the wrath of God by cruel deeds, [Col. 0651A] but he was not even permitted to accomplish what he had devised; rather, he was immediately cut off at the very beginning of his fury.** Thus Gallienus issued an edict of indulgence to the Egyptians in A.D. 272 with the utmost precision, the feast of Easter being at hand . . . Thereafter no one is suspected of persecution until Aurelian. Yet Sulpicius Severus, a man otherwise much devoted to fables, passed over even Aurelian himself. And rightly so. For it was merely contemplated by Aurelian, not put into execution. This is indicated clearly enough by Lactantius and Eusebius, writers closest to those times. What could be clearer than Lactantius’s words? “But he was not even permitted to accomplish what he had devised; rather, immediately,” etc. Similarly Eusebius says of the same Aurelian: “Already he was being stirred by certain plans, as though he were about to raise a persecution; and there was much talk of this among all. But as he was already on the point of it, and, so to speak, almost setting his signature to documents against us, divine justice overtook him, all but pulling him away from the undertaking by the elbows.” Thus Aurelian was merely impelled to stir up persecution against Christians; and only a rumour of it circulated [Col. 0651B] as of something not yet brought to completion. Eusebius also said that he was “about to” do it, and that, “so to speak,” he was nearly signing the edicts when he was overtaken by God. He had not yet therefore stirred up persecution; he had scarcely even signed the edicts when he was punished by God. God checked his attempt with his arm held back. The matter therefore had not yet advanced beyond an attempt; he had not yet inflicted the blow which he had threatened with raised arm. DODWELL.

**But he was not even permitted to accomplish, etc.** Dodwell adduces this passage of Lactantius and says: “If Aurelian was not permitted to accomplish what he had devised, as Lactantius relates, it follows necessarily that no martyrs were made by his decree.” Yet Dodwell’s position is destroyed by this very passage and by those following it. Lactantius, who was closest to these times, says indeed that Aurelian could not accomplish what he had devised, but he does not say that he was not permitted to begin it. He adds immediately that he did begin the persecution: “rather, he was immediately cut off at the very beginning of his fury” [Col. 0651C]—not, therefore, before its beginning, but before he could complete it and bring it to an end. The following words confirm this more strongly: “His bloody writings had not yet reached the more distant provinces, and already he himself lay bloodied on the ground.” They had therefore reached provinces nearer to Thrace, where he was killed. By these words Lactantius also confirms what is reported in Eusebius’s *Chronicle* and in Orosius: that some interval of time passed between the decree of persecution and Aurelian’s murder. PAGIUS, in whom there is much more worthy of reading on this subject.

**He was immediately cut off at the very beginning of his fury.** Aurelian was killed, it seems, one or two months after issuing the edict of persecution. PAGIUS.—Thus the persecution was exceedingly brief, even though he called it by that name: at most two months. But, the learned man continues, it lasted after Aurelian’s death for several months, that is, throughout the six-month interregnum; and any Christians who then suffered martyrdom are said in the martyrologies to have suffered under Aurelian [Col. 0651D], because they were killed by force of his decree. Thus again PAGIUS.

**To the more distant provinces.** That is, the remotest provinces. For Thrace has not yet been named by our author, so that with Pagius one may understand provinces lying beyond Thrace. Maucroix, “to the most distant provinces,” is of the same opinion as we are.

**Writings.** That is, edicts—the rendering of Maucroix—or “edicts against Christians,” the fuller interpretation of the Bishop of Salisbury. Know only that writings of this kind seem to be called by another name, *letters*, in chapter 10, no. 22, in these words: “and, having sent letters to the commanders, he ordered even soldiers to be compelled to abominable sacrifices”; there read what we have noted.

**Coenophrurium.** “But while he was travelling, he was killed at Coenophrurium, a stopping-place between Heraclea and Byzantium, by the treachery of his secretary and by the hand of Mucapor.” Oxford and Cambridge editions, from Vopiscus. Add Baluze, col. 307, and Columbus, 397.

[Col. 0652A] **Which place is in Thrace.** But what sort of place? “A village,” says Maucroix, that is, a country settlement. Ferrari’s *Geographical Lexicon* had preceded him: “Caenophrurium, Castelnovo, as the Greek name itself signifies, a village of Thrace, on the Propontis, between Byzantium . . . and Heraclea . . . where the Emperor Aurelian was killed, according to Eutropius.” Vopiscus called it a *mansio*, a stopping-place, in the words just cited; the meaning of that word will be discussed in its proper place below.

**Killed by his friends.** Oxford and Cambridge editions, from Vopiscus: “It happened, as events are fatally wont to happen, that he rendered Mnestheus—whom he had employed as secretary of confidential affairs, his freedman, according to some—more hostile to himself by threats, because he had suspected him of I know not what. Mnestheus, knowing that Aurelian neither threatened without cause nor, when he had threatened, forgave, drew up a short list of names, mixing those with whom Aurelian was genuinely angry with persons against whom he had conceived no harsh intention,” etc.—The man whom Vopiscus calls Mnestheus is called by Zosimus Eros, “appointed as messenger of replies brought from outside,” as we formerly noted on the first book of Zosimus. The same editions. Add Columbus, col. 397.

**They acted . . . against God.** English translation: “They acted against God.”—Literally, “They acted against God”; this confirms what we said at the end of chapter 5. Compare Columbus, col. 397; Sallust uses similar language of the ancient Romans: “Each best man preferred to act rather than to speak . . .”

## CHAPTER VII

**Diocletian.** He was proclaimed emperor in A.D. 284—not later, as Scaliger incorrectly maintains—and this occurred not at the Palilia, or 21 April, as very many believed before Petavius’s *Doctrine of Times*, but on 17 September, if one follows with Pagius the author of the Alexandrian Chronicle; or on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, that is, 20 November, if one prefers Baluze’s Diocletian chronology. See Petavius, book XI, [Col. 0652C] *On the Doctrine of Times*, chapter 30; finally Pagius’s *Criticism on the Annals of Baronius* at A.D. 284, nos. 3–4.

**The inventor of crimes and contriver of evils.** MAUCROIX: “A wicked prince, and author of all our evils.”—As though the final words of the passage were “and contriver of all our evils.” English translation: “That was the Contriver of all our late miseries.”—Likewise as though the received reading were “inventor of all our latest evils.” Both translations, I think, meet the difficulty which Tollius will touch upon at chapter 9, col. 666. Add Columbus, col. 397. Lactantius, in chapter 7 of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, teaches us what kind of character Diocletian possessed . . . Yet Eusebius testifies that Diocletian favoured Christians in the earlier years of his reign. In book VIII, chapter 1, while describing the great glory attained by the Christian religion before the persecution begun in A.D. 302, he says: “The emperors’ goodwill toward our people may be proof of this: they entrusted even provinces to them to govern, freeing them from every fear of sacrificing because of the particular goodwill with which they were disposed toward our religion. What need is there to speak of those who moved in the emperors’ palaces? What of the emperors themselves?” etc. These matters must be referred here. PAGIUS, at A.D. 284, no. 9.

**The whole world.** You will shortly see it called Diocletian’s kingdom; it must therefore be understood simply of the Roman Empire, as must likewise the word *world* used shortly afterward without qualification.

**Avarice and timidity.** An example of his avarice occurs in Vopiscus’s *Numerian*, when he was staying among the Tungri. Oxford and Cambridge edition.—Baluze cites the passage from Vopiscus, col. 307. But do you wish here for a notable proof of Diocletian’s timidity? Continue reading what our author says. “For,” he says, “he made three men partners in his rule.” If any reason was ever decisive, this is one. Compare the passage from Aurelius soon to be adduced: “Because the burden of wars pressed more urgently,” etc.; also the most distinguished Graevius on [Col. 0653A] chapter 8, no. 6; and finally what we say on chapter 9, col. 664, and chapter 10, col. 668.

**He overturned the whole world.** In the Latin acts of the passion of the holy martyrs Tarachus, Probus, and Andronicus—who certainly suffered, sooner or later, under Diocletian and Maximian Herculius—one reads: “Maximus said, ‘You curse the emperors, O wicked head, who have bestowed a lasting and nourishing peace.’ Andronicus said, ‘I have cursed and do curse the powers and blood-drinkers who have overthrown the world.’” Since this was said courageously while those emperors lived and before a Roman governor, this writer deserves still greater credit when, after the death of both, he makes similar assertions.

**For he made three men partners in his rule.** Maximian, surnamed Herculius, in A.D. 285; Constantius, surnamed Chlorus; and Galerius Maximianus, surnamed Armentarius, in A.D. 293. Oxford and Cambridge editions.

Add Baluze, col. 307; Cuper, col. 482; Columbus, col. 398; and Pagius’s *Criticism* at A.D. 292—when, according to Pagius, though not in the following year, [Col. 0653B] Constantius Chlorus and Galerius Maximianus were made Caesars by Diocletian.

**His rule.** As though the subject concerned the dominion and power of a king properly so called, rather than an emperor who administered the world. But since, as we have already seen, Roman emperors were called kings, at least in the third century, their dominion and power also sometimes received the name of kingdom. Aurelius Victor says of Diocletian’s own reign: “After celebrating the twentieth year of his kingdom, in better health he relinquished the care of the commonwealth.” Compare the Latin translation of Eusebius’s Chronicle by Jerome: “Tiberius makes Drusus a partner in his kingdom”; likewise, “Philip made his son Philip a partner in his kingdom.” The translators rendered the word here simply as “empire.”

**When the world had been divided into four parts.** See how, in a truly notable passage of Aurelius Victor: “Because the burden of wars . . . pressed more urgently, as if the empire had been divided, all Gaul beyond the Alps was entrusted to Constantius”—this is the first part—“Africa and Italy to Herculius”—the second—“and the Illyrian coast as far as the strait of Pontus to Galerius”—there is the third. “Valerius retained the rest.” Here you have the fourth. Consider, then, whether Spain did not fall among the other territories to Valerius Diocletian.

**Which the former princes had held alone, etc.** English translation: “The former emperors.” That is, former emperors. An excellent commentary. For among the ancients *emperor* and *prince* are interchangeable terms, even when the greatest emperors are under discussion. Compare what is said on chapter 14, no. 10.

**Of those receiving.** English translation: “Of those who received his pay.” That is, those who received wages from him.

**Of those giving.** The same translation: “Of those who paid his taxes.” That is, those who paid the taxes imposed upon them.

**The enormity of the assessments.** Thus in Spartianus’s *Caracalla*, “the enormity of the pay”; in Pontius’s *Life of St Cyprian*, “the enormity of a longer interval”; and in the Novels of Theodosius, “the enormity of the palatine exaction”; finally, in Julius Capitolinus’s *Gordian III*, concerning Philip the Arab, “who did not restrain himself in the novelty and enormity of his fortune” [Col. 0653D].

**Assessments.** Taxes. Oxford and Cambridge editions. Add Baluze, col. 307.

**The fields were abandoned.** See Baluze, col. 307.

**And cultivation.** Perhaps the text was *et culta rura*, “and cultivated lands”; although the received reading is not bad either. TOLLIUS.

**The provinces too were cut into fragments.** Augustus left the Senate a summary of the Empire; from Strabo, Tacitus, and Pliny we understand what it was like. No emperor is recorded as having altered the distribution of provinces until Hadrian. We learn from Appian that Hadrian did make some changes. But whatever distribution of provinces he eventually left to posterity seems to have remained again until Diocletian. For Diocletian, together with his Caesars, made a new division of the provinces. Lactantius reports in his golden little book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* [Col. 0654A] that under his rule the provinces were cut into fragments. DODWELL, *Dissertation on Cyprian* XI, no. 23.

**Many governors.** See Cuper, col. 482, and Columbus, col. 378.

**Offices.** That is, officials. Oxford and Cambridge editions.—Compare Du Cange’s *Glossary*, under *Officium*, and Graevius below, chapter 8. But that lower-ranking officials must be meant here is shown both by the preceding mention of governors, to whom those officials were subordinate, and by comparison with Pollio’s passage on the two Gallieni, where prefects and masters of palace offices are mentioned thus: “When he went to the gardens bearing his name, all the palace offices followed. The prefects went also, and the masters of all offices attended.”

**To press upon.** Thus also in book VII, *On the Happy Life*, chapter 19: “For, having captured the world, he will press upon it with great armies of robbers”; and above, book III: “Yet he pressed upon the necks of his subjects for a very long time.” Florus, book II, chapter 6, concerning Scipio: “Thus it came about that he drove Hannibal, clinging to and pressing upon Italy, away.” But I see that the most distinguished Columbus has already assembled many more examples on chapter 3 [Col. 0654B], col. 395. TOLLIUS.

**Rationales.** The procurators of the emperors, whose task was to secure for the fisc property escheating or left vacant in the provinces. Oxford and Cambridge editions.—Lampridius in the *Life of Alexander Severus* clearly shows that *rationales* are in fact the same as imperial procurators: “Whenever he wished either to assign governors to provinces, appoint overseers, or establish procurators—that is, rationales—he posted their names.” Concerning the same *rationales*, I find in the Code: “The rationalis shall decide cases pertaining to the fisc, all extortions being forbidden”; and elsewhere: “If you prove that the property occupied by the fisc belongs to your master, our rationalis will follow the public law.”

**Masters.** See Columbus, col. 400, and also what is to be said on chapter 14, no. 18.

**Deputies of prefects.** The deputies of the prefects of royal cities did not have such authority that they might do the same things as the prefects whose place they held. Thus a broader [Col. 0654C] authority was now given here, that they might carry out the will of the Prince. TOLLIUS.

**To all of whom.** Perhaps one should read, “under all of whom.” GALE.

**Civil acts.** That is, judicial acts rendering decisions in civil cases; and likewise shortly afterward, condemnations and proscriptions mean judicial acts concerning condemnations and proscriptions. Those who performed such acts were called *actuarii* and *actuales* by the ancients. Aurelius Victor: “So many factions of clerks flourish . . . in the army.” The glosses of Philoxenus and others: “Actuarius, a practical recorder”; “actual knowledge, practical [knowledge].” Compare Cuper, col. 483, and Columbus, col. 400.

**But only condemnations, etc.** How “only condemnations and proscriptions”? That is, how did they do nothing but condemn and proscribe, if, as follows, proscriptions alone were frequent? Again, how “only condemnations and proscriptions,” when there were evidently civil acts, however rare? Should one read: “under all of whom civil acts were very [Col. 0654D] rare, but condemnations and proscriptions frequent,” omitting *tantum* (“only”)? Certainly the whole difficulty of the passage would disappear. Yet there will, I think, be some to whom this adverb seems rather superfluous, as in this passage from Justin’s epitome: “I consider it the duty of an ungrateful citizen,” says Trogus, “if, after he has illuminated the deeds of all nations, he should remain silent about his own country alone”; although the passages are not perfectly alike.

**Proscriptions.** This word may be understood both of persons driven into exile and of their goods confiscated to the fisc. TOLLIUS.

**Exactions.** See Columbus, col. 400.

**These things too.** Read, “Nor are these things either [to be endured].” ALLIX.—Rather, “Neither are these things either [to be endured],” which departs less from the old manuscript. And long before I saw the most learned man’s conjecture, I wondered, as my friends know, that it had occurred to no one, so easy and necessary was the correction. For what matters connected with Diocletian’s government of the commonwealth are named and enumerated in the preceding passage? Are they in any respect tolerable things, so that our author, continuing the list, could add: “These things too can be endured”? By no means; rather, they are altogether intolerable things: namely, “the enormity of the assessments, the continual exactions of countless things, and in the exactions injuries not to be endured.” From this it is clear that there should immediately have followed: “nor can these things either be endured.”

**For supplying soldiers.** That is, for providing soldiers’ pay. PAGIUS.—Likewise Oxford and Cambridge editions, following Baluze, who has further material on this point, col. 308.—*Ad exhibendos milites.* In later Latin, *exhibere* means to feed or support. Justin, book XI, chapter 10: “supporting life wretchedly”; that is, sustaining oneself wretchedly. Graevius, whom you should also consult on this matter at chapter 11, no. 2.

**By various injustices.** Thus Salvian, book V: “For by what other things were the Bagaudae made, if not by our injustices, if not by the wickedness of judges,” etc.

**A law of prices.** See Baluze, col. 308, and Columbus, col. 400.

[Col. 0655B] **Until the law.** See the same authors, in the same place.

**In supplying labourers, craftsmen, and all carts, whatever they may be, etc.** I think a conjunction has fallen out. Lactantius seems to have written: “In supplying labourers, craftsmen, carts, and all things whatever necessary for construction works.” The *-que* was swallowed up by the following syllable in *quaecumque*. They were compelled to supply not only labourers, craftsmen, and carts, but also every other implement required for constructing works. GRAEVIUS.

**All things whatever.** Here too a conjunction is lacking. Read therefore, “and all things whatever.” TOLLIUS.

**Here a basilica, here a circus, here, etc.** In place of *hic* (“here”), I think one should read *hinc* (“from here”) everywhere. GALE.

**Here a mint.** See Cuper, col. 483, and Columbus, col. 400.

**Here [a factory] of arms.** See Cuper, col. 483.

**A great part of the city is departed.** For “a great part of the city is made to depart.” Citizens were driven out of private buildings whose sites were to be absorbed into the emperor’s construction projects; as though the city had been captured, they were compelled to depart and seek other dwellings. TOLLIUS.—“A great part of the city is departed.” Read, “by a great part of the city they depart,” or “a great part of the city is cut down.” ALLIX.—*Exceditur*: read *exeditur*. GALE. Allix too elsewhere.

**Of the city.** Of Nicomedia, which Diocletian strove to make equal to Rome, as follows. Oxford and Cambridge editions. The most learned translators agree, for they do not even mention the word “city,” but put Nicomedia in its place. Compare Baluze, col. 308.

**Thus he was always madly extravagant.** “So madly expenceful was he.” English translation. Literally, “He was so foolishly lavish.”—*Dementabat*: “He raved,” namely, with an unbounded passion for building. TOLLIUS.—Maucroix says nearly the same. Add Cuper, col. 401, in Columbus’s note on this passage.—*Dementabat*: perhaps *dementabatur*? ALLIX, though elsewhere he unreservedly says that *dementabatur* should be read.—For my part, I do not doubt that our author wrote the compound *demutabat* (“altered”) for the simple *mutabat* (“changed”), because he had recently used *mutari*, in this sense: “But the reason why Diocletian more than once demolished and altered works already completed was that he sought to make Nicomedia equal to the city of Rome.” Thus he first mentioned Diocletian’s frequent alterations to his buildings, and then gave the reason for them, which I have stated and which is very plain and apt. *Demutare* means the same as *mutare*. Plautus:

> . . . or if they alter your character by their habits;

for “change” or “transform,” as appears from the preceding verse:

> If you wish to transform your character by your habits.

But prose authors also used the verb *demutare* and its verbal noun *demutatio*. Apuleius, though in a sense somewhat different from that which we follow here, says: “Although your very ugly face differs very little from that of tragic Thyestes”; that is, differs. Pliny, however, uses *demutatio* in exactly the meaning in which Latin writers usually employ *mutatio*: “No animal is thought more fearful than the chameleon, [Col. 0656A] and for that reason [it is thought] to have a changeable variation of colour,” at least according to the older editions. For it must be admitted that the newer editions print *mutationis*, perhaps among other reasons because of the unusualness of the word. It is certainly surprising that editors have made no mention of the ancient reading.

**Permitted by custom.** See Baluze, col. 308.

## CHAPTER VIII

**What of his brother?** Namely, Diocletian’s. PAGIUS, at A.D. 291, no. 2.—Correctly, although that designation must be carried back from the beginning of chapter 7.

**His brother Maximian.** Not by nature but by imperial office; for Diocletian was a Dalmatian, Maximian a native of Pannonia. “You have mingled different bloods with affections,” says Mamertinus in his panegyric. “Your brotherhood is not accidental but chosen.” Oxford and Cambridge editions.—“Maximian, his associate in the Empire,” MAUCROIX.—That is, Maximian, his associate in administering the empire; with this agrees the English translation: “His Colleague in the Empire,” his colleague in imperial rule. [Col. 0656B] Compare Baluze, col. 308; Cuper, 483; Columbus, 401.

**Who was called Herculius.** Maucroix’s translation closes the first period of this chapter here: “Maximian, his associate in the Empire—what likeness had he not to him?” The Abo edition likewise closes it thus: “What of his brother Maximian, who was called Herculius?” But these matters derive from the excellent guide, the eminent Cuper, whom see, col. 485.—“Who was called Herculius.” The *Compendium of Roman History* published by Pomponius Laetus, where the subject is also treated more fully: “They gave themselves surnames. Diocletian was called Jovius, Maximian Herculius, as though the one were heir of Jupiter, the other of Hercules.” But Aurelius Victor says otherwise, and more credibly, in the *Caesars*: “To this man [Maximian] the surname Herculius was later added in honour of the deity, just as Jovius was added to Valerius [Diocletian]; whence the name was also given to military auxiliary units greatly surpassing the ordinary army.” Add Cuper, on “who was called,” col. 485; and Columbus, under *Herculius*, col. 401.

**Not unlike him?** Remove the question mark. [Col. 0656C] GALE.—Cuper rightly wished it transferred from here to the passage just cited; thus, after the writer had turned to Maximian Herculius with the question, “What of his brother Maximian, who was called Herculius?”, he briefly answered himself: “Not unlike him”; that is, he was not unlike Diocletian.

**For they could not have remained united in so faithful a friendship unless there had been, etc.** This is said rhetorically for “For they could not have remained united in so faithful a friendship unless there had been”; and so on. For they were no longer alive. Thus the English translation is excellent: “Nor could they have been cemented into so entire a friendship, if they had not been,” etc. Maucroix’s translation comes to the same thing: “Unless they had had the same inclinations, the same thoughts, the same desires, could they have lived in such perfect harmony?”

**For they could not have remained united in friendship.** That well-known saying of Sallust in the *Catiline*: “For to desire the same things and to reject the same things—this, and this alone, is firm friendship.” TOLLIUS.

**In both, etc.** See Baluze, col. 310.

Hoc solum differebant, quod avaritia minori, etc. [Col. 0656D] “That, in avarice, the lesser…” The Abo edition, together with the Oxford edition of 1684 and the Cambridge edition of the following year, reads *quod avaritiae minori*. *Avaritiae* should be read. Vossius, soon to be supported by others, so holds.

Hoc solum differebant, quod avaritia minori, etc. With Baluzius I suspect that there is a corruption in this passage; for the construction of the words has been dislocated. Yet I cannot agree with that most learned man, who judges the words corrupt and depraved because Lactantius would otherwise contradict himself, since he writes elsewhere that Maximian was not especially diligent in preserving the wealth supplied to him by the very wealthy provinces of Africa and Spain. For why should Maximian not be considered more rapacious, Diocletian more grasping? Especially since Maximian was savage in spirit, cruel in avarice, and in this respect at least surpassed his partner in empire.

Accordingly, until its meaning is better established, I restore the passage thus: “They differed only in this: that the one who was less avaricious—that is, Maximian—had more [while the more avaricious had less, but more fearfulness], but more courage, not for doing good, but for doing evil.” Thus the intermediate words, enclosed in brackets and detached from the preceding words, seem to me to furnish the meaning which this passage requires. The Oxford edition of 1680, from which the English translation may be said to differ only in words.—The Bishop of St Asaph reads: ‘That the one less avaricious had more, but more timidity; whereas the more avaricious had less [Col. 0657A], but more courage,’ etc.” This reading is indeed clearer; but if it is admitted, Lactantius will not be consistent with himself, since below he describes Diocletian as fearful and unnerved in every disturbance. SPARK in the Oxford edition of 1684, and likewise in the Cambridge edition, after the remarks just reproduced from the earlier Oxford edition.—All who have laboured to cleanse this little work have perceived that this passage is corrupt and dislocated, and have employed various remedies. Perhaps Lactantius wrote:

> They differed only in this: that one had greater avarice, but also more timidity; while the other had less avarice, but more courage—not for doing good, but for doing evil.

[Col. 0657B]

I would not venture to guarantee that this is Lactantius’ own hand; nevertheless, I am persuaded that this reading departs less far from it, if one considers what precedes and follows. He says that Diocletian had the greater avarice, but also the greater timidity. Hence in the preceding chapter he said that Diocletian had overthrown the world by both avarice and timidity. Because of that timidity he admitted three men into partnership in the empire; they multiplied the armies and exhausted the Roman Empire. He then adds examples of his avarice. Maximian, however, he represents as less avaricious but prodigal, and bolder in doing evil—namely, in killing very wealthy senators and carrying off maidens. I later saw that the most learned Columbus was of nearly the same opinion. GRAEVIUS.—I read: “They differed only in this: that the one less avaricious had more, but also more timidity; whereas the more avaricious had less, but more courage—not for doing good,” etc. GALE.—Let us likewise indulge in conjecture toward understanding and restoring this passage. [Col. 0657C] What if *minori* and *majori* were ancient marginal notes, first written, as usual, in the margin of the book and afterward, by ill fortune, admitted into the author’s words? What if the author originally wrote:

> They differed only in this: that one had more avarice, but more timidity; the other less, but more courage—not for doing good, but for doing evil?

Then it would certainly have been easy to understand the earlier *altero* as referring to the younger brother, and the latter to the elder brother, since this writer is unquestionably treating Diocletian and Maximian Herculius as brothers. Likewise, an annotator could easily have placed *minori* and *majori* immediately in their proper places in the margin, if, building on what he believed were firm foundations from the ancients, he held Diocletian to have been younger in age and Herculius older.

The grounds chiefly before me are two. One is from Cassiodorus’ Chronicle: Diocletian and Maximian Herculius laid aside the purple in the same year because of age, after Diocletian, as Eutropius relates, had urged Herculius to withdraw into private life and entrust the post of guarding the commonwealth to men fresher and younger. The other is that, according to Zosimus, Maximian Herculius not only died a natural death like Diocletian, but died several years earlier. No one is ignorant how often scholars complain that marginal notes have wrongly crept into authors’ texts; and, I think, a most evident example of the fact will occur in what immediately follows. We know elsewhere from Victor’s *Epitome* that Diocletian lived sixty-eight years, while Maximian Herculius died at only sixty. Add Baluzius, col. 311, and Columbus, col. 401.

Subjacerentque opulentissimae provinciae vel Africa, vel Hispania. What? If Africa alone, for instance, lay subject to him, did several very rich provinces lie subject to him, rather than merely one? The manuscript, therefore, should read: “And the very wealthy provinces of Africa and Spain lay subject to him,” as the most distinguished interpreters [Col. 0658A] have been led to read, contrary to the authority of that manuscript and of Aurelius Victor alike. Or at least it should read: “And the very wealthy provinces of Africa or Spain lay subject to him,” in the genitive case. But the received reading is such that, after mention is first made not of one province but of several, they suddenly collapse into a single Africa or Spain.

Further, since Aurelius Victor, writing on the Caesars under the Emperor Julian, knew well that, with the empire as it were divided, all Gaul beyond the Alps had been entrusted to Constantius, Africa and Italy to Herculius, and the Illyrian coast as far as the straits of Pontus to Galerius, while Valerius (Diocletian) retained the rest—among which Spain must therefore be included—who would believe that our Caecilius, who lived much nearer to the times of Maximian Herculius, did not know the same facts, or, what comes to the same thing, could not discover and state whether Africa or Spain, in addition to Italy, lay subject to Herculius?

He therefore wrote simply, as the matter itself demands: “For, since he held the very seat of empire, and very wealthy provinces lay subject to him” [Col. 0658B]—that is, the general province of Africa, in which several smaller provinces were included—“he was not so diligent in guarding wealth,” etc. But someone born long after our author, who did not know or did not sufficiently recall which provinces our author had precisely meant, yet wished incidentally to elucidate the passage for himself or others, noted in abbreviated form in the margin beside the words *opulentissimae provinciae*, “either Africa or Spain,” that is, “such as Africa or Spain.” From this there later arose and was written into the text the reading upon which we comment. Learned men, however, as the following remarks will show, take another view—something which must be admitted.

Dodwell, in Dissertation XI on Cyprian, *On the Scarcity of Martyrs*, no. 75, thinks that at this time there were no martyrs in Spain because Constantius governed it. Victor, in *On the Caesars*, writes that Italy and Africa obeyed Maximian Herculius, but says of Constantius: “With the empire as it were divided, all the territories beyond the Alps in Gaul were entrusted to Constantius.” Therefore [Col. 0658C], because Victor does not assign Spain to other jurisdictions, the most learned Dodwell thinks that Spain, Britain, and Gaul were entrusted to Caesar Constantius. From this he infers that there were no martyrs in Spain, since no edict of Constantius intervened, and the magistrates of Urbicus, lacking the power of the sword, could crown no one with martyrdom.

But Victor’s cited words show only that Constantius governed Gaul; Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, ch. 8, teaches that Spain was subject to Maximian Herculius: “For since he held Italy, the very seat of empire—Herculius, that is—and the very wealthy provinces of Africa or Spain lay subject to him, he was not so diligent in guarding the wealth with which he had an abundance at hand.” PAGI, on the year of Christ 303, no. 10.

Non erat in custodiendis opibus tam diligens. “He was not so careful in the management of his treasure as was necessary.” English translation.—That is, he did not show as much diligence in guarding wealth as was necessary. More simply, *tam diligens* may mean “very diligent.” [Col. 0658D] Suitable authors not infrequently use *tam* elegantly for *valde*, “very.” Pliny, *Natural History* VII.49: “M. Caecilius Rufus and C. Licinius Calvus were born on the same day, both indeed orators, but with so different an outcome”; where nothing could ever be more *tam dispari*, “so different,” than *valde dispari*, “very different.” Likewise Plautus in the *Mostellaria*, act IV, scene 2, line 9:

> You make him fierce because his master loves you so much.

On this verse Taubmann rightly explains *tam* as “very,” confirming it by the cited passage of Pliny and others.

Non deerant locupletissimi Senatores, etc. A device well known to Aurelian, as Vopiscus relates: “It is also said that he possessed such cruelty that he would bring against very many senators a fabricated charge of conspiracy and usurpation, in order that he might more readily kill them.” Oxford and Cambridge editions. Compare Baluzius, col. 311.

Qui subornatis indiciis, etc. I had stumbled over this [Col. 0659A] passage and therefore thought it should be explained, among other passages, from Livy: “To create odium against Marcus Fulvius, he introduced into the Senate Ambracian envoys suborned with accusations”; that is, to accuse, since *crimen* often means in Cicero the accusation itself, or an indictment on charges. But the knot can be solved much better in another way, as you will now see.—To “suborn evidences” (*subornare indicia*) is to suborn witnesses (*indices*). Thus *conjugia* for spouses, *servitia* for slaves, *officia* for those who perform duties, and a thousand similar instances that may easily be amassed. Nothing is more certain. Suetonius, for example, in his *Augustus*, uses *consilia semestria*, “half-yearly councils,” for half-yearly councillors. GRAEVIUS.—The English translation agrees: “Accused by some witnesses that were suborned to swear against them,” etc.; that is, accused by several suborned witnesses.

Effoderentur assidue lumina senatus. “That the lights of the Senate should continually be dug out.” Justin uses almost the same phrase concerning the Athenians captured by the Lacedaemonians. And our author, V.12: “Finally, let their hands be cut off, their eyes dug out.” Below, ch. 36: “Thus the eyes of confessors were dug out.” TOLLIUS. [Col. 0659B] Add Baluzius, col. 311, and Cuper, col. 485.

Jam libido in homine pestifero. Heinsius rightly saw that one should read: “Now lust, destructive in the man,” etc. GRAEVIUS.

Non modo ad corrumpendos mores, etc. The sense will be clearer if you read *mares*, “males.” Although the progression may appear less fitting from the crime of sodomy to the abduction of maidens, among Romans the latter crime was nevertheless considered greater than the former. BURNET.—Long before he was Bishop of Salisbury, and before we received, together with the others, Colomesius’ note to be added shortly. Compare Cuper, col. 485.—Nothing is more certain than the splendid conjecture of the most learned Burnet. GRAEVIUS.—All the more, let me add this: if we consider the matter more closely, the author’s progression does not proceed simply from the crime of sodomy to the abduction of maidens, as the expression of that most distinguished man somewhat too strongly suggests, but from the crime of corrupting males to that of violating daughters of noble families. Thus Maximian inflicted force upon the latter by having intercourse with them, but not upon the males, whom he had first gained for himself by entreaty, payment, or other seductions. [Col. 0659C] In this sense *corrumpere*, “to corrupt,” is certainly less than *violare*, “to violate,” especially when the violation concerns daughters of the foremost families, as it does here. Nor should one doubt that the distinction is the same in Aurelius Victor: “he corrupted the marriages of nobles,” concerning Carinus, who pursued the wives of soldiers; and “after forcibly defiling very many,” concerning Victorinus.—Our friend John Battely, Archdeacon of Suffolk, a most eminent man and domestic chaplain to the most reverend Archbishop of Canterbury, most keenly scented out that *mares*, rather than *mores*, must be read. The reverend Dr Burnet does not differ from him in his English translation of this little work. COLOMESIUS.

Verum etiam ad violandas prim. fil. Thus he was in truth [that is, he went even so far as to violate the daughters of leading men],, as the Emperor Julian says of him in the *Caesars*, “in every way licentious in the affairs of Aphrodite” (*τὰ εἴς ἀφρωδίτην παντοίως ἀσελγής*).—“In the debauching of daughters …” English translation.—Sparing the ears, I suppose, since *violandas*, “to be violated,” signifies much more here.

Felicitatem imperii. See Cuper, col. 485.

Si libidini, et cupiditati malae nihil denegaret. Such were the habits of the man who afterward persecuted the Church. PAGI, [Col. 0659D] on the year of Christ 291, no. 2.—*Si libidini*: Cicero in Nonius: “For the grave mistresses of thought, infinite lusts, compel and command certain things; and because they can in no way be satisfied or sated, they drive all those inflamed by their enticements toward every crime.” TOLLIUS.

Constantium. Understand Constantius Chlorus, one of those three whom Diocletian is said in ch. 7, no. 6, to have made partners in his rule: “He made three partners of his rule.” On those words we have noted in which year after Christ’s birth this happened to each. Compare Baluzius, col. 312, and Columbus, col. 402.

Orbem. Namely, the world which Diocletian is said in ch. 7, no. 8, to have divided into four parts: “with the world divided into four parts.” See the notes. “The whole empire.” English translation. That is, the entire empire; the sense is, if I see rightly, excellently expressed. Maucroix, on the contrary, took it as the whole or universal world: “Worthy to command the whole universe.”

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 0660A]

Alter vero Maximianus, etc. “As for Galerius, Diocletian’s son-in-law.” MAUCROIX.—In Latin: “concerning Galerius, Diocletian’s son-in-law.” Not badly, if we look to other historians; but perhaps not so well, if we look to our author. To explain: that other Maximianus, to whose history our author now hastens, is very frequently called Galerius by Latin historians, so that they may distinguish him more readily from Maximian Herculius. This occurs whether they also add the name Maximianus or not. In the first manner we read in Eutropius, book IX: “Diocletian made Maximian Herculius Augustus from Caesar. Maximian Galerius was born in Dacia, not far from Sardica”; and again in Aurelius Victor, though in another order: “Galerius Maximianus, whose byname was Armentarius,” etc. In the second manner, after a few intervening words, the same author says: “The Illyrian coast as far as the straits of Pontus was entrusted to Galerius.”

But, as Maucroix seems not to have observed, this writer has somehow [Col. 0660B] refrained throughout the whole work from calling him Galerius. Instead, he either employs other distinguishing marks—for example, shortly below, “whom Diocletian had taken as his son-in-law,” and in ch. 10, “Caesar Maximianus,” and so on—or none at all, as in ch. 19: “There was,” he says, “a high place … on whose summit Maximian himself had assumed the purple.” This refers to Galerian Maximianus, as will be clear from the remaining sequence of the work. In this latter way the Emperor Julian speaks of the two Maximiani together in the *Caesars*: “Then Diocletian, taking with him the two Maximiani and my grandfather Constantius”; here you see no other names for either Maximian. Add Baluzius, col. 312, and Cuper, col. 486.

In what year this Maximian, now under discussion, was advanced by Diocletian to the administration of the state and made Caesar has been said above, sufficiently, on ch. 7, no. 7.

Quem sibi generum Diocletianus, etc. Eutropius, *Roman History*, book IX: “Diocletian made Maximian Herculius [Col. 0660C] Augustus from Caesar; Constantius and Maximian Caesars … and, in order to bind them also by family connection, Constantius took Theodora, Herculius’ stepdaughter, while Galerius took Valeria, Diocletian’s daughter.”

Non his duobus tantum, etc. The order and sense are: “He was worse not only than these two evil rulers whom our times experienced, but than all who ever existed.” Compare the most learned translators.—“These two”: that is, Maximian and his father-in-law, as Maucroix sought to explain in his translation.

Huic bestiae. See Baluzius, col. 312.

Efferitas. Read *et feritas*, “and savagery.” Oxford and Cambridge editions; likewise Vossius, Boherellus, and Gale. Add Columbus, col. 402.

Cum mater ejus. “Born of rustic parents, a herdsman, whence his surname.” Oxford and Cambridge editions, from the *Epitome* of Aurelius Victor.

Transdanuviana. Other editions have *Transdanubiana*. By all means see Cuper on the words “his mother Romula.”

In Daciam novam. That is, Aurelian’s Dacia: namely, that part of Moesia [Col. 0660D] into which Aurelian had transferred the peoples whom he had withdrawn from Trajan’s Dacia. Oxford and Cambridge editions.—From Baluzius, of course, where see the rest, col. 312. See also Cuper, col. 486.

In Daciam novam. See the Anonymous *Excerpts on Constantine*, p. 659, book I. GALE.

Amne. Read: “by the river Danube.” Oxford edition of 1680, p. 108, in the later-occurring emendations.

Confugerat. Read *confugerit*, “had fled.” TOLLIUS.—No need. Terence:

> By Pollux, do you know that a son has been born to Pamphilus?  
> I pray the gods that he may survive, since he himself is of good character,  
> and since he feared to wrong this excellent young man.

Here, after *cum*, used by Lesbia to give the reason for her wish [Col. 0661A], one should not read *non veritus sit* but *veritus est*, because *cum* is here used in the sense of *quoniam*, “since.” Our author elsewhere similarly writes: “Since he could not endure the freedom of the Roman people, he broke out,” where someone would vainly wish to emend, according to ordinary usage, *non posset*. Elsewhere again: “Since he saw that nothing was accruing to him from it except the name, he replied,” etc., not *videret*. See the passages.

Statu. The Abo edition reads *status*. Compare Columbus, col. 402.—More correctly: “of lofty stature,” as others have also perceived. TOLLIUS.

Caro ingens. See Baluzius, col. 313.

Actibus. “His actions.” MAUCROIX.—He undoubtedly understood these as bodily movements and gestures, from which Donatus, in his commentary on Terence, calls a scene *actuosa*, “active,” when it consists more in gesture than in speech.

Metuebat acerrime. *Aeneid* I: “Or fear was keen.” GALE.

Narseus rex Persarum. See Cuper’s very ample Epistle 1 to the likewise most distinguished Voetius, col. 580.

Concitatus domesticis exemplis, etc. “Being encouraged by the success that his grandfather Sapor had against Valerian.” English translation.—Almost word for word: [Col. 0661B] “Encouraged by the successful outcome of his grandfather Sapor’s campaign against Valerian”; an excellent paraphrase and sense.

Avi sui Saporis. See Cuper, col. 486.

In omni tumultu meticulosus. *Tumultus*, from Cicero’s Eighth Philippic: “The disturbance is so great that a greater fear arises, whence even the name *tumultus* has been derived.” These words begin to illuminate this passage considerably, where Diocletian’s timidity—and, so to speak, proneness to fear—appears not merely joined to every disturbance but arising from every disturbance.

But can Narseus’ expedition, arriving and thirsting to seize the East with great forces, be counted among disturbances? Certainly, I say, if not according to the Roman usage by which from Cicero’s time onward *tumultus* generally denoted something less than war and battle—Florus, III.18: “But this was more a disturbance than a war”; Curtius, VI.5: “It was more a disturbance than a battle”; the cited Philippic: “Some thought that the name of war should not be introduced in the motion; they preferred to call it a disturbance” [Col. 0661C]—then at least according to the usage by which the ancient Romans particularly termed their most serious wars, namely Italian and Gallic wars, *tumultus*, because of the greater fear they aroused in the Roman people.

The reasons are these. First, Cicero, in his letters to Atticus, called by the name *tumultus* that great Parthian war which, during his proconsulship in Cilicia, he saw threatening the commonwealth, extending the ancient Roman linguistic usage beyond Italian and Gallic wars. His words are:

> “Today the Parthians winter in Cyrrhestica, and a very great war threatens. For Orodes, son of the Parthian king, is in our province; nor does Deiotarus, whose son is promised the daughter of Artavasdes, doubt … that he himself will cross the Euphrates with all his forces at the beginning of summer. But on the very day when Cassius’ victorious letters were read in the Senate, mine announcing a *tumultus* were read.”

Second, if the passages cited from our author and others are compared even lightly, it will appear that the Persian *tumultus* of our author—that is, [Col. 0661D] Narseus’ expedition under Diocletian, which this writer seems here to have numbered among mere disturbances—is called by Aurelius Victor now a Persian attack, now a severe shaking of the East by the Persians, now simply a war. Conversely, what Eutropius seems simply to have called a Persian *tumultus* under Carus was called a Persian war by the same Aurelius, concerning those who had invaded Mesopotamia.

Our author in the passage before us: “Diocletian, as he was fearful in every disturbance.”

Aurelius Victor, *On the Caesars*: “At the same time the Persians violently shook the East, Julianus and the Quinquegentiani Africa … And because the mass of wars, mentioned above, pressed more severely … the Illyrian coast as far as the straits of Pontus was entrusted to Galerius … and a province was entrusted to Caesar Maximian, so that, leaving its borders, he might advance into Mesopotamia to repel Persian attacks.”

[Col. 0662A] Eutropius, book IX: “While Carus was waging war against the Sarmatians, news having been received of a Persian disturbance, he departed for the East and performed notable deeds against the Persians.”

Aurelius Victor again, *On the Caesars*: “Because, after Probus’ death became known, the barbarians had opportunely invaded, Carus sent his elder son to defend Gaul and immediately proceeded with Numerian’s company into Mesopotamia, because it was subject to a Persian war as if by custom.”
