Finally our author, ch. 23: “A census,” he says, “sent once into the provinces and cities, with assessors spread everywhere and disturbing everything, presented the dreadful appearance of a hostile *tumultus* and captivity.” Since, when he joined hostile *tumultus* with dreadful captivity, scarcely anything other than hostile war can be meant by hostile *tumultus*. Therefore we believe there can be no doubt that in this chapter also he includes Narseus’ expedition under the term *tumultus*.

Animique disjectus. The eminent Columbus correctly reads *dejectus*, “dejected.” For *animi disjectus* means mentally disordered, without concentration of mind or care for necessary matters. TOLLIUS.—The most learned [Col. 0662B] Boherellus and Gale saw the same.

Non ausus est obviam tendere: sed hunc, etc. I wish those who shortly will affirm that scarcely any ruler of greater courage than Diocletian ever existed would prove from reliable writers that Diocletian dared what our author denies. For if they cannot show this, and if on the contrary Aurelius Victor establishes that events happened as they are here narrated, why should we not believe that Diocletian was fearful and cast down in spirit?

Thus Aurelius Victor says: “In these times, meanwhile, Jovius departed for Alexandria; a province was entrusted to Caesar Maximian, so that, leaving its borders, he might advance into Mesopotamia to repel the attacks of the Persians.” And again, a little later, indicating the true time of Galerius’ Persian expedition: “When those lands were more vigorously reclaimed, a new war was undertaken, very serious and destructive.” By “the lands more vigorously reclaimed,” he means the lands of Egypt, which Valerius Diocletian reclaimed, after [Col. 0662C] Achilleus had once been defeated, only by defiling all Egypt with proscriptions and slaughter, as we shall hear below from Eutropius. By “the very serious and destructive war” undertaken while those lands were being reclaimed, he means the war entrusted to Galerius against the Persians—very serious and destructive in that Galerius was severely beaten by the Persians on the first occasion.

If anyone thinks it should be replied that Galerius was sent against the Persians for the very reason that Diocletian himself had set out against Achilleus, who had invaded Egypt: first, it has always been natural to rulers of greater courage to undertake the repelling and conquest of the greater enemies themselves. Carus, as we have just heard from Eutropius, while waging war against the Sarmatians, upon news of the Persian *tumultus*, departed for the East and performed notable deeds against the Persians. And Diocletian ought at all times to have judged the Egyptian campaign insignificant beside the Persian.

For Aurelius Victor writes concerning the Persian war: “While the Egyptian lands were [Col. 0662D] being more vigorously reclaimed by Diocletian, there arose a very serious war. But in Egypt Achilleus was routed with ease.” Further, if we attend, as we should, to Victor’s cited words, together with Pagi’s discussion of Eumenius’ panegyric addressed to Caesar Constantius after the British victory, also to Hydatius, the author of the Alexandrian Chronicle, and Libanius, then either Egypt had already become entirely quiet, its fury laid aside, and Diocletian, after defeating Achilleus, was merely defiling it with proscriptions and slaughter when he entrusted a province to Caesar Maximian so that, leaving its borders, he might proceed into Mesopotamia to repel the Persian attacks; or, if Egypt had not yet been completely quiet, it had certainly been wholly pacified long before the Persians were truly defeated by Galerius. Yet Diocletian remained in the East—a point in which we shall now state the sense.

Per Armeniam misit. The Persians had invaded Mesopotamia, a province of the Roman Empire. Hence, as [Col. 0663A] Eutropius relates, Galerius Maximian’s first battle with them occurred between Callinicum and Carrhae. Now, when Diocletian had as it were divided the empire among himself, Constantius, and the two Maximiani, he entrusted Galerius with the Illyrian coast as far as the straits of Pontus. Thus Galerius could not more conveniently move an army against the Persians, leaving his borders, than through Armenia, adjoining Mesopotamia, which they had invaded. For other matters see Baluzius, col. 313.

Ipse in Oriente subsistens. The expression is undoubtedly very emphatic; yet, unless I am greatly mistaken, this writer’s purpose was by no means to distinguish Armenia, through which Diocletian sent Galerius against the Persians, or Mesopotamia, which they had invaded, from the East. For Aurelius Victor says of this campaign, “The Persians were shaking the East”; and Eutropius similarly: “Narseus was bringing war upon the East.”

The author’s purpose, rather, was sharply to censure and reveal Diocletian’s faint-heartedness: while the Persians were violently shaking the East [Col. 0663B]—Aurelius indeed adds that adverb—he did not move from Alexandria, where he had gone and which itself was likewise included under the designation of the East, or, if one prefers, the eastern provinces. He was content, in a word, to send a lieutenant against the Persians, although he himself ought to have gone to meet the enemy. Thus in this passage “himself remaining in the East” means the same as: “himself, while standing in the very theatre of war, planting his foot far—immeasurably far—from the enemy.”

Yet, to speak candidly, I think the text should read *ipso in Oriente subsistens* (“he himself remaining in the East”), rather than *ipse*, as hitherto printed. “The East, moreover, in the organization of the Roman Empire, lest we seem to extend the East too widely, comprises from the time of Vespasian onward all the provinces extending from Thrace through Egypt and Asia Minor to the Euphrates and Tigris,” says the most illustrious de Marca in his *Concordia*, book I, ch. 4. Compare the *Notitia Imperii*, in which Egypt, both Armenias [Col. 0663C], and Mesopotamia are listed among the provinces once subject to the Prefect of the East.

Aucupans exitus rerum. Here *aucupans exitus rerum*, “watching for the outcomes of events,” has the same force as *scrutari res futuras* (“to investigate future events”) and *venturas quaerere* (“to seek coming things”) at the beginning of ch. 10, concerning sacrifices. Dodwell, Cyprianic Dissertation XI, no. 68. I would rather take *aucupans* simply as “observing,” for these words of Cicero: “Especially since so many watch Sulla’s occupation and hunt for an opportunity, so that, as soon as he looks away, they may attempt something of this kind.” In this passage scarcely anyone, I think, can doubt that *observent* and *aucupentur* are synonymous.

Ille insidiis. *Insidiis usus*, “employing treachery,” seems preferable. TOLLIUS.

Quibus mos, etc. Namely, his wife, concubines, and royal household. This was an ancient Persian custom, concerning which see Curtius in his *Life of Alexander*. Compare Columbus, col. 402. TOLLIUS.

Difficiliter. Examples of this adverb may perhaps be rare, but they are not lacking. Cicero, book IV of the *Academica*: “Why not also ‘very probable’? Why then not ‘such that it is difficult to distinguish from the truth’?” [Col. 0663D] Elsewhere in the same book: “But how do you understand it, that if something can be similar to it, it follows that it can also be distinguished only with difficulty?” Thus *difficile* and *difficulter* are merely more common. The glossaries of Polyxenus and others give *difficulter* as δυσκόλως, δυσχερῶς, “with difficulty.”

Fugatoque Narseo rege. Yet Galerius’ first encounter did not turn out especially fortunately. “Meanwhile,” says Baptista Egnatius, “against Narseus, king of the Persians, Galerius was at first unsuccessful; then, after his forces had been restored—and anger also giving him spirit because, after suffering defeat, he had been compelled to run on foot for a thousand paces beside Diocletian’s carriage—he won an outstanding victory, routing Narseus, killing a great part of the Persians, and capturing the concubines together with all the royal treasure.” Oxford and Cambridge editions.—Others differ. Dodwell, for example, holds that Galerius had already been defeated by Narseus in two battles when in turn he defeated and routed Narseus. For the rest concerning this, consult Cuper, col. 487; Baluzius, col. 313; and finally Pagi, on the year of Christ 297, where, if I now see sufficiently, he demonstrates that the Persians were defeated by Caesar Galerius [Col. 0664A] in that year.

Reversus, etc. In the year of Christ 302, as that distinguished man indeed places it in his Cyprianic dissertations. But while Dodwell, in Cyprianic Dissertation XI, no. 68—rather, 70—defers Galerius’ return from the Persian expedition to the year 302, “he departs from the right path,” says Pagi in his *Historical-Chronological Criticism*; Pagi himself assigns it to the year of Christ 297, no. 4, which see.

Cum praeda, etc. See Cuper, col. 488.

Sibi attulit superbiam, Diocletiano timorem. That is, Diocletian feared that Galerius, excessively elated by his success, might someday avenge upon him the insult he had received from him, when after the campaign against the Persians had gone badly Diocletian compelled him to run for a thousand paces beside his carriage; as our author will show below that indeed later happened. TOLLIUS.

Diocletiano timorem. Rather, I think, fear arose from that arrogance which, as you have just read, Maximian brought upon himself. For, as follows immediately, Galerius [Col. 0664B] was raised to such pride after this victory that he now began to reject the title of Caesar. Thus Diocletian had great cause to fear that Galerius would soon seize the authority of Augustus and, because of the run beside the carriage mentioned by Tollius, deprive his father-in-law of it—which later occurred. Cuper differs also, col. 489.

As he was now beginning to decline, etc. Thus also the Abo edition, and our author again in chapter 10, “if they had declined.” All the rest have “he was declining.” See Columbus, if you wish, col. 402. — “As he was now beginning to decline the name of Caesar.” Thus, therefore, he had hitherto been accustomed to be called *imperator* neither in letters sent to him, nor in other salutations, nor finally in ordinary conversation—a point very much to be noted. For according to Pagi, Caesars indeed in A.D. 197 were not yet styled *imperatores* . . . but from the following year, and therefore from 198, when Severus exhibited the Quinquennalia, it is certain, he says universally (*katholou*), that Geta and subsequently other Caesars, although they were adorned neither with tribunician power nor with proconsular imperium, were called *imperatores* [Col. 0664C]. But our Caecilius says the contrary concerning Galerius, who, according to Pagi, defeated Narses in A.D. 297: “so that he was now beginning to decline the name of Caesar,” by which, doubtless, Galerius had not refused to be called for about six years before that victory.

But the matter is much more certain on other grounds from this author. For in what immediately follows he says: “When Maximian heard that name, namely Caesar, in letters addressed to him, he would cry out with a grim expression and a terrible voice: ‘How long a Caesar?’” And in chapter 18, Diocletian, replying to his son-in-law Galerius when he wished to compel him to abdicate the empire, said that it was unbecoming that, after the great splendour of so lofty a station, he should fall into the obscurity of a humble life . . . “But if he desired to obtain the name of *imperator*, since he had not hitherto possessed it, nothing prevented all of them from being called Augusti.” Indeed, the very explicit assertion near the end of this chapter is that Galerius was not called *imperator* before he stripped his father-in-law of the purple: “But I defer speaking of his deeds, lest I confuse the times. For only after he received the name of *imperator*, his father-in-law having been stripped of office, did he then begin to rage.” The unquestionably genuine order of these words is: “For only after, his father-in-law having been stripped of office, he received the name of *imperator*, did he then,” etc.

What more? If it is worth the labour—as it is—to compare individually the chapters in which our author speaks of Galerius Maximian, already made Caesar, before Diocletian’s abdication, with those in which he mentions the same Galerius after Diocletian had laid aside the purple, it will plainly appear that our author calls Galerius Maximian *imperator* more than once after the said abdication of Diocletian—for example in chapter 24—but never before it. Before that time he calls him either the other Maximian, whom Diocletian had adopted as his son-in-law, as at the beginning of this chapter; or simply Maximian, as once in chapter 20 and twice in chapter 19; or Maximian Caesar, as at the end of chapter 10; or finally, most simply, Caesar: once each in chapters 9 and 17, twice at the end of chapter 11, and three times in chapter 14 [Col. 0665A].

This being so, let the most distinguished Pagi consider how it can be certain in every respect that which he stated without qualification: that Caesars from A.D. 198, although adorned neither with tribunician power nor with proconsular imperium, were called *imperatores*. So much points to the contrary in our author concerning that very Maximian who, by Pagi’s calculations, was created Caesar in A.D. 292 and at the same time endowed with tribunician power. We, indeed, shall readily reconcile in its proper place the words of chapter 14—referring to Diocletian and Galerius Maximian, still Caesar—“that two emperors were almost burned alive in their own house,” with what we have hitherto observed from our author’s expressions. See, therefore, what will be said on chapter 14.

**The name of Caesar.** “Caesar was the presumptive heir of the Empire.” MAUCROIX. — As if to say: he who was Caesar was considered the future heir of the empire. See, if you desire more, the most distinguished Baluzius, col. 313; the most ample Cuper, [Col. 0665B] on “And Narses having been put to flight”; the same in the preface, col. 301; and finally the letter of the most learned Noris, appended to the said Preface.

**He began to behave most insolently.** It has already been said above what this means: namely, precisely what is commonly said among us: *Il commenca à agir très-insolemment* [“He began to behave very insolently”]. Nor is it substantially different in chapter 21: “And because he could not openly command this, he acted in such a way as himself also to deprive men of liberty.” It is merely that one sometimes finds *se superbissime agere* (“to conduct oneself most arrogantly”) in the same sense. Julius Capitolinus, in *Gordian* 3: “Having therefore assumed the empire, when Philip conducted himself most arrogantly against Gordian,” etc. Nor do the same writer’s words concerning Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher depart from this manner of expression: “He was prefect of the Latin festival; in which office he showed himself conducting himself most excellently in place of the magistrates . . .”

**That he was begotten by Mars.** Victor’s *Epitome* puts it somewhat differently, though it conveys the same insolence: “He dared insolently to affirm that his mother, after the manner of Olympias, mother of Alexander the Great, conceived him through intercourse with a serpent” [Col. 0665C]. Oxford and Cambridge edition. — More pertinent, therefore, are the remarks made above by the most learned Cuper on this passage, col. 489.

**His mother Romula.** From that Romula, as though from a maternal great-grandmother, Romulus, that other son of Maxentius—of whom, as Pagi says, there is no mention anywhere—received his name, according to Pagi; Pagi elsewhere believes that he was killed at Constantine’s command. See his *Critica* at A.D. 312, no. 5. See also Cuper on the same Romula, col. 489.

**His father-in-law having been stripped of office.** Cuper must be consulted here also, col. 490.

**And to despise everything.** As, naturally, those accustomed to act most insolently do; and our author shortly before represented this as Galerius’ fault.

**Everything.** I would prefer “the name.” GALE.

**For before his accession Diocles was his name. When he was overthrowing the commonwealth, etc.** The passage is corrupt. Maucroix’s punctuation and emendation, as appears from his translation, is: “Diocles—for that was Diocletian’s name before his accession—when [he was overthrowing] the commonwealth”; and later: “Diocles (that was the name borne by Diocletian when he was [Col. 0665D] a private person) employed such counsels.” I do not reject this. Yet the author’s wording may also have been: “Diocletian—for Diocles was his name before his accession—when [he was overthrowing] the commonwealth,” and what follows. See Baluzius, col. 313.

**To despise everything. For Diocles, etc.** Learned men perceived that these words do not cohere well; I think also that Gale corrected them rightly: “to despise the name.” Thus the passage seems to be constituted: “To despise the name Diocli. For thus he was called before his accession.” *Diocli* for *Dioclis* also occurs in Cicero, *Against Verres*, Act V, as in Cornelius Nepos, “Themistocles, son of Neocles.” Likewise they said *Aristoteli* for *Aristotelis*, *Ulyssi* for *Ulyssis*, and hundreds of similar forms. GRAEVIUS.

**He was overthrowing the commonwealth by such counsels and such associates.** This too is false. For scarcely was there a prince better, more useful to the commonwealth, wiser, and greater in spirit than Diocletian—apart from the stain of the persecution which he initiated and cruelly prosecuted. TOLLIUS. — There is indeed something, reader, which this most learned man here concedes unprompted [Col. 0666A]. But because, when he asserts that Diocletian was otherwise an excellent prince, most useful to the commonwealth, most prudent, and finally of the greatest spirit, he seeks only to deprive our author of all credibility, consider, I pray, whether Tollius or this writer deserves greater credit.

“Diocletian,” Eutropius testifies in precisely these words, “defeated Achilleus, besieged in Alexandria, after nearly eight months, and killed him. He made harsh use of victory: he defiled all Egypt with grievous proscriptions and slaughter.” You may read very similar things in Suidas, under Διοκλετιανός (*Diocletianus*), and even more inhumane things in Baptista Egnatius, in his account of Diocletian and Maximian Augustus.

“What am I to say of this,” Vopiscus now exclaims in *Aurelian*, “that so few good princes have existed, although there have already been so many Caesars?” He shortly adds: “For from Augustus to the princes Diocletian and Maximian, the public register records the succession of those who wore the purple. But among them the best were Augustus himself, Flavius Vespasian, Titus, Cocceius Nerva, the divine Trajan, [Col. 0666B] the divine Hadrian, Pius and Marcus Antoninus, Severus the African, Alexander son of Mammaea, the divine Claudius, and the divine Aurelian. For Valerian, although he was excellent, appeared unfortunate to all. You see, Terentianus, I pray, how few good princes there are.”

There, however, what is very notable is not merely that Diocletian is not numbered among the good; the evident reason is that he lacked clemency, the primary endowment of emperors. For Vopiscus continues, returning to his own divine Aurelian, whom he had shortly before reckoned among the best: “Many place Aurelian neither among good nor among bad princes, because he lacked clemency, the primary endowment of emperors.” Thus Diocletian did not possess the goodness suggested by Tollius, who excepts from Diocletian’s life only the stain of the persecution initiated and cruelly exercised.

Further, from that division of the empire by which, as we saw above, Diocletian entrusted Africa and Italy to Herculius, “a great evil of taxes was imposed upon the Italian part,” says Aurelius Victor with the utmost explicitness in *The Caesars*: “For whereas all had administered the same function and in moderation, so that the army and emperor, who were always present wholly or for the most part, might be supported, a new law was introduced concerning payments. What was tolerable under the moderation of those times indeed advanced into ruin” [Col. 0666C]. And according to Eutropius, “Herculius was openly fierce and of uncivil disposition, indicating his harshness even by the terror of his countenance; indulging his own nature, he complied with Diocletian in all his more severe counsels.”

By such counsels and such associates, therefore, as our author says, Diocletian was truly overthrowing the commonwealth: harmful, I say, to the commonwealth together with them, even if without them he might have been useful to it in the highest degree. For it is altogether plain that the association to which I refer is stressed here—a point which the most distinguished man does not seem to have noticed. Compare the response of Andronicus to the prefect of Egypt, cited above: “I cursed, and I curse, the powers and blood-drinkers who overthrew the age.”

[Col. 0666D] Moreover, Eutropius again writes: “Constantius was not only beloved but also revered by the Gauls, especially because under his rule they escaped Diocletian’s suspect prudence and Maximian’s bloodthirsty rashness.” Diocletian’s prudence, therefore, was not truly praiseworthy, since Eutropius joined it to Maximian’s bloodthirsty rashness and called it “suspect prudence” in a bad sense: that is, suspicious prudence, or prudence always miserably suspecting and fearing something or other. Those who escaped it were accordingly regarded as most fortunate.

Finally, that Diocletian made three men partners in his rule was, if we consult Aurelius Victor, done because the weight of wars pressed too strongly. Therefore Diocletian did not possess that great spirit for which Horace, for example, praised Augustus:

> Since you alone sustain so many and such great concerns,  
> defend Italy by arms, adorn it by morals,  
> and reform it by laws . . .

[Col. 0667A]

On the contrary, he possessed a spirit truly petty and unequal to bearing the burden of the commonwealth. Another, indeed graver, argument for this point will be brought forward below in chapter 10.

**Since he deserved every punishment for his crimes.** See what bitterness of hatred, what desire to flatter princes, can accomplish. Therefore, in most of what follows, our author deserves no more credit than Eusebius in the *Life of Constantine* and in that part of the *Ecclesiastical History* which encompasses Constantine’s times. TOLLIUS. — Rather, see to what a preconceived opinion once adopted can carry a man. For what can it be but crimes—crimes such as are here briefly indicated, that is, Diocletian’s own crimes—when, according to Aurelius Victor, Eutropius, and others, long before the persecution Diocletian was the first of all after Caligula and Domitian openly to allow himself to be called Lord, and to command that he be adored and addressed as a god; when, according to Eutropius too, after defeating Achilleus he defiled all Egypt with slaughter; when, moreover, as Aurelius Victor testifies, his faith toward friends was not sufficiently honourable; and finally when, whenever he resolved upon those many inhumane and harsh measures and wished at once to satisfy his own severity by means of another’s odium, he called Herculius into counsel before all others [Col. 0667B]—“since he deserved every punishment for his crimes.”

Add that, even if our author had most plainly lied concerning Diocletian’s crimes, he ought not for that reason to lose all credibility in other matters. Otherwise, certainly, no credit will henceforth be due to Livy, Sallust, Cornelius Tacitus, and similar writers. Why? Because, as Vopiscus warns, no writer, so far as history is concerned, has failed to tell some lie. “I maintain, on the contrary,” he says, “that there is no writer who, so far as history is concerned, has not lied in some respect”; indeed, he reveals in what particulars Livy, Sallust, Cornelius Tacitus, and finally Trogus are convicted by manifest witnesses. The passage occurs near the beginning of *Aurelian* and, as you see, is not merely relevant but highly noteworthy [Col. 0667C].

**He reigned with the highest prosperity.** See Baluzius on these words in chapter 17, “prosperity departed from him,” col. 324.

**But what reason had he for persecuting?** What we said above concerning that compressed manner of expression is confirmed by a similar passage of Tertullian in *To Scapula*, chapter 4: “Arrius Antoninus, while persecuting vigorously in Asia, found all the Christians of that city presenting themselves before his tribunals of their own accord.”

## Chapter X

**While he was acting in the regions of the East.** Perhaps at Alexandria, but perhaps also elsewhere, whether in Egypt or outside Egypt. For although in our judgment Diocletian was residing at Alexandria—or, if perhaps not in that metropolis, at least somewhere in Egypt—when he commanded Galerius to lead his army through Armenia against the Persians, he certainly did not remain permanently thereafter at Alexandria or in Egypt. This is evident, to omit other points, first because, after Galerius, according to Eutropius, had been defeated by the Persians in the first battle and had set out toward Diocletian, he met Diocletian while Diocletian was travelling: “Having been defeated and setting out toward Diocletian, when he met him,” etc. It is evident also because, as the same author continues, the place where Galerius, after defeating the Persian king in turn and driving him into the furthest wildernesses of his realm, was received with great honour by Diocletian was situated in Mesopotamia:

> “Soon afterward . . . having assembled his forces . . . he again fought Narses in Greater Armenia, with immense success . . . Having defeated Narses . . . he drove him into the furthest wildernesses of his realm. Therefore, returning in triumph, he was received with great honour by Diocletian, who was then staying in Mesopotamia with his guards.”

Whether Diocletian had already come to Mesopotamia before that second battle, or, as I would rather believe, came after hearing of Galerius’ victory, while Galerius meanwhile was driving Narses to the extremity of his kingdom. It will therefore be preferable, I think, here to understand “in the regions of the East” generally as the East with the most distinguished interpreters, rather than to guess at some particular region of the East where the sacrifices soon to be mentioned were performed at the demand of timid and superstitious Diocletian. For in the *Saracenica*, p. 102 of the edition prepared by Sylburg, ἕως Δαμασκοῦ, “as far as Damascus,” and ἐπὶ τὰ μέρη Δαμασκοῦ, “toward the regions of Damascus,” have exactly, or nearly, the same force. See Cuper, col. 491.

**As was his way through fear, etc.** Galerius had not yet defeated Narses, nor had he therefore been received with the highest honours in Mesopotamia by Diocletian, when the events that our author will now recount happened in the eastern regions—that is, when Diocletian resorted to the immolation of so many cattle in order to learn the future. “Diocletian was altogether in the greatest fear, since Galerius had already been defeated in two battles by Narses; accordingly, he judged that recourse must be had to his native superstition.” DODWELL, *Cyprianic Dissertation* XI, no. 68.

**Through fear.** It may also be read “from fear.” [Col. 0668B] “Lactantius wonderfully twists all Diocletian’s actions toward the worse and perverse side. What Alexander the Great, Julius Caesar, and the best and bravest princes and commanders did in accordance with solemn custom, he turns into a fault in this man as an argument of fear. Diocletian certainly seems to me to have been entirely free from fear: he raised himself by his own valour to the very summit of supreme power and, not unwillingly and under compulsion—as Lactantius relates, though that is scarcely credible—but freely and voluntarily, despising the vanity of human affairs, which is the mark of the greatest spirit, abdicated it.” TOLLIUS. — On the learned man’s emendation, see Columbus above, col. 402. But let Tollius himself consider what he undertakes in the rest. For he contends that Diocletian investigated the future by solemn custom, not fear, and that he abdicated the empire through greatness of spirit, not fear.

Aurelius Victor, by contrast, in *The Caesars*, associates that investigation of the future by Diocletian and his abdication of the empire alike with fear:

> “Yet while Herculius and Valerius Diocletian were doing these things, they were not without faults. For Herculius . . . while Valerius’ faith toward friends was not sufficiently honourable, out of fear of discord he thought that the tranquillity of their shared rule could be disturbed by disclosures. Hence too the city’s strength was, as it were, cut short, the number of the praetorian cohorts and the populace under arms being reduced. On this account many believe that he laid down the empire. For, an investigator of coming events, when he discovered by fate that internal calamities and, as it were, some crashing downfall of the Roman state were impending, after celebrating the twentieth year of his reign, being the stronger man, he cast aside the care of the commonwealth.”

[Col. 0668C]

Whatever Tollius—or even Aurelius himself in what follows—may say, this was the conduct of a fearful spirit, not finally of the kind which Horace required in his great-souled man when he sang, among other things:

> The just man, steadfast in his purpose,  
> though the shattered world should fall upon him,  
> will be struck by its ruins undismayed.

**An investigator of future events.** See Cuper, col. 492, and Columbus, col. 402.

**And in their livers.** Read “their,” feminine: *earum*. BOHERELLUS. — Correctly, since “he was sacrificing cattle” preceded; nor does Ennius’ verse stand in the way:

> To give one living beast to her husband,

since *pecus, pecudis* was in use among all as a feminine noun.

**Then certain of the attendants, etc.** From this passage Baluzius, col. 314, draws an argument that this book is genuinely Lactantius’, because similar material occurs in *Institutions* IV.27:

> “For when they sacrifice to their gods, if someone bearing a marked forehead stands by, the rites by no means prove favourable, nor can the consulted seer give an answer. And this was often the chief cause of persecuting righteousness among wicked rulers. For when certain of our attendants stood by while their masters were sacrificing, having placed the sign upon their foreheads, they put their gods to flight, so that they could not portray the future in the entrails of beasts. When the soothsayers understood this, urged on by those same demons whom they invoked, they complained that profane men were present at the rites and drove their rulers into fury, that they might assail the temple of God.”

Oxford edition, 1680 [Col. 0669A].

Yet this argument is not so strong that by its force alone it can establish this book as Lactantius’, since, as the learned man correctly observes, someone else might have borrowed these words from Lactantius. Oxford edition, 1684.

**Then certain of the attendants.** The passage is by no means easy, if we carefully consider the supplement now required. For either some of Diocletian’s attendants must necessarily be understood as such, or some ministers of the sacrifices in the proper sense; and either group must have known the Lord as well, that is, have been Christians. “Then certain of the attendants, knowing the Lord,” etc.

If first—that is, if “certain attendants” means some of Diocletian’s servants or courtiers, as the translators understood it (“Some of his officers, who were Christians,” MAUCROIX; “But some of his courtiers, that were Christians,” English translation)—rather than some of the actual ministers of sacrifice, the words of Lactantius just cited do not indeed conflict: “when certain of our attendants stood by while their masters were sacrificing.” But the following words in this chapter seem strongly to oppose this: “Then, in raging anger, he commanded not only those who ministered at the rites, but all who were in the palace, to sacrifice.” For you hear, “those who ministered at the rites,” not “those who ministered to Diocletian.” Thus in the earlier statement, “certain of the attendants, knowing the Lord,” they can scarcely be anything other than some of the ministers of sacrifice properly so called—especially because they are there seen standing beside one sacrificing. For that reason they resemble that comic pseudo-Sosia to whom Jupiter says in Plautus’ *Amphitruo*:

> See that these matters are attended to,  
> just as you understand that I wish,  
> and that you minister to me while I sacrifice.

[Col. 0669C]

But if the passage must now be understood of ministers of sacrifice, and Christians at that, how could the faithful persuade themselves to minister at rites of that sort? But on these matters again in the following column.

**Knowing the Lord.** That is, men who knew who the Lord Jesus was and also believed in him: Christians, in one word, as the translators correctly render it. Thus in Lactantius, *On the Blessed Life*, chapter 20: “Those therefore who knew God will be judged,” where shortly before he had said, “those who have been occupied in the religion of God”; and by the opposite expression, chapter 24: “Those who did not know the Lord of the world.” Nor is it otherwise in the New Testament, whether one consults the Greek sources or the Vulgate translator: Acts 19:15, τὸν Παῦλον ἐπίσταμαι, “I know Paul”; and John 1:31, 33, Κἀγὼ οὐκ ᾔδειν αὐτόν, “And I did not know him,” again in the Vulgate. This perhaps is also the reason why our author spoke in the way that he did.

It is certain, at any rate, as the most distinguished Graevius observed here, that more polished writers said *ignorabam eum* (“I was unacquainted with him”) instead of “I did not know him.” Cornelius Nepos, in *Aristides*: “He replied that he did not know Aristides.” Suetonius, in *Vitellius*: “Those asking who he was. For he was unknown.” I add to the examples of a most friendly man this passage from Terence’s *Eunuch*:

> What? Did those men not know you? After I showed them your character  
> and praised you according to your deeds and virtues,  
> I obtained it.

[Col. 0669D]

**While they stood beside one sacrificing.** A deed altogether unworthy of Christians; but for that reason more credible, because they belonged to the emperor’s court, and more odious examples too are readily available. Hadrian’s letter in Vopiscus’ *Saturninus*:

> “Hadrian Augustus, to Servianus, consul, greetings. I have thoroughly learned the Egypt which you praised to me . . . it is frivolous, unstable, and flying about at every movement of rumour. Those who worship Serapis are Christians; and those devoted to Serapis call themselves bishops of Christ. There is no chief of the Jews’ synagogue there; no Samaritan; no Christian presbyter; no astrologer; no soothsayer; no anointer”—that is, no one who is not an astrologer, a soothsayer, and an anointer. “The patriarch himself, when he comes to Egypt, is compelled by some to worship Serapis and by others Christ.”

Origen, *Homily 7 on Joshua*:

> “And those too who, for example, though Christians, celebrate the festivals of the Gentiles and introduce anathemas into the churches; who investigate men’s lives and deeds from the courses of the stars; who consult the flight of birds and other such things formerly observed in the world—these bring the anathema of Jericho into the Church and defile the camp of the Lord.”

Consider now, I pray, whether those from the body of Christians who judged it lawful to stand beside Diocletian’s sacrifices would not readily have persuaded themselves that it was lawful also to minister at them. Our author certainly does not contradict this.

**They placed upon their foreheads, etc.** That is, as Lactantius explains in the *Institutions*, they inscribed upon their foreheads the sign of blood—that is, of the cross which shed blood—or, more plainly, if you prefer, and largely with Tertullian, they repeatedly traced their forehead with the sign of the cross by placing a finger upon it. For Tertullian says in *On the Soldier’s Crown*:

> “At every advance and movement, at every coming in and going out, when clothing and putting on shoes, at baths, at meals, at lights, at beds, at seats—whatever activity we undertake—we mark our forehead with the sign of the cross.”

[Col. 0670B]

Since you see that this present custom, well known to all, of so many Christians has long prevailed in the Church on the authority not of one but of many, most ancient and weighty witnesses, take care, reader, lest those among us who abstain from this practice be thought or said for that reason to be wholly outside the bosom of the Church. “For if you demand a law of Scripture for this discipline,” Tertullian continues immediately, “you will find none. Tradition will be presented to you as its author, custom as its confirmer, and faith as its observer.”

And if what he further adds in defence of the said rite—“Tradition will be presented to you as its author, custom as its confirmer, and faith as its observer”—proved that our people, who do not mark their forehead with the sign of the cross, had renounced the faith, it would prove the same of their opponents as well, since they do not observe several other disciplines of the ancient Church mentioned in that very passage and defended by the same reasoning of Tertullian. For where today do they “offer to infants, or adults who have been immersed three times, a taste beforehand of the concord of milk and honey”? Or where do they “consider it unlawful to worship kneeling on the Lord’s Day”? Yet concerning these rites Tertullian speaks no less expressly: “If you demand a law of Scripture for these and other disciplines of this kind, you will find none. Tradition will be presented to you as its author, custom as its confirmer, and faith as its observer.”

Let those who call themselves Catholics κατ’ ἐξοχήν, “in the pre-eminent sense,” admit therefore, even against their will, that all who refuse to observe each individual discipline or tradition of the primitive Church are not thereby necessarily strangers to Christ’s faith. But this is incidental, and intended to answer in two words that rather recent French author [Note: Col. 0670D]

> The title of the book is: *The Honours of the Holy Cross, justified by Scripture and the Fathers, etc., for the conversion of Protestants, for the instruction of new converts, and for the edification of all Catholics*. Bordeaux, 1636.

[Note: Col. 0670D]

> A futile answer: for who does not perceive the difference between those usages, of which the former are indifferent, whereas the latter expresses the principal mystery of religion?

who thinks that those whom they call Neophytes, and other Protestants, cannot be called Catholics unless they have learned to place the sign of the cross upon their foreheads.

The Greek author Theodoret uses the same expression in the remainder of the passage, *Ecclesiastical History* III.4. His words are:

> Ἐκείνων δὲ (sc. δαιμόνων) μετὰ τῆς συνήθους φαντασίας ἐπιφανέντων, ἠνάγκασε τοῦτον (Ἰουλιανόν) τὸ δέος ἐπιθεῖναι τῷ μετώπῳ τοῦ σταυροῦ τὸ σημεῖον.

> “But when those demons appeared in their customary form, fear compelled Julian to place the sign of the cross upon his forehead.”

**The immortal sign.** That is, if we choose to follow Maucroix, “the adorable sign of the cross.” For his version is: “Some of his officers, who were Christians and were present at these profane ceremonies, marked their foreheads with the adorable sign of the cross” [Col. 0671A]. But who can endure this? “Immortal is that which is not by itself capable of death, or which is defended from death through the care of another,” says Macrobius in the *Dream of Scipio*. The glossaries of Philoxenus and others give: “immortals, ἀθάνατοι; immortal things, ἀθανάσια; immortal, ἀθάνατος; immortality, ἀθανασία.” But nowhere has anyone explained *immortalis* or *immortale* as “adorable,” or προσκυνητόν (“fit for veneration”).

[Note: Col. 0671D]

> An inept argument.

Further, Minucius Felix expressly says in his *Octavius*, “We neither worship nor pray to crosses”; and Ambrose likewise:

> “Let Helena have something by which she may recognize the Lord’s cross. She found, therefore, the title. She adored the King, certainly not the wood, since this is the error of the Gentiles and the vanity of the impious. But she adored him who hung upon the wood, as written in the title.”

If Ambrose truly declared this concerning the wood of the cross, and Minucius concerning all crosses without exception—as there can be no doubt—how much more is it true of the sign of the cross. Maucroix should therefore have abstained from his translation, which no moderately fair-minded person who has even heard in passing of the controversies long stirred concerning the adoration of the cross will deny to be unfaithful and proceeding from excessive party zeal [Col. 0671B].

But to come closer to the matter. Lactantius says:

> “It will happen at the beginning of the holy kingdom that the prince of demons will be conquered by God. But when the thousand years of the kingdom—that is, the seven thousand years—begin to end, he will again be released and, sent forth from custody, will emerge. He will stir up all the nations then under the rule of the righteous to make war upon the holy city. An innumerable multitude of nations will be gathered from the whole world, and it will besiege and surround the city. Then the final wrath of God will come upon the nations and destroy them to a man. First he will shake the earth most violently; by its movement the mountains of Syria will be split and the hills collapse into chasms; the walls of all cities will fall. God will cause the sun not to set for three days and will set it aflame. Excessive heat and great burning will descend upon hostile and impious peoples; there will be rains of sulphur, hailstorms of stones, and drops of fire. Their spirits will melt in the heat; their bodies will be crushed by the hail; and they themselves will strike one another with the sword. Mountains will be filled with corpses and plains covered with bones. But for those three days the people of God will be hidden beneath the hollows of the earth, until God’s wrath against the nations has completed the final judgment. Then the righteous will come out from their hiding places and find everything covered with corpses and bones. Those who are to be safe amid this extreme necessity and plague of the whole world will be only those who have marked upon the upper part of their body the sign of the true and divine blood.”

[Col. 0671C]

Lactantius elsewhere calls this sign “immortal,” as does our Caecilius: “But because the demons can neither approach those in whom they see the heavenly mark nor harm those whom the immortal sign has fortified, as though by an impregnable wall, they attack them through men.” It is therefore clear what both authors—if they are not one author but two—understood by the “immortal sign of the cross”: namely, something by which, in the judgment of the “good Fathers,” God’s people could be protected against temporal and eternal death. This we do not believe, I admit [Note: Col. 0671D]:

> Therefore the Fathers of earlier centuries also, whom he contemptuously calls “good Fathers,” think the same as we do; we glory in having them as our guides, since he concedes them to us.

But since without controversy not even the opponents themselves give Lactantius credit concerning all the matters which we have just deliberately adduced from Book VII of the *Institutions*, they must necessarily pardon us if we do not heed Lactantius, our author, or similar writers concerning the power of their immortal sign as much as they would wish.

**By which act the demons were put to flight.** Those who enjoy such things may see Theodoret among others, *Ecclesiastical History* III.3, where that Julian the Apostate is said similarly to have put demons to flight after he had been led by a certain diviner into a temple of idols, and there the deceiving demons had appeared in terrible form, as they were accustomed, at the invocation of a diviner. See also, not to name more now, Lactantius, *Institutions* IV.27, a good part of which has been cited above by others [Col. 0672A].

**The rites were disturbed.** See Cuper, col. 492.

Trepidabant aruspices. That is, they moved their heads, hands, indeed their whole bodies about the victim, and acted with a certain disordered haste, so as to see the customary signs in the entrails—something which the French admirably express in one phrase: *Les Aruspices se trémoussoient* [“the haruspices were fidgeting”]. Yet this was not restless running about, as will be clear from what follows; nor was it necessarily done in fear, as we shall show in the same place, although it is far more likely that the haruspices feared they would not find in the entrails the signs for which they searched. Here, however, we attend to the native meaning of the word. Palmerius: “*Trepidare* is to hasten, to busy oneself strenuously, and … to move about in circles.”

[Col. 0672B] Varro, *On Agriculture*, III.16: “They take the sign for removing the honeycombs from the bees themselves, when their bellies are full; and when they have doubled the hives, they infer from the bees whether they make a buzzing within, and when they go out and hurry abroad.” For this last word Aristotle has κινεῖσθαι—κινεῖσθαι ἐξιούσας, καὶ εἰσιούσας, “moving as they go out and go in”—and Theodore Gaza elegantly rendered the Greek term by “a whirling movement in going out and coming in.”

Let a not insignificant confirmation be added from Festus and etymology. “*Trepit*,” says Festus, “means *vertit*, ‘turns’; whence *trepido*, *trepidatio*, because in agitation the mind turns.” Thus *trepit* derives from the Greeks’ τρέπω, among whom indeed we encounter τὸ τρέπειν a thousand times in the sense of the Latin *vertere*, “to turn.” This being so, why should not *trepido* and *trepidatio* likewise derive from it as so many frequentatives—that is, as though they were *trepito* and *trepitatio*, or, in Latin terms, *versito* and *versitatio*, “turn repeatedly” and “repeated turning”? So that, I say, from its earliest origin *trepidare*, written with *d* in place of *trepitare* with *t*, meant nothing else [Col. 0672C] than repeatedly τρέπειν—turning oneself this way and that. Since fearful people do this almost continually, and likewise those who do something rather hastily, the Romans subsequently used *trepidare* for “to fear” and “to hurry.”

Thus surely Varro, in the most proper and excellent sense of ordinary language, said *foras trepidant*, “they hurry abroad,” meaning “they turn themselves in every direction,” or “move about,” in order to go out. The words in our author, *trepidabant aruspices*, may also aptly signify what we have just said. See chapters 12 and 17.

Relevant to Varro’s use of *trepidare* is this passage from Phaedrus, IV.5:

> When the mice, defeated by the army of weasels,  
> Fled and hurried about the narrow hollows;

where the most recent interpreter wrongly paraphrases it as “they were afraid near the dark caves,” whereas it means that they were hastening to rush into the narrow entrances of the caves. So too Sallust, *Jugurtha* 67: “They hurried toward the citadel of the town, where the standards and shields were.” GRAEVIUS.—But what, then, are the *Aruspices*? For Maucroix’s translation reads: *Les Sacrificateurs étonnés, s'écrièrent*—“The astonished sacrificers cried out.” A little later in the same translation, however, *Magister ille aruspicum Tagis* is rendered *Tagis un des Augures*, “Tagis, one of the augurs”; while in the English translation neither passage has a rendering resembling either of these, but both simply read “The Diviners.”—

According to Festus, *harjuga* was the name given to a victim whose attached entrails were inspected. Thus *aruspices*, or rather—with aspiration—*haruspices*, were properly a class of diviners who foretold the future from the inspection of a *harjuga*, or, as others write, a *haruga*, that is, a sacrificial victim. This entirely accords with what follows. But since the terms *haruspices* and *haruspicy* have long been obsolete among modern peoples, the distinguished translators doubtless preferred familiar, though less precise, words to barbarous literal renderings.

I only wish that Maucroix had refrained from the word *Augures* in the latter [Col. 0673A] passage. For augurs never foretold the future, after the manner of haruspices, from the entrails of sacrificed birds; rather, they did so from their flight, their song, or finally their feeding, when food was offered to chickens taken out of their coop, so that there might result the “solemn dance” (*tripudium solistimum*). Cicero, *To Aulus Caecina*: “I do not therefore augur for you from the bird’s flight, nor from the ill-omened song of the *oscines*, as is done in our discipline, nor from solemn feedings …”

Nor did they see the customary signs in the entrails. That is, for example, entrails with a head. I infer this from Cicero’s passage: “For when the most ominous entrails have been headless—than which nothing seems more dreadful—the next victim is often accepted with the most favorable result.” I have singled out this sign, among many that could easily be adduced, because this same passage of Cicero, which mentions it, silently indicates that the sacrifice was not accepted whenever that sign was lacking in the victims offered. We shall presently discuss acceptance of sacrifice (*litatio*) and immolation.

As though they had not obtained a favorable sacrifice, they sacrificed more frequently. Therefore, if we wish to speak more exactly, *litare* and *immolare* differ from one another. Plautus confirms this in the *Poenulus*, Act II:

> May the gods make miserable every pimp who, after this day,  
> Shall ever sacrifice any victim to Venus,  
> Or offer any grain of incense.  
> For I, unhappy man, today sacrificed six lambs  
> To my most wrathful gods, yet I could not  
> Make Venus favorable to me.  
> Since I cannot obtain a favorable sacrifice, I went away at once  
> In anger …

And a little later in the same act:

> If, by Hercules, that has ever happened, then may Jupiter make me  
> Always sacrifice, yet never obtain a favorable sacrifice.

Finally, Cicero, *On Divination*, II: “What? When sacrifice is offered to several gods, how does it happen that one obtains favorable acceptance with some and not with others?” According to Festus, moreover, *immolare* is to consecrate a victim sprinkled with *mola*—that is, softened spelt—and salt; but *litare* is to render propitious, as Plautus has just explained, or, in Macrobius’s words in the *Saturnalia*, “to appease a divinity by performing a sacrifice.” [Col. 0673C]

And yet among the Fathers one quite often finds *litare* in the simple sense of “to sacrifice.” Sulpicius Severus, speaking of the book of Leviticus, which is wholly concerned with prescribing sacrificial rites, says: “Then follows the book of Leviticus, in which the precepts for sacrifice are handed down.” Elsewhere, and much more explicitly: “Again the Hebrews, corrupted by the evil of long peace, sacrificed to idols.” This must indeed be understood as “sacrificed,” without any implication either of propitiation or of a vow obtained; for immediately afterwards comes, “and punishment was soon at hand for the sinners,” while shortly before it is preceded by the synonymous phrase, “the people began to sacrifice to idols in a profane rite.”

That master of the haruspices, Tagis. The most learned Baluzius thinks these words were spoken in an oratorical manner, because Tages was once famous among the Tuscans for the highest skill in haruspicy. Oxford and Cambridge editions.—“Tages that was set over the Diviners”; *Tages, qui praepositus erat Divinis*. English translation. Add Baluzius, col. 314, and Cuper, col. 492.—

Tagis. Thus both Paris editions—the Latin edition of Baluzius, I mean, and Maucroix’s French edition—together with the Aboensis edition. The others read *Tages*. Columbus defends the former reading, col. 403. The latter, however, if, as I think, it refers to that ancient Tuscan haruspex, is supported by the following passages. Fulgentius: “Labeo, who expounded the Etruscan disciplines of Tagetes and Bacchetis in fifteen volumes.” Cicero, *On Divination*, I: “But why say more? Let us consider the origin of haruspicy … A certain Tages, it is said, appeared in the territory of Tarquinii when the earth was being ploughed and a furrow had been cut rather deeply; and he addressed the man who was ploughing. This Tages, moreover, as the Etruscan books relate,” etc. Then, after a few intervening words: “But if that Tages was a man, how could he have lived buried beneath the earth?”

He therefore says that the sacrifices do not give an answer because, etc. The same thing was said to the Emperor Julian by a haruspex. GALE.—Christians were regarded as most hostile to magical operations. Hence Alexander the false prophet took care that Christians should be excluded from his mysteries. Hence Macrianus the magician drove Valerian into persecution. Hence Diocletian was likewise driven by his own Tages, as Lactantius calls him. Hence Julian arranged for the martyr Babylas to be removed from Daphne, because he considered Christians hateful to his gods, and consequently believed that none of his rites could proceed properly unless Christians were removed. DODWELL, *Dissertation on Cyprian*, XI, no. 30.

Profane persons. That widely known formula of those performing sacred rites: “Away hence, away, you profane persons.” TOLLIUS. Add Cuper, col. 492, and Columbus, col. 403.

Then, in raging anger. Diocletian, namely. This is so although the preceding words concern the master of the haruspices and Diocletian has not hitherto been named even once in this chapter—a point sufficiently worthy of notice. But what can one do? The following words necessarily require it, as everyone must admit. Accordingly Maucroix, in order to remove every ambiguity, rendered it: *Dioclétien en fureur*, “Diocletian in a fury”; and the English version likewise: “Upon which Diocletian being enraged.”

[Col. 0674B] He ordered not only those who administered the rites, but all, etc., to sacrifice. Maucroix: *Commanda non-seulement à tous les assistants, mais encore à tous ceux qui se trouvèrent dans son palais, de sacrifier*—“He ordered not only all those present, but also all who were found in his palace, to sacrifice.” First, since in antiquity not everyone present at pagan rites administered those rites, and since the beginning of this passage does not speak of all persons attending the rites but only of those administering them, the learned man’s translation is already plainly broader than it ought to be. Secondly, since in that translation Diocletian, once stirred to anger, appears to have wished not merely those initially present at the rites, but without exception everyone found in the palace, to sacrifice, whereas chapter 15 shows, on the contrary, that Diocletian’s rage raged not against everyone but against his household alone:

> “The emperor therefore raged now not only against his household, but against all men; and he compelled first of all his daughter Valeria and his wife Prisca to be defiled by sacrifice”—

it is again clear that Maucroix extended the sense of our passage further than was proper.

Finally, concerning all those in question—that is, those who were in the palace at the time of Diocletian’s sacrifice and were ordered by Diocletian to sacrifice—he also ordered that punishment should be inflicted by beatings if they refused; for the text follows: “and that, if they declined, they should be punished with beatings.” But not all men, or men of every rank, were customarily subjected to whips and beatings when they had offended; nor is it even slightly plausible that such a punishment was decreed, for example, against Diocletian’s daughter Valeria, his wife Prisca, those courtiers who attended the emperor’s court in the discharge of office, or the more distinguished companies of household servants. For all these reasons, and also because near the beginning of this chapter mention is made of certain attendants who stood by while Diocletian sacrificed—“Then certain attendants, as they stood by one sacrificing”—we cannot, I confess, avoid thinking that the following words, “he ordered not only those who administered the rites, but all who were in the palace, to sacrifice,” apply to all and only Diocletian’s attendants, in this sense:

Then Diocletian, raging in anger, wished and compelled not only those among his attendants—some of whom knowingly confessed Christ, others unknowingly—who had until then stood by while he sacrificed, to sacrifice; but also all the rest who belonged to the same household of attendants and might be found here and there in the palace occupied with various duties. See, moreover, how correctly, if these words are understood thus, it was later written in chapter 15: “The emperor therefore raged now not only against his household, but against all men, and first of all his daughter,” etc.

If they declined. The Aboensis edition gives the same reading. Others read *si detrectassent*.

To be punished with beatings. Maucroix: *Il condamna au fouet*—“He sentenced them to the whip.”—As though the author’s words were “to be beaten with scourges or rods.” Nor is the English rendering otherwise: “and ordered those to be whipped who should refuse to do it.” I entirely agree, if only because of the passage in chapter 21, where stretching on the rack is joined with beating. For who that has read even one play of Plautus does not know that slaves were customarily stretched out when they were to be beaten with scourges or rods? Add Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, VIII.3, where, discussing the various kinds of contest in which martyrs struggled during Diocletian’s raging persecution, he mentions some whose bodies were torn by lashes: ὁ μὲν μάστιξιν αἰκιζόμενος τὸ σῶμα, ὁ δὲ etc., “one having his body tortured with whips, another …”

And letters having been given to the commanders. Thus the emperor entrusted the responsibility for that persecution against the soldiers not to one man alone, as Dodwell expressly maintained, but to several. This is all the more so because the words of Eusebius upon which that most learned man relied are: Ὡς γὰρ ὁ στρατοπεδάρχης ὅ τίς ποτε ἦν ἐκεῖνος, ἄρτι πρῶτον ἐνεχείρει τῷ κατὰ τῶν στρατευμάτων διωγμῷ. Eusebius indeed says there, word for word: “When a certain commander, whoever he was, first began [Col. 0675B] to persecute the soldiers,” and what follows; but he does not likewise say, “that that commander alone was the prefect to whom Diocletian sent letters on the matter.”

Commanders. This was indeed the title of a military rank, and they ranked after the tribunes, though they were in charge of a cohort just as tribunes were. Oxford and Cambridge editions.—*Aux généraux de ses armées*, “to the generals of his armies.” MAUCROIX. See Baluzius, col. 315.

Letters. That is, if one wishes, edicts. For Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, VIII.2, calls the edicts which Diocletian subsequently sent in every direction against Christians after these letters to military commanders—and the first of which is more than once called an edict in this work—simply γραφή and γράμματα, “a writing” and “letters,” or at most βασιλικὰ γράμματα, “imperial letters.” Hence Valesius did not hesitate, even in the final passage, to translate: “But not long afterwards other letters again arrived.” I myself would prefer to make some distinction between the letters to commanders, of which our author speaks here, and the edict of which he speaks in chapters 13 and 14.

He ordered soldiers also to be compelled, etc. Eusebius’s statement in the *History* that the first stage of the persecution was directed against soldiers must be understood from the *Chronicle*. In the seventeenth year of Diocletian, year 2217 from Abraham, he says: “Veturius, commander-in-chief, persecutes Christian soldiers; from that time the persecution against us begins gradually.” The edition of Pontacus places this two years earlier; Prosper of Aquitaine, three years earlier; as do the acts of the centurion Marcellus, if the consular year in those acts—Faustus and Gallus—is genuine, which Antonius Pagi denies. But the Scaliger edition establishes the date entirely correctly. Lactantius agrees, for he arranged everything in the most exact chronological order … What the most learned Pagi adduces to the contrary from the acts of Marcellus is certainly suspect and cannot in any respect be compared with the reliability of Lactantius. DODWELL.—

The persecution against Christians began with soldiers, as not only Eusebius, speaking in the *Chronicle* of Veturius the commander-in-chief, and in *Ecclesiastical History* VIII.1 and 4, but also Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapters 9 and 10, testify … Since Veturius began to persecute soldiers in the year 298, that persecution did not occur before that year. PAGI, on A.D. 297, no. 3.

The persecution against soldiers began in the year 298, as Prosper rightly says in the *Chronicle*. The same PAGI, on A.D. 298, no. 2, and 302, no. 3; see them for the arguments by which he contends against Dodwell that the martyrdom of St. Marcellus the centurion ought not to be removed from that year.—But here a difficulty arises: whether Eusebius, among others, could rightly have written that Diocletian’s persecution first began with those in military service—ἐκ τῶν ἐν στρατείαις ἀδελφῶν καταρχομένου τοῦ διωγμοῦ, “the persecution beginning from the brethren in military service”—when, according to our Caecilius, it more truly began with those attendants who knowingly confessed the Lord and whom Diocletian ordered and compelled to sacrifice.

The answer is easy. It did indeed begin with those attendants of Diocletian; but Eusebius, because this affair was undertaken in a disorderly manner and as it were within private walls, and perhaps against very few Christians—for only certain persons knowingly confessing the Lord had stood by when Diocletian began to sacrifice—preferred to date the beginning of the persecution from the persecution of the soldiers. The letters alone which Diocletian sent to the commanders, bearing the character of edicts, rendered that persecution incomparably more widely known and memorable than the domestic persecution, just as publicly promulgated edicts of rulers are better known and more noteworthy than their private commands. Add Baluzius, col. 315, and Cuper, col. 493.

That those who had not obeyed should be dismissed from military service. So, as we previously cited from Sulpicius Severus in another matter: “Licinius, because he contended with Constantine for the empire, ordered his soldiers to sacrifice; those refusing, he dismissed from military service.” But, Sulpicius continues, although there is now a great difference between our author and Sulpicius Severus, this was not reckoned among the persecutions; so slight was the matter that it did not reach the level of wounds upon the Churches. Conversely, according to our author, as we shall presently see, Diocletian is said to have initiated the persecution of Christians precisely because, by letters sent to the commanders, he ordered soldiers to be compelled to perform abominable sacrifices, so that those who did not obey should be cashiered.

That those who did not, etc. Thus edicts of persecution were issued against soldiers, but they were not yet bloody. For it follows: “Thus far his fury and anger proceeded, and he did nothing further against the law or religion of God.” Yet Eusebius teaches that some suffered, although not pursuant to the emperor’s edict but from the individual cruelty of an official; he teaches this, however, so as to suggest that they were altogether very few. DODWELL, *Dissertation on Cyprian*, XI, no. 69.

Thus far his fury and anger proceeded, etc. At that time, namely, and in the said letters. For afterwards Diocletian issued far harsher edicts, directed not only against Christian soldiers but against all believers, and sent them to provincial governors. Thus, even if, as in the excellent observation of the most learned Joannes Fridericus Gronovius, *hactenus* sometimes means “not thereafter,” that meaning cannot possibly suit this passage, as what follows will show.

Then. That is, after the persecution of the soldiers had been decreed. PAGI, on A.D. 302, no. 4.

After an interval of some time. Namely, four years. For the most learned men who thought Lactantius indicated that the persecution of soldiers began in 302 and that in the following year one against all Christians was decreed were mistaken. In explaining this history, Eusebius and Lactantius must be compared with one another, and one explained by the other; for they disagree on very few points. Since Eusebius expressly joins the persecution of soldiers in the *Chronicle* with the year of Christ 298, and indicates in the *History* that several years elapsed between the beginning of the persecution against soldiers and that of the universal persecution, there can be no doubt that Lactantius’s words concerning Diocletian—“then,” that is, as has been said, after the persecution of soldiers had been decreed, “after an interval of some time, he came to Bithynia”—must be understood of an interval of several years, not several months. PAGI, on A.D. 302, [Col. 0676D] nos. 3 and 4.

He came to Bithynia to winter. Diocletian, namely; and to the city of Nicomedia, which was the imperial residence. He withdrew there toward the end of that year—understand 302—and there the universal persecution of Christians was planned. For although not only Baronius, but Petavius in *On the Doctrine of Times* and several other learned men placed the beginning of Diocletian’s persecution in this year, 302, Lactantius’s book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* finally settled the controversy and showed Valesius’s opinion to be certain. In his notes on Eusebius, Book VIII, Valesius demonstrated so solidly that it began only in the year 303 that I am astonished that, after his notes had been published, persons could still be found who thought otherwise. PAGI, on A.D. 302, no. 3. Add Baluzius, col. 315.

Maximianus Caesar also. Galerius Maximianus. English translation.

[Col. 0677A] He arrived inflamed with wickedness. Thus Lactantius, *Institutes*, VII.1: “inflamed with love of power.” So likewise there, chapter 17, and in our author, chapter 14, “inflamed with anger”; but especially Cicero, *Against Verres*: “He himself, inflamed with wickedness and frenzy, came into the forum”; and elsewhere: “That man suddenly comes forth from the praetorium, inflamed with wickedness, frenzy, and cruelty.”

The foolish old man. That is, Diocletian, as the preceding words show; and hereafter you will see him called now an unthinking old man, now a feeble old man, and now simply an old man.

He had made a beginning. Livy uses a similar phrase: “The beginning of the conspiracy was made from the marriage of Harmonia …”

## CHAPTER XI

His mother was, etc. I read: “His mother was a woman exceedingly superstitious.” Since she was a worshipper of the gods of the mountains, [she sacrificed] with banquets, and so forth. ALLIX.

His mother. That is, the mother of Maximianus Caesar, whom our author mentioned a little before. For if we refer this to the foolish old man, of whom he speaks later, the whole logic and truth of history oppose it. —*La mère de ce prince*, “the mother of that prince.” MAUCROIX.—That is, the mother of that prince, while the matter still remains obscure and ambiguous. Add Baluzius, col. 315.

Of the gods of the mountains, etc. This is a most corrupt passage. I know what learned men have offered, both to emend and to explain it. It is certain that mountains, no less than rivers, trees, and the earth, were regarded and worshipped as gods. The god Carmel is well known from Tacitus and Suetonius; the most learned Gaspar de Montoza, Marquis of Agropoli, eminent among Spain’s highest nobles both in rank and in broad and varied learning, published a very learned dissertation on him. The Syrian promontory called θεοῦ πρόσωπον, “the face of God,” for this reason, is also well known.

Yet I strongly doubt that Lactantius wrote thus; for who could persuade himself that the woman was a worshipper of the gods of all mountains? I therefore think Lactantius wrote *Deae montium cultrix*, “a worshipper of the goddess of the mountains,” or *deorum matris cultrix*, “a worshipper of the Mother of the Gods.” As the eminent Gisbertus Cuper had already noted, Cybele is called by the former title in Maecenas.

The subsequent words are confused, as are many others in this little work. But they seem to me capable of being recast and restored to their proper order as follows:

> “His mother was a worshipper of the goddess of the mountains. Since she was a woman exceedingly superstitious, she sacrificed almost every day and supplied her fellow-villagers with banquets and feasts.”

When the ancient pagans had performed sacred rites, they prepared a feast from the portion which they did not burn, inviting those to it to whom they wished well. Lactantius relates that this superstitious worshipper of Cybele did this almost daily and thus, as it were, supported by these meals the villagers among whom she lived. *Vicani* are people living in the same village, a word found in Livy and Cicero. *Exhibere* means “to maintain” or “support.” Justin, IX.2: “Atheas blamed the harshness of the climate and the barrenness of the soil, which scarcely supports the Scythians with food, though not rich in estates …” The same author, Book XXII: “She sustained life by the endurance of prostitution.” The ancient jurists spoke similarly, as that distinguished man in rank and learning, Jacobus Bongarsius, showed by examples in his note on the former passage of Justin. GRAEVIUS.

[Col. 0677D] A worshipper of the gods of the mountains. Maucroix’s translation: *Avait une dévotion particulière pour les dieux des montagnes*—“She had a special devotion to the gods of the mountains.”—That is, she worshipped particularly the gods of the mountains. The English translation likewise understands the passage in this sense: “was particularly addicted to the devotion of the Gods of the mountains.” Thus neither understands it of mountains as gods, but of gods of the mountains. On this question and others, see above Cuper, col. 493; Baluzius, col. 317; and Columbus, col. 403.

A woman exceedingly superstitious. Since she was. I prefer: “Since she was a woman exceedingly superstitious.” GALE.

Since she was. The name of the city has dropped out. Perhaps it was Nicomedia. TOLLIUS.

Since she was, with feasts, she sacrificed almost every day, and supplied her *vicarii* with banquets. There is a passage in Julius Capitolinus, in his life of Antoninus Pius, which I shall transcribe because perhaps it may shed some light on this pericope: “He shared private and public banquets with his friends; nor did he perform any sacrifice through a deputy, except when ill.”

With feasts. The distinguished GALE preferred to read “to demons” (*daemonibus*).—There is reason to suspect that something similar occurred to Maucroix, since he translated: *Il se passait peu de jours qu'elle ne sacrifiât à ses divinités fabuleuses*—“Few days passed on which she did not sacrifice to her fabulous divinities.”

She supplied her *vicarii* with banquets. I suspect a corruption, although Baluzius either concealed or passed over it. With a slight alteration one may read, *vicariis suis epulas exhibebat*, “she supplied her deputies with feasts”; unless one prefers, *vicarios suos epulis adhibebat*, “she admitted her deputies to feasts.” One or the other seems necessary. Oxford and Cambridge editions.

Her *vicarii*, etc. Read, *vicarios suos epulis exhibebat*, “she entertained her own villagers,” that is, those living in the same village. John of Salisbury, *Polycraticus*, VIII.22: “Therefore teach pagans also to make contributions for such ministries, and let the villages of pagans offer the first fruits of the crops.” Thus *vicani* are those who dwell in villages of this sort. TOLLIUS.

Her *vicarii*. *À ses domestiques*, “to her household servants.” Maucroix; that is, to her dependents.—“Her officers.” English translation. That is, if Salvian’s word may be used, her officials.—Her *vicarii*. I restore: *victimariis suis*, “her victim-slayers.” GALE.

She supplied with feasts. It should read, “she supplied feasts.” GALE; ALLIX.

The Christians abstained. *Les chrétiens évitaient sa table*, “the Christians avoided her table.” Maucroix. That is, Christians abstained from her table.—I would prefer, in accordance with the preceding words, to supply with the English translation “from those feasts”: “The Christians would not assist at those entertainments.” But why, do you suppose, did they abstain? Was it because of the idols themselves, which they believed to be something, as Paul speaks in 1 Corinthians 10:19? Or rather because, in their judgment, that celebrated apostolic decree concerning things sacrificed to idols and similar things was still to be observed in the Church: “It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose upon you no greater burden than these necessary things: that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols,” etc. Acts 15:28–29.

It is doubtless difficult to divine the matter. But if the former, the reason for abstention was certainly necessary and wholly just. For if, according to the apostle’s commands (1 Corinthians 10:27 ff.), one ought to abstain from things sacrificed to idols for the sake of another person’s conscience, when that person is not fully persuaded that idols are nothing, how much more for the sake of one’s own conscience?

But if the latter, the believers of the fourth century were so far from being obliged by the apostolic decree to abstain from every consumption of things sacrificed to idols that, because the Jewish commonwealth had already been overthrown for one or two centuries and Moses no longer had those who, according to the custom, read and expounded him in every town on every Sabbath, that decree had by that very fact long become void and was not thereafter to be observed by Christians. For from the beginning it rested upon no other foundation than this: that Moses had, from ancient generations, those who proclaimed him κατὰ πόλιν, “in every city,” namely because he was read in the synagogues every Sabbath:

> “Symeon has declared how God first visited the Gentiles, to take from them a people for his name; and the words of the Prophets agree with this … Therefore I judge that those of the Gentiles who turn to God ought not to be troubled. But we should write to them to abstain from pollutions of idols, from sexual immorality, from things strangled, and from blood. For Moses has from ancient generations those who proclaim him in every town, since he is read in the synagogues every Sabbath.”  
> —Acts 15:14 ff.

Therefore, since after this judgment of James it is evident that foods sacrificed to idols would never have been forbidden to Christians unless all those readings—and the expositions—of Moses, which had from ancient times been customary every Sabbath in every city and synagogue, had continued after Christ’s ascension to heaven without any obstacle from divine providence, it necessarily follows that Christians were free to abstain from observing the prohibition as soon as Moses ceased to have persons reading and expounding him in the synagogues in that manner. This happened long before Diocletian’s persecution. Once the cause has been removed, the effect is removed. This matter, insufficiently observed alike by the Fathers and by the Greek Churches, produced those many canons and practices of which Suicer briefly treats under αἷμα, “blood,” in his *Ecclesiastical Thesaurus*, and of which perhaps we shall treat more fully elsewhere, if we live.

Hence she conceived hatred. Because they silently reproached her for vain superstition. See what we have collected to this effect in our notes on Lucian’s *On Calumny*. TOLLIUS.

To remove the men. A concise expression, like Justin’s, XXXVIII.1: “Mithridates, having inaugurated parricides by the death of his wife, resolved to remove the children of his other sister Laodice, whose husband he had killed by treachery”—that is, to kill them, with the verb changed so as not to use the same one repeatedly; and a few words later, “that through the same man, his son, he could be removed”—that is, killed—through whom he had killed his father, the later verb already made clear by the earlier one.

The full phrase would have been “to remove men from the midst,” “from among,” or “from the world of living things.” Livy, for example, in Book IV of the Punic War: “Thraso having been removed from the midst”; and Cicero, *For Roscius*: “They show … that this man can very easily be removed from the midst”; and again there: “Do they not seem to have removed this man from the world of living things?” But others too sometimes used *tollere*, “remove,” simply for *e medio tollere*, “remove from the midst,” that is, “kill.” The Vulgate, John 19:15: “Take away, take away, crucify him”; and the unknown author who marked Nero’s impiety, in killing his mother, and Aeneas’s filial piety, in carrying his father from Troy on his shoulders, by the same word:

> This man removed his mother; that man removed his father.

This writer seems to imitate that usage when in chapter 46 he says “they lift up shields,” meaning “raise them” or “lift them from the ground”; and later in our author, “they decided that the enemies of the public religions should be removed,” that is, killed.

Having held counsel together, etc. Baluzius and both translators rightly understand only Diocletian and Galerius, Diocletian’s son-in-law. For, as we have just learned concerning Romula, mother of Maximianus Caesar, that she conceived hatred against the Christians because they abstained from her feasts and urged her son to remove them, it is nevertheless certain that Romula too was not admitted to the deliberation whose history now begins. It was in fact held only between the old man, or emperor, on one side—Diocletian—and the rash man, Caesar, on the other—Galerius Maximianus.

Hence a little later the singular is used: “For a long time the old man resisted his fury,” not “their fury”; and again subsequently: “Yet he could not turn aside the madness of the rash man,” with no mention whatever of the mother. That this passage speaks of counsel held throughout the winter between Galerius and Diocletian shows that Maximianus Caesar flew to Bithynia as soon as he learned that Diocletian had gone there to winter; see chapter 10 near its end.
