Throughout the winter. Namely, that of the year 302, according to Pagi, whose words on that year, no. 3, are: “In this year the question of persecuting Christians was considered throughout the whole winter.”

The old man. That is, as Maucroix interprets, Diocletian: *Dioclétien résista longtemps*, “Diocletian resisted for a long time,” etc.—Correctly. For there can be no question here of Maximianus Herculius, the other old man among the emperors. At that time there were in the Roman Empire two preeminent old men, κατ’ ἐξοχήν: Valerius Diocletian and Herculius Maximianus, both Augusti and emperors. Hence chapter 12: “When both old men were holding their eighth and seventh consulships”; and chapter 20: “Maximianus”—understand Galerius—“after expelling the old men, accomplished what he wished.” But because this passage concerns Diocletian and Galerius Maximianus alone, and because Diocletian was an old man chiefly in relation to Galerius, our author did not hesitate simply to call Diocletian “the old man”; for the same reason he will do so again in chapter 19.

His. That is, Maximianus’s. English translation.

[Col. 0680A] **Showing how much, etc.** It is surprising that those for whom the credibility of this book is suspect have not asked here how these facts became known to our author, when, as the preceding remarks indicate, no one was admitted, and all supposed that deliberations concerned only the supreme interests of the state, as has just been stated. But an answer was ready, had they asked. For although Diocletian and Galerius Maximian had for a long time admitted no one to their deliberations, a few judges and a few military men were eventually admitted, whose opinion they chose to test, as will appear from what follows. This being so, it is not merely more than probable that Diocletian—whose disposition recoiled from the bloody persecution of Christians, and whose habitual practice it was to satisfy his own severity through another’s odium—began, before everything else, to set forth to that assembly the arguments by which, as stated here, he had tried throughout the winter to turn Galerius from his purpose of persecution, and the replies Galerius had persistently made to him; and then to ask them frankly which man’s reasoning they judged the weightier. It is also highly likely that among those advocates, judges, or military men there later emerged one or more persons well disposed toward Christ’s people (for some held that Christians ought not to be destroyed), who sooner or later reported the entire affair to our Caecilius, or at least to other friends of his; and from them it subsequently came to this writer’s knowledge.

**“The whole world would be disturbed.”** As above, chapter 7: “He overturns the whole world”; and interpreters have rightly understood this in both places to mean the Roman Empire.

**“And be poured out.”** For *et fundi*, “and be poured out,” as elsewhere the conjunction often seems to be absent. TOLLIUS.

**“That they were accustomed willingly to die.”** Hence such voluntary cries as: “I am a Christian; I wish to die.” This pious zeal grew so heated that Mensurius, bishop of Carthage, held that the honour of martyrdom ought to be denied to persons who had offered themselves to death without being summoned. Oxford and Cambridge editions.

**“They willingly die.”** Indeed, they sought death even when it was not threatened. See Tertullian, *To Scapula*, and other writers of that period on the subject. TOLLIUS.—When Sabinus, prefect of Egypt, was sitting with his assessors, and a certain Christian seemed to yield somewhat to tortures and gradually relax from his former firmness of spirit, others at the same time ran up to the tribunal, restrained him, and, though no one questioned them, confessed themselves Christians. Diocletian opposed this very fact to Galerius, who was urging persecution: Christians were accustomed willingly to die. DODWELL, Dissertation XI, no. 92.

**“If he prohibited only palace officials and soldiers from that religion.”** “All who serve in the palace may be called *Palatini*,” says the scholiast on Julian the predecessor, cited by Cange in his *Glossary*, under *Palatini*. But since here *Palatini* are distinguished from soldiers, it is clear that another meaning must be considered.

Cange continues: “*Palatini*” means the nobles and grandees of the palace, called *primores palatii* (“chief men of the palace”) in the Life of St Genulphus; *palatini principes* (“palatine princes”) in the Saxon poet under the year 782; *palatinus [Col. 0680D] senatus* (“palatine senate”) in Claudian, *On the Fourth Consulship of Honorius*; and *proceres palatii* (“magnates of the palace”) in the charter of Robert, king of France, of 1029. Shortly thereafter he adds that, under the Roman emperors, *Palatini* were those who collected the revenues belonging to the *res privata* and the sacred largesses; concerning whom both Codes contain the title *On the Palatines of the Sacred Largesses*. He immediately confirms this from the scholiast on Julian the predecessor, in whom *palatini* are those belonging to the Count of the Private Estate or to the Count of the Sacred Largesses.

But if in this place we understand by *palatini* nothing other than palace nobles or counts of that sort, what becomes of the masters and judges whom we shall shortly see in Diocletian’s palace? Chapter 14: “Finally, all who were masters in the palace, being granted authority, tortured [them]”; and chapter 17: “Suddenly there was grief in the palace—mourning, tears, the trembling and silence of the judges.” Was Diocletian, I ask, unwilling that these should in any way be prohibited from the Christian religion, but only the great palatines and soldiers? That is absurd. Again, if here the name *palatini* must mean only palace nobles or the counts of either order, Diocletian must then have given no further thought whatsoever to the household servants and attendants with whom he had begun the persecution—an absurdity no less great. In the present passage, therefore, we think that *palatini* denotes both all Diocletian’s household, as so many inhabitants of the palace, and, in addition, all who were adorned with some dignity connected with the palace.

**“To turn him aside.”** I would prefer *flectere*, “to bend.” Thus shortly afterward: “Nor indeed was the Emperor bent so as to give his assent”; and in chapter 25: “Unless his friends had bent him from that madness,” where I would prefer *flexissent* to *deflexissent*. TOLLIUS.

**“A headlong man.”** That is, an inconsiderate man; for which Maucroix, without circumlocution, interpreted Galerius—who is certainly attacked and meant here: “All these reasons could not bend the obstinacy of Galerius.” We spoke shortly before, on chapter 9, of this kind of interpretation.

[Col. 0681B] **“For he was of this malignity.”** Hence, in Vopiscus’s *Numerian*, “a man shrewd and subtle, always of deep counsel, sometimes shameless.” Oxford and Cambridge editions.

**“He summoned many into council.”** But if this is so, why does our author, six or seven words later, say: “A few judges and a few military men were therefore admitted”? We think that the original reading was: *in consilium alios advocabat*, “he summoned others into council”—that is, others besides himself. The immediately following words favour this: “that whatever wrongdoing he himself committed might be ascribed to the fault of others”; nor does the purer idiom of Latin stand in the way. Cicero, *On Duties*, I.1: *Nos autem quantum in utroque genere profecerimus aliorum esto judicium*—“but let the judgment of others be as to how far we have progressed in either kind,” that is, of persons other than myself. Add the elegance of the expression: “he summoned others into council, so that to the fault of others, etc.” Moreover, if in *multos* the first letter is discarded as though rashly repeated from the ending of the preceding word *consilium*, clear traces appear of the reading which, unless I am mistaken, we restore—or at least propose to the learned with our own hesitation. For until now, so far as I can see, no one has managed to resolve this difficulty.

**“A few judges and a few military men were therefore admitted.”** Just as judges are here rightly distinguished from military men, so, in effect, judges are distinguished from soldiers in chapter 17 in these words: “The faces of the judges changed to cheerfulness. There were some who suspected that his death was being concealed until Caesar should arrive, lest perhaps the soldiers should make some disturbance.” Yet in chapter 22 we find the combined and very elegant designation *judices militares* (“military judges”) applied to one and the same persons: “Military judges, untrained in humane letters, dispatched into the provinces without assessors.”

**“That they ought to be removed.”** “That they had to be exterminated.” MAUCROIX.

**“And those who thought otherwise.”** So read all editions except the first, in which, from a manuscript codex, one finds *et qualiter sentiebant*, “and how they thought”; but this is erroneous, as Baluz[i]us himself first saw and noted.

**“Of the man.”** That is, of Maximian. English translation.

**“The Emperor.”** Both translators render more directly and clearly: Diocletian.

**“And he sent a diviner to the Milesian Apollo.”** Eusebius recounts this story in Book II of the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 1. PAGIUS, on the year of Christ 302, no. 3.

**“He was therefore led away from his purpose.”** Too concisely, as the translators rightly perceived. Both, though it is not obscure to whom these words refer, considered that, because Apollo of Miletus and the diviner sent to him had been mentioned last and immediately before, either the word “Emperor” or Diocletian’s proper name had to be supplied in their translations. “Thus the Emperor was compelled to yield.” MAUCROIX.—“Upon this Diocletian yielded.” English translation.

**“When Caesar wished that they should be burned alive, etc.”** Thus Galerius was exceedingly cruel, and concerning him Dodwell rightly says, though in other words:

> For if there is any evil here, ah, there is the chief source of this matter.

The words are those of a most learned man: “Then in the year [Col. 0682A] 304, if we trust Eusebius, severer edicts followed, by which ‘all persons everywhere in each city were ordered to sacrifice and pour libations to the idols’ [πάντας πανδημεὶ τοὺς κατὰ πόλιν θύειν τε καὶ σπένδειν τοῖς εἰδώλοις ἐκελεύετο]. At that time Eusebius relates that Timothy, after innumerable tortures, was at last consumed by a slight and slow fire. These edicts plainly bear Galerius as their author, whom Lactantius says wished those who refused sacrifice to be burned alive, while Diocletian was still administering the Empire.”

## CHAPTER XII

**“A propitious [day].”** “Of good omen.” MAUCROIX. That is, of favourable omen: “auspicious,” English translation; that is, begun under favourable auspices.

**Terminalia.** “The Terminalia,” says Varro, “because that day was appointed the last day of the year.” For February was the twelfth month; and when intercalation occurs, the last five days are deducted from the twelfth month. Festus. Terminus, according to Varro, was a god consecrated by Tatius; according to others, by Numa Pompilius. So that Romans, content with their own possessions, should not covet those of others, Numa enacted a law concerning the marking of estates by boundaries. Oxford and Cambridge editions.—“Terminalia: the festival of the god Terminus.” English translation. That is, the feast of the god Terminus.

**“On the seventh day before the Kalends of March.”** Maucroix’s translation says “23 January,” that is, 23 January—an obvious and utterly intolerable printers’ error for “23 February,” as may be established even from the following observations of learned men.—“Within five days of the end of February,” English interpretation; as though one said, “on the sixth day before the end of February.”—“On the seventh before the Kalends of March.” The persecution therefore began on 23 February, as is also clear from chapter 48 of the same book. After the long ignorance of so many centuries, Lactantius in his book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* has taught us not only the year but also the month and day of this persecution with certainty. PAGIUS, on the year of Christ 302, no. 5.

**“So that, as it were, a boundary might be set to this religion.”** The author’s meaning is entirely clear. But who has used “to set a boundary” in the sense of “to put an end,” as he does? I lack an example. Although perhaps no one has said *terminum imponere* as they say *finem imponere*, it is nevertheless clear that Lactantius, by this mode of expression, alludes to the word *Terminalia*, on which this persecution began. Since he saw that the expression was somewhat harsh, he softened it with the little word *quasi*, “as it were.” GRAEVIUS.

**“That day was the first, etc.”** From Virgil, *Aeneid* IV. BALUZIUS, in the margin of the first edition.

**“Both for themselves and for the whole world.”** That is, for the emperors and all nations, according to Maucroix; for this is his rendering: “for the emperors and all nations.” But it is better understood with the English translation as though the author’s words were “both for themselves and for the whole Empire”: “not only on them, but on the whole empire.” We have already said enough elsewhere on this point.

**“While the two aged men were holding their eighth and seventh consulships.”** That is, in the year 303, when Diocletian entered upon his eighth and Maximian upon his seventh consulship, and in which year the persecution consequently began with certainty. PAGIUS, on the year of Christ 302, no. 5. Somewhat fuller light is supplied by Maucroix’s translation: [Col. 0682D] “Under Diocletian’s eighth consulship and Maximian Herculius’s seventh.” That is, under the eighth consulship of Diocletian and the seventh of Maximian Herculius; whereas the English translation gives: “in the seventh and eighth consulate of the two ancient emperors”—that is, in the seventh and eighth consulships of the two aged emperors, reversing, for some unknown reason, the order in which our author named and numbered the two consulships together.

**“The two aged men.”** Correctly so, though they were not yet decrepit. I prove both points from Cassiodorus, who under Diocletian’s tenth consulship—that is, the consulship Diocletian subsequently entered in the year of Christ 307—writes:

> Diocletian X and Maximus VII. Under these consuls, Diocletian at Nicomedia and Maximian at Milan laid aside the purple on account of the infirmity of age.

I prove it again from Book IX of Eutropius, whose words are: “When Diocletian, feeling himself less fit to govern the Empire because of advancing age, urged Herculius to retire into private life and entrust the post of safeguarding the state to younger and more vigorous men, his colleague reluctantly obeyed.” Moreover, both lived for no few years after laying aside the purple.

**“To the Church.”** This manner of speaking had already been introduced in the fourth century after Christ’s birth, so that Latin and Greek Fathers used the name *ecclesia* for a building consecrated to Christian worship. Our author shortly afterward: “The Church could be seen from the palace.” Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VII: “Theotecnus, the bishop of that city, approached Marinus, drew him away at some length in conversation, took him by the hand, and led him to the CHURCH [Θεότεκνος ὁ τῇδε Ἐπίσκοπος ἀφέλκει (Μαρῖνον) ποσελθῶν δὶ ὁμιλίας, καὶ τῆς χειρὸς λαβῶν ἐπὶ τὴν ΕΚΚΛΗΣΙΑΝ προᾷγει]. Having placed him within by the very sanctuary [ἁγίασμα],” etc. That is, as Valesius translates: “Theotecnus, bishop of the city, approached Marinus and, drawing him farther away through conversation, led him by the hand to the church. And when he had placed him within at the altar itself,” and what follows. Similar examples occur very frequently in Eusebius and in writers of the fifth century. Yet in the same fourth and fifth centuries Christians also called their sacred buildings *templa*, “temples.” Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, Book V, chapter 2: “When I had been summoned to teach rhetoric in Bithynia, and it happened that at that same time the temple of God was destroyed . . .” Augustine, Sermon 255 *On Time*: “Although the holy temples which we see constructed from wood and stones are sacred, the temples of our hearts and bodies are more precious in God’s sight . . . Temples of wood and stones are fashioned by human skill; temples of bodies are fashioned by the hand of the heavenly craftsman himself.” And the emperors Theodosius and Valentinian Augustus, in a rescript to Antiochus, Praetorian Prefect, use the terms interchangeably: “Let the temples of the supreme God stand open to those who fear [him]; nor do we decree that only altars and the surrounding oratory of the temple—which encloses churches within a fourfold enclosure of walls—are appointed as a refuge for those who flee thither”; and so often subsequently.

**“Having set out with the commanders.”** So read all editions except the Oxford edition of 1684 and the Cambridge edition of the following year, which read: “the prefect [went] to the church with the commanders.” Indeed Sparke, who edited the former, comments excellently on this passage: “Formerly *profectus* was read, a word with which nothing suitable occurs.”

**“Having set out with the commanders.”** There is no sense. Therefore one must read *praefectus*, “prefect,” etc., says the Right Reverend Burnet, bishop of Salisbury; hence his translation: “the Prefect,” and what follows.—“*Profectus*. Read *praefectus*. Thus chapter 16 mentions Flaccinus the Prefect.” GALE.—“I read *Praefectus*.” ALLIX.—“To the church, the prefect.” See Pliny’s letter to Trajan and Justin Martyr’s *Apology*. TOLLIUS.

**“The rationales.”** “The officers of the treasury.” MAUCROIX.—“The receivers.” English translation.

**“An image of God is sought.”** As among pagans, who thought temples could not exist without images. Oxford and Cambridge edition.—As was done by the Romans under Pompey, after the capture of Jerusalem. TOLLIUS.—This undoubtedly derives from Tacitus: “The first Roman to subdue the Jews was Gnaeus Pompey, who entered their temple by right of conquest. Hence arose the common report that within there was no image of a god, but an empty sanctuary and vain mysteries.”—“An image of God is sought.” The bishop of Salisbury: “Nor [was it] that the Christians had any images in their temples, as Lactantius himself testifies, *On the Origin of Error*, Book II, pp. 65, 66, 67, 107; but the heathens, having images in all their temples, were ready to conceive the same of them.” That is, not because Christians had any images in their temples—for Lactantius himself testifies to the contrary in *On the Origin of Error*, Book II, etc.—but because images stood in all pagan shrines, pagans could readily form the same notion concerning Christians.—“An image of God is sought.” Good; but it is not found, a point very much to be noted. None is named in the immediately following list of things found, but only Scriptures. “The Scriptures found are burned.”—To this belong two conclusions of Pagius, certainly not undeserving of praise and not useless for our people, though neither is yet of the clearest good faith. One is: “It is therefore credible that images were little used by Christians during approximately the first four centuries, throughout which the abominable religion of demons in idols and the most cruel harassment of the Christian name continued their course.” The other is: “Therefore, in the controversy concerning images, one ought to follow rather the examples and institutions of the later Church than those of the earlier.” Those who consult the former passage will see why, in this matter at least, I should have wished to find somewhat more good faith in that very distinguished man: namely, because he gratuitously added that images had nevertheless been in some use before the fifth century, though not common or frequent; yet he proved this by no example.

**“An image of God is sought.”** “They seek the idol of God.” Maucroix. [Note: He speaks in accordance with the pagans’ conception, and aptly according to their system. Hence any argument drawn from this is utterly weak.] Literally, “the idol of God is sought.” This is well put. For an *idolum* is therefore also an image of the true God. Let those who wish to turn the second precept of the Decalogue—“You shall not make for yourself an idol”—to the defence of images of the Most Holy [Col. 0684B] Trinity consider how, even with their interpretation, they can prove that idols are indeed unlawful, that is, images of things or gods which do not exist [οὐκ ὄντων], but that images of the true God are altogether lawful. For Maucroix in our passage renders *simulacrum Dei*, “image of God,” namely of the supreme and only true God, by *idolum Dei*, “idol of God”; and in his marginal note he calls by no other word the images which pagans thought existed in Christian temples: “They believed that Christians had idols in their temples.” That is, *Credebant Christianos habere idola in suis templis*. Moreover, the idols which pagans possessed they were persuaded were images not of beings that do not exist [τῶν οὐκ ὄντων], but of beings that do exist [τῶν ὄντων].

**“The Scriptures found are burned.”** From this arose the term *traditor*, applied against those who, through fear of punishment, handed over the Holy Scriptures to imperial judges. Oxford edition of 1680, likewise the Cambridge edition.

**“Plunder is granted to all.”** Better: “All things are given over as plunder.” [Col. 0684C] TOLLIUS.

**“There is seizing, agitation, running about.”** *Trepidare*, therefore, in the sense touched upon above, signifies something different from running about, as we observed there: one is agitated in a single place—or perhaps sometimes around that same place—whereas one runs about through several places. Terence’s verse confirms this:

> “I perceive agitation, running up and down,”

which makes the distinction between agitation and running about most manifest, as between a movement much smaller and a greater one. Further, *trepidatur* very plainly sometimes occurs without any fear at all, as we noted additionally on chapter 10, p. 603; for with the persons of whom our author now speaks—“there is seizing, agitation”—the safest possible authority to plunder and seize had previously been granted in Diocletian’s name. “Plunder is granted to all. There is seizing, agitation.” Varro’s previously cited “agitation of bees” likewise confirms this: certainly no greater fear comes over them when they bustle out of their hives than when they enter them again. Not to mention Livy’s passage to the same effect: “What? The enemy had drawn up their battle line in complete leisure, had recovered their spirits, and stood each man in his ordered ranks; whereas we then had to bustle suddenly in forming the line.” And again shortly afterward: “But not even on that very day was battle joined, though neither consul nor king wished it: not the king, because he was not going to attack men exhausted, as on the preceding day, by their journey, nor men agitated in drawing up their line and scarcely yet formed; nor the consul, etc.” You rightly observe that *trepidare* is often taken without the notion of fear. For it often means to be in commotion and to exert oneself from every side in entering, departing, attacking, or violently assailing something. GRAEVIUS.

[Col. 0685A] **“There is seizing, agitation, running about.”** Maucroix: “Some seize, others faint with fear, others flee.” As though the Latin first read: “Some seize, others are overcome by terror, others scatter in flight”; and as though Christians had already gathered in the Nicomedian church early in the morning, and some of them, after the doors were torn down, had fainted in terror while others had been driven hither and thither in flight—whither the other translations also tend. But besides the objections already noted in passing against these hypotheses, let us add this: the author’s words are by no means, “There is seizing, agitation, flight”—forgive the word—but “There is seizing, agitation, running about”; thus they do not properly apply to persons fleeing, but to persons running about. Add that the Christians of Nicomedia had not yet assembled in their church on that day, so much so that it was necessary to tear down the doors because they had not yet been opened. For to say that they were torn down because Christians within were attending to their worship behind closed doors would be absurd: partly because our passage makes no mention of Christians found within after the doors were torn down, but only of Scriptures; partly because, since the Christians at Nicomedia had hitherto possessed their church openly and with the magistracy’s permission, there was no reason for them to hold their assemblies behind closed doors; and finally because these three expressions—“there is seizing, agitation, running about”—most plainly apply not to different persons but to the same persons, that is, to all those to whom plunder had been granted. I would therefore much rather translate in French: “Some seize, others bustle about, others run hither and thither,” than as Maucroix chose to translate. Let the learned judge.

**“For the Church was situated on high.”** Perhaps by chance, but perhaps also by design. For Jews of old deliberately built their synagogues in elevated places, though they had not done so from the beginning; and pagans did the same with a large part of their temples. Concerning the Jews, the matter is most certain from very many canons of what might be called Rabbinic law, which prescribe that synagogues be built in the highest part of cities and be higher than the other buildings, in imitation, doubtless, of the Temple at Jerusalem, which was established upon a mountain. As for pagans, the Greeks, for example, placed temples of Aesculapius, whom they appointed over health, in lofty and pure places. “Why,” asks Plutarch in the *Roman Questions*, “is the shrine of Aesculapius outside the city? Is it because they think life outside the city healthier than within it? For the Greeks too, not unreasonably, place sanctuaries of Aesculapius in pure and lofty locations.” And Vitruvius: “For sacred buildings, of those gods under whose protection the city appears most particularly to be—Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva—sites should be assigned in the highest place, from which the greater part of the walls may be seen.”

“But,” someone will say, “it is incredible that Christians erected the church in question on high for any similar reason.” I grant it; but perhaps, then—if one supposes anything intentional in the matter—it was because the earlier Christian assemblies had been held *ἐν ὑπερῴοις*, that is, as it is commonly translated, “in upper rooms,” almost literally, “in the upper places.” See Acts 1:12 and following, and likewise 20:7–8. I would rather leave the reason entirely uncertain, especially because, just as Jews did not at every time build their synagogues in elevated places, nor pagans always erect their shrines on high—Vitruvius, to omit others, immediately after the words cited above says: “But for Mercury, in the forum; or, as also for Isis and Serapis, in the marketplace; for Apollo and Father Liber, beside the theatre; for Hercules, in cities without gymnasia or amphitheatres, beside the circus; for Mars, outside the city but by the field; and for Venus, by the gate”—so Christians likewise did not continually place their churches upon mountain summits, but sometimes in low valleys, sometimes on the shores of seas and rivers, and in other places, as Hospinian long ago observed. Let this alone be established: Evagrius also mentions a *τέμενος* or *ναός*, that is, a temple, which he saw, built in the fifth century for Symeon Stylites, about three hundred stadia from Theopolis, on the very summit of a mountain.

**“Whether fire ought rather to be set beneath it.”** Rather than what? For this seems to be the force of the adverb, and the common Latin usage, such that the author could not have failed to write: “whether fire ought rather to be set beneath it than that it be demolished,” or, better, “whether it ought to be demolished or whether fire ought rather to be set beneath it.” We therefore do not doubt that one of these, or some similar form, must be read.

**“After a fire had been made.”** An entirely Latin expression. Caesar, *Gallic War*: “And so much harm was done to the enemy by devastating the fields and setting fires.” Other examples are readily available.

**Praetorians.** “A considerable body of guards.” English translation. That is, a great body of attendants and protectors of the imperial person.

**“Yet they levelled that very lofty [building] to the ground in a few hours.”** Anyone learned in Latin knows that *tamen* cannot stand here, not to say that *editissimum*, “most lofty,” requires a noun. I do not approve *tutamen*, “protection,” which some think ought to be substituted. I have thought that it should read *culmen illud editissimum*, “that most lofty structure.” For *culmina* are temples and all higher buildings; and this church was such a building. Justin, XXIV.8: “That the god had come and that he had seen him leaping down into the temple through the open high gables [culminis].” The same, XXVIII.3: “When day began to approach, and the rising sun shone upon the highest rooftops [culminibus] of the city.” Statius, in the *Birthday Poem for Lucan*:

> You will speak of the infamous fires  
> Of the guilty lord over the high buildings of wandering Remus.

“The high buildings of Remus” are temples and other buildings into which Nero sent fire when he burned Rome. The same author, *Thebaid* IX:

> . . . whether he now keeps watch, fixed beneath a lofty roof,  
> Or hangs as a glory in an ancient grove.

That is, whether they suspended the spoils of the captured lion in a temple or in a grove. Other examples are readily available. [Col. 0686C] GRAEVIUS.—Maucroix supplied “temple,” Burnet “building,” each in his own translation.—“Yet that most lofty, etc.” I have no doubt that *templum*, “temple,” should be substituted for *tamen*. Lactantius himself establishes my conjecture in *Divine Institutes*, Book V, chapter 2, where he calls a building dedicated by Christians to divine worship “the temple of God.” So too at the beginning of this little book. COLOMESIUS.—At the same place, “Yet that most lofty.” The received reading can be defended. Nevertheless I would prefer *tandem*, “at last,” for which I recall that *tamen* has sometimes been used. But “that most lofty temple,” or “shrine,” may also be read not inappropriately. For *tutamen* scarcely finds a place here. TOLLIUS.—“*Tamen*. Read *culmen*, or *cacumen*.” GALE.—“‘That [tamen]’—there is a gap or corruption there.” ALLIX.—I wholly agree. But it is astonishingly uncertain which reading is preferable. Formerly, because the latter appealed to me, I did not dislike reading *fanum*, “shrine,” which also occurred to Tollius, or in Latin letters the Greek *temenos*, that is, “temple”; and I have not yet repented of either conjecture. For Cange’s claim that Christians used *fanum* as their proper term for pagan temples, though many passages of the ancients suggest it, is not universal. Concerning the Jewish temple, the Christian translator of 2 Maccabees 14:33 renders the Greek, “Unless you hand Judas over to me bound, I shall level this house of God to the plain” [ἐὰν μὴ δέσμιόν μοι τὸν Ἰούδαν παραδῶτε, τόνδε τὸν τοῦ θεοῦ οἶκον εἰς πεδίον ποιήσω], as follows: “Unless you hand Judas over to me bound, I shall bring this shrine [fanum] of God down to the plain.” And concerning both the temple of Christ’s body and that at Jerusalem, the author of the treatise *On Mounts Sinai and Zion*, written against the Jews, says: “In the likeness of which temple, namely Solomon’s, Jesus said that his flesh was, saying to the Pharisees: ‘Destroy this shrine [fanum], and in three days I shall raise it.’ And the Pharisees said: ‘This shrine was built in forty-six years, and will he raise it in three days?’ But Jesus spoke of the shrine [fanum] of his body.” Add from Aldhelm, or rather from Gronovius’s *Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers*:

[Col. 0687A]

> Do you not know that those are temples [templa] of God, your . . .?

The manuscript reads:

> Do you not know that [they are] shrines [fana] of God, etc.

As for *temenos*, the second correction of our *tamen*, that word does not indeed occur, except in Greek letters and among Greeks, in the sense of “temple”—for example, in Dio Cassius concerning the temple at Jerusalem, “defending the sanctuary [τέμενος] of their God” [ὑπὲρ τοῦ τέμενους τοῦ θεοῦ ἀμυνόμενοι]; and in Evagrius concerning the temple of Symeon Stylites: “I desired to see the temple [τέμενος] of that holy man” [Ἐπόθουν τὸ τέμενος τούτου δὴ τοῦ ἁγίου θεάσασθαι]. Yet, in a word, nothing is more frequent in the writings of the Fathers than Greek words written in Latin letters. John Frederick Gronovius, *Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers*: “Cerda,” he says, “forbids *cyclus* to be written and instead wants *ciclus*, as though it were contracted from *circulis*. I wonder at the reasoning. Was it harder to take *cyclus* from the Greeks than *orama*, *protus*, *tetra*, and countless other words of that kind?” Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, Book VII, chapter 23: *qua de anastasi*, for *qua de ἀναστάσει*, that is, “concerning the resurrection”; and again shortly afterward: *Anastasim mortuorum futuram esse consentiunt*, “they agree that there will be a resurrection of the dead,” for *ἀνάστασιν*, in the same sense. Our author below, chapter 23: “Apollo and Asclepius are invoked,” from the Greek Ἀσκληπιός, instead of the Latin Aesculapius. Most plainly again, in chapter 2: *epinicium sanctum et sempiternum*, “a holy and everlasting victory-song,” for ἐπινίκιον. Orosius, Book VII, chapter 7, concerning Nero: “He often seemed to himself to have surpassed heralds [cerices], cithara-players, tragic actors, and charioteers,” not *Ceritos* or *Scenicos*, as the first editions read, but *Cerycas*, Greek κήρυκας, as that genuine passage of the Hieronymian Chronicle shows: “Nero is crowned at Olympia, surpassing heralds [cericas], cithara-players, tragic actors, and charioteers in varied competition.” In the *Passion of Saints Perpetua and Felicity*: “Welcome, *tegnon*,” for τέκνον, “child.” Elsewhere later: “On the day before we fought, I see in a *horomate*,” for *in ὁράματι*, “in a vision.” Again elsewhere: “And I see him rolling in the *afa* against the Egyptian,” for *in ἀφῇ* (“in aphē”; precise sense uncertain); and again later: “We heard a united voice saying, ‘*Agios, Agios, Agios*,’ without ceasing”—ἅγιος, ἅγιος, ἅγιος, “Holy, Holy, Holy.” Compare the beginning of Cyprian’s address *For the Martyrs*, and likewise the address he delivered on the day of his passion: lest now Lucretius’s *equum durateum*, “wooden horse,” be for δουράτεον, “wooden”; Pliny’s *probata*, that is, πρόβατα, “sheep”; and let me pass over six hundred other examples of the kind. But this passage is perhaps mutilated rather than corrupt.

## CHAPTER XIII

**“On the following day.”** Namely, 24 February. Eusebius, however, in Book VIII, chapter 2, writes that the edict was posted in March, as the feast day of the Lord’s passion approached. The author of the Alexandrian Chronicle gives 25 March, Easter Day itself. But the very distinguished Baluz[i]us reconciles these accounts as follows: the edict was first posted at Nicomedia, where Lactantius lived, as in an imperial city, on 24 February; then it was sent to the other cities of the Empire, posted in March in the place where Eusebius then lived, in Palestine in April, and at Alexandria or elsewhere on Easter Day itself. I shall shortly show that this conjecture is certain. PAGIUS, on the year of Christ 302, no. 5.

**“The edict was posted.”** *Proponere*, “to post,” is the same as *proscribere*, “to publish by posting”: to make something known publicly by affixing a notice, decree, or other written document. In Justin, “to post symbols” means to place inscriptions on public monuments for reading. But who does not know such things? GRAEVIUS.—“An edict was published.” Maucroix. Literally, and in present usage, “it was made public”; this is also the sense of the English translation: “An edict was published.”—Writers of the better age sometimes said more fully *proponere in publico* and *in publicum*, “to set forth in public.”

**“That persons of that religion.”** Namely, the religion our author called divine at the end of chapter 2: “He replied as an enemy of the divine religion”—in a word, Christians, whom he had also called so directly three times shortly before. Accordingly Maucroix renders it directly here: [Col. 0688A] “All who professed the Christian religion”; and the English translation even more simply: “The Christians.”

**“Should be subjected to tortures, etc.”** Therefore, as we noted above concerning beatings, various classes and ranks of persons had previously been exempt from torture.

**“Every legal action against them should be active.”** Rather: “Every action against them should be active.” GALE.—This emendation occurred not only to me, but also to the distinguished author of the English translation, as appears from the words: “All actions were to be received against them.” Unless he also judged that *valeret*, “should be valid,” ought to be read instead of *caleret*, “should be pressed more vigorously,” along with the most eminent Cuper. At one time I also suspected that the original read, with greater emphasis: *adversus eos omnes omnis actio caleret*, or *valeret*: “against all of them every legal action should be active,” or “valid.” Nor otherwise are all exceptions met in the words immediately preceding: “They should be deprived of every honour and dignity; they should be subjected to tortures, from whatever order or rank they came.”

**“To bring suit concerning things taken away.”** Supply *iure*, “at law,” as in the familiar verse:

> “There will be a tribunal through which it will be permitted to bring suit at law.”

For in another sense, though with a very similar phrase, our author says below in chapter 39: “She replied . . . that she could not treat of marriage in that mournful attire.” But just as here *agere* means “to proceed at law and in court,” so *actio* means “a forensic action” in the words: “Every legal action against them should be active.” Hence the English translation rightly gives: “might not sue for thefts or robberies.”

What of the edict, and so forth. The account occurs in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, chapter 6 (rather, 5). Yet nowhere is the name mentioned more explicitly than here. Oxford and Cambridge editions.

“A certain man.” *Un particulier* [“a private individual”].—MAUCROIX. As though one said: “a certain private person”; which accords least of all with Eusebius’s words [Col. 0688C]: Τῶν οὐκ ἀσήμων τις, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἄγαν κατὰ τὰς ἐν τῷ βίῳ νενόμισμένας ὑπεροχὰς ἐνδοξοτάτων, “one of no obscure standing, but indeed most eminent according to the distinctions customarily recognized in life.” But Baluzius must certainly be consulted on this matter.

“He tore down.” Read *deripuit* (“he tore down”), as below, chapter 28. TOLLIUS.—“He tore down and tore to pieces.” The narrative of Symeon Metaphrastes concerning Polyeuctus may not inappropriately be referred to here: when Decius and Valerian were emperors, he received their edict against Christians from the hands of Nearchus, read it through, spat upon it as he read, and then finally shattered it into tiny fragments and consigned them to the winds.

“While mockingly saying that the victories over the Goths and Sarmatians had been placed before it.” That is, I suppose, that the emperors were as barbarous as the Goths and Sarmatians from whose defeat they had acquired their titles. Oxford and Cambridge editions.—“Mocking the surnames ‘Gothic’ and ‘Sarmatian,’ which the emperors arrogated to themselves.” MAUCROIX. Literally: “mockingly deriding the designations of the Goths and Sarmatians which the emperors arrogated to themselves.” [Col. 0688D]—“And rallied the emperors, who had put among their titles that they had triumphed over the Goths and the Sarmatians, that they acted like those whom they pretended that they had subdued.” English translation. As though one said: “And he mocked the emperors, who in the preface to their edict had boasted, among other things, that they had triumphed over Goths and Sarmatians, because they acted no differently from those whom they claimed to have subdued.”

“Placed before.” I read: *propositas* (“set before [them]”). It is said ironically: that is, although subjected, Christians were now in the position of Goths and Sarmatians to be conquered. BOHERELLUS.—This can be supported by the Abo edition, in which *propositas*, not *praepositas*, was printed long ago. But, lest you should not know it, the exceptional and most closely associated colleague Graevius believed that something of weightier significance, ὕπουλον (“hidden, insidious”), lay concealed here, which cannot be brought to light without a better manuscript—as in many other passages of this work. I agree.

“And immediately brought forth.” Namely, into court or before the magistrates. [Col. 0689A] The translators took it simply as “he was seized.”—“He was taken.” MAUCROIX.—“He was presently seized on.” English translation.

“Racked.” That is, mangled by torture. So also in chapter 27: “Parents and husbands were racked, so that they might betray their daughters, their wives, and their possessions.” TOLLIUS.

“Legally roasted.” “In accordance with the laws enacted by the Augusti,” says Baluzius. Cambridge edition.—Ὡς ἂν μὴ συντόμως ἀπαλλαγείῃ, καταβραχὺ ἀνηλίσκετο, “lest he should be released quickly, he was slowly consumed,” Eusebius in the passage cited; that is, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, chapter 6, continue the Oxford editions, although the words cited from Eusebius do not at all concern the martyr in question, but another, named Peter, τῶν βασιλικῶν παίδων ἓνα, “one of the imperial servants,” or, in Valesius’s rendering, “one of the emperor’s chamberlains.”

“Legally roasted.” “He was put upon the grill.” MAUCROIX. Literally, “he was placed upon a gridiron”; but I do not see how this can be borne or defended.—“Legally roasted.” Rather, “very slowly roasted”; chapter 21: “Laws having been given that, after torture, the condemned should be burned with slow fires.” GALE.

[Col. 0689B] “With admirable endurance,” etc. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, chapter 5: Τὸ ἄλυπον καὶ ἀτάραχον εἰς αὐτὴν τελευταίαν διετήρησεν ἀναπνοήν, “He maintained cheerfulness and tranquillity of mind to his final breath.”

## CHAPTER XIV

“But Caesar.” A briefer and more obscure identification of the person; and learned men have already variously attempted to remedy this defect.—“But Maximian.” That is, “But Maximianus.” English translation.—“Galerius Maximian Caesar.” MAUCROIX.—“But Caesar, namely Galerius Maximianus.” Pagius, on the year of Christ 302, no. 6. Compare what we said above on chapter 9.

“He is not satisfied.” Elegantly and rhetorically, for “he was not satisfied”; the clearest indication of this is the following period: “He prepares to attack Diocletian by another means,” not “he prepared”; whereas otherwise one could scarcely refrain from emending the text. Yet the most learned translators have not badly rendered both places with past-tense words: “Galerius [Col. 0689C] Maximian Caesar was not satisfied with the severity of this edict. He devised, etc.” “But Maximian was not satisfied with the severity of this Edict, so he resolved.”

“The provisions of the edict.” In the edict of which our author speaks there were, if not various sections, at least various classes and heads of persecution to be instituted against Christians: namely, that persons of that religion should be deprived of every honor and rank; that they should be subjected to tortures, from whatever order or rank they came; and so on, among the matters recounted in the preceding passage. And now this author, in my judgment cleverly, calls these individual heads “the provisions of the edict.” The cited recent translations understood “the severity and harshness of the edict,” as is clear also from the concluding clause of the preceding note.

“He prepares to attack.” So chapter 36: “For he was preparing to do what he had done in the eastern regions”; and Terence, *Phormio*, prologue:

> He prepares to deter him by abuse, lest he write.

“That he might impel him toward the purpose of a most cruel persecution.” Must this be explained with the translators as meaning that he might force him to decree and resolve upon a most savage persecution? “So that this audacity might compel the emperor to swear the ruin of the Christians.” MAUCROIX. “That so he might engage him in an unrelenting persecution.” English translation. I should rather understand it as though our author had written quite plainly: “For Galerius Maximianus, in order to induce Diocletian to undertake the most cruel persecution which he himself had first proposed, etc.”

“He set fire to the palace through hidden agents.” I believe Lactantius wrote *occultis ministeriis* (“through secret instrumentalities”); this had also occurred to Nicolaus Heinsius. GRAEVIUS.—I judge that the punctuation should be made lighter after *ministris*: “through hidden agents, he set fire to the palace,” etc. GALE.—I too had considered it in this sense: he set fire to the palace through the agency of agents whom for this purpose he had concealed—that is, whom he had ordered carefully to hide themselves. Nor, I think, is there anything to prevent *occultis* [Col. 0690A] here from being as good a participle, meaning “concealed,” as it is commonly thought to be a noun formed from a participle.

“He set fire to the palace through hidden agents.” Eusebius, book VIII, chapter 6, confesses that he does not know by what accident it was started; Constantine, however, in the *Oration to the Assembly of the Saints*, chapter 25, says that the palace caught fire when struck by lightning. PAGIUS, on the year of Christ 302, no. 6.

“The Christians were accused.” As under Nero, when Rome was burned by him. TOLLIUS.—It would be preferable, I think, to refer this to Galerius Maximianus Caesar rather than to the uncertain report of the city of Nicomedia: namely, that Galerius, after some portion of the palace had once been burned, approached Diocletian in order effectively to impel him toward his intended most cruel persecution, and immediately denounced the Christians to his father-in-law as public enemies, proceeding with great vehemence, as we shall shortly hear, to say that “they had conspired with the eunuchs to destroy the emperors, and that two emperors had almost been burned alive in their own house.”

[Col. 0690B] “And with immense hostility,” etc. Delete the preposition. For Latin writers simply said *ardere invidia, ira, odio* (“to burn with envy, anger, hatred”). TOLLIUS.—The learned man’s observation is sound. Livy, for example: “When the senators burned with envy . . .”; and similarly Cicero to his brother Quintus: “The matter burns with hostility.” Yet I would rather make the preposition which Tollius wishes deleted into the temporal adverb *tum* (“then”): “And when some part had burned, the Christians were accused as public enemies; and then, with immense hostility, the name of Christians burned together with the palace.”

“They had conspired,” etc. According to the distinguished translators, these are the words of common report; but to me they are rather Galerius’s words, as we have already touched upon, and what follows will confirm it. The punctuation of the Abo edition is better: “They, after holding counsel with the eunuchs, had plotted to destroy the emperors,” and what follows.

“To destroy the emperors.” Namely, Diocletian Augustus and Galerius Maximianus Caesar. For at that time [Col. 0690C] Galerius was not merely staying at Nicomedia with Diocletian, but living with him in the same palace, as very many considerations show. In speaking thus, Galerius made the title *princeps* common to himself and his father-in-law, the Augustus; this was initially permitted by the usage of the age, in which Caesars were called *principes* no less than the Augusti themselves. We are also dealing with that Caesar who for some time had been unable to bear the designation Caesar; hence his question in chapter 9: “How long [shall I remain] Caesar?” There is therefore nothing surprising so far—unless it be surprising that there is talk here of destroying them at a point where mention is made of burning them, indeed of their almost having been burned. But this is easily resolved. In good authors, those who lose their lives, however they lose them—by illness, fire, or another cause—are said to be “extinguished.” Cicero, in the *Dream of Scipio*, chapter 3: “Yet I asked whether he himself and my father Paullus lived, and the others whom we believed extinct”; that is, dead. Livy, book VIII: “In another region of the world fortune extinguished the young Alexander the Great, undefeated in war, by disease.” Thus our emperors could likewise be “extinguished,” even by burning.

“Two emperors.” “Two Emperors.” English translation, without the article; its complete text is: “and that two emperors were well nigh burnt alive.”—“The two emperors.” Maucroix, with the article: “And that they had nearly burned the two emperors alive.” The addition of the article indicates, reader—whether you know it or wish it or not—that Diocletian and Galerius Maximianus were then both, under the Roman imperial arrangement, emperors or Augusti, and that no one else at that time possessed comparable power and title. But Galerius Maximianus was not yet properly Augustus, but Caesar, as the most learned Cuper points out. The two who then, under the later arrangement of the Empire, were the true and sole emperors were Diocletian and Maximian Herculius. The Parisian French translation is therefore wrong, [Col. 0691A] and the English, on the other hand, entirely correct. “But,” you say, “Galerius counts himself among the emperors: ‘two emperors had almost been burned alive in their own house.’” Correct: he does count himself among them. For the quoted words are not those of our Caecilius, nor of the Nicomedian populace, but truly of Galerius. Why, then, do you suppose he counted himself among them, unless because, ever since Narses’s defeat, he rejected the title Caesar—though he was Caesar—and wished to speak of himself as emperor? Compare what was said on the preceding page.

“In their own house.” That is, in the palace: both because of what we observed in chapter 3 concerning Domitian, said to have been killed “at home,” though all the best historians report that he was slain at Rome in the Palace; and especially because of the repeated interpretation of this expression found in this very chapter: once shortly before, in the words “the name of Christians burned together with the palace”; and again in these, “Finally, those who were in the palace . . .”—a most explicit explanation of *in their own house*. The translators render it more than literally: *dans leur propre maison*, “in their own house”; that is, in their actual private home.

“He always wished to be thought,” etc. Terence describes Chremes in this way in the *Self-Tormentor*; Menedemus mocks him on that account. TOLLIUS.—The more usual form of expression was: “who always wished to seem shrewd and intelligent.”

“He could suspect nothing.” “Yet he did not suspect this artifice at all.” MAUCROIX; as though one said: “he entertained not the slightest thought of Galerius’s treacherous deceit.”—“Could not be brought to give any credit to this.” English translation. That is, he could not be induced to give it any credence.

“He immediately ordered all his own people to be racked.” I should prefer, with Columbus: “He immediately began to rack all his own people.” See Baluzius for the reasons.—“All his own people.” That is, the entire household of his domestics; as is evident if you compare this passage with the words that shortly follow, and also with the beginning of chapter 15. For what does this first statement mean—“He ordered all his own people to be racked . . . while no one tortured Caesar’s household”—unless Diocletian’s household was racked, while Galerius’s household was tortured by no one? “All his own people,” therefore, are now Diocletian’s household. [Col. 0691C]—Then: “Therefore,” says our author at the beginning of chapter 15, “the emperor raged, now not merely against his own household, but against everyone; and he compelled first of all his daughter Valeria and his wife Prisca to be defiled by sacrifice.” From this it is now entirely clear not simply how many escaped that first slaughter of Diocletian’s, but who they were: all who were not properly among Diocletian’s household servants—such as his daughter Valeria, his wife Prisca, the judges, whom he will presently add, all alike, and everyone who was a *magister* in the palace. It is also plain that “all his own people” in our passage means nothing other than the whole household of Diocletian’s domestic servants, and those not of the rank of *magistri* but of a lower order. In this manner, too, the ancient word *familia*, strictly speaking, included slaves, but not likewise offspring or children.

“He sat himself down and roasted the innocent with fire.” “From his chair he watched these innocents being burned.” Maucroix.—That is, from his seat he watched the innocent being [Col. 0691D] roasted by fire. But, as the Latin reads and as what follows shows, Diocletian did not merely watch them being roasted: he himself roasted them.

“Finally, all the *magistri* who were in the palace.” “All those who had power of life and death.” Maucroix.—Literally, “all those who had the power of life and death.”—I do not approve. For that plainly confuses the *magistri* with the judges, who were mentioned earlier. Besides, if, as Maucroix implies, those *magistri* possessed by virtue of their office power over life and death, why was extraordinary authority given them to torture? For it immediately follows: “having been given authority, they tortured”—authority of the kind that they had not previously possessed, from which they were called *magistri*. I would therefore understand entirely that kind of *magistri* who, for example, are called by writers of the lower ages *masters of the chamberlains*, *masters of the doorkeepers*, *masters of the slaves*, and so forth. I admit that some difficulty may arise from the passage of Pollio quoted above: “When he went to the gardens bearing his name, all the Palace offices followed. The prefects went too, and the masters of all offices were in attendance.” For in those words one should not understand, for example, masters of the household of slaves dwelling in the emperor’s palace, but masters of all the palatine offices, that is, of those performing offices in the palace. Yet we believe the answer is either that the palatine offices themselves are included under the general name of the imperial household, and that our Caecilius therefore dealt with them too when, as what follows shows, he discusses the servants of Diocletian’s household; or rather that he distinguished servants of the lesser imperial household specifically from palatine officials. Pollio’s words will then not be contrary to him, since the former intended only masters of palatine offices, [Col. 0692A] while the latter only masters of Diocletian’s lesser household, who also lived in the palace. “All the Officers of his Household.” English translation. As though one said: “all the overseers of his household.” Compare Cuper above, [Col. 0692B] letter 1. Moreover, if one wishes, the whole passage can be punctuated more elegantly from the Abo edition as follows: “Likewise all the judges, finally all the *magistri* in the palace, having been granted authority, tortured.” Baluzius should be consulted on these final words in two places.

“They were competing to see who would discover something first.” That is, who would extract something from those being tortured as to who had been the author of the fire. But they heard nothing from anyone, because Caesar’s household was not being tortured—the household in which were those concealed agents through whose agency Galerius had applied firebrands to the palace, so that he might load the Christians with the odium of this crime. GRAEVIUS.

“They were competing,” for “they competed.” So chapter 15: “Their judgment in matters so great was not awaited,” for “was not being awaited.” And for a similar reason Vitruvius, book II, chapter 8: “As for brick walls, provided that they stand plumb, nothing is deducted.”

“Was discovered.” That is, in the sense in which something is said to be discovered when it is manifest and ascertained by us. Therefore no special distinction need be acknowledged here between the preceding verb *invenire* (“to find”) and *reperire* (“to discover”), such as learned men have sometimes rightly or wrongly established elsewhere between the two words. They are synonyms here; and our author used the latter only because he had used the former immediately before. Compare what we noted on chapter 7.

“While no one tortured Caesar’s household.” Namely, Caesar boasting that Christians were certainly and beyond doubt the source of the evil, and that none of them had ever been admitted or tolerated among his own servants, whereas, on the contrary, a great number of them had long been tolerated and then existed in Diocletian’s household. For we do not doubt that by “Caesar’s household” one must understand the servants of Galerius Caesar. Ulpian: “The designation *familia* includes slaves; that is, those in service, even if they are said to be free, or are in good faith serving us though belonging to another.” And in Terence’s *Self-Tormentor*, act IV, scene 3, Syrus says:

> Bring all Bacchis’s maidservants over here to your house quickly.

And Chremes in the following scene:

> To support that woman with that household?

[Col. 0692D] “Galerius’s house.” MAUCROIX. Literally, “Galerius’s home,” with “home,” as is clear, used for household servants; a usage not uncommon among us.—“Maximian’s family.” English translation: that is, Maximian’s household, with a different designation of the person, but not yet sufficiently precise, to say what the fact requires, since at that time not one Maximian alone was famous in the Roman Empire but two: one a Caesar, whom it would therefore have been expedient to call “Maximian Caesar,” for fuller distinction; the other an Augustus.

“He was present and pressed on.” “He was present at everything.” MAUCROIX, preserving the force of the imperfect tense and plainly suggesting that Maximian Caesar had already been present before. [Col. 0693A] “He came and stood by Diocletian.” English translation. Literally, “he came and stood beside Diocletian,” as if Galerius had only then arrived and had not been present earlier—contrary to what we have established in more than one place above. But we established it, among other reasons, from the natural character and meaning of both imperfects; and we see no reason to depart from it.

“To cause the anger of the thoughtless old man to burn itself out.” This is an exceedingly elegant translation. It is all the more pleasing here because the discussion concerns the burned palace and Diocletian’s anger thereby kindled. He calls him “thoughtless” because he had allowed Galerius to impose upon him so shamefully. TOLLIUS.—“To burn itself out,” in the sense in which the word sometimes means “to cool down,” as in these words of Philip, king of Macedon, sitting as judge between his two sons in Livy: “At times hope came over my mind that your anger might burn itself out and suspicions be cleared away.” “To be abated.” English translation in our passage. As though one said, “to be diminished, to decline,” which amounts to the same thing. Otherwise, certainly, as many passages in Cicero show, *deflagrare* means “to be utterly consumed by fire.” Phaethon “was consumed by a thunderbolt,” *On Duties*, book III. And against Antony: “He [kindled] the torches by which the house of Lucius Bellienus, having been set on fire, burned to the ground.”

“After fifteen days had intervened.” “A fortnight after.” English translation, using a distinctive idiom of the language: as though one said, after fourteen nights, or after the fourteenth night.

“Having contrived the fire.” So chapter 37: “While he was contriving these things,” and chapter 29: “he was planning flight.”

“But [or, ‘that’] was discovered more quickly.” The Abo edition has *id celerius animadversum* (“that was discovered more quickly”), Columbus’s emendation—or rather, according to the learned man, not doubtful—because *sed* (“but”) immediately preceded. But that reason is exceedingly weak. Our author likes this particle and repeatedly uses it in many places. Chapter 23: “But others were sent after others, as though they were going to find more. And it was always doubled for those who found nothing, but added whatever pleased them.” Chapter 25: “But he devised this: that he should name Severus, who was more mature in age, Augustus; [Col. 0693C] Constantine, however, not emperor, as he had been made, but Caesar, etc.” At the end of chapter 27 and at the beginning of the following chapter: “so that it should be called not the Roman Empire but the Dacian. After his flight, when the other Maximian had returned from Gaul, he held the empire jointly with his son. But the young man . . .” So elsewhere too.

“Then Caesar.” “And then Maximian.” English translation; that is, “then Maximianus.” See what was said above.

“Having prepared for departure in the middle of winter, he burst forth.” Yet chapter 11 says that Diocletian deliberated with Galerius throughout the whole winter; chapter 12, moreover, says that the persecution began toward the end of February; fifteen days afterward the palace burned, so Galerius could not have departed before nearly the end of March. Sparke, in the Oxford edition of 1684, and subsequently in the Cambridge edition derived from it.

The learned man’s difficulties are excellent, though not most serious; they are not new to me either, but you will seek their solution in vain in translations or other learned studies. Maucroix, for example: “Caesar, although it was the middle of winter, hastened his departure.” That is: “Caesar’s departure and journey were sudden and hasty, although it was midwinter.” Similarly the English translation: “Maximian, though it was in the midst of winter, left Nicomedia on the same day on which this second fire was raised, protesting, etc.” That is: “Although it was midwinter, Maximian left Nicomedia on the very day on which that second fire was kindled.” As you see, these tighten the proposed knots rather than untie them. The punctuation must be altered so that they disappear: “Then Caesar, having arranged his departure through the middle of winter, burst forth, declaring on the same day,” etc. The sense is: Then Caesar, who throughout the winter had secretly caused everything required for his departure to be prepared with most wicked intent, burst forth as though unexpectedly; and at the same time he wickedly gave this reason for his sudden exit—that he did not wish to be burned alive—although he had resolved to leave Nicomedia even before that fire. Add what was said on chapter 17.

## CHAPTER XV

“The emperor.” Namely, he who truly—indeed, preeminently, ἐξόχως—was emperor: in a word, Diocletian, as he was called by his own name in the preceding chapter. I would not mention this, had the phrase “two emperors had almost been burned alive in their own house” not also occurred there; that is, had Maximian Caesar not called himself emperor in those words as well. And this writer likewise says of Diocletian in chapter 11, “the emperor was not even then persuaded to give his assent,” although, according to him in chapter 7, Diocletian had already then made three men partners in his rule and one of them—namely Maximian Herculius—an emperor. But the latter was nevertheless only Diocletian’s subordinate. Compare the Bishop of Meaux at the beginning of chapter XIII of Revelation.

“Now not merely against his own household.” Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, chapter 6, confirms Lactantius’s statement that Diocletian raged against his household. PAGIUS, on the year 302, no. 8.

“But against all.” That is, against every class of persons or people, as the translators render it very well.—“He compelled his daughter Valeria and his wife Prisca to be defiled by sacrifice.” They were therefore Christians. Thus indeed the Acts of Saint Marcellus and the Passion of Saint Susanna, in which Diocletian’s wife is called Serena and his daughter Artemia. Perhaps they bore two names. Let scholars determine the matter. COLOMESIUS.—From Lactantius’s words we learn that both Diocletian’s wife Prisca, whose very name had been unknown to us, and his daughter Valeria, wife of Galerius Maximianus, were Christians . . . Eusebius had indicated this, indeed, in book VIII, chapter 1, but in more obscure words, mostly not understood by his translators. His words are: Τί δεῖ περὶ τῶν κατὰ τοὺς βασιλικοὺς λέγειν οἴκους, καὶ τῶν ἐπὶ πᾶσιν ἀρχόντῶν οἳ τοῖς οἰκείοις εἰς πρόσωπον ἐπὶ τῷ θεὶῳ παῤῥησιαζομένοις λόγῳ τε καὶ βίῳ, συνεχώρουν γαμεταῖς καὶ παισὶ καὶ οἰκέταις, μονονουχὶ καὶ ἐγκαυχάσθαι ἐπὶ τῇ [Col. 0694C] παῤῥησὶα τὴς πίστεως ἐπιτρέποντες: “What need is there to speak of those in the imperial households and of governors over all, who permitted their wives, children, and servants, openly and in word and life speaking boldly for the divine teaching, almost even allowing them to boast in the frankness of their faith?” PAGIUS, on the year 302, nos. 7 and 8.

“Valeria.” Valeria, daughter of Diocletian by his wife Prisca, was married to Galerius Maximianus in 292, when she was at least twelve years old. It is certain that she outlived Galerius, as the most learned Baluzius observed in his notes on Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 15 . . . Indeed, both Valeria and Prisca survived Maximian Augustus, who died in 313, as I shall demonstrate below from the same Lactantius, chapter 50. PAGIUS, on the year of Christ 294, nos. 2 and 3.—“Prisca.” Prisca married Diocletian before he became emperor, since Valeria, as has just been said, was married to Galerius Maximianus in 292, when she was at least twelve years old. That Prisca, her mother, was then alive is certainly inferred from this, that she survived long afterward and was only put to death in 313, after Licinius’s victory over Maximian. It is likewise certain that Diocletian had no wife other than Prisca throughout his reign, whatever Baronius, Henschenius, and Papebrochius may have alleged to the contrary from certain Acts of saints; for they had not seen Lactantius’s book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*. PAGIUS, on the year of Christ 294, no. 3.—“His daughter Valeria and his wife Prisca,” etc. What the distinguished Cuper observed regarding these two Augustae in chapter 1 is admirably illuminated by Lactantius, book V, chapter 13: “Since human beings can sin and be defiled, but cannot be turned away from God; for truth prevails by its own power.” What immediately follows there likewise sheds light upon this passage: “For herein too the wickedness of those men is convicted who imagine that they have utterly overthrown God’s religion if they have defiled people; since it is possible to make satisfaction to God, and no worshipper of God is so evil that, if given opportunity to appease God, he will not return—and indeed with greater devotion. For consciousness of sin and fear of punishment make one more religious; and faith restored by repentance is always much firmer.” Thus Valeria and Prisca seem to be counted among those doing penance, since Diocletian compelled them by force to place incense upon the altars. Very fine are the words our author immediately adds there: “If therefore they themselves, when they believe their gods angry with them, nevertheless believe that they can appease them with gifts, sacrifices, and incense, why then do they suppose our God so harsh, so unappeasable, that one who has unwillingly and under compulsion offered libation to their gods seems no longer able to be a Christian? Unless perhaps they think that those once defiled will change their minds, so that they will begin of their own accord to do what they did under torture.” See below concerning Maximian’s new policy, chapter 37. TOLLIUS.

Add Cuper’s letter, which you will find immediately before our notes.

“The eunuchs were killed.” Among them was Peter, who, ἀπρὶξ ἐχόμενος τῆς προθέσεως, ἐν αὐταῖς ταῖς βασάνοις νικηφόρος ἀπέδωκε τὴν ψυχήν, “clinging firmly to his purpose, victoriously gave up his soul amid the very tortures.” Oxford and Cambridge editions, from Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, chapter 6.

[Col. 0695B] “Through whom the palace itself had previously stood.” An obscure passage. ALLIX.—Indeed, if I judge rightly, corrupt; perhaps one should read: “through whom he himself had previously breathed together with the palace,” in the sense in which it is familiar among us to say: *Il ne respire que par lui*—literally, “he breathes only through him”—of a man who seems to live not through himself but through another, so great is his attachment to the other and, so to speak, the former’s being brought to life through the latter. For *conflare*, properly speaking, is “to breathe together.” An old glossary: *Conflare*, συμπνέειν. And Latin writers used *flare* for “to breathe,” “to draw breath,” and “to breathe out the soul carried on breath.” Plautus, *Mostellaria*:

> You there—if you wish to consider this saying,  
> It is not easy to breathe and swallow at once.

If this interpretation pleases, “palace” will stand for “palace people,” or persons belonging to Diocletian’s palace, just as ancient writers frequently use “town” for townspeople, “house” for household servants, “kingdom” for inhabitants of a kingdom, and similar terms.—“Whose counsels [Col. 0695C] had been so useful to him.” MAUCROIX.—That is, “whose counsels had been so useful to him.”—“By whose directions the whole affairs of the palace had been conducted before this edict.” English translation. As though one said: “By whose service and management all the palace’s affairs had been administered before that edict.”

“Presbyters and ministers were seized.” Our author mentions such a seizure above, in chapter 3, where he speaks of our Lord Jesus Christ being seized by the Jews in order that they might punish him: “He gathered the disciples whom fear of his seizure had put to flight.” Cicero, *Philippic* 2: “When the seizure of the guilty was mine, the punishment was the Senate’s.”—“Priests and ministers of the altar were arrested.” MAUCROIX. Literally, “presbyters and ministers of the altar were seized.” But our author makes no mention of an altar; and the distinguished canon might just as well have supplied “table,” had any supplement been necessary. Chrysostom, Homily 3 on the Epistle to the Ephesians: Πῶς ἔμεινας, καὶ οὐ μετέχεις τῆς τραπέζης; “How did you remain and yet not partake of the table?” Indeed, Basil the Great, Epistle 73, speaking of those who had some years earlier represented themselves as orthodox, said: “Ask them whether Basilides, companion of Ekdikios, is now orthodox; why, when returning from Dardania, they overturned his altars in the territory of the Gangrenes and set up their own tables.” Ἐρωτήσατε οὖν αὐτοὺς, εἰ ὀρθόδοξος νῦν Βασιλείδης, ὁ κοινωνικὸς Ἐκδικίου, διὰ τί ἀπὸ Δαρδανίας ἐπανιόντες, τὰ θυσιαστήρια ἐκεινοῦ ἐν τῇ χώρα τῶν Γαγγρηνῶν κατέστρεφον, καὶ ἑαυτῶν τράπεζας ἐτιθεσαν. And this would be as though the practice had prevailed in the fourth century that the sacred tables of heretics were called θυσιαστήρια, “altars,” while those of the orthodox were simply called τράπεζαι, “tables,” and *mensae*; though I do not wish this to be asserted on my authority. My sole point is that Maucroix had no reason to supply “altar” rather than “table” in our passage—indeed, no reason to supply either, since the ministers in question are indisputably deacons, and deacons are called by the Fathers sometimes ministers of the episcopate and Church, sometimes ministers [Col. 0696A] of God, sometimes ministers of Christ, and sometimes simply ministers, as will shortly appear.—“Presbyters and ministers.” “Presbyters and deacons.” English translation. That is, presbyters and deacons.—Entirely correct. See Du Cange’s *Glossary*, under *Minister*, where, among other examples, he offers this notable one from the poem of Commodianus entitled *To Ministers*:

> Deacons, ministers of Christ—  
> (that is, *diacones*, or, in more Latin form, *diaconi*)—  
> perform your ministry chastely;  
> therefore carry out the commands of the Master, ministers, etc.

“And they were condemned to confession without any proof.” “And without proof or confession.” MAUCROIX. That is, “without any proof or confession.” As is clear, this emendation occurred not only to that distinguished man but also to others.—“To confession.” Read “or confession.” It is known what “confessed defendants” are in law, and that no one is usually condemned without confession. TOLLIUS.—I emend: “or confession.” GALE.—With the good leave of these most learned men, I think the error lies elsewhere; and instead of *sine ulla probatione* (“without any proof”), I judge that one should read *sine ulla prolatione* (“without any postponement”), that is, without delay or ἀναβολή. Plautus, *The Braggart Soldier*:

> It is easy: three hundred excuses can be assembled:  
> “He is not at home; he went for a walk; he is asleep;  
> he is dressing; bathing; lunching; drinking; he is occupied;  
> there is no work; he cannot.”  
> However many postponements—provided only that now, by the first route,  
> we bring in . . .

On which passage Taubmann rightly says: “However many *prolationes*, postponements, ἀναβολαί.” Note also Cicero’s *prolatio rerum* in his letters to Atticus, for the suspension of business. But what then will it mean to be condemned “to confession” without any delay or postponement? The answer is easy. Presbyters, for example, when seized, were condemned as soon as they confessed that they were presbyters, with no intervening delay. This was to be “condemned to confession.” Nor is it a different mode of speaking when Christ says in Matthew 12:41 that the Ninevites repented εἰς τὸ κήρυγμα Ἰωνᾶ, [Col. 0696C] “at Jonah’s preaching.” Or perhaps you may prefer what we once considered, though it now pleases us less: “to be condemned to confession” is to be condemned to martyrdom, because, as Du Cange rightly observed and demonstrated with various authorities, “those who ended their lives in martyrdom for Christ, whom they openly confessed and testified to, were also formerly called confessors.” This is so true that, according to the episcopal ceremonial, book I, chapter 12, “the place which is usually under the principal altar in most churches, where the bodies of holy martyrs rest,” is called not only *martyrium* but also *confessio*: “which is called a martyrium, or confessio,” etc.

“With all their own.” We said above what we thought of a similar phrase. Here, however, its meaning is broader than before. There, to be sure, one was to understand not children or wives, but at most all household servants; here, as must be inferred from what follows, household servants and others besides—who can these be, if not wives and children?

Deducebantur (“they were led away”). Better, *ducebantur* (“they were led”), as often elsewhere. TOLLIUS.—Above all, the passage in chapter 51 supports this: “The women, therefore, were led to punishment with the immense spectacle and pity occasioned by so great a disaster.” For those of whom our author now speaks were likewise being led to punishment, as is clear from the immediately preceding words: “Persons of every sex and age were seized for burning.” Yet, since among sound authors one finds *deducere in carcerem* (“to lead into prison”), *deducere ad extremum casum* (“to lead to the final extremity”), and similar expressions, perhaps the ordinary reading need not be disturbed. Strictly speaking, if you prefer our former interpretation of the whole passage, *ad confessionem*, that is, “to martyrdom,” must be understood in common before either reading. Nor do the translators differ in sense: “They were made to pass through the hands of the executioners.” MAUCROIX. “Were condemned and executed.” English version. But today we believe that *deducebantur* itself [Col. 0697A] may properly be understood as “were led away to punishment.” See what was said on these words at the end of chapter 40, “thus situated among the wedges,” etc.

“Persons of every sex and age,” etc. This is, as regards the sequence of the narrative, a passage most difficult to understand, unless, just as learned men hold that in this clause of Revelation 18:13, *καὶ κτήνη, καὶ πρόβατα, καὶ ἵππων, καὶ ῥαιδῶν, καὶ σωμάτων, καὶ ψυχὰς ἀνθρώπων*—“and cattle, and sheep, and horses, and carriages, and bodies, and souls of human beings”—*anthrōpoi*, literally “human beings,” are distinguished from *sōmasi*, “bodies,” as persons of free condition from slaves, so here by “persons of every sex and age” we understand all persons of free condition belonging to the household of the presbyters and deacons whom our author had begun to mention, and thus each one as distinct from the household servants of whom he shortly afterward speaks. Thus, continuing the history of the persecution and explaining more precisely how presbyters and ministers were led to martyrdom with all their people, he says that “the presbyters and deacons, with their wives and children of every sex and age, were seized for burning” [Col. 0697B] “and burned in groups”; then, shortly afterward, that their servants, millstones having been tied about their necks, were drowned in the sea; next, that persecution also violently fell upon the remaining people of Nicomedia; and finally, that cruelty was likewise practiced in the provinces subject to the elder Maximian or to Constantius—whether against Christ’s servants or against their meeting places—no less than at Nicomedia, at the command of one and merely with the connivance of the other.

“And in groups,” etc. It seems one should read: “But the servants were surrounded in groups by a ring of fire, and, with millstones tied,” etc. Oxford and Cambridge editions.—Read rather, “but in groups”; and punctuate after *ambiebantur* (“they were surrounded”). Our author has something similar in Book V, chapter 11: “As one man in Phrygia who burned the entire people together with the meeting-house itself.” TOLLIUS.
