“And in groups.” I believe that *et* arose from *sed* (“but”), and that, in my judgment, the entire passage should be established thus: [Col. 0697C] “Nor were they [burned] singly, because the multitude was so great, but in groups they were surrounded by fire; the servants (with millstones tied about their necks) were drowned in the sea.” GALE.

“Servants.” “Their servants.” English version. Literally, “their slaves or servants”; this strongly confirms what we have just proposed, namely that the most learned man did not suppose that the emperor’s household servants were meant here. Yet he seems otherwise to have understood the servants not of the presbyters and deacons but of other people: “Some presbyters and deacons were seized … Persons of all ages and of both sexes were burnt … and their servants were cast into the sea.”

“With millstones tied about their necks, they were drowned in the sea.” This punishment, then, was not peculiar to Palestinians, as Jerome falsely maintained on Matthew 18:6, and Casaubon after him—at least as regards the manner of drowning (*katapontismos*); nor, as the learned man correctly showed from Polybius, was it regarded by the Greeks as among the most severe penalties. Jerome’s words are: “But when he said, ‘It is expedient for him that an ass’s millstone be hung about his neck,’ he speaks according to the custom of the province, in which this was among the ancient Jews the punishment for greater crimes: they were submerged in the deep with a stone tied on.” Casaubon’s passage is: “Matthew 18:6: *Καὶ καταποντισθῇ ἐν τῷ πελάγει* [‘and be drowned in the sea’]. What St Jerome notes, that a punishment peculiar to Palestinians, *katapontismos*, is intended here, ought not to be understood as though other nations did not employ this punishment, but should rather be referred to the manner of drowning indicated here. For that the Greeks used this kind of punishment against the most wicked persons is sufficiently clear from the Histories. Diodorus Siculus, Book XVI: *Ὁ δὲ Φίλιππος τὸν μὲν Ὀνόμαρχον ἐκρήμασε, τοὺς δὲ ἄλλους ὡς ἱεροσύλους κατεπόντισε* [‘Philip hanged Onomarchus, but drowned the others as temple-robbers’]. But the rationale and procedure differed from that among the Palestinians. For the Greeks did not tie a stone about the neck, but put the offender into a leaden vessel; as we learn from this passage of Athenaeus, Book XIV: *Πάτροκλος* [Col. 0698A] *οὖν ὁ τοῦ Πτολεμαίου στρατηγὸς ἐν Καύνῳ τῇ νήσῳ λαβὼν αὐτὸν, καὶ εἰς μολιβδίνην κεραμίδα ἐμβαλὼν, καὶ ἀναγαγὼν εἰς τὸ πέλαγος κατεπόντισε* [‘Patroclus, Ptolemy’s general, seized him on the island of Caunus, put him into a leaden jar, carried him out to sea, and drowned him’]. Moreover, Polybius, Book II, teaches that this punishment was not regarded as one of the severest: *Ἀλλ’ ὅμως τοιοῦτος ὢν οὐδενὸς ἔτυχε δεινοῦ, πλὴν τοῦ καταποντισθῆναι διὰ τῶν ἐν ταῖς Κεγχρεαῖς πεπραγμένων* [‘Yet, villain though he was, he suffered nothing dreadful except being drowned, because of what had occurred at Cenchreae’].” Thus even the Greeks, contrary to Jerome’s opinion, sometimes drowned their guilty persons with a stone tied about the neck, contrary to Casaubon’s belief.

“Upon the remaining people.” “In all other places.” English version. That is, “in all other places.”—I prefer to understand it of the remaining Christian people of Nicomedia.

“The prisons were full.” Namely, of those whom they had compelled to sacrifice; that is, those whom they saw had strongly refused and whom they had therefore recognized as most devoted adherents of the Christian faith.

“The prisons were full of wretches.” MAUCROIX. Literally: “The prisons were full of miserable persons.”

[Col. 0698B] “Lest anyone rashly,” etc. That is, lest justice be administered to anyone without his being identified and known. See here the Acts of Crispus in Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. III, p. 423. GALE.—By the edict mentioned by our author in chapter 13, it had among other things been provided that Christians could not bring actions for injury, adultery, or stolen property. Hence, I think, arose the expression now before us: “lest justice should be administered to anyone rashly”; that is, lest judges inadvertently hear and determine the case of some Christian. Maucroix agrees entirely: “For fear that, without thinking of it, justice might be rendered to them”; and the English version more obscurely: “And that no man might have the benefit of the Law that was not a Heathen.”

“In the *secretaria*.” “In judicial courts.” Oxford and Cambridge editions.—“In the very Courts of Justice.” English translation, in the same sense.—“In the registries.” MAUCROIX.—Incorrectly. For *secretaria* were properly places in which judges heard and sat in civil or criminal cases, [Col. 0698C] while there, among the litigants, some sat and others stood according to their rank or lowliness. The Code, Book III, title 24, law 3: “He shall also have permission to sit in some part of the *secretarium* which appears lower than the judges but higher than the litigants”; and final section: “They shall obtain the right of sitting, when an investigation of a criminal complaint is conducted in the *secretaria* of the judges.”

“So that litigants should first sacrifice, and then,” etc. Both the adverb of sequence *prius* (“first”) and the demands of clear sense entirely require that *ita* here be understood not in its common sense, “for that reason,” “in this way,” or the like, but as “then,” Greek *eita* or *epeita*. For what would it mean that litigants should first sacrifice and state their cases “thus,” by sacrificing? Could they, I ask, state their cases by sacrificing? And why insert *prius*, which, as already said, is an adverb of sequence, in this phrase, “an altar was set up, so that litigants should first sacrifice,” if they were to state their causes while sacrificing, rather than afterward? Clearly, therefore, the altar was set up so that litigants should first—that is, before everything else—offer incense or something else to false deities, and afterward, when the sacrifices had been completed, plead their cases. Nor is the usage otherwise at the end of chapter 47: “Thus he resumed his garment,” where *ita* means “then”: he dared, namely, to resume his purple garment. More explicitly in chapter 49: “But first he gorged himself with food and wine, as men do who believe that this is the last thing they will do. And thus he drank the poison”; that is, afterward or then he drank the poison. Add, by way of confirmation, Acts 28:14, which itself should be elucidated from these examples: *ἤλθομεν εἰς Ποτιόλους, οὗ εὑρόντες ἀδελφοὺς, παρεκλήθημεν ἐπ’ αὐτοῖς ἐπιμεῖναι ἡμέρας ἑπτά, καὶ οὕτως εἰς τὴν Ῥώμην ἤλθομεν*—“We came to Puteoli, where, having found brethren, we were asked to remain with them for seven days; and then we came to Rome”; not, as in the Vulgate, “And so we came to Rome,” unless one also assigns to “so” the force of “then.” Add [Col. 0699A] again this clause from 1 Corinthians 11:28: *δοκιμαζέτω δὲ ἄνθρωπος ἑαυτόν, καὶ οὕτως ἐκ τοῦ ἄρτου ἐσθιέτω*—“Let a person examine himself, and then eat of that bread.” Here likewise it should be translated in a new manner: “But let each person examine himself, and then eat of that bread.” Finally, not to bring forward more instances now, add also 1 Thessalonians 4:17: *Ἔπειτα ἡμεῖς οἱ ζῶντες, οἱ περιλειπόμενοι, ἅμα σὺν αὐτοῖς ἁρπαγησόμεθα ἐν νεφέλαις εἰς ἀπάντησιν τοῦ κυρίου εἰς ἀέρα, καὶ οὕτως πάντοτε σὺν κυρίῳ ἐσόμεθα.* If we wish to translate correctly, this means: “Then we who are alive, who remain, shall be caught up together with them in clouds to meet the Lord in the air; and afterward we shall always be with the Lord.” Such also is the force of the Ethiopic version.

“And now letters had been sent to Maximian and Constantius, that they should do the same.” It is therefore true that the edict was posted first in the imperial city, before the other cities of the empire, indeed first in the East before the West. PAGIUS, on the year of Christ 302, no. 7.—“To Maximian.” It would be surprising if our author, who shortly will call this same Maximian “the elder Maximian” for purposes of distinction [Col. 0699B], had not also here, in a much more suitable place, given him the title “elder” for the sake of a similar distinction—or rather “Herculius” or “Augustus.” Certainly no other Maximian is meant than he who was known by those names.—“To Maximian.” “To the other Emperor.” English version. That is, to the other emperor.

“It was not awaited.” That is, “it was not expected,” as was said above concerning a similar passage.

“Lest he should appear to dissent from the commands of his elders,” etc. This is stated briefly for “lest he should appear to dissent from the commands of his elders”; that is, from what the emperor Diocletian and Maximian, likewise Augustus—both elders of Constantius, who at that time was merely Caesar—ordered to be done in the provinces subject to them. For to understand instead what the same emperors, or Diocletian as emperor and Maximian as Caesar, might have ordered Constantius Caesar to do is contrary to sound reason. First, because nowhere do we read that Maximian Augustus instructed Constantius by letter to do the same as himself. Second, because Maximian Caesar was so far from being Constantius Caesar’s superior in the Roman empire at that time that, on the contrary, both being Caesars, they were equals. The translators avoided the difficulty: “As for Constantius, lest anyone should think that he did not approve the emperors’ decision.” MAUCROIX.—“But Constance, that he might not seem to dissent from those that were in rank above him.” English version.

“Meeting places.” The words *conventiculum* and *conventicula*, now most odious terms, the eminent Cange incautiously maintained were originally and properly applied to heretics; nevertheless, they sometimes also meant meeting places of civil or ecclesiastical assemblies of better standing, as here, or the assemblies themselves. Of civil gatherings, Cicero, *On His House*: “Since our ancestors wished that the urban plebs also should have meeting places and, as it were, certain councils.” The same, *For Sestius*: “Those who first excelled in virtue and outstanding counsel, recognizing the teachable character and capacity [Col. 0699D] of human nature, gathered scattered people into one place … then they enclosed with walls, under law both divine and human, the matters comprising common advantage, which we call public affairs; the gatherings of human beings, later called states; and their connected dwellings, which we call cities.” Of ecclesiastical gatherings, to cite no more, Lactantius, *Institutions*, Book V, chapter 11: “Some rushed headlong to kill the righteous, as one man in Phrygia who burned the whole people together with the meeting-house itself.” Maucroix’s rendering is therefore justified here: *quelques églises*, “some churches”; whereas the English is: “the houses where the Christians held their assemblies”—houses in which Christians held their gatherings.

“He allowed [them] to be pulled down.” Namely, by the populace or by the prefects. Hence Lactantius, chapter 24, speaking of Constantine now as Augustus: “Having assumed imperial power, Constantine Augustus did nothing before restoring Christians to their worship and to their God. This was his first enactment: the restoration of the holy religion.” For, as Dodwell correctly observes in Cyprianic Dissertation XI, “On the Scarcity of Martyrs,” no. 75, Constantine would have had nothing to do if nothing had been altered in the affairs of Christians by his father Constantius. Therefore what Lactantius writes is true: “Constantius, lest he should seem to dissent from the commands of his elders, allowed the meeting places—that is, the walls that could be restored—to be pulled down.” PAGIUS, on the year of Christ 302, nos. 7 and 8.

“But he preserved unharmed the true temple of God, which is in human beings.” He is therefore not to be counted among the most savage persecutors of the early Church, as the distinguished bishop of Meaux, Bossuet, did repeatedly not long ago, when, through the seven *kephalai* (“heads”) in Revelation 13 and the seven *basileis* (“kings”) in Revelation 17, he wrote that this group of Roman emperors should be understood as persecutors noteworthy for one reason or another: Diocletian, [Col. 0700B] Maximian Herculius, Constantius Chlorus, Galerius Maximian, Maxentius, son of the first Maximian, and Licinius. But let him hear himself refuted by the great critic and historian of his own party, under the name of Baronius.

“Baronius supposed that, while the persecution endured, Gaul overflowed with the blood of martyrs. Yet it seems certain that it had no place in those regions where Constantius ruled; for Lactantius expressly affirms this in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 15,” etc. PAGIUS, on the year of Christ 303, no. 7.—Add the same author there, no. 8, where he reconciles histories that protest the contrary.

## CHAPTER XVI

“The whole earth.” That is, all the provinces of the empire, as Maucroix correctly says. For in the fourth century the whole world in its entirety, from East to West and South to North, was not subject to the Augusti and Caesars, but only a large part of it. Therefore, even if the Gauls about to be excepted were included, nothing other than the entire Roman empire could be meant. We have touched upon similar hyperboles (*hyperbolai*) of this kind above in their appropriate places.

“Except Gaul.” How fortunate Gaul then was, good God, and how deserving of congratulations for that exception—not complete and absolute, indeed, but such as our author had before his eyes! For Constantius, as just related, “allowed the meeting places—that is, the walls which could be restored—to be pulled down; but preserved unharmed the true temple of God, which is in human beings.” Accordingly, such being the facts, Gaul did experience persecution so far as churches were concerned—because the populace raged, and Constantius did not prevent it—but none involving blood, because Constantius himself resisted it.

“But Eusebius, at the end of his book *On the Martyrs of Palestine*, learned men say, affirms that ‘all Italy and Sicily, indeed Gaul too, for the full first two years of the persecution endured *pólemon*, war’”—supply, “the war of persecutors.” I admit it. But Eusebius could easily have meant, as regards Gaul, no other war than that which for two years was waged there, without any command from Constantius and through the reckless license of the populace, solely against the walls of sacred buildings, not against persons. First, because assaults upon basilicas and inanimate temples are also wars, if we attend to this author’s or others’ mode of speaking. The Acts of the Martyrs Saturninus, Felix, and Others: “It was resolved, therefore, [Col. 0700D] … to address the cause of this war … For in the times of Diocletian and Maximian the devil declared war upon Christians in this manner: that he should demand the holy testaments of the Lord and the divine Scriptures to be burned, overthrow the Lord’s basilicas, and forbid sacred rites and most holy assemblies to be celebrated for the Lord.” And our author above, in chapter 12, recounting the first onset of the Diocletianic persecution, which was directed solely against the church at Nicomedia, says: “When that day dawned, suddenly … the prefect came with commanders, tribunes, and treasury officials; the doors having been torn down … the Scriptures found were burned, plunder was given to all … Then the praetorians came in battle formation,” etc.

Second, because in the *Book of Petitions*, which before our time the eminent Baluzius cited from Optatus, the Donatists emphatically assert: “Constantius exercised no persecution among the other emperors, and Gaul was free from this crime.” Finally, because Eusebius, who must be consistent with himself, praises Constantius in precisely these terms, as a ruler “who had nowhere taken part in the war stirred up against us Christians; who had kept the worshippers of the true God living under his rule free from every harm and molestation; lastly, who neither tore down the buildings of the churches nor undertook anything else against the faithful”: *τοῦτε καθ’ ἡμῶν πολέμου μηδαμῶς ἐπικοινωνήσας, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοὺς ὑπ’ αὐτὸν θεοσεβεῖς ἀβλαβεῖς, καὶ ἀνεπηρεάστους φυλάξας, καὶ μήτε τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν τοὺς οἴκους καθήλων μήθ’ ἕτερόν τι καθ’ ἡμῶν καινουργήσας.* He therefore merely allowed, to return deservedly to our author’s words, churches to be torn down; he himself undertook nothing concerning them or Christians.

I know how many histories of Gallic cities and provinces mentioned by Baluzius go in a wholly different direction. But I think few learned persons will judge them worthy of being heard in preference to this Author and Eusebius, who can be brought into agreement so conveniently both with himself and with our author. Consult now, if you wish, Dodwell, Cyprianic Dissertation XI, nos. 75 and 77, and Pagius on the year of Christ 303, nos. 7 and 8.—“And except Gaul, from the East,” etc. The better punctuation is that of the Abo edition: “and, except Gaul, from the East …”; or Gale’s: “and (except Gaul) from …”

“Three most cruel beasts.” The names of the persecutors meant by our author occur above in Baluzius. Here, moreover, are the reasons why ancient Christians believed themselves entitled to attack their persecutors of every rank with such reproaches. Lactantius, *Institutions*, or *On Justice*, Book V, chapter 11: “Therefore those persons, who conform to the character of their gods, because justice is burdensome and harsh, violently exercise against the righteous the same impiety they employ in other matters. Nor without reason are they called beasts by the prophets. Accordingly Marcus Tullius aptly says: ‘For if there is no one who would not prefer to die rather than be changed into some form of beast, even though he retained a human mind, how much more miserable is it to be savage in mind under a human form? To me it seems so by as much as mind is more excellent than body.’ Thus they despise the bodies of beasts, though they themselves are more savage; and they are pleased with themselves because they have been born human beings, though they bear nothing of humanity but its outline and outer form. For what Caucasus, what India, what Hyrcania ever reared beasts so monstrous and bloodthirsty? Since the rage of every wild animal lasts only until its belly is full, and, when hunger is satisfied, immediately subsides, that is the true beast at whose one command

> Dark blood is shed everywhere, everywhere cruel  
> Grief, everywhere fear, and manifold image of death.  

[Col. 0701D] No one can describe as it deserves the savagery of this great beast, which, lying in one place, nevertheless rages throughout the whole world with iron teeth; and it does not merely tear apart human limbs, but crushes their very bones and rages even against their ashes, lest any place for burial remain—as though those who confess God sought to have people come to their graves, rather than to attain God themselves. What savagery, what frenzy, what madness is this: to deny light to the living and earth to the dead? I say, therefore, that nothing is more miserable than those persons whom necessity has either found or made ministers of another’s fury, attendants upon an impious command. For that was not an honor or an advancement in rank, but a man’s condemnation to the slaughterhouse and God’s condemnation to eternal punishment.” Let those who, writing among us about that supposedly pious expedition of the Bimachians, appeal to the patience and moderation of the earliest Christians now say whether anything of this sort ever escaped any one of us.

[Col. 0702A] “Not to me,” etc. Restore confidently, with Gale and three editions:

> Not if I had a hundred tongues, a hundred mouths.

For it is a Virgilian verse from *Aeneid* VI, as Baluzius noted in the margin; but it has been mutilated through a copyist’s carelessness, or perhaps ignorance, since he did not know that a verse ought to stand here. In this example you have a most evident reason why those who read this author ought to attend not only to corrupt words that may be found in him, but also to omissions.

“I could recount every name of punishments which the judges inflicted.” Write *quas* (“which [they inflicted]”), not *quae*. For “to inflict the name of a punishment upon someone” cannot be good Latin, although the learned man just cited has close together *poenarum nomina* (“names of punishments”) and *poenas* (“punishments”). Sparke, Oxford edition of 1684, and the Cambridge edition derived from it.

“Against the prefect Flaccinus.” Of Bithynia. Oxford and Cambridge editions.

[Col. 0702B] “No small murderer.” This is *meiosis*, as Maucroix perceived very well; like “a man not altogether merciful” in chapter 15, concerning Maximian Herculius, whom Eutropius expressly reports to have been openly savage and inclined to every harshness and cruelty. Similar also is the passage in Matthew according to the Vulgate translator: “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means the least among the rulers of Judah.”

“Then against Hierocles,” etc. Lactantius, *Institutions*, Book V, chapter 2, is excellently illuminated by this passage, where the sharp-sighted bishop John Pearson, of blessed memory (*ho makaritēs*), saw that Hierocles was mentioned, though silently, in his most learned Prolegomena on Hierocles. COLOMESIUS.—But Baronius had noticed it before Pearson, as may be learned from Baluzius. This Hierocles, a pagan judge, wrote against Christians while God’s temple at Nicomedia was being overthrown, and governed Bithynia before the prefecture of Egypt, with which, as Valesius teaches in his notes on Eusebius, he was honored; see *On the Martyrs of Palestine*, [Col. 0702C] chapter 5. PAGIUS, on the year of Christ 302, nos. 9, 10, and 8, at the end.

“An author and adviser for carrying out the persecution.” *Persecutionem facere*, “to carry out persecution,” was an expression of those times, as can be established from Acts 8:1: “And on that day a great persecution took place in the Church,” and again from Lactantius’s words cited by Baluzius on this passage.

“For nine times he was subjected to tortures and various torments.” How only nine times during the entire tenure of the three governors mentioned, who succeeded one another?—Roman governors especially fixed as days for punishment those on which, according to custom, the most numerous assemblies of the whole province were expected. Among these were the days on which circus games and gladiatorial spectacles were to be given … If any persons had been condemned to beasts or to gladiatorial combat against one another, they certainly produced them at those very games. And that they could suffer on no days other than the days of the games themselves we infer from the letter of the Smyrnaeans on Polycarp’s martyrdom. The people of Smyrna asked the Asiarch Philip to let loose a lion upon Polycarp. Philip replied, *μὴ εἶναι ἐξὸν αὐτῷ, ἐπειδὴ ἐπληρώκει τὰ κυνηγέσια*—“that it was not permitted to him, since he had completed the beast-hunts.” … Since the cycles of public games could not recur very frequently, neither did the occasions of public punishments recur frequently. During the whole two years in which Eusebius reports Agapius kept in custody—from the second year of the persecution, that is, to the fourth—he was brought out of prison only three times and led in solemn procession with criminals into the stadium. And during the whole six years Donatus, though three governors succeeded one another—Flaccinus, Hierocles, and Priscillian—was nevertheless subjected only nine times, and no more often, to tortures and various torments. DODWELL, Cyprianic Dissertation XI, no. 89.

“Zabulus.” “The Devil.” Thus we find *Zacones* used for *Diacones* (“deacons”); indeed *Zeta*, if I remember correctly, occurs in Pliny the Younger for *Dieta*. Oxford and Cambridge editions.

[Col. 0703A] “You triumphed over the world with its terrors.” The received text has, “triumphing over those principalities in himself.” Aurelius Victor: “He twice defeated the Achaeans in battle and handed them over to Mummius to be triumphed over.” Finally Tertullian, though using a compound verb: “We never more thoroughly triumph over those demons than when we are condemned because of the steadfastness of our faith.”

“Yoking triumphant conquerors beneath your chariot.” This was suspect to Nicolaus Heinsius, now among the saints (*tō nyn en hagiois*), not only because one finds in Latin writers a horse yoked to a chariot, though the logic of Latin does not oppose yoking a chariot itself, but also because *subjugare* immediately follows: “For, conquered by your courage, they have been subdued.” The ingenious man therefore preferred: “yoking triumphant conquerors to your chariot.” For who does not know that Latin writers say *jungere* and *subjungere currui*, or *ad currum jumenta*—“to yoke animals to a chariot”? Virgil, *Eclogues* V:

> Daphnis began to yoke Armenian tigers to his chariot.

Instituted. [Col. 0703B] GRAEVIUS.

“When rulers rule.” I read, “when rulers are subdued” (*cum dominatores domitantur*). GALE.—The translators give the same sense and therefore a similar correction: “It is a true triumph to conquer the conquerors of nations.” MAUCROIX.—“This is true victory, when those who have conquered the world are subdued.” The bishop of Salisbury.

“By an impious command.” According to Cange, *jussio* denotes a command, especially that of a ruler. This is entirely true, as the examples adduced by that learned man establish, and we confirm it by these. Proconsul Anulinus to Saturninus: “You acted contrary to the command of the emperors and Caesars.” And Lactantius, *Institutions*, Book V, chapter 11: “That is the true beast, at whose one command:

> Dark blood is shed everywhere.”

The Greek Fathers use the corresponding term *keleusis* (“command”) in a similar matter: Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VII, chapter 11: *ἐκ τῆς κελεύσεως τῶν Σεβαστῶν ἡμῶν*—“by the command of our Augusti.” And just as our author here calls the imperial order of which he speaks an “impious command,” so elsewhere ancient Christians—lest more recent people be thought to lack examples from good men—called a spade a spade in such matters. The Acts of the Martyrs Saturninus and Others: “the army of the Lord God shuddered at the sacrilegious command.” Lactantius, in the passage just cited: “attendants upon an impious command.”

“By steadfast faith.” That is, firm faith, such as confessors and martyrs of old, for example, possessed in standing firm in faith. Cyprian, in his letter concerning Mappalicus: “This most blessed martyr now, and the others who shared the same struggle and were his companions, steadfast in faith,” etc. Shortly afterward he called such faithful persons *stantes* (“those standing”) in a single but notable word: “I likewise hope and exhort … that by your joy you may dry the tears of Mother Church, who laments the falls and deaths of very many; and that, by the prompting of your example, you may strengthen the constancy of the other *Stantes* [‘those standing’].” I would prefer *vestri* (“of you”) to *vestra* (“your”). Again in Letter VIII: “who are placed … amid the numerous slaughter of those languishing and the scanty number of those standing.” The expression, I believe, first arose from the idea of “very many who had fallen and had been prostrated,” to whom he thought it elegant to oppose “those standing”; then from the words of 1 Corinthians 16:13, *στήκετε ἐν τῇ πίστει*—“Stand firm in the faith”; and finally from the fact that in many places the Latin *stare* and Greek *stēkein* denote resistance to attackers.

“Mulciber stood for Troy; Apollo [stood] for Troy.” Paul in Galatians 5:1: *Τῇ ἐλευθερίᾳ οὖν ᾗ Χριστὸς ἡμᾶς ἠλευθέρωσε στήκετε*—“Stand firm, therefore, for the freedom by which Christ made us free.” For we believe this clause should be translated thus, rather than in the usual manner, “Stand firm, therefore, in the freedom,” and what follows.

“This is a soldier.” I would prefer “This is to be a soldier”; supply *est* (“it is”). [Col. 0704A] TOLLIUS.—I too had conjectured that it should be read thus, or at least, “This too is a soldier of Christ.” The received reading seems in comparison with either emendation insufficiently elegant and scarcely worthy of that polished work. Yet it may anciently have been written: “This is to be a disciple of God; this is to be a soldier of Christ.”

“Let no snare induce [you].” It seems preferable to read *induat* (“clothe [you]”). TOLLIUS.—I would prefer “let no rack induce [you]” (*nullus equuleus inducat*); that is, persuade you, or something of that sort. For there follows, “let no pain conquer [you], let no torture afflict [you],” with which the idea of the rack coheres excellently, whereas that of a snare does not. Cicero, *For Roscius*: “He induced someone by money, influence, hope, and promises”—that is, he persuaded or enticed him. And in the second *Philippic*: “I make no complaint of Dolabella, who was then driven, deceived, induced”—that is, persuaded. This emendation pleases us all the more because there is some ground for suspecting that it occurred also to the most learned Gale.

“He did not dare to contend with you further.” The monstrous courage of Christians usually broke the ferocity of persecutors, so that they did not dare to rage further … And just as Christians were elevated beyond measure by victory, so their adversaries, cast down by the hope of victory, abstained from all assault. Thus Lactantius says of his Donatus: “Finally, after those nine most glorious battles, in which Zabulus was conquered by you, he did not dare further to contend with you, having so often experienced that you could not be overcome,” etc. DODWELL, Cyprianic Dissertation XI, no. 92.

“To contend with you.” Thus above, on the preceding page, in Cyprian’s opening words: “This most blessed martyr now, and the others who shared the same struggle.” And elsewhere: “He himself—the Lord—wrestles in us, he himself contends, he himself in the contest of our struggle,” etc.

*Victrix corona.* “The victorious crown.” English translation. Literally, “the crown of victory,” with the sense expressed most clearly; likewise in the Acts of the Martyrs Saturninus the Presbyter, Felix, and others, “bearing the victorious palm in their passion”; and Cicero, in his letters to Atticus: “on the day when Cassius’ victorious dispatches were read in the senate.” [Col. 0704C] Finally Ambrose, Letter 29: “To this man you will entrust the victorious standards, to this man the labarum.”—But, lest we leave this point sooner than is proper: what crown did our Caecilius mean to have been prepared for his Donatus, after he had fought so many battles with the devil? A purple one, or a white one? For the most distinguished Beckius, discussing the memorials of holy martyrs and confessors in general, stated: “For these valiant soldiers and athletes of Christ a crown is prepared: for the martyr, indeed, a purple one of roses; but for the confessor, a white one of lilies, according to Cyprian, Letter VIII, and his commentator Rigaltus in the notes.” Yet, may that most learned man pardon what I am about to say: he does not seem ever to have read, or at least attended to, the letter of Cyprian which he cites. For in it Cyprian so far from making the white crown of which he speaks peculiar to confessors, so far from proposing it to confessors alone as something to be received specially for confession, first proposes it to be received for good works; then to each of the brethren, or members of the Church; lastly, as that by which “the Church was already at that time white, though it did not yet possess confessors or martyrs through Decius’ persecution, but only brethren distinguished by good works.” The Cyprianic passage in question is too illustrious—indeed, here too necessary—to be omitted, though somewhat long. It runs as follows:

“If the battle-line summons you, if the day of your contest arrives, serve as soldiers bravely, fight steadfastly, knowing that you fight under the eyes of the Lord who is present, and that through confession of his name you attain to his glory: he is not such as merely to look upon his servants; but he himself also wrestles in us, he himself contends, he himself both crowns and is crowned in the contest of our struggle. But if, before the day of your contest, peace should supervene through the Lord’s mercy, your will nevertheless remains entire [or, preferably, *may remain*], and your conscience glorious. Nor should any one of you be grieved as though inferior to those who before [Col. 0705A] you endured torments and, having conquered and trampled down the world, came to the Lord by a glorious path: the Lord is the searcher of kidneys and hearts; he sees hidden things through, and beholds what is concealed. His testimony alone suffices for earning God’s crown—he who is to judge. Therefore both conditions, dearest brethren, are alike lofty and illustrious. The one is safer: to hasten to the Lord through victory’s consummation; the other happier: having received leave after glory, to flourish in the Church amid praise. O our blessed Church, which the honour of divine condescension so illumines, which the glorious blood of martyrs adorns in our times! Formerly it was white in the works of the brethren; now it has become purple in the blood of martyrs. Its flowers lack neither lilies nor roses. Let each now strive for the most ample dignity of both honours, that they may receive crowns either white through good works or purple through suffering. In the heavenly camp both peace and battle-line have their flowers, by which Christ’s soldier is crowned for glory.”

Thus unsound is the division of heavenly crowns which the most distinguished Beckius wished to suggest and establish from Cyprian—into “purple crowns of roses prepared for martyrs, and white crowns of lilies to be received by confessors”—as though Cyprian had regarded those white crowns as being as proper and peculiar to “confessors, who, when questioned by the judge, confessed Christ, yet experienced neither prisons nor torments, much less the punishment of death itself,” as the purple crowns are to martyrs who shed blood for Christ. On the contrary, according to Cyprian’s meaning, not even the most valiant confessors have any claim to white crowns unless they shine through good works; and, again, any brethren whatever, provided they are eminently holy, have as much claim to white crowns as even the most glorious confessors who have not lacked good works.

*In praesenti.* What is meant—“in the present world,” or “at the present time”? Certainly the words *saeculo* (“world”) may have dropped out through the excessive haste of a copyist; and one must admit that a greater contrast appears between “the present world” and the kingdom of God, of which shortly afterward follows, “yet it is reserved entire for you in the kingdom of God,” than between “the present time” and that same kingdom of God. But because the Greeks often said concisely and elegantly ἐν τῷ παρόντι (*en tō paronti*, “in the present”) for ἐν τῷ παρόντι χρονῳ (*en tō paronti chronō*, “at the present time”), and the Latins likewise said *in praesenti* for *in praesenti tempore*, it will be better, I think, to recognize a similar expression here. Cicero, for example, to Caelius: “I have written this to you at present, so that you might hope to attain what you had wished for.”—“Though it was not given to you then.” English translation; as though the author’s words were: “though you did not receive it then, or at the time then present.”

“It is reserved entire for you in the kingdom of God, in proportion to your virtues and merits.” On the reservation of a similar crown there is a notable passage in Paul’s Second Epistle to Timothy 4:7–8: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will render to me on that day; and not to me only, but also to those who love his appearing.” But concerning the cause or reason which our author touches upon [Col. 0705D] for that reservation (“in proportion to your virtues and merits”), we shall speak at some point, God willing, in a separate dissertation, since the matter requires fuller treatment.

## CHAPTER XVII

“Having therefore perpetrated this crime.” That, namely, of which our author speaks in chapters 12, 15, and 17, or by which it came about that the whole earth was vexed. Those who know English may compare the translation of the Reverend Bishop of Salisbury: “Diocletian being now engaged into this wicked design, and having succeeded so well in the execution of it.”

“He immediately proceeded to Rome.” That is, in the year 303; PAGIUS, on that year, no. 2.

“The day of the *Vicennalia*.” The ceremonies to be performed at the beginning of the twentieth year of his reign; Diocletian joined to them, in order to make them more splendid, the triumph over the Persians which had hitherto been postponed. Baluzius calculates the chronology thus. [Col. 0706A] It is admitted by all that Diocletian began to reign at the end of 284, as Petavius has clearly proved; and it is evident from many passages of Lactantius that the persecution was set in motion in 303, so that it falls in the nineteenth year of Diocletian’s reign, as that most learned man discusses more fully immediately before the *Acta Vicennalia*. Oxford and Cambridge editions.

The *Vicennalia*, and festivals of that kind, were customarily celebrated on the anniversary of the accession. If it happened that they had to be either anticipated or postponed—which often occurred—a day of the same denomination as the anniversary on which the empire had been assumed was selected, or the festival was held on the anniversary of the colleague’s accession to imperial power. PAGIUS, on A.D. 284, no. 7.

The *Vicennalia*, as Maucroix observes in the margin of his translation, were a festival of many days for celebrating the twentieth year of Diocletian’s reign.

“Which was to fall on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December.” Hence the English translation of this passage states, and Baluzius defends, that Diocletian was made emperor on such a day—that is, according to our way of reckoning, 20 November—nineteen years earlier. [Col. 0706B] Pagius, however, takes a different view, as follows.—“Given the rule which we established in the first part of the Hypatian dissertation from Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 17—that the *Decennalia* and festivals of that sort were held either on the anniversary of the accession, or on the anniversary of colleagues, or at least on a day bearing the same designation as that upon which the anniversary of accession fell—it is established . . . that Diocletian, who was proclaimed emperor on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, therefore deferred the *Vicennalia* in 303 to the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, because in that year he had adorned Maximian Herculius with Caesarean imperial power on the same day; otherwise he would have held those solemnities, not on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, but on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October. Thus the exact anniversary of the Caesarean imperial accession of Maximian Herculius is now certain: I have shown that he was proclaimed Caesar on the twentieth day of November, or the twelfth day before the Kalends of December.” PAGIUS, on A.D. 284, no. 7, toward the end and beginning.—See also the same author on A.D. 298, no. 2; on A.D. 303, no. 2; and on A.D. 304, no. 12.

[Col. 0706C] “Since he could not endure the liberty of the Roman people.” Better, “because he could not endure liberty,” etc. Otherwise one might read *posset* (“could”) for *poterat* (“could”). TOLLIUS.—No: the reading of the old manuscript is sound; and here *cum* means “because,” as was already observed on chapter 9.

“He burst forth from the city.” Slightly differently above, at the end of chapter 14: “Then Caesar, having prepared for departure in midwinter, burst forth”; namely, it is used absolutely, much like Cicero’s expression in the Second Catilinarian: “He has gone, departed, escaped, burst forth.”

“To whom his ninth consulship was assigned.” This was done in 304: PAGIUS, on that year, no. 2.

“He advanced as consul at Ravenna.” Ravenna lay on the Adriatic Sea, and was formerly one of the foremost cities of Italy.

“He contracted a mild but lasting illness.” Let those more skilled determine whether Latins say *trahere morbum* (“to draw out an illness”) in the sense of “to fall ill.” For *trahere morbum* means to prolong or extend an illness so that it lasts longer, as one says *trahere bellum*, “to prolong a war,” *obsidionem*, “a siege,” or *iter*, “a journey.” I think a syllable has fallen out, and that Lactantius too, in accordance with the practice of correct writers, wrote [Col. 0706D] *morbum levem ac perpetuum contraxit*, “he contracted a mild and lasting illness.” GRAEVIUS.—“He drew out a mild but lasting illness.” Write: “he contracted a mild but lasting illness.” BOHERELLUS. TOLLIUS.—For *ac* (“and”), I read *at* (“but”). GALE.

“And he was distressed throughout the whole journey.” That is, by the illness mentioned immediately beforehand. This is the more likely because we have seen above that Tertullian employs the very term *vexatio* (“affliction”) for an illness, in these words: “like those who, having contracted an affliction in the more shameful parts of the body, avoid the attention of physicians.” This summary, not to omit the point, greatly supports the preceding alteration of *traxit* into *contraxit* made by learned men.

“Thus, after the summer had passed.” Namely, of A.D. 304. PAGIUS, on that year, no. 2.

“He came to Nicomedia by a circuit along the *striga* of the bank.” This passage is corrupt. Yet Baluzius, relying on I know not what authority, understands by *per ripam strigam* the shore of the Propontis. But to me, since conjecture is required, a more plausible remedy seems capable of being drawn from the fact that Strigonium, a city of Pannonia situated on the Danube where it flows toward the Black Sea, may, with a slight alteration of the corrupted passage, provide at least some cure. What especially favours this conjecture is that Diocletian came to Nicomedia not by a direct route but by a circuit. Therefore one should write *ripae Strigoniae*, “the bank of Strigonia,” until something else presents itself to which this conjecture must yield. SPARKIUS, Oxford edition, 1680.—“I had thought this passage corrupt. But now, better informed, I judge that nothing should be altered; since *striga* is a technical term of the surveyors (*gromatici*), and, according to them, what extends lengthwise is called a *striga*, while what extends in breadth is called a *scamnum*. In agricultural matters, according to Festus, it signifies a furrow made in a single drawing.” The same SPARKIUS, Oxford edition, 1684.—“Of the *striga* of the bank.” Namely, the bank of the Danube, on which Galerius says, in the following section, that he had struggled for fifteen years against barbarian peoples. For the use of the word *striga*, both in surveying and military terminology, see the learned dissertation of Dodwell, [Col. 0707B] printed at the end of the Oxford edition of Lactantius, 1684. The memory of this *ripa striga* seems today to survive in the name Strigonium, a city situated on the bank of the Danube. Cambridge edition.—“By a circuit along the *striga* of the bank.” That is, along the bank of the Danube, which was the ancient frontier of the empire, where were the Illyrian frontier-defences, called *strigae*, as Dodwell learnedly demonstrates in his separate dissertation *On the Ripa Striga*. PAGIUS, on A.D. 304, no. 2.—“Of the *striga* of the bank.” I read *ripae Istricae*, “of the Istrian bank,” whether one understands the river Ister or the Istrians at the Adriatic Gulf. For Diocletian, intending to travel from Ravenna to Nicomedia, ought to have embarked; but, being ill, he preferred, in order to avoid the inconveniences of navigation, to make a circuit through the Adriatic toward the Veneti and Istrians, or even to the bank of the Ister, that is, the Danube. BOHERELLUS.—“By a circuit along the *striga* of the bank.” I judge that Heinsius rightly emended this to *ripae Istricae*, meaning that he came through Illyricum, Pannonia, and Dacia to Constantinople, and then, after crossing the Bosporus, to Nicomedia. The *ripa Istrica*, [Col. 0707C] whence *Dacia Ripensis*. The term “circuit” indicates that he did not proceed directly to Nicomedia, but extended his journey by detours. GRAEVIUS.—For *strigae*, I prefer *Istricae*. GALE.—It should read: *Frigiae* [“of Phrygia”]. VOSSIUS.—Emend to *Phrygiae*. Oxford edition, 1680, p. 108, and perhaps thence the most distinguished author of the English translation: “Having come round the Coast of Phrygia.”

“As the illness had now grown severe.” Read: “as the illness was now growing more severe.” For it had previously been mild. TOLLIUS.—“It had been mild,” I admit; and the learned man’s emendation also seems considerably strengthened by two passages of Virgil, one in Book XII of the *Aeneid*:

> He, rising higher, hurled with trembling hand  
> the weapon snatched up against his foe.

The other is in Book XI:

> Then, rising higher, through the warrior’s arms  
> and through his bones, he drives the mighty axe  
> and redoubles the wound upon him as he prays and pleads much.

[Col. 0707D] Yet because of this third passage in the same book:

> But the wounded serpent twists its winding coils,  
> bristles with raised scales, and hisses from its mouth,  
> rising high,

the received reading may very well be retained. For, especially since in those Virgilian examples the true order of words is *insurgens altior*, “rising higher,” and *insurgens arduus*, “rising high,” so too in our passage the sense is not “a severe illness, and it rising,” but “an illness rising severely,” that is, one which, from being mild as it had been before, was becoming severe.

“Whichever way [or, wherever] he saw himself being pressed.” Here there is a corruption. ALLIX.—“Whichever way.” I read: *utcumque*, “however.” Oxford edition, 1680.—I read: *quo utcumque*, “wherever, in whatever way.” Oxford edition, 1684, and the Cambridge edition after it.—“Whichever way he.” Read: *quo cum se*, “when he found himself thereby.” COLOMESIUS.—Emend: *quo cum se*, or *quo utcumque se*; for *quo* must be retained. BOHERELLUS. GALE.—“Whichever way he saw himself being pressed.” This is worthless. Nicolaus Heinsius and Joannes Columbus long ago rightly saw that the reading should be: *quo utcumque se premi videret*, “wherever, in whatever way, he saw himself being pressed.” Or perhaps he wrote: *quo cum undique se premi*, “when he saw himself pressed on every side,” etc. GRAEVIUS.

“He was carried out.” Namely, in a litter into public. TOLLIUS.

“So that around [the circus],” etc. The ancient glosses: “*Circus* and *circuitus*; κύκλος ἐν ᾧ ἱπποδρομίαι γίνονται, ‘a circle in which horse-races are held’; ἱππικὸς τόπος, ‘an equestrian place.’” The same glosses elsewhere: “ἱππικὸς τόπος, *circus circensis*; ἱππικὸν, *circum*; ἱππόδρομος, *circus circensis*, *circus*; ἱπποδρομία, *circenses*.” Hence without doubt the English translation gives, for *Circo*, “the Mippodrome” [i.e. “Hippodrome”]. Yet in circuses, to mention this in passing, not horses only but boxers too were exercised, and many other spectacles were exhibited. Ovid, *Tristia*, Book IV, Elegy 9:

> The circus still lies idle, yet the fierce bull  
> scatters the sand and now strikes the ground with hostile hoof.

The same, *Fasti*, Book IV:

[Col. 0708B]

> When nearest Eos has looked upon victorious Rome  
> and the banished star has yielded its place to Phoebus,  
> the Circus will be renowned with procession and a host of gods.

And Onuphrius Panvinius, concerning, for example, the Circus Maximus at Rome: “That many types of spectacle were customarily held by the ancients in the Circus Maximus will be evident to anyone who investigates the commentaries of the ancient annals. As I considered and examined these matters more carefully from the same records, eight kinds presented themselves to me: the chief and proper one, the chariot or equestrian race; gymnastic or athletic contests; procession; the Game of Troy; hunts; cavalry and infantry battles; naval battles; and sometimes stage-plays.” Therefore, I think, Maucroix did better to retain the word *Circus* in his translation.

“In the year completed after the *Vicennalia*.” Therefore in A.D. 304, after the twelfth day before the Kalends of December; for, as we saw above, Diocletian celebrated the twentieth anniversary of his reign in A.D. 303 on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December. And to the point that he dedicated the circus in question not during the year of the *Vicennalia* while it was running, but after it had already elapsed, this observation of the most learned Pagius is sufficiently relevant: “Baths, temples, and other public works were customarily begun at the beginning of a five-year period and dedicated when it was completed, as is clear from many examples.”—“Completed.” I prefer “ended.” Tollius.

“Thus overcome by weakness.” Supply *est* (“he was”), from what precedes. BOHERELLUS.

“Through all the gods.” That is, supplicatory prayers were offered to the gods through all the temples. See Suetonius and Plutarch on Pompey’s illness, and likewise Velleius. Lactantius uses the same phrase in chapter 36: “And they offered sacrifices through all their gods daily”; that is, in all the temples. TOLLIUS.—To me also, in both passages, “through all the gods” has the same force as “through all the temples” in that passage of chapter 15: “Judges dispersed through all the temples.” It is a figure of the kind found in these verses of Martial:

[Col. 0708D]

> Why do you seek from Phoebus? Minerva’s chest has money;  
> she is wise, she alone lends to all the gods.

“Through all the gods,” as the great Gronovius observed, means the gifts of all the gods—wisdom, beauty, power, finally whatever things the other gods are said to give; and Minerva’s one chest *lends*, that is, confers or bestows, each of them. Thus now, and indeed with better right, all the gods are all the temples of the gods. The reason is that daily, in a similar fashion, we see innumerable names of saints used: for example, “Saint John” for the temple of Saint John; “Saint Mary” for the church of Saint Mary; and so for the rest. Indeed, in the writings of the ancients, Μαρίαμ Θεοτόκον (*Mariam Theotokon*, “Mary Mother of God”), and even in the New Testament, according to critics of the greatest renown, τὸν Δία (*ton Dia*, “the Zeus”) are used for the Church of Mary the Mother of God and the temple of Jupiter. Cyril, in his letter to the clergy and people of Alexandria: Ἴστε τοίνυν, ὅτι κατὰ τὴν ὀγδόην καὶ εἰκάδα τοῦ Παυνὶ μηνὸς, ἡ ἁγία σύνοδος γέγονεν [Col. 0709A] ἐν τῇ Ἐφέσῳ ἐν τῇ μεγάλη ἐκκλησίᾳ τῆς πόλεως, ἥτις καλεῖται Μαρία Θεοτόκος· “Know, therefore, that the holy Synod was held at Ephesus, in the great church of the city which is called Mary Mother of God, on the twenty-eighth day of the month Pauni.” Acts 14:13: Ὁ δὲ ἱερεὺς τοῦ Διὸς τοῦ ὄντος πρὸ τῆς πόλεως αὐτῶν, etc.: “But the priest of Zeus, whose [temple] was before their city,” etc. On these words see the critics mentioned below.

“That prayer might be made for his life.” This passage also shows that Scioppius wrongly criticized this manner of speaking, and it clears Phaedrus—a writer of the best, or nearly the best, age—of the charge of barbarism and vulgarity which he fastens upon him for saying: “They do not refuse the loss; they only pray for life.” Lactantius, moreover, has above been censured as a writer below the standard of his age. Why, Cicero himself speaks thus in his speech to the Quirites concerning his return: “Finally, he did not merely ask you, but even beseeched you, for my safety.”

“On the Ides of December.” Namely, of A.D. 304. PAGIUS, on that year, no. 2.

[Col. 0709B] “The agitation of the judges.” That is, “terror,” according to the interpreters. I prefer to understand it of those frequent movements and lesser comings and goings which are customarily seen outside a person’s bedchamber when someone is dying or has recently died, and when there is an interest in concealing his death. Compare what we said above on the native sense of *trepitare*.

“In the whole city,” etc. So Suetonius, in *Julius Caesar*, chapter 39: “He gave spectacles of various kinds: a gladiatorial show, and games also throughout the whole city by districts.”

“Until Caesar.” That is, by joining the supplements of the translations, as is fitting: “until Caesar Maximianus Galerius.” He was the Caesar for whose sake, as Diocletian’s son-in-law, it was more likely that Diocletian’s alleged death would be concealed.

“On the Kalends of March.” Namely, of A.D. 305. PAGIUS, on A.D. 304, no. 2.

“He appeared.” Thus in the following chapter, by a double contraction, *quaesisset* for *quaesivisset*, and *redisse* for *rediisse*.

[Col. 0709C] “Having been lulled by death, he had recovered his soul.” How can one who has been lulled by death recover his soul except by some divine power, like Lazarus? Either this word was wrongly inserted by some smatterer who did not know the force of *sopire* (“to lull”), or one should read: *pro mortuo sopitus*, “lulled as though dead”; that is, he was merely unconscious, as if he were dead; when he was accounted dead, he was merely unconscious. *Pro mortuo*, “as though dead,” as in Caesar, *nihil pro sano loqui*, “to say nothing as a sane man.” In Justin, “Victor seemed to flee as though defeated.” Those are called *sopiti* who, through a fainting of the mind, also temporarily lose bodily sensation, so that they lie as though dead. Livy, Book I: “Tanaquil addresses the people; she commands them to be of good courage; the king had been stunned by a sudden blow; the iron had not penetrated deeply into his body; he had now returned to himself.” This passage is nearly identical with Lactantius’. Tarquinius is said to have been stunned by a blow; Diocletian was rendered unconscious by the force of illness. The former was said to have “returned to himself”; the latter truly “recovered his soul,” which is the same as “he returned to himself.” Livy again, Book XLII: “First the friends, then the guards and servants, rushed to the king’s body, raising him up, [Col. 0709D] unconscious from the wound and sensing nothing. Yet they perceived that he lived, from warmth and breath remaining in his breast; there was slight, indeed almost no, hope that he would survive.” Those lulled by sleep, a wound, or illness awaken and return to themselves; those lulled by death sleep that iron sleep from which they are never awakened in this world. GRAEVIUS.

“Lulled by death,” etc. Although the Vulgate, Judges 4:21, not inelegantly joins sleep with death in these words, “He [Sisera], joining sleep to death, fainted and died,” yet I am certain that the double emendation of this passage was deservedly proposed by my most learned colleague. But what if, meanwhile, we read somewhat nearer the old text: “And he, on the Ides of December, having been lulled for death, had recovered his soul”? That is, he had been rendered unconscious as one who seemed about to become the prey of death. Certainly the expressions *debiti morti*, “owing to death,” Wisdom 12:20—“For if you punished with such care the enemies of your servants, [Col. 0710A] who were owing to death”—and the following verses of the *Aeneid* favour our suspicion:

> Many bodies of cattle are slaughtered round about for death.  
> (*Aeneid* XI)

> He himself does not deign to lay his adversaries low for death.  
> (*Aeneid* XII)

For what difference can there be, whether in syntax or indeed in sense, between “to be laid low for death,” or “to lay low for death,” “to be slaughtered for death,” and “to be lulled for death”? Add other expressions of the Vulgate translator in which persons may be seen now destined for death, now bearing fruit for death, and others of this sort.

“Yet not the whole [mind].” This is elegant and witty. Thus people are said to be diminished in mind and spirit when illness has taken away their entire use thereof. See Suetonius on Claudius. TOLLIUS.

“For he became mad.” Διὰ τὴν τῆς ἀφροσύνης βλάβην, μιᾶς εὐκαταφρονήτου οἰκήσεως καθειργμῷ ἐτιμωρήθη: “Because of the injury of his folly, he was punished by confinement in a single contemptible dwelling.” Constantine, *Oration to the Assembly of the Saints*, chapter 25.

## CHAPTER XVIII

[Col. 0710B] “Caesar.” Namely, Galerius Maximianus. PAGIUS. Likewise the English translation.

“Not that he might congratulate his father.” That is, as Maucroix very well renders it, not that he might congratulate his father-in-law on the restoration of his health. For Diocletian was only the father-in-law of Galerius Maximianus, whom Diocletian had taken as his son-in-law, as our author stated above in chapter 9. Hence the same author shortly afterward: “His father-in-law too feared him most intensely.” Thus this passage, in which one who was merely a father-in-law is called “father” in historical narration, may conveniently be applied to resolving various difficulties of Sacred Scripture, which we shall discuss elsewhere in a formal treatment, God willing.

“He had lately come into conflict with Maximian,” etc. Undoubtedly one must read, “with Maximian.” Nor should one suppose that Lactantius, according to the character of his age, spoke so barbarously. TOLLIUS.—If, as I think, the first hand wrote “he had lately contended something against old Maximian,” it was an elegance of Latin borrowed from Greek. For Greeks frequently said, among other expressions, ἀμφισβητεῖν τινί (*amphisbētein tini*), literally, “to contend something with someone,” for “to contend with someone about something.” Thus in Propertius, Book I, Elegy 13:

> Yet let not these things contend against my love,

for “contend with my love”; precisely as Ovid in the *Metamorphoses*:

> . . . Antigone, who once dared to contend  
> with the consort of great Jupiter.

“And he had intimidated him by instilling fear of civil wars.” By a similar fear, as we heard above from Aurelius Victor, many formerly wished Diocletian too to have laid down imperial power. Indeed, this explicit judgment of Aurelius Victor—“Valerius Diocletianus, a scrutinizer of coming events, when he learned that internal calamities and, as it were, some crash of the Roman state were impending by fate, celebrated the twentieth year of his reign and, being the stronger man, cast off the care of the commonwealth”—is not lightly confirmed by what our author narrates here and below. [Col. 0710D] Theodorus Metochites, in the almost final book of his Roman history, supplies another reason for the abdication of the two Augusti, but one plainly not very plausible.

“Saying that he was already an old man, already less vigorous, and incapable of administering the commonwealth.” Saturninus in Vopiscus: “Add that every age is censured in imperial power. Is someone old? He seems incapable,” etc. We have stated above the other points to be noted here.

“He put forward the example of Nerva, who had transferred the empire to Trajan.” Learned men entirely agree that Nerva transferred imperial power to Trajan. But whether Nerva did this by wholly abdicating himself, or merely by sharing the imperial power with Trajan, the highly learned Dodwell, Pagius, and others do not agree in the same manner. “He abdicated when he made Trajan *autokrator*,” says Dodwell in the appendix to the Cyprianic dissertations, no. 40; and the most distinguished translators render the passage thus: [Col. 0711A] “He cited for him the example of Nerva, who relieved himself of the empire in favour of Trajan.” MAUCROIX.—“He set before him Nerva’s example, who resigned the Empire to Trajan.” English translation. On the other hand, Pagius says, on A.D. 97, no. 3, that he did not abdicate. Indeed, it is evident from Pliny that Nerva did not abdicate, and everything Victor wrote about Nerva is monstrous; and Lactantius did not say that Nerva laid down the empire, Pagius continues, nos. 4 and 5—although, remarkably, Victor expressly wrote in *The Caesars*: “When Nerva saw that the empire could not be administered except by men younger and stronger in body and mind, in the sixteenth month he abdicated himself from it”; and our author likewise in this chapter: “He at the same time put forward the example of Nerva, who had transferred the empire to Trajan.” “But he said . . . that Nerva . . . since he could not bear the weight and care of such great affairs, whether through age or inexperience, had cast away the helm of the commonwealth and returned to private life, in which he had grown old.”

It seems to me that this controversy cannot be better settled than by carefully distinguishing, on the one hand, the empire—that is, the very administration of the commonwealth—from the title of Augustus, the guards of the imperial person, the emperors’ occupancy of palaces, and similar things; and, on the other, by maintaining that Nerva abdicated and did not abdicate in different senses. That is, he abdicated so far as concerned government of the commonwealth, committing its whole helm to Trajan and returning so far to private life; and in this sense the cited words of Victor apply: “he abdicated himself from it.” But he did not abdicate as regards the emperor’s title, because he retained it even after the aforesaid laying down of imperial power; and this among other matters is indicated by the passage in Pliny’s panegyric: “You seemed a private man, Trajan, so long as another was emperor”—namely, Nerva, still bearing the emperor’s title. Nor did he abdicate in respect of the imperial mode of life, because he continued after that same adoption of Trajan to imperial power to enjoy it, living, for example, with Trajan in the palaces of the Augusti; as is indicated by the words of the other Victor in the *Epitome*: “Nerva adopted Trajan in the place of a son and into a share of imperial power; with him he lived for scarcely three months.”

[Col. 0711C] But perhaps the most distinguished Pagius will object: if Nerva adopted Trajan only into a share of the empire, how can Nerva be said to have abdicated from the whole empire—that is, from the entire government of the commonwealth? Because, I reply, he did not wish, for example, to be stripped of the purple or to lose the title of emperor; therefore, when Trajan’s adoption was under consideration, he declared that Trajan was being adopted by him only into a share of imperial power, even though he had afterward resolved to lay the entire weight of the commonwealth upon Trajan’s shoulders and in fact did so after the adoption. In this respect, then, he differed from Diocletian: he did not lay down everything simultaneously and at once, as Diocletian subsequently did—namely, the administration of the empire, purple, imperial title, palaces, and the rest of that kind—but only imperial cares and anxieties, retaining the honours.

Indeed, that Diocletian permanently took leave, from the very first day of his abdication, of the emperors’ purple, palaces, and other such prerogatives is attested first by our author in chapter 19: “Diocletian cast upon him his own purple, which he stripped off, and became Diocles again”; then by Eutropius, Book IX, at the end: “Diocletian, as a private man, grew old in distinguished leisure at a villa not far from Salonae; employing the unprecedented virtue of being the only man, after the founding of the Roman Empire, voluntarily to return from so great a height to the state and civil condition of private life. It therefore happened to him, as to no one after the birth of humankind, that, though he died a private man, he was nevertheless enrolled among the gods.” Nerva too was certainly enrolled among the gods, as is evident even from Pliny’s panegyric alone. But since Nerva had died with the title and status of emperor, and was not similarly a private man, Eutropius says: “It happened to Diocletian, as to no one after the birth of humankind, that, though he died a private man, he was nevertheless enrolled among the gods.” Hence all that we have said thus far concerning this distinction—that Nerva abdicated and did not abdicate in different senses—is most strongly confirmed. But we shall return to these matters below. Either the passages of writers must be reconciled in this way, as you aptly do, or one must admit that their opinions differ so that one or the other is mistaken. GRAEVIUS.

[Col. 0712A] “But he said,” etc. Namely, Diocletian. PAGIUS, on A.D. 297, no. 3. Likewise the translators.

“He said to him that it was unbecoming.” Am I mistaken, or had our author rather written: “he said, and that it would be unbecoming”? Thus Columbus had already partly corrected it before us.

“Of lofty eminence.” There is a notable passage on the eminence of princes and kings in Suetonius, *Caligula*, chapter 22: “He was not far from immediately assuming the diadem and converting the appearance of a principate into the form of a monarchy. But, warned that he had surpassed the eminence of both princes and kings, he began from then on to claim divine majesty for himself.” There, “he had surpassed the eminence of princes and kings” means that he had been raised above that highest dignity of kings. So also in Curtius, “you surpass human eminence” means “you have been raised above that supreme summit of human dignity”; and in Livy, “they are citizens of the same eminence” means that they are established in the same high dignity. Thus *fastigium* in these contexts means dignity, ἐξοχή (*exochē*, “eminence”), ὑπεροχή (*hyperochē*, “superiority”), and similar terms. Trebellius Pollio, in the passage we cited earlier, called the supreme authority and lofty eminence of Roman emperors “the greatest summit on earth,” using a similar expression. Our author above mentions Decius as advanced to the principal—that is, Augustan—eminence; and shortly afterward, in this chapter, he will mention Constantine as most worthy of Caesarean eminence. From such eminences derive the two *fastigatissimi consulares* in Sidonius, Book I, Letter 9, as though “most eminently exalted,” that is, according to Cange’s excellent interpretation, raised to the highest eminences of dignities; and *fastigatissima felicitas* in the same Sidonius, Book II, Letter 4, for “supreme happiness.”

“That it was less safe,” etc. The plans and examples of Sulla and Augustus are not obscure. See also below, at the end of chapter 20. TOLLIUS.—Although, as here, it has more often been dangerous to lay aside the purple, sometimes it was nevertheless less safe not to assume it. Flavius Vopiscus on Saturninus: “When he began to think that it was not safe for him to live as a private man, having laid aside the purple, he was clothed and adored by the soldiers surrounding him in a wife’s robe taken from the statue of Venus.” Here *deposita* means “removed” and “taken off.”

[Col. 0712C] “In so long a reign.” Namely, one of twenty years and more.

“Had acquired.” That is, had gained for himself. The simple verb for the compound; as is certain even from the fact that no one voluntarily attracts the hatred of many people to himself, but always endures it unwillingly. Compare what we said above on chapter I.

Nerva, however, having reigned for one year. That Nerva reigned for more than one year, whichever calculation of the two Victors one follows, is beyond doubt. For, according to the younger Victor in the *Epitome*, Nerva reigned thirteen months and ten days. The elder Victor, moreover, says in *On the Caesars*, as indeed the printed and manuscript codices have long transmitted it: “What man was more prudent or more moderate than Nerva of Crete? [Col. 0712D] When, in extreme old age, among the Sequani . . . he had assumed the empire at the discretion of the legions, and saw that it could not be administered except by men stronger and more vigorous in body and spirit, in the sixteenth month he abdicated it.” But, to avoid prolixity, Victor had originally written in the latter passage: “Nerva abdicated it in the fourteenth month.” A copyist, however, transposed the numerical sign and wrote “in the sixteenth month”; and subsequently, when the numerical signs had in the course of time been omitted, it was written “in the sixth and tenth month.” This, in so many words, was recently pointed out by the most learned Pagi, who most happily reconciles the two Victors in this manner. And further, although Nerva, according to either passage in the Victors, reigned at least thirteen months and ten days, Diocletian could nevertheless, in order the more effectively to refute his own son-in-law, make mention of only one year, rounding the number. Besides, since the passage in which we are now engaged is manifestly corrupt, nothing prevents the author’s [Col. 0713A] original reading from having been: “Nerva reigned only about one year, and, when the burden,” etc.

Nerva, however, reigning for one year. I read: “Nerva, however, reigning for one year.” The letter *m* has often been omitted. BOHERELLUS.—“Nerva . . . reigning.” Those are right who prefer “Nerva reigning.” TOLLIUS.—For my part, I should prefer, if no greater alteration is required: “Nerva, however, reigned for one year,” etc. . . .

Could. For which one finds *cuiret* in Lucretius in some places, with *c*, and made trisyllabic for metrical reasons.

To have cast aside the helm of the commonwealth. That is, with respect to the care and bearing of the weight of such great affairs, of which our author spoke immediately before; not, however, with respect to the title and position of ruler, as we have explained above.

To have returned to private life. Inasmuch as he no longer administered the commonwealth. Otherwise, indeed, he was not rendered private by such a laying aside of cares to the extent that he died as a private person; rather, he died emperor, as we have shown from Victor’s *Epitome*.

[Col. 0713B] If he desired to attain the name of Emperor. Galerius Maximianus, therefore, had not yet attained this title, as we have inferred and established at length above.

That they should be called Augusti. Why should it not rather be, “that they should be called emperors”? For the discourse seemed to be proceeding in no other direction: “But if he desired to attain the name of Emperor, there was nothing to prevent all from being called Emperors.” Maucroix replies in two words in the margin of his edition that Augustus and Emperor are the same thing; moreover, for this reason, that eminent man translates τὸ “if he desired to attain the name of emperor,” etc., as though the author’s words were “if he desired to attain the name of Augustus”; and similarly, in the English translation, τὸ “that all should be called Augusti,” as though our author had written “that all should be called emperors.” It cannot be denied that in the Code six hundred prefaces of this kind precede laws: “The Emperors Diocletian and Maximian, Augusti”; “The Emperors Carus, Carinus, and Numerian, three Augusti”; “Emperor Constantine Augustus.” Yet the very fact that in those prefaces [Col. 0713C] or inscriptions Diocletian, for example, and Maximian were called not merely emperors, but first emperors and then, as a title of honour, Augusti, is to me a most weighty argument that this author once wrote: “But if he desired to attain the name of Emperor, there was nothing to prevent all from being called both Augusti,” as though Diocletian had said: “Not only does nothing on my part prevent the title of Emperor from being given even to Caesars; nothing also prevents those same men from being called Augusti.”

He had already longed for it. I prefer: “He had already longed for it in hope.” GALE.—On conjecture the learned men have here printed *inhiaverat* (“had longed for”), while testifying that the manuscript read: “He himself had already found”; from which one would not depart very far if one wrote: “He had already seized upon it in hope.” I am fully persuaded that Lactantius wrote *spe* (“in hope”) for *ipse* (“he himself”), as Columbus observed. For writers regularly say that one seeks or seizes imperial power in hope. What *ipse* can mean here, no one can say. It is entirely pointless. GRAEVIUS.—The reading should be: “He had already seized upon it in hope.” Vossius, and, following his indication, the Oxford edition of 1680, p. 108, among the later corrections. I confess that I would prefer, partly on the authority of the old reading and partly because the sense seems more suitable: “He had already found it in hope.” For Galerius was being offered the bare attainment of the imperial title: “But if he desired to attain the name of Emperor,” etc.; whereas he had already, in hope, found the whole world—that is, he already hoped that he had found the empire of the whole world, or, if one prefers, a way by which he might become master of the whole world. Thus at the beginning of chapter 20: “Maximian, after expelling the old men, had accomplished what he wished and claimed that he was now almost sole lord of the whole world. For he despised Constantius, though he had necessarily to be named first, because he was mild by nature and hindered by bodily infirmity. He hoped that he would shortly die; and, if he did not die, it seemed easy to strip him even against his will.”

Since he saw that from it there would accrue to him either nothing but the name, or much, [Col. 0714A] etc. The sense requires that one read: “or not much.” The Oxford and Cambridge editions.—Thus also Tollius and Allix. Vossius, according to Colomesius: “Since he saw that either nothing, or not much beyond the name, accrued to him from it.” Finally Gale, as one may partly see with one’s eyes and partly infer in one’s mind: “Since he saw that nothing but the name and disturbance accrued to him from it,” and what follows. I judge the first correction, being the simplest of all, preferable to the others—unless one should rather read: “since from it either nothing but the name, or not much, accrued to him . . .”

Saw. Read: “should see.” TOLLIUS.—On the contrary, “saw” stands well enough, as has just been said.

His own arrangement, etc. That is, his own plan for governing the commonwealth. Oxford and Cambridge editions.

That there might be two greater men in the commonwealth. That is, as the English translation puts it plainly, two emperors, who were also Augusti; Gale wished, moreover, that “greater” should be written with a capital M.

Likewise two lesser men. That is, as Maucroix now puts it without circumlocution, two Caesars; the learned man adding in the margin, if not in Spartianus’ very words, at least in accordance with his sense in *Aelius Verus*: “Caesars were designated as heirs of Augustan majesty.” “The Caesars were the presumptive heirs of the empire”; a point he had also noted earlier at chapter 9.

Between two. Supply from what follows, “equals”: “That harmony could easily be maintained between two equals”; this must be understood of two emperors properly equal. For Diocletian had proposed to Galerius that in future there should be four equal Augusti; Galerius, however, was arguing against his father-in-law on that matter.

That he might no longer be the lesser and last. That is, as the preceding words show, not merely that he might no longer be the lesser and last among the lesser men, but that he might no longer be Caesar and the last of the Caesars. For he was one not among the greater men, who were emperors, but among the lesser, who were Caesars; and even among these he was not first, but second—and thus fourth among those whom the Roman world at that time saw established at the summit of sovereign rank. [Col. 0714C] Do you want a most authoritative witness? Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, chapter 5, mentioning the edict posted at Nicomedia by command of Diocletian Augustus but at the instigation of Galerius Caesar, says: “As soon as the edict against the churches had been posted, a certain man of no obscure station . . . tore that edict, as impious and criminal, apart with his own hands.” Δυοῖν ἐπιπαρόντων κατὰ τὴν αὐτὴν πόλιν βασιλέων, τοῦ τε πρεσβυτάτου τῶν ἄλλων, καὶ τοῦ τὸν τέταρτον ἀπὸ τούτου τῆς ἀρχῆς ἐπικρατοῦντος βαθμὸν: that is, “while two emperors were residing in the same city, one of whom was senior in comparison with the others,” namely Diocletian, “while the other held the fourth rank of authority after him,” namely Galerius.

That fifteen years had already passed in Illyricum or at the riverbank, etc. This is Baluze’s correction in his second edition. For the reading of the old codex, as that eminent man observed, is: “That fifteen years had already passed Illyricum or at the riverbank . . .” It was therefore rightly printed in this way in the Paris, Oxford, Cambridge, and Åbo editions, [Col. 0714D] although the passage is certainly of such a kind as to require a healing hand, which learned men have variously applied as follows:

[Col. 0715A] “That fifteen years had passed during which [he was] in Illyricum”: Cuper, Gale, Allix.  
“That fifteen years had passed since [he went] into Illyricum”: Boherellus, Dodwell.  
“That fifteen years had passed [since] him into Illyricum”: Boherellus, Gale, Allix.  
“That fifteen years had passed . . . in Illyricum”: Baluze.  
“That fifteen years had passed . . . in Illyricum, that is . . .”: the same Baluze.  
“That fifteen years had passed . . . in Illyricum, him . . .”: Sparke.

And these, moreover, are the reasons which some of them have offered for their emendations.

It should be written: “in Illyricum, with [him] at the bank of the Danube.” Baluze writes, “in Illyricum, that is, at the bank,” a construction which does not seem sufficiently clear. For just as our author had earlier said, “he had fought with the old Maximian,” so the reading “he wrestled with barbarian peoples” cannot be maintained. The particle *cum* (“when” or “with”) must either be used again, as we do, or at least be prefixed once to the word *relegatus* (“banished”). SPARKE, in the Oxford and Cambridge editions.—“Fifteen years into Illyricum.” Correct: “fifteen years when [he went] into Illyricum”; this particle had dropped out because of the preceding syllable. TOLLIUS.

Of the Danube. As above, “Transdanubian.” Thus the first edition of all, and the Åbo edition; the others have “of the Danube.” See Cuper on “Romula, [his] mother.”

Wrestled. Rather, “was wrestling.” TOLLIUS.—Indeed, thus near the end of chapter 11, *reluctari* (“to struggle against”), as everyone says, not *reluctare*, which, so far as I know, no one has ever used.

Whatever he had said to the writer. Far too concisely put, to say what is true, instead of “whatever Galerius had said to the writer,” or something similar; namely, in that conflict of conversation concerning which our author speaks near the beginning of this chapter. Elsewhere in him there are not a few traces of the faulty brevity which I note.
