By him. That is, by Galerius Maximianus, as may be read in the English translation and as the words just cited could suggest.

[Col. 0715B] Tearful. Here too I place as much confidence in Lactantius as those who place very little or none at all. For his whole purpose is to describe or portray Diocletian for us as a timorous woman. But whence did he obtain this scene? I wonder that anyone can be so credulous; Lactantius is a liar. It is not likely that these events, which the emperors conducted between themselves alone, were recorded in public records. Then, if they occurred within the secret walls of the bedchamber, who saw Diocletian weeping? Who heard the remarkable dialogue that follows? I suppose Lactantius was hidden behind the hangings and thus entered in his notebooks what he heard—unless someone wishes foolishly to suppose that he received these details from some half-Christian little servant. TOLLIUS.—Please, use fair language. The matters then transacted between the Emperor Diocletian and Caesar Galerius were not transacted by them alone, as the learned man chose to state. Whether they occurred within the secret walls of the bedchamber or not, they took place in the presence of several witnesses—[Col. 0715C] certainly Constantine and Daia, as will appear from what follows. Now those two were at that time either far from Diocletian and Galerius or nearby. If nearby, why does Tollius ask: “Who saw Diocletian weeping, and heard this remarkable dialogue of the chapter?” For those two saw Diocletian tearful and heard his conversation with Galerius; and each or one of them later related, more or less, what they had seen and heard. But if, as is more likely, to speak candidly, they stood at a distance, nonetheless, if they were within the chamber, they could have seen Diocletian’s tears. Finally, even if they neither saw nor heard even a γρὺ (“a grunt”) of all that our author records, I ask Tollius whether those who have successfully committed such acts do not tend to boast and confess, at least to intimates, what they have done—indeed, to recount every detail down to the minutest particulars? This is by no means uncommon. In our author, for example, in chapter 30, Maximian [Col. 0715D] Herculius, after cutting down the eunuch whom he supposed to be Constantine, he leapt up exultantly and proclaimed what he had done. Thus, in this way—learned men among whom our author has not lost credit may elegantly say—when Galerius at last extracted the empire from his unwilling father-in-law by his stratagems, he pleasantly recounted to his friends, laughing at how he had wrung out the old man, and acting both parts; whence later the whole affair was conveyed to our author. As for the rest, we have shown elsewhere, in the appropriate places, that Diocletian really was timorous.

It remained that the Caesars should be chosen by the common counsel of all. After the immediately preceding words—“Let it be so, if this pleases you”—which are those of Diocletian reluctantly assenting, Diocletian had continued in one breath, as the following words indicate, if not in precisely these words, at least in similar ones: “It remains that, by the common decision of all—that is, of myself and Maximian Herculius, as well as of you and Constantius Chlorus—Maxentius, the son of Herculius, and Constantine, the son of Constantius, who is here present, should be chosen as [Col. 0716A] Caesars”; that is, elected. And immediately thereupon Galerius: “What need is there of deliberation, since it is necessary that whatever we do should please those two?” “Certainly so. For their sons must be named.” And at once Diocletian responds: “What then is to be done?” Galerius, without delay and referring first to the named Maxentius: “That man,” he says, “is not worthy. For he despised me when I was a private man,” and what follows. This is the genuine, complete, and uninterrupted sequence of the conversation, of which you have thus far seen a part, reader; the rest will follow. But our author, in order that the persons whom Diocletian proposed for election as Caesars might be better understood, first compressed Diocletian’s rather lengthy proposal about the selection of the new Caesars into a few words, and thought it should be presented in his own words rather than Diocletian’s. For if they were truly Diocletian’s words, they would have been: “It remains that the Caesars should be chosen by the common counsel of all”; whereas our author says: “It remained that the Caesars should be chosen by the common counsel of all.” Then, somewhat later, he explained [Col. 0716B] at length, in this observation of many lines, who had in fact been proposed: “Now Maximian had a son, Maxentius,” etc. Thus he interrupts the sequence of this dialogue once and again unexpectedly and, I confess, rather inconveniently. But what is one to do? That the matter stands thus is evident; and, I know, those who wish to flee elsewhere in order to extricate themselves will not deny it. Add that examples are not lacking both of such transitions from direct to indirect discourse, or conversely, and of similar quasi-parenthetical insertions (παρενθέσεις), which very often serve to clarify matters, though sometimes they are quite inconvenient. The order observed in the formula for those who convert from the religion of the Saracens to the Christian faith is this: “You who today come from the Saracens to the Christian faith, not by any force or necessity, nor by deceit or pretence, but loving Christ and Christ’s faith with all your soul, a pure and earnest heart: I renounce the whole religion of the Saracens and anathematize Mohammed.” Genesis 4:25: “And Adam knew his wife again, and she bore a son, and called his name Seth: ‘For the Lord has restored to me another seed in place of Abel, whom Cain killed.’” Nor is it otherwise at Genesis 41:51–52, and again at 1 Samuel 4:20, and so in other places.

[Col. 0716C] It remained, etc. Maucroix seems certainly to have constructed his translation of this passage by changing the first word, *supererat* (“it remained”), into *supererit* (“it will remain”), and the last, *legerentur* (“should be chosen”), into *legantur* (“should be chosen”), thus: “It will remain that the Caesars should be chosen by the common counsel of all.” But leaving aside that multiple correction, if Diocletian continued in this simple fashion—that is, without the least identification of Maxentius and Constantine, Maxentius because he was Herculius’ son and Constantine because he was Constantius Chlorus’ son—how could Galerius immediately reply: “What need is there of deliberation, since whatever we do must please those two? Certainly so; for their sons must be named”? These words clearly indicate that Diocletian’s mention of the selection of the new Caesars was not at all vague and general; rather, the sons of particular men were designated to Galerius, precisely those whom we have already more than once called by their names and whom the first editor also understood with us, as we shall note in its place. Let the reading, therefore—which also seemed right to the most reverend Bishop of Salisbury—be accepted in its entirety; and let the passage itself be regarded not as a part of Diocletian’s reply to Galerius, but as this author’s words representing in his own manner that proposal of Diocletian. Moreover, it is entirely possible that immediately after this period—“It remained that the Caesars should be chosen by the common counsel of all”—our author once added: “Diocletian had continuously touched on this point; indeed, for that purpose he had mentioned Maxentius, son of Herculius, and Constantine, son of Constantius. But the other suddenly said: ‘What need is there of deliberation, since it is necessary,’” etc. For not merely individual words, but sometimes lines, and occasionally several lines, are often missing from manuscript codices, as learned men know.

[Col. 0717A] By the common counsel of all. What we have already said on these words is confirmed by the English translation, “by the concurring advices of all the four,” that is, “by the common agreement of those four,” since its author plainly understood no others than Diocletian, Herculius, Constantius, and Galerius, whom we have named. Compare the passage in Eusebius concerning the martyrs of Palestine, in which Procopius, ordered by the governor to sacrifice to four emperors—τοῖς βασιλεῦσι τέσσαρσι σπένδειν—is ordered to sacrifice to that very tetrarchy.

What need is there of deliberation, etc. These are Galerius’ words rejecting Diocletian’s proposal, as the distinguished translators have not failed, more or less, to explain.—Read: “What need,” he says, “is there of deliberation?” GALE.

Those two. Maximian Herculius and Constantius. TOLLIUS.—Likewise the translations, in other words.

Certainly so. For their sons must be named. It follows clearly, therefore—as Baluze most rightly saw [Col. 0717B] but others obscure, which is why this matter must be reconsidered—that Diocletian proposed that Maxentius, son of Herculius, and Constantine, son of Constantius, should become Caesars, lest the sons of rulers live as private citizens. It is likewise manifest, therefore, that these are not Diocletian’s words, as Maucroix believed, nor this writer’s words, as another celebrated translator held, but the words of Galerius mocking Diocletian’s proposal. For surely, if they could be attributed to Diocletian, there would have had to precede, for example: “What need is there of deliberation, since whatever we do will be most pleasing to those two?” And again, if they could with any likelihood be attributed to this author, they would at least have to be: “And certainly their sons had to be named,” using the imperfect tense suitable to a historian offering his judgment about a past event. But, on the contrary, we have the present: “Certainly so. For their sons must be named.” This can in no way be the language of a judging historian, but is plainly the speech of a man derisively receiving another’s words.

Now Maximian had, etc. That is, the elder Maximian, as the translators rightly supplied.

Maxentius. He is called savage and inhuman in Aurelius Victor; dear to no one, not even to his father or to Galerius, his father-in-law. Oxford and Cambridge editions.

The son-in-law of this Maximian himself. That is, the son-in-law of this Maximian Caesar himself, of whose conflict with Diocletian Cecilius is now silently speaking. Yet how much better he would have written: “Now the elder Maximian had a son, Maxentius, son-in-law of the younger Maximian”; this is the force of the English translation. Or: “Now the elder Maximian had a son, Maxentius, son-in-law of Galerius,” as Maucroix translated it.

Was accustomed to adore. That is, as Maucroix translates, “to honour.” Although this interpretation is not without use for men of our side, who have long and rightly proposed and defended a similar interpretation in many passages of the ancients against opponents, we cannot admit it here in any way, because the honour of adoration in the strict sense was formerly granted to several emperors. Aurelius Victor, in *On the Caesars*: “Diocletian was the first of all, after Caligula and Domitian, to permit himself to be called Lord, to be adored, and to be addressed as a god.” Vopiscus, in *Saturninus*: “When he began to think that it was not safe for him to live as a private person, having taken off the purple, he was clothed from the statue of Venus in his wife’s gown, and, surrounded by soldiers, was invested and adored”—on that occasion, namely, when Diocletian wished to be continually adored. Add the English translation: “he would not pay the wonted respect of adoration.” I once doubted whether the alternative reading *solitus esset* (“was accustomed to be”) ought not be preferred to the received *solitus sit* (“is accustomed to be”); it could easily have arisen from *us* and *sit*. Let learned men judge.

Constantine, most virtuous, etc. [Col. 0718A] A commendation much older than Christianity. Cicero, *Philippics* XIII: “Antony, unaware that whatever false things he said against the most virtuous young man [Caesar], truly rebounded upon the memory of his own youth.” Again, *For Flaccus*: “Whom you have known as a most modest young man, a most upright man in a very great province . . .” And again in the same place: “They are men from all Asia, most frugal, most upright, and far removed from Greek luxury and frivolity.” I thought the latter examples especially worth citing because, while they make sufficiently clear what should be understood by *sanctissimus*, whether of a man or a young man—namely, a person endowed with exceptional virtue, which is also the precise sense of the English translation in our passage—Maucroix nevertheless translated it in our passage in the quite different sense “a young man of great promise.”

Most worthy of that high rank. That is, of that lofty rank of Caesarean dignity, to which new men had to be advanced.

And was desired by private persons. Rather, “was greatly desired by private persons.” GALE.—This too I had long ago conjectured should be read.

[Col. 0718B] And he was then present. Let Tollius hear this plainly. Therefore the emperors were not conducting between themselves alone the matters treated in Galerius’ assault. I know that, according to each translation, Constantine was merely present somewhere in Diocletian’s court—that is, among the courtiers, at a place more or less distant from where the father-in-law and son-in-law were debating these matters—not in the same place with them. But why, by adding this or that phrase, make Constantine absent from the place of conversation, when, if our author is taken as he stands, he was plainly present in that very place, and no reason can be advanced why he should not have been equally present there with Daia, whom Galerius will shortly point out to his father-in-law?

[Col. 0718C] What then is to be done? Diocletian’s words; our author, as I have noted, now returns to the remaining sequence of the discussion he had begun, after the fairly lengthy digression in which he thought it necessary carefully to explain whom Diocletian had briefly named to Galerius as Caesars to be selected by the common judgment of all.

“That man,” he says, “is not worthy.” These are now Galerius’ words, referring by “that man” to Maxentius, of whom he speaks. “That man . . . is not worthy.” Namely, Maxentius. TOLLIUS.—Correct; and likewise the translators, who have most properly substituted the name itself for the pronoun. If anyone asks why Galerius did not likewise use the name, the answer is that it was not equally necessary. For Diocletian’s direct proposal—which our author partly suppressed and partly transformed into indirect discourse—would approximately have been: “It remains that Maxentius, son of Herculius, and Constantine, son of Constantius, should be chosen as Caesars by the common counsel of all.” A little later Galerius could therefore reply of Maxentius, without any obscurity of speech, “That man is not worthy,” because Maxentius was the first named by Diocletian.

But this man is lovable, etc. Diocletian’s reply, now contending only for Constantine, whom Diocletian, when he uttered “But this man,” and the rest, [Col. 0718D] pointed out with his finger, since he was present, whether standing nearer or not. Diocletian certainly spoke of him as present, unless Constantine was at the same time indicated. Therefore I wish the translators had preferred not to name Constantine, but to preserve and convey the force of the pronoun.

That he may be judged better and more merciful than his father. That is, better even than his father, etc., as Maucroix has explained very well. For Constantine’s father Constantius truly was a good and mild ruler. Our author, chapter 20: “He despised Constantius, though he had necessarily to be named first, because . . . he was mild by nature,” etc.

That dancer, drunkard, etc. These are highly disparaging terms borrowed from the stage. Thus Clitipho in the conclusion of Terence’s *Self-Tormentor*. TOLLIUS.

He faithfully rendered. Read: “he presided.” Oxford edition of 1680, p. 108, among the later corrections. [Col. 0719A] Likewise Gale and Allix. Cuper and Columbus differently.

I sent [him] to Maximian. Supply Herculius, or “the elder,” with the translators.

That he may be clothed by him. Juvenal: “His wife clothes the dictator.” GALE.—The remaining points needed here must be sought in Baluze, Cuper, and Columbus.

Pointing out Daia. Therefore he too was then present, and before their eyes, if not under their hands.

Daia. Aurelius Victor: “Born of the sister of Armentarius, and before his imperial elevation called by his true name Daza.” Oxford and Cambridge editions. Add Baluze and Columbus.

A certain half-barbarian young man. I am strongly inclined to believe that our author wrote rather: “a certain half-bearded young man” (*semibarbatum*). Cicero’s letters to Atticus contain the well-known *barbatuli* (“young men with slight beards”), and his speech *For Caelius* distinguishes bearded men from *barbatuli*. Moreover, *adulescens* for *adolescens* occurs frequently in ancient monuments.

[Col. 0719B] Maximinus. See Baluze on “he ordered Maximinus,” and likewise on “pointing out Daia.”

Already for himself as well. Read: “For Diocletian also.” GALE.—Likewise the most reverend Bishop of Salisbury, as appears from his translation: “For Diocletian,” etc.; word for word, “For Diocletian also.”

He had partly changed the name for the man’s sake. Read: “for the sake of the omen.” Oxford and Cambridge editions, followed by Gale.—Instead of the words “for the man’s sake,” one should read with the English edition “for the sake of the omen.” From this most certain emendation we learn that, when Diocletian proclaimed Galerius Armentarius Caesar in the year 292, he partly changed his name and ordered him to be called Galerius Maximianus, regarding it as a favourable omen because the loyalty of Maximian surnamed Herculius toward him had never failed. Moved by this example, Galerius Maximianus, when in the year 305 he proclaimed Daia Caesar, changed his name entirely and wished him to be called Galerius Maximinus after his own name. “For Galerius Maximinus was born of the sister of Armentarius and, before assuming imperial office, was called by his true name Daza,” says Victor in the *Epitome*. [Col. 0719C] Hence neither the names Armentarius nor Daza are ever found on coins, inscriptions, or other public monuments. PAGI, on the year of Christ 292, no. 2, and 304, no. 3.

Because Maximian. Namely, Herculius. PAGI, on the year of Christ 304, no. 3.—“Because Maximian.” Perhaps, “because [of] Maximian,” etc. BOHERELLUS.

You see to it. A formula expressing disapproval of something. Nothing is more frequent in Tertullian and writers of this age. TOLLIUS.

Will accrue. Rather, “will happen.” GALE.

CHAPTER XIX.

[Col. 0719D] They proceed, etc. That is, with great pomp, such as might be seen, for example, in processions of consuls, Diocletian and Galerius Maximianus went out from Nicomedia on the first day of May toward the place which our author will shortly describe. Compare Cuper on “the consul proceeded.” *Proceditur* (“they proceed”) for *procedunt* (“they proceed”): namely, the rulers just mentioned with their attendants. So in what follows, *eo pergitur* (“they make their way thither”) for *eo pergunt* (“they make their way thither”), in a similar sense; and near the end of the chapter, *tum descenditur* (“then they descend”) for *tum descendunt* (“then they descend”). Many other instances might be added.—“Everything having been settled, on the first of May they came to the execution.” MAUCROIX. As if one said: what they had so decided, they carried into effect on the Kalends of May.—“All things being thus concerted in secret, on the first of May this great affair came to be declared.” English translation. As though the Latin now read: “When these things had been settled in secret in this manner, on the Kalends of May they were done openly and publicly.” I greatly fear that neither sense can be accepted.

All were looking at Constantine. Namely, in the procession itself; that is, while they were still travelling to the place [Col. 0720A] immediately to be described, a rumour having spread among the people that new Caesars would be appointed that day. “All” here, as frequently elsewhere, means “almost all”; except that it now means almost all of those who accompanied the rulers and escorted them to the place toward which they were proceeding.

There was no doubt. Namely, that Constantine would become Caesar; another example of excessive brevity in this writer, rightly avoided by the translators. “No one doubted of his elevation.” MAUCROIX.—“Not doubting but the nomination must fall on him.” English translation.

The leading men among the soldiers. Rather, “the foremost men among the soldiers,” as in chapter 21, “the foremost men of the cities,” etc. Gale and Columbus.

Outside the city. Outside Nicomedia. Maucroix’s translation. Pagi confirms this.

On whose summit Maximian himself had assumed the purple. That is, Maximian Herculius, who had been Caesar until the year 286 and who, in that year, [Col. 0720B] when public necessity required it, was called Augustus and invested with tribunician power, as ancient inscriptions show. This proclamation occurred on the Kalends of April, as is recorded in the Fasti of Idacius, and it was at Nicomedia, about three miles outside the city, as Lactantius teaches us in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 19. There, speaking of the abdication of Diocletian and the same Herculius, he says: “There was a high place about three miles outside the city, on whose summit Maximian himself had assumed the purple,” etc. This proclamation was therefore made near Nicomedia, as the distinguished Noris had inferred even before the work *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* came to light, from Law 6, *On the Authority of Instruments*: “Given at Nicomedia, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February, under Maximus II and Aquilinus”—that is, in the year 286, when Diocletian, wintering at Nicomedia and preparing there a war against the Persians, proclaimed Maximian Augustus at Nicomedia on the Kalends of April. PAGI, on the year of Christ 286, no. 2.

[Col. 0720C] Maximian himself. That is, Armentarius. Oxford and Cambridge editions. Accordingly, they understood not Maximian Herculius, with Pagi and Noris, but Galerius, with Maucroix. See how our author’s brevity has driven learned men into opposing camps, and how truly Horace wrote: “I strive to be brief; I become obscure.” Indeed, in Maucroix’s translation not even the name Maximian is seen, but only the single designation Galerius: “At the summit of which Galerius had been honoured with the purple.”

The purple. The English translation adds “imperial”: “the imperial purple,” either solely to make it known that this passage concerns the Emperor Maximian Herculius, not Caesar Galerius Maximianus, or also to establish some distinction between the purple of emperors and that of Caesars.

With the image of Jupiter. That is, with a statue of Jupiter. Both translators, from whom Cuper rightly does not depart.

An assembly of soldiers is summoned; the old man says, etc. The passage is undoubtedly corrupt, and learned men have attempted its correction in various ways, which we set out as follows:

[Col. 0720D] “An assembly of soldiers is summoned. In it the old man addresses the soldiers with tears.” Åbo edition.—“It is summoned. The old man receives with tears. He addresses.” Anonymous commentator on the column.—“It is summoned. The old man rises with tears; he addresses.” TOLLIUS.—“Let it be summoned,” says the old man with tears. He addresses. GALE.

The old man says. Others, namely Columbus, read “in which the old man,” that is, in the assembly; but the account requires an asyndetic verb. Read therefore: “the old man rises.” TOLLIUS.—He would, I think, have pronounced differently if he had seen the last conjecture.

He addresses the soldiers that he, etc. Rather: “He addresses the soldiers: that he is infirm . . .” GALE.—Provided, moreover, that the punctuation after “tears,” which we have just presented, is adopted.

He seeks rest after his labours. More elegantly, I think, it would have been: “that he seeks rest,” etc. And it would be surprising if *se* had not been absorbed by the final syllable of the preceding word.

[Col. 0721A] The utmost expectation of all [was] what, etc. The Åbo edition punctuates: “The utmost expectation of all: what he would bring forth”; and the distinguished Gale punctuated in the same way.

He Proclaims Severus and Maximianus Caesars. Severus and Maximinus were named Caesars in the year 305, not in the present year (306), as is established by what we said under the year 304. Moreover, that appointment was made not in Italy, as Socrates mistakenly states, followed by Baronius, but at Nicomedia, as I showed there from Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*. Thus, on one and the same day—namely, the Kalends of May in the year 305—Diocletian and Herculius abdicated; Galerius and Constantius were proclaimed Augusti; and Severus and Maximinus Caesars, as was demonstrated in that place. Socrates and Theophanes, as well as Eutropius, erred in writing that Galerius did not create both men until after he had arrived in Italy. Idacius also errs in the *Chronicle* when he says that the abdication occurred in 304, on the Kalends of April. All this is certain from the evidence we have already presented. PAGIUS, on A.D. 306, no. 4.—Add the same author on A.D. 304, nos. 5 and 6, and likewise Baluze.

All Are Astonished on the Tribunal. Constantine Was Standing Above. In my opinion, you will punctuate much better with Columbus and the English version after *omnes* (“all”), and with us after *astabat* (“was standing”), as follows: “All are astonished. Constantine was standing on the tribunal. Sus . . . . .” The basis for the former punctuation may be seen partly in Columbus and partly at the beginning of this chapter, in these words: “All were looking at Constantine . . . . . The soldiers present, and the foremost soldiers selected and summoned from the legions, rejoiced with their attention fixed upon this one man,” etc. We give the basis for the latter immediately below.

Above (*susum*). In the upper part. The ancients said *susum* for *sursum*, “upwards.” Oxford and Cambridge editions, after Baluze from Du Fresne.—*Susum*: perhaps *sursum*? This is probable. ALLIX.—*Susum*: thus the ancients used it for *sursum*. PAGIUS.—To me it seems that neither *astabat susum* nor *astabat sursum* can be read [Col. 0721C]. For, if either were read, Constantine would have been standing in the upper part of the tribunal, as they explain it. But how could he then have obstructed the drawing forward into the middle of Daia, who stood behind Galerius Maximianus? Constantine had to be pushed aside for this to occur, as our author immediately continues: “Before the sight of all, Maximianus, stretching his hand backward, drew Daia forward from behind, Constantine having been pushed aside,” etc. . . . “and placed him in the middle.” It is altogether clear that Constantine was by no means standing in the upper part of the tribunal, as learned men understand through their *susum* or *sursum*; rather, he was standing beside him in the proper sense—that is, he occupied Maximianus’ right or left side—so that Daia, who was behind, could not conveniently be drawn into the middle unless Constantine had first been pushed aside. Besides, when they speak of an upper part of the tribunal, they plainly imply that the tribunal was sloping or descending, with Diocletian seated or standing with Galerius in the front section and Daia behind. That hypothesis not only greatly increases the difficulty just raised [Col. 0721D], but is entirely implausible because, as matters stand, it is evident that Diocletian laid aside the purple nowhere except where Maximianus himself had taken it—whichever Maximianus one chooses to understand. Yet, as we have just seen, one or the other Maximianus took it on the summit of an elevated site three miles from the city; and they proceeded to the same place in order to proclaim the new Caesars. Hence the tribunal there was surely not built on a slope but, conforming to the terrain, was level and flat, without any upper or lower part. Therefore *susum* must be joined to the old manuscript’s *schedae*, as it stands, with the following words, if any sense can be made from it—which I do not believe—or altered into something else, in accordance with examples to be given shortly and again a little later.—*Susum*: I read *confusus*, “bewildered,” so that it is: “Constantine was standing bewildered.” GALE.

To Ask Questions, or to Hesitate, etc. Read *instare*, “to press forward.” [Col. 0722A] VOSSIUS.—*Sciscitari* (“to inquire”) comes from the conjecture of the most learned man, namely Baluze. The manuscript has *stare*, and in the margin *haesitare* (“to hesitate”). I would not condemn the marginal reading; for *haesitare* means “to doubt” in Latin: “They doubted among themselves,” that is, inwardly in their minds. *Sciscitari* is too far removed from the traces of the old codex. GRAEVIUS.—*Sciscitari*: more correctly, *haesitare*, which the most learned Baluze found in the manuscript’s margin. For inquiry can scarcely have had a place here, since reverence for the emperors imposed silence. Yet I think the little word *illi* has fallen out, so that it was: “They hesitated among themselves.” TOLLIUS.—I hear what the most learned man says about inquiry, and I do not protest against it. But if reverence for the emperors left no room for questioning, there was certainly room for whispering. Therefore, we have long believed that *susum stare*, two words, should be made into *susurrare*, “to whisper.” “Then he suddenly proclaimed Severus and Maximinus Caesars. All were astonished. Constantine was standing on the tribunal. They whispered among themselves whether Constantine’s name had been changed.” It is as though our author had written in other words that the whole assembly was amazingly astonished at the names of Severus and Maximinus [Col. 0722B]: for they heard proclaimed as Caesar not Constantine—the sole object of their eager joy and hopeful wishes a little earlier—but Severus and some Maximinus whom they did not know. Immediately, indeed, because they recognized no one named Maximinus and saw Constantine standing at one side or the other of Galerius, they suspected perhaps that Constantine’s name had been changed to Maximinus and whispered among themselves: “Has Constantine’s name been changed, and is he henceforth to be called Maximinus?” The English version strongly supports this: “All people were amassed; and since Constantine was standing by, some began to ask whether he had changed his name into Maximin.”

He Drew Him Forward from Behind. Livy uses it similarly in Book VIII, *On the Punic War*: “They were drawn naked into the middle.” In such examples, *protrahere* and *protrahi* properly mean “to draw” and “to be drawn forward”—*tirer en avant*, as our countrymen say every day [Col. 0722C]. Nor is the force of the same prefix otherwise in Cicero’s *progredi*, where, after Quintus Fabius Labeo or someone else, he says: “that they preferred to retreat rather than advance”; or below in our author, chapter 11, in *promoti*: “And lest they be snatched from the executioners’ hands by the people’s onrush, they were moved forward in military fashion,” etc. See the passage and notes.

And Having Removed His Private Garment. Thus Baluze now prints, instead of *et exuto vestem privatam*, the reading of the old manuscript, first presented by that eminent man and afterward adopted by other editors. From this arose the following emendations and attached notes.—Read *exutum*, “having stripped him”; for this refers to Maximinus. BALUZE, at the end of the Paris edition.—Read *exutum*. It refers, indeed, to Maximinus, the son of Galerius’ sister. Oxford edition of 1630; likewise Cambridge, 1685.—Read *exutum veste privata*, “having stripped him of his private garment”; it refers, indeed, etc., as just stated. SPARKE, Oxford edition, 1684.—The immediately following words, “the purple . . . which he took off,” show that Sparke emended better than all the others.

[Col. 0722D] He Placed Him in the Middle. Why not rather *constituit in medio*, “placed him in the midst,” as Cicero and others so often say *ponere in medio*, *proponere in medio*, and hundreds of expressions of that sort? Surely the last letter of *medium* owes its origin to the first letter of the following word, *mirari*.

Diocletianus Put His Own Purple upon Him, Which He Took Off. Diocletian laid aside the purple at Nicomedia on the Kalends of May, 305, according to Lactantius; Eusebius also agrees, despite forgetting himself elsewhere . . . Although Lactantius alone ought to count for as much as all others, there are nevertheless other considerations that commend his credibility in this matter. DODWELL, Dissertation XI on Cyprian, no. 73.—You must consult him to see what other evidence he means and adduces; it is too extensive to transcribe here.

The Purple upon Him, etc. We have said that Diocletian laid aside the purple on 1 April A.D. 305 if one follows Idatius, or on 1 May if Lactantius is heard. On that same day Maximinus was made [Col. 0723A] Caesar. For Diocletian clothed him in the same purple which he himself removed; and Lactantius likewise indicates that this occurred with the other Caesar, Severus, at the hands of Maximianus Herculius. Yet Eusebius assigns a different birthday to both, namely 20 November—precisely the day which Lactantius assigns to Diocletian—unless perhaps we should suspect some hidden significance in the words, *κατὰ τὴν λεγομένην αὐτοῦ γενέθλιον ἡμέραν*, “on his so-called birthday,” as though it were said that it was merely called, but was not truly, his birthday . . . It is certain from Lactantius that Diocletian laid down power and Maximinus assumed it in one and the same—not merely year, but day. DODWELL, the same Dissertation XI on Cyprian, no. 78.

Diocles Was Made Again. That is, by returning to private life, which he had lived before his imperial accession and when he was still called Diocles. But did Diocletian, as the English version states, at the same time return to his former name, so that he no longer wished to be called anything but Diocles? Or was he also called Diocletian, either by himself or others, after his abdication, as in this passage of Jerome: “Diocletian died not far from Salona, in his villa at Spalato” [Col. 0723B]? This is surely a matter for the most eminent Bishop of Meaux, Bossuet, to investigate most thoroughly. In one place he maintained that the fatal number of the apocalyptic beast is found in the name Diocletian; elsewhere he derived the same number from the numerical letters of *Diocles Augustus*, and displayed it thus: *DIoCLes AVgVstVs*, DCLXVI.

It is established in my view that Diocletian never had a proper name—in private life, after acquiring the empire, or finally after his abdication—in which, if one looks to the Latin numerical letters by the method of that most celebrated prelate, the number he calls fatal might be found. Before the empire, as our author stated above, he was called *DIoCLes*: the numerical letters, which we have therefore printed in capitals, amount only to DCLI. After entering upon the empire, however, he was no longer called Diocles but Diocletianus, as everyone knows. This outstanding writer himself witnesses to this, since whenever he treats matters pertaining to Diocletian’s reign, he everywhere calls him Diocletianus and nowhere Diocles. See chapters 7, 9, 12, 14, 17, 18, and this very passage a little earlier. But from the name *DIoCLetIanVs* the number DCLXVI cannot in any way result; only DCLVII can emerge. Finally, after Diocletian had laid aside the purple, he was called either Diocles again in the old fashion, or still Diocletian according to the later usage. Neither name, as is apparent from what precedes, will ever suffice to make up the beast’s number.

I know that, if to the private name the Bishop of Meaux’s full hypothesis adds once [Note: [Col. 0723D]

“The name of Diocletian before he became emperor was Diocles. He was called Diocles before his empire (*Lactantius, On the Deaths* 9). Then he laid aside the purple and became Diocles again (*ibid.* 19). To make him an emperor—who here is what St John indicated by the beast—one need only add to his personal name Diocles the title *Augustus*, which emperors were indeed accustomed to append to their names. At once one will see, at a glance, in the Latin numerical letters—as is fitting, since an emperor of Rome is concerned—the number 666: *DIoCLes aVgVstVs*, DCLXVI.”

] the title *aVgVstVs*, the number DCLXVI will suddenly appear, as he says. But, not to say much: who can tolerate, in this argument, that the title *aVgVstVs* should be joined and presented to educated people otherwise than all ancient monuments require it to be joined and exhibited? In them, contrary to what that most learned man falsely suggests, one nowhere finds Diocles Augustus of Diocles after he attained the empire; rather, one finds either Diocletianus Augustus, as in Spartianus: “It is in my mind, Diocletian Augustus, greatest of all emperors,” etc.—with similar forms in Capitolinus at the end of the lives of Verus and Macrinus—or *Imperator Diocletianus Augustus*, as always in the headings of legal texts promulgated by Diocletian [Col. 0724A], either alone or with Maximianus Herculius. For example, in Book VIII, Title 7 of the Code: “Emperor Diocletian Augustus to Camerius. Let no one be compelled unwillingly to act or to accuse.” And in Book I, Title 11: “The Emperors Diocletian and Maximianus Augusti.” So too in a thousand other places. Yet the number produced in Latin from *DIoCLetIanVs aVgVstVs* is not DCLXVI but DCLXXII; and the number likewise produced from *IMperator DIoCLetIanVs aVgVstVs* is not apocalyptic either, but nearly three times greater, namely MDCLXXIII. Thus the eminent man misleads and is himself misled. And by this very fact almost his entire Commentary on the Apocalypse, which rests chiefly on this now-refuted hypothesis, is undone [Note: [Col. 0724D]

“He may be mistaken; he does not deceive. For he says, not perhaps true things, but highly plausible ones.”].

Then They Descend. From the mountain, as Maucroix added? I would prefer, “from the tribunal.” For the tribunal is mentioned immediately before. It is also much more likely that the great figures we saw in that scene—Diocletian, Galerius, and Daia—are intended, rather than [Col. 0724B] those figures together with all the spectators, which Maucroix seems to have implied: “They come down from the mountain . . .”

Through the City. Here too Maucroix’s version substituted the proper name Nicomedia for the common noun “city”; and the English version, in imitation of it, has “through Nicomedia.”

The Veteran Emperor. Since he had reigned for twenty years. From this chapter the reason why Diocletian abdicated is clear; Lactantius was the first to disclose this secret of history. For he formed that plan after launching the persecution, returning from Rome, and completing the *vicennalia*, when a severe illness unsettled his mind. Oxford and Cambridge editions.

Immediately a Shield-Maker. Labbé’s glossaries: “*Scutarius*: a shield-maker holding a military rank” (*ἀξίωμα στρατιωματικὸν φέρων ἀσπιδοποιός*). The term therefore has a double sense: at times it denotes a maker of shields, which suits this passage; at times a man invested with military rank, whom the same glosses shortly afterward undoubtedly call *scutigerulus*, Greek *ὁπλοφόρον*, “weapons-bearer.” Interpreters have taken it in this latter, not inappropriate sense as referring to a common soldier. Yet elsewhere the same glossaries define *scutarius* as “a military office” (*ἀξίωμα στρατιωματικόν*) [Col. 0724C].

Protector. The Basilica glosses: “*Primoscutarii*, defenders, who are now called *protectores*” (*Πριμοσκουτάριοι, ὑπερασπισταί, οἳ νῦν λεγόμενοι Προτίκτορες*). A *protector* is an emperor’s bodyguard. This order was instituted by the younger Gordian. SPARKE, Oxford edition of 1684, adding himself that this came from Suicer.—*Protector*. The Basilica glosses: “*Primoscutarii*, defenders, who are now called protectors.” They were called protectors because they protected the emperor’s side. This order was instituted by the younger Gordian. See Meursius’ *Glossary* and Valesius, notes on Ammianus Marcellinus, p. 34, Paris edition of 1681. Anonymous author of the Cambridge edition.

But let readers more devoted to truth (*φιλαληθέστεροι*) see whether the assertion which learned men, following Cedrenus, make here [Col. 0724D]—that the order of protectors was instituted by the younger Gordian—is not among the reasons that led Casaubon, when dealing with the Gordians, to cry out: “What nonsense Cedrenus chatters in the history of the Gordians!” For Suicer’s passage includes: “They were instituted by the younger Gordian, as Cedrenus reports, p. 211: *Μετὰ δὲ τούτον ἐβασίλευσεν Ἰουνίωρ μῆνας τρεῖς, ὃς πρῶτος ἐποίησε Κανδιδάτον, καὶ προτίκτορας*.” “After him, namely Pupienus, Junior ruled for three months. He was the first to establish candidates and protectors.” Yet Spartianus, in his life of Caracalla—who ruled before the younger Gordian—attributes protectors to Caracalla. His words are: “I travelled through Thrace with the praetorian prefect. Then, when he was crossing into Asia, he ran the risk of shipwreck, his mast having broken; so that he descended into a small boat with his protectors” [Col. 0725A].

Protector. “Bodyguard.” MAUCROIX.—By this he accurately expressed for our countrymen the proper force of the word.

He Received the East to Be Trodden Underfoot. These and many similar passages may be offered to youth as examples for stirring up indignation. TOLLIUS.—A similar expression occurs in Cicero, *Philippics* 2: “In the same tribunate, when Caesar, departing for Spain, had entrusted Italy to this man to be trampled underfoot, what was his progress through the journey?”

No Longer a Shepherd of Flocks, but of Soldiers. Christ addressed Peter and Andrew in much the same way, Matthew 4:19, saying, *Δεῦτε ὀπίσω μου, καὶ ποιήσω ὑμᾶς ἁλιεῖς ἀνθρώπων*: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men.” TOLLIUS.

## CHAPTER XX

Maximianus. Maucroix has Galerius instead, apparently lest the ambiguous name Maximianus provide any occasion for error.

After the Old Men Had Been Expelled. That is, as Maucroix explains, after the abdication of Diocletian and the elder Maximianus.

What He Willed, He Did. “Maximian having now effected which he had projected.” English translation. This confirms Columbus’s excellent emendation—which changes *et fecit* (“and did”) to *effecit* (“accomplished”)—even in the eyes of those who do not know English.

He Claimed to Be Now Sole Master of the Whole World, etc. That is, of the whole Roman Empire, according to the English version; what follows shows that it is preferable to Maucroix’s.

He Claimed to Be. I can scarcely believe that this was originally written. I would prefer *esse rebatur*, “he considered himself to be”; Maucroix too may seem to have read this: “Galerius believed himself master of the universe.”

Because He Was Mild by Nature. This is praise with which it would surely be strange for Constantius Chlorus to be honored here if, as the eminent Bishop of Meaux most recently held, this writer counted Constantius among the major persecutors of the Church. For what is less likely—indeed, more contrary [Col. 0725C] to nature—than to commend as mild by nature one whom one considers to have made a name for himself in persecuting the faithful? Rather, since our author now attributes to Constantius Chlorus such a disposition not without praise, and elsewhere expressly states that he differed from Diocletian and both Maximiani; indeed, since he declares him worthy to hold the world alone, says that he preserved unharmed the true temple of God, which is in human beings, and finally records that he did not perish miserably like all the other enemies of God but received, in his own bed, the rest of life which he desired: rather, I say, on account of all this he should be regarded by this author as one of the Church’s fosterers and defenders, rather than—because of certain utterly empty exceptions—as one of the Christians’ enemies and persecutors.

Illness. Thus in chapter 22, *valitudinis*. Other editions have *valetudine*. On this matter consult Dausque, in his work on orthography, under *Valetudo, Valitudo*.

To Lay Aside. Supply “the purple,” as concisely in chapter 18 above: “that it might be put on by him.” What was necessary has been noted at greater length on that passage [Col. 0725D].

If by Three. Namely, by his three colleagues in imperial office.

He Himself. That is, as the English version rightly explains, Maximianus; for our author no longer speaks of Constantius but of Galerius Maximianus, as what follows shows.

To Govern Everything. I would not dislike the nearby word *gerenda* in place of *regenda*. Likewise, I believe, Orosius, Book VII, chapter 4 should be emended to read *geri*, “to be done,” rather than *regi*, “to be ruled”: “And so that most praiseworthy moderation of Caesar Tiberius was gradually changed, as punishment for the Senate’s opposition. For whatever he did at will, it was a pleasure to be ruled.” Compare Cicero’s passage from *On Duties*, where some read: “But as long as the republic was governed by them”; others, including Graevius, a man of most weighty judgment, prefer: “But as long as the republic was conducted by them.”

Lest He Name His Son, So That Later, etc. I would prefer: “lest he name his son, and later proclaim him Augustus and brother in Constantius’ place.”

And Having Appointed His Son as Caesar in His Place, etc. The passage is obscure through excessive brevity. Our author certainly means that Galerius Maximianus planned, after he had once completed that celebration of the *vicennalia*, first of all to promote Severus from the rank of Caesar to that of Augustus; then to appoint his son Candidianus—he will shortly be called so—as Caesar in Severus’ place, that is, to bestow Severus’ Caesarian rank upon him; and finally, once this was done, to lay aside the empire following Diocletian’s example. For Candidianus did not yet possess either the authority or the name of Caesar when Galerius proposed this; rather, he was long intended as Severus Caesar’s replacement. Therefore perhaps one should read: “and having appointed his son in the place of a Caesar”—that is, in the place of one of the Caesars—since his father Galerius was contemplating making him not Augustus after the *vicennalia*, in the place of some Augustus, but simply Caesar.

His Son. Born of a concubine. For by Valeria, being barren, he had no child. Oxford and Cambridge editions.—[Col. 0726B] His son. Galerius Maximianus’ wife was Valeria, daughter of Diocletian . . . Galerius Maximianus had no son by her, for she was barren, as Lactantius teaches in chapter 50. He therefore speaks here of Candidianus, who is named shortly afterward. PAGIUS, on A.D. 304, no. 6, and A.D. 311, no. 12.

Who Was Then Nine Years Old. That is, he was to be so. Therefore Candidianus was then of the same age as Maximinus’ son in chapter 1, namely eight years old; for Maximianus died before the *vicennalia*, chapter 35. TOLLIUS.—Undoubtedly better and simpler are the interpreters who understand: “who was then only nine years old.”

And He Himself Should Lay It Aside, Thus When, etc. Punctuate: “and he himself should lay it aside. Thus when,” etc. GALE.—The original wording, I think, was: “and he himself should lay it aside, and thus . . .,” in this sense: he too should lay it aside, and then, “when the supreme power of the Empire,” and what follows.

The Second-Rank Name of Caesar. Because it was the other and primary title, which emperors still used, following the example, for instance, of Emperor Octavius Augustus Caesar, in the headings of edicts. This is clear from the edict which Galerius Maximianus issued in A.D. 311: “Emperor Caesar Galerius Valerius Maximianus . . . Augustus . . . And Emperor Caesar Flavius Valerius Constantine . . . Augustus . . . And Emperor Caesar Valerius Licinianus . . . Augustus,” etc. I have called the title Caesar primary, among other reasons, because emperors who assumed it did not assume it alone; instead, as the cited heading shows, they joined it to the explicit titles *Imperator* and *Augustus*, which were superior titles belonging to those who held supreme authority. Conversely, when they wrote to the two subordinate rulers, who by Diocletian’s arrangement were intended as assistants to their superiors, they addressed their letters with the title Caesar alone. Thus our author above, chapter 9: “After this victory, Galerius Maximianus was raised to such pride that he now disdained the title Caesar. When he heard it in letters sent to him, he cried out with a fierce countenance and terrible voice: ‘How long [Col. 0726D] Caesar?’” Accordingly, here “the second name of Caesar” has a connotation of lesser and subordinate rank. For the primary sense, this observation of Theodore Metochites may not be inapposite: that all Roman emperors were called Caesars after Julius Caesar . . . *ἕως Ἰουλίου Καίσαρος, τοῦ μὴ γεννηθέντος· τῆς γὰρ μητρὸς αὐτοῦ θανούσης ἐν τῷ ἐννάτῳ μηνὶ τῆς ἐγκυμονίας αὐτῆς, τὴν κοιλίαν αὐτῆς ἀνατέμνουσι, καὶ σῶον αὐτὸν ἐκεῖθεν ἐκβάλλουσιν, ὅθεν Καῖσαρ ἐλέγετο ἀφ᾽ οὗ καὶ πάντες Ῥωμαῖοι βασιλεῖς Καίσαρες προσηγορεύθησαν*: “Down to Julius Caesar, who was not born; for when his mother died in the ninth month of her pregnancy, they cut open her belly and brought him out alive. Hence he was called Caesar, and after him all Roman kings were called Caesars.”

These Plans Showed Him This. Lactantius certainly did not write thus; not even country people who spoke Latin once spoke so. Lactantius’ hand wrote: “His plans tended to this end.” The final syllable of *ejus* (“his”), separated by an earlier scribal error, adhered to the following *tendebant*, so that *ei ustendebant* was first written, whence *ostendebant* arose. GRAEVIUS.

## CHAPTER XXI

[Col. 0727A]

Having Therefore Obtained the Highest Power. Namely, because he had obtained the Augustan power, which had long been the greatest of all human powers. For example, Athenagoras, at the beginning of the *Apology* which he presented in the Christians’ name to emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus, perhaps in A.D. 166, and inscribed—on this matter I follow the judgment of the most learned Pagius and Toinard—*Αὐτοκράτορσιν, Μάρκῳ Αὐρηλίῳ Ἀντωνίνῳ . καὶ Λουκίῳ Αὐρηλίῳ Κομμώδῳ ἡ ὑμετέρα, μεγάλοι βασιλέων, οἰκουμενη . . .* That is, in Gesner’s translation: “To the Emperors Marcus Aurelius, etc., whose empire, greatest kings, is acknowledged far and wide throughout the world.” Or, better in view of what follows: “To the Emperors Marcus Aurelius Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus . . . in whatever part, greatest of kings, the world is yours”—reading, that is, not merely *ἡ* with rough breathing, but *ᾗ* with circumflex and iota subscript. Consult the passage. Indeed, when the Maximianus here discussed became Augustus from Caesar—this is, as Maucroix rightly supplied, the younger Maximianus, or Galerius—then [Col. 0727B] the authority of the Augusti so greatly exceeded that of the Caesars under Diocletian’s arrangement that, according to our author in chapter 18, the two Augusti held supreme power, while the Caesars served only as assistants. Thus, if later Augusti and Caesars were jointly called *βασιλεῖς*, “kings”—as, for example, in Eusebius concerning the martyr Procopius: *ὡς δὲ καὶ τοῖς βασιλεῦσι τεσσάρσι σπένδειν ἐκελεύετο*, “when he was ordered to pour a libation to the four kings”—that expression, insofar as it concerned the Augusti, should be understood as *βασιλέας τελειοτάτους*, “most perfect,” or supreme kings; whereas, insofar as it concerned Caesars, it meant only imperfect kings of inferior rank. Eusebius provides this distinction in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VIII, chapter 13. Narrating how Constantine the Great, after his father’s death, was promoted by the soldiers from the position of Caesar, which he had previously held, to a higher rank, he says that they proclaimed him *βασιλέα τελειότατον καὶ Σεβαστόν*, “a most perfect king and Augustus”: *Βασιλεὺς Κωνστάντιος . . . τέλος εὐδόκιμον καὶ τρισμακάριον ἀπείληφε τοῦ βίου . . . τελευτήσας. τούτου παῖς Κωνσταντῖνος εὐθὺς ἀρχόμενος, βασιλεὺς τελειότατος καὶ Σεβαστὸς πρὸς τῶν στρατοπέδων . . . ἀναγορευθείς.* “Emperor Constantius . . . having died, received an honorable and thrice-blessed end of life . . . His son Constantine, immediately upon beginning his rule, was proclaimed by the armies a most perfect king and Augustus.”

He Directed His Mind toward Harassing the World Which He Had Laid Open to Himself. In my opinion the passage is too badly damaged to be sufficiently repaired merely by punctuating it, with the Aboensis edition and also Pagius and Gale, as follows: “He directed his mind toward harassing the world, which he had laid open to himself.” You should therefore, if you trust me, punctuate and emend at once: “He directed his mind toward harassing the world—the purpose which he himself had laid open.” That is, the purpose which he had openly and everywhere disclosed to the whole world, by praising from the very time of his victory over the Persians the Persian custom about to be discussed—so that no doubt remained that he formerly wished to harass everyone—he applied and directed toward actually harassing the world. Read quickly what follows [Col. 0727D].

Let Them Enslave Themselves. *Servitium*, and more frequently *servitia*, in the plural of multitude, sometimes means slaves themselves. Cicero, *Verrines* 7, after asking, “Was there no uprising of slaves in Sicily under Verres as praetor?” shortly adds: “Yet I suspect that a slave body began to stir in several places in Sicily.” The same author, *Against Catiline* 4: “To overthrow the foundations of the republic, he summoned the Gauls, enlisted slaves, summoned Catiline.” Elsewhere again: “The Allobroges are solicited, slaves are stirred up, Catiline is summoned.” Here I would prefer to understand by *per servitium*, “through slavery,” in light of this passage of Livy: “That a needy man be seized and put in chains by right of liberty, who had enslaved his free person.” That is, what our author calls “to enslave oneself” Livy explains as “to enslave one’s free body.”

As a Household. That slaves are properly meant here by *familia* is made beyond doubt both by the preceding words, “that they should enslave themselves to their kings,” and by what we noted above on the corresponding passage in chapter 14: “For no one tortured Caesar’s household” [Col. 0728A].

From the Time of That Victory. In imitation of Alexander the Great, who after conquering the Persians ordered himself to be adored in the manner of Persian kings, whose customs he had adopted. TOLLIUS.—Gale reasonably wished to place punctuation both before and after “from the time of that victory.”

Thus He Acted. Perhaps rather *satagebat*, “he was busily striving”? GALE.—I do not believe so. For, as we have seen and noted elsewhere, our author is not unaccustomed to use the two words *agere* and *facere* intransitively, in the very sense in which we regularly say *agir* in French. For example, in chapter 9: “Thereupon he began to act most insolently.” We explained this very point in passing at that passage. I add now, by way of confirmation, a very similar passage from Cyprian’s letters: “And in the Acts of the Apostles we read: ‘The multitude of those who believed acted with one soul and mind.’” Finally, the English translation likewise assists us here: “yet he behaved himself so as etc.” [Col. 0728B].

That He Also. Substitute *ipsam*, “that she also.” TOLLIUS.—I am surprised that this seemed necessary to the learned man, since the received reading provides a plainer and more suitable meaning: “that he also”—that is, he too, following the example of Persian kings, etc.

Not Only Decurions Were Tortured by Him. Although Constantine later enacted a law allowing decurions to be tortured in a charge of forgery. Oxford and Cambridge editions.—They say, after Baluze, from Baronius; but to state the matter as it is, this is too abbreviated and scarcely relevant unless the rest of Baluze’s remarks, which they omitted, is added.

Men of Distinguished and Most Perfect Rank. These were honorary ranks, as is evident from Theodosian Code, Book VI, Title 37. We have already said in our notes on Zosimus, Book II, that Constantine formerly added the rank of *spectabiles*. Yet this passage is especially illuminated by another twofold passage in Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, Book V, chapter 14: “No one is poor before God except one lacking righteousness; no one rich except one full of virtues; no one distinguished except one who has been good and innocent; no one most illustrious except one who has generously performed works of mercy; no one most perfect except one who has fulfilled every degree of virtue.” Thus no one can doubt that Lactantius used these words in their then-common and popularly accepted sense [Col. 0728C]. Oxford and Cambridge editions.

Men of Most Perfect Rank. They must surely be regarded, in the period of which our author speaks, as among the leading men of cities, just as he expressly says, “the leading men of cities, men of distinguished and most perfect rank.” But note, please, from the following title of the Code, “Concerning the rank of the *perfectissimi*,” that later even bakers and people of that kind obtained certificates of the rank of *perfectissimus*, and that it was therefore necessary to decree that they should not enjoy it: “Emperor Constantine Augustus to Paternus Valerianus. Let those who have obtained certificates of the rank of *perfectissimus* enjoy them, if they are free from servile condition and are not liable to the fisc or the curia; if they have not been bakers or engaged in any trade; if they have not purchased office through venal influence; and if they have not managed another person’s property” [Col. 0728D].

And Indeed in Slight and Civil Cases, etc. The passage has been separated from what precedes more than it should have been, and is not better joined to what follows. For in what way could those distinguished and most perfect men have seemed deserving of death in slight cases? Rather: “They were tortured in slight and civil cases. But in graver and criminal cases, if they seemed deserving of death, crosses stood ready. Shackles, however, were prepared if they were judged to have deserved a punishment less than death.” Everything should therefore be recast as follows, even though both translations followed the received punctuation: “Not only decurions, but even the leading men of cities—men of distinguished and most perfect rank—were tortured by him, and indeed in slight and civil cases. If they seemed worthy of death, crosses stood ready. But if not, etc.” And, lest you be unaware, the most eminent Gale supports us in almost every respect [Col. 0729A].

But If Not. “At least.” MAUCROIX. As though our author had written: “If they seemed worthy of death, crosses stood ready, or at least shackles were prepared.” But why shackles at least, if they were deserving of death? Why, I ask, would crosses not always be used? Therefore *sin minus* clearly does not refer to the immediately preceding words, so as to mean, “If not, crosses stood ready.” Rather, as we touched on above, it refers to the more distant words, “if they seemed deserving of death”; its meaning is: “But if they were thought to have merited some punishment less than death.” This is undoubtedly what the most reverend Bishop of Salisbury meant when he translated, “and for lesser transgressions he put them in irons”: “And for lesser offenses he cast them into chains, or shackles.”

In the *Gynecaeum*. That *gynaecaea*, by force of the word, signify places assigned to women’s work is beyond dispute. But here I should rather believe that the infamous slavery of lust is indicated, such as the emperor of the Ottomans still exacts from women in his public [Col. 0729B] brothel. And that no other tasks were performed there is sufficiently indicated by what immediately follows concerning Maximian’s lust. Oxford and Cambridge editions.—For my part, since I have been unable to find, even within the thirtieth chapter, the matters said immediately to follow concerning the lust of the emperor Galerius, and since I see that in our present chapter this Author’s particular purpose is to show how Galerius, once he had acquired the power of Augustus, harassed the world and deprived men of liberty, I should judge it far more probable that the *Gynecaeum* now in question, into which our author records that freeborn and noble matrons were carried off, was some public weaving workshop, such as Du Cange will now describe for us, rather than Galerius’s public brothel, as the cited editions put it, or, as the English version has it, his seraglio. Du Cange, therefore, among other things, under the word *Gynaeceum*, with a diphthong in the second syllable—which is undoubtedly the better spelling—writes:

> “Under the Roman emperors there existed *Gynaecea*, or public weaving workshops [Col. 0729C] in which the workmen called *Gynaeceiarii* laboured in weaving garments, being otherwise of a servile condition; so much so that criminals and persons accused were sometimes sent to these places as a punishment. Sozomen, book I, chapter 8, testifies this concerning men; John Chrysostom, in his letter to the younger widow, vol. VI, p. 300, concerning women.”

Maucroix, as he noted in the margin of his translation: “The *Gynaeceum* was a place into which women were shut up for punishment and disgrace.”

*In stabulo* [“in a stable”]. I prefer *in sabulo* [“in the sand”]. GALE.

“To which no slave was ever usually stretched.” That is, according to Maucroix’s translation: “to which not even a slave was stretched,” “although not even slaves were fastened there”. Perhaps because of what follows, from which it appears that the punishment of slaves, since they had no rank, was fire. Our friend David Martin, the reverend gentleman, preferred: “to which no one except a slave was ever [stretched],” etc.; I should not wish to condemn this reading.

*Lusorium*. Amphitheatres, where public games were exhibited. Oxford and Cambridge editions. A theatre or amphitheatre [Col. 0729D] where public games were held. PAGIUS.—*Lusorium*. Here *lusorium* is not an amphitheatre in which combats with beasts were staged, but a domestic place in the palace, assigned to pleasure and beneath Maximian’s dining-room or triclinium. For it follows: “nor did he ever dine without human blood.” Hardly anyone is unaware of that abominable and savage Roman delight in feeding dinner-guests with gladiators’ blood; Lipsius discusses it more fully in the *Saturnalia*. Maximian, however, amused himself with bears of monstrous savagery in their place; hence our author calls this shedding of human blood his “delight.” Perhaps indeed the condemned man was exposed to introduced bears in the dining-room itself, which Lactantius here mockingly calls a *Lusorium*. TOLL.

“He kept bears,” etc. Do you wish to know why the feet of the beast which John, *Apocalypse* XIII.1–2, says he saw were like a bear’s feet? Because Galerius Maximian, our author reports, kept bears extremely like himself in savagery and size [Col. 0730A], says the illustrious Bossuet on that passage of John—except that he also presses the preceding words into the service of his own argument: “Galerius also had a body corresponding to his character: lofty in stature, immense in flesh, spread out and swollen into a dreadful bulk.” Indeed, if the bishop is to be believed, this little book is almost a continuous commentary on the *Apocalypse*.

“He kept bears,” etc. See Ammianus Marcellinus XXIX.3. GALE.—No doubt referring to those words found in Columbus.

“He had selected.” What if it were “he had reared”? GALE.—Few, I think, will accept this. Bears “selected throughout the whole period of his reign” means bears not merely sought out and acquired from every quarter over a long period, but bears more bulky and savage than very many others, and therefore specially selected by a lover of beasts of this kind.

“He ordered one to be brought by name.” That the words “to lead” and “to bring” ought not lightly or indiscriminately to be used is plainly shown by the Plautine passage—or should I call it a joke?—in which Calidorus, speaking of Pseudolus, whom he brings to Charinus, says: “I have brought him.” Pseudolus immediately rebukes him angrily: “What? You have brought [carried] him?” Then Calidorus corrects himself and placates the man: “I meant to say, I have led him here.” Since it must surely be agreed that Calidorus’s error was spontaneous, yet malicious and employed for the sake of a joke, the question may now be asked in what spirit he used it: whether Calidorus, by saying on the first occasion not “I have led him here” but “I have brought him,” intended to jest about Pseudolus as though he were a child; or rather, for example, as though he were a calf, since calves and similar four-footed livestock are customarily carried, bound by the legs, upon men’s shoulders. For my part I decidedly incline to the latter view. But however that may be, the bears of Galerius were of such savagery and size—indeed, extremely like his own savagery and size, as was said a few lines earlier—that it is by no means probable Galerius wished bears to be brought to him bound together by all four legs. Is *afferri*, then, used by our author for *adduci* (“to be led”), as the idiom of not a few languages today [Col. 0730C] would readily permit? I should not think so. Rather, Galerius ordered that one bear or another should be conveyed to him by name in a wooden or iron cage, just as, in the memory of our forefathers, Tamerlane carried Bajazet about shut in an iron cage. Tatian, certainly, discussing Alexander the Great in his *Address to the Greeks*, says:

> Ὅστις, inquit, Ἀριστοτελικῶς πάνυ, τὸν ἑαυτοῦ φίλον διὰ τὸ μὴ βούλεσθαι αὐτὸν προσκυνεῖν καθείρξας, ὥσπερ ἄρκτον ἣ πάρδαλιν περιέφερε.

“That man who, in a thoroughly Aristotelian manner, imprisoned his friend because he would not worship him, and carried him about like a bear or a panther.” Maucroix therefore translates quite literally: *Quand il voulait passer le temps, il ordonnait qu'on en apportât quelqu'un*—“Whenever he wished to amuse himself, he ordered one of them to be brought.”

“Men were exposed to these [bears],” etc. Ruinart argues thus on this passage, p. 61 of the preface which he prefixed to his genuine *Acts of the Martyrs*: as though the men now said to have been exposed to Galerius’s bears to be devoured were never taken from the body of the pagans, but on every occasion from the company of Christians; and as though this happened so frequently that the most savage emperor never dined a single day without the human blood of believers; and as though, again, our author in this passage dealt only with Christians, but very few of them, in agreement with Dodwell’s view in *On the Scarcity of Martyrs*. Indeed, after Ruinart has once introduced our author’s words in his own manner:

> “As often as he [Galerius] wished to amuse himself, he ordered one of these [bears] to be brought by name. Men were exposed to them, not exactly to be eaten, but to be swallowed; and when their limbs were torn apart, he laughed most sweetly,”

the learned man immediately adds on his own account: “Nor did this happen rarely, or only on festival days, as Dodwell contends.” He then adds from our author’s words: “For [Galerius] never dined without human blood.”

But first, nowhere in Dodwell’s entire dissertation *On the Scarcity of Martyrs* will one find that he wished only Christians to be understood by the “men” in this passage; in it the most distinguished man did not discuss or even touch in the slightest degree the question whether those men were pagans or Christians. Secondly, what Ruinart not merely suggests but explicitly affirms—namely, that they were Christians alone—is so far from being clear or certain from our author that, on the contrary, the matters related a little earlier at the beginning of this chapter can establish that they were much more probably pagans than Christians. For who were those men there, toward whom Galerius is said to have acted so as himself to take liberty away from men? Christians only, or principally? Not at all; rather, the inhabitants of Roman territory, and therefore, speaking universally and more correctly, pagans:

> “For,” our author relates, “after conquering the Persians, whose rite and custom it is to devote themselves to servitude under their kings, while the kings use their people as a household, this impious man wished to introduce this custom into Roman territory. From the time of that victory he shamelessly praised it. And because he could not openly command it, he acted so as himself to deprive men of liberty. First of all, he took away their honours,”

[Col. 0731B] and the rest which follows. Therefore, those men whose liberty and honours were thus taken away under Galerius’s rule were not properly Christians, but rather, as I have said, pagans. Or if perhaps certain Christians also experienced vexations of this kind, certainly not insofar as they were Christians, but insofar as they were inhabitants of Roman soil, like the pagans. For this very reason, moreover, the “men” whom our author now relates to have been exposed to Galerius’s bears to be swallowed ought chiefly to be judged pagans as well. Ruinart should therefore consider whether, when he judges that Dodwell has from partisan zeal misused no small company of ancient writers in support of his scarcity of martyrs, he himself may not, in the present passage, have misused them against Dodwell from a similar zeal. That we are not led by the same motive may be shown by the observations we have made more than once above against that most learned Englishman, and long before Ruinart’s cited preface saw the light. But altogether, in this controversy over the scarcity of martyrs, if I see anything, error is committed both within the walls and outside them, as the saying goes: while Dodwell admits fewer than he should, Ruinart in turn introduces more than is fair.

*Obsorbendi* [“to be swallowed”]. The Abo edition, and more recently Ruinart also, read *absorbendi*. On this correction see the most learned Cuper.

*Objectabantur* (“they were exposed”—men to these bears). Our author, ch. 24: “Under the pretext of exercise and sport he had exposed him to beasts”; similarly the *Fragment on Constantius Chlorus*: “Galerius exposed him [Constantine] to many dangers beforehand.” Yet examples of the frequentative form itself, as it is called, used in a similar sense are not rare. Virgil, *Georgics* IV:

> *Et corpora bello*  
> *Objectant.*

“And they expose their bodies to war.”

The same author, *Aeneid* II:

> *Et rursus caput objectare periclis.*

“And again to expose one’s head to dangers.” I refrain from adducing more for the sake of brevity.

“When their limbs were torn apart.” A Lactantian expression. *Institutes* V.1: “No one can adequately describe the savagery of this great beast, which . . . with iron teeth . . . tears apart not merely the limbs of men, but,” etc.

“For those without rank, the punishment was fire; and he had permitted exile first against the Christians, laws having been issued.” Unless one writes *permissa* [“having been permitted”], I do not know what will become of the meaning of this passage. Oxford and Cambridge editions.—No one fails to see that the passage is defective. But after *fuit* (“was”) one must read, as Nicolaus Heinsius also saw: *Id exitii primo adversus Christianos* [“this instrument of destruction, first against the Christians”]. The opening of the following chapter teaches that he first employed this punishment against Christians, then against others: “What he had therefore learned by torturing Christians, he practised against everyone through habit.” Yet the passage has not been fully cleansed. For who would believe that the most eloquent of the early Latin doctors of the Church wrote: *permisit id exitii adversus* [Col. 0732A] *Christianos*—“he permitted this destruction against Christians”? Nor should it be *legibus datis* (“laws having been given”), but *latis* (“laws having been enacted”); and in place of *permiserat* I believe Lactantius wrote *prompserat*. The whole passage must therefore be reconstructed thus:

> “For those without rank, the punishment was fire. This instrument of destruction he had first brought forth against the Christians, laws having been enacted that, after tortures, the condemned should be scorched with slow fires.”

“To bring forth destruction,” as in Tacitus, *Annals* XII.59, “But Claudius was driven by the contrivances of that same Agrippina to bring forth every kind of savage measure”; and *Annals* IV.57, “when he brought forth cruelty and lust in his deeds, concealing them in hidden places.” GRAEVIUS.

“For those without rank,” etc. Or rather: “For those without rank, the punishment was fire (and exile, which he had first permitted against Christians), laws having been issued,” and what follows? Or perhaps: “For those without rank, the punishment was fire, not exile (which he had first permitted against Christians),” etc.? I prefer: “For those without rank, the punishment was fire (not that of exile, which had first been permitted against Christians), laws having been issued,” and what follows. GALE. [Col. 0732B]—“For those without rank,” etc. The punctuation should be: “For those without rank, the punishment was fire and exile. First against the Christians . . .” ALLIX.

“And he had permitted exile first against the Christians.” There is no place here for exile. I read: “and he had first set an example against the Christians” (*et exemplum primo adversus Christianos praemiserat*). This is confirmed by the opening words of section 22. Everything intervening should be understood of Christians. BOHERELLUS.—*Et exilii*. More correctly read *et illam*, namely, the punishment of fire; for exile has no place here, as can readily be proved from the opening of the next chapter. TOLLIUS.—I prefer: “For those without rank, the punishment was fire. And from among them he had first permitted [it] against Christians, laws having been enacted,” etc., in this sense: thus far the punishments of those prominent by some rank have been discussed. But all who had no rank, whenever they were to be punished, were burned alike; except that, since there were two classes of these obscure persons—one consisting of Christians, the other of pagans—the Christians were the first upon whom Galerius began to inflict punishment by fire. “He seems to mean that Galerius first permitted the punishment of fire against Christians,” says the most learned Cuper on this passage; and what else is this than to state precisely what we state? Compare the opening of the immediately following chapter. Columbus and Dodwell, in Dissertation XI of the *Cyprianic Dissertation*, no. 74, take another view; but their conjectures have not yet, as is apparent from what has been said, won our approval.

“And extinguished.” That is, with respect to the lamps first blazing, but not with respect to their heat; for those torches were lit and extinguished for no other reason than that immediately after their extinction, while still burning hot, they might be applied to burn each individual limb with slow fire. This is explained excellently in the English translation, but most badly suppressed in Maucroix’s.

“Which happened at last. Then throughout a long day,” etc. Read: “Which happened at last, when throughout a long day.” Pagius, at the year of Christ 305, no. 7; and before him the Oxford and Cambridge editions. [Col. 0732D] The Abo edition has: “which happened at last, when, throughout a long day, all the skin having been boiled away, the force of the fire,” etc.; but it would, I think, have punctuated better: “when, throughout a long day, all the skin having been boiled away, the force of the fire had penetrated to the inmost organs.”—“Which happened at last, when throughout a long day . . .” Ruinart’s preface to the *Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 61.—I read: “Whom at last he killed, when . . .” GALE.

“Then, after a pyre had been made, he was burned. The bodies now burned, the bones collected,” etc. Read: “Then, after a pyre had been made, they were burned. After the body had now been burned, the bones were collected.” Oxford edition of 1684, likewise Cambridge; also, as the most distinguished Graevius informed me, Nicolaus Heinsius; finally Gale.

“The bodies now.” The word *ubi* (“when”) or *postquam* (“after”) is lacking. TOLLIUS.—I should agree, were it not far more probable that our author had once written, with singular elegance: “Then, after a pyre had been made, bodies already burned were burned.” That is, bodies which the executioners had already burned with slow fire were burned with most fierce and extensive fires. For immediately before came: “which happened at last, when, throughout a long day, all the skin having been boiled away, the force of the fire had penetrated to the inmost organs”; and a little above: “Laws having been given, or enacted, that after tortures the condemned should be burned with slow fires. When they had been bound, a gentle flame was first applied beneath their feet for so long that the hard skin of the soles, contracted by the fire, was torn away from the bones.”

I know that no explicit mention precedes of bodies already burned, and that, strictly speaking, there is otherwise some difference between *uri* (“to be burned”) and *cremari* (“to be cremated”), as these words of Minucius Felix indicate: “How many of our people have endured, without any cries, not merely their right hand but their entire body being burned, cremated?” But first, that this strict distinction between *uri* and *cremari* is not always maintained is sufficiently testified, I think, by Labbe’s glossaries, where at p. 45, col. 1, and p. 197, col. 4, one reads: *cremo*, καίω; *cremat*, φλέγει; *uro*, καίω . . . φλέγω—that is, the Greek renderings common to both Latin words, καίειν and φλέγειν, show how frequently *cremare* and *urere* are synonymous. Secondly, although our author has made no explicit preceding mention of bodies already cremated, he has certainly mentioned bodies to whose inmost organs the force of the fire had penetrated; and to be burned in this way is not merely to be burned, but, among other things, to be cremated. For *cremari* without qualification is one thing, and, to use Pliny’s expression, *cremari in cineres* (“to be cremated into ashes”) another: this happens, for example, to the more serious criminals who are cremated after a pyre has been made and whose entire bodies, except usually a few bones, consequently turn to ashes.
