Thus, in this author’s proper usage, to be cremated after a pyre has been made differs from being cremated by slow fires—or, what is the same, “being burned by such slow fires that eventually all the skin is boiled away and the force of the fire penetrates to the inmost organs.” Therefore, if I judge correctly, the misplaced punctuation of a copyist first corrupted the remarkable elegance of the passage; and now learned men, with their “after the body had already been burned,” make it still more corrupt. What follows may then begin with a capital letter: “The collected bones, crushed into powder, were cast.”

“Into river and sea.” The Abo edition reads: “into rivers and sea” [Col. 0733C]. Gale likewise.—“River”: perhaps “rivers.” Oxford edition of 1684, and Cambridge following it.—“Into river and sea.” Others rightly read “into rivers or the sea.” TOLLIUS.—Columbus must certainly be consulted here on the words, “when throughout a long day.”

## CHAPTER XXII

“He exercised [them] against all.” That is, “against all his subjects,” according to Maucroix’s translation; but simply “against others,” according to the English. Yet, both because of the notes on the preceding chapter and because of what will shortly be said, I prefer to interpret: “Indiscriminately against pagans and Christians, provided that they were to be punished, possessed no rank, and were not members of his household or dependants.”

“No punishment with him was light,” etc. The Oxford and Cambridge editions say this derives from Baluz’s correction, because the manuscript reads *Nulla poenis eum levis*; Baluz himself admits and avows this in the relevant place. But might not the alternative reading be drawn just as suitably—indeed, more suitably—from the manuscript: *Nulla e poenis eorum levis* (“None of their punishments was light”), referring, that is, to the Christians mentioned immediately before: “What he had therefore learned by torturing Christians”? I cannot help believing this, because in that way our author, who near the end of the preceding chapter spoke only incidentally of Christians without rank burned during Galerius’s reign, would then proceed deliberately to the whole body of Christians. He would say, if not in precisely the same words, yet in equivalent terms, that no one ought, because mention has been made only of the most grievous punishment of certain Christians, to infer that the case was very different for the rest—as though, for example, the remainder were only banished to islands, thrown into prisons, or condemned to mines; for none of their punishments was light: not islands, not prisons, not mines [Col. 0734A], but fire, crosses, beasts. Though these things could most truly be said by this writer of Christians considered in particular, the contrary cannot be true of Christians and pagans taken together—that Galerius inflicted upon them no light punishment. For fetters and prisons belong to the lesser kinds of punishment; and in the preceding chapter, speaking of the leading men of cities, whom no one would commonly claim to have been Christians, our author says: “If they seemed worthy of death, crosses stood ready. If not, fetters were prepared”—a punishment surely extremely mild.

I add that, lest anyone now suppose the discourse returns to those persons without rank of whom it spoke briefly above—“For those without rank, the punishment was fire”—their punishment was, as is clear even from that, fire; but our author is now treating of persons against whom Galerius raged not by fire alone, but by these three means: fire, crosses, and beasts. Therefore, in my judgment, the narrative more suitably concerns the whole body of Christians than any other persons; and if this is true, then it will also plainly be better to read: “None of their punishments was light,” rather than, as commonly read, “No punishment with him was light.” It greatly assists this view that, to say nothing of poets, writers of ancient prose rather frequently used *Deum*, for example, in place of *Deorum*, *Januarium* in place of *Januariorum*, and almost invariably *nummum* in place of *nummorum*; so copyists could easily have written the abbreviated *eum* in place of *eorum*. Mamertinus, in his panegyric of Maximian Herculius: “With the gods’ indulgence I shall say it: not even Jupiter himself,” etc. Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXII: “Thus, when the day of the Kalends of January had arrived,” etc.

“Light.” Ruinart’s preface to the *Acts of the Martyrs* has *lenis* (“gentle”), whether printed against his intention or deliberately, as elsewhere. I should not wish to condemn it too strongly. Yet it does not please me, because since our author shortly afterward wrote, “Now these things were light to them,” it is clear that *poena levis* (“a light punishment”), not *lenis* (“a gentle punishment”), preceded. We shall say more of this again in its place.

[Col. 0734C] “Not islands, not prisons, not mines,” etc. That is, as we have already noted after the English translation: not banishment to islands, not imprisonment, not condemnation to mines, but to fire, to the cross, to beasts.

“Not mines.” That is, mine-shafts, to which criminals were relegated, as by Dionysius the tyrant to the stone-quarries. TOLLIUS.

“With him they were daily.” A little earlier came: “he exercised [them] against all.” And I should gladly believe that the original reading here likewise was: “against them they were daily”—that is, against Christians—and with a full stop after “daily”; the reason for this immediately follows.

“And easy.” In what good sense our author could say, for example, that beasts were “easy things” to that man, that is, to Galerius Augustus, I confess is not clear to me. Indeed, even if one reads, “Fire, cross, beasts, were daily and easy against them,” I should find it difficult to digest the statement that beasts, among other things, were called easy against Christians. Therefore, and because mention will shortly occur of several lighter punishments taken from Galerius’s household, I think the text should read: “His household, his dependants,” etc., so that our author may pass from the punishments of outsiders to the penalties and corrections of those in his own household. I also considered this correction: “Against them they were daily and customary.” But that seems somewhat further removed from the old manuscript.

“Administrators.” Labbe’s glossaries: *Administrator*, διοικητικὸς; *administro*, διοικῶ, διακονῶ; *administratio*, διοίκησις, οἰκονομία. Thus household stewards and ministers of this kind may readily be understood here: *ses officiers* (“his officers”). MAUCROIX.—But the illustrious Burnet preferred to understand those to whom Galerius entrusted the management of his own affairs.

“They were corrected by the spear.” Supply: in cases which were not capital, and when it was necessary only to correct conduct. For it follows: “In a capital case,” etc.

“It was conferred almost as a benefit.” Closer to the old text, one would correct it as: “It was conferred as a benefit.” GALE.—Correct. For *loco* is Baluz’s addition.

“Now these things had been light to them.” I prefer: “Now these things here,” etc. BOHERELLUS.—I correct: “Now these things were light in comparison with those.” GALE.—I think the fault lies not in *his* but in *fuerant*, for which *fuerunt* should be written. “Now these things were light to them,” in this sense: so severe were the punishments which Galerius Maximian inflicted on all persons, both pagans and Christians, to be considered—and in fact considered—outside his household, that the punishments he inflicted on his dependants by correction with the spear, or even by cutting off the head, were reckoned light by those dependants. What immediately preceded supports this: “Punishment by the sword was conferred upon very few, almost as a benefit.” Moreover, there is, as I mentioned above, a palpable opposition between that earlier manuscript reading, however it is ultimately corrected, “No punishment was light to him,” and the present passage, “Now these things had been light to them.” *Ce que je m'en vais dire [Col. 0735B] n'est rien au prix*—“What I am about to say is nothing by comparison.” MAUCROIX.—As though the author’s words were: “But now these things are light in comparison with those.” “Eloquence was extinguished,” etc. “Yet all these were small matters.” English translation. As though the present text of our author were: “Now these things were light,” without the pronoun *his*.

“Jurists.” That is, according to the English translation, legal experts: “All that were learned in the law.”

“Letters, however, among the evil arts,” etc. Cuper must again be consulted, where I have already mentioned him.

“Were cursed.” Passive, as shortly “were measured,” and above, “were ruled.” TOLLIUS.—Many examples could also be adduced from other writers of better standing. Cicero, for example, against Antony: “You had brought from home a crime meditated upon.” Horace, *Odes* I.1: “Wars detested by mothers”; Justin, book VII, chapter 3: “the king’s command having been carried out.”

“Military judges,” etc. That is, these judges were not civilian and learned in the law; rather, contrary to all custom and reason, they were men of military rank who did not even know what humane letters were. This recalls to my mind, among other things, those verses of Ennius:

> Wisdom is driven from the midst; affairs are conducted by force.  
> The good orator is despised; the rough soldier is loved.  
> They contend not with learned speeches but with abuse;  
> stirring up enmities, they mingle among themselves,  
> they press their case not by joining hands in law, but rather with iron,  
> and seek sovereignty, advancing with sheer force.

## CHAPTER XXIII

“It was of all.” I prefer: “It was the beginning.” GALE.—This greatly pleases me.

“The census into the provinces,” etc. Tertullian, *On Flight in Persecution*, chapter 12: “So many remedies are daily provided for increasing the treasury—from censuses, taxes, contributions, and military payments”; where, although one may not clearly see what he understood under each term, one nevertheless sees that he did not wish censuses properly so called to be confused with the others. Maucroix, in the margin of his translation: *Une imposition [Col. 0735D] sur les personnes, sur les bêtes, sur les terres labourables, arbres fruitiers, vignes*—“A tax upon persons, animals, arable lands, fruit-bearing trees, and vines.” That is to say: some imposition laid upon persons, livestock, fields, fruit trees, and vines.

“Sent once.” Rather, “sent at the same time.” GALE.—This I again strongly approve, even on account of the preceding words: “That was the beginning of public calamity and common grief.” Thus, if you now punctuate after *missus* (“sent”), as the Abo edition does, or even somewhat more strongly than it does, you will have, in my opinion, a passage excellently established in this form: “But that was the beginning of public calamity and common grief: the census was sent into provinces and cities simultaneously.” Then, “With the census-assessors,” etc. The English translation likewise favours this at almost every point: “He also took care to involve the whole Empire into a general calamity, and under a common grievance, by the new Tax that he laid both on the Cities and Provinces.”

“With the census-assessors,” etc. Lest you should be surprised that those who elsewhere are very often called *Censores* are here called *Censitores* by our author, Ulpian himself repeatedly uses our author’s term, derived from the ancient word *censio*: “The census-assessor ought to admit such equity as accords with his office, so that a man unable for certain reasons to enjoy the benefit recorded in the public registers may be relieved. Therefore, if a portion of land has perished through a chasm, he ought to be relieved by the census-assessor. If vines have died or trees withered, it is unfair that that number should be entered in the census. But if he has cut down trees or vines, he is nevertheless ordered to declare the number that existed at the time of the census, unless he proves to the census-assessor his reason for cutting them down.” We judged this passage, although rather long, so much the more worthy to be transferred here because it will also be useful under another heading for understanding what follows.

“There were the dreadful appearances of hostile tumult and captivity.” The sense may readily be that at one and the same time two different images of events presented themselves to the eyes throughout the Roman Empire: one, namely, of hostile tumult—that is, war, as we noted earlier regarding the words “as he was fearful in every tumult”; the other, of dreadful captivity. Yet let the learned reader consider whether perhaps the adjective *horrendae* (“dreadful”) belongs rather to the nominative plural *species* (“appearances”) than to the genitive *captivitatis* (“of captivity”), in this order: “There were dreadful appearances of hostile tumult and captivity.” Whatever reading may please, our author says again in chapter 24: “When he had resolved, after establishing censuses, to devour the world, he advanced to such madness that he would not allow even the Roman people to be exempt from this captivity.”

“The fields were measured *glebatim*.” I see no one who has said what it is to measure fields *glebatim*. Indeed, translators render it as though the word *glebatim* were wholly absent; yet it is certain that it occurs in the manuscript, and that it contributes greatly, in one way or another, to representing the enormity of Galerius’s census. What then are fields measured *glebatim*, or what can they more probably be? For first, the thing itself is impossible to do, and is not at all like that mentioned by the jurist Paulus in these words: “What we have said—that possession must be acquired both physically and mentally—must not be understood to mean that one who wishes to possess an estate must walk around every clod; rather, it suffices that he enter any part of the estate, provided that in mind and intention he wishes to possess the whole estate as far as its boundary.” Certainly anyone wishing to buy even a very large estate can easily walk around all its clods together and at once, without entering any part of it, by walking around its whole perimeter. But who could ever measure every individual clod in all the fields of the Roman Empire? Yet that is the explicit force of the phrase: “The fields were measured *glebatim*.” Surely no one. And if someone supposes this written as a most invidious hyperbole, our author will then have added by a similar hyperbole: “vines and trees were counted,” although the latter words have no more the flavour of hyperbole than the former. But that there is no hyperbole whatever in these latter words is shown by the census-form, devised and prescribed from the time of Ulpian, by which those possessing vineyards or acres of olive trees were obliged to declare how many vines they had in each vineyard and likewise how many trees in every acre of olive grove:

> “The census-form provides that lands be entered in the census thus: the name of each estate; in what city and district it lies; its two nearest neighbours; how many *iugera* of arable land there are which have been sown during the preceding ten years; how many vines the vineyard contains; and how many *iugera* and how many trees the olive grove contains.”

*Digest*, book L, title 15, no. 4, §1. There is no need to repeat here what was a little earlier excerpted from the same Ulpian. Accordingly, our author seems no more able to have written “the fields were measured *glebatim*” hyperbolically in the present passage, but rather to have recounted historically what actually occurred. On this very matter I now offer the following conjecture.

That kind of payment which senators formerly rendered to the Emperor on account of their estates was, among other names, called *gleba*, and “senatorial *gleba*”; likewise *aurum glebale* (“glebal gold”) and *aurum oblatitium* (“offered gold”), because it was exacted from senators not as a regular tax or assessment but as a sort of offering, as is most certain partly from both codes of law and partly from the letters of Symmachus and Synesius. Therefore I should readily believe above all that the lands for which senators paid this *gleba* acquired the designation *glebati*, or *glebatici*, or perhaps even *glebatitii*. Further, because this senatorial *gleba* was called offered gold—that is, as though it were voluntarily brought into the treasury—the lands had not been subject to measurement in earlier censuses; but Galerius’s census at last abolished this ancient immunity, so that thereafter senators were compelled to pay their *gleba* in proportion to the quantity and measure of each estate. For all these reasons taken together, and particularly in order to note the enormity of the census wherever he could, this writer finally wrote, I conjecture, one letter fewer than is commonly read, the present reading having very probably arisen over time from the beginning of the following word: *Agri glebati metiebantur*—“The *glebate* fields were measured” [Col. 0737B]. Or perhaps rather: *agri glebatici* or *glebatitii*.

However that may be, *glebatus* can be formed from *gleba*, and *glebaticus* or *glebatitius* from *glebatus*, just as *barbatus* is formed from *barba*, and *oblatitius* from *oblatus*, *adscriptitius* from *adscriptus*. For we have already encountered *aurum oblatitium* in this very subject; and serfs bound to the soil (*servi glebae adscriptitii*) are well known to all. Moreover, the adjective *glebaticus* itself occurs in the will of Perpetuus, bishop of Tours, who died at the end of the fifth century, where he mentions places of *glebatica* and transferable servitude. Thus, if one now wishes to read *agri glebatici* instead of *agri glebatim*, the final word will not be without precedent. Such are my contributions on this passage for the present, while we await better ones from learned men. For we were the first to raise a difficulty concerning the received reading.

Metiebantur (“were measured”). Tollius above said that it is passive; the following examples confirm this. Arnobius: “If the sun is larger than the world, is it measured by the breadth of one foot?” Cato, chapter 146: “Give, by the oil-measure, ten pounds of ointment.” Curtius, book III: “Then from the money of Babylon … the infantrymen’s pay was measured out at two hundred denarii each.”

Vines and trees were counted. That is, by the census officials, contrary to the old census procedure, under which, just as those possessing anything themselves assessed their property according to their right when making their declaration—for Ulpian says in the appropriate place, “Let the declarant himself assess everything”—so it was likewise their duty to count their own vines and trees for purposes of declaration, and afterwards to declare the number. This is evident from the following: “If he has cut down trees or vines, he is nevertheless ordered to declare the number that existed at the time of the census.” Compare the words of the census form cited on the preceding page.

The heads of persons were registered in the cities, the urban, etc. I would prefer: “The heads of persons were registered in the cities,” with a colon; then, “the urban and rural commons were brought together.” GALE.—Either manner of reading may certainly find its admirers and defenders. The first does so because the received punctuation itself naturally suggests the sense which the most eminent Cuperus follows in these words: “Census officers, scattered everywhere.” The other, on account of the following note in the editions published at Oxford and Cambridge: “This passage of Lactantius confirms Gothofredus’s conjecture, who inferred from Book II of the Theodosian Code, *On the Census*, that some alteration had been made by Galerius in Lycia and Pamphylia—namely, that the urban populace was subjected to the poll-tax.” For you see how that observation supports the first member of Gale’s punctuation: “the heads of persons were registered in the cities.” I shall say something further. At the very beginning of this Section came: “A census was dispatched at once into the provinces and cities”; that very clause also considerably supports Gale’s second punctuation: “the urban and rural commons were brought together.” Yet we prefer to follow the common reading with Cuperus rather than Gale’s, for the reason to be stated at the end of the next note.

Brought together (*adunatae*). As one and undifferentiated body, they were assessed in the same manner. TOLLIUS.—“Brought together.” I emend: “made equal” (*adaequatae*). GALE.—As though the meaning were that formerly such a distinction had existed between the urban and rural commons that farmers were assessed but citizens of towns were not; but that this distinction eventually ceased, when persons’ heads were registered in the cities themselves, and both classes came to be treated equally. No one fails to see that this interpretation depends entirely on the aforesaid alteration in punctuation. Yet, without changing anything, another suitable sense, different from that, can be established. For competent authors properly say that things and persons are “brought together” (*adunari*) when, having first been scattered, they are afterwards gathered into one bundle or place. Pliny, book XIX, chapter 2: “The plucked spartum, gathered in bundles into a heap for two days, is on the third day untied, spread in the sun, and dried; then it returns beneath cover in bundles.” Justin, book V, chapter 9: “Greece was filled with Athenian exiles; when even this refuge was taken away from the wretched … all made their way to Argos and Thebes … Thrasybulus … having gathered the exiles together, occupied the fortress of Phyle.” Finally, our author at the end of chapter 15: “For the soldiers had been scattered through different regions, and the pressure of time did not allow them all to be gathered together.” Thus our author could readily, and in the best Latin usage, say both of the common inhabitants of cities and of the immense multitude of country people—who from ancient times had been dispersed through the fields and had come into the cities for the census—that the urban and rural commons had been brought together in the cities; that is, assembled. Especially since nearby other places are named where, at that time, country dwellers were most miserably brought together with townspeople: namely, all the market-places.

All the market-places. The Abo edition reads, “all the market-places” (*fora omnia*), which is also Gale’s emendation and ours. Add column 413, on chapter 23.

In groups of households. Not in the way in which our author earlier used *familia* for slaves in this clause (chapter 14): “Nothing anywhere was found, since no one tortured Caesar’s household”; or elsewhere (chapter 21): “This is the custom among the Persians, that they dedicate themselves to the service of their kings, and their kings treat their people as a household.” Rather, it is used as the word *familia* among the ancients sometimes embraces the father of a household, offspring, and slaves alike, as these following words most clearly show: “Each person was present with children and slaves.”

Every most faithful slave was tortured against his master. Contrary to the rule of law, which forbids slaves to be interrogated concerning the person of their masters. Oxford and Cambridge editions.

If everything failed, etc. The passage is obscure and ambiguous. For either our author means to say: if all these things—namely, the hanging of children against parents, the torture of every most faithful slave against masters, and of wives against husbands—had at last extracted no confession, then the persons themselves were tortured against themselves, because the other measures had been in vain. Or, as I prefer, the sense is: if there were persons against whom, because they now lacked wives, children, and slaves, or because they had never possessed any such persons, neither wives, children, nor slaves could be tortured, then they themselves were used against themselves and pressed by the most severe torments.

[Col. 0738D] Things which they did not possess were entered. That is, even those things which, compelled by tortures, they declared themselves to possess, although they did not in fact possess them, were entered in the census registers. Hence shortly afterwards: “And it was always doubled, not because they found them, but because they added them as they pleased, lest they seem to have been sent in vain.” TOLLIUS.

Things which they did not possess. I prefer: “which they did not confess.” GALE.

The interpretation which Tollius now draws from the received reading is most plainly supported by Maucroix, who translated: “And when pain had wrung some avowal from their mouths, it passed as true.” Nor, to speak candidly, do I see why it should be displeasing.

No exemption on account of age or health. It seems that through copyists’ fault a *nulla* (“no”) was once omitted, and that Lactantius wrote: “No exemption on account of age, no exemption on account of health.” Nicolaus Heinsius preferred: “No exemption on account of age or health.” GRAEVIUS.

[Col. 0739A] No exemption on account of age, health. More elegant: “No exemption on account of age, none on account of health.” For our author likes to speak in this way, as in chapter 16: “whom no enemy may conquer, no snare entrap”; and in almost the same manner, chapter 21: “whose is this rite, this custom.” TOLLIUS.

Health (*valitudinis*). And here again all the other editions have *valetudinis*. Since they persist in doing this, as if their editors believed that the reading of the old manuscript could by no means be defended, observe, contrary to our earlier conclusion, what Dausquius noted on this matter in his *Orthographica*: “They produce from Horace *dura valetudo* [‘severe ill-health’]. I accept it. But since forms vary almost infinitely in spelling—since *Genitrix* is written with *i*, and *Genetrix* with *e*—why not also *valitudo*? Certainly the supine is *valitum*, whence Livy, book XXXV, has *valiturus*, lest they throw something else at us in a dream. And I observed that Vulcanius always prints *valitudo* with *i* in Apuleius, and Lipsius writes it so; thus it occurs in the most correct Paris edition of Justin.” Thus far Dausquius; had he lived today, he would surely have known that the other spelling pleased Graevius, most learned in Latin, more. For that reason we prefer it; and Dausquius himself would certainly not hesitate to set it before the usage of Lipsius and Vulcanius.

The sick and infirm were carried in—on chairs, presumably, or litters, like those of whom Acts 5:15 says: “… so that they might carry the sick out into the streets and lay them on beds and pallets.” Beza: “… so that they brought the sick out into the streets and laid them on beds and pallets.”

Years were added to children; deducted from old people. Here is the reason for both practices from Ulpian, *On Censuses* (*Digest*, book L, title 15, §3), where he says: “It is necessary to state one’s age in making the census, because age grants certain persons exemption from the burden of tribute. Thus, among the Syrians, males from the age of fourteen and females from twelve are liable to the poll-tax until their sixty-fifth year. Age, however, is considered at the time of the census.”—“Years were added.” Thus again Baluzio’s old parchment, which has likewise, at the end of chapter 35, *adiciebantur* and, in order to transfer him from second place to fourth, *reiceret*. All other editions have *adjiciebantur* and *rejiceret* in their respective places. “In these words (*adjicio, ejicio, injicio*), the second syllable must be written with two *i*s, not one,” says Gellius, book IV, chapter 17. But “the practice of inscriptions and authors is not uniform,” says Dausquius in turn in the *Orthographica*, under *adjicio*.—Indeed, *adicere* is the ancient spelling for *adjicere*, found, learned men testify, in books of every highest authority, says the anonymous author of the Notes on Dictys Cretensis.

What conquerors had done to the conquered by right of war, those things he, etc. Thus Baluzio now prints it. Earlier, with the manuscript, he had: “What the ancients had done to the conquered by right of war, he also …” Nor indeed do other editors differ, although, as will shortly be seen, neither emendation is recent.—“What the ancients.” Read: “what conquerors.” Baluzio’s first edition, in the additions; likewise the Oxford edition of 1680, at the end.—“And he.” It should read: “those things he.” Oxford and Cambridge editions.

Whom Trajan had imposed upon the Dacians. Under him, after two campaigns, Dacia was reduced to a province and thereby made tributary. Oxford and Cambridge editions.

A conqueror imposed it as a punishment. Learned men therefore rightly substituted the word “conquerors” for “ancients,” which is read in the manuscript.

And payment was given for life. Who can understand these words as they stand? Emend at my risk: “And goods were given for life” (*merces pro vita dabantur*). The goods (*merces*, plural of *merx, mercis*), not wages (*merces, mercedis*). The sense is: because the poll-tax was so great that they paid for their heads whatever money they possessed, they were compelled, whenever necessities of sustenance had to be purchased, to give their wares for food. Thus *merces* is a plural, not a singular. As for *ad vitam*, “for sustenance” or “for food,” Terence will provide an example if you seek one, in the *Phormio* (Act II, scene 2, verses 16–17):

> A poor man, whose livelihood depended on his labor,  
> generally kept himself in the country.

[Col. 0740A] Hence the latest paraphrast rightly explains: “A poor man who sought his livelihood by rural labor and work.” In this respect Latin *vita* plainly corresponds to Greek βίῳ (*biō*), which denotes both life and sustenance indiscriminately. Maucroix, if you prefer to follow him: “The freedom to breathe was bought at the price of money.” Literally: “The liberty of breathing was redeemed with silver.” The English translation, if perhaps it may please you more, is: “After that all men were thus listed, then so much money was laid upon every man’s head, as if he had been to pay so much for his life.” That is: after all had thus been enrolled, such a sum of money was imposed upon each person’s head as though the issue had been the redemption of each person’s life.

By the same census officers. Thus in chapter 31, “concerning these same men”; in chapter 34, “as pleased these same persons”; and in chapter 48, “when you perceive that it has been granted by us to these same persons”—indeed, in that final chapter, “to these same Christians” occurs three times. I would not observe this unless this author seemed here to have condemned alike Ennius’s *isdem*, Cicero’s *eisdem*, and others’ *iisdem*, while preferring to all of them *hisdem*, “a match for many others.” Yet Cicero makes no mention of this form in the *Orator*, where, setting forth his judgment concerning the three earlier modes of expression, he says: “Ennius approved *in templis isdem* [‘in the same temples’]; but *eisdem* was more correct, though *eisdem* was less rich. *Iisdem* sounded ill. Custom has obtained permission to err for the sake of pleasantness.”

[Note: Col. 0740D. After Cicero’s time Ovid too approved it in this verse: “Under the same masters you will behold the house.”]

And it was always doubled, etc. I confidently say that there is no sense unless you punctuate thus: “And it was always doubled by them—not by finding [it], but by adding as they pleased, lest they seem to have been sent in vain.” That is: they always diligently doubled the taxes and similar matters, not because they found more things for which payment was due, but because they added more at will, lest they seem to have been dispatched for nothing. For just before came: “Others were sent after others as though they were going to find MORE.” Hence shortly afterwards “not finding” is said briefly for “not finding more,” by implication from the common element (*ἀπὸ τοῦ κοινοῦ*); and again shortly thereafter, “but adding as they pleased,” for “but adding more, as they pleased,” in the same fashion.

And no less was paid. The Abo edition has “and nonetheless” (*nihilominus*). So too Gale.

Nor even to die free of charge. The Cambridge edition has *saltem* rather than *saltim*; on this spelling difference consult Dausquius in the *Orthographica*. The Abo edition also punctuated this whole passage well thus: “so that it was now permitted neither to live nor even to die free of charge.”

Secure from every kind of wrong. The reading of the old sheet is: “Secure from every kind of wrong and atis.” From these last letters Baluzio, in the first edition, made *injurietatis*, not without defending the word; and all later editors down to the present printed the same. Yet shortly afterwards, in the additions, he warned that it should be read “secure from wrong,” and that his earlier note on this passage should be deleted. Therefore do not consult that earlier note above, but another in its place, column 338; nor read here any longer *injurietatis*, but “secure from wrong.”

[Col. 0740D] *Injurietatis*. Baluzio wished to establish this unusual word in legal Latin on the authority of several examples, but in a vain effort, as he himself acknowledges; for in the corrections appended to the end of his work he declares that “secure from wrong” is beyond doubt the reading. Oxford and Cambridge editions.

But an impious man. It will be more biting if you read it ironically, “but a pious man”; and I think Lactantius wrote so. TOLLIUS.—I would not deny it, although shortly I shall conjecture that one should read not “merciful” but “merciless.”

He took pity on them. This is an expression of those times. TOLLIUS.—Nicolaus Heinsius emended: “He pitied them.” GRAEVIUS.—The Abo edition and Gale punctuate after “them.”

So that they might not be in need. I should be surprised if the sense were not “so that they might lack nothing,” that is, might be in need of nothing; just as the Vulgate at 1 Corinthians 11:22: “You shame those who do not have,” for “those who have nothing.”

So merciful a man. I prefer: “I see a merciful man.” GALE.—The sense requires us to read: “O merciful man!” Elsewhere in Terence occurs, “Can a man be so graceless and unfortunate …?” But that mode of speaking has no place here. TOLLIUS.—In my judgment, a better emendation is: “But, O merciless man, who …” This is supported by the preceding reading, “an impious man,” if it is to be retained; nor is it inconsistent with Tollius’s “pious man,” if, as I believe, it is to be accepted. For after our author has called Galerius a pious man ironically, he then calls him by his true name—as though correcting himself—merciless.

Thus, while he took precautions. Read: “Thus, while he takes precautions,” as the most distinguished Columbus also saw. Otherwise *subterfugeret* [“he evaded”] should be replaced by *subterfugiat* [“he may evade”]. TOLLIUS.—I further thought that punctuation was required after “thus,” in this manner: “Thus, while he takes care lest …”

Of wretched men. What? Were there no wretched women among the wretched at that time, that our author should mention only wretched men? Or did Galerius spare wretched women while not sparing wretched men? But none of this is necessary. The author’s hand undoubtedly wrote: “Thus, while he takes care lest anyone evade the census by the pretence of begging, he kills, against every law of humanity, a multitude of truly wretched persons.” That is, he contrasts the truly wretched with those persons of feigned beggary from whom Galerius did not wish anyone to escape the census.

## Chapter XXIV

Now it drew near. Although our author uses this verb again in chapter 46, and although the Vulgate uses it five times in its respective passages (Judges 19:9; Isaiah 41:1), I nevertheless more readily believe that from its original character it was poetic rather than prose. For, for example, one instance occurs in Plautus’s *Truculentus* (Act II, scene 6), and fourteen in Virgil; by contrast, none in Cicero, Suetonius, or Justin.

Now it drew near. Read: “Now it was drawing near.” TOLLIUS.

Wrongly, I think, since immediately afterward the perfect tense is again used: “and the appointed time came.” Maucroix, however, follows Tollius, lest I deceive anyone: “But the time of divine justice was approaching.”

His affairs were dissolving and slipping away. Virgil, *Aeneid* II:

> The hope of the Danaans slips away from him  
> and, having slid backward, is borne back.

GALE.

While he is occupied. Why not rather: “While he was occupied”? For these certainly seem to cohere poorly: “He had not yet turned his mind to it, while he is …” But in any case *nondum animum intenderat, dum esset*—that is, “he had not yet turned his mind to it, while he was,” or “when he was,” or “meanwhile while he was,” etc.—is of the same kind as Virgil at the beginning of the *Aeneid*:

> Having also suffered much in war, while he founded a city.

And he awaited his death. There is an elegant play on this word in Quintilian: when a son accused of plotting parricide said that he did not await his father’s death, the father replied, at once wittily and sternly: “No, I would rather that you did await it.” TOLLIUS.

When he was seriously ill. That is, as the English translation excellently renders it, “when Constantius was gravely sick.” So Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* II: “The limbs suffer severely,” for “are in very bad condition; are very ill.”

He had demanded him back in vain. Baluzio testifies that these words do not occur in the old manuscript. But since the sense would have been incomplete without some supplement, none could be added more suitably than what is supplied by the Fragment concerning Constantius Chlorus, where it is read: “Constantine, a hostage with Diocletian and Galerius, served bravely in Asia under them. After Diocletian and Herculius had laid down imperial power, Constantius demanded him back from Galerius. But Galerius exposed him to many dangers beforehand.” Oxford and Cambridge editions.

For he had often attacked the young man by plots as well. Delete *in*, as elsewhere too. BOHERELLUS.

Young man. Yet earlier he was called an adolescent. For in chapter XVIII: “Constantius also had a son, Constantine, a most holy adolescent”; and again in chapter 29 he will be denoted by the word *adolescens*: “The adolescent trusts Maximian Herculius as experienced and old.” Correctly. But for our author, as is not uncommon among others, *juvenis* and *adolescens* are synonyms. And, more notably, he understands “young man” to mean a man already thirty-five years old, or at least about thirty-four years completed. Constantine was indeed born in A.D. 272, as Pagius observed before us (*Critica Baroniana*, on A.D. 337, no. 2). And in Dodwell’s Cyprianic Dissertations (namely the eleventh, no. 67), Lactantius in our chapter calls Constantine *juvenis* in A.D. 306. If this is true, as certainly it is, then not only is the number of years we have stated established; this passage can moreover shed considerable light upon many difficulties of history.

Lest he stir up civil arms against himself and, what he feared most, the hatred of the soldiers. Therefore, as we said before, no one acquires others’ hatred except by gaining it through ungrateful conduct, as we explained there in different words. Here, moreover, lest you be unaware of it, the most distinguished Gale and Pagius (*Critica Baroniana*, on A.D. 306, no. 5), and before both the Abo editor, rightly judged it worthwhile to punctuate after “civil,” thus: “Lest civil arms against himself—and, what he feared most—”; with what follows.

Under the pretext of military exercise. See Sallust, *Jugurthine War*, concerning Micipsa’s approaching death and Jugurtha. But here the conjunction *and* is lacking, having been absorbed by the preceding syllable; therefore read: “and under the pretext of exercise.” TOLLIUS.—What precedes absolutely requires this reading. For “he had also attacked him by plots” came before, after which words a second *and* must follow. We ourselves have already suspected in two other places that the same conjunction was similarly absorbed, and have restored it as best we could.

He had exposed him to wild beasts. “He had exposed Constantine to a lion.” MAUCROIX.—As though our author wrote not “to wild beasts” but “to a lion,” or “to a wild beast,” in the singular; whereas he used the plural, and from this it is highly probable that Galerius, who attacked Constantine not once but often with human plots, likewise exposed him to wild beasts not once but repeatedly. The English translation agrees with us: “he had engaged him to encounter with Wild Beasts.”

At the very turning-point. Virgil, *Aeneid* I:

> He will not cease at so great a turning-point of affairs.

GALE.

“At the very turning-point,” that is, at the very crisis or moment of opportunity for deliverance. Servius on the preceding verse of Virgil: “Either he said this demonstratively: not even to such an extent—that is, he will not cease even for a brief occasion; or it should simply be understood: he cannot cease amid so great an opportunity of affairs.” It is drawn, as the saying goes, from the proverb, “The matter is at its hinge,” that is, at a crisis. The English translation aptly renders it: “In the last and critical moment,” almost literally, “at the final and decisive moment.”

For more often. Some word is lacking after *saepius* (“more often”): for example, *rogatus* (“when asked”) or *sollicitatus* (“when urged”), if one trusts Boherellus; *repetenti* (“when demanding him back”), if one trusts Tollius.—“For more often.” *Saepius* is corrupt, for he gave the seal not often but only once. Read: “For later” (*serius*). GRAEVIUS, likewise GALE.—With the good leave of those most learned men, I preferred—and still prefer—“and more often,” linking it to what precedes in this manner: “who rescued him from his hands at the very turning-point, and more often besides.” Then shortly afterward: “When he could no longer refuse for a long time.” Thus, in a word, just as our author has said that Constantine was often attacked by the plots of Galerius, or of others whom he had placed in charge of this, and likewise exposed to beasts more than once, so he also observed that Constantine was rescued more than once from Galerius’s hands when he was in extreme danger.

When he could no longer refuse [for a longer time]. The manuscript, and consequently all editions that had hitherto been published, read: “when he could no longer refuse for a long time.” Except that in the very first edition Baluzio placed, at the end of the work in the errata list, the correction that you see printed here. The judgments of learned men concerning the old sheet’s reading follow.

“When he could not kill [him] secretly for a long time, etc.” Read: “when he could not kill him secretly for a long time.” Earlier he related that Constantine had often been attacked by plots. GRAEVIUS.—Boherellus reads “when he could not refuse for so long”; Gale emends “when he could no longer refuse”; Tollius prefers “when he could not refuse for a longer time.”

I preferred: “When he could no longer refuse for a long time,” so that the order and sense are: when he could no longer continue refusing Constantine to his father for long; and this because he had already refused him longer than he could still refuse him for long.

A seal. Interpreters have understood this differently. Maucroix: “Galerius gave him his leave and signed it with his hand,” as though our author’s words were: “he gave him a pass of leave, signed in his own hand.” The English translation: “A pass, which had the seal put to it.” That is, a leave-pass furnished with a seal.

Intending to hold him back (*retentaturus*). Gale wishes *retenturus* (“intending to retain”) to be read. This is certainly plainer and could very suitably have been used by our author. But he either used *retentandi* because it is sometimes employed for simple *retinere*, “to retain.” Cicero, book I, *On Divination*:

> For all retain the portent in mindful recollection.

That is, they retain it. Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXIX: “with no one advising better things or holding him back,” that is, likewise, restraining him. Finally Aurelius Victor, *On the Caesars*: “Since the burden of wars … pressed more urgently, the empire was as though divided: all Gaul beyond the Alps was entrusted to Constantius; Africa and Italy to Herculius; the Illyrian coast as far as the strait of Pontus to Galerius; Valerius held back the rest”—plainly, if ever anything was, for “held.” Or he used it because, since Galerius had already often detained Constantine under this or that pretext, there arose from this a certain necessity of using a frequentative verb rather than another. Or finally because Latins not infrequently express by *retentare* the very efforts by which we try to hold back persons striving to leave us, or things that are difficult to preserve. Of persons, Plautus, *Asinaria*, Act III, scene 3: “Why do you now hold me back?” The same author, *Rudens*, Act III, final scene: “Do you still hold [me] back?” Of things, the life of Antony in Athanasius, volume II, p. 450, Commelin edition: “In sum, we must perceive that even if we wish to hold on to our riches, by the law of death we are torn unwillingly away from them.” I add incidentally, although I know it is irrelevant to this passage, that among the ancients *retentare* is also found for simple *tenere*, “to hold.” Spartianus, at the beginning of the *Aelius Verus*: “It is my intention, Diocletian Augustus, to write of as many princes as possible, not only of those who held the first place in this office which you govern,” that is, possessed it.

He might be detained. Better: “he might be held back,” as shortly before “intending to hold him back” is read. TOLLIUS.

He hastened to depart. Ovid, *Fasti* VI: “… though you hasten, Caesar, to conquer.” Sulpicius Severus, at the beginning of his *Sacred History*: “those who hastened to learn divine matters through a concise reading.”

Through many stopping-places. That stations for overnight lodging (*mansiones*) and halting-stations (*stativae*) had much in common cannot be denied. First, for example, public horses were kept at both. Our author says of the former in this very passage: “Having removed all the public horses through many stopping-places.” Of the halting-stations, or stations, Thomas Magister in Du Cange’s Latin Glossary, under MANSIO: “The public fields at the various places are stations”; Du Cange: “houses where public horses were also kept.” Secondly, at both alike, persons who had undertaken a journey for private reasons commonly took food. Finally, as Lampridius will now show, even in military expeditions stopping-places and halting-stations were arranged at fixed intervals along routes, serving to receive and refresh the troops. Yet they otherwise differed from one another, contrary to the view apparently held by the most distinguished Du Cange. Lampridius, in *Alexander Severus*: “He undertook military expeditions … The secrets of wars were kept silent; but the days of travel were publicly posted, so that an edict hung up two months beforehand, in which was written: ‘On that day, at that hour, I shall leave the city; and, if the gods will, I shall remain in the first stopping-place;’ then, in order, the stopping-places; then the halting-stations; then where provisions were to be received.” Accordingly, at halting-stations, around midday and not for long—whence their names *stationes* and *mutationes*, and in Greek ἀλλαγῶν (“changes”)—both soldiers and any others travelling either by emperors’ order or on private business halted and took food. At stopping-places, however, they halted toward evening and throughout the whole night. Du Cange rightly says on this subject: “Among Latin writers, *mansio* is called the place where they rested for the night after completing a day’s journey; hence it is very often taken for a single day’s journey.” This is confirmed by the Disputation of Archelaus, bishop of Mesopotamia, against Manichaeus (at the end of Sozomen, Valesius edition), near its beginning: “Turbo … delivered the letter he had received to the person whom Mani had instructed, having completed the whole journey in five days … during which he endured much labor and hardship. For whenever, toward evening, he arrived as a stranger at lodging … they even drove Turbo from their inns, not granting him even water to drink. As he endured these things daily, and worse, from those who presided over the stopping-places and lodgings in the several places, etc.”

When he had deliberately slept until midday. “Who deliberately did so? Who wished to pursue Constantine?” Nicolaus Heinsius once asked, as Graevius, his distinguished colleague, testifies; Heinsius therefore held that Lactantius had written “as usual” (*consueto*). But let us in turn ask the most learned shade: who would have wished Galerius to pursue Constantine, when he did not at all know that Constantine had departed? Galerius rather deliberately slept—or lay in bed and pretended to sleep—until midday, because the day before he had ordered Constantine to depart the next morning after receiving his instructions. By sleeping until midday on the following day, he thought that he was at least trying to hold Constantine back, if he was not actually holding him back, since Constantine had departed after supper the previous evening; he was ignorant of his departure and thought to gain a day for himself. The received reading is therefore sound, unless I am greatly mistaken, and should be retained.

So that he might have him brought back. Spartianus, in *Caracalla*: “He had his brother killed in the Palace.” Nor does Mamertinus speak very differently (*In Praise of Maximian Augustus*): “That laurel gained by the nations bordering Syria whom you conquered, and that Rhaetian and that Sarmatian laurel, Maximian, caused you to triumph with pious joy.” The Vulgate, Matthew 5:45: “That you may be children of your Father … who causes his sun to rise upon the good and the evil.” Several similar examples occur in Plautus’s *Persa* and *Epidicus*.

The public post had been stripped bare for him. Zosimus, book II: “At the stations, he mutilated the horses maintained by the public treasury as soon as he reached the station, leaving them useless, and used those standing ready at the next stations.” Oxford and Cambridge editions.

Stripped bare. Perhaps rather “cut off” (*truncatus*) or “now given” (*jam datus*)? GALE, who also added: “See Ammianus, book XXX.”

He could scarcely hold back his tears. See again the same place, and Cuperus’s very full discussion there.

Who, having commended him to the soldiers, handed over imperial power into his hands. Am I mistaken, or is the sense: he commended Constantine to the soldiers before his arrival, so that after his own death they might create him emperor; then he himself handed to Constantine the purple, the insignia of imperial rank, into his hands? This may certainly be the case, just as in the following words concerning Esther: “And it happened on the third day that Esther was clothed with kingship”—for this is the literal sense of the Hebrew. The meaning is: “But on the third day Esther was clothed in royal garments,” as the Vulgate interpreter rendered it excellently; or, as the Septuagint translated: “And it happened on the third day that Esther put on royal garments.” Nor do the matters which we shall adduce from Dodwell in the following column oppose this.

He handed over imperial power into his hands. Namely, Augustan imperial power. For Lactantius ordinarily denotes nothing else by the name “imperial power.” DODWELL, *Cyprianic Dissertation* XI, no. 85.—He ordinarily does; yet in this work Caesar’s authority too is sometimes signified by the same word. I do not say this as though I think our author is now speaking of Caesar’s authority; but because, in fact, in chapter 18, when the choice of two Caesars was being discussed, and Constantine had been mentioned by Diocletian as most worthy of that height, Galerius immediately bestowed upon that Caesarean power the straightforward designation of *imperium*, in these words: “He is not worthy. For if he despised me as a private man, what will he do when he has received imperial power?” The use of this word by this writer is therefore not invariably of Augustan imperial power; it varies.

And so forth. That is, “and in this manner.” For here *ita* is not used in the sense of “then,” as elsewhere. Rather, Constantius Chlorus, who had greatly desired to hand the purple to his son with his own hand, and had said, for example, that, once he had done this, he would die without any longing for life, received on his bed the rest from life which he desired, after he had in fact handed imperial power to Constantine. This manner of speaking, especially because it occurs in this author, can and ought to cause no small difficulty for the most distinguished bishop of Meaux, who considers Constantius Chlorus among the great persecutors of the Church. For our author, as the final words of the first chapter indicate, did not simply propose in this little work to deal with the authors of persecutions, but chiefly to explain by what punishments the severity of the heavenly Judge avenged itself upon them.

Thus above, in chapter 2, concerning Nero: “Yet he did not go unpunished. For God regarded the vexation of His people. [Col. 0745C] Cast down therefore from the height of imperial power, and hurled from on high as a helpless tyrant, he suddenly appeared nowhere, so that not even a place of burial on earth appeared for so evil a beast.” And in chapter 3, concerning Domitian: “He ruled in safety . . . until he stretched out impious hands against the Lord. But after he had been urged by the prompting of demons to persecute the righteous people, he was delivered into the hands of his enemies and paid the penalty. Nor was it sufficient vengeance that he was killed at home: even the memory of his name was erased”; and so forth concerning the rest. But when he says that Constantius Chlorus received the rest from life which he had desired, what, I ask, does he say that suggests the severity of the heavenly Judge, rather than the great kindness and mercy of God? Clearly, then, Constantine’s father was not, for this writer, one of the more notable persecutors of the Church. [Col. 0745D]

Still less was he such for Maucroix, whose translation reads: *Il expira doucement comme il avait souhaité*—“He died gently, as he had wished.” Indeed, he was much less so for Eusebius, who called the death of Constantius *τέλος τοῦ βίου εὐδόκιμον καὶ τρισμακάριον*, “a praiseworthy and thrice-blessed end of life.” I know from chapter 5 of this book that the enemies of God do not always receive a recompense proportionate to their crime. But neither our author nor Eusebius anywhere counted Constantius among the enemies of God. Let the most learned prelate therefore consider how he can know Constantine’s father better than those two contemporaries of Constantius Chlorus could have known him.

For among other matters Bossuet reports after Eusebius that the martyr Procopius was commanded to sacrifice to four emperors, and thus to Constantius Chlorus, one of them. But this fact, I say, together with the rest which he has advanced for his company of persecutors, was as well known, as all will admit, to Eusebius as to the bishop of Meaux. Yet Eusebius most explicitly excluded Constantius Chlorus from the number of the Persecutors and assigned him a thrice-blessed death. Indeed, see, what is more, Ruinart’s Preface to the *Acts of the Martyrs*, in which he frankly concedes that no martyr existed under Constantius’ rule, while urging against Dodwell only the religious assemblies which Constantius allowed to be destroyed and Diocletian’s edicts which, according to Ruinart, were published in Gaul while Constantius was still Caesar and were not rescinded by him after he became Augustus. These may be marks of a prince excessively compliant and not resisting persecution as he ought, but not of one who himself persecutes. We have already said more on this matter above.

Moreover, that Constantius Chlorus died in the year of Christ 306, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August [25 July], as Idatius in the *Fasti* and Socrates have it, is established by the evidence I adduced in Dissertation *Hypat.* ch. 2, no. 19. Nor is Socrates, as some very learned men thought, inconsistent in book I, chapter 1, where he says that Constantius died on the first year of the 271st Olympiad, which is completed in the current year of Christ 306, in July. For Socrates, after the manner of many Easterners, who begin all eras in September, begins the [Col. 0746B] second year of Olympiad CCLXXI only in September of this Christian year, as I show elsewhere. Neither Scaliger nor Petavius nor Calvisius was able to solve this difficulty. In his book on the Greek writers of Byzantine affairs, part I, chapter 1, nos. 19 ff., Hanke argues at length that Constantius died in the preceding year and that Constantine was raised to the imperial office in that same year. But his foundations were overturned by us in the cited Dissertation, although we had not seen that book when we published it.

“Constantine, having assumed the imperial power, Augustus,” etc. His father Constantius, himself Augustus before Galerius, made him Augustus. Immediately upon his father’s death the army also proclaimed him Augustus; by the custom of those times, that army possessed the right of proclamation. Galerius, however, opposed the title of Augustus and confirmed for him only the dignity of Caesar. For Lactantius writes that Galerius contrived “that, by naming Severus Augustus, he should order Constantine to be called not emperor, as he had been made, but Caesar together with Maximinus, in order to cast him down from second place into fourth”—Maximinus himself, of course, being placed before him. That he actually did this is also clear from the Alexandrian *Fasti* of the Usserian manuscript, whose author was, I believe, Theon of Alexandria, who brought them down to the year of the Lord 372.

There, for the consuls of the year 307, recognized by the Eastern Empire, we read: *Σεβῆρον σεβαστὸν καὶ Μαξιμιανὸν Καίσαρα*, “Severus Augustus and Maximian Caesar”—that is, our Maximinus, whose first consulship Baluze could not discover; for writers of that period often confuse these names with one another. Constantine therefore moderated his use of the title Augustus for a time, as we learn also from the panegyric of an anonymous author contemporary with those times.

DODWELL, *Diss. Cyp.* XI, no. 85. [Col. 0746D]—This passage from Eumenius’ panegyric upon Constantine may strongly confirm it: “O Britain, fortunate and now happier than all lands, which first beheld Constantine Caesar!” Yet I judge it more correctly, because thus the whole narrative of our author will hang together better, that Constantine was first created emperor of the Gauls by his father, as Orosius expresses it. Then, after his father’s death, he was proclaimed by the soldiers *βασιλέα τελεώτατον καὶ σεβαστόν*, “a most perfect king and Augustus,” in Eusebius’ words. Thirdly, by virtue of the supreme power which he saw had been conferred upon him by his father and the army, he immediately issued, with the title Augustus prefixed, an edict in favour of the Christians in Gaul, restoring them to the public worship of their God.

All this occurred before Galerius had received from Britain any report of Constantine’s succession to his father’s place, and hence before he could have devised what will be recounted in the following chapter. Only when, a few days later, the laurel-crowned image of the new Augustus had been brought to the evil beast did Galerius begin to devise that Severus, who was of more mature age, should be called Augustus, and thus that Constantine’s imperial power should be reduced to Caesarian rank. Constantine, after he had understood Galerius’ intention somewhat later, abstained from the title of Augustus which he had previously assumed, until Galerius, abolishing the name of Caesars, ordered Constantine and three others to be called emperors, as we shall see at the end of chapter 32. Add Toinard’s note on this passage.

“He did nothing before restoring the Christians to their worship and their God.” Therefore his father Constantius had permitted public worship of Christ to be prohibited for them, as we explained above and as, before us, the very distinguished Dodwell and Pagi had also inferred.

“To restore.” “Might restore”: Gale; likewise Toinard on this passage, in the author’s words. They accordingly wish these words to be understood as though the construction were: “He did nothing before he might restore the Christians to their worship and their God.”

“The restoration of the holy religion.” “Restored”: the Abo edition, which Boherellus wished to correct in this way.

[Col. 0747B] “The restoration of the holy religion.” What if, rather, we should read, “what belonged to them restored to their holy religion,” or “the temples restored”? GALE.—I reject nothing. But what if nevertheless nothing needs changing, and here *restituta*, used substantively, means “restoration,” as in the Raphelengian edition of Apuleius, in this title: “THE ADDRESS (*ALLOCUTA*) OF HERMES TRISMEGISTUS ON THE NATURE OF THE GODS TO ASCLEPIUS, with Apuleius, as some maintain, as translator”? There *allocuta* most plainly signifies “an address,” and indeed the word *allocutio* is found in some manuscripts in its place. So too in Tertullian we find *defensam* for *defensio*, that is, “defence” or “vindication”; in Cyprian, *remissam* for *remissio*, “remission”; in John of Girona, *relatam* for *relatio*, “report”; and so with others. Let the learned judge.

## CHAPTER XXV

“His laurel-crowned image.” That is, according to the English translation, his image with the insignia of imperial dignity placed upon it; or, if it must be rendered literally, with its emblems: “His image, with the characters of the imperial dignity upon it.” From this, anyone can infer what Constantine had been made by his dying father, or at least by the army after Constantius’ death: Augustus, or only Caesar.

“His image was brought.” From Herodian we learn that this custom originated with Elagabalus. TOLLIUS.

“To the evil beast”: Galerius Maximianus, namely. PAGIUS, who joined together what the translators had separately supplied for purposes of explanation. Maucroix’s translation indeed has Galerius for “the evil beast,” while the English has Maximianus.

“He deliberated long whether to receive it.” “The matter was nearly at the point that he,” etc. The reading is certainly tolerable enough. Yet this alternative reading might equally well, if not better, be adopted from our author: “He deliberated long whether to receive it, or to burn both it and the man who had brought it. The matter was nearly at the point, had not his friends,” and what follows.

“Friends.” “His ministers,” says Maucroix, as if our author had written: “Those who assisted him in administering the empire.” Correctly. For, as the distinguished Graevius observed on Justin I.5, the *friends* of kings were formerly those who served as their counsellors. See the passage, where many examples are gathered on this subject.

“Unknown Caesars”: Severus, namely, and Maximinus Daia. This is certain and clear from chapter 19: “Then suddenly the old man Diocletian proclaimed Severus and Maximinus Caesars. All were astonished. After a few words had intervened, Maximian, before all present, stretched his hand backwards and drew Daia forward from behind . . . stripped off his private dress and placed him in the midst. All wondered who he was, whence he came,” and what follows.

“The image.” “The statue,” says the English translation. Since its author had previously rendered the same word at the beginning of this chapter literally as “image,” he shows either that he makes no distinction between statues and images, or at least that he thinks the discussion in neither place concerns a flat painted portrait sent by Constantine to Galerius, but, for example, a cast statue. Yet, on the contrary, one or two passages warn us that statues and images should not be confused in our author. Such are these. In chapter 44: “The emperor Constantine learned of Maximinus’ perfidy, discovered letters, found STATUES AND IMAGES.” Likewise chapter 42: “At the same time the STATUES of the old Maximian were torn down by Constantine’s order, AND THE IMAGES in which he was depicted with him were removed.” Compare the very learned annotations, characteristically so, of the most distinguished Cuperus on this latter passage.

“Into partnership”: in the empire, of course, as the translators rightly supplied.

“His plans were already disturbed.” Those recounted in chapter 20. TOLLIUS.

“And he could not name another beyond the number, as he had wished.” Nowhere do we see in our author that Galerius ever wished to confer the name and power of Caesar or Augustus upon anyone beyond the prescribed number; indeed, we see the opposite most plainly three times in what precedes. Namely, in chapter 18: “He replied that Diocletian’s arrangement ought to be preserved forever: that there should be two senior men in the state holding supreme power, and likewise two junior men to assist them.” Then in chapter 20, in two passages: first, where, if the matter concerns creating a third Augustus beyond the number, we left Galerius waiting for Constantius to die, so that, once he had died, he might name Licinius—his friend from their old mess companionship, familiar with him from his first military service, and the man whose counsels he employed in all administration—Augustus and brother in his place; and again, where, if the question is of creating a third Caesar beyond the number, Galerius is likewise left by our author contemplating the future conferral of Caesarian rank upon his son Candidianus, not because there would then be three Caesars in the Roman Empire, but only two, since Galerius simultaneously planned to lay down imperial power and to make Severus, one of the Caesars, a second “Augustus, so that Licinius and Severus might hold the supreme power of the Empire, while Maximinus and Candidianus might bear the secondary name of Caesars, and he, surrounded by an impregnable wall, might pass a secure and tranquil old age.”

Since this is so, and since all his designs truly tended to that end, what can these words now mean: “And he could not name another beyond the number, as he had wished”?

Maucroix’s translation is: *Il ne pouvait nommer un troisième César contre la disposition de Dioclétien*—“He could not name a third Caesar contrary to Diocletian’s arrangement.” But it is certain from what has just been said that Galerius never contemplated naming a third Caesar, and again from these words in chapter 20: “He did not wish to make Licinius Caesar, lest he should name his son, and so that later he might name him Augustus and brother in Constantius’ place.” Moreover, the two words found in the manuscript, *ut voluerat*, “as he had wished,” appear nowhere in Maucroix’s translation.

The English reads: “Nor could he now make another Emperour supernumerary”; that is, “Nor could he make another emperor beyond the number.” But Galerius had not even once previously made such a supernumerary emperor, as that translation suggests; nor had he ever contemplated creating any such person, as we have just shown; nor, finally, does the same translation any more preserve the two words *ut voluerat*. What then? Must they be wholly removed, as words intruded into this passage by copyists under an evil fate? Or should they rather be retained, while the corruption lies elsewhere? I think it lies elsewhere. My conjecture, in one word, is that the true text of the entire passage was once: “His plans were already disturbed, and he could not name another self within the number, as he had wished” (*nec poterat alterum se intra numerum nuncupare, ut voluerat*); that is, Licinius, his greatest friend, whom he regarded as another self.

For Galerius had previously in fact resolved, as we have already recalled from chapter 20, to appoint Licinius, his friend from their old mess companionship and familiar from his first military service, in Constantius’ place immediately upon Constantius’ death, and to name him Augustus, thus preserving Diocletian’s arrangement in every respect. But while matters stood thus, Constantine succeeded to his father’s place contrary to Galerius’ expectation. Galerius could therefore no longer name Licinius, his other self, within the number, as he had wished.

You will find *alterum me*, “another me,” in a similar sense more than once in Cicero’s letters. For example, writing to Gaius Caesar: “See how fully I have persuaded myself that you are another self to me, not only in matters pertaining to myself, but also in those pertaining to my friends”; and to Atticus: “Here pardon me; for I accuse myself much more, and then you, as another self.” Again elsewhere: “He said that he would be another self to me in all matters”; and again to Brutus: “Setting out for you, as for another self.” What then? When in Cicero’s *Laelius* a true friend is said to be as another same self—for “he is indeed,” he says, “as another self”—could *alter idem* ever mean anything other than what we French say every day, *un autre soi-même*, “another self”? I acknowledge, meanwhile, that the received reading of our passage, *alterum extra numerum*, differs no slightly from the emendation we propose, *alterum se intra numerum*. But, as you have seen, the author had necessarily to be reconciled with himself; and we draw this reconciliation as best we can from the work itself. If anyone has a better one, we shall not reject it.

[Col. 0749B] “That he might name Severus, who was of more mature age.” At the time of year when these events occurred, Constantine was in his thirty-fifth year. For they occurred after the eighth day before the Kalends of August, the day on which Constantius Chlorus died; and Constantine, as we have previously maintained with Pagi, had been born in the year of Christ 272, on the third day before the Kalends of March [27 February], or at the latest on the day before the Kalends of April [31 March]. Let him who can infer from this how many years Severus had already lived at the time in question. Certainly, if he was not older, he had scarcely completed fewer than thirty-five.

“But that Constantine should be called not emperor, as he had been made, but Caesar,” etc. Our author, as you see, strongly maintains his view that Constantius handed imperial power to his son Constantine and made him Augustus. And the administration of those times becomes more probable to me the more I consider it: the first among the Augusti was generally able to do everything in such matters. Now Constantius was the senior Augustus, as is certain from the beginning of chapter 20. The words are: “For Galerius despised Constantius, although he necessarily had to be named first.” Why, then, should Galerius, after Constantius’ death the senior Augustus in relation to Constantine, not have thought that he could alter what Constantius, senior Augustus in relation to Galerius, had done to his son Constantine by his own right—and have actually altered it in the manner now recounted? Yet the most learned Cuperus thinks otherwise, lest I conceal it.

I add that, since our author here establishes so great a distinction between an emperor and a Caesar when he says that Constantine “should be called not emperor, as he had been made, but Caesar together with Maximinus,” this strongly confirms what we have stated above against Pagi from this very writer.

Nor, conversely, is what we have said above concerning the difference of the two terms overturned because the same Constantine who at the end of the preceding chapter was called Augustus is now called emperor in the conclusion of this chapter. For, just as Christians daily call the one God “Best” in one sense, “Greatest” in another, and sometimes jointly “Best and Greatest,” so in antiquity the titles Augustus and emperor were applied to the same man, though under different conceptions. Here, lest you be unaware, we have “emperor” rather than “Augustus” concerning Constantine because in the immediately preceding words we had “Augustus” concerning Severus, and our author likes to vary phrases and terms as far as possible.

“But Caesar.” What the most learned men have noted here concerning the Caesarian, so to speak, birthday of Constantine is readily available. I would not contend with them concerning it. Yet I cannot persuade myself that in Herwart’s ancient calendar, where the eighth day before the Kalends of January [25 December] is entered as *Natalis Invicti*, “the birthday of the Unconquered,” Constantine’s birthday is meant. This is not only because, whereas that calendar mentions three birthdays of Constantine, it always calls them *Natalis Constantini*, “Constantine’s birthday,” never *Natalis Invicti*; but especially because the eighth day before the Kalends of January was commonly called the birthday of the Sun and the New Sun.

Chrysostom, at the end of his homily on the Nativity of John the Baptist: “What they call the birthday of the Sun—and the Sun of righteousness, of whom the prophet Malachi speaks,” and what follows. For they believed that on this day, the eighth day before the Kalends of January, which they took as Christ’s birthday, daylight increased and nighttime darkness diminished, and that therefore the Sun, beginning to return to us from the hemisphere of the Antichthones, was as it were reborn. Eucherius of Lyons—or Eusebius, if that is who he is—in Homily 2 on the Nativity: “For today [25 December] the losses of night pass into the gains of day. Today night, as its darkness fails, is diminished, and the day is lengthened by the light added to it [perhaps read: ‘with added light’], so that, as the author of light is born, after that night of unbelief which had covered and veiled the whole world has been scattered, our faith may shine like the day.” Below: “The predecessor and maker of all ages chose this day for His birth, so that as it advanced in light, it might advance [Col. 0750B] also in dignity.”

For this reason this day was held in great honour among the pagans, as also among certain Christians—not only because of Christ’s birthday, but because of the Sun’s. Leo the Great, Sermon II on the Nativity of Christ: “Remain steadfast in the faith in which you have been established, lest that same tempter, whose domination Christ has already excluded from you, again deceive you by some snares and corrupt by the art of his deception the very joys of this present day, mocking simpler minds through the pernicious persuasion of certain persons, to whom this day of our festival appears worthy of honour not so much because of Christ’s Nativity as because of the rising, as they say, of the New Sun. Their hearts, wrapped in darkness and alien from every increase of true light, are still imbued with the errors of most foolish paganism.”

Ambrose, Sermon 16, teaches that this day was called the New Sun; and Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, ch. 21: “To others the natural year seems to begin from the new sun, that is, from the winter solstice,” etc. Many ancients held that the winter solstice fell on this day. Pliny, book LIX, chapter 25: “All these variations”—of the equinoxes, solstice, and winter solstice—“occur in the eighth parts of the signs. The winter solstice in Capricorn falls approximately on the eighth day before the Kalends of January.” Servius, on Virgil, *Aeneid* I, noted that the winter solstice ends on the eighth day before the Kalends of January: “The winter solstice ends on the eighth day before the Kalends of January.”

Therefore, on this day the pagans celebrated the birthday of the Sun, while most Christians in the second and third centuries of the Christian era celebrated the birthday of our Saviour—the practice they still maintain. Hence that ancient calendar says *Natalis Invicti*, namely, of the Sun. This was indeed its constant epithet, as in an ancient inscription in my possession: “To the unconquered Sun, to Apollo.” See the most distinguished Cuperus. GRAEVIUS.

Compare also Pagi’s *Critique of Baronius’ Annals*, on the year of Christ 306, no. 12; above all, John Hardouin’s *Antirrheticus on the Ancient Coins of Colonies and Municipia*, addressed to Jean Foy-Vaillant, pp. 65–66, and again near the end, in the additions; likewise again in the “Address to the Reader” which that distinguished man appended in a somewhat later work after the *Embolus on the Canon of Tours*.

“Maximinus.” Maucroix has *Maximien*, that is, Maximian. I should be surprised by this, were it not better attributed to a printer’s error than to the translator’s intention. For the subject is Maximinus Daia, as both the reading of the old manuscript and chapter 19, along with very many other passages, partly indicate and partly prove.

“In order to cast him down from second place,” etc. Thus already the first edition of Baluze. All the others have *rejiceret*, “should cast down,” rather than *reiceret*.

## CHAPTER XXVI

“His affairs were settled.” Correctly. For from chapter 26: Galerius Maximianus’ plans had previously been disturbed; and among other usages, in Latin affairs are said to be *componi*, “set in order,” when, after being disturbed as here, precautions are taken to prevent their falling into disorder. For *turbari*, “to be disturbed,” and *perturbari*, “to be thrown into disorder,” differ from one another no less than *purgare*, “to cleanse,” and *perpurgare*, “to cleanse thoroughly,” and the other words of that kind. Cicero, *On Duties* I: “We must take care not to fall into disorder before reason sets our minds in order.” And our author below, chapter 29, after mentioning in the preceding chapter the calamities suffered by the state when its condition was disturbed: “Herculius set out,” he says, “against the enemy of his son Maximian, as though to discuss with him the settlement of the condition of the commonwealth.”

Nor are the old writers’ expressions unlike these, where you see the verb *componere* used whether the matter concerns things displaced from their proper position and restored to their former state, or other things insufficiently ordered for this or that purpose and needing to be arranged better. Of the former kind Virgil, *Aeneid* I:

> Whom I— . . . but it is better to SETTLE the troubled waves.

Of the latter, our author in chapter 46: “On the previous morning he FORMED the battle-line.” And Livy: “The battle was fiercer in onset and spirit than it was FORMED in any order.” Except that there we have not simply *compositior*, “more ordered,” but *compositior ullo ordine*, “more ordered in any formation”; perhaps not without considerable indication that the ablative *ordine*, “in order,” must everywhere be understood in its literal or metaphorical sense in the preceding passages.
