“Another terror was brought to him.” That is, another report that frightened him. For our author would scarcely have immediately added, by way of explanatory expansion (*ἐπεξηγήσεως*), that Maxentius, Galerius’ son-in-law, had been made emperor at Rome; and later, in different words indeed but giving the reason for his movement, that Maxentius had been invested with the purple, when “Upon receipt of this report” immediately follows. Clearly, then, “terror” here is used for a terrifying report. And this terror was another, that is, a second and new one, for Galerius, because, as we have seen, the earlier report brought to the evil beast with Constantine’s laurel-crowned image was that “Constantius had handed imperial power to his son.” Maucroix therefore rightly renders: *On apporta à Galérius d'autres nouvelles qui le remplirent de terreur*—“Other news was brought to Galerius which filled him with terror”; and the English translation concisely: “He received a new alarm.”

“Maxentius was made emperor at Rome.” “Take care,” says the distinguished Toinard on these words, “not to understand *imperator* here in the sense of Augustus, as Maxentius himself later became in the end of chapter 32.” He immediately adds: “For here *imperator* means nothing but Caesar; for below, Maxentius included, it is written: ‘And he hated the man, and could not make three Caesars.’” I confess, however, that I see no need for the caution prescribed by this most learned man. On the contrary, the few soldiers who are shortly said to have invested Maxentius with the purple at Rome, without opposition from the people, seem to me much more to have made Maxentius Augustus than Caesar by thus investing him.

First, since they were taking from Severus an imperial power which he held as Augustus, not as Caesar, it naturally follows that those soldiers conferred Augustan dignity upon Maxentius rather than merely Caesarian dignity. For that they truly wished to take from Severus, in favour of Maxentius, not merely a portion of imperial power, to be administered thereafter by Maxentius under the bare name of Caesar, but the whole power, is indicated by these words which follow shortly: “Galerius summoned Severus and urged him to recover the Empire”—the whole Empire, therefore, which had been taken from Severus in Maxentius’ favour.

Secondly, if the soldiers in question had endowed Maxentius only with Caesarian power, Maxentius could have had no right to name his father Herculius “Augustus for the second time,” since such designations properly belonged to Augusti, not Caesars. Yet, as the following words again testify, “Maxentius sent the purple to his father Herculius and named him Augustus for the second time.” Finally, as we learn by comparing chapters 28 and 32, Galerius had not yet ordered Maxentius and, at the same time, three others to be called by the name of emperor when Maxentius’ own authority—which had, very recently, restored his father Herculius’ Augustan authority to its former position—already surpassed that Augustan authority of his father. He therefore was not a mere Caesar when he restored it to Herculius, but Augustus, and in a sense even more than Augustus.

[Col. 0752A] Toinard therefore plainly disrupts the whole sequence of our history, if one may say so, when, from what we read below—“and Galerius Maximianus hated the man, and, with Maxentius included, could not make three Caesars”—he infers that the soldiers mentioned made Maxentius nothing other than Caesar. For by those words our author does not touch in the least upon the kind of authority granted to Maxentius at Rome in that revolt of the Praetorians; rather, he tells what came into Galerius’ mind upon first receiving the report of their action, and what nevertheless, for two reasons, he could not bring himself to undertake or do.

First of all, then, since it is worthwhile to recount the whole affair in order: the few soldiers left in the camp at Rome, having found an opportunity, invested Maxentius with the purple and thereby made him not Caesar but Augustus. Eutropius is explicit on this point, in book X: “Meanwhile at Rome the Praetorians, having stirred up a revolt, proclaimed Maxentius, the son of Herculius, who was staying not far from the City on the public road, AUGUSTUS.” Nor did they take merely an imperial seat from Severus, but, as far as lay in their power, the entire Empire.

But shortly afterwards, when news of this event was brought to Galerius, he considered whether, by the same means by which he had made Constantine—whom Constantius had made Augustus in dying—a mere Caesar by right of the senior Augustus, he should likewise make Maxentius, whom the soldiers had established as Augustus, a mere Caesar. After considering this plan more or less in his mind, he finally rejected it for two reasons. One was that he hated Maxentius intensely and, because of that hatred, could not bring himself even to name him Caesar. The other was that, in addition, under Diocletian’s venerable arrangement described in chapter 18, there could not be three Caesars at once in the state.

Accordingly, turning to another course, he summoned Severus, urged him to recover the Empire, and sent him with Maximian Herculius’ army to overthrow Maxentius, so that Maxentius might be excluded from every form of imperial power. Finally, after Severus’ expedition against Maxentius, Maxentius had not merely failed to be defeated, but his forces had more than doubled; Severus had perished; and Maxentius’ authority now exceeded even the authority of Herculius Augustus, recently restored to his former position. At that point, I say, Galerius judged that he could not safely wish to confer the simple title of Caesar upon a man of such power—neither safely for Maxentius nor sufficiently safely for himself—and furthermore wished to take from Maximinus Daia all hope of supreme power. Abolishing the name of Caesars, he therefore named himself and Licinius Augusti, but Maxentius and Constantine sons of Augusti; nevertheless, not long afterwards, on the occasion mentioned at the end of this chapter, he granted them the title of emperor as well.

“Maxentius was made emperor at Rome.” As is clear from Lactantius, chapter 46—or rather chapter 44—Maxentius was proclaimed emperor at Rome on the sixth day before the Kalends of November [27 October]; and, according to the same Lactantius, chapter 46—or more correctly chapters 26 and 25—Galerius did not receive the news that Maxentius had been called emperor until after he had named Severus Augustus and Constantine Caesar. PAGIUS, on the year of Christ 306, no. 11.

“When he had resolved”: Galerius Maximianus, namely. The former of these names is supplied by the French Parisian translation, the latter by the English.

“To devour the world.” A *συμπλοκή* (“interweaving”) of figurative expressions, felicitously explained by the translation last cited as: “to exhaust the wealth of the whole Empire.” Cicero’s passage in *On His House* may also serve here as a commentary: “For I do not suppose that, after my departure, you had devoured in hope and greed the fortunes of all wealthy men, the revenues of all provinces, and the property of tetrarchs and kings,” etc.

“Sprang forward” (*prosilivit*). The manuscript has *prosiluit*, as may be inferred from Baluze’s first edition, which later editors followed. I wish indeed that the later revision of that distinguished man had not changed this perfect tense. For why, when *prosiluit* was no less in use among Latin writers than *prosilivit*? Livy, book VIII of the Punic War: “Hasdrubal, roused by the shout of the cavalry . . . sprang from his tent.” The same elsewhere: “The king, almost stunned by the marvel, sprang from his seat.” And before him Virgil, *Aeneid* V:

> . . . all, without delay,  
> SPRANG FORWARD from their bounds.

What is more: if *prosiluit* could not be retained, I think it ought rather to have been changed to *prosiliit*, which you will encounter below in chapter 30, than to *prosilivit*. But, as I have already said, the reading of the old manuscript is sound; and the verb *prosilire* had three perfect forms at once: *prosilui, prosilivi,* and *prosilii*. Compare what is to be said in chapters 30 and 49.

“From this captivity.” That is, “from this tribute,” if we follow Maucroix’s version:

> Galerius carried his madness so far as to wish to subject even the Roman people to this tribute.

Or, “from this tax-assessment,” if we follow the English:

> Maximian proceeded to that pitch of madness that he would not so much as grant the city of Rome an exemption from this tax.
[Col. 0753B] we choose to follow it. Nor indeed can it be denied that, among writers of the eleventh and twelfth centuries, *captiones* and *capturae* denote such things. But, besides the fact that these words belong to a very late period, they also differ greatly from the word *captivitas*. Therefore, in my judgement, it is far preferable here to understand by *captivitas* a mark or token of captivity. Not that the Roman people were in fact captives, but that they were treated by Galerius as captives. For our author above, in chapter 23, speaks of the same censuses, and expressly anticipates what we now say concerning the meaning of this passage: “The census,” he says, “once sent into the provinces and cities, with assessors scattered everywhere and stirring everything up, presented the appearance of a hostile uproar and a dreadful captivity.”

Moreover, if in the words, “he advanced to such madness that he would not even wish the Roman people to be exempted from this captivity,” we rightly take *captivitas* to mean the mark or token of captivity, some light may thence be cast upon Paul’s passage to the Corinthians, where interpreters commonly take ἐξουσία (*exousia*) as an indication of authority. The sentence is: “A woman ought to have authority upon her head” (1 Cor. 11:10).

At about the same time he had also removed the camps. This passage has been understood in various ways by learned men.

That is, he had greatly reduced the number of the Praetorian soldiers. Maucroix’s translation reads: “At the same time he had extremely weakened the number of the Praetorian soldiers.”

That is, he had taken away certain privileges from the Praetorian cohorts. The English translation, as appears from these words: “He had also at the same time made an attempt upon some of the privileges of the Praetorian bands.”

“He had removed.” I would prefer, “he had transferred.” GALE.—“He had removed the Praetorian camps.” That is, in part. For he cannot be said to have removed altogether those by whom he was made emperor. For according to Zosimus, “having enlisted as agents of the undertaking those whom they call Praetorians, he was raised by them to the imperial throne, after solemnly promising to reward with great gifts those who had granted him this.” The Oxford and Cambridge editions. Baluzio and Cuper agree with them.

My contribution is that everything will be perfectly clear if, instead of “At about the same time, etc.,” we read with only a different order: “At the same time he had almost removed the Praetorian camps.” That this should be done is suggested first by what follows immediately: “The few soldiers who had been left at Rome in the camps.” For if in fact few soldiers had been left in the camps at Rome, Galerius had therefore almost removed the Praetorian camps—this is our reading—not altogether removed them, as the received arrangement of the words suggests. And secondly, since it is certain that our author did not write in the preceding passage, in the plural number, “These were the causes of his disturbance,” but in the singular, “This was the cause of his disturbance,” it is certainly preferable that the two things from which the sedition in question arose should have happened at precisely the same time, because thus they formed, as it were, one cause of that disturbance, rather than occurring at different times. For this reason also I would judge that “At the same time, etc.” should be read rather than “At about the same time.”

*Nancti.* Thus also in Baluzio’s first edition. The others have *nacti*. See in every case what Columbo observes above on this matter.

“Certain judges having been killed.” Among them he killed Abellius, “the prefect of the city.” Oxford and Cambridge editions. This addition is drawn from Zosimus.

“Certain judges.” These judges were not ordinary civil judges, but household officials of the emperors and military judges, of whom above in chapter 22: “Military judges, unversed in humane letters, were sent into the provinces without assessors.” The same persons are also mentioned in chapter 17, where [Col. 0754B] Diocletian’s illness is discussed. TOLLIUS.

“Who was aroused.” That is, according to Maucroix’s interpretation, who was already ill-disposed towards Galerius; and according to the English translation, who was greatly enraged. But I would rather explain it as one who at that very time could be seen in agitation and causing disturbances—on account, namely, of those assessors whom he had heard were being appointed to be sent to Rome to register the populace. In French, with a manner of speaking no less idiomatic than concise, *soulevé*.

“They had clothed Maxentius with the purple.” It seems to have been corrected to “they had clothed Maxentius in purple.” GALEUS.

“He was troubled,” etc. That is, Galerius, according to Maucroix; Maximian, according to the English translation. Baluzio rightly combines both.

“Yet not excessively frightened.” This expression should be noted, though perhaps no one today has better felt its force than the French, among whom—although, strangely enough, Maucroix translated otherwise—it is most familiar to say in exactly so many words, *et toutefois pas trop épouvanté* [“and yet not too frightened”]. We use it properly when someone, as here, is moderately disturbed but his mind is not rendered incapable of discerning what needs to be done. Our author employs a similar expression below, in chapter 40: “not too close to Augusta”; see the notes there.

“The man.” For this, Maucroix has inserted “Maxentius” in his translation as a kind of commentary.

“And he could not make three Caesars.” That is, in addition to Constantine and Maximinus Daia, whom he had already made Caesars, although with very different dispositions, the arrangement discussed above by Baluzio and Cuper did not permit him to add a third by raising Maxentius, out of the ordinary course, to the height of the same Caesarean rank.

“To have done once what he wished.” Namely, when he unwillingly made Constantine Caesar: this is Maucroix’s interpretation.

“He urges him to recover the empire.” Namely, his own. For *recipere* here means not to accept something which is only now given to you, as the English translation suggests, but to recover something which you had already possessed, as Maucroix translated excellently and as the most learned Cuper will explain to you. Yet, to conceal nothing, I should have wished that Maucroix’s translation, which is simply, *il l’exhorte à recouvrer l’empire* [“he urges him to recover the empire”], had included the possessive: *il l’exhorte à recouvrer son empire* [“he urges him to recover his empire”]—that is, *hortatur ad recuperandum suum imperium*—lest it seem to imply that Severus was the senior Augustus, which certainly he was not.

“He sends him with Maximian’s army.” Namely, that of Herculius, or the senior Maximian; Maucroix supplied the latter for clarity in his translation, and not without reason, as will shortly appear. The English translation likewise points out for understanding what follows that this same Maximian was Maxentius’ father. But Maxentius, as the following words will show, did not know what Galerius Maximian was plotting against him, when Severus was thus sent by him against Maxentius, with the army of his father, Maximian Herculius, to subdue him.

“Maxentius, conscious to himself of so great a deed.” That is, of having assumed the purple without the senior Augustus’ counsel, and at the same time usurped sovereignty over Italy, which Galerius had assigned to Severus together with the West.

“Although by right of paternal inheritance he could bring the soldiers over to himself.” The sense is: although it did not seem at all impossible to him that he might bring his father’s soldiers over to his own side by right of inheritance, if they should be led by Severus against him. These paternal soldiers are the same as those called Maximian’s army a few lines earlier.

“Maximian his father-in-law.” That is, Galerius; Maucroix also preferred to state this, suppressing the author’s words, in order to clarify the narrative.

“He sought how far.” Consult Columbo on the force of this adverb.

“To fortify himself against the impending danger.” The same learned man defends this phrase there, with various examples.

[Col. 0755B] “To his father.” Namely, the senior Maximian, as Maucroix added in his translation.

“Dwelling in Campania after laying down the empire.” Zosimus says: “Rightly distressed over his son Maxentius, he set out from Lucania, where he then was, and went towards Ravenna.” Baluzio reconciles these statements by saying that Herculius had indeed withdrawn to Lucania when he laid down the empire, but that, when these events occurred, he had come into Campania. Oxford and Cambridge editions.—Nor does Baluzio say otherwise. Yet the actual facts, and the two translations by the most distinguished interpreters, clearly show that the words of this passage, as hitherto understood, signify something quite different. The French: “He sends the purple to his father, the elder Maximian, who, after his abdication, had his residence in the countryside.” The English: “So he sent the purple to his father, who had lived in Campania ever since his resignation of the Empire.”

What if, therefore, in this passage, as sometimes in Cicero, *post*, followed by a comma, and elsewhere in countless places, has the force of *postea* [“afterwards”]? And what if in our author, again in imitation of Cicero—who used *ego morabor te* for *ego te expectabo* [“I shall wait for you”] in the Letters to Atticus—*depositum imperium in Campania moranti* was said for “waiting after laying down the empire”? Then certainly no greater difficulty will remain than if we had most plainly: “To his father afterwards, waiting in Campania after laying down the empire,” etc. That is, as soon as Herculius heard how the Praetorians at Rome had proclaimed his son Maxentius Augustus, he hurried with the utmost speed into Campania from Lucania, where he had been growing old in private life ever since laying aside his unwelcome purple; yet he wished to remain within the borders of Campania until he learned whether his son would grant him the opportunity to resume the purple.

Eutropius is also very helpful, although recounting each point less distinctly, in these words: “Meanwhile, at Rome the Praetorians, having stirred up a disturbance, proclaimed Augustus Maxentius, the son of Herculius, who was staying not far from the city on the public road. On receiving this news, Maximian Herculius, raised to the hope of recovering the lofty position which he had unwillingly lost, hurried to Rome from Lucania, which he had chosen as his residence in private life, growing old amid its most pleasant estates.” I therefore approve, to conclude in this way, this punctuation: “To his father, dwelling in Campania after laying down the empire, he sends the purple.” Nor is this unlike Cicero’s: “An hour later, they condemned a certain Antiochus Gabinius,” etc.

“He calls [him] Augustus twice.” Toinard explains this expression in its proper place.

“And he who had laid it aside unwillingly.” Namely, the purple, by a very close *apo koinou* construction. For *imperium* [“empire”] preceded and could equally well be understood according to Latin usage; but that is more remote.—“And who.” Read: “and because.” GALE.

“He gladly seized it.” Namely, the same purple. Baluzio says much more on this matter.

[Col. 0756A] “Meanwhile Severus proceeds.” *Vadere* is sometimes said of enemies advancing armed and with the intention of fighting. Virgil, *Aeneid* II:

> Each man arms himself with fresh spoils.  
> We advance mingled with the Danaans, not by favour of our gods,  
> And, encountering many battles through the blind night,  
> We heap them up.

And Livy likewise, Book III: “They therefore advance to battle from their own side, take up again the position from which they had yielded, and in a moment not only is the battle restored, but the Sabine wing is even forced back.” Indeed, one sometimes finds it used even of those who, already fighting, move themselves here or there. Ennius, Book VIII of the *Annals*, in verses quoted above:

> Not by a hand-to-hand contest according to law, but rather by the sword  
> They seek again the issue and seek the kingdom;  
> They advance with solid force.

And Livy similarly, Book XXVI: “When unexpectedly Numidians and Spaniards with elephants burst into the Roman camp, the elephants, advancing through the middle of the camp, caused destruction among the tents, with the enormous noise and flight of beasts breaking their tethers.” Thus you may dispense altogether with Columbo’s emendation.

“And they surrender themselves to him against whom they had come.” Correct: “and to him against whom they had come they surrender themselves.” GALE.—I too had made this correction, because our author is remarkably fond of asyndeton. Yet he could also have written: “and they surrender themselves to him, or to that man, against whom they had come,” and other expressions of that kind.

“But Maximian, now having resumed the empire, meets him.” Namely, the senior Maximian, which both interpreters reasonably thought should be supplied.—In the current year (306), Maximian Herculius, who after laying down the empire had been residing in Lucania, was summoned to Rome by his son Maxentius while he was in Campania, and was again proclaimed Augustus by him, as we have already said from Lactantius, chapter 26. That this occurred in the present year is established not only from the cited chapter of Lactantius, but also from his ordinary consulship in the following year (307), assumed according to the first rule governing Caesarean consulships. PAGIUS, *Critica Baroniana*, on A.D. 306, no. 13.

“By whose arrival he fled to Ravenna.” Zosimus says that he was killed at Tres Tabernae, but captured at Ravenna. GALE.

“By Maximian.” Namely, him who will soon, at the beginning of chapter 27, simply be called Herculius, and thereby distinguished from the other Maximian. The passage is: “But Herculius, when he knew Maximian’s madness.” From this the fair-minded reader may judge in passing how many places in this little work are not merely somewhat obscure but obscure indeed, and how much better it would have been for both the author and us if he had everywhere called Herculius, for example, Herculius, and Galerius likewise everywhere Galerius.

“And he returned the robe and the purple to the same man from whom he had received them.” This passage is notable for more than one reason. For first, as we saw above, Severus was sent by Galerius to Maximian Herculius in order that Herculius might clothe him in purple—for the elder Maximian in chapter 18 and Maximian Herculius are the same man. From this passage we learn that this actually took place, and consequently that Severus received the purple from Herculius. Secondly, and more importantly, Severus, who thus received the purple from Herculius, had been made only Caesar when he received it. But when he returned the same purple to Herculius, he had recently been made Augustus by Galerius, as was stated at the end of chapter 25.

Thus the purple of the Augusti does not appear to have differed from that of the Caesars, since Severus, having received from Herculius the purple as the insignia of Caesarean power, returned the same purple to Herculius, from whom he had received it, when he had become Augustus. I add a relevant point: when Diocletian, in chapter 19, put off the purple which he had hitherto worn as Augustus and senior Augustus, and wished at the same time to make known to the assembly of soldiers he had convened the man whom he had almost ceased proclaiming, together with Severus, as the new Caesar, by placing the purple before their eyes, he did not throw over Maximinus Daia a purple different from the one he removed, but the very same one: “Diocletian threw over him his own purple, which he had taken off, and became Diocles again.” We do not know whether we have thereby said enough in answer to the question of the most learned Cuper, mentioned above. Yet the observations we have now made could scarcely have been omitted, nor do we recall anything to the contrary capable of outweighing them.

“Both the robe and the purple.” Columbo asks above whether this is a *dia dyoin*. He denies it, believing instead that an inner and an outer garment are meant. I, on the contrary, consider it a *hen dia dyoin*, meaning only one garment, which was at once purple and outer, on the basis of these words of our author compared together:

> The elder Maximian … in order that he might deceive Constantine, lays aside the royal robe. Chapter 29.

> The elder Maximian … when he now thought that Constantine had entered the territories of the barbarians, suddenly puts on the purple. In the following passage of the same chapter.

Nor, evidently, did the most learned interpreters think otherwise. The French translator rendered “the robe and the purple” simply as *la pourpre* [“the purple”], corresponding word for word to *purpuram*; while the English translator rendered it “the imperial purple.” This latter openly confirms what we have just said concerning the undifferentiated purple of Caesars and emperors, in calling “imperial” the purple which Severus received when he became Caesar from Herculius: “and gave back the imperial purple to him from whom he had received it.”

A celebrated example of the figure here mentioned, should anyone seek one, is Virgil’s:

> … of the liquor which we pour from bowls and gold,

that is, “from golden bowls,” as Servius says; and elsewhere:

> a heifer veiled for the victor with gold and fillets,

that is, likewise “with golden fillets.” So also in the Acts of the Apostles, according to the better judgement of learned men, “having brought bulls and garlands to the gates,” that is—as Beza among others translates—when he had brought garlanded or crowned bulls to the entrances.

[Col. 0757C] “Having done this, he obtained nothing else,” etc. It is undoubtedly preferable, with the Abo edition and again with both translations, to remove the punctuation after *facto* and read in a single breath: “Having done this, he obtained nothing else but a good death.” “That cowardice could obtain for him only a gentle death.” MAUCROIX.—“But all that he could obtain by this submission was a gentle death.” English translation.

“Good,” that is, gentle, as Maucroix has just rendered it; the immediately following words confirm this: “he was compelled to die gently.”

“For his veins had been cut.” “His neck was broken with a noose,” according to Zosimus. Oxford and Cambridge editions.

“To him.” I would prefer “to himself.” GALE.

“He was compelled to die gently.” Namely, in A.D. 307. PAGIUS, on A.D. 306, no. 10, at the end.

“From this point [he began] to persecute his own.” Read: “From this point he began to persecute his own,” since he had previously raged only against Christians. BOHERELLUS.

[Col. 0757D] “From this point [he began] to persecute his own.” The defect in this most corrupt passage will easily be remedied if, with Nicolaus Heinsius, we read: “From this point he began to persecute his own.” *Ab hoc* means “after this.” In *capite* for *coepit*, as many wrote it, there has been an error through transposition of letters. GRAEVIUS.—“From this point [he began] to persecute his own.” Add *coeperunt* [“they began”]. But perhaps more has fallen out. TOLLIUS.—There is a lacuna here. ALLIX.

## CHAPTER XXVII

“But Herculius, when he knew Maximian’s madness.” A summary apparently clear, but truly obscure because the Maximian now under discussion is wholly different from the one denoted by that name in the immediately preceding passages. Moreover, that Maximian of the preceding passage is now unexpectedly called Herculius. Seeking to remedy this obscurity, the distinguished Maucroix and Burnet translated it as though our words were: “But the elder Maximian, when he knew Galerius’ madness” (*Le vieux Maximien, qui connaissait la fureur de Galérius*); and as though the received reading were: “But Maximian the elder, when he knew the madness of the younger Maximian” (“But Maximian the elder knew well the madness of Maximian the younger”).

“With Maximinus added.” Oxford edition of 1680, p. 108, in the corrections that had occurred too late. Maucroix followed the received text in his translation; Burnet followed the correction. See above in the Notes on this passage and on chapter 18 what Toinard says of each reading.

“With forces doubled.” For which, with almost identical sense, you will find “with strength doubled” at the end of chapter 46.

“Against which resistance could in no way be made.” With a period and comma. GALE.—I think it should be corrected: “With which resistance could [in no way be made],” etc. BOHERELLUS.—This is very pleasing, except that our author could also have written: “Against which resistance could in no way be made: and, after fortifying the city,” or even “and after fortifying the city”; thus the conjunction may have been absorbed by the preceding word. But I know that polished ears will less approve the latter mode of reading.

“Having fortified the city, and carefully equipping hostile undertakings.” There is an error here. ALLIX.—A corrupt passage, which scarcely seems capable of restoration otherwise than by reading: “Having fortified the city, and diligently attending to, or pressing on with, enterprises on the march.” Oxford and Cambridge editions.—The passage is utterly corrupt. How it may be cleaned is uncertain. Heinsius conjectured: “Having fortified the city, and carefully informing himself about hostile enterprises”; that is, carefully investigating and inquiring what plan the enemies were adopting. GRAEVIUS.—Correct: “Having fortified the city, and no less carefully equipped with necessary things”; or, if this does not please, “and no less carefully supplied with fresh troops.” TOLLIUS.—I correct: “Having fortified the city, and carefully instructing his friends with commands”; or, “and diligently attending to, or pressing on with, matters against the enemy.” GALE.—I would prefer: “Having fortified the city, and carefully equipping [it] with things suitable against enemies,” provided that “things suitable against enemies” means not hostile suitable things, but things suitable for repelling and driving enemies from the walls—*des choses propres pour des ennemis*, as the French say daily word for word—such as scorpions, catapults, and other devices of that kind in former times. Hirtius, Book V: “He had a great supply of scorpions, catapults, and other missiles which are usually prepared for defence.”

“By the marriage of his younger daughter.” Maucroix’s translation, or rather paraphrase, is: “by the marriage of his daughter Fausta”—that is, “by the marriage of his daughter Fausta.” Correctly. Compare Baluzio and also Toinard on this passage.

“Meanwhile he.” Galerius. MAUCROIX.—The other Maximian. English translation.

“He approaches the city.” Namely Rome; the interpreters reasonably and plainly supplied this in their translations, from what follows and from common Latin usage.

“To besiege the walls.” I believe that the learned man, whose name I shall suppress because the matter is uncertain, preferred “to surround the walls.” But no change is needed. “To besiege Mutina,” “to besiege Cologne,” “to besiege a town”—or, as some manuscripts have it, *circumsidere*—and other such expressions are familiar to Cicero in the *Philippics* and elsewhere, for “to blockade” and similar terms.

“And he judged her.” Virgil, *Eclogue* I:

> I, foolish one, thought her like ours, Meliboeus—  
> Like ours, etc.

TOLLIUS.

“A father-in-law attacked his son-in-law.” That is, Galerius Maximian attacked Maxentius, as these words of chapter 26 can show: “Maxentius, conscious to himself of so great a deed … thinking … that it could happen that Maximian, his father-in-law … might himself come with his army to attack him.” Add, however, what the most learned Cuper records from Tristan.

“And because the Roman soldiers, having transferred their standards to Rome.” The Abo edition has changed the punctuation, in my judgement, from the best to the worst: “And because the Roman soldiers, having transferred their standards to Rome, abandoned the empire.”

“They abandoned the empire.” Namely Galerius’, which Maucroix did not think superfluous to explain: “They revolted against Galerius.”

“With their spirits cast down.” It would be better to read “with their spirits lowered.” BOHERELLUS, likewise GALE, from whom Columbo does not differ.—Both *dimissis* and *demissis* can here be read and conveniently explained, but the former is better. *Dimittere animos* means to lay aside and cast away pride. One says rather *dejicere animum* than *animos*. TOLLIUS.—“With their spirits cast down.” Nothing is truer than Columbo’s correction, “with their spirits lowered.” For the following words show with what lowered spirit he prostrated himself at the soldiers’ knees. Latinity does not know what *dimittere animum* means. GRAEVIUS.

“Until by enormous promises he bent their minds.” This is from Baluzio’s second thoughts. For his first edition, followed afterward by the others, had represented in the author’s words the reading of the manuscript thus: “Until, by enormous promises, a fortunate spirit, of whom …” Hence arose the following notes or explanations of scholars.

“A fortunate spirit, of whom.” An error lies hidden here. ALLIX.—The correction is easy: “He bent their minds.” Oxford and Cambridge editions.—“At last the greatness of his promises touched some of them.” MAUCROIX.—From whose conjecture it was formerly written: “Until by enormous promises he bent the minds of certain persons, or of some persons.” Add Baluzio, Columbo, and Toinard.

“If with a few.” The interpreters vary here: one understands a few cavalrymen, the other a small body of soldiers. “If cavalry had been sent after him.” MAUCROIX.—“If he had been pursued by ever so small a body.” English translation.

“Supplies.” Things necessary for food. Oxford and Cambridge editions, and likewise the interpreters.—*Utensilia* are provisions, resources necessary for subsistence. Tacitus, *Annals* I.70: “They spent the night without supplies, without fire.” See what the eminent Johannes Fredericus Gronovius noted there. GRAEVIUS.—“Supplies.” This sense of the word is noteworthy. TOLLIUS.

“Whereby pestilential.” Read: “By which pestilential.” TOLLIUS.

“Women were corrupted.” Namely, by force, as in the preceding passage: “He gave the soldiers authority, when scattered as widely as possible, to plunder or violate everything.” Soon follows the synonymous expression concerning virgins: “virgins were violated.” Thus the distinction which we believed and established might occur in chapter 8 between *corrumpere* and *violare* in a similar subject is not invariably maintained. “Women were forced,” the English translation; this is used only of women violated, or corrupted, by force.

“Parents and husbands were tortured, that they might betray their daughters, their wives, and their property.” *Extorqueri* is commonly used not of persons but of things; *torqueri*, however, of persons. In a word, things are generally extracted by torture, persons are tortured. In the former manner, “to extort money,” “to extort fifty Attic talents,” “to extort iron,” “to extort assistance,” occur in Cicero along with very many similar expressions. In the latter, our author above in chapter 14: “All the judges, indeed all who were masters in the palace, having received authority, tortured [men]”; and shortly afterwards: “Nothing anywhere was discovered, since no one tortured Caesar’s household.” Likewise in chapter 21: “Not only decurions but even the foremost men of the cities were tortured by him”; and similarly in chapter 23: “If everything else failed, they themselves were tortured against themselves.”

We must therefore either take the compound *extorti* here for the simple *torti*, on the same principle by which the Latins use *territus* and *exterritus*, *pavidus* and *expavidus*, and other expressions of this kind almost interchangeably; or the meaning is that in that circumstance parents and husbands were tortured so severely that Galerius’ soldiers finally extracted from them where they had hidden their daughters, wives, and property. Cicero speaks in a nearly similar sense in the *Tusculans*: “Since you have extorted from me that I confess.” Let the learned choose whichever they prefer.

“In this manner he withdrew to his own territories.” “Thus Galerius regained the lands subject to his rule.” MAUCROIX.—Thus Galerius withdrew to the lands under his rule.

“He had ravaged everything in hostile fashion.” Therefore Vorstius’ annotation on Sulpicius Severus is sound, when at the beginning of the *Sacred History* he applies the name “harassments” to the first persecutions of Christians: “To harass, as Asconius teaches, signifies the infliction of a great calamity. Authors everywhere join the word with terms which certainly signify a great calamity, writing ‘to harass and destroy,’ ‘to plunder and harass,’ ‘to devastate and harass,’ ‘to harass and despoil.’” For here too we have “to ravage everything in hostile fashion”; and hence the emendation proposed above by Baluzio is less necessary.

“He wished his title to be changed.” See the same author there.

“But Dacian.” Since he himself was of Dacian origin. Oxford edition of 1580; likewise Oxford 1684 and Cambridge 1685, except that the latter two additionally direct that *Dacicum* be read.—“Dacian.” Others read *Dacicum*. [Col. 0760B] But the received reading may be defended by the author of the *Historia Augusta* in the life of Maximinus, who calls him *Thraciscum* [“Thracian”]. TOLLIUS.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

“After his flight.” That is, after Galerius Maximian had left Italy in this way, as may be gathered from the various observations which the learned have contributed on this passage.—“After that he had left Italy in this manner,” English translation.—“After the flight of Galerius.” MAUCROIX.—“His,” namely Galerius Maximian. PAGIUS.

“The other Maximian.” Therefore he of whom above in chapter 8: “What … of Maximian, who is called Herculius?” and who elsewhere is so often called the elder Maximian in this little work, indeed in Maucroix’s translation of this very passage.

“Had withdrawn from Gaul.” Namely into Italy, from which he had, on the contrary, withdrawn into Gaul a little before: “And he was expelled from the city of Rome like another Superbus.”

“He held the empire jointly with his son.” Namely Maxentius. PAGIUS. And this according to the English translation, “in that part of the empire”—that is, in that part of the empire which the same translation shortly before called Italy, and into which our author silently placed Maximian Herculius, at the beginning of this chapter, when he said that he had withdrawn from Gaul, that is, returned.

“Since the son’s authority was prior and greater.” One may understand *esset* [“was”]; but it is more convenient and clearer to add it. TOLLIUS.—“Since.” I correct: “because.” GALE.—My conjecture is that it should be corrected to *quippe tum* [“since then”], so that our Caecilius may signify by this temporal adverb that there had once been a time when Maxentius’ authority—which, after he had restored the empire to his father Herculius, was prior and greater than his father’s authority—was not of that kind, but inferior and less.

“Who had also restored the empire to his father.” I take this as though our author had written, “exercising which authority to such an extent,” or “by which authority he had also restored the empire to his father and named him Augustus twice.” For *etiam* [“also”], the Abo edition, whether by accident or someone’s design, has separately *et jam* [“and now”]. If anything were to be changed, I would prefer to read *qua* for *qui*: “by which authority he had also”—understand “authority”—“restored the empire to his father.” Nor perhaps did the author’s hand write otherwise.

“That he might claim his own for himself.” That is, if we interpret Maucroix’s translation somewhat freely, that he might claim and recover what had been his; but literally, “that he might recover his ancient inheritance”: *De se mettre en possession de son ancien héritage*. This pleases me greatly, even because of that passage from Victor, already cited more than once: “When the empire was divided, all Gaul beyond the Alps was entrusted to Constantine; Africa and Italy to Herculius.”

“Because the soldiers were,” etc. From Herculius’ old army, whom he believed he would easily draw to his own side. Oxford and Cambridge editions.—Undoubtedly more correctly, in imitation of the most learned Cuper, read: “because they were his soldiers, who had abandoned Severus,” in this sense: Herculius regarded as properly his, not his son Maxentius’, that portion of Maxentius’ soldiers which had shortly before revolted from Emperor Severus, having raised their standards, and surrendered themselves to Maxentius, against whom they had come. Thus it was highly likely that those who, because they had formerly belonged to the father, had defected to the son after deserting Severus, would likewise defect from the son to the father as soon as an opportunity arose.

“To his son.” To Maxentius. Maucroix’s translation.

“That prince of calamities.” That is, according to the English translation: “The chief occasion of all the calamities,” etc.—the principal cause of all the calamities. For Maucroix, *auctor* [“author”] and *princeps* [“chief”] did not have different meanings in this place; he translated as though the latter word were entirely absent: “having called him the author of public calamities, he tears the purple from him.” It is certain that they do not differ greatly, if indeed they differ. I infer this from Cicero’s expressions: “chief of the war,” “chief of the killing,” “chief and architect of the crime”; and similarly Caesar’s: “chief of the crime and instigator of the war.” In these, not only may *auctor* be substituted everywhere for *princeps* in an excellent sense, but one also sees that “chief of the crime” and “architect of the crime” are synonymous, as likewise “chief of the war” and “instigator of the war.”

“He stripped [him],” etc. On account of this he endured the soldiers’ sedition and reproaches. Eutropius, Book X. Oxford and Cambridge editions.

“The purple.” “The imperial purple.” English translation—that is, the purple of the emperor. This accords excellently with the beginning of chapter XXVI: “Suddenly another terror was brought to him: his own son-in-law Maxentius had been made emperor at Rome.” Yet it does not thereby undermine what we concluded above by comparing our author with himself.

“Stripped.” Thus also the Abo edition. The others have *exutus* [“stripped”]. Nor otherwise above, at the end of chapter 4, “stripped and naked.”—Read *exutus*. ALLIX.

“Elder.” This word is inconveniently absent from the Abo edition; I note this for those who use it.

[Col. 0761C] “Like another Superbus.” Namely Tarquinius, the last king of the Romans. PAGIUS.—“Like another Tarquin.” MAUCROIX.—That is, like another Tarquinius. “As Tarquin the Proud.” English translation: that is, as Tarquinius Superbus.

“Superbus.” The Abo edition has *Superbus*, with a capital letter at the beginning, as Gale also wished it to be written.

“He was expelled.” The substantive verb should be deleted here as tasteless and redundant. TOLLIUS.—Rather, it should be retained and has no fault; I think what I shall now say will make this clear.

## CHAPTER XXIX

“Returning again into Gaul.” Namely, in A.D. 307, around August, as is understood from the little work on the prefects of the city, first published by Cuspinian and Onuphrius, then by Bucher. PAGIUS.

“Where, having remained for a while, he departed to the enemy,” etc. The substantive verb should more elegantly be inserted after *profectus*. TOLLIUS.—Either, with the addition of the other *est*, one must read: “where, having remained for a while, he departed to his son’s enemy”; or one must punctuate: “where, having remained for a while, he departed,” etc. BOHERELLUS.—Likewise as regards the latter punctuation. I have no doubt that, for the reasons to be given immediately, the latter is far preferable to the former.

He set out against the enemy of his son Maximian. That is, against the other Maximian. English version.—That is, against Galerius in Pannonia, as Maucroix translated it. I grant everything. For it is entirely certain from Zosimus and others that the matter concerns Galerius Maximian (who, being distinct from Maximian Herculius, was therefore truly the other Maximian), then residing at Carnuntum in Pannonia, and that Herculius set out for and arrived before him. I ask only how Herculius could, on his return—as he did—from the city of Rome into Gaul, set out for Carnuntum. For those travelling from Rome to Gaul turned their backs entirely upon Carnuntum; nor did Herculius merely set himself upon the road toward Gaul, so that, for example, upon arriving at Milan, he abandoned the journey undertaken and then began to make for Pannonia. Rather, he actually returned into Gaul, and indeed remained in Gaul for some time after his return; nor was it until after that stay that he set out against Galerius, the enemy of his son: “Returning again into Gaul, where he stayed for a little while, he set out against Maximian, the enemy of his son.” Hence, even if unwilling, one must again ask how Herculius could, at the very time when he was returning from Italy into Gaul and did not cease to proceed toward Gaul, set out for Carnuntum, a town of Pannonia to which he was turning his back.

No scholar has, I shall not say solved, but even touched this difficulty. Yet, I think, a change in the received punctuation, traced back a little further, will solve it easily, in this manner: “Disturbed by the anger and outcry of these soldiers, the impious old man was driven from the city of Rome, like another Tarquin the Proud, while returning [Col. 0762B] again into Gaul, where, having stayed for a little while, he set out against Maximian, the enemy of his son.” Thus Herculius held the assembly in which he tore the purple robe from Maxentius’ shoulders not in Rome itself, but outside the city—perhaps even far from it—in one or another town of Latium, say in the territory of the Hernici; for, as related above, “he summoned the people and the soldiers.” Afterwards, disturbed by the anger and outcry of the soldiers, who were profoundly indignant at his act, he suddenly formed the plan of returning into Gaul by way of Rome. Soon thereafter he was driven out of Rome itself like another Tarquin the Proud; and this occurred while he was carrying out that plan—that is, while he was in fact returning to Gaul by way of Rome. He subsequently reached Gaul; and, after remaining there for some time, finally made his way into Pannonia to Galerius Maximian, the enemy of his son. You see, unless I am greatly mistaken, with how little effort a by no means insignificant sequence of events holds together; likewise, how, contrary to Tollius’ opinion, the *est* after *exactus* (“was driven out”) is neither inept nor redundant; and finally, how there is likewise no need to supply a second *est* after *profectus*, but only to punctuate: “where, having stayed a little while, he set out,” etc.

On arranging the condition of the Commonwealth. The expression is very proper, as we observed above at the beginning of chapter 26. Please see that note. Elsewhere it is extremely similar to Sulpicius Severus’ phrase, shortly afterwards, “when domestic affairs had been arranged” (*rebus domi compositis*). The whole passage, so that you may judge better, reads as follows: “Not long afterwards Tirhakah, king of the Ethiopians, invaded the kingdom of the Assyrians. Upon receiving this news, Sennacherib, turning to the defence of his own possessions, raging and crying out that victory was being snatched from him although he was a victor, abandoned the war. He sent a letter to Hezekiah, threatening amid insulting language that shortly, after domestic affairs had been arranged, he would return swiftly for the destruction of Judaea.”

“He conferred with him.” Not in the sense in which *disputare* is commonly understood, but in that established from Cicero, as you may see above in Cuper’s Notes, and happily expressed in the translations of Maucroix and Burnet as follows: “Under the pretext of conferring with him about the affairs of the empire.” [Col. 0762D] MAUCROIX.—“He pretended that he went to concert with him,” etc., English translation. In both translators this amounts in Latin to: as though they might exchange and adopt counsels concerning the affairs of the empire.

His kingdom. That is, as the English translation rightly gives it, that part of the empire which had fallen to Galerius: “his share of the empire.” For it is certain that it was not properly called a kingdom. Yet, just as in those times Emperors and Caesars were sometimes styled kings, so their dominions were also called kingdoms.

Excluded from his own, wherever he came. According to Aurelius Victor—and our author did not deny it in chapter 8—the portion of the empire which Diocletian committed to Herculius’ administration was bounded by Italy and Africa. Yet nowhere does our author, after once mentioning in chapter 26 the empire reassumed by Herculius, name Africa even slightly as Herculius’ kingdom, or as the kingdom to which he set out and from which, wherever [Col. 0763A] he came, though it was his own, he was excluded. Rather, he names Italy alone, which Herculius wished to claim as his own; then Gaul, into which he fled twice. We therefore do not doubt that the kingdom from which he is now said to have been excluded wherever he came must properly be understood as Italy: whether no other part of his former empire was restored to Herculius through his son—which I should readily believe—or Africa was restored along with it, as the most distinguished Cuper seems above to prefer, and as Pagius perhaps would not deny. For in his *Critica Baroniana*, under AD 336, no. 12, he expressly states that Felix, the praetorian prefect to whom Law 21 of the Theodosian Code is addressed, was prefect of the praetorium of Italy in such a way that the prefecture of Africa was also included within it.

“Wherever he came.” It has no sense unless you separate it from the preceding member and make it the beginning of the following period. ALLIX.—I thought that an excellent sense could be derived without changing the received punctuation, in this way: there was no city in Italy to which Herculius attempted to withdraw that did not shut its gates against him; and thus, wherever he came, he was excluded from his own kingdom—that is, from the kingdom which he had once governed alone and which had been entrusted to him by Diocletian’s arrangement, and which he afterwards held jointly with his son, as though by right of postliminy.

Diocles was present there. That is, with the Maximian to whom Herculius was previously said to have set out, and consequently with Galerius Maximian; or, what comes to the same thing, at Galerius’ court, if with Maucroix you wish to attend to the sense rather than to the preceding words: “Galerius had recently summoned Diocles to his court,” etc.

Diocles. This is the first occasion given to our author for speaking of Diocletian after that passage in chapter 19: “Diocletian cast his purple upon him, having stripped it off himself, and became Diocles again.” Hence, when we now hear him called not Diocletian but Diocles, it appears to follow that Diocletian, on laying down the purple, returned to his former designation, Diocles [Col. 0763C]. Especially since we similarly read in chapter 37: “For if Diocles or Maximian left anything behind”; and again in chapter 52: “Where now are those magnificent and illustrious titles of Jovians and Herculians, renowned among the nations, which were first assumed by Diocles and Maximian?” Take care, however, not to infer anything of the kind too incautiously. For in chapter 41 our author will again call him not Diocles or Diocletes, but Diocletian, in these words: “Augusta, however, having been banished into certain deserted solitudes of Syria, secretly made known her calamity to her father Diocletian.” Eutropius likewise says of the same man after his return to private life: “Diocletian, in private life, grew old in distinguished leisure at a villa not far from Salona.” Not to cite more now, add the passage from Jerome quoted above. Maucroix, as though correcting our author—or uncertain what he ought rather to choose—writes: “Galerius had recently summoned Diocles, or Diocletian, his father-in-law, to his court”; word for word: Galerius had recently summoned Diocles, or Diocletian, his father-in-law, into [Col. 0763D] his court.

For my part, I should not wish to decide what ought rather to be chosen. But whatever name Diocletian ought to bear, or was in fact called, after his abdication of the empire, he was certainly then either Diocles again, without another addition, as when our author wrote above, “he became Diocles again”; or Diocles, or Diocletian, again a private citizen, if mention of his condition must also be added; or Diocles, or Diocletian, a second time a private citizen, in the manner in which those who formerly held a second consulship among the Romans were called second consuls; [Col. 0764A] or finally Diocles, or Diocletian, twice a private citizen, just as Herculius above in chapter 26 was called twice Augustus. And the numerical letters in all these expressions will no more yield the fatal number of the Apocalyptic Beast, should anyone wish to ponder that matter after the example of the Bishop of Meaux, than they did in the other expressions mentioned above. I add this lest that eminent man perhaps suppose that he can escape by some avenue. See the notes appended at the foot of the page.

[Note: [Col. 0764A]

Recently summoned by his son-in-law, in order that, etc. If what the same bishop alleges concerning chapter 13 of the Apocalypse were true, Diocletian had made all the other emperors down to Licinius and was, as it were, the father and source of them all. Indeed, according to the distinguished bishop, after Diocles had abdicated the empire and renounced the title of emperor, some power of creating others was in a manner retained for him. Accordingly, the bishop continues, Galerius Maximian summoned Diocletian to himself when he wished to confer the title of Augustus upon Licinius. But first, as is clear from chapter 24, it was not Diocletian but Constantius Chlorus who named Constantine Augustus and handed the empire over to him. Likewise, it was not Diocletian but Galerius who named Severus Augustus at the end of chapter 25. Nor was it Diocletian but the hands of the praetorian guards who made Maxentius emperor in chapter 26. Nor again was it Diocletian but Galerius who urged Severus to reclaim the empire and in fact compelled him to do so, in the same place. Nor, again, was it Diocletian but Maxentius who twice named Herculius Augustus, again in that place. Finally, in the following chapters it will not be Diocletian but Galerius who suddenly orders three men, besides himself and Licinius already Augusti, to be counted as emperors, having abolished the title of Caesars and, with it, Diocletian’s former arrangement, in chapter 32. Indeed, it will appear from those same chapters that all these things were done not only without Diocletian being present, but without his even being consulted. Nor should I add that Severus too, entirely without Diocletian’s knowledge, was sent by Galerius to Herculius before Diocletian’s very abdication, so that he might be clothed with the purple by Herculius. Therefore, what we reported at the beginning of this note from the observations of the cited bishop on John’s Apocalypse must be mere dreams of a man carried away by zeal for a cause. Thus Diocletian was summoned by Galerius for this simple and proper reason when, in his presence, he wished to confer the empire upon Licinius: that the inauguration might be more solemn.

By his son-in-law. By Galerius. MAUCROIX.

That he might confer the empire upon Licinius. Baluzius here undertakes a long discussion concerning the year in which Licinius became emperor: some assign it to 307, others to the following year. Their chief argument is that Galerius could not have traversed so great an extent of lands within so few months. To this, however, one may reply that Galerius’ restless and fierce disposition, especially inflamed by desire to retain the empire, quickly broke through barriers that would have checked minds somewhat more composed. Oxford and Cambridge editions.—Baronius rightly wrote that Licinius was named Augustus in the current year, 307, [Col. 0764D] and we demonstrated it in our *Dissertation on the Consular Fasti*. Hence Hydatius errs in the *Fasti*, where he reports that this dignity was conferred upon him in the following year. Yet both rightly noted that this designation took place at Carnuntum in Pannonia, on 11 November. But Licinius was first called Caesar and, not long afterwards, Augustus, as I have shown there. PAGIUS, *Critica Baroniana*, under AD 307, no. 14, where there is further material on this subject.

Having been substituted in Severus’ place. Those who prefer “into Severus’ place” are right. TOLLIUS.—I should indeed judge that more correct. [Col. 0765A] For Florus, for example, book I, chapter 6, writes: “Therefore, after Tarquinius’ death, with the queen’s support, Servius Tullius was substituted into the king’s place.” But, in a word, whereas writers of the better age commonly said *in manum tradere*, “to hand over into the hand,” *in matrimonium postulare*, “to seek in marriage,” and countless other expressions of this sort, our author, by contrast, as did Sulpicius Severus and the Vulgate translator of the Bible, not infrequently said *in manu tradere*, *in matrimonio postulare*, *in matrimonio accipere*, and likewise in other cases. Thus below, in chapter 35: “having commended his wife and son to Licinius, and handed them over into his hand”; and in chapter 39: “having sent envoys ahead, he seeks her in marriage”; and in Sulpicius Severus, book I, chapter 9: “Jacob burned with love for the maiden and sought her for himself in marriage,” etc.; and again, chapter 43: “Ahab, having received Jezebel, daughter of Ethbaal king of Sidon, in marriage, set up an altar and groves for the idol Baal.” Yet elsewhere he writes: “Moses, having stayed with Jethro, received his daughter Zipporah in marriage”; and elsewhere again: “Saul gave his daughter Michal to a certain Phalti [Col. 0765B] in marriage.” Since Fathers of the more polished fourth century of Christianity used both phrases indiscriminately, along with other similar instances in the same author, the wording of this passage ought not, in my judgement, to be rashly interpolated. Compare what we shall observe on chapters 35 and 39.

Thus it happens in the presence of both. Namely, Diocletian and the old man Maximian, as Maucroix reasonably supplied or explained, both from what precedes and from what immediately follows. For immediately afterwards follows “the old man Maximian,” and shortly before Diocles preceded.

Thus at one time there were six. The passage is doubtless corrupt or mutilated. For what does “there were six” mean, when no word preceded that can already be understood in the plural and, as they say, supplied *apo tou koinou* (“from the common element”)? Both translators supplied *emperors* as a supplement: “There were therefore then six persons who bore the name of emperor.” MAUCROIX.—“And now there were all at once six emperors,” [Col. 0765C] English translation. I wonder—not without reason—that the word is not found in the neuter gender in the whole beginning of this chapter, indeed not even in the whole preceding chapter 28. But not all those governing the Commonwealth at that time were yet emperors: under Diocletian’s old arrangement, confirmed by Galerius, some were emperors and others Caesars. If you doubt this, look through all of chapter 32. You will understand that, far from six emperors presiding over the Commonwealth once Licinius had been named emperor, the distinction between Caesars and emperors continued for some time. Indeed, the name of Caesar was not truly removed until, after some lapse of time, Maximinus wrote to Galerius that he had been hailed Augustus by the army and Galerius, upon receiving this letter, finally ordered that the four who, besides himself, administered the Roman empire under this or that right and title should thereafter also be called emperors, as we shall establish in its place. Since this is so, how could the sense of the words “thus at one time there were six” be “thus at one time there were six emperors”? Rather, with leave for conjecture, our author wrote: “Thus at one time six men presided”—namely, over the Commonwealth, of which mention is made in the preceding section: “as though to confer with him concerning the arrangement of the condition of the Commonwealth.”

Thus at one time there were six. Namely, Herculius, Galerius, Maximinus Daza, Constantine, Maxentius, and Licinius. Oxford and Cambridge editions.

The old man Maximian, his plans frustrated. “Maximian, disappointed of his hope.” MAUCROIX.—In Latin: Maximian, whom his own hope had disappointed. It will doubtless be better explained from the following verses of Terence:

> P. Come now, good sir, what do you say? Do you see that by your counsels  
> I have been made wretched and entangled?  
> D. But I shall now free you.

See the commentators, if you have leisure or need.

[Col. 0766A] He was also planning a third flight. The passage has been understood variously by translators. Maucroix uses the present: “he prepares for a third flight”; literally, “he prepares a third flight.” Not badly, since in expressions of this kind verbs in the present and imperfect tenses elegantly have the same force. Servius elsewhere, on *Aeneid* I:

> Often the Danaans, Troy abandoned, desired  
> To devise flight.

“To devise,” he says, “that is, to prepare.”

The English translation, however, uses the past tense: “Fled again for the third time”; thus introducing Herculius not as preparing flight after some more or less extended interval, but as already fleeing. I suspected that our author wrote *Tertiam quoquo fugam moliebatur*, “He was devising a third flight, whithersoever [he might go],” that is, he was considering to what place he should depart, among the many which came to mind, and meanwhile was preparing the things necessary for flight. Cicero, *On Divination* II: “Thus, whithersoever the Stoics turn themselves,” etc.

[Col. 0766B] Full of evil contamination and crime. Heinsius preferred “full of evil thought and crime.” He thought that “contamination” had no place here. “He reveals these evil thoughts in the following words.” GRAEVIUS.—“Contamination. Correct me at my own risk, and read ‘thought.’ Surely contamination has no place here; nor do the passages brought forward by the most distinguished Colombus, p. 380, col. 1, help.” TOLLIUS.—“Contamination. Thought. Thus in book V of the *Institutes*, §12, On Justice.” GALE.—Yet in the cited passage of Lactantius, not only does the word “thought” nowhere appear in any case in my editions; the received reading also seems to yield excellent and perfectly intelligible sense: “Is innocence among you so utterly destroyed that you judge it unworthy even of a simple death, but regard it as worse than every crime not to commit any crime, and to keep one’s heart pure from all contamination of wickedness?” Judge for yourself.

“That Constantine [was] emperor.” Yet by Galerius’ leave he could not as yet be called emperor, but only Caesar. Our author, however, plainly regarded Constantius’ arrangement, mentioned at the end of chapter 24, as prior to Galerius’ arrangement, mentioned likewise at the end of chapter 25. Therefore, just as he says above immediately after Constantius’ death, “Having assumed the empire, Constantine became Augustus,” so now, more than a year after that same Constantius’ death, he calls Constantine emperor. You will shortly see several similar expressions in this very chapter. Thus this writer might at some time have counted five emperors before Galerius abolished the name of Caesars, but not six, because Maximinus Daza until then enjoyed only the name or title of Caesar.

His son-in-law. Since he had married Fausta, Maximian’s daughter. Oxford and Cambridge editions.

The son of his son-in-law. That is, the son of Constantius, who, having repudiated Helena, married Theodora, the daughter—or, according to others, stepdaughter—of Herculius. Oxford and Cambridge editions.

With evil intent. Which is opposed to good faith. See Brissonius’ formulae. TOLLIUS.

“Evil intent is when one thing is done and another pretended.” Julius Paulus, *Sentences Received*, title 9.

The royal garment. Which shortly will be called by the other name, the purple robe: “He suddenly takes the purple”; and Lactantius similarly says: “Among the Romans, the garment of purple is the mark of assumed royal dignity,” *Institutes* IV, chapter 7. This strongly confirms what we said above.—“The imperial ornaments.” Maucroix; literally, “imperial ornaments,” in the plural.—“The imperial habit.” English translation; that is, “the imperial garment,” in the singular.

The nation of the Franks was under arms. That war with the Franks of which Lactantius speaks does not appear to be different from that which Eusebius mentions in *Life of Constantine*, book I, chapter 25, where he says that Constantine crossed over against the British peoples. PAGIUS, *Critica Baroniana*, under AD 307, no. 7.—But then in AD [Col. 0767A] 307 the Franks would already have overrun all Gaul and settled in Gallic Britain, which I do not recall ever reading anywhere; whereas Einhard and others say quite different things. Add Baluzius on the words “having left behind part of the soldiers,” and Cuper, whom I would rather follow.

Gallic Britain received this name around AD 460, when, in the time of Placidius Valentinian, Rivalus, fleeing the domination of the Angles, crossed into Gaul with a great multitude of Britons, occupied the territories of the Veneti and Osismii, and named the region Britain after his own people. GRAEVIUS.

Barbarians. “The Emperor Valentinian wished the Franks to be called, in the Attic tongue, from their ferocity, hardness, and boldness,” says Ivo of Chartres at the beginning of his *Chronicle of the Kings of the Franks*. This would greatly illuminate the present passage, where our author simply calls barbarians the same people whom he shortly before called Franks, if this book and many other ancient monuments did not prove and establish that the name Franks is older than the times of either Valentinian. But was the designation “barbarians” therefore milder for this author when he spoke of Gauls? Certainly not. For he called the Carpi “barbarians” disparagingly in chapter 4, and the Persians in chapter 5, in precisely the same spirit in which elsewhere he speaks of barbarian lust, natural barbarism, some barbarian son-in-law, barbarian slavery, and similar things.

The young man believes. “This young prince.” MAUCROIX.—Not badly, provided you do not understand “prince” of a very young man. Constantine was then about thirty-six years of age. Compare what was said on chapter 24.

The emperor. Constantine, namely; Burnet rightly preferred, for clarity’s sake, to repeat the name rather than speak more obscurely with our author by changing the designation.

The man is overpowered. That is, the old man Maximian, as the translators have in part made clear; indeed, the very man who shortly before had planned to overpower Constantine. For the preceding words are: “He persuades [Constantine], who suspected nothing, not to take the whole army with him . . . so that he himself, the old man Maximian, might have an army which he could seize, and that he, Constantine, might be overpowered because of the small number of his soldiers.”

[Col. 0767C] Which especially did not become him. Because he was Constantine’s father-in-law, had been the father-in-law of his father, Constantius, and was an emperor of advanced age whom Constantine had received with every honour—indeed, in the place of a father, because Augusti were called the fathers of Caesars. TOLLIUS.

Then suddenly the gates behind him are opened and the soldiers admitted. The sense is entirely clear, provided that neither event is understood to have occurred strictly behind Herculius, but in a remote quarter of the city to which he was turning his back. The basis and necessity of this observation are evident of themselves.

The rebel emperor is dragged before the emperor. Observe how our author continues to attend rather to the arrangement of others than to Galerius’ arrangement. Certainly, if you compare that passage of chapter 26—“Afterwards Maxentius sends the purple robe to his father, namely Herculius, who was staying in Campania after laying down the empire, and names him Augustus twice”—with this passage of chapter 32—“Galerius, defeated by their obstinacy, abolishes the name of Caesars and calls himself and Licinius Augusti, Maxentius and Constantine sons of Augusti”—you will understand that Herculius was so far from being regarded as emperor by Galerius for some time that in this almost final arrangement of Galerius no mention is made of Herculius, much less of him as emperor.

The impious father. A father in the proper sense, by reason of his daughter Fausta, whom Constantine had married. “Impious” means cruel, inhumane, merciless, just as, conversely, “pious father” is used of a kind, humane, and merciful father. Cicero: “No less pious toward me than a father toward his sons.” Thus the Latins did not speak solely of the piety or impiety of children toward parents, but also of parents toward children. Indeed, near the end of this book, in chapter 52, our author will praise God’s eternal piety—that is, mercy—toward his flock.

[Col. 0768A] He hears of the crimes which he committed, etc. That is, as soon as he was brought before Constantine, Constantine reproached him for having behaved not as a father and father-in-law toward him, but wickedly, impiously, and treacherously. Then his garment was removed; and finally, after he had thus been rebuked, his life was spared.

Garment. The royal garment, namely. Maucroix translates straightforwardly “the purple”; Burnet, “the imperial purple.”

## CHAPTER XXX

Thus, having lost the honour of emperor and father-in-law. That is, Herculius Maximian, having lost in that manner the honour which Constantine and others had previously given him generally as emperor, and which Constantine had additionally shown him as father-in-law. This is confirmed both by the following words, “unable to endure humiliation”—from which it is clear that henceforth Herculius lacked not merely the purple but also the ceremonial respect and deference of courtiers, and was finally reduced to the lowliest condition of life [Col. 0768B]—and by the statement in what precedes that Constantine, showing him no honour, rebuked Herculius as a wicked man, an impious father, and a treacherous father-in-law.—“Maximian deprived of the title of emperor and father-in-law.” Maucroix, thus supposing that the words refer simply to the lost designations of emperor and father-in-law.—“But Maximian, having lost both the dignity of an emperor and the regard paid to him as a father-in-law,” English translation; explaining the lost honour of emperor as the loss of imperial dignity, and the lost honour of father-in-law as the loss of Constantine’s respect toward Herculius as his father-in-law. This interpretation differs little from our author’s and is nearly the same as it.

Because he once went away unpunished. Move the full stop before “because” to after “unpunished.” BOHERELLUS. Likewise Gale.—I suspected that the conjunction *et*, frequently absorbed elsewhere by preceding words, had likewise been absorbed here before *quia*; consequently I would read: “And because he once went away unpunished, he summons,” etc.

He summons his daughter Fausta. “He flatters his daughter Fausta.” MAUCROIX.—I wonder, since there is so great a difference between *vocare* (“to call”) and *blandimentis sollicitare* (“to solicit with blandishments,” “to flatter”). Besides, it is also evident from the words immediately following that blandishments were only Herculius’ second device, by which he attempted to win his daughter to his side. He first of all summoned her—that is, he caused her to be summoned to himself and brought it about that she came.

He promises [her] a worthier husband. Let Colombus be consulted on this passage.

He asks that the bedchamber, etc. The Abo edition has it somewhat differently: “He asks that the bedchamber be left open and that she allow it to be guarded less carefully.”

She promises that she will do it, and immediately reports it to her husband. “But Fausta, having anticipated the attempt and informed Constantine of it, Herculius, despairing because he had fallen from all his fortunes, died of illness at Tarsus.” Zosimus rightly says this of the plot; but, as we observed long ago, he confuses Herculius with Maximinus Daza, whom the Epitome of Victor testifies to have died a natural death at Tarsus. But we shall consider that later. Oxford and Cambridge edition.

She immediately reports it to her husband. To Constantine. MAUCROIX.

That he might be caught in manifest crime. I would prefer “in the act of crime.” TOLLIUS. This also seems to have occurred to Maucroix: “Everything is arranged to catch the traitor in a manifest attempt.”—If anything must be emended, I would prefer: “that the criminal might be caught red-handed.” For Cicero, *Against Verres* V, says: “I catch … a thief caught red-handed diverting the whole grain supply.” Yet why should the received reading not stand well, when Cicero elsewhere in the same speech against Verres wrote: “Therefore the man’s avarice, greed, crime, dishonesty, and audacity are now caught—caught red-handed”; and again elsewhere, *For Cluentius*: “Oppianicus’ crime, clearly established and detected [Col. 0769A].”

A certain lowly eunuch is substituted, to die in place of the emperor. A notable act, though, to tell the truth, I do not sufficiently see its fairness or necessity. I know only a similar example in the *History of the Maccabees*, book III, near the beginning of chapter 1, as follows: “A certain Theodotus, intending to carry out the plot …” In Latin: “But a certain Theodotus, intending to execute the treachery, took with him the strongest of the armed men entrusted to him by Ptolemy and went by night to Ptolemy’s tent, in order to kill him unawares and so put an end to the war. But Dositheus … having removed him, placed a certain obscure man in the tent, who happened to suffer punishment in his place.”

He. Maximian, whom for that reason the translators preferred to name.

Suitable for the plot. That is, suitable for his treacherous undertaking. Maucroix renders it too simply: “suited to his design.”

To have seen a dream. A phrase upon which you should consult Cuper, and in which *se* after *vidisse* may easily elsewhere be lacking, having been absorbed by the preceding word.

He enters armed. The crime of Darius, who wished to overpower and kill his father Artaxerxes by night because he had denied him Aspasia, was not unlike this; nor was its outcome different. TOLLIUS.

The eunuch having been cut down. That is, as the translators rightly render it, killed. For shortly afterwards follows: “The corpse of the slain man is brought out of the bedchamber.” And although *obtruncare*, strictly speaking, means to make a body a trunk by mutilating, for example, its head and arms, it sometimes also means simply to kill in whatever manner. Plautus, *Aulularia*, act III, scene 4:

> I seize a club; I cut down the cock, the manifest thief.

Here the word *manifestarius* must be noted because of what immediately follows.

He leapt forward. More correctly, “he leaps forward.” TOLLIUS.

[Col. 0769C] He declares what he committed. Read “what he had committed,” or “what he committed.” The same editor.

A manifest murderer. Compare the passage from Plautus just cited.

“Or hard flint, or the Marpesian cliffs, should stand.” From Virgil, *Aeneid* VI. GALE. Likewise the Paris edition, in the margin.

“Cautis.” “Cautes” (“cliffs”). Abo edition and Pagius.

“And from a lofty beam he ties the noose of a hideous death.” Zosimus, on the contrary, in book II of his *History*, says: “Herculius died of illness at Tarsus.” But Sylburgius long ago remarked on those words: “Sigonius reports from others that he was strangled at Massilia by Constantine’s order.” Compare what was said above, previous page, col. 1, and what will shortly be said, following column.

“And the noose of hideous death,” etc. A verse of Virgil from *Aeneid* XII, as Baluzius first noted in the margin of the Paris edition.

Death. The Abo edition writes *lethus*, with an aspirate. Festus, Varro, and many others later approved that spelling, deriving the word from Greek *lēthē*, which means “forgetfulness” in Latin. But Priscian preferred to write *letum* without an aspirate and derived it from the archaic *leo* for *deleo* (“I destroy”). Since even among modern scholars the highly learned Manutius and Joseph Scaliger judged his opinion more probable, there was certainly no reason to interpolate the spelling of the old manuscript.

He celebrated vows for twenty years. That is, the *Vicennalia*. Lactantius alludes to the Roman custom of making vows for the ruler’s health and prosperity in solemnities of this kind, as is clear from Pliny’s letters to Trajan. Such vows are also expressly found on ancient coins: *VOTIS XX, MULTIS XXX*—“Vows for twenty [years], for many thirty.” Other coins read: *SIC X, SIC XX*, that is, “thus the Decennalia, thus the Vicennalia.” The anonymous author of the Cambridge edition adds that this is drawn from Valesius on Eusebius, *Life of Constantine* IV.47.

For twenty years. The word “reign” is lacking before these words. Otherwise the *per* in the preceding phrase would have to be changed to *in*. TOLLIUS.—Both translators strongly support this or some similar conjecture. “Thus this great emperor, master of the world for twenty years.” MAUCROIX.—“Thus this great emperor, who in the long course of a twenty-year reign,” English translation.
