A detestable life. A most odious epithet, as this passage of Cicero indicates: “There is between children and parents an affection which cannot be broken except by a detestable crime.” *Laelius, or On Friendship.*

He ended it. At Massilia, as Eusebius in the *Chronicle*, Victor in the *Epitome*, and Orosius in the *History* teach. PAGIUS, *Critica Baroniana*, under AD 307, no. 8. Compare what was said above, previous page, col. 1.

## CHAPTER XXXI

After this. After the emperor, or after the time? For the expression is elliptical; and the matter is doubtful not only from what precedes and from Latin usage, but also from the translations of this passage, which openly depend upon one or the other supplement. “After God had avenged his religion and his people upon the old Maximian.” MAUCROIX.—Literally: “after this old man Maximian,” etc.—“In the next place.” English translation: plainly as though our author had written “after these things” or “after this.” I prefer this interpretation, since the most distinguished Graevius similarly explained *ab hoc* at the end of chapter 26, and Greek authors are not unfamiliar with using *ek toutou* in the sense of *ek toutou kairou*, “from this time.” For example, John 19:12: “From that time Pilate sought to release him.” Beza: “From that time Pilate tried to release him”; but the Vulgate, in a single word: “Thereupon Pilate sought,” etc.

To the other Maximian. That is, in Maucroix’s translation, to Galerius. Correctly so, since our author is now turning his discourse to the final and disastrous fortunes of Galerius Maximian; hence “the other Maximian,” because the emperor whose hideous death had just been recounted also bore the name Maximian. But was the first Oxford edition likewise correct in advising, among its later corrections, that one should read “to the other Maximian, Galerius”? I suspect that the learned man to whom the received reading was displeasing wished “to the other Maximian” to be replaced by “to Maximian Galerius”; this is not without rationale. Yet the author nowhere speaks in that manner; whereas Galerius had already, at the beginning of chapter 9, been called “the other Maximian,” to distinguish him from Herculius. We therefore believe that no alteration is now needed.

The author of the persecution. Therefore one of those authors mentioned above, at the end of chapter 2: “If, from the beginning when the Church was established, I shall set forth who were the . . . authors . . . and by what punishments the severity of the heavenly Judge avenged itself upon them.” In that passage we do not doubt that after *authors* one must supply the word *persecutions*, or, if one prefers, *persecution*, because of the complete phrase here, “the author of the persecution.” Let Bal. be added there for other reasons.

So that in him also He might display the force of His majesty. Compare that passage in the same chapter 2: “that the most high God might display His power and majesty in . . . destroying His enemies and those of His name.”

Now he too was concerned with conducting [the celebration], etc. For Diocletian had, of course, celebrated his Vicennalia eight years before. Maucroix: “This prince, following Diocletian’s example.” See chapter XVII.

Who long before, etc. This gap seems to be supplied thus: “and who long before, etc., in order that he might pay what he had promised.” Oxford and Cambridge editions.

In order that he might pay what he had promised. Thus correctly emended. These promises concern the soldiers, to whom, with the Vicennalia imminent, he had promised, as customary, a *congiarium*, or donative. In order to make good these promises, new assessments were necessary. TOLLIUS.—I read: “and, since he had long afflicted the provinces by assessments of gold and silver, in order that he might pay what he had promised; he also, etc.” GALE.—I would prefer: “and since he had long afflicted the provinces by assessments of gold and silver [Col. 0771A] imposed, he, so that he might pay what he had promised, also,” and then what follows; so that *he* follows *having done*, and *so that* follows *what*. Or simply: “and who had long afflicted the provinces by assessments of gold and silver imposed, so that he might pay what he had promised, also . . .”

Assessments of gold and silver having been imposed. Livineius, on this passage of Pliny in Trajan’s *Panegyric*: “Nor, oppressed by new assessments, do they fail in payment of their former taxes,” says that there are altogether three kinds of fiscal payment: the *Canon*, a fixed and ordinary tax; the *Oblation*, that which is offered voluntarily; the *Indiction*, that which is newly imposed. Asconius mentions this in his commentary on *Against Verres*, IV.

That he might pay what he had promised, also in the name of the Vicennalia, etc. These words are badly corrupted; the damage seems removable if we rewrite them: “That he might render what he had promised, and under the empty name of the Vicennalia he inflicted a second axe-blow.” To “render Vicennalia” means to hold, celebrate, or exhibit them. Suetonius, *Domitian* 4: “He had established a college from which, chosen by lot, they should perform the office of president and exhibit exceptional hunts [Col. 0771B] and scenic games.” Terence, *Andria* 3.1: “If he had attacked me unprepared at a real wedding, what games he would have given me!” For *reddere* often means “to give,” as in Columella, VIII: “There is no greater safeguard even for a most worthless man than the daily exacting of work: that the allotted tasks may be rendered, that the overseer may always be at hand.” And XI, chapter 2: “The overseer shall take care that the allotted tasks are rendered”; that is, that they perform, give, and supply what is imposed upon them. Celsus, book XCIV, *On the Meaning of Words*: “Although the word *rendering* has the meaning of giving back, it nevertheless also admits the meaning of simply giving.” Thus, “to render entrails.” Virgil: “We render the smoking entrails”; and “to render vows,” meaning to perform them, is a conventional expression.

Subsequently, from the word *inani* (“empty”), the final letters *ani* fell away and adhered to the preceding little word *etc.* Hence arose *etam*, and then *etiam*. The “empty name of the Vicennalia” is so called because he vainly promised the Vicennalia and extorted money under their name, though he did not celebrate them. At the end, *afflixit* (“afflicted”) cannot be tolerated, since “he had long afflicted the provinces” had just preceded; not to mention the awkwardness of the phrase “to afflict an axe.” But one may “inflict an axe-blow,” as in the familiar expression “to inflict an axe upon the leg.” The Oxford editors perceived the sense when they explain it as: “he inflicted a second wound.” He clearly means that most bitter exaction of which he speaks in what follows. GRAEVIUS.

Also in the name of the Vicennalia. Delete *in*. GALE.—Perhaps it could be retained, though apparently superfluous, were there not other objections. I establish this from Jerome: “And Cain was building a city, and he named it after his son Enoch.” Here the preposition is plainly redundant.

He inflicted a second axe-blow. Without sense. ALLIX.—The passage is corrupt. PAGIUS.—That is, “he inflicted a second wound.” Oxford and Cambridge editions.

Axe. *Axe.* Abo edition. Though this is more correct, Columbus nevertheless rightly rejects it.

By this harassment. As learned men, following Gellius, have observed concerning the *Passion of Saints Perpetua and Felicity*, *vexare* is a mild word and denotes slight inconvenience. Nor is this badly said, provided it is understood only of particular passages—for example, that in the said *Passion*: “My father, provoked by this word, rushed at me as though to tear out my eyes; but he only harassed me.” Yet that this meaning is by no means constant we have not only already shown, but what immediately follows here will also declare and confirm.

Of the human race. Relevant here is something which I remember reading in Florus, or a similar writer of Roman history, approximately in these words: “the human race,” that is, “the Roman people.” At present I cannot more precisely identify or cite the passage.

Of all the offices. “All the taxmasters.” English translation. That is to say, all who had been set over exacting money; or, in a single word, tax-collectors. Thus our author shortly afterwards: “No threshing-floor was without a collector”; and Caesar, *Civil War*, III: “The province was full [Col. 0772A] of lictors and commands, crowded with prefects and collectors.” But I believe Cuperus explains it differently, and better, at the end of his observation on this passage.

It was uncertain whom they should satisfy first. “Pardon,” etc. Thus Baluze, in this second edition, employs the punctuation and correction which he had proposed in the errata of the first. For in the first edition that most distinguished man had caused the following to be printed from the manuscript codex as the author’s words: “It was uncertain whom they should satisfy first; pardon, and what follows.” Accordingly, the Oxford and Cambridge editions, some years later, had no other reading. The Abo edition alone has, in a different arrangement: “whom they should satisfy first, pardon not being available.” I myself do not readily grasp the meaning of these words.—I emend: “whom they should satisfy first among persons uncertain [of payment].” GALE. This coheres excellently with what precedes.

No pardon was available to those who did not possess [the means]. Thus Baluze now again prints it, whereas he previously, and the other editors after him, had printed: “no exemptions from refraining were available to those who did not possess [them],” and the rest; consequently with no punctuation at all after *nullas* (“none”). This gave occasion to the learned notes below.—“Although the old manuscript offers the reading which we gave, since it is certain that it is unsound, it may perhaps not be an empty conjecture to suppose that it should be read thus: ‘No pardon was available to those who did not have the means to endure multiple tortures,’ unless, and what follows.” BALUZE, in the errata of his first edition.—Baluze thus emends the passage: “No pardon was available to those who did not have the means to endure multiple tortures.” It seems to me it should be read: “Pardon: for those who did not possess [the means], no refraining,” etc. Oxford and Cambridge editions.—“No pardons [were available] to those who did not possess [the means]”; without sense. ALLIX.—Correct: “Indeed, for those who did not possess [the means], there was no way,” etc. Unless someone prefers the singular, “for one possessing,” because *circumsepto* follows shortly; though I would prefer to change that to *circumseptis*. TOLLIUS.—I thought it could not be read and punctuated better than in either of these ways: “No pardon from refraining was available to those who did not possess [the means]. Multiple tortures, unless it were produced,” etc. That is: tax-collectors had been strictly ordered not to refrain from those who would firmly say, “I have nothing to furnish”; hence whenever they heard this from anyone, they applied multiple tortures, unless what did not exist were immediately produced. Or, as today with Baluze: “No pardon [was available] to those who did not possess [the means].” Supply “was given,” in this sense: those who had nothing to produce could never obtain from the soldiers of the offices remission of the demand. What follows opposes neither sense, but rather confirms either; as does what we showed above, from the cited passage of the Vulgate, namely that “not to possess” is the same as “to possess nothing.” For the latter sense, Quintilian’s passage is especially apposite: “I have sinned; I ask pardon,” where pardon is remission of fault or sin. Then likewise chapter 35: “Yet he did not receive . . . pardon for his crime from God.”

To endure multiple tortures. An old sheet has: “To refrain from multiple tortures.” Not only have all editions hitherto published faithfully reproduced this reading, [Col. 0772D] but Gale also believed it could conveniently be explained.

Circumsepto. The word is suspect to Tollius, as he himself just testified; he would certainly prefer *circumseptis* in its place. I once suspected the wording of the entire passage to have been: “to endure multiple tortures, unless what did not exist, or was enclosed under many guards, were immediately produced. Then immediately: ‘There was no opportunity to breathe,’ etc.” Read again what precedes, if you doubt whether all the parts cohere suitably.

Frequent conflict over these same persons, whether by the judges themselves or by the soldiers of the judges. I punctuate and supply: “Frequent conflict over these same persons, whether by the judges themselves of the soldiers, or by the soldiers of the judges.” GALE.—Entirely ingenious, in my judgment. Yet Gale’s meaning seemed to me to emerge from the received reading even without supplementation. Moreover, it has already been said above that *de hisdem* is used for *eisdem*, “over these same persons.”

How tolerable these things are. The passage is dislocated. ALLIX.—

[Col. 0773A]

Perhaps one should restore: “Although it is intolerable,” etc.

Baluze reads: “Although it is intolerable,” with, as it seems to me, an interrupted sense. Therefore it should be written: “Since these things are intolerable.” Oxford and Cambridge editions.—I emend: “Although these things are intolerable.” Boherellus, likewise Graevius, on the entire passage, in these words:—

“How tolerable these things are: that food won by men’s labor should be snatched from their labor; yet in some way tolerable by the hope of future things.” These words, as they stand in the books we have thus far seen, are intolerable, because no sane Orestes will swear that any sound meaning can be extracted from them. See whether they are not sounder if, as Lactantius very probably wrote, you read: “Although these things are intolerable—that food obtained by men’s labor should be snatched from men’s lips—yet [they are] in some degree tolerable through hope of future things.” In place of *labore* (“labor”), I have restored *labro* (“lip”), namely, from which they were going to eat. The familiar saying is well known: “Many things fall between the cup and the upper lip.” Food “obtained by labor” is food acquired, just as Horace a thousand times uses *quaerere* (“to obtain”):

[Col. 0773B]

> It is no lesser virtue to preserve what has been gained than to gain it.

I formerly approved this emendation to Heinsius. GRAEVIUS.—“How tolerable these things are.” I read: “Although these things are intolerable.” For he has in view food obtained and brought back from ploughing and from the vintage. Wine too is counted among foods. In the first clause he regards the diversity of foodstuffs; in the second, the very act expressed by the phrase, “that food gained by labor should be snatched from men’s mouths.” TOLLIUS.—I correct: “Oh! how intolerable it was,” etc. GALE.—“How much more intolerable these things are.” Pagius, under A.D. 311, no. 10, whether deliberately or through a printer’s error.—I preferred to all these: “O wicked man! Are these things tolerable?” and what follows—with apostrophe, namely, and interrogation. First, because our author shortly afterwards uses a similar apostrophe and interrogation: “Whence then, O most mad tyrant, shall I provide this?” Then because that emendation comes closest of all to the reading of the old manuscript. For how little separates “*quae quam*,” or rather, as copyists wrote it a thousand times, “*quae quam*,” from “*o nequam*” (“O wicked man”)? Finally, because, since the question concerns not one kind of food snatched away but several kinds, the author could quite aptly exclaim: “O wicked man! Are these things tolerable—that food acquired by labor should be snatched from men’s lips or mouths?” For this is the true order of the words. Let others pronounce upon the whole matter, not I. I add only Cicero’s not dissimilar exclamation in the letters to Atticus: “O Sestius’ letter-carrier, you wicked man!”

That food gained by labor should be snatched from men’s mouths. Thus the two Oxford editions and the Cambridge edition have long read. Baluze, moreover, had already led the way with his conjecture in the often-praised errata. But the old book finally has: “food gained by labor snatched from the labor of men,” with simple *e*; and hence the Paris edition with the Abo edition: “food gained by labor snatched from the labor of men,” with the diphthong, and something further. Beware, however, of understanding any food here other than that suggested by the preceding words “threshing-floors” and “vintages”: namely bread and wine, food indeed coming back from ploughing and vintage, as Tollius spoke shortly before; and likewise food in the proper sense, as he rightly observed.

Yet [it is] tolerable (or endurable) in some manner, or through hope of future things. Let the most learned men who accept this reading and each explain it in his own fashion forgive what I shall say: I judge that it cannot be accepted. Rather it should be rewritten: “Yet [it is] tolerable in some manner, or through hope of offspring (*foeturarum*).” Those who till the soil in regions fertile in wine and grain ordinarily sustain—or at least can sustain—hunger by three kinds of resources: bread, or grain, which is the yield of the threshing-floor; wine, which is the yield of the vintage or winepress; and finally offspring, or the increase of animals. For the increase of animals is called *foetura* by Latin speakers, and the young themselves are *foeturae*. Pliny: “The best breeding is after the vernal equinox”; and Virgil, *Eclogue* 7:

[Col. 0774A]

> If offspring has filled out the flock, be golden.

Servius comments: “If I have as many lambs as sheep; for this is what it means for a flock to be filled out through breeding. For *foetura* is increase, that is, the offspring itself.” Hence, as Stephanus explains, certain animals are said to *superfoetare* (“conceive again while pregnant”) when, after conceiving one offspring through intercourse, they conceive another in addition to the first; it too is commonly brought forth in due time one or two days, or even several days, after the first has been emitted. This second delivery, as it were a new birth, is called *superfoetatio*.

But for farmers, if their ordinary foods, bread and wine—each returning from ploughing and vintage at great labor—are snatched even from their mouths, that act, however intolerable by nature, nevertheless becomes bearable if they hope otherwise to live from the offspring, that is, the young, of animals; because, in this sense, the breeding of cattle, for example, differs from the breeding of sheep. A notable passage of Caesar, *Gallic War*, VII, supports this: “When the army was afflicted by the greatest scarcity of grain, . . . to such an extent that for several days the soldiers lacked grain and sustained extreme hunger by driving in cattle from more distant villages.” But if I am mistaken, here is how the translators rendered it: “They consoled them with the future.” Maucroix. Almost word for word: “They said that they should hope for better things hereafter, and so consoled them.” “Yet all this was softened by the hopes that were given of what the emperor was to do in his twentieth year,” English translation. That is: “Yet all this was alleviated by the hope held out of the benefits with which the emperor would favor them in his twentieth year.”

What of clothing of every kind, what of gold, what of silver? The passage, as is apparent even from the translators’ rendering, is mutilated or corrupt. “Can one do without furniture or clothing?” MAUCROIX.—“Who can do without household goods or clothing?” “It was expected that men should appear in rich clothes, and bring much gold and silver along [Col. 0774C] with them.” BURNET.—That is to say: men were obliged to celebrate the said Vicennalia dressed in costly garments and adorned with much gold and silver placed about them. And Galerius expected this to occur.

It seemed to me that some verb proper to the exaction of assessments had fallen out, such as “is accordingly demanded”: “What clothing of every kind is demanded? What gold? What silver?” Namely, for clothing and adorning the emperor’s attendants, soldiers, and others, in the name of conducting the more solemn Vicennalia. What follows certainly is: “Whence then, O most mad tyrant, shall I provide this?” That is, “shall I furnish it, shall I give it”; this more than suggests that a demand for furnishing some object had preceded. And that the discussion can now very well concern the collection of assessments is likewise proclaimed by these words at the beginning of this chapter: “who had long afflicted the provinces by assessments of gold and silver imposed . . . also, in the name of the Vicennalia, inflicted a second axe-blow”—namely, new assessments of gold and silver. This is especially so if the end of the chapter is also considered: “Who therefore was not ruined in his property, so that riches which had been under his rule might be scraped together for a vow which he was not going to celebrate?”

Whence then, O most mad [tyrant]? These words are better [read] as immediately above: “Are not these things?” What was necessary concerning the apostrophe has already been said.

Who therefore was not ruined in his property, so that riches, etc.? From these words it is clear with what magnificence the Vicennalia and festivals of that kind were celebrated by emperors, since huge exactions were customarily made for this purpose. PAGIUS.

Which he was not going to celebrate. Because he did not reach the twentieth year of his reign. Oxford and Cambridge editions; the latter adds: see Section 30.

It is clear from these words that Galerius Maximian did not celebrate the Vicennalia of his Caesarean rule, although, had they been held in the proper year, they should have been celebrated in the current year 311, in which the sixth year after the celebrated Quindecennalia was beginning. For the Vicennalia of Galerius Maximian’s Caesarean rule fell in this year, though he deferred them until the following year, as we shall see from Lactantius, chapter 3, having meanwhile assumed the consulship. PAGIUS.

## CHAPTER XXXII

Licinius having therefore been proclaimed emperor. After Severus had been removed, Galerius gave the imperial power to Licinius, placing him in Severus’ position—namely the Augustan imperial authority; for we have demonstrated that this had been granted to Severus . . . and, it seems, with the same purpose of depressing Constantine, so that he might accordingly give Licinius precedence over Constantine. DODWELL.

Maximin. Before becoming emperor, he was called Daza. These are Victor’s words in the *Epitome*.

Angry, he would not consent either to be Caesar or to be named in the third place. Not indeed because there were then three Caesars in the Roman Empire and Maximin was third among them; for there were only two, namely Maximin, by the joint arrangement of Diocletian and Galerius, and Constantine, by Galerius’ own act in disapproving the final will [Col. 0775B] of Constantius. Rather, in a word, Maximin no longer wished to be called Caesar but Augustus. Nor did he wish, as Augustus, to be named only in the third place in the titles of edicts, after Galerius and Licinius; rather, he wished to be second and Licinius thereafter third, in this order: Galerius Augustus, Maximin Augustus—Licinius Augustus; not, as he saw would follow from Licinius’ recent proclamation by Galerius: Galerius Augustus, Licinius Augustus, Maximin Caesar. The English translation briefly expresses the same sense: “Maximin resented it extremely, and would neither be contented any longer with the title of Caesar, nor allow Licinius the precedence.”

Angry. Anonymous Cambridge editor. See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, VIII.13, edition of Valesius.

He therefore often sends envoys to him. Namely, Galerius Maximian. PAGIUS. Thus combining the different supplements of the translators.

[Col. 0775C]

Let him preserve his arrangement. “[The arrangement] by which Licinius was proclaimed emperor.” Oxford and Cambridge editions.—I add: “and by which Maximin had formerly been proclaimed Caesar by Diocletian, with Galerius suggesting and supplying the man.” See chapter 17.

Let him yield to age, etc. “And to induce him to pay the respect that was due to Licinius’s age and to his gray hairs.” English translation; in this sense: let him yield to Licinius’ age and honor his gray hairs. Toinard agrees. But Baluze understands it quite differently.

But he raises his horns more boldly. Namely Maximin, as the English translator explained.

He contends by prescription of time, etc. A legal topic still famous today in civil as well as ecclesiastical affairs, and already so in both, as those skilled in sacred and profane history know.

He despised his entreaties and commands. Read: “he despises.” TOLLIUS.

His. Maximian’s. English translation.

The beast is grieved and bellows. Perhaps: “The beast is grieved and roars.” NIC. HEINSIUS.

Beast. In place of this word, read “Galerius” in Maucroix’s translation and “the tyrant” in the English. Many similar expressions occur above, for example at the beginning of chapters 4 and 9.

Because he had made him an obscure Caesar in order that he might obey him, yet he, etc. I read: “because, although he had for that reason.” BOHERELLUS. Likewise Gale and Allix.—Unless someone should prefer to be content with transposition, reading: “because he had made him obscure . . . Caesar,” corrected as: “because, although he had made him an obscure Caesar.” TOLLIUS.—Perhaps: “because he whom he had made an obscure Caesar for this purpose, that he might be obedient to him, nevertheless, forgetting such a great benefit,” and what follows. *Eum* (“him”) cannot stand when *is* (“he”) follows. NIC. HEINSIUS.—It follows, I admit. But what if the conjunction *and* is missing before *is*, having been absorbed into the preceding word, as so often elsewhere? Would *eum* still be intolerable? On the contrary, it would not impede a plain and convenient meaning. Especially if, at the same time, *adeo* (“so very”) is read for *ideo* (“for this reason”), in this manner: “The beast is grieved, and bellows—or roars—because he had made him, though so very obscure, Caesar, that he might obey him, yet he, forgetful of so great a benefit, wickedly opposed his will and entreaties.” Those few words in chapter 19 place Maximin’s utterly contemptible obscurity beyond all dispute: “Daia, lately raised up from cattle and woods.” We therefore believe that by both corrections we have restored the author’s hand.

He might wickedly oppose. We said incidentally above that piety and impiety can apply to sons. Caesars were called sons by the Augusti, as is certain from chapter 20 and the learned observations upon it. Hence our author says of Maximin Caesar, who despised the commands of Galerius Augustus: “yet he wickedly opposed his will and entreaties.”

Conquered by obstinacy. Who was conquered, and by whose obstinacy? For learned men differ on both questions. “Maximin was conquered by his own obstinacy,” say one or two—namely Toinard and Pagius, in the *Dissertation on the Consuls*, p. 138, and in the *Critique of Baronius* under A.D. [Col. 0776B] 307, no. 14. Except that in the latter place “Maximian,” through an error, was printed for “Maximin.”—We shall continue to do as we have done so far. We stand with the latter opinion, principally for three reasons.

The first is that all these actions—abolishing the name of Caesars, then calling himself and Licinius Augusti, and finally naming Maxentius and Constantine sons of the Augusti—were by their nature proper and genuine functions of the senior Augustus, not of a mere Caesar still, such as Maximin necessarily must have been, according to those who say he proclaimed himself Augustus. The second is that it is so improbable that Maximin undertook by his own initiative and in one bold stroke to arrange all three matters that, although, according to Eusebius, Maximin styled himself Augustus, he nevertheless never dared announce this in a letter to Galerius as something done by himself, but as something done by the army. “Maximin,” our author will shortly say, “later writes, as though reporting, that in the recently celebrated Campus Martius he had been proclaimed Augustus by the army.” The third, finally, is that since, according to his own account, Maximin wrote only to Galerius that he had been proclaimed Augustus by the army, and did not add, I say, that he had thereafter abolished the name of Caesars and called Maxentius and Constantine sons of the Augusti, those two actions—“He abolishes the name of Caesars; he calls Maxentius and Constantine sons of the Augusti”—can no longer be referred except either to that same army or to Galerius. But that they should be referred to the army is not permitted, even apart from pressing the silence of the letter, by the fact that no mention of Maximin’s army appears before the present passage. He therefore plainly referred them to Galerius. These arguments, I think, add no little weight to those of the learned men whose guidance we follow.

“He abolishes the name of Caesars”: namely Galerius, for the reasons just stated, so that those adopted into the hope of imperial office should thereafter refrain from that name and Maximin might thus be excluded, say the Oxford and Cambridge editions here, following Baluze.

He abolishes the name of Caesars. It therefore still remained in force, as we have elsewhere inferred from these words, not without cause. Let Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, VIII.13, be added: “After this, Licinius was declared Emperor and Augustus by the common vote of the rulers. This greatly grieved Maximin, who until then was still called only Caesar by everyone.” Baluze’s translation. But was he the only one? Certainly so according to our author, by whom Maxentius in chapter 26, and Constantine more than once in chapter 29, and others, are called emperors. But Galerius reckoned the numbers of Caesars and emperors differently, and Toinard above calculates according to Galerius’ understanding.

Maxentius and Constantine [he calls] sons of the Augusti. “By which Maximin was quite shut out.” English translation. Literally: “By this act, or in this manner, Maximin was entirely excluded.” But Baluze suspects that this passage is corrupt in the name of Maxentius. Columbus and Cuperus judge it mutilated.

As though reporting, etc. The force of the words is to be noted; it is certainly much weaker than if our author had written “announcing.” Thus Maximin still acted cautiously and not without a degree of deference toward the senior Augustus. It is consequently less likely that Maximin dared simultaneously and all at once to usurp the rights of that senior Augustus in all the many matters of which we spoke on the preceding page.

In the recently celebrated Campus Martius. Nicolaus Heinsius thought that the word *ludo* (“games”) had fallen out: “in the Campus Martius, at games recently celebrated.” Nothing seems to me to have fallen out. It means that the field was “celebrated,” that is, thronged by a great multitude of people, whether for a public spectacle, a hunt, or games. Thus in an old calendar an asylum is said to be “celebrated”; and in Ovid the nearby grove of Hylernus is “celebrated,” that is, visited by very many people, as sacred places are customarily frequented at solemn festivals. The Campus Martius is said to be celebrated in no different manner than Mucius’ doorway in Cicero: “The doorway of Quintus Mucius is celebrated daily by the greatest throng of citizens”; and Cicero himself, *To Atticus* IV.1: “A like crowd and applause attended me as far as the Capitol.” Maximin, moreover, could have been proclaimed Augustus in the Campus Martius even while absent; perhaps, therefore, a Campus Martius outside Rome should not be sought. GRAEVIUS.—“In the recently celebrated Campus Martius”: a phrase of that period. That is, on a solemn day, or at the assembly in which consuls were created. This had formerly been done in the Campus Martius. This was the day on which he himself was declared consul for the eighth time and Maximin for the second; Maximin used this occasion of his honor to seize the dignity of Augustus. This act, moreover, occurred in the eastern territories, as is clear from chapter 36. TOLLIUS.

He received it. What? That message. Maucroix. Likewise the English translation; perhaps [*it*] was absorbed into the preceding *recepit*: “He received it, etc.”—He: namely Galerius Maximian. PAGIUS.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

[Col. 0777C]

Now the eighteenth year. Of his reign. The translators mean the Caesarean rule of Galerius Maximian, begun on the first of March, A.D. 292 (for 392 was printed erroneously). PAGIUS, *Critique of Baronius*, under A.D. 311, no. 11. Columbus likewise above. Baluze disagrees with them.

God struck him with an incurable affliction. Therefore in the year 309, in which he began his eighteenth year. PAGIUS. But Baluze understands the matter differently in the same place. On the remaining points consult Cuperus and Columbus.

A grievous ulcer in, etc. Zosimus: “an incurable wound.” Oxford and Cambridge editions; only the latter adds: See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, VIII.16.—A grievous ulcer: *cacoethes* [a malignant condition]. TOLLIUS.

The physicians cut, treat. At first sight I thought one should read “cut, cauterize.” Now nothing seems to require alteration. BOHERELLUS.—That the word *treat* must be retained is shown by the following passage, after a few intervening words: “A new treatment from the beginning.” But see what Columbus wishes inserted here.

The physicians cut, treat. “The surgeons cut, excise.” MAUCROIX.—Literally: “the surgeons cut, cut out.” Nor can it certainly be denied that by *physicians* our author properly meant that kind of physician who treats wounds and is called a surgeon from manual operation. But who has ever used *curare* (“to treat”) in the sense of “to excise”? I add that shortly afterwards, in this same chapter, *fovere* (“to foment”) and *curare* (“to treat”) are joined as synonyms, where *fovere* most certainly does not mean “to cut.”

When a scar has already formed, the wound is cut open. Baluze formerly, and the other editors after him: “The wound cuts open the scar that has already formed”; except that Baluze’s emendation now preferred (for each reading partly corrects the old book) had long ago been proposed by himself at the end of his first edition, and the Oxford edition of 1680 also expressly approved it with this note: “It should be read: ‘When a scar has formed, the wound is cut open.’” The judgment of my most distinguished colleague on Baluze’s other emendation follows.

“The wound cuts open the scar that has formed.” Latin usage requires the reading: “the wound reopens the scar that has formed.” I removed a similar error in the letters to Atticus. GRAEVIUS.—Wound: concerning an ulcer which, improperly treated and not completely healed, had eaten away some small vein. Otherwise a wound is a division of skin and underlying flesh with blood; an ulcer is accompanied by pus. TOLLIUS.—The remaining matters relevant to this passage are found above in Baluze and Columbus.

Yet the blood scarcely stops. Rather, “only with difficulty at last,” etc. BOHERELLUS.—I correct to *tandem* (“at last”). GALE.—Who nevertheless says elsewhere that *tamen* is used for *tandem*, as often in Marcellinus.

Yet it is brought [to healing]. Read *tamen* (“yet”). Oxford edition, 1684; likewise Cambridge.—Again *tamen* for *tandem*. BOHERELLUS.

Again, at a slight movement of the body . . . etc. Nicolaus Heinsius astutely, and later the Oxford editors, saw that the gap should be supplied thus: “Again wounded by a slight movement [Col. 0778B] of the body.” GRAEVIUS.—Supply *motu* (“movement”). Oxford and Cambridge editions.

Wounded. I emend: “is wounded.” GALE.—“Having been wounded.” It is astonishing that they hesitated over so easy a conjecture. Read: “when the wound has reopened.” TOLLIUS.—Those who wish may obey this command. But I fear that such conjectures are no easier to prove to others than to venture. Gale’s alternative is certainly more tolerable.

He himself grows pale. The translator: “He turns pale.”

The masters yielded, Chiron son of Philyra and Melampus son of Amythaon. From *Georgics* III, whereas it had previously been incorrectly read “Phyllides, Cirona, Metonius, Melamphius.” Cambridge edition, likewise Oxford, 1684.—Correctly. For so reads Baluze’s first edition and the Oxford edition of 1680. But later editions have:

> The masters yielded,  
> Chiron son of Philyra, and Melampus son of Amythaon,

without doubt following the note in the smaller Oxford edition concerning the old reading:

“‘Phyllides, Cirona, Metonius, Melamphius.’ A most corrupt passage, and the punctuation is exceedingly bad. Baluze seems, as though it were sound, to recognize no error; and, what is especially astonishing, he reads the earlier names separately, although they must undoubtedly be joined. For poets everywhere testify that Chiron was the son of Philyra; hence in Virgil he is called ‘Philyrides.’ Hesiod likewise, in the *Theogony*, concerning the same man:

> . . . and Chiron, son of Philyra, reared him in the mountains . . .

One must therefore read ‘Chiron son of Philyra.’ In place of ‘Metonius, Melamphius,’ moreover—names which Baluze seems to acknowledge as those of physicians—substitute ‘Melampus son of Amythaon.’” Virgil, *Georgics* III. Oxford edition, 1680.

Distinguished physicians are drawn from every quarter. I do not doubt that here too one should read *contrahuntur* (“are gathered together”), as I showed above that one should read *contraxit morbum* (“contracted a disease”) for *traxit*, which occurs in the books. GRAEVIUS.

Recourse is had to idols. “One has recourse to idols.” This has no difficulty whatever. But because above we thought Maucroix should not be passed over negligently, where he translated *simulacrum Dei quaeritur* (“the image of God is sought”) as “They seek the idol of the god,” while adding in the margin: “They believed Christians had idols in their temples”; and because it might appear to someone that the illustrious canon of Rheims was speaking in both places from the pagans’ viewpoint rather than his own, we add, as occasion now permits, that our argument against Maucroix will always retain its force, until he or anyone else shows that *idola* among pagans were sometimes representations of gods who existed nowhere in reality. No one, I think, will ever prove this. If the matter truly is such that it cannot be shown, then there is a powerful argument against the celebrated distinction between *idolum* and *simulacrum*, or *imago*: when our author, speaking of the true God, had written “the image of God is sought,” Maucroix, as already stated, translated: “They seek the idol of the god.”

Apollo provides a remedy. Indeed, Apollo does not provide a remedy. GALE. — The immediately preceding words do not conflict: “The evil is aggravated into something much worse.” Yet see whether an excellent sense may be derived from the received reading and the whole passage: “Apollo teaches a remedy; it is used; the evil becomes worse.” MAUCROIX. Literally: Apollo teaches a remedy; it is applied; the evil increases.

Apollo provides a remedy. That is, he teaches a remedy. Virgil: “Give us, Tityrus.” “Give” means “teach us,” just as *tradere* [to impart] does. Conversely, *accipere* [to receive] means “to learn.” GRAEVIUS.

The whole lower region wastes away into corruption. That is, all the lower parts of the body through which we discharge excrement are dissolved by putrefaction; as shortly afterward: “the second destruction had produced a greater abundance of decaying viscera”; and in chapter 35: “when the limbs of his whole body were already melting away, he was consumed by a dreadful wasting disease.” Suetonius, *Vitellius* 10: “He even dared to assert in a loathsome voice that certain persons recoiled from the decay of corpses.” [Col. 0779B] We note more than one example elsewhere. GRAEVIUS.

With the marrow repelled, the disease recedes inward. Here “marrow” denotes the flowing humours which, being checked inwardly by repelling remedies, produced a new evil through putrefaction; hence the worms which arose. TOLLIUS. — I correct: “The disease, repelled by remedies, recedes inward.” GALE. — Nicolaus Heinsius thought that one should read: “With remedies repelled,” that is, when the disease did not admit treatment or remedies. But it seems to me that, from the preceding word *curare* [to treat], its final syllable was twice repeated by a careless copyist, and that one should write: “With the vital parts struck.” For God had struck the lower genital region with an incurable blow, as he says at the beginning of the chapter; now the *medullae*, that is, the vital parts, are struck. Thus those loved from the depths of the heart are said, in the comic poet’s phrase, “to cling in the marrow.” GRAEVIUS. — I embrace this alone, though other readings had occurred to me which I might have defended from the ancient authorities.

[Col. 0779C] The stench spreads not only through the palace, but through the entire city. Baluze reads: “The foul smell spreads not only,” etc. The easier emendation, however, is: “But the smell.” The Oxford and Cambridge editions, followed by Pagius. — Read: “But that smell,” or: “But the smell goes.” VOSSIUS. — I read: “But the smell goes not only through the palace, but also through the whole city.” The Greek article in *etiam* [also] has been confused with that in *totam* [whole]. BOHERELLUS. — I emend: “The smell [pervades] the whole, not only through the palace, but,” etc. GALE. — Nicolaus Heinsius conjectures: “But the smell goes not only through the palace, but through the whole city.” What if we read: “But the dreadful smell spreads not only through the palace,” and what follows? GRAEVIUS.

When the outlets of excrement and urine, eaten away by worms, had already become confused. The reading of the old book, followed hitherto by all editions except the Åbo edition, is: “When the outlets of excrement and urine had already become confused. Eaten by worms,” etc. Only recently Baluze had suggested, at the end of volume II of the *Miscellanea*, the emendation which he wished now to be adopted in the author’s words; and the following judgments of scholars upon the old wording have also appeared.

The outlets of excrement and urine. Eaten by worms. Read: “the outlets of excrement and urine eaten away by worms.” Oxford edition of 1660. — Read: “The outlets of excrement and urine [were] eaten away by worms.” Or, if you prefer: “He was eaten away by worms,” preserving the earlier punctuation. Oxford edition of 1684, likewise Cambridge. — “Eaten by worms.” Read: “He is eaten,” etc. Åbo edition, and GALE. — Along with me the distinguished Columbus saw that *comestur*, that is, “is eaten,” should be read. TOLLIUS. — A passage of Seneca confirms it: “Thus they eat among them, thus they drink.”

“Together he raises dreadful cries to the stars,” etc. The Åbo edition:

> Together he raises dreadful cries to the stars,  
> Such as the bellowing when a wounded bull flees the altar  
> …

This restoration, which Gale and the other two editions did not merely propose in their notes, they also confirmed from *Aeneid* II. [Col. 0780A]

Cooked and warm animals. Correctly so; for from these, and especially from bacon, worms are drawn out from corrupted limbs. TOLLIUS. — I do not object. But, lest you be unaware, the translators are very different. Maucroix, namely: “Living animals or warm meat were applied to him.” *Animalia viva aut calida caro apponebantur* [Living animals or warm flesh were applied]. But the other renders as follows: “Some living animals, and others that were boiled”: *Viva aliquot animalia, tum et alia elixa* [some living animals, then also others boiled]. To avoid too much surprise, compare Columbus above.

When these had been unbound. Maucroix understood it as though our author had written: “Cooked and warm animals were applied to the flowing lower part, so that the heat might draw out the little worms. But, after his wounds had thus been cleaned, so that no little worm appeared any longer, an immeasurable swarm welled forth: *Mais, quand on en avait nettoyé ses plaies, il en ressortait une fourmilière* [But when his wounds had been cleaned, an ant-hill came out of them].” But what could be plainer than that these animals were not laid upon the wounds without bandages, by whose aid they might be better applied to the ulcerated parts [Col. 0780B] and remain in position? Therefore the animals were bound together with the wounds; and, when afterward the bandages were removed, the animals themselves too were unbound. For in a thousand passages *resolvere* means to unfasten what had been bound. Our author, chapter 46: “Licinius’ men lay down their shields and unfasten their helmets.” And Ovid, *Fasti* III, concerning the Sabine women carried off:

> He had given the signal; they obey, and loose their hair;

whence, a few verses later, of the same women:

> With hair unbound they reached the middle of the field.

Lactantius, *Epitome*, chapter 15: “But the prince of demons himself, author and contriver of evils, being bound with chains of fire,” etc. “But when the thousand years had passed, and the prince of demons had been unbound.”

An immeasurable swarm welled forth. Namely, in those animals which had been unbound, applied for drawing out Galerius’ little worms, and to which this swarm had adhered successfully; contrary to Maucroix’s interpretation just given.

Of decaying viscera. More correctly, as others have it, “of viscera decaying.” TOLLIUS. — See Columbus, whom he indicates, and indeed his other conjectures also.

A second destruction. I emend: “a fruitful destruction.” GALE.

The lower part, swollen like a bladder and without any shape of feet, had spread out. That *discreverat* is certainly corrupt. For, first, swollen things do not distinguish. Then, if *discreverat* had any place by reason of its meaning, it would have been necessary to write: “He had distinguished the lower part … swollen like a bladder.” Although, as the learned man notes (namely Columbus), *discrescere* may be taken for *decrescere* [to decrease], what swollen things ever decrease? I therefore think Lactantius wrote: “The lower part, swollen like a bladder and without any shape of feet, had increased.” Justin XI: “A remarkable swelling of spirit increased.” Livy I: “Growing boldness.” GRAEVIUS. — *Discreverat*, from *discresco*, not from *discerno*. This word is rare. It means to expand by swelling. TOLLIUS. — *Discreverat*. I correct: *discrepuerat* [had become different]. GALE.

For an entire year. Namely, from the final months of A.D. 309, and therefore for a year and several months, which Lactantius disregards. Pagius, in the *Critica Baroniana*, on A.D. 311, no. 11.

Add Cuperus and Columbus, likewise Norisius in the letter which the most worthy Cuperus deservedly wished appended to his preface.

He was compelled to acknowledge God. See another example in Antiochus in the author of the history of the Maccabees. TOLLIUS.

Of a new pain. Perhaps read: “by a new force of pain.” Pagius, in the place just cited. — Columbus well: “and by a new force of pain,” unless someone prefers “immense” to “new.” TOLLIUS.

Columbus himself, and Cuperus after him, differ somewhat nevertheless.

Of a new pain. I emend: “and by force of pain.” GALE.

[Col. 0781A] God’s temple. For which the English translation has: “the Church of Nicomedia,” *templum Nicomediae*.

He sent an edict of this… Write: “He sent an edict of the following kind.” NIC. HEINSIUS, and likewise Gale. We shall express doubt elsewhere. That it was sent, or dispatched, from Serdica to Nicomedia—and not before March of A.D. 311, although Valesius and other learned men so held, but after the Kalends of March of that same year—was asserted and proved by Pagius for that year in the *Critica Baroniana*, nos. 12 and 13; we agree with him. Compare Norisius’ letter cited above.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

“Among,” etc. See Eusebius, book VIII, chapter 17. Oxford edition of 1684, likewise Cambridge. — Correctly. For there we have the present letter, translated by Eusebius himself, as he says, *ἐπὶ τὴν ἐλλάδα γλῶτταν κατὰ τὸ δυνατόν*, *μεταβληθεῖσαν*: that is, translated into Greek as far as possible. But what must by no means be omitted here is that this letter, to which our author attached not even one word of the preface, has in Eusebius a notable and very lengthy one, as follows: *Αὐτοκράτωρ Καῖσαρ Γαλέριος Οὐαλέριος Μαξιμῖνος*, etc. That is, in Valesius’ translation:

> “The Emperor Caesar Galerius Valerius Maximianus, unconquered, Augustus, Supreme Pontiff, Greatest Germanicus, Greatest Egyptian, Greatest Thebaic conqueror, Greatest Sarmatian conqueror, for the fifth time Greatest Persian conqueror, for the second time Greatest Carpic conqueror, for the sixth time Greatest Armenian conqueror, Greatest Medic conqueror, Greatest Adiabenic conqueror, invested with tribunician power for the twentieth time, acclaimed imperator for the nineteenth time, consul for the eighth time, father of his country, proconsul. And the Emperor Caesar Flavius Valerius Constantine, pious, fortunate, unconquered, Augustus, Supreme Pontiff, invested with tribunician power for the fifth time, imperator for the fifth time, consul, father of his country, proconsul. And the Emperor Caesar Valerius Licinianus, pious, fortunate, unconquered, Augustus, Supreme Pontiff, invested with tribunician power for the fourth time, imperator for the third time, consul, father of his country, proconsul: greetings to their provincials.” [Col. 0781B]

This preface is indeed notable in that, of the four emperors whom Galerius had commanded, more than three years earlier, to be counted as emperors together with him, only two are named in the cited preface—Constantine and Licinianus, otherwise Licinius—while Maxentius and Maximinus Daia are entirely omitted. For what follows from this except that the statement is removed from truth which the distinguished Bishop of Meaux made plainly and in express words in his exposition of the Apocalypse, in order by every device to make Constantius Chlorus a persecutor:

> It is known that the emperors, though they divided the provinces among themselves, nevertheless governed them as forming one single body of empire. The names of all the emperors were inscribed in the dating clauses of all public acts, wherever they were made; general orders too were issued in the name of all.

That is: the names of all emperors were prefixed and inscribed to all public acts, wherever they were drafted and published; likewise, general commands were issued in the name of all emperors.

Pagius, I know, adds in his place, after the words of the cited preface: “But the names of Constantine and Licinius occur in that edict of Galerius Maximianus because it was issued with their consent.” Yet, to say nothing else, from where, I ask, could it ever be proved that Diocletian prefixed Constantius’ name together with his own to the edicts he issued against Christians, unless the very preface of the edicts were produced—which, as I now recall, is impossible? And even if it were produced, how could it be established that those edicts were issued with Constantius’ consent, when we have previously learned from our author that in matters so great the opinion not only of Constantius but not even of Herculius Maximianus himself was awaited? The words are in chapter 15: “And letters had already been sent to Maximianus and Constantius, that they should do the same. Their opinion was not awaited in matters so great.” [Col. 0781D]

Moreover, when scholars list the names of the four emperors whom Galerius at last wished to share his common title with him, they commonly place Licinius before Constantine; whereas the said preface puts Constantine before Licinius. This too deserves more than slight notice.

Always for the interests. Should *semper commodis* be read as one word, *sempercommodis* [always-serviceable], as in Terence’s *Andria*:

> I wondered what would happen if this went on so; and yesterday I feared where her perpetual mildness would lead;

and there are similar examples elsewhere. Certainly, the order of words used by our author seems to require it. For this was the true and natural order: “Among the other matters which we always arrange for the advantage and benefit of the commonwealth.” Maucroix’s translation is evidence, if you do not believe me: *Quoique nous ayons toujours travaillé avec beaucoup d'application au bien et à l'utilité de l'Etat* [Although we have always laboured with great diligence for the good and benefit of the State].

We arrange. In that age, *disponere* [to arrange], *dispositio*, and *dispositiones* were very familiar terms, whether the subject was the more solemn decrees and constitutions of the emperors or their other, less weighty wishes and intentions. In the former sense our author above: “His ordinance ought to be observed forever”; and in the words: “Let him observe his ordinance.” The notes on those passages should be consulted, if necessary. In the latter sense, Lampridius in *Alexander Severus*:

> “The days of his journeys were publicly posted, so that an edict hung up two months beforehand, in which it was written: ‘On such a day, at such an hour, I shall depart from the city; and, if the gods will, I shall stay at the first station …’; and this continued until the barbarian frontier was reached. For from there onward nothing was announced, and all travelled so that the barbarians might not know the Roman plan. It is certain, however, that he never failed to do what he had proposed, though he said: ‘I do not wish my plans to be sold by courtiers.’”

Then, after a few intervening words:

> “And because mention has arisen of making plans public, whenever he wished either to appoint governors to provinces, or set men over offices, or appoint procurators—that is, rationales [financial officers]—he posted their names, exhorting the people, if anyone had any accusation against them, to prove it by manifest facts; if he did not prove it, he should undergo the penalty of death. And he said it was serious that, when Christians and Jews (note the distinction) did this in the proclamation of priests who were to be ordained, it should not be done in the case of provincial governors, to whom both the fortunes and the lives of men were entrusted.” [Col. 0782B–C]

Here, reader, you may incidentally observe certain matters, not to be neglected, concerning the older and stricter discipline of pagans, Christians, and Jews, relating to the election of this or that man to civil or ecclesiastical dignities. It is certainly established that elections of this kind, even when not yet confirmed and completed in every respect, were sometimes also called *dispositiones* [appointments/plans].

And to provide this also, that Christians who [follow] their ancestors… As though he said: We had not simply intended to correct everything according to the ancient laws and the public discipline of the Roman Empire out of regard for those Christians who had in no respect abandoned their original sect, and whom it was accordingly in our interest, as the chief adversaries of the Romans’ public religion, to bring back to sound minds through renunciation of Christianity; but we had intended also to provide with respect to those Christians who had abandoned the said sect of the ancient Christians, splitting into various heresies—so far were they from appearing to us more worthy of some indulgence on that account that, on the contrary, they seemed less worthy. “For by what reasoning,” etc. [Col. 0782D]

Sect. Religion. The translators, since they had to represent Galerius as speaking, would, I think, have done better to retain the word “sect,” however odious.

Return to sound minds. Namely, by themselves renouncing, in favour of paganism—which alone was, for Galerius, the good religion—the whole of their Christianity, whatever its character.

For by a certain reasoning, etc. I once thought, before comparing Eusebius’ version with this passage, that it should be emended: “For there was a certain reason why so great a will had seized those same Christians,” and what follows. But afterward, because of these words of Eusebius, spoken interrogatively, *Ἐπείπερ τίνι λογισμῷ* [For by what reasoning, etc.], we saw that one should rather read: “For by what reasoning,” with what follows, in this sense: “For, we once said, by what reasoning did so great a will seize those perverse followers of Christianity, and so great a folly occupy them, that they do not follow the institutions of the old sect which perhaps the first ancestors of those pseudo-Christians established, but according to their own judgment—and just as it had finally pleased the first founders of Christian worship—make laws for themselves which they may observe, and gather various peoples in different places?” Galerius therefore touches incidentally here upon the reasons why he had previously been unwilling for even those deserters of the original Christian sect to be tolerated any longer. [Col. 0783A]

That they should not follow those ancient institutions which perhaps, etc. Either one must read: “that they should follow neither those ancient institutions, nor those which perhaps …,” or the sentence becomes very obscure and ambiguous, since “according to the ancient laws” has preceded—that is, the ancient laws of the Gentiles—and shortly follows “that they should turn themselves to the ancient institutions,” which can be referred to both the Gentile and the Christian religion. Yet Maximianus and the other emperors did not by their edicts compel Christians to a more exact observance of the true Christian religion, but to its renunciation and to the worship of idols. I agree, however, with the most illustrious Cuperus in his explanation of this passage, and think that all this must be understood of the ancient worship of Gentile divinities. TOLLIUS.

Ancient. That is, the Christians, from whose simplicity they had departed. Eusebius attributes the tenth persecution to this cause, when envy everywhere grew, slanders and the contests of bishops among themselves wretchedly tore the Church apart. Oxford and Cambridge editions, the latter adding only at the end: “See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, chapter 1.”

Which perhaps their first ancestors had established. As though he said: which perhaps not even the old founders of Christianity simply, but those very persons from whom they trace the origin of their lineage, prescribed. He conjectures, for example, that those apostles, well known even to the Gentiles, might once have had such descendants as, through a series of grandchildren, produced the heterodox Christians of whom Galerius is now speaking—if we may speak with Plautus. [Col. 0783C]

But according to their own judgment, etc. He undoubtedly understands the sects and internal disputes into which the people bearing the Christian name had then been divided. GRAEVIUS.

And just as it pleased them, so they made laws for themselves which they might observe. A passage truly to be noted for understanding this chapter. For what is the first sense unless this: that in the same manner they made laws for themselves to observe as had previously been done by others at their own pleasure? Now, whom else could Galerius generally have understood as persons who had made laws concerning religion for themselves from mere caprice, except Christians, since the Romans regarded their religious enactments not as decisions of human will but as the counsels of the goddess Egeria? And finally, whom else among Christians could Galerius particularly attack when he said, “And just as it pleased them,” except the first founders of the Christian religion; and, in what follows immediately, “thus they made laws for themselves which they might observe, and gathered various peoples in different places,” except deserters from that old Christian religion? Let it therefore be concluded that it had never occurred to Galerius to compel such apostates from Christianity, by his edicts, to a more exact observance of the true Christian religion, but [that he intended] to compel or induce absolutely all adherents of Christianity, whether purer or less pure, to renounce it and worship idols. At one time this passage seemed to me capable of some further elucidation by changing the word order as follows: “And thus, as it pleased them, for themselves,” and what follows. [Col. 0783D]

In different places. I supply “places” or “assemblies.” GALE. [Col. 0784A] — Yet Eusebius himself also has *ἐν διαφόροις* [in different …] without a substantive. — “In the provinces.” Maucroix; that is, in provinces.

Our command. Our edicts. The translators. — Add what we noted above on chapter XIV.

That they might return to the institutions of the ancients. What we have already said, preceding page, column 2, plainly shows—and what we shall continue to show on the following page—namely, that these words cannot at all refer to both Gentile and Christian religion, but pertain solely to the ancient Roman religion, contrary to Tollius’ recent position. The most worthy Cuperus agrees with us.

Many were brought into subjection by danger. Namely, the danger they would have incurred if they had not obeyed Galerius’ edict, because it was accompanied by threats of very severe penalties. — *A quoi plusieurs ont déféré par crainte* [To which many submitted from fear]. MAUCROIX. That is, many were subjected by fear.

Many also were cast down. I would conjecture, were Eusebius’ version not an obstacle, that the author wrote not *deturbati* [cast down] but *deturpati* [disfigured], referring, namely, to Christians whose eyes were gouged out, hands amputated, feet mutilated, noses or ears cut off under Galerius’ edict. First, because we shall see at the end of chapter 36 that Maximinus dealt similarly with confessors in the East. Secondly, because that they were then miserably disfigured is beyond doubt after this passage of Suetonius in *Caligula*: “Whenever handsome, long-haired men came before him, he disfigured them by shaving the back of their heads.” Finally, because, if the reading *deturpati* for *deturbati* were once admitted, an appropriate distinction would emerge between being disfigured and being brought into subjection by danger; whereas no such necessary distinction appears between being brought into subjection by danger and being cast down, since they seem to amount to exactly the same thing. But Eusebius’ words are decisive: *πλεῖστοι δὲ ταραχθέντες, παντοίους θανάτους ὑπέφερον* [but very many, being troubled, endured every kind of death], literally: “But very many, being disturbed, suffered deaths of every kind.” Thus we should not lightly believe that the reading of this passage ought to be changed—especially since, as appears from the same Eusebian words, it is not whole but mutilated. Let some new manuscript codex therefore be discovered before I venture to say what our author intended here. Maucroix: *Plusieurs aussi n'y ayant pas voulu obéir, ont été punis* [Many others also, having been unwilling to obey, were punished]: so that I do not know what he divined should be read. [Col. 0784B–C]

And since very many. I correct: “But indeed.” GALE.

Nor observe the God of the Christians. Why so, if the Christians of the older and more exact sect still had their public assemblies in which, under Galerius’ edicts, they might lawfully worship Christ? They did not, therefore; and this will become still clearer from what follows. Yet, what cannot be denied is that the most worthy Cuperus takes a different course.

Having regard to the consideration of our most mild clemency. What, I ask, is “to behold the consideration”? Beyond doubt the final letter was erroneously written twice. Lactantius wrote: “Having regard to the consideration of our most mild clemency, and to the perpetual custom.” GRAEVIUS. — Nothing is more certain than the distinguished colleague’s emendation, which had also occurred to me. Many ancient passages confirm it. Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History* II.25: “Then Demetrius, having renewed the alliance with the Jews, in consideration of the disaster inflicted by Tryphon,” etc. The same, *Dialogue* 2, on the virtues of St Martin, chapter 13: “But she, the virgin, did not relax the bonds of her most steadfast resolve, not even in consideration of Martin.” Justin VIII.8: “After these events, it happened by chance that two brothers, kings of Thrace, chose him as judge of their disputes, not out of consideration for his justice, but because each feared that he might add his strength to the other.” I observe only that the same ancients sometimes wrote not simply *contemplatione* [in consideration], but *in contemplatione* [in consideration of]. The *Libellus Precum* of Faustinus and Marcellinus: “We beseech your clemency, most pious emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius, that you may deign to read these things tirelessly in consideration of Christ, the Son of God, who sustains your Empire.” And Maucroix renders it literally here: *en contemplation de notre très-douce clémence* [in consideration of our most mild clemency]. [Col. 0784D–0785A]

That they may again be Christians. That is, that those who had secretly been Christians for some time, and had formerly been Christians openly, may again be Christians publicly. Their assemblies had thus previously been scattered by Galerius’ edicts and their sacred buildings demolished, so that no Christians, orthodox or heterodox, appeared any longer who professed any form of Christianity. Maucroix briefly: *C'est pourquoi nous leur permettons l'exercice de la religion chrétienne* [Therefore we permit them the exercise of the Christian religion].

And restore their meeting places. That is, let them hold their assemblies, according to the translators: *Et de tenir leurs assemblées* [And to hold their assemblies]. MAUCROIX. “To hold their assemblies.” English translation. — I would rather interpret *conventicula* as the places of assemblies and understand *componant* as “let them build,” in the sense in which Virgil, *Aeneid* III, says:

> On what safe land you may build a city.

The end of chapter 48 confirms this: “When these letters had been posted, he also exhorted them orally that their meeting places should be restored to their former state. Thus from the overthrow of the Church to its restoration there were ten years,” etc. [Col. 0785B]

Contrary to discipline. Namely, that which almost at the beginning of this Letter he called the public discipline and ancient laws of the Romans. “Contrary to the established discipline.” English translation. Literally, “contrary to settled discipline,” which I do not doubt must be referred to the same thing. Add Cuperus on the words “But another…”

But another letter. *Par une autre Déclaration* [By another declaration]. MAUCROIX. “By another ordinance.” English translation. — “I do not distinguish between a letter and an edict,” Pagius says in a similar case. Nor does this author seem to have distinguished them more here, since at the end of the preceding chapter he called an edict what is now called a letter of Galerius: “he sent an edict of the following kind”; and likewise at the beginning of the next chapter: “This edict is posted at Nicomedia.” We think that, if things are to be called by their proper names, this document, on account of the final part of its preface, *ἐπαρχιώταις ἰδίοις χαίρειν* [greetings to their provincials]; then on account of this very clause, “But in another letter we shall signify what they ought to observe,” which could not so well be inserted into Galerius’ edict; and finally on account of the very name “letter,” bestowed on this document by Galerius—we think it should rather be called, and truly was, strictly speaking, a letter rather than an edict. Yet from it, with a few omissions and alterations and with the addition of the governor’s public notice, an edict properly so called was to be, and shortly afterward was, prepared. Observe, please, how much the final words of Licinius’ letter to the governor of Bithynia—given below in chapter 48 and commonly called Licinius’ edict concerning the restoration of the Church—support this:

> “But in order that the form of this ordinance of our benevolence may come to the knowledge of all, you should cause these writings, when set forth in your public notice, to be posted everywhere and brought to everyone’s knowledge, so that this ordinance of our benevolence cannot remain hidden.” [Col. 0785C–D]

Then immediately afterward: “When these letters had been posted”; and just before the beginning: “He ordered that letters of the following kind, addressed to the governor concerning the restoration of the Church, be posted.” Compare the similar passage in the Letter of Emperor Maximinus to Sabinus, which Eusebius gives in full, *Ecclesiastical History* IX.9: *ἵνα δὲ αὕτη ἡμῶν ἡ κέλευσις εἰς γνῶσιν πάντων τῶν ἐπαρχόντων τῶν ἡμετέρων ἔλθῃ, διατάγματι ὑπὸ σοῦ προτεθέντι τὸ κεκελευσμένον ὀφείλεις δηλῶσαι*. That is, in Valesius’ translation: “Furthermore, in order that this command of our Majesty may become known to all our provincials, you shall see that our injunction is published by an edict posted by you.”

What they ought to observe. Who? Christians or judges? I had thought Christians were meant because of the preceding words: “That they may again be Christians and restore their meeting places, provided that they do nothing contrary to discipline.” Maucroix preferred to understand it of judges: *Par une autre déclaration nous ferons savoir à nos officiers de justice la conduite qu'ils doivent tenir envers eux* [By another declaration we shall make known to our judicial officers the conduct they must observe toward them]. [Col. 0786A]

## CHAPTER XXXV

This edict. Understand it of the foregoing letter of Emperor Galerius, after it had been put into the form of an edict by the governor of Bithynia, who commonly resided at Nicomedia.

It is posted at Nicomedia. That is, it is published in that town by the public notice of the same governor.

At Nicomedia. The first two editions of this little work, namely the Paris edition of 1679 and the Oxford edition of 1680, have *Nicomediae*; hence the latter, in the corrections which came later: “Read: *Nicomediae*,” as Allix also observed.

On the day before the Kalends of May. On the thirtieth day of April. Maucroix’s translation. “On the last day of April.” English translation. All three amount to the same thing.

On the day before the Kalends of May. If I see anything, it must be read: “on the day before the Kalends of February.” TOLLIUS. — Since in the heading of the aforementioned edict Galerius Maximianus is called holder of tribunician power for the twentieth time, it is established that it was issued after the Kalends of March in that current year, 311, on which Galerius entered upon his twentieth tribunician power. That it was issued after that day is also made certain from Greek coins in Goltzius. For the last coin on which the year of his Augustan rule is marked bears the characters L Z, that is, the seventh year. For since, according to Lactantius’ testimony, he was proclaimed Augustus on the Kalends of May in 305, on the Kalends of May of the current year of Christ he began the seventh year of his Augustan reign. Therefore, since the same emperor promulgated that edict when already failing, it appears that Lactantius’ statement is corroborated by Galerius Maximianus’ coins, and that Valesius wrote wrongly in his notes on Eusebius, as did other learned men, in saying that the edict was issued before March. PAGIUS, in the *Critica Baroniana* on A.D. 311, nos. 12 and 13; there he also learnedly indicates the other error from which that error improperly flowed. See the passage: it is worth the effort. [Col. 0786B–C]

At last, after the completion of the seventh year of persecution and at the beginning of the ninth, Galerius’ edict appeared, by which the persecution was wholly extinguished, between the Kalends of March, when he had begun his twentieth tribunician power, and the day before the Kalends of May, when Lactantius says it was posted at Nicomedia. DODWELL, *Dissertatio Cyprianica* XI, no. 82.

He himself, etc. Namely Galerius Maximianus. Pagius. The translators too, in their own manner, since one uses Galerius’ name itself in place of the pronoun and the other Maximianus’.

He himself consul for the eighth time, and Maximinus consul for the second time. At Rome … in 311, until September, no consuls had been publicly proclaimed … But in Gaul, Spain, and the other provinces beyond the Alps belonging to Constantine’s empire, Maximianus Galerius alone was named consul in that same year, 311. Thus one reads in the Fasti of Idacius and in the consular fragment published by Bucherius, p. 250: *MAXIMIANO VIII, SOLO* [Maximianus, eighth time, alone] … In Greece, Macedonia, Dacia, and the other provinces of Illyricum, in Thrace and Bithynia, which obeyed partly Emperor Galerius Augustus and partly Emperor Licinius, the consuls were said to be Galerius Maximianus for the eighth time and Maximinus for the second time. I recently learned this from the golden little book of Lactantius Firmianus, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, published by the most learned Stephanus Baluze from the distinguished library of the most illustrious M. Colbert … for he writes in chapter 35 that the edict on behalf of Christians, proposed by Maximianus Galerius a few days before his death, was posted at Nicomedia on the day before the Kalends of May, he himself consul for the eighth time and Maximinus consul for the second time. Norisius in Pagius, *Critica Baroniana* on the said year of Christ, 311, no. 3; and this from Norisius’ fourth dissertation *On the Pisan Cenotaphs*, chapter I, §1.

But because, first, Prosper in his *Chronicle*, Victorius in the Paschal Canon, Cassiodorus, the author of the Alexandrian Chronicle, and others place Licinius as colleague with Maximian for his eighth consulship in that year, the distinguished Noris continues in the cited *Critica* [Col. 0787A], immediately adding: “Perhaps in Pannonia, Raetia, and Noricum, where Licinius ruled, he had likewise associated himself as colleague with Maximinus.” Then, what is much more weighty, and has hitherto been noticed by no one: Galerius in that very year, in the preface of the letter from which the edict now under discussion was drawn up, not only expressly joined that same Licinius to himself as colleague in the consulship, but moreover joined Constantine, whom he names even before Licinius, entirely omitting that alleged second consulship of Maximinus. Eusebius’s words, rendered in Latin, are as follows:

> “The Emperor Caesar Galerius Valerius Maximianus . . . consul for the eighth time . . . and the Emperor Caesar Flavius Valerius Constantine . . . . . consul . . . and the Emperor Caesar Valerius Licinianus . . . consul, father of the fatherland, proconsul, to his provincials, greeting.”

How then can our author say, “when he [Galerius Maximian] was consul for the eighth time, and Maximinus for the second,” rather than, according to the aforesaid preface of Galerius, “when he [Galerius Maximian] was consul for the eighth time, and Constantine and Licinius were consuls”? Let the learned decide. I myself now find nothing [Col. 0787B] that satisfies me, nor do I discover anything adduced by them.

For as regards these conjectures of the distinguished Pagius: “That Licinius Augustus was added as colleague to Galerius Maximian in March of the year 311, and is called consul in the Edict of Galerius Maximian; but that not long afterwards Maximinus Augustus II was colleague of the same Galerius Maximian, as is clear from Lactantius’s words, *ipso octies, et Maximino iterum consulibus*”; so that this consulship of Licinius was by no means ordinary but suffect—first I ask why Galerius, if this was so, named Constantine consul in the said preface in the second place, but named no Maximian likewise as consul. I ask next how Galerius could have appointed Licinius as his suffect colleague in the ordinary consulship in March of A.D. 311, if, according to Norisius in the preceding discussion, no consuls were published at Rome in A.D. 311 until September, before which Galerius had already been dead for quite some time. Thus not all the difficulties of this passage have been removed by Pagius. Perhaps, however, we shall soon be permitted to see them happily unraveled in the latest work of the distinguished Norisius, which we hear has reached the eminent Cuper from Italy, and at which we heartily rejoice.

**“When he was consul for the eighth time, and Maximinus for the second.”** The English translation reads: “in Maximian’s eighth consulship, and Maximin’s third.” Literally: “in Maximian’s eighth consulship and Maximin’s third.” Would that the very learned man who judged that one must have recourse to this correction—easy to defend as necessary, namely the substitution of *tertium* (“third”) for *iterum* (“a second time”)—had somewhere given his reason for it. For we do not know upon what foundations it rests, especially in view of what follows immediately.

**“Maximinus, consul for the second time.”** Of this second consulship, as also of the first, there is no mention in the other fasti; so that here we rely on the authority of Lactantius alone. Our Lydiat places Galerius as consul for the eighth time without a colleague. The Oxford and Cambridge editions add at the end: “See Valesius’s notes on Eusebius, book IX, chapter 11.”

[Col. 0787D] From Lactantius, who was then living at Nicomedia, it is clear that Maximinus was consul for the second time in 311. Norisius, as cited above.

From Dodwell’s Greek excerpts, p. 102 of the Appendix to the Cyprianic Dissertations, smaller Oxford edition: “In the year 307 we read that the consuls were Severus Augustus and Maximian Caesar.” He means Maximinus by the one whom he calls Caesar. Thus we have Maximinus’s first consulship, sought in vain elsewhere by the distinguished Baluzius. [Col. 0788A] Yet obscure traces of this consulship also remain in the book on the prefects of the city. For there we read the consuls recorded for 307, down to April, as follows: “Maximian VII and Maximian.” This latter Maximian is none other than our Maximinus. For not only later writers but monuments contemporary with that age confuse these names, calling Maximinus “Maximian,” and Constantius “Constantine.” Dodwell, Appendix to the Cyprianic Dissertations, no. 1.

**“Then, when the prisons had been opened,” etc.** Certainly in each individual city, as the passage of Rufinus cited by Baluzius attests; yet it would be surprising if prisons at Nicomedia are not specially meant here, in view of the preceding words: “This edict is posted at Nicomedia.”

**“You were released from custody with the other confessors.”** We have already shown above what follows from this against the distinguished editor of the Martyrology of the German Church.
