**“When prison had served as your home for six years.”** We have said that Diocletian laid aside the purple on 1 April 305, if we follow Idatius; on 1 May, if we follow Lactantius . . . From the year in which Diocletian abdicated, however, persecution continued at Nicomedia until Galerius’s recantation: from the Kalends of May 305 until the day before the Kalends of May 311. We infer this from Lactantius, who writes at this time that his Donatus was released from prison, when prison had served him as a home for six years . . . Throughout that six-year period Donatus, under three governors succeeding one another—Flaccinus, Hierocles, and Priscillian—was subjected to tortures and various torments nine times, but no more often. For, just as the occasions of the games of the Roman Empire could not recur very frequently, so the occasions of public punishments did not recur frequently. DODWELL, *Cyprianic Dissertation* XI, nos. 78, 80, and 89.

**“When this had been done.”** That is, by the promulgation, or literally the publication, of the aforesaid Edict. English translation.

**“With his wife and son.”** Valeria, daughter of Diocletian, and [Col. 0788C] Candidianus. Oxford and Cambridge editions.—“His wife and children.” MAUCROIX. As though our author’s words were “with his wife and children,” which greatly surprises me.—The wife of Galerius Maximian, Pagius says in the place we touched upon very briefly above, was Valeria, daughter of Diocletian. Because of Licinius’s savagery she fled to Maximinus, by whom she was treated most shamefully . . . Galerius Maximian had no son by her; for she was barren, as Lactantius teaches, chapter 50. These words therefore must be understood of Candidianus, whom Lactantius says in the same place was born of a concubine, adopted by Valeria, and betrothed to the seven-year-old daughter of Maximinus Augustus. As Lactantius relates, chapter 20, his father intended to make him Caesar after celebrating his *vicennalia*. But he was killed by Licinius in 313, in the sixteenth year of his age. PAGIUS, *Critica Baroniana*, under A.D. 311, no. 12.

**“He was consumed by a dreadful wasting disease.”** Relevant here is a notable passage from the Anonymous Valesianus, produced by Pagius in his *Critica Baroniana* under A.D. 311, no. 12, in the following form: “Moreover, we learn from the Anonymous Valesianus that Galerius Maximian fell ill and died at Serdica, [Col. 0788D] who, after speaking of Licinius’s creation as Caesar, says: ‘Then, having left him in Pannonia, he himself returned to Serdica, where he was seized by a grave illness and wasted away so that he died when his entrails had opened and putrefied.’”

**“And this became known at Nicomedia ( . . . ) of the same month.”** As to supplying the gap in the manuscript codex—which Baluzius has at last taken care to represent in the manner you see—learned men hitherto, not surprisingly, had thought only of how to insert something into this passage, which they recognized as mutilated. Hence arose the suspicion mentioned by Cuper and Columbus in their notes: namely, that one should read, “And this became known at Nicomedia in the middle of the same month”; and this had formerly suggested to us too that the final part of the name *Nicomediae* might serve, if, we said, the *to* [Greek article] in *medio* had been swallowed up through the copyist’s carelessness after the preceding word *Nicomediae*. But now, since the defect in this passage must be attributed not to a copyist but to all-devouring time, it is equally [Col. 0789A] possible that two words—“toward the end” or “at the end”—or one word, “on the Ides,” or others of this sort, are missing, rather than “in the middle.” Let those who can consult the manuscript codex see what the extent of the gap, or the surviving traces of letters, if any remain, more readily allow. The English translation indeed has: “before the end of May,” which literally is *ante finem Maii*.

**“Of the same month.”** That is, of May, from the Kalends onward. Oxford and Cambridge editions.

**“Of the same month.”** That is, May. PAGIUS.

**“With the Kalends of March impending.”** Namely, of the following year, A.D. 312, on the Kalends of March, the anniversary of his accession as Caesar; on that day he had resolved to celebrate those solemnities which had been postponed because of his continual illness. PAGIUS.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

**“Upon receiving this news.”** Namely, news of the death of Galerius Maximian. PAGIUS.

**“Having arranged relays from the East, he sped onward.”** As though he meant: he used the utmost speed, employing horses which, immediately after receiving the news, he had ordered to be ready for himself and his men at fixed stations; and so he covered the great distance from the East, where he had learned of Galerius’s death, to the provinces he was preparing to seize, as if in uninterrupted flight. Do you want a similar example and a not dissimilar expression? “But he, making use of incredible speed, arrived at his father, already failing,” our author said in chapter 24 concerning Constantine, when a few lines earlier he had said of the same man: “Having removed all the public horses at many posting stations, he flew onward.”

“He took post-horses and made haste into the East.” MAUCROIX. He therefore thought that, instead of the received reading, *dispositis ab Oriente cursibus pervolavit* (“having arranged relays from the East, he sped onward”), one should rather read, *dispositis cursibus pervolavit in Orientem* (“having arranged relays, he sped onward into the East”). But please consider how much this conflicts with chapter 19: “Daia, moreover—who is also Maximinus—‘raised recently from tending flocks and the woods . . . received the East to trample underfoot.’” He therefore ought to have sped away from the East. This is also required by the end of chapter 38.

[Col. 0789C] **“That he might occupy the provinces and, while Licinius delayed, claim everything for himself as far as the Chalcedonian strait.”** “With the purpose of taking advantage of Licinius’s absence and seizing all Asia as far as the sea of Chalcedon.” MAUCROIX. As though our author had written: “that, in Licinius’s absence, he might claim all Asia for himself as far as the strait,” etc. But first, what could be clearer than that, in this rendering, not two but one single goal of Maximinus’s journey is assigned: namely, invading all Asia as far as the Chalcedonian strait while Licinius was absent? Whereas according to our author, Maximinus had proposed to himself not one goal but truly two in that headlong journey: first, to claim particular provinces for himself, whatever Licinius might do—that is, even if he made the greatest haste; secondly, not only those provinces but all territories as far as the Chalcedonian strait, if Licinius should happen to delay for a time: “that he might occupy the provinces and, while Licinius delayed, claim everything for himself as far as the Chalcedonian strait.” This, then, is the first defect in Maucroix’s translation. The second and third are, undoubtedly, that he renders *provincias* more freely as “all Asia,” and *morante* as “absent.”

**“That he might occupy the provinces,” etc.** “To take into his possession all those Provinces: and as Licinius lingered, he possessed himself of all to the straits of Thrace.” English translation. As though our author’s words were now: “that he might occupy (all those) provinces and, while Licinius delayed, he claimed everything for himself as far as the Thracian strait.”—I would have preferred to retain *vindicaret* (“might claim”), which the very reverend translator thought plainly must be changed to *vindicavit* (“claimed”); and in place of the two words which he supplied before *provincias*, and which we have taken care to enclose in brackets, we suspected that *propinquas* (“nearby”) or *proximas* (“nearest”) had rather dropped out through a copyist’s fault.

**“The Chalcedonian strait.”** Since it lay on one side between Thrace and on the other side the Bithynian city of Chalcedon, this is why the English translation had “the straits of Thrace” instead of the Chalcedonian strait.

[Col. 0790A] **“For the present.”** That is, “time”; just as the Greeks often say *ἐπὶ τοῦ παρόντος* and *ἐν τῷ παρόντι*, omitting the nouns *χρόνου* and *χρόνῳ*, for “at the present time.”

**“He removes the census.”** The census instituted by Galerius Maximian, concerning which see chapter 31. See Justin, book I, on the Magi conciliating the Persian people to themselves in the same manner. TOLLIUS.—*Sustollit.* The Abo edition has *sustulit* (“removed”).—I should not wish this change made, since Plautus, Lucretius, and Catullus have used the word *sustollendi*. The last, for example, in the *Marriage of Peleus and Thetis*:

> And the twisted ropes raise the gleaming sails.

Nor, therefore, will Columbus’s argument above for his emendation be very strong.

**“Discord between.”** Read: “Discord thence arose between,” etc. TOLLIUS. Both translators likewise rendered it so.—“The two emperors almost came to a rupture.” MAUCROIX.—“By this means the two Emperors were now on ill terms.” English translation.

[Col. 0790B] **“But peace was made on definite terms,” etc.** Since Maximinus, in a letter written to Sabinus after the death of Galerius Maximian, teaches that he had been at Nicomedia in the preceding year, as may be seen in Eusebius, it is clear that on Galerius’s death Maximinus occupied Asia and Bithynia, which Galerius had retained together with Illyricum and Thrace. Indeed, Baluzius infers in his notes on the cited passage of Lactantius that Bithynia passed into Maximinus’s right and dominion, from the martyrdom of Saint Lucian of Antioch, recounted by Eusebius, book IX, chapter 6. PAGIUS.

**“In the strait itself.”** That is, in the Bosporus strait itself. Maucroix’s translation.—That is, in the sea itself. English translation.—Perhaps it is simpler to supply from the preceding context: “the Chalcedonian [strait].”

**“He returns.”** Namely, Maximinus. PAGIUS.—The translators agree, in whose versions one finds Maximinus’s very name in place of the pronoun. It need only be noted that, since our author uses not the past tense *rediit* (“he returned”) but the present *redit* (“he returns”), the discussion is by no means now of Maximinus’s completed return to the East, but [Col. 0790C] simply of a return undertaken and begun. This will presently be confirmed.

**“Secure.”** That is, trusting that he was now secure: “reckoning that he was now secure.” English translation.

**“And he becomes such as he had been in Syria and Egypt.”** That is, in the provinces which he had recently added to his empire, as he returned through them to the East, he acted as he had previously acted in Syria and Egypt. Maucroix likewise gives the same sense: “And his conduct was like that which he had followed in Syria and Egypt.” But the English translation differs: “and so he governed Syria and Egypt just as he had done formerly.” Literally, that would mean: “and he continued to govern Syria and Egypt in precisely the same manner in which he had formerly begun.”

**“First of all, he revoked the indulgence granted to Christians under the common *tutelo*,” etc.** Baluzius says that this means “by common consent,” and testifies that he has not encountered the word elsewhere. Why, then, should it not be regarded as corrupt, with *tutela* (“protection”) substituted for it by an easy change? For “common protection” will scarcely signify anything else here [Col. 0790D] than a certain safeguard of the recently issued edict, upon which Christians could thereafter rely more safely in practising Christian worship. The very reverend man reads *titulo* (“title”). Oxford and Cambridge editions.

**“Tutelo.”** The Abo edition has *titulo*.—Read *titulo*. VOSSIUS.—*Tutelo* for *titulo*. ALLIX.—“And though the Christians were now received under the protection of the government, yet he broke all this.” English translation. Almost literally: “He violated the indulgence by which Christians had been entrusted to the common protection of the magistrates.”—I think that the old reading was: “First of all, he removed the indulgence granted to Christians together with the protection of the wall”; and I explain it thus. Galerius, as appears from his first letter—or what is the same thing, from chapter 34 of this little work—had, when nearly dying, already offered this most ready indulgence in the Christians’ affair: that Christians might again exist and restore their places of assembly. But Galerius, as is certain from the same chapter, was about to indicate in another letter to the judges what was further to be observed in matters concerning Christians. The occasion and necessity of such matters did not, indeed, simply require that the letter tell judges in which places Christians might thereafter openly live and publicly erect their temples; but it could not happen otherwise than that such places would be assigned either inside or outside city walls. Now scarcely anything is more probable than that Galerius, in his later letter, informed the judges that it was his pleasure that, just as Christians had earlier . . . . erected several of their churches in cities by permission of emperors, and as people always otherwise lived more safely in cities because, among other protections, they had the protection of walls, than in the countryside, Christians should be permitted to reside within the walls of every town for greater security and there restore their places of assembly.

And indeed that Christians previously had churches within city [Col. 0791B] precincts is proved by the Nicomedian church alone, which our author mentions in chapter 12. What follows immediately—the instigated embassies of cities asking that Christians not be permitted to build places of assembly within their cities—again most clearly indicates that Christians had previously been allowed, through Galerius’s letters to judges, to build temples inside pagan cities. Thus Galerius had granted Christians not merely the indulgence discussed above, but also the protection of walls for both their dwellings and their places of assembly; hence Maximinus afterwards removed the indulgence granted to Christians together with the protection of the wall.

This at least is my opinion on this passage, partly for the reasons now given, partly because, while among learned men some understand *communi tutelo* as “by the common consent of the emperors,” and others emend it to *communi titulo*, that is, as they explain, “under the prescribed names of Galerius, Constantine, Licinius, Maximinus, and Maxentius,” neither party can produce the requisite common consent of the emperors [Col. 0791C]—whether the question is of the genuinely common consent of all five emperors, or only of the consent of some among them. If it is genuinely common consent, the first three names indeed occur in Eusebius in Galerius’s preface, which we have mentioned so often; but the last two do not likewise occur, and thus no consent of all the said five emperors can be established. But if it is the common consent of only three or two of them, Eusebius indeed mentions such consent in the cited place, but our author does not. For in the preceding passage he has mentioned not merely no consent by Maximinus, but no emperor at all who consented to the aforementioned indulgence; he mentions Galerius alone, who sent it. Thus scarcely anything harsher can be conceived than this expression: “Maximinus removes the indulgence granted to Christians by common consent, whether under protection or title,” if at last some common consent is to be understood in which he himself, according either to Eusebius or to our author, had no part.

Finally, in support of the “protection of the wall” of which we speak, there are the four kinds of enclosure for protecting a farm, described by Varro, book I of *On Agriculture*: “Now I shall speak concerning the enclosures made for protecting a farm, or a part of one. There are four kinds of such protection: one natural, another rustic, a third military, a fourth constructed.”

**“Having instigated embassies,” etc.** Eusebius says, *Αὐτὸς αὐτῷ καθ᾽ ἡμῶν πρεσβεύεται*—“he himself sends an embassy to himself against us”—in book IX, chapter 11; see Valesius’s notes there. Cambridge edition.

An edict of Galerius appeared . . . after the eighth complete year of persecution and at the beginning of the ninth, by which the persecution was wholly extinguished, between the Kalends of March [in 311] and the day before the Kalends of May [of the same year] . . . This peace did not last even six whole months. Thereafter Maximinus turned to seeking new devices and pretexts for restoring the persecution. First, he barred Christians from cemeteries. Then he instigated embassies from cities to petition him, as though requesting a great favour, that Christians be expelled—especially at Antioch, where Theotecnus, the city curator, an eminent impostor, set up a new image of Jupiter Philius, consecrated by magical arts, and fabricated an oracle of it, ordering Christians to be expelled from the city and its entire territory . . . He received these embassies at Nicomedia in the same year in which Galerius died, but toward its end, after he had occupied Galerius’s dominion as far as the Chalcedonian strait and arranged peace and friendship with Licinius on definite terms. This is established by Maximinus’s own edict, issued at the end of the following year, 312, in favour of Christians. But the indulgence granted to Christians by Galerius must also have been revoked in this year, if that peace lasted less than six complete months. DODWELL, *Cyprianic Dissertation* XI, no. 82.

Maximinus, in a letter which, as we shall say, he wrote in the following year, 312, to Sabinus, prefect of his praetorium, and which Eusebius reports in book IX, chapter 9, says: “When in the preceding year”—that is, 311—“I had happily entered Nicomedia, the citizens of that city approached me while I was staying there, carrying images of the gods and earnestly begging that men of this sort should not be permitted to dwell at all in their city”; and more besides, which remarkably illuminate what we have related above from Lactantius: events in this and the following year in the case of Christians, hitherto shrouded in many obscurities. PAGIUS.

Here, therefore, you see a notable example of embassies of this kind being instigated in such a manner.

**“In a new fashion, he appointed one chief priest in every city,” etc.** As though, in other words, he had written: “In a new fashion, he made one chief priest in each city.” Hence, in my view, the novelty of the act: previously pagans had sometimes had *ἀρχιερεῖς* (“high priests”) and priests appointed over provinces or cities, but not one in every individual city.

**“Who should also offer sacrifices every day through all their gods.”** No one will persuade me that Lactantius wrote this. The word *dies* (“days”), which preceded *deos* (“gods”), dropped out because of similarity of letters, as often happens. Once it had been omitted, because there was nothing to which *omnes* (“all”) could apply, they refashioned *diis suis* (“to their gods”) into *deos suos* (“their gods”). Lactantius wrote: “who should offer sacrifices every day through all days to their gods,” as in the following chapter, “sacrifice was offered on every single day.” “Through all days every day” is pleonasm, as “now already often” in Plautus, “afterwards then” in the same author, “to repeat again” in Suetonius, *Caesar* 2, and “old aged wine” in the *Curculio*. But if this displeases anyone, one might read: “who should offer sacrifices every day through all the shrines to their gods.” GRAEVIUS.

**“Through all their gods.”** That is, through all the temples of their gods, or in all temples, Tollius said above; and with him we cannot yet wholly reject this interpretation, whether because of our author’s twofold expression in chapter 17, “that prayer should be offered through all the gods for his life,” or because of Livineius’s observation on the ancient panegyrics which we later encountered, and by which what we noted in the cited passage appears to be considerably strengthened. Cicero, *Letters to Atticus* IV.1 and *For Publius Sestius*, called the Nones of Sextilis the birthday of salvation because on that day a shrine was consecrated to him on the Quirinal; and Martial elegantly says, “You created Mercury on the Ides of May,” because a temple was then dedicated to him, as Livy, book 2, and Festus wrote; or finally because we are not yet sufficiently accustomed to this pleonasm, “they should offer sacrifices every day through all days.” We certainly believe the latter conjecture of the distinguished colleague, to which he himself gives preference, should be preferred. But it must not be omitted that the eminent Cuper also explains the received reading, though differently from us.

**“By their service.”** I should prefer “by their direction.” GALE. *Ministerio*, “the assistance.” English translation; that is, “by aid, help.”

**“They should see to it [that] Christians should not build.”** Namely, temples, as Maucroix interpreted it: “they were to prevent Christians from building temples.”—I emend: “they should see to it that Christians build nothing.” GALE.—There will doubtless be those to whom this word order [Col. 0793A] seems preferable: “they should see to it that Christians build nothing.”

**“Should worship.”** I prefer “should assemble.” GALE.

**“By his own right.”** “By his authority.” Maucroix; as if one said, “on his own authority.”

**“And this was not enough, unless he also set over the provinces, from a higher rank of dignity, individual quasi-pontiffs, and both of these,” etc.** This passage is not merely difficult but, if I see rightly, very corrupt; and it has moreover been understood in entirely opposite ways by the translators. Maucroix, apparently because of the final word *utrosque* (“both”), thinks that Maximinus appointed not one but two pontiffs together over each province: “Not content with this ordinance, he established two pontiffs in each province to keep an eye upon the others.” On the other hand, according to the translation of the very reverend Burnet, not two but only one pontiff was appointed by Maximinus’s command to each province. His words are: “And not contented with this subordination that he had settled among the priests, he ordered [Col. 0793B] one in every province to be over all the priests of the province.” Their sense is: Not content merely to subject one chief priest to the other priests in each city, he further appointed one in each province who should be superior to all the priests of the province.

First, because of the express words “and both of these,” we cannot but believe with Maucroix that the passage concerns two persons appointed, in Maximinus’s design, over each province to administer religious affairs. Secondly, because of the word *quasi* in the phrase “individual quasi-pontiffs,” we cannot but conclude, against Maucroix in turn, that his two properly so-called pontiffs must be rejected. Further, since our author has stated above that Maximinus, in a new fashion, conferred the dignity of chief priest in every city upon some one of its leading citizens, we do not doubt any more that the same Maximinus set over each province two men of this dignity, each of whom was nevertheless a quasi-chief-pontiff. Finally, should someone object, “But where does the word ‘two’ appear?” I answer: it is not only concealed in the word *utrosque*, but it is more than likely that it formerly stood after the ablative *gradu* in this form: “And this was not enough, unless he also set over the provinces, from a higher rank of dignity, two men, each a quasi-pontiff”; then “both of these,” with what follows. Thus, at length, that word dropped out through the ill-starred copyist’s excessive ignorance or haste, together with the similarity between *dus* and *duos*—unless some better reconciliation can be offered which we can embrace.

**“With white cloaks.”** In the form of a military cloak or white tunic, sometimes bordered with gold; this was worn only by the ministers of emperors. Maximinus certainly shared these court garments with the high pontiffs. Oxford and Cambridge editions.—The English translation has the same sense: “He ordered them to wear that sort of white habits edged about with gold, which might only be worn by the chief officers of the court.”

**“Chlamydes”: “mantles.”** Maucroix; that is, cloaks.

**“But he was preparing to do in the eastern regions what,” etc.** That is, according to the English translation: “But he was preparing to do against Christians in the other provinces what he had already done in the East.” Maucroix, however, interprets it: he was preparing to do in the West also the things which he had done in the East.

**“While he professed clemency only in outward appearance.”** The persecutors of whom we speak, those under Diocletian, placed the praise of this clemency in sparing life while tearing out the right eyes and disabling the left hamstrings with red-hot iron. Hence, once these mutilations began, since they had been devised to preserve life, martyrdoms were probably rarer. DODWELL, *Cyprianic Dissertation* XI, no. 81.

[Col. 0794A] **“He forbade the servants of God to be killed,” etc.** Namely, in the East. For in other regions Maximinus was merely preparing to do the things he had done in the eastern regions, as our author has just said; and therefore he again says of him at the beginning of chapter 37: “While he was planning this, he was deterred by Constantine’s letters.” But, not to conceal the matter, I nevertheless do not see how it could formerly have been elegantly written here as we now have *dierum* (“of days”); and I accordingly suspect the old reading was: “There he forbade the servants of God to be killed,” with the later understanding that “there” meant the eastern regions.

**“He ordered them to be disabled.”** Here, that is, “to be mutilated,” as each of the four examples which follow shows. Not every disabling is mutilation; rather, as Casaubon properly observes, in correct Latin *debiles* (“disabled persons”) are those whose limbs have become *ἄχρηστα* (“useless”), or who are prevented by some defect from using all the limbs of their body. Such, for example, were those confessors whose left hamstrings had, Dodwell just said, been disabled with red-hot iron. But here, as I said, true mutilations are under discussion [Col. 0794B]. The same Dodwell confirms this elsewhere in the following words: “Thus he returned to the aforesaid mutilations of bodies, which, although they made many confessors, made no martyrs.”—“He had them maimed.” MAUCROIX.

**“Therefore the eyes of confessors were gouged out,” etc.** It is indeed true that after the edict issued by Galerius Maximian in favour of Christians, Maximinus, upon receiving it, ordered the judges to refrain from attacking Christians. Yet he suppressed Galerius’s constitution, and merely ordered the governors of provinces through Sabinus, prefect of his praetorium, in bare verbal instructions, to restrain the persecution against them, as Eusebius recounts in book IX, chapter 1, where he also recites the letter written by Sabinus to the governors of the individual provinces. But, as the same Eusebius says in chapter 2, he did not permit this condition to continue for even six complete months, and Maximinus left nothing untried to overthrow the peace. Thus the persecution of Christians which Lactantius recounts as renewed around November—for that is the sixth month after Galerius’s death—and therefore around Maximinus’s *quinquennalia*, which fell in that month, was renewed. PAGIUS.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

**“While he was planning this, he was deterred by Constantine’s letters.”** Maximinus now seemed to have found for himself a most excellent opportunity to avoid odium: as though compelled by the embassies of cities—and by *θεσπίσμασι* (“oracular pronouncements”)—to revoke the edict of peace. For in reply to those decrees of the cities he wrote that Christians should be expelled . . . Everything was already ripe for persecution, had Constantine not deterred him . . . Since we have established that those edicts of persecution were issued after May, in 312, when Constantine was already moving against Maxentius, Constantine nevertheless deterred him by letters as soon as he learned of it, at that very time; Lactantius writes that Maximinus was thereby compelled to dissemble. Lactantius, section 37. And rightly so. For Constantine was the first of the Augusti, whom, under the administration of those times, all the other emperors, both Caesars and even Augusti, had to obey. DODWELL, *Cyprianic Dissertation* XI, nos. 83 and 85.

**“While he was planning this,” etc.** “The letters of Constantine repressed these acts of violence.” MAUCROIX. Literally: “Constantine’s letters checked those violent acts.” But according to this rendering, at the time when Maximinus was deterred by Constantine’s letters, at Maximinus’s own command the things previously done under his rule in the East would have been done in the recently acquired provinces also; and so, for example, at Nicomedia, through the cruel agency of the governor and other officials, he would already have been gouging out confessors’ eyes, amputating hands, cutting off feet, slicing off noses or ears. This certainly is not so, even because of our author’s words: “While he was planning this”—that is, as just before he had said, “preparing to do”—“he was deterred by Constantine’s letters.” He therefore dissembled.

Constantine’s letters. The letters in question have perished; but it cannot be called into doubt that Constantine and Licinius issued two constitutions, one in this year, 312, and the other in the following year, and that the earlier of these was transmitted to Maximinus in the current year—although Baronius and other most learned men have mentioned only one edict. For, after Maxentius had been defeated—whose overthrow and death belong to this year, 312—the Emperor Constantine and his colleague Licinius, by unanimous agreement, promulgated a most complete and ample law in favor of the Christians; and they transmitted to Maximinus, who even then ruled in the eastern regions and pretended to be their friend, the news of their victory over the tyrant, and indeed the law itself, as Eusebius says, Book IX, chapter 9 . . . Moreover, in the later Constitution of Constantine and Licinius reported by Eusebius, Book X, chapter 5, the earlier constitution, issued in this year 312, is mentioned more than once, as Valesius learnedly explains in his notes on that edict, where he also shows the distinction between the two. The second edict was issued at Milan . . . the first in an uncertain place; yet it seems to have been promulgated at Rome, where Constantine spent the remainder of this year [Col. 0795B]. I think Lactantius was speaking of the aforementioned letters in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 37, where, after recounting the persecution stirred up by Maximinus against the Christians, he says: “While he was plotting these things, he was deterred by Constantine’s letters.” PAGIUS, *Critica Baroniana*, on the year of Christ 312, no. 8 and preceding.

“He was deterred.” Namely, only to the extent we have stated, not in every respect. For although Maximinus was deterred in provinces outside the East from, for example, gouging out the eyes of confessors, as he had decreed, Eusebius nevertheless testifies in Book IX of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 9, that, after letters written by Maximinus himself to Sabinus, prefect of his praetorian guard, he did not permit Christians to hold assemblies or build churches, although Constantine and Licinius had indicated in letters sent to him that they granted these things to the Christians. These final words are Pagius’s, in the cited passage, no. 8.

[Col. 0795C] “And yet if anyone fell [into his hands].” That is, into his hands, or those of his agents; as in chapter 16: “For when you had fallen into the hands of Flaccinus the Prefect . . . then into those of Hierocles . . .” etc. Maucroix preferred the latter supplementation, “But when a Christian fell into the hands of the ministers of his cruelty.”

“He was secretly drowned in the sea.” Thus he did not dare openly to tear Christians to pieces, as he had done before; but neither did he diligently seek them out. For Lactantius says, “if anyone fell [into his hands],” so that necessarily very few fell into his hands. DODWELL, *Dissertation on Cyprian*, XI, no. 87.

“He was secretly drowned in the sea.” A similar expression occurs in chapter 50: “There he had often ordered chaste women to be drowned.” Indeed, with almost exactly the same syllables in chapter 15: “They were drowned in the sea.”

“Secretly.” Secretly and at night. The English translation: that is, secretly and by night.

“And he had been the first to devise this: that all the animals,” etc. Baluzius understands this as concerning the private use of food in the palace. For a general edict concerning the eating of *eidōlothyta* (εἰδωλόθυτα, food sacrificed to idols) had already been established under Decius and Galerius Maximian. Oxford and Cambridge edition.

“And he had been the first to devise this.” As, in the administration of justice above, chapter 15, Diocletian and Maximian had devised that litigants should first sacrifice and then plead their cases. Therefore he immediately adds: “Similar also to his master in his other practices,” for so it must be read with the most illustrious Cuperus. TOLLIUS.

“That all the animals on which they fed should be sacrificed at altars, not by cooks but by priests.” Related to this—though we do not mean it to be altogether similar—is what we read in Samuel: when on one occasion the Israelites had routed the Philistines, and the people, turning to the spoil, had taken sheep, oxen, and calves, which they ate after first slaughtering them on the ground with the blood, Saul immediately ordered, so that the people should no longer sin against Jehovah by eating blood, that a great stone be rolled to him. Then he ordered that anyone thereafter wishing to slaughter such animals should bring them to him, to be killed, plainly, at that stone. The whole people consequently brought their oxen in their hands until nightfall, and they were slaughtered there. Moreover, an altar to the Lord was built by Saul on that occasion—indeed the first of all that he made. Since this is so, what is more likely than that Saul is said to have built an altar at that time because he immediately raised the great stone which he had caused to be rolled to him in the form of an altar, so that the Israelites might slaughter their animals beside it, and thus the animals which they desired to eat were sacrificed at an altar?

“And absolutely nothing was placed upon the table unless it had either been offered in first-fruits, or sacrificed, or sprinkled with unmixed wine.” *Delibatum* means food prepared for supper, from which a certain portion had been taken and offered to the gods. They were accustomed also to make libations of food. Silius Italicus, Book VII:

> He distinguished the sweet feast; and his chaste table,  
> Unstained by any blood, brought the gifts of Ceres,  
> [Col. 0796B] and first wiped away Vesta’s honor on every side,  
> And cast the libations into the midst of the flame.

This is what Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities* IV, calls τὰς ἀπὸ τῶν δείπνων ἀπαρχὰς ἁγίζειν, “to offer the first-fruits of meals.” “Sacrificed” means that which had been cut from a victim offered to the gods for a feast, as they used to cut up and burn a part of the victims, reserving another part for the feasts of priests and sacrificers. “Sprinkled with unmixed wine,” namely the wine with which they were accustomed to make supplication, so that these foods might as it were be consecrated. For who does not know that the ancients customarily made supplication with incense and wine, even amid feasting? Horace, *Odes* IV.5, on Augustus:

> At the second table he receives you as a god.  
> With many a prayer, with wine poured out before you,  
> He follows you and mingles your divinity  
> With his household gods.

GRAEVIUS.

“Or sprinkled with unmixed wine.” Wine which was poured over the foreheads [Col. 0796C] of sacrificial victims. See Servius on Virgil. But the libation customarily made into the hearth or onto the ground, concerning which the most learned Baluzius writes, is a different rite from this. TOLLIUS.

“So that whoever had been invited to dinner,” etc. Julian likewise in John of Salisbury, Book VII, chapter 21. The same [Tollius].

“Then.” This word is absent in the Abo edition, and might easily indeed be absent from them all. Yet why should we reject it, since it is found in the manuscript codex and is not altogether superfluous?

“Similar to his master.” Namely Galerius, as Maucroix’s translation anticipated: “He strove to resemble his master Galerius.” That is, he tried to be like his master Galerius.

“The granaries of private persons were shut; their storehouses were sealed.” A passage to be noted. For granaries and storehouses, if one must speak properly, differed from one another; hence Isidore, Book XV, chapter V, wrongly conflated them in these words: “*Apothecae*, or granaries, may be called, word for word from the Greek, repositories or places of storage, because men store in them the fruits of their labor. Hence also, in Greek speech, we call a plentiful stock of stored goods ἐνθήκη.”

“Storehouses.” *Boutiques*. MAUCROIX. That is, workshops or shops.—But workshop, storehouse, and shop differ greatly, says Gerard John Vossius in his *Etymological Dictionary*, shortly explaining the matter thus: In a workshop an article is made by craftsmen. From there it is carried for keeping into a storehouse; those who sell from the storehouses are called merchants, and sometimes, with an addition, wholesale merchants. From storehouses goods are sent to shops so that they may there be offered for sale; but only shops sell retail, and those who run them are called shopkeepers. Thus it may appear that the most learned man understood by *apotheca* what the French call *un magasin*; nor would he elsewhere say that *apotheca* is a general word assigned by jurists and others to receptacles for wines, oil, books, and similar things.—“Storehouses: in which wines are stored.” Consult the notes on Phaedrus. [Col. 0797A] TOLLIUS.—A most fitting interpretation. For just as in chapter 31, “there was no threshing-floor under Galerius without a tax-collector, nor any vintage without a guard,” so later under Maximinus, in the same category of things, granaries were shut and wine-cellars sealed. It follows that Maximinus was in fact similar to his master Galerius, as was said shortly before.

“Debts due in future years were exacted.” Certainly not money, but taxes in grain and wine, as what follows shows: “Hence famine in the fields,” etc.; “hence an unheard-of dearth.”

“In future years.” “Of the year to come,” the English translation; as though one said, “for the coming year.”—I preferred the plural number both on account of the authority of the old book and because, if the obligations which I have just mentioned were exacted not simply for the next year but for future years, the unheard-of dearth of which our author is shortly to speak could more readily arise from satisfying them.

“Hence famine, the fields not bearing.” I emend: “Hence famine for farmers who were not producing.” GALE.—I had considered whether it might be read: “Hence a sharp famine for those supplying the aforesaid obligations,” ἀπὸ τοῦ κοινοῦ [from the common construction]. Since these obligations were partly paid in grain, it could scarcely fail that those who in the year of Christ 312 supplied Maximinus with those requisitioned grain subsidies for several years would afterward suffer severe famine. Terence, *Phormio*, Act I, scene 1:

> My chief friend and fellow-countryman Geta  
> Came to me yesterday. He still had with me  
> A very small remainder of money from an account  
> Long outstanding, that I might settle it. I settled it; I bring it.

This is an example of a debt brought in.

“Herds of cattle and flocks were seized from the fields for the daily sacrifices,” etc. Something is missing. GALE.—Some words are missing here. For these words do not cohere with what follows; the latter concerns soldiers, to whom grain-rations had now become distasteful because excessive quantities of meat from the daily sacrifices were sent to them. TOLLIUS.—It certainly does concern them. But what if this passage is corrupt rather than mutilated, and nothing else is required, at least to connect the following properly with what precedes, except that we should presently emend *suos* (“his own”) for *eos* (“them”), with several learned men named in the following note?

“With which he had so corrupted them,” etc. “With which he fed his Domesticks and his Souldiers so copiously, that they come to despise the corn, that was brought them for their provision, so that without any care they threw it often out of doors.” The English translation has this sense: “With which [sacrifices] he had so corrupted his household and his soldiers that they despised the grain brought to them as their ration, and often threw it out of doors without any concern.”—The author’s words are corrupt here. Maucroix, in the margin of his translation.

“With which them.” Place a stop before *quibus*, and read: “With which [things] his own [people].” That is, “with which things.” BOHERELLUS.

“So that they despised the ration.” That is, the grain ration alone; for it is clear from what precedes that they did not at all despise the flesh of cattle and flocks, but on the contrary had become disgusted with grain because of the abundance of that meat. Further, not only does the English translation quoted in the preceding note support this, but also the levy of supplies mentioned by our author in chapter 31; for there no herds of cattle or flocks are included under the designation *annona* (“ration” or “provision”), as will be clear to those consulting the passage. Yet the most illustrious Cuperus interprets our author differently.

“And they poured out.” “And they might pour out.” Oxford and Cambridge editions.—For my part, in view of what follows, I thought preferable: “He poured out money,” namely military money, or the money which, as Asconius says, was customarily paid from the treasury by the military paymasters to the quaestor for soldiers’ wages. Finally, the familiar phrase *aere dirutus miles*, “a soldier stripped of his pay,” shows that *aes* (“money”) without qualification was not infrequently so called: it refers to a soldier whose wage was not given because of disgrace, but was instead confiscated into the treasury, not placed in the soldier’s purse.

“With all lawsuits.” The Abo edition reads: “With all the soldiers.”

[Col. 0798A] “With lawsuits.” There is an error here. ALLIX.

“Lawsuits.” Read: “soldiers.” VOSSIUS.—Read: “soldiers” or “attendants.” Oxford and Cambridge editions.—I would rather read “with all his attendants” than “with all his soldiers,” because an emperor cannot be said to have conferred those gifts on all alike, since he gave only money even to common soldiers and recruits, though they too were soldiers. TOLLIUS.

“With lawsuits.” I emend: “while [he was rewarding] his companions.” GALE; which comes to the same thing.

“Should expunge.” “Should expunge” [singular]. Abo edition.—There is an error in this passage, not only in the number of the verb but also, in my judgment, in its meaning. Therefore one should write *excoleret*, “should cultivate” or “should caress.” This conjecture is confirmed by the passage from Rufinus, Book VIII, chapter 17, cited by Baluzius: “Thus he distributed, as it were, mountains of gold gathered together to his intimates and attendants.” For *expungere*, when joined to soldiers, means nothing other than striking them from the military roll and discharging them from service. Oxford and Cambridge editions.—“Should fill up,” perhaps. TOLLIUS.—I correct: “should milk dry” (*emungeret*). [Col. 0798B] GALE.—I preferred Tertullian’s word *expingeret*, that is, “should adorn,” or something of the kind. In *On Women’s Dress*, chapter 7, he says: “How blasphemous it is if you who are called priestesses of chastity go about dressed or painted in the manner of unchaste women”; and a few words later: “Because Tamar had painted and adorned herself, she seemed to Judah’s suspicion to sit for hire.” He similarly uses the word often elsewhere. Indeed, in the final chapter we believe it may be read, by analogous reasoning, “how he now adorned [them] with costly garments and golden coins,” since he said: “Clothe yourselves with the silk of uprightness, the fine linen of holiness, the purple of modesty. Thus adorned, you shall have God as your lover.” By “golden coins” I understand gold medallions hung from the neck, such as one sometimes sees many people wear in princes’ courts.

“For that he gave away the property of the living,” etc. Related to this is Salvian’s saying: “Robbers are accustomed to use this proverb, that they say they have given [life] to those from whom they have not taken life.” Oxford and Cambridge editions.

“To his own as a gift.” Therefore learned men correctly restored *suos* (“his own”) for *eos* (“them”) on the preceding page.

“I do not know whether I should think that he ought to be thanked.” “I do not know whether he does not deserve some praise.” MAUCROIX.—Therefore he judged that one should rather read “whether he ought not to be thanked” than “whether he ought to be thanked.”

## Chapter XXXVIII

“But that capital vice, beyond all who have existed, a desire for corruption,” etc. The passage is badly corrupted, but easily restored. I read and punctuate merely: “But that capital vice in him, beyond all who have existed,” or perhaps also, “But that capital vice in him—and beyond all who have existed—was a desire for corruption, which I do not know how to describe except as blind and unbridled.” That is: this was the capital vice in Maximinus, far beyond all mortals who ever lived: he suffered from a blind and unbridled desire to corrupt the weaker sex. The Abo edition and Gale punctuated after *fuerunt* with us; but the former elsewhere does so most badly, and in no way in this fashion: “But that capital vice, and beyond all who have existed; a desire for corruption,” etc.

“To express [it] in proportion to its indignation.” Read: “that the matter be expressed,” etc. Oxford and Cambridge editions.

“In proportion to its indignation.” That is, according to the English translation, in proportion to the indignation which this ought to arouse: “for the indignation which this must give.”

“In proportion to its indignation.” I emend: “in proportion to its worthiness.” BOHERELLUS.

“In proportion to its indignation.” Read: “in proportion to its shamefulness.” TOLLIUS, likewise GALE.

“Eunuchs, procurers, searched everywhere.” A most elegant asyndeton, like that in Dictys of Crete, Book V, *On the Trojan War*: “Thus each one, many together, according as each encountered [them], approached them kindly.” I observe, moreover, that both examples show that nothing prevents us from using, in Paul, 1 Corinthians 7:22, instead of the received punctuation, “ὁ γὰρ ἐν κυρίῳ κληθεὶς δοῦλος, ἀπελεύθερος κυρίου ἐστίν,” this other punctuation which I have long used: “ὁ γὰρ ἐν κυρίῳ κληθεὶς . δοῦλος, ἀπελεύθερος, κυρίου ἐστίν”; “For the one called in the Lord as a slave is a freedman, the Lord’s.” For the sense or connection of the whole passage certainly does not stand in the way; rather, the entire sequence clearly shows that it strongly favors this reading: “Let each remain in the calling in which he was called. Were you called as a slave? Do not be concerned; but if you can also become free, make use of it rather. For the one called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord’s freedman; likewise the one called free is Christ’s slave.” More on this elsewhere, God willing.

“Women of noble rank.” Why not rather “noble matrons,” with Rufinus in Baluzius? Here certainly women are distinguished from virgins: “Garments were removed from noble women, and likewise from virgins.” Yet in Latin *foeminae* are not only those joined to husbands, but also virgins. Labbe’s glossaries: *Foemina*, θήλεια, a word commonly interpreted by *foeminea*, “that which is of the female sex,” which is also applicable to virgins.

[Col. 0799B] “They were inspected limb by limb.” The Persians once had, and the Turks and likewise the Persians today have, a not dissimilar license. TOLLIUS.

“He had refused.” “He had declined.” Oxford and Cambridge editions.—But our author has already used *detractaret* in chapter 9, and likewise *detractassent* in chapter 10.

“Adulterer.” The Abo edition reads “adultery,” incorrectly.

“Under this minister there was no integrity of chastity unless,” etc. “Under this monster, ugliness was the sole refuge of modesty.” MAUCROIX.—“Under this monster, there was no other security for modesty but ugliness.” BURNET.—It is therefore clear that, for the first words “under this minister,” they read “under this monster.” And indeed not badly, since the received reading cannot be sustained. In what good sense could “under this minister” be said of the man who was emperor, and of whom our author shortly afterward says, “under such a prince”?—“Under this minister”: that is, a priest, ironically. TOLLIUS.—If perhaps the learned man took *pudicitiae* as a genitive dependent on *ministro*, “minister of chastity,” I well recall what I cited above from Tertullian concerning priests of chastity: “How blasphemous it is if you who are called priestesses of chastity go about dressed or painted in the manner of unchaste women.” But by what reasoning our author could call Maximinus, in great irony, a minister of chastity—that is, in Tollius’s interpretation, a priest—I neither see nor understand. Partly because “minister of chastity” and “priest of chastity” are not the same expressions; partly because, as the rest of this chapter is very serious, this portion can scarcely be ironic. I therefore think that either one should read, with the most distinguished interpreters, “under this monster there was no integrity of chastity”; or, proceeding somewhat further on the same path, “under this monster of unchastity there was no integrity unless,” etc.

“In all marriages he was a first-taster.” Namely, in those in which the new bride was not remarkably ugly, as the preceding exception requires.

[Col. 0799D] “First-taster.” Travelers who have gone through the farthest parts of Africa and India report that there is there a widespread custom whereby the virginity of brides is first sampled by kings or priests. Indeed, in Africa, if I remember rightly, in the kingdom of Mozambique, strangers are invited, with much complimentary language, to perform this office for husbands or bridegrooms. Among us, however, I read some years ago in a public notice posted in the taverns of Utrecht concerning a noble estate which included among its other rights and privileges the right of deflowering newly married brides—though this could be redeemed from the lord of the place by money. TOLLIUS.

“Diminished.” Baluzius—in the errata index of his first edition; for in this edition, p. 332, col. 2, he reads quite differently—would prefer “unwilling,” for no reason known to me. For since Maximinus was a first-taster at all weddings, *imminutas* means nothing other than “previously deflowered.” Oxford and Cambridge editions.

“His companions.” “The great lords.” MAUCROIX; that is, magnates. “His courtiers,” the English translation. That is, his courtiers.

“He imitated . . . They imitated.” Abo edition; likewise PAGIUS.—I emend: “They were initiated.” GALE.—Supply: “They imitated his example and . . .” Oxford and Cambridge editions.—I correct and supply: “They committed adultery freely, and [with] citizens’ [wives].” ABBOT OF ST HILARY, canon of Beauvais.

“They violated the beds of their subjects.” An elegant and modest form of expression, very familiar indeed to Scripture; Maucroix says more directly, without such circumlocution: “they treated the wives and daughters of their subjects with the same insolence.” Yet rightly so. Thus Genesis 49:4: “You ascended your father’s bed; you defiled my couch,” meaning, “you lay with Bilhah, my concubine.” Nor is Paul’s sense unlike in Hebrews 13:4: “Let marriage be honorable in all, and the bed undefiled”—or, with the Vulgate, “the marriage-bed unstained”; for fornicators and adulterers God will judge.

“They were not permitted to refuse.” Read: “nor was the father permitted to refuse.” VOSSIUS.—The English translation agrees: “The father durst not refuse it.” [Col. 0800B] Literally, “nor did the father dare refuse.”

“An attendant at his side.” I prefer “by his side,” whence *latrones*, as though *laterones*, soldiers at one’s side. TOLLIUS.

“All his guards.” MAUCROIX.—“Domestics or guards,” English translation.

“By the Goths.” These inhabitants of the bank of the Ister, taking advantage of the occasion, invaded the father’s neighboring province and expelled its inhabitants. Oxford and Cambridge editions.

“At the time of the vicennalia.” Namely, those of Diocletian. This is rightly supplied in the English translation: “in the twentieth year of Diocletian’s reign.”

“They surrendered themselves to Maximian.” Read: “They had surrendered themselves.” TOLLIUS.

“To Maximian.” Rather, “to Maximinus.” MAUCROIX: at least this is to be inferred from his translation, “they gave themselves to Maximin.”

“Protectors.” Namely, because he himself, whose attendants and guards-at-his-side—or by-his-side—they were, had formerly been a protector. Chapter 19: “But Daia, recently raised from the sheep and woods, was immediately a shield-bearer, then a protector,” etc. We have already said what we had to say concerning protectors on that passage. Add only, if you have leisure, Gruter’s inscriptions, p. 371, Inscription VI; p. 542, Inscriptions VII and VIII; and elsewhere.

[Col. 0800C] “He made the East a laughingstock.” Correctly. For it is consequently sound, as we argued above, that chapter 36 begins: “When Maximinus received this news, he sped through the East by arranged relays in order to occupy the provinces”; and the final words of chapter 19 agree strikingly: “But Daia . . . received the East to be trodden down and crushed,” with this clause of our author: “He made the East a laughingstock.”

## Chapter XXXIX

“That he thought it lawful [to do] whatever he had desired.” The story of Julia and Caracalla may be referred to here. TOLLIUS.

“Had desired.” In imitation of Cicero, who says in the speech for Quintius, “as you have always exceedingly desired,” and in the *Philippics*, “[he] desired the affection of citizens and glory,” although elsewhere he uses “had desired” and “they had desired” and many similar forms. What then? In our author *prodisset*, *obiisset*, *dormisset*, *quaesisset*, *sepelisset*, *redisset*, and others of this kind, are most familiar and almost perpetual.

“Not even from the Augusta, whom he had recently called mother,” etc. That is, according to the English translation, not even from the Empress Valeria, Maximian’s widow, whom he had acknowledged as his mother by adoption: “He had acknowledged the Empress Valeria, that was Maximian’s widow, his adopted mother.”

“After the death of Maximian.” “After the death of Galerius.” Maucroix’s translation.

“To him.” To Maximinus. The same [translation].

“In his regions.” Therefore, in the eastern regions, just as our author spoke at the end of chapter 36, when dealing with Maximinus and the regions where Maximinus lived and ruled before Galerius’s death. But I think it very rare that the region in which someone lives should be called “his regions,” except when we address that person face to face or by letter: “I shall make a journey into your parts”; “I was still in your parts,” and similar expressions.

[Col. 0801A] “A wicked creature.” As in chapter 4: “the accursed creature Decius.”

“The woman was still in black garments.” “Although the princess had not yet left mourning.” MAUCROIX. Literally: “Although the Augusta had not yet laid aside mourning.” And indeed not badly, since the French everyday expression *quitter le deuil* corresponds to the Latin phrase *lugubrem vestem deponere*, “to lay aside mourning dress”; that is, as they otherwise express it more fully, *ses habits de deuil*. Thus we use “mourning” for garments or a garment of mourning—that is, appropriate to mourning, bearing witness to and signifying mourning. Yet, to say this in passing, it is surprising that Maucroix did not instead translate, *Elle était encore en noir* (“She was still in black”), since the Latins sometimes say, as here, *in atris vestibus esse*, “to be in black garments,” elsewhere *atratum esse*, “to be clothed in black,” and elsewhere again *pullatum esse*, and since our people commonly and equally well say both *être en noir* (“to be in black”: *in atro esse*, or *in atris*, with *habitu* or *vestibus* understood) and *être en deuil*, “to be in mourning”—that is, likewise to be dressed in mourning habit or mournful garments. But do other peoples speak so too? Certainly the Jews do, if no others; this is the point to which I intended properly to bring the matter, because of the following Scriptural passages, which shed light on what we have stated.

Ezekiel 7:27: “The king shall mourn, and the prince shall be clothed with grief.” That is, with garments of grief, suitable to grief and becoming a grieving prince, such as, for example, the sackcloth mentioned in Jonah 3:5–6: “The men of Nineveh believed in God, proclaimed a fast, and clothed themselves in sackcloth, from the greatest to the least. And word came to the king of Nineveh; and he arose from his throne, cast away his garment from him, clothed himself in sackcloth, and sat in ashes.” Again Ezekiel 26:15–16: “Thus says the Lord God to Tyre . . . All the princes of the sea shall descend from their thrones; they shall remove their robes and cast off their embroidered garments; they shall clothe themselves with trembling; they shall sit upon the ground, and, terrified at your sudden fall, shall marvel.” That is, they too shall be clothed in garments signifying an astonished mind. Conversely David says, Psalm 29:12: “You have turned my lamentation into dancing for me; you have loosed my sackcloth and girded me with joy,” when he meant to say, “you have girded me with garments of joy,” or garments displaying joy, which otherwise were customarily white in Judaea in that age. Ecclesiastes 9:7–8: “Go then, eat your bread with joy and drink your wine with gladness, because God is pleased with your works. Let your garments always be white.”

Compare, if you have leisure, the remarkable passage near the end of Cicero’s speech against Vatinius, where Tully says among other things: “I also wish to know from you . . . with what intention you acted so as to recline at the banquet of Quintus Arius, my friend, wearing a dark toga? . . . Who ever dined clothed in black? . . . when so many thousands of men reclined at table, when the master of the feast himself, Quintus Arius, wore white, you brought yourself into the temple of Castor, clad in black with Gaius Fidulus and your other furies, a funerary apparition,” etc.

[Col. 0801D] “Woman.” The word is sometimes contemptuous, as when Chremes in Terence, addressing his wife Sostrata, says, “Oh! Will you persist in being a woman?” Elsewhere it is often an expression of anger, as when Christ in John’s Gospel, speaking indignantly to his mother, says: “What have I to do with you, woman?” Here, however, since there is no occasion for contempt or anger in our Caecilius, *mulier* plainly serves in place of the pronoun “she” or “that woman,” just as in these verses of Horace:

> Has a husband just authority over both  
> The guilty matron and her seducer—or a more just authority over the seducer? Yet he neither changes  
> His dress nor his place, nor sins from above,  
> When the woman fears you . . .

There the final words mean nothing other than “when she fears you.” Learned men before us have observed this; indeed, elsewhere *homo* (“man”) similarly occurs for “he” or “that man.”

“Woman.” “The Princess.” MAUCROIX, repeating the title Augusta which preceded.

“He seeks [her] in marriage.” Read: “he seeks [her] for marriage.” BOHERELLUS, GALE.—This fault has often crept into Lactantius’s little work through scribal error: the ablative was written for the accusative. Correct, therefore, and read *in matrimonium*. TOLLIUS.

“In that funeral attire.” That is, attire of the dead, if one compares these few words from ancient glossaries: Νεκρικός—though one should rather read Νεκρικόν—“funeral”; Νεκρικόν, “funereal”; “pertaining to the dead.” “Pertaining to the dead” is what concerns a dead person or is used on account of a dead person.

“With the ashes still warm,” etc. Lucan has almost the same thing at the beginning of Book III:

> You led me, Magnus, your wife, through joyful triumphs;  
> The fortune of the marriage-bed has changed. Ever doomed by fate  
> To drag powerful husbands into ruin,  
> Cornelia, the concubine, married a still-warm pyre.

CUPERUS.

[Col. 0802B] When I saw that the most illustrious man, among other things which he had elsewhere noted on this passage with his exceptional learning, had simply stated that the ancient Romans were very careful lest their own or others’ corpses be cremated or buried mutilated, while I recalled that Paul the Deacon had written most explicitly among the fragments of Festus: “A limb was said to be cut off from a dead person when one of his fingers was removed; it was preserved so that the funeral rites might be performed for it, while the rest of the body was burned,” I believed—as indeed happened—that the learned man would take it in good part if I asked by letter how he thought Paul’s cited words should be reconciled with the contrary testimonies of Apuleius, Statius, and the others which he had adduced.

Not long afterward he replied, with his customary kindness, that I had not raised the question about Paul’s passage inopportunely; but after considering the matter, he thought and conjectured briefly as follows. First, the practice mentioned by Paul was indeed very ancient, but not perpetual, since no writer other than Paul made explicit mention of it. So far as one may guess, it had long since fallen through the passage of time into such disuse that it had entirely become obsolete in the centuries in which, for example, Statius and Apuleius lived. Nor did it then seem credible to him that the same rite, however long it lasted, had prevailed everywhere at once. For whenever a finger was thus cut off from the dead, nature was in some degree violated; therefore very many, without doubt, recoiled from that usage. Certainly the Greeks never did anything of the kind; and the Romans under the first emperors were much less superstitious than before. Besides, time has always possessed marvelous force and power to alter such superstitions. Finally, Kirchmann too seemed to think that the ancient practice under discussion had not endured longer than Cuperus himself did, as these words of his testify: “It is also likely that the limb which, as we have said above, was removed for the purification of the household and was not placed in the urn with the rest of the body, was in ancient times, so long as that custom lasted, buried in the earth during these same funeral rites.” These, reader, are the matters which we thought should be translated for your sake from French into Latin, lest perhaps the same scruple which troubled us should trouble you when you come to the preface of the most illustrious Cuperus.

[Col. 0802D] “His father.” Namely, by adoption, referring *ejus* (“her/his”) to Maximinus understood; as Maucroix rightly translates, “the adoptive father of Maximinus.” For “father” is not here used in the sense in which Constantius is properly called Constantine’s father in chapter 24; nor in that in which Diocletian is called Galerius’s father—that is, father-in-law—in chapter 18; but in the true sense in which one who has adopted someone, whether already born or not yet born, is customarily called that person’s father. I gladly refer to this Mary’s saying: “Behold, your father and I have sought you sorrowing,” Luke 2:48. Compare the English translation of this passage: “his adopted father.”

“Then [he said] that he would act impiously,” etc. “And besides, he could not do so without injustice,” MAUCROIX.—Thus *impie* means “unjustly.” To me, however, it rather means “inhumanely” or “cruelly,” just as at the end of chapter 29 an *impius pater* is a cruel, inhuman, merciless father.

“Let him repudiate [her].” Not because he was in fact then repudiating Valeria, or had already repudiated her; for the preceding words are: “he would cast out his wife, if he obtained [Valeria].” Rather, it is because he was contemplating repudiating her. Thus *repudiet* means “he wishes to repudiate,” or something of the sort; just as in the next chapter *necabatur* means “was destined for death,” as the whole sequence of the passage will confirm.

Without custom, without precedent, to take another husband.

To the points which I note on chapter 39 and in the letter to the most distinguished Voetius, concerning the second marriages of Empresses, I can now add that others did not follow Valeria’s example. For Eudocia, wife of Constantine Ducas, who became emperor in A.D. 1059, although she had promised the dying emperor in writing that she would not enter a second marriage, took as her second husband Romanus Diogenes, the patrician, duke and commander of Sardica; and he was at the same time made emperor. [Col. 0803B] Galla Placidia, daughter of Theodosius the Great and wife of King Ataulf, having been sent back by Wallia, was given in marriage by her brother Honorius to Flavius Constantius the patrician in A.D. 418, although Placidia had initially refused him. Indeed, Faustina, wife of Marcus Antoninus, surnamed “the Philosopher,” was not of that mind. For she conspired with Cassius to make him her husband, and agreed with him that, “if anything should happen to Antoninus, he should obtain both her and supreme power” (*ἄν τι ὁ Ἀντωνῖνος πάθοι, καὶ αὐτὴν καὶ τὴν αὐταρχίαν λάβῃ*), as we read in Dio.

Julia, after the death of L. Septimius Severus, married Caracalla, whose stepmother she was, according to the testimony of Spartianus, Victor, and Eutropius. Yet Tristan, vol. 2, argues at length that this history should be counted among fables, and that Julia was not Caracalla’s stepmother but his mother. These two examples, therefore, do little to refute Valeria; but Lucilla Augusta, daughter of Antoninus the Philosopher and Annia Faustina, supplies us with a third, and a most evident, example. She was given in marriage to L. Aurelius Verus, who was made partner in the imperial power and Augustus by Lucilla’s father. After her husband’s death, before the period of mourning had ended, Marcus caused her to marry the private citizen Claudius Pompeianus. [Col. 0803C] Capitolinus, ch. 20:

> “Before the period of mourning had elapsed, he gave his daughter to Claudius Pompeianus, the aged son of a Roman knight, of Antiochene origin and not sufficiently noble; afterward he made him consul twice, although his daughter was Augusta, and the daughter of an Augusta.”

There are, however, certain considerations which in this very matter lend some support to Valeria’s cause. For Lucilla did this not of her own will, but unwillingly. Capitolinus: “But Faustina and she herself, who was given in marriage, accepted this marriage unwillingly.” Unless someone judges that Lucilla obeyed her father reluctantly because Pompeianus was aged and insufficiently noble; for otherwise, being a forward woman and by no means a stranger to Venus’s allurements, she would not seem likely to have refused a marriage more suited to her rank.

Further, it should be observed that Galerius Maximianus, after the senior Augusti Diocletian and Maximian Herculius had laid aside the purple, occupied their place together with Constantius Chlorus; whereas L. Aurelius Verus was always the junior Augustus. [Col. 0803D] Now it is established that the junior Augusti treated the senior ones with great reverence, so that they were, as it were, their Caesars and legates, and consequently were not endowed with so extensive authority and power, though they used the same titles and insignia. Indeed, this is evident from the history of M. Aurelius and L. Aurelius Verus itself, as Henr. Dodwell excellently demonstrates in his learned dissertation, *On the Primitive Succession of the Roman Pontiffs*, ch. 14. CUPERUS.

I should be extremely unfair if I did not frankly acknowledge and most plainly profess how learnedly and carefully this most distinguished man has argued here and elsewhere, on both sides, concerning the second marriages of Empresses before and after Valeria. Yet this difficulty still remains: why did Valeria so peremptorily deny that any woman previously of her rank and title had taken another husband, when several examples to the contrary were already available in her age? If anyone thinks it should be said [Col. 0804A] that perhaps those examples were wholly unknown to Valeria, or at any rate were not sufficiently present to her mind when she answered Maximinus’s envoys, either alternative might easily be true.

Meanwhile, I wish that some new manuscript copy of this book might be found. For what if the old reading were *maritum ex filiis alterum experiri*, “to take another husband from among the sons,” as in Pliny: “Yet I remember that I was assigned an advocate from among the judges”? Valeria certainly already had at that time two sons—not born from her, but at least adopted by her and her husband Galerius: namely Candidianus, whom she had adopted, being born of a concubine, because of her barrenness—these are the words of chapter 50—and afterward Maximinus as well. Though he had properly been adopted by Galerius (whence Valeria shortly before said: “while the ashes of her husband, his father, were still warm”), he was thereby also Valeria’s son. Hence our author says of him very recently: “he could not even restrain himself from the Augusta,” whom he had just called mother. Thus Valeria would indeed have taken another husband from among her sons, had she been joined to Maximinus in a second marriage.

This is all the more so because, when formerly Maevius, for example, was expressly adopted by one of the spouses, Maevius was at the same time called the son of the other spouse. Chapter 35: “After a few days, Galerius, having commended his wife and son to Licinius”—supply *his own son*, namely Candidianus—“and delivered them into his hand,” etc.; although, strictly speaking, Candidianus was not the adopted son of Galerius but of Valeria. But here again the example of Julia, who after Severus’s death married her stepson Caracalla—or, as others prefer, her son—troubles the matter inconveniently. Therefore I do not see where I can securely set my foot.

**Homini.** For this the English translation has *Maximino*; but Maucroix has *Imperatori*, “the Emperor.” From what has been said above, it can suitably be understood as *illi*, “to him.”

**Mulierem, etc.** Thus the English translation. That is, it confirms our preceding note.

**Spadones in tormentis necat.** “He kills eunuchs under torture.” The preposition here is superfluous and should be deleted. TOLLIUS.—“He causes her slaves to die under tortures.” MAUCROIX. Literally: “he has her servants killed under tortures.”—“He tortured some of her eunuchs.” English translation. That is, he tortured some of her eunuchs to death.

**Ipsam cum matre in exilium, etc.** Namely with Prisca, Diocletian’s wife. PAGIUS.

**Amicas ejus.** “Their female friends.” MAUCROIX. That is, their friends, contrary to the authority of the book; indeed contrary to the authority of almost the entire following chapter, where not Prisca’s but Valeria’s friends alone are enumerated and described. The most distinguished English translator is therefore better: “such women as were dearest to her.” That is, briefly, “her friends.”

## CHAPTER XL

**Suspicabatur.** Maximinus, of course, as the translators rightly supplied.

**Dat negotium Praesidi Eratineo, ut, etc.** “He gives the task to the governor Eratineus, that,” etc. Cicero, *In Verrem*: “He gives a certain friend of his the task … that he should take careful precautions.” Tullius elsewhere used this phrase as well, and together with him Caesar, Terence, and Sallust. *Dare negotium* is like entrusting a province, giving instructions, and similar expressions.

**Quarum altera Vestalem famulam virginem Romae reliquerat.** “One of whom had left in Rome one of her maids to be a Vestal.” MAUCROIX. As though our author had written: “One of whom had left in Rome one from the number of her own female servants as a Vestal virgin.”—“A Vestal household virgin.” Rather, “a Vestal daughter, a virgin.” BOHERELLUS.—The English translation agrees in this manner: “The one was mother to one of the vestal virgins of Rome.” That is, one was mother of one of the Roman Vestal virgins. But Cuperus differs still further.

**Non minus Augustae proxima.** Thus also the Abo edition. All the others, with the manuscript, have *non nimis*, “not very”; hence scholars have now gone off into various conjectures.

**Non nimis.** I think it should be restored as *nonnihil*, “somewhat.” Anonymous writer in the Oxford and Cambridge editions.—I emend: *non minus*. GALE.—“No less close to the Augusta.” Thus learned men rightly read it, as Heinsius also conjectured it should be read. [Col. 0805A] A woman is called *proxima Augustae*, “close to the Augusta,” when she was among the Augusta’s friends admitted to her inner circle; as there was a *proximus epistolarum*, head of the correspondence bureau, a *proximus memoriae*, head of the memoranda bureau, and a *proximus libellorum*, head of petitions. That rank was called *proximatus* in the Theodosian Code. Salmasius has noted much upon these matters in his remarks on Lampridius’s *Alexander Severus*. GRAEVIUS.—“And was the Empress’s kinswoman.” English translation; that is, she was or had been among the Augusta’s relatives.—“The other had no great intercourse with the Empress.” MAUCROIX. Literally: “The other had no great familiarity with the Augusta.”—Correct in my judgment, though it could have been translated still better: “But she did not approach the Empress too closely.”

In a word, of Valeria’s three friends whose unhappy end our author recounts in this chapter, Valeria loved the first as a second mother, as we have just seen; she was thus her friend admitted to the most intimate circle. The second, though not openly, was nevertheless secretly intimate with Valeria. The third, though herself also among Valeria’s friends, was nevertheless [Col. 0805B] far less intimate than the other two, and therefore did not approach the Augusta so closely: *non nimis Augustae proxima*, “not too close to the Augusta,” in that sense; as in chapter 26, *nec tamen nimium territus*, “yet not excessively terrified.”

**Necabatur.** That is, to speak with Ammianus, she was being pressed toward execution: “But whatever had pleased Caesar’s implacability, as though weighed as law and right, was immediately pressed to be carried out.” Ammianus, book XIV, near the beginning.

**Non ad judicium, sed ad latrocinium.** That is, as Maucroix translates it, not before a judge, but before a brigand.

**Invenitur quidam Judaeus, etc.** By the same contrivance, namely, whereby two false witnesses had formerly been found among the Israelites against Naboth, 1 Kings 21; and whereby afterward men were likewise found among the Jews at Jerusalem who said that they had heard Stephen speak impiously against Moses and God, Acts 6.

**Adversus insontes mentiatur.** That is, he is willing to lie at the requisite time and place, imputing adultery to the innocent women [Col. 0805C] and saying that he himself had had intercourse with them. Hence shortly afterward: “Nor is the promised immunity paid to the adulterer.”

**Judex aequus et diligens.** Said ironically. Oxford and Cambridge editions.—The irony is the same as that by which Cicero often praises Verres when speaking of his singular injustice, by which he oppressed the innocent. TOLLIUS.—I scarcely doubted that the ancient reading had been *judex acutus et diligens*, “a sharp and diligent judge.”

**Extra civitatem cum praesidio, ne lapidibus obruatur, protulit.** He brought out that Jew beyond the city with a guard, lest he be overwhelmed with stones—Eratineus fearing stoning by the people if the Jew delivered such false testimony against most honorable matrons within the city. But, I confess, the most distinguished translators take it otherwise: both refer *ne lapidibus obruatur*, “lest he be stoned,” to Judge Eratineus, who feared for himself; and the English translator further supplies after *protulit* the pronoun “them,” or “those women”—namely Valeria’s three friends—indeed as though all had already been condemned within the city and merely remained to be led beyond the walls to the place of punishment.

“The Judge, fearing that he would be stoned if he conducted this trial in the city, went out from it accompanied by armed men.” MAUCROIX.—“The Judge who condemned them upon this evidence, carried them out of Town to their execution with a Guard; for he was afraid that he should have been stoned by the people.” English translation. I can scarcely believe all this to be consistent with what follows, where torture is inflicted on the Jew only after he has finally been brought outside the city, in order that the said women might be brought to trial and condemned.

**Nicaeae.** The Abo edition has *Niceae*, as indeed in Justin, XII.8, where the Juntine editions read *Niceam* for *Nicaeam*, which is deservedly the received reading.

**Inrogantur tormenta Judaeo.** “Tortures are inflicted upon the Jew”; as in chapter 1, *mortem superbis inrogare*, “to inflict death on the proud.”

**Deum quae jussus . . . loqueretur, pugnis, etc.** This gap was thus filled by a most reverend man: “While he brought accusations, as he had been ordered, the women, if either spoke in her own defense, etc.”—I would prefer: “While he spoke, as he had [Col. 0806A] been ordered, as though reluctantly, etc.” ABBAS A S. HILARIO.—The gap seems capable of being filled conveniently thus: “While he publicly uttered what he had secretly been ordered.” NIC. HEINSIUS.—I punctuate and supply: “Tortures are inflicted upon the Jew while he speaks what he had been ordered to say. The innocent women are restrained by blows, etc.” GALE.—I suspected that the older reading was rather: “Tortures are inflicted upon the Jew; and while he spoke what he had been ordered”—that is, to say or answer—“the innocent women are restrained by blows and ordered to be led away.”
