**Duci jubentur.** Namely, to punishment; as our author shortly afterward says, “led to punishment,” and Justin XII.11: “Alexander himself led thirteen men, seized by his own hand, to punishment.” For *duci* and *deduci*, simply used, very frequently have that sense. Tertullian, *To Scapula*, final chapter: “When Arrius Antoninus in Asia was vigorously persecuting, all the Christians of that city presented themselves before his tribunal in a body; and when he ordered a few to be led away, he said to the rest: ‘You cowards, if you wish to die, you have cliffs or nooses’” (*ὦ δειλοί, εἰ θέλετε ἀποθνήσκειν, κρημνοὺς ἢ βρόχους ἔχετε*). Pliny in his letter to Trajan: “I asked … whether they were Christians; those who confessed I asked a second and third time, threatening punishment; those who persisted I ordered to be led away.” And our author above, chapter 15: “The presbyters and ministers were seized and, without any … being condemned, were led away with all their households.” We no longer approve, therefore, the other supplementation of that passage which we formerly believed could be drawn from what preceded. Compare Cuperus under *coercentur*, and Buchner on Pliny’s cited words.

**Contraxerat.** “Had drawn [them] to this spectacle.” MAUCROIX. That is, had attracted [them] to this spectacle.—“Had brought together.” English translation. That is, had assembled or united, which is better. For in Cicero, Livy, and others, *contrahere viros, milites, auxilia, pecuniam* is the same as to assemble, unite, or collect; just as, conversely, *distrahere* is sometimes to divide or separate. Florus, I.3: “For when those three Curiatii had been wounded and two Horatii killed, the surviving Horatius, adding stratagem to courage in order to divide the enemy, feigned flight”; that is, to divide, separate, or something similar.

**Promoti militari modo instructi velites et sagittarii prosequuntur.** Thus Baluzius long ago conjectured at the end of his first edition. For previously the author’s words, together with the manuscript, read: *promoti militari modo instructibile mens essagitari prosequuntur*; this is also the reading of the first Oxford edition. From it soon emerged the readings of other editions and likewise various observations of scholars, which I shall now set out.

“*Promoti militari modo instructibile menses sagittarii prosequuntur*.” Abo edition.—“*Promoti militari modo instructibile mens efflagitari prosequuntur*.” Oxford edition of 1684, likewise Cambridge, and Pagius, *Critica Baroniana*, at A.D. 312, no. 11.—“*Promoti militari modo instructibile*, etc.” Thus Baluzius reads: “The light-armed troops, arrayed in military fashion, advance, and the archers follow,” because both are soldiers of light armament. Oxford and Cambridge editions.—It should be read: “Those promoted, arrayed in military fashion, and the Viennese archers follow.” [Col. 0806D] VOSSIUS.—“*Promoti militari modo instructibile mens essagitari proseq.*” The text is monstrously corrupt; learned men have labored in various ways to amend it. Lactantius’s words seem to me to have been: “Military officers, arrayed in military fashion and equipped with weapons, follow them with arrows.” *Promoti* are military commanders promoted through lower grades to their ranks, as Lucan says:

> “Promoted by rank, he bears the Latin vine-staff.”

GRAEVIUS.—I correct: “Those promoted, arrayed in military fashion, aiming arrows, follow.” GALE.—I emend: “Horsemen, arrayed in military fashion, go before, and archers follow.” ABBAS A S. HILARIO.—“*Instructibile mens essagitari*.” It has no sense. It should be read: “Armed … swords, [and] archers.” ALLIX.—My contribution was that it should be emended: “Those posted in advance, arrayed in military fashion and equipped with javelin and sword; the archers follow.” The sense is this: Those placed before those matrons, equipped in military fashion with javelin and sword, proceeded as a first line; immediately following them came a second line of archers. And indeed, since the next words are, “Thus, placed between columns of armed men, they were led to punishment,” it is manifest that Eratineus employed two companies of armed men, lest the said matrons be snatched from the executioners’ hands: one to go before them while they were being led to the place of punishment, and another to follow them.

And because Mamertinus expressly says in his thanksgiving for the consulship: “Arms, therefore, and young men with swords and javelins are not a guard for the body, but a certain customary ornament of imperial majesty,” it is, I say, equally clear evidence that, according to our reading, the arms of the first troop could properly have been javelins and swords, since Mamertinus, their contemporary, joins javelins and swords—the same thing—when speaking of imperial guards; likewise Ammianus at the beginning of book XVII: “Accordingly, several fell, pierced by javelins and swords.”

**Inter cuneos armatorum.** Therefore all were infantry, contrary to the learned man’s preceding proposal. [Col. 0807B] For wedges consisted of a multitude of infantry arranged in wedge formation, so that such a wedge in battle proceeded narrower at the front and broader behind, according to Vegetius, book II.

**Nec adultero impunitas promissa persolvitur.** That is: the Jew who had falsely declared himself an accomplice in the matrons’ adulteries, after Eratineus had first assured him that he would not only suffer no penalty for that fictitious adultery but that all offenses for which he might deservedly have been prosecuted and punished would be forgiven in consideration of the false testimony he was about to give, was nevertheless unable to enjoy the immunity promised him. For he was in fact guilty of other crimes, as is stated in this chapter, though entirely innocent of every act of adultery with the noble women mentioned—whence our author says at the end of the preceding chapter, “he condemns her friends on a fabricated charge of adultery.” “That wretch, who had declared himself accomplice in their adulteries, did not enjoy the immunity promised.” MAUCROIX.

**Aperuit omne mysterium.** That is, if this is to cohere with what follows, he began to disclose it—by murmuring, for example, something which those standing nearer could hear, or even by crying out. Our countrymen commonly say word for word, *il découvrit tout le mystère*, “he disclosed the whole mystery”; therefore I wonder that Maucroix, in order not to translate the word *integram* simply, added from his own invention: *il découvrit tout ce mystère d’iniquité*, “he disclosed all this mystery of iniquity.”—*Aperuit*: read *aperit*. TOLLIUS.

**Sub extremo spiritu inquit omnibus qui videbant, innocentes occisas esse testatur.** I judge Lactantius wrote: “At the last hour, with restless breath, he testifies to all who saw that innocent women had been killed.” *Sub extrema*, namely, “at the final hour.” NIC. HEINSIUS.—It seems to me that *inquit* should be deleted. GRAEVIUS.—*Inquit.* These words are superfluous (*παρέλκει*), unless perhaps one should read *inquirentibus*, “to those inquiring.” Oxford edition of 1684, likewise Cambridge.—For *inquit* I read *inique*, “wickedly.” GALE.—“At his last breath, he says.” Perhaps it was written, “at his last departing breath.” Yet I would prefer: “at his last breath, while all groaned,” etc. [Col. 0807D] TOLLIUS.—I emended: “and at his last breath, restless (*inquies*) or agitated (*inquietus*), he testifies to all who saw that innocent women had been killed.” Ammianus certainly, book XXIX: “Procopius indeed, a restless man,” etc.; and Justin, XLIV.2: “A people swift in speed, with a restless spirit.”

## CHAPTER XLI

**Augusta vero.** Valeria, namely, Galerius’s widow. PAGIUS.—“The Empress Valeria.” MAUCROIX.

**Mittit ille legatos.** Diocletian, namely, to Maximinus; both translators supplied the latter.

**Eum.** Namely Maximinus, introduced for clarity in the English translation.

**Is quoque imperfecta legatione.** It should be read: *perfecta legatione*, “when the embassy had been completed.” NIC. HEINSIUS.—I corrected: “He likewise, to him, when the embassy had been completed,” etc., so that *illi*, through the lapse of time, became *im*, while preserving somehow the individual strokes of the letters.

## CHAPTER XLII

[Col. 0808A]

**Eodemque tempore.** Read: *Eodem quoque tempore*, “at the same time also.” TOLLIUS.—Columbus likewise suspects that this should be read.

**Senis Maximiani.** Namely, Herculius. PAGIUS.

**Senis.** And indeed, lest the following words perhaps deceive you, long since dead. The final words of chapter 30 attest this: “Thus that greatest emperor of the Roman name, Maximian Herculius … having his most arrogant throat crushed and broken, ended his detestable life by a base and ignominious death.”

**Et imagines cum quo pictus esset detrahebantur.** I emend: “And images were taken down from the place in which he had been depicted.” GALE.

**Et imagines.** Perhaps *illius*, “of him,” is missing, because of what follows. SPARKIUS, in the Oxford edition of 1684.

**Cum quo.** Read *ubicumque*, “wherever.” VOSSIUS.—The reverend man restores *ubicumque*, as do the Oxford and Cambridge editions, whether they understood Vossius or someone else.—The English translation supports this: “any where set up.” But Cuperus differs, and I prefer his view.

**Senes ambo.** Namely Herculius and Diocletian. PAGIUS.—Correct. Yet Herculius had already, as I just noted, been dead for a considerable time; Diocletian, however, was still alive and seeing. Of both, while alike living, our author above, chapter 12: “When that day had dawned, the two old men were holding the consulship, for the eighth and seventh time.” More briefly in chapter 20: “Maximianus [Galerianus], after expelling the two old men, accomplished what he wished,” etc.

**Cum videret vivus.** Diocletian, namely, named at the beginning of the preceding sentence, whose name the author of the English translation rightly repeats here: “Diocletian seeing this affront.”

**Quod nulli unquam Imperatorum acciderat.** For it had otherwise been customary for the images of condemned emperors to be cast down, smeared with mud, and thrown down the Gemonian stairs, as Casaubon proves from Plutarch. Oxford and Cambridge editions.

**Duplici aegritudine affectus.** Namely, of mind and body. [Col. 0808C] For his body undoubtedly suffered from some illness when such irreverent treatment began to be inflicted upon the images shared by Diocletian and Herculius. Compare the words of Cuspinians which Baluzius has produced.

**Jactabat se huc atque illuc.** In imitation of Peleus’s son mourning his friend, of whom Juvenal speaks. TOLLIUS.

**Viginti annorum felicissimus Imperator.** The passage must be understood cautiously and favorably, since either Diocletian’s prosperity had already entirely departed before the nineteenth year was complete, or at all events it departed shortly after the twentieth began. For it had departed not merely before Diocletian celebrated his vicennalia—which were celebrated on the first day of the twentieth year, or at the latest after two months of that year had very recently elapsed—but even before Diocletian had begun his journey from Nicomedia to Rome for their celebration. For our author says above in the clearest terms: “Therefore, after this crime had been perpetrated, Diocletian, since prosperity had now departed from him, immediately proceeded to Rome [Col. 0808D] to celebrate there the day of his vicennalia, which was to fall on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December.” Since that journey was very long, and prosperity had already departed from Diocletian when it was undertaken, Diocletian plainly ceased to be a most prosperous emperor while the nineteenth year of his reign was still running. How then was he “a most prosperous emperor for twenty years,” if one speaks strictly? For other difficulties, consult Cuperus.

**Ad humilem vitam dejectus adeo et proculcatus injuriis, atque in odium vitae dejectus.** Who could believe that in the same sentence so eloquent a writer used the same word *dejectus*, “cast down,” twice? Nic. Heinsius conjectured that in the former place it should be written *ad humilem vitam redactus*, “reduced to a humble life.” But since Latin ears can scarcely bear *in odium vitae dejici*, “to be cast down into hatred of life,” while *ad humilem vitam dejici*, “to be cast down to a humble life,” is said excellently, I judge that it should be written *in odium vitae deductus*, “led into hatred of life.” GRAEVIUS.

[Col. 0809A]

**Dejectus adeo.** Rather, by three words: *dejectus a Deo*, “cast down by God.” BOHERELLUS, likewise Gale; this had long been our own conjecture as well.

**In odium vitae dejectus.** I would prefer *adductus*, “brought.” For *dejectus* immediately precedes. TOLLIUS.

I correct: *deductus*, “led.” GALE.—I emend: *devectus*, “brought down.” BOHERELLUS.—I prefer this both because it differs less than the others from the received *dejectus*, and because, since the subject is a man who had once been emperor, there would thereby be an elegant, though tacit, contrast between Diocletian formerly advanced (*provectus*) to the imperial summit—for thus our author says in chapter 4, “as though Decius had been advanced to that imperial summit for this very purpose”—and the same Diocletian brought down (*devectus*) even to hatred of life.

**Fame atque angore confectus est.** “He perished through hunger and anguish.” Some report that he died of dropsy, others by poison; Suidas says by hanging. Whatever the case, it is certain that he died in A.D. 312, before the marriage of Licinius and Constantia. Here Baluzius rebukes Victor, who asserts that Diocletian swallowed poison after being invited to that celebration, because he feared a dishonorable death. Oxford and Cambridge editions; the latter adding: “See Valesius’s notes on Socrates’ *Ecclesiastical History*, book I, ch. 2.”

Until now it was believed that Diocletian’s death occurred in this year, A.D. 316; for so it is written by Zosimus, by the author of the Alexandrian Chronicle, and by Idacius in his fasti, who under this year’s consuls records that Diocletian died at Salonae on the third day before the Nones of December. But after Lactantius’s book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* was published, there can be no doubt that he died at the beginning of the year 313; for Lactantius, immediately after recounting his death, being about to speak of Maximinus’s destruction, says in chapter 43: “One enemy of God still remained, whose end and ruin I shall now append. Diocletian, therefore, died before Maximinus …”

Victor, however, in the *Epitome*, supports Lactantius as to the year of death, although he differs concerning the manner of death: “He lived,” he says, “sixty-eight years, of which he spent nearly nine in private life. He was consumed by a death which, as was sufficiently evident, was voluntary through fear. For, when summoned by Constantine and Licinius to the marriage festivities, he had excused himself on grounds of old age, as unable to attend; having received threatening replies accusing him of having favored Maxentius and of favoring Maximinus, and fearing an ignominious death, he is said to have taken poison.” That final detail is reported by Victor only as rumor and is very uncertain. But in other respects Lactantius and Victor agree not only that Diocletian and Maximian abdicated in A.D. 305, as I have shown in its place, but also that Diocletian was removed in A.D. 313, before Licinius’s marriage and Maximinus’s death. For from A.D. 305 to A.D. 313, counting each incomplete terminal year as a whole, there are nine years during which Diocletian led a private life. PAGIUS.

## CHAPTER XLIII

**Unus jam supererat de adversariis Dei.** Namely Maximinus, according to this English addition: “Namely Maximin.” “Maximinus Daza.” Oxford and Cambridge editions.—All are correct; although, surprisingly, in this entire chapter, where Maximinus is discussed expressly and at length, Maximinus’s name does not appear even once. But those whom our author calls “enemies of God,” Maucroix not badly interprets as “enemies of the Christians.” And further, when Baluzius drew up a catalogue of those same enemies of God, he did not anywhere include Constantius Chlorus among the others—an observation I make against the most distinguished bishop of Meaux.

**Exitum.** The Abo edition has *exitium*, “destruction,” for an uncertain reason or authority. Columbus says nothing of this emendation in his notes. It is certain that, wherever it comes from, it should not be despised; *exitium* also combines excellently with *ruina*, “ruin.” But why should the received reading not meanwhile be better retained, in view of the similar passage in chapter 1: “Those who had overthrown the holy temple fell by a greater ruin; those who had tortured the righteous poured out their guilty souls, deserving heavenly plagues and torments … It seemed proper to bear witness concerning this end, so that,” etc.

**Quia praelatus ei a Maximiano fuerat, etc.** Namely when Galerius Maximianus—who is beyond all doubt the Maximianus of this passage—had named Licinius emperor, passing over Maximinus. Hence our author at the beginning of chapter 32: “Therefore, when Licinius had been named emperor, Maximinus became angry and did not wish to be called Caesar or named in the third place”; and a little later: “he argues from priority in time that he ought to be preferred, since he had first assumed the purple.”

**A Maximiano.** “By Galerius.” MAUCROIX: “Although he had conceived jealousy against Licinius, whom Galerius had preferred to him.”

**Licet nuper cum eo amicitiam confirmasset.** Namely, the friendship of which our author speaks in chapter 36: “But peace and friendship are arranged upon definite conditions; on the strait itself a treaty is made and right hands are joined.”

**Et ipse Legatos, etc.** I do not understand what *et ipse*, “he too,” means here, since no mention has preceded of anyone who had first sent envoys to the city of Rome. I therefore emend: *eo ipse*, that is, “therefore he himself”; or *eo ipso*, that is, “for that very reason,” followed by “envoys,” and what comes next. Cicero similarly says in *On Ends*: *hoc ipso, quod adest*, “by this very thing which is present.”

**Ad urbem misit.** “He sent [them] to Rome.” English translation.—*Misit*: more correctly, *mittit*, “he sends.” TOLLIUS.

**Occulte.** Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, VIII.14: “making a secret compact of friendship with the ruler at Rome” (*πρὸς τὸν ἐπὶ Ῥώμης φιλίαν κρύβδην σπενδόμενος*). Cambridge edition.

**Scribit etiam familiariter.** That is, amicably; the sense is that Maximinus not only sought Maxentius’s friendship but employed most friendly language in seeking it. Maucroix: *avec beaucoup d’honnêteté*, “with much courtesy,” as though the Latin were *cum multo verborum honore*, or *verbis honorificentissimis*, “with most honorable words.” But *familiariter* is certainly, in a thousand similar places, a word of friendship, not of honorific address. Terence, for example, in the *Heautontimorumenos*, act I, scene 1:

> “Yet either your virtue, or the neighborhood—which I regard as akin to friendship—causes me to advise you boldly and familiarly.”

Cicero, *On Friendship*: “For nothing is more disgraceful than to wage war with one with whom you have lived on intimate terms.” Finally, Pliny in his letters: “I myself am witness that he loved me intimately.”

**Fit amicitia.** Namely, with very few people, as usual, initially aware and participating; thus, one might say, within private walls.

**Utriusque imagines simul locantur.** Namely, immediately after that friendship was established, as a public testimony to the matter and at the same time to Maxentius’s joy at it.

**Maxentius tanquam divinum auxilium libenter amplectitur.** What does he embrace? Maximinus’s alliance, as Maucroix supplied? “Maxentius regarded this alliance as aid sent from heaven.” But Maximinus’s alliance would then have been named in what precedes, so that it could be recalled from the common context. Yet there we see only Maxentius’s alliance mentioned. Or does he embrace Maximinus’s envoys? Or, with the English translation, Maximinus’s offered friendship? But our author had already finished speaking in the preceding words of Maximinus’s envoys and friendship, and had moved on to the images of Maximinus and Maxentius placed together: “The envoys are graciously received, friendship is established, and the images of both are placed together.”

Therefore, if we seek the true sense of this passage, Maxentius, in our author’s view, rather gladly embraced the images of Maximinus that had been sent him, as though they were divine aid, than any other thing: “Maxentius gladly embraces [them] as divine aid.” Especially since it was customary among the Romans, for example, to regard the image of Pessinus as divine aid; hence Herodian calls the statue *διοπετές*, “fallen from heaven.” Moreover, if what we have just set forth is true, the images of Maximinus sent to Maxentius were received unlike the image which Constantine had once sent to Galerius. For Galerius long deliberated whether to receive Constantine’s image, as we saw in chapter 25, and the matter almost came to the point that he would burn both it and the man who had brought it; in the end he received it with great reluctance. Maxentius, by contrast, embraced the Maximian images as divine aid.

**Jam enim bellum Constantino indixerat.** Namely in A.D. 311. For the war between Constantine and Maxentius began not in A.D. 312 but in the preceding year, since the anonymous author of the panegyric addressed to Constantine, ch. 21, testifies that that expedition lasted a year; and Eutropius, book X, says: “That war was set in motion in Constantine’s fifth year.” But Constantine’s fifth year ended on 24 July, A.D. 311; and therefore the war against Maxentius began in that year. Lactantius rightly says, “For he had already declared war on Constantine,” although Eutropius in the cited passage says: “In the fifth year of his reign Constantine initiated a civil war against Maxentius.” For that war had in fact been declared by Maxentius, as Zosimus, book II, also teaches us in these words: “Maxentius was seeking occasions for waging war against Constantine and, pretending to grieve over his father’s death, alleged that Constantine had furnished the cause of it …” Nazarius too, in his panegyric addressed to Constantine Augustus, chs. 9–12, imputes that war to Maxentius and praises Constantine’s prudence at length for avoiding it. From Pagius’s *Critica Baroniana*, under A.D. 312, no. 2.

**Senem illum.** That is, as Maucroix translates, “that old man Maximian,” who is certainly under discussion and who was otherwise Maxentius’s father.

Detestable (or destructive), etc. That is, detestable and hated. The Oxford edition of 1680, likewise the Cambridge edition, refers it to the discord just mentioned. — “That is, detestable and hateful.” Oxford edition, 1684; which, if it is not a typographical error, pertains to that old man. — *Intestabilem*: read *detestabilem*. VOSSIUS. [Col. 0811C] Likewise Gale says, “after the manner of ‘the detestable’ (*τοῦ detestabili*),” at the end of chapter 49. — Yet *intestabilis* is also found in Sallust in the sense of “detestable” and “accursed.” The passage is: “Unless, because in so great a disaster a shameful life with an unblemished reputation seemed preferable to him, he appears wicked and accursed.” — *Intestabilem*. Since the manuscript has *xtabilem*, I judge that one should read: “to have feigned an inexpiable discord.” GRAEVIUS.

“To have feigned discord with his son.” Arts of this kind had already been known from the time of Tarquinius Superbus; nor is what is read in Suetonius’s *Life of Augustus* dissimilar. TOLLIUS.

“But that is false.” “Nor is that false.” GALE. — Entirely contrary to what follows; I do not understand it. For why did Maximian Herculius wish genuinely to claim for himself and his son the empire of the whole world, if, according to what follows, his intention was to restore himself and Diocletian to the throne after both his son and the others had been destroyed? If only that most learned man had explained his thought!

## CHAPTER XLIV

[Col. 0811D] “Now set in motion,” etc. Namely, from the year 311, as was just noted at greater length.

“Between them.” It is said obscurely; the translators make it perfectly clear: “between Maxentius and Constantine.”

“He had recovered his father’s army from Severus.” See Constantine’s *Oration to the Assembly of the Saints*, chapter 25, and Valesius’s notes thereon, Cambridge edition.

“His father’s”: Maximian’s. MAUCROIX.

“His own proper [army].” A usage not to be passed over by lovers of better Latinity; for I have seen some of them doubt even about the inscription on the coin minted three years ago here at Utrecht in the name of the so-called refugees: *OMNES UT PROPRIA VISCERA EXCEPTI*—“all received as their own entrails”—as though some faulty Gallicism lay within it. Yet, as is clear, the manner of speaking *suus proprius*, “one’s own proper,” was not faulty even among the Latins. The following examples confirm it. Julius Capitolinus, in *Antoninus Pius*: “He lived on his own proper estates, variously and according to circumstances.” Lactantius, *Institutions*, book V, chapter 11: “Others, through their own proper hatred against the just.” Vopiscus, in *Firmus*: “Marius Maximus … included Avidius … not in his own proper books, but in those of others.” Indeed Cicero himself, *On the Orator*: “Crassus by a certain ability peculiar to himself, not common to orators”; and in his letter to Terentia, with a first-person possessive pronoun: “The calamity is shared by both of us; but the fault is my own proper fault.” Elsewhere, however—which must not be denied—he inserted a conjunction. Thus in the *Tusculan Disputations*: “Each matter must be treated by its own proper and its own arguments.”

“He had recently drawn [them] out from Moors and Italians.” Read *exstruxerat*, “had drawn them up.” Thus above, chapter 12: “the battle-line having been formed.” TOLLIUS. — I emend: *contraxerat*, “had assembled.” GALE.

“The soldiers of Maxentius prevailed.” For some time, from the passage of Justin below [Note: [Col. 0812D]

Book XIII, chapter 3: “When the cavalry had done the same, the infantry, indignant that no share in deliberations had been left to them, proclaim Aridaeus, Alexander’s brother, king. When this was reported to the cavalry, they send two of the leading men, Attalus and Meleager, as envoys to calm their feelings; these men, seeking power through the flattery of the mob, abandon their embassy and side with the soldiers. Then all, armed, rush into the palace to destroy the cavalry; upon learning this, the cavalry, in alarm, withdraw from the city and, having pitched camp, begin in turn to terrify the infantry.”

], where a continual contrast is observable between Alexander’s surviving infantry and cavalry, I had inferred that Justin’s phrase *militibus consentiunt*, “they side with the soldiers,” could mean nothing other than “they side with the infantry”; and consequently that Latin writers sometimes used the term *milites*, “soldiers,” to signify infantry as distinguished from cavalry. Learned men before us observed that many passages in Livy establish the same point. But undoubtedly there is nothing here to confine the designation “Maxentius’s soldiers” in that way. Let us therefore understand rather Maxentius’s infantry and cavalry together, in accordance with the best-known and most common usage of the word. For example, Justin, book XII, chapter 5, says: “Alexander exhorts the soldiers to write to their own [people],” when Alexander wished to ascertain the views not only of the infantry, who held a rather harsh opinion of him, but also of the cavalry. The same historian elsewhere says: “Then, advancing against the enemy, Alexander forbade the soldiers from plundering”; and this unquestionably includes not merely the thirty-two thousand infantry in Alexander’s army but also his four thousand cavalry, as what follows shows. Add the passage of our author, read near the beginning of chapter 45, together with Cuper.

“Prepared for either outcome.” Understand: a decisive outcome—swift death or joyful victory—according to Horace:

[Col. 0812C]

> They clash in battle: in a moment of an hour  
> swift death comes, or joyful victory.

A passage of Justin, book VI, chapter 7, confirms this: “For when they saw among what circumstances and for what causes they were taking their stand, they resolved that they must either conquer or die.” Indeed, Cicero’s letter to Toranius is an eloquent commentary on this passage: “Although, when I was writing to you, either the end of this most disastrous war seemed to be approaching or something already seemed to have been done and brought to completion, nevertheless I recalled daily that, in so great an army, you alone had agreed with me and I with you, and that we alone had seen how much evil there was in that war, in which, with all hope of peace excluded, victory itself would be most bitter: if defeated, it would bring destruction; if victorious, slavery. And so I—whom those brave and wise men, Domitius and Lentulus, then called timid (and I was indeed so; for I feared that those things would occur which did occur)—now fear nothing and am prepared for every [Col. 0812D] outcome. When it seemed that something could be guarded against, I grieved that this was neglected; but now, with all things overturned and no progress possible by counsel, one course alone seems available: whatever happens, to bear it calmly, especially since death is the end of all things.”

“Constantine, resolved upon whatever might happen.” MAUCROIX. — “Having resolved to put all to hazard,” English translation.

[Col. 0813A] “The Mulvian Bridge.” Today, Ponte Mole. MAUCROIX. — *Mulvii*: *Milvii*. PAGIUS. — Read *Milvii*. Cambridge edition. — Read *Mylvii*. ALLIX.

“On the sixth day before the Kalends of November.” Write *a. d. sextum*, etc. TOLLIUS. — As is clear from Lactantius, Maxentius was proclaimed emperor at Rome on the sixth day before the Kalends of November—that is, 27 October … I had previously suspected that the passage was corrupt and that one should read “on the fifth day before the Kalends of November.” But the entry in the *Book of the Prefects of the City*—“on the sixth day before the Kalends of November, Annius Anulinus, day 34, P. V.”—removes this suspicion. PAGIUS.

Constantine defeated Maxentius on the sixth day before the Kalends of November, according to Lactantius. Nor does the calendar of Constantius published by Bucherius differ greatly. In it we have, for the fifth day before the Kalends of November: “Defeat of the tyrant”; for the fourth: “Arrival of the deified one”—provided, however, that by “the tyrant” Maxentius rather than Licinius is meant, as is certainly most likely. DODWELL.

In the ancient calendar written under Constantius, indeed, under the fifth day before the Kalends of November occurs “Defeat of the tyrant,” [Col. 0813B] and under the fourth day of the same month “Arrival of the deified one”; but these words must be understood not of Maxentius and Constantine, but of Licinius and Constantine, as is clear from the *Book of the Prefects of the City*. For under the year of Christ 312 it says that Aradius Rufinus was created prefect of the City on the fifth day before the Ides of February, and Annius Anulinus on the sixth day before the Kalends of November. Therefore Maxentius was defeated on the sixth day before the Kalends of November, and another prefect of the City was appointed by Constantine. Nor should that passage be explained otherwise. Those, therefore, who wish the quoted words of the Constantian calendar to be interpreted of Maxentius are mistaken. PAGIUS.

“The quinquennial celebrations were coming to an end.” That is, as Maucroix notes, the fifth year of Maxentius’s reign: “The fifth year of Maxentius’s reign.” The English translation agrees: “The 27 of October was now near, which was the Anniversary of Maxentius’s coming to the empire: and now his fifth year was almost out.” — “The quinquennial celebrations were coming to an end”: festivities customarily celebrated on the anniversary of accession. PAGIUS. [Col. 0813C] — Lactantius teaches us that the sixth day before the Kalends of November, or 27 October, was the anniversary of Maxentius’s accession, since emperors celebrated their quinquennial observances and such festivals on the day on which they had assumed power. The same writer elsewhere.

“He was warned in a dream.” This is a special word. For those to whom God commands something in a dream are said to be *moneri*, “warned.” See ancient inscriptions. TOLLIUS.

“The heavenly sign of God.” A remarkable circumlocution for the cross—unless one prefers to explain it as a sign seen by Constantine in the sky, namely an image of the cross, as some have related [Note: [Col. 0814D]

The following comparison is impious—impious in expression.

]. This stratagem of Constantine was no less ingenious than that of Philip of Macedon, by which he crushed the sacrilegious Phocians. TOLLIUS. — “The heavenly sign of God”: “the adorable sign of the cross.” That is, “the sign of the cross to be adored.” MAUCROIX. A rather freer paraphrase, surely, and one that betrays an interpreter excessively devoted to a partisan interest. — “The Divine Mark, the Sign of the Cross,” English translation; as though one said, “the divine emblem, the sign of the cross.”

[Col. 0813D] “And thus he joined battle,” etc. That is, “and then” or “thereafter.” For Christ did not intend Constantine to join battle at the very time he was marking God’s heavenly sign on the shields, and therefore—if one must speak more plainly—not during the marking; rather, he was to mark them first, and then, once the shields had been marked with the said letter, fight. Compare what we observed above, and also that passage of Spartianus in his *Severus*: “He accused Cincius Severus of having attempted to poison him, and thus put him to death”—that is, “then put him to death,” as the circumstances demand and Erasmus long ago noted. See again what we shall say on the words in chapter 49, “And thus he drank the poison.”

“And, with the upper stroke bent around, he marks Christ on the shields by means of the transverse letter X.” Baluzius says that this should be understood to mean that Christ’s monogram was curved [Col. 0814A] at the head of the labarum, as we see on ancient coins. Oxford and Cambridge editions. — “And the transverse letter X”: I would prefer “and the transverse letter X,” accusative. BOHERELLUS. — I punctuate: “And, with the transverse letter X, its upper stroke bent around, he marks Christ on the shields.” GALE. — That most distinguished man has corrected it excellently: “By curving round the upper head of the transverse letter X, he marks Christ on the shields.” TOLLIUS.

“Christ”: read “Christ [accusative].” Abo edition; and I too had conjectured that this should be read. — “And he has an X painted on his shields with a circumflex accent, which signifies Jesus Christ.” MAUCROIX. Carelessly stated. For, strictly speaking, the curved X does not abbreviate “Jesus Christ,” *Ἰησοῦς Χριστός*, but *Χριστός* alone—Latin *Christus*. — “And ordered the letter X with the letters of the name of Christ mixed in a monogramme, to be drawn on all their shields,” English translation.

“Without the emperor”: without Maxentius. English translation.

“He advances with an equal front.” In a thousand passages *concurrere* means to fight or engage in battle. For example, Horace in the verses quoted above:

> Service in war is better. What then? They clash in battle: in a moment of an hour swift death comes, or joyful victory.

And Justin, book III, chapter 5: “Accordingly they engaged with such courage that rarely, if ever, was there a bloodier battle.” But elsewhere the same word often means to run somewhere together or to make one’s journey at a rapid pace. Thus Justin, in the same book and chapter: “The Lacedaemonians too rush all the more unitedly to arms.” And our author, chapter 45: “Maximinus moved his army from Syria in the most severe winter, and, doubling the stages, hastened into Bithynia with his column exhausted.” Here I understand “to advance with an equal front” as meaning: to go to meet them with the same confidence and eagerness with which the enemies come against you; so that there is not yet any discussion of the battle of the two armies, which only shortly afterward begins in these words, “They fight with utmost force on either side.” Rather, it properly concerns the movement of Constantine’s soldiers, who themselves too confidently [Col. 0814C] and swiftly ran forth against the Maxentians advancing from the opposite side. Finally, the distinction here between *concurrere*, “to rush together,” and *pugnare*, “to fight,” is no smaller than, in Justin, book IX, chapter 8, that between “to run against the enemy” and “to join battle,” in this passage: “It was his father’s custom even to run from the banquet against the enemy, to join battle,” etc.; and these two things certainly differ greatly.

“And the commander is reproached”: Maxentius is reproached. The translators.

“As though he were a deserter of the public safety.” That is, as each person customarily calls the welfare of the party he follows “the public safety.” And later, by the most just judgment of God, that commander and persecutor was such a deserter: when he saw that the affair in the battle in which he was present was proceeding otherwise than he expected, he threw down the purple, put on a slave’s garment, fled, and crossed the strait. Thus one half of the army was cut down, while the other either surrendered or took flight, because the deserting emperor had deprived them of shame at desertion. What follows in chapter 47 will name him [Col. 0814D] Maximinus.

“And when suddenly the people—for at his birthday [the] Circensian games … and with the prescribed voice cry out.” Some words are missing. PAGIUS. — The passage is mutilated. ALLIX. — These words must be supplied and punctuated thus: “And when suddenly the people (for they had celebrated Circensian games on his birthday),” etc. Oxford and Cambridge editions.

“And when suddenly.” Read: “When suddenly.” BOHERELLUS. — Nicolaus Heinsius thought that health could be restored to the miserably corrupted passage if it were read: “And suddenly the whole people—for he was exhibiting Circensian games on his birthday—cry out with one voice.” GRAEVIUS. — Read: “And when suddenly the people (for he was exhibiting Circensian games on his birthday) cry out with one voice.” Here “birthday” is the day on which he assumed imperial power, which our author just before said was imminent; where *imminere*, “to be imminent,” must be understood of the immediately following day. Thus above, chapter 35, he said “with the Kalends of March impending,” that is, immediately following. On that birthday our author says that the quinquennial period had ended, that is, the first five-year period of the reign was complete; when that had elapsed, games were at last held on the birthday itself, the first day of the subsequent second five-year period. Those who explain *quinquennalia* otherwise and take it to mean the solemn festival itself are mistaken. TOLLIUS. — I proposed: “Then—or, suddenly—the people, for he was giving Circensian games on his birthday, cry out in a loud voice that Constantine cannot be defeated”; so that from the two words *dabat*, “was giving,” and *edita*, “uttered,” the meaningless *debita* was produced by an unskilled and hasty copyist. “To give Circensian games,” like Cicero’s “to give birthday festivities,” and Pliny’s “to give a most magnificent show.” But *edita voce*, “with a voice uttered,” is like Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, book II: “What cries does Sophocles utter here in the *Trachiniae*?” The native force of the word *subclamare*, or, as others write, *succlamare*, supports this, for it properly means “to shout in response.” Livy, book VI from the founding of the City: “I beseech you … think of me as one citizen shouting in response from the middle of the assembly.” The same author, book III: “While Verginius cried these things, the crowd shouted in response that they would not fail either his grief or their own liberty.” Moreover, the *Circenses*—supply *ludi*, “games”—are, according to the English translation, spectacles of the hippodrome: “the spectacles of the Hippodrome.”

[Col. 0815B] “By which cry.” Read “By this” or “By that.” Oxford and Cambridge editions. — Retain “by which.” BOHERELLUS.

“To inspect the Sibylline books.” “The Book of the Sibyls.” MAUCROIX; that is, “the book of the Sibyls,” in the singular number, contrary to what was altogether required. See, for example, Lactantius, *On False Religion*, chapter 6. The English translation is therefore more correct: “The Sibylline books.”

“The enemy of the Romans.” A perplexing expression, whose mystery Cuper explains.

“The bridge behind him is cut.” And at his own command, if Maucroix is to be believed, so that the necessity of conquering might add courage to his army: “He has the bridge broken behind him, so that the necessity of conquering might give more courage to his army.” Yet what follows seems strongly to oppose this: “He himself, turned to flight, hastens to the bridge, which had been broken,” since it is in no way likely that Maxentius hastened to that bridge to escape for any reason other than because he believed it unbroken. If this is indeed probable, therefore, he had not ordered it to be broken.

“And the hand of God was over the battle-line.” The passage is ill preserved, as even the freer translations of the interpreters not slightly indicate. “But God favoured Constantine.” Maucroix. That is, “but God favoured Constantine.” — “And the hand of God appeared over the armies,” English translation. Literally, “and the hand of God appeared over the armies.” — Perhaps one should read: “And the hand of God moved stealthily through the battle-line.” That is, it extended itself here and there through the ranks of those fighting, secretly exerting its force against Maxentius’s soldiers. For *acies* often means a fight or battle. Cicero, to Torquatus: “For although no one can foretell what outcome the battle-line will have, nevertheless I see also the outcome of the war.” And, *Tusculan Disputations*, book II: “Brave men do not feel wounds in battle.” Moreover, “to move stealthily through the battle-line” is like Claudian’s “to move stealthily beneath the mountains” in these verses:

[Col. 0815D]

> All native rivers whatsoever steal beneath  
> Italian mountains and drink deadly Alpine frosts.

“The Maxentian is overthrown.” Namely, the soldier. Yet I would prefer the plural: “The Maxentians are overthrown.” TOLLIUS.

“The Maxentian”: rather, “the Maxentian battle-line.” BOHERELLUS.

“Is overthrown”: “is trampled down.” GALE. — “Maxentius was beaten,” Burnet’s translation; so that he seems plainly to have emended both manuscript readings in this manner: “Maxentius is trampled down.”

“He discovered letters.” Namely, among Maxentius’s papers: “Among Maxentius’s papers he found Maximinus’s letters.” English translation.

“He found statues and images.” Namely, imperial ones, which Maximinus had sent to Maxentius. The same translation. — Add [Col. 0816A] what we have above partly said and partly indicated concerning the distinction between statues and images.

“The Senate decreed to Constantine, for his courage, the title of the first name, which Maximinus claimed for himself.” Because he had been made Caesar before Constantine. PAGIUS. — “The Senate did Constantine the honour to order his name to be put first in order, before the other Emperours.” English translation, in this sense: the Senate decreed in Constantine’s honour that his name should be placed before the names of the other emperors—say, in the preambles of edicts. — To speak frankly, I do not see how the Latin words can bear that sense. I would therefore willingly correct them as follows: “The Senate decreed to Constantine, for his courage, the title of the first divinity, which Maximinus claimed for himself”—that is, a title or epithet of Maximinus, used by Maximinus and always one of Jupiter’s principal appellations; so that thereafter Constantine might be called not simply Emperor, but “Greatest Emperor” and “Constantine the Great.” The end of the chapter confirms this, where you will find not “Then, upon learning of the Senate’s decree, Maximinus was so inflamed with grief that he openly professed hostilities and uttered insults, mingled with jokes, against the emperor first, or of the first name,” but “against the greatest emperor.” Secondly, not a few inscriptions in Gruter’s collection confirm it, inscriptions which the Romans publicly displayed in Constantine’s honour after Maxentius’s defeat. For example, that of Constantine’s arch, still to be seen at Rome:

> TO THE EMPEROR CAESAR FLAVIUS CONSTANTINE THE GREAT,  
> PIOUS, FORTUNATE AUGUSTUS,  
> THE SENATE AND PEOPLE OF ROME.

It confirms it again that in those times not only was the aforesaid appellation *Maximus*, “Greatest,” one of Jupiter’s titles—as Maximinus’s rescript to civic decrees against Christians and countless other inscriptions attest—but Jupiter was also at that time the first divinity of the Romans, as inscriptions in a thousand places show. Finally, it confirms it that, since we have seen Galerius Maximian nine times arrogate to himself titles of *Maximus*—“Greatest Germanic conqueror,” “Greatest Egyptian conqueror,” “Greatest Thebaid conqueror,” and so forth—nothing is more credible than that Maximinus, following Galerius’s example, claimed the same epithet for himself on some such ground, or even simply sought the title *Maximus*. Those able may consult the coins on the matter.

“The Senate decreed to Constantine, for his courage, the title of the first name.” Hence Constantine dealt authoritatively with Maximinus. DODWELL. — After Constantine received by decree of the Senate the title of the first name, which Maximinus arrogated to himself because he had been made Caesar before Constantine, he dealt authoritatively with Maximinus. Maximinus was therefore compelled in this year, 312, to write that letter to Sabinus which Baronius wrongly assigns to the following year. PAGIUS.

“When the news of the victory of the liberated city had been brought to him,” etc. That is, unless I am mistaken: when news had been brought to him of the victory of the city of Rome now liberated and hitherto victorious—because the Roman people regarded as its own the victory Constantine had won over Maxentius—Maximinus received it no otherwise than if he himself had been defeated. Indeed, at last the Romans rejoiced deeply in that victory as though they themselves had conquered. Hence earlier: “When the most bitter war had at last been concluded, Emperor Constantine was received with great joy by the Senate and people of Rome.” Surely “a victory having been brought” elegantly means “news having been brought of a victory won”; and the interpreters sufficiently recognized this, although they did not explain how the victory of a liberated city could properly be said to have been brought, when it was not truly the city but, on the contrary, Constantine fighting against it and Maxentius who had won.

“The news of that great event having been brought to Maximinus.” MAUCROIX. That is, when news of that great event had been brought to Maximinus. — “Who was as much struck with the news that was brought to him [Col. 0817A] of Rome’s being thus freed from tyranny, as if it had been a defeat given himself,” English translation. That is, Maximinus, when news had been brought to him that Rome had been freed from the rule of a tyrant, received it no otherwise, etc.

“He received it no otherwise than if he himself had been defeated.” After Maximinus received news that Maxentius had been defeated, he grieved exceedingly. “But he,” Eusebius says, book IX, chapter 9, “when he learned these things, first indeed, being a tyrant, groaned deeply. Afterwards, however, etc.” PAGIUS.

“He uttered [insults] against the greatest emperor.” Note well. For, as we have gathered above, it was truly and newly decreed by the Senate in Constantine’s favour that henceforth he should be surnamed “Greatest Emperor.” I think *Maximus* should therefore be written with an initial capital, rather than, as commonly, with a lower-case letter. The remaining points relevant here have been stated quite recently.

## CHAPTER XLV

[Col. 0817B]

“Constantine, having settled affairs in the city, set out for Milan in the following winter.” Constantine defeated Maxentius on the sixth day before the Kalends of November, according to Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 44. That day is commonly called 27 October. Thus Constantine entered Rome on 29 October. He did not complete two months in Rome. For Nazarius says of Maxentius and Constantine: “Whatever evil that deadly domination had inflicted during the whole six-year period, care lasting scarcely two months healed.” A law of Constantine in the Theodosian Code likewise agrees: he issued it at Rome at the beginning of December, though he was about to leave Rome immediately. DODWELL.

Since Nazarius writes in the panegyric he delivered to Constantine, chapter 23, that he healed by care lasting scarcely two months whatever evil had been done, it is clear that, after the affairs of the city had been settled, Constantine went from Rome to Milan at the beginning of the following year, in order to give his sister Constantia in marriage to Licinius. I say “at the beginning of the following year,” [Col. 0817C] because in book I of the Theodosian Code, *On the Census*, it is stated: “Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February at Rome, in the fourth consulship of Constantine Augustus and the third of Licinius,” namely in the year 313. Constantine was therefore still in Rome in January, unless *dat.* (“given”) should be read *PP.* (“posted”), with some editions. PAGIUS.

“Constantine, having settled affairs in the city, set out for Milan in the following winter,” namely the winter of 313. Pagius puts the same thing elsewhere, apparently adhering to the same hypotheses. Yet it must first be noted that this eminent man was not consistently in agreement with himself, as his words under the said year, no. 2, testify: “Constantine came to Milan at the end of the preceding year, 312, or the beginning of the current one, 313, and bestowed his sister Constantia in marriage upon Licinius.” Moreover, Pagius did not merely doubt at what exact time Constantine left for Milan after winning victory over Maxentius; rather, the victory gained on the sixth day before the Kalends of November, Nazarius’s statement that “whatever evil that deadly domination had inflicted during the whole six-year period, care lasting scarcely two months healed,” and finally our author’s phrase “in the following winter,” whose easy sense may be “when winter was immediately at hand,” seem altogether to require us to conclude that Constantine set out from Rome for Milan about the middle of December. Especially since, for instance, the Paris edition of the Theodosian Code published by Nivellius in 1586 in no way represents the first law *On the Census* as having been issued at Rome; rather, it simply gives it as posted, as follows:

> Emperor Constantine Augustus to the people. Since the record-keepers of cities, through the influence of the powerful, transfer the burden to the lower classes, we command that whoever proves himself burdened shall acknowledge only his former declared assessment, etc. Posted on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February at Rome, in the third consulship of Constantine Augustus and the third of Licinius.

This could certainly have occurred while Constantine was absent from Rome and residing at Milan, just as much as if he had actually been present at Rome.

[Col. 0818A] “He set out for Milan.” Under the consuls of this year, Constantine, emperor for the ninth time, and Licinius, emperor for the seventh. It is certain from a law, the first *On Summoning to Possession*, issued there on the sixth day before the Ides of March and reported in the Theodosian Code, that Constantine was still at Milan in March 313. PAGIUS.

“Licinius arrived at the same place in order to take a wife.” Namely Constantia, whom Constantius Chlorus, Constantine’s father, had begotten by Theodora, the stepdaughter of Herculius; she was thus Constantine’s sister by the same father. Licinius had already been betrothed to her, as was mentioned above in chapter 43: “Yet when Maximinus heard that Constantine’s sister had been betrothed to Licinius, etc.” — Licinius came to Milan, I think, early in December for the marriage. DODWELL. — I would judge that it happened rather at the beginning of the following year. Yet, whenever it occurred, once Constantine and Licinius had successfully met near Milan for the wedding—as we learn from this chapter and chapter 48—they also discussed there, incidentally, all matters pertaining to public advantage and security. Among other things which they saw would benefit many people, they believed that the foremost measure to be arranged was to grant both Christians and all others free power to follow whatever religion each wished.

Constantine afterwards left Milan, while the year 313 was still declining, and returned to Gaul and the lower German frontier, where he was at Trier. There he prevented and checked the crossing of Franks and barbarians over the Rhine, as the anonymous author of the panegyric addressed to Constantine, chapter 21, testifies … Hence, as Gothofredus observes in his *Chronology of the Theodosian Code*, several constitutions were subsequently issued by him at Trier in November and December of this year. Licinius, however, returned from Milan to Illyricum, as the Anonymous Valesianus relates. PAGIUS.

“In winter raging as severely as possible.” Am I mistaken, or is this reading corrupt? Should one read instead either simply “although winter was raging as severely as possible,” or, with one additional word supplied by the manuscript, “in winter, although it was raging as severely as possible”? Let learned men consider. Cuper and Columbus explain it as sound.

“He hastened into Bithynia.” I think: “he ran into Bithynia.” GRAEVIUS. — Read: “he advanced rapidly into Bithynia.” TOLLIUS. — But we have, I think, already established above that our author uses *concurrere* to mean “to proceed in the company of one or more persons” and “to advance at a more or less hurried pace or on a hurried journey.” This passage in chapter 25 may confirm it: “warning him of the danger which all the soldiers, against whose wishes unknown Caesars had been made, would have incurred for Constantine and would have rushed to him with the greatest eagerness, if he had come armed.”

“Having immediately crossed the strait.” Namely, the Thracian strait, as the English translation correctly supplies: “having crossed the straits of Thrace.” It is commonly called the Thracian Bosporus.

“Yet neither force nor promises availed anything.” The passage was perhaps not wrongly considered mutilated by Columbus.

“Through whom there was opportunity to send messengers and letters [Col. 0818D] to the emperor.” The interpreters understood it in different ways. The French translation takes it as though our Caecilius had written: “through which there was sufficient time to send messengers and letters to Licinius”—“The city had already been besieged for eleven days, a sufficient period for informing Licinius of the events taking place.” The English translation, however, treats the author’s words as though they were: “which days Maximinus had assigned to the besieged so that during them they might inform the emperor of his condition and that of Byzantium”—“they had eleven days assigned them, for advertising the emperour.” Let learned persons choose whichever of these senses they prefer. Yet the truer view, I think, is that, since our author contains not the slightest mention of any such time granted by Maximinus to the Byzantines, the meaning is not simply that during the eleven days of siege, while they were hard pressed on every side by Maximinus’s encircling army, the Byzantines had an opportunity to send messengers and letters to Licinius; rather, they actually found a way to do so, even against Maximinus’s will. Thus, after that period, they did not surrender to Maximinus without Licinius’s awareness or expectation.

“When the soldiers distrusted not the loyalty, but the small number.” Whose loyalty or small number? The word “garrison” seems to be missing, or at least some similar genitive: “When the soldiers distrusted not the loyalty, but the small number, of the garrison.” — For “having despaired,” I read “having defected.” GALE.

“From there he advanced to Heraclea.” Namely Maximinus, although that name must be supplied from nearly the beginning of the chapter. By Heraclea understand Heraclea of Thrace, which will shortly be called by its other name, Perinthus. Ptolemy: *Πέρινθος, ἤτοι Ἡράκλεια*, “Perinthus, or Heraclea.” An anonymous poet:

> Great Perinthus,  
> which it once was, changed its ancient name to Heraclea.

Compare what is to be said below.

“On a hurried march.” Pliny has a not dissimilar expression in his *Panegyric*: “He increases and augments by honours hastily conferred.” But a very similar phrase occurs in the eminent Johannes Fredericus Gronovius: “He says that he used a voyage undertaken in haste, from necessity rather than judgment,” when, that is, he had emended a passage in Dictys Cretensis from his own ingenuity and a manuscript codex alike: “The envoys arrive at Troy in a few days; nor do they then find Alexander in the place. For he, having imprudently used a voyage undertaken in haste, etc.” Indeed, Justin may not unreasonably seem to have used *festinato*, “in haste,” elliptically from the full phrase *festinato itinere*, “on a hurried march,” in these words: “Phraates then began to regret having dismissed Demetrius; when he had sent squadrons of cavalry in haste to bring him back, Demetrius, etc.” Elsewhere, in the same sense, he wrote “they sent [them] on a hurried journey.”

“Having received Perinthus in surrender.” That is, Heraclea; for Heraclea of Thrace was so called to distinguish it from other cities of the same name, as Valesius notes on Ammianus, book XXII. PAGIUS.

“Having received [it] in surrender.” Correct, as several times above, to “into surrender.” TOLLIUS; likewise Boherellus. — Countless examples certainly support this. For instance, Justin, book XII, chapter 6: “Dabas received [them] into surrender”; likewise chapter 7: “He receives all the peoples of that region into surrender”; and chapter 9: “He received the Hyrcanians and Sileans … into surrender.”

“He advanced eighteen miles to a stopping-place.” That is, arranging the words as Maucroix does: “He advanced eighteen miles to a stopping-place”—“he advances six leagues to meet the enemy”—and I had also judged that it should be construed in this way. Yet I further wondered whether perhaps, after or before *mansionem*, “stopping-place,” one ought to supply an ordinal numeral in this or a similar manner: “he advanced eighteen miles to the first stopping-place.” For it is immediately followed by a second ordinal: “nor could he proceed further, Licinius already occupying the second stopping-place.” Let learned men judge; I affirm nothing.

“Eighteen miles.” “Six leagues,” Maucroix; literally, six *leucae*, each of which consequently comprises three ancient Roman miles.

“Miles.” The old manuscript everywhere, insofar at least as can be gathered from Baluzius’s edition, has *mile*, not *millia*; this supports those who, with Varro, Eutropius, and others, derive the word *miles*, “soldier,” from *mile*, “a thousand,” in this way: “He selected a thousand warriors, who were called *milites* from their number.” Eutropius, book I, on Romulus; and Isidore, book IX, chapter 3, more clearly: “A soldier is called *miles* because there were formerly a thousand in one number, or because one is selected from a thousand.”

Licinius, now holding the second posting-station, at the same distance in miles, who, having collected, etc. Thus today, after Vossius, Baluzius reads; whereas earlier, with the manuscript codex, he had in the author’s words: “Licimo [Licinius], now holding the second posting-station, being distant by as many soldiers and having collected them”; except that shortly afterwards, by conjecture, he had noted in the list of errata that it should be read: “Licinius, now holding the second posting-station, distant by as many miles, and having collected them”; whence presently Spark, in the first Oxford edition: “The most reverend gentleman (Vossius) reads: ‘Licinius, now holding the second posting-station, distant [Col. 0820A] by as many miles, who, etc.’ This Baluzian emendation seems clearer.” Moreover Columbus too followed the Vossian reading in the Åbo edition; and, as regards the old wording, here is in addition what learned men have printed in its place or noted upon it.

**Licinius now holding the second posting-station.** “Licinius, now holding the second posting-station.” PAGIUS.

**Licinius now holding the second posting-station.** Read: “Licinius, now making for the second posting-station”; that is, pitching camp. Suetonius, *Galba* 12: “more favourably disposed toward Cn. Dolabella, beside whose gardens he was encamped.” Virgil:

> Here the band of Dolopians, here fierce Achilles was encamped.

This sense of the word is extremely familiar, and especially proper, among writers of every kind. GRAEVIUS.

**Holding, being distant.** The passage is mutilated. ALLIX.—“Being distant by as many soldiers and having collected them,” etc. The passage is corrupt. PAGIUS.

**By as many soldiers, and having collected them . . .** I read: “by so many miles, and having collected them,” etc. GALE.

[Col. 0820B] **Having collected from the neighbourhood as many soldiers as he could.** *As many as he could*, in the Greek manner, for *as many as he was able*—namely, to collect. TOLLIUS.

**He.** Maximinus. English translation.

**He himself.** Licinius. MAUCROIX.

**For the soldiers were scattered.** Licinius’s soldiers, of course, as both translators supply.

**All were assembled.** As above: “in the cities the urban and rural populace were assembled”; a phrase which we illustrated from Pliny and Justin. We now add the following examples from Justin. Book II, ch. 12: “The entire allied fleet having been assembled.” Book VII, ch. 1: “The nations of diverse peoples having been assembled.” Book XI, ch. 5: “Then, having assembled the army, he loads the ships.”

## CHAPTER XLVI

**As the armies were approaching.** So at the beginning of ch. 24: “The judgment of God has now drawn near to him”; see the notes on that passage.

**That, if he obtained victory.** That is, in Maucroix’s rendering, *won* it: *S'il remportait la victoire* [“If he won the victory”].—Very well. For what else can *to obtain victory* mean but, as Latin speakers commonly said, to win, attain, or achieve it? But who besides our author has used the expression *capere victoriam*? For I have observed no example of it anywhere.

**While resting.** *En songe* [“in a dream”]. MAUCROIX. That is, in dreams. Justin’s passage is pertinent here: “After this, Cambyses saw in sleep that his brother Smerdis would reign. Terrified by this dream,” etc.—“In his sleep.” English translation. That is, while asleep. I prefer this. Not merely because shortly afterwards follows, “when sleep had then been dispelled,” but especially because, although people commonly see many things in their rest by dreaming, strictly speaking, resting is not dreaming, but sleeping. Cicero, for example, *Against Verres* 6: “When I came there, the praetor was asleep.” Compare Lactantius’s most elegant passage:

> For the body, while the faculty of sensation is awake, though it lies motionless, is nevertheless not at rest, because sensation burns within it and quivers like a flame, holding all the limbs tightly drawn to itself. But after the mind has been diverted from attention to the contemplation of images, then at last the whole body is relaxed into rest. The mind is diverted by blind thought when, compelled by darkness, it has begun to be alone with itself; while it is intent upon the matters of which it thinks, suddenly sleep steals upon it, and thought itself gradually declines into neighbouring images. Thus it begins also to see the things it had set before its eyes. Then it proceeds further and finds diversions for itself, lest it interrupt the body’s most healthful rest.

**The supreme God.** When the true God is meant, scarcely any epithet occurs more frequently in Lactantius’s unquestioned writings. Hence, in their respective places: “the might and power of the supreme God”; “that man was created by the supreme God in a certain illustrious condition”; “yet that the worship due to him was not rendered to him as supreme Father”; “that there is a Son of the supreme God, endowed with the highest power”; “that the Erythraean Sibyl began her poem from the supreme God”; “that the ordering of the supreme God proceeded from the beginning in such a way that it was necessary,” etc.; “that the supreme God had raised up Constantine to restore the dwelling-place of justice and to protect humankind”; “that the providence of supreme divinity had advanced him to the imperial summit”; finally, lest excessive abundance of examples weary you: “that man, unless he has known the supreme God through him who was sent, will suffer punishment.” Yet, a point worthy of some notice, the same epithet occurs no less often in this little work, proportionately to its size. For in chapter 1: “That they might know to what extent God supreme displayed his power and majesty in . . . destroying . . . the enemies of his name”; in our passage, “that he might pray to God supreme”; and in chapter 47, “God supreme delivered them up to enemies to be slaughtered.” That these considerations, among others, indicate Lactantius as the author of this little book also cannot be doubted.

**When he seemed to himself to have risen, and stood beside the one who was admonishing him, then he taught him how and with what words he should pray.** Of this passage, which perhaps many have regarded as perfectly sound, I see two emendations proposed by learned men: one involving only a single letter, the other consisting of several emendations together. I correct it: “when he seemed to himself to have risen, and stood beside her, who remained, then,” etc. BOHERELLUS.—Read: “He seemed to himself to rise, and to stand beside the one who was admonishing him. Then,” followed by what comes after. TOLLIUS.—We judge the first to be far preferable to the other, if only because it alters the reading of the old codex as little as possible.

**A notary, etc.** That is, according to both translators, one of those who served Licinius as confidential secretaries: *Un de ses secrétaires* [“one of his secretaries”]. MAUCROIX. “One of his secretaries.” English translation.

**To be summoned.** That is, to be employed. Alternatively, *accersiri* or *acciri* [“to be called for”] may be read. TOL.

**Supreme God, we beseech you, etc.** We did not add the threefold address in this prayer, “supreme God,” to the other expressions in this treatise which may vindicate it for Lactantius [in the preceding column], because these addresses ought to be regarded as having not even a human author properly speaking, but an angelic one, as is clear from what precedes.

**In several little documents.** That is, just as a slip on which someone sets forth in very few words in the forum or on the doors of temples that he has found something and will return it to its owner is called a *libellus* by Ulpian in the *Digest*: “Many persons also commonly do this: they post a notice stating that they have found something and will return it to the person who has lost it.” Nor was a bill of divorce, the βιβλίον ἀποστασίου (*biblion apostasiou*, “document of divorce”) concerning which our Lord speaks in Matthew 19:7, much longer—or certainly not much longer—than the prayer in this chapter, since a bill of divorce had to be written in only twelve lines, neither more nor fewer, as may be learned from the Rabbis cited by Lightfoot on Matthew 5:31.

**And they are sent through the prefects and tribunes, that each may instruct his own soldiers.** I understand. But to whom, exactly, were they sent, who afterwards and immediately, having received copies of the said prayer, were each to teach their own soldiers to pray to God supreme? For concerning people of this sort there is the deepest silence in the received reading. Either it must be said that something is missing, for example, *to the centurions*, thus: “and they are sent through the prefects and tribunes to the centurions, that each may instruct his own soldiers,” if *to send through prefects and tribunes*, in the most ordinary idiom, means to send by the agency of prefects and tribunes. Or, as I prefer, one must hold that, just as in Justin, book VIII, chapter 3, *to send through kingdoms*, and elsewhere in Latin *to send through streets and crossroads*, mean precisely the same as *to send to kingdoms* or *to send to each individual street and crossroads alike*, so here *to send through prefects and tribunes* properly means to send to each individual prefect and tribune, so that those who were prefects and tribunes over the soldiers might become their instructors with respect to that prayer [Col. 0822A]. Nor indeed did the translators understand it otherwise.—*Que l'on distribue aux colonels et aux capitaines, pour l'apprendre à leurs soldats* [“That it be distributed to colonels and captains, for them to teach it to their soldiers”]. MAUCROIX. Literally: the copies of the prayer are distributed to prefects and tribunes, so that each may teach it to his soldiers. “Which were sent about to all the Officers, etc.” English translation. Literally likewise: the copies of the prayer were sent to all officers.—On prefects and tribunes, their differences and the force of their titles, see Cuper and Columbus.

**Their courage grew, etc.** This stratagem of Licinius was no less excellent than Constantine’s, discussed above. Sertorius employed much the same artifice in Plutarch; nor are Scipio’s retreat into Jupiter’s temple or Numa’s visits to the goddess Egeria of a different kind. TOLLIUS.—But how does Tollius know that neither Constantine nor Licinius truly dreamed what they professed, so that such things must be deemed mere stratagems? Is he, like Joseph in Egypt of old, *Tzophnathpahaneach*—that is, in Matthathias’s rendering, κρυπτῶν εὑρετής (*kryptōn heuretēs*, “discoverer of hidden things”)? Yet Joseph, son of Jacob, acknowledged that God sends dreams even to Gentiles; this Tollius does not seem to admit.

**The emperor appointed the battle for the day of the Kalends of May.** Which emperor? Licinius or Maximinus? The English translation names Maximinus most expressly: “Maximin resolved to give battle on the first of May.” Nor should the Oxford and Cambridge editions be understood otherwise in the annotation which they shortly add below. But what could be clearer, since the Licinian soldiers have just been mentioned—“The courage of all grew, believing that victory had been announced to them from heaven”—than that the following words, “the emperor appointed,” refer directly to their emperor, Licinius? Especially because what will be read a few lines below expressly establishes that Maximinus had not wished to fight on the Kalends of May themselves, but a day earlier—on the preceding day, to use our author’s words. I admit, meanwhile, that the matter, viewed from another angle, is not altogether free of difficulty; but it is not insoluble, as will appear from what follows.—**For the day of the Kalends of May.** Read: “to begin on the day,” or rather, “for the day of the Kalends of May.” TOLLIUS.—What Columbus thinks at the end of his note—that *to appoint a battle for a certain day* may somehow be tolerated, ἀντὶ τοῦ [instead of] *to appoint a battle for that day*—does not so displease me that I do not consider it very close to the passage in chapter 38 where the Goths are said to have surrendered to Maximian, “the evil of humankind,” for *to the evil of humankind*, as is plain: *au grand intérêt de l'empire* [“for the great interest of the empire”]. MAUCROIX.—I would therefore judge that nothing should here be interpolated. The French would say: *Il résolut la bataille pour le premier jour de mai* [“He resolved upon battle for the first day of May”]. Nevertheless, we neither can nor should conceal that Cuper, and Columbus too at the beginning of his note, take another view.—**For the day of the Kalends of May.** On that day he was made emperor in the year 305; and because eight years have now elapsed from that point, this strengthens what was said above concerning the date of Diocletian’s death. Oxford and Cambridge editions; the latter adding further: “See Valesius’s annotations on Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, final chapter.”—But certainly wrongly—though other matters, which I am not now discussing, may be correct—that in the editions mentioned, and in Baluzius himself before them, the emperor in these words, “the emperor appointed,” is Maximinus. For Licinius should rather be understood, as we have just shown and shall further demonstrate.

**Which completed the eighth year of his proclamation.** I do not see what can ever conveniently be made of this passage unless it is read with a supplement: “which completed the eighth year of the proclamation of his enemy,” or “of his adversary,” or something of that sort. The first reason is that in this way the words “the eighth year of his proclamation” will no longer seem to refer to the same emperor of whom our author has just said, “the emperor appointed”—Licinius, that is, as we have just argued—the battle for the day of the Kalends of May. The second is that those Kalends of May did in fact complete the eighth year of the proclamation of Maximinus, Licinius’s enemy; but not of Licinius, as I think anyone can show. And the third, finally, is that precisely because those Kalends were the birthday of Maximinus’s rule, Licinius could very aptly appoint battle for that day, so that, just as Maxentius had earlier been defeated on the birthday not of Constantine but of himself, Maximinus likewise might be overcome on the very anniversary of his own reign. But how, conversely, could it properly be said that Maximinus appointed battle for the day of the Kalends of May, which completed the eighth year of his proclamation, in order that he might be defeated especially on his own birthday, as Maxentius had been defeated at Rome? For if, as is proper, one must speak not from the outcome but from Maximinus’s intention, Maximinus did not at all wish to be defeated, but to conquer; nor did he wish it on the Kalends of May themselves, but a day earlier, as will shortly be related. I would therefore suppose that this passage, like many others in this little work, is mutilated and requires some supplement such as those proposed above.

**Which completed the eighth year of his proclamation.** Thus these events occurred in the year 313, when the eighth year of his Caesarean rule was completed on the Kalends of May. PAGIUS.

**That he might be defeated especially on his own birthday.** Maximinus, of course; and although this was already noted in a rather inappropriate place, it should be observed again here, if only because the English translation has expressly supplied that name.

**Just as he was defeated at Rome.** That is, Maxentius. PAGIUS.—Compare the English rendering: “It happened, that as Maxentius was defeated at Romae, etc.” Likewise Baluzius and Toinard.

**Maximinus wished to go forth earlier.** I correct: *prodire* [“to advance”], or *perire* [“to perish”]. GALE.—I preferred the latter, in this sense: “But Maximinus wished to fight one day earlier and therefore, considering the matter from its outcome, to perish earlier.”—“Only Maximin would needs anticipate his own ruin; for he would needs fight the day before it.” English translation. Literally: “Only Maximinus did not wish to anticipate his own ruin. For he did not wish to fight on the day preceding it.” Thus it is evident that the eminent translator read, among other things, *Maximinus noluit* (“Maximinus did not wish”) in place of *Maximinus voluit praeire maturius* (“Maximinus wished to go forth earlier”). I can conjecture no more.

**It is announced in the camp, etc.** Perhaps *in* should be deleted, as elsewhere. BOHERELLUS.

**The soldiers take up arms, etc.** Licinius’s soldiers, of course, as they will simply be called shortly afterwards. Nor do the translators differ.

**Which they call Serenum.** A place in Thrace between Hadrianopolis and Heraclea, against Zosimus, who relates this battle as fought in Illyricum. Oxford and Cambridge editions.

**They unfasten their helmets.** Namely, by undoing the knots of the straps by which helmets were fitted and fastened to the head so that they would not fall off. Helmets (*cassides*), as Isidore notes, were made of metal plate; *galeae* of leather, with this distinction, according to Joseph Scaliger: those made of dogs’ skins were properly called κυνέαι (*kyneai*) by Greek poets; those of wolves’ skins, λύκειαι (*lykeiai*); and those of cats’ skins, γαλέαι (*galeai*), “helmets”—for γαλέη, in prose γαλῆ, means “cat.” But this is undoubtedly especially worthy of notice: Licinius’s soldiers uttered the prayer they had been taught only after removing their helmets and thus with heads uncovered. Either because the angel of God himself, who had instructed Licinius in the words with which he was to pray, had at the same time prescribed that this be done—for it had preceded: “Then he taught him how and with what words he should pray”—or because nature herself teaches that every man who prays to his God with covered head thereby dishonours his God. Paul certainly says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “Every man praying . . . with his head covered dishonours his head”; and a little later: “For a man ought not to cover his head, being the image and glory of God,” εἰκὼν καὶ δόξα θεοῦ ὑπάρχων (*eikōn kai doxa theou hyparchōn*), which, God willing, I shall explain elsewhere as it is commonly misunderstood. “Cooked and warm animals were placed beside the flowing seat, so that the heat might draw out little worms. Once these were released, an immeasurable swarm poured forth.” Likewise this passage of Justin: “He demanded the yoke of a wagon; when it was brought, he cut the straps with a sword, and thus, the fastenings having been undone, found the heads hidden in the knots.”

[Col. 0824A] **Now full of courage.** That is, of martial courage, commonly known by the name of fortitude and opposed to cowardice.
