Nothing is more familiar to Justin, although in book IX, chapter 2, he calls it not simply *virtus* but *virtus animi*, “courage of spirit,” in these words: “The Scythians are esteemed for courage of spirit and hardness of body, not for wealth,” than to call it elsewhere *virtus* without any addition. Thus in the same book shortly afterwards: “Although the Scythians excelled in courage and numbers, they were defeated by Philip’s cunning”; and in the following chapter: “The Athenians . . . were defeated by Macedonian courage”; and book V, chapter 11: “Throughout so great stretches of travel they defended themselves by courage as far as their country’s borders”; and book XII, chapter 1: “When King Agis saw his men turning their backs, having dismissed his bodyguards so that he might seem inferior to Alexander in fortune, not in courage, he made such slaughter of the enemy that at times he put whole columns to flight”; to which many similar examples might be added. “The Souldiers being now wonderfully animated.” English translation. That is, when the soldiers had now been greatly encouraged.

**They lift their shields.** “They took up their Schields.” The same meaning. Literally, they raise their shields. The sense is indeed excellently expressed, but there is no necessity on that account to read it thus. For *tollere* often means to lift from the ground, or from a level surface. Cicero, *To Atticus*: “What if you should wish it, you ask? Come now, who is there to whom wishing is not permitted? But I think this very wishing more miserable than being lifted onto a cross”—which, as everyone knows, was done only by lifting one from the ground. The same writer, *On Duties*, book III: “The Sun said to his son Phaethon—to return to fables—that he would do whatever he wished. He wished to be lifted into his father’s chariot; he was lifted up, to his ruin.” Here likewise *tolleretur* means “he should be lifted from level ground.”

## CHAPTER XLVII

**Maximinus went around the battle-line, etc.** His own, or Licinius’s? Certainly not his own. For, as will shortly appear, Maximinus had gone so far from his own troops when he went around the battle-line in question that, when the Licinians made an attack upon him, he was forced to flee back to his own men: “An attack is made upon him, and he flees to his own.” Therefore he had not previously been going around his own troops, but Licinius’s troops, all of them. We add this because, as things stand, our author seems altogether to have explicitly distinguished the battle-line he mentions from the Licinian soldiers of whom he has just spoken: “Maximinus goes around the battle-line, and now seeks to win over the Licinian soldiers by prayers, now by gifts.” Therefore the battle-line is the entire army of Licinius, including both all officers and all ordinary soldiers together; but the Licinian soldiers are only the rank-and-file, so that Maximinus went around Licinius’s whole army, consisting of officers and ordinary soldiers, but sought to win over only the ordinary soldiers, as more disposed to desertion, now by prayers, now by gifts. “These things are written in several little documents and sent through prefects and tribunes, that each may instruct his own soldiers”: these are the words of the preceding chapter, from which the distinction just proposed derives considerable support [Col. 0824D].—*Maximin tournait autour des bataillons de Licinius, et tâchait de les ébranler par ses prières et par ses promesses* [“Maximin went around Licinius’s battalions and tried to shake them by his prayers and promises”]. MAUCROIX.—As if the received reading were: “Maximinus goes around Licinius’s battle-line and seeks to win it over now by prayers, now by gifts.”

**So great a number of legions . . . so great a force of soldiers was cut down by a few.** Justin uses a similar expression somewhere.

**None remembered his name, none his courage, none his former rewards.** Horace on Crassus’s soldier, book III, ode 5:

> The Marsian and Apulian grew old in arms  
> under a Median king, forgetful  
> of the sacred shields, of his name and toga,  
> and of eternal Vesta.

TOLLIUS.

**None his courage.** That is, his fortitude; and consequently in the same sense as in the preceding chapter: “They, having recited the prayer three times, were now full of courage”; and again as in chapter 44: “The senate decreed to Constantine, for the sake of his courage, the title of first”—shall I say “name” or “divinity”?—“which Maximinus claimed for himself.”

**To a death devoted.** Here *devota mors* is an appointed death, as in Virgil, *Aeneid* I:

> Especially unhappy, devoted to a future pestilence,  
> the Phoenician cannot satisfy her mind and burns as she gazes;

that is, destined for a love which would prove fatal to Dido.—*À une mort volontaire* [“to a voluntary death”]. Maucroix. That is, “to voluntary death,” with the meaning felicitously explained.

**God supreme.** As above, “that he might pray to God supreme,” which we have illustrated to the best of our ability in its place. Baluzius and Cuper will provide you with more.

**He cast off the purple.** At the end of the chapter he will call it simply “garment”: “Thus he resumed the garment.” But it is clear that in both places a purple garment is meant. Relevant to this is the fact that the garment which Mark once and again in the account of Christ’s passion calls πορφύρα (*porphyra*), literally “purple,” “and they clothe him in purple,” chapter 15, verse 17; “and when they had mocked him, they stripped him of the purple,” in the same chapter, verse 20, John in two passages alike calls ἱμάτιον πορφυροῦν (*himation porphyroun*), that is, word for word, “a purple cloak”: “they put a purple cloak around him,” chapter 19, verse 2; “Jesus therefore went out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple cloak,” likewise verse 5. Our author above, much as here: “Diocletian placed his own purple upon Daia, which he himself had taken off.”

**Having put on a servant’s garment, he fled.** Eusebius confirms this, book IX, chapter 10, and book I of *The Life of Constantine*, chapter 58. PAGIUS.

**He crossed the strait.** The same strait, of course, as in the preceding discussion: “But Maximinus, having immediately crossed the strait, approached the gates of Byzantium in arms.” The difference is that, when Maximinus crossed that strait the first time, he was hastening from Bithynia into Thrace to seize whatever provinces or cities of Licinius he could; whereas on the second occasion he was returning, conversely, from Thrace into Bithynia, to withdraw within his own borders. I infer this from chapter 45 and from these words of Eusebius: οὕτω ἔπειτα αἰσχύνης ἔμπλεως ὁ τύραννος ἐπὶ τὰ καθ᾽ ἑαυτὸν ἐλθὼν μέρη πρῶτον μὲν ἐμμανεῖ θυμῷ, etc. That is: “Thus then the tyrant, having come, full of shame, to the parts of his own empire”—for this is the literal Greek—“first indeed raged in spirit,” and what follows. Add Baluzius, and after him, if you wish, Pagius in the *Baronial Critique* for the year of Christ 314, no. 5.

**And in the army, etc.** Better: “But in the army.” TOLLIUS.—I read: “And so one half of the army was overthrown. The other half either surrendered or turned to flight.” BOHERELLUS.—The English translation comes very close: “for now the one half of his Army was destroyed, and the other half either fled or rendered it self.” For one half of his army had already been overthrown, and the other half had either surrendered or taken flight.

**For the deserter emperor had taken away their shame at deserting.** Deserting what? “His interests,” says the same translation; as though one said, his party or his cause. Yet *desertor imperator* means “an emperor who deserted his army.” “And since the emperour had deserted his Army, the souldiers were not at all ashamed of deserting his interests.”

I preferred to repeat here in a general sense the word *battle* which preceded: “for the emperor, a deserter of battle, had taken away their shame at deserting battle.” How shameful such desertion was for both emperor and soldiers is shown both by the most odious designation “deserter,” with which Maximinus is now branded, and by that notable commendation of the Athenians in Justin, book IX, chapter 3, although they were slain in battle: “Yet they did not fall forgetful of their former glory; for, wounded in front, all as they died covered with their bodies the positions entrusted to them for defence by their commanders.” Indeed, what had escaped my memory: in the same Justin, book XXII, chapter 8, “a king who deserts his army is a singular example of disgrace.”

**But he reached Nicomedia on the Kalends of May—that is, in one night and one day—on another night.** After *day* some word is missing, the name of the posting-station at which Maximinus arrived on the Kalends of May—that is, in one night and one day—and from which he reached Nicomedia in the depth of night. BOHERELLUS.—After *day*, *to the strait* is missing. TOLLIUS.

**He reached Nicomedia on another night.** Read: “in the depth of night.” ALLIX.—What if nothing is missing and nothing is corrupt except the order of the words, so that the genuine order was once: “But he reached Nicomedia on the Kalends of May, that is, in one night, one day, and another night.”

**One hundred and sixty miles.** *Soixante lieues* [“sixty leagues”]. Maucroix. That is, sixty leagues; whereas, if he had wished to be consistent with himself, he should have written only *cinquante-trois lieues*, fifty-three leagues.

**And having hastily seized his children, etc.** That is, having seized them rapidly or with utmost haste. Livy uses it in the same sense: “More nearly an excuse for crossing as necessary than a boast of having seized, as though the first opportunity, an opportunity snatched up.” But perhaps Christ does not use it otherwise in Matthew 11:12: Ἀπὸ δὲ τῶν ἡμερῶν Ἰωάννου τοῦ Βαπτιστοῦ ἕως ἄρτι, ἡ βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν βιάζεται, καὶ βιασταὶ ἁρπάζουσιν αὐτήν (*From the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and violent men seize it*). The Vulgate: “But from the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and violent men snatch it.”

**He made for the East. But in Cappadocia, etc.** That is, he had first determined to withdraw into the East properly so called, and therefore to pass beyond Cappadocia and make for Syria, for example, from which not long before, as though it belonged to him, he had moved an army into Bithynia to invade, if possible, the neighbouring provinces of Licinius. But when, on the march, he unexpectedly gathered not a few soldiers in Cappadocia, both from the fugitives and from the East, he halted in Cappadocia for some time. While I mark this boundary, I do so among other reasons because of the passage in Zosimus which you will find in Baluzius. From these matters, even if I say nothing, you understand that Cappadocia was not included by this author within the notion of the East in its specific sense.

[Col. 0826C] **Thus he resumed the garment.** *Ces légers secours lui donnèrent le courage de reprendre encore la pourpre* [“These slight reinforcements gave him the courage to take up the purple again”]. MAUCROIX. That is, briefly, “thus he resumed the purple.”—“And there he took the purple again,” English translation; as though the received reading were, “there he resumed the purple.”—In any event, either “there he resumed the garment” should be read, or, as I prefer, the sense is: “Then he resumed the garment,” just as we have already noted more than once above that τὸ *ita* means “then” or “afterwards.” Compare, should you require still more examples, Justin, book V, chapter 3 at the end; likewise book XI, chapter 7, also at the end, lest I enumerate further instances again.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

**Having accepted and distributed a portion of the army.** Of his own army, or of the enemy’s? For the translators differ. I understand it, with Maucroix, to mean the enemy’s army; because if the discourse concerned a portion of Licinius’s own army accepted from Licinius and at the same time distributed among various cities, say, he would by no means next say, “he transported the army into Bithynia,” but “he transported the other part into Bithynia”; for one who deliberately leaves behind a part of his own army no longer has an army to transport, but only the remaining part of the army. But our author’s narrative is explicit: “Licinius, having accepted and distributed a portion of the army, transported the army into Bithynia a few days after the battle.” Add that, since at the end of the preceding chapter he expressly wrote of Maximinus’s army—“One half was overthrown, while the other half either surrendered to Licinius or took flight”—the two statements fit together excellently: some portion of Maximinus’s army wished to surrender to Licinius; Licinius first willingly accepted it into surrender, then shortly afterwards prudently distributed it among various divisions or companies of his own soldiers; and only then transported the army, now consisting of his own troops and Maximinus’s, into Bithynia.

[Col. 0827A] **On the day of the Ides of June.** On the day of the Ides of June letters concerning the restoration of the Church were indeed posted at Nicomedia and sent to the governor, as Lactantius testifies; but they had been issued at Milan in the same year, namely 313 of Christ, around March, as Constantine and Licinius expressly state in them. PAGIUS.

**On the day of the Ides of June.** *Le treizième de juin* [“the thirteenth of June”]. MAUCROIX.—That is, on the thirteenth day of June. “On the thirteenth of June,” English translation: these are merely different ways of marking the same thing.

**When Constantine and he himself were consuls for the third time.** Namely, in the year of Christ 313. PAGIUS.

**Concerning the restoration of the Church.** Namely, the Church at Nicomedia and the others which had been destroyed during the preceding ten years throughout Bithynia, of which Nicomedia was the chief city. For the Nicomedian Church had indeed been the first of all to be destroyed and levelled to the ground, as is certain from chapter XII; but that the same afterwards happened to many others across the broad region of Bithynia is clear even from the fact that our author, after setting out in this chapter Licinius’s letter to the governor of Bithynia, immediately adds: “When these letters had been posted, he also urged verbally that the meeting-houses be restored to their former condition.” As you see, mention is made of several meeting-houses, or, what is the same thing, churches, to be restored—not of the Nicomedian Church alone.

**Letters.** Eusebius sets these out in book X, chapter 5 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, from the Latin language in which they were first published, as he himself teaches. PAGIUS.

**Letters.** That is, according to the rendering of each translator, an edict. And Pagius indeed expressly says in this very connection: “Here I do not distinguish an epistle from an edict.” But, speaking precisely, there is some difference between edicts and letters of emperors addressed to governors, as we have already shown, unless I am mistaken; and it will appear more fully again from what is to be said on almost the final words of this chapter.

**Given to the governor.** But which governor? Of Nicomedia or of Bithynia? For both words have preceded: “he transported the army into Bithynia . . . and having entered Nicomedia,” etc. Maucroix understood the governor of Nicomedia: *On l'adressa au président de Nicomédie* [“It was addressed to the governor of Nicomedia”]. But the Code of Justinian strongly opposes this supplement, from which it is clear that governors were governors of provinces. See, for example, book I, title 40, laws I and II. Add also Salmasius on the writers of the *Historia Augusta*. Nor does it object that in our author, chapter 40, Eratineus, who is shortly afterwards called governor, is called judge in what follows. For by the same Code, those who governed provinces were also judges; or, as Lactantius suggests to us in the epitome, not merely governors of provinces but likewise governors of the laws. His words are: “For the governors of the laws themselves were corrupted by rewards and gifts.” Hence the French, who simply translate *praeses* as *président*, were deservedly reproved in their place by the most distinguished Cuper.

**He ordered them to be posted.** But not without a proclamation by the governor, as Licinius himself will command almost at the end of the appended letter, in order that an edict based on Licinius’s letters might be prepared according to the instructions given, as Pliny’s letter to Trajan below will confirm.

**Since happily, etc.** See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book X, chapter 5. Cambridge edition.

When we had met at Milan. In my judgment, this did not occur before about the beginning of the first month of A.D. 314. First, because Nazarius states that Constantine, by an effort of nearly two months, healed all the harm which the deadly six-year domination of Maxentius had inflicted upon the city of Rome; and this followed immediately upon his victory over Maxentius, won on the sixth day before the Kalends of November—that is, 27 October. It is therefore apparent that Constantine remained in Rome at least until the middle of December. Secondly, because Rome, from which Constantine had to depart for the appointed place, Milan, lay at a very great distance; Constantine could scarcely have arrived conveniently at Milan before the beginning of January [Col. 0828A].

I know that Baluzius infers from the Code of the Emperor Justinian, Book XI, title 57, law 1, that Constantine did not leave Rome before the end of January, since the usual subscription of the law reads: “Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February at Rome, in the third consulship of Constantine Augustus and the consulship of Licinius.” But we have already noted that other manuscripts read thus: “Published on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February at Rome, in the fourth consulship of Constantine Augustus and the third of Licinius”; hence, contrary to what that most distinguished man thought, the subscription from which he argued against the equally distinguished Dodwell not only does not strike at the heart of the case, but nothing whatever can lawfully be inferred from it because of the variant reading, which no more places Constantine personally at Rome than elsewhere.

Add that, if that law had truly been issued at Rome by Constantine on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February—that is, on 18 January A.D. 314—it would follow that Constantine had healed, not in an effort of nearly two months, as Nazarius explicitly affirms, all the evils inflicted during the entire six-year rule of Maxentius, but in nearly [Col. 0828B] three months. Therefore Constantine, departing from Rome, and Licinius, from Illyricum, met at Milan in January 314, after not much of that month had elapsed, rather than as it was passing—for example, in February of the same year or in December of the preceding year, 313. See meanwhile what Dodwell wrote on both sides of the question in Dissertation XI on Cyprian, no. 86.

At Milan, etc. There was framed the decree concerning peace, preserved for us in Latin today by Lactantius in chapter 48. They immediately sent it to Maximinus together with news of the victory. But he, “wishing not to appear to yield to others,” as Eusebius tells us, issued a new edict “on his own authority.” For he yielded with great reluctance and unwillingness to the senatorial decree by which Constantine was proclaimed Augustus of the first rank. DODWELL.

Security. Tranquillity. MAUCROIX. As though there were absolutely no difference between these words; but that this is not so is shown by two kinds of passages in Cicero. One consists of passages in which *securitas* and *tranquillitas* are named as things distinct from one another, though not greatly so. The other consists of passages in which Cicero supplies differing definitions of the two terms.

Of the first kind are these: *On Duties*, Book I, chapter 20: “We must be free from every disturbance of the mind—from desire and fear, as also from distress, pleasure of mind, and anger—so that tranquillity and security may be present.” *On Ends*, Book V: “But the security of Democritus, which is a kind of tranquillity of mind,” etc. The following passages belong to the second kind. *Tusculan Disputations*, Book IV: “Those who divide the mind into two parts make one participate in reason and the other devoid of it; in the part participating in reason they place tranquillity, that is, calm and untroubled constancy.” Book V of the same work: “But can anyone possess that security most eagerly desired and sought after—I now call security freedom from distress, in which the good life consists—who either has, or may have, a multitude of evils?”

[Col. 0828D] “That the divinity, placated and propitious in its heavenly abode, may prove favourable to us and to all who are established under our authority.” I suspect a corruption. I therefore read: “That, by divine agency indeed, etc., it may be able to render [the divinity] propitious.” Sparkius, I think, in the Oxford and Cambridge editions.—Instead of *quod quidem divinitas*, perhaps read *quod quidem divinitus*, etc. BOHERELLUS.—Lactantius’ words are unsound. The remedy is uncertain. I thought they would be more tolerable if recast thus: “that indeed the divinity, placated and propitious in its heavenly abode, may be favourable to us and to all who are established under our authority.” GRAEVIUS.—Read: “that the divine power of the deity,” and shortly afterward *posset* instead of *possit*. TOLLIUS.—I should write either: “that indeed the divinity, placated and propitious in its heavenly abode, may be favourable to us and all who are established under our authority,” accepting a neglect of syntax; or: “that indeed the divine power in its heavenly abode,” etc. In ancient books *divinitas* certainly means “divine power.” Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXVII, chapter 7: “‘Act more sparingly,’ said Eupraxius, ‘most pious of princes; for those whom you order to be killed as criminals, the Christian religion reveres as martyrs—that is, as persons acceptable to the divinity.’” And in the Code the Emperor Justinian says: “By propitious divinity the Roman Empire has been entrusted to us.” GALE.

“That the supreme divinity, whose religion we obey with free minds, may be able for us,” etc. Words worthy of notice. For if Licinius, as must be certain, understood Jupiter by the “supreme divinity” of which he speaks, then it was to Jupiter, not to the God of Christians, that he and his entire army uttered the prayer mentioned above: “Supreme God, we beseech thee. Holy God, we beseech thee,” and what follows. Thus, if perhaps any fraud was involved in the matter, that prayer cannot be said to have been composed in honour of the supreme God of Christians by this Caecilius or by other writers.

With free minds. “Voluntarily.” MAUCROIX; that is, of their own accord, or literally, willingly.—Correctly. For to whom could it occur to interpret it as “licentiously”? How strange, O supreme God of Christians, that through thee it was permitted to a pagan man, who worshipped not thee but a god of no account, openly and with free minds to obey the religion of a false divinity, while today the same is not permitted to so many thousands of thine who desire publicly to worship thee, the true God, in spirit and truth! But thy judgments are a great abyss, O King of Saints.

[Note: [Col. 0829D]

Observe the ridiculous exclamation of a raging heretic.

]

“Your devotedness” (*dicationem tuam*). That is, “your dignity” (*dignationem*). Oxford and Cambridge editions.—That is, “you.” The translators.—Read *dignationem*. ALLIX.

“After all conditions whatsoever had been removed.” Baluzius, a man of most polished intellect and learning, explained this correctly. Hence he shortly afterward says that he has granted them a free and unrestricted opportunity to practise religion. Compare the preceding edict of Maximinus, where this opportunity is restricted and checked by fixed laws: “provided,” he says, “that they do nothing contrary to discipline,” etc., matters contained in the letter given to the judges. TOLLIUS.

[Col. 0829C] “Concerning the name of the Christians,” etc. Is this in the same sense as in chapter 14: “The name of Christians burned amid great hostility together with the palace”? Or is it by circumlocution for “concerning Christians,” as the translators briefly understood it, and before them Eusebius in this rendering, *peri tōn Christianōn*, literally, “concerning Christians”? I would prefer: “concerning the divine power of Christians” (*super Christianorum numine*), for which I shall shortly give my reason.—The text must be supplied and corrected from Eusebius’ Greek, Book X, chapter 5, as follows: “the provisions contained concerning the name of Christians, and all matters which seemed altogether harsh and foreign to our clemency, shall be removed; and now freely and simply each person,” and what follows.—Far be it from me to judge the translation of Eusebius’ words, which the most learned man proposes as suited to this passage, less responsive to the Greek for any reason other than that it begins “concerning the name of Christians,” whereas the Greek simply has *peri tōn Christianōn*: “concerning Christians” or “about Christians.”

But what if, while Eusebius made the Latin—whatever it was—more concise in translating it into Greek, the following Latin had, conversely, been more concise than Eusebius represented it in Greek? In one word, I suspect this, both because in Greek *ta skaia* can readily mean “trifles” or “pettifoggeries” (*skaios* means, among other things, foolish, stupid, full of disturbances, difficult), and because it is at the same time entirely certain that what is *severa* in Latin may very well be rendered by a Greek writer as *praotētos allotria*, “foreign to gentleness.” I suspect this, I say, for both reasons, and also for this third reason: the reading “they seemed trifles and harsh measures” does not depart very far from the old “they seemed, now to take care and,” and perhaps the earlier wording of our passage, if traced a little further back, was:

> “Wherefore your devotedness should know that it has pleased us that, after all conditions whatsoever had been removed which, in the earlier letters sent to your office concerning the divine power of Christians, seemed trifles and harsh measures, each one of them simply [Col. 0830A] …”

or something of that kind, such as: “they seemed pettifoggeries and harsh measures.”

Eusebius’ words, that the whole matter may be better understood, are formulated thus:

> “It was consequently fitting for us to write back that, all restrictions having been entirely removed which were contained in our earlier letters sent to your piety concerning the Christians, and all things which seemed very harsh and foreign to our gentleness having been withdrawn, now each of those who have adopted the same purpose of observing the Christian religion may observe it freely and without error, free from any annoyance.”

“Now to take care (or now truly) and.” Read: “Now take care that.” Oxford and Cambridge editions, likewise Allix.—I correct: “You must now take care that.” BOHERELLUS.—“Now to take care.” Read more correctly: “Now let them be revoked.” TOLLIUS.

“Who maintain the same will to observe the religion of Christians.” I prefer, with the Oxford and Cambridge editions: “Who maintain the same will to observe religion,” etc.

“Let them strive to observe that very thing.” What is “that very thing”? As matters stand, nothing has preceded to which it can grammatically refer except “Christians.” But it is absurd that Licinius should have wished to establish by edict that Christians should continue to observe the name of Christians, if they wished. For what could observance of the Christian name have been to Christians? Therefore in the preceding words, unless we are greatly mistaken, one must read: “concerning the divine power of Christians.”

“Let them strive” (*contendant*). Rather, “let him strive” (*contendat*). TOLLIUS.

“Your devotedness.” Rather, “your dignity,” as above. BOHERELLUS, likewise ALLIX.

“So that each may have free opportunity to cultivate what he chooses.” The editions praised at the bottom of the page are undoubtedly better: “So that in cultivating, each,” etc.

“May have what each chose.” Read: “may have what each shall choose.” GRAEVIUS.

“Which (or because) … honour, nor to any religion anything from us.” Thus it must be supplied: “Because we do not wish anything to appear to have been taken away by us from any honour or from any religion.” Oxford and Cambridge editions.—But this too requires correction, and not in one way only. The proposed supplements are otherwise supported both by Eusebius’ words in Columbus and by these words of chapter 13: “On the following day an edict was posted, providing that the people of that religion should be deprived of every honour and dignity.”

[Col. 0830C] “In the person of Christians.” *Eis to prosōpon tōn Christianōn*, Eusebius. That is, as Valesius translates it, “in favour of Christians”; whence one might not without reason suspect that the author wrote “in favour of Christians,” not “in the person of Christians.”—“With relation to the Christians.” English translation. That is, “with respect to Christians.”

“The same places to which they had formerly been accustomed to assemble.” Read: “those places”; and no differently a little below, where *consueverunt* (“they were accustomed”) is read. Here, however, the text has *consueverant* (“they had been accustomed”), but less correctly. TOLLIUS.

“They appear earlier to have bought something either from our treasury or from some other person whatsoever.” Rather, “some persons.” BOHERELLUS; likewise GALE. Correctly.

“Let them restore [them] as quickly as possible.” Put a full stop after *reddant* (“let them restore”). BOHERELLUS.—That this must absolutely be done is demonstrated by everything, especially Eusebius’ punctuation properly understood, which is also supported by that of the Åbo edition: “let them restore [them] as quickly as possible to those same Christians. Moreover,” etc.

“As quickly as possible” (*quantocius*). In Gemma it occurs for “quickly,” “as soon as possible.” But I seek an author. GERARD JOHANN VOSSIUS.—I am surprised that, besides the two ancient authors already cited before us by Columbus, partly correctly and partly incorrectly—namely Sulpicius, *Dialogues* III, chapter 5, and the Vulgate translator at Genesis 45:19—Mamertinus also, no insignificant writer, employed the same word in this passage: “Although, greatest Emperor, I ought publicly to offer thee thanks in the name and judgment of all, I shall nevertheless now omit for the most part those deeds which thou hast accomplished for the highest good at home and abroad, so that my speech may arrive as quickly as possible at matters peculiar to itself.” For it is plainly clear that the reading must be thus, not “with all speed” (*quanto totius*); not to mention Braulio, a seventh-century author, who says in the preface to the *Life of Saint Aemilianus* that it might be read as quickly as possible [Col. 0831A] in the celebration of his Mass. Let this then be an adverb which, if not of the best standing, is nevertheless of far better standing—and of the same period—than the most learned man supposed. Especially since Licinius shortly afterward again orders that his command be fulfilled as quickly as possible.

“Also even those who bought [them].” At first sight I suspected that this was corrupt and that one should read: “Moreover, even those,” etc. But I now change nothing. TOLLIUS.—“As they please.” But long ago the distinguished Gale changed *etiam* (“also”) to *iam* (“now”) in the margin of his copy; and below likewise did the man of highest rank and learning, Petrus Valerus Diazius. I conjectured, induced by more than one reason, that the earlier reading was *et ita* (“and thus”) instead of *et deinde* (“and then”). First, because in this way everything coheres suitably: “Those who have purchased Christian meeting-places in whatever manner, let them restore them as quickly as possible. Those who have received them as gifts, let them likewise restore them as quickly as possible. And then let both parties consider indemnity, as may seem equitable to them.”

The second reason, no less strong, is that Eusebius does not seem to have read otherwise than as we emend. For what do these words mean:

> “So that, if they restore [them] as quickly as possible to those same Christians, then—that is, afterward—either those who purchased the same places or those who received them by gift, if they request anything from our beneficence, may approach the provincial governor administering justice,”

unless this very sense? But we have already shown, with many examples, that both Greek *houtōs* and Latin *ita* are not unusually used for *eita*, “then,” or “afterward.” And the fact that we have now supplied the adverb *ei* (“if”) before *aitōsin* in Eusebius’ passage is shown to be necessary not only by comparison with our text, “if they think,” but also because Eusebius does not immediately follow with *proselthōsi te*, or something similar, but without any conjunction has *proselthōsi*, “let them approach,” so that it plainly depends upon the preceding *hopōs*, “so that.”

[Col. 0831C] “Or those who will have received [them] as gifts.” Rather: “those who had received [them] as gifts.” GALE.

“If they consider that they should seek something from our beneficence, let them request a vicar.” This is a rather difficult passage, both because the learned disagree about its soundness and punctuation and because some, with Eusebius, understand by “vicar” a definite person, while others understand not a person but some substitute thing. The entire issue may be briefly stated thus.

I think it should be written: “If they desire something in recompense from our beneficence, let them request it.” Diazius. I formerly believed that this passage was mutilated and should read: “If they think that something may be hoped for from our beneficence, let them request compensation.” But I now change nothing, and understand *vicarium* as that which Christians considered due to them in return for the restoration of their property, as the distinguished Diazius did. He shortly afterward calls it indemnity. TOLLIUS.—Read thus: “If they think something should be demanded from our beneficence, let them request compensation.”—I merely punctuate: “If they think, let them request some compensation from our beneficence.” Gale; likewise Columbus.—“Let them request a vicar.” *Proselthōsi tō epi topōn eparchō dikazonti*, Eusebius. That is: “let them approach the governor who administers justice in that province.” Valesius.—“Let them request a vicar,” namely, one who administers justice. Oxford and Cambridge editions.—“They shall apply to the vicars.” MAUCROIX. That is to say: they will ask the vicars to provide for their interests, as he notes in the margin of his translation: “Vicars were lieutenants of the praetorian prefect,” which I can translate no better than “vicars of the praetorian prefect.”—“They shall go to some magistrate.” English translation. Literally: “They shall approach some magistrate.”

[Col. 0831D] We may be permitted, even after the opinions of so many learned persons on this passage have been reported, to offer our own judgment, such as it is. Either the reading evidently followed by Eusebius—“If they request anything from our beneficence, let them apply to the Vicar”—is correct and genuine; and then not only is the current reading, “if they think,” plainly corrupt, but also *aliquid* (“anything”) belongs not to the following word *vicarium* (“vicar”), but to the preceding verb *petiverint* (“they request”), exactly as in the Greek, *aitēsōsi ti*; and thus “Vicar” must mean some person such as the eminent Cuperus indicated.

Or Licinius’ letter formerly read, in words, as we now have it: “If they think, let them request some compensation from our beneficence”; and then one must necessarily adopt at once Columbus’ punctuation and interpretation: “If they think, let them request from our beneficence some compensation,” understanding indemnity of whatever sort. Or finally, this punctuation, which no one has hitherto considered, must be adopted: “those who had received [them] as gifts, if they think [that they may claim] something from our beneficence”—that is, if there can nevertheless be persons who wish to settle accounts with us concerning the price of a thing which we gave them from our mere beneficence—“let them request something compensatory,” that is, something to take the place of the former gifts. Let those who read this choose what they prefer. For my part, I judge Eusebius’ reading preferable to the others, although “to think about a matter” must have been a very familiar Roman expression, and it is not unusual for *benevolentia* to be used not of the disposition of benevolence itself but of its token or favour. Thus, for example, Spartianus says of Caracalla: “He was neither slow in letters nor inactive in favours.” Compare Diazius, Baluzius, Cuperus, and Columbus, should more evidence be needed.

[Col. 0832B] “To the body of Christians.” “To the Christians.” English translation. Literally, “to Christians.”—Correctly. For just as “the Sabines” and “the body of the Sabines” are wholly interchangeable in Livy, in these words: “Being descended from the Sabines, and fearing that, because after the death of P. Tatius no king had ruled from their side, they might lose their share in sovereignty in an equal partnership, they wished a king to be created from their own body”—that is, one who was from among the Sabines—so in this letter of Licinius, “Christians” and “the body of Christians” are entirely synonymous and interchangeable expressions, which he merely varied so as not always to say “the same Christians.” Yet below, instead of “to the body of Christians,” one sees in one place in the same translation: “The Corporations or Assemblies of the Christians,” that is, “the bodies” or “assemblies of Christians”; and elsewhere again: “The Bodies corporate of the Christians,” that is, “the colleges” or “societies of Christians.”

“Not into those places.” Delete *in*. BOHERELLUS; likewise Gale.—The preposition must be deleted here, as I have also advised above. TOLLIUS.

“They were accustomed.” “Had used.” English translation. That is, “they had been accustomed.”—I do not reject this, even because of the preceding words: “if the same places to which they had formerly been accustomed to assemble.” Nor, I think, did Tollius reject it in relation to those words.

“Belonging to the right of their body.” That is, according to the English translation, belonging to them as a common body: “That belonged to them as a Body corporate.” For who could tolerate a literal translation such as “as to a corporate body”?

“Restore all these things according to the regulation which we have set forth above, without,” etc. Insert a slight pause after *comprehendimus* (“we have set forth”), which must be explained in the same sense as *comprehensum est* (“has been set forth”) in what follows. BOHERELLUS.—Emend: “we have set forth, and let them [restore] these things without,” etc.; this word appears to me to have fallen out. Otherwise one must read “which we have set forth,” as shortly afterward: “as has been set forth above.” TOLLIUS.—I preferred, partly with our Boherellus, to whom the Åbo edition also agrees, and partly by changing the order further, though slightly: “You shall order all these things to be restored to those same Christians—that is, to their body and assemblies—according to the regulation which we have set forth above, without any ambiguity or controversy whatsoever.” In this way the reading will be sound and most coherent with little effort.

“We are.” “The highest.” Åbo edition. Most corruptly.

“With our prosperous successes.” I would prefer: “with our prosperous successes,” or “with our successes flowing prosperously.” TOLLIUS.

[Col. 0833A] “But in order that the form of this ordinance of our beneficence may reach the knowledge of all, you must publish these writings by your proclamation, post them everywhere, and bring them to the knowledge of all.” Licinius now calls his enactment “this ordinance” and “these writings”; shortly before he had called the same thing “his command,” and indeed tacitly “his statute” and “his ordinance.” But it should be noted that nowhere did he likewise call it an edict; nor did our author, who, on the contrary, once and again used only the name “letters” to designate this disposition of Licinius.

First, near the beginning of this chapter: “Licinius ordered letters of this kind, given to the governor concerning the restoration of the Church, to be posted”; and again, almost at the end: “By these letters.” Hence a not unwelcome question now arises, whether the interpreters here, and many others elsewhere, both ancient and modern, correctly call this an edict. I should not think so, if we speak with greater precision. Rather, they are genuine letters with commands sent to a particular governor of Bithynia, from which he was at once obliged to extract the orders and then “to draw up and publish his edict, according to those commands, with a proclamation added.”

[Col. 0833B] Licinius himself says this in the present passage in the clearest words: “But in order that the form of this ordinance of our beneficence may reach the knowledge of all, you must publish these writings by your proclamation, post them everywhere, and bring them to the knowledge of all.” Pliny said it still more plainly before him, Book X, Letter 97, to Trajan: “When these things had been done, it had been their custom [the Christians’] to depart and to assemble again for a meal, ordinary and harmless; but that they had ceased to do even this after my edict, by which, according to your commands, I had forbidden associations.” Here you see not only that Trajan’s commands and Pliny’s edict are described as different things, but also that the emperor’s commands were the material of the governor’s edict; and for that reason Pliny called it not Trajan’s edict but his own: “after my edict.”

Before proceeding, we should frankly acknowledge that, in citing Pliny’s words in this argument, we are indebted to the letter of the eminent Cuperus to the distinguished Graevius, dated 7 April 1691. In confirmation of his note on this passage, he says: “An elegant passage to this effect occurs in Pliny, Book X, Letter 97: ‘When these things had been done, it had been their custom to depart and to assemble again for a meal, ordinary and harmless; but that they had ceased to do even this after my edict, by which, according to your commands, I had forbidden associations.’ For from this, most distinguished Father,” he continues, “the governor publicly testifies that he himself received an edict of this kind.” Thus far the most illustrious Cuperus.

“He also urged [them] by word.” Licinius, namely. PAGIUS.—And without any circumlocution: “When the edict was published, Licinius did likewise by word of mouth entreat all persons,” etc.

“Meeting-places.” “The churches.” Maucroix. That is, churches.

“Thus from the destruction of the Church.” Namely, of Nicomedia, according to the English translation: “And from the destruction [Col. 0833D] of the church of Nicomedia”; but Maucroix is undoubtedly better, following the Latin sense: “Thus from the ruin of the Church.” Compare chapter 3: “The Church was restored to its former state.”—“From the destruction of the Church”: that is, from 23 February A.D. 303. PAGIUS.

“Until its restoration.” “To the rebuilding of it.” English translation. That is, “until the restoration of it,” namely, the Nicomedian church.

“Until its restoration.” That is, until 13 June A.D. 313, on which day the edict concerning the restoration of churches was posted at Nicomedia. PAGIUS.

“Ten years, approximately four months.” The persecution therefore began on the seventh day before the Kalends of March. If from this one subtracts the time until 13 June, when this edict was posted, it will be found that ten years, three months, and nineteen days elapsed—that is, ten years and approximately four months. Oxford and Cambridge editions.

“Approximately four months.” Namely, three months and nineteen days. Thus peace was restored to the whole Church only in the year 313. PAGIUS.

## CHAPTER XLIX

“But the following Licinius,” etc. Correct and read: “with Licinius following.” TOLLIUS.

“The tyrant.” The English translation has “Maximinus,” whom it is certain is meant.

“He withdrew as a fugitive.” I would prefer “he retreated.” TOLLIUS.—What need is there for alteration? Terence, *Eunuch*, Act I, scene 2:

> I cannot obtain this from him, save that  
> at least you grant me two days’ leave to withdraw.

And in the *Mother-in-Law*, Act IV, scene 2:

> Here I see that I am undeservedly disliked; it is time to withdraw.

Thus the Latin *concedere*, used absolutely, means among other things “to yield” or “to give someone room by departing.” This latter phrase is also used by Terence in the *Self-Tormentor*, Act IV, scene 2:

> SY. Order him  
> to go away from here somewhere. CL. Where am I to go from here? SY. Wherever  
> you please; give them room.  
> Go take a walk.

“He seeks.” I prefer, with Columbus, “he sought.” TOLLIUS.

“Fortifications there,” etc. Rather, “and fortifications there,” as the distinguished Columbus also thinks should be read. TOLLIUS.—You may consult Columbus himself, if there is still any need.

“To block the route.” Licinius’ route, namely; the English translation added this for clarity.

“And from there, the victorious men breaking through toward the right.” I punctuate: “and from there, toward the right, the victorious men breaking through.” GALE.

“He was terrified (or he was attacked).” I think Lactantius wrote “he was attacked.” GRAEVIUS.

“He was terrified.” Above, “the supporter of Maxentius is driven into terror”; this verb likewise seems to me more correct here than the other. TOLLIUS.

[Col. 0834C] “Refuge.” “Escape.” GALE.—Yet competent authors also use *refugium*. Cicero: “He was the harbour and refuge of kings, peoples, and nations, and of the senate.” Suetonius: “He punished all of them with exile, lest anyone have any refuge in such treachery.” Nor was our author averse above to the verb “to flee for refuge”; his words in chapter 47 are: “An attack is made upon him, and he flees back to his own people.”

“As those are wont who in this final,” etc. Examples occur in Florus and Livy. GALE.—It is remarkable how closely relevant is another, wholly parallel passage of Lactantius, from *On the Blessed Life*, which until now we, along with the other commentators, had passed over: “As each sees himself approach in advancing years toward old age that day on which he must depart from this life, let him consider how pure he departs, how innocent he comes before the judge; not as certain persons do, relying on blinded minds, who, when the powers of the body are already failing, are reminded of their last necessity only in order that they may devote themselves more greedily and more ardently to satisfying their lusts.”

“And thus he drank poison.” Therefore he did not perish by a simple death, as Victor’s epitome relates. Oxford and Cambridge editions.

“And thus.” That is, “and afterward,” a sense which we wished earlier to indicate. The translators agree: “After which he took the deadly draught.” MAUCROIX. “And then he took poison.” English translation. But perhaps nothing can better show that *sic* is sometimes an adverb of sequence than this passage of Vulcatius Gallicanus on Avidius Cassius: “My mother Faustina thus urged your father Pius in the rebellion of Celsus: that he should first preserve loyalty toward his own people, then toward strangers.” Since the matter itself speaks, I add no word. Let Cicero alone be heard, using “first” and “afterward” in a similar sequence and meaning: “I consult first for the safety of the citizens and afterward for their dignity.”

“He could not [do so] at the time.” An example may be added by those who wish to collect passages in which *praesens* does not refer at all to the present time of now, but to the time then present [Col. 0835A]—thus, if one may say it in one word, a present past—such examples occurring in Cicero and others.

“Torments.” Cicero too will not fail those seeking an example. *Philippics* XI: “Nor indeed are the tortures of executioners more grievous than are sometimes the torments of diseases.”

“Insupportable.” I do not know whether anyone before our author ever spoke thus. But certainly this epithet cannot be defended from Cicero.

“Earth dug up with his hands,” etc. That is, as the English translation excellently expressed it, earth excavated by his hands: “He ate earth which he dug up with his hands.”

“As he struck his head against the walls.” Namely, through impatience under his tortures. For already four days of madness had passed. Suetonius similarly represents Augustus striking his head against doors through grief at the loss of Varus’ legions, in *Augustus*, chapter 23. See that passage and Casaubon’s notes upon it; likewise what Baluzius notes above.

“His eyes sprang from their sockets.” “While he was still alive, the pupils themselves leapt spontaneously from his eyes; Maximinus was in such a condition.” Chrysostom, in the oration *On Saint Babylas against the Pagans*. See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IX, chapter 10. Cambridge edition.

“He began to see God with ministers in white garments,” etc. “He saw God surrounded by his angels.” Maucroix, who therefore evidently wished the text to be corrected to: “He began to see God surrounded by ministers.”—“A vision represented him to his imagination as standing to be judged by God, who seemed to have hosts of ministers about him, all in white garments.” English translation. As though the earlier reading had instead been: “He began to see God, surrounded by ministers in white garments, judging him.”

“Ministers in white garments.” Of the same Maximinus, Simeon Metaphrastes in Surius, vol. VI, p. 929, says that he was scourged by angels. COLOMESIUS.

“Then, as though compelled by tortures, he confessed.” Namely, “that he had done [these things],” supplied from the common construction, as the translators understood it. Unless, with the distinguished Gale, one prefers to supply “Christ” from what follows, punctuating: “Then, as though compelled by tortures, he confessed Christ.”

[Col. 0835C] “He breathed out his guilty spirit.” Baluzius rightly observes in his notes that Maximinus did not immediately die and reach Tarsus, but endured extremely severe pains for some time; thus he does not seem to have died before August. For, since he had to travel several miles in order to reach Tarsus, a city of Cilicia, and first halted in Cappadocia and then in the narrows of Mount Taurus, where he constructed fortifications and towers to ward off the pursuing attacks of Licinius’ forces, it could scarcely have happened that one who arrived at Nicomedia on the Kalends of May reached Tarsus before the following July. Thus Maximinus does not appear to have died before August. PAGIUS.

## CHAPTER L

“Having gained control of the whole realm.” Namely, in the year 312. PAGIUS.

In the first place Valeria, whom, etc. Thus today the most illustrious Baluzius, who had previously, following an old slip, printed “in the first place Valerius, whom”; whence shortly afterward Sparke, in the Oxford edition of 1680: “It should be written,” he says, “following the correction of the reverend gentleman, ‘Valeria, whom.’” Thus Baluzius’s painstaking search for Valerius is in vain. This judgment, repeated again later in subsequent editions, is endorsed above, not unwittingly, by Baluzius, likewise by Cuper, and also by the English translation in this form: “For Licinius being now settled in the Empire, gave order to put both Valeria and Candidian to death.” Yet apart from this edition there is none which does not, with the manuscript codex, have in the author’s words “Valerium quem.” And, what is more noteworthy, that the manuscript reading can stand perfectly well is maintained and argued by Pagi in his *Baronian Criticism*, as follows.—“In the first place Valerius”: namely Valerius Valens, of whom we spoke under the year 306, no. 14 (indeed, 15), thus: “At almost the same time at which Alexander, who held the office of praetorian prefect [Col. 0836A] of Africa, was made emperor at Carthage, Valens was created emperor,” says Victor in his epitome; after relating Maximian’s death, he adds: “Valens is punished with death by Licinius.” Lactantius speaks of this Valens in book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 50, as the most learned Abbot Louis du Four first observed in a letter written to me. There Lactantius, after recounting Maximinus’s death, says: “Licinius, having gained supreme power, first ordered Valerius to be killed, whom Maximinus in anger had not dared to kill even after his flight, when he saw that he himself must perish.” Nor can it be doubted that this Valerius is the same as the Valens mentioned by Victor, since Goltzius, among the coins of the Thirty Tyrants who afflicted the Roman commonwealth during Gallienus’s reign, records this one: ΑΥΤ. Κ. πΟΥ. ΟΥΑΛΕΡ. ΟΥΑΛΕΝΣ. CEB. L. A., that is, “Emperor Caesar Publius Valerius Valens Augustus. Year one.” Yet that coin belongs altogether to Valerius Valens, killed by Licinius’s order, and not to the Valens who, after Valerian was taken captive by the enemy, seized tyranny [Col. 0836B] (as Pollio testifies, book *On the Thirty Tyrants*, chapter 19), although Mediobarbus attributes it to this Valens, who ruled briefly in Macedonia. PAGI, cited above, under A.D. 314, no. 12, and 306, no. 15.

Compare now, first of all, Toinard, who agrees and argues in support; then Maucroix’s translation, which likewise does not dissent: “For first Licinius has Valerius put to death”; in which, as the sequel and the genius of the language together show, Valerius rather than Valeria is understood; finally, the most distinguished Cuper, who raises various objections to Pagi and his followers in his letter to the most illustrious Voetius.

Likewise Candidianus. The manuscript codex, which all earlier editions had followed, likewise has “Candidianum.” But certainly it must either be corrected, with Baluzius, again to “Candidianum”; or, with us, by introducing an adverb of sequence, “then Candidianus”; or, by almost a mere transposition of letters, “afterward Candidianus.”

[Col. 0836C] Candidianus. The son of Galerius and a concubine, as Maucroix observes in the margin of his translation.—“Candidian was her adopted son, for his mother was a concubine of Maximian.” English translation. Literally: Candidianus was Valeria’s adopted son; for his mother was Maximian’s concubine.

Valeria. In place of this woman’s name, through a gross typographical error, “Valerius” is read in Pagi’s *Baronian Criticism*, under A.D. 314, no. 12, where this entire chapter is transcribed. Compare only the same work under A.D. 303, no. 6.

Yet “the woman.” Perhaps “the woman immediately,” or “for the woman.” TOLLIUS.—I emend: “The woman at last.” GALE.

“When she learned that he was alive.” Who is meant, and what is the sense? For the translators differ astonishingly on both points.—“This lady, having learned that Candidianus was not dead.” Maucroix. That is, when the woman had learned that Candidianus was not dead.—“She had no sooner got the news of Maximinus’s death, etc.” English translation. That is, the woman had scarcely received news of Maximinus’s death. [Col. 0836D]—For my part, first of all—and I ask that this be taken in good part—it seemed to me that there could be no sense whatever in speaking here of Maximinus. What further I think, I shall say shortly.

“Alive.” I read “victorious.” But I understand the preceding “him” to mean Licinius. BOHERELLUS.—“Alive”: restore “victorious.” GALE; likewise Colomesius.—It should read “victorious” and refer to Licinius. “Had learned” should likewise be corrected for “learned”; and shortly afterward “had mingled herself” for “mingled herself.” TOLLIUS.—It seemed more plausible that “had escaped by force,” or simply “had escaped,” should be read: so that, after Licinius had ordered Candidianus killed, Candidianus, aware of the order, found a way on the first occasion to escape from the place where he was to be slaughtered; and Valeria, having learned that he had happily broken out from there, changed her dress and joined the entourage of her adopted son, in order to observe his fortune.

“His entourage.” Here again, according to mutually opposed hypotheses of the interpreters, the translations go in opposite directions: the French, namely, explaining it of Candidianus’s companions; the English, of the court—that is, the courtiers—of Maximinus, who had most recently died: “She had no sooner got the news of Maximinus’s death, then she came to his Court in disguise.”

“Because at Nicomedia.” I write, “He who, when…” Sparke, in both Oxford editions; and the Cambridge edition is not different.

“Because at Nicomedia.” Read with Columbus: “he who, because at Nicomedia…” TOLLIUS.

“And she, upon hearing of his death.” That is—as Maucroix explains every point, though the matter is by no means obscure—when Valeria had heard of Candidianus’s death. Compare, if it is worthwhile, what we noted on the word *exitus* [death, departure].

“Who all.” But only two were mentioned above: Candidianus and Severianus. TOLLIUS.—Rather, three: Candidianus, Severianus, and before both, Valerius, or Valeria, according as at the beginning of the chapter one prefers to read: “Licinius, having gained supreme power, first [ordered] Valerius … [whom Maximian] had [Col. 0837B] not dared to kill,” or “first Valeria”; and it is remarkable that this woman or man should be overlooked by Tollius after such explicit words.

“Fearing him as an evil.” That is, according to the English translation, “fearing him as an evil man”: “looking on him as an ill man.”—It should be read: “fearing him as a rival.” GRAEVIUS.—Perhaps: “fearing him as angry.” TOLLIUS.—I suspected that “fearing [him] as an evil” is a phrase taken from common usage, like the French expression: *il le craignait comme la peste* [he feared him like the plague].

“Before Valeria (or, except for Valeria), who willingly, etc.” But above it has already been said that Licinius fled. See what learned men noted on chapter 39. Therefore you would more rightly change τὸ *volens* [willing] into *nolens* [unwilling], with Cuper. Hence it is clear that Maximinus was inflamed by no less avarice than lust in seeking marriage with Valeria. TOLL.

“Before Valeria, who willingly, etc.” Thus all the interpreters, so that those who consult them will understand immediately.

“His own son, the eldest, being eight years old.” Delete *suum* [his own]. BOHERELLUS.—Perhaps more correctly: “a son then just reaching eight years.” TOLLIUS.—I emend: “his eldest son, now eight years old.” GALE.

“Their mother.” Maximinus’s wife, concerning whose name there is profound silence among scholars. Oxford and Cambridge editions.

“She was cast into the East.” Into the Orontes. Abo edition. “Into the River Orontes.” That is, into the river Orontes. English translation.

“The East.” It should be written: “the Orontes,” that is, a river of Syria, or “a torrent,” following the correction of the reverend gentleman praised above. Oxford and Cambridge editions.—Read “torrent,” or rather “Orontes.” ALLIX.—Read “Orontes.” VOSSIUS.—Maucroix literally: “Their mother was thrown into the East,” which very few will doubtless approve.

“There he had often ordered chaste women to be drowned.” “There to be drowned,” as above in chapters 15 and 37, “to be drowned in the sea”; hence I think the most learned man who deletes τὸ *ibi* [there] should be given less heed.

“She.” Correct and read “he”: namely, Maximian. [Col. 0837D] Look back to chapter 38: thus the law of retaliation befell him, so that his own wife died by the same punishment by which he had ordered other men’s wives killed. TOLLIUS.

“She.” Both translators followed this reading.

“Thus all the impious,” etc. John of Salisbury, in the *Polycraticus*, book VIII, chapter 19, on Domitian: “And because Domitian tore apart the Church of God, indeed the whole empire as well, he too, by God’s same judgment acting upon him, was torn apart.” TOLLIUS.

## CHAPTER LI

“Fifteen months.” “During the space of eighteen months.” English translation: as though our text read “eighteen months”; I do not perceive the reason for this discrepancy.

“In plebeian dress.” “In the habit of a Peasant.” The same [Col. 0838A] translation. Literally, “in the dress of country people,” which is somewhat freer.

“With her mother.” Namely Prisca. PAGI.

“She paid the penalty.” With no charge at all fabricated against her: such is the opinion of the most distinguished man. I could scarcely believe it, both because of the very term “penalties” used here, and because of what follows, where both women are said to have been led to punishment—and a most severe one. For each had her head cut off, and shortly thereafter their bodies were thrown into the sea. Add that we have not seen even Valeria’s friends condemned in the preceding passages unless adultery had first been fabricated against them, namely at the end of chapter 39.

“Thus their chastity and rank proved their ruin.” Because Valeria had refused to marry both Licinius and Maximian. TOLLIUS.—But even in that age, for example among women, it was therefore regarded as part of chastity to have been the wife of only one man. For it is known to everyone from Tertullian’s book *On Monogamy* that in his own time he, together with the Montanists, required monogamy in both sexes. Meanwhile, it should be observed that the rank which our author mentions here [Col. 0838B] was indeed equally fatal to mother and daughter—or, what is the same thing, to Prisca and Valeria—according to the English translation; but the added mention of chastity pertains specifically to Valeria. The words are: “so fatal did their Dignity and Valeria’s chastity prove to them.”

## CHAPTER LII

“All these things I relate on the testimony of those who know them, so that, etc.” After *loquor* [I relate], I supply *et* or *atque*: “and thus I judged that the deeds as they occurred should be committed to writing.” BOHERELLUS.—Similarly the English translation: “and I have thought fit to write them just as they were transacted.” Cuper, however, differently.

“[So that it] might not corrupt the truth.” *Non* [not] would better be absent. BOHERELLUS.

“Mercy” (*pietati*). That is, clemency, kindness. See the notes on Ausonius. TOLLIUS.

“He looked upon the earth.” As in chapter 5: “For God looked upon the affliction of his people.” Therefore, cast down from the height [Col. 0838C] of imperial power, etc.

“Where now are those magnificent and illustrious titles of the Jovians and Herculians among the nations, which first, etc., flourished?” It should be noted, lest this seem written too rhetorically and contrary to historical truth, that our author does not simply ask, “Where now are the titles of the Jovians and Herculians?” as though, after Diocletian and Herculius had once died, no one ever used them again in any manner; but: “Where now are those magnificent and illustrious titles of the Jovians and Herculians among the nations, which, first assumed insolently by Diocletian and Maximian and afterward transmitted to their successors, flourished?” Thus he denies only that they were equally magnificent and illustrious among the nations, and still flourishing while he wrote, as they had first been under Diocletian himself and Maximian Herculius; and this is altogether certain.

“Of the Jovians and Herculians.” As though they derived their lineage from Jupiter and Hercules. Oxford and Cambridge editions.

[Col. 0838D] “Maximian.” Namely the one whom we have just called Herculius. For the other, Galerius Maximian, bore the cognomen Jovius, in imitation of Diocletian; and here, moreover, the discussion concerns him who first bestowed upon himself the name Herculius.

“Namely, the Lord destroyed them and erased them from the earth.” Inasmuch as Diocletian and Maximian themselves, who had first so insolently assumed the cognomens, the one Jovius and the other Herculius, and through whom these titles at the same time became so illustrious and magnificent among the nations, were divinely removed from the land and number of the living.

“Let us celebrate with daily and nightly prayers.” I would prefer “let us entreat.” For *celebremus* [let us celebrate] occurs a little earlier. BOHERELLUS.—The learned man who supervised the Abo edition thought that something was missing before “with daily [prayers],” and wished this marked with an asterisk.

“That he may preserve his mercy also for his servants, etc.” Read: “that he may preserve his mercy and, now propitious and gentle to his servants, [Col. 0839A] [may avert] all snares, etc.,” deleting τῷ *ut*. TOLLIUS.—For *servet etiam* [may preserve also], I restore *servet aeternam* [may preserve everlasting]. BOHERELLUS.—What if the author’s own hand wrote rather: “that he may preserve his mercy again and again, propitious and gentle to his servants”? Then afterward, “that [he may avert] all snares,” and what follows; and finally, with *ut* [that] elegantly repeated a third time without conjunction, “that [he may protect] the flourishing [churches],” and what follows.

“Of the Devil.” *Zabuli*, as earlier. GALE.—Namely in chapter 16, in two places.

“That he may guard the flourishing Churches in perpetual peace.” The reading of the old codex and of all editions hitherto is: “that he may guard the flourishing Church of perpetual peace.” [Col. 0840A] But that reading had long ago been corrected, as you now see it printed, by the most illustrious Baluzius in the errata of his first edition, and afterward by others with him, or differently, as I set out below.

“Church of perpetual peace.” Write: “the Churches in perpetual peace.” Oxford and Cambridge editions; likewise Allix.

“That he may guard the flourishing Church of perpetual peace.” I have no doubt that one should read: “That he may guard the perpetual peace of the flourishing Church”; this was also the opinion of Nicolaus Heinsius, as I once learned from the lips of the greatest and most beloved man, when I discussed this passage with him while he was still living. GRAEVIUS.

[Col. 0839]

# DISSERTATION ON THE BOOK OF LUCIUS CECILIUS, *ON THE DEATHS OF THE PERSECUTORS*, ADDRESSED TO DONATUS THE CONFESSOR, HITHERTO ATTRIBUTED TO LUCIUS CAECILIUS FIRMIANUS LACTANTIUS

*(BY DOM LE NOURRY)*

## PREFACE

[Col. 0839B]

We have been led to publish this dissertation anew with fresh efforts chiefly for two reasons, neither of slight importance. First, throughout this second volume of our apparatus, and in no small part of the preceding one, we have examined by what arguments, and arguments of what wholly invincible force, the most ancient defenders of the Christian religion demonstrated its truth against the pagans. It therefore seemed that one thing remained to be established: what was the outcome of such great struggles, and what the victory. Cecilius, moreover, has made this plain to all in this book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*. For his whole purpose in it is to disclose what and how great penalties the enemies of the Christian name suffered at the hands of Almighty God, the avenger [Col. 0839C] of crimes, and what an admirable triumph our true religion achieved over the impious superstitions of the Gentiles. We therefore judged that this dissertation should be appended to our preceding dissertations as their complement, so that those who in them have watched the battles of learned champions may in this one see and admire the victories and triumph.

Moreover, several most distinguished men, to whose wishes, because of their outstanding learning and singular goodwill toward us, we think it wrong not to respond, have urged us in speech and writing to reprint this dissertation. For they do not think it enough that some have been compelled openly to admit that the two names Firmianus Lactantius were rather boldly added to the title of this book against the testimony of the one surviving manuscript codex. [Col. 0839D] Nor do they yet judge it sufficient that many have thought that the arguments by which this book is shown to have been falsely attributed to Lactantius outweigh the arguments advanced by defenders of the contrary opinion. They even add that it is not enough that some have subscribed to our opinion in published writings. But they further demanded that we answer a certain writer who has attempted to weaken the force of our arguments by his own judgment rather than by sound reasons. We could therefore no longer resist their wish, or rather command. Accordingly, we shall examine and refute in their proper places in this dissertation the objections made against us by that learned writer, while wishing, nevertheless, that nothing be detracted from the honor due to him. From him, however, and from others who never wish to abandon an opinion once preconceived, we ask this one thing: if at any time they undertake again to examine or refute our arguments, let them not diminish their force, but deign to set them forth [Col. 0840C] as they are proposed by us. Then, if they refute them rightly and establish and confirm their own position by other reasons of greater weight and importance, we shall yield quickly and willingly. For we have openly professed, and still profess, that in writing our purpose and aim are none other than that the truth, if possible, may be perceived by all.

# CHAPTER ONE

Analysis of this book; and concerning its sole manuscript codex, title, argument, and why and at what time it was published by Lucius Cecilius.

## ARTICLE ONE

Analysis of this book.

[Col. 0840D] Although this book is composed with such brevity of style that it can quickly be read through by all, nevertheless, because there occur in it very many passages shamefully corrupted, gaping with lacunae and mutilated by accident, while others are obscure and exceedingly difficult to understand, we have judged that an analysis of it should be provided, so that less experienced readers may more easily [Col. 0841A] understand those matters which its author has treated with no small ambiguity and with various verbal circumlocutions.

1. From the very beginning of this book, Cecilius addresses Donatus and asserts that the prayers of him and of the other confessors were heard by God, who, having restored peace to the Christian Church, had restored to it its former splendor. But those who had raged against it, he says, were overthrown by rulers divinely raised up and paid, by a death worthy of their crimes, the penalty for their offenses to God, the most just judge and avenger of crimes. He promises that he will demonstrate this in the present book.

2. Before beginning with Nero, he briefly explains how, at the end of the reign of Caesar Tiberius, Christ died under the consulship of the two Gemini, [Col. 0841B] was restored to life on the third day, instructed his disciples in divine precepts, and afterward was taken up into heaven. Then his eleven disciples, having added Matthias and Paul, laid the foundations of the Church in all provinces and cities over twenty-five years. But afterward Peter, having performed certain miracles and converted many from the errors of the Gentiles to the true faith of Christ, Nero ordered him to be crucified and Paul to be killed. Yet that cruel tyrant was suddenly removed from the midst of men for so great a crime, and no place of his burial was ever found. Hence certain deranged persons invented that he had been preserved, so that at the end of the world he might be the forerunner of Antichrist.

3. After several years had intervened, Domitian reigned long and safely. But when he began to harass Christians, he was immediately killed in his own house. After his murder, the Senate annulled his acts, his images were destroyed, his honorary inscriptions overthrown, and thereafter the Church of Christ flourished more vigorously under good rulers during a long period of peace.

4. After many years Decius indeed broke this peace, but not with impunity. For, having joined battle with the Carpi and lost the greater part of his army, he himself was killed; and his unburied body became food and fodder for beasts and birds.

5. After this Valerian indeed shed much Christian blood, though for a short time; but he long paid the penalty of such inhumanity with the greatest disgrace. For Sapor, king of the Persians, by whom he had been captured in war, never mounted a horse or a chariot unless he set his foot, not without insults, upon [Col. 0841D] Valerian’s back. Indeed, when Valerian died in this most shameful servitude, his skin was stripped off and hung in a barbarian temple as an everlasting memorial of so great a disgrace.

6. Aurelian, however, was in no way moved by this example and issued bloody laws against Christians. But scarcely had these reached the more distant provinces when he lay dead at Coenofrurium in Thrace.

7. Having touched lightly upon these matters, Cecilius comes to Diocletian and speaks much more fully of him and of the other emperors down to Constantine the Great and Licinius. Diocletian, he says, the inventor of crimes and contriver of evils, corrupted everything through avarice and timidity. For he made three men partners in the Roman Empire, which he divided into four parts; and they, in order to assemble and maintain great armies, utterly crushed all the provinces, divided into fragments, by immense levies, tributes, and taxes, trampling even more sacred laws underfoot. Yet Diocletian, with greater and insatiable avarice, would not allow his treasuries to be diminished, and amassed other riches through countless exactions and capital punishments. With wealth thus most unjustly extorted, he scarcely satisfied his boundless desire to construct circuses, basilicas, houses, palaces, a mint, and weapons. Such was his desire that he wished Nicomedia to rival Rome.

8. Nor was Maximian Herculius altogether unlike him, except that he was not so concerned with preserving wealth. But by unbridled lust he weakened and corrupted morals, and wherever he journeyed he tore the daughters of leading men and other virgins from their parents’ sight and violated them.

9. Although Cecilius has related more about Constantius in this book, he nevertheless warns us there that he passes him over for the present because, wholly unlike all the others, he was worthy to hold the reins of the whole Roman Empire. He therefore turns to Maximian Galerius, Diocletian’s son-in-law, worse than all the rest. Born of a Transdanubian mother, terrifying through his inborn barbarity and monstrous bodily bulk, he struck fear into everyone by his appearance, words, and deeds. Diocletian therefore feared everything from him, especially after he won a notable victory over Narses, king of the Persians. For then he became more insolent, disdained the name Caesar, and wished to appear born of Mars.

10. Cecilius says no more there of Galerius’s wicked deeds, lest he disturb the order of time, and thus explains the cause of the persecution of Christians stirred up by Diocletian, previously called Diocles: when, in the East, Diocletian was sacrificing cattle to false gods, demons were put to flight by the sign of the cross made by certain bystanders; the rites were thrown into confusion, and repeated slaughterings of victims were ineffectual. The chief of the soothsayers, however, attributed this great confusion and disturbance of the rites to the Christians standing by. Whereupon Diocletian, raging in anger, first ordered all persons in the palace, and even the soldiers, to be compelled to sacrifice.

11–12. He then came to Nicomedia, whither Maximian Galerius hastened. Overcome by the complaints and instigations of his mother, who was astonishingly superstitious, Galerius pressed Diocletian most fiercely to remove Christians utterly. But Diocletian resisted him long, until, after holding consultation throughout the winter with friends, judges, and others concerning the matter, he yielded only after the response of the Milesian Apollo had been received. Yet he did not wish any Christian to be punished by death.

13. But on the seventh day before the Kalends of March, when the Terminalia were celebrated, he set out with commanders and tribunes and proceeded to the church. Its doors were broken down; the image of God was sought in vain; the sacred Scriptures were burned; and the whole church was razed to the ground. On the following day an edict against Christians was promulgated; it was torn up by a certain man, who for that reason was burned after various tortures.

14–15. Galerius, however, not at all content with the provisions of this edict, arranged for Christians to be accused of the burning of the palace—set on fire by his own agents—and of treason, in order to inflame Diocletian further against them. Therefore Diocletian, so that those guilty of such a great crime might be identified, ordered very many innocent people, whether he was present or absent, to be tortured, racked, and tormented by fire. Galerius, still inflamed with anger, contrived another fire fifteen days later. But when it was quickly extinguished, he departed in midwinter, lest, as he said, he be burned alive.

16. Diocletian therefore, then raging with monstrous fury against all, compelled his wife Prisca and daughter Valeria, while his prefects compelled others, to be defiled by impious sacrifices. Those who refused—people of every sex and age—they killed by various kinds of death and tortures hitherto unheard of. Meanwhile letters were sent to Herculius and Constantius that they should do the same everywhere. Herculius obeyed this exceedingly cruel command; but Constantius allowed only the meeting houses to be destroyed and kept the people unharmed. Christians throughout the whole world, except in Gaul, were then tortured by punishments so many and so great that no one could ever describe them. Donatus, however, endured various most bitter torments of whippings, claws, fire, and iron under the prefect Flaccinus and the governors Hierocles and Priscillianus, with truly wondrous and unconquered patience.

17. Diocletian, however, began to be afflicted with deserved calamities for so great crimes. For a few days after celebrating at Rome, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, his twentieth anniversary, he came to Ravenna in order to assume there his ninth consulship. Then, with rain and cold raging, he was seized during that journey by a slight illness. After spending the summer there, he made his way to Nicomedia by a circuitous route along the bank of the Striga, in order to dedicate the Circus there.
