But while still on the journey, his illness so returned that shortly after his arrival in that city he was believed to be dead. Nor could he dispel the suspicion of his death until he showed himself to everyone on the Ides of December—yet so that no one could recognize him any longer. Although he was better, he nevertheless raved at fixed hours.

18–19. A few days later Galerius, who had already frightened Herculius by raising the specter of civil war, flew there. In a long conversation, which Cecilius presents in full, between him and Diocletian, he finally persuaded the latter, though with difficulty, to abdicate after new Caesars had been created. The wretched Diocletian therefore, with tears and groans, proclaimed Severus and Maximinus Daia Caesars on the Kalends of May, rejecting Constantine; and, having removed the purple from himself, he clothed Maximinus in it. Having laid it aside, he again became Diocles and returned to his homeland.

20. But Galerius, having attained supreme rule, despised Constantius because of his infirm health. He had already resolved that after Constantius’s death, which he hoped would come shortly, he would make Licinius emperor and his own nine-year-old son Caesar, and that, after celebrating his own twentieth anniversary, he would leave Severus and Licinius as Augusti, Maximinus and Candidianus as Caesars, and spend a secure and tranquil old age after laying down imperial power.

21–23. Meanwhile, intent on harassing the world, he planned indeed to reduce the Romans to slavery after the fashion of the Persians. But because he did not dare do so openly, he first removed the honors of noble men and ordered the leading citizens of towns to be tortured, respectable and noble matrons to be carried off into the women’s quarters, and others to be thrown before his eyes, for amusement, to the fiercest bears he possessed. Finally, that most savage tyrant was accustomed never to dine without human blood having been shed. Christians were first driven into exile under laws issued by him; but afterward they were burned limb by limb with slow fires, and their bodies, reduced to ashes and cinders, were thrown into the sea and rivers. Moreover, no punishment was slight under him, not only for Christians but for all pagans as well. Eloquence and letters were likewise extinguished by him; advocates were removed; jurists were banished or killed; and all laws were ruined. Furthermore, he oppressed men of every age and rank with such taxes and poll taxes, exacted even for the dead, that very many perished by hunger. Only beggars remained; because they were unable to pay, he ordered them gathered together, placed in small boats, and drowned in the sea.

24. Meanwhile, Constantius, seriously ill, requested by letter that his son Constantine be returned to him by Galerius, who had often tried to take Constantine’s life. The tyrant pretended to grant the request and gave Constantine, whom he wished to keep, authorization to depart the next day. But immediately after dinner Constantine escaped, committed himself to the hazards of the journey, and, removing the public horses at every posting station so that no one could pursue him, flew to his father. From the hands of his father, now on the point of death, he received the empire and immediately issued his first law in favor of the Christian religion.

25–26. Galerius, however, shortly afterward received with the greatest displeasure Constantine’s laureate image, brought to him according to custom; he made Severus emperor and Constantine Caesar. But the soldiers, angered because Galerius had abolished the praetorian camp, and the Romans, most impatiently enduring the dreadful census officials sent to register the populace, clothed Maxentius in purple. Therefore Galerius sent Severus to Rome with the army of his father Herculius against the new Caesar. But when Severus came nearer to the walls of the City, he was deserted by his own men and fled to Ravenna. Fearing that he would be handed over to Herculius, who had most willingly resumed the purple of Augustus offered by Galerius, Severus laid down his own purple and, with his veins cut, lost his life together with his empire.

27. But Herculius, in turn fearing Galerius, came into Gaul to win Constantine to himself through marriage with his younger daughter. Galerius himself attempted in vain to invade Rome, hitherto unseen by him. For, since the legions detested so great a crime, he feared Severus’s fate and, taking flight, returned to his own seats after leaving Italy to be most cruelly ravaged by his soldiers.

28–29. Thereupon Herculius returned from Gaul to Rome, where he held joint rule with Maxentius. But because in a public assembly he had torn the purple from Maxentius’s shoulders, he was expelled from that city like Tarquinius Superbus. He therefore went through Gaul to Galerius, intending, under the pretext of reconciliation, to kill him and despoil him of his kingdom. But when he learned that Licinius had been made emperor by Galerius in Diocles’s presence, he again fled to Constantine. In order more easily to deceive him, he laid aside the purple and persuaded Constantine, still a young man, to set out with a few soldiers against the barbarians. Not long afterward, this wicked traitor resumed the purple, plundered Constantine’s treasuries, fled, and seized Massilia. But Constantine, returning with remarkable speed, besieged the city; after peace was offered in vain, he captured Herculius and, having stripped him of the imperial dress of rebellion, did not wish to deprive him of life.

30–32. Yet no better for this, Herculius laid other snares for Constantine. But when these were exposed by Fausta, he had a eunuch cut down in Constantine’s place. Therefore he was compelled to pay the penalty for so great a crime by hanging. Meanwhile, in order to incur great expenditures in celebrating his twentieth anniversary, Galerius overwhelmed everyone with intolerable taxes. But, overcome by the stubbornness of Maximinus, who most bitterly resented being named third among the Caesars, Galerius abolished the title of Caesar, called himself and Licinius Augusti, and called Maxentius and Constantine sons of the Augusti. But Maximinus replied that he had been acclaimed emperor in the Campus Martius.

33–35. Galerius was then in the eighteenth year of his reign when he was struck by a horrifying and incurable wound in the lower part of his genitals. Our Cecilius describes at length this disease and the remedies uselessly applied for a whole year. There he presents the edict issued by Galerius when he was near death, in favor of the Christian religion and in order to appease God. When it was promulgated at Nicomedia, Donatus was brought out of prison with the other Christian confessors. Galerius, having handed over his wife and son to Licinius’s custody, died consumed by a dreadful wasting disease.

36–37. Then, on receiving news of Galerius’s death, Maximinus abolished the census and entered Bithynia, so that he might more easily bring all the provinces as far as the Chalcedonian strait under his dominion. A quarrel then arose between him and Licinius; they were already preparing to go to war, but they made peace on that very strait under fixed terms. With matters thus settled, Maximinus returned more secure and turned his mind to torturing Christians. He therefore ordered their eyes gouged out and their hands cut off, and immediately established new priests of his gods in the provinces to compel these same disciples of Christ to perform impious sacrifices. Yet deterred from persecuting Christians by Constantine’s letters, he dissembled, but allowed them secretly to be drowned in the waves of the sea. Moreover, in order to kill them by hunger or contaminate them with prohibited foods, he was the first of all to order every animal we eat to be sacrificed at the altars of the gods, and everything necessary for food to be consecrated by libation, sacrificed, or sprinkled with wine. Finally, he oppressed not only Christians but all others with such taxes that, after famine had arisen from this and all that Diocles and Herculius had left had been swept away, he granted human beings mere use of life, like a bandit, as a great benefit.

38–42. But that lust of his, described by Caecilius, was so utterly unbridled [Col. 0846B] that the chastity of no freeborn woman or virgin could be safe, save perhaps through ugliness. Moreover, being the first to taste every marriage-bed, he gave over to marriage with any petitioner the virgins whom he had himself corrupted, and the women of rank violated by others. Those who refused were subjected to violence by his bodyguards, nearly all of them Goths, by whose agency he made the Romans and the East a mockery. Indeed, that wicked man banished Augusta, who begged to be spared marriage with him, hither and thither together with her mother. Her female companions he falsely condemned for adultery. Caecilius particularly recounts three noble women among them who, falsely and undeservedly accused of this crime by a certain Jew, were led away to execution amid ranks of armed men. The shameless Jewish calumniator [Col. 0846C] was afterwards affixed to the gibbet and thereby publicly declared their innocence, though too late. When Diocletian asked through various embassies that Augusta, banished into the deserts of Syria, be restored to him, Maximinus always refused. At the same time, by Constantine’s order, the images and statues of Herculius and of the still-living Diocletian were overthrown. Consequently Diocletian, struck by intolerable grief and weary of life, brought death upon himself through hunger and anguish.

43–44. Thus Maximinus alone remained of all God’s adversaries. Since he altogether distrusted the betrothal of Licinius and Constantine’s sister, he sent ambassadors to Rome and made an alliance with Maxentius, who desired nothing more. Maxentius was then staying at Rome and had declared war upon Constantine. [Col. 0846D] But when battle with the enemy was required, terrified by a certain oracle, he did not dare to set foot outside the City. He therefore sent generals who, equipped with forces greater than Constantine’s, prevailed in the first assault. Constantine, however, having taken courage, moved his soldiers closer to the City opposite the Milvian Bridge; and, having seen the heavenly sign of the cross and marked it upon the shields, he entered the contest, in which the combatants fought with equal spirit. This was announced at Rome, and a sedition arose: Maxentius was reproached, and at the Circus games it was shouted aloud that Constantine could not be conquered. Moved by these cries and by an answer received from the Sibylline Books, the tyrant advanced into battle. The fighting was renewed; he was terrified and put to flight, and while striving to escape, [Col. 0847A] he was thrown from the bridge into the Tiber. Constantine the victor was received in the city of Rome with the greatest joy and honored by the Senate with the title of foremost rank. But Maximinus, although he heard these things not without the deepest grief, could not refrain from wholly ill-timed insults and jests.

45–47. Constantine settled affairs in the City and came to Milan. While there the marriage of his sister and Licinius was being celebrated, Maximinus led his army from Syria into Bithynia in the severity of winter, though his column was utterly exhausted. Nevertheless, he crossed the strait and, after eleven days of siege, brought Byzantium under his power, and shortly afterwards Heraclea. Licinius hastened up and, having passed Adrianople, came to meet him, though with inferior [Col. 0847B] forces. Therefore, seeing that battle would take place within a few days, Maximinus vowed to his Jupiter that, if victorious, he would exterminate the Christians. Licinius, resting on the night before battle, learned from an angel a prayer which, if uttered, would enable him to defeat the enemy. Then Maximinus moved camp and, scorning Licinius, with whom he had held discussion, could never be brought to accept peace. On the day before the Kalends of May they came to blows, and Licinius’s soldiers attacked the enemy in the first onset. No less an assault was made upon Maximinus himself, as he tried to win them over with prayers and gifts; he was compelled to flee back to his own men. Meanwhile his battle-line was cut down without resistance: one part of the army was overthrown, the other turned to flight. Defeated, Maximinus cast aside the imperial purple and, putting on a slave’s dress, fled with the utmost speed [Col. 0847C] to Nicomedia. From there he hurriedly carried off his wife and children and, with a few companions, came into the East. Gathering soldiers from the fugitives, he halted in Cappadocia, where he resumed the purple.

48. A few days after this battle, Licinius had transferred his army into Bithynia. Entering Nicomedia himself, he first gave thanks to God, by whose aid he had conquered; then, on the Ides of June, he published the solemn edict for the restoration of the Christian religion, as it is set forth here by our Caecilius. He further urged that the Christians’ meeting-places be restored to their former condition. Thus peace was restored to the Christian Church after ten years and several months of persecution.

49. Thereafter Licinius drove Maximinus out from the defiles of Mount Taurus and besieged by land and sea Tarsus, whither he had fled. Terrified, despairing alike of refuge and safety, Maximinus swallowed poison. But, having first gorged himself with food and wine, he was tortured for four days by the most severe pains in his vitals, even to madness; and, having invoked Christ in vain, he breathed out his guilty spirit in a loathsome manner of death.

50–51. “Thus,” says our author, “were all the persecutors of the Christian religion destroyed, so that absolutely neither stock nor root of them remained.” For Licinius ordered Valerius to be killed; Candidianus, adopted by Valeria; Severianus, son of Severus; Maximinius’s eight-year-old son; and his seven-year-old daughter, betrothed to Candidianus. Valeria, [Col. 0848A] who had fled after following Candidianus and after his death, was finally seized at Thessalonica and beheaded with her mother, because of her chastity and status.

52. Caecilius further declares that he committed all these events to writing as they occurred, lest their memory perish or truth be corrupted thereafter by other writers. He then exhorts all men, and Donatus by name, to give eternal thanks to God for the extirpation of the persecutors of Christians and for peace restored to the Church, and to pray to Him that He may preserve the flourishing Churches in perpetual tranquillity.

## ARTICLE II

On the manuscript codex of this book: how imperfect it is, and how shamefully it was corrupted by a copyist wholly ignorant of the Latin language.

The fate of this little book, like that of very many others, was plainly unjust. For many centuries it lay buried in the corners of libraries, unknown to anyone, struggling with cockroaches and moths. But in 1678 the most distinguished M. Foucault—then royal procurator in Aquitaine and now Count of the Consistory—found its manuscript codex in the former monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict at Moissac, or the Abbey of a Thousand Monks, which for several years has been inhabited by what are called secular canons. Without the slightest delay, this eminent man sent it, together with several other works found there, to the illustrious Jean Colbert, administrator of the realm, [Col. 0848C] who, out of his supreme devotion to letters, ordered this book, together with others sought from every quarter, to be deposited in his library. Accordingly Étienne Baluze, who then directed that very rich library, obeyed the nobleman’s orders and, in the following year, 1679, arranged for this book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* to be printed from that sole codex.

He informed us, however, that this codex itself was complete indeed, but infected with many errors, and appeared to have been copied about eight hundred years earlier by an incompetent person. Yet because several editors of its later editions complained that they had been denied even the opportunity to inspect the same codex once, we judged that a brief specimen of it should be presented at the beginning of this dissertation, so that all might recognize its form and age. M. Charles Duchesne, now librarian of the Colbert Library, a man commendable to all no less for piety than learning, supplied us with it at the command of the illustrious Abbé Colbert.

In the specimen of the Colbert codex, we have ordered the almost complete first page to be printed with the utmost accuracy, represented in precisely the letters and characters in which the entire work was written by the scribe. What you will see omitted in the second and third lines cannot be read, having been erased beneath a coating of some adhesive substance. The shorter gaps on the same page were caused by rot and decay, by which [Col. 0849A] its outer portions were torn away. Other lacunae altogether similar, and arising from the same cause, are found in several other places in this book. We considered it necessary to note this at least once because the editors of the second and subsequent editions of this book, being unable to know the extent of these gaps, almost always expended useless effort in filling them with conjectures.

Moreover, from this specimen you may observe that the words *Serius quidem, sed graviter, ac digne*—“Late indeed, but gravely and worthily”—have been omitted from all editions down to our own. No mention of this omission has been made anywhere. Yet they did not sufficiently notice that a single copyist’s error underlies it: he wrote *seruit* for *serius*, changing the final letter *s* to *t*. But no one fails to see how necessary these words are to Caecilius’s design and how they are connected with what follows.

A little later the printed editions read: “And to inflict upon the same man, by a death-worthy vengeance, punishment upon the proud, impious, and persecutors.” But this has been freely invented. For in the manuscript codex nothing else appears to be written except: “and that the same judge should inflict deserved punishments, by a worthy judgment [*digna judice*, or *digno judicio*], upon the impious and persecutors.” Nothing else indeed appears written in the codex, and these words certainly serve the author’s purpose clearly enough.

A few things, though indeed only few, occur in this book which the copyist added, unless it be said that he omitted something placed before them by Caecilius. Such certainly are the words, “From this point [he began] to persecute his own” (*Ab hoc capite suos persequi*, ch. 26), which have no connection with what precedes or follows [Col. 0849C]. Whatever else was removed, added, or transposed in that codex will be noted in its proper place, lest we repeat the same things.

But throughout the same codex we shall show very many passages that have been vitiated and utterly corrupted not only by the copyist’s usual carelessness, negligence, or excessive haste in writing, but also by his great ignorance of Latin. Would you like this demonstrated now by merely a few examples? Please attend to these words in which Caecilius speaks of noble women who, though innocent, were nonetheless led away to execution: “Lest they be snatched from the hands of the executioners by an assault of the people, [the remainder of the transmitted text is corrupt and materially uncertain: *promoti militari modo instruc tibile mens essagitari persequuntur*]” (ch. 40). Who, having received the first elements of Latin, could ever have written in such a manner? No sounder is another passage of our Caecilius, where he discusses the inhuman exactions of the emperor Maximinus: “Herds of cattle and flocks were carried away from the fields for daily sacrifices; [the remainder of the transmitted wording is corrupt and materially uncertain: *quibus eos adeo corruperat, ut aspernarentur annonam, et effundebant passim sine delictu, sine modo culites universos, quorum numerus ingens erat, pretiosis vestibus nummis expungerent*]” (ch. 37).

If you please, we shall add a third example, taken from the place where the following is written about Herculius, fearing the madness of his son Galerius: “[The transmitted wording is corrupt and materially uncertain: *Urbe munita, et rebus ceptis inimicis diligenter instructis proficiscitur in*] [Col. 0850A] Gaul” (ch. 27). Finally, the copyist’s supreme incompetence is most clearly proved by other words transcribed by him in this form: “*Cessere Phillides, cirona, metonius melamphius*” (ch. 33). For there Caecilius cites the verse of Virgil:

> The masters gave place:
>
> Chiron, son of Philyra, and Melampus, son of Amythaon.  
> (*Georgics* III, at the end)

Since, then, this sole codex of Caecilius’s book, infected with so many and such great errors, has hitherto been found, must we not frankly acknowledge that this book, copied by so ignorant a hand, has reached us neither uncorrupted nor wholly complete? We know indeed that certain learned men have expended no little labor in seeking to heal all these wounds. But more often they have offered nothing but mere conjectures, so uncertain and so mutually discordant that no one would dare assert whether any one of them—or which of them—has found our author’s true reading. Other codices, more correct than the Colbert codex, or at least one other free of the same errors, are therefore needed if this book of our Caecilius is to be restored to its former and uninjured condition.

## ARTICLE III

On the true and genuine title and subject of this book.

We can surely learn the title of this book with greater certainty from no other source than the Colbert codex which alone, as we have said, survives. In it the heading is: “The book of Lycius Caecilius [or Lucius Caecilius: *y* being written for *u*, as is customary] on the deaths of the persecutors.” Those who supervised publication of its editions, altogether persuaded that this was the very book which Jerome (*Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 121) testifies was composed by Firmianus Lactantius *On Persecution*, added to this title both names of Firmianus Lactantius. Nor was there lacking one who, with equal authority, joined in his commentaries on this book the twofold designation, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, noted in the manuscript codex, and *On Persecution*, recorded by Jerome. Yet no one has ever been permitted to change the title of a book not composed by himself, unless he shows more clearly than the noonday sun that it has been corrupted by unfaithful copyists. But since no one has hitherto shown, as will be said below, that the title of the book in question has been corrupted, it undoubtedly ought to have been retained as it appears in the Colbert codex.

[Col. 0850D] Further, if the subject of this book is explained by its heading, as it ought to be, it may be inferred that throughout the book it treats of the deaths of tyrants who cruelly persecuted Christians in the first centuries of the Church. Yet it is not understood sufficiently distinctly and explicitly who these men are: whether all persecutors of the Christian Church, or only some of them. For ten persecutions are commonly enumerated by the author of the Eusebian Chronicle, Paul Orosius, Sulpicius Severus, and others. Augustine lists them, not so much as his own as according to the opinion of all writers of his age, as follows: “They reckon the first persecution as that carried out by Nero; the second by Domitian; the third by Trajan; the fourth by Antoninus; the fifth by Severus; the sixth by Maximinus; the seventh by Decius; the eighth by Valerian; the ninth by Aurelian; the tenth by Diocletian and Maximian.” But Caecilius wholly omits four of these ten persecutions—namely, those which Augustine and others testify were stirred up from Domitian down to Decius. If you ask why he was so profoundly silent concerning them, we shall give you the reason in his own words: “At that time the Church suffered no assaults of enemies, and stretched forth her hands to East and West.” Now we do not inquire whether this is true; but from it one certainly and plainly infers that Caecilius’s purpose in this book was not to discuss the deaths of every persecutor of the Church, but only of several—namely, of those who, on account of their crimes, as he declares both at the beginning and end of this book, and on account of their most savage cruelty toward Christians, paid the penalty in a miserable end.

Nor did he intend to discuss in exactly the same manner those whose deaths he describes. Of the first, from Nero to Diocletian, he speaks so briefly in the five chapters after the opening of his book that he seems to have wished only to touch upon them very lightly. He truly devotes the greater part of the book to setting forth the final persecutors of the Church—Diocletian, Herculius, Galerius, Severus, Maxentius, and Maximinus—their dreadful cruelty toward Christians and pagans alike, and their other crimes, for which they deserved punishment by a most wretched death.

[Col. 0851C] Thus Caecilius’s sole aim in composing this book was, after a very brief account of the persecution stirred up against Christians by those earlier emperors and of their destruction, to explain at greater length the savage cruelty of the later persecutors toward those same Christians, their abominable crimes, their disastrous deaths, and how, when they had finally been extinguished by divine vengeance, the Church of Christ achieved a wholly wonderful triumph. Certainly no person unpossessed by prejudice can fail to admit that the true and genuine title of this book appears to be *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, to which nothing should ever have been added.

## ARTICLE IV

By what reasons Caecilius was moved to write this book, and at what time he published it.

Caecilius gives two reasons why he was moved to write this book (ch. 52). The first is lest the memory of such great events should perish—that is, of the punishments and deaths by which tyrants and persecutors of the Christian religion miserably ended their lives, and of how, after they had been removed from the scene by God’s most just judgment, as we were just saying, Christ’s triumphant Church recovered peace and a splendor greater than before.

The second reason is that, should anyone afterward wish to write a history of these tyrants, truth should not be corrupted by him, either by concealing their sins against God, as Caecilius himself says, [Col. 0852A] or God’s justice against them. From both these reasons it may certainly be inferred that Caecilius held that no Christian writer, at least down to his own time, had either composed or made public such a history.

“What then?” you will say. “Had not many writers previously published, more than once, acts of martyrs and apologies for the Christian religion?” Certainly; but they could not have written these without recounting the tyrants’ shameful deeds, crimes, savagery, brutality, and the most grievous punishments which, owed to such crimes, they endured from the avenging God through a disastrous death. Did Caecilius, then, not know this? Not at all. Rather, he denies only that there had hitherto been published—or had come into his hands—a particular history dealing chiefly with the cruelty, crimes, and deaths of the persecutors, especially the last of them. Nor is this surprising, since he indicates that he composed this book shortly after the death of the emperor Maximinus. But the date of this writing must be investigated more precisely.

First, it is now established that Caecilius’s book is dedicated to Donatus the Confessor, who, at the beginning of the persecution aroused by Diocletian, was cast into prison and suffered many torments for six years because of his profession of the Christian religion; he is reported to have been finally released in 311, after the edict issued by the dying Galerius in favor of that religion.

Secondly, our author declares (chs. 43 and 50) [Col. 0852C] that the emperor Maximinus was the last of all the tyrants who harassed Christians. No less clearly does he state that Maximinus and all the other enemies and persecutors of the Christian Church were so defeated and overthrown by divine vengeance that neither stock nor root of them remained; or, as Eusebius says, “*mē genos, mē sperma, mēdeti leipsanon*”—“neither race, nor offspring, nor any trace of their name” (*Oration in Praise of Constantine*, ch. 9, p. 629)—remained any longer upon the earth. Moreover, at the beginning and end of this book he openly proclaims, with the fullest testimony of gratitude, that peace has been restored to Christians and that Christ’s Church has been restored to its former condition and splendor. Yet Maximinus died in A.D. 313, or at the latest in 314. Further, Caecilius speaks of Licinius and Constantine as still united in treaty and friendship, and nowhere makes even the slightest mention of enmities that arose between them. Finally, he nowhere places Licinius among the persecutors of the Church; indeed, he indicates not obscurely that Licinius favored Christians, and he gives in full the edict said to have been issued by him in their favor in January 313. Therefore, after that year, and before Licinius began to rage against Christians, this book was published by Caecilius—unless he himself deceives us. Yet if the author of the Eusebian Chronicle and other writers whom we have cited elsewhere (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 4, art. 1) are to be trusted, Licinius expelled Christians from his palace in 319 or 320; consequently more learned critics date the beginning of the persecution raised by him from that point. Caecilius therefore composed this book within the interval between 313 and 320.

But in what precise year he put the finishing touch to it is indeed more difficult to say. For Sozomen left it written (*Ecclesiastical History* I.7, p. 408) that, after the battle of Cibalae, in which Licinius was defeated by Constantine, then his enemy, in October 314, Licinius wholly changed his disposition and afflicted Christians and their priests with various penalties in order to trouble Constantine, their supporter. He therefore then began to attack them. Eusebius likewise (*Life of Constantine* I.5, p. 446) gives us a speech delivered by Licinius before that battle of Cibalae, in which he instructed his soldiers that, if the gods whom they had hitherto worshipped granted victory, they would always be honored by all; otherwise Constantine’s God was to be worshipped. Yet this does not establish that he then raised a public persecution against Christians; rather, it suggests that he was still undecided whether to reject or uphold their religion. Moreover, these private actions of Licinius could have remained unknown to Caecilius, who was farther away.

But Caecilius himself plainly declares that after the aforementioned edict of Licinius in favor of the Christian religion, issued in 313, there followed, in August or September, the death of Maximinus and Candidianus. He then relates that, after Maximinus’s death, Valeria, daughter of Diocletian, wandered for fifteen months through various provinces with her mother Prisca, in plebeian dress, [Col. 0853C] and that both were afterwards condemned to death (chs. 48 ff.). They therefore died around the end of 314, as will be explained more fully below. This book, then, had not yet appeared. But since it ends there, may it not reasonably be concluded that Caecilius published it at this very time, when he had as yet learned nothing either about the battle of Cibalae or about a persecution raised by Licinius against Christians? This book therefore appears to have been written by him about the end of 314, or shortly thereafter.

# CHAPTER II

On the author of this book, Donatus the Confessor to whom it is dedicated, and the three judges by whose command he was subjected to various punishments for confession of Christ.

## FIRST ARTICLE

[Col. 0853D]

Arguments are proposed by which very many have thought that this book might be ascribed to Firmianus Lactantius.

The title of this book, represented by us precisely as it is written in the sole Colbert codex, most plainly shows that Lycius—or Lucius, with the letter *y* written for *u*, as is customary—I mean Lucius Caecilius, is truly its author.

> [Note: Cf. the inquiry prefixed to the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, in which this opinion of Nurry is opposed by very powerful arguments.]

But who he was may not unreasonably be called into doubt. For no one even moderately versed in ancient history is unaware that the gens Caecilia was once highly distinguished among the Romans. All who sprang from it bore the name Caecilius, with some agnomen added to distinguish them from one another, and sometimes also a cognomen. After the Christian religion had been established, moreover, the name Caecilius was common to several persons. For we have shown that a certain Caecilius is introduced in Minucius Felix’s *Octavius*, who, rejecting the pagan religions which he had vainly attempted to defend, most willingly accepted Christianity (*Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 1, art. 3). Jerome also mentions another Caecilius (*Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 67, p. 119), a presbyter of the African Church, through whom Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, was brought to the Christian faith and took this same surname Caecilius. [Col. 0854B] Finally, in several of Cyprian’s letters we read the name Caecilius in the superscription (*Cyprian*, letters 7, 57, 63, 67, 70).

Although these and many others, eminent in learning and piety, bore that name, Baluze, followed by nearly all others, believed that he had certainly and clearly discovered Lucius Caelius, or Caecilius, Firmianus Lactantius to be the author and originator of this book, no less than of the other works which we have discussed. He was so persuaded of this that, without any scruple, he prefixed the four names Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius to the first edition of this book, and others did likewise in subsequent editions. Nor was he in the least troubled that the two latter names were omitted in the ancient and sole Colbert codex—the names by which Lactantius is distinguished, as by a characteristic of his own, from all others called Caecilius or Caelius. For, he says, they were omitted by an inattentive copyist, just as Sirmond observed in a similar case regarding Sidonius.

He states that three arguments led him to ascribe this book to Lactantius and unhesitatingly inscribe it with Lactantius’s name. First: when Jerome enumerates the genuine works of Firmianus Lactantius, he includes among them one book *On Persecution*. This, Baluze says, is the very work now at issue (*Baluze, Notes on the title of this book; Jerome, Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 80, p. 121).

His second argument he drew from the style of this book, which seemed to him altogether Lactantian. He confirms this by verses of Virgil inserted in this book, just as they are in Lactantius’s genuine works.

Finally, he derives a third ground of argument from various modes of expression found word for word in this book as in Lactantius’s other books.

Baluze thought that only one objection could be made to arguments so many and so manifest, as he believed them: that Lactantius is called not Caecilius but Caelius in the commonly printed editions of his works. Yet he answers that this difficulty is of so little weight that it ought not move anyone at all. For in Colbert manuscript 507, containing various books of Lactantius, he is called Caecilius; whereas in two others, 1003 and 1495, and likewise in the very ancient Oxford manuscript, this and another praenomen are omitted and he is simply called Firmianus Lactantius. Nevertheless, the editors of two later editions of this book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, the Oxford and Cambridge editions, were not moved by Baluze’s answer and chose to prefix the name Caelius, not Caecilius, to its title.

These, then, are all—and no more—the grounds of argument on which Baluze and other learned men have hitherto attempted to attribute this book to Firmianus Lactantius. We have stated them in such a way that nothing at all has been subtracted from their force, but rather something added. Yet although they seem most compelling to Baluze and all the rest, Baudry thought otherwise (*Baudry, notes on chs. 1 and 2*), though he did not explain why or on what grounds. Given our disposition toward candor and frankness, we cannot conceal that arguments more numerous and of far greater strength than the foregoing are available to us—arguments which provide no small ground for doubt whether this book was really composed by Firmianus Lactantius. We shall set them forth in our usual candid and straightforward manner, so that all, laying aside every prejudice, may more easily understand what may be determined with greater certainty concerning the author of this book.

## ARTICLE II

Arguments drawn from the title of this book are produced, from which it seems possible to conclude that Firmianus Lactantius was not its author.

The book’s very title supplied us with the first reason for doubting whether it ought to be attributed to Firmianus Lactantius. It has two parts: the first gives the author’s name; the second, the subject of the book. Yet both parts show that Firmianus Lactantius was not its author. For no name other than Lucius Caecilius is written in it. Lactantius, however, was called by these four names: Lucius Caelius, or Caecilius, Firmianus Lactantius. The distinguished Christoph Matthäus Pfaff informed us that in the most ancient manuscripts of Lactantius’s works—the Bobbio and Oxford codices, eight Turin codices, the Ambrosian, Modena, and two Florentine manuscripts—both praenomina, Lucius Caelius or Caecilius, are wholly omitted. With regard to the French codices: in the royal manuscript formerly belonging to Puteanus, written seven or eight hundred years ago, the title of the *Divine Institutes* is: “Firmianus [Col. 0855D] Lactantius, *On False Religion*.” Afterwards: “Here begins the second book of Lactantius Firmianus.” At the end: “Of Caelius Firmianus, the *Institutes* … ends.” At the foot of the book *On the Wrath of God* appears: “Of Caecilius Firmianus, *On Wrath* … ends”; and of the book *On the Workmanship of God*: “Of Caecilius Firmianus … ends.” In another royal manuscript, formerly of Fleury and written about nine hundred years ago: “Here begins the book of Firmianus’s *Institutes*,” etc.; and in the margin, in the same hand: “Of Caelius Firmianus, *On Religion*”; and at the end: “Of L. Caelius Firmianus”—and in the same way at the end of the third, fourth, and fifth books. There are further codices in the Colbert Library, but much more recent ones, as we explained in our dissertation on Lactantius’s books. Only one, however, presents the four names Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius.

Do you see that the complete name Caecilius is written in the Colbert codex alone? For in the Puteanus manuscript we read *Caeli* and *Caelii*, and in two other places *Cecili*; but the copyist certainly erred somewhere in writing these names. Who would say that the authority of a single manuscript, written by the wavering or mistaken hand of a copyist, and of another very recent one, should be preferred to that of many more numerous, older, and better manuscripts? May it not therefore rightly be concluded that it is at least legitimately doubtful whether Caecilius or Cecilius is one of the four names by which Lactantius is called? But if this is uncertain, it plainly follows that in the title of the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* only one of those four names, namely Lucius, is certainly found. The second, Caecilius, is at least ambiguous and doubtful, as we have said. The latter two, Firmianus and Lactantius, are wholly absent. On what grounds, then, could this book so confidently be inscribed, in its editions, with Lactantius’s four names?

But come: tell us, I pray, what prevents us from accepting the title of our codex and believing that a certain Lucius Caecilius was the author of that book? Have we not clearly shown that many men, and men by no means undistinguished, were called by the same name Caecilius and lived in the same age as our author? No certain reason can be offered why this book could not have been composed by one of them. It therefore could not be asserted without great rashness that it was published by Firmianus Lactantius, whose two names are not written in this book’s title and whose third name must at least be doubtful.

“But who,” they ask, “is this Lucius Caecilius?” We in turn ask those who demand this: who are the authors of the many books of which only one copy survives, and which are known to us solely by the name prefixed to them? Should their genuine treatises therefore be taken away from them and ascribed to another who bore one only of their several names?

Setting aside, then, that utterly frivolous demand, Baluze and others contend that the two names Lactantius and Firmianus were omitted from the title of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* by an inattentive copyist. But this is supported by no argument whatsoever, nor do we see how it could have happened. For the title was written in red and in what are called majuscule letters. Who does not know that copyists exercise greater care in writing such titles and authors’ names than in copying anything else? They form such letters singly, slowly, and in a special manner, not with a running pen. It should further be noted that this book was copied by a scribe who corrected many words which he had first corrupted. Certainly, if anything were missing from the book’s title, he ought with much greater reason to have corrected it.

Still, grant, if you please, that both names Lactantius and Firmianus were omitted by a copyist inattentive and thinking of something else—a thing which could scarcely, or indeed hardly at all, have happened. Did he never afterwards reread the title, lest it diminish the price of a book undoubtedly intended for sale? [Col. 0857A] Was it never read even by someone else who reminded him of the omitted names? For then he would at least have written them in the margin, as we have seen done in another manuscript of Lactantius.

But Baluze says that Sirmond noted a similar omission in his observations on the books of Sidonius. Yet he does not indicate what it was. Is it perhaps the one published by Sirmond concerning this title: “Book One of the Letters of C. Sollius Apollinaris Sidonius”? There that learned man observes that in certain, though not all, manuscripts the name Modestus is added. But immediately in the same place he warns us that this latter name is nowhere mentioned in Sidonius, unless perhaps he seems to allude to it where, writing to Oresius, he says that he would rather be thought *modestus* (“modest”) than witty. [Col. 0857B] Who does not see that this omission differs greatly from the one alleged in the title of Caecilius’s book? For the designation Modestus was a fifth name, not Sidonius’s proper name; it was very rarely attributed to him, and only in some manuscript codices. One must therefore find the title of some other book in which the author’s own distinctive names have been omitted.

But perhaps someone will object and insist that Sirmond himself further observes (*Preface to Sidonius on Proper Names*) that, while the Roman republic stood, eminent men were called by several names, of which the proper name was the first. After the overthrow of the republic, however, a custom was introduced, he says, by which they placed each person’s proper name after the others, [Col. 0857C] or imposed one drawn elsewhere at will, and more often derived from the affections of relatives. That most learned man admits that in some book titles this later custom was departed from. Thus, for example, the writer on agriculture bore four names: Palladius, Rutilius, Taurus, Aemilianus. Yet although Isidore cites him by this last name as if it were his proper name (*Origins*, beginning of Book XVII), most call him simply Palladius. Cassiodorus likewise had four names; but some, wholly rejecting the name Senator, which they thought an epithet, called him simply Cassiodorus. Yet, Sirmond continues, through the negligence of copyists striving for brevity, only the proper name of certain authors—that is, their last name—was inscribed on their books.

[Col. 0857D] But what bearing does this shrewd observation of Sirmond have against us? For there he warned us that hurried copyists had omitted authors’ first names and written only the last. Here, however, the question is not of an author’s first names, but of the last names, which they contend were omitted by the copyist, whether rightly or wrongly. Moreover, Lactantius was never called Lucius, or merely Lucius Caecilius, in the title of any book or by any author. Therefore, however hastily the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* is imagined to have been written out, the names Firmianus and Lactantius ought rather than Lucius and Caecilius to have been written in its title.

Further, Sirmond expressly declares that this error which he noted was the error of a few [Col. 0858A] copyists. But if it belonged to a few, may anyone infer from this that the same carelessness belonged to the particular copyist who transcribed the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*? But tell us, please, why he rather than so many other copyists, by whom all or some of Lactantius’s separate treatises were copied, omitted his two principal names and wrote one out of two others—something which, as we have said, is highly doubtful? Until you plainly demonstrate this, is it not far more probable—indeed, not to say more certain—that the author of the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, called by the two names Lucius Caecilius alone, was quite different from Firmianus Lactantius?

Nor do we think those others deserve more attention who [Col. 0858B] insist that Lactantius is frequently called by Firmianus alone, or Lactantius alone, or by both names. For since each of those names was proper to him, he is sufficiently distinguished from all other writers by both, or by either one alone.

If we turn to the second part of the title, which contains the subject of this book, it can likewise be concluded from it that the book is not wholly deservedly assigned to Firmianus Lactantius. For it is represented only, and in no fuller form, by the words *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*. Yet no one has ever shown or said that Lactantius composed a book entitled *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*.

Baluze and others nevertheless contend that this inscription is wholly identical with that of the book [Col. 0858C] which Jerome (*Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 80, p. 121) testifies was published by Lactantius himself under no title but the simple one *On Persecution*. But by what argument, I ask you, did Baluze—endowed, as everyone knows, with such great learning—or others afterwards prove this? By none whatever. Why, then? Did they suppose that *On Persecution* and *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* were so plainly one and the same book that no argument, not even the slightest, was necessary to establish it? But who would immediately trust them when they make such an assertion? To us these titles certainly seem to designate entirely different subjects, which necessarily required wholly different treatment. For one who composes a book *On Persecution*—that is, the persecution of Christians—must undoubtedly explain in it what and how great torments and punishments they endured for professing their religion, [Col. 0858D] and how they defended it even to their last breath and most cruel extermination. Yet these matters could have been described without any, or with only the slightest, mention of the death of any persecutor or of the public affairs of the pagans. Caecilius, on the contrary, in our book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, treats in an altogether similar manner of the afflictions of pagans and Christians. Then, from the beginning of the book, he openly declares that he published it in order to make known to all by what punishments the severity of the heavenly Judge exacted vengeance upon those persecutors of Christians, and how they, though late, yet grievously and deservedly, paid to the supreme God the penalties due for their crimes—God who, in extinguishing and destroying them, displayed his power and majesty. Throughout the entire book he aims at that subject and does not depart from it for another. Therefore the subject of the two books, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* and *On Persecution*, is different.

Nor should you say that Jerome is one of those who often erred in citing book titles from memory. For he cited not only this one book of Lactantius but several others. On what grounds, then, can it be said that he suffered a lapse of memory in listing this one alone? Moreover, if his memory failed him there, why do they misuse his false authority in assigning this book to Lactantius?

Furthermore, with what confidence [Col. 0859B] can it be asserted that the treatise *On Persecution* and that *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* are one and the same? For we know what this book of Caecilius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, contains; but what was written in Lactantius’s book *On Persecution* we entirely and utterly do not know. We suffered its loss a very long time ago, and only its title, identified by Jerome, remains. That outstanding teacher did not state what Lactantius discussed in it, nor has anyone else thus far been able to know it. Until that book is found, therefore, or someone who has read it shows us with certainty what it contains, no person can rightly and properly affirm that it is the same as the book of our Caecilius. But let us, if you please, proceed to other arguments of no less weight.

## ARTICLE III

[Col. 0859C]

Other arguments are set out by which it may be demonstrated that this book did not proceed from Firmianus Lactantius; and the objections to them are refuted.

Certainly no argument by which this book is assigned to Lactantius seems of less force and weight than that which very many have hitherto thought can be drawn from its author’s style and manner of writing. For from this it can manifestly be demonstrated that it was never written by Firmianus Lactantius. To make this clearer and easier to grasp, one must observe that the difference, rather than the similarity, of style and expression provides far surer grounds for judging whether different [Col. 0859D] books proceeded from one and the same author. For several writers could have attained, or at least imitated, another’s style and method of writing. But no one, in composing several books, has employed a mode of expression wholly unlike and entirely different. Yet such a discrepancy of diction and language is found everywhere in the books of Caecilius and Lactantius.

Those who have perused this book of our Caecilius more carefully and attempted to elucidate it with their notes and observations are compelled to admit that Caecilius’s concision, and the brevity of his language, are defective and altogether obscure. Indeed, in many places it is enveloped in such obscurity that those who have tried to explain such dark passages in observations or in French and English translations completely disagree among themselves. There is no need to gather here every example of these more obscure passages and of the varying opinions in explaining them. For they occur frequently, and we shall note several later. Who, then, will not agree with us that these learned men ought either to charge Lactantius with the defect of this faulty brevity or deny him this book? Yet no one has hitherto detected this defect of language in Lactantius’s genuine works. What follows from this, then, who cannot see?

But come now: let us plainly demonstrate not only how obscure our Caecilius’s concision is, but also how greatly his manner and style of expression differ from Lactantius’s. First, then, Caecilius [Col. 0860B] speaks as follows of Christ’s first disciples (ch. 2): “Throughout all provinces and cities they sent forth the foundations of the Churches.” What author of good Latin ever said, as they claim Lactantius did, “to send foundations” (*mittere fundamenta*)? Certainly not Lactantius, who wrote more aptly: “They laid the foundations of the Church everywhere” (*fundamenta Ecclesiae ubique jecerunt*; Lactantius, *Institutes*, Book IV, ch. 21). Will you say that an ignorant copyist erred there, writing *miserunt* (“sent”) for *jecerunt* (“laid”)? First, this is imagined without evidence. Secondly, if you judge that every barbarism and improper expression occurring in this book should be attributed to copyists’ incompetence, by what reasoning can you maintain that Lactantius’s manner of expression is easily recognizable in this very book, when you admit that the sole copy surviving to this day is disgracefully corrupt?

A little later Caecilius (ch. 3) discusses the death of the second persecutor of the Church. Yet nowhere—not once—will you find him explicitly naming Domitian, by whom that persecution was raised. Is this how Lactantius kept his readers’ minds in suspense in his books, leaving them to guess, not without difficulty, whom he means?

Then Caecilius says: “Sapor, king of the Persians, who had captured the emperor Valerian, whenever he wished to mount either a carriage or a horse, ordered the Roman to bend down and offer his back; and, setting his foot upon his back, he said that this was the true image, reproaching him with laughter, not what the Romans painted on tablets or walls.” Who, I ask, has ever noticed a phrase like this in Lactantius’s genuine books? Let him produce one, if he wishes, and we yield. Baudry certainly admits, first, that he had encountered no example of the phrase “setting his foot upon his back” (*imposito pede super dorsum ejus*) except in the Vulgate translation of Holy Scripture, which no one has ever called similar to Lactantius’s style. Secondly, Baudry declares that he could scarcely, indeed hardly at all, grasp the meaning of the words “he said that this was the true [image]” (*illud verum esse dicebat*). Will others, then, less learned or less attentive in reading this book, grasp it more easily? Some authors, however, think they have discovered that the particle *non* (“not”) was wrongly inserted there by a copyist; if it is removed, the author’s meaning will not be obscure. But what follows? We do not ask whether, with that particle removed, the sense is clearer; rather, whether this whole phrase proceeded from Lactantius, who is regarded as a Christian Cicero. I truly do not know whether anyone with a taste for Ciceronian elegance would ever have said it.

Do these words of Caecilius concerning the emperor Galerius (ch. 9) more strongly savor of Lactantius’s style: “But I postpone speaking of his deeds, lest I confuse the times. For after he received the title of emperor, once his father-in-law had been stripped [of office], he then at last began to rage and despise everything; for before the imperial office he was called Diocles”? What connection, I ask, is there among these words, even though they are joined by the conjunction “for”? What place is there for Diocles’ changed name, or the mention of that change? Some suspect [Col. 0861B] that the text has a gap or has been corrupted. Thus here and elsewhere they accuse of corruption the passages and statements they cannot excuse. For they also regarded as disgracefully corrupt the no clearer and no easier-to-explain words of Caecilius in which he sets out the distinction between Diocletian and Herculius: “The sole difference,” he says (ch. 8), “was that in the one there was more greed, in the other less; but in the greater [man] less, yet more fearfulness; and more spirit, not for doing good, but evil.” Nor, owing to like obscurity, does the integrity of these words about Galerius’s mother seem any less suspect to them: “She was a most superstitious woman, who, since she was such, sacrificed almost daily with banquets and offered feasts to her servants” (ch. 11). Yet in all those passages there is absolutely no sign of corruption and no trace whatever of it in the manuscript codex. Let it be so, nevertheless. Suppose these and other dark, ambiguous, and most difficult passages to explain—found everywhere, which we omit for brevity—were defiled, corrupted, adulterated, mutilated, or transposed by a copyist. What, I ask, will you conclude from this, except that it cannot certainly be affirmed that Lactantius is the author of this book until another wholly sound and uncorrupted manuscript is found?

What, further, of the fact that several passages, clouded with equal obscurity, cannot be charged with any corruption? After the last words quoted, Caecilius goes on to narrate the hatred for Christians conceived by Galerius’s mother and transferred by her to her son. He then immediately adds: “Therefore, after they had held counsel together throughout the whole winter … the old man long resisted his rage.” [Col. 0861D] Tell us, please, to whom do you think Caecilius’s opening words refer? To Galerius’s mother, of whom he had just spoken? By no means (ch. 10). For there he is not speaking of her, but of Galerius and Diocletian, whose discussion he had wholly interrupted much earlier.

Again, later he says of Galerius (ch. 14): “Then Caesar, his departure having been prepared in the middle of winter, broke forth.” Who would not think these words mean that Caesar suddenly fled Nicomedia, where he had been staying, in midwinter? Various interpreters of Caecilius have certainly thought this was his meaning. But wrongly. For we see that he had previously said: “Having held counsel with Diocletian throughout the whole winter.” The true sense of those words, therefore, is that Galerius prepared in midwinter all that was necessary for his departure. Where did Lactantius ever speak in this way?

Would you like other examples of more obscure language? Read, if you please, what Caecilius relates of the same Galerius’s terrible exactions (ch. 24): “Tax assessors were sent, one upon another, as though they were going to discover more. And their number was always doubled when they found nothing, but added whatever they pleased.” Has anyone hitherto noticed a similar and such an obscure mode of writing in Lactantius’s genuine books? Elsewhere Caecilius has the following equally obscure words concerning noble women falsely accused of adultery and led to execution (ch. 40): “A certain Jew is found … who may lie against [Col. 0862B] the innocent. A just and diligent judge proceeded outside the city with an escort, lest he be overwhelmed with stones.” Of whom, do you think, is “lest he be overwhelmed with stones” said? Of the Jewish accuser or of the unjust judge? These words are plainly so obscure and ambiguous that some have judged them to refer to the former, others to the latter. Yet by adding one word—“he” or “that man,” or something similar, in no way opposed to the author’s affected brevity—all obscurity and ambiguity could have been removed.

Continue, please, and read how Caecilius narrates that the statues and images of Diocletian and Maximian Herculius were overthrown by Constantine. “At the same time,” he says, “the statues of the old man Maximian were torn down by Constantine’s command, along with the images in which he was painted with him. And because both old men were painted together, the images of both were also taken down together.” Would Caecilius not have been able to write more clearly and briefly, omitting the words “with whom he was painted”: “At the same time, the statues and images of Diocletian and the old man Maximian, painted together,” etc.? [Col. 0862C] This would surely have been clear and perspicuous, and readily understood by all. What would have hindered the brevity at which he aimed?

We would certainly never finish speaking if every example of equal ambiguity and obscurity had to be transcribed. Nor is that truly necessary. For who does not plainly see, from what we have reported, that Caecilius’s style is wholly alien to Lactantius’s plain, lucid, and clear style?

But because it is exceedingly difficult to root out from many minds their welcome opinion concerning the singular work of a most learned and ancient writer, as it seemed to them—a work lost for so many centuries and at last found by them—we shall add another example which, even by itself, may persuade every fair-minded judge that this book was composed in such a manner that it openly cries out that it had an entirely different parent from Lactantius. We draw this argument from the conversation in which Galerius compelled Diocletian to lay aside the purple and imperial rank. First Caecilius recounts certain milder words of Galerius and Diocletian’s opposing replies. Then our author continues as follows (ch. 18): “Having heard this, the feeble old man, who had already received letters from Maximian, writing whatever he had said …” [Col. 0863A] Who is this Maximian, I ask, and what had he said? You will not understand unless you turn your mind back to what had been said earlier: Galerius had previously quarrelled with Maximian Herculius, whom he frightened by raising the specter of civil war. Caecilius then continues: “And he had learned that the army was being enlarged by him; weeping, he said: ‘Let it be so, if this pleases you. It remained that Caesars should be chosen by the common counsel of all.’” Of all whom? For he had mentioned Maximian Herculius alone long before. Yet by these ambiguous words Caecilius meant Diocletian, both Maximian—Herculius and Galerius—and Constantius, of whom he had been silent for a long time.

But let us follow our author, who returns directly to the dialogue he had begun, in this fashion: “What need is there of counsel, when it is necessary that whatever we do should please those two”—who are not named there either. “Exactly so. For it is necessary that their sons be named.” Whose words are these? Of one man alone? Not at all. The earlier words are Galerius’s, and the latter Diocletian’s reply to him: “Exactly so.” Then, with the dialogue still interrupted and once more without mention of the speaker, Caecilius continues: “What then shall be done? G[alerius]: ‘That man is unworthy. For if he despised me when I was a private citizen, what will he do when he has received imperial power?’ D[iocletian]: ‘But this man is lovable, and will rule so that he will be judged better and more merciful than his father.’ G: ‘Thus it will come about that I shall not be able to do what I wish. Therefore those must be appointed who are in my power, who fear me, who do nothing except at my command.’ D: ‘Whom then shall we make [Caesars]?’ G: ‘Severus.’ D: ‘That dancer, drunkard, and sot, for whom night is day and day night?’ G: ‘He is worthy, because he has served the soldiers faithfully; and I sent him to Maximian to be invested by him.’ D: ‘So be it. Whom will you give as the other?’ G: ‘This one,’ he said, pointing to Daia … ‘he showed loyalty with the utmost religious solemnity.’ D: ‘Who is this whom you offer me?’ G: ‘My kinsman.’ D, groaning: ‘You do not give me men to whom the guardianship of the republic can be entrusted.’ G: ‘I have tested them.’ D: ‘You will see to it, since you are about to assume the government of the empire.’”

Continue, if you wish, and in the words following this dialogue you will encounter the same defect of overly obscure expression. Who, unless with the utmost concentration he weighed every word of this dialogue, would readily recognize what was said by Diocletian or Galerius? This indeed seemed so difficult to very many that some, in the editions they supervised, and others in their observations, judged that the initial letters, as you see, of each speaking emperor’s name should be prefixed to his words. But why, I ask, add these letters and reproduce the whole dialogue in notes? No reason can doubtless be offered other than that learned men well understood how difficult it was to distinguish the words of the emperors in conversation. Yet what could more easily have entirely removed that difficulty than adding the name of the speaking emperor repeatedly, wherever it was especially needed? What harm would that have done to brevity of expression, however refined? But such, without doubt, was Caecilius’s natural disposition, which reveals itself in his writing, as does that of others. Therefore someone rightly reminded us that our author had fallen into the defect of expression censured in this line of Horace:

> I strive to be brief;  
> I become obscure.

(*Horace, Art of Poetry*, v. 25.)

But who ever detected this defect of such obscure and ambiguous brevity in Lactantius’s writings? Nothing, indeed, is more contrary to the eloquence and perspicuity recognized by all in his books, as we have shown elsewhere (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. I, art. 2). [Col. 0864B]

What then should one make of a certain more recent writer who, while leaving the matter to the reader’s investigation, nevertheless professes that he found nothing in this entire passage unworthy of Lactantius? Why does he leave to the reader’s judgment what he preempts by his own? Ought he not rather to await the reader’s unbiased judgment, to which he appeals—as we in turn appeal to him? From anyone who has leisure, we ask only this: that he compare this book, however short, fairly with the shorter *Epitome* of Lactantius’s works recently published by the most learned Pfaff; and unless he acknowledges with us that the style of the two is very different, we shall gladly subscribe to his view.

We know, indeed, that one and the same writer varies his manner of expression according to the diversity of subjects and compositions: one style in writing histories, another in letters, another in speeches, another in polemical disputations. But no writer who, like Lactantius, excels in eloquence and in the grace of clear and perspicuous expression has ever, in any composition—even one treating a subject however different from those of his other works—fallen away everywhere from an elegant, plain, and open manner of writing into so great a defect of obscurity.

Yet we seem to hear some objecting that in this book of Caecilius there are more passages than those we have cited where he speaks clearly and perspicuously, and with no less elegance of language than Firmianus Lactantius. Let that be granted. Yet neither can it be denied that in the passages we have transcribed, and in many others, there is such obscurity of difficult and uncultivated expression that it alone suffices entirely to deny this book to Lactantius.

And certainly, just as, as we have said, a certain similarity of style found in two books is insufficient to conclude that they were composed by the same author, so all the more surely and manifestly does discrepancy and dissimilarity of style prove that their authors are different. For who does not know that it has often happened that one writer imitated another so well that he seems to have written Latin in precisely the same manner? Did not some writers, especially those of the same period, possess the Latin language so well—which is not an infinite labor—that one can scarcely distinguish by whom their books were written? Similarity of language, therefore, is not so forceful and weighty that diverse treatises should be assigned to one and the same writer on that basis alone. Conversely, dissimilarity and difference of style far more certainly and effectively demonstrate that certain treatises proceeded from different writers. We infer that Lucius Caecilius’s manner of writing differs from Firmianus Lactantius’s because the latter published various books, in which, although he treated diverse and many difficult subjects, the same style and the same elegant, polished mode of expression are found throughout them all. We possess, however, only one small work of Caecilius, in which he discusses historical matters alone. In it he sometimes speaks clearly and neatly, and, if you wish, elegantly; but more often ambiguously, confusedly, and most obscurely. Such a divergent manner of writing in a single, short composition can arise from no other cause than that Caecilius was either of mediocre talent or not yet sufficiently practiced in composing books. He therefore cannot be called Lactantius.

Thus Baluze and others object to us in vain that expressions wholly similar are frequently found in this book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* and in Lactantius’s genuine treatises. For similar modes of expression are found in writers of middle and even late Latin, as well as in Cicero. Can it therefore be concluded that Cicero’s genuine books were composed by them? No person of sound mind would ever say so. In order, therefore, to prove on any plausible grounds that this book was written in the same style as Lactantius’s true works, one would undoubtedly have had to identify words and expressions so distinctive of Lactantius that he alone, and no others, employed them. But who has yet demonstrated this? Even if it were demonstrated, one might say that it occurred by chance or that those expressions were drawn from the same sources. Finally, from very few—or indeed, if you wish, from many—similar expressions in Lactantius and Caecilius, it can never be inferred that the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, everywhere suffused with terse, ambiguous, difficult, and altogether obscure expression, belongs to that same Lactantius who spoke elegantly, plainly, and perspicuously in all his other books.

[Col. 0865D] Nor should those be heard who press the claim that this book of Caecilius must be attributed to Lactantius because verses of Virgil are inserted in it, as in Lactantius’s books. For Virgilian verses are similarly cited in books by other authors, sacred as well as profane. Nor should anyone find it remarkable if two—or even many—writers alike quoted in their works Virgil’s poems, which were in everyone’s hands.

## ARTICLE IV

Other arguments, drawn from various opinions of Caecilius, are set out to show that this book was not written by Firmianus Lactantius.

We cannot sufficiently wonder by what reasoning certain learned men persuaded themselves that the man to whom this small work *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* is addressed is the same Donatus to whom Lactantius dedicated his book *On the Anger of God*. Those two Donati are so unlike one another that, apart from their name, they seem to have absolutely nothing in common. This can evidently be proved from the date of each book and from the deeds of the one and the other Donatus. For the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, as we showed above, was completed either about the end of the year 313 or at least before Licinius began to persecute Christians. But the Donatus of whom Caecilius speaks there had been thrown into prison with other confessors in A.D. 305, and for six years afterwards, until the year 311, had endured many torments for confessing Christ. The Donatus to whom Lactantius dedicated his book *On the Anger of God*, however, was not yet sufficiently established in Christian doctrine. For Lactantius feared (*On the Anger of God*, chs. 1 and 22) that, deceived by the authority of men who thought themselves wise, he might fall into the error of those who made God so immovable that he could be stirred neither to anger nor to favor. Indeed, Lactantius wrote his book *On the Anger of God* for him so that he might learn how to refute these impious men. He was therefore not yet sufficiently imbued with this doctrine, in which, as Lactantius says, the sum and hinge of religion and piety consists. But who could readily persuade himself that Donatus, a most holy martyr, who most steadfastly endured the various torments of word, claw, iron, and fire for confessing the Christian religion, and had nine times triumphed over the tyrant, did not know whether God is moved to anger against the wicked and to favor toward the pious?

Nor should you answer that Lactantius composed the book *On the Anger of God* when Donatus had as yet suffered nothing for confessing Christ, or doubted, or did not sufficiently know what should be held concerning God’s anger and favor. For apart from the extreme difficulty of proving this, one would have to say that Lactantius published the book *On the Anger of God* before or around the year 305—when Donatus, shut up in prison and either ignorant or uncertain what God’s anger was, ought to have feared it less than whatever wounds tyrants might inflict upon him. But in the preceding dissertation we showed that the book *On the Anger of God* was published much later, about the year 321. Therefore the outstanding confessor of Christ, Donatus, whom Caecilius adorns with the highest praises, must be altogether different from the man to whom Lactantius offered the book *On the Anger of God*. They are thus mistaken who think that the two Donati are one and the same, and from this wrongly infer that Lactantius was the true author of these two books. But if that argument is taken from them, may it not with better reason be concluded that, just as the Donati differ in profession and time, so the authors of these books—Caecilius and Lactantius—are two and different persons? Who that martyr Donatus was we shall explain more fully in the following article.

Moreover, this very book of Caecilius supplies us with several further arguments by which it is demonstrated that it was composed by someone other than Firmianus Lactantius. First, as we have noted, Lactantius is accustomed in his books to cite other books which he had already published or intended later to compose. Yet neither is this book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* cited in Lactantius’s genuine works nor is any treatise of Lactantius cited anywhere in this book of Caecilius. Many occasions, however, arose in which this book might—and indeed ought—to have cited Lactantius, or Lactantius’s books Caecilius, if their author were one and the same. For, to omit much else, did not an exceedingly fitting—indeed, necessary—occasion arise to cite this book, or in it the other books *On the Divine Institutions*, where each discussed the tyrants’ most savage cruelty, the terrible punishments of martyrs, and their invincible endurance borne even unto death? Why, then, did Lactantius, contrary to his custom, not refer us from one book to the other, unless this book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* was written not by him but by another writer?

Nor should anyone object that this implies that all works of writers not cited in their other books are false and spurious. We are speaking of writers who are accustomed to cite their other books and, when an appropriate and necessary occasion for citation presents itself, do not pass it by—as Lactantius does.

But we can press still more strongly the fact that this book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* presents as certain not a few matters which are contrary to Lactantius’s opinions or could by no means have been said by him. Such, without doubt, are the things Caecilius reports concerning the year in which Christ was crucified, his thousand-year reign, the Sibyls, and the peace of the Church, which he asserts suffered no attacks from pagan enemies between the death of the emperor Domitian and Decius.

Furthermore, there is no room whatever for doubt that Lactantius, as we said in its proper place, was summoned by the emperor Diocletian to Nicomedia and taught rhetoric there. He was still living in that city when the church of Nicomedia was burned by that emperor’s command. Afterwards, finally, in his extreme old age, he was summoned to Gaul by Constantine the Great and instructed Constantine’s son, Caesar Crispus, in Latin literature. Since all these things, as we have seen, are certain, it could not have been unknown to Lactantius while he was still residing at Nicomedia what Diocletian, Galerius, and Constantine the Great did in that city, or how Diocletian laid aside both the purple and the rank of emperor.

Yet Caecilius wrote many things in his book about this most celebrated abdication which are so improbable, and so contrary to writers more worthy of credence, that certainly no one could say that they were transmitted by Lactantius, who could not have been ignorant of what had occurred. For by what reasoning, pray, could he have described as true the conversation of Diocletian and Galerius mentioned by us, in which are exaggerated Diocletian’s weakness of spirit—scarcely tolerable even in women—his timidity, cowardice, tears, and groans? Who will readily be persuaded [Col. 0868A] that Lactantius said that Constantine, present while the emperors were conversing, accompanied them so far as the place where he knew—or at least had no slight ground for doubt—that he would be most disgracefully deprived of Caesarean rank? Finally, who will not find it difficult to persuade himself that Lactantius asserted that Diocletian, compelled by Galerius’s threats and menaces, relinquished the empire, whereas nearly all writers, even contemporaries, affirm that he laid it down voluntarily?

“But,” someone will object, “Caecilius is admitted to have been a contemporary of Lactantius. Therefore he could know as well as Lactantius what was taking place at Nicomedia. And what wonder if he did not report the same things as other writers of the same age, when they very frequently disagree among themselves?” Yet, although it be granted that both [Col. 0868B] Lactantius and Caecilius lived in the same age, it is not equally certain that both lived at Nicomedia when Diocletian abdicated the empire there. It is indeed established that Lactantius was then living there, as we have sufficiently proved elsewhere. But no one has ever shown that Caecilius came thither or was present there at the end of Diocletian’s reign. Indeed, the very things which, as we have said, he narrates concerning the manner in which Diocletian resigned imperial rank in that city sufficiently prove that he was far away from it. For they are so remote not only from the judgments of contemporary writers, but also from every appearance of probability, that they cannot be believed to have been recorded by someone who was then residing in the same city as Diocletian. But these matters and others like them will be more fully explained by us below, [Col. 0868C] in a more fitting place.

As to how much weight and force all the arguments we have thus far advanced possess, and whether they rightly establish that Firmianus Lactantius was not the author of the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, we willingly leave this to the judgment of all who, setting prejudices aside, sincerely pursue truth. But from them, unless our judgment deceives us, it has certainly been plainly demonstrated that there is very great reason to doubt whether Caecilius, the author of this book, is the same person as Firmianus Lactantius. If this is so, then both names, Firmianus Lactantius, ought certainly not to have been added to its title; rather, it should have been left as it appears in the sole Colbert manuscript.
