Therefore, throughout this dissertation we have judged that this [Col. 0868D] writer ought to be called by no name other than Lucius Caecilius, or, for brevity’s sake, simply Caecilius.

Moreover, whatever may be pronounced concerning this author, we must always acknowledge that we owe much to those who brought this book out of the densest darkness, in which it had lain for so many centuries, into public light. For it seems, as has been said, to have been composed by an ancient writer; and many things occur in it which were either omitted by others or by which their opinions may be confirmed.

## ARTICLE V

Concerning Donatus, to whom this book is dedicated, and the three judges—Flaccinus, Hierocles, and Priscillian—by whose command he was subjected to various punishments because of his confession of Christ.

In the preceding article, unless we are wholly mistaken, we made it clear to everyone that there were two distinct Donati: one to whom Lactantius’s aforementioned book *On the Wrath of God* is addressed, and the other to whom this book of our Caecilius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, is dedicated. Yet who this latter Donatus was, scarcely any writer other than Caecilius himself can teach you. But when he discusses the persecution raised by Diocletian against the Christians, he addresses that same Donatus thus:

> “What need is there to recount those things, especially to you, dearest Donatus, who beyond all others experienced the storm of the turbulent persecution? For when you fell into the hands of Flaccinus, a prefect, no small murderer; then of Hierocles, from vicarius made governor, who was the author and counsellor of the persecution; and lastly of Priscillian, his successor, you furnished to all an example of unconquered courage. For nine times you were subjected to tortures and various torments; nine times you conquered the adversary by your glorious confession. In nine battles you defeated Zabulus [the Devil] with his satellites; by nine victories you triumphed over the world with its terrors. . . . Neither blows, nor claws, nor fire, nor iron, nor the various kinds of tortures availed anything against you. . . . Finally, after those nine most glorious combats in which Zabulus was defeated by you, he did not dare to engage you further, having learned through so many battles that you could not be overcome. And when the victorious crown was ready for you, he ceased to challenge you further, lest you should now receive it. Although you have not received it [Col. 0869C] in the present life, it nevertheless remains unimpaired for you and is reserved in the kingdom of God in return for your virtues and merits.”

You have surely heard what torments Donatus endured for Christ’s confession, how great they were and for how long, by whose unjust judgment they were inflicted, and with what steadfast courage he bore them.

Caecilius then relates that an edict favourable to Christians was issued by the emperor Galerius when he was near death; afterwards he again addresses Donatus in these words: “Then, when the prisons were opened, dearest Donatus, you were released from custody with the other confessors, since for six years prison had served you as a dwelling.” He further added that this edict was posted at Nicomedia on the day before the Kalends of May, in the eighth consulship of Galerius and the second of Maximinus—that is, in the year of Christ 311, as we shall show below. Donatus, therefore, six years earlier, [Col. 0869D] as stated—that is, in the year of Christ 305—had been thrown into prison and tortured by so many and such varied torments.

For this reason Caecilius calls him and others tortured in like manner by the glorious name of confessors. Cyprian, as some have observed, bestows this name, which he uses very frequently in his letters, upon those who, when questioned by pagan judges, steadily professed Christ to be the true God without undergoing any penalties. With far greater right, therefore, Caecilius bestowed this name and title of so great an honour upon Donatus and others who, for that same confession of Christ, were so long racked by diverse and dreadful tortures.

[Col. 0870A] As for the judges mentioned by Caecilius, by whose altogether inhuman cruelty Donatus was thrown into prison and mangled by so many punishments, some think that Flaccinus was then governor of Bithynia. Although they offer no reason for this opinion, they seem to have adopted it because they supposed that Donatus underwent the punishments just mentioned in that province—indeed at Nicomedia or not far from that city. Others, however, think that this Flaccinus was prefect of the Praetorian Guard, perhaps with better reason. For he is distinguished from the other two judges, who are called governors. The governors of provinces and cities were indeed customarily called prefects, but with the name of the province or city over which they presided, or some additional designation. Flaccinus, [Col. 0870B] however, is called simply, and as it were by antonomasia, “the prefect.” To whom could this designation better apply than to the Praetorian prefect?

The other two, Hierocles and Priscillian, his successor, are called by Caecilius governors—that is, directors and rulers—of the province, undoubtedly, in which Donatus resisted their unjust fury. They suppose this occurred in Bithynia, as we have already noted. Yet we read that Epiphanius recorded that Hierocles was then prefect at Alexandria when Diocletian and Maximian were raging against the Christians. Moreover, Eusebius relates that the martyr Aedesius, by command of the governor of Alexandria, whose name he suppresses, was cast into the sea. In the Greek Menaion also Hierocles is called governor of Egypt. But he could have held the office of governor at different times not only in Bithynia but also in Egypt. Finally, he is said to be the man who, when he had rashly attempted to defame the Christian religion in public writings, gave Lactantius, as we have noted elsewhere, occasion to compose his books of the *Divine Institutions*. This whole opinion rests upon certain conjectures; and though the matter itself is not thereby demonstrated with certainty, these nevertheless either seem sufficiently probable or contain nothing wholly inconsistent with truth.

Finally, the third judge is called Priscillian by Caecilius. But in the Roman Martyrology we read that at Nicaea in Bithynia, during Diocletian’s persecution, Antonina was ordered by the governor Priscillian to be beaten with rods, suspended on the rack, torn in the sides, burned with flames, [Col. 0870D] and finally killed by the sword. Let more learned critics determine and pronounce whether he is the same man whom Caecilius mentions.

Thus, by the impious command of these judges, Donatus was tortured with the punishments we have mentioned because of his confession of Christ. Caecilius (Caecilius, chs. 1, 35, and 52) repeatedly addresses him as “dearest.” He was therefore joined in the closest bond of friendship with that most holy confessor, whose wondrous endurance amid so many torments we have thus far had no writer other than Caecilius to celebrate.

Moreover, our author added that it was a pleasing spectacle to God when he saw the victorious Donatus yoking to his chariot not white horses or huge elephants, but especially the conquerors themselves. In these words he alludes to the Roman emperors’ custom of harnessing, or even hitching beneath, white horses or elephants to their triumphal chariots. Therefore someone suspects that Caecilius’s text should read *subjungentem* (“hitching beneath”) rather than *subjugantem* (“yoking”), but this ought to have been proved by the authority of another manuscript or writer. Bulenger has adduced many examples of emperors triumphing with white horses and elephants; Onuphrius Panvinus and his interpreter Johannes Maderus confirm them, and anyone may readily consult their books.

# CHAPTER III

Concerning the various editions of this book and the observations and notes upon it by various scholars.

## ARTICLE I

Concerning the various editions of this book.

The first edition of this book, as we have already said, is owed to the most distinguished Stephen Baluzius, who in Paris in 1679, at the beginning of the second volume of his *Miscellanea*, made it public from that sole manuscript codex preserved in the Colbert Library. Since the author’s text in this manuscript book was very frequently corrupted through the great incompetence of a scribe ignorant of Latin, as has already been observed, Baluzius candidly and frankly declares that he corrected those passages whose emendation was easy and obvious, but left others untouched where, as he says, the boldness of correction was not free from danger. Whether [Col. 0871C] he kept his promise, judge from what we have noted concerning some omitted words and other matters.

When this first edition of a singular book, lost for so long a time, had been received with great applause by all, many people eagerly arranged for it to be reprinted afterwards in different parts of Europe. The second edition thus appeared at Oxford in 1680. Paul Baudrius wished us to be informed that the author of the preface prefixed to this edition was John Fell, bishop of Oxford. In it that distinguished man declares that he had from time to time restored this badly mutilated book, so often gaping with lacunae, partly by his own conjectures and partly by those of the most learned men, the bishop of St Asaph and Isaac Vossius.

[Col. 0871D] The third edition of this book then appeared in the same city, through the care of Thomas Spark, at the end of the complete works of Lactantius, in 1684. But he warns us in the preface that, through either his own carelessness or that of the printers, the publication of this book had laboured under the press for three years. In the same year John Columbus published this book, printed at Åbo in Finland by Johannes Winter.

In the following year, this same book was again brought before the public from the Cambridge press together with all the works of Firmianus Lactantius. Nothing new was added in that edition, except one or two brief notes, undoubtedly proceeding from the man who supervised it but concealed his name.

Thereafter Paul Baudri caused the book again to be published at Utrecht on the Rhine in 1692, with all the notes and observations of others which had thus far been published or remained unpublished, and which he himself had written or friends had sent and communicated to him.

Finally, at Paris in 1710 we prepared a new edition of this book in order to satisfy the entirely fair wishes of those who desired it to be printed exactly as it was written in the sole manuscript which no one besides Baluzius had collated. For they rightly judged that its lacunae and gaps could then be more certainly filled, and its corrupt and [Col. 0872B] obscure passages more easily corrected and explained.

Nor were there lacking others who desired that this book, translated into the vernacular, should become public property. Maucroix, abbot of Saint-Hilaire and canon of the cathedral church of Reims, published a French translation of it at Paris in 1680.

Burnet, bishop of Salisbury, later translated it also into English; and shortly afterwards another person, who did not wish his name to be known to us, produced from that very translation another French version, published by the press of François Halma at Utrecht in 1687. Yet the principal—or perhaps sole—aim of this French translator was to administer to the French the poison of treason which Burnet had offered to English Protestants in his preface. But it is not our purpose to pursue these two heterodox men, who deviate no less from truth than from our subject. For we do not think it lawful to detain readers with matters irrelevant to our argument, matters long ago adequately and abundantly refuted and utterly overthrown by Dom Denis de Sainte-Marthe, now prior of our royal abbey of Saint-Germain, and by other most learned men. And indeed, what sound-minded person would not condemn as utterly intolerable rashness those who dared to compare our most Christian King, because he removed the public liberty to profess a heresy extorted by civil arms, with Diocletian, Galerius, Maximinus, [Col. 0872D] and other tyrants, who most cruelly slaughtered the defenders of the most holy Christian faith—a faith founded by the blood of Christ the Lord himself and of his disciples, and by wondrous divine works?

## ARTICLE II

Concerning the notes and observations of various scholars upon this book.

There are very few books upon which so many notes and observations have been written in proportion to their small size. Baudrius compiled from them a huge volume, in which he inserted all of them in their proper places, both published and unpublished. Among those published, some were printed together with Caecilius’s book and others separately. Some, too, in letters sent to friends; others in books composed on another subject; and still others in some particular dissertation, endeavoured according to their ability to explain and interpret certain obscure passages of this book.

Shorter notes on this book were written by Thomas Spark, Georgius Graevius, Elias Boherellus, Thomas Gale, Peter Alix, Paul Colomiès, Vossius, Maucroix, Burnet, Antonio Pagi in his critical study of Baronius’s *Annals*, and Dodwell in his Cyprianic dissertations. Not content with these, the latter also published a separate dissertation on the *ripa striga* mentioned by our author.

Longer ones were written by Stephen Baluzius, Gisbert Cuper, John Columbus, Nicolas Toinard, Jacob Tollius, and Paul Baudrius. Moreover, in certain letters, Valesius, Diazius, Stephen Baluzius, and Gisbert Cuper attempted to correct or elucidate several passages of our Caecilius.

All into whose hands these writings may come will readily judge their value and usefulness. There is therefore no need to introduce our own judgment, which can scarcely ever be made without offending someone. Yet we think there is no one who does not recognize how great were their learning, sagacity, and talent in explaining the more obscure passages of our author or correcting corrupt ones. But neither will anyone deny that certain of these notes are of lesser importance and attend to grammar far more than was fitting; while others are more diffuse, and their authors stray too far from Caecilius’s purpose or run wholly beyond the course, doing something altogether different from what can contribute even slightly to their author’s design or explanation. No one, moreover, was bolder than Tollius, who everywhere rashly accuses our author of error and therefore is often, and deservedly, soundly castigated by Baudrius—though of the same sect, yet a man of better faith. Tollius’s rashness is the more blameworthy because he frankly declares that his notes are hasty work, composed quickly and without books, briefly for the benefit of a bookseller.

# CHAPTER IV

New notes and observations upon this book; and first concerning Christ the Lord and his disciples.

## ARTICLE I

[Col. 0873D]

An examination of what Caecilius transmitted concerning the time and year in which Christ the Lord died, and whether his opinion on this matter was the same as Lactantius’s.

Since this whole book is historical, its author repeatedly professes that he follows chronological order in it (ch. 9). At times, however—as often happens to other writers of histories—he departs from it (chs. 9 and 11), but in only one place does he warn us of his digression (ch. 17). In our notes, therefore, we shall follow in his footsteps; but we shall endeavour, according to our capacity, to examine, unravel, or confirm together rather than separately, lest some confusion arise, those things which he has preserved in memory in various places about Christians and each [Col. 0874A] emperor, things less easy to understand or more worthy of notice.

Caecilius begins his history (ch. 2) from the death of Christ our Saviour as follows: “In the last times of Tiberius Caesar, as we read written, our Lord Jesus Christ was tortured by the Jews, after the tenth day before the Kalends of April.” In the manuscript codex: “after the tenth day before the Kalends of April, under the consulship of the two Gemini.” But Firmianus Lactantius, in his genuine books of the *Divine Institutions*, spoke somewhat differently (Lactantius, *Divine Institutions*, IV.10): “Herod was under the reign of Tiberius Caesar, in whose fifteenth year, that is, under the consulship of the two Gemini, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April” (in the two older royal manuscripts and in certain other codices: “on the tenth day before the Kalends of April”), “the Jews crucified Christ.” Baluzius and the others, however, all exert themselves to reconcile these two passages and show that they were written by one and the same author.

Certainly it is altogether certain and manifest that the same year of Christ’s death is indicated by Lactantius and our Caecilius, under the consulship of the two Gemini—that is, Lucius Fusius Geminus and Lucius Rubellius Geminus. But this was not the peculiar opinion of Lactantius and Caecilius alone; it was also that of Tertullian, as we have shown above, and of many other earlier Fathers of the Church, as all acknowledge.

Yet these words of Caecilius, “in the last times of Tiberius Caesar,” are wholly alien either from Lactantius’s expression or from his opinion. For if Caecilius said this of the twenty-second and subsequent years of Tiberius’s reign, while Lactantius spoke with him of the fifteenth year of that reign, he speaks incorrectly and contrary to Lactantius’s manner. For Tiberius, who reigned seven or eight years afterward, had then completed only the second portion of his reign. These therefore cannot be called his last times. But if Caecilius by those words indicates the eighteenth year of Tiberius’s rule, he will indeed speak somewhat more aptly, but he wholly departs from Lactantius’s opinion, which we have explained elsewhere.

Moreover, the following words of Caecilius still seem to conflict with Lactantius: “After the tenth day before the Kalends of April.” For Lactantius wrote, “On the seventh day before,” or, according to certain manuscripts cited by us, “on the tenth day before the Kalends of April.” Yet Baluzius contends that the two modes of expression signify the same thing. For, he says, the Romans were not accustomed, when saying “after the Kalends,” to designate the days following them, but those preceding them. He further thinks it can be proved by these words of the jurist Paulus that the two forms of writing, “before” and “after the Kalends,” designate one and the same thing: “A yearling dies on the last day of the year; and customary speech makes this clear: ‘on the tenth day before’; ‘after the tenth day before the Kalends.’ Nor are eleven days signified by either expression.” [Col. 0875A] But if these words of Paulus are not wholly sound and intact, as Baluzius himself and others admit, what certain conclusion can be drawn from them?

Baluzius nevertheless replies that, whatever difficulty may lie in those words, it is removed by the authority of Lactantius, who said in one and the same sense in the books of the *Divine Institutions* and in this book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*: “before” and “after the tenth day before the Kalends.” But we have already shown that it is by no means certain that this latter book was composed by Lactantius. Nor is it more established whether, in the two books, whoever may be the author of the latter, these words are actually used in one and the same sense.

But grant, if you wish, that they are taken in the same meaning: then the sense of the words “after the tenth day before the Kalends” will be this: “after the tenth day which the Kalends will follow.” But who has ever spoken thus—Paulus or any ancient writer? Let them produce such a writer for us, and we shall gladly yield.

For this reason many were not persuaded. They prefer to accuse the ancient copyist of the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* of error or incompetence, and suspect that our Caecilius wrote *ante* (“before”), not *post* (“after”), the tenth day before the Kalends. Correctly, indeed, if this can be established by the sufficiently strong authority of some manuscript. For one may often know what an author ought to have said; but who would dare, against the testimony of a single manuscript and without the certain evidence of others, to determine what he actually wrote—whether well or badly, clearly or obscurely?

[Col. 0875C] Finally, Caecilius relates that Christ was crucified in the last times of Tiberius Caesar, “as we read written.” Where, pray, is this read as written? Is it in the sacred books of the New Testament or in those of ancient ecclesiastical authors? In Luke’s Gospel alone (ch. III, vv. 1, 21) it is written that many Jews and Christ the Lord were washed in the waters of the Jordan in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar’s reign. Caecilius did not have these words in view unless, with Lactantius, Clement of Alexandria, and others cited by us elsewhere, he believed that Christ died in the same year in which he was baptized by John. But even if he aimed at those statements of the Evangelist, it still cannot rightly be concluded from them, as we have already said, that Christ died in the last times of Tiberius. Moreover, if Caecilius did not attend to Luke’s Gospel, we shall most gladly learn from others what writers he cites and whether their works survive.

## ARTICLE II

Concerning the things which Caecilius records as having occurred from Christ the Lord’s restoration to life until his ascension into heaven.

Caecilius continues his begun discussion of Christ thus (ch. 2): “When Christ had risen, on the third day after his death, he assembled his disciples,” namely in Galilee, so that there, as Matthew says, they might see him restored to life (Matthew 28:10 [Col. 0876A] and 16). “And for forty days,” our author continues, “he remained with them,” or, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles (1:3), “He presented himself alive after his passion by many proofs, appearing to them for forty days and speaking concerning the kingdom of God.”

Then, in Caecilius’s words, “Christ opened their hearts and interpreted the Scriptures, which until that time had been obscure and veiled.” Lactantius himself (*Divine Institutions*, IV.15) says: “The birth and passion of Christ revealed the mysteries, as also the sayings of the prophets, which, though read by the Jewish people for a thousand five hundred years and more, were nevertheless not understood until Christ interpreted them by word and deeds.” If you maintain that these words ought to be referred to the fulfilled predictions of the prophets concerning that same Christ the Lord, we shall not object. Yet Lactantius himself afterwards confirms more expressly the statements of our Caecilius in these words (*ibid.*, IV.20): “After Christ’s death, when the disciples had gathered again, he opened to them the sacred writings of Scripture—that is, the mysteries of the prophets—which could in no way be perceived before he suffered, because they announced himself and his passion.” We know with what rashness Gallaeus dared in his notes to charge Lactantius there with error. But in our dissertation on the books of Lactantius we repressed and restrained the futile efforts of this rash man.

Our author, however, continues his discussion as follows [Col. 0876C] (Caecilius, ch. 2): Christ, restored to life, “ordered” and instructed his disciples “for the preaching of his dogma and doctrine, establishing the solemn discipline of the New Testament. When this office was completed, a storm-cloud enveloped him and, taking him from the sight of men, carried him away into heaven.” So he writes; and though in this book he strives for a marvellous brevity of expression, as we noted above, he is nevertheless more expansive than Lactantius, who said more briefly (*Divine Institutions*, IV.21): “Having arranged for his disciples the preaching of the Gospel and of his name, a cloud suddenly surrounded him and raised him into heaven.”

There can be no doubt that both writers intended by their earlier words to signify what the Evangelists Matthew and Mark record as delivered by Christ to his disciples when he was soon to ascend into heaven. Matthew indeed says (Matthew 28:19): “Go therefore and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit; teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you.” Mark says (Mark 16:15): “Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature. He who believes and is baptized shall be saved.” This, then, is the doctrine for the preaching of which Christ, as Caecilius said, ordained—or appointed—and instructed his disciples; or which, in Lactantius’s words, was ordained and arranged by Christ for his disciples.

Some, however, think that Caecilius’s subsequent words [Col. 0877A] (Caecilius, ch. 2), “establishing the solemn discipline of the New Testament,” refer to what we quoted from Matthew and Mark and designate sacred baptism, which in the early times of the Church was customarily administered solemnly on the sacred days of Easter and Pentecost. Why should they not refer also to all other things pertaining to the doctrine of the Christian religion itself? For, as follows from the cited words of both Evangelists, Christ instructed his disciples not only to baptize all nations with solemn baptism but also to preach the Gospel and teach all to observe whatever he had previously commanded them. And this is Caecilius’s meaning can be inferred with no little clarity from what he added there concerning these same disciples of Christ: “They were dispersed throughout the whole earth to preach the Gospel, as their Master and Lord had commanded them.”

Finally, some think that Caecilius spoke somewhat too freely in the words: “A storm-cloud enveloped him.” For, they say, he should not have departed from Luke’s sacred text, where it is written, νεφέλη ὑπέλαβεν αὐτόν, “a cloud received him” (Acts 1:9); nor from Mark, ἀνελήφθη, “he was taken up” (Mark 16:19); nor from Luke, ἀνεφέρετο, “he was borne up” (Luke 24:51). This manner of speaking, they say, wholly excludes a storm. Therefore Cyprian speaks better (*On the Vanity of Idols*, near the end): “He was taken up into heaven, surrounded by a cloud”; and Lactantius, cited shortly above (*Divine Institutions*, IV.21): “A cloud suddenly surrounded him and raised him into heaven.” But because the sacred writers did not altogether plainly state how Christ was raised to heaven by a cloud—whether calmly and slowly, or swiftly and with a certain impetus—Caecilius wished to explain this in his own words. Whether, and how far, he departed through this interpretation from the true sense of the Evangelists must be demonstrated by those who criticize him so boldly.

Again, Toinard rebukes him because in the same place he wrote somewhat improperly that Matthias and Paul were taken by the eleven disciples of Christ into Judas’s place. For the former is said to have been chosen by lot in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 1:25 ff.; 9:15 ff.; 13:2), and the latter selected by Christ. But our author, speaking thus for brevity’s sake, seems to signify nothing else than that Matthias and Paul, each in his own time, were admitted by the other apostles after the disastrous death of Judas the traitor to apostolic rank. Yet no one will doubt that he speaks as obscurely as he speaks briefly. For Paul was admitted into their sacred college by Matthias as well as by the other eleven Apostles.

## ARTICLE III

Whether Caecilius rightly said that the Gospel of Christ had been disseminated through all regions of the earth at the beginning of Nero’s or of Decius’s reign.

After Christ ascended into heaven, his disciples, says Caecilius (ch. 2), were scattered throughout [Col. 0878A] the whole earth to preach the Gospel, as Christ himself, as we have said, commanded. For twenty-five years, from Christ’s ascension into heaven until the beginning of Nero’s reign, they laid the foundations of churches in every province and city, or, as Lactantius wrote (*Divine Institutions*, IV.21), cited above by us, everywhere. That the foundations of churches were laid by the Apostles, no one fails to know and freely acknowledge.

But someone may ask what Caecilius meant when he so emphatically declares that at the beginning of Nero’s reign the Apostles disseminated the Gospel throughout the whole earth and laid the foundations of Christian churches in every province and city. Did he mean throughout absolutely the entire earth, including all its remotest recesses? Certainly not; his words must not be pressed with such literal exactness. For he later affirms no less plainly that, from the death of Domitian—who reigned long after Nero—until the beginning of Decius’s reign, there were good Roman emperors under whose rule the Church spread so extensively in East and West (Caecilius, ch. 3) “that there was now no corner of the earth so remote that the religion of God had not penetrated it, nor any nation living with such savage customs that, having embraced the worship of God, it was not softened toward works of justice.” In Nero’s time, therefore, the Christian religion had not yet penetrated all those places.

But some rise up and contend that these later words of Caecilius too are wholly and entirely false. For, they say, he did not know that America was a fourth part of the earth, and he, like Lactantius, as we have observed elsewhere, denied the antipodes. How then, unless hyperbolically (ὑπερβολικῶς), could he assert that under Decius there was no corner of the earth so remote in which the Christian religion had not been disseminated? We are truly astonished that learned men should seriously raise this objection to us. For whenever ancient Fathers of the Church who denied the existence of antipodes and to whom America was unknown recorded that the Christian religion had spread everywhere on earth, they designated no regions of the earth except those which they believed inhabited by human beings.

Nor can Origen be objected to us with greater right (Origen, *Homilies on Matthew*, 29), since he testifies somewhere that, up to his own times, no word of Christianity had been heard by many peoples, not merely barbarians but other nations as well. For Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History*, III.1), from another of Origen’s books, shows that the Apostles and disciples of Christ were dispersed throughout the whole world in order to announce his Gospel to all human beings.

Yet, someone will object, however doubtful Origen’s opinion on this matter may seem, Augustine nevertheless, in replying without hesitation to Hesychius, who maintained that in his own age the world had been filled with the Gospel, stated that there were innumerable peoples in Africa—as he had learned with the utmost certainty—to whom Christ’s Gospel had not yet been preached (Augustine, Epistle 199). Therefore, he held that what was said by the apostles—“You shall be my witnesses even unto the uttermost part of the earth” (Acts 1:8)—was promised [Col. 0879A] not to them alone, but to the whole Church, which is to endure until the consummation of the age. He judged likewise that Paul’s words, taken from the Psalmist—“Their sound has gone forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” (Romans 10:18)—must be understood such that, although they are in the past tense, they denote the future, as do other similar prophetic utterances.

Yet there were also those who believed that, in Caecilius’ own age, and even earlier, the Gospel had been spread through every part of the earth. For what, I ask you, could be clearer or more explicit than these words of Tertullian (Against the Jews, book 7, chapter 7):

> “In whom else have all the nations believed, if not in Christ, who has now come? For in whom have other nations believed: the Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and those dwelling in Mesopotamia, Armenia, Phrygia, Cappadocia; those inhabiting Pontus, Asia, and Pamphylia; those residing in Egypt and in the region of Africa beyond Cyrene; the Romans and their inhabitants; then also the Jews in Jerusalem; and the other nations besides: the various peoples of the Gaetulians, the many territories of the Moors, all the boundaries of the Spains, the diverse nations of the Gauls, places of the Britons inaccessible to the Romans yet subject to Christ, and the Sarmatians, Dacians, Germans, Scythians, and many hidden nations, provinces, and islands unknown to us and too numerous to enumerate; in all these places the name of Christ, who has now come, reigns … in all these places dwells a people bearing Christ’s name.”

And shortly afterwards:

> “Christ’s kingdom and name extend everywhere; everywhere they are believed in; everywhere they are honoured by all the nations enumerated above; everywhere he reigns; everywhere he is worshipped; everywhere he is equally bestowed upon all.”

No less clearly, though somewhat more briefly, Lactantius wrote (Divine Institutes, book IV, chapter 26): “No nation is so barbarous, no region so remote, that his passion—that is, Christ’s—or the sublimity of his majesty is unknown.” Elsewhere he says: “From the rising of the sun to its setting, the divine law has been received; and every sex, every age, nation, and region, with united and equal minds, serve God” (ibid., book V, chapter 23). But elsewhere we have shown more fully concerning this writer and how he argues from this fact for the truth of the Christian religion [Col. 0879D].

Add also Eusebius (Ecclesiastical History, book IV, chapter 7), who expressly attests that, under the emperor Hadrian, the Church flourished throughout the whole world like the brightest stars, and that true faith in Christ the Lord prevailed among every nation.

What, moreover, of Chrysostom, who interprets Paul’s words to the Colossians—“Which has been preached in all the earth” (Colossians 1:23)—as referring to that same Gospel propagated everywhere? He observes there that the Apostle wrote not “which is preached,” but “which has been preached.” Nor is he alone in thinking that the Apostle’s words must be understood in this proper and natural sense; others, both ancient and more recent, hold the same. Yet we shall not conceal that many others saw in them a certain hyperbole, or rather a synecdoche, by which the greater part is taken for the whole. Still, it cannot be denied that our Caecilius had supporters and adherents of his opinion, who were surely persuaded that, under the emperor Decius, the Christian religion had been dispersed through every part of the world. Yet by this manner of speaking they included only those regions which, as we have said, they believed were actually inhabited by human beings.

## ARTICLE IV

What Caecilius thought concerning Peter’s arrival at Rome; the time when he held the supreme pontificate in that city; the miracles performed there by him; and the death of Peter and the Apostle Paul.

We have already shown that scarcely anything in the whole of ecclesiastical history is established with greater certainty than Peter’s arrival in the city of Rome, which our Caecilius rightly affirms. It is therefore astonishing that anyone can still be found who, though not daring wholly to deny it, now asserts that there remains some ground for doubting it. For whom, I ask, can there be any ground for doubt? Certainly for no one except those who, blinded by utterly invincible obstinacy, have never been willing to yield to the most certain authority of ancient and modern writers—and indeed even of those themselves who, as we shall show elsewhere, remain stubbornly devoted to new heterodox sects.

On the other hand, many persons—and especially these same heterodox writers—welcomed with open arms what our Caecilius added: “When Nero was already reigning, Peter arrived at Rome” [Col. 0880C]. For, they say, by these words we are at last freed from the long-standing error of Peter’s twenty-five-year Roman pontificate. But this old opinion, which they now call an error, must be explained a little more fully.

Eusebius testifies (Ecclesiastical History, book II, chapter 15) that Peter came to Rome in the time of the Emperor Claudius in order to oppose Simon Magus. Jerome writes (Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers, chapter 1) that this occurred in the second year of that emperor, in A.D. 43 (Eusebius, Chronicle, under the year 43), or, as others prefer, in 42 or 44; and that Peter there occupied the sacerdotal chair for twenty-five years [Col. 0880D]. Yet they do not suppose that the prince of the apostles remained in Rome throughout that whole period. Rather, they hold that he afterwards returned to Jerusalem, and then, in A.D. 68 or 69, returned from there to Rome, where he was put to death with the Apostle Paul by Nero’s command.

But scholars have observed many things which seem to conflict with and oppose this opinion [Col. 0880D]. In A.D. 44, as Eusebius indicates (Ecclesiastical History, book II, chapter 10), Herod Agrippa, shortly before departing this life, committed the Apostle Peter to prison, as we read in Acts (12:4). In the same year, as is recorded in the Eusebian Chronicle (under the year 45), a famine arose, likewise foretold by Agabus in Acts (11:28); and after the death of Herod it still continued, as may be gathered from Josephus (Jewish Antiquities, book XIX, chapter 7, and book XX, chapter 3). At that time Paul, as may also be gathered from Acts (11:30; 12:25), brought to Jerusalem alms collected by the disciples. Moreover, Josephus testifies that this famine and Herod’s death occurred in the fourth year of the Emperor Claudius. Finally, Apollonius, quoted by Eusebius (Ecclesiastical History, book II, chapter 18), related from ancient tradition that Christ had commanded his apostles not to leave Jerusalem during the twelve years following his ascension to heaven. Others, however, suppose themselves to have escaped all these difficulties by positing various journeys of Peter from Jerusalem to Rome and from Rome to Jerusalem.

As soon as the book of our Caecilius was published, certain modern writers wished to prefer its testimony to the authority of Jerome and all the rest, openly declaring that Peter’s supposed journeys before Nero’s reign were as fictitious as his twenty-five-year Roman pontificate was improbable. Yet they do not think this harms the primacy of the Roman Church in any way. That primacy, they say, was instituted and established not by some fixed number of years during which Peter presided over that Church, but by the establishment there of the episcopal see and its confirmation through the shedding of his blood. Accordingly, Papebroch openly and plainly taught (Chronological-Historical Essay) that Peter placed the Roman and supreme pontifical chair only in the fiftieth year of Christ and the tenth of Claudius’ reign [Col. 0881C]. But he attempts to establish this from grounds other than the authority of our Caecilius.

Let us now examine, if you please, whether our author himself in fact favours this second opinion, which opposes the Apostle Peter’s twenty-five-year Roman pontificate. First, he asserts that, from Christ’s ascension into heaven to the beginning of Nero’s reign, the apostles were dispersed through various provinces for a period of twenty-five years and laid the foundations of the Church. Second, he says that Peter came to Rome when Nero was already reigning there. But he does not say that it was then for the first time, nor that Peter had never gone there before. Since he everywhere, and especially in this place, strives for the utmost brevity, there seems no room for doubt that he counts Peter among the other apostles who preached the Gospel in various provinces. But if that is what he intended to imply, why may not Peter also have made a journey to Rome earlier in the course of his travels? Might it not be said that Caecilius omitted Peter’s earlier arrival in that city because he hastened to announce the death inflicted on him at Nero’s command, and the punishments that the wicked emperor suffered precisely on account of that crime? Besides, even if he had stated most explicitly that Peter came to Rome only once and not before Nero’s reign, should his testimony, if he alone were not the genuine Lactantius, have been preferred with such acclamation to the authority of Eusebius, Jerome, and the other ancient writers?

But as true and certain as Peter’s residence in the city of Rome is, so firm and settled must be what our Caecilius added (Caecilius, chapter 2): that Peter performed certain miracles there by divine power. Yet he said no more about these miracles of Peter. Some, however, in their lengthy notes on this passage investigate whether Caecilius speaks of real or invented miracles of Peter. What incurable itch for writing notes so led their minds astray? Does not Caecilius there declare that he speaks of miracles which Peter performed by power given to him by Him—that is, by God? Does he not openly indicate those miracles by which Peter converted many to righteousness and established for God a faithful and stable temple—that is, the Roman Church, gathered from those persons whom he had converted to the Christian religion? Who could ever call into doubt whether miracles performed by divine power, through which many are converted to righteousness, are genuine? Can Christ’s Church be founded and established by miracles other than true miracles performed by divine power?

Finally, Nero, Caecilius continues (chapter 2), fastened Peter to a cross and killed Paul [Col. 0882B]. Baudrius, however, wished the word *gladio*, “by the sword,” to be inserted before *interfecit*, “killed,” in the text, and attempts to prove this by various arguments. But additions of this kind ought not to be made without the authority of some manuscript. For Origen, cited by Eusebius (Ecclesiastical History, book III, chapter 1), likewise said simply of Paul: ἐν τῇ Ῥώμῃ ἐπὶ Νέρωνος μεμαρτυρηκότος, “having undergone martyrdom at Rome under Nero” [Col. 0882C]. Yet he had previously said that Peter was crucified there (ibid., book II, chapter 25). Eusebius, Tertullian (On Prescription, chapter 36; Apology, chapter 5; and Scorpiace, chapter 15), and many others, however, testify quite clearly that Peter was killed by the punishment of the cross and Paul by the sword.

# CHAPTER V

The statements transmitted by Caecilius concerning Christian morals and certain of their doctrines are examined.

## ARTICLE I

How greatly Christians abhorred things sacrificed to the gods of the Gentiles; whether the Emperor Maximinus was the first to order food offered for sale to be first consecrated to the gods before being placed on tables; and concerning a most distinguished martyr who was burned alive for tearing up Diocletian’s edict.

Nothing was more important or dearer to Christians than to observe with the utmost zeal the precepts of the true religion which they had embraced [Col. 0882D]. Therefore, they took the greatest care not to be defiled by any Gentile rite or even the slightest shadow of idolatry. Thus Caecilius reminds us (chapter 11) that, while the mother of the Emperor Galerius daily feasted on banquets—that is, on food falsely sacrificed to some god—the Christians, wholly abstaining from them, persevered in fasting and prayer. For they knew from the apostolic and divine command, concerning which we have spoken elsewhere, that all *idolothyta*—that is, things offered to some false god—were altogether and utterly forbidden to them.

Accordingly, Maximinus, so that he might compel them to violate this law and so that very many might either be polluted by these impious meals or perish from hunger, “was the first to devise,” in Caecilius’ words (chapter 37), “that all animals which he ate should be sacrificed at the altars, not by cooks but by priests; and that nothing whatsoever should be placed upon the table unless it had either been tasted in libation, sacrificed, or sprinkled with wine, so that whoever was invited to dinner might depart from it polluted and unclean.” So it stands in the Colbert manuscript; and nothing there, whatever anyone may say, is redundant or superfluous. We have explained elsewhere what is meant by food “tasted in libation” and “sprinkled with wine.”

Some doubt, however, whether Caecilius correctly said that this was established first of all by Maximinus [Col. 0883B], and whether he is to be understood as speaking generally of every kind of animal, or only of those served at Maximinus’ own table. For Eusebius relates (Martyrs of Palestine, chapter 9) that Maximinus commanded by public edict that all persons—men and women, slaves and children—should be compelled to eat the flesh of sacrificial victims; that every article for sale should be defiled with the libation of sacrifices; and that guards should be placed before public baths, as if in ambush, to pollute bathers there by accursed sacrifices. Yet some think it may be inferred from certain Acts of the Martyrs that Decius had ordered this earlier. They therefore suppose Caecilius’ meaning to be that Maximinus was the first to devise, or command, that only members of the imperial household, not all others, should eat only meat and food from animals previously sacrificed to the gods. And Caecilius’ words seem indeed to point in that direction: “all animals which he ate,” namely, Maximinus himself along with those who customarily reclined at his table. Yet because he adds, “nothing whatsoever should be placed upon the table,” the expression may perhaps seem general and to encompass everyone’s tables. But if after the word “table” one must understand “his own,” Caecilius’ words concern those who lived in Maximinus’ palace and reclined at his daily banquets. We fear, however, that this exception is more subtle than true. For if Decius had previously ordered that nothing but things consecrated to the gods should be placed on tables, his edict undoubtedly encompassed his own table as much as those of others. And the more savage the cruelty of this emperor, Maximinus, and the other tyrants, the greater, surely, was the constancy and courage of the Christians, borne with wholly unconquered spirit amid hunger and other dreadful torments. What could those have feared who were accustomed willingly and eagerly to undergo death for Christ’s faith?

Although this is most clearly demonstrated by what we have often observed in the preceding dissertations and shall observe below [Col. 0883D], we cannot pass over the example mentioned by our author of a certain most distinguished martyr who, when Diocletian’s and Galerius’ edict against Christians was posted in a public place, “though,” says Caecilius, “not rightly, yet with great courage tore it down and rent it apart [Col. 0884A], mocking as he said that victories over the Goths and Sarmatians had been posted. Immediately brought forth, he was not only tortured, but also *legitime coctus* [‘lawfully cooked’], and finally burned, after displaying admirable patience.”

The same story was recounted by Eusebius (Ecclesiastical History, book VIII, chapter 5):

> “First, as soon as the edict against the churches was posted at Nicomedia, a man of no insignificant standing, but highly conspicuous for the pre-eminence of secular honours, moved by a certain divine zeal and stirred by fervour of faith, tore down that edict of Diocletian and Galerius, which had been affixed in a public and prominent part of the city, and with his own hands rent it apart as impious and wicked. This he did while the two emperors were residing in the same city: the one, the senior Augustus, Diocletian, held the first rank of the imperial order; the other, Galerius, the fourth. Thus, since he was the first in that city to become famous through such a deed, he immediately endured the punishments that it was believable should be inflicted upon him after so great an act of boldness, preserving joy and tranquillity of mind until his last breath.”

Valesius thus translated Eusebius’ Greek words into Latin [Col. 0884B]; they are sufficiently clear and readily accessible, and it would be both lengthy and useless to transcribe them here.

You see, however, that Eusebius’ narrative is indeed longer but clearer than that of our Caecilius. For it is not easy to understand what Caecilius means by saying that the martyr tore up the edict “mocking that victories over the Goths and Sarmatians had been posted.” Various interpreters therefore explain this obscure passage in entirely different ways. Some think it derides the titles “Gothicus” and “Sarmaticus” assumed by the emperors; others, their vain display of victories over the Goths and Sarmatians; others, their barbarity equal to that of the Goths and Sarmatians whom they had conquered; and still others, that something greater and graver lies concealed in Caecilius’ text, which cannot be divined without another manuscript. Yet might it not be said that, by this bitter mockery, the martyr openly reproached that cruel decree as not truly an edict of Roman and pious emperors, but as some document proclaiming either the bloody victories of Goths and Sarmatians or the fictional and imaginary Roman victories over Goths and Sarmatians defeated by them?

But since it is irony, it is undoubtedly less important to know what our author intended by it than to understand these two words concerning the same martyr: *legitime coctus* [Col. 0884D]. He records various kinds of torments by which this most holy martyr was tortured. Brought before the tribunal and first “tortured”—that is, though he did not deny the deed, he was interrogated concerning it under great torments. Thus Caecilius says below: “Parents and husbands were tortured, that they might betray their daughters, wives, and wealth.” Seneca too says (Epistle 66): “tortured bit by bit through prolonged tension of the sinews.” Second, the martyr is said to have been *legitime coctus*, that is, according to the French translator of this book, placed upon a gridiron—a view rejected by others. But Prudentius writes of Saint Lawrence placed upon a gridiron (Hymn on St Lawrence, lines 409 ff.):

> The prefect orders him to be turned over;
>
> Then he says: “It is cooked; eat,
>
> And test whether raw or roasted
>
> Is the more agreeable.”

Yet it may be said that not everything called “cooked” was placed upon a gridiron [Col. 0885A]. Some think that *legitime coctus* means “cooked according to laws enacted by the emperors,” that is, burned. And indeed, among jurists, the adverb *legitime* signifies what is done in accordance with legal rule, or in the ordinary manner. Thus “lawful gladiators” and “lawful festivals” are spoken of. But since this martyr is said to have been killed at the beginning of the persecution raised by Diocletian, it would be necessary to prove that a law had then been issued by which Christians were to be burned with a slow fire. Our author Caecilius, however, records that this was later enacted by Galerius (chapter 21). Who, then, could previously have correctly written in the stated sense that a martyr had been *legitime coctus* merely by a sentence pronounced by a single judge? Therefore some suspect that *lentissime*, “most slowly,” should be read, but contrary to the authority of the manuscript. Until another, more correct manuscript is found, consider, I ask, which one—or what combination—of these two interpretations seems more acceptable to you. Whatever may be decided, Caecilius says much more clearly of that most unconquered martyr: “Finally he was burned, with admirable patience.”

If you ask who that most illustrious Christian athlete was [Col. 0885C], we shall answer that nothing more certain is available than what we have reported from our Caecilius and Eusebius. Eusebius expressly affirms that this man was highly conspicuous for the pre-eminence of secular honours. But the most learned Baluzius charges him with error here. Why? Because, says Baluzius, Firmianus Lactantius, the author of the book under discussion, was then residing at Nicomedia. Therefore he could not have been ignorant of the martyr’s name. Moreover, it concerned the Christian commonwealth to make that name known to all if he had been distinguished by such great pre-eminence of rank. But I shall detain you only briefly, most learned sir. Tell us, I ask, whether it was less proper for Lactantius—whom we shall now grant you to be the author of this book—to omit the martyr’s name because of secular dignities than because of so illustrious a martyrdom? “Firmianus Lactantius,” you say, “did not know his name because he was an obscure man.” But, I reply, he could not have been unknown, because he was a most celebrated martyr, who ended his life by a death so glorious not only to himself but to all Christians, in the city where the emperors and Lactantius himself, as you say, were dwelling. It therefore greatly concerned the Christian commonwealth that Lactantius should make the name of that utterly unconquered martyr, even if otherwise a wholly obscure man, known to all Christians and Gentiles, so that the latter might be confounded and the former more ardently inflamed to defend their religion. Perhaps Eusebius and Caecilius omitted his name because it was then sufficiently well known to everyone.

In ancient martyrologies written from the ninth century onward, we read that this martyr is called John [Col. 0886A]. But their authority is entirely uncertain, and they cite Rufinus (Ecclesiastical History, book VIII, chapter 5), who in his translation of Eusebius’ history gave no name at all. Nor is Papebroch’s opinion more certain: he thinks this is George, the most celebrated martyr. For he tries to confirm that view only by certain conjectures which appear to others of slight weight and wholly insufficient to prove it. It is enough, therefore, candidly to confess that this martyr’s name is as unknown as his struggle for Christ’s faith was glorious, and his victory illustrious.

## ARTICLE II

Concerning the Christians’ supreme power over demons, whom they drove away by the sign of the Lord’s cross during sacrifices performed by Diocletian; and whether, and how, it was lawful for them to be present at these pagan sacrifices.

The Christians’ power over demons was exceedingly great, and they exercised remarkable authority over them [Col. 0886B]. Demons were driven away by the sign of the cross alone. Caecilius furnishes us with a truly remarkable example of so great a power (chapter 10). When Diocletian, he says, “was sacrificing animals in the regions of the East, namely at Nicomedia, certain of the attendants, knowing the Lord, while they stood by as he sacrificed, made the immortal sign upon their foreheads. When this was done, the demons were put to flight and the rites were disturbed. The haruspices were alarmed and did not see the customary indications in the entrails; and, as though they had not obtained a favourable sacrifice, they repeatedly offered sacrifices. But the victims again and again slaughtered revealed nothing, until that master of the haruspices, Tagis, whether by suspicion or sight, said that the rites gave no answer because profane persons were present at the sacred ceremonies.” We have shown in another dissertation that Lactantius likewise recorded this same event in the genuine books of the Divine Institutes.

The fact that some believe an argument may be drawn from this to attribute the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* to Lactantius will seem to others of little weight [Col. 0886D]. The story was sufficiently well known and widely circulated to be recorded by writers of different ages as well as of the same age. Moreover, Lactantius (Divine Institutes, book IV, chapter 27) did not describe it in exactly the same way as Caecilius. Nor did he say, as our author does, that the pagan priests repeatedly and vainly renewed the sacrifice of animals.

Finally, Caecilius’ account seems much more obscure than Lactantius’. Caecilius writes: “Certain of the attendants, knowing the Lord, stood by.” But who, I ask, were these attendants: attendants of Christ, Diocletian, or the sacrifices? Those ambiguous words can certainly be explained in just as many ways. Lactantius entirely removed this obscurity when he wrote: “Certain of our attendants.” Perhaps, however, Caecilius read in Lactantius’ text what is written in two older royal manuscripts: “Certain of the attendants from among the worshippers of God,” and rendered it by the words “knowing the Lord.” But even if this is so, should he therefore have written in such a fashion that scarcely anyone could understand him?

But another difficulty arises [Col. 0887A]: how could Christians—and, more seriously, ministers of Christians—have dared to be present at pagan sacrifices? Tertullian resolves this knot with the following words (On Idolatry, chapter 16), which had first been corrupted but were emended by Rigaltius from Agobard’s manuscript:

> “Sacrifices are associated with [weddings]. If I am invited, and neither the title of an office attached to sacrifice nor the discharge of my service is involved, let me go as far as I please. Would that I could go as far as I pleased indeed; nor could we see things that it is unlawful for us to do. But since the Evil One has so encircled the world with idolatry, it will be lawful to be present at certain things in which we are rendering services to a person, not an idol. Certainly, if called to a priesthood or sacrifice, I shall not go; for that is the proper service of an idol. But neither shall I serve in such things by counsel, expenditure, or any other assistance. If I stand by because I was called for a sacrifice, I shall be a participant in idolatry; if another cause joins me to the person sacrificing, I shall be merely a spectator of the sacrifice.”

Tertullian therefore teaches that it is surely desirable that no Christian should be present at pagan sacrifices, which it was never lawful for him to perform. But because Christians, living among pagans, were compelled by their duties or servitude to follow them to temples and sacrifices, they were allowed to be present if they had not been summoned to the sacrifice itself and were discharging certain due services not to an idol but only to a human person—for example, their master [Col. 0887C]. They were then not participants in the sacrifice, but merely spectators. Accordingly, in another book he teaches (On Spectacles, chapter 9) that no prohibition derives from locations:

> “For a slave may enter even temples themselves without danger to discipline, if compelled by some straightforward necessity which does not pertain to the business or service proper to that place.”

Yet this indulgence was undoubtedly regarded as a concession to weaker persons because of pressing necessity, one that others of greater strength rejected with high courage.

The Christians who accompanied Diocletian while he sacrificed to his gods made the immortal sign of Christ’s cross upon their foreheads [Col. 0887D]. Lactantius likewise calls it the “immortal sign” (Divine Institutes, book IV, chapter 27), by which Christians fortified their foreheads as with an impregnable wall. We have discussed elsewhere, in our dissertation on Lactantius’ genuine books, the most ancient Christian custom of making the sign of the cross upon the forehead and its remarkable power for driving away demons.

This sign of the cross is called immortal by both our Caecilius and Lactantius, not only because it is invincible against demons and can never be conquered by them, but also because, as Lactantius says (Divine Institutes, book IV, chapter 26), it brings salvation to all who have inscribed upon their foreheads the sign of blood—that is, of the cross upon which Christ shed his blood [Col. 0888A]. Do you hear why he calls the sign of the cross immortal, and from where he derives its unconquerable power? Namely, from Christ’s own blood, which, fastened to it, he poured out for human salvation. Who but a heterodox person, wholly ensnared by the false errors of his sect, can deny that this doctrine is altogether sound and true?

## ARTICLE III

Concerning the sign of the Lord’s cross that appeared to Constantine the Great, by whose power he won a remarkable victory over Maxentius; with a discussion of sacred images.

Caecilius calls the sign of the cross not only immortal but also heavenly [Col. 0888A]; so great is its power that Constantine the Great’s army, armed with it, won a remarkable victory over the tyrant Maxentius in a wondrous manner. Caecilius briefly describes what the sign was, how it was formed, and by whose command (chapter 44):

> “Constantine was warned in a dream to mark upon the shields the heavenly sign of God and thus join battle. He did as commanded, and with the letter X turned crosswise, its upper head bent around, he marks Christ upon the shields.”

He is, as usual, rather brief and obscure. But Eusebius describes this much more clearly as follows (Life of Constantine, book I, chapters 28–29, p. 422):

> “At midday, when the sun was declining toward the west, he affirmed that he saw with his own eyes a trophy of the cross formed from light, σταυροῦ τρόπαιον ἐκ φωτὸς συνιστάμενον, set above the sun, bearing this inscription: Τούτῳ νίκα, ‘By this conquer.’ At this sight both he himself and the soldiers who followed him as he travelled somewhere—I know not where—and who were spectators, were greatly astonished. Meanwhile, he said, he began to doubt what this apparition might signify. As he pondered and considered the matter long and deeply, night at last came on. Then Christ God appeared to him in sleep with the sign that had been shown in heaven, and commanded him to have a military standard made in the likeness of that which he had seen in heaven and to use it as a saving defence in battles.”

Eusebius there certainly and openly affirms that he received this account from Constantine himself, who, lest anyone doubt so remarkable a sign, confirmed it by the sanctity of an oath [Col. 0888D]. After Eusebius, we also read the same things recorded by Socrates and Sozomen.

No one should be troubled that Caecilius says the sign of the cross was shown once to Constantine in a dream, while Eusebius says it was shown twice: first to him awake and to his soldiers in daylight, and later to him alone while sleeping at night. For our author, who, as we have said, everywhere pursues brevity of expression, thought it enough to relate only one of Constantine’s visions, the one which removed every scruple and doubt from him while he was still uncertain.

With comparable brevity, but with such obscurity that there are almost as many interpretations of Caecilius’ words as there are heads [Col. 0889A], Caecilius depicted that sign of the cross. Some even suspect that his text is corrupt. But perhaps some light is cast on this dark passage by the Eusebius already cited (Life of Constantine, book I, chapter 31), who describes the sign as Constantine ordered it to be made:

> “A long spear, overlaid with gold, bore a transverse crossbar in the shape of a cross. At the summit of the spear was placed a crown woven of gems and gold, in which Christ’s name was represented by only its first two Greek letters, namely Χ and Ρ, the letter Ρ being crossed through the middle by the Χ: Χιαζομένου τοῦ Ρ κατὰ τὸ μεσαίτατον. A purple banner, gleaming with gold and gems, hung from the crossbar; and at its upper part, beneath the very sign of the cross, was a golden portrait, painted to the chest, of Constantine and his children.”

But Eusebius there describes not only the cross seen by Constantine but also the golden and jewelled ornaments by which he subsequently adorned it. For he relates that at first nothing appeared to Constantine except a sign of the cross formed of light in the sky. The other features were added afterwards by him, except undoubtedly Christ’s monogram, or the first two Greek letters by which his whole name is signified. Caecilius seems to indicate these two first letters of Christ’s name joined together with the words: “with the letter X turned crosswise, its upper head bent around.” But the letter P, which is the second letter of Christ’s name, may perhaps have been omitted by a copyist because he did not know it was a Greek capital and thought the first letter to be Latin. Caecilius thus indicates the sign of the cross with Christ’s monogram in the form in which it is very frequently represented on coins and other most ancient monuments.

Who, then, can be of so patient a disposition as to endure without any disturbance the stubborn audacity of certain heterodox persons, who, while proscribing and detesting this cross of Christ and all other sacred images, rashly assert that in that sign no image of the cross was represented, but only the name of Christ? What could be imagined more rash and false? What testimony is clearer and more certain than that of Eusebius, who had himself seen with his own eyes what that sign was like: “It also happened to us once to receive it with our eyes.” [Ὃ δὴ καὶ ἡμᾶς ὀφθαλμοῖς ποτὲ συνέβη παραλαβεῖν.] Yet he expressly affirms it to be a σταυροῦ τρόπαιον, “trophy of the cross,” and a σημεῖον, [Col. 0889D] “sign.” “But,” they say, “not the cross, but Christ, is the Saviour of the world.” What follows from this? Can it therefore be established, against the authority of Eusebius and of all others, that the object of which we speak was not truly the sign and image of Christ’s cross?

Still less tolerable is the scarcely credible shamelessness of Tollius, who dared publicly to assert that this image of Christ’s cross shown to Constantine was a stratagem, to be referred to the military deceptions of the ancient emperors. But that most shameless man is rightly rebuked by his associate Baudrius. By what reasoning, pray, do you suppose Tollius there proved it? By none whatever. And indeed what could he bring forward against that sign of the cross, which not Constantine alone but also all [Col. 0890A] the soldiers accompanying him saw so plainly that, upon seeing it, they were greatly astonished, as Eusebius says (Eusebius, ibid., ch. 28)? But more on this later.

Yet perhaps you will think it doubtful whether certain associates of Tollius himself have not surpassed his rashness. For he did not venture utterly to deny that this event occurred, but interprets it in the most absurd manner. Others, however, in order to show that it is either false or at least uncertain, object that Eusebius makes no mention of this sign in his Ecclesiastical History. But what argument, I ask you, could be more futile or feebler? Is it not sufficient for establishing the truth of any matter that a witness wholly worthy of belief once affirm, emphatically, that nothing is more certain and true? Is his silence [Col. 0890B] in one book to be preferred to his explicit and express affirmation of it in another work?

“But,” they say, “what need was there for Constantine to confirm by an oath that he had seen the sign of the Lord’s cross, if an almost countless multitude were witnesses of so wonderful a miracle?” But when, I ask, did he swear this oath? Was it in the presence of those same soldiers? Not at all; rather, as Eusebius says, a long time afterwards, and therefore before certain others who had not seen this heavenly sign, or at least doubted whether Constantine related the truth.

A more recent heterodox writer nevertheless insists that the sign was a natural phenomenon, which so carried Constantine—who was doubtless not deeply versed in astrology—away in admiration that he wrongly thought it divine. [Col. 0890C] Were all the soldiers as well, and all the others who accompanied him in such great numbers, deceived by the same ignorance? Were the words τούτῳ νίκα, “By this conquer,” likewise natural; and was the inscription of the first letters of Christ’s name a chance occurrence? Certainly no person of sound mind could ever conceive this. Yet Eusebius, however vainly that writer protests, plainly and explicitly affirms that Constantine the Great saw and read both these words and those letters. Who would not place faith in Eusebius, who was alive at the time, rather than in a rash writer of our own age, supported by no authority?

Therefore neither he nor others are any longer to be heard when they still wrongly object that this history is described somewhat [Col. 0890D] differently by Sozomen, Philostorgius, and certain other later writers than by Eusebius and our Cecilius. For who does not know that some writers recount certain deeds and events more fully, while others do so more briefly? Would anyone therefore dare to accuse them of falsehood? Moreover, the writers cited nowhere deny that Constantine the Great saw the sign of the Lord’s cross; indeed, they rather establish and confirm it.

Finally, some gratuitously invent that Christ’s name was not represented in that wonderful sign. But they are refuted not only by the testimony of the most ancient writers, but also by that of their own associates, cited shortly below. Yet what wonder if men led by error contradict one another? Nor does it help others at all to have said that the sign had previously been affixed to military standards and banners. For even if this were demonstrated by them more clearly than daylight, it would never follow that neither Constantine nor his army truly saw the trophy of Christ’s cross, formed from light and set above the sun.

But it is shameful to linger over refuting these futile subtleties of heterodox persons, who strive by every means whatsoever to overthrow all sacred images of Christ’s cross and other images. Yet however madly they may be carried away against them, neither these men nor anyone else in possession of his senses will ever deny the truth of what Eusebius adds (Book I, *Life of Constantine*, ch. 31): “Constantine the emperor always used this saving sign [τούτῳ μὲν τῷ σωτηρίῳ σημείῳ] as a defence against the hostile forces of every enemy, [Col. 0891B] and ordered other signs fashioned in its likeness to be borne before all his armies.” Eusebius thus plainly declares that the sign of Christ’s cross is salutary to all, and that all Christians held it in great honour and regarded it as a defence. Who, moreover, would withhold belief from him as he recounts things done publicly, of which he was himself an eyewitness? Accordingly, we may throw at the haters and enemies of this saving sign what Prudentius once said to the pagan Symmachus:

> You, Queen—that is, Rome—must willingly acknowledge my standards,  
> In which the image of the cross either shines adorned with gems,  
> Or is displayed on long spears in solid gold.  
> By this sign the unconquered avenger Constantine, having crossed the Alps,  
> Loosed miserable servitude. [Col. 0891C]  
> (Prudentius, *Against Symmachus*, Book II, §§18–19.)

The Iconoclasts nevertheless press their point and again object against the use of other sacred images that, according to our Cecilius (Cecilius, ch. 12), the pagans found absolutely no image of God in the church at Nicomedia while they were destroying it, although they sought one most diligently. But the false opinion had taken root in the minds of the pagans—as we have observed elsewhere—that Christians truly worshipped an ass’s head. What wonder, then, if the pagans did not find in that church the Christians’ God, the *Onochoites* (“ass-god”), as we have noted Tertullian called him, though they had diligently sought him? Further, even if Christians then possessed no image of God, as being invisible, does it rightly follow that they rejected [Col. 0891D] every other sacred image of Christ and of the rest who had lived most holy lives? Certainly, we have already demonstrated sufficiently clearly that Christians retained the image of Christ’s cross, which they honoured with devout reverence and were accustomed to carry before their armies. We have discussed the religious veneration of sacred images in our preceding dissertations.

## ARTICLE IV

Concerning the churches of the ancient Christians, their goods and possessions, the merits of good works, and whether Cecilius transmitted anything concerning Christ’s thousand-year reign on earth.

It is more certain than certain that Christians constructed great and spacious churches before the reign of Diocletian. For shortly before we saw—and this will later be explained more clearly—that the church at Nicomedia is mentioned most explicitly not only by our Cecilius but also by Lactantius (*Institutions*, Book IV, ch. 27); at the beginning of the persecution stirred up by Diocletian, it was razed to the ground. Eusebius further testifies (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book VIII, ch. 1) that no one can adequately describe the innumerable multitude of persons then daily resorting to faith in Christ, the great number of churches in individual cities, and the very frequent concourses of people into them.

Nor did Christians possess only their churches or ecclesiae, but also other goods and possessions belonging to their corporate body—that is, to their civil community [Col. 0892B] and association. For in the edict of Licinius and Constantine the Great, reproduced in full by our author (Cecilius, ch. 47), these words occur:

> “And since it is known that these same Christians possessed not only the places in which they were accustomed to assemble, but also other property belonging to the right of their corporate body—that is, to their churches—and not to individual persons, you shall order that all these things, under the law set forth above, be restored without any hesitation or dispute whatsoever to the same Christians, that is, to their corporate body and congregations.”

Eusebius, however (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book VII, ch. 30), relates that the emperor Aurelian, appealed to by Christians, ordered that the heretic Paul of Samosata be expelled from the house of the Church [τῆς ἐκκλησίας οἴκου] and that this house be handed over to those to whom the bishops of the Christian religion in Italy and the bishop of Rome should write. Elsewhere he records (*Life of Constantine*, Book II, ch. 39) that Constantine the Great similarly commanded that everything judged rightly to belong to the churches—whether houses, possessions, lands, gardens, or any other things—be restored, without any diminution of the legal right pertaining to ownership.

It is also worth observing here what we read that our Cecilius taught about the merits of good works. Of Donatus and other confessors of Christ, who in defence of his faith had endured various tortures with wondrous and unconquered patience, he writes (Cecilius, ch. 1): “By their glorious confession they sought an everlasting crown for the merits of their faith.” You see [Col. 0892D] how expressly he proclaims the merit of faith and asserts that an everlasting crown is obtained by it. But Columbus replies that the verb *mereri* is often used in the sense of obtaining, attaining, or receiving by lot, so that it signifies an outcome rather than a right or worthiness—or even an outcome as well as, not merely, right and worthiness. Granted: that word is sometimes used in this sense by good authors. The question, however, is not about them, but about the sense in which Cecilius employed it. Certainly he does not take it to mean the outcome of faith. In what sense, indeed, could a man of sound mind say that Christ’s confessors sought an everlasting crown through the outcome, rather than the right and merit, of their faith? Did this happen by mere chance and fortuitous outcome? Further, even if we granted Columbus that *meritum* here signifies outcome, [Col. 0893A] what would follow? What could that outcome of faith be except faith’s very merit, through which Christ’s confessors sought an everlasting crown? Baudrius’s candid admission is therefore more commendable, although he belongs to the same sect as Columbus: he frankly declares that these words of our Cecilius, and certain others of the ancient Fathers of the Church, are to be understood concerning the reward and merits of good works.

Nor did Cecilius assert this only there. Elsewhere, after recounting the various torments endured by the same Donatus for maintaining Christ’s faith, he says: “An unspoiled crown is reserved for you in the kingdom of God in return for your virtues and merits” (same author, ch. 16). Does not Cecilius here most openly state the cause and reason—namely, virtues and merits—why a crown was reserved for him in the kingdom [Col. 0893B] of God? Thus sound and orthodox doctrine concerning the merits of good works could not have been asserted and explained more clearly. The aforementioned Baudrius had promised us that he would expound it in a separate dissertation, but death forestalled him and he did not fulfil his promise. We, however, in our preceding dissertations, have set it forth to the extent of our ability as opportunity arose.

Finally, let us observe that some suppose the thousand-year reign of Christ is indicated by our author where he says (Cecilius, ch. 2) that at the end of the world there will be a holy and everlasting beginning of Christ when he begins to descend. On the contrary, others think, with much better reason, that by these words this same thousand-year reign of Christ on earth is utterly destroyed and overthrown. For a millennium cannot be everlasting. But if this were Cecilius’s true opinion, he certainly cannot be Lactantius, who, as we saw elsewhere, strove with all his strength vainly to affirm that false reign of Christ. We know that this passage of Cecilius is mutilated and gaping; but the blank spaces are very short, and cannot in any way seem to have contained anything by which that thousand-year reign of Christ might be denoted.

## CHAPTER VI

Concerning the first persecutors of the Christian Church and their destruction.

## ARTICLE I

How rightly Cecilius asserts that the first persecution of Christians was raised by Nero Augustus; how improperly Tollius accuses him of falsehood because he traces the cause of this persecution to the preaching of the apostle Peter and asserts that Nero’s body lacked burial; and on what ground Cecilius charges with delirium those who invented that the same Nero would be the forerunner of Antichrist.

Cecilius first (Cecilius, ch. 2) assigned Nero the first place among all persecutors of the Christian Church: “He was the first of all,” he says, “to persecute the servants of God.” But, as some observe after Augustine (*City of God*, Book XVIII, ch. 52), was there not earlier, after Stephen had been killed by the Jews, a great persecution, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 8:1), in the Church which was at Jerusalem? Did not Herod, before Nero, kill with the sword James the brother of John and put Peter in prison? (ibid. 12:1 ff.) Were not Christians also expelled from Rome with the Jews by the emperor Claudius? Certainly. But Augustine himself also reminds us in that place that Christian writers accustomed to count ten persecutions of the Church begin the first from Nero’s time. Nor is this surprising. For the persecutions preceding Nero’s were not general, but were stirred up only in Judaea, or else only a few were swept away in their heat.
