Thus our Cecilius follows the common opinion of those who dated the beginning of the general persecutions from Nero. Since this cannot be unknown to anyone, we shall now cite only Tertullian (*Apology*, ch. 5) and Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, ch. 25), who reproduces his words. That African writer addresses the pagans themselves thus:

> “Consult your records: there you will find that Nero was the first to rage with Caesar’s sword against this sect, then especially rising at Rome; yet we even glory in having such a founder of our condemnation.”

In another book (*Scorpiace*, ch. 15), where he mentions the slaying of Stephen and James, he immediately adds: “We read the lives of the Caesars: Nero was the first to bloody the rising faith at Rome.” In both places he refers pagans to the records of their own writers, namely—as many have thought—to the books of Cornelius Tacitus. Why not, as we saw in its place, and surely with no less justice, to the lives of the Caesars written by Suetonius, or to public records? In these, or in other pagan books, Tertullian asserts that it was recorded that Nero was the first to rage with Caesar’s sword against Christians—that is, the first of all Roman emperors who raged against Christians with Caesar’s sword. Nothing prevents us from saying that Cecilius is to be understood in this sense, since in this book he discusses, as we have said, the disastrous deaths of persecutors. Some also thought Nero’s persecution was called the first because it was the first raised after the Church had been established at Rome and in other parts of the world. But the other explanation, even if it differs altogether from this, seems closer to our author’s intent and purpose.

Nero therefore began then to rage against Christians when, Cecilius says (Cecilius, ch. 2), he noticed that through Peter’s preaching a great multitude of people were daily passing from the worship of idols to the Christian religion. But Tollius there boldly accuses Cecilius both of falsehood and bad faith. Fine words, I pray you, my Tollius! Does not Cecilius openly profess at the end of his book (ch. 52) that he wrote everything in it according to the faithful accounts of those who knew? “But,” you say, “the times do not fit; and this persecution was consequently raised by Nero in order that the odium for the burning of the City might be transferred to Christians.” But tell us again, my Tollius: why do the times not fit? We have, unless we are mistaken, sufficiently proved that Peter was crucified at Rome by Nero’s order. For what reason, moreover, except because this prince of the apostles brought many to Christ’s religion by both preaching and miracles? Are not Peter’s death and the beginning of the Neronian persecution joined together in Eusebius’s books (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, ch. 25; *Chronicle*, year 69), and by other writers?

“But,” someone will say, “Cornelius Tacitus (*Annals*, Book XV), and later Sulpicius Severus (*Sacred History*, Book II, after the middle), expressly assert that Nero, in order to abolish the rumour that he had set fire to the City, produced culprits and inflicted the most elaborate punishments on those whom, hated for their offences, the populace called Christians”—thus speaks the pagan Tacitus. But why, I ask, were Christians hated by the pagan populace except for their religion, which they had received from the apostle Peter preaching at Rome? Further, was Nero’s sole reason for persecuting Christians that he might shift to them the accusation of setting the City on fire? On the contrary, Suetonius (*Life of Nero*, §16), in his life of Nero, first recounts that Christians were tortured with punishments because pagans considered them a class of men given to a new and criminal superstition. Much later he describes how Rome was burned by Nero’s command. But in that second passage there is no mention whatsoever either of Christians or of odium first directed against them because of that fire. And what if Cecilius followed Suetonius and did not attend to the words of Tacitus? No one would rightly accuse him of bad faith for that reason. Besides, Tacitus himself added in the same place: “A vast multitude were convicted upon their information, not so much of the crime of arson as of hatred for the human race.” He therefore declares that they were tortured more for hatred of the human race than for the crime of arson. Where then is Cecilius’s bad faith or error, when he had authors whom he followed and whom others followed later?

But Tollius not only there accuses Cecilius of bad faith and error; elsewhere he still censures him and other ancient Christian writers as men accustomed, as he says, to lie splendidly. This might be endured if he charged some men, subject as they were to human weakness, with some error. But who can patiently hear so many and such great men accused, without any reason advanced, of splendid falsehood—of asserting in public writings something contrary to their conscience and conviction? But, to set aside others who are not at issue here, where is this splendid lie of Cecilius? Tollius replies that it is found where he wrote of the punishments inflicted by the most just God upon Nero for the most unjust persecution of the Christian people:

> “Cast down from the height of empire and hurled from his summit, the powerless tyrant,”

and a little earlier:

> “The execrable and guilty man”—by which final adjective he elsewhere means wicked, cruel, and impious—“suddenly disappeared, so that not even a place for burial in the earth could be found for so evil a beast.”

Could these things, then, be said only by a man lying shamelessly? After Nero laid violent hands upon himself, were not various reports spread concerning his death? Did not many believe that his death was feigned and that he continued to live afterwards? Certainly we read this recorded by Cornelius Tacitus (*Histories*, Book II, near the beginning):

> “At the same time, when Galba was reigning after Nero, Achaia and Asia were falsely alarmed as though Nero were coming, owing to varying reports about his end, and because many invented and believed that he was alive.”

He then added that a freedman resembling Nero gave himself out to be the true Nero. Suetonius likewise says: “Twenty years later, when I was a young man, a person of uncertain rank arose who claimed to be Nero; his name was so favourably received among the Parthians that he was strongly supported and was surrendered only with difficulty” (*Life of Nero*, at the end). From these passages of Tacitus and Suetonius Casaubon infers that there were three false Neros. To this may be added that Augustine and Sulpicius Severus, to be cited below, record that many thought Nero had not truly been killed but preserved, in order that he might return to this world at its end.

You will press, however, that Suetonius and others affirm so openly and certainly that Nero killed himself and was subsequently buried that no man of sound mind can call it into doubt. Granted. Yet from this you cannot accuse Cecilius or others of bad faith or splendid lying, but only of error: they may have been unwittingly deceived by false reports or by the testimony of others, such as the Sibyl, whom our Cecilius himself praises.

For he then continues as follows (Cecilius, ch. 2): “Whence certain delirious persons” (the manuscript [Col. 0896C] codex has *deleri*, but the final letter *e* appears stained and corrected), “believe that he was transferred and preserved alive, the Sibyl saying that a matricidal fugitive would come from the ends of the earth; so that, because he was the first to persecute, he might likewise be the last to persecute and precede the coming of Antichrist.” Nor were they few, if we believe Jerome (*Commentary on Daniel*, ch. XI, 27), who speaks somewhat differently from our Cecilius: “Many of our people,” he says, “think that, because of the greatness of his cruelty and depravity, Domitian, a Nero, will be Antichrist.” Augustine, moreover, writes: “Some suspect that Nero himself will rise again and will be Antichrist. Others think he was not killed, but is hidden alive, in the vigour of the age in which he was when he was believed dead, until he is revealed in his own time and restored to his kingdom. But such great presumption astonishes me” (*City of God*, Book XX, ch. 19).

Although Augustine thus rejects this opinion, Sulpicius Severus nevertheless testifies that Martin, bishop of Tours, had embraced it. For when questioned concerning the end of the world both by Sulpicius himself and by his other disciples, Martin replied, as Sulpicius says (*Dialogues*, Book II, final chapter), “that Nero and Antichrist would first come; that Nero would rule in the western region, having subdued ten kings; and that persecution would be carried out by him, so that he might compel the idols of the nations to be worshipped . . . and finally that Nero himself would be killed by Antichrist.” Again, elsewhere (*Sacred History*, Book II, concerning Christ), Sulpicius writes that it was the opinion of many that Nero would be Antichrist. Then, after inserting several matters, he says:

> “It is uncertain whether Nero killed himself. Certainly, his body was destroyed. Hence it is believed that, even if he pierced himself with the sword, he was preserved after his wound had been healed, according to what is written of him: ‘And the wound of his death was healed’; he is to be sent at the end of the age, that he may exercise the mystery of iniquity.”

On the same matter Cuperus (*on the cited passage of Cecilius*) reproduced several verses by Commodianus, copied from a book he regards as rare; but this book was printed again in the final volume of the *Library of the Fathers*, published at Lyons.

Moreover, Cecilius intended us to observe that those ancient writers had fallen into this false opinion because, as we have already noted, the Sibyl said that a matricidal fugitive would come from the ends of the earth. Among the published Sibylline verses we read:

> Ἤξει δ᾽ ἐκ περάτων γαίης μητροκτόνος ἀνήρ  
> Φεύγων ἠδὲ νόον, ὀξὺ στόμα μερμηρίζων,  
> Ὃς πᾶσαν γαῖαν καθελεῖ, καὶ πάντα κρατήσει.
>
> A man, murderer also of his mother, will come from the ends of the earth,  
> A fugitive, breathing fury and devising sharp utterance;  
> He will destroy all lands and rule over all things.  
> (*Sibylline Oracles*, Book V, vv. 364 ff.)

And in another book:

> . . . . . Ἵν᾽ ὅταν γ᾽ ἐπανέλθῃ  
> Ἐκ περάτων γαίης ὁ φυγὰς μητροκτόνος ἐλθών,  
> Ταῦθ᾽ ἅπασι διδούς πλοῦτον μέγαν Ἀσσίδι θήσῃ.
>
> So that, when the fugitive murderer of his mother returns  
> From the ends of the earth,  
> Giving these things to all, he may make Asia abundantly wealthy. [Col. 0897C]

But our Cecilius brands this opinion with no less grave a mark of censorious severity than Augustine does. For our author not only refutes it but also calls its adherents, as we have said, delirious. He nevertheless admits that these writers assented to so false an opinion because they believed it supported by the authority of the Sibyl. Cecilius therefore was persuaded that in this matter the Sibyl had been no less delirious than her followers.

Perhaps someone will ask whether he is the same Lactantius who, as we saw in its place, confirms by very many verses of the Sibyls those things which he believed would certainly come to pass at the end of the world. For would he have made so much of their authority if he had thought them delirious, when he makes use of their testimonies concerning Nero, which are by no means wholly obscure? But above we showed that Lactantius cited Sibylline poems against pagans because they were persuaded that these poems possessed divine authority. Whether, however, the genuine Lactantius ever wished entirely to weaken this *ad hominem*, as they call it, argument by charging them with delirium, let others judge.

## ARTICLE II

Concerning Domitian, the second persecutor of the Church, his destruction, and the overthrow of his images and titles of honour.

Cecilius passes (Cecilius, ch. 3) from the first persecution of the Christian Church to the second, stirred up by Domitian. But throughout this entire account he never once calls him, as we observed above, by his proper name. First, he relates that Domitian arose after an interval of several—that is, twenty—years after Nero, and that he was no lesser tyrant than Nero. Tertullian, after speaking of Nero as noted above (*Apology*, ch. 5), immediately added these words, cited and translated into Greek by Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, ch. 20): “Domitian too had attempted it, a portion of Nero in cruelty.” And in another book (*On the Pallium*, ch. 4): “I refrain from designating a Caesar more impure than *Physione*, and more effeminate than Sardanapalus—indeed, a sub-Nero.” Moreover, as Eusebius still testifies (*ibid.*, ch. 17), Domitian himself boasted that he was the successor to Nero’s impiety, war, and hatred against God. Petilianus, in Augustine (*Against the Letter of Petilian*, Book II, vol. IX), calls him the greater part of Nero. Nor did Christian writers alone call him another Nero; pagan poets did as well. Hear, pray, Juvenal (*Satires*, V, vv. 37 ff.):

> When the last Flavian was already mangling the half-living world,  
> And Rome served the bald Nero.

Ausonius, following him, wrote:

> Titus, fortunate in the brevity of his reign, was followed  
> By his brother, whom his own Rome called the bald Nero.

Yet, Cecilius continues (Cecilius, [Col. 0898C] ch. 3), that cruel emperor reigned for a very long time and securely, until he stretched out impious hands against the Lord. In what sense, you may ask, is one said to have reigned for a very long time who ruled only fifteen years, as Eusebius says (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, ch. 20), and, according to some, a few months in addition? Is it because, apart from Augustus and Tiberius, he both reigned longer and more securely than the other preceding emperors? Or because a most savage tyrant’s reign, completed over fifteen years, is exceedingly long? How weighty these reasons are, or whether Cecilius erred, I ask you to determine and pronounce.

But when that intolerable tyrant, prompted by demons, set his mind near the end of his life to persecuting Christians, then, our author says (Cecilius, ibid.), he was delivered into the hands of his enemies and paid the penalty. For in the fourteenth year of his reign, Jerome says (*Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, §9), that Domitian stirred up the second persecution after Nero, as is confirmed by the author of Eusebius’s *Chronicle* (*Chronicle*, year of Christ 95). Eusebius himself writes (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, ch. 17) that Domitian, after many proofs of his cruelty, finally stirred up the second persecution against Christians. Many also think that it is indicated by these verses of Juvenal, *Satires* IV, at the end:

> But he perished after he had begun to be feared by cobblers;  
> This harmed him, drenched as he was in the slaughter of the Lamiae.

They suppose that by the name “cobblers” Christians are indicated by the satiric poet, as men of slender means and the lowest populace. We know indeed that some writers consider this persecution to have been raised earlier; but their argument is as slight as those we have reported are weighty.

That impious tyrant paid his due penalty to God, the avenger of his crimes, when he was killed at home, as Cecilius says. For we read these very words of Suetonius (*Life of Domitian*, §16) concerning his death: “Having dismissed everyone, he withdrew to his bedroom, and there was killed.” How and by whom he was killed, if you desire to know, you can readily learn from Suetonius’s subsequent account:

> “Stephen, Domitilla’s procurator . . . with his left arm wrapped in wool and bandages for several days as if it were ill, in order to avert suspicion, at the very moment of the plot introduced a ruse. Claiming to have evidence of a conspiracy, he was admitted; and while Domitian read the document handed him and was astonished, Stephen stabbed him in the groin. As he was wounded and resisted, Clodianus, a cornicularius, Maximus, Parthenius’s freedman, Saturius, a decurion of the chamberlains, and a certain gladiatorial trainer attacked him and butchered him with seven wounds.”

The same is related in Dio’s *Epitome*. And, to omit Philostratus (*Life of Apollonius*, ch. 10), who recounted the affair somewhat differently, and others, Eutropius certainly relates (*Roman History*, Book VII, at the end) that he was killed in the palace. Finally, Pliny (*Panegyric on Trajan*, near the middle, §49), after vividly setting before all eyes Domitian’s horrible cruelty and ferocity—he calls him a most savage beast—adds these words concerning his death:

> “Yet within the very walls and ramparts by which he seemed to defend his safety, he enclosed treachery, ambushes, and God, the avenger of crimes. Punishment moved and broke through the guards, and burst in through narrow and blocked approaches just as through open doors and welcoming thresholds. Far from him then were his divinity, those secret bedchambers, and savage retreats, into which fear, pride, and hatred of men drove him.”

Nor was this dreadful death of the most cruel emperor sufficient vengeance for his crimes. For although he had constructed, Cecilius says (Cecilius, ch. 3), many wonderful works enumerated by Suetonius (*Life of Domitian*, §5) and in Eusebius’s *Chronicle* (*Chronicle*, year of Christ 90), and even the Capitol, as Plutarch still testifies (*Life of Publicola*), the Roman senate so persecuted his name that it left no trace either of his images or of his titles. Suetonius indeed records (*Life of Domitian*, §23) that the senate was so delighted at Domitian’s death:

> “that, with the senate-house filled in a contest of acclamations, it did not refrain from assailing the dead man with the most insulting and bitter cries; it ordered ladders to be brought in, and his shields and images to be taken down before it and dashed upon the ground there; finally, it decreed that his inscriptions everywhere be erased and all memory of him abolished.”

Or, as Eusebius says (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, ch. 20), καθαιρεθῆναι τὰς Δομιτιανοῦ [Col. 0900A] τιμάς: “all titles of honour of Domitian were to be abrogated”; or, as Macrobius writes (*Saturnalia*, Book I, ch. 12), “his ill-omened name was to be erased from every bronze or stone.” Then, as Dio says (*Epitome, on Nerva*), his golden and silver statues were removed, producing a great sum of money.

## ARTICLE III

Whether Cecilius rightly said that Roman emperors from Domitian until Decius were good princes, and that the Church of Christians then suffered no assaults from enemies; and whether it may consequently be inferred that Lactantius was not the author of this book.

After Domitian’s death, “many and good princes,” Cecilius says, “held the helm and government of the Roman Empire” (Cecilius, ch. 3); and then the Church, restored to its former [Col. 0900B] condition, suffered no assaults from enemies. There are, as is evident, two propositions here of our Cecilius. The first asserts that from Domitian’s death to Decius’s accession there were good princes ruling the Romans. But with his customary audacity Tollius does not hesitate once again to charge Cecilius with disgraceful lying, because he affirmed as true something which he knew to be false.

But Tollius himself either truly lied or had not read these words of Zosimus (Zosimus, *History*, book I, after the beginning), who, after saying that Domitian had been killed by Stephen, a freedman, continues thus: “Good men, having assumed the supreme power—Nerva, Trajan, and after him Hadrian, the pious Antoninus, and the pair of brothers Verus and Lucius—undertook the correction of many abuses.” These, indeed, are the very emperors who reigned after Domitian. Yet Zosimus, just as does our Caecilius, expressly calls them good men. And what abuses, I ask, does he affirm were corrected by them, if not Domitian’s cruel edicts against pagans and Christians alike? Eusebius (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, ch. 20) plainly testifies that writers of that time recorded that those whom Domitian had sent into exile were recalled by Nerva and their property restored. Then the same Eusebius (ibid., [Col. 0900D] book IV, ch. 9) provides Hadrian’s edict, which stipulated that Christians should not be punished without a stated charge. Finally, he praises the extraordinary benevolence of the emperors before Diocletian’s age: after removing every fear of being compelled to sacrifice, they not only entrusted Christians with the government of provinces, but even allowed them to move about in their palaces, profess their religion, and build churches in which they could safely and securely devote themselves to their sacred rites. Do you see how falsely and rashly Caecilius is charged by Tollius with lying because he called these rulers good princes?

“But,” Tollius continues, “Caecilius himself lied for the purpose of showing by this falsehood that all the persecutors of the Church died miserable and accursed deaths.” Yet if Tollius reads that book attentively, he should surely take care lest he himself, rather than Caecilius, be convicted once more of falsehood. For that same Caecilius (Caecilius, ch. 5), shortly after the words cited by us, states most explicitly that the emperor Valerian was destroyed by a new and extraordinary form of punishment and death: “That,” he says, “there might be for posterity an example that the adversaries of God often receive a recompense worthy of their crime.” Here, as elsewhere, he designates the persecutors of the Church by the name “adversaries of God.” Therefore he plainly admits that they received a recompense proportionate to their crimes not always, but often. Thus he had not undertaken to prove that every persecutor whatsoever of the Christian Church met, in Tollius’s words, with a miserable death.

Moreover, we have made it clear that Caecilius’s purpose in this book [Col. 0901B] was not to write the history or recount the deaths of all the persecutors of our Church, but only of many of them, and especially of the later ones—namely Diocletian and others who most unjustly harassed Christians down to Licinius’s time. We may further add what we read written by Cyprian (*To Demetrianus*): “Never does wicked crime rise up against our name without divine vengeance immediately accompanying it.” Do you want something still more explicit? Here are Jerome’s very words: “But we,” he says, “shall say that all”—let Tollius hear, *all*—“not merely some persecutors who afflicted the Church of the Lord, to say nothing of future torments, have received even in this present age what they have done” (Jerome, *Commentary on Zechariah*, ch. XIV, v. 18). Had Caecilius said this, what tragedies, good God, Tollius would have raised! But he did not say it, and is unjustly accused of falsehood by that same Tollius.

A greater difficulty, therefore, arises from the second proposition of this same Caecilius. He unhesitatingly affirms that under the Roman emperors who held the helm and government of the Roman Empire from Domitian down to Decius, the Christian Church suffered no assaults from its enemies—that is, from the pagans. Dodwell indeed holds that it was then troubled by no general persecution decreed through imperial edicts. But in this matter he found, beyond the rest, a most vigorous opponent in our Theodoric Ruinart.

Whatever may be determined concerning general persecutions of the Church [Col. 0901D], Dodwell himself and all others are compelled to admit that Christians in these times were most cruelly tortured in various persecutions which they call local. Yet at that time almost countless martyrs, as Ruinart and others have shown, shed their blood for Christ’s faith. What then? Eusebius, and earlier Tertullian (*Apology*, ch. 2), as we have seen in its place, relate that the emperor Trajan, when Pliny the Younger consulted him as to what should be done with Christians, replied that they were not to be sought out, but, if brought before the authorities, ought to be punished. By this reply, therefore, a persecution was established against Christians, at least when they were brought forward. And who can doubt that many of them were in fact brought before judges by their most hostile pagan enemies, and condemned by those judges to death? Moreover, Pliny, Eusebius himself testifying (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, ch. 33), consulted Trajan on this matter for no other reason than that he had been moved by the great multitude of martyrs being put to death. But what need is there to summon these and other witnesses and writers? Pliny himself alone is sufficient (Pliny, book X, letter 101), who wrote to Trajan in these words: “The matter seemed to me worthy of consultation, especially because of the number of those endangered. For many of every age, every rank, and both sexes too, are being called into danger and will be called. For the contagion of this superstition has spread not only through the cities, but also through villages and rural districts; yet it seems possible to arrest and correct it.”

[Col. 0902B] Who can rightly doubt that very many came into this danger and were most cruelly tortured and killed for Christ’s faith? We are indeed not unaware that Tertullian, as we have elsewhere observed, recorded that Marcus Aurelius added a penalty—and a harsher one indeed—or, as Eusebius says (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, ch. 5), threatened capital punishment against those who accused Christians. Yet Melito and Apollinaris, as Eusebius himself (ibid., book IV, ch. 13), and also Jerome (*Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, chs. 24 and 26), testify, presented apologetic books to this very emperor, openly complaining that Christians were tortured and cruelly mangled with impunity by pagans. What, moreover, of the earlier complaint, made for this very reason, by Justin Martyr and Athenagoras, as we have seen elsewhere, before Antoninus Pius; and by Quadratus, disciple of the apostles, and Aristides before Hadrian, as Jerome relates (Jerome, *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, chs. 19 and 20)? Is not the same point further demonstrated by the books of Theophilus of Antioch and Tatian, of whom we have treated elsewhere, published in defense of the Christian religion? Finally, besides many others, we have plainly shown by the reliable testimony of Justin Martyr and Clement of Alexandria how great was the multitude of martyrs during the reigns of Antoninus and Severus.

We should certainly never make an end of speaking if all the evidence that most clearly proves this had to be set forth. [Col. 0902D] We shall therefore add only that, not merely during Marcus Aurelius’s reign did persecution against Christians arise—or, according to others, at least rage fiercely—but Severus too, in Eusebius’s words (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, ch. 1), “stirred up persecution against the Churches” (*Severus diōgmon kata tōn ekklēsiōn ekinei*). Then throughout the churches everywhere, Eusebius continues, glorious martyrdoms were accomplished by athletes contending for piety. Did Caecilius not therefore stray wholly from the path, when he plainly and utterly contradicts so many writers of such great authority, both contemporaries and others?

Perhaps someone will answer that he too had his defenders and supporters to follow. [Col. 0903A] For Melito of Sardis, in the *Apology* cited by Eusebius (ibid., book IV, ch. 26), as we have noted, openly testified that Nero and Domitian alone had endeavoured to malign our religion, and that they had accordingly been corrected and reproved by their successors. Tertullian, however (*Apology*, ch. 5), as we have observed in its place, after mentioning the persecution stirred up against Christians by these same emperors and the laws issued against those same Christians, immediately demands of the pagans that they produce thereafter some conqueror of Christians. He then lists emperors succeeding Nero and Domitian—Trajan, Hadrian, Vespasian, Marcus Aurelius, Antoninus Pius, and Verus—who corrected their impious edicts and promulgated no laws against Christ’s disciples.

But if our Caecilius paid attention to these writings of Melito and Tertullian, he certainly did not grasp their intention and meaning. For both, and especially Tertullian, there argue against pagans who, in order to excuse the slaughterhouse they exercised upon Christians, openly declared that they were bound by their laws, which commanded that Christians be tortured and butchered even without a hearing. Tertullian and Melito therefore rightly refute them, because emperors after Nero and Domitian had corrected their most unjust laws. Neither, however, says that those laws had been altogether repealed by them.

Furthermore, Marcus Aurelius did not openly remove punishment from persons of this sort—that is, Christians—as Tertullian says (*loc. cit.*), but only dispersed it. Although, therefore, neither Marcus Aurelius nor the other Caesars and Augusti mentioned by Tertullian issued laws against Christians, this nevertheless did not prevent very many Christians from being tortured and killed in different parts of the world. For the pagans were persuaded that the general and ancient laws, by which every new religion was forbidden, still remained in force. By their authority alone, therefore, they thought it lawful for themselves to rage against Christians; and in fact, as we have said, they did rage against them in a savage and dreadful manner.

Whatever may be determined concerning the laws of these emperors, it is most certain that very many Christian martyrs were butchered by various punishments and tortures after Domitian’s reign and before that of Decius. Caecilius therefore could not, except falsely, infer from the words of Melito, Tertullian, and others that the Christian Church suffered no attacks from enemies under the rulers succeeding Domitian.

Now if this is false, perhaps there will not be wanting some who suppose that it may thereby be established that this book of Caecilius is wrongly ascribed to Firmianus Lactantius. For it will undoubtedly seem more plausible to them that it proceeded from another author of a later age who, having misunderstood the words of Melito, Tertullian, or some other writer, struck upon this rock of error. Yet Caecilius might have been deceived by a scarcity of books, a lapse of memory, or false reports. But if he truly erred, by what reasoning, I ask, can he be said to be this very Firmianus, whom all admit had already, from the very time of the emperor Diocletian, been illustrious for a great reputation for knowledge and learning, and was by no means moderately versed in both the secular and ecclesiastical history of his own time?

## CHAPTER VII

On other persecutors of the Christian Church.

## ARTICLE I

On the persecution stirred up by the emperor Decius, and his disastrous death.

Caecilius, passing over those good emperors of whom we have spoken, comes from Domitian to Decius. Of him he records nothing else than that he fell immediately [Col. 0904B] after beginning, from the outset of his reign, to rage and revel madly against Christ’s Church: “For,” says our author, “after many years”—that is, one hundred and fifty years and somewhat more—“there arose the accursed beast, Decius.” He marks him by that exceedingly infamous name because of his extreme cruelty against Christians. Among others, Prudentius (*Against Symmachus*, book II) introduces Rome singing thus:

> Nero first, after murdering his mother,  
> drank apostolic blood; with the slaughter of the pious  
> he polluted me, and cruelly branded me with his own crime.  
> After him Decius, revelling amid severed throats,  
> fed his mad frenzy.

Hilary too (*Against Constantius*, §§4 and 7; *Against Auxentius*, §3) especially compared the Decian persecution with the Neronian. But it is not now our purpose to pursue at greater length what our author judged should be passed over.

Caecilius further said that Decius, after initiating persecution against Christians at the beginning of his reign, fell immediately; because, says Eusebius (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, ch. 39), he was killed before completing even the second year of his reign. Yet Aurelius Victor (*Epitome*) informs us that he ruled for thirty months. But the more learned critics of our age judge that the beginning of his reign should be placed before October of the year 249, and its end in November 251, after the commencement of the third year of his reign. They think their opinion may be confirmed by certain inscriptions presented by Goltz, Gruter, and Pagi.

How and by whom that emperor was killed, our Caecilius (Caecilius, ch. 4) describes in these words: “Setting out against the Carpi, who then occupied Dacia and Moesia, he was immediately surrounded by barbarians and destroyed with a great part of his army; nor did he even deserve the honor of burial, but, stripped and naked, lay as food for wild beasts and birds.” But Constantine the Great, in Eusebius (Eusebius, *Oration of Constantine*, ch. 24), expressly declares that he was struck down on the Scythian plains; Orosius (*History*, book VII, ch. 21), that he was killed in the midst of the barbarians; Zosimus (*History*, book I), that he was embedded in the mud of a marsh; Aurelius Victor (*Epitome*), that he was drowned in the depths of a marsh; Zonaras (*Annals*, book XII) [Col. 0905A], that he was buried in mud in a marsh—so that, as these latter two report, his corpse could not be found. Finally, the Eusebian *Chronicle* (Eusebius, *Chronicle*, at A.D. 252) says that he was killed at Abritus, or, as Jordanes says (*On the Deeds of the Getae*, ch. 18), near Abritus, a city of Moesia. You clearly see whose tracks our Caecilius follows, and why he added that Decius’s body lay as food for beasts and birds.

## ARTICLE II

On the persecution of the emperor Valerian, his disgraceful servitude, and the skin stripped from him after death.

Not long after Decius’s death, says Caecilius (Caecilius, ch. 5)—that is, around August of A.D. 253—Valerian was made emperor. Seized with a like rage against Christians, he shed much blood of the righteous—that is, of Christians—though for a short time. Eusebius relates more concerning this persecution (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chs. 10 and 11) from Dionysius’s letter to Hermammon. In it he wrote that none of the preceding rulers had embraced Christians with so much humanity and goodwill as Valerian had at the beginning of his rule. Indeed, he says, his entire household so abounded with pious persons that it seemed to be a Church of God.

But afterwards, through the persuasions of a certain master of magicians in Egypt and an archisynagogue, he turned his mind to torturing these Christians most cruelly. Then, says the same Eusebius, was fulfilled John’s prediction in the Apocalypse: “And there was given to him a mouth speaking great and impious things; and power was given to him to act for forty-two months” (Apocalypse, ch. 13, v. 5)—that is, for two years and six months, during which he exercised the utmost cruelty against Christians. Optatus (*On the Donatist Schism*, book II, §8) indeed said that the Church’s persecution under Decius and Valerian was like the lion, one of the four beasts which Daniel saw rising from the sea (Daniel, ch. VII, v. 4).

But Valerian paid for such great and unjust inhumanity by a form of penalty and punishment altogether singular and hitherto unheard of. “For,” says our author (Caecilius, ch. 5), “having been captured by the Persians, he lived in most disgraceful servitude”; or, as Eutropius (*Brief History of Rome*, book IX) and Aurelius Victor (*Epitome on Valerian*) relate, he grew old in ignoble slavery; [Col. 0905D] while the Chronicle of Eusebius and Cassiodorus says (Eusebius, *Chronicle*, at A.D. 258; Cassiodorus, *Chronicle*): “He grew old in miserable servitude.” For the king of the Persians, Shapur, says Trebellius Pollio (*On Valerian*), spoke with him as with a cheap and contemptible slave. Finally, in Zosimus’s words (*History*, book I), “having been reduced to the status of a captive, he ended his life among the Persians in that condition, leaving the Roman name with the greatest disgrace among posterity.”

To the disgrace of slavery was added this: according to Constantine the Great, he was paraded about loaded with chains, wearing a purple cloak and the remainder of the imperial dress. [Col. 0906A] Moreover, he was compelled to offer his back to Shapur, so that, as Caecilius says, by placing his foot upon Valerian’s back, the king might mount either a horse or a vehicle. If you seek another witness to so great an indignity, here is Aurelius Victor (*Epitome on Valerian*) and his very words: “As long as he lived, Shapur, king of that province, used, with Valerian bent over, to place his foot on his neck in mounting his horse.” Let us add, if you please, Orosius (*History*, book VII, ch. 22), who relates it thus: “The emperor of the Roman people grew old in most ignominious captivity among the Persians, sentenced throughout his life to this continual degradation of infamous service: he himself, bent down, was always to lift the king mounting his horse, not by the king’s hand, but by his own back.”

Lest any insult should be lacking to so great a disgrace [Col. 0906B], the proud Shapur, while trampling on the wretched emperor, reproached him with laughter: this, Caecilius continues (Caecilius, ch. 5), was the real thing, not what the Romans painted upon panels or walls. By these obscure words he means that Shapur said that the victories painted by the Romans on panels or walls were fictitious or much smaller, as Gregory Nazianzen observes (*Oration 3 against Julian*, near the middle); but that his victory over the Romans was real or greater, proved most plainly every time that, about to mount his horse or vehicle, he placed his foot upon Valerian’s back.

Although that disgraceful captivity lasted long, the miserable emperor, Caecilius says (ibid.), found no avenger of so great an injury, nor was he ever reclaimed by anyone, not even by his own son Gallienus. But Trebellius Pollio wrote of Gallienus (*On Valerian*) that, when he learned of his father’s most disgraceful captivity—over which many either murmured or grieved—he rejoiced and answered some persons: “I knew that my father was mortal.” Yet Pollio, contrary to our Caecilius’s view, presents us there with three letters in which the kings Betsoldus, Baserus, and Artabasdes demanded Valerian’s release from Shapur. For this reason these letters seem to have been wholly unknown to Caecilius, unless one can prove that his words mean nothing else than that Valerian was not reclaimed by any Roman person or Roman subject.

Furthermore, lest the mark of so great a disgrace inflicted upon the Roman name and its living emperor should ever be effaced, Shapur, says our author, ordered Valerian’s skin to be stripped off after his death, dyed red, and hung in a barbarian temple. Accordingly Constantine the Great, in his oration to the assembly of the saints, addresses Valerian in these words reported by Eusebius (Eusebius, *Oration of Constantine to the Assembly of the Saints*, ch. 24): “By command of Shapur, king of the Persians, your skin was stripped from you and preserved; you furnished for beholding an everlasting trophy of your calamity.” The Greek reads: “By command of Shapur, king of the Persians, having been flayed and preserved, you set up an eternal trophy of your misfortune.” Peter the Patrician (*Extracts on Embassies*) says the same, although Agathias (*On the Deeds of Justinian*, book IV) seems to indicate that Valerian’s skin was torn off while he was still alive.

## ARTICLE III

On the persecution stirred up against Christians by the emperor Aurelian, and his death.

Aurelian, not terrified by Valerian’s punishment, so great and infamous, or forgetful of his crimes and penalties, provoked, says Caecilius (Caecilius, ch. 6), God’s wrath by cruel deeds, undoubtedly against Christians. But suddenly he experienced that same God, whom he had already grievously offended, as the avenger of his crimes. For his bloody writings—that is, his cruel edicts against Christians—had not yet reached the more distant provinces, and already, says Caecilius, he himself lay bloodied on the ground at Caenophrurium, a place in Thrace. Eusebius relates (*Oration to the Assembly of the Saints*, ch. 24) that, while rushing through Thrace in a frenzy, he was slain in the middle of the public road and filled the furrows of the public highway with impious blood. According to the same Eusebius (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, ch. 30), he ruled the Romans for six years; Orosius (*History*, book VII, ch. 23) subtracts six months from this, and some modern writers subtract a full year.

Thus, near the end of his life, as Caecilius and the authors cited by us report, he began to rage against Christians by bloody writings; or, as Eusebius says, by “edicts composed against us.” But while, Eusebius continues, he was, so to speak, subscribing these laws, divine justice took vengeance upon him—even before they had reached the more distant provinces, as our author says.

[Col. 0907C] This persecution begun by Aurelian was therefore very brief. Yet it is surprising that some unhesitatingly assert that no martyrs were then made. For when Caecilius wrote that Aurelian’s edicts had not reached the more distant provinces, he indicates clearly enough that they had been published in nearer places. There seems, surely, no room for doubt that pagans—and especially the priests and sacrificial ministers of the gods—when these laws were promulgated, abused them to put to death many Christians tortured by the customary punishments. Indeed, we learn from Eusebius (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, ch. 30) that Aurelian was prompted by certain counsels to stir up persecution against Christians, and that while he was still alive a rumor of this was spread everywhere. And who would not readily persuade himself that the pagans, given this opportunity to satiate their hatred of Christians, did not then spare their blood?

Caenophrurium, moreover, mentioned by Caecilius, commonly called Castel-Novo, is a village of Thrace in which Aurelian was indeed killed, as was just said. For in the Chronicle of Eusebius (Eusebius, *Chronicle*, at A.D. 276) we read: “When Aurelian had stirred persecution against us, lightning struck him”—so too Orosius (*History*, book VII, ch. 23)—“and his companions; and not long afterwards he was killed between Constantinople and Heraclea, at Caenophrurium on the old road.” Vopiscus (*On Aurelian*) says: “While he was travelling near the station of Caenophrurium, which lies between Heraclea and Byzantium, [it was] through the malice of his secretary”; or, as Eutropius wrote (*Breviary*, book IX), “he was killed through the treachery of a member of his household.” Vopiscus adds that this secretary was called Mnestheus and, fearing the threats of his master, forged the emperor’s handwriting and wrote down his own name and those of certain friends, as though Aurelian had determined to kill them. Thus those men, deceived by a wicked slave, killed Aurelian himself by the hand of Mucapor, as Vopiscus also says (*loc. cit.*). Is this not what our Caecilius signifies in these rather obscure words (Caecilius, ch. 6): “He was killed by his friends through a certain false suspicion”?

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0908B] On the final persecutors of the Christian Church, and first on Diocletian.

## ARTICLE I

On Diocletian’s three names, Diocles and Jovius; his native land, avarice, and timidity; on the other emperor and two Caesars created by him through timidity; whether he gave Spain to Constantius to govern; how he oppressed all by exactions and taxes; on his great prosperity until he began to harass Christians; and whether he was better and more useful to the state than other rulers.

Before Diocletian had been raised to the supreme dignity of emperor, he was called Diocles, says Caecilius (Caecilius, chs. 9 and 19). We have already observed that this passage appears, perhaps not without reason, to be mutilated and gaping in several places. For, to provide a sense and some connection of words, it would certainly seem necessary to read: “But Diocletian, who before his reign was called Diocles, when he [took control of] the state” (Caecilius, ch. 9), etc. But who would dare, without another manuscript, to affirm that these are the true and genuine words of our Caecilius?

Whatever the case, after laying aside the purple together with the imperial office, Diocletian, says our author, became Diocles again—that is, he became such as he had been before his reign, a private person. For it is not likely that he then resumed the name Diocles. Certainly, although Caecilius afterwards calls him once or twice by that earlier name, elsewhere he still calls him Diocletian.

That the name Diocles was originally given him may be learned from these words of Aurelius Victor in the *Epitome* (Aurelius Victor, *Epitome on Diocletian*): “Diocletian, a Dalmatian, freedman of the senator Anulinus, was named Diocles after both his mother and the town Dioclea; but when he assumed the power of the Roman world, he converted his Greek name into a Roman one.” This is fully confirmed by Paul the Deacon, to be cited shortly. Hence some think that in the text of Vopiscus (*On Numerian*), where he reports a druidess as saying to Diocletian, before he had been proclaimed emperor, “Diocletian, you are too avaricious,” one should read *Diocles* instead of *Diocletian*. But this should have been supported by at least some authority. Others think that certain words of Libanius (Libanius, *Oration* 12, *To Theodosius*) may prove that the name Diocles was restored to Diocletian after he abdicated the empire. Not badly, indeed, if they had shown that Libanius was truly speaking there of Diocletian. Yet however the matter stands, when our Caecilius said that he became Diocles again after laying aside the imperial dignity, he seems there rather to denote his return to private life than to allude to the restoration of his earlier name.

Moreover, Diocletian also adopted, according to Caecilius (Caecilius, ch. 52), the surname Jovius, just as the elder Maximian adopted that of Herculius, so that the former might be believed descended from Jupiter and the latter from Hercules. Concerning both surnames Aurelius Victor (Aurelius Victor, *On the Caesars*, on Diocletian) has recorded: “To Maximian there was added the surname derived from the worship of the divinity Hercules, as to Valerius”—that is, Diocletian—“that of Jovius. From this name was also given to the military auxiliaries, exceptionally distinguished in the army.” This appears still more clearly not only from writers of ancient panegyrics, but also from many coins on which these names are inscribed and each emperor is represented adorned with the insignia of Jupiter and Hercules. The learned Dom Anselm Banduri, connected with us no less by friendship than by fellowship, displays various coins of this kind in his work *On the Coins of the Emperors*.

Aurelius Victor, whom we cited a little earlier, likewise added there that Diocletian was a Dalmatian by origin. Yet as great as is the agreement of writers on this matter, so varied are their opinions as to the place in which he was born. For these are, as we said, the words of Aurelius Victor (*Epitome on Diocletian*): “Diocletian, a Dalmatian, of a mother and town alike named Dioclea.” From these words they think it indicated that he derived from Dioclea or Dioclea. But relying on the testimony of Paul the Deacon (Paul the Deacon, book X, *History of Diocletian*), some think that he speaks there of Diocletian’s mother. For after the words, “Of a mother, town, and name alike Dioclea,” he immediately adds: “From their names, until he assumed the empire, he was called Diocles.” But they judge the sense of these words to be that Diocletian’s mother was Dioclea both by town and by name, and that he received both names from her. Let others decide whether Paul, who transcribed Victor’s words, speaks more clearly or more truly.

But Caecilius, like very many others, certainly asserts that Diocletian, after laying aside the purple, returned to his native country. Yet, as the author of the Eusebian *Chronicle* says (Eusebius, *Chronicle*, at A.D. 317), “He lived as a private person at an estate near Salonae, and there grew old in distinguished leisure.” Eutropius’s words are almost the same (*Breviary*, book IX, at the end). Socrates (*Ecclesiastical History*, book I, ch. 2) says, “He died at Salonae, a city of Dalmatia.” The Aurelius Victor cited by us above (*Epitome on Diocletian*) relates that, when Herculius and Galerius urged him to resume the empire, he replied: “Would that you could see at Salonae the vegetables planted by my own hands!” Therefore many think Diocletian was born at Salonae; and because that city was not far from Dioclea, perhaps the various opinions concerning his native place arose from this.

Diocletian, however, is called by Caecilius (Caecilius, ch. 7) “the inventor of crimes and contriver of evils”—namely, those by which he ruined everything, attacking not only Christians but pagans also. If you ask Caecilius how this was done, he immediately answers: “By avarice and timidity he subverted the world”—that is, the world under Roman, and therefore his, dominion.

We have already heard the druidess reproach him for the vice of avarice. Nor should you say that it was counterbalanced by his boundless desire for building, noted by Caecilius himself shortly afterwards, and by his great munificence, through which he ordered palaces, basilicas, circuses, armories, and mints to be built, and finally wished Nicomedia to be made equal to Rome. For he amassed immense riches through dreadful exactions, as will shortly be said; and, Caecilius further says, in insatiable avarice he was unwilling ever to diminish what he had stored in the treasury.

Timidity, as is customary, accompanied his avarice. For in every disturbance, as our author says (ibid., ch. 9), he was plainly fearful. Aurelius Victor, however, writes (*On the Caesars*, on Diocletian): “Valerius”—that is, Diocletian—“showed too little honourable faith toward friends, from fear indeed of dissensions, while he thought that the tranquility of their partnership might be disturbed by disclosures.” But our Caecilius charges Diocletian with timidity, of which a fuller discussion is to follow, because he made three others participants in his rule: Maximian Herculius, Constantius Chlorus, and Maximian Galerius. For he admitted them to partnership in the empire at the time when he himself had most to fear. Throughout the whole world, as Eutropius says (*Breviary*, book IX), affairs were disturbed; or, as Aurelius Victor observes (*loc. cit.*), the burden of wars pressed hard. Yet he did not add these partners and associates in rule at the same time. For, as many report, he named Herculius Augustus in the year 286, and Constantius and Galerius Caesars in 292. We shall discuss this below.

Having summoned them into partnership in his rule, he divided the world in this manner: assigning a part to each, he reserved one quarter for himself. “For,” says Victor (*loc. cit.*), “all the Gauls beyond the Alps were entrusted to Constantius; Africa and Italy to Herculius; the Illyrian coasts as far as the strait of Pontus to Galerius; Valerius Diocletian retained the rest.” Yet if our author is to be believed, Maximian Herculius, besides Italy, in which he had the seat of his empire, had under him the richest provinces, either Africa or Spain. Julian the Apostate (*Oration* 2) indicates that Spain, or “the western Iberians,” was given to Constantius. There thus seems to be no slight disagreement between our Caecilius and these two writers. For neither Aurelius nor Julian could possibly have been unaware under whose jurisdiction Spain fell. Can it therefore be answered, in order to untie the knot of this difficulty, that Caecilius uses the particle *vel* not conjunctively but disjunctively, because Spain, ravaged by wars and at the beginning of the divided empire, was assigned by name to no one? But whether the matter stands thus, or which of these writers erred, we leave for others to decide.

With the Roman Empire thus divided into four parts, both the two Augusti and the two Caesars strove to raise from the peoples subject to them a larger army than earlier rulers had maintained. Therefore, to provide for the soldiers, as Caecilius says (Caecilius, ch. 7)—that is, to furnish them with pay and provisions—the provinces were plundered by immense exactions; and the strength of the cultivators was so exhausted by the enormity of the *indictions*, or taxes, that the fields, untilled, were abandoned.

Aurelius Victor likewise (Aurel. Vict., *De Caesaribus*, at Diocletian), after describing that division of the Roman Empire, says: “Hence a vast evil of tribute was imposed upon the Italian portion. For, since all administered the same public service in an orderly manner, in order that the army and the emperor, who were always present either wholly or for the most part, might be maintained, a new law of assessments was introduced.”

Moreover, in order to extort a greater abundance of money and wealth, Diocletian divided the provinces into fragments and various parts, and multiplied the prefects of the treasury [Col. 0911C] and the collectors of tribute. “The number of governors,” says Caecilius (Caecil., ch. 7), “that is, rulers of individual provinces, and of offices,” or officials and those who discharged official duties, “as well as of rationales,” that is, procurators of the fisc who presided over matters of the sacred treasury, “and also of magistri,” was increased by him. Concerning these, as also concerning the others mentioned there by Caecilius, consult the law of Constantine the Great, Gothofredus’s notes upon it, and the observations of the latter and of Panciroli upon the *Notitia Dignitatum*. Moreover, the exaction of money and revenues was so great that, as Caecilius again testifies (Caecil., ch. 7), many perished for the sake of their wealth and possessions, since these were evidently seized from them together with their lives.

But because Diocletian, as we have already said, wished to adorn Nicomedia with a magnificence equal to Rome’s [Col. 0911D], any owner in that city whatsoever of either a more highly cultivated estate or a more splendid building was exposed to a ready accusation and punished capitally. Thus the citizens of Nicomedia, utterly crushed by those immense taxes, departed thence; and so “a great part of the city is evacuated,” as we read in a manuscript copy of Caecilius’s book—that is, a large part of those same citizens is compelled to leave this city, as though it had been captured by enemies—unless Caecilius wrote *excedit*, “goes out” or “departs.”

Everything set forth thus far concerned Christians no more than pagans and all others placed under Diocletian’s rule. Yet, when he was overturning the commonwealth by such plans, says Caecilius (ibid., [Col. 0912A] ch. 9), and with such associates—when he deserved every punishment for his crimes—he nevertheless reigned in the highest prosperity so long as he did not defile his hands with the blood of the righteous, that is, Christians. All readily acknowledge that he reigned in the highest prosperity until he persecuted Christians. But Tollius denies that the commonwealth was overthrown by his policies and accuses our author of falsehood in this matter: “For scarcely,” he says, “was there a prince better, more useful to the commonwealth, more prudent, or of greater spirit than Diocletian.” Granted, he may have been more prudent than others. Yet his prudence was certainly wicked and evil. For his malice, as Caecilius observes (ibid., ch. 10), was such that he performed what was good by his own will alone, but what was evil by the counsel of others, to whom the whole perversity of the undertaking might be ascribed. And indeed Eutropius (*Breviary of Roman History*, bk. IX) calls him shrewd, subtle in intellect, and well-mannered; yet he wished to satisfy his own malice through the odium incurred by others.

How, then, can he be called better than other emperors, when, through insatiable avarice, as we have seen, and through most cruel exactions, he devastated all lands, cities, and provinces, and took from rich and very wealthy persons both their possessions and their lives?

Eutropius further relates that Diocletian, after defeating Achilleus—certainly before he raged against Christians—used that victory harshly and stained all Egypt with grievous proscriptions and slaughter. Orosius agrees with Eutropius (*Histories*, bk. VII, ch. 25) and adds: “Using victory without restraint, he gave Alexandria over to plunder and stained all Egypt with proscriptions [Col. 0912C] and slaughter.” Eutropius adds (loc. cit.) that Herculius, indulging his native ferocity, followed Diocletian in all his more severe counsels. Tollius is therefore mistaken; or he should have shown that scarcely any prince had been better than Diocletian, or more useful to the commonwealth. How, moreover, he ceased to be fortunate as soon as he began to harass Christians must now be explained.

## ARTICLE II

### On the preliminaries and beginning of the persecution stirred up by Diocletian against Christians: for what reason, and by what counsels, he was prompted to harass them

Our Caecilius (Caecil., ch. 10) has explained [Col. 0912D] in the following manner why Diocletian was roused against Christians: “He was sacrificing cattle to his gods in the regions of the East”—that is, at Alexandria or in Egypt, as some suppose; or, as others hold, at Antioch, where certain laws issued by him at that time are mentioned. But, out of the fear discussed earlier, as an investigator of future events—or, as Aurelius Victor says (*De Caesaribus*, at Diocletian), of impending events—he sought knowledge of the future in the livers of these cattle. Yet, when some of those present made the immortal sign of the cross upon their foreheads, the demons were put to flight; the rites were disturbed and repeated in vain; and they returned absolutely no answer. The master of the haruspices, named Tagis by our Caecilius (Caecil., ch. 10)—the man presiding over the inspection of the entrails of sacrificial animals—said that there was no cause for this silence other than the presence of profane persons, that is, Christians.

Now, since this name was derived from Tages, the inventor of haruspicy, as we observed in another dissertation, the chief haruspex was afterwards called by that name. But whereas our Caecilius says that the response concerning the demons’ silence was given by Tages, or the master of the haruspices, Lactantius (*Divine Institutes*, bk. IV, ch. 27) reports that it was given not by him alone but by the haruspices. Some have thought that this response of one or several haruspices is identical with that by which Apollo, according to Eusebius (*Life of Constantine*, bk. II, ch. 50), was said to have declared, not through a human mouth but from some dark cave, that he was prevented by righteous men from uttering true oracles. But [Col. 0913B] it may be questioned whether the account related by Caecilius and that related by Eusebius are one and the same. For our part, we are readily persuaded that they are two distinct accounts. For Caecilius seems later to speak of Apollo’s response, as we shall shortly see.

Nevertheless, both Eusebius and Caecilius assert that this silence, imposed upon the demons by Christians, was the true reason why Diocletian began to rage and rave against them. “Immediately,” says Eusebius, “he composed bloody edicts with blood-stained, murderous, so to speak, sword-points”: *διατάγματα λύθρων μιαιφόνοις, ὡς εἰπεῖν, ἀκωκαῖς συνέταττε* (Euseb., ibid., ch. 51). He commanded the judges to direct their minds toward devising more cruel forms of punishment.

Caecilius (Caecil., ch. 10) therefore says that, raging with anger, Diocletian first ordered—letters having been issued for this purpose—that soldiers and all who were in the palace should be compelled to perform abominable sacrifices. And Eusebius indeed relates (*Ecclesiastical History*, bk. VIII, ch. 1) that the persecution began with Christians serving as soldiers. Yet our author seems there rather to indicate that this was only a prelude to the persecution. For he adds that this occurred then, but that Diocletian did nothing further at that time against the religion of God. In the Eusebian *Chronicle* (at A.D. 302) the following is recorded: “Veturius, master of the army, persecutes Christian soldiers, persecution against us now beginning gradually from that time onward.” Caecilius further warns us that this occurred some time before Diocletian came to winter in Bithynia. [Col. 0913D] Some think these events took place in the year 298, four years, that is, before the general persecution began in 302, as the *Chronicle* of Eusebius notes. But we fear that Caecilius’s cited words cannot bear this explanation, especially because he said that Diocletian fell from the height of prosperity at the time when he undertook to harass Christians. For by these words he seems to indicate that Diocletian then laid aside the imperial dignity, as will become clearer from what follows.

Caecilius next relates (Caecil., ch. 11) that, after some time had elapsed, Diocletian came to Nicomedia, a city of Bithynia, and Galerius hastened there. Spurred there by the complaints of his superstitious mother, Galerius most vehemently urged Diocletian to destroy Christians, but did not easily bend his mind. For Diocletian, after holding counsel throughout the whole winter with Galerius alone, tried—as the manuscript reads—to turn aside the madness of this headlong man. He said it was enough that the Palatines—that is, as was said shortly before, those dwelling in the palace—and soldiers should be prohibited from the Christian religion. Since Galerius pressed him, “a few judges,” says Caecilius, “and a few military men were admitted to the council,” and they gave their opinion against Christians.

But why, one may ask, are they called “few” here, when Caecilius had just said that Diocletian was accustomed to summon many persons to council in a similar matter? Some therefore think that *alii*, “others,” should be read in place of *multos*, “many,” but this is contrary [Col. 0914B] to the plain testimony of the manuscript. Nothing, however, need be changed in the text; and its reading can be shown to be sound from the fact that a few judges selected from one order and a few from another would make up many persons. Yet it must be admitted that Caecilius speaks of an exceptional matter, still secret, which at that point did not permit, I think, so large a number of advisers to be admitted to council.

Diocletian, however, had not yet acquiesced in the judgment of Galerius and the judges concerning the torture of Christians. He therefore sent a haruspex to Milesian Apollo, who answered, says Caecilius, “as an enemy of the divine religion.” This is all he says, and no more concerning that response of Apollo. Consider, however, whether this may be the response quoted a little earlier from Eusebius (*Life of Constantine*, bk. II, ch. 50), in which Apollo declared that his oracles were hindered by righteous men.

Diocletian could resist no longer in the face of all these counsels and Apollo’s response. He therefore permitted Christians to be afflicted, but on the condition that no one’s blood should be shed. Galerius, on the contrary, wished them all to be burned alive.

## ARTICLE III

### In what year, month, and day Diocletian began to torture and persecute Christians

Diocletian was holding his eighth consulship (Caecil., ch. 12), and Maximian Herculius his seventh, when Diocletian decreed that Christians and the Christian religion should be utterly removed and completely overthrown. Diocletian himself was then in the nineteenth year of his reign [Col. 0914D]. For our author (ibid., ch. 17) later relates, as we shall see, that he went to Rome to celebrate there, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, the day of his vicennalia. He immediately adds that he rushed out of the city as the Kalends of January approached, on which his ninth consulship was to be conferred. Now, in the year 284, on the seventeenth of September, according to the opinion of more expert critics, he was made emperor. Therefore the twentieth year of his reign fell in A.D. 304, when he assumed his ninth consulship. Thus he began his eighth consulship and nineteenth regnal year in A.D. 303, when he undertook more cruelly to torment and persecute Christians.

Moreover, Caecilius (Caecil., ch. 48) expressly declares that this persecution of Diocletian lasted ten years and approximately four months, namely, from the destruction of the church at Nicomedia until the promulgation of Licinius’s edict for its restoration. But this church was restored on 13 June 313. It was therefore demolished in 303, on 23 February, as will shortly be explained. Thus the persecution of Christians began in that year and month.

Although these matters seem clear and manifest to many, some nevertheless think that this persecution was begun in the preceding year, 302. For Augustine records (*Against Cresconius the Donatist*, bk. III, ch. 27) that the Council of Cirta was convened in the consulship of Diocletian for the eighth and Maximian for the seventh time, on the fourth day before the Nones of March. Elsewhere, however, he himself says that certain persons were crowned with martyrdom in February, thirteen months before that council. But hear his very words in this second passage: “The records of the martyrs, which showed the time of the persecution, were drawn up in the consulship of Diocletian for the ninth and Maximian for the eighth time, on the day before the Ides of February; but the episcopal acts of the decree of Cirta were drawn up after their consulship, on the third day before the Nones of March. Thus thirteen months are found to intervene, certainly more than the eleven which the Catholics had formerly answered through less careful calculation. But the office, in making its mistaken answer that a month intervened, regarded the consulship as the same one, and did not notice ‘after the consulship,’ where another year was already in progress.”

Thus Augustine admits there that the office, or official, erred and did not sufficiently notice that another year was then being reckoned, after Diocletian’s ninth consulship had elapsed. That year, therefore, ought to have been A.D. 305. Since there is an open contradiction between these two Augustinian passages, no one will deny that either a copyist or an official erred in one of them; and he could more easily have erred in the former than in the latter. Hence nothing at all certain can be inferred from these two passages of Augustine, unless it is clearly shown in which one the error occurred.

Furthermore, the martyrs mentioned by Augustine are said to have died for confession of Christ thirteen months before the Council of Cirta, celebrated in Diocletian’s eighth consulship, on the fourth day before the Nones of March. Yet Diocletian’s first edict was issued at Nicomedia on 24 February 303. What follows from this except that those martyrs departed this life before that edict? And yet the Donatists inferred the time of that persecution from their acts. Thus the argument drawn from these passages of Augustine is as weak as it seems certain that the Diocletianic persecution arose in A.D. 303.

Caecilius (Caecil., ch. 12) identifies the day of that year and the first day of the persecution as the festival of the Terminalia, ordinarily celebrated on the seventh day before the Kalends of March, or 23 February. For Macrobius says (*Saturnalia*, bk. I, ch. 13): “The Romans intercalated not after February was completed, but after the twenty-third day, that is, after the Terminalia had been celebrated; they then appended the five remaining days of February after the intercalation.” On these matters, in addition to the ancient Roman calendars, consult Varro (*On the Latin Language*, bk. V) and Augustine (*City of God*, bk. VII, ch. 7). We ourselves have touched upon them elsewhere.

Against this opinion of our Caecilius, however, Eusebius may be objected (*Ecclesiastical History*, bk. VIII, ch. 2), who dates the beginning of this persecution raised by Diocletian in the nineteenth year of his reign, in the month of Dystrus—which the Romans call March—as the feast-day of the Lord’s Passion was approaching; or, as Rufinus translates (*Ecclesiastical History*, bk. VIII, ch. 2), when the feast-day of the Lord’s Passion was imminent. But the Eusebian and Alexandrian *Chronicles* (at A.D. [Col. 0916B] 384), and Theodoret’s *Ecclesiastical History* (bk. V, ch. 39), note the day of Easter itself, or of the saving Passion. Others reply that Easter in Diocletian’s nineteenth year did not fall on 25 March but on 18 April. They therefore hold that these writers should be understood as referring to the first edict against Christians, according as it was promulgated earlier or later in their respective provinces. But this edict must be discussed shortly.

## ARTICLE IV

### On the church at Nicomedia, demolished at the beginning of the persecution by Diocletian’s command; on this emperor’s edict against Christians immediately promulgated; on the first and second fires in the imperial palace; on their author; and on the manner in which Galerius tried thereby to inflame Diocletian to more cruel harassment of Christians

When the first day of persecution, noted by Caecilius (Caecil., ch. 12), as just mentioned, had dawned—or rather had begun to dawn—

> That day, the first of death and the first of evils,  
> Was the cause.

So Virgil sang, as quoted by our author without naming him (*Aeneid*, bk. IV, v. 169). “For suddenly,” he says, “while the light was still uncertain,” that is, before sunrise, “he came to the church with commanders, tribunes, and rationales.” The manuscript indeed has *pfectus*, that is, *profectus*, “having set out,” but this makes no sense unless something has been added or understood. For Diocletian cannot be understood there, since he is later said to have remained in his palace [Col. 0916D]. Instead of *profectus*, therefore, it seems preferable to read *praefectus*, perhaps “the praetorian prefect,” or at least one of those prefects who, according to custom, attended Diocletian while he was staying at Nicomedia. Whoever this prefect was, he came with the others mentioned above to the church; after the doors had been torn off, they sought the image of God, as observed above, but found none. The sacred Scriptures, undoubtedly of the Old and New Testament, found by them were burned—Scriptures which it was then customary to keep in churches.

Caecilius immediately adds: “Plunder is granted to all.” But once the sacred Scriptures had been burned, what plunder, pray, could have remained in those Christian churches for pagans to carry off? Sacred vessels, ornaments, benches, stools, chairs? It would not at all have been a useless undertaking if our Caecilius had at least briefly touched upon these things. For such items must have possessed some value, since our author declares that they were seized by those pagans. If anyone nevertheless clearly proves that the captured plunder was nothing other than copies of the sacred Scriptures, which the pagans, as Eusebius soon to be cited explains, burned in the middle of the forum, we shall not wholly resist. Yet no one will deny that Caecilius’s language is altogether obscure.

Meanwhile, while these things were being done in the church at Nicomedia, “they themselves were on watch,” that is, Diocletian and Galerius, viewing the church from their palace. For a long time they debated with one another whether fire should be applied to it. But Diocletian forbade it, lest the neighboring houses, and then some part of the city, should be consumed in that fire. Therefore the praetorian soldiers leveled that very lofty temple to the ground within a few hours.

But Lactantius, in his genuine works, as we have shown elsewhere, clearly testifies that he was then in Bithynia, namely at Nicomedia, teaching rhetoric when that temple was destroyed. Why, then, if Caecilius truly was Lactantius (Lactant., *Divine Institutes*, bk. V, ch. 2), he did not now also say that he was an eyewitness of this destruction, we leave for others to examine. Eusebius, however, certainly did not pass it over in silence, but wrote: “All these things were fulfilled in our times, when we saw with our own eyes the sacred buildings leveled to the ground and utterly overthrown, and the sacred books of the divine Scriptures burned in the middle of the forum”: *αὐτοῖς ἐπείδομεν ὀφθαλμοῖς* [Col. 0917C]. Nevertheless, in his oration on the praises of Constantine, he made no further mention of his own presence, and narrated the event more briefly and simply: “These men, recently, *πρὸ μικροῦ*, tearing down houses of prayer from their very heights to the ground and uprooting their foundations themselves, presented to spectators the image of a city taken in war” (Euseb., *Oration on the Praises of Constantine*, ch. 9).

But let us follow our Caecilius (Caecil., ch. 13), if you please. “On the day after,” he says, “the Church of Nicomedia had been utterly destroyed, Diocletian decreed in a public edict that Christians should be deprived of every honor and dignity; that all, without any exception, should be subject to torture; and that legal action should be effective against all, while they themselves should be unable to bring suit for injury, adultery, or stolen property, and should possess neither freedom nor a voice.” Eusebius, however, reports somewhat differently (*Ecclesiastical History*, bk. VIII, ch. 2): the edict first decreed that churches be razed to the ground and the sacred Scriptures burned; secondly, *καὶ τοὺς μὲν τιμῆς ἐπειλημμένους ἀτίμους, τοὺς δὲ ἐν οἴκετίαις, εἰ ἐπιμένοιεν ἐν τῇ χριστιανισμοῦ προθέσει, ἐλευθερίας στερεῖσθαι προαγορεύοντα*.

Rufinus translates this into Latin: “If anyone among us were protected by the prerogative of some honor, that privilege being removed, he should remain infamous; if any slave remained a Christian, he could not obtain freedom.” Valesius, however: “That persons of rank should be marked with infamy; but persons in households should be deprived of liberty if they persisted in the profession of the Christian faith.” We give both differing interpretations of Rufinus and Valesius because some learned men support the one, others the other. The entire difficulty lies in explaining the words *τοὺς δὲ ἐν οἰκετίαις*, “those in households.” Some think that slaves cannot be meant, since they cannot be deprived of a liberty which they lack. Others maintain that Rufinus, close to Eusebius’s age and skilled in Greek, understood both the force of Eusebius’s words and what was done in his time. Moreover, otherwise no penalty would be designated in that edict against Christian slaves. Yet although slaves cannot be deprived of liberty, they can sometimes obtain it. What therefore prevents this possibility from having been removed from them by Diocletian’s edict, so that all Christians without exception were either marked with infamy or consigned to perpetual slavery?

Whatever Eusebius’s meaning may be, our Caecilius certainly makes it plain that freedom was taken away from all Christians by this edict, so that every opportunity to complain in court concerning injury done to them, adultery, or stolen property was taken away, although legal action against all of them—*omnis* in the manuscript—was effective, that is, exercised with the greatest diligence. For Cicero also wrote (*Letters to Atticus*, bk. IV, ep. 16): “The courts are active,” *judicia calent*. But what if *valeret*, “was valid,” is to be read, and Caecilius’s meaning here is that all opportunity for Christians summoned before a tribunal to defend themselves before judges was removed, although every action, denunciation, and accusation brought against them by pagans was valid and admitted?

That edict of Diocletian, however—which is not given in full either by our Caecilius (Caecil., ch. 14) or by Eusebius—did not please Galerius, who considered it too mild. Therefore, in order to inflame Diocletian’s mind toward more cruel torture of Christians, he set fire to the palace through certain secret agents and arranged for Christians to be accused of this fire with equal odium and calumny. Eusebius, however, relates (*Ecclesiastical History*, bk. VIII, ch. 6) that the fire arose by some unknown accident, but that Christians were declared and publicly proclaimed to be its authors by a false public rumor. Yet in another work of this same Eusebius (*Oration of Constantine to the Assembly of the Saints*, ch. 25), Constantine the Great testifies that Christians were in fact accused of that fire, although he himself, together with others then living at Nicomedia, had seen with his own eyes that the palace was set ablaze by lightning and by a certain heavenly fire, as men knowledgeable in these matters had foretold. But if our Caecilius was then staying at Nicomedia, as Constantine was, this ought to have been entirely well known to him. Why, then, did he pass it over in such complete silence? Was it because, when the palace began to burn from lightning, Galerius immediately sent secret agents to intensify the fire? Could Caecilius, as a scrupulous adherent of brevity, have presented one cause of this fire and omitted the other? But how that most ardent herald of divine vengeance could wholly omit so striking an example of heavenly fire punishing the enemies of Christians, let others explain to us.

Whatever the cause of this silence, Eusebius (Caecil., ch. 14) attests that Christians were then killed by sword, fire, and other punishments. Caecilius, however, has recorded in writing that Diocletian, inflamed with anger, since he could not—or pretended that he could not—suspect that Christians were guilty of that fire, ordered all his own people, namely the Palatines and household servants, to be tortured, so that whoever might be convicted as guilty of so great a crime should suffer deserved penalties. But his attempt was wholly futile, because he had left wholly untouched the household of Caesar, that is, Galerius, to which those incendiaries and wicked men belonged.

But Galerius himself, who did not allow Diocletian’s anger to burn itself out—that is, to cool and diminish—contrived another fire. Yet we find no writer besides Caecilius who mentions it. Nor is this surprising, someone may say; for, as Caecilius notes, it was extinguished very quickly. Then Galerius himself, pretending to fear that he would be burned alive, rushed out of Nicomedia, having prepared for departure “in the middle of winter,” says our author. What, then, does he mean by “in the middle of winter,” when he had previously said that Galerius held counsel with Diocletian throughout the whole winter?
