The sense, therefore, as we observed above, is that Galerius secretly prepared in midwinter all things necessary for the flight which he was then planning.

## ARTICLE V

[Col. 0919C]

### How Diocletian raged against Prisca and Valeria; against the most powerful eunuchs, and who these were; likewise against presbyters and ministers with all their households; against persons of every sex and age; and against household servants; and with what cruelty he and other judges attempted to compel all to sacrifice to false gods

Galerius was persuaded, and not falsely, that Diocletian would, after his own sudden flight, be stirred up more fiercely to torture all Christians. And in fact Diocletian “burned with such anger,” says Caecilius (Caecil., ch. 15), “not only against his household servants, but even against all, that first of all he compelled his daughter Valeria and his wife Prisca”—of whom we must speak later [Col. 0919D]—“to be defiled by sacrifice.”

Then come the very words of our author (ibid.): “The most powerful eunuchs, through whom the palace, and Diocletian himself, formerly stood secure, were killed.” In a manuscript copy stands *eda*, a corrupt and abbreviated reading; some would read: “Certain eunuchs were killed, whose power in Diocletian’s palace was very great, and through whom Diocletian himself had formerly stood secure.” But these persons do not seem sufficiently to have considered how varied are the meanings of the adverb *quondam*. Good writers use it not only to denote past time, but also in the sense of “sometimes” and “always,” as Servius notes on this verse of Virgil, *Aeneid*, bk. II, v. 678:

> I am left behind, once called your wife.

Thus he says elsewhere: “*Quondam* embraces three tenses, as does *olim*.” Caecilius’s meaning, therefore, may be that the eunuchs were then the most powerful, because they were greatly loved by Diocletian and consequently both the emperor himself and the palace were sustained through them.

If you ask who these were, we reply that almost everyone thinks there is no room for doubt that they had professed the Christian religion. Baluzius thinks that one of them was Peter, whose celebrated martyrdom is described by Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History*, bk. VIII, ch. 6). Why should Dorotheus, Gorgonius, and others mentioned in the same passage by that historian not also be numbered among them? He calls them *τοὺς Βασιλικοὺς παῖδας*, that is, “the king’s chamberlains,” as Rufinus translates, or “chamberlain boys,” as Valesius has it. Who indeed does not know that almost all such chamberlains of kings or emperors were eunuchs? Hence the more learned critics judge that Caecilius speaks of these chamberlains, concerning whom Eusebius wrote: *Οἱ καὶ τῆς ἀνωτάτω τιμῆς παρὰ τοῖς δεσπόταις ἠξιωμένοι, γνησίων τε αὐτοῖς διαθέσει τέκνων οὐ λειπόμενοι*—“Men who were indeed distinguished by the highest privilege of honor before the emperors and were loved by them no less than sons.” These words certainly confirm what we said just above: that Caecilius calls them “the most powerful” (Caecil., ch. 15) because the palace and the emperor himself were sustained through them.

Caecilius continues: “The presbyters and ministers were arrested and condemned without any proof, *ad confessionem*.” In the Colbert manuscript we read *ad confessione*, but this must undoubtedly be emended to *ac confessione*, “and by confession,” if they were truly condemned because of the previously mentioned fire in the palace. But if they were condemned for confession of the Christian faith, as is more probable, perhaps the text read *ob confessionem*, “on account of confession,” namely confession of the Christian religion alone, so that they were condemned without any other proof. “And with all their own,” the author adds, that is, with other inferior ministers of the Church or their household servants, “they were led away”—supply, “to punishment.”

Further, Caecilius continues: “Persons of every sex and age were burned in groups, fire having been set around them; household servants, millstones bound to their necks, were sunk in the sea.” It is not easy to say what is meant here by “household servants”: whether persons of every sex and age; or the household servants of presbyters and ministers; or rather those enrolled in the *schola domesticorum*, some of whom held office in the forum, while others were bound by military oath, and some among them always attended the emperor. Gothofredus and Valesius discuss all these at greater length. Let fair judges of matters decide which explanation of Caecilius’s obscure expression is truer.

What more need be said? “Judges,” he continues (Caecil., ch. 15), “were dispersed through all the temples, compelling everyone to sacrifice.” Whom does “everyone” mean? Pagans? For we saw shortly before that Prisca and Valeria were compelled to perform these sacrifices. For it is not certain, as will be said below, whether they were truly Christians. But if Caecilius designates pagans, it certainly cannot be denied that, by saying “everyone,” he includes Christians also, of every rank and sex.

Yet we cannot wholly approve the inference drawn from this by a certain most learned man: that Christians then frequented pagan temples while preserving the faith of Christ, in order, by rendering some cult and honor to false gods, to escape punishment and a death by no means uncertain. For we have already shown from Tertullian’s testimony that Christians entering pagan temples were permitted only to observe sacrifices being performed there, but were in no way to participate in them or to render any honor whatsoever to counterfeit divinities. Who would dare to assert, without the most certain grounds, that Christians treated these laws as nothing? Moreover, our Caecilius openly declares that judges used force upon Christians to make them offer sacrifices to the gods in temples; but he does not say—indeed, he appears plainly rather to deny—that they were defiled by any sacrifice or any kind whatsoever of impious worship.

The learned man nevertheless presses his case. Does not this immediately follow: “The prisons were full; unheard-of kinds of tortures were devised” (Caecil., ch. 15)? But with whom, he asks, were the prisons full, and against whom were unheard-of kinds of torture devised, except against Christians whom pagans had discovered to have rendered some honor to the gods, in order to escape the most dreadful punishments? But who could readily be persuaded that the prisons were then full of such false and deceitful Christians? Who would not rather admit that they were said to be filled with those who openly and boldly refused to worship the pagans’ false gods and to sacrifice to them in pagan temples and elsewhere? But if anyone is not yet willing to yield to these reasons, let him hear Eusebius, a witness beyond doubt worthy of trust in this matter: *Μυρίου πλήθους ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ καθειργνυμένου· καὶ τὰ πανταχῇ δεσμωτήρια ἀνδροφόνοις, καὶ τυμβωρύχοις πάλαι πρότερον ἐπεσκευασμένα, τότε πληρούντων ἐπισκόπων, καὶ πρεσβυτέρων καὶ διακόνων, ἀναγνωστῶν τε καὶ ἐπορκιστῶν· ὡς μη δὲ χώραν ἔτι τοῖς ἐπὶ κακουργίαις κατακρίτοις αὐτόθι καταλείπεσθαι* (Euseb., *Ecclesiastical History*, bk. VIII, ch. 6): “An innumerable multitude of persons everywhere was consigned to custody; and prisons everywhere, once assigned to murderers and tomb-robbers, were then filled with bishops, presbyters, deacons, readers, and exorcists, so that there was no longer any room left there for those condemned for crimes.” Who could find it probable that all these persons—and even others, if one wishes—who shared their punishments, or most of them, were cast into prison because they had either genuinely or falsely, merely pretendedly, worshiped the gods or sacrificed to them?

Finally, Caecilius relates (Caecil., ch. 15) that altars were set up in the *secretaria*, that is, in the praetoria and places where judges customarily sat, so that litigants might plead their cases only after first offering sacrifice. “Lest,” says this same Caecilius, “justice should be administered rashly to anyone”—that is, lest justice should rashly be administered to any Christian, who could not be heard for any reason whatsoever unless he had first sacrificed to the gods [Col. 0922A]. For they judged it an utterly rash act if any Christian were ever admitted by any judge to state his case otherwise. Thus Christians in the provinces subject to Diocletian’s rule were tortured in a manner wholly dreadful. This, indeed, you will find asserted and reported in the passage from Eusebius just cited. But what was done in the other provinces, let us now consider, if you please.

## ARTICLE VI
How great was the slaughter of Christians, by Diocletian’s command, in the provinces subject to Galerius and Herculius; and, conversely, how Constantius allowed churches to be destroyed, yet kept Christians in Gaul unharmed and exempt from persecution.

[Col. 0922B] Since the Emperor Galerius was, as we have said, a most vehement author and instigator of the persecution stirred up by Diocletian against the Christians, there is plainly no room for doubt that in his own provinces he tortured and killed Christians with greater cruelty than did the other emperors. But this will be explained more clearly below in its proper place. Yet, in order that the Christian religion, together with its adherents, might be utterly destroyed throughout the world, Diocletian, sending letters to Maximian Herculius and Constantius Chlorus, ordered them to rage against the Christians in the same manner as he himself did. Herculius, however, “not at all merciful,” says Caecilius, “but a most cruel man,” willingly obeyed in Italy. In Italy alone? Did he not also do so throughout Africa, which, as we observed above, had been assigned to him? Surely, we think, no one will ever deny it. For Optatus of Milevis testifies (Optat., bk. I, §13) that Africa—and Eusebius adds other provinces to it (Euseb., *On the Martyrs of Palestine*, ch. 13)—was shaken and most cruelly harassed by this tempest of the most dreadful persecution. Caecilius therefore named Italy alone, either because it was the chief seat of Herculius Augustus, or because, while staying there at that time, he there began to persecute the Christians.

Under these rulers, therefore—Diocletian, Herculius, and Galerius—whom Caecilius calls three most savage beasts, “the whole earth,” he says, was harassed: that is, all the territory subject to their rule and laws. Moreover, they harassed Christians with such savagery and inhumanity that Caecilius (Caecil., ch. 16) declares true what Virgil sang, *Aeneid* VI, vv. 620 ff.:

> Not if I had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths,  
>   
> . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .  
>   
> Could I run through every name of punishments.

And indeed Eusebius (Euseb., *Ecclesiastical History*, bk. VIII, ch. 6) frankly acknowledges that the slaughter of Christians at that time was so great as utterly to exceed every capacity for speech. But these matters are made still clearer and more evident to all from what we have elsewhere brought forward from the true Lactantius.

As regards Constantius, when he received Diocletian’s letters, he allowed the “meeting places,” that is, “the walls,” as Caecilius says—that is, the churches and temples of the Christians, which could be restored—to be destroyed, lest, Caecilius adds in the same place, [Col. 0923A] “he should seem to dissent from the commands of his elders” (*maiorum*). But whose elders, pray? Not Herculius, to whom Diocletian had written likewise. Not Galerius, who, being still Caesar, could certainly not be called his elder. What, then, if the reading were *maioris*, “his superior”? Everything would certainly stand well. Yet if you more obstinately maintain that the reading *maiorum* must be retained, we shall immediately and readily agree with you, if you establish this properly. But from it one may not without reason infer that the names not only of Diocletian but also of another emperor were inscribed upon the law issued against Christians. For then Caecilius could call them Constantius’ elders. But what is one to do in a matter so obscure, where only one manuscript survives, and that one everywhere infected with errors?

[Col. 0923B] However this may be, Constantius cared little to obey the commands of these elders. For, although he allowed—and did not order—the churches to be destroyed, nevertheless he kept wholly unharmed the Christians, who, as Caecilius still says, are the true temple of God. For he exercised no persecution against Christians, as Optatus of Milevis testifies (Optat., bk. I, §22), nor was he ever a participant in the war stirred up against us, as Eusebius puts it (Euseb., *Ecclesiastical History*, bk. VIII, ch. 13). Indeed, “the pious emperor,” Eusebius says, “obtained a most blessed end of life,” having kept safe and free from injury those under his authority who worshipped God:

> Τοὺς ὑπ᾽ αὐτὸν θεοσεβεῖς ἀβλαβεῖς, καὶ ἀνηπηρεάστους φυλάξας, καὶ μήτε τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν τοὺς οἴκους καθελὼν, μηδ᾽ ἕτερόν τι καθ᾽ ἡμῶν καινουργήσας.

“Having preserved the worshippers of the true God who lived under his rule immune from every injury [Col. 0923C] and calumny; and having neither overthrown the buildings of the churches nor undertaken anything against our people.” Nor, content to have said this once, does he fail to repeat it a second and a third time.

What then, someone will object, does not Eusebius there expressly affirm, contrary to the opinion of our Caecilius, that no church was destroyed by Constantius? But let him, I pray, note what Caecilius says there: not that the churches of the Christians were destroyed by Constantius’ order or direction, but that he allowed them to be destroyed—that is, did not prevent the pagans from destroying them. His toleration was therefore compelled, lest he should appear utterly to oppose the commands of Diocletian, or of his elders, as has been said. In this sense, then, Eusebius could quite rightly say that the buildings of Christian churches were not overthrown by him.

Moreover, Caecilius writes (Caecil., ch. 16) that the whole world, except Gaul, was harassed by the other three rulers. Since Gaul had fallen under the authority of Constantius, as we have said, it was not tossed and shaken by any storm of persecution. We have already heard Optatus and Eusebius, who testify that he was in no way a participant in the persecution raised against us. But this is demonstrated still more plainly by the remarkable comparison—which must not be passed over—that Eusebius himself makes (Euseb., *Life of Constantine*, bk. I, ch. 13) between Constantius and the three emperors named above:

> They had undertaken to storm the churches [Col. 0924A] of God, level them to the ground, and obliterate the houses of prayer together with their very foundations. But he kept his hands pure and unstained by their impious wickedness and showed himself in no way like them. They had defiled the provinces subject to them with the slaughter of God’s worshippers, men and women alike, as with a kind of civil war. But he always kept his mind pure and inviolate from such a crime. They, by accumulating the evils of a most impious superstition, first enslaved themselves and then all their subjects to the deceits of most wicked demons. But he, the author and standard-bearer of the deepest peace within the boundaries of his empire, allowed his subjects to serve divine worship without any disturbance.

This is from Valesius’ translation; in his edition you may easily read, if you wish, Eusebius’ somewhat longer Greek wording. [Col. 0924B]

By what reasoning, then, someone will ask, did the same Eusebius elsewhere assert (*On the Martyrs of Palestine*, ch. 3) that the western provinces, and Gaul specifically—Γαλλίαν—had endured the fury of the war scarcely for the first two complete years of the persecution:

> Ὅσα . . . οὐδ᾽ ὅλοις ἔτεσι δυσὶ τοῖς πρώτοις τοῦ διωγμοῦ τὸν πόλεμον ὑπομείναντα.
>
> “which . . . had endured the war for not even two whole years at the beginning of the persecution.”

Does he not there openly admit that Gaul, at the beginning of this persecution, endured the pagans’ fury for scarcely those two full years? Did he, then, in writing this, suffer some human lapse and plainly contradict both himself and our Caecilius? Can it be said that, when composing this book, he did not know what had occurred in Gaul? Some answer that, because Constantius was then occupied in waging war against the barbarians, he was not in a position to suppress every assault by pagans who cruelly attacked Christians living in that province. This may indeed be confirmed by certain Acts of martyrs, if they are true and genuine, in which we read descriptions of their glorious slaughter for confession of Christ. Others think that Eusebius’ words signify nothing else than that persecution was quieted in Gaul after two years, though some persons nevertheless then gained the palm of martyrdom.

But what if it be said that Constantius, at the very outset of the persecution, was unable to restrain the madness [Col. 0924C] and fury of pagans raging against Christians—not because he was occupied in war, but because he was only Caesar and therefore subordinate to Diocletian and Maximian Herculius? Since the pagans were then armed with the bloody edicts of the emperors, Constantius could not prevent them from destroying certain churches of Christians and massacring many of their members by diverse and dreadful punishments. On that interpretation Eusebius may certainly be reconciled both with himself and with our Caecilius. For if, contrary to Constantius’ will, the pagans in mad fury destroyed certain Christian churches and killed many Christians, these things were done against his will. Indeed, so far as lay within his power, he prevented them; and accordingly he kept those Christians safe and was not a participant in the persecution stirred up against them.

Nor will anyone have any room still to object to us the various Acts of martyrs which enumerate a great number of persons [Col. 0925A] killed for Christ’s faith. For however certainly you demonstrate that their multitude in Gaul was great, we shall always answer that all were tortured and killed against Constantius’ will and despite his resistance. To this is added that the more discerning critics of our age rightly, and not altogether without reason, challenge the credibility and genuineness of many of these Acts and charge that the number of martyrs in them has been enlarged.

## ARTICLE VII

On Diocletian’s vicennalia; when they were celebrated at Rome; why he left that city in haste; how, arriving at Ravenna and seized by a slight illness, he assumed there his ninth consulship; in what sense he is said then to have made his way to Nicomedia “by the bank-striga”; and how, being overcome by death there, he fell into madness.

After the fire of the most savage persecution had been kindled, devouring Christians in almost all the provinces of the Roman Empire, as has been said, Diocletian went to Rome in order to celebrate there, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December—that is, on 20 November in the year 303—his vicennalia, or twentieth year of rule, with Maximian Herculius, of whom we must speak later. Yet Eusebius writes (Euseb., *On the Martyrs of Palestine*, chs. 1–2) that this festival day of the vicennalia was celebrated at Antioch on 17 November. On neither date, however, had Diocletian’s vicennalia been completed, because, as we have already noted, he was made emperor on 17 September 284 [OCR reads “384”]. Many learned men therefore prefer the authority of our Caecilius to all the others, and think that Diocletian, following the examples of others and wishing to spare expense, postponed that festival until 20 November, so as to celebrate his vicennalia together with those of Maximian Herculius and at the same time to hold with him a public triumph over Narseh, king of the Persians, whom they had defeated. There are nevertheless some who suspect that the author of the Caecilian book erred in copying the number, and that one should read, instead of *XII Kal. Dec.*, “15 Kalends,” that is, 17 November. But who would dare affirm this with certainty without the testimony of another, better manuscript?

[Col. 0925C] However that may be, Diocletian, as Caecilius says (Caecil., ch. 17), could not endure the freedom of the Roman people—that is, undoubtedly, the reproaches, insults, and abuse with which they publicly assailed him because of his pride and his ambition for divine honor. Therefore he hastily fled Rome, even though the Kalends of January were now approaching, and could not remain in the city another thirteen days. He then came to Ravenna. But throughout the journey, according to our Caecilius, although he travelled chiefly in a litter, amid bitter cold and rain he fell into a mild yet persistent illness. On the Kalends of January, in the year 304, he entered upon his ninth consulship at Ravenna. But while there he continued always to suffer from that mild illness; after the summer had passed, he departed thence and went to Nicomedia “by the circuit of the bank-striga” (*per circuitum ripae strigae*), as Caecilius says.

It is truly remarkable how much these latter two words have exercised the ingenuity of learned men of our age. Dodwell wrote a distinct and entire dissertation concerning them, appended in certain editions to the end of this Caecilian work. In it he endeavors to prove that *striga* is a term of land-surveyors, transferred from military encampment to the allotment of colonial lands, and that it signifies the boundary and limits of fields, and formerly of camps. He then similarly seeks to show that the Danube was the boundary of the Roman Empire. From this he concludes that the phrase *ripae strigae* designates the bank of the Danube. He accordingly supposes that these two words of Caecilius permit the inference that Diocletian was carried in a litter from Ravenna as far as the Danube bank, then conveyed by ship down the Danube, winding here and there, and arrived by way of the Euxine Sea at Nicomedia. [Col. 0926B]

But although Dodwell had shown more clearly than daylight that *striga* denotes the Danube rather than another river, and that the word *ripae* was added because that river bends here and there and was the frontier of the Roman Empire, he nevertheless did not persuade many that Diocletian, while ill, was transported to Nicomedia by a long and perilous voyage through the Danube cataracts and the storms of the Euxine Sea.

Others therefore judge that he was conveyed from Ravenna to Nicomedia by land, not by the shorter route, which was more difficult, but by the longer and easier route, namely along the bank of the Danube. The entire difficulty therefore lies in the word *strigae*. They consider it corrupt in the manuscript; but they differ completely as to how it should be corrected. Some suspect that *Strigoniae* should be restored; others, *Phrygiae*; others, *Histriae* or *Histricae*; and still others, *Istricae*, that is, “Danubian.” For the Danube, as everyone knows, is also called the Ister. If Diocletian travelled along the Danube bank, this last opinion certainly seems more plausible than the rest. For the Danube takes the name Ister where it turns toward its mouths, and from there Diocletian could have been carried to Nicomedia.

Throughout that whole journey, however, Diocletian’s illness relapsed so severely, and at Nicomedia so overwhelmed him, that on the Ides of December he was considered dead. Yet at that time, “overcome by death,” says our author, “he had recovered his breath.” But what, some ask, can these words, *morte sopitus*, mean except “dead”? Since Diocletian was still alive, they therefore judge that one should read *pro mortuo* (“as dead”) or *morti sopitus* (“overcome unto death”). But what if Caecilius spoke somewhat improperly and intended to signify a profound swoon, by which Diocletian was for some time deprived of every vital sense, and was thus as if overcome by death, or unto death? Certainly he continues thus: “He had recovered his breath, but not wholly. For he became mad, so that at fixed hours he was insane, and at fixed hours recovered his senses.” [Col. 0926D]

Would you like this madness of Diocletian established for you by the testimony of another writer? Eusebius is at hand (*Ecclesiastical History*, bk. VIII, ch. 13), who records that, scarcely after the completion of the second year of the persecution, he fell into a certain severe illness:

> Ὑφ᾽ ἧς δὴ καὶ τὰ τῆς διανοίας εἰς ἔκστασιν αὐτῷ παρήγετο,

“by whose force he was removed from the state of his own mind.” Constantine the Great (*Oration to the Assembly of the Saints*, ch. 25) testifies that after the cruelty of the bloody persecution, Diocletian was condemned by his own judgment, *διὰ τὴν τῆς ἀφροσύνης βλάβην*, “because of the affliction of madness,” and, confined in some mean dwelling, paid the penalty for his crimes. Nor are there lacking those who believe that Diocletian is indicated, though unnamed, by Chrysostom (*Against the Gentiles and on Babylon*), where, discussing the various punishments of tyrants, he records that one of them died *μανέντα*, “having been driven mad.”

But Diocletian, to dispel the suspicion of his death, appeared in public on the Kalends of March, namely in the year 305. Yet because he had wasted away through illness for almost the entire year, he could scarcely be recognized by anyone. [Col. 0927B]

## ARTICLE VIII

On the conference in which Galerius compelled Diocletian to resign the empire; whether he properly proposed to him the example of the Emperor Nerva; how great were Galerius’ insolence and Diocletian’s timidity in this conference; whether Caecilius rightly asserts that Constantine was present there; and whether Diocletian, at Galerius’ prompting and compulsion, abdicated the empire.

Not many days after the Kalends of March just mentioned, Maximian Galerius hastened to Diocletian, who was gravely ill, to compel him to resign the empire. Although Caecilius, as we have often said, pursues the utmost brevity everywhere, he nevertheless transcribed a long conversation between them, through which Diocletian was at last, though most reluctantly, brought to lay aside the dignity of emperor. Galerius therefore, as our author relates, first undertook gently and amicably to persuade him of this; he pointed to the weakened strength of old age and of a body almost exhausted by illness, and to the example of Nerva, who had surrendered the empire to Trajan. But Diocletian replied that it had been easy for Nerva, after one year of rule, to return to private life, in which he had grown old; but for himself, who had ruled so long, this was neither fitting nor sufficiently safe, owing to the enmities he had incurred from many persons.

But how, you will ask, does Caecilius assert with such confidence that Nerva had laid aside the imperial dignity? Does not Eutropius (*Roman History*, bk. IX) openly declare that Diocletian was the only person, after the founding of the Roman Empire, who returned from so lofty an eminence to private life? Does not Pliny (*Panegyric of Trajan*, §§9–10), who flourished at that time, congratulate Trajan precisely because, while Nerva lived, he was his associate and partner in the empire in such a manner that he appeared a private person to himself?

Others, however, think that Pliny’s words are to be understood not at all of Nerva’s empire but of his life. For immediately in the same passage he added: “Your prayers were heard”—namely, Trajan’s—“but only insofar as it was beneficial to that best and most holy old man, whom the gods claimed for heaven, lest after that divine and immortal act he should do anything mortal.” [Col. 0928A] Yet some maintain that these words were spoken and elaborated by Pliny because Trajan ruled with Nerva for three months. Others, on the contrary, insist that the same Pliny wrote to Tacitus that he had been praised by Nerva, then already a private man, because in the case of Baebius Massa, exiled by Domitian, he had done something resembling ancient practice. Others answer that this letter was indeed written by Pliny while Trajan actually ruled, but that he speaks of the case of Baebius Massa, which had been conducted earlier, in the year of Christ 93, when Domitian was emperor and Nerva still a private citizen.

Yet however obscure Pliny’s words may seem, these words of Aurelius Victor are equally open and clear:

> “When Nerva, in extreme old age, had assumed imperial power at the discretion of the legions, and saw that it could not be administered except by successors stronger in body and mind, he abdicated it in the sixteenth month.”  
> —Aurelius Victor, *On the Caesars*, under Nerva.

From this, moreover, it can be inferred either that a rumor circulated or that some believed that Nerva, already close to death, yielded the empire and for some time—though a very short one, as Dio Cassius and others testify—led a private life (Dio, *Epitome*).

Galerius, then, inflamed by an unrestrained desire to rule, thought it sufficient for deceiving the old man, gravely ill as he was, to propose Nerva’s example. It could easily have happened that Diocletian, having not examined the matter closely enough and disturbed by Galerius’ discourse, answered that Nerva had abdicated the empire after holding its reins for only one year. For in this at least Diocletian seems to have erred: he told Galerius that Nerva had reigned only one year, whereas Aurelius Victor, just cited, testifies that he ruled six months besides; or, as others cited elsewhere by us say, four additional months.

After this Caecilius relates how Galerius and Diocletian continued their conversation, and how Galerius passed to threats, by which Diocletian, terrified, was at last forced to lay down the empire and, rejecting Constantine, to create Severus and Maximinus Caesars. We have set out the greater part of this conversation above in such a way that there is no need to describe it again.

Yet we cannot now pass over certain points without observation. First, one notes in this dialogue such great insolence and ferocity in Galerius as one does weakness and timidity in the aged Diocletian. Galerius advanced to such impudence that, among other things, he said that he had already sent Herculius—without consulting Diocletian, to whom he was speaking—to proclaim Severus Caesar. Diocletian, though superior to him, is said to have borne this most patiently and not even murmured. Perhaps, however, one may answer that the former fault, insolence, ought not without reason to be attributed to Galerius, certainly a barbarian and most ferocious man who already coveted the whole world, as Caecilius says (Caecil., ch. 18); and the latter, weakness, to the aged Diocletian, scarcely recovered from the gravest illness of body and mind. [Col. 0929A]

Perhaps more difficult is what our Caecilius there mentions concerning Constantine the Great: he was present when Diocletian and Galerius were talking together. Where, pray, was he present then? In Diocletian’s palace, as some please; or in the very bedchamber where he spoke with Galerius, as others have thought? In support of this second view may be brought forward the statement that shortly afterward Galerius is said to have shown Diocletian Maximinus Daia, who was presently to be proclaimed Caesar. For if this man was present in their chamber, why not Constantine also, who is asserted to have been present there? Yet if he had truly stood in that chamber, he could undoubtedly have inferred, from the emperors’ words or gestures, that he was to be rejected from the dignity of Caesar. But the fuller and subsequent words of Caecilius himself seem altogether to oppose this, as we shall show below.

Moreover, however you may extricate yourself from this difficulty, you will immediately fall into another no less serious. For if Diocletian, weeping, as Caecilius says (Caecil., ch. 18), groaning, entirely weak, and resisting, stripped himself of the imperial purple and dignity, how, pray, could Aurelius Victor write that Diocletian laid down the empire not at Galerius’ prompting but from fear of dissensions; not in infirm health, but when stronger both in mind and body?

> “For, being a discerner of coming events, when he learned that by fate internal calamities and, as it were, a certain crash threatened the Roman state, after celebrating the twentieth year of his reign he, stronger in health, laid down the care of the Roman people, having with great difficulty brought Herculius to the same decision.”  
> —Aurelius Victor, *On the Caesars*, under Diocletian.

But Victor adds in the same place that another opinion, held by others, was false; the true view, he thinks, is that Diocletian, endowed with an outstanding nature, descended to common life in contempt of ambition. Neither he, therefore, nor other defenders of this opinion considered Diocletian’s abdication forced or compelled, whether by weakness or by fear of Galerius.

[Col. 0929D] Eutropius, indeed, relates (*Abridgment of Roman History*, bk. IX) that Diocletian yielded an empire which he felt himself unequal to governing, together with Herculius, whom he had previously persuaded to do so, though with difficulty. You see, therefore, how openly he testifies that Diocletian voluntarily and of his own accord laid aside the imperial purple.

If you wish, however, you will hear Eumenius (*Panegyric of Constantine*, §15) speaking much more clearly:

> “But that divine man,” he says—Diocletian—“who was the first both to share in empire and to lay it down, does not repent of his counsel and deed, nor does he think that he has lost what he voluntarily transferred.”

Indeed, Eumenius further intimates there that this emperor had previously sworn with Herculius in the temple of Capitoline Jupiter that they would abdicate the empire together.

Do you still desire another witness? We shall give you Constantine the Great, who, if our Caecilius is to be believed, had seen Diocletian strip himself of the imperial purple. For in his own *Oration to the Assembly of the Saints*, Diocletian is said afterward to have lived as a private man, *αὐτὸς ἑαυτοῦ καταψηφισάμενος*, “having condemned himself by his own judgment” (in Eusebius, *Oration to the Assembly of the Saints*, ch. 25). But is such language recorded or handed down of an emperor driven by Galerius’ ferocity and threats to cast aside the supreme dignity of empire? Who would say that the authority of Constantine the Great and of the others cited by us is less than that of Lucius Caecilius?

[Col. 0930B] Yet many, someone will object, maintain that he laid down the empire either because of the inactivity and weakness of old age, as Eutropius, cited a little before, says; or because of a disorder of a deranged mind, as Constantine the Great, likewise cited just now by us, says; or finally, as the anonymous author of the panegyric says, because advancing years or failing health compelled him to sound the retreat. May it not therefore be inferred that he did this voluntarily, though old age and infirmity prompted him to make this abdication? Perhaps correctly, if Galerius, without inspiring any fear, had led him to lay aside the purple.

Yet you will press the point: what prevented Diocletian, persuaded at last not so much by Galerius’ threats as by his friendly words, from willingly and voluntarily renouncing the empire? But what also prevented, another will object, the other writers from describing that insolent conversation between Galerius and Diocletian, or at least making some mention of it? Yet the question is not about matters that might have happened, but about those which actually occurred. Nearly all explicitly affirm that Diocletian, weakened by old age and bodily infirmity according to some, but according to others still sound in strength and even stronger, laid down the empire freely and voluntarily, with no one else compelling him. But this opinion plainly and completely opposes Caecilius’ words, in which he declares most openly that Diocletian, after Galerius’ threats, relinquished the imperial dignity in tears and groans. For however one may say that he gave forth groans and tears, who will readily persuade himself that these were marks of a man yielding not under compulsion but freely and willingly? We leave it to sincere investigators of truth to decide whether Lactantius, who was then staying at Nicomedia, would have passed over in such profound silence, as Caecilius did, Diocletian’s voluntary abdication. [Col. 0930D]

## ARTICLE IX

Where and how Diocletian clothed Maximinus in the purple and, rejecting Constantine, proclaimed him and Severus Caesars; whether Caecilius’ account of this is true; to what place Diocletian withdrew after laying down the empire; and where Licinius was made emperor in his presence.

After the conference mentioned in the preceding article, in which Diocletian, prompted by Galerius, had at last decided, as Caecilius says, to lay down the empire, both emperors and Constantine, attended by the soldiers wintering at Nicomedia and by their leading men, came from that city on the Kalends of May in the year of Christ 305 to a place about three miles distant. This place, says our author (Caecil., ch. 19), was elevated; upon it stood a column bearing an image of Jupiter—that is, a statue and effigy—and Herculius, of whom we shall speak below, was remembered to have assumed the purple there.

At this place Diocletian, addressing the soldiers from a tribunal, suddenly proclaimed Severus and Maximinus Daia Caesars. Galerius then, after rejecting Constantine, drew Maximinus from behind and placed him in the middle, stripped of his private clothing. Without delay Diocletian clothed him in the purple which he himself had taken off. All were astonished and amazed that it had occurred so suddenly and unexpectedly: both because they did not know who Maximinus was or whence he came, and because they thought Constantine was going to become Caesar.

But he had already been rejected at the famous conference at which, if Caecilius is to be believed, he had been present. If he truly attended that conference, with what face, someone will ask, did he dare to ascend with the emperors to that lofty place, where he knew certainly that he was to be rejected with the utmost disgrace? Did Caecilius not therefore err throughout, or lend too ready an ear to false rumors? For the Anonymous Valesianus expressly reports that Severus and Maximinus were made Caesars while Constantine knew nothing of any such thing. But later, and in a more suitable place, we shall investigate whether there is any means by which, once these difficulties are removed, Caecilius’ opinion may be defended or established. [Col. 0931C]

Meanwhile let us proceed and consider whether what our Caecilius recounts regarding the two Caesars created by Diocletian is more true. For the Anonymous Valesianus unhesitatingly affirms that they were proclaimed Caesars not by Diocletian but by Galerius: “Galerius made these men—namely Severus and Maximinus—Caesars.” This view is plainly confirmed by these words of Eutropius: “Galerius created two Caesars: Maximian, or Maximinus, whom he set over the East; and Severus, to whom he gave Italy” (Eutrop., *Abridgment of Roman History*, bk. X, beginning). From this some light is shed upon Socrates, who says similarly:

> Δύο καθιστησιν Καίσαρας, Μαξιμῖνον μὲν ἐν τοῖς κατὰ τὴν ἐῳαν, Σεβῆρον δὲ ἐν τοῖς κατὰ τὴν Ἰταλίαν.  
> “He appointed two Caesars: Maximinus in the eastern regions, and Severus in those of Italy.”  
> —Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, bk. I, ch. 2.

This cannot, certainly, mean that Galerius made one Caesar in the East and the other in Italy at the same moment, though they were so far apart; rather, he himself proclaimed one in the East and had the other proclaimed in Italy through someone’s agency, or, more probably, assigned both to these provinces of the Roman Empire. For this reason, unquestionably, our author added (Caecil., ch. 19) that Maximinus received the East “to tread down and crush.” Finally, the Eusebian Chronicle contains: “Maximinus and Severus were made Caesars by Galerius Maximian.” In certain manuscripts of this Chronicle and in printed editions, however, an error occurs where this proclamation of the Caesars is placed in the second year after Diocletian’s and Herculius’ abdication, contrary to the testimony of the other manuscripts.

[Col. 0932A] What then, someone will ask: do these statements not conflict with Caecilius’ view? For he expressly asserts that Maximinus was clothed in purple by Diocletian and proclaimed Caesar in Galerius’ presence, while Galerius had previously sent Herculius to have Severus likewise proclaimed Caesar by him in Italy. But since our author no less clearly affirms that both inaugurations took place at Galerius’ instigation and prompting, can it not on that account—and for this very reason—be said that they are ascribed to Galerius alone by Eutropius, the author of the Eusebian Chronicle, Socrates (*Ecclesiastical History*, bk. I, ch. 2), and, if you wish, others also?

Diocletian, after laying aside the purple in this manner, became Diocles again, as our author says; that is, Diocletian returned to the private life which, before assuming the empire, he had lived under the name Diocles, as we said above.

When Maximinus had been made Caesar, Diocletian immediately descended from the tribunal and high place mentioned a little earlier and, riding in a carriage through the city—that is, Nicomedia, Caecilius says (Caecil., ch. 19)—was carried off to his homeland. We discussed that homeland above: some think it Dioclea or Doclea, others Salonae.

Yet he did not remain there permanently. For when Herculius came to Galerius, “Diocles was there,” says Caecilius (Caecil., ch. 19), having recently been summoned by his son-in-law Galerius, that he might, in his presence, give the empire to Licinius—something he had not done before. But our author entirely keeps silent as to the place where Herculius met Galerius, leaving others to guess. The Anonymous Valesianus, however, undoubtedly speaks more plainly: “Galerius made Licinius Caesar in Illyricum.” If you ask in what city, you will learn from Eusebius’ Chronicle: “Licinius was made emperor by Galerius at Carnuntum.” It is a city of Pannonia, situated on the banks of the Danube, which Zosimus (*History*, bk. II) wrongly confuses with Carnutes, a city of Celtic Gaul. Moreover, Galerius made Licinius Augustus not merely in the presence of Jovius—that is, Diocletian—but also after calling him into counsel, as Aurelius Victor says (*On Constantius and the Armenians*). Herculius, who had come there, either assented to Licinius’ inauguration or did not dare to refuse his assent. [Col. 0932D]

## ARTICLE X

Whether the things Caecilius relates concerning Diocletian’s private life are true; and whether he died consumed by grief and hunger because the return of his exiled daughter Valeria was denied him and his statues had been overthrown.

Diocletian, returning from Carnuntum to Salona, [Col. 0933A] grew old there in distinguished leisure, if we believe Eutropius (Eutropius, *Breviarium*, book IX, at the end, and book X); nor could he ever, as the same Eutropius, Aurelius Victor (*Epitome on Diocletian*), and Zosimus (*History*, book II) testify, be induced to resume the purple offered him by the other emperors. Eumenius indeed (*Panegyric of Constantine*, §15) celebrates this in the following words, some of which we have already quoted:

> “But that divine man, who was the first both to share imperial power and to lay it down, does not repent of his counsel and action, nor does he think that he has lost what he voluntarily transferred. Truly happy and blessed, whom the dutiful services of so great princes honour in private life. And he too, supported by the yoke of manifold rule, is gladly sheltered by your protection; knowing that you have grown from his stock, he rightfully claims your glories as his own.”

Nevertheless, in that leisure, however distinguished, he experienced many adversities, if one trusts Cecilius (Cecilius, ch. 41) [Col. 0933B]. For, first, neither by repeatedly dispatched envoys nor by renewed entreaties could he ever obtain from Maximinus the return to him of his daughter Valeria Augusta, who, as will shortly be said, had been banished with her mother to the deserted wildernesses of Syria.

Moreover, while still alive, he saw, as Cecilius says, his own statues and images, and those of his colleague Maximian Herculius, overthrown and destroyed by order of Constantine the Great—something which, as Cecilius himself adds in the same place, had never happened to any emperor. But someone will confront us and object: by what right, then, did Eumenius, whom we have just cited, in a public address delivered in the presence and hearing of Constantine the Great himself, extol in such great praise the latter’s supreme reverence toward Diocletian [Col. 0933C], if, by the command of that same Constantine, the statues and images of Diocletian himself were cast down? Did Cecilius therefore err there also? This objection would not be foolish if it were rightly proved that Eumenius delivered that oration after Diocletian’s death. For Cecilius writes, as will presently be seen, that Diocletian died shortly after the overthrow of his statues. Yet that panegyric is said to have been delivered in the year 310, and Diocletian to have departed this life three years later. Eumenius himself, certainly, seems to mention Diocletian as though he were still living. Finally, Cecilius sufficiently and plainly intimates that it was not the statues and images of Diocletian alone, but the combined statues and images of him and Maximian Herculius, that were torn down and removed—especially out of hatred for the latter [Col. 0933D]. Hear, if you please, our author’s own words:

> “The statues of the aged Maximian were torn down by Constantine’s order, and the images in which he was painted were taken away. And because the two old men were generally painted together, the images of both were removed together.”

Constantine therefore seems to have ordered the destruction of no images other than those of Herculius. That these were in fact destroyed we shall show in its proper place. But since it could scarcely—or rather, not at all—have happened that Constantine did not know that the images of Herculius and Diocletian were painted together, he undoubtedly ordered them all to be overthrown. How this, then, can stand with the profound reverence for Diocletian which Eumenius so highly praised in that same Constantine, perhaps others will teach us.

[Col. 0934A] But someone else may yet rise against our Cecilius and object that it is false for him to assert that Diocletian was the first of all men to see his images destroyed while he was alive. For Tacitus (*Histories*, book III, near the end) expressly declares that the emperor Vitellius, before he was killed, saw his statues falling. Can it be said in Cecilius’ defence that Vitellius saw those statues falling in a manner different from Diocletian’s seeing his? Vitellius’ statues, as Tacitus writes in the same passage, were overthrown in a great popular tumult. Diocletian, however, saw his images cast down by order of the emperor Constantine, but without any popular sedition.

Yet although Diocletian saw his images cast down not so much to disgrace himself as Maximian Herculius, he could not, if one believes Cecilius, endure so great an affront with composure [Col. 0934B]. He then, indeed, resolved that he must die. But what form of voluntary death, do you suppose, did he choose? Hear, I beg, Cecilius himself once more:

> “Trampled beneath insults and cast into hatred of life, he was finally consumed by hunger and anguish,”

that is, by grief and sorrow. But Cecilius mentions no other insults except the overthrow, in the manner we have described, of his images and Maximinus’ refusal to restore to him his exiled daughter. And certainly these affronts do not seem so great that Diocletian—who, as we have said, was growing old in distinguished retirement—ought thereby to have fallen into so monstrous a hatred of life.

What then of the fact that other writers offer different, and very different, accounts of his death [Col. 0934C]? Eusebius says (*Appendix* to book VIII) that he was **Μακρᾷ καὶ ἐπιλυποτάτῃ τῇ τοῦ σώματος ἀσθενείᾳ διεργασθείς**, “worn out by a long and most grievous bodily illness.” He does not say what that illness was, or whether he fell into it through grief, despair, or the frailty of old age. Jerome, however (*Commentary on Zechariah*, book III, ch. 14, v. 18), places him among those tyrants who, because they had afflicted Christ’s Church, were punished by a cruel death. But what Jerome said there specifically about him cannot be determined.

In the *Epitome* of Aurelius Victor, Diocletian’s death is described in these words:

> “He lived sixty-eight years, of which he spent almost nine in the common condition [of private life]. He was consumed by death, as was sufficiently apparent, through voluntary fear. For when he had been summoned by Constantine and Licinius to the wedding festivities, he excused himself on grounds of age, as unable to attend; and, having received threatening replies in which he was reproached for having favoured Maxentius and for favouring Maximian, he suspected an ignominious death and is said to have swallowed poison.”

[Col. 0934D] Did, then, the sad sight of his demolished statues and images increase this fear? Can it also be said that, after taking poison, he thereafter refused all food? Aurelius Victor, moreover, does not affirm as certain what we have cited from his book, but himself warns us that it was handed down only by report and the testimony of others.

If we descend to later writers, we at once encounter the author of the Alexandrian Chronicle [Col. 0935A], who recorded in writing: “Galerius Maximianus”—Diocletianus should be read—“suffering grievously at Salona from dropsy, **ὕδρωπι δεινῷ** [“a terrible dropsy”].” Suidas, on the other hand, says of the same Diocletian and of Maximian, his son-in-law (Suidas, under Διοκλητιανός):

> **Καὶ ὁ μὲν ἐσφάγη ὑπὸ τῆς συγκλήτου, ὁ δὲ ἀπήγξατο.**

> “The one was slain by the Senate; the other hanged himself.”

But from what source he drew these statements, since he is wholly silent about it, is indeed very difficult to say. Whether our Cecilius came closer to the truth than the others, let others judge. Meanwhile, we shall proceed to examine what he relates concerning Prisca, Diocletian’s wife, and Valeria, his daughter.

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 0935B] Concerning Prisca, Diocletian’s wife, and his daughter Valeria.

## ARTICLE I

How seldom Prisca and how frequently Valeria are mentioned by ancient authors; whether both professed the Christian religion.

Although Valeria, Diocletian’s daughter, is often mentioned by ancient authors, his wife Prisca is very rarely mentioned. We know indeed that this emperor’s consort is called Serena in certain Acts of saints, and Alexandra in others. But these Acts seem, and rightly so, neither genuine nor authentic. In the pontifical records published by Anastasius she is further called Eleutheria, and in a very ancient manuscript of those records, Leutheres. Yet this rests solely on the testimony of the writer of these records [Col. 0935C]. Our Cecilius, however, names her Prisca; but whether with better right, and whether she bore several names, we shall gladly learn from more learned men.

Diocletian by his wife had a daughter, Valeria, whom, as we shall show below, he gave in marriage to Maximian Galerius when he made him Caesar and partner in his imperial power. Galerius, moreover, having cut down, as Aurelius Victor writes (*On the Caesars*, in the section on Armentarius), immense forests and directed the grove of Peltona among the Pannonians into the Danube, wished a province to be called Valeria after his wife. Ammianus Marcellinus supports this view (*History*, book XIX, ch. 11), recording that the province was so named in honour of Valeria, Diocletian’s daughter [Col. 0935D]. There exists, moreover, in the royal cabinet this bronze coin of the second size, which we acknowledge that we received from our most devoted friend Anselm Banduri; he will shortly publish it, along with many others, not without learned observations.

But when Diocletian first began, as we have seen, to rage against Christians with monstrous cruelty, “First of all,” says Cecilius (Cecilius, ch. 15), “he compelled his daughter Valeria and his wife Prisca to be defiled by sacrifice.” Why, then, did he compel them to sacrifice to the gods? Was it because they were Christians, or in order to compel them, though devoted to pagan superstitions, to furnish others with an example of performing these impious sacrifices [Col. 0936A]? Learned men certainly hold different opinions on this question. Some judge that they really had embraced the Christian religion. They consider that their opinion can be supported by these words of Eusebius, though, as many acknowledge, they are rather obscure:

> **Τί δεῖ περὶ τῶν κατὰ τοὺς βασιλικοὺς λέγειν οἴκους, καὶ τῶν πᾶσιν ἀρχόντων, οἳ τοῖς οἰκείοις εἰς πρόσωπον ἐπὶ τῷ θείῳ παῤῥησιαζομένοις λόγῳ τε καὶ βίῳ συνεχώρουν, γαμεταῖς, καὶ παισί, καὶ οἰκέταις, μονονουχὶ καὶ ἐγκαυχᾶσθαι ἐπὶ τῇ παῤῥησίᾳ τῆς πίστεως ἐπιτρέποντες· οὓς ἐξόχως καὶ μᾶλλον τῶν συνθεραπόντων ἀποδέκτους ἡγοῦντο.**

Valesius translates them thus:

> “What need is there to speak of those who lived in the imperial palaces, or of the emperors themselves? They gave their household members—their wives, children, and servants—the liberty to practise before themselves, freely in word and deed, what belonged to their religion [Col. 0936B]; permitting them, as it were, to glory and make display of themselves because of this liberty of their faith, and embracing them with a special affection beyond all their other attendants.”

In his notes, however, Valesius criticizes Christophorson, who interpreted the Greek noun **γαμεταῖς** (*gametais*, “wives”) as referring to the emperors’ wives. For the following words of Eusebius seem to him wholly opposed to that sense.

Yet both the translation of Valesius and that of Christophorson seemed too free to Toinard, who thinks Eusebius’ Greek should be rendered in Latin as follows:

> “What need is there to speak of those who were in the houses of the emperors, and of those who ruled over all? They allowed their own people freely to conduct themselves before them in matters concerning God [Col. 0936C], both in speech and manner of life—wives, children, and servants, almost to the point of permitting them also to glory in the free profession of the faith—and they held these in especial favour above their other fellow-servants.”

He contends that the word **οἰκείοις** (*oikeiois*, “household members”) is there, as it were, generic, embracing the **γαμετάς**, **παῖδας**, and **οἰκέτας**—the wives, children, and servants—of the emperors [Col. 0936C]. From this he concludes that Prisca and Valeria were Christians. This interpretation can be confirmed by the authority of Rufinus, who explains Eusebius’ Greek words in Latin thus:

> “Some of the Roman rulers permitted their wives, attendants, and whole household not only to believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, but also to act in the faith with all confidence and freedom.” (Rufinus, book VIII, ch. 1.)

[Col. 0936D] Cuperus, however, thinks that by Eusebius’ words **ἐπὶ πᾶσιν ἀρχόντων** he means not emperors, or those set over everyone, but praetorian prefects—or rather chamberlains and others like them—who presided over all the others dwelling in the palace. For Eusebius shortly afterward plainly indicates that one of these was Dorotheus, another Gorgonius, and that they had permitted their household members and wives freely to profess the Christian religion.

But Eusebius seems there to deal only with the liberty which emperors, and not their other officials, had granted Christians to practise their religion publicly and openly. Further, these officials dwelling in the imperial palace could not have given this permission to their wives and household members unless the emperors themselves assented, or had first granted the same liberty to their own wives [Col. 0937A]. For who does not know the usual way of courtiers and palace officials: that they do almost nothing publicly except what pleases kings? It is therefore more probable that Eusebius means that, before Diocletian stirred up the persecution against Christians, the emperors gave the wives of their household members, and much more their own wives, liberty to practise their religion.

Even if this were so, however, it may still be disputed whether Prisca and Valeria really embraced Christianity before Diocletian began to harass Christians. Baluzius flatly denies it, because Cecilius quite clearly testifies that Prisca and Valeria did not dare resist Diocletian’s impious edict. But if they really professed the Christian faith, why did they so readily defile themselves with the abominable sacrifices of pagans, showing themselves more timid than other Christian women and children, who confessed their faith with such fortitude even to the most dreadful destruction? Add to this that they are frequently mentioned later in this book of Cecilius; yet nowhere is there any trace whatsoever of Christianity having been embraced by them [Col. 0937B]. Indeed, they are said to have been killed not because of this religion, but, as we shall shortly say, because of their rank and chastity.

Others nevertheless argue that they were Christians, or at least favoured Christians, from their having been compelled to sacrifice to the gods of the pagans. Pagans, indeed, sacrificed to their gods not unwillingly and reluctantly, but voluntarily and of their own accord. But what if, after this sinful sacrifice, they did not repent, or concealed their repentance through fear?

Nor should one object that Cecilius shortly afterwards added (ch. 15): “Judges compelled all persons, throughout all temples, to sacrifice.” For these words are wrapped in no less obscurity than most of his other expressions. If by “all persons” he includes pagans as well as Christians, it cannot be concluded that Valeria and Prisca were Christians. But if that term is taken in an accommodated sense, as meaning all Christians and referring to them, it will rightly be inferred that they had in fact given their names to the Christian religion. We must therefore admit that our author’s expression is highly ambiguous [Col. 0937C], and that scarcely anything certain can be concluded from it. [Col. 0937D] Perhaps, however, he spoke thus because at that time it was as well known to everyone as it is now unknown whether Prisca and Valeria were Christians; yet Cecilius certainly ought to have explained this more clearly to posterity.

## ARTICLE II

Concerning Valeria and Candidianus, adopted by her because of sterility; why, after the death of Galerius her husband, she fled to Maximinus after leaving Licinius, and rejected Maximinus’ marriage proposal. Concerning the black garments worn by widows during mourning; and whether no emperor’s wife had ever previously married a second husband.

Because of sterility, Valeria had borne no children to her husband, the emperor Galerius [Col. 0938A]. She therefore adopted Candidianus, his son by a concubine, as her own. When Galerius was dying, he commended both Candidianus and Valeria to Licinius and placed them in his hands. We have received these facts from our Cecilius. But more difficult to explain is what he in turn relates concerning Valeria, Candidianus, and Severianus, son of the emperor Severus:

> “Having long feared Licinius as an evil, they preferred to be with Maximinus, especially because Valeria, willing to yield to Licinius by her own right all the inheritances of Maximian Galerius, had refused the same to Maximinus.”

Do not these words mean that Valeria remained with Licinius after the death of her husband Galerius? Yet he had previously said:

> “[Col. 0938B] After the death of Maximian Galerius, Valeria came to him, Maximinus, thinking she would live more safely within his territory, especially because he had a wife.”

Can one reply that her stay with Licinius was very brief, and that she immediately fled to Maximinus, with whom she hoped to be safer? But if that is so, why did she wish to yield all Galerius’ property to Licinius? Some therefore suspect that Cecilius’ text should read *unwilling*, not *willing*. Yet the Colbert manuscript reads: *Volenti Licinio*, “to Licinius wishing [it].” Consider, however, whether this sense can ever be elicited from it: Licinius wished to seize all Galerius’ inheritances, and Valeria therefore immediately fled from him in order to take refuge more safely with Maximinus, who had a wife. But who would recognize Lactantius’ style here?

Valeria, however, did not obtain from Maximinus the security she desired [Col. 0938C]. For that most lustful man wished to marry her, having put aside his own wife—the very woman whom he had recently called mother. Why, then, did he call her mother, except as a title of honour and because she had been the wife of Galerius Augustus? Since Galerius, as we have said, had made Maximinus Caesar, Galerius was called by him father, and consequently his wife mother. Valeria herself replied to the envoys who sought her hand in Maximinus’ name that, while her husband’s ashes were still warm and she wore a widow’s mourning garb, it was not lawful for her to think of a second marriage.

Plutarch records a law of Numa Pompilius (*Life of Numa*, vol. I) which prohibited any widow from marrying another man before roughly ten months had elapsed after her husband’s death. Ovid, moreover, not only gives the reason for this decree but also mentions the funeral and mourning attire, as our author calls it, which the widow was required to wear during that time [Col. 0938D]:

> The period sufficient for the mother’s womb  
> To bring the child to birth,  
> He fixed as a sufficient span of time.  
> Through as many months from her husband’s funeral  
> The wife bears in her widowed home  
> The sorrowful tokens of widowhood.  
> (*Fasti*, book I, vv. 33 ff.)

Therefore she had to remain a widow during these months, because she might be pregnant when her husband died. If you desire more, you may also consult Brissonius and Gothofredus (Brissonius, *On the Law of Marriage*, at the end; Gothofredus, note on law I, *On Second Marriages*, vol. I of the *Theodosian Code*, p. 281 ff.).

It is established that men wore black clothing when mourning their dead wives [Col. 0939A]. For, apart from the countless number of witnesses, Propertius sang:

> Who, then, saw you bowed at my funeral?  
> Who saw your dark toga grow warm with tears?  
> (Propertius, book IV, elegy 6, to Cynthia, v. 27)

The case of widowed women may therefore be more difficult. In his commentaries on the books of Cornelius Tacitus, Lipsius cites various authors: some state that such women passed the period of mourning in dark or black clothing; others, in white and bright garments, or purple garments interwoven with golden ornaments. He considers them to be reconciled thus: Roman women, while the republic endured, wore dark clothing, and under the emperors white. If anyone asks the reason for this alteration, Lipsius replies that it was no other than the luxury of Roman matrons, who scorned white garments as less costly [Col. 0939B]. Nor is he much moved by the authority of Apuleius, who mentions a grieving widow, a matron covered in dark clothing. Lipsius thinks that Apuleius there referred either to the ancient custom or to that which was still usually observed in the provinces.

But the testimony of our Cecilius (Cecilius, ch. 39) wholly opposes this conjecture. For he plainly and explicitly declares that the empress Valeria wore black garments during her mourning. Must we then say that Roman widows used white, black, or purple clothing, of greater or lesser cost, according as they wished to display greater or lesser grief for the death of their husbands? Yet read also, if you please, Ferrari’s observations on dark mourning garments (*On Clothing*, book I, ch. 23) [Col. 0939C].

Valeria’s second reason for rejecting marriage to the emperor Maximinus is that she thought it wicked, *without custom, without precedent*, to take another husband. But these words are no less difficult to explain than the foregoing. For this general proposition means that no empress until then had been bound in a second marriage. Yet Cuperus, Toinard, and others produce examples of empresses who married another man after their husbands’ deaths. Some therefore suspected that Cecilius’ text had read: “another husband from among his sons”; but distrusting this certainly very weak conjecture, they are compelled to admit that they do not see where they can securely plant their foot.

We are aware that some cite Tertullian (*On the Prescription against Heretics*, ch. 40, and *Exhortation to Chastity*, ch. 13), who teaches that it was not lawful for the chief pontiff of the pagans to take a second wife [Col. 0939D]. But emperors were chief pontiffs. Others, however, think Tertullian is speaking of the *Flamen Dialis*, to whom remarriage was forbidden, as Gellius and Plutarch attest (*Attic Nights*, book X, ch. 15; *Roman Questions*, question 50). Further, this prohibition does not entail that remarriage was without custom and precedent. Let us add, if you please, that our Cecilius speaks not of emperors but of their wives, for whom the practice and rationale could have been different.

[Col. 0940A] Some, therefore, reduced to straits, maintain that this difficulty can be resolved only by Valeria’s ignorance: she knew of no second marriages of empresses. But what if she thought such marriages had been celebrated either against the empresses’ will, or contrary to ancient custom, and without a precedent that was to be praised—in fact, by a wholly perverse precedent? Yet we dare affirm nothing certainly, but leave these matters to the judgment of others.

## ARTICLE III

Concerning the exile of Prisca and Valeria; the execution and death of three noble women, friends of Valeria; and a certain Jew who falsely accused them of adultery.

Because Valeria had rejected Maximinus’ marriage proposal, as we said shortly before [Col. 0940B], she was sent, says Cecilius (Cecilius, ch. 39), into exile here and there with her mother Prisca; her property was seized, her attendants taken away, and eunuchs put to death under torture. Cicero likewise wrote, as we may note in passing: “We have received the report that Zeno of Elea was killed under torture” (*On the Nature of the Gods*, book III).

Three noble women, whom Valeria cherished with singular affection, likewise experienced Maximinus’ fury. The first was a woman of the highest rank, who already had grandchildren through her sons while they were young men. Since Valeria loved this woman as a mother, Maximinus suspected that it was by her counsel that Valeria had spurned and rejected the marriage he had offered her.

The second, likewise noble, had left at Rome, says Cecilius, a virgin handmaid of Vesta, secretly then intimate with Valeria [Col. 0940C]. But whose handmaid, I ask, was she? Was she servant of the goddess Vesta, or of that noble woman? For Vestals were called both handmaids and maidservants of the goddess Vesta, as Apuleius and Augustine testify (Apuleius, book VI; Augustine, *City of God*, book IV, ch. 10). But since the mention of this Vestal contributed little to the matter, some accordingly thought she was the handmaid of that noble woman, others her daughter. The opinion of the latter might perhaps seem more probable if it were supported by at least some reasoning. But whatever one may pronounce, one must admit that the discourse and customary manner of speaking of Firmianus Lactantius are not enveloped in so great obscurity.

The third woman had a senator for her husband—these are Cecilius’ words—“not too closely connected with the Augusta.” The Colbert manuscript reads *non nimis*, “not too [closely],” and this certainly should not have been altered in some editions. For the second woman is called Valeria’s secret intimate; this woman, then, could be called “not too close,” just as Galerius was earlier said to be “yet not excessively terrified.” Moreover, both women were killed not so much because of friendship with Valeria as on account, says our author, of their exceptional bodily beauty [Col. 0940D] and chastity. Cecilius’ meaning, therefore, seems to be that these two women were united to Valeria by a bond of friendship and connection less close than that of the first matron; but that an occasion was seized from this slight friendship in order that they might be put to an infamous death because of their beauty and chastity.

[Col. 0941A] Furthermore, because those three noble women were conscious of no crime, they bribed a certain impure and criminal Jew, a false witness, by promising him pardon for his crimes. At Nicaea, before the governor Eratineus, he accused them of adultery [Col. 0941A]. The most unjust judge, however, brought him outside the city with a guard, in Cecilius’ words, “lest he be overwhelmed with stones.” Some refer these final words to the judge himself; others, with what appears the stronger reason, to the Jew.

Then, Cecilius continues, the Jew was tortured, while “those things which he had been ordered . . . . . . might speak, [they] were restrained by the torturers with blows.” In the blank space, two or three words, for the most part, have been cut off at the beginning of the page, and thereafter is written *oquerentur* [part of *loquerentur*, “might speak”]. Hence it may be conjectured that the reading should be: “while the Jew declares what he had been ordered to say, the women are restrained by the torturers with blows lest they speak.” Eusebius indeed testifies (*Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, ch. 3, and *Martyrs of Palestine*, ch. 1) that many martyrs were struck and battered in the mouth lest they answer their accusers and judges.

Those women, condemned to death, were led to execution through ranks of armed men, lest the people—moved by such great injustice and by the tears of one woman’s husband—should rush upon the executioners and rescue them from their hands [Col. 0941B]. Finally, the promised immunity was denied to the false witness himself, the adulterous Jew—that is, as some conjecture, one who had falsely claimed to have committed adultery with these women. But if this is so, he was fastened to the gallows not only for that invented adultery but also, as was said a little earlier, for other crimes. While there he yielded up his wicked life, he publicly—but too late—revealed the innocence of those noble women.

[Col. 0941C] From the deserted wildernesses of Syria, to which she had been banished, Valeria informed her father Diocletian of her misfortune. But he could never, as we have said, obtain her return from Maximinus by any entreaties. After the death of that same Maximinus, Valeria came to Nicomedia in altered dress in order to observe Candidianus’ fate. But when she heard that he had been killed by Licinius’ order, she fled at once. Cecilius is wholly silent as to whether she had her mother Prisca as companion in her flight and journey. Yet shortly afterward he records that, having wandered here and there for fifteen months in plebeian attire, she was finally seized at Thessalonica with her mother and that both were eventually beheaded [Col. 0941D].

It may be doubted, moreover, whether our author counts these fifteen months from the time when Valeria was driven into exile by Maximinus in the year 312, or from the time when, after Maximinus had been defeated by Licinius and Candidianus killed by his order, she took flight. But the beginning of these fifteen months must beyond doubt be reckoned from this latter time. For only then, and not earlier, was Valeria compelled to exchange royal garments for plebeian dress and seek safety in flight. Maximinus, defeated by Licinius, died in the year 313, about August. Valeria, therefore, and her mother Prisca were killed by the cruel command of that same Licinius—now raised to the summit of imperial power—about the end of the following year [Col. 0942A]; and their bodies, if one believes our author, were cast into the sea.

## CHAPTER X

Concerning the emperor Maximian Herculius.

## ARTICLE I

When and where Maximian Herculius was made emperor; his accord with Diocletian; the extent of his greed, cruelty, and lust; and where he first laid down imperial power.

The elder Maximian was called Herculius, as Cecilius (chs. 8 and 52) and all others readily acknowledge. He had claimed that surname for himself in honour of Hercules, as we have observed above, or rather in order that he might be believed descended from him [Col. 0942B]. He was admitted by Diocletian to partnership in imperial power in the year of Christ 385, according to some; or, as others think, he was proclaimed only Caesar in that very year, and emperor and Augustus in the following year, 386.

If you ask our Cecilius where he was clothed with the imperial purple, you will receive from him this answer: “There was a high place outside the city”—Nicomedia—“about three miles away, on whose summit Maximian himself assumed the purple.” Yet writers of our age dispute, with no slight contention, whether Cecilius there speaks of the former Maximian, Herculius, or of the latter, Galerius. Some think these words should be understood of the former, many others of the latter. Nevertheless, all of them, with fairly unanimous agreement, admit that Herculius himself, as the Alexandrian Chronicle has it, was created emperor at Nicomedia [Col. 0942C]. Afterwards he is called Diocletian’s brother by Cecilius. For emperors, though not related by blood, used to address each other by the name of brothers.

Although Herculius was not joined to Diocletian by blood relationship, he was nevertheless like him. For, says our author, in both there was one mind, the same thought, equal will, equal judgment. They ruled with great concord of wills and judgments. Mamertinus greatly extols their common and particular harmony (*Panegyric of Maximian*, §41, and *Genethliacus*, §7). Yet Herculius, as the lesser followed the greater, obeyed Diocletian in persecuting Christians and in every harsher policy, as Eutropius testifies (*Breviary of Roman History*), down to his abdication of imperial power [Col. 0942D].

Thus, Cecilius continues, they differed only in this: the lesser had more greed, but the greater less; the greater, however, had more timidity. He meant the greater greed of Herculius because, even if he was not as diligent as Diocletian in guarding his wealth, he accumulated it with the utmost injustice and cruelty. Whenever he lacked money, he seized it from the wealthiest senators, whom he ordered to be punished by death through the wicked subornation of witnesses. Nor was it difficult for him to amass boundless riches in a very short time by such evil arts, since he had under his rule the most affluent provinces—Italy, Africa, and Spain—as we have explained above [Col. 0943A].

Cecilius calls him not only greedy (Cecilius, ch. 15), but “a man not very merciful.” For how far removed he was from mercy no one can fail to see from what has just been said. If anyone nevertheless wishes this to be further proved, let him hear Eutropius (in the passage cited), speaking thus of him:

> “Herculius was manifestly and openly cruel, alien from moderation and companionship; by the terror of his appearance and countenance he displayed harshness.”  
> (The same, book X, p. 229; Zosimus, p. 673.)

Eutropius later repeats this in other words and further accuses him, like Zosimus, of faithlessness.

Herculius burned with no less heat of lust than of greed and cruelty [Col. 0943B]. For it was not enough for that pernicious man to corrupt morals—this is indeed how the manuscript reads—against every law human and divine; he also violated the daughters of leading men and virgins torn from their parents’ sight. In a word, he thought the happiness of his imperial power consisted in denying nothing to lust.

If you do not believe Cecilius when he says this and seek another witness, we shall give you Aurelius Victor, by whom Herculius’ unbridled lust and other vices are noted in these words in the *Epitome*:

> “Aurelius Maximianus, surnamed Herculius: fierce by nature, ardent in lust, foolish in counsel, rustic in origin.”

And in his work *On the Caesars*:

> “He was driven by such lust that he did not restrain the stain of his mind even from the bodies of hostages.”

But if from this you infer that Cecilius’ text should read *males* rather than *morals*, as some have proposed, you will plainly act against the authority of the manuscript and against the progression by which Cecilius moved from the general corruption of morals to the particular violation of virgins [Col. 0943C]. For these are his exact words:

> “Already lust in this pernicious man extended not only to corrupting morals, which is hateful and detestable, but even to violating the daughters of leading men.”

We therefore wonder how that fictitious emendation—or rather, corruption—of the Ceciliane text could have entered the minds of men whose morals are not wholly corrupted.

No one, moreover, will find it surprising that this emperor, corrupted by lust, unchastity, and so many other vices, considered that he must always comply with the wishes of Diocletian, to whom he was similar [Col. 0943D], especially when Diocletian wrote to him that he too should persecute the Christians. And indeed, having received his letter, he willingly obeyed throughout Italy, as our author says (ch. 15), being a man not particularly merciful. Who, even if we were wholly silent, could not most readily perceive by how many and how great tortures very many Christians in the provinces under his command were racked, and shed their blood for the invincible confession of their religion? Yet if you still wish to hear our Caecilius, he will tell you—having cited the verses of Virgil quoted above—that this man, Diocletian, and Galerius were three most cruel beasts, who raged against the Christians from east to west with such fury that no words could adequately describe it. Therefore no one can doubt that Herculius, a man far from merciful, then gave free rein to his inborn savagery and never spared Christian blood.

Yet although, as we have said, he was more daring than Diocletian, Galerius frightened him, in order to compel him to lay down the supreme dignity of emperor, by fear of civil arms. Herculius therefore sent letters to Diocletian, reminding him both of Galerius’s designs and of the army which Galerius had in fact enlarged after his threats. From our Caecilius we learn that these letters of his were delivered to Diocletian; but what Diocletian himself replied, Caecilius passed over in profound silence. Nevertheless, he indicates clearly enough that Herculius, after receiving the reply, divested himself of the purple, with which he clothed Severus, just as Diocletian, as stated, clothed Maximinus with his own [Col. 0944B].
