The author of the Eusebian Chronicle explains where and when this occurred in these words: “In the second year of the persecution, Diocletian at Nicomedia and Maximian at Milan laid aside the purple.” But we have already discussed this abdication above; Severus and Maximinus must be considered below.

## ARTICLE II

How Maximian Herculius, having resumed the purple, freed Rome from siege and came to Constantine, whom, after giving his younger daughter to him in marriage, he attempted to deceive; concerning his second return to Rome, where he vainly attempted to deprive Maxentius of imperial power and was thence ignominiously expelled.

[Col. 0944C] Herculius abdicated the supreme dignity of emperor and Augustus not willingly, if one believes Caecilius, but altogether against his will; or, as we have already noted from Eutropius, after Diocletian had persuaded him to do so with difficulty. Accordingly, as Eumenius testifies, he was ashamed to imitate the remarkable moderation of Diocletian himself, who had so gloriously retired to private life. Nor is this at all surprising. For he was indeed, as Caecilius says, desirous of revolution; and, in Zosimus’s words, φύσει ὤν, φιλοπράγμων καὶ ἄπιστος—by nature restless, or willingly making trouble for others, and untrustworthy. Therefore, after laying aside imperial power, while he was staying in Campania, he again seized the purple sent to him by his son Maxentius, who feared Severus; and he did so with as much delight [Col. 0944D] as he had formerly laid it aside unwillingly.

He then met Severus, who was besieging Rome—or, as Eutropius says, flew thither from Lucania—and entered the City after it had been freed from siege. But he feared that he might be unable to resist Galerius, angered by Severus’s death and perhaps advancing against him with Maximinus and doubled forces. Therefore, after fortifying the City and carefully equipping the undertakings begun against the enemy, he set out for Gaul. This is how the manuscript has it, but it is most corrupt and makes no sense. Thus each editor has attempted to emend the passage according to his own judgment. But who would dare assert what the true reading is without another, better manuscript? Caecilius’s meaning nevertheless seems to be that Herculius, leaving the City fortified [Col. 0945A] and well supplied with things captured from the enemy, set out for Gaul.

Did he then come there to Constantine, who was staying there, so as to win him to his party by marriage to his younger daughter? In our manuscript the phrase reads, “by marriage to the younger family,” doubtless through a scribal error similar to the earlier one. Zosimus, however, relates that after Severus’s death Herculius came to Diocletian (Zosimus, *History*, book II). But when he had vainly urged him to resume the purple, he says, he hastened across the Alps to Constantine. He gave his daughter to Constantine by this wicked stratagem, in order to compel him to attack Galerius. That this wife of Constantine the Great was named Fausta is acknowledged not only by Zosimus, but by Eutropius and all others (Eutropius, *Breviary of Roman History*, book X [Col. 0945B]). Why Caecilius called her Herculius’s younger daughter is highly uncertain, unless perhaps he thought that Herculius’s elder daughter was his stepdaughter Theodora, born of his wife Eutropia and wife of Constantius, Constantine’s father. For Aurelius says in the *Epitome*: “From Eutropia, a Syrian woman, he begot Maxentius and Fausta, Constantine’s wife; and he had given his stepdaughter Theodora to Constantius, Constantine’s father.” The emperor Julian, moreover, extols this Fausta with great praise (*Oration* 1), and Constantine the Great is said to have begotten by her his son Constantius, whom he preferred above the others.

Herculius’s wicked hope of deceiving Constantine was, however, entirely frustrated. Therefore he immediately made his way to Rome to his son Maxentius, as just mentioned [Col. 0945C]. There he did indeed share imperial power with him, but Maxentius’s authority was greater. Thus that impious father, torn by envy, stripped the purple from his son’s shoulders in a public assembly. But the soldiers, abhorring such treachery, supported the son and expelled the father from Rome as a Superbus—that is, as a Tarquin. We have further witnesses to this most disgraceful deed, first the anonymous author of the panegyric addressed to Constantine the Great, who relates it thus: “He himself,” Herculius, “who was believed to be his,” Maxentius’s, “father, having attempted to tear off the purple rent from his shoulders, realized that his destiny had passed into that disgrace.” Our second witness is Eutropius (*Breviary*, book I), whose words are: “Herculius, the father of Maxentius, addressed the army in its midst and attempted to depose his own son from imperial power, but received a mutiny and many reproaches from the soldiers.” Zonaras nevertheless teaches us (*Annals*, book XI, §33) that some others narrated this somewhat differently, though he does not name them. Socrates differs still further (*book I*, ch. 2), recording that when Herculius attempted to kill his son, he was prevented by the soldiers. This belief was readily formed by those who saw him tear the purple from his son.

## ARTICLE III

How Maximian Herculius, having returned to Constantine, again laid aside the purple, then deceived Constantine and assumed it for the third time; how he afterwards seized [Col. 0946A] Marseilles, from which he was expelled by Constantine; by what devices he finally attempted to kill him, paid the penalty by the noose, and concerning the overthrow of his statues.

Driven from Rome with such disgrace and ignominy, Herculius returned to Gaul and pretended to be at odds with his son Maxentius, as though he had been expelled from rule by him, as Eutropius relates (*Breviary*, book X). But our Caecilius entirely denies that he fabricated this in order to claim for himself and his son, as he says, the empire of the whole world. For his purpose was that both he and Diocletian should be restored to sovereignty. Yet Caecilius maintains deep silence about the part of Gaul to which he went, and whether he came as far as Constantine. Consider, however, whether one would wholly miss the mark in inferring from this that, after a very brief stay in the first provinces of Gaul, Herculius saw the approaches to Constantine closed and insufficiently safe, and did not wish to complete the journey he had begun [Col. 0946B].

Be that as it may, he remained for some time in Gaul, says Caecilius; then, having changed his plan, he went to Galerius, who was then staying with Diocletian at Carnuntum in Pannonia, intending, under the appearance of a false reconciliation and of settling the condition of the state, to deprive Galerius of sovereignty and life. But whichever route he took, Caecilius says, he was shut out from what was his own—that is, from the towns and cities under his authority. Anxious and disturbed, he returned to Constantine, his son-in-law, as Caecilius says, and the son of his son-in-law. For, as we recalled a little earlier, Constantine had then married Fausta, daughter of Herculius, [Col. 0946C] and Constantius, Constantine’s father, had married Theodora, Herculius’s stepdaughter. But this criminal father-in-law, to deceive Constantine more easily, laid aside royal dress and dignity. Indeed, by this feigned abdication he persuaded Constantine—who no longer suspected any fraud—that a smaller force would suffice to defeat the barbarians. Constantine had scarcely entered the barbarians’ territory with a few soldiers when Herculius resumed the purple; with the utmost treachery he plundered Constantine’s treasuries, crossed Gaul, and occupied Marseilles, which was to serve as his stronghold. But Constantine flew there with marvellous speed, and the soldiers returned to him. He then surrounded Marseilles with a siege and addressed Herculius graciously, while Herculius answered him with abuse and insults. Meanwhile the city was taken and the imperial purple stripped from Herculius; yet, after he had been reproved, his life was spared. Thus our Caecilius.

But Eumenius the orator narrates these matters more fully (*Panegyric to Constantine*, §14 ff.). Constantine, he says, had received Herculius after he was expelled from Rome, driven from Italy, and ejected from Illyricum, into his provinces, forces, and palace. Yet this most ungrateful man, who had usurped imperial power for a third time after twice laying it down, first came to Arles and then to Marseilles, having tested the loyalty of the soldiers. Constantine pursued him with a most faithful army, travelling from the Rhine to the Saône and Chalon, then down the Rhône; with almost incredible speed he arrived at Arles, already abandoned by Herculius, and then at Marseilles, where the latter had shut himself in [Col. 0947A], and surrounded it with siege. His soldiers were already ready to storm the city when Constantine sounded the recall and granted pardon to Herculius and the others. Eumenius delivered this speech, indeed, in Constantine’s own presence. Nor does he seem to differ greatly from Caecilius, except that the former gives a fuller, the latter a briefer, account.

Such, as our author continues, was the treachery of Herculius, utterly forgetful of so many benefits, that he incited his daughter Fausta, Constantine’s wife, to lay new snares for her husband. She indeed pretended at the time to comply with him, but meanwhile informed her husband of these matters. Thus Herculius, secretly admitted in the dead of night into Constantine’s bedchamber, slew a eunuch in Constantine’s place [Col. 0947B]. But Constantine confronted him, exulting in so great a crime, with a band of armed men and granted him the power of choosing a free death; Herculius chose to meet it by the noose. Caecilius does not expressly identify the place of this fatal catastrophe, but seems sufficiently to imply that it occurred at Marseilles. Several others state this openly.

Eutropius, however (*Breviary*, book X), omitting Herculius’s various betrayals, relates that after he had vainly attempted, as stated, to deprive Maxentius of rule, he came to Constantine in Gaul, in order to kill him by prepared ambushes when an opportunity offered. When these plots were exposed by Fausta, Eutropius continues, he fled to Marseilles, where, having been overcome, he paid the penalty for so great a crime by a most just end. Eusebius says that he “ended his life by hanging himself,” ἀγχόνῃ τὴν ζωὴν ἀπορρήξας (*Supplement*, book VIII; likewise book VIII, ch. 13): he broke off his life by the noose, which elsewhere he calls the foulest kind of death. In his *Chronicle* he says: “Herculius Maximian, exposed by his daughter Fausta because he was preparing a plot against her husband Constantine, was killed while fleeing at Marseilles” (*Chronicle*, A.D. 310). Orosius also reports the same [Col. 0947C] (Orosius, book VII, ch. 28). Aurelius Victor, who in one place records that he perished by a death worthy of his crimes, says elsewhere much more plainly: “Besieged by Constantine at Marseilles and then captured, he paid the penalty with a final mode of death, his neck broken by the noose.” You see by what witnesses Caecilius’s opinion is supported. Eutropius is therefore mistaken when he records that Herculius died at Tarsus from disease after the plots revealed by his daughter Fausta, and there wrongly confuses him with Maximinus. Finally, Caecilius added that this wretched emperor ended his detestable life by so ignominious a death after celebrating the vows of twenty years—that is, the festival of the *vicennalia*, or the twentieth year of his reign. Hence the already cited Aurelius Victor: “He died at the age of sixty, in his twentieth year as emperor.”

Moreover, our author relates that, at Constantine’s command, Herculius’s statues and images were destroyed in such a way that images of Diocletian, displayed with them, were cast down at the same time. These are our author’s words: “The statues of the old man Maximian were torn down by Constantine’s command, and images of Diocletian, as we saw above, with whom he had been depicted [Col. 0948A], were taken down” (Caecilius, ch. 42). Eusebius recorded the overthrow of these statues and images of Maximian Herculius in these words: πρώτου δὲ τούτου τὰς ἐπὶ τιμῇ γράφας, ἀνδριάντας δὴ, καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα ἐπ᾽ ἀναθέσει νενόμισται, ὡς ἀνοσίου καὶ δυσσεβεστάτου καθῄρουν (*Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, ch. 13; and *Life of Constantine*, book I, ch. 47): “He was the first whose honorific inscriptions, namely statues, and all such monuments as customarily are set up in dedication, were pulled down as those of a sacrilegious and most impious man.” Elsewhere he repeats the same statement, except that there the text reads πρὸ δὲ τούτου, “before this.” Christophorson rendered this as “before death,” doubtless because he read the Greek πρὸ δὲ τούτου. Rufinus, on the contrary, wrote in Latin: “So that after his death his statues and images were removed” [Col. 0948B]. Our Caecilius seems to follow Rufinus’s view, since he had described the death of Maximian Herculius much earlier. He reports only concerning Diocletian that Diocletian, while still alive, saw his own images cut down and destroyed. But we have dealt with these matters above.

# CHAPTER XI

On the Emperor Maxentius.

## FIRST ARTICLE

On the parents of the emperor Maxentius; the nature and extent of his vices; how, where, and by whom he was made emperor; in what sense he and Constantine the Great are called sons of Augusti; what the salutation of a king was; [Col. 0948C] and what the name *privatus* signifies.

In the preceding articles we cited various writers who state that Maxentius was the son of Maximian Herculius. Eusebius and Zosimus likewise call him τοῦ Ἑρκουλίου παῖς, “son of Herculius” (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, ch. 14; Zosimus, *History*, book II). Aurelius Victor indeed says that he was born to Herculius by Eutropia, a Syrian woman; but at the same place he adds: “They report that Maxentius was substituted by a woman’s device, to retain the affection of a husband troubled from childhood by the omen of a most wicked undertaking.” And indeed, the anonymous Valesian author says concerning his origin, when inquiry had been made, “his mother confessed in reply that he had been fathered by a certain Syrian.” The anonymous author of the panegyric soon to be cited asserts this with greater certainty. Yet this same anonymous writer, no less than Aurelius Victor and our Caecilius, expressly declares at the same place [Col. 0948D] that Maxentius was the son-in-law of Maximian Galerius. Therefore, on the coin produced by Baronius (Baronius, A.D. 306, §23, vol. III), Maxentius is rightly proclaimed the son-in-law of Maximian—not of Herculius, as some supposed, but of Galerius.

If you wish to know what kind of man Maxentius was, hear Caecilius (ch. 18): “A man,” he says, “of ruinous and evil disposition, so proud and obstinate that he was not accustomed to adore”—that is, to greet by bending the knee or kissing—“either his father Herculius or his father-in-law Galerius.” This is clear from various laws of the Theodosian Code, Gothofredus’s notes upon them, and Panciroli’s observations on the *Notitia of the Dignities of the Roman Empire* [Col. 0949A]. Aurelius Victor further records that Maxentius was fierce, inhuman, cowardly, unwarlike, and far more horrible in lust. But Eusebius, and later Socrates and Suidas, attack his ungovernable lust, monstrous cruelty, and other vices much more vehemently (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, ch. 14; *Life of Constantine*, book I, ch. 33 ff.; Socrates, book I, ch. 2 ff.; Suidas, s.v. Μαξέντιος). Yet we cannot omit the comparison of Maxentius with Constantine the Great made by the anonymous author of the panegyric addressed to Constantine, in which both Constantine’s virtues and Maxentius’s vices are vividly described. “Maxentius,” he says, “was the supposititious son of Maximian,” Herculius; “you were the son of pious Constantius. He was marked by the most contemptible depravity, his limbs distorted and lax, and even his name”—undoubtedly Maximian—“mutilated by a fraudulent alteration; you were attended by your father’s piety. Lest we begrudge him a falsely claimed lineage, impiety attended him; clemency attended you. Cruelty attended him; chastity devoted to marriage alone attended you. Lust polluted by every form of sexual corruption attended him; divine precepts attended you. Superstitious crimes attended him; finally, the expiatory crimes of temples plundered, the senate slaughtered, and the Roman people killed by famine attended him; [Col. 0949B] you were attended by the abolition of false accusations, the prohibition of informers, preservation, and rejoicing over the blood of a murderer.” It is therefore no wonder that Aurelius Victor says that Maxentius was never dear to anyone, not even to his father or to his father-in-law Galerius.

Nor should it be any more surprising that Galerius did not wish him to be called Caesar by Diocletian, as Caecilius reports. Galerius gave this reason for his refusal: “He who despised me as a private man—what will he do when he receives imperial power?” Galerius clearly complains that he was despised because Maxentius, as observed shortly before, refused to adore him. Cuperus gives many learned notes on the term *privatus*; but who does not see that it is opposed to the titles Caesar and emperor, as in this verse of Plautus (*Captives*, act I, scene 3, v. 63):

> “He who was once such an emperor is now a private man.”

But the Praetorian soldiers, observing that Galerius, who had abolished their camp, was hateful and odious to the Roman people because of excessive exactions [Col. 0949D], made Maxentius emperor at Rome. This is fully established by the testimonies of Aurelius Victor, the anonymous Valesian author, and the author of the Eusebian Chronicle. Eusebius himself nevertheless recorded that he seized τὴν ἐπὶ Ῥώμης τυραννίδα, “the tyranny at Rome” (*Chronicle*, A.D. 208 [probably an OCR error for 308]), though it was undoubtedly conferred upon him by the Praetorians. And Zosimus relates (*History*, book II) that he was placed upon the royal throne, εἰς τὸν βασίλειον θρόνον, by those whom he calls πραιτωριανούς, “Praetorians.” Yet if one follows Eutropius (*Breviary of Roman History*, book X), he was not acclaimed emperor by those Praetorians at Rome itself, but not far from the city of Rome, namely in the countryside where he was staying [Col. 0950A].

Some learned men dispute whether Maxentius was then made emperor or merely Caesar. Their disagreement arises from these words of our Caecilius concerning the emperor Galerius: “Overcome by obstinacy, he abolishes the name of Caesars and calls himself and Licinius Augusti, and Maxentius and Constantine sons of Augusti.” Some have thought that Caecilius is here speaking of Maximinus, who, overcome by obstinacy—that is, carried away by the force of his own obstinacy—proclaimed himself emperor together with Licinius, as Eusebius says (*Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, ch. 13); and that he intended Maxentius and Constantine, who were sons of Augusti by birth, to be called by that honorary designation. Thus he removed the name of Caesars from these three. But many others maintain that Caecilius’s words denote Maximian Galerius, as the entire sequence of his discourse plainly indicates. For he speaks of Maximinus a little later, and the title of Caesars could not have been removed by Maximinus himself, who was not yet emperor.

Others, however, suspect the name Maxentius here. “Why,” they ask, “is he mentioned here?” Why not, others reply, if Galerius then called him Augustus or son of Augustus? Some therefore believe that *Maxentius* should be retained and the name *Maximinus* added. But perhaps they have not sufficiently noticed that Caecilius, in narrating this designation as sons of Augusti, makes no mention of Maximinus, because Galerius then quite rightly excluded him from this dignity. For he saw Maximinus, utterly forgetful of the many benefits he had received from him, resisting him with the utmost audacity [Col. 0950C].

Accordingly, nothing in Caecilius’s text (Caecilius, ch. 26) appears to need alteration if it asserts that Maxentius, son of an Augustus either by birth or, if one prefers, by adoption, was then called Augustus and emperor by Galerius. For, as we have said, the Praetorians had already placed him upon the royal throne. Moreover, our author had earlier plainly declared that Maxentius sent the purple to his father Maximian Herculius, whom, he says, he named Augustus twice. But how did he name Herculius Augustus twice unless he himself had already been Augustus and emperor? To this is added what we read in Eutropius: not Maxentius alone but Constantine too, likewise a son of an Augustus, were then in fact Augusti and emperors. For these are his exact words: “Thereafter the state was held by four emperors: Constantine and Maxentius, sons of Augusti; Licinius and Maximian”—read, “Maximinus.” Did he not therefore speak of them there as true emperors? For those who were called sons of Augusti merely by honorary designation possessed no power to govern the state [Col. 0950D].

From what has been said, then, a twofold sense may be drawn from Caecilius. The first is this: Galerius calls himself and Licinius Augusti, while calling Maxentius and Constantine not emperors but only sons of Augusti. But because these latter two were, as said, long before sons of Augusti by birth, Caecilius’s words may be interpreted in a second way: Galerius wished himself and Licinius, together with Maxentius and Constantine, sons of Augusti, to be emperors. Consider, I ask, and decide which of these two interpretations of our author’s meaning and words is truer. What follows, however, seems clearer: that Galerius then abolished the title of Caesars. But how, pray, was it abolished? Was it abolished so that this title should thereafter be given to no son of an Augustus as a definite expectation of imperial power? For he left the rank of Caesar to Maximinus, undoubtedly for no other reason than that he could not take it from him [Col. 0951B].

After this, when Maxentius had been acclaimed emperor by the army, Galerius, as Caecilius reports in the same place (ch. 32), ordered all four emperors to be reckoned, doubtless in addition to himself, who was first among them all. Thus Galerius himself also proclaimed Maxentius emperor, just as Maximinus had already been proclaimed emperor by the soldiers; that is, he approved their election. Therefore no one should be surprised if our author left it written that several men were made emperors not once but twice and three times.

## ARTICLE II

Whether and why Maxentius, delivered from the snares laid for him by his father Herculius, declared war on Constantine; concerning his alliance with Maximinus; the immense size of his army; his superstition; and his first battle against Constantine.

We have shown above with how great treachery and how great a fault of most ungrateful spirit Maximian Herculius vainly attempted to strip his son Maxentius of the imperial purple, with which he himself had nevertheless again clothed him not long before. Delivered from the plots of this most unjust father, Maxentius declared war on Constantine the Great after his father’s death and pretended that he wished to avenge his father’s death. This is indeed the view not only of our Caecilius (ch. 43), but also of Zosimus (*History*, book II). By contrast, Adrian Valesius believes (*French Affairs*, book I) that Constantine made war upon Maxentius because he had overthrown his statues at Rome. But this opinion is entirely refuted by Nazarius (*Panegyric*, §§6, 8, and 13), another anonymous author of a panegyric, and Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History*, book IX, ch. 9; *Life of Constantine*, book I, ch. 26), who firmly assert that Constantine undertook this war wholly unwillingly, only after gentler remedies had been offered, and for no reason whatever except to free Rome from Maxentius’s tyranny [Col. 0951D]. He wished, therefore, to make peace with Maxentius; but Maxentius not only wholly rejected it, but further provoked Constantine himself by cutting down and trampling upon his revered images. Nevertheless, that most excellent emperor disregarded the insult done to himself and resolved only to vindicate the liberty of the Romans.

Meanwhile Constantine betrothed his sister to the emperor Licinius. But this relationship was suspect to Maximinus, who feared that they were joined against him by it. Therefore he sent Maxentius his image and envoys, and gave them letters in which he sought to enter into an alliance with him. Maxentius accepted all this most willingly, regarding it as aid sent to him by heaven against Constantine, his enemy. As a sign of the alliance agreed, he placed the image received from Maximinus alongside his own. For it was the custom of Caesars and emperors, after their inauguration, to send their images to one another; if they approved the election, they arranged for these images to be joined with their own. Herodian testifies (*History*, book V, ch. 567 [materially uncertain citation]) that the emperor Elagabalus sent his own image to the Romans to be placed in the middle of the curia [Col. 0952B], in order to test with what disposition it would be received by the Roman senate. Some therefore think that the origin of the later custom by which a new emperor sent his image to others should be traced to this event. But Cangius, and we ourselves below, say more concerning that custom.

When civil arms had been set in motion, Constantine, intending to fight Maxentius, established his camp in the fields near Rome. “Maxentius’s army,” says Caecilius, “was larger than Constantine the Great’s.” This is confirmed by the author of the panegyric delivered in praise of Constantine. Zosimus expressly asserts (*History*, book II) that Constantine’s army consisted of ninety thousand infantry and eight thousand cavalry, but Maxentius’s of one hundred and seventy thousand infantry and eighteen thousand cavalry [Col. 0952C]. Eusebius more briefly (*Ecclesiastical History*, book IX, ch. 9; *Life of Constantine*, book I, ch. 37), and the anonymous author of the panegyric likewise, wrote more than once that the multitude of armed men in Maxentius’s army was innumerable.

Yet although he was equipped with so great a number of forces, and one so much greater than Constantine’s, Maxentius remained inside Rome, having received an answer from experts in magical arts that he would perish if he went beyond its gates. For, as Eusebius testifies (*Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, ch. 14; book IX, ch. 9; *Life of Constantine*, book I, chs. 27 and 36), this wicked man zealously pursued those impious arts and deceptions, and trusted them more than the goodwill of his subjects; he did not dare set foot beyond the gates of the City. The anonymous author of the panegyric whom we have just cited says: “That foolish and wicked animal dared never go outside the walls. For he was warned thus either by prodigies or by omens of his own fear.” But Zosimus expressly states (*History*, book II) that he sacrificed victims to the gods and consulted haruspices and the Sibylline books about the outcome of the war, and was deceived by their misleading response.

Eusebius, the anonymous panegyrist, and Nazarius, whom we have cited, mention several battles between Maxentius and Constantine in various regions of Italy. But our Caecilius (ch. 44), passing these over, comes to the battle in the aforesaid fields near Rome, where the two emperors fought after bringing their standards together. In this contest, he says, “Maxentius’s soldiers had the advantage, until afterwards Constantine, strengthened in spirit and prepared for either outcome, moved his forces nearer to the City, opposite the Milvian Bridge; the manuscript reads *Milvi*.” The Milvian, or Molvian, Bridge, now commonly called the Ponte Molle, was built on the Via Flaminia about two Roman miles from the city of Rome. But among those who mention this earlier battle one can scarcely find any writer other than our Caecilius and the author of the *Politeia of the Holy Fathers Metrophanes and Alexander*. The words of this writer himself concerning Constantine, who could not persuade Maxentius to abstain from impious deeds, are found thus in Greek in Photius: Ἅπτεται πολέμου καὶ συμπλακεὶς μάχῃ, τὰ πρῶτα μὲν ἐγγὺς γίνεται τοῦ λαβεῖν τὸ ἧττον (*Bibliotheca*, cod. 216): “He undertook war and, engaging in battle, at first came close [Col. 0953B] to suffering defeat.” But this seems to have been only a slight skirmish: even if Maxentius’s soldiers had some advantage, Constantine was by no means hindered thereby from moving all his forces nearer to the City, opposite the Milvian Bridge.

## ARTICLE III

Whether what Caecilius reports concerning the battle in which Maxentius was defeated by Constantine the Great is true; concerning the bridge from which he was hurled into the Tiber; the year in which he died; and whether this occurred after his *quinquennalia* had been completed.

After the battle recounted in the preceding article, Caecilius says (ch. 44): “The day was approaching on which Maxentius had assumed imperial power; it was the sixth day before the Kalends of November”—that is, 27 October—“and his *quinquennalia* were ending” [Col. 0953C]. On the following night Constantine saw the heavenly sign of the cross, concerning which we have discussed above, and ordered his army to be armed and fortified with it. Then the enemy met him and crossed the Milvian Bridge. They came to blows and fought with the utmost force on both sides, but with an entirely uncertain outcome. A disturbance therefore arose in the City, and the people in the circus reproached Maxentius, who was staging games there on his birthday. Alarmed by this, he ordered the Sibylline books to be consulted; in them, as the already-cited Zosimus testifies, it was found that the enemy of the Romans would perish. Maxentius allowed himself to be persuaded that Constantine was indicated by this answer. He therefore came into battle line and crossed the bridge, which was cut apart behind him. On seeing this, the battle grew fiercer; turned to flight and crushed by the multitude of fugitives, he was hurled from the bridge into the Tiber and drowned. Thus Caecilius describes this battle, the death of Maxentius, and the victory of Constantine the Great.

But in this account, many may perhaps find it not very credible that Caecilius (ch. 44) says Maxentius gave public games in the circus in his own presence on the very day when battle was raging so fiercely almost at Rome’s walls. For who would believe that the emperor and Roman people were occupied with games and entertainments while a formidable enemy was fighting at the City’s gates? But this passage of Caecilius is mutilated and corrupt; without the aid of another manuscript, we cannot know what he actually said.

Furthermore, what Caecilius reports in this account concerning the Milvian Bridge seems to be related somewhat differently by other writers [Col. 0954A]. Eusebius relates (*Ecclesiastical History*, book IX, ch. 9; *Life of Constantine*, book I, ch. 38) that Maxentius had built a bridge of boats, indeed very solidly, but in such a fashion that it could be cut apart and that Constantine, crossing it, could easily be thrown into the river. The opposite happened: Maxentius, defeated, fled over this bridge; but the contrivance gave way under his feet, and he fell into the stream with many others and was drowned. Zosimus (*History*, book II), Libanius (*Oration* 3, vol. II), Protagoras (in Photius, cod. 62), and the author of the *Politeia of the Holy Fathers Metrophanes and Alexander* likewise record this. But Aurelius Victor reports that Maxentius was “caught while crossing the Tiber by the snares which he had set”—perhaps the text should read “for the enemy”—“at the Milvian Bridge.” But in the *Epitome* he speaks somewhat more clearly: “A little above the Milvian Bridge, while hurrying to enter a bridge made of ships at the side, he was plunged into the depths by a fall from his horse.” Thus you see that this writer distinguishes two bridges: the Milvian Bridge, and another built of boats and ships [Col. 0954B]. Maxentius is said to have been thrown into the Tiber from this second bridge, which he himself had constructed for Constantine’s destruction. Whether these two bridges were not distinguished by others because of their proximity, noted in the cited *Epitome* of Aurelius Victor—listen further to Eutropius, in order to judge more confidently—who says very briefly that Maxentius was defeated at the bridge called Molvian. Prudentius also identifies the same bridge in these verses:

> Witness, Molvian Bridge, of the Christian leader advancing upon the City,  
> hurling the tyrant, caught, into the pools of the Tiber.  
> (*Prudentius, Against Symmachus*)

Nazarius (Nazarius, *Panegyric*, §30) makes no mention of any bridge; nor does the anonymous Valesian author, whose words on the death of Maxentius, defeated by Constantine, are these: “Maxentius, having gone out from the City, chose a plain above the Tiber on which to fight. There, being defeated and all his men put to flight, he was thrown from his horse into the river amid the crush of the crowd that hemmed him in.” Finally, the uncertain author of the panegyric addressed to Constantine has handed down that Maxentius, shut in by the narrow confines of the Milvian Bridge, vainly attempted to escape over the steep ground of the farther bank and was swallowed by the whirlpool of the Tiber [Col. 0954D].

You have, then, heard the differing accounts of writers concerning Maxentius’ fall, his plunge into the Tiber, and the bridge from which he fell into that river. Whichever account you pronounce the truer, it must certainly be admitted that all of them plainly establish that this tyrant, defeated by Constantine and submerged in the waters of the Tiber, did indeed perish. But Cecilius, like Bucherius, asserts—as we have observed—that he died there on 28 October in the year 312, the day, he says, on which his *quinquennalia* ended. Yet, according to Aurelius Victor, it was in the sixth year of his tyranny—not merely begun, indeed, but completed after an idle six-year period, or *sexennium*, if you credit the uncertain author of the panegyric mentioned shortly before: “So that,” he says, “he marked the very day of his birthday [Col. 0955A] by his final slaughter, lest, by beginning it, he should violate that sevenfold number, sacred and religious.” This is read as repeated by that author a little later, and more than once, as also by Nazarius. May it not then be quite reasonably inferred that our Cecilius is to be understood as referring to Maxentius’ completed *quinquennalia*, although those festivities were celebrated either at the beginning or the end of the sixth year of his reign, and were sometimes transferred to another day? But Dufresne, Cardinal Noris, and Pagi, who cites them, treat these matters more fully; you may consult them.

## CHAPTER XII

### On the Emperor Maximian Galerius

### ARTICLE I

[Col. 0955B] On the homeland, parents, savage barbarity, and enormous bodily bulk of Maximian Galerius; on the superstition of his mother Romula; on a difficult passage of Cecilius concerning this matter; on the victory won by Galerius over Narses; and on the title of Caesar, which he insolently rejected.

Maximian Galerius was of Dacian origin, as Cecilius indicates more than once (*Cecilius*, chs. 9, 23, and 27); or, as Eutropius says (*Breviary*, book IX), Maximian, who was called Galerius, derived his stock from Dacia, not far from Sardica; and, as we read in the Epitome of Aurelius Victor, from Dacia Ripensis, while in Victor’s books he is placed in Illyricum. For this reason, as our author elsewhere relates, he once attempted to change the name of the Roman Empire, so that it should be called the Dacian Empire.

[Col. 0955C] He derived his origin, however, from parents who, as Aurelius Victor says, were farmers; and he himself was a herdsman. Doubtless for that reason he was first surnamed *Armentarius* (“herdsman”). But Diocletian, as Cecilius says, had already changed his name in part on account of a man: because Maximian performed his loyalty with the utmost devotion. That is, Diocletian wished Galerius, after rejecting the name Armentarius, to be called Maximian in honour of Maximian Herculius, because he had shown him loyalty with the utmost devotion. Yet some think that our Cecilius’ passage ought to be corrected, and that instead of *jam . . . hominis* one should read *nam . . . ominis*. But this must be confirmed by the authority of at least one manuscript. For this passage of Cecilius is enveloped in his customary obscurity.

[Col. 0955D] Doubtless clearer are these words of his concerning Galerius’ mother: “His mother, a woman from beyond the Danube, had fled into New Dacia after crossing the river, when the Carpi were ravaging the region.” Her name, moreover, as our author further says and Aurelius Victor confirms, was Romula; and for this reason Galerius, as is noted by him, wished the place where he was born to be called Romulianum. Yet such was the impiety of this most ungrateful son that, our author continues, he defamed his mother with a sexual slander, so that he might appear descended from the gods. For, in the words of the same Aurelius Victor, “he dared insolently to assert that his mother Romula, after the fashion of Olympias, mother of Alexander the Great, had conceived him through intercourse with a dragon.” Alexander foolishly boasted this, as Julian the Emperor says among others (*Oration* 1), in order that he might be believed the son [Col. 0956A] of Jupiter Ammon; Galerius, however, that he might be believed the son of Mars.

It is therefore no wonder if this man, born of such rustic parents, or, as Cecilius puts it (ch. 9), “this beast had an innate barbarous savagery, alien to Roman blood.” In the Colbert manuscript we indeed read *barbaries efferitas*; but some suspect that *barbaries et feritas* (“barbarity and ferocity”) was written, and this emendation is not altogether implausible. What that inborn ferocity of the most savage barbarians was in Galerius, and how dreadful was his bodily bulk, our author describes in these words: “His body suited his character; he was tall in stature”—so the manuscript reads—“his flesh enormous, spread and swollen to a frightful [Col. 0956B] size; in short, in speech, deeds, and appearance, he was an object of terror and dread to all.” And indeed Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, ch. 16; *Life of Constantine*, book I, ch. 57) has recorded that his entire body, owing to excessive abundance of food, had grown into a certain boundless corpulence. Yet Aurelius Victor calls him handsome in body and, despite a rough and rustic sense of justice, sufficiently praiseworthy; and Eutropius calls him a man of good character. But these statements must undoubtedly be understood of his youth and of the time before he was Caesar, or attributed to flattery. For Aurelius Victor himself admits that he possessed little humanity, no more than his colleague did.

Diocletian, moreover, “took him as son-in-law,” says Cecilius [Col. 0956C] (ch. 9). For when, as we saw above, he was proclaimed Caesar by Diocletian, he then gave him his daughter Valeria—of whom we have spoken earlier—in marriage, and compelled him to repudiate his first wife. Eutropius and Aurelius Victor likewise record these facts.

Romula, Galerius’ own mother, as has been said, was most devoted to the impious cult of the pagans and a worshipper of the gods of the mountains—that is, of gods set over mountains, or to whom mountains were consecrated, or who were said to dwell in them, such as Cybele and others, of whom Ovid sang in *Fasti*, book III, vv. 315 ff.:

> We are rustic gods, and we rule upon the lofty  
> mountains; Jupiter has dominion in his own abodes.

[Col. 0956D] We shall discuss these elsewhere. This woman, then, being very superstitious, says Cecilius, “would sacrifice with sacrificial feasts almost daily and would furnish banquets to her *vicarii*.” Christians abstained. This is precisely what we read in the Colbert manuscript; yet all acknowledge that the passage is corrupt. Very many have tried to apply a remedy to it, but in vain. Now *daps*, according to Festus, “among the ancients meant a religious offering, performed either at winter sowing or in spring. The word is derived from Greek, among whom this kind of banquet is called δαίς [*dais*, ‘feast’].” Livy, however, relates that a sacrifice was once performed with an exceptional ox taken from the herd, with the Potitii and Pinarii employed in the service and sacrificial feast; and that it happened by chance that, when the Pinarii had eaten the entrails, they came to the remainder of the [Col. 0957A] sacrificial feast. Servius, moreover, observes twice or thrice that *dapes* are feasts of the gods, whereas *epulae* are feasts of human beings.

Consider, then, what sense of Cecilius may be drawn from this, and whether it is this: Galerius’ mother was a worshipper of the gods of the mountains; this very superstitious woman sacrificed almost daily with sacrificial feasts offered to the mountain gods, and provided banquets from the same offerings to her *vicarii*, that is, those who acted in her stead; or to her *vicani*, that is, the inhabitants of the village where she was sacrificing. Christians abstained from these banquets. But whatever the true reading of this text may be, Cecilius there clearly declares that Christians abstained from Romula’s feasts, lest they be defiled by sacrificial offerings made to a false divinity. Such, then, were Galerius’ parents, from whom he derived rustic barbarity, just as from his impious mother he had sucked in vain superstition concerning the gods with his milk.

Although Aurelius Victor calls him an outstanding and fortunate warrior, and Eusebius says that he was endowed with military experience, he was nevertheless initially defeated by Narses, king of the Persians, as both Eutropius, Aurelius Victor, Ammianus Marcellinus (*Ammianus*, book XIV, ch. 11, and book II), the author of the Eusebian Chronicle (*Eusebius, Chronicle*, under A.D. 301 and 303), Orosius, Zonaras (*Annals*, book XII), and others have recorded. But when the contest was renewed, he won a notable victory over him. He then returned to Diocletian, who had first received him with the deepest disgrace, bringing booty and spoils; he inspired fear in him and afterwards most insolently rejected [Col. 0957C] and scorned the name of Caesar.

### ARTICLE II

How Galerius compelled Diocletian to rage against Christians and to relinquish the Empire; what he then reproached him with; with what injustice he attempted to deprive all men of liberty; and how, contrary to the laws, he ordered decurions, leading citizens, *egregii*, and *perfectissimi* to be tortured; noble matrons to be carried off to the women’s workhouse; household guards and administrators to be punished with the spear; and persons to be flogged to be stretched upon a stake in a *stabulum*.

We have, unless we are mistaken, explained sufficiently clearly by what evil arts, and how wickedly, Galerius impelled Diocletian to harass and most cruelly kill Christians. Nor have we shown less clearly how, if our Cecilius is to be believed, he compelled him [Col. 0957D] to resign the Empire and to create Severus and Maximinus Caesars. Then Galerius himself sharply reproached Diocletian, who paid no heed, that “fifteen years had now slipped away while he was relegated in Illyricum, or on the bank of the Danube, struggling against barbarian peoples.” These are Cecilius’ words in both printed editions and the manuscript, except that the manuscript reads: “into Illyricum, that is, to the bank of the Danube . . . was struggling.” But there some things appear to have been omitted and others added to the text. For after “fifteen years” there has been omitted “since when,” or “from what persons,” or something similar. If, however, you read as in the manuscript, “that is, to the bank of the Danube,” these words may perhaps have been appended by Cecilius himself, for purposes of explanation, to Galerius’ words which he reports. But Baluze and others afterward preferred to write “or to the bank,” so that Galerius meant that he had been relegated either to various regions of Illyricum or to the bank of the Danube, by which Illyricum was, of course, separated from other provinces. If you wish to know more about its boundaries, you may consult Cellarius.

After Diocletian and Maximian Herculius had laid aside the supreme imperial dignity in the manner we have seen, Galerius considered himself master of the state. He wholly despised Constantius, the one man who could oppose him, both on account of his gentleness and mildness and because of his weak bodily health; this led him to the quite certain expectation that Constantius—of whom we shall speak later—would soon die, or might at least easily be deprived of the purple and the Empire. Nothing, therefore, was then nearer to his heart than to exercise a cruel dominion over all, and, after celebrating his *vicennalia*, or twentieth year of rule, and after appointing emperors and new Caesars, to pass a secure and tranquil old age.

He consequently directed all his mind and thoughts toward afflicting everyone, Christians and pagans alike. First, indeed, he wished to introduce among the Romans the custom by which the Persians devote themselves in servitude to their kings, while their kings, says Cecilius, use the people like a household (*familia*; the manuscript wrongly has *milia*). Whence, someone may ask, had he learned that this was a Persian custom, a point which has not been observed in the many notes on this book of his? Let him consider, I pray, whether the following words of Hystaspes, Darius’ father, to Cyrus, cited from Herodotus (*Histories*, book I, §210), are to be understood of this custom: “Far be it, O King, that any Persian man should plot against you . . . For you have made the Persians free instead of slaves, and masters of all instead of being ruled by others.” Ὃς ἀντὶ μὲν δούλων ἐποίησας ἐλευθέρους Πέρσας εἶναι, ἀντὶ δὲ ἄρχεσθαι ὑπ᾽ ἄλλων, ἄρχειν ἁπάντων: “You who, instead of slaves, made the Persians free; and instead of being ruled by others, made them rule all.” We do not, however, dare to assert with certainty that these words plainly prove that the Persians had formerly been slaves of their kings. But because it was not in Galerius’ power to place the Romans under the yoke of slavery, he attempted to take liberty away from them.

Furthermore, under him, “not only decurions but also leading men of cities, *egregii*, and *perfectissimi* were tortured.” [Col. 0958D] Decurions were the prefects and chiefs of each order, which was called a *decuria*. But just as there were various kinds of them, so too were there various duties and offices, which you will find described by Gothofredus and others. By a law of Constantine issued in 317, these men, together with the *egregii* and *perfectissimi*, are included in one provision:

> “Those who have served in the palace, and those to whom provinces have been entrusted—since they have deservedly obtained the honours of the rank of *perfectissimus* or *egregius* through the most distinguished administrations—likewise those who, appointed decurions or leading citizens, have fulfilled all the public duties of their native city, ought to enjoy the dignity granted them. But if a decurion, having obtained by favour the dignity of *perfectissimus*, or the rank of two-hundred-thousand or one-hundred-thousand [*ducenae* or *centenae*], or the rank of *egregius*, seeks to evade his council, then, after the loss of his letters patent, he shall be restored to his former condition; so that, having undergone examination regarding all honours and public duties, he may obtain some prerogative in accordance with municipal law.”

The ranks of *perfectissimus* and *egregius*, therefore, could be conferred only upon those who had served in the palace or discharged the most distinguished provincial administrations. They enjoyed several privileges, among which was immunity from corporal punishments, torture, and judicial interrogation. But on these matters Gothofredus says more in his annotations on the Theodosian Code; Valesius, in his notes on Ammianus Marcellinus, says more on the rank of *perfectissimus*; and we ourselves have treated both ranks elsewhere. Galerius, however, overthrowing these and other laws, ordered decurions, *egregii*, *perfectissimi*, and the principal men of cities—that is, their chiefs and nobles, the foremost citizens—to be fastened to crosses if they deserved death, and otherwise to be tortured and kept in fetters.

Moreover, freeborn and noble matrons were carried off to the *gynaeceum*, a chamber and more secluded place in houses where women carried out weaving and women’s work. Galerius therefore ordered freeborn and noble women to be banished to this place as a mark of disgrace and infamy. But Constantine the Great granted freedom to all women who had been reduced to bondage in the *gynaecea*. Various laws concerning the workers of the *gynaecea* survive in the Theodosian Code; you may consult Gothofredus’ commentaries on them.

[Col. 0959C] “Household guards and administrators,” Cecilius continues, “were punished with the spear,” that is, put to death. The *domestici* were men divided into various corps who served more intimately within the palace, although some were sometimes sent to the provinces. Various laws concerning them still occur in the Theodosian Code, on which Gothofredus likewise makes many observations. He also says more concerning the administrators or officials mentioned in the same passage by Cecilius. They were of three kinds: first, the higher officials or judges; second, those of middle rank, called *spectabiles*; third, the lowest, called *clarissimi*. You see, however, by what punishment Galerius wished them and the *domestici* to be punished: namely, by the spear, struck by which they were killed.

Further, if anyone was to be flogged, “four stakes,” says Cecilius, “stood fixed in the *stabulum*, to which no slave had ever been accustomed to be stretched.” [Col. 0959D] One critic prefers *in sabulo* (“on the sand”) to *in stabulo* (“in the station/lodging”), but gives no reason. He perhaps supposed that *stabulum* here means a place where herds and cattle are stalled and kept. Yet it is sometimes used for an inn or lodging-place, as in Cyprian (*Epistle* 68), and sometimes for any station or place where someone is accustomed to dwell and remain. Some support this with the following line from Virgil, *Aeneid*, book VII, v. 512:

> He seeks the lofty dwelling, and from the topmost roof  
> of the station sounds the pastoral signal.

If our Cecilius used *stabulum* in this sense [Col. 0960A], it doubtless denotes some public place where persons to be flogged were tied to stakes and beaten; and, as he says, no slave had ever before been accustomed to be stretched on them. Some wish to insert *nisi* (“except”) before *servus*, but with no authority whatever. Without this or any other alteration of the text, is not our author’s meaning sufficiently plain? No one whatsoever—not even a slave—had ever previously been accustomed to be stretched on those stakes. Cecilius will thus appear to mark Galerius’ cruelty more emphatically.

### ARTICLE III

The many and dreadful tortures by which Galerius killed Christians and others; and how he attempted to exterminate all letters and learned men, and to establish military judges.

No one will doubtless be surprised that Galerius, so ferocious and superstitious, raged far more cruelly against Christians than against all others. But everyone will marvel, and hear with horror, at the many tortures and punishments by which he mangled them. Our Cecilius indeed speaks of them as follows: “For those without rank, the punishment was fire; and at first, against Christians, he had permitted that of exile, but, after laws had been issued, [he ordered] that the condemned should be burned in slow fires after torture.” Nearly everyone unhesitatingly maintains that this passage is corrupt and depraved, since they perceive no reason why exile should be mentioned there. Yet it is scarcely credible how much the writers of *scholia* [Col. 0960C] have laboured in restoring this text. Some suspect that *exitii* (“destruction”) should be written instead of *exilii* (“exile”); others propose *exilium quod*, some *exemplum*, others *illum*, still others *ex illis*. Some think *permissa* should be read instead of *permiserat*; others, *promserat*. Finally, some suppose that only the punctuation should be changed, by placing a full stop before the word *primo*.

We, however, are more readily persuaded that the reading of the ancient manuscript should be retained until another, more correct one is found. From it, given our author’s excessive concern for brevity, as we have said, the following sense can be elicited: “For those without rank, the punishment was fire; and Galerius had at first permitted the punishment of exile against Christians; but later, after laws had been issued, he ordered that the condemned should be burned in slow fires after torture.” For, since that most inhuman tyrant had previously been unable to obtain from Diocletian permission for Christians to be burned alive, he was initially compelled to comply with Diocletian, who did not wish Christian blood to be shed. Thus Galerius for some time, following Diocletian’s example, had undoubtedly permitted the punishment of exile against Christians, as Cecilius says.

But after he obtained supreme dominion, as we have said, he then gave free rein to the savagery and madness innate to him, which he had hitherto restrained unwillingly. Accordingly, by laws issued, he ordered all Christians to be burned in slow fires after torture. Who can hear Cecilius’ account without deep emotion of the dreadful and monstrous cruelty with which this was done? “A gentle flame,” he says, “was applied beneath [Col. 0961A] their feet, until the hardened skin of the soles, contracted by the fire, was torn away from the bones.” Anacharsis too, in Cicero, spoke of the “hardened skin of the soles”; by this term is signified the thicker part of the sole, or lower part of the foot. Cecilius therefore says that, when Christians were tortured by Galerius’ order, the hardened skin of their soles—the lowest part of their feet—was torn from the bones by a slow fire. Then burning and extinguished torches were applied to individual limbs and to every part of the body without exception. And lest the Christian martyr, tortured in this way, should die sooner because his throat became parched by excessive heat and dryness, his mouth and face were drenched with cold water. Finally, after these most cruel tortures, that Christian martyr, as Cecilius says, gave up his spirit when, throughout a long day, his entire skin having been boiled away, the force of the fire had penetrated to his innermost organs [Col. 0961B]. Nor was the fiercer-than-beasts frenzy of this most savage tyrant yet satisfied by that horrible torment: he further ordered the bodies to be burned again after death and, reduced to ashes, cast into sea and river. But we have discussed these and other similar punishments of Christian martyrs—punishments that could have been devised by a diabolical rather than human frenzy—more fully in another dissertation.

Accustomed thus to torture and kill Christians, this foul man, in all cruelty and inhumanity, tortured others also with the same savagery. “For,” says Cecilius, “he afflicted no one with any light punishment; but fire, the cross, and beasts were for him everyday and easy [punishments].” Yet this entire passage has certainly been corrupted through the great ignorance of a copyist. For in the Colbert manuscript we read the following words: *Nulla poenis eum levis, non insola, non in carceris, non metella; sed ignis, crux fere in illa erant cotidiano . . . et facilia.* [Col. 0961C] The space marked by dots is blank there, but nothing seems ever to have been written in it. Everyone has attempted to correct this shamefully corrupted passage according to his own judgment, yet no one has produced anything altogether certain and established. But our author’s meaning appears to be that Galerius employed no light punishment, such as exile, deportation to an island, imprisonment, or condemnation to work in the mines; but punishments by fire and the cross were everyday and easy for him—that is, if the text is to be read thus, he was accustomed to decree and impose them on everyone as readily as he did daily and very frequently.

Then the same manuscript reads: “In this capital punishment, punishment and execution by the sword was granted to very few as though it were a favour, to those who, because of former merits, had obtained a good death.” Through a copyist’s carelessness, in the last two words a stroke was omitted which ought to have been placed over the final two letters as a double *m*. In printed editions, however, the word *poena* (“punishment”) and the conjunction *et* (“and”) are omitted. But what if only the word *poena* has been transposed, and the text is read: “In a capital case, punishment and execution by the sword,” etc.? Would not our author’s expression then be sufficiently clear, with the same meaning as if those words were omitted, and with the same sense? For his words signify quite clearly [Col. 0962A] that, in a capital case—that is, for those condemned to death in whatever fashion—punishment and execution by the sword were granted, as though a favour, to very few indeed, and only to those who, on account of merits, had obtained a good death: that is, a gentler, milder, and less cruel one. For in this sense he uses the same words below.

This, then, was the greatest mercy of the most savage tyrant, who had stripped himself of every trace of humanity. Indeed, his dreadful cruelty had proceeded so far that, whenever he wished to amuse himself, he ordered a certain bear, by name, from among those he maintained, to be brought forward, and men were thrown to it to be devoured. Do you hear how execrable and hitherto unheard-of was the amusement of this most inhuman [Col. 0962B] tyrant, who thus played with human blood? We are not unaware that the Emperor Valentinian the Elder, according to Ammianus Marcellinus (*Ammianus Marcellinus*, book XXIX, ch. 3), possessed two she-bears, faithful guards of his person but devourers of men; one was named Golden Mica, the other Innocence. But Ammianus Marcellinus does not there say that Valentinian, for amusement, threw men to these bears as Galerius did.

Certain learned men have debated among themselves whether our Cecilius meant that Galerius ordered not only Christians but also pagans to be killed after being mangled by all the kinds of tortures and punishments mentioned thus far. Yet, when we carefully examine all his words and what precedes and follows them, it seems to us that Cecilius is speaking there of all who had come under the power of Galerius himself, pagans as well as Christians. He exercised monstrous cruelty upon them, but could never satisfy it. Yet you should not, together with some who stray far from the truth, infer from this that the number of martyrs is diminished. For we have seen with what frenzy and rage Galerius raved against Christians. He therefore spared their blood less because they had despised the worship of false gods than he spared that of pagans; and without doubt he slaughtered a greater number of the former than of the latter by the punishments we have described.

That intolerable tyrant persecuted not only human beings [Col. 0962D], but letters too and all learned people, with implacable hatred. “For eloquence,” says Cecilius, “was extinguished by him”—namely, the eloquence taught in public schools. For he immediately adds concerning forensic eloquence: “Advocates were removed.” These words, as is clear from what follows, include all advocates who pleaded the cases of others in court. He then continues: “Jurists, or legal experts, were either banished or killed.” If anyone asks us who can properly be called a jurist, we shall answer in Cicero’s words: “I would call him one who is skilled in the laws and the custom by which private persons conduct themselves in the state, and is skilled in giving legal opinions, conducting actions, and drawing legal safeguards.”

[Col. 0963A] Galerius, moreover, plotted to exterminate not only these men but all learned persons and learning together. “For learning,” says our author, “was counted among evil arts, and those who knew it were worn down and detested as enemies and foes.” By *litterae* our author means philosophy and the other liberal disciplines, which Galerius proscribed as *malae artes*, “evil arts”—that is, magical arts, as Cuperus interprets; or why not also poisonous arts? More probably, however, he regarded them as harmful and pernicious to the state. Nor should anyone be at all surprised that this emperor, because of his innate ferocity and barbarity, as has been said, wished utterly to abolish all learning and learned people.

After expelling jurists and those skilled in law, he sent into [Col. 0963B] the provinces military judges, untrained in humane letters, or, as Cicero says, devoid of common learning and cultivated refinement (*On the Orator*, book II). He sent them without assessors or advisers, so that they alone might render judgment contrary to law and right. From what Suetonius (*Life of Tiberius*, §33; *Life of Galba*, §14) and Lampridius (*Life of Alexander Severus*, after the middle) have recorded concerning assessors, some light may be cast upon this passage of Cecilius. But many laws concerning them occur in the Theodosian Code, especially that in which the Emperor Constantine is reported to have enacted the following against this audacious and most unjust abuse:

> “It has been determined that provincial governors shall decide disputes in civil cases, even if soldiers have undertaken or initiated the litigation.”

See Gothofredus’ annotations on this and the other laws cited here.

But whatever may be said concerning these military judges sent out by Galerius, some certainly charge our Cecilius here with an error into which Lactantius, who could not have been ignorant of the events then occurring, could not have fallen. For if Cecilius had asserted that learned men, and especially jurists, had been removed by Galerius, then Lactantius could not have done so. Diocletian, they say, protected them and issued various edicts in their favour in his own and Galerius’ names; and certainly no one has yet recorded that these were annulled by Galerius either before or after Diocletian’s death. Thus, they say, Cecilius’ credibility falters, and he himself is charged with falsehood, unless you prefer another guarantor and defender of his opinion. Whether it is sufficient in his defence to observe the barbarity and savagery of that most cruel emperor, we leave for others to decide. Perhaps some will suspect that Galerius has been confused, in an anachronistic manner, with Licinius, of whom we shall speak below. But would Lactantius also have confused them?

### ARTICLE IV

On the immense and utterly intolerable exactions, assessments, poll taxes, and tributes by which Galerius overwhelmed all his subjects and reduced them to extreme poverty; and on the beggars whom he ordered drowned in the sea.

It was not enough for Maximian Galerius to rage and revel in such dreadful slaughter against all Christians [Col. 0964A] and pagans; he also reduced every one of his subjects to utter poverty by immense exactions and taxes. For a census was sent throughout all provinces and cities “once”—so the manuscript reads, signifying irrevocably. The census assessors, whose business it was to impose and collect taxes, and concerning whom much is found in the Theodosian Code, devastated and plundered everything in a manner utterly lamentable. Fields, indeed, were measured plot by plot—not *glebati*, nor *glebatii*, nor only the lands of senators, as some suppose, but the land of all persons, according to each individual’s plot and share. Vines and trees were even counted, in order that these wicked men might extort a greater assessment from them. In addition, animals of every kind were counted by them and entered in public registers, and a tax was exacted for each individual animal. Human heads too were registered, so that money might be paid for every head and person.

We know, indeed, that some have thought this capitation assessment to mean not merely each human head or person, but also the estates, possessions, other goods, and resources of every individual. But our author undoubtedly enumerates all these things separately and therefore distinguishes them from one another.

But will someone ask whether Galerius introduced anything new by this registration of fields, persons, and other things? Does not Ulpian observe that this registration was much older? Quite rightly. But, besides the fact that it had long been discontinued and was revived by Galerius, this assessment was increased to an immense degree and, with the utmost inhumanity, imposed and extorted from those who had previously been exempt and from others who were unable to pay. For from Ulpian, already cited, we learn that boys under fourteen, girls under twelve, and all persons over sixty years of age were subject to no tribute. By contrast, Galerius would allow no exemption at all on grounds either of age or health. Yet, lest he should seem to have cast off every appearance of humanity toward children and infirm old people, while they nevertheless did not enjoy the tax exemption supposedly granted, the assessors subtracted years from the old and added them to the young. But there may have been another reason why years were added to children: namely, so that they could give testimony against their parents and concerning the seizure of their property. For children before the age indicated by us were not qualified to give such testimony, as Ambrose writes concerning Agnes, virgin and martyr: “All were astonished that she should already be a witness to divinity, though by reason of age she could not yet be mistress of herself.” Consult our observations on that passage, if you have leisure and inclination.

Nor did Galerius burden and oppress the Romans less than others with these immense exactions. He also sent assessors to register them and imposed upon them the same assessment which Trajan, after conquering their Dacian ancestors in their continual rebellions, had imposed as a penalty [Col. 0965A]. No writer other than our Cecilius has hitherto been cited as mentioning this assessment. Yet, after imposing it, Galerius dared to do to the Romans what the ancients—so the Colbert manuscript reads—had done by right of war to the conquered. Many think that not *veteres* (“the ancients”) but *victores* (“the victors”) should be read there, because Cecilius is speaking of Trajan as conqueror. But even if we read *veteres*, as in the cited manuscript, *victores* must always be understood, since the phrase “to the conquered by right of war” immediately follows. Therefore nothing seems to require alteration in the text. Our author’s meaning appears to be that Galerius exacted from the Romans that assessment which not only the ancients had imposed by right of war after victory, but which Trajan also imposed upon the Dacians as punishment for their continual rebellion and revolt.

The assessors, moreover, for whom nothing was dearer than to satisfy Galerius’ incredible greed and cruelty, tortured all free and enslaved persons, townsmen and country dwellers, sons and parents, husbands and wives, with torture, flogging, and the rack, in order to make them all reveal their property in turn. After their declarations, more was entered against each person than he truly possessed, and by this cruel fraud the assessment was increased. New assessors, moreover, were sent, one group upon another; and, in order to squeeze out still greater sums, they exacted taxes even for the dead, either because they refused to believe those who said that the persons were dead, or because they compelled witnesses brought forward by them to confess that those persons, although already dead, were still alive [Col. 0965C].

Finally, says Caecilius, “wages were paid for life.” Thus in the manuscript codex. But Baudry thinks it should be corrected to *were paid*, so that Caecilius’ meaning is: the poll-tax was so great that, once money had been exhausted, wages, or any marketable goods, were given in exchange for life—that is, for sustenance and food. But what if, retaining the reading of the old codex, one says that the money of the poll-tax is signified as the price paid for life—that is, in order that one might be allowed to live and not be deprived of life? It is therefore no wonder that Constantine the Great, whose generosity and piety were as great as Galerius’ cruelty and avarice, abolished this wholly intolerable poll-tax by an enacted law. Indeed, by that very law those things may be confirmed [Col. 0965D] which our Caecilius so confidently asserts concerning those immense and execrable exactions of Galerius.

But when the goods and resources of all had been taken away with such inhumanity, beggars alone, surely, remained—persons whom, Caecilius says, misery and misfortune had made secure from every kind of injury of age; thus in the manuscript codex. Yet all acknowledge that the word *aetatis* (“of age”) is corrupted. Baluze therefore wrote *injurietatis* in place of it and of the preceding *injuriae*; but, upon more careful consideration, he wished, with others, to correct it: “secure from every kind of injury.” This yields an excellent sense, and nothing further need be desired except confirmation from the authority of another, better manuscript. But that most savage emperor begrudged these most miserable people even this security amid their utter calamity [Col. 0966A]. For, contrary to every law of humanity, he ordered them to be carried out in little boats and drowned in the waves of the sea. Nor will followers of our Caecilius allow it to be objected that so atrocious and horrible a crime was omitted by other writers. For, they will say, no one can deny that those writers omitted many things which, for the sake of brevity, they judged should be passed over in silence. Caecilius himself, however, did not state when these things occurred. Yet he declares most plainly that Galerius, toward the end of his life, overwhelmed everyone with new and unheard-of exactions, in order to procure the expenses needed to celebrate his vicennalia.

Nor did the insatiable greed of that most cruel tyrant, who seized everything, stop there. “No one,” says Caecilius, [Col. 0966B] “can recount how monstrous at that time was the exaction, especially of provisions.” Indeed, soldiers—or rather, as he calls them, executioners—of the *officia*, that is, officials discharging the duties of judges and magistrates, clung to every individual. Those utterly foul cutthroats and marauders plundered and laid waste everything, leaving laborers nothing for subsistence. Even from those who possessed nothing more they granted no pardon, and by various tortures tried to wring from them what did not exist. This, indeed, seems to be the meaning of our author (Caecilius, ch. 31), although his text in the manuscript codex is plainly corrupt.

He goes on and says that these things, however intolerable, could nevertheless somehow have been endured through hope of crops in the following year. But even this, [Col. 0966C] the sole thing left to the wretched, was wholly taken away by Galerius’ most criminal attendants. For they demanded garments of every kind, gold, and silver, which it was necessary to buy by selling the crops. Thus Galerius consumed the goods, wealth, resources, and even the standing crops of all under the empty pretext of the vicennalia, which in fact he was not to celebrate. For his power and fortunes had already begun to collapse, as we shall explain later.

## ARTICLE V

The plots which Galerius laid against Constantine the Great; what was the *sigillum* which, having received it, Constantine returned to his father; with what grief Galerius learned that Constantine and Maxentius had been made emperors and received Constantine’s laurelled portrait; how he attempted to besiege Rome; with what confusion, on departing from there, he allowed Italy to be ravaged by his soldiers; and how he proclaimed Licinius and Maximinus emperors.

Just as Galerius despised the emperor Constantius, as we have said, so he feared his son Constantine. Therefore, while Constantine was still young, he often assailed him by secret plots, as Caecilius says and Eusebius confirms (*Life of Constantine*, I.20). For, our author continues, under the pretext of training and sport he exposed him to wild beasts—or, as Praxagoras says more clearly in Photius, to a savage and ferocious lion—and to several other dangers, as the Anonymous Valesianus likewise has testified. But all these matters must be separately examined and explained by us below at greater length.

[Col. 0967A] That intolerable tyrant further held Constantine, as will also be explained more clearly below, at Rome, if Aurelius Victor is to be believed—or rather at Nicomedia, as the already cited Praxagoras says—as a hostage. Meanwhile Constantine’s father Constantius, seized by a mortal illness, wrote several letters to Galerius himself, asking, as the Anonymous Valesianus also testifies, that his son be sent back to him. But the inexorable Galerius turned a deaf ear for so long that, exhausted by the urgent entreaties of the gravely ill father, he could no longer deny him his son. He then gave Constantine a *sigillum* as the day was already declining, and ordered him to set out on the following day after receiving his instructions.

If anyone asks what that *sigillum* was, Baluze, relying on the authority of Du Cange, answers that it was a letter of dismissal authenticated by a seal. But Du Cange there cites writers of late Latin. We, however, shall more readily prove that the term signifies an *evection* (*evectio*), frequently mentioned in the laws of the Theodosian Code: namely, a diploma or authorization, validated in writing and by seal, for obtaining the public post; and Constantine in fact obtained it, as will later be shown. That it is indicated by the term *sigillum* is proved by the very words of our author, in which the *sigillum* is distinguished from Galerius’ instructions—that is, undoubtedly, the letters by which he was to inform Constantius that he had sent back his son Constantine and of other matters.

Galerius, however, supposed that Constantine would await these instructions on the next day, as he had ordered. [Col. 0967C] Therefore he pretended to sleep until midday, so that he might delay Constantine on some pretext. But Constantine, having received the *sigillum* on the previous day, immediately after supper hastened with the utmost speed to his father; and, as will be said below, having killed the public horses at many posting-stations along the way, he flew to him. When Galerius learned this, he was so overcome with grief that he could scarcely restrain his tears. His sorrow was greatly increased when he learned that Constantine had been made emperor by his father Constantius. He therefore came very close to ordering the man who had brought, according to custom, Constantine’s laurelled portrait to be burned alive. Yet, urged by the counsel of his friends, he received Constantine’s portrait and sent him the purple robe, as we shall explain later.

But another report again alarmed him: Maxentius had been made emperor through a certain faction of the Praetorian soldiers, whose camp, as we observed above, he had almost entirely abolished. Yet he was not wholly dismayed; he sent Severus to Rome to conquer that city and Maxentius, who was residing there. But after Severus had been defeated and killed, Galerius invaded Italy and attempted to besiege Rome and Maxentius within it. Since, as Caecilius says, he had not previously seen Rome, he brought with him a smaller number of troops than was proper; consequently, he could not surround by siege a city far larger than he had thought. He therefore abandoned all hope of breaking into it.

But we seem to hear someone who will delay us as we hasten from this siege of Rome to other matters [Col. 0968A], and who will object that Caecilius is wrong to deny utterly and absolutely that Rome had hitherto been seen by Galerius or that he knew its extent. “For who,” he will say, “does not know that Aurelius Victor—or at least the person who abridged his history—plainly asserts, as we said a little earlier, that Constantine, still a youth and therefore before these events, was retained as a hostage by Galerius in the city of Rome under the pretext of religion? But where could Galerius have held him hostage except with himself in this very city? As is clear from what has already been said, was Constantine not far too suspect to him for Galerius to leave him alone at Rome? Further, the same Constantine, still young, fought bravely in Asia as a hostage with Galerius, according to the testimony of the same Anonymous Valesianus. Why not also at Rome?”

He will then press the point more vigorously: “Suppose, if you wish, that this is wholly false. How could Galerius, an emperor who remained in Italy at least for some time, then never have seen Rome—not even once? But even if you demonstrate with complete certainty that he had never seen it, you will hardly persuade anyone that Galerius believed, as Caecilius relates, that this city was not much larger than the towns he knew. For who ever, unless he were the most insane of emperors, undertook to besiege a city without having fully ascertained its breadth and length, the garrisons and defenses by which it was fortified, and by what number of forces and what engines it could be taken? If, however, you show that all these things—though very easy to learn—were entirely unknown to Galerius, we shall not oppose either you or Caecilius.”

Please give attention, moreover, to what the Anonymous Valesianus, whom we shall shortly cite, records: Galerius came to Rome with immense forces, which our author nevertheless asserts were insufficient to surround its walls. See, therefore, whether there is any disagreement between them.

Some legions, however, detesting the unworthy crime of Galerius in attacking Rome and Maxentius within it—his own son-in-law—deserted him. The remaining soldiers were already wavering. Broken by fear, he threw himself at their feet; by enormous promises he bent their minds, and he sought safety in flight. Nor did Caecilius alone commit this expedition of Galerius to writing, but many others also, including the Anonymous Valesianus [Col. 0968D], whose words are these:
