> “Galerius came to Rome with immense forces, threatening the destruction of the city, and pitched camp at Interamna on the Tiber. He then sent Licinius and Probus as envoys to the City, asking in conference that the son-in-law with the father-in-law—that is, Maxentius with Galerius—should obtain what he desired by entreaties rather than arms. When this proposal was rejected, he learned that, through promises, the men of Maxentius had abandoned his own side; disturbed by this, he turned back.”

Similarly, though more briefly, Aurelius Victor states that Rome was besieged by Galerius; but, fearing that his own men would desert him, he departed from Italy—or, as another writer says, retreated in haste. Zosimus also records that, when he perceived the soldiers’ dispositions toward him to be insufficiently loyal, he returned to the East without engaging in battle, namely to his own residence, as Caecilius says [Col. 0969A].

So that he might not be intercepted by enemies in his disgraceful flight, or that they might not have, as the same author says, equipment—that is, things necessary for food and use—he granted his soldiers permission to ravage Italy wherever they travelled, or, as the Anonymous says, to provide his soldiers with whatever booty they could. They plundered, despoiled, and laid waste everything by robbery and crime.

Later he came to Carnuntum, a city of Illyricum, and there, in the presence of Diocletian and Maximian Herculius, as we noted above, granted imperial authority to Licinius. “Thus at one time,” says Caecilius, “there were six to whom imperial power had been granted”: Maximian Herculius, Maximian Galerius himself, Maxentius, Constantine, Licinius, and Maximinus. [Col. 0969B] If there is no error in Caecilius’ text, he here uses the term *imperium* to designate the rank alike of Caesar, Emperor, and Augustus; for Maximinus was then only Caesar. We subsequently read in our author: “When Licinius had been named emperor, Maximinus”—in the manuscript codex, *Maximianus*—“was angry and did not wish to be called either Caesar or to be named in the third place.”

Eusebius supports our Caecilius (*Ecclesiastical History*, VIII.3), declaring openly that Licinius was proclaimed Augustus and emperor by the common counsel of the emperors—undoubtedly Diocletian, Galerius, and Herculius:

> “This,” he continues, “Maximinus bore with great displeasure, since hitherto he had been called by everyone merely Caesar,”  
> *μόνον Καίσαρα παρὰ πάντων εἰσέτι τότε χρηματίζοντα*  
> “being still then styled by all only Caesar.”

Neither entreaties nor envoys repeatedly sent could induce Galerius to soften the spirit or break the anger of this ungrateful and obscure man, whom he had made Caesar. Conquered therefore by his obstinacy, Galerius removed, as was said earlier, the title of Caesars and, although unwilling and distressed, named him and three others emperors.

## ARTICLE VI

On Galerius’ final and shameful illness and the edict which, being now close to death, he published in favor of the Christians.

Galerius was in the eighteenth year of his reign and was thinking of celebrating his vicennalia, when God, the most just avenger of crimes, struck him with a thoroughly shameful affliction [Col. 0969D]. It was, says our Caecilius, a fistulous ulcer in the lower part of his genitals; it afterwards grew and spread more widely. Our author then describes the various remedies applied by doctors and surgeons with futile and ineffective effort, and cites for this purpose these verses of Virgil without naming him:

> The masters yielded—  
> Chiron, son of Philyra, and Melampus, son of Amythaon.  
> (*Virgil, Georgics* III, end.)

We have already shown how greatly these words were corrupted through the incompetence of a copyist. Our author means, moreover, that the physicians withdrew in despair of Galerius’ recovery.

Yet other eminent men, he continues, were brought in from every quarter [Col. 0970A]—and *trahuntur*, “are dragged,” is not badly said, that is, unwillingly and against their will. But since they, like the others, achieved nothing, the miserable emperor fled, with no more fortunate result, to the idols of false gods and to Aesculapius and Apollo. “Apollo,” says Caecilius—that is, the priests of this false god—“prescribes treatment,” doubtless assigning medicines to heal his ulcer; but these, like the remedies later suggested by other doctors, proved altogether useless. For “the cancer,” Caecilius says—that is, gangrene—“meanwhile spreads; the malady increases; worms are produced; and the flesh dissolves into putrefaction. Then the stench,” in the words of our author, “pervades not only the palace but the entire city.”

No one, certainly, fails to see that this passage is corrupt; but there are as many proposed meanings for emending it as there are heads. Those may perhaps be closer to the truth who think it should read, “But the stench.” Certainly, if by *odor*, as Pliny notes (*Natural History* IX.7), one may understand nothing other than contaminated air, may it not be more easily understood why Caecilius says that this most foul stench, or contaminated air, pervaded not only the palace but the whole city? “But,” you will ask, “how did it pervade an entire city, certainly not a small one?” We shall therefore not at all oppose those who demonstrate that there is considerable hyperbole in these words of Caecilius, through which he expresses more forcefully how foul-smelling was that most horrible odor exhaled from Galerius’ ulcer. Racked by most acute pains:

> At once he raises dreadful cries to the stars,  
> like the bellowing of a wounded bull fleeing the altars.  
> (*Virgil, Aeneid* II.222.)

[Col. 0970C] These too are verses of Virgil, cited by Caecilius neither in their entirety nor with the author named.

Finally, certain cooked and heated animals, wrapped in bandages, were applied to the ulcer so that the heat might draw out the worms. But from this an even far greater multitude of worms was generated. Thus, through putrefaction, his entrails and every part of his body wasted away with emaciation; his lower part swelled in the shape of a wineskin, and his feet lost their form and appearance.

Other writers described this illness of Galerius more briefly or more fully. Aurelius Victor says that he was consumed by a pestilential wound; the *Epitome* says that his genitals were consumed; Eutropius, that he suffered from an incurable wound; and the Anonymous Valesianus, that he wasted away from a severe illness and at last died when his entrails had opened and putrefied—or, as Jerome suggests, when his flesh was decaying [Col. 0970D]. Chrysostom records that the corrupted private parts of this same Galerius produced worms, and that doctors applied fat foreign birds to his putrefying limbs to cure the ulcer; after they had vainly tried to extract the worms, he breathed out his soul many days later.

Earlier Eusebius had recorded that there suddenly arose, as doctors call it, an abscess around the middle of the more hidden parts of the body, followed by a suppurating and fistulous ulcer from which an incredible multitude of worms poured forth. They devoured his innermost organs so that the great mass of his body dissolved into decay and presented a horrible spectacle to those standing by. He adds [Col. 0971A] that several physicians were summoned; but, because they either could not endure the excessive stench or could provide no remedy, they were cruelly put to death. Rufinus and, later, Paulus Orosius add that one of these doctors boldly declared that he was being consumed by this incurable disease because he had tortured Christians with as much cruelty as injustice.

But he was compelled at last to acknowledge God as avenger less by the exhortations of this doctor than by the violence and pains of the disease, which lasted a full year. Reduced to the utmost extremity, he promised that he would restore the temple of the true God and make satisfaction for his crime; or, as Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History* VIII.17) puts it somewhat more clearly, that he would rebuild the churches of the Christians and put an end to their persecutions [Col. 0971B]. He immediately drew up an edict in favor of these Christians and wished it published in every province.

Caecilius presents this edict to us in full, as does Eusebius, who testifies that he translated it from Latin into Greek, and Rufinus, who testifies that he translated it from Greek into Latin. If, moreover, you compare all their Greek and Latin wording, you will readily observe that their meaning and sense are the same. Therefore some think that we must credit Caecilius with our present possession of this edict in Latin. Eusebius, however, supplies the heading of this edict with the emperors’ names, omitted by Caecilius, though not altogether complete and perfect, as some think [Col. 0971C].

Others further observe that the edict is altogether insulting and abusive toward Christians. Yet at its end Galerius orders Christians to pray and entreat their God for his own welfare and that of the state. But what wonder if Galerius and his ministers, utterly blinded by pagan errors, ineptly contradicted themselves in one and the same edict? At Nicomedia, says Caecilius (ch. 35), it was posted on the day before the Kalends of May, when Galerius himself was consul for the eighth time and Maximinus for the second. Eusebius also notes this eighth consulship of Galerius. Some identify him as sole consul; others, both ancient and modern, suppose that his colleague was not Maximinus but Licinius. Nor are there lacking those who maintain that the latter was substituted for Maximinus [Col. 0971D]. Yet no one has yet certainly demonstrated edicts bearing the name of any substituted consul. Moreover, Caecilius quite plainly declares Maximinus, no less than Galerius, to have been an ordinary consul of that year. For this reason the judgment of our Caecilius appears more probable to some learned writers of our age. See, if you please, Cardinal Noris, Pagi, and Tillemont.

## ARTICLE VII

Where and when Galerius died, after commending his wife and daughter to Licinius; and concerning his son Candidianus.

Although Galerius issued the edict in favor of the Christian religion in the manner we have described, his repentance was not sincere, as is clear even from this edict itself. It is therefore no wonder that he could not obtain from the most just God restoration of bodily health, which one Innocentius obtained when, having been brought by a similar disease into extreme danger of death, he was healed, according to Augustine, by his own tears and prayers and those of a bishop and other ministers of the Church.

That wicked and unrepentant emperor, therefore, a few days after publication of the edict just mentioned, having commended to Licinius, as Caecilius says (ch. 35), his wife and son and handed them over, as they say, from hand to hand, was consumed by a dreadful wasting disease. He immediately continues his account thus: “And this became known at Nicomedia on [day omitted in the manuscript] of the month, when the vicennalia were to take place, with the Kalends of March impending.” Thus, certainly, we read in the manuscript codex, where through a copyist’s carelessness the day of the month mentioned by Caecilius has been omitted [Col. 0972B].

From these words of Caecilius we infer, first, that Galerius died not at Nicomedia, but after he had returned to Serdica, if the Anonymous Valesianus is to be believed. Second, that the emperor Licinius stood beside the dying Galerius there, since our author says that Galerius placed in his hand there the wife and son entrusted to him (Caecilius, chs. 35 and 36). Third, that Galerius departed this life in May, after having been either Caesar or Augustus and emperor for nineteen years and two additional months. For Caecilius indicates that his vicennalia were to occur on the Kalends of March in the undoubtedly following year. Indeed, in the heading of the edict cited by Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History* VIII.17), which, as we said shortly before, was issued by him, we read: “Emperor for the nineteenth year,” *Αὐτοκράτωρ ἐννέα καὶ δέκατον*—that is, undoubtedly in the nineteenth year of his reign, already begun.

Where we read in the Anonymous Valesianus, “He ruled eighteen years,” we should reasonably understand “complete and finished years.” Nor does Aurelius Victor appear to hold any other view when he distinguishes the years during which Galerius possessed the rank either of Caesar or Augustus: “His imperial rule was five years; Constantine’s, one year; though both had exercised the power of Caesars for thirteen years.” Five and thirteen years make eighteen. Yet in Eusebius’ *Chronicle* we read: “Galerius Maximian dies in the twenty-first year of his reign” [Col. 0972D]. But perhaps a copyist erred in writing the numerals, or the author of the *Chronicle* counted the first and last year, though the latter was plainly incomplete. More clearly, however, that same *Chronicle* places Galerius’ fatal death in AD 311, while more expert chronographers place it in the preceding year, 310.

Galerius had had a son by a concubine, who was called Candidianus. Valeria, Galerius’ wife, concerning whom we have said more, later adopted him because she suffered from sterility. He had already reached his ninth year when Diocletian abdicated in 305. His father then intended, after celebrating his own vicennalia, to set him in his place and create him emperor [Col. 0973A]. But at this very time he himself perished by the miserable death which we shall shortly recount. As he lay dying, therefore, unable to do anything further, he commended this Candidianus to Licinius, as has been said, and handed him over into his care.

After this Candidianus came to Nicomedia, where Licinius seemed to hold him in honor; Licinius then betrothed to him a seven-year-old daughter of Maximinus. Yet, trusting too much in Licinius’ feigned favor, he was killed by him when he feared nothing of the sort. It would be difficult, indeed, to find any writer other than our Caecilius who has mentioned this Candidianus. Thus his credibility rests on Caecilius alone, until another witness or guarantor for these matters is produced.

# CHAPTER XIII

[Col. 0973B] On the emperors Severus and Maximinus.

## ARTICLE I

The country and vices of Severus; by whom and how he was made Caesar and then Emperor; the manner of his death after he had besieged Rome and been deserted by his own men; and concerning his son Severianus.

We have observed how Galerius proposed to Diocletian that Severus, a native of Illyricum, as Aurelius Victor says, should be made Caesar. But Diocletian himself at first rejected him as, in Caecilius’ words, “a drunken dancer, to whom night was day and day night.” Nor without reason. For, according to the Anonymous Valesianus, he was obscure both in character and birth, a drunkard, and a friend of Galerius. No one, therefore, will wonder that Galerius, whom we have seen to be a thoroughly depraved man, wished to have as friend and have made Caesar one so like himself [Col. 0973C].

Nevertheless, Galerius presented Diocletian with some argument that induced him to assent to Severus’ appointment. For he openly and emphatically said that Severus was worthy of imperial power because he “*praebuit* faithfully to the soldiers”—that is, as some suppose, he faithfully supplied money and pay to the soldiers, or other things which Galerius himself had entrusted to him for distribution among them. But where, pray, will you find the verb *praebuit* used thus by itself? Some therefore want it emended to *praefuit* (“he commanded”), which gives an easier and better sense but has no manuscript authority. Whatever the case, Galerius, wholly distrustful of this argument, immediately added that he had already sent Severus to Maximian Herculius, to receive from him the purple of Caesar [Col. 0973D]. This was done at Milan.

Accordingly, since Diocletian could no longer prevent it, he laid down, as we have said, the purple and imperial power at Nicomedia, and made that Severus and Maximinus Caesars. Eutropius (*Breviarium* X), as also others, relates that Galerius then gave Italy to Severus to govern. Socrates (*Ecclesiastical History* I.2) supports this, though here he differs from Eutropius: Socrates says Galerius went into Italy, whereas Eutropius says that he remained in Illyricum.

But after Galerius had compelled Diocletian, if our author (Caecilius, ch. 20) is to be believed, and Maximian Herculius to yield imperial power, he had intended, upon completion of his vicennalia—that is, after the twentieth year of his reign—to install Severus as emperor in his own place. But when, as we said, the laurelled image of Constantine, to whom his dying father had entrusted imperial power, was brought, he then seriously considered proclaiming Severus emperor and Augustus and placing him before Constantine, as being younger in age. But while entertaining this design, he was informed that Maxentius had been proclaimed emperor by a faction of the Praetorian soldiers. Therefore, having summoned Severus immediately, he persuaded him by his exhortations to receive imperial power and go forth against Maxentius, residing at Rome.

Severus accordingly obeyed Galerius’ will without delay and advanced with an army to the walls of that city. But there [Col. 0974B] he was deserted by his soldiers, as our Caecilius and the unknown author of the panegyric addressed to Constantine testify; and, when Herculius arrived, he fled and shut himself up with a few men at Ravenna. Yet fearing that he would be surrendered to Herculius, he sent back to him the garment and purple, as Caecilius says (ch. 26)—or, as the manuscript codex has it, “the purple garment”—namely to Herculius, who, as was said a little earlier, had actually clothed him in this purple of Caesar. But by that disgraceful abdication he obtained nothing except permission to die gently by having his veins opened. Caecilius thus reports that Severus lost his life along with his imperial office. But let us now see, if you please, what others have recorded on the matter.

First, Eutropius relates that Severus Caesar was sent by Galerius to besiege Rome and Maxentius there; deserted through the treachery of his own men, he fled to Ravenna, where he was killed. Zosimus, without mentioning a siege of Rome, writes that the same Severus Caesar was sent by Galerius to wage war against Maxentius. He set out from Milan, according to Zosimus, with Moorish units. But Maxentius, who had corrupted the greater part of the soldiers with money, easily defeated him as he approached; Severus fled to Ravenna, strongly fortified and well stocked with provisions. Herculius quickly came there; when he realized that Severus could not be forced out, he deceived him by oaths and persuaded him to depart for Rome. But on the road, at the place called Tres Tabernae, Maxentius laid an ambush; Severus was captured and, *βρόχῳ τὸν τράχηλον ἀρτήσας, ἀνεῖλεν*, “he killed him by fastening a noose around his neck” [Col. 0974D].

The Anonymous Valesianus does not differ greatly from this view, expressing it in these words:

> “When Severus led an army against Maxentius by Galerius’ command, he was deserted by his own men and fled to Ravenna. Herculius was summoned there on behalf of his son Maxentius; by perjury he deceived Severus and handed him over to custody, led him to the City in the garb of a captive, and had him guarded in the imperial estate on the Appian Way, at the thirtieth mile, namely at Tres Tabernae. Later, when Galerius was advancing into Italy, Severus was put to death.”

Do you see how greatly these writers differ from Caecilius?

Aurelius Victor seems to favor Caecilius more strongly. He says that Galerius Armentarius, as soon as he learned that Maxentius had become emperor, commanded Severus Caesar, who happened to be near the City, to take up arms swiftly against him. But, he says, “while he was operating around the walls, he was deserted by his own men, whom Maxentius had won over by the lure of rewards; fleeing and besieged at Ravenna, he died.” Yet in the *Epitome* attributed to him we read: “Severus was put to death by Maximian Herculius at Tres Tabernae near Rome, and his body was placed in the tomb of Gallienus, which lies nine miles from the City by the Appian Way” [Col. 0975A].

But how, you will ask, can Aurelius Victor assert that he died at Ravenna when in the *Epitome* he is said to have been killed at Tres Tabernae, thirty miles from Rome? Did the writer of this *Epitome* think that Aurelius Victor himself, his own author, ought to be corrected? Perhaps no one will consider this wholly remote from the truth. For writers of such abridgments have more than once tried to correct matters in which they thought their authors mistaken.

These differing opinions perhaps arose because Severus, fraudulently and perjuriously lured from Ravenna by Herculius, was secretly led, in changed dress, to Tres Tabernae, where ambushes had been prepared. Since this was known to few, some thought he had been killed at Ravenna, others elsewhere. Perhaps the disagreement among writers about the manner of his death flowed from no other source.

Severus left a son, whose name is said to have been Severianus. He had already reached vigorous adulthood [Col. 0975C] when Licinius defeated and routed Maximinus in the battle which we shall recount below. Yet Severianus followed Maximinus as he fled from the battlefield. After Maximinus’ death, the victorious Licinius condemned him to death, because, says Caecilius, he had contemplated assuming the purple. By Licinius’ order he was brought before public judges, and, after they had pronounced sentence, his head was cut off as one convicted of treason and aspiring to the purple. But those who can produce corroborators of this history other than Caecilius will do us a great service.

## ARTICLE II

The country, various name, parents, occupation, and drunkenness of Maximinus; how he became a shield-bearer, protector, tribune, Caesar, and emperor; and what the Campus Martius was.

Maximinus, like Severus, was a native of Illyricum, as Aurelius Victor says. But our author expressly asserts that he was initially called Daia—or rather Daza—that he was by occupation a herdsman, and that he was related to Galerius. The *Epitome* of Aurelius Victor states no less clearly: “Galerius Maximinus, born from the sister of Armentarius, and before his accession called by his true name Daza . . . of pastoral birth and upbringing” (*Epitome of Aurelius Victor*, under Maximinus). His name had been changed not long before he became Caesar. For Caecilius adds concerning his proclamation as Caesar: “Maximian Galerius had recently ordered him to be called Maximinus after his own name.”

[Col. 0976A] In the Colbert manuscript codex, however, *Maximianus*, not *Maximinus*, appears almost everywhere; but Baluze calls this an obvious error. Nevertheless, in Eutropius’ *Breviarium* and in other works to be cited below, it is written *Maximianus*. It therefore does not appear to be merely the error of one copyist; one must acknowledge that some at times called him Maximianus, after Galerius’ own praenomen.

As for his origin and occupation, the previously cited Aurelius Victor testifies that he was born from the sister of Armentarius, as has been said, but that he was also of pastoral birth and upbringing, the same as Galerius Armentarius himself. This is established and confirmed by the words of our Caecilius soon to be cited [Col. 0976B].

Victor further adds that he was excessively fond of wine, so that when drunk he ordered things which, sober on the following day, he ordered to be corrected. We likewise read in the Anonymous Valesianus: “Thus Galerius”—read, or understand, *Maximinus*—“was so drunken that, while intoxicated, he ordered things which ought not to be done; but, warned by the prefect, he decreed that no one should carry out his orders after dinner.” Eusebius also reports the same, describing his other vices, of which we shall speak more fully below.

Above we showed how, when, and where Diocletian—compelled by Galerius, if Cecilius is to be believed—made this Maximinus Caesar. Thus, “recently raised from cattle and woods,” [Col. 0976C] says Cecilius, “he was immediately a shield-bearer, then at once a protector, soon a tribune, and on the next day Caesar; he received the East to trample down and crush.” He is said to have been “recently raised from cattle and woods” because, as we have already observed, he was a herdsman and a rustic. He was immediately made a shield-bearer (*scutarius*). The shield-bearers were soldiers accustomed, as Zosimus relates, to attend the emperor. Ammianus Marcellinus, Gothofredus, and Pancirolus discuss them more fully and enumerate their various corps.

Thereupon Maximinus at once became a protector. Honorius the emperor explains what protectors were in these words: “Those who undertake armed military service bear the duty not only of defending their own bodies, but also of protecting our person; whence they have received the name of protectors.” See, if you wish, [Col. 0976D] Gothofredus’s commentaries on this law, Valesius’s observations on Ammianus Marcellinus, and the already-mentioned Pancirolus.

As soon as Maximinus had become a protector, he was shortly afterwards proclaimed tribune, as Cecilius says. No one is unaware that there were various kinds of tribunes; nor can there be doubt that our author calls Maximinus a military tribune. Gothofredus and Pancirolus, already cited by us, have made many observations concerning such tribunes and their duties. Vopiscus has provided us with a copy of a letter from the emperor Valerian to Mulvius Gallicanus, prefect of the praetorian guard, written in these words: “Perhaps you marvel that I have made a beardless man tribune, contrary to the ordinance [Col. 0977A] of the divine Hadrian; but you will not marvel greatly if you consider Probus, truly upright though a young man.” Yet Galerius—or, if you prefer, Diocletian at Galerius’s prompting—made Maximinus tribune, a certain young man, as Cecilius says (ch. 18), half-barbarian (*semibarbarus*); and so the manuscript reads. Baudrius, however, would prefer *semibarbatum*, “half-bearded,” because Cicero calls young men *barbatuli*, “little-bearded.” *Barbatuli* is indeed correct, but not “half-bearded.” Cecilius seems to have called Maximinus half-barbarian because he had recently been raised from cattle and woods—one who, Cecilius continues, knew neither military service nor the commonwealth, now a shepherd no longer of cattle but of soldiers.

Although he was wholly unworthy to be suddenly raised, against ancestral custom and institutions, to these ranks of dignity, he was nevertheless, [Col. 0977B] as Cecilius says, made Caesar on the following day and received the East “to trample down and crush.” For Galerius, as Eutropius and Socrates relate, set him over the East; later, surrounded by barbarian Goths, he held it in derisive mockery, as Cecilius puts it—though the manuscript reads most poorly *indibria*.

Moreover, Galerius assigned this half-barbarian, thus elevated to such dignities contrary to established laws, the first place among Caesars, and Constantine the Great the second. Yet when Licinius was proclaimed emperor, proud Maximinus flared up with such anger that he scorned to be called Caesar and assigned third place; neither Galerius’s envoys nor his entreaties could ever bring him back to a sounder mind. Galerius then repented of having made him Caesar, but in vain. [Col. 0977C] For Maximinus afterwards wrote to him that he had been proclaimed Augustus at the recently celebrated Campus Martius. Should you seek another witness to this proclamation, Eusebius is readily available, who recorded:

> After Licinius had been declared Augustus: “These things greatly grieved Maximinus, who until then was still called only Caesar by all. Yet he, being above all else tyrannical in disposition, seized the dignity for himself and became Augustus by his own act” (*Ταῦτα Μαξιμῖνον δεινῶς ἐλύπει … σεβαστὸς ἦν αὐτὸς ὑφ’ ἑαυτοῦ γεγονώς*; Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VIII.13).

“But Maximinus bore this with extreme displeasure, since until then he had been called Caesar only by all. Therefore, endowed beyond others with a tyrannical temperament, he proclaimed himself Augustus.”

But Eusebius does not indicate the place where he arrogated to himself this supreme Augustan power. Our true Cecilius [Col. 0977D] (ch. 32) expressly says: “at the recently celebrated Campus Martius.” What this Campus Martius was is disputed among scholars with no slight contention. Some think it was so called from the multitude of people who flocked there for a public spectacle, hunting, or games. Others regard it as a phrase of that age indicating a festival day or the assemblies at which consuls were created. Some think it denotes the festival day on which soldiers were gathered together for exercise or some other purpose. Finally, others interpret it as military assemblies at which soldiers and armies were reviewed whenever the emperor commanded.

If we too may add our conjectures to all these, [Col. 0978A] we shall say that these words signify the *Equiria*, festivals so called from the racing of horses, as Varro says (*On the Latin Language* V). “On that day,” he continues, “horses run in the Campus Martius.” Festus observes that these were games instituted by Romulus for Mars through horse-racing, held in the Campus Martius (*On the Meaning of Words*, s.v. *Equiria*). Earlier Ovid sang (*Fasti* II, at the end):

> And now two nights remain of the second month,  
> And Mars drives swift horses yoked to their chariots.  
> From the race the name *Equiria* has remained,  
> Which the god himself beholds in his own field.

These games, therefore, being dedicated to Mars, were celebrated in the Campus Martius at the end of February, as we read noted not only by Ovid but also in ancient Roman calendars (*Roman Calendars*, vol. VIII, *Roman Antiquities*). [Col. 0978B] Is it not indeed quite likely that our Cecilius’s words designate this day of the Equiria, on which horses customarily raced in the Campus Martius, so frequently mentioned by writers? We may further add that, in the time of Gregory of Tours (*History of the Franks* II.29), the name Campus Martius was still in use. On this day Maximinus was made emperor in a Campus Martius situated in Egypt or Syria, as may be inferred from the following words of our Cecilius (chs. 32, 33, and 36). If you ask in what year, we answer: in 310, because Galerius was then, as Cecilius wrote in the same place, in the eighteenth year of his reign. In the following year, 311, he died at Sardica, as we have said.

## ARTICLE III

[Col. 0978C]

How Maximinus, after Galerius’s death, attempted to invade the provinces; made peace with Licinius; abolished the indulgence granted to Christians by joint protection; why he established chief priests everywhere, adorned in white cloaks; ordered Christians’ limbs to be mutilated; and required all animals offered for sale to be sacrificed by pagan priests.

As soon as news of Galerius’s death was brought to Maximinus, he immediately hastened forth to claim for himself the provinces and everything as far as the Chalcedonian strait. Having entered Bithynia, he immediately abolished the census tax in order to win popular favour. Then, when discord arose between him and Licinius, they nearly went to arms. But, upon fixed terms, a treaty and peace were concluded by both at that same Chalcedonian—or Thracian—strait, or Bosporus. Eusebius mentions this peace, which was later broken (*Ecclesiastical History* IX.10). [Col. 0978D]

Thereafter Maximinus, more secure and returned to the East, “first of all,” says Cecilius, “abolished the indulgence granted to Christians by joint protection.” That is, he removed the permission which Galerius, as we observed a little above, had given Christians when near death: to build churches and profess their religion. Eusebius indeed attests (*Ecclesiastical History* IX.1) that Maximinus had not dared openly to oppose this edict, though it displeased him. Accordingly, henceforth making no mention of the edict, he merely instructed judges and governors orally not to harass Christians any further, and signified that others should do likewise. Eusebius there supplies us with a copy of Sabinus’s letter on the matter.

In the text of our Cecilius, some judge the word *tutelo* corrupt. Baudrius thinks both it and the preceding *communi* should be corrected thus: *cum muri tutela*, “with the protection of a wall,” that is, with authority to construct churches within city walls. He attempts to establish this with much, but vain and useless, labour. For by Galerius’s very edict Christians were granted permission not only to build churches within city walls but also openly and publicly to practise their religion wherever they might be. It was further commanded that no annoyance be caused them on that account, and that those imprisoned should be released. [Col. 0979A]

Others therefore suspect that *communi titulo*, “under a common title,” should be read, because our author seems to refer to the imperial constitution mentioned shortly before, inscribed with their names—that is, with a common title. Finally, some think Cecilius wrote *communi tutela*, “by common protection.” This may perhaps not be inept. In the manuscript the final letter *o*, instead of *a*, seems to have slipped from the copyist’s hand and been placed beneath the preceding *l*. Moreover, certain laws in the Theodosian Code use the phrases *tutela publica*, “public protection,” or *juris publici tutela*, “protection of public law.” Can it not therefore be inferred that our Cecilius, speaking of an imperial law, could have used this noun employed by jurists and others? Consider, I pray, and pronounce which of these conjectures seems closer to the truth. [Col. 0979B]

Moreover, in order to remove this indulgence and peace granted to Christians without incurring the odium of the emperors, Maximinus, as Cecilius says (ch. 36), instigated embassies from cities, which petitioned that Christians should not be allowed to build meeting-houses or churches within the cities: “so that,” says our author, “he might appear compelled”—or, as the manuscript has it, “compelled and impelled by persuasion”—to do what he was going to do. Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History* IX.2, 4, 7, 9), who testifies that this tyrant, enemy of honour and of every good, could endure the Christians’ peace for only six months, repeatedly mentions these petitions. He also transcribed two letters in which Maximinus himself assented to the petitions and ordered Christians to be tortured and tormented. [Col. 0979C]

Furthermore, “by a new custom,” says Cecilius (ch. 36), he “made chief priests in every city and one in each province from among the leading men, who should perform sacrifices through all their gods”—that is, in all their temples, as we observed elsewhere—daily; and should ensure that Christians did not build, supply “churches,” nor worship publicly or privately, understand “their God,” but should compel them to sacrifice to false gods or bring them before judges. But hear Eusebius relate this as follows:

> “He established priests of idols in every place and city, and over them a high priest in each province—some one of those distinguished in civic life through every public service—assigning to him a military guard and escort” (*Ἱερέας τε εἰδώλων … μετὰ στρατιωτικοῦ στίφους, καὶ δορυφορίας ἐκτάσσων*; Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VIII.14).

Later he repeats nearly the same thing:

> “Thus priests of images in every city, and in addition high priests appointed by Maximinus himself, were established—especially those who had excelled in civic offices and become illustrious through all public services” (*Ἱερεῖς δῆτα κατὰ πόλιν τῶν ξοάνων … καθίσταντο*; Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* IX.4).

Can it not rightly and reasonably be concluded from these words that, just as one principal priest or high priest was established by Maximinus in each place and city, so also in each province, to compel Christians to offer impious sacrifices to false gods? [Col. 0980A–B]

After this Cecilius says: “And he ordered both kinds”—that is, the high priests placed over provinces as well as those placed over other places and cities—“to go about adorned with white cloaks.” For Servius seems to imply in his notes on this verse of Virgil that they wore purple, at least when sacrificing:

> “…and his mantle blazed with Tyrian purple.”  
> (*Aeneid* IV.262; Servius ad loc.)

Elsewhere he notes that the *trabea*, or toga, common to augurs and to the priest of Jupiter or Mars, was made of scarlet and purple. Read, if you wish, [Col. 0980C] the fuller observations made by Albertus Rubenius.

Maximinus therefore granted these priests, who compelled others to sacrifice to the gods, two prerogatives and privileges: first, that they should everywhere preside over the rest; second, that they should proceed adorned in white cloaks, by which they might be distinguished from all others. For other priests, see Gothofredus’s commentaries on the Theodosian Code.

Lest excessive cruelty against Christians provoke the other emperors, this wicked man affected a certain appearance of clemency. He forbade Christians to be killed, but ordered them to be maimed. Accordingly, says Cecilius, their eyes were gouged out; their hands and feet amputated; their noses and ears cut off. Eusebius likewise reports this (*Life of Constantine* I.58; *Ecclesiastical History* VIII.12), recording that this was a new form of punishment devised by Maximinus, which elsewhere he attributes to the tyrants’ false humanity. As soon as he issued the law ordering Christians’ limbs to be mutilated, the right eye of almost innumerable men, women, and children was immediately gouged out, and their knees were disabled by iron and cautery. Eusebius (*Martyrs of Palestine* 8) includes among them one hundred and thirty thus mutilated in Egypt. Later many attended the Council of Nicaea carrying on their bodies these “stigmata of Jesus Christ,” as Theodoret puts it. Paphnutius too was one [Col. 0981A] “of those,” says Rufinus, “whom Maximinus, after gouging out their right eyes and cutting the left knee, condemned to the mines.” The author of the *Polity of the Holy Fathers Metrophanes and Alexander*, cited by Photius, relates the same; but both texts read *Maximianus*, not *Maximinus*.

Yet in the meantime, deterred by letters from Constantine the Great and compelled to dissemble, he discontinued the daily sacrifices in his palace. But if any Christian was encountered anywhere, he was secretly drowned in the sea. Eusebius declares elsewhere (*Ecclesiastical History* VIII.8) that Maximinus, after peace had been granted to Christians, displayed the treachery and craftiness of his mind and could not be moved by the letters of Constantine and Licinius, until divine justice pursued him. [Col. 0981B]

Finally, that Christians might be defiled by the abominable superstitions of the pagans, this most wicked man was the first to decree “that all animals,” says Cecilius (ch. 37), “which he ate should be sacrificed at the altars, not by cooks but by priests; and that nothing at all should be placed upon the table unless it had either been offered in preliminary tasting,” that is, unless a portion had been offered to the gods, “or sacrificed, or sprinkled with unmixed wine.” These matters have already been expounded and explained by us above. There, moreover, we made clear on Eusebius’s authority that Maximinus sent edicts through every province ordering not only guards to be stationed before public baths, to defile bathers with execrable sacrifices, but also all merchandise in the market to be polluted by impious libations, so that everyone might eat flesh sacrificed to a false divinity. [Col. 0981C]

## ARTICLE IV

Concerning the immense exactions and taxes by which Maximinus utterly crushed all persons, pagans as well as Christians.

Maximinus was inflamed not only with blind fury against Christians, but also against all pagans whom he held under his dominion and power. He oppressed every one of them with new and utterly intolerable exactions and taxes. “In other matters too,” as Cecilius says (ch. 37), “he resembled his master. For whatever Diocles or Maximianus”—namely, Galerius—“had left, he scraped away, shamelessly taking [Col. 0981D] everything.” Perhaps *magistris suis*, “his masters,” should be read there, namely Diocletian and Galerius, who are mentioned in the passage. Copyists sometimes omit the last letter of a word, especially when the same letter follows. The word *reliqui* seems superfluous because of the subsequent *reliquerunt*, “they left.” We have already shown how great were the taxes exacted by Diocletian and Galerius. But Maximinus seized with still greater cruelty everything they had left behind.

For he compelled debts to be paid for future years; and for this reason, these are Cecilius’s words (ch. 37), “private storehouses were closed, warehouses sealed”—that is, chambers in which not only wine, as this term frequently denotes, but also grain used to be stored—[Col. 0982A] were shut and secured with seals, lest anyone remove anything from them except for the emperor. And thence arose famine, Cecilius continues, “though the fields bore crops.” This is how the manuscript reads, and with good sense: although the fields bore abundant fruits, people nevertheless perished of hunger, because Maximinus’s agents seized all wine and grain with savage cruelty, to sell them in other regions for the benefit of the public treasury.

Some, however, have added to Cecilius’s text the particle *non*, though enclosed in brackets, before *ferentibus*, “bearing”; thus they obtain this sense without doubt: that nothing was left to farmers with which they could thereafter sow and reap, and therefore the fields produced nothing. Yet nothing should be added to a text without certain authority when, as we have seen, another good sense can be drawn from it. Eusebius, moreover, relates (*Ecclesiastical History* IX.8) that, after this same Maximinus had published an edict against Christians, an unexpected famine occurred, followed by plague. He attributes it, however, to rains which had not fallen in winter as usual. [Col. 0982B]

Cecilius then continues:

> “Herds of cattle and flocks were seized from the fields for the daily sacrifices; by these he so corrupted them that they despised the grain supply and poured it out everywhere without distinction or measure, while *lites universos* [corrupt; perhaps ‘soldiers’ or another class], whose number was immense, *expungerent* [uncertain] all things with costly garments and gold coins; he gave silver to common soldiers and recruits, and honoured barbarians with every kind of largesse.”

We have transcribed all this because various scribal errors are apparent there, although it is thus written in the manuscript, except that *largitionibus* stands for *largitionis*, and very badly so. Some therefore suspect that *suos*, “his own,” should be restored in place of *eos*; then *effunderent*, “they poured out,” for *effundebant*; others propose *aes effundebant*, “they poured out bronze.” For *lites* some propose *milites*, “soldiers”; others *satellites*, “attendants”; some *comites*, “companions”; others *divites*, “the wealthy.” Finally, for *expungerent*, one proposes *expungeret*, another *expleret*, another *excoleret*, nor is there lacking one who would emend it to *expungeret*. From this single example learn how fertile human ingenuity is when men attempt to devise the true reading of a corrupted text. Yet it cannot be asserted with certainty whether any of them has yet reached the mark. [Col. 0982C–D] Whichever of these emendations you choose, you will scarcely produce from it a clear and certain sense. Another manuscript must therefore be sought, so that all may, if possible, be correctly restored.

Meanwhile, in order that Cecilius’s meaning and intent may be understood, it should be observed that he distinguishes four classes of persons. First, those whom Maximinus, seized for the daily sacrifices already mentioned, so corrupted and filled with food sacrificed to a false deity that they despised and poured out the grain supply. The second class was that of his principal soldiers, household retainers, or, if you prefer, flatterers, to whom he distributed costly garments and gold coins. The third was that of common soldiers and recruits, to whom he gave silver. The fourth, finally, was that of barbarians, whom Maximinus honoured with every sort of largesse. From these observations it may be inferred that this is the sense of our Cecilius: Maximinus bestowed individually upon all these persons everything mentioned by us, which he had ordered extorted through the greatest and most excessive taxes and exactions. [Col. 0983A]

Please do not suppose that we gratuitously invent this interpretation of Cecilius’s words, which are certainly anything but Lactantian. For it can quite appropriately be supported and established by these words of Eusebius concerning the same Maximinus:

> “After this he harassed and oppressed not one city or region only but all the provinces subject to his rule with most grievous exactions and assessments of gold, silver, and money, and with repeated and varied condemnations. He also despoiled every wealthy man of ancestral and inherited possessions, and gave huge riches and heaps of money to his flatterers, *τοῖς ἀμφ’ αὐτὸν κόλαξι* (Rufinus), his familiars and attendants … He allowed soldiers to indulge in luxury and softness. But he instructed governors and commanders, as partners in his tyranny, to exercise every rapacity and greed against provincials.”

What we have related concerning Galerius has further shed light on the explanation of all that our author and Eusebius say; Maximinus, as we observed earlier, imitated both Galerius and Diocletian and scraped together all that each had left. Finally, Cecilius added (ch. 37) [Col. 0983C] that all the property of the living was plundered by this cruel tyrant, after the manner of merciful robbers, who seem merciful only when they plunder others’ goods, wealth, and money while leaving their lives safe and unharmed.

## ARTICLE V

Concerning Maximinus’s unrestrained and depraved lust.

All Maximinus’s crimes, however great, were surpassed by his most wicked and depraved lust. If you ask how great it was, Cecilius answers (ch. 38): “The magnitude of the crime exceeds the office of speech.” These are also Lactantius’s exact words in his genuine works (*Divine Institutes* VI.23). But you should not infer from this that this book was composed by Lactantius himself. For this mode of expression is not so unusual or extraordinary that two writers could not use it, or one derive it from the other. Moreover, the immediately preceding words of our Cecilius are wholly alien to Lactantius’s style: “And yet he cannot express it in these words because of his indignation.” Even if, as some think, *exprimi*, “to be expressed,” were read there, it would not thereby produce Lactantian diction. For what does *pro indignatione* mean—that is, “because of indignation,” anger, and wrath? Perhaps *pro indignitate*, “because of its enormity,” would be better. But who would dare assert that this is Cecilius’s true reading? [Col. 0983D]

He says that Maximinus’s utterly unrestrained and untameable lust cannot be explained in any words. He deprived every noble woman, or any virgin of more distinguished beauty, of chastity. Fathers and husbands had to withdraw, lest they be thought to obstruct the abduction of their daughters and wives. Yet all women were first inspected limb by limb, “lest any part of the body,” says Cecilius (ch. 38), “should be unworthy of the bedchamber.” Suetonius relates that Antony reproached Octavian Augustus with “sought-after terms,” that is, adulteries sought through friends who stripped and inspected married women and women of mature age, “as though Throanius the slave-dealer were selling them” (*Life of Augustus* 69). Therefore all the women abducted were truly stripped and their limbs inspected before they were carried off. See, if you wish and have leisure, the observations written on this passage of Suetonius. [Col. 0984A–B]

If a woman who was to be presented to Maximinus refused to be stripped, she was drowned, as though guilty of treason. In earlier times the crime of violated majesty was punished by various penalties, and later by the sword and confiscation of all property to the treasury. But Maximinus preferred that those chaste women be submerged.

He had additionally introduced the most shameful custom that no one should marry without his permission, and that he himself should first taste every woman about to be married. Yet, if we trust Herodotus, the same custom prevailed among the Andyrmachidae, peoples of Africa. Why say more? Maximinus gave freeborn virgins, once defiled, to his slaves as wives. Whatever some may contend, the manuscript actually reads *imminutas*, that is, corrupted, no longer whole and untouched. Plautus too sang:

> “No other person has impaired my chastity.”

Firmianus Lactantius likewise takes this word in the same sense.

Moreover, the example of this most criminal emperor was followed not only by his companions, who with impunity violated the beds of their own [a noun is missing in the manuscript at the beginning of the page, perhaps *colleagues* or something similar]; but anyone whatsoever also abducted the daughters of persons of middling station at will. If parents resisted, they either had to perish or, if they wished to survive, were compelled to give their daughters in marriage to barbarians—the attendants of Maximinus who had committed themselves to him. If you ask who these barbarian men were, we answer that Jordanes indeed records [Col. 0984D] that, with Gothic aid, Herculius defeated the Quinquegentiani, Maximian defeated the Parthians, and Galerius, as we have said, defeated and routed Narses king of the Persians. But our author undoubtedly speaks of Goths, because he immediately added that Maximinus had recruited from their nation his own attendants, guards, and protectors. Finally, we have seen with what cruelty that impious man ordered Valeria, the recently bereaved widow of the emperor Galerius, to be killed because she steadfastly refused his illicit marriage.

## ARTICLE VI

Why and how Maximinus declared war on Licinius and was defeated; how he fled into the mountain passes of Taurus, and then attempted to defend and secure himself at Tarsus in Cilicia.

Maximinus had made peace with Licinius in the manner explained above. But when he learned that Licinius had been betrothed to Constantine’s sister—against whom he had already declared war—he regarded this kinship as all the more suspect because Diocletian, at Galerius’s prompting, had, as we said earlier, made Licinius emperor while passing him over. Therefore, as was also observed before, he secretly made an alliance with Maxentius, who was in all things, as Eusebius says, like himself. When he afterwards learned that Maxentius had been defeated by Constantine and that the Senate had granted this victor the title of first emperor, he burned with such grief [Col. 0985A–B] that he openly professed hostility.

Eusebius indeed records that he then conducted public business dishonourably; puffed up with exceptional arrogance towards his colleagues in the empire, he claimed for himself first place among them in titles and honours; and then, mad with desperation, broke the treaty made with Licinius and undertook a wholly implacable war.

When, therefore, he learned for certain that the marriage of Licinius and Constantine the Great’s sister was being celebrated, and that both were occupied with its arrangements, he quickly moved his army from Syria. By forced marches he came first into Bithynia, then, having crossed the Thracian strait, reached the gates of Byzantium. But amid the fierce cold of winter, snow, and rain, his army was greatly weakened. He attempted in vain to corrupt Licinius’s soldiers by promises and gifts. Yet, abandoned by assistance and distrustful of their small numbers, they surrendered Byzantium to him after eleven days’ siege. He then brought Heraclea, formerly called Perinthus, under his power. [Col. 0985C]

From there, Cecilius says, he had advanced eighteen miles to the first halting-place, when Licinius went out to meet him at Adrianople and thence at the second halting-place, equally distant from Heraclea by eighteen miles. Since Maximinus had seventy thousand soldiers and Licinius only thirty thousand, Licinius had decided rather to delay than fight. But their armies were close to one another, and neither could any longer avoid battle. Maximinus therefore vowed a vow to Jupiter: if he gained victory—Cecilius uses this improper expression—he would immediately extinguish the Christian name. Licinius, on the other hand, as will be said below, commanded that the true God be invoked in prayers dictated to him by an angel. [Col. 0985D]

On the day before the Kalends of May, Maximinus moved his camp, and his army and that of Licinius advanced against one another in opposing battle-array, separated only by a barren plain called Serenus. The emperors then conferred about peace; but Maximinus utterly rejected it. Battle was therefore joined, and Licinius’s men rushed upon the enemy with such force that, when they had slaughtered them to extermination, Maximinus himself was compelled to flee in a slave’s clothing. Such is our Cecilius’s description of the battle.

Zosimus, however, relates (*History* II) that both sides fought fiercely *ἐν Ἰλλυριοῖς*, “in Illyricum,” and that at first Licinius’s soldiers seemed broken and defeated; but when the battle was renewed, Maximinus was defeated and put to flight. Eusebius writes (*Ecclesiastical History* IX.10; *Life of Constantine* III.58) that, confident in the assistance of demons and the multitude of his troops, he entered the contest. But because he was utterly deprived of God’s help and support, the greater part of his army was routed and destroyed, while the remainder went over to the victor. Forced therefore to provide for his safety, Maximinus put on a slave’s dress and, hiding himself through fields and villages, barely escaped at last from the hands of the enemy. [Col. 0986A]

You see, then, that Zosimus differs here from Eusebius and our author in reporting that Licinius appeared at the first encounter to have been overcome by Maximinus, whereas the others report that Maximinus’s soldiers were slaughtered with impunity and scarcely dared defend themselves. Yet Zosimus does not assert that this actually occurred, but only that it perhaps appeared so to some who had been deceived by a false rumour. As to his addition that the battle was fought in Illyricum, from which the plain of Serenus seems distant, some accuse him of error. But perhaps these have not sufficiently considered that various boundaries are assigned to Illyricum; on these, you may consult Strabo and Appian, already cited by us (*Geography* VII; Appian, *Illyrian Wars*). [Col. 0986B]

Having escaped in flight, Maximinus reached Nicomedia “in one night,” says Cecilius (ch. 47), “and one day and another night”—that is, in roughly twenty-four hours—although the battle-site, namely the plain of Serenus, was one hundred and sixty miles away, or somewhat more than fifty leagues if three miles make one league. If we trust geographers, the journey is still longer. But it cannot certainly be stated what system Cecilius used in calculating leagues and miles, or whether the copyist erred in transcribing the figures, though they are complete. In any event, Cecilius clearly indicates the extreme haste of fleeing Maximinus and the very long journey that he completed in a few hours. Nor should this wholly surprise you: fear, as they say, had given wings to the fugitive. [Col. 0986C]

At Nicomedia he hastily took with him his wife, children, and a few attendants from the palace; then, having gathered soldiers in Cappadocia, he resumed the emperor’s clothing. Cecilius seems here to indicate that Maximinus fled as far as the borders of Cappadocia, where it is separated from Cilicia by Mount Taurus. For he subsequently relates how, as Licinius approached, Maximinus, who had remained some time in Cappadocia, again fled from there into the passes of the same Mount Taurus. Having constructed fortifications and towers there, he attempted to block Licinius’s route. Yet from there he was “driven to the right,” in Cecilius’s words; but the manuscript reads *detorsum*, perhaps *detrusus*, “thrust out,” or *depulsus*, “repelled.” Finally, he fled for refuge to Tarsus, a city of Cilicia, into which he had escaped through the gorges of Mount Taurus. [Col. 0986D]

## ARTICLE VII

[Col. 0987A]

Concerning Maximinus’s disastrous death, how long he reigned, and in what year he died.

Nothing, certainly, did Maximinus gain by fleeing to Tarsus. There, besieged by Licinius by land and sea and with all hope lost, he swallowed poison. But first, being, as we have already said, an utter drunkard, he followed the example of condemned men mentioned by Zenodotus and Suidas, cited by Erasmus, and gorged himself with food and wine, by which the force of the poison was initially repelled. Yet once it penetrated his vital organs, he was tormented by such pains that, driven by insane frenzy, for four days he devoured earth which he had dug up with his hands. He struck his head against the walls with such violence that his eyes [Col. 0987B] sprang from their sockets. Having lost his sight, he at last began to see God, says Caecilius (ch. 49), judging him through white-clad attendants. Some wish the word *circumdatum* (“surrounded”) to be understood here; others supply the particle *cum* (“with”), and take “white-clad attendants” to mean angels. But did not Caecilius rather allude to the order of the *candidati*, which was senatorial, and from which candidate quaestors and praetors were chosen? Caecilius’ meaning, then, is that Maximinus then saw God passing judgment upon him through ministers clothed in white garments, like the order of the *candidati*. This order of *candidati* is mentioned in various laws of the Theodosian Code; see Gothofredus’ observations upon them, and Panciroli’s work on the *Notitia Dignitatum*. Whatever be decided concerning these *candidati*, Maximinus certainly implored in vain the mercy of the true God and of Christ the Lord. By that detestable kind of death, guilty as he was—so our Caecilius speaks, and not merely once—he breathed out, that is, gave up, his wicked and accursed spirit.

If anyone asks what other writers have recorded concerning the death of this same Maximinus, he will first learn from Eutropius that, plotting revolution, Maximinus made war upon Licinius in the eastern regions and, at Tarsus in Cilicia, anticipated the impending end by a sudden death. Zosimus, however, writes that, defeated by Licinius, as we have said, he went through the East into Egypt—which is difficult to believe—and at last died at Tarsus: ἐν Ταρσῷ τελευτᾷ, “he died at Tarsus.” Aurelius Victor stated more briefly that he perished near Tarsus; and the *Epitome* added, “by an ordinary death” (*morte* [Col. 0987D] *simplici*). Jerome (on Zechariah 14:12), when discussing the deaths of persecutors, testifies that some of them had their eyes waste away. Whom else did he more clearly designate by these words than this most cruel Maximinus? For, besides our author, Chrysostom, naming this very man expressly (*On St Babylas, against the Gentiles*), reports him as one of those tyrants who died a miserable death and whose pupils sprang from their places. Epiphanius likewise records the same thing (*On Weights and Measures*, §20), though in his text, as also in that of Zosimus, *Maximianus* is read for *Maximinus*.

But these matters are more fully described by Eusebius [Col. 0988A] (*Ecclesiastical History*, IX.9; *Life of Constantine*, II.58). For he makes it clear that the same Maximinus, after being routed in battle and taking to flight, enacted in favour of the Christians the law which Eusebius reproduces in full; and that he was punished severely indeed, though more mildly than he deserved. In the second battle, doubtless near Tarsus, he hid himself indoors; and, struck by a blow from heaven, he burned with pains throughout his entire body so great that he rolled prostrate upon the ground. Through hunger and a certain hidden fire divinely introduced, he wasted away to such an extent that, his bones laid bare by emaciation, he wholly lost his former shape and appearance. Finally, confessing his crimes and calling for death, he breathed out his soul. Thus Eusebius describes this final illness and fatal [Col. 0988B] death of Maximinus; yet he makes no mention of the poison which Caecilius asserts that Maximinus drank. Consider, I pray, whether this may be said to have been omitted by him because it was unknown to him; or whether, if he knew it, he perhaps believed that Maximinus, having drunk poison, was destroyed and killed by it as though by a hidden fire divinely introduced.

Moreover, Aurelius Victor, whom we have cited, maintains that this unfortunate emperor perished after a reign of two years as Augustus; but the *Epitome* says: “He was Caesar for four years, then Augustus in the East for three years.” In one of these two passages, as you see, there is an error. Our Caecilius, however, plainly declares that Maximinus’ first battle with Licinius was fought when he was completing the eighth year of his reign on the first of May. Afterwards he fled to Tarsus, as has been said. Therefore, after several months had elapsed, perhaps around August, he died there—in the year of Christ 312, as some think; 314, according to others; or finally, as seems more probable, in 313. We have already noted that Diocletian clothed him with the purple of a Caesar on the first of May, 305, and that in 310 he was proclaimed Augustus in the Campus Martius—if, however, credit is to be given to our Caecilius, as we said above (this chapter, art. 2). Later writers hold that he was proclaimed emperor from 307, others from 308; and he held that highest dignity for five years and more, until his death.

## ARTICLE VIII

[Col. 0988D] On Maximinus’ wife and children, and their fatal deaths.

We have already observed that Maximinus, fleeing from the battle, came to Nicomedia, whence he took with him his wife and children, whom he had previously left there, and made them companions of his flight. We have also made clear how that wicked emperor wished to repudiate this very wife of his in order to marry Valeria after the death of her husband Galerius. Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History*, I.2) mentions several children of Maximinus, whom he had made participants in imperial titles and images. But after Maximinus died in the manner we have described, Licinius, by whom he had been defeated, [Col. 0989A] ordered all of them to be killed. Eusebius adds that, when they had thus been put to death, images both of them and of their impious parent were broken and obliterated. These, and no more, were the facts which Eusebius committed to memory concerning them.

Our author, however, going further, elsewhere mentions several sons of Maximinus; but elsewhere says: “Licinius destroyed Maximinus’ own son Maximus, aged eight, and his daughter, seven years old” (ch. 47). “But their mother was first cast into the East.” Some suppose there are corruptions in this text. For some believe that the word *suum* (“his own”) has been omitted; others would read *filium natu maximum* (“his eldest son”), or *filium tum maxime* (“his son at that very time”); others, finally, *filium in Cilicia* (“his son in Cilicia”). Yet we fear that they have not sufficiently attended to the cited words of our Caecilius himself, and indeed of Eusebius. For each notes several children of Maximinus, whom Eusebius testifies were made by their father, while he lived, partners in the imperial power, as we have just said. But our Caecilius (chs. 47 and 50), although at the former place he too mentions several children of Maximinus, nevertheless names at the latter place only one son, eight years old, and a daughter seven years old, both killed by Licinius’ order. Yet nowhere does he say whether this son of Maximinus was called either emperor or even Caesar by his father. But if the eight-year-old is called older in age than Maximinus’ other sons, who will find it credible that others, far younger in age, were created emperors or Caesars by him, as Eusebius says?

[Col. 0989C] Might one answer that this son of Maximinus is called *Maximus* by our author, not because of his age, but because that was his proper name? But grant, if you wish, that all these things are true. Still, for what reason, pray, does Caecilius now (ch. 50) mention this one alone, and not the other sons of Maximinus whom Eusebius declares to have been killed by Licinius’ command? Was not Caecilius’ purpose in this book, as we have observed, openly to show all that the tyrants who devastated Christ’s Church with such fury paid the punishments due to them by God’s most equitable judgment in such a way that no stock or root of theirs remained? Why does he mention only one, while omitting the others whom Eusebius maintains were killed by Licinius’ order?

[Col. 0989D] Nor should you say that Caecilius mentions several children of Maximinus, namely his son and daughter, who were slaughtered at Licinius’ command. For Eusebius speaks of those children of Maximinus whom he had made participants in his imperial rule. But this cannot at all be said of his seven-year-old daughter. Consider, therefore, how Caecilius can be reconciled with himself and with Eusebius. And if you contend that this error must be laid to the incompetence or negligence of the man who copied his book, teach us, I pray, exactly how this error is to be corrected.

As for the wife of the emperor Maximinus, she was cast into the East, as our Caecilius says—the East in which he had ordered several women to be drowned. Some, however, have thought that the text should read not *Orientem* (“the East”) but *Orontem* (“the Orontes”). For this is a great river of Syria, frequently called the Orontes by geographers and other writers. But this emendation may perhaps seem unnecessary to others. For in Hegesippus (*On the Destruction of Jerusalem*, III.13) and Isidore, who follows him (*Origins*, XIII.21), we read concerning this very river: “From the course of its source they called this river the East” (*Orientem*).

# CHAPTER XIV

On the Emperor Licinius.

## ARTICLE I

On Licinius’ homeland, parents, vices, and intimacy with Galerius; whether Galerius made him Caesar and emperor at the same time; and whether, at his death, Galerius entrusted his wife and son to him.

Licinius was a native of Dacia, according to Eutropius and also Socrates—of New Dacia, according to the Anonymous Valesianus—but, as that writer adds in the same place, of rather low birth. Aurelius Victor indeed records that he sprang from a family of farmers and country people. Our Caecilius relates that he was a “friend from long shared military quarters and an intimate from his earliest service” of the emperor Galerius, “whose counsels he employed in governing all things”; or, as Zosimus and Socrates say (*Zosimus, History*, II; Socrates, cited passage), an old friend, intimate, and comrade in quarters; and, finally, as Eutropius records, known and esteemed by Galerius both through longstanding association and through vigorous labours and services in the war which he waged against Narses. For that reason Galerius wished to raise him to the supreme height of imperial power; but at first he did not wish to make him Caesar—these are Caecilius’ words—lest he call him son; rather, he intended later to proclaim him Augustus and brother in the place of Constantius, whose imminent death he expected. For it was customary for Caesars to be called sons by emperors and Augusti, just as emperors were called brothers by other emperors.

Our author has committed little, indeed almost nothing, to writing concerning Licinius’ vices, either because he did not know them or, more probably, because he judged them better left unspoken. For through the zeal, work, and piety of Licinius, no less than of Constantine the Great, as he relates, the Christian religion was restored to its former condition and achieved a truly remarkable triumph over the tyrants. Moreover, Caecilius ended this book after the edict granted by Licinius in favour of Christians, and before Licinius began to persecute and harass them. Is it not, then, very likely that he did not wish, by recording Licinius’ vices, to diminish the glory rightly due to one whom he recognized as the Church’s chief liberator for so illustrious an act?

Nevertheless, as we have just said, Caecilius acknowledges that Licinius was the friend, intimate, and counsellor of the most criminal Galerius. That friendship, intimacy, [Col. 0991A] and association could undoubtedly bring him little credit. Elsewhere our Caecilius calls him sparing in giving. But in this milder mode of speech he seems rather to extenuate something of Licinius’ vice of avarice than to censure it as it deserved. For other writers attack both this and his other vices far more sharply. Hear the Anonymous Valesianus: “He raged,” he says, “with crime, avarice, cruelty, and lust, killing many for their riches and violating their wives.” Eusebius also testifies that, in addition to this wicked lust, no measure restrained his sordid parsimony, nor could his desire of possession be satisfied. “For,” he says, “suffering from a kind of Tantalic disease, although he had filled his treasuries with an immense abundance of gold, silver, and wealth, he nevertheless groaned and still complained of his poverty.” Aurelius Victor further records that his parsimony was rustic, and that the servile tortures of innocent and more distinguished philosophers seemed to him too mild. In his *Epitome* he paints him in these colours: “Most wretched of all through his craving for avarice, not free from venereal luxury, exceedingly harsh, by no means moderately impatient, hostile to letters, which through excessive ignorance he called poison and a public plague—especially forensic practice.”

When the emperor Galerius learned that Constantius, already at the point of death, had handed over the empire to his son Constantine, he then bestowed the supreme imperial dignity upon Licinius, bound to him by such close ties of friendship. We have already shown above [Col. 0991C] how, in what city, and in whose presence he made him emperor. Learned men, however, are in doubt whether he was then inaugurated only as Caesar, or both as Caesar and emperor. Valesius once thought that he was made Caesar in 308 and emperor in 311. He was led chiefly to this assertion because Galerius, in the edict written shortly before his death, made no mention of Licinius. But upon more careful examination he recognized, both from manuscripts and from Nicephorus, that Licinius’ name had in fact been inscribed in this edict.

Some therefore hold that he was proclaimed Caesar for at least some time before he was made Augustus. Others think it can be inferred from our Caecilius that he was called emperor only. For he expressly affirms that Galerius, as we have just said, did not wish to proclaim him Caesar lest he call him son. But what prevents him from having been made Caesar and Augustus on one and the same day, or on two successive days? We have indeed already observed that Maximinus was made a guardsman, protector, and tribune on one day, and Caesar on the next. Thus Galerius need not have feared calling him son then. Finally, on this interpretation Aurelius Victor and the Anonymous Valesianus, who say that he was made Caesar, may easily be reconciled with the others. Nor do the various journeys of Maximianus Herculius, who attended this inauguration, conflict with this opinion. Although they seem to require some delay, that man, being most avid for power, could have accomplished them with the utmost diligence and speed.

Whatever the case in this matter, the more expert critics agree that Licinius was hailed emperor on 2 November 307, not without the greatest jealousy on the part of Caesar Maximinus. Later he was present with Galerius at Sardica, as we have related above, when Galerius was dying; there Galerius commended and entrusted to him his wife and son.

## ARTICLE II

On the discord and peace between Licinius and Maximinus; on the betrothal and marriage of Licinius with Constantia, sister of Constantine the Great; on the subsequent breach of peace between Licinius and Maximinus; on their battle; and on the prayer dictated to Licinius by an angel, notwithstanding Tollius’ assertions, and his remarkable victory.

After Galerius’ death such discord arose between Licinius and Maximinus that they nearly came to arms. But, as we have observed, they made peace on stipulated terms at the Thracian strait, though it was to endure only a short and scant time. For Maximinus, unable to bear being thus preferred before him, once he learned that Constantia, sister of Constantine the Great, had been betrothed to Licinius, concluded that they were binding themselves together against him by this alliance. The suspicion was further increased by the marriage, celebrated at Milan in 313, as is thought, to which city Licinius had been summoned by Constantine. For we read in the *Epitome* of Aurelius [Col. 0992C] Victor: “Constantine joins his sister Constantia in marriage to Licinius, summoned to Milan.” And Maximinus did not without entirely just cause regard this alliance with suspicion. For Constantine, as Zosimus relates, Μεταπεμψάμενος, Λικίνιον ἐν τῷ Μεδιολάνῳ, κατεγγυᾷ τὴν ἀδελφὴν τούτῳ Κωνσταντίαν, ἣν καὶ πρότερον αὐτῷ δώσειν ὑπέσχετο, τῆς πρὸς Μαξέντιον δυσμενείας κοινωνὸν ἔχειν βουλόμενος: “Having summoned Licinius to Milan, he gave him his sister Constantia in marriage, whom he had earlier promised to give him, wishing to have him as a partner in his hostility toward Maxentius” (*Zosimus, History*, II). If you desire another witness besides, we shall immediately provide the Anonymous Valesianus, whose words on this same marriage and alliance are these: “When Constantine had recovered Italy, he attached Licinius to himself by this alliance: Licinius took Constantia, Constantine’s sister, as his wife at Milan.”

Accordingly, Maximinus, whose secret alliance with Maxentius we have already noted, as soon as he learned that both emperors were occupied with the marriage ceremonies, led an army from Syria, as we have also related above, into Bithynia; he brought Byzantium and then Heraclea into submission. But Licinius came to meet him, having assembled as many troops as he could. When battle was imminent, an angel dictated to him, while he rested at night, a prayer which, once recited, would secure victory. Upon waking, he ordered notaries to write it down in full, as our author gives it, [Col. 0993A] and a copy to be distributed to every soldier. Made more eager by this, they offered the written prayer three times after the emperor before entering battle upon the Campus Serenus. Then, when Maximinus could not be induced to make peace, they attacked their enemies with such force that, as we have said, the latter were annihilated to the last man and Maximinus barely escaped by flight.

But at this point Tollius, as though stationed between the battle lines, holds us back. He boldly declares that this prayer, like Constantine’s vision of the cross in a dream, was nothing but a stratagem to inflame the soldiers more fiercely for battle. Yet the shameless rashness of this over-bold man is rightly and deservedly rebuked by Baudrius, a man of the same sect; for Tollius produced no reason for his empty conjecture and reckless assertion. Moreover, who does not know that dreams of this sort are recorded in Holy Scripture as divinely sent not only to the patriarch Joseph and other pious men, but even to pagans? It must nevertheless be acknowledged that other writers are profoundly silent concerning this prayer. But it should not therefore rashly be dismissed as deceit and stratagem; and certainly no one can deny that Licinius gained this signal victory over the most impious tyrant Maximinus only with the help of the divine power. Something more will be said below concerning these visions.

## ARTICLE III

On the edict which Licinius published for the restoration of peace to the Christian Church.

After defeating Maximinus in the manner we have seen, Licinius distributed a great part of Maximinus’ army, which had fled to him, crossed the Bosporus, and came to Nicomedia. There he first gave immortal thanks to God for the victory gained. Then, Caecilius says, he ordered Letters—that is, an edict—for the restoration of peace to the Christian Church to be promulgated. It was issued on the Ides of June, that is, on the thirteenth of that month, in the third consulship of both Licinius and Constantine—that is, in the year of Christ 313. It is reproduced by our author, as also by Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History*, X.5), who declares that he himself translated it from the Roman language into Greek. Eusebius, however, prefixed and transcribed a brief introduction omitted by Caecilius. For the latter began only from the words in which Constantine and Licinius state that they had met at Milan and, after carefully examining many matters—or, as in Eusebius, πάντα ὅσα, “all things whatsoever”—bearing upon the public good, had judged it necessary above all to establish that everyone should be free to follow whatever religion he wished: “So that the divinity,” says Caecilius (ch. 48), “in its heavenly seat may prove appeased and propitious toward us and all who are placed under our authority.” But everyone sees that these words are corrupt and yield no sense. They therefore seem to be corrected from Eusebius as follows: “that whatever divinity and heavenly power there is may be able to be propitious toward us . . .”: Ὅπως, ὅ τι ποτέ ἐστι θειότης καὶ οὐρανίου πράγματος ἡμῖν εὐμενὲς εἶναι δυνηθῇ.

[Col. 0994A] The emperor therefore orders that no one be denied the liberty to embrace whatever religion he chooses: “so that the supreme Divinity”—these are still the emperor’s words transcribed by Caecilius—“whose religion we obey with free minds, may show in all things its accustomed favour and benevolence.” The words enclosed in brackets are not found in Eusebius’ text. Eusebius, however, writes τὸ θεῖον, “the divine power”; Caecilius says *summa Divinitas*, “the supreme Divinity.” By these words Jupiter is not meant, as some suppose, but He whose divinity is supreme—that is, beyond doubt, the true and highest God. This may readily be inferred from the words cited above.

The emperor continues: “Therefore your devotedness should know that it has pleased us that, all conditions whatsoever being removed which seemed to have been set forth earlier in written instructions sent to your office concerning the name of the Christians,” they may observe their religion without any molestation.
