Some suspect that *dignationem* should be written here instead of *dicationem*, but wrongly. For *dicatio* is a title of honour given to governors and proconsuls, as is clear not only from Anulinus’ report in Augustine (*Letter* 88), but also from various laws of Constantine the Great promulgated at about this time. What Caecilius calls *conditiones* (“conditions”), Eusebius calls αἱρέσεις (*haireseis*). Valesius admits that this word is obscure, but thinks that it denotes Jews, Samaritans, Marcionites, and other heretics, who are permitted by this law to follow their own faith. Yet we have seen in one law of the Theodosian Code *navalem haeresim* and, in the next, *navalem functionem*. There *haeresis* denotes not a sect deviating from the true faith but a function and public duty. Whatever may be decided about the word *haeresis*, by which Eusebius rendered the Latin *conditiones*, in this edict itself *conditiones* seems to be used in its natural sense for provisions and agreements concerning Christians and others, previously contained in other rescripts sent to the governor, and removed and repealed by this edict.

Some further think that the following words, “now take care . . . contend,” are still corrupted, and that they should read: “which seemed altogether absurd and harsh,” or, according to others, “wholly perverse and alien from our clemency.” They seek to confirm this emendation because Eusebius wrote in Greek: Ἄ τινα πάνυ σκαιὰ, καὶ τῆς ἡμετέρας πρᾳότητος ἀλλότρια εἶναι ἐδόκει, “which seemed wholly perverse and alien from our mildness.” But he who translated this edict, as has been said, from Latin into Greek may have added certain matters for explanation and παραφραστικῶς, “paraphrastically.” It is therefore difficult to say what Caecilius’ true reading is, since here, as also shortly afterward, something seems to have been omitted through the copyist’s carelessness. Until another and better manuscript is found, we think it sufficient that the full sense of this edict may be known from Eusebius.

Nor is it easy to say what those writings previously sent to the governor, mentioned there, may have been. Some think they designate the law enacted by Maximinus after he had been defeated and put to flight by Licinius, which Eusebius reproduces in full. But that law, enacted after his flight, appears later than Licinius’ edict. Thus the emperor indicated another law, perhaps now lost. Some have further thought that the adverb *quantocius* (“as speedily as possible”), used there, is not good Latin. Others remind us that writers of the seventh century of the Church use it. But perhaps they have overlooked that the same word occurs in a law of the emperor Honorius, which scholars have noted was enacted in the year of Christ 395.

Moreover, some suspect that the words following that adverb are not only corrupt but difficult to understand: “Let them restore [them] as speedily as possible, even those who shall have received them as a gift; if they think anything [due] from our benevolence, let them apply to the Vicarius, so that provision may also be made for them through our clemency.” Some propose correcting *etiam* to *et jam* (“and now”), others to *et ita* (“and thus”); and *dono erunt* to *dono fuerunt* (“were given”) or *dono erant* (“were held as a gift”). Likewise, for *putaverint*, some propose *optaverint* (“shall wish”), while others wish to add *poscendum* (“to be requested”). Finally, some think *vicarius* means the things to be restored or, in jurists’ language, compensation; others mean some person acting for a judge or prefect and determining the reparation of loss. Eusebius, however, renders this more clearly in Greek:

> Εἴ τινες κατὰ δῶρον τυγχάνωσιν εἰληφότες τοὺς αὐτοὺς τόπους, ὅπως εἰ τοῖς αὐτοῖς χριστιανοῖς τὴν ταχίστην ἀποκαταστήσωσιν οὕτως, ἢ οἱ ἠγορακότες τοὺς αὐτοὺς τόπους, ἢ οἱ κατὰ δωρεὰν εἰληφότες αἰτῶσί τι παρὰ τῆς ἡμετέρας καλοκᾳγαθίας, προσέλθωσι τῷ ἐπὶ τόπων ἐπάρχῳ δικάζοντι, ὅπως καὶ αὐτῶν διὰ τῆς ἡμετέρας χρηστότητος πρόνοια γένηται.

“If any have received those same places as a gift, they are to restore them immediately to the Christians. If any who bought those places, or received them as gifts, wish to request something from our clemency, they shall approach the prefect administering justice in that province, so that, through our graciousness, provision may also be made for them” (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, X.5). If anyone nevertheless contends that the Greek Eusebius did not adequately understand the meaning of the Latin words, then, unless he proves this correctly, a correction of Caecilius’ text from another manuscript should rather be awaited than indulgence given to idle conjectures.

At the end of this enactment, the emperor, as Caecilius says, further commands that it be published by a proclamation of the governor and thus brought, under that authority, to everyone’s knowledge. Eusebius, however, makes no express mention of this proclamation, but only of the publication of the same law everywhere. By *programma* is meant a publicly displayed notice upon which that edict of Licinius or of the governor was to be written—the edict by which the governor was to publish the emperor’s commands conveyed in letters sent to him. Finally Caecilius adds: “When these letters had been posted, he also exhorted verbally”—Licinius, namely—“that the meeting-houses,” that is, as we have often said, the churches [Col. 0996A] of the Christians, “be restored to their former condition.” Whom did Licinius exhort but the governor to whom, as Caecilius had previously said, these letters were addressed? He therefore gave these letters into the hand of this governor, then residing at Nicomedia, or ordered them sent to him.

Moreover, our author intended to inform us there that this edict put an end to the most cruel persecution which Diocletian had stirred up against the Christians. He thus specifies the whole duration of it: “Thus, from the destruction of the church until its restoration, there were ten years and approximately four months.” What church is meant there, pray, except that of Nicomedia, which was destroyed at the beginning of Diocletian’s persecution and restored after Licinius’ edict? For, as we have seen, he begins the account of that persecution with the destruction of this church. From that point, therefore—from the seventh day of February 303, when this church was demolished and Diocletian began to persecute Christians—until Licinius’ edict, issued on 13 June 313, ten years, three months, and nineteen days are reckoned. But Caecilius preferred to say “approximately four months” and deemed it of less consequence to state the number of days elapsed beyond the third month.

## ARTICLE IV

How Licinius pursued Maximinus and compelled him to take his own life at Tarsus in Cilicia; and how, after gaining supreme power, he extirpated the whole stock of the former tyrants and all their children—first concerning Valerius.

After staying at Nicomedia for several days after issuing the edict discussed above, Licinius then set out with his army to pursue Maximinus. In the passes of Mount Taurus, as we have explained, Maximinus had fortified himself with strong ramparts and towers. But driven thence by Licinius, he finally fled to Tarsus. Nor was he safer there. For, besieged by the army of Licinius by land and sea, he was compelled to inflict upon himself the death discussed above.

Licinius, having gained supreme power, rooted out the remaining stock and progeny of the tyrants who had raged with such inhumanity against Christians. “For first,” says Caecilius, “he ordered Valerius to be killed—Valerius whom Maximinus, although enraged and even after his flight, when he saw that he himself must perish, had not dared to kill. . . .” This is precisely the reading in our manuscript and in the first edition of this book. Yet later critics argue among themselves with the greatest intensity about this Valerius. Some, believing that no Valerius existed then, suppose that our author’s text was corrupted by a copyist and that it ought to read *Valeriam quam* (“Valeria, whom”), not *Valerium quem* (“Valerius, whom”). They suppose this Valeria to be the wife of the emperor Galerius, who, after her husband’s death, refused the emperor Maximinus’ offered marriage, as we have said, and was therefore sent by him into exile, stripped of all property, companions, and servants, wandering here and there through the deserts of Syria. For, they say, it is as certain that Maximinus was angry with this Valeria as it is unknown at whom else he could have been angry.

If you object that Caecilius describes Valeria’s death later, they reply that he touches upon it there only briefly, but subsequently describes it far more fully and distinctly. In a not dissimilar manner, they say, he there mentions the death of Candidianus, of whom he nevertheless speaks later as still alive. Accordingly, many, moved by these arguments or because they did not know who Valerius was, have caused *Valeriam quam* to be written in Caecilius’ text without any hesitation.

[Col. 0997B] Others, on the contrary, rise up boldly and contend that the name Valerius must be retained and that nothing in Caecilius’ text should be changed. For they are persuaded that he is Valerius Valens, who on a Greek coin reproduced by Goltz is called ΑΥΤ. Κ. ΠΟΥ. ΟΥΑΛΕΡ. ΟΥΑΛΕΝC. CEB. E. A.: “Emperor Caesar Publius Valerius Valens Augustus, first year.” They also think there is no room for doubt that he is the very person of whom Aurelius Victor wrote in the *Epitome*: “Thereafter Licinius is made Augustus; in like manner Alexander is made emperor at Carthage; and in like manner Valens is created emperor. Their end was as follows.” Victor then immediately recounts the ends of Severus, Maximianus Galerius, Maximianus Herculius, Alexander, and Maxentius, and continues: “Valens is punished with death by Licinius.” Here, they say, Aurelius Victor joins the death of Valens, just as our Caecilius does, with the death of Maximinus. From this they infer that this Valens is the same as the one called Valerius Valens on the aforementioned coin of Goltz. His first name was Valerius, as one descended from the family of Diocletian, and he took Valens as his cognomen. Having laid down this foundation, they assert without hesitation that he was made emperor and Augustus when Maximinus was defeated and overthrown by Licinius in 313.

They further carefully note that this Valens Valerius is improperly confused with another Valens, whose coin is displayed by Mediobarbus, and with a third Valens whom Licinius created Caesar after being defeated by Constantine in the battle of Cibalae. The former Valens usurped tyranny while Galerius was emperor, and Ammianus Marcellinus calls him the Thessalonican. For these are his own words concerning Gallienus: “Though repeatedly and truly assailed by conspiracies of treason, he sometimes punished rather mildly the crimes which brought about the deaths of Aureolus, Postumus, Ingenuus, Valens surnamed the Thessalonican, and many others” (*Ammianus Marcellinus*, XXI.16). But the Valens represented on Goltz’s coin is not called Thessalonican. The latter Valens, moreover, is called only Caesar, not Augustus and emperor, by the Anonymous Valesianus and Zosimus; and shortly thereafter he was stripped of his rank and reduced to private status. For Zosimus’ text has the word ἀναιρεθῆναι, which signifies not only “to be killed” or “put to death,” but also “to be deposed” and “to be deprived of authority.” It remains, therefore, they say, that this Valens whom Aurelius Victor and our Caecilius mention is the one who, killed by Licinius’ order, is called Valerius Valens in Goltz’s cited coin. They do not allow it to be objected that no mention of him is ever made elsewhere. For likewise no mention is made of Julian, a tyrant under Diocletian, except in Libanius; nor of Perpenna Licinius, another tyrant, except on a single coin.

Yet this whole opinion rests on no other foundation than the authority of Aurelius Victor, who links the death of Valens with that of Maximinus, and on a single coin represented by Goltz, as has been said. But these considerations may perhaps appear of no great weight to others [Col. 0998B], who will observe that Aurelius Victor himself there confounds several matters, and recounts together and conjointly the deaths of this Valens and of other emperors, as we have said, in such a way as to follow no chronological order whatsoever. For he places Galerius before Herculius, although Galerius is said to have died in 311 and Herculius in 310. Moreover, although he joins the death of Maximinus with that of Valens, he nevertheless says nothing there of how much time intervened between the two. Nor is it indicated on Goltz’s coin at what time that Valerius Valens reigned or departed this life. Finally, Cecilius plainly declares that the Valerius in question was descended from the stock of those emperors and tyrants who, during Licinius’ reign, persecuted Christians. Yet no one has hitherto shown us that that Valerius Valens was begotten by one of them. Nor should you say that the name Valerius was peculiar to those who derived their origin from Diocletian’s family. For you must still demonstrate either that this name was never given to any except men of that lineage, or that Valerius Valens was truly descended from Diocletian’s blood. The foundations of this opinion therefore totter, and are not established by sufficiently firm grounds of reasoning for one to conclude from them that Valerius Valens was the man whom Licinius ordered to be put to death before the battle of Cibalae.

Wherefore, if the name Valerius was actually written in the text of our Cecilius, as it appears to have been, and neither Cecilius himself nor a copyist erred in writing his book, [Col. 0998D] it must be beyond doubt that this man derived his origin from one of those persecutors of the Christian Church whom we have hitherto mentioned. But if you ask us from which of them he sprang, and whether he was in truth called Valerius Valens, we shall frankly answer that this is unknown to us; and that he should be counted among those of whom, as the defenders of the foregoing opinion admit, mention occurs only once in the writing of some author or upon some coin. We can therefore determine nothing certain concerning him unless the unshaken authority of Cecilius is first established.

Moreover, Licinius ordered not only this Valerius but also Candidianus, Prisca and Valeria—Diocletian’s wife and daughter, respectively—and besides these [Col. 0999A] Maximinus’ wife, his eight-year-old son and seven-year-old daughter, and finally Severianus, the son of Severus, to be killed. But we have discussed all these in their proper place.

## CHAPTER XV

On the emperors Constantius Chlorus and Constantine the Great.

## ARTICLE I

How outstanding were the virtues of Constantius Chlorus; when he was made Caesar and son-in-law of Maximian Herculius; whether and how, during the persecution, he kept Christians unharmed in Gaul while permitting the churches to be demolished; why he became the first emperor although despised by Galerius; how he handed the empire over to Constantine upon his return to him; and where he died.

[Col. 0999B] We have hitherto deferred our discussion of the emperor Constantius Chlorus, lest what must be said of him and of his son Constantine the Great should be too widely separated from one another. But after our Cecilius has exposed the vices of Diocletian, Herculius, and Galerius, he continues in the same place (chap. 8) as follows:

> I pass over Constantius, since he was unlike the other tyrants and persecutors of the Church, and worthy to hold the world alone, or to rule the entire globe.

The briefer this statement, certainly, the greater is its commendation of so great a man, and indeed its highest praise. Although our Cecilius did not there pass him over wholly without reason for this cause, he nevertheless interspersed many matters concerning him as occasion subsequently arose; these must be examined and elucidated by us. Thus, our author elsewhere [Col. 0999C] (chap. 20) calls him “a man mild by nature.” Eutropius, whose testimony in this matter surely cannot be of doubtful trustworthiness, calls him “an excellent man, of most eminent civility,” beloved by the Gauls and even revered by them; a man who sought not the advantages of the treasury, but promoted the wealth of provincials and private persons. Later Cecilius calls him the son-in-law of Maximian Herculius, and rightly so. For when Diocletian created him Caesar in the year 292, as we noted above, he was then compelled, as Eutropius writes, to repudiate his former wife and marry Theodora, Herculius’ stepdaughter.

Our author further relates (Cecilius, chap. 15) that Diocletian, as soon as he had begun to rage against the Christians with the monstrous cruelty already described, sent letters to the same Constantius, commanding him to do what he himself did. But having received these letters, Cecilius says, “lest he should seem to dissent from the commands of his superiors, he permitted the meeting-houses—that is, the walls of the churches, which could be rebuilt—to be demolished; but he kept unharmed the true temple of God, which is in men,” that is, in Christians. In this passage of our author the reading is indeed *majorum* (“of his elders/superiors”); but we have already observed that perhaps *majoris* should be read—that is, of Diocletian, who had made him Caesar and was therefore his superior. We have also there considered upon what grounds our author could say that Constantius, lest he should seem to dissent from the commands of his superiors, permitted the walls of Christian meeting-houses or churches to be destroyed, [Col. 1000A] and yet was not thereby wholly opposed to Eusebius.

We likewise endeavoured, to the best of our ability, in the same place to explain in what sense he immediately added: “Therefore the whole earth was harassed, except Gaul,” over which, of course, Constantius ruled. For we made plain that Eusebius seems in some places to subscribe to this opinion of our author and elsewhere to oppose it. But with the greatest diligence we could employ, we investigated what Eusebius’ true mind and judgment were, and what the genuine sense of his words was. If we have attained our aim, we have clearly shown, unless we are mistaken, that he cannot justly be accused of a wholly absurd contradiction; and that he can be reconciled both with himself and with our Cecilius, so that there is no discord or disagreement between them, but perfect agreement and mutual harmony. Let us now proceed, if you please, to other matters.

After Diocletian and Herculius had abdicated the imperial power, as Cecilius relates (chap. 20), and as we have elsewhere seen, Constantius obtained the first rank of emperor and Galerius the second; or then, as Eusebius says (*Life of Constantine*, II.18), Constantius “was proclaimed first Augustus and emperor” (*πρῶτος Αὔγουστος καὶ σεβαστὸς ἀνηγορεύετο*). Certainly Eutropius and Zosimus name him first, before his colleague Galerius. Yet Galerius despised him because of his innate gentleness and the weakness of his bodily health at that time; or, to use Cecilius’ words, because “he was hindered by bodily infirmity.” Galerius therefore entertained a strong hope that he would soon [Col. 1000C] die, or at least that he would deprive him of the empire.

But not long afterwards—and perhaps sooner than Galerius himself thought—he received letters from Constantius, now ill, as we have said, requesting that his son Constantine be sent back to him. Galerius did not dare longer refuse him to his father, who had repeatedly made this request. He pretended to permit Constantine to return to his father, but in fact wished to keep him back. Constantine nevertheless secretly escaped from Galerius’ palace, as we have said, and hastened to Constantius with incredible speed. He arrived, Cecilius says, “when he was already failing; and Constantius, having commended him to the soldiers, handed over the empire through his hands, and thus found in his bed the rest from life which he desired.”

Eusebius similarly relates that Constantius, lying in the palace and royal bedchamber under a fatal illness, sprang from it in order to embrace with both arms his son, whose arrival he had not expected. Having then arranged everything, he handed him the administration of the empire and departed from this life by a happy death. The same is asserted no less clearly by the anonymous author of the panegyric delivered before Constantine himself and Maximian.

Eutropius and Aurelius Victor, however, to whom Zosimus and the anonymous Valesian writer appear to lend support, expressly affirm that Constantine, after his father’s death, was created emperor by the Praetorians and by the efforts of all [Col. 1001A] who were present. But Julian the Apostate, in his oration addressed to Constantius, the son of that same Constantine the Great, states no less plainly that he attained the highest dignity of the empire both by his father’s judgment and by the vote of all the armies. From this, undoubtedly, a reconciliation of the foregoing opinions may readily be made. For if Constantine’s election by his dying father was freely and spontaneously confirmed by the army and all the rest, what prevents one from saying that he was made emperor by them all? Nor should you suppose that we have invented this gratuitously. For Eumenius addresses Constantine himself in a public panegyric thus:

> Clearly, you were chosen emperor by your father’s decision.

Then shortly afterward:

> As soon as he had been taken from the earth, the whole army agreed upon you; the minds and eyes of all marked you out. And although you had referred the supreme matter of the state to the senior emperors, they nevertheless anticipated their judgment by their zeal—a judgment which those emperors soon afterward approved. The soldiers, serving the public welfare rather than your own wishes, cast the purple upon you in tears as soon as your first appearance gave them access to you.

If anyone should inquire more curiously where Constantius laid down his life, we reply that Cecilius, Eusebius, and others have passed it over in silence. But Aurelius Victor recorded that he died in Britain. Eutropius says: “At Eboracum, a city of Britain.” The anonymous Valesian writer relates that Constantine “came to his father Constantius at Bononia, which the Gauls formerly called Gesoriacum,” and that Constantius died in Britain. Gesoriacum is frequently mentioned by ancient writers—Suetonius, Pliny, Mela, Eumenius, and others. But there are diverse opinions as to which city it was. Some think it was Calais; others, more plausibly, Bononia in Picardy. Consult the observations and notes of various scholars on these authors.

The opinion of the anonymous Valesian writer just cited is confirmed by Eumenius’ words to Constantine himself: [Col. 1001C] “At the very moment when your father was crossing over to Britain, and the fleet was already setting sail, your unexpected arrival shone upon him.” Must it not therefore be said, in order to reconcile Eutropius with the opinion of the others, that Constantius, revived by his son’s sudden and unexpected arrival, recovered somewhat from his illness, embarked with him on the ship, and reached Eboracum, where he died on 15 July in the year 306? To this may be added that Eumenius shortly afterward addresses Britain in these words: “O fortunate Britain, now more blessed than all lands, which first beheld Constantine as Caesar.” But if Britain first beheld him as Caesar, then undoubtedly he was made Caesar there by his dying father. For he is reported to have died in the place where he named him Caesar.

## ARTICLE II

On the parents, birthplace, exceptional bodily and mental gifts of Constantine the Great; where he was educated; the great envy felt toward him by others, especially Galerius; and the plots by which they sought his ruin.

What we discussed in the preceding article and earlier sufficiently demonstrates to all [Col. 1002A] that Constantine was the son of Constantius Chlorus, as our Cecilius records. But since Cecilius is silent as to the mother from whom and the place where he was born, he has given us—who follow in his footsteps—no occasion to investigate the matter more carefully. It will therefore suffice to note that the opinion which seems more certain and has now prevailed is that Constantine was born of Helena, his mother, as the anonymous Valesian writer says, in the town of Naissus.

Our Cecilius first speaks of him in the dialogue between Diocletian and Galerius, already mentioned by us, in which they debated at Nicomedia concerning the appointment of new Caesars. There he speaks of him in these exact words:

> Constantius had a son, Constantine, a most upright young man and most worthy of that summit of empire; he was loved by the soldiers for his distinguished and handsome bodily appearance, military diligence, honourable character, and singular affability, and desired by private persons.

So many writers, ancient and recent alike, besides Eusebius the eyewitness (*Life of Constantine*, I.12), have celebrated these outstanding virtues and remarkable gifts of Constantine’s mind and body with such emulation that there is plainly no need to recount them more fully. Nor should you think they have been exaggerated by those writers. You will find the same qualities publicly recorded by others: namely, by the anonymous author of the panegyric already cited, Eutropius, Aurelius Victor, and Praxagoras in Photius. No suspicion of flattery can attach to them all.

Before the aforesaid conference between Diocletian and Galerius in 304, Constantine, according to our author, [Col. 1002C] “had long before been made tribune of the first rank by Diocletian.” We have already spoken of these tribunes. Yet from this and other words of our Cecilius it may be inferred that Constantine, though still a young man, had long been admitted to Diocletian’s court, having been sent thither by his father for education, as Praxagoras and Zonaras testify. If we believe the anonymous Valesian writer: “As a hostage under Diocletian and Galerius, he fought bravely under them in Asia.” Indeed, Galerius, Aurelius Victor says, retained him hostage in the city of Rome under the pretext of religion. Praxagoras, whom we cited a little earlier, states no less plainly that Constantine was sent by his father, not to Rome but to Nicomedia (*εἰς Νικομέδιαν*), to the emperor Diocletian; there, if we believe Cecilius, he was present at the aforementioned conference of Galerius and Diocletian. May it not be inferred that, while still young, Constantine accompanied these emperors jointly or separately in the places where they stayed or to which they occasionally went? But what need is there of conjectures? Did not Eusebius expressly say that, while still a youth and adorned with youthful down, he stood, like Moses, in the very residences of the tyrants, among whom he was held in the highest honour?

But their esteem was undoubtedly far from sincere. For Eusebius further says that, shaken by envy and fear, they sought, whenever an opportunity offered, not only to harass him with insults, but also laid snares for him once and again; through God’s providence he discovered and escaped them. Galerius envied him much more intensely. Therefore, as the anonymous Valesian writer relates, he exposed him to many dangers; or, as we have already observed our author to report, he likewise plotted against him, though secretly and covertly, lest he provoke against himself civil arms and the hatred of the soldiers, by whom Constantine, as was said shortly before, was loved. If anyone wishes to know what these plots were, let him first hear our Cecilius, who affirms that Constantine was exposed to wild beasts under the pretext of sport and exercise. He committed to memory no further details concerning these beasts. But Praxagoras, quoted by Photius, relates that Galerius induced Constantine to fight a savage lion, which he killed—not, Zonaras says, without divine assistance. Nor did Galerius expose him only to this but to other no less [Col. 1003B] fearful dangers of combat. But if you do not altogether trust us, hear, I pray, the anonymous Valesian writer recounting this in these exact words:

> When still a young cavalryman in service against the Sarmatians, he seized a fierce barbarian by his hair, pulled tight, and brought him captive to the feet of the emperor Galerius. Then, sent by Galerius, he entered a marsh on horseback and made a path for the others against the Sarmatians; having slain many of them, he brought Galerius the victory.

## ARTICLE III

Whether Constantine the Great was present at the conference of Diocletian and Galerius, as Cecilius relates; whether he learned that Caesars were to be appointed; and whether he knew that he himself was to be disgracefully rejected from this appointment.

So far were the splendid deeds of Constantine the Great which we have recounted from extinguishing the envy of Maximian Galerius that they inflamed it much more. For he completely dissuaded Diocletian, when discussing with him the abdication of imperial power and the appointment of new Caesars, from proclaiming Constantine himself Caesar. At that time he could not conceal the intensity of his malevolence and envy. For although Constantine is said by our Cecilius to have been present at the oft-mentioned dialogue of Diocletian and Galerius, although Diocletian himself maintained that he was lovable, more merciful, better in every respect, and worthy of empire, Galerius nevertheless openly and plainly resisted Diocletian, and with no small impudence forbade him [Col. 1003D] to make Constantine Caesar. Indeed, contrary to the expectation of all who desired that this most distinguished dignity be conferred upon Constantine, he tried to subject him to the utmost humiliation. For after Constantine had followed Galerius and Diocletian for three miles from the city of Nicomedia, as we have said, and had mounted the elevated tribunal with them, Galerius most indignantly repulsed him; and after rejecting him, Diocletian proclaimed Severus and Maximinus Caesars. Thus our Cecilius describes the appointment of the Caesars and Constantine’s rejection, unprecedented up to that time.

Yet this account presents difficulties by no means slight, which must now be explained more fully. In what sense could Cecilius say of Constantine, “He was then present” (Cecilius, chap. 18), when Diocletian conferred with Galerius? Was he in the emperor’s bedchamber, as some suppose, or in his palace, as others have thought? Certainly not in the palace, for Cecilius’ words appear to indicate that he was nearer at hand. Nor in the bedchamber, since Constantine could have perceived from their words, or at least from their gestures and signs, what they discussed with such agitation of mind. But if he had any inkling that he was to be rejected from the dignity of Caesar, how did he accompany them to the place where he knew that he would endure so great and public an injury? Indeed, if he had so much as the slightest suspicion, how did he dare rashly expose himself to such disgrace? Should we not rather believe the anonymous Valesian writer, who transmitted in writing that Severus and Maximinus were then made Caesars, Constantine knowing nothing of the kind?

Will it suffice, in order to untie the knot of this difficulty, to say that he was present not in Diocletian’s bedchamber or palace but in some separate place belonging to him, or in the city of Nicomedia? For Cecilius could in this sense contrast Constantine with Severus, who was very far away. But if he is truly contrasted with Severus, he could certainly be called present to Diocletian and Galerius—that is, much nearer to them than Severus, but sufficiently distant not to hear them speaking. Yet others will object that Cecilius’ expression would be wholly improper. Moreover, they will say, Cecilius quite plainly and manifestly declares [Col. 1004C] that Galerius then showed Diocletian, and as it were pointed out with his finger, Maximinus Daia, soon to be made Caesar after Constantine had been rejected. Therefore Maximinus stood in Diocletian’s very bedchamber, before the eyes of Diocletian and Galerius. But if he was in their bedchamber, Constantine—of whom Cecilius plainly said, “He was then present”—was undoubtedly not far away.

But suppose, if you will, that Constantine was at a very great distance both from Maximinus and from Diocletian and Galerius. You will immediately encounter another difficulty. For while Diocletian and Galerius were fiercely disputing, Constantine, as Cecilius unhesitatingly affirms, was present either in the palace or at least in the city of Nicomedia. When their conference had ended—though it could have been heard by at least some persons—Constantine followed them for three miles to the place where he was to be rejected from the dignity of Caesar. How, I ask, could it have happened that he, beloved by all, was not warned by anyone after the conference of the two emperors and throughout this whole journey that new Caesars were to be appointed, nor suspected that he himself was to be excluded from their number? Could he not most readily infer it from the emperors’ silence alone concerning that appointment? Why then did he follow them and voluntarily, rashly expose himself to so degrading a rejection? Will you answer that he possessed so brave and great a spirit that he prudently concealed this rejection and insult? But let others weigh what value and force this or any other answer has, and whether it suffices to maintain, without any guarantor or defender—and indeed against the plain testimony of the anonymous Valesian writer—Cecilius’ account of Constantine’s presence.

Yet someone will still press the point and finally object to us that the anonymous Valesian writer erred, but our author did not. This must, however, be proved by some argument at least. Moreover, Cecilius’ view involves no small obscurity and is difficult to explain, since, as we have said, it appears inconsistent with and opposed to itself. Perhaps other, more acute critics will untie all these knots; we shall await their judgment upon the entire controversy. They will also do us a great favour if they point out similar modes of expression, shrouded in equal obscurity, in the genuine books of Firmianus Lactantius.

## ARTICLE IV

[Col. 1005B] How Constantine returned, against Galerius’ will, to his father Constantius, now on the point of death; and whether he was made Caesar and emperor by him or by others.

Constantius, afflicted by a very severe and fatal illness, wrote many letters, as we have already observed, to Maximian Galerius, requesting that his son Constantine be sent back to him. But even by repeated letters and prayers he could scarcely ever obtain this from Galerius. For, as Cecilius says, “when he could no longer deny [it] after a long time”—a manuscript reads *diu necare non posset*, “could not kill [him] for a long time”—“he gave him the seal as the day was already declining.” All acknowledge that these words of our author are corrupt; and some suspect that after the adverb *saepius* (“often”) one should add *rogatus* (“having been asked”), *sollicitatus* (“having been urged”), or *repetenti* (“to one repeatedly requesting”), and that *diutius* should be read for *diu*. But who would dare assert what the true reading is without another, better manuscript? Cecilius’ sense seems to be that, when Galerius could no longer continue refusing Constantius, repeatedly requesting his son, he gave Constantine the seal, of which we spoke above, [Col. 1005C] and permission to return to his father on the following day. Yet he still wished to detain him, or at least to write to the emperor Severus that he should detain him on the journey; but his plans were vain, and his hope failed him.

For Constantine, having received the seal, departed immediately after supper and, as our author says, “having removed all the public horses from many posting-stations, sped away.” Aurelius Victor explains and confirms this more clearly in these words:

> Constantine, contriving an escape, killed the public draft animals wherever he travelled in order to frustrate his pursuers, and reached Britain.

Likewise the anonymous Valesian writer says:

> With the utmost haste, and after cutting the hamstrings of the post-horses behind him, he crossed the Alps and came to his father Constantius.

Zosimus writes in Greek in a not dissimilar way: “Whenever he reached a station, he mutilated and rendered useless the post-horses maintained by the state” (*Τοὺς ἐν τοῖς σταθμοῖς ἵππους, οὓς τὸ δημόσιον ἔτρεφεν, ἅμα τῷ φθάσαι τὸν σταθμὸν, κολοβῶν καὶ ἀχρείους ἐῶν*); and so he came to his father, appearing, Eumenius says, to have flown there not by public transport but by some divine speed.

[Col. 1006A] Thus he came to his father Constantius, whose strength was nearly spent. As he was dying, Constantius commended him to the soldiers, as Cecilius says (chap. 24), and handed the empire over to him through his hands. After Constantius’ “death,” Aurelius Victor says, “with the efforts of all who were present, but especially Erocus, king of the Alemanni, who had accompanied Constantius as an auxiliary,” Constantine “assumed the imperial power.” Learned writers dispute whether he was then proclaimed merely Caesar or emperor. Eusebius, indeed, unhesitatingly affirms that he was left by his father as successor in the empire and adds: “Constantine, from the very beginning, was greeted by the soldiers as a most complete sovereign and Augustus” (*Κωνσταντῖνος εὐθὺς ἀρχόμενος, βασιλεὺς τελειώτατος καὶ σεβαστός*; Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, IX.14). Elsewhere Eusebius writes that his father left him “the inheritance of the empire” (*τὸν κλῆρον τῆς βασιλείας*). Julian the Apostate states that the empire was given him after his father’s death by the vote of all the armies.

The anonymous Valesian writer, Zosimus, and Eumenius, however, maintain that he was made Caesar. To this may be added the anonymous author of the panegyric, who addresses Maximian Herculius thus:

> O Maximian, how divine was your judgment, when you wished this Constantine to be your grandson by legal adoption, your son in rank of majesty, and also your son-in-law.

That is, when he gave him his daughter Fausta in marriage, as will be said below. But if he was then his son in rank of majesty, it follows that he was at that time merely Caesar. For Caesars, as we have already observed, were called sons of the Augusti, just as emperors were called their brothers. Moreover, the same author had said shortly before that on the day of this marriage the name of emperor was added to Constantine Caesar.

Yet the orator himself appears to settle this dispute in the words with which he addresses Constantine:

> Such is your great maturity that, although your father left you the empire, you were nevertheless content with the appellation of Caesar and preferred to wait, until the same man who declared your father Constantius Augustus should likewise declare you Augustus.

May it not rightly be inferred from this that Constantine the Great’s moderation and modesty were such that, although he had been made Augustus and emperor by his father and the whole army, he nevertheless chose at that time, content with the name of Caesar, not to be called Augustus and emperor? For we read earlier that the same orator said:

> Constantine, through your father-in-law, the title of emperor was added to you.

Moreover, when his laurelled portrait was conveyed to Galerius in the customary manner, as we have said, Galerius received it unwillingly and named Constantine not emperor, as he had been made, but, after sending the purple, Caesar in the fourth rank—that is, after Galerius himself, Severus, and Maximinus. It is therefore unsurprising that in the provinces governed by these men Constantine was given only the name of Caesar, by which he is called on various coins shortly to be reproduced by our learned Anselm Banduri.

## ARTICLE V

[Col. 1007A]

How greatly Constantine favoured Christians; why Maximian Herculius came to him, betrothed and married to him his younger daughter; why he returned to him; what plots he prepared against him while Constantine was about to fight the barbarians; how, after capturing Massilia, Constantine granted him pardon; how Herculius afterward vainly attempted to kill him in his bed; and what remarkable victory Constantine gained over Maxentius after seeing the miraculous sign of Christ’s cross.

Constantine the Great, Cecilius says (chap. 24), upon assuming imperial power, “did nothing before restoring Christians to their worship and to their God. This was his first enactment: the restoration of the holy religion.” Thus it reads in the Colbert manuscript, where some suspect that several words are corrupt and strive to amend them by conjecture. But what if they are the words of the author himself, who does not speak with the greatest elegance? Should they not first prove that they did not proceed from him before perhaps wasting effort in correcting them? Whatever the case, his meaning appears to be this: from the very beginning of his rule Constantine the Great restored the Christian religion and, by issuing a law, restored Christians to the worship of their true God. Nor is it surprising that he then imitated his father, who, as we have seen, showed Christians very great and earnest favour. This could indeed be demonstrated most clearly by a certain discourse of Lactantius, inserted among his genuine works, in which he congratulates Constantine on this account. But, as we have shown in its proper place, it is not yet sufficiently established whether that discourse was ever written by Lactantius himself.

Whatever judgment may be made concerning it, after the emperor Severus had been killed not long afterward, as has been noted, Maximian Herculius came into Gaul to Constantine. To draw him to his own party against Galerius, he betrothed to him his younger daughter Fausta, as we have also explained, and afterward gave her to him in marriage. At the celebration of this marriage the panegyric was delivered by the anonymous author; printed together with others, it is in everyone’s hands.

After this Maximian Herculius departed for Rome, where, as we have already observed, he wrongly attempted to deprive his son Maxentius of the imperial power. When he had been driven thence because of that most shameful crime, [Col. 1007D] he returned to Constantine, who was then staying in Gaul. With the same treachery by which he had sought to deceive his son, he tried to deceive his son-in-law. To ensnare him more easily, he laid aside the royal robe. Constantine, no longer doubting the sincerity of his intentions, was persuaded by him that the Franks could be defeated with a few soldiers. But as soon as Constantine had entered the territory of these barbarians with forces smaller than was fitting, Herculius, as we have said, resumed the purple, corrupted the troops left behind by money plundered from Constantine’s treasury, and fled to Massilia.

Some think that this war which the Franks waged with Constantine is none other than that mentioned somewhere by Eusebius (*Life of Constantine*, I.25). Others deny it and maintain that it was the war which Constantine finished with them a little before he conquered Maxentius. However that may be, no one will doubt that this war is described by Eumenius, who moreover confirms there what our Cecilius relates concerning the astonishing speed with which Constantine returned against Herculius and, after taking Massilia, spared his life, though first stripping him of his royal dress. Since we have already explained these matters, they need not now be repeated. We have also made clear how that criminal Herculius, not rendered better thereby, entered upon another plot, in concert with his daughter Fausta, then Constantine’s wife, and wrongly attempted to kill in his bed the man to whom he was bound by such great benefits. When Fausta disclosed these plots to Constantine, Herculius paid the penalty of his extreme treachery by the most shameful manner of death, as we have already seen.

Cecilius then relates that Galerius, abolishing the title of Caesar, called Maxentius and Constantine sons of the Augusti and also emperors. But we have examined this elsewhere as well, together with his subsequent statement that Maximinus was deterred by Constantine’s letters from the new persecution which he had stirred up against Christians. Finally, we have recounted how Constantine, after betrothing his sister Constantia to Licinius, defeated and routed Maxentius, who had made war upon him, under the leading sign of Christ’s cross, which had appeared to Constantine by divine agency. There we made clear what that miraculous sign of the Lord’s cross was, whatever its precise nature, [Col. 1008C] and with how vain and fruitless an effort recent heterodox writers have tried to attack this divine vision of Constantine the Great. We also showed no less clearly that Tollius, who rashly declared it should be classed among military stratagems, was deservedly rebuked by Baudrius, although Baudrius was a man of the same sect.

But that reckless writer again attacks his critic in another book. For he objects, not without sharp but wholly ill-timed mockery, that quite a few kings—and above all a certain king of Portugal and Antigonus, successor of Alexander the Great—used a similar stratagem. The former boasted that he had seen the same thing as Constantine the Great. Antigonus, however, pretended that he had seen a pentagon, an image of salvation, upon which was likewise written [Col. 1008D]: “In this sign you will conquer.” In this manner Tollius argues not only against the sign of the cross seen by Constantine himself, but also against the prayers dictated to the emperor Licinius by an angel, as we have seen above. Moreover, Tollius himself boldly proclaims that he judges historical matters far more certainly and accurately than Baudrius.

But who would not marvel at the absurd and insipid argument of this new critic, who so foolishly parades his learning? The visions of the king of Portugal and of Antigonus, he says, were fabricated and false, mere military stratagems; therefore those of Constantine the Great and Licinius were likewise so. What sound-minded person ever argued thus? Indeed, if such reasoning were permissible, another might argue in the same way: Pharaoh’s magicians performed by magical arts the same miracles as Moses; therefore Moses’ miracles are false and wrought by magical arts. [Col. 1009A] Yet no one, unless wholly irrational, would reason thus. For who does not know that one narrative may be true, even though another wholly similar to it has been transmitted in writing as false? Can one man’s lie undermine truth handed down by another? But we have demonstrated above, with the clearest evidence, that Constantine the Great’s vision was genuine. Therefore Tollius’s folly deserved rather to be scorned than seriously refuted, unless it were to be feared that it might deceive some unbeliever, or that he might suppose we had passed it over because it could not be answered.

## ARTICLE VI

[Col. 1009B] On Constantine’s triumphal entry into the city of Rome; the title of highest rank decreed to him by the Roman senate; how long he afterward remained in Rome; where he gave his sister Constantia in marriage to Licinius; and the peace and tranquillity restored to the Christian Church by both.

After his victory over Maxentius, won not without a great miracle, Constantine was received at Rome amid the utmost rejoicing of the senate and Roman people. An anonymous author of a panegyric delivered to Constantine thus described his glorious entry into the City—or rather, his triumph:

> “The very buildings, as I hear, seemed to be shaken, and the height of the roofs appeared to rise, wherever your Divinity was borne along in the slow movement of the chariot. [Col. 1009C] So great was the crowd of people, so dense the press of senators, that they both advanced and held you back. Those who could see you more closely were happy; those farther away called out your name; those whom you had passed regretted the place they occupied. Everywhere, some withdrew, others followed; an innumerable multitude contended, surged with varied impulse, and declared that after the disaster of six years so much spirit still remained to the Roman people. Some even dared to beg you to stop, and to complain that you had reached the palace so quickly; and when you had entered, they not only followed you with their eyes, but almost burst through the sacred threshold itself. Then, crowding about on every side, they waited, watched, wished, and hoped for the moment when you would come out, so that they who had been freed from siege might be seen besieging him by whom they had been freed.”

Nazarius likewise says:

> “Since the founding of the City, no day has dawned upon the Roman Empire on which rejoicing was, or ought to have been, so unrestrained and so remarkable; no triumphs were ever so joyful as those which the antiquity of the annals has consecrated in writing.”

He says more there about that same triumphal entry, as does Eusebius; but it would take too long to transcribe it, and it can very easily be read in their books.

Nor did the Roman senate think it enough to have loaded Constantine with such great honors; it also decreed to him, on account of his valor, the title of highest rank, as Caecilius calls it. But there is no single opinion as to the meaning of these words. Some think that they designate the name and title *Maximus*, which was then decreed to Constantine for his valor. For, they say, [Col. 1010A] Constantine is there called *Maximus*, as he was afterward on coins and public inscriptions. Moreover, several other emperors assumed this title for themselves. Yet because it was also a title of Jupiter, some conjecture that Caecilius’s text should read *numinis* (“of divinity”), not *nominis* (“of rank” or “of name”). But when did the Roman senate honor its emperors by any public decree with this title, whether of first or second divinity? Did this conjecture not require at least some proof?

Others therefore think that Caecilius’s words have no other meaning than that the Roman senate gave Constantine the title of highest rank—that is, the title of Emperor—so that he should thereafter take precedence over Maximinus, who had been made Caesar long before him. In confirmation of this view may be cited Eusebius’s report that Maximinus had reached such a pitch of arrogance that he claimed for himself the first place among the emperors in their titles. But the senate judged that this was to be assigned to Constantine’s valor. Furthermore, our Caecilius declares that this was precisely the title of rank which Maximinus claimed for himself, doubtless alone and in preference to the other emperors. Yet he certainly assumed the title of first emperor because he had, as we have said, been made Caesar before them all. Nor should one say that, when that decree of the Roman senate was announced to Maximinus, he was so inflamed with grief that, openly professing hostility and uttering, as Caecilius says, insults mingled with jesting against “the greatest emperor,” he called him “greatest” in bitter mockery, [Col. 1010C] thereby insulting the Roman senate which had decreed to Constantine, for his valor, the title of highest rank, or of first emperor. For Caecilius seems beyond doubt to have called him *Maximus* in his own words, not in those of the senate, because by his outstanding virtues Constantine surpassed not only Maximinus but all others as well.

After this, that most excellent man settled affairs in the city of Rome, as our Caecilius relates, with whom Zosimus, Eusebius, and others agree. If you wish to know how long he remained at Rome in order to settle them, please listen to Nazarius: “Whatever evils the deadly rule of Maxentius had inflicted during the whole six-year period, the care of scarcely two months healed.” Constantine therefore stayed at Rome for about two months, namely until 28 December of the year 312, as the more learned chronographers have noted. [Col. 1010D] Nor do two laws promulgated by Constantine at Rome on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February conflict with this opinion. For those laws add *P. P.*, that is, “posted” or “published in the city of Rome.” But they could have been posted there after Constantine had already departed. Indeed, our Caecilius (chap. 45) immediately adds these exact words: “In the following winter he hastened to Milan.”

There he joined in marriage to Licinius his sister Constantia, whom he had promised to Licinius. Zosimus writes that Constantine, having summoned Licinius to Milan, gave him his sister Constantia, whom he had previously promised to give him. If you want another witness, here is the Anonymous Valesianus, whose words are these:

> “After Maxentius had been overthrown and Constantine had recovered Italy, he caused Licinius to be joined to himself by this alliance: Licinius married Constantia, Constantine’s sister, at Milan.”

But we have discussed this marriage above.

All these things, and no more concerning Constantine the Great, our Caecilius committed to memory. Yet in continuing his discussion there, he makes plain and evident to all, as we have shown, how Licinius afterward destroyed Maximinus and all the others descended from the stock of tyrants and most cruel persecutors of the Church, so that no branch or root of them remained alive. But at the beginning of this book he openly and expressly proclaims that the emperors—or, as he calls them, the princes—namely Constantine [Col. 1011B] [Col. 1012A] the Great and Licinius, were raised up by God, greatest and best, to annul the bloody edicts of the tyrants and most savage persecutors of the Christian Church, and to grant Christians throughout the world subject to their empire the supreme peace and tranquillity so long desired. Then not only were their impious edicts against Christians extinguished, but also the magnificent and ridiculous titles of *Jovians* and *Herculians*, as our author himself calls them, which Diocletian and Maximian Herculius, as noted above, are said arrogantly to have assumed. Finally, Caecilius himself indicates that nothing is more earnestly desired by him than that the Churches then flourishing should preserve forever the peace granted them by Licinius and Constantine the Great.

[Col. 1011]

# DOGMATIC INVESTIGATIONS CONCERNING LACTANTIUS, OR CONCERNING HIS METHOD OF THINKING AND ARGUMENTATION IN MATTERS OF RELIGION

# CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 1011C]

On religion considered in general.

## ARTICLE I

On the derivation of the terms *religion* and *superstition*, and whether Cicero gave the true etymology of each term.

Before discussing matters that pertain specifically to the Christian religion, we must examine what Lactantius committed to writing concerning religion itself, taken generally. To begin with the name itself: he thinks it derives not from *relegere* (“to reread” or “retrace”), as Cicero thought, but from *religare* (“to bind”). For he argues against the Latin orator concerning its etymology as follows:

> “Bound by the bond of piety, we are bound to God; whence religion itself received its name—not, as Cicero interpreted it, from *relegere*. In the second book of *On the Nature of the Gods* he says thus: For not philosophers alone, but our ancestors also, distinguished superstition from religion. For those who spent whole days praying and sacrificing so that their children might survive them were called superstitious. But those who reconsidered and, as it were, carefully reviewed all things pertaining to the worship of the gods were called religious, from *relegere*, just as *elegantes* comes from *eligere*, and *diligentes* from *diligere*. For in all these words there is the same force of *legere* as in *religiosus*. Thus it came about that *superstitiosus* became the name of a fault, and *religiosus* the name of praise.” (Lactantius, *Institutions*, IV.8)

These words are indeed transcribed verbatim from Cicero’s cited book (*On the Nature of the Gods*, II), except for the words which follow the word “called”: “That designation afterward became more widely extended.” [Col. 1012C]

But our Lactantius wholly rejects this etymology and interpretation of both terms as given by Cicero. For, he says, if superstition and religion consist in worshiping gods in this manner, there will be little or rather no difference between them. For if praying to the gods and sacrificing to them once for the safety of one’s children, so that they may survive, is good and religious, then to pray and sacrifice more often, even the whole day, for the same safety of one’s children is neither evil nor superstitious. Conversely, if praying and sacrificing more often is counted a fault, so also is doing so once.

Again, what could fathers more honorably or justly desire and ask than that their children should remain alive after them? Superstition, therefore—which, Cicero admits, is the name of a fault—does not derive from this.

Lactantius consequently concludes (*Institutions*, IV.28) that religion is the worship of the true God, and superstition the worship of false gods. He adds: “What matters is what you worship, not how you worship or what you pray for”; that is, it matters altogether whether you worship the true God or fictitious gods. In this religion differs from superstition, not in the manner—that is, whether you pray once or repeatedly, for one hour or for whole days; for this contributes nothing to distinguishing superstition from religion.

But Lescaloperius, when he endeavors to elucidate Cicero’s cited book by his commentaries, contends that many things in Lactantius’s observation cannot escape just criticism. First, [Col. 1013A] he faults Lactantius because he denies that superstition and religion consist in the worship of gods. For all theologians admit that superstition differs from religion not merely because someone worships a false god, but because he also worships the true God in a manner neither due nor fitting. Therefore Lescaloperius cannot calmly tolerate Lactantius’s assertion: “What matters is what you worship, not how you worship.” For the true God may be worshiped and honored with a false and unworthy worship.

But as Lescaloperius said these things, with Lactantius’s leave, so let us, with Lescaloperius’s leave, say that perhaps he did not sufficiently understand Lactantius’s meaning. For that excellent man refutes Cicero because Cicero wished those to be called superstitious who prayed to the gods and sacrificed to them all day long that their children might survive them. Yet the pagans were not called superstitious precisely because they prayed to their gods for the safety of their children, but because they supplicated and sacrificed to them throughout the entire day. Lactantius therefore rightly asserts that the distinction between superstition and religion does not lie in this longer or shorter prayer.

Lescaloperius replies that this was not Cicero’s meaning: Cicero merely presents the common etymology of the term *superstitious* and leaves it for the judgment of all. But what does this contribute against Lactantius’s argument? Did Cicero not himself report the words by which he explains and interprets what had been handed down by philosophers and ancestors? Certainly, since Cicero does not reject it, does he not seem to approve it rather than leave it indeterminate and undecided? [Col. 1013C]

Lescaloperius presses his objection: What is best to do once is not always best to do more often, as various examples show. But he raises this objection in vain. For the discussion concerns only those who prayed to the gods. Who would deny that, if it is best to pray to them once, it is likewise best to pray to them more often?

Moreover, just as Lescaloperius’s excessive partiality toward Cicero, whom he comments upon, perhaps made him more hostile to Lactantius than was fair, so, where Cicero is no longer at issue, he is more equitable toward Lactantius. For he frankly admits that the etymologies of the two names, religion and superstition, offered by Lactantius and others, are not to be rejected. And rightly so. Lactantius confirms the first with these verses of Lucretius, of which he transcribed only the final words:

> First, because I teach concerning great and difficult matters,  
> and proceed to free the mind [variant: “minds”] from the tight knots of religions.  
> (Lucretius, I, near the end)

Servius supports this in commenting on Virgil’s verses:

> Even then dreadful religion, of the place, terrified the fearful country-folk.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid*, VIII.349)

For he added this explanatory note there: “Religion, that is, fear: religion is so called from that which binds the mind.” Augustine likewise says: “Tending toward the one God, and binding our souls to him alone—from which religion is believed to have received its name—let us be free of every superstition.” (*On True Religion*, chap. 55.) [Col. 1014A]

We know that Augustine elsewhere does not reject Cicero’s etymology of this word; and other etymologies of *religio* and *religiosus* are supplied by the aforementioned Servius, Festus, Macrobius, and Aulus Gellius (*Attic Nights*, V.9). But it is enough for us to have shown that Lactantius had several supporters and defenders of his opinion. We may add one observation made by Betuleius: Lactantius uses the plural *religiones* in an unfavorable sense (*Institutions*, III.9 and 30; IV.3). Yet, while it must be admitted that he commonly and almost everywhere uses it in that sense, the singular term is also occasionally used by him in the same meaning.

As for the term *superstition*, Lactantius readily grants Cicero that it arose from the word *superstes*, “survivor”; but he differs from him in not thinking that it should be understood of children whom parents desire to survive them. He wishes it to be understood of the surviving memory of the dead, or of the image of deceased parents, whom the pagans worshiped as gods by a new rite. He proves this by Virgil’s verse (*Aeneid*, VIII.188):

> Vain superstition, ignorant of the gods of old.

On this verse Servius noted: “He says two things: We worship Hercules neither because we think every religion true nor because we are ignorant of the ancient gods. For among both Athenians and Romans provision had been made that no one should introduce new religions. … Therefore it is vain because it is superstition ignorant of the gods,” doubtless by introducing new gods contrary to the laws of the commonwealth. [Col. 1014C] Cicero records that law in these words: “Let no one hold gods separately, nor new gods, nor foreign gods, unless publicly admitted; let them not be privately worshiped.” For those who worshiped the ancient and public gods, as our author says (*Institutions*, IV.28), were called religious. But enough of these matters: anyone who desires more should consult Vossius’s *Etymologicon*.

Certainly, no one will deny that Lactantius’s conclusion drawn from these points is undoubtedly true:

> “Therefore those are superstitious who worship many and false gods; but we are religious, who entreat the one and true God.” [Col. 1014D]

In what manner and rite the true God ought to be worshiped, he does not explain there, because it did not serve his purpose. But he explains it fully in the sixth book and elsewhere, as will become clear to all from what follows.

## ARTICLE II

What true religion is, and by what inseparable bond it is united with justice and wisdom.

The matters argued in the preceding article plainly demonstrate that Lactantius locates religion in the knowledge and worship of the true God. But that worship must be true, devout, just, holy, and such as is owed to the true God, the supreme Father of all. “For in the recognition and worship of God,” he says, “the sum of all things consists: in this lies all hope and salvation of man; this is the first step of wisdom—that we may know who our true Father is; that we may pursue him alone with due devotion; that we may obey him, serve him with utmost devotion, and place every act, care, and work in winning his favor.” (*Institutions*, VI.9.) What could be said more splendidly or clearly concerning the worship of God and true religion? Does he not define with the greatest clarity what the true worship of God and true religion are? Earlier he had said, no less correctly:

> “This is heavenly religion: not that which consists of corruptible things, but that which consists in the virtues of the mind, which arises from heaven. This is true worship, in which the mind of the worshiper presents itself unstained before God.”  
> (*Ibid.*, VI.2)

Would you hear him speak the same thing again? Here are further words of his:

> “Whoever obeys all the heavenly precepts is a worshiper of the true”—or, as is rightly read in the most ancient royal manuscript, “a true worshiper of God”—“whose sacrifices are gentleness of spirit, an innocent life, and good deeds.”  
> (*Ibid.*, VI.24)

Many passages to this effect might be assembled, but they should be reserved for the place where we discuss sacrifice.

No one therefore ought to find it surprising that Lactantius constantly affirms that this religion—the knowledge of the one supreme God and the worship due to him—cannot be separated from justice and true wisdom. Although this is sufficiently clear and plain, he proves it by various considerations, first by the definition of justice itself. Justice, he said, is nothing other than the devout and religious worship of the one God (*Ibid.*, V.7); that is, it is true religion itself. He therefore rightly declares that the two adhere to one another in such a way that one cannot be removed without the other immediately being taken away. Hence he says again: “The expulsion of justice must be considered nothing other, as I have said, than the abandonment of divine religion” (*Ibid.*, V.6). [Col. 1015C] But he had already established this by various testimonies of poets and ancient philosophers (*Institutions*, V.5, 6 ff.). For they repeatedly sang that justice lasted down to Jupiter’s time and remained as long as religion—that is, the worship of the true God—stood and endured. But afterward, when this worship and religion were extinguished by the introduction of the worship of false gods, justice too was removed and every evil subsequently flooded in. He clearly shows that this must be regarded not as poetic fiction but as truth. Therefore he rebukes Cicero, who endeavors to prove by this verse that justice flew away from earth to Jupiter’s heavenly kingdom:

> And in Jupiter’s realm and part of heaven she took her seat.  
> (Cicero, fragment)

For justice could not take her seat in the realm of one who drove his father from his kingdom, pursued him by war, and cast him as an exile throughout the whole world.

But the same justice, Lactantius says (*Institutions*, V.7), was brought back to earth by Christ, together with her inseparable companion, religion and the devout worship of the true God. Therefore he sharply reproves the pagans (*Ibid.*, V.8), who in their writings lamented that justice was still in exile from the world and wished that she might descend from heaven. She stood before their very eyes, and they could easily receive her, if they put away the worship of false gods and wickedness and began to worship the true God. [Col. 1016A]

Nor is it greatly to be wondered at if those who did not know the true God did not recognize justice either: “For he who does not know God,” he says, “must necessarily also be ignorant of justice” (*Ibid.*, VI.9). He gives this reason: civil law, established by men, varies according to their customs; but justice, uniform and simple, can be set forth by God alone. Once it is recognized, God, its author, must be recognized; and where he is recognized, true and due worship must be rendered to him.

Ignorance of the true God was all the less excusable in human beings because, with greater reason, both the ancient philosophers and Cicero himself admitted that man was truly born for justice. Our author demonstrates this by the words of the same Latin orator: “But of all matters discussed in the disputations of learned men, nothing is surely more excellent than that we understand plainly that we are born for justice” (*On the Laws*, I). These are Cicero’s exact words, transcribed from the first book of *On the Laws*. Yet our author cites the same words in another book (*On the Anger of God*, 14), and from them confirms that man was created for the sake of religion and justice. He shows clearly that this is true because man was created by God with an upright bodily stature, endowed with mind, reason, speech, and the capacity to rule over all other things, in order that he might acknowledge, contemplate, worship, and love his Creator, proclaim his majesty, and be subject to him. [Col. 1016C] You see, therefore, how rightly Lactantius concludes from all this: “Therefore no religion is true except that which consists in virtue and justice” (*Institutions*, VI.25). For this reason, justice can never be severed from true religion. For justice belongs properly to religion, as he asserts elsewhere (*On the Anger of God*, 7), and to justice the worship of God is assigned.

He was no less convinced that wisdom, in exactly the same way as justice, is united with religion, so that it can never be separated from it. At the very beginning of the *Divine Institutions*, he teaches that the impious superstitions and greatest errors of the pagans arose because they knew neither themselves nor the end to which life should be directed, nor how it should be lived. “I briefly define,” he says, “the sum of this knowledge thus: no religion is to be undertaken without wisdom, and no wisdom is to be approved without religion” (*Institutions*, I.1). If one is separated from the other, neither will any longer be true religion or wisdom. But listen to him, if you please, explaining this with the greatest clarity (*Ibid.*, III.11):

> “God willed human nature to be desirous and eager for two things, religion and wisdom. But people err because they either undertake religion while omitting wisdom, or devote themselves to wisdom alone while omitting religion, though neither can be true without the other. Thus they fall into multiple religions, but false ones, because they have abandoned wisdom, which could have taught them that there cannot be many gods; or they pursue wisdom, but a false wisdom, because they have omitted the religion of the supreme God, who could have instructed them in knowledge of the truth. Thus people who undertake either one separately follow a path astray and full of the greatest errors, since in these two inseparably connected things are contained both man’s duty and all truth.”

If you wish to know the arguments by which he supports this teaching, we shall first adduce the one which he sets forth in these words: “All human wisdom lies in this one thing: that he know and worship God. This is our doctrine; this is our judgment” (*Ibid.*, III.30). But religion, as he teaches, is nothing other than the knowledge and worship of the true and supreme God. Therefore, according to his judgment, true wisdom and religion are one and the same, and cannot be separated from each other. For, he says, “It is the same God who must be understood, which belongs to wisdom, and honored, which belongs to religion” (*Ibid.*, IV.4). He confirms this again by the following argument (*Ibid.*, IV.3): “In worshiping we must be wise—that is, know what and how we ought to worship. In being wise, we must worship—that is, fulfill in reality and action what we know.” Wisdom and religion, therefore, cleave to one another by an inseparable bond. When they are thus joined, one God is worshiped, and our life and every action are directed to one head and one supreme end.

Moreover, he says (*Ibid.*), “To be wise is nothing other than to honor the true God with just and devout worship.” But this is precisely true religion, which so honors God. “Therefore religion is in wisdom, and wisdom in religion.” [Col. 1017C]

Further, what of this: God, as our author rightly says (*Ibid.*, IV.4), must be understood and known. But this is wisdom itself. When he is known, he must thereby be honored; and this is religion’s duty (*Ibid.*, VII.9). Therefore wisdom and religion can never be separated from each other. He does, indeed, admit that wisdom comes first and religion follows. For one must first know God and afterward honor him. Yet they are like two streams flowing from the same source, and one force belongs to the two names: by one, understanding is signified; by the other, action.

Why then, you may ask, did he say: “Wisdom concerns sons, which demands love; religion concerns servants, which demands fear”? Does he not indicate by these words some distinction between them by which they are truly separated? Not at all. For in the same place he concludes that they are joined together. He had first shown that there can be only one God, who is both Father and Lord of all; and therefore each of us is both his son and his servant. Since he is our Father, we must love and honor him; since he is Lord, we must worship and fear him. God is known by wisdom and worshiped by religion; and by both he is loved as God and feared as Lord. As these acts, then, so religion and wisdom are joined by the closest bond.

Someone may object: Does not Lactantius seek to establish his opinion concerning the true anger of God from the fact that, just as religion can never exist without fear, so God cannot exist without anger? “There is no fear,” he says (*On the Anger of God*, 8 and 11), “where no one is angry”; and afterward, “religion cannot exist where there is no fear.” But who would say that fearing God when angry is the same as following him with a son’s love? Yet who does not know that a father is both loved and feared by his son? Fear, therefore, is neither contrary to love nor always excludes it. Moreover, even if filial fear of God, as our theologians call it, and servile fear were entirely different, what prevents both from being included in religion? Does not a man, as both God’s son and servant, worship him as Father and fear him as Lord through the same religion? But Lactantius’s opinion concerning the anger of God, and whether it is true, will be examined later in its proper place.

## ARTICLE III

[Col. 1018B]

Religion was not introduced because of fear, but instituted by God and implanted in man, who for that reason has an upright body, is called in Greek ἄνθρωπος (*anthrōpos*), and is distinguished from beasts especially by religion; contrary arguments of Epicurus are answered.

Although Lactantius, as we have just seen, said that there is no religion where there is no fear, he nonetheless expressly declares that those wholly miss the way who thought religion had been instituted by wise men for the sake of fear and terror, in order more easily to deter unlearned people from sins. These are his very words, by which he condemns their impious error with this mark of infamy:

> “False also is that opinion [Col. 1018C] by which they think that religion was instituted by wise men for the sake of terror and fear, so that unlearned persons might restrain themselves from sins.”

Therefore he utterly overturns this absurd opinion, because the wisest of all philosophers and the founders of the greatest schools among them constantly taught that the world was created by an omnipotent God and governed by his providence. Therefore God, the Creator of humankind as of the world, must be acknowledged and worshiped by them. Yet, as we have said, religion wholly consists in this acknowledgment and worship of God. It was therefore not introduced by any mortal man, but was innate with man himself, as our author rightly says (*Ibid.*, 14). For all are compelled to admit that the highest honor and supreme reverence are due to this God, as Creator and Ruler of the world and humankind. Indeed, he created the world for the sake of man, just as he created man for his own sake: namely, that man might know and worship him (*Institutions*, VII.6). But true religion, as we have said, is nothing other than the knowledge and worship of the true God. Religion therefore was instituted by God himself, not in order to instill some foolish fear, but in order to honor God.

Our author confirms, repeats, and emphasizes this not merely in one place but frequently. Besides the passage cited, he wrote elsewhere:

> “We are born on this condition: that we render just and due service to God who begot us; that we know him alone and follow him. Bound by this bond of piety, we are bound to God, whence religion itself received its name.”  
> (*Institutions*, IV.28)

From our very birth, therefore, we are bound to God by religion, by which we know, worship, and follow him, and obey his will and commands. [Col. 1019A]

To this is added that not only is the human mind implanted by God so that it may know and venerate him, but man is continually reminded of this duty even by the upright posture of his body, formed by God himself. Our author asserts this not only once but very frequently in various books, and corroborates it with the testimony of the pagans themselves. For in the second book of the *Divine Institutions*, chapter 1, he says: “While the other living creatures look downward to the ground with their bodies bent, God raised man from the earth to the contemplation of his Creator.” He shows that this had been sung by the ingenious poet, as he calls him, namely Ovid, in the following verses:

> While all other animals look downward upon the earth,  
> he gave man an uplifted face and commanded him to see the heaven  
> and raise his erect countenance toward the stars.  
> (Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, I.80 ff.)

In Ovid, however, *tuēri* (“to behold”) is read instead of *vidēre* (“to see”). Lactantius adds that man is called in Greek ἄνθρωπος (*anthrōpos*) because he looks upward. The Greek word, as some think, derives from ἄνω ῥέπων, “inclining upward”; or, as others prefer, from παρὰ τὸ ἄνω ἀθρεῖν, “from looking upward”; or, according to the author of the *Great Etymologicum*, from ἄνω θρεῖν, that is, “to look upward.” This last is more consonant with the opinion of our Lactantius.

Therefore elsewhere he argues thus:

> “Those who do not embrace religion are earthly, because religion is from heaven. … It profits man nothing, therefore, to have been formed so that with an upright body he looks at heaven, unless with an upright mind he beholds God and his thought is wholly engaged in hope of everlasting life.”  
> (*Institutions*, III.27) [Col. 1019C]

See, then, whether he does not mean this in fewer words where he exhorts man to know the sacrament of his birth—that is, the upright posture of his body—by which he is admonished, as by the symbol and sacrament of his form, to look down upon the earth and behold heaven and God.
