But if you wish this to be proved, we shall produce other words of his, in which he expressly declares that man alone of all creatures is an animal “whose body,” he says, “raised from the earth, whose lofty face and upright posture seek its origin and, as though scorning the lowliness of earth, strive upward … and, mindful of the condition in which God made him excellent, looks to his Maker. Trismegistus most rightly called this contemplation θεωρία (*theōria*), which does not exist in mute animals” (*Ibid.*, VII.9). Do not the words “mindful of his condition,” or of his creation—by which God made his body upright so that he might look to his Maker—plainly enough declare what he meant by the sacrament of man’s birth?

We would truly never finish speaking if we were to transcribe entire all the passages in which he taught and established this point. It is therefore enough to have noted the principal passages which occur in his other books.

Who has ever dared oppose so sound and right a doctrine, so suited to human nature, unless he were an atheist or an Epicurean philosopher, [Col. 1020A] who confessed God merely in words and utterly abolished all religion? Such a man, our author says, objected: “What benefit, then, does human worship”—that is, religion itself—“bring to God, who is blessed and in need of nothing?” (Institutions, Book IV, ch. 5.) Although Lactantius does not there name the man who said this, it is nonetheless clear that he means Lucretius, whose verses, in which he foolishly sang this, he had cited shortly before:

> What profit can our gratitude bestow  
> upon the immortal and blessed gods?  
> (Lucretius, Book V, v. 165 ff.)

And earlier:

> Moreover, it is fitting to praise the gods  
> for their praiseworthy work.

But Lactantius declares that he had sufficiently answered this foolish objection [Col. 1020B] when he repeatedly stated that God created humanity in order that human beings might contemplate Him and His works, understand them, wonder at them, proclaim them, and pursue Him with due reverence. Moreover, he had shown that this was not merely his own view, but that of the pagans themselves. If he did not cite more authorities, the reason undoubtedly is that, except for those whom we have noted, all regarded this as true, certain, and acknowledged.

Cicero was readily available for him to praise, and perhaps Lactantius follows him without naming him, when Cicero says: “God first raised human beings from the earth and set them high and upright, so that, looking upon the heavens, they might attain knowledge of the gods. For human beings are from the earth, not as its inhabitants and dwellers, but almost as spectators of the things above and heavenly, the spectacle of which belongs to no other kind of living creature.” (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book II.) Cicero had also committed the same point to writing in the *Tusculan Disputations* and elsewhere (*Tusculans*, Book I).

Yet Lactantius did not stop there. By another mode of argument he showed that religion is inborn and innate in humankind. Indeed, he considers this to be either the sole, or at least the principal and greatest, distinction between human beings and beasts. “The distinction,” he says, “between man and the dumb animals lies either solely, or certainly most greatly, in religion.” (*Institutions*, Book II, ch. 3.) Elsewhere: “There is no other animal that has any knowledge of God; and religion is almost the only thing that distinguishes man from brute beasts.” (Book VII, ch. 9.)

He attempts to defend and establish his opinion both by Cicero’s authority [Col. 1020D] and by reason. He had indeed cited Cicero in the passage just mentioned. But earlier he reported Cicero’s words as follows: “For this reason Cicero’s judgment is true: ‘Of so many kinds of living creatures,’ he says, ‘there is none besides man that has any knowledge of God; and among men themselves there is no nation so uncivilized, so savage, that—even though it does not know what sort of God it ought to have—does not nevertheless know that it ought to have one. From this it follows that a person recognizes God who, as it were, remembers whence he has sprung.’” (*Institutions*, Book III, ch. 10.) These words are transcribed from the first book of Cicero’s *Laws*, to which Lactantius refers us elsewhere; and there he adds: “For man alone has been endowed with wisdom, so that he alone may understand religion. And this is either the chief or the sole difference between man and dumb animals.” (*On the Anger of God*, ch. 7.)

But hear, I pray, by what reasoning he proved this. Everything, he says (*Institutions*, Book III, ch. 10; *On the Anger of God*, ch. 7), apart from religion, which appears distinctive of man, is either shared with other animals or at least plainly similar to something found in them. If speech is said to be peculiar to man, dumb animals also recognize one another by their sounds and disclose their inward disposition. Thus there is in them some likeness of speech. If laughter, arising from joy, appears peculiar to man, signs of joy are found in animals’ ears, eyes, mouths, and cheerful expression. If nothing is more peculiar to man than reason and forethought for the future, animals also possess a certain appearance of intelligence and thought, by which they open various exits from their hiding places, so that, when besieged and danger threatens, they may provide for their safety by flight. Ants and bees, moreover—as Lactantius proves from Virgil’s verses—gather in summer what they foresee will be necessary for their sustenance during winter.

He passes over many examples in the several classes of animals that closely resemble human ingenuity. He thought those he had related entirely sufficient to draw this conclusion: “If, then, in dumb animals also there is found a likeness of all these things commonly ascribed to man, it is evident that religion alone is that of which no trace whatever, nor any suspicion, can be found among dumb animals.” (*On the Anger of God*, ch. 7.)

But Isaeus observes in his notes on Lactantius that, [Col. 1021C] when composing the *Institutions*, Lactantius thought that man was distinguished from brute beasts by religion alone, because he then followed the opinion of Pythagoras, Plato, and certain others, who believed that brute animals possessed reason. Later, however, when he published *On the Anger of God*, Isaeus thinks that he had then recovered from this error. And indeed, in the earlier books Lactantius spoke thus: “For my part, I think that reason has been given to all living creatures, but to dumb animals only for preserving life, and to man for its propagation. And because reason itself is perfect in man, it is called wisdom; this makes man outstanding in that he alone has been granted to understand divine things.” (*Institutions*, Book II, ch. 10.) In *On the Anger of God*, however, he seems to ascribe to dumb animals only a likeness of all things belonging to human reason and ingenuity. [Col. 1021D]

Nevertheless, we fear that Isaeus did not fully and thoroughly ascertain our author’s meaning. For in Books II and VII of the *Institutions*, cited by us shortly before, Lactantius openly declares that man differs from dumb animals solely, or especially, in religion, because man, being possessed of perfect reason, can have religion, whereas brute animals cannot, since they can possess only imperfect reason. Therefore his meaning and opinion seem to have been no other than that brute animals possess some imperfect reason—or, rather, merely a likeness and appearance of reason—given to them only for preserving life. Accordingly, since religion alone has absolutely no trace, not even the least, [Col. 1022A] among brute animals, Lactantius inferred that it is by religion that man is more clearly and evidently distinguished from them. Whatever the case, if he erred and corrected his error, the modesty of a candid and truthful man, his sincere love for preserving truth, and his supreme zeal ought certainly to be praised.

Since religion, then, is thus innate in human beings, and since they are naturally desirous and eager for it, just as for wisdom—as Lactantius says (*Institutions*, Book III, ch. 10)—what wonder if he concludes that those who abolish it deprive man of his own proper and distinctive good? “Therefore those philosophers,” he says, “who wish to free minds from every fear abolish religion also, and deprive man of his own proper and distinctive good.” (Ibid., ch. 10.) By these words he censures Epicurus, of whom he says elsewhere: “All religion is dissolved, if we believe Epicurus when he says” (Book II, v. 56 ff.):

> For the whole nature of the gods must necessarily  
> enjoy immortal life in fullest peace,  
> removed from our affairs, etc.

You see clearly that Lucretius’ verses are there cited under Epicurus’ name. Lactantius had elsewhere warned us (*On the Workmanship of God*, ch. 6) that all Lucretius’ ravings belong to Epicurus. Cicero expressly ascribed this impious error to Epicurus. Moreover, this same pagan orator, when a disciple of Epicurus objected: “But Epicurus also wrote books about holiness and piety,” replies: “But how does he speak in them? You would say that you were listening to Coruncanius or Scaevola, chief pontiffs, not to one who has utterly abolished all religion at its root; who has overthrown the temples and altars of the gods, not with his hands, as Xerxes did, but with arguments. For why should you say that gods ought to be worshipped by men, when gods not only do not care for men, but care for nothing whatever and do nothing?” (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book II.) Shortly afterward he repeats this in other words and then adds that, in Epicurus’ book on holiness, composed for the sake of detestable popularity, we are being mocked “by a man not so witty as unrestrained in license of writing,” who “abolishes the gods in fact and retains them in speech.” Cicero had indeed said this earlier.

Lactantius, however, who attacks and uproots this most absurd error—rejected by all others—with still greater sharpness, draws a twofold conclusion from the foregoing discussion. First, religion was not instituted because of fear, [Col. 1022D] since it is naturally implanted in human minds and God willed human nature to desire and seek it. Second, the same religion must be served, since the consensus of the whole human race establishes that it must be embraced. But because many religions had invaded the world, we must consider which Lactantius thinks to be true, and which all must choose and embrace.

## CHAPTER TWO

The arguments by which Lactantius demonstrates that the Christian religion alone is true are examined.

### ARTICLE ONE

Lactantius’ arguments demonstrating the truth of the Christian religion from the oracles of our sacred prophets are examined: they foretold that Christ, the Son of God, would become man and be born of a virgin.

Since all human beings are bound, as stated, by so great a necessity to undertake and embrace religion, it is surely established that they must embrace no religion other than that which is true and which honors and venerates the supreme God with true and due worship. Lactantius demonstrates, by various and invincible arguments (*Institutions*, Book IV, chs. 23–25), that this religion alone is the Christian religion. He argues first from the fact that Christ was sent as ambassador and messenger by God the Father, in order to restore justice, which no longer existed on earth; and, having spread throughout the whole earth by word and example the true and pious worship of God, to build a new temple—that is, to found, teach, and establish the true religion. In order to institute it and fulfill the office of teaching, God willed Christ to descend to earth, as He had decreed, and to be clothed in human flesh.

But since pagans and others could deny that Christ had truly been sent by God and had established the true religion, Lactantius proves this most clearly (*Institutions*, Book IV, ch. 10) by the authority of the sacred prophets. Many centuries before Christ’s birth, they foretold that the Son of God would one day receive a human body from a virgin, be born of David’s family, work miracles, proclaim the worship of the true God throughout the earth, die nailed to a cross, and finally return from death to life on the third day. But these matters could not have been foretold by those sacred prophets in the very manner in which they occurred unless they had been inspired by the divine Spirit. No sane person can ever deny that these divine oracles, which received their fulfillment, demonstrate certainly and evidently both that Christ was truly sent by God and that the Christian religion founded by Him is true.

Accordingly, Lactantius first shows that these prophets foretold many centuries beforehand that Christ, the Son of God, would be born of a virgin. He began with these words of Solomon (*Institutions*, Book IV, ch. 12): “Solomon says thus” (the oldest royal manuscript and Betuleius’ edition: “Solomon says thus in the nineteenth ode”; another royal manuscript, somewhat later than the former, and several others: “Solomon says thus in the nineteenth psalm”): “The womb of the virgin was weakened, and received a fetus; and in great compassion the mother and virgin was burdened.” But many have already observed that this passage is not found in our sacred Bibles. Betuleius suspects that it was one of the five thousand songs which the author of Third Kings attests were composed by Solomon: “And his songs were five thousand” (III Kings 4:32).

Gallaeus thinks that Lactantius cited words he had heard from others but had not himself read; yet he peddles trifles as conjectures. For by what argument does he attempt to prove this? “The Fathers,” he says, “often cite passages which you will seek in vain in the books of the sacred Bible.” [Col. 1024A] Does it therefore follow that Lactantius reported them without reading them, merely because he heard them from others? Who ever argued in such a fashion?

But Isaeus brings this passage under suspicion of falsity. He does not believe that these words were written in any canonical book of Scripture, since the blessed Virgin experienced no pain in the conception and birth of Christ the Lord. Yet the word *infirmatus* (“was weakened”) seems to be taken by Lactantius in a favorable sense, not in the adverse sense that would imply the Virgin’s womb was weakened so that she suffered some pain. For by these words Solomon, or whoever wrote them, declares that she conceived by the divine Spirit without any contact with a man, became a mother in great compassion, and remained a virgin. Was not the customary pain of women giving birth excluded by so great and unheard-of a miracle? Yet although the words can be explained in a favorable sense, there will still be those who think Lactantius drew them not from a genuine book of Solomon but from some apocryphal work. For, they will ask, how could so clear and manifest a prophecy of Mary’s unimpaired virginity have been passed over by Irenaeus, Epiphanius, Jerome, and others, who undertook with all their powers of intellect to defend her virginity against heretics who denied it?

More familiar to everyone, therefore, are the words of Isaiah which Lactantius further cites (*Institutions*, Book II, ch. 12): “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb” (many manuscripts: “in the womb”), “and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel” (Isaiah 7:14). Cyprian likewise cites it thus (*Against the Jews*, Book I, §9; Epistle 9). The clearer, as our author says, this prophetic testimony concerning Christ’s birth from a virgin is, the more certain it ought to be. Christians had received it from the Jews, their own and Christ the Lord’s bitterest enemies. Therefore those Jews, however obstinate, and all others, necessarily ought to acknowledge and receive this testimony of Isaiah, like all the other testimonies of our sacred prophets, as true and plainly divine, as we shall show below.

Nor could it be objected that Christ was called not Emmanuel but Jesus. Isaiah called Him Emmanuel in order to signify by this term that God would one day be with us. But Christ, born of a virgin, was truly God with us. Lactantius seems to have taken these points from Tertullian, who contends against the Jews with the same Isaian oracle (*Against the Jews*, ch. 9) and refutes their frivolous answer thus:

> Therefore the Jews say: “Let us test this prophecy of Isaiah and compare whether the name first proclaimed by Isaiah applies to the Christ who has already come. … Isaiah certainly proclaims that He must be called Emmanuel. … But,” they say, “the one who came was not born under such a name. …” Yet we, on the contrary, thought they should be admonished to examine also the coherence of this chapter. For its interpretation is added: Emmanuel, “God with us,” so that you may consider not merely the sound of the name but also its meaning. The sound—Emmanuel—is Hebrew and belongs to its own nation; but its meaning, “God with us,” comes through a common translation. I ask, then, whether this expression “God with us,” which is Emmanuel, has been realized in Christ from the time Christ shone forth. And I think you will not deny it at all. For those who from Judaism believe in Christ, when they say Emmanuel, signify that God is with us. Thus it is established that He has already come who was proclaimed as Emmanuel, because what Emmanuel signifies has come—that is, God with us.

We have transcribed this entire passage, though somewhat lengthy, because it makes clearer what our Lactantius reported more briefly. Tertullian added more there, but since it does not pertain to our purpose—however worthy it is of reading—we omit it. [Col. 1025B] In another book as well (*Against Marcion*, Book III, chs. 12–13), he repeats the same points and rebukes those Jews who falsely and dishonestly claimed that Isaiah’s words signified not that a virgin but a young woman would conceive. In the first volume of our *Apparatus*, where we discussed the writings of Justin and Irenaeus, we refuted that perverse explanation. See also Eusebius (*Demonstration of the Gospel*, Book II, §39; Book III, §2; Book VII, §3), Jerome, Huet (*Demonstration of the Gospel*, proposition 9, ch. 9), and other interpreters of sacred Scripture.

Lactantius then shows that Christ’s coming was again foretold by this oracle of the Psalmist: “Truth has sprung from the earth” (Psalm 84:12). He establishes this in the following way: “Because God, in whom truth is, assumed an earthly body in order to open the way of salvation to earthly beings.” Irenaeus, however (*Against Heresies*, Book III, ch. 5), judged that by these very words not only Christ’s birth from a virgin, but also His return from death to life, was announced: “David,” he says, “prophesying His generation from a virgin and His resurrection from the dead, says: ‘Truth has sprung from the earth.’” But Jerome, in the fourth book of his commentaries on Isaiah, interprets the Psalmist’s same words concerning Christ’s human birth thus (Jerome, *On Isaiah* 11:1 ff.): “He who speaks in the Gospel, ‘I am the light, the life, and the truth,’ and of whom it is said in the Psalms, ‘Truth has sprung from the earth, [Col. 1025D] and righteousness has looked down from heaven,’ was made for us by God wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption.” Later again (ibid., on Isaiah 45:1): “Let the clouds rain down the righteous one—or righteousness—upon the world; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Savior, of whom the Psalms sing: ‘Truth has sprung from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven’; or, according to the Septuagint: ‘The earth has brought forth mercy and righteousness together,’ so that sinners may obtain mercy and the righteous their rewards.” Whoever desires more should consult interpreters of sacred Scripture and learn from them that the truth announced by the psalmist is Christ, who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

Lactantius returns to Isaiah and proves, from these words, that Christ’s coming was also foretold elsewhere by him: “But they did not believe … and He Himself fought, and remembered the days of old, He who raised up from the earth a shepherd” (Isaiah 63:10–11). In the Septuagint one reads: “He Himself fought against them and remembered the days of old, He who brought up from the sea, ἐκ τῆς θαλάσσης, the shepherd of the sheep.” The final words of the Vulgate differ from both of those renderings: “He remembered the days of old, Moses and His people. Where is He who brought them up from the sea with His shepherds?” But Lactantius, who read “shepherd” in his sacred text, says that this is He of whom Isaiah had previously said: “Let the heavens rejoice above, and let the clouds put on righteousness; let the earth be opened and put forth the Savior. For I, the Lord God, created Him” (Isaiah 45:8). The Septuagint reads: “Let heaven rejoice above, and let the clouds scatter righteousness; let the earth germinate and bring forth mercy, and let it produce righteousness together. I am the Lord who created.” We have just heard Jerome cite these words from the same version. But the Vulgate reads: “Drop down dew, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the Just One; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Savior, and let righteousness arise together. I, the Lord, created Him.” We have reported the varying renderings of these words of the sacred prophet so that each reader may more readily understand which Lactantius followed. All the ancient Fathers of the Church and interpreters of sacred Scripture everywhere consider Isaiah’s words to concern Christ made man, as does our Lactantius. Since they confront us in such number and with such unanimity, we judged it wholly useless to name them here.

With the same unanimity they teach that Christ’s human birth was further foreshadowed by these words of the same Isaiah, which Lactantius next cited (*Institutions*, Book IV, ch. 12): “Behold, a child has been born to us, and a son has been given to us, whose dominion is upon His shoulders, and His name has been called Messenger of Great Counsel” (Isaiah 9:6). Here Lactantius adheres more closely to the Septuagint. Cyprian also does so (*Against the Jews*, Book II, §21), except that at the end he wrote “Messenger of Great Thought.” The notes nevertheless observe that one manuscript reads “Messenger of Great Counsel.” Lactantius argues from this: “For this reason He was sent by God the Father: that He might reveal to all nations under heaven the holy mystery of the one true God, taken away from the faithless people who repeatedly sinned against God.”

Tertullian, however, argues against the Jews from this passage as follows: “What wonder if He does not speak of the Son of God? … What king ever carries the insignia of his power upon his shoulder, rather than a diadem on his head, a scepter in his hand, or some mark of his distinctive dress? But Christ Jesus alone, the new King of the ages, bore both power and exaltation of new glory upon His shoulder—namely, the cross.” (*Against the Jews*, ch. 11; *On the Flesh of Christ*, ch. 14.) He repeats the same words elsewhere to refute Marcion. In yet another book (*Against Marcion*, Book III, ch. 19), he refutes not only Jews but also heretics [Col. 1027A] who denied that Christ was either true God or true man, by Isaiah’s later words: “He is indeed called the Angel—that is, Messenger—of Great Counsel: this is a title of office, not of nature. For He was to announce to the world the Father’s great design concerning the restoration of man. Yet He is not therefore to be understood as an angel such as Gabriel or Michael. For the son of the lord of the vineyard is sent to the cultivators, just as the servants are sent to seek the fruits. But the son will not therefore be counted one of the servants because he performed the office of servants in succession.” (*On the Flesh of Christ*, ch. 14.) Finally, he concludes his argument with these words: “What more? Hear Isaiah still crying out: ‘Not an angel, nor an envoy, but the Lord Himself saved them.’” Jerome and Eusebius interpreted these and the preceding words of Isaiah in the same manner (Jerome, in the cited commentary on Isaiah; Eusebius, *Demonstration of the Gospel*, Book VII, ch. 3); you will not regret reading Eusebius, who relates much that is noteworthy.

Lactantius continues (*Institutions*, Book IV, ch. 12), and shows further that Daniel foretold not only Christ’s first coming but also His second coming at the end of the world. For, he says, Daniel prophesied both in these words: “I beheld in a vision of the night, and behold, one coming in the clouds of heaven like a son of man, and He came even to the Ancient of Days. And those who stood by offered Him, and kingdom, honor, and dominion were given Him; and all peoples, tribes, and tongues shall serve Him; and His power is eternal, which shall never pass away, and His kingdom shall not be destroyed” (Daniel 7:13). Our author rebukes the Jews from this passage, because they denied that Christ was the true Messiah on the ground that He was born from a human being. In these few words the prophet plainly foreshadowed Christ’s two comings. The first, indeed, when he says: “one coming like a son of man.” By this manner of speech he signified that Christ would assume human form and mortal condition in order to teach human beings justice and truth. By the subsequent words of the same Daniel, our author shows that Christ’s second coming is foretold—although “kingdom was given Him,” and what follows, may be understood of both comings of Christ.

Tertullian, however, employing this same testimony of the sacred prophet (*Against the Jews*, ch. 14; *Against Marcion*, Book III, ch. 7), which he reports with several variant readings, proves against the Jews and Marcion that only Christ’s latter future coming is designated, while the former is designated by another prophecy of Isaiah. Cyprian follows Tertullian (*Against the Jews*, §26), transcribing Daniel’s words with readings that differ further from both. Jerome, however, in his commentary on the cited passage of Daniel, seems rather to refer them to Christ’s first coming. Lactantius adds (*Institutions*, Book IV, ch. 22) that the same prophetic words also signify that Christ, raised from the dead, would afterward ascend into heaven.

Again, Lactantius expressly affirms that Jeremiah foretold that Christ would become man when he uttered this oracle: “And He is a man, and who shall know Him?” But the editors of notes upon our author’s works observe that these words are found neither in Jeremiah’s nor in Baruch’s prophecy. Yet they undoubtedly sought them in the Vulgate rendering, where they read differently, rather than in the Septuagint, which reports them in Greek in the same manner as our author, and later Epiphanius did (Epiphanius, *Heresies*, 54, §4). And what then? The same prophetic testimony has been transcribed in exactly the same Latin words by Tertullian in several of his books (*Against the Jews*, final chapter; *On the Flesh of Christ*, ch. 15; *Against Marcion*, Book III, ch. 7), and by Cyprian (*Against the Jews*, §10), Ambrose (*On the Institution of Virgins*, ch. 16), and others.

Yet Jerome’s remarks on this passage of Jeremiah must not be omitted: “The Hebrew word *Enos* is written with four letters: aleph, nun, waw, and sin. If it is read *Enos*, it means ‘man’; if *anus*, ‘unsearchable’ or ‘desperate,’ because no one among men can discover the human heart. Symmachus rendered this passage thus: ‘The heart of all is unsearchable; but what man is there who can find it?’ Some of our people are accustomed, with good intention indeed but not according to knowledge, to use this passage against the Jews, saying that the Lord and Savior is man according to the dispensation of assumed flesh, and that no one can know the mystery of His birth. … But it is better to understand it simply: no one knows the secrets of thoughts except God alone.” From this whole discussion Jerome concludes that Christ is God, since, as the Evangelist testifies, He knew the secret thoughts of human beings. But the most ancient Fathers of the Church, following the rendering of the Seventy-Two—who themselves were Jews—considered these words likewise to be understood of Christ.

What more? Lactantius says (*Institutions*, Book VI, ch. 13) that Isaiah also foretold Christ’s future humanity by these words: “And God shall send them a man, and he shall save them, and, judging, shall heal them” (Isaiah 19:20). But certain writers of notes on this passage of Lactantius again warn us that these words too are absent from Isaiah’s book. What then? Could they not have read in the Vulgate edition of sacred Scripture and in Jerome’s commentary, as we have: “And He shall send them a savior and defender, who will deliver them” (Jerome, on the cited passage of Isaiah)? Is not the same meaning indicated by those words and by the words transcribed from Lactantius? Did they require anything more explicit? They should therefore have consulted the Septuagint, where they would have read: “Καὶ ἀποστελεῖ αὐτοῖς ἄνθρωπον, ὃς σώσει αὐτούς· κρίνων σώσει αὐτούς”—“And He shall send them a man who will save them; judging, He shall save them.” You see plainly what diligence was shown by certain heterodox persons who had charge of editions of Lactantius’ works. Jerome, moreover, and other ancient Fathers of the Church openly profess that this passage is to be understood of Christ.

To all these prophecies of our prophets Lactantius adds (*Institutions*, Book VI, ch. 13) the most celebrated oracle of Balaam, which he cites under the name of Moses, its narrator, as follows: “Moses also speaks thus in Numbers: ‘A star shall arise from Jacob, and a man shall rise from Israel’” (Numbers 24:17). The Vulgate has: “and a rod shall rise from Israel.” Cyprian presents it in exactly the same words as our Lactantius (*Against the Jews*, Book I, §10). But Irenaeus writes (*Against Heresies*, Book III, ch. 19): “A star shall arise from Jacob, and a leader shall arise from Israel.” Justin Martyr likewise gives it in Greek (*Dialogue with Trypho*), also under Moses’ name: “ἀνατελεῖ ἄστρον ἐξ Ἰακώβ, καὶ ἠγούμενος ἐξ Ἰσραήλ”—“A star shall arise from Jacob, and a leader from Israel.” Eusebius likewise (*Demonstration of the Gospel*, Book IX, §2), except that he adds the word “καὶ ἀναστήσεται,” “and shall rise.” There he discusses judiciously and at length this and other oracles of Isaiah and of other prophets concerning the human nature to be assumed by Christ. You will certainly not waste your effort if you consult him, as well as the many other Greek and Latin Fathers of the Church whom it would take too long to name individually. Meanwhile, let us follow our author as he relates further prophetic oracles concerning Christ.

### ARTICLE TWO

The prophetic oracles by which Lactantius demonstrates that Christ was foretold to be born from David’s family, and whether he rightly said that the city of Jerusalem received its name from Solomon.

[Col. 1029C] Lactantius continues (*Institutions*, Book IV, ch. 13), producing several oracles of our sacred prophets which expressly foretold that Christ would not only assume human nature but also be born from David’s family. He first demonstrates this by the following twofold prophecy of Isaiah: “And in that day there shall be a root of Jesse, and He who shall arise to rule the nations; in Him the nations shall hope, and His rest shall be in honor” (Isaiah 10:11). And elsewhere: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of God shall rest upon Him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and godliness; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill Him” (Isaiah 10:11). You see that our author has cited the two passages in an order somewhat reversed from that of the prophet.

Cyprian presents the former as follows (*Against the Jews*, Book I, §12): “And in that day there shall be a root of Jesse, who shall rise to rule all nations; in Him the nations shall hope, and His rest shall be honor.” The Septuagint likewise. But the Vulgate differs somewhat: “In that day the root of Jesse, who stands as a sign to the peoples—to Him the nations shall seek, and His sepulcher shall be glorious.” Paul the Apostle also cites it (Romans 15:12), more in accordance with the Septuagint rendering, and teaches that these words foretold Christ’s birth from David’s stock and His rule after calling all nations to Himself.

The second passage is described almost the same way in both the Septuagint and Vulgate versions. Cyprian had cited it in precisely the same words and for the same purpose as Lactantius (*Against the Jews*, Book II, §11). Before them both, however, Tertullian argued from it against the Jews as follows: “And since the virgin from whom Christ had to be born, as we have mentioned above, was to derive her lineage from David’s seed, Isaiah the prophet plainly says in what follows: ‘And a rod shall be born from the root of Jesse’—that is, Mary—‘and a flower shall rise from his root. …’ For the fullness of spiritual proofs applied to no person except Christ, likened to a flower because of grace, but reckoned from Jesse’s stock, through Mary—that is, deriving His descent from it. For Mary was from the town of Bethlehem and from David’s house, as she was entered in the Roman census, and Christ was born from her.” (*Against the Jews*, ch. 9.) Tertullian also argues from this against heretics who thought wrongly about Christ, and repeatedly refutes their errors elsewhere. Similarly, Eusebius (*Demonstration of the Gospel*, Book II, §19; Book III, §1; Book VII, §3) proves from both Isaian testimonies that Christ was to be born from the root of Jesse and David’s seed. Since his discussion is too long to transcribe entire here, we indicate the locations in his books so that anyone may consult them. It would be no less lengthy to cite later writers; therefore, omitting them, we refer you to Jerome (in the cited commentary on Isaiah) and Eusebius (*Demonstration of the Gospel*, Book VI, ch. 33), who discuss this question admirably.

Moreover, Lactantius, in order to slay the pagans with their own sword, says that the flower mentioned by Isaiah is the one designated by the Sibyl—whose authority they could not diminish—in these words: “Ἀνθήσει δ᾽ ἄνθος καθαρόν,” “And a pure flower shall blossom” (Book VI of the *Oracles*, v. 8). In an old royal manuscript of Lactantius’ books this is rendered in Latin: “But a pure flower shall bloom”; and the words are found in the published Sibylline Oracles.

Nor did our author stop there (Lact. ibid.); he further demonstrates the same point by these words of the prophet Nathan, cited thus by him and by Cyprian (Cyprian, *Against the Jews*, II.11): “Likewise, in the book of **βασιλειῶν** [*Basileiōn*] (two most ancient royal manuscripts: *Basilion*; Cyprian: *In Basileion*),” that is, “of the Kingdoms, the prophet [Col. 1030D] Nathan was sent to David when he wished to build a temple for God: And the word of the Lord came to Nathan, saying: Go and say to my servant David: Thus says the Lord Almighty” (this word was omitted by Cyprian), “You shall not build me a house for dwelling in” (Cyprian adds, “it shall be”), “when your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I shall raise up your seed after you” (Cyprian adds, “who shall be from your womb”), “and I shall establish his seed” (Cyprian: “kingdom”). “He shall build me a house in my name, and I shall establish his throne for ever; and I shall be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son; and his house and his kingdom shall obtain steadfastness for ever.” Cyprian further adds, in [Col. 1031A] “my sight.” He had previously cited the same passage, though for a different purpose. These words occur in the Second Book of Kings, as stated—that is, in the Second Book of Samuel (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 7:4, 5, 12, 13, 14, 16); but both Cyprian and Lactantius have omitted several words inserted there in the sacred text.

By various arguments Lactantius refutes the Jews who wished these words to be understood not of Christ but of Solomon. For, he says, the prophet was speaking of one who was not to be born until David had rested with his fathers. Yet Solomon had been born before then. Next, by this prophetic oracle the person whose dominion was to be perpetual is expressly designated. Solomon, therefore, is not meant, since he reigned for only forty years. Finally, the temple built by Solomon was destroyed. Thus it was not Solomon’s temple, that of David’s son, but the temple of Christ, Son of God, that was indicated: namely, the Church founded by him, which will endure for ever not in walls but in the hearts of faithful people.

Tertullian had earlier argued against Marcion in precisely the same way (Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, III.20): “Nathan the prophet in the Second Book of Kingdoms”—these are his own words—“makes a declaration to David concerning his seed: ‘It shall be,’ he says, ‘from his own womb.’ If you expound this simply of Solomon, you make me laugh. For David will appear to have given birth to Solomon. Or is Christ signified here also: the seed of David from that womb, who was to be from David—that is, from Mary? Indeed, Christ rather was to build the house of God [Col. 1031C], namely the holy human being in whom the Spirit of God would dwell in a more excellent temple; and Christ rather was to be reckoned the Son of God than Solomon, David’s son. Finally, the throne for ever and the kingdom for ever suit Christ better than Solomon, a temporal king. Moreover, God’s mercy did not depart from Christ; but God’s wrath came upon Solomon also after his luxury and idolatry. For He raised up against him Satan, the Idumaean enemy. Since, therefore, none of these things applies to Solomon but to Christ, the basis of our interpretations will be certain, the very outcome of events proving that the things foretold were proclaimed concerning Christ.” Augustine agrees with Tertullian and our Lactantius (Augustine, *City of God*, XVII.8.3), as do very many others.

[Col. 1031D] “But Lactantius,” someone may perhaps object, “in ranging much further than Tertullian and Augustine (Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, IV.13 and 18), struck upon a certain rock of error. For he asserts not only that the Jerusalem Temple was built by Solomon, but also that he called the city Jerusalem after his own name.” Yet this city, founded long before Solomon’s time, had received its name. For, to pass over its frequent mention in the books of Joshua and Judges (Joshua 10, 11, 12; Judges 1, 19), Josephus (*Antiquities*, VII.2.3) relates that Jerusalem, Ἱεροσόλυμα [*Hierosolyma*], was captured by David and subsequently restored. He then adds: “Accordingly David, after expelling the Jebusites, was the first to give the city its name from himself; for in the time of Abraham, the founder of our race, it was called Solyma.” In another book (*Jewish War*, VII.18), however, he relates that it was built in Abraham’s time by Melchizedek, but adds that it was called Jerusalem by him, whereas it had previously been named Solyma.

Jerome likewise writes that it derived its name from the Jebusites, and that David, after exterminating them, made it the metropolis of the province of Judaea: “Because,” he says, “he bought the site of the Temple and left the costs of its construction to his son Solomon. Josephus relates that this is the Salem written of in Genesis under King Melchizedek” (Jerome, *Hebrew Questions*). There he surveys the opinions of the ancient Fathers of the Church, and adds that several authors whom he names expressly handed down [Col. 1032B] “that Melchizedek was a Canaanite, king of the city Jerusalem, which was first called Salem, afterwards Jebus, and finally Jerusalem” (Jerome, *Letter to Evangelus*). Yet he did not say at what times its name was changed. He nevertheless goes on to criticize Josephus and others who believed Salem to be Jerusalem and the latter name to be a compound of Greek and Hebrew. Suidas, however, thinks that it was called Jerusalem by Melchizedek.

Eusebius (*Preparation for the Gospel*, IX.34) records that Eupolemus committed the following to writing concerning the Jerusalem Temple built by Solomon:

> Προσαγορευσθῆναι δὲ πρῶτον μὲν τὸ ἀνάκτορον, ἱερὸν Σολομῶνος· ὕστερον δὲ παρεφθαρμένως τὴν πόλιν ἀπὸ τοῦ [Col. 1032C] ἱεροῦ Ἱερουσαλὴμ ὀνομασθῆναι· ὑπὸ δὲ τῶν Ἑλλήνων φερωνύμως Ἱεροσόλυμα λέγεσθαι.

“But first that sacred building was called Solomon’s temple. Afterwards the city itself was called Jerusalem, through a corrupt and altered form of the Temple’s name; and the Greeks subsequently called it Hierosolyma, by a similar and compound designation.”

You see, certainly, that there was no single opinion concerning the one who first gave Jerusalem its name, and that Lactantius lacked no defender of his own opinion.

But even if you convict him of error in this matter, you must nevertheless admit that he proves sufficiently, not indeed by every prophetic oracle he might have advanced, but by many—and the most certain—of the sacred prophets, that Christ would be born from a virgin and from David’s family. No less clearly he demonstrates that the eternal priesthood of the same Christ the Lord was foretold. This must now be examined.

## ARTICLE III

### By what prophetic oracles Lactantius demonstrates that the everlasting priesthood of Christ, author of true religion, was foretold

It did not suffice Lactantius to demonstrate by what clear and explicit oracles of the sacred prophets the altogether wondrous birth of Christ from a virgin and David’s family had been foretold. He proceeds further and shows that his everlasting priesthood was likewise predicted by them no less clearly. First, therefore, he proves (*Divine Institutes*, IV.14) that it was plainly foretold in these words of the Psalmist: “Before the morning star [Col. 1033A] I begot you. The Lord has sworn and will not repent: you are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109 [110]:4–5). Yet the latter three words are absent from two most ancient manuscript codices of the royal library. But that these words were truly spoken by the sacred bard concerning Christ is expressly asserted by the Apostle in his Epistle to the Hebrews (Hebrews 5:6).

Accordingly Tertullian argues thus: “This too is added here concerning him: ‘You are a priest for ever.’ Now Hezekiah was neither a priest nor eternal, even if he had been one. ‘According to the order,’ he says, ‘of Melchizedek.’ What has Hezekiah to do with Melchizedek, priest of the Most High, and indeed uncircumcised, who blessed circumcised Abraham after he had received the offering of tithes from him? But the order of Melchizedek will suit Christ, since Christ, God’s own and lawful high priest, pontiff of the uncircumcised priesthood, was then established among the nations, by whom he was rather to be received; and when he comes at the last, he will deem the circumcision and Abraham’s race worthy of acceptance and blessing, having then made himself known to them” (Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, V.9). Jerome treats this still more fully (*Letter to Evangelus*), after citing the words of both the Psalmist and the Apostle. Eusebius likewise does so in his *Demonstration of the Gospel* (IV.15), though more briefly in his commentary on the Psalms. Such also, in complete agreement, is the interpretation of Hilary (*Tractate on Psalm* 149), Cyprian, to be cited shortly, and others.

[Col. 1033C] Although David’s testimony, confirmed as we have said by apostolic authority, ought to suffice even the most obstinate person, Lactantius (*Divine Institutes*, IV.14) further proves the point by these words written in the First Book of Kings: “And I shall raise up for myself a faithful priest, who shall do all that is in my heart; and I shall build him a faithful house, and he shall pass before me all his days” (1 Kings 1:2). Cyprian likewise writes (*Testimonies against the Jews*, I.18) that Christ’s everlasting priesthood is prefigured by these words and by the preceding words of the Psalmist.

Lactantius further adduces (*Divine Institutes*, IV.14) this very clear testimony of Zechariah, as he calls it: “And the Lord God showed me Jesus” (both the older royal codices of Lactantius and Cyprian, *Testimonies*, II.14, have “Jesus”) [Col. 1033D] “the great priest standing before the face of the Angel of the Lord . . . And behold, a brand plucked from the fire; and Jesus was clothed in filthy garments and stood before the face of the Angel . . . If you walk in my ways . . . you shall judge my house . . . Hear therefore, O great priest” (Zechariah 3:1 ff.).

Lactantius makes it plain, therefore, that those are wholly deceived who think these words were spoken of Jesus son of Nave, that is, Joshua, or of Jesus the priest, son of Jozadak. Neither was defiled; neither, like a brand plucked from the fire, endured any adversity; neither stood in the presence of God and the angels. Finally, Zechariah spoke not of past events or of those dead men, but of some future man. But insofar as these things do not at all fit either of those Jesuses, so certainly do they altogether fit Jesus Christ. For he, clothed in a filthy garment—that is, human flesh—was extinguished like a brand by the fire of torments and the punishment of the cross. Moreover, Zechariah speaks of him who, after walking in God’s ways and fulfilling his will, would receive judgment and everlasting dominion. Now Christ alone, abolishing the false worship of gods and establishing true religion, fulfilled his Father’s will and command; and therefore, our author says, he received the dignity of an everlasting priest, the honor of supreme king, the authority of judge, and the name of God.

Justin Martyr (*Dialogue with Trypho*) presses the same words of Zechariah against Trypho and makes plain that the divine prophet spoke these things beforehand concerning Christ, not Joshua or another. Since his interpretation is rather lengthy, we refrain from quoting it and refer you to his readily available book. Meanwhile hear Tertullian (*Against the Jews*, 14), who explains the cited passage of Zechariah concerning Christ’s two advents and adds much that wholly accords with our Lactantius’s explanation:

> “In Zechariah,” he says, “in the person of Christ himself—indeed, in the mystery of his very name—the true high priest of the Father, Christ Jesus, is portrayed in a double guise for two advents. In the first, he is clothed in filthy garments, that is, in the lowliness of passible and mortal flesh, while the devil opposed him—the instigator, namely, of Judas the traitor, who had also tempted him after his baptism. Then, stripped of his former filth and adorned with a long robe, mitre, and clean turban, he is displayed as having attained glory and honor: this belongs to the second advent. Nor can you call him the son of Jozadak, who was never at all clothed in filthy garments but was always adorned with priestly attire and was never deprived of the priestly office. But this Jesus, Christ, the high priest of God the Father, came in his first advent in human and passible form, in lowliness even unto suffering; he himself also became in every respect a sacrifice for all of us. After his resurrection, clothed in the long robe, he was called priest for ever of God the Father.”

He repeats this, nearly in the same but fewer words, against Marcion (*Against Marcion*, III.7).

Cyprian (*Against the Jews*, II.13), however, interprets these things, like our author, of Christ’s first advent. But Jerome especially ought to be read (Jerome, *Commentary on Zechariah*, I, on the cited passage), for he admirably shows that the Jews wrongly and falsely explain Zechariah’s words concerning Jesus the priest, son of Jozadak, and that they must be understood of Christ Jesus. Eusebius likewise demonstrates at no less length and with no less clarity that they were spoken of the same Christ (*Demonstration of the Gospel*, IV.16).

Since, then, all these predictions concerning not only Christ’s altogether wondrous birth but also his everlasting priesthood were true and attained their fulfillment, no one can ever deny that they were uttered by the divine Spirit, that Christ was in fact sent by God, and that the religion he established is true. Lactantius [Col. 1035A] confirms this most remarkably by further oracles concerning Christ’s death. Let us therefore now, if you please, proceed to examine them.

## ARTICLE IV

### On other oracles of Apollo of Miletus, the Sibyls, and our sacred prophets, by which the impious Jewish conspiracy against Christ, the various torments to be inflicted upon him before his death, the manner of his death, the eclipse of the sun at his death, and his return to life were foretold; and how greatly these establish the truth of the Christian religion

Lactantius (*Divine Institutes*, IV.13) passes to other oracles in which Christ’s death, its circumstances, the miracles then performed, and his return from death and the underworld had been predicted. He plainly shows that these oracles were uttered not only by our sacred prophets, but also by other seers, Apollo of Miletus and the Sibyls, who possessed the highest authority among the pagans. He cites these three verses of Apollo of Miletus concerning Christ’s future mortal life and death:

> Θνητὸς ἔην κατὰ σάρκα, σοφὸς τερατώδεσιν ἔργοις,  
> Ἀλλ` ὑπὸ Χαλδαίων κριτῶν ὅπλοις συνάλωθεὶς,  
> Γόμφοις καὶ σκολόπεσσι πικρὴν ἀνέτλησε τελευτήν.

“He was mortal in the flesh, wise in wondrous works; but, seized by the weapons of Chaldaean judges, he endured a bitter end through nails and stakes.”

The Latin version in the royal manuscript no. 3736 of our Lactantius’s works is not word-for-word: “He was of a mortal body, wise in signs of works and wonders; seized under Chaldaean judges, pierced, he completed a bitter end” (*Ancient Oracles*, §5). These verses occur in printed collections of ancient oracles, but were drawn from our Lactantius. Yet Apollo of Miletus’s oracles are not infrequently mentioned by ancient writers. Besides Herodotus (II.178), Strabo (*Geography*, IV), Mela (*On the World*, I.17), Pliny (*Natural History*, V.20), Apuleius (*Metamorphoses*, IV), and others, Sozomen (*Ecclesiastical History*, I.9) testifies that Apollo replied to the Emperor Licinius, when consulted about the outcome of a war, by citing verses of Homer.

Lactantius observes that Apollo, by the customary deception of demons, called Christ’s body mortal and his works prodigious, so that pagans might believe him not to be God and might attribute the miracles he performed to magical arts and powers. Yet, in calling Christ mortal, Apollo did not dare to deny his divinity. Further, although by deceitful falsehood he wished to conceal that Christ’s miracles were performed by divine power, truth nevertheless compelled this very Apollo to call them prodigious; and, as we shall show below, to acknowledge that they were performed not by any magical arts but by God’s power. Finally, in calling Christ wise, he declares both that Christ’s teaching is wise and that those who follow it are wise.

Our author cites far more extensively (*Divine Institutes*, IV.18) verses of the Sibyls (*Sibylline Oracles*, I and VI), by which they had sung of most of Christ’s torments before death: that he would be altogether silent, defiled with spittle, struck with blows and scourges, crowned with thorns, given vinegar and gall to drink; that the Temple veil would be rent; that darkness would cover the brightest day; and finally that Christ would undergo the most cruel death [Col. 1036A], yet on the third day return from death and the underworld to life. But all these things, which our Lactantius recorded in Greek Sibylline verses, cannot be more aptly reproduced in Latin than in the words of Augustine (*City of God*, XVIII.23), who excerpted them from our Lactantius and confirms his meaning:

> “Lactantius inserts in his work certain Sibylline prophecies concerning Christ, although he does not state which Sibyl. But the passages he himself set down separately, I thought should be set down together as one lengthy passage, whereas he mentioned several short ones. ‘Thereafter he shall come into the wicked hands of unbelievers. They shall give God blows with unclean hands and shall spit forth poisonous spirits from their defiled mouths. He shall simply give his holy back to blows; and, receiving fists, shall keep silence, so that no one may recognize what Word he is or whence he came, that he may speak to those in the underworld; and he shall be crowned with a thorny crown. They gave him gall for food and vinegar for thirst; they shall display this table of inhospitality. For you, foolish one, did not recognize your God, who plays upon the minds of mortals; but you crowned him with thorns and mixed bitter gall. The veil of the Temple shall be rent, and at midday there shall be a very dark night for three hours. And he shall die by death, having received sleep for three days; and then, returning from the underworld, he shall first come to light, showing the beginning of resurrection to those recalled.’ Lactantius employed these Sibylline testimonies piecemeal throughout the course of his argument, as seemed demanded by the points he wished to prove. We have inserted nothing, but have joined them in a single sequence and have taken care to distinguish them only by headings—provided, that is, that subsequent copyists do not neglect to preserve them.”

Augustine undoubtedly transcribed this from the manuscript of Lactantius’s works which he had before him. Yet he cited the Sibylline oracles only in Latin, whereas in most of the oldest and more recent manuscripts and printed editions of Lactantius’s works they are given only in Greek. The Latin translation of the Sibylline oracles offered by Augustine is identical with that which, as we have already said, we read word for word opposite the Greek text in the second, most ancient royal-library manuscript of Lactantius’s works. You will find the Greek Sibylline oracles translated into Latin in printed collections of their books; but they were collected and transcribed from our Lactantius and other writers, even though some have thought that certain passages do not occur in them.

But Lactantius (*Divine Institutes*, IV.16), not content with citing these oracles concerning Christ accepted by the pagans, further shows clearly that our prophets, by inspiration of the divine Spirit, prophesied the same things and more concerning him. For, besides the fact that Christ himself predicted Judas’s betrayal—on which Eusebius says more (*Demonstration of the Gospel*, X.2–3)—and his own death, the Psalmist certainly prefigured the Jews’ impious conspiracy to put him to death in the words in which he sang that blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked. Justin Martyr (*First Apology*) teaches that these words are to be understood in the same way as Lactantius understands them. Tertullian (*On the Shows*, 3), however, although he applies them to forbidden pagan spectacles, nevertheless admits, because the meaning of sacred Scripture is varied and manifold, that they may also seem to have been spoken concerning that righteous man who did not share in the counsel and assembly of Jews deliberating on the Lord’s death.

Moreover, Lactantius (*ibid.*) judges that Solomon wrote more than a thousand years earlier, in the Book of Wisdom, concerning this conspiracy against Christ: “Let us beset the righteous man, because he is troublesome to us” (Wisdom 2:12 ff.). He transcribed the entire passage, as Cyprian had earlier done (*Against the Jews*, II.14, p. 40), and likewise did not doubt that it should be understood of Christ, whom the Jews were to kill. Here he follows his master Tertullian (*Against Marcion*, III.22), who judged that those words should also be explained in this sense.

Furthermore, Isaiah, Lactantius says (*Divine Institutes*, IV.18), had announced, as certainly as explicitly and not shortly beforehand, the scourges, blows, and spitting with which Christ was to be beaten and defiled before death. He cites (*ibid.*) these exact words of the sacred prophet: “I am not rebellious, nor do I resist; I gave my back to scourges and my cheeks to the palm; but I did not turn away my face from the foulness of spittle” (Isaiah 50:5). Cyprian (*Against the Jews*, II.13; *On the Good of Patience*, near the end) transcribed precisely these same words and interprets them likewise concerning Christ. So also Tertullian (*Against Marcion*, III.5; *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, 20), excepting the latter words, which he renders: “But I did not turn away my face from spitters.” The Septuagint: “from the shame of spittings”; the Vulgate: “But I do not resist; I did not turn back; I gave my body to those striking me and my cheeks to those plucking them; I did not turn away my face from those reviling and spitting upon me.” Jerome, at the beginning of Book XIV of his *Commentary on Isaiah*, reproves the Jews who wished these things to be understood of Isaiah, and shows, as do Justin Martyr (*First Apology*) and Irenaeus (*Against Heresies*, IV.68), that they were spoken of Christ.

Further, Lactantius (*Divine Institutes*, IV.18) teaches that this too was designated by these words of the Psalmist: “Scourges were gathered against me, and they knew not; they were dispersed and were not pierced with remorse; they tested me and mocked me with mockery, and gnashed their teeth over me” (Psalm 34 [35]:15–16). Although the Jews, as Eusebius says (*Commentary on this Psalm*), tried to explain these words of David, he and the other interpreters—whom it would take too long to name—judge in complete agreement that they were foretold concerning the suffering Christ the Lord. And the sacred narrative of the Evangelists makes it utterly clear that they were then fulfilled in him.

Lactantius continues that Isaiah also indicated the utter silence of the suffering Christ in these words: “Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearers is voiceless, so he did not open his mouth” [Col. 1038A] (Isaiah 53:7). The eunuch of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, was reading these words of Isaiah when Philip approached him; Philip demonstrated so clearly that they had been written concerning Christ that the eunuch embraced faith in Christ. What wonder, then, that all our writers—Justin Martyr (*Dialogue with Trypho*), Irenaeus (*Against Heresies*, IV.41), Tertullian (*Against the Jews*, 9 and 13), Cyprian (*Against the Jews*, II.15), Athanasius (*On the Incarnation of the Word*), Jerome (on the cited passage of Isaiah), and others—subscribed to this most evident interpretation?

Again, Lactantius says, the sacred Psalmist had sung that Christ would be given gall and vinegar to drink. For he said: “They gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.” Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, and Ambrose share this interpretation (Ambrose, *Commentary on Luke*, X.124). Tertullian (*Against the Jews*, 10 and 13) rebukes the Jews, who deny it in blind obstinacy, as follows:

> “So that the things predicted by the prophets as to befall him through you might be fulfilled, the Spirit of Christ himself already sang in the Psalms . . . ‘They put gall in my drink, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink’ . . . Having endured all these things, he did not suffer in any way for some act of his own, but in order that the Scriptures from the mouths of the prophets might be fulfilled.”

But Eusebius, in his commentary on this Psalm, and others treat the matter more fully.

Our Lactantius then adduces various testimonies from the same sacred prophets by which they foretold that Christ the Lord would be killed by the Jews. Yet the most difficult of all is the passage which he transcribed from the book of Ezra:

> “And Ezra said to the people: This Passover is our Savior and our refuge. Consider, and it shall rise in your heart, because we must humble him in a sign; and afterwards we shall hope in him, lest this place be deserted for everlasting time, says the Lord, God of hosts. If you do not believe him and do not heed his proclamation, you shall be a mockery among the nations.”

Justin Martyr (*Dialogue with Trypho*), who cited this entire passage in Greek, observes, as we have noted elsewhere, that it had been cut from Ezra’s text by the Jews—that is, from the books which he had read. Certainly neither he nor our Lactantius would have advanced it with such confidence against pagans and Jews unless they had read it in the books of Ezra which they had before them. There are nevertheless some who openly say that these words were fabricated by Christians, though through a certain pious fraud, by which they might more easily bring pagans and others to faith in Christ. But those who accuse the most ancient Fathers in this manner perhaps employ not a pious but a malicious fraud, in order to weaken their authority. For, I ask you, what need had Justin and Lactantius of that pious fraud? Was this the sole testimony in all the books of the sacred prophets and in the whole of sacred Scripture concerning Christ’s death? In that case, such a pious fraud might have been useful. But many other passages met them everywhere—as they did Justin Martyr, concerning whom we have spoken elsewhere, Eusebius (*Demonstration of the Gospel*), [Col. 1039A] and others—by which the same things were predicted no less clearly.

Certainly our Lactantius (*Divine Institutes*, IV.17) did not set down all of them, but selected several which, as we shall explain, are no less clear and manifest. First, these words of Isaiah express them: “In his humiliation judgment was taken away. Who shall recount his generation? For his life shall be taken from the earth; he was led to death because of the crimes of my people. And I shall give the wicked for his burial and the rich for his death, he who committed no crime and spoke no deceit with his mouth. Therefore he shall obtain many, and he shall divide the spoils of the strong, because he was delivered up to death and was numbered among evildoers; and he bore the sin of many and was delivered up because of their crimes” (Isaiah 52:8 ff.). Cyprian (*Against the Jews*, II.15) cites this in the same way and for the same reason, apart from a few variant readings, especially this: “Because his soul was delivered up to death.” But he also omits several words inserted in Isaiah’s sacred text. Tertullian (*Against the Jews*, 10 and 12), though transcribing fewer words from this same passage of Isaiah, interprets it in the same sense concerning Christ and rebuts Jewish obstinacy. This had likewise been the view earlier of Irenaeus (*Against Heresies*, IV.40) and later of Jerome (on this passage in Isaiah) and others.

Lactantius next (*ibid.*) further proves the point by these words of David: “They shall hunt for the soul of the righteous and condemn innocent blood; and the Lord became my refuge” (Psalm 93 [94]:21–22). Huet (*Demonstration of the Gospel*, proposition 9, chapter 126) and some others do not doubt that these words are to be understood in the same sense. Yet it must be admitted that far more others explain them concerning righteous people whom the ungodly habitually harass.

More apt, therefore, for proving this are the words of Jeremiah that Lactantius cites (*ibid.*): “Lord, make known to me, and I shall know. Then I saw their plans. I was led as a spotless lamb to sacrifice. They devised a plan against me, saying: Come, let us put wood into his bread, and let us root his life out of the earth; and his name shall no longer be remembered” (Jeremiah 11:18–19). In [Col. 1039D] the two most ancient royal codices, “without malice” is written instead of “spotless.” This is likewise the reading in Cyprian (*Against the Jews*, II.15), who set down the entire passage in the same manner and sense. In the Septuagint it is written in Greek, ὡς ἀρνίον ἄκακον [*hōs arnion akakon*], “like an innocent and pure lamb.” Neither Cyprian nor Lactantius follows this Greek translation entirely word for word (*kata podas*).

Our author further says that “wood” means the cross and “bread” signifies Christ’s body. Tertullian likewise says: “Concerning this sign of the cross God also gives an intimation through Jeremiah, which you were to say: ‘Come, let us put wood into his bread, and destroy him from the land of the living, and his name shall no longer be remembered.’ Certainly wood was put into his body. For thus Christ revealed it, calling bread his body, whose body the prophet formerly prefigured in bread” (Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, 10). He repeats the same elsewhere (*Against Marcion*, III.19). What need is there to cite many others here, when Jerome, at the end of Book II of his *Commentary on Jeremiah*, expressly declares this to have been the consensus of all the churches, which confess that these things were said by Christ under the person of Jeremiah? We have also already observed that Justin Martyr enumerates this passage among those which the Jews undoubtedly removed from the sacred codices—not from all of them, but perhaps from the one he alone had seen.

Lactantius continues (*ibid.*), teaching that this further prophecy concerning the same cross of Christ is, in his view, more plainly proclaimed by these words of Moses: “Your life shall be hanging before your eyes, and you shall fear by day and by night and shall not believe in your life” (Deuteronomy 28:66). Cyprian transcribed this passage in precisely the same words and explains it in the same way. Tertullian (*Against the Jews*, 11 and 13) had preceded both, but through a lapse of memory thought that the words had been transcribed from Exodus rather than Deuteronomy. Yet this did not prevent very many, including Augustine (*Against Faustus*, XVI.22), Procopius (on this passage in Deuteronomy), and Leo the Great (*Sermon* 8 *on the Passion*), from subscribing to his interpretation. We know that some accuse them on this account of error, because others do not consider this to be the genuine meaning of Moses’ words. But who does not know that one and the same passage of sacred Scripture has various meanings: one, as they say, literal; another, such as this one, prophetic?

Further, Lactantius (*Divine Institutes*, IV.18) believes that the same cross of Christ is indicated by these words of Moses in the Book of Numbers: “The Lord is not suspended as a man, nor does he suffer less as a son of man” (Numbers 23:19). We are not unaware that this passage is presented differently in the commonly printed Bibles. But it is no less certain to us that Cyprian (*Against the Jews*, II.20) not only explains it in the same sense, but also transcribes it in precisely the same words, except that he writes “God” instead of “Lord.” Who can doubt that both read these words in their own biblical codices as they transcribed them?

[Col. 1040D] Perhaps greater difficulty attends the words Lactantius adds shortly afterward: that Solomon foretold, in these words, the most disastrous destruction of Jerusalem as vengeance, in his view, for the holy cross: “But if you turn away from me . . . Israel shall be for destruction and reproach” (manuscripts: “reproach” . . .), “because they forsook the Lord their God, persecuted their king beloved by God, and tortured him in great humiliation; for this reason God brought these evils upon them” (3 Kings [1 Kings] 9:6 ff.). Although most of these words seem to have been taken from the Second Book of Kings or from Chronicles, the words, “and persecuted . . . in great humiliation” (Chronicles 7:19 ff.)—the only words bearing upon Lactantius’s argument—are found in neither book. Moreover, in both books the words that are found are not Solomon’s, but God’s words to Solomon. Must it not therefore be said either that copyists erred in transcribing Lactantius’s text, or that Lactantius himself suffered a lapse of memory, unless it can be proved that he excerpted these words from some biblical codex different from ours?

Yet even if Lactantius (Lactant., *Institutions*, IV.18) had adduced certain testimonies from the sacred Scriptures which seemed to him alone, and not at all to others, to have been spoken concerning Christ, it must nevertheless be certain that he also brings forward others which no sound-minded person could ever deny to have been truly foretold concerning Christ [Col. 1041B]. For, besides those already mentioned, undoubtedly of this sort is that which, following Cyprian, he introduced from the book of Zechariah: “Zechariah,” he says, “also handed down these words: ‘And they shall look upon me whom’ (Cyprian, *Against the Jews*, II, §20: ‘upon whom’) ‘they pierced’” (Zech. 12:10). For who indeed will deny that these words must be understood of Christ, after John the Evangelist most expressly affirmed (John 17:37 [apparently 19:37]) that, when Christ died, the Scripture had been fulfilled which said: “They shall look upon him whom they pierced”? The testimony of this divine writer is of such authority that it seems superfluous to cite others besides. Yet if anyone still wishes to consult Jerome (Jerome, on the cited passage of Zechariah), he will undoubtedly not regret the effort.

[Col. 1041C] With no less evidence, certainly, is the same point demonstrated by the words of the Psalmist which Lactantius next adduces (*ibid.*): “They pierced my hands and my feet; they numbered all my bones. But they themselves looked upon me and saw me; they divided my garments among themselves, and cast lots over my clothing” (Ps. 21 [22]:18–19). Cyprian likewise (*Against the Jews*, II, §20) interprets these words in precisely the same sense. But the Psalmist, as Lactantius says, spoke these words not of himself, who suffered nothing similar, but, inspired by the divine Spirit, foretold Christ. Tertullian likewise says: “Scripture says in the Psalms: ‘They destroyed’ [he had first written, ‘they dug’] ‘my hands and feet; they numbered all my bones. But they looked upon me and saw me . . .’ [Col. 1041D] David did not suffer these things, so that he could rightly seem to have said them of himself; but Christ did, who was crucified” (Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, chs. 10 and 13). Indeed, he expressly asserts that the passion Christ was to undergo is sung throughout that entire Psalm without exception. And, to pass over many others, Justin Martyr (*Dialogue with Trypho*) and Eusebius (*Evangelical Demonstration*) expound the whole Psalm and each of its verses concerning these same final torments and death of Christ. Matthew (Matt. 27:35) and John (John 19:24), moreover, teach that what had been foretold in the same Psalm about his garments being divided by lot then came to pass.

At that very time, Lactantius says (Lactant., [Col. 1042A] IV.19), when Christ freely and willingly breathed out his life, the light of the sun failed and all things were enveloped in darkness for three hours. Yet the prophet cited by him had foreshadowed this in these words: “And it shall come to pass in that day, says the Lord, that the sun shall set at noon, and the day of light shall be darkened; and I shall turn your feast-days into mourning, and your songs into lamentation” (Amos 8:9–10). Cyprian (*Against the Jews*, II, §23) cited this prophecy in the same way, except that before “songs” he added “all.” Irenaeus, however, somewhat differently: “In that day, says the Lord, the sun shall set at noon, and there shall be darkness over the earth in the day of light . . . and all your songs into lamentation. They plainly announced that setting of the sun which occurred from the sixth hour when he was crucified” (Irenaeus, IV [Col. 1042B] *Against Heresies*, ch. 61). Tertullian too (*Against the Jews*, ch. 10) presses this prophecy against the Jews, who denied that it should be understood of Christ: “For Amos the prophet announces what happened at his passion, namely, that midday was darkened, saying: ‘And it shall come to pass in that day, says the Lord, the sun shall set in the middle of the day, and the day of light shall be darkened over the earth; and I shall turn your days into mourning and all your songs into lamentation.’” Hence he wrote elsewhere: “Certainly those considered it an eclipse who did not know that this too had been foretold concerning Christ. Yet you have the account of that cosmic event in your archives” (the same, *Apology*, ch. 21). Finally, he argues from the already cited oracle of Amos against Marcion, just as against the Jews (the same, *Against Marcion*). [Col. 1042C] Jerome, however (Jerome, on the cited passage of Amos), explains it both of the Jews’ captivity among the Assyrians and Chaldaeans and of Christ the Lord crucified. But what is surprising in this, since we have already observed that our sacred text has several meanings and interpretations, all of which no one can rightly deny to be true?

Nor was it enough for our sacred prophets to foretell to all Christ’s death and what happened at that time, unless they had also foretold the mystery of his resurrection, without which, as the Apostle says (Paul, 1 Cor. 15:17), our faith would be vain. Lactantius proves that this was clearly foretold by them (Lactant., IV.19) with these words of the Psalmist: “You will not leave my soul among the dead, nor give [Col. 1042D] your Holy One to see destruction” (Ps. 15 [16]:10). Cyprian had previously set down the same words in writing (*Against the Jews*, II, §24), except for the last word, in place of which he put “corruption.” This prediction is so clear and manifest that the Apostle Peter, in his first discourse to the Jews (Acts 2:25 ff.), plainly demonstrates that it was perfectly fulfilled not in David, who had died and been buried among them, but in Christ, restored from the dead to life. Paul likewise shows precisely the same thing in his address to them (Acts 13:35 ff.). Therefore, since this oracle is confirmed by the authority of such great Apostles, to strengthen it by the testimony of others would be as lengthy as it would be useless. For to whom, pray, will one who does not believe them ever give credence?

Lactantius does not stop there, but proves the same thing again with these words of the same Psalmist: “I slept and took sleep, and I rose again, because the Lord has helped me” (Ps. 3:6). Cyprian too gives these words, word for word (*Against the Jews*, II, §24). Justin Martyr (*First Apology*, alternatively the second) and Irenaeus (IV *Against Heresies*, ch. 15) assure us that Christ, speaking in David’s person, uttered these words concerning his death and return to life.

Moreover, the prophet Hosea had clearly foretold, not in one oracle only but in two, that this same Christ would one day return to life. For he had said: “This is my wise son, because he will now resist in the affliction [Col. 1043B] of his sons; and I shall deliver him from the hand of the dead. Where is your judgment, O death, or where is your sting?” (Hos. 13:13–14). Here he follows, as usual, the interpretation of the Seventy, though not without certain variant readings. The Apostle Paul, as everyone knows, cited the latter words of the prophet in his letter to the Corinthians (1 Cor. 15:54). Therefore Jerome (III *Commentary on Hosea*, ch. 13) drew this conclusion from the words of the Apostle cited by him: “Therefore, what he interpreted of the resurrection of the Lord, we can neither interpret otherwise nor dare to do so.”

Another testimony of Hosea, cited by Lactantius in the second place, is expressed thus: “He will give us life after two days; on the third day” (Hos. 6:2). [Col. 1043C] Cyprian also transcribed these words verbatim (*Against the Jews*, II, §25), and he, Tertullian (*Against the Jews*, ch. 15; IV *Against Marcion*, ch. 44), and later Jerome (on the cited passage of Hosea), as well as others, interpret them similarly.

Finally, Lactantius adds that Daniel foretold that Christ, restored from death to life, would ascend into heaven. But we discussed this prophecy a little earlier.

Who, then, does not now understand with what right Lactantius said (Lactant., IV.14) that “all the prophets”—that is, our sacred prophets and others whom the pagans regarded as seers—“announced concerning Christ that, born bodily from David’s stock, he would establish for God an everlasting temple, called the Church, [Col. 1043D] and would summon all nations to the true religion of God”? For it could not be that so many oracles—concerning Christ’s altogether wondrous birth from a virgin and from David’s family; his supreme priesthood; the utterly unjust conspiracy of the Jews against him; his most dreadful tortures; his terrible death; and his return to life—foretold long beforehand, should have proceeded from anyone but the divine Spirit. Thus it follows as certainly as it does clearly from them that Christ was sent by God his Father to bring human beings from the false and impious worship of gods to the true religion which he founded. Therefore neither Jew nor pagan, unless struck by incurable blindness, can deny that this is a most certain [Col. 1044A] and invincible argument for demonstrating the Christian religion. But Lactantius advances other arguments of no less weight, which must now be examined.

## CHAPTER III

How Lactantius asserts and confirms the truth of the Christian religion from Christ’s genuine miracles, which had been foretold by our sacred prophets and others.

### ARTICLE I

With what evidence Lactantius shows that Christ’s religion is true, confirmed by genuine miracles designated by Isaiah and the Sibyl.

Lactantius derives another argument for asserting and proving the truth of the Christian religion from Christ’s miracles: both because they were performed by him truly and through divine power, and because the sacred prophets and others had in fact foretold them long before they occurred. For God communicates neither the inspiration of his Spirit nor the more powerful part of his divine power for performing true miracles to others, except in order to uphold truth and to convey and establish sound and true teachings. Therefore the religion which Christ founded by genuine miracles—foretold long beforehand and performed by himself through divine power—must wholly and necessarily be true and holy.

But Christ, Lactantius says (Lactant., IV.4), performed “very great powers,” which Apollo, mentioned earlier by us, called “wonder-working,” “not by magical tricks, which display nothing true or solid, but by heavenly force and power, which had long before been sung of by prophets announcing them.” For wherever Christ went, he healed every sort of sufferer—paralytics, the lame, the blind, the mute, lepers, and others—not by hand or medicines, but by word and command alone, in a single instant [Col. 1044C]. Indeed, in the same manner he also restored the dead to life. Now Isaiah had announced that such sick persons would be restored by Christ to their former health. The following prophecy of his was quoted by Lactantius, and earlier by Cyprian: “Strengthen the feeble hands, and comfort the weak knees” (the oldest royal manuscript reads *consoldamini*; Cyprian, *Against the Jews*, II, reads “exhort”); “you who are faint-hearted, do not fear.
