Our Lord will render judgment. He himself will come and save us. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall hear. [Col. 1044D] Then the lame man shall leap like a stag, and the tongue of the mute shall be made plain” (Isa. 15:3 ff. [materially uncertain citation; likely an OCR error]). Here neither Lactantius nor Cyprian adheres wholly either to the Septuagint or to the Vulgate, but to another version somewhat different from both. Jerome collected the variant readings of each (Jerome, X *Commentary on the cited passage of Isaiah*) and openly showed that what is said there had its fulfillment in Christ and the Apostles. Earlier Tertullian (*Against the Jews*, ch. 9; *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 20; IV *Against Marcion*, chs. 10 and 12) refutes from this passage the almost incredible obstinacy of the Jews and of Marcion, and demonstrates that these things were foretold of Christ and truly performed by him.

Indeed, the Sibyl, whose credibility pagans could not impugn, sang of the same miracles of Christ in these verses, which Lactantius (IV.16) cited in Greek and which are rendered in Latin thus in the royal manuscript: “There will be resurrection of the dead; the course of the lame will be most swift; the deaf will hear; the blind will see; and those who do not speak will speak” (*Sibylline Oracles*, VIII.226 ff.). Moreover, the same Sibyl had sung in one verse that Christ would do these things by his word alone:

> Πάντα λόγῳ πράττων, πᾶσάν τε νόσον θεραπεύων.  
> Accomplishing all things by a word, and healing every disease.

(*The same, after the Acrostic; Lactantius, cited passage.*)

The writer of the aforementioned royal manuscript rendered this in Latin: “Doing all things by a word, and curing every infirmity.” Lactantius very aptly observed that it was no wonder Christ wrought wonders by a word (the royal manuscripts: “would work”), since he himself was the Word of God, supported by heavenly force and power [Col. 1045B].

He continues and says that five thousand people, perishing from hunger in the wilderness, were satisfied by Christ with only five loaves and two fishes. We discussed these in the preceding dissertation. Yet what, our author asks (Lactant., cited passage), can be said or done more wonderful than this (*Sibylline Oracles*, VIII.302 ff.)? The Sibyl had likewise foretold this event in these verses which he transcribed and which are found similarly in published editions of the Oracles, apart from some variant readings.

Furthermore, Christ not only walked dry-shod upon the waves of the sea, but also calmed the storms of that sea by his word. Lactantius adds: “Not as the poets falsely say that Orion walked upon the sea, [Col. 1045C] who, with his body submerged, rose above the waves at the shoulder.” Betuleius, followed by Gallaeus, observes here that this is the half-line of some poet; but neither identifies him. Yet with little effort they could have learned that it is Virgil’s, whose verses are these (*Aeneid*, X.763 ff.):

> When mighty Orion walks with his feet through the vast pools of mid-Nereus, cleaving a path, he rises above the waves at the shoulder.

Who can doubt that Lactantius points to and ridicules these words? See Servius’s notes on those verses and on Book I of the same *Aeneid*, Natalis Comes, and others.

Lactantius again shows (IV.15) that these things had long ago been designated in the songs of the Sibyls, which we read in their various books. Although he transcribed them only in Greek, they are rendered in Latin in the royal manuscript, so often mentioned by us, as follows: “He will restrain the winds; he will tread the raging sea under foot, pacified by the pledge of peace. And again, somewhere she said: He will walk upon the waves, remove human infirmity, make the dead rise, drive away many pains, and from the bread of one *perion* there shall be a satisfying of men.” Here *perionis* is written because the Greek reads πέρης ἄρτου, that is, “of a sack and a bag of bread.” But some printed editions read ῥίζης, others πηγῆς, “a spring”; perhaps πήρης is better: from one bag or sack of bread, by which the small number of loaves is more clearly denoted. In any event, we have often furnished curious and learned readers with the Latin rendering in the aforementioned royal manuscript of Lactantius’s works, so that they may more easily see how it differs from others and which Greek words have been corrupted [Col. 1046A].

But let us see what pagans and Jews objected against the authority of Christ’s so many and hitherto unheard-of miracles. First, they replied that the songs of the Sibyls had been composed not by them but by us—that is, by Christian writers—under a deceptive title.

Lactantius (IV.15), however, shows this answer to be futile and empty. For Varro, Cicero, and the ancients mention the Erythraean Sibyl and others. Christians, moreover, had transcribed from the books of those authors the testimonies which they cite; their trustworthiness could not be doubted, since they had died before Christ became man [Col. 1046B].

The Jews, however, with undoubtedly greater audacity and rashness, loudly asserted that Christ had indeed performed these miracles, but entirely by magical arts. No greater slander, our author says, could be imagined. For Christ, as he puts it, “began to perform very great powers not by magical tricks, which display nothing true or solid”—that is, nothing true or beneficial and useful to others. For things performed by magic or by the deceptions of demons are done solely in order to deceive people. Christ’s miracles, however, were performed by divine force and power, not by any evil art but, as we have said, by a word alone, in order that people might be brought to worship the true God and embrace true religion. Further, the Jews could not deny [Col. 1046C] that Christ had performed these miracles, just as they had been foretold in their secret writings—that is, the books of the Old Testament. And by whom had they been foretold long beforehand, if not by men, as we have seen, inspired by the divine Spirit, who could harm no one, deceive no one, and could never lie? Finally, we have shown elsewhere that Arnobius and others refuted and overthrew this most foolish accusation, not merely of the Jews but of pagans too.

Lactantius therefore rightly concludes (IV.13 and 15) that Christ, through such great miracles and prodigies, earned credence both as a truthful envoy sent by God and as divine himself. Indeed, they were the surest indications of heavenly power, by which, clearer than the noonday sun, he proved true the religion which he founded and established. But Lactantius further demonstrates most clearly, from other miracles of Christ by which he put demons—the authors of magical arts—to flight, that these deeds were performed by him not through any tricks or contrivances of magicians but wholly by divine power, and that thereby the truth of the Christian religion is remarkably strengthened. These matters, however, must be examined in the following article [Col. 1046D].

### ARTICLE II

How invincibly Lactantius demonstrates the truth of the Christian religion from demons put to flight by Christ, by his name, and by the sign of the cross.

So far was Christ from performing miracles by the tricks and arts of magicians or demons that both he himself [Col. 1047A] and his disciples drove demons to flight by wondrous power and cast them out of the bodies of people whom they possessed. Now, as Lactantius rightly argues (IV.27), “It must be that religion is true which knows the nature of demons, understands their cunning, repels their force, and compels them, subdued and subjected by spiritual weapons, to yield to it.” These demons are either friends of Jupiter, Aesculapius, and the other gods whom pagans worship, joined to them by some bond, or, conversely, enemies hostile to them. If they are joined together, and, as Homer says (*Iliad*, I.221), Jupiter is associated with demons; if poets and philosophers call them now demons, now gods, how shall we distinguish them from one another, so as to worship and honor them duly as distinct? But if the eminent gods of the pagans are truly enemies and foes of demons, why do they not put them to flight, and why do they not possess the same power as Christ and his disciples to cast them out? What force or power will these gods have if demons are not subject to them? Why, too, are demons driven away in Christ’s name, but not in the name of Jupiter or of the other gods, unless it is because they fear Christ but not false gods? And certainly, where they are worshipped, they pretend to be gods; where they are adjured by Christians, they are compelled openly to confess that they are demons. Why is so disgraceful a confession forced from them, unless they are struck by great fear of the Christians who adjure them?

But let us hear Lactantius himself, if it pleases you, relating all this—and indeed not once only: “They fear the righteous,” he says, that is, worshippers of God; “adjured in his name, they depart from bodies. At their words, as though beaten with whips, demons not only confess themselves to be demons but also reveal their names—the very names worshipped in temples. And this they often do before their own worshippers, certainly not to disgrace their religion but their own honor” (two very ancient royal manuscripts read “and their own honor”), “because they can lie neither to God, by whom they are adjured, nor to the righteous, by whose voice they are tormented. Thus, uttering very loud howls, they cry out that they are being beaten and burned and are just about to depart” (II.15; IV.27; V.21). Elsewhere we have noted and explained the same reports from Minucius Felix [Col. 1047C].

But if such is the fear of demons, who fraudulently turn people away from veneration of the true God toward the impious worship of false gods; if such is the weakness both of those gods and of the demons; but, conversely, if Christians, who worship the true God, exercise such dominion over demons and have such power to drive them away—does it not follow most certainly that the Christians’ religion is as true as the pagans’ is false?

Lactantius presses the argument still more strongly and makes it clear that the same demons were filled with extreme terror even by the sign of the cross; when it was made, just as when they were adjured in Christ’s name, they were immediately cast out from the bodies of people which they held possessed. Our author recounts this not as something uncertain or obscure, but as something very well known and entirely certain to all people of his own time. “Now,” he says, “his followers”—namely, Christ’s—“expel those same unclean spirits from people by both the name of their master and the sign of his passion” (Lactant., IV.27). Nor did they turn these wicked spirits to flight secretly and in concealment, but openly and publicly, even while pagans themselves sacrificed to their gods. For if, as he says, someone stood by wearing a forehead marked with the sign, they could by no means obtain favorable omens, or, as Virgil, cited by him, sang (*Georgics*, III.149):

> Nor can the consulted seer give responses.

He emphatically asserts that this happened not once or rarely, but frequently. For he immediately adds that this was often the chief reason why evil emperors persecuted righteousness—that is, Christians [Col. 1048A].

Yet he selected one memorable example from among many, which he set forth in these words: “When certain of our attendants” (in the two older royal manuscript codices, instead of “our attendants,” we read “some worshippers of God”) “stood by their masters while they sacrificed, they put the sign upon their foreheads and drove their gods away, so that they could not portray the future in the entrails of the victims. When the haruspices perceived this, urged on by those same demons ‘whom they sacrifice to’” (the noted royal codices read *prosecrant*; one, in a second hand, *consecrant*; the Florentine edition, *prosequerant*), “complaining that profane—that is, Christian—persons were present at the rites, they drove their rulers to madness in order that they might purify” (the aforesaid royal manuscripts and many others, both older and more recent, together with the latest edition, read “might attack”) “the temple of God, and might themselves be polluted by sacrilege, which would be expiated by the most severe punishments of persecutors” [Col. 1048B–C].

The two different manuscript readings yield a double sense for Lactantius. If one reads “might attack the temple of God,” it will mean the temple at Nicomedia, which, at Diocletian’s command, as Lactantius himself later relates, was attacked and destroyed. But if one reads “might purify the temple of God,” the sense will be that the pagans might expiate the temple of their god, which they believed had been defiled by Christians.

Whatever Lactantius’s true reading may be, it is plainly understood from it that demons were terrified and put to flight by Christians making the sign of the cross. Lucius Caecilius recounts this more fully in his book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, where he explains to us why Emperor Diocletian began to rage against Christians. There we read: [Col. 1048D] “Then certain attendants, knowing the Lord, while they stood by one who was sacrificing, put the immortal sign upon their foreheads. When this had been done, the demons fled and the rites were thrown into confusion. The haruspices were alarmed, seeing none of the customary marks in the entrails; and, as though they had not obtained favorable omens, they sacrificed repeatedly. But the victims continually slain showed nothing, until that master of haruspices, Tages, whether by suspicion or sight, said that the rites did not respond because unclean persons, namely Christians, were present at the sacred acts. Then, raging with anger, he ordered not only those ministering at the rites but all who were in the palace to sacrifice, and ordered that those who refused be punished with beatings. He also sent letters to the commanders, ordering soldiers as well to be compelled to perform the abominable sacrifices, so that those who did not obey should be discharged from military service” (Caecilius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, ch. 10). You see clearly how emphatically both affirm that pagan rites were disturbed when Christians made the sign of the Lord’s cross, and that Diocletian, present there, then ordered persecution of these and other Christians [Col. 1049A].

Although the testimony of both Lactantius and Lucius Caecilius, as we have shown elsewhere, concerning demons put to flight by the sign of the cross is wholly certain and cannot rightly be called into doubt by any sound-minded person, yet if anyone asks that this be proved to him from elsewhere, we shall first give him Athanasius as witness. He openly testifies that, when the sign of Christ’s cross is made, demons and gods are struck dumb as though dead, and their magical tricks are rendered ineffectual:

> Τῷ δὲ σημείῷ τοῦ σταυροῦ πᾶσα μὲν μαγεία παύεται, πᾶσα δὲ φαρμακεία καταργεῖται.  
> “But by the sign of the cross every magical art ceases, and every spell is abolished.”

(Athanasius, *On the Incarnation of the Word of God*.)

Accordingly Cyril of Jerusalem exhorted the Christians committed to his care: “Let us not, then, be ashamed of Christ’s cross; but if someone else conceals it, do you openly mark it upon your forehead, so that the demons, seeing the royal sign, may flee trembling far away.”

> Μὴ τοίνυν ἐπαισχυνθῶμεν τῷ σταυρῷ τοῦ Χριστοῦ, ἀλλὰ κἂν ἄλλος ἀποκρύπτῃ, σὺ φανερῶς ἐπὶ μετώπῳ σφραγίζου, ἵνα οἱ δαίμονες τὸ σημεῖον ἰδόντες τὸ βασιλικὸν, μακρὰν φύγωσι τρέμοντες.

(Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catecheses*, IV, §10.) “For,” he says, “the invocation of another crucified person does not drive away demons.”

[Col. 1049C] Nor did Gregory Nazianzen express less clearly the divine power of this saving sign of the cross and of Christ’s invoked name in these verses:

> . . . . Ἐγὼ Χριστοῦ λάχος οὔνομα σεπτὸν  
> Πολλάκι μοῦνον ἔειπον· ὅδ` ᾤχετο τηλόθι δαίμων  
> Τρύζων, ἀσχαλόων τε, βοῶν σθένος ὑψιμέδοντος·  
> Ἢ σταυροῦ μεγάλοιο χαράγματι, μηδὲ μένοντι,  
> Ἠέρα μέσσον ἔγραψα, τύπος δὲ ἔστησε τρόπαιον.

> I myself, Christ’s renowned portion, often by uttering his revered name alone drove out demons, shrieking, groaning, and crying out the strength of the God who rules Olympus on high; or I traced the middle air with the mark of the great cross, and this sign raised a splendid trophy over the foe.

(Gregory Nazianzen, *Poem* 61.)

What is more, that man, undoubtedly most worthy of belief, and after him Theodoret (III *Ecclesiastical History*, ch. 3), provide us with the celebrated example of Julian the Apostate, than which nothing could ever be desired more effective for showing the power of the sign of the cross over demons. For that impious emperor, as they testify, after abandoning the Christian religion, descended into an underground and dreadful shrine, attended by only one companion, in order to devote himself to magical arts. But terrified by unfamiliar sounds, foul odors, and fiery apparitions, “he fled,” says Gregory, “to the cross and the old remedy; with it he marked himself against the terrors, and summoned as his helper the one whom he persecuted,” namely Christ. “The sign prevailed; the demons yielded, and the terrors were driven away. What followed? The wretch regained his breath, conceived boldness again, attacked again; again [Col. 1050A] the same terrors pressed upon him; again the sign was applied, and the demons became quiet.”

Since pagans could not deny these public facts, known to all, by what reasoning, do you suppose, did they attempt to weaken them? They replied, Lactantius says (IV.27), that the gods did this not from fear (incorrectly in the printed editions, “by assent”) but from hatred. Please do not imagine that our author invented this freely in order to refute it more easily. For the already cited Gregory Nazianzen and Theodoret make us more certain that the priest of the rites who clung to Julian’s side, replying to Julian himself as he greatly marveled at the power of the cross, said: “We became an abomination to them, not a terror”; or, as Theodoret writes: “The demons did not fear, as you suppose, but withdrew because they abhorred your act.”

But Lactantius thoroughly overturns this foolish quibble. For if gods or demons had possessed any power, it would have been fitting—indeed undoubtedly necessary—that they should not flee those whom they hated and detested as fortified with the sign of the cross, but rather should inflict present punishments upon them. For this shameful flight was the surest indication of the victory Christians had won over those very demons. Therefore no one could deny that the Christians’ religion was as true as it was victorious, since they put demons to flight and subdued them by the sign of the cross alone [Col. 1050B].

Who, therefore, would not wonder at Gallaeus, just as at the other adherents of his party, enemies of the saving sign of the cross, who observes on this passage of Lactantius that he attributed more to the sign of the cross than was fitting, since he said it terrified demons? For, I ask you, what did he attribute to it in excess? “Demons,” says Gallaeus, “were not terrified by the sign of the cross, but by the cross itself—that is, by the death of Christ put to death on the cross.” But that eminent man ought first to have proved most clearly that the writers, not of doubtful credibility, whom we have cited so far, had lied. Gallaeus neither proved this nor took care to prove it. Yet if Julian, that impious apostate, no longer a sincere follower of Christ—if indeed he ever was one—drove away demons, as we said, merely by placing the sign of the cross upon his forehead, it must be all the more certain that true and pious disciples of Christ drove them away by this alone [Col. 1050C].

Gallaeus presses the point: Paul wrote in his letter to the Hebrews that the devil was destroyed by Christ’s death. What follows from this? Does it follow from these words that demons were not put to flight by the sign of Christ’s cross alone? Quite the contrary: because Christ destroyed the devil by his death, it surely follows that the sign of his cross is terrifying to the devil and demons.

The heterodox man further insists that Lactantius did not say demons were expelled by the bare sign of the cross, but by both the master’s name and the sign of his passion—which, he says, we also grant. It is well that he finally grants what he could no longer deny. But if demons were expelled by both Christ’s name and the sign of his cross, then that saving sign certainly had some power to expel them. For why else would it have been employed in vain? Yet Lactantius immediately added what Gallaeus seems to have concealed not without fraud and deceit: while pagans were sacrificing, demons took flight when attending Christians placed the sign of Christ’s cross upon their foreheads. But there Lactantius, like the others whom we have cited, made mention of the sign of the Lord’s cross alone. Moreover, all Catholics openly profess, whatever heterodox slanderers may prattle to the contrary, that this power of the sign of the cross derives not from the sign by itself but from the divine power of which it is an instrument [Col. 1051A].

### ARTICLE III

The arguments of pagans are refuted, by which they vainly attempted to prove that Apollonius of Tyana had performed miracles like Christ’s, or even greater ones, or that these miracles had been fabricated by the Apostles for profit.

As greatly as the Christian religion is established by Christ’s true and certainly astounding miracles, pagans have, with equal boldness and effort, so often as vainly repeated, endeavored to deny or weaken them. One of them, whose name Lactantius spared and whom we have shown above to have been Hierocles, undertook by a peculiar but entirely empty and futile argument to depress and diminish all Christ’s miracles. Since he could not deny them, he wished to show—these are Lactantius’s words—that Apollonius had performed miracles equal or even greater (Lactant., V, *Divine Institutions*, ch. 3). This Apollonius of Tyana was a famous follower of Pythagorean philosophy, flourishing toward the end of the first century of the Church, as is noted in Eusebius’s *Chronicle* (Eusebius, *Chronicle*, at A.D. 96). Philostratus composed eight books, which still survive, on his life, in a style, as Photius says, clear, pleasing, and concise. There various and very great miracles are recounted, of which Photius himself lists a few; he concludes his narrative thus: “Having fabulized many other things like these, full of folly, he expends in eight books all the effort of his utterly vain labor.”

> Παραπλήσια τούτοις ἀνοίας μεστὰ καὶ ἕτερα πλεῖστα τερατευσάμενος· ἐν ὁκτὼ δὲ λόγοις ἡ πᾶσα αὐτῷ τῆς ματαιοπονίας σπούδη κατηνάλωται.

From this history of Philostratus—or rather, from the fables invented by him—Hierocles seized an opportunity in his books, which, as we noted, he had entitled with the false title *Philalethes* (“Lovers of Truth”), to compare improperly the miracles of Apollonius with those which Christ performed by divine power [Col. 1051D]. Thus, by this foolish comparison, not only he but other pagans as well subsequently attempted to diminish, and even utterly to undermine, the authority of Christ’s miracles. For in the fifth century Marcellinus proposed certain questions for Augustine to resolve, and begged him to deign to answer those who “bring forward among us their Apollonius, and Apuleius, and other practitioners of magical art, whose miracles they maintain were greater” (Augustine, Ep. 136). These men undoubtedly appear still bolder, since they supposed that miracles performed not only by Apollonius, as Philostratus boasted, but also by Apuleius, were equal—and even greater—than those performed by Christ [Col. 1052A]. But because no one could deny that this Apuleius was an impious man and had been accused of magic, Lactantius (ibid.) wittily ridicules Hierocles thus: “It is surprising that he passed over Apuleius, of whom many and wonderful things are commonly related.” But he subsequently refutes him seriously, replying that, if the miracles attributed to Apollonius were true, he ought to have been worshipped by all as a god. He therefore presses Hierocles thus: “Why then, O madman, does no one worship Apollonius as a god—unless perhaps you alone do, being of course worthy of such a god?”

“But,” you will ask, “how could Lactantius maintain this? Did not Xiphilinus record that the same Apollonius was held in great honour by Antoninus Caracalla, and that he *καὶ ἡρῶον αὐτῷ κατασκευάσαι*—‘constructed a heroon for him’—that is, erected for him a monument, or built a basilica for him as for a hero?” Vopiscus indeed relates that Apollonius appeared to Aurelian after the capture of the city of Tyana and advised him to act more mercifully. He then adds: “Aurelian knew the countenance of the venerable philosopher, and had seen his likeness in many temples [Col. 1052B]. Finally, struck with astonishment, he immediately promised him both an image, statues, and a temple” (Vopiscus, *Life of Aurelian*, about the middle).

“But if that emperor fulfilled his promises, a temple to Apollonius was built before Lactantius’ time. And what else do the images and statues of him seen in temples indicate, except that they were placed there for him as for a god?” Yet this still requires proof. For who does not know that statues and images of persons other than gods were erected in pagan temples? And certainly Xiphilinus says that Caracalla made for him a monument not as for a god, but as for a hero [Col. 1052C].

However the matter may stand, Lactantius shortly afterwards explains his meaning more clearly, when he attacks his adversary thus: “Since you say both that he was worshipped by some as a god, and that his image was set up under the name of Hercules Alexicacus, and that even now he is honoured by the Ephesians” (Lactantius, ibid.). Hierocles undoubtedly derived this from Philostratus’ history (Philostratus, IV.3). Does not Lactantius therefore rightly infer that Apollonius was regarded as a god only by certain persons, who nevertheless worshipped him not under his own name but under another’s—namely, that of Hercules Alexicacus, or, as Philostratus said in Greek, *ἀποτρόπαιος*, “the repeller and averrer of evils” [Col. 1052D]? If any others honoured him as a god under his true and proper name, they were very few: perhaps only one, namely Hierocles himself, as Lactantius had said in jest and mockery.

But Hierocles himself replied that Apollonius had been more modest than Christ: although, as he babbled, he had performed miracles greater than Christ’s, he nevertheless had not arrogated to himself the name of God. Lactantius, however, utterly demolishes this vain refuge of falsely assumed modesty. For who, he asks, does not desire the remembrance of his name to be immortal? Certainly the greatest kings and other men have sought to secure this for themselves through magnificent portraits, statues, and tombs. Indeed Hierocles himself, by publishing his books—though they are a detestable memorial of his talent—had sought nothing else than immortality of name [Col. 1053A]. It is therefore foolish to suppose that Apollonius rejected what all desire, when Hierocles said that he had been worshipped by some as a god.

Our author next openly proves from this that Apollonius’ miracles were false (Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, V.3), because it was established that he devoted himself to magical arts, by which he seemed to have done something beyond the ordinary order of nature. For it must plainly be attributed to these abominable deceptions that, as Hierocles after Philostratus handed down to posterity (Philostratus, VIII.4), when Apollonius stood before the tribunal of judges and was shortly to suffer the penalties due from Domitian, he suddenly vanished from the sight of all and appeared no more [Col. 1053B]. Hence Eusebius rightly concludes (*Against Hierocles*) that he was a magician not because he underwent trial, but because he escaped and deceived the judges, the emperor, and the spies surrounding him. Jerome argues in a similar way against the Marcionites, who falsely asserted that Christ had been born only fictitiously and in appearance: “Apollonius of Tyana, it is written, when he stood before Domitian in the council chamber, suddenly ceased to appear. Do not equate the power of the Lord with the tricks of magicians, so that what was not may seem to have been” (Jerome, Letter to Pammachius against the Error of John of Jerusalem).

For this reason Augustine judges that the pagans who dared compare this Apollonius and Apuleius—men devoted to magical arts—with Christ are wholly to be ridiculed, although it seems more tolerable that they compared these men with Christ rather than with their own most wicked gods. In reply to Marcellinus, who, as we said shortly before, had asked him about this, he writes: “Who would not think it worthy of laughter that they attempt to compare Apollonius and Apuleius, and the other most skilled practitioners of magical arts, with Christ, or even to prefer them to him? Though it is more tolerable that they compared these men with him rather than with their gods. For Apollonius was far better—this must be admitted—than that author and perpetrator of so many adulteries whom they call Jupiter” (Augustine, Ep. 138 to Marcellinus, §18) [Col. 1053C].

In another letter or book, where he refutes pagans who mocked as wholly unbelievable the account that Jonah was three days in the belly of the whale, Augustine unhesitatingly calls Apollonius a magician and declares that the miracles attributed to him rest upon no trustworthy authority: “And yet, if Apuleius of Madaura or Apollonius of Tyana were said to have done what is written concerning Jonah—men about whom, without any reliable authority, many marvels are boasted, although demons too perform some things resembling those of holy angels, not in truth but in appearance, not by wisdom but plainly by deception—yet if, as I have said, such a thing were narrated of these men, whom they commendably call magicians or philosophers, laughter would no longer crackle upon their lips, but conceit” (Augustine, Ep. 102, Question 6). Please attend for a moment to what this eminent doctor there openly and plainly affirms: that the miracles of both Apollonius [Col. 1054A] and Apuleius are boasted of on no trustworthy authority. Nor without reason. For those attributed to Apollonius were committed to writing by Philostratus, as we observed—a writer of wholly uncertain credibility, to say no more. Augustine next says that they are called magicians, or, commendably, philosophers. How rightly he said this may be inferred from Jerome’s testimony that Apollonius was called a magician by the common people, but a philosopher by the Pythagoreans: “Apollonius,” he says, “whether that magician, as the populace calls him, or philosopher, as the Pythagoreans say” (Jerome, Ep. 50 to Paulinus).

Moreover, it was not the populace alone that called him a magician. Lucian relates (*Alexander, or the False Prophet*) that a certain evil-worker and wicked impostor, likewise the teacher of the magician Alexander, had been among those who associated with Apollonius of Tyana and knew his entire “tragedy”: *καὶ τὴν πᾶσαν αὐτοῦ τραγῳδίαν εἰδότων* (“and knew his entire ‘tragedy’”) [Col. 1054B].

Lactantius presses the pagans still more strongly on this point: only a few and insignificant prodigies of Apollonius were reported by them, even as Hierocles admitted; whereas Christ, he says, performed innumerable and so many miracles that one book would not suffice to embrace them all (Lactantius, IV.15). In this manner of speaking he undoubtedly imitated John, who wrote at the end of his Gospel that he did not suppose the world itself could contain the books that would have to be written if Christ’s individual deeds were recorded (John 21:25). By these words he unquestionably indicates that Christ’s deeds and miracles, worthy to be individually committed to immortal memory, were innumerable [Col. 1054C].

Further, Christians, as Lactantius continues (V.3), recognized and openly professed Christ to be the true God, not merely because he had performed so many and such great miracles, but also because they had learned with the utmost certainty that these very things had been foretold by the sacred prophets, as already stated, inspired by the divine Spirit. But neither Apollonius nor Apuleius ever performed true miracles; nor has anyone anywhere testified that these had been announced by any divine prophet before they occurred. Whoever wishes to read more about Apollonius should consult Huet (*On the Demonstration of the Gospel*, proposition IX, ch. 147), and the work of a more recent writer, lately composed in French [Col. 1054D].

Nevertheless Hierocles, that most shameless enemy of Christians, persisted in asserting that the things related in Sacred Scripture were false, self-contradictory, invented and deceitfully disseminated by Peter and Paul and Christ’s other disciples—men untrained and uneducated, most of whom earned their living by fishing and referred everything to gain. But our Lactantius quickly and easily dismisses this utterly foolish calumny (V.2–3). For if they were untrained and uneducated, they lacked both the craft and the will to invent. Moreover, was it not learned and cultivated men—Plato, Aristotle, and other philosophers—who sometimes taught things mutually contradictory and inconsistent [Col. 1055A]? Yet everything handed down by Christ’s disciples fits together everywhere and fully agrees with itself.

Nothing could be more absurd than to say that they were sowers of falsehood for profit and advantage. For they followed a manner of life devoid of all pleasure and utterly despised everything counted among the goods of this mortal life. Indeed, for Christ’s faith and religion they not only endured death with the utmost constancy, but Christ and they themselves also foretold that they would die for his cause and that all their followers would suffer bitter and abominable things. But we have already discussed all this in the preceding dissertation.

What then is to be concluded from this entire discussion except that every miracle performed by Christ was entirely true, and that he performed them not through certain evil arts but solely by divine power and authority [Col. 1055B]? And if Christ was endowed with divine power—as no one except a man blinded by mad obstinacy can deny—it must necessarily be admitted that the religion founded by him is true.

## CHAPTER IV

Other arguments by which Lactantius establishes the truth of the Christian religion are examined.

## ARTICLE I

How clearly Lactantius demonstrates the truth of the Christian religion from the abolition of the Jewish law and the establishment, spread, and holiness of Christianity.

[Col. 1055C] The truth of our religion is demonstrated not only by arguments drawn from the life of Christ, its author, and his wholly wondrous works, but also by others that may be derived from the establishment, spread, and holiness of religion itself (Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, IV.11 and 17). For it had been foretold by the sacred prophets and by Moses himself that God would send his Son from heaven, who would abolish Jewish circumcision, as will be said below, and their law, and establish a new law to be spread throughout all lands. The same prophets had also foretold that righteousness, rejected by the Jews, would be transferred to the nations that had not known it. Who would not admit that things thus foretold are true [Col. 1055D]?

Lactantius says that the prophet Malachi—“Malachiel” according to two very ancient royal manuscripts; or, according to Jerome (*Preface to Malachi*), “Malachi,” and according to Augustine (*City of God*, XX.25), “Malachias or Malachi”—indicates this in these words: “I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord, and I do not accept sacrifice from your hands” (Malachi 1:10; Cyprian has “I shall accept”; the Septuagint and Vulgate, “I shall receive”); “for from the rising of the sun to its setting my name shall be glorified among the nations” (Cyprian, “has been glorified”; the Septuagint, “is great”; the Vulgate, “has been glorified”). Hardly any of the ancient Fathers of the Church fail to interpret this testimony of Malachi as concerning the rejection of Jewish sacrifices and the subsequent establishment of the new Christian law and its unbloody sacrifice [Col. 1056A]. It would therefore be superfluous to transcribe the words of every one individually; it will suffice to cite the books and passages of Justin Martyr (*Dialogue with Trypho*), Irenaeus (IV, *Against Heresies*, ch. 32), Tertullian (III, *Against Marcion*, ch. 22, and book IV), Cyprian (place cited), Eusebius (at the end of book I of the *Demonstration of the Gospel*), and Jerome (on the cited passage of Malachi).

Lactantius further confirms this by the Psalmist’s prophecy: “Likewise David in Psalm XVII: ‘You will set me as head of the nations; a people whom I did not know shall serve me’” (Psalm 17:44). So too Cyprian, according to the Corbie manuscript and according to others, has “has served me”; and he similarly proves from these words that the nations destined to believe in Christ were designated. Tertullian writes: “As we have shown above that the old law and carnal circumcision were foretold to cease, so too the observance of the new law and spiritual circumcision shone forth in the duties of peace. ‘For,’ he says, ‘the people whom I did not know served me; in hearing of the ear they obeyed me’: the prophets announced it. But what people, ignorant of God, except ours, who did not know God? And who heard through hearing of the ear except ourselves, who, leaving idols, were converted to God?” (Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, ch. 3) [Col. 1056B]. But for the words of that psalm and the whole psalm, Augustine should especially be read (*City of God*, XVII.16).

Lactantius teaches that the same thing is announced no less clearly in these words of Isaiah: “I come to gather all nations and tongues; and they shall come and see my glory. And I shall set a sign upon them, and shall send from among them those who have been saved to nations far away, which have not heard of my glory” (Cyprian: “which have not heard my name nor seen my glory), “and they shall proclaim my glory among the nations” (Isaiah 66:18). Here Lactantius omitted what we noted from Cyprian (*Against the Jews*, II, §22), and what is found in the Septuagint translation. Yet both also omitted some other matters contained in that version; nevertheless they explain the words cited by them in the sense we have stated. Jerome likewise does so, among others, though he treats the passage much more fully (Jerome, commentary on the cited passage of Isaiah) [Col. 1056D].

The aforesaid words of Isaiah also signify, not obscurely, that Christ’s true religion, spread throughout the whole world, would be received by all nations. Our author further considers this declared (Lactantius, ibid., ch. 12) by the words of Daniel of which we spoke shortly before: “To him were given kingdom, honour, and dominion, and all peoples, tribes, and languages shall serve him” (Daniel 7:13). For these have obtained their effect, since Christ, Lactantius says, “now has perpetual authority, when all nations and all languages venerate his name, confess his majesty, follow his teaching, [and] imitate his life” [Col. 1057A]. Elsewhere he says: “No nation is so barbarous, no region so remote, that either his passion”—Christ’s, namely—“or the sublimity of his majesty is unknown” (Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, IV.26). Finally, in yet another place: “From the rising of the sun,” he says, “to its setting the divine law has been received” (V.13). Who can deny that the religion is true which has been spread throughout the world in precisely the manner that the prophets, inspired by the divine Spirit, had foretold long before? But we have seen and examined this argument treated somewhat differently and more fully by Arnobius.

Moreover, in confirmation of his proposition Lactantius (III.10) adduces other testimonies of the same sacred prophets, by which they openly announced that Christ, having rejected and disinherited the Jewish people, would make Christians heirs of his kingdom. He first takes these words of Jeremiah: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I shall complete a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, not according to the covenant which I made with their fathers on the day when I took their hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; because they did not remain in my covenant, and I neglected them, says the Lord” (Jeremiah 31:31–32) [Col. 1057B]. These are found in the Septuagint translation and in Cyprian (*Against the Jews*, I, §11), who interpreted them as our Lactantius did. Tertullian also argues from them in two books against the Jews and Marcion (*Against the Jews*, ch. 3; *Against Marcion*, IV.1), though in those two places he reports Jeremiah’s words differently. But the cause of this variation was undoubtedly nothing other than that he sometimes gave them merely from memory, as happened more than once with other Fathers of the Church. Jerome, however, on the cited passage of Jeremiah, unhesitatingly affirms that the Apostle Paul had previously used this testimony, and that all ecclesiastical writers afterwards judged it fulfilled at Christ’s first advent, when the Gospel succeeded the Old Testament.

Lactantius considers a second prediction of this future succession to be expressed in these words of Jeremiah: “I have abandoned my house; I have forsaken my inheritance” (the Septuagint adds: “I have given my beloved soul”) “into the hands of its enemies. My inheritance has become to me like a lion in the forest. It raised its voice against me” (the Septuagint, “over me”), “therefore I hated it” (the Septuagint, “I have hated it”) (Jeremiah 12:7–8) [Col. 1057D]. By “inheritance,” Lactantius says, a kingdom is not meant, but the ungrateful and impious Jewish heirs, to whom Christ became like a lion—that is, prey—when they put him to death by the punishment of the cross, after first raising against him their voice, that is, the sentence of death. Jerome and others, with great unanimity, subscribed to this interpretation of the prophetic words.

Lactantius further infers that Christians called and substituted by Christ from among the nations in the place of the Jews are called the children of those Jews themselves [Col. 1058A]. He further confirms this by a Sibylline verse, which in the second, older royal manuscript we read thus in Latin: “The blessed divine race of the Jews, of those who are heavenly.” But Gallaeus attacks this with malicious spite because our author said that Christians are called children of the Jews; for Paul, he says, plainly distinguished Jews from Gentiles (Galatians 3:7, 29; 4:31). What then, good sir? Has your innate hatred of the ancient Fathers of the Church blinded you? For how could you forget or conceal that Christians are called by the same Apostle the seed of Abraham and children of him and of the free woman, that is, Sarah?

Therefore, setting aside the rubbish of this foolish scholiast, let us follow our Lactantius (ibid.) [Col. 1058B]. He again proves his assertion by this prophecy of Isaiah (Isaiah 42:6–7), where, he says, the supreme Father speaks to the Son: “I, the Lord God, have called you in righteousness, and I shall hold your hand and strengthen you” (the Septuagint and Cyprian, *Against the Jews*, II, §7: “I shall make you strong”), “and I have given you as a covenant of my race” (Septuagint: “as a covenant of the race of Israel”), “as a light of the nations, to open the eyes of the blind, to bring the bound out of bonds, and those sitting in darkness out of the prison-house.” By these words he thinks it is signified that we, formerly like blind persons and shut in prison, ignorant of God and truth, were enlightened by him, released from evil bonds, and admitted to the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom.

Tertullian had the same understanding. Hear him, if you please, disputing against the Jews: “Look,” he says, “at all the nations, now emerging from the abyss of human error to the Lord God the Creator and to God his Christ; and, if you dare, deny that it was prophesied. The promise immediately confronts you. . . . As he says through Isaiah: ‘Behold, I have given [you] for the ordering of my race, as a light of the nations, to open the eyes of the blind’—that is, of those who err—‘to release the bound from bonds,’ that is, to free them from sins, ‘and those sitting in darkness from the prison-house,’ that is, from death, namely the darkness of ignorance” (Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, ch. 12) [Col. 1058C]. What, I ask, accords more closely with Lactantius’ argument? Does he not seem to you to have drawn it from this Tertullianic source? Who then will deny that the religion of Christ’s followers is true, when prophets and Christ himself announced that they would be divinely substituted for the disinherited Jewish people? On these matters one should read Justin in the *Dialogue with Trypho*, Eusebius, *Demonstration of the Gospel*, IX, p. 443 ff., and others [Col. 1058D].

Nor are only those predictions concerning the establishment and spread of Christianity that attained their result evidence of its truth. The holiness of that religion itself, its teachings and precepts, faithfully observed throughout their entire lives by those who professed it, confirms its truth in a truly remarkable manner. For the whole religion of Christians, Lactantius says (V.9), commands what else except that they should live not merely without crime and stain, but piously and holily? It cannot be, he continues, that persons who do not err in all the acts of their lives should err in religion itself, which is the head and sum of all things [Col. 1059A]. Who indeed will not admit that it is altogether impossible for the very great multitude of Christians, such as already existed in Lactantius’ age, to persevere consistently throughout their lives in true piety and holiness unless the institutions, precepts, and teachings to which they diligently obeyed were pure and sound? Yet Christians, as we have repeatedly shown and shall say again below, lived such a life; pagans certainly did not. Therefore the religion of the former was as true as that of the latter was false.

## ARTICLE II

How clearly Lactantius asserted the truth of the Christian religion from the most terrible sufferings of the martyrs, endured with the utmost constancy to their last breath of life, not without the aid of divine grace.

Another argument for vindicating the truth of the Christian religion, undoubtedly no less powerful than the others, was supplied to Lactantius by the unconquerable constancy of innumerable martyrs of every age, sex, and condition, with which they everywhere defended it to their final breath. Although they were very often tortured by every kind of punishment, including the most cruel that human fury could devise, their constancy and their commitment to the religion once embraced could never be shaken. But let us hear our Lactantius, if it pleases, speaking beautifully, as is his way, on this matter: “Since the divine law has been received from the rising of the sun to its setting, and every sex, every age, nation, and region serves God with united and equal minds, and since the same patience and the same contempt of death are found everywhere, they ought to have understood that there is some rational ground in this matter, which is defended to the death not without cause” (Lactantius, V.13) [Col. 1059C].

For how could so great a consensus of so many Christians—so different in age, sex, and condition, and living in regions so remote from one another—and so great a united resolve in defence of their religion, have existed unless they had been completely persuaded by the most invincible arguments that it was true and had been instituted not by any human ingenuity but by God himself? So great a multitude of people could not all have erred, unless perhaps one says that they all reached such folly that by unanimous agreement they preferred the most grievous tortures and death, which they could very easily have avoided, without reason to every advantage and to life itself [Col. 1059D].

But this wholly remarkable courage of the martyrs deserves somewhat more attentive consideration. Pagans admitted that Christians were most peaceful people, imitators of the just, who, as Lactantius says, did good and just deeds. Yet with such injustice and ferocity they tortured them merely on account of faith in Christ; and with such, and such truly wonderful, patience did these innocent men of utterly blameless life endure every punishment inflicted upon them. For impious judges, tyrants, and executioners, contrary to every law and duty of humanity, condemned, mangled, and killed them without even hearing their case, solely because of the Christian name [Col. 1060A]. Indeed, by assailing their lives, property, and children with sword and fire, they surpassed in horrifying brutality the very wild beasts, wolves, and serpents, as our author puts it. He further expresses this in a verse of Virgil, without naming him:

> Wolves, or  
> Ravagers in the black mist, whom the wicked  
> Fury of the belly has driven, blind.

(*Aeneid* III.354 ff.)

But the most savage enemies of the Christian name were made brutal not by a cruel hunger of the belly, like beasts, but by the more cruel fury of the heart; nor did they ravage innocent people in a black mist, but in open plunder. Nor was it enough to torment the living and kill them by the most dreadful punishments: with horrible cruelty they also mocked their bodies after death [Col. 1060B].

So thoroughly diabolical was the injustice of the pagans that, if any Christian, through fear of pain or death, abandoned the heavenly sacrament—that is, Christ’s religion—and sacrificed to false deities, they praised him and “heaped honours upon him,” that is, as we said elsewhere (*Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. VIII, art. II), increased and multiplied them. But those who persevered in professing the true religion they called impious and, as we observed (*ibid.*, ch. XII, art. I), desperate; against them they brought all the strength of slaughter. Hence Lactantius declares (V.11) that these most inhuman tyrants are rightly called beasts by the prophets—undoubtedly our prophets. For, he says, they were more savage than beasts and retained nothing human except their features and outward form. Yet, he says, according to Cicero’s testimony, nothing is more miserable than they (*Cicero, Fragments*, II, p. 36) [Col. 1060C].

It is worth while here to report what he relates concerning the unheard-of cruelty and brutality of a certain most cruel tyrant, whom he calls only “the beast” (Lactantius, V.11): “That is the true beast, at whose single command

> Dark blood is shed everywhere.  
> Everywhere cruel  
> Mourning, everywhere fear, and the many image of death.

(Virgil, *Aeneid* II.647; II.268 ff.)

Here he combined several verses of Virgil, as he customarily does, suppressing the poet’s name, and taken from different books—unless one prefers to say that the copyists erred. He continues: “No one can adequately describe the savagery of this great beast, which, lying in one place, nevertheless rages throughout the whole world with iron teeth, and not only tears apart men’s limbs but crushes their very bones and rages against their ashes, lest any place for burial remain” [Col. 1060D].

By the name “beast” he undoubtedly denotes the impious and cruel Diocletian, of whose and other similar acts of unspeakable inhumanity toward Christians Eusebius records many examples (*Ecclesiastical History*, VIII.3 ff., pp. 293 ff.). What Lactantius especially writes—that that savage emperor raged against the ashes of slain martyrs—may be confirmed by the testimony of the already cited Eusebius (ibid., VIII.6, p. 298), who records that the bodies of Dorotheus and Gorgonius, imperial chamberlains, after having been committed to fitting burial, were removed from their graves and cast into the sea, lest anyone should worship them as gods when buried in tombs [Col. 1061A]. Tertullian also denounces and attacks a similar pagan fury directed against the buried bodies of martyrs (*Apology*, ch. 37). We shall discuss this below in its proper place. Lucius Caecilius, as we noted elsewhere (*Dissertation on Lucius Caecilius*, ch. XII, art. III), relates that Galerius, who ruled with Diocletian, showed the same savagery and ferocity. If, therefore, anyone should rightly prove that our author designates both emperors by the name “beast,” he will lead us all the more easily to his view, since it is more certain that laws issued against Christians were inscribed in the name of both emperors [Col. 1061B].

Our author continues (ibid.), asserting that Diocletian’s attendants and officials devised such numerous and grievous kinds of torture for tormenting and killing Christians that no one could recount them and no number of volumes could contain them. He nevertheless lists some there; these are sufficiently confirmed by the cited Eusebius (ibid., VIII.7 ff.), but it would take too long to give them one by one. Yet the man whom Lactantius mentions must not be passed over in silence: one of those most ferocious men, he says, was driven headlong into bloody slaughter and in Phrygia burned the whole population together with their meeting-place. Eusebius describes this as follows: “Certainly armed soldiers surrounded a certain city of Christians in Phrygia with a siege; and, having set fire to it, they burned the whole place, together with men, women, and little children calling upon Christ the Lord” [Col. 1061C].

Valesius and others—indeed Gallaeus as well—admit that Eusebius and Lactantius narrate the same event. Consider, then, whether in Lactantius (ibid., ch. II) *conventiculum* (“assembly-place”) means the same as Eusebius’ Greek word *πολίχνη*, that is, “small town.” But observe what Lactantius himself had said shortly before: when he was teaching rhetoric at Nicomedia in Bithynia, it happened that at the same time the temple of God was destroyed. Did he then mean that both a temple and an entire small town were destroyed?

Moreover, after Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History*, VIII.12) had listed at length the various punishments by which Christians were tortured, he concluded his narrative thus: “To commemorate each martyr by name would be lengthy and difficult, not to say wholly impossible.” Lucius Caecilius has also transmitted more concerning this persecution of Diocletian and that burned meeting-place in his book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*; we have sought to explain these matters in our dissertation on that book (*Dissertation on Lucius Caecilius*, ch. VIII, art. IV ff.) [Col. 1061D].

But let us follow, if you please, our Lactantius (V.11), who expressly affirms that the insatiable cruelty of certain persons advanced so far that they ordered careful treatment, as he says, to be given to those under torture, so that their limbs might recover for further torments and fresh blood be restored for punishment [Col. 1062A]. Eusebius also testifies somewhere (*Ecclesiastical History*, VIII.11) that certain martyrs, revived by various remedies of their attendants, proceeded more confidently toward death. In our already cited dissertation on the book of Lucius Caecilius (*Dissertation on Lucius Caecilius*, ch. XII, art. III), we showed that the emperor Galerius, by this false compassion—which was itself more cruel than cruelty—prepared our martyrs for new and repeated tortures.

Some, however, Lactantius continues, most criminal murderers, whether from excessive hatred of Christians, from an inborn savagery of spirit, or finally in order impiously to flatter the emperors, dared to interpret their cruel edicts through still crueller elaborations, and to set out in detail [Col. 1062B] by what punishments Christians ought to be tortured. But it is pleasing to hear Lactantius himself speak:

> “Most criminal murderers,” he says, “enacted impious laws against the pious. For sacrilegious imperial constitutions are read, and unjust juridical disputations. Domitius, in the seventh book *On the Office of the Proconsul*, collected nefarious rescripts, in order to teach by what penalties those who professed themselves worshippers of God ought to be punished.” (Lactantius, loc. cit.)

From Eusebius, moreover, we learn (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, ch. 2) that, in the nineteenth year of Diocletian’s reign, in March, about the feast-day of the Lord’s Passion, two laws were issued. The first commanded that churches be razed to the ground, sacred codices burned, persons of rank who persisted in the profession of the Christian faith branded with infamy, and commoners deprived of liberty. [Col. 1062C] Not long afterward, a second law ordered that all bishops of the Churches everywhere be cast into chains and compelled, by whatever means at last, to sacrifice to the gods.

Yet in Caecilius’ book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, we read that Diocletian enacted a law on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, providing that all Christians, of whatever order or rank, should be deprived of every honour and dignity, and subjected to any punishments whatsoever. But we have discussed these matters in our dissertation on this book of Caecilius (*Dissertation on Lucius Caecilius*, ch. VIII, art. IV).

The Domitius cited by Lactantius is thought to be Domitius Ulpian, tutor of the Emperor Alexander, who had published ten books *On the Office of the Proconsul*, now lost. From these books you will find several passages transcribed [Col. 1062D] in the *Digest* (book I of the *Digest*, title 15, and elsewhere). But consider, I beg you, and decide whether he is indeed the person of whom our author speaks, or another jurist living under Diocletian.

Yet he certainly and most deservedly condemns as harsher than every torture the false indulgence of certain governors, who, with feigned humanity and clemency, pretended that they did not wish to torture Christians, in order more easily to extort from them a repudiation of their religion. Nor had he merely learned from others that some extraordinarily flattered themselves because their administration had been bloodless in this respect; rather, he says: “I myself saw in Bithynia a governor wonderfully elated with joy, as though he had subjugated some barbarian nation, because [Col. 1063A] one man, who for two years had resisted with great courage, seemed at last to yield.”

Eusebius relates that these same pagans employed every device in order falsely to persuade some that other Christians had finally sacrificed to the gods: “Thus,” he says, “the enemies of piety greatly valued even seeming to have achieved what they wished” (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, ch. 3). He adds, however, that this succeeded but poorly against Christ’s most steadfast martyrs.

But as deceitful as the leniency of these certainly very few persons was, so dreadful was the ferocity of almost all the others. Far more savage than beasts, they continually devised new tortures, more atrocious than the rest, by which they might torment and kill Christians more cruelly than before. If you hesitate to give us complete credence, [Col. 1063B] you will surely not deny it to Lactantius, who writes as follows concerning things which were still being done in his own time, and which he had either himself seen or learned with the utmost certainty:

> “The punishments of God’s worshippers have been seen, and are still seen, throughout the world; and, in torturing them, new and unprecedented torments have been devised. For the mind recoils from recalling the kinds of death, since the butchery of savage beasts has raged beyond death itself.” (Lactantius, *Institutes*, book VI, ch. 17)

He says “beyond death,” therefore, just as he had earlier said that they raged against the ashes of the martyrs.

We do not think that any sound-minded person can fail to see most clearly, from this most certain account of so many and such great punishments, endured by Christians with such constancy, that their religion is true [Col. 1063C] and that of the pagans false. For that religion is plainly proved false whose adherents, with the utmost injustice and contrary to every right of divine and human law, killed Christians—entirely innocent persons and worshippers of the true God—without any hearing whatsoever, solely because of their name, by those tortures which, as Lactantius says, the mind recoils from recalling. True religion cannot coexist with crime and injustice.

Conversely, that religion is true whose adherents, distinguished by piety, fairness, and integrity of conduct—plainly evident even to their enemies—endured all these punishments, even to death, with wholly remarkable constancy and, as Lactantius further affirms (*ibid.*, book V, ch. 17), not by necessity but willingly. Nothing was easier for them than, even once, or even falsely, renouncing their name, not merely to escape all those tortures [Col. 1063D] but also to obtain temporal rewards, honours, and dignities.

Moreover, what sound-minded man, when he saw martyrs enduring the many and most cruel torments of every sort of punishment with wonderful and wholly unconquered patience, was not compelled immediately to admit that, as Lactantius says, not even patience itself can sustain such great sufferings without God? For neither robbers nor men of robust body can bear such mutilations so patiently; rather, they cry out, groan, and are overcome by pain. Why then? Because, says our author, they lack inspired patience. But if the patience of our martyrs surpassed human powers, if it was inspired in them by almighty [Col. 1064A] God—as we have also shown in our earlier dissertations (*Dissertation on Minucius Felix’s Octavius*, ch. VI, art. IV)—it follows most evidently that the Christian religion is true.

A new strength and confirmation is added to this argument by the fact that the number of Christians was not merely not diminished by these punishments and slaughters of our most unconquered martyrs, but continually increased more and more. Such, indeed, and so universal a contempt for torments and death plainly persuaded others that there was undoubtedly something wholly extraordinary and divine in their religion. Consequently, from the very source from which it ought to have been overthrown, it struck deeper roots and became more firmly established and more widely disseminated.

[Col. 1064B] Certainly, instructed by this almost incredible patience of the martyrs, educated and uneducated alike recognized that their religion was true, and founded not upon human ingenuity but upon the help and power of God himself.

> “For when the populace sees men torn apart by various kinds of tortures, and, amid wearied executioners, maintaining unconquered patience, they judge—as is indeed the fact—that neither the agreement of so many nor the perseverance of those dying is vain, and that patience itself cannot overcome such great sufferings without God.” (*Ibid.*, book V, ch. XIII)

Or, as he later said more briefly: “The religion of God increases the more it is oppressed.” For very many people, after examining and understanding why Christians endured these things so patiently, rightly detested the utterly unjust cruelty of tyrants; and, having ascertained the wonderful patience and courage of the martyrs, they acknowledged their innocence [Col. 1064C] and the truth of the religion which they defended so steadfastly.

Tertullian likewise (*Apology*, ch. L) argues against the pagans in defence of the Christian religion, and boldly declares in a public writing that the dreadful cruelty of tyrants was an attraction by which others were drawn to profess that religion. Those who saw the punishments by which martyrs were tortured sought the reason for them, and readily recognized their innocence; recognizing it, they embraced the Christian religion. Thus, as Tertullian says, the blood of the martyrs was the seed of Christians, and the surest proof of how true their religion is. [Col. 1064D] In our earlier dissertations, moreover, we have shown how other Fathers of the Church set forth, explain, and confirm this argument for the Christian religion.

## ARTICLE III

The contrary arguments of the pagans are resolved: those by which they attempted to prove that Christians ought to be brought back by force, punishments, and tortures to the religions of their ancestors; and that God would be unjust if he allowed them to live in want and poverty.

Although the diminished population of pagans and the astonishing multiplication of Christians demonstrated the truth of our religion with such evidence as we have described, the more obstinate pagans, moved not at all by this or other reasons, objected that ancestral religions must be maintained and that Christians ought rightly and deservedly to be compelled by force and tortures, since it could not be done otherwise, [Col. 1065A] to retain them. Lactantius, however, readily admits (*Institutes*, book V, ch. 19) that one ought to remain in that ancestral religion which worships the true God and is defended by willingly enduring every torture and inflicted death; but not in that which prohibits the worship of the true God and attempts to defend itself by killing innocent people. For the latter is the practice of unjust persons, the former that of just persons.

Nothing, indeed, is more voluntary than religion. God truly loves no one unless he is freely loved by that person; he hears no one praying unless that person comes to prayer of his own accord and from the heart. “Religion,” therefore, in Lactantius’ words, “cannot be compelled. The matter must be conducted by words rather than blows, so that there may be willing choice.” Tertullian had earlier said: “No one wishes to be worshipped unwillingly, [Col. 1065B] not even a human being.” And afterward: “It would seem unjust for free persons to be forced unwillingly to sacrifice. For in every other performance of divine service, a willing mind is required” (*Apology*, chs. 24 and 28). But we shall discuss Tertullian further below.

Christians, therefore, understanding these things well, compelled no one to embrace their religion or kept anyone in it against his will; but they taught, proved, and demonstrated that it alone was true. Accordingly, our Lactantius, like Cyprian (*Treatise to Demetrianus*), challenges all pagans to arm themselves, without any force or wrong, with all the eloquence at their command, to engage Christians at close quarters, examine each of their teachings, and refute them if they can. He further asks them clearly to demonstrate [Col. 1065C] what was the origin of their gods and rites; by what rite those gods should be honoured; and what reward awaits persons in their worship, or punishment in their contempt.

But however great their eloquence, they never dared to determine these things, lest, by revealing the birth, deeds, death, and tombs of their gods—whom no one could deny had been mortal—they should plainly be convicted of the utmost folly. Christians, by contrast, however unlearned and inexperienced, demonstrated most eloquently the truth of their religion and the holiness of all its institutions. What else, then, is to be concluded from this, except that, as Lactantius says, the thing itself and truth speak: theirs is the true religion, that of the others false?

He still pierces the pagans with a most acute weapon, because they openly clamoured that Christians should be punished even for this reason alone: that they utterly destroyed the religions of their ancestors. Yet, he says, Christians did not overthrow those religions more than the Egyptians, who worshipped as sacred shameful beasts and certain things too indecent to mention, concerning which we have spoken elsewhere and shall speak further below. Nor did they abolish them more than the pagans themselves, who, while worshipping their gods in temples, mocked them in theatres, as we have shown elsewhere. Nor, finally, did they overthrow them more than Epicureans and other philosophers, who most shamelessly and ignorantly taught that there were no gods, or that, if there were any, they cared for nothing, or that all things had arisen of themselves—matters which we have sufficiently treated elsewhere. Thus there was no reason why the pagans should dismiss unpunished all these people who mocked or denied their gods, [Col. 1066A] while raging and rioting with such cruelty against Christians, worshippers of the true God, as though they were destroyers of true religion.

Further, he acknowledged that religion and the worship of the gods were destroyed by these persons alone, and that the gods alone were therefore injured by them; then, says Lactantius (*Institutes*, book V, ch. 20), it was for the gods to avenge their own injuries. Unless indeed they were deprived of power and divinity, they had no need of human assistance to exact punishment from their enemies.

And certainly Cicero reports that this had been enacted in his own—that is, the ancient Roman—laws: “Let piety be practised; let wealth be put away.” Whoever does otherwise, according to the text of Cicero himself (*On the Laws*, book II) and an older manuscript of Lactantius’ works, “God himself will be the avenger.” [Col. 1066B] Therefore Cyprian attacks the same pagans in the same manner and in these words:

> “If there is any divinity and power in your gods, let them themselves rise up for their own vengeance; let them themselves defend themselves by their own majesty. Or what can they bestow upon those who worship them, when they cannot avenge themselves upon those who do not worship them? Be ashamed to worship those whom you yourself defend; be ashamed to hope for protection from those whom you yourself protect.” (Cyprian, *Treatise to Demetrianus*)

But in our earlier dissertations we observed how greatly the pagans were pressed by this argument.

Moreover, by compelling Christians to sacrifice to the gods, pagans could confer no benefit at all upon anyone—not upon the gods, certainly; for what is wrung from an unwilling person is not a sacrifice but an execration. And what is more, those are not gods who wish to be honoured in this fashion by unwilling persons, as we said [Col. 1066C] a little earlier. To this must be added that no one who is not out of his mind can demand such a thing.

Nor did pagans deserve well of Christians by this force and violence. For no benefit is conferred upon one who is unwilling and refuses it. Nor should one say that it is the duty of piety to provide for the welfare of all persons, even unwilling ones. For it is genuine cruelty, not piety at all, to suppose that one is providing for the welfare of others who refuse to worship false divinities, by torturing, crushing, destroying, and killing them unless they adore those divinities. Christians therefore did not use force even against the least person who refused to worship the true God, to make him worship him against his will. For they knew with the utmost certainty that one who does not worship God as is fitting will someday himself pay the penalty for his impiety.

[Col. 1066D] Yet the pagans persisted: if the gods ought to avenge injuries done to them, then the God of Christians too, if he is true and almighty, ought to have prevented his worshippers from being tortured with such great sufferings. Yet he not only silently permits this, but even permits others, by whom he is never worshipped, to be rich, wealthy, happy, and to ascend to the highest ranks of every dignity. But we have already seen how this argument, or perpetual complaint of the pagans, is refuted and answered by Minucius Felix.

Our Lactantius replies that pagans who reason thus measure everything by the body, desire, and pleasure, rather than by the mind, in which alone, he says, the human being is. If they used their mind and right reason, [Col. 1067A] they would surely recognize that the goods of the body are as fleeting and fragile as the body itself, whereas the goods of the mind are, like the mind itself, solid and everlasting, since they are situated in virtue alone.

Further, God, as our author continues, allowed Christians to be afflicted by want, poverty, sufferings, and punishments for various reasons, though always just ones: lest, like the transgressing Jews of old, becoming sluggish through ease, they should fall into luxury; that their faith and devotion might also be tested; that pagans, once they understood the reason for their admirable patience, might abandon the impious worship of gods and the number of Christians continually increase; and finally, that this most just God himself might reward their constancy and virtue with eternal happiness, and subject their most unjust persecutors to everlasting punishments.

[Col. 1067B] Tertullian had earlier said for this reason: “God permits us to suffer these things” (*Apology*, ch. 50), because the injustice of tyrants who tortured and crushed Christians was a certain proof of the latter’s innocence; and Christians, by shedding their blood for the confession of that same true God and Christ, obtained both forgiveness of all sins and eternal happiness. But Tertullian must still be considered later.

## ARTICLE IV

Other pagan arguments are answered: arguments drawn from the falling away of certain Christians, from the constancy of Regulus and Mucius in bitter death, and from their claim that Christians were the cause of public calamities.

[Col. 1067C] The blind and untamed obstinacy of the pagans had not yet been overcome by so many and such great considerations of reason, or by the weight of the arguments thus far set out. For they still objected to us that the courage of our martyrs was not so admirable, since many, yielding to tortures, had fallen away from our religion. But lest anyone complain that the force of this argument is diminished, we shall add what Eusebius recorded concerning them:

> “Others, not few—*myrioi alloi* (μυρίοι ἄλλοι), ‘very many others’—broken in spirit and weakened, fell at once, at the very first onset, through fear.” (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, ch. 3)

Yet if these are compared with the countless number of others who persevered and were put to death by dreadful torments, they must be admitted to have been few. For, as Lactantius rightly asserts, from the rising of the sun to its setting the Christian religion had been embraced; and every nation, sex, and age, everywhere serving God with the same patience and equal courage, despised every kind of torture. Eusebius, in the same cited passage, recounts how great was the number of those martyrs who most steadfastly died for their religion by every kind of punishment.

Further, he plainly declares that many were indeed broken in spirit through fear, *apo prōtēs probolēs* (ἀπὸ πρώτης προβολῆς), “at the very first onset,” as Valesius translates; yet he does not deny that they returned to a sound mind. Lactantius states this most expressly:

> “There is no worshipper of God so evil that, when given the opportunity, he will not return [Col. 1068A] to appease God,”

that is, to the religion of Christ, “and indeed with greater devotion” (Lactantius, *Institutes*, book V, ch. 13). Therefore, just as their defection, extorted by the most dreadful punishments, was an example of human frailty, so their voluntary repentance was surely a miracle of outstanding virtue; and upon seeing it, a new body of people continually joined the Christians.

Cyprian advances much on this point (*On the Lapsed*), and although it is somewhat lengthy, it will not be useless to transcribe it here. Thus he writes:

> “He may complain of tortures who has been overcome through tortures; he may offer the excuse of pain who has been conquered by pain. Such a person may ask and say: ‘I indeed wished to contend bravely, and, mindful of the sacrament, I took up the arms of devotion and faith; but, fighting in the encounter, I was conquered by various torments [Col. 1068B] and long punishments. My mind stood firm and strong, and my soul struggled long against torturing pains. But when the cruelty of the most harsh judge was renewed, when now the already exhausted and wearied body was at one time torn by whips, at another beaten by clubs, at another stretched on the rack, at another dug open by claws, at another scorched by flame, my flesh deserted me in the struggle; the weakness of my body gave way; it was not my mind but my body that failed through pain.’ Such a cause may quickly advance toward pardon; such an excuse may be pitiable. … Thus those defeated in the first encounter he restored as victors in the second battle, so that those who had formerly yielded to flames became stronger than flames, and overcame from the very source by which they had been overcome.”

Again, in another book (*On the Unity of the Church*), he writes:

> [Col. 1068C] “The holiness and dignity of confessors was not immediately diminished because the faith of certain persons had been broken. … The greater and better part of the confessors stands firm in the strength of its faith and in the truth of the Lord’s law and discipline. … Indeed, they gain greater praise for their faith precisely because, separated from the perfidy of those who had shared in the fellowship of confession, they withdrew from the contagion of crime.”

These things certainly suffice to answer the pagan argument, until another occasion is given us to discuss the case of those called the *lapsed*. Meanwhile, both these treatises of Cyprian and the letters he wrote on the same subject may be read.

Again the pagans pressed the claim that the courage and constancy of Regulus and Mucius had been no less great than those of our martyrs. One offered himself to the enemy for a certain [Col. 1068D] death; the other thrust his hand into a burning brazier. But Lactantius replies that this comparison is frivolous and wholly absurd. Regulus offered himself to the enemy because he was ashamed to live as a captive. Mucius, captured by enemies, thus provided for his desperate safety by this deed, so that he received a pardon which he certainly had not deserved. We have already treated both Regulus and Mucius.

But what relevance had these things against Christians? Not merely very many of them, as Lactantius rightly rebuts, but the weak and frail sex, and persons of every age and condition, as we have said, endured having their whole bodies torn apart and burned, not from necessity but voluntarily, with wholly wonderful constancy. [Col. 1069A] How illustrious and praiseworthy this was even the pagans themselves could not deny. For their philosophers, though certainly not by their own example, as our author says, were compelled publicly to confess that true virtue is that by which a wise person cannot be torn away by any terrors from the resolve not to do anything unjust.

Nor could they, or anyone else, say that the Horace cited by our author was mad when he sang:
