> The just man, steadfast in his purpose,  
> Is not shaken in his firm mind  
> By the frenzy of citizens commanding what is wrong,  
> Nor by the countenance of a threatening tyrant.  
> (*Horace, Odes*, book III, ode 3)

[Col. 1069B] Lactantius further confirms this with these words of Seneca: “The highest virtue, in their view, is greatness of soul.” These words are thought to have been copied from Seneca’s lost book entitled *Fortuitous Things*, which Tertullian, as we shall see in its place, cites by name. You will find those words among the fragments at the beginning of the same works of Seneca.

Finally, Lactantius judged that the pagans ought no longer to be heard, since with nearly incredible audacity and importunity they never ceased to cry out that Christians must be destroyed, as being the cause of all public calamities. He utterly rejects this shameless calumny, however frequently repeated and not without the greatest weariness. Yet in a few words he overthrows it completely and makes plain that the pagans themselves, by whom false gods were worshipped, were the authors of these calamities. [Col. 1069C] For if the true God alone were worshipped and his laws diligently observed, there would surely be no wars, no dissensions, jealousies, frauds, robberies, adulteries, sexual violations, or other crimes introduced by the impious worship of gods. Therefore not Christians, diligently obeying their laws, but the pagans themselves, guilty of so many crimes, were the cause of public calamities. But we have already shown (*Dissertation on Arnobius*, ch. 6, art. 1 ff.) by what arguments Arnobius overturns that foolish pagan refutation; and later we shall see how Tertullian refutes it.

Who then, whether Jew or pagan, whose mind is sound in a sound body, can deny that the Christian religion is true? [Col. 1069D] For its defence, as we have sufficiently proved, its adherents—boys, men, and women of altogether remarkable and universally acknowledged innocence and integrity—endured so many and such great punishments, which the mind recoils even to recount, not under any necessity but with a courage of spirit as truly real as it was voluntary, and not without divine aid. We have also examined how Arnobius demonstrated the truth of the Christian religion from that same wholly unconquered courage of the martyrs. Now, however, we must investigate what has been handed down and affirmed in Lactantius’ books concerning it and its holy institutions and teachings. But first let us see what he determines and declares concerning its sacred writings.

# CHAPTER V

[Col. 1070A]

Concerning the sacred books of the Old and New Testament and their authors, from whom Lactantius drew the institutions and teachings of the Christian religion.

## ARTICLE I

Concerning the division of Sacred Scripture into the Old and New Testament, and the divine inspiration of the sacred prophets.

Having shown by what and how powerful considerations of reason the truth of the Christian religion was asserted and established by our Lactantius, we must now examine what its institutions and teachings are, and from what sources they were drawn. These sources are undoubtedly none other than all the books of [Col. 1070B] our sacred Scriptures and the oracles of our prophets, from which he drew, as we have seen, an invincible argument for asserting the truth of our religion. It is therefore worthwhile to investigate what he has handed down and determined concerning them.

All this Scripture, he says (*Lactantius*, book IV, ch. 20), is divided into two Testaments. The first contains the books of both the Law and the Prophets, which set forth all those things that preceded Christ’s coming and death. These books are therefore customarily called the Old Testament. The second comprises those things which, after Christ rose again, were committed to writing by the Evangelists, apostles, and his other disciples; and for that reason [Col. 1070C] the name New Testament was applied to them. But these matters, thus related by our author, being well known to everyone, require no longer explanation.

He then says that Jews use the Old Testament just as Christians use the New. Yet do not suppose that he believed the New Testament to be of use only to the latter, just as the Old was to Jews alone. For he immediately adds that the Testaments are not different, but altogether one and the same. He proves this in two ways. First, because the New is the fulfilment of the Old. That this is true follows plainly from the matters by which we have shown above that the predictions delivered by our sacred prophets concerning Christ’s birth, life, death, and the substitution of Christians in place of Jews did indeed have the fulfilment predicted.

Second, he confirms this because Christ is the same testator in both Testaments. [Col. 1070D] These words certainly support the opinion of Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, and other ancient Fathers of the Church, as we have seen in its proper place, who taught that the Son of God, Christ the Lord, made himself visible to Moses and the ancient patriarchs, and that he poured out our sacred prophets’ predictions through his divine Spirit. Therefore he strikes the pagans with no light blow, since they wrongly denied that those prophets had been filled with the divine Spirit. Indeed, he openly shows that this was why the same prophets described many future things as though they were past or accomplished before their eyes.

[Col. 1071A] Nor could it be objected that they uttered these things when seized by some mad frenzy. For, says our author, no one so deranged—that is, so alienated from his mind—can truly foretell future events and speak coherently. Yet what our sacred prophets had foretold concerning Christ the Lord not only actually came to pass, as we have seen, but all their words mutually cohere and agree so fully that no prophet ever contradicted himself or another.

In addition, we have shown that they wholly lacked any motive or will to deceive, or any desire for gain, by which false prophets are led. For while carrying out the office entrusted to them by God, content with food obtained for the moment and abandoning all things not absolutely necessary for the [Col. 1071B] preservation of life, they rebuked the crimes and corrupt morals of the Jews with such confidence and freedom that the Jews, offended by this, most cruelly murdered some of them. Lactantius, after Cyprian, proves this through the most evident testimonies of Elijah, Jeremiah, and Ezra. One prophet alone is named by him: Isaiah, whom the Jews cut with a saw and killed with dreadful inhumanity. But we have discussed this most atrocious murder elsewhere. Therefore no sound-minded person can deny that prophets of this kind uttered all those oracles under the inspiration of the divine Spirit, oracles which their fulfilment demonstrated to be true after a very long time. Thus no pagan could with any right withhold belief from them.

## ARTICLE II

[Col. 1071C]

Concerning the antiquity of Sacred Scripture; and first, whether Lactantius correctly determines when and how Moses delivered the Israelites from Egyptian slavery; what he maintains concerning the Angel preceding them and dividing the water; concerning the miracles performed in the wilderness by Moses himself; where and why he gave the law to the Israelites; and when, after the name of the Hebrews was changed, they began to be called Jews and their land Judaea.

Since nothing lay more near the hearts of pagans than to weaken the authority of our sacred Scripture, they sought to shake it by at least some wedge. Accordingly, they objected to Christians not only the matters we have refuted above, but also that it was new and recently fabricated. [Col. 1071D] Lactantius therefore, to make plain the antiquity of the sacred prophets, which, as he says, ought to be investigated by all, begins the matter from its origin: namely, from the migration into Egypt of our forefathers, the chiefs of the Hebrews.

He makes clear to us how God, after they had long been oppressed there under the intolerable yoke of slavery, freed them, with Moses appointed as their leader, after four hundred and thirty years. But in two very ancient royal manuscripts and certain others, as also in the Roman edition of these books of Lactantius, the reading is “three hundred and thirty.”

There therefore arises a question as to which reading is true, and what Lactantius understands by the term “our forefathers.” [Col. 1072A] For in the book of Genesis a different number of years is given in these words: “It was said to him [Abram]: Know beforehand that thy seed shall be a stranger in a land not its own; and they shall subject them to slavery and afflict them for four hundred years” (Gen. XV.13). In Exodus: “The dwelling of the children of Israel in Egypt”—the seventy-two elders [the Septuagint] add, “and in the land of Canaan”—“was four hundred and thirty years” (Exod. XII.40). In the Acts of the Apostles: “And God said to him [Abraham]: Because his seed shall be a sojourner in a foreign land, and they shall subject them to slavery and maltreat them for four hundred years” (Acts VII.6). Paul, however, writes to the Galatians concerning the same years: “But this I say: the covenant confirmed by God, the Law, which was made after four hundred and thirty years” (Gal. III.17).

[Col. 1072B] You see, then, that in certain sacred books four hundred years are counted, while in others thirty years in addition to those four hundred are assigned. Besides these sacred writers, Josephus recorded the following:

> “They left Egypt in the month Xanthicus, on the fifteenth day of the moon, *met’ etē triakonta kai tetrakosia* (μετ᾽ ἔτη τριάκοντα καὶ τετρακόσια), in the four-hundred-and-thirtieth year after Abraham our father came into Canaan; and two hundred and fifteen years after Jacob’s migration into Egypt, *diakosiois pros tois diapente eniautois hysteron* (διακοσίοις πρὸς τοῖς διάπεντε ἐνιαυτοῖς ὕστερον).” (Josephus, *Antiquities*, book II, ch. 6)

But Augustine, to omit other interpreters of Sacred Scripture and chronographers, explains the beginning, number, and end of these years as follows:

> “The four hundred years, indeed”—namely, in the words cited from Genesis—[Col. 1072C] “are stated on account of the roundness of the number, although they are somewhat more, whether they are counted from this time or from the birth of Isaac, on account of Abraham’s seed, concerning which these things are predicted. For, as we have already said above, four hundred and thirty years are counted from Abraham’s seventy-fifth year, when the first promise was made to him, to Israel’s departure from Egypt, years of which the Apostle makes mention.” (*Augustine, City of God*, book XVI, ch. 24)

That is, in the very words which we transcribed a little earlier. But he treats the matter more fully in another book, proposes various opinions on it, and regards as true the view of Eusebius, who said: “When Abraham was seventy-five years old, he was deemed worthy of divine speech and of the promise made to him; from that time [Col. 1072D] to the return of the Hebrew nation from Egypt, four hundred and thirty years are reckoned” (*Augustine, Questions on Exodus*, question 48; Eusebius, *Chronicle*, book I). Augustine says that these are the years mentioned in the words of Paul and Moses in Exodus cited above.

These matters we have related so that everyone may understand that Lactantius took the beginning of his narrative from this year of Abraham, if, as is more probable, his text reads, “after four hundred and thirty years.” For, since he is treating of those persons by whom the future works of Christ as man were foretold, he surely ought to have begun with the promise made by God to Abraham himself. But if anyone should maintain and prove that our Lactantius wrote, “after three hundred and thirty years,” then he must be said to have reckoned their beginning [Col. 1073A] from the time when the patriarch Jacob descended into Egypt with his sons. Moreover, from this too it may be inferred whom he intended to denote by the name “our ancestors.”

Our author describes the manner in which the Hebrews were led out of this Egyptian captivity as follows: “Moses led the people through the midst of the Red Sea; an Angel going before them and dividing the water. . . . . . . as the poet says:

> The curved wave stood round in the form of a mountain.

This verse is from Virgil’s fourth book of the *Georgics*.

But Gallaeus carps at this account of Lactantius concerning the Angel going before the Israelites and dividing the water. For, he says, we read in the book of Exodus that the Angel went [Col. 1073B] behind them, and that the waters were dried by a blowing and scorching wind, after Moses had stretched out his hand over the sea. Yet the criticism of this man, who everywhere and continually gnaws at his author with venomous tooth, is so foolish that Spark rightly rejected it. For the pillar of light went before the Hebrews as far as the shore of the Red Sea; and there it divided its waters after Moses had stretched out his hand over it.

Lactantius then relates the miracles which he performed in the wilderness, though neither all of them nor in the very order in which they are described in the sacred writings. When he recounts God’s altogether wondrous benefits toward the Israelites, he calls manna a rain of heavenly food. But they, he says, impiously ungrateful and wholly forgetful of such great benefits, fell into luxury and Egyptian idolatry [Col. 1073C] and fashioned, as he puts it, “the golden head of a bull, which they call Apis. . . . . .”: that is, they fashioned the head of a bull which the Egyptians, as we have observed elsewhere, called Apis.

But God, angered at the ungrateful people, our author continues, punished them with severe penalties and subjected them to the law given through Moses. Again Gallaeus quarrels with Lactantius and objects that this is false, if Lactantius, as he seems to do, signifies that the law was promulgated as punishment for this sin. For before the people, as he argues, had fashioned the calf, Moses had already ascended the mountain to receive the law. But did Gallaeus sufficiently consider that Moses ascended this mountain once and again, and that after his second descent from it he gave the Hebrews the two tablets [Col. 1073D] of the law? For then he had been offended by their crime before subjecting them to the law.

Moreover, Lactantius thinks that this law was given not on Mount Zion but on Mount Oreb [Horeb] (Lactantius, Book IV, ch. 17). This is likewise handed down by Malachi, and afterwards by Irenaeus (Irenaeus, Book IV *Against Heresies*, ch. 21) (Malachi 4:4). Nor should this seem surprising to you. For from Moses himself and Jerome we learn that this mountain is called by two names, now Sinai, now Choreb [Horeb] (Exodus 31:18; Deuteronomy 19:1, 2; Jerome, Letter to Fabiola, *On the Twelve Stations*). Some, however, suppose that Oreb, or Horeb, or Choreb, is the summit of Mount Sinai; others, its western part; others, its eastern part. [Col. 1074A] Finally, others think that there are two adjoining mountains, and call Oreb the lower Sinai.

More difficult indeed is what Lactantius immediately adds: that the Israelites, after settling in a certain desert region of Syria, lost their old Hebrew name, and began to be called Jews, and the land they inhabited Judaea, because, he says, “the leader of their company was Judah.” For who, you will argue, was this Judah, leader of the Hebrews in the Syrian wilderness? And who does not know how varied are the opinions concerning the first origin of the Jewish name? Josephus, whom certain more recent critics also support, thinks that both names, Jews and Judaea, were imposed upon the Hebrews and their nation after they returned from Babylon and were restored to their former places. Epiphanius [Col. 1074B] believes (Epiphanius, Book I *Against Heresies*, §§ 2 and 3) that they were thus named after the tribe of Judah, composed of a race of devout men, and in the times when David, Solomon, and his son Rehoboam reigned at Jerusalem. But others, with Augustine, think that the designation Jews and Judaea arose from Judah (Augustine, Book XV *City of God*, ch. 9), son of the patriarch Jacob. Some have further thought that this name should be derived from the fact that the tribe of Judah, while the rest hesitated or lost confidence, was the first to follow Moses through the midst of the waves of the Red Sea. What wonder, then, if, amid so many opinions on this matter, Lactantius adopted some singular view different from them all? Yet he seems to derive the name Jews and Judaea and its origin from that Judah [Col. 1074C] who is recorded to have conquered the Canaanites and Perizzites and destroyed many cities, Jerusalem in particular.

## ARTICLE III

How many years Moses preceded the fall of Troy; and concerning the age of the other prophets, and of the kings or rulers under whose dominion they flourished; how many years after the Trojan destruction David and Solomon reigned, and how many are reckoned from then to the time of Christ; whether Zechariah was the last prophet, and how many years elapsed from his time to Christ’s death; and how correctly Lactantius concludes from this chronology that the sacred seers uttered all their oracles concerning Christ long before he became man.

[Col. 1074D] Lactantius thought, and rightly so, that the age of Moses and of the other prophets could be known with greater certainty from no other source than the specified time in which the kings and rulers lived and reigned, under whose dominion those prophets are said to have flourished. Therefore he considers that time must be investigated, although he judges that no great difficulty arises in uncovering it. For every prophet testified under which king or ruler he lived and committed to writing those things which, inspired by the divine Spirit, he had learned long before they occurred.

But it is preferable first to hear Lactantius himself speaking of Moses: “Many writers,” he says, “have published books on times, beginning with [Col. 1075A] the prophet Moses, who preceded the Trojan war by nine hundred years” (Lactantius, Book IV, ch. 5). In both most ancient royal manuscripts, however, *scriptos* (“written”) is read instead of *scriptores* (“writers”), not very well indeed, but with the same sense. Of greater consequence, therefore, is their common reading, “seven hundred” instead of “nine hundred” years. For it is exceedingly difficult to say whether either of these readings, or which of them, is true.

For who would dare to determine with certainty for us which writers he cites? Later he indeed teaches that the whole sequence of times is gathered from Jewish, Greek, and Roman histories. But since he calls none of their writers by name, it is no more certain whom he followed. For concerning the age of Moses and by how many years he preceded the Trojan war, there are almost as many opinions as there are heads. We have already spoken of these matters in the *Chronography of Clement of Alexandria*. Yet if someone demonstrates that Lactantius indicated the smaller number of years, we shall not reluctantly give him our support. For to refute the false pagan opinion concerning the more recent date of Moses, the number he gave was certainly altogether sufficient. Nevertheless, we cannot omit to observe that the number of years indicated by Lactantius is not far from the calculation of Tertullian and Josephus (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 19; Josephus, Book I *Against Apion*). Tertullian, as we shall see in its proper place, relates that Moses was contemporary with Inachus and preceded the fall of Priam, or the destruction of Troy, by about a thousand years. Josephus, however, reckons a thousand years beyond the number which Manetho thought had elapsed between the Israelites’ [Col. 1075C] departure from Egypt and the Trojan war.

Having thus established the age of Moses, Lactantius continues (Book IV, ch. 5) and says: “When he had governed the people for forty years, as we read in our sacred codices, he had as successor Joshua” (or, as is written in the two royal codices, Jesus), “who held the leadership for twenty-seven years.” This is also the opinion of Clement of Alexandria, who calls him in Greek Ἰησοῦς (*Iēsous*), and of Augustine, who calls him Jesus Nave [Jesus son of Nun]. Josephus too calls him Jesus, but says that he governed the Hebrew commonwealth for twenty-five years, πέντε καὶ εἴκοσι (*pente kai eikosi*). But concerning Joshua’s rule and the number of his years, see our edition of the chronology of Theophilus of Antioch and Clement of Alexandria.

Lactantius continues (ibid.): “Thereafter they were under Judges for three hundred and seventy years.” But Clement of Alexandria, after enumerating the years for which the individual Judges ruled the Hebrews, thus gives their total sum: Ὧν ὁ πὰς ἀριθμὸς ἕως τοῦ Σαμουὴλ γίνεται ἔτη τετρακόσια ἑξήκοντα τρία, μῆνες ἑπτά (*Hōn ho pas arithmos heōs tou Samouēl ginetai etē tetrakosia hexēkonta tria, mēnes hepta*): “Their whole number down to Samuel is four hundred and sixty-three years, seven months.” But there he includes ninety-three years during which Israel was held captive under foreign kings. If you remove that number of years, there remains the number which Lactantius [Col. 1076A] assigns to the Hebrew Judges. Nevertheless, one must fear that copyists of Lactantius’ books, in transcribing numbers written only in Roman characters, may have erred, as is not unusual. Consider, therefore, whether Lactantius deliberately omitted these years of captivity because he is speaking only of the period of the Hebrew Judges. Or what if, being little concerned to provide a most exact calculation of these years, he always gave smaller numbers, lest he afford pagans or others even the slightest occasion for cavilling?

For afterwards he says: “Then, their constitution having been changed, they began to have kings; during whose rule, for four hundred and sixty years” (two older royal manuscripts and other excellent witnesses read, “for 450 years”) “down to the reign of Zedekiah,” and the Babylonian captivity. But Clement of Alexandria says: “From the kingdom of David to the captivity carried out by the Chaldeans were four hundred and fifty-two years, six months; but according to our exact calculation, four hundred and ninety-two years, six months, ten days” (Clement of Alexandria, Book I *Stromata*). You certainly see that an even greater number is indicated there than in the royal manuscripts of our Lactantius’ works. We treat of these matters in the already cited chronography of Theophilus of Antioch and Clement of Alexandria.

Finally Lactantius says: “In the seventieth year afterward, Cyrus the Great” (both royal manuscript codices add, “restored the captive Jews”) “restored them to their lands and homes; and at the same time he assumed power over the Persians, as Tarquinius Superbus did at Rome.” At the end [Col. 1076C] of the second book of Chronicles and the beginning of the first book of Ezra (2 Chronicles 36:22–23; Ezra 1:1), the end of the Babylonian captivity is likewise set in its seventieth year and in the first year of Cyrus, king of the Persians. On this matter Josephus, Eusebius, the author of the Eusebian chronicle, and very many others—and we ourselves in the chronology of Clement of Alexandria—have written.

But by what reasoning, someone will object, did Lactantius say that Tarquinius Superbus began to rule the Romans at the same time? For Eusebius placed no small interval of time between the beginnings of Cyrus’ reign over the Persians and Tarquinius’ reign over the Romans. But learned chronographers posit three beginnings of Cyrus’ reign over the Persians, one of which was when, having gained possession of the whole empire of Asia, he ended the Jewish captivity. Thus Lactantius may be reconciled with others in some fashion.

These words of Lactantius concerning the age of David and Solomon are also not free from difficulty: “The latter, who reigned afterward, preceded the destruction of the city of Troy by one hundred and forty years” (Lactantius, Book IV, ch. 8). For there is scarcely any room to doubt that either Lactantius’ memory or the copyists’ carelessness failed here. For the common opinion of chronologers is that Solomon was later, not earlier, than the Trojan destruction by no fewer than one hundred and forty years. How, then, can he be called earlier by the same number or more? Yet Isaeus thinks that the knot of this difficulty can be untied [Col. 1077A] by the authority of one of the Vatican codices, in which *alterum* (“the latter,” accusative) is read instead of *alter* (“the latter,” nominative). For then Lactantius’ words will have this sense: “The ruin of the city of Troy preceded the latter—that is, Solomon, who reigned after David—by one hundred and forty years.” This is not bad, if the reading of this not very ancient manuscript were strengthened by the testimony of older ones. Nevertheless, we shall not be unwillingly persuaded that the reading of that Vatican codex is true, since the final two letters of the name *alterum* could easily have been omitted by an earlier scribe and subsequently by others. Whether this is indeed so, let others judge, so far as we are concerned.

The copyists seem, however, to have transcribed more accurately the number of years which Lactantius assigned from the reign of David and Solomon to the death of Christ. For he says of David: “The Spirit of God spoke through him, who was to suffer after one thousand and fifty years. For so many years are collected from David’s reign to Christ’s cross.” And of Solomon he had earlier said: “From Solomon to the time when the event took place,” that is, when Christ was fastened to the cross, “there were one thousand and ten years. We invent nothing; we add nothing.” Correctly indeed. For if you subtract the forty years of David’s reign, precisely one thousand and ten years are in fact to be reckoned from Solomon, his son and successor, to Christ’s death. But if you ask whether this opinion of our author is true, we shall answer that the ancient chronologers count somewhat more years, as is clear from the chronology of certain persons set forth by us elsewhere. Yet some exceedingly learned modern scholars hold that 1,047 years, or a little more or less, elapsed from the time when David was inaugurated king to Christ.

Lastly, Lactantius (Lactantius, ibid.), following Theophilus of Antioch (Theophilus, Book III *To Autolycus*), relates two things concerning the prophet Zechariah. First, that under King Darius, in the second year of his reign, in the eighth month, he committed his oracles to writing. And rightly so. For he expressly declared this very date of his prophecy at the beginning of his own book. But from the time, Lactantius continues, when Zechariah lived, to the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, in which Christ was crucified, nearly five hundred years are reckoned; since Zechariah came to maturity in the age of Darius and Alexander [Col. 1077D] not long after Tarquinius Superbus was expelled (Zechariah 1:1; Lactantius, Book IV, ch. 14). These statements agree sufficiently with the respective chronographies of Eusebius and Clement of Alexandria, which we have reconciled elsewhere. Eusebius himself, in another book, counts 493 years from the time when Zechariah prophesied to Augustus, emperor of the Romans. Therefore Lactantius correctly marks nearly five hundred years from the same time of Zechariah to the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar.

Second, Lactantius calls Zechariah the last of the prophets. But does not Clement of Alexandria affirm (Clement of Alexandria, Book I *Stromata*) that Malachi was later than this same Zechariah—or, as he himself puts it, μεθ᾽ ὃν ὁ ἐν τοῖς δώδεκα Ἄγγελος (*meth’ hon ho en tois dōdeka Angelos*), “after whom was Angelus among the Twelve”? Do not Eusebius and Augustine also call the final prophets three together (Eusebius, *Chronicle*, at year 4497; Augustine, Book XVIII *City of God*, ch. 35): Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi? Finally, was not the last place in the sacred Bible given to Malachi, not Zechariah? It may not inaptly be answered that these three prophets are named together by many because they were contemporaries. But they think the final place in the sacred Bible was assigned to Malachi because he does not exhort the Jews to build the temple, but rebukes them for corrupt morals and the depravity of divine worship.

In any event, Lactantius composed this whole chronology of the Hebrew Leaders, Judges, and Kings for no other purpose than to show that the sacred prophets uttered their oracles concerning Christ and the religion established by him long before Christ himself was born and died. Although this chronology might not seem worked out to every legal nicety, it is nevertheless evident from what has been said that his opinion is true and can be demonstrated as certainly as clearly. First, as was said shortly before, our sacred prophets testified under what king or ruler they published their oracles. Then, if Zechariah—or, if you prefer, Malachi—the last of the prophets lived roughly four hundred years before Christ, it follows most plainly that the other prophets flourished under earlier Hebrew leaders and kings at a still more remote time before Christ the Lord. Therefore Lactantius, [Col. 1078C] in order to consult brevity, did not name the others besides Zechariah. It was indeed enough for him to name this last prophet, or one contemporary with the last.

If you desire more concerning the age of each prophet, consult the first book of Clement of Alexandria’s *Stromata* and his chronography, which we have compared with others. Read also, if you wish, the first book of Cyril of Alexandria *Against Julian*, and among more recent chronologers Scaliger and Petavius—the latter on doctrine, the former on the correction of times—and the chronologies published in the English Polyglot Bibles and elsewhere in Latin and French.

Finally, Lactantius rightly concludes from the matters hitherto discussed that sacred Scripture is unjustly charged with novelty by the pagans. “For the prophets,” he says, “are found to be older even than Greek writers” (Lactantius, Book IV, ch. 5). This is certainly true if he speaks of Moses. For we have repeatedly shown in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus* that he is the most ancient of all writers. But just as it is certain that he and some other prophets preceded Greek writers, so too it seems not at all doubtful, as may be inferred from the more accurate chronologies of Eusebius and others, that some of them were older than Zechariah. Yet since Lactantius’ proposition is not definite, and it is not sufficiently understood whether he includes absolutely all prophets, there is no need to undertake a longer discussion of the matter. To demonstrate the antiquity of sacred Scripture it was enough for him to prove [Col. 1079A] that Moses and certain other of our sacred seers were older than Greek writers, lived long before Christ’s human birth, composed their books, and delivered true oracles.

## ARTICLE IV

Concerning the books of Moses and Joshua, who was first called Auses and then Joshua; the books of Kings, or *Basilion*; and the books of Ezra and Nehemiah.

To turn to what Lactantius (Lactantius, Book IV, ch. 5) committed to record concerning certain books of the Old and New Testament, it is useful to observe that he calls Moses not only a prophet, but also one to whom the first place is assigned by many among those who published treatises on times. But what books on times, I ask, did Moses compose except Genesis and the others commonly ascribed to him?

And certainly, no doubt imitating Cyprian, he expressly attributes the book of Numbers to him. For he says, “Moses in Numbers: ‘The Lord is not suspended as a man, nor does he suffer threats as a son of man.’” Both transcribed this not from the Vulgate but from the translation of the seventy-two elders. Lactantius even cited under Moses’ own name the words of Balaam, recorded in the same book of Numbers, in this manner: “Moses speaks thus in Numbers: ‘A star shall arise from Jacob.’” Moses, therefore, is said to speak—not in his own words, indeed, but in Balaam’s—because, while writing this book, he faithfully reported them all.

He also claims the book of Deuteronomy for Moses as its true and genuine [Col. 1079C] author, once and again. Hear, please, how emphatically he affirms it (Lactantius, ibid., ch. 17): “But Moses himself . . . . . . . left written in Deuteronomy: ‘And the Lord said to me: I shall raise up for them a prophet’” (Deuteronomy 18:15). And again a little later (Lactantius, ibid.): “Likewise Moses himself: ‘In the last days the Lord will circumcise your heart.’” Afterwards also: “More plainly Moses himself prophesied thus in Deuteronomy: ‘And your life shall hang before your eyes’” (Deuteronomy 30:6).

Thus he unhesitatingly attributes this book to Moses, as well as the others ascribed to him, just as Cyprian and the other most ancient Fathers of the Church did. Who, then, can patiently endure the audacity of certain moderns who deny that Moses was the author either of these books, of the entire [Col. 1079D] Pentateuch, or of the greater part of them? But elsewhere we have refuted their mad recklessness.

In exactly the same way Lactantius asserts the book of Joshua (Lactantius, Book IV, ch. 17), which we have bearing his name. For after the words of Moses cited immediately above, he continues thus: “Likewise Jesus Nave, his successor: ‘And the Lord said to Jesus: Make for yourself very sharp stone knives’” (Joshua 5:2). Our author deliberately added “his successor,” that is, Moses’ successor, lest there be any ambiguity in the name. Cyprian, however (Cyprian, Book I *Against the Jews*, §8), is read as citing the same words thus: “Thus in Jesus Nave.” But in the preceding article we saw that this same successor of Moses was called by both names. Before both of them Justin Martyr, without any opposition from Trypho, cited many words from the same book thus: ἀπὸ τοῦ βιβλίου Ἰησοῦ (*apo tou bibliou Iēsou*), “from the book of Jesus,” or Joshua.

Lactantius observes, however, that this prophet had previously borne another name: “When he was first called Auses,” he says, “Moses, foreseeing the future, ordered him to be called Jesus.” Justin Martyr (Justin, *Dialogue with Trypho*) and others repeatedly noted this change of name. But Tertullian must not be passed over (Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, ch. 9, and Book III *Against Marcion*, ch. 16), in whose footsteps our author seems to have walked. For he says: “When Auses, son of Nave, was appointed Moses’ successor, he was certainly transferred from his first name and began to be called Jesus.” [Col. 1080B] He repeats this elsewhere, and in both places teaches, like Lactantius, that this Jesus or Joshua was a figure of Jesus Christ. What they say concerning the name Auses is drawn from the book of Numbers, where we read, according to the translation of the seventy-two: Καὶ ἐπωνόμασε Μωϋσῆς τὸν Αὐσῆ, υἱὸν Ναυή, Ἰησοῦν (*Kai epōnomase Mōysēs ton Ausē, huion Nauē, Iēsoun*): “And Moses renamed Ause, son of Nave, Jesus.” But the Vulgate has: “And he called Osee, son of Nun, Joshua” (Numbers 13:17). If you wish for more, read Eusebius (Eusebius, Book IV *Evangelical Demonstration*, §17), who discusses the matter admirably. Jerome nevertheless maintains that *Ause*, which signifies nothing, is wrongly written in Greek and Latin codices (Jerome, Book I, Commentary on Hosea 1:1), and that *Osee* should be written, which has the same meaning as “Saviour.”

[Col. 1080C] Lactantius further transcribed certain words from the books of Kings (Lactantius, Book IV, ch. 11), the first, second, and third; in many editions of his works these are called in Greek Βασιλειῶν (*Basileiōn*), in two older manuscript codices of the royal library and in the Roman edition *Basilion* in Latin characters; while Cyprian calls them *Basileion*, and earlier Tertullian calls them *Basiliarum* and *Basilicarum*, or rather *Basilaeorum*. We have thought it necessary to note this because in the royal manuscript codices of Lactantius’ books the words of Greek authors cited by Lactantius are written in Greek, as we have already said. Why, then, was this one word, *Basilion*, not likewise written in Greek letters? There seems to be no other reason except that the copyists found it so written in older codices. Consider and decide, if you please, whether in the age of Lactantius, Cyprian, and Tertullian these books of Kings were commonly cited and named in this way.

It seems beyond doubt that our author (Lactantius, Book IV, ch. 18) read in his codex of the sacred Bible not only the name of Ezra prefixed to his book, but also these words, “This Passover is the Saviour,” etc., which he transcribed and thought had been spoken concerning Christ, as we saw above. Elsewhere, however, we observed that Justin Martyr was altogether persuaded that these very words of Ezra had been cut from the sacred text by the Jews. But Justin was doubtless speaking of the Jews who inhabited the same region as himself. Yet our Lactantius doubtless did not know them; otherwise he certainly would not have passed over in such complete silence this opportunity to reproach them with so great a fraud.

It is therefore not surprising that Lactantius, who had read those words in his sacred codices, openly calls Ezra a prophet. But someone may perhaps wonder that not only he, but even earlier Cyprian, cited under the name of Ezra certain words found in the second book bearing the name of Nehemiah. For Lactantius reports them in this manner: “Ezra also the prophet, who lived in the same times as Cyrus, by whom the Jews were restored” (Ezra could certainly not be identified more clearly), “speaks thus: ‘They rebelled against you and cast away your law.’” But certain critics of no mean reputation answer that this book is cited under Ezra’s name by Lactantius and other most ancient Fathers of the Church because it contains the deeds accomplished jointly by him and Nehemiah. Further, our author seems to have been led especially by the fact that the two books are distinguished not by Hebrews and Greeks but by Latins alone. For, to use Jerome’s words: “Among the Hebrews the accounts of Ezra and Nehemiah are compressed into one volume” (Jerome, Preface to Ezra).

## ARTICLE V

Concerning the Psalms; the books of Ecclesiasticus, Wisdom, and Proverbs, ascribed to Solomon; and certain words cited by Lactantius which are now lacking in the sacred text. [Col. 1081C] Concerning the books of Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, Hosea, Amos, Micah, Malachi, and Zechariah; the opening words of John the Evangelist; Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians; and the Apocalypse.

Lactantius (Lactantius, Book IV, ch. 9) most expressly calls David king, prophet, and author of divine hymns, or psalms. Nor does he assert that this was only his own and the Christians’ view, but also that of the Jews, who, as he says, read him especially among—or, as the older royal manuscripts have it, beyond—the other prophets. Yet if the hymns written by David are divine, he surely composed them while inspired by the Spirit of God; and for that reason Lactantius rightly calls him a divine prophet. Moreover, since the things he prophesied concerning Christ occurred in fact in precisely the manner in which they had been foretold, as we have already shown, who would deny that they were announced by the prompting of the divine Spirit?

Lactantius seems to have subscribed to the opinion, discussed by us elsewhere, of those who attributed all the psalms to David. For David is called the writer of the divine hymns without exception, and none are cited except under David’s own name. We have seen many thus cited: namely Psalms 1, 3, 15, 17, 21, 32, 4, 44, 68, 71, 84, 93, 109, and [Col. 1082A] 126. We have treated above, especially in the preceding chapter, of the verses of these psalms cited by him; and shall treat of them below when a more suitable occasion arises. Lactantius declares no less emphatically that Solomon—or *Solomon*, as we read in many manuscripts—the son of the aforementioned David, was, like his father, a prophet. Nor is this surprising. For he was persuaded that the books written by Solomon, like those by David, were composed under the inspiration of the divine Spirit, and that many things concerning Christ were foretold in them, as indeed they later occurred.

He attributes the book of Ecclesiasticus to this same Solomon, no differently from Cyprian. For the words he transcribed from this book he presents as follows: “Solomon shows that he”—namely Christ—“is the Word of God. . . . . [Col. 1082B] ‘I came forth from the mouth of the Most High.’” Lest anyone doubt that these words were taken from that book, Cyprian declares it expressly: “In the same Solomon, in Ecclesiasticus: ‘I came forth from the mouth of the Most High.’” And these words are indeed found in this book of Ecclesiasticus, concerning which we have spoken elsewhere.

That Solomon wrote filled with the Spirit of God, Lactantius teaches us (Lactantius, Book IV, ch. 6) when he also attributes to him the book of Proverbs. For these are his very words: “He is the Son of God, who spoke through Solomon, the wisest king, filled with the divine Spirit, the following words: ‘God created me at the beginning of his ways.’” But Cyprian (Cyprian, Book II *Against the Jews*, §1) says: “In Solomon, in the Proverbs: ‘The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways.’” By the name *Paroemiae* [Proverbs] he rightly indicates the book of Proverbs, where these words actually occur. We shall discuss this book elsewhere, and below we shall discuss the words transcribed from it.

Lactantius (Lactantius, Book IV, ch. 16), still following Cyprian, likewise unhesitatingly affirms that the book of Wisdom proceeded from Solomon himself. For both cite several passages written in this book with Solomon’s name prefixed. Lactantius indeed says: “Solomon in the book of Wisdom used these words: ‘Let us lie in wait for the just man, because he is disagreeable to us,’ etc.” (Wisdom 2:12). Earlier Cyprian (Cyprian, Book II *Against the Jews*, §14) had said: “In the Wisdom of Solomon: ‘Let us lie in wait for the just man, because he is disagreeable to us,’ etc.” But he cited this book in the same way not merely there, but repeatedly in the following [Col. 1082D] book as well. We have discussed this book elsewhere.

We cannot pass over without some observation two further testimonies cited by Lactantius under the name of this same Solomon, which are not found in his published books. The first is expressed by him in these words: “The womb of a virgin became weak and received a fetus; and she became pregnant, and the virgin became a mother in great mercy” (Lactantius, Book IV, ch. 12). We have treated of this testimony above. The other is one in which our author reports the following words of Solomon as if they were God’s own: “But if you turn away from me, says the Lord,” etc. But we have already noted that more is cited there than is found in the sacred text.

[Col. 1083A] Lactantius also collected many predictions and sayings from Isaiah and Jeremiah, fewer from the books of Daniel, which he constantly attributes to those prophets, in the common consensus of all except those wholly blinded by voluntary obstinacy. Since we discuss the sayings of these prophets in their proper place where necessary, it is now only useful to note that a passage of Jeremiah is cited in editions of Lactantius under this heading: “Likewise Isaiah thus prophesied concerning the abolition of circumcision” (Lactantius, ibid., ch. 17). The editors of the scholia observe there that this is an error of Lactantius’ memory. But why not rather of the copyists? For in the older royal manuscript codex 3736 we read: *Item de circumcisione solvenda eseias item prophetavit.* Who would not detect here the copyists’ carelessness and error? An unlearned copyist, therefore, who knew no Latin, being unable to read or understand the name *Hieremias* [Jeremiah], wrote *eseias item*, entirely without sense.

Lactantius undoubtedly cites the little book of Baruch under Jeremiah’s name, as many others did, because Baruch was, as we have said elsewhere, Jeremiah’s secretary and scribe, and because, as Jerome says, “the little book of Baruch is commonly joined to the book of Jeremiah in the edition of the Seventy” (Jerome, Prologue to the Commentary on Jeremiah).

When Lactantius acknowledges that the book we have inscribed with the name Hosea was written by Hosea himself, he unhesitatingly calls him the first of the twelve prophets, namely those commonly called the Minor Prophets. Why, then, you ask? Were not Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, and Micah, according to Jerome’s testimony (Jerome, Book I, Commentary on Hosea 1:1), σύγχρονοι (*synchrónoi*), contemporaries with him? Certainly. But Jerome answers in the same place that Hosea is called the first of them all because the Lord spoke in Hosea earlier than in them and the others.

Lactantius likewise assigns to Amos, Micah, Malachi, and Zechariah the prophecies bearing their names. But since they themselves testify that they wrote them, and writers of the New Testament have cited certain of their words, sometimes even with their names prefixed, who would dare, without the greatest rashness, to deny that they were written by those same men under the prompting of the divine Spirit?

[Col. 1083D] From the books of the New Testament likewise, he thus reports the opening words of the Gospel composed by John, expressly naming him: “John too has handed down thus: ‘In the beginning was the Word’”; yet he does so in order to confirm, by David’s and Solomon’s authority, what he had undertaken to prove: that God from God could be generated by the utterance of voice and spirit. We have, moreover, discussed this Gospel more than once in the first volume of our *Apparatus*.

Our Lactantius also sets forth the commands of the apostle Paul as having been delivered to Christians by God Himself (Lactantius, Book VI, ch. 18): “God,” he says, “commanded that the sun should not set upon our anger.” But where did God command this, unless when Paul wrote to the Ephesians: “Be angry and do not sin; let not the sun set [Col. 1084A] upon your wrath” (Eph. 4:26)?

Finally, Lactantius seems to have excerpted several passages from the book of Revelation where he discusses those things that will occur at the end of the world. But since he has not named either the book or its author, perhaps there will not be wanting those who maintain that he drew these matters from elsewhere and from other books. We have therefore not judged it necessary to pursue that matter more fully now, since we think that what will be said below can make it clearer to everyone.

## ARTICLE VI

### Why and how Lactantius uses testimonies of Sacred Scripture to instruct Christians and to refute Jews and Gentiles

Lactantius made excellent use of the divine authority of the Old and New Testaments: of the Old, indeed, against Jews and Gentiles; but of both, for the instruction of Christians generally. For, since both Testaments are accepted by Christians, he instructs them in true doctrine and in divine institutions and precepts. He employs the oracles and pronouncements of the Old Testament against the Jews in order to demonstrate Christ’s twofold coming, and that, apart from this very Christ, another Messiah is awaited by those Jews in vain. Lactantius admirably indicates in these words how weighty are the arguments drawn from those sources against them: “A testimony borne by enemies themselves is sufficiently strong for proving the truth” (*Divine Institutions*, Book IV, ch. 12). For these most hostile enemies of Christians could not be more securely overcome than by their own weapons—that is, by the same Scriptures which they [Col. 1084C] had supplied to Christians as wholly divine. Nor could they object that these had been corrupted and falsified by Christians. Christians, indeed, drew nothing from them that had not been written and handed down by the Jews themselves.

Yet such was their obstinacy and perversity that, while reading them daily, they closed the eyes of their minds, lest they should understand what was clearer than the light of the sun. Hence Lactantius says: “Those who committed these acts possessed these writings; those against whom these things were spoken read them. But even now the heirs of their name and crime both possess them and, in their daily readings, proclaim aloud their own condemnation, foretold through the mouths of the prophets; yet they never admit it into their hearts—which itself is also part of their condemnation.” Indeed, they were so driven by blind [Col. 1084D] fury that, as Justin Martyr says, they persecuted Christians with implacable hatred, because Christians proved most irresistibly from those very Scriptures that Christ had come:

> Ὅπερ μὴ νοήσαντες οἱ ἔχοντες τὰς βίβλους τῶν πρωφητῶν Ἰουδαῖοι, οὐκ ἐγνώρισαν, οὔτε παραγενόμενον τὸν Χριστόν . ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡμᾶς τοὺς λέγοντας παραγεγενῆσθαι αὐτὸν, καὶ ὡς προεκεκήρυκτο ἀποδεικνύντας ἐσταυρῶσθαι ὑπ` αὐτῶν, μισοῦσι  
> (Justin, *Apology* I.)

“Because they did not understand this, the Jews who possess the books of the prophets did not recognize Christ even when He was present. Moreover, they hate us who assert that He has come, and who demonstrate that He was crucified by them, just as had been foretold by prophecies.”

[Col. 1085A] Therefore Lactantius rightly draws this conclusion against these Jews, who crucified Christ and stand refuted by the authority of their own sacred prophets: “What more can now be said concerning their crimes than that they were then blinded and seized by an incurable frenzy—since, though they read these things daily, they neither understood them nor could avoid doing what they did?” (Lactantius, Book IV, ch. 19). They were, namely, blinded by a frenzy as voluntary as it was blind. Indeed, such was their perversity that they could not—or would not—recognize their crime even through the heavenly portents displayed at Christ’s death, as had been announced by their sacred seers.

Nevertheless, Lactantius and the other defenders of the Christian religion did not lose all their labour in refuting them. For by the most evident and invincible force of the arguments which he had drawn from the sacred oracles of the prophets, he and our other writers led many Jews, and far more Gentiles, to the profession of Christian faith.

It was therefore not without reason that our author sometimes likewise contended against the Gentiles by the authority of the same Scripture (*ibid.*, Book I, ch. 5; Book V, ch. 14; and *On the Wrath of God*, ch. 22). Although they rejected it, they could not deny that it had not been fabricated by Christians, but received from the Jews, their enemies; nor could they deny that their own philosophers and others had drawn not a few teachings from our sacred writers, as we have shown more than once. Thus, in one place, he plainly shows that humankind was created by God after all the other creatures, just as Ovid had sung after our sacred writings [Col. 1085C] (*ibid.*, Book II, ch. 8). Likewise, God is proclaimed one by them, as by the Sibyl, and righteous persons are to be restored to life. Elsewhere he again uses the authority of Sacred Scripture against the same Gentiles, where he shows that its various doctrines are wholly consonant with right reason. All these points will become plain and evident to everyone from what will be said below.

Moreover, above we have demonstrated as clearly as possible, unless we are mistaken, that our same author also establishes the truth of the Christian religion against the heathen by means of the oracles of the sacred prophets—prophecies which, after long intervals of time, obtained precisely the outcome which they had foretold [Col. 1086A]. Since they could not have predicted these things in such a manner without the inspiration of the divine Spirit, no heathen in possession of his senses could deny that they deserved credence.

Accordingly, the Gentiles were no longer to be heard when they argued that our prophets ought to be despised or rejected because they spoke in a simple, unpolished, uncultivated, and barbarous manner. For eloquence alone, Lactantius says (*Divine Institutions*, Book V, ch. 1), serves the age, not truth, and seeks something embellished. Yet he does not deny that God, by whose Spirit our sacred writers composed their books, could have employed elaborate, polished, and elegant expression. But, he says, “divine providence wished those things which are divine to be free from ornament, so that all might understand the things which He spoke to all” (Book VI, ch. 21). Further, he rightly maintains that God spoke in Sacred Scripture as was fitting. But attend, I pray, to Lactantius’ own words: “For it was not fitting that, when God spoke to man, He should support His utterances with arguments, as though He would not be believed. Rather, as was proper, He spoke as the greatest judge of all things, whose role is not to argue but to pronounce” (*ibid.*, Book III, ch. 1). How true this is can readily be demonstrated from the laws of the Gentiles themselves; from Cicero and others who collected them, it is wholly plain to all how simply those laws were written [Col. 1086C]. But we have already discussed these matters sufficiently above and in our other dissertations.

Finally, Lactantius taught that, for the establishment and demonstration of every particular matter—that is, of all the doctrines and precepts of the Christian religion—we possess the testimonies of the divine voice, which we understand to be expressly uttered in our sacred Scriptures. How true this is, and in what manner he affirms it, must next be examined.

Volume back matter

## APPENDICES TO THE WRITINGS OF THE HOLY ROMAN PONTIFFS MARCELLINUS, MARCELLUS, EUSEBIUS, AND MELCHIADES MENTIONED IN VOLUME VI

[Col. 1085]

## FIRST APPENDIX: TO SAINT POPE MARCELLINUS

### FIRST LETTER [Note: [Col. 1085D] Both are spurious.], OF POPE MARCELLINUS TO BISHOP SALOMON

[Col. 1085D]

The error of those who say that the Father is greater than the Son, etc., is refuted.

Marcellinus, bishop of the holy Catholic Church of the city of Rome, to Salomon, fellow bishop: greeting in the Lord.

The letters transmitted to us through your deacon demonstrate how commendably you are moved for the truth of the Catholic faith (St Leo, Letter 93), and how diligently you devote the service of your pastoral office to the Lord’s [Col. 1086D] flock. By them you have taken care to bring to our knowledge what diseases of error have lately arisen in your regions. For the language of the letter, the sequence of the memorandum, and the text of your little book declare that certain persons, deceived by error, say that the Father is greater than the Son because sacrifice is offered to the Father alone; that the Son has no share in a common operation with the Father; and that the prophetic statement, “Let the nations know that Thou, whose name is God, Thou alone art the Most High over all the earth” (Psalm 82), was spoken of the Father alone. Or again, they say that the Son is inferior because He Himself, hanging upon the cross, said: “My God, my God, why hast Thou forsaken me?” (Matt. 27). To these persons a fitting and appropriate answer should be given (Ithacius, *Against Varimadus*, ch. 51): namely, that, just as to the Father, so also to the Son, sacrifice was offered by priests in many and various ways, not only in Christian times but also in ancient times. The prophet Daniel says: “There is no place,” say the three youths, “to sacrifice to Thy name and to find Thy mercy; but may we be received in a contrite soul and a spirit of humility. And, as the burnt offerings of rams, bulls, and fat lambs, so may our sacrifice be before Thee today, that it may please Thee” (Dan. 3).

And that you may recognize the Son as the one to whom these three youths confessed that they had offered sacrifice, learn this from the confession of the very king and tyrant who commanded that they be cast into the fiery furnace. He declared that he saw a fourth joined with the three in the very blaze of the raging furnace: “Did we not,” he said, “cast three men bound into the furnace?” And they said to him: “Truly, O king.” And he said: “Behold, I see four men unbound and walking in the midst of the fire; and the appearance of the fourth is like the Son of God” [Col. 1087C] (*ibid.*).

The same Son of God speaks through the prophet, saying: “Kings shall offer gifts to Thee” (Psalm 67). And, to teach that He had said these words concerning the Son of God, He said: “The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of Arabia and Saba shall bring presents; and all kings shall worship Him; all nations shall serve Him” (Psalm 71). That we may show that all these things mentioned above were offered to Christ, the Son of God, we prove them to have been fulfilled at the birth of the same Son of God according to the flesh, as the Gospel confirms: “When Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judaea in the days of King Herod, behold, Magi came from the East to Jerusalem, saying: ‘Where is He who has been born King of the Jews?’” And below: “Entering the house, they found the child with Mary His mother; and falling down, they worshipped Him; and opening their treasures, [Col. 1087D] they offered Him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh” (Matt. 2).

Therefore, the sacrifice offered by Christians at the sacred altars is offered in common devotion not only to God the Father, but also to the Son; for it can be offered neither to the Father without the Son, nor consecrated to the Son without the Father. That the Father and Son possess a common operation is taught as follows (the same Ithacius, ch. 52): God is said to have made the first human being, a formed creature, in the power of their common operation, in the image of God, Scripture saying: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1). Likewise: “Let us go down and confuse their language there” (Gen. 11). And: “The Lord rained from the Lord fire and sulphur upon Sodom” [Col. 1088A] (Gen. 19). And in the Gospel: “My Father works until now, and I work” (John 5). Likewise: “The works which I do are not mine, but His who sent me, the Father’s” (John 7). All these things show not a divided power of Father and Son, but declare a single operation of divinity. And one who carries out the Father’s work is not believed to be alien from the Father’s works.

If, however, you knew from the Gospel that the Son of God is called the Most High (the same Ithacius, ch. 53), you would never, in disparaging the Son, apply to God the Father alone this testimony: “And thou, child, shalt be called the prophet of the Most High” (Luke 1). And that the Son is believed to have dwelt inseparably with the Father in the highest places is confirmed by Solomon’s testimony: “I, Wisdom,” he says, “have dwelt in the highest places, and my throne is in a pillar of cloud” (Ecclus. 24). And in Psalm 91: “But Thou, O Lord, art Most High for ever, for behold, Thine enemies shall perish.” For when the devil, lifted up in pride, set his throne in the highest places against the throne of his Creator, he dared to utter this with impious mouth: “I will place my seat in the north; I will ascend,” he says, “above the stars of heaven; I will sit upon the lofty mountains, and I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). Likewise in Solomon: “Do not say: ‘I have sinned; and what sorrowful thing has happened to me?’ For the Most High is a patient requiter” (Ecclus. 5).

If you do not wish to turn the hearing of your heart toward the divine Scriptures which teach that the Son is called the Most High, believe at least the devil, who wished to establish a seat for himself against the throne of his Maker. That you may recognize that the Son was not wholly forsaken by the Father, as you suppose [Col. 1088C], He Himself set down this testimony concerning Himself in the Gospel: “The Father who sent me is with me, and He has not left me alone, because I always do the things that please Him” (John 8).

Accordingly, we command, by way of precaution, that every care and vigilance be kept awake, lest the faith be rashly handled or violated. There is now no place for ignorance; let no one employ the excuse of former simplicity. Shame is necessary for one who sins knowingly; and what he has incurred by his speech must be reformed by knowledge. Hold these things, brother, and teach them (Hormisdas, Letter 24). Would that the joys of your presence had fallen to our lot, for a fuller satisfaction of speech, so that we might rejoice to enjoy both your conversation and presence, whom we have first embraced in writing. Nevertheless, most beloved brother, you have proved with what affection you venerate the Christian [Col. 1088D] faith: for you desire, without any transgression, to preserve those matters which pertain to the rules of the Fathers and to Catholic commands; rejecting wandering and harmful doctrine, you hold fast Catholic and apostolic precepts, and teach and preserve the rules of right faith.

These things, dearest brother, and other matters (the same, Letter 25) contained in the rules of the Fathers, let us meditate upon with undivided reflection in our lips and hearts; and, as it is written, let us recount them to our children, that they may meditate upon them in their hearts, sitting at home, walking on the way, sleeping and rising; for blessed in the Lord is he who meditates on His law day and night (Psalm 77). The teacher of the Gentiles, following this practice and instructing his disciple, exhorts him: “Meditate on these things; be occupied in them” (1 Tim. 4), adding “the fullness” [thus also in the manuscript codex of Justus]: “Attend to thyself and to the doctrine.” For if we apply ourselves without interruption to the instruction of the faithful, we are separated from vices, since devoted care for the divine work leaves no room for human error (Hormisdas, Letter 79). But if the matters stated above are held fast with strong roots, if there is no departure from paternal tradition, if challenges are firmly met, then the purpose of the wicked is nullified and the faith and constancy of the good are strengthened.

Given on the eighth day before the Ides of September [6 September], in the consulship of Diocletian for the sixth time and Constantius for the second time, most illustrious men (A.D. 296).

### LETTER II, OF POPE MARCELLINUS TO THE EASTERN BISHOPS

[Col. 1089B]

That a layman may not accuse a cleric.

I. That disputes arising among Christians are to be brought before the Church and lawfully decided by ecclesiastical persons. II. That a superior ought not to be judged by an inferior, nor may bishops impose any prejudice upon the pontiff by whom they are proved to have been consecrated. III. That no cleric, without the permission of his bishop, may presume to summon anyone before a secular court; nor may a layman accuse any cleric. IV. That an unjust judgment made by judges through fear or command of a king is invalid; and that the enactments of unbelievers shall be annulled.

Marcellinus, bishop, to all his most beloved brethren, the bishops established throughout the eastern provinces.

What is so sweet to one who is concerned as the knowledge that those things which I desire concerning you have become known to me? What is more suitable to religious institutions than that priests preserve peace among themselves—the peace which by their office they must proclaim to others? [Note: [Col. 1089D] Hormisdas, Letter 65, which alone, in the judgment of learned men, overturns and proscribes all the wares of Pseudo-Isidore.] With full rejoicing, I confess, I received your letters concerning the love which is among you and the peace of the churches. Of your own accord, you have conveyed to me whatever I could have urged and whatever I could have advised. May God confirm this, which He has wrought in us (Psalm 67); and may He Himself, by the mercy through which He redeemed us, bring about for the salvation of souls those things which He has commanded to be done. In return for these so good tidings, we too render the holy service of messengers [Note: [Col. 1089D] “In return for the service of religious messengers,” whatever …]. Whatever we share with the Easterners—whom, having been restored to the body and unity of the Church, we long ago reported in letters sent through the aid of our God—we again communicate to you when fitting, with the evidence renewed. Soon, in response to our edict, an embassy was sent by the Easterners: it hoped with certainty and consulted with certainty. [Col. 1089D] But, concerning these matters, we shall make a summary of what was to be said, sending you rather the replies themselves for your instruction, lest, over the greater expanse of lands, either opinion claim anything for itself or error assume anything, when, for confidence in the facts, it is enough to hold to the truth itself.

But as regards the substance of our letter, it was proper indeed to satisfy your desires more fully. Therefore [Note: [Col. 1089D] Here begin the customary songs of the *Mercator* [i.e. Pseudo-Isidore].] know that [Col. 1090A] you ought to abstain from persecution of brethren and from every dispute, Scripture saying: “The servant of God ought not to quarrel” (2 Tim. 2); nor ought anyone to harm another. Rather, by your rebukes correct all persecutors of the Church and of her servants, as the Apostle testifies: “Rebuke, exhort, reprove” (2 Tim. 4).

I. Therefore, whatever disputes arise among Christians should be brought before the Church and settled by ecclesiastical persons.

II. A superior cannot be judged by an inferior; nor can bishops impose any prejudice upon the pontiff by whom they are proved to have been consecrated. If such a thing is found to have been presumed, it is beyond doubt without force [Col. 1090B] and cannot in any way be counted among ecclesiastical enactments.

III. No cleric of any rank may, without the permission of his own pontiff, presume to summon anyone before a secular court. Nor may a layman accuse any cleric. Yet detractions, accusations, and persecutions among Christians are to be especially avoided; for although we are few in comparison with others, if we are united in mind, we shall more easily resist adversaries. For the holy protomartyr Stephen was being stoned, but Jesus was receiving the blows. Therefore each person must take care not to judge or punish anyone unjustly. And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Judge not, that ye be not judged; for with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged” (Matt. 7).

Hence too the teacher of the Gentiles speaks, saying: “This therefore I say and testify in the Lord: that you no longer walk as the Gentiles walk, in the vanity of their mind, having their understanding darkened, alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their hearts; who, having despaired, have given themselves over to licentiousness, unto the practice of all uncleanness and covetousness. But you have not so learned Christ, if indeed you have heard Him and have been taught in Him, as truth is in Jesus: that you put off, according to your former manner of life, the old man, who is corrupted according to the desires of error. But be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth. Therefore, putting away [Col. 1090D] falsehood, speak truth, each one with his neighbour, because we are members one of another. Be angry, and do not sin. Let not the sun set upon your anger. Give no place to the devil. Let him who stole steal no longer; rather, let him labour, working with his hands that which is good, so that he may have something to give to one suffering need. Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth, but only what is good for the edification required, that it may give grace to those who hear. And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption. Let all bitterness, wrath, indignation, clamour, and blasphemy be removed from you, together with all malice. But be kind and merciful toward one another, forgiving one another, as God in [Col. 1091A] Christ also forgave you. Be therefore imitators of God, as most beloved children, and walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave Himself for us, an offering and sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling savour.

“But fornication and all uncleanness or covetousness must not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints; nor obscenity, foolish talk, or coarse jesting, which is out of place, but rather thanksgiving. For know and understand this: that every fornicator, unclean person, or covetous person—which is idolatry—has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. Let no one deceive you with empty words; for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the children of unbelief. Therefore do not become partners with them. For once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light—for the fruit [Col. 1091B] of light is in all goodness, righteousness, and truth—proving what is pleasing to God. And do not participate in the unfruitful works of darkness; rather, expose them. For it is shameful even to speak of the things done by them in secret. But all things that are reproved are made manifest by the light; for everything made manifest is light. Therefore He says: ‘Awake, thou who sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light.’ See therefore, brethren, how carefully you walk: not as unwise persons, but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil. Therefore do not become foolish, but understand what the will of God is. And do not be drunk with wine, in which is debauchery; but be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking among yourselves in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord [Col. 1091C], always giving thanks for all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God and the Father; submitting to one another in the fear of Christ.”

For the Catholic Church defends everything that is irreproachable [Col. 1092A] (Canon IX of Nicaea, cited in the sixth Roman council under Symmachus). Therefore it is not lawful for the emperor, or for anyone maintaining piety, to presume anything contrary to the divine commands, nor to do anything that conflicts with evangelical, prophetic, and apostolic rules.

IV. For an unjust judgment and an unjust determination, imposed by judges through fear of or command from a king, shall not be valid. Nor shall anything stand that has been done contrary to the established teaching of the Gospel, prophets, or apostles, or contrary to their successors or the holy Fathers. And whatever has been done by unbelievers or heretics shall be wholly annulled (thus far the sixth council under Symmachus). But stand firm in the faith; act manfully; and let all [Col. 1092B] that you do be done in love. For this reason, as the Apostle says (1 Cor. 16; Eph. 5), “I bend my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, that He may grant you, according to the riches of His glory, strength to be fortified through His Spirit in the inner person; that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts, you being rooted and founded in love; that you may be able, with all the saints, to comprehend what is the breadth, length, and depth [height], and also to know Christ’s love which surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled unto all the fullness of God. Now to Him who is able to do all things superabundantly beyond what we ask or understand, according to the power at work in us—to Him be glory in the Church and in Christ Jesus, throughout all generations, for ever and ever. [Col. 1092C] Amen.”

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of September [9 September], in the consulship of Diocletian for the seventh time and Maximian for the sixth time, most illustrious men (A.D. 299).

[Col. 1091]

## SECOND APPENDIX: TO SAINT POPE MARCELLUS

[Note: [Col. 1091D] For his see … was transferred by the Lord’s command. Just as Peter was sent in A.D. 35 to confirm those who had received the word of God in Samaria, so also, by the judgment of all the apostles, the prince of the apostles himself was dispatched in A.D. 39 to Antioch, the chief city and metropolis of all Syria. Thence, after designating but not yet instituting Evodius as successor, he departed for Rome. He arrived in the city in the second year of Claudius; and there, on 18 January, A.D. 45, while Claudius’ second year was still in progress, he established the Roman Church and transferred to it, together with his person, every right of the supreme pontificate.]

### FIRST LETTER [Note: [Col. 1091D] Both are spurious.], OF POPE MARCELLUS TO THE BISHOPS OF THE PROVINCE OF ANTIOCH

On the primacy and authority of the Roman Church, etc.

Marcellus, to all his most beloved brethren, the bishops established throughout the province of Antioch.

Bearing, according to the Apostle, the care of all the churches (2 Cor. 11), we must be mindful of the divine grace bestowed upon us [Col. 1091D]. Through the mercy of His condescension, He raised us to the summit of the priestly office (Acacius, letter of Constantinople to Pope Simplicius), so that, adhering to His commands and stationed as watchmen in a certain lookout-post of His priests [Col. 1092C], we may forbid what requires concern and teach what must be followed (Pope Hilary, letter to Ascanius). Therefore, in letters sent through our deacon Boniface, we admonish you that the evils which spring up be cut off, wrongful deeds [evils] corrected, and good things pursued; and that the examples and decrees of our Fathers be imitated. We therefore ask you, brethren, to teach and think nothing other than what you received from the blessed apostle Peter and the other apostles and Fathers. For you were first instructed by him; therefore you ought not to abandon your own father and follow others. For he is head of the whole Church, to whom the Lord said: “Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16), and the rest.

For his see was first among you; thereafter, at the Lord’s command, it was transferred to Rome, over which, with divine grace assisting, we preside today. Nor ought you to depart from its ordering; to it all major ecclesiastical affairs have been commanded to be referred, by God’s disposing grace, so that they may be regularly ordered by that see from which they took their beginning. But if your Antiochene see, which was formerly first, yielded place to the Roman see, no see exists that is not subject to its jurisdiction. To it, as to a head, according to the decrees of the apostles and their successors, bishops who wish—or whom necessity requires—must have recourse and appeal, that they may receive from it protection and release, from which they received instruction and consecration. This must by no means be denied to any bishops; rather, they must be permitted to go freely, without any restraint, excommunication, condemnation, or despoilment.

At the same time, they established, under the Lord’s inspiration, that no synod should be held apart from the authority of that same see; nor should any bishop accused of any crimes be heard or judged except in a lawful synod convened at the proper time by apostolic authority. For, as was briefly stated above, the judgments of bishops, the business of the highest causes, and all doubtful matters (Socrates, Book II, ch. 8) must be conducted and concluded by the authority of the Apostolic See. And all provincial matters are to be reconsidered by the judgment of this holy, universal, and apostolic Church, if the pontiff of this Church commands it. Nor is anyone permitted, without prejudice to the Roman Church—to which reverence must be preserved in every cause—to abandon those priests [Col. 1093C] who, by divine will, govern the churches of God in the same province, and flee to other provinces, or undergo or seek the judgment of bishops of other provinces. Rather, once all bishops of the same province have assembled, judgment shall be concluded by the authority of this see; yet, as said before, it may be dealt with through its vicars if it so pleases, and whatever has been done unjustly must be reformed.

[Note: [Col. 1093D] Notes of Severinus Binius on columns 1093–1094: “They established that no synod …” In this passage blessed Marcellus writes that it was established by apostolic canon that no general councils should be celebrated apart from the judgment of the Roman pontiff. The First Council of Nicaea renewed the same rule, as the Alexandrian synod testifies in its synodical letter to Felix, and as Julius I testifies in his letter to the Easterners. There, citing this canon, he reproved them because they had held a council at Antioch without his consent. Hence, at the first session of the Council of Chalcedon, Dioscorus of Alexandria was ordered not to sit among the bishops, because he had dared to convene a synod without the authority of the Apostolic See. “That,” it says, “has never been permitted; it has never been done.” And rightly so. For a council is not otherwise lawful unless it has been assembled in the name and authority of Christ. A general council called by Peter and Peter’s successors is called by one who possesses, through Christ’s grant, the authority to convene it; the case differs with a council called by Roman emperors. For it was not to Tiberius or subsequent emperors, but to Peter and his successors, that the words were spoken: “Feed my sheep; feed my lambs.” Therefore the statement of Pelagius II in his first letter to the Easterners is most true: “The authority to summon general synods was granted to the Apostolic See as a singular privilege to blessed Peter.” So also is the statement of Emperor Valentinian, who, as Sozomen relates (Book VI, ch. 7), when bishops asked him to permit them to hold a council, replied: “It is not lawful for me, who am numbered among the laity, to investigate such matters too curiously; let the priests, to whom these matters belong, meet in whatever place they wish.” Below, in its proper place, we shall refute the objection made by opponents: that the Councils of Nicaea, Sardica, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon were convened or called respectively by Constantine, Constantius, the elder Theodosius, the younger Theodosius, and Emperor Marcian. See Bellarmine, *On Councils*, Book I, chapters 12 and 13.]

The pastoral care of our office therefore admonishes us both to aid the destitute and to reform everything neglected or wrongly done (St Gregory, Letter 51, Book VII; St Leo, Letter 97), so that that fire which the Lord, when He came, sent upon the earth, stirred by the frequent movement of correction [Col. 1094A] or frequent meditation, may grow warm enough to burn, and be so kindled as to give light.

For it must often be said and done that evils springing up ought to be cut off with brotherly charity, so that good things may find the widest possible room to grow and increase.
