Therefore, as the apostle James says (ch. III): “Let not many of you become teachers, my brethren, knowing that you incur a greater judgment. For we all stumble in many things. If anyone does not stumble in word, he is a perfect man; he is also able to guide the whole body with a bridle. Now if we put bridles into horses’ mouths so that they obey us, we guide their whole bodies. Behold also ships: though they are great and are driven by strong winds, they are guided by a small rudder wherever the impulse of the helmsman directs. So also the tongue is indeed a small member, and boasts of great things. [Col. 1094B] Behold how great a fire kindles how great a forest. And the tongue is a fire; the tongue is constituted in our members as a world of iniquity, defiling the whole body and setting ablaze the wheel of our birth, itself set ablaze by Gehenna. For every kind of beast and bird, reptile and other creature, is tamed and has been tamed by human nature. But no human being can tame the tongue: it is a restless evil, full of deadly poison. With it we bless God and the Father, and with it we curse human beings, who have been made in God’s likeness. From the same mouth proceed blessing and curse. These things, my brethren, ought not to be so. Does a spring send forth sweet and bitter water from the same opening? Can a fig tree, my brethren, produce olives, or a vine figs? Neither can salt water produce sweet water.

[Col. 1094C] “Who among you is wise and instructed? Let him show by good conduct his works (his activity) in the gentleness of wisdom. But if you have bitter zeal and contention in your hearts, do not boast and lie against the truth. For this wisdom does not descend from above, but is earthly, animal, and diabolical. For where zeal and contention are, there are instability and every evil work. But the wisdom which is from above is first indeed chaste, then peaceable, modest, compliant, consenting to what is good, full of mercy and good fruits, judging without dissimulation. And the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make [Col. 1095A] peace.”

> [Note: [Col. 1095D] Severinus Binius’s Notes on columns 1095–1096]  
> **The Letter.** The matters written here, which cohere little with one another, indicate that this letter, written in the year 308, received some addition from without. Do not be surprised that Maxentius is addressed by the pontiff in this letter as though he were nearly a Christian: for, at the beginning of his seizure of power, he pretended that he would embrace the Christian religion, and exerted himself with the greatest zeal to bind Christians’ affections to himself by benefactions, to the end that he might in every respect secure against the emperor Constantine, who was most devoted to Christians, the empire he had seized. “Maxentius,” says Eusebius, Book VIII, [Col. 1096D] ch. 26, “who undertook to seize tyranny at Rome, at his very entrance upon rule craftily pretended both that he embraced our faith, in order to please the Roman people and win them over by flattery, and ordered those subject to his authority to relax the persecution against Christians; and he displayed so great an appearance of piety that he seemed to everyone humane and very gentle in comparison with those who had previously held power.” See Baronius, year 308, no. 24.

“Therefore, having girded the loins of your mind, be sober, and hope perfectly in the grace offered you at the revelation of Jesus Christ, as children of obedience not conformed to the former desires of your ignorance; but according to him who called you, the Holy One, be yourselves also holy in every manner of life, because it is written (Lev. XIX; 1 Pet. I): ‘You shall be holy, because I am holy.’ And if you call upon as Father him who judges without respect of persons according to each one’s work, conduct yourselves during the time of your sojourning in fear, knowing that you were redeemed not with corruptible gold or silver from your vain way of life handed down by your fathers, but with the precious blood of Christ Jesus, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot; foreknown indeed before the foundation of the world, but manifested in the last times [Col. 1095B] for your sake, who through him are believers in God, who raised him from the dead and gave him glory, so that your faith and hope might be in God.

“Having purified your souls in obedience to charity, in brotherly love, love one another earnestly with a sincere heart; having been born again, not from corruptible seed but incorruptible, through the word of the living and enduring God. For all flesh is as grass, and all its glory as the flower of grass. The grass has withered, and its flower has fallen; but the word of the Lord endures for ever. And this is the word that has been preached to you. Therefore, putting away all malice and all deceit, hypocrisies, envies, and all detractions, like newborn infants desire the rational milk without deceit, that by it you may grow unto salvation, if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is sweet. Coming to him as to a [Col. 1095C] living stone, indeed rejected by men but chosen and honoured by God, you yourselves also, like living stones, are built up as spiritual houses (perhaps: “a spiritual house”), a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. Therefore Scripture contains: ‘Behold, I place in Zion a chief cornerstone, chosen and precious; and he who believes in him shall not be put to shame.’ To you therefore who believe is honour; but to those who do not believe, ‘the stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner,’ and ‘a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence’—to those who stumble at the word and do not believe, for which also they were appointed.

“But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of acquisition, that you may proclaim the excellences of him who called you out of darkness into his marvellous light. Therefore, beloved, be prudent and watch in prayers. Above all [Col. 1095D] have continual mutual charity among yourselves, because charity covers a multitude of sins. Be hospitable to one another without murmuring, each one, as [Col. 1096A] he has received grace, administering it to one another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God. If anyone speaks, let him speak as the utterances of God; if anyone ministers, let him do so as from the strength which God supplies, so that in all things God may be honoured through Jesus Christ, to whom belong glory and dominion for ages of ages. Amen.”

Given on the Kalends of April, when Maxentius and Maximus, most illustrious men, were consuls.

> [Note: [Col. 1095D] In the year 309, seventy-four days after the death of St Marcellus, which occurred on 16 January.]

## LETTER II OF POPE MARCELLUS I TO THE TYRANT MAXENTIUS

He admonishes the tyrant to cease raging against Christians.

Marcellus, bishop of the holy apostolic and catholic city of Rome, to Maxentius.

Charity, the teacher of all good things (St Gregory, Letter 114, Book VII), which seizes nothing belonging to another, does nothing harsh, nothing disorderly, nothing factional, nothing that conflicts with divine honour, harms one’s own soul, or detracts from a neighbour’s advantage—forgetful of itself, seeking not what is its own but what belongs to God or neighbour (Phil. II), envying no one, providing for all, not raging but sympathizing, not grasping but giving, not murmuring but bearing all things equably—if it dwelt perfectly in you, you would restrain your mind from evils, cease raging, stop persecuting God’s Church and his saints, set a limit to tyranny, curb fury, attend to humanity, embrace moderation, and strive to enjoy better goods. For charity (St Gregory, ibid.) exercises hearts and strengthens the senses, so that nothing difficult, nothing burdensome, but everything done becomes sweet; for it is its characteristic to nourish peaceful things, preserve what is united, [Col. 1096C] join what is divided, correct what is crooked, and strengthen the other virtues by the protection of its perfection.

Therefore the Apostle, admonishing all concerning it, speaks thus (1 Cor. XIII): “Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not charity, I have become as sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal. And though I have all prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and though I have all faith so as to remove mountains, but have not charity, I am nothing. And though I distribute all my goods to feed the poor, and though I deliver my body so that I burn, but have not charity, it profits me nothing. Charity is patient, is kind. Charity does not envy, does not act perversely, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek its own, is not provoked, thinks no evil, does not rejoice in iniquity but rejoices together with truth. It bears all things, [Col. 1096D] believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Charity never fails.”

> [Note: [Col. 1097D] Severinus Binius’s Notes on columns 1097–1098]  
> **“You therefore, who persuade us …”** The reason why Marcellus wrote to Maxentius is this: although Maxentius had hitherto favoured all Christians, especially those living in Rome, and for some time had pretended to be an adherent of the catholic faith, after the deaths of Severus and Alexander, judging his power sufficiently secured, he disclosed the impiety concealed within and tried by certain blandishments to draw Marcellus, then living at Rome, from the Christian faith to the worship of idols. The outcome may be seen above in the Life of Marcellus.  
> **“Therefore, a synod …”** The words which follow down to the passage, “We command you to know these things, by whom we are persecuted most hostilely,” etc., seem to have been added from elsewhere and fraudulently inserted, because there was no reason or occasion to write to Maxentius on this subject. Baronius, at the place cited above.

Whoever, therefore, is grafted into its root (the same Gregory, same letter) does not fail in greenness or become barren of fruits, because a work made effective by the love of fruitfulness is not lost. Although charity has now dried up in the persecutors of the Church and servants of God, it nevertheless flourishes in its lovers and in those who suffer for righteousness’ sake. Concerning them Truth himself testifies, saying: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. V). And elsewhere: “If they persecuted me, they will persecute you also” (John XV). For we, and all the Lord’s priests—those, namely, who are his true priests—choose rather to be persecuted for righteousness and the true faith, and to suffer for Christ’s name, than to be enriched by great wealth, abound in the most abundant honours, and lack the heavenly kingdom. For these things are temporal; those [Col. 1097B] eternal. These are perishable and pass away in an hour; but those are everlasting and will remain without end.

You therefore, who persuade us to abandon divine worship, depart from the right faith, and sacrifice to gods: it would be better for you first to show yourself changeable and exhort all to hold the teachings of faith and the ministries of divine worship as our holy fathers, the apostles, preached and taught that they had received them. For it is the part of a good prince and a religious king to restore churches which have been broken and divided (or: shaken or torn apart), build new ones, and honour and protect God’s priests.

> [Note: [Col. 1097D] Distinction 96, “It is the part of a good prince.” Accordingly, it should be noted that few supreme pontiffs have hitherto not established these things.]

Hence we read that the holy apostles and their successors established under divine attestation that persecutions ought not to occur, disturbances ought not to be inflicted, those labouring in the Lord’s field ought not to be envied, nor should the stewards of the eternal King be expelled.

> [Note: [Col. 1097D] The edict of the emperors Valentinian and Valens, ch. 9, Book VII of the Tripartite History, has *great*. See the passage.]

But if any have been expelled or stripped of their possessions, first all things taken from them by enemies or persecutors must legally be restored, and their own sees, with everything belonging to them, regularly restored; and afterward, at a suitable time, they are to be summoned to a duly convened synod. Nor may anyone, before these things have been done, answer concerning himself according to the statutes mentioned above, or, if he sees himself oppressed, give an account of the accusations against him. But once these matters have been duly performed and all his own affairs freely arranged, then, if it seems just (“just”: 3 q. 9, *Non oportet*), let him answer his accusers; and, if necessary, let him receive no small respite, so that he may investigate what is objected to him, lest, deceived by some fraud, he fall innocently. For no one ought to be judged or condemned before he has legitimate accusers [Col. 1097D] present and receives an opportunity to defend himself and clear away the charges. Hence the prophet says: [Col. 1098A] “Before you have examined, judge no one.”

Therefore, in the fact that bishops and the other servants of God suffer persecution, it is not so much they themselves who suffer persecution as he whose office they perform, as it is written: “He who touches you touches the pupil of my eye” (Zech. II). And elsewhere: “He who has saddened you has saddened me” (2 Cor. II). “And he who does wrong shall receive what he has unjustly done” (Col. III). Therefore, although you can kill our bodies, you cannot kill our souls; nor can you take away the ranks divinely conferred upon us.

Therefore you cannot regularly hold a synod of bishops without the authority of this holy see, although you may be able to assemble certain bishops; nor can you condemn any bishop who has appealed to this apostolic see before a final sentence proceeds from here. For if laypersons employ petitions of appeal in public courts, how much more may priests do the same, since they are above them? Of them it has been said: “I said, you are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High.” Therefore no bishop accused of any crimes whatsoever is to be heard or judged except in a legitimate synod, at its proper time, summoned by apostolic or regular authority, lest an innocent person be condemned or lose communion.

We read that blessed Clement, instructed by the apostles themselves, determined that laypersons or suspect persons ought not to accuse bishops, nor should credence be given to accusers issuing from an enemy’s household; and we confirm the same, because such persons now frequently seek, out of hostility, to disturb those who live and believe rightly. Accordingly, the person, faith, life, conduct, and [Col. 1098C] suspicion of accusers must first be examined in detail; then the matters alleged must be faithfully considered, because nothing ought to be done before the life, suspicion, and hostility of the accusers have been investigated. And if they are not of good conduct, or are laypersons, manifest enemies, or stained by hatred, they are by no means to be admitted to accuse bishops.

We command you to know these things—you by whom we are persecuted most hostilely—so that you may guard yourselves against them and cease persecuting those who minister to God, by whose prayers earthly wars are calmed and God is reconciled to sinners. And if you choose rather further to persecute us than to please God, we choose rather to endure persecution than to see ecclesiastical order thrown into confusion, being exhorted by the voice of Truth itself and thus testified to: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. X). And again: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me. For whoever wishes to save his life shall lose it; but whoever loses his life for my sake shall find it. For what does it profit a man if he gain the whole world and suffer loss of his [Col. 1098D] soul? Or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul? For the Son of Man will come in the glory of his Father with his angels” (Matt. XVI), “and then he will render to each according to his work” (his works).

> [Note: [Col. 1099D] Severinus Binius’s Notes on columns 1099–1100]  
> **“When Maxentius and Maximus, most illustrious men, were consuls.”** Since no consulship of Maxentius is recorded in the fasti, the civil war that broke out among the emperors may have been the cause: that is, each of the three emperors may have appointed consuls independently according to his own decision, without agreement with the others. For above, in the author of the *Liber Pontificalis*, in the Life of Marcellus, and likewise below in the Life of Miltiades, explicit mention is made of Maxentius’s second and fourth consulships. Baronius, at the place cited above.

These things are greatly to be feared and avoided by you, by whom the Church of God and its ministers are harassed and suffer persecution. To such persons the Lord speaks threateningly through the prophet, saying (Ps. XLVIII, from St Jerome’s version): “Man, though in honour, does not remain; he is likened to beasts, he is made equal to them. This is their way: their folly; and after them those according to their mouth shall run. Like sheep they are set in hell; death shall feed upon them. And the upright shall subdue them in the morning, and their form shall be consumed in hell, after their dwelling. Yet God will redeem my soul from the hand of [Col. 1099B] hell when he receives me. Do not fear when a man has grown rich, when the glory of his house has been multiplied. For when he dies, he will take none of it; his glory will not descend after him. Although he blesses his soul in his lifetime—they will praise you when you prosper—he shall go in to the generation of his fathers; unto the end he shall not see light. Man, when he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared to beasts and became like them” [the transmitted text adds, uncertainly: “and he shall be silenced”].

And elsewhere (Ps. LI, from the same version): “Why do you boast, O mighty one, in the mercy of God all day long? Your tongue has devised treachery, like a sharp razor working deceit. You have loved evil more than good, falsehood more than to speak righteousness. You have loved every devouring word, O deceitful tongue. But God will destroy you for ever; he will terrify [Col. 1099C] you and pluck you from your tent, and uproot you from the land of the living. The righteous shall see and fear, and shall laugh at him. Behold the man who did not make God his strength, but trusted in the abundance of his riches, strengthened himself in his snares. But I, like a living olive tree in the house of God, have hoped in the mercy of God for ever and ever. I will confess to you for ever, because you have done it; and I shall await your name, because it is good in the sight of your saints.”

All these things have been said for your destruction, but for our strengthening, lest we perish. We write these things to you, therefore, because we are debtors to you, the Lord saying: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matt. V; Rom. XII). And elsewhere Scripture says: “If your enemy is hungry, feed [Col. 1099D] him; if he thirsts, give him drink. For in doing this, you heap coals of fire upon his head.”

Supported by these authorities, we desire to bear peacefully the war which you stir up against us (St Leo, Letter 54), so happily under the protection of the Lord’s right hand, which protects us and fights for us, that, Christ triumphing, there may be one victory for all true priests; and that, with the light of truth shining forth, only the darkness of error, together with its authors, may be driven away. For God’s counsel is not in human power. For the Lord is just, and all his judgments are just; and all his ways are mercy, truth, and judgment. In the hand of God is power over the earth, to whom every iniquity is detestable. In the hand of God is power over humanity, and upon the face of the scribe they shall set his honour. God has destroyed the memory of the proud and of those acting unjustly, and has not forsaken the memory of humble and good persons.

But everyone who rightly worships God holds this for certain: if his life is under trial, he will be strengthened (or: crowned); if in [Col. 1100B] tribulation, he will be delivered; if indeed under correction, he will attain mercy. Therefore do not delight in our destruction, because after a storm God makes calm, and after tears and weeping he pours out exultation (Job III). Blessed be the Lord God of our fathers, who, when he has been angry, will show mercy, and in the time of tribulation forgives sins. Great is the Lord for ever, and he himself will rule us through the ages (Ps. XLVII), because his kingdom endures for ages of ages. Amen.

Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February, when Maxentius and Maximus, most illustrious men, were consuls.

> [Note: [Col. 1100C] 17 January, in the year 309, the day after the death or burial of St Marcellus.]

## DECREE OF POPE MARCELLUS I, TAKEN FROM GRATIAN

> [Note: [Col. 1100D] The author of the Gloss on Gratian attributes this to Martin, to whose times it seems more suited. 20, question I, *Illud autem statuendum*. It is cited by Gratian and the author of the Gloss as *Palea*, but it exists in nearly all ancient copies without the name *Palea*.]

[Col. 1100C] Persons confined in monasteries against their own will are not to be retained.

We judge it should be established that, if children have been offered to a monastery while under age, or have received the sacred tonsure or veils, then in their fifteenth year they should be admonished by their superiors and questioned verbally whether they wish to remain in that habit or not. If they profess that they wish to remain, they may by no means subsequently embrace an opportunity for repentance. But if they wish to return to secular dress, permission to depart must by no means be denied them, because it is quite useless for forced services to be rendered to the Lord.

[Col. 1101]

## APPENDIX III: TO SAINT POPE EUSEBIUS

## FIRST LETTER OF POPE EUSEBIUS TO ALL THE BISHOPS OF GAUL

> [Note: [Col. 1101D] All are fabricated and spurious.]

1. Laypersons are forbidden to accuse priests; likewise those in any way subject to them.  
2. Which accusations ought not to be heard by ecclesiastical judges; and which accusers are to be excluded from accusation.

Eusebius, to his dearest brethren, beloved in the Lord and God, all bishops established throughout the provinces of Gaul.

I have received the letters of your Holiness with great thanksgiving (St Gregory, Book II, Letter 36), rejoicing, indeed, in your welfare but deeply grieved at your oppression. For as you have indicated (variant: *however*), concerning what ought to be done with converted heretics, know that we receive by the laying on of hands those who have been baptized in faith in the Holy Trinity.

### I

But concerning accusations against clerics, regarding which you have written, know that from the time of the apostles it has been observed in this holy city that accusers and accusations not admitted by the laws and customs of foreign jurisdictions (Hadrian, collection of canons 11) are excluded from accusations against clerics. Likewise, it has hitherto been observed and established that laypersons do not accuse bishops, because they are not of the same manner of life (see Hincmar, ch. 24 of Book LV). Indeed, certain of them are very hostile to bishops, since their life and conduct ought to be secluded and removed from lay activities. Nor ought they to be assailed by those who refuse to imitate their chastity and [Col. 1101C] gravity, especially since bishops do not receive such persons in accusations brought according to their own wishes.

Concerning these persons—that is, concerning their own cultivators and servants—the Lord says to laypersons and to all who persecute them: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act maliciously against my prophets” (Ps. CIV). And Holy Scripture itself says: “He who touches you touches the pupil of my eye” (Zech. II). Foreseeing such dangers and others like them, the holy fathers forbade laypersons engaged in secular affairs to accuse priests. Likewise, they excluded slaves and free persons, persons subject to public or private assessments, and all infamous persons from the same accusation or obstruction. For carnal persons ought not to be permitted to persecute spiritual persons, nor those entangled in crimes or engaged in secular affairs to defame, [Col. 1101D] attack, or bring an accusation against bishops. For if the apostles or their successors had permitted this, very few would have remained to serve the Lord in priestly rank.

Therefore we too, following in the footsteps of the fathers, for the salvation of God’s servants, withdraw from all persons whom public laws do not admit to accusation the permission also to attack another person (Ennodius, *Apology for Symmachus*, from canon 7 of the Second Council of [Col. 1102A] Carthage). And let no accusations prohibited by secular laws be heard by ecclesiastical judges.

### II

Accordingly, those to whom flawless and polished perfection has not been imparted ought to keep silent concerning such matters, so that they are neither mutilated (variant: “discussed”) nor advanced. Nor may those who are suspect either in catholic faith or by reason of enmity be admitted to prosecute the aforesaid persons, because unbelief in profession and enmity commonly impede truth (Anianus, on the Sentences of Paul, title 15, sentence 2). Nor are those to be believed or admitted who voluntarily confess the crimes of others. Therefore their truth must be examined carefully; what a voluntarily produced voice cannot possess in them, a rigorous torturer must exact from its hiding places by diverse tortures, so that, while bodies are subjected to punishments, what was done may be investigated faithfully and truthfully.

Therefore, I ask you, turn your attention first to public laws and then to judges, who can and wish to speak justly in defence of all (variant: “to state their own case thus”). For shall we—whom God’s service, after rejection of such matters, has made free; who either despise or deride such insults, outrages, or contempt; concerning whom it is written by the Apostle regarding servants and common people (variant: “vulgar persons”): “Remember that your Lord and theirs is in heaven” (Eph. VI)—be recalled to these evils of the age? Must we do what, when another does it, we maintain to be profane? Shall that which would defile the sight through the ministry of another’s command and hand be carried out by our own authority?

Do not retain throughout all the churches this disposition, after the manner and nature of rapacious wolves. For after a bloody inquiry has perhaps defiled us in accordance with their desires, they will not obtain in these matters the result at which they aim (variant: “at which you aim”), the prophet saying to us (variant: “to you”): “Let us put a ring in their nostrils and a bridle on their lips, and bring them back to the right way” (Isa. XXXVII). For, as the same prophet declares (Isa. XLI), those who say, “They shall be as though they were not, and the men who oppose us [variant: you] shall perish,” are opposed.

For undoubtedly infamous are those who attack bishops, all who arm themselves against fathers, trample upon churches and their priests, flee from public battles, despise God’s commands, or are stained by any mark of infamy. Following the fathers’ institutions, we too withdraw from all such persons the permission to attack [Col. 1102D] bishops, because God so hates those who persecute fathers (Proclus to Domnus) as invaders of fathers, who are branded with infamy throughout the world and are therefore justly and canonically rejected.

There is now no need for lengthy admonition. We ought to cover over hatred for those already lost, concerning whose authors nothing remains that may be condemned (variant readings materially uncertain: “we ought to cover over … concerning whose …”). Concerning such persons the Lord speaks through the prophet (Isa. XXX), saying: “Rejecting the word, you have hoped in calumny and tumult, [Col. 1103A] and have leaned upon it. Therefore this iniquity shall be to you like a breach.”

Again the prophet cries concerning such persons (Isa. LVII): “Come here, seed of adulterer and fornicator” (variant: “offspring of the adulterer and fornicator”). “Over whom have you mocked? Against whom have you opened wide your mouth and thrust out your tongue? Are you not children of wickedness, a false seed?” Let the wicked cease henceforth to fabricate falsehood against the simple by fraud. “Keep,” says the prophet (Ps. XXXIII), “your tongue from evil and your lips from speaking deceit. Depart from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it. The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous and his ears upon their cry. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth.” And shortly afterward: “Malice shall kill the wicked, and those who hate the righteous shall be condemned.”

Although we suffer much from such people, beloved, let us love one another, because charity is from God. Everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God. Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is charity. In this the charity of God appeared in us: that God sent his only-begotten Son into the world, that we might live through him. In this is charity: not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son as propitiation for our sins. Beloved, if God loved us, we also ought to love one another. No one has ever seen God. If we love one another, God remains in us, and his charity is perfected in us. By this we understand that we remain in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit. And we have seen and testify that the Father sent his Son as Saviour of the [Col. 1103C] world. Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in him and he in God. And we have known and believed the truth which God has in us. God is charity; and whoever remains in charity remains in God, and God in him. In this charity is perfected with us, so that we may have confidence on the day of judgment: because as he is, so also are we in this world. There is no fear in charity; rather, perfect charity casts fear out, because fear has punishment. But whoever fears is not perfect in charity. Therefore let us love God, because God first loved us. If anyone says, “I love God,” and hates his brother, he is a liar. For whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see? And we have this command from God: that whoever loves God should also love his brother.

[Col. 1103D] Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God; and everyone who loves him who begot loves also him who has been born of him. By this we have known (Vulgate: “we know”) that we love God’s children: when we love God and keep his commandments. For this is the charity of God: that we keep his commandments. And his commandments are not burdensome, because everything born of God conquers the world. And this is the victory which conquers the world: our faith. Who is the one who conquers the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God? This is he who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ—not in water only, but in water and blood. And the Spirit is the one who testifies, because Christ is truth. For there are three who bear testimony: spirit, [Col. 1104A] blood, and water; and these three are one. If we receive human testimony, God’s testimony is greater. For this is God’s greater testimony: that he has testified concerning his Son. Whoever believes in the Son of God has God’s testimony in himself. Whoever does not believe the Son makes him a liar, because he does not believe the testimony God has borne concerning his Son. And this is the testimony: that God has given us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life. I write these things to you so that you may know that you will have (Vulgate: “have”) eternal life, you who believe in the name of the Son of God. And this is the confidence which we have toward him: that whatever we ask according to his will, he will hear (Vulgate: “hears”) us. And we know that he hears [Col. 1104B] us whatever we ask. We know that we have the requests which we ask from him. If anyone knows that his brother is committing a sin not unto death, let him ask, and life will be given to the one sinning not unto death. There is a sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it. Every iniquity is sin, and there is sin unto death. We know that everyone born of God does not sin; but God’s begetting preserves him, and the evil one does not touch him. For we know that we are of God, and the whole world lies in the evil one. And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true God and may be in his true Son. This is the true God and eternal life” (1 John IV–V).

“Because of their evils many powerful persons have been greatly oppressed, and glorious persons have been delivered into others’ hands. But God’s blessing hastens toward the righteous person’s reward, and in swift honour (Vulgate: “hour”) his advance bears fruit. Blessed is the man who has not fallen by a word from his mouth and has not been stung by the sorrow of sin” (Ecclus. XI and XIV).

Know, beloved, that, because of the piety which must be shown toward you as servants of God (St Leo, Letter 46), I have graciously received all your petitions as beneficial to the catholic faith, in order that through their effect Christian peace also may be restored and impious error abolished. And if anything further concerning such matters or matters like them must be determined, let a report be sent quickly to us, so that, after our care has examined their character, it may determine what should be observed.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of August, Constantine (variant: Constantius) being consul (variant: Constans).

## LETTER II OF POPE EUSEBIUS TO THE EGYPTIANS

> [Note: [Col. 1104D] A manuscript adds: “Alexandrians.”]

[Col. 1104D]

Concerning bishops who have been despoiled of their property or driven from their sees: unless they are restored in full, they are not to be judged; and concerning the calling of synods, in which they are to be heard by all the bishops of their province.

Eusebius, bishop of the Roman and apostolic Church, to his beloved brethren, unanimous in Christ’s charity, joined by the bond of charity, serving the Lord throughout Alexandria and Egypt and holding the right faith: greeting in the Lord.

Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our tribulation, so that we too may be able to console those who are in every affliction through the exhortation by which we ourselves are exhorted by God. For just as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds. But whether we are afflicted, it is for your exhortation and salvation; or whether we are exhorted, it is for your exhortation and salvation, which also works endurance of the same sufferings that we too endure. And our hope concerning you is firm, knowing that, as you are companions in the sufferings, so also you shall be in the consolation.

The old things, beloved, have passed away; and behold, new things have come into being. But all things are from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation: namely, that God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not reckoning their offences against them; and he placed in us the word of reconciliation. Therefore we act as ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us. We beseech you for Christ’s sake: be reconciled to God. Him who knew no sin, he made sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him. And, assisting, we exhort you not to receive the grace of God in vain. For he says: “At an acceptable time I heard you, and on a day of salvation I helped you.” Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation. Giving offence to no one in any respect, lest our ministry be blamed, but in all things let us show ourselves as ministers of God: in much patience, in tribulations, in necessities, in distresses, in beatings, in prisons, in tumults, in labours, in watchings, in fastings, in chastity, in knowledge, in long-suffering and kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in unfeigned charity, in the word of truth, in the power of God; through the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left; through glory and dishonour, through ill report and good report; [Col. 1105A–C] as deceivers, yet truthful; as unknown, yet well known; as dying, and behold, we live; as chastened, yet not put to death; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as needy, yet enriching many; as having nothing, yet possessing all things.

Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians; our heart is enlarged. You are not constrained in carnal things (Vulgate: “in us”), but you are constrained in spiritual things (Vulgate: “in your own affections”). But having the same recompense—as to children I speak—be enlarged also yourselves. Do not bear the yoke with unbelievers. For what participation has righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement, moreover, has Christ with Belial? Or what share has a believer with an unbeliever? What consent has the temple of God with idols? For you are the temple of the living God, as the Lord says: “Because I shall dwell in them and walk among them, and I shall be their God, and they shall be my people. Therefore go out from their midst, and separate yourselves from their midst,” says the Lord; “and touch nothing unclean, and I shall receive you; and I shall be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me,” says the Lord Almighty. Therefore, having these promises, most dear ones, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting sanctification in the fear of God (2 Cor. 1, 5, 6, 7). [Col. 1105D]

Correct your error, brothers, and guard yourselves from every stain of error, so that you may be able to offer a pure gift to God. Do not persecute the servants of God; do not defame or accuse bishops, because God willed that they should be reserved for his own judgment. For he himself gave an example that he did not will them to be corrupted or accused by men or by men of depraved life: when, by himself (St Gregory, *Moralia*, book 25, ch. 14), and not through another, he drove the priestly merchants from the temple, overturned the moneychangers’ tables with his own scourge, and drove them from the temple. And as he says elsewhere: “God stood in the assembly of gods; but in their midst he judges gods” (Ps. 81). Therefore, whoever accuses or condemns bishops accuses God’s ordering, while pursuing earthly rather than spiritual things.

For the cause of faith and charity (St Leo, ep. 34), upon which Christian salvation rests, compels me to labour with great solicitude, fearing lest perversity, which should have been cut off in its beginnings, become, through the passage of time, both more obstinate and more deeply rooted. For it is exceedingly hostile (St Leo, ep. 40, ch. 3), and inappropriate, that those who harass bishops or the remaining true priests by their persecution should indiscriminately be mixed among those bearing the name of Catholics; since, not abandoning their condemned impiety, they are themselves condemned by their own perversity. Such persons ought either to be struck down for their perfidy, or to be released (variant: “made to labour”) for the sake of pardon. For just as it is full of piety (the same author, cited work, ch. 2) that the Lord’s charity be restored—or, variant, returned—to the oppressed, so it is just that the authority of one who disturbs all things be cut off.

I wonder, most dear ones, why you are so quickly moved and transferred from your own judgment (Gal. 1), when it is written: “Do not go after your desires, and turn away from your own will. If you grant your soul its desires, it will make you a joy to your enemies. Do not take pleasure in crowds, nor even in small gatherings; for their commission is at hand” (Vulgate: “for it is continual”). “Do not become a mediocre man in contention arising from lending at interest, when you have nothing in your purse; for you will become envious of your own life. A drunken workman shall not become rich; and he who despises small things shall fall little by little. Wine and women cause wise men to apostatize and rebuke the sensible; and he who joins himself to fornicators shall be wicked. Rot and worms” (Vulgate: “worm”) “shall inherit him; he shall be raised up as a great example, and his soul shall be removed from the number. He who believes quickly is light of heart and shall be diminished; and he who sins against his own soul shall moreover be held in contempt” (Vulgate: “shall have [it]”). “He who rejoices in iniquity shall be marked; and he who hates correction shall have his life shortened; and he who hates talkativeness extinguishes malice. He who sins against his own soul shall repent; and he who delights in malice shall be marked. Do not repeat an evil and harsh word, and you shall not be diminished. Do not disclose your thought to friend or enemy; and if you have committed an offence, do not uncover it.” [Col. 1106A–D]

“For he will hear you and keep watch over you; and, as though defending the sin, he will hate you and thus will cling to you” (Vulgate: “will be present to you”) “always. Have you heard a word against your neighbour? Let it die within you, confident that it will not burst you apart. At the sound of a word a fool goes into labour, like the groaning in the birth of a child. As an arrow fixed in a fleshy thigh, so is a word in the heart of a fool. Rebuke a friend, lest perhaps he did not understand; and, when he has committed an injury and did not understand, he may say: ‘I did not do it.’ Or, if he has done it, lest he add to doing it again. Rebuke your neighbour, lest perhaps he did not say it; and if he did say it, lest perhaps he repeat it. Rebuke a friend, for an accusation often arises; and do not believe every word. There is one who slips with his tongue, but not from the heart. For who is there who has not offended with his tongue? Rebuke your neighbour before you threaten him; and [Col. 1107A] give place to fear of the Most High. For all wisdom and knowledge are the fear of God, and in all wisdom is the ordering of the law. There is no wisdom, nor knowledge, nor good thought except in it. The prudence of sinners is wickedness, and in it is abomination; and there is a fool who is diminished in wisdom.”

> [Note, Col. 1107D:] This passage is read thus in the Vulgate: “And there is no wisdom in the discipline of wickedness; and there is no thought of the prudence of sinners. There is wickedness, and in it abomination,” etc.

“Better is a man who lacks wisdom and is deficient in understanding, yet fears God, than one who abounds in understanding and transgresses the law of the Most High. There is a kind of skill which is certain, and it is itself unjust; and there is one who utters a certain word, telling the truth. There is one who wickedly humbles himself, while his inward parts are full of deceit. For there is a righteous man who subjects himself excessively through great humility; and there is a righteous man who bows his face and pretends not to see what is unknown. And if he is prevented from sinning through weakness of strength, when he finds an opportunity of doing evil, he will do evil. A man is known by his appearance, and the sensible man is known by the encounter of his face. The clothing of the body, the laughter of the teeth, and a man’s walk declare concerning him. There is a false rebuke in the mouth” (Vulgate: “anger”) “of an insolent man; and there is a judgment that is not proved good; and there is one who is silent, and he himself is prudent. How good it is to rebuke rather than to be angry, and not to hinder one who confesses in prayer! The desire of a eunuch has deflowered a young woman: so does one who by force execute an unjust judgment. How good it is for one rebuked to show repentance! For thus you shall escape voluntary sin. There is one who is silent and is found wise; and there is one hateful because he is rash in speaking. But there is one silent because he lacks understanding for speech; and there is one silent because he knows the fitting time. A wise man will be silent until the proper time, but the wanton and imprudent man will not keep the time. He who uses many words harms” (Vulgate: “will harm”) “his own soul; and he who unjustly assumes power to himself shall be hated.” [Col. 1107B–C]

“There is advancement in evil for an undisciplined man, and there is a discovery that results in loss. There is a gift that is not useful; and there is a gift whose return is double. There is diminution on account of glory; and there is one who shall lift up his head from humility. There is one who redeems much at a small price, and one who repays it sevenfold. A wise man makes himself lovable by his words; but the favours of fools shall be poured out. The gift” (Vulgate: “giver”) “of a fool will not be useful to you, for his eyes are sevenfold. He will give little and reproach much; and the opening of his mouth is an inflammation. Today one lends, and tomorrow demands; such a man is hateful. A fool will have no friend, and there will be no glory” (Vulgate: “favour”) “for his good things. For those who eat his bread have false tongues. How often, and how many, will mock him? For he distributes neither what ought to be possessed with right judgment, nor likewise what ought not to be possessed. The stumble of a false tongue is like one falling from a pavement; thus the falls of evil men shall come quickly. An ungrateful man” (Vulgate: *acharis*, “without grace/favour”) “will be like an empty tale continually in the mouth of the undisciplined. A parable shall be rejected from the mouth of a fool, for he does not utter it at its proper time. There is one prevented from sinning by” (Vulgate: “through”) “poverty, yet in his repose he shall be pricked. There is one who will lose his soul because of” (Vulgate: “through”) “shame, and will lose it through an imprudent person; indeed, through regard for persons he will destroy himself. There is one who, because of shame, promises for a friend” (Vulgate: “promises [to] a friend”) “and has gained an enemy for nothing.” [Col. 1107D–1108A]

“A wicked reproach is a lie in a man, and it will be continually in the mouth of the undisciplined. The persistence of the lying man praises a thief” (Vulgate: “a thief is better than…”); “but both shall inherit destruction. The habits of men are a lie without honour, and their shame is with them without interruption” (Ecclus. 18, 19, and 20).

We admonish you, brothers, unceasingly to pursue in the charity of Christ those things which are mutually beneficial to men. Likewise we beseech you in the Lord to walk worthily of the calling by which you were called, with all humility and meekness, with patience bearing one another in charity, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. One body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling; one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God, the Father of all, [Col. 1108B] who is above all, and through all, and in us all. But grace has been given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift. Therefore he says: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men” (Ps. 67). But what does “he ascended” mean except that he also first descended into the lower regions of the earth? He who descended is himself also he who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things. And he himself gave some as apostles, others as prophets, others indeed as evangelists, and others as pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of Christ’s body, until we all meet in the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, in a perfect man, in the measure of the maturity of Christ’s fullness; so that we may no longer be little children, tossed about and carried around by every wind of doctrine, [Col. 1108C] through the wickedness of men, through craftiness directed toward the deception of error (Eph. 4).

For it is unjust rashly to judge the hidden things of another’s heart (Prosper, *Sentences*, 21); and it is sinful to reproach from suspicion one whose works alone appear good. Therefore the sheep entrusted to their shepherd (Fifth Roman Council under Symmachus) ought neither to rebuke him—unless he has departed from the right faith—nor can they accuse him in any manner; for the deeds of shepherds are not to be struck by the sword of the mouth (variant: “sheep”), although they may seem secretly deserving of rebuke. We say these things because we have found in your writings that some bishops in your regions have been accused by their own sheep: some, indeed, on suspicion, and others for a definite reason; and consequently that some have been despoiled of their property and others driven from their own see.

You should know that they can be summoned neither to a provincial synod nor to a general one, nor be judged in any matter, before all that has been taken from them has been restored by law to their authority (variant: “before everything is peacefully restored”). First, therefore, all things must be restored to them by law, and the churches taken from them restored to them with every privilege belonging to them (variant: “with every privilege of their own”); and afterward they must be allowed, not a narrow span of time, but as much time as they appear to have been despoiled or expelled, before they are summoned to a synod and heard by all the bishops whatsoever (variant: “by each bishop”) of their province. For one who has been despoiled or expelled cannot either be summoned to a case or be judged, since one already stripped bare does not possess the privilege by which he might be despoiled. [Col. 1108D–1109A]

Therefore it was decreed even in antiquity that the possessor, or the chief party (variant: “the first [party]”), must restore to the former possessor, before a suit is contested, all possessions, everything taken from him, and all fruits. And elsewhere it is written: “He who has suffered violence shall receive all things in the state in which they were, and shall hold securely what he possesses.” And elsewhere, in the synodal decrees of the Fathers and the edicts of kings, the following ordinance is read: all things are to be restored to bishops despoiled or ejected; they are to be restored immediately by the authority of bishops, and thoroughly recalled to the places from which they withdrew, if before their accusation or regular summons to a synod they are known to have lost, through any condition of time, deceit, captivity, the force of greater powers, or through any unjust causes, the property or possessions of the Church or their own property or substance; and so forth.

There is also a decree in the ancient statutes of the Church that one who invades another’s property shall not escape unpunished, but shall restore everything with increase. Hence it is also written in the Gospel: “If I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold” (Luke 19). And the laws of the secular order provide: whoever steals another’s property shall restore tenfold to the person whose property was plundered what was taken away. And in the divine law we read: “Cursed is everyone who moves the boundary-mark of his neighbour.” And all the people shall say: “Amen” (Deut. 28). Therefore such acts must neither be presumed without punishment nor carried out without their own condemnation. (Thus far are the words of Pope Symmachus in the council cited.)

Pursue peace, and not another’s injury or injustice, among yourselves and toward all. But, doing the truth in charity, [Col. 1109C] let us grow in every respect into him who is the head, Christ: from whom the whole body, joined and knit together through every joint of supply, according to the working measured to each individual member, produces the growth of the body for its own edification in charity. Finally, most dear ones, rejoice and be made perfect; receive exhortation, be of one mind, keep peace, and the God of peace and charity shall be with you (Heb. 12; Eph. 4). May the Lord preserve you both now and unto the day of eternity (2 Pet. 3). Amen.

Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of October, Constantine (Constantius), most illustrious consul.

## EPISTLE III OF POPE EUSEBIUS, ADDRESSED TO THE BISHOPS OF TUSCIA AND CAMPANIA

Concerning persons of ill repute not to be admitted as witnesses; concerning those said to be of ill repute; and concerning heretics who have been duly baptized, who, if they return to the faith, are to be received through the laying on of hands [Col. 1109D]—which laying on of hands is shown to belong solely to the high priests.

Eusebius, to all his most beloved brothers, the bishops established throughout Campania and Tuscia.

Blessed be the Lord our God, who (Hormisdas, Ep. 25) through His mercy enriched the Roman Church with the priesthood of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and granted us mutual charity in showing the way among those around us (on account of the universal care which belongs to us by the privilege of that same Church), so that we who cleave together in the firmness of faith may also be joined in the desired delight of correspondence; and so that, while we reach even to you through the service of letters, we may also stir your hearts by apostolic admonitions to religious worship [Col. 1110A]; and while we repay to our love—or to the hope of our love—as it were a certain debt, we may show our full affection toward God.

Let us therefore, most beloved brethren, join continual and humble prayers; and, imploring our God with the tears of mouth and heart, let us beseech Him in unceasing supplication that, in teaching and in deed, we may cleave to Him whose members we desire to be, and that we may never turn aside by a wandering path from that way which is Christ, lest we unhappy ones be justly abandoned by Him whom we wickedly forsake. By the aid of heavenly favor, this can happen to us on this principle: if we preserve apostolic doctrines and the commands of the Fathers. For our Lord says: “He who loves me will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14).

And although these words, spoken generally, may suffice either for avoiding errors or for keeping the catholic faith, nevertheless we know it to have been ordained by the apostles and their successors (Sixtus, Saying 250; Hadrian, Collection, ch. 67) that accusations against teachers ought not to be received; that foreign tribunals ought not to be held (Theodosian Code, IX.1, constitution 10); and that no one ought to be bound by the judgment of any judge other than his own (Justinian Code, VII.48, constitution 4). For Christ is the head of the Church. Priests are Christ’s vicars, who perform an embassy in the Church in Christ’s stead (Hormisdas, Ep. 25, already cited). Therefore whatever injury is done to them pertains to Christ, who said: “He who hears you hears me; and he who rejects you rejects me. And he who rejects me [Col. 1110C] rejects him who sent me” (Luke 10).

These things, brethren, are terrible and must be considered and guarded against with the utmost diligence: both for the sake of those who endeavor to destroy themselves through greed, avarice, or envy, lest they fall into the depths or encounter such evils; and because of the persecutions of the Church and of her servants—those who, according to the voice of truth, have eyes yet do not see, and have ears yet do not hear, nor understand what pleases God.

Following, therefore, in all things the apostolic rule and proclaiming all its ordinances (John, epistle, chapter in the booklet after Hormisdas, Ep. 51; 3, question 5, *Constituimus cum*), for the protection of bishops—whom God has called pillars of the Church—and of the other true priests, confirming the venerable enactments of the Fathers, we decree again with all the bishops who are with us [Col. 1110D], as we find it formerly decreed, that murderers, evildoers, thieves, sacrilegious persons, robbers (Hadrian, Collection 63, in the second decree of Pope Eutychian), adulterers, incestuous persons, poisoners, persons under suspicion, criminals, household servants, perjurers, those who have committed abduction, borne false witness, or resorted to sacrilegious persons [read *sortilegos*, “diviners,” by Latinus’s conjecture] and diviners, and persons like them, are by no means to be admitted to accusation or testimony. For they are infamous and must rightly be rejected, because their voice is deadly. A deadly voice (Theodosian Code IX.6, constitution 3) ought in every respect to be prohibited rather than heard.

The danger threatening teachers must therefore always be most carefully avoided and shunned; and they must be sustained and protected by all, as the Lord says: “What you did to one of the least of mine, you did to me” (Matt. 25). For the first safeguard is to preserve the rules of right faith and never in any way to depart from the Fathers’ determinations (Hormisdas, *Rule of Faith*, after Ep. 9 and Ep. 51). Nor can the judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ be omitted, who says: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16). And what has been said is proved by the outcome of events: for in the Apostolic See catholic religion has always been preserved free from stain.

Therefore, beloved, let the voice of Holy Scripture also be heeded: “Learn to do good” (Isa. 1), “and avoid evils” (Prov. 16), and be instructed in the Fathers’ rules [variant: “always”], as it is written:

> My son, if you have means, do good to yourself,  
> and offer offerings worthy of God.  
> Remember that death does not delay,  
> and that the covenant of Hades has been shown to you.  
> The covenant of this world shall die by death.  
> Before death, do good to your friend;  
> and according to your ability, stretch out your hand and give to the poor.  
> Do not deprive yourself of a good day,  
> and let no portion of a good gift pass you by.  
> Will you not leave your pains and labors to others in the division of the lot?  
> Give and receive, and justify your soul.  
> Before your death, work righteousness,  
> for in Hades food cannot be found.  
> All flesh grows old like grass,  
> and like a leaf putting forth fruit upon a green tree.  
> Some are born and others fall away;  
> so it is with the generation of flesh and blood:  
> one comes to an end and another is born.  
> Every corruptible work will fail in the end,  
> and he who performs it will go with it.  
> But every chosen work will be justified,  
> and he who performs it will be honored in it.  
> Blessed is the man who dwells in wisdom,  
> who meditates upon his righteousness,  
> and in understanding considers the circumspection of God;  
> who devises her ways in his heart  
> and understands her hidden things;  
> who follows after her as an investigator  
> and stands in her paths;  
> who looks through her window  
> and listens at her door;  
> who rests beside her house  
> and fixes a peg in her walls;  
> who sets his little dwelling by her hands,  
> and good things will rest in his dwelling forever;  
> who sets his children under her shelter  
> and dwells beneath her branches.  
> He shall be protected beneath her branches from the heat  
> and shall rest in her glory.  
> 
> He who fears the Lord will do this [Vulgate: “good things”];  
> and he who holds fast to righteousness will obtain her.  
> She will meet him like an honored mother  
> and receive him like a wife from his virginity.  
> She will feed him with the bread of life and understanding  
> and give him the water of saving wisdom to drink.  
> He will be established in her and will not be moved;  
> she will hold him fast and he will not be put to shame;  
> she will exalt him among his neighbors.  
> In the midst of the Church she will open his mouth,  
> fill him with the spirit of wisdom and understanding,  
> and clothe him with a robe of glory.  
> She will heap joy and exultation upon him,  
> and he will inherit an everlasting name.  
> Foolish men will not lay hold of her,  
> but discerning men will meet her.  
> Foolish men will not see her,  
> for she is far from pride and deceit.  
> Lying men will not remember her,  
> but truthful men will be found in her  
> and will attain [Vulgate: “success”] even to the vision of God.  
> Praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner,  
> for wisdom has gone forth from God.  
> For the praise of God’s wisdom shall stand  
> and abound in the faithful mouth,  
> and the Sovereign will give it to him.  
> 
> Do not say, “It is from the Lord”:  
> for do not do what he hates.  
> Do not say, “He has led me astray”:  
> for he has no need of wicked men.  
> God hates every abomination of error,  
> and it shall not be loved by those who fear him.  
> From the beginning God created man  
> and left him in the hand of his own counsel.  
> He added his commandments and precepts.  
> If you wish to keep the commandments [Vulgate: “If you wish to keep the commandments”],  
> they will preserve you,  
> and enable you always to render pleasing faithfulness.  
> He has set before you water and fire:  
> stretch out your hand to whichever you choose.  
> Before man are life and death, good and evil;  
> whichever pleases him shall be given him.  
> For the wisdom of God is great,  
> mighty in power,  
> seeing all things without ceasing.  
> The eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him,  
> and he knows every work of man.  
> He has commanded no one to act wickedly  
> and has given no one license to sin.  
> For he does not desire a multitude of faithless and useless children.  
> 
> Do not delight in wicked children if they multiply,  
> nor take pleasure in them if the fear of God is not with them.  
> Do not trust their life,  
> and do not look to their labors.  
> For one who fears God is better than a thousand wicked children;  
> and it is better to die childless  
> than to leave wicked children.  
> By one wise person a homeland will be inhabited,  
> and by three wicked persons it will be abandoned.  
> My eye has seen many other such things [Vulgate: “such things”],  
> and my ear has heard things mightier than these.  
> In the assembly of sinners fire will blaze,  
> and wrath will blaze in an unbelieving nation.  
> The ancient giants did not pray for their sins,  
> who were destroyed because they trusted in their strength.  
> He did not spare their sojourning, but struck them  
> and cursed them for the pride of their speech.  
> He did not have mercy on them, destroying the whole nation,  
> those who exalted themselves in their sins.  
> Likewise the six hundred thousand foot-soldiers  
> who assembled in the hardness of their hearts:  
> even if there had been one stiff-necked man,  
> it would be remarkable if he had gone unpunished.  
> For with him are mercy and wrath,  
> mighty in forgiveness and pouring out wrath.  
> As is his mercy, so is his correction.  
> He will judge a person according to his works.  
> The sinner will not escape through plunder,  
> nor will the patience of one who practices mercy be delayed.  
> Every act of mercy will make room for each person  
> according to the merit of his works  
> and according to the understanding of his sojourning.  
> 
> Do not say, “I shall be hidden from God,  
> and who from on high will remember me?  
> In a great people I shall not be known:  
> for what is my soul amid so immense a creation?”  
> Behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens,  
> the abyss, the whole earth, and all that is in them  
> will be shaken in his sight—  
> mountains together with hills and the foundations of the earth.  
> When God looks upon them, they will be shaken with trembling.  
> Yet in all these things the heart is senseless;  
> every heart is understood by him.  
> Who understands his ways,  
> or the storm [Vulgate: “storm”] which no human eye has seen?  
> For very many of his works are hidden;  
> but who will recount, or endure, his works of righteousness?  
> For the covenant is far from some,  
> and the investigation of men is at the consummation.  
> He who is deficient in heart thinks evil [Vulgate: “vain things”];  
> and an imprudent, wandering man thinks foolish things.  
> (Ecclus. 14–16)

Therefore, brethren, let no evil speech proceed from your mouth, but only such as is good for the building up of need, so that it may give grace to those who hear. And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption. Let all bitterness, wrath, indignation, shouting, and blasphemy be removed from you, with all malice. But be kind to one another, merciful, forgiving one another, as God also in Christ forgave you (Eph. 4).

Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children; and walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a fragrant odor. But fornication, every impurity, or greed must not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints; nor obscenity, foolish talk, or coarse joking, which are unsuitable, but rather thanksgiving. For know this and understand it: every fornicator, impure person, or greedy person—which is idolatry—has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. Let no one deceive you [Col. 1113B] with empty words. For because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the children of disobedience. Therefore do not become sharers with them.

For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light—for the fruit of light consists in goodness, righteousness, and truth—testing what is pleasing to God. Do not participate in the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather expose them. For it is shameful even to speak of the things done by them in secret. But all things that are exposed are made visible by light; for everything made visible is light. Therefore it says: “Awake, sleeper; rise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you.”

See therefore, brethren, that you walk carefully: not as unwise persons but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil. Therefore do not become foolish, but understand [Col. 1113C] what the will of God is. And do not be drunk with wine, in which is debauchery, but be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking to yourselves in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs [Col. 1114A], singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord, always giving thanks for all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God the Father, submitting to one another in the fear of Christ (Eph. 5).

We command you solemnly to celebrate the feast of the discovery of the Cross of our Lord Jesus Christ—which was recently discovered, while we held the helm of the holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Nones of May—on the aforesaid calendrical day of its discovery.

[Note, Col. 1113C–1114D: **“Therefore the Cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, which was discovered recently while we held the helm of the Holy Roman Church …”** It can be established with the greatest certainty, as Surius says in his marginal notes, that the additions to this letter concerning this matter are spurious and inserted from outside. The Cross of the Lord was not discovered in the time of Pope Eusebius. Eusebius testifies (*Ecclesiastical History* III.46) that Helena embraced Christianity after Constantine. If Constantine was not yet Christian in the time of Pope Eusebius, how could Helena, still a worshipper of the gods, have been so intent upon finding Christ’s Cross? In addition, the common judgment of the Fathers and historians affirms that after the Council of Nicaea, Helena, then eighty years old and divinely instructed in a dream, directed by very ancient Jews and by Christian helpers, advisers, and informants, discovered the Lord’s Cross amid the great joy of those seeking it on 14 September; it was miraculously distinguished from the crosses of the thieves.

This is affirmed among the Fathers by St Paulinus, Ep. II to Severus; St Jerome, Ep. to Paulinus, *On the Institution of Monks*; St Ambrose, funeral oration for Theodosius; St Chrysostom, Homily 84 on John; Andrew of Crete, homily on the Exaltation of the Holy Cross; and, earlier than these, Cyril of Jerusalem, Ep. to Constantius. Among historians it is likewise affirmed by Eusebius, *Chronicle* and *Life of Constantine* III.29; Jerome, *Chronicle*; Prosper, *Chronicle*; Sulpicius, *Sacred History* II; Rufinus I.7–8; Theodoret, *History* I.18; Sozomen II.1; Socrates I.17; Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks* I.26; Nicephorus VIII.29; and Emperor Justinian’s Novel 28. I pass over a thousand other later writers. See Baronius, year 311, no. 41; likewise year 326, no. 42 and following; Gretser, *On the Cross* I.54 and following.

**Feast of the Invention [Discovery].** The author and founder of this feast, celebrated by the Latin Church on 3 May, are uncertain. For what is read here and in Gratian, canon *Crucis*, distinction 3, *De Consecratione*—that Pope Eusebius instituted the feast—is not probable, since the Cross was discovered not under Eusebius but under Sylvester, as shown above. The Greeks do not have this feast in their Menologion because, as Baronius says in his notes on the Roman Martyrology for 3 May, they count it among movable feasts. For on the third day after the Lord’s resurrection they celebrated the resurrection of the Cross: that is, when, as though rising from concealment through the zeal and work of the Empress Helena, it began to be made renowned by miracles. See Baronius at the cited place.]

[Note, Col. 1114C: *De consecratione*, distinction 3, “The Cross of the Lord.” This indeed conflicts with the consensus of historians, as was also said above; it has therefore been stitched onto this passage from elsewhere. Indeed, the entire letter is fabricated.]

Likewise, we decree that all heretics who are converted by God’s grace, who were baptized as believers in the name of the Holy Trinity, and who hold the rule of the Roman Church, are to be reconciled through the imposition of hands. The sacrament of the imposition of hands must likewise be held in great veneration, since it cannot be performed by anyone except the highest priests. Nor is it read or known that, in the time of the apostles, it was performed by persons other than the apostles themselves; nor can or ought it ever be performed by persons other than those—as has already been said—who hold their place. For if it is attempted otherwise, it shall be considered invalid and void and shall never be reckoned among the ecclesiastical sacraments.

For the rest, brethren, rejoice and exult in the Lord, so that, enlightened and strengthened by the grace of the Holy Spirit, you may be able, with the Lord’s help, to reach the pastures of eternal life and lead your own people there. May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit always be with us all. Amen.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, in the consulship of Constantine [variant: Constantius], illustrious consul.

[Note, Col. 1114C: Both chronological designations are suspect.]

[Col. 1115]

## Appendix IV, to Saint Pope Melchiades

[Note, Col. 1115D–1116D: **“For this privilege has been established for this holy see from apostolic times.”** That the causes of bishops are to be referred to the See of the Roman Church was established by Apostolic Canons 73 and 74, and the same has been confirmed by the decretal letters of nearly all pontiffs.]

## Letter of Pope Melchiades to All the Bishops of Spain

[Note, Col. 1115D: Learned men consider it forged.]

[Col. 1115]

Concerning accusations and disputes; that no one should be hostile toward another; baptism and the bishops’ imposition of hands; whether either of these is sufficient without the other, or seems greater.

I. On referring judgments concerning bishops, or major causes, to the Apostolic See; and that no one should be prevented from appealing to it.  
II. Which is the greater sacrament: the imposition of bishops’ hands or baptism?  
III. On fasting on Sunday and Thursday.

To the most beloved brethren Marinus, Benedict, Leontius, and the other bishops established in Spain and in those regions: Melchiades (Melciades or Miltiades).

The words of the apostolic command are that we ought to be without offence toward Jews and Gentiles (1 Cor. 10). Whoever is a Christian preserves this with all the strength of his soul. [Col. 1115B] Since this is so, no small danger before God may await the person who refuses to show this even to believers. For how greatly these matters grieve us who wish no one to perish—matters which strike Christian minds through Christian authors—the Lord’s own word in the Gospel testifies. For the Savior himself says that it is better for one who causes one of the little ones to stumble to be submerged in the depth of the sea (Matt. 18; Luke 17). Therefore let us ask what punishment awaits him for whom we read that such a penalty is preferable.

Accordingly, beloved, these words must be weighed and guarded against very carefully, lest eternal things be lost for temporal ones, enduring things for perishable ones, and, for the most trifling temporal things, everlasting joys be lost—which God forbid. Therefore we ask and beseech you that no one harm another, nor be hostile or injurious to another [Col. 1115C], but that—according to the apostle—each bear the other’s burdens, so as to fulfill the law of Christ (Gal. 6). “Do not judge one another”; but rather, according to the same apostle, “judge this instead: never to put a stumbling block or offence before a brother” (Rom. 14).

Always and before all things inquire diligently, so that you may decide with justice and truth [variant: “charity”]. Condemn no one before a true and just judgment [variant: “condemning no one beforehand”]. Judge no one according to the estimation of suspicion; but first prove the matter, and afterward pronounce a charitable judgment. And what you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another.

[Note, Col. 1115D: Here the letter begins in Justel’s manuscript.]

Remember always the Lord’s saying: “Do not judge, and you will not be judged; do not condemn, so that you will not be condemned” (Luke 6). “For with the judgment with which you judge, [Col. 1115D] you will be judged” (Matt. 7). Do not judge bishops; do not condemn them without the authority of this See [variant: “seat”]. If you do so, your judgments will be invalid, [Col. 1116A] and you will be condemned. For this privilege has been established for this holy See to preserve [variant: “to be preserved”] from apostolic times, and it remains inviolate to the present day.

The bishops, therefore, whom the Lord chose for himself as eyes and willed to be pillars of the Church, and to whom he also gave the power of binding and loosing, he reserved for his own judgment; and he entrusted this privilege, in his own stead, solely to blessed Peter, the keeper of the keys. This just prerogative of his accrues to the See [variant: “Which prerogative succeeded …”], to be inherited and retained in future ages, because even among the blessed apostles there was a certain distinction of authority. Although the election of all was equal, it was granted to blessed Peter to be preeminent over the others and prudently to order the causes and questions brought to complaint [Col. 1116B] concerning them. We believe this was so ordained by God’s ordering, lest all their successors [variant: “their successors”] claim all things for themselves, but so that greater causes—such as those of bishops—and matters requiring more weighty care might always flow to the one See of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles; that they might receive the conclusion of judgments from the place whence they received the beginning of their institutions, lest they ever differ from their own head.

### I.

If any one of you sees himself oppressed, let him appeal to this See and have recourse here, as custom has always ordained; for we willingly sympathize with them and gladly, as the Lord grants, will render assistance. Nor, brethren, should anyone be prevented [Col. 1116C] or rebuked who wishes to share in our communion; rather, let him be given help in coming.

[Note, Col. 1116D: What follows through §11 is absent from Justel’s manuscript.]

For the rebuke inflicted by the many is sufficient for each person, so that, according to the apostle, you should rather forgive and console him, lest he who is in distress perhaps be swallowed by excessive sorrow (2 Cor. 2). Therefore, as he says, I beseech you to confirm love toward him.

We silence the mouth of those who would accuse priests or testify against them, whom we know to be dead not by human but by divine words; for “the faithless man is dead in a living body” (Saying of Sixtus 6, Rufinus’s translation). Nor should a faithful person come under suspicion [Sayings 168–169 of the same author], so as to say or do what he does not wish to suffer. If anyone is faithful, let him see that he does not speak falsely or lay snares for anyone. It is easy [Sayings 176, 291, 203 of the same author] to deceive a human being, but not God. He is not wise who harms another. And one who is faithful wills no evil.

For by these things—by harming and by helping—we can recognize the faithful and the faithless person, as Truth itself says: “A good man brings forth good things from the good treasure of his heart; and an evil man brings forth evil things from the evil treasure of his heart” (Matt. 12). “For the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart” (Luke 6). For the Lord says on our behalf through the prophet: “I myself will judge those who judge you” (Isa. 49). And again he said to his servants: “Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not be afraid of their blasphemies” (Isa. 31).

The prophet also sings of such persons, saying:

> Not so the wicked,  
> but like dust which the wind drives away.  
> Therefore the wicked shall not rise in judgment,  
> nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous;  
> for the Lord knows the way of the righteous,  
> but the way of the wicked shall perish.  
> 
> Why have the nations been troubled,  
> and the peoples meditated vain things? [Col. 1117B]  
> The kings of the earth shall arise,  
> and the rulers shall take counsel together  
> against the Lord and against his Christ:  
> “Let us break their bonds  
> and cast their yoke from us.”  
> He who dwells in heaven shall laugh;  
> the Lord shall mock them.  
> Then he shall speak to them in his wrath  
> and trouble them in his fury.  
> (Pss. 1–2)
