And elsewhere he says:

> The wickedness of the ungodly is in the midst of his heart;  
> there is no fear of God before his eyes.  
> For he dealt deceitfully against him in his sight,  
> so that his iniquity might be found unto hatred.  
> The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit;  
> he has ceased to consider doing good.  
> He devises iniquity on his bed;  
> he stands in a way that is not good;  
> he does not reject evil.  
> 
> O Lord, your mercy is in heaven, reaching to the clouds.  
> Your righteousness is like the mountains of God; [Col. 1117C]  
> your judgments are a great abyss.  
> You will save humans and beasts, O Lord.  
> How precious is your mercy, O God!  
> The children of Adam shall hope in the shadow of your wings.  
> They shall be intoxicated with the richness of your house,  
> and you shall give them to drink from the torrent of your delights.  
> For with you is the fountain of life;  
> in your light we shall see light.  
> Draw out your mercy to those who know you,  
> and your righteousness to the upright in heart.  
> Let not the foot of pride come against me,  
> and let not the hand of the wicked move me.  
> There the workers of iniquity have fallen;  
> they have been driven out and could not rise.  
> (Ps. 35 [36])

Most of what is cited here follows Jerome’s version.

We have heard from certain brethren, against whom you were exceedingly hostile, that quarrels and discord exist among you. Therefore we have written these things to you, commanding that you hold them as the Apostolic See commands you to hold them. Thus also the Lord’s forerunner, answering soldiers who questioned him in the Gospel, said: “Do violence to no one, make no false accusation, and be content with your wages” (Luke 3). For he does violence to a person who unjustly troubles him.

For the present, let these things suffice concerning these matters. But if you need fuller instruction, provided life continues, send word and it will be sent to you.

[Note, Col. 1118B–C: *De consecratione*, distinction 5, “The Holy Spirit who [comes] upon”; also in Ivo’s *Decretum*, book I.]

II. Concerning those matters about which you asked to be instructed—namely, whether the greater sacrament is the laying on of bishops’ hands or baptism—know that both are great sacraments. And just as one is performed by the greater authorities, that is, by the chief bishops, which cannot be accomplished by lesser ones, so it too must be held and venerated with greater reverence. [Col. 1119A] [Note: [Col. 1120D] [Notes of Severinus Binius on columns 1119–1120] Confirmation belongs to the completion of baptism. Confirmation is called the completion of baptism not only here, but also in the Council of Elvira, canon 77, likewise by Dionysius the Areopagite, *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, ch. 4, part 3 of that chapter, where he calls it “the most holy completion of divine generation.” Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, book II, ch. 2, calls it likewise “the spiritual seal which remains after the font, so that completion may occur.” This is certainly not because baptism without confirmation confers no grace, or because it does not fully and perfectly remove the baptized person’s sin, but because through confirmation an increase and strengthening of grace is added to the baptized person, for the constant profession of the faith received in baptism. Suárez, vol. III, disputation 34, on confirmation, section 2. Fasting on the Lord’s day. See what we have said in the notes on Apostolic Canon 65 and the others.] But these two sacraments are so joined that they can by no means be separated from one another, except when death intervenes; and one cannot duly be completed without the other. For one, if death intervenes, can save without the other; but the other cannot.

Hence it is written: “In those days, says the Lord, I shall pour out [Note: [Col. 1119C] Eucherius, homily on Pentecost, commonly but falsely attributed to Eusebius of Emesa; its author is said by some to be Faustus. From this the reader may learn that much gold lies hidden in the wares of our merchant.] of my Spirit upon all flesh” (Joel 2). Let us observe the highest riches of God’s goodness. What the laying on of hands grants individually to neophytes being confirmed, the descent of the Holy Spirit then bestowed universally upon the peoples of believers (variant: *upon the people*). But since we have said that the laying on of hands and confirmation belong to the completion of baptism, and that it can effect something in one who has already been regenerated in Christ, perhaps someone thinks to himself: What [Col. 1119B] profit is the mystery of confirmation to me after the mystery of baptism? (variant: *the ministry of the confirmer*). Or, as I see it, we did not receive everything from the font, if after the font we need the addition of a new kind [of grace]. Not so, beloved. Let your charity attend.

Just as military order requires that, when an emperor has admitted someone into the number of soldiers, he not only mark the man whom he has received, but also equip him with suitable arms for battle: so, in one who has been baptized, that blessing is a fortification. You have given him a soldier; give him assistance for military service. What advantage is it if one of his parents bestows great property upon an orphan (variant: *little child*), unless he also takes care to provide him with a guardian? Thus the Paraclete is guardian, consoler, and tutor for those regenerated in Christ. Therefore the divine word says: “Unless the Lord guards [Col. 1119C] the city, the one who guards it keeps watch in vain” (Ps. 136 [137]).

Therefore the Holy Spirit, who descends upon the waters of baptism in a saving inpouring, grants fullness at the font for innocence, and in confirmation supplies increase for grace. And because those who are to live throughout their whole age in this world must walk amid invisible enemies and dangers, in baptism we are regenerated for life; after baptism we are confirmed for combat. In baptism we are washed; after baptism we are strengthened. But although the benefits of regeneration suffice for those who are to depart at once, the aids of confirmation are nevertheless necessary for those who are to live. [Col. 1120A] Regeneration by itself saves those who are immediately to be received in the peace of the blessed age; confirmation, however, arms and equips those reserved for the contests and battles of this world. But whoever, after baptism, reaches death unstained, with the innocence he has acquired, is confirmed by death, because after death he cannot sin.

Here, if perhaps we should also wish to inquire what benefit the coming of the Holy Spirit brought to the apostles after Christ’s passion and resurrection, the Lord himself plainly explains it to them. “What I say to you,” he says, “you cannot bear now. But when that Spirit of truth comes, he himself will teach you all truth” (John 16). Do you see that when the Holy Spirit is infused, the faithful heart is enlarged toward wisdom and constancy? Accordingly, before the descent [Col. 1120B] of the Holy Spirit the apostles are frightened, even to denial; but after his visitation they are armed, even to martyrdom, with contempt for safety.

Accordingly, through Christ we are redeemed; through the Holy Spirit we are illuminated, built up, educated, instructed, and perfected by the gift of spiritual wisdom, so that we may be able to hear that voice of the Holy Spirit: “I shall give you understanding, and shall instruct you in this way in which you shall walk” (Ps. 31 [32]). From the Holy Spirit we receive the power to become spiritual, because “the natural man does not receive the things that are of the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2). From the Holy Spirit we receive the power to discern wisely between good and evil, to love what is just and reject what is unjust; to resist malice and pride; and to withstand luxury, diverse enticements, and shameful and unworthy desires. [Col. 1120C] From the Holy Spirit we receive love of life and ardor for glory, so that, set aflame by God, we may be able to raise the mind from earthly things to things above and divine. [Note: [Col. 1120C] Thus far the orator, whoever he was, outstanding in Gallican eloquence.]

III. No one ought to observe a fast on the Lord’s day [Note: [Col. 1120C] The so-called *Apostolic Constitutions*, book V, final chapter, above.] or on the fifth day, so that there may be a true and not false distinction between the fasting of Christians and that of Gentiles, between those who truly believe and unbelievers and heretics. Hence it is written: “What share has Christ with Belial? Or what share has the faithful person with the unbeliever? But what participation has righteousness with iniquity?” (2 Cor. 6). And [Col. 1121A] again: “Do not be yoked together with unbelievers” (2 Cor. 6).

Furthermore, brothers, see that no one deceives you by empty words, nor through philosophy and empty deceit according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world and not according to Christ. For in Christ the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily, and you are made full in him, who is the head of every principality and power. In him you were also circumcised with a circumcision not made by hands, in the stripping off of the body of flesh, but in the circumcision of Christ; buried with him in baptism, in which you also rose through faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead. And you, when you were dead in transgressions and in the foreskin of your flesh, he made alive together with him, forgiving you all transgressions; blotting out the written bond of decree that stood against you and was contrary to us; he removed it [Col. 1121B] from the midst and nailed it to the cross. Stripping the principalities and powers, he made a public display of them boldly, triumphing over them in himself.

Therefore let no one judge you in food or drink, or concerning a part of a feast day, or a new moon, or sabbaths—things which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is Christ’s. Let no one defraud you, taking pleasure in humility and the worship of angels, entering into things he has not seen, vainly puffed up by the understanding of his flesh, and not holding fast the head, from which the whole body, through [the Vulgate: “joints and ligaments”] joint and connection, being supplied and built together, grows into an increase of faith. If, therefore, you died with Christ to the elements of this world, why do you still make decrees as though living in the world: “Do not touch; do not taste; do not handle”—all things that perish through their use—according to the commandments and teachings of men? These [Col. 1121C] indeed have an appearance of wisdom in superstition and humility, and in not sparing the body, but not in any honor toward the gratification of the flesh (Col. 2).

Therefore, if you have risen together with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; set your minds on the things above, not on things upon the earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you too shall appear with him in glory. Therefore put to death [Col. 1122A] your members which are upon the earth: fornication, impurity, lust, evil desire, and covetousness, which is the service of idols; because of these the wrath of God comes upon the children of unbelief. Among them you too once walked, when you lived with them. But now put away from yourselves every (Vulgate: *all*) anger, indignation, malice, blasphemy, and shameful speech from your mouth. Do not lie to one another, stripping off the old human being with his deeds and putting on the new, the one renewed in knowledge according to the image of him who created him; where there is neither Jew nor Gentile, circumcision nor foreskin, barbarian nor Scythian, slave nor free, but Christ is all things and in all.

Therefore put on, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, hearts of mercy, kindness, humility, [Col. 1122B] modesty, patience; bearing with one another and forgiving one another, if anyone has a complaint against anyone; just as Christ forgave you, so also you [must forgive]. But above all these things, have charity, which is the bond of perfection. And let the peace of Christ flourish in your hearts, to which you were also called in one body; and be grateful. Let the word of God dwell in you abundantly: in all wisdom teaching and admonishing yourselves with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing to God in your hearts with grace. Whatever you do in word or deed, do all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks to God and the Father through him (Col. 3).

You, most beloved, do not grow weary in doing good. But if anyone does not obey the apostolic words, mark that person, and do not associate with him, so that he may be ashamed. Yet do not regard him [Col. 1122C] as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother (2 Thess. 3). May the God of peace grant you to think the same thing toward one another and toward all; and may he himself be always with you in every place. Amen (Rom. 15).

Given on the Kalends of March, in the consulship of Volusianus and Rufinus, most illustrious men. [Note: [Col. 1122C] In the year 314, when Melchiades had already died, about three months earlier, on 10 December 313.]

Henry Dodwell’s dissertation on the *ripa Striga*. 175  

§ I.—This bank was not of the sea but of a river. Ibid.  
§ II.—*Striga* is a surveying and military term. Ibid.  
§ III.—Roman camps were for the most part square. The front of permanent camps faced east; that of mobile camps, the enemy. Ibid.  
§ IV.—Accordingly, the ancients called the front of a camp *striga*, its side *latus*, and its bench *scamnum*. 177  
§ V.—Roman colonies were laid out according to military discipline. The *strigae* of colonies were their *praetenturae*. Ibid.  
§ VI.—The boundaries of fields, camps, and especially Roman provinces were rivers. Ibid.  
§ VII.—The Danube was the frontier of the Illyrian *praetenturae*. The riparian Illyrian provinces took their name from the bank of that same Danube. Ibid.  
§ VIII.—The same is proved from the very numerous permanent camps on the Danube’s bank, and from history. The character of the fortifications of Roman *praetenturae*. Tertullian is explained against Rhenanus. Ibid.  
§ IX.—The same point from Attila’s province taken from the Romans. 179  
§ X.—The Romans sometimes, but rarely, crossed the Danube’s bank. 180  
§ XI.—The belief in the fated boundaries of empires hindered them from crossing it often. Nevertheless, in Diocletian’s age they retained no province beyond the Danube. Ibid.  
§ XII.—This reference to the *ripa Striga* accords with Diocletian’s plan and journey. Ibid.  

Henry Dodwell’s chronology of the persecutions, interwoven, as chronological method required, with Stephen Baluze’s Diocletian chronology. In addition, the consuls of each year and other events have been included. 181 ff.

Chapter I.—Analysis of this book; its sole manuscript codex, title, and subject; and why and when Lucius Caecilius published it. 840  

Article I.—Analysis of this book. Ibid.  
Article II.—On the manuscript codex of this book: how incomplete it is and how shamefully corrupted by a copyist utterly ignorant of Latin. 848  
Article III.—On the true and genuine title and subject of this book. 850  
Article IV.—The reasons which prompted Caecilius to write this book, and the time when he issued it. 851

Article I.—Arguments are set forth by which very many have thought that this book might be claimed for Firmianus Lactantius. Ibid.  
Article II.—Arguments drawn from the title of this book are advanced, by which it appears capable of being established that Firmianus Lactantius was not its author. 855  

[Col. 1128]

Article III.—Other arguments are presented by which it can be demonstrated that this book did not proceed from Firmianus Lactantius, and the objections to them are answered. 859  
Article IV.—Other arguments drawn from various opinions of Caecilius are presented, showing that this book was not written by Firmianus Lactantius. 865  
Article V.—On Donatus, to whom the book is dedicated, and on the three judges Flaccinus, Hierocles, and Priscillianus, by whose command he suffered various punishments for confessing Christ. 868  

Chapter III.—On the various editions of this book, and the various observations and notes upon it. 871  

Article I.—On the various editions of this book. Ibid.  
Article II.—On various persons’ notes and observations upon this book. 872  

Chapter IV.—New notes and observations on this book; first, concerning Christ the Lord and His disciples. 873  

Article I.—An examination of what Caecilius relates concerning the time and year in which Christ the Lord died, and whether Lactantius held the same opinion on this matter. Ibid.  
Article II.—On the acts which Caecilius records as having occurred from Christ the Lord’s return to life until His ascension into heaven. 875  
Article III.—Whether Caecilius rightly said that Christ’s Gospel was disseminated throughout all parts of the world at the beginning of Nero’s, or Decius’, reign. 877  
Article IV.—What Caecilius thought concerning Peter’s arrival at Rome, the time when he held the supreme pontificate in that city, the miracles he performed there, and the deaths of himself and the apostle Paul. 882  

Chapter V.—An examination of what Caecilius relates concerning Christians’ customs and certain of their doctrines. Ibid.  

Article I.—How greatly Christians abhor things sacrificed to the gods of the nations; whether the emperor Maximinus was the first of all to command that food for sale be first offered to the gods before being placed upon tables; and concerning the most noble martyr who was burned alive for tearing up Diocletian’s edict. Ibid.  
Article II.—On Christians’ supreme power over demons, whom they put to flight at sacrifices performed by Diocletian through the sign of the Lord’s cross; and whether and how it was lawful for them to be present at these pagan sacrifices. 886  
Article III.—On the sign of the Lord’s cross which appeared to Constantine the Great, and through whose power he gained his remarkable victory over Maxentius; also on sacred images. 890  
Article IV.—On the churches and possessions of early Christians; on the merits of good works; and whether Caecilius related anything concerning Christ’s thousand-year reign upon earth. 891  

Chapter VI.—On the first persecutors of the Christian Church and their deaths. 893  

Article I.—How rightly Caecilius asserts that the first persecution against Christians was stirred up by Nero Augustus; how absurdly Tollius therefore charges him with falsehood because he attributes the cause of this persecution to the preaching of the apostle Peter; and asserts that Nero’s body lacked burial; and on what grounds Caecilius charges with madness those who invented that Nero would be the precursor of Antichrist. Ibid.  
Article II.—On Domitian, the second persecutor of the Church, his death, and the destruction of his images and honorary inscriptions. 897  
Article III.—Whether Caecilius rightly said that Roman emperors from Domitian to Decius were good rulers, that the Christian Church then suffered no assaults from enemies, and whether Lactantius’ non-authorship of this book can be inferred from this. 900  

Chapter VII.—On other persecutors of the Christian Church. 904  

Article I.—On the persecution of the Church stirred up by the emperor Decius and his disastrous death. Ibid.  
Article II.—On the persecution by the emperor Valerian, his disgraceful servitude, and the removal of his skin after death. 905  
Article III.—On the persecution against Christians instigated by the emperor Aurelian and his death. 907  

Chapter VIII.—On the last persecutors of the Christian Church; first, Diocletian. 908  

Article I.—On Diocletian’s three names, Diocles, Jovius, and Diocletian; his country, avarice, and timidity; another emperor and two Caesars appointed by him out of timidity; whether he gave Spain to Constantius to govern; the exactions and taxes by which he oppressed all; his great prosperity until he began to harass Christians; and whether he was better and more useful to the state than other rulers. Ibid.  
Article II.—On the preliminaries and beginning of the persecution instigated by Diocletian against Christians; its cause and the counsels by which he was induced to harass them. 912  
Article III.—In what year, month, and day Diocletian began to torture and persecute Christians. 914  
Article IV.—On the church at Nicomedia demolished at the beginning of the persecution by Diocletian’s command; on his edict against Christians immediately published; on the first and second fires in the imperial palace; on who caused them; and on how Galerius tried thereby to inflame Diocletian to persecute Christians more cruelly. 916  
Article V.—How Diocletian raged against Prisca and Valeria, against the most powerful eunuchs—and who these were—likewise against presbyters and ministers with all their households, and against persons of every sex and age; also against household servants, and by what cruelty he and other judges tried to compel everyone to sacrifice to false gods. 919  
Article VI.—How great a slaughter of Christians, at Diocletian’s command, occurred in the provinces subject to Galerius and Herculius; whereas Constantius permitted churches to be demolished, yet kept Christians in Gaul unharmed and free from persecution. 922  
Article VII.—On Diocletian’s vicennalia, and when they were celebrated at Rome; why he departed thence in haste, came to Ravenna, and, seized by a slight illness, assumed there his ninth consulship; in what sense he is said thereafter to have hastened to Nicomedia by the *ripa Striga*, and there, overcome by illness, to have fallen into madness. 925  
Article VIII.—On the conference in which Galerius compelled Diocletian to resign the empire; whether he rightly proposed to him the example of the emperor Nerva; the great insolence of Galerius and timidity of Diocletian in that conference; whether Caecilius rightly asserts that Constantine was present and that Diocletian, urged and compelled by Galerius, abdicated the empire. 927  
Article IX.—Where and how Diocletian clothed Maximinus in purple and proclaimed him and Severus Caesars, rejecting Constantine; whether Caecilius’ view on this point is true; to what place Diocletian retired after relinquishing the empire; and where Licinius was made emperor in his presence. 930  
Article X.—Whether the things Caecilius relates concerning Diocletian’s private life are true; and whether, because his exiled daughter Valeria was denied return and his statues destroyed, he wasted away from grief and hunger and died. 932  

Chapter IX.—On Diocletian’s wife Prisca and his daughter Valeria. 935  

Article I.—How rarely Prisca and how frequently Valeria are mentioned by ancient authors; whether both professed the Christian religion. Ibid.  
Article II.—On Valeria and Candidianus, adopted by her because of barrenness; why, after the death of her husband Galerius, she left Licinius and fled to Maximinus, and rejected his marriage proposal; on the black garments of widows during their period of mourning; and whether no emperor’s wife had ever previously married a second husband. 937  
Article III.—On the exile of Prisca and Valeria; the execution and death of three noblewomen, friends of Valeria, and of a certain Jew who had falsely accused them of adultery; and the execution and death of Prisca and Valeria themselves. 940  

Chapter X.—On the emperor Maximianus Herculius. 942  

Article I.—When and where Maximianus Herculius was made emperor; his accord with Diocletian; the extent of his avarice and lust; and where he first relinquished the empire. Ibid.  
Article II.—How Maximianus Herculius, having resumed the purple, freed Rome from siege and came to Constantine, whom he tried to deceive after giving his younger daughter to him in marriage; on his second return to Rome, where he vainly tried to deprive Maxentius of the empire and was then disgracefully expelled. 944  
Article III.—How Maximianus Herculius, having returned to Constantine, again laid aside the purple; how, after deceiving Constantine, he assumed it a third time and subsequently occupied Marseilles, from which he was expelled by Constantine; and finally by what treacheries he attempted to kill him, paid the penalty by the noose, and had his statues destroyed. 945  

Chapter XI.—On the emperor Maxentius. 948  

Article I.—On the parents of the emperor Maxentius and the nature and extent of his vices; how, where, and by whom he was made emperor; in what sense he and Constantine the Great are called sons of the Augusti; what the royal salutation was; and what the name *privatus* (“private person”) signifies. Ibid.  
Article II.—Whether and why Maxentius, rescued from plots laid against him by his father Herculius, declared war on Constantine; on his alliance with Maximinus; on the enormous size of his army; on his superstition; and on his first battle against Constantine. 951  
Article III.—Whether what Caecilius relates concerning the battle in which Maxentius was defeated by Constantine the Great is true; how Maxentius was cast from the bridge into the Tiber; in what year he died; and whether it was after the completion of his quinquennalia. 953  

Chapter XII.—On the emperor Maximianus Galerius. 955  

Article I.—On the homeland, parents, wife, savage barbarity, and monstrous bodily size of Maximianus Galerius; on the superstition of his mother Romula and a difficult passage of Caecilius concerning it; on Galerius’ victory over Narses; and on the title Caesar, which he arrogantly rejected. Ibid.  
Article II.—How Galerius compelled Diocletian to rage against Christians and to surrender the empire; what he then reproached him with; the injustice with which he tried to deprive all of liberty; and how, contrary to the laws, he ordered decurions, leading citizens, distinguished and most eminent men, and noble matrons to be tortured, the latter dragged into the women’s quarters (*gynaeceum*); household servants and administrators to be corrected with the spear; and men to be stretched for flogging upon a post in the stable. 957  
Article III.—The number and horror of the tortures by which Galerius killed Christians and others; and how he tried to exterminate all letters and learned men, and establish military judges. 960  
Article IV.—On the immense and wholly intolerable exactions, censuses, poll taxes, and tributes by which Galerius crushed all his subjects and reduced them to utter poverty; and on beggars whom he ordered drowned in the sea. 963  
Article V.—The plots Galerius laid against Constantine the Great; what the *sigillum* was, upon receiving which Constantine returned to his father; Galerius’ grief when he learned that Constantine and Maxentius had been made emperors and received Constantine’s laureate image; how he attempted to besiege Rome; the disorder with which, on departing thence, he allowed Italy to be ravaged by his soldiers; and how he named Licinius and Maximinus emperors. 966  
Article VI.—On Galerius’ final and shameful illness, and the edict which he then published in favour of Christians. 969  
Article VII.—Where and when Galerius died after entrusting his wife and daughter to Licinius; and on his son Candidianus. 971  

Chapter XIII.—On the emperors Severus and Maximinus. 973  

Article I.—The homeland and vices of Severus; by whom and how he was made Caesar and afterwards emperor; the manner of his death after Rome had been besieged; and on his son Severianus. Ibid.  
Article II.—On the homeland, various names, parents, occupation, and drunkenness of Maximinus; how he became a guardsman, protector, tribune, Caesar, and emperor; and what the Campus Martius was. 975  
Article III.—How, after Galerius’ death, Maximinus attempted to invade provinces, made peace with Licinius, and rescinded the indulgence granted to Christians under a common title; why he everywhere appointed high priests adorned with white cloaks, ordered Christians’ limbs mutilated, and required all animals offered for sale to be sacrificed by pagan priests. 978  
Article IV.—On the immense exactions and tributes by which Maximinus utterly oppressed everyone, pagans and Christians alike. 981  
Article V.—On Maximinus’ unbridled and ruinous lust. 983  
Article VI.—Why and how Maximinus declared war on Licinius and was defeated; how he fled into the passes of Mount Taurus; and how he afterwards tried to defend and protect himself at Tarsus in Cilicia. 985  
Article VII.—On Maximinus’ disastrous death, the length of his reign, and the year in which he died. 987  
Article VIII.—On Maximinus’ wife and children, and their disastrous deaths. 988  

Chapter XIV.—On the emperor Licinius. 990  

Article I.—On Licinius’ homeland, parents, vices, and intimacy with Galerius; whether Galerius made him Caesar and emperor at the same time; and whether, as he was dying, Galerius entrusted his wife and daughter to Licinius. Ibid.  
Article II.—On the discord between Licinius and Maximinus and the peace they made; Licinius’ betrothal and marriage to Constantia, sister of Constantine the Great; the subsequent rupture of peace between Licinius and Maximinus; their battle; the prayers dictated to Licinius by an angel, whatever Tollius may say; and Licinius’ remarkable victory. 992  
Article III.—On the edict which Licinius published for the restoration of peace to the Christian Church. 993  
Article IV.—How Licinius pursued Maximinus and compelled him to kill himself at Tarsus in Cilicia; and, having gained supreme power, extirpated the entire remaining stock of the tyrants and all their children—especially Valerius. 996  

[Col. 1131]

Chapter XV.—On the emperors Constantius Chlorus and Constantine the Great. 999  

Article I.—How outstanding were the virtues of Constantius Chlorus; when he became Caesar and son-in-law of Maximianus Herculius; whether and how he kept Christians unharmed in Gaul during the persecution while permitting churches to be demolished; why he became the foremost emperor despite Galerius’ contempt; and how, when Constantine returned to him, he transferred the empire to him, and where he died. Ibid.  
Article II.—On the parents, homeland, exceptional bodily and mental gifts, and education of Constantine the Great; the great envy directed against him by others, especially Galerius; and the plots by which they assailed him. 1001  
Article III.—Whether Constantine the Great, as Caecilius relates, was present at the conference of Diocletian and Galerius, knew that Caesars were to be appointed, and knew that he himself would be disgracefully excluded from that nomination. 1003  
Article IV.—How Constantine returned, against Galerius’ will, to his father Constantius, who was on the point of death; and whether his father or others made him Caesar and emperor simultaneously. 1005  
Article V.—How greatly Constantine favoured Christians; why Maximianus Herculius came to him, betrothed his younger daughter to him, and joined her to him in marriage; why he returned to him; the plots he prepared against Constantine while the latter was about to fight barbarians; how Maximianus, after Marseilles was taken, obtained pardon from Constantine; how he later vainly tried to kill Constantine in bed; and what remarkable victory Constantine gained over Maxentius after seeing the wondrous sign of the cross. 1007  
Article VI.—On Constantine’s triumphal entry into the city of Rome; the title of pre-eminence decreed to him by the Roman Senate; how long he afterwards remained in Rome; where he gave his sister Constantia in marriage to Licinius; and the peace and tranquillity restored to the Christian Church by both rulers. 1009  

Dogmatic inquiries into Lactantius, or concerning his manner of thinking and arguing about religion. 1011  

Chapter I.—On religion considered generally. Ibid.  

Article I.—The derivation of the names *religio* (“religion”) and *superstitio* (“superstition”), and whether Cicero gave the true etymology of each. Ibid.  
Article II.—What true religion is, and the inseparable bond by which it is joined with justice and wisdom. 1014  
Article III.—That religion was introduced not because of fear, but instituted by God and implanted in man, who for this reason has an upright body and is called in Greek ἄνθρωπος (*anthrōpos*, “human being”); that humanity is principally distinguished from beasts by religion; and that Epicurus’ contrary arguments are answered. 1018  

Chapter II.—An examination of the arguments by which Lactantius demonstrates that the Christian religion alone is true. 1022  

Article I.—An examination of Lactantius’ arguments demonstrating from the oracles of our sacred prophets that the Christian religion is true, inasmuch as they foretold that Christ, the Son of God, would become man and be born of a virgin. Ibid.  
Article II.—The oracles of the sacred prophets by which Lactantius demonstrates that it was foretold Christ would be born from David’s family; and whether he rightly said that the city Jerusalem received its name from Solomon. 1029  
Article III.—The prophetic oracles by which Lactantius demonstrates that the everlasting priesthood of Christ, author of true religion, was foretold. 1032  
Article IV.—Other oracles of Apollo, the Milesians, the Sibyls, and the sacred prophets, by which the impious Jewish conspiracy against Christ, the various tortures to be inflicted upon Him before death, the manner of His death, the eclipse of the sun at His death, and His return to life were foretold; and the extent to which the truth of the Christian religion is established thereby. 1035  

Chapter III.—How Lactantius asserts and confirms the truth of the Christian religion from Christ’s true miracles, foretold by our sacred prophets and other seers. 1044  

Article I.—How clearly Lactantius shows the truth of Christ’s religion, which He confirmed through true miracles indicated by Isaiah and the Sibyl. Ibid.  
Article II.—How incontrovertibly Lactantius demonstrates the truth of the Christian religion from demons put to flight by Christ, by His name, and by the sign of the cross. 1046  
Article III.—Refutation of pagan arguments by which they vainly tried to prove that Apollonius of Tyana performed miracles like, or even greater than, those of Christ, or that these had been invented by the apostles for gain. 1051  

[Col. 1132]

Chapter IV.—Other arguments by which Lactantius establishes the truth of the Christian religion are examined. 1053  

Article I.—How plainly Lactantius demonstrates the truth of the Christian religion from the abolition of the Jewish Law and the institution, propagation, and holiness of Christianity. Ibid.  
Article II.—How forcefully Lactantius disclosed the truth of the Christian religion from the most dreadful punishments of the martyrs, endured with the utmost steadfastness to their final breath of life, not without the help of divine grace. 1059  
Article III.—Contrary pagan arguments are answered: they tried to prove that Christians ought to be brought back to the religions of their ancestors by force, penalties, and torture, because God would be unjust if He permitted them to live in want and poverty. 1064  
Article IV.—Other pagan arguments are answered, drawn from the falling away of certain Christians, the constancy of Regulus and Mucius in bitter death, and their assertion that Christians caused public calamities. 1067  

Chapter V.—On the sacred books of the Old and New Testaments and their authors, from which Lactantius drew the doctrines and teachings of the Christian religion. 1070  

Article I.—On the division of sacred Scripture into the Old and New Testaments, and the divine inspiration of the sacred prophets. Ibid.  
Article II.—On the antiquity of sacred Scripture; first, whether Lactantius rightly determines when and how Moses liberated the Israelites from Egyptian slavery; what he maintains about the angel who went before them and divided the water; about the miracles wrought in the wilderness by Moses; where and why he gave the Law to the Israelites; and when, after the name Hebrews was changed, they began to be called Jews and their land Judaea. 1071  
Article III.—How many years Moses preceded the fall of Troy; the dates of the other prophets and of the kings or rulers under whose reign they flourished; how many years after Troy’s fall David and Solomon reigned; how many years are counted from then to Christ’s time; whether Zechariah was the last prophet; how many years passed from his age to Christ’s death; and how rightly Lactantius concludes from this chronology that the sacred seers issued all their oracles concerning Christ long before He became man. 1074  
Article IV.—On the books of Moses and Joshua, who was first called Auses and afterwards Joshua; on the books of Kings, or *Basileion*; and on the books of Ezra and Nehemiah. 1079  
Article V.—On the Psalms; the books of Ecclesiasticus, Wisdom, and Proverbs, attributed to Solomon;
and concerning certain words cited by Lactantius which are now lacking in the sacred text. On the books of Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, Hosea, Amos, Micah, Malachi, and Zechariah; on the opening words of John the Evangelist; on Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians and the Apocalypse. 1084 Art. VI.—Why and how Lactantius employs the testimonies of Sacred Scripture to instruct Christians and to refute Jews and Gentiles. 1084 Appendices to the writings of the holy Roman pontiffs Marcellinus, Marcellus, Eusebius, and Miltiades, mentioned in volume six. 1085 First appendix, to Saint Pope Marcellinus. Ibid. First letter of Pope Marcellinus to Bishop Solomon. Ibid. The error of those who say that the Father is greater than the Son, etc., is refuted. Ibid. Second appendix, to Saint Marcellus. 1089 Letter II.—Pope Marcellinus to the Eastern bishops. Ibid. That a layman may not accuse a cleric. Ibid.

I.—On disputes arising among Christians being brought before the Church. Ibid.

II.—That one greater ought not to be judged by one lesser, nor may bishops inflict any prejudice upon the pontiff by whom they are shown to have been consecrated. 1090

III.—That no cleric should presume, without his bishop’s permission, to summon anyone before a secular court; nor may a layman accuse any cleric whatsoever. Ibid.

IV.—That an unjust judgment rendered by judges through fear of a king or at his command is invalid, and that the enactments of unbelievers shall be abolished. 1091 First letter of Pope Marcellus to the bishops of the province of Antioch. 1092 On the primacy and authority of the Roman Church, etc. Ibid. Second letter of Pope Marcellus I to the tyrant Maxentius. 1096 He admonishes the tyrant to cease raging against Christians. Ibid.

# INDEX OF NOTABLE SUBJECTS AND WORDS CONTAINED IN THE WORKS OF LACTANTIUS

[Note: [Col. 1133] In this index, Roman numerals I and II refer to *Patrologia Latina* volumes 6 and 7. Arabic numbers refer to Migne’s columns.]

## A
ABDERE, ABDITUS, for *abscondere*, *absconditus* (“to hide,” “hidden”), II, 599.  
ABDICARE, what it signifies, I, 327.  
ABDICATIO FILII, what the disowning of a son signifies, I, 457.  
ABDOMEN, whence its name is derived, II, 59. — What internal organs it encompasses, ibid.  
ABELLIUS, who he was and how he was killed, II, 236, 343.  
ABEUNT IN PROFUNDUM (“they sink into the deep”): submerged cities, I, 742.  
ABJURARE (“to abjure”), I, 636.  
ABNEGARE LUCEM ANIMIS (“to deny light to souls”), that is, to kill, I, 708.  
ABOMINABILIS (“abominable”), a Lactantian word, I, 813.  
ABRITTUM, *aburtum*, and *abyrtum*: the same place, II, 441.  
ABSCIDI, what it means, I, 186.  
ABSQUE, for *praeter* (“except”), I, 483.  
ABSTINENTIA, what it is, I, 420.  
ABSTINERE is rightly joined with the accusative case, ibid., and 951, 952.  
ABICTI, used in place of *uti* (“to use”), I, 166.  
ACADEMICS. They abolished knowledge, I, 355 and ibid., 336. — Their origin, ibid. — Wherein they erred, 360. — The source from which their school flowed, 439. — Their doctrine, 604.  
ACCEDERE ad religionem (“to join a religion”), I, 713, 714.  
ACCENSI soldiers, whence so called, I, 928.  
ACCIPITER (“hawk”). Worshipped by the Egyptians, I, 786.  
ACCIUS NAVIUS, an augur, I, 288.  
ACCUSATIONE FORTUNAE consolari se (“to console oneself by accusing Fortune”), I, 583.  
ACHILLEUS assumed the purple in Egypt, II, 491. — In what year he was defeated by Diocletian, 492.  
ACIES, for battle or engagement, II, 262, 815.  
The Acts of Saint Maurice and his companions are spurious, II, 311. — Likewise those of Saint George, 318, 321. — When, and by whom, the Acts of Pilate were composed, 466, 540.  
ACTIO, for a legal action, II, 658.  
ACTUARII and *actuales*: who were so called, II, 654.  
ACTUS, for *actio* (“action”), II, 114. [Col. 1154]  
ACUMINARE (“to sharpen”), II, 732.  
ADAM. On his life in paradise, I, 322. — Whether he lived there free from labours, 322, 323. — On his fall and repentance, 323. — Expelled from paradise, ibid. — The condemned opinion maintaining that he died because of his carnal condition, 931.  
ADDICTI and NEXI: who were so called, I, 637.  
AFFERRE and ADDUCERE: not to be used indiscriminately, II, 750.  
ADGAUDERE (“to rejoice with”), I, 462.  
ADICERE, archaically for *adjicere* (“to add”), II, 739.  
ADMINISTRATORES: who they were, II, 230, 734.  
ADOLESCENS and JUVENIS, synonyms, II, 742.  
ADON, probably struck by a boar [source reads *agro*], I, 208.  
ADORATION. In the rite of adoration, it was customary to bring the hands to the mouth, I, 135, 136.  
ADORARE, for bowing oneself deeply, II, 223.  
ADULESCENS, for *adolescens*, II, 719.  
ADULTERY. What it is, I, 719. — Roman laws are blameworthy in this matter, ibid. The penalty for adultery: when it began to be capital, II, 549.  
ADVERSARIUS, for the devil, II, 191, 471, 600.  
ADUNARI: what things are said to be united, II, 738.  
AEACUS, judge of the underworld, I, 804.  
AEDILES formerly restrained the frenzy of sellers, II, 400.  
EGYPT: in what sense it may be called the East, II, 491, 663.  
The AEGEAN Sea: what it is and whence so called, I, 182.  
Αἰγίοχος (*Aegiochos*): why Jupiter was so called, I, 240.  
EGYPTIANS. Their priests shaved the whole body, I, 235. — Authors to be consulted on their superstitions, 282. — What sort of year they had, 325, 647, 934. — By what name their land was formerly called, 327. — They were the first to contemplate and worship the stars, 328. — Among them rains are absent or rare, 329, 533. — They were the first to hand down transmigration of souls, 405. — The drowning of them and of Pharaoh in the Red Sea, 470, 471, 785. — On their worship of animals, 620, 786. — They worshipped the sun under Jupiter’s image, 621. — Whether the Jews received from them the custom of embalming bodies, 772. [Col. 1155]  
AEOLIANS change Δ into Ζ, II, 408.  
AEQUALIS: with what it agrees, II, 93.  
AEQUITAS, for equality, II, 417 and ibid. — It is a part of justice, 597, 598. — Wherein it consists, 598.  
AES, when used without qualification, denotes military pay, II, 797. — Who was called a soldier discharged *aere* (“by payment”), ibid.  
AESCULAPIUS: his birth and upbringing, I, 160. — By what deeds he earned divine honours, ibid. — Why he perished after being struck by lightning, ibid. — His native country and burial place, ibid. — Why he was called Epidaurian, ibid. — Whether he invented medicine, 213. — Summoned from Epidaurus, he freed Rome from plague, 290, 921. — His history, 894, 895.  
Aesculapius bearded, I, 273. — A cock sacred to Aesculapius, I, 417.  
AESOPHAGUS, called the gullet, II, 49. — Its nature and use, ibid. — Called the stomach by some, ibid.  
AESTIMARE sometimes means the same as *numerare*, or to make a conjecture from a number, II, 422.  
AETERNUS, that is, perpetual, I, 592.  
AFFECTS. The opinion of the Stoics and Peripatetics concerning them, I, 688 ff. — Refuted, 692 ff. — The same affects were given to animals and to human beings, 690. — Their seat, according to Ovid, 689. — Virtue lies in mastering them, 689. — What their true use is, 690, 705. — In what sense they compel us. — Heretical opinions concerning the proposition that they must be mastered.  
AFRICANUS (Scipio). Why celebrated, and placed among the gods, I, 211, 212.  
ἀγάλματα and ἀνδριάντες; ἀγαλματοποιός and ἀνδριαντοποιός: how they differ, II, 550, 551.  
EGAPIUS. His martyrdom during the Diocletianic persecution, II, 322.  
AGATHOCLES, king of Sicily. On his exploits in Africa, I, 233.  
AGERE, for *facere* (“to do”), II, 665, 728. — For *jure agere* (“to bring a legal action”), 688.  
AGESILAUS, Pluto, I, 173.  
AGDIR, or *abdir*: a stone, or a goddess worshipped in the image of a stone, II, 496. — The same as the stone which Saturn is said to have devoured in place of Jupiter, 497.  
AGDUS, the stone-god, II, 496.  
Ἀγρανόμοι (*agranomoi*): who were so called among the Greeks, II, 400.  
The PASCHAL LAMB, a figure of Christ among the Jews, I, 530.  
ALAGABUS, a stone-god: in what form, II, 497.  
ALAMANNI, slain by Constantius near Langres, II, 504.  
ALBESCERE, for *pallescere* (“to grow pale”), II, 246.  
WHITE horses: see HORSE.  
ALBUNEA, a Sibyl, I, 144.  
ALCIBIADES. Whether he was Socrates’ disciple, I, 414.  
ALEXANDER, tyrant of Africa: where he was defeated, II, 555.  
ALEXANDER THE GREAT never traversed Africa in his victories, II, 555. — Why his soldiers were blinded by Milesian Ceres, I, 291 and ibid.  
ALEXANDRA. Fables concerning her marriage to Diocletian and Christianity, II, 321, 542.  
ALTITUDO, for depth, I, 995.  
ALTRINSECUS, for “on the other side,” II, 35.  
AMALTHEA is believed to have nursed Jupiter in infancy, I, 240.  
AMALTHEA, a Sibyl, I, 143.  
AMALTHEA, a nymph, I, 240.  
AMAZONS. Whence their name, I, 158.  
AMBRACIOTES, I, 408.  
AMBROSIA, the food of the gods among poets, II, 282.  
AMBURI, AMBUSTUS, II, 408.  
AMERICA. Whether the apostles preached the Gospel there before Nero’s reign, II, 643, 644.  
FRIENDS OF KINGS: who were so called, II, 397, 747.  
AMISENIANS worshipped Serapis, II, 416. — On their twofold era, ibid. — Granted freedom by Julius Caesar, ibid. How they later sought freedom for themselves, 447. — A third era falsely attributed to them, ibid.  
Ἀναβολεύς (*anaboleus*): what it was among the Greeks, II, 478.  
ANACHARSIS, a Scythian, learned philosophy, I, 431.  
ANASTASIS, for resurrection, I, 806.  
ANAXAGORAS. His opinion concerning God, I, 134. — When he was born, ibid. — Authors on him, ibid. — His error in assigning the human end, 371 ff. — He called snow black and ingenious, 424 ff. — He asserted that all things were enveloped in darkness, 438, 439. — He equated man with beasts, II, 92, 93. — He predicted that a stone would fall from the sun, 496.  
ANAXIMANDER. His opinion concerning the magnitude of the moon, I, 425.  
ANAXIMENES. What he thought concerning God, I, 134. — Authors on his teaching, ibid.  
ANCILE: to carry the sacred shield, I, 242.  
ANGELS. Their name is one of office, I, 149. — They do not wish to be worshipped, 150 and ibid. — Called sons of God by Lactantius, 296. — How they were sent by God for the protection of humankind, 330. — Their intercourse with women, 330, 938. — On the time of their creation, 922. [Col. 1156] — Lactantius did not say that they are sons of God by nature, 925, 926. — They are called sons of God in Scripture, ibid. — Which authors taught that they are corporeal, 938 ff. — They entirely lack every body, 939. — In them there is a more perfect mode of understanding, 963.  
ANGUIMANUS: why the elephant is so called, II, 26.  
SOUL. It is situated in heat or fire, I, 309, 322. — How it arises from God, 319 ff. — It has dominion over the body, 322. — Its office, ibid. — Its food, 323. — Its origin is from heaven, 345. — Whether it is born with the body, 405 and ibid. — The pre-existence of souls and their being a portion drawn from the divine essence, 750. — They are not from God, but by God, ibid. — Whoever prefers the life of the soul must necessarily despise bodily life, 754. — Who taught that it is immortal, 960 ff. — Plato’s arguments are set forth and refuted, 961 ff. — Its eternity is demonstrated, 764 ff. — Lactantius seems to imply its resurrection, 769 and ibid., 806. — Its desires are eternal, 770. — Arguments advanced against its immortality are refuted, 771 ff. — Why it cannot be dissolved, ibid. and 776. — It neither grows in children, nor flourishes in youths, nor diminishes in old people, 772 ff. — It is not the same as the mind, ibid. — It falls ill through the body’s contagion, 775. — It is not a part of the body but is in the body, ibid. — It is contained in the substance of the blood as light is in oil, ibid. — The immortality attributed to it by Pythagoras is ridiculed, 776. — Testimonies of Hermes and the Sibyls on its eternity, 777, 778. — On the summoning of souls from the underworld, 778 ff. — Aristoxenus’ opinion concerning the nature of the soul, 779. — How, being immortal, it can nevertheless feel punishment, 798 ff., 1011. — The error is noted of those who think that the punishments and rewards of souls are deferred until the day of universal judgment, 802, 1012 ff. — In what sense poets say that souls return from the underworld, 804. — The opinion that they are of God’s substance: by whom defended and by whom condemned, 927. — Who held that souls of the righteous would, after the universal judgment, be introduced into the earthly paradise, 932. — In what sense it may properly be said that souls derive their origin from heaven, 943. — The soul is not contained in the body as something is in a vessel or in a place, 1005. — Who believed it fiery, II, 34, 35. — Various opinions concerning its nature, 68. — How it is infused into the body, 69. — Whether it is the same as the mind, 70. — Whether it is generated by parents, 73.  
ANIMA, for a living creature, I, 306.  
ANIMALS. On their shape and limbs, II, 24. See BEASTS and BRUTES.  
ANIMARI, for receiving a soul: a rare word, I, 310.  
ANIMIS, for *animabus* (“souls”), I, 708.  
MIND. What its office is, I, 265, 321. — From it comes knowledge in man, I, 360. — With what enemies it must fight, 378 ff. — The difference between its conflict and that of the body, 379. — The principle of heaven is in it, 636. — The union of minds is stronger than that of bodies, 667. — What its power and rationale are, 696. — Its works are eternal, 770.  
MIND. See SOUL.  
ANNICULUS: who is so called, II, 382, 383.  
ANNONA militaris: what is to be understood by it, II, 541.  
YEAR. What kind it was among the Egyptians, I, 325, 934. — On its diversity among nations, 325, 647 ff. — The years lived by those before the Flood were equal to ours, 934.  
The YEAR OF THE LORD’S PASSION, I, 474.  
ANTE, for *post*, frequently used by Lactantius, I, 277. — *Ante decimum Kalendas* for *decimo Kalendas*, ibid. Whether *ante diem decimum Kalendas* and *post diem decimum Kalendas* have the same force, II, 302, 383, 607.  
ANTHROPIAN heretics, I, 542, 990.

VALITUDO for *valetudo* (“health”). II, 739. VANILOQUENTIA, empty talk. 146. VARRO. VENARUM SECTIO, cutting of the veins: what kind of death it is. II, 519. VENDERE ANIMAM SUAM PUBLICE, “to sell one’s life publicly,” namely in gladiatorial combat. I, 579. VENERARIUS. 617. VENENATUS, for pernicious. 566. VENTER, the belly. On it, and what kind is praised by authors. II, 47. VENTI, winds. On their use and utility. 117. VENUS instituted the art of prostitution, I, 207. — Worshipped in Syro-Phoenicia, II, 279. — Under what form Venus Urania was worshipped at Athens, 497. — Paphian Venus, under the form of a pyramid, ibid. — Her obscenity and lusts, I, 207. — On her affair with Mars, ibid. — A temple to Venus Calva (“Bald Venus”) was consecrated by the Romans, 225. — Under what name the Lacedaemonians dedicated a temple and statue to armed Venus, 225, 906. — Venus Limnesia presides over harbors, 236. — Who first established a temple to her, ibid. VERBENA, customarily used in sacrifices, 727. — Whence the name, ibid. — How much distinction it possessed at Rome, ibid. VERBUM DEI, “Word of God”: see FILIUS DEI. VERITAS, truth. The value of its knowledge, 111. — How much men of outstanding intellect sought it, ibid. — Why they did not attain it, 113. — It lies hidden in obscurity, ibid. — Why it is despised by the learned and hated by the unlearned, ibid. — No food for the mind is sweeter than knowledge of it, 118. — Who harden themselves against it, ibid. — How great its power is, 130. — Why men of the highest intellect did not reach it, 137. — It is sufficiently adorned by itself, 349. — Who said that it lay submerged in a well, 439. — It is bitter and hateful to all, 528. — Why it needs suitable heralds, 551. — Why it produces hatred, 576. — Who, with their eyes shut, kick against it, 737. — It has been almost wholly divided among philosophers and sects. 759. Truth: the stages by which one ascends to it, II, 81 ff. — It can never be discovered by human senses. 112. VERRES plunders the temples of Sicily, I, 275. — Whether a ruinous punishment was inflicted upon him for his crimes [Col. 1203], 276. — How he died, ibid. VERSURAM SOLVERE, what it means. 299. VERSUS. Among the Latins any lines were called *versus*. 297. VERUS (Lucius), emperor: in what year he died, II, 459. — He did not reach the tenth year of his reign, ibid. — In what year he was raised to the empire, ibid. VESICA, the bladder: how it draws urine, 52. — Which animals do not have the use of it, ibid. VESTA. VESTIRE, “to clothe”: likewise, to invest with the insignia of supreme authority. II, 334, 411. VETERANI, who they are. I, 115. VETERANUS REX, “veteran king”: an elegant expression for Diocletian after he had laid down the empire. II, 334. VETERNUM, the same as lethargy. I, 774. VETUS VETUSTUM VINUM, “old, very old wine”: an ancient pleonasm. II, 792. VEXABILIS. I, 751. VICANI, those dwelling in the same *vicus* (“district” or “village”), so called. 677. VIRGINES, “virgins”: included among women by the Latin term, 255. — What it means “to diminish a virgin,” ibid. VIRTUS, virtue. By what rite it should be worshipped, I, 223. — It is not God but God’s gift, ibid. — It is not the highest good, 369, 377. — Its power and function, 377. — If it contains any baseness, it ceases to be virtue, 370. — No reward worthy of it is found on earth, 379, 609. — What that reward is, 380. — What it accomplishes in attaining the highest good, 382. — Its exercises and means of strengthening, 383. — In what sense virtue alone can produce the blessed life, 434. — It bears no fruit where it is mortal and perishable, 435. — Its sole reward is immortality, ibid. — If an adversary is lacking, whether it should be regarded as nonexistent, 443, 570. — It alone can be judged the true good, 496. — It cannot be deprived of its reward, 610. — Philosophers did not define it rightly, 649. — Whether it can be taught, 650. — In what it consists, 651, 654. — It follows knowledge, 651. — Its way is simple, narrow, and arduous, 659. — Without faith it does not exist, 663. — Once hope of immortality is removed, it is sought in vain, 665. — It is not mercenary, 673. — By what stages it ascends to the highest summit, 685. — On the distinction of virtues and vices, 687. — The rewards of the latter are temporal, of the former eternal, 735. — No one favors virtue except one able to follow it, 737. — Its way does not admit those bearing great burdens, 738. — In what sense it cannot be called according to nature, 766. — Why it is perpetual whereas vices [Col. 1204] are not, 767, 768. — Why so few embrace it. 885. VIRTUS, virtue. Whence it is named, II, 57. — It is tested and established through evils, 137. — *Virtus*, said simply of military valor. 824. VISCERA, internal organs. VITA, life. How earnestly it is sought by all, I, 381. — No one despises it except in hope of a longer life, ibid. — In it one must seek wisdom and be wise, 396. — The opinion of those who flee it as an evil is refuted, 411. — In it all things are brief and perishable, 601. — On the two paths by which life must proceed, 641. — Its course was compared by the ancients to the letter Y, ibid. — By what life is sustained, II, 49. — On the long life of certain people, 370. — *Vita*, for livelihood or food. 739. VITALIS VIR, a thrifty man. I, 686. VITAM VIVERE, “to live life.” II, 96. VITELLIUS, emperor: while still alive, he saw his own images abolished. 427. VOLUPTAS, pleasure. II, 148. VOTUM CELEBRARE, “to celebrate a vow”: of festivals in which vows were made for the safety of the emperors. 244, 356, 769. VOX, voice. It does not exist without mind, and is improperly attributed to souls, I, 714. — Also attributed to brute animals by Aristotle, ibid. — Why the Greeks called it αὐδή (*audē*), II, 36. — On its origin and cause, 49 ff., 62. — How philosophers defined it, ibid. — Its instruments, ibid. VULCAN. Why he was believed to be fire, I, 185. — How he was thrown down onto the island of Lemnos, 195. — Why he was numbered among the gods, 213. — The invention of fire and iron is attributed to him, ibid. — Regarded by many as Tubal-cain, ibid.
